speaker: BERNANKE
text: Cathy has been a regular participant since August 1994.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will have an opportunity later in the fall to say goodbye to Cathy more officially, but I think this will be a good opportunity to thank you for your collegiality and for thirteen years of tremendous contributions to the FOMC.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It has been truly an honor and an incredible experience, something I never expected to happen and a joy through the ups and downs and ins and outs of every meeting.

text: So I thank everybody around the table who has been here and made it that way.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 It is hard to follow that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Today, I want to focus on the significant rise in long-dated Treasury yields that has occurred since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you can see in exhibit 1, Treasury yields have moved sharply higher over the past six weeks, although they have recovered a bit in the past few days.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At two-year and longer maturities, the shift in the yield curve has been nearly parallel, with yields roughly 50 basis points higher over this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen in exhibit 2, the rise in nominal ten-year Treasury yields has been accompanied by a rise in ten-year TIPS yields.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because the rise in nominal yields has been slightly larger than the rise in real yields, forward breakeven inflation rates have risen a bit since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, exhibit 3 shows the trajectory of the breakeven inflation rate five to ten years in the future estimated using nominal Treasury and TIPS yields.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This measure has risen more than 20 basis points from its trough in May.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So how does one explain the rise in nominal and real Treasury yields and the increase in breakeven inflation?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In my opinion, there is one very compelling explanation—market participants generally believe that the downside risks to growth have diminished, and this has led to (1) a sharp shift in monetary policy expectations and (2) a modest change in investors’ assessment of inflation risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But other factors 1 Material used by Mr. Dudley is appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: also played a role, including mortgage convexity hedging and, perhaps, the gradual shift in the appetite of foreign central banks away from U.S. Treasury securities toward other assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 4, monetary policy expectations as embodied in the Eurodollar futures market have shifted sharply since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In May, a drop of more than 50 basis points in Eurodollar rates was anticipated to occur by the end of 2008.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, currently the Eurodollar futures strip is virtually flat—indicating that market expectations are close to neutral through 2008.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This shift in expectations is also evident in responses to our survey of primary dealers.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Using exhibits 5 and 6, we can compare the dealers’ forecasts before the May 9 meeting with their forecasts before our meeting today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The green circles represent the average forecast of the dealers; the size of the blue circles indicates the frequency of different forecasts; and the horizontal dark lines represent market rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen in these exhibits, over the intermeeting period the dealer forecasts have moved upward, but much less than market expectations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This presumably reflects the fact that the market rate represents the mean of potential outcomes whereas the dealer forecasts are modal forecasts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, the smaller shift evident in the dealer forecasts may reflect the fact that dealer forecasts tend to lag changes in market expectations when expectations are changing rapidly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen in these two exhibits, much of the dispersion evident in the forecasts toward lower rates has vanished since the May 9 FOMC meeting, and the skew to the downside has disappeared.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Dealers who had forecasted a flat or higher federal funds rate path generally did not alter their forecasts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, dealers who had earlier anticipated easing have eliminated or dramatically scaled back those expectations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, the blue circles evident in exhibit 5 at rates of 3.5 percent and 4.0 percent are not present in exhibit 6.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The dealer forecasts support the notion that expectations are changing mainly because market participants are less worried about downside risks to growth rather than because they think that the growth rate of real GDP will likely be stronger.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: With the exception of the current quarter, in which GDP forecasts have been revised upward sharply following a very weak first quarter, the real GDP forecasts of dealers have generally not changed materially through 2008.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is illustrated in exhibit 7.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Instead, as shown in exhibit 8, dealers are now, collectively, more certain about the growth outlook—in other words, the downside risks to growth have diminished.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The reduction in the downside risks to growth may also be important in explaining the modest rise in breakeven inflation measures.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If the downside risks to growth have diminished, then a corollary may be that the upside risks to inflation have increased.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In that case, investors should show more interest in purchasing inflation protection.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The breakeven inflation measure calculated from nominal Treasury and TIPS yields has several components, including expected inflation and the premium paid by investors for inflation protection.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In assessing the rise in these breakeven inflation measures due to diminished downside risks to growth, it is unclear how to apportion the rise in the overall breakeven inflation measures between a higher premium for inflation protection and higher expected inflation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In theory at least, reduced downside risks to growth might reasonably be expected to push both components a bit higher.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Three other factors behind the backup in Treasury yields bear mentioning.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, the shift in monetary policy expectations and the rise in longer-dated yields have been a global phenomenon.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When yields are rising elsewhere, that shift should put some upward pressure on U.S. long-term rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, mortgage-related convexity hedging may have exacerbated the speed and magnitude of the rise in yields.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A rise in yields causes expected rates of prepayment on lower-coupon fixed-rate mortgages to fall, which lengthens the average duration of mortgage portfolios.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Mortgage servicers, the housing-related GSEs, and other mortgage holders respond by selling long-dated Treasury securities and long-dated interest rate swaps to reduce the average duration of their holdings.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 9 shows that most conventional fixed-rate mortgages are below current mortgage rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As rates rise, these mortgages get further “out of the money.” This lowers expected prepayment rates and lengthens duration, and people react by hedging.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As long-term rates keep rising, the effect of higher interest rates on duration gradually lessens as the rates on most outstanding mortgages fall further below current market rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The effect of mortgage convexity hedging is evident in the relative underperformance of ten-year Treasuries, which is one of the preferred hedging vehicles versus mortgages, relative to other Treasury maturities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The week ending on June 13 had the biggest rise in longer-term Treasury yields.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 10, this was also the week in which ten-year Treasury yields rose the most compared with five-year and thirty-year Treasury rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To the extent that mortgage convexity hedging pushes up nominal ten-year Treasury yields more than other yields, then it may also temporarily distort breakeven inflation measures.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, diminished appetite among central banks for Treasury securities may have also been a factor behind the rise in longer-dated yields.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Central bank buying was often a featured part of the story when bond term premiums were unusually narrow.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Foreign central banks may have played a role in the recent rise in bond term premiums.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 11, the growth rate of Treasury custody holdings at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York has slowed sharply since April.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But it is important not to push this point too strongly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although foreign central banks with the largest foreign exchange reserve holdings are diversifying their portfolios away from Treasuries, they still appear to be extending the average maturity of those Treasuries that they hold, which implies a continued bid for longer-dated Treasuries from this source.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Turning now to other market developments, the most striking aspect of this period of rising Treasury yields has been the limited effect that this rise has had on the risk appetite of investors in most other markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is in sharp contrast to the reduction in risk appetites that occurred in a broad array of asset classes in late February and the first half of March.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, as shown in exhibit 12, the rise in long-term yields has not caused the U.S. equity market to retrench.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 13, until the past week or so, corporate debt spreads have been relatively stable.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, in the foreign exchange markets, the carry trade remains alive and well.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One way to see this is in exhibit 14, which illustrates the change in the value of the yen against high- yielding currencies such as the Australian dollar and New Zealand dollar as well as against the U.S. dollar and the euro.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, in the late February selloff, the yen rallied, and the high-yielding currencies sold off sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, during the recent rise in interest rates, the yen weakened and the high-yielding currencies appreciated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Similarly, as illustrated in exhibit 15, although volatility in the U.S. Treasury market moved up sharply (shown by the rise in the MOVE index), volatility in the equity and foreign exchange markets remained quite low.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the foreign exchange markets, movements between the major currencies continue to be driven mainly by changes in expected interest rate differentials.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 16 shows the movement in the spreads between the September 2008 Eurodollar futures yield versus Euribor futures for Europe and Euroyen futures for Japan.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen here, interest rate expectations shifted more sharply upward in the United States relative to Japan than relative to Europe.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Not surprisingly, as shown in exhibit 17, the dollar appreciated more sharply against the yen than against the euro over this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The yen’s weakness, which has been persistent but stealthy, may begin to receive more attention.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: After all, as shown in exhibit 18, while the nominal yen/dollar exchange rate has fluctuated in a relatively narrow range in recent years, the real effective yen exchange rate has declined sharply over this period—a rate of decline that may be intensifying.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, in May the real effective exchange rate of the yen—as estimated by the BIS—had fallen to its lowest point since the early 1980s and had declined nearly to half of its early 1995 peak.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the June BIS data are not yet available, the rate of depreciation has likely increased over the past month.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although calm generally pervades U.S. financial markets, there is one important exception worthy of note.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The subprime mortgage space is still very unsettled—hurt both by poor housing market fundamentals and by the problems of two hedge funds sponsored by Bear Stearns.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 19 shows the behavior of the spread on the ABX 06-2 index, which is an index based on a basket of credit default swaps on underlying cash securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, the spread has increased to a new high, and underlying CDS spreads have also increased.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There is a danger that forced liquidation of illiquid subprime-based securities could exacerbate the pressure on this market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, it should be noted that the Bear Stearns-sponsored hedge funds that are in trouble are not particular large; the problems of these hedge funds appear to be mostly exceptional rather than the norm; and the counterparty exposures generated by these hedge funds are broadly distributed and have already shrunk sharply in size.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That said, there still are risks that forced selling could drive market prices down sharply, leading to lower marks for other portfolios of assets related to subprime mortgages.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This, in turn, could lead to margin calls, investor redemptions, and further selling pressure in this market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of lessons learned, three points come to mind.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, high credit ratings don’t fully capture measures of risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The ratings are based on the risk of default, not the market risks associated with illiquidity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, highly leveraged portfolios of highly rated but illiquid assets are subject to significant market risk that the ratings may obscure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the performance of some of these complex securities is very sensitive to the correlation of returns.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As correlations move higher, the subordination protection offered to senior tranches in complex securities such as CDOs, and CDO- squared products—CDOs of CDOs—can evaporate quickly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because the ratings for the tranches within such products are typically established on the basis of historical correlations, the default risk for some of these tranches may be understated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, marked-to-model asset valuation may artificially smooth returns and obscure risk— both to portfolio managers and to investors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The health of the broader CDO and CLO (collateralized loan obligation) markets may rest on this same fragile set of assumptions—that credit ratings fairly capture risk and that historical correlation relationships will continue to apply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This implies the potential for problems: If investors questioned these assumptions in the subprime area, they could also rethink their assumptions about these risks in the broader markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Such a development might lead to considerably less buoyant conditions in the corporate debt and loan markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It could be noteworthy that some of the indexes that reference credit default swaps in the corporate debt and loan markets have shown some deterioration in the past week.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, there were no foreign operations during this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I request a vote to ratify the operations conducted by the System Open Market Account since the May FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, I am very happy to take questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the breakeven inflation rates, the five-by-five rose more, I believe, than either the five or the ten arithmetically because the ten rose more than the five and it’s in the spread.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It seems odd that a change in the near-term growth outlook would have significant implications for five-to-ten-year inflation expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there technical issues there as well as in mortgage hedging, or is it just the way you calculate these spreads with the differences in liquidity and so on?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I think there is an issue.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You have to wait for the market to settle down.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To the extent that you are taking a snapshot at a time that more convexity hedging is influencing the ten-year and the five-year has not caught up, that can be a phenomenon.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, people in the marketplace say that people in the nominal Treasury markets are different from the people who invest in TIPS, and so the behavior of the two can diverge for short periods.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would be more confident if a month from now we saw the same uptick in five to ten years of forward inflation as we do today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am not convinced it will necessarily persist.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It may be that real yields and nominal yields will eventually equilibrate as these two markets come back into balance.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So my own view would be that it bears watching, but I wouldn’t reach strong conclusions about it at this stage.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there other questions for Bill?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: My memory of the Long-Term Capital Management situation was that the dollar amount that went into the original program that the investment banks put together when they started to manage the situation wasn’t that much bigger than the money that Bear Stearns is throwing at its hedge funds, yet the effect on the market seems to be very, very different.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Having been around during the Long-Term Capital episode, I know that there were real concerns that the domino effect was going to be enormous because of the market uncertainty and the lack of liquidity and so forth across a wide range of instruments.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Is it the range or the nature of the instruments?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: How would you see the two situations and compare them because clearly this one, for all you can read and understand and even in your own presentation, doesn’t seem to be that much of a systemic issue.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I think there’s a difference in terms of people’s assessment of how much risk Bear Stearns is actually taking on in terms of their hedge fund.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: My understanding is that they are extending credit, and they are basically taking out the credit that was extended by the counterparties for the less highly leveraged of the two funds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They are hoping that they still have equity—that the assets of the hedge fund are essentially going to exceed the value of the loan that they are making.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So they’re feeling that, if all goes well, they are not going to be out any money.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: My memory of Long- Term Capital Management, and somebody can correct me if I’m wrong, is that the people who came into that pool were putting up equity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it is quite different in terms of what was actually being contributed in these two cases.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Bear Stearns is just replacing the counterparty borrowings with its own line of credit.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: But then they managed it so that they did come out ahead over a period of time—at least that’s my memory.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I was going to follow up on Cathy’s point, but I think Don is, too.

speaker: KOHN
text: I was going to do the same.

speaker: KOHN
text: I was just going to remark that the situation was quite different.

speaker: KOHN
text: LTCM followed the Russian debt default.

speaker: KOHN
text: The markets were already in considerable disarray.

speaker: KOHN
text: All those correlations had already begun to turn, and then on top of that you had the fire sale effects of LTCM.

speaker: KOHN
text: You can see some of that in the subprime market, where this thing is concentrated.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is just not spread out now, and the whole market situation was very different at that time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think there is a presumption in the Long-Term Capital Management case that a lot of people had similar positions in place.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the Bear Stearns case, we certainly don’t have all the information at this point, but the general thought at this time is that there are not a lot of other people with the same positions in place.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vice Chairman, did you have a comment?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I agree with all of that, but the relative size is much smaller—much narrower in the type of positions to which they’re exposed.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The state of the world is dramatically different.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Direct exposure of the counterparties to Bear Stearns is very, very small compared with other things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: These guys are making a loan against a set of positions—a right to those positions—not equity, and what they realize in the value of those positions over time will be determined.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: They think there is positive value in that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So the situation is dramatically different.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It does not mean that you should view it as particularly reassuring.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You know, these people were exceptionally experienced in the mortgage credit business, and there were smart people in LTCM, too.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: That was the general opinion.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But these guys were regarded as very smart people, who knew the business well, and this is just a good example of how little one can know in some sense and what leverage does to your exposure to liquidity risk.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In this case, people were just not willing to give them the time to realize whatever value might be in these positions, and this is just a natural consequence of leverage.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: People think they had substantially less leverage than LTCM had in some sense, but that is hard to measure.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I would argue that there are similarities in that, with Long-Term Capital, most of the stress-testing had been just computer-model driven.

speaker: FISHER
text: Then when actual market prices began to be quoted, you saw the deterioration.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is clearly the case here.

speaker: FISHER
text: The ABX is a technical index.

speaker: FISHER
text: For a lot of the CDO-squared market, nobody knows what the values, as opposed to the prices, really are.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is a difference between price and value.

speaker: FISHER
text: Price is what you pay; value is what you get.

speaker: FISHER
text: I suppose one charitable interpretation of this, Bill, would be that the good thing about this situation is that we actually may be creating a real market to determine value on these things or at least price relative to value.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I think the phenomena are similar, and I would argue—having been in the business, although the business wasn’t as sophisticated when I used to be in it—that this has broader dimensions than those we had before.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you look at the growth rate of these instruments—again, without any underlying sense of what you ultimately can cash in if you’re pressed—it has been a straight upcurve.

speaker: FISHER
text: The numbers are quite huge.

speaker: FISHER
text: Again, I was once a hedge fund manager—I know all the tricks that are played there, including, by the way, the valuation of underlying securities—in a day when the business was less sophisticated than it is now.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t feel I understand this issue.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t know about my other colleagues around the table, but you did kindly send someone down to brief our staff on this.

speaker: FISHER
text: They came out with more questions than they did answers, but it was very helpful.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am worried that we will be asked publicly at different intervals and perhaps starting now what our opinions and perspectives are.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m also worried about giving the wrong answer.

speaker: FISHER
text: I wonder if there is not a way—not during this meeting but at some point— that all the principals at this table can be briefed so that we can understand and have a common approach to this issue.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t think the issue is contained.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do think there is enormous risk.

speaker: FISHER
text: I hope that something good comes out of this, but speaking personally, I would like to understand this better, and I hope that we all understand it very well in case a negative scenario obtains.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We can monitor the situation here and in New York.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know, Vincent, if we have any reports or materials that we can share with President Fisher.

speaker: REINHART
text: Well, Bill and I can get together.

speaker: FISHER
text: Maybe we could just have a common briefing.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it would be very helpful, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think, Richard, you need to be in a position to offer an opinion on what happened in Bear Stearns in particular.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think you need to or want to be in the business of doing that in that particular case.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Regarding a broader understanding about the implications of what we see in these markets, Bear Stearns is relevant also in some broader sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is obviously value in trying to make sure that people have as much understanding as they can.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My suspicion is that you are going to find yourself where most people are on this, which is with some differing mix of unease and reassurance that you’re not going to resolve fundamentally until we get through the next period of excitement.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, again, Tim, I would suggest that we not comment on this.

speaker: FISHER
text: None of us should comment on it.

speaker: FISHER
text: But (1) it would be good to have an understanding, and (2) if it gets worse, more intense, or troublesome, the Committee will have to respond in some way, and it would be nice to at least have a common understanding as we go down this path.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s my suggestion or request.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are a couple of themes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that the subprime problems are still being worked through the financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second is that subprime is an example of a broader class of structured products that are difficult to value, and that creates some uncertainty in the markets in periods of stress.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am always in favor of more understanding, but for this Committee, what I know about this now suggests that there isn’t any reason for us to be involved.

speaker: LACKER
text: I compliment Vice Chairman Geithner on not serving sandwiches in this case.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree with Vice Chairman Geithner—there’s a certain danger of our commenting on stuff like this and leading people to believe that we feel some responsibility for damping or otherwise minimizing the effects of changes in market prices on the changes in other market prices.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are happy to share all the information we have about the specific case and its broad implications with everybody—in confidence, of course.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, I need a motion to ratify domestic operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will turn now to the economic situation, and we call on David Wilcox.

speaker: WILCOX
text: 2 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: WILCOX
text: My colleagues and I will be referring to the packet entitled “Staff Presentation on the Economic Outlook.” Your first exhibit summarizes our economic forecast.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As shown in the top panels, we have edged up our forecast for the growth of real GDP this year and next.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Taken by itself, the increase in interest rates that Bill Dudley mentioned was a negative for our growth outlook, but it was outweighed by a variety of other factors, including the higher stock market, the upward revision to wages and salaries, and the more favorable composition of real growth during the first half of this year.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As shown in the middle pair of 2 Material used by Mr. Wilcox, Ms. Liang, and Mr. Leahy is appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: WILCOX
text: panels, we have trimmed our forecast of the unemployment rate—partly in response to the latest readings on this series and partly in light of the slightly stronger outlook for real output—and we now have it ending 2008 just below 5 percent, our estimate of the natural rate.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As shown in the bottom right panel, core PCE inflation in the current quarter appears to be running at an annual rate of 1.4 percent, considerably less than the 2.2 percent we expected as of the May Greenbook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: However, as I will discuss later in more detail, we have interpreted most of that good news as likely to prove transitory and so have taken down our forecast for core inflation over the projection period only 0.1 percentage point.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Exhibit 2 turns to the market for single-family housing.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The yellow stripes in the top left panel mark major downturns in single-family housing starts since 1970.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As can be seen in the box to the right, the current contraction now ranks among these major episodes in terms of magnitude.

speaker: WILCOX
text: It differs importantly from previous ones, however, in terms of its origins because this one did not result from a round of monetary tightening aimed at taking economic activity down to bring inflation under control.

speaker: WILCOX
text: That difference has important implications for the likely contour of the recovery.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In earlier episodes, once the desired reduction in inflation appeared to be in train, the policy rate was brought back down and longer-term interest rates often came down as well.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But this time, as shown in the middle left panel, with policy assumed to hold at its current position, we are not banking on any reduction in mortgage interest rates from here forward, suggesting that the housing recovery may be more subdued than it often has been in the past.

speaker: WILCOX
text: One factor that poses some downside risk is the overhang of unsold homes, shown in the middle right panel.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Months’ supply remains at a very high level.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As we illustrated in one of the alternative simulations in the Greenbook, the contraction in the housing sector could be a good deal deeper than the one in our baseline if builders decide to bring inventories down more quickly.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Another factor that will be important in shaping the recovery is the pace of sales, shown in the bottom left panel.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In light of the tighter conditions in the subprime loan market and the recent backup in rates, we have sales moving a little lower over the next few months but then stabilizing and beginning to edge up around the turn of the year.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The data on both new and existing home sales that were released earlier this week were consistent with our Greenbook forecast.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I should also note the situation with regard to the price of single- family housing.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As you know, home prices have decelerated greatly, and over the projection period, we have them remaining close to their current levels on a national-average basis.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But our ability to judge the alignment of prices with fundamentals is limited, to say the least, and a substantial move downward is certainly possible.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The bottom right panel illustrates that risk by presenting the estimated valuation error according to the very simple model that we showed you two years ago in our special presentation on housing.

speaker: WILCOX
text: To be sure, other models deliver different answers, but this one judges the misalignment of the price-rent ratio to be historically large.

speaker: WILCOX
text: If prices break more sharply because builders decide to clear out inventories more quickly, construction activity might well recover faster, even as other consumer spending is crimped by the damage to household balance sheets.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Which effect would predominate in terms of overall aggregate demand is not entirely clear.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Exhibit 3 focuses on business fixed investment.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As shown in the top left panel, sales of medium and heavy trucks have more or less fallen off a cliff thus far this year, reflecting the influence of new EPA regulations that took effect on January 1, and this has been an important factor holding down overall equipment spending.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We think that this dynamic should be coming to a close over the next few months and are looking for truck purchases to begin trending up sometime during the second half of this year.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As shown in the top right panel, orders and shipments of nondefense capital goods hit an air pocket around the turn of the year, apparently driven down in part by the trials of the motor vehicle and construction industries.

speaker: WILCOX
text: However, the orders and shipments data for March and April—the latest that were available to us when we were putting together the Greenbook, encouraged us to think that a rebound of at least modest proportions is in train, and this morning’s release came in close to our Greenbook expectations.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Moreover, surveys of business conditions, including the two orders-based indexes shown in the middle left panel, suggest that businesses concur that the situation has brightened somewhat in the past few months.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As shown in the first line of the middle right panel, we are projecting that, over the next six quarters, equipment investment will post respectable—if unspectacular—increases.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Two of the variables conditioning that view appear at the bottom of the page.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As shown on the left, we expect real business output to grow a little more slowly over the forecast period than in the preceding few years, suggesting—all else being equal—somewhat more modest growth in investment than in earlier years.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Similarly, as shown on the right, we expect the user cost of capital for high-tech equipment, the red line, to continue to decline at about the average pace of the past few years, and we expect the user cost for non-high-tech equipment, the black line, to be about unchanged, much as it has been over the past year and a half.

speaker: WILCOX
text: All in all, these factors point to a steady outlook for business investment.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Exhibit 4 takes a slightly longer term perspective on the inflation outlook by comparing our current projection to the one that we had in the January Greenbook—the last time you submitted projections for a Monetary Policy Report.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As shown in the top left panel, since January we have revised up our near-term forecast for overall PCE price inflation but not our longer-term outlook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Part of the near-term revision is due to faster food price inflation— the top right panel—which in turn reflects, among other things, the greater pressure that ethanol production has placed not only on the price of corn but also the prices of other foods that are produced using corn as an input, such as beef, dairy, and poultry.

speaker: WILCOX
text: By the end of this year, though, we assume that the livestock and poultry sectors have adjusted to the higher level of corn prices, so we have food prices coming back in line with core inflation.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Another part of the upward surprise in overall PCE inflation is due to a steeper climb in consumer energy prices—the middle left panel—reflecting crude oil prices that have been running about $10 per barrel above our January assumption and refinery outages that have kept utilization below typical levels.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But as with food, we have energy price increases moderating greatly over the projection period.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Excluding food and energy—the middle right panel—core PCE price inflation has looked a little tamer thus far this year than we expected in January.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Nonetheless, our projection for core inflation next year is unrevised, on net, relative to the January Greenbook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The absence of any net revision since January reflects a mix of considerations.

speaker: WILCOX
text: For one thing, not all the news related to inflation has been good; both import and—as I just noted—energy prices have been running higher than we expected and thus have been generating more upward pressure on inflation than we had foreseen.

speaker: WILCOX
text: For another, some of the recent good news seems likely to prove relatively short- lived.

speaker: WILCOX
text: For example, as shown in the bottom left panel, nonmarket-based prices, which account for about 20 percent of the core index, have been rising less quickly thus far this year than we expected in January.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Historically, however, fluctuations in nonmarket prices have not conveyed much information about the future behavior of this series, so we have trimmed our projection for the increase in this component of prices over the second half of this year by only a tenth.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As shown to the right, both tenants’ rent—the black line—and owners’ equivalent rent, or OER—the red line—have decelerated lately but, as shown by the bars at the bottom of the panel, OER has slowed by noticeably more.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Historically, differences of this magnitude have not persisted long—see, for example, the bulge that emerged and then disappeared in 2003; moreover, these divergences have tended to be resolved in favor of tenants’ rent.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Accordingly, we expect the increases in OER over the projection period to look more like the recent increases in tenants’ rent rather than the other way around.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In the end, these influences happen to roughly offset one another, leaving our core inflation projection for next year unchanged from January.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Exhibit 5 focuses on the recent behavior of inflation expectations and, as noted in the top left panel, asks whether those expectations have moved above levels that were typical from mid-1996 through mid-2004—a period when actual core PCE inflation was mostly between 1 percent and 2 percent.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As noted in the last bullet in the box, the answer varies by series.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In the next three panels, I use shaded bands to indicate levels of each series that were typical during the eight-year reference period—the darker bands marking the middle 50 percent of the series’ observations and the lighter bands marking the middle 80 percent of the observations.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As shown in the top right panel, the short-term expectations measure from the Michigan survey of households has indeed been tending to run above the levels that were typical of the earlier period.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Roughly, those higher readings seem to reflect the steep climb in energy prices over the past few years.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In contrast, as shown in the middle left panel, longer-term inflation expectations from that survey have remained remarkably stable.

speaker: WILCOX
text: They have drifted slightly higher relative to the levels that were typical during the reference period, but even so the latest reading sits just at the edge of its 50 percent band.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The middle right panel shows a measure of short-term inflation expectations from the Philadelphia Fed’s Survey of Professional Forecasters; the most recent reading on this series is near the center of its 50 percent band.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As you know, the measure of ten-year expectations from the SPF, not shown, has mostly been stuck at 2.5 percent since 1998 and was slightly below that in both the first and the second quarters of this year.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Unfortunately, the TIPS market is too young to allow an apples-to-apples comparison on the basis used here.

speaker: WILCOX
text: On the whole, however, we interpret the evidence as suggesting that inflation expectations have been quite stable recently.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We assume that they will remain so over the projection period and thus will not be an important influence on the inflation contour this year and next.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The bottom left panel plots our projection of the unemployment rate and our estimate of the NAIRU.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We expect the small amount of upward pressure currently being generated from this source to be relieved over the projection period as the unemployment rate drifts up and resource utilization eases.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The bottom right panel summarizes our inflation outlook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Relative to the May Greenbook, our forecast for core PCE inflation in 2007 as a whole is down 0.3 percentage point; as I noted earlier, our forecast for the second half of this year and for next year is down only a tenth.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Nellie will continue our presentation.

speaker: LIANG
text: The next four exhibits focus on financial conditions in the corporate and household sectors.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the black line in the top left panel of exhibit 6, operating earnings per share for S&P 500 firms for the second quarter are currently forecasted by analysts to be up about 5 percent from a year ago, a deceleration from the 9 percent pace in the first quarter.

speaker: LIANG
text: However, in view of the sparseness of earnings warnings thus far, we expect second-quarter earnings to top analysts’ forecasts by a few percentage points.

speaker: LIANG
text: As noted to the right, for the year as a whole, analysts are forecasting 8 percent growth in earnings per share (EPS), not very different from the Blue Chip Consensus and the staff’s forecast.

speaker: LIANG
text: For 2008, however, analysts appear to anticipate that EPS growth will pick up to 11 percent, whereas we project that profits will flatten as margins get squeezed by rising unit labor costs.

speaker: LIANG
text: Even adjusting for a typical bias in analysts’ views, our outlook is a little more guarded.

speaker: LIANG
text: The middle panels use analysts’ forecasts to assess equity valuations.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the blue line in the left panel, the trend-forward earnings-to-price ratio for S&P 500 firms has stayed near its level of the past several years, and the gap between it and the real Treasury perpetuity yield—the equity premium shown by the shaded area—narrowed a touch in the past few months as yields rose.

speaker: LIANG
text: But the premium remains close to its average of the past twenty years, suggesting perhaps that investors still are mindful of the risks of investing in equities.

speaker: LIANG
text: However, this caution seems to be less the case for smaller stocks.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown to the right, a simple metric of valuation—the forward price- earnings ratio—shows that valuations of smaller companies, the red line, are on the high side of their range of the past two decades.

speaker: LIANG
text: Relative to valuations of larger firms, shown by the blue line, small-cap valuations also appear on the high side.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the red line in the bottom left panel, risk spreads for high-yield bonds have fallen on net in recent quarters and currently stand near record lows.

speaker: LIANG
text: To assess the risk premium on high-yield bonds, we subtract from this spread the compensation for expected losses from defaults that would be required by risk-neutral investors.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the black line, expected losses have been low for the past few years, and the risk premium, the gray shaded area, is narrow at about 120 basis points.

speaker: LIANG
text: Low risk spreads and risk premiums may be supported by the exceptional quality of corporate balance sheets.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown to the right, the ratio of debt to assets for publicly traded speculative-grade firms, the red line, is just off its twenty-year low.

speaker: LIANG
text: The ratio for investment-grade firms, the black line, continues to edge down.

speaker: LIANG
text: Exhibit 7 examines corporate leverage.

speaker: LIANG
text: Some analysts have expressed concern that low risk spreads are encouraging firms to ramp up debt, which will lead to a sharp deterioration in corporate credit quality in the future.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the green bars in the top left panel, share repurchases have risen sharply since 2003, far outpacing the rise in dividend payments, the blue bars.

speaker: LIANG
text: Cash-financed acquisitions, including leveraged buyouts (LBOs), the yellow bars, have also risen.

speaker: LIANG
text: The table to the right characterizes the effects of large repurchases on leverage in 2005 and 2006.

speaker: LIANG
text: Firms with large repurchases, defined as more than 5 percent of assets, had earnings that equaled 9 percent of assets, row 1, higher than earnings of 6 percent at firms with limited or no repurchases.

speaker: LIANG
text: Row 2 shows that high-repurchase firms boosted their debt ratios 2 percentage points, in contrast to the decrease of 1 percentage point at other firms.

speaker: LIANG
text: Even so, the increase raised the debt ratio to only 22 percent at large-repurchase firms, below the average for other firms.

speaker: LIANG
text: Thus, repurchases to date do not suggest material damage to credit quality and would seem likely to do so going forward only if firms were pressured to continue to pay out cash despite weaker profits.

speaker: LIANG
text: LBOs tend to involve much more debt than share repurchases, as firms typically have debt-to-asset ratios of more than 65 percent right after an LBO.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the middle left panel, the issuance of speculative-grade bonds for mergers and acquisitions, including LBOs, the dark portion of the bars, has risen notably, and originations of speculative-grade loans for M&A, shown to the right, have shot up.

speaker: LIANG
text: The sharp rise in loans reflects in part greater demand, particularly for collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), by institutional investors, who are estimated to have purchased more than half of these loans last year.

speaker: LIANG
text: One reason for the greater demand could be the relatively attractive risk-return tradeoff of loans relative to bonds, illustrated in the bottom left panel.

speaker: LIANG
text: Returns on leveraged loans in recent years, the black line, are only modestly lower than returns on high-yield bonds, the red line, but are significantly less volatile.

speaker: LIANG
text: Thus, as noted in the inset box, Sharpe ratios— defined as mean excess returns to standard deviation—are higher for loans than for bonds.

speaker: LIANG
text: We expect that institutional investors will continue to pursue loans until expected returns decline, perhaps through tighter spreads or lower recovery rates on loans.

speaker: LIANG
text: Financial data generally are not available for firms taken private; views of examiners and rating agencies can be used to gauge the effect of LBOs on credit quality.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the black line in the right panel, the most current, and still preliminary, reading on the share of syndicated loans outstanding that were adversely rated shows almost no change from the previous year and remains low.

speaker: LIANG
text: For corporate bonds, the share rated B minus and below, the red line, stayed in its recent range at the end of the first quarter.

speaker: LIANG
text: Although these measures provide a bit of comfort, it may take some years to fully assess whether the operating efficiencies attained through LBOs will be sufficient to cover the higher debt obligations.

speaker: LIANG
text: Exhibit 8 focuses on household financial conditions.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the top left panel, the ratio of net worth to income is estimated to be up on net through the current quarter, largely on stock market gains.

speaker: LIANG
text: While we expect this ratio to decline in coming quarters as house prices flatten and stock prices advance more slowly, it remains high by historical standards.

speaker: LIANG
text: Moving to the right panel, delinquency rates on consumer loans at banks, auto loans at finance companies, and most mortgages have edged up in recent months but do not suggest signs of stress.

speaker: LIANG
text: Overall, most households appear to be in good financial shape.

speaker: LIANG
text: However, there are strains among some subprime mortgage borrowers.

speaker: LIANG
text: As can be seen in the middle left panel, delinquency rates on subprime adjustable-rate mortgages, the solid red line, have climbed sharply and in April moved up again, while those on other mortgages have remained low.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown to the right, early-payment delinquency rates—at least three missed payments within six months of origination—on adjustable-rate loans rose further in April, though they remain modest for prime and near-prime types, the blue line.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the bottom left panel, we estimate that new foreclosures were started at an annual rate of 1.3 million in the first quarter.

speaker: LIANG
text: Subprime mortgages, the red bars, accounted for more than half of the starts.

speaker: LIANG
text: As noted to the right, foreclosure starts in states with high unemployment, like Ohio, Michigan, and Indiana, continued at a high rate but were little changed from the fourth quarter.

speaker: LIANG
text: The sharpest increases were in four states— California, Florida, Nevada, and Arizona—accounting for more than the nationwide increase, as house prices in those states decelerated.

speaker: LIANG
text: To predict foreclosure starts, we have developed a model of national rates that regresses state-level rates on house price growth, unemployment, the share of loans that are subprime, interest rates, and other variables.

speaker: LIANG
text: This model predicts that foreclosures will continue to rise and reach a bit more than 1.4 million for 2007 as a whole and 1.5 million in 2008, under the Greenbook assumption that national house prices will be roughly flat this year and next.

speaker: LIANG
text: There is unusual uncertainty right now about a forecast given the unprecedented reach of the subprime market in recent years.

speaker: LIANG
text: Some sources of that uncertainty are discussed in exhibit 9.

speaker: LIANG
text: The top four panels present information on interest rate resets on subprime adjustable-rate mortgages, based on a very recently acquired dataset of more than 2 million 2/28 and 3/27 loans that were outstanding as of March of this year.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the top left panel, we estimate that as of the end of the first half of this year, 36 percent of the loans have already had their first interest rate reset.

speaker: LIANG
text: Another 25 percent will face their first reset in the second half of this year, and 21 percent will do so in the first half of 2008.

speaker: LIANG
text: Characteristics of interest rate resets for this snapshot of mortgages are noted in the right panel.

speaker: LIANG
text: The data indicate that, for mortgages close to their first reset date, the initial rate averages about 7.35 percent.

speaker: LIANG
text: Most contracts specified the “fully indexed” rate as the six- month LIBOR plus a margin, which averages 6 percent, and most had caps on the size of each adjustment.

speaker: LIANG
text: The diagram at the middle left presents a progression of interest rates that borrowers about to reset likely will face, based on mortgages that were reset in the past year.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the red line (a slightly stylized version of the actual data, the gray line), the jump in the rate at the first reset date is sizable, almost 2½ percentage points, resulting in a new rate of 9¾ percent.

speaker: LIANG
text: The first reset rate almost never jumps to the fully indexed rate, the blue horizontal line, because of the various caps on increases.

speaker: LIANG
text: But rates are subsequently reset every six months, and as shown on the second reset date, the rate rises another 1 percentage point.

speaker: LIANG
text: Our data suggest that a borrower would not reach the fully indexed rate in the original mortgage until twenty-four months after the first reset (not shown).

speaker: LIANG
text: As noted to the right, however, many borrowers historically have refinanced their mortgages before the first reset date or shortly thereafter.

speaker: LIANG
text: In our sample, 25 percent of mortgages had one reset, and only 12 percent had a second reset.

speaker: LIANG
text: The expected resets in coming months highlight a risk to the outlook for subprime credit quality.

speaker: LIANG
text: Fewer borrowers currently have the ability to refinance because of less home equity accumulation, higher interest rates, and tighter credit conditions.

speaker: LIANG
text: However, many lenders are working with borrowers to modify their loans.

speaker: LIANG
text: In addition, our most recent data indicate that, while credit conditions have tightened, financing remains available.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the bottom left panel, spreads on new subprime MBS issues have eased from their peaks in April, although they have moved up in recent weeks, triggered by concerns related to losses at Bear Stearns’s hedge funds.

speaker: LIANG
text: Subprime mortgage originations, the full height of the bars in the right panel, while down substantially from record highs in late 2005, are not inconsiderable.

speaker: LIANG
text: Moreover, funds appear to have been available both for refinancings, the blue bars, and for home purchases, the green bars.

speaker: LIANG
text: My colleague Mike Leahy will continue.

speaker: LEAHY
text: As you know from the Greenbook, recent news on foreign economic activity has been generally upbeat, supporting our view that growth abroad will continue at a solid pace.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The top panel of exhibit 10 shows our weighted average of total foreign GDP growth and our outlook.

speaker: LEAHY
text: If our forecast is borne out, foreign growth will soften slightly over the forecast period, to about 3½ percent, which is also our current best guess of the rate of foreign potential growth.

speaker: LEAHY
text: As you can see from the chart, rates of growth of 3½ percent (the thin horizontal line) or better are not unprecedented, but a stretch of five consecutive years, like that from 2004 to 2008, would be unusual.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The chart also shows foreign growth maintaining most of the momentum it developed over the past couple of years even as U.S. growth has taken a more substantial step down.

speaker: LEAHY
text: This is also a bit unusual.

speaker: LEAHY
text: However, as shown in the middle left panel, foreign domestic demand gained strength throughout the current expansion, leaving foreign economies less dependent on demand from the United States.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Foreign investment spending, in particular, has been picking up.

speaker: LEAHY
text: As shown to the right, fixed investment spending as a share of GDP has moved up a couple of percentage points since 2003.

speaker: LEAHY
text: With foreign activity expanding slightly faster than potential, it is not surprising that we are seeing signs in some foreign economies that labor market slack is dwindling.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The unemployment rate in Japan, shown in the bottom left panel, is at a nine-year low; in Canada, the rate is at a thirty-year low; and the euro-area rate is also at a multiyear low.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Tight labor market conditions are less apparent in emerging- market economies, although we are hearing stories of labor shortages in certain sectors in China, where growth has been extremely rapid.

speaker: LEAHY
text: What is more apparent is that in markets for oil and other primary commodities, shown in the bottom right panel, demand has outstripped available supply, driving prices higher.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Supply capacity is expanding, however, and we are projecting, consistent with futures markets, that commodity prices will flatten out by the end of the forecast period.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Before they do, our forecast calls for oil prices to rise a bit further over the remainder of 2007 and 2008.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Food commodity prices are projected to move slightly higher on average as well, in part as energy-related demand for grains remains strong.

speaker: LEAHY
text: If this forecast is realized, oil and energy prices should impart in coming quarters noticeable but only moderate upward pressure on headline consumer price inflation abroad.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In part this is because the projected increase in oil prices is relatively modest, at least compared with what we’ve seen in recent years.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In addition, the direct effect of oil prices on consumer prices in many cases is damped by tax structures or more-active government intervention in energy markets.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The top panels of exhibit 11, which examine the pass-through of crude oil prices to gasoline prices, provide some evidence of how such pass-through varies across countries.

speaker: LEAHY
text: These panels present local-currency prices of unleaded gasoline and imported crude oil over the past couple of years or so, plotted on a ratio scale so that vertical distances correspond to percent changes in prices.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Looking across the panels, you can see that the price of imported crude oil in local currency—the black line at the bottom of each panel—moves similarly across countries.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In contrast, the prices that consumers pay at the pump—the red lines—are less volatile in the foreign economies shown than in the United States and have moved up more slowly.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In part, this reflects some differing movements in refinery and distribution margins, which are represented by the gap between imported crude oil prices and retail gasoline prices excluding taxes (the blue lines).

speaker: LEAHY
text: This is most noticeable for Japan, where margins are proportionally higher and more of the increase in crude oil prices was absorbed than in the United States and the other countries.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In addition, higher gasoline taxes abroad have inserted a greater wedge between the pre-tax price and the retail price of gasoline—the difference between the blue and the red lines.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Accordingly, increased crude oil prices have pushed up retail gasoline prices proportionally less abroad than in the United States.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The middle left panel presents some calculations of the rates at which the changes in crude oil prices were passed through to the retail gasoline prices between September 2004 and March of this year, the most recent observation I have for these countries.

speaker: LEAHY
text: During this period, rates of pass-through were lower abroad, particularly for Japan and Germany, the countries with relatively high taxes.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The smaller pass- through of oil prices to retail gasoline prices abroad has also shown through to broader measures of consumer energy prices.

speaker: LEAHY
text: As shown to the right, consumer energy prices in Canada, Germany, and Japan have increased less than those in the United States over the past four years.

speaker: LEAHY
text: An extra factor holding down energy price inflation in Canada over this period was the substantial appreciation of the Canadian dollar, which made imported energy relatively cheaper.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Overall, this suggests that the effects of past increases in global energy prices on headline inflation, as well as on consumer sentiment and inflation expectations, were likely smaller abroad than in the United States.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In many emerging market economies, gasoline and other retail energy prices are controlled or subsidized, so that energy-related fluctuations in consumer prices, if they occur at all, tend to be gradual.

speaker: LEAHY
text: For this group of economies, what has left a bigger imprint on headline consumer price inflation in recent months is the global rise in food prices.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The black line in the bottom left panel shows that food price inflation in Mexico has been heavily influenced in recent years by enormous, weather-induced swings in domestic tomato price inflation, shown in red (of course).

speaker: LEAHY
text: This year, however, food price inflation has not followed tomato price inflation down.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Rather, it has been sustained in part by a sharp acceleration in prices of tortillas and other corn products, shown by the green line, which are responding to the fuel-related surge in the global price of corn.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Food price inflation in China, shown to the right in black, has also been boosted by higher grain prices, as higher feed costs, along with an outbreak of swine flu, have driven up meat and poultry prices.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Prices for corn and other grains are forecast to level out by the end of 2008, after they have increased enough to align supply and demand growth.

speaker: LEAHY
text: A risk, of course, is that further rapid expansion of demand might continue to outstrip that of supply, making food price inflation more persistent and more likely to spur inflation in other sectors.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The Bank of Mexico cited such a risk following its policy tightening in April, and China’s authorities have raised concerns that food prices may exert upward pressure on wages.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Evidence for emerging market economies that inflation pressures might already be spreading outside the food and energy sectors is limited so far, however.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The top left panel of exhibit 12 shows core inflation rates in four of our largest emerging market trading partners.

speaker: LEAHY
text: China’s core rate (in blue), which excludes only food, shows no sign of wider inflation pressures.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In Brazil, inflation has declined substantially over the past few years, despite a slight uptick recently.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Core inflation in Korea has been trending upward, but it is still low.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Mexico’s core inflation rate has edged up toward 4 percent, a rate that concerns Mexican authorities, but this upward trend may merely reflect the fact that core inflation in Mexico does not exclude processed food such as corn tortillas.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The advanced foreign economies appear to be exhibiting more broadly based inflation pressures.

speaker: LEAHY
text: As shown on the right, in Canada, the euro area, and the United Kingdom, core inflation has been on a rising trend since the middle of 2006 or earlier.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In response, the central banks in all three economies, as well as the Bank of Japan, are expected to tighten policy in the near term.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Core inflation is still in generally acceptable ranges, however, except perhaps for the Bank of Japan, for which it might be too low, and market sentiment does not indicate concern that inflation pressures are going to rise substantially.

speaker: LEAHY
text: As you can see from the middle left panel, ten-year government bond yields in the major markets have all risen since the beginning of the year.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Except for Japan, most of the increases in nominal yields (the first column) can be attributed to higher real yields, shown in the second, which is consistent with stronger prospects for growth.

speaker: LEAHY
text: The table to the right shows that survey measures of inflation expectations for the year 2007 rose moderately for Canada between December and June and a bit less for the United Kingdom, whereas the measures fell off some for the euro area and Japan.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Longer-run inflation expectations as of the most recent survey date in April were still locked in at rates consistent with inflation targets in Canada, the euro area, and the United Kingdom.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Our outlook for headline inflation abroad, shown in the bottom panels, reflects a diminishing inflationary impulse from oil and other primary commodity prices as they flatten out over the forecast period.

speaker: LEAHY
text: It also incorporates the view that some further monetary policy tightening will be needed to restrain domestic demand and guide inflation in each economy toward its price stability objective by the end of the forecast period.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Your last two international exhibits focus on the extent to which external adjustment is under way.

speaker: LEAHY
text: A little more than a year ago, in May, was the last time we forecast that the U.S. current account deficit in 2007 would exceed $1 trillion.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Since then, as shown in the top left panel of exhibit 13, our outlook for the current account has improved substantially, so much so that currently we don’t see the deficit reaching $1 trillion within our forecast period.

speaker: LEAHY
text: As shown to the right, much of the improvement has come through an improved outlook for the trade balance.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Two likely suspects fail to provide the answer.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Given the recent strength of foreign growth, one might have thought that a year ago we were perhaps too pessimistic on foreign activity and consequently undershot on U.S. export performance.

speaker: LEAHY
text: However, as shown in the middle left panel, our outlook today for foreign economic activity is very similar to what we had in mind a year ago.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Similarly, the decline over the past year in the broad real dollar, shown to the right, which has helped curb the deterioration in the trade balance, has turned out to be not much different from our forecast a year ago.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Part of the answer, it turns out, is that, even though the assumptions we fed our model for exports have not proved much off the mark, our model forecast for core exports, shown at the bottom left, failed to catch the unusually strong growth of exports in 2006.

speaker: LEAHY
text: We attribute this miss to the composition of foreign demand rather than its overall magnitude.

speaker: LEAHY
text: As shown in the table to the right, the largest contributors to growth of U.S. core exports in 2006 were in the categories of capital goods (line 2) and industrial supplies (line 3).

speaker: LEAHY
text: With capital goods making up a large fraction of core exports, the rise in foreign investment as a share of GDP (mentioned earlier) likely provided a boost to core exports above that indicated by our aggregate measure of foreign GDP.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Similarly, the global commodity boom likely favored U.S. exports of industrial supplies.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Additional factors behind the improved outlook for the U.S. current account are described in exhibit 14.

speaker: LEAHY
text: One is the lower path of U.S. real GDP, shown in the top left panel, which prompted real imports of core goods, shown to the right, to expand along a shallower trajectory than we had predicted last year.

speaker: LEAHY
text: A third factor, illustrated in the middle left panel, is that we did not forecast the dip in the price of oil in the second half of 2006, which reduced the value of oil imports substantially.

speaker: LEAHY
text: These three factors explain the bulk of the upward adjustment in our forecast for the trade balance in 2007.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In addition, the improved outlook for the current account reflects an upward revision to net investment income, shown in the middle right.

speaker: LEAHY
text: This adjustment results from a number of factors, including new data on U.S. holdings of direct investment abroad, new procedures for determining interest payments to foreign holders of U.S. Treasuries, and a change in the methodology used to record interest flows on cross-border holdings of other fixed-income securities.

speaker: LEAHY
text: As a result of these surprises, the external accounts have clearly improved.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Going forward, we expect the current account deficit to resume widening nonetheless as interest payments on the net external debt mount.

speaker: LEAHY
text: But the combination of solid, demand- driven foreign growth and weaker U.S. growth has led the external accounts to make a more positive contribution to U.S. GDP growth in the near term, as shown in the table.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In our current forecast, shown in the rightmost column, we project that the arithmetic contribution of real net exports to GDP growth should be roughly neutral starting in the second half of this year, as strong foreign growth helps sustain real export gains that match those of real imports.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was an excellent report.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have time now for some questions for our colleagues.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Aircraft constitute what share of capital goods exports, and might they have something to do with the competitive situation, particularly between Boeing and Airbus?

speaker: LEAHY
text: Aircraft are an important factor in this.

speaker: LEAHY
text: In the fourth quarter of last year, Boeing was essentially exporting all the aircraft it could produce; so coming into the first quarter, we didn’t get much more because there weren’t any more to sell.

speaker: LEAHY
text: But that issue has been important.

speaker: LEAHY
text: I don’t know to what extent Boeing has benefited from the fact that Airbus has had some hard times, but I suspect it has gotten some benefit from that.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Aircraft are roughly 5 percent of exports.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Five percent of capital goods or of total exports?

speaker: JOHNSON
text: More like 20 percent of capital goods and 5 percent of exports.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to take David back to exhibit 5 and try to pin him down, although I am not very hopeful.

speaker: LACKER
text: You took us back to the period from 1996 to mid-2004, in which inflation, by the core PCE measure, was between 1 and 2 almost all the time—I think the only exception was basically the last few months of 2001.

speaker: LACKER
text: Core inflation averaged something like 1.6 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: You take these three survey measures there and look at them.

speaker: LACKER
text: What I took away from your assessment was that you view these as roughly consistent with that period.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I would say that the answer differs by series, so that if you tend to favor the short-term Michigan series shown in the top right, you might get a more alarming picture.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But, for example, the Survey of Professional Forecasters’ ten-year- ahead series is all the way at the other end of the spectrum, having been essentially rock solid at 2.5 percent, and these other series fall somewhere in between.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Obviously, this analysis is extraordinarily simple and doesn’t take into account other factors that may have been at work over that eight-year reference period that are not operating now.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But the hope was that, on a very rough and ready basis, this might be broadly indicative and that an eight-year period might capture some variation in other factors that were influencing inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am wholly on board with you there.

speaker: LACKER
text: What I was most curious about was what you took away from this for your core inflation outlook, which you have going to 2.0 real soon and staying there, and whether you view current expectations as broadly similar to this period and your forecast as consistent with that period?

speaker: LACKER
text: Or do you view expectations and your forecast as potentially at variance with that period, or some combination of the two?

speaker: WILCOX
text: I think we view the current constellation of expectations measures as not providing much impetus either upward or downward on inflation—it is just not going to be an important factor shaping the contour of inflation in our view.

speaker: LACKER
text: A question I had—and maybe Vince can help with this— is that the TIPS measures obviously don’t go back that far; and going back only as far as they go, my sense is that most analysts don’t view them in the earliest period in which we have quotations as representing prices and markets liquid enough to give us a sense.

speaker: LACKER
text: I guess 2003 is around the borderline of the reliability period.

speaker: LACKER
text: In 2003, those TIPS spreads for the next five years were down well into the 1 to 2 percent range, very close to 1½ percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: Do you folks view the TIPS spreads in the year or two leading to 2003 as something out of which we should take any information about inflation expectations?

speaker: WILCOX
text: Well, there is a picture in the lower right panel of chart 1 in the Bluebook.

speaker: LACKER
text: It goes back only to ’04, doesn’t it?

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, I was looking at Greenbook Part 2, page II-35, and it goes back to ’01.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In my conversations with some of the TIPS analysts on our staff, they suggested, as consistent with your statement, that 2003 was, roughly speaking, the period in their view in which the TIPS market emerged into the modern era with some tighter pricing.

speaker: LACKER
text: So there is some informational content there.

speaker: LACKER
text: Are you giving me some comfort in that regard?

speaker: REINHART
text: I think the thing to note, President Lacker, is that, if you look at the term structure of TIPS compensation, the five-year, five-year-forward in that has been a whole lot more stable.

speaker: REINHART
text: The quotes you are looking at are very much influenced by the first five years.

speaker: REINHART
text: In fact, at the end of 2001, again in 2002, and in the middle of 2003, the first five years’ inflation compensation fell below 1½ percent.

speaker: REINHART
text: Yes, the TIPS inflation-compensation measure.

speaker: REINHART
text: During the same period, however, the five-year, five-year-forward basically bounced up and down around 2½ percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the longer-run expectations maybe weren’t so anchored or weren’t tied to the middle of this period.

speaker: LACKER
text: But we had a period in which there was an indication that expectations over the near term were around 1½.

speaker: LACKER
text: I guess the thing I would be curious about, and maybe Vince’s presentation is a more appropriate time to address this question—I would be happy to defer it until then—is that viewing 1996 to 2003 as sort of a distinct period in which we nailed things between 1 and 2 for a while suggests thinking about the transition from ’03 forward a couple of years as a transition out of price stability defined that way and whether we can take any lessons from that for the potential costs of a transition back to a period like that.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just wanted to thank Mike, in particular, for that excellent presentation on the international dimension of this.

speaker: FISHER
text: It was sterling, or euro, or whatever the expression would be in terms of its excellence.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have a tutorial question about the export figures.

speaker: FISHER
text: I assume services are not included in core exports.

speaker: LEAHY
text: No, that is just goods.

speaker: FISHER
text: Are our service exports increasing more rapidly than our non- service exports?

speaker: FISHER
text: Would they be a possible source of explanation for the improved trade balance?

speaker: LEAHY
text: They are a possible source.

speaker: LEAHY
text: They were my fourth factor, if I had gone on longer.

speaker: LEAHY
text: They were neck and neck with the oil imports in terms of their contribution to the improved outlook for trade.

speaker: FISHER
text: That was an excellent presentation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Just a question about scale—regarding exhibit 8, serious mortgage delinquency rates—when you refer to adjustable rates going to almost 12 percent of loans, is that of adjustable-rate loans?

speaker: HOENIG
text: What is the total dollar value the 10 percent is against?

speaker: LIANG
text: The serious delinquency rate is for the pool of adjustable-rate subprime loans, and they represent about 9 percent of the outstanding mortgages.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Okay—and the total outstanding mortgages are what dollar amount?

speaker: LIANG
text: There is $10 trillion in mortgages outstanding.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is what I thought.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I just wanted to make sure.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But to make sure that is right, the red lines are subprime?

speaker: LIANG
text: The red lines are subprime.

speaker: LIANG
text: Subprime adjustable-rate loans are about 9 percent of outstandings, and subprime fixed loans are another 5 percent of outstandings.

speaker: LIANG
text: That would be 9 percent of the $10 trillion in total mortgages.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although the percentages are by number of mortgages rather than by value, I think.

speaker: LIANG
text: By dollar it is very similar.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Also, on exhibit 8, the net worth chart in the top left-hand corner—I thought I heard you say that this was high by historical standards.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So there are two things here—the stock market has been strong, and then housing prices have been very weak.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I assume if you run this out into another year, the line is going to keep going down as well.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I was just wondering if you could expand on this.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Is this higher than you expected it to be at this particular time?

speaker: LIANG
