text: If we had started this series in the early ’90s, this would be the high.

speaker: LIANG
text: We have the stock market bubble of 2000 in here, and it has come off, but it is 5½.

speaker: LIANG
text: Even at the end of the projection period, it is 5½ times disposable income.

speaker: LIANG
text: Before ’96, it would have been about 3½ or 4.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We do indeed forecast it to continue to decline over the next year or so, in large measure because, as David shows in his chart, we still think this house price adjustment has to proceed further before we get into a better equilibrium.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Our assumption on the stock price, of course, is pretty neutral because we have it going up pretty close to the overall rate of nominal income, so I think the downward tilt is being driven mostly by the house price story.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: On a longer-term trend basis, where would you expect it to stabilize or to level out?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Take this for what it is worth, which isn’t a whole lot.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It drops just a bit; it is between 5½ and 5¼ over the longer haul and just gradually declines back in that direction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Hoenig, I think I interrupted you.

speaker: HOENIG
text: This is the number of loans—then do you have any idea what the percentage of the dollar amount of loans is in delinquency?

speaker: LIANG
text: We think there is probably $900 billion to $1 trillion in adjustable- rate subprime mortgages outstanding.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wasn’t sure I heard correctly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What was the average ratio of wealth to disposable income over the ’90s roughly?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The number I recall is 4.6 as the long-run average since the ’80s.

speaker: STERN
text: I want to go back to the surprise in net exports once again.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t quite remember the argument, but it seems to me we used to worry a lot about small foreign elasticities of demand for U.S. goods and services when the dollar declined or when income growth differentials changed.

speaker: STERN
text: Has what we have seen lately affected your view about that?

speaker: LEAHY
text: I would say it hasn’t affected our view in the sense that we haven’t changed the elasticities that we are using on the basis of this one year’s observation, but it points in the right direction.

speaker: LEAHY
text: I mean, we are getting a little bit more “umph” from foreign growth than we thought before.

speaker: LEAHY
text: Whether it is going to be a one-time miss related to aircraft—there was some temporary investment surge in foreign economies, and we are a capital goods exporter, and we are just taking advantage of that, and it is going to go back—or whether it persists is a little too early to tell.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: We have updated the elasticities since ten years ago.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: When you first heard us nattering on about the unsustainability of the U.S. current account situation, we had perhaps a more extreme view of those elasticities.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: If you drop out the 1970s and you restrict your estimates to a more recent period, you tend to get elasticities that move toward each other a little.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But the basic asymmetry is still there, and we haven’t responded to 2006 in some specific way.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: We’re letting a little more time go by to see what happens going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In exhibit 9, the average initial rate on the stock of mortgages that you are looking at for resetting over the next couple of years is about 7⅓ percent.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: What is roughly the current rate for subprime fixed-rate loans?

speaker: LIANG
text: It is around 9 percent.

speaker: LIANG
text: If you get on the Internet and try to find a subprime fixed-rate loan, it would be about that.

speaker: LIANG
text: We can’t find an official series, but roughly 9.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So they are facing a 2½ percent payment shock if they stick with the mortgage.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But if they were able to switch to a fixed-rate product, it is about 1½ percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no other questions, Vincent, could I call on you to talk about the economic projections?

speaker: REINHART
text: As was evident in the survey responses summarized in the memo of June 15 on your attitudes toward the economic projections, there seems to be broad agreement among you on the key features of the process.

speaker: REINHART
text: Where there was not, including about sharing forecasts, the specification of the monetary policy assumption, and the characterization of uncertainty, the Subcommittee on Communications tried to find common ground.

speaker: REINHART
text: The result was reflected in the survey on the economic outlook for this meeting, which I will discuss with the aid of the material distributed with the cover “Economic Projections of FOMC Participants.” As can be seen by comparing the bolded with the italicized numbers in the first exhibit, there were only minor changes in your projections of real GDP growth, the unemployment rate, and core PCE inflation over the next two and one-half years from those you submitted in May.

speaker: REINHART
text: Given the favorable data over the intermeeting period, you raised your real growth forecasts a notch and lowered the core PCE inflation forecasts for 2007.

speaker: REINHART
text: Still, as plotted in the top panel of exhibit 2, the red bars showing the central tendency of your forecasts indicate that most of you anticipate that GDP growth will be somewhat soft this year but will pick up a bit over 2008 and 2009.

speaker: REINHART
text: Although the submissions were not specific about potential output growth—and not all of you would agree that it is even a useful concept—this expansion of real output would seem initially to be slower than that of capacity in that the central tendency for the unemployment rate (the second panel) edges higher.

speaker: REINHART
text: With resource markets less taut and perhaps some transitory factors ebbing, core PCE inflation (the third panel) drifts down.

speaker: REINHART
text: In this experiment, you were asked for inflation readings coming from two measurement systems.

speaker: REINHART
text: The historical wedge between inflation measured by the core PCE price index and the total consumer price index is about ½ percentage point.

speaker: REINHART
text: The central tendency projections for those two series in 2008 and 2009 are about that far apart, leading to the inference that you are not forecasting significant changes to the relative prices of energy and food.

speaker: REINHART
text: The subcommittee suggested forecasting these two inflation series in the spirit of experimentation.

speaker: REINHART
text: Sometime in the next two days, you might want to express how useful you found that part of the experiment.

speaker: REINHART
text: Another notable feature of your projections is that the differences among them widen, rather than narrow, the further into the future you forecast.

speaker: REINHART
text: This suggests a diversity of views as to key attributes of the economy as well as where you believe inflation should be headed in the long run.

speaker: REINHART
text: As for the assumption about monetary policy underlying these outcomes, about two-thirds of you indicated general agreement with the path laid out in the Greenbook.

speaker: REINHART
text: As for the others, there were explanations advanced for being on either side of the staff assumption.

speaker: REINHART
text: 3 Material used by Mr. Reinhart is appended to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: REINHART
text: You were also asked to provide a qualitative characterization of your uncertainty about your outlook.

speaker: REINHART
text: The results for real GDP growth are given in the top panel of exhibit 3.

speaker: REINHART
text: Somewhat surprisingly, there was no Lake Wobegon effect, and the preponderance of responses viewed the real GDP growth outlook as just about as uncertain as has been the case on average over the past twenty years.

speaker: REINHART
text: As shown in the bottom panel, a majority of the submissions indicated that the risks around the projections for GDP growth are judged to be broadly balanced.

speaker: REINHART
text: This contrasts with the indication in the May minutes that, although the risks to economic activity had “diminished slightly,” they were still “weighted to the downside.” For some, the incoming news may have led to a reassessment of the risks to economic growth.

speaker: REINHART
text: For others, it may reflect a view that the main downside risks to activity are concentrated in the near term and those risks further ahead are broadly symmetric.

speaker: REINHART
text: To shed light on this issue, participants might want to address the main risks to economic growth and whether they are still judged to be weighted to the downside as had been the case in your May discussion.

speaker: REINHART
text: Some more detail about your forecasts of the unemployment rate is provided in exhibit 4.

speaker: REINHART
text: A majority of the projections embody a more muted rise in the unemployment rate than in the Greenbook forecast, the dashed vertical lines.

speaker: REINHART
text: This smaller expected increase may partly reflect the stronger outlook for GDP growth suggested by many of your projections.

speaker: REINHART
text: But then again, it may not: [laughter] From the comments in the narratives about the likely strength of trend growth, it is not clear that the projected growth in output relative to trend is expected to be materially more robust than that suggested by the staff’s forecast.

speaker: REINHART
text: Does the more modest projected rise in unemployment reflect a difference in views from the staff’s about the rate of growth of potential output, the unemployment rate associated with no change in the inflation rate, cyclical movements in productivity, or other factors?

speaker: REINHART
text: Exhibit 5 provides a tally of the year-by-year inflation outlook.

speaker: REINHART
text: A majority of the projections have a more benign medium-term outlook for core inflation than that suggested by the staff’s forecast.

speaker: REINHART
text: But the responses to the question about the appropriate path of interest rates indicate that for a majority of projections this does not stem from a significantly tighter stance of monetary policy than assumed by the staff.

speaker: REINHART
text: Likewise, the projections for GDP growth and unemployment do not appear to imply greater economic slack than expected by the staff.

speaker: REINHART
text: For some, this more marked moderation in inflation may reflect a judgment that more of the rise in core inflation reflects the effect of temporary influences, such as the rise in energy prices and owners’ equivalent rent, that are likely to abate over the forecast period.

speaker: REINHART
text: For others, it may reflect an assessment that the NAIRU is lower than that assumed by the staff or that inflation expectations may edge lower over the forecast period, perhaps pulled down by Federal Reserve communications.

speaker: REINHART
text: You might wish to exchange views about the main factors contributing to the expected moderation in inflation in your forecasts.

speaker: REINHART
text: As to where inflation is headed in the longer run, many of you indicated that the third-year projections (the bottom panel) reflect to a considerable degree your policy goal rather than initial conditions.

speaker: REINHART
text: If that is the case, the central tendency reveals that most of you individually define the inflation rate that best fosters the dual mandate to be 1½ to 2 percent when measured by the core PCE inflation rate.

speaker: REINHART
text: Given your apparent beliefs about future movements in the relative prices of food and energy, discussed earlier, you would also seem to think that total PCE inflation should place within a range of 1½ to 2 percent.

speaker: REINHART
text: As for the process from here on, if you would like to change your forecast in light of the discussion at this meeting or data received since you prepared your projection, we ask that you submit your revision to the Secretariat by close of business Friday.

speaker: REINHART
text: Unless we are instructed differently as a result of the discussion tomorrow, the staff will draft a minutes-style narrative description of the economic projections.

speaker: REINHART
text: This will be a standalone document that will circulate with the draft minutes on the regular schedule as was the case in May.

speaker: REINHART
text: One last point: Your final exhibit gives the traditional presentation of your economic projections that will be made public in the Monetary Policy Report and included in the published minutes.

speaker: REINHART
text: If you want to change your submission, please let us know by Friday.

speaker: REINHART
text: How you judge the usefulness of this exhibit compared with the forecasts compiled for the experiment presumably will be one topic for discussion tomorrow.

speaker: REINHART
text: That concludes my prepared remarks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thanks for reminding us that this projection counts in some sense, right?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also, I think it is very useful for us to have the discipline of thinking about how our projections fit together.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Vincent?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, then we can begin our economic go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Who would like to go first?

speaker: YELLEN
text: Data relating to both economic activity and inflation during the intermeeting period have been encouraging.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Economic indicators have strengthened considerably, and recent readings on core inflation have been quite tame.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although a portion of the recent deceleration of core prices likely reflects transitory influences, the underlying trend in core inflation is still quite favorable.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I view the conditions for growth going forward as being reasonably solid.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The main negative factors are tied to housing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The latest data don’t point to an imminent recovery in this sector, and I fear that the recent run-up in mortgage rates will only make matters worse.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition, housing prices are unlikely to rise over the next few years and, indeed, may well fall, and the absence of the housing wealth gains realized in the past should damp consumption spending.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I agree with the Greenbook that the recent run-up in bond and mortgage rates reflects primarily a shift in market expectations for the path of policy and, therefore, implies only a small subtraction to my forecast for growth in 2008.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In my view, the stance of monetary policy over the next few years should be chosen to help move labor and product markets from being somewhat tight today to exhibiting a modest degree of slack in order to help bring about a further gradual reduction in inflation toward a level consistent with price stability.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The stance of monetary policy will need to remain modestly restrictive, along the lines assumed in the Greenbook and by markets, in order to achieve that goal.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My forecast is for growth to be around 2½ percent in the second half of this year and in 2008, slightly below my estimate of potential growth, and for the unemployment rate to edge up gradually, reaching nearly 5 percent by the end of next year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Under these conditions, core inflation should continue to recede gradually, with the core PCE price index increasing 2 percent this year and 1.9 percent in 2008.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This forecast is predicated on continued well-anchored inflation expectations and the eventual appearance of a small amount of labor market slack.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition, special factors such as rising energy prices and the sustained run-up in owners’ equivalent rent that have boosted inflation should ebb over time, contributing a bit to the expected decline in core inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In terms of risks to the outlook for growth, I still feel the presence of a 600-pound gorilla in the room, and that is the housing sector.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The risk for further significant deterioration in the housing market, with house prices falling and mortgage delinquencies rising further, causes me appreciable angst.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, the repercussions of falling house prices are already playing out in some areas where past price rises were especially rapid and subprime lending soared.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, in the Sacramento metropolitan area east of San Francisco, house prices shot up at an annual rate of more than 20 percent from 2002 to 2005.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Since then, however, they have been falling at an annual rate of 3½ percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Delinquencies on subprime mortgages rose sharply last year, putting Sacramento at the top of the list of MSAs in terms of the changes in the rate of subprime delinquencies.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Research by my staff examining metropolitan areas across the country indicates that the experience of Sacramento reflects a more general pattern.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They found that low rates of house price appreciation, and especially house price decelerations, are associated with increases in delinquency rates even after controlling for local economic conditions such as employment growth and the unemployment rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One possible explanation for these findings is that subprime borrowers, especially those with very low equity stakes, have less incentive to keep their mortgages current when housing no longer seems an attractive investment, either because prices have decelerated sharply or interest rates have risen.

speaker: YELLEN
text: These results highlight the potential risks that rising defaults in subprime could spread to other sectors of the mortgage market and could trigger a vicious cycle in which a further deceleration in house prices increases foreclosures, in turn exacerbating downside price movements.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The risks to inflation are also significant.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition to the upside risks associated with continued tight labor markets, a slowdown in productivity growth could add to cost pressures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although recent productivity data have been disappointing, I expressed some optimism at the last meeting about productivity growth on the grounds that at least some of the slowdown appeared to reflect labor hoarding and lags in the adjustment of employment to output, especially in the construction industry.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Data since that meeting have reinforced my optimism concerning trend productivity growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In particular, new data in the recently released Business Employment Dynamics report suggest that productivity growth may have been stronger than we have been thinking.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This report, which includes data that will be used in the rebenchmarking of the payroll survey in January, shows a much smaller increase in employment in the third quarter of 2006 than is reported in the payroll survey; it, therefore, implies a larger increase in output per worker.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A second risk to inflation is slippage in the market’s perceptions of our inflation objective.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although inflation compensation over the next five years is essentially unchanged since our last meeting, long-run breakeven inflation rates implied by the difference between nominal and indexed Treasury securities are up about 20 basis points.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, our analysis suggests that this increase reflects in good part an elevation in risk premiums or the influence of various—let me call them “idiosyncratic”—factors of the type that Bill Dudley mentioned, such as a possible shift in the demand by foreign central banks for Treasuries or special factors affecting the demand for inflation-indexed securities and not an increase in long-run inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We base this conclusion on the fact that long-run breakeven inflation rates have also climbed in the United Kingdom—a country where inflation expectations have been remarkably well anchored over the past decade and where inflation has been trending downward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The fact that breakeven inflation rates rose in both countries, despite their different monetary policy regimes, suggests that a common explanation is needed rather than one specific to the United States.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think this conclusion is supported by the Board staff model that attributes about half of the movement in breakeven inflation to risk premiums.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That said, our understanding and estimates of risk premiums are imprecise, so we must continue to monitor inflation expectations very carefully—of course, along with everything else.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Conditions in the Seventh District have changed little since my last report.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Overall activity in the District is lagging the nation, mainly because of the continued difficulties of what we now call the Detroit Three, formerly known as the Big Three, [laughter] and their suppliers.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: But other sectors of our region are doing better—notably, a number of manufacturers outside autos—and consumer spending is moving forward at a moderate rate.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Looking at the outlook for the national economy, the Greenbook baseline forecast has growth recovering to potential and core inflation stabilizing at 2 percent.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Our outlook is not much different.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: We see growth returning close to potential.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Assuming that monetary policy maintains its slightly restrictive stance, we think inflation will edge a shade below 2 percent by 2009.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: That would be a good outcome, and I sure hope we get it.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: The biggest news since the May FOMC meeting is the adjustment in financial conditions.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: The change in fed funds futures brings market expectations into better alignment with what I think will be the appropriate path for monetary policy.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I’m not sure, however, how much restraint we can expect from the increase in long-term interest rates.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: As the Chairman heard from our directors last week, the effects can be muted by ample liquidity in the financial markets.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: One of our directors, who heads a large private equity firm, says that he does not see much of a change in the lending environment.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Financing for even high-risk projects continues to be readily available at quite favorable rates and terms.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Notably, such loans are being made with few covenants and no automatic default triggers.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Of course, the housing market remains a risk.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Like the Greenbook, we continue to expect large declines in residential investment through the end of this year, and I remain concerned that builders may need to cut back even more to reduce the high inventory of unsold homes.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Our Detroit Branch director, who is CFO of Pulte Homes, noted that two-thirds of their sales usually occur between the Super Bowl and Memorial Day.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Sales this year in that period were sluggish and relatively unresponsive to price discounting.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Accordingly, he is not looking for a turnaround in housing markets before ’08.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Another director, the head of U.S. Gypsum, agreed that it would be ’08 before we could expect a pickup in housing.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: With regard to consumer spending more generally, some contacts noted the impact of higher gasoline prices.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: A developer of malls and shopping centers downgraded his expectations for the rest of 2007, but he is not overly pessimistic and is expecting retail sales in the second half to remain near their first-half pace.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Both GM and Ford believe that the higher gasoline prices are holding down the overall level of motor vehicle sales in addition to moving the mix of sales away from SUVs and toward cars.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: At this point, they believe that higher interest rates are having only a marginal effect on demand.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Both are predicting that total light vehicle sales will be about 16.5 million units in 2007.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: That is the same as the pace predicted by the participants in our annual outlook symposium that we held in Detroit earlier this month.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: But the rest of the manufacturing is doing better than autos.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Producers of heavy machinery and agricultural equipment continue to report strong demand.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: The Chicago purchasing managers’ report, which is confidential until its release this Friday, was 60.2 in June; that reading is down only a bit from its very high one of 61.7 in May.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Some of this strength reflects strong growth abroad, which is fueling the demand for U.S. products, as we talked about during the chart show.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Indeed, I think that there may be some upside risks to the GDP forecast from faster-than-expected export growth.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Labor markets continue to be strong, and we heard the usual stories about selected labor shortages and associated increases in wages.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: One exception is the soft demand for temporary workers, but this could be normal for a mature business cycle.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Turning to prices, our contacts seem to be a bit more pessimistic about the prospects for inflation.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: We heard concerns that higher energy prices would boost transportation costs and that the demand for food stuffs from abroad and the booming domestic ethanol market are pushing up food prices.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: In contrast to the anecdotes, the incoming data on core inflation were better than expected.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Our indicator models revised down a tenth or two from the last round; they now have core PCE inflation being about 2 percent this year and next and then edging down to 1.8 or 1.9 in 2009.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Without any meaningful resource slack, this improvement would require a comparable adjustment in inflation expectations, which may be difficult given a prolonged period of core inflation at or above 2 percent.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So I continue to think that the predominant risk remains that inflation will not moderate as expected.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Fifth District’s economy has picked up since the last meeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: Retail sales rose briskly in June following several months of flatness, and shopper traffic increased more broadly as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: Of particular interest, building supply and furniture retailers report better sales.

speaker: LACKER
text: Big-ticket sales remain generally weak, however, with domestic brand automobile dealers continuing to note soft sales.

speaker: LACKER
text: Activity at District services firms added to an already healthy pace of growth, with revenues and employment expanding somewhat faster in June.

speaker: LACKER
text: In May, our manufacturing sector finally joined in the general manufacturing pickup that began a few months back in other regions.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our indexes for shipments and new orders swung well into positive territory after having spent the entire year well down in the negative region.

speaker: LACKER
text: This rebound appears to be broadly based, with most industries posting stronger readings.

speaker: LACKER
text: Housing sales and construction remain weak in most parts of the District, though home prices have been more resilient, with very modest gains reported in most areas and lower prices in only a few.

speaker: LACKER
text: In contrast, the commercial real estate sector appears to be fairly strong, with both leasing and construction looking solid.

speaker: LACKER
text: Regarding inflation, our survey measures suggest that price trends in the services sector remain moderate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our manufacturing numbers, however, consistent with President Moskow’s report of anecdotal information, indicate significant price acceleration, on both the product and the input sides.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the national level, the new information on the real economy we have received since the last meeting has been fairly positive.

speaker: LACKER
text: In particular, I’m heartened by the recent reports on business investment and manufacturing, which appear to confirm our expectations that the softness we were seeing a few months ago would prove to be transitory.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consumer spending also continues to expand, although not as rapidly as earlier in the year.

speaker: LACKER
text: Housing, of course, continues to be the main drag on spending, and the most prominent source of uncertainty about the real outlook.

speaker: LACKER
text: My sense is that the uncertainty is receding, however.

speaker: LACKER
text: Construction numbers have more or less moved sideways since the beginning of the year, in contrast to the sharp fall we saw in the first three quarters of last year.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it looks to me as though we’re nearing a bottom in housing activity, albeit a bottom that may slope gently away from the steep cliff we descended last year.

speaker: LACKER
text: At this point, I think the risk of encountering another cliff has become relatively small.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have also received favorable readings on core inflation for the past three months.

speaker: LACKER
text: This has brought the twelve-month core PCE number down to 2.0 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: While this news is good, we should react cautiously, of course.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have seen several months of favorable data before only to see several months of unfavorable numbers.

speaker: LACKER
text: Moreover, the Greenbook points to a number of special factors suggesting that the second quarter’s better inflation performance is likely to be transitory.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am inclined to agree with that assessment, and so I think we could well see core inflation rise again.

speaker: LACKER
text: Measures of near-term inflation expectations have not moved much in recent months.

speaker: LACKER
text: They all still point to PCE inflation expectations of 2 percent or so.

speaker: LACKER
text: Moreover, five-year, five-year-ahead inflation compensation has moved up ¼ percentage point, for whatever reason, since just before our last meeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: All this makes it hard to be confident that we are going to see a sustained decline of inflation below 2 percent anytime soon.

speaker: LACKER
text: The good news on the real side, however, suggests that we are making progress toward seeing downside risks diminish enough for us to do something about inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, for the sake of consistency, I will refer to my report at the last two meetings on what I call the Goldilocks porridge classification system.

speaker: FISHER
text: I reported last that the international economy was hot, and it remains so as we saw in the excellent slide presentation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I reported that the domestic economy was cold.

speaker: FISHER
text: I believe it remains so, in contrast I think to the previous two interventions, at least from a growth perspective.

speaker: FISHER
text: I also reported that the Eleventh District, home of the NBA champions, vanquishers of the—shall I say “more cavalier”?—Fourth District, [laughter] was just right.

speaker: FISHER
text: It remained so in relative terms.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would say that it has weakened somewhat and cooled somewhat in absolute terms.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just want to comment quickly on the international side of the domestic economy, with the hopes of adding on the margin to the staff’s excellent work in the Greenbook, the Bluebook, and the presentations we had earlier.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the international side, I was pleased that for the first time, at least since I have been a member of this august body, the last minutes reported that the participants expressed “some concern that the strength of global demand could contribute to price pressures at home” and noted “heightened levels of capacity utilization in those countries.” We didn’t talk about capacity utilization in your excellent report.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just wanted to add that our work in Dallas and my CEO contacts continue to validate the phenomenon that we are getting closer to capacity constraints abroad.

speaker: FISHER
text: Research by the Dallas staff, imperfect as it is, confirmed continued growth overseas, resulting in a tightening of capacity around the world, as does the work of JPMorgan, one of the few places in the private sector that we find has spent a good deal of time contemplating this issue.

speaker: FISHER
text: Anecdotal reports from CEOs and CFOs confirm this trend.

speaker: FISHER
text: The rest of the world is reported to be offering more fertile soil for growth and investment, as I think President Moskow pointed out.

speaker: FISHER
text: Shippers tell me that tonnage demand for dry bulk is running at a rate significantly higher than last year, driven by underlying demand outside the United States and despite slower rates of growth of shipments to the United States.

speaker: FISHER
text: You also see this in ship charter rates remaining high.

speaker: FISHER
text: Freight rates, which don’t have a spot market and are much more difficult to measure, appear to be rising in terms of their volume expansion and in shipments to Europe from the Pacific—certainly at a faster rate than those shipments from the Pacific to the United States.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of the largest engineering logistics firms in the world reports that, with the exception of downstream oil and gas investments, power, and an as yet unannounced nuclear power plant that will be built in the United States, their bookings and substantial backlog are “all driven by non-U.S. demand, with cost escalation not only of commodity inputs but of the building blocks and their materials, such as compressors and pumps, and so on, despite the leveling-off of the price of steel.” On the cost side, the head of the United States’ largest importer of consumer goods—without mentioning the name of the retail company—[laughter] reports that cost pressures, as you indicated before in your presentation, coming from China are leading them to “aggressively seek to shift imports to other country sources; in certain sectors, China is becoming too pricey.” At home, business operators to whom I talked are more equivocal about growth prospects for the economy, Mr. Chairman, than I expected.

speaker: FISHER
text: The CEO of one of the largest rails describes the economy as “lethargic.” The CEO of one of the largest IT firms “doesn’t see much sequential growth.” The CEO of an airline, which is not Southwest Airlines, says that “domestically, the seasonally adjusted revenue for the industry line is flat.” A usually ebullient CEO of one of the nation’s largest broadcasters said that “while Q2 is always the slowest quarter, this one is slower than normal.” The CFO of one of the flagship express shippers reports that B2C is growing at 3 to 4 percent rates of volume expansion after several years of 7 to 8 percent rates of growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: But there has been no pickup in the second quarter over the first quarter seasonally adjusted, and “it just seems to be as flat as it can be across the board in all segments.” A leading restaurateur with thirty years in the business notes that he is experiencing a combination of soft top line and rising costs for the first time in his history of operating.

speaker: FISHER
text: For added measure, the CEO of a very large retailer describes demand as “flatter than a pancake.” He and retailers at the higher price points report that shoppers are moving away from the malls to closer-to-home retailers because of transportation costs and financial insecurity.

speaker: FISHER
text: They make fewer trips, and they buy larger volumes per trip.

speaker: FISHER
text: President Yellen, I won’t depress you with the soundings from the two largest public homebuilders.

speaker: FISHER
text: I only half jokingly recommended that they take all sharp objects off their desks and seal their windows.

speaker: FISHER
text: Their situation is reported to have gone from bad to worse.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of the interesting data points is that they represent 27 percent of the homebuilders.

speaker: FISHER
text: The remainder is in private developers’ hands.

speaker: FISHER
text: They suggest that the rapidity with which those private developers report their stress is certainly much less than the publicly held companies, in part because they are afraid of their lenders.

speaker: FISHER
text: Therefore, those shoes have yet to drop, which is not an encouraging sign.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the price front, I hear two common complaints across the board.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, labor remains tight and pricey except in the homebuilding sector, where there has been some relief for obvious reasons.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second—and I think very importantly—food prices driven by corn oil are creating significant cost pressures for all crops, including substitute crops.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of the most astute contacts I have—a leading banker, not a restaurateur or a food person—says that adding ethanol to what he called a tectonic shift in demand for corn, wheat, and other food stuffs stemming from the addition of two billion people—new consumers moving up the food chain (no pun intended)—may place corn at the center of the inflation paradigm in the new century.

speaker: FISHER
text: One commonly voiced concern might influence business investment in capital expenditures.

speaker: FISHER
text: I keep hearing from each CEO, “What are we going to do with our capital?” Reports are increasing of competition from rates on the longer end of the yield curve, above 5 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: Boards of directors are reluctant to embrace the concept that eighteen months out the U.S. economy’s sun will shine more brightly than it is shining currently, and concerns linger about the costs and the availability of labor for domestic cap-ex purposes.

speaker: FISHER
text: In summary, Mr. Chairman, statistically we may have a second-quarter snapback driven by inventory adjustment as predicted by the Board staff and by my own staff.

speaker: FISHER
text: But my soundings with business leaders—again, no doubt imperfect—provide some cognitive dissonance.

speaker: FISHER
text: I didn’t hear a single one of twenty-six interlocutors who would agree with the baseline case as stated in the Greenbook.

speaker: FISHER
text: Most would agree with the alternative cases that were presented, which were quite thoughtful.

speaker: FISHER
text: I used the term “dyspeptic” in describing the mood of corporate leaders the last time we met.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would say the mood, Mr. Chairman, remains sour, and perhaps it has become more sour.

speaker: FISHER
text: I remain relatively pessimistic on growth and skeptical about inflation and the utility of reliance on the core measurement in guiding our deliberations.

speaker: STERN
text: Regarding the national economy and real growth, it seems to me that recent developments are unfolding to a considerable extent largely as anticipated.

speaker: STERN
text: Growth was positive but subdued over the four quarters ending in the first quarter of this year.

speaker: STERN
text: It apparently snapped back discernibly in the current quarter, and my forecast is for sustained growth around trend going forward.

speaker: STERN
text: In examining the twelve-month period spanning the last three quarters of last year and the first quarter of this year, it is apparent that the slowing of aggregate demand went beyond the housing sector and, in fact, was fairly broadly based.

speaker: STERN
text: To be sure, residential construction activity contracted persistently and substantially over those four quarters.

speaker: STERN
text: In addition, spending on equipment and software barely advanced, federal government outlays were soft in real terms, and there was a significant inventory correction.

speaker: STERN
text: In most cases, with the likely and perhaps obvious exception of residential construction, there are reasons to believe, based on some of the indicators that David Wilcox covered this afternoon as well as materials distributed before the meeting, that these components of demand—that is, spending on equipment and software, federal government outlays, and inventories—will strengthen going forward.

speaker: STERN
text: I thought it was particularly heartening, as noted in Part 2 of the Greenbook, that apparently the inventory overhang in construction supplies and in autos has been worked off, which suggests that we should see improvement in those sectors going forward.

speaker: STERN
text: As I have commented before at recent meetings, I think the outlook for nonresidential construction, for net exports, and for consumer spending remains positive, although not unduly exuberant.

speaker: STERN
text: All of this fits reasonably well with my view of what we should expect from productivity gains going forward, as well as increases in employment and hours worked.

speaker: STERN
text: So, overall, I think the outlook for the real economy is promising and favorable.

speaker: STERN
text: As to inflation, there has been, as everybody has noted, some moderation in the core measures recently.

speaker: STERN
text: I expect this performance to continue, not necessarily on a month-by-month basis but over time.

speaker: STERN
text: Overall, my reading of monetary policy is that it is moderately restrictive.

speaker: STERN
text: As a consequence, that should feed into a further, gradual diminution of inflation along with ebbing of some of the transitory factors that pushed it up for a time.

speaker: STERN
text: I would add that anecdotes from our business contacts don’t suggest any changes in pricing power or acceleration of inflation at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: Now, of course, risks to the outlook abound, as they always do, and many have already been mentioned.

speaker: STERN
text: Several relate, of course, to housing—construction activity, home prices, mortgage-related paper, and so forth.

speaker: STERN
text: Then, you can add uncertainty associated with energy prices, the run-up in long-term interest rates that has already occurred, and I am sure a few things that I haven’t enumerated.

speaker: STERN
text: I wouldn’t want to sound overly complacent or sanguine, but I would observe that many of these risks are not new.

speaker: STERN
text: Many of them are already built into the Greenbook or other forecasts.

speaker: STERN
text: In any event, if one of them were to occur in isolation, I would doubt that it would have a profound effect on the outlook that I have described.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The pace of growth in New England, at least as measured by employment, remains below that of the nation.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Indeed, since the trough of the last recession, New England’s jobs have grown at less than half the pace of the nation as a whole.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Some of this is the traditionally slower pace of job formation in the region, and some is undoubtedly the result of the kind of industries— telecommunications and technology more generally—that were hardest hit in the 2001 recession and have yet to recover fully.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: But some of it also revolves around issues of supply.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Almost every firm, large or small, comments on the difficulty of finding skilled labor.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: There is also reason to believe that, at least relative to the rest of the nation, the supply versus demand imbalance may be a particular issue in the region.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: This comes from the Conference Board’s online job-posting measure, which for some time has shown New England as having the highest number of advertised job openings relative to the size of the labor force.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Contacts report that they are willing to offer—and do offer— higher pay to get the skills they need, but finding the workers is harder to do and takes longer than earlier in the cycle.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Another issue that came up again in our round of contacts is the pervasive rise in the cost of almost any metal, but especially copper and aluminum.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Contacts at one very large diversified company speculated about China’s stockpiling valuable metals.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Whatever the cause, worldwide demand is strong, and prices are rising for all types of metal inputs.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Some firms report progress in passing on those price increases.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Indeed, larger manufacturing companies appear to be buoyed, if not driven, by strength in foreign markets.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: One firm reported that their booming aircraft business required such long hours and continued stress on skilled workers to figure out ways to meet demand that employee turnover had tripled.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Not surprisingly, year-over-year manufactured exports for the region rose in the first quarter.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Elsewhere, news in the region has been fairly positive, with business confidence rising and commercial real estate markets good and improving throughout.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Residential real estate markets remain slow.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Regardless of what measure is used, the region’s home prices appear to have slowed more than the nation’s.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: However, although we had led the nation—this is not something in which you want to lead the nation—in the rate of rising foreclosure initiations, especially for those related to subprime mortgages, the pace of this growth has subsided.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Indeed, initiations of subprime foreclosures went down in the region most recently.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Moreover, in the most recent data on home sales, the Northeast was a bright spot.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I have speculated before that the New England residential real estate market could be bottoming out.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Such thoughts may remain in the category more of a hope than a certainty, but perhaps the pace of decline is slowing.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Finally, while consumer confidence has been bouncy recently, probably from concerns about gasoline prices, demand seems reasonably strong as gauged by local retailers.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Software and IT firms are showing considerable strength, and at least in our region, so is temporary help.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Coincident indicators of regional health also show solid growth for all six states.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: In sum, the region appears to be doing fairly well; and except for residential real estate, there are perhaps growing signs of price and resource pressures, in that regard not unlike the nation as a whole.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Turning to the nation, I was pleased to see that incoming data validated the substantial pickup in second-quarter growth that we, along with the Greenbook, had forecasted.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Indeed, outside of residential investment, incoming data have depicted an economy that is growing at a relatively healthy pace.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Data on shipments and orders of capital goods have improved, consumer demand seems relatively well maintained despite high gas and soft home prices, and payroll data show little sign of dwindling labor demand.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Markets have at last decided to adopt the Committee’s more positive outlook on economic prospects, and credit was repriced as a result.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I view this event as healthy.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It has tempered our GDP forecast slightly, but the continued ebullience of equity markets is an important offset.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: As I noted at our last meeting, we find ourselves a bit more optimistic than the Greenbook about trends in residential real estate, based on new housing starts and data on new home sales most recently, and we have moderated the pace of decline of residential investment for the second quarter just a bit relative to our May forecast.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The April value of nonresidential construction put in place was a clear positive as well.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The health of the rest of the world continues to surprise, and we, like the Greenbook, expect little drag from net exports over the forecast period.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Turning to projections for 2008 and 2009, the factors shaping our outlook haven’t changed much.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: We continue to see output accelerating mildly as the housing situation moderates and more of the underlying strength of the economy shows through.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: This is tempered a bit both by rising long-term interest rates and by our expectations that consumers will mend their ways a bit—consume less and save more.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: This hasn’t shown signs of happening yet.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: By the end of 2009, GDP is about at potential, unemployment has ticked up a bit but remains below 5 percent, and core inflation moves down gradually to 2 percent—again, not much change and certainly within the central tendency of members’ forecasts.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: One obvious risk to this forecast lies in housing, as everybody has said.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: But as I noted at our last meeting, the longer there are no obvious spinoffs from the subprime problem to the wider economy, the more that particular risk seems to ebb.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Indeed, as we have yet to see the saving rate pick up with the moderation in consumption over what would be expected by the fundamentals, there may be some upside to growth.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Pressures from abroad—worldwide expansion of somewhat larger size than we expected—do raise some upside issues, both for growth and for inflation.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: On the inflation side, it is true that the April and May core data were encouraging.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: However, those numbers were dominated by temporary rather than permanent effects, at least in our view.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So we haven’t moderated our forecast of core inflation, as have the Greenbook authors, albeit they moderated it only in a very minor way, and I remain concerned about upside risks.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Headline CPI inflation has been strong.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The unemployment rate and widening concerns about input costs suggest that pressures to raise prices might have grown, and strong growth worldwide affects not only input prices but the value of the dollar as well.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: If anything, since our last meeting, I think that risks related to growth have abated and have become more balanced and risks regarding inflation have grown.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Thus, as we look over the next two and a half years, our forecast sees policy staying somewhat restrictive given the inflation risks and then easing a bit in late 2008 or 2009 to a level closer to its equilibrium rate.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Finally, continuing some thoughts I began to articulate at our last meeting, as we think about policy, we also need to be concerned about financial stability.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: This is particularly true given what we’ve seen in the markets for credit derivatives.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: We’ve talked before about how high levels of liquidity and low interest rates worldwide cause much reaching for risk, much reaching for return, and related risk-taking.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: While the Bear Stearns hedge fund issue may well not have legs, the concerns regarding valuation of the underlying instruments do give one pause.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Can markets adequately arrive at prices for some of the more exotic CDO tranches?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: What happens when the bottom falls out and positions thought to be at least somewhat liquid become illiquid?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Is there a potential for this to spread and become a systemic problem?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Maybe not, and I am not advocating our taking any action as a central bank.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: But I do think the size of the credit derivatives market, its lack of transparency, and its activities related to subprime debt could be a gathering cloud in the background of policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I will spend just a couple of minutes extra on the District this time because, generally speaking, our District economy continues to perform very well despite the weakness in the housing sector.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Energy and agriculture remain very strong, and manufacturing remains generally strong although we have seen some leveling-off of that in the past month.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The strength in these three sectors has helped spur broad-based job growth throughout the District and a significant tightening of our labor markets and their conditions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Many of our contacts report labor shortages and higher wage pressures.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Demand for skilled labor remains very strong, and some firms have limited hiring plans because of the unavailability of qualified workers.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To bolster recruiting, a few companies have partnered with vocational schools to offer industry- specific training programs to try to fill the gap.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Since our last meeting, hiring announcements, which we try to track, have outpaced layoff announcements by a margin of 6 to 1.

speaker: HOENIG
text: One anecdotal piece of information—we have some fairly large engineering firms in Kansas City that build power plants globally, including in China, and also ethanol plants.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Last year, one CEO told me that they hired 2,100 engineers and were unable to fill 900 positions on a global basis.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So there is a lot of activity going on out there.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Construction activity remains mixed, with weakness in residential construction balanced by strength in commercial construction.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the residential side, we have seen some pickup in sales, but high inventories have limited new construction.

speaker: HOENIG
text: For us, problems with subprime loans are concentrated in Colorado and in a few other areas.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But because of the strength in energy and agriculture, some parts of the region are actually experiencing a housing boom, with strong home-price appreciation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Relative to the total market, that is small, but it is a rather sharp contrast.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Conditions in agriculture are the best in recent years.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Spring rains have alleviated drought conditions in much of our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Strong demand and limited supplies continue to boost farm commodity prices and farm incomes.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, we are also beginning to see the effects of higher livestock and crop prices on retail food prices themselves.

speaker: HOENIG
text: An additional concern is the sharp rise in land prices throughout much of our District.

speaker: HOENIG
text: First-quarter cropland values in the District rose roughly 12 percent above year-ago levels, and ranchland values have strengthened as well, that much or perhaps a little more.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our contacts in the real estate industry indicate that some of the recent surge in land prices is speculative in nature, and some District bankers have expressed concern about the bubble in farmland values driven in part by the ethanol boom that we have heard about.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In recent examination reports, our supervision staff have begun to see some increases in nonperforming real estate loans, and that includes some pickup in other real estate owned as well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: These developments are very preliminary, but they are reminiscent of an earlier time, and we are trying to pay a little more attention to that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the national outlook, data released since the last meeting support the view that growth will pick up over the year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I have been encouraged by the recent pickup in retail sales and by positive news on employment and personal income.

speaker: HOENIG
text: At the same time, the recent increase in longer-term interest rates, if sustained, is likely to damp growth somewhat in the period ahead.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In particular, the rise in the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate may deepen and prolong the ongoing housing slump.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The combined effects of weaker growth in the first quarter and the rise of long-term rates have led me to lower my estimate of growth in 2007 to about 2.3 percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I expect growth of 2.7 in ’08 and 2.8 in ’09.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I now think the risks, perhaps, are roughly balanced.

speaker: HOENIG
text: While the downside risk from housing remains, the outlook for other sectors, as others have reported, has appeared to improve.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Markets seem to have adopted this view as well, as removal of the expected policy easing has contributed to the flattening of the yield curve at this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In terms of the inflation outlook, recent data have been favorable, with core CPI on a twelve-month basis down to 2¼ percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I expect continued moderation over the year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In particular, if owners’ equivalent rent continues at the slower pace of the past three months, it will help bring down the twelve-month core inflation number over time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Despite these recent improvements, I continue to believe that upside risks to inflation remain.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The possible pass-through of recent energy and food price inflation to core inflation may slow progress toward lower inflation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, pressures from resource utilization and slow productivity growth, if that happens to be the case, could affect that outlook as well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Finally, I am somewhat concerned with the recent uptick in longer-term inflation expectations.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have talked about the TIPS five-year, five-year-ahead breakeven inflation rate; as mentioned in the earlier briefing, it has increased about 20 basis points over the past month.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So in light of these factors, I believe it is important that we continue to signal to the markets that current inflation rates are not acceptable over the longer term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a twenty-minute coffee break and then resume.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: News from the Fourth District is little changed from my last report.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The District economy continues to be weighed down by weakness in the housing market, and there is general consensus among my contacts that the housing sector has not yet seen bottom.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: To date, adverse spillovers from housing to other sectors of the economy have not been observed, although this remains a significant risk to the outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: While I have heard some reports from my business contacts that the labor market is strengthening, the official data still do not show net employment growth in the region.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My projections for the national economy still call for growth to resume to a more typical expansionary pace as we move beyond 2007.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My projection for GDP is slightly stronger than what is seen in the latest Greenbook because of my assumption for slightly stronger growth in potential.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Obviously, I don’t make that judgment with great confidence.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, the business leaders I talk with tell me that their plans to expand capital are consistent with a pickup in productivity growth from its recent cyclical low.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This includes the Cleveland Cavaliers—[laughter]—a franchise which, as many of you know, experienced a substantial productivity shortfall against the San Antonio Spurs a couple of weeks ago.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Here, too, we are projecting a good rebound, so to speak, in 2008.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In the meantime, I would like the record to show that I am making good on my wager with President Fisher.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I brought with me a selection of Cleveland’s finest, and I will present those to Richard after this meeting with my heartfelt congratulations.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am putting this back, because it feels funny having a beer bottle in my hand.

speaker: FISHER
text: If this were the Australian Reserve Bank, it would be okay.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also extend my heartfelt congratulations to the Spurs on their fourth and final NBA championship.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Now, turning to inflation, I am hearing reports of upward price pressures across a handful of industrial commodities, and notably for metals.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But wage pressures remain modest.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Nevertheless, for the first time in more than a year, I am hearing from my business contacts that they are concerned about inflation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: They are bringing inflation concerns up with me, and they are telling me that they concur with the Committee’s assessment that inflation remains a risk.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: To be sure, there were many positive signs in the May CPI report.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The traditional core CPI beat expectations, and while the trimmed mean estimators that we produce in Cleveland were a little higher than the measure excluding food and energy, even those indicators were consistent with the moderation and the longer-term inflation trend we expect to see.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Looking at the core measures enables me to be encouraged by the May CPI report.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But that view is a rather hard sell to a public that saw headline CPI inflation rise 8½ percent at an annualized rate last month.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Indeed, our readings of the underlying inflation trend and what people are feeling in their wallets have been at odds for many years now.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I understand that our policies are not well advised or even equipped to address transitory price movements.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But at some point, large and persistent price disturbances, such as we have seen in energy markets, warrant our attention.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: If these isolated price pressures become more generalized and enter into consumer and business decisionmaking, we could easily find ourselves living in the Greenbook’s “drifting inflation expectations” scenario.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In summary, I think the housing market still presents a risk that the economy may not resume a more typical growth trajectory over the forecast period.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Nonetheless, that concern is trumped by the risk that we may yet lose the public’s confidence that we are making sustainable progress against inflation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Therefore, I continue to believe that the predominant risk going forward is that inflation will fail to moderate as expected.

speaker: POOLE
text: Let me talk first about some of the anecdotal reports.

speaker: POOLE
text: A contact with a large software company suggested that the IT industry is doing fine.

speaker: POOLE
text: Labor is very tight because technical people are in such scarce supply.

speaker: POOLE
text: This company is expanding development facilities in China and India.

speaker: POOLE
text: They are not allowed to import the labor they need, and so they will send the operations abroad.

speaker: POOLE
text: My contacts with transportation industry people get the same information that Richard Fisher is emphasizing.

speaker: POOLE
text: Movement of goods is just really, really flat.

speaker: POOLE
text: The over-the-road trucking industry is actually taking down capacity, selling off the older, less efficient trucks.

speaker: POOLE
text: In the express business, UPS is taking down capacity.

speaker: POOLE
text: FedEx is more optimistic, probably taking market share.

speaker: POOLE
text: A contact with the fast food industry says that their business volume is down.

speaker: POOLE
text: The whole industry is down.

speaker: POOLE
text: Sales revenues are up a bit, but it is because of price increases.

speaker: POOLE
text: The casual dining industry is down even more.

speaker: POOLE
text: There is sort of a disconnect here between the overall view of the economy, I think, and the anecdotal reports that come from the movement of goods.

speaker: POOLE
text: Of course, the most cyclical part of the economy is always the goods part.

speaker: POOLE
text: The services part is much more stable.

speaker: POOLE
text: Perhaps what is going on here is simply what is also in the Greenbook’s second-quarter numbers, because the goods part of the economy—consumption—is pretty flat.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think consumption is only—I forget the exact number—1.6 or something.

speaker: POOLE
text: That is an annual rate.

speaker: POOLE
text: You have to divide that by 4 to tell you what is actually going on in the quarter itself.

speaker: POOLE
text: Of course, the housing industry continues to decline.

speaker: POOLE
text: So maybe these anecdotal reports really are consistent with what is going on and what is in the Greenbook picture.

speaker: POOLE
text: The Greenbook picture makes a lot of sense to me.

speaker: POOLE
text: Let me talk a little more about housing.

speaker: POOLE
text: The staff presentation had a point that I want to underscore—that the housing downturn is unlike any other that we have had.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think the chart went back to 1972, but you could go back before that.

speaker: POOLE
text: If you look at the housing downturns and the recessions of the 1950s, they were all related to a very standard cyclical pattern.

speaker: POOLE
text: Interest rates would rise, housing—starts, permits, construction—would start to turn down well before the cycle peak, and then housing would start to recover after the cycle peak as interest rates came down.

speaker: POOLE
text: The current situation is completely different from that standard pattern.

speaker: POOLE
text: Here we had a housing boom driven by a period of very low interest rates.

speaker: POOLE
text: The period really got started when we were holding the fed funds rate at 1 percent.

speaker: POOLE
text: Then you had a lot of these financial innovations and subprime mortgages that added a sector to the market that hadn’t traditionally been there.

speaker: POOLE
text: Interest rates came up, housing prices are flattening out, and my concern is that there is a lot more to go.

speaker: POOLE
text: This is an asset market that does not work anything like securities markets.

speaker: POOLE
text: It is completely different from the stock market and the bond market.

speaker: POOLE
text: Housing starts and permits peaked in the early part of last year, and the adjustment really got under way.

speaker: POOLE
text: But if you think about how much of the adjustment is complete—well, there is not much sign that much is complete because the inventory of unsold new houses is close to its peak.

speaker: POOLE
text: There is no convincing evidence that it is really starting to come down.

speaker: POOLE
text: We have seen some bankruptcies of builders, but not very many.

speaker: POOLE
text: A lot of banks—I know from our contacts—are putting pressure on their builders to sell out their houses and pay off the loans.

speaker: POOLE
text: The same thing is true of “the ground,” as the real estate people like to put it.

speaker: POOLE
text: Builders are stopping their development of new land for housing developments because they don’t have the financing to support it anymore.

speaker: POOLE
text: The banks are starting to turn off the credit spigot because these companies are getting pretty close to the edge.

speaker: POOLE
text: They have laid off a large number of workers, but they have to sell out their inventory.

speaker: POOLE
text: Still, the number of months’ supply that they are sitting on is abnormally high; it really hasn’t come down.

speaker: POOLE
text: We also know that prices in this market respond with a very substantial lag to the underlying determinants of prices.

speaker: POOLE
text: So prices of existing homes are only gradually adjusting, and I think there is probably more of that to go.

speaker: POOLE
text: We know that there will be a lot more resets of these adjustable-rate mortgages.

speaker: POOLE
text: The projections are that a lot more defaults than we have yet seen will occur in that area.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I think that we have a long adjustment to go here.

speaker: POOLE
text: Whether that will spread into the rest of the economy, I don’t know.

speaker: POOLE
text: I share the Greenbook estimate that probably there won’t be major fallout, but it seems to me that the risk there is significant.

speaker: POOLE
text: I just wanted to underscore that point because I think this risk is by far the biggest that we face at this time.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I would like to speak earlier next time, so I don’t have to give credit to so many of the previous speakers—[laughter] including President Poole, who really said a lot of what I have to say.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There wasn’t much change in the Sixth District economic picture during the intermeeting period, particularly regarding things that are relevant to the national outlook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I am not going to devote a lot of time to discussing across-the-board conditions in the District.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My staff’s outlook— and my outlook—for the national economy doesn’t differ much from the Greenbook analysis and forecast, so I also won’t detail small differences between those two forecasts.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The Greenbook outlook reflects the baseline expectation of a diminishing drag on real growth from residential investment.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Since our forecast largely agrees with the Greenbook, we obviously see the most likely playout of the housing correction similarly.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, as suggested in the Greenbook’s first alternative simulation, we may be too sanguine.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think this is really President Poole’s message about a recovery in the housing sector.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That is to say, the downturn in residential investment will be deeper and more prolonged and possibly involve spillovers.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I would like to devote my comments, in a cautionary tone, to this particular concern.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Credit available for residential real estate purchases is contracting, and the credit contraction, specifically in the subprime mortgage market, has the potential to lengthen the transition period required to reduce housing inventories to normal levels.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This tightening of credit availability, along with higher rates, may affect the timeline of the recovery.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One market of concern is the starter home market.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The subprime mortgage market has been a major credit source for first-time homebuyers—although, as has been mentioned earlier, subprime mortgages are a small portion of the aggregate stock of mortgages.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Subprimes were 20 percent of originations in 2005 and 2006, and if you added alt-A nonprime mortgages, you would get 33 percent of originations in the past two years.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In many suburban areas, like those around Atlanta and Nashville in my District, much home construction was targeted at first-time buyers.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We have heard anecdotal reports from banking and real estate contacts in our region that tighter credit conditions have aggravated the already sluggish demand for homes.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The country’s largest homebuilder—there may be a debate with President Fisher—[laughter] so one of the country’s largest homebuilders, headquartered in Miami, reported on Tuesday a 29 percent drop in homes delivered and a 7.5 percent drop in average prices.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But that is combined with a 77 percent increase in sales incentives.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: They attribute their negative sales experience to rising defaults among subprime borrowers and higher rates.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That company’s CEO said that he sees no sign of a recovery, and he provided guidance of a loss position in the third quarter.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Because of the major role that homebuilding—and, I might add, construction materials, particularly in forest products—plays in the Sixth District economy and because of some tentative signs of spillover, we will continue to monitor these developments in our District very carefully.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I stated at the outset, we share the basic outlook described in the Greenbook, but observation of the housing sector dynamics in the Sixth District has raised our level of concern that the national housing correction process may cause greater-than-forecasted weakness in real activity.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: If that is the case and inflation gains prove transitory, as suggested in the Greenbook commentary, we may be dealing with a far more challenging policy tradeoff than we are today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Since our last meeting, the news in the Third District economy has been mixed but, on balance, slightly more positive than the previous report.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The District continues to grow at a moderate pace, and we expect that pace to continue.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The bright spot since our last meeting is a rebound in regional manufacturing activity, which had been flat for the past six months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In June, the Philadelphia Business Outlook Survey index of current activity rose sharply—18 percentage points—from a level of 4.2.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is the highest level it has obtained since April 2005.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The index of new orders also showed a sizable jump, and capital spending plans firmed in the survey.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Respondents also expected further improvement in manufacturing activity over the coming months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Job growth in the region, however, was somewhat slower over the past two months compared with earlier in the year, but we really didn’t expect much since payrolls seemed to rise much more rapidly than expected during the first quarter.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Year-to-date payroll growth is running about 0.6 percent at an annual rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That rate is slower than the national average but is fairly typical of our region, where population growth is rather flat.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Labor force participation is rather flat as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Unemployment rates, however, remain low in our three states, and firms still report having difficulty finding both skilled and unskilled workers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is no surprise, as everyone has said, that residential construction in our region continues to decline and remains weak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The value of contracts for residential buildings has fallen more than 30 percent in the region during the first five months of this year compared with last year at this time—but that, we have to remember, was near the peak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Real estate agents and homebuilders generally report slowing of sales in May.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While the number of existing homes for sale on the market has increased, average selling prices have not changed much.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would characterize the nonresidential real estate market in the region as fairly firm, although construction is not as strong as last year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Office vacancy rates continue to fall, and in Center City Philadelphia, they dropped to 10 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They were about 17 percent just around eighteen months ago.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Real estate firms report that overall demand for industrial space continues to be robust and that vacancy rates for this type of space are near record lows in some markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Rental rates continue to rise, particularly for warehouse space, and rents are at a record high in those areas.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I take these reports as indications of continued expansion in economic activity going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Interestingly enough regarding building, I had two observations from CEOs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One is CEO of a building supply company that manufactures throughout the United States and has sales of almost $10 billion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: He said that, remarkably, even with what is going on with homebuilding, his sales are holding up very, very strongly and they are doing very, very well this year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Another CEO, whose company produces products mostly for residential cabinetry and other types of things, one of the largest in the country, says that, while new home sales for his work are way down, they have largely been offset by remodeling activity—people have substituted remodeling for buying a new home.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As long as I’m reporting anecdotes here, I will pass on one other anecdote, for what it is worth, about trucking.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I listened to President Fisher and President Poole talk about volumes in trucking.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Just as an observation, an executive who runs a trucking company throughout the country told me that one thing that has happened in trucking is that, rather than shipping boom boxes, they are shipping iPods.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is true of a lot of consumer goods.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Instead of shipping large CRT screens, they now ship flat panel displays.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So even while the volume of goods is being reduced, gasoline prices are high, and they are laying off truckers and downsizing the volume, the value of what they are shipping has been maintained pretty well.

speaker: PLOSSER
