text: So he was noting a dynamic of value versus volume here, which I thought was very interesting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the inflation front in the District, prices for industrial goods continue to increase, but retail price increases have not been widespread.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, many of our business contacts continue to express concern over rising energy costs and food prices and the effect on their businesses and the consumers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I interpret this to mean that they continue to be puzzled by our focus on core inflation when they see that overall inflation is what affects the consumer and their businesses, and they seem to doubt core inflation’s value as a policy objective or a measure of underlying inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They may be wrong in that, but it tells me that, if they continue to be confused by how we view core inflation and what we use it for, we might need to improve our communication to the public about how we think about it and why we focus on it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the national level, I have become more comfortable with the economic situation as the year has progressed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At our meeting in May, we were beginning to see some positive signs regarding both real economic activity and inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Durable good orders were up, allaying some concerns about the first quarter’s weakness in business investment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Improved ISM numbers were signaling that the slowdown in manufacturing might be ending; and although housing markets remained weak, there were limited signs of any significant spillovers to other sectors.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At that time there were signs that core inflation might be moderating.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As a consequence, I expressed hope that in the coming months those data would be reinforced.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Fortunately, from my perspective, those hopes have been largely realized.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Coming into this meeting, we have received more positive news on the economy, and I have become somewhat more confident that the economy is on track to return to near-trend growth later this year as the effect of the housing correction moderates, albeit very slowly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, data received to date suggest that we will see a substantial rebound in real GDP growth this quarter, as the Greenbook has noted.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: After several months of stagnation, manufacturing activity seems to have picked up, and business fixed investment is moderately strengthened.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Labor markets remain firm, and yet in recent quarters we have noted a seeming disconnect between strong labor markets and weaker GDP growth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, we now may be getting some hints that this puzzle is more apparent than real, and I want to reinforce the point that President Yellen made earlier in that I think two factors suggest this.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, from December to May the household survey showed almost no employment growth whatsoever, whereas the establishment survey showed 1.2 percent annual growth during that period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Second— and again as President Yellen noted—the Business Employment Dynamics report came out.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It was only for the third quarter of last year, but it showed about 155,000 fewer jobs created in the third quarter than we thought.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What is important about that report is that it arguably does a better job of tracking the birth and death of firms in the data, and so there is some reason to believe that, while this is suggestive, the payroll employment that we have been seeing may not be as strong as perhaps we thought, and that may make some of this puzzle less of a concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, as President Yellen pointed out, it is also relevant for the longer term because, if employment wasn’t as strong as we thought, productivity is going to end up being higher than we thought, and it will help resolve some of that slowdown in productivity.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think there are various hints that that may be the direction that we are headed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my own forecast, I see slightly more underlying strength and so a somewhat faster return to trend growth than the Greenbook does.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The current stance of monetary policy is maintained.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I see strength in personal income, a strong balance sheet (as we saw earlier today), strong equity markets, and a resiliency already shown by consumers despite the lower home equity values and higher gasoline prices, suggesting that there is probably slightly more momentum in consumer spending than suggested in the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am modestly more optimistic about the labor market than the Greenbook—modestly, as I anticipate less of a downturn in labor force participation rates than is built into that forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The rise in long-term interest rates reflects the market’s upgrading of its assessment of the economy’s strength going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, as has been noted a couple of times, that uptick in long-term interest rates has been, I won’t say a worldwide phenomenon, but certainly widely spread in many countries around the world, which may be saying that global growth is more stable, predictable, and positive than perhaps we thought.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, this is not to say that I do not see risks around this growth forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, as everyone else does, I see housing as the biggest downside risk that we face.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There is still considerable uncertainty out there, and I do not want to underestimate the risk.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Housing inventories remain high, and I do not see any strong evidence of pickup in demand.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite the problems in subprime lending markets, however, I think the financial sector remains healthy—healthier now than it was perhaps in the early ’90s with the previous housing boom.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am more comfortable with the notion that there will be no spillovers into other parts of the economy, and thus I have become more comfortable with forecasts of return-to- trend growth in the second half of this year and into ’08.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the inflation front, higher energy prices have led to an acceleration of headline inflation, but there has been some improvement in core inflation measures in recent months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The three-month growth rates in the core CPI and the core PCE have been decelerating since February.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although these developments in inflation are encouraging, I remain cautious about extrapolating too much from recent data.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: During this cycle we have seen periods of deceleration reversed a couple of months later.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, the Greenbook expects that much of the favorable readings on core PCE inflation will prove transitory.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I remain concerned that our core inflation rates may not continue their recent drift down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would also caution that headline inflation, as I noted earlier, has remained stubbornly high.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, in approaching my forecast, I have assumed that the appropriate policy path was one that would return the economy to steady-state growth and to my inflation target by the end of the forecast period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given my outlook on the underlying strength of the economy and an inflation goal of 1.5 percent for the PCE, it should not be surprising that my forecast incorporates a slightly tighter policy path than the Greenbook does.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In particular, in my forecast the federal funds rate rises 50 basis points, to 5.75 percent, by early ’08.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As progress is made on bringing down inflation starting in the second half of ’08, the fed funds rate moves down, ending at about 5 percent by the end of 2009.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This policy path reflects my view that, unless we take further action by additional firming or an announcement or both that commits us to an inflation goal that is lower than the market currently expects, which seems to be about 2.5 percent, I believe it will be difficult to sustain an inflation rate that is in keeping with my view of price stability.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe this can be accomplished with relatively little effect on real growth in 2008.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My assumption in the model with which I’m working is that, once we begin to raise rates, the markets will quickly recognize our commitment to lower inflation and expectations will move down accordingly, mitigating the real output effects of this modest tightening.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The movement down in expectations could be expedited by the Committee’s explicitly announcing the target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This view of expectations formation is more heavily weighted to forward-looking elements than to distributed-lag elements of past inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: By the way, I want to applaud the staff for their work on inflation dynamics.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I thought it was an excellent piece of work.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I found the discussion very helpful and a step in the right direction, both conceptually and empirically.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In any event, the bottom line for my forecast is that I anticipate that the economy will grow just below trend of 3 percent in 2008 and at trend of 3 percent in 2009, and we achieve an inflation goal of 1.5 percent by the end of the period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, this forecast is based on my desired inflation objective, which may not be representative of other members of the Committee.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If there were a common objective that differed from my own view, then my presumed appropriate policy path might be different.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given this observation and the lack of an agreed-upon goal, I think we need to be concerned about how the public will interpret these forecasts, but I will save my thoughts on that for the next go-round.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The outlook looks a little better, I think.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The United States looks okay, and the world looks very strong.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Housing here seems as though it will get worse before it gets better, but the rest of the economy seems to be doing reasonably well—with output and investment spending perhaps a bit firmer than we thought they would be and employment growth and income growth looking reasonably good.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have not significantly changed our central projection.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We still see an economy growing around 3 percent over the forecast period, about our estimate of potential, with core PCE inflation falling just below 2.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This assumes a path for the nominal fed funds rate that is flat for several more quarters, essentially the same as in the Greenbook and in the market now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The risks to this outlook, though, have changed.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We see less downside risk to growth but still believe the risks to our growth forecast are weighted toward the weaker outcomes.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Although the recent inflation numbers have been good, they probably exaggerate the moderation of underlying inflation, and we see, therefore, continued upside risk to our inflation forecast.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I still think this latter risk should remain our more consequential concern.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Relative to the Greenbook, we have a bit more growth because of our higher estimate of growth in the labor force and a bit less inflation, but these differences are small, smaller than they have been, and they do not have significant implications for our views on monetary policy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The markets’ perceptions of fundamentals have in some respects moved in our direction in the past few weeks.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I say “in some respects” because we need to be attentive to the rise in implied inflation that you see in TIPS.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our view and the markets’ view of the expansion, the risk to the outlook, and implications for monetary policy have converged.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This means that the effective stance of monetary policy is a little tighter than it was.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: A few important issues going forward: On the growth front, I still think that the probability of weakness exceeds that of strength.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is still a significant risk that we will see a more substantial adjustment of house prices, perhaps drawn out over a sustained period of time with greater adverse effects on confidence and spending.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course, if employment and income growth stay reasonably strong, the effects of that potential scenario should be manageable.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If not, we will have more to worry about.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I note that some major financial institutions are now starting to report signs of rising delinquencies in consumer credit products outside mortgages such as automobile loans and leases.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is the first time that I have heard that report in a significant sense, and maybe it is a sign of some vulnerability ahead.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The strength of demand growth outside the United States has been helpful, and we agree with the Greenbook that it looks likely to continue for some time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But things could be kind of bumpy out there, particularly in places like China, and monetary policy in much of the world is only now starting to move short-term real rates higher into positive territory.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the inflation front, it seems early to declare satisfaction or victory, not particularly because of the recent reacceleration in headline inflation but just because of the role of transitory factors in the recent moderation in core and the rise in breakevens in TIPS.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We cannot be fully confident yet that a constant nominal fed funds rate at current levels will deliver an acceptable inflation forecast.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We do not, in my view, need to try to induce right now a further tightening of financial conditions to push core inflation down further and faster.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But we need more time before we can justify shifting to a more balanced risk assessment of inflation or something equivalent, something that would have the effect, for example, of indicating satisfaction with current levels or of suggesting that the risks are balanced around the path of inflation that we see in our central tendency projections.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: With financial markets, we are at a delicate moment.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The losses in subprime are still working their way through the system.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Rating agencies are likely to downgrade a larger share of past issues, more than they have already.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The marks that people show indicate that both hedge funds and dealers in a lot of this stuff may still have a way to go to catch up with the movement in market prices.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This dynamic itself could induce a further reduction in willingness to finance new mortgages.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You could see pockets of losses in the system, liquidity pressures in hedge funds and their counterparties, and further forced liquidations.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is possible that we will still have a bunch of that effect ahead of us, even if no big negative shock to demand occurs and induces a broader distress in consumer credit.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We could also see it spread to commercial real estate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We could see a broader pullback from CDOs and CLOs as well, either from a general erosion of faith in the rating models—as Bill said, it is a possibility—or from just concerns about liquidity in those instruments.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We could see a sharp, substantial widening of credit spreads provoked by an unanticipated default or two or just a general reassessment of risk at current prices.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: A very large amount of LBO financing that is yet to be closed, distributed, and placed is still working its way through the system.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As in the past, we could see a deal or two get hung, the music stop, and that force some broader repricing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: People get stuck with stuff they don’t want to hold or did not expect to hold.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think we now see more sensitivity in markets about the prospect of a diminished appetite among the world’s savers and central banks to increase their exposure to the United States, or at least we see more sensitivity to the perception out there that the dynamic might be unfolding.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You can see a bit of all this in some spreads, in some reports of resistance to further erosion in covenants, in some reduced appetite for new bridge book exposure to leveraged lending.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You can see it in some changes in margin terms in some instruments vis- à-vis some counterparties.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: For now I think it is a relatively healthy, still pretty modest, and quite contained shift toward a more cautious assessment of risk, but these things generally don’t tend to unfold gradually.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On balance, though, I think we are in a pretty good place in terms of policy, in terms of the market’s expectations about policy now, and in terms of how we have been framing the balance of risks to the outlook.

speaker: KOHN
text: My projection was closely in line with that of the Greenbook, modestly below-trend growth for a few quarters, held down by a prolonged weakness in housing.

speaker: KOHN
text: As that drag abates, the economy picks up to potential and is held back from overshooting that potential by various factors, including the rise in the saving rate and slightly lower growth of government spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: Under these circumstances, core PCE inflation holds in the neighborhood of 2 percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do not really see much to push it one way or another at this point.

speaker: KOHN
text: The economy is producing very near its potential, as close as we can figure.

speaker: KOHN
text: Inflation expectations have been moving in a narrow range.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some of the transitory factors, such as owners’ equivalent rent, that we’re expecting to come down to reduce inflation have already done that to a considerable extent.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I don’t see them, moving forward, as having a big effect.

speaker: KOHN
text: Given the limited pass-through of energy and commodity prices into core prices, I would not expect much downward pressure on inflation from a leveling-out of those prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that we are around 2 percent and that we will probably stay there, at least for a little while.

speaker: KOHN
text: In terms of risks, the recent data on capital goods, orders and shipments, and manufacturing activity suggest, as many have remarked, some reduced downside risk from business attitudes on spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: They do not suggest a great deal of strength in business capital spending, however.

speaker: KOHN
text: The fundamentals are less favorable than they were a couple of years ago, and the most recent data, which we received today, suggest a pretty flat or a modest upward tilt to capital spending in the second quarter.

speaker: KOHN
text: The data weren’t that strong, but they do suggest that what I feared in May—that we were in the midst of a cyclical adjustment that was going to make capital spending much weaker—has certainly abated.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with many others around the table that housing is a significant downside risk to the forecast, given the high level of inventories despite a major reduction in starts over the past year and the price-to-rent ratio being as high as it is.

speaker: KOHN
text: The further slide in housing may be gentle, as President Lacker said, but I do not think we’ve seen the bottom yet.

speaker: KOHN
text: You can go a long way at a gentle slope.

speaker: KOHN
text: We also have not yet really seen the full effects of the tightening in subprime credit terms or, obviously, of the recent increase in mortgage rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also see a big downside risk from consumption.

speaker: KOHN
text: The Greenbook has the growth of consumption sustained despite an increase in saving rates as the growth in disposable income exceeds the growth in GDP—and that is with the labor share recovering and the business profit share declining.

speaker: KOHN
text: I see two downside risks to that.

speaker: KOHN
text: One is that the saving rate will rise faster as the housing weakness feeds through both in terms of wealth effects and in terms of reduced availability of credit as terms tighten and there is less equity to borrow against, particularly for liquidity-constrained households.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also continue to see a downside risk to equity prices, although I have certainly been wrong so far.

speaker: KOHN
text: Nellie’s table presenting the difference between the staff’s forecast of profits and the market’s forecast of profits showed a huge difference for next year.

speaker: KOHN
text: So though I think the basic outlook is fine, I still see some downside risk on that side.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the inflation front, I, like others, see the better-than-expected core inflation as a hopeful sign; but it is recent and may be affected by temporary factors, and I do not think we need to get too enthusiastic about it.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do see several upside risks to inflation: the high level of total headline inflation, which could erode inflation expectations; business resistance to any erosion of profit margins as unit labor costs pick up; the high levels of resource utilization in the United States; and the tighter global conditions of demand on potential supply that others of you have mentioned.

speaker: KOHN
text: Let me say a word or two about my year-three projections.

speaker: KOHN
text: I projected output growth at 2½ percent, the unemployment rate at 4¾ percent, and core PCE inflation at 1.9 percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: I certainly saw my output and employment projections as a sense of what the steady state was.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the unemployment rate, I do think the odds are better that the NAIRU is lower than that it is higher than the staff’s 5 percent assumption.

speaker: KOHN
text: This judgment is partly based on the very moderate pickup in the employment cost index, and average hourly earnings growth has actually been coming off recently.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the behavior of core inflation, I don’t see much evidence that we are significantly beyond potential now, although I recognize that, with a very flat Phillips curve, it could be a long time before one figures that out.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I had growth of potential at 2½ percent, which is below what I infer to be the central tendency of the Committee.

speaker: KOHN
text: Regarding my reading of the decline in productivity growth, productivity over the past five quarters has been growing significantly below the staff’s estimate of 2½ percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some of it is cyclical.

speaker: KOHN
text: There could be a revision, as Presidents Plosser and Yellen have suggested.

speaker: KOHN
text: I confess to having asked David Wilcox about this at the break, and he said that the data are kind of ambiguous here and that it is much too early to predict a significant downward revision to employment.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I hope you are right.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, some of the recent slowdown certainly must be cyclical, though I would have thought that labor hoarding and things like that would be much less in today’s flexible labor markets, with so much more use of temporary workers than there has been in the past.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would think that the cyclical effects on productivity would be muted, that businesses would move pretty promptly to adjust their labor forces to output.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I wonder how much cyclicality there is.

speaker: KOHN
text: The big uncertainty is in the construction industry and in the fact that construction employment hasn’t come down.

speaker: KOHN
text: We don’t quite understand why it hasn’t come down more.

speaker: KOHN
text: So perhaps productivity will pick up.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I still would look at the staff’s 2½ percent as having even just a little more downside than upside risk to it, given the fact that we have had more like 1 to 1½ percent in the past four or five quarters.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I stuck with the staff’s forecast of 2½ percent potential GDP.

speaker: KOHN
text: In some sense, our view of what the potential growth rate is isn’t all that important for monetary policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: We ought to be looking at the gap.

speaker: KOHN
text: We ought to be looking at the pressure of the level of production on the level of potential GDP.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I don’t think it’s quite that easy.

speaker: KOHN
text: We don’t know what that gap is.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have seen that the surprises over the past year or two have been in the behavior of the unemployment rate and capacity utilization relative to growth.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we do tend to look at our estimates of potential growth and the actuals coming in relative to those estimates and pass judgment on what’s happening to the output gap even when the unemployment rate doesn’t move.

speaker: KOHN
text: We just need to remember that potential growth is an entirely estimated number that we will never observe, and we need to be aware that it might not be quite as high as the central tendency indicates that my colleagues on the Committee apparently think it is.

speaker: WARSH
text: Regarding overall economic growth, my own macroeconomic views are not inconsistent with the central tendency of the projections that were pulled together for this meeting.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the staff and the participants around the table deserve significant credit for being stubborn about the moderate-growth hypothesis while markets have been on all sides of it.

speaker: WARSH
text: The markets appear ready to look through the second-quarter GDP growth number, which appears to be a bit above trend.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’d say that we have gotten some credit from the markets for being stubborn and stubbornly right on our economic forecast, but they certainly haven’t given us their proxy, and I would not expect them to do so.

speaker: WARSH
text: They happen to share our views for now is what I would say, and I wouldn’t expect that situation to remain over the forecast period.

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, neither should our intention be to somehow get these curves to match over the coming several quarters.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the inflation picture, though it has improved a bit—and I am trying not to disregard very good news—I must say that it strikes me as thoroughly unconvincing.

speaker: WARSH
text: To me, inflation, in our old statement language, remains the predominant risk.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am less certain that core will continue the recent trend.

speaker: WARSH
text: I do believe that headline inflation may be telling us something in terms of secular trends around energy and food that we can’t dismiss, and the warnings from some of the other signals that we would see as rough proxies for inflation are still very real.

speaker: WARSH
text: Regarding what the financial conditions are telling us about growth, it strikes me that, from all the data we have received between our last meeting and this, financial conditions might be as different as any other sets of data that we received.

speaker: WARSH
text: My view is that financial conditions are still supportive of growth, but somewhat less so.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is hard to determine at this point how much, but let me take a stab at doing just that.

speaker: WARSH
text: Since we last met, as Bill said at the outset, we witnessed ten-year Treasury yields increase on the order of between 30 and 50 basis points.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am not uncomfortable with that incremental tightening of policy in the financial markets, but we have to be careful of what we wish for.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the explanation from our staff here in Washington and Bill and the staff in New York is right, which is that markets have not come to a rosier view of the future.

speaker: WARSH
text: All they have really done is to take out the downside risk that came out of the first quarter.

speaker: WARSH
text: As the data came in a bit above expectations, that insurance bet that they had—that we were wrong and would have to cut rates—really lost credibility.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think their central view of the economy now is not one that roars back but one that is quite consistent with the moderate growth story.

speaker: WARSH
text: The financial markets have indeed tightened policy somewhat.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even since the time that the Bluebook was produced last week, spreads have apparently widened in addition to the risk-free rate being somewhat higher.

speaker: WARSH
text: But this is all happening in very real time, and my report a week ago would have sounded quite a bit different from the one today.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have witnessed increased term premiums and greater volatility across many, if not all, financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: Both the MOVE index for Treasuries and the VIX for equities are high relative to the averages of the past year but are still fairly reasonable over a somewhat broader period—say, the last five years.

speaker: WARSH
text: Term premiums I would characterize as returning to more-normal levels—but, again, not out of line with history.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have seen in the Bluebook that credit default swap (CDS) spreads and other spreads had widened, but that yet hadn’t happened in the high-yield market, where apparently there was some narrowing of spreads.

speaker: WARSH
text: That has changed rather dramatically in the past four or five trading days.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m sure Vince will share more information on this tomorrow.

speaker: WARSH
text: But the CDS spreads really occurred first; then there was a lag to high-yield spreads.

speaker: WARSH
text: In the past two weeks, investment-grade CDS spreads have widened about 7 basis points, high-yield CDS spreads have widened about 20; a relatively new index of loan CDS spreads has widened about 65 basis points; and most, if not all, structured products, even assets wholly unrelated to the housing markets, have been undergoing some spread widening.

speaker: WARSH
text: As I mentioned, high-yield spreads appear to be catching up to CDS spreads, and with the incredible flow of deals in the market, I would guess that the trend continues.

speaker: WARSH
text: We’re seeing higher financing costs and slightly tougher terms for LBOs; the latter is a remarkable new development.

speaker: WARSH
text: M&A prices, probably for the first time since I have been sitting at this table, appear in the markets to be coming off their levels.

speaker: WARSH
text: So when auctions for properties of publicly traded companies are occurring, the price between initial indications of interest and final bids for the first time may actually be coming down.

speaker: WARSH
text: Interest coverage ratios cannot go much below where they have been in this cycle.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is 1.2 or 1.3 times, but again, as the risk-free rate has gone up, as spreads have widened, you can buy just a little less debt for that.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a result, equity players that do not want to compromise their equity returns can pay a little less for these properties.

speaker: WARSH
text: Whether this phenomenon is very short term, like the phenomena we heard about after the tumult in late February and we returned to in the heady days of the capital markets, I do not know.

speaker: WARSH
text: This may just be a temporary preference shift toward quality and toward higher volatility and a return to the “glory” days, but I tend to think not.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is a tough call, and I reserve the right to change my judgment.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that the new supply that’s coming into the markets, most of which needs to get priced before the markets slow down in August, will test the markets’ resilience, will test prices, and will test terms.

speaker: WARSH
text: Up to this point we have seen very little reduction in liquidity, but we are seeing a few deals being pulled from the market.

speaker: WARSH
text: Pricing power appears to be coming back to investors, and negotiations around prices and terms seem significantly more balanced than they have been in a very long time.

speaker: WARSH
text: Some of the instruments that we have sort of giggled about around this table—the pay-in-kind notes with optional cash payment— seem to have lost some traction in the market in the past week.

speaker: WARSH
text: I do not know whether they will return, but I take this new discipline in the markets as an encouraging sign.

speaker: WARSH
text: So what is going to be the resulting effect on prices, terms, and conditions?

speaker: WARSH
text: That is something we will have to judge; but financial conditions, as I said at the outset, are perhaps somewhat more restrictive than they were, but they should still be quite supportive of growth.

speaker: WARSH
text: At the outset I talked about the risk on the inflation front.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me build on a couple of remarks that Vice Chairman Geithner made about risks now in the financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: If the problems that we have seen around structured products that have come out of the Bear Stearns scenario are really about the subprime markets and subprime collateral and housing, there’s not much to worry about.

speaker: WARSH
text: But to the extent that the story is really about structured products—products that have not been significantly stress-tested—then there is a risk that the financial markets may react and overreact.

speaker: WARSH
text: That scenario will bring up reputational risk issues.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even financial intermediaries that are in the agency business are relearning the lesson that agency business is not free—that there are, in fact, dissynergies from being in the principal investment business and the agency business under one marketing name.

speaker: WARSH
text: We are learning a lot about what the markets believe about the transparency of prices, particularly in times of financial distress.

speaker: WARSH
text: Of course, in times of distress, the correlations among all these assets do not look as they do in models, and that is something that will play itself out.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that Tim rightly referenced the role of gatekeepers in the credit agencies, who I suspect are going to have a fairly rude awakening over the next six to nine months.

speaker: WARSH
text: As I also said, regarding this financial innovation, which on net is of great benefit to us, we will really see some of the products tested.

speaker: WARSH
text: Along with the products, moreover, the market participants’ behavior will be tested, perhaps in this upcoming period, as never before.

speaker: WARSH
text: So the financial markets are a friend on this, but there is greater risk than there was when we last met.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The last time we met, there seemed to be a bit of increased uncertainty about a potential downdraft on economic growth, and now some of that concern about that downturn seems to be no longer there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some intermeeting data have come in a little more on the upside, and obviously the markets have changed their expectations and seem to agree with that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think the strength in the labor market and in consumption, although facing some challenges, is still at a reasonable level.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It does seem that we are getting some signs that investment is coming back.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Recent durable goods numbers, which came out today, perhaps raise some questions of that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have had a couple of good months and now a bit more of a challenge.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But when you smooth through, I think, exactly as Governor Kohn suggested, that we’ll have moderate growth going forward, a forecast that I think is consistent with the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Strength in nonresidential construction, as we have heard around the table, has also provided us with a bit more optimism for investment in general.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But investment is obviously closely tied to where productivity is going because, if we don’t have investment, particularly in the high-tech areas rather than just in the construction sectors, it is going to be hard to sustain high productivity growth.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: When we get the revised numbers on July 27 and we also get advance GDP, we’re going to get a lot of information about that, and I think there is still a lot of uncertainty as to exactly where productivity is going.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I will defer my comments until the next meeting because we will have those numbers by then.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Regarding consumption, we have been having the offsetting wealth effects of the recently robust equity asset market and much less robust housing asset market, continuing strength in the labor market, and as the Greenbook points out, increasing disposable income because we’re having incomes grow faster than productivity growth, at least right now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That suggests that we might maintain a reasonable support for consumption growth, but again, as Governor Kohn said, there are potentially some challenges here.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But now I want to discuss the big challenge that everyone keeps talking about, which is the housing market.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It has become obvious that the transition is going to be quite a long one and potentially a painful one, perhaps more in individual pockets and for individual families than for the macroeconomy.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It will not just disappear after the third quarter of the year or even the fourth quarter of the year.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I would think in four different ways about how housing can have a broader effect on the economy.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: First is obviously the direct effect on prices.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The Case-Shiller ten-city index suggests that the prices will fall about 3 percent over the next year.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now, that’s roughly where the market was just before the issues in subprime arose at the end of February, and it is actually better than it was last fall.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So the markets don’t think that there will be an enormous challenge with respect to prices, at least in these ten markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But as President Poole mentioned, sometimes the prices even in these improved indexes, like the Case- Shiller index, may lag what’s going on and may not accurately reflect the underlying actual values that people can realize.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So there still may be more challenges even though the index suggests that house prices are down only 3 percent.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is also interesting to look at the delta, the change in the index.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We haven’t really seen much from that, which I think is heartening, but it is still something that we have to watch out for.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Second are the indirect effects, the wealth effects.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I mentioned, there have been offsetting wealth effects from the equity markets and the housing market.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: More broadly, there can be confidence effects on spending and on saving behavior.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So far we haven’t seen a lot of evidence of that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As Vice Chairman Geithner mentioned, there have been anecdotal reports of challenges in other areas of consumer credit, although so far no real systematic data suggest that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Even if there is a little movement up, in almost all the typical indexes we use, many of which were mentioned in the briefing, we are at lows or are much lower than usual historically.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So even with the small movement up, there are not necessarily enormous challenges; but these effects also have to be watched.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A third very important potential effect of this long transition is a response by us or by lawmakers that could make the transition even longer and more difficult.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As a number of you know—and all of you have been facing pressure on some of these things—we will be putting out the subprime adjustable-rate mortgage guidance that we put out for comment just at the end of February.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Our timing couldn’t have been better for getting that out—we did it just as the problems were becoming more of an issue publicly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I hope the guidance will be out by the end of this week.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We are proposing guidance that subprime adjustable-rate mortgages have underwriting at the fully indexed rate.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I do not think that’s going to be much of a shock to the markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The markets have largely moved there already.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This was true from some early statements by Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, some of the major players who were not underwriting at the fully indexed rate are simply not there anymore— they are bankrupt—and some of the other players who were not doing it have changed their standards.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As we know from the survey of senior loan officers, standards have been rising.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That is not to say that it won’t have some effect, but relative to where the market has already moved, the effect is not going to be significant.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The other major guidance is for giving a prepayment penalty grace period of sixty days so that people will have at least sixty days before the reset to refinance their mortgage.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s unclear from the studies we have done at the Board and from looking around how much of an effect that will have on the initial rate or the so-called teaser rate.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It seems that changing their ability to do that from zero to thirty to sixty days is unlikely to have an enormous effect on the teaser rate, but that is something that is uncertain.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There are some states that already outlaw prepayment penalties or have restrictions on them.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There is not a lot of evidence suggesting that it is more difficult to get financing in those states.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Again, these guidelines are untested, but I don’t think they will have an enormous effect on the market, but they are obviously something to watch.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As you well know, we have put out an interagency letter suggesting that servicers and lenders work very closely with distressed borrowers to try to work things out and keep people in their homes.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Doing so is in the interest of the people in the homes; it is virtually always in the fiduciary interest of the loan servicer and of the lender.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we have been making progress on accounting issues that have been making it difficult for some servicers to do this, and we are working very closely with the SEC and with FASB on some of these things.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We may be making progress in giving comfort to the servicers who want to do some restructurings that would help keep people in their houses and would ultimately be better for the individuals and for the owners of the securities.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have also had the HOEPA hearings here in which we talked about the potential for rule writing in several areas, such as requiring escrow for taxes and insurance, some regulation or restriction of prepayment penalties, and various other things.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That would be down the line, but again, we are thinking that this is unlikely to have a major effect relative to where the markets have already moved.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Fourth and finally, there has been a lot of interest in the effect of subprimes in the housing market not only on the mortgage market but also more generally on the financial markets, as Governor Warsh and Vice Chairman Geithner pointed out.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Fortunately it seems that liquidity is largely being maintained in the mortgage origination market.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There are still fairly robust amounts of subprime and alt-A originations occurring.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They obviously are going to be declining over time because there are fewer being made; but they were at an unusually high level in 2006, and so it’s a natural part of the transition process that they would go down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There has been a very significant increase in spreads, as has been mentioned by the previous speakers, and there’s much more tiering of risk.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is not just that the Bs are all the same; it is where they originate.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The markets are looking through the packages to see what’s in them, which is very, very valuable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Increased volatility and higher pricing in these markets and the higher long-term interest rate will be a bit more of a challenge for people doing refinancing, although we’re now down to about 5.08 for the ten- year, off 20 to 25 basis points from the high of the other week, and so it may not be quite as much of a challenge.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But there is also a legal risk in this market because, if some problems become larger, there could be concern about what the new instrument really means and what you have actually purchased.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If legal risk is there, the markets will start to run away from these things.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Then you may have some severe liquidity problems.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I do not think that we see those challenges yet, but it is one indirect effect on the financial market of some of these issues.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Just quickly on inflation—most people have said that we’ve seen some moderation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is a little too soon to declare victory.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As we said in the initial briefing, when we drill down into the components and look at owners’ equivalent rent, we may get some nasty surprises going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some numbers have gone down, but owners’ equivalent rent may come back up a bit.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I don’t think we can say that the temporary elevation in that area has passed and that we can move on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think some challenges are still there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Fortunately, expectations still seem reasonably well contained.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I think that there may be some challenges going forward as the economy continues to grow at least at a moderate pace, and some of the temporary factors are not necessarily completely behind us.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We still have to look for potential price pressures going forward.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My view of what has been happening in the economy is that we have been basically going through a rebalancing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We had a sector that was clearly bubble-like with excessive spending, and now we are getting the retrenchment, which is taking a bit longer than we expected.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But the good news is that we are going through a rebalancing in which we are just moving resources to other sectors and that is actually going much along the lines that we want to see.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The problem in a rebalancing episode is that you are always worried about the risk that is possible because these transitions don’t always occur smoothly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that we were much more worried about that—at least I was more worried—at the previous meeting.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we have been seeing that the rebalancing is actually going along pretty well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, although the housing market is very weak, very much along the lines of the Greenbook forecast, it hasn’t surprised us this particular period.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s just that it is pretty bad.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But the risks are actually fairly balanced on housing because we do not see it as very strong and that is part of the process of undoing the previous excesses.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Another very important thing is that we have not seen any surprising spillovers from the housing market.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As time goes on and nothing really bad happens, we become more confident that, in fact, the downside risk isn’t there either.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have also seen that the investment sector has been looking a little stronger.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Again, that really did concern me at the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Yet we have had some reasonable numbers; they are not spectacular, but I think the downside risks have dissipated.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the bottom line is that I see the economy as rebalancing and doing it in a fairly good way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, from a long-run perspective, this is a good thing and not a bad thing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The downside risk has dissipated, and the risks are now quite balanced.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I am quite comfortable with the Greenbook forecast on this, which is that we have growth somewhat below trend but moving back toward trend, and I see that there has been a shift in a positive direction and the risks are not excessively on the downside but are much more balanced.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When I look at the inflation picture, I am in a way pleased with the recent numbers because there is no strong indication that we are far from potential output and, in particular, there is a little indication that the tightness in the economy certainly will be unraveled.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: According to our forecast, not much is going on in that area, so what’s going on in inflation expectations will be dominant.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I mean, given that inflation expectations have been pretty well anchored around 2 percent, although there is some uncertainty, I thought that we would have a return to 2 percent numbers a bit more quickly than the original Greenbook forecast showed.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I was really pleased because the Greenbook has basically moved closer to the picture that I had all along; so now I’m very comfortable with the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In contrast to some other people, I think the risks are pretty balanced.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Now, maybe that is not really different because of the people who have inflation going below 2 percent, and I don’t see that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I believe it’s going to be 2 now and it’s going to be 2 for a while unless we make a concerted effort to change inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Then there is the whole issue of how we might go about doing that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But given the current environment, my view is that risks are fairly balanced.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Other people are saying that there is risk on the upside, but I think that’s because they just have slightly lower numbers regarding where they think inflation will be.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But probably when we look at it from that perspective, it is about the same.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So right now I think the economy is evolving in a pretty reasonable way, and I’m sure we will be surprised in one direction or another in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you, and thanks to everyone.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me try to give a quick summary, and if I misrepresent you, please let me know.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Participants’ expectations for growth were varied, but most people expect to see strengthening over the remainder of this year and into 2008 and 2009.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The principal source of downside risk is housing, which remains weak, perhaps in part because of problems in mortgage markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, significant spillovers have yet to emerge from the housing situation, and other components of demand appear to be strengthening and thereby offsetting the drag from residential construction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A number of participants referred to the strength of the global economy, which is stimulating U.S. exports but also leading to increases in costs of energy and metals.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Investment has picked up from a bit of a pothole and is growing now at a moderate pace with particular strength on the commercial real estate side.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inventories are mostly aligned with sales and manufacturing seems to be strengthening overall.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumption seems likely to grow at a steady but not exuberant level, with factors such as gasoline prices and slower house appreciation creating some drag but strong employment and incomes acting as supports.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Indeed, the labor market continues to be strong, although there are some measurement issues that were noted, with unfilled demands for highly skilled workers and with some signs of wage pressures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Overall, the risks to output seem roughly balanced around the path of a gradual increase in growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Participants did note the increase in long-term interest rates, which tended to align market policy expectations with those of the Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Higher long-term interest rates and some other changes in financial markets may be slightly restrictive but probably not substantially so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some also noted risks in financial markets, including the aforementioned risks associated with the subprime sector, but also more-general concerns about structured credit products and the possible effects of a decline in liquidity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, I would note also, as some others did, that a bit of cooling in the financial markets might not be an entirely bad thing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Recent core inflation numbers have been favorable, and most of you see continued moderation in inflation resulting from mildly restrictive policy, the ending of some temporary influences, and slower increases in shelter costs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, a few of you have suggested that some of the recent improvement in core inflation is transitory, and they noted upside risks, including resource utilization, possible pass-through from energy and commodity costs, slower productivity growth, and the possible effect of high headline inflation on inflation expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: High capacity utilization—and “globally,” President Fisher—is also a source of possible inflation pressure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is President Fisher a source of inflation?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All in all, there still seems to be general agreement that the risks to inflation remain to the upside and remain the predominant concern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is that a reasonable summary?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me present just a few essentially random thoughts at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First of all, from my perspective, the biggest puzzle about what’s happening is the behavior of the labor market, which is continuing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unemployment is at least not falling anymore, but it remains stable at a fairly low level.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My scenario for the soft landing plus some moderation of inflation involves some cooling of the labor market from here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I still think it will happen, but admittedly, there is only the slightest suggestion so far that it is happening.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, we have not yet seen the decline of construction employment, which I have continually referred to and continue to expect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There have been a number of discussions about why we haven’t seen that response yet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some have noted the possibility that a lot of the workers are undocumented and, therefore, are not being counted by the usual measures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, they seem to have been counted when the market was expanding.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is a little puzzling why suddenly they are not being counted.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thus I still think there will be some moderate softening in the labor market over the next year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If that does not happen, then we will be at some risk of higher upside growth than we anticipate and higher inflation pressures than we anticipate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So for me that is a central thing to look at.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think in talking about this, it is important to note how uncertain we are about what the natural rate of unemployment is and that entire concept.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Judging from the FOMC’s 2009 projections, most of us think that the natural rate may be a bit below 5 percent, and I would note that the unemployment rate was in the mid to low 4s for four years in the late 1990s and has been in that range now for about two and one-half years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is not entirely evident where the natural rate is, and it does make some difference obviously.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I expect to see some moderation in the labor markets, and I believe that is critical to our scenario.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Like everyone else, I think the housing situation continues to involve downside risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would reiterate what President Poole said—that this is an asset market; that therefore price changes are inherently, at least to some extent, unpredictable; that a lot is going to depend on confidence, which is going to depend on results, which is going to depend on confidence; and therefore, that we need to be very careful, just the same as with inflation, about declaring victory too soon on the housing front.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, there is an interaction between the mortgage market and financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There has been discussion of that already today, but there is the potential for some trigger to lead to what would amount to an effective tightening in financial markets, which would affect not only housing but also potentially, for example, corporate credits.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although that remains just a risk, I think it’s one we need to keep in mind.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with the general view around the table that, except for housing, the economy looks to be healthy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Capital spending is not going gangbusters, but it does seem to have come back to some modest trend.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I also agree with what a number of people said about the strength of the world economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We shouldn’t get too carried away with the export sector.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What we’re hoping for here is that net exports will not be a net drag on growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nevertheless, that is an improvement over the past, and the strong world economy should on net be helpful to our economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Like everyone else, I’m encouraged about the incoming inflation data.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree that some of these good numbers may be partially transitory.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, when you analyze this, there has been a decided step-down in the past three or four months in the shelter component.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would make two observations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that, excluding shelter, core PCE inflation is now at the lowest number since the end of 2003; if the shelter numbers of the past three months were to persist, then that would automatically arithmetically give us some additional progress on inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, that may not happen.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Clearly we have month-to- month variations, as we have mentioned many times; but I think some slack could combine with some more moderation in rents.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the inflation expectations issue, I thought David Wilcox’s graphs were very instructive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do very much believe that inflation expectations influence actual inflation and that the anchoring of inflation expectations is very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I don’t think they’re anchored at 2.000; I think that they’re anchored at a general range somewhere around 2 percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What David’s graph showed was that the level of expectations that we observe seems also to be consistent with 1.8 or 1.7.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I don’t think that’s an absolute barrier, though I concede that expectations play an important role.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Two, I would also just comment about the statistical issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I was among a number of people who talked about the statistical significance of the change in inflation that we have seen and noted that these month-to-month changes are subject to a lot of variable shocks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But let me just say that I think it’s probably worth noting that, in the classical statistical significance tests and everything we’re doing here, we’re Bayesian decisionmakers, and we’re trying to make a decision based on our best estimate of where we are at a given moment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Even if we concluded that inflation’s decline is not statistically significant in a classical sense, we still ought to act as if there has been some decline in inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As a thought experiment, I would ask what we would be saying now if we had gone up 0.6 percentage point from where we were in May.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that would have led to a somewhat different tone around the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So while acknowledging the statistical variability and the transitory nature, I think that there has been some improvement and that it is showing through into our thinking about the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One last thought—a number of people have mentioned the distinction between core and total inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree that our communication on this issue really needs some work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I was just in Chicago, and several people, including directors and employees, asked me, “Don’t you guys drive?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Don’t you eat?” Clearly, we understand why we do this, but I think we need to improve our communication on that particular front.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s a little segue into what we’ll be talking about tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if you will bear with me—I know it is six o’clock, but I’d like to ask Vincent just to give us a brief introduction to the monetary policy discussion we’ll be having tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That will save us some time tomorrow and give us a chance to think overnight about the subject.

speaker: REINHART
text: 4 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: REINHART
text: Two personal notes to start: First, I am the last person between you and British food, which means that I’m not sure whether it is in your interest for me to speak quickly or slowly.

speaker: REINHART
text: Second, this week marks the first anniversary of the Committee’s last policy action—the quarter-point firming that brought the federal funds rate to 5¼ percent.

speaker: REINHART
text: Paper is the traditional 4 Material used by Mr. Reinhart is appended to this transcript (appendix 4).

speaker: REINHART
text: present, and my gift to you is the material labeled “FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” The intermeeting period saw considerable upward revision to investors’ expectations for the setting of monetary policy.

speaker: REINHART
text: As the shift from the dotted to the solid line shows in the top left panel of the first exhibit, the path of the expected federal funds rate rotated up, posting increases of 15 basis points at the end of this year and about 50 basis points by the end of next year.

speaker: REINHART
text: The starting point for both the May 8 and the June 26 lines, though, is the same: Market participants continue to believe that you will keep the federal funds rate at 5¼ percent at this meeting.

speaker: REINHART
text: Judging by the Desk’s survey of primary dealers, you are also expected to keep the wording of the statement mostly intact.

speaker: REINHART
text: Not much of this rise in market yields occurred in narrow windows surrounding the release of economic data and speeches by monetary policy makers.

speaker: REINHART
text: Rather, the economic data, which ran somewhat stronger than anticipated, and Federal Reserve communications, with the steady repetition of the assessment that upside risks to inflation remained, seemed to induce a rethinking of the economy’s prospects and the attendant need for monetary policy support.

speaker: REINHART
text: This rethinking is most evident in the middle left panel, which shows that the latest primary dealer forecasts of the federal funds rate at year-end (the blue bars) have shifted notably compared with the survey forecasts just before the May meeting (the dashed line).

speaker: REINHART
text: The revision to investors’ views was associated with the increase of 20 to 50 basis points in the nominal Treasury yields plotted in the right panel (and seen as the shift from the top dotted black line to the solid black line).

speaker: REINHART
text: The pricing-out of near- term policy ease probably explains the now-shallow portion at the front part of the yield curve.

speaker: REINHART
text: The rise in nominal yields can mostly be attributed to an increase in real yields of 30 to 50 basis points, shown in the lower portion of the same panel.

speaker: REINHART
text: Our term-structure models suggest that virtually all the rise in real yields is due to fatter compensation for bearing risk.

speaker: REINHART
text: Because the shifts in the two sets of yield curves did not match, the spread between the nominal and the indexed yields, which measures inflation compensation, widened somewhat at longer maturities.

speaker: REINHART
text: Here, too, the models suggest that some of that larger gap reflects a higher risk premium—this time for bearing inflation risk—leaving their estimates of inflation expectations only modestly higher.

speaker: REINHART
text: In recent days, concern about risk-taking, brought into the spotlight by the problems of two hedge funds managed by Bear Stearns, reversed some of the upward tug of yields imparted by the revision to the outlook for the economy and policy.

speaker: REINHART
text: As can be seen in the bottom left panel, the cost of credit protection for subprime mortgage pools packaged over the past 1½ years has risen over the past few weeks as the fear of a fire sale of the collateral seized by lenders to the Bear Stearns funds depressed prices and raised concerns about a more general spillover to other entities and markets.

speaker: REINHART
text: These fears also seem to have set off flight-to-safety flows that pulled Treasury yields lower in recent days.

speaker: REINHART
text: As noted in the table at the bottom right, the ten-year Treasury yield had risen about 50 basis points from the May meeting to when we put the Bluebook to bed (the first column).

speaker: REINHART
text: The outbreak of skittishness in recent days trimmed several basis points off that run-up (the second column) and put equity prices into the red.

speaker: REINHART
text: I wonder if the recentness of these events, which unfolded after much of the staff briefing work was wrapped up and your own interventions were mostly written, means that they have not been completely incorporated into your outlook.

speaker: REINHART
text: If so, this nervousness in financial markets probably adds to the list of reasons for keeping a low profile in your policy action at this meeting by ratifying prevailing expectations—that is, to choose the unchanged policy stance of alternative B in the Bluebook.

speaker: REINHART
text: Some of the other reasons are the subject of exhibit 2.

speaker: REINHART
text: In the staff forecast, summarized in the top left panel, output growth runs a bit below that of its potential in the near term, and inflation settles in at 2 percent.

speaker: REINHART
text: If you find that both a plausible and an acceptable outcome, you might also align yourself with the policy assumption of an unchanged federal funds rate upon which that forecast is based.

speaker: REINHART
text: Moreover, you were satisfied with keeping the funds rate at 5¼ percent at your May meeting.

speaker: REINHART
text: If you have filtered the incoming economic information in a manner similar to the staff— seen in the Greenbook as a slight upward revision to the growth of real GDP and a slight downward revision to core PCE inflation—you probably also believe that circumstances have not changed enough to warrant a recalibration of policy.

speaker: REINHART
text: It is true that financial market restraint has ratcheted up somewhat as investors’ forecast of the federal funds rate path has risen—proxied in the top right panel by the year-end expected federal funds rate in futures markets—but the staff expected this to happen over the next year or so, which has been a sentiment shared by some of you at the past few meetings.

speaker: REINHART
text: The adjustment in financial markets over the intermeeting period now brings market pricing into better alignment with the Greenbook assumption— shown by the black dots—and that this adjustment took place on a more compressed schedule than expected should probably not make for a material change to the outlook.

speaker: REINHART
text: As seen in the middle panel, the current real federal funds rate, at 3¼ percent, matches the Greenbook-consistent estimate of its equilibrium level.

speaker: REINHART
text: That is, if maintained, the current real rate would be consistent with the output gap closing within three years, at least in the Greenbook outlook.

speaker: REINHART
text: An unchanged nominal funds rate at this meeting is also consistent with many policy rules, including an estimated one that captures your practice over the past twenty years and that is plotted as the solid line in the bottom left panel.

speaker: REINHART
text: Of course, if you take into account forecast uncertainty, as is done by the light and dark green regions, you can pitch a pretty large tent with such policy rules.

speaker: REINHART
text: There is less doubt about the course of monetary policy in financial markets.

speaker: REINHART
text: As shown by the red bars at the bottom right, options on Eurodollar futures imply a distribution for the federal funds rate six months from now that is tightly clustered around the current setting.

speaker: REINHART
text: Here might be another reason for keeping the fed funds rate unchanged today: For all this year you have been hinting that prevailing market expectations for the fed funds rate were too low.

speaker: REINHART
text: Now that market participants have adjusted in your desired direction, you might not want to surprise them.

speaker: REINHART
text: Many of you noted that problem with the version of table 1 that circulated in the Bluebook, a subject discussed in exhibit 3.

speaker: REINHART
text: In the May statement, inflation was characterized as “somewhat elevated,” as in row 3 of the left column.

speaker: REINHART
text: But favorable data since then have put the twelve-month change in core PCE inflation at 2 percent, a level that some of you might find tolerable.

speaker: REINHART
text: As yet the Committee has not spoken with one voice on the subject.

speaker: REINHART
text: We dropped that contentious phrase in the Bluebook and softened the balance-of-risks language as well.

speaker: REINHART
text: As a result, the release of the wording in the Bluebook version of alternative B would likely trigger a decline in money market yields.

speaker: REINHART
text: The new version of alternative B in the right column turns the heat back up somewhat by inserting in row 3 words to the effect that the Committee is not convinced that the present step-down in inflation will persist.

speaker: REINHART
text: This draft also makes clear in row 2 that the characterization of recent economic growth is based on the first half of this year and returns the language in row 4 to that used in the May statement.

speaker: REINHART
text: Even if you are willing to keep the funds rate at 5¼ percent for now, you might foresee policy action sometime soon, in which case the changes to the statement probably do not represent your views.

speaker: REINHART
text: In particular, as shown in the top left panel of exhibit 4, the unemployment rate (the red line) has bounced around 4½ percent for almost a year.

speaker: REINHART
text: If you believe that this represents a taut labor market, you may be concerned about inflation pressures, particularly given that the manufacturing sector seems to have gone into a higher gear, as shown by recent readings on the ISM’s new orders index, the black line.

speaker: REINHART
text: You might not be alone in being concerned about inflation prospects.

speaker: REINHART
text: As plotted in the middle left panel, five-year, five-year-forward inflation compensation has risen 30 basis points from its recent low.

speaker: REINHART
text: It might be noise, it might be a wider risk premium, or it might be increased inflation expectations.

speaker: REINHART
text: If it is the last, you may want to position yourself now for policy firming sometime soon on the theory that an early demonstration of your displeasure with a rise in inflation expectations will effectuate a less costly decline.

speaker: REINHART
text: Some suggestions for doing so were offered in alternative C in the Bluebook, a few highlights of which are given in the bottom left panel.

speaker: REINHART
text: In particular, the alternative C draft reverses the order of the description of economic activity in row 2 to downplay the qualification “despite the ongoing adjustment in the housing sector.” More important, it retains the judgment that “core inflation remains somewhat elevated” and gives more reasons that inflation many come under pressure.

speaker: REINHART
text: If you have a frame of mind favorable to finer shades of meaning, you can always try dialing down the modifier of elevated inflation from “somewhat” to “slightly.” More substantial changes might be required if you are inclined toward alternative A, arguments for which are shown in the right-hand column.

speaker: REINHART
text: Regardless of the reason behind the run-up in market yields, households borrowing to buy a house now face higher mortgage rates (as shown in the top panel).

speaker: REINHART
text: This may both dissuade potential new purchasers of homes and disappoint those households that were hoping to refinance on more-favorable terms as the lock-in periods on their extant ARMs end.

speaker: REINHART
text: Both will act as a drag on spending and perhaps more substantially so than in the staff forecast.

speaker: REINHART
text: Months’ supply of new homes, plotted in the middle right panel, has edged higher.

speaker: REINHART
text: The staff projection has the feature that the efforts of builders to bring inventories back into line will be a drag on production for some time but that residential investment will begin to turn up by the second half of next year.

speaker: REINHART
text: However, this is a projection, and if you are more pessimistic on that score or want to give greater weight to downside possibilities from a risk-management standpoint, you might want to show some leaning toward policy ease in the statement.

speaker: REINHART
text: The language of the draft statement in alternative A may do so.

speaker: REINHART
text: As summarized in the bottom right panel, that draft pointed to “ongoing weakness in the housing sector” in row 2, excises the reference to “somewhat elevated” inflation in row 3, and moves the risk assessment to balance in row 4.

speaker: REINHART
text: The pieces of what I have just been talking about have been put together in your last exhibit, which represents an ever-so-slightly revised version of table 1 that circulated on Monday.

speaker: REINHART
text: In particular, in row 3 of alternative B, the word “sustained” has been inserted in the middle sentence to raise the bar as to what it takes for the Committee to be convinced that inflation has moderated.

speaker: REINHART
text: That concludes my prepared remarks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any questions for Vincent?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no questions, then we’ll adjourn.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll see you at the dinner, and we will begin at 9:00 a.m. June 28, 2007—Morning Session

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The GDP figures came out this morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: David, would you like to comment?

speaker: WILCOX
text: The BEA published this morning their so-called final estimate of GDP for the first quarter.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Top line came in slightly lower than we had been expecting in the Greenbook—0.7 percent compared with the 1 percent that we had been expecting.

speaker: WILCOX
text: There were small misses in a smattering of categories, including equipment and software investment, net exports, and inventories.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Our snap reading, though, is that this release will have little, if any, implication for our outlook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: What we lost in the first quarter in inventories, for example, we might be inclined to regain in the second quarter in our projection.

speaker: WILCOX
text: So we think that our projection for real activity will not change as a consequence of this release.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We did get the upward revision to core PCE prices that we had been expecting on the basis of the revision to the PPI for medical services.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Core PPI was revised up from 2.2 to 2.4 percent.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The core PCE price index for the first quarter was revised up, exactly as we had been expecting on the basis of the PPI revision.

speaker: KOHN
text: May I ask, Bill, whether there has been any reaction in financial markets to this?

speaker: DUDLEY
