text: I think that people are taking this in stride.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The first quarter is old news.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So, on your estimate, what we will be seeing tomorrow when we get the details on prices will be in line with what you have been expecting?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There was nothing here to make you change your view of that?

speaker: MR.WILCOX
text: We don’t know the details of what we will get tomorrow, but there is nothing here to condition our expectation any differently from what we had before.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are well advanced in our deliberations here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We heard from Vincent yesterday on the action in the statement, and so we are prepared for the go-round.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think what I heard yesterday was consistent with what I was thinking myself.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are in a pretty good spot, macroeconomically and policywise.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have moderate growth; low core inflation, which is not rising and could possibly be falling, suggesting an underlying balance of demand and potential supply that is in pretty good shape.

speaker: KOHN
text: Total inflation is high, but unless the futures markets are wrong again, total inflation should come down to core, and core is telling us that the balance is about right.

speaker: KOHN
text: I didn’t hear anything yesterday in the forecast or in the anecdotes—some were strong and some were weak—to contradict this picture or to suggest that we have any need to adjust policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I strongly support alternative B.

speaker: KOHN
text: Markets now roughly agree with our outlook, at least in terms of their expectations for the federal funds rate and judging from our submissions on the forecast process.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think we should be trying to change those expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I share everyone’s concerns around the table about the risks on inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: Even if I don’t always share everyone’s goal for where we might be going in the next few years, I think the risks are clearly pointed to the upside given the tightness of domestic and foreign markets and the increase in headline inflation, which could feed through to inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I like the alternative B language as it was handed out by Vincent yesterday.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is consistent with yesterday’s discussion that focuses on the forecast of inflation in sections 3 and 4.

speaker: KOHN
text: It reflects our unease about whether recent improvements will be sustained.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it should leave expectations approximately where they were, although I don’t have any confidence whatsoever in that judgment—I have been wrong too often for too many years on these things.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think it has the virtue of reflecting our discussion yesterday.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have one suggestion for sentence 3 in section 3, which I think makes it a little closer to last time in terms of wording.

speaker: KOHN
text: In the second sentence—“however, a sustained moderation in inflation”—well, is that core or total?

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we should go back to “inflation pressures”: “However, a sustained moderation in inflation pressures has yet to be convincingly demonstrated.” That is what we talked about last time—inflation pressures.

speaker: KOHN
text: Then, “moreover, the high level of resource utilization has the potential to sustain those pressures.” I don’t think we need the word “inflation” twice.

speaker: KOHN
text: So with that small amendment, I think alternative B language should do the trick.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I agree with Governor Kohn.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am in favor of alternative B, of holding the rate where it is.

speaker: FISHER
text: The point that he just made may cover a suggestion I had because I was thinking about what I heard yesterday at the table.

speaker: FISHER
text: One, in our discussion of inflation, I heard some concern about core inflation qua core inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I was going to suggest that the first sentence be modified slightly to say that “readings on core inflation have improved modestly in recent months, but measures of overall inflation have remained stubbornly high.” Then, I would strike “however” and just say “a sustained moderation in inflation pressures has yet to be convincingly demonstrated.” I believe that is what I heard yesterday.

speaker: FISHER
text: The other music to my ears, but I think it also reflects reality—and I hear it more at the table—would be amending slightly the last sentence in that section 3 to read, “Moreover, the high level of global and domestic resource utilization has the potential to sustain inflation pressures.” That is what we said.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is what we discussed.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it would show that we’re tuned in to what’s going on, and that would be my recommendation.

speaker: FISHER
text: Otherwise, I would leave the rest of alternative B unchanged.

speaker: LACKER
text: Before I talk about policy, let me just note that it has been a tremendous pleasure being a colleague of President Minehan over the years and being an immediate neighbor of hers—[laughter]—at Federal Open Market Committee meetings.

speaker: LACKER
text: For one thing, she has done a great job as buffer between me and the President of the New York Bank.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Not always easy, I might add.

speaker: LACKER
text: For another, I have gotten an up-close view of some really dazzling jewelry.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Please take that out of the transcript.

speaker: LACKER
text: Core inflation has come down recently.

speaker: LACKER
text: But as I mentioned earlier, my sense is that it could well rise again.

speaker: LACKER
text: In any event, it doesn’t seem likely to fall much further.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I think we have to position ourselves to do something about inflation when we are more certain that the soft patch is behind us.

speaker: LACKER
text: I support the actions in alternative B. I support Vince Reinhart’s language from yesterday.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am sure there will be more amendments put on the table.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t want to start now by commenting on everything that has been put on the table.

speaker: LACKER
text: I will just say that, as we recognized at our last meeting, if inflation fell, we would have a problem characterizing inflation, and core PCE inflation has indeed fallen and could well go below that number on Friday, according to the staff.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it seems appropriate to recognize that improvement.

speaker: LACKER
text: The difficulty, of course, is how to do so in a way that respects the fact that we haven’t yet decided whether our objective for inflation is 1½ or 2 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is what motivated my letter to the Committee last week.

speaker: LACKER
text: I didn’t think the first draft of alternative B was sufficiently agnostic on the question.

speaker: LACKER
text: My advisers and I put our heads together, and we couldn’t figure out a way to rewrite the statement to acknowledge the decline but not tip our hand toward preferring one objective or another.

speaker: LACKER
text: So that is why in my letter I proposed that we go ahead and make a decision by choosing between language consistent with 1½ and language consistent with 2.

speaker: LACKER
text: After all, we are widely seen to want an inflation rate between 1 and 2, and we communicated that via language in our statement expressing displeasure with inflation below 1 and, more recently, expressing displeasure with inflation above 2.

speaker: LACKER
text: Sure enough, however, some people with far more expertise in the mysterious art of drafting FOMC statements seem to have found a way around this, and the revised statement seems to finesse this pretty well—the language “moderation in inflation has yet to be convincingly demonstrated.” In other words, we don’t have to say how we feel about 2 percent inflation because we are not really sure that inflation is 2 percent yet.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, I think this will finesse the problem for the time being.

speaker: LACKER
text: Assuming that it does finesse the issue—and that is sort of a big “if”—I don’t think we are likely to be able to finesse this issue forever.

speaker: LACKER
text: If core inflation does spend some time near 2 percent, as the Greenbook forecasts, then eventually it will become convincingly demonstrated that inflation is indeed 2 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: More broadly, the lack of a decision about our objective will continue to pose difficulties both for our statement and our deliberations, and I think it is going to be increasingly unsatisfactory to say we are still thinking about it.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I hope we can make progress on that soon.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, I am very comfortable with our current stance at 5¼ percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that it is, as I have said before, modestly restrictive and that it will take us over time to a lower inflation rate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the statement itself, I have a couple of comments.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am a little uncomfortable with the language used in the output rationale because we use the term “moderate” to describe growth for the first half of this year and coming quarters and this suggests that there will not be much change in growth going forward as we use “moderate” in both places.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I would like, if we could, to have something in there that will describe the pickup in activity from the second quarter on that we have talked about.

speaker: HOENIG
text: This would improve the characterization.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is just a suggestion.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I know how hard it is to craft these things, but it is something to think about.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the inflation rationale, I’ll make two points.

speaker: HOENIG
text: One, I think the statement carries pretty well—that is, inflation has come down recently, but we are not yet confident that progress will be maintained.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Two, on a twelve-month basis, core inflation is higher than I find acceptable over the longer term, and would like to see further progress toward price stability.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Perhaps President Fisher’s suggestions would take us closer to my preference in terms of something more explicit that promotes further progress in reducing inflation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That would improve the statement.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But, as I said, crafting these things is pretty difficult.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I can live with the language as it is, and those are just suggestions to think about as we go forward from here.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, like others, I think the case for alternative B is convincing.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t think we have any reason to contemplate changing the fed funds rate target at this point or trying to change market expectations about what we are up to.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as the language is concerned, something that came up at the last meeting was not to make any more changes than are necessary.

speaker: STERN
text: Some changes clearly are appropriate here because of the incoming data and the way they have influenced the outlook.

speaker: STERN
text: With that as a guiding principle, I think alternative B as drafted is fine.

speaker: STERN
text: I might have a mild preference for the suggestion that Governor Kohn made.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that on the margin it is an improvement, but I can live with B as drafted.

speaker: STERN
text: I think we are into nuances here that probably matter more to us than to anyone else.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am not so sure about that.

speaker: POOLE
text: I support alternative B, and I also support the slight revision in the wording that Governor Kohn recommended.

speaker: POOLE
text: One thing that I worry about and that I hope we can make clear in the minutes—clearly, we couldn’t do it in the statement—is that we have been in an unusual period.

speaker: POOLE
text: If you look at Greenbook Part 1, the evolution of the staff forecast, the staff forecast for both ’07 and ’08 has changed remarkably little since last September.

speaker: POOLE
text: There has been a 0.1, 0.2, or 0.3 here, but very, very little change.

speaker: POOLE
text: Ordinarily over this span of time you get some information that changes your outlook in some significant way.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would hate to see us encourage the market to think that our projected path of 5¼ percent for the fed funds rate is carved in stone.

speaker: POOLE
text: We need the market to respond to incoming data, as we will have to do when we have some data that really move us off dead center.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I hope that we would emphasize—and it has sort of drifted into insignificance here—that “future policy adjustments will depend on the evolution of the outlook.” I think it is very important that the market understands that.

speaker: POOLE
text: It gets into the broader discussion of communications, but I hope the minutes will emphasize the importance of that part of our statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have seen some change in policy expectations, obviously, in the intermeeting period.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I am very comfortable with the policy stance—keeping the rate at 5¼ percent.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I think policy is in the right place.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: It is moderately restrictive but not restrictive enough to cause us any problems, particularly in the housing area.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: In terms of the statement itself, I am comfortable with alternative B, as written or as modified by Don Kohn.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: We could talk a bit more about where that word “pressure” should be when you compare it with the last statement that we had, but that is a very minor point.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: The key in this statement is dealing with the fact that core inflation, according to our forecast, is going to be 1.4 percent in the second quarter.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: It was 2.4 in the first quarter, 1.4 in the second, and then it goes back up to 2.2 and 2.2.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: That is really the key because, when you see inflation improving and then going back up again and juxtapose that against the longer-term forecast that we have come up with, which shows some improvement in inflation over time in ’08 and ’09, it is a delicate balance as to how we present this in the statement.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I think the way alternative B has been formulated captures that.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I had suggested a slightly different approach.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I don’t feel strongly about this, but you could also take that first sentence in section 3, which says “readings on core inflation have improved modestly in recent months” and just add the phrase “but part of the improvement may be transitory.” But as I said, I am comfortable with either formulation here.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I think it accomplishes the same objective.

speaker: POOLE
text: The minutes should certainly make that point because the staff has emphasized that this may be transitory.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As people said before, I, too, am in favor of keeping the fed funds rate at 5¼ percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The economy does seem to be rebounding in the second quarter.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The lingering uncertainty over housing suggests that now is not the right time to take more-aggressive action.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am in agreement with that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, the most current readings on core inflation, while they have been good—just to reiterate the point—I, too, believe there is a lot of evidence that it may be transitory, and we have to be very careful about the fact that headline inflation has not been very cooperative recently.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation expectations remain somewhat high from my perspective, and based on our previous discussions, that is a worry for me.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do tend to favor our announcing an inflation target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am not yet convinced that we will see inflation expectations where they need to be to achieve my goal by the end of 2009.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we look at the projection narratives prepared by the Committee members, we see that a majority believe that the flat fed funds rate will get us to a PCE core inflation of 2 percent or slightly less by 2009.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If my own goal were 2 percent, I might be more comfortable with a flat fed funds rate going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, even the Greenbook suggests that there is a model where that could happen.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The bottom line is that I think we can’t avoid the elephant in the room.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How can we sensibly talk about the forecast and appropriate policy choices, either in real time, as we do today, or prospectively, when we can’t articulate or agree upon what our objective is?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the absence of agreeing on a numerical long-run inflation objective, we, as individual members, face increasingly difficult choices in arriving at an appropriate policy stance in any given meeting and even greater difficulty conveying our Committee’s decision to the public in an informative and transparent manner.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Individuals could be advocating different policy paths either because they have different models of the economy or different inflation goals or both.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At a minimum, I believe it would help our internal deliberations—and it would certainly help mine—if the causes of these differences in our projections were more transparent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we are thinking about our forecast as a communication device, this would seem to even be more imperative.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That brings me to language.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think the language in the revised alternative B is incredibly well crafted and it tries to get around the problem that we are facing in dealing with what we meant by “elevated” and how we think about this going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Citing growth over the past two quarters as having been moderate is a step in the right direction because it encourages the public and the markets to look through shorter-run, transitory movements.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Similarly, we need to be looking through transitory movements in inflation as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As several of you have pointed out in your comments on the proposed statement language before the meeting and as Vince pointed out in our last FOMC meeting, how we characterize the inflation outlook in our statements going forward is becoming increasingly an issue since we have not agreed on what our objective is.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have two related concerns.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The first is that, in eliminating “elevated,” we run the risk of signaling to the market that we are satisfied with the current rate of inflation, even though we haven’t communicated what that means.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are we looking forward twelve months?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are we looking backward at the past three months or the past twelve months?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are we basing our judgment on forecasts of the next twelve months?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are we concerned only about the core PCE, or are we concerned about headline PCE or some version of the CPI that is relevant to our concept of inflation?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I said yesterday, my concern is that there is considerable confusion in the marketplace about why we focus on core and what it means to us and how we communicate that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Internally, we are not clear on these issues, so how do we expect the public to divine our meaning when we are not willing to do it internally?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In essence, I think there will be a great deal of speculation, even with this language, about what we mean.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Will the market conclude what we think it should, or will we just accept whatever the market divines our intentions to be?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My second concern about changing the language dramatically is that it might convey to the market the notion that we are satisfied with inflation at current levels.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We may reveal through our projections next month that we actually are forecasting inflation to be lower than it is today on a twelve-month basis.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This was the point that President Yellen made in her memo.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It creates somewhat of a contradiction in how we describe our current views.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If the market infers that we are satisfied with a year-over-year core at 2 percent and then our forecasts come in at 1.8 or whatever, I think that will send some confusing messages.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the other hand, releasing the forecast later may clarify for the market what we are expecting and that may be the interpretation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But there is no way for us to know what the outcome of that is without being more specific about what our objectives are.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Why do we want to create that much confusion and speculation in the marketplace about what we mean?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I understand the desire to extricate ourselves from the language about core inflation, but I think we are being unnecessarily confusing and cryptic in our choice of language, and it will be difficult for us to control those expectations given the way we are trying to manage the language.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am not going to get engaged in all the details of the wording.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There must be people who are better at that than I am.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I would just like to conclude by noting that, even if we are successful—and, indeed, we may be with the current language in alternative B—in wordsmithing ourselves around this delicate problem, it is not going to go away.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We will continue to grapple with it in this environment—and we are going to continue to be pushed by the markets, by commentators, to clarify what in fact we mean.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So the problem isn’t going to go away even if we sort of finesse our way around it in the short run.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also support the policy action in alternative B. I have some of the same concerns that President Lacker and President Plosser, and also President Yellen in her letter, raised about the increasing difficulty in characterizing inflation without having a clear sense of the Committee’s longer-term objective on inflation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also mentioned yesterday that I have some concerns about claiming that inflation has moderated at the same time that we see the headline measure rising.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I find this to be a real problem, and I therefore like the suggestion that President Fisher made.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, I am concerned about introducing yet another concept or another measure of inflation in our statement.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I hope that through the minutes we will be able to raise our concern about the headline measure staying stubbornly high.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But without further communication, introducing yet another concept, or another measure of inflation, in our statement is going to confuse markets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I support making as little change as we can to the statement, and I am comfortable with the way the most recent alternative B is presented—although I can also support Governor Kohn’s suggestion about the word “pressure.” So I support alternative B, with some of the minor changes that Governor Kohn has made.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I, too, am in favor of keeping policy where it is.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: As I stated yesterday, I see the risks around growth as better balanced than they were, even given the potential for the housing problems to be deeper and longer-lasting than we might have expected earlier in the year.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I remain concerned about the risks that inflation will not continue to moderate, but I am not wed, as I have said many times, to a particular low number.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I would be as happy at 2 as at 1½ and perhaps even happier given that levels that start with 1 seem to have downside risks—or at least they did the last time we were there.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I am concerned, however, about the pressures on the economy, whether you think of them in terms of headline inflation or in terms of the components of headline, particularly energy costs, tight labor markets, and a growing world.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I think, although we may not want to put it in the statement, that Richard is right—our economy is subject to pressures from the rest of the world at this point and, related to that, the falling dollar.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: A lot of things could take inflation from its current moderate level and push it back up, and that I would be very concerned about.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It is true that financial conditions have tightened slightly, so markets are starting to do a little work for us.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: But I believe that we need to continue with policy in a slightly restrictive stance to provide some insurance that the inflation pressures in the economy stay moderate.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Staying with current policy is a good balance between the prospects we see for moderate growth and the prospects we also have recognized around the table for the potential for inflation pressures to get worse.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I support alternative B’s language.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I want to say two things.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: First, the more substantive concern—I think that Governor Kohn’s thoughts about inflation pressures are slightly better than the current language.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I was attracted to the “transitory” language that I think President Moskow raised first, and we fiddled around with it a bit in Boston, but I have been convinced that “convincingly demonstrated” and “transitory” are equivalent.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So I don’t want to battle about that at this table.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The statement in section 3 is headed in the right direction, and I would be in favor of its current form or the form that Governor Kohn suggested.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Second, I may be the only one sensitive to this, but in section 2 we have two sentences that start with exactly the same words.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I never wrote that way when I was in school.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: There is an easy way to make that sentence a little better from an English composition point of view.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: But, again, that is tricky to argue about at the table, so I guess I am fine.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: How about something like “Economic growth proceeded at a moderate pace”?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: There are many ways to do it.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I know that there are some objections to this, but you could say, “Despite the ongoing adjustment in the housing sector, the economy appears to have grown at a moderate pace over the first half of this year and seems likely to continue growing moderately over the coming quarters.” You could make it one sentence—it is simple, it is shorter, and it reads better.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are talking about the economy, so mentioning it twice seems to be reasonable.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: We have two sentences starting exactly the same way, though.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: In any event, this is a nit in the overall scheme of things.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I, too, favor alternative B and the current policy stance.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My interpretation of the discussion around the table yesterday is that we see encouraging signs that the current policy appears to be producing the desired directional effects at least, or intermediate effects, so it seems to be working.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There is still a fair degree of uncertainty, and based upon my long experience, I think it is a normal amount of uncertainty.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So the current policy deserves being held.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding the policy statement, I favor the wording in revised alternative B that was distributed by Vince yesterday afternoon because I think it captures the key points— the ones that are important to me at least—and they are moderate growth prospects, mention of the housing sector, better inflation readings and prospects of continued moderation (though it is still too early to draw definitive conclusions), continued inflation pressures, and a continued weighting to inflation risks with no suggestion that the current levels around 2 percent are acceptable for the long term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So for that set of reasons, I favor the wording as presented.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I certainly agree that policy is well positioned, and we should leave it exactly where it is.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Markets have come around to our view, and I think our objective in the statement should be to keep market expectations aligned with our view and not to change them.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In terms of the statement, I think that the current draft is very much improved relative to the Bluebook, and I have no problem in supporting the current language.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like Governor Kohn’s proposal; I think that it is a worthwhile change.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I do, however, share many of President Plosser’s concerns and think that we will have a lot of difficulty going forward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Markets are wondering what our long-run inflation objective is.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They will certainly note the omission of the term “somewhat elevated.” It will raise a question about whether, if core inflation were to stabilize at 2 percent, we would be satisfied with that or we would want to see it move lower.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This statement is very cleverly crafted, and I think it succeeds in finessing that issue for today.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t have a problem, really, with finessing it for today.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My own proposal was designed to say to markets something that I thought we could say without actually coming to full agreement, even within the Committee, about whether we have a single long-run inflation objective.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even if we don’t go announce a numerical inflation objective, our statements need to be consistent with the projections that we will be issuing publicly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: President Plosser pointed out that we will be issuing a two-year projection that does show inflation coming down.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It seemed to me that we could therefore remove the term “elevated” and still say, as our projections in a couple weeks will confirm, that the Committee expects underlying inflation to come down further without saying exactly how far.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I don’t feel strongly about such language, and I think alternative B does a good job of resolving the problem for today.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We will wait until another day, when we will have to face this again.

speaker: WARSH
text: Like many of you, I see no reason to materially change market expectations about our policy action.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is important that we not appear more comfortable with either the level or the trend of inflation than we actually are.

speaker: WARSH
text: Any nods in that direction in the statement are ripe to be misinterpreted, and the process of fixing any such nod would be tricky.

speaker: WARSH
text: Yesterday Vice Chairman Geithner said that financial markets are in a delicate place, and I would say that is particularly relevant in the context of this statement.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I would try not to mess with market expectations, given what we know about the state of our financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: All that having been said, I support alternative B. I like Governor Kohn’s amendment, and I still think we are running a bit of a risk in suggesting to the markets that we are more comfortable.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I don’t think there is really much we can do at this point to mitigate that risk more than the Kohn amendment suggests.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I mentioned yesterday, I think we have seen some very welcome signs of moderation, but it is certainly too early to declare a victory.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That is certainly very clear in the Greenbook, as many of you emphasized.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I also agree with Governor Kohn that we are in a reasonably good spot with moderate growth likely going forward and inflation and inflation expectations reasonably contained.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is reasonable to think that they may be going down, but there’s a lot of uncertainty, and most of the uncertainty is to the upside.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is sensible to acknowledge reality, and we should take out the word “elevated” so that we are not seen as inflation nutters.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We should acknowledge that some of the numbers have come down but be careful about saying that we are done, we are happy, or we are satisfied.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I mentioned yesterday, an upturn in owners’ equivalent rent could be coming.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There could be some uncertainty about pass-through to core of the higher energy prices that we have been seeing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There is continued strong world demand, and there could be some lagged pass-through effects of the previous declines in the dollar.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I see all those as risks to the upside, and so I think it’s important to convey that we are still concerned about those things.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That said, I am very supportive of where we are with alternative B, in terms of both the policy and the message that is coming from it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The type of amendment that Governor Kohn mentioned is one that I very much support for a number of reasons.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One, as he mentioned, it is more forward looking.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it is much better to talk about a sustained moderation in inflation pressures rather than inflation, because that gets us out of explaining specifically what we mean by “inflation.” It’s a little bit more general.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we had a clear goal, it would be beneficial.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Given that we don’t have a clear goal, I think talking about pressures is good.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It also has the value of being forward looking.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Two, the amendment fits with President Stern’s notion that we should try to keep as much in parallel with the previous statement.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So mentioning moderation in inflation pressures—I’m not sure I wrote down properly whether Governor Kohn suggested in the final sentence of section 3 “the potential to sustain those pressures,” taking it back parallel to what we had before, or whether he said “sustain inflation.” So I would certainly agree with “those pressures.” Three, putting in “pressures” gets us out of the potential for getting stuck.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Here we are saying “sustained moderation in inflation has yet to be convincingly demonstrated.” Well, if we take that out at some point, then we will be admitting that it has been convincingly demonstrated, or at least markets might interpret us as saying that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that gets us into a bit more of a box than I would like, and so talking about inflation pressures avoids the market’s taking an implication that if we remove that at some point we have said, “Okay.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is convincingly demonstrated when for six months it is below X or below Y.” I think since we haven’t articulated a goal yet, we don’t want to get into that box, but I do think that would be one of the values of articulating a goal.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I support alternative B with the amendment that Governor Kohn suggested, so I am very comfortable with that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The real issue for me here is one that I think has been expressed by several others, what President Plosser called the “elephant in the room,” which is that writing the statement is getting harder and harder.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that we have a brilliant fudge this time around, but it is not going to work forever.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There are two senses in which I have a problem with this statement.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is the issue of the appropriate level of inflation that we should be shooting for.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is really two separate questions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is what we do about communication outside, but there is also an issue about consensus inside the Committee.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I would find it much easier to agree to statements of certain types if, in fact, there were a consensus.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As many of you know, I am actually comfortable with an inflation number of 2 percent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On the other hand, if the Committee comes to consensus for a lower number, I would be more than happy to be comfortable with that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, I would be willing to have a statement that would reflect a lower number.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I sense that this is true for other members of the Committee—some who might be caught on the dovish side with 2 percent while some members are on the hawkish side at 1½.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But the difference between the hawks and the doves here is extremely slight.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, from more than five feet away, you couldn’t tell the difference between a hawk and a dove.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s one issue that is very important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think it is going to become more and more difficult as we go forward, as long as inflation evolves in the way that we expect.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I mean, we could have bad news—inflation could actually start rising—and we’d have a different kind of a problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But let’s hope we don’t get into that problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We want dealing with the good news to be the problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second issue relates to core versus total.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am quite concerned about the emphasis on core, not because I don’t think it is very important to communicate about core, particularly when you get a big shift in something like energy prices and you don’t want to unhinge inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that context, we need to talk about core so that people understand that the currently high inflation rates, in terms of things they care about—going to the gas station or going to the supermarket—are not actually something that should change their long-run inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s why the use of the core measure makes a lot of sense.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The problem is, as I read the research, that no one measure of core will always be good.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, the core measure that we have evolved to has a lot of history behind it, but it is not clear that it will be the best measure in all cases.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There are certain alternatives that I think will work in some cases—a trimmed mean may sometimes be appropriate, but at other times it will not.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think there will be a key problem, as has been discussed today, which is that at times one core measure may make more sense than another core measure.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Our whole discussion is very much in terms of a particular core measure that excludes food and energy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That measure will sometimes be problematic for telling us about long-run trends, particularly if we think that energy changes are more permanent or crazy policies about ethanol may be having a more permanent effect in terms of food prices.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In this context, we are going to have to deal with exactly this issue going forward.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also, a problem is that people do consume a lot of food and energy, and it is very peculiar to act as though we don’t care about that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think that we have to grapple with these issues.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: They are part of our communication issues.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The bottom line is that we are fooling ourselves if we think that we are going to get away forever with not dealing with them.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We will have to figure out some way of doing this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that we can do it because, in my reading of what people on the Committee have been saying, the differences here are actually fairly minor.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is the outside world that wants to make them into a big deal because doing so sells newspapers.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we do need to get to some consensus on these issues so that the outside world sees that the Committee actually has unity rather than differences.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Mishkin and others have referred to communication issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d just point out that we will be addressing some of those later this morning.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I actually agree with—and am happy associating myself with—much of what has been said.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I am totally comfortable with alternative B as amended by Don or with the Kohn-Kroszner amendment because you don’t need to repeat “inflation” twice in the end, [laughter] and I think we should keep the rate as it is.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Tim, I’m sorry, I heard my name but I didn’t hear what you said about me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Change the word “inflation” to “those.”

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Several of you put on the table a bunch of broader questions about communication going forward, which I would like to talk about now, but I think we should defer that until we come to the later conversation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I am fine with alternative B as amended.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I do think that a lot of you made many interesting suggestions about the language.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But there is much virtue in making minimal changes at the meeting because, even if they sound small, I think it is hard in the few minutes we have before we vote to really step back, take stock, and ask whether we altered the balance in ways that we fully intended to be understood.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Thus I would be for minimalism in changes at the table generally unless we have something really consequential that we are trying to shift in the statement.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In that spirit, I would keep the changes small and stay with a modest amendment to alternative B.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we appear to be in considerable agreement about the policy action.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is a good thing, I guess.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Not only are we in agreement, but also the bond market is in agreement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would just note that, in fact, the bond market is acting as an automatic stabilizer, responding to news, as we have discussed before.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we are in a very good place, and our forecasting process has served us very well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In that respect, I think this might be an appropriate time to congratulate the staff, including Dave Stockton, Karen Johnson, Vincent Reinhart, and the research directors at the Reserve Banks who are here, for their tremendous contributions to this process, which has really been instrumental in helping us find the right level of policy and in building a lot of credibility in the market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So thank you very much for your outstanding work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to the statement also, I didn’t hear a lot of dissent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First of all, let me say that I think Governor Kohn’s amendments in section 3 are very much to the point— so that would be “a sustained moderation in inflation pressures.” First, the word “pressures” dilutes to some extent the attention to the monthly numbers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, as a number of people have said, it is a broader concept, and it can be construed as including some of the headline issues and the oil, commodities, and so on prices that we are concerned about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think it is definitely an improvement, and so I would like to recommend it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On section 2, just a couple things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that I would hesitate to try to indicate growing strength in the second half, for a couple of reasons.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, at least in terms of the Greenbook, that acceleration is relatively modest—certainly not at all a definite uptick.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: By continuing to use the language of “moderate pace,” I think we signal that we are not going to take the second quarter as necessarily indicating a new reacceleration of growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We think that the second quarter represents, at least partly, a transitory increase in the growth rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, Professor Minehan [laughter] was correct about the quality of writing in the section.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The last statement began with the term “economic growth.” I am kind of ambivalent about whether or not to do this, but we could say, “Economic growth appears to have been moderate during the first half of this year, despite the ongoing adjustment in the housing sector.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A little more variation—is that acceptable?

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Could you read that again?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The proposal is, “Economic growth appears to have been moderate,” and then it goes on, as it says here, “during the first half of this year, despite the ongoing adjustment in the housing sector.” I see nodding, so I think that is accepted.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There is a tense question.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The first half of the year isn’t over.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, I mean, that is no different from what we already have.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s the word “appears,” which is fine.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The content is no different.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is everyone okay with the language?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Well, at least that solves the instant problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You do know that English professors get paid very little money.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: That is what I’m going to—very little money.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think President Minehan is entitled to her change, given that she is valedictory in this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So with that change—“Economic growth appears to have been moderate during the first half” et cetera—that would be my recommendation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any further comments?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On section 3, can somebody just read that complete section as now amended?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The entire statement: “The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to keep its target for the federal funds rate at 5¼ percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Economic growth appears to have been moderate during the first half of this year, despite the ongoing adjustment in the housing sector.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The economy seems likely to continue to expand at a moderate pace over coming quarters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Readings on core inflation have improved modestly in recent months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, a sustained moderation in inflation pressures has yet to be convincingly demonstrated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Moreover, the high level of resource utilization has the potential to sustain those pressures.” The last section is the same.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is just one observation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The second sentence of section 3, where we talk about capacity utilization, seems to be redundant once you put “inflation pressures” in the first sentence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, look at the May statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have been doing that for a while now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any other questions or comments?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, I’d like to call for a vote.

speaker: SMITH
text: I will be reading the directive from page 29 of the Bluebook.

speaker: SMITH
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: SMITH
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with maintaining the federal funds rate at an average of around 5¼ percent.” And the risk assessment: “In these circumstances, the Committee’s predominant policy concern remains the risk that inflation will fail to moderate as expected.

speaker: SMITH
text: Future policy adjustments will depend on the evolution of the outlook for both inflation and economic growth, as implied by incoming information.” Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes President Hoenig Yes Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes President Minehan Yes Governor Mishkin Yes President Moskow Yes President Poole Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The coffee is not yet brewed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So why don’t we go on to the next phase of the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We turn to Vincent to discuss communication issues.

speaker: REINHART
text: 5 Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for giving me the normal role as speed bump.

speaker: REINHART
text: In that effort we are now handing out material to which we will be referring.

speaker: REINHART
text: If someone will let me know when the doughnut truck comes, I’ll pick up 5 Material used by Mr. Reinhart is appended to this transcript (appendix 5).

speaker: REINHART
text: The Subcommittee on Communications began its work only fifteen months ago, [laughter] which seems like yesterday (at least in geological time).

speaker: REINHART
text: Given the considerable discussion the Committee has had since then on its communication policies, it seemed appropriate to take stock.

speaker: REINHART
text: In particular, I sent around a list of questions designed to elicit your views on the potential roles of the survey of economic projections, the minutes, and the statement in refining your dialogue with the public.

speaker: REINHART
text: The material with the cover, “FOMC Communications,” is designed to help to organize this discussion.

speaker: REINHART
text: With regard to the enhanced economic projections process, the survey results circulated on June 15 reported general support for the key features of the process, with three notable exceptions, given at the top of exhibit 1.

speaker: REINHART
text: The subcommittee tried to address those concerns in the modified projections process used for this meeting.

speaker: REINHART
text: So the first question listed at the top of your first exhibit boils down to, how did they do?

speaker: REINHART
text: Did the changes address the concerns you expressed in answer to the May survey?

speaker: REINHART
text: In particular, some of you preferred not to share your forecast submissions, mostly on the grounds that it might make the discussion of the economic outlook at the meeting more inflexible.

speaker: REINHART
text: But some of you held that sharing was important, both to help inform your internal deliberations and as a source of material for the forecast write-up.

speaker: REINHART
text: As a compromise, the submissions were circulated on an anonymous basis, with an opt-out clause that one of you took this time.

speaker: REINHART
text: Some of you were concerned about specificity—particularly in writing down an explicit path for the federal funds rate and in quantifying uncertainty.

speaker: REINHART
text: Those questions were turned into qualitative ones that asked for comparisons with the staff policy assumption and historical uncertainty.

speaker: REINHART
text: Another process question is item 2.

speaker: REINHART
text: In what form should the projections be released?

speaker: REINHART
text: Debbie Danker’s memo identified the three options listed in the exhibit, which basically differ by the extent to which the narrative description is tailored to suit different purposes.

speaker: REINHART
text: Option 1 is one-size-fits-all: The staff would produce a single document describing your economic projections, which would be dropped into the Committee-approved minutes and repeated verbatim in the Board-approved Monetary Policy Report.

speaker: REINHART
text: The chief advantages of this option are that the vetting process is tried and true and that there will be consistency across Federal Reserve documents.

speaker: REINHART
text: The disadvantage is familiar to anyone who has bought clothes off the rack in a big box retailer—the fit will not be perfect across documents.

speaker: REINHART
text: Option 2 opens the door to some variety.

speaker: REINHART
text: The Committee-approved minutes would include a brief description of the forecasts, as is the practice now.

speaker: REINHART
text: A separate document would give a fuller account of the projections.

speaker: REINHART
text: In that case, there would be more flexibility as to who approves the document and when it is released.

speaker: REINHART
text: This poses a tradeoff that has come up in previous discussions in that the earlier the narrative is released, the more useful it will be in explaining the policy decision but the more complicated the governance process will be.

speaker: REINHART
text: Option 3 is the bespoke alternative in which separate, complete discussions would be prepared for the minutes and the Monetary Policy Report.

speaker: REINHART
text: The fit will be better, but carrying it out will be more expensive, and even subtle differences may draw attention.

speaker: REINHART
text: The third question asks when the projections should be finalized.

speaker: REINHART
text: The choices essentially are the day of the meeting, the end of the week of the meeting, or as late as practicable to be close to the official release of the document.

speaker: REINHART
text: But you have a more fundamental question to answer first.

speaker: REINHART
text: What is the purpose of the economic projections?

speaker: REINHART
text: If they are supposed to help explain your most recent policy choice, they should be conditioned on the same information set that the policy decision is.

speaker: REINHART
text: That is, they should be finalized as soon as possible after the meeting so that they are not contaminated by post-decision information.

speaker: REINHART
text: That is the rule we now use for the minutes.

speaker: REINHART
text: If, in contrast, the Committee’s objective is to release an up-to-date assessment that sheds light on future policy actions, then the individual projections should be nailed down only close to publication day.

speaker: REINHART
text: The middle ground of closing the books on the projections a few days after the meeting seems unsustainable to me, particularly if the narrative description is to be included in the minutes.

speaker: REINHART
text: The first time an important piece of news hits within the window between policy decision and update deadline, the explanation of the policy action will become muddled.

speaker: REINHART
text: Some immediate feedback on that score will be helpful because the schedule for this round allows for your projections to be updated through close of the week.

speaker: REINHART
text: If so, you would seem to have to incorporate Friday’s chockfull data calendar.

speaker: REINHART
text: Do you really want to do that, particularly as it may lead to confusion in the minutes about what you knew and when you knew it?

speaker: REINHART
text: The next exhibit focuses on the minutes.

speaker: REINHART
text: You have 2½ years of experience under your belt in publishing the minutes three weeks after the day of the policy decision.

speaker: REINHART
text: In that time, the document has received more attention from you in the editing process and from market participants and the press on its release compared with the previous regime of delaying publication until after the next meeting.

speaker: REINHART
text: How do you assess the benefits and costs of further expediting the minutes?

speaker: REINHART
text: The benefits, listed at the left, are the same as discussed in 2004.

speaker: REINHART
text: A document made public closer to the day of the decision will be more of an aid to the private sector in understanding the current outlook and the prospects for policy.

speaker: REINHART
text: In that regard, you will be able to use that material from the minutes for public statements more promptly.

speaker: REINHART
text: A speedier release may facilitate making the post-meeting statement shorter or less substantive.

speaker: REINHART
text: I point out, though, that my sense in 2004 was that a few of you supported expediting the minutes in the hope that the statement would subsequently be shortened, but that did not pan out.

speaker: REINHART
text: To appreciate the costs listed at the right, you should understand that we use the three weeks after the meeting partly to accommodate your busy schedules and partly to provide a cushion so that the drafting iterations can converge without a dissenting vote.

speaker: REINHART
text: The costs, then, would include your increased effort to ensure that your schedules align with that of the drafting and approval process for the minutes.

speaker: REINHART
text: You should also recognize that less drafting time might lead to more compromises that make the minutes less informative so as to avoid dissent, and more staff resources will be needed to prevent errors.

speaker: REINHART
text: Simply put, with fewer hours, we need more eyes looking at the document.

speaker: REINHART
text: Of course, the decision on expediting the minutes further may interact with other potential decisions on communication policies, especially those regarding the enhanced projections process.

speaker: REINHART
text: In particular, if you decide to include a narrative description of your forecasts in the minutes, you may want to delay any speeding-up of the minutes until you are comfortable with the new process.

speaker: REINHART
text: You may also want to consider ways to make drafting and commenting easier.

speaker: REINHART
text: That is the subtext underlying question 5.

speaker: REINHART
text: How do you assess the current content of the minutes, including the staff’s description of recent data?

speaker: REINHART
text: Some time ago, it was suggested that the first eight to ten pages, which provide a backward-looking review of recent economic data, be relegated to an annex.

speaker: REINHART
text: In a similar vein, it could be described explicitly as a staff summary—with its production perhaps even linked up mechanically to a modified Part 2 of the Greenbook.

speaker: REINHART
text: That way, you would be responsible for commenting only on the forward-looking and policy portions of the document, and some of the pressures on staff time could be relieved.

speaker: REINHART
text: If you have any other views on the content of the minutes, today probably would be an appropriate time to raise them.

speaker: REINHART
text: The last exhibit raises issues that have not been addressed for some time, namely the role of the post-meeting statement.

speaker: REINHART
text: Some of you might consider the statement as a vehicle designed only to convey coarse signals about policy, with more-nuanced information provided in subsequent communications.

speaker: REINHART
text: Others might see it as important that the statement be able to stand on its own as a reasonably complete explanation of the Committee’s monetary policy decisions and intentions.

speaker: REINHART
text: What is the appropriate role of the statement in light of the changes to the Committee’s other communication devices (question 6)?

speaker: REINHART
text: The statement’s role, which can be described in terms of a monetary policy rule, has varied over the years.

speaker: REINHART
text: At times the statement has provided hints about the odds on future action by characterizing the left-hand side of the policy rule—that is, by directly addressing the path of the federal funds rate.

speaker: REINHART
text: At times the statement has described the right-hand side of the policy rule—that is, the risks to the dual macroeconomic objectives.

speaker: REINHART
text: That is another way of stating question 7: If you believe that the statement should provide guidance about the outlook, should that guidance be couched in terms of the policy interest rate or the dual objectives?

speaker: REINHART
text: If you decide to describe the economic outlook, you will have to settle on the policy assumption underlying that projection, as in question 8.

speaker: REINHART
text: The conditioning possibilities include the appropriate path of monetary policy, some reading on market expectations, or an unchanged policy rate.

speaker: REINHART
text: This choice may interact with the role you envisage for your economic projections in explaining policy decisions.

speaker: REINHART
text: As for question 9, your ambition regarding the complexity of the statement will determine how much time needs to be devoted to drafting.

speaker: REINHART
text: Because of constraints as to how long you can meet as a group, a complicated statement necessitates pre- meeting consultation.

speaker: REINHART
text: That may get the nuance right, but it may also force you to settle on a policy view before you have had the benefit of consulting with your colleagues on the Committee.

speaker: REINHART
text: Moreover, it shifts some of the policy discussion out of this room, for which a transcript is kept and minutes are produced, and into informal back channels.

speaker: REINHART
text: A statement that could be agreed upon mostly within the confines of these four walls is probably one that is short and relays a routinized risk assessment, given your long-held view that “nineteen people cannot edit the statement on the fly.” Question 10 raises one last governance issue: Who owns the statement?

speaker: REINHART
text: At the inaugural of the age of statements in 1994, the Committee formally directed the Chairman to explain its policy action.

speaker: REINHART
text: Over the years, the statement has come to be viewed as a Committee product, with the words sometimes viewed to be at least as important as the immediate policy action.

speaker: REINHART
text: But you still vote only on the policy action and the risk assessment.

speaker: REINHART
text: Should that continue, or should you be asked to vote on the statement in its entirety?

speaker: REINHART
text: These three sets of questions are interrelated, and there is no obvious place to wade into this thicket.

speaker: REINHART
text: One possibility would be to conduct two go-rounds on these issues, with the first covering your views on the enhanced forecast and the minutes and the second addressing the statement.

speaker: REINHART
text: The first two issues are closely related and perhaps closer to closure.

speaker: REINHART
text: I suspect that you are closer to the beginning of your discussion of the statement than to the end.

speaker: REINHART
text: That concludes my prepared remarks.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Vince, it’s a little unclear from what you’ve circulated what the subcommittee is recommending or presuming about the pieces of material that would go into the Monetary Policy Report.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Do you want to say just a little about options there?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I assume you want people to comment on that question, too, and that goes to the core of this next stage of evolution in the transparency.

speaker: REINHART
text: That’s a complicated governance issue because it relates to both what the Committee approves potentially and what the Board approves because the Monetary Policy Report is by law a report of the Board of Governors explaining the monetary policy actions of the Committee.

speaker: REINHART
text: The short answer is that it depends on what you want.

speaker: REINHART
text: One possibility—that’s option one—is to write a narrative included in the minutes, have it approved by the Committee, and then essentially lift that out and make that a significant chunk of Part 1 of the semiannual Monetary Policy Report.

speaker: REINHART
text: Then the words would be the same in both places.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Those choices I think I understand, but I was really thinking about the pictures.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You circulated a whole different set of new things, innovative pictures that showed dispersion, uncertainty, balance of risk, histograms, and so forth.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I guess you don’t need to answer this question, but do you want people to react, in the first round at least, with a view on which pictures we think should be part of the narrative?

speaker: REINHART
text: If you don’t express a view here, you’ll have a chance in commenting on what the staff proposes.

speaker: REINHART
text: Our intention was to take a small subset of those charts and tables that were essential for explaining the central tendency projections themselves and the dispersion of views and to put them into the narrative.

speaker: REINHART
text: The draft that we would circulate to you would have that information, and from there, we could take your comments.

speaker: REINHART
text: About the same size as the last draft we circulated, which was, in fact, circulated as an appendix in Debbie Danker’s memo.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I meant the graph showing the evolution of the central tendency with things plus the histograms?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That’s what I meant by subset.

speaker: FISHER
text: Excuse me, but the histograms we’re talking about are the individual differences?

speaker: REINHART
text: Well, that’s what we circulated last time in the draft write- up of the May discussion.

speaker: FISHER
text: So you would have the central tendency analysis that we have and then further amplification, which would show individual differences of the nineteen members of the Committee.

speaker: REINHART
text: Potentially that’s what we would have.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m just trying to understand what we’re going to talk about.

speaker: REINHART
text: The staff draft of the June narrative will be similar in structure to the May narrative.

speaker: REINHART
text: That, however, is only the first draft.

speaker: REINHART
text: Given that we intended it to be similar in structure to the May narrative, then we would include a couple of histograms.

speaker: REINHART
text: We also added in this package a revised picture of the central tendency—you know, the red bars and the box and whiskers chart.

speaker: REINHART
text: We intended to include that.

speaker: REINHART
text: So we didn’t view any material upgrade in the pictorial description of the forecast.

speaker: REINHART
text: We tried to come up with as fat a package as we could for your internal discussion so that you could see how the individual forecasts of your colleagues vary and also are related—for instance, between the unemployment rate and the growth rate and between the inflation rate and the unemployment rate.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I think Governor Mishkin preceded me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re having questions for Vincent now.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: This is just an intervention.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I had President Poole first and then Governor Mishkin.

speaker: POOLE
text: Vince, in thinking about the possible benefits of accelerating the release of the minutes, can you name a time when that would have produced a benefit?

speaker: POOLE
text: I understand the cost because we all understand the costs, but I don’t know of any case in which releasing the minutes five days earlier would have bought us anything.

speaker: POOLE
text: At any rate, we need to think that through before we bear all those costs.

speaker: REINHART
text: The particular cases that I can imagine would be employment reports.

speaker: REINHART
text: If it takes five fewer business days—and that might be a little speedier than the staff can actually deliver—any cutting of those business days, particularly if it gets past that Friday, produces the chance that there would be another employment report between your policy decision and the release of the minutes.

speaker: REINHART
text: This also interacts with the Chairman’s testimony schedule, which is something we have to think about.

speaker: REINHART
text: Do you want to be in the position of having the minutes more likely to be out before his testimony, or would you prefer to have the minutes out after the testimony?

speaker: REINHART
text: I can imagine both benefits and costs associated with that.

speaker: POOLE
text: It probably would be helpful if we could have more detail with regard to how that might work and how often those cases would arise because the costs would occur continuously.

speaker: POOLE
text: As you emphasized, there are also some risks to accelerating the minutes because doing so reduces the amount of time to think it all through and make sure that nothing has slipped through inadvertently.

speaker: REINHART
text: There were a couple of statistics in Debbie’s memo in particular about how it interacts with the standard semiannual testimony schedule.

speaker: POOLE
text: Another observation somewhat in the same vein—regarding the economic projections, as I commented earlier, we have been thinking about this during a period in which the forecast hasn’t changed much.

speaker: POOLE
text: The situation has been pretty benign from the point of view of anybody who has been doing this for very long.

speaker: POOLE
text: One thing that I think we need to work on is how this would have worked—would it likely have been constructive—at a time like the fall of 1998, the time of September 11, 2001, or the time in early 2001 when the economy was sinking really rapidly?

speaker: POOLE
text: We need to work on those cases and not just think about the projections in the context of the relatively benign period that we’ve had.

speaker: POOLE
text: I realize that that involves more staff work, but it seems to me essential that we think all of that through before we start to do it.

speaker: POOLE
text: One other comment: I view the whole communication process that we’ve been going through as incremental, and I’m a little worried that we’re biting off too much at once here.

speaker: POOLE
text: We should think about a really pared down set of releases here if we’re going to expand the process with the idea if all that works well, then we’d take the next step.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just say that there’s going to be a go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Everyone will have an opportunity.

speaker: POOLE
text: Well, I’m sort of asking him to reflect on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Mishkin, do you have a question?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Yes, I do have a question—just a clarification.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One thing that we talked about early on when you gave us information was that there is the information regarding our views about whether risk was greater or less than usual and about the skewness of the risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You might also want to include in the documents that would go out information to guide people on what is normal so that you would have the things that we actually sent out, which was either a picture or the table showing the forecast errors.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Is it your view that part of it would be not only the charts that we actually responded to but also the background information?

speaker: REINHART
text: I believe the table of uncertainty was one thing that the subcommittee viewed as useful to include, not the three big fat bars that showed uncertainty variable by variable.

speaker: REINHART
text: That was useful background for writing the paragraphs in the narrative that talked about the Committee’s perceptions of risks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m just trying to remember—did the table have the uncertainty for the variables?

speaker: REINHART
text: The table had historical variability coming from a couple of different sources.

speaker: REINHART
text: That would be a reference table in the write-up.

speaker: REINHART
text: The narrative would say, “In the Committee’s view, current uncertainty was about at historical experience.” Then in the narrative description of the risks, we’d use the information that you provided about the asymmetries of those risks.

speaker: REINHART
text: I don’t think we envisioned showing a particular chart.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Right, but the key idea is that we do have a table with actually some numbers as part of the document.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I have one question and a plea.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The question is, Have we decided about how many times we’re doing these forecasts and I just missed the decision?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Will we be meeting four times a year?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s what we have to discuss.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It didn’t seem to fall into this huge list of things.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The plea is, Please tell us what you want us to focus on first.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: There’s so much stuff here that goes into the heart of every communication issue that we’ve talked about over more than the past eighteen months.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Do you have in mind a plan of action for which you need us to weigh in on something first and then other things second and third?

speaker: KOHN
text: Our hope was that we could come close to closure on enhanced projections.

speaker: KOHN
text: That led naturally into the minutes because the projection’s write-up would be in the minutes.

speaker: KOHN
text: The statement would be put off for a second round, and I personally wouldn’t be surprised if we never got to the second round.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we should focus first on the projections—what’s in them—and then how they might relate to the production of the minutes.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So really to home in on what we all want to see out of the projections is job number one.

speaker: KOHN
text: We would like to come out of this with some decisions made about the way forward.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Is the subcommittee making a recommendation on any of these?

speaker: KOHN
text: All along we’ve viewed our job as bringing things to the table and helping the FOMC to make the decisions and not making recommendations, and we’ve stuck with that.

speaker: KOHN
text: Janet is rolling her eyes.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This may get us slightly ahead of ourselves, but I think it’s important to what we’re asked to do now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It makes sense to get people to focus on how comfortable they are with what has been on the table regarding the range of options on projections and to say what they’re comfortable with and what they’re not comfortable with.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But as I see this plan, you’re still building in some time for refinement over the next several months to get this to the point where it’s ready for prime time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I don’t think you’re asking people—you really can’t because you’re not quite there yet—to commit right now to views on all specific attributes of this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It seems to me you’re a step short of that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Broad elements of the package on projections would then provide a basis for the subcommittee and the staff to refine this further over the next several months.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That’s what I understood the plan to be.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think you’re right, Cathy—there’s a lot here.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You can get a lot from asking people to give that broader orientation and still recognize that this is going to need a little refinement.

speaker: KOHN
text: As Vincent pointed out, we’ll have another round, a practice round this time and maybe even another one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there other questions for Vincent?

speaker: KOHN
text: I had, Mr. Chairman, a timing question.

speaker: KOHN
text: Vincent, you said that including the write-up of the projections with the minutes—either as a separate document or integrated—might argue for not shortening the time.

speaker: KOHN
text: But how could we do that with the Chairman’s testimony?

speaker: KOHN
text: Doesn’t that actually force the shortening of the time?

speaker: REINHART
text: Well, I would make a distinction between when the Committee approves the document and when the Committee releases the document publicly.

speaker: REINHART
text: You might not want, for instance, to release the minutes before the Chairman’s testimony because it does sort of step on that message.

speaker: REINHART
text: But if the write-up is in Committee-approved minutes and a Board-approved Monetary Policy Report, you’re going to have to figure out a mechanism by which the Committee signs off on the write-up so that it will be the same in the report.

speaker: REINHART
text: The possibilities are that if it is an annex or a drop-in portion of the minutes, the Committee may very well need to have two editing schedules—that is, comments on the narrative would have to be finalized by a certain date so that it could go into the report and comments on the complete minutes could take longer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Pianalto, do you have a question?

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Yes, I have a question on the timing of the Chairman’s testimony.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Are those dates set by law?

speaker: REINHART
text: The law says no later than February 20 and July 20.

speaker: REINHART
text: In practice, the Committee sometimes allows for some slippage.

speaker: REINHART
text: The last few times it has tended to be earlier than that.

speaker: REINHART
text: So that does put a T in terms of your planning horizon.

speaker: REINHART
text: You also have some flexibility about when you schedule the meetings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I understand that the doughnut truck has arrived.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So give us a twenty-minute break for coffee, and we will continue this discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We had some hurried consultation during the break about how best to proceed with this discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Breaking with our usual practice, we decided that it might be best for me to begin and to provide you with my sense of a broad schematic of how I see us going forward with our communications, in particular with the projections, which I view as being central to our plan.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I note that people can justifiably complain that they haven’t had enough preliminary information for this discussion, which I’m about to give you.

speaker: BERNANKE
