text: But let me also say, first, that there will be, of course, opportunity to react in the round to follow and, second, that we will continue to poll you and to consult with you and that we’re not going to be finalizing this for some time yet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in the interest of trying to give you something to react to, let me just present an overview of how I see this going.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The extended projections that we have been experimenting with can be a central critical element of a new and expanded communication strategy that will, in fact, address many of the concerns that were raised today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll be very explicit about that as I go through this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, what are the elements of these expanded projections?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, I recommend that we extend the projection horizon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have used a third year in our experiment so far.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that might be the right solution, but let me just leave open for discussion the possibility of either using a fourth year or replacing the third year with a third through fifth year average or something of that sort—sort of a long-term average.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, I recommend that we release this projection quarterly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would mean approximately quarterly because the calendar is not conducive to an exact quarterly release schedule.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would mean that two of the projections would appear in the context of the Monetary Policy Report.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is not a central concern, but my thought at this point would be that we should revisit the Monetary Policy Report and try to make it more informative.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a lot that we could do to make it better—to include more information, include boxes, and essentially make it a more-effective publication.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would be, as now, twice a year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Perhaps on the off quarters we could have a small release of some sort, or we could include the projections in the minutes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s one of the issues that we need to discuss as we go forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Third, I think that in our projections we ought to project a total inflation measure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As many people have noted, there is confusion—and even some resentment, I would say— about what appears to be our excessive attention to core inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Projecting a total inflation measure throughout the projection would, first of all, clarify that our definition of price stability is in terms of total inflation and would give us opportunities to explain in this document, in speeches, and elsewhere not only why we do look at core inflation, how we use core inflation, and its role as a forecasting mechanism but also—as President Fisher and others have mentioned—that it’s not a necessarily sufficient statistic and that we should look at other things as we try to forecast overall inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would go even further here—just, again, to be concrete.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ve wavered myself on thinking about which particular measure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ve had discussions with the staff, and I am not wedded to anything in particular at this point, but currently I am leaning toward suggesting that we use the PCE deflator as our measure of inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s a technically better measure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It uses chain weighting and has a lower weight on shelter costs, which have their obvious problems.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has disadvantages: There is a significant nonmarket component, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: An argument can be made for the CPI on the grounds that it is better known although, as has been pointed out to me, if we begin to really focus on the PCE, it may endogenously become better known.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Another point to make here is—and I don’t want to get too distracted with this—that since there is a fairly stable wedge between the PCE and the CPI, we might be able to use the CPI in some of our communication as long as we’re clear that we are not picking and choosing as far as our objective and our definition of price stability are concerned.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Another component of the projections that we have been doing, which I think is very valuable, is adding a considerable amount of both qualitative and quantitative information to our projection.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That includes, in particular, our explanation of the qualitative material that we have been submitting—describing the forecast, the risk to the forecast, the sense of uncertainty that we have, and so on—and I think that will be very valuable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I said, we can combine this with other supporting information.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are various ways to do this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There could be a separate document four times a year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It could be in the minutes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I suggested one possibility, which is to include it in the Monetary Policy Report twice a year and keep it in the minutes or as a separate document on the off quarters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me talk a bit about what this would accomplish for us, and then I will summarize that at the end.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First of all, the public is very hungry for information about the Federal Reserve’s outlook and our sense of the risks to the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have, as I have noted before, the best forecasting group in the world.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have useful information to add to the debate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: By providing that information, I think we can help people make better decisions and understand policy and the economy better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, the more we are forced to explain our predictions and our forecasts, the more credible we’ll be and we’ll be inviting discussion, reaction, and debate that will, I think, make our projections better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One of the advantages of transparency is that we begin to interact more with the outside world.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, I think we should assume optimal monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I had some other ideas before, but in the end, I think that’s the right thing to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: An important implication of assuming optimal monetary policy is that the projections therefore become essentially, as everyone understands, a plan for how we propose to steer the economy, if you will— subject, of course, to all the qualifications of uncertainty, forecast problems, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It gives an explicit road map with reference to both sides of our mandate about how we expect our policies to move the economy toward our objectives over the next three years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that’s very important for a number of reasons, such as accountability and transparency.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But let me give you an example of where I think it’s particularly useful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One issue we have been discussing is the appropriate period for achieving price stability, and two suggestions are out there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is sort of the standard Bank of England approach, which says that we have a two-year horizon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have certain concerns about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, it doesn’t necessarily take into account, at least not explicitly, the state of the real economy, the initial conditions, how far we are from price stability, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Another possibility is to say, well, it’s just an aspirational number.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t have any particular schedule for getting there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: People have raised the obvious objection: Where’s the discipline?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Where’s the credibility associated with that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, as we understand this, we can explain to the public that the projections go a long way toward solving this problem because they show how far out we think we have to go to get to what we and the public view as being reasonable levels of price stability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it does in a very important way solve the problem of the appropriate horizon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, I should add a point that will come up, which is that one could object that the projections are not the same as a Committee forecast.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are not going to come together and make a single forecast that the entire Committee buys into, except to the extent that we do have consensus building, which we will have over time in our meetings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That aspect of it could be viewed as a lack of clarity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, the aggregation process does reflect unique features of the Federal Reserve, including its institutional structure, the large size of Committee, the geographical dispersion of its membership, and our longstanding willingness to accept and encourage diverse views within the Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we won’t be forcing some kind of artificial consensus.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be opportunity for disparity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, I would recommend that we provide information to the public about the cross- sectional distribution, as we already do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But my inclination—and people can react—would be to provide the entire cross-sectional distribution to convey the sense of uncertainty or the sense of dispersion of views, and that will be informative in the same way that the votes in the BOE’s Monetary Policy Committee are informative.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, as in the case of the Bank of England and other banks, even though we won’t be having a common forecast, nevertheless—as I think we have already seen— the preparation of our individual forecasts does create a certain amount of discipline and has been useful for us in thinking about our forecast.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A very important question is what is conveyed by the third-year projections, and I think that they are at the heart of the innovation created by this step.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Assuming that we’re not too far from the steady state initially, which I think characterizes our current situation, it is evident that the third-year projections—or, alternatively, the third through fifth or however we decide to do it—reveal a lot of information about our views on sustainable long-run growth; our views on sustainable unemployment; and, of course, our views of what price stability is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I simply take note of the fact that the latest projections show the central tendency of the Committee’s inflation objectives to be 1.5 to 2 percent on the core PCE deflator.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I actually—and I’m speaking entirely for myself—would be not at all displeased if that became known as the Federal Reserve’s comfort zone or informal definition of price stability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, it’s a compromise among different views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, I realize that I’m complicit in the 1 to 2 percent comfort zone, but I do note that the lowest twelve-month core PCE, in 2003, was 1.27.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think we’d be comfortable with inflation rates below 1 percent even though we’re obviously willing to tolerate inflation rates slightly above 2.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not symmetrical, and I think that the comfort zone revealed by our third-year forecast would be reasonable and would provide useful information.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some would be concerned that we’re also providing information about the Committee’s views on sustainable growth and sustainable unemployment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am not that concerned about it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that a transparent Committee should do that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, for those who are concerned about possible risks, I’ll point out that Committee projections will have a lot of dispersion that probably will essentially encompass most reasonable estimates of these variables.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Moreover, there will be forecast errors around those projections, and as we get information about productivity and other factors, we will be able to update those estimates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think that they will be a major constraint.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that they will, in fact, just provide some information to the public.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I note that some participants have talked about an opportunistic approach to disinflation, which still seems to have some adherents around the table—that is, people who may say, “Well, I’m sort of for 2 percent now, but I can see over time, if the opportunity arises, very gradually moving down to 1½ and so forth.” Obviously, the revealed preference shown by the third-year projection doesn’t distinguish between those things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One thing that might happen—and I don’t think it’s necessarily a bad thing—is that, if opportunistic disinflation happens and those individuals therefore lower their projections, the Committee’s projection might drift down a bit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think it would drift up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there would be a strong resistance to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it would be responding appropriately to changing conditions, and I don’t think it would change very much; so the fact that it would not be literally rigid is not necessarily a problem to me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some thought will have to be given to vocabulary, how we describe these things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that I will myself want to talk about the Committee’s projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not quite right to call them a target because we will not have agreed universally and chosen a number once and for all.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That being said, I think that the normative implications of the number will not be missed by the public, and that it will do a lot to clarify people’s views on what the Committee is trying to do and will also be useful for internal discussions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, in testimony, speeches, and the like, I would use the projections as my reference point as I talk about what the Committee is trying to do, where we are heading, and what we think is the best way to get there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me summarize what I think this component of our communication strategy could do for us, noting that some other things could come in the package—perhaps faster minutes, changes in the statements, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But let me just talk about what I think is best for us.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, it is going to allow us to provide considerably more information to the public and in a more timely way because it will be quarterly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, it will give us an opportunity to clarify how quickly we intend to move toward our objectives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It will give us a way to deal with the problem of the horizon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those of you who were at the St. Louis Fed’s conference on inflation targeting in 2003 might remember a paper by Board staff members Jon Faust and Dale Henderson in which they talked about inflation targeting as being focused on the mean of the objective but needing also to focus on the variance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What they mean by that is the speed with which misses are fixed and that some regimes are not adequately constructed to deal with that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, this would allow us to be very explicit and very accountable about how we return to our objectives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Third, it would allow us, again, to move to total inflation as our objective and to clarify how we use core inflation as an input into forecasting total inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Fourth, it would clear up the current confusion about comfort zones and individual views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re not going to take a vote on the particular number, but I think a reasonable way to proceed is to consider the range of third-year projections as being a kind of consensus view of what most of us think is an appropriate measure of price stability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I think the normative implications will be clear.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Fifth, it will improve our internal discussion and decisionmaking.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In fact, it has highlighted some problems that we have in our communications and in our coherence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This will help, I think.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Sixth, it respects the Fed’s unique institutional structure, the nature of its Committee, its governance procedures, and its attention to diversity of views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Moreover, it builds explicitly on a communication device that we’ve been using for thirty years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In that respect, it will look in some sense as incremental even though I think it’s very substantive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I think with its incremental nature, the transition risks—be they market risks, political risks, and so on—will be more moderate than they would otherwise possibly be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So this is an outline.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I know that some of you may think that this is a bridge too far.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some of you will think that I’ve only started on the road to Damascus here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I said, there will be an opportunity now to go around as you talk to give any reaction you might have to this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also, I have not been very specific about the questions raised in exhibit 1 that Vince put out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: These things bear on the details, but I’m pretty flexible about them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I’d like to see the minutes moved up if possible, consistent with doing all of what I’ve described.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Otherwise I’m pretty flexible about this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just say a few other things about going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This, together with the other elements, is part of an ongoing process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re not going to lock this down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will ask the subcommittee to continue in existence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Certainly we’re going to have to move forward, if we all agree that this is the direction that we want to go, to implement the details of the minutes, the Monetary Policy Report, the collection of this information, and so forth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to talk about the whole package, whatever we come to, in the fall—that is, in the next three or four months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will surprise Don by saying this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It would be very nice if I could have something to point to in October, but it’s certainly possible and I think it’s very important for us to move deliberately.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If that’s not possible to do in a safe and clean way, then we could wait until January to actually deliver some product.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is a question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that what will happen is that we will see the reaction we get.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will see how the public and the markets respond.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We may have to take further steps.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When we see how this goes, the markets and the public will tell us what they need to know that we’re not yet telling them, and then we can move it still further if we need to.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But my sense is that, with some of the details that we need to work out—and your comments are more than welcome, as they are with the entire vision—as a central part of a package, this would move us in a good direction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I’m going to stop there, and we’ll have a go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Did you have an intervention?

speaker: HOENIG
text: I have just a question.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In communicating the projections, what are you suggesting there, Mr. Chairman?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Is it four times a year that we would put the projections out with commentary?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me give Governor Kohn a chance to lead off as the chairman of the subcommittee, and then we’ll have a full go-round.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with and strongly support the path that you’ve outlined for us for the reasons you’ve articulated so nicely.

speaker: KOHN
text: Let me add a few things and then give a few specifics.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think this would be a very important contribution to enhancing the understanding of the public, the markets, and the legislators about what we’re doing and why.

speaker: KOHN
text: Just to emphasize something that you just mentioned, Mr. Chairman, this systematic approach to thinking about the risks and the symmetries and the asymmetries around the risks will be very useful in our communication with the public, and a systematic and regular approach to talking about the changes in the forecast will be very useful to explaining to the public how our forecast is evolving.

speaker: KOHN
text: From my perspective, these explanations are among the most important things that we can do.

speaker: KOHN
text: The write-up that President Hoenig was asking about is key here.

speaker: KOHN
text: To my mind, the forecast is really a framework for putting all of our explanation, our write-up, in place, and is a disciplining process for explaining our thoughts about how and why the economy is evolving.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it’s more those explanations than the specific numbers that we use to educate the public about what we’re thinking, how we think things are developing and, looking at the risks and the uncertainties, how we’re likely to react to incoming information.

speaker: KOHN
text: This would put that endeavor on a much more systematic track than it has been in the past when it has relied from time to time on ad hoc speeches by the Chairman or on mentions of it in the announcements, minutes, or whatnot.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think this will be very good.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with you that the third-year forecasts are mostly people’s preferences for the long run.

speaker: KOHN
text: I admit to being that opportunistic disinflator to whom you were referring.

speaker: KOHN
text: Maybe there are others around the table.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wrote down 1.9 for year three, and I might prefer something a little lower over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: But given the starting place, I thought the welfare benefits of going down to 1.8 or 1.7 or even 1.6 or 1.5 were less than the welfare costs of the potential unemployment that we would incur doing that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m also somewhat skeptical about the credibility bonuses from making announcements.

speaker: KOHN
text: But obviously, I wouldn’t have written down a number that wasn’t very heavily influenced by my objective over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: So the public will be correct in interpreting those third-year numbers as pretty much where the individual members of our Committee want to go even if it’s not exactly the right number.

speaker: KOHN
text: I note that the 1.5 to 2 that’s in our forecast is not that wide a range.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s narrower than the inflation targets of some countries, like New Zealand and Australia.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it won’t contribute that much to uncertainty.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also note that in Mike Leahy’s charts yesterday the inflation compensation changes in the United States over the past couple of months were about the same as in the inflation-targeting countries.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think there’s a huge amount of uncertainty about what we’re doing.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, some people might think that the inflation expectations are tied at too high a level—I think that President Plosser pointed that out.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I don’t think that the public is afflicted with a whole lot of uncertainty about what our objectives are relative to some other, inflation-targeting countries.

speaker: KOHN
text: I see this as sort of a risk-management approach to talking about our long-run inflation objective.

speaker: KOHN
text: We get this out there, see what the reactions are, see what kinds of questions there are, and then proceed.

speaker: KOHN
text: If it looks as though the right thing to do is to actually vote in the Committee about what our long-run objective is, we can do that then.

speaker: KOHN
text: But we haven’t gone that extra step, which we will never be able to take back again if there’s some sort of reaction that we haven’t anticipated.

speaker: KOHN
text: The Federal Reserve is in a very different place relative to our democratically elected representatives than a lot of other central banks.

speaker: KOHN
text: We report to the Congress.

speaker: KOHN
text: We don’t have a Minister of Finance or a Chancellor of the Exchequer that intercedes between us and the Congress.

speaker: KOHN
text: The Congress has given us goals in words and not in numbers, fortunately.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wouldn’t want them to give us goals in numbers.

speaker: KOHN
text: There were some numbers in the Humphrey-Hawkins Act, which on the unemployment rate were potentially quite damaging if we had gone for them.

speaker: KOHN
text: They haven’t asked us to put numbers on these goals.

speaker: KOHN
text: They haven’t looked at this for ten years, but in the mid-’90s when the Senate looked at this, they didn’t go anywhere with it.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think we are out in front by doing this.

speaker: KOHN
text: If there were to be a backlash against even this limited step, then at least we wouldn’t have committed to something that might provoke a bigger backlash.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I see this as a step toward possibly specifying price stability numerically, a step that helps to manage the risk that it might provoke some reactions that we would have trouble living with.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I’m very strongly in support of the path you outline.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the subcommittee needs from the rest of the Committee some answers even before we get to the specifics here.

speaker: KOHN
text: So, do you agree that we ought to proceed with an enhanced projections process like the one we’ve been going through the past two times?

speaker: KOHN
text: We might have some specifics.

speaker: KOHN
text: Should we do it four times a year?

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we should, but not everybody might.

speaker: KOHN
text: Are we doing approximately the right variables, noting that we’ll have to adjust our price variables?

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with you, Mr. Chairman, that adding total inflation to the core is a very good idea, and we ought to use the same index for both of those, whatever it might happen to be.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we’ll do some adjusting.

speaker: KOHN
text: Do you agree that there ought to be a write-up of these projections more or less like the one that the staff has produced, approved by the FOMC so that it is an FOMC document, and released to the public?

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, we might discuss exactly what’s in that document.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like you, Mr. Chairman, I kind of like the histograms of how many people were lined up at the particular answers to give a sense of the dispersion of views on the Committee; they are much easier for me to look at than the central tendencies and the broad range things, but not everybody might agree.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think there are some questions even before we get to “Are you satisfied with the general thrust of where we’re going?” I think that’s what we really, really need to know more than other things.

speaker: KOHN
text: Let me address some of the things in exhibit 1.

speaker: KOHN
text: I like the sharing of forecast submissions anonymously.

speaker: KOHN
text: I guess I’m concerned that if it was by name, it would potentially be harder to change your mind at the meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: It would put pressure on those submitting to have more-elaborate submissions.

speaker: KOHN
text: My sense was that I got the information that was important to me about where people generally were.

speaker: KOHN
text: I thought the way we provided information on the federal funds rate path was useful as well.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to recognize that as we go forward with this—I hope we go forward with this—there will be public pressure on us to release the underlying federal funds rate path.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we need to go into this with our eyes open.

speaker: KOHN
text: That pressure will be there, but we need to resist that pressure.

speaker: KOHN
text: The process that we used last time worked pretty well.

speaker: KOHN
text: But let’s be aware that there are risks associated with releasing what we think is the path of the federal funds rate going forward.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some central banks are doing that now, small central banks or small countries in the north and the south, in the Antipodes and up in Scandinavia.

speaker: KOHN
text: Let them experiment with this for a while and see how the market reacts and how that interfaces with their own decisionmaking processes before we go down that path.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also like the change in characterizing uncertainty in the risks around the forecast.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is, here’s a table.

speaker: KOHN
text: How do you feel relative to that table?

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the table will help the public understand how little we know about the macroeconomy.

speaker: KOHN
text: One thing that concerns me about the projections process and delivering these things is the decimal point—to the right of the decimal point.

speaker: KOHN
text: There’s a bit of a risk that we would be perceived as knowing that there’s some difference between 1.7 and 1.8 percent inflation—that we can really determine it—and I think that including the table will tell people that’s not really the case.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think it is important that the table be in there.

speaker: KOHN
text: Regarding in what form the projections should be released, your thought for two times in an enhanced Monetary Policy Report—in February and July—and two other times—either in the minutes or in a separate document released around or just before the minutes, but really just being that enhanced write-up—strikes me as right.

speaker: KOHN
text: So two updates that are very compressed and not much more than what we agree on and then the two Monetary Policy Reports in which they would be embedded strike me as the right way to go.

speaker: KOHN
text: In terms of finalizing the projections, as I think Vincent noted, I’m of the view that we shouldn’t be updating our projections except from what we hear at this meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: The projections we release are how we explain what we did; why we did it; and when we sat around this table, how we saw the path forward that influenced our decision.

speaker: KOHN
text: As for information that comes in after we leave this table, we will not have had an opportunity to digest it or to discuss it and its implications among ourselves.

speaker: KOHN
text: So, yes, if we want to update our projections after the meeting, I would have a very narrow window, and the update would be based on the information you heard at the meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: In terms of the minutes, as indicated by my question to Vince, as a general principle I’d like to shorten the time before they come out.

speaker: KOHN
text: President Poole, I can’t speak to a specific advantage of dodging one piece of data or another, but the minutes are a very good, nuanced view of what we discussed and why we made the decision.

speaker: KOHN
text: I found it always very helpful to have them out there when I give a speech or answer questions, particularly when I answer questions from the audience and I can’t control what I’m saying.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’ll clean that one up in the transcript.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the sooner we get the minutes out there the more helpful they will be for the public and for all of us who are out in the public, but we can’t put so much pressure on this process that we don’t have an appropriate review.

speaker: KOHN
text: The words will be even more important, particularly four times a year.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m not quite sure how all of this fits together with your testimony and all that, but if we can, I think we ought to shorten the time.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the minutes have approximately the right level of detail in them now.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some central banks give much more detail about what one view was and another view was and what one person said and another person said; but with nineteen people sitting around the table, that would be impossible.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think we’re there.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also I like the idea that President Poole suggested a couple of years ago and I think Vincent did as well, of taking that stuff about the past, the first eight pages or so through the staff forecast and making that a staff document.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we could say, “As background for the meeting, the staff prepared or supplied the Committee with the following information.” However they want to do it—if they want to make it part Greenbook or whatever, it is their thing.

speaker: KOHN
text: At the least, that takes it out of our hands.

speaker: KOHN
text: It helps us with the editing process.

speaker: KOHN
text: It helps them with the editing process.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think that would be a helpful innovation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am sorry to have gone on so long.

speaker: LACKER
text: We were asked to comment on a long list of questions concerning economic projections, the minutes, and the statement.

speaker: LACKER
text: In addition, Governor Kohn has put out the broader question of the general thrust of the direction we’re going in, and I’d like to focus my remarks on the latter.

speaker: LACKER
text: Frankly, right now I think the most important question regarding the release of our projections concerns the relationship of these communication devices to our inflation objective.

speaker: LACKER
text: Everything else is more or less small potatoes right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe it would be a mistake to release our projections without agreeing on it and communicating a Committee inflation objective.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s inevitable; in fact, it’s intended the way you described it, Mr. Chairman, that participants’ third-year inflation projections will be interpreted as the equivalent of an objective.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think this would be problematic without an explicit statement of an objective for a number of reasons.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, our projections display a nontrivial dispersion, admittedly a narrow range, but market participants are going to have a keen interest in whether we believe a 1.9 percent inflation rate, say, is too high or just about right.

speaker: LACKER
text: Financial market participants already believe that there’s a dispersion of the Committee members’ preferred inflation rate and that it lies between 1½ and 2 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: I note that showing that every individual preferred inflation rate spans a range of 1½ to 2 percent is not equivalent to the Committee’s deciding that its collective preferred inflation rate is for anything within a band of 1½ to 2 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I don’t think this is going to enhance the clarity of the public’s understanding of our intentions much at all.

speaker: LACKER
text: Second, communicating our inflation objective via three-year-out projections would accomplish little by way of enhancing any commitment since we’d release the projections anew three or four times a year with the implication that our implied objective could change over time.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’ll remind you again about my brother-in-law doing retirement benefit projections, just to make the important point that a significant part of the value of an announced objective is to reduce long-run uncertainty about inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Third, our inflation projections would be displayed alongside exactly analogous projections for unemployment and GDP growth in an exactly analogous way.

speaker: LACKER
text: This would confuse people about the economics of monetary policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: In that context, how do we convey that we do not have numerical targets for unemployment or growth?

speaker: LACKER
text: How do we convey that inflation is a variable that we control in the medium and long run, but we cannot peg growth or unemployment at any one number in a sustained way?

speaker: LACKER
text: In other words, how do we remind people that the long-run Phillips curve is virtually vertical?

speaker: LACKER
text: A related consideration is that, if we present our projections this way and do not clearly state our inflation objectives, it’s not hard to imagine someone in the Congress trying to hold us as accountable for our unemployment projection as for our inflation projections.

speaker: LACKER
text: This would be a dramatic step backward for us, I think.

speaker: LACKER
text: Fourth, and probably the most pressing and immediate problem in my view, publishing our projections this way will do nothing to improve the clarity of our internal deliberations or to alleviate the problems we have and will continue to have in writing statements in the absence of an agreed-upon objective.

speaker: LACKER
text: For these reasons, I believe that the release of economic projections containing participants’ forecasts for inflation three years out would be a poor and ineffective substitute for an explicitly articulated objective and would be problematic without such an objective.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, let me be clear.

speaker: LACKER
text: I do think we should move ahead in this direction, and I applaud your leadership, Mr. Chairman, for putting something on the table today at the outset of the discussion.

speaker: LACKER
text: I just think we should do this in conjunction with the inevitable other step of agreeing on what we’re about here in the Committee.

speaker: LACKER
text: I can appreciate the sensitivity to the likelihood that various politicians may react to our communication of an explicit numerical objective; but over the past thirty years, politicians have reacted to many of our actions that were integral to our successes over that period.

speaker: LACKER
text: We should decide honestly what we believe is best for the country and communicate it clearly and with confidence.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So, President Lacker, is it your view that if we’re not at this point prepared to announce a quantitative definition of the Committee’s long-term objective, that we should not do a third-year projection?

speaker: HOENIG
text: I very much support the proposal that you’ve outlined here.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think it does not tie our hands as individuals, which was one of my concerns originally.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It allows us to do our work as members of this Committee and to put our information out there for our colleagues and for the public to judge, and I think that’s very important as individuals on the Committee.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that the third-year projections are helpful.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They do take on the tone of a goal.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There’s no question about that, but I don’t think that it’s necessarily bad at all for us as individuals; and I don’t necessarily think the fact that we have differences is bad for us as a Committee so long as we’re clear about our analysis for that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I’m very supportive of that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would move the minutes up if at all possible.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think they have served us well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We still work very hard on the statement, but the minutes have de-emphasized the importance of the statement because they clarify, and the sooner you can clarify through the minutes, the better the public is served.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So, yes, we should proceed.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I like four times a year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Now, how do we do it in terms of the description and so forth?

speaker: HOENIG
text: That’s something I think we’ll experiment with over time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I really do like the histograms.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think they give a very clear piece of information to the public and to each of us.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I’m very supportive of them as well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The variables you have are just about right.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I prefer the CPI, as I have in the past, but I certainly wouldn’t fall on my sword about it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think getting this out is more important than whether we do the CPI or the PCE.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I do think total inflation is very important—it helps clarify things for the public and allows us to explain the difference between it and core.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If I had my choice, I’d stay away from the fed funds rate path.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Appropriate policy or the way you have described it is fine.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Using uncertainty in explaining it is extremely important because it is an uncertain business over time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would not have revisions; they distort what we had coming in.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The minutes should describe parts of the discussion and clarify things for us as we go through it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So redoing the projections afterward serves no real useful purpose to my mind.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think we should move forward on this as you’ve described it here.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I like your summary of what doing it accomplishes.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I, too, want to thank you for putting this proposal on the table.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I think it will help this discussion, and I find myself agreeing with everything you recommended actually.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I can’t find anything to disagree with.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: But let me mention a few nuances.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: On the question of whether it is helpful to do this in the absence of a quantitative inflation objective, I think that on balance it is.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: It does move the ball forward.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: In line with Bill Poole’s question earlier, it’s an incremental step, but a very significant incremental step forward and one that on balance will help provide more information.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: If at some point in the future the Committee decides to have a quantitative objective, it would be an important part of that process.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: In any case, you’d have to do it as well.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: On the questions that Don Kohn asked us to comment on specifically, I think that, yes, we should proceed with the enhanced projections and four times a year is a good way to do it.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I like the total inflation approach, looking at it on a long-term basis, because it clarifies the confusion between core and total, and over time they should clearly be the same.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Regarding the write-up, my recommendation is to put it as an appendix to the minutes to keep it as simple as possible.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I think that putting it as an appendix simplifies it because then you can just lift it out and use it those two times a year for the Monetary Policy Report, and it just eliminates any possibility of confusion between the two.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: If the timing of your testimony before the Congress is such that you need an expedited process for that appendix, it’s easier to do it that way.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: It just simplifies it for everyone, and there’s just less risk of confusion.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I think it would be easier for the staff as well.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I like the idea of the three to five years, by the way, for the longer term.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: That is helpful in terms of explaining this to the public.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I know some people are concerned that it raises questions about what potential output is and so on, but you’re giving a range, and I think it helps just to explain the complexity of this.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Having the longer-term period would be helpful as well.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Getting back to Vince’s specific questions here—should we share them?

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I like the way you’ve used the fed funds rate path, and I like the uncertainty and risk.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: About finalizing projections, I agree completely with what Don said.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: The information should be what we have in hand at the time of the meeting because we all should have the same cutoff point for the projection, and that’s the logical cutoff point, and then maybe give people a day or two to update them or modify them based on what they heard at the meeting.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: But it should be a very clear cutoff—the day of the meeting.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: About expediting the minutes, I guess I would have one disagreement here.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I disagree with Don on this.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: The benefits of expediting them would be very minor compared with the potential costs in terms of additional staff resources that would be needed.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I think we have it just about right now.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Again, if you shorten the schedule, you can’t lengthen it again.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So I would just keep it where it is now.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I just mention one other little aspect, and that relates to the histograms.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I agree we should use them—they will show the outliers in the projection, which is fine.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Again, using them shows the diversity of views.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: There is a risk here that some of the outliers may over time want to move more to the center, but so be it.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I don’t think that is a great risk, but I think it is something we should recognize might occur here.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So on balance, I think the proposal you have put forth is very, very good, and I agree completely with it.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I, like President Moskow, find it very difficult to find any disagreement with what you propose.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I’m very supportive of the approach you’ve laid out for the reasons that you articulated so clearly.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I support extending the forecast period.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: You mentioned going to a third year; you also suggested maybe a three- to-five-year average.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I’m leaning toward the three-to-five-year average because I had proposed a five-year extension of the forecast period—the two years that we currently use and then adding the fifth year.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But your three-to-five-year average makes perfect sense to me.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I’m very supportive of using a total inflation number.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: President Hoenig mentioned that he had a preference for the total CPI and so do I for the reasons that you mentioned: It’s a measure that the public currently understands, and it gets a lot of publicity.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But as you point out, if we start using the PCE deflator, the public will start to focus on that measure.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I like the approach of having quarterly releases of our projections.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Last year we saw that when we release our forecasts only twice a year, they can become outdated rather quickly.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So giving more information on a quarterly basis would allow us to keep our forecasts more current.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I would like us to spend more time talking about whether we assume an optimal policy because, as Governor Kohn pointed out, we’re going to get pressure to release our fed funds rate path because people are going to want more clarification of what we mean by “appropriate” monetary policy or “optimal” monetary policy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Finally, I like the fact that your approach retains the current structure of the Federal Reserve System and allows us to give our own forecasts, letting the public see the diversity of opinion around that forecast.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We are going to have to discuss when it will be appropriate for us to talk about our individual forecasts because, once we start to give the public more information about the Committee’s views on certain things, the public will want to find out where the differences are.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Then we will have to have some agreement about whether it’s appropriate to talk individually about how we see our differences from the Committee.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But these are details that we can talk about with more time.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In general, I’m very supportive of the approach that you’ve laid out today.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I know we’ve been asked to answer some of Vincent’s questions and respond to some proposals that Governor Kohn put out, and I’ll just make a few comments.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do want to proceed with the projection.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I mentioned that quarterly would be fine.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Regarding when the projections should be finalized, I support doing it at the end of the week and using the same rules that we use for the minutes currently—not to bring in new data that we receive.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In terms of the benefits and costs of further expediting the minutes, I think, like President Moskow, that the benefits are minor compared with some of the costs.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The current process is giving more time for members to give thoughtful input into those minutes, and I wouldn’t want to change that.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Those items complete my comments.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As some others have said, I want to applaud your leadership in laying out a proposal for how we think about this.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s important to have a framework on the table for thinking about where we want to be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would add that generally I agree with almost everything you said.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it’s a good way forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I view this as a step, not the end game.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s part of a process in which we evaluate what we’re doing and how we do it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While I share in principle President Lacker’s concern about the potential risks associated with doing this without agreeing on explicit objectives, I’m willing to bear those risks because, since most people around this table know where I’d like to be in terms of that, I think the risks are acceptable in the short run as a means of getting us to that ultimate objective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that this will help us as a Committee become more comfortable with being more transparent and more communicative and that the process in itself will help us get to where I think we ought to be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So from that standpoint I’m very supportive of this direction.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I support going through with it under the guidelines and broad outline that you described.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As to some of the specific things that Governor Kohn mentioned and we talked about, as I said, I want to proceed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think four times a year is right.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The details of the Monetary Policy Report to the Congress are just a detail.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We can work them out.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Somebody is better at figuring that out than I am.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that shouldn’t be considered a stumbling block.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I support moving to total inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I said both yesterday and earlier today, I think that’s important.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m marginally indifferent between total PCE and total CPI.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Earlier I had advocated the CPI.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m still perhaps at the margin, but to me that’s not a big issue one way or the other.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I agree on the timing—the forecast and the projections ought to be based on information available at the meeting, not subsequent information.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, that’s very important in what we’re trying to communicate about our decisionmaking process.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m fairly happy with the way the staff has crafted the language.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think they have done a pretty good job of capturing the sense.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m rather indifferent about whether we incorporate it into the minutes directly or we make it an addendum.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Again, I think the markets and this group can live with it either way, and people who read the minutes will come to understand and accept it one way or another.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The two points with which I have some trouble or perhaps a little disagreement with Governor Kohn’s comments concern the optimal policy and whether we reveal what’s implicit in the fed funds rate forecast going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that revealing a dispersion or the varying underlying policy assumptions that people are using going forward helps on the issue of uncertainty—that the world is uncertain and that our understanding of the way the macroeconomy works is uncertain.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: By revealing that some underlying sets of assumptions that we on the Committee are making to get to this set of objectives are different could actually be very helpful in reinforcing the view that the future is uncertain.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Therefore, rather than locking us into some path, it may end up, in fact, opening up options to us in a way that we might not have had before.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think there’s actually potential information there that we’re providing to the marketplace that may be valuable.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Giving this area a bit more thought might be worthwhile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The second point is one that President Pianalto just mentioned, and it just occurred to me after she mentioned it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I realized that, if we submit these forecasts anonymously and if they’re reported anonymously, even though the dispersions and so forth are reported in the minutes, we as presidents and as Board members are out giving speeches all the time about our outlook for the economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the end of the day, we are unlikely to stop giving out information about what our views are.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s a little like hiding it over here, but everybody is out talking about what their view is anyway.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I’m not sure we are buying anything real by being anonymous about our forecasts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess I’m in favor of revealing more rather than less—revealing more about our uncertainties or our assumptions underlying the future path of the fed funds rate and having that information convey some uncertainty—and being more transparent, because we are anyway, about what our individual forecasts may have been in talking about that outlook.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: May I ask a clarifying question before I speak?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This really goes to the remarks of President Moskow and to the relationship between a narrative to accompany the projections and the description in the minutes.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If you did that model, which as I understood it, President Moskow, is to incorporate a narrative as an appendix to the minutes, how then would the description of the outlook that is in the minutes now—the narrative description of the central tendency of the Committee that now goes in the minutes—relate to the narrative description about the projections?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What would be the relationship be between those two things, if you did them as separate but linked documents?

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Obviously, the two would have to be drafted very carefully to make sure that they are in concert and that there are no inconsistencies in them.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: But I think doing so is clearly manageable because one is a set of longer-term projections and the other is a discussion of the shorter-term outlook.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So that is the distinction.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You would say the minutes are the description of the near-term outlook that underpins our judgment about the decision at the meeting, and the annex would be more of a focus on the description of the medium term?

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Yes, whatever the timeframe is for the projections.

speaker: WARSH
text: Isn’t there a third alternative?

speaker: WARSH
text: The minutes are what we actually discussed, and the other thing is a story.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think President Moskow’s question really relates to whether or not we are going to try to weave what we actually discussed into some coherent story or try to make the minutes really be what I suspect they were originally intended to be, which is what the color and commentary of our discussion were?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I would just note, Vice Chairman Geithner, that Jim Clouse wrote a version of the minutes that did a pretty good job of integrating them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It gave the projections with the long-term overview and the underlying forces, et cetera, and then the rest of the minutes, as is our wont, in sort of a sector-by-sector discussion of mostly developments in the near term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But you raise a good question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we should keep that in mind.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, may I ask—was that the draft that Ms. Danker sent around?

speaker: REINHART
text: Yes, the appendix to Debbie Danker’s memo is the draft that Jim Clouse prepared.

speaker: REINHART
text: I think the Vice Chairman is correct in that, of course, there would be some repetition in the discussion of the minutes just because the sector-by-sector discussion of the near-term conjuncture is going to be somewhat similar to the longer- term structure of the three-year or the three-to-five-year forecast.

speaker: REINHART
text: But they would serve different purposes, and that repetition might not be unhelpful.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So, Mr. Chairman, I am very supportive of the path you laid out.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it basically is the optimal balance today between what the consensus of the Committee will bear now on the merits and what our unique institutional structure as a central bank permits.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Now, your view and the Committee’s view of that balance may change over time, but I think what you described has to be pretty close to the optimal balance of those needs today.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What is the objective of this exercise?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think I am completely comfortable with what you and Don said in terms of the broad objectives of what we are trying to achieve through these enhanced projections.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think fundamentally that it is important to recognize that we are not principally trying to give a lot of detail about dispersion and variance within the Committee.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What we should try to do mostly is to give more texture around the central tendency view of the Committee about the likely evolution, the desirable evolution, of the economy over a two-to-three-year, maybe longer, period so that people have a better sense of what informs our basic judgments about the appropriate stance of monetary policy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We should make sure that we keep to that objective as we think about what to put into a proposal regarding enhanced projections.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the specifics, I am fine with a third year.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would like to discuss a little further the merits of three years versus three to five years.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the tradeoffs between the two are very interesting, and I want to say something about that in a bit.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I am fine with quarterly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I agree that we should have projections on both headline and core and that they should be based on the same index, not different indexes.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Before we decide to go to PCE and core PCE, again, we should discuss how to think about what it will be like to live in a world where we still have TIPS paying the CPI.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We still have a whole bunch of survey-based measures reporting the CPI.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we’re going to give a lot more emphasis to the medium-term implicit objectives of the Committee in some quantitative sense like this, we should think through whether it will work or be comfortable over time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I agree that this should be done on a view of optimal policy that is undisclosed for the reasons that have been put in favor of that, although I think President Plosser did a nice job of explaining the alternative view.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would also be in favor of expediting the minutes on the grounds that I think there is a lot of virtue in saying that you want to have a short period between what we say about what we did and why we did it and the greater narrative texture that has to come in the minutes.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The longer the gap between those two things is, the greater the risk that you have two events with signaling impact on monetary policy rather than one.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is complicated to do and must have some cost, but I’d say that a bias toward collapsing the two as close as possible is the right bias.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the third-year question, Mr. Chairman, you talked about how you would describe what people should infer from the third-year projection about the objectives and preferences of the members of the Committee individually.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My own bias would be to still try to qualify heavily whatever we say about the meaning of that third year.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we believe, as you’ve said many times I think, that one wants to think about the period for bringing inflation back down to objective as something that will probably have to vary based on the circumstances, it is really important not to set up a dynamic in which people view that third-year projection as our fixed objective for that horizon.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We want to have a fair amount of flexibility for a view of the appropriate path of inflation over time to change meeting to meeting and not be too locked into a judgment about that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I would say that I am inclined to keep that softer for all the reasons the proponents of a flexible horizon have laid out.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is virtue in laying out the central tendency of the Committee’s view about what the appropriate path is likely to be today, but there may be circumstances in which we want to be above target or objective for a longer time than three years.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, our view about that path might actually vary meeting to meeting.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I would want to soften that up a little.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But as we elaborate the package and the drafts of how this gets presented, people will have a chance to look at whether the balance is right.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On dispersion and what we say about dispersion across the Committee, I think the histograms have a lot of appeal, and I have been in favor of them and of disclosing them in the past.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I am a little worried about the following: There is some risk that they are demystifying.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Either the dispersion is going to look too wide, or it is going to get kind of narrow.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we had to decide today, I would be inclined to say for this next step that we should use the narrative description rather than the histogram to characterize dispersion.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One reason is that we don’t have nineteen people doing independent, fully fledged, internally consistent forecasts with a fully elaborated view that is independent of the Greenbook’s view of the structure of the economy and its evolution.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are not like the respondents to the Survey of Professional Forecasters in some sense, and so to have a histogram presented of nineteen different views with this degree of diversity and what goes into that gives probably a bit too much emphasis to the quantitative number of the individual views with which people come to the table.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But they are very appealing as a device for conveying uncertainty, so that’s the virtue.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would say maybe start with trying to put more texture into a narrative description rather than in a histogram.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The issue about the relationship between the narrative description that would accompany the projections and the minutes is something we need to think through more carefully.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I’m still uncomfortable in that I think what we want to do is to try to give people a little more sense of the story that defines the central tendency of the Committee about the likely desired evolution of the economy—of output and inflation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The part of the minutes that talks about the outlook shouldn’t be too narrow and shouldn’t be too short in its horizon.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In many ways, we are making a broad judgment about the forecast horizon at every meeting.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t know what the solution to this is, but I would think through the relationship a bit more carefully, and my inclination is to go for integration.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Four times a year we do minutes like today, and four times a year we do something that has more texture, more detail, and a little bit more on the medium term and has some tables accompanying it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, what we should try to do is give people more of a sense of the view of the central tendency of the Committee that informs that judgment about the appropriate stance of monetary policy over time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: To view them as separate, distinguished things leaves me slightly uncomfortable, so I think the topic deserves some more thought.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On timing, Mr. Chairman, in terms of it launching in October versus January, I think we should defer to your basic judgment about what makes sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My view is that you should set a dynamic in motion now that gives you the option of doing it in October if people are comfortable enough by that time and if it looks as though the state of the world at that point would be conducive to this kind of announcement.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think that you want to make sure before we go forward that you have a good sense of how we’re going to describe this, what it’s really going to mean, and how we handle all the obvious complicated questions that we’re going to get.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Will it leave us with an unmanageable set of problems internally in how we think about decisions on monetary policy or externally in terms of the ambiguity it still leaves in the market about what our objective is?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Let me just say a few things about that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think it is right to say that the market is fixated particularly on the question about whether our implicit view about what we’d like to see inflation do over time is 1.5, 1.75, or 2.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think what the market wants, really, more than anything is to know what we are going to do with the fed funds rate [laughter] at the next meeting, the meeting after that, and the meeting after that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: They would like to know more about what we think about the economy, but really what they want to know is what we are going to do with monetary policy tomorrow.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very important—as you read that people complain about the ambiguity we live with today, have lived with for several decades, and are likely to live with in the future about what we are going to do to inflation over time—to remember that what they want to know is what we are going to do with the fed funds rate tomorrow.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My own sense is we can manage, as we have managed in the past, with a framework that leaves the present degree of ambiguity about our objective unresolved.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is a lot of value and flexibility in that ambiguity.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t view it as a particular vice.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think that there is any compelling evidence to support the view that the burden that ambiguity presents today is unmanageable—certainly not relative to the past two decades.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course, we can evolve further.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As the Chairman said, we should view this as an evolutionary process.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We should be prepared to revisit over time each judgment we make and to continue to explore whether there are things we can do beyond this to improve the way monetary policy works in the United States.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I think it’s not right to think about this as the beginning with a clear evolution for something beyond this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is also not right to view this as the end.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think you should view it as this is what is next, and we’ll continue to think through things that might help us do monetary policy better over time.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I, too, would like to thank you very much for presenting your thoughts at the beginning of this discussion.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It was extremely helpful to my thinking through what comments I wanted to make at this meeting.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I have also found Governor Kohn, Vice Chairman Geithner, and everybody else who has talked very helpful in thinking through some of these issues.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I am very much in favor of the forecast process that we are working on.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I don’t think we have it totally right yet, but I think we’re headed in the right direction.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It’s a great balance because, as opposed to establishing right now an inflation objective that would sit out there for all time—maybe that’s the direction in which you want to head in the future—it characterizes over a longish term—and I am attracted more to three years than to three to five years—how we see the balance of things working out in the economy and what we think it is possible to do with our inflation objective over that period, given the other factors that we need to think about in the economy and that are important, both to us and to everybody within our economy.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So using these forecasts and putting a third year out there that describes what the balance of things would be given an appropriate policy path is something with which I could be very comfortable.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I like the way that Vice Chairman Geithner talked about beginnings and ends.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: One thing that I’ve been struck by in this whole communication process is how hard it is to move backward once one starts to do something.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It is nearly impossible to take it away.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So as we think about beginnings and ends, we need to be very careful about taking a step at a time.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Even though it might seem reasonable to take five steps, we should try one, see how it works, and then move on from there.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Giving a forecast four times a year; going to three years, not three to five; and showing the balance of things and the range in which the Committee would see those things turning out would be, I would say in harmony with Vice Chairman Geithner, “a good step.” I agree with four times a year—that’s a good frequency.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I was kind of drawn to some of Vice Chairman Geithner’s thoughts about whether or not to integrate this with the minutes.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I came into the meeting thinking that it would be better as a separate document appended to the minutes that, if the timing worked out well, could be put into the Monetary Policy Report or could stand on its own.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I tend to think of the minutes as a discussion of what happens at the meeting, focused on what we used to think of as the foreseeable future, which never was three years.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It was always two or three meetings ahead, shaping the stance of policy over the near term.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So I was on the same wavelength as President Moskow.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The minutes describe a set of circumstances around which one is shaping current policy.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Of course, they are related to the longer run, but that is a story that can be told somewhat independently and might be told better independently than woven into the minutes.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: But I think there is a need to think more about that—Vice Chairman Geithner had some interesting thoughts.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I think anonymity is useful at this time—again, I am thinking that, once one takes a step forward, it’s hard to go back.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I like the histograms myself.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: However, I think if we accompany at least the first round of these forecasts with histograms, it will be somewhat like throwing red meat at a tiger.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: We have had those boring tables in the Monetary Policy Report for thirty years.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: You know, the variance in the range, the outliers—they have been there the whole time.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The market could have made a lot out of that, but it never did, not too much anyway.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I think that we might be better off with a more boring approach as a first step into this four times a year—say we did it, write what it was about, give the table, but don’t give all these red histograms that seem to beg everybody to worry about the outliers.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I don’t think that is going to be helpful to us in terms of discussing things.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I know we are probably running short of time, and I can’t go through all these questions in the same amount of detail.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Let’s see, on that basis, I think that we should go forward four times a year and forecast a three-year time horizon.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I like the idea of total inflation.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Every time we have talked about this I thought that, if we are going to set a target, it should be in terms of a longish term in total inflation.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I would be more inclined to the CPI.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I should mention that I heard your comment that, if we focus on PCE, sooner or later everybody else will.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: That’s what we thought about ten years ago when we started talking about PCE, and over time people haven’t.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: PCE is there, but the CPI still is very, very common in terms of how people talk about inflation and the economy, and things are still linked to the CPI.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I do think that we need to give a little more thought to either the CPI or PCE, and looking at the total as well as the core is very valuable.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I don’t think that we should update our forecasts on anything other than what we heard at the meeting.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: There haven’t been many updates in the past.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I wouldn’t expect there to be that many in the future, so I would think either the same day of the meeting, the next day, or the following Friday, depending on when the day of the meeting is.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Fine, give people time to update their forecasts based on what they heard at the meeting but not on new data that are out there.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Let me see if there’s anything else.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: In terms of the benefits and costs of further expediting the minutes, I agree that there would definitely be costs to doing so.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: There may, however, be a benefit in that we might be able to get to the objective that we initially had of trying to make the statement after the meeting more streamlined.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: To me, that would be a significant benefit of expediting the minutes.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: We could focus the statement on what we did and why we did it and not try to make that a vehicle for some longer-term reference, but rather leave that to the minutes and then four times a year to the forecast.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So I think there is a benefit to expediting the minutes.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: From a process point of view, people have to be able to get encrypted information on their Blackberrys and not be forced to carry their laptops with them every single place they go.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: If we expedite the minutes, that will become even more of a burden, I think.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: In a memo, Vince talked about delegating approval.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I would not do that.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The principals have to be the ones to approve the minutes.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: If we decide to expedite them, we have to facilitate that process so that the principals can weigh in in a timely way on the minutes.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Did I miss something that somebody wants to hear about?

speaker: KOHN
text: We’ll ring you up in retirement.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: How about the Red Sox?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: My prediction is that they will stay in first place through the All-Star break.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I think that’s safe enough.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I also want to say that I am very supportive of what the Chairman and the Vice Chairman said.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I really think this threads the needle for getting, as Vice Chairman Geithner said, the right balance.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We get to provide more information with greater clarity and greater accountability, and I think it will also lead to greater credibility without being perceived as inflexible or challenging the dual mandate.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some of the questions and concerns that I raised in my interventions earlier indicated that I was supportive of an inflation goal, but I said it was a close call.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: For me, this is not a close call.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It really addresses a lot of the potential concerns that I had.

speaker: KROSZNER
