text: I also think it’s extremely good in putting us on the proper evolutionary path.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As you well know, everything at the Fed moves at a pace that is likely to be measured [laughter], and so this should operate on that same pace.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It allows us to understand how the new numbers will be perceived.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As a number of people said, it is very hard to move back, but this gives us some experimentation and a clear movement forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It allows us to think about appropriate risk management, as the Vice Chairman said, at least at this stage, particularly given that not everyone is on board with a particular number.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Even if everyone were on board with a particular number, I think a more difficult thing would be that, if you are away from that number, what the right path is to get to it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I actually think that is the most difficult thing to get consensus on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This gives us a little more flexibility on that without making any particular commitments.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It provides some credibility without raising something that could potentially be more problematic.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, it allows us to harden this if we so choose.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we’re finding that we’re not getting the credibility benefits that we might hope from this, we can go forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On the specifics, I think there is consensus on many of the things that have been said, so I won’t go through the individual pieces.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Just let me mention a couple of things.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Actually, along the lines of what the Chairman said about focusing on PCE and the endogenous response that there will be more focus on it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that is, to some extent, correct.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I also think that there may be some issues on existing contracts, and so it is an important point to think about.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The point that President Lacker raised is also an important one to think about: How are these different numbers going to be perceived?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, we are focusing a lot on the particular number for inflation, but we are putting these other numbers out in the same format in the same way.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This raises questions about growth goals, employment goals, the NAIRU, and Phillips curve tradeoffs, about which we certainly—or at least I certainly—wouldn’t feel comfortable in making commitments.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That actually leads me to desire to put out just a third-year forecast rather than a three-to-five-year forecast, at least at this point because I think it reduces the chance of misperception and allows for greater flexibility of how we want to characterize it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It allows us to go forward and characterize it more as a goal, if we so choose and there isn’t confusion.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But if we say three to five years, it is hard to step away from that being a particular goal.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I am not saying that we don’t want to do that down the line.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But at this stage I think I’d feel a bit more comfortable in sticking with the pace that is likely to be measured and just adding a year on that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Again, on this endogenous response, if we do this quarterly, we are likely to generate a request for quarterly testimony from the Chairman, and that response becomes more and more likely the more independent we make this document.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I’m not saying that anything is wrong with that, but I think we should just be aware of it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The Chairman should be aware of what he is getting himself into [laughter] and make sure that he feels comfortable with that, although I don’t see any problem with it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I just think that it is important to think about.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With respect to the question about whether or not it should be anonymous, I think it is valuable to have the projections out there but to have them be anonymous.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The main reason for anonymity is, as you well know, that a reporter will ask, “Don’t you think that President X is completely wrong?” Talk about red meat in front of a tiger.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That is exactly what people like to look for.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They like to look for dissent.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Although there could be some benefits, I see attribution as mostly a downside— trying to generate dissent among people, which I think is not particularly productive.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I do broadly like the idea of expediting the minutes.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Getting information to the market sooner and when it is fresher is more valuable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I am sensitive to concerns about the downside risks of people being unable to weigh in and of excess burden on the staff.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So we have to get that balance right.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But all other things being equal, I prefer sooner rather than later.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Making sure that we are available to give feedback or can get minutes securely in a more expedited process is a relatively small price for the nineteen of us to pay to provide fresher information to the public.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With that, I would also say that we shouldn’t revise our projections beyond the day of the meeting because the minutes should be about the meeting.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They shouldn’t step on or confuse things, and expediting them makes that kind of revision even more sensible.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I am very much on board with this type of proposal.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, you spoke of the road to Damascus.

speaker: FISHER
text: I was thinking about the movie “What About Bob?”—not because of my own neuroses about this exercise but because I think it is important to proceed with baby steps, step by step.

speaker: FISHER
text: President Minehan’s point is cardinal: It’s very hard to go back once you move forward.

speaker: FISHER
text: As I wrote in my memo of June 4, I believe it was, I think that you have summarized one of the most important things that we can do as a Committee, and that is to get a useful and credible inflation metric.

speaker: FISHER
text: Not only do I applaud the overall outline that you started us off with—and, again, thank you for bringing that outline to the table because it organized the conversation—but also I am a big believer in the need for us to come up with an inflation metric that is credible.

speaker: FISHER
text: Tim’s point on the PCE versus the CPI is very important to consider.

speaker: FISHER
text: As I have said before, I am more in favor of the CPI, but I do think we need to think that decision through in terms of the different instruments that are out there in the market and the precedent that has been set.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, I just want to make a couple of points.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the road to Damascus, we have to think of what the milestones are going to be.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to be careful that we don’t labor under a conceit of false precision.

speaker: FISHER
text: I worry sometimes that, when we look at these histograms—and I want to come back to the histograms in a second—the reality is that only 20 basis points separate these things.

speaker: FISHER
text: The further we go out in the time horizon— you know the old saying that you only put something three points to the right of the decimal point to show that you have a sense of humor—we have to be very, very careful not to imply that we have ultra precision.

speaker: FISHER
text: We don’t have ultra precision; this is a judgmental business.

speaker: FISHER
text: So that is one point I would like to make.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have very mixed feelings about the histograms.

speaker: FISHER
text: After listening to this conversation, I would suggest that we start with the central tendency analysis—the table that was put together.

speaker: FISHER
text: The problem with histograms, besides giving us a sense of false precision, is something that a couple of the Presidents and Governors pointed out or hinted at and Governor Kroszner just pointed to but I thought that he didn’t go far enough.

speaker: FISHER
text: Even if we do it anonymously, if we were to publish these, the press is going to poke and poke and poke—the red meat argument that President Minehan gave—and ask, “Who are the outliers, and why?” Once the press starts doing this, it is just a matter of time before a Congresswoman or a Congressman does the same thing.

speaker: FISHER
text: We row as a crew, as a team, and I want to be very careful that we don’t take any risk to undermine the unique aspect of this body.

speaker: FISHER
text: We sit around this table.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have differences of opinion.

speaker: FISHER
text: I noticed Governor Kroszner pointed to me when he said, “This guy is wrong.” It was just the way you were pointing.

speaker: FISHER
text: I realize that sometimes I am a total outlier here, but that is in the spirit of the comradeship that exists at this table.

speaker: FISHER
text: You put this out for the public, and I think you run certain risks of undermining the authority of this Committee, the authority of the Chairman, and the integrity of the process.

speaker: FISHER
text: The federalist process that we have is of value.

speaker: FISHER
text: Let’s be careful that we preserve it and don’t make this like every other Washington institution, because we are unique in the nature of our integrity.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just a couple of other comments.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m very wary, as I outlined in my letter, of being open about the fed funds rate path we envision.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is our central policymaking instrument.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we were to forecast it, I worry that we are going down a slippery slope.

speaker: FISHER
text: We would be under pressure to validate our forecasts by our actions, and I think we need to preserve some of the mystery that surrounds them.

speaker: FISHER
text: I remind you that FF does stand for “full frontal,” so I want to be careful, again, not to give the markets a full frontal view but to preserve some of our power.

speaker: FISHER
text: With regard to the frequency with which we do this exercise—again, if we do it baby step by baby step, I would like the Governors to be mindful of the fact that the Presidents run businesses.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have other things to do.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think Vice Chairman Geithner pointed to that indirectly.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is not the only thing we do.

speaker: FISHER
text: We don’t have our own models.

speaker: FISHER
text: If Governor Kohn and the Bank Affairs Committee are willing to give us a few billion dollars more to build our own models, then we are happy to take the money.

speaker: FISHER
text: But the realism is that we key off the staff and off the FRB/US model.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you really look at all these numbers that were given out, not a whole lot of variation is there.

speaker: FISHER
text: We need to acknowledge the fact that we don’t have the wherewithal and that a lot of this is guesswork.

speaker: FISHER
text: The further we go out, the more it is guesswork.

speaker: FISHER
text: One last point: I like your suggestion, Mr. Chairman, of the three to five years.

speaker: FISHER
text: As I have made clear, I have the opposite fear of President Lacker’s.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that what President Lacker suggests puts us right into an argument with the political authorities about what our employment target is.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is a nice way to skirt the issue of formal inflation targeting and, in my view, inevitably being forced by the Congress into employment targeting.

speaker: FISHER
text: I support your suggestion that we use a three-to-five-year range.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is a nice, elegant way to get us out of a possible box.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet if we decide to go down that road in the future—again, in this “What About Bob?” baby-step approach—we can do that later.

speaker: FISHER
text: I wouldn’t start out there.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think there are too many risks.

speaker: POOLE
text: Clearly, from the discussion so far— and my prediction is that it will continue this way—there is a tremendous amount of support for the outline that you have presented, and I share that.

speaker: POOLE
text: I want to focus on two points that Richard raised and maybe hit them a little harder.

speaker: POOLE
text: First, on the fed funds path, the fed funds rate is the policy instrument.

speaker: POOLE
text: We don’t want to confuse the public about the difference between the policy instrument and the policy goals.

speaker: POOLE
text: If we want to present something, we ought to present the policy rule by which the fed funds rate is determined.

speaker: POOLE
text: We don’t know how to do that beyond the broad outlines of the Taylor rule, and that is the point that we should be emphasizing.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I am very opposed to presenting a fed funds rate path because I think it is really going to confuse our communication.

speaker: POOLE
text: Now, on the issue of false precision, I want to use an analogy because I hope that it will help to explain this issue.

speaker: POOLE
text: Let me use a GPS analogy.

speaker: POOLE
text: If I did my calculation correctly, GPS coordinates usually show up on your instrument down to a thousandth of a minute of longitude, let’s say.

speaker: POOLE
text: If I did my calculation correctly, that’s about six feet.

speaker: POOLE
text: For some policy purposes, perhaps locating the piers on a suspension bridge, you would really like another digit.

speaker: POOLE
text: But the GPS instrument can’t produce that other digit.

speaker: POOLE
text: If you were to try to do it with repeated trials, you would just get random garbage.

speaker: POOLE
text: Therefore, if you are locating bridge piers, you have to use a different measuring device.

speaker: POOLE
text: Now, Don said, “What is the difference between 1.9 and 1.8?” Well, that is beyond the measurement accuracy of a lot of the data.

speaker: POOLE
text: It is not just that it doesn’t have very much policy relevance, but it is really beyond the measurement accuracy, and we have multiple measures of inflation.

speaker: POOLE
text: We take the PCE index, and we look at it with and without the nonmarket components.

speaker: POOLE
text: Those relationships change, and therefore we are really making a mistake if we force ourselves to make these judgments to 0.1 percentage point.

speaker: POOLE
text: In the projections, we ought to round these things off to the appropriate number of significant digits.

speaker: POOLE
text: Standard scientific practice is not to present measurements that run beyond the accuracy of the measuring instruments.

speaker: POOLE
text: So what is the appropriate number of significant digits in this business?

speaker: POOLE
text: If you look at the nature of the revisions, the multiple measures, and so forth, I would propose that for GDP and inflation it is probably 0.5 percentage point.

speaker: POOLE
text: For the unemployment rate, it is maybe 0.25 percentage point.

speaker: POOLE
text: But we are really going to tie ourselves in knots over stuff that is like the fourth digit on your GPS instrument.

speaker: POOLE
text: It just doesn’t have any measurement validity to it.

speaker: POOLE
text: Part of the problem in presenting the histograms that are organized around these very fine intervals is that they will display differences that are totally insignificant and don’t amount to anything.

speaker: POOLE
text: But if we present it, people will start thinking that we must think it means something.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I think we really will aggravate the communication process, and therefore we ought to look at what the appropriate number of significant digits is.

speaker: POOLE
text: I am not trying to obfuscate the differences.

speaker: POOLE
text: I am trying to make sure that we focus on differences that are genuine.

speaker: POOLE
text: If we have a real difference that is 0.5 percentage point apart, well so be it.

speaker: POOLE
text: There is no reason in my view that we shouldn’t present it and explain it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I strongly support the proposals that you have laid out.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I appreciate your doing so.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They have helped focus this discussion.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Besides agreeing with the proposals, I also agree with the reasoning that you have set out as to why this is the right step and why it is an important step.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It doesn’t go all the way to having a single agreed-upon inflation objective, but I do think it’s a major step in that direction.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the political realities and sensitivities and the differences of opinion and comfort level with moving wholly in that direction, I think this is a very constructive step.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It moves us forward, and it doesn’t preclude other measured steps later on.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It would worry me to take this step if there were a huge difference among us about the quantitative definition of an appropriate price stability objective.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But it is clear that the range of difference is not very broad; 1½ to 2 in the grand scheme of things seems to me to be very minor.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Certainly, at this point going out to a third year, it seems to me, will be very informative to the public.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I really like the idea that, having talked about our individual comfort zones, we will be able to get out of the current phase of being very reluctant to talk about this topic at all.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It would be good to express in our own speeches something that reflects a Committee objective.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think that 1½ to 2 as a range of what we think of as price stability is adequate and will be useful.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It will let us clearly explain our objectives and our strategy for using monetary policy to achieve them, which is something we really haven’t done much of, and I think that’s a good thing to do.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am really torn about your proposal about whether or not we should go beyond three years.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We are lucky at this point that we are awfully close to the range that we think we would like to be in.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But if at some future date we were a lot further from the objective, I could easily imagine—given my own view of the tradeoffs between the employment and inflation goals—that three years would be an insufficient period for you to look at my projection and see what my view of price stability was.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So at some future date, having a range as short as that could be problematic.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, going from three to five years has a disadvantage in that we will, in effect, be laying out something that the Congress is likely to view as an employment goal or an unemployment goal, and I am worried about taking that step.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I am really torn about it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Just a bit on a few specifics—I think that four times a year is appropriate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like our sharing our projections among the Committee members; it has been helpful in understanding what other people think and in facilitating our own discussion.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the staff has done a wonderful job of producing the narrative.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A major thing that we can provide to the public is to lay out our reasoning about the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is being nicely done, and I think we really have that in good shape.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like the idea of a total inflation number.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like the CPI because of its familiarity but could certainly live with the PCE as well.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like “appropriate policy.” There have been a lot of concerns in the Committee about projecting the fed funds rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In the past I have been where President Plosser is now in terms of wanting to reveal that to the public, but many good reasons have been advanced in our discussions about why we shouldn’t do that, at least for now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to the concern that, if we are very specific in our own submissions, it will eventually become public, my own feeling is that, in this round, just asking people “Do you agree with Greenbook?” or “Are there any significant differences?” has been quite informative and is sufficient.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like the treatment of uncertainty in this round.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Asking people to put down their own numbers was false precision—I really didn’t like that.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Providing some table of model-based or forecast-based historical averages is very helpful if combined with some qualitative discussion.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am a little worried about the histograms.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They are nice graphical devices.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But are they really informative about something we want to inform the public about?

speaker: YELLEN
text: I share some of the concerns that have been expressed about outliers and whether or not we want to focus attention on them.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to timing of the forecasts, I really think we should not be adding information in those projections that goes beyond what we had at the meeting.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It will be very confusing if we try to do so.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I feel that we should have the projections finalized either on the day of the FOMC meeting or shortly thereafter but not based on any additional information.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to publication, I agree with President Moskow’s thoughts that putting the projections out as an appendix to the minutes is desirable, though we will have to be careful about what we say in the discussion.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We can then also include them in the Monetary Policy Report.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I do like the idea of expediting the minutes, especially if we figure out a way to be able to read them on our Blackberrys.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We ought to be able to do that—most of the compression in time to cut it down to two and a half weeks comes in terms of our own response time.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think that we can respond quickly, especially if we can get them while we’re traveling.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like the idea of being able to use the minutes in our speeches.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have not yet talked about the statement, but I think getting the minutes out more quickly will also take a little pressure off the statement.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If the staff can find a way to write the first part of the minutes and we can present it as the staff’s information that they brought into the meeting, that will also take a burden off the minutes, and I hope it will take some burden off the staff.

speaker: WARSH
text: I also think that your straw-man proposal really does strike the right balance, and I strongly support it.

speaker: WARSH
text: We probably owe it to you between now and the fall, or whenever you feel appropriate to be able to go forward with an announcement, to keep our discussion in this room.

speaker: WARSH
text: Our confidentiality around this discussion for the past year has been incredibly helpful, and it does strike me that your ability to frame something that fairly represents your views and our views without having any of it previewed by us, wittingly or unwittingly, is awfully important.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of additional reasons that I think we have the right balance in your proposal, there has been a discernible difference in the markets in putting data- dependence into practice.

speaker: WARSH
text: In seeing how the financial markets have reacted to data sets and how they have struggled with what those data have meant, I think that they seem to have come a long way from a year or two years ago in understanding how we process data, rather than looking at the width and depth of our briefcases or the winks and nods of our statements.

speaker: WARSH
text: I can’t help but think that we have really made some progress down that path.

speaker: WARSH
text: By putting the projections first and foremost on our list of deliverables to come, we are going to continue to ask them to do their own homework as opposed to relying on us.

speaker: WARSH
text: If we were to go a step or two beyond that at this point, we might undermine some of those good market practices that are starting to bear some fruit.

speaker: WARSH
text: The markets judge us by our actions and not by our words, and that is why I must say that I don’t think any of these iterations or any of these proposals that we have discussed is a panacea in and of itself.

speaker: WARSH
text: These proposals and iterations constitute an appropriate framework for us to continue our dialogue with the markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: By taking this next step we are going to put some of our words into action by generating these projections quarterly and seeing what responses we get.

speaker: WARSH
text: I tend to think that we are going to learn quite a bit through that process.

speaker: WARSH
text: As others have said, while the economic environment is apparently benign, I think that the political environment and the financial markets are probably somewhat less so.

speaker: WARSH
text: Maybe that suggests to me another reason for taking appropriate steps and not going beyond them at this point.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, I don’t think the financial markets are asking for more than your proposal suggests.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think Tim has it right in some ways—they are still just asking for the answer key.

speaker: WARSH
text: What we are doing here is finally telling them that we are not going to give them the answer key but that we will tell them more about what we’re thinking.

speaker: WARSH
text: That will be more than sufficient to that constituency, and over time we can revisit what we are doing.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of details, I will refer to only three items.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, on whether we should be making our projections under appropriate policy or sharing a fed funds rate path, I am incredibly concerned that policy forecasts would be misunderstood to be policy commitments.

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, I think that would undermine much of the good work that we’ve done.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, regarding the anonymity of projections and the points that President Fisher made, I am a little uncomfortable with even these numbers of 1 through 19 with each of our projections because I think that the veil that we have around us could well be pierced.

speaker: WARSH
text: Another way for us to get the benefit of that might be for us to individually submit our projections to the staff.

speaker: WARSH
text: Then when the staff circulates them for us to review, they would have the projections aggregated to the extent that we can see granularity but not be listed as numbers 1 through 19.

speaker: WARSH
text: Obviously, that can be done a lot of ways.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I am very concerned that, if we were to go with individual projections, we would have calls and speculation that would make us all hunker down and somehow explain why we are where we are and be somewhat less interested in hearing where our colleagues are or in modifying our projections over time.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I would favor even a step back on anonymity—but only enough, obviously, to give us a view of where our colleagues are.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, the question that requires probably the most time among the issues that have been raised is the third year versus some three-to-five-year average.

speaker: WARSH
text: I could change my views on this, but my instinct is that, if we were to adopt a three-to-five-year window for that set of data, it might look just a little too cute.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would prefer that we all do our best to say, “This is about projections.” As we get into a third year, our crystal balls are cloudier than they are over shorter periods.

speaker: WARSH
text: Over time, if we were to do that with a third year, in our own ways and our own speeches, we could be elaborating on what that third year means to us.

speaker: WARSH
text: To some of us it might be aspirational.

speaker: WARSH
text: To some of us it might be opportunistic.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I would hesitate to go further than that at this point.

speaker: WARSH
text: But, again, I think this is the right path forward, and obviously discussion will continue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser had an intervention.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just want to make one comment about the issue of the fed funds path.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Both Vice Chairman Geithner and Governor Warsh made a comment about the markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: When I hear you talk about the markets, I am struck that it is a very narrow definition of what the markets care about.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You are looking at it in the context of what the financial markets care about is only what the funds rate is—what our path is going to be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that is much too narrow a way to think about what we are trying to do here.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To say that they don’t care about inflation and that they care only about the funds rate is a slippery slope.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Whether it is just a financial adviser who is worried about inflation planning for his clients or people who are investing long term and trying to make decisions about housing or other things, I think it does go back to inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is not just about what the markets think the fed funds rate is going to be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In that regard—I am going to go out on a limb a bit here—to the extent that longer-term decisions or the prices of longer-term assets, such as longer-term bonds, move frequently with short-run funds rate decisions—sometimes more, sometimes less—that really tells us something about what they are expecting the path to be in the future.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They are trying to infer something about our future path from one decision.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To the extent that we can provide some more certainty or shape to that path as it relates to our inflation objectives or our inflation ranges that we want to talk about, we are going to change that dynamic between short and long rates in a way that will remove some of that uncertainty and some of that speculation about what the path is going to be, even though we can at the same time convey some uncertainty about our individual perspectives about that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think we want to be careful not to become too focused on what tomorrow’s market response will be and what they care about because I think it goes beyond just that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just wanted to share that with the group.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I could just add to that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I had a similar reaction to Vice Chairman Geithner.

speaker: LACKER
text: When we targeted money supply growth, markets reacted to money supply growth figures because they thought we were going to react to money supply growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: If Red Sox victories influence a fed funds rate setting, the market would react to the Red Sox.

speaker: LACKER
text: Obviously, we are going to manipulate the fed funds rate in response to inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think that is going to drop off the table anytime soon.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it sort of sounds great to say that they don’t care about inflation, that they care about the fed funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, they are going to care about inflation if they care about the fed funds rate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Perhaps I could say my piece again, just so he didn’t misinterpret it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course they care about inflation, and of course they care about whether we are going to competently deliver acceptable inflation outcomes over time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My only point was to say that even if you gave them clarity on an objective at a certain horizon, in quantitative terms, fundamentally they would still want to know how you are going to achieve that, and you are still going to leave unmet their principal demand.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course they care about inflation, and we care about inflation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I believe that the differences they are concerned about today—a central tendency that has a 50 basis point spread on it—are small compared with the uncertainty that they would like us to resolve about how we are going to react to stuff.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What they really want is something that I don’t think we can fundamentally give them.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: They really want more certainty than we have at any given time about how we are going to react to a changing world, and they would like us to resolve the mystery in what the future will hold about the evolution of the economy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is important to recognize that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But you are right, of course they care about inflation and how we’re going to react to inflation.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I would just like to add a comment in favor of uncertainty for the markets.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Uncertainty is important in how markets work.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Uncertainty is critical to market participants forming their own views about the future and managing the risks as they see them in the future.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Everybody talks about the famous Greenspan put.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: We know Greenspan is going to be there to save us if the market overdoes it, so let’s just play into the rising market because the Fed will save us if everything tanks.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: That is an overdone argument, but I have heard it made.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: If we give people a policy path, no matter how we characterize it, they are going to take that as far more a given than we could ever really commit to, and they are going to make bets on that basis.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: When those bets don’t work out, it is going to be another version of the Fed leading them down the garden path.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I really think we should not go there.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: We should encourage some uncertainty in markets about what our actual policy path is going to be, given that over a three-year period or a three-to-five-year period the range of the Committee’s preferences around inflation is within some narrow band.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Let the markets figure out what they think incoming data prescribe in terms of policy and make their bets on that basis.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I think a certain degree of uncertainty is absolutely healthy for markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: I thank Vice Chairman Geithner for clarifying his views.

speaker: LACKER
text: I couldn’t agree more that there is a vast range of uncertainty out there about which we can’t help markets and they can’t help us.

speaker: LACKER
text: We would all like to know more about the future.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is why it is imperative, to me at least, that we focus on resolving the uncertainty we can resolve.

speaker: LACKER
text: Foremost on that list would be our coming to terms with decisions that we eventually will have to make about our intentions.

speaker: LACKER
text: Just leave it at that.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, I, too, strongly am in favor of the direction you have proposed, Mr. Chairman, and the reasons that you laid out for moving in this direction.

speaker: STERN
text: I would urge us to move as promptly as is practical down this path.

speaker: STERN
text: I am fairly flexible about many of the specifics that would accompany this path because I think there is more than one way to skin the cat and I think it is important that we get there.

speaker: STERN
text: Before I get to some of the specifics, let me just say that I went back and looked at a fairly recent chronology of our changes to communication going back to 1994.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t know whether I got everything; all actions were not equally significant; and of course, we don’t have the counterfactuals, so we don’t know what would have happened had we not taken these steps.

speaker: STERN
text: But I think it is fair to say that all our increases in communication, beginning with the press releases back in 1994 up through the expediting of the minutes and so forth, with the benefit of hindsight have worked out well.

speaker: STERN
text: They have worked out well in part because we give these things pretty careful consideration and long deliberation before we move ahead.

speaker: STERN
text: I think we have done that in this case as well, and so we are well positioned now to move ahead with this.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as some of the specifics go, yes, I would be in favor of the quarterly frequency.

speaker: STERN
text: For now I would favor sticking with the three-year horizon.

speaker: STERN
text: I am not particularly opposed to a longer one, but at least to date I think the three-year horizon would be a significant advance.

speaker: STERN
text: It seems to have worked out reasonably well as far as the trial runs are concerned, and I would do that.

speaker: STERN
text: In terms of the general shape of the latest trial run, the level of anonymity, and so forth, that was all fine with me, so I wouldn’t see any need to make any particular changes with regard to that.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to the form in which the projections should be released, I think I would come down in favor of President Moskow’s suggestion as some sort of appendix to the minutes.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that will give us more flexibility over time and it will not be a big problem to make sure that whatever we say in the minutes is consistent with those projections.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that is a manageable issue, so I would favor that.

speaker: STERN
text: I would also favor cutting off the projections as soon as possible after the meeting for a couple of reasons.

speaker: STERN
text: One is that not doing it raises the potential for confusion of what we know and when we know it, which we can and should avoid.

speaker: STERN
text: I also think that we don’t really want to put much emphasis on high-frequency data.

speaker: STERN
text: Just because you get one or two more observations, most of the time they don’t make much difference; but even when they seem to indicate a significant departure from what we had expected, they are subject to revision or the next observation we get a day or two later may work in the opposite direction.

speaker: STERN
text: It just doesn’t seem to me that there is a lot of advantage to emphasizing them.

speaker: STERN
text: I would be in favor of expediting the minutes, but I think I would defer that for now, just because we are talking about some major steps.

speaker: STERN
text: We ought to get those in place first, and we can come back and think about expediting the minutes shortly thereafter, assuming that this all works out well, if that’s what we want to do.

speaker: STERN
text: There are probably good reasons to do it at the end of the day, but I don’t view that as quite as important as some of the other things we’re talking about at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: With that, that’s all I want to say.

speaker: STERN
text: I think we are in the process of making some significant progress here, and I am encouraged by that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I, too, applaud your putting a concrete proposal on the table.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: With a Committee of nineteen, and as many moving parts as this could have, we could end up with a camel when we wanted a horse, and therefore having something concrete to react to is very helpful.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Having said that, I have looked at this question both at the strategic level and at the tactical level.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Let me just comment on the strategic level first.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The way I process the question is that it is based on principles in some respect, and some of the principle-based objectives are (1) transparency in governance is a best principle in general, and this moves in that direction; (2) it should enhance accountability; (3) it should enhance public confidence in our credibility; and (4) it should enhance the influence on outcomes—that is to say, it should have a grounding in results and the optimal outcome should involve somewhat less risk.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am trying to process the thrust of my decisions through that strategic prism.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I asked myself under what circumstances this could backfire, and I think the answer is perhaps that in periods of very rapid change, volatility, turbulence, severe shocks, and the aftermath of severe shocks, we could find this degree of explicitness and degree of openness problematic.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But I don’t think we can manage to those kinds of contingencies.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think we have to manage more with a view of normal times.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I see here in the Committee some tension, as we address this question, between a mystique model of effectiveness, which perhaps optimizes flexibility and gives us an opportunistic posture and, therefore, is built around closed deliberation and a transparent, explicit, exposed, “out there” model.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: They both have some benefits in terms of our ultimate effectiveness.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I view it as a bit of a balancing act between those two.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But, as I said, I support the thrust because I think the principle of transparency and accountability trumps that of maximum flexibility, if those two things under certain circumstances are opposed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am influenced, Mr. Chairman, by your and Don Kohn’s sense that this is incremental.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is a step and, therefore, is adjustable.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It may not be reversible, but it is at least adjustable, and that means that we can tweak the overall tactical aspects of it to get it to work as efficiently and as effectively as possible.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As to some of the specifics, yes, we should proceed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Four times a year seems right, and I think we have to line it up with the Monetary Policy Reports.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I like the idea of total inflation because I think that is where people live for the most part.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I see the narrative best done as an addendum.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding anonymity, I would say that not being anonymous might be too much disclosure, so I support anonymity.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On the third year, I think of the third year as a statement of intentions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is our intended steady state, if we can get there.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I do see a tradeoff there: Having a single third year is more consistent with accountability, but it puts credibility a bit more at risk.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So as I listen to the debate on that, I am somewhat influenced by Vice Chairman Geithner’s approach of allowing for more flexibility in the outyears.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This is not a moon landing.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We can’t be precise in where it comes out in the thirty-sixth month.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We are in a world of shocks and uncertainty, so I, on balance, favor the idea of buying us some flexibility in the three-to- five-year timeframe.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I like the qualitative characterizations, particularly of uncertainty, for the same reasons.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am not terribly in favor of accelerating the minutes for now.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We could do that at a later date, after we have refined and nailed down some of the other moving parts here.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I don’t think it buys us enough at this time, so I would view that as a refinement that might be made at a later date.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Let me leave it at that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I share many of President Lacker’s concerns, but I come to a different conclusion because I strongly support this proposal.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is a major step, but it is incremental.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I’d like to go through some of the issues that President Lacker discussed because I think that they relate to where we may be heading in the future and how we may have to handle things now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The concerns that he raised are very, very important ones.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The first is that a third-year or a three-to-five-year projection does not reflect a commitment.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We know that there are some very strong benefits to having a commitment.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: A particular thing that’s important here is that being opportunistic in terms of changing what our view is of where we will head in the future creates very bad expectations dynamics.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, it creates an anti-stabilizing influence rather than a pro-stabilizing influence because, when you overshoot, you might tend to have higher projections.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Similarly, when you might undershoot, you might lower projections.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This has become an issue, by the way, in other countries.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In countries that have inflation targets, when they were undershooting for a long time, people actually pushed them to lower the inflation goal.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Doing that turns out to have very negative effects on the economy because, when you get a negative shock to the economy, people lower their expected inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That raises the real interest rates and means that you have a contractionary impulse.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s very problematic and a serious concern that we have to worry about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’ll talk about how I think we can deal with some of these issues.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Second, I also very much worry about the issue of the projections.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Although they have the benefit of giving information about what people’s views of our inflation goals are, they could be interpreted in relation to output and unemployment as also being speed limits, goals, or whatever.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In the end, that is a very dangerous thing to happen.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The third thing that I think is an important concern is that, without a consensus of this Committee, it is much harder to deliberate.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It will be much harder to write our statements.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have been struggling with this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am willing to go along on this for a period of time because we are still not there yet, and a question is whether we can get to a consensus.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I am willing to hold off.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But there will be a point at which some of us may say, “Gee, I can’t sign on to that statement unless a consensus is built.” I think that problem could become serious in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So how do we deal with these issues?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The reason that I’m comfortable with this step at this point is that through speeches we can clarify some of these issues.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So, for example, if we go with this approach, I would give a speech and say that, although some information is here about inflation objectives, we should not think about it as having information about unemployment or output objectives because we have much uncertainty about what potential GDP or the NAIRU is and, furthermore, we can’t control either.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think that we can clarify some issues in speeches.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m sure that the Chairman will do it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The point that I think is relevant, and the reason I am discussing these issues, is that people have to realize that, even though this step is exactly the right way to proceed, it will still leave us with problems, and the reality is that we will have to deal with them.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The advantage of proceeding this way is that it gives flexibility, particularly to the Chairman for dealing with the political considerations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Eventually we will have to go to a numerical inflation goal.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Not doing so will get more and more untenable over time.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: A question is, What is the right time to do it?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What is the right time in terms of the political environment?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What is the right time in terms of where the economy is?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So people have to be aware that this is really a first step.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: To be honest, I will not be satisfied with this as the end game.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: At the same time, the question is, When would be the appropriate time to move forward from here?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We will have to use our best judgment on this question, and the Chairman will have to use his judgment as well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I am very supportive of this proposal, but I want to make clear that I think that we’re not settling the issues.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m sure we will have to deal with them in the future, and I think we will deal with them in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So those are the general issues.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Let me go to some of the specifics.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The issue about the horizon is really very tricky.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am very comfortable right now with a three-year horizon because things are working out pretty well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Thank goodness the economy has been coming out pretty much in line with our forecasts—that we actually have inflation coming down and that it is very close to what the goal of anybody on this Committee would be because we are all between 1½ and 2 percent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Given a goal of 1½ or 2 percent and a three-year horizon, we should get approximately there.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I do not think there’s a problem now with a three- year horizon.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, I don’t see this as stable because, God forbid, there could be cases when we get shocks and where we are substantially away from where we want to be, and then a three-year horizon will not be adequate.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: President Yellen and Vice Chairman Geithner made this point.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The issue here is that doing three years now is fine, but we will have to rethink this in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: At some point, we may have to go to a longer horizon, or the alternative will be that we will have objectives—so it is one or the other.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think people know where I stand on that issue—I have a preference.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Right now, I’m actually very comfortable with three years because three years plus a long-run inflation goal will provide the information that people need.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If we don’t have a long-run inflation goal, then at some point, if things don’t go right, we may need a five-year horizon as well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I get concerned about providing a federal funds rate path.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am known as a person who is very pro-transparency, but I wrote a paper called “Can Central Bank Transparency Go Too Far?” The problem here is exactly the one that Governor Warsh and others have mentioned.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Even though we know that, when you put out a path, it is completely contingent on events and a lot of uncertainty is around it, making that clear to the public is very hard, particularly to politicians who want to use things in their own way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s amazing, when you testify in the Congress, you’ll say something, and then they will try to use whatever you say in a way exactly opposite to what you said.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Everybody knows it is exactly opposite, but they will do it anyway.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So you have to be very careful with what you put out there.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This has been a problem with other central banks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The Swedes actually had problems when they first announced their path because they didn’t clarify the uncertainty and some problems arose in the marketplace.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We shouldn’t rule it out in the future, but it is a tough thing to think about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: For the time being, I would certainly not advocate it, and I have serious concerns about it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On the issue of the CPI versus the PCE, a lot of details are here, and my view is to let the subcommittee decide.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’ll go with whatever they want here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do have a preference for the CPI, but it is very slight—I don’t even think it’s a second order issue, maybe third order; it’s not really critical.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: An advantage is that CPI is better known.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Vice Chairman Geithner mentioned it is actually involved in a lot of contracts.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One reason that the CPI is used is that it is not revised.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That turns out to be the reason that I lean to the CPI rather than the PCE.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think the PCE is a slightly better measure, but the CPI is not revised, which will make our lives simpler because we know that we’re making decisions ex-ante with the information we have now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, when the PCE gets revised, people can second-guess you.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We’ve had this in the past, when our PCE was getting very close to 1 percent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It turned out to be revised quite a bit upward, and then people said, “Gee, why weren’t you tougher on inflation?” So I think that using the CPI has a political-economy advantage, even if there is a slight disadvantage from a technical viewpoint.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I share some people’s concerns about the histograms.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I love to see the histograms.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: They were very useful to me.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I like them because they provide information and actually show that there is less diversity.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What was remarkable about them—and I don’t think that this will be a problem in the future—is how close we generally are.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that actually will help dissipate some of the issues in the press.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But, again, I don’t feel particularly strongly about this issue.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: A very important issue that comes up here is where we put the enhanced projections into our documents and their relationship to how quickly we do the minutes.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I lean toward having the projections as a separate document in some form, either as an addendum or whatever, because I think it gives us a lot of flexibility.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am going to say something that may get me an IED (improvised explosive device) in my office later on, but we’ll talk about that in a second.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There is also an issue about the times of the testimonies, which are happening two times a year.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I suspect that we will end up with testimonies four times a year, and in that context it may be difficult to have the full minutes done within three weeks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We will definitely need to expedite the enhanced projections.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, if we have the flexibility of having a separate document, we may be able to do one and then do the other; that way we can basically relieve some of the pressure on people.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We’re going to end up having to speed up the process on that part of the picture, so separating them to some extent has the advantage of giving us more flexibility.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the last issue, for which I may get the IED in my office and which I think is going to happen even if I didn’t propose it, is that I think there really is an advantage to having these enhanced projections as part of a Monetary Policy Report that is issued four times a year.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My suspicion is that we will be in a situation when we do this that the Congress will likely want testimony more often.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am sorry for the Chairman here, but I would welcome the increased testimony because it gives us a bully pulpit from which to provide more information to the markets and to tell them our point of view.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I wouldn’t have to do the testimony, but there is a little work because, as a Board, we have to go over the testimony.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m going on vacation, so we have to do a conference call about the testimony.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I will have to do that four times a year, so there is a little cost for me but more for the Chairman.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Having a Monetary Policy Report with these enhanced projections will actually be a plus.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Again, it gives us an opportunity to express our views, and I suspect that it will actually end up improving the quality of the Monetary Policy Report.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It could be an important part of our communication process.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Now, let me mention an issue so that I don’t get the IED but instead just a water gun shot at me by the staff.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have a really serious problem right now in that our staff at the Board is getting severely overwhelmed by work.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is of great concern to me and, I think, to other members of the Board.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The situation is such that, if we don’t fix it, I think the staff will break.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This means that we have to think about the products that the staff produces for us.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Do we absolutely need them?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Even if we like them a bit, if they’re very costly to produce, do we need them?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This will be an issue going forward.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The process that we are talking about now will increase work for the staff.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If we do a Monetary Policy Report four times a year, it will be even worse.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We may need to think about what goes on in terms of FOMC documents.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Can they be done in a more efficient way?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Do we need certain information?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What is the most efficient way to run a research operation?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The issue here also is that there has become a discrepancy in terms of the workload for the Board staff versus the research staff at the Banks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that it is great that the Banks actually have the research that is coming from them, which has greatly improved over time.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is a major positive for the System.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But the discrepancy in terms of workload, which is killing our staff—if in fact their work is increasing relative to that of the Banks—is not a healthy situation for the System in the long run.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So one of the things that I am proposing is more work in a sense, but the Committee will need to think about the issues of how we can use our staff more efficiently to continue to provide us with all the services we need, so that the quality of work does not decrease.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If it’s done right, it can improve the quality of work for us and can actually take some of the pressure off the staff.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I’m doing this so that I don’t end being a victim of Jihadism, but I actually strongly believe it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, first of all, let me thank everyone for extremely thoughtful and helpful remarks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will be looking at them, the staff will be looking at them, we will proceed with this process, and we will try to converge to the document that ultimately will be the one that will be the format that we will be using.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we will be in touch with you about perhaps further questions, and we will be doing another trial run for the next meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We do want to have a few thoughts from you on the statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me propose the following.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s take a half-hour break for lunch.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When we come back—I’ve conferred with Governor Kohn about this—let me just ask you to answer two questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One, in light of these proposed changes, are you happy with the statement, or is there a change that you would make?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Two, are you happy with the approval governance—the process by which we now construct the statement?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The answer could be yes-yes, no-no, [laughter]—clearly 3:00 p.m. is the drop-dead deadline—but I hope that we can have a very quick and efficient go-round on those two questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let’s take a break for lunch now and come back in half an hour.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, thank you for the very useful discussion before lunch.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just remind you that we need to keep this discussion within this room.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It would be destructive to the whole process if we had it leak out in the next few months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we appreciate your doing that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The last item of business is just to do a go-round on the statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Remember there are two questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, given where we seem to be going on using projections and the other elements we discussed, do you think that the statement is okay?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What suggestions do you have for changing it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, do you have any comments on the consultative governance issues?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Who would like to begin?

speaker: HOENIG
text: As far as the statement now goes, the way I would phrase it is that I can live with what we have.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If I may anticipate President Minehan just a little bit, I would like to see it simpler and shorter as we go forward, especially if we can move the minutes closer to the meeting date as we discussed here earlier.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That would enable us to do that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the governance, I think the way we do it right now is fine.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we are going to have the statement as it is now structured, the process seems to be working, and I don’t see any need, again, to vote on it.

speaker: KOHN
text: Could I add to the governance question the issue of what we vote on as a Committee?

speaker: KOHN
text: Should we vote on the whole statement or just the first and fourth sections as we do now?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Well, I guess the way I would answer that is I would not change the way we do it now because I’m not sure if it’s the first or the fourth section.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the practical implication is that it really wouldn’t be legitimate if we agree with that to dissent on the description of the economy or inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we agree on that—but we will hear what people have to say.

speaker: STERN
text: I’m basically happy with the statement as it is now.

speaker: STERN
text: It’s not exactly where I thought I would come out, honestly.

speaker: STERN
text: But if you look at it, it’s really pretty straightforward and does what it needs to do—by which I mean that it provides a concise, but I would say valuable, rationale for the decision.

speaker: STERN
text: That has to include, and it does, something that’s forward looking a bit because obviously with the lags in policy we’re not just making decisions based on looking in the rearview mirror.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t think it’s too long.

speaker: STERN
text: It’s only, if I counted this up right, seven sentences or something like that.

speaker: STERN
text: That doesn’t strike me as excessively long.

speaker: STERN
text: In fact, other things being equal, I would probably be in favor of adding to it rather than reducing it, but I don’t think it’s worth the effort based on my experience around this table in recent years.

speaker: STERN
text: So I think it does what it should do and does it reasonably effectively.

speaker: STERN
text: I have no inspirations, I guess, for how to improve it in any significant way.

speaker: STERN
text: I do think it will continue to evolve just as the economy, the outlook for the economy, and the position of policy do.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as governance is concerned, I would prefer voting on the entire statement, but I don’t think that the current system is so badly broken that we absolutely, positively need to do something about it.

speaker: STERN
text: But it seems as though we spend a fair amount of time on it, so I don’t know why we wouldn’t at the end of the day vote on it.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think the statement is okay.

speaker: POOLE
text: I am a little concerned that we modify it case by case.

speaker: POOLE
text: Today we had this issue about “elevated” or “somewhat elevated” and how would we change that without giving a message that we don’t intend.

speaker: POOLE
text: I don’t know whether we can craft language that would avoid that sort of case-by-case issue.

speaker: POOLE
text: It seems to me that after we go through the projections exercise, we might want to come back to that.

speaker: POOLE
text: On governance, I could go either way.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think it’s okay the way it works because we fully discuss the issue.

speaker: POOLE
text: If there’s sentiment to vote on the full thing, that’s fine, too.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I’m basically happy with the statement the way it is now.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like President Stern, I was leaning on the side of making it shorter, but when I started to look at where I would cut, it was very hard to come up with places to cut.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I don’t think that adopting some of the changes that you outlined earlier will shorten the statement.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: It could change how we characterize elements of the statement, especially the rationale section.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: When we talk about economic growth, we can characterize it more as it relates to the central tendency projections that we’ve provided.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Then when we characterize inflation, rather than using words like “remains elevated” or “will moderate further,” the public will have the benefit of our projections on a quarterly basis, and it might be easier then to describe how we view the inflation situation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Then also by adopting a total measure for inflation, it will be easier and, again, clearer when we’re saying words like “inflation” or “inflationary pressures.” The public will better understand what measure we’re looking at.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I don’t think that the new approach or the revised approach would change the length, but it might help us in the communication process, and I’m happy with the way that we’re doing the risk assessment in the statement now.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In terms of governance, I think that the public views the statement as a product of the Committee deliberations, and for that reason I think having the Committee vote on the full statement would be helpful.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In that regard, Vice Chairman Geithner made a comment earlier about if we go that approach, let’s make fewer changes at the table and focus on giving our input to the statement before the meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: If we do some of the editing at the table, we don’t have time to reflect on how those changes will be interpreted.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So having fewer changes at the table would be helpful.

speaker: LACKER
text: I like the statement as is.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was one of those who, when we considered accelerating the release of the minutes, thought that it would take some weight off crafting the statement, which we could shorten.

speaker: LACKER
text: Alas, I was incorrect, and that was sort of hopeless.

speaker: LACKER
text: I sort of like the length the statement is now.

speaker: LACKER
text: It does a reasonable job with what it does, with one exception—the last section, the so-called balance-of-risk assessment.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’ve argued this many times when we’ve talked about this.

speaker: LACKER
text: The intention is to convey the likely next direction of interest rate changes.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our general practice has been—there have been some exceptions—to describe the risks to the things we care about, and we invite people to deduce what we think of as the likely next direction of interest rate moves by inverting our policy reaction function somehow.

speaker: LACKER
text: I always thought that was problematic, needlessly obscure, and I liked the times when we crafted that statement fairly directly and explicitly with phrases like “policy firming.” About the balance-of-risk assessments, I hesitate to put something else on the table, but we ought to think about the directive, too, because the balance-of-risk assessment came into the statement because it was in the directive and there was a tilt statement in the directive that originated in the ’80s as a way of providing the Committee’s sense of constraint on the Chairman’s discretion to make intermeeting moves.

speaker: LACKER
text: That’s my understanding of how it arose.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then it came to be about the next meeting when we did intermeeting moves, and now it’s just sitting there in the directive, and I don’t know what good it does in the directive really.

speaker: LACKER
text: You know, we don’t make intermeeting moves.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t know what our understanding is about discretion about intermeeting moves.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that we’re supposed to have a conference call with everybody.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I don’t know why we need this little directive in there, and it seems to me you could just take it out of the directive.

speaker: LACKER
text: About governance, I’m in favor of voting on the whole thing.

speaker: LACKER
text: I remember talking at one point with I think it was you, Mr. Chairman, and others about how it is backward for us to talk about the statement—to do negotiations about the statement—a week before we even talk to each other or read the Greenbook.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I don’t think that’s so problematic.

speaker: LACKER
text: It doesn’t end up putting our feet in cement really, and I think we’ve been able to have sufficient flexibility during the meeting despite what we said the week before.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I don’t view that as terribly problematic.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Regarding the first question, the statement, I think the process is working well at this point, and so I don’t see any need for major changes in it.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Given the consensus on moving forward on these projections, I think that fits in quite well with the existing process we have for the statement.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: My feeling is to minimize forward-looking comments in the statement.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: We never used to do this, and then we got into it with phrases like “considerable period,” and “patience,” and so forth, and then we evolved to a statement in which we say “future policy adjustments depend on the evolution of the outlook for inflation” and so forth, and the data coming in.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So we don’t really have a forward-looking statement currently, but my preference is to use forward-looking statements only when it really is important to serve a specific purpose for the Committee.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I tend to agree with Jeff Lacker that you could drop the last part of the statement.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: On the governance issue, it seems artificial not to vote on the entire statement because we spend so much time talking about all parts of it.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So on balance I would say, yes, we should vote on the entire statement.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: One issue was raised in the background material about whether the statement should be the Chairman’s or the Committee’s.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I think it should be the Committee’s.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: It would put the Chairman in an awkward position not to have it as a statement of the Committee.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: If it wasn’t a statement of the Committee, people would try to pull us apart by asking us questions individually as to whether we agree with “the Chairman’s statement.” So I think the process we have now is just right and that it should be a Committee statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just to clarify your comment on forward-looking language, your examples were about policy, like “considerable period” or whatever, but not necessarily.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Does your comment apply to statements like “output is going to grow at a moderate pace?”

speaker: MOSKOW
text: No, I should have clarified that.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: No, in terms of comments in the statement about the outlook for the economy, yes, I think that’s fine.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I was thinking of the outlook for policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also had a two-hander on that.

speaker: KOHN
text: So in terms of things like “predominant concern,” which is kind of forward looking for what our concern is in the future, would you have that or would you cut out the whole fourth section?

speaker: MOSKOW
text: No, when appropriate, I would keep that.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: But I was thinking primarily of the last sentence that we had happen there.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: My recollection is that it evolved from “a considerable period” to “patience” and so forth, and then we got into “it will depend on the outlook for inflation and economic growth.”

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not sure I heard you clearly, Mike, but I want to clarify: I was advocating eliminating the risk assessment from the directive, but I would keep that section in the statement.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Well, thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the statement is just about right.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like the current length and structure.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would not want to see a great deal more detail in it about our assessment of the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think that should wait for the minutes, but I don’t think there’s anything that’s in the statement now that we should cut.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The statement has evolved; and we have in practice avoided doing something formulaic in terms of the balance of risks.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We do not have the same language all the time.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We sometimes use forward-looking policy language and sometimes we don’t.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we should avoid anything formulaic and just do what’s appropriate in the given conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: When we were on a path of raising the fed funds rate from 1 percent, and we had every expectation that we would be involved in a series of steps over time, it would have been highly artificial to avoid indicating in the statement that this was our expectation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It was important to signal it using forward-looking language.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I wouldn’t want to take forward-looking language off the table.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It doesn’t seem too important now when our own expectation is for a flat path.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I think the statement is working well.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’m really amazed at how well the process of drafting the statement is working too.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Initially when we started getting into circulating ideas about it before the meeting, I thought, “Oh, this is going to be chaotic and spin out of control.” I’ve been amazed at how thoroughly constructive it has been—that by the time we walk in here and have the statement, it has actually evolved a fair amount.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it has always been an improvement, and we have been able to have drafting sessions, and they have worked out surprisingly well.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the governance, I think this thing has accidentally fallen into a governance hole, and it needs to be cleaned up.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The Committee should vote on the whole statement.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That’s what the outside world thinks now; they just haven’t noticed that we don’t.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I’m relatively happy with the statement.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Along the lines that Presidents Yellen and Moskow discussed, I would try to stay away as much as possible from forward-looking language or commitments.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: There’s a time and a place—2003 going forward: Moving from 1 percent up was a unique occurrence, I think.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So I would really focus the statement, as we mostly do now, on what we did and why we did it.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Why we did it has a forward-looking component to it.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It has to depend on what we expect the economy to look like in the future and where we expect inflation to go.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Something referencing both of those things has to be in there.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: If I had my druthers, I’d be agnostic about whether or not we do an assessment of risk each and every time; rather, consider what that adds to or possibly subtracts from in terms of the statement.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So I wouldn’t be committed to doing a section 4 each and every time.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It’s really good, to the extent we can do it, to stay away from formulaic language and to focus the statement as much as we can on what the realities are at the time of what we did and why we did it.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: In terms of process, with anything edited by nineteen people, the process is not always optimal.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Getting a little sense of where the staff is the week before is helpful.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: It has allowed people, myself included, from time to time to weigh in, to actually be heard before the meeting and to make some changes to the draft statement that we look at in the meeting.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I can understand the desire not to do too much editing around the table.

speaker: MINEHAN
