text: However, I thought that one of the reasons that we went to more two-day meetings was so we could all get a read on what others were saying and thinking on the one day, think about it and any implications it had for what we said and how we said it overnight, and then bring those thoughts to the table the next day.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I always thought that there was a lot of logic to the process and that it probably adds to rather than subtracts from the amount of comments around the table, particularly when you find yourselves in a bit of a tenuous or dicey situation with regard to how to characterize how people are feeling about things.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So I think I’d be willing to bear a little more noise around the table rather than a little less.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: On the governance issues, I think this started as the Chairman’s statement because nobody had the stomach for nineteen people editing.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: So it was better to let it be the Chairman’s statement, and therefore we didn’t have the right to edit it.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Now, of course, we edit it, so it doesn’t seem reasonable to me not to vote on the entire statement.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I think it’s easy enough to make that change.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The whole thing is so esoteric anyway that I can’t imagine that anybody aside from us knows that we don’t vote on it or has even focused on it.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The idea that people are going to dissent on the statement?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: We’re not dissenting on policy.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I find it difficult to think that dissenting on the statement is going to be a big issue, but it is always possible, I suppose.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: Were there any other governance issues?

speaker: MINEHAN
text: I think I probably said this.

speaker: MINEHAN
text: The current approval process is difficult; but given the ability to look at some form of a draft the week before, to be able to think overnight, and provide some substance to the editing process the next day, I think it works okay.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I think the statement should be a statement of the Committee.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t have any problem with the current governance structure, although I think it does make sense for everybody to vote on it since we hammer it out anyway.

speaker: FISHER
text: I wouldn’t change the language.

speaker: FISHER
text: We do have one sentence that we always repeat, which to me is a given—that our future policy actions will depend on the evolution of the outlook, et cetera, et cetera.

speaker: FISHER
text: I guess we should say that every time, but I’m not sure we have to say that every time.

speaker: FISHER
text: Otherwise, I’d keep it the same, although I promise to continue to lobby for the word “global” from here to infinity.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like the others, I think the statement has basically evolved into a very good place.

speaker: KOHN
text: I sometimes worry that the process of putting a statement together by nineteen people will mean that there’s too much inertia in the process.

speaker: KOHN
text: But so far, maybe because the economy hasn’t jerked around very much recently, we’ve been able to keep up.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I do think we need to make sure that the language doesn’t lag the events or, if events start to move, we’ve got to be willing to change the language even though it’s hard here.

speaker: KOHN
text: I like the way the balance-of-risk section has evolved from talking about what’s going to happen to the funds rate—I agree with President Yellen that it was appropriate in the particular circumstances—to talking about the right-hand side of the Taylor rule—that is, what’s going to happen to the output or inflation gaps.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think that’s positive.

speaker: KOHN
text: It gives a little very vague guidance about what the Committee is most worried about, and I think that’s probably helpful to the markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is then elaborated in the minutes, but it fills a three-week gap before the minutes come out.

speaker: KOHN
text: Certainly if we changed our minds about where we saw the risks to the economy, we would probably want to tell people about that before those minutes come out.

speaker: KOHN
text: So basically you’re in a pretty good place here, and it will continue to evolve.

speaker: KOHN
text: We just have to allow it to continue to evolve.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the governance side, I think the editing is also going pretty well.

speaker: KOHN
text: When we got into the pre-meeting editing, I was a little concerned that the decisions were going to move outside the room.

speaker: KOHN
text: But the process has evolved in a way that we get close to what the final statement is in these pre-meeting sessions, and then we can fine-tune the language at the meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: That’s probably where we need to be if we’re going to put out a statement.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I’m comfortable with where we are there.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that most people outside this room think that the Committee is responsible for the whole statement, and we probably ought to acknowledge that by making the Committee responsible for the whole statement.

speaker: KOHN
text: But if we do that, we ought to understand among ourselves that the hurdle for dissenting on words should be very, very high or else we will get ourselves into a governance mess.

speaker: WARSH
text: I like the statement format and process and, like Governor Kohn, think that the governance, while it is not urgent to change, will catch up with the reality and with the expectation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Much as Gary Stern has said, as an academic I was never particularly enamored of the statement.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But actually having seen how it evolves, how it is built—usually when you see the way the sausage is made, that upsets your stomach, but it has actually been the opposite.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Maybe I have been eating the sausage for too long now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I’ve been taken in by it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I think, as Governor Kohn has said, it has evolved in a way that many of the elements that I was more critical of a few years ago are not there now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it operates in a perfectly reasonable way.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some people have mentioned how the statement could change if we speed up the minutes.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’re never going to speed up the minutes beyond say a week.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Even if we were to get it to a week, which I don’t think is feasible, the statement can’t change all that much.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have to convey the information that’s in the statement.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t think we can say, “Well, gee, because next week we’re going to say something, we can just cut it down to two sentences or three sentences.” As long as there’s a week in between, and I can’t imagine there being any less than a week in between, the statement is going to have the kind of information that it has in it, which I think has evolved in a perfectly reasonable way.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On governance, since the process is working, I don’t really see the need to change it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There’s a possibility that down the line that concurring opinions could be put out so that people agree to whatever the monetary policy movement is but, like the Supreme Court, write their own statement.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Since the process seems to be working well without leaving that possibility for coming in, I don’t see that it’s necessary to make the change, although I’m open on that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In terms of this issue of forward-looking language, I’m quite comfortable with the statement and with forward-looking language so long as it’s on the right-hand side of the Taylor rule in terms of what’s going on with output and inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m actually not a fan of forward-looking language in terms of the federal funds rate, and in fact, I differ from some people on this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I really didn’t like it, even during the unusual period when there was some concern about deflation—in that context, it did have elements that people might have interpreted as a commitment.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It turned out that nothing bad happened because the economy evolved in a reasonable way, but I can think of scenarios during that period, particularly in 2004 and so forth, when it might have been a real problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So you do have the statement at the end that we’re always contingent on events.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I like that statement; but what I don’t want to see is moving from that to what we did in that period, except in the most unusual circumstances.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: At the beginning it was justifiable in terms of concerns about deflation, but it actually had real potential problems that did not arise, but I think we got lucky.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I’m very comfortable with where we are right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think the editing process is going well in terms of the meeting—there is fine-tuning going on, but it’s done in a very constructive way, and I think it’s working well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In terms of governance, I guess I lean toward the idea that we should vote on it, for the following reason.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When you think about doing policy, it’s not just what you do today that’s important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What you are signaling about the future is every bit as important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is the whole issue that the Chairman has worked with Mike Woodford on—the issue of managing expectations is not just what you do with the federal funds rate now; it’s also the path.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, the projections that we are talking about doing are very much consistent with that way of thinking.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the reality is that, from a policy viewpoint, what we say in the statement is as important as what we do in voting on the federal funds rate.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Indeed, since I’ve been on the Board, that’s been really the only issue because we really haven’t had much debate about the federal funds rate decision.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So in that sense, if it is really important and it is a key part of policy, it makes sense for us to vote on it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m not worried about the issue of dissents because the point that you made, Governor Kohn, that there should be a very high barrier is exactly the way people have been proceeding.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The barrier is fairly high for the federal funds rate decision, but in this case even more so.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s just a couple of words, and if you dissent, well, to be honest, then you’re a jerk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t see any jerks here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So my feeling is that I don’t think we’re going to have a big problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I’m actually quite comfortable with moving in that direction.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have to put those words in the minutes so that they get out there sooner than five years.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’ll be an outlier in terms of the transcripts five years from now; they’ll say, “Oh, God, Rick is here.”

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It may horrify everyone at the table that before I joined the Committee, I didn’t actually parse this statement every few weeks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I don’t have a lot of historical perspective, but I’m basically okay with the way the process works now.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think that the inclusions in the statement all serve a purpose.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’m not sure I fully understand the right and the left side of the Taylor rule, Rick, but maybe afterward you can explain that to me.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I view this statement as having a short term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: If there are forward-looking statements, they are short term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: They signal the next meeting or two, but not much more than that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding the governance or the voting issues, I think we should vote on the whole thing, and if we ever need to have a tie breaker, I guess I would revert to its being at that time the Chairman’s statement.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But in normal circumstances, we all vote and agree, and that’s it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I, too, am relatively new to this process of watching the sausage being made.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have to confess up front that I’m a bit schizophrenic about this because I’m really of two minds in terms of the direction I think about, and I’m persuadable either way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Part of me, as Jeff said, has argued that maybe the forecasting exercise is going to take some pressure off all the nuances and the time we spend on the statement.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As Governor Kroszner mentioned, no matter how soon we get the minutes out, it’s going to be tough to do that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I’m sympathetic to that argument.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My view is that the minutes really provide the nuance of what goes on in the Committee, and I think that’s incredibly important.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The only thing I worry about in terms of the statement is that it can’t provide that nuance and it gets so much attention in the marketplace so immediately so that part of me says either we want to enrich the statement and get rid of some of the inertia that’s in it, and make it longer or just make it shorter.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So a part of me says that maybe what we really ought to say in the statement is just section 1 and section 4 and let the nuance of how we got there and what our views are be elaborated in the minutes.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So a part of me says that it would be a simplification that tells the markets what we did and how we view the assessment of risk as we look at the economy, but it doesn’t try to tell them all of the details of what went on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We let the minutes do that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I can live with the statement with way it is, but I think there might be some advantages in simplifying it so that we don’t spend so much time arguing over the nuances of the rationales and other things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Besides that, we’d get capacity utilization out of there if possible and just go with the overall assessment of the risk, and then let the minutes speak for themselves in terms of the nuances of the discussion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the governance question, I agree with everybody else.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that it has been implicitly a statement of the Committee.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Committee ought to vote on it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If you took sections 2 and 3 out, there would be a lot less wordsmithing and a lot less worrying about whether the words were exactly right and what each of us might have meant or preferred to say.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So it might even make it easier to have a Committee vote on that, and they’d have to worry about fewer things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Those are just some thoughts.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the statement has been evolving sensibly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The process is basically working.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think we need to lock ourselves into any fixed view of the optimal structure of the statement over time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We should be open to changing it if it suits our purposes in specific circumstances.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Obviously, shaping expectations about the stance of monetary policy is a vital part of what we do.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I’m pragmatic on all the questions about whether or not to have forward-looking language.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There are some circumstances in which it may make sense in the future as it has in the past.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Those should be exceptional circumstances, and using it should be done very carefully and thoughtfully.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But we do not need to commit not to use it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I also think the basic structure of saying something implicitly about the forecast, the outlook on which our decision is based, is very important.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So we should have something in there that refers to the expected path of output and inflation and the risks to that generally as part of the signal.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Without that, you’d lose a lot of value.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think I’d still be open to experimenting further as we have been doing with introducing a bit more forward-looking view about the outlook for demand and inflation as part of the statement, even though that will be hard to do well.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On governance, I have a very different view.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that we really should stay in this governance limbo that we now have.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s very important to recognize that we’ve had a huge amount of turnover in this Committee.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s important to give the Chairman the flexibility to ultimately be the arbiter of the nuance in the statement without having to go through a process in which he will have to figure out whether he’s prepared to have a vote with significant dissent in that context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Right now we have a process in which the Committee has substantial input into the shape of the signal that’s in the statement.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The minutes actually say that the Committee agreed that the statement should say X. It’s clear that the Committee is implicated in the statement.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The Chairman is obviously very deferential to the views of the Committee in shaping it, but we’re close to 80 percent of the way in having a formal endorsement by the Committee of the statement.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t see any virtue in going the next 20 percent and a lot of virtue in preserving the possibility for the Chairman to say, “My sense is that we should do X,” (I know that’s not acceptable to all of you) and not have that come with something that forces a vote in that context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just don’t think the balance we have now is problematic, but I can envision a circumstance in which the state of the world, the state of the Committee, or a bunch of other things might make a formal vote unnecessary and tilt the balance in a way that may not make sense for the institutional structure we have.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You know, we have a group of nineteen, not of seven.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Fundamentally the Fed model institutionally is based on a strong Chairman, and I’d preserve that particular remaining piece of that model.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any other comments?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, again, we’ll review the transcript and see what steps we need to take.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Once again, thank you for your very useful comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next meeting is Tuesday, August 7.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there is no other business, then we’re adjourned.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We start off today with some welcomes and farewells.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would first like to welcome Eric Rosengren, the new President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have known Eric for about twenty years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We used to be squash partners.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I won’t say who won.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We know who wins now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I admire Eric—he has been a multitasker: He has been very successful as a researcher and as a bank supervisor, and he is no slouch with respect to monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we look forward to your contributions, Eric.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Sadly, today we have to say farewell to President Michael Moskow of Chicago.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Michael has sat at this table since 1994, which we have calculated is a total of 104 FOMC meetings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Mike has been involved in public policy off and on since 1969 in many capacities, and he has seen both the good times and the bad times.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will have a luncheon today after the meeting to honor Mike, but let us memorialize in the transcript that we thank him for his many contributions and wish him the very best.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I will make some comments later on, but I just want to add that I counted 104 meetings, too.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: It has been a privilege and an honor to serve on this Committee, and I will miss the intellectual stimulation, the camaraderie, and the spirit of doing what is best for the American people.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Today is also Vincent Reinhart’s final FOMC meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vince went to work at the New York Fed in 1983 and came to the Board— PARTICIPANT.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, he gets docked for...

speaker: KOHN
text: Make sure he submits a leave card.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, let me make a couple of other announcements, and then we’ll move on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First of all, in the days when Don Winn was the head of the Congressional Liaison Office, it was customary for him to present during the luncheon after the meeting an update on congressional matters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Laricke Blanchard, whom I think most of you know, is now the head of the Congressional Liaison Office.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We would like to begin that tradition again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have lunch, of course, for President Moskow, but if there are a few minutes after the adjournment, Laricke will provide us with a short update.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: He has already circulated a written summary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if we don’t get to the update, at least we will have the summary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the future we are going to try to have a congressional update at every meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, on communications, the subcommittee sent a memo to the Committee on July 25.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Broadly speaking, the recommendations were that we should now focus on expanding the FOMC projections as our next step in increasing transparency, that we submit trial-run projections in September as we did for August and live projections, so to speak, for the October meeting, and that we vote in October to approve this step.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My sense from June was that there was a general agreement on this approach.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We would like to give you several more opportunities to comment and to discuss details.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will poll you between now and the September meeting on remaining issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In September, there will be an agenda item for final discussion of various issues that might come up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In October, we will have another opportunity to talk about it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like, if possible, to take a vote at the October meeting, which would be followed by a roll-out about three weeks later, with a press release and with a speech by me, and then by the information in the minutes that would come out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is where we are.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, we will have an opportunity to talk about the program on an agenda item in September.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The subcommittee also recommended, based on the discussion we had earlier, that we vote on the entire statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to make that also an agenda item in September.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have asked Scott Alvarez, our General Counsel, working with Monetary Affairs, to provide us with a memo that will address two issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, what is the legal status?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What specific action do we have to take to allow the Committee to vote on the full statement?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, it would be worthwhile to have them take one more look to see whether there are any unintended consequences.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, would this inhibit us in any way if there were intermeeting moves or any special steps being taken?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the plan would be to have a brief discussion in September on this memo, to take a vote, and, if we agree, the full statement would be subject to a Committee vote.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Today, let’s stay with the old process, which still allows a vote on the balance- of-risk assessment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me raise an item of business here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Since Vince Reinhart clearly has disappeared, we need to vote for a replacement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to nominate and elect a new secretary and economist to the FOMC whose position would be valid until the first regularly scheduled meeting of 2008.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would you like to make a nomination?

speaker: KOHN
text: I nominate Brian Madigan, with pleasure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, all in favor say “aye.” Opposed?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will wait until Vince appears.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: He may be looking at financial markets this morning, and so we will wait until he appears to bid him farewell.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s go ahead, then, to the authorization for Desk operations and turn it over to Bill Dudley.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you all know, there has been considerable financial market turbulence since the last meeting: Problems in subprime mortgage credit have persisted and intensified; credit-rating agencies have begun to downgrade asset-backed securities and CDOs (collateralized debt obligations) that reference subprime debt; the problems in subprime have spread into the alt-A mortgage space and into parts of the prime mortgage market; corporate credit has been infected, with high-yield bond and loan spreads moving out sharply; and stock prices have faltered.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although markets generally have been functioning well in terms of liquidity and the ability to transact, there have been some important exceptions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The nonconforming residential mortgage market and the structured-finance product markets—especially the CDO and CLO (collateralized loan obligation) markets—have been significantly impaired, and there are concerns about the ability of some asset-backed commercial paper programs to continue to source funding via that market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a consequence, market expectations with respect to monetary policy have shifted sharply, with market expectations consistent with considerable monetary policy easing over the next year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Market participants are worried about the effect of tightening credit standards on housing and about the deterioration in the market function in structured finance, which could broaden and be self-reinforcing, ultimately damaging the macroeconomy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am going to be referring to this handout as we go through these comments.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In tracing the source of the turmoil that we have experienced recently, we find that the deterioration of the subprime mortgage sector continues to play an important role in several ways.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, the deterioration in underlying credit quality continues unabated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 1, delinquencies of more than sixty days for recent ABX index vintages have continued to move higher, and the pace of deterioration—measured by the steepness of the curves—has, if anything, worsened.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Note that the newest vintage—07-2, so the second half of 2007—does not show any benefit from improved underwriting standards.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That stems mainly from the fact that the pipeline to build these securities is relatively long—with the average loan referenced by this index more than six months old at this point.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It also may reflect the fact that this newest vintage gets—in contrast to earlier vintages—less benefit from earlier home- price appreciation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a consequence of this poor credit performance, ABX spreads have continued to widen sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is shown in exhibit 2, which shows the performance for ABX BBB- tranches across vintages, and exhibit 3, which shows the performance for the various tranches of the 07-1 vintage.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The deterioration in the 1 Materials used by Mr. Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: higher-rated tranches has been much more severe than earlier in the year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In part, this greater deterioration reflects the fact that loss estimates have been trending higher, putting the higher-rated tranches more in harm’s way.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It also reflects efforts to hedge subprime risk by going short these indexes by people who can’t liquidate securities easily.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Translating these ABX spreads back into price, July was a very rough month for ABX.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Price declines of 20 points or more occurred in the ABX BBB- tranches of some more-recent vintages.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the disturbing delinquency trajectories shown in exhibit 1 have caused the rating agencies to downgrade a significant number of residential asset-backed securities and CDOs that have exposure to the subprime sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, most of the downgrades apply to vintages before 06-2.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For more- recent vintages, the loss experience is worse but still hard to estimate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This means that many more downgrades lie ahead.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, some of the credit-rating agencies have made changes to their structured-finance rating models.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That, combined with huge marked-to-market losses even in highly rated subprime tranches, has led to a fundamental reevaluation of what a credit rating means and how much comfort an investor should take from a high credit rating on an opaque structured-finance CDO or CLO product.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problems in subprime have spread into other mortgage markets, including alt-A, certain types of prime residential mortgage products, and commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Countrywide, for example, announced a deterioration in its second-lien prime mortgage book.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Meanwhile, American Home Mortgage, which had operated primarily in the alt-A and nontraditional prime mortgage space as both a large monoline mortgage issuer and a REIT investor, was forced to shut down its operations last week and filed for bankruptcy yesterday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Market liquidity for nonconforming residential mortgage products is poor, and this has contributed to a further tightening in underwriting standards.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, a number of mortgage originators indicated that they will no longer offer 2/28 and 3/27 adjustable-rate mortgage products, and some have indicated that they will not buy any alt-A mortgages originated by brokers.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the same time that we have seen turmoil in the subprime market, it has spread into the corporate sector as well.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Credit spreads in the corporate sector have also widened sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, in July, high-yield corporate bond spreads widened about 150 basis points (see exhibit 4).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Similarly, the spreads on key hedging indexes that reference credit default swaps on corporates have also gone up sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, in July the spreads on three of these major indexes rose nearly 200 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is illustrated in exhibit 5.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The ITRAXX crossover index references fifty European nonfinancial names with ratings below BBB- or at BBB- and on negative watch.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The high-yield CDX index references credit default swaps on 100 high-yield U.S. names.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The LCDX index references credit default swaps on 100 U.S. leveraged loans.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast to the residential mortgage sector, corporate credit fundamentals still look good.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, as shown in exhibit 6, corporate default rates for both investment-grade and below-investment-grade borrowers have been at very low levels.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, as we saw in the subprime market, readily available credit can depress default ratios.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One should expect that the tightening of credit standards in the corporate sector would generate some rise in default rates independent of other developments.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Nevertheless, other measures also underscore the positive fundamentals of the corporate sector—in contrast to the poor fundamentals in residential mortgages.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, global growth has been unusually strong with little volatility, and corporate profit margins are unusually wide, both in the United States and elsewhere.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the slowdown in profit growth expected for the United States has been milder than anticipated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This can be seen in the rise in the median equity analysts’ bottom-up earnings forecasts for the S&P 500 companies for 2007, which is shown in exhibit 7.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It was falling through about April.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Since then, expectations for this year have actually increased, and they have been increasing recently, even over the past month.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So how does one explain the contagion to corporate credit from the subprime market given the disparity in fundamentals between these two sectors?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the answer is complex, one factor stands out: There has been a loss of confidence among investors in their ability to assess the value of and risks associated with structured products, which has led to a sharp drop in demand for such products.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The loss of confidence stems from many sources, including the opacity of such products; the infrequency of trades, which makes it more difficult to judge appropriate valuation; the difficulty in forecasting losses and the correlation of losses in the underlying collateral; the sensitivity of returns to the loss rate and the degree of correlation; and the problem that the credit rating focuses mainly on one risk—that of loss from default.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The CLO and CDO markets have facilitated the transformation of low-rated paper—for which there is a limited investor appetite—into a high proportion of high- grade-rated debt.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, in a typical CLO structure, the underlying loan quality averages a rating of about B.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yet through the magic of structured finance and the corporate rating agencies, the resulting CLO tranches are rated predominately investment grade.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 8 shows the structure for a representative CLO: More than two-thirds is AAA-rated debt, and 87 percent is investment grade.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The loss of confidence among investors in the ability to assess the value and risks associated with this structured product has led to a sharp drop in CDO and CLO issuance.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 9, CLO and CDO issuance plummeted in July.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is very important because the CLO and CDO markets represent the bulk of the demand for non- investment-grade debt.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: With this demand falling away at a time when the forward supply of high-yield corporate loans and debt exceeds $300 billion by some measures, a huge mismatch between demand and supply has developed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The underlying problem is that the depth of the market for non-investment-grade rated loans and debt—excluding CDO and CLO demand—is far shallower than the market for investment-grade products.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Where do we go from here?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Presumably buyers and sellers in the corporate sector are in the process of finding appropriate market-clearing prices.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But it may take time for the market to settle down, especially given the August doldrums that are upon us.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, we still may have further scope for market dislocations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: After all, some single-strategy hedge funds that emphasize corporate credit may have been caught out by the sharp widening in spreads that has occurred over the past few weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When such results become known, investor redemptions could follow— leading to forced selling to generate the cash to fund these redemptions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In addition, the asset-backed commercial paper market is very skittish in two areas—structured investment vehicles and extendable commercial paper programs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yesterday at least two commercial paper programs were subject to extension.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is not clear whether or to what degree these extensions will further unsettle the commercial paper market, but that is clearly a risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The effective shutdown of the CDO and CLO markets has, in turn, raised questions about the sustainability of the strong bid by private equity firms to conduct leveraged buyouts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This uncertainty has undoubtedly been a factor behind the recent weakness of the U.S. stock market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The importance of the buyout bid can be seen in the relative underperformance of the Russell 2000 index compared with the S&P 500 index during the past few weeks (see exhibit 10).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problems in corporate credit and the virtual shutdown of the CLO and CDO distribution mechanism have caused investors to reevaluate both the business opportunities and the risks associated with large investment and commercial banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Investment bank and commercial bank shares have underperformed the broader stock market indexes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In addition, as shown in exhibit 11, the CDS spreads for the major investment and commercial banks have widened considerably over the past month.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The CDS spreads for financial guarantors have widened as well, even though the exposures of these firms appear to be concentrated in the most senior portions of the subprime and structured-finance debt structures.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Perception of the strength of the financial guarantors could prove important given the key role that they play in some markets, such as the municipal debt sector, that lie far afield from either the subprime mortgage market or the corporate debt markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Only in the past few weeks have the problems in the subprime and corporate debt markets led to broader risk-reduction activities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These risk-reduction efforts are similar to the adjustments that we saw in late February and early March.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A matrix that shows the correlation of returns across different asset classes over the past few weeks (see exhibit 12) looks very similar to the correlation matrix that we saw following the late February risk-reduction period (see exhibit 13).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It looks very different from the very calm period we had from late March through the first part of July, which is shown in exhibit 14.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the adjustments are not uniform across markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In some ways, the risk reduction that we are seeing this time is a little more U.S. specific, a little more corporate credit specific, and a little more mortgage specific.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, as shown in exhibit 15, implied volatility in interest rate swaps—the SMOVE index—and in equities—the VIX index—has climbed well above the late February peak.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, the foreign exchange markets have experienced a less-pronounced rise in volatility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the United States, the turmoil in financial markets has been accompanied by a shift in monetary policy expectations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 16 illustrates the Eurodollar futures strip.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, the futures curve has shifted down about 40 basis points since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are back where we were before the May FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Currently, market prices imply a bit more than 50 basis points of easing by year-end 2008.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The shift in expectations appears to reflect, in part, a revival of the “downside risks to growth” idea rather than that the Federal Reserve will absolutely cut interest rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This can be seen in several ways.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The shift in market expectations implicit in Eurodollar futures yields has not been accompanied by a substantial change in dealer forecasts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 17 and 18, which show the federal funds rate projections of the primary dealers before the June and the current FOMC meetings, the average dealer forecast and the range of dealer forecasts have not changed much over the past six weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Instead, a gap has opened up between the average dealer forecasts, represented in the exhibits by the green circles, and the forecasts implicit in market yields, represented by the horizontal black lines.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The most recent dealer survey does not capture the minor forecast changes that occurred late last week.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, two dealers with tightening forecasts pushed back the timing of the first tightening, and one dealer with an easing forecast moved it closer and increased the magnitude (not shown in exhibits 17 or 18).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The dealers’ forecasts are modal forecasts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, the expectation embodied in market yields represents the mean of the distribution of expected outcomes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Presumably, it includes some possibility that the current market turbulence could lead to a weaker growth outcome and a reduction in the FOMC’s federal funds rate target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Options on Eurodollar futures contracts 300 days forward show a sharp downward skew in the distribution of rates (see exhibit 19).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the mode is at 5.25 percent, the same as it was before the June meeting, the probability distribution has shifted down drastically below that 5.25 percent mode.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it may not be correct to say that market participants now expect much more monetary policy easing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Instead, a more proper characterization might be that the perceptions of downside risks have reemerged, and this characterization is reflected in the downward skew below what is still a 5.25 percent modal forecast for the Eurodollar rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There were no foreign operations during this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I request a vote to ratify the operations conducted by the System Open Market Account since the June FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, I am very happy to take questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you for a very good report, Bill.

speaker: POOLE
text: First, does the New York Fed have what I might call material nonpublic information about firms that would suggest that there is more difficulty than we see in the newspapers?

speaker: POOLE
text: The other question has to do with the distribution of views among dealers about probable Fed policy.

speaker: POOLE
text: There is obviously an arbitrage relationship between, let’s say, a two-year Treasury and these futures markets.

speaker: POOLE
text: My sense is that probably what is going on here—and I will use the two-year as the example—is a flight to safety.

speaker: POOLE
text: People are trying to shore up their liquid assets in case they have to sell some stock into the market, so they are trying to hold more of that.

speaker: POOLE
text: But there is no easy way for those on the other side of that market to go short and push that yield back to where the best-informed people think it will be once we are past this turmoil.

speaker: POOLE
text: So what we may be seeing is less a reflection of expectations about future policy actions than a flight to liquidity as a desperate effort— “desperate” may be too strong—to shore up the liquidity of a balance sheet, and there is no easy way for people to go on the other side.

speaker: POOLE
text: Those are the two questions I have.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Let me take the second question first.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You know, it’s certainly possible that, when people want to hedge their risk in areas where they can’t easily sell the assets, they would buy something that will perform well if those assets continue to deteriorate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One thing to do would be to buy Eurodollar futures or Treasury securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So, at least temporarily, those yields may not fully reflect what the market expectations are.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That said, the Eurodollar market is a very deep market, and if one thought that the Fed was not going to do what the market priced in, there certainly would be the ability of people to take the other side of the bet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it’s sort of hard to know exactly how big or long-lasting the effects that you are talking about could actually be.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the short run, that kind of thing certainly goes on.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If I can’t sell the bad asset that I hold, then I will buy something that will perform well if the bad asset deteriorates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: People actually do talk about that on the trading side.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As far as the issue of material nonpublic information that shows worse problems than are in the newspapers, I’m not sure exactly how to characterize that because I guess I wouldn’t know how to characterize how bad the newspapers think these problems are.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We’ve done quite a bit of work trying to identify some of the funding questions surrounding Bear Stearns, Countrywide, and some of the commercial paper programs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There is some strain, but so far it looks as though nothing is really imminent in those areas.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, could that change quickly?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, one question that we’re following with Bear Stearns is what their clients do in terms of continuing to want to do business with them.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, if people start to pull back in their willingness to do business with Bear Stearns, the franchise value of the company goes down, and that exacerbates the problem.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One thing that we have heard about Bear Stearns is that they have approached a number of major commercial banks about a secured line of credit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We don’t know what the outcome will be, but they are clearly trying to get even better liquidity backstops than those they have in place today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But as far as we know, they have enough liquidity—and Countrywide as well at this moment.

speaker: FISHER
text: Let’s go back to your previous comment on the second question of President Poole.

speaker: FISHER
text: Another standard reaction is to sell things that are more liquid when you can’t unload things that are less liquid.

speaker: FISHER
text: One thing I am curious about—and I don’t know if we have the data, but this is the question—in terms of CDO/CLO issuance, do we know how much is held by non-U.S. investors?

speaker: FISHER
text: For example, I have been told—and I don’t know if this is correct—by a senior partner at Goldman that, since ’03, most of the mezzanine CDOs were issued or sold to Asians or to Europeans.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m wondering if we are aware of any tripwires by which we might have overseas the kind of reaction I just described, which is selling assets that might be more liquid to cover the illiquidity of something they’re stuck with.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would be interested to do a little work, if we can, on CDO issuance and how much is held here.

speaker: FISHER
text: It seems to me to be common sense that, given that surplus liquidity has come from abroad—and we have talked about the surplus of saving a great deal and the Chairman has talked about it a great deal—that may well be where a lot of this risk resides, and we should be aware of it.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would posit that probably the same is true for asset-backed commercial paper.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is really the CDO market not asset-backed commercial paper that I am most concerned about.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: President Fisher, I have a tiny bit of information in that regard.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Once a year there are surveys taken of U.S. liabilities to foreign holders, and they are done security by security.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: We went looking for the securities that had been downgraded—by Moody’s I guess it was, or maybe it was both Moody’s and S&P—in CDO packages to see if we could find them.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: We found a certain fraction of them in the survey, which meant that the others that we didn’t find were not held abroad because the custodians didn’t report them as foreign owned.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Of the fraction of the securities that were actually found, 40 percent were owned abroad, which implied about a 10 percent ownership of all the downgraded securities.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Not all of the securities, but all of the downgraded securities.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: A meaningful number—but not a huge number, not 50 percent, not more than half, but a fraction—were in the survey; of those, 40 percent of the total outstanding were what was held abroad.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: However, not all countries are forthcoming with what they own, and it is certainly possible that the system doesn’t capture all foreign ownership.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: China, for example, is very unforthcoming.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But our liability survey doesn’t depend on their answering the questions; it depends on custodians answering the questions.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: So I would say it’s significant, but I think I come away from this information thinking that perhaps we are exaggerating a bit how much of it is abroad.

speaker: FISHER
text: It might be interesting to look at the issuance dates of those, if we were able somehow to analyze the issuance dates.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: This survey, which we basically have received just recently, is dated June 2006.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: So there is always a lag of several months to a year in the information that you can get out of this survey.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But the survey itself is very comprehensive.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Where the securities are held abroad is also very important.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If they are held in a hedge fund that is highly leveraged, that is one thing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If they are held in a central bank reserve account, that is a small loss against all their other assets, so it wouldn’t have any consequence.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So if you talk to the dealers, they’ll say, “Well, we know whom we sold the things to initially, but we don’t know what happens after that.” I would expect, though, that most of the stuff probably resides with the initial person because, as we have seen, these instruments are not particularly liquid and so I don’t think that they pass on that far.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If you did a survey of the dealers, you might be able to make some headway in terms of figuring out whom they sold them to originally.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It might be a fair approximation of where they reside today.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have one other quick question, and that is that I want to make sure I understand what you’re saying.

speaker: FISHER
text: It seems to me from this presentation that this is not just a matter of price; it is also a matter of structure and covenants.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I guess I would characterize the situation as people having lost faith in the structured-finance product, especially the high-grade AA/AAA product that they thought was safe and therefore not subject to much market risk or liquidity risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They found out otherwise, and so there is a total reevaluation of that market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a consequence, since the vehicle that was used to turn non-investment-grade corporate debt and into investment-grade debt is sort of broken, now they have to sell a lot of non-investment-grade debt directly and find people who are willing to hold it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think about the situation as that demand has lessened at a time when supply, just by bad luck and timing, is exploding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The market should clear, because the fundamentals in the corporate sector are good as opposed to bad, but at a much higher price.

speaker: FISHER
text: Thank you for an excellent presentation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The credit derivative swaps for Countrywide and some of the other mortgage providers spiked up very appreciably at the end of last week, and they were accompanied by announcements that the companies were having no trouble rolling over their financing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Some of the Boston hedge fund managers have observed that one dependable correlation has been that the announcement of no problem seems to be highly correlated with the actual problem’s occurring with a lag of one to two weeks.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I am curious whether you are worried about the possibility that Countrywide and some of the largest mortgage lenders might have difficulty in the next two weeks rolling over financing, which would obviously have a broader impact.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Their problem is that they have a very large mortgage finance subsidiary and a small thrift.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If the mortgage finance subsidiary were in the thrift, then there would be other ways of financing all their assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So far they are able to maintain their liquidity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But a lot of this is about perception, and that could change at any time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The good news about Countrywide is that people view them as having a strong franchise.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They also have a very large loan-servicing portfolio, which might actually be worth a bit more because the duration of those mortgages is extending.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They are not just a mortgage originator whose business has evaporated; they also have other parts of their business, which I think people view as potentially quite valuable.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: One area that you talked a bit about was the commercial paper market.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: That made me uneasy because this segment is different from the other segments of the market that you were talking about, and obviously that short-term financing is crucial to companies.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I wonder if you could expand on your comments there.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Two areas of the asset-backed commercial paper market are being closely scrutinized, which means that a whole bunch of the asset-backed commercial paper market is fine, such as the asset-backed commercial paper with backstops—you know, credit card receivables.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That area is fine; it is not a problem.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One difficult area is the extendable commercial paper programs that are funding some of the stuff that is very illiquid right now.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The risk is that investors, typically money market mutual funds, will look at the situation and say, “Gee, if they can’t roll over commercial paper, my commercial paper investment will automatically be extended to a longer maturity.” They are worried about the headline risk of that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They are also worried—and it is hard to know how worried—that there is no guarantee that the extended commercial paper would necessarily trade at par.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If it traded below par, then they would have to worry about breaking the buck, which is the last thing they want to do.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the risk is that the investors, who are quite risk averse in the commercial paper market in this area, will pull back and that very pulling back will cause extension.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is what was happening yesterday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Apparently a couple of commercial paper programs were extended.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, does extension mean anything really necessarily bad?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It hasn’t happened before, and so we really haven’t experienced how this extension process is going to work.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These programs are backstops in various forms.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the end of the day, the commercial paper holders should come out whole; but until that is demonstrated, you can imagine that the extensions could cause other people to pull back.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So there is a risk of a cascading of extensions that has crossed all of these extendable commercial paper products.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You know, it is an interesting tension right now because the large investors know that, if they don’t roll, they’ll probably be extended.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So at the current time, most of them are continuing to roll so that they don’t get stuck with extended commercial paper.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But this situation is very fragile day to day.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second area is more complex—structured investment finance vehicles that basically fund pipelines of highly rated CDO and CLO kind of stuff.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I can’t say I fully appreciate exactly how this structure works, but basically there is some risk that the collateral values of these structures could fall below certain thresholds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In that case, the securities would have to be liquidated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Again, commercial paper investors are saying, “Do I really want to see what this means?” So they are pulling back from that market as well.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of the two, the extendable commercial paper issue seems to be the more immediate one in the market’s attention, but the SIV asset-backed commercial paper is also an ongoing issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there other questions for Bill?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, we need a vote to ratify domestic market operations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I move we ratify those operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We just want to acknowledge you.

speaker: REINHART
text: Ever since you gave the guards guns, I didn’t really have any choice.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We want to acknowledge your final meeting, Vincent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has been six years since Vincent was elected Secretary and Economist to the Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You took that role only three or four weeks before September 11, and your steady hand during that crisis was invaluable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unfortunately, against all good advice and after only eighty-two FOMC meetings—a record which to his credit he has achieved without prompting accusations of steroid use—[laughter] Vincent is insisting upon returning to civilian life.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So today is an appropriate occasion upon which to express our gratitude, Vincent, for your sage advice, your thoughtful guidance, and your undoubtedly well-deserved admonitions to the Committee over the years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vincent’s legacy, of course, will live on in the meeting transcripts from his tenure, as the transcripts become public over the next few years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, in the May 2004 transcript, Vincent is caught using the words “cattle prods” in reference to a possible experiment involving bond market traders.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In 2005, he suggested that the FOMC as a group was incapable of agreeing on something as straightforward as the color of an orange.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Notwithstanding that, Vincent, the Committee does agree on this: You have our heartfelt thanks and our best wishes for the next stage of your career.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, we can go to the economic situation, and I will call on David Wilcox.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In putting together the Greenbook forecast for this meeting, we adjusted our outlook in five ways in response to the developments that Bill Dudley has just described.

speaker: WILCOX
text: First and foremost in terms of its implications for real activity, we took on board the implications of the decline in the value of equities since the June Greenbook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Second, we adjusted our home-price forecast down a notch, both in response to slightly disappointing indicators of home- price appreciation during the second quarter and in recognition of the bleaker conditions in housing markets more generally, including the developments in the subprime mortgage market.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In all, we took the level of home prices down 1½ percent by the end of 2008, with about one-third of that amount representing our response to the incoming indicators and two-thirds reflecting the other considerations.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In combination and allowing for some relatively minor offsets, the reduction in equity values and home prices took about $1 trillion off the balance sheet of the household sector and weakened our outlook for consumer spending through the usual wealth- effect channels.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Third, we further adjusted our forecast of real PCE to allow for a direct effect of interest-rate resets.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We estimate that 4.7 million variable-rate subprime loans are scheduled to undergo interest-rate resets over the next year and a half.

speaker: WILCOX
text: If all these resets were to take full effect, they would result in extra interest payments cumulating to about $12 billion between now and the end of 2008.

speaker: WILCOX
text: For several reasons, however, we think that $12 billion figure represents a loose upper bound on the likely effect of resets on consumption spending.

speaker: WILCOX
text: For example, even in today’s relatively more hostile financial environment, some households will succeed in refinancing into a prime mortgage with a lower rate; others will sell their property and become renters rather than bear the additional debt service payments; and some who remain in their homes with no refinancing will have the financial wherewithal to shield their spending from a dollar-for-dollar reduction in response to the increase in debt service payments.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In light of these considerations, we took consumer spending down by half the amount of the reset-induced payments.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Fourth, we adjusted down our forecast for new-home sales to allow for the unusual restraint that the tightening in mortgage-borrowing conditions since the last Greenbook will likely impose on the demand for new homes.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The adjustment we made this time followed similar downward revisions in March and June; together, these three revisions were calibrated to unwind the boost to mortgage originations that we think was provided by nonprime lending in 2005 and 2006.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Overall, we took the trajectory of new-home sales down 6 percent this round—half in response to the mortgage developments and half in response to the disappointing pace of sales data for June.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Having cut the pace of sales, we then also took down the rate of new construction in the forecast to keep inventories of unsold new homes from bulging too much further.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Finally, we trimmed our forecast for investment in equipment and software a bit on the theory that the increase in spreads that investment-grade and especially non- investment-grade firms now are facing might reflect greater uncertainty in the business climate and that they might respond to that uncertainty by being a little more reluctant to invest.

speaker: WILCOX
text: To be sure, the econometric evidence supporting this hypothesis is not rock solid, but it did strike us as suggestive enough to warrant a modest adjustment.

speaker: WILCOX
text: All told, these responses to the more hostile financial climate took about ¼ percentage point off our forecast for the growth of real GDP over the second half of this year and next, with about half of that amount reflecting the changes working through the traditional wealth channel and the remainder representing the combined influence of the three less traditional adjustments.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Could the implications of the financial situation for the real economy be even worse than we have built into the baseline?

speaker: WILCOX
text: I almost invariably resist the temptation to declare that uncertainty about the real economy is greater than usual, but the current situation strikes me as the exception that proves the rule.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In the “Alternative Scenarios” section of the Greenbook, we sketched three situations in which economic activity would be markedly weaker than in the baseline.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In the first, residential investment drops 10 percent relative to baseline by the middle of next year, and home prices drop a total of 20 percent in nominal terms over the next year and a half—unprecedented in modern times but not outside the realm of possibility, as it would merely return the valuation of the housing stock to the level predicted by one of the house-price models that we track.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The second scenario adds a deterioration in consumer sentiment, giving the meltdown in the housing sector an additional vehicle for spilling over into consumer spending more generally.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In both of these scenarios, financial conditions deteriorate relative to baseline but only to the extent judged “normal” by the model in light of the weaker overall economy.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The third scenario adds a further and more virulent deterioration in financial conditions, with a 10 percent decline in equity values and a 100 basis point widening in the spread on investment-grade securities.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In the third scenario, we nearly—though not quite—succeed in generating a recession despite a substantial easing of monetary policy.

speaker: WILCOX
text: On the other hand, could it be better?

speaker: WILCOX
text: A key objective in putting together this forecast has been to ensure that risk lies on both sides of the baseline forecast.

speaker: WILCOX
text: For example, yesterday’s market rebound is a reminder that stranger things have happened than for calm to break out in financial markets.

speaker: WILCOX
text: One cannot rule out that, six months or a year from now, we will look back on this episode much as we look back on the flare-up in February of this year or as we look back on the stock-market break in 1987, with a sense of surprise that the financial event did not leave a greater imprint on the real economy.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Even if the financial markets do not heal themselves quickly, consumers may prove more willing to postpone the increase in the saving rate that we have assumed in the baseline; businesses may aim to build the investment share of GDP back much closer to the levels that it attained in the late 1990s; and home sales may recover more quickly than we have assumed.

speaker: WILCOX
text: A second challenge that we faced in putting the forecast together—more routine than the task of factoring in the implications of financial-market developments—was to take account of the annual revision to the national income and product accounts.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As you know, the BEA revised down the growth of real GDP ⅓ percentage point, on average, in 2004, 2005, and 2006.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Conveniently, this time around, the BEA made only very small adjustments to their estimates of PCE inflation.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Because the NIPA revision gave us no new reason to revise our previous assessment of the pressures in product markets, we took our estimate of potential output down in line with actual GDP, thereby maintaining the gap between the two at its previous level as of the end of 2006.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In line with our custom in years past, we carried the revision to the growth of potential through into the forecast period.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As a result, we now have potential output increasing 2¼ percent in both 2007 and 2008.

speaker: WILCOX
text: A virtue of the approach that we have taken in revising the supply side of the projection is that it leaves most of the variables you care about undisturbed.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Thanks to the BEA, inflation is essentially unrevised.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Because we moved potential down in line with actual, the GDP gap and the unemployment rate trajectories are also essentially unrevised.

speaker: WILCOX
text: And with real interest rates and the GDP gap about the same as before, r* is also roughly unrevised.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In short, if you make your policy decisions based on expected inflation and expected resource utilization, your policy choices after the revision should be about the same now as they were before the revision, provided that you see the prospects for resource utilization as roughly the same now as they were before the revision.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The one variable that is different, of course, in the projection as well as in history, is the growth rate of real GDP.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But a conventional analysis would view the revision to that variable as something you simply have to accept—not something you can do anything about.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In a statement that will strike you as reminiscent of “other than that, Mrs. Lincoln…,” I would summarize the nonfinancial news that we received during the intermeeting period as having been remarkably consistent with our June projection.

speaker: WILCOX
text: On the downside, the most notable development, to be sure, was in home sales, both new and existing, confirming the recent step-down in housing demand.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Pending home sales—our most reliable near-term indicator of existing-home sales— rebounded in June, but to a level that is still well below its average in the first quarter.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Even so, were it not for the substantial disruption on the lending side, the portrait of the housing sector that we would be reporting to you today would be substantially the same as the one we presented in June.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Elsewhere, the data on orders and shipments of nondefense capital goods in June were a little softer than we had expected.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The slowdown in light-vehicle sales in July to 15.2 million units at an annual rate raises a warning flag, but we are inclined at this point to interpret that result as a temporary pause rather than a harbinger of much weaker spending ahead.

speaker: WILCOX
text: All that said, last Friday’s employment report once again showed a little more momentum in hiring than we had expected, and initial claims for unemployment insurance in the two weeks since the July survey week have remained low, giving no sign of any material deterioration in labor-market conditions.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The increase in the unemployment rate to 4.6 percent in July was not a surprise given the moderate pace of growth, on average, thus far this year.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Moreover, the indicators that we have in hand put manufacturing IP on track to post a solid increase in July.

speaker: WILCOX
text: All told, the real economy seems to have entered the period of intense financial-market turbulence with, if anything, a little more momentum than we would have projected at the time of the June meeting.

speaker: WILCOX
text: On the inflation front, the picture looks very much the same as it did at the time of the June Greenbook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We still see the bulk of the improvement in core PCE inflation during the second quarter as likely to prove transitory.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In a nod to the relatively favorable recent monthly readings, we trimmed our forecast for the second half of this year by 0.1 percentage point despite a number of factors that could put slightly greater upward pressure on inflation, including the slower pace of structural productivity growth, the higher level of commodity prices, and the uptick of a tenth in the Michigan measure of long-term inflation expectations.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Next year, as energy prices turn down slightly, inflation expectations remain well contained, and pressures on resource utilization ease slightly, we continue to have core inflation edging down to a rate of 2 percent; and we have top-line inflation dipping slightly below the core rate to 1.8 percent for the year as a whole, before coming back up in line with the core over the next two years.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Karen will now continue our presentation.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The financial market turmoil over the intermeeting period has not been confined to U.S. markets.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In today’s financially globalized world, events in one asset market frequently have consequences in other markets and other countries; both the level and the volatility of asset prices abroad have moved with U.S. asset market developments.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Equity prices are generally down, although not in China.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Yields on long-term sovereign fixed-income securities are also generally down.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: CDS spreads, corporate bond spreads, EMBI+ spreads, and similar measures are generally up.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: With so much action happening in global financial markets, you might have expected some major revisions to our outlook for foreign real growth and inflation.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Yet with the exception of revisions to some second-quarter numbers because of surprises from incoming data, the baseline forecast this time is little changed from that in June.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Two reasons for the lack of significant macroeconomic consequences in the rest of the global economy from these financial events seem particularly noteworthy.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: One is that there is no sector abroad in any of the major regions that corresponds to the U.S. housing sector and its direct ties to credit problems related to subprime mortgages.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The second reason is that we do not observe any telltale signs, such as overexpansion by one or more industries or fragile household balance sheets, that would suggest that some repricing of risky assets and perhaps some restraint in credit creation would trigger significant changes in real economic behavior of firms or households.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The global economy expanded strongly in the first half of this year with the underlying strength broadly distributed across regions and sectors.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: As a result, it is in robust condition and is likely able to withstand the adjustment proceeding in financial markets without substantial risk to continued real expansion or creation of inflationary pressures.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Of course, we cannot be certain that continued or more- intense disorderly conditions in financial markets will not trigger a negative macroeconomic reaction, nor do we know for sure that problems are not already present but are not yet visible to us.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: So we see the events of the past several weeks as giving rise to an abundance of downside risk to our forecast of real activity rather than to changes in the baseline.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Despite a basically unchanged outlook for the rest of the global economy, two elements of the international forecast merit some further discussion: global oil market developments over the intermeeting period and the staff’s judgment that U.S. real imports of goods and services will expand at a rate about 1 percentage point lower than we projected in June.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: On July 31, the spot price for WTI rose above $78 per barrel and attracted attention for having reached a new peak value.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Although that price subsequently moved back down somewhat, the spot WTI price was about $7 per barrel higher on the day we finalized the Greenbook forecast than it was on the comparable day in June.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In part, the upward shift in the spot WTI price reflected an unwinding of most of the unusual discount for WTI relative to Brent and other grades of oil that persisted from mid-March until recently as a result of large inventories of WTI at certain locations.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: By comparison, the spot price for Brent crude oil rose nearly $4 per barrel over the same interval.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The upward pressure on spot prices appeared to arise from the supply side, with production restraint by OPEC a factor.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: However, although prices moved up noticeably at the front of the curve, futures prices for oil dated later this year and early next year moved up much less; and futures prices for crude oil in late 2008 and beyond actually moved down.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: As a consequence, the oil futures curve returned to what is called “backwardation,” meaning that the spot price is above futures prices, which tend to flatten out at more- distant dates.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Putting all this together, our forecast for the U.S. oil import price is more than $4 per barrel higher for the very near term than it was in June, but it is little changed over 2008.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: So the impact of higher oil prices on our trade deficit is limited.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Whereas some upward push to consumer prices abroad might result from the recent increases in crude oil prices, our expectation, based on futures markets, that they will prove transitory means that few sustained pressures on inflation should result.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Our forecast for the growth of total U.S. imports of goods and services has been revised down about 1 percentage point for the second half of this year and nearly that much for next.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The resulting annual growth rates of 2¾ percent in the near term and 3 percent next year are about 3 percentage points below the growth we are projecting for real exports of goods and services.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Although in the near term slightly weaker projected imports for oil and natural gas are part of the story, further out weaker growth in imported core goods and services largely account for the revision.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: For these two categories, the downward revision reflects the changes in this forecast to the projected level of the dollar and to the path for U.S. real GDP.

speaker: JOHNSON
