text: We have made some small adjustments to our outlook for the constituent currencies in our broad dollar index that by chance are offsetting, leaving the staff forecast for the rate of depreciation of our real broad dollar index going forward about the same as in June.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: However, the depreciation of the dollar that has already occurred since your June meeting resulted in a downward shift in the current-quarter starting value for our forecast path of about 1¼ percent.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: That real depreciation works to restrain imports of core goods and of services somewhat, especially in the near term.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Parenthetically, it also has a stimulative effect on our exports of core goods and services.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The lower path for U.S. GDP growth going forward is the primary explanation of our downward revision to projected import growth.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: With U.S. GDP now expected to grow at an annual rate of 2 percent, rather than 2½ percent, imports of both core goods and services decelerate more than in proportion, as our best estimate of the income elasticities for each of these categories is above 1.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Of course, the baseline path for U.S. real GDP takes into account the lower imports and the simultaneous nature of the determination of GDP and its components.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But the information contained in the annual revision to past U.S. GDP growth and the prospect of lower potential GDP going forward was “news” to our import model and led us to make the downward revisions I have just described.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: With growth of real exports of goods and services revised up only slightly, their positive contribution to real GDP growth is just a bit more positive.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In contrast, the negative contribution from real imports is now significantly smaller in absolute value.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: As a result, the overall arithmetic contribution from real net exports to real GDP growth over the forecast period is positive at an annual rate of about ¼ percentage point.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Such an outcome would mean that real net exports have contributed or will contribute positively to real GDP growth in each of 2006, 2007, and 2008.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: From the perspective of real GDP, a positive contribution from real net exports is one very reasonable criterion for external adjustment, should it be sustained.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Brian will now continue our presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2 I will be referring to the handout labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Trial-Run Projections.” As in shown line 1 of the top panel of exhibit 1, the central tendency of your current forecasts for real GDP growth for the second half of 2007 is 2.0 to 2.7 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Combined with the BEA’s estimate of 2.0 percent growth in the first half, your projections imply a central tendency for the year of 2.0 to 2.3 percent, down 0.2 percentage point from the June trial run.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The growth rates for 2008 and 2009 were revised down by a similar amount and now center on about 2.5 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As can be seen by comparing rows 3 and 4, the central tendencies of the projections for the unemployment rates at the end of 2007, 2008, and 2009 are essentially the same as in June.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The downward revisions to real GDP growth together with the unchanged forecasts for unemployment suggest that, like the staff, many of you revised down your estimates of potential GDP growth about ¼ percentage point.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Still, as in June, FOMC participants generally are a bit more optimistic than the staff about potential growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, many of you made those points in your forecast narratives.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in row 5, the central tendency for core PCE inflation for the second half of 2007 is 1.9 to 2.1 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Together with the 1.9 percent rate for the first half, this implies a central tendency of 1.9 to 2.0 percent core inflation for the 2007 as a whole, down slightly from the June projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendencies for the next two years are nearly identical to those in June, with the midpoint edging down over time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendencies for total PCE inflation, line 7, collected for the first time in the current exercise, are similar to those for core inflation for 2008 and 2009.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendencies of your projections for core inflation this year and next lie just below the corresponding staff forecasts, and the central tendencies of your projections for unemployment late this year and next are also just below the staff forecasts.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: These comparisons suggest that many of you have a somewhat lower estimate of NAIRU than the staff’s estimate of 5.0 percent, a point that some of you made explicitly in your narratives.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In earlier discussions of the role that your projections might play in enhancing the Committee’s communications, some of you noted that extending the time horizon for your projections would give the public more information about your estimates of potential GDP growth and your judgments about optimal or acceptable trend inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To the extent that argument is correct, the 1.1 percentage point range of your projections for GDP growth in 2009, shown in line 1 of the middle panel of exhibit 1, suggests noticeable dispersion in your views of potential growth, though those growth rates may also be affected by projected adjustments toward inflation rates that you see as desirable.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The range of your projections for total inflation in 2009, line 7, is not quite as wide, suggesting somewhat greater commonality in your views about the rate of inflation consistent with price stability; and the range for your core inflation forecasts in 2009, line 5, is a bit narrower, remaining at 1.5 to 2 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2 Materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the bottom panel, most of you again characterized the appropriate path for the federal funds rate as broadly similar to the Greenbook assumption.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As in June, a few of you assumed a modestly lower path for the federal funds rate, evidently reflecting expectations of more-favorable aggregate supply conditions than in the Greenbook forecast, while two assumed an increase in the fed funds rate later this year or early next year (followed by a reduction) to foster more disinflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Exhibit 2 summarizes the results on uncertainty and skews.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You were asked to characterize your judgment of the uncertainty attached to your projections relative to levels of uncertainty over the past twenty years and to indicate your judgment of the risk-weighting around your projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the top two panels, about two- thirds of you see uncertainty about growth as broadly similar to that experienced historically and see the risks around your growth projections as broadly balanced.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Compared with the situation in June, however, a few more of you see greater uncertainty than historically; and a few more view the risks as tilted to the downside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Similarly, with regard to the outlook for unemployment, not shown, noticeably more of you than in June see the risks as tilted to the upside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With respect to core inflation, the middle two charts show that almost all of you again judge that the uncertainty attached to your projections is similar to past levels, while the number of you who see the risks as tilted to the upside edged down.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the bottom panels, your judgments about the uncertainty and risks for total inflation are nearly the same as those for core inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I would like to end on a personal note.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As the Chairman noted, Vincent Reinhart will be leaving us.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Vincent joined the Board’s staff in 1988.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For a while, Debbie Danker and I oversaw Vincent’s work, but before long Don and the Board recognized prodigious talent, and eventually the tables were turned.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Chairman has already indicated how the Board and the FOMC have benefited from Vincent’s unparalleled expertise and work ethic.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But I want to note that we on the staff have benefited equally, from Vincent’s generous contributions to our research, current analysis, and policy work and from his insightful and creative approaches to day-to- day management issues.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, Vincent’s eclectic wardrobe was useful to the staff in generating random numbers for stochastic model simulations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On any given day, for any given occasion, whether he would choose to show up snazzy or shabby was perfectly unpredictable.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Vincent, all members of the Federal Reserve staff have been proud to be associated with you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re now open for questions for the staff.

speaker: FISHER
text: I noted Karen’s comments about the globalized interlinkages with financial markets, and I have a simple question for maybe Karen.

speaker: FISHER
text: In terms of the alternative scenario that was sketched for greater housing correction to spill over to confidence in financial markets, in that discussion and in that model or simulation, when you talk about equity prices, stresses in the debt markets, and further weakness in aggregate spending, are you talking about the United States only?

speaker: LACKER
text: David, when you were describing the implications of the GDP revisions for your assessment of the output gap, you said that you essentially marked down potential by the same amount as realized growth recently based on your assessment of pressures in product markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: In case we wanted to try it at home, I was wondering if you could say a little more about what data that assessment of pressures in product markets relies on?

speaker: WILCOX
text: It relies on a variety of considerations, but ultimately I would say it relies on inflation performance.

speaker: WILCOX
text: One way that we have of assessing whether our gauges of resource utilization are moving off track is to look back and see whether our inflation models that incorporate those measures of resource utilization are overpredicting or underpredicting.

speaker: WILCOX
text: It’s an imperfect mechanism, to be sure, because the impulse from resource utilization to inflation is very weak; therefore, an error in estimation on our part of the pressures on resource utilization would show up in a discrepancy in the inflation projection that could easily be lost in the noise.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But that’s probably the main approach that we take to attempting to gauge ultimately whether or not we’re off base.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In putting together our assessment of the output gap, we also attempt to maintain some alignment of that measure with the gap between the unemployment rate and the natural rate or the NAIRU.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Our analysis of the NAIRU factors in as well a more fundamental inspection of things like demographic influences, including disability rates and the age composition of the population.

speaker: WILCOX
text: So there is an effort to bring to bear an independent analysis of some of the economic determinants that might be moving the NAIRU up or down.

speaker: LACKER
text: I guess my question was motivated by my sense that estimates of the current output gap tend to play an important role in your outlook for near-term inflation trends.

speaker: LACKER
text: To the extent that the current estimate of the output gap is derived from current inflation, I am wondering if it provides less independent information than current inflation about future inflation than one might otherwise have thought.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I would make two remarks regarding that.

speaker: WILCOX
text: First, quantitatively, in fact, the output gap doesn’t play a very large role in shifting our projection of inflation.

speaker: WILCOX
text: If one does a sort of retrospective decomposition of the factors that were generating inflation over the past ten, fifteen, or twenty years, during the period of the great moderation, gaps in resource utilization are at most a modest contributor to the variance in inflation.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Econometrically speaking, a very important determinant of inflation variability is just shocks that push inflation and that our model has no ready attribution for.

speaker: WILCOX
text: So they are not directly attributable to relative energy price movements, relative import prices, resource utilization, or inflation expectations, but just stuff happening that moves inflation around.

speaker: WILCOX
text: So your point is correct in principle, but quantitatively, I think it has a very modest influence on our current projection.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Second, we enforce a good deal of smoothness so that we are not, by any means, soaking up the residual in the inflation equation that emerges in one period by saying, “Oh, that must have reflected a variation in potential output growth” in order to drive the residual to zero.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We are allowing that residual to persist and to inform our assessment of potential output growth only over time and with an accumulation of evidence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll begin our economic go-round then.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For President Rosengren’s benefit—as you probably know, if we have a comment or a question for a speaker, we use a two-handed symbol for an intervention.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to begin the go-round today with President Moskow.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Conditions in the Seventh District have changed little since our last meeting.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: We continue to lag the nation largely because of difficulties in the auto industry.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Our contacts thought that the U.S. economy had softened a little since June but that international sales continue to be strong.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: They also voiced continuing concerns about input cost pressures.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: There is no good news to report on residential construction.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Some of my contacts again pushed back their expectations on when housing markets would begin to improve and are now saying later in 2008.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: We did hear some upbeat comments from our directors about nonresidential construction in the District, but manufacturers of heavy equipment indicated that they were seeing less demand for products that are used in nonresidential construction.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: We also heard some less-optimistic reports about consumer spending.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: A major shopping center developer and operator scaled back his expectations for the second half of this year and now thinks that spending will be softer than in the first half.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: In addition, a large national specialty retailer saw a broad-based slowing in its sales over the past six weeks.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Still, no one was overly pessimistic.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: In our own forecast, we assume that the weakness in consumption relative to trend during the second quarter was largely transitory, perhaps a reaction to the run-up in gasoline prices.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Regarding the motor vehicle sector, the major topic of discussion is the current labor negotiations and the possibility of a strike in September.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I get the sense that the odds of a walkout are small because both the automakers and the UAW think that a strike would be very damaging.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: As our director who heads the Michigan AFL-CIO noted, a strike would be mutually assured destruction.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: The UAW realizes that the negotiations are occurring against the backdrop of very bad economic conditions in the traditional automaking regions.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: For example, since 2000, Michigan has lost 400,000 jobs.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: That’s an 8½ percent decline in employment.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: A strike would be seen as just adding to these economic woes.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So from all my discussions with management and labor, my impression is that the climate for change underlying these negotiations is stronger than it has been in the past, but I am not sure how big a move the UAW leadership thinks it can get approved by its members.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Of course, the major development affecting the forecast since the last round is the turmoil in credit markets that we were talking about earlier.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Our director who runs a major private equity firm made a number of interesting comments regarding the difficulties that banks were having selling off loans that had been made to risky borrowers with extremely beneficial terms, such as covenant-lite and an option to accrue interest charges.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: The bottom line is that he thought that after the current shakeout there would be fewer buyouts and that pricing and terms would become more reflective of risk.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Going forward, it seems likely that the market will favor so- called strategic buyers, the nonfinancial firms that are looking for acquisitions that would directly enhance the efficiency and scale of their business operations.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So while we are concerned about the negative implications of tighter credit conditions, markets may now do a better job in pricing the tradeoff between risk and return, which is a positive development.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So how might these financial developments affect the real economy?

speaker: MOSKOW
text: If sustained, the fallout of credit market jitters on the stock market and other assets would weigh on spending through the standard wealth-effect channels.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: With regard to the credit markets themselves, the key question is how many of the deals that are now being canceled or scaled back would have resulted in an expansion of business activity as opposed to simply transferring ownership.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Given the modest changes in interest rates on higher-rated debt, continued growth in C&I lending, and ample internal funds of nonfinancial firms, the cost of capital for most investment projects probably has not risen substantially.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So the first-order effects on spending will likely be limited.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Of course, this could change quickly in the current volatile markets, and we will need to monitor these developments carefully, or should I say you will need to monitor these developments carefully.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: However, right now, putting all these factors together, we view the developments in credit markets as a risk to the near-term forecast but not a reason to lower the outlook for growth very much.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: That said, we, like the Greenbook, have marked down our assumptions concerning potential.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: We now see potential as a bit above 2½ percent.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: However, relative to potential, our forecast for real activity is not much different from last round.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: We see growth averaging close to potential in the second half of ’07, which is stronger than the Greenbook, but running a touch below potential in ’08 and ’09, which is similar to the Greenbook.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Our inflation forecast also has not changed much since June.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: We still see core PCE prices increasing a shade below 2 percent by 2009.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: But I must say I remain concerned about the inflation forecast.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: The standard list of upside risks—the lack of resource slack, cost pass- throughs, inflation expectations—these could break the wrong way and require a policy response.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: So, if potential output growth is, in fact, significantly lower than our earlier assessment, then you could face some challenges in calibrating policy as the economy and economic agents adjust to the lower trend in productivity growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Data on inflation during the intermeeting period have continued to be encouraging, but the prospects for economic activity have become dicier.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The results for GDP in the second quarter as a whole actually took on a positive tone, with final sales mainly accounting for the healthy growth rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But the quarter ended on a weak note, with disappointing data for housing consumption and for orders of core capital goods.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, the big developments since our last meeting were in financial markets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I read them as pointing to weaker growth going forward and greater downside risk.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The market for mortgage- backed securities is now highly illiquid, and there are indications that credit problems are spilling beyond the subprime sector.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It thus seems likely that lending standards will tighten for a broader class of borrowers in the mortgage market.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The drop in equity prices and rising rates on most risky corporate debt are further negatives for growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There are some offsets to these negative factors, including the decline in the dollar and, most important, the steep reduction we have seen in risk-free rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On balance, however, I expect these offsets to be only partial, providing a cushion against future weakness, because I interpret the decline in Treasury rates during the intermeeting period primarily as a reflection of weaker growth expectations and a correspondingly lower path for the expected future fed funds rate and not a consequence of the fall of the term premium.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The jump in oil prices since our last meeting is a further factor weighing on aggregate demand.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As a result of these considerations, I have lowered my growth forecast for the second half of this year ½ percentage point, to just over 2 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This rate is moderately below my estimate of potential growth, which I now put at about 2½ percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Going beyond this year, the outlook depends on one’s assumption concerning appropriate monetary policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I consider it appropriate for policy to aim at holding growth just slightly below potential to produce enough slack in labor and credit markets to help bring about a further gradual reduction in inflation toward a level consistent with price stability.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Barring a more serious and prolonged tightening of credit market conditions or a general liquidity squeeze, I would keep the fed funds rate modestly above its equilibrium level to accomplish this goal.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, I now see the fed funds rate as well above the neutral level.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I think it likely that the fed funds rate will need to fall appreciably over the next few years.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My assessment of the neutral federal funds rate declined during the intermeeting period for two main reasons—first, because of the tightening in financial conditions associated with the reassessment of risk now taking place and, second, because of the NIPA revisions, which suggest slower structural productivity growth and, in all likelihood, correspondingly slower growth in aggregate demand.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I thus think that a larger decline in the fed funds rate will be needed over time than in the Greenbook baseline to achieve a soft landing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A key development during the intermeeting period was the downward revision of real GDP growth over the 2004-06 period.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This adjustment reinforces the work of productivity experts at the Board and elsewhere who had previously found evidence of a slowdown in underlying productivity growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The revision in actual productivity was big enough to lead us to lower our estimate of growth in both structural productivity and potential output, although our estimates remain above those in the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition to tighter financial conditions, lower structural productivity growth was the reason that we lowered our forecast for real GDP growth to 2¼ percent in 2008.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As a result, the unemployment rate edges up in our forecast, reaching nearly 5 percent by the end of next year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The modest amount of slack that this entails should help bring about the desired gradual reduction of inflation in the future.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Readings on core PCE prices have been quite tame for some time now, rising only 0.1 percent in each of the past four months.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although a portion of the recent deceleration in core prices likely reflects transitory influences, the underlying trend in core inflation still appears favorable.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We anticipate that the core PCE price index will rise 2 percent this year and that core inflation will gradually ebb to around 1.8 percent over the forecast period.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This forecast is predicated on continued well-anchored inflation expectations and the eventual appearance of a small amount of labor market slack, as I just mentioned.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For some time now, I’ve thought an argument could be made that the NAIRU was a bit lower than assumed in the Greenbook, and the new evidence that structural productivity growth has been lower than we thought for more than three years reinforces this view.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It means that the relatively good inflation performance over this period occurred despite the upward pressure that must have been operating because of the deceleration in structural productivity.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In any event, I also expect to see modest downward pressure on inflation in the next couple of years from the ebbing of the upward effects of special factors, including the decline in structural productivity, energy and commodity prices, and owners’ equivalent rent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In terms of risk to the outlook for growth, the housing sector obviously remains a serious concern.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We seem to be repeatedly surprised with the depth and duration of the deterioration in these markets; and the financial fallout from developments in the subprime markets, which I now perceive to be spreading beyond that sector, is a source of appreciable angst.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, financial conditions have deteriorated in markets well beyond those connected with subprime instruments or even residential real estate more generally.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It appears that participants are questioning structured credit products in general, the risk assessments of the rating agencies, and the extent of due diligence by originators who package and sell loans but no longer hold a very sizable fraction of these originations on their own balance sheets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The Greenbook has long highlighted, and we have long worried about, the possibility and potential consequences of a broader shift in risk perceptions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With risk premiums having been so low by historical standards, it would hardly be surprising to see them rise, making financial conditions tighter for any given stance of monetary policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: While it remains possible that financial markets will stabilize or even reverse course in the days and weeks ahead, the possibility that the financial markets are now shifting to a historically more typical pattern of risk pricing is very much on my radar screen.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Should this pattern persist and possibly intensify, it will have very important implications for policy.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, at the past few meetings I have spoken about my District as having strong growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have asked questions about the strength of the growth in the national economy, and I have described the global economy from the standpoint of the way the staff here writes about it and the way we do our own work as “hotter than a $2 pistol.” Nothing has really changed since my last intervention.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would note that, unlike President Moskow’s District, our District is unusual on the other side: We are not experiencing the kind of decline in home prices that is being experienced elsewhere.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’re suffering from widespread labor shortages, for both unskilled and skilled labor.

speaker: FISHER
text: We believe that we are seeing significant labor hoarding in our District.

speaker: FISHER
text: Unemployment is strikingly and historically low in the two major cities of Dallas and Houston at 4.1 percent, in Austin at 3.5 percent, and along the border areas unprecedentedly in the low single digits.

speaker: FISHER
text: Salaries for accountants in our District are up 5 to 8 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: Law firms—I note that there are 1.2 million lawyers in America and 1.1 million people who work in the auto industry from parts to final assembly, which is a statement on our society—[laughter] are raising first- and second-year annual compensation by double digits for their new lawyers.

speaker: FISHER
text: So there is still price inflation in the service sector.

speaker: FISHER
text: We perceive, through our discussions with CEOs around the country, that while there has been a net downward movement in the more-robust measurements of price inflation—the trimmed mean—there still are some threats on the inflation front.

speaker: FISHER
text: For example, the CEO of Wal-Mart USA told me yesterday that, internally, when they evaluate their comparable store measurements, the comps are being driven by inflation, not by volume.

speaker: FISHER
text: As for the demand for ships—if you read the Wall Street Journal yesterday or from the interviews I have had with large shippers, the bulk carriers are trading at record highs.

speaker: FISHER
text: The Baltic index is at a record high, driven by exports of iron ore, pulp, and other products to voracious Chinese demand and by the return of exports from China to a voracious European demand.

speaker: FISHER
text: Container shipments are up 20 percent year over year in terms of European imports.

speaker: FISHER
text: The price pressures being exerted there seem to be invading other areas.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of the more interesting observations was what has happened recently in terms of the pricing of paper products being led by SCA, which is a European corporation.

speaker: FISHER
text: Kimberly-Clark and the others have fallen in line.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are asking for double-digit increases.

speaker: FISHER
text: So although we are seeing some mitigation of price pressures, I am nonetheless concerned that, given the international dynamics, we still have the potential for price increases and a bit of resistance to what I would like to see.

speaker: FISHER
text: In terms of economic growth nationally, I just want to comment on some things that the staff presented.

speaker: FISHER
text: I thought the Greenbook was excellent.

speaker: FISHER
text: I did speak to two of the five largest publicly held builders.

speaker: FISHER
text: They report that all-in, with incentives, their prices have been marked down an average of 25 to 35 percent from a year ago.

speaker: FISHER
text: For example, in the Imperial Valley of California, homes selling for $550,000 to $600,000 have been now marked down to $400,000 to $450,000.

speaker: FISHER
text: The builder with the most experience—forty years of experience—who has lived through all kinds of cycles is of the strong belief that we are in the second year of a five-year correction.

speaker: FISHER
text: Like the point that you made, President Yellen, this is of great concern.

speaker: FISHER
text: So net from the Dallas Fed standpoint, we have lowered our expectation for second-half growth to 2 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are still concerned, despite the encouragement of marginal movement, on the inflation front.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’d like to leave the discussion of the economy there and just turn to the previous discussion we had and the references made by President Moskow and President Yellen.

speaker: FISHER
text: This may be a bit harsh, but if you look at the front page of the Wall Street Journal from this morning, I see what I call the “Churchillian maxim” at play, which is, “I shall fare well in history because I shall rewrite that history.” Whether you use Greg Ip to rewrite the history or you rewrite it yourself, no amount of rewriting of history will exonerate us if we are not prepared for the more-dire scenarios that were presented by the staff.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would ask that we do some scenario preparation in terms of, should we encounter increased financial market turbulence, what actions we might take to deal with it.

speaker: FISHER
text: For example, it is not clear to me that a widespread opening of the discount window solves the problem given the structure of what I call “ersatz credit” that is then spread throughout the system.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s not clear to me that even dealing, for purposes of the present meeting, with the fed funds rate is the issue because it is not an issue of just pricing in the marketplace.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s a structure issue, and it’s a covenant issue.

speaker: FISHER
text: I started my career, Mr. Chairman, with Herstatt.

speaker: FISHER
text: That was not an auspicious beginning.

speaker: FISHER
text: I lived through the corrections of the S&L market, portfolio insurance, the crashes of ’87, ’97, and so on.

speaker: FISHER
text: When you sort through them, all of them have a common basis, and that is a search for greater yields or greater return, leverage in order to achieve that return, and some assumption of risk mitigation leading to what I call “rational complacency.” I believe that’s at play presently.

speaker: FISHER
text: I agree fully with President Yellen that it presents a significant risk.

speaker: FISHER
text: However, I want to exercise great caution in interpreting these signals.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we have to be extremely careful about what we do and what we say.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just to show my hand, I would not be in favor of cutting the federal funds rate at this juncture.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we have to analyze the language carefully.

speaker: FISHER
text: But my request is that, in addition to our exercise on communication, we take a serious look at the various scenarios that might obtain, so that no one could ever accuse us of being unprepared in case the worst obtains.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just to respond very briefly, we do have a group here at the Board working with other economists and financial experts throughout the System that does scenario analysis and does monitor the markets, and we certainly are quite attuned to these issues.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The reports that I am hearing from business leaders in the Fourth District lead me to conclude that the pace of economic activity hasn’t changed a great deal since our last meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, the uncertainties surrounding the business climate seem to have risen measurably.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The troubled housing sector is still weighing on the region, as it is nationally.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I now have little doubt that this theme is going to recur throughout the balance of the year and perhaps well beyond.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My view of the housing sector conforms closely to the way housing is depicted in the Greenbook baseline, but I have had many conversations in the past few weeks with anxious industry insiders, who believe that housing markets are likely to worsen substantially over the balance of the year with the possibility of significant spillovers to other sectors of the economy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The stories they tell me sound a lot like the greater housing correction scenarios that are depicted in the Greenbook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Indeed, casualties in the mortgage markets are rising, and I am hearing more and more that the fallout from housing is affecting deals in other sectors of the economy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: For example, I talked with a CEO who runs a large national real estate development company.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: He told me that some of his projects are being held up by his investment banker’s inability to price deals and to bring them to market.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Where the deals can be priced, risk spreads have widened across a range of issuers and financial instruments.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This CEO’s comments are very much in line with the points that Bill Dudley made in his report earlier this morning.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Because of these uncertainties in financial markets, some of my contacts confirm that they have been reevaluating their capital formation plans.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: They are trimming their projections of some of the projects that they are going to put on the books, and that led me to trim my projection for business fixed investment accordingly.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Even with this adjustment, however, I am concerned that the pattern of business investment that I have incorporated into my GDP projections for this meeting may still be somewhat optimistic.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This is a risk to the outlook that was not on my radar screen at our last meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The June retail price measures gave us more evidence that the inflation trend may be coming down.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Inflation moderated in the second quarter, as measured by the median CPI and the 16-percent trimmed mean that we produce at the Cleveland Fed.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am not yet persuaded that this progress will be sustained, but the patterns in the June data were promising.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My projection for inflation in the outyears of the forecast are actually a little more favorable than what is in the Greenbook baseline, primarily because I still expect a bit more potential GDP growth than the Greenbook envisions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I am feeling more comfortable about the inflation risks than I have felt for a while but less comfortable about the real-side risks.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My overall risk assessment is moving closer into balance.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Nevertheless, I still think that inflation is the predominant risk we face today.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, as best I can judge, recent readings on the economy are generally consistent with anticipation of moderate growth and some gradual diminution or at least no deterioration in inflation.

speaker: STERN
text: Second-quarter GDP readings, as far as I can tell, contain no big surprises.

speaker: STERN
text: In particular, the components of aggregate demand that were expected to bounce back after periods of sluggishness or, in some cases, correction—inventory accumulation, spending on equipment and software, and federal government outlays—all in fact did bounce back as anticipated.

speaker: STERN
text: The labor market report for July was positive, and anecdotes and indicators in our District are generally quite consistent with the tenor of that report.

speaker: STERN
text: The labor market appears to be healthy.

speaker: STERN
text: Job availability appears to be ample.

speaker: STERN
text: The labor market overall, I would say, is strong.

speaker: STERN
text: Of course, all of that is by way of background because that information has been overshadowed in recent weeks by what I think are three or four developments of greater significance, one of which is the revision to the NIPA accounts.

speaker: STERN
text: The GDP and productivity data and, in particular, the downward revision to productivity may have significant implications for the longer-term performance of the economy.

speaker: STERN
text: I won’t dwell on that now.

speaker: STERN
text: Dave Wilcox covered some of that earlier.

speaker: STERN
text: There was also an upward revision to the personal saving rate, which possibly has implications for the outlook for consumer spending going forward, and I will come to that briefly in a moment.

speaker: STERN
text: Of course, the big headlines have been the turbulence in the financial markets and all the uncertainty associated with the duration of the repricing and the adjustments that are under way and their quantitative significance for the performance of the economy going forward.

speaker: STERN
text: This turbulence in the financial markets is likely the most significant development for the short-term performance of the economy and possibly for policy.

speaker: STERN
text: But at this point, it is very difficult, to put it mildly, to assess its effects for reasons I alluded to earlier— namely, that we don’t know how long this will last and what will follow in its wake.

speaker: STERN
text: Even if we knew the duration, would we be—at least would I be—all that confident that we could go from that to the magnitude of the effects on the economy?

speaker: STERN
text: So all of that suggests to me that we should have a good deal of caution at the moment.

speaker: STERN
text: Since we don’t, it seems to me, know enough to act decisively, we certainly don’t want to overreact or to act wrongly in these circumstances.

speaker: STERN
text: These developments really have taken hold forcefully in the past several weeks.

speaker: STERN
text: The situation has not been so dramatic for any extended period of time.

speaker: STERN
text: Returning to the saving rate for a moment, I am quite cautious about drawing implications for consumer spending on the basis of a judgment about whether the saving rate is likely to go up or down.

speaker: STERN
text: An argument has been popular in some circles that, with the negative saving rate as reported until recently in the data, the implications for consumer spending were likely that spending was going to be sluggish going forward because the negative saving rate couldn’t persist.

speaker: STERN
text: It seems to me that the argument now, at a minimum, has to be less compelling, and so, other things being equal, we might be tempted to become more optimistic about consumer spending.

speaker: STERN
text: That could be swamped, of course, by the negative wealth effects coming out of the adjustments in the financial markets and the tighter financial market conditions as well.

speaker: STERN
text: On net, I guess I come out where I usually do on this—that it is mostly a matter of employment and incomes—and so far so good on that score.

speaker: STERN
text: Finally, and this is the fourth development that I will mention—although I don’t think it’s as important as the other three, but I did want to comment on it—it looks as though, as part of the revisions to the NIPA accounts, the increase in unit labor costs will be revised up for the previous three years—that is, for ’04, ’05, and ’06.

speaker: STERN
text: Now, this is a matter of correlation and not causation, but it does appear that there is a pretty high correlation in the short run between unit labor costs and inflation.

speaker: STERN
text: That observation flashes a bit of a warning light on our expectations of a fundamental slowing of inflation over time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, the Tenth District economy overall continues to perform well, with strength in energy and agriculture partially offset by the weaknesses in residential construction.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Developments since the last meeting include some softening in District manufacturing activity similar to that shown in the July ISM survey numbers and in other regional Reserve Bank indexes.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have also seen a slowing in overall employment growth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In contrast, consumer spending seems to be holding well in spite of higher gasoline prices.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Indeed, reports from District directors and business contacts indicate a strong summer tourism season with increased air traffic and higher hotel occupancy rates throughout the western part of our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The recent slowing in District employment growth has been somewhat surprising to us, given the activity in much of our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Since the beginning of 2004, District employment growth has been running around 2 percent, and in the past few months has slowed to about 1½ percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Geographically, the slowdown has been most notable in Wyoming, New Mexico, Colorado, and Oklahoma, and anecdotal information suggests that the slower growth is due more to a shortage of skilled and semi-skilled labor than to any weakening in demand.

speaker: HOENIG
text: This anecdotal information is supported by new regional information on employment costs by the BLS.

speaker: HOENIG
text: According to them, recent employment cost increases in these states have been well above increases nationally and in other parts of our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Construction activity remains mixed, with weakness in residential construction offset to some extent by strength in commercial construction.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Just an aside, when you talk about things that are on the horizon, we are a little concerned about commercial real estate because it is very hot right now and there is a fairly large portion of it on the books of the banks in our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the residential side, there is considerable variation across our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In some areas where energy and agriculture are strong, housing activity is actually above normal.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In other parts of the District, however, both national and local developers are experiencing the most difficult conditions in some time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In most District metro areas, inventories of unsold homes continue to rise, but the rate of increase has diminished somewhat in recent months.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to the national outlook, data released since the last meeting support the view that growth will pick up over the year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Compared with the Greenbook, I am more optimistic about both the near-term outlook and longer-run growth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Specifically, I think second-half growth is likely to be around 2½ percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Growth in 2008 and 2009 is likely to be near potential, which we estimate to be around 2¾ percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Housing obviously constitutes the major downside risk to growth over the next few quarters.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am not yet convinced, however, that recent financial market volatility and repricing of credit risk will have significant implications for the growth outlook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It is still reasonable at this point to think that the recent volatility will prove transitory, and the repricing of credit risk is, in that sense, desirable.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am also encouraged by the results of the July senior loan officer survey, which suggests no general tightening of bank credit conditions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Like the Bluebook, I think that Treasury yields are likely to move back up once the markets feel more comfortable about the state of the economy and credit conditions and realize that policy easing is not likely to be forthcoming.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Although weakness in housing and tighter credit conditions have increased the downside risk to output, I believe that strength in consumer spending, exports, and government spending will help maintain moderate growth in the period ahead.

speaker: HOENIG
text: With regard to the inflation outlook, recent data on core CPI and PCE continue to be favorable.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, I am expecting some pass-through of higher energy prices to temporarily boost core measures over the second half of this year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, pressures from resource utilization and slow productivity growth remain.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Thus, despite recent improvements, I continue to believe that some upside risk to inflation remains.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Since our last meeting, the news in the Third District has been generally positive.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Economic activity continues to expand in the tri-state area but at a less rapid pace than at our previous meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our Business Outlook Survey indicates that the District’s manufacturing output continued to expand in July, although at a somewhat slower pace than in June.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The June measure, you may recall, was more than 18 in our Business Outlook Survey, the highest level that it had been since April 2005.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In July the index dropped to a little over 9, although it was still significantly positive.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Shipments of new orders increased in July, and the outlook for manufacturers’ own capital spending plans remains positive and is at a level typical of an expansion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Firms in our survey generally see improvements in their businesses coming in the second half of the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Residential construction, however, continues to be very weak in the region, but we have not seen, at least according to OFHEO indexes, any absolute price declines in our area.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is confirmed by our business contacts, who report that they have not seen steep or broad-based declines in house prices, except for properties along the Jersey shore, where the boom was most prevalent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At our last meeting I characterized the nonresidential investment market as firm, and that characterization continues today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Office vacancy rates in the Philadelphia region remain very low and declining, and rents in office and warehouse spaces remain at a record high.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although reports on retail sales in our region have been mixed, sales appear to have improved somewhat in late June and early July, especially at higher-end retail establishments.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Bank lending has continued to advance but at a more moderate pace than at the time of our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our banking and other business contacts indicate that banks have money to lend to customers with good credit ratings, and so I don’t get the sense that area businesses are facing a credit crunch of the normal type.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Banks are comfortable with their lending standards and do not expect to make any big changes along this dimension in the foreseeable future.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: For the most part our banks were not in the subprime business and obviously don’t intend to start now, [laughter] and thus they have not seen an appreciable deterioration in their balance sheets or in those of the businesses to which they lend—their customers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Clearly, there is nervousness, but as yet there seem to be few consequences for the real economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: June employment growth in the region was below trend, but the region’s unemployment rate remains relatively low.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our staff expects employment to continue to grow at a moderate pace going forward and expects the region’s unemployment rate perhaps to rise modestly by the second quarter of next year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yet businesses continue to report tight labor markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One very large builder, who is headquartered in our area and who builds mostly high-end homes, has actually reported that he cannot finish a number of homes that he has under contract and that buyers are waiting to move into.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Because of the crackdown on illegal immigrants, who do a lot of the landscaping, a lot of roofing work, and all the labor that goes into finishing these homes, he cannot hire these workers, and so he actually has to put off closing deals because he cannot find workers to complete the homes.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the inflation front in the District, employment costs in the Northeast are increasing at about the same pace as in the nation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Area manufacturers continue to report higher production costs, but there is relatively little evidence of pass-through of those higher costs to customers as they see it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Consumer prices are growing more slowly in the region than in the nation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So in summary, the Third District economy continues to expand at a moderate pace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While there is nervousness caused by the recent volatility in the financial markets, businesses do not yet see that affecting their current growth or prospects for future growth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Business contacts as well as the Philadelphia staff expect this moderate pace of expansion to be continued in the coming months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the national level, the news has been mixed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the positive side, employment and income growth remain solid.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Manufacturing output continues to improve, and core inflation and inflation expectations remain contained, although both remain higher than I would like to see in the long run.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the negative side, news on business fixed investment and housing has been disappointing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: After encouraging signs of stabilization early in the year, the sales of both new and existing homes have continued to decline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Sales of homes declined 6.6 percent in June and almost 8 percent in the second quarter.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the time of our last meeting, I expressed the view that I was getting hopeful that economy was on track to return to near-trend growth later this year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Setting aside the issue that our perception of long-term trend growth in real GDP may need reassessment in light of the benchmark revisions, as we’ve been discussing—and I’ll return to this point in a moment—the recent data on housing are suggestive of a weaker third quarter and perhaps fourth quarter as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Though I think the underlying steady-state demand for housing is lower than the pace of housing demand before we saw the downturn begin, which implies that much of the adjustment in housing supply is part of a healthy adjustment to a new equilibrium, the stock of unsold homes continues to cause a drag on residential investment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also think that there is some risk of temporary weakness in business fixed investment going forward simply because of increased uncertainty.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So the return to trend growth, which I think will happen within the forecast period, may be delayed by a few quarters and may not get under way solidly until late in the first half of next year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You know the old saying: “If you can’t forecast well, forecast often.” The biggest economic news headlines since our last meeting have focused on the volatility of the financial markets and the repricing of risk.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am inclined to put minimal weight on the current financial conditions for a slowdown in the pace of economic activity going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although risk spreads have widened in the past three weeks or so, the cost of capital for high quality borrowers has hardly changed and remains relatively low by historical standards.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This suggests to me that what we are seeing in the marketplace—at least right now but which could change, as we’ve all noted—is a change in the relative price of various measures of types of risk.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The cost of capital for some borrowers is increased, but demand for business investments that originate from large corporations with good credit ratings has not changed and is not likely to be adversely affected very much in the repricing of risk, if that’s what this represents.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This news was reinforced to me by my conversations with area bankers, as I mentioned earlier, who say that they have plenty of money to lend to good credit risks.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There is no evidence of a general credit crunch from their point of view.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My general view regarding the limited nature of the credit repricing is reinforced by the fact that default rates on auto loans, credit cards, and other types of consumer debt instruments have not changed much, suggesting that the spillover effects, at least to date, have not been very measurable.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, I think that the decline in the subprime market is primarily a result of lax underwriting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Those lenders are now paying the price, but we must be very careful not to act or appear to act in a way that supports bad bets or lax underwriting standards without more widespread evidence of systemic problems affecting the real economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Let me now turn to what I think is a more fundamental factor for gauging the strength of the economy going forward and, therefore, the appropriate stance for monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the most recent Greenbook, the Board staff revised down the rate of growth of structural productivity more or less in line with the reduction in real GDP growth, as we have been discussing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is certainly reasonable to think that this new information about the pace of real GDP growth during the past three years contains information about the rate of growth of structural productivity going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But that is not an infallible signal.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my thinking about how monetary policy needs to be set, distinguishing temporary decreases in the rate of growth of productivity from permanent decreases is a critical piece of the puzzle.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A transitory decrease would not affect the steady-state equilibrium real rate to my mind.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But a permanent decrease would imply a lower steady-state equilibrium real rate and, thus, a lower natural rate for the federal funds rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If the equilibrium real rate is lower, holding the fed funds rate constant, of course, would imply an implicit tightening of monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am still grappling with the implications of these benchmark revisions for future productivity growth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At this point in my forecast, I’m assuming that the revisions imply a rebenchmarking of the growth rate of structural productivity, but that rebenchmarking or that lowering of the trend rate of growth of real GDP is not enough so that core inflation can decelerate toward price stability in the next two or three years or so under a constant fed funds rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But the reduction in the growth rate of structural productivity does feed through to a somewhat looser required path of the fed funds rate through 2008 to 2009.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my forecast, appropriate policy has the fed funds rate rising to 5½ percent in the first quarter of ’08, holding steady there for two or three quarters, and then gradually drifting down toward a more neutral rate consistent with lower inflation expectations and lower trend output growth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: With this path of the fed funds rate, I expect the economy to return to near potential real GDP growth in the first or the second quarter of 2008.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I expect the housing correction to continue through the first half of 2008, but the drag lessens over the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I expect the core inflation rate to be somewhat higher in the second half of the year than in the first half, but I expect the economy by 2009 to grow near its potential growth rate, which I now assume to be 2.8 percent, about 0.2 percent lower than I had last time, with the unemployment rate close to its natural rate of 5 percent and core inflation at about 1.5 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have two other brief comments I’d like to make about our forecasting exercise and some information I think is relevant.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We continue to focus on the PCE price index, and I have some objections to that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I continue to believe that the CPI is a better measure, if for no other reasons than that it is more familiar to the public and that it is not revised.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We were lucky this time in the GDP revisions that the PCE price index was not revised very much, and I think we run the risk that focusing too heavily on a measure that does get revised can cause us some difficulty.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also have some concern about the empirical ability of core PCE to actually be a very good predictor of headline PCE inflation at the end of the day.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I am still struggling with our choice of the index there.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The other item that I would like to emphasize—and it was driven home to me in a meeting with some reporters in the not-too-distant past—is that I do believe that moving toward measures of uncertainty that include some fan charts would be useful.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was hesitant at first about that in part because getting appropriate measures of uncertainty that are internally consistent across all our forecasts and all our models would be very difficult.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yet some, what I would view as very sophisticated, journalists continue to confuse the issue of the range of our forecasts and our central tendencies with the issue of uncertainty or certainty.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They do not understand that our central tendency is an agreement about what our point forecast is but that it may reveal very little or nothing about the degree of uncertainty in our forecasts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think it is very important that we quantify that in some way to be clearer and to eliminate some of that confusion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I see a two-handed intervention.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Charlie, could I ask you about the issue of the fan charts?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As I understood the proposal, the fan charts would be in there, but we would not be producing our individual fan charts.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think you are absolutely right.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I strongly agree with you that it is important to have something that is visually dynamic to get across uncertainty for many, many reasons, particularly to get people to understand that, even when we don’t get it exactly right, we may still actually be doing a very good job and then, of course, to evaluate us in a more reasonable way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, I am encouraged that that is going to be the case.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I think it is a question of nuance.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One of the issues that I wonder about here is that for us to do a communal fan chart would be extremely difficult technically.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the question is how we get across the issue of uncertainty in a very graphic way, and I think it can be done by producing information along the lines that the proposal mentioned.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I think we will need to see examples.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I would recommend that the subcommittee or whoever will be involved with the staff give us some different ways of doing it so that we can actually get some polling information on people as to whether or not this is effective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This point was driven home to me by somebody who I thought was fairly sophisticated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: He saw the central tendency narrow and thought that therefore we were more certain about what our forecasts were.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is not just the media.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Think about the financial analysts who are writing about this all the time—and they get paid a lot more than we do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The two things are not completely unrelated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there is a lot of uncertainty, then there will be more divergence of views as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They could be negatively correlated actually.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Just because our point forecasts converge does not mean that our uncertainty about that forecast is decreased.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It just means that there is more agreement.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My basic view of appropriate policy is little changed from the previous meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: None of the intermeeting developments yet compel me to change my view that our focus should remain on reducing inflation and inflation expectations.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The outlook for GDP growth remains acceptable, especially in view of the recent downward revisions in the data and the associated lowering of estimates of growth potential.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Our baseline outlook is consistent with that of recent months, but the new concern is obviously the financial markets that clearly are skittish about spillovers from the subprime market and about contagion in credit markets spreading beyond structured products.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Evidence within the Sixth District is consistent with this basically stable and positive outlook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Florida is seeing some notable spillovers from their problems in real estate, but some of these problems are idiosyncratic to the state—for example, the widespread inability to get wind and storm insurance.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The rest of the District has not seen serious spillover into the broader economy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Just like the Greenbook, we view the fundamentals of the economy to be stable.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Although the residential real estate market may take some time to stabilize, the problem seems generally contained.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Our model suggests slightly stronger growth than the baseline Greenbook throughout the forecast period.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Our trend growth rate has not been reduced quite as much as the Greenbook’s, and our inflation forecast is not as favorable.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: At this juncture, we are not ready to give much weight to some of the more extreme alternate Greenbook scenarios.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We certainly recognize more uncertainty and volatility than at the last meeting, but we’re still expecting results essentially in line with the baseline Greenbook forecast.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the past few days, I have had substantive conversations with some well-positioned credit market observers, including managers of large investment portfolios, suggesting that the skittishness of financial markets is not likely to abate until later this fall.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: They have suggested that the choppiness in financial markets will be the rule in the near term and, very important, that the threshold for what constitutes a shock is now much lower than usual.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I believe that the correct policy posture is to let the markets work through the changes in risk appetite and pricing that are under way, but the market observations of one of my more strident conversational counterparts— and that is not Jim Cramer [laughter]—are worth sharing.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This party sees problems in the subprime structured debt market spreading to the CLO leveraged-loan market and, in a knock-on effect, to repo and commercial paper markets as well as to investment-grade corporate credit.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This party points to nonprice rationing, commercial paper rollover risk, and general CDO contagion caused by the damaged credibility of rating agencies and contraction of collateral values.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This party argues that treating the widening of credit spreads as normalization ignores substantial subsurface potential dislocations as evidenced by the collapse of American Home Mortgage Corporation.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: All that said, another counterpart noted a large pool of money now on the sidelines that is ready to provide financing for reasonable deals if prices fall low enough.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Importantly, a large portion of this money comes from reliable long-term sources of investment, pension funds and insurance companies.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Notwithstanding some descriptive rhetoric, this is not the credit crunch of the late 1980s, when the traditional financial intermediaries were strained for capital.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The traditional investors are still out there with substantial liquidity, and they are just temporarily on the sidelines for understandable reasons and, barring further shocks, should return to the markets in force later this fall.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The dislocations in the financial markets call for a posture of vigilant monitoring of developments but nothing more for now.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding the balance of risks, it is early to materially adjust the weighting of GDP downside versus inflation upside risks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But I have heightened concern, as many of you do, about the continuing housing sector weakness combined with some potential of credit market turbulence in time affecting business investment and consumer confidence and thereby the real economy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Boston staff forecast is broadly consistent with the Greenbook forecast, with export-led growth being significantly offset by weakness in residential investment, resulting in a gradual increase in the unemployment rate and core PCE inflation settling around 2 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Boston staff forecast is somewhat more optimistic on residential investment but also has somewhat higher potential than the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My own view is that residential investment is likely to be as weak as in the Greenbook forecast but that potential may be closer to Boston’s estimate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Taken together, weak residential investment and somewhat stronger productivity, along with the possibility that construction employment will be more depressed going forward, may result in more of an upward drift in unemployment, helping to reduce some of the concerns with labor market pressures on inflation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, given the similarities in the forecasts, well within standard errors, at this time it is probably more important to highlight the risks to the forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It is notable that the rather benign outlook of the forecasters is in marked contrast to the angst I hear when talking to asset and hedge fund managers in Boston.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The angst is new and reflects heightened concerns with the financial ramifications stemming from subprime mortgages.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Recent developments in residential markets are of potential concern.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: They have been raised by many around the table.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Over the past several years, large homebuilders have been able to increase their market share.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given the use of subcontractors and with little obvious economies of scale, the primary advantage of large homebuilders would seem to be access to external finance, which allows them to purchase large tracts of land.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: When housing and land prices were rising, particularly in fast growing areas of the country, this access provided a significant advantage over the small builders that could not tie up significant resources in land.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, what provided a competitive advantage in the first half of this decade now places a significant strain on large homebuilders.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A large investment in land whose price is falling is aggravating the problem these builders have with unsold inventory and depressed prices for new homes.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Not surprisingly, the largest homebuilders, which account for nearly a quarter of homes sold, have equity prices trading lower than at any time in the past year, and recent earnings announcements have highlighted significant write-downs in land values.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The low equity prices of homebuilders seem broadly consistent with residential investment remaining quite weak well into 2008.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Financial market disruptions are likely to be a further impediment to the housing market and potentially provide a channel for problems to extend beyond residential investment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A number of financial instruments, such as the 2/28 and 3/27 mortgages that were widely used last year, are no longer readily available.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Furthermore, the originate-to-distribute model has been disrupted by the heightened uncertainty surrounding CDOs and CLOs that we heard about earlier this morning.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There seem to be two significant developments.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, the liquidity of these instruments has declined, making valuation assessment difficult.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As lenders have made margin calls, forced liquidation of collateral in illiquid markets has further depressed the market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While of concern, I would hope that this is only a short-run effect.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The second development of concern is that many investors have been relying on rating agencies to evaluate credit risk but the underlying credit risk is relatively opaque and the correlations between tranches may not have been fully appreciated.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If investors have lost confidence in the rating agencies to accurately assess credit risk for structured products, the market could be impeded until confidence is restored.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Since similar structures are used for financial instruments besides mortgages, getting secondary market financing for a broader range of financing needs could be difficult, and external financing for some borrowers could be affected.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This has been reflected in the widening spreads for riskier corporate bonds, where the spreads have widened from unusually low levels and are still relatively narrow compared with earlier periods of significant financial disruption.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While recent problems are not compelling enough for me to have a significant disagreement with the forecast presented in the Greenbook, the risks surrounding that forecast on the downside have increased.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I remain concerned that higher oil prices, a falling dollar, and tight labor markets pose upward risks to the forecast of inflation, but recent events have significantly raised my estimate of the risk of a slower economy than I would have predicted a few weeks ago.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m informed the coffee is ready.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we break until 11 o’clock?

speaker: POOLE
text: At the beginning of the break, two of our leaders made a special point of indicating that I was first up after the break.

speaker: POOLE
text: I guess that was an invitation to be fast and quick.

speaker: POOLE
text: My overall impression from my business contacts is that things are more of the same rather than anything very much different.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would note that the financial market upset is too recent to have affected the plans of companies operating in the real economy.

speaker: POOLE
text: Obviously financial firms are scrambling.

speaker: POOLE
text: There seems to be something of a disconnect between my trucking industry contacts and what I see in the industrial production numbers.

speaker: POOLE
text: The industrial production numbers suggest that goods production is rising; I don’t know how they’re moving, but they don’t seem to be moving by truck.

speaker: POOLE
text: One big over-the-road trucker says that loads are down 8 percent year over year.

speaker: POOLE
text: The company has already cut trucking capacity 10 percent.

speaker: POOLE
text: He expects another cut of 4 percent by the end of this year.

speaker: POOLE
text: He’s trimming capital spending next year for trucks.

speaker: POOLE
text: Obviously they see the business as being pretty slack.

speaker: POOLE
text: Incidentally, nobody is talking about any particular labor market pressures.

speaker: POOLE
text: Another big company probably best known for the color of its brown trucks [laughter] says that the industry overall is flat year over year.

speaker: POOLE
text: It believes that the outlook is somewhat more optimistic than recent experience.

speaker: POOLE
text: The international business is booming.

speaker: POOLE
text: The Asia-Pacific region is shipping an awful lot of goods to both the United States and Europe.

speaker: POOLE
text: My contact noted something that I thought was sort of interesting.

speaker: POOLE
text: He said that there is some diversion from air freight to water transport—I guess because of the enormous cost difference, but it suggests that there may be a little easier inventory situation or something that is making that diversion make sense.

speaker: POOLE
text: This company is very much in a cost-cutting mode because they have a big infrastructure, demand is relatively slack, and they have a lot of cost built in; and so the only thing they can do when they can’t build volume in the short run is to cut costs.

speaker: POOLE
text: That company’s major competitor is much more optimistic and has capital spending plans for fiscal ’08, which ends in May of next year, up 20 percent from this year and sees a pretty strong business situation at least going forward.

speaker: POOLE
text: A contact in the restaurant industry says that restaurant prices are rising everywhere and volumes are falling, but overall business conditions are about the same.

speaker: POOLE
text: The restaurant industry has been seeing that.

speaker: POOLE
text: A contact with a major software firm is pretty optimistic.

speaker: POOLE
text: PC sales are running at or above expectation.

speaker: POOLE
text: My contact pointed out particularly that the quality of receivables has actually improved.

speaker: POOLE
text: They’re not seeing any problem with collecting on the software that they sell, and 94 percent of the customers are current on making payments.

speaker: POOLE
text: Even that is something of an underestimate because a lot of purchasers initiate the payment at the end of a thirty-day due period, and so the payment doesn’t come for another couple of days, despite our brilliant electronic clearing of payments.

speaker: POOLE
