text: A comment about the housing industry: Obviously the subprime issue is going to have a relatively permanent effect.

speaker: POOLE
text: It is just changing the characteristic of this industry.

speaker: POOLE
text: Underwriting was too lax, and that is changing.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think it is somewhat surprising that the builders have not scaled back more quickly—that they continue to sit on such a large inventory.

speaker: POOLE
text: Part of the reason is that, once a builder has started a development and has put all the infrastructure in place—the roads, the sewers, the water, and all of that—the only way to get anything out of that investment is to complete the subdivision.

speaker: POOLE
text: In addition, a subdivision that stops is a bad signal for prospective buyers because they don’t want to move into something that is sitting there mostly idle.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I think the builders have an intense interest in trying to complete these projects.

speaker: POOLE
text: But what that means, of course, is that, as they complete those projects, they are not initiating a lot because they’re taking, as Richard pointed out, some pretty big price concessions in many cases, and so they are probably not going to be initiating as many projects in the future.

speaker: POOLE
text: My own bet is that the financial market upset is not going to change fundamentally what’s going on in the real economy.

speaker: POOLE
text: First of all, bank capital is not impaired.

speaker: POOLE
text: So unlike in some past cases, when losses on real estate impaired bank capital and thus affected the lending in areas that had nothing to do with real estate, I don’t think that’s the case this time.

speaker: POOLE
text: Second, the fact that some LBO deals fall through isn’t going to change what those companies are producing.

speaker: POOLE
text: The fact that the ownership hasn’t changed doesn’t change the company’s profit-maximizing level of production in the short run.

speaker: POOLE
text: Obviously, that could change, but it seems to me that the best information that we now have is that this financial market upset is going to settle out and not have major repercussions on the real economy, putting the housing part aside.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the Fifth District we continue to see moderate economic growth, though it has been uneven across sectors in recent weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Manufacturing activity rebounded somewhat in June and July after several months of weakness, with our indexes showing increases in new orders and shipments.

speaker: LACKER
text: Activity at District services firms advanced at a steady pace, with solid revenue growth and a broader pickup in hiring.

speaker: LACKER
text: The retail sector, however, has lost much of the momentum reported last month, as softness in big-ticket categories continues to constrain revenue growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the employment front, District labor markets are increasingly taut, given steady hiring activity and slower labor force growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: In addition, in contrast to the Eighth Federal Reserve District, contacts continue to report rising wage pressures and difficulty finding qualified workers.

speaker: LACKER
text: Housing markets remain weak across much of the District.

speaker: LACKER
text: However, commercial real estate activity remains healthy, with steady demand reported for office and industrial space.

speaker: LACKER
text: Some contacts, however, have expressed concern about slower activity in the retail segment of that market.

speaker: LACKER
text: Turning to prices, our July surveys indicate increased inflation pressures.

speaker: LACKER
text: The average current rate of increase of manufacturers’ prices has moved up for both raw materials and finished goods over the past few months, reversing the decline seen earlier this year.

speaker: LACKER
text: Price pressures on the services side have picked up as well, though expectations for future prices eased somewhat in the July report.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the national level, we continued to receive fairly good news on inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: After annualized rates of monthly core PCE inflation above 2 percent at the beginning of the year, we’ve now had four months of readings below 2.

speaker: LACKER
text: But there are still abundant reasons for caution, as President Moskow, for example, noted.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’ll mention the Greenbook, which cites transitory factors—apparel and owners’ equivalent rent, for instance—that have contributed to the recent moderation.

speaker: LACKER
text: The passing of these damping forces could well push core inflation back up in the near term.

speaker: LACKER
text: So although I think we have reason to take some comfort from recent inflation numbers, and I do, I want to wait to see more evidence, especially as growth moves back toward trend.

speaker: LACKER
text: I still think the prospects for a return to trend growth are reasonably good, and my assessment of trend is still a bit higher than the Greenbook’s, in part because I’ve not revised my estimate of productivity growth much in response to the GDP revisions.

speaker: LACKER
text: Obviously, there are downside risks to be concerned about, and financial market activity since the last meeting obviously raises some concerns.

speaker: LACKER
text: As far as we can tell at this point, the heightened turbulence of the past month is all pretty closely related to subprime and nontraditional mortgages and the leveraged financing of private equity buyouts in the corporate sector.

speaker: LACKER
text: These two market segments are relatively new, and they represent the latest manifestation of the broad, ongoing wave of financial innovation that we’ve been seeing over the past few decades.

speaker: LACKER
text: Because these two markets are so young, one would expect participants’ risk assessments to be more uncertain and thus be more sensitive to what is learned from market events and incoming news.

speaker: LACKER
text: That said, developments in the past month have certainly been quite dramatic, and it looks less like rapid learning than it does rapid unlearning of what was previously viewed as known—although that, too, is of course a form of learning.

speaker: LACKER
text: The implication of these revised risk assessments for the economic outlook and for policy depend on whether they affect business investment or household spending on consumption or new housing.

speaker: LACKER
text: At this point the answer to that question is not yet clear, but it’s worth noting that, by many measures, corporate credit quality seems to remain pretty good by historical standards, and the buyout movement, as President Poole just noted, seems to have been more about restructuring liabilities and governance arrangements and less about funding capital spending.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it’s not obvious why there should be dramatic effects on business investment.

speaker: LACKER
text: PCE was fairly soft last quarter, and this softness could be a harbinger of more-sustained weakness.

speaker: LACKER
text: The second-quarter softness may well be a one-time phenomenon, however, reflecting both the sharp rise in gasoline prices in the first five months of the year and some payback from the strong spending growth in Q4 and Q1.

speaker: LACKER
text: Moreover, the outlook for household income looks pretty good, with labor market conditions fairly firm and consumption gains showing no sign of slowing down.

speaker: LACKER
text: In addition, household net worth is coming off a relatively high base.

speaker: LACKER
text: Neither of these fundamentals seems likely to be seriously threatened by the repricing that’s in train.

speaker: LACKER
text: Housing, on the other hand, continues to be the predominant area of concern regarding real spending, and financial market developments have only heightened that concern.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Greenbook paints a fairly pessimistic picture.

speaker: LACKER
text: The decline in residential investment accelerates over the remainder of year and continues into next, and the inclusion of three “greater housing correction” alternative scenarios suggests that the staff is especially concerned, justifiably so in my view, with the downside risk to their outlook.

speaker: LACKER
text: But even though the housing market has definitely deteriorated, the outlook for housing is quite uncertain in my mind, and I continue to think that a more moderate decline is also possible and that housing could be somewhat less of a drag on growth than the Greenbook forecasts.

speaker: LACKER
text: At this point, however, the reassessment under way in secondary markets regarding housing-related credits still has a way to go, and until that process plays out, it’s going to be hard to gauge the resulting magnitude of repricing at the retail level.

speaker: LACKER
text: About all I conclude at this point is that the outlook for housing is still awfully uncertain right now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The balance of risks has changed since our last meeting—significantly, in my view.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Overall spending by households and businesses is weaker.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Housing, of course, is significantly worse, and the underlying pace of productivity growth and potential growth seems lower.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In addition, financial market developments have deteriorated with a very broad based increase in risk premiums, decline in some asset prices, pockets of liquidity pressures, and some disruption in mortgage markets and high-yield corporate credit markets.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: These developments in financial markets, even though they represent a necessary adjustment, a generally healthy development, have the potential to cause substantial damage through the effects on asset prices, market liquidity, and credit; through the potential failure of more-consequential financial institutions; and through a general erosion of confidence among businesses and households.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If this situation were to materialize and these effects were to persist, they could have significant effects on the strength of aggregate demand going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The process now under way in financial markets could take some time to resolve, and finding a new balance could take a while.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have modified our forecast in ways similar to the changes to the Greenbook.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have a slightly weaker second half of ’07 and a slightly lower estimate of growth in ’08 and ’09, reflecting a downwardly revised estimate of potential growth.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our growth numbers for ’07, ’08, and ’09 look roughly like 2½ rising to 2¾ percent.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our inflation forecast is essentially unchanged, with core PCE inflation moderating to slightly under 2 percent over the forecast period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our differences with the Greenbook are not trivial, but they seem well within the somewhat greater uncertainty we now face about the outlook for growth.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The negative skew in our view of the risks to the outlook suggests a somewhat downward slope to the path of the fed funds rate going forward, to the appropriate stance of monetary policy, rather than the flat path assumed by the Greenbook.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So even if financial market conditions stabilize and credit markets, particularly the mortgage markets, find equilibrium relatively soon and start to open up again, the growth risks have shifted a bit more to the downside around the lower expected path.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In contrast, if the disruption in credit markets persists and liquidity markets are further impaired, then we face the prospect of a significantly weaker path to aggregate demand.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Inflation risks in our view, however, remain slightly tilted to the upside, but these types of risk are very different.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The inflation risks are modest and manageable.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We characterize them as skewed to the upside in part because of the differences across the Committee as to our desired individual long-run views about the inflation level, in part because of our differences as to what’s an acceptable period for bringing core inflation down to that objective, and in part because of different views about the structure of inflation dynamics in this economy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The risks to markets and ultimately to growth are very different.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There’s a much longer negative tail in terms of the range of potential outcomes, and those risks are going to be harder for us to manage, partly because they depend on confidence.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Because of these differences, I think it’s hard to counterpoise these two risks against each other and assess the balance between them.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course, as always, we should weigh each by their probability, their effects, and our capacity to manage those effects.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that the probability of a bad inflation outcome has diminished from what we would have said two quarters ago and the probability of an adverse growth outcome has increased.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As I said, the latter risk is interesting and complicated in part because it might be harder to manage.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I want to make two points in this regard.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: First, a number of you have said that we want to see more evidence of adverse effects on aggregate demand before we change our view about the appropriate path of monetary policy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t really think that’s the right way to think about this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we took that approach, we’d inevitably be too late.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just as we think about inflation risks by looking forward and looking at expectations, we need to be forward looking and thinking about the potential implications of these dynamics of financial markets on the growth outlook.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The information we have now about what’s happening in markets and about the implications for credit markets and ultimately for confidence and demand is very stale and uneven.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My second observation about this challenge is that what makes it hard is partly that you are seeing a combination of things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You are seeing a loss of confidence in the capacity of investors to assess underlying risk in mortgage markets in part because of uncertainty about what housing prices are going to do and in part because of uncertainty about correlations in losses across households.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You are also seeing a collapse in confidence, as Bill described it, in how to value complex structured credit products, probably from the loss of faith in ratings and from the changes ahead in ratings methodology and in actual ratings.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You’re also seeing the difficulties that investors and counterparties now have in evaluating the risk in exposure to financial counterparties, and you’re seeing in some ways reflecting all of this a diminished willingness to finance what’s relatively high quality paper.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We live in a system in which risk has been transferred much more broadly, but a lot of that risk has gone to leveraged funds that have much less capacity to absorb this kind of shock without facing a lot of liquidity pressures.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The combination of these things means that you’re seeing some impairment in the natural dynamic by which, when prices adjust, you have new people coming in willing to buy at those low prices.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But these challenges in information and in diagnosing what’s happening in markets mean that the process is not working as quickly as you might have thought in mortgages and in high-yield corporate credit.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You can see this sort of skew in the risks reflected, I think sensibly, in the change of market expectations about the fed funds rate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You can see this balance in the distribution that Bill described, where you see a sharply negative skew in expectations about the path on the downside, and you see that come also in the context of relative stability of inflation expectations.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That shift of mean expectations, in the distribution, does not come with any sense that the consequence might be some erosion in confidence about our capacity to keep inflation expectations down.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Now, in terms of policy, I personally wouldn’t want to lean against the change in market expectations that we’ve seen so far, even though it has moved a long way in a short time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s really important to give ourselves more flexibility than we now have to respond to what could be a rapidly deteriorating overall environment; that’s just pragmatically essential, given that the range of foreseeable monetary policy actions we’re likely to confront has broadened very substantially relative to where we were a quarter ago.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The challenge, of course, is to figure out a way to acknowledge and to show some awareness of these changes in market dynamics without feeding the concern, without overreacting, about underlying strength in the fundamentals of the economy as a whole or in the financial system.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That is a difficult balance, but I think it requires some softening of the asymmetry in our assessment of the balance of risks now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: An advertisement in response to a bunch of points made so far, including by President Fisher—the Morning Call that Bill Dudley’s staff runs from New York is a very good, fairly textured prism of what’s happening across these markets.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: They do a good job of trying to integrate a bunch of the anecdotes and the facts, and it’s the most efficient device any of us have to check in about that evolving balance.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It won’t satisfy everybody’s demand to have as much information as is out there, but it’s a fairly efficient way to get a pretty good picture, and so I commend that to you.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s a really good, thoughtful, and reasonably deep collection of wisdom in the markets today.

speaker: KOHN
text: Building on what the Vice Chairman just said, I have been listening in on that Morning Call.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’ve found it very useful, and it’s certainly an opportunity to ask questions if you have them.

speaker: KOHN
text: My forecast for the most likely outcome for output over the next few years is close to that of the staff—growth a little below potential for a few quarters, held down by the housing correction, and the unemployment rate rising a little further.

speaker: KOHN
text: Although some recent data for housing, consumption, and capital spending have been a bit to the soft side, we need to view those data against the background of a lower path for potential GDP and recall the tendency we’ve seen over the past several quarters for short runs of data that are a little hotter or a little cooler than we expected.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think this is sort of what it feels like when the economy is running at about 2 percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: I see a number of reasons to think that moderate growth remains the most likely outcome going forward.

speaker: KOHN
text: First, as President Stern has stressed from time to time, is the natural resilience of the economy, its tendency to grow near potential unless something is pushing it one way or another.

speaker: KOHN
text: If anything, this resilience has probably increased over the past couple of decades, reflecting more- flexible labor and product markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: Second, global growth remains strong, supporting the growth of exports.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think this growth should be undermined by the fact that some unknown quantity of losses in the U.S. mortgage market is being absorbed by investors overseas, and the recent declines in the dollar will reinforce the effects of good foreign demand for U.S. goods and services.

speaker: KOHN
text: Third, the most likely factor to throw the economy off its potential is the financial markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: My most likely forecast assumed that the credit markets would begin to settle down over coming weeks with some, but limited, net tightening of conditions.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’ll return to the subject in a bit, but my outlook in this regard does rest fundamentally on the very strong financial condition of the nonfinancial business sector and commercial banks and my expectation that most households accounting for the vast bulk of consumer spending will not find credit availability newly constrained.

speaker: KOHN
text: Finally, a resumption of growth in consumption should be supported by moderate growth in jobs and household income as the rebound in productivity is limited by the slower path for trend productivity and as income shares shift a little toward labor.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also assumed that households would not face a repeat of the rise in gasoline prices that has taken something out of recent consumption demand.

speaker: KOHN
text: Then moderate growth in consumption along with good export markets should, in turn, support business investment spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: I expect this path for output to be associated with core inflation remaining in the neighborhood of 2 percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: If energy prices follow the path in futures markets, total inflation would come down to 2 percent as well.

speaker: KOHN
text: Basically I don’t see anything in my central tendency forecast for the economy that would push inflation very much one way or another.

speaker: KOHN
text: The economy produces around its long-run potential.

speaker: KOHN
text: My NAIRU was 4¾ percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: Inflation expectations as best we can judge are anchored at something like 2 percent PCE inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m encouraged that the most recent data on prices have tended to confirm that core inflation remains fairly low.

speaker: KOHN
text: Most measures of compensation also do not show a marked acceleration that might be associated with producing appreciably beyond the economy’s sustainable level of production.

speaker: KOHN
text: Risks around my inflation forecast remain to the upside, provided that output follows my most likely path.

speaker: KOHN
text: The recent run-up in energy prices could still feed through to expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: The damped increase in productivity growth implies greater pressure on business costs and margins.

speaker: KOHN
text: Historically, nominal wages have tended to respond more sluggishly to changes in trend productivity than do prices, and this could be especially the circumstance when workers have seen real incomes held down by higher energy prices and business profit margins have been high.

speaker: KOHN
text: At the same time, like many around this table, I think that the downside risks around the forecast of moderate growth and production going forward have increased.

speaker: KOHN
text: For some time I thought that the risk of a shortfall from our central tendency outweighed the risk of an overshoot, mainly centered on housing and consumption.

speaker: KOHN
text: But the financial developments of the last intermeeting period have appreciably increased those risks.

speaker: KOHN
text: As many have remarked, and Bill said so nicely, problems have spread from the subprime sector to a good part of the mortgage market more generally, including a severe restriction on securitization of nonconforming mortgages.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some business credit has been affected.

speaker: KOHN
text: Spread are widening across a broad array of instruments and ratings.

speaker: KOHN
text: This has occurred in an atmosphere of greatly increased volatility and uncertainty, partly related to the questions about the pricing of complex structured credits that weren’t well understood and compounded by a loss of confidence in the rating agencies.

speaker: KOHN
text: The uncertainty is also a reflection of the perception that activity and prices in the housing market have not yet shown any signs of beginning to stabilize.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that we need to keep our focus on the effects of these developments and the financial markets on the economy, not on the distribution of wealth in the financial sector.

speaker: KOHN
text: The relationship of financial markets to real activity is multifaceted, not easily modeled with interest rates and stock prices, especially when markets are reconsidering risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: Tightening nonprice terms of lending, the reduced availability of credit, and simply the pervasive sense of uncertainty about the price of assets and cash flows can also affect spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: In such an environment, it wouldn’t be surprising if businesses and households postponed capital investments.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that this reassessment is a fundamentally healthy but somewhat messy correction to more-sustainable term and risk premiums.

speaker: KOHN
text: The most likely outcome is that it will be limited in duration and effect, and that’s what I assume for my forecast.

speaker: KOHN
text: Well-capitalized banks and opportunistic investors will come in and fill the gap, restoring credit flows to nonfinancial businesses and to the vast majority of households that can service their debts.

speaker: KOHN
text: In the end, credit conditions will be tighter than they were a little while ago, for the most part justifiably so, and the effect on output will probably not be very large.

speaker: KOHN
text: To be sure, the latest episode comes on top of a rise in term premiums over the May to June intermeeting period.

speaker: KOHN
text: As a consequence, financial conditions have tightened noticeably in the past few months, even abstracting from market disruptions of the last week.

speaker: KOHN
text: The federal funds rate has been as high as it has been in part to offset the accommodative effects of low volatility and tight term and credit premiums.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that, even in the relatively benign adjustment scenario, we’ll need to look at whether that rate is still sufficiently supportive of economic activity.

speaker: KOHN
text: But in the circumstances—that is, the benign adjustment—that reassessment can await further information about aggregate demand and further assurance that inflation will remain low.

speaker: KOHN
text: I assumed an easing of policy in 2008 and 2009 in my projections to take account of this.

speaker: KOHN
text: But we can’t know how the market situation will evolve.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also believe that there’s a non-negligible chance of a prolonged and very messy adjustment period that would feed back substantially on confidence, wealth, and spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: With the rating agencies discredited and markets vulnerable to adverse news on the economy, the period of unusual uncertainty could be prolonged.

speaker: KOHN
text: The greatest risk is in the household sector, where uncertainty about valuations of mortgages could continue to feed back on credit availability, housing demand, and prices in a self-reinforcing cycle.

speaker: KOHN
text: Moreover, as lenders and borrowers revise assumptions about house prices even further, credit from home equity lines of credit and mortgage refinancings will become even less available and more expensive, putting to the test the hypothesis that I have been working under—that the feedback from housing on consumption can be approximated by a wealth effect, not something more serious working through housing equity withdrawal.

speaker: KOHN
text: As I noted, I don’t think this is the most likely outcome, but this tail of distribution is a lot fatter than it was only a month or so ago.

speaker: WARSH
text: As many of us have discussed around this table and many of you already mentioned today, it has finally happened.

speaker: WARSH
text: Per earlier discussions, the much-anticipated repricing of risk is upon us, and I think what we all have quickly recognized, then and now, is that the diagnosis was the easy part.

speaker: WARSH
text: More difficult is to figure when the symptoms would manifest themselves; harder still is to understand the second- and third-order consequences; and perhaps most difficult is to determine whether any treatment is needed or whether, as the Hippocratic oath suggests, the patient will recover on its own.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even orderly repricings have fat tails, as Governor Kohn mentioned, and what we find in the marketplace is complacency replaced very quickly by deep concern.

speaker: WARSH
text: Certainly, this recent market turmoil looks particularly pronounced in contrast to previous periods when trees appeared to grow to the sky and markets were priced for perfection in a world that seemed to most of us to be decidedly imperfect.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me discuss two distinct matters—first, the state of the financial markets, building on the presentation from Bill, Tim, and others, and then the harder part, the impact on the broader economy—before trying to summarize the situation.

speaker: WARSH
text: The financial markets have really provided wind at the back of the broader economy throughout this most recent period, even until a month ago.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the open question, and the hardest, is whether those financial markets will prove sufficiently resilient—that is, whether the underlying shocks to the economy that might occur are exacerbated by this financial market situation or whether the worst of the outcomes are made less severe by the financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: Perhaps it is best to review the dynamics of different asset markets to assess their implications for credit availability during the forecast period.

speaker: WARSH
text: The threat is that these different asset classes increasingly look correlated, particularly in times of distress.

speaker: WARSH
text: Certainly, the events of recent weeks culminating in trading late Thursday and Friday of last week are troubling, driven by a combination of factors: first, symbolized perhaps by one financial institution that has unwittingly called its own liquidity into some question; second, a function of a reduction in confidence in markets themselves—a pullback in liquidity—with considerably less trust in underlying valuations, underlying collateral, and the underlying structure of markets themselves; and third, an expectation, at least in the mortgage markets, that there is still another leg down and so one way bets, at least for a period, appear insufficient to bring other opportunistic capital in at this point.

speaker: WARSH
text: The pullback was manifested in the difficulty of rolling over extendable commercial paper, as Bill and others have said, a lack of bid for anything mortgage related, a lack of trust in credit ratings, and a fear of using financial institutions as counterparties.

speaker: WARSH
text: The next period in my judgment holds out some promise, but not a guarantee, of opportunistic capital.

speaker: WARSH
text: Certainly, there are big fund raisings by investment banks and other private pools of capital at remarkable leverage levels, giving the potential that the pools of liquidity that are on the sidelines could quickly find their way back into the game.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me now turn to different asset markets to try to assess when we will know how they will figure themselves out and make sure that we are able to get some judgments before it is too late.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I will spend a moment on the bank and leveraged-loan markets, a couple of moments on the subprime market, and another moment on a third bucket of assets, which might be everything else, as we are trying to figure out whether there is real spreading.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, in the bank and leveraged-loan market, the volume of loans, as many of you know, is somewhere between $220 billion and $320 billion of committed capital in the pipeline.

speaker: WARSH
text: The underlying credits still appear quite strong, and I will tell you that I have a reasonably high degree of confidence that, in spite of the distress, these markets should work themselves out between now and the next FOMC meeting.

speaker: WARSH
text: We certainly won’t see any return to the markets that people have gotten used to over the past several months and years, but I would be surprised if we didn’t see opportunistic capital coming into these markets and bidding prices.

speaker: WARSH
text: Just to give you some idea, off that denominator of capital committed, we might see losses on the order of $30 billion or $50 billion.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say that’s a fairly conservative estimate.

speaker: WARSH
text: Bank debt, which is the most secured, might have discounts of 3 to 5 percent, should bids find their way into the market in the coming days; leveraged loans and high yields, discounts of about 10 percent; and second lien mortgages, discounts of 15 to 20 percent.

speaker: WARSH
text: Almost all of these are largely related to risk premiums, not credit quality.

speaker: WARSH
text: Real money is still in these businesses.

speaker: WARSH
text: Some of the hot money that was discussed earlier, some of these CLO buyers, are no doubt gone for some time.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the most encouraging thing is the new funds that have begun capital-raising campaigns, even over the past weekend, looking to buy the distressed securities, market-force the commercial institutions that have been having it on their books, and mark it to market.

speaker: WARSH
text: Remarkably, many of the same commercial banks are prepared to stand behind these new leveraged investments with leverage of about 4 to 1.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I would expect that market to increase pretty quickly.

speaker: WARSH
text: Market functioning there is thus, in my judgment, likely to improve.

speaker: WARSH
text: Some deals are certainly likely to blow up, relieving some of these banks of their commitments.

speaker: WARSH
text: But in this market, because there are multiple gatekeepers and because valuing the underlying credit strikes me as not that time-intensive or taxing a process, it is likely in my judgment that, come fall, we will come to some new equilibrium.

speaker: WARSH
text: I can be far less confident, however, about the subprime mortgage market.

speaker: WARSH
text: My base case assessment there has a much lower confidence level, both in terms of timing and in terms of outcome.

speaker: WARSH
text: The subprime market has about $1.4 trillion in outstandings, and there is considerably less certainty about the underlying credit.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is harder to measure and appraise the underlying pools.

speaker: WARSH
text: Recovery rates will be still harder to find.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a final note, which might have struck the markets last week, apparently more fraud is endemic to these pools, making valuation increasingly difficult.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a result, I am less comfortable about suggesting what the underlying losses might be.

speaker: WARSH
text: They might be $100 billion.

speaker: WARSH
text: They could be considerably more.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m also less confident that there will be opportunistic capital coming back to these markets over the next thirty or sixty days.

speaker: WARSH
text: With another leg down, it could take considerably longer.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a result, I am quite a bit less confident that the market functioning will return as rapidly as we would hope.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am more concerned that, unlike the multiple gatekeepers we find in the leveraged-loan markets, for those that relied on the single gatekeepers, the credit-rating agencies, given that their credibility has been shot, it is much harder to see that this market will unwind itself in a rather calm and comforting environment, at least over the balance of 2007.

speaker: WARSH
text: The final set of asset markets I’d speak a moment about is “everything else.” What about everything else that is subject to structured products?

speaker: WARSH
text: What about everything else that is subject to complex financial instruments?

speaker: WARSH
text: Some questions arose late last week about the market integrity regarding those.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think it is just too hard to judge how that is going to work out.

speaker: WARSH
text: We are seeing losses showing up in some very unlikely places.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’d like to say that what we have witnessed over the past week is transitory, but for that set of asset markets, it is probably hardest for me to come to a broader judgment.

speaker: WARSH
text: So what are the effects, then, on the broader economy?

speaker: WARSH
text: I agree with the point that President Stern made earlier that this judgment is extremely hard to make.

speaker: WARSH
text: I also agree with Governor Kohn’s judgment that there is a very real downside risk if some of these financial market turmoil issues persist.

speaker: WARSH
text: If I look at some of the credit channels and at financial intermediaries and ask whether they are under stress, I see more dispersion of risk among similarly situated institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: Some commercial banks may well be under more distress than others.

speaker: WARSH
text: I have no doubt that some investment banks are under more distress than others.

speaker: WARSH
text: We see some of this dispersion in credit default swaps and some of it in equity prices, but my sense is that the underlying fundamentals of their core businesses are very different from each other and from their competitors than they’ve been at any point in this cycle.

speaker: WARSH
text: For some of them to take losses on their own balance sheets of $3 billion, $4 billion, or $5 billion, as an investment bank, might not be hard to do when many of them have been picking up market share and using their own proprietary trading and agency businesses to steal customers and revenue from others.

speaker: WARSH
text: But for the balance, I think it is unclear how it is going to result.

speaker: WARSH
text: With many of the investment banks’ quarters ending in August, the markets are going to put genuine pressure on them to come clean with their losses.

speaker: WARSH
text: I expect most, if not all, of them to do so.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think come mid- September we’ll have a clearer sense of what their own marked-to-market models suggest.

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, not principally their regulators but I suspect the markets are going to push them to come clean with what their losses are.

speaker: WARSH
text: Large financial institutions I would expect, though with less confidence, to take writedowns of their portfolios of leveraged loans and writedowns to some extent of their mortgage products to try to assure the investing community of their financial positions.

speaker: WARSH
text: I hope that the process would work out this fall, but as I mentioned, I’m less comfortable that we’re going to get that kind of transparency with the regulated commercial banks than with some others.

speaker: WARSH
text: Private pools of capital are also undergoing a real shakeout.

speaker: WARSH
text: For those with liquidity pressures, which will tend not to be the largest hedge funds or private equity funds, we will read about their problems, and we will read about their closings, over the coming weeks and months.

speaker: WARSH
text: The good news is that the largest among them have used the period of strong liquidity over the past year to more or less have quasi-permanent capital to term out their loans and provide capital so that they could take advantage in this period.

speaker: WARSH
text: I understand that there has been very little spike in margin calls where most of the assets rest in the hedge fund community.

speaker: WARSH
text: So for many of us who have talked about hedge funds bringing resilience to these markets, this is really a time of testing.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the early news for the largest among them is quite positive.

speaker: WARSH
text: Many of you have talked about what the other transmission mechanisms are for having GDP effects.

speaker: WARSH
text: The wealth effect is real.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have lost about $1 trillion in market capital in the past twenty trading days, and that can’t be discounted.

speaker: WARSH
text: Questions about board room confidence and cap-ex in the second half of this year are equally real.

speaker: WARSH
text: My sense is that we are going to finally use that excess cash on balance sheets that many of us have long talked about.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, with respect to consumer confidence, though I think the recent data suggest that it’s positive, I suspect that the next set of data we get will show a retreat from those numbers.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is very hard to judge how real consumers are going to react here.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me make two final comments.

speaker: WARSH
text: Opportunistic capital is a key here to a smooth transition.

speaker: WARSH
text: It’s key to ensuring that what happened in the financial markets doesn’t seep its way into the real economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: Of the equity investors that were using loose credit markets to get equity returns, the most sophisticated are focusing on and looking for equity returns in the debt markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: So many investors previously investing in equity are now looking to the debt markets, where they see a risk-reward tradeoff that is better than it has been in a long time.

speaker: WARSH
text: That gives me some confidence that opportunistic capital will come back to some of these markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: That said, rating- sensitive buyers will no doubt pull back given that ratings are less authoritative.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I will end where I began, which is looking at economic fundamentals.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think Governor Kohn talked about how the capital markets, the financial markets, and the labor markets have proven to be absolutely core to the resilience of the broader economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: To the extent that there is now an unfortunate timing between weakness in the financial markets and some potential weakness in underlying credit, we can rely less on the financial markets to come to the rescue, should that circumstance occur.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I was looking back at my notes of the past few meetings and noted that the position we are in is a bit like that in the May meeting, at least the way in which people are characterizing things—that economic fundamentals still suggest moderate growth for the intermediate term but that uncertainty has gone up dramatically.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Then, in the June meeting, we said that uncertainty went down, and now we’re saying that uncertainty has gone up again.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So we seem to have a little volatility just like the markets do, but obviously, we are responding to what the markets are doing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Clearly, there are key downside risks.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The risk that I’ve mentioned many times before that concerns me and that we now have more data on is productivity and potential growth.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With the revisions since ’03, the compounded growth rate of productivity is down to 1.4 percent from 1.8 percent.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The revision is fairly significant over this period.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I am not ready to go quite as far as the Greenbook has gone in marking down potential, but I do think that it is a real possibility, and it is very closely linked to my concerns about investment, which obviously the financial market volatility has affected.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Orders and shipments of durable goods have been a bit choppy, and we haven’t seen the kind of rise that we would expect, given the balance sheets and given all the other sorts of strength that we would otherwise see in the economy.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Nonresidential investment has been strong, and there is still some strength in mining and drilling, but I have a lot of concerns outside that area.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As a number of people have mentioned, there is little change in the actual cost of capital, even though spreads have risen, because the Treasuries have gone down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But with more uncertainty and more volatility, as Governor Warsh and others have mentioned, undoubtedly that is going to weigh heavily in the board room.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is going to weigh heavily on capital expenditure plans.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So all other things being equal, businesses are likely to be a bit more cautious going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But that caution with respect to investment and the slowing of the investment recovery make it harder to be optimistic about a rebound in productivity growth.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So that’s something that I watch very closely because I think it is a very, very important effect.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On the consumption-saving balance, certainly we still have very robust labor markets— average growth of 120,000 private-sector jobs per month this year, which is a step down from last year but still a robust level.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have a transition from a sort of cushion of the strong equity market offsetting the negative wealth effect in the housing market.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now, if they become more correlated—and, in particular, more correlated and both go down—that obviously would raise some concerns about slowing consumption growth and increasing saving.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I think that is something to be very mindful of.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With respect to housing and financial markets, in the senior loan officer survey with respect to mortgages, when you drill down into it, both in April and in July more than 50 percent of the senior loan officers reported that they are tightening credit standards for subprime, and about 15 percent are for prime.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The depository institutions are pulling back, and we have certainly heard reports that some of the large institutions are no longer offering 2/28s or 3/27s.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There has also been a tightening outside the depository institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The reason for part of the tightening is that some of the mortgage providers are simply no longer there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have had dozens of smaller providers of credit go out of business, and the ones that are still there are obviously changing their underwriting standards.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As President Rosengren mentioned, we are seeing some questions about the originate-to-distribute model.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We are also seeing volatility on the financial market side.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But part of that volatility, as a number of people have expressed, is about concerns about what is going into those securities in the originate-to- distribute model.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That may raise some questions in the long run about how much we’re going to see this market come back.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I share Governor Warsh’s concerns, not only from the point of view of the financial markets but also regarding the structure of mortgage markets—that we may be seeing a little less of that kind of structure than we have seen in the past.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So that, combined with the tightening of standards more broadly, may make financing more difficult to get.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This, of course, is occurring in many parts of the country—not all parts but many parts—where housing inventories are very high and in some cases are still rising.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, that puts a lot more pressure on the housing market, and I think the drag from the housing market, as many of you said, is likely to continue.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Fortunately, the financial market volatility is coming at a time of relative strength in corporate balance sheets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Debt-to-asset ratios have been declining, and liquid assets as a percentage of total assets have been high.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That provides much more of a cushion, much more insurance.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As President Poole mentioned, the banking system is in a dramatically different state from when we had challenges before in the housing market or major challenges in financial markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The major banks have very high, relative to historical trends, capital-to-asset ratios in excess of the required minimums.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They have been very, very profitable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If you look at the largest banks—and I was just looking at some that were most involved in the leveraged-loan market—they each have tier 1 capital on the order of $80 billion to $90 billion.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The earnings for each over the last year are $25 billion to $35 billion.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There is also a lot of discussion of the amount of highly leveraged loans in the pipeline—on the order of $300 billion.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But unless they have to take losses on that $300 billion, which is not going to happen, they have very thick capital cushions and very high earnings.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So at least for the foreseeable future, this will just be more a challenge to their earnings than a challenge to capital.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That is extremely important because the banking system can provide a critical automatic stabilizing mechanism, as it did in 1998, when there are liquidity challenges.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In 1998 we had the Asian crisis that spread to Latin America, then the Russian crisis, and LTCM.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There were some parallels to what we are seeing now: Risk spreads were rising very dramatically after a period of near-record low levels, and we saw the yields on Treasuries go down quite a bit because that’s where people were going.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But what was happening in the system was that people were pulling money out of various funds and instruments and putting it into the banking system.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So the banks do act as liquidity providers and liquidity insurers, and I think we’re starting to see a bit of that now with people pulling out of some of these instruments and so more is flowing into the banks.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s a little early to tell.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We haven’t gotten enough data on that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But anecdotal reports are consistent with exactly what happened in 1998.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As people need an alternative to commercial paper or other short-term sources of credit, it can be very helpful that the banking system will have more liquid resources to do that, and obviously it’s a strong capital environment.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, as Governor Warsh mentioned, there are more large private pools of capital to step in to bid for the LTCMs, if such things happen.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: When we look back to LTCM, only one offer was on the table— from Warren Buffett—and there were a lot of questions about how serious that offer would be.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now a number of players have the wherewithal to be the equivalent of that in this market, which has the potential to be quite helpful.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There are obviously more potential downside risks, but a lot of stability exists in the banking system to deal with some of these risks and, given the strength of the balance sheets, should be helpful in the short or the intermediate run.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With respect to inflation, as many people have mentioned, a number of risks are still skewed to the upside, with robust global growth, potential pass-through, some previous high energy prices, and a lower dollar.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I still think that there is much more of a potential upside skew to inflation than a downside skew.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Basically, I would start taking my first steps, but just very first steps, a little more toward a balance of risk because of the greater downside to growth.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Although there are still upside risks to inflation, as Vice Chairman Geithner mentioned, overall we might want to think of moving a little more toward a greater balance of risk but still with a predominant concern for inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Well, except for the fact that we have had a benchmarking of potential GDP downward and greater weakness in housing, my forecast is basically similar to my forecast at the last FOMC meeting and is consistent with the Greenbook forecast—that we would have a return to trend growth a bit later than we had expected but by mid-2008 and 2009.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In regard to the issue of inflation, let me just provide a little information on the model that I’m thinking about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You know that I think a key driver of inflation, of course, is inflation expectations, and that there are good arguments to say that they are grounded around 2 percent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have been seeing numbers continually coming in that are very consistent with that, which gives me more and more confidence that, in fact, inflation is gravitating strongly to this 2 percent level.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I want to talk a bit about the issue of output gaps because I think that it is important, even if you think that inflation expectations are extremely important, not to have a deus ex machina view of the inflation process, which is that inflation is caused by expected inflation and then where does that come from?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think that resource utilization is important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, the problem is that what is really important is not just current resource utilization, which is what we tend to put in our econometric specifications, but also the future expected path of resource utilization and output gaps.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, one problem here is that it is hard to measure.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also, if you are doing monetary policy right, then there is an expectation that you are going to do the right things to eliminate those output gaps.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, that is exactly what is in our forecast and exactly what our policies have been doing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So one reason I think, in the current juncture, that it is not critical to talk about output gaps a whole lot is that basically we are doing the right thing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That context gives me further reason for saying, given our forecast, that a 2 percent inflation number is where we are heading, just not now, and that the trend is solidly in place.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we are going to stay there for the foreseeable future, unless we screw up somehow, and we are not going to do that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One key point that makes me a little different from the Committee on inflation is that I do not see the upside risks as being greater than the downside risks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I really do see the risks as being quite balanced on inflation—again around this 2 percent number.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Yes, we do have some temporarily good news, and it is going to be unraveled a bit, but it is still consistent with the 2 percent overall trend.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In terms of output gaps and future expectations, I don’t see those getting people thinking that we’re going to have too tight resource utilization.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Let me turn to the issue of the financial markets because, obviously, that is the big gorilla sitting at the table.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t see what is happening now as a direct spillover from the subprime market.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is very consistent with the way that Bill was talking about this issue.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, the media are making the subprime market into the whole story, but I think it is just not the right story.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The subprime market is really a very small percentage of the total credit markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What I think is much more important is that people are questioning and reassessing the quality of the information that exists in financial markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The point of the subprime market is just that we now trust the credit-rating agencies less.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Basically what I think is happening in a way is quite a good thing: We were concerned that the markets were a little too optimistic, that there was too much opacity, and that people weren’t worried about it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Now, in fact, they are worried about it, and I think that is fundamentally a healthy situation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also, the parts of the market that are having the problem are the most opaque parts, it is not clear that they are particularly important to the things we really care about in terms of our policies, which is what will happen to aggregate demand and, therefore, to both inflation and output.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So at this point, I take the view that this could all end very well and could in the long run make the situation healthier, and this view is consistent with what Governor Kohn was pointing out.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I do worry that this reassessment could actually find more—what’s the right word?— skeletons in the closet or bad things happening than were expected.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In the past, we’ve seen that, when the quality of information gets questioned and people don’t think the marketplace is providing the right information, headwinds in the economy can become quite significant.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The most recent episode that I am thinking about, of course, is the episode of Enron and its aftermath, in which a key reason that the economy was so slow to recover was that the quality of information was impaired.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Then, people realized that the markets in fact did have some slight elements of financial instability—again, not too serious because the banking system was in such good shape.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We could have a similar situation occurring now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the sort of bad scenario that I see is an Enron-type scenario, not something much worse than that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we really have to keep on top of this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It means, I think, that there are greater downside risks to the forecast.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The survey of all of us indicates that people are now much more worried about downside risks than they are about upside risks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that is absolutely right, and, in fact, it could get a lot worse.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the way I would view the situation is that right now we should be pretty calm, but we want to monitor it very carefully and be ready for some potentially bad things to happen and just hope that they don’t.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The kind of scenario that we’re seeing in the Greenbook is one that is going to play out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you, and thank everyone.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I want to make a comment following the remarks of Governor Warsh and Governor Kroszner related to the calendar of potential market stabilization and the leveraged-loan market.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Both of you cited a backlog of $300 billion or something maybe slightly less than that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In one conversation I had, a market observer cited $470 billion and argued that it would take well beyond our September meeting, into October and November, before the market would clear in that particular part of the market.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So to connect this comment to Governor Geithner’s comment about maintaining some flexibility as we go into the fall and observe the markets, we have different estimates out there of how much backlog there is, and therefore we are likely to be still facing a great deal of uncertainty at our September meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you for the useful discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As usual, I am going to very briefly summarize what I heard.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will be happy to take any comments on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then I just want to make a few short points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, most of the key points have been made.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most participants expect growth to remain moderate over the forecast period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Despite lower household wealth resulting from weaker house and stock prices, consumption is likely to continue to grow as labor markets remain strong, real incomes increase, and gasoline prices moderate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Business investment should also grow moderately, although lower productivity and higher volatility could be drags on investment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Commercial real estate, in particular, may be slackening, but it retains good fundamentals.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The global economy is strong.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Industrial production is expanding at a reasonable pace.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, downside risks to growth were noted and perhaps received somewhat greater emphasis than at past meetings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most notably, housing appears to have weakened further, with sales of new and existing homes declining and inventories of unsold homes remaining high.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Homebuilders are experiencing financial strains, and there is downward pressure on home prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Spillover on consumption spending is not yet evident but is a possible risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In this regard, developments in credit markets received considerable attention.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the positive side, the repricing of risk and the reevaluation of underwriting standards seem appropriate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Liquidity still exists, credit is still being extended, and markets may work out their problems on their own.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A lower dollar and lower long-term Treasury rates also tend to offset financial tightening.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, higher risk premiums, tougher underwriting, and greater uncertainty may constrain housing and investment spending, leading to broader macroeconomic effects.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In more-pessimistic scenarios, dislocations in credit markets may last awhile and have a more substantial effect on credit availability and costs for businesses as well as for homebuyers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The possibility of contagion or severe financial instability also exists.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Many participants took note of the NIPA revisions and their implications for productivity growth, consumer saving, and unit labor costs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Meeting participants tend to put potential growth at higher rates than the Greenbook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Views on inflation are similar to those in previous meetings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Recent readings are viewed as reasonably favorable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, risks to inflation remain, including the possible reversal of transitory factors, tight labor markets, the high price of commodities, and higher unit labor costs resulting from lower productivity growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In all, the risks to inflation remain to the upside.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is my summary of what I heard.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m sure a lot more could be said.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let me just make a few additional comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There have been two very important developments since the last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first was the downward revision to the NIPA growth numbers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not obvious yet, of course, how much of that reflects a permanent decline in productivity and how much is transitory.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But certainly the best guess is that some of it is more long term in nature.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the main point I’d like to make is that the implications of this downward revision for inflation and monetary policy, except perhaps in the very short run, are not obvious.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The question is, What is the effect of the lower productivity growth on aggregate demand?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have examples of both types of phenomena.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the late ’90s, the pickup in productivity growth stimulated a very strong boom working through the stock market, consumption, and investment, so it led to an overheating economy, whereas in the earlier part of this decade, productivity growth picked up again but with weak aggregate demand.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We had a jobless recovery associated with that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it remains to be seen exactly how aggregate demand will respond to these developments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think that perhaps that in the very short run, given wage behavior and unit labor costs, if I had to choose, I would say that there is a slight bias toward higher inflation and tighter money.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the longer run, you would expect to see lower long-term rates because of slower growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second issue that has been widely discussed around the table is the financial market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is an interesting question why what looks like $100 billion or so of credit losses in the subprime market has been reflected in multiple trillions of dollars of losses in paper wealth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it’s an interesting question about what is going on there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there are three reasons that the financial markets have moved in the direction they have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, there has been a widespread repricing of risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is, obviously, a healthy development, particularly if there is no overshoot, which is a possibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But all else being equal, it is restrictive in terms of aggregate demand, and it makes our policy tighter than it otherwise would be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second reason for the changes in markets is that there has been a loss of confidence in the ability of investors to evaluate credit quality, particularly in structured products.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is an information fog, as I have heard it described.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is very much associated with the loss of confidence in the credit-rating agencies.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think one of the implications of this is that some of the innovations we have seen in financial markets are going to get rolled back.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are going to see more lending taken out of originate-to- distribute vehicles and put back onto portfolio balance sheets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the question is how much effect this adjustment process will have on the availability of credit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The third reason that I think the markets have reacted as much as they have is concern about the macroeconomic implications of what is happening.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, there is a fear that subprime losses, repricing, and the tightening of underwriting standards will have adverse effects on the housing market and will feed through to consumption, and we will get into a vicious cycle.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That certainly is reflected in the expectations of policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am not going to go through all the things that are going on now in the markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You have had very good reviews of that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, the markets right now are not functioning normally.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some conduits of credit are simply closed or frozen.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A number of companies are having difficulties with short-term finance, and so, per President Fisher’s comment, we are watching those things very carefully.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are prepared to use the tools that we have to address a short-term financial crisis, should one occur.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the longer term, of course, our policy should be directed not toward protecting financial investors but, rather, toward our macroeconomic objectives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then the question is what the long-run implications of the financial market adjustment will be for the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the odds are that the market will stabilize.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most credits are pretty strong except for parts of the mortgage market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But even so there will be notably tighter credit, tighter standards, probably some loss of confidence in markets, and higher risk premiums that will on net be restrictive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This restrictive effect could come in various magnitudes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It could be moderate, or it could be more severe, and we are just going to have to monitor how it adjusts over time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, there is a bit of a risk—and tail risk has been mentioned not only in a financial sense but also in the macro sense—that, if credit is severely restricted so that we get feedback from lower house prices, for example, into the financial markets, that situation would be difficult to deal with.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those are the two major issues that people have talked about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just very briefly on the overall assessment—on the output side, economic growth looks a little softer to me, mostly because of housing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are also some slightly worrying developments in terms of automobile demand, which suggest some weakening in consumer spending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But there are some strong elements as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also the labor market has marginally softened.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The unemployment rate is about 25 basis points above its recent low; so there has been some movement, and I still expect to see some reduction in construction employment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think there is a bit more softness and there are a few more downside risks to output than at our last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Like others, I think the recent inflation data are moderately encouraging.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I continue to see risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you’re not satiated with risks, I’ll add one more, which is that if the housing market really weakens and people go back to renting, we could get the same phenomenon that we saw last year, by which rents are driven up and we get an effect working through shelter costs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I agree with those who still view the risk to inflation as being tilted to the upside.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no comments or questions, let me turn now to Brian to discuss the policy action.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I’ll be referring to the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” Financial markets have experienced exceptional strains over the intermeeting period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Bluebook provided a thorough review of these developments through Thursday, and I had intended to provide only a brief summary of and update on those developments, as in exhibit 1, and some thoughts on their implications for monetary policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But given the extensive discussions of this topic so far this morning, those points seem all to have been made, and I will turn directly to a discussion of policy alternatives.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As noted at the top of exhibit 2, the risk of weakness in aggregate demand stemming from tighter credit conditions and disruptions in credit flows formed part of the rationale for the 25 basis point easing of alternative A that was presented in the Bluebook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even if your views about the modal outlook are similar to the Greenbook baseline forecast, you may be concerned that the deterioration in credit conditions, the significant increase in market volatility, and potential declines in confidence have tilted the risks to growth distinctly to the downside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You may also see the recent spate of soft spending indicators as having raised the likelihood of sluggish growth in aggregate demand.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The considerable gap between the Greenbook-consistent real federal funds rate, the dashed green line in the panel to the right, and the range of model-based estimates of the equilibrium real federal funds rate, shown in red, may add to questions about the possibility of weaker growth than in the staff forecast and reinforce your belief that some easing of policy is appropriate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, you may be more optimistic than the staff about either productivity growth or the NAIRU or both.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, as I mentioned earlier, several of you noted just such optimism in the narratives accompanying your trial-run projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The financial stimulus from a policy easing, of course, would help support growth directly.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A policy action might be highly potent in current circumstances, possibly helping to buoy consumer and business confidence in a period when sentiment may well be deteriorating.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You may 3 Materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: also believe that the inflation outlook would support a near-term policy easing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Core inflation readings have been relatively subdued in recent months, wage growth seems to have remained moderate, and labor market pressures may be starting to ease, although the evidence on that score is so far quite limited.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the staff forecast, core inflation converges toward 2 percent, an outcome that, judging by your projections, some of you would find acceptable—and your forecasts suggest that you think the odds favor a prompter and slightly steeper decline in inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In contrast, as noted in the bottom left-hand panel, you may concur with the Greenbook forecast for spending and prices, given its policy assumptions, but judge that the forecasted trajectory for inflation is too slow and leaves inflation at a level that is too high to foster optimal economic performance.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If so, you may be inclined to firm policy ¼ percentage point, as in alternative C. The decline in core inflation in the Greenbook is slight and slow.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the bottom right panel, the optimal control simulation in the Bluebook based on a 1½ percent target for core PCE inflation suggests an increase in the federal funds rate of about ¾ percentage point over the next year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Credibility or learning effects that might flow from a policy firming, as in the simulation, could limit the output and employment sacrifice necessary to foster a lower path for inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, you may agree with the staff’s baseline assumption that the effects of current market strains will prove temporary, that markets will soon resume clearing, albeit at higher and perhaps more- rational and more-sustainable spreads, and that the restraint on aggregate demand will be modest.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, you might see the risks to the inflation outlook as tilted to the upside, given high levels of resource utilization and increased energy prices.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative B, discussed in exhibit 3, may be seen as an appropriate balancing of the considerations motivating alternative A, on the one hand, and alternative C, on the other.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under this alternative, the Committee would leave the stance of policy unchanged today.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement would acknowledge the recent volatility of financial markets and tighter credit conditions but would also convey an expectation that moderate growth will likely continue.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Core inflation would be characterized as subdued in recent months but subject to upside risk.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee would expressly refer to increased downside risk to growth but indicate that its predominant policy concern remains the risk that inflation will fail to moderate as expected.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A rationale for alternative B is laid out in the upper left-hand panel.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the baseline Greenbook forecast, the economy expands at a moderate pace, resource pressures ease slightly, and core inflation ebbs to 2 percent with the federal funds rate held at its current level through next year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That forecast may be close to your own view about the modal result, and you may see it as an acceptable outcome.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown to the right, optimal control simulations based on the Greenbook baseline and an assumed core inflation objective of 2 percent would suggest leaving the federal funds rate unchanged for the rest of the year before easing slightly.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Returning to the left- hand panel, holding steady at this meeting would also be consistent with the Committee’s past behavior as captured by the estimated outcome-based and forecast- based policy rules presented in the Bluebook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You may also believe that alternative B represents a suitable weighting of the risks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, even if you are a bit more optimistic about potential growth and the NAIRU than the staff, you may nonetheless see maintaining the federal funds rate at its current level as an appropriate risk-management approach, given the upside risks to inflation and the higher costs should they be realized.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Careful consideration of the most recent developments also may incline you toward alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In particular, even if the incoming data and increased financial market strains of recent weeks incline you to believe that the downside risks to growth have increased, you may be quite unsure about the extent of those risks and not wish to exaggerate them.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As suggested by yesterday’s developments, it is not inconceivable that markets will soon begin to right themselves and that the Greenbook baseline assumption of only modest financial restraint will prove correct.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In these circumstances, watchful waiting may be the best approach in order to allow more information to accumulate that will enable you to better assess the likely eventual adjustments of market prices and flows and the appropriate policy response.

speaker: MADIGAN
