text: Indeed, you may be especially concerned about the risk of overreacting (or being perceived as overreacting) to temporary market developments—particularly if you see a significant probability that markets could misinterpret changes in the stance of policy, or in your words, as an indication that you place a higher priority on financial market stability or economic growth than on price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, your inflation concerns may not have diminished much, if at all, over the intermeeting period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: While the most recent core inflation readings have been relatively low, you may concur with the staff that some of that good performance will likely prove transitory.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, overall inflation has remained high, and with resource utilization elevated, you may be worried that high rates of overall inflation could allow inflation expectations to move higher.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement associated with the revised version of alternative B is provided in the bottom panel.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Given the volatile market conditions of late, getting a reliable read on market participants’ expectations at this point is difficult, but an announcement roughly along these lines seems to be anticipated by most market participants.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Notably, the statement explicitly mentions downside risks to growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That mention may be seen as opening the door a crack to future easing or at least giving the Committee greater scope to move in that direction.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although only a minority of market participants apparently expect the Committee to point explicitly to downside risks to growth, a sizable market reaction to the inclusion of such a reference in paragraph 4 seems unlikely, as the Committee still would state that inflation risks are its predominant concern.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The final exhibit is an updated version of table 1 for your reference.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Changes relative to the Bluebook are shown in red.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions of Brian?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let’s begin our go-round.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, Mr. Chairman, against this background of skittishness, my best advice would be to recognize, to an extent, in our statement what is going on in the marketplace, what ails the marketplace.

speaker: FISHER
text: The best guidance would be that we must not ourselves become a tripwire.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we have to show a steady hand.

speaker: FISHER
text: I rather liked the reference to the Hippocratic oath earlier, “Do no harm.” I think we can best accomplish this by acknowledging market turbulence and yet not implying that we are given to a reaction that might create a moral hazard.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m particularly mindful of the discussion in the press and by security analysts of a so-called Bernanke put, and I want to make sure that we do not take any action or say anything that might give rise to an expectation that such is to occur.

speaker: FISHER
text: Therefore, I would suggest that alternative B offers the best policy response.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is, I am in favor of keeping the rate where it is.

speaker: FISHER
text: The wording in the second paragraph acknowledges that there has been volatility in the markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it addresses the points Governor Kohn made about growth in employment, incomes, and a robust global economy.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’ve waited a long time to see the word “global” in these statements.

speaker: FISHER
text: Whether it gets left in or not, it does reflect reality.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m mindful of President Geithner’s point of softening a little, and yet that is where I worry that we might become a bit of a tripwire.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would under normal circumstances be somewhat inclined toward the last paragraph in alternative A, and yet I didn’t hear around the table, nor do I fully believe myself, that things are exactly roughly balanced.

speaker: FISHER
text: I take the point that was made just now in the presentation that, by saying “downside risks to growth have increased somewhat,” we are opening the door.

speaker: FISHER
text: The only refinement that I might suggest is that we soften a little the word before “policy concern remains the risk that inflation will fail to moderate as expected.” By taking out the word “predominant,” I would leave that up for consideration.

speaker: FISHER
text: I actually talked to somebody about this earlier; I want to acknowledge that.

speaker: FISHER
text: But otherwise I would stick with alternative B, again, mindful that we are dealing with a skittish market situation and yet acknowledging the fact that a sense around this table is that there are risks to growth, that we are making progress on inflation, and yet there is no convincing evidence that we have completely turned the corner on the latter front.

speaker: POOLE
text: It’s clear that the markets are very skittish.

speaker: POOLE
text: I haven’t heard anyone suggesting that we should be changing the fed funds rate, and I believe we should keep it steady.

speaker: POOLE
text: So what is important now is what we say rather than the federal funds rate.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think that the market is looking to us for leadership, but we have to define exactly what that means in a difficult market situation.

speaker: POOLE
text: I start by saying that we need to view the current market situation not as unique but as a particular example of a class of events.

speaker: POOLE
text: Each one has unique characteristics, but this is part of a not-uncommon thing that happens.

speaker: POOLE
text: It happens every now and then.

speaker: POOLE
text: So what should our response rule be to events like this, not how should we respond to this particular case?

speaker: POOLE
text: I think there are two things that we need to do, given what we know at the moment, which obviously may change.

speaker: POOLE
text: What we know at the moment is, in the current situation, we ought not to give any hint that we are trying to suggest a policy change at our next meeting because I don’t think we have enough information to say that such a hint would be appropriate.

speaker: POOLE
text: Second, we want to make clear to the markets our readiness to respond to the situation should the environment change so that response by us would be helpful.

speaker: POOLE
text: Now, if we were to hint or if the markets were to view what we say as hinting, we could produce a positive market outcome this afternoon.

speaker: POOLE
text: Where do we go from there?

speaker: POOLE
text: Would we, having given such a hint inadvertently or on purpose, want to actually carry through at our next meeting?

speaker: POOLE
text: That will depend on what we know at the next meeting, but in the meantime we would have created a market dynamic that would not be at all helpful.

speaker: POOLE
text: Reducing the fed funds rate 25 basis points at the next meeting or the one after that is not going to fix the subprime market.

speaker: POOLE
text: That market is changing permanently from a situation of really very poor underwriting, and the market will fix it in due time and sort it out.

speaker: POOLE
text: I favor basically alternative B and the language there, but I am concerned about paragraph 4, that the market could interpret “although the downside risks to growth have increased somewhat” as our effort to give a hint that we see a cut in the rate ahead.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I would like to suggest a little different way of doing that.

speaker: POOLE
text: If you look in paragraph 2 at the sentence that begins with “nevertheless,” I would insert a sentence immediately ahead of that which says, “Consequently, the downside risks to growth have increased somewhat.” That follows the discussion of the situation in the market, credit conditions, and so forth.

speaker: POOLE
text: Then I would leave the last paragraph the same as it was last time.

speaker: POOLE
text: The point of doing that is to make clear that the downside risks to growth have increased somewhat, but nevertheless, the economy seems likely to continue to expand at a moderate pace.

speaker: POOLE
text: That was what I would suggest we do so that we do not inadvertently give a hint.

speaker: POOLE
text: We are aware that the markets are upset.

speaker: POOLE
text: We are making that very clear, but there is no intent to give a hint of policy action in our minds at our next meeting.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, I guess the thing that strikes me first about the current situation is that the incoming news on core inflation has been promising.

speaker: STERN
text: At least as far as I’m concerned, the inflation outlook is satisfactory.

speaker: STERN
text: So that, in and of itself, suggests no change in policy.

speaker: STERN
text: Now, if we append to that the financial market turmoil and the adjustment that is under way there, that does raise the risk to real growth.

speaker: STERN
text: I think we have pretty well acknowledged that in this discussion.

speaker: STERN
text: But in my view, that shouldn’t prompt a change in the federal funds rate target at this meeting for the reasons I cited earlier having to do with the substantial uncertainties associated with all of this and, of course, I would be lax if I didn’t mention the resilience of the underlying economy that has been demonstrated through the period of the great moderation.

speaker: STERN
text: I do think it’s important, though, that we use the language to make sure that the public is aware that we are aware of what is going on here.

speaker: STERN
text: Alternative B, as drafted, largely does that.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t think we should feel constrained at this point, as we sometimes do, to try to make the changes to the language as few and far between as possible.

speaker: STERN
text: I’m pretty comfortable with alternative B as drafted.

speaker: STERN
text: In fact, I might be prepared to go even a little further than B, something closer to a balanced risk statement, but I don’t feel strongly enough about it to insist on that, even if I could.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we have a couple of issues in front of us today.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, do we react to the recent inflation numbers?

speaker: LACKER
text: I have been pleased by the recent reports, as I said, coming in better than expected, but there seems to be a substantial chance that the improvement we have seen is temporary and that we will get some higher figures later this year.

speaker: LACKER
text: Moreover, inflation expectations remain above where I’d like them to be, so I don’t think we should relax our characterization of inflation in this statement.

speaker: LACKER
text: A second question we face is how to react to the recent turmoil in financial markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we need to be careful to maintain our focus on the implications of market developments for the anticipated paths of inflation and real spending.

speaker: LACKER
text: At this point, I don’t see those implications being substantial enough to warrant a policy response on our part or a change in our sense of the likely near-term policy path, though obviously this assessment may change as events unfold.

speaker: LACKER
text: Absent evidence of such implications, our financial stability responsibilities can be met quite adequately through the automatic supply of reserves under the Desk’s operating procedures for targeting the overnight federal funds rate or through the supply of reserves to solvent institutions at the discount window.

speaker: LACKER
text: Unfortunately, the recent behavior of the fed funds futures market and recent financial press commentary suggest that some market participants, perhaps thinking back to 1987 or 1998, believe that financial market turbulence per se will induce us to respond with interest rate cuts.

speaker: LACKER
text: Even if we did cut rates to counter financial market volatility, financial market jitters might take some time to dissipate.

speaker: LACKER
text: We may be reluctant to undo such rate cuts in the meantime, and we would run the risk that policy then becomes too easy and we get behind the curve.

speaker: LACKER
text: My main concern is the risk that our communication today might mislead markets into thinking that we may cut rates in response to asset-price volatility per se, absent any expectation of sustained effects on the real economy or inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Accordingly, I believe the statement language should acknowledge the recent developments as in the second part of alternative B but not go any further.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m concerned about paragraph 4 and adding the passage about downside risks to growth increasing.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m concerned that it may go a bit too far in that direction.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that the minutes should acknowledge the problems in subprime and private equity markets, and I also think the minutes should educate financial markets that the mitigation of volatility in asset prices is not an FOMC objective.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I didn’t know I raised my hand, but I’ll go anyway.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I certainly don’t want to recommend a change in the fed funds target at this point, Mr. Chairman, so I agree with alternative B in terms of the fed funds rate portion.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I do want to go on record, since this is my last meeting, as saying that I’m not agreeing with alternative B because I’m comfortable with a 2 percent quantitative guideline for inflation.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: But I am, on balance, comfortable with alternative B. I am concerned about inflation.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I think the improvement that we see may be transitory, as I mentioned.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: As President Stern mentioned in his earlier comments, unit labor costs will likely be increasing, and I think that, although the forecast on inflation looks promising, there could be significant risks that it might go higher.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: In terms of the developments in the financial markets, I think we have all talked about them extensively.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: There is nothing more to be said there.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: At this point, it is a period of watchful waiting.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I would agree with President Lacker, with his comment about paragraph 4 of taking out the phrase that the downside risks to growth have increased somewhat.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I would prefer to see it in the minutes rather than in the statement, and I would prefer to have paragraph 4 exactly as we had it at the last meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As I said earlier, I do think that the risks to the outlook for economic growth have increased while the risks to the outlook for inflation have moderated but are still to the upside.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I found the suggestion on page 25 of the Bluebook that we might want to mix and match the alternative A and B language appealing, but I did think that changing our statement in that way could convey a greater shift in our risk assessment than I believe is warranted today.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I think the revised version of alternative B makes the modest but important adjustment of acknowledging the recent change in credit conditions in the rationale section, and it signals the greater downside risks to growth in the risk assessment section.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I support our alternative B—that is, no change in the fed funds rate today and the language that is in the revised version.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the inflation news has continued to be encouraging, but the risks remain on the upside.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to growth, the prospects have worsened, and I think there is greater downside risk for the reasons that we have discussed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the market response to these events is not inappropriate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They perceive a greater likelihood that we will need to cut the fed funds rate sooner and more deeply than seemed likely only a few weeks ago, and I think we should essentially try to leave those expectations in place today to indicate that we intend not to respond to asset prices or to the problems of particular dealers or financial institutions directly but to assess the economic consequences of the turmoil.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So the question is, What is the right language to do that?

speaker: YELLEN
text: The alternative B language that is proposed is trying to achieve exactly what I think is appropriate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I agree with the goal of alternative B. I’m simply concerned about some of the actual language that is proposed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Particularly I worry about the language in paragraph 4.

speaker: YELLEN
text: When you say “although the downside risks to growth have increased somewhat, the Committee’s predominant policy concern remains the risk that inflation will fail to moderate,” that’s like saying—perhaps because I respond so strongly to the word “predominant”—that, yes, we see greater downside risk, but we don’t care; we remain totally focused on inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That’s how it comes across to me.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t think the intention is to make it that way.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I would make two proposals to soften it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think what we need to do is dial it down, but I do think that inflation risk remains to the upside.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would second two suggestions that have already been made.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would second President Fisher’s suggestion that we remove the word “predominant” from paragraph 4.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We might say, “The Committee remains concerned about the risk that inflation will fail to moderate as expected.” Now, I do think the downside risk has increased on the growth side.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’m not sure it is actually necessary to say so explicitly, and I think dialing down paragraph 4 by simply removing “predominant,” along with the additional language that is proposed in line 2, might be sufficient.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I think that we actually do agree that downside risks have increased.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If we want to express that, I would endorse President Poole’s suggestion that we move the language about downside risks to paragraph 2, saying something after “for some households and businesses, and the housing correction is ongoing.” We could then say, “Although the downside risks to growth have increased somewhat, nevertheless the economy seems likely to continue to expand at a moderate pace.” So we would get it in there.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Basically we would say that we see it, but nevertheless we think most likely the economy will grow at a moderate pace.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If financial turbulence diminishes and markets stabilize, not having downside risks to growth in paragraph 4 and continuing to express some asymmetric bias, some worry about inflation, we’ll be comfortable living with that going forward, and it is a good summary of where we are.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So those are my suggestions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, a couple of things.

speaker: HOENIG
text: First, I am satisfied with the current policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that for the moment our concern should still be on inflation, and I think our policy is designed to address that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In saying that, I also recognize—from my own observations and from what I’ve heard here today—that more downside risks are emerging and that we have brought the risks more in balance, I guess is the way to say it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Complicating that, of course, are the tighter credit conditions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think they are probably transitory, but we won’t know that for a while yet—maybe by the next meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That leads me to conclude that I am comfortable with alternative B and its language because I think it recognizes this dynamic and puts it out there for the public.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I would stick with what we have in alternative B and then see how we develop between now and the next meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am certainly comfortable with maintaining the fed funds rate where it is, so I’m supportive of that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think the real key here is language.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What are we trying to convey to the markets?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How far can we go, acknowledging what many people share—a sense of some increased risk—without creating another set of concerns in the marketplace?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So the language is the tricky piece here.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’ve waffled a bit in my feelings about this.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m inclined to be about where I think Bill Poole and Janet Yellen are—moving the downside risks into paragraph 2 as opposed to putting them in the assessment of risk.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would be supportive of that tone.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Also, in response to some of Jeff’s comments in his earlier memo on this, I actually prefer the language of repricing of risk rather than of tightening credit conditions simply because it emphasizes that this is partly a relative price adjustment that is going on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I don’t want to take a strong stand on that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Only one other word concerns me, and I’d like to raise the issue here.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In paragraph 3, which nobody has talked about yet, in the first sentence, “readings on core inflation have been relatively subdued in recent months” is a change in the language from our previous statement, which says, “improved modestly recent months.” I worry a little about the word “subdued” because I think it becomes very close to making some kind of normative judgment about the level of inflation that we are happy with.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m uncomfortable about that particular change in the language because it, again, might imply some normative statement without the Committee’s agreeing on what we view as being subdued or not.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I’d like to suggest that we change that back to what it was before because, if we want to convey stability and some continuity here, there are places to change, there are places not to change, and I would rather change fewer words than more words going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That would be the only additional suggestion I would make.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I, too, feel that we should hold the rate, so I am concerned principally with the way the statement plays to the various audiences, particularly the market.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The posture we should take is to acknowledge, while not reacting prematurely to, the turbulence in the financial markets and the subdued or the improved inflation numbers, and we should make an effort to maintain some flexibility.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I am a bit torn on paragraph 4 between President Poole’s suggestion, which I have some sympathy for, and the concern that paragraph 4 will come across as ritualistic repetition of what we’ve said every month for several months and, therefore, will convey a sense that we’re not paying attention to what’s going on in the market.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I come out ambivalent on that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I can support President Poole’s suggestion, but on balance I guess I like the statement in alternative B as it is.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I support leaving the target for the fed funds rate at 5¼ percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, the news since the last meeting would seem to be more elevated downside risk to economic growth.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This elevated risk reflects the baseline growth for real GDP as 2 percent (a considerable reduction from the previous Greenbook), greater uncertainty about the evolution of the housing market, and concern about the fallout from financial market disruptions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given the greater downside risk, I would prefer language in the assessment of risk paragraph from alternative A, though I do like the modification to alternative B that was made, and I am worried about an interpretation of a Fed put for financial markets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So although I’d prefer the risk assessment in alternative A, which more accurately reflects my assessment of risks, I could certainly accept removing the word “predominant.” That would be my second choice.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My third choice would be to bow to those who have a better understanding of nuanced language, since that is certainly not my expertise, though I hope I will develop it over the years, and I could live with the alternative B language as my third choice.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like the others, I think keeping the federal funds rate where it is is the right thing to do.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need, as others have said, to watch the situation carefully and see how it evolves.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we’re trying to do two things with this statement, as others have remarked.

speaker: KOHN
text: One is to make people aware that we’re aware that a major market event has occurred and to say that we’re looking at it and trying to assess its implications for the outlook but that it hasn’t really—not yet, anyhow—caused a major change in our fundamental assessment of where the economy is going.

speaker: KOHN
text: The second thing we are trying to do is make sure that we have a flexible platform we can move from over the next couple of meetings or even, should it become necessary, in the intermeeting period.

speaker: KOHN
text: So one can see this going in lots of different directions—the markets getting much more turbulent with implications for the outlook and we need to move in the intermeeting period or things settling down and we go back to inflation as the predominant risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: The incoming data on demand and production remain consistent with the central forecast.

speaker: KOHN
text: As I and some others noted, we could end up coming out of this and easing policy somewhere down the road, but not right away.

speaker: KOHN
text: I thought the language of alternative B did both of those things.

speaker: KOHN
text: It reinforced the sense that moderate growth going forward was where we thought things were going because we added the “supported by solid growth in employment and incomes and a robust global economy.” So we have some rationale for that, which we didn’t have before.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also thought that paragraph 4 was a really accurate reading.

speaker: KOHN
text: I was actually a little surprised through the go-round just how, almost universally, people said that the downside risks to output have increased but that they were still most concerned about inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I thought that paragraph 4 turned out to be presciently—on the part of the Chairman, Brian, or whoever drafted it—a really accurate view of where the Committee was.

speaker: KOHN
text: My concern about moving the first piece of that into paragraph 2 is that then we have one risk in paragraph 2.

speaker: KOHN
text: We haven’t done that before, right?

speaker: KOHN
text: The risks to output and to inflation have all been talked about in paragraph 4.

speaker: KOHN
text: Another risk is in paragraph 4, the risk to inflation, and that is an asymmetry of how we discuss risks.

speaker: KOHN
text: It was intended to soften the risk, but I think it strikes me as creating a precedent that in the future will be hard to live with, when some risks are in some paragraphs and other risks are in other paragraphs.

speaker: KOHN
text: Another thing we could do is move the inflation risk into paragraph 3 and not come down one way or another.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think the Committee wants to come down on the inflation side—in terms of predominant risk or main risk—and the Committee isn’t quite ready to go to balance.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it seems to me that paragraph 4, as written, really captured the center of gravity of the Committee.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I am in favor of that.

speaker: KOHN
text: One word on the moral hazard and the concern about being seen as reacting: I am not worried about it.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we have kept our eye, through the past twenty years, on the macro environment.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have adjusted policy to stabilize the economy, to bring inflation down, and we were pretty darn successful in all of that.

speaker: KOHN
text: Asset prices go up, and asset prices go down.

speaker: KOHN
text: Anybody who bought a lot of high-tech stock, betting on the Greenspan put, is still waiting to recover their money.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think it ever existed.

speaker: KOHN
text: I really don’t care what people say; I care about what we do, and we just need to keep our eye on those macro implications.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, as I said in my presentation, I think the connection between the financial markets and the macroeconomy is pretty complicated and runs through confidence and other things, too.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I’m not really worried about a moral hazard from acting.

speaker: KOHN
text: Should markets continue to be turbulent and we see that turbulence in the future—I agree with the Vice Chairman that we have to be forward looking in this—such turbulence has the potential for adversely affecting the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we should go ahead and act.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we basically did the right thing in ’87 and ’98, and I don’t think we need to apologize for it.

speaker: WARSH
text: Before diving into alternative B, I’d say part of the reason that we are trying on different clothes around the language in alternative B is that we have an odd juxtaposition of growth and inflation at this time.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is because the growth risks seem to be driven largely by a financial market situation that we still don’t totally understand, and we even have some disagreement about how quickly we will come to that understanding.

speaker: WARSH
text: So unlike our typical juxtapositions, when we have intermediate concerns about inflation and about growth, here it strikes me that the differences are in timing and in magnitude—that is, if the downside risk from the financial markets happens soon and we’re in the middle of it and we just don’t see it yet, boy, we might know it soon and that could have very ugly outcomes.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think there are differences here.

speaker: WARSH
text: I also think there are differences in our power.

speaker: WARSH
text: Our power over inflation is pretty darn good, and we can exercise that kind of judgment.

speaker: WARSH
text: Our power over getting in the middle of these markets by moving rates ¼ percentage point or moving our language is harder for me to decipher.

speaker: WARSH
text: That’s why I think the suggestions about the language of alternative B are good ones, and they are hard for us to all wrestle with.

speaker: WARSH
text: The reason I come down for alternative B as written is that it strikes me that we have two goals.

speaker: WARSH
text: One is to be as clear as we can be with the markets, notwithstanding their expectations of what we see, and I think alternative B does that.

speaker: WARSH
text: The second goal is trying to buy ourselves some insurance and some flexibility.

speaker: WARSH
text: I worry that, if we were to drop “predominant,” which has become part and parcel of their view of where we are, it might turn out that these markets are benign and this isn’t the storm I talked about just a moment ago, and it will be hard to go back to that word.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t know how we go back to “predominant” in September or in the meeting after that if we have dropped it.

speaker: WARSH
text: So in some ways I think the question is, as in the Poole approach, Do you drop “predominant” and move the downside risks to paragraph 2, and is that roughly equivalent to alternative B as is?

speaker: WARSH
text: The reason I do not think so is that alternative B as is provides us with more flexibility to end up dropping the downside risks if that eventuality comes to pass.

speaker: WARSH
text: So for the reasons that Governor Kohn has given, I think we probably have the right construct here in alternative B.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I also support keeping the fed funds rate unchanged, and I very much agree with the way that Governor Kohn was thinking about what we’re trying to achieve.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So let me just describe why I think that alternative B as is largely achieves that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The key to my thinking about the decision on changing the statement is, first, whether something has materially changed so that the markets will realize that, when we change the statement, we do so because something has actually happened and, second, whether it gives us the flexibility going forward to make another change if new information comes in.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So, for example, in paragraph 2, acknowledging the volatility and talking about credit conditions, about the housing market, and then about the offsetting factors of employment, growth in income, and global demand—all those things are relevant.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The new things—the financial markets and credit conditions—have been there a bit but are now more important than they were before.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So we’re acknowledging things that actually have happened in the intermeeting period.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I also like that it gives a bit more color about what’s going on and how we’re thinking about things, and each piece is one that we can easily leave, add to, or take back, and that is very valuable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I like the formulation of paragraph 2 because it both acknowledges new information that has come in and does so not in a way that suggests fear or excess concern but just sort of acknowledges various factors, particularly the financial conditions in the context of others on the upside.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The balance is, I think, very nice.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On paragraph 3, I agree with President Plosser that it is not clear to me that we had new information so that we would want to change the characterization.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I see nothing wrong with the characterization that we have there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I am not as concerned as President Plosser is that it makes more of a value judgment.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But my question is just why we have made the change.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I am happy with either way, but using my criterion that if no information is new why change, I am not quite sure why we changed it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it is fine either way.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On paragraph 4, I think it is very important to take a step toward balance without going all the way toward balance because it is much too early to tell, as many people have said.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Putting the downside risks there makes a lot of sense because of the tradition of the structure.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Again, I don’t see any reason to change the overall formulation or the overall structure at this point, particularly when the markets are jittery.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t think we should be going about a sort of structural change in the statement.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Even if ultimately we might want to think about it, I do not think this would be the time to do it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, I like that it is very easy to put on and take off, so that if growth does come back up, we can easily remove the language.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If growth goes down, we can move toward balance of risk very easily there if we want to, and as Governor Warsh said, if we drop “predominant,” we cannot get that back.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I feel that we are not at a stage—or at least from the discussion around the table and from where I am—where we should do that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, I think you would have a very strong reaction in the markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If the markets saw that we both acknowledged the downside risk and took out “predominant” or even just took out the word “predominant,” that would indicate a much stronger risk and be a much stronger signal that we are going to move more quickly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I do think that this statement as is will lead to a slight increase in expectations of a cut a little earlier, but that’s perfectly acceptable because I can’t see any better way to get the balance right.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Obviously I agree that we should not have a change in the federal funds rate.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I want to talk about the statement.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When I think about the statement that I would write, a key thing from my viewpoint is just to ask what the inflation objective is because it really affects the statement in a major way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I believe that a 2 percent goal is reasonable for reasons that I have discussed before.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that context, inflation has moderated, and so I would have difficulty saying that we are concerned that it has not moderated when I think, in fact, it has.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I do have to say that I think we want to stick with alternative B as it is written here for two reasons.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The first reason is that I am actually in a conflicting situation because it is not clear whether I should think about writing a statement that’s appropriate for Governor Mishkin or a statement that’s appropriate for the Committee as a whole.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We are going to have to deal with this challenge.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When I read the projections, it’s clear to me that I’m on the high side, that my 2 percent is higher than the median, which is around 1¾ or 1.8.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I would not have difficulty accepting an inflation objective of 1.8 as long as the Committee came to a consensus.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that the issue of writing the statement is much more difficult when we don’t have consensus of the Committee.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is creating a problem for me in terms of thinking about how to get involved in the internal deliberation on what the statement should be, and that will be important in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do not think that now is the time to deal with that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So one of the issues then is let’s deal with that at some point in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second reason is the issue of what is going on in terms of the financial markets and what kind of impression we give outside.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I agree with Governor Kohn that we have not been operating under a Greenspan put or a Fed put.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is very clear to me that we have not been doing so, except that I think an impression has been created, and I would like to mention that I am a little less sanguine about what was done in the past.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that one mistake was made, perhaps because I’m looking at it ex post.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When the Fed lowered interest rates 75 basis points in the LTCM episode, it was a brilliant stroke.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It was exactly the right thing to do.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But when you think about an operation like that, which was basically to restore confidence to the markets and was very much like a classic lender-of-last-resort operation, we know that you want to put in liquidity; but when the crisis is over, you want to take it out.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: At that time, I was quite critical that the Fed did not then remove the 75 basis point decline, and I think it created an impression—I don’t know about a Greenspan put, but there was some element of that—and it is very hard to dissipate that impression.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Maybe it is true that people said we weren’t trying to do that, but we did create some kind of impression along those lines.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think the issue of perception still is important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that context, it is very important that we not give the impression that we are responding to financial markets now because the discussion here has been that we are very concerned that this might be a problem in the future but right now it is not affecting our forecast in a major way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s exactly what we have to communicate to the public and the markets; and in that context, changing the statement too much in moving toward balance will create problems along those lines.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If I were not worrying about these issues, I would take the word “predominant” out of the statement.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, I might even take out the issue that I’m worried about, that we say inflation has not moderated.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But given the current situation, I think it is best that we stick with “predominant.” That we mention downside risks to growth and then the “predominant” side in terms of inflation does create an element of balance.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Thus I think there is a potential issue that we have to worry about in future statements and that we will have to grapple with.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I hope that this Committee could come to a consensus on what our inflation objective is so that we can have a more coherent discussion of these issues; however, I do not think this is the time to pursue that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I support alternative B as written.

speaker: LACKER
text: About classic lender-of-last-resort operations, we asked people at the Open Market Desk how much additional reserves it takes to lower the federal funds rate ¼ percentage point.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is on the order of a couple of ten million—so 75 basis points added maybe $100, maybe $150 million in that instance.

speaker: LACKER
text: You know, I’d venture that that was probably trivial in terms of adding liquidity to the market after LTCM.

speaker: LACKER
text: The real effect it had was altering the then-current and expected path of the real overnight federal funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: As you know, Rick, the classic lender-of-last- resort option had to do with the 1900s and preventing interest rates from spiking above current rates, not from adding reserves or driving down interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I think it is a confusion to link things like what we did in ’87 or ’98 to the classic lender-of-last-resort operation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But there’s always an issue about what we mean by the word “classic.” What I’m thinking about here is that a lender-of-last-resort operation is really about restoring confidence.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It can be done without actually putting any liquidity into the system.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If you look at a successful lender-of-last-resort operation, just the announcement that you will be a backstop for the system has tremendous impact.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, this is one reason that what was done in ’87—with Greenspan not actually sitting in the tub that morning but getting up early and announcing before the market opened that the Federal Reserve was going to be a backstop—was extremely important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m thinking of it in that context, which is that we wanted to provide information to the markets, which was that we were going to be there and that we were not going to be the Bank of Japan and allow something to spiral out of control.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly, it was basically taking out insurance, saying that the Fed will be there.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Once you don’t need insurance anymore, there’s a really strong argument to take it away.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I’m not talking about this in terms of liquidity per se but what we are trying to do in terms of expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That episode was important for doing the right thing, which was critical to the way the financial markets recovered; but I think a problem was created when we didn’t reverse it in the same way that, when you actually do a lender-of-last-resort operation, you put liquidity in and you take it out.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s the sense in which I mean putting lower interest rates in and then taking them out when the crisis is over.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me get us back to the statement.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just quickly, I think we are actually all in a fairly similar place, not far apart in our basic diagnosis, and that’s good, given the complexity of our decisions going forward in some sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We want to soften slightly the asymmetry in our current statement to give us a bit more flexibility and to show some awareness of the change in the reality out there.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Quickly on the statement, first, I agree that, on the question of how we characterize and how we display some recognition of financial market developments, the reference to volatility itself may not capture it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Somebody suggested that we say something instead about going to “risk premium” or something more generally, and I think that might be slightly better—a small point.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The second question is whether we should revert to June on the inflation readings in response, I think, to the right observation by President Plosser that this does convey more comfort with a level than the previous wording did.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I would be fine going back to June, but I could also live with this because it conveys a sense that the readings have been and continue to be reasonably favorable.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I would be fine with the way it is, but I could go back to the June language.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the question about whether we refer explicitly to downside risks to growth, which we’ll be doing for the first time—a sort of consequential act—and, if so, how we do it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would have been fine leaving it implicit rather than introducing it explicitly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think Don is right: If we’re going to do it, unless we’re going to change the structure of the statement significantly and put some risk assessment on growth in paragraph 2 and some risk assessment around inflation in paragraph 3, then we need to leave it in paragraph 4.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So, again, on the risks to growth, I’m okay with putting that language in.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it’s consistent with the broad objectives.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I guess my preference would have been to leave it implicit.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Finally, on “predominant,” my own view is that we should not repeat “predominant” and that we would be better off simply stating that the Committee remains concerned about the risks or concerned that inflation will fail to moderate as expected.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think the arguments for sticking with “predominant” are that compelling.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think that taking it out constrains our options going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is true that it’s a shift in some broad sense, but I don’t think we need to say so starkly now that we’ve looked at this set of risks—very different types of risk, some very fast moving, very uncertain, and some slower moving, probably manageable over time—and say that we weighed that balance and we think the latter risks continue to predominate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that’s the substance of the argument we face.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it would be better to slightly soften that further.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Having said all of that, I can live with alternative B as drafted.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: May I make a two-handed intervention?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Could I ask a question of Brian?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: “Predominant” is a key word.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So what do you think might be the response of the markets if we leave it in or take it out, in terms of two elements.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is the issue of how the markets would think about the future evolution of our policy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Two is how the media might read whether we are reacting to the distress in the financial markets.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, as I said earlier, it’s a little hard to judge market reactions right now, given the flux in financial markets.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That said, I do think that the introduction of “downside risks,” as an explicit phrase in the statement will obviously not be overlooked by market participants, [laughter] and I think that they will see it as at least some slight shift in the Committee’s body English.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With regard to “predominant,” that’s just another step in the same direction—and I think maybe even a bigger shift.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think it is a bigger shift.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think if the first is one unit, the second is maybe two units in terms of how far you go.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: I just have another objection to taking out the word “predominant.” I don’t think the sentence makes any sense if you take it out.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: You have to put something in.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: You cannot say that it is our only problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You really have to rewrite the sentence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me try to evaluate this with your guidance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I agree with Brian that this is one of the toughest ones to write and to assess the response.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you read the commentary, expectations are all over the map, and so it is very difficult to know how this will be taken.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t pretend to know.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me start with something easy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that President Plosser is absolutely right.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is no reason to change paragraph 3 without a reason.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So unless anyone has concerns, I’d like to change paragraph 3 back to the June language.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Regarding the tougher question—and President Yellen, President Poole, and others have raised an interesting possibility—again, without much confidence I am going to resist it for the following reasons.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first reason is mostly that it is complicated, [laughter] and it moves things around in ways that will make it even harder for the market to understand what we’re trying to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Another reason is that the statement “although the downside risks to growth have increased somewhat,” if we follow your advice and put it after the new sentence in paragraph 2, will essentially say that the financial markets are the reason that the downside risks have increased, whereas there are other factors—the housing market, automobile sales, and things of that sort—that could be viewed as increasing the downside risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I guess that’s my recommendation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On “predominant,” I think the word has been neutralized to a significant extent by its use.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You may recall that we used the phrase “predominant policy concern,” and we changed the second sentence, and the market based on that decided that we had gone all the way to balance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My concern is that, if we get rid of “predominant” and if we mention the downside risks to growth anywhere, that will be viewed as having gone mostly to balance, and I don’t think that’s where we are right now as a Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have one thought, which may have come too late in the day here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is going back to paragraph 2, “financial markets have been volatile in recent weeks.” President Geithner raised the idea of changing that to something about risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One small concern I have, and it would have been good had we put this in earlier, is that the phrase refers to something going on in the markets per se and not an effect of the markets on the economy, which heightens some of the put risk a little.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: An alternative would be to replace that first phrase with something like “investors have demanded greater compensation for risk.” That would be a market development that evidently affects yields and borrowing costs.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Are you saying that you would then get rid of “credit conditions have become tighter”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “Investors have demanded greater compensation for risk, credit conditions have become tighter for some households and businesses.” All right.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is not clear whether probability distributions over the fundamentals have shifted or whether the probability distribution over marginal utility has shifted.

speaker: LACKER
text: Do you see what I mean?

speaker: LACKER
text: It is not clear whether their attitudes to a given risk have changed or their assessments of the magnitude of the risks have changed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Oh, I see what you’re saying.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, actually the way I phrased it was intentionally not to say that risks have increased but rather to say that the price of risk has increased.

speaker: LACKER
text: But that says one of them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But that’s what I want it to say.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is not clear that it isn’t just a widening of the probability distribution over the relevant outcomes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t see any snowball.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: “Risk premiums in financial markets have increased, credit conditions have tightened for some households”—it is true that you don’t really know what the source of the increase in risk premiums is, but it is true that risk premiums have increased.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Volatility itself is not particularly interesting from a policy perspective, and as many people have said, we’re not here to damp volatility.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The considerations relevant to the macroeconomy and to financial market stability in some sense are what happened—and that’s a different way of saying it.

speaker: LACKER
text: No, it encompasses both of what I was referring to, and so that would be a way to do it.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would agree with that.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, that doesn’t say that pricing has changed.

speaker: FISHER
text: Let me give you an example.

speaker: FISHER
text: Kimberly-Clark last week went to market on $2 billion in debt.

speaker: FISHER
text: They couldn’t move it unless they had a change-of-control provision.

speaker: FISHER
text: So it is part of the risk premiums, but we’re not seeing pricing per se.

speaker: FISHER
text: I like the wording that President Geithner has suggested.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Yes, in principle I think that is a good way to characterize what’s going on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But going back to the criteria that I was using, in many cases the risk premiums have simply moved close to historical levels from record lows.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So if they stay at historical averages over time, that’s not necessarily something that’s wrong or problematic.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It may be very difficult to take that phrase away if risk premiums stay where they are in at least some of the markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t think that’s necessarily a bad thing, and I’ve heard a number of people around the table suggest that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In certain markets, they have been above historical averages, but in many markets they have simply moved to the historical average, and I am just a bit concerned about being able to take that away.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, just to say “have increased” and then have the next phrase say “credit conditions have become tighter” also makes no value judgment on whether they’re appropriate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Kohn, do you have a comment?

speaker: KOHN
text: I see why you want to take out “volatile,” and I agree with that.

speaker: KOHN
text: Unlike President Lacker, I think it is important to keep credit conditions in there because it’s more than just price.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I was a little concerned that saying “risk premiums have increased and credit conditions have become tighter” puts it all on price.

speaker: KOHN
text: Suppose we didn’t have the phrase in red.

speaker: KOHN
text: We just had “owing to developments in financial markets, credit conditions have become tighter,” or “reflecting recent developments in financial markets, credit conditions have become tighter.”

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I am okay with that.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: You could just go back to the original language in the Bluebook.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: It says essentially the same thing.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: Just change the sentence around.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that is a good idea.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit conditions are becoming tighter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We saw that in the bank surveys before any of this happened.

speaker: MOSKOW
text: That is in the Bluebook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I understand, but I think that some acknowledgement of the effects of financial market developments in the recent weeks on the economy is needed just to make sure that people understand that we’re awake.

speaker: KOHN
text: So the proposed language is “risk premiums” and “financial markets”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “Have increased, credit conditions have become tighter.” And the housing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I just want to point out, Mr. Chairman, that those two clauses seem to overlap to a considerable degree, “tighter risk premiums” and “tighter credit conditions.” It’s not clear to me precisely what distinction we’re trying to draw there.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Well, “credit conditions” is more general because it can encompass both price and nonprice.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So it raises a question in my mind as to why the first clause is necessary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, think of it as being market-traded assets, and “credit conditions” sounds like mortgages, retail type of credit provision.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I’m okay if you want to put “premium,” the Vice Chairman’s language, in there.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But I think that the markets have become more volatile, and nothing is wrong with saying that, and credit conditions have tightened, which is a fact, and people are thinking about the volatility of the markets.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So that is on their minds.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We’re acknowledging it, as you said, and so I was comfortable with the language.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just get a sense around the table, if I could.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think President Hoenig makes the point that volatility in financial markets could be viewed as having an effect on the economy through uncertainty and those sorts of factors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One option is “financial markets have been volatile in recent weeks.” The second option is “risk premiums in financial markets have increased.” Who wants “volatility”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Who wants to make the change?

speaker: KOHN
text: You have the deciding vote.

speaker: LACKER
text: One factor for me is that “volatility” is a very broad term, and “risk premiums” refers to a narrow set of markets, and this way shifts the focus off equity markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I apologize profusely for bringing this up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we just leave it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So after all the discussion, my proposal is to follow President Plosser and to replace paragraph 3 with the June version.

speaker: DANKER
text: I’ll read the directive wording from the Bluebook and the balance of risk assessment from Brian’s handout.

speaker: DANKER
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: DANKER
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with maintaining the federal funds rate at an average of around 5¼ percent.

speaker: DANKER
text: “Although the downside risks to growth have increased somewhat, the Committee’s predominant policy concern remains the risk that inflation will fail to moderate as expected.

speaker: DANKER
text: Future policy adjustments will depend on the outlook for both inflation and economic growth, as implied by incoming information.” Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes President Hoenig Yes Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes Governor Mishkin Yes President Moskow Yes President Poole Yes President Rosengren Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next meeting is September 18.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me remind you that we will be discussing briefly on September 18 and in October the communication issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me ask you, please, to be reticent about discussing this; please be nontransparent about transparency [laughter] in our discussions so that we don’t front-run ourselves too much.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m going to adjourn formally, but if you can tolerate a few extra minutes at the table, we would like to give Laricke a chance just to give us a very quick update on congressional matters, and then we will move upstairs for lunch for President Moskow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d like to welcome Charlie Evans to the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: He has been attending these meetings since February 1995, certainly ahead of me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d also like to thank Cathy Minehan in absentia [laughter] for being willing to postpone her celebratory lunch until the next meeting, but we will do that in October.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first item of business is to select associate economists.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With Brian Madigan becoming the secretary and Mr. Evans taking on a new role, we need to appoint two associate economists: Jim Clouse from the Board and Dan Sullivan from Chicago have been nominated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do I have a motion?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s turn now to the Desk operations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’ll be referring to the handout that you have in front of you.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In my mind, there are three key questions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, how did the problems in the subprime mortgage area—with losses that probably will ultimately turn out to be in a range of $100 billion to $200 billion—lead to such broad market distress?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, what is the cause of the dysfunction in U.S. and European money markets?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, how far along are we in terms of the adjustment process—in other words, when might we anticipate a resumption of normal market function?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Turning to the first question, the losses in subprime mortgages had wide-ranging effects because the poor investment performance made investors much less willing to invest in structured-finance products more generally.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Investors lost confidence because highly rated securities that referenced subprime assets performed poorly and because investors found it difficult to value complex structured-finance products.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This loss of confidence triggered several broader developments: the inability of mortgage originators to securitize nonconforming mortgage loans; the rapid 1 Materials used by Mr. Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: contraction of the asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) market; the virtual shutdown of the collateralized debt obligation (CDO) and collateralized loan obligation (CLO) markets; the sharp shifts we saw into and out of Treasury-only versus prime money market mutual funds, which in turn disrupted the Treasury bill market; and the anticipated pressure on bank balance sheets and the upward pressure on term funding rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The pressure on bank balance sheets is coming from three major sources.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, investor demand for securitized non-agency mortgage-backed securities has dried up.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Bank originators now have to hold such loans in their bank portfolios.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, bank backstop liquidity facilities have been triggered as investor appetite for asset-backed commercial paper has fallen sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, banks are expected to have difficulty syndicating the bridge loans that they provided to finance leveraged buyouts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of these three sources of pressure, the rollup of ABCP programs has been, in my view, the most important.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The magnitude of the potential funding requirement is the largest, and how much will come back onto bank balance sheets is very uncertain.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The constraint on mortgage loan origination can be seen most visibly in the widening of the spread between fixed-rate prime jumbo mortgage loan rates and conforming mortgage loan rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you can see in exhibit 1, the spread has widened from around 25 basis points to around 100 basis points in recent weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The sharp contraction in the ABCP market began when commercial paper investors became aware that their investments could be vulnerable to loss but were uncertain as to the extent of their exposure in particular programs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This fear of loss had a legitimate basis for those ABCP programs that finance mortgage-related assets without full bank credit enhancement.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: An inability to roll over these programs in the current market would force the liquidation of the assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the current market, that could lead to investor losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problem started in extendable commercial paper market programs, where the credit enhancement backstop by banks was typically either absent or less than 100 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problem then quickly migrated to structured-investment vehicle (SIV) programs, which suffered from similar shortcomings.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: From there, the problem spread as risk-averse investors started to shun the entire asset class.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Asset-backed commercial paper rates rose for those programs that were able to roll over their outstanding commercial paper.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is shown in exhibit 2, which compares unsecured and secured commercial paper rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The volume of outstanding asset- backed commercial paper shrank sharply as some issuers were unable to roll over their maturing paper.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 3 illustrates the downtrend in the volume of outstanding ABCP.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 4 shows the maturity structure of outstanding asset-backed commercial paper and highlights the high proportion of paper that is now being rolled on an overnight basis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The pressure on the asset-backed commercial paper market was temporarily exacerbated by the behavior of money market mutual fund investors, who shifted funds last month from prime money market funds to Treasury-only money market funds (see exhibit 5).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because the total assets in money market mutual funds are nearly four times the size of outstanding Treasury bills, these flows led to a large, albeit mostly transitory fall in Treasury bill yields.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is shown in exhibit 6.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The good news is that the money flows into the prime money mutual funds have stabilized.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This reflects greater discernment among investors about the risks associated with different types of asset-backed commercial paper and the widening yield differentials between prime and Treasury-only money market funds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is noteworthy that those areas of the asset-backed commercial paper market with underlying structural problems—primarily the extendable, SIV, and SIV-lite portions of the market—represent only a small proportion of total asset-backed commercial paper outstanding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, as shown in exhibit 7, SIV programs represented only about 7 percent of the asset-backed commercial paper market before the recent sharp contraction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, as shown in exhibit 8, much of the asset-backed commercial paper market does not finance residential mortgage asset-backed securities, so there is less uncertainty about the underlying value of the assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, much of the market has solid credit support, with 100 percent bank credit enhancement.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This suggests that, as time passes, investors will gradually be able to distinguish between the different types of the ABCP programs and stability will return to the multi-seller, bank-sponsored programs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Already, the pace of contraction of the overall ABCP market has slowed significantly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, the extendable and SIV programs are likely to continue to be under pressure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The third source of balance sheet pressure stems from the sharp contraction in CDO and CLO issuance.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen in exhibit 9, CDO and CLO issuance volumes have plummeted in recent months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The virtual closure of the CDO market has led, in turn, to a virtual cessation of high-yield debt issuance—illustrated in exhibit 10.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These developments have created uncertainty for commercial and investment banks about their ability to syndicate the large volume of loan and debt commitments that they have made to finance private equity buyouts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These institutions are faced with the prospect that they may have to carry such loans on their books for an extended period at a discount to par value.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Syndication will be more difficult because the ability to transform a large proportion of these obligations into marketable investment-grade products through the alchemy of structured finance is not currently an available option.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This pressure on bank balance sheets—both existing and anticipated—has led to significant dysfunction in financial markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, primary dealers have pulled back in their willingness to finance the security positions of investment banks, hedge funds, and other leveraged investors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 11 illustrates the median repurchase-rate bid-asked spread by primary dealers for three types of collateral— GSE MBS, prime MBS, and high-yield corporate debt—at overnight, one-week, and one-month maturities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, there has been an upward trend in bid-asked spreads, especially at the one-month maturity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 12 illustrates the median haircuts applied against such collateral.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Again, there has been an increase, which has been particularly pronounced at the one-month maturity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the same time, this balance sheet pressure and worries about counterparty risk have led to a significant rise in term borrowing rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Banks that are sellers of funds have shifted to the overnight market to preserve their liquidity, and this shift has starved the term market of funds, pushing those rates higher.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 13, the spread between the one-month LIBOR and the one-month interest rate swap rate has widened sharply, and the one-month LIBOR has generally traded considerably above the anticipated level of the overnight federal funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The same pressure on funding rates has been also evident in euribor rates (see exhibit 14).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rise in term rates has pushed banks that depend on funding from the interbank market into the overnight market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In addition, these depository institutions have turned to the Federal Home Loan Bank system as a source of term funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, FHLB advances rose $110 billion in August.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, despite the 50 basis point reduction in the spread between the discount rate and the federal funds rate target, the dollar value of discount window borrowings remains modest, as shown in exhibit 15.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This reflects the lower cost of FHLB advances, the ability to borrow at longer terms from the FHLB, and the lack of stigma in using such advances as a source of funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So where do we go from here?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Clearly, the adjustment process is far from over.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Asset-backed commercial paper programs are still being rolled up, and there is considerable uncertainty about how difficult it will be to roll some of this paper over quarter-end.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, it remains unclear what proportion of leveraged loan commitments commercial and investment banks will be able to syndicate and at what price.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Despite the big backlog and the end of the August doldrums, there has, as yet, been little syndication activity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The good news, of course, is that as time passes, the uncertainty about bank balance sheet pressures and funding requirements should lessen.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, investors’ ability to distinguish between “good” and “bad” ABCP programs and structured-finance products should continue to improve.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The bad news is that the stress caused by the forcible deleveraging of the nonbank financial sector could lead to further losses accompanied by headlines that could further damage investor confidence.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the increased reliance by banks on overnight funding increases rollover risk and may limit the willingness of banks to expand their balance sheets to accommodate the deleveraging of the nonbank financial sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the mortgage sector, depository institutions will undoubtedly—at the right price—take up the slack in the prime jumbo mortgage market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But nondepository institutions are unlikely to be able to originate and securitize nonconforming mortgages in appreciable volume for some time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The tone in financial markets has improved a bit in recent days.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Nevertheless, we still appear to be in an environment in which the dominant theme is risk aversion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This can be seen in a matrix that measures the correlation among the price movements in the major asset classes (see exhibit 16).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In times when markets are calm and untroubled, the correlation coefficients are generally low.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you can see in the exhibit, which examines these correlations since the August 7 FOMC meeting, the correlation coefficients have been very high recently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the foreign exchange markets, two developments are worth noting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, the turmoil in money markets did impair the functioning of the foreign exchange swap market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This made it more difficult for banks in Europe that are structurally short of dollars to obtain the dollar funding needed to fund their assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In recent days, this market function has improved.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the dollar has weakened.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 17, the dollar has fallen to a record low against the euro.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But don’t be too impressed by that headline.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On a broad trade-weighted basis, the decline of the dollar has been modest, with a decline of less than 1 percent from the last FOMC meeting and a fall of slightly more than 4 percent from the start of the year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, this softness in the dollar does not appear to signal any fundamental shift in the willingness of foreign investors to hold dollar-denominated assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Instead, it appears to be driven mainly by changing interest rate expectations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 18, the exchange rate of the dollar versus the euro has continued to track changes in expected short-term interest rate differentials between the United States and Europe.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Not surprisingly, our dealer survey reveals a large decline in short-term rate expectations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibits 19 and 20 compare the dealer surveys before the August 7 FOMC meeting and before the current FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The green circles represent the average of the dealer forecasts, and the blue circles represent the range sized by the number of dealers at each value.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, the average of the dealer modal forecasts for mid-2008 has fallen more than 60 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Market expectations—as reflected by the solid bold lines—have declined about the same amount and remain below the average dealer modal forecasts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: With respect to the outcome of this meeting, a slight majority of dealers expect a 25 basis point reduction in the target federal funds rate rather than a 50 basis point cut.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Only one dealer expects no change in the federal funds rate target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Uncertainty about the short-term interest rate path has also increased.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is evident both in the dealer survey and in the probability distribution of rate outcomes implied by options prices on Eurodollar futures.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen in exhibit 21, the probability distribution of rate outcomes has become much broader since the August 7 FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, open market operations since the last FOMC meeting warrant some discussion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you know, in early August, following persistent upward pressure on the federal funds rate and an extraordinarily large reserve-adding provision by the ECB, we aggressively added reserves on August 10.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That provision of reserves did break the upward pressure on the federal funds rate, and the federal funds rate traded notably soft over the remainder of that two-week reserve maintenance period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Since that time, we have attempted to pull back on our provision of reserves in order to push the federal funds rate back up toward its target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Notice that the blue bars in exhibit 22, which measure daily excess reserves before borrowing, have been generally in negative territory over the past month.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although we have had some success in pushing the effective federal funds rate higher, it has generally traded over the past month below the 5¼ percent target.

speaker: DUDLEY
