text: Our efforts to push the federal funds rate back toward the target have been undermined by several factors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, expectations about the possibility of an intermeeting cut in the federal funds rate target have caused the federal funds rate to trade somewhat soft.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, in recent days, the effective rate has been held down somewhat by expectations of a rate cut at today’s meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the narrower margin between the discount rate and the federal funds rate target makes it more difficult to push up the effective federal funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The upper band of the corridor above 5¼ percent is now half as wide as before even as the lower bound for the federal funds rate remains at 0 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The lower discount rate acts as a cap on how high the federal funds rate can climb when reserves are tight.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, we have had bad luck in the sense that most of our forecasting misses in terms of autonomous factors that affect reserves—such as float, Treasury balances, currency demand, and borrowings at the window—have caused us to inadvertently leave more reserves in the banking system than we had intended.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Our difficulty in pushing up the effective rate can be illustrated by our experience last Wednesday, the last day of the two-week reserve maintenance period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Despite a consistently stingy provision of reserves that resulted in $5 billion of overnight primary credit borrowing for the day and $7.2 billion in total borrowing, the effective rate for that Wednesday was 5.18 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would note, though, that in the past two days we have actually pushed the funds rate effectively up to its target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There were no foreign exchange operations during this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I request a vote to ratify the operations conducted by the System Open Market Account since the August 7 FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, I am very happy to take questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any questions for Bill?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I appreciate your comments on this last point, but I think that the fact that the fed funds rate has been trading so low for so long is problematic.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Certainly around August 9, when we started the interventions, that’s all understandable.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But the Committee made it very clear at that time that it wasn’t changing the targeted funds rate, and yet for the past month it has been essentially below.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So in my mind that has raised three questions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One is a technical question about our ability to actually target the fed funds rate using the procedures that we have in place.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We continue to quote a price target and try to control it using quantities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I still believe it would be a lot easier just to set the price target and buy and sell.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That’s an operational question that I think is on the table for another day.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It also raised the question to me as I watched it going on why the Desk did not choose to intervene more frequently during the day to be more aggressive when they saw that their forecast for the day’s balances was not accurate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There is nothing that says you can’t go back in during the day to help rectify some of that, and I’d like some explanation as to why we didn’t do that or whether that’s an option.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The third question is actually a more serious one because it combines a technical issue and a philosophical one.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think allowing the fed funds rate to trade so low for so long away from our target really creates a credibility problem for this Committee.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It puts us in an awkward position now because, in effect, it hasn’t gone unnoticed by the investment community.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some have called it a “stealth” rate cut that is already in effect.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some have said that the Fed has already cut the fed funds rate, and it puts the Committee’s decision today in a somewhat awkward position because people look back and say, “Well, they have already done it.” So I think it is important that we think about mechanisms and ways to ensure—at least going forward—that, if the Committee has a target, we can be successful in achieving it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I’d just like some further enlightenment there, if I could.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Turning first to your first question, why we do it the way that we do—well, with the new authority to pay interest on reserves, we are going to take a pretty broad look at the whole issue of how we target the federal funds rate and how we manage reserves more generally.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think that’s a legitimate question, and it is going to be done as part of that process.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, the way we do it today is based on a sort of historical evolution that started when the Fed did not reveal what the federal funds rate target was.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think it’s probably fair to say that four or five years from now, when we have that new authority, we may be doing things quite differently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of the issue of going back in later in the day, the problem there is that we don’t really know what’s happening to the autonomous factors until the next morning.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So we don’t know exactly how we’re doing in terms of tracking the reserve provisions relative to our forecast in real time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But you see the rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We do see the rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We could be more aggressive and push people to the window, but I think it is important in this environment not to be contributing to market turmoil.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We felt that the right thing to do was to err on the side of not pushing people forcibly to the window when the market was under some distress.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would also say that the fed funds rate, while it has traded soft, it hasn’t traded that soft.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The effective rate so far this month has been 5.08, and I think that, coming into this meeting, we have pretty much eliminated from the minds of people in the markets that there was a stealth easing, especially in light of where the federal funds rate has been trading over the past week.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I don’t see that as a significant issue for this meeting.

speaker: FISHER
text: Bill, I just want to make sure that I understand what you said in your excellent presentation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think I heard you say that, as time passes, investors in the markets will become more discriminating.

speaker: FISHER
text: Already we’re seeing signs of returning stability.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m trying to differentiate between what we had earlier—serious counterparty risk and phobias— and what we have now—which seems to be concerns about balance sheet risk.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to understand better the distinction between the two.

speaker: FISHER
text: I read Egon’s briefing last night, which by the way was very, very solid.

speaker: FISHER
text: What I read was that the largest banks are well positioned to absorb even larger exposures than they currently anticipate, and the number in that document was $1 trillion—a significant number for five banks to absorb.

speaker: FISHER
text: Given what you just presented to us—I think I interpreted you correctly—the concern about counterparty risk is diminishing, but it is still there.

speaker: FISHER
text: The balance sheet risk issue is somewhat defined, although there are uncertainties—you mentioned them yourself.

speaker: FISHER
text: There’s headline risk, which cuts two ways, by the way, and I want to talk about that during my other intervention.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is also a surprise loss that might occur.

speaker: FISHER
text: Could you distinguish for us whether or not we’ve seen a reduction in counterparty risk, and if so, could you define it somewhat?

speaker: FISHER
text: How serious is the balance sheet risk from your perspective against the background of the briefing we received last night, which indicated that it appears to be manageable?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, it’s difficult to sort out exactly how much of that term premium that we see in the term funding markets represents counterparty risk versus balance sheet constraints.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think in the United States that it is probably more of a balance sheet issue.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In Europe it’s probably more counterparty risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The general sense is that the U.S. banks are very healthy and, as you note, well capitalized.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, the fact that you still have quite a bit of room before you hit that boundary of “well capitalized” doesn’t mean that the banks aren’t concerned about potential balance sheet pressures.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problem they have right now is that they can’t really size with any accuracy how much will be coming onto their balance sheets over the next few months through asset-backed commercial paper, through bank conduits, and through other things for which they may be on the hook that they didn’t expect to be on the hook for.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I wouldn’t take the boundary line of “well capitalized” versus “not well capitalized” as the constraint.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the constraint actually starts to bind quite a bit before you get to that point.

speaker: FISHER
text: We talked about the conduit question somewhat on the calls.

speaker: FISHER
text: Again, I assume we’ve done sensitivity analysis to the degree that we can in terms of the potential for having to absorb some of that risk and bring it onto the balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The analysis that has been done has suggested that the banks are well capitalized and should, with one or two exceptions, be able to handle this balance sheet expansion reasonably well; but they can’t say that with absolute certainty.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Another thing happening is that there is a potential problem on the earnings side.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You can imagine a worst case scenario in which you can’t syndicate any of the loans and then the loans have to be marked down significantly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That has an earnings consequence.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So then the balance sheet is going to be affected not just by what’s happening in terms of the assets but also by what’s happening in terms of the capital.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the uncertainty about it will probably turn out to be more of a problem than the actual reality, but it’s going to take time for us to find out what the actual reality is.

speaker: FISHER
text: May I ask one more question, Mr. Chairman?

speaker: FISHER
text: At the last meeting I asked about commercial paper risk in Europe and got nods of not a great risk.

speaker: FISHER
text: Is there anything that you see or that you can think of that we don’t know or that hasn’t been in this presentation that would indicate significant potential for risk?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would hesitate to say that I know with any great clarity that there’s nothing else there in Europe.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we have all been a bit surprised by the size of some of the conduits that some European banks were sponsoring relative to their capital.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would be very hesitant to say that we have transparency regarding that marketplace and know with certainty that there’s nothing else there.

speaker: STERN
text: I would like to return to the issues that President Plosser raised, which I think are very serious for this Committee.

speaker: STERN
text: Maybe the question is what you would have done differently with the benefit of hindsight to have come closer to the target.

speaker: STERN
text: My “back of the envelope” calculation starting with August 9 or August 10 is that maybe the fed funds rate averaged about 5 percent—so a full ¼ percentage point below the target.

speaker: STERN
text: If you felt constrained to enter the market later in the day because of concerns about adding to turmoil, you certainly could have consulted with the Committee about the tradeoff there.

speaker: STERN
text: But it does seem to me that, when we establish a target, we have an obligation to achieve that target.

speaker: STERN
text: Obviously, early in the period erring on the side of generosity was no problem, but it seemed to me that we gave away some degrees of freedom, shall we say, by the way things proceeded.

speaker: STERN
text: I find that of considerable concern.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I would just reemphasize the fact that we did try to be stingy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Our ex ante provision of reserves was less than what we thought that the market needed, and we thought that would push up the federal funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We do not have control over all the factors that affect the demand for reserves, and unfortunately they consistently came in on the side of adding more reserves into the system than we intended.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That said, we have been pretty consistently trying to push back on the market to get the effective federal funds rate back toward the target, and I think we can say that we made it by the meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think there are very few people in the market today who believe that there’s a stealth easing in the market.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just to reinforce what Bill said—of course, we spent a lot of time thinking through exactly the risks that you are worried about in this context, and we’ll have a lot to reflect on in terms of the nature of the regime and what the legislative authority gives us going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think that Bill and his people really had just a simple choice, which was— particularly at that point late in August and early in September—whether they should have acted in a way that raised the possibility of having fed funds trade significantly above target over this period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If you look at the experience of the other central banks managing this situation in the past six weeks or so and what happened when they prematurely acted in a way that ended with having their rates trade substantially firm to target and the effects of that on behavior and the market, I am completely confident that our guys erred in the right direction.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I also don’t believe, just to reinforce what Bill said, that anybody serious in the markets viewed what the Desk was doing and the behavior regarding where fed funds were traded as having a signaling effect or as constraining the flexibility of the Committee.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is true that you had a bunch of people in mid-August talking about that possibility and wondering whether they should read the very soft trading of fed funds as an indication of the stance of monetary policy going forward, but I think that got sucked out of the market relatively quickly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, I think you’re raising absolutely the right questions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We grapple with those questions every day.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We basically made the judgment that to adopt a much more aggressive stance in being stingy with the reserves at various points in this period would have created too much risk of fed funds trading firm relative to target at a moment when psychology and confidence were very, very fragile.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I really think the experience of other central banks was a good counter example of the cost of the alternative strategy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Now, of course, we will have a chance over time to go back and do a much more detailed review.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Another thing I would say about coming in later in the day is that it’s very important to have some stability in the basic framework with which the Desk operates, particularly after what we did the week before August 17 and on August 17.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: To have a lot of changes at the same time in the standard operating procedures of the Desk would have created more risk of uncertainty about what we were doing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We were trying to find a balance between the imperatives of a relatively steady hand and the risk that you are phrasing in absolutely legitimate questions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We’ll have a chance to reflect on a lot of things after this period, but my own view is that they made exactly the right judgment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One complexity in this whole period is that there is a surprisingly large demand for dollars in Europe, which of course is early in the day.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the fed funds rate was opening very, very high, very tight, and then there were judgments about how to bring it down during the peak trading period of the U.S. markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That led to guesses about how many reserves to inject before the end of the day.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the dysfunction in the normal interbank market process—precautionary demand for dollars in Europe—led to some very unusual stresses early in the day, which complicated Bill’s job considerably.

speaker: FISHER
text: We still love Bill, by the way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Oh, we all love Bill.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For the record, I laughed.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to ask about the term funding market, and I want you to help us understand what we know about that.

speaker: LACKER
text: In typical times, like before this, do we know how much lending was done at term in the fed funds market?

speaker: LACKER
text: Do we know what names were typically involved—is there a flow across the banking system of some particular structure—and what kind of spreads are typical?

speaker: LACKER
text: Then, what have we been observing now, in contrast?

speaker: LACKER
text: Related to this, do we know what names are borrowing at term now?

speaker: LACKER
text: Do we have a sense of the extent to which the elevated spread is a risk premium or some other effect?

speaker: LACKER
text: Are people who are borrowing at term tapped out at the Home Loan Bank?

speaker: LACKER
text: Does that have some significance in the term market?

speaker: LACKER
text: Is there an interaction between options at the Home Loan Bank and the term market?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the question about volume, there’s no question that volume went up considerably in the overnight market—about 20 percent, as near as we can judge over this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Since the term market was mostly shut down, especially in term fed funds, there has been very little in term fed funds trading.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You can almost infer that most volume is done overnight but probably 20 percent or so is done term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Almost all of that crowded back into the overnight market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So there was an increase, as near as we can measure, of about 20 percent in overnight fed funds activity over the past month compared with normal.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, in terms of who is actually borrowing at term—well, very few people were actually borrowing at term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There was probably a bit of a “lemons” problem in the term market in the sense that—because term rates were elevated and those rates were not very attractive economically—your wanting to borrow in the term market was a sign that you were probably not in good shape in terms of your own liquidity position.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that contributed to the shutdown of the term market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because of the economics really—why are you doing that unless you’re in bad shape and you really need the funds?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that contributed to the shrinking of the term market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Really two things were going on.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One, banks that had the funds to lend didn’t want to lend term because they weren’t sure what they would need that money for down the road, depending on what was going to come onto their balance sheets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Two, people who wanted to borrow term were the least attractive borrowers.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That caused the market to essentially dry up over this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think it is starting to come back.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We’re not back to normal because obviously the term rates are still somewhat elevated relative to the overnight rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it’s still not that attractive from an economic perspective, but it is certainly more attractive than it was even a week ago.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I could just follow up, I know the Desk tracks overnight fed funds trades, and you get from the dealers the quantities at different rates in order to calculate the effective rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Are you inferring term volume from that, or do we have any other independent quantitative sources on the volume of term funding?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I haven’t actually seen any volume data on term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They may, in fact, exist.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: What we did, though, is look at the volume in the overnight federal funds market, and we saw that go up about 20 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So if you start with the premise that the banks that have excess funds to lend aren’t going to change much month to month, you can pretty much infer that most of it is coming out of the term market.

speaker: LACKER
text: Both large banks in our District have gone from being net borrowers to being large net lenders.

speaker: LACKER
text: One, in fact, says it’s the largest in the market and lends $10 billion to $15 billion every night overnight, and they used to borrow a couple of billion dollars every day.

speaker: LACKER
text: Could something like that account for the volume in the funds market?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, obviously that moves in that direction, but if I remember correctly, the number on the volume of the fed funds market is in the $400 billion to $500 billion range.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Twenty percent on that kind of level is quite a bit bigger than what you’re seeing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That would include brokered trades and nonbrokered trades.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But, Mr. Chairman, if I’m not mistaken, I think that the term market for interbank liquidity is largely offshore in Europe, not in fed funds onshore.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I’m not sure that helps when we get into this context.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was asking about the demand.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was curious about what we know about the domestic part.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our research people have tried to figure out whether they could infer or take from Fedwire data other indications of who’s lending at what maturities and who’s borrowing at what maturities and what the balance is.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My own sense from looking at this, and maybe I just haven’t figured it out yet, is that it doesn’t give you the kind of clarity that you were looking for.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s an over-the-counter market, and in most over-the-counter markets we do not have the kind of volume data we would like to have.

speaker: LACKER
text: Just one tiny thing—in the overnight market, from the brokers, we have volumes traded at different rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: For the term fed funds rate, which is showing up in a graph or two—I can’t remember where—does that come off broker screens?

speaker: LACKER
text: We don’t have trades on that, do we?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t know the answer to that.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: There is not a regular data source.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there other questions for Bill?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, I need a vote to ratify domestic open market operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: May we turn now to the staff presentation on the economic situation?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Dave Stockton and Karen Johnson will start with the economic overview, and then Brian will make a few comments on the projections that we submitted.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: “This has been a far from placid time.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, the intermeeting period has been marked by financial tumult of such a magnitude as to significantly alter the outlook for the economy.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: A deeper retrenchment in U.S. stock markets, more-cautious credit provision, and more-serious disruptions to economic growth abroad are now expected to combine to produce a sharper deceleration in output than we had projected in August.” These words were taken from the first page in the Greenbook of September 1998.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: While the particulars obviously differ in many important respects from that period, we once again face substantial financial turbulence; and once again, we have marked down our projection of real activity on the expectation that recent financial developments will impart considerable restraint on activity in the quarters ahead.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Before explaining these changes, let me read to you from the first page of another Greenbook, and I quote: “[T]he economy has continued to exhibit remarkable dynamism, generating hefty gains in employment and income.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have tacked about ¾ percentage point onto our previous forecast of first-quarter real GDP growth, and the evident momentum of domestic demand has led us to elevate our projection for output growth over the near term a bit as well.” That passage was taken from the Greenbook of March 1999, just six months after the onset of that period of financial disturbance.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Needless to say, the experience of that episode was not lost on us as we approached the construction of the current forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But neither were the episodes of the summer of 1990 and the fall of 2000, when we thought financial and other factors would result in a period of below-trend growth but that outright recession would be avoided.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So the question is, Are we projecting too much or too little weakness in real activity over the next several quarters?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Answering that question has two aspects.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One is whether we have correctly gauged the magnitude of the potential restraint on real activity arising from the recent developments in mortgage and other credit markets.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other is whether we have appropriately assessed the underlying strength of the economy being subjected to those shocks.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think it’s fair to say that part of our mistake in 1998 was a failure to appreciate just how strong the U.S. economy was as we entered that period.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Could we be making that mistake again?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The incoming data did lead us to revise up our estimates of the growth in real GDP in the second and third quarters by ¼ and ½ percentage point, respectively.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Most notably, consumer spending has surprised us to the upside.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Last Friday’s report on retail sales provided another positive innovation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Although the spending figures for August were right in line with our expectations, the upward revision to July suggests that the growth of real PCE in the third quarter will be about ¼ percentage point stronger than we projected in last week’s Greenbook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Elsewhere, the growth of exports has continued to outstrip our expectations, providing greater impetus to domestic production.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That added impetus may help explain factory output, which has also been a bit stronger, on net, than anticipated in our August projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Manufacturing IP excluding motor vehicles is estimated to have fallen 0.3 percent last month, but that decline came on the heels of upward-revised increases of 0.7 percent in June and July.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are now projecting manufacturing IP excluding motor vehicles to have increased 4¾ percent in the third quarter, a bit more than in our August forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Not all the news, however, has been favorable.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Despite a rebound in motor vehicle sales in August, the automakers still found themselves with uncomfortably high inventories at the end of the summer and have announced substantial reductions in assembly schedules for the fourth quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In our projection, the cut in motor vehicle production lops ½ percentage point off the growth of real GDP in the fourth quarter, about ¼ percentage point more than we had earlier expected.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The labor market report also was a bit weaker than we had penciled into our projection at the time of the August FOMC meeting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Private payrolls increased just 24,000 last month, which, combined with downward revisions in June and July, left the level of employment about 100,000 shy of our expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nevertheless, we didn’t attach a great deal of signal to the employment report in terms of its implications for real activity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, despite the fact that real GDP was coming in close to our expectations most of this year, we had been fairly consistently surprised to the upside by employment.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For the most part, we had attributed that surprising strength to an unusual degree of labor hoarding that was resulting in a more-pronounced cyclical sag in productivity than is typical.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now that the employment figures have softened, we are inclined to let much of that softness show through in higher labor productivity rather than weaker output.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Still, there is no denying that labor demand over the past three months now looks a bit weaker than we expected.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We see the incoming data taken together as suggesting that there was a bit more strength to the expansion through the summer than we had earlier recognized.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we have seen little to suggest that the economy was either gathering any momentum or seriously faltering as we entered the period of increased financial turbulence.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, getting the starting point right for the projection is important.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the main action in this forecast has been our reaction to developments in mortgage and other credit markets.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I would love to dazzle you this morning with precise scientific estimates of the effects on spending and activity of difficulties involving subprime mortgages, structured-investment vehicles, leveraged loans, and the like.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But, sadly, that will not be the case.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Rather, because you seem to be on the brink of joining me in the humbling world of forecasting, I thought that I would invite you to don your hair nets and white butcher smocks and join me for a tour of the sausage factory.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The difficulty we confronted in this forecast is that, even after decades worth of research on credit channels and financial accelerators—much of it done by economists at all levels in the Federal Reserve System—the financial transmission mechanisms in most of the workhorse macro models that we use for forecasting are still rudimentary.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As a result, much of what has occurred doesn’t even directly feed into our models.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But that doesn’t mean that it isn’t important.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, the residuals in our main spending equations seem to be negatively correlated with measures of financial stress.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In other words, our models tend to overpredict spending in periods of financial disturbance.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: To be sure, that general tendency is not evident in all episodes.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Shortfalls in spending were sizable in the “headwinds” period of the early 1990s and in the aftermath of the stock market collapse in the early part of this decade.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we have found little evidence of any material effects on spending during the 1998-99 episode.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In very broad terms, we were guided in our revisions to the forecast by the average historical tendency of these spending equations to overpredict in periods of financial stress.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As for the specifics, we made adjustments in those areas that seem most likely to be affected in this particular episode.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Housing, of course, is at the epicenter of the current financial shock.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In response to the intensifying problems in mortgage markets and the increasingly bleak anecdotes, we slashed our housing forecast significantly further.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We now expect new home sales to drop another 18 percent by the end of this year and single-family starts to drop another 25 percent by early next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If this forecast comes to pass, this housing downturn will come close to matching in severity that of the late 1970s and early 1980s.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Underlying this projection is an assumption that nonprime originations will remain virtually dead in coming months and stage only a modest and partial rebound over the next year and a half.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We also expect some of the spillover that we have seen recently in prime jumbo mortgages to persist for a while, though the effects on housing demand from this part of the market are likely to be much smaller.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, in contrast to the partial recovery in nonprime mortgage originations, we are expecting a full recovery in jumbo mortgages to occur by early 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, our estimates of the effects emanating from nonprime and jumbo markets are subject to considerable uncertainty—in terms of both depth and duration.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As for the rest of the economy, we don’t think it will escape entirely unscathed by the recent turmoil in financial markets, and we have made some modest downward adjustments also to business investment and consumer spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In particular, we have marked down a bit our forecast for nonresidential construction on the expectation that higher borrowing costs and tighter underwriting standards will hold down the volume of commercial real estate lending and construction activity in coming quarters.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In that regard, we have already seen some increase in “busted contracts” for commercial property transactions.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Like the effects in residential mortgage markets, the restraining influences on commercial construction are assumed to fade by the end of next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have also revised down our projection for equipment spending, but here the story is a bit different because we are not really anticipating a spillover that will result in significant funding problems for most nonfinancial firms.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Rather, in previous forecasts, we had incorporated an extra dollop of spending growth to reflect the general strength of corporate balance sheets and the tendency of some of our models to underpredict equipment spending over the past few years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: With heightened uncertainty and less favorable financial conditions, we have moved the E&S forecast down closer to the models in both our August and our September forecasts.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Finally, we made a modest downward adjustment to our consumption forecast, in part to account for the likelihood of some tightening of terms and standards on consumer lending and for the possibility that weaker home prices may make it more difficult or expensive for households to finance consumption through the equity in their homes.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We also assume that there will be some hit to consumer sentiment in an economy with a weakening labor market, ongoing strains in financial markets, and continuing downbeat news on house prices, home sales, and foreclosures.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The restraint imposed by these factors is assumed to fade over the next year—again, on much the same schedule as we are expecting the financial restraints to lessen.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think we have the sign right here, but I must admit that this element of our forecast seems the most problematic to me.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: To be sure, we’ve already seen a fall in consumer sentiment that, if sustained, would imply a drag on spending going forward that is at least as large as is incorporated in our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Still, the direct fallout of recent developments for the cost and availability of consumer credit could be quite limited, and consumer sentiment could recover more quickly than is assumed in the baseline.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I would be more worried about the upside risks of this aspect of our projection if I didn’t also see some sizable downside risks to other elements of our baseline forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: First, even with the 5 percent decline we have projected over the next two years, house prices will remain at historically high levels relative to rents.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: With foreclosures increasing, there is a clear risk that the drop in home prices could well be deeper and faster than we expect.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Second, implicit in our forecast is the assumption that we are experiencing the worst of the financial turmoil now; there would seem to be more downside risk than upside risk to this assumption.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Finally, we are still projecting what amounts to a very soft landing: The unemployment rate rises by a few tenths, growth converges to potential, and inflation levels out near current rates.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Such an outcome would be nearly unprecedented.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Turning to our inflation forecast, we did not receive any news that materially affected our outlook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Both headline and core PCE prices in July came in a bit lower than we had been forecasting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For the most part, the key conditioning factors governing our inflation projection changed little over the intermeeting period.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Food and energy prices were nearly unrevised; nonoil import prices were a touch lower, reflecting lower commodity prices; and most measures of inflation expectations have been roughly unchanged.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The only adjustment of note in our inflation forecast was the ¼ percentage point reduction that we made in our estimate of the NAIRU.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We did so because of some tendency of our wage and price equations to overpredict inflation over the past few years and because we’ve seen a continuation of some of the structural forces in labor markets that we thought had lowered the NAIRU in earlier periods.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The adjustment also better aligns our estimate of the NAIRU with other readings of labor market tightness.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: All told, some slack in resource utilization now emerges in this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: However, because the estimated slope of our aggregate supply function is quite flat and inflation expectations are expected to remain reasonably well anchored, this change is pretty small potatoes for our price forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, it trimmed only 0.1 percentage point from our forecast of overall and core PCE price inflation in both 2008 and 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That concludes my tour of the sausage factory.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I hope it was somewhat revealing, though I recognize that sausage factories can test the convictions of even the most ardent proponents of full transparency.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Karen will now continue our presentation.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In the International Division, we, too, were challenged to assess the avalanche of events and information that arrived during the intermeeting period and to make our best judgment as to how these developments would affect the rest of the global economy and the U.S. external sector.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: One striking feature of the baseline forecast that resulted is the difference between prospects for the industrial countries and those for the emerging-market economies.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: For the industrial countries, the surprises in the latest data were generally negative, and considerable financial turmoil has been evident in the markets in the euro area, the United Kingdom, and Canada.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In contrast, the most recent surprises in economic data for the emerging-market economies have generally been positive, and so far there has been little evidence of financial disruption in those countries.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: We have revised down total foreign growth a bit less than ½ percentage point for the second half of this year and ¼ percentage point for next year.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: This downward revision is due entirely to revisions to projected average growth in the industrial countries.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The foreign industrial countries are largely being spared the direct effects of contraction in the residential construction sector so far.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But they are vulnerable to negative effects on the pace of overall economic activity from increased volatility and impaired functionality in financial markets.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: As market participants have demanded higher returns for risky assets and have withdrawn from some exposures, many asset prices in Europe and Canada have fallen sharply.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: As in the United States, these developments have had implications for bank balance sheets and earnings, as banks have experienced calls on lines of credit or have taken other steps in response to funding difficulties of conduits and other entities sponsored by them.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Some markets have experienced severe disruption, particularly European ABCP and a portion of the Canadian ABCP market.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Although it is too soon for us to have actual data on the consequences of stresses being put on bank balance sheets, we think it is likely that some constraint on credit extension will result.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In addition, business and consumer confidence could well be impaired by the general awareness of heightened risk and uncertainty as strains persist in financial markets.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: We have very little historical experience on which to base a projection of the magnitude of these effects.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Our downward revision of the forecast for real GDP growth in the industrial countries in response to recent financial market events has been small, but we acknowledge that recent financial events have been severe and have lasted long enough that they likely will have some effect on domestic demand in the affected countries.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Other channels of transmission from developments over the intermeeting period are more straightforward.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The downward revision to U.S. real output growth causes us to lessen projected export demand growth in our trading partners; for Canada, this channel could be particularly strong.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In exchange markets, the intermeeting period has seen upward pressure emerge on the euro, with the dollar-euro rate reaching new highs.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: This euro appreciation should weaken demand by other countries for exports from the euro area.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The downward revision of real growth in the United States and in other industrial countries should, in turn, reduce demand for exports from emerging- market economies.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Economic indicators of activity from months before August have also led us to revise down projected growth in the major foreign industrial countries.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In Canada, both retail sales and real manufacturing shipments fell in June.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In Japan, second- quarter real GDP growth has been revised to show a decline of more than 1 percent at an annual rate, and industrial production and real household expenditures fell in July.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In the euro area, some moderation in expansion is implied by recent data: Real GDP decelerated in the second quarter, and a number of measures of business sentiment, some of which contain responses after August 9, have moved lower.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Taking all this together, we revised down our outlook for real GDP growth in the foreign industrial countries, with the change for the second half negative ½ percentage point at an annual rate.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Accordingly, we now expect that monetary tightening measures in those countries this year and next, which we and the markets had been projecting in August, will not occur except in Japan.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The upward revision of our figure for average second-quarter real GDP growth in the emerging-market economies from 6 percent at an annual rate to about 7½ percent is indicative of the magnitude of positive surprises we received about activity in these regions.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The news was broadly based across Asia, Latin America, and other areas.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Importantly, at the time of the August Greenbook, we had already received data on China’s nearly 15 percent real growth in the second quarter, so the developments underlying this upward revision arose outside China.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Our forecast calls for real growth in the emerging-market economies to slow to a more sustainable pace of nearly 5 percent over the forecast period from the very rapid second-quarter outcome.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: We judge that, going forward, the upward boost provided by faster activity earlier this year is about offset by the implications of the weaker outlook for the United States and other industrial country economies, and so our projection for real expansion in the emerging world is about unchanged from August.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: At this time, we do not see sufficient evidence of financial stress in these countries to warrant incorporating into the forecast restraint from credit channels or from confidence effects.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: We do recognize that there are risks to the moderately strong forecast we have for the emerging-market economies.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: On the upside, with the pace of growth so strong in China, we may once again find that the government is unable to put in place sufficient restraint to cause a discrete step-down in real output growth there.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: However, Chinese stock prices have continued to rise very sharply, and we see a possible downside risk to growth from a bursting of that bubble with consequent effects on real spending.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: It is also possible that we are underestimating the spillover of contractionary pressures from the industrial countries onto activity in the rest of the world.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: For example, one channel by which such forces could weaken activity in Mexico more than we now expect is through reduced remittances.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: With the U.S. construction sector particularly weak, earnings of immigrant labor and remittances to Mexico could be reduced, and the result could be a slowing of growth in Mexico by more than we have forecast.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Another element of the forecast worth a brief mention is the price of crude oil.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The price for spot WTI recently surged above $80 per barrel as recent data on U.S. inventories and some signs of hurricane activity led market participants to bid up prices for very near term oil.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: However, prices further out on the futures curve have moved down since August, and our overall path for the price of U.S. oil imports is little changed to down slightly by the end of 2008.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: With the futures curve showing pronounced backwardation, the spot price is very sensitive to unfolding news.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Should a serious hurricane or some other factor threaten near-term production, we could see an outsized reaction in the spot price of crude oil.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: With the shock to the global economy this time arising largely in the U.S. economy, it is fitting that we might look to the rest of the world to provide some support to overall demand, some contribution to stabilizing global economic activity in general, and some help in damping rather than augmenting fluctuations in U.S. economic activity.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: As we now read the evidence, such an outcome is likely this time.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Strength in the most recent data has led us to revise up projected real export growth in the third quarter.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Although foreign GDP growth has been revised down a bit, thereby weakening exports, the dollar is on a path slightly lower than in August; and relative prices should provide a bit more boost to exports than we previously thought.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: All in all, the contribution to U.S. real GDP growth from exports should be somewhat more positive over the forecast period than we expected in August despite the global financial turmoil.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: If the Greenbook forecast is realized, net exports should make a positive arithmetic contribution to U.S. real GDP growth of about ⅓ percentage point during the second half of this year and about ¼ percentage point next year.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Brian will now continue our remarks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2 I will be referring to the table in the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on September Trial-Run Projections.” I will first focus on the near term.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The upper panel of the table shows the forecasts for the second half of the year that are implied by the estimates that you submitted for the first half of 2007 and your projections for the year as a whole.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Participants revised down their expectations for real GDP growth in the second half of 2007 by several tenths of a percentage point.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you cited the steeper-than-expected downturn in housing markets and tighter credit conditions as key factors.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The downward revision to output growth was accompanied by a slight upward revision to the unemployment rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your forecast for total inflation in the second half of this year was revised down noticeably, but the central tendency for core inflation was unrevised.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Almost all of you conditioned your outlook on near-term monetary policy easing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A slight majority characterized the Greenbook’s assumption of a 50 basis point near-term reduction in the target funds rate as appropriate monetary policy, but almost as many think a somewhat larger cumulative decline will prove appropriate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The lower panel shows your annual forecasts.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendency for GDP growth in 2008 was revised down about ¼ percentage point and now centers on about 2¼ percent rather than 2½ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendency for the unemployment rate at the end of the year revised up 0.2 percentage point.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your total inflation forecast for next year edged down 0.1 percentage point, but the central tendency of your core projections was unchanged.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You also again characterized your views of uncertainty relative to historical norms and skews.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Those views presumably apply primarily to the relatively near term outlook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you again see risks to growth as tilted to the downside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In contrast, almost all of you now see inflation risks as roughly balanced rather than as tilted to the upside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A majority of you judge that the uncertainty attending the prospects for economic activity is greater than has been typical in the past.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Looking further ahead, the projections for 2009 changed little.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For the first time, you submitted forecasts for 2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The forecasts for those years and your commentary suggest that most of you see actual and potential GDP growth over that period at around 2½ percent, a bit above the staff’s estimate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The unemployment rate hovers just below 5 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: (Let me note at this point that in the table there is a typo in the 2009 column for the unemployment rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendency of August projections should read 4.7 to 5.0 percent.)

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With the unemployment rate just a bit above the 4¾ percent that a number of you have identified as your estimate of the NAIRU, both core inflation and total inflation are expected to edge lower in the out years—at least if you squint hard and focus particularly on the lower bound of the central tendencies.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your forecasts for core and total inflation in 2009 are essentially unrevised—not surprisingly, if you view those forecasts as reflecting to an important 2 Materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The relatively narrow central tendencies and ranges for total and core inflation in 2009 and 2010 suggest substantial agreement in your views on this score.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Mr. Stockton has been reading Upton Sinclair, I think.

speaker: EVANS
text: Dave, your presentation seemed to hit on all the right points with regard to the forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am reminded, though, that Chicago is no longer the hog butcher capital of the world.

speaker: EVANS
text: Still, I have a forecasting question.

speaker: EVANS
text: In the briefing yesterday, you quantified the financial stress effects on GDP growth that you talked about this morning as about ½ percentage point in the second half of this year and about ½ percentage point in 2008.

speaker: EVANS
text: Having read the alternative simulations for a number of years, I know it is not uncommon for an alternative that starts off with financial difficulties to have a small effect on the outlook, then there is a layering on of the consumer sentiment and it drops off a little more.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I am curious about sorting out these components with an idea toward, if the policy action were taken as a form of insurance against these risks, what the early warning signs that those insurance reasons are really no longer critical would be.

speaker: EVANS
text: Would we quickly see objective measures of the turnaround?

speaker: EVANS
text: Is consumer sentiment the key?

speaker: EVANS
text: Presumably, financial conditions would be a little more evident in their improvement.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In this particular forecast, the housing revision is basically all driven off our assumptions about the difficulties in financial markets.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There are no additional sentiment-type effects there.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On commercial real estate, I’d say pretty much the same thing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As I noted in my briefing, the area where we have ventured into a looser sort of approach would be on the consumer spending side, where we are not really expecting a significant amount.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We would expect some restraint on consumer lending and consumer borrowing associated with tighter underwriting, so there will be some increase in cost.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But I don’t think those effects are likely to be large.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Here we are relying more on an assumption that some disturbance to consumer sentiment will persist into next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One thing that I would be looking for—for that piece of the forecast to be wrong and, therefore, for there to be more underlying strength in the economy—would be a quicker rebound in consumer sentiment and a moving up to the low 90s in relatively short order.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That piece of what we built into the forecast would look to be questionable and might be worth a couple of tenths on the level of GDP next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other area where I would be looking if I were in your shoes and auditing our forecast is that we are expecting the labor market to be quite weak moving into the fourth quarter and, by the end of the fourth quarter, no employment growth, basically flat employment.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Thus far, we have seen some uptick in initial claims for unemployment insurance.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That seems consistent with some of the slowing that we have already seen.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But I think we would have to see a further rise there to be consistent with the weakness that we are expecting in the labor markets.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If that were not to occur, it would suggest, again, that we are likely to be off the mark on the weakness in activity that we are projecting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I would say that those two areas would be at the top of my list for monitoring the weakness of the forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The factory sector would be the final area where I think, again, we get relatively timely information—some of it physical product data, not just data based on the labor market.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are expecting things to be a little weaker than they were in the middle of the summer but not so weak as they were in August.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: However, if we saw continued strength there, I think that would suggest some inconsistency with the weakness of our forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My first question was very much related to what Charlie just asked.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First let me say that I appreciate the tour of the sausage factory.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It was a little bloody, but I want to commend you in that I think it was a fairly balanced way of looking at what the risks are in various places.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I want to come back to my interpretation of what you just said.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Your answer to President Evans sounded to me as though a significant part of your downward revision, particularly to consumption, was the factor of consumer sentiment, which is looming rather large in this forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While you’ve revised down some other things, it sounded as though you were saying that consumer sentiment is a particularly sensitive and difficult thing to forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We know it is very volatile; it can change rapidly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I heard you say that in the forecast you have implicitly reduced consumer spending and held it low for a period of time into the forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Am I misinterpreting your answer there?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I mean, we expect some recovery.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We weren’t expecting that August figure to prevail through the forecast period.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If that were to occur, we would be looking at an even weaker outlook than we are seeing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, in all these things, I don’t want to make it sound too precise, but we do think underwriting standards and the cost of consumer credit are likely to increase, and that rise is likely to impinge on consumer spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In our models, the fed funds rate shows up in our consumption equation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have some consumption equations that we run with consumer credit rates.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: They don’t actually do any better than our standard equation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So we have added a little for something that we think is outside the model on consumption, probably operating through the credit channel.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But I don’t want to deny that in some sense, again, if we saw a significant rebound in consumer sentiment from its current levels into the low 90s, it would be inconsistent with what we are currently forecasting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That would be a significant change from the standpoint of how you are viewing the forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That would raise the forecast, as I said.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My impression from studies and empirical work is that consumer sentiment usually is a much bigger coincident indicator than it is a forecasting tool.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Yes, it helps for forecasting near-term consumption.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But you are right, I don’t think the low level of consumer sentiment that we have seen through the middle of September is telling us a great deal about where consumer spending will be early next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There is not a lot of predictive content that way.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Therefore, in some sense, to be consistent with the forecast, we would have to continue to expect that consumers are going to be worried and more downbeat.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, while I would say that’s obviously a significant source of uncertainty, I don’t think that’s necessarily unreasonable in an environment where there will continue to be a lot of bad news and where the bad news is compounded with a weakening labor market and some things that could lead to some extra-model type of restraint.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The other question I had has more to do with the NAIRU and employment issues.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wish you could clarify a bit for me—the downward shift in employment numbers for the past three months is for me significant.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the same time, I say to myself, “Well, you know, now it is about at the level that the Board has been forecasting all along.” In your previous discussions you have talked about participation rates and other things, and now the level seems to be about where you had been predicting it all along.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yet you still interpret that as bad news from the economy point of view.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would like a little discussion of that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The second thing is that, at the same time, you have lowered the NAIRU.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am a bit puzzled and would like a little discussion about the interaction between those two things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Finally—and you may have said this, but I may have missed it—if you had not changed the NAIRU, would inflation have been 0.1 or 0.2 percentage point higher over the forecast period?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Or what would it have been?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just need a little clarification.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On that last point, I think it probably would have been a little higher.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But if we hadn’t revised the NAIRU, we might also have had a higher unemployment forecast going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It wouldn’t be just like “everything else equal” if we lowered the NAIRU.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think it did contribute to a slightly larger output gap in this forecast, but also contributing to the larger output gap in this forecast was a weakening of activity relative to potential that we are assuming is going to be driven by this.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are really splitting hairs because, as I indicated, we changed the forecast only 0.1 in each year, but it would have been a little less than that had we not changed the NAIRU.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the first point about our interpretation of employment, I was trying to convey a sense that a lot of people were very surprised at how weak employment was.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have been expecting weak employment.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think we were less surprised.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We also, as I indicated, had written off some of this weakness in employment as sort of extracyclical labor hoarding, and we hadn’t really bought in fully to that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We let that show through in lower labor productivity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now that we have actually seen some of the weakness that we were expecting all along, we don’t think there was as much labor hoarding as we previously thought.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So it wasn’t as big a surprise.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Still, there is just no denying the fact that the labor market report was weaker.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Even if we had gone back to where we were, we weren’t expecting things to be that weak.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I think there was some small negative signal attached to the labor market report but probably not as much as would be suggested by the market reaction.

speaker: POOLE
text: What do we know about the likelihood of an auto strike, what might come out of it, and how long it might last?

speaker: POOLE
text: Second, Karen, my sense is that the financial markets in the United Kingdom are probably the most disrupted of any of the industrial economies.

speaker: POOLE
text: Perhaps you could comment a bit more on that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So thus far—unless something has happened while we have been sitting here that I don’t know about and you do—I think things look reasonably encouraging on the labor front with the auto negotiations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are not expecting a strike; in fact, we are expecting them to work through the final details.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, the creation of the trust fund for health expenditures is one of the biggest remaining issues.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the fact that it is still on the table and is still being actively discussed leads us to think that a strike is not likely at this point.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The situation in the United Kingdom is an unfolding drama that is just a soap opera in many respects.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: At the root there seem to be some severe differences of opinion of what the right response is to situations in the markets.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In the beginning, there was virtually no explicit action by the Bank of England to counter heightened demand for liquidity on the part of banks in U.K. markets.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: So the spreads of overnight pound LIBOR, relative to target, opened up widely, and they were not addressed.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: They were allowed to just sort of sit there.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The term pound market had a problem, too.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Of course, many of the dollar issues that we have spoken of— and that Bill talked about—are really being captured as a London phenomenon.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But you might say that, from the point of view of the Bank of England or the U.K. economy, these dollar issues are somewhat separate from the domestic economy.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: There is some truth to that, but also the institutions are involved, the institutions have obligations, and the shocks to the institutions reverberate back into the domestic economy, it seems to me.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: That process went on for a while, and it is to some degree a function of the way the Bank of England manages its reserves and the system of reserve market interaction that exists.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: It has, among other features, a monthly timetable, not a two-week timetable; so even though the Bank of England operates daily in the sense that we do, it ties its own hands a bit each month.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Toward the end of the month in which August 9 occurred, it announced that the subsequent month it was going to ease things just a bit in response to a lot of pressure both perhaps from disagreements inside the bank and criticisms of the bank.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: It has taken some steps to provide for greater flexibility within its existing system than it had for the three weeks before the month turnover in August.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Indeed, the Bank of England did a two-day operation last night, or this morning U.K. time, which is the first temporary extra injection of reserves it had done on this basis.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: So it is moving in the direction of introducing flexibility into the market that was not there on August 9 and wasn’t there for some time after August 9.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: I think there is a great concern in the Bank of England, or certainly in the person of Mervyn King, with the moral hazard aspects of enabling the markets to solve their problems and deal with the consequences of their own decisions by the Bank of England’s providing them more liquidity.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: That lies behind some of his reluctance.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: On the other hand, we now have the Northern Rock issue.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: That is somewhat distinct from the problems of overnight lending or even term lending, in that Northern Rock has been questionable for a while, has been looked at for a while, has been kind of talked about a bit, but has not really been on anybody’s radar screen for a while.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: It is an institution that funded itself to an exceptional extent in wholesale markets as opposed to from a deposit base, and yet it had grown to be a very, very large mortgage lender in the United Kingdom.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: One might say that it is a bad coincidence that somehow Northern Rock hit a turning point this month, but that is perhaps going too far.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: I think the fact that the wholesale markets were disrupted had to interact with its business plan, had to be part of the reason that concerns that have been festering for a while became acute, and so forth.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The actions that the Bank of England took with respect to Northern Rock were really from its lender-of-last-resort institution-based mechanisms as opposed to market concerns.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But they came out basically on the same day.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: They announced that they were going to introduce flexibility into their reserves management system, and a different announcement was all about Northern Rock.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: They got it wrong on Northern Rock, quite understandably.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: That, too, was a function of their deposit insurance system, which is now under review because it is prone to this sort of thing.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: It was just, if you will, one thing after another, all of which are interacting.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: We have revised down somewhat our U.K. GDP forecast.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In general, the industrial countries are where we see the weakness.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: That economy was, in terms of domestic demand, pretty strong.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: We think it can absorb some of this.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But the set of factors is very complex—some of them are deep and structural, like the way they do deposit insurance; some of them have been ongoing for a while; and some of them are related to this crisis.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: I think the differences of opinion among the Financial Services Authority, the Treasury, and the Bank of England aren’t helping, the differences of opinion within the Bank of England aren’t helping, and the situation remains to be totally sorted out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I see a two-handed intervention.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Just a question, really, for Bill and Brian.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One thing that is positive about all of this—although maybe I’m wrong about it—is that the spillovers into the other markets outside the United Kingdom have been very, very minor.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Normally, what’s happening in the U.K. context would be an information shock that could trigger problems.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The good news here is that, if anything, the markets have actually gotten a little better since this whole episode occurred, and it has been contained in the U.K. context.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Is this a fair assessment?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, I agree with that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is really an important issue.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Three weeks ago, if this had happened, I think there would have been a different market reaction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The market reaction has been very mild.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They seem to be able to sort it out as a specific problem pertaining to Northern Rock and the U.K. regulatory regime, not something that applies to a broader market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I agree with that.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But, I have to say—as when President Fisher asked that question about whether we know what we don’t know, to which, of course, the answer is always “no”— [laughter] five days ago, I wouldn’t have brought up Northern Rock.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: So, I can’t promise you that there aren’t—

speaker: FISHER
text: Previously Newcastle, should have been called Sandcastle.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The Spanish banks, for example, and the Spanish mortgage market are places, if I were going to dig deeper and look for hidden problems, that are a possibility.

speaker: FISHER
text: I won’t ask a silly question like the one I asked before.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just have two quick questions, one for Dave, and the other for Karen.

speaker: FISHER
text: When we look at the labor situation, from an analytical standpoint, it seems to me that there is cognitive dissonance between that and what we are hearing anecdotally.

speaker: FISHER
text: What I’m hearing anecdotally—and I will talk a bit about that in a minute, but I’d like your viewpoint—are still complaints about labor shortages, from bank tellers to chemical workers to hotel maids, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.

speaker: FISHER
text: You see it in the Beige Book.

speaker: FISHER
text: You hear it from the CEOs with whom I’ve talked.

speaker: FISHER
text: You see it District by District.

speaker: FISHER
text: How do you square these two corners, Dave?

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s my question for you.

speaker: FISHER
text: Then, for Karen, my question is this: You talked about the non-industrial country growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would submit, by the way, that those are the industrial countries now in terms of how they are fueling their growth; what we call “industrial” countries are service-driven economies.

speaker: FISHER
text: Setting that aside, you talked about the impact on growth, and you mentioned oil in particular.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would like to get your views on the potential inflationary impact from the kind of demand growth that we are seeing and the growth that you are projecting elsewhere in the world.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The way I square the corners is that, even by our estimates, the labor market is still tight.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The 4½ percent unemployment is still below the 4¾ that we are estimating the NAIRU to be.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Even on our forecast of the labor market, the unemployment rate doesn’t get to the NAIRU until the middle of next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So it wouldn’t surprise me if some complaints about availability of labor linger for a while here.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The labor market, even with our weak employment forecast, only gradually begins to loosen up.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Really not until next year would we have something approaching an equilibrium in the labor market and then beyond that before we got some slack.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think there is sort of a level versus a change issue here.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The current state of the labor market is tight, even though we are forecasting it to deteriorate going forward.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: I think there are some inflation risks out there.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In general, Mexico, say, or Brazil—some of the countries that target inflation—are operating pretty near their target, maybe even a tiny bit above it.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: One of the pre-August but sort of persistent problems we have been facing for about six to nine months, maybe even for a year, has been to understand food prices.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Why does everybody say that our inflation is up but it is food prices?

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Sometimes it’s hog disease in China, and sometimes it’s an allusion to biofuel issues or other kinds of one-off things that you might see in some emerging-market countries.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But the strength of demand in these economies—and Asia is really operating at a very high level of capacity and at a very strong growth rate—raises the potential for upward pressure on prices in some of these countries.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Now, China is obviously an outlier in this regard, right?

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The numbers are crazy; the numbers aren’t trusted.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Again, the government says it is food.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But if most of the food is domestically produced and food is approximately one-third of the weight in their CPI, maybe that’s where you ought to look.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The most important thing you can do with respect to trying to achieve an inflation objective would be to do something about food prices, either by addressing your supply-side policies or by doing something about the rate of money growth or both.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: So China is a unique case in this regard.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: I think people are very skeptical about some of the data.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: People fear that the inflation problem might be even worse.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: It has always seemed to me that the obvious solution to China’s problem is to let the exchange rate rise.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: It would solve many, many ills, including lowering food prices and getting the inflation rate down.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: I don’t hold out much hope for that.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In places where markets are more effective and where monetary policy works in ways that look more like our experience in the service-sector economies, we are probably going to see some monetary tightening continue to be in place.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Some of those countries are experiencing a little exchange rate appreciation, and that will help.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But I think they are operating with as much inflation as they really want.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The industrial countries probably won’t be doing some of the tightening that we had in mind for them and that the markets anticipated, but some of these emerging markets—India, for example—need to continue tightening, and they need to be very alert on their monetary policy.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: There could be some cases in which their policies aren’t able to do the job or they don’t move quickly enough.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, we are ready for our economic go- round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For President Evans’s benefit, we do have two-handed interventions as a possibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s like the discount window—rarely used but there if you need it.
