speaker: KOHN
text: Is there a stigma, Mr. Chairman?

speaker: HOENIG
text: As far as where conditions are today, I’ll keep my remarks short since they don’t differ a great deal from the Greenbook, Part 2, and the remarks of others.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the District itself, our District continues to do economically well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Energy obviously is a strong factor.

speaker: HOENIG
text: For agriculture, we have even adjusted the earnings numbers up dramatically since February.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Manufacturing has shown strength in August, and services seem to be good.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The surveys we’re doing also suggest those are continuing to do reasonably well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: My outlook in terms of what the reaction is or what we’re seeing in the economy for the national economy is not unlike that, except that the data are more mixed, as described by others.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I won’t go into that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The issue is not so much where we are.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It’s where we’re going to be six and nine months from now, and the issues around that are issues of uncertainty.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Banking conditions in our region, and I think more broadly, are good.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The issues there, as we will talk about later, are issues of balance sheets, liquidity, and such things, which are important considerations to the economy going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That will be an important discussion.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As we survey our businesses looking forward, we see the effects of some of the uncertainty where people, in a broad cross-section, are saying that they have not pulled back on their capital spending or in their hiring plans generally but are in a little more of a wait-and-see mode.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So there is a tendency to want to hold back, and the effects of that are really up in the air.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that’s important for us to consider.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Also, we have seen backing- off from funding commitments that were there.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Just like others, we’re seeing that as well in our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As a result, looking forward, we have reduced our outlook, but not anywhere near as dramatically as the Greenbook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that we will get through this transition and that the economy has enough momentum that it will go forward if confidence hasn’t been lost.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I don’t have quite as pessimistic an outlook going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The other element is the inflation outlook, and I think that inflation should remain relatively modest.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The thing that struck me is that the real rate has increased as inflation has come down over the past year since we last held, and so real rates are actually tighter.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That should have a favorable effect on the inflation outlook and also its own slowing effect in the economy, and I think that will be a very important part of our discussion going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: With that, I’ll just stop for the time being.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, Mr. Chairman, with regard to our District, we continue to grow apparently faster than the rest of the country.

speaker: FISHER
text: There are signs of overbuilding, particularly in the multiresidential and some commercial sector areas.

speaker: FISHER
text: I will give you one data point that focuses the mind, and then I’d like to go on to a broader discussion.

speaker: FISHER
text: In the city of Austin, Texas, between 2000 and 2007, fifty condominium units priced at $1 million or more came on the market.

speaker: FISHER
text: Over that seven-year period, forty of them sold.

speaker: FISHER
text: There are now more than 560 coming onto the market.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have seen a significant boom in construction in all the major cities of our District, and that does give me pause.

speaker: FISHER
text: Nonetheless, we continue to speed along, driven not so much by energy as by medicine and the service sector.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I continue to expect that we will outpace the rest of the country.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are seeing some decline in terms of advanced airline bookings as they affect our District, but they’re not that different from the rest of the United States.

speaker: FISHER
text: What I’d like to address is the broader issue.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I am a little confused as to why we are talking about the economic situation and then skipping a beat before we talk about the proposed discount window facility.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do see the two going hand in hand.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’d like to suggest that we’re navigating a very narrow passage here in something of a fog.

speaker: FISHER
text: David, I think, was honest about that.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the one side is a serious risk of overcompensating in our navigational course and incurring a moral hazard or overcompensating for what is a perceived risk in uncharted waters.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the other side, I think we run the risk of biting off our employment growth responsibility to save our inflation-fighting face.

speaker: FISHER
text: So on the starboard shore we hear a siren called “Very Large Financial Institutions,” which infer that a reduction in the fed funds rate will rescue them from peril, however self-inflicted that peril may have been and despite the fact that they’re well capitalized according to the reports that we have put together.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the other shore, we are relying on navigational charts or uncertain landmarks or—as you said, David—rudimentary tools that are giving us mixed readings.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m going to argue today that we should ease by 25 basis points, Mr. Chairman—I’m just showing my hand early—and indicate through our words that we might tilt the rudder a bit further if needed.

speaker: FISHER
text: Further, I am going to argue that we should defer discussion of the new discount window, and we can get to that later.

speaker: FISHER
text: My concern is that if we fail to ease, we risk steering into a recession, but if we shift the tiller too radically on the fed funds side, I believe that we risk tacking onto that siren call that I mentioned earlier and that we will indulge rather than discipline risky financial behavior.

speaker: FISHER
text: What I’m about to talk about I base on a rather in-depth sounding, just to kill the naval analogy once and for all in this discussion.

speaker: FISHER
text: I sent you and the Vice Chairman a list of the people I consulted.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is also based on what we’re hearing from our economists in the District and in our Bank and, very importantly, on what the Greenbook and the Bluebook have said.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is no question that our contacts report a slowing in the pace that occurs through the third quarter, and they do detect a pulling in of the horns in terms of cost controls; budgetary planning; and U.S. capital expenditures as opposed to foreign cap-ex, which they’re still planning to expand significantly—all in light of the press given to the subprime debacle, financial turmoil, and just a general sense of caution.

speaker: FISHER
text: However, there are some very bright spots, and I’m going to go through these at a bit of length because I think they’re important to recognize.

speaker: FISHER
text: AT&T, for example, a local but significant company says, “We’ve had the best quarter we’ve had on the consumer side, and on the business side it’s the hottest August in history.” Their average revenue per user has risen for the past two quarters after declining for the past two and a quarter years.

speaker: FISHER
text: Texas Instruments, an international company, reports “continued growth on the consumer side, robust industrial growth”—I’m quoting their CFO—and “strong industrial demand” and is struggling to meet demand.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just to go to the other extreme, Brinker International is a middle-income restaurant chain that employs 120,000 and operates throughout the country.

speaker: FISHER
text: Other than weakness in Southern California and Florida, traffic increases in July and August, seasonally adjusted, were “the best in twelve months.” Wal-Mart reports, according to their CEO for U.S. operations, that August was “a perfect retail month.” They’re experiencing no problems with suppliers and no shortage of supply inventory.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are feeling cost pressures from China, which I’ll turn to in just a minute.

speaker: FISHER
text: Disney reports record attendance in their theme parks, very high advanced bookings through next spring, and very strong broadcasting revenues.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are hearing the same from the other broadcasters and companies like Time-Warner, and needless to say, Exxon is a happy place right now.

speaker: FISHER
text: The law firms that we have begun to survey rather thoroughly, reminding ourselves that there are more lawyers than there are auto workers in America, are experiencing a boom in business.

speaker: FISHER
text: In short, if you take the summary offered by the CEO of Time-Warner, who also sits on a significant bank board, as many people know, he says, “I see softness but not precipitous change, whereas the bank board I sit on keeps yelling ‘Incoming.’” From a real Main Street perspective, he said that the changes are marginal.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, to be sure, there are some weaknesses being reported.

speaker: FISHER
text: The one utility I talked to at length is TXU.

speaker: FISHER
text: The housing market has left a bit of a slowdown in demand.

speaker: FISHER
text: Hookups by big industrials, however—steel, aluminum, et cetera—are running very good loads according to their CEO.

speaker: FISHER
text: UPS reports that the package line has been flat to slightly up, with a pickup occurring in July and August.

speaker: FISHER
text: The volume declined 0.2 percent in the first and second quarters, yet that’s against a “gee whiz” first quarter of 2006.

speaker: FISHER
text: July and August have picked up 0.8 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: According to their CFO, “We have not seen an impact from the credit crunch.” The CEO of MasterCard reports a softening, but nothing falling off the cliff.

speaker: FISHER
text: Then JCPenney, which is a middle-third retailer, sees retrenchment in discretionary spending, the so-called appointment shopping.

speaker: FISHER
text: Their back-to-school season was one of the strongest they have seen recently.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you dissect, say, Cisco’s and EDS’s data, you see a significant cutback in IT expenditures by financial institutions, which you would expect—what they call the “big box” financial houses, Citi, Morgan, et cetera—and yet, according to John Chambers, rock solid growth in commercial and service-provider categories.

speaker: FISHER
text: In summary, underlying economic growth, from the standpoint of anecdotal evidence from the contacts I’ve talked to, is stronger than it would appear from the press or from most prognosticators.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that’s one important point to take into consideration.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is also very important, Mr. Chairman, to think of how people react to what they’re seeing.

speaker: FISHER
text: There’s no doubt an effort, if you’re worried about the future, to tighten up on cost of goods sold and to reduce your head count.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet everybody is complaining that there’s a massive shortage of labor in every one of the companies I spoke of but one.

speaker: FISHER
text: The other thing is that you change your strategic approach.

speaker: FISHER
text: One relief that’s been provided here is that the private equity firms have been taken out so that bids of, say, seventeen times EBITDA, which is an actual case, with no due diligence, are no longer the case.

speaker: FISHER
text: Four of the companies I spoke with are now able to make strategic acquisitions, and they plan to proceed.

speaker: FISHER
text: The point is that the economy is not grinding to a halt.

speaker: FISHER
text: I won’t mention lawyers again in this discussion except here, but see how they’re being hired now.

speaker: FISHER
text: Akin Gump, very large firms—they are working on strategic acquisitions, and you can see a ramp- up in the volume that’s occurring there.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I think that’s an important thing to consider.

speaker: FISHER
text: Another very important point to consider is that price pressures have not disappeared.

speaker: FISHER
text: I believe they are being maintained by global demand.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m going to give you just a couple of reference points, and then I’ll stop.

speaker: FISHER
text: As you know, I like to quote the Panamax shipping rates.

speaker: FISHER
text: When we last met, the spot daily rate for a Panamax ship—again, the dry bulk carriers—was $59,000 a day.

speaker: FISHER
text: Port utilization is running at a record high.

speaker: FISHER
text: After ten years of deflation, the major retail sources from China, according to Wal-Mart and other interlocutors, report cost increases running at 2 to 4 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: After ten years of deflation, they’re now inflating slightly.

speaker: FISHER
text: (Although I said I wouldn’t mention lawyers, but just so you know, for the first time in history in Los Angeles, New York, and Dallas, all beginning lawyers start at $160,000.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think they are raising it to $180,000 in all markets.)

speaker: FISHER
text: Sara Lee—from an agflation standpoint I think this is important and I think we have to be aware of the public perception—just announced a 5 percent increase in the cost of bread, and they announced that they “may hike another 5 percent at the end of the month.” The spread between wheat and corn, Mr. Chairman, is the widest it has been.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is usually $2.00 to $2.50; it is now $6.00.

speaker: FISHER
text: Cooking oil prices, milk prices—even the Italians went on a one-day strike to protest the price of pasta.

speaker: FISHER
text: It wasn’t successful, but that’s what they did.

speaker: FISHER
text: The firms respond by “weighting out” the increased prices by putting less in the package here in the United States.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to mention again that we’re hearing widespread reports of labor shortages, and I do worry, Dave, that it somehow just doesn’t square.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think your report certainly was elucidating, but it does have implications for how fast consumption can fall off, if indeed we’re suffering from a labor shortage.

speaker: FISHER
text: Finally, there are price pressures that ensue from the booming construction markets in China.

speaker: FISHER
text: Chinese demand for skilled labor last year, year over year, was up 100 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: They’re building a huge shipbuilding market and so on.

speaker: FISHER
text: So, Mr. Chairman, I am concerned, first, that while we have made progress by any measurement, including our beloved trimmed mean measure of the PCE in Dallas, that we’re just beginning to make such progress and that there are risks out there and we need to acknowledge them.

speaker: FISHER
text: They stem largely from global demand.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, I’m very concerned that we’re leaning the tiller too far to the side to compensate risk-takers when we should be disciplining them.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I’m going to conclude not with a sailing analogy but with a football analogy.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t think it’s time to throw a “Hail Mary” pass.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it’s time just to continue to move up the field, running the ball as we’ve been doing, and I would strongly recommend a rate cut of only 25 basis points and no more.

speaker: FISHER
text: If, indeed, we accompany it with a change in the primary credit facility, then I think we have to have a very serious discussion of how far we’re willing to go on the fed funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The news about the Italian strike is concerning me considerably.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Fisher, you raised a legitimate issue, which I think I should address now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will this afternoon be discussing this auction credit facility with a possible swap that would allow the Europeans to provide term dollar funding as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This work has been going on for a few weeks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has been very intensive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The staff has done a great job, but as you know and as Bill explained, the financial market conditions have improved somewhat in the past few days, and so we view it—I view it and I think the Board views it now—as a relatively close call as to whether such a facility is needed at this juncture.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I would propose to do is discuss it as planned on the agenda.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We would like to have a thorough discussion and, if the Committee approves the contingent permission, to use it should market conditions appear, in our judgment, to warrant it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But just because, as you point out, there is some interaction with the monetary policy decision, I’d just like to say that, at this point, it is not by any means a certainty that we will go ahead and apply that particular agency.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: FISHER
text: I look forward to that discussion.

speaker: FISHER
text: If they are, indeed, tied together, then I would be making a very strong argument against a 50 basis point cut if it were tied at the same time to this facility.

speaker: FISHER
text: So thank you very much for that clarity.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On balance, the data and the anecdotal evidence in our District say that the economy continues to expand and advance moderately, but the pace may have slowed somewhat since June.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Readings of our Business Outlook Survey of regional manufacturing have been very volatile this summer.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You may recall that in June, our activity index rose to 18, which was its highest value since April 2005.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The index fell to 9 in July and to 0 in August.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The September survey, conducted during the first two weeks of September, remains confidential and will not be announced to the public until this Thursday at noon—so these are really new data.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, we finalized it only yesterday.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It indicates some recovery in general activity, new orders, and shipments.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The general activity index rose from 0 to 10.9.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: New orders and shipments indexes also improved.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Another piece of good news from the manufacturers’ capital spending plans is that they remain positive, with the index at a level typically seen during expansions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Plans to increase capital spending were common among nearly all the major manufacturing sectors covered by our survey.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Consistent with this, our respondents generally see improvements in their business activity coming over the next six months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In September we asked a special question about whether the recent changes in the construction and financial sectors had any adverse effects on their business or their business plans.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: About two-thirds of the respondents said there was no impact on their orders or shipments.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: About 11 percent reported a substantial decline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Most of these firms were housing-related industries.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One was in auto parts, and one was in apparel.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Similarly, three-quarters of the respondents had no change in their capital spending plans, and only about 9 percent expected to cut back substantially on their capital spending relative to plan over the rest of the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My reading of this is that the manufacturing sector in the region is holding up pretty well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In contrast, residential construction activity in the region continues to deteriorate, and we are expecting to see declines in house prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Earlier these declines were seen only at the Jersey Shore, but now they seem to have spread a little more widely in the District.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Interestingly enough, homebuilders reported reducing prices to stimulate sales but with relatively little success.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Several contacts told us that they were more concerned about the negative effects on buyer psychology of recent financial market developments than they were about the availability of mortgage financing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That our region has been largely less dependent on subprime lending than some other areas may be part of the reason for that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nevertheless, none of our contacts in the real estate industry were willing to forecast when the demand for housing was going to pick up.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nonresidential construction has also softened somewhat in our region, as indicated by the value of contracts, but that’s a very volatile number.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: These data tend to be revised up; but the decline still is quite pronounced, and it bears watching.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the same time, vacancy rates remain very low in the Philadelphia area, and so the demand seems to be there, but the contracts are down for the moment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Employment growth over the three-state region ending in July remains below trend in New Jersey and Delaware and kind of flat in Pennsylvania.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some firms continue to support what has already been said—difficulty in finding qualified workers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One of our board members runs a temporary employment agency that goes through tens of thousands of people every month.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: She said that there has been an uptick in walk-in traffic of people applying for employment, particularly skilled workers, but in fact, there has been no falloff whatsoever in the demand from firms looking for these people.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So she has seen no decline in demand for these workers, but she has seen a little uptick in the supply coming through their office.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our three-state unemployment rate remains relatively low and below that of the nation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nonetheless, July unemployment rates in our three states were a little higher than we saw earlier in this year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The inflation picture for the District has changed little since our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Wage increases have been moderate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Several firms report large increases in benefit costs but not an acceleration of those benefit costs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The prices of industrial goods are increasing, but retail price increases haven’t been as widespread as they were earlier.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In summary, our region’s inflation has not accelerated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Economic activity in the Third District continues to expand, but its pace has perhaps slowed somewhat.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our business contacts generally expect activity to remain slow but on an upward trend and are more uncertain about the outlook than they were, but their plans seem to be in place.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One board member spent a great deal of time talking to a number of CEOs and CFOs about capital spending plans, and it was funny.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: He said that they said, well, everybody thought there was going to be a capital spending program reduction.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They weren’t planning a reduction, but they knew somebody else who was.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It was very hard to find the person who was actually doing it, but everybody thought that someone else was doing it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So it was a little anecdotal.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The national economy looks more vulnerable to me than it did six weeks ago, but it would be a mistake—and I think Dave Stockton did an excellent job of reminding us—to count out the resiliency of the U.S. economy at this early stage.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think there can be a tendency in the midst of financial disruptions, uncertainty, and volatility to overestimate the amount of spillover that they will exert on the broader economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: For example, the rate cuts after the stock market crash in 1987 were reversed fairly quickly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Unfortunately, we have very little hard data as yet to help us gauge the potential size or persistence of the impact on real activity of the August turmoil, and early signs may be fraught with noise and overreaction to headlines.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think we have to be very careful.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, it is possible that disruptions will further restrain the already weak housing market by reducing the supply of mortgage credit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nonconforming mortgage rates, even to prime borrowers, remain elevated, but conforming rates to prime borrowers are actually lower right now.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Reduced lending in the alt-A and subprime market is not a surprise.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It has been difficult to obtain those loans since the early part of this year, and I think that is not a big change.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The biggest surprise, at least for me, is that the impact on the obtainability of mortgages to homebuyers of the recent disruptions has been in the area of nonconforming jumbo mortgages.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yet the availability of these mortgages and their rates are likely to settle back down more quickly to normal levels since most of the people borrowing at the jumbo rates tend to be closer to prime borrowers than to subprime.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, as banks take some action to bring some of these risky assets back onto their balance sheets, we may look forward to further restraints on credit because they don’t want to push their capital ratios any harder than they have, and so that may have a diminishing effect.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But putting aside any financial market effects, signs of stabilization in the housing markets that we saw early this year just have not been sustained, as we all know.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Home prices have decelerated and have been falling in certain localities, and that’s likely to continue.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Incoming data suggest that the downturn in housing may be both more prolonged and somewhat deeper than certainly I had earlier anticipated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The question has been whether this decrease in housing wealth would spill over into consumer spending, regardless of the source of the decrease in housing wealth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The argument has been that the strength in the labor markets and the stock market gains would continue, and continued personal income growth would buoy the consumer and mitigate those declines.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I remind everybody that, even though the market is down heavily in August, it is still up roughly 5 percent for the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So it wouldn’t be a tank unless something further happened.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: August nonfarm payroll surprisingly fell by 4,000 jobs in August, as we know.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wouldn’t be too surprised to see this number revised up.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Loss of government jobs concentrated in local education took a very big hit, and this might be overstating the seasonal adjustment factors that are going into this in the timing of the starts of the school year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Still, there was weaker private payroll growth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There’s no question about that, and the revisions done in June and July were down substantially.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, nonfarm payroll gains have averaged about 44,000 over the past three months, whereas private payrolls have been a little more than 70,000 for the past three months, and that’s weaker than we’ve seen during the rest of the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There’s no question about that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the positive side, business spending remains fairly solid, but our hard data are somewhat stale and may be a little sketchy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although not in the data yet, there’s some risk of temporary weaknesses in business fixed investment going forward simply because of the increased uncertainty inherent in financial market disruptions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So far most of the firms we’ve talked to, as I said earlier, say that their capital spending plans remain in place, and only a few nonmanufacturing firms have mentioned not canceling but just delaying them until the market has settled down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Risk premiums have increased from abnormally low levels, which is probably beneficial.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This has raised the cost of capital for some firms; but for most firms, financing for capital spending remains available.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Many banks say that they have lending available and that they will lend to good customers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, most capital expenditures by businesses, in fact, are internally financed, and so the turmoil in the credit markets may not have as much spillover on capital spending as we might otherwise expect.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So unless there’s a sharp decline in business sentiment, which could occur if the financial market turbulence worsens, I don’t expect to see that much of a pullback in business investment spending, except possibly in the very, very near term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On balance, I believe that within the forecast period we can see a return to trend growth, which I still estimate at about 2¾ percent, somewhat higher than the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I still think that’s the most likely outcome, but I now expect that return to be delayed by a couple of quarters given housing, and it won’t be under way until certainly late in 2008.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I admit there’s still considerable uncertainty surrounding that forecast, and I certainly see that there’s a possibility of particularly bad outcomes, some of which the Greenbook scenarios have laid out.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also expect that some of the indicators we receive over the next few months are likely to be weak, but not necessarily weaker than many of us have already built into our new forecasts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, because of the financial markets disruptions, the August data won’t be particularly helpful or useful in reading the trends in the economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it’s going to be crucially important for us to convey to the public that we are forward looking, that we expect to see somewhat weaker data coming in, but that they may not necessitate a further change either in our forecast or in our policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Only when we accumulate sufficient new information that causes our forecast to deviate from our already lowered projections do we want to revise our forecast and perhaps our policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think this is a point that we need to make very clearly to the public, if not in our statement, which we should try, then in the minutes and in our speeches as we go out.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it would be detrimental to our cause and to good policy if the public expected us to react to each piece of incoming data.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the inflation side, I see that recent readings on core inflation have moderated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Headline inflation remains quite elevated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t think that we can afford to be sanguine.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I continue to see underlying inflation pressures, as has already been articulated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Long-range inflation expectations have been stable, but I’m concerned as we go forward with potential rate cuts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m concerned about their remaining stable, particularly when we may be lowering rates without being clear about what our inflation goals are.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, I think the current situation clearly shows the benefit of having an explicit inflation goal.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: By anchoring those expectations, an explicit goal would mean less of a tradeoff between our two goals and so might make this policy decision easier and even perhaps more effective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, while my forecast has built in some near-term policy easing partly to offset the anticipation of tighter credit conditions, I believe that we might find ourselves in a position sometime during ’08 in response to rising inflation of having to raise the fed funds rate back up.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We need to be particularly careful now with our communications regarding any policy action we take, but I’ll save that discussion for the policy go-round.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Readings on core inflation during the intermeeting period have continued to be encouraging, and the downward trend has persisted long enough that I’ve lowered my inflation forecast slightly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With the weaker outlook for growth, I also see less upside inflation risk emanating from cyclical pressures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to economic activity, I’ve downgraded my forecast for growth in the fourth quarter by about the same amount as Greenbook and lowered it only marginally, a bit less than Greenbook, in 2008.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The downside risks to this forecast are substantial and worrisome.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The downward revision to my forecast reflects three factors: first, incoming data bearing on the outlook; second, my assessment of the likely impact of the financial shock that’s been unfolding since mid-July; third, the offsetting effect of the policy changes I consider appropriate in response to the first two forces.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My forecast assumes that the fed funds rate will fall to about 4½ percent in the fourth quarter.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In other words, my forecast is premised on timely actions by the Committee to mitigate much of the potential damage.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Let me begin by commenting on the economic data that we have received since early August.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Some has certainly been positive.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Growth in the second quarter was revised upward, suggesting more momentum heading into the current quarter, and most indicators of consumer spending and business fixed investment were also robust.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Like most observers, I’ve concluded that these data taken together support a small upward revision in my estimate of third-quarter growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, recent data on housing and forward-looking indicators relating to this sector suggest even greater weakness in residential investment than we previously anticipated.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Manufacturing activity recently turned down, and importantly to me, the August employment report showed a marked deceleration in payroll employment growth over the past three months, suggesting that the financial shock hit an economy possessing quite a bit less momentum than I had factored into my previous forecast.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Moreover, survey measures of consumer confidence are down, and these results probably do incorporate early effects from the recent financial shock.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, the most important factor shaping the forecast for the fourth quarter and beyond is the earthquake that began roiling financial markets in mid-July.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Our contacts located at the epicenter—those, for example, in the private equity and mortgage markets—report utter devastation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Anecdotal reports from those nearby—for example, our contacts in banking, housing construction, and housing-related businesses—suggest significant damage from the temblor.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, a large furniture retailer with stores in Utah and Nevada has seen sales fall off, and he has tightened credit terms for his customers and has already frozen his hiring and investment plans.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In contrast, our business contacts operating further from the epicenter appear remarkably unfazed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Luckily for them and for us, the financial quake has thus far produced at most minor tremors in their businesses.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is still too early to expect the ripple effects to be noticed by our contacts or to show up in the spending data.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We could take a wait-and-see approach to the financial shock, incorporating its impact on our growth forecasts only after we observe its imprint in the spending data.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But such an approach would be misguided and fraught with hazard because it would deprive us of the opportunity to act in time to forestall the likely damage.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This means we must do our best to assess the likely effect of the shock.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The simplest approach is to rely on our usual forecasting models.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, as David emphasized in his remarks, the shock has not affected to any great extent the financial variables that are typically included in our macro models.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Since we last met, there have been only small net changes in broad equity indexes and the dollar.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, risk spreads in credit markets are up across a broad range of instruments and for most borrowers, both corporate and households.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But there has been an offsetting drop in Treasury rates so that key rates appearing in our models—the interest rate on conforming mortgages and the interest rate facing prime corporate borrowers—are little changed or even slightly lower.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is riskier corporate borrowers and households seeking nonconforming mortgage loans, including jumbos, that have seen their borrowing rates rise over the past few months.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But importantly, it is the drop in Treasury yields, about 50 to 100 basis points since early July, that has thus far shielded so many borrowers from higher interest rates, and of course, this drop reflects the market’s expectations that the Committee will ease the stance of monetary policy rather substantially.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I noted, my forecast assumes that we will plan to ease by around 75 basis points by year-end in line with market expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even under this assumption, I see movements in interest rates alone as adding to a modest tightening of financial conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But, of course, an evaluation of the likely economic impact from the financial shock must also take into account changes in credit availability and lending terms even though these variables rarely appear explicitly in forecasting models.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is apparent that the availability of lending of some types, including subprime and alt-A mortgages, has diminished substantially or disappeared entirely.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Moreover, banks and other financial institutions are imposing tighter terms and conditions across a broad range of corporate and household lending programs.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, FICO cutoffs have been raised and maximum loan-to-value ratios lowered in many mortgage programs according to our contacts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In part, these changes reflect the pressures that banks and other financial intermediaries are experiencing in the context of severe illiquidity in secondary markets for nonconforming mortgages and other asset-backed securities, asset-backed commercial paper, and term loans in the interbank market.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Many of the liquidity problems now afflicting banks and other financial market participants will presumably be resolved at least eventually, but it’s hard to believe that markets will return to business as usual as defined by conditions in the first half of this year even after that occurs.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For one thing, many of the structured credit products that became so widely used may prove to be too complex to be viable going forward, and this would more or less permanently reduce the quantity of credit available to many risky borrowers.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Moreover, if the financial intermediation that was routinely conducted via asset securitization and off-balance-sheet financing vehicles ultimately migrates back onto the books of the banks, borrowing spreads and lending terms are likely to remain tighter given current limitations on bank capital and the higher costs of conducting intermediation through the banking sector.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Most important, the recent widening of spreads appears to reflect a return to more-realistic pricing of risk throughout the economy; this development may be positive for the long run, but it will be contractionary in the short run.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Similar to the Greenbook, we’ve incorporated these financial developments into our projection by revising down our forecast for residential construction and home prices.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But as we all know, housing is a small sector, so a major question is to what extent the financial shock will spread to other parts of the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We see a large drop in house prices as quite likely to adversely affect consumption spending over time through a number of different channels, including wealth effects, collateral effects, and negative effects on spending through the interest rate resets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A big worry is that a significant drop in house prices might occur in the context of job losses, and this could lead to a vicious spiral of foreclosures, further weakness in housing markets, and further reductions in consumer spending.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Several alternative simulations in the Greenbook illustrate some of the unpleasant scenarios that could develop.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A final concern is that the uncertainty associated with turbulent financial markets could make households and businesses more cautious about spending, causing some investment plans to be put on hold and some planned purchases of houses and consumer durables to be deferred.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So at this point I am concerned that the potential effects of the developing credit crunch could be substantial.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I recognize that there’s a tremendous amount of uncertainty around any estimate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I see the skew in the distribution to be primarily to the downside, reflecting possible adverse spillovers from housing to consumption and business investment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Most of the economic data we have for this meeting reflect the economy before the liquidity issues in August.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The employment report, while probably not wholly reflective of the problems and affected by some anomalous seasonals, nonetheless provides evidence that labor markets were slowing at the outset of the financial problems.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given the layoffs that are being announced by financial services firms and the potential for continued difficulties in construction, some further easing of labor markets seems quite likely.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Although we do not have housing starts and permits for August, the outlook for the second half of 2007 is likely to deteriorate further than forecasters had predicted before the liquidity issues.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There is good reason to believe the staff forecast that residential investment will remain weak well into 2008.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Stock prices of all the major homebuilders have continued to decline since our last meeting, and the credit derivative swaps for several of the largest homebuilders are at levels that reflect a very high probability of default.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The news from the financial markets has improved marginally from the last meeting, but I still have some significant concerns.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Certainly, some of the financial anomalies have abated, such as the extremely low rates for short-term Treasury securities, and there are some tentative signs of improving liquidity.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, these improvements are tenuous, and the ability to raise funds in a number of short-term financial markets remains quite difficult.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would just highlight a few of the financial anomalies that are reflective of the situation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Usually, the overnight Eurodollar trades very close to the overnight fed funds rate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Both are overnight dollar loans between financial institutions on an unsecured basis.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Over the past month, the funds for overnight Eurodollars have frequently been trading much higher than overnight fed funds.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This highlights the difficulty that some European financial institutions are having borrowing in dollars and the unwillingness of many financial institutions to arbitrage these spreads if they involve credit exposures to European financial institutions, even for overnight.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: These difficulties worsen when the maturities extend out to one to three months.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Both the one-month and three-month LIBOR rates have remained very elevated, particularly given that the fed funds futures during this period have indicated a market expectation of falling federal funds rates over the next three months.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The elevated LIBOR rate tightens credit for a variety of domestic borrowers and could affect areas that are already troubled.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: For example, many subprime mortgages are tied to the LIBOR rate as are many loans that have been used to finance leveraged buyouts.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A second example is the significant swelling of bank assets in August.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The monthly growth rate for bank C&I loans was 2.6 percent and for other loans and leases was 6.3 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: These are among the largest monthly increases in thirty years.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As in other periods of liquidity strain, bank balance sheets become particularly important.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As banks honor loan commitments and agreements to provide liquidity support, their balance sheets grow.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My concern is that bank obligations will continue to expand bank balance sheets in September and crowd out other investment opportunities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Many financial market participants are very concerned about the next two weeks, despite some recent easing of conditions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Some investors are not willing to lend except overnight.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The asset-backed commercial paper market has remained under stress, and the rollovers have been for shorter maturities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There is significant concern that holders of commercial paper may be reluctant to hold asset-backed commercial paper on their balance sheets at the end of this month, and rumors abound about whether money market funds and other short-term investors will continue to hold commercial paper for structured products, particularly of the SIVs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So we have a situation of a very weak housing sector, some evidence of slowing employment growth, and a period of extended illiquidity that may get worse before it gets better.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The tail risk of liquidity problems and economic problems has grown, and we clearly want to avoid outcomes by which declines in prices for houses and for financial assets tied to the housing sector could create more-severe economic outcomes.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The fact is that we do not have much experience with periods of extended illiquidity, especially when the housing sector is so weak.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So taking out insurance against these risks seems entirely appropriate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The decision is made easier, in my view, because I see the risk of unacceptably high inflation resulting from such an action as being quite low.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My hope is that with appropriate easing of policy the liquidity issues will abate as we start the fourth quarter.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The reports that I am hearing from my business contacts reflect a sudden and a significant deterioration in their evaluation of the business climate.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The data in hand, except for the troubling August employment report, have not been especially dire, and neither are the impressions I get from the business community regarding their current pace of economic activity.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In fact, by most accounts, business activity in the Fourth District, outside of the residential real estate market, remains reasonably positive, and the Beige Book report that we submitted for this meeting reflects that view.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In most cases, the sharp downward reassessment of the business situation that I am now hearing from my contacts describes greater unease over what may happen and not what has happened.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As we discussed earlier, our forecast models are not well equipped to accommodate the role that shifting expectations play in shaping the economic outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Nevertheless, the sharp falloff in business confidence that I am hearing from people in many sectors in the District has had a material influence on the economic projections that I submitted for this meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The market for real estate is still declining, perhaps even in a freefall, according to the descriptions I have been getting from people across the sector, including real estate professionals, developers, and manufacturers of home construction supplies and materials.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I don’t pretend to have a very confident forecast of where the bottom of the residential real estate market lies, but the industry sources that I am talking to have convinced me that we should anticipate that this process will play itself out for a considerable time to come.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Moreover, and unlike my last report to the Committee, my business contacts are now fearful that we are going to see a spillover from the declines in the residential real estate market, and they now expect some amount of retrenchment by consumers.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I have incorporated some of that sentiment into my outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The most noteworthy development affecting my economic projection, however, has been the deterioration in business confidence and the effect that deterioration may have on capital expansion plans.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The diminished confidence in the outlook that business leaders are reporting to me has had a significant negative effect on my outlook for investment.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like the Greenbook, I have scaled back my growth outlook to reflect a considerably softer trajectory for business fixed investment.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Even with a monetary policy response, the combination of weaker consumer and business spending has led me to mark down my GDP projection for next year nearly ½ percentage point, to 2 percent.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Meanwhile, the incoming inflation report continues to point to a gradual disinflation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The usual caveats about inflation forecasts apply, of course, but I am not seeing in the data—and I am not hearing from my business contacts—the same concern over rising prices that I heard in the spring.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My outlook for inflation hasn’t changed that much since July.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am still expecting core PCE inflation to be just under 2 percent.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But I am more confident, if just a little, that we are seeing the progress toward price stability that we had hoped to achieve.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I believe that the risks to the outlook, given no change in our policy, have shifted decisively toward potential rapid deterioration in the real economy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Some of that deterioration may reflect the unwinding of earlier financial imbalances, and every prudent effort should be made to allow that process to run its course.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But the moral hazard caveat does not diminish the significance of the falloff in business sentiment that I have heard since our last meeting, and so I am concerned that we have seen greater risk to the economic outlook since our last meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the Sixth District, we indulge ourselves with the conceit that our District looks a lot like the nation as a whole.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We have 45 million consumers and an industrial composition that does resemble the country, so you can process my regional remarks with that conceit in mind.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Housing markets continued to deteriorate in August in the Sixth District.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Housing market weakness was most pronounced in Florida, as you might expect, followed by Atlanta and middle Tennessee.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The consensus view is that the recent tightening in mortgage credit availability will exacerbate the region’s housing market problems, and most regional contacts believe that housing markets will continue to weaken, bottoming out no earlier than mid-2008, and some see a much longer adjustment period.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Aside from housing, real economic readings in the Sixth District were mixed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Anecdotal feedback across a number of industries suggested that business spending has not yet slowed markedly, but the majority of contacts indicated that they are now approaching new capital spending more cautiously.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That said, most contacts acknowledge that tighter credit standards have not significantly affected business capital investment outlays.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Reports of factory activity were mixed, with defense and export industries doing well, while industries linked to housing were predictably weak.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Transportation contacts indicated ongoing weak domestic demand.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Consumer activity in the District was flat to slightly up in August compared with a year ago.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Housing-related home product sales were especially weak, as were auto sales.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Perhaps the most notable change from previous months was a turn to pessimism on the part of directors, reflecting their soundings of business contacts in their communities.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I will mention that we have five Branches, so we actually get director feedback from more than forty directors across the District.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Sixty percent believe that economic activity will be slower six months out, twice the percentage recorded in July.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Even factoring out idiosyncratic conditions in localities such as south Florida and the Gulf Coast, the outlook, based on these anecdotal reports, has turned to the negative.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: To summarize my regional comments—current fundamentals are mixed, and the outlook is pessimistic.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In our view, the economic outlook has changed since the last meeting, and the balance of risk has clearly shifted to the downside.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We do not see a near-term recession as a high likelihood, but we do anticipate that growth will approach trend much more slowly with employment edging up as a consequence.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So in direction and tone, if not magnitude, we are in agreement with the Greenbook, but our forecast differs from the Greenbook baseline forecast in the depth of the below-trend growth, ours being somewhat milder because we condition our forecast on deeper cumulative cuts in the fed funds rate over the coming months.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Turning to capital markets, my recent conversations with a number of capital market participants suggest that the adjustment process in financial markets is far from complete.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Their anecdotal feedback reflects a range of views about the severity of the current problems and the outlook for stabilization.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Here is the overall picture I gleaned from these conversations.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Some debt markets have firmed a bit.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The leveraged-loan market, for example, is likely to renew trading in the coming weeks, but structured-debt security markets are not yet clearing.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The principal reason—and this has been mentioned earlier by Bill and others—that debt markets remain illiquid is weak counterparty transparency and, therefore, uncertain counterparty risk, as well as uncertainty regarding the performance of collateral pools that back securities.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The process of achieving adequate clarity and stabilization of the markets will likely take many more weeks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Markets will remain volatile while the condition of heightened uncertainty persists.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There has been some spillover into markets that are unrelated to structured debt and subprime, but creditworthy borrowers are getting credit.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There is sufficient buyer liquidity currently on the sidelines awaiting greater clarity regarding counterparties, market pricing of securities, and the depth and scope of the difficulties.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Widespread deleveraging, particularly by SIVs and hedge funds and nonbank entities, is occurring and is likely to continue.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One party argued, however, that all the news of financial distress has not pushed risk spreads to the extremes of historical bands.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This party argued, “We are experiencing a painful adjustment from excessively high leverage to more-rational or more-realistic pricing in line with historical averages.” But all contacts believe—and this is perhaps not unexpected—that prolonged credit market problems will affect the broad economy, mostly through the consumer credit channel.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I believe our decision today boils down to whether we cut ¼ percentage point or ½ percentage point, obviously in combination with careful wording of the statement that conveys a rationale focused on economic fundamentals while signaling some recognition that the problems in the capital markets have the potential to deliver a credit shock to the broad economy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I consider it appropriate to adjust the federal funds rate to the now-weaker economic outlook, and I support a 50 basis point move with the rationale that at least 25 basis points of that represents recognition of a lower equilibrium rate and the remainder is a preemptive, preventive measure designed to renew confidence, facilitate conditions that resolve uncertainty, and shorten the necessary adjustment timeline in a deleveraging financial sector.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is a fair question whether the process of information revelation—that is, removing uncertainty—will be accelerated by an aggressive rate cut.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My view is that this action, along with other liquidity actions, removes the psychological barrier—that being the concern that the Fed might fail to ensure enough upfront liquidity and might be pursuing an inadvertently tight policy, compounding problems by putting undue stress on the real economy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think a distinction can be drawn between trying to influence the psychology around dangerous financial sector circumstances and bailing out the markets, and care should be taken to reflect this in the minutes.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Let me add that I agree with the earlier comments of President Fisher that we perhaps should be looking at any policy move in the context of a total package that includes the auction credit facility.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I do have, let’s say, some sympathy for the view that the total package must be discussed.

speaker: LACKER
text: Recent information from the Fifth District, both from contacts and from our survey responses, suggests that growth in economic activity in our District has slowed in recent weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: The survey indicates that retail sales have weakened, with big-ticket categories such as automobiles and building materials leading the way.

speaker: LACKER
text: Shopper traffic has trailed off somewhat as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: Services firms report slower revenue growth and less optimism about demand going forward.

speaker: LACKER
text: Activity in some District housing markets has slowed markedly in the past two to three weeks, and some formerly healthy markets are now showing signs of weakness.

speaker: LACKER
text: One contact in Charlotte, for example, says that sales agents there are saying the same things they were saying in Atlanta several months ago.

speaker: LACKER
text: Residential foreclosures are more widespread, though they appear to be concentrated or overrepresented among investors rather than owner-occupants.

speaker: LACKER
text: Mortgage activity has fallen off in the past several weeks, according to our contacts.

speaker: LACKER
text: While standards have tightened for marginally qualified applicants, it is reported that mortgages remain readily available for creditworthy borrowers.

speaker: LACKER
text: The CEO of a nationwide title insurance company reports that their open orders have been trending down in recent weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: He also says that they are seeing an increase in cancellations of title insurance orders because people are applying for more than one mortgage in the current climate.

speaker: LACKER
text: In contrast, commercial real estate conditions appear generally healthy, although recent reports suggest that closer scrutiny is being given to marginal project proposals.

speaker: LACKER
text: Conditions in manufacturing also look positive, shipments and new orders continue to expand, and hiring indicators for this sector have edged higher.

speaker: LACKER
text: District price pressures remain at about the same level they have been in recent months.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me say that, broadly speaking across our contacts, we have heard in the past week or two more reports mentioning a sense of gloom.

speaker: LACKER
text: This echoes what Presidents Pianalto and Lockhart said.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the other hand, one contact in Charlotte, who has had a lot of successful experience in real estate markets, said that compared with past crises this is a walk in the park.

speaker: LACKER
text: Maybe that is just because he has made his.

speaker: LACKER
text: It may be particular to this situation, so I don’t want to make too much of that.

speaker: LACKER
text: The national economic data that we have received since our last meeting point pretty clearly to a weaker economic outlook for real growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: The employment report is a prominent example.

speaker: LACKER
text: Slower growth in the months ahead would weigh on income growth and consumption, although the Greenbook’s outlook for income remains pretty healthy.

speaker: LACKER
text: Recent reports on housing activity have also been quite disappointing.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the key question is the effect on the housing market and broader economic activity of the recent financial market turmoil.

speaker: LACKER
text: I won’t survey what has happened; Presidents Yellen and Rosengren and Mr. Dudley did an excellent job on that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I will just comment that it seems, broadly speaking, as if we are on a traverse from a configuration of intermediation that placed a fairly heavy reliance on fairly complicated and structured products and rating agencies’ assessments of those.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is a traverse that is obviously going more rapidly and is fraught with more peril than the path that took us to the configuration we are coming from.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it is hard to know how much of an effect this turmoil will have on housing.

speaker: LACKER
text: I suspect that a lot of the slowdown was already in train before the middle of August.

speaker: LACKER
text: I base that thought on the fact that many mortgage rates rose earlier in the summer than August, though the jumbo market is an obvious exception to that.

speaker: LACKER
text: Beyond housing, any projections of real effects from events in financial markets seem like guesswork at this point.

speaker: LACKER
text: My sense is that, while we may see some marginal slowing in business investment, the effects are likely to be small because I don’t think the marginal cost of funding for most businesses has gone up much and we aren’t hearing reports of wholesale tightening of lending standards in the corporate sector.

speaker: LACKER
text: I haven’t heard that from around the country either.

speaker: LACKER
text: I expect consumer spending to grow more slowly than in recent years, but not too dramatically so.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that there is a fair amount of uncertainty about the size of the housing wealth effect and that household net worth overall remains fairly high relative to income at this point.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I noted earlier, the Greenbook’s projection for disposable income isn’t too bad, so that would support consumption growth at least at a moderate pace going forward.

speaker: LACKER
text: Overall, then, I come out a touch above the Greenbook, with real growth about 2 percent in the second half and then gradually returning to trend.

speaker: LACKER
text: Of course, I have been expecting less of a slowdown than the Greenbook for about a year now.

speaker: LACKER
text: It turns out that, although we have both been too optimistic, the Greenbook has been closer to reality, so my confidence in my forecasting ability is waning here.

speaker: LACKER
text: The inflation numbers have been encouraging.

speaker: LACKER
text: Core PCE inflation averaged under 1.4 percent for the past five months, and overall PCE inflation was under 2 percent for both June and July.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am particularly pleased that TIPS inflation compensation has not increased even as market participants have marked down their expected funds rate path in the midst of the recent turmoil.

speaker: LACKER
text: That said, it still looks as though market participants expect inflation to settle near 2 percent rather than lower, as I would prefer.

speaker: EVANS
text: To date, economic conditions in the Seventh District have changed little since our last meeting.

speaker: EVANS
text: We continue to expand at a modest rate, as reported in the Beige Book two weeks ago.

speaker: EVANS
text: Even after accounting for continuing declines in the housing sector, most of my contacts thought the national economy had softened.

speaker: EVANS
text: Outside of housing, they generally reported a modest deceleration rather than an abrupt change in conditions.

speaker: EVANS
text: Retailers thought that continued high energy prices were holding back consumers, but demand was not seen as deteriorating sharply.

speaker: EVANS
text: A similar slowing was reported on the hiring front.

speaker: EVANS
text: For instance, Kelly and Manpower experienced softer demand for temporary workers, but again this was not characterized as a general pullback in hiring.

speaker: EVANS
text: Many contacts added that finding skilled workers remained difficult, as President Fisher mentioned.

speaker: EVANS
text: In terms of the business outlook going forward, several directors and other contacts noted that many in the business community were apprehensive about the prospects for growth.

speaker: EVANS
text: They were concerned that these worries might soon begin to weigh more heavily on actual spending.

speaker: EVANS
text: For example, in the motor vehicle sector, both Ford and General Motors cautioned that the August sales numbers overstated the underlying strength in demand for vehicles.

speaker: EVANS
text: They thought some selective incentive programs had boosted the sales figures.

speaker: EVANS
text: I asked all my contacts about the effects of the turmoil in credit markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: Though it is still early, none of them thought that the recent financial turbulence was causing creditworthy nonfinancial firms to have unusual difficulty in finding adequate financing.

speaker: EVANS
text: As several people have said, many business people suggested that the situation is much better than what they hear from financial commentators on Wall Street.

speaker: EVANS
text: Of course, we heard many examples of difficulties from financial market contacts, and several have spoken about that already.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning to the national outlook, three broad developments since our August meeting have influenced my views on the economic situation.

speaker: EVANS
text: First, financial conditions have become more restrictive.

speaker: EVANS
text: Second, the incoming data suggest a greater decline in housing and a somewhat weaker labor market.

speaker: EVANS
text: Third, inflation prospects have improved to the point where my outyear projections are within a range that many participants would view as consistent with price stability.

speaker: EVANS
text: These projections embed a path for the federal funds rate that is similar to the Greenbook assumption.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to financial conditions, I think it is useful to consider the situation relative to an assessment of a neutral or an equilibrium federal funds rate.

speaker: EVANS
text: Taking into account the slower growth of structural productivity, a neutral rate is likely between 4½ and 4¾ percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: The Greenbook-consistent rate is in this range.

speaker: EVANS
text: Until recently, one argument for keeping the target funds rate at 5¼ percent had been to offset otherwise accommodative conditions.

speaker: EVANS
text: As recently as June, we had very low risk premiums and ample liquidity for all types of private borrowing, including large commitments for private equity deals.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, of course, overall financial conditions have tightened and in some markets have turned very restrictive.

speaker: EVANS
text: Clearly, this restrictiveness is a downside for growth.

speaker: EVANS
text: Whether it is as large as ½ percentage point, as the Greenbook assumes, is uncertain.

speaker: EVANS
text: In any event, the ongoing repricing of risk also adds a good deal of uncertainty to the forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: You all know it is very difficult to forecast the impact of such financial turbulence.

speaker: EVANS
text: Recent history and Dave Stockton remind us of this.

speaker: EVANS
text: In the early 1990s, restrictive credit due to depositories’ capital adequacy problems had a significant impact on real economic activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: In contrast, in the fall of 1998, we thought financial conditions would impinge a good deal on the real economy, but 1999 turned out to be a very strong year for growth.

speaker: EVANS
text: Bottom line—and we all recognize this—we need to be careful how we react to the current financial situation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning more specifically to the outlook for growth, our Chicago forecasts have tended to be somewhat more optimistic than the Board staff forecast, and we remain so.

speaker: EVANS
text: That said, the incoming data have been softer than we expected.

speaker: EVANS
text: So we marked down our assessment of residential investment again, but not as much as the Board staff did—again, and the decline in payroll employment caused us to lower our near-term outlook somewhat.

speaker: EVANS
text: As long as the financial difficulties are contained, and that is our working assumption, we expect growth to return to potential by the second half of 2008, and we have a higher potential output growth rate than the Board staff.

speaker: EVANS
text: However, I admit that the risks seem weighted to the downside of this projection.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to inflation, the improvement in core PCE inflation earlier this year appears to have a bit more staying power than we thought it might.

speaker: EVANS
text: If aggregate demand does weaken, as expected, then there is less risk of inflationary pressures arising from constraints on resource utilization.

speaker: EVANS
text: Energy prices, though, are a concern.

speaker: EVANS
text: My contacts do not seem to have much difficulty passing cost increases through to their customers.

speaker: EVANS
text: Overall, however, we have core PCE inflation edging down to 1.8 percent next year and remaining near that rate in 2009.

speaker: EVANS
text: I see the risk to this inflation forecast, conditioned on the outlook for growth, as being fairly well balanced.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s put President Poole between us and the coffee break.

speaker: POOLE
text: I’m going to be brief.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s a question of how desperate you are.

speaker: POOLE
text: I have just a few anecdotes here.

speaker: POOLE
text: My contact in the trucking industry says that things are very, very glum there.

speaker: POOLE
text: Volume is down 11 percent, year over year.

speaker: POOLE
text: Shipping rates are down 5 percent, and this is very general in the trucking industry.

speaker: POOLE
text: We get the same story from the trucking side of FedEx and UPS.

speaker: POOLE
text: But the small package side of FedEx and UPS is doing somewhat better.

speaker: POOLE
text: In fact, the August and September numbers— September to date, obviously—are actually a little better than the July numbers.

speaker: POOLE
text: They have not changed their outlook for the holiday season, and so it is not a real buoyant outlook, but they haven’t changed it at all in response to the financial market upset.

speaker: POOLE
text: A contact in the fast food industry had an interesting comment that actually came out of Wal-Mart.

speaker: POOLE
text: Wal-Mart is reporting a very significant drop in money transfers to Mexico.

speaker: POOLE
text: That is probably reflecting the number of Mexicans who work in the construction industry.

speaker: POOLE
text: A contact with a major software firm is really completely different.

speaker: POOLE
text: They are seeing very buoyant revenues.

speaker: POOLE
text: They are seeing IT sales running above the Gartner forecast.

speaker: POOLE
text: They track sales, and the weekly sales—this is as of Friday the week before last—were doing very well; in fact, they were accelerating.

speaker: POOLE
text: A comment about the consumer market: A new release of software for an apparently popular game has very strong pre-orders.

speaker: POOLE
text: Business sector demand is uniformly strong across small, medium, and large businesses.

speaker: POOLE
text: International demand is very strong.

speaker: POOLE
text: There were no bad pockets in this business at all was the report that I received there.

speaker: POOLE
text: My summary view on the outlook is that, if the financial market upset goes away or settles down in a few weeks, the outlook for next year is going to appear more or less as it did last June before the financial market upset began, with of course some major exceptions or revisions.

speaker: POOLE
text: Housing is, unambiguously, going to be weaker.

speaker: POOLE
text: The nonprime market is gone, I think, for the foreseeable future.

speaker: POOLE
text: Maybe some of the alt-A market would start to come back, but the subprime is gone for the foreseeable future, and housing-related goods—appliances and furniture—presumably are going to reflect the housing weakness.

speaker: POOLE
text: If the market disruption continues, the fallout for the real economy will grow, and it is very hard to know how that might turn out.

speaker: POOLE
text: As you were discussing, things like the surprises going on in the United Kingdom come along in a very unpredictable fashion with unpredictable results.

speaker: POOLE
text: I view the Greenbook forecast as reflecting a mean with a certain probability of a stronger outcome, more like the one we had in June perhaps, and then, of course, a certain probability of a weaker outcome.

speaker: POOLE
text: Our job is to raise the probability of that stronger outcome without raising the probability of higher inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Sorry to have put you on the spot there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a break until 11:30?

speaker: STERN
text: Let me make a few comments about current economic conditions and then talk a bit about the outlook.

speaker: STERN
text: By way of overview, I will say that I largely agree with the Greenbook, both about the current quarter and about the near-term outlook, in any event.

speaker: STERN
text: The current quarter does look as though it is going to turn out to be certainly respectable real growth of 2½ percent or perhaps a bit more.

speaker: STERN
text: The anecdotes from our District that relate to the third quarter seem to be consistent with that.

speaker: STERN
text: Employment has been sustained, and if anything, the reports of the scarcity of skilled labor have probably increased.

speaker: STERN
text: In fact, some of our directors have speculated that perhaps the aggregate employment gains have been restrained by that availability issue.

speaker: STERN
text: The largest bank in our District and several others say that, based on what they are seeing, consumer spending and consumer unsecured borrowing are proceeding normally.

speaker: STERN
text: Repayments are proceeding normally, and credit quality on the consumer side is in good shape.

speaker: STERN
text: The one exception to what I would describe as a generally positive picture is what we are hearing in the nonresidential construction sector.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t want to make too much of this, but I have a sense that it is significant.

speaker: STERN
text: Some of the large developers in the District have reported that, because of the change in financial conditions that has occurred in the past month or two, some projects are clearly being postponed.

speaker: STERN
text: Whether they will ultimately be cancelled remains to be seen, but there certainly have been some effects there.

speaker: STERN
text: Turning to the outlook, I think that the outlook for real growth over the next several quarters is less favorable than it was formerly.

speaker: STERN
text: I admit that it’s a stretch to get there, if we rely on our familiar models to produce that result.

speaker: STERN
