text: In fact, something more like paragraph 4 in alternative D would suit me better, but perhaps a simpler way would be to rewrite paragraph 4 as follows.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is just a suggestion—it’s a little shorter: “With this action, the Committee judges that the downside risks to economic growth are now roughly balanced by the upside risks to inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Committee will continue to monitor incoming economic information relative to the outlook and act as needed to foster price stability and sustainable economic growth.” That is a little shorter and conveys the kind of balance that I think is important.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In some versions of the statement, we have had a little too much of a temptation to promote the idea that we can fine-tune the economy, and I think that’s a dangerous and slippery slope.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: With regard to the rationale, I’m happy with paragraph 3 on inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, I noticed that there was no capacity utilization in that statement, which pleases me no end.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You know, we have to take small victories when we can.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would like to see some changes to paragraph 2.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In particular, I’d like us to say a little less about the disruptions in the financial markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think this has the potential to confuse people—that our move is being taken as a desire to bail out bad actors—and that could feed into moral hazard.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We are moving because our outlook for the broader economy is weakening.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The tightening of credit conditions may have the potential to affect the real economy, and that’s why we are acting preemptively.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would again try to simplify paragraph 2, and I suggest the following language: “Economic growth was moderate during the first half of the year; but labor market strength has moderated, and the housing correction appears to have intensified and may be exacerbated by the tightening of credit conditions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Today’s action is intended to help forestall some of the potential adverse effects of those events on the broader economy and to promote moderate growth over time.” Finally, as I said earlier, I believe it will be very important to communicate, in the minutes and perhaps our speeches going forward, that our forecast incorporates weak data in the near term and, although we may individually have different views as to what that near term might look like, that forecast has been incorporated in our funds rate assessment and we intend to alter our bias or our policy only if our forecast changes appreciably in the months to come.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think there’s a general consensus that we should ease.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: To me the question is not whether to ease but how much is appropriate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: To ease by 25 basis points, I think, could be justified by slow housing and weakening labor markets in the absence of any financial turmoil.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, I’m concerned that a 25 basis point ease today might very well need to be followed by another ease, quite possibly before the next meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given the economic slowing we have seen and the additional slowing that is already likely as a result of the increase in many short-term interest rates, I prefer a more aggressive approach.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A 50 basis point reduction will offset some of the tightening that has already occurred in short-term interest rates and will reduce the likelihood that the most pessimistic outcomes for housing prices and residential investment will occur.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Furthermore, it seems appropriate insurance against tail events given that inflation pressures are unlikely to be a problem given the current economic outlook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Alternative B in conjunction with other actions designed to improve liquidity seems the most appropriate given the current economic outlook.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’ve already said that I don’t see that the risk is on the inflation front right now, although clearly we have to keep monitoring inflation, and that the serious risk is the nonlinear downward spiral that could occur.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, the big problem is really the issue of information revelation and price discovery.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I want to point out that there are really two sources of this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is that it’s very difficult for the market to figure out what the value of assets in these structured products is.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly, that will take a long time to work out, and it is not something that monetary policy can do anything about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second source of the problem of price discovery is the fear that, in fact, we might have a severe economic downturn, and we can do something about that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So in this context a cut is not controversial because everybody is coming to the conclusion that we should cut the federal funds rate by 50 basis points and, in particular, that we want to get ahead of the curve to indicate to the markets that we are on top of this and that we are trying to remove the downside tail that we’re particularly worried about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I want to talk a little about a somewhat longer-run perspective on monetary policy strategy and how we might proceed from here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The way I think about this is that the situations we have to deal with fall into two camps.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The normal situation is when things are fairly linear, when we don’t have financial disruptions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that case, there is a lot of reason to have what has been characterized in the academic literature as policy inertia—that is, the idea that, when you move the federal funds rate, you don’t move it back quickly and, in fact, you have very persistent federal funds rate moves.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Indeed, I think that is the right thing to do under normal circumstances.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly, there’s an issue that moving a very short-term interest rate will not have an effect unless people expect it to persist.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Because the longer-run part of the term structure is more relevant to people’s decisions in terms of spending, there’s a very strong case for pursuing things in a persistent way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also, there is always a problem that, when you reverse, people may say, “Gee, you didn’t know what you were doing, and you had to change your mind?” So there’s always this issue of flip- flopping that you have to be concerned about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The other situation is exactly the environment we’re in, when you really have to take out insurance against something that has the potential to create a downward spiral that’s hard to control.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s particularly imperative in that situation that you get ahead of the curve.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, there’s a very strong case to make sure in that situation that you emphasize to the markets that you are trying to take out insurance against the downward spiral.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But if you are successful, things may start to turn around, and if things go the right way, which is what you hope happens, then you want to reverse course.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So in the projections that I provided, I did something that was unusual.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think I was the only person to have a rate reversal in the projections.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I had us going down 50 at this meeting.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I thought there was a possibility—though I hope not—that we might have to go 50 at the next meeting and, if we did, that would certainly be enough, and then we would move back up afterwards.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So in this context, I think that we really do have to think in terms of potential reversals and, therefore, to not be scared of overshooting a bit.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There tends to be a lot of inertia in the way we do monetary policy—it is well documented.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There’s even inertia in general, just in that we have nineteen participants at a table.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As an academic, I mentioned to Don Kohn at one point that sometimes I think these meetings have elements of faculty meetings, and that is not always something that you enjoy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Some of you guys may not have experienced that, but it’s a lot of fun.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think the bottom line here is that we have to be prepared to think about being much more aggressive, not just now but even in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, I do want to point out that this does not mean that we should have an alternative that indicates that we are going to do further cuts in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I strongly advocate alternative B because, by aggressive action now, we may start turning the markets around and, if that’s the case, then it will not be necessary for us to quickly do more.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So we do not want to say to the markets that we have to keep on going when we’re hoping that we won’t have to keep on going.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that’s extremely important in thinking about where we are right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Another issue in terms of an extremely aggressive policy and then possibly doing reversals is the moral hazard context.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Again, I think this is a communication issue.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have a slight disagreement with President Plosser in that I think we have to talk about the financial market disruptions because it is very important to indicate that, in being very aggressive, we are not losing sight of our inflation goals and that this is a case of worrying about the downside tail that we have to deal with and really showing that we’re on the ball in that context.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So we’re in a slightly different situation from the normal one, and I would advocate keeping the discussion of financial disruptions in our statement the way we have it now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As you know, I’m an advocate of two-day meetings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Michelle informs me that our true drop-dead time is 1:45.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we do need, please, to be efficient.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Well, in my earlier remarks I stated my reasons for supporting 50 basis points, so I will play Calvin Coolidge here—that is, 50 basis points, alternative B. It’s important that we neither signal further actions nor suggest that we’re through and that we preserve some flexibility because of the uncertainty.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given the shift that I am projecting in economic outlook, I think that a more decisive action is called for today, and I support a 50 basis point cut in the fed funds target rate.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In the past few meetings I was in favor of setting our fed funds target rate above neutral to secure progress for disinflation, but that stance no longer seems compelling.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Recent inflation reports have been encouraging, and my outlook for inflation shows inflation remaining in an acceptable range.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Furthermore, an above-neutral stance does not seem prudent given my projection for economic growth.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I’m in favor of moving our policy stance back to neutral.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Obviously it is difficult to know exactly where that is; but if the economy is in the midst of a rapid adjustment, I would prefer not to be behind the curve.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I would prefer not to be chasing neutral down.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Gradualism has its place, but in this instance I would prefer a more aggressive move today and to not leave markets with an expectation of a long sequence of moves, as others have already noted.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I prefer the language of alternative B.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Yes, we may see a great falloff in confidence and a further deterioration in the economic outlook, but the recent business pessimism that I talked about earlier may also prove to be unfounded.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Therefore, I’d prefer not to lock ourselves into further rate reductions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also like the uncertainty language that’s been added to the new version of alternative B. I think, again, with the 50 basis point move today there’s a good chance that we’ll be close to neutral, and that’s exactly where I think we should be with the uncertainty that many of us see in the outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also take very seriously the risk of undermining the appropriate pricing of risk in financial markets that we face.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The long-run success of a decisive move today pivots on the ability to make clear that we take such action in recognition of the current economic environment and that it is not a rush to protect investors from poor past business decisions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I support a clear statement that, should be we later find ourselves in calmer financial waters and stronger economic winds, we will move quickly to affirm our commitment to achieving and maintaining price stability.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Now, because of this preference for downplaying the financial market disruptions, I think a simple way to remove at least one reference to them is to end paragraph 2 after the word “arise”—so “today’s action is intended to help forestall some of the adverse effects on the broader economy that might otherwise arise.” That gets rid of one reference to disruptions in financial markets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Also, the last part of that statement on promoting moderate growth over time almost gets lost in that language, so it might be simpler to just end the paragraph after “arise.” Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the actual signs of softness we’ve seen are significant enough to warrant a 25 basis point cut in the fed funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: I expect that the slowdown is going to be a little less severe than that in the Greenbook, and I’m concerned about the likelihood of inflation’s remaining above my objective.

speaker: LACKER
text: Arguments for a larger cut appear to rest on the possibility that financial turbulence since last month could cause significant further reductions in real activity.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that’s certainly a plausible possibility, and we can’t rule it out at this point.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I don’t see it as extremely likely, and so my preference is for a cut of 25 basis points.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would describe that preference as a mild one, and I could support a 50 basis point cut.

speaker: LACKER
text: I just have this hunch that a 50 basis point cut might make it easier for us to resist a further cut two meetings down the road.

speaker: LACKER
text: Whichever we choose, though, I’m very concerned about how we justify our actions, and I share the concerns of Presidents Plosser and Pianalto about paragraph 2.

speaker: LACKER
text: That language motivates the cut as a way of taking out insurance against the possible effects of financial market turmoil.

speaker: LACKER
text: I worry that, if we tie our actions too closely to the expected effects of financial market conditions, as much as we are concerned about this, we may make it harder to respond appropriately down the road if the data indicate that we should take back some rate reductions.

speaker: LACKER
text: The sense of fragility in financial markets could well persist, and as long as it does, so will the possibility that financial market volatility could create a drag on spending and growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: The persistence of that fragility could hold us back from reversing course if we find that real indicators and inflation data indicate that we ought to.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we do reduce the target rate by 50 basis points, I think we should remove the tilt.

speaker: LACKER
text: I liked the original version of alternative B that was circulated in the Bluebook.

speaker: LACKER
text: As drafted now, it talks about uncertainty, and one could argue that’s a mean-preserving spread, but I think in the context it’s going to be read as the equivalent of a downward tilt.

speaker: EVANS
text: Given my outlook for growth and inflation and my assessment of the neutral federal funds rate, I can readily agree to 50 basis points in cuts on a cumulative basis.

speaker: EVANS
text: I came into this meeting having a slight preference for alternative C and doing 25 basis points today with an expectation of 25 at the next meeting.

speaker: EVANS
text: I thought that that would take us to a point at which more data would come out and it would be more likely that we could perhaps stop at a 4¾ percent fed funds rate.

speaker: EVANS
text: Obviously, if we cut 50 basis points today, and I have no disagreement with that, I think it is then a little more difficult to stop there.

speaker: EVANS
text: I agree with some of the previous comments that any action beyond that should be based on incoming data that we don’t expect.

speaker: EVANS
text: That is kind of difficult from a communication standpoint.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I’m fine with alternative B.

speaker: EVANS
text: In fact, the language is fine.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’d just like to take a minute to talk about risk management.

speaker: EVANS
text: We talked a lot about that in terms of tail risk and nonlinearities and insurance, and I think this is quite appropriate in the current environment.

speaker: EVANS
text: But we have to continue to ask, What happens in the more likely event that things turn out better than these tail events?

speaker: EVANS
text: That’s why they’re called tail events.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I agree with Governor Mishkin that we have to be very careful to think about taking them back.

speaker: EVANS
text: If we respond aggressively to address financial conditions beyond our dual mandate goals, we should be prepared to retrace that pattern of federal funds rate cuts if conditions calm.

speaker: EVANS
text: With respect to the comments that Governor Kroszner made about inflation, I think you have to be a little careful.

speaker: EVANS
text: My memory of ’98 was that we actually had a tightening bias when the Russian default–LTCM came in.

speaker: EVANS
text: We cut 75 basis points.

speaker: EVANS
text: By the spring, we were debating whether or not we should tighten.

speaker: EVANS
text: By the June meeting, we did begin to tighten, and we went up to 6½ percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: My memory of core CPI in 2000 is that it increased about ¾ percentage point.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think there was some divergence between PCE and CPI over that time period.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is something to keep in mind, but I can support 50 today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Evans joins the table with twelve years of experience already.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’ll be glad if you don’t tell how many years of experience I have around this table.

speaker: KOHN
text: I support the action and the language of alternative B for the reasons that have been given by many others around this table.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that the odds favor a significant reduction in aggregate demand owing to the financial conditions we’ve all been talking about.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with Governor Mishkin that part of the disruptive effects of the financial conditions are the small chance of a very adverse effect—the sort of interactions you were talking about, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: Holding back and doing just 25 in that context would be a mistake.

speaker: KOHN
text: Going ahead and doing 50 will largely relieve some uncertainty.

speaker: KOHN
text: With regard to some of the comments about language, the discussion of credit conditions in financial markets in paragraph 2, I guess my read of what we talked about today was just this, and it seems to me that the way it is now is very transparent.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s a nice replication of the discussion we have had, and so I don’t see a need to subtract language about financial markets from this.

speaker: KOHN
text: With regard to the balance of risks in paragraph 4, also consistent with our discussion is the sense that there’s a huge amount of uncertainty about how things are going to evolve, both the markets and the effect on the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t feel as though I know enough to say that the risks are balanced.

speaker: KOHN
text: The range of outcomes is just too wide, and there’s very little central tendency in it.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I’d be very uncomfortable with a statement saying that I kind of thought the risks were balanced.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am much more comfortable with a statement that says there is a lot of uncertainty out there and that’s uncertainty around the economic outlook.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think the current language in paragraph 4 is also a nice representation of the discussion we had today and consistent with our ignorance.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m not concerned about the moral hazard issues.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think our job is to keep the economy at full employment and price stability and let asset markets fluctuate around that.

speaker: KOHN
text: There will be winners and losers.

speaker: KOHN
text: The Congress told us to have maximum employment and stable prices, and that’s what we should be about here.

speaker: KOHN
text: Sometimes that means you need to move to keep employment maximum or prices stable, and we need to take account of the asset markets but not worry about the effects of those actions on asset markets per se.

speaker: KOHN
text: Holding back—inertia—because of concerns about moral hazard would be a serious mistake.

speaker: KOHN
text: We shouldn’t hold interest rates higher than they need to be in order to impose additional cost on borrowers to teach lenders a lesson.

speaker: KOHN
text: Too many innocent bystanders would be hurt in that process.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I strongly support the Bluebook alternative B. I think a 50 basis point cut right away is appropriate, and I like the language.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My reasons for supporting this action are, first, that inflation has been quite well behaved.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’m pretty sanguine about the future.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Second, I think the available economic data that preceded the financial shock are separate from it and support a fed funds rate cut entirely on their own.

speaker: YELLEN
text: You can see that just by looking at the backward-looking Taylor rules in the Bluebook, which suggest that the fed funds rate in the third and fourth quarters should be well below where it is now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In part, inflation has come down, and as President Hoenig and others have pointed out, that’s raised the real fed funds rate—so a real rate of 3¼ percent now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the stance of policy is unnecessarily restrictive, and that is before recent developments.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Third, of course, is that the financial shock has made financial conditions more restrictive.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even if things sort themselves out, I think the conditions will remain more restrictive.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I thought the Bluebook gave us a good method for seeing how much more in showing that the Greenbook implicit equilibrium funds rate has declined 50 basis points since August; that says to me that a 50 basis point cut is not too much to try to neutralize the shock and try to forestall it from damaging the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I contemplate the issue of 50 today or 25 with the presumption that we would do 25 more in October, I find myself strongly favoring 50 today.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we should be taking a forward-looking approach and trying to forestall damage.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I agree with Governor Mishkin that, should developments later on call for us to reverse what we have done, we should not hesitate to do it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I really don’t like the message that a 25 basis point cut would essentially send to markets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It would seem to say, “Well, why did we do 25 basis points today?

speaker: YELLEN
text: It’s because we want to wait and monitor incoming data and see what effect the shock has.” I think that’s an unwise message to send.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, it says that the policy is reactive rather than forward looking, and I hope we’re going to be coming out with a communication package that sends a rather different message.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Also, I really don’t think we’re going to see that much in the spending data over the next six weeks that’s going to be convincing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am also very concerned about the asymmetric nature of the risks that we face and the possibility of the type of nonlinear, negative dynamics that Governors Mishkin and Kohn and you, Mr. Chairman, have mentioned.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like the language in the statement.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it’s very well crafted.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like the idea of discussing forestalling negative effects and our hope and sort of optimism that we’ll be able to do it by sufficient action today.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t like the idea of putting out a statement today that says there are continuing asymmetric downside risks.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It leaves us open to the question, “If you think that, then why didn’t you do more?” I agree with Governor Kohn.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like the risk assessment because I honestly don’t know exactly what the risks are.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like the approach that we’re going to watch and do what is appropriate as events unwind in the future, and I don’t want to have to say that I now feel the downside risks are essentially balanced with other risks to inflation.

speaker: POOLE
text: I favor a cut of 50 basis points, and I think that the alternative B language does what we need it to do.

speaker: POOLE
text: It’s very much in our interest that the markets settle down sooner rather than later.

speaker: POOLE
text: I also think that the moral hazard argument in this context is simply wrong.

speaker: POOLE
text: It’s wrong because if you take an insurance company context, there the issue is that the policyholder takes action that is adverse to the interest of the insurance company.

speaker: POOLE
text: It’s in our interest and it’s in the economy’s interest that the markets settle down sooner rather than later.

speaker: POOLE
text: We want subprime paper to trade.

speaker: POOLE
text: If it’s 30 cents on the dollar, okay.

speaker: POOLE
text: Nobody is talking about subprime paper trading at 100 cents on the dollar or 98 cents on the dollar.

speaker: POOLE
text: We want the market to function so that the positions can be adjusted and so that we can go back to a normal situation in which the paper trades for what it’s really worth.

speaker: POOLE
text: If the data and the anecdotal information justify going down 50 and going down only 50, our best chance to make that stick is actually to do it all at once because, if we can leave rates unchanged in our October meeting, that sets the default option for the following meeting also to be no change rather than further action.

speaker: POOLE
text: So it seems to me our best chance of avoiding an overreaction is to do 50 now and then make the case that we’re waiting to see how all of that works and we don’t think that as time goes on it will probably be necessary to do anything more.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, I favor meaningful action today, so that’s a 50 basis point reduction in the fed funds rate target along the lines of alternative B. I think I pretty well laid out the reasons for that in my earlier comments.

speaker: STERN
text: I think the financial disruptions do matter for the short-term path of the economy in a negative way.

speaker: STERN
text: My judgment is that it is likely to be nontrivial, and so we should respond to that, especially when underlying inflation seems to be moving in the right direction and, if anything, moving a little more rapidly than I earlier anticipated.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to language, well, it’s very tempting to carry on about that and make Michelle even more nervous, [laughter] but I’m convinced as I listen to the conversation that beauty really is in the eyes of the beholder.

speaker: STERN
text: I would make only two comments.

speaker: STERN
text: First, the language in alternative B is basically fine with me.

speaker: STERN
text: I think the final paragraph, the assessment of risk, leaves our options open, which to me is what we’re trying to do.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t have a conviction about what we’re going to want to do in October, and I don’t worry very much about whether at some point down the road—I don’t think it’s going to be all that soon because I don’t think we’ll have enough evidence—we will decide we need to reverse some or all of whatever we wind up doing.

speaker: STERN
text: That’s okay, too, because we’ll be able to explain that fairly readily when the time comes.

speaker: STERN
text: Second, I don’t understand these suggestions to take out references to financial market conditions.

speaker: STERN
text: We devoted a lot of time to talking about that subject today and at the last meeting, and so to act as if it somehow hasn’t been important in what we’re considering here just doesn’t make sense to me.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, Mr. Chairman, I already presented my position.

speaker: FISHER
text: Like President Evans, I came into this room expecting to argue for a 25 basis point cut.

speaker: FISHER
text: Unlike President Evans, I’m still there.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just want to record, since I’ve already lost the battle, two points.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think Vice Chairman Geithner said it right.

speaker: FISHER
text: Governor Kohn is absolutely correct.

speaker: FISHER
text: We should be guided by what we think is going to happen in the economy and not be pushed around by the markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s one reason I’m in favor of 25 basis points and not 50, with an eye open to possibly moving further later.

speaker: FISHER
text: But the point that Vice Chairman Geithner made that I think is relevant here is that we should direct policy not to insulate but to facilitate.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that’s a key point.

speaker: FISHER
text: Another is that we need to demonstrate credibility that we have a feel for what’s happening in the markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: On that basis, we need to at least be mindful that this is the first decision to move under the new FOMC.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m a little worried, despite my enormous admiration for President Yellen, about her interpretation of what is reactive.

speaker: FISHER
text: Indeed, we might be viewed as being reactive by moving 50 basis points.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that’s a real risk.

speaker: FISHER
text: What we say, therefore, is very important—not just in the statement but also in our subsequent minutes and speeches, as President Plosser said.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m, therefore, a little sensitive to two references to developments in financial markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yes, that’s what we talked about, but getting ahead of the curve, we can state it too strongly and look as though we’re just way too reactive, particularly given that this is the first decision to cut.

speaker: FISHER
text: As President Rosengren said, there’s no question that we’re going to ease; the question is how much.

speaker: FISHER
text: The only suggestion I would have on the wording is to refer to the financial markets once rather than twice.

speaker: FISHER
text: The other thing I would ask to be reassured on, Mr. Chairman, is that, if we’re going to go to 50 basis points, it is not a lock that we will put forward the new credit facility because I think doing that simultaneously with 50 basis points would basically confirm that we are reactive and that we’re overreacting to the markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: Just a quick point on moral hazard—I think there are fair concerns about it.

speaker: WARSH
text: The losses that have been felt in the markets in the past six weeks— that money is gone.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is not coming back.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is true that some of these institutions will find new ways, create new products, buy assets cheap, but that lesson has been learned.

speaker: WARSH
text: I won’t say forever [laughter] because that is an awfully long time, but it is changed for purposes of this cycle.

speaker: WARSH
text: Profit profiles of all these financial institutions are now fundamentally different.

speaker: WARSH
text: Nondepository institutions are looking at their access to capital in a dramatically different way, thinking about whether they have business models that work.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think it overstates our ability to suggest that, whether we move 50 or more over the ensuing months, we would somehow fix that and make things like they once were.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think the moral hazard argument in this context is really a straw man that I just wanted, after Governor Kohn’s comment, to kick one more time.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of the stance of monetary policy, as we’ve discussed, the equilibrium rate here is a function of fed funds and a function of what’s happening in the real capital markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: The real capital markets are fundamentally different, and so a reduction in the fed funds rate today of 50 basis points may or may not be sufficient to find some new equilibrium.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we will need to continue to evaluate that as we go forward.

speaker: WARSH
text: Bottom line on the statement, I support alternative B and the 50 basis point reduction.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the markets will have some genuine consternation this afternoon and in the ensuing days in figuring out what we mean by paragraph 4.

speaker: WARSH
text: As others have said, there is some ambiguity, but I suspect it is inevitable given that we really don’t know what our next actions will be.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I support alternative B as written.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I mentioned before, from a risk- management perspective I think it’s very sensible to make a 50 basis point cut.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have an environment in which the economy has been growing modestly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some of the numbers that we’ve seen recently—the lower numbers in the labor market in the revisions from the previous months as well as from August—presumably had nothing to do with the August financial turmoil or I think it’s highly unlikely that the August numbers had anything to do with it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The housing market was turning down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So even though we have been growing a little more strongly, we’re really coming in facing headwinds in some important markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As the Chairman mentioned, the interaction between those two leads to a potential for downside risk, particularly in light of the financial market turmoil that we’ve been seeing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it’s important to be aware of that and to take that into account in undertaking our monetary policy actions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, as I’ve mentioned before and as others have mentioned, even given the dramatic changes that we’ve seen in the past month in market expectations about what we are going to do, we have not seen an uptick in inflation expectations in terms either of surveys or of the markets, which heartens me that a 50 basis point action is unlikely to have a large negative effect on expectations about the future path of inflation, particularly, I think, given the language in alternative B. I don’t see this at all as being reactive.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One thing that I’m extremely pleased to see is that the FOMC did not have an intermeeting cut.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that would have been seen as reactive.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The LTCM situation was worked out in late September.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There was the meeting with the 25 basis point cut, and then there was the concern with another 25 basis point cut that came after that, and then the following meeting they did it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There was an intermeeting move.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That seemed much more reactive.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think our approach has been very level-headed, and that is one thing that has allowed the expected inflation rates to stay stable even as they expect us to cut the policy rate.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I’m very much heartened by that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Then with respect to what Charlie and others have brought up about reversals, that’s very important.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Exactly as President Evans said—pardon me for reverting to your civilian name—[laughter] certainly what happened was that, by June, the FOMC decided to reverse and then in the next three meetings reversed the 75 basis points.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The FOMC went up to 6½ percent, and only about six or seven months later dramatically reversed that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Many people ex post have said moving up that much was ill-advised.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Even before September 11, the FOMC had dropped interest rates approximately 400 basis points in a very short time, suggesting a very rapid reversal.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I’m not sure that it was necessary to go up to those heights to forestall inflation pressure.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So in this circumstance, I’m very supportive of alternative B. I think it will be read well by the markets that we’re aware of what’s going on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’ve waited until our meeting, and we’ve left our options open in alternative B, honestly admitting that we are uncertain about what is going forward and leaving open the possibility of future actions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Taking a stronger action now has the potential to help unlodge the logjam in the markets, and we may have to take fewer actions in the future.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I support, Mr. Chairman, cutting the fed funds rate 50 basis points today and the language in alternative B, and I cede the rest of my time to you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you very much, everyone.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The one person at the table who I know is going to be right is President Hoenig, who says that whatever we do is going to be criticized.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I can write the Wall Street Journal editorial for tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just want to say that I think that moral hazard is a terribly misunderstood idea and that as the central bank we have a responsibility to help markets function normally and to promote economic stability broadly speaking.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are not in the business of bailing out individuals or businesses.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As long as we make that distinction, I think we’re fine, but it may be history that agrees to that rather than the newspapers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I do advocate 50 basis points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The modal assessment of the Greenbook suggests that at least 50 basis points are needed to restore a pre-financial-crisis neutrality.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There have been some differences about how severe this is likely to be, but something on that order of magnitude seems about right.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There seem to be significant tail risks, and I think some insurance is worthwhile.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Quite frankly, I thought about the alternative C option—25 basis points and a downward bias.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One of the concerns I have would be that turmoil during the intermeeting period would sort of force us to come in and do the next 25, and I would rather say that we did what we had to do—we are moving at the meeting—and let the markets absorb that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I also want to agree with Rick and others who have noted that we should be prepared to take this back, and I state that for the record.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the statement, I prefer alternative B. I have struggled with President Pianalto’s interesting suggestion about deleting the last clause in paragraph 2.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess in the end I would prefer to leave it as it is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What this is doing is two things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, we’re trying very much to clarify in this paragraph that what we care about are the effects on the broader economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is, financial market disruptions have occurred, but we are trying to ameliorate the effects on the broader economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, we need in some sense to play a little defense in that this is a sharp change from the statement of August 7.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What has changed since August 7?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, clearly, the most obvious thing that has changed is the financial market situation, which in turn has fed through to housing and other parts of the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to the assessment of risks, I think what the market wants to hear is that we get it, that we’re here, that we are ready to move as needed, and that we pay attention to both parts of our mandate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think that it’s a little premature to make that a balance of risks, and the inherent flexibility here is useful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker’s comment that this is actually a downside balance of risks is an interesting one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It might be taken that way to the extent that markets think that the economy will deteriorate much further and the Fed will have to respond.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But our perspective is that we will respond as needed, and we should be careful to emphasize that in public—in the minutes and elsewhere.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s my recommendation—50 basis points and alternative B.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, could you please call the roll?

speaker: DANKER
text: I’ll be reading the directive from page 35 of the Bluebook, and the assessment of risks from the table distributed today.

speaker: DANKER
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: DANKER
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with reducing the federal funds rate to an average of around 4¾ percent.” Then: “Developments in financial markets since the Committee’s last regular meeting have increased the uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Committee will continue to assess the effects of these and other developments on economic prospects and will act as needed to foster price stability and sustainable economic growth.” Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes President Evans Yes President Hoenig Yes Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes Governor Mishkin Yes President Poole Yes President Rosengren Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We can recess now for half an hour for lunch.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Board of Governors will vote, but the rest can recess for lunch.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: During lunch, our Congressional Liaison person, Laricke Blanchard, will give us an informal update on congressional matters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will try to reconvene around 2:00.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we reconvene our meeting?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Item 5 on the agenda is communication.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have a couple of things to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Scott Alvarez and his colleagues have prepared a memo, which you received, on the issue of voting on the full statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Could you give us a brief overview, Scott, and then I’d like, if possible, just to get a sense of the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I hope we don’t have to get into a lengthy discussion.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: I was delighted to hear this morning that employment of lawyers is now a factor in assessing the robustness of the economy.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: I recommend that in the Committee’s drive for transparency, however, the FOMC not disclose this new factor because undoubtedly there will be those among my colleagues in the legal profession who will sue for a more prominent and permanent place in the Committee’s forecasting models.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Today, I’ve been asked to address an element of the Committee’s governance.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Over time, a consensus appears to have developed that the Committee would prefer to change its current practice of approving only the assessment of risk portion of the policy announcement issued after each Committee meeting and instead approve the entire statement.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: If that is the Committee’s desire, there are several methods for achieving that result.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Each method has advantages and disadvantages.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: A key concern in choosing an alternative involves the amount of flexibility that the Committee wishes to retain to allow other methods for announcing its decisions, especially in emergency, intermeeting, and special circumstances.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: A second key concern is how much attention the Committee wants to draw to its change in practice.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The first and simplest alternative would be for the Committee just to begin voting on the entire statement along with the policy action.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: This approach maintains the maximum flexibility for the Committee to alter its practice in different situations and to adjust the content of the statement.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: This approach also maintains the flexibility of the Chairman to issue a statement in times of emergency or special need.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: If the Committee chooses this alternative, the Committee also controls the amount of prominence that it calls to this change in the minutes.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: If the Committee believes this change is significant, it may include a robust discussion in the minutes.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: If it views the change as not significant, it may have no or only a brief notice in the minutes.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: A second and slightly more formal alternative would be to adopt a nonbinding resolution outlining the Committee’s desired new practice.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: A nonbinding resolution provides a more formal vehicle than the first alternative for explaining the change in voting practice in the minutes.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: At the same time, because the resolution would be nonbinding, it retains the flexibility of simply voting on the matter.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The remaining two alternatives are the most formal and involve adopting a binding resolution or changing the Committee’s rules to require Committee approval of statements issued at each regularly scheduled meeting.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: These alternatives are more binding because they require further deliberate Committee action to change the practice in the future.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: A rule change would also be very visible because, in addition to an explanation in the Committee’s minutes, a rule change entails publication in the code of federal regulations.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: This would attract attention in part because the Committee’s rules currently do not address voting practices beyond the requirements of a quorum.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: A formal resolution or a rule change may hold an advantage for a member who wants to delineate publicly the exact content of the statement.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: On the other hand, were the Committee to desire to retain flexibility to alter the content of the statement, a rule or resolution would have to be carefully crafted to ensure that flexibility.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: A binding resolution or a rule change could also limit the flexibility of the Committee and of the Chairman to speak about the FOMC’s actions.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: To date, the Chairman has retained the flexibility to speak for the Committee in emergency and other situations.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Indeed, the statement was originally a statement of the Chairman, not of the Committee.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: If the Committee desires to retain this flexibility and yet adopt a binding resolution or rule, the resolution or rule could be drafted to maintain that flexibility.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: I would be happy to entertain any questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any questions for Scott?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, it appears that one thing we can do is just do it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Precedents have been pretty effective in this Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, our circulation of table 1 has become a regular modus operandi.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, if others would like to go further, that’s fine with me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is it the sense of the Committee that simply beginning to adopt this action would be adequate?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My sense of the table is, then, that we will just begin the practice at the next meeting of voting on the entire statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That, of course, raises the possibility for dissent based on the statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have to use good judgment on that particular decision.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there is dissent on the statement, Scott, it would be explained in the minutes?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s the same practice we use for a dissent on the action.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t feel strongly, but would it make more sense to have this change be consistent in time with changes in communication strategy more broadly?

speaker: WARSH
text: Now, recognizing this is not of the same import, but rather than have a question be raised and then have to explain it through our communication folks and others, I wonder whether this might not just be sort of a housekeeping footnote as part of a broader communication rollout.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, if our communication schedule continues along current lines—and we can discuss that next—it would in fact be in these minutes that we made this decision, right?

speaker: KOHN
text: Well, if we’re just going to do it, we haven’t had a vote yet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So would it be okay if we just put this in the October minutes, reflecting the first time we took that action?

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: This would be just a discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In that case, it would be part of the overall description.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is an agenda item at this meeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: We could just say that this is our sense at this meeting of what we’re going to do now and just leave it at that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we also have another element coming up right now— an update by Governor Kohn on the communication strategy.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The Committee needn’t take a formal position today on what it does, particularly if the discussion suggests that the Committee simply wants to act when the time is right.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: So the minutes could be very general.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t attach much substance to this.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think very many people even know or care or would view this as a change.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All else being equal, we’ll try to get it into the October minutes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But if it turns out to be a problem, we’ll address it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Don, do you want to update us on the projections?

speaker: KOHN
text: We are planning right now to go live with the enhanced projections process after the October meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: The plan is to have a speech by the Chairman in early November, and then the forecast and its narrative would be published with the minutes of the October meeting, so three weeks into November.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would have to say that’s a planning presumption, and we are going to proceed on that basis.

speaker: KOHN
text: But who knows what the circumstances will be when we get to the October meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: The Committee could well reconsider whether that is the right time to add a new way of communicating about the future, if it’s an unsettled time.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we can discuss it again.

speaker: KOHN
text: No votes or final decisions today, but just to alert you about the planning process going forward.

speaker: KOHN
text: The subcommittee sent out some recommendations in terms of the variables, and that’s what we used for this dry run.

speaker: KOHN
text: What we would like from you is, if people have comments on the whole thing or on the particular variables that we used, to hear them.

speaker: KOHN
text: We also sent out some material on uncertainty and how that is portrayed.

speaker: KOHN
text: The most important thing to lock in soon is what variables we are going to ask you to use for the October meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: We will have a two-day meeting in October.

speaker: KOHN
text: We can discuss things further.

speaker: KOHN
text: We can discuss what the box on uncertainty might look like when it comes out in November.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we don’t really need to have a detailed discussion on that—though if you have comments, they would be useful.

speaker: KOHN
text: But we do need to lock in the variables.

speaker: KOHN
text: So the floor is open for anybody who wants to bring something to the attention of the Committee.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I was completely fine with the proposal.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The only thing it mentioned that I would slightly differ on is that I would like the box on uncertainty to come out with every forecast narrative—you know, the four times a year deal.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The negative is that it would be the same each time, so there would not be much that is new.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But when you look at inflation reports that people have done, they frequently have a box that’s the same each time.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In my view, the issue of making sure that people understand that there’s a lot of uncertainty about our forecast is so critical that, even if they ignore a bit because we’re putting it out every time and it’s just a standard part of the package, I think it is extremely important.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I feel generally comfortable with the trajectory you’re on and with the evolving shape of this thing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is one issue still where it seems to me we don’t quite have it right, which is that the narrative description does not, because it really cannot, describe the story that is reflected in the central tendency of the forecast.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So the narrative is really more a repetition of the numbers and of what is in the tables around dispersion, and that is probably because we haven’t given the staff a way to talk about or let us talk about the story that underpins it in some sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Since a central value in this innovation to the communication regime is to give a bit more texture to the story that underpins the central tendency, it would be worth exploring whether we could figure out a way to design our discussion so that the staff could write a narrative in a way that does a better job of allowing that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: With that exception, that qualification, it seems as though what you laid out, Don, makes sense.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the staff shouldn’t hesitate to talk about different points of view.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is not at all necessary to come up with or try to manufacture a consensus narrative.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I didn’t mean to suggest not having anything that reflects the dispersion of views or the uncertainty around those views.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But right now it’s so skeletal that it doesn’t add much value to the tables, and it gives in some ways less texture than what is in the minutes, frankly, about the outlook over time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If the central purpose of this is to animate the set of judgments about the evolution, we could do it a little better that way.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is complicated because we have all sorts of different conditioning assumptions that underpin our forecasts.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: When those conditioning assumptions vary, you can’t really tell much from what the variance in the forecast is.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We don’t ask people to give a modal and an expected forecast and the difference between the two, even though we ask them about the balance of uncertainty in that sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So it is hard in some sense, Mr. Chairman, but I didn’t mean to suggest you would want to do that because you want to try to force a consensus view.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A lot of us this morning discussed tail risk, and it does seem that the tables we have right now might not capture the nature of tail risk that actually was critical to a lot of that discussion.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Some things that are related to your ability to forecast variables are tied to uncertainty.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But looking forward, there are also the kinds of risks, which I don’t think we’re capturing, that were central to some of our discussion.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Is there a way to capture tail risk or the distribution—kind of like the scenarios that are done in the Greenbook, but, in effect, what people were talking about with tail risk?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I don’t think we’re quite there yet, and I don’t know that we need to do it for the first round.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But we need to give some more thought to what tail risk means and what we actually mean when we talk about insurance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have a section on the risks, though, right?

speaker: KOHN
text: It should be possible in that context.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s hard to think about exactly how to do that in terms of the survey, but certainly that’s exactly where the narrative would have a lot of value because it’s really hard to do it just in terms of some kind of standard survey.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I hope that in the future we won’t have many discussions like today’s, but we might.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Maybe that could be handled in the narrative.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Yes, it gets to the texture that Tim was getting at.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I was thinking about maybe having a question that tries to capture it so that we could at least respond to it if it’s an important point for us to cover.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our last item is approaches to stabilizing money markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me make, if I might, just a few introductory comments about where this came from and what we’re asking of you today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As we have been thinking about various money market issues, two things have come up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that there have actually been a surprisingly large number of problems in dollar markets in Europe—that is, banks that need dollar-based funding.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Debbie reminds me that this is a joint Board-FOMC meeting and that I need a motion.

speaker: KOHN
text: I move to close the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first issue is the need for dollar funding and dollar term funding by European banks, which has caused problems in Europe but also has bled over to some extent to dollar markets in the United States.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have been in conversations at various times with Europe about a swap arrangement that would provide dollars to Europe to address this issue, but the issue has not yet, obviously, been brought to you as a Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second issue that we have been looking at is how to address the stigma of the discount window.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there ways to provide liquidity that would help normalize money markets, particularly term money markets, and would allow banks to make use of the enormous amount of collateral they have at the discount window, but would avoid the stigma and create a more efficient system?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The solution that the staff came up with on that was to have an auction facility that would essentially set an endogenous price and, because it was an auction, it might look more like a good business proposition rather than like a move of desperation and, therefore, would not have the same stigma.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there are these two separate issues—the auction facility as a way of addressing the stigma of the discount window and the swap as a way of getting dollars into the European dollar markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some conversations that I had, in particular with President Trichet of the European Central Bank, came up with the possibility of combining these two things, essentially having auctions simultaneously in the United States and in Europe, and then using the swap markets to provide the dollars to the extent that the ECB would like to have them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Swiss National Bank expressed interest in joining this as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In a moment you will be hearing from the staff a few details about these proposals.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, let me just say a couple of things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, one thing on governance is that the rules here are that the auction credit facility requires an amendment of regulation, which is a province of the Board, so in that respect it’s a Board decision.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, obviously, the Bank presidents are very much involved in this because it would involve discount window management, and therefore, I think it’s fair for us to have the discussion of this from the perspective of the entire Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, the swaps would be, of course, a decision of the FOMC, and they obviously would need a vote.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We began working on this some weeks ago when the markets were in a particularly stressful condition, and our hope was to try to normalize those markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I said earlier today, the markets seem to be getting better, and this may not be the exact moment that we want to be doing this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, it might be a good idea to have this process or, alternatively, the two separate processes—we could do either one without the other—available should market conditions demand it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So what I would like to propose is that we have a presentation; some comments, discussion, and questions from you; and we’ll get a sense of the Committee in terms of where you are on this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I will commit to is that we won’t take any votes today, but before using either option or a combination of both options, we will have a videoconference and ask for your formal approval of the swaps and at least your consent to the ACF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we are not planning to implement this immediately, but we would like to have the possibility of having it as an option, should money markets seem to require it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So with that, let me turn to the staff.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Could I ask a question?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What does a closed meeting mean, Scott?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Does it mean there’s a transcript, with a normal release, or there’s no transcript?

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The FOMC continues to be in meeting, and so what is happening here is part of the transcript of the FOMC.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: But on top of that is a Board meeting.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The Board meeting has only minutes.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Those minutes are very summary.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The current plan is that they won’t be released until after Thursday.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But the minutes of the FOMC meeting will be released in two weeks?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They will be very general—something like there was a discussion of means to address money market issues.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Explore the range of options to address.

speaker: LACKER
text: Maybe this isn’t the appropriate time, but do you envision that approval by Reserve Bank boards of directors would be required for this facility?

speaker: LACKER
text: Is that part of the governance, or is that maybe a question for later?

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Well, the auction credit facility doesn’t require the approval of the Reserve Banks.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The Board is required to set the rules for lending under 10B, which is what we’ll explain in the program.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: However, the interest rate on loans under the credit facility would, of course, be established by the Reserve Banks and reviewed and determined by the Board.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: So depending on the governance of the different Reserve Banks, it may be that the interest rate that is the result of the auction would be something that the board of directors would want to recommend.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Our proposal, as you’ll hear it later on, will be that the boards of directors adopt the process rather than a particular interest rate, and that would allow the auction to continue over time.

speaker: LACKER
text: So they would have to act to make the rate they set determined by this process.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Like seasonal credit works today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t you go ahead and make your presentation, and then we’ll take questions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your introductory remarks and the questioning and some answers that we just had covered some of the points that I was going to make in my introductory comments.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It has been a long day already, and you received a detailed memo.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So in view of that, we thought we would abbreviate our briefings relative to what we had initially planned.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In response to recent developments, as you know, the staff has proposed consideration of a set of responses that could be coordinated with actions of foreign central banks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We distributed considerable material to you on Friday, the gist of which is proposing an auction credit facility and swap lines for foreign central banks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I’d like to note that a large number of staff here at the Board and at the New York Fed contributed intensive work to that document and to planning for the facility more generally, and I’d like to mention Pat Parkinson and Myron Kwast, whose names were inadvertently omitted from the list of authors.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under the proposed facility, the Federal Reserve would auction blocks of collateralized twenty-eight-day discount window credit to institutions eligible to borrow from our primary credit program.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As the Chairman said, based on discussions with the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank, we understand that those institutions are interested in conducting parallel auctions of term dollar credit to institutions located in their jurisdictions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Those institutions have requested, but to date only on a preliminary basis, the establishment of reciprocal currency swaps lines on which they would draw to fund the extensions of dollar credit under such auctions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We have provisionally assumed that $20 billion of twenty-eight-day ACF loans would be auctioned each week over the course of four weeks, building up to a maximum of $80 billion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The ECB would, similarly, auction up to $40 billion, and the Swiss National Bank would auction up to a total of $20 billion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Jim Clouse was going to present a briefing providing additional background on the markets and the pros and cons of the proposal, but we have decided to skip that at this point in the interest of time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Jim could answer questions on that if you’d like.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But you may not have had a chance to absorb the details of the implementation, and the Reserve Bank Presidents in particular as well as the Board members may be interested in them.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Sandy Krieger will talk a little about that, and then Karen Johnson will wrap up with some comments on the swap line.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: I will discuss at a high level some of the operational aspects of the auction credit facility.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Yesterday, SCRM (Subcommittee on Credit Risk Management) members and discount window officers at your Reserve Banks talked together about the operational details.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Although they have had only hours to learn and to think about this, they seem to be comfortable with the basics and are helping to work out the open items.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: So, how would this work?

speaker: KRIEGER
text: First, the watchwords for implementing this program would be “simple and robust.” This means employing many of the procedures that we already use locally to extend discount window credit.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The discount staffs have the necessary expertise to receive and to screen bid information.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The local Reserve Bank 4 Materials used by Ms. Krieger are appended to this transcript (appendix 4).

speaker: KRIEGER
text: staff members are in the best position to know the bidders in their District.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: They would use many of the same procedures they use to accept discount window loan requests.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The applications we use to determine adequate collateralization for discount window loan requests would be used to determine acceptability of auction bids, with a supplemental calculation to screen for the excess of collateralization we would be requiring for ACF credit.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The discount window “hotline” telephone infrastructure—a number with multiple lines known to depository institutions (DIs) in each District— would be used for Reserve Bank staff to receive and confirm bids and awards from DIs in the District.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The SCRM members and discount window officers are working now with Board staff members on a communication plan for outreach to DIs should this facility be implemented.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Let me now walk you briefly through the auction cycle that is in the handout.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: We have been contemplating that on Friday at noon the Board would announce the terms of the next auction.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: It would include, for example, “On Monday, October 1, 2007, there will be an auction for up to $20 billion of twenty-eight-day funds, to be issued on Thursday, October 4, 2007.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Bids may be submitted to local Reserve Banks between times X and Y on the auction date.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The minimum bid size will be $50 million, and the minimum bid rate will be Z percent.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The auction results will be announced on Wednesday, October 3, at 10 a.m. eastern time.” Details pertaining to the eligibility, the bidding, and the award procedures would be defined in an announcement posted to the Board of Governors’ website, and discount window staff would be available on the announcement date to answer calls to their local hotlines regarding the terms of the specific auction.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: On the morning of the auction date (typically a Monday), the Reserve Bank staff would perform the necessary calculation to determine the maximum bid size for the eligible DIs in their District, based on collateral pledged.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Also on the auction date, Reserve Bank staff members would receive and confirm or reject phone bids during the announced bidding window, following defined procedures.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: After the close, the Reserve Bank staff would submit formatted information to the auction agent by encrypted e-mail.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Next, the auction agent would combine the information from the individual Reserve Banks.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: A first step would be to constrain the separate bids from branches of the same foreign banking organization to comply with single-bidder rules.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The administration of the other elements of the auction allocation is straightforward.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: A predefined process would award partial allocations at the stop-out rate when bidding at this rate exceeds the maximum amount expressed in the auction announcement.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The auction agent would communicate the awards back to Reserve Banks on Tuesday afternoon, and the Reserve Bank staff would check these against the stop-out rate information that the auction agent provides.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: On Wednesday, the Board would publicly announce the auction results and post this information to its website.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: At that point, Reserve Banks would begin to notify the DIs in their respective Districts that submitted winning bids of the awards they would receive the following day and the rate they would be charged.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: On Thursday, Reserve Banks would post the term credit to the automated application that they currently use for extensions of credit.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Unless otherwise requested by the DI, the credit would be posted to the DI’s reserve account at the end of the day.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: I have covered most, if not all, the details in the table of auction terms and the auction dateline that are in your handout, and I will turn to Karen to continue our presentation.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: In conjunction with the establishment of the ACF, the staff proposes that the FOMC authorize temporary reciprocal currency arrangements with the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: These facilities would provide dollar financing for parallel credit auctions for euro area and Swiss banks, which the staff understands would be conducted in a manner broadly similar to that provided for U.S. banks by the ACF, which Sandy just described.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The proposal is for swap arrangements that would authorize the ECB and the SNB to draw up to $10 billion and $5 billion, respectively, each week with individual draws for a period of twenty-eight days.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Cumulative totals may reach $40 billion for the ECB and $20 billion for the SNB.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The swap arrangements would expire after six months unless renewed.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The purchases of U.S. dollars with foreign currency would be based on the prevailing spot exchange rate, and the ECB and the SNB would charge their banks and pay interest on the swap at the rate established each week by the U.S. auction.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: These temporary swap arrangements are proposed so that dollar funding problems now faced by European banks, particularly at terms longer than overnight, can be addressed in a parallel manner and at the same time that dollar funding problems of U.S. banks are addressed.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Improved conditions in European dollar trading would guard against the spillover of volatility in such trading to New York trading and could help reduce term funding pressures in U.S. markets.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Establishment of these swap lines in parallel with the ACF could have broad, positive confidence effects.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Given the financial positions of these two central banks, the swap lines would involve virtually no credit risk on our part.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: By providing dollars to the ECB and the SNB to use in their efforts to address the term dollar funding problems in Europe, we benefit the credit markets without ourselves providing support to banks overseas.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for the staff?

speaker: FISHER
text: Just so I understand this, let’s say Paribas shows up at our auction window.

speaker: FISHER
text: Can they also show up at the European window, or are we going to make sure that there’s no duplication?

speaker: FISHER
text: How do you make sure there’s no duplication so that foreign banks might get an advantage or vice versa?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: They will be able to bid in both, President Fisher.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Just as our banks will be able to bid in both.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s why I said vice versa.

speaker: FISHER
text: So for certain banks, holding companies, or organizations, there is really more than the stated limit, right?

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Well, the Europeans are going to impose a structure.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: It’s not “no limit”; it’s the sum of the two.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just wanted to make sure that that was the case.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Two things, one related to that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On the first page, you said that you consolidate all the foreign banking organizations.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So in the United States they would just operate as one, even though they may have different subsidiaries, and they will be treated as one organization, even if formally they have multiple organizations in the United States.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Under the single-bidder guidelines, they’d be treated as one.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: But for extensions of credit, that’s done at the local Reserve Bank.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: So their bids would be combined and treated as one, and then they would be disaggregated so the loans could be booked at the local Reserve Bank.

speaker: FISHER
text: But again, for Paribas, for example, which can come to our discount window, the total sum would be 20 percent for any single credit across the System, even though it might be pieced out by Bank.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Second, in terms of the timing of the auction itself, are there any challenges because of some of the delays here?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This seems like a somewhat slower process than some other auctions that are run—the bids are submitted on Monday, and the notification isn’t until Wednesday.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: We’ve given ourselves a lot of time just because of the uncertainty associated with it, with an opportunity to change it if we were to do this over time with learning.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So you have the flexibility, if you get used to it, to be able to do it almost in real time.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The preference is for settlement always to be on Thursday, so we can time it with open market operations and, to the extent that this is or is not combined with actions in Europe, with some time parameters that might be sensitive to European time zones.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: But in terms of how long it takes to run a somewhat automated and somewhat manual auction, we don’t really know.

speaker: KRIEGER
