text: We don’t anticipate that it will be that complicated, but we’re giving ourselves a little flexibility in the beginning.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One point in this regard, Governor Kroszner, is that we’ll be taking the bids over the telephone.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That just means that there is going to be a certain amount of time depending on how many bidders show up.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It’s not a fully automated process.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think that this is a very creative solution to thinking about the stigma issue and providing liquidity to the market, so I applaud the effort to try to broaden the tools that we have to think about these kinds of issues.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: When I was thinking about how this might actually work, I did come up with a couple of operational questions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My thought was that if we had this auction, who would be the most likely to want to take the money out?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I could imagine a situation in which you would have five borrowers taking out the full $20 billion.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If those five were Countrywide, Washington Mutual, and three European banks, it would certainly give the perception that we were focused on financial institutions that had significant risks.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of worrying about markets as opposed to institutions, I think there is a potential perception issue.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So my first question related to that is the following: You picked 20 percent of the auction; but if you picked a smaller percentage of the auction that any one institution could take, by broadening out the number of institutions, I think there would be more of a perception that it was designed for markets rather than for institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Now, I am aware that the offset to that is that you might not take down the whole auction.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So the less that any one institution can take, the greater is the risk that you’re not fully subscribed, or you presumably could change the amount.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But I’d like to hear at least some thought as to how you came up with 20 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The second issue is that when we think about the discount window, which is primarily for overnight loans, there seems to be a bit of ambiguity in terms of whether you are primary or secondary credit, and in this situation I think it starts becoming important.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: When I think of an institution like Countrywide having a $4 billion loan, the OTS views them as a 2-rated institution, and I don’t know how we would view them if we were regulating them.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I do know that the markets seem to be assessing them as being a good bit different from a 2-rated institution.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So when we’re thinking about an institution that we might have concerns about giving 23A exemptions and an institution that might have difficulty raising funds because the market perception is that they are very, very risky, how comfortable are we with the way the discount window thinks about primary and secondary credit for institutions that the financial markets at least think have a high probability of a fall?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My third question ties to the European banks.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It seems for the European banks that the ECB is better positioned to make the credit evaluation of whether they are risky or not risky and the equivalent of our primary-secondary distinctions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given that the European banks have the option to borrow, assuming that the swap did go through, it would seem preferable that they borrow in Europe rather than borrow here because I think about the incentives going forward.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If a European bank that has financial problems that, say, the German authorities and the German Bank are aware of but we may not be fully aware of borrowed $4 billion from our liquidity window, I wonder what the incentives are for either the institution or the regulator to fully disclose the nature of the problems.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I’d like to get your sense of why you think it necessary for U.S. banks to have access in both locations and for European banks to have access in both locations.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Those were the three questions that I had.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Well, starting with the last question, I think the sense is that it’s a dollar funding problem.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Obviously, the markets are deepest here, so that’s part of the interest in offering it here to the broad range of institutions and the institutions that need it.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: It is also related to your question about the limits.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: One thing we did was to look at what the Treasury does as an auctioneer.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: They have a 35 percent limit.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: So we were working down from there, trying to see how low we felt comfortable going and not departing from what are typical auction norms.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: Also, if this is really meant to facilitate funding for those who need it, is there a possibility that, if you go too low, you won’t have the desired impact?

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Could I add a couple of thoughts before you move on to the next thing?

speaker: JOHNSON
text: The concerns of the sort you raised are part of the reason that the swap is being proposed at all.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Consider just doing the ACF.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: These are duly licensed depository institutions in the United States.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: If we were to create the ACF but to say that no duly licensed DI in the United States with a foreign parent could participate, that’s a huge change in our national treatment policy.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: So without a decision to really change the way we approach licensed entities in the United States, we don’t have a way of distinguishing foreign parent organizations from domestically licensed DIs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But we would know whether they have access to an ACF facility in Europe or an ACF facility here, and it would seem as though saying that you have access to an ACF facility somewhere would not exclude, say, the Canadians or the Japanese but would exclude the Europeans if they were participating in the same program.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: I’ll leave that to the lawyers to decide.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: But I am suggesting that by creating a swap, the staff had a presumption that the Europeans could work with the ECB and a certain hope, if nothing else, that they would work with the ECB.

speaker: JOHNSON
text: Otherwise, with no swap, we have basically put them back in the position that they are getting this directly from us.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If I could just make two points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One reason that you might want to let them borrow in both places is that their collateral may be in both places, and they may have different availability of collateral in the two locations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second reason is that your goal at the end of the day is to get the money to those who most need it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To the extent that you put constraints on the system, you are going to make it more difficult for the money to get to the people who value it the most.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We make that distinction already in the discount window with primary and secondary.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So if you are at a CAMEL rating of 4 or 5, we normally would not allow you to borrow as a primary credit.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we are taking the discount window as an analogy, yes, we want to give it to the people who need it, but we don’t want to give it to the people who need it so much that they are about to fail.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: No, I think we all agree on that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think it’s clear in the documentation that to be eligible to bid you have to be eligible to borrow at the primary credit facility.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: To be eligible to bid in the auction, as it’s designed, you have to be eligible to borrow from a Federal Reserve Bank at the primary credit facility.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Now, if you are an institution that is migrating across states of the world and ratings in the midst of this four-week program, then we’d face some awkward decision in that context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think that Karen’s response is right, which is that in general, in the world today, we have a lot of large institutions that are essentially dollar based, that live with a big mismatch between the access to liquidity in the currency where they may need it and the liquidity that the home country central bank is willing to provide.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In that context, being open to respond to requests for a swap is a way to help limit the risk you referred to, which is that we don’t want to live in a system where, if there’s substantial dollar-based liquidity needed at a non-U.S. institution, if the only option that exists is for us to be the ones providing liquidity, then that would not be a terrific situation for us or for the home country central bank and its supervisor, probably because they will be better at making the liquidity-solvency judgment in some sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You would want them to have the means to actually respond to that need, if they think it’s appropriate, without having the entire burden for that come on us.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the other hand, they exist here in the United States as depository institutions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: They have a set of not rights but expectations about what they can borrow and what kind of liquidity insurance they can get from us, and we can’t change those in the middle of the game.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Mishkin had a question.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Actually, great minds think alike.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The first question you asked was exactly the one I was going to ask.

speaker: FISHER
text: The degree to which this new Lombard facility’s bidding process would avoid the stigma issue is unclear.

speaker: FISHER
text: Could you repeat to me how this deals with the stigma issue?

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s my first question, and then I have another one after this.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, partly by auctioning credit, so institutions are coming to the Federal Reserve voluntarily and paying a price that is market based.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Another point is that the institutions are regarded as generally sound.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: They have to meet a certain qualification standard to get to the discount window, and we would be taking certain steps in terms of our reports to try to distinguish this from other discount window credit.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Now, that said, I think we have to admit that we’re not sure the degree to which this would deal with the stigma issue.

speaker: FISHER
text: I mean, aren’t they still saying that they are distressed?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: No, the economics are better because you have to think about the minimum rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The minimum rate is the swap rate plus 10 basis points, which is well below one- month LIBOR and well below the one-month term fed funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So there is that room in- between.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You could actually criticize a bank for not participating in this.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They are somehow leaving money on the table by not taking advantage of this.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m sure the small banks will.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s why they’re not going to like it.

speaker: FISHER
text: In other words, this is a big institutional facility.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Just as long as you need 50 million bucks.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, you have to have $63 million, if you’re using the ratios you’re using, in collateral.

speaker: FISHER
text: So there is that aspect.

speaker: FISHER
text: I understand that’s what it was meant to address.

speaker: FISHER
text: My second question derives from the first, and that is, could you give us a little background on the staff’s discussion on having tighter standards?

speaker: FISHER
text: I gather there was some discussion of that in terms of coming to the ACF and being well capitalized but also well managed.

speaker: FISHER
text: Why the distinction, and what is the state of play of that argument as opposed to the regular requirements for going to the discount window?

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We did consider imposing a higher standard, something like “well capitalized and well managed”—the financial holding company type standards—and two concerns were raised.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: One is that it has the same problem that President Rosengren referred to that we have to rely on the exam rating and the capital adequacy determination by another regulator.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We don’t get out of that problem by raising the standards, and most of the institutions that were referred to actually fit into the higher standard.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: So it didn’t achieve very much.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The second thing is that there was some concern that it might have a blackballing effect.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: For folks that were between the standard for primary credit and the higher standard that we were setting, it might indicate that the Federal Reserve felt those folks were weaker.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Those may in fact be people we want to get some funding to.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: They’re the ones that seem to be struggling with liquidity, and this might make their problems worse because the market will perceive that the Fed wouldn’t even be willing to lend to them under the facility.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Just kind of on this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There is a description of this as somewhat prequalifying.

speaker: HOENIG
text: You have to be available for primary credit.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Third, it’s in pretty rough times as far as when you’re borrowing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I’m not sure you’re going to get rid of the stigma problem with this, and you’re going to go through a lot of gyrations to do something that then you’re going to have to unravel.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Are you sure that you want to do this?

speaker: HOENIG
text: If I were introducing this, I think I’d be more inclined to introduce it in good times, so that you get a perspective going that is less subject to wide interpretation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That’s a little concern I have as much as anything.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any other questions before we take general comments?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Quickly, as a follow-up to that—if you are successful in getting rid of the stigma problem, then does the discount window effectively disappear?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But there might be pressure for it to disappear because this certainly would be more desirable than the discount window.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s cheaper, and there’s no stigma.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But this is a temporary program.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Deposit insurance, I’ll remind you, in 1933 was temporary.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: But when you have that inadvertent overnight overdraft that you are facing, you can’t wait until the weekly auction.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You are capping the amount in a way that you could not reasonably decide you’re going to cap total access to the discount window.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, this wouldn’t substitute at all for secondary credit, by construction.

speaker: KOHN
text: In my thinking about the stigma point, the time line is an important part of that.

speaker: KOHN
text: If you have to submit your bid on Monday to get awarded on Thursday, this is not the action of a bank that’s desperate for funding.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the stigma comes because, at the discount window, apart from bidding strongly at the end of the day and then ending up paying this penalty rate, you don’t have anywhere else to go.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it seems to me this auction facility looks much more like a liability-management facility than it does a facility for banks that absolutely have to get funds, given that there’s a three-day or four-day wait until you get them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we start our go-round?

speaker: LACKER
text: I’ve been thinking a lot about this since I heard about it last week.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to start by complimenting the staff at New York and the Board who wrote the summary memo.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it does a very good and balanced job of articulating the costs and benefits of this proposed facility.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was going to say that they undoubtedly did it in a compressed timeframe, but then I heard you guys have been working on it for weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: But in any event, my hat is off to them.

speaker: LACKER
text: I very much agree with the staff that weighing the costs and benefits to reach an assessment about the desirability of this is inherently a difficult judgment.

speaker: LACKER
text: For me the critical question concerns the normative implications of what we’re seeing in the marketplace for term funding and the normative implications of this proposed intervention.

speaker: LACKER
text: Banks that are borrowing at term now are paying up for insurance against the eventuality that their funding costs rise—for example, because of a deterioration in their perceived creditworthiness.

speaker: LACKER
text: Banks that have viewed themselves as more at risk are naturally willing to pay more for such insurance, and some reports suggest, as Mr. Dudley did this morning, the presence of an adverse-selection problem in the sense that borrowing at term reveals oneself to be a borrower of high risk, and so only high-risk borrowers are willing to pay more.

speaker: LACKER
text: Banks that are reluctant to lend at term are placing a high value on being able to use their liquidity to accommodate assets that may come on their balance sheet soon.

speaker: LACKER
text: We had a lot of discussion about this in the morning.

speaker: LACKER
text: Balance sheet capacity appears genuinely to be a scarce valuable commodity these days.

speaker: LACKER
text: That’s consistent with the notion that raising bank capital is expensive in the current environment.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the adverse-selection story is worth considering seriously in this context because it’s the interpretation of what we’re seeing that provides the best hope for this being an intervention that improves market functioning in the microeconomic sense of the term.

speaker: LACKER
text: But if adverse selection is what has impaired the functioning of the term market in this normative sense, then there must be lower-risk banks that are unwilling to borrow at the same high rates as high-risk banks but that are rationed because they’re unable to distinguish themselves from high-risk banks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, if this is the case, the only way to improve market efficiency by lending is to lend more than the current volume of term lending because otherwise we’re just going to lend it to the current term-lending borrowers and none of these rationed-out, lower-risk banks are going to get access to it.

speaker: LACKER
text: In other words, if we do lend through an auction facility to draw in disadvantaged borrowers to try to reach them with credit, we can do so only by subsidizing the high-risk borrowers as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, I’ll mention that, from the discussion this morning, my understanding is that we have very little idea what the volume of that term lending is.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I don’t see how we chose this number and how we can be confident that it’s going to do this and reach through the high-risk borrowers to pick up the low-risk borrowers.

speaker: LACKER
text: More broadly, I’m not sure I see how this facility could improve the normative functioning in the market.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’re going to auction off only the same contracts that market participants are capable of offering now, only we’re also going to subject ourselves to the additional constraints imposed by our single-price auction format.

speaker: LACKER
text: So we’re not improving on any contract out there.

speaker: LACKER
text: The only unique attribute we would appear to bring is our ability to subsidize lending terms.

speaker: LACKER
text: We could conceivably improve market functioning if adverse selection is the right story here by doing something that market participants are incapable of doing, and that would be compelling borrowing by everybody or by a set of people to achieve a superior pooling allocation.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I don’t think we want to do that.

speaker: LACKER
text: Or we could conceivably improve market functioning by acting on information that’s superior to that of market participants—a knowledge of the creditworthiness of institutions, for example.

speaker: LACKER
text: But it isn’t clear that this is a key part of the proposal either, because institutions have to be rated 3 or above to get access and I think virtually all the currently affected institutions in these sorts of high-risk and low-risk categories are in the 3 or above categories already.

speaker: LACKER
text: A related point here is that, if we really think information constraints are at the heart of the problem, it might be better to address this problem by addressing those constraints directly by using our supervisory authority to encourage and facilitate greater transparency.

speaker: LACKER
text: So my sense is that this facility would just subsidize borrowing banks without doing anything to mitigate underlying informational asymmetries or any other type of market friction that I can think of.

speaker: LACKER
text: That means to me that this proposal raises the usual moral hazard concerns.

speaker: LACKER
text: The staff memo was very clear and articulate about those.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think there’s a danger with this facility of raising expectations that, in the future, significant increases in interbank funding spreads are going to be ameliorated by central bank intervention.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we raise that expectation, we’re going to undermine to some extent market mechanisms for assessing the relative risk of institutions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m a little worried that if this does not produce a demonstrable effect on relevant market conditions, it could erode confidence in us, and I feel so especially in light of our previous change in discount window policy, which I think is widely viewed as having had little substantive effect so far.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that’s the view out there.

speaker: LACKER
text: I also worry that this could complicate the resolution of failing institutions whose condition, as Vice Chairman Geithner suggested, deteriorates while they’re borrowing from this auction facility.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would put us in a very awkward place.

speaker: LACKER
text: As Governor Kohn said, this isn’t like a one-day emergency kind of thing—it takes some time.

speaker: LACKER
text: But some institutions in questionable situations, some problem institutions, look for term funding and are willing to wait four days to get it and know enough about their condition to line it up ahead of time.

speaker: LACKER
text: I worry about this sounding like a cloak for the ECB, for us to give money to the ECB, and I worry about President Rosengren’s issues as well, and I’d be more comfortable with the swap line than I am with the domestic facility.

speaker: LACKER
text: If those foreign authorities want to extend credit and have the knowledge and capacity to do so, and it’s on their dime and they’re bearing the credit risk and they want to borrow the dollars from us, I see that as a reasonable step for a central bank to take.

speaker: LACKER
text: I also worry about valuing collateral.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think that our mechanisms for doing that are robust and strong, especially in the current environment with at least standard haircuts.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, I can appreciate the broader problem articulated by the staff and others that banks that are constrained in the term funding market might tighten borrowing terms for consumers and businesses and that might have real economic consequences.

speaker: LACKER
text: But if that’s the problem, I think it would be better for us to just cut the funds rate rather than alter the relative funding costs of different banks.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is essentially what we did today.

speaker: LACKER
text: We cut the funds rate to offset the macroeconomic effects of higher credit spreads.

speaker: LACKER
text: Just a final set of comments.

speaker: LACKER
text: More broadly, I’ve been hoping for some time that banking policy in our country was moving slowly but surely toward greater reliance on market discipline and away from forbearance and subsidization.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’ve been hoping that we as a central bank would gradually move away from things that are tainted with credit allocation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Times like these don’t come around very often—you know, once a decade—and my sense is that the precedent we set here is going to be remembered for a long time and it’s going to affect market behavior for a long time to come as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: In my opinion, we ought to look at these episodes of market stress as an opportunity to make some reputational progress on the time-consistency problem that is at the heart of moral hazard.

speaker: LACKER
text: So for me the balance of considerations weighs heavily against this proposal, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me echo what you first said and congratulate the staff on an enormous amount of work and a terrific presentation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do want to just say a word, President Lacker.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most of your arguments are premised on the idea that markets are basically in some kind of equilibrium and we’re just messing with the equilibrium.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s a longstanding tradition, both in central banking and in theoretical analysis, that you can have periods when there is insufficient cash in the market and prices are, therefore, driven away from fundamentals by the lack of cash.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What central banks do is provide cash against collateral.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I refer you, for example, to Franklin Allen and Douglas Gale’s new book, Understanding Financial Crises, in which they present a model with exactly that property.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The moral hazard issue is the following: There is a good reason to allow some deviation of cash-based valuations from fundamentals because it creates incentives for providing sufficient liquidity and rewards those who have sufficient liquidity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But beyond a certain range, the models as well as central banking experience suggest that, when you have a fire sale type of situation, then the central bank can be useful by providing cash against that collateral.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Essentially this process would take $140 billion of undervalued, hard-to-sell, or illiquid assets onto the central bank’s balance sheet and provide term liquid funding in its place, which I find totally consistent with Bagehot and the traditions of central bank lending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, the question arises whether the market is in sufficient distress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If it’s not, then we’re in the first regime where some deviation of values from fundamentals is legitimate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If the market is in extreme distress, I think—I repeat what I said before—there can be situations in which markets are simply not functioning well and there could be a lot of reasons for that in which case the central bank could help the market function better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree that some of these issues about bid size and so on do confuse the issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to make a strong distinction between helping these markets to function better—we can address, for example, some of the counterparty risk because we have all this collateral in our discount windows—and helping or bailing out any individual institution.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with you that we certainly want to avoid that perception if at all possible.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think it does reduce stigma, and it would likely reduce the spread during a time of crisis.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would want it spread out among a larger number of institutions than just five because I do worry about that potential.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While I know that in your documentation you highlighted that there wouldn’t be a way to identify the institution, my guess is that, given that this is a new facility, there may be congressional hearings, and I wouldn’t be surprised, particularly if only five institutions borrowed from it, if we’d have to at least be prepared for the possibility that it would become more public than under normal circumstances.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So in these terms, I think the haircuts that we think about for a twenty-eight-day period are a little different from the haircuts you might take overnight, in which case we’re going to have to make sure that we really are collateralized sufficiently so that we’re not taking risks, since that is a principle of the discount window.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I worry a bit about whether our primary-secondary distinction was designed for this, and we might want to at least rethink exactly how we classify primary versus secondary credits.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: During times of distress, this would be a way to try to provide liquidity, but it might also be worth at least thinking about some of the potential issues during those times of stress.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Again, I’ll echo praise for just the incredible work that the staffs have done—a very clever way to address some specific problems that we’re facing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One is the stigma problem, and two, as I mentioned earlier, is the source of the uncertainty.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We don’t really have the tool to get at that directly; we can get at it only very indirectly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With the 1998 situation, there was another way to get at that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some people thought it was a good way; some people thought it was a bad way.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We won’t debate that, but the market perception was that a particular institution was at the heart of a lot of the uncertainty, and if you could resolve that, you could reduce that uncertainty significantly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also the interventions by the IMF and other organizations dealt with some of the international uncertainties.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With the traditional tools that we have, we’re somewhat hampered in trying to get at that, so I think this is a very clever way to try to do so.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But really my comments echo what President Rosengren has said.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: When we start to move from doing overnight to doing term funding, we may need to rethink what kind of collateral we have.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, we’re now using 80 percent of collateral rather than 100 percent of collateral.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That’s certainly a step in the right direction.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We need to think about whether we need “well capitalized and well managed.” That creates some challenges in trying to differentiate this from the overnight lending facility, and as Mr. Alvarez said, it raises some issues with respect to singling out institutions that make one hurdle but don’t make the other hurdle.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we need to think about it very carefully because the potential challenge both from an optics point of view and a substantive point of view is that, in the short run, we want to help out institutions in certain ways by providing funding but we don’t want to be helping out those that have not taken appropriate actions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In extreme circumstances like those we have now, as the Chairman said, one could certainly say that we’re out of equilibrium on pricing a lot of the assets, pricing the collateral, pricing the value, or pricing issuances by certain institutions, and so it is extremely important that this be short term and that those kinds of considerations be brought to the fore and thought through very carefully and have the potential to be altered over time if we don’t feel we’re having sufficient haircuts.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we do feel that certain institutions may transit from one rating to another within twenty- eight days, we need to be prepared to think about how to respond because it raises questions for a least-cost resolution of institutions that may be going down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I do think this is an extremely creative approach to try to get at something that we otherwise didn’t have easy tools to get at.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It may create a longer-term issue of an expectation that this kind of thing will come out again or that there will be another type of clever innovation that will deal with the next market problem so that people don’t have to worry about those market problems.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But that’s a very difficult tradeoff to make.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I can support this as addressing the short-term problem, and I think we can largely deal with some of those longer-term issues if we do stick to our guns and make it temporary and if we clearly articulate what we’re trying to get at.

speaker: HOENIG
text: One of the appealing things about it is that it broadens options, and I think that, any time you are in a set of circumstances where you have to find solutions, broadening your options is good.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I appreciate the fact that we are not voting on this today because I think it deserves a little further thought, especially about the unintended consequences.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There are advantages to saying it is temporary, but I’m not sure that there aren’t also some disadvantages from that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There are advantages in trying to remove the stigma, but I’m not sure what other hazards you create because, if you don’t pre-qualify, what have you said to the world about that as well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So there are lots of uncertainties around this that I would appreciate more time to think though before we actually begin to implement it.

speaker: POOLE
text: The staff did a fine job of designing and explaining.

speaker: POOLE
text: I want to concentrate on the issues that I have.

speaker: POOLE
text: I’m pleased that we’re not about to launch it.

speaker: POOLE
text: If we had, one of my concerns is that the United Kingdom is left out, which I assume is by choice, but it might still create a whole lot of issues for the United Kingdom.

speaker: POOLE
text: I’m sure there would be a lot of questions in the market— Why didn’t you do it?—or whatever.

speaker: POOLE
text: It might have added pressure there that would not only have complicated the U.K. situation, but it might have ended up complicating our own situation.

speaker: POOLE
text: That might still be an issue if we go this way in the future.

speaker: POOLE
text: I’m concerned that the method of setting the minimum bid rate is not really transparent.

speaker: POOLE
text: As I gather from reading, we’ll tell the market the number, but we won’t say what the reference rate is.

speaker: POOLE
text: Are we going to announce that it’s tied to the overnight swap rate?

speaker: POOLE
text: I had understood that we were not going to.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: It was based on a market rate for term funding.

speaker: POOLE
text: But weren’t we going to announce that this overnight index swap—

speaker: KRIEGER
text: No, I don’t think that had been the plan.

speaker: POOLE
text: But then the first time that you change that rate you are going to raise a whole lot of questions—Well, how did you decide how to change it?

speaker: POOLE
text: I’m more worried about the transparency of setting it that way because it is bound to raise questions about where that rate comes from.

speaker: POOLE
text: How did you decide on this one?

speaker: POOLE
text: It might be particularly true if that rate ends up being below the target federal funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is news to me, by the way, because the logic of this was that the normal spread between the overnight index swap and term funds is about 10 basis points.

speaker: POOLE
text: Yes, but that depends on the market’s expectations of where the funds rate is going to go.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the OIS captures that—the one-month OIS.

speaker: POOLE
text: I understand that, but that can be different from the current target rate that’s in effect right now.

speaker: POOLE
text: This rate could be below the current target rate, and that seems to me to create an issue that we are going to have to be prepared to explain, and I’m not so sure that’s going to be easy to explain.

speaker: POOLE
text: At any rate, I’ll leave that on the table for the moment.

speaker: EVANS
text: Are you saying that the minimum rate is going to be a secret?

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, they’ll figure it out.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Won’t they figure it out almost immediately?

speaker: STERN
text: If they’re going to figure it out, why don’t we tell them?

speaker: KRIEGER
text: The question is whether you identify a particular market rate that you’re pegging or whether you say you’re looking at market-based rates.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: I think that’s a decision variable of this program.

speaker: EVANS
text: I just didn’t realize this was as highly confidential.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: But you have the auction announcement.

speaker: KRIEGER
text: You must tell the bidders ahead of time what the minimum rate acceptable is.

speaker: POOLE
text: You’ll tell them the basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They should figure out pretty quickly what this rate means.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would suggest that we not get too involved in this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we ought to be as transparent as possible.

speaker: POOLE
text: No, but I just say that I think there’s a transparency issue here that might have to be explained.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I’ll just leave that on the table to be talked about.

speaker: POOLE
text: There is certainly a risk that this facility will not be—well, maybe this would not be a wrong judgment—available to small banks, and the large banks would be getting access to discount window funds at a rate potentially well below that available to small banks.

speaker: POOLE
text: If this were to become a political controversy with some of those who are less friendly to us in the Congress than others, it would complicate the value of this.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would hate to see us get embroiled in a political controversy over this because we were discriminating against 98 percent of the banks in the Eighth Federal Reserve District as well as some of the other Federal Reserve Districts.

speaker: POOLE
text: If we were to launch this, if we were voting today, this would create a big issue in terms of our directors because we would be announcing to the directors what discount rate they would have to set under the Federal Reserve Act.

speaker: POOLE
text: So if we are preparing to do this in the future, I think it is very important that we have material prepared and that we take it up with our directors in advance so that they will know what we will be asking of them because this could be a very big problem.

speaker: POOLE
text: We need to make sure that we have the directors on our side and that we have prepared them so that, if we have to do it, they will know what the reasoning is.

speaker: POOLE
text: Finally, once the dust settles, assuming that we don’t need to do this before the markets return to a reasonable normality, I don’t see any reason that we couldn’t have this well planned and actually run a trial or maybe even have a trial once a year or something like that so that the banks and the markets understand how this works.

speaker: POOLE
text: Then you can pull it out of your pocket if you really need it in crisis circumstances.

speaker: POOLE
text: Everybody would have understood it because you would have actually done it.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, a lot of what I have thought about this since I realized we weren’t going to do this immediately has been addressed by the previous individuals who have spoken.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’d just like to touch on a few points.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, like everyone else, I want to congratulate the staff for excellent work.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s also very well balanced in the way that the pros and the cons are argued.

speaker: FISHER
text: Bagehot and the Lombard facility not withstanding, it seems to me that, if we proceed down this path, we have to position it so that it’s a refinement of what we did in August rather than a confession of failure or insufficiency.

speaker: FISHER
text: That would be point number 1.

speaker: FISHER
text: Still, President Lacker made some very good points, and part of this gets to what President Poole just mentioned, and that is that some political risk, in addition to the risk of failure, is there and we have to acknowledge that it may not work.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have some concerns about the value of collateral and the automaticity, as it were, in this kind of new facility and our ability to value complicated collateral.

speaker: FISHER
text: My biggest concerns are the ideas, as President Lacker put it, that we’re subsidizing foreign banks without really doing anything to mitigate hazard.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that roughly translates what he said, which gets me to the point of President Poole’s comment.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have to be mindful of the risk of being perceived as (1) helping a limited number of very large money center banks and (2) bailing out the Europeans.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t think the public understands that.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you look at my discount window, there are five banks that could meet these collateral requirements, the $63 million minimum.

speaker: FISHER
text: Some Districts have less; some Districts have more.

speaker: FISHER
text: Our backbone at the Federal Reserve in terms of our political support is the community banking system.

speaker: FISHER
text: To be sure, we all understand that we have systemic responsibilities, but the idea that we might be facilitating these huge institutions or “bailing out” the Europeans is just a risk I think we need to be aware of, and if we proceed, we’re going to have to figure out how to manage that.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m not against a swap line, another point that President Lacker made.

speaker: FISHER
text: Usually I would expect President Lacker to be against a swap line, but he’s not against the swap line.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m not against the swap line.

speaker: FISHER
text: It does beg the question of whether we couldn’t do a swap line and work with the existing facility but for the fact that we think that the existing facility is insufficient.

speaker: FISHER
text: Again, I would present this, if we proceed, as a refinement.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I would like more time to think about this.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m grateful that you’re giving us more time to think about it, and I, again, would like to consider the governance aspects of it.

speaker: FISHER
text: But those are the questions that I have at this juncture.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s a very creative proposal, and I agree basically with the comments that President Rosengren and Governor Kroszner said about it.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s important that the collateral be appropriate and well established, and it’s definitely better if we don’t have simply a small number of borrowers.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s also important we know that we hit our funds rate target because this is, you know, tied to the effective federal funds rate.

speaker: EVANS
text: So if we’re really soft on that, then it’s going to be an even better opportunity for everyone.

speaker: EVANS
text: But as I think about it, it seems as though this is an opportunity to narrow the spread to 10 basis points instead of the 50 basis points that we actually have on the discount window, except for the eligibility requirements.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I can support this as a temporary facility, but I’m glad that we’re going to have more time to think about it.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I, too, want to congratulate the staff on a creative proposal.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think I need more time to think about this, but let me offer, just to some degree, speculative remarks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: They’re speculative because it has been a few years since I’ve even been around a treasury of a money center bank, but I do think I have some feel for it.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: First, looking at it from the market perspective, lengthening the maturity of liabilities and then, in train, assets is desirable.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Clearly, that will assist financial stability, which is our objective here.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The sub-objectives are to reduce stigma and to unstick the market from its short-term orientation.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I try to put myself in the shoes of a bank treasurer thinking about whether or not to use such a facility.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The way that large bank treasuries work, or at least worked when I was close to them, is that you have essentially what is called an MCO, or maximum cumulative outflow, schedule, which is a schedule of liability maturities going out for 360 days or more.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Today’s picture on the margin—that is to say, in the money markets, noncore deposits, the things basically where banks are funding themselves on the margin—spikes very early.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It’s dramatically early, and then it tails off, and it seems to me that the treasurer would think about this by asking, “What MCO gain do I get from using this?” It is just a matter of days—maybe two or three days, not twenty-eight— because you’re just adding it to a mix of liabilities that you already have.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The offset of that would be the reaction of the market, the stigma question, as they perceive a bank using this—that is, whether there would be some countervailing reaction.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It’s probably not insignificant no matter how hard we try that, when you use the lender of last resort as a funding source, you are using the lender of last resort as a funding source.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So if I were a treasurer, I would be making a kind of calculation as to whether I was really gaining from an MCO point of view any significant comfort relative to the direction I thought the market was going.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My own hope is that this issue will improve dramatically in the second half of October.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This week and next week, I believe, we are going to go through the broker-dealer disclosures, and then in mid-October, we’ll get the large bank and other bank disclosures, and the market transparency should improve, it seems to me, reasonably strongly in that period.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So it is conceivable that we’ll have different circumstances in the second half of October regarding the market’s being so terribly short term at this time.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So, again, I am trying to think this through as a treasurer would think it, and I think there are some market dynamic considerations that a treasurer would have to think about, which suggests maybe not using it except in really extreme market circumstances.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My inclination after reading the memo over the weekend was to be supportive of the proposal.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, given some of the comments that I’ve heard from my colleagues today, I welcome the additional time to think about some of the concerns, especially some of the issues that President Rosengren raised about only five institutions borrowing.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I have some of the same concerns that President Hoenig raised about whether introducing a proposal like this during these times really does address the stigma issue.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Then the memo also raises the issue that there is a risk that such a program would exacerbate the moral hazard problem, and I’m concerned about this.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But I heard a lot of comments today around this table that, in terms of financial stress, it’s critical that we do the right thing and play the appropriate central bank role.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So, again, I like other comments that were made earlier.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We have a great staff, a skilled staff, which came up with a very creative proposal, and my inclination is to support it.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am pleased that we have the additional time to think about some of these issues so that I can better understand some of the concerns that were raised.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Actually, I do have some sympathy for this proposal.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it is very creative.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But there are a lot more people around this table who know a lot more details about this market, how it works, and how treasurers work than I do, and I will certainly defer to their judgment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I have a couple of points that I’d like to make.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: President Hoenig made the point that really gives me a little pause as I absorb this.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What I’m really worried about is the law of unintended consequences, and I don’t know what they are right now.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Many of you around the table have raised some possibilities that this could exacerbate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think President Poole’s suggestion about creating a tension between large and small banks about who has access to this could prove to be a problem.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also agree that it might be unusual, but it would be troubling if, in fact, we ended up lending money in this facility going below the targeted funds rate, which would be maybe unlikely but would complicate our lives in other dimensions as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also worry a bit as I look at the market—and this probably has more generally to do with provisions of liquidity—that part of the problem here is price discovery.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Where are the risks, how much are they, and how do we price them?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I worry a bit, too, about the degree to which providing liquidity shuts down or slows down the price-discovery process, which is something that we really want to get done.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t know how to answer that question, but it’s one that I just sort of struggle with in trying to think about whether we are hampering the process of price discovery, by slowing it down and making it easier for people, or are we moving it along at a faster rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t know the answer to that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The last point, I think, is more of a policy question.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Again, President Hoenig, I think, made it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we view this as a temporary tool, which I think is fine, it is important that we lay out in our own minds under what circumstances in the future we would decide whether or not to implement this tool and how we decide.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What criteria do we have?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We need something a little more objective than just whenever we want to.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I worry a bit that by failing to do so we will abandon some expectations about how the market will react to this and when they might expect us to use it or not.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Do I know what the consequences of that will be?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m struggling with those kinds of questions, so having a little more time to think through some of these things would be very helpful.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, at this time, my bottom line on this proposal is that it’s okay, but I’m not altogether enthusiastic.

speaker: STERN
text: It’s okay because I think having another arrow in our quiver is not a bad idea, and so to have done the work and put this forward strikes me as clearly constructive.

speaker: STERN
text: I’m not enthusiastic because I didn’t find the case for it that compelling, and let me elaborate on that a minute.

speaker: STERN
text: I probably would have thought it more compelling a week or two ago, but the markets seemed to be working a bit better, and I think it’s to our advantage to let that unfold, assuming it continues to do so.

speaker: STERN
text: More broadly, I think there’s a question of whether the pricing that we’re seeing in the term funding market is something that we really should be addressing.

speaker: STERN
text: Maybe, given all the concerns and everything else, that pricing is perfectly fine at the moment and will adjust over time to something more normal without any action on our part.

speaker: STERN
text: If so, that would strike me as preferable.

speaker: STERN
text: But the real question for me at the end of the day is that it seems as though the ultimate justification for something like this has to be related to our macroeconomic objectives.

speaker: STERN
text: Do we believe that, say, a malfunctioning in the short-term funding market is going to have significant macroeconomic consequences?

speaker: STERN
text: Is it going to make the economy behave significantly worse than perhaps the economy otherwise would have behaved?

speaker: STERN
text: My answer to that is “perhaps,” but I don’t really have a real conviction about that.

speaker: STERN
text: So that’s why I come out, at the moment anyway, with “Yeah, this could turn out to be useful,” but it’s hard for me to get really enthusiastic about it.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think this is aimed at addressing a serious problem that I’m afraid we’re losing sight of a bit.

speaker: KOHN
text: The piling-up of financing in very short term vehicles is an issue for financial stability.

speaker: KOHN
text: Partly this is, yes, the term rates are elevated, and if this were just a risk premium on certain counterparties, I don’t think that would be a big deal.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I do feel that there has been a malfunctioning in the markets: As is typical in a financial crisis or panic, people have fled toward liquidity and safety in Treasury bills and overnight lending, and the normal arbitrage that happens across markets just isn’t happening.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s great that the markets seem to be getting better, but if they continue to malfunction or if it gets worse again, I think there’s a serious problem.

speaker: KOHN
text: The problem is that all these banks are being financed in the one-day to four-day area, and it leaves them open to huge rollover risk and huge liquidity risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: In turn, because they have this risk, they’re more reluctant to lend.

speaker: KOHN
text: They’re more reluctant to use all that capital that you saw in the chart the other day.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it is having a potential macroeconomic effect, and I completely agree with President Stern.

speaker: KOHN
text: We would do it because there’s a macroeconomic effect and because there is a financial stability effect.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think there is an issue here that we can’t shrug off.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that the facility would attract those banks that need it most.

speaker: KOHN
text: That’s what auctions do, right?

speaker: KOHN
text: That’s why they’re designed that way, and I think that’s fine.

speaker: KOHN
text: For the most part, with one exception, that’s the way it would have the maximum effect of relieving some of these issues.

speaker: KOHN
text: You bring in the folks who need it the most, and it relieves some of their problems.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is a problem regarding the borderline institutions that people have been talking about, and if an institution is in transition from being sound to being not sound, this is an issue.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s an issue for two reasons.

speaker: KOHN
text: One is that it could facilitate the runoff of uninsured liability holders, and the Congress has told us not to do that, and we shouldn’t do it.

speaker: KOHN
text: That’s a moral hazard problem.

speaker: KOHN
text: The second is that it might allow the banks that aren’t being run well to make that last bet—to do some other things that would put them at greater risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think those would be very, very rare institutions that are in that kind of spot where they’re just placing the final bet before going out of business.

speaker: KOHN
text: So the borderline institution is a bit of a problem, but I’m not sure it’s as big a problem as others have said.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think this would have a chance of success.

speaker: KOHN
text: When arbitrage isn’t working, you have very strong preferred habitats.

speaker: KOHN
text: People want to lend short, and other people want to borrow long, and the Fed would be stepping into that breach in some sense where the markets aren’t working.

speaker: KOHN
text: We would be supplying Treasury bills and, to a certain extent, doing matched sale-purchases or reverse RPs or whatever they call them these days, borrowing from the public at the very short term, and we would be extending the term credit.

speaker: KOHN
text: In a sense, we would be stepping in for the arbitrage that’s not happening, and that would relieve pressures on these markets at least a little.

speaker: KOHN
text: It has a chance of having some second-round effects of helping those banks that want to use their capital do so more than they are already.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t know that it would remove the stigma.

speaker: KOHN
text: As I said, I think the auction process, making it a totally separate discount window, and having the long period over which it has to happen makes it look very, very different from a discount rate loan.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the moral hazard issue, of course, this isn’t doing anything really to relieve people who made subprime loans.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s not going to change the price of those assets, so it’s not really affecting that in any moral hazard way.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s not aimed at individual institutions.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s more like open market operations than it is like the old form of discount window lending.

speaker: KOHN
text: Even when normal functioning is restored to markets, banks will be paying for the liquidity insurance that they wrote.

speaker: KOHN
text: There’s no relief on the credit side.

speaker: KOHN
text: They’ll still have to tie up capital, making good on the liquidity insurance, forgoing more-profitable opportunities.

speaker: KOHN
text: It would reduce, perhaps at least a little around the edges, the extra cost of financing this liquidity insurance that they sold that comes from the disruption of the markets, from the fire sale aspect.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that, if we thought that the markets weren’t improving and it would have a feedback effect on financial stability, stepping in would be worthwhile.

speaker: KOHN
text: That’s the classic central bank thing to do—to step in and relieve some of the extra panicky pressures on the markets to get them functioning again.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I guess I don’t see an important moral hazard issue or, to the extent that there is a moral hazard issue, I think it would be more than offset by the benefits to the macroeconomy of the functioning of financial markets, should we decide that this were needed if those markets weren’t working.

speaker: WARSH
text: Very briefly, when I think back about a week ago to maybe one of the darker days that we’ve had in the past six weeks, there were so many more institutions that were funding themselves on an overnight basis that it wouldn’t take much imagination for us to get very fearful very soon if there were some kind of shock that made it impossible or much more difficult for them to fund themselves twenty-four hours later.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think the ACF would have held great promise then to be useful in addressing some of the headline risks that could very quickly have had systemic implications.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the ACF holds great promise now.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’ll highlight only one question, which is timing.

speaker: WARSH
text: I share the view put forth by President Stern that, to the extent we see these markets improving on their own terms, which is something we’ve seen in recent trading days, we wouldn’t want to do anything to stop that momentum.

speaker: WARSH
text: If we had hit the button today, it may well be that they would have had to take stock of this new instrument and compare it to the other alternatives they have, and that improvement could have potentially been delayed.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the other hand, if we wait until these markets deteriorate to where they were a week ago, the efficacy of hitting the button then would also be less than ideal.

speaker: WARSH
text: So my own sense on timing—and it’s something that the Chairman will, I think, brief us all on if we get to that point—is to the extent that we see that momentum has stopped and we see the ground weakening below us, then we might have to make a risk-adjusted call at that point.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t think it will be a very easy or a very apparent one.

speaker: WARSH
text: But on balance, I think that the macroeconomic possibilities are pretty scary, which makes me suggest that we would lean forward on this.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I also want to congratulate the staff.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This is a very clever and targeted intervention, and it’s a very nicely put together proposal.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it’s something that’s good to have available.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’m glad that we’re not planning to put it in place instantly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It does have the potential to address the stigma issues that banks have coming to the discount window.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Really, the spike in the spread between term and overnight loans in the interbank market has been quite sizable, and it’s obvious that that has been complicating the difficulties that banks have had in managing liquidity.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have also been concerned, given how many other borrowing rates are linked to LIBOR, that if the spread remains elevated, it has the potential to spill over into the rates that a lot of borrowers pay.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think this has a chance in succeeding and reducing that spread and bringing LIBOR down, but it’s not 100 percent obvious to me that it will succeed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it does depend on your interpretation of exactly what that spread represents, whether it’s credit risk or liquidity risk.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I read the proposal, I thought it really didn’t make the case in a powerful way to me that the inability of banks to fund at term was creating systemic risk.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It seems to me that, given a proposal of this magnitude that involves coordinating central bank intervention and has a chance of not succeeding, we ought to be doing it to address something that we regard as an important systemic risk.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The comments that Governors Kohn and Warsh made have convinced me, as we have discussed this, that there could very well be systemic risks here and that we might, if things get worse again, want to put this into place.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I found that discussion very useful.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It seemed to me that the case that was actually made in the document in a sense was more a monetary policy case that banks facing these funding pressures would likely raise rates and that would have macroeconomic consequences.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That then suggests to me, Well, why don’t we use the federal funds rate more?

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is a more general tool to remove those pressures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I share the concern that we will be perceived as bailing out a small set of weak institutions, including Washington Mutual, Countrywide, and others that may be associated with the crisis.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Especially if we’re using this overnight index swap rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It has been sitting here, I guess, around 4.80, 4.76, or something like that, which if we had had this facility in effect would be below the funds rate and would raise questions about why we were lending so cheaply.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One way or another, I would certainly be happy to approve a swap agreement with the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank to provide them with dollar funding whether we go ahead or not, if that’s desirable.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that this proposal has an important advantage in that it is channeling funds to a place where they are most needed, so it has macroeconomic consequences.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If you think about it, open market operations are a very blunt tool.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Here you are actually able to direct credit to a market that isn’t working.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have a LIBOR market that really is not working; it clearly has spreads that are way out of line.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When people talk about what’s going on in the market, they basically say, “Yes, there’s an arbitrage opportunity, but there’s so much risk that I can’t take advantage of it.” That is something that I think is important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: For example, my understanding of commercial real estate deals is that all the deals are done off of LIBOR, and so this actually is an important market.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Do I think this will solve the problem of price discovery in general?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I do think that this is an important market that is having important macroeconomic implications, and going in and doing something about it can have very strong benefits.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There are some tricky issues.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The issue I really worry about the most is the 20 percent number, where we might have five guys, and everybody knows that some people will be politically problematic for us.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So maybe you might want to think about whether that 20 percent number is exactly the best number.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s why I was going to ask the same question that you asked, and now that we have some time, I would encourage the staff to think about exactly that issue.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Another element here is important—which is that we’re saying to the marketplace that we’re not just thinking about using monetary policy tools; in fact, because it is a credit problem, we’re thinking creatively about how to use credit tools as well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that regard, there’s an advantage that we are thinking outside the box and trying to deal with this another way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Let me give you an analogy to something that we did on August 17.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On August 17 we pulled out the discount window.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We did it with a 50 basis point penalty.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You know, you look at it, and in one sense it was not a success.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It didn’t make a big difference in terms of the numbers.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It wasn’t bad, but I’ll tell you, when you asked people out there whether it was a positive thing to do, they’d say, “Oh, yeah.” It really sent a very, very good signal.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My sense is that this may not completely solve the problem— there are some issues about how much should be taken up—but I think that it would send a signal that we’re on the ball.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It has another element, which I’m a bit sensitive to, that there is criticism that we are too academic here because some of us have worn tweed coats.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So that you know, the Chairman used to come to the New York Fed meetings and would wear those patches on the outside of his coat.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I actually like that look and have my assistant professor corduroy suit.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But here we are trying to think very practically in a creative way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It also has an advantage for this institution at this juncture because we are thinking about market issues and dealing with very specific details in the markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that’s something that we’ve gotten across to some extent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We’re ready, and I think this would help.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I’m not saying absolutely that we definitely should use this, but I think Governor Warsh talked about this exactly right.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If we’re seeing that there’s some stalling, that these spreads are not improving, then this is an option that will have benefits.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just a few quick things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: First, I should say that the concerns and questions you all put on the table are the right set of concerns and questions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Some of them can be resolved by tweaking the design of things, but some of them we will not be able to resolve with changes in design, and we’ll have to decide whether or not we want to live with those things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it’s important to recognize that, even though we’ve had ten days of pretty steady improvement in the willingness and ability of financers to differentiate across different sets of institutions and different sets of instruments, et cetera, and the process is encouraging, we should not take too much comfort from that yet.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This process could go on for some time, we are still in a quite fragile situation, and the situation could get more fragile again easily and quite quickly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We may need at that point to escalate in terms of the range of things that we’re prepared to do in that context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We need to be very open to thinking about practical, creative ways to address some of the limitations not just in our tools and the relative stigma attached to them but in the tools of the other central banks in the major financial centers.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We now exist with a very complicated set of limitations and asymmetries in those limitations, and I think that mix together does not leave us optimally positioned or with the flexibility to deal with the kinds of things we’re facing in these markets.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So it’s going to require that we be open, practical, and creative in thinking through the optimal way to navigate through those kinds of things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It would be very hard to know outside the circumstance what hierarchy of choices is going to look most appealing to us—whether in the event the swap alone would be ideal or feasible, whether something at the discount window alone would be ideal or feasible, or some other things would be.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s just hard to know.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think you have to recognize that we’re all going to be in a world of second, third, or fourth best just because nothing looks terrific now relative to those problems.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are not going to be able to clarify for ourselves fully what the effect might be and whether we can manage some of the risk of unintended consequences, not just in terms of future incentives but also in terms of signaling effect.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I’m sure we all know that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But some of the things that you raise today we would face in the moment and would not be able to resolve definitively.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is also true that we may need to move very quickly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We may not have a lot of time, and we may need to do something multilateral just because, even though this has a lot of manifestations in dollar funding markets, it’s not solely a dollar issue and it’s obviously not solely and maybe not even principally a funding issue around U.S. financial institutions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So we may need to be open to doing something together.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That will, of course, mean we may need to compromise in terms of what may be optimal for our optics or for our design of the economics of the thing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I think those of you who welcomed the fact that you would have more time to think through this shouldn’t take too much time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This may be a situation in which you will have to resolve your ambivalence quickly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You may not be able to resolve it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So thank you very much.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I appreciated this discussion a great deal.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I did not hear a great deal of opposition to the principle that the Federal Reserve at times should help markets function when they are in a state of panic or otherwise in serious dysfunction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in that respect, I think that this is the kind of tool that under some circumstances might prove quite useful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You did raise a large number of practical issues, political issues, optical issues, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You all said that you wanted to think about it, and I’m going to take you up on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Please consult with your staffs, and then let me to please ask our staffs in New York and Washington to see if some of these issues can be addressed, and let us continue to think about under what circumstances this might be useful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You know, just because you have a hammer doesn’t mean that every problem is a nail, right?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we do need to think further about the circumstances under which this kind of intervention would improve market functioning and reduce financial stress in an appropriate way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Fortunately, it does not appear that we need to act today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But as Vice Chairman Geithner points out, markets are fragile and the possibility that we might come back to you in three days or a week or two weeks or whatever should not be discounted.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So thank you very much for your comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next meeting is October 30 and 31, a two-day meeting, and we will also have Cathy Minehan’s farewell lunch at that meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This meeting is Karen Johnson’s last.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: She attended her first meeting in 1991 and has been a regular participant for the past ten years, so she has ninety-one total FOMC meetings to her credit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Karen has been briefing the FOMC on international financial and economic matters since she became head of the International Finance Division in 1997, and she has done a great job of covering about 95 percent of the world’s population and about two-thirds or more of the world’s economic activity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also, as the head of IF, she has logged an awful lot of miles to World Bank–IMF meetings, the BIS, and elsewhere.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: She has given me a lot of good advice on jetlag, I can assure you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: She is going to finance her retirement with frequent-flyer miles.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, Karen, I am sure every member of the Committee would like to join me in thanking you for your dedication and your excellent advice and counsel.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have the less pleasant duty of reminding everybody about the Wall Street Journal article on our communications policy that appeared some time ago.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think anybody actually leaked the story, because the way Greg Ip works is that he goes around and talks to each person and gets a little of the story and then builds it up in that way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nevertheless, I think it is obviously bad for our institution when our internal deliberations become public, and so let me just ask everyone, please, to be especially careful about maintaining confidentiality.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For our first item today, in light of Karen’s retirement, we would like to propose Nathan Sheets to be an economist for the FOMC until the first meeting of 2008.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do I have a motion?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Next, we turn to Bill Dudley.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am going to miss Karen as my fellow scribe at the BIS.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: She also was the person who identified who was actually speaking.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Two crosscurrents have dominated financial markets since the September 18 FOMC meeting: (1) greater discrimination by investors with respect to credit quality across asset classes versus (2) ongoing deterioration in credit quality within the class of mortgage-related assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the one hand, underlying market function has generally improved.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, investors have shown greater ability to differentiate between the corporate and the mortgage sectors and between different types of products such as collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) versus collateralized debt obligations (CDOs).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Most of the asset-backed commercial paper market is no longer under duress, bank funding pressures have abated somewhat, and the issuance of CLOs and high-yield debt has increased.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the other hand, those areas more closely linked to the U.S. housing sector remain under pressure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This includes the subprime mortgage market, the mortgage-backed securities market, and financial entities—such as mortgage and financial guarantors—that have significant exposures to these asset classes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The tension between the improved ability of investors to discriminate among risky assets versus the deteriorating fundamentals is illustrated in the performance of the ABX indexes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These indexes measure the cost of buying protection on different tranches of particular vintages of mortgage-backed securities that hold subprime mortgage loan assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I will be referring to the handout in front of you.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 1 shows the performance for the 07-01 vintage—that is, mortgage-backed securities originated mainly during the second half of 2006.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, the prices of the lower-rated tranches have continued to plunge in response to rising delinquency rates for subprime loans and the virtual shutdown of the subprime mortgage market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, the performance of the AAA-rated tranche has held up better, especially until very recently.

speaker: DUDLEY
