text: This suggests that investors are more carefully distinguishing between the implications of widespread subprime losses for those tranches, such as AAA, that are in a senior position in the structure versus lower-rated tranches, where the losses may well be large enough to wipe out their value altogether.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Similarly, investors appear to be doing a better job of discriminating between the different types of asset-backed commercial paper programs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Those with high-quality, diversified 1 Materials used by Mr. Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: collateral or strong bank support or both are performing well.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, those programs with less solid support—mainly SIV and extendible programs—in which the commercial paper holders are more vulnerable to loss continue to hit liquidity and capital triggers and are gradually being wound down.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 2, the overall asset-backed commercial paper market has been contracting recently at a much slower pace than earlier in the summer.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, secured commercial paper rates have narrowed significantly relative to the overnight index swap rate and relative to top-quality unsecured commercial paper (exhibit 3).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The ability of banks to securitize assets also appears to have improved.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, as shown in exhibits 4 and 5, CLO and high-yield debt issuance has picked up.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, CDO issuance remains very depressed relative to the level of issuance earlier in the year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Investors have lost confidence in this product as market prices have plunged and the rating agencies have begun to cut their ratings, often very sharply, on many outstanding CDOs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Market participants are more willing to buy corporate debt for three reasons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, the underlying fundamentals in the corporate sector remain good.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the underlying assets are much easier to value.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, investors are more willing to trust the credit ratings in this area.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rating agency models have been battle-tested over a much longer period and have been shown to be robust across a broad range of environments.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, the ability of banks to securitize nonconforming mortgage loans remains impaired.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Nevertheless, spreads between jumbo and conforming mortgage loan rates have come in a bit (see exhibit 6).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This may reflect diminished pressure on bank balance sheets from other sources.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Overall, term funding pressures for banks have diminished as banks have gained greater clarity about their future funding needs and the need for excess liquidity has diminished.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Nevertheless, term funding pressures still persist.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen in exhibit 7, although the spreads between one-month LIBOR and the one-month overnight index swap rate and three-month LIBOR and the three-month overnight index swap rate have narrowed, these spreads remain high relative to the level of spreads evident at the beginning of the summer.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 8 shows the same spreads for Europe—they have also come in but remain higher than normal.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the credit default swap (CDS) spreads for the large investment banks and the large commercial banks narrowed following the last FOMC meeting, much of this improvement has been reversed over the past two weeks as the housing outlook has deteriorated further and as the earnings announcements for several major financial institutions have disappointed investors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Similarly, the CDS spreads for mortgage insurers and financial guarantors have widened.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These CDS spreads are shown in exhibit 9.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The broader bond and equity markets have generally shown improvement.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the fixed income market, credit default swap spreads have fallen somewhat for the high- yield debt market (see exhibit 10), and the U.S. equity market has largely recovered over the past couple of months (see exhibit 11).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Interestingly, despite the poor earnings of the financial sector and the outlook for slower U.S. growth, earnings expectations of equity analysts for 2007 have declined only slightly, and the decline in 2007 has been offset by an upward revision to 2008 earnings estimates (see exhibit 12).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the demand for downside protection in the equity market has diminished.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 13 examines the relative cost of buying a put versus a call.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A positive skew is consistent with a greater cost of downside protection.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although a significant positive skew persists, it is now much lower than it was immediately before the September 18 FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibits 14 and 15 summarize the incomplete transition away from risk-reduction behavior by financial market participants.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 14 shows the correlation of daily price movements and yield changes across the different asset classes for the time interval between the August and the September FOMC meetings.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, the correlations were very high— indicating that risk aversion was the dominant impulse among investors—with most of the correlations over this period exceeding an absolute value of 0.5.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These are shaded in blue in the exhibit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, the same correlations since the September 18 FOMC meeting, shown in exhibit 15, have come down but remain much higher than during the first half of the year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Two other market developments deserve a brief mention before I turn to dealer expectations concerning monetary policy and a brief look at inflation expectations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, crude oil prices have shot higher.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There is considerable disagreement among market participants about how long the higher prices will last and the factors behind the price surge.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although some argue that it is speculative, others point to more- fundamental drivers such as inventory drawdowns, geopolitical uncertainties, and dollar weakness.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Regardless of the cause, the effect on the macroeconomy has been modest up to now because higher crude oil prices have not fed through meaningfully into product prices.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is because the so-called crack spread—the margin between the value of the refined products produced from that crude oil and the cost of crude oil supply—has come down sharply, as shown in exhibit 16.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The narrowness of the crack spread implies that further increases in crude oil prices, if forthcoming, would likely feed through into product prices.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the dollar continues on its gradual downward course.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the dollar has reached new lows against the euro and the Canadian dollar, the overall pace of the decline as measured by the broad trade- weighted index has not changed much from the trend exhibited earlier in the year (see exhibit 17).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The dollar’s trajectory still appears to be driven mainly by interest rate differentials.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This can be seen in exhibit 18, which shows the dollar versus the euro relative to the Eurodollar–EURIBOR interest rate differential.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, there is little evidence that the dollar’s slide has made investors less willing to participate in the long end of the U.S. bond market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You can see that by the fact that U.S. 10-year Treasury note yields are still fairly low, trading around 4.4 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Market expectations about monetary policy have shown considerable variability since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 19 tracks the implied probability of different target rate outcomes at this meeting calculated from the option prices on federal funds futures contracts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen in the exhibit, the probability of a 25 basis point cut has fluctuated in a wide range.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The most recent survey of primary dealers, conducted ten days ago, shows a slight tilt toward a 25 basis point cut at the current meeting, with eleven dealers expecting a 25 basis point cut, nine expecting no change, and one expecting a 50 basis point reduction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Since that time a number of dealers have shifted camp.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Currently, a more informal survey by the Desk indicates that nineteen out of twenty-one dealers expect a 25 basis point rate cut at this meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibits 20 and 21 show the primary dealer forecasts for the federal funds rate before the September and the current FOMC meetings.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, the dealers’ forecasts for the federal funds rate path are currently a bit lower than before the September 18 meeting—partially reflecting the fact that the FOMC easing of 50 basis points at the September meeting was of greater magnitude than the cut embodied in the average dealer forecast.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, the gap between the dealers’ forecasts and the expectations embodied in market rates has narrowed over the past six weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, considerable disagreement about the rate path remains.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One year out, the dispersion of the modal dealer forecasts remains very wide.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Inflation expectations increased following the 50 basis point rate cut in September.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, the degree of widening is sensitive to how the forward breakeven inflation rate is calculated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 22 shows the five-year, five-year- forward implied inflation rate as estimated by the Board staff versus the five-year, five-year-forward breakeven inflation rate as estimated by Barclays Bank, a major participant in the TIPS market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen in the exhibit, typically these two measures move together.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: More recently, however, they have diverged a bit, with the Board staff measure showing a more persistent increase following the September FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The two measures differ in the securities that they use to compare nominal versus inflation-adjusted yields—with the Board staff using a smoothed yield curve based on off-the-run nominal Treasuries and the Barclays measure using the on-the-run nominal five-year and ten-year Treasury notes to compare with the five- year and ten-year TIPS notes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, liquidity differences among Treasury securities are hard to model.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, it is difficult to be confident of the accuracy of such adjustments.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This argues that one should not completely dismiss the Barclays measure when the two measures are behaving differently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This might especially be true when no rise in long-term inflation expectations is evident in other measures, such as the University of the Michigan’s survey of consumer sentiment or the Desk’s own primary dealer survey.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, I want to discuss briefly the Desk’s performance in implementing the FOMC’s directive from the last meeting for a 4.75 percent federal funds rate target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In this respect, let me make two observations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, in contrast to the previous intermeeting period, in which the effective rate traded below the target for much of the period, the average effective rate has been extremely close to the target since the September 18 meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 23 shows the cumulative effective rate relative to the target since the last meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, as shown in exhibit 24, there has still been more day-to-day volatility in the federal funds rate than earlier in the year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This pattern likely reflects several factors, including the demand by European banks for funds early in the day and the reduced spread between the discount rate and the target federal funds rate, which has altered the banks’ demand for reserve balances.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There were no foreign operations during this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I request a vote to ratify the operations conducted by the System Open Market Account since the September 18 FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, I am very happy to take questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Bill?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then, may I have a motion to ratify?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know if we will have the same luck over on this side.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me turn to Dave Stockton to begin the economic situation report.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: From a forecast perspective, it’s been a pretty wild ride over the intermeeting period, with our outlook for activity shifting sharply at various points in the process in response to large swings in the stock market, the exchange value of the dollar, and the price of crude oil.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: A couple of weeks ago, with the incoming data stronger, the stock market up substantially, and the dollar down noticeably, we were looking at a forecast that had economic growth moving materially above potential later in the projection period.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It appeared that, after taking you for a tour of the sausage factory in my September briefing, I would need to issue a recall of that last batch of sausages even before the arrival of their typically short expiration date.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In the event, the stock market retraced most of its earlier increase, and some of the improvement in financial conditions that had occurred immediately following the September meeting was subsequently reversed.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As a consequence, our forecast changed relatively little, on net, over the past six weeks.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The growth of real activity is higher in the near term, but in 2008 and 2009, the stimulative effects on GDP growth of the lower dollar are offset by the restraint on incomes and spending imposed by the higher path for oil prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We expect the growth of real GDP to slow from a 2¼ percent pace this year to a 1¾ percent pace in 2008 before edging back up to a 2¼ percent rate in 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The period of below-trend growth late this year and next year results in some easing of pressures on resource utilization, and core inflation moves roughly sideways at just under 2 percent over the forecast period.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: To my mind, recent developments raise three big questions about our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: First, does the broad-based strength that we have seen in the data on spending and activity over the intermeeting period suggest that we have overestimated the restraining effects on aggregate demand emanating from the recent financial turbulence?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Second, is the staff missing signs of greater restraint on aggregate demand that will weigh more heavily on activity in the period ahead?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Finally, with oil prices up sharply, the dollar having depreciated, and resource utilization a touch tighter, why is our forecast for core inflation about unchanged?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Let me start with the question about whether the strength in the incoming data casts doubt on our estimates of the restraining effects of financial turbulence.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There can be little denying that, almost across the board, the readings on economic activity have been stronger than our expectations in September.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In terms of domestic spending, the largest upside surprises have been in consumer spending, and much of the upward revision reflects data on activity after the financial turbulence had already begun.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Overall consumer spending was stronger than we had expected in August, and the available information on retail sales and on sales of motor vehicles suggests that real PCE exceeded our expectations for September as well.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At this point, we know very little about October.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Chain store sales have softened somewhat but only by enough to make us comfortable with the meager monthly gains in spending that we are projecting for the fourth quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Our discussions with the automakers suggest that sales this month have remained reasonably steady.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: All told, third-quarter growth in consumption looks stronger than we had expected, and spending appears to be headed into the fourth quarter with a bit more momentum.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In the business sector, stronger purchases of motor vehicles led us to raise our forecast of equipment spending in the third quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other components of E&S came in close to our expectations, though last week’s data on orders and shipments of capital goods, which we received after the Greenbook was completed, were also a bit stronger than we had anticipated.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The incoming data on construction put in place are consistent with our projected sharp slowdown in the growth of nonresidential structures after a surge in the second quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But even here, the data have outflanked us to the upside, with surprising strength in commercial construction, factory buildings, and telecommunications structures.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Taken together, stronger consumption and investment account for only about half of the upward revision that we made to real GDP growth in the third and fourth quarters.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The external sector accounts for the other half.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In particular, continuing a pattern we have seen during much of this year, the growth of exports once again exceeded our expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We estimate that real exports increased at an annual rate of nearly 17 percent in the third quarter, about 3½ percentage points above our September forecast, and we have marked up export growth in the current quarter as well.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The greater strength in both foreign and domestic demand led us to revise up the growth of real GDP in the second half of this year about ½ percentage point, with annualized growth rates of 3¼ percent and 1½ percent in the third and fourth quarters, respectively.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So, do these fairly broad-based upward surprises in spending and activity suggest that we overreacted in the extent to which we marked down our projection in response to the recent difficulties in financial markets?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It certainly seems a legitimate possibility.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: However, we think it would be premature to make that call.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As Bill noted, financial market conditions have improved somewhat over the intermeeting period but remain far from normal.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In terms of credit provision, the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey revealed a sharp jump in the fraction of banks reporting tighter terms and standards on loans to businesses and households, a development consistent with the restraint on spending that we have built into our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Consumer sentiment remains depressed relative to overall economic conditions, perhaps because of worries about financial developments.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For now, although we have slightly trimmed the magnitude of the turmoil effects on aggregate demand, the more important adjustment in this forecast has been to push more of the restraint into next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At the other end of the spectrum of worry is the second question that I posed earlier: Have we missed some significant signs of potential economic weakness in the developments of the intermeeting period?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Financial market participants seem to have reacted to the news of the past six weeks by marking down the expected path for the fed funds rate, whereas our forecast and policy assumptions are nearly unchanged.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Is it possible that we are missing signs of an impending downturn in aggregate activity?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Of course, the prudent and accurate answer to that question is always “yes.” But if that turns out to be the case, it won’t be for lack of attention.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At present, it is difficult to find evidence in high-frequency indicators that the economy is in the process of turning down.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Initial claims for unemployment insurance have remained relatively low, motor vehicle sales are reported to have been well maintained at least through mid-October, commodity prices are firm, reports from purchasing managers continue to suggest modest expansion, and few anecdotes outside the housing sector sound as though we’ve moved past a tipping point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If we are missing something important, it seems more likely to me that we could be facing a more-grinding period of subpar economic performance associated with a deeper and more-protracted adjustment in the housing sector.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It might seem a bit surprising to point to housing as a major downside risk when this has been one aspect of our forecast that was right on the mark over the intermeeting period; we had expected steep declines in sales and starts, and that is what we got.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But I would counsel you not to take too much comfort from that observation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In our forecast, we expect sales and starts of new single- family homes to decline another 8 percent before bottoming out around the turn of the year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The projected configuration of starts and sales is consistent with a dropback in the months’ supply of unsold new homes from an estimated peak of 8½ months early next year to 4½ months by the end of 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Residential investment continues to fall through the middle of next year and only edges up thereafter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But it is not difficult to envision a more painful period of adjustment.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We know a huge inventory imbalance still exists in the housing sector.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If, in response to that imbalance, house prices register steeper declines than the ones we are forecasting, prospective purchasers could experience an even greater fear of buying into a declining market, reinforcing the housing sector’s drag on aggregate activity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, sharply lower prices could have more-serious implications for the ability of households to refinance existing mortgages and could impair the performance of mortgage markets more broadly.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Those strains, as they have in recent months, could spill over into other areas of the financial markets.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As we showed in a couple of alternative simulations in the Greenbook, a steeper decline in house prices and construction activity could result in a path for the fed funds rate that does not differ materially from the one that appears to be currently built into market expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We remain comfortable with our baseline projection for housing, but it is still easier to see sizable downside risks than sizable upside risks to this aspect of our forecast, and that suggests to me that our modal forecast of GDP still has more weight to the downside than the upside.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That said, given the strength over the intermeeting period of the incoming data outside housing, that downward skew is probably less pronounced in this forecast than in the one we presented in September.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Turning to the price projection, the question I posed at the outset was why our forecast of core price inflation is largely unchanged given higher oil prices, a lower dollar and tighter resource utilization.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: With respect to resource utilization, both the GDP gap and the unemployment rate suggest only slightly tighter product and labor markets than in our previous forecast, and given the flatness of our aggregate supply curve, the effect on prices over this period is negligible.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As for the lower dollar, we see higher import price inflation in the near term in line with the recent depreciation, but these effects quickly play through.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: More broadly, the available evidence continues to suggest that exchange rate pass-through to import prices is quite low, which in turn mutes the effects on broader prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The indirect consequences of higher oil prices are a bit more consequential, and all else being equal, would have added about a tenth to our core price projection in 2008.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But not all else was equal.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The incoming data on core PCE prices were again slightly more favorable than we had expected.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The surprise in this intermeeting period was largely in nonmarket prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: More broadly, the deceleration that we have observed in core PCE prices over the past year has been greater than can be explained by our models, and we have carried a bit larger negative residual forward in this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As a consequence, we expect core PCE price inflation to move sideways at a 1.9 percent pace in 2008 and 2009, unchanged from our previous forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Overall price inflation is projected to move down from 3 percent this year to 1.8 percent in 2008 and 1.7 percent in 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The deceleration in overall prices reflects some decline, on net, in energy prices over the next two years and a dropback in food price inflation to a rate closer to that of core consumer prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the whole, I’d characterize the risks around our inflation forecast as roughly balanced.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan will continue our presentation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Although the foreign economies appear to have grown at a moderate pace during the third quarter as a whole, indicators for September and October suggest that the recent financial turmoil may yet leave an imprint on activity in some countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Perhaps the most striking evidence on this score has been the ECB’s survey of euro-area bank lending.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the third quarter, this survey showed the sharpest shift toward tightening in its five-year history, along with evidence of more- stringent credit standards for business and housing loans.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, we have seen downward moves in surveys and measures of sentiment in the euro area, particularly in Germany, although these indicators have generally remained in expansionary territory.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the United Kingdom, the growth of mortgage lending continued on a downward path in September, and a recent Bank of England survey suggests a tightening of corporate credit conditions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: All in all, we see this (admittedly fragmentary) evidence as broadly consistent with our assumption in the September Greenbook that fallout from the financial turmoil is likely to exert some drag on growth over the next several quarters in the euro area, the United Kingdom, and Canada.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This assessment, however, is marked by significant upside and downside risks—as it is still too soon to gauge these effects with much confidence.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As in our previous forecast, we do not see the turmoil weighing directly on activity in Japan or the emerging-market economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: More generally, the contours of our forecast remain similar to those in September.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Recent data have confirmed our expectation that average economic growth abroad declined to about 3½ percent in the third quarter, cooling from the very rapid rate in the first half of the year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We see growth edging down further in the current quarter, to just over 3 percent, and remaining at about that pace in 2008 and 2009.

speaker: SHEETS
text: After the Greenbook went to bed, we received Chinese GDP data, which according to our seasonally adjusted quarterly estimate grew at an annual rate of just over 8 percent in the third quarter—a little slower than we had expected and down from the 14 percent rate in the first half of the year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This deceleration appears to have been led by a slowing in investment and a smaller contribution from the external sector.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Going forward, economic growth in China should remain below its previous double-digit pace, as the Chinese authorities take further action to cool the country’s booming real estate market and the rapid growth of bank lending.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition to uncertainty about the eventual effects of the financial turmoil on real activity, other risks to our generally favorable foreign outlook are worth noting.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First on this list is the possibility of a softer-than-expected performance from the U.S. economy.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Although there is talk in some quarters about so-called decoupling—that is, that the foreign economies may now be less linked to developments in the United States than has been the case in the past—the jury is still out on this point.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Although domestic demand does appear to have firmed in some foreign countries in recent years, a marked slowing in U.S. growth would affect the rest of the world through trade channels (particularly Canada, Mexico, and emerging Asia) and, as highlighted by the recent turmoil, probably through financial channels as well.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As a second risk, house-price valuations in many advanced economies appear elevated.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given that, a correction in housing markets abroad—with potentially sizable accompanying wealth effects—strikes us as an important downside risk for some countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Third, although we see average foreign inflation remaining well behaved, at near 2½ percent over the next two years, inflation risks cannot be dismissed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: After several years of exceptionally strong economic growth, the foreign economies on average are now operating near potential, and resource constraints may be more binding than we currently envision.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, food prices have moved up in many countries, and the prices of oil and other commodities are at high levels.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indeed, recent developments in oil markets seem to pose intensified risks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The spot price of WTI is trading today at nearly $92 a barrel, up $5 since the Greenbook went to bed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Since your last meeting, the spot WTI price has climbed $13 per barrel, while the far-futures price has increased about $10 per barrel.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It suffices to say that underlying supply-demand conditions in the oil market are exceptionally tight.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Over the past several years, as the global economy has expanded briskly, oil production has increased only sluggishly—reflecting both OPEC supply restraint and diminishing production from OECD countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Against this backdrop, the price of oil has been driven up further in recent weeks by reports of decreasing inventories (at a time of year when such stocks are typically on the rise) and by intensified concerns about the stability of Middle East oil production, triggered by tensions between Turkey and Iraq and by concerns about U.S. relations with Iran.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We see OPEC’s plans to expand production 500,000 barrels per day beginning on November 1, even if fully implemented, as unlikely to go very far in defusing the tightness in the market.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Futures markets call for WTI prices to remain elevated, in the neighborhood of $80 per barrel, through 2015.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I conclude with some upbeat news on U.S. external performance.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Exports continue to surprise on the upside, having shown exceptional strength in the July and August trade data, as exports of aircraft, autos, and agricultural products have all expanded briskly.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Consequently, as Dave mentioned, real exports of goods and services are now thought to have surged at a pace of 17 percent in the third quarter, up 3½ percentage points from the last forecast.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We estimate that real imports in the third quarter grew at a comparatively modest rate.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Taken together, these data suggest that net exports made an arithmetic contribution of 1¼ percentage points to U.S. real GDP growth in the third quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Going forward, we see export growth moderating to just under 8 percent in the current quarter and proceeding at a solid 6½ percent average rate through the next two years.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Relative to our September forecast, the path of export growth is up nearly 2 percentage points in the fourth quarter and by lesser—but still sizable—amounts in 2008 and 2009.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This higher projection reflects stimulus from recent declines in the dollar, which have exceeded our previous projections.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The broad dollar index has dropped more than 3 percent since your last meeting.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But in addition to support from the weaker dollar, we now see greater underlying strength in exports than we had previously thought.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our projected path for imports, in contrast, is little changed from the last Greenbook.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Import growth is slated to bounce up in the current quarter, largely because of a seasonal rebound in oil imports.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Thereafter, the projected strengthening of U.S. growth and a deceleration in core import prices should provide increasing support to imports.

speaker: SHEETS
text: All told, we see the external sector making a neutral contribution to U.S. real GDP growth in the fourth quarter, contributing 0.4 percentage point to economic growth next year, and returning to neutrality in 2009 as imports accelerate.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Thus, to the extent that our forecast materializes, large negative contributions from net exports might very well be a thing of the past.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Brian will now continue our presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2 I will be referring to the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on October Projections.” The table shows the central tendencies and ranges of your current forecasts for 2007 and the next three years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Where available, the central tendencies and ranges of the projections last published by the Committee―those submitted for inclusion in the July Monetary Policy Report―are shown in italics.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2 Materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Notably, a majority of you conditioned your current projections on an easing of monetary policy, with most of that majority apparently seeing lower rates as appropriate either imminently or within the next six months or so.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even with that assumed easing, your GDP growth forecasts for 2007 have been marked down slightly since last June, and your outlook for next year has been revised down more substantially.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Many of you noted that last summer’s NIPA revisions led you to lower your estimate of potential GDP growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you cited the intensification of the downturn in housing markets, the turmoil in financial markets, and higher oil prices as factors leading you to scale back your expectations for actual growth in 2007 and 2008, though some participants commented that rising net exports could provide support to aggregate demand.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendency of the economic growth forecasts for 2008 is now 1.8 percent to 2.5 percent, below the central tendency of 2½ percent to 2¾ percent in June.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Perhaps partly because you expect easing whereas the staff assumed an unchanged stance of policy, the central tendency of your economic growth projections is above the Greenbook forecast of 1.7 percent for real economic growth in 2008.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That difference may also reflect your somewhat more optimistic view of potential growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is worth noting that the divergence among your views concerning the outlook for next year has widened substantially: The width of the central tendency, for example, at nearly ¾ percentage point, is about three times that in the June projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The downward revision to the outlook for GDP growth was mirrored in a small upward revision to the unemployment rate: The central tendency of the projections for unemployment at the end of this year is around 4¾ percent, and it centers on a rate just under 5 percent at the end of next year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Based on the comments that some of you have made about sustainable rates of unemployment and on your longer-run unemployment projections, many of you apparently predict the emergence of a small amount of slack by the end of next year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With incoming data on core inflation a bit better than you had expected and with some slack likely next year, the central tendency of your projections for core PCE inflation is down noticeably for 2007 and is a shade lower for 2008; most of you now see core inflation below 2 percent in both years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your near-term forecasts for total PCE inflation are higher than those for core inflation, reflecting surging energy prices and, in some cases, an expectation of continued brisk increases in food prices.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With regard to the uncertainties in the outlook, most of you see the risks to growth as tilted to the downside—even with an assumed easing of policy—and judge that the degree of uncertainty regarding prospects for economic activity is unusually high relative to average levels over the past twenty years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your commentaries highlighted downside risks arising from the possibility that financial market turmoil and tighter credit conditions could exert unexpectedly large restraint on household and business spending and that the downturn in housing could prove even steeper than currently anticipated.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A slight majority perceived the risks to total inflation as broadly balanced, and a more sizable majority judged that the risks to core inflation are in balance; in both cases, those in the minority saw the risk to inflation as tilted to the upside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As the experience in the September trial run highlighted, the Committee’s policy statement will need to be reviewed carefully for potential inconsistencies with the risk assessments submitted with the projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will return to that issue tomorrow.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Turning to the longer-horizon forecasts, you expect real GDP growth of around 2½ percent and unemployment slightly above 4¾ percent in both 2009 and 2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Judging from your forecast narratives, these projections are close to your estimates of the economy’s potential growth rate and the level of the NAIRU.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The former is a bit higher than the staff estimate of about 2.1 percent potential growth, and the latter is close to the staff estimate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For 2009 and 2010, all of your core inflation forecasts are in a range of 1½ to 2 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A couple of you expect rising prices of food and energy to keep total inflation above 2 percent in 2009, but all of your forecasts for total inflation are within a range of 1½ to 2 percent in 2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Many of you state that you view your projections for inflation in 2010 as consistent with price stability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for our colleagues?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Dave, this is about the Greenbook forecast—I was going to say existentialism, but I am not sure that is quite right.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Dave, is the Greenbook forecast something we should view as a modal forecast, as I think you implied, or the expected value of the range of plausible scenarios that might have—

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Well, I would say this is a modal forecast, and as I indicated, I think there is probably more downside mass than upside mass in that probability distribution at this point.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Is the monetary policy path that you reveal in the Greenbook based on the modal forecast?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Thinking about our forecast as a modal forecast is correct.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If I could ask one more question.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In the Greenbook, you reveal the usual assumptions for what you anticipate for total credit growth, and you show it decelerating significantly over this period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: How does the deceleration you are anticipating look compared with a range of previous periods in which the U.S. economy was slowing significantly or periods following substantial financial distress?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: For example, if you compare it with 2001-02 or 1990-91, is it a modest deceleration in credit growth, or does it look large compared with that?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Well, I should get the facts before I answer your question in terms of exactly how this compares with both the 2000 period and the 1990 period.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We could certainly do that and circulate it to the Committee.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, in our forecast we have credit growth decelerating not just because overall activity is decelerating but because we think there will be some important restraints on credit availability going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Most of that, of course, is on the mortgage side, but some of it is on the business credit side as well.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That said, we are not forecasting a deep credit crunch.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If you were more concerned that that was what you were facing, I don’t think this forecast is consistent with it.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This forecast is consistent with some unusual restraint on the availability of credit, principally on the mortgage side but more broadly elsewhere, but not truly a deep or strong headwind type of episode in which there is substantial impairment going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As I noted at the last meeting, even the restraint that we do have on the credit side fades over the coming year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have two brief questions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One, in business investment, particularly equipment and software, you have somewhat of a rebound in the early half of ’08, and then it falls off again in the latter half of ’08.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given the way you have the recovery in housing coming in the middle of ’08 and presumably some of the credit- tightening cycle gradually diminishing, why is business investment falling off again in the latter half of ’08?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The second question, just to get them both out on the table, is that you are predicting that a 25 basis point unexpected boost to the fed funds rate would result in a fall in equities of about 2 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, the papers I have read randomly about that suggest that such an estimate is probably a bit on the high side.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just wonder where that number came from.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We took that estimate from a paper by Ben Bernanke and Ken Kuttner.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I thought that was 5.3 percent for 100 basis points, right, which would be a decline of a little over 1 percent, not 2.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Of course, we have multiple estimates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just read the wrong one

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We felt that in the past we did not typically worry about that sort of surprise effect, given that overall our ability to predict asset prices is so limited to begin with.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This seemed stark enough that we thought we should probably lean in that direction.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Whether we are too large or too small I don’t know.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It’s not a very significant or consequential effect.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, we are not pretending to forecast all the things that might happen if you were not to ease at this meeting in terms of how the financial markets might take that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’re just trying to take the biggest pieces, and that’s where we were.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It looks to me as though some of the investment piece has to do with the idiosyncrasies of our forecast of the high-tech area.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The underlying core piece of E&S spending follows pretty much a standard accelerator path, where things slow down more evenly through next year and then begin to pick up with the overall pickup in activity toward the end of next year as we move into 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I think your basic intuition about what you should have seen is there.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have some slowdown in high-tech spending that sort of progresses.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In transportation, in particular, things are especially weak in the first half of this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: They pick up a little in the beginning of next year and then slow down again, and that really is more based upon our forecast of motor vehicles and our forecast for aircraft production.

speaker: POOLE
text: I guess the first is more a comment than a question.

speaker: POOLE
text: When we look at the net exports—and I think you commented on that in terms of the outlook—it seems to me that most of it is really coming on the import side, which I assume is importantly related to domestic demand and consumption.

speaker: POOLE
text: Looking at the annual data—I’m looking at page 24 in Part 1 of the Greenbook, which has the annual data over a string of years—export growth is actually slowing in terms of percentage growth year over year.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I guess the way that I would put it is, To what extent is the lower growth in imports really driven by lower aggregate consumption rather than a genuine improvement in the current account?

speaker: POOLE
text: Another question is really quite separate, and I think it will tie into our later go-round here.

speaker: POOLE
text: I don’t have a good sense of the relative importance of your anecdotal information in modifying your outlook compared with the underlying data that you follow so thoroughly and so expertly.

speaker: POOLE
text: To what extent do you modify the views based on the data, the model, and your reading of the numbers by your anecdotal information, your business contacts?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So do you want me to start with that?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the anecdotal side, as I think about the revisions that we’ve made to the forecast of this most recent period, by which we have taken down the level of GDP nearly ¾ percentage point for our estimate of the effects of the financial disturbance, I don’t know whether you’d call that based on anecdotal or on actual data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It felt pretty much like guesswork with a few anecdotes at the time of the last meeting, when we had some measures of financial stress that were significant and we knew on the data side, in terms of the impairment to the mortgage markets, that something very significant was going on.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The housing side was about half the adjustment that we made.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I guess I’d just say that a big chunk of that was probably data based, but some guesswork was involved in how much restraint on housing activity would come from the cutbacks in mortgage availability that were going to occur in the subprime market.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In terms of the consumer side last time, we really had very little to go on, except a hint that maybe consumer sentiment had weakened somewhat.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Since then I think we have accumulated a little more evidence in favor of our hypothesis that possibly some restraint on spending will occur going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Consumer sentiment has remained low relative to what we think the other macro fundamentals would suggest.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We think that there is a correlation between the residuals of explaining consumer sentiment and our consumption equation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So that correlation, in addition to the senior loan officer survey—again, I don’t know whether you consider that anecdotal evidence or systematic data, but there’s a very substantial and widespread uptick in the tightening of terms and standards for both business and household loans—gives us more confidence that what we thought were pretty sizable effects that we built into the forecast have some credible basis.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, there are still some touchy-feely kinds of things that we’re looking at.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For example, with the assistance of the Reserve Banks, we did the survey of our Beige Book contacts on capital spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I can’t say that we didn’t make some adjustment to our E&S forecast on the basis of those anecdotes, but again, those anecdotes gave us a little more confidence that something may be happening on the capital spending side going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I wish I could tell you that, yes, three- tenths of this is anecdotes and seven-tenths is data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There’s a big gray area between the kinds of information that we gather versus the GDP data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If you ask how the GDP data alone influenced our outlook, as I noted in my briefing, those have been pretty clearly to the upside, and we haven’t yet seen any hard evidence in the actual spending data outside the housing sector that we’re getting any restraint.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So that remains a forecast based upon these other shreds of evidence that we think support some notion that there will be a weakening going forward.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In response to your first question, I think the answer is that it’s the improvement in the net export contribution in the current account that’s being driven by both a strengthening of exports and a softening of imports.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The net export contribution or the direct contribution of exports to GDP growth has risen roughly 25 basis points over the past couple of years—so about ¼ percentage point.

speaker: SHEETS
text: By the same token, the arithmetic negative drag from imports has been reduced about 40 basis points.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think it’s strictly an arithmetic computational thing.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Your observation that it’s more imports than exports is absolutely right, comparing 2007 with where we were several years ago.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But certainly for the third quarter and for the second half, exports have been extraordinarily strong, and imports have been softer than maybe they were a couple of years ago but not extraordinarily weak.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So in the near term, it’s more an export story.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Then the other point is that certainly you’re also correct that the softening of imports that we’ve seen over the past few years has been driven in large measure by the softening of U.S. domestic demand, and that’s probably—I don’t have an exact decomposition here—on the order of two-thirds of the softening in imports.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, we’re ready for our economic go- round.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I will talk a little about the District this time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It continues to perform well, with ongoing weakness in the housing sector offset by strength in agriculture and energy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As has been true for a while, construction activity remains mixed, with weakness in residential construction offset by continued strength in commercial construction.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In terms of residential construction, both the number of single-family permits and the value of residential construction contracts declined in September, and home inventories rose with slower home sales, as is happening elsewhere.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, District home prices measured by the OFHEO index edged up in the second quarter and remain stronger than in the nation as a whole.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the commercial side, after a robust spring, construction activity has slowed but has remained solid.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Energy regions, such as Wyoming, report strong activity.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But even in the non-energy regions, activity remains solid.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Office vacancy rates were stable, and absorption rates declined.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, developers reported more-stringent credit standards, and they expected credit availability to remain tight.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Consumer spending softened in September.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mall traffic was flat, and retailers reported that sales were down slightly.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, auto dealers reported that sales fell further in September as high gasoline prices cut demand for our SUV sales and for vans.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In other areas, though, activity appears to remain at least moderate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: For example, travel and tourism remain healthy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, manufacturing activity picked up slightly in October.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Solid increases among producers of durable goods offset a weakening among producers of food, chemical, and other nondurable goods.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Even so, purchasing managers remain optimistic about future activity, as most forward-looking indexes strengthened or held steady.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Finally, we continue to see strength in agriculture and energy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: District producers are selling a bumper crop at high prices as poor crop conditions in the rest of the world trimmed global inventories and boosted export demand.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, robust meat demand kept cattle and hog prices above breakeven levels.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The sharp rise in farm income led to a surge in farm capital spending in the third quarter and is expected to rise further in the fourth quarter.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to the national economy, my outlook for growth is basically unchanged from our last meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Generally speaking, economic indicators have been a bit stronger over the intermeeting period, as described here, but financial markets continue, obviously, to exhibit some stress.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The senior loan officer survey suggested moderate tightening of credit conditions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is consistent with our estimates of slower growth in the current quarter.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As before, though, I remain more optimistic than the Greenbook about both the near-term outlook and the longer-run growth potential for the economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Specifically, I think growth over the forecast period will average about 2½ percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: My forecast is based on maintaining the fed funds rate at its current level of 4¾ percent through the middle of next year before reducing it to its more neutral level late next year or early 2009.

speaker: HOENIG
text: With regard to trend growth, I continue to expect a decline in potential growth from about 2¾ percent to 2½ percent by 2010.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Disappointing housing data have led me to mark down my near-term forecast for residential investment.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I continue to expect that residential investment will decline through the first part of next year before turning up in the second half.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Also, after strong growth in the first half of this year, nonresidential construction is likely, perhaps, to slow significantly over the next year and a half.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Supporting growth in the near term will be moderate growth in consumer and government spending along with strength in exports driven by the lower dollar and robust foreign growth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to the risks to the outlook, I believe they remain on the downside as far as real output but have not worsened noticeably since our last meeting, especially with that action.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I believe that construction, both residential and nonresidential, and slower consumer spending from higher energy prices constitute the main risks to the outlook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: With regard to the inflation outlook, recent data on core inflation continue to be, as noted here, favorable.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I expect core PCE inflation to average about 1.8 percent over the forecast period—remember, assuming no change in the fed funds rate—but I also expect that overall PCE inflation next year will moderate as the effects of higher food and energy prices wear off.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, I do remain concerned about the upside risk to inflation as well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Greater dollar depreciation and higher energy and commodity prices, along with greater pass-through from all three, could push inflation higher for a period of time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, I am also concerned about the implications of the gradual upcreep in the TIPS measures of expected inflation for the long-run path, and I am receiving more anecdotal information, in discussions with individuals in our region, about a change in expectations about inflation as they continue to deal with some rising prices in materials and other goods.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There has been little change in the District economic conditions since our September meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Except for housing, activity is expanding at a modest pace, somewhat below trend.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our business contacts are cautious, generally expecting slow growth to continue over the next quarter, but they remain fairly optimistic for business conditions six to twelve months out.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Payroll employment continues to expand at a slow pace in our three states, which partially reflects slow population growth, and so the unemployment rate remains slightly below that of the nation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Retail sales have generally held up, but there are divergent views among retailers regarding holiday sales.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: High-end stores expect a very strong finish to the year; lower-end merchants are more cautious.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Housing construction and sales continue to decline, but the pace of that decline is in line with the expectations at our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The value of nonresidential building contracts has declined more sharply in our region than in the nation as a whole.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nevertheless, I would characterize nonresidential real estate markets as firm.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That office vacancy rates are declining and commercial rents are rising suggests a positive outlook for commercial construction going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: According to our business outlook survey, manufacturing activity in the District has been increasing at a modest pace for the past several months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The general index of economic activity moved down slightly, from 10.9 in September to 6.9.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Shipments and new orders also weakened slightly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Staff analysis suggests that our manufacturing index, which precedes the release of national industrial production numbers, provides useful information in forecasting monthly manufacturing IP and total IP.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That forecasting model is predicting a rise in both manufacturing IP and total IP in October.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: About two-thirds of the District manufacturers and service-sector firms we have polled said that recent changes in financial conditions have not prompted any change in their capital spending plans, and the other firms are about evenly split as expecting a slight decrease or a slight increase over the next six to twelve months compared with the past six to twelve months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, in speaking with my business contacts, I do hear a sense of continuing caution among businesses in their capital spending plans.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The manufacturers seem to be a bit stronger than the service firms, perhaps reflecting a more robust export market, which many of them are participating in.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: District bankers, in general, continue to express concern over housing and mortgage lending but see commercial and industrial lending as fairly stable and proceeding about as they had expected.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There has been little change in the District’s inflation picture since our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Firms continue to report higher benefit costs, but other wage pressures have moderated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our manufacturers reported having to pay higher prices for many inputs, particularly energy-related inputs and petroleum-based products as well as agricultural commodities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They have passed on many of those increases in terms of higher prices to their consumers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While retailers report only modest price increases for many products, food prices are generally higher.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In summary, since our last meeting, there has been little change in the economic conditions in the District or in the outlook for the region.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Overall, business activity in the region is advancing at a fairly modest pace, and most of our contacts expect that pace to continue for the next quarter or so.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But in general, firms in the District remain optimistic about business six to twelve months from now.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Turning to the nation, the economy appears less vulnerable to me than it did at the time of our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Financial markets have improved somewhat, as Bill Dudley was telling us.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Conditions are not back to normal yet in all segments of the market, but the markets that are still under stress are the same ones that were under stress last month.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Subprime and jumbo mortgages and asset-backed commercial paper are the ones that still are struggling.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Price discovery still plagues many of these markets, and I suspect it will take some time before the markets can sort things out and trading returns to normal.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That does not mean that the ultimate agreed-upon market prices for some of these assets will bear any resemblance to what they looked like before August.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, they probably won’t, but that’s not necessarily a bad sign or a cause for concern; it may even be a healthy development.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We haven’t seen disruption spread to other asset classes for the most part, and the level of stress in financial markets seems to have fallen even as volatility remains high.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The spread of jumbo over conventional mortgage rates remains elevated, reflecting some concern, I think, about the risk that expensive homes may face greater price declines than other homes, but the premium is less than it was in September.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Both investment-grade and non-investment-grade corporate bond issues have increased.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Financial institutions have begun to write off some of their investments and take the losses.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This has weighed heavily on equity markets, but I view the write-downs as a necessary part of the process toward stabilization in the markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Earnings reports from nonfinancial firms have actually been pretty favorable.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not saying that we are out of the woods yet, but in my view the risks for a serious meltdown in financial markets have lessened somewhat since our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The news on general economic activity has improved somewhat since our last meeting as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, some of the data have come in better than expected.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Employment was revised up, and retail sales data suggest that consumer spending remains resilient, despite the downturn in housing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Like the Greenbook, my outlook for the economy has changed little since our last meeting, when we acted preemptively and lowered rates to “forestall some of the potential adverse effects of financial market disruptions and the expected intensification of the housing correction on the broader economy.” Housing investment and sales continue to decline but about as expected in our forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: After all, the rapid reduction in subprime lending is exacerbating the decline in housing demand and thus home sales, contributing to the slower recovery of that sector.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Other sectors of the economy have performed about as I expected, with little evidence as yet of any major spillovers from housing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Oil prices have moved higher than expected since our last meeting, as has been discussed, but it is unclear to me yet how permanent that increase will be or how much of a drag it might be on activity.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The oil price rise is likely to show through to headline inflation in the coming months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although core inflation measures have improved since the beginning of the year, the rise in energy prices has the potential to put upward pressure on core inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, while inflation and inflationary expectations have been stable to date, I suspect that inflation risks are now more to the upside than they were in September.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The forecast is an important context for our policy, in my view.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have stressed in the past year that we are data driven and respond to the evolution of our forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In general, like the Greenbook, as I said, my forecast of the economy going forward is little changed from my September view.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I see that growth returns to trend, which I estimate to be about 2.7—a little higher than the Greenbook—late in 2008 as the housing correction runs its course and the financial market turbulence unwinds.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Core PCE inflation remains slightly below 2 percent next year and moderates toward my goal of 1½ percent by 2010.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I built in a 25 basis point easing sometime in early 2008 to bring the funds rate back down to a more neutral level, and in my baseline forecast I assume a constant funds rate thereafter.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That forecast, however, is contingent on inflation and inflationary expectations remaining well behaved.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Having said that, I repeat my caution that inflationary pressures are somewhat elevated at this point, and we run the risk that inflationary expectations may become unhinged if the markets suspect that we have lessened our commitment to keep inflation contained.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, I don’t rule out the possibility that we may have to reverse course and tighten policy sometime in 2008 or 2009 in order to achieve consistency between my target rate of inflation of 1½ and inflationary expectations.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Boston forecast is very close to that of the Greenbook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With the constant federal funds rate assumption, the economy is very close to full employment, and core inflation is close to 2 percent at the end of 2008.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Such an outcome is consistent with what I would hope to achieve with appropriate monetary policy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, while this is an expected path that seems quite reasonable, the distribution of risks around that outcome for growth remains skewed to the downside.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Our forecast, like that of the Greenbook, expects particularly weak residential investment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Problems in financing mortgages, expectations of falling housing prices, and more-severe financial stress for homebuilders are likely to weigh heavily over the next two quarters.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In fact, our forecast for residential investment has become sufficiently bleak that there may actually be some upside risk to it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Somewhat surprising to me has been the lack of spillover to the rest of the economy from the problems in residential investment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I remain concerned that falling housing prices will further sap consumer confidence and cause a pullback in consumption, though to date there is little evidence of a significant effect of the housing problems on consumer spending.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Similarly, I would have expected the financing problems that have aggravated the housing situation to have caused a sharper reduction in investment in general and in nonresidential structures in particular.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, so far these remain risks rather than outcomes.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Thus, while I am worried about the downside risks, I am reminded that forecasters have frequently overestimated the consequences of liquidity problems in the past.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: On the financial side, there have definitely been improvements in market conditions, though markets remain fragile.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Particularly worrisome has been the announcement of significant downgrades of tranches of CDOs and mortgage-backed securities with large exposure to the subprime mortgage market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Not only have the lower tranches experienced significant downgrades, but a number of the AAA and AA tranches have been downgraded to below investment grade.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Some investors cannot retain below-investment-grade securities and are forced to sell these securities in an already depressed market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The number of the downgrades, the magnitude of the downgrades, and the piecemeal ratings announcements all are likely to call into further question the reliability of the ratings process.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If many high-grade securities tied to mortgages are downgraded to below investment grade, some investors may conclude that repricing of even high-graded tranches does not reflect a liquidity problem but rather a substantial reevaluation of credit risk.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Thus, I am concerned that continued widespread downgrades may make recovery in the securitization market more difficult, particularly for nonconforming mortgages, with a consequent increase in the financing cost of these assets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I also remain concerned that the asset-backed commercial paper market remains fragile.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While investors seem to be distinguishing between conduits whose structure or underlying assets are quite risky, my sense is that money managers are watching the market quite closely.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I continue to hear concerns over the possibility that some money market funds will experience losses that will not be supported by their parents, resulting in increased investor concern with the safety of money market funds more generally.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: On balance, the data both on the real economy and on financial markets have improved since our September meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That improvement makes it more likely that the economy will continue to recover gradually from the financial turmoil.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, both the real and the financial risks remain skewed to the downside.

speaker: FISHER
text: Like the global economy, the Eleventh District is slowing, but relative to the other Districts it remains very strong.

speaker: FISHER
text: Our retail sales improved in September.

speaker: FISHER
text: Nonresidential and commercial construction remains elevated.

speaker: FISHER
text: Service- sector job growth strengthened significantly in September, and our staff estimates that 18.2 percent of the jobs created in the country year to date were created in the State of Texas.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just wanted to mention that.

speaker: FISHER
text: Needless to say, wages are rising because of labor shortages, a decline in immigration, and the increase in minimum wage.

speaker: FISHER
text: I will stop with the Texas brag and now go on to the national economy.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think President Rosengren just gave an excellent summary of the financial markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would add only the following—that with regard to credit markets, the hardening of the arteries or the blockage of the aorta or whatever cardiovascular analogy we want to choose to describe what happened is no longer as severe and life-threatening as it appeared to be in August.

speaker: FISHER
text: As mentioned by the staff, whether it is net bond issuance of investment-grade securities or C&I loans et cetera, the markets are moving toward pricing assets according to what they will sell for rather than what their hypothetical mathematical modeling value might posit.

speaker: FISHER
text: There was a startling statement in the Financial Times on Friday morning.

speaker: FISHER
text: Somebody, otherwise forgettable, said, “Corporate treasurers are no longer buying things they don’t understand.” Imagine that.

speaker: FISHER
text: Investors are coming home from lala land.

speaker: FISHER
text: To be sure, we’re not out of the woods quite yet, as President Plosser and President Rosengren mentioned.

speaker: FISHER
text: The situation remains real, but we’ve gone beyond suspended reality.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you will forgive me, you might say we have gone from the ridiculous to the subprime.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let the transcript say “groan.”

speaker: FISHER
text: By that I mean, by the way, that the subprime market is a focus of angst, which it should be, but the ridiculous practice of the suspension of reason in valuing all asset classes, if not over, is in remission.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have a long way to go before full recovery and must acknowledge that shocks regarding access might occur.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am confident, as I have said in previous meetings, that—just to be polite—some cow patties might show up in the punchbowls of some portfolios, perhaps especially in Europe and Asia.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I would submit, Mr. Chairman, that we are on our way back to markets priced by reason rather than by fantasy.

speaker: FISHER
text: So, while we must remain ready to act as needed, I think it is appropriate to focus our discussion today and tomorrow foursquare on the economy, and I want to turn to that now.

speaker: FISHER
text: The wealth effect of the severe markdown in housing is as yet incalculable and worrisome.

speaker: FISHER
text: As the Greenbook states and my sounding with CEOs confirms, there are as yet no appreciable, let alone debilitating, signs of spillover into the rest of the economy.

speaker: FISHER
text: The economy has been weakened.

speaker: FISHER
text: You see it in the rails and trucking and retail.

speaker: FISHER
text: It has not shown signs of succumbing as much as one might have expected to the full-blown virus that is afflicting housing.

speaker: FISHER
text: As Dave mentioned, going back to July, banks in our District and everywhere else have reported tightening terms and standards on loans to businesses and households.

speaker: FISHER
text: The overall sentiment or mood of the country, as reported by the press and the surveys, is sour.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet we haven’t seen sharp increases in initial claims, low PMI (purchasing managers index) readings, or sharply falling durable goods orders.

speaker: FISHER
text: Households are still reasonably optimistic about their job prospects.

speaker: FISHER
text: Consumer spending continues to grow, albeit at a slower pace.

speaker: FISHER
text: The CEO of Disney started his discussion with me this time by saying, “I hate to be the bearer of good news,” and went on to cite an internal survey they recently completed that shows that families plan to spend liberally on vacations, despite setbacks in presumed housing prices, as well as strong ad statistics for their broadcasting network.

speaker: FISHER
text: There remain widespread reports of labor shortages, not just in our District but also elsewhere.

speaker: FISHER
text: The bottom line, Mr. Chairman, is that, there is clearly a fat left tail on growth—the economy is growing slower.

speaker: FISHER
text: But the economy is growing at a positive pace.

speaker: FISHER
text: Some might say that it has slowed to a sustainable pace.

speaker: FISHER
text: In part, this is due to infrastructure investment, spending on nondefense capital goods that is better than expected, decent if not robust E&S demand, fiscal stimulus, and strong export performance that we talked about earlier, assisted by superior demand growth abroad, facilitated by a progressively weaker dollar.

speaker: FISHER
text: I note that we meet the day after the trade-weighted dollar celebrated a post–Bretton Woods low—not an easy thing for a strong dollar man to note.

speaker: FISHER
text: Certainly, there is a risk that downward economic momentum will emerge.

speaker: FISHER
text: I worry about the plight of the big, populous states like Florida and California under the crush of the housing implosion.

speaker: FISHER
text: I take note of the reports from UPS, the rails, and the truckers as to the deceleration in year-over-year trends in pre-holiday shipments.

speaker: FISHER
text: I realize that Wal-Mart same-store growth has slowed, that mall traffic is down, and so on.

speaker: FISHER
text: But not a single one of my thirty-five CEO interlocutors, except for the homebuilders, felt that the economy was at risk of falling off the table.

speaker: FISHER
text: Fluor and the other big builders—or logistics organizers, as I like to call them—report a booming domestic infrastructure business, especially in the petrochemical sector.

speaker: FISHER
