text: The technology folks, as manifested by the earnings reports of Microsoft, Apple, and others, continue to find that demand is brisk.

speaker: FISHER
text: Cisco’s CEO confirms that business with all but the financial institutions “has begun to flow again” after being laid low by the uncertainty of August.

speaker: FISHER
text: The airlines report volume conditions as “less bad” than they were in the third quarter.

speaker: FISHER
text: UPS’s CFO, about to become CEO, who serves on President Lockhart’s board, is concerned, like the rails, about consumer holiday demand, and notes that trans-Pacific shipments into the United States have slowed.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet when he digs deep into the data, he will tell you that the tech side looks good.

speaker: FISHER
text: So the net effect is that, while nowhere near robust, “domestically, conditions have not materially worsened.” Except for housing and Bill’s two law firms, we are not hearing of significant lagging of receivables or collectibles.

speaker: FISHER
text: Many of my interlocutors, however, worry about prices, as do our staff members in Dallas.

speaker: FISHER
text: We differ significantly, Mr. Chairman, from the central assumption of the Greenbook in our views on headline inflation looking forward.

speaker: FISHER
text: I noticed you cocking an eye in my direction, Brian, when you were talking about the outliers.

speaker: FISHER
text: The Greenbook has a 3 percent number for PCE inflation for this year, followed by a deceleration, to a pace of 1.8 percent in 2008 and 1.7 in 2009.

speaker: FISHER
text: We in Dallas are not as confident that we will continue to experience a disinflation of the momentum of the PCE.

speaker: FISHER
text: Partly this stems from concerns expressed anecdotally by big importers like Wal-Mart, who report stiffening Chinese prices, by the CEO of JCPenney, who is planning for cost increases of goods imported from China on the order of 3 to 4 percent next year, and by the users of pulp and recycled waste paper that are set to announce a 5 percent increase in essential paper products effective in February, having just announced a double-digit increase not too long ago.

speaker: FISHER
text: Our concern at the Dallas Fed stems from two more-pervasive sources than that anecdotal evidence I just cited, and those are food and energy, for which we anticipate a more pernicious pass-through effect from recent rapid price increases of underlying commodities.

speaker: FISHER
text: The concern we have for food is encapsulated in the eye-popping chart on page II-30 of Part 2 of the Greenbook.

speaker: FISHER
text: You have to have a hawk’s eye to see this chart from that end of the table, but it shows an incredible divergence between food prices and the core PCE.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now this pattern has a historical precedent.

speaker: FISHER
text: A spread of this magnitude between food prices and core indexes occurred on several occasions between 1951 and 1980.

speaker: FISHER
text: In 1973, the gap was 20 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: In 1974, the gap was closed when the CPI rose up accordingly.

speaker: FISHER
text: But we have not seen a gap of this nature in over a quarter-century.

speaker: FISHER
text: Wholesale food prices are up 6.3 percent for the year to date.

speaker: FISHER
text: Through September, the CPI for food is up 5.7 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: As mentioned by one of the previous interlocutors, milk and green grocery prices are rising at double-digit paces.

speaker: FISHER
text: This goes beyond ethanol, Mr. Chairman, as a driver of shifts in crop rotation and production.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is occurring against a ramping up of the caloric intake of a few billion new eaters in China, India, and elsewhere.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is hardly encouraging, and it injects a modicum of doubt in predicting a significant decline in PCE inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: We spoke about energy price dynamics earlier.

speaker: FISHER
text: They further cloud the picture.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you talk to Exxon or Independence, they will tell you that there is no problem in finding oil, in refining it, or in delivering the final product.

speaker: FISHER
text: They will, however, note that there are two key impulses at work.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, there is no evident slowdown in demand growth according to them— that is, domestically—and the appetite in the BRICs (Brazil, Russia, India, and China) and in the developing countries was described as voracious.

speaker: FISHER
text: An enormous amount of infrastructure in chemical plant capacity is being constructed everywhere, from the Gulf Coast of the United States to the Middle East to China and Singapore, in order to be nearer to either feedstock or growing final demand.

speaker: FISHER
text: Any analysis of the income elasticity of demand for oil in low but rising income nations like China and India points to demand for oil that will grow even faster than their slightly slower but still rapidly growing income levels.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, price pressures on crude at the margin are compounded by noncommercial activity, which we did not talk about earlier.

speaker: FISHER
text: Noncommercial contracts, the busywork of what are called “city refiners” in the industry—that is, the city of London and the financial exchanges—have of late been running at triple their traditional volume according to Exxon’s CEO, driving oil through $90.

speaker: FISHER
text: Thus far, gasoline and distillates, which is where the pass-through rubber hits the consumer price road, have been tame in response.

speaker: FISHER
text: Bill discussed the low crack spread, for example.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet our models at the Dallas Fed for retail gasoline prices envision increases above $3 a gallon next year if crude stays above $85, which we consider a reasonable probability.

speaker: FISHER
text: Similarly, price pressures for distillates are increasingly probable.

speaker: FISHER
text: Finally, while currently high inventories continue, it is noteworthy that natural gas prices have reversed their summer slide downward to $5.50 per million Btu and are now quoted at $7 at the Henry Hub.

speaker: FISHER
text: All this gives me, Mr. Chairman, a sense of discomfort, like that expressed by President Hoenig and President Plosser, on the headline inflation front and is a reminder that the balance of risk is not necessarily skewed only toward slower growth.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Are we permitted to question?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Richard, you described vividly the bunch of forces working on headline inflation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But since you identified yourself as a negative outlier on the inflation forecast, it seems to me your headline forecast is still for significant moderation in headline inflation in ’08.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Am I wrong in that?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: At least I infer from this that you’re not showing an acceleration in core PCE inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I am talking about a spread being maintained between the two, and I am concerned about it, depending on where we are going to go in terms of our communication exercise, which we will talk about tomorrow.

speaker: FISHER
text: But we don’t show as much relief on PCE inflation as the Greenbook indicates nor as the central tendency indicates, and I wanted to explain why.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Over the past week or so, we have been following the devastating fires in Southern California.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They have burned over 500,000 acres, destroyed nearly 2,000 homes, and inflicted seven deaths and sixty injuries.

speaker: YELLEN
text: These were large fires, even by California standards, but they were by no means the largest in recent memory; and, of course, the loss of life and economic costs pale compared with Katrina.

speaker: YELLEN
text: While the fires have seriously affected the lives of many individuals, they do not seem likely to show up in the macroeconomic data.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Turning to the national economy, developments since we met six years—six weeks ago—actually, it seems like just two weeks ago—[laughter] generally have been favorable and the risks to the outlook for growth have eased somewhat.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I think it is too early to say that we are out of the woods.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The inflation news has continued to be favorable, but some upside risks have become more prominent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to economic activity, we have raised our forecast for growth in both the third and the fourth quarters in response to incoming data, even though the pace of deterioration in the housing sector has been more severe than we expected and the problems associated with housing finance seem far from resolution.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We agree with Greenbook that residential investment is likely to continue its severe contraction for at least a few more quarters.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We also agree with Greenbook that the rest of the economy has held up reasonably well, at least so far.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Exports have been strong, and while business fixed investment seems to be slowing, it should still make a robust contribution to growth in the second half of this year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to consumer spending, most aggregate data suggest only a modest deceleration so far.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Such readings help to allay our concerns about potential spillovers from housing to consumption, but they don’t completely assuage them.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Survey measures of consumer confidence are down sharply since the financial turmoil began, and most indexes of house prices show outright declines.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the current state of the housing and mortgage markets, bigger declines going forward are a distinct possibility.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, the Case-Shiller futures data for house prices point to larger declines in the months ahead.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A sharp drop in house prices would likely crimp consumer spending over time through wealth and collateral effects.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Some of my directors and other contacts are also raising warning flags about consumer demand.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, the CEO of a large well-known high-end retailer said that the company’s sales are softening and that the company is having to work diligently to control inventories.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In his view, the consumer has pulled back.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The CEO of a Southern California bank observed a number of his clients talking about a drop in discretionary consumer purchases.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The bottom line is that consumption spending seems to be all right for the time being, but there is a real risk that households may cut back on spending more than expected in response to higher oil prices, a slower economy, and economic uncertainty.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I agree with President Rosengren’s assessment of financial markets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Strains appear to have eased a bit on balance since our September meeting, with interbank lending markets showing some improvement and spreads on asset-backed commercial paper declining.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But structured credits related to mortgages remain quite troublesome, and liquidity conditions and Treasury bill markets are still at times strained.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My impression is that, despite having moved in a positive direction over the past six weeks, these markets remain vulnerable to shocks, and so the economy remains at risk from further financial disruptions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Both survey evidence and anecdotal evidence have confirmed that banks are tightening lending standards across the board.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Tighter terms and conditions are being applied to a range of business lending, including commercial real estate, and on most household lending from prime and nonprime mortgages to auto and home equity loans.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The main financial variables that are commonly included in formal macroeconometric models appear to have changed since the onset of the financial shock—say, in late June—in ways that should have roughly offsetting effects.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Oil prices are markedly higher, which should restrain consumer spending, and the stock market is roughly unchanged since June in spite of the financial turmoil.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A weaker dollar should have a positive influence on growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Mortgages rates on jumbo loans and the rates facing the riskiest corporate borrowers are higher, but many private borrowing rates are down because of the decline in Treasury yields.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, the current levels of Treasury yields, as well as the stock market and dollar, reflect at least in part the market’s expectation that the Committee will ease the stance of monetary policy at this meeting.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Underlying our forecast is the policy assumption that the Committee will cut the funds rate another 25 basis points at this meeting.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In assessing the appropriate path of the stance of policy, I took a number of considerations into account.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, core consumer inflation currently is at a level that I consider consistent with price stability.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Second, unemployment is very near my best estimate of the full employment rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In the context of a Taylor-type rule, these considerations imply that the real funds rate should be near its neutral level.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In fact, any version of the Taylor rule you prefer, with whatever rates you want to put on inflation versus the gap, will give you the same recommendation because all the terms are zero and drop out, except for one—the equilibrium real rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, we cannot know the level of the real equilibrium rate with certainty.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Defined in terms of the PCE price index, our best estimate is in the range of 2 to 2½ percent, which is well below the current real rate of about 3 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would like to highlight two additional points here.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, the actual real rate has been boosted over the past six months or so by declines in short-term inflation expectations, whether one measures them by lagged inflation, by surveys of expected inflation over the next year or so, or by forecasts of inflation including the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Second, one important aspect of the financial turmoil is that it probably represents in part a movement toward a more reasonable pricing of risk, as seen in the rise in risk spreads.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This development tends to push the equilibrium real funds rate down toward the lower portion of the range I just cited.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The bottom line is that in my view, even without the contractionary effects of recent financial developments, an appropriate stance of monetary policy would involve further declines in the fed funds rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have assumed that the funds rate drops to 4½ percent by the end of this year and to 4¼ by the end of next year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My assumed path ends in the same place and embodies the same medium-term assumption concerning neutral as FRB/US, on which the extended Greenbook forecast relies.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The only difference concerns timing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We assume a more rapid path to the long run than the Greenbook does.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Our forecast shows real GDP growth gradually picking up to around 2½ percent, our estimate of potential, by the end of next year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, given that the financial shock is not yet resolved, I think the downside risks to this forecast predominate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With regard to inflation, I expect core PCE inflation to remain around 1¾ percent over the next several years.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The probable appearance of a small amount of labor market slack is likely to help hold down inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition, I expect that, with inflation remaining below 2 percent, inflation expectations will edge down as well, reinforcing our success.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I hope that this result will be aided by the release of our extended forecasts and the greater awareness of where we would like to see inflation settle down.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I see the risk to my inflation forecast as moderate and mainly to the upside in view of recent increases in oil and food prices, declines in the dollar, and a slower rate of structural productivity growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So, in summary, I think the most likely outcome is that the economy will move forward toward a soft landing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I see downside risks to economic activity and some upside risks to inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But in view of continuing questions about the effects of the financial market shock, I am more concerned about the activity side of things right now.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like many others around the table, my report to this Committee in September indicated a sharp deterioration in business confidence.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My business contacts were concerned about what may happen.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: During the intermeeting period I heard less about what may happen and more about what is actually happening.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My contacts who are linked to residential real estate have seen a further and, in some cases, sharp drop-off in business activity.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My banking supervision and regulation staff told me just a few days ago that they’re now seeing a sudden and sizable percentage increase in nonperforming loans at a number of large banking companies in my District.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: To be sure, nonperforming loans had been at extremely low levels, and most of the sharp rise can be traced to mortgage and construction development lending.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But I’m now beginning to hear reports that bankers are experiencing some loan performance problems outside their real estate portfolio.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The CEO of a large, major bank in my District has also reported difficulty in securitizing the student loans that they’re making, forcing them to keep those loans on their books and to make adjustments elsewhere in their balance sheets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: To what extent these banking conditions are affecting overall bank lending is not obvious, but clearly there has been some disruption to the channels of intermediation, and I am now beginning to hear reports of some spillover to other sectors of the economy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: A growing number of retailers tell me that they have seen a noticeable decline in spending since mid-September in items ranging from autos to apparel.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: While my reports from the business community reflect a falloff in business conditions from what we submitted to the Beige Book just a few weeks ago, they don’t necessarily indicate a significant deviation from the slowdown that was already built into the economic projections that I submitted in September.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In preparing for this meeting, I found it difficult to judge whether the reports of weakness that I am hearing represent an unfolding of the September projection or additional deterioration in the outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In the end, I have only minor differences with the Greenbook projection in the near term and, like the Greenbook, made only minor revisions to my forecast.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I see economic activity a bit softer than the Greenbook for the remainder of 2007, but I project slightly better growth in 2008.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like the Greenbook, I have assumed an unchanged path for the fed funds rate over the forecast period.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The recent rise in oil prices has caused me to push up my near-term PCE projection, but inflation expectation projections remain anchored around 2 percent.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I see a small upside risk to the near-term inflation projection as a result of the continuing dollar depreciation; but on the whole, I continue to judge our inflation risks as reasonably balanced.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I would like to conclude by echoing the sentiments of others around the table.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Considerable strains in the financial sector remain, and further turmoil in markets is a distinct possibility.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think that, in this environment, households and businesses can easily be spooked—excuse the Halloween pun—and I don’t think it would take much additional tightness in credit markets to push my fragile near-term growth outlook even lower.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So this concern continues to be the predominant risk to my outlook.

speaker: LACKER
text: Conditions in the Fifth District’s housing sector continue to deteriorate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Sales have weakened further across most areas, and starts have pulled back sharply.

speaker: LACKER
text: Inventories are rising in part, we hear, because some residential investors have run short on patience and are listing their properties.

speaker: LACKER
text: The housing correction has been particularly acute on the outer edges of the Washington, D.C., metro area, and contacts from the area anticipate that additional slowing in more-central markets is likely.

speaker: LACKER
text: In addition, reports of home-price reductions are becoming more common around my District.

speaker: LACKER
text: Until recently the weakness looked to be mostly contained in housing, but spillovers into other sectors are beginning to appear.

speaker: LACKER
text: For example, our survey of the Fifth District manufacturing sector—which, by the way, is larger than the Philadelphia and New York manufacturing sectors combined—[laughter]

speaker: LACKER
text: —and we don’t appear in Part 2 of the Greenbook—posted notably weaker readings for October.

speaker: LACKER
text: Drilling down into the details, much of the softness can be traced to housing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We can’t help it if you have no predictive content.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Chair is calling for order.

speaker: LACKER
text: Conditioning on the Philadelphia index, we actually have marginal predictive value for the national ISMs.

speaker: LACKER
text: A modest housing spillover into business investment plans seems to be unfolding as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the recent Board-commissioned survey of capital investment plans, our District was among those in which more businesses plan to trim rather than boost spending in the months ahead.

speaker: LACKER
text: Again, a more detailed look reveals that most firms planning reductions have ties to housing.

speaker: LACKER
text: Reports on retail sales in the District remain soft, with sales of automobiles and building materials notably weak.

speaker: LACKER
text: In addition, an executive from a major transportation firm headquartered in the District told us that freight volumes, both rail and trucking, are now at the lowest level since the 2001 recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: Although in a number of District markets commercial real estate activity remains healthy, we are hearing scattered reports of commercial construction projects being shelved.

speaker: LACKER
text: One director from D.C. said that commercial development there “doesn’t have the pulse it had six weeks ago.” The turmoil in financial markets has not appreciably constrained business lending in our District, however.

speaker: LACKER
text: Contacts generally describe credit as readily available to creditworthy borrowers, but some say spreads have widened a bit.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the price front, our monthly measures suggest some moderation in growth despite ongoing complaints of higher input costs.

speaker: LACKER
text: At our last meeting, I was more optimistic than the Greenbook on the national economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: A significant part of the difference was related to housing, where I saw greater probability of the drag receding sooner.

speaker: LACKER
text: Longer term, I had a somewhat higher estimate of trend productivity growth, which supported a somewhat stronger outlook for household consumption.

speaker: LACKER
text: The main shift in my perspective since the last meeting is that I am now at least as pessimistic as the Greenbook about prospects for housing bottoming out anytime soon.

speaker: LACKER
text: The 10 percent fall in housing starts in September was certainly eye catching, and it indicates that the weak summer housing market tailed off further toward the end.

speaker: LACKER
text: In our District, and this seems to be true elsewhere as well, the housing downturn appears to have spread into many formerly unaffected markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is hard for me to believe that any discernible stabilization is likely before the spring, when the seasonal pickup in housing activity typically takes place.

speaker: LACKER
text: Even then a prolonged period of depressed activity seems more likely than any noticeable bounceback.

speaker: LACKER
text: Other recent news suggests a bit more demand-side fallout from the housing market than I had been expecting.

speaker: LACKER
text: Manufacturing production was sluggish in August and September, and durable goods orders have shown only modest growth, especially outside the aircraft industry.

speaker: LACKER
text: I mentioned a minute ago that our survey of the Fifth District manufacturing sector—which, by the way, is larger than the Philadelphia and New York manufacturing sector—[laughter] is showing a significant slowdown for October, particularly in housing-related industries.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consumer spending has been a source of stability during this housing correction, and I expect that to remain true over the forecast period.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think household spending will generally expand in line with disposable income, but even though consumption advanced broadly in the third quarter, it now seems we’re in for a bit of a slowdown this quarter.

speaker: LACKER
text: In that regard, I’m feeling sympathy for what President Yellen said.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’m less sanguine overall about the near-term outlook for growth at this meeting, although that may just represent catching up on my part to the Greenbook’s past level of gloominess.

speaker: LACKER
text: Having said all that, I do believe that the effects of this summer’s financial market adjustments are likely to be limited; and out beyond the middle of the next year, I’m, again, more optimistic than the Greenbook and for the usual reasons.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that productivity growth and, thus, real income growth will be somewhat higher than in the Greenbook forecast, and my outlook for the personal saving rate is centered on its current value rather than a steady increase.

speaker: LACKER
text: Inflation appears to have ticked up a bit in September, at least according to the CPI.

speaker: LACKER
text: Still, year-over-year core PCE inflation remained reasonably contained, and I’ve been struck by the extent to which TIPS inflation compensation has held relatively steady in recent months, especially given our easing move last month and the run-up in oil prices.

speaker: LACKER
text: While I would like to see inflation come down further, I’m somewhat more comfortable about inflation than I was at the beginning of the year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I have noted in the past, the industrial mix in the Sixth District looks a lot like the country as a whole.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The regional data and anecdotal information show that, although the Sixth District economy is still expanding, the pace is marginally weaker than it was in September.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In earlier meetings I commented on the severity of the housing situation in the District.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There is no improvement in sight for the housing market, and there are signs that the sharp decline in residential construction is spilling over into nonresidential real estate segments, such as shopping center development.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Employment growth is softening as well.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Although the largest negative effects are in construction-related sectors, the slowdown in job growth appears to be fairly broad based.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The broad contour of our national forecast is similar to the Greenbook baseline.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Like the Greenbook, our forecast includes a slowing in business investment.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Based on our survey of District business contacts, it appears that the low levels of expected capital expenditure are due mainly to pessimism about the pace of economic activity rather than restrictive credit conditions per se.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Specifically, financial market turbulence does not appear to have directly affected economic activity, but it has created a greater uncertainty about the outlook for the economy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As a consequence, the majority of my directors and business contacts are reporting very little in the way of plans to increase capital expenditures in the coming year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Where business investment is discretionary, most respondents report a wait-and-see posture.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: More positively, the weaker dollar does appear to be having a positive effect on exports from the region.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: For the year to date, the dollar value of exports through the Sixth District ports was up 35 percent through August, whereas import growth was only 21 percent.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Not coincidentally, the majority of businesses that indicated they were increasing capital expenditures over the coming months were exporters.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the run-up to this FOMC meeting, I again made calls to a few financial market participants, and they reflected a range of institutional and market perspectives.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A synthesis of this opinion is consistent with the views that were expressed earlier by Bill Dudley and others.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There’s a widespread view that persistent volatility in credit markets is bound to negatively affect the general economy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Credit market conditions have improved somewhat, but stability may be a long way off.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A second wave of volatility may accompany incoming details regarding mortgage delinquencies caused by rate resets in 2008, and there’s a suspicion that third-quarter writedowns may be followed by substantial further losses recognized at year-end.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Also, as referenced in the Bluebook, there is skepticism about the M-LEC (master liquidity enhancement conduit) proposal from several angles.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In summary, our soundings of the economy, informed by formal modeling work, point to a continued slowing of the economy that will likely persist well into next year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Anecdotally, credit constraints outside the housing sector do not appear to be a major factor at this stage.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But uncertainty created by financial market turbulence does seem to be acting as a constraint, and I believe that the heightened uncertainty regarding the economic outlook for 2008 warrants consideration of insurance against this downside risk.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: With respect to the outlook for inflation, I agree with the view expressed by others that recent developments in energy prices, if they persist, make it likely that we are about to enter another period in which headline numbers substantially exceed the trends suggested by core measures.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Because of this, I feel it’s appropriate to characterize inflation risk as having increased.

speaker: EVANS
text: The Seventh District economy appears to be expanding at a moderate rate, similar to what I reported at our last meeting.

speaker: EVANS
text: As we talked with business contacts, we heard mixed reviews regarding activity across different sectors of the economy.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the downside, everyone in the construction industry, from builders to suppliers, had grim assessments, and our contacts with the Detroit Three characterize the vehicle market as mediocre.

speaker: EVANS
text: Another negative is on the labor front.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our contact at Manpower reported that demand for temporary workers was down a lot.

speaker: EVANS
text: He said that the current market felt almost as it did in 2001.

speaker: EVANS
text: Kelly’s assessment was not quite so negative, although they did say that some indicators were flashing yellow.

speaker: EVANS
text: Of course, the BLS has been showing declines in temp help employment since early 2006, and most other indicators point to a healthy labor market.

speaker: EVANS
text: Indeed, we continue to hear about firms trying to cope with shortages of skilled workers.

speaker: EVANS
text: For instance, a couple of heavy- equipment manufacturers based in Illinois said that they were recruiting engineers from the Detroit area.

speaker: EVANS
text: There were other upbeat reports on activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: United Airlines said that all their markets were quite good, apparently better than President Fisher was reporting earlier.

speaker: EVANS
text: They noted the bookings for business travel, which can be an indicator of business’s more general willingness to spend, remained strong in October and November.

speaker: EVANS
text: International bookings also were extremely good.

speaker: EVANS
text: We heard numerous reports of strong export demand—for example, for machine tool manufacturers and heavy-equipment producers.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to the financial situation, I continue to hear that there is a disconnect between Wall Street and Main Street.

speaker: EVANS
text: Importantly, except for construction, our contacts do not see nonfinancial firms being constrained by a lack of access to credit or by the pricing of credit.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning to the macroeconomy, the news on economic activity that we’ve received over the past six weeks has been better than the downside scenario that we feared.

speaker: EVANS
text: Indeed, it has been better than what we had assumed in our baseline forecast in September.

speaker: EVANS
text: Like the Greenbook, we have raised our outlook for growth in the second half of 2007 about ½ percentage point.

speaker: EVANS
text: Residential investment does look a bit worse than we thought, but consumption came in a good deal stronger than we had expected.

speaker: EVANS
text: Also, the incoming news about labor markets, including the revisions to employment in August, points to continued support to household spending from growth in jobs and income.

speaker: EVANS
text: Unlike the Greenbook, we marked up the outlook for activity a bit in 2008 and 2009.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our current projection sees growth recovering to a little above potential in the second half of next year and in 2009.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to inflation, the incoming price data have been positive, and we have revised down our forecast for inflation a bit, to about 1¾ percent in 2008 and 2009.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think the risks to this forecast are two-sided.

speaker: EVANS
text: Some of our statistical models translate the incoming data into quite low forecasts for inflation in 2009 and 2010 if you take them at face value.

speaker: EVANS
text: But higher costs for energy and other materials, the weaker dollar, and potential pressures from resource utilization still pose some risk that inflation will come in higher than we currently are forecasting.

speaker: EVANS
text: For me, the positive inflation developments are an important ingredient allowing us to focus on risk management.

speaker: EVANS
text: Since risk-management considerations have played a key role in our policy decisions, it is important to think about how the risks to the forecast have changed since September.

speaker: EVANS
text: Last time and today, Dave Stockton cited several downside risks to watch for: an intensified fallout from the problems in mortgage finance onto housing demand; a substantial drop in consumer sentiment; and a spillover from financial market disruptions to business spending.

speaker: EVANS
text: These high-cost scenarios are possible, but I think their likelihood is smaller than they were in September.

speaker: EVANS
text: We have been pessimistic on housing for a while, and for once, despite Dave Stockton’s warning, I am encouraged that the Greenbook’s forecast for 2008 has not been marked down materially.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is a small comfort, but just a bit.

speaker: EVANS
text: The economy outside of housing seems to have entered the fourth quarter with more momentum than we had thought it would.

speaker: EVANS
text: Importantly, consumption growth has been solid even though there has been another downtick in sentiment.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the financial front, the Greenbook points to the special Beige Book capital spending questions and to the senior loan officer survey as signals that we could expect more spillovers to nonfinancial activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: Tighter standards for C&I loans are definitely news, but they are hardly surprising.

speaker: EVANS
text: The real news will be next quarter.

speaker: EVANS
text: Looking at previous surveys, we had one bad quarter in 1998, and then it came down, and then the later tightening was part of the increase in the fed funds rate.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I think that the next quarter will be very informative and important.

speaker: EVANS
text: In assessing how risks have changed, these surveys need to be balanced against the improvements we have seen in credit markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: While I continue to be concerned about collateral damage from the credit markets to real activity, I still think the problems in financial markets are likely to remain largely walled off from the nonfinancial economy.

speaker: EVANS
text: So on balance, the economic outlook has improved, and the risks of financial contagion have diminished somewhat since September, although they haven’t disappeared.

speaker: STERN
text: There really have not been any significant changes in economic conditions or trends in the District.

speaker: STERN
text: The special survey we did on financial conditions and whether the changes there had affected capital spending plans suggested that plans, at least for firms in our District, were largely unaffected.

speaker: STERN
text: Contacts with insight into the shipping industry do report that exports are very strong, stronger than at least they had anticipated.

speaker: STERN
text: That, of course, is consistent with what we have been seeing in some of the aggregate data.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as the national economy is concerned, I agree with the Greenbook’s assessment of the incoming information that we received since the last Committee meeting.

speaker: STERN
text: I won’t rehash it here, except to say that the surprises have been positive, a bit on the upside, and I think we still—at least at the aggregate level—haven’t seen generalized spillovers from the contraction in housing activity or prices on overall economic activity.

speaker: STERN
text: I also agree with the Greenbook’s assessment of the outlook for the economy for the next two or three quarters.

speaker: STERN
text: I think growth is likely to be subdued as a consequence of the changes in financial conditions that we’ve seen.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as prices are concerned, core inflation seems to me to be relatively well contained at least on a year-over-year basis, and I expect that performance to be maintained as long as we pursue appropriate policy.

speaker: STERN
text: Looking at the overall economic outlook beyond the next two or three quarters, I think there is a reasonable chance, given recent developments and recent actions, that by the middle of next year, say, we’ll be looking at real economic growth of something close to what the economy has averaged over the past six years—that is, the period 2002 through 2007.

speaker: STERN
text: This is a bit more favorable, a bit higher, than the Greenbook outlook, and as best I can judge, the Greenbook is more conservative than I am about the nonconsumption, nonresidential investment components of aggregate demand.

speaker: STERN
text: Put another way, those components add a bit less to aggregate demand in the Greenbook than I would expect.

speaker: STERN
text: But my real point is that I don’t think it is a great stretch to see pretty respectable growth by the middle of next year.

speaker: STERN
text: My reading of the projections package that was briefly discussed earlier suggests to me that at least some have the same view.

speaker: STERN
text: Of course, that improvement could occur even sooner given the uncertainty associated with forecasting short-term perturbations in the economy.

speaker: POOLE
text: I want to concentrate on the outlook for the nonhousing part.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think the housing sector is obviously in miserable condition, and the issue as to where that’s going to go really depends on how much of it spreads to other parts of the economy.

speaker: POOLE
text: Now, I have a contact with a large software firm, and the headline there is that things are going great—in fact, going gangbusters, I would say.

speaker: POOLE
text: Computer hardware sales nationally are running at 14 to 16 percent above last year, about 3 percentage points above expectation.

speaker: POOLE
text: Business IT growth is around 12 percent.

speaker: POOLE
text: Computer gaming software is strong.

speaker: POOLE
text: Just overall a very bullish outlook there.

speaker: POOLE
text: Capital expenditures at this company are up about 35 percent this fiscal year over last fiscal year and are expected to be up another 15 percent in fiscal 2009.

speaker: POOLE
text: So the outlook is uniformly very, very strong.

speaker: POOLE
text: The company says it is behind in hiring and has lots of unfilled positions partly as a consequence of turnover.

speaker: POOLE
text: Now, all the other contacts were pretty downbeat.

speaker: POOLE
text: UPS is expecting a peak season that is milder than in the previous years; my contact believes that the economy is not going into a negative but is clearly slowing down.

speaker: POOLE
text: The company is leasing eleven fewer aircraft this year.

speaker: POOLE
text: To meet the peak, they always lease extra planes for shipping.

speaker: POOLE
text: They are probably holding about steady on capital outlays.

speaker: POOLE
text: My contact at FedEx says that the outlook is very soft, not much buildup toward the holiday peak.

speaker: POOLE
text: The retailers that they talked to are anticipating a softer season, not an absolute decline, but slow growth.

speaker: POOLE
text: International business remains very strong.

speaker: POOLE
text: This company is reducing capital expenditures by 10 percent from its previous expectation.

speaker: POOLE
text: My contact in a major company in the trucking industry says that we are in a recession, the worst he has seen in twenty to forty years.

speaker: POOLE
text: The company is reducing its fleet size by 10 percent, is cutting capital spending quite substantially, and has no good news.

speaker: POOLE
text: A contact with a major money center bank said that the bank’s analysis of credit card usage indicates that sales have been flat in some areas and are declining in others.

speaker: POOLE
text: Credit card usage for department store and catalogue sales has been declining.

speaker: POOLE
text: In an e-mail I received after that conversation, my contact painted a weaker picture than had been discussed the previous day.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think that there are other comments around the table suggesting that the anecdotal reports are a bit on the weak side.

speaker: POOLE
text: Now, to me there is a puzzle in the market’s assessment of the outcome of this meeting.

speaker: POOLE
text: The market has essentially bid in a probability of 1.0 of either a 25 or a 50 basis point cut.

speaker: POOLE
text: If I were simply following the flow of news, the general flow of news putting housing aside has been okay, maybe a little stronger than expected, and following this fed funds futures market for a long time, it does respond to the current information.

speaker: POOLE
text: The flow of data clearly moves that market, and if that were all that were driving the market, I guess I would have anticipated a 50-50 split between no change in the fed funds target and down 25 basis points.

speaker: POOLE
text: So why has the market bid in such a high probability of a cut at this time?

speaker: POOLE
text: I’ll offer a hypothesis, which is that a number of people who are players in this market, like my contact at a large bank, are looking at news and saying that the proprietary inside information they have on what’s going on leads them to believe that the overall economy has a soft tone to it that is not yet showing up in the data that we follow.

speaker: POOLE
text: I’m throwing out that hypothesis.

speaker: POOLE
text: I don’t know what other hypothesis to offer, but it does seem to be a reasonable one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have been extraordinarily efficient today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a coffee break and come back at 4:30?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just want to start by saying in defense of the Empire State that there is no way—the only way that Richmond could be bigger than New York and Philadelphia is if you don’t count the substantial business we have in the manufacturing of financial products.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s a lot smaller business than it used to be.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As the Chairman said at the Economic Club of New York, it is likely to emerge stronger.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the outlook looks about the way it did in September.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just a few quick points.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Financial market conditions are substantially better than during the peak of the panic in mid-August; but the improvement, as many of you said, is still quite limited and uneven.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Sentiment is still quite fragile, and I think we still seem likely to face a protracted period of adjustment ahead as the markets work through the substantial array of challenges remaining.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Growth in the United States and in the world economy in my view seems likely to slow— more here, of course, than elsewhere.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Here, even though the nonhousing, non-auto parts of the U.S. economy don’t yet show significant evidence of a considerable slowdown of actual or expected demand, I think that still seems likely.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In our central scenario, though, housing construction weakens further.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Housing demand slows further because of the tightening of credit conditions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Consumer spending slows a bit, and businesses react by scaling back growth in hiring and investment, and this produces several quarters of growth modestly below trend.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that growth outside the United States is likely to slow a bit.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It will slow toward potential, if not all the way to potential, in those economies that have been growing above potential.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Although the world is larger in relative terms and somewhat less vulnerable to a U.S. slowdown than it once was, it seems to me very unlikely that domestic demand in the rest of the world will accelerate as domestic demand slows in the United States.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So the risks to this outlook for U.S. growth still seem to lie to the downside.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The magnitude of the downside risks may be slightly less than in September, but they remain substantial.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the main source of this downside risk to growth is the interaction between expectations of recession probability and the credit market dynamics.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As the outlook for housing deteriorates and the recession probability stays elevated, financial institutions and investors stay cautious.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That caution, in turn, slows the pace of recovery in markets—in asset-backed, securitization, and structured-credit markets—and in credit growth more broadly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As expectations adjust to anticipate a longer, more-substantial period of impairment in markets, then recession probability at least potentially increases.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that the underlying inflation numbers and the measures we use to capture underlying inflation do not suggest any meaningful acceleration in underlying inflation, and we still expect the core PCE to run at a rate below 2 percent over the forecast period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In some ways, though, the inflation outlook now feels a bit worse.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It feels worse because of the modest rise in breakevens that we saw following our last meeting and because of sentiment in markets around gold, commodity and energy prices, and the dollar.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The fact that breakevens at long horizons have risen or failed to fall as monetary policy expectations have shifted down is not the most comforting pattern out there.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I think we need to be very careful not to encourage any sense in markets that we’re indifferent to those potential risks.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Having said that, I think the risks to that inflation forecast are roughly balanced.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The range of tools we have for measuring equilibrium combined with what you see in financial market expectations suggests that monetary policy, to assess the real short-term interest rate, is at or above most estimates of neutral and, therefore, is still exerting some modest restraint on growth.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The expectations now built into markets imply too much easing over the next eighteen months, more than I think we’re likely to have to do.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think the appropriate path of monetary policy lies under the Greenbook’s assumption.

speaker: KOHN
text: In broad outline, the situation is evolving as we anticipated in our last meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: Spending outside of housing has been well maintained.

speaker: KOHN
text: The housing market is very weak.

speaker: KOHN
text: Financial markets have been returning more toward normal functioning, banks have tightened credit terms and standards, and core inflation has remained low.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it is the nuances around each of these that complicate our decision at this meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: As Dave Stockton and others pointed out, spending outside housing has been a bit stronger than expected.

speaker: KOHN
text: Paths of consumption and investment, along with employment, seem to be moderating going into the fourth quarter, but gradually.

speaker: KOHN
text: Importantly, the data for September haven’t been especially weak, and these could have potentially been affected by the financial tightening, increased uncertainty, and reduced consumer confidence that followed the events of August.

speaker: KOHN
text: With growth in the third quarter likely to be at or above 3 percent and no material change in the output gap for several quarters now, it does appear that the real funds rate of 3 percent plus that persisted since mid-2006, while quite high relative to historical averages, was not far from the equilibrium real rate at that time, given the low level of long-term rates, the ready availability of credit at historically low spreads, and the high level of wealth relative to income through this period.

speaker: KOHN
text: It seems somewhere between difficult and impossible to calibrate the effects on aggregate demand of the rise in long-term rates last spring, the tightening of credit conditions of the past few months, and the expected decline in housing prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: The staff has judged 50 basis points of easing—we did that at the last meeting—to be enough to keep the economy near its potential in the context of the relatively solid incoming data.

speaker: KOHN
text: That doesn’t seem unreasonable, though it does leave the fed funds rate at the higher end of its historical range.

speaker: KOHN
text: Nonetheless, I see a couple of reasons for important downside risks to such a growth forecast.

speaker: KOHN
text: First, though the housing market was roughly in line with staff forecasts, builders have made only a little progress in reducing inventory overhangs.

speaker: KOHN
text: Moreover, reports suggest that downward price pressures are increasing—for example, the constant quality new home index declined in the past two quarters.

speaker: KOHN
text: Market expectations for the Case-Shiller index revised down, suggesting that the drop in house prices could be steeper than the moderate drop assumed in the staff forecast.

speaker: KOHN
text: Substantial decreases in house prices would at some point revive the demand for housing.

speaker: KOHN
text: At the same time, that decline threatens greater spillovers from wealth effects on consumption and from tighter credit conditions as lenders react to threats to their capital from declining collateral values.

speaker: KOHN
text: Second, although financial markets are improving in many respects, the trajectory is gradual, uneven, and subject to reversal.

speaker: KOHN
text: We saw this just in the past couple of weeks, when adverse housing data, downgrades of highly rated mortgages and senior tranches, and earnings warnings caused some risk spreads to widen out.

speaker: KOHN
text: The secondary markets for nonconforming mortgages are still quite disrupted.

speaker: KOHN
text: Clearly, uncertainty about the pricing of many of the assets in question, about the amount of credit that will get put back to the bank balance sheets, and about the size and location of the losses that have to be taken continue to make lenders very skittish.

speaker: KOHN
text: In this environment, I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see a further tightening of credit availability at banks in the coming months.

speaker: KOHN
text: The developments in housing and financial markets are also likely to weigh on business spending plans, as we saw hinted at in the capital spending revisions that some of the Reserve Banks reported, and for households as evidenced by the low confidence surveys.

speaker: KOHN
text: These downside risks are strong enough that I think they will persist even if we ease slightly tomorrow.

speaker: KOHN
text: Besides the influences I already cited, my judgment in this regard takes account of market expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: The markets’ implied r* has been below the staff’s and, I think, the Committee’s implied r* for some time now, but the gap seems to have widened considerably.

speaker: KOHN
text: In an environment of increased uncertainty about the outlook, such disparities perhaps aren’t surprising, and we can’t substitute market participants’ judgment for our own, but I did take a little signal from the extent of the pessimism about aggregate demand that I inferred from the interest rate path in the market relative to the staff’s path in the Greenbook.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think r* is quite as low as President Yellen was suggesting—it is perhaps in the 2 to 2½ range since term premiums are still low; and even with house prices declining, the wealth-to-income ratios are still pretty high, and the dollar has been falling.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I did assume a slight easing of monetary policy sometime in the fourth quarter in my projection.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also projected low, stable core and ultimately total inflation, but I do see some upside risks around this outcome if the economy follows its most likely path.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is still producing at a high level of resource utilization, and some measures of compensation and labor costs have been rising.

speaker: KOHN
text: Core CPI inflation on three-month and six-month bases has accelerated even if the acceleration hasn’t shown through to the PCE measures.

speaker: KOHN
text: Increases in energy and commodity prices, along with recent declines of the dollar, are also a risk factor—less from their direct effects on prices, which are likely to be small, but more because they could suggest a potential for a more inflationary psychology that could feed through to expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: Our decision tomorrow will involve weighing these risks, the extent of the relative risk to our dual objectives, and the potential costs of missing in either direction in the context of the market conditions and expectations built into markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: I thought I’d just talk about four subjects today: first, spend a few more moments on the capital market conditions, which Bill did a great job of summarizing; second, talk about financial intermediaries; and third and fourth, talk briefly about implications for growth and inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of the capital markets, I think it is important that we judge their state today not from where they might have been two weeks ago or from where they might have gotten ahead of underlying reality—if you look at credit spreads and equities—but from where they were before we last met or from where they were in the darkest days of August.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think these markets are at the very high end of what are reasonable expectations for improvement.

speaker: WARSH
text: As Governor Kohn suggests, it doesn’t mean that they can’t reverse themselves.

speaker: WARSH
text: It certainly doesn’t mean that they are solid—plenty of fragility is there.

speaker: WARSH
text: But all things considered, as a function of both time and Fed policy, there is, indeed, better sentiment; bid-asked spreads have narrowed; price discovery is at work; and differentiation and tiering are very real.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’d highlight a few markets that have gone into the category of being on more solid ground.

speaker: WARSH
text: Bill referred to the interbank funding markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: The multiseller bank-sponsored conduit is performing well.

speaker: WARSH
text: Prime auto finance paper has gone through quite a volatile period in the past couple of months but has now found its way to the good side, where I think those markets are increasingly open.

speaker: WARSH
text: High-quality paper is increasingly being received on terms that don’t look dramatically different from the way they would have looked before August.

speaker: WARSH
text: Another example is credit card receivables.

speaker: WARSH
text: Of course, as many others around this table have pointed out, there is no panacea.

speaker: WARSH
text: Serious problems remain in some asset markets, particularly housing and certain parts of structured finance.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I note that might be for good reason.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’d hesitate to call this poor market functioning.

speaker: WARSH
text: By and large, it may be that some investors don’t like the outcomes, but as the asset-backed commercial paper markets have separated the haves from the have-nots and the have-nots are without bank sponsorship and have poorer quality assets and poorer disclosure, they are having a hard time finding and securing bids.

speaker: WARSH
text: Another example might be some large financial institutions that are rolling over more of their funding on a shorter-term basis than they desire.

speaker: WARSH
text: There may be good reasons for that, and as we think about our policy tools tomorrow, we shouldn’t try to come to the rescue with any fixes for institutions that may not have been managed well or, at least, may not have had a capital structure that fit the risks.

speaker: WARSH
text: There are a couple of other indicators of continued concern.

speaker: WARSH
text: Obviously, the Treasury bill market has been quite volatile and is a pretty good reminder to us that these markets are not back to anything that we’d even want to consider normal.

speaker: WARSH
text: Another indicator that I look to in evaluating whether the capital markets are coming back to some normalcy is the percentage of cash holdings in money market mutual funds.

speaker: WARSH
text: In the pre-July period, money market mutual funds, particularly those that hold these prime-plus securities, would hold 5 to 10 percent of their assets in cash.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the darkest day in August, that was up to 45 percent.

speaker: WARSH
text: By and large, my sense is that the average now is something in the mid-20s.

speaker: WARSH
text: That suggests that there might be requests for redemptions and liquidations for which they need to keep cash available, but they are feeling a little better about their prospects and about some of the paper that they’re holding.

speaker: WARSH
text: On balance, I’d say it’s pretty easy for us to sit here and judge improvement.

speaker: WARSH
text: It’s a lot harder for us to judge success.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think President Plosser talked about the normalization in these markets, and we must hesitate to think that the markets before their August turmoil were normal.

speaker: WARSH
text: Risk premiums were abnormally low, and access to credit perhaps unusually easy.

speaker: WARSH
text: So in judging the success of time in our policy prescriptions, I think we’re having a hard time—at least I’m having a hard time—figuring out what are the new steady-state outcomes that are trying to be achieved.

speaker: WARSH
text: These markets appear delicately balanced between fear and greed.

speaker: WARSH
text: One example of greed, as we discussed in previous meetings, is some of the pay-in-kind, or PIK, securities with toggle features in the high-yield market.

speaker: WARSH
text: One of them was priced just last week between 97 and 98.

speaker: WARSH
text: So some of these corporate credits may well have improved in the eyes of the market beyond what we think might be sustainable.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the other side is fear.

speaker: WARSH
text: A new paradigm is trying to take root in the markets, but the risk of reversal remains very real.

speaker: WARSH
text: The marks on many leveraged loans look good.

speaker: WARSH
text: But if you judge the financial institutions that hold this paper, they are rushing to get the paper to market as soon as they possibly can, perhaps with a view that the corporate credit conditions won’t hold at these levels.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, let me talk briefly about financial intermediaries.

speaker: WARSH
text: As we discussed before, after the tumult in mid-August, many of them retrenched.

speaker: WARSH
text: Then many of them tried to re-liquefy.

speaker: WARSH
text: At that time they were trying to revalue their securities.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now they are probably somewhere in the process of revaluation, review, and refinement.

speaker: WARSH
text: Some of them, after the earnings announcements of the past couple of weeks, might be going back to step 1 and trying to understand what the risks are and what their liabilities are.

speaker: WARSH
text: Some of the improvements that we saw in the capital markets after our September 18 meeting might have been upended or seemed so by a couple of announcements from a leading investment bank and commercial bank that represented a negative surprise to the markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: A couple of explanations are possible for why the market seemed to react not just with respect to the securities of those two banks.

speaker: WARSH
text: Were the losses and risk-management systems particular to those banks that called the risk management into question, or were they illustrative of losses to larger segments of their peer group owing to poor risk-management systems?

speaker: WARSH
text: It was probably a combination, but I guess the key question for me is whether we are seeing impairment of the entire financial sector or simply the realignment of the competitive landscape.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the answer is the latter, but I’m not certain.

speaker: WARSH
text: The best-in-class comparables among commercial banks and investment banks seem to suggest that bifurcation is at work.

speaker: WARSH
text: If you look at the credit default swaps, at the profits, and at the share prices for the best in class of this group, they seem to have come out of the scare of a couple of weeks ago stronger and more profitable and, frankly, in much better shape.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would have thought that those sorts of entities would be putting opportunistic capital to work in a hurry, particularly when many of their competitors are down.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m afraid that is not the case.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even they are playing defense in this market.

speaker: WARSH
text: We talk, I talk, about the resilience of our capital markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: What they tell many of us, I think, is that the way for them to be resilient is to be exceptionally prudent here.

speaker: WARSH
text: The risk-reward tradeoff for them suggests that this is a time to be careful.

speaker: WARSH
text: You can’t succeed if you don’t survive, and I suspect that many of them are still quite jarred by recent events.

speaker: WARSH
text: The profitability of most of these financial institutions has been significantly called into question.

speaker: WARSH
text: I suspect that the losses in the fourth quarter are going to look particularly bad, but I would expect that many of these financial institutions are asking themselves the question of what business they really should be in after all.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, let me speak briefly about the implications for economic growth.

speaker: WARSH
text: To me there is no question that we have less market uncertainty than two months ago, and the prospects of some really bad tail events have dissipated somewhat; but there is still caution, as Vice Chairman Geithner said.

speaker: WARSH
text: Certainly, large multinational nonfinancial companies, excluding housing, seem to be holding up well, as represented by their bottom-up S&P earnings forecast for the fourth quarter of next year, and certainly there’s good news to report, as President Poole suggested, from many in the tech sector.

speaker: WARSH
text: Housing is, of course, as bad as the Greenbook has long suggested.

speaker: WARSH
text: So at the end of the day in terms of trying to judge what’s going on in the real economy, we go back to a discussion the Greenbook highlighted for us, which is the state of the consumer.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even though on balance I am a bit more optimistic than the Greenbook for GDP growth for the balance of ’07 and ’08, I have to admit that the conclusion that consumer sentiment has taken a hit seems, at least from my reading and my discussions with some business leaders, to be backed up by some very disappointing consumer spending for October.

speaker: WARSH
text: Having surveyed a few of the credit card companies, I think that it looks to many of them that October spending is really not at comforting levels.

speaker: WARSH
text: Nominal spending excluding fuel for their consumer base appears flat to down over the past four weeks.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is, I think, a rather remarkable outcome.

speaker: WARSH
text: Delinquencies have also ticked up a bit, but I would say that’s probably less disconcerting to me than what the credit card companies seem to be reporting as a proxy for retail spending.

speaker: WARSH
text: The key over the medium term, however, is job growth and real disposable income, in my judgment more important than the negative wealth effects from housing.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn to the final issue for discussion—at least on my list—which is inflation risks.

speaker: WARSH
text: At the end of this six-week period, I must admit to being considerably less sanguine about inflation prospects and risks than the Greenbook.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is true that incoming data have not been bad at all.

speaker: WARSH
text: Some have even been pretty good, and inflation expectations are seemingly anchored.

speaker: WARSH
text: But as Governor Kohn suggested, I worry a lot about inflation psychology and the real effect of importing inflation given dollar weakness and the effect of commodity price increase pass-throughs on a breadth of products.

speaker: WARSH
text: Given the massive liquidity on the sidelines, given uncertainty in the global capital markets and the current political calendar, and given the rather large and growing expected discrepancies in interest rate differentials between us and our trading partners, I worry about outsized moves between the U.S. dollar and foreign currencies.

speaker: WARSH
text: A disorderly move in the dollar could prove very costly, even undermining foreign direct investment in the United States and perhaps threatening to unanchor inflation expectations, particularly if the judgments of this Committee aren’t well understood by the markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: I have never been a big believer in looking at artificial levels for prices or at charts to figure out where we should worry.

speaker: WARSH
text: Nonetheless, I must say a euro-dollar move beyond 150 strikes me as a level that the markets will be paying keen attention to.

speaker: WARSH
text: We’ll obviously talk about the policy tradeoffs involving these risks in the next round.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I very much agree with Dave’s characterization of the Greenbook as a modal forecast, and I think it is an excellent and perfectly reasonable modal forecast.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As almost all of us have said, the data are coming in a little stronger.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We will have a fair amount of momentum going into the fourth quarter.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We will have a significant drag from housing in ’08.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The financial markets outside of housing have generally had fairly significant improvement, although a lot of brittleness remains.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A very clear example of that is how the markets seemed to flatten out in the past week or so and certain markets backed up a bit, and thus the risk spreads are widening.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is also interesting to note that, when the first earnings reports that were fairly negative were coming out, there was a positive market reaction because it was sort of a relief that they were owning up to the challenges.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now that more information is coming out, some of which is more negative than had been expected, the market’s reactions have been more negative, and some of the risk spreads have been widening.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That suggests that a lot of concern is still out there, and a lot of people are waiting for the other shoe to drop.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I will note that I am sure that other shoe will have been manufactured in Richmond.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Since this was a modal forecast, I want to think about a downside scenario, one on which I put a reasonable amount of probability mass and one that I think we should seriously consider.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A number of people have talked about bank balance sheets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Generally, there has been less concern about them than before.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One of the big issues that we had focused on earlier was leveraged lending.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That seems to be working itself out reasonably well without much incident.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There is obviously a lower new flow on, but the new flow does have covenants, et cetera.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So that seems to be working out reasonably.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: ABCP, SIVs, conduits—there is still uncertainty about how much may come onto the balance sheets, although there is a lot more comfort with the extent of the call on the capital that is there, but there is still uncertainty as to how much might be called.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: You know, the SIVs seem to be working themselves down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They are shrinking through orderly asset sales.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But, of course, what are they doing?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They are selling the best assets first, so the potential challenges are still left behind.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: For the banks, the conforming mortgages are easy to get off the balance sheets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There seems to be a debate about whether banks are choosing not to get nonconforming ones off the balance sheet or whether they can’t get them off the balance sheet.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Many organizations that have a lot of capital seem to be just originating these wholly on the balance sheet and waiting for better pricing, as we have heard reports from other institutions saying that they are ready, willing, and able to buy at a good price and the supply just isn’t there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Nonetheless, there is still much more carefulness in the underwriting of those loans.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, the jumbo mortgages, the nonconforming mortgages, are more important than they used to be because housing prices have run up so much around the country: $417,000 doesn’t buy you as much house anymore, even in parts of the country that don’t have or traditionally have not had particularly high housing prices.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That raises a concern about a squeeze through the mortgage markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I see that the consequence of the financial turbulence is primarily highlighting issues in the mortgage markets, as a number of people have said.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, as I think the Greenbook and Bluebook pointed out, it is not a problem for highly rated or even just moderately well rated corporations to get funding.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That is not a challenge right now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It seems mainly to be coming through the housing market.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I see a potential for a slow-burn scenario coming and for the housing market to slowly play itself out because we are going to have continuing negative shocks.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: More than 400,000 resets are going to be coming every quarter, starting with this quarter, through 2008.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As a number of people have noted, we have much higher credit standards than before.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Many of the people who were supplying subprime loans no longer exist, and those who are supplying them are supplying them at much, much higher standards.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We will be proposing and putting out new rules.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The Congress is considering new rules.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This is all casting a pall over people who might potentially be supplying credit into some of these markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The delinquencies and foreclosures are clearly going to continue rising at least for a few quarters, probably—as analysis by some people at the Board suggests—peaking in mid-2008.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But there is still a lot of uncertainty with respect to that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So it is going to continue to put more and more challenges in this market.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: All of these things coming together could put a lot more pressure on housing prices.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we have been seeing some significant declines in housing construction, but I see a potential for a reasonable likelihood of a much larger negative house-price effect than what the Greenbook has.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As a shred of evidence for that, the incredibly illiquid Case-Shiller index that is traded on the Mercantile Exchange, if you look forward, for a number of markets they have a cumulative decline of 20 percent over a couple of years.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now, the number of players may be no more than the number of fingers that I have, but still it is a piece of data suggesting that it could be lower.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The anecdotal reports are that real housing prices are much lower than the indexes are indicating.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Certainly, in the new market, they are throwing in a lot of extras, add-ons, et cetera, and the inventory may actually be larger because the anecdotal reports are that a lot of people are taking their houses off the market, so they are not formally included in the enormous inventories that are out there but may well be potentially there for supply.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So what does this suggest going forward?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, from a risk-management perspective, we ought to be thinking about buying insurance against this downside scenario.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: What is the cost of insurance?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As most people have mentioned, we have seen some gradual slowing and expectations are still being contained but, as Governor Kohn pointed out, there is a bit of an uptick in the CPI, which is definitely worrisome.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But what is the risk?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, let us think about the upside risk.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I go back to 1998, when the FOMC cut 75 basis points.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Growth was 4.5 percent in 1998 and 4.7 percent in 1999.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I mentioned last time, we saw very little increase in inflation—actually a decline in core inflation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I looked at the core PCE in addition to the core CPI that I reported last time, and that was effectively flat at 1.4, 1.6 percent in ’98 and ’99 and then 1.6 percent again in 2000.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The potential benefit of buying a little insurance now is that, given that a lot of these challenges may be peaking in mid-2008, it may have some effect down the line.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It provides perhaps a bit more insurance against some of the negative shocks that we may be hearing about.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If those other shoes do drop over the next few months, then we have a lower downside risk for broader financial turbulence.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, by mid- 2008, if the scenario that I am describing or the other negative scenarios that people have described, aren’t materializing, we can take back some of these moves.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My forecast is actually quite similar to the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In terms of inflation, I see a little faster movement back to 2 percent, where I think inflation expectations are grounded, but the difference is very minor.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do think the risks are quite balanced around that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In terms of economic growth, I am fairly comfortable with the Greenbook forecast, maybe a smidgen less sanguine in the next two quarters but really not very different.

speaker: MISHKIN
