text: However, in terms of the issue of potential downside risk, I do think that, given the policy path that the Greenbook assessed, there are substantial downside risks and they come from several sources.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One source is that the financial market disruptions have led to some tightening of lending standards.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that could have some potential effect on business investment.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The housing market is pretty grim.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We still have a big inventory overhang, and there is a question about whether that large inventory overhang is going to lead to even fewer housing starts than the Greenbook has forecasted.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Furthermore, it has raised the issue about house prices, which have spillovers into household spending.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The spreads for commercial real estate are still very high, and so there is a question about whether commercial real estate will be as strong as it has been.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is a bit worrisome as well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Consumer confidence has not deteriorated too much, but it has been on a path of deterioration.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So, again, I worry a little about what the consumer might do.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In general, I worry more about these downside risks, given the policy path of keeping the federal funds rate constant.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What about the financial markets and their disruptions?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Well, I think that there are two elements to the disruption in these big, widening credit spreads.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is the valuation risk: All of a sudden people realized that they didn’t know as much about what kind of assets were in portfolios and how complicated the structures were in terms of those assets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly, the solution to that problem is price discovery.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We see that happening, but it is going to be very slow.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So that problem, in terms of the credit markets, will take a fair amount of time to resolve.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second element is what I call macro risk, which is the concern about a downward spiral: The problems in the credit markets will lead to a weakening of the economy, which then makes price discovery harder to do, which means that you have wider credit spreads, which then make things worse.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, that’s the issue with the tail risk that all of us have been talking about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think the policy change that we did in September clearly had a big impact.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It did exactly what we wanted it to do.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is almost a textbook case in doing what we wanted it to do—it took out a lot of the macro risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It didn’t take out the valuation risk, which is getting better but very slowly over time.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So looking at this issue and thinking about going forward in terms of the credit markets, I am a little worried that credit markets are still quite skittish.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is the danger that macro risk could come back.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So there is a question about shoes dropping.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There is an issue about what we might do at this meeting, and then there are issues about what might actually happen that people don’t know about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One thing that is sort of surprising is that, when you look at what is happening in credit spreads, they seem pretty reasonable in their steady but very slow improvement.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But then, you sense some discomfort—in particular, the reaction to the Treasury superconduit has not been very positive.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If it worked, it would actually reveal information because it would look like the way that the old clearinghouses used to work, when they would combine assets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Randy knows all about this because he studied this stuff.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You pool your assets, then you monitor each other, and then you actually create information that makes the markets work better.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that is what the Treasury was trying to get at.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But the skepticism in the markets is such that they think this could be used to hide information about assets and that other shoes may be dropping in this regard.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This does not give me a lot of confidence, and so I worry very much at this juncture, which I think is a critical one, that a policy move could have an effect of sending the credit markets in a bad direction.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is something we have to take into account tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me try to summarize this discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is a little harder than usual.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Broadly, the macroeconomic news came in slightly better than expected during the intermeeting period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing has been very weak, as expected; but consumption, investment, and net exports were relatively strong in recent months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the aggregate data, there is yet no clear sign of a spillover from housing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most participants expect several weak quarters followed by recovery later next year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The risks remain to the downside but may be less than at our last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One issue, given all these factors, is determining the equilibrium short-term interest rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial market conditions have improved somewhat since our last meeting, with investors discriminating among borrowers and with the process of price discovery proceeding.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was general agreement that conditions are not back to normal and that it would be some time before that happened.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some suggested that a risk of relapse remains, should credit quality worsen or further bad news be disclosed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Lending conditions have tightened, particularly for mortgages, and securitization remains impaired.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is not yet much evidence that this tightening is affecting business borrowing, however, although financial conditions may have somewhat increased uncertainty among business leaders.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Views on how consumption would evolve were mixed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumer sentiment is on the weak side, house prices are down, and oil prices are up, which suggests some weakening ahead.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, the labor market remains reasonably solid, which should support consumer spending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Anecdotal information about consumer spending was unusually mixed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some saw evidence of growing weakness in consumption.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This evidence included weak reports from shippers and credit card companies.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Others saw the consumer side as slowing a bit but generally healthy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Investment, including investment in commercial real estate, may also be slowing somewhat; but again, the evidence is mixed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Manufacturing growth appears to be moderating.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other sectors— including energy, agriculture, high-tech, and tourism—are doing well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Core inflation has moderated, and there was generally more comfort that this improvement would persist.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was less concern expressed about tightness in labor markets and wage pressures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Energy prices and food prices could lead total inflation to rise, perhaps even into next year, and there is the risk of pass-through to the core.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Similar concerns apply to the dollar and to export prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some, but not all, TIPS-based measures of inflation expectations have risen, and survey-based measures have been stable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most participants saw inflation risks to the upside, but at least some saw them as less pressing than earlier this year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, again, as usual, it is hard to be the last person to speak, but let me make just a few comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, as always, the Greenbook was very thoughtful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The authors have done a good job of balancing the risks, and I find their forecast very plausible as a modal forecast.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing does seem to be very weak, of course, and manufacturing looks to be slowing further.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But except for those sectors, there is a good bit of momentum still in the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Having said that, I think there is an unusual amount of uncertainty around the modal forecast, maybe less than in September but still a great deal.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me talk briefly about three areas: financial markets, housing, and inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A lot of people have already spoken about financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Market functioning certainly has improved.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our action in September helped on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, commercial paper markets are working almost normally for good borrowers, the spreads are down, and volumes are stable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One concern that we had for quite a while was that banks would be facing binding balance sheet constraints because of all the contingent liabilities that they had—off-balance-sheet vehicles, leveraged loans, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That problem seems to be somewhat less than it was.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some of the leveraged loans are being sold off, some of the worst off-balance-sheet vehicles are being wound down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there is generally improvement in the financial market, certainly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the past couple of weeks there has been some deterioration in sentiment, and I see that as coming from essentially two factors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, there were a number of reports of unusually large and unanticipated losses, which reduced the confidence of investors that we had detected and unearthed all the bad news.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This problem will eventually be resolved, but clearly we still have some way to go to clarify where people stand.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other issue, which I think is more pertinent to our discussion, is about economic fundamentals.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was a very bad response, for example, to Caterpillar’s profit report, and so the market is appropriately responding to economic fundamentals as they feed through into credit concerns.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: From our perspective, one of the key issues will be the availability of credit to consumers and firms going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My sense—based on my talking to supervisors, looking at the senior loan officer survey, and talking to some people in the markets—is that banks are becoming quite conservative, and that is what Kevin said.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is not necessarily a balance sheet constraint but more a concern about renewed weakness in markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is also a concern about the condition of borrowers, about credit risk, and the demands of investors for very tight underwriting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, of course, tight underwriting is not a bad thing; it is a good thing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But from our perspective, we need to think about its potential implications for growth and, if you like, for r*.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The biggest effect of the tighter underwriting, of course, has been on mortgage loans, although we have seen a bit of improvement in the secondary market for prime jumbos, which is encouraging if that continues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is the area in which vicious-circle effects, which Vice Chairman Geithner and others have talked about, is most concerning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: House prices, according to the Greenbook, are projected to fall 4½ percent over the next two years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Clearly, there is some downside risk to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If house prices were to fall much more, that would feed into credit evaluations, into balance sheets, back into credit extension, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think there is a risk there, as Governor Kroszner and Governor Mishkin also discussed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The corporate sector is not much of a problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Good firms are issuing debt without much problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t really have much read on small business, but I have not heard much complaining in that area either.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to consumers, my guess is that we are going to see some effects on consumers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Certainly, home equity loans and installment loans have tightened up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We can see that in the senior loan officer survey.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t see that yet for credit cards, but since a lot of credit cards are used by people with subprime credit histories, I suspect that we will see some tightening there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I do expect to see some effect on consumers from credit conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As has already been mentioned, an area we also need to note is commercial real estate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financing conditions have already tightened there quite considerably, and spreads are much wider.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The senior loan officer survey shows the tightening of terms and conditions that matches previous recessions, and CMBS issuance has dropped very significantly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You can debate whether or not this tightening is justified by fundamentals.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the one hand, vacancy rates remain low, and rents are high.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, it is still also true that price-to-rent ratios are quite high.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you calculate an equity risk premium for commercial real estate analogously to the way you calculate one for stocks, you would find that it is at an unusually low level, which would tend to suggest that prices may fall.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is uncertain, I would say.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Certainly one area in which we might see further retrenchment in commercial real estate is the public sector: Tax receipts are slowing, and that might affect building decisions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I do think this is another area in which we will be seeing some effects from credit tightening.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I should be clear—the Greenbook already incorporates a considerable slowdown in commercial real estate, but that means it will no longer offset the residential slowdown.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just want to make one comment about housing, which I think we all agree is a central source of uncertainty, both for the credit reasons I have discussed and in terms of prices, wealth, and other issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just make one point that I found striking anyway, which is that—at least from the Greenbook—the forecast of a strengthening economy by next spring and the second half of next year is very closely tied to the assumption that housing will turn around next spring.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, if you look at all the final demand components for the economy, other than housing, in 2007 those components contributed 3.5 percentage points to GDP.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: According to the Greenbook forecast, in 2008 all those components together will contribute 2.0 percentage points to GDP.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the fact that GDP doesn’t slow any more than 0.6 comes from the assumption that the negative contribution of housing next year will be much less than it was in this year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is certainly possible—again, I think the Greenbook authors have done a good job of balancing the risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But as we have noted, we have missed this turn before, and it could happen again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me just note that as an important issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we do miss on that turn, the other forecast errors for consumption and so on obviously would be correlated with that miss.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, let me talk for a moment about inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to share the concerns that some people have noted.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you wanted to be defensive about inflation, you could point out that the movement in oil prices and the dollar and so on is in part due to our actions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it is also due to a lot of other things—for example, the dollar in broad real terms is about where it was in the late ’90s.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In that respect, it is perhaps about where it should be in terms of trying to make progress on the current account deficit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Similarly, with oil, a lot of other factors besides monetary policy are involved.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That said, I share with Governor Warsh the concern that the visibility of these indicators day after day in financial markets and on television screens has a risk of affecting inflation psychology.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do worry about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we should pay attention to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I do think that is a concern, and we obviously need to take it into consideration in our policies, in our statements, and in our public remarks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have one more comment on housing before ending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In thinking about the turnaround for housing next year, Governor Kroszner talked about resets and those sorts of issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We spend a lot of time here at the Board thinking about different plans for refinancing subprime borrowers or other borrowers into sustainable mortgages.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have looked at the FHA and other types of approaches.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A very interesting paper by an economist named Joseph Mason at Drexel discusses, at a very detailed institutional level, the issues related to refinancing, in terms both of the servicers’ incentives and of the regulatory perspective.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Mason points out that there are some serious regulatory problems with the massive refinancing effort, including consumer protection issues, because refinancing can be a source of scams.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are also issues of safety and soundness because refinancing can be a way to disguise losses, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you read that paper, I think you will be persuaded—at least I am becoming increasingly persuaded—that a significant amount of refinancing will not be happening and that we will see substantial financial problems and foreclosures that will peak somewhere in the middle of next year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that is an additional risk that we ought to take into account as we think about the evolution of housing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those are just a few comments on the general outlook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just note, we will adjourn in a moment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be a reception and a dinner, for those of you who wish to stay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be no program or business, so if you have other plans, feel free to pursue them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A number of pieces of data, including GDP, will arrive overnight, and we will begin tomorrow morning with a discussion of the new data.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Perhaps that will help us in our discussion of policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s start with Dave Stockton, who will bring us up to date on the overnight data releases.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: 3 We left at your place—and I hope you will find—a table showing the GDP release numbers relative to the Greenbook forecast that we had.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I thought I would start out by just walking you through that for a minute and giving my impressions of what its implications are.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you can see, there was an advance estimate of third-quarter GDP of 3.9 percent—that was 0.6 percentage point above our estimate for the third quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Looking at the second line of the table, you can see final sales.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We were actually surprised a bit to the downside—just a tenth—by final sales.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The real area of surprise in this release, if you look further down the table to the level in chained 2000 dollars, was the change in nonfarm inventories.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The BEA has a much higher estimate for third-quarter inventory investment than we do.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Typically that change doesn’t carry a great many implications for us going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If anything, if we hold inventory investment at the level that we projected for the fourth quarter, the higher level that they are estimating for the third quarter would actually lead to a reduction in our estimate of fourth-quarter GDP.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Going back just briefly to the components of final sales, as you can see, two areas explain most of the small downside surprise that we had in final sales.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Personal consumption came in at 3 percent versus the 3.2 percent we were estimating, and equipment and software expenditures came in at 5.9 percent versus the 7.4 percent that we were estimating.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One other area that came in a bit below our expectations was net exports, which is down there in the “level” area.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan tells me that his folks would not be inclined to take all of the lower estimate, so they would probably be carrying a slightly higher number for net exports going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: 3 The materials used by Mr. Stockton are appended to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We had two small offsetting upward revisions.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One that was big in percentage change difference was nonresidential structures, for which the BEA is estimating 12.3 percent versus 3.7 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That miss was principally in drilling and mining, which would have been a big surprise to us in the second quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The BEA has some proprietary information on drilling and mining.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I must say the big increases that they are showing for the past two quarters seem at odds with what we can see in the data that we look at for rigs in use and foot-drilled.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nevertheless, there is not really any strong reason to doubt that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Going to the very bottom part of the table, you can see for core PCE an upside surprise of 0.2 percentage point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That was all in the nonmarket component of PCE prices, the part in which the BEA is making various imputations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In fact, the market part of the core PCE came in 0.1 percentage point below our expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, we don’t typically give a great deal of weight to nonmarket prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So that is the GDP release.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I would say, obviously, it was stronger.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t see any reason necessarily to doubt this number.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It will be revised as data come in.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In looking at their estimates for September, for which they are missing data, we could quibble a bit on net exports and on inventories.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Those quibbles would be largely offsetting, so if we had had this release in hand, today we would probably be showing a number something close to 3.9 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We had two other important pieces of information this morning.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One was the ADP survey of private payroll employment growth.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Their estimate for the gain in private payrolls in October is 106,000.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is above the 50,000 that we implicitly had built into our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, this has significant information content in terms of its predictive content for payrolls; they have improved their methodology over the past couple of years as they have gotten into this.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: While I don’t think we would move our estimate all the way to their 106,000, we would certainly raise it from the 50,000 that we have—probably to 75,000 or 80,000, at least, for an estimate of payroll employment growth in October.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other piece of data that came out this morning was the employment cost index.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It is showing hourly compensation for private-sector workers up at an annual rate of 3.1 percent in the third quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is considerably below our estimate of 3.8 percent through the third quarter and leaves the twelve-month change in that measure of hourly compensation flat at 3.1 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So that basically is showing no signs of any acceleration whatsoever.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, a lot of detail will come out later today and tomorrow in terms of the underlying data and assumptions behind this GDP release.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So right now I am really shooting from the hip, but I will shoot away anyway.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As I indicated, I don’t think we would necessarily fight the BEA on the 3.9 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We would probably mark down our fourth-quarter estimate from the 1.4 percent that we had in the Greenbook to 1.2 percent, with a smaller contribution coming from inventory investment.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, we would probably raise our level of inventory investment a bit but not enough to prevent the swing from becoming a little more negative going into the fourth quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That change, if we were at 3.9 in the third quarter and 1.2 percent in the fourth quarter, would boost the second half from 2.4 in the Greenbook to about 2.6 and raise the year as a whole from 2.3 to 2.4.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On PCE prices, I don’t think we would really do anything to our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We would take the third-quarter estimate on board, but we would keep the growth rates of both total PCE prices and core PCE prices unchanged in the fourth quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So we would be adding somewhere between 0.1 to the second half and 0.05 to the year as a whole.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That might cause the year as a whole to round up just a bit.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think that is basically where we would be.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In going back to my remarks of yesterday, I think that these releases—certainly the GDP release—would not have affected in any important way our basic take on the data, which was that the incoming data have been stronger than we had expected at the time of the last meeting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we still see good reasons for thinking that GDP growth will slow significantly going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If we do get 106,000 on payroll employment for October as in the ADP data, the extent of that slowing will probably be a little less than we thought in terms of the overall level of GDP going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In terms of the downside risk, I think we are still looking at a housing sector that has a significant amount of overhang and downside risk and that could be a bit worse than we’re expecting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Shifting gears completely—Vice Chairman Geithner asked yesterday about debt growth in our forecast and how it compared with the early 1990s and the earlier part of this decade.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I have left a chart of that at your places.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you can see, our forecast has a bigger drop-off in debt growth than we have experienced so far in this decade but not nearly so large as the one that we experienced in the late 1980s and the beginning of the 1990s.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, I would characterize this forecast as not really having what you would call a full-blown credit crunch but as having some significant restrictions on credit provision going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I will take whatever questions you might have, and I will do my best to answer them.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I just wanted to ask—and this is a question based on ignorance—you’ve talked about nonresidential structures, and you mentioned drilling and mining.

speaker: FISHER
text: One thing that has impressed me in talking to some of the bigger logistics companies— Fluor, Bechtel, Zachry—are the enormous numbers in what I mentioned earlier—the infrastructure developments in the Gulf Coast area and somewhat in the heartland, I think all the way up to President Hoenig’s District.

speaker: FISHER
text: The numbers are quite large, and they continue to surge.

speaker: FISHER
text: Would that be part of this nonresidential structure investment number?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Yes, most of that would be part of this nonresidential structure figure.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But since we don’t know exactly what proprietary information the BEA has, I’m not quite sure what is included in the number.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But conceptually, that should be there.

speaker: FISHER
text: And the weight of construction and mining is what?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Drilling and mining in the overall economy is very small.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yes, that’s what I thought.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I mean, nonresidential structures contribute about 3½ percent; drilling and mining I could get for you.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think the two combined are something like that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Yes, it’s a small piece.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I had a follow-up question on nonresidential structures.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: You talked about drilling and mining, and I was wondering about the other parts of commercial real estate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I don’t know if you had a chance to look at it, but the reason I ask is that, if you thought financing was starting to become a problem and you do have very weak nonresidential investment going forward, you would expect to start seeing it there.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I’m wondering if anything was in that breakout.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I have a second question, which is that you didn’t mention durable goods.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But if I thought that credit problems, particularly subprime and other things, were starting to create issues, I would expect to start seeing more imprints in the data for some of the durable goods.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So was seeing durable goods a little stronger in the consumption figures a surprise at all?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We don’t have the details yet.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In fact, a construction-put-in-place release will come out later today and will provide us with a bit more insight into the composition of the non-drilling-and-mining component.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I don’t really know what is happening there in terms of this particular figure.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In terms of durable goods, given what we’ve seen, I think that it would still be early at this point for any credit restriction to have left much of an imprint on capital spending or durable goods orders.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are looking for that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have been a little surprised at the strength there, so I think that would be part of a question mark in our own minds as to whether we have overestimated the restraint.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But as I said yesterday, given the data that we currently have in hand, I think it is probably too early to see a significant mark yet from the credit restraint.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If we don’t over the next three or four months, that will more seriously call into question our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, we have not built in a very large capital spending effect from the financial turmoil because we basically think corporate finance is still looking pretty good.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There may be some pockets of stress and some difficulties with tighter terms and standards in bank lending, but that is not the big area in which we are expecting constraint.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It really is the household sector.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Mr. Chairman, I would just like to take this opportunity to remind the Committee that you will have the opportunity to revise your projections that you submitted a few days ago in light of the information available through the time of this meeting—of course including the data that were released this morning.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We would need to get your revised projections by close of business tomorrow.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 4 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will be referring to the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” That package includes two versions of table 1: The first is the version that was discussed in the Bluebook, and the second is a revised version dated October 31.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The revised table presents basically the same policy alternatives as the Bluebook version but with some changes in the rationale and risk assessment sections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To review, alternatives B and C contemplate leaving the stance of policy unchanged today, but they differ importantly in their assessments of risk: Alternative C characterizes the downside risks to growth as roughly offsetting the upside risks to inflation, whereas alternative B indicates that the downside risks to growth are the Committee’s greater policy concern.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative A, in contrast, eases the stance of monetary policy 25 basis points and indicates that the Committee assesses the risks to growth and inflation as roughly in balance.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In discussing these alternatives, I will basically be working from right to left across the two versions of the table.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As Dave Stockton discussed yesterday in response to a question from Vice Chairman Geithner, the Greenbook projection is a modal forecast.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Without consideration of risks, the Greenbook analysis would seem to support the Committee’s selection of alternative C. In that forecast, which is conditioned on the federal funds rate remaining at 4¾ percent, economic growth slows in the near term, and below-trend growth over the next few quarters closes the small positive output gap that the staff sees as currently prevailing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Maintaining the present stance of monetary policy leads to a gradual strengthening of the expansion over 2008 and 2009 and by enough to leave the economy producing at its capacity.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Core inflation stays under 2 percent, while total inflation runs a bit lower, reflecting declining energy prices.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Judging by your projections, most of you would find such a trajectory for inflation satisfactory, at least for the next couple of years if not over the longer term.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your projection submissions, however, as well as your comments yesterday, suggest that many of you see less vigor in aggregate demand than the Greenbook does as well as appreciable downside risks—an outlook that might argue against alternative C. The Greenbook provided several alternative simulations involving greater weakness in housing and larger fallout from financial stress that illustrate some prominent risks to spending; they suggested that the path of the federal funds rate might need to run ¾ percentage point or more below baseline should such weakness in aggregate demand eventuate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The choice of alternative B could be consistent with a modal expectation along the lines of the Greenbook coupled with appreciable concerns about downside risks and a judgment that you need to await additional information before deciding whether to ease policy further.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As noted in alternative B, section 2, of either version, the statement would in effect explain the decision to stand pat, first, by recognizing that economic growth last quarter was solid and perhaps conveying the implicit suggestion that the economy was likely to continue to expand at an acceptable pace, even if growth were to slow temporarily; second, by noting that strains in financial markets have eased somewhat on balance; and third, by indicating that the domestic 4 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 4).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: economy apart from housing has proven resilient and that the global economy remains strong.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: At the same time, the statement would indicate that the Committee is concerned about downside risks to growth, explicitly citing the potential effect of tightening credit conditions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Regarding inflation, the language would be identical to that used in September.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement would conclude by indicating that, on balance, the Committee saw the downside risks to growth as the greater policy concern.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As Bill Dudley noted, the market was all but certain as of yesterday that you will ease policy today 25 basis points.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Today, in response to the economic data released earlier, intermediate and longer-term interest rates have risen somewhat; however, futures quotes still suggest that investors now see high odds that you will ease policy today.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus, the announcement of an unchanged stance of policy would come as a considerable surprise to markets.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To be sure, the assessment under alternative B that the downside risks are the greater policy concern and its implication that further easing might well be forthcoming before long would soften the blow.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But a selloff in bond and equity markets would no doubt ensue.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, financial asset prices could remain volatile for a time, as investors attempted to recalibrate their expectations of the probable path of monetary policy going forward.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Concern about such market reactions clearly would not persuade you to ease policy at this meeting if you judged that an unchanged stance of policy would likely be more consistent with maximum employment and stable prices, and hitching monetary policy to market expectations would make for extremely poor economic outcomes.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But especially in circumstances of persisting financial strains, concern about unnecessarily adding to those strains might incline you a bit more toward easing, as in alternative A, if you were already strongly leaning that way today based on your view of economic and financial fundamentals.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As I noted yesterday, your economic projections suggest that most of you believe that the stance of policy should be eased within the next six to twelve months, and many of you indicated that some easing was appropriate imminently.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You may see several reasons for preferring to move earlier rather than later.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In particular, you may think that a timely reduction in interest rates could be valuable now in buoying household, business, and investor confidence.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Yesterday the Chairman noted the possibility of a vicious cycle involving a deteriorating macroeconomic outlook and tightening credit conditions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: By bolstering confidence in the outlook, easing policy as expected could help reduce concerns about deteriorating economic fundamentals and declining asset values.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Beyond reducing the risks of nonlinear responses, easing policy as expected by market participants would support growth of aggregate demand over time through the usual channels.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, you may also be worried about a possible increase in inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Such concerns may reflect a variety of factors—the further sharp increase in oil prices of recent weeks, the depreciation of the dollar, accelerating unit labor costs, and perhaps the relatively high level of resource utilization.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But given the recent good inflation performance, you may feel that downside risks to growth are the more immediate danger and believe that further easing today to address those risks is warranted.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You may also believe that, should the easing eventually appear to have been unnecessary, you could act as quickly to remove stimulus as you did to put it in place.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If you were inclined toward easing policy another 25 basis points at this meeting, you would need to confront the question of the appropriate statement language.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In both versions of alternative A, the first two sentences of section 2 are similar to those proposed for alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But rather than emphasizing remaining downside risks, the statement would then repeat most of the “help forestall” language used in September.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The language proposed for the inflation paragraph in both versions is identical to the corresponding paragraph suggested for alternative B; again, the language shown in the October 31 version suggests a bit more concern about inflation risks than the September language.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, both versions of alternative A would characterize the upside risks to inflation as roughly balancing the downside risks to growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This indication might well lead market participants to reduce the nearly two-thirds odds that they currently place on another quarter-point easing in December and might trim the extent of the overall easing of policy anticipated over the next year or so.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus, implementation of alternative A also could prompt some further backup in market interest rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In closing, let me remind the Committee that the September trial run highlighted the potential for inconsistencies between the results of the projections survey and the Committee’s statement.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your latest forecast submissions indicated that, while a minority of you sees the risks to inflation as skewed to the upside, a slight majority perceives the risks to total inflation as broadly balanced, and a more-sizable majority judges that the risks to core inflation are in balance.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: These results could be seen as incongruent with the draft statements for some of the alternatives.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, alternative A references upside risks to inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Several considerations might explain this apparent inconsistency.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, your responses on skews in the projections survey may capture only the subjective probabilities that you attach to various outcomes, while you may see the statement language as capturing not only the odds but also the economic costs associated with those outcomes.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Or perhaps the upside risks to inflation referenced in the statement should be interpreted as reflecting the views of all members not just of the majority who saw inflation risks as balanced, thus encompassing the views of those in the minority who see upside inflation risks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, I am worried about the possibility that some of you may have provided your numerical projections under the assumption of appropriate monetary policy but may not have applied that assumption as well to your individual risk assessments.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In your upcoming remarks, you may wish to address whether there is any tension between your own views of the distribution of risks and the risk assessments in the draft statements.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Brian, do I have it correctly that the blue shows the change between the Bluebook and the current version?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the only changes from the Bluebook in A-3 and C-3 are that there’s a more expansive description of the inflation risks, and in A-4 there is simply the phrase “after this action.” Those are the only changes from the Bluebook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any questions for Brian?

speaker: EVANS
text: Brian, we don’t have a long history of announcing the risk assessments contemporaneously with the decision, so I’m curious as to your take on the likely response.

speaker: EVANS
text: In alternative B, section 4, it says that the Committee views the downside risks to economic growth as the greater policy concern, and I think you said that markets would likely see a funds rate decline as forthcoming.

speaker: EVANS
text: What has been our experience when we have invoked this type of risk and what has the actual policy been afterward?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I’m not sure I could answer that without doing a fair amount of research, President Evans.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: My sense is that, as I think I indicated in my remarks, for the policy decision today there is effectively 23 basis points or so of easing still built in.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So there would be a considerable surprise in that dimension.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: According to a chart that I am looking at, the biggest upside surprise in the federal funds rate that we have experienced since the era of policy announcements began in 1994 has been more on the order of 12 basis points.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So that dimension of alternative B would, I think, be pretty significant.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I don’t really know how much the assessment of risks might moderate the shock.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think there would be some moderating effect there, but it would be limited.

speaker: EVANS
text: So as I thought about this briefly, it seemed to me as though it’s not unusual for us to say that, because of the risks of higher inflation, we don’t feel we’d take action in subsequent meetings for quite some time.

speaker: EVANS
text: But when we have had this type of assessment—I think there have been only a couple of opportunities—usually we’ve had a decline pretty quickly thereafter.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the market takes the upside risk to inflation as more what central bankers have to say.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Right, and I think that the downside risk would be viewed as more a hint of the way that the central bank is leaning.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I don’t think they are symmetric.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I just wanted to ask you for a little more detail about the market’s reaction to the GDP numbers and the ADP data.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You said that it’s the same.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Can you be just a little more precise?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Is there any movement at all in terms of the assessment of the federal funds rate cut at this meeting?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A very small one, I think.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: November fed funds futures were up 1 basis point, December was up 2 basis points, January fed funds were up 2 basis points, and then as you go further out they are 4 to 5.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Breakevens were up about 3 basis points across the curve.

speaker: FISHER
text: One just came to mind.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are talking about very recent futures expectations.

speaker: FISHER
text: In light of what you just discussed, what has been the range in the intermeeting period in terms of the odds of a 25 basis point cut?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think it has been as low as 30 and as high as—it’s nested, because there is some probability on 50 and some probability on 25.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But if you look at the Cleveland Fed, I think it has ranged from about 30 to about 80.

speaker: FISHER
text: So it has been all over the lot.

speaker: FISHER
text: My question really is maybe not so much of Brian but just to inform a decision here, or at least to inform an input.

speaker: FISHER
text: There was some discussion yesterday of strong hints about the need to have insurance—that is, insuring against the risk of downside economic growth that might be more dramatic than we would like.

speaker: FISHER
text: We did cut rates 50 basis points at the last meeting.

speaker: FISHER
text: David, when do you assume that kicks in—other than the psychological effect?

speaker: FISHER
text: I infer from the numbers in the Greenbook that you see it begin to have an effect on the kind of economic growth we were supposing sometime in the second half or at the end of the second quarter of next year.

speaker: FISHER
text: Or what is the lag?

speaker: FISHER
text: We have already bought an insurance policy.

speaker: FISHER
text: The question is, Is it enough?

speaker: FISHER
text: So I’m curious as to what your assumption is as to when that actually takes grip in the economy.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The mean lag is about four quarters, so you get about half of the effect in the first year and the other half of the effect in the second year; and that, at least according to the models, feeds in relatively smoothly over that period.

speaker: FISHER
text: Did it bump up your estimate for the second half of next year in terms of economic growth from where it would have been had we not cut rates 50 basis points?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any other questions?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just a follow-up on your comment about thinking about the release and of uncertainty and risks around inflation and unemployment—it looks as though the nomenclature that we’ve used in the assessment of risks was in part intended to get at the direction of policy in the future.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It does seem a little awkward if the language that we’re using in the assessment of risks looks different from these fairly stark histograms.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Since we haven’t gone through this experiment before, seeing histograms that aren’t consistent with our statement seems like an awkward start.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, one point to make is that the histograms aren’t in the public release.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: They won’t see those data per se.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The histograms will be published—yes?

speaker: YELLEN
text: Not the asymmetry of the risk, but it will be described.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think this emphasizes the importance of the point that Brian made about the opportunity everybody has to revisit their submissions, particularly in terms of how they think about the risks to the forecast in the wake of a possible move in monetary policy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We haven’t talked about this in much detail before, but if the expected path of monetary policy in the near term changes between when you submit and when we clarify, then that might change a bit and, I would think, would affect what those histograms might look like in terms of the balance.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It won’t affect them dramatically, but it will affect them a little.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I’m not sure it will make them converge fully to the way alternative A, section 4, is written now.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just to follow up on that—we submitted this last Friday, right?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I don’t know if people will know when we submitted it, but it’s not a huge amount of time between when it was submitted and when we are making an announcement.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So if there were a larger span of time, I would think that awkwardness wouldn’t be as great.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think your point about the awkwardness is right.

speaker: POOLE
text: I have a process question.

speaker: POOLE
text: In this go-round, are we going to talk just about the policy decision in the statement, or are we supposed to include the discussion of the projections?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s a separate agenda item.

speaker: POOLE
text: So it will be a separate discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any other questions for Brian?

speaker: LACKER
text: While the intermeeting period has seen a mix of good news and bad news, a substantial amount of good news, the net effect on my near- term outlook, as I said yesterday, has been negative, stemming largely from the continued slide in housing.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have come around to the view that the slump in housing activity is going to be deeper and more prolonged than I had thought.

speaker: LACKER
text: Many of you have read the intermeeting news as positive on the outlook.

speaker: LACKER
text: My sense of my shift in views is that I have come closer to the median view of my colleagues around the table about the second-half outlook.

speaker: LACKER
text: Taking all of this on board, my assessment would be that, even given the 50 basis point reduction in the fed funds rate at the September meeting, the current funds rate is probably somewhat more restrictive than is desirable.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I would favor a 25 basis point reduction in the fed funds rate at this meeting, along with a statement that contains no tilt, as in alternative A; and I endorse the passages in blue that highlight the inflation risks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me first comment on market expectations.

speaker: LACKER
text: You know, they have to influence our decision, but we need to be careful about that, obviously.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think we should ever be afraid of disappointing expectations or putting a new outlier in Brian’s chart.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the same time, those expectations are a fact, and we have to take into account the likely effect of our action on markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I think Governor Kohn said yesterday, they do contain within them some market assessment, some information, that we can’t ignore or that we ignore at our peril.

speaker: LACKER
text: So that had some influence on my decision as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m thinking that there may be a need for an increase sometime next year if the economy strengthens more than in the staff forecast.

speaker: LACKER
text: In addition, I have not lost sight of the risk of inflation increasing.

speaker: LACKER
text: In particular, I’d take this opportunity to endorse the public statement of Governor Kohn that an increase in inflation would not be in the public interest.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That would be intrepid of you.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, I’m hoping that inflation drifts down enough so that pessimists about adjustment costs will swing around to endorsing a lower numerical objective for inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we see signs of firming inflation or firming growth early next year, I would hope for a firmer policy stance accompanied by appropriate communications.

speaker: LACKER
text: So my preference today is a component of a preferred policy rule that has us responding with alacrity should things firm next year.

speaker: LACKER
text: That concludes my statement, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I’ll take just a second here because I realize how difficult today’s decision is and that it involves balancing contrasting and rather elevated risks.

speaker: HOENIG
text: One risk is that the current housing and financial environment will cascade the real economy immediately into a slowdown, and that would cost output and jobs and prove after all to involve little effect on rising inflation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To do nothing in this instance, I realize, would at least seem to be a poor choice.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The other risk, however, is that inflation is less contained than we would like to think.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Aggregate demand is at least holding and looks firm.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Commodity prices, not just energy, show a rising trend and are unusually high.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The dollar has depreciated, as Brian pointed out, and if it continues to fall, will add to further inflationary pressures.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Unit labor costs are increasing, and these inflationary factors are real and show themselves to be present in TIPS measures and in terms of expected inflation, as I mentioned yesterday, in a lot of anecdotal discussions that I have had.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To ease further in this instance would also seem to be a poor choice.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I realize that the intensity of these two countervailing forces complicates our decision, and I know that I might be only one view on this, among others who have a different view.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But as I see it, we are having to choose a policy that involves tradeoffs around these two choices.

speaker: HOENIG
text: One choice is to ease now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We would take an action that is oriented toward the short run, and the immediate easing could be looked at as an insurance policy, as I have heard it described, designed to mitigate further the possibility that the current upheaval in the housing and financial markets will lead to an unwanted slowdown in the real economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If the economy strengthens, as President Lacker has pointed out, we can always reverse that easing—so we tell ourselves.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The other choice is to hold firm now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Inflationary risks, as I’ve described above, are real; and while they are unlikely to affect us in the short run, they most certainly could affect us in the longer run if we continue to ease.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If inflation above acceptable levels gets entrenched into the U.S. and global economies, make no mistake—as we all have experienced, this has happened before.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It doesn’t jump in—it’s a little at a time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Also, if we ease today and things don’t turn immediately, we will be reset for another discussion of what the market expects when we come to December.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The cost to remedy inflationary momentum later is also high— indeed, as we all know.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So what is the better choice, then, when adjusted for long-run and short-run considerations regarding these elevated risks?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Personally, I think that we should hold where we are.

speaker: HOENIG
text: When I analyze how the U.S. and global economies are performing and look at the projections for these economies that we shared here, I judge this to be the better long-run decision.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We moved rates down significantly at our last meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Indeed, we front-loaded the action to ensure a strong result.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Also, we are very close to neutral, if not there, I realize, and we need to be slightly firm if we are to hold inflation and inflationary expectations better in check.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It strikes me that inflation is at the higher end of what most individuals prefer.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we need to move down, we can do so later.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It is, in fact, easier to lower rates than to raise them back up.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our issue today, I think, remains for the moment principally liquidity, and we should remind the world that we have stepped up to this issue and reassure it that we are ready to meet the need further—and other needs, if necessary.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But for now the risks on both sides of this policy decision are elevated, and we need to wait, watch, and be ready to act depending on how events play out.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As to the statement, then, I prefer alternative B for the most part.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would prefer something along the lines in paragraph 4 that “financial markets remain uncertain,” and then “thus the Committee will continue .

speaker: HOENIG
text: .” or paragraph 4 in alternative C. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You prefer C-4 to B-4, is that what you said?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Well, what I really prefer is that we go back to our last statement but say, “Financial markets obviously remain uncertain, and we will watch them.

speaker: HOENIG
text: .,” and then bring in “the Committee will continue to assess the effects of financial and other factors,” without the downside risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is basically the September assessment.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with President Hoenig that this is a difficult decision between staying where we are—and I would have downside risks to growth on that—or moving 25, but with more-balanced risks.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it’s difficult—we are balancing a number of very difficult things here.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the one hand, the incoming data, as Dave has emphasized, have been, if anything, stronger than we anticipated on the real economy and include data for September and some hints for October in here.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the other hand, many members of the Committee, myself included, have a sense that the real interest rate is still a little to the high side of where it needs to be to promote full employment and stable prices over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: We expect the output gap to move over the next couple of quarters, as housing holds down growth relative to potential.

speaker: KOHN
text: We expect inflation to stay low and inflation expectations, if anything, perhaps to edge down as people realize that inflation is going to stay at 2 or below.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wonder whether the 50 basis points we did last time was enough to offset the tighter credit conditions that have developed and the market disruptions that are going to impede, particularly, the secondary markets for nonconforming mortgages for some time.

speaker: KOHN
text: This stuff isn’t going to go away soon, and it’s going to weigh on demand.

speaker: KOHN
text: Partly as a result of this sense, many of us think that the risks to growth are on the downside but are still worried about inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: The risks to growth on the downside are compounded, as the Chairman and Brian pointed out, by the sense that financial markets are still fragile and there is the tail risk of getting into the feedback spiral between concerns about the real economy and reactions in financial markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: Not the most likely outcome, but certainly a tail risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: As I tried to square several circles at the same time, I came down on alternative A: reducing 25 basis points but going to risks being roughly balanced.

speaker: KOHN
text: I see this as preemptive but not open ended.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that combination of preempting some of the tail risk, getting a little ahead of the possibility, and buying this insurance is helpful.

speaker: KOHN
text: But going to roughly balanced risks takes out the open-ended sense that we’re on a path toward ever-lower interest rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: I see the incoming data for inflation as consistent with this.

speaker: KOHN
text: Inflation has been low even with today’s data.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the core PCE has been low; the CPI is up a little but not much.

speaker: KOHN
text: I found the ECI data kind of interesting this morning.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have been a little concerned about labor costs creeping up, which you could see from some of the compensation data.

speaker: KOHN
text: But the ECI is a good, consistent measure over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is not totally comprehensive.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also, the fact that there is no increase in the growth rate of the ECI to me is pretty encouraging that underlying cost pressures are not building.

speaker: KOHN
text: By emphasizing our concerns about inflation—that the risks are roughly balanced—we are signaling that we are not buying into the full extent of the market expectations for our easing, and I think that is a good thing.

speaker: KOHN
text: The “roughly balanced” language will raise the hurdle a bit for ourselves to ease again in December if we have some weak data, but it won’t raise it so high that, if the data are really weak, we can’t react in a constructive way to change it.

speaker: KOHN
text: So putting all of this together and admitting that it is a close call, I think that alternative A—roughly balanced risks—minimizes the deviations from where we want to be, helps us send the signal about what we think might be coming and what our concerns are, and comes closest to furthering economic performance toward our objectives.

speaker: KOHN
text: I certainly agree with President Lacker that alacrity will be required.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think I actually called it “nimbleness” in the speech I gave—I want to quote myself again—and that will be very much in the forefront as we go forward next year, I agree.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One of my life-long purposes has been to make the world safe for ambivalence and indecision.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Well, I’m gaining ground this morning.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Having said that, I prefer that we reduce the federal funds rate target 25 basis points.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My thought process is that the softening of economic activity, at least in some sectors, and the lower estimates suggest that the neutral rate of interest may be falling.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The downside risks to economic growth and the evidence of lingering liquidity issues are to me good arguments for taking steps that insure against an inadvertently restrictive policy stance.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: With regard to the policy statement, I am going to continue to use the inexperience excuse as long as I can, even though we have some newer members.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But just a few remarks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The language in the rationale section of alternative A most closely reflects my assessment of the situation, but I am not entirely comfortable with any of the options for the assessment of risk.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The real economic outlook faces uncertainties on the downside that are difficult to characterize.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Because of that, I am skeptical that we can credibly claim near-term downside growth risks to be roughly in balance with upside inflation risks, as is done in alternatives A and C. That said, I worry that the wording in alternative B would be interpreted as a rather significant loss of confidence in the economy and a signal that another rate reduction is probable in the near term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: At this point, I’d prefer not to send a signal that another rate cut is most likely in December.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Since our last meeting, expectations were centered on no change in the fed funds target today until a string of weak housing and earnings reports moved the probabilities strongly in the direction of a rate reduction.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Thus, judging from the evolution of market expectations since our September meeting, the assessment of risk language in our last statement was sufficient to convince financial market participants that our decision on the funds rate is being driven by incoming data.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I said, I think the assessment of risk statement should try to recognize the uncertainties inherent in our growth forecasts—and those uncertainties are greater than those associated with our inflation forecast—but without tilting expectations in favor of a future rate cut.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I said in my remarks yesterday, it is quite possible that we will enter another period in which headline inflation numbers exceed the trend suggested by core measures.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: If that is even a short-lived problem, my opinion is that—and this is based on the Bluebook version—we would be well served to note that fact by adopting the language in alternative C, section 3.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, I do note that the new language, as presented this morning, in alternative A, section 3, is quite helpful because it largely incorporates the language in alternative C. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: POOLE
text: Two weeks ago I was pretty adamant in my own mind that the recommendation I would be offering was no change, but I have reluctantly tilted in the other direction and favor a 25 basis point cut.

speaker: POOLE
text: I have changed my mind because of really two things.

speaker: POOLE
text: First, in my discussions with our directors, in my phone calls before the meeting, and around the table yesterday, I think there has been fairly pervasive anecdotal information indicating a soft economy—not disastrously weak but just soft, certainly softer than the hard data that have been coming in.

speaker: POOLE
text: Second, the financial markets are still unsettled, and with the markets putting a very high probability on action, I am concerned about the effects of violating that market expectation.

speaker: POOLE
text: I ask myself how big a risk it would be to violate the market expectation, and I am not really sure.

speaker: POOLE
text: But I am not sure that I want to find out either.

speaker: POOLE
text: It is just not a risk that I really want to run.

speaker: POOLE
text: That said, it is very important that we understand—I think everybody does, but I want to state it—that there can be no equilibrium in the economy if all we ever do is follow the market expectation.

speaker: POOLE
text: We have to get out front, and we have to help define what that market expectation is going to be.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think there are a number of things that we could do coming up to the December meeting not only in the statement but also in speeches and comments that we make.

speaker: POOLE
text: I favor the alternative A language for the most part, but I am a little concerned about the assessment of risk statement.

speaker: POOLE
text: If it is really true that upside risk to inflation is mantra, then what is operative in the statement is downside risk to growth in terms of shaping market expectations about the Committee’s direction in the future.

speaker: POOLE
text: As I try to think through the downside risks to growth in the coming weeks or the next few months, we can’t really do anything about what is going to happen in the remainder of the fourth quarter or the first part of next year.

speaker: POOLE
text: But when I think about the period over which the policy action makes a difference, I am not sure that the risks are really skewed to the downside.

speaker: POOLE
text: We could well see the recovery of normal market processes proceeding, plus the lower interest rates, giving more or less equal probability in the second, third, or fourth quarter of next year of a 50 basis point upside surprise or a 50 basis point downside surprise in the growth rate of GDP.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I would like to see us work on the language for paragraph 4.

speaker: POOLE
text: Given that paragraph 3 includes risks to inflation, we might concentrate just on the growth risk, and we might say something like, “After this policy action, the upside and downside risks to economic growth in coming quarters are roughly balanced.” Because I think this will be the thing that the market keys off of in terms of a hint about our future policy or likely policy direction.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would like to see us go as far as we can in the direction of saying that we think we’ve done enough, at least for the time being.

speaker: POOLE
text: Let’s sit, wait, and see what happens, providing that the information comes in more or less as expected and we don’t have any big surprises on that.

speaker: POOLE
text: Looking further ahead, we are at a point where we are really within reach of bringing the inflation rate down to about 1½ percent on a long-run basis.

speaker: POOLE
text: We’re also at a point that, in coming meetings, we could throw that option away.

speaker: POOLE
text: If we go too far or hang on with lower rates too long, then we’re going to end up eighteen months from now looking at a situation in which we have rekindled some inflation pressures.

speaker: POOLE
text: So this is a critical time in terms of not going too far and also of being willing to take back some of these cuts.

speaker: POOLE
text: I guess the way I look at it is that, if 5¼ percent was the appropriate funds rate in July or June, before the financial distress really took hold, it probably can’t be too far off where we want to be once the financial turmoil is largely over.

speaker: POOLE
text: We are going to end up substantially below that if we cut 25 basis points today.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I think it’s important that we not go too far and that we try to set market expectations that we have this much longer run view and that we’re not just reacting to the very short run data on the real economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The last time we sat around this table, I and many of you argued for what the markets described as a surprisingly aggressive 50 basis point rate cut.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At that time, the baseline Greenbook forecast was for 25 basis points, 25 in subsequent meetings, and then flat thereafter.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our rationale was that we were trying to act preemptively, trying to get ahead of the curve, to limit some of the potential spillover effects from what we then believed to be a weakening housing market, perhaps a somewhat softer labor market, and the financial turmoil.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We also argued that higher-than-normal tail risk loomed out there, that it was associated with the financial market meltdown, and that it warranted aggressive action to help forestall the possibility of that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the forecast that we submitted in September, and we all submitted a forecast, the appropriate policy varied.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nine of us submitted appropriate policy as being consistent with the Greenbook, which was 25, 25, and then constant.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of the remaining eight, seven of us had a 50 basis point cut in September, which we did.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Many of those, including myself, had some further cuts to the funds rate but further out in the economy, more like in ’08, later in ’08, and ’09, as we move toward more-stable inflation, expectations coming down, a recovered economy, and so forth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was certainly in that camp as well, and in fact, most people ended up with a funds rate forecasted at either 4¼ or 4½ percent—little differences but not much.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In September, only two of us anticipated appropriate policy as dropping 75 basis points before the end of ’07.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, we all have the luxury, fortunately, of changing our minds in response to data and other things, and certainly all of us are doing our best to read the tea leaves of the economy, both aggregate and within our regions, and that influences the color and texture that we put around our forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We all work very hard at that, and I respect those efforts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I think it is important that, as a Committee, we enforce discipline and systematic behavior on ourselves as our views evolve, particularly as those views influence policy choices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Without that discipline, without that systematic behavior, I find it very difficult to figure out how I am going to communicate to the public about what monetary policy is doing and why.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It makes both our commitment and our credibility, either to inflation or to employment growth, more difficult to substantiate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It makes transparency in general more difficult.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: All of those things—commitment, credibility, and transparency—are important elements of what contributes to a stable economic environment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now I have tried to impose that discipline about policy on myself by focusing on the incoming data, trying to focus on how those data cause me to revise my outlook for the real economy, not for tomorrow or next month particularly but for the coming quarters.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: After all, the monetary policies we have just been talking about operate with somewhat of a lag.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In that sense, I think there has been a lot of discussion by myself and others around the table that we are data- driven, that we are forecast-based in how we think about our policy choices, and that we try to take a somewhat longer run view.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that view is important to communicate to the public.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I suspect that at the end of our last meeting—certainly I can speak for myself—many, if not most, of us probably would not have anticipated that we would cut again at this meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Perhaps some of you did.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Certainly, your appropriate policy paths in our forecast at the last meeting didn’t suggest that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But we wouldn’t have anticipated cutting unless we thought that the outlook for the economy had noticeably deteriorated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So what has really happened since the last meeting?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, the collective forecasts that we submitted—in terms of risk assessments, ranges, medians, and however you want to look at them—hardly budged.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Greenbook forecast didn’t change very much.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The economy generally had better-than-expected news on many fronts—not hugely better but certainly the surprises were on average to the upside for most of us given our forecast from last time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I thought we generally agreed that the risk of serious financial meltdown, while perhaps it hadn’t vanished, had mitigated at least somewhat.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As a consequence, neither the Greenbook nor our collective FOMC forecasts moved very much.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To the extent that they did, they actually moved up a little.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Based on that forecast and on the data that came in, I’m in a very troubled position in figuring out how to justify in my mind additional rate cuts at this meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Had this meeting been held two weeks ago, as President Poole suggested, before the market’s reaction to the write- downs in some of the financial institutions, before the fairly dramatic flip-flop in the fed funds rate futures market about the assessment of a future rate cut, I certainly would not have been in favor of a rate cut at that time, and I suggest that each of you should ask yourself the question that Bill did: Would I have chosen to cut rates at that time?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I certainly would have also resisted the temptation, arising from those data and what has happened over the past two weeks, to be in any great rush to think we needed to call a special meeting of the FOMC to consider additional rate cuts.

speaker: PLOSSER
