text: My attitude would have been that these financial markets are volatile and they are bouncing around an awful lot, we understand that there are risks, but let’s wait and get the data on the real economy and see how it is evolving and make appropriate decisions at the time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What worries me is that we run the risk of being whipsawed here by market expectations or by the financial markets that are moving around in a very volatile way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That leaves me with some concern that we may be putting ourselves in a position of either responding too much to these volatile markets or being accused by markets of being bullied by the financial markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So at this point, my take is to say that we are going to get a lot of data between now and December.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We are going to get two more employment reports, as we have discussed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We are going to get some more information about retail sales and consumption.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would prefer to keep my own approach to discipline-based policymaking by looking at the forecast and waiting for the data to tell me whether my forecast deteriorated significantly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If it has, I will be the first to argue for an additional rate cut in December if I think it is called for.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Right now we have a difficult time justifying a decision.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On what grounds are we going to justify it, particularly in a more systematic fashion?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that creates problems for us.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As we have already been discussing, it is creating somewhat of a problem in the language of the statement, and I will come back to that in a minute.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I also think that, without a very articulate rationale in the data and in reasoning that supports a systematic approach to policy, we run the risk of being capricious or arbitrary.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we are in a situation, as Kevin Warsh said yesterday and Tom Hoenig spoke about, when many of us view inflation risks as more fragile perhaps than they have been recently, particularly more fragile in an environment in which we are cutting rates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that we run the risk, more so now perhaps than in other times, that inflation expectations might be at risk.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t want to raise those inflation expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They are much harder to get down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You can’t act nimbly to deal with movements in expected inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also think we have to ask ourselves the question—and this ties into the balance of risks issue—if we choose to cut today when our forecast hasn’t declined and suppose the data between now and December look as they have for the past six weeks—kind of in line with what we expected, not much different one way or another with nothing really falling out of bed or booming—on what basis in that meeting would we choose or not choose to cut again?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At this meeting we have had a hard time grappling with the criteria that we are using.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we are not very explicit about those criteria, we could find ourselves in the same boat next time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think this is related to Tom’s point that, once we start on the path of making explicit what our expectations are or what the market is going to be expecting us to do without having a firm basis for saying we are doing this because of X or Y, we are going to find ourselves in an awkward position in December.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I share Brian’s concern about the assessment of risk language in alternative A being balanced when it seems to be out of touch with the way the Committee has described things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Again, I think that puts us in an awkward position of trying to balance those two things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So with that, I appreciate the time, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On net, I am troubled by a cut today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would much prefer to wait until December and to assess the data that come in.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If a 50 basis point cut in December is required, so be it; but I feel as though we would have a firmer basis then for making that decision.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Let the record show I am asking this with a smile.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: President Plosser, you are not really suggesting that your colleagues, if they have evolved in their view, are undisciplined, unsystematic, or capricious in their rationale for that evolution, are you?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: No, I am just saying that the communication of that rationale is tricky, and I did say that people are making their best efforts to make their forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I explained my view of how I discipline my forecast and how I discipline my policymaking.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just to clarify about the submission you presented— you have, as I think you said yesterday, a 25 basis point cut early in the year, in the first quarter?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First quarter perhaps, but that was conditioned on inflation and inflationary expectations remaining well behaved.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I found the choice between alternatives A and B to be a tough call.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’ve struggled with this over the past week, and in the end I find the arguments for alternative A for a 25 basis point rate cut more persuasive.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have several reasons for this judgment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, as I argued yesterday, further action to my mind is appropriate, even leaving aside the recent financial shock.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With output near potential and inflation near my objective, the stance of policy should be close to neutral, and while we can debate exactly what the equilibrium real interest rate is—that’s an important discussion to me—it appears that, even after our action in September, policy is somewhat restrictive.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I agree with President Plosser’s view that we need to maintain some consistency in our thinking over time, and I would say that I expressed this identical view at our last meeting and said at that time that I did envision a 75 basis point cut during 2007.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So my views haven’t changed, and the data that we have seen in the intermeeting period haven’t suddenly pushed me in the direction of this move—instead, if anything, slightly away from it, but I regard those data as largely uninformative.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So my views really haven’t changed about this, but it seems to me that the argument that we should be moving toward neutral does allow for quite a bit of flexibility in the timing of an additional rate cut.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It doesn’t have to be something that we do in October.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We could do it in December, or it could wait until January.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So that argument in and of itself doesn’t completely persuade me that we have to do it today.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I do think it would be prudent to act today for a couple of reasons.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The first has to do with the effects of the financial shock of the summer.

speaker: YELLEN
text: When we came into the meeting last month, we faced credit conditions that were quite restrictive, and our goal was to offset that shock to avoid a significant economic slowdown.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the favorable inflation results over the previous six months did give us the flexibility to take strong action, which we did.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My judgment is that we have had some success so far.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Financial conditions appear to be easier than they were in September, and arguably, as I said yesterday, I think we may have roughly neutralized the shock.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But an important element in our success has been the decline in Treasury rates along with the further decline we’ve seen in the dollar and the increase in equity prices since we last met.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Those changes are supported by the market’s expectations that we will ease further at this meeting and beyond.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In other words, if we don’t ease today as the market expects, then rates may move up, and that raises concern to my mind about whether we will have accomplished the goal of offsetting the restrictive effects of the recent financial shock.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A second reason for easing today is the asymmetric nature of the risks we face in achieving our goals.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I do see some upside risk to inflation although I have not read the recent increase in five-to-ten-year inflation compensation as really reflecting a market perception of a deterioration in long-term inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In my view, the more serious risk is the one that our Chairman discussed yesterday of unleashing negative nonlinear dynamics in the real and financial economy that could be difficult to reverse.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Conditions in housing markets and their possible implications for housing prices and, in turn, consumption are at the center of these concerns.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition, although liquidity in financial markets has improved, I think the markets are still rather fragile and subject to further sudden disruptions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’m comfortable with the wording in alternative A, including the balance of risk assessment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Through the fed funds rate being 25 basis points lower, I do see the upside risk to inflation as being roughly balanced with the downside risk to growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the statement does give us sufficient flexibility to respond in whatever way we need to, and that includes the possibility of taking back some of this easing should there be upside surprises.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I do think that it’s important to signal to markets that this is not yet another step in a planned series of continuing rate cuts.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I, too, find myself torn between alternative A and alternative B and have been anguishing over them much of the last week figuring out where I come out.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The economic outcome detailed in both Boston’s and the Board’s forecasts with no change in interest rates seems reasonable.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The evidence since the last meeting indicates that there may have been more strength in the real economy than we expected in the third quarter; and financial markets have been recovering, but they are certainly not back to normal.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The risks are clearly on the downside, and our forecast expects a weak fourth quarter.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So certainly an argument for alternative B is to cut when it is clearer that the fourth quarter will be weak or we have data of more-significant collateral damage from the housing sector.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The argument for alternative A would seem to be that we should take out more insurance against the downside risks.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The costs for such action are not great; and given the downside risk, some additional insurance is not unreasonable.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, we have discussed the modal forecast at some length, but our rigor around the tail is quite limited, making it difficult to determine how often and how much insurance should be taken out against downside risk.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Thus, I prefer to wait until there are more data that the economy is weakening, which I think is likely to happen.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just to comment on the assessment of risks—when I look at the uncertainty in terms of GDP growth, I think of the histograms.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If the major concern we have is downside pressure on prices of housing, which is my concern—that housing prices continue to decline and housing gets much worse—I think 25 basis points is probably a small premium to pay.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But I doubt that I would change where I would put the weighting even with a 25 basis point cut.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think the housing scenario that is detailed in the Greenbook will still be there whether or not we cut the 25 basis points, and my guess is that between now and December we’ll have more confirmation that it is a concern.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Whatever we do in terms of the language, we need it to be consistent and accurate, and I am a little worried about the language in alternative A being consistent and accurate with what we are going to portray in our uncertainty of risks if we show those histograms.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So if we’re showing the histograms, regardless of whether or not we have a 25 basis point cut, I think the alternative B language is more consistent with at least what we put down.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Unless people think that, with the 25 basis point cut, there is a big shift in the uncertainty and the risks to GDP growth, I do worry about how that will play out in the market and what kind of a tension there will be.

speaker: LACKER
text: If the language in alternative A, section 4—the assessment of risk—were simply about the likelihood of rate changes in either direction and didn’t say anything about growth and inflation, would you view that as inconsistent with the assessments in our projection?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If the goal is to try to convey that we aren’t necessarily going to cut rates again, that is different from an assessment that there’s a downside risk that housing will get much worse.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So whatever we put in that should reflect what we actually want to convey and certainly shouldn’t be inconsistent with histograms that we’re going to be publishing at the same time.

speaker: LACKER
text: I asked this, Mr. Chairman, because I’ve said this before on a couple of occasions: The awkwardness about the assessment of risk statement is that it talks about rates but it talks about them using a code about growth and inflation rather than talking about the rates themselves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just for clarification—and, Brian, you can correct me—we are not going to publish the histogram showing the risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will describe verbally, generally speaking, the Committee’s views.

speaker: EVANS
text: I find myself in agreement with so many things that have been said already, no matter how the conflict may appear.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is a close call.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think it’s a tough decision.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have, frankly, gone back and forth in thinking about the nuances here.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is the case that the data have been better than I expected at the time of our September meeting.

speaker: EVANS
text: The ADP report this morning sort of continues that.

speaker: EVANS
text: It didn’t have to work out that way, but 106,000 is a pretty strong number.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m still trying to figure out exactly how to project that to payroll employment.

speaker: EVANS
text: The bad news that we have seen in terms of surveys has hardly been surprising, given our views and what we would have expected in September.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I found myself grappling with many of the ideas that President Plosser was talking about earlier in terms of data dependence and our decision and discussion in September.

speaker: EVANS
text: One view is that 50 basis points in September was seen as enough, and we would be judging our future actions on the basis of deterioration in our forecast— data that come in worse than that or some information about risks that are hard to quantify but we thought would be important.

speaker: EVANS
text: I haven’t seen the impetus for that.

speaker: EVANS
text: Then the other view is the risk-management perspective.

speaker: EVANS
text: Maybe many people, President Yellen included, thought that more than 50 was required but only 50 in September was really achievable without startling markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: So there’s a tension there.

speaker: EVANS
text: Mr. Chairman, I really enjoyed your speech in St. Louis, when you talked about different responses to different types of uncertainty.

speaker: EVANS
text: With the sort of standard Brainard response, when the economy might be changing but we have a lot of uncertainties, we go slowly and we look at it.

speaker: EVANS
text: Juxtaposed against that are other types of risk, such as the financial risks, where things could be moving much more quickly and we don’t fully appreciate the potency of policy and what we can do against certain tail risks.

speaker: EVANS
text: In that case, the robust control type of approach suggests that we should do more; then in the event that we find that policy is very effective, we can reverse it.

speaker: EVANS
text: Of course, reversing it is important—we talked about that last time, too.

speaker: EVANS
text: It seems to me that we’re close to the limits of initial risk management.

speaker: EVANS
text: That’s how I’ve thought about this, and I thought that Governor Kohn’s comment that we shouldn’t view this as an open-ended commitment to risk management was very important.

speaker: EVANS
text: After all, how can you ever argue that more insurance won’t help against some catastrophe, some unforeseen tail risk that hasn’t yet happened?

speaker: EVANS
text: There is a lot of value to setting a benchmark stopping point for how you would respond to that tail risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: Then if other evidence intervenes to make you reassess the likelihood of that tail risk or the cost of it, then there’s reason to do more.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I think there’s value to putting the benchmark out there.

speaker: EVANS
text: Another way to stop this insurance is if we end up balancing the risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: The actions taken move our inflation risk up, and we’ve had some concerns about that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m actually pretty comfortable with the inflation risks, and people have reminded me that I’m pushing this pretty far.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’ve taken more comfort from our ability to forecast inflation than perhaps others would—it seems to have a pretty reasonable trajectory.

speaker: EVANS
text: But as we continue to move toward more- accommodative policy in the hopes of addressing a tail risk, I think those risks go up, too.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I looked at table 1 and I struggled with the rate decision, it seemed to me that the balance of risks was more important, and what got my attention early on was the risk assessment under alternative A. I thought it was important to project our assessment that risks were a little more balanced.

speaker: EVANS
text: I can easily imagine that we’ll have reasons to reduce the fed funds rate because we think that r* is lower, but it’s purely opportunistic to take advantage of that now.

speaker: EVANS
text: We could have done that several meetings ago, but we can do it opportunistically.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I’m okay with the action of 25 basis points today, and I think that the balanced risk assessment is important.

speaker: EVANS
text: We probably do need to think about the linkages with our projections; I hadn’t really taken full account of that myself.

speaker: EVANS
text: That will put me and, I hope, many of us much closer to the views that President Plosser expressed in terms of data dependence because I think that the risks will be balanced in how the data continue to roll out in the intermeeting period.

speaker: EVANS
text: So thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I take the view that a cut today is justified on the basis that keeping rates where they currently are leaves us with a lot of downside risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s exactly what I’ve been hearing from other people.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If there is, in fact, downside risk, why not move today?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I would be very troubled by not changing and still using the language in alternative B because it says there’s a lot of downside risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Then there is the problem of why we are sitting there and not doing anything.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On just the straight economic issues, I think that a cut could be justified.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, I was one of the people who advocated a cut at this meeting.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, I was being a bit—I don’t know what the right word is—flamboyant when I suggested a cut of 50 basis points and then that we might move back up 25 basis points.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I was trying to make the point that I was very concerned about the macroeconomic risk, the potential for a downward spiral of financial disruption leading to problems in the real sector and then feeding back on the financial markets, and really felt that we needed to keep ahead of the curve.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What is key is that the response to our actions on September 18 was almost textbook perfect in the sense that the markets really got the message that we were not going to be asleep at the wheel.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As a result, the macro risk was taken out of these markets, and we achieved exactly the kind of signaling that we intended.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So clearly I do not feel that we need to get ahead of the curve in that sense, the way I did last time.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also very important in my thinking about the macro issues is that I think inflation expectations are contained.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have been able to achieve that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, there is a bit of concern about inflation compensation having gone up in terms of the spread between nominal rates and TIPS.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But the analysis that I’ve heard from people who are much more knowledgeable about the way yield curves operate is that the way to interpret this is that there’s an increase in uncertainty about what inflation would be.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I hope that our communications strategy will help in that regard.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, that provision of information will actually help the markets in the current environment.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Furthermore, the Michigan survey has, if anything, gotten better in terms of inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I always get a little nervous about asking regular people what they think because if you ask them what they’re watching on TV, they’re never going to tell you that they’re watching Vanna White.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: They’ll tell you that they’re watching ballet or the History Channel.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I don’t see a problem there, and that the ECI numbers came in the way they did also gives me some confidence on the inflation front.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am very concerned about Charlie’s issue—I always call President Plosser “Charlie” because we have known each other such a long time—about being led by the markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is very important that we not get into that box.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I worry about that, but I am a bit less worried about it in this context in that we affirmed last meeting that we were not being led by the markets because we sure as heck surprised them.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the fact that we don’t surprise them this time to me does not create a pattern that we’re just doing whatever the market tells us.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I also want to raise a consideration that I think deserves some emphasis, which is thinking about scenarios of what may happen.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This relates to what Bill talked about, but I want to be a little more explicit.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I want to ask myself what might happen as a result of our policy actions today and what the implications might be for the economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, let’s think about the case of our doing alternative B.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that case, I think there is a significant probability that the markets would react quite negatively and that the macro risk that we took out by our action on September 18 might creep back into the credit markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m actually very worried about the skittishness of the credit markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When you’re in a financial-disruption type of world, things are much more nonlinear.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I would have no disagreement at all with Charlie on the issue that, if you are in a normal situation, then you definitely do not want to be led by the markets at all.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I think that we do have to worry about market considerations a bit more in the current situation, when we could have a negative reaction to what we do.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That creates problems in the credit markets, and then that weakens the outlook for the economy and there is an issue about what do we do then.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If we then cut in December and cut more than 50 basis points, that’s really bad.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Or if we don’t cut and things head south, that could be very, very problematic.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I do not think that cutting today will have very negative effects on inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, I do think that the issue of going forward is very important, and this relates to the statement.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I strongly agree that we need a much stronger balance and an indication that our action today—if we do what I suggest, which is to cut 25 basis points—does not mean that we expect to cut at the next meeting or further out.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We really need to make that very clear.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The statement will be one part of it, although I worry very much about the issue that we always put much too much weight on the statement and that we don’t have other means of communicating.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m not sure what to do about this; I’ve been thinking about it and haven’t come up with any good answers.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But there are issues in terms of how other central banks communicate things beyond the statement that are hard to communicate with fifteen words rather than something more extensive.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So my view—and it is reflected in my projections—is that, if we cut 25 basis points, it’s not clear to me that the balance of risks is so much to the downside.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think the risks to the downside have been very substantially eliminated—not that they aren’t still there to some extent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think they are but not really as much, and I think that is true of the actions on September 18 and today.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Because I’m never very precise in my language—as you know, I tend to say pitiful things— somebody will craft this much better than I do.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I’m wondering about the assessment of risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Let me make a suggestion, although I’m not sure this is the best way to do it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We need to emphasize that it’s not just the upside risks to inflation but also the downside risks to the economy that have lessened.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is also important when we have a 25 basis point cut not to say to the markets that we’re so worried about the economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One possibility might be, for example, to say that “the Committee judges that after this action the upside risks to inflation roughly balance the somewhat reduced downside risks to growth.” So we would not be saying that there isn’t some downside risk but that it’s not really as strong as we thought.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s certainly not as strong as we thought on September 18.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I think that, with this kind of reduction in rates, it would reduce the risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s a little past 10:30.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we recess until 11:00?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s recommence with President Fisher.

speaker: FISHER
text: Flying home last time I thought it would have been nice to have been at the Bank of China and cut 37½ basis points.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t want to repeat what has already been said at the table because so much has been said.

speaker: FISHER
text: But it is important to note that, since we last met, the data on the economy are stronger.

speaker: FISHER
text: Some of us have expressed concerns about inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: Credit markets, as I said yesterday, are at least in remission, if they haven’t fully recovered, and are in better shape than they were.

speaker: FISHER
text: Listening to the arguments, I took particular note of President Poole’s comment that he’s not sure that he wants to find out what the market reaction would be if we did not cut rates 25 basis points.

speaker: FISHER
text: I lived through three market corrections as a market operator, 1974-75, 1987, and 2001.

speaker: FISHER
text: I lived through a dollar crisis as a public servant in the U.S. Treasury.

speaker: FISHER
text: And I haven’t heard a person yet talk about some of the risk.

speaker: FISHER
text: The Riksbank, by the way, last night and the Mexicans raised rates; but more important, the Europeans are talking tough because of their concerns about inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am worried about the pernicious effects of inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think President Hoenig hit the nail on the head when he said it’s easier to lower than to raise.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would simply counsel, since I don’t have a vote, that we should consider the value of keeping our powder dry.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s very dangerous in my opinion for policymakers to be driven into a cul-de-sac by futures markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: In response to the question I asked earlier, the markets have been all over the lot.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am worried that we have too much of a discussion about what markets expect of us since the fed funds rate is designed—as you have made very clear in your speeches, Mr. Chairman—to affect the economy and should be so driven.

speaker: FISHER
text: So were I to have a vote today, I would be thinking along the lines of Presidents Hoenig, Plosser, and Rosengren in terms of their expression.

speaker: FISHER
text: Everybody has been grappling with this issue.

speaker: FISHER
text: We would make a great wrestling team.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are thinking very hard about these matters.

speaker: FISHER
text: But in the balance of risks that I see, given the improvement in the data, I’m tempted to consider the value of another cut as insurance against weakness.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet we took a huge step last time—we took out a double-barreled shotgun—and it seems to be reflected in the data that the staff projected.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m a little worried not so much of being accused of being asleep at the wheel but of having our foot too heavily on the accelerator if we cut 25 basis points.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I, like several of my colleagues who have gone ahead of me, find myself torn between alternatives A and B. I also wrestled with many of the issues that President Plosser articulated so well.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I left our September meeting thinking that the 50 basis point cut pretty much put us close to where we needed to be given our outlook, and my outlook hasn’t changed much in the past six weeks.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As I said yesterday, I’m not certain about whether the weakness that I’m hearing or have heard about during this intermeeting period is simply evidence of the business conditions that are unfolding as I thought they would or whether there is more weakness than I anticipated in September and more weakness than I have reflected in my projection.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The Committee has said repeatedly and for good reason that our decisions are going to be dependent on the incoming data, and as many have already said, the data seem to be confirming my outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But financial markets do remain on edge.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Moreover, many of the incoming data are backward looking and, hence, don’t provide me with great comfort when we’re trying to ascertain what might lie ahead.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The projection that I submitted for this meeting, as I said yesterday, is rather fragile, and it wouldn’t take much additional market turmoil or deterioration in household and business confidence to push my near-term growth outlook even lower.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I think this risk is the predominant one that we face today, and it is a risk that has weighed heavily on my deliberations for this meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The assessment of risk language in alternative B addresses these concerns, and I was contemplating supporting no change in the fed funds rate and the language in alternative B.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, in the climate that we find ourselves, I believe that just saying that the risk to the outlook is to the downside isn’t enough.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do think that we should be taking out some insurance against possible further deterioration in the near-term outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I support a 25 basis point cut in the fed funds rate target today, and I support the language that’s embodied in alternative A. I believe that the language does acknowledge the likely slowdown in the economic expansion.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: It also acknowledges that, if we take this action today, the risks are roughly balanced, and importantly, it suggests that further policy easing may not be forthcoming.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also like the language that was added regarding the recent inflation numbers.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Finally, as Governor Mishkin pointed out, it is difficult to express all of these issues in our short statement.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: It seems to me that we can draw some comfort from the fact that the minutes will be providing the public with a greater understanding of the different views that were expressed today and some of the challenges that I wrestled with.

speaker: STERN
text: As I commented yesterday, I think there’s a respectable chance that by the middle of next year or so the economy will be growing again at a reasonable rate, and because of the lags between our actions and their effects on the economy, there is not a lot we can do about what happens in the intervening period anyway.

speaker: STERN
text: It seems to me that those kinds of considerations are at the heart of something like the case for alternative B.

speaker: STERN
text: There has been some progress in the financial markets, and that step—that is, taking no action today—would in my view be consistent with long-term achievement of the dual mandate.

speaker: STERN
text: But I am an economist.

speaker: STERN
text: So on the other hand, financial conditions are still unsettled, and it’s difficult to know the degree of restraint that changes in the cost and availability of credit relative to conditions back in June will have.

speaker: STERN
text: It might well be prudent—this is the case for alternative A—to take additional steps today to err on the side perhaps of doing too much since it seems to me that it is inevitable that a lot of uncertainty is associated with the economic outlook.

speaker: STERN
text: Weighing those two cases, I come down in favor of alternative A but with misgivings, and let me share those misgivings.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that there is some chance that financial conditions will remain unsettled for several more months at a minimum, and so in some sense that part of the environment may not change very much in the next few months.

speaker: STERN
text: You pointed out yesterday, Mr. Chairman, that an important ingredient in the Greenbook forecast is a cessation of the drag from housing roughly around the middle of next year.

speaker: STERN
text: Let’s suppose that, in fact, turns out to be precisely correct.

speaker: STERN
text: That’s all well and good, but we won’t recognize that it has actually happened with any degree of confidence, given the flow of data, probably before August or September at the earliest even if the anecdotes get a little more positive.

speaker: STERN
text: So I can see a situation in which the circumstances we confront over the next series of meetings don’t look very different from the circumstances we’re confronting today.

speaker: STERN
text: I think we have to be very careful of not letting good intentions on a decision-by-decision basis get into what turns out to be a policy error as a consequence of an accumulation of those kinds of decisions.

speaker: STERN
text: It’s the time-inconsistency problem obviously, and that gives me some pause even though I come out at the moment in favor of alternative A.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as directive language, for a variety of reasons that others have expressed, I am uncomfortable about characterizing the balance of risks the way they are characterized in alternative A. I think that a way we might consider going, although it’s not the most elegant solution, is perhaps just to drop that first sentence under alternative A.

speaker: STERN
text: We succeeded at the last meeting in making it clear that we were data dependent, and you had significant swings in probabilities of funds rate reductions over the intermeeting period.

speaker: STERN
text: I think this would leave us in that circumstance.

speaker: STERN
text: As President Pianalto pointed out, we have the minutes coming out, and we may well have the communications package, including the narrative, coming out with it.

speaker: STERN
text: Obviously there’s a three- week lag, but it seems to me that that would be an effective way of communicating what we want to communicate and perhaps of putting the attention on that communications package, which I think would turn out to be valuable.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Gary, I’m a little puzzled here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m not sure I understand.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What I understand from your reasoning is that the key issue is that you don’t want to give an impression that we are going to keep on cutting.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So if you take that first phrase out, you’ve taken out any issue of balance of risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My view is that the markets would interpret this as actually indicating that the Committee would be more likely to cut in the future.

speaker: STERN
text: If you look at the language from the last meeting, we were careful not to pre-commit to anything, and it seemed to me that the markets understood the data dependence.

speaker: STERN
text: I forget the precise numbers, but I guess the probability of a ¼ percentage point cut ranged from 30 percent to 100 percent, or more when you think of it in terms of bigger cuts, too.

speaker: STERN
text: It seems to me that the proof of the pudding is in the eating.

speaker: STERN
text: That seemed to work out okay.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But in this case, if we do alternative A, we will have cut.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, I don’t follow that.

speaker: STERN
text: We cut even more significantly at the last meeting.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me be the most recent but, I guess, not the last to say that this is a close call.

speaker: WARSH
text: I suppose I take more comfort in that than some around the table because I am pleased at the progress though it is not perfect and we’re not even back to an honest view of normal in the financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: That it’s a close call suggests to me that the data in the financial markets are normalizing.

speaker: WARSH
text: I guess the alternative of a close call would have been to have this be an easy call, and I suspect that the only way this would have been an easy call would be if we continued to have bad data and bad sentiment in the market.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think we’re in the realm of a close call and we shouldn’t completely rue that situation.

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, that’s probably a function of the resilience of the economy, the resilience in the markets, some time and patience, and maybe even a little good monetary policy.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I’m okay with that, I think.

speaker: WARSH
text: The judgment that we make on moving or not moving ¼ percentage point today matters, but it strikes me as being considerably less important than what the future path of policy is expected to be in the capital markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think that the most important judgment we make is in the fourth paragraph rather than the first paragraph.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me spend a moment on what the financial markets are telling us with a degree of certainty which, speaking for myself, is quite surprising.

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, I think they have responded to real data over the past couple of weeks.

speaker: WARSH
text: They haven’t changed their probabilities based on utterances from the Chairman or from any of us, and I take some comfort in that.

speaker: WARSH
text: I might disagree with what they’re saying, but I don’t think that they’re just giving us a mirror image of our own views.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I take what they’re saying and the certainty with which they have taken on board that we’re going to move today.

speaker: WARSH
text: It’s not dispositive, nor should it be, but the debt capital markets, at least, think that the economy is worse—worse than the Greenbook and worse than many of us feel.

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, I would say that I have to take that on board without giving it too much predictive capability.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that Brian is right—given the fragility in the financial markets and given the surprise that we had for them last time, I wouldn’t want our judgments today to add to that volatility, which I think would be quite possible.

speaker: WARSH
text: In sum, I would say that I support alternative A as written on this revised page.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that, absent having strong language in alternative A, section 4, it would look to some as though the markets dictated this outcome.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think A-4 and robust balance of risk language is important so that the markets don’t believe incorrectly that we succumb to what their wants are.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that previously, including at our last meeting, when we spoke about uncertainty, they seemed to understand what that was—that it wasn’t that we’re just calling it uncertainty but we really have cuts ahead.

speaker: WARSH
text: For better or for worse, they’ve now learned a lesson.

speaker: WARSH
text: Uncertainty with even pretty good data led us to cut this time, if we end up adopting alternative A.

speaker: WARSH
text: So if we use that same uncertainty language, I don’t think it would have the effect that it had last time of letting folks be on both sides of the bet on whether we would have continued actions.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I’m comfortable with alternative A, paragraph 4.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is a way of addressing market expectations and addressing our uncertainties by insurance, but being very clear to the markets that they ought not prejudge nor have we prejudged the outcome next time.

speaker: WARSH
text: The references to inflation risks there and in alternative A, paragraph 3, are useful to address some of the broader concerns we have about commodities and the foreign exchange value of the dollar.

speaker: WARSH
text: So with that, I think that alternative A is the right thing to do and that it does preserve for us plenty of ability to call it as we see it when we meet next.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I discussed yesterday, I take very much a risk- management approach.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I also like the way that President Evans characterized that risk- management approach as your having to think about the costs and the benefits and very much focus on the potential costs.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So in thinking about the best way to go, I think about if we do or don’t move, then what are the downside risks to each?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’ve seen, as many people have said, a lot of progress in the financial markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have also seen a little backing up of some of that progress and a flattening out over the past couple of weeks.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In particular, the one set of markets that we haven’t seen as much progress in as certainly I would like is housing-related markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That is for me the most direct channel between financial turmoil and the real economy.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I described yesterday, my tail risk scenario is sort of a slow-burn scenario.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is not one in which this financial turmoil will get out of control and we will have an incredible mess so we need to cut interest rates to prevent it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that was more the concern and focus in our previous meeting.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have seen improvement, although I don’t think we’ve seen normalization, particularly in the housing markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Given that we’ve had some but not full normalization and then given that we have resets coming and the tightening of credit standards, the elimination of a lot of subprime lending, the rules that we are going to put out, and the rules that the Congress is considering, regardless of how carefully we craft them or whether or not the Congress makes progress, the effect on the housing market will undoubtedly be somewhat chilling.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I see a potential slow-burn scenario in which it is valuable to be buying some insurance against that as early as possible.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: These problems may be peaking toward the middle of next year, because that’s when they have the most potential to have a negative effect on housing prices, which, as others have described, could have this sort of simultaneity issue or vicious cycle aspect that could lead things to go down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Given that we have those conditions and we have that potential going forward, it seems worthwhile to buy that insurance now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: What is the cost of doing that?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Of course, it is in terms of inflation and inflation expectations.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As the markets have changed their expectations about what we’re likely to do at this meeting and even as they have dramatically changed their path of future policy moves, there’s very little evidence that inflation expectations, at least up to the five-year horizon, have moved up significantly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There is a question of how to interpret that longer-term change in inflation expectations; I take it very seriously, and I think we have to try to understand it better.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I don’t think that there’s an enormous cost in terms of moving now versus six to nine months from now to buy more insurance against what I see as a challenge from the recent financial market turbulence.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think there is also a concern, which President Poole raised, that if we have a fairly large surprise to the markets, it could reduce or even reverse some of the progress that has been made in some of the markets, potentially forcing us to move more than we would like at the next meeting.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So that said, I think it is very important and very valuable that we make a move now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As other have said, it is a close call because we have to worry about the cost with respect to inflation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One way to contain that cost, as a number of people have said, is to clarify the path going forward, to show that what we’re doing now is responding not to current data but to the forecast about the data.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously when the markets were expecting GDP at 3.1 and it comes in at 3.9, we’re not saying that we’re reacting to current market data by making a cut.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we are thinking about the potential future effect and then trying to give some guidance through a balance of risk statement.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I’m open to a modification of that statement to try to convey that we think we don’t necessarily need to do more with respect to the challenges that are coming now but we’re going to continue to remain vigilant and look at things like the housing market and other markets that have potential to have negative ramifications for the whole economy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the economy is slowing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Even the nonhousing part of the economy is slowing a bit.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Housing prices are still obviously sliding down.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We don’t really claim to know much about where they’re going to end up or where we are in that process, but it seems that they are falling and probably at an accelerating rate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our modal forecast—“our” meaning from the submissions—is for an economy that slows further and runs below trend over several quarters.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But if you just look at the size of the bars on the submissions, the size of that bar about downside risk to growth is very high, much higher than the bar about upside risk to inflation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is a huge amount of uncertainty about what equilibrium is and where short-term interest rates should be over time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think it is fair to say that we are now at the high end of, if not slightly above, most of those estimates of where equilibrium is.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Therefore, it seems to me sensible that most of our submissions had a downward slope to the path of the fed funds rate going forward over this period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The question then is not principally whether to move but when and what signal of a change or no change should come.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it is a very close call, and everything that I say I say with a lot of unease and discomfort.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If the choice is to stay firm but to signal more explicitly than we did in September that we’re likely to move further, that seems to me just a bad choice.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it is likely to amplify many of the risks that you are all worried about and it probably would make people more tentative about coming in and doing what they’re going to do to let this thing work through the markets because they will be living with our acknowledgement of substantial downside risk without action and uncertainty about whether we’re going to move.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think you might argue that a decision not to move with an explicit asymmetry in the balance of risks to growth would lower the path going forward and add to that uncertainty in some sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I do not think that the markets are so fragile now that they could not take an adverse surprise of this magnitude, even though it is a very, very large adverse surprise relative to recent history.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think that’s a good argument for moving.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the best argument is that we’re still in the midst of what is a very delicate and consequential asset-price adjustment in the U.S. economy with a fairly dense, thick, adverse tail on the potential implications about the evolution in housing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The Chairman spoke eloquently early in the year—I think it was early in the year, but maybe it was late last year—about the pattern of history and the acknowledgement that weakness tends to cumulate, and you don’t really have a lot of experience with sustained periods of below-trend growth without falling into a more substantial rise in unemployment rates.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Those risks have to be substantially greater when you have an economy going through this kind of asset-price adjustment.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I found these charts discouraging, not reassuring, in the sense that we’re anticipating a slowdown in the rate of growth of credit for the economy as a whole that’s comparable to ’01.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the pressure on bank balance sheets is probably—it’s hard to make these statements with any certainty—greater than it was in ’01.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: At least a reasonable expectation is that it’s going to be bigger than it was in hindsight in ’01, and I think you have a much more substantial impairment to the functioning of what Kevin calls debt capital markets—the industry around the design of securitization and structured finance, et cetera, which has been so important to the way credit gets originated and moved.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That disruption could take a long time to resolve, and I think that just has to amplify the density of the adverse tail and the growth outcome, certainly with more uncertainty at this time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that it is hard, but the better course of valor is to move today, and I like the language in alternative A.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Let me just go quickly through the arguments against it that I find most compelling.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The best argument against is the fear that many of us spoke about—that even though the inflation numbers have been reasonably reassuring and we haven’t seen substantial erosion in inflation expectations that we can measure, there is a bit of deterioration in the feel, in the psychology.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have to be very careful that we don’t add to that through our actions or people’s expectations about how we’re going to behave going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But we should take some comfort from the fact that the market is pricing in more than 100 basis points of easing over the next two years.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You have to believe that a fair amount of that is already reflected in breakevens, reflected in what people are willing to pay for insurance against adverse inflation outcomes, and reflected in the dollar.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It doesn’t mean that if we validate part of those expectations you won’t see erosion, but we should take some comfort from that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have been through three years of very substantial relative price shocks in energy prices, commodity prices, and some other things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Those hit an economy that was growing over the period above most estimates of potential, and we have had pretty good performance of underlying inflation and inflation expectations in that context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So even though we look forward and we see what’s happening in commodity prices, energy prices, and the dollar as posing some potential risk of upside pressure on input costs, that is hitting the economy in a very different state.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The experience of those last couple of years should give us a fair amount of confidence in the judgments we bring as to how we think about inflation going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think we have less uncertainty around an inflation forecast than we would have had two or three years ago and still substantial uncertainty around the growth forecast inevitably given what the economy is going through.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The balances suggest that it is better to move today because of that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As I said, I’m comfortable with the language in alternative A. I would be comfortable with Governor Mishkin’s amendment to A—I think that helps a bit.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I have a lot of sympathy for all the arguments against the first sentence in alternative A in any form, but on balance, I would say that we just don’t want to take the risk that, by omitting some statement like it, we cause people to price in a steeper slope to that path going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is something that we should try to avoid, and the best way to achieve that is the language in A.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, it has been said many times, but this is very, very close, and I’ve thought about it quite a bit, obviously.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a lot of sympathy for President Plosser’s very clear analysis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There have been good data since the last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have talked about the importance of spillovers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have not so far seen evident spillovers from housing into other sectors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We did take a preemptive action in the last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think not immediately, but some of the factors like input costs are there, and market expectations alone are obviously not a reason to move.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All of those things are valid, and I have thought about all of them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So why do I favor a cut?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most of the arguments have been made.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The downside risks are quite significant, if the housing situation, including prices, really deteriorates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think part of the difference between what the market sees about housing and what we see is that we are a little more sanguine about price behavior than the market is, and a decline in prices has effects both on consumers and on the credit system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that risk is fairly important and may swamp some of the other issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is some new information that is relevant.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The senior loan officer survey and other information suggest that credit conditions are tightening and that this will have an effect, I believe, in some significant markets, certainly including housing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other information, like consumer sentiment and consumers’ views of the labor market, suggests some slowing and some weakening.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The decline in sentiment in the markets in the past two weeks is very interesting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On one level I feel as though we failed to communicate somehow; however, I don’t know exactly where the mistake was.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The markets seem to be responding to information about earnings reports and projections of future activity and so on, both in the financial sector and in the real sector, and as a number of people have said, I don’t think we can entirely ignore that information.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think there are some good reasons on the real side to take out a bit more insurance, as has been said.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with the Vice Chairman that the credit markets probably could stand the surprise, but they have become somewhat more uncertain, and I think their basic problem is macro uncertainty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has to do with concerns about tail risk, and that is something that we can, I think, address a bit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The point has been made a number of times, first by President Yellen, that the current rate could be construed as being slightly restrictive and that creates an argument for a somewhat lower rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: An additional argument is that the core inflation rate has come down some since last year, and so the real federal funds rate on that basis has gone up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, an argument that I would bring to you is about tactics, and the Vice Chairman also alluded to this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most of the paths that we submitted include a path for policy that is perhaps slightly lower than the current one, and the question is how we do this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we take alternative B, which I think is the most obvious alternative, on the one hand we don’t take an action and on the other hand we express alarm about the economy and say we’ll probably be cutting in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That makes calibrating how the longer-term expectations will respond to that very difficult.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it would, on balance, tighten expectations a bit because we didn’t act, but it does create some uncertainty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The advantage of alternative A, even as we take a cut, is that we will, I hope, curb expectations for sustained additional cuts through several mechanisms.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, in the economic growth paragraph, we have switched language from actions “intended to help forestall”—very indirect—to “should help forestall,” suggesting that we are now more confident in our ability to prevent bad outcomes in the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, we have—and this will certainly be noticed—taken note of energy and commodity prices, among other factors, and we have highlighted our concerns about inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Third, the rough balance of risks certainly indicates that we are not eager to cut again quickly unless the data clearly support it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So a lot of this is tactical, about how to take control of expectations— you know, how to manage the market’s views of our policies.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I just felt a bit more comfortable with taking the action but then using that to recalibrate our balance of risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For what it is worth, 75 basis points of easing has been pretty much the standard Fed medicine for financial crises ever since 1970 or so; in that respect we are in good company.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s my recommendation—25 basis points with alternative A.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: With the Mishkin amendment or without?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What exactly was the Mishkin amendment?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It was to add a phrase before the downside risks to growth to say, “The Committee judges that the upside risks to inflation roughly balance the somewhat reduced downside risks to growth.” It would give a flavor that, in fact, our actions have reduced the downside risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, by saying that the action “should help forestall” instead of “is intended to forestall” I think we address that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I didn’t feel strongly about this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It was just maybe I’ll do it in speeches afterward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other comment that came up, I think President Hoenig and President Stern mentioned it, is not exactly softening but emphasizing the uncertainty that surrounds our judgment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So another possibility, and I have always regretted making suggestions on the statement, is that we could take the first sentence from the September paragraph 4, cut out the phrase “since the Committee’s last regular meeting,” and say, “Developments in financial markets have increased the uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, the Committee judges that .

speaker: BERNANKE
text: .,” and we could put that at the beginning of the assessment of risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess my prejudice is, unless there is strong sentiment, to stay with what we have because that is what people have talked about.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the problem with that is that developments of financial markets on balance since the last meeting have been reassuring.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The disruptions are more contained, and so I don’t think that works.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, Ms. Danker will call the roll.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s just note for the record that for the first time we will be voting on the entire statement.

speaker: DANKER
text: I will start with the directive from the Bluebook.

speaker: DANKER
text: The language is as follows: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: DANKER
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with reducing the federal funds rate to an average of around 4½ percent.” Then the statement, which I will not read in its entirety, is as written under alternative A in the revised October 31 table that was handed out.

speaker: DANKER
text: Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes President Evans Yes President Hoenig No Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes Governor Mishkin Yes President Poole Yes President Rosengren Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I need to have the Board for a moment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just address quickly the last item on the agenda, which is communications.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On October 19, you received a memo from the subcommittee that describes the latest round of changes to the projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I won’t repeat what they are, but if there are questions, we can take them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t believe we received any comments on this round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll talk in a moment about getting this ready for prime time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But what I’d like to talk about now is, as I discussed in September, asking the Committee for a consensus to release these projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They would be released with the minutes of the current meeting on November 20, which is one day less than three weeks because Wednesday is the day before Thanksgiving.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we would release it on Tuesday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The necessary explanation of the projections—what they mean and how to interpret them—would be in a speech that I propose to give on November 14.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That speech would be preceded by a press release from the FOMC describing the plan in general terms.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You received copies of the press release.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Michelle, do we have other copies?

speaker: SMITH
text: It was not changed from what you received.

speaker: SMITH
text: I have extra copies if you need one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If anyone needs a copy, Michelle is happy to give you one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would talk in general terms about this approach, why we’re doing it, what the implications are, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d be happy to share my draft remarks with anyone who would like to look at them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me be clear—I do not plan to reveal any of the data from the projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They would be released to the public for the first time in the minutes, and so it would obviously be very important for everyone not to release that information.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Your speech is November 14?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My speech is November 14, and the release of the minutes will be on November 20.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would give people some time to digest the ideas.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The press release would be on the morning of November 14 before my speech.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On previous occasions when the FOMC has announced communication changes, they have followed the meeting by some weeks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not unusual for that to happen.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are questions about timing, whether we should think about doing it later.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We had some discussions about this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My own view is that this was the most convenient time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: January would run into the monetary policy hearings, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are serious problems in the markets or anything like that, I am prepared to add material about the markets or to substitute another speech—to do whatever is necessary to address that issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I do think that, besides the natural rhythm and the fact that we are about as far as we are going to get in fine-tuning this, the fact that this has appeared in the press suggests that we should just go ahead and get it out soon, if possible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In a moment I’m going to ask you for your comments, and then I’ll ask you for your consensus—first, on releasing the material and, second, on the speech and the rollout of the press release.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just say that, as Brian indicated, we do have until tomorrow close of business to revise our projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is the real thing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Please take a look at your projections in light of this morning’s data and in light of the discussion today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the future we will not be doing this every meeting, only four times a year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in that respect it won’t be such a burden as I know it has been.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I urge you please to do that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me now open the floor for any comments or questions about projections, the rollout plan, or anything.

speaker: POOLE
text: Brian talked about the skewness, which I gather we are going to describe in words but not use the histogram.

speaker: POOLE
text: I have the following question about the skewness.

speaker: POOLE
text: I was one of those who said “broadly similar,” and here’s how I would look at it.

speaker: POOLE
text: You start with some point estimate.

speaker: POOLE
text: Let’s make it simple—next year, fourth quarter to fourth quarter.

speaker: POOLE
text: You ask yourself how far down you would have to move the point estimate such that the probability to the right and the left would be about the same.

speaker: POOLE
text: If the amount that you would have to move that point estimate is a fraction of a standard error, then I would interpret it, roughly speaking, as that there are symmetrical risks.

speaker: POOLE
text: I just have the suspicion that people who are talking about “weighted to the downside” are in a way mixing up the first moment and the third moment of the probability distribution.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I worry that, as I think Brian was worrying, that this will give a message that’s going to interfere with the communication that we also want to offer about the policy path.

speaker: POOLE
text: That’s the best way I can think about it—to ask about how far you would have to move your point estimate to make the probability to the right or left roughly the same.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would also note that the Greenbook, for example, has reduced the point estimate for next year ¾ percentage point from June to now, roughly speaking.

speaker: POOLE
text: Maybe I can even ask Dave about whether he thinks the distribution around the current point estimate is very skewed, and I could also go on and ask how far down he would have to move that point estimate to make the probability to the right and left about the same.

speaker: POOLE
text: The other point that I want to make—and it is really in many ways a much more important point—is that, when we disclose the 2010 inflation projection and presumably, Mr. Chairman, at the February monetary policy hearings—assuming that some member of the Congress actually asks you a question related to monetary policy, which is not a given—[laughter] a very logical question either then or sometime in the future would be where you personally stand, what your number is in that projection.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would very much like to know that answer in advance because I would be more than happy to conform my estimate, which I regard as a target, to the number that you would throw out.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think there’s an issue here.

speaker: POOLE
text: In an inflation projection for 2010 that varies from roughly 1.5 to 2, the numbers are materially different, and I think that question is going to come back at us over and over again.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I won’t say any more about that, but I do believe that I would hate to be in a position of having to explain why my number is different from yours.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, let me say first on the mode and the median, you make a good point on the first issue about risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The question to ask yourself is, Given your most likely forecast, on which side are the largest and most costly deviations most likely to occur.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In which direction are the risks skewed?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is the way to think about it.

speaker: POOLE
text: Well, I would keep separate the cost from the distribution itself.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: No, I don’t think so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think you ought to put in some costs—

speaker: POOLE
text: I’m not saying I would ignore the costs, but maybe we need to be clear about what this probability distribution is supposed to mean.

speaker: POOLE
text: I thought that this was supposed to mean simply the weights that I would give on various possible outcomes in terms of the probability that the forecast might be 1 percentage point below or 1 percentage point above the central tendency, however I described it.

speaker: POOLE
text: Now, I agree that a full analysis requires that you also add the costs to those, but I would interpret that as not being part of the projections process for GDP and inflation but rather you’d fold that in through the policy decision as to how you weight those various possible outcomes.

speaker: POOLE
text: But I have interpreted it all along as being really a statement about your probability distribution on the outcomes unweighted by the severity of the outcome.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the answer would be pretty similar in either case.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we can discuss this at another time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On your second question, I think I’m kind of a special case because people will overweight what I say if I give a number.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I would not give a number, and what I would say is that what matters are the views of the broad Committee, and I don’t want to distinguish myself from the broad Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is a Committee decision process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If individuals want to give their numbers, I suppose that’s okay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I would urge you to consider the externality a bit, which is that there will be some desire to figure out who is where on the distribution in order to assess who is holding which type of policy preference and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Certainly many of us have often given our views of what price stability is and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think I want to prohibit that, but my recommendation would be to be a little fuzzy, a bit careful about being too precise and too sharp about that number.

speaker: POOLE
text: Well, it won’t really matter very much with me because I will be out of here before too long, but I have long been on record as bringing the number down, and so I can’t back off that.

speaker: POOLE
text: That’s what I believe, and so I’m going to keep that.

speaker: POOLE
text: But I’ll disappear from the calculus next spring anyway.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I appreciate your answer.

speaker: FISHER
text: The one worry I have had about this exercise, which is much better the way it is now expressed and presented—I think it is ready for prime time—is that we might be divided as to our individual instincts.

speaker: FISHER
text: We do operate as a Committee.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have said this a million times, but I’d like to reiterate it.

speaker: FISHER
text: To me it’s the last bastion of integrity here in Washington.

speaker: FISHER
text: To go down a path of who is saying what just threatens to tear us apart, and I would urge your response on everybody else as well.

speaker: FISHER
text: Thank you for the spirit in which you answered that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Has there been any reaction to the Greg Ip story?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Have we received any feedback from the principal audience for the projections?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yes, and there have been no problems.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The response has been positive.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I want to come back to President Poole’s question.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: President Poole, you said a fraction of a standard error.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: How large a fraction of a standard error would you want to use as a basis?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Really, I’m not sure what the standard error is in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But just in terms of how you think about this, how large a fraction of the standard error?

speaker: POOLE
text: Well, I was one of those who put down B—that both the distribution and the skewness were broadly similar to the past twenty years.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I came out that way.

speaker: POOLE
text: I was trying to offer a way to think about this issue and, for those who believe that the probability distribution is way over on one side, a way to think about it: How far would you have to move that point estimate?

speaker: POOLE
text: I wasn’t trying to give the answer; I was trying to give a way to approach the question.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, maybe we should clarify just this one point.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Did you leave the question about—I don’t know what this chart is called; it is not going to be in the addendum to the minutes—what those bars show about the balance of risk?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Is it about just the probability of the outcome or about the probability of outcome and the costs or consequences of the outcome?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: May I ask the staff, do you have institutional memory on this question?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I am not sure what the question is exactly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is the skew that determines the risks simply the probability of outcomes, or is it the probability weighted by the cost of certain outcomes?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, I think it is a matter of how the members interpreted it in responding.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The memorandum to the Committee asks whether the risks around your projection for each variable are weighted to the upside, weighted to the downside, or broadly balanced.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the balance of risk statement in the announcement has had the utility weight on it; there have been times when the Committee was more concerned about falling to one side or another.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I at least interpreted the forecast as simply whether there were skews to one side or another.

speaker: KOHN
text: If I may have the floor to talk a bit to President Poole’s point.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we do say in the statement that there are upside risks to inflation and downside risks to growth.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I would be concerned if the whole Committee shifted to the middle because then I think we would be contradicting the announcement that we made, so I think your point is good.

speaker: KOHN
text: I mean, you ought to be sure that you really do think there is downside risk to growth and upside risk to inflation, or whatever, and adjust it for the policy choice that we made today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The utility cost is relevant in the statement, and you can’t take a balance of risks unless you compare them in terms of cost.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is no other metric by which you can compare them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in that case, it has to be cost-weighted.

speaker: BERNANKE
