text: But I think it is more or less equivalent—the univariate answers you are giving about mode versus median.

speaker: POOLE
text: But if we view the projections as being a statement just about the probability distribution of the various outcomes, this might be an important point for you to explain in the speech that you give because the whole thing is labeled projections—I guess we have been calling it a “projections exercise”—and so I have interpreted that as a discussion of the numbers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we won’t go too far wrong by interpreting it as a probability distribution in the shape of the probability distribution for outcomes.

speaker: POOLE
text: That’s the way I have interpreted it.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the risk of introducing further moments of the probability distribution into the discussion, have we been instructed as to whether our projection is a mean or a maximum-likelihood estimate?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think our standard procedure is that it is a modal.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The memorandum to the Committee says, “Please provide your projections of the most likely outcomes,” et cetera.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m sorry, President Plosser, we have kept you waiting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t have any comments.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just wanted to say that I think the staff has done a great job and the subcommittee has done a great job.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is a very important step forward for us, and I am strongly supportive of it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I want to thank Governor Kohn, Janet Yellen, and the other members of the subcommittee for getting us here and you for taking this step forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe that, as we go through this time after time, it will be refined.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We will stumble over a few things and the language is going to be tricky, but I just want to commend the Committee for taking this step.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me also commend Governor Kohn, President Stern, and President Yellen for their excellent work.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I just want to return to the point that the Chairman, President Poole, and President Fisher raised.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In my conversations, people have expressed different views at this juncture about what the optimal long-run inflation rate is.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: People know that I am a 2 percent kind of guy, and I know good people here who are 1½ percent kinds of guys.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But in talking to people about this, I hear a lot more consensus and that people don’t feel strongly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I would be in concert with what President Poole said.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If the Chairman said, “How about X?”, I would be more than happy to say, “Giddyap, I am with the Chairman.” So, again, my colorful language.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But the key point here is that I think it would be very helpful at this juncture that people really not emphasize differences but that, in fact, there really is consensus on this Committee.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That takes one of two forms.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is if you had something in the past, that’s fine; but you can say that you had that in the past but you are actually comfortable with where the general Committee is, and that way you can soften it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Two is a case in which somebody like me has not actually publicly talked about an inflation goal.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that case, I would keep my mouth shut on the issue.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In terms of this initial launch—again emphasizing the fact that there really is a lot of consensus on the Committee because we know that the press loves to create the opposite of consensus because it sells newspapers—the more we can be supportive and to the extent that we can look unified on this, the better off we are.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I sense that is actually where the Committee is, so I would encourage it in this process.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I just wanted a clarification.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In the explanation, will we say that the projections are based on what we have done?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: For example, today, given that we are having a policy move and I am not sure that everyone around the table had anticipated that move today in their path, will we be articulating that these are not the numbers that we came into the meeting with, but these are the numbers that we think after the policy action has been taken?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yes, let’s do that because it will be more consistent with the statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me ask everyone to rethink their risks conditional on our policy move today.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Sorry, Mr. Chairman, two points.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One is a concern to which I have no solution.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The chart that is now called chart 1, which has evolved over time, has a slight disadvantage, because it doesn’t have fans around it because we all didn’t like the fans, of having the sense of a pretty narrow range of likely outcomes for the future.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just wonder whether anybody is uneasy, given the relatively low probability that we are going to end up within those over time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t have a solution to this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I was wondering whether, if you changed the scale—[laughter].

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is a concern with no real suggested solution—I apologize.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My second point is more significant.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Bill, I think you asked a good question.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, another question that is interesting is, when asked whether the world should interpret the central tendency of the Committee at a three-year horizon for PCE inflation as the rate that is consistent with the Committee’s long-run view of price stability, how will you answer it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It represents the diversity of views on the Committee about that, with the additional caveat that not everyone may necessarily believe that we will approach their ideal level of price stability even in three years, conceivably.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is a mixture of elements, and that’s what I will talk about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, if you would like to look at the speech—

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that is consistent with how it is described and what is discussed, but it just goes to the point that, Bill, you raise, which is for some of you your optimal horizon is always going to be two years or three years.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But you said all that could be said, I think, about that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I’m sorry, but I need to understand what you just implied.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Are we to go back now and redo our projections for this meeting under the assumption that we took the action today?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you wouldn’t mind, yes.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: And appropriate policy going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But it’s not what I based my decision on.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Tom, if you took a view about what appropriate policy was last Friday and you have a chance now to assess, in light of what the Committee did, what appropriate policy is going forward, whether that has changed, and what implications that change has for your forecast—isn’t that the way to say it?

speaker: HOENIG
text: But the whole point of the process was to prepare us for this meeting, and now I am going to go back and reassess the process I went through in light of what took place in this meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If everyone is comfortable with doing that, then I would be happy and able to do it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: At least I understand that we are all going in the same direction that way.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I am fine with it, as long as that is what, in fact, we’re doing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But the Greenbook won’t be changed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This confuses me a bit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wasn’t quite clear—I thought I was, but I guess I wasn’t.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We can do whatever we want as long as we all agree to do the same thing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If that’s it, then I’ll go back and do it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I just want to make sure that’s what we all agree we’re going to do.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If that is, then fine; but I didn’t have that understanding before you made that statement.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Is there an inconsistency in adjusting a forecast after the meeting when the minutes are the minutes of the meeting and the forecasts informed the judgments that were expressed in the meeting?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: No, I don’t think so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is based on the information in the meeting, including the data we received this morning.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’m not sure I see minutes reflecting subsequent actions or subsequent decisions.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’re releasing this with the minutes?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re releasing it with the minutes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not part of the minutes.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It’s like an annual report that has updated information in it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As long as everyone is doing the same thing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I hope, President Hoenig, that you won’t be in this situation too often.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I’ve got a long record, and I haven’t been in this situation too often.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But I have been in this situation before.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any other questions or comments?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: May I have the sense of the Committee to proceed with the release?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I appreciate it, and I appreciate everyone’s hard work and cooperation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think this is a very important step, and I am very pleased with the outcome.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just describe now the sequence of events.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will now give you the date of the next meeting, and I will adjourn the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Laricke Blanchard is here to talk briefly about congressional issues for us, and the lunch for Cathy Minehan begins at 12:30.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So our next meeting will be Tuesday, December 11.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to start by thanking the Committee for the very useful discussion we had last week, although I must say that videoconference is not the most intimate format.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: People raised a number of important reservations about the TAF, including the fact that capital, perhaps more than liquidity, is the issue now; issues about the size of it; and concern about stigma.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that those points are well taken and that we need to be modest in our expectations about at least the initial effect of this facility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, as I indicated last week, I think that it will perhaps provide a platform for us to create a more flexible tool that will allow us to use our discount window facilities in a more effective way as we go forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the near term, it has also provided a good vehicle for us to cooperate with other central banks, and I would like to update you on that now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, the Board did approve the TAF on Friday by notation vote, as we expected.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, we have been in communication with the whole G-10 about these matters and have widespread support from our colleagues for this action.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, I believe that you have a draft press release that will be very similar to what will be released tomorrow morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s at 8:30 a.m. now?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It will be a joint release of five central banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The press release will have a common first paragraph, as you see in front of you, and then each central bank will describe its own actions in more detail, followed by web links to the other central banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, the European Central Bank will take the $20 billion in swaps that we approved last week and will do two essentially noncompetitive auctions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is, they will allocate $20 billion in two tranches to European banks needing dollars at the price that clears the U.S. TAF, so they may have to ration or otherwise allocate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Swiss National Bank will also do a $4 billion one-time auction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s see, they are going to do an actual auction.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think with a reservation price.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: With a reservation price is our understanding.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The minimum bid will be one-month OIS.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So they have the same auction plan that we have, essentially.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, we are being joined by the British, who are doing two auctions of £10 billion each before year-end.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: These are sterling auctions, not dollar auctions, but they are in fact of the same actual size as ours—an indication of the appreciation of the pound.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, the Canadians were already planning to do some auctions before the end of the year, and they will simply join us in announcing those at the same time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, the Japanese and the Swedes, although not planning anything in the near term, will issue statements supporting our actions and affirming their willingness to support liquidity as necessary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I think our expectations should be modest.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is not a one-shot deal.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will continue to try to address these problems, but I am hopeful that the international aspect of this will also be at least somewhat reassuring to markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be, I think, a bit of disappointment today that we don’t cut the discount rate spread; but by tomorrow morning, I hope that will be resolved one way or another.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A few people have asked about informing their boards.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have no objection to your informing your board if you wish in advance of the announcement—so long, of course, as it is with the usual confidentiality rules.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I might suggest to you to consider is that perhaps a compromise between doing nothing and informing your whole board might be to give a call to your chairman sometime today and just give a heads-up, if you choose.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am just indicating that we have no objection, to your doing that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is one piece of business remaining associated with this, which is that we have to approve the $4 billion swap request from the Swiss National Bank.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I would propose to do is allow Bill to begin his report on Desk operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Subsequent to that, we can take questions, either on the financial conditions that Bill describes, on any of these aspects, and then I would like, along with the ratification of operations, to ask you at that time also for a vote on the swap.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if there is no question or comment at this point, I will turn to Bill.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I will be referring to the exhibits that you should have in front of you.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Over the past few months, the outlook for residential housing has continued to darken.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Rising inventories and tightening credit standards have led to outright declines in home prices in many major housing markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The deterioration in the subprime mortgage space continues.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 1, delinquency and foreclosure rates for subprime mortgages continue to rise very quickly; and as before, the degree and the pace of deterioration are much worse for more recent vintages (see exhibit 2).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But most important, the problems in residential mortgages can no longer be thought of as a subprime or even an alt-A mortgage problem.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 3, delinquency and foreclosure rates on prime mortgages have moved up sharply in recent months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The ongoing deterioration in the housing market has had a number of important implications.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The first important development is that highly rated collateralized debt obligation (CDO) tranches—including so-called super-senior AAA-rated tranches— are now vulnerable.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is because these tranches typically are backstopped, in part, by lower-rated subprime ABS tranches and other mortgage-related securities product.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For highly rated CDO tranches to be protected against loss, it is important that the average loss rate on the underlying collateral stays relatively low and that the correlation in loss performance among the different assets that underpin the CDO stays low.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Unfortunately, for many of the CDOs issued in 2006 and 2007, these conditions no longer apply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As housing has deteriorated, not only have expected loss rates climbed, but the correlation among the assets within CDOs has also moved sharply higher.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This has occurred because a growing proportion of BBB-rated and A-rated ABS tranches now appear likely to suffer losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At a 10 percent average 1 Materials used by Mr. Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: loss rate on subprime ARMs, many BBB- and A-rated tranches are likely to survive.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There is a dispersion of loss rates—say between 5 percent and 15 percent—that helps keep correlations low.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But at a 15 percent loss rate, the same degree of dispersion protects many fewer tranches than before.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Instead, most of these tranches will become impaired.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As this occurs, the correlation rate will climb sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The net result is that CDO tranches that were thought to be safe become highly vulnerable to losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibits 4 and 5 illustrate the sensitivity of CDO performance to the mortgage loan-loss rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These exhibits summarize a study by UBS of a large number of CDOs brought to market in 2006 and 2007.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 4 shows how sensitive the performance of the CDO market is to changes in underlying mortgage loss rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The base case scenario assumes a relatively favorable loss experience.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, in the base case, losses for subprime mortgages are assumed to be about 11 percent for both 2006 and 2007 vintages.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In this case, total loss estimates for mezzanine CDOs are around 20 percent and less than 5 percent for high-grade CDOs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the base case, the losses for the super-senior tranches are trivial.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But when loss estimates increase 50 percent above the base case, loss estimates on the CDO tranches climb much more sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, the average losses for the mezzanine CDOs triple, rising six times faster than the rise in underlying loan losses, and expected losses on the super-senior mezzanine CDO tranches soar.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In this case, they are anticipated to lose about one- half of their value.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 5 focuses on how a relatively modest change in the loss rate on the underlying mortgages leads to a sharp shift in the distribution of losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the base case, the super-senior tranches of most CDOs are expected to suffer no losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, at the higher loss rate on the underlying mortgages, about half the super-senior tranches are expected to lose more than half their value.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The CDO market is now fully implicated in the housing crisis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rating agencies are now downgrading many CDOs, and the magnitude of the downgrades is often quite large.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, the value of many CDOs has fallen sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This has led to (1) large write-downs at some major financial institutions and (2) questions about the financial health of the financial guarantors that ensure some of the super- senior CDO tranches and that have other exposure to the residential mortgage market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 6 illustrates the large movements in two of the major financial guarantors’ share prices and credit default swaps over the last few months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moody’s recently indicated that MBIA—generally perceived as one of the stronger players—is “somewhat likely” to need to raise more capital to avoid a credit-rating downgrade.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: MBIA announced yesterday that they are raising $1 billion in equity capital from Warburg Pincus.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The total outstanding volume of asset-backed commercial paper has begun to contract more rapidly again (see exhibit 7).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This contraction appears relatively broad- based—it is not just an SIV story.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Master Liquidity Enhancement Conduit (MLEC) continues to move slowly forward, with the syndication process having just started.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the MLEC is not likely to be very large.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: SIV assets have already shrunk sharply, and some banks have already taken SIV assets back on their own balance sheets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The difficulties of the SIVs have affected some money market investment funds—with the State of Florida’s Local Government Investment Pool the most notable casualty in this regard.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fortunately, most money market funds that have SIV exposure are backed by strong parents that have been willing to lend support, at least up till now.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second key development—the deterioration in the performance of the broader mortgage market—has had its own set of effects on the financial sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, it has led to significant loan-loss provision charges and mark-to-market losses for the two major housing GSEs—Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The result has been a sharp decline in their share prices and a substantial rise in the cost of credit default swaps for these institutions (see exhibit 8).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the mortgage insurers have also been implicated, with even more substantial share price declines and increases in the cost of credit default protection (see exhibit 9).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In addition, the big thrift institutions remain under pressure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yesterday, for example, Washington Mutual announced large loan-loss provisions and other write-downs and slashed its common stock dividend.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For commercial banks, the consequence of CDO write-downs and of rising mortgage and other loan losses has been even more pressure on capital ratios and on balance sheets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, corporate debt spreads have increased markedly over the past few months (see exhibit 10).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rise in high-yield debt spreads is important for banks that still have significant leveraged-loan exposure that they hope to distribute to the capital markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The widening in spreads suggests a risk of further mark-to-market charges for banks for these exposures.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So is there any good news in any of this?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would emphasize four aspects that might provide some modest reassurance.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, market participants know a lot more now than they did before.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Thus, fear is diminishing, which implies less risk of a crisis developing from this source.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, although there remain considerable uncertainties on many fronts—such as the magnitude of mortgage losses, the degree of further tightening of credit availability, and the fate of some thrifts and mortgage and financial guarantors, I believe we may have finally defined the broad dimensions of the crisis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Most of those who are likely to be implicated may already have been identified, with the CDO debacle the latest installment that has widened the circle of participants.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The issue now seems to be shifting toward severity from dimension.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, the market is resolving some aspects of the crisis on its own.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, the level of SIV assets has shrunk sharply since August.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fourth, several major financial institutions, in addition to MBIA and Washington Mutual, have raised capital from disparate sources.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Citigroup and UBS are raising funds from sovereign wealth funds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: E*Trade raised funds from a major hedge fund.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have raised capital through preferred stock issues.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The willingness of opportunistic investors to make such commitments may limit the balance sheet squeeze somewhat and put a floor—albeit a low one—under asset prices.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Let me turn next to market expectations about the path of short-term interest rates at this meeting and beyond.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 11 shows expectations for the current meeting, calculated from options prices on federal funds rate futures.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, the probability of a 25 basis point cut has climbed to about 70 percent, and the probability of no change in the target federal funds rate has fallen virtually to zero.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 12 and 13, expectations for subsequent rate cuts have increased considerably since the October meeting, whether one looks at the yields implied from federal funds futures contracts or from Eurodollar futures contracts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Looking out to the end of 2008, rate expectations have fallen more than 50 basis points since the October FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Eurodollar futures rate for December 2008 implies more than 100 basis points of additional easing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Our survey of primary dealers also shows a sharp shift downward in rate expectations since the October FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown by comparing exhibit 14 with exhibit 15, the average of the dealer modal forecasts for the federal funds rate target in the first quarter—the green circles in the exhibits—fell about 30 basis points, and the average of the dealer modal forecasts does not differ meaningfully from market expectations at that time period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, longer term, the primary dealers’ forecasts seem to anticipate less easing than market participants.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But this may reflect more the downward skew to rate expectations that pulls the mean below the mode rather than a more fundamental difference in expectations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As has been the case for several months, there is a very wide dispersion of forecasts one year ahead, with the primary dealers’ modal forecasts now ranging from 2.5 percent to 4.75 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Despite an expectation of more-aggressive easing, inflation expectations appear to be well anchored.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 16 shows two measures that I discussed at the October FOMC meeting—the market- based Barclays measure of five-year, five-year forward inflation versus the Board staff measure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, although the gap between these two measures has remained much wider than earlier in the year—presumably reflecting, in part, a climb in the liquidity premium for on-the-run nominal Treasuries—both measures have moved down a bit since the October FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, a very brief discussion of the Desk’s open market operations is warranted.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As seen in exhibit 17, which shows the cumulative effective federal funds rate since the last meeting, we have managed to keep the federal funds rate close to the target on average.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But it hasn’t been easy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you can see, the rate did trade a bit soft to the target early in the intermeeting period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, we continue to see upward pressure on the federal funds rate early in the day—reflecting a strong bid by European banks— and much greater intraday and day-to-day volatility than before August.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There were no foreign operations during this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I request a vote to ratify the operations conducted by the System Open Market Account since the October 30-31 FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I also request a vote to ratify the swap agreement with the Swiss National Bank that Chairman Bernanke discussed earlier.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, I am very happy to take questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Bill on financial conditions or for Bill or me on the TAF proposal?

speaker: POOLE
text: I have an observation, and that is, Bill, that most of your presentation has to do with spreads rather than with the absolute level of rates.

speaker: POOLE
text: Although it is true that spreads remain wide, the absolute level of the high-quality rates in general has come down, I believe.

speaker: POOLE
text: Prime mortgage rates are down, and it seems to me that if we look only at spreads then, of course, our actions to reduce the federal funds rate target may not show up for quite some time.

speaker: POOLE
text: In fact, I think most people have the sense that spreads had gotten too narrow and they may end up being elevated for a long time even as a “permanent” matter.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I think it is very important to look at the level of rates as well as the spreads, and I insert the comment—and I notice you’re nodding your head “yes”—that the rates on high-quality paper have in general come down.

speaker: POOLE
text: The rates on riskier paper are perhaps higher than they were, let’s say, in July.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, I think that is correct.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If you look at chart 10, which shows corporate credit spreads, you have a widening of about 50 basis points in investment-grade corporate spreads at a time that long-term—you know, ten-year—Treasury note yields have come down by I think a little larger magnitude.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, in the high-yield debt market, you have a widening of spreads of 200 basis points just in the last month and a half or two months, which is much more dramatic than any decline that we have seen in Treasury rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: I asked the staff to put together a table—the table III-T-1 that we get in the Greenbook—and compare rates with August 6.

speaker: KOHN
text: It turns out that all the rates are about the same as they were on August 6 for the bond yields, and equity prices are essentially unchanged, maybe down or up—actually up—just a tick.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I would say that the 75 basis points of easing we did and the additional 100 that the market has priced in since August 6 have had no effect on the cost of long-term credit to corporations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it is probably worth observing that the spreads probably also are correlated with nonprice terms.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it may not be an exactly neutral change.

speaker: FISHER
text: Bill, we talked a bit about this on the phone yesterday, but on the four relatively optimistic points that you mentioned, the fourth point, which is what I call the substitutability of capital, we are seeing new sources.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of them is measurable, which is the GIC in Singapore.

speaker: FISHER
text: But do we have any sense of the dimension that is available for substitution, and is there a way to get a better sense of measurement?

speaker: FISHER
text: I just want to preface this by saying that we went through the petrodollar issue in 1974.

speaker: FISHER
text: Some of us were very involved in that exercise.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is a much more sophisticated business right now, and we have much more sophisticated investors.

speaker: FISHER
text: What we don’t know—or I don’t know and I would be curious whether we know at the New York Desk—is how big this money is and how much is available to be tapped.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I guess I would say two things.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think you are absolutely right that the sovereign wealth funds are of significant size and are growing rapidly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think that you really have to distinguish between the equity side and the debt side of things.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The commitments that you are seeing from the sovereign wealth funds seem to be equity investments, and they are equity investments that have occurred only after share prices fell very sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If you look at debt spreads in the United States, debt spreads in Europe, and debt spreads throughout the world, they have widened.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it doesn’t look as though the sovereign wealth fund money is providing much help for that sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It would be surprising if it were big enough, given the constraints on bank balance sheets globally, that they could come in and fill the gaps.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think, on the equity side, the sovereign wealth funds are pretty important.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They are providing some floor on equity prices, but only after the equity prices of some of these financial firms have gone down very significantly in value.

speaker: FISHER
text: Nonetheless, they can restore tier 1 capital, as we saw in the case of UBS.

speaker: FISHER
text: I mean, that is how markets work.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is a good development that we are actually finally seeing banks raise capital.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think you were seeing that until last month.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would say that there was stigma associated with raising capital, and then things got progressively worse, so banks were just forced to raise capital despite the stigma associated with it.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, I wanted to thank you for at least raising four rays of dim sunlight.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Bill, the trouble with the mortgage insurers has been a development since our last meeting, and I am curious—Do they have the capability for raising capital?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Will raising capital correct or help them get their ratings back to AAA, or is it more complicated than that?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I have read some concerns about the effect, for example, on municipal markets if the guarantors cannot in fact maintain their ratings.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So do you have some insight into their ability to raise capital and correct the potential for a downgrade?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The risk to the municipal market is really through the financial guarantors, not so much the mortgage insurers.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The fact that MBIA was able to raise $1 billion of equity capital yesterday for, I think, about one-seventh of their book value—so it is a fairly large capital commitment relative to the size of the company—is an important development.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You saw that MBIA stock yesterday rose more than 10 percent because it basically was a confirmation, at least in the minds of some people in the market, that MBIA was a viable business and that someone was willing to put $1 billion of new capital in.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that was reassuring to the market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Generally, the people I have talked with suggest that the barriers to entry into those businesses are pretty high.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second thing that is happening is, obviously, as you see this distress, their pricing power on new business is actually improving.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That would suggest that there is a reasonable chance that these firms will be recapitalized, but it depends on how far down the path they are toward serious problems.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have talked to one of the large mortgage insurance companies in some detail, and their view is that their pricing power actually is improving—that their own ability to work their way out of this thing is getting better all the time right now.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Even though they are taking some very large hits in the near term, their outlook actually has improved in recent months, partly because of this.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This was just to reinforce that point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, we need to vote to ratify domestic operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We also need a vote on the Swiss request for a currency swap.

speaker: POOLE
text: I vote against the swap for the same reason that I did before, which I would like to amplify, if I may, just for a moment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t you make your comment, and then we will take a roll call vote.

speaker: POOLE
text: As I said in our conference call, foreign central banks have ample amounts of reserves.

speaker: POOLE
text: The swap is, therefore, in my view not necessary.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would like to make one other observation.

speaker: POOLE
text: In the past, the swaps have been most often used in conjunction with operations to intervene in the foreign exchange markets.

speaker: POOLE
text: I worry that we may get a reaction in the market, given the concerns in Europe about the value of the dollar, that would say that this is a precursor to some sort of coordinated intervention in the foreign exchange market.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would be very opposed to the intervention, I think it would upset things quite substantially, and I would worry that the market concerns that there might be intervention coming would upset the situation on this announcement.

speaker: POOLE
text: So those are my concerns and why I vote against.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will, of course, announce a swap in the context of our plan to address money market issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to the issue of their reserves, I think there are two reasons for having the swap.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that for technical reasons it is easier for them to segregate their foreign exchange reserves from the money they would use in this auction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They felt it was bureaucratically easier for them to do it this way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, this obviously gives us—which is very important for our monetary control—sort of a clear marker in terms of what the size of this operation will be, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But your points are well taken.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, Debbie, could you please read the resolution?

speaker: DANKER
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee directs the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to establish and maintain a reciprocal currency arrangement for the System Open Market Account with the Swiss National Bank in an amount not to exceed $4 billion.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Committee authorizes associated draws on the arrangement up to the full amount of $4 billion.

speaker: DANKER
text: The swap arrangement shall be for a period of up to 180 days, unless extended by the Committee.” Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes President Evans Yes President Hoenig Yes Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes Governor Mishkin Yes President Poole No President Rosengren Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let us turn now to the economic situation and Dave Stockton.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We had a great deal to contend with over the intermeeting period, and the forecast has changed in some important ways.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nevertheless, the basic story underlying our projection remains largely unchanged.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The fallout from the slump in the housing sector, the ongoing turbulence in financial markets, and elevated energy prices result in subpar growth over the next several quarters.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: With some further easing of monetary policy, a leveling-off of oil prices, and a gradual improvement of financial conditions, growth picks back up toward potential in 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The gap in resource utilization that opens up over the next several quarters, in combination with the anticipated flattening-out of energy prices, puts total and core inflation on a mild downtrend over the longer haul.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Overall, our forecast could admittedly be read as still painting a pretty benign picture: Despite all the financial turmoil, the economy avoids recession and, even with steeply higher prices for food and energy and a lower exchange value of the dollar, we achieve some modest edging-off of inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I tried not to take it personally when I received a notice the other day that the Board had approved more- frequent drug-testing for certain members of the senior staff, myself included.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I can assure you, however, that the staff is not going to fall back on the increasingly popular celebrity excuse that we were under the influence of mind- altering chemicals and thus should not be held responsible for this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: No, we came up with this projection unimpaired and on nothing stronger than many late nights of diet Pepsi and vending-machine Twinkies.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: While our basic story hasn’t changed much, the events of the past six weeks have resulted in a considerable darkening of our outlook for activity over the next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In particular, the incoming data have been weaker than expected, the projected path of household net worth has been revised down owing to lower prices for both equities and houses, oil prices average about $7 per barrel higher than in our previous forecast, and the brief improvement in financial conditions that we experienced in September and October has been reversed in recent weeks.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As a consequence, we now project that real GDP will be about flat in the current quarter after having increased at an annual rate of 5 percent in the third quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Although the sharp swing in activity from the third to the fourth quarters is exaggerated by some wide fluctuations in inventory investment, we are reading the incoming data as suggesting that there has been a greater downshift in the underlying pace of growth than we had previously anticipated.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Furthermore, we expect activity to remain sluggish next year, growing 1¼ percent, nearly ½ percentage point less than in our October projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In 2009, real GDP is projected to grow at a 2.1 percent pace, a touch below our previous forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Most of the disappointing news that we have received over the past six weeks has centered on the household sector, most especially on residential construction.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Single- family housing starts came in a bit below expectations, and permits plunged, suggesting some further intensification of the decline in construction activity in the months immediately ahead.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, substantial downward revisions to estimates of new home sales for earlier months indicate that housing demand has been weaker than we previously thought.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Meanwhile, conditions in mortgage markets have deteriorated further and appear likely to remain impaired longer than we had projected in October.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nonprime markets remain moribund, spreads on jumbo mortgages have widened further, and spreads on conforming mortgages to Treasuries have increased.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: These developments along with the weaker incoming data on sales and starts led us to mark down our housing forecast once again.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We now expect that sales and starts will post a further drop of nearly 10 percent by early next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, we have delayed our projected recovery in starts until 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As a consequence, the contraction in residential investment is now expected to subtract over ½ percentage point from the growth of real GDP next year, about ¼ percentage point more than in our October projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In addition to these softer readings on housing activity, the incoming data on consumer spending also have surprised us to the downside.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Real outlays are now estimated to have been nearly flat between August and October, rather than increasing modestly as had earlier appeared to be the case.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That subdued pace seems consistent with the slump in consumer sentiment that has followed in the wake of the increased financial turbulence.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We now project that real PCE increased at a 1¼ percent pace in the current quarter, 1 percentage point less than in the October Greenbook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t want to overstate the strength of our case that a noticeable slowing in consumer spending is under way.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Light motor vehicle sales ran at a 16.2 million unit pace in November, an observation that creates a bit of tension with the survey reports of bummed-out consumers.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, it wouldn’t take much more than a few modest upward revisions to earlier months or a pop in spending in December to undermine this part of our story.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That said, the picture doesn’t seem likely to us to brighten much soon.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The recent jump in oil prices, coupled with a restoration of currently narrow gasoline margins, points to steep increases in retail energy prices that will take a bite out of the purchasing power of household incomes and further restrain overall consumer spending in coming months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Furthermore, with the lower level of the stock market and a downward revision to our house-price forecast, household net worth is expected to exert more of a drag on consumer spending over the next two years than in our previous forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: While we don’t expect a dramatic shift, we are anticipating that households will face tighter standards and more-expensive terms for consumer credit.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: All told, we are projecting real PCE to increase 1½ percent in 2008, about ¼ percentage point less than in our October projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In contrast to the almost uniformly weaker-than-expected data on the household sector, the information that we have received on business spending has been more mixed.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Investment in high-tech equipment has been well below our expectations, especially for communications equipment.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That observation squares with some reports we have heard that orders for high-tech gear from financial institutions have fallen off.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Other equipment spending has come in close to our expectations, with the recent data on orders and shipments consistent with our projection for some modest slowing in capital spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The data also have been mixed for nonresidential structures.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As I noted at the last meeting, the GDP data for the third quarter pointed to stronger drilling activity than we had earlier anticipated, and we have revised up our projection for this category in response to both the incoming data and the higher projected path for energy prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For nonresidential buildings, the October data for construction put in place were a bit below our expectations, and we have lowered our near-term projection of activity in this sector.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Beyond the near term, we have reduced our forecast for both equipment spending and nonresidential investment.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Most of that revision reflects an expected endogenous response of investment to the slower growth of final sales and business output in this projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we also have made some small allowance for what we expect to be less favorable financing conditions and greater uncertainty over the next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Taken as a whole, the spending data have clearly fallen short of our expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It might appear that, like the spending data, last week’s labor market report was also a downside surprise for us; after all, we noted in the Greenbook that we had penciled in an increase of 100,000 for private payrolls in November.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: However, we did that only grudgingly after seeing the ADP survey last Wednesday morning, and basically we did not allow that change to alter any other important aspect of our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In fact, the payroll employment figures are slightly stronger than we expected at the time of the October Greenbook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, I still see the generally firm conditions in labor markets as suggesting some upside risk to our view that the economy is in the process of slowing sharply.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Let me now turn to the inflation forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Total PCE prices are projected to increase at an annual rate of 3½ percent in the current quarter, about ¾ percentage point above our previous forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Most of that revision reflects higher retail energy prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we have also raised our projection of core PCE prices for the third and fourth quarters by ¼ percentage point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That adjustment resulted from the upward revisions made by the BEA to nonmarket prices in earlier months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, we had been consistently surprised by the mild increases in nonmarket prices that had been reported since the spring.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As a concession to those persistent errors, a couple of forecast rounds ago, we pushed off the reacceleration of those prices into 2008.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Well, we should have stuck with our earlier story because the revised data now show that those prices picked back up in late summer and early fall.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Our slight upward revision to core PCE prices in 2008, from 1.9 to 2.0 percent, reflects the indirect effects of the higher oil prices in this projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We continue to believe that the pass-through of energy prices is small, but not zero.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other major influences on our price projection have remained relatively tame.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Although the exchange value of the dollar has fallen a bit, global prices for non-oil commodities have revised down as well, leaving the forecast for core non-oil import prices roughly unchanged.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Increases in labor compensation remain subdued.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: And taken as a whole, readings on inflation expectations have not changed much.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The Michigan survey measures of inflation expectations are up some, the Survey of Professional Forecasters was flat, and inflation compensation as inferred from TIPS has edged down slightly.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: With some slack emerging in labor and product markets in the second half of next year and with energy and import prices projected to decelerate, we are forecasting a slight drop in core price inflation from its projected pace of 2 percent this year and next to 1.9 percent in 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In contemplating our forecast, you might be concerned that our relatively benign muddle-through scenario is increasingly looking like the average of two considerably less benign outcomes—one in which the economy proves considerably more resilient, growth bounces back more quickly, and inflation picks up by more than we are projecting and another in which we drop below stall speed and the economy experiences outright recession.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: While I would readily acknowledge those risks, I still see something like our forecast as the more plausible outcome at this point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At the September meeting, I quoted from the Greenbook of March 1999, in which we had raised the white flag of surrender on our story that the financial turbulence of the autumn of 1998 would significantly restrain the growth of the economy.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We could be making that mistake again, but it seems less likely to me now.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In particular, one important feature of the episode of the late 1990s was that we were almost immediately fighting the incoming data, much of which came in well above our expectations over the final months of 1998 and early 1999.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: By contrast, as I have noted today, the recent data seem to be lining up comfortably with our projection of slower growth ahead.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I also noted in September the possibility that we could be facing a situation similar to the fall of 2000, when we were forecasting a period of muddling through but were, in fact, on the brink of a mild recession.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, this possibility certainly can’t be ruled out.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But here, as well, there are some noteworthy differences from that earlier episode.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In particular, through the fall of 2000, we were receiving increasingly grim stories, especially from manufacturers, about the dismal state of order books and a sharp shift in business psychology.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At the time, we didn’t have the conviction to embrace those anecdotes given the strength of the official data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I’ll be interested to hear your reports today, but my sense is that the anecdotes from businesses, while mixed, are not sharply at variance with the data at present.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Both seem to be pointing to slower growth but not to a serious retrenchment in activity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For these reasons, we are inclined to stick with our muddle-through story for now.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan will continue our presentation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our reading of the recent data suggests that economic activity abroad decelerated toward the end of the third quarter and has remained on a decelerating path thereafter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the euro area, the United Kingdom, and Canada, this softening of activity appears to reflect—at least in part—increasing drag from the ongoing financial turmoil.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, in the euro area, business and consumer confidence have weakened some in recent months, PMIs for both the services and manufacturing sectors have declined, and recent readings on retail sales and industrial production have softened.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the United Kingdom, indicators of sentiment and retail sales also have slipped of late, and a slowdown in the housing sector is now under way—with declines in net mortgage lending, mortgage approvals, and major indexes of house prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In response, the Bank of England late last week cut its key policy rate 25 basis points, to 5½ percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Bank of Canada also lowered its policy rate a notch last week, citing concerns about financial market turmoil.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In assessing the impact of the financial turbulence, we continue to see little evidence that the emerging-market economies are being significantly affected.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Over the past month or so, debt spreads for many of these economies have risen, and their equity markets have given back some ground, but these moves are relatively mild when viewed from a longer-term perspective.

speaker: SHEETS
text: All told, foreign growth is projected to step down from an average rate of nearly 4½ percent during the first three quarters of this year to below 3 percent in the current quarter and early next year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition to headwinds from the financial turmoil, this slowing reflects policy actions in some countries (particularly China) to rein in above-trend growth, as well as the softer pace of activity in the United States.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Thereafter, we see foreign growth rising back to a rate of 3¼ percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This outlook is weaker over the next few quarters than in our October projection, in line with the lower U.S. forecast.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, given the renewed market turbulence, we now see the drag from financial developments as likely to be larger and more protracted than we had previously assumed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We continue to believe that these effects will be felt mainly in the advanced economies, but an important downside risk to our forecast is the possibility that the emerging-market economies may be more affected than we now expect.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On Friday, we received revised Japanese GDP data for the third quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The latest estimate cuts growth in the quarter to 1.5 percent at an annual rate, down 1 percentage point from the initial reading.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, this growth can be attributed entirely to net exports, as domestic demand contracted for the second consecutive quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Residential investment plunged in the third quarter, as new building regulations temporarily weighed on spending.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our forecast calls for domestic demand to bounce back quickly, but downside risks are increasingly evident; for example, the profitability of small and medium-sized companies has recently deteriorated, labor market conditions seem to be softening, and wages continue to contract.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The spot price of West Texas intermediate approached $100 per barrel in late November, but mounting concerns about the near-term outlook for global activity have since pushed the price back below $90 per barrel.

speaker: SHEETS
text: At that level, spot WTI is down a few dollars per barrel since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Continued concerns about the longer-term supply-demand balance, however, have kept the far-futures price at its late-November level, near $87 per barrel—up about $7 since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nonfuel commodity prices fell sharply in the third quarter and have continued on a downward trajectory.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The prices of copper and nickel have plunged, driven by concerns that rising inventories may signal a softening of global demand for these commodities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The price of zinc has fallen as well.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, however, the prices of food commodities, including wheat, corn, and soybeans, have continued to rise.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This run-up in food prices, coupled with high oil prices, has stoked inflation in a number of countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For example, in the euro area, twelve-month headline inflation has jumped from 1.7 percent in August to 3 percent in November, led by food and energy prices, thus prompting the ECB to leave policy on hold at its meeting last week.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Going forward, this rise in inflation may continue to limit the ECB’s willingness to ease policy, as fallout from the financial turmoil weighs on activity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the United Kingdom, however, a recent rebound in inflation to slightly above the Bank of England’s 2 percent target—driven in part by rising food prices—did not deter last week’s policy move.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indeed, in cutting rates, the BoE noted that “higher energy and food prices are expected to keep inflation above the target in the short term.” In China, food price inflation is running at more than 15 percent and has pushed overall inflation to 6.9 percent in November.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The pace of inflation has elicited a range of policy responses from the authorities, including a move over the weekend to further increase reserve requirements.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our forecast sees global food and oil prices soon leveling off in line with quotes from futures markets, and this would contribute to a welcome moderation of inflationary pressures in a number of countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Since the last FOMC meeting, the dollar has strengthened on balance, rising 1 percent on average against the major currencies and ½ percent in broad nominal terms.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notwithstanding this reprieve from dollar depreciation, we continue to see the current account deficit—which still exceeds 5 percent of GDP—as a key factor that is likely to weigh on the exchange rate going forward.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Thus our forecast incorporates some modest further real depreciation of the dollar.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, this depreciation comes entirely against our emerging-market trading partners, and we have slightly raised our projections for the pace at which the renminbi and several other emerging Asian currencies appreciate against the dollar.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I conclude with a few words about the U.S. external sector.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We expect that export growth, following its red-hot 19 percent performance in the third quarter, will moderate to a still-strong pace of around 7 percent in the current quarter and through the next two years, as exports are supported by past declines in the dollar and still- solid foreign activity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Import growth in the current quarter will be sustained at its moderate third-quarter rate by a seasonal rebound in oil imports, but import growth is expected to fall off during the first half of next year, in line with the softer pace of U.S. activity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Thereafter, imports are projected to gradually accelerate, as growth in the United States firms.

speaker: SHEETS
text: All told, we see net exports making positive arithmetic contributions to growth of 0.1 percentage point in the fourth quarter of this year, 0.5 percentage point in 2008, and a little over 0.1 percentage point in 2009.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That concludes our prepared remarks, and we are happy to take questions.

speaker: FISHER
text: Actually, Mr. Chairman, I have a statement disguised as a question.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am glad on the international side that we raised the issue of food price inflation, not because it is on the cover of The Economist but because we discussed it at our last meeting.

speaker: FISHER
text: What is curious to me, David, is that there is only one line on page 13 of the Greenbook.

speaker: FISHER
text: It says, “At the same time, agricultural producers are expected to step up output of farm products, and that should help bring consumer food price inflation more in line with core inflation.” My statement is that, given our communication exercise, we are drawing more attention to headline PCE.

speaker: FISHER
text: My question is, Do I understand it correctly that the food weight in the PCE is twice that of energy and in the CPI is 1½ times that of energy?

speaker: FISHER
text: Therefore, why are we not talking about food price inflation as it affects headline inflation numbers, and why do we spend so much time on energy relative to food?

speaker: FISHER
text: Or are we just not worried about food?

speaker: FISHER
text: The second question—by the way, on the international side, as well as the domestic side—is, What is the basis for our optimism that food prices will come down against the background of the demand that you have described on the international side?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In fact, we devote, I would imagine, a surprising amount of resources to it.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have an agricultural economist whose job is to follow those developments and report on them.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It is his view—and based on both the futures prices and some of the modeling that we have done—that we will see a deceleration going forward in retail food prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, futures prices basically are projecting a flattening-out.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I assume that is part of what is in Nathan’s forecast as well.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are not trying to outguess the markets in that regard, and the reports that we have received on agricultural production look relatively favorable for the coming year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, most of that is a bit of winter wheat at this point and not much more in terms of production, although we have seen some significant rebuilding of both flocks and livestock herds that suggests that we are on the right track in terms of an output response to the higher prices that we have seen in the past year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Markets are tight, and I think there probably is some asymmetry in the risk surrounding the food price forecast, in that it is easier to see some possibility of stock-out problems if there is any shortfall in production over the coming year, than that there would be some massive boom in agricultural production that will depress prices sharply.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But I do think—and in the Greenbook Part 2 quite often, especially in the autumn, when we are actually doing a more careful accounting of the harvest—we devote a fair amount of attention to resources to it.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We can certainly do even more going forward.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Just to underscore what Dave has said, our forecast is driven largely from the quotes from futures markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So, really, the question boils down to, Why in the world do the futures markets expect the prices of these foodstuffs to decline?

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think a key factor is that there are some important temporary developments that have driven up food prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There have been adverse weather conditions in a number of Asian economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For example, in China, they had floods earlier this year that have significantly driven up vegetable prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, there has been a sustained drought in Australia that has driven up wheat prices significantly.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It has been several years that we have seen these drought conditions in Australia.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It is an open issue as to whether that goes away in 2008 or 2009, but the expectation is that at some point that is going to abate somewhat.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So we can point to temporary factors.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There has also been a significant imprint on the food prices of a move to ethanol in the United States, and that has driven up the price of corn.

speaker: SHEETS
text: At the same time, some acreage that had been in soybeans has shifted to corn, and that has reduced the supply of soybeans and driven up that price as well.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But it is our view and I think the view of the futures markets that over time you are going to see some of these effects balanced out, and the acreage production will be distributed in a way that will help bring these prices down.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, you could get more acres brought into production of these foodstuffs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The final point that I want to emphasize here is that there are also some important structural factors that are driving up food prices, two that I think are worth mentioning.

speaker: SHEETS
text: One is that you have a lot of people in these emerging-market economies who are a lot wealthier than they were ten years ago, and they want to eat better, and the world is going to have to find a way to produce more and higher-quality agricultural goods.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It is imaginable that there will be some upward pressure on price through that transition.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The second important factor that I think is structural is we have seen a sustained and now an apparently permanent increase in the price of oil.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It takes a lot of petroleum to produce these goods, so that is a longer-run factor that may contribute to higher agricultural prices.

speaker: FISHER
text: Thank you for your thorough answer.

speaker: EVANS
text: Dave, I have two questions, I suppose.

speaker: EVANS
text: The first one is that the Greenbook GDP forecast has come down a good bit since October.

speaker: EVANS
text: At the same time, the Greenbook-consistent short-run equilibrium real funds rate was revised down ¾ percentage point.

speaker: EVANS
text: How much independent information is there between these two observations?

speaker: EVANS
text: I mean, the equilibrium real funds rate is the rate which, if maintained for some period of time, would get us back up to potential growth.

speaker: EVANS
text: So the fact that you have marked that down suggests that you would have a lower real rate.

speaker: EVANS
text: The second question is this: We were expecting the economy to slow during the current period.

speaker: EVANS
text: Expectations of slowing versus slowing that is revealed in the data are very important for how we think about the outlook—maybe you said this, but I don’t recall it.

speaker: EVANS
text: Could you give me an idea of how in the Greenbook your assumptions have evolved since October with regard to prospective losses due to mortgage foreclosures and the write- downs that the banks are expected to take or have announced on this?

speaker: EVANS
text: Do you have some numbers in mind on how things have changed in that regard and how that might be influencing your housing outlook?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In response to your first question about whether there is independent information in that estimate of the equilibrium funds rate for the Greenbook-consistent measure, the answer is that there is no independent information.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It’s just a transformation of the revision in the GDP outlook into interest rate space.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, obviously, we provide a few other measures in that table, some based on a large-scale econometric model and some on smaller-scale models.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Those have come down, too.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I don’t think our forecast is doing something different from, well, what those other models suggest.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In response to your second question, our forecast of housing activity going forward is not driven by the foreclosures.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The foreclosure forecast that we have is driven importantly by the house-price developments, and there we have marked down our house-price forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We would expect some increase in foreclosures, and obviously that would have some feedback on overall lending and conditions of bank balance sheets.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In general, since the October forecast, we have built in more broadly about ¼ percentage point to the level of GDP in additional restraint on spending coming from the increased overall financial turmoil—not just in the housing markets, but we’ve taken down a little our forecast of consumption and our forecast of business fixed investment too.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Basically, looking at the past correlation between measures of overall financial stress and the residuals of our spending equations, there’s considerable correlation there.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is, our standard models, as I noted in the past, have very rudimentary financial transmission mechanisms in them—mostly a few interest rates, a few asset prices, housing, equity, and the exchange rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In the past, periods when we’ve seen significant increase in financial stress have also been associated with significant shortfalls in spending, and we’ve tried as best we can to build that in.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Most of that effect overall is in housing—over half of it—but some of it we think will spill over elsewhere.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Those bank balance sheets are going to be impaired.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We think there will be some restraint on lending going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But, boy, it’s a lot of guess work!

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the housing side, I do think we can go through more-careful calculations of the implications of the shutdown of the nonprime market and the current impairment in the jumbo markets, but beyond that, I’d say we’re very loosely calibrating it.

speaker: POOLE
text: Dave, I want to lump together all the various forms of financial distress here—the mortgage market, auto loans, credit card loans, and maybe even business failures.

speaker: POOLE
text: If my memory serves correctly (and it may well not), if we look at the history of business cycle fluctuations, all those different forms of financial distress rise after a business cycle peak when we have increases in unemployment and actual declines in GDP.

speaker: POOLE
text: Assuming that we are not after a business cycle peak right now, it appears that we have a great deal of financial distress ahead of— I’m hoping it remains ahead of—a business cycle peak.

speaker: POOLE
text: So this is a very atypical situation in the context of U.S. business cycle history.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t actually know in terms of the lag between financial stress and activity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: They look very contemporaneous in many cases, and in some cases, obviously, they are past leading indicators of economic activity, such as the Stock-Watson index, which ultimately didn’t work all that great, but for a while it looked as though various quality spreads and term spreads had some leading indicator value.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I’m not totally sure about whether or not this looks incredibly unusual in that the stress might have increased.

speaker: POOLE
text: I’m talking particularly about the delinquencies, foreclosures, and business failures because I think that they usually occur on the way down during the contraction phase of the business cycle and ordinarily those measures look their best close to a business cycle peak.

speaker: POOLE
text: That’s what I remember, but I haven’t gone back and reviewed it, but from just my memory of looking at a lot of business cycle data over the years.

speaker: POOLE
text: That would say that, if my observation is correct, this is quite an unusual situation—unless of course we are past the peak or right at the peak.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This is obviously a situation in which, in some sense, the financial stress is the shock to the system rather than the endogenous response to some other shock, either an aggressive tightening of policy or some other type of aggregate demand shock.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So in that sense this particular configuration, I think, sort of fits with the situation we’re currently facing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously we’re not forecasting a business cycle peak.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So in our forecast, we’re not yet saying that we’re on the downside of a business cycle.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have a growth recession in this forecast and nothing more than that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If we were to get a true cyclical downturn, I think you could obviously expect that to have some very considerable effects on foreclosures, business failures, and so forth; that channel or mechanism would amplify the downturn in this particular episode.

speaker: STERN
text: Dave, I’m having difficulty reconciling the employment and hours data for the current quarter with your forecast of no growth whatsoever.

speaker: STERN
text: It seems to me that, even if domestic final demand doesn’t grow or grows little, we still have inventories and exports that could take up whatever output turns out to be, and we don’t know very much about those two components for the current quarter, if I understand the situation right.

speaker: STERN
text: Alternatively, obviously you can get a very bad productivity number, and that would square the circle.

speaker: STERN
text: But I’m wondering what we know in particular about inventories and exports that would lead us to something as weak as this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In the forecast, in fact, we do square the labor market with our forecast of weak GDP with basically flat labor productivity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, that’s coming on the heels of a quarter in which we had a 6 percent increase in nonfarm business labor productivity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That’s a huge gap, and I don’t think in some sense that the level of productivity that we’re forecasting here is at all at odds with the basic trend that we’ve been seeing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, when you ask me what we know about inventories and net exports, I’ll let Nathan speak to the net export side of things.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On inventories we know virtually nothing at this point, and this forecast is actually predicated on non-motor-vehicle inventory investment stepping up.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have some offset in some sense built into this forecast on the non-motor-vehicle side, that there will be some, we think, unintended accumulation of inventories in the fourth quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously the standard error around our forecast is very large, and it includes much higher numbers on inventories, which if that were to be the case, would obviously not bode well for activity going forward because we certainly don’t see inventories currently as so lean that they need to be rebuilt.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As I indicated on the final sales side, at this point we do have, I think, enough data in hand to make us pretty comfortable with the notion that there’s going to be a considerable slowing in final demand in the current quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan, do you want to say anything?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Yes, just to echo what Dave said, we have very little hard data so far, essentially no hard data for net exports for Q4.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We will be receiving the October trade data later this week.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So at that point we’ll start getting a bit more insight into it.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That said, we see the contribution from net exports falling off from a substantial 1.4 percentage points in Q3 to just a touch above 0.1 in Q4, and that’s driven by a moderation in export growth and continued 4 percent import growth.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But obviously there’s a lot of uncertainty around those projections.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have sort of a longer-run question that I’d like to pose.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was looking at the alternative scenarios in the Greenbook, and one of the things that I was looking at was the funds rate path that was described as the market-based forecast for the funds rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It drops almost 150 basis points, or 100-plus basis points, between now and the middle or end of next year.

speaker: PLOSSER
