text: One consequence of that, though, seems pretty benign—that there’s not much change in the inflation forecast at least through 2009; it changes only about 0.1 percentage point—and there are some positive effects on output, particularly in ’09.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It appears, at least within this period, that 100 basis point rate cuts seemed to be pretty much free.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I guess my question to the staff is, Is there a price to be paid for that, and if I run the forecast out beyond 2009, will any of those prices or those consequences appear in the forecast for inflation?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If so, how long would I have to look before I saw them in the model?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t think you’d need to look much farther than the horizon that we’re showing here to see that, in the context of the staff’s view about activity, that path for the fed funds rate would probably not be sustainable because in some sense our IS curve is considerably stronger than the market’s currently.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If it makes you feel a little better, we are planning on incorporating the extended forecast into the Greenbook next time, and we want to take these alternative scenarios and push them out because we recognize that one of the weaknesses in the relatively short period that we have here is that much of the interesting action in these often takes place just beyond the time frame that we’re showing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I think that will help.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That would be very helpful to put in some perspective what tradeoff in the costs we might see.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We should make some progress there.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My first question is an extension of President Evans’s question.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Dave, there are two things to your monetary policy assumption in the Greenbook.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One is that you lowered the path 50 basis points over the forecast period, but the way you did it was sort of interesting.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You did 25 now, and you did the rest just at the point where I think in your forecast the economy is coming back up toward trend growth.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Can you say a little about the shape of that path?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In some sense that reduction in the middle of 2009 goes back to President Plosser’s point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’re trying to get on track so that when we actually show the extended Greenbook, we have been following, roughly speaking, the optimal control simulation on a 1¾ percent inflation target.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The 25 basis points up front is in some sense dealing with the current weakness in overall activity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The 25 basis points in 2009 really reflects the fact that, at that point, inflation is coming down a little and you’ve opened up an output gap.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: You have an unemployment rate at 5 percent, and you can start a process then, according to that optimal control, of lowering the real funds rate to encourage growth to move above potential and eventually reduce the unemployment rate back toward the NAIRU.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I recognize it’s going to be a cosmetic—I mean, not a cosmetic but a small analytical wrinkle—that might be more confusing than enlightening.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But, as you know, in the Greenbook extension memo that we circulate, we do see the fed funds rate coming down to 4 percent or below in the extended Greenbook part.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So it really is more to try to stimulate growth to above potential once you have inflation moving down.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: May I ask one follow-up question?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In the note for the Board that you circulated on Monday, Dave, you said that the magnitude of the credit crunch you’re contemplating is roughly comparable to the unusual weakness of private spending seen during the headwinds episode of the early 1990s.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is sort of interesting because you think that capital at banks going into this period is much stronger than going into the 1990–91 period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Corporate balance sheets, based just on the crude leverage ratios, are much healthier today than they were then.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the other hand, banks are a smaller share of the financial system, and you could say that the nonbank part looks kind of weak.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The FHLB is growing very dramatically, taking up a fair amount of the room left by the shrinking of the nonbank sector.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: GSEs have less room to grow.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I was curious about how you thought about the comparison.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You didn’t seem to like the comparison.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So the headwinds of the 1990–91 period—that was a calibration we used for the “credit crunch” scenario in the Greenbook.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Oh, it’s just the alternative scenario.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In our baseline forecast, we don’t have what I would call a real credit crunch.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have some tightening of terms and standards in a period of financial stress that we think will depress spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But if you’re really thinking that we are on the verge of something that looks more like the 1990–91 period, then I think that credit crunch scenario gives you a better sense of the dimensions of the demand shock.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, as we discussed at the Board meeting yesterday, and Governor Kroszner suggested, we might want to think about elongating that particular shock.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We piled a big shock into a relatively short time, and certainly another reasonable alternative—if you were in a situation like that—would be that you would face a longer period of weak demand but not necessarily that sort of recessionary type of scenario that we showed there.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I was looking at the alternative simulations and the credit crunch scenario and trying to make sense of what financial markets are thinking about in terms of the expected fed funds rate path, it seems as though you need that credit crunch scenario to get to that type of path, and that’s not where you are.

speaker: EVANS
text: Then there are also other scenarios that are slightly stronger, which I think are in line with more Blue Chip types of forecasts, too.

speaker: EVANS
text: So there really is a disconnect in a lot of this.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Well, I think, as we showed in the alternative scenarios, something like either the credit crunch or the greater housing correction scenarios—in the real world obviously wouldn’t necessarily be shocks that would be independent of each other—but either one of those two scenarios is constructed to produce something that looks similar to what the markets might be thinking.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: And we don’t think those scenarios are unreasonable.

speaker: HOENIG
text: David, in listening to this, I have a question.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As you are looking at and projecting forward, we’re talking about a fed funds rate path that comes down, and yet we’ve talked a great deal about inflation rising temporarily in some views.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The question I have is, Does it give you pause?

speaker: HOENIG
text: How do you analyze the risk that you are lowering rates in an environment of rising inflation on a global basis?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Do you have any concerns about the risk?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Are you reevaluating the risk of how stable inflationary expectations might be in that scenario?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously in our baseline forecast we don’t really have a pickup of inflation, even headline inflation, beyond the very near term.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So we do think that, in the next quarter or two, we’re going to be looking at some pretty large headline numbers that will be reflecting the jump in energy prices and some lingering increases in food prices.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Right, and you’re saying the slowdown in the economy makes that temporary?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The slowdown in the economy helps in the sense that we do think opening up an output gap is going to limit and eventually bring down some of those inflation pressures.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In terms of the risks surrounding the forecast, I think an important element in the baseline forecast is that taking on futures markets for both energy and food—and those markets are expecting almost an immediate flattening-out and even oil prices coming down just a bit—is probably more important in some sense over the next year or so in terms of relieving inflation pressures.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Certainly our experience in the past several years is that we don’t know any better way to do it.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It’s not as though the futures markets have done a great job for us; they’ve always been forecasting that things were going to be flattening out right around the corner.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So if you were skeptical about whether that was going to occur, you might be concerned about whether or not you could experience some continued upside surprises there.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, we’ve been encouraged in looking at inflation expectations, because we haven’t yet seen any really broad-based deterioration, and we think things have to date been reasonably well contained.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In our forecast, that continues.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This forecast does not assume that there will be any deterioration of inflation expectations going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If we saw that, it would be at odds with what we’re seeing now and would probably lead us to revise up the forecast.

speaker: YELLEN
text: At the time of our last meeting, I held out hope that the financial turmoil would gradually ebb and the economy might escape without serious damage.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Subsequent developments have severely shaken that belief.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The bad news since our last meeting has grown steadier and louder, as strains in financial markets have resurfaced and intensified and as the economy has shown clear signs of faltering.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition, the downside threats to growth that then seemed to be tail events now appear to be much closer to the center of the distribution.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I found little to console me in the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Like the Board staff, I have significantly marked down my growth forecast.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The possibilities of a credit crunch developing and of the economy slipping into a recession seem all too real.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Conditions in financial markets have worsened.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Rates on a wide array of loans and securities have increased significantly since our last meeting, including those on term commercial paper, term LIBOR, prime jumbo mortgages, and high-yield corporate bonds.

speaker: YELLEN
text: CDS spreads from major financial institutions with significant mortgage exposure, including Freddie and Fannie, have risen appreciably.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition, broad stock indexes are down nearly 5 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: At the same time, measures of implied volatility in equity, bond, and foreign exchange markets have all moved up, reflecting the greater uncertainty about the economy’s direction.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The most recent data on spending have been discouraging as well.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Data on house sales, prices, and construction have been downbeat, and foreclosures on subprime loans have moved even higher.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even with efforts such as those facilitated by the Administration to freeze subprime rates, foreclosures look to rise sharply next year, which may dump a large number of houses on a market already swamped with supply.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This will exacerbate the downward pressure on house prices and new home construction from already elevated home inventories.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, the ten-city Case-Shiller home-price index has declined more than 5 percent over the past year through September, and futures contracts point to another sizable decline over the next twelve months.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am particularly concerned that we may now be seeing the first signs of spillovers from the housing and financial sectors to the broader economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although the job market has remained reasonably healthy so far, real consumer spending in September and October was dead in the water, and households are growing more pessimistic about future prospects.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The December reading of consumer sentiment showed another decline, and the cumulative falloff in this measure is becoming alarming.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Gains in disposable income have been weakened.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With consumer sentiment in the doldrums, house prices on the skids, and energy prices on the rise, consumer spending looks to be quite subdued for some time.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This view is echoed by the CEO of a national high-end clothing retailer on our board, who recently emphasized to us that the positive chain store sales data in November were in fact artificially boosted by the Thanksgiving calendar shift and that the underlying trend for his business has worsened notably.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My modal forecast foresees the economy barely managing to avoid recession, with growth essentially zero this quarter and about 1 percent next quarter.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I expect growth to remain below potential throughout next year, causing the unemployment rate to rise to about 5 percent, much like in the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This forecast assumes a 50 basis point decline in the federal funds rate in the near future, placing the real funds rate near the center of the range of estimates of the neutral rate reported in the Bluebook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I should emphasize that I do not place a lot of confidence in this forecast, and, in particular, I fear that we are in danger of sliding into a credit crunch.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Such an outcome is illustrated by the credit crunch alternative simulation in the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although I don’t foresee conditions in the banking sector getting as bleak as during the credit crunch of the early 1990s, the parallels to those events are striking.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Back then, we saw a large number of bank failures in the contraction of the savings and loan sector.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In the current situation, most banks are still in pretty good shape.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Instead, it is the shadow banking sector— that is, the set of markets in which a variety of securitized assets are financed by the issuance of commercial paper—that is where the failures have occurred.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This sector is all but shut for new business.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But bank capital is also an issue.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Until the securitization of nonconforming mortgage lending reemerges, financing will depend on the willingness and ability of banks, thrifts, and the GSEs to step in to fill the breach.

speaker: YELLEN
text: To the extent they do, that will put further pressure on their capital, which is already under some pressure from write-downs on existing loans and holdings of assets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Banks are showing increasing concern that their capital ratios will become binding and are tightening credit terms and conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Several developments suggest to me that this situation could worsen.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition to the problems plaguing the adjustable-rate subprime mortgages, delinquencies have recently started to move up more broadly—on credit card and auto loans, adjustable-rate prime mortgages, and fixed-rate subprime mortgages.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My contacts at large District banks tell me that, because the economy continues to be reasonably healthy and people have jobs, things are still under control.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But if house prices and the stock market fall further and the economy appears to be weakening, then they will further tighten the lending conditions and terms on consumer loans to avoid problems down the road, and these fears could be self-fulfilling.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If banks only partially replace the collapsed shadow banks or, worse, if they cut back their lending in anticipation of a worsening economy, then the resulting credit crunch could push us into recession.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This possibility is presumably increasingly reflected in CDS and low-grade corporate bond spreads.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Thus, the risk of recession no longer seems remote, especially since the economy may well already have begun contracting in the current quarter.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, the December Blue Chip consensus puts the odds of a recession at about 40 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This estimate is within the range of recession probabilities computed by my staff using models based on the yield curve and other variables.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Turning to inflation, data on the core measure continues to be favorable.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Wage growth remains moderate, and the recent downward revisions to hourly compensation have relieved some worries there.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I mentioned, I expect some labor market slack to develop, and this should offset any, in my view, modest inflationary pressures from past increases in energy and import prices and help keep core PCE price inflation below 2 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Continued increases in energy and import prices pose some upside risk to the inflation outlook, but there are also downside risks to inflation associated with a weakening economy and rising unemployment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: To sum up, I believe that the most likely outcome is for the economy to slow significantly in the near term, flirting with recession, and I view the risk to that scenario as being weighted significantly to the downside.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In contrast, I expect inflation to remain well contained, and I view those risks as fairly balanced.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think I took the same pessimism pill as President Yellen this morning.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Greenbook makes very somber reading, and I would make several observations about the forecast it provides.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, Greenbook forecasts of two successive quarters of growth below 1 percent are quite rare, and often in the past have occurred shortly before or during recessions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, the 70 percent confidence interval for the Greenbook projection of GDP, using historical forecast errors, has a negative lower bound.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Third, I would note that when the unemployment rate rises at least ½ percent, it tends to rise much further than just ½ percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That is, historically, when we have unemployment rates rise ½ percent, we have subsequently found ourselves in a recession.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: These observations indicate that, while a recession is not forecast in the Greenbook—as David has been careful to state—the probability of a recession is clearly elevated.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: At our last meeting, the housing market was very soft, but weakness in other components was not yet reflected in the data.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But now we have some evidence that consumption and investment may also be slowing, and residential investment may be even weaker than we thought.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While incoming data have generally been weak, some higher-frequency data, like the recent labor report, might be consistent with a stronger outlook than the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, I am concerned that housing prices may actually fall more than assumed in the Greenbook, potentially resulting in consequences that are difficult to forecast with models using only postwar data.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I am also sympathetic to the view that disruptions in financial flows have the potential to result in significantly more weakness than would result from an econometric model that does not capture significant liquidity disruptions, in part because the occurrence of such events is quite rare.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Added to these concerns is the current state of financial markets both here and abroad.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The elevated rates for term lending, even over relatively short maturities, indicates significant risk aversion by market participants.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Financial institutions with very low probabilities of default, as measured by credit default swap rates, are nonetheless having difficulty securing term lending over year-end.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Bank supervisors of large financial institutions are beginning to report correlations in nonperforming experiences of auto, credit card, and mortgage loans.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Geographic regions hard hit by mortgage defaults are also experiencing rising default rates in other types of loans.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Portfolios that are not highly correlated during good times can become highly correlated during bad times, and the initial trends being reported in bank supervision are not encouraging.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would also highlight this as one of the instances in which bank supervision is providing some very relevant input into thinking about the macroeconomy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Finally, I would highlight several institutional concerns that could have broader implications.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, financial guarantors, as was highlighted earlier, have credit default swap rates inconsistent with their AAA rating.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Significant downgrades would further depress CDOs but also disrupt the municipal bond market and force some banks to fulfill agreements to purchase securities that do not maintain at least an AA rating.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, there is the potential for significant further announcements of downgrades of assets related to SIVs and CDOs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Money market funds are currently experiencing inflows.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, those flows could quickly reverse if investors lose confidence in their ability to redeem money market funds at par.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Third, I would note that for securities like lower-grade bonds that have not previously shown elevated risk premiums, those premiums are now becoming quite elevated, providing evidence that what was initially a liquidity concern is now becoming a more widespread and generalized concern about the state of the economy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With core inflation a little below 2 percent, and future reductions in labor market pressures likely, we have the flexibility to respond aggressively to slowing economic growth and the ongoing financial turmoil.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This seems to be the appropriate time to take significant further action, knowing that, should the economy perform much better than we currently anticipate, we could be equally nimble in raising rates as appropriate.

speaker: POOLE
text: Just before the meeting I learned something about how we select the order.

speaker: POOLE
text: There are a bunch of us sitting with Debbie, and most people seem to want to go toward the end.

speaker: POOLE
text: Debbie apparently has been in touch with too many econometricians because she said it is “overdetermined.” Anyway, here I am.

speaker: POOLE
text: Let me start with some of the anecdotal reports.

speaker: POOLE
text: It is pretty clear that the anecdotal reports that I am getting from large national firms on the goods side of the economy are coming in on the soft side.

speaker: POOLE
text: The holiday season, according to UPS, is coming in about 2 percentage points below projection; and UPS and FedEx are revising down somewhat their longer-term projections and their capital spending plans.

speaker: POOLE
text: My FedEx contact said that the less-than-truckload business is, in his terms, pitiful.

speaker: POOLE
text: My contact with a large trucking company, J.B.Hunt, said that the company is cutting its capacity.

speaker: POOLE
text: Its volume is down 13 percent from a year ago.

speaker: POOLE
text: The company has reduced capacity 13 percent over the past twelve months and will cut another 12 percent.

speaker: POOLE
text: That is, after all, a full one-quarter cut in capacity of that company.

speaker: POOLE
text: Hunt is selling its trucks.

speaker: POOLE
text: Many of them are going to Russia, interestingly enough.

speaker: POOLE
text: Perhaps the only good news from this company is that drivers are plentifully available, which has not been so true in the past.

speaker: POOLE
text: In the quick-serve restaurant business, there is a ray of hope.

speaker: POOLE
text: The projection is that food prices will increase much more modestly than they have been doing this year, but they said that most people in the restaurant business are pessimistic.

speaker: POOLE
text: On the other hand, a large software company reports that it is optimistic.

speaker: POOLE
text: The sales of PCs are good, gaming devices and software are doing well, and cap-ex plans are substantial—nothing being cut back there.

speaker: POOLE
text: A contact with a large money center bank said that the bank’s analysis of its consumer credit card business indicated that the increase in thirty-day delinquencies is entirely explained by what is going on in Florida, California, and Nevada, and delinquencies in the rest of the country are about unchanged.

speaker: POOLE
text: A general comment on the business outlook: We have a lot of specific news—and certainly Janet talked about some of that—that is pretty negative.

speaker: POOLE
text: I have an inherent optimism about the economy, which is hard to put any real flesh on the bones I guess, but I think that the economy in the longer run is inherently strong and resilient.

speaker: POOLE
text: A lot of the adjustments in the credit markets I believe are under way.

speaker: POOLE
text: We see it with a lot of the recapitalizations that are taking place and the initial shock back in July and August.

speaker: POOLE
text: There are a lot of smart people with sharp pencils who are digging into their situations, deciding what to write off, and then getting on with things; and they are past the initial scramble.

speaker: POOLE
text: So those things together give me some sense of optimism.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would also note that, although many households are certainly stressed, there does seem to be a lot of discretionary spending taking place—consumer electronics, for example, are pretty strong.

speaker: POOLE
text: There was an article in the newspaper noting that the hot items this Christmas season are GPS navigation devices.

speaker: POOLE
text: To add one of these to your car hardly seems to be an essential expenditure.

speaker: POOLE
text: Computer games are another example.

speaker: POOLE
text: I bought my GPS a long time ago, and I don’t play computer games.

speaker: POOLE
text: But at any rate, flat panel TVs, a lot of stuff like that, suggest that many households are not on the edge of being highly stressed.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I don’t know where to come out on this.

speaker: POOLE
text: I guess that my outlook has more variance to it than usual, and it seems to me that, when we get to the policy discussion, what we need to do is to find a way to react promptly to the surprises that I think are inevitably ahead of us.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is the sale of a used truck to Russia an export or a capital inflow?

speaker: POOLE
text: Well, it is not current production, so it is not an export.

speaker: LACKER
text: Economic conditions in the Fifth District appear to be generally sound but with some notable areas of weakness.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our survey readings on the services firms indicate continued moderate growth in November, and our index of manufacturing activity gained a few points following a sharp decline in October, though it remains in neutral territory.

speaker: LACKER
text: A number of our contacts reported that the weaker dollar is providing a boost to manufacturing exports, and I have noticed a definite increase in the number of coal trains rumbling by my office on their way from West Virginia to port.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the other hand, our merchant contacts were much less optimistic about their sales prospects going into the holiday season.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our retail sales survey indicator slid another 8 points, pulled down by significant declines in big ticket sales and shopper traffic components.

speaker: LACKER
text: District housing markets continue to weaken overall, with distinctly more-pessimistic tones in some markets, particularly around the D.C. area, although there are a couple of areas that are still reporting decent activity to the south.

speaker: LACKER
text: In commercial real estate, reports from the retail and industrial markets are generally upbeat.

speaker: LACKER
text: One former director, whose firm owns a sizable portfolio of retail properties throughout the East Coast, described the sector as in the best shape he has seen in his lifetime, and he is by no means a young man.

speaker: LACKER
text: Industrial leasing appears to be in good shape, even tight in some markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the office market, however, contacts in Maryland and the Carolinas report slower office leasing activity in October and early November.

speaker: LACKER
text: The community bankers I have talked with say that portfolios are still quite clean but that they are scrutinizing deals much more carefully in the current environment.

speaker: LACKER
text: They also complain that large banks are raising deposit rates and competing more intensely for deposits.

speaker: LACKER
text: At large banks, the cost of capital has increased, and they are responding accordingly by reevaluating the profitability of various lines of business.

speaker: LACKER
text: This does not appear to have resulted in any wholesale cutback in lending but more in a tightening of terms in selected market segments.

speaker: LACKER
text: I view the information from our District as fairly consistent with my economic outlook at the national level.

speaker: LACKER
text: Housing investment continues to contract, and the overhang of unsold homes and general tightening of credit terms suggest a quite prolonged period of relatively depressed activity.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consumer spending clearly has slowed.

speaker: LACKER
text: For the months of September and October, real consumption showed almost no growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: While early reports on the holiday shopping season are notoriously slippery, it seems clear that shoppers are far from ebullient, perhaps with the exception of these GPS toys.

speaker: LACKER
text: This seems consistent with the virtual absence of growth in real disposable income over the past two months and the flattening-out of household net worth in the third quarter.

speaker: LACKER
text: Job growth has shifted down to a more modest pace over this year, and revisions to the payroll series, when we finally get them, seem likely to make the slowdown look bigger.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it wouldn’t surprise me if consumer spending came in fairly tame next year.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am expecting a slowdown in consumer spending growth, however, not a sharp pullback.

speaker: LACKER
text: Labor markets are still fairly tight.

speaker: LACKER
text: Household net worth is still at fairly elevated levels.

speaker: LACKER
text: So while the increase in the saving rate projected by the Greenbook for next year is plausible, I think consumer spending could come out on the high side of that forecast.

speaker: LACKER
text: A key factor in the outlook and a key source of uncertainty is the continuing drama in credit markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: Large banks are bringing impaired assets onto their balance sheets and are facing a higher cost of capital and increased funding costs.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would seem reasonable to expect them to respond by tightening terms of credit for households and business borrowers, implying a further drag on spending.

speaker: LACKER
text: The magnitude of this sort of fallout is still quite uncertain.

speaker: LACKER
text: Reduced credit flows appear so far to be less a reduction in credit supply than in demand.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is, they appear to reflect a genuine deterioration in borrower creditworthiness in some segments.

speaker: LACKER
text: Residential real estate fits this description as does some, though not all, commercial real estate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Beyond these sectors, we have seen some evidence of yield spreads widening, but the cost of credit to investment-grade nonfinancial firms is low and has been falling along with the risk-free rate, at least until very recently.

speaker: LACKER
text: The flow of credit to such firms seems to have been holding up well, as has the nonmortgage consumer credit flow.

speaker: LACKER
text: So at this point, it does not look as though an indiscriminate, across-the-board credit crunch is taking place, although marginally higher credit costs may exert some additional drag on spending growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: Overall, then, I do see a weaker outlook for growth in the near term, and the timing of the return to trend is going to depend somewhat on the bottoming-out of the housing cycle, which unfortunately appears to be getting even more remote each time we meet.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we have a more protracted slowdown ahead of us, as seems likely now, we need to be careful not to lose sight of inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Core PCE inflation has edged up over the past two months, and it now appears likely to move above 2 percent for a time.

speaker: LACKER
text: Overall inflation, of course, has been higher on average over the last year, and we have seen a slight upward trend in five-year- forward inflation compensation since earlier in the year.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, the behavior of energy and food prices over the past several years calls into question the standard presumption we make that overall inflation is going to return to the core inflation trend in a reasonable period of time.

speaker: LACKER
text: That points to the possibility that inflation may give us more trouble ahead.

speaker: EVANS
text: Coming out of our October meeting, I expected a period of subpar growth stretching into the middle of 2008.

speaker: EVANS
text: Since I was anticipating some soft data, it was not obvious to me that the outlook had worsened until later in the intermeeting period.

speaker: EVANS
text: A lot of the data that we have cited are financial items that are difficult to assess and are somewhat unusual for the current period.

speaker: EVANS
text: But the incoming information has caused us to mark down our outlook further, although we don’t see growth declining as far below potential as in the Greenbook baseline forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: Although housing continues to weaken, that by itself did not cause a substantial revision to our outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: The bigger factor was a noticeable weakening of consumption.

speaker: EVANS
text: PCE was basically flat in September and October—I guess dead on arrival.

speaker: EVANS
text: The financial headlines are taking their toll on consumer sentiment, and higher energy prices are lowering real incomes.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is not clear, however, that we are seeing a major sustained pullback in consumption; but, of course, that is arguable.

speaker: EVANS
text: The limited information we have about November—motor vehicle sales and the chain store data—suggest at least modest gains in consumer expenditures.

speaker: EVANS
text: I realize that the chain store sales could be a bit artificial.

speaker: EVANS
text: I was talking to one of my business contacts who has a significant presence in retail, and I am accustomed to hearing that, “Well, the Christmas season is a bit short this year, so that could be a problem.” But I actually caught him this time saying, “Gee, it’s so long this time that people seem to be losing interest.” On balance, I think the fundamentals for consumption are still reasonably good.

speaker: EVANS
text: Importantly, although they may be somewhat lagging, the payroll numbers are still consistent with decent growth in wage income, and the unemployment rate remains low.

speaker: EVANS
text: Elsewhere, foreign growth remains good, which along with the lower dollar should support continued growth in exports.

speaker: EVANS
text: We have seen some softening in capital spending as well, but the usual indicators still point to moderate gains in investment.

speaker: EVANS
text: These developments seem reasonably consistent with what I heard from business contacts.

speaker: EVANS
text: Most of them think that growth is slowing, and they are more cautious, but I would summarize their views as guarded and not alarmist.

speaker: EVANS
text: Furthermore, many say that their improved inventory control methods are preventing an inventory cycle from exacerbating the current situation, and they bring this up without my prompting.

speaker: EVANS
text: So to me their comments do not yet suggest a sharp curtailment in real economic activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: Of course, the financial markets continue to weigh negatively on the outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: In my view, the biggest concerns are the large markdowns on structured securities and the volume of assets that may be returning to banks’ balance sheets.

speaker: EVANS
text: These effects appear to be larger than the banks had planned for as of October and could have a significant impact on lending capacity.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is an important downside risk to the real economy, as the Greenbook highlights in many places.

speaker: EVANS
text: That said, when I talk with my business contacts, there continues to be a disconnect between the credit conditions they report facing and the turbulence we see in money and credit markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: Outside of lending for residential and nonresidential construction, my CEO contacts at nonfinancial firms do not report much change in credit costs or availability.

speaker: EVANS
text: We have heard this from a number of sources.

speaker: EVANS
text: For example, two of the larger banks in our District said they have not changed terms to borrowers, and they expressed relatively sanguine views of lending conditions overall.

speaker: EVANS
text: For the time being, some lenders report offsetting a portion of their higher funding costs by taking a hit on their interest margins.

speaker: EVANS
text: Credit conditions for construction-related industries are another matter.

speaker: EVANS
text: A major shopping center developer who has been one of the largest issuers of commercial mortgage- backed securities indicated that this market has dried up completely.

speaker: EVANS
text: However, the developer has been able to obtain financing from other traditional sources, such as life insurance companies.

speaker: EVANS
text: He is paying similar interest rates, he says, but the terms include lower loan-to-value ratios.

speaker: EVANS
text: So there is some credit effect, but he still has access for the moment.

speaker: EVANS
text: That is a bit like what President Lacker was suggesting.

speaker: EVANS
text: He said the switch is not a big deal for him currently, but if it continues for too long—say, for more than six months or so—it would then weigh more heavily on his business activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: The evolution of such developments will obviously be an important thing to watch over the next few meetings.

speaker: EVANS
text: I would just note that I don’t often look at the Duke University survey of CFOs.

speaker: EVANS
text: But as I looked at it—and I don’t have a great deal of experience— it did seem to indicate that they had higher spending plans on average from their September survey for capital expenditures and technology spending.

speaker: EVANS
text: It wasn’t a great bit, but given all the negative headlines associated with the credit conditions—which are unweighted, whereas these spending plans are weighted—that was a bit of a surprise.

speaker: EVANS
text: Putting all of this together, we have marked down our current quarter and 2008 real GDP forecasts 0.4 percentage point, which is pretty significant.

speaker: EVANS
text: We now have growth next year of 2¼ percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: We expect growth to improve to our assessment of potential thereafter, namely about 2½ percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: This forecast assumes two policy easings, similar to but sooner than the Greenbook, and it is shaded toward the “stronger domestic demand” alternative scenario, which has less financial restraint on PCE and business fixed investment than in the Greenbook baseline.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning to inflation, our forecast is for PCE inflation to settle in at 1.8 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: This continued favorable projection for inflation is important for my policy views now.

speaker: EVANS
text: We think resource utilization likely will be about neutral for inflation over this forecast period.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our GDP projection does not result in appreciable resource slack over the forecast period.

speaker: EVANS
text: Even under the weaker Greenbook scenario, the GDP gap remains less than ½ percentage point.

speaker: EVANS
text: But there are upside risks.

speaker: EVANS
text: The most recent data on core prices have been a bit higher.

speaker: EVANS
text: The lower dollar could put pressure on prices, and my business contacts remain concerned about the cost of energy and other commodities.

speaker: EVANS
text: Finally, at least by the Board staff calculations, five-year forward TIPS inflation compensation has moved up to the range that it was in during the spring of 2006, a period when we were more concerned about the inflation outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: I wouldn’t put too much weight on this particular inflation expectation development at the moment, but it may be looming ahead.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I continue to see upside risk to inflation, which if realized would complicate our policy reaction to developments on the growth and employment side of the ledger.

speaker: STERN
text: It probably goes without saying that I think the main development since the last FOMC meting has been the renewed deterioration in some of the financial markets.

speaker: STERN
text: In the absence of that—that is, had financial market conditions either stabilized or continued to improve as they had from the September to October meetings—we would be probably having a somewhat different conversation this morning.

speaker: STERN
text: We would be talking more about parsing the recent incoming macro data and talking about whether the economy was slowing as anticipated or a little more or a little less.

speaker: STERN
text: We should remember, we were expecting a significant slowing in the rate of growth, and that in fact does seem to be occurring.

speaker: STERN
text: But, as I said, I think the financial market developments have been the dominant ones.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as the economic outlook is concerned, my view of the next few quarters is for growth a bit better than that in the Greenbook for a couple of reasons.

speaker: STERN
text: One is that I think the incoming data, as always, are noisy, and I am reluctant to put a lot of weight on them.

speaker: STERN
text: Second, it seems to me that some of the underlying fundamentals, particularly the labor market data, present a more favorable picture of the outlook than the spending numbers at the moment.

speaker: STERN
text: But it seems to me that the risks are clearly on the downside, and they are on the downside because of financial market conditions.

speaker: STERN
text: Perhaps the most interesting anecdote I came across in the intermeeting period was that about two weeks ago we had a meeting with about fifteen leaders from firms in the financial services industry in the Twin Cities.

speaker: STERN
text: There was a good deal of concern among, I would say, virtually all the participants in that meeting, and it wasn’t so much about year-end funding and that kind of thing.

speaker: STERN
text: It was really about the economic outlook, and it had to do with the fact that some markets are not working or are barely working at the moment.

speaker: STERN
text: There is no doubt that in their own businesses they are all tightening terms and other conditions.

speaker: STERN
text: They believe that is appropriate, but they wouldn’t argue that it isn’t going to have an effect on spending.

speaker: STERN
text: They also believe that at least some of their customers are acting in anticipation of that.

speaker: STERN
text: That is, they are starting to cancel or at least delay spending plans, believing that they aren’t going to be able to find financing or at least find financing at terms they would like.

speaker: STERN
text: So it seems to me that we are in an environment, as far as financial conditions are concerned, where that poses a very real downside threat to what otherwise might be a pretty acceptable economic outlook.

speaker: STERN
text: Just a word about inflation.

speaker: STERN
text: I haven’t changed my outlook for inflation going forward.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t have a sense from the incoming information that there is any compelling reason at the moment to do so.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The conversations that I have had with my business contacts indicate that business conditions in our region have clearly softened since the last meeting and perhaps even more than what is reflected in the Beige Book report that we prepared just a few weeks ago.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: A sense of pessimism about the economic outlook seems once again to be sweeping over our business community, and it is not just the financial community.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This is a decided change from what I was hearing in October and is clearly an added threat to our already fragile outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My banking supervision staff reports that the District banks continue to address the risks in their portfolios by shifting focus away from residential and commercial real estate and by requiring more collateral, stronger covenants, and better debt-service coverage in their deals.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But our examiners are not reporting that capital positions of our financial institutions have been impaired such that they cannot accommodate sound projects.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: A few of the corporate CFOs I talk with say that credit commitments are more difficult to come by.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The CEOs of the Fourth District financial institutions advise me that what we are facing is a liquidity squeeze and not at present a credit crunch.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: That said, these bank CEOs have expressed concern that their capital positions could become impaired if the current pressure for more liquidity forces them to sell some of their assets at large discounts.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The incoming data for the economy appear to be unfolding reasonably close to my October projection.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I was fairly pessimistic about our near-term growth prospects, and that pessimism seems to have been well founded.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So the economic data by themselves haven’t been enough to push me off the forecast trajectory that I submitted at our last meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But as I noted earlier, I do observe a sharp drop in business confidence across a broad collection of industries, not just those tied to residential real estate.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: What I am hearing sounds more substantial than the transitory slowing that I was projecting just six weeks ago.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: What I am hearing from my business contacts is probably more aligned with the prolonged slow growth outlook that I now see in the Greenbook baseline, or worse.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am somewhat thankful that I didn’t have to submit a projection for this meeting because I am torn between what my mostly data-driven model says and what I am hearing from my business sources.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: About the only thing that I can say with much confidence is that the reemergence of liquidity pressures, combined with the deterioration in business confidence, has increased the downside risk to growth.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think it is prudent to address that risk with our policy decision today, but I will hold my comments about our policy moves for later in the meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think President Stern framed it well in bringing focus to the effect on our thinking that the financial markets are having.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As many have said, the central question is not whether the economy is softening but whether it is softening beyond the range that underpinned the policy decision in October.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’d add to that a range of questions related to financial markets, particularly the question of whether the deterioration in the financial markets changes the prospects for achieving financial stability, the potential for spreading to a wider array of financial markets and institutions, the potential for spillover to the general economy, and the compounding of the already heightened degree of uncertainty.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: All of these weigh heavily on my thinking.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Like the Greenbook projections, Atlanta’s forecast has been revised down as a result of incoming data since the last meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I just point out, speaking only for ourselves, that these downward revisions of previous forecasts and our general outlook have been a pattern over recent months.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The current situation is extremely difficult to read—which is another way of saying that uncertainty around our forecast has increased yet again.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Contributing to this uncertainty is the continuing, if not accelerating, gap between the anecdotal information and the views I’ve received from Wall Street versus Main Street.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The expectations of financial market participants have deteriorated and can be characterized as extremely serious.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, the message I get from directors and representatives of nonfinancial businesses outside the housing sector, though relatively pessimistic, has not changed substantially since our October meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my conversations with financial market contacts, to varying degrees I heard the persistent and growing apprehension concerning the spread of turmoil to an expanding set of affected markets and institutions and a wondering of what will be the next shoe to drop.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One consistent message is the belief that the recent volatility and increase in term spreads cannot be entirely explained by the year-end problem.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Most of my contacts agreed that year-end balance sheet concerns are adding to market stress, but no one expressed confidence that getting past year-end will bring much reduction of concerns over counterparty weakness, asset values, and secondary market liquidity.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Most expect financial market turmoil to be protracted, with increasing risk to the general economy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Almost all my contacts noted that deteriorating housing values are a root cause, feeding problems in the markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This view holds that the adjustment in prices and inventory required to stabilize the housing sector will take many months to play out, and until that occurs, the value of structured financial instruments and the solvency and liquidity of structured investment vehicles will be uncertain.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There remains a great deal of skepticism that arrangements like the super SIV and the Treasury’s rate freeze plan will have much tangible effect.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The issue of SIV restructuring and support by sponsors is a growing focus of concern because of their linkage to money market funds as well as their contribution to a general contraction of credit availability.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In sum, my contacts in the financial industry uniformly express the belief that things will not get better any time soon and may well get worse.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: While recognizing that a rate reduction does not directly address the information problems in the markets, there is widespread sentiment that lower costs of funds will help.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Turning to the anecdotal inputs from contacts in my District, there is some divergence of views between contacts directly affected by the housing sector, including bankers, and others.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Bank loan activity remains particularly weak in real estate segments.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Trucking, large retailers, auto dealerships, and businesses supplying building materials and household durables were identified as segments where loan volumes are slipping.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Industrial warehouse markets have weakened in some metro areas as subcontractors have exited.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Bankers also expect that consumer credit exposures in credit cards, auto loans, prime mortgages, and HELOCs will see a combination of credit deterioration and demand contraction in 2008.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The anecdotal messages from other contacts are less dire.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We took great care in our information-gathering this round to probe hiring expectations, investment plans, and credit availability conditions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Though credit conditions do seem to have tightened, we still are not hearing that they are preventing planned spending.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Spending and hiring plans remain on the weak side, but no more so than was the case at our October meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Consistent with the Greenbook projection for exports, we heard that spending from abroad, including international tourism and condo-purchase activity, continues relatively strong.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: At the branch board meeting in Miami, I heard that Russians are the latest foreign buyers of condos.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So combine that with President Poole’s comment on trucks, as a child of the Cold War, I think it is very ironic that our bailout is coming from the Russians.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On the employment front, the demand for workers in sectors such as hospitality and energy remains quite strong, but overall plans appear to be more cautious.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The trend in regional labor data mirrors the slowing trend in the national statistics.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Each FOMC round my staff provides a summary sentiment index of expected economic conditions over the next six months based on responses of directors and contacts.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Relative to the October meeting, that index is little changed, with the majority expecting flat or slower growth.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: When I combine the somewhat, but not dramatically, worse data inputs since the last meeting with the anecdotal and survey information from regional and other markets, I’m left with a view that economic fundamentals, current and prospective, have not yet fallen off a cliff.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That being said, there’s not much of a case to be made for any risk assessment other than one weighted to the downside.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my view, the potential for protracted and growing financial market troubles should weigh heavily in the policy decision, and though recent core inflation readings are acceptable, I continue to be concerned about the ongoing divergence between headline and core inflation.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Until they converge, price pressures cannot be removed from the watch list.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But overall I see more uncertainty and, therefore, more downside risk in the real economic growth picture.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There has been little change in the economic conditions in our District since the October meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Except for housing activity, manufacturing and other businesses are expanding at a modest pace, somewhat below trend.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our business contacts are a little less optimistic about growth in the near term than they were earlier in the fall primarily because of uncertainty surrounding the outlook rather than any immediate change in their business activity.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’ll begin by reporting on what our contacts say about credit conditions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Business contacts as well as our board of directors have told me that credit activity has changed very little.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Creditworthy borrowers, as far as they were concerned, have had no problem accessing credit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Banks have reported some tightening of lending standards, but mostly that has occurred for real estate developers and in residential mortgages.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some loan demand has dropped because of businesses’ uncertainty about the future, as I suggested earlier.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is, businesses seem to be a bit more cautious.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But banks do not appear to be conserving capital.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, they’re actively seeking good credits.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To quote one of my directors, “The crunch on Wall Street has not hit Main Street.” A couple of bankers I spoke to, one representing a very large regional bank and another a very large community bank, expressed the view that they were actively seeking to regain market share from the larger banks because they did not engage in the same off-balance-sheet financing of riskier debt that the large banks did and so they were not facing either capital or funding constraints.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some bankers acknowledge that consumer credit quality seems to have deteriorated slightly, but they reminded me that this was from very good levels.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So the defaults and delinquencies remain well within historical norms.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Turning to the economy, payroll employment continues to expand at a somewhat slow pace in our three states, yet the unemployment rate is still 0.4 percentage point below that of the nation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Retail sales picked up in November.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, retailers generally said they met their expectations for the Thanksgiving weekend.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, these sales seem to have been boosted by fairly heavy discounting, according to them; and despite the reasonable showing to date, retailers are wary and uncertain for the holiday season.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Housing construction and sales continue to decline, but the pace of that decline is in line with the expectations at the time of our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nonresidential real estate markets remain firm in our District.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Office vacancy rates continue to decline, and commercial rents are rising.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: New contracts for commercial real estate have declined, however; but with the decline in vacancy rates and with rising rents, the outlook of many developers is not as negative as the current level of spending would suggest.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: According to our Business Outlook Survey, manufacturing activity in the District has been increasing at a modest pace for the past few months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The index of general activity moved up slightly, to 8.2 in November from 6.8 in October.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is actually about the same average level that the outlook survey has maintained over the past two years.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Shipments and new orders moved up slightly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, optimism regarding the outlook over the next six months declined.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s a common theme of many of our business contacts that their businesses have not changed much, but they seem to be reacting to the steady stream of negative news, and it is affecting their outlook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, the CEOs of several very large industrial firms in our District report business to be very strong both domestically and overseas, and the CEOs have seen little effect of the turmoil on Wall Street on their ability to obtain credit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, last time I said that there had been little change in the District’s inflation picture.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, we have started to see evidence of increased price pressures.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Business Outlook Survey’s prices-paid index has risen considerably since the beginning of the year and has doubled since August.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The index for prices received has also more than doubled since August, rising sharply in both October and November.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Also retailers have noted spreading price increases for imported goods, and a wide range of industries are reporting increases in energy and transportation costs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Firms continue to report higher health care costs, and at the same time, wages continue to be moderate, they say.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In summary, economic conditions have changed little since our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The business activity in the region is advancing at a moderate pace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Credit constraints experienced by the large money center banks have not appreciably affected the banks in our District or their lending practices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In general, firms in the District remain cautiously optimistic about their businesses six months from now but not so much as they were last month.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Price pressures have increased on the input side related to energy and commodity costs; more generally, many firms are now prepared to raise their own prices and are looking to do so in the near future, and the financial conditions of our banks remain good.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Turning to the nation, financial market conditions, especially those associated with the big money center banks, have clearly deteriorated in recent weeks.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Until the end of October, spreads were gradually declining.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It seems that the potential for a serious meltdown was monotonically declining.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, since early November, as we all pointed to, a number of financial institutions, subprime mortgages, jumbo mortgages, asset-backed commercial paper, below-investment-grade bonds, and LIBOR have experienced increased spreads.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Volatility has risen as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Clearly, risk premiums have risen for certain classes of assets, and investors have fresh concerns about the way credit market conditions are evolving.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Overall, the recent financial developments suggest that it will take longer before conditions are “back to normal” in all segments of the market.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I’ve said before, I continue to believe that price discovery still plagues many of these markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It now looks as though it will take a little longer before these markets can sort things out and return to normal.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Financial institutions continue to write off some of the investments and take losses.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I view these write-downs as a necessary and healthy part of the process toward stabilization.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Infusions of capital in some financial institutions, I think, are encouraging and helpful to the process.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This does not mean that the ultimate agreed-upon market prices for some of these assets will bear any resemblance to what they did before August.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But that’s not necessarily a bad sign, nor is it a cause for concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In general, it may be a very healthy development.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The news on economic activity has softened somewhat since our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Among the negatives, of course, the housing market and residential investment continue to decline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Foreclosures have continued to grow at unprecedented rates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Firms have become a little more cautious in their investment plans.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Consumer spending has softened slightly, and real disposable personal income declined in October.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Oil prices have moved higher.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the brighter side so far, there is some evidence of spillovers from the financial and housing markets to the broader economy, but I believe it is limited.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Net exports and business fixed investment have been surprises on the upside.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Finally, and most important, the labor market still looks pretty solid.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Foreclosures and consumer weaknesses appear to be heavily concentrated in those states where the housing boom and thus the housing price declines have been most pronounced—especially California, Nevada, and Florida—and in those states, such as Ohio and Michigan, that are feeling the effects of the decline in automobile manufacturing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As President Poole indicated, credit card delinquencies were up but highly concentrated in California, Nevada, and Florida.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, based on such observations and the news that I hear from my District, I sense that the stresses in the economy vary significantly by region, and we must be mindful that the weaknesses on Wall Street are in those states that have exaggerated housing volatility and may not be representative of the rest of the economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To be sure, we must be wary of continued deterioration and spillovers, but at this point my assessment is that they remain concentrated in a few regions and are not as widespread as some of the aggregate data might suggest.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s important to note that, for a good part of the forecast for the fourth-quarter GDP, it’s payback for strong inventories and net export numbers in the third quarter.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I note that, absent payback and despite the worsening news, economic growth would be on the order of 2 percent higher.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To put this differently, the news since the last meeting has not altered the overall GDP forecast for the second half of 2007.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The news has clearly altered the Greenbook’s forecast for 2008, especially for the first half of the year but also extending into the second half of 2008.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The forecast calls for explicit spillovers from financial markets and the housing sector to the broader economy, to consumption, to fixed investment, and so forth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I should note, however, that most private sector forecasters are significantly less pessimistic than the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Blue Chip survey, our just-released Livingston Survey, our Survey of Professional Forecasters, and several of the major forecasting firms that have issued forecasts in the last couple of weeks see weakness extending into the first and maybe the second quarter of 2008 but a much more rapid bounceback in the second half of 2008 than is suggested in the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: These private sector forecasts are more in line with my own view.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While the news on growth is somewhat on the downside, the news on inflation is on the upside.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Readings on core inflation have been stable over the last few months, but headline inflation rates have risen sharply, with increases in energy and commodity prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The broader scope of these commodity price increases and their breadth suggest that perhaps there are more-generalized inflationary pressures out there rather than these isolated relative price shocks.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I will note that the core PCE inflation rate for March to June was 1½ percent; and in every three-month window subsequently, the inflation rate has risen monotonically, now reaching 2.26 percent for the latest three-month period from August to October.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This comes after fairly steady declines in core rates during the first half of the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my comments on the Third District, I noted the greater prospects for price increases indicated by our manufacturing firms.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also am going to cite another statistic from the same survey that President Evans referred to—Duke University’s CFO Magazine survey.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The survey to which he referred was a survey conducted in late November and early December of more than 600 CFOs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the survey, the average price increase that these CFOs were estimating for their own products in the coming year was 2.8 percent, and that was up from just 2 percent in the previous quarter.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, it appears that firms are beginning to be more interested in increasing prices and are more able to do so than they were just a few months ago, even though the same CFOs were more pessimistic about the economy than they were in the last quarter.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Another piece of news on inflation expectations comes from the Livingston Survey, which was just released yesterday.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There the forecast of the average annual change for the CPI for 2007 to 2008 moved up from 2.3 percent to 3 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This, of course, partially reflects the behavior of oil prices during the past several months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The December-to-December forecast, on the other hand, also rose, but only slightly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, overall, the economy is weak but only slightly more so than I anticipated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Volatility in the financial markets continues, and the repricing of risk has not progressed as smoothly as I would like to see.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nevertheless, the spillovers from the financial turmoil seem geographically concentrated, and broader spillovers appear limited to date.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I view inflation expectations as fragile and see evidence that price pressures are growing and that more and more firms feel that price increases are coming and are supportable.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we will have to be very careful not to presume that just because price expectations and prices have remained contained that they will continue to be so, independent of our actions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I’ll start on the local level.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Overall our District economy continues to perform generally well, with ongoing weakness in the housing sector being offset by strength in agriculture, energy, and manufacturing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have seen some slowing in employment growth over the past few months, but this appears in part to be a supply consideration.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our directors and business contacts continue to report that the labor markets are, in fact, tight across much of the District with shortages of both skilled and unskilled labor and rising wage pressures.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There is some reduction in employment, obviously in the housing sector, but that is being offset by these other considerations.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would also note that manufacturing activity remains basically solid, with manufacturers reporting strong export orders.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The District’s manufacturing index moved upward in November and still points to moderate growth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, District manufacturers’ capital spending plans actually rose but remained below most of last year’s readings on balance.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to spending, general retailers reported a rebound in sales in the latter part of October and early November.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Automobile dealers, on the other hand, did report weaker sales and have also become more pessimistic on future sales.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Travel and tourism continues to expand in our region, with District airline traffic figures solid, particularly in the Denver area.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Likewise, hotel occupancy figures have continued to increase from already strong levels in the region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As has been true for some time, housing activity, as I said, remains soft.

speaker: HOENIG
text: For example, the value of residential contracts dropped again in October, and the rate of decline in residential permits steepened again in the past few months in our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Offsetting this weakness in housing, though, is considerable strength in agriculture and energy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: District energy producers continue to expand their capital investments as they are relatively confident that oil and gas prices will remain firm over the longer term.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In fact, their capital expenditures have been slowed by a continuing shortage of labor and access to some equipment.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our larger regional banks are still reporting fairly good conditions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The deal flows seem to be coming through, although they are looking at those carefully, just given the environment that they find themselves in on a national level.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Finally, price pressures remain mixed.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Most businesses report rising input costs, both labor and materials, but differ in their ability to pass those costs on at this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In transportation, input costs are passed through one for one through customer surcharges.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Other businesses continue to find it a little more difficult to pass through the higher costs, but they are beginning to push harder on that as we talk to them.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Let me turn to the national outlook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Weakness in incoming data and continuing stress in financial markets obviously are noteworthy, and others have noted that here today.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Compared with the Greenbook, however, I see stronger growth in both the short run and the longer run.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I expect fourth-quarter growth to be closer to 1 percent, not the zero percent in the Greenbook, and the economy to strengthen slowly through a good part of 2008, starting out slowly obviously and then picking up as we go through the year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Comparing my views with those in Greenbook, the basic difference appears to be largely in some of the judgmental adjustments in the Greenbook concerning spillovers from the housing and financial stress to consumer spending.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The current Greenbook forecast, as others have noted, is similar to the Blue Chip Bottom Ten forecast, which suggests to me that it might be better seen as the downside risk outlook not necessarily the most likely outlook at this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The first half of 2008, as I said, is likely to be somewhat slower than I previously projected because of the high energy prices and continued drag from housing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, I expect that growth will gradually strengthen as we move toward the end of 2008 and then remain there through the rest of the forecast period.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Having said this, I realize that the downside risk to economic activity does remain elevated.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The housing slowdown could be deeper and last longer, and continuing financial turmoil could further affect consumer and business spending.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, while financial factors remain a risk to the outlook, in my view the economy, though it will grow below its potential, can weather these forces and is being supported by the policy actions that we have taken in the past two meetings.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Against this outlook for economic growth, let me turn now to the inflation outlook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Year- over-year overall and core inflation rates have risen.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, Greenbook’s 2008 forecast for overall and core PCE inflation has increased since our last meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: While below-trend growth in the near term may exert some downward pressure on inflation, the combination of higher prices for oil, commodities, and some services and dollar depreciation should place upward pressure on both overall and core inflation going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Over the past several years, the pass-through of dollar depreciation and higher oil prices to inflation has been limited in part because of longer-term inflation expectations remaining, as we said, anchored.

speaker: HOENIG
text: My concern is that, if we continue to lower the fed funds rate into a rising inflation environment and the dollar continues to depreciate, these expectations may become unhinged perhaps more quickly than we would like to think.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In this environment, I think we should not lose sight of not just the downside risk to the real economy but also some very serious upside risk to inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, Mr. Chairman, having listened to various views starting with President Yellen, on the one end, and President Plosser, on the other, and President Hoenig on inflation, I was thinking that Edward R. Murrow said that anybody who isn’t confused really doesn’t understand the situation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m confused, and I don’t understand the situation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would like to report what I see, however.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, in terms of my District—in sharp contrast to the Twelfth District, because I think they are two extremes, or, say, Florida, in President Lockhart’s District— employment growth has slowed.

speaker: FISHER
text: I mention this because last time I mentioned a data point, which is that within our District—actually in one state—year to date we may have created up to one-fifth of the jobs in this country.

speaker: FISHER
text: We were growing our employment base at 3.9 percent in the first quarter.

speaker: FISHER
text: We expected it to slow to 3.1 in the third quarter and then to slow down to the high 2s as we approached the end of the year.

speaker: FISHER
text: Housing prices in our District are appreciating, and we’re benefiting from what we call the California diaspora—that is, particularly the techies and others, who are pushing up prices in Dallas and Austin.

speaker: FISHER
text: Finally, one point to bear in mind is wage pressure.

speaker: FISHER
text: Oil and gas extraction represents only 2 percent of the employment of Texas, despite how everybody stereotypes our state.

speaker: FISHER
