text: It might be worth noting that many market participants expect the Federal Reserve to augment its monetary policy action today with some announcement regarding the discount window—for example, a reduction in the primary credit spread.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As the Chairman noted earlier today, the absence of such a reference in today’s announcement could prompt some investor disappointment; but given your monetary policy action under alternative B, the effect on market interest rates seems likely to be limited, and presumably, any effect today will be reversed tomorrow.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If the Committee is already persuaded that the economic outlook has weakened more sharply than in the Greenbook or if it has become significantly more concerned about the downside risks to growth, it might prefer the 50 basis point easing of alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee might see the larger move at this time as warranted particularly by risk-management considerations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Greenbook presented two alternative scenarios—a “greater housing correction” and a “credit crunch”—that illustrate downside risks and suggest that the Committee may need to ease markedly further over coming quarters.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the case of the credit crunch scenario, for example, the estimated version of the Taylor rule calls for a funds rate that troughs at 2.6 percent, well below the low point currently built into market interest rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the second column, the language suggested for alternative A explicitly cites both a weaker outlook and greater downside risks in explaining the relatively large policy move.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As in alternative B, the language on inflation would be nearly unchanged from that employed in October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But in section 4 of alternative A, the Committee would indicate a judgment that—following the further reduction in interest rates—the upside risks to inflation roughly balance the downside risks to growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Or the risk language shown in red in section 4 of alternative B could instead be employed under alternative A; this might be appropriate if the Committee felt that the same elevated risks that motivated it to ease 50 basis points also suggested that it was difficult to weigh the remaining risks after the action.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In either case, short- and intermediate-term market interest rates would likely decline noticeably under alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In contemplating the pros and cons of alternative A, one consideration might be whether the Committee views this combination of sharp easing and the associated language, particularly the version coupled with an inconclusive risk assessment, as likely to lead market participants to worry about what information the Committee might have that would lead it to take such a substantial step, and so undermine investor confidence.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If, in contrast, the Committee saw the downside risks to growth as somewhat greater but was not yet convinced that the outlook had deteriorated substantially and remained concerned about inflation prospects, it might consider implementation of alternative C. As indicated in the right-hand column, under this alternative the Committee would maintain the stance of policy at this meeting but conclude that the downside risks to growth now are the predominant concern.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With overall inflation on the high side and upward pressures stemming from energy prices and dollar depreciation, members might be concerned that policy easing could go too far.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The stance of policy has already been eased 75 basis points despite only limited evidence to date that economic weakness is spreading to a significant degree beyond the housing sector.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, as some of you suggested, the incoming indicators of slowing growth over the intermeeting period may be broadly in line with what you expected in October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If so, the Committee may feel that its monetary policy actions to date—and, at the margin, the establishment of the TAF as well as swap lines with foreign central banks—probably will provide sufficient insurance that financial problems will remain contained and will not greatly restrict the availability of credit to households and businesses.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus members may believe that further easing is not and probably will not be necessary.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, members may find worrisome the prescription of the optimal control simulation in the Bluebook that a slight degree of policy firming would be appropriate over coming quarters if the Committee were pursuing a 1½ percent long-run objective for inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even with such unease about inflation prospects, though, the Committee may be sufficiently concerned about the current threat to growth to judge that, on balance, the risks are tilted to the downside with an unchanged stance of policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will conclude by responding belatedly to a question that President Evans posed at the last meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: He asked what the experience has been with including an indication of downside risks in the policy statement.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In particular, would markets likely see such a risk assessment as signaling a likelihood of an imminent policy easing?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Answering the question on the basis of the historical record is not entirely straightforward, partly because the Committee’s practices have evolved over time; as President Evans noted, it has been only since 1999 that the Committee has released a risk assessment or some other form of a tilt along with its announcement.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Despite some qualifications, the basic answer seems to be, not surprisingly, that the risk assessments have been predictive of future Committee action.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The experience from December 2000 through January 2002 makes this point clearly.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: During that period, at fourteen meetings in a row the Committee indicated that “the risks are weighted mainly toward conditions that may generate economic weakness in the foreseeable future.” In eleven of those fourteen instances, that indication was followed by a policy easing at the next meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Later, toward the end of 2002, one of two indications of downside risk was followed by an easing, and in June 2003, a different balance of risks—one concerned with disinflation—was followed by an easing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: All in all, it seems reasonable to judge in current circumstances that maintaining the stance of policy while assessing that the risks are tilted to the downside, as under alternative C, would lead market participants to continue to put high odds on future policy easing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But the absence of policy action at this meeting despite nearly unanimous expectations of policy easing would mean that the expectation of a downtilt in rates would begin from a notably higher level and might be less steep, prompting a significant upward shift in short- and intermediate-term interest rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That concludes my prepared remarks.

speaker: EVANS
text: Brian, thank you very much for that answer.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have a clarifying question because I’m not quite sure I caught, in the way you talked about the economic risks in section 4 of alternative B, how they could be added.

speaker: EVANS
text: One thing that I wanted to ask about is that in section 2 there’s no mention of downside economic risks.

speaker: EVANS
text: At least the five or six times I read it, I couldn’t find it.

speaker: EVANS
text: That seems different from alternative C and alternative A, and also the October statement, at least in the balance of risk, mentioned downside risks to growth.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is there a particular message that we’re thinking about sending with that?

speaker: EVANS
text: I guess part of the question is that, without some mention of expected slowing, are we maybe undercutting our November forecast that we published?

speaker: EVANS
text: It seems natural that there would be some discussion about how things have slowed relative to what we were expecting.

speaker: EVANS
text: I mean, that might be one way that those forecasts would be interpreted and used.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I lay that out as a question.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: President Evans, in response to your first question, the suggestion for section 4 of alternative B would be to add after the “Recent developments…” sentence, “On balance, the Committee sees downside risks to growth as having increased, but it must also remain attentive to the upside pressures on inflation.” With regard to your other question, I think that characterizing whether the slowing in economic growth right now is what you anticipated may be a little difficult.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is relatively early in terms of the information that’s available for the fourth quarter, so it may be difficult to pin that down very precisely.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Weakness in economic data reported since the last meeting, continued financial turmoil, and a forecast that places us uncomfortably close to a recession calls for action, and my strong preference is for the decisive action reflected in alternative A.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With well-anchored inflation expectations and the possibility of unemployment rising above our estimate of the NAIRU, the risks to inflation from this action seem quite low.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, the possibility that the economy will soon be in a recession is too high, and our action should be significant enough to substantially reduce that risk.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to policy, I also favor alternative A, a 50 basis point rate cut.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Let me explain my reasoning.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Otherwise I certainly agree with what President Rosengren said.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, I think the equilibrium real rate of interest is low relative to its long-run average.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The range of medium-run measures of r* reported in the Bluebook is between 1.8 and 2.3 percent, and this range includes the Greenbook-consistent measure and the staff’s Kalman filter model estimate of 2.1 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Market perceptions of future real interest rates are also very low, with yields on five-year Treasury inflation-indexed bonds now below 1¼ percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the headwinds from financial market turmoil and the more general reassessment of risks that is taking place in global markets are good reasons why the equilibrium real rate may be low in the current situation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We do have historical precedence for this.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, Kalman filter estimates of r* fell noticeably during the credit crunch of the early 1990s.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the current state of the economy with inflation near a level consistent with price stability and resource utilization near its equilibrium level, policy should be close to neutral, which implies a nominal funds rate of 4 to 4¼ percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The forecast and risk assessment must also enter the analysis.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With an assumed 25 basis point cut at this meeting, the Greenbook foresees the economy barely skirting a recession, so any more bad news could put us over the edge; and the possibility of getting bad news—in particular, a significant credit crunch—seems far from remote.

speaker: YELLEN
text: To my mind, the risk to the forecast and the risk of a vicious cycle, in which deteriorating financial conditions and a weakening economy and house prices feed on each other, argue for adopting a risk-management strategy that, at the very minimum, moves our policy stance to the low end of neutral—namely, a cut of 50 basis points—and I think it argues for doing so now rather than taking a “wait and see” approach and lowering it only grudgingly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This may not be enough to avoid a recession—we may soon need outright accommodation—but it would at least help cushion the blow and lessen the risk of a prolonged downturn.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I should also say that my recommendation assumes that the implementation of the TAF, even if it succeeds in improving liquidity in the money market, will not appreciably alleviate macroeconomic conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Regardless of the policy actions taken at this meeting, I think we need to be very careful in these unsettled conditions about how we communicate our assessment of risks and likely future policy actions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We should maintain maximum flexibility so that our future actions can, in Governor Kohn’s well-chosen words, be nimble.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If the Committee chooses to cut the funds rate 50 points, I would favor the assessment of risks from section 4, alternative B, in table 1.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This appropriately leaves open what the future policy will be and stresses that it depends on developments.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If the Committee goes with the 25 basis point cut, then I would support using the assessment of risks from section 4, alternative C, which states clearly that the predominant concern is the downside risk to growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Otherwise I fear that market participants may mark up their expected path for policy over the next year, leading to further erosion in financial conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Finally, I would suggest that, given the long period of time between today and the next FOMC meeting, we be open to the possibility of a special intermeeting videoconference to assess economic and financial developments, and this meeting could also benefit from an assessment of the effects of the TAF once it’s in place.

speaker: LACKER
text: I favor a ¼ point reduction in the funds rate and the language of alternative B.

speaker: LACKER
text: Perhaps more than usual I think it is important to preserve some flexibility now to respond to incoming information.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would not be surprised if we want to reduce the funds rate another ¼ point at the end of January, but I don’t want to send a signal that would encourage market participants to presume another cut then.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I guess I am in the “grudgingly” camp to which President Yellen referred.

speaker: LACKER
text: Besides, I would welcome a permanent move away from the balance-of-risk-assessment machinery.

speaker: LACKER
text: I do believe we face a good-sized risk of things unraveling and substantially weaker growth in the near term.

speaker: LACKER
text: But my sense is that the risk just isn’t large enough to make me want to support 50 basis points now.

speaker: LACKER
text: While I wouldn’t be surprised with a January rate cut, I don’t think it should be a foregone conclusion.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we need to be more deliberate about such actions as we go forward.

speaker: LACKER
text: The magnitude of the fallout from our mortgage problems could be substantially clearer in the first half of next year.

speaker: LACKER
text: If the fallout turns out to be smaller and more manageable than we fear, the downside risks to growth prospects could dissipate, even though we still would be working through a bulge of mortgage resets and defaults.

speaker: LACKER
text: Some of us have given a warning that we may need to reverse course promptly and raise rates should conditions improve.

speaker: LACKER
text: You know, it is always attractive to comfort ourselves as we cut interest rates and to promise ourselves that we are willing to do so, but there always seems to be a reluctance to start a sequence of funds rate increases after a series of rate cuts.

speaker: LACKER
text: The usual thing is a fear of sort of an exaggerated reaction in the yield curve.

speaker: LACKER
text: These pressures are likely to be especially acute if, when the time comes, we are still in the midst of significant distress among subprime mortgage borrowers and the housing market.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I think we need to be realistic about prospects for reversing field.

speaker: LACKER
text: To the extent that such pressures would be hard to resist—and I think they would be—we should be very cautious, more cautious than we otherwise would be, about lowering rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: Another reason to be cautious is that overall inflation is well above our targets.

speaker: LACKER
text: As David Stockton pointed out, we have a record of forecasts for food and energy prices based on futures market prices coming in too optimistic over the past several years.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we need to be concerned about that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am concerned that market participants might have come to believe that we have placed our concerns about inflation entirely on hold for the duration of the housing market difficulties we face.

speaker: LACKER
text: Such a lexicographic reaction function is what led to the stop-go policy pattern in the pre-1979 era.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I believe it would be a mistake to take our eyes entirely off inflation right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am doubtful that a forceful restatement of our assessment of upside inflation risk will be very effective in that regard.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have been doing that, and I think it is falling on increasingly deaf ears.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that we may come to believe that action is required to back up that sentiment.

speaker: LACKER
text: If inflation drifts up or overall inflation doesn’t come down, I think we need to be prepared to respond to real weakness less than we otherwise would have before.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would say that when Governor Mishkin talked about the importance of maintaining long-anchored expectations about inflation, I agreed with that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that is more vulnerable than others do, and so if it were on the table, I would support maintaining the rate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think inflation risks are elevated.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am uneasy about lowering rates into a rising inflation environment, and I think we should have allowed more time for the 75 basis points to work.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Having said that, however, I also acknowledge that the downside risk to growth may be larger than I judge it to be.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There is a lot of evidence out there right now, and I have heard it from around the table.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Thus, I can accept the 25 basis point cut, if that is the Committee’s preferred action.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would be very uneasy with a 50 basis point cut at this time, and I do not think a 50 basis point cut is warranted in conjunction with tomorrow’s announcement of a term auction facility.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that would send a signal to financial markets that we view the outlook as more dire than it is, thus adding to financial turmoil rather than alleviating it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I ask the Committee to keep that very carefully in mind as we go forward with this discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Hoenig, did you have a view on the statement?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to the statement, I think the language in alternative B is the right language, regardless of which—A, B, or C—we choose.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think in particular I would prefer that we not assess a balance of risk and instead simply state that recent events have increased the uncertainty on output and inflation.

speaker: POOLE
text: I favor alternative B, including the language, and let me outline how I get there.

speaker: POOLE
text: First, I think that it is important to recognize that the Greenbook outlook already takes account, as best we can or as best the staff can, of a lot of the dismal financial news that is out there.

speaker: POOLE
text: There is a probability distribution around that.

speaker: POOLE
text: We don’t want to double-count the financial distress.

speaker: POOLE
text: It is already in the baseline forecast, and we don’t want to think of all the weight of the financial distress effect as being down from there.

speaker: POOLE
text: So there could be an outcome that is certainly stronger than the Greenbook outcome.

speaker: POOLE
text: In fact, I think it is true historically, if you look at forecast accuracy, any forecaster, including the Greenbook staff, does not have a standard error all that much below a very naïve outlook that just says that GDP will grow at potential.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I believe that there is genuine weight above the Greenbook forecast in the probability distribution, and I think the Greenbook forecast is a very good baseline for our discussion.

speaker: POOLE
text: Second, clearly, should the unemployment rate rise significantly, credit problems are likely to multiply rapidly.

speaker: POOLE
text: We could have a great deal of distress that would accumulate, possibly very quickly.

speaker: POOLE
text: On the other side, should the nonhousing sectors prove more resilient than the Greenbook forecast, we could be faced by upside surprises, especially on inflation.

speaker: POOLE
text: Certainly, I would come down hard on the side that following a policy that temporizes on inflation only builds in a much deeper problem in the future, and it is better to take the medicine early, if necessary, to deal with inflation.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would also note that, over next year, there will be an increasingly high bar on any change in the federal funds target.

speaker: POOLE
text: There is an election in November.

speaker: POOLE
text: I have tremendous confidence in the nonpolitical outlook of every single member of the Committee, every single participant; indeed it is a very deep part of the culture of the institution.

speaker: POOLE
text: Nevertheless, there are tricky issues involved with maintaining the appearance of impartiality, and I think historically during an election year there is a strong presumption to try to stay as low key as possible.

speaker: POOLE
text: The way you do that is not change the fed funds rate target at all unless there is a really good case, and that is increasingly true as you come up to the November election.

speaker: POOLE
text: So as we go through the year, there is going to be an increasingly high bar, it seems to me, and if we overshoot on the easing side, it may be difficult to come back until ’09.

speaker: POOLE
text: I think that every cut is likely to be permanent through next year in any event.

speaker: POOLE
text: That tells me that we should pursue a strategy—I say “we,” but it is more “you” because the next meeting is my last.

speaker: POOLE
text: Not quite after that meeting.

speaker: POOLE
text: It is still a little cold.

speaker: POOLE
text: But my instinct is that we have demonstrated a willingness to act decisively when there is a very good case in the data.

speaker: POOLE
text: So if data come in with very bad employment reports, additional financial distress, and all of that, I don’t think there is any question that the market will then anticipate decisive action.

speaker: POOLE
text: That wasn’t so true back in August, by the way, but the fact that there was a 50 basis point move in September has conditioned the market to respond differently.

speaker: POOLE
text: I would be in favor of a strategy that says at this point, if we indeed go down another 25 basis points, we will have cut the target by 100—a strategy that is very open but in a sense follows the market.

speaker: POOLE
text: Now, if it turns out that we have a lot of weak news in the weeks ahead, the market is going to build in further rate cuts.

speaker: POOLE
text: It will do a lot of the work for us without our having to be out front.

speaker: POOLE
text: You will get the benefits brought forward because the market is going to bid those in, and therefore, I think a strategy that tries to follow the data, to demonstrate a clear willingness to respond to the incoming information, gives us the best chance for stability over the coming year.

speaker: POOLE
text: Despite the memo that I distributed, which I think was an option that we should consider, I think that we should not have any balance of risks view because it is highly desirable to leave everything very open.

speaker: POOLE
text: Meeting by meeting, we, or you, will have to decide whether the case is being made from the data.

speaker: POOLE
text: Of course, I think that the speeches and other communication will be very important to try to explain the strategy and the process by which we assess and respond to the data, maintaining always a longer-term view and not getting carried away with the most recent observations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I support the action and language of alternative B. I think rates are too high right now to support the economy’s remaining near full employment and higher than they need to be to contain inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: When we left the meeting last time, we thought we might be where we needed to be, but that was premised on a lack of spillovers outside the housing sector and improving financial markets, and both of those have proven not to be the case.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think we need to move.

speaker: KOHN
text: How much is a tough question.

speaker: KOHN
text: If we were to do 25, we would still have restrictive policy based on the staff forecast because 25 basis points moves the unemployment rate above full employment.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it is still on the restrictive side, even with 25 in the Greenbook.

speaker: KOHN
text: Of course, we would be outrageously tight relative to the markets’ expectations of what we need to do.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think 25 basis points still leaves us a little on the tight side, and I suspect we will have to do more over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I am comfortable doing 25 at this meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: There is just a huge amount of uncertainty about how the financial markets are evolving, especially before the end of the year.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we will have a little better sense of what the net deterioration is when we get past the year-end, into January, and see what effect, if any, our auction facility has.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some of the signs we have had in the incoming data haven’t been that negative—the employment report—which is a really key report, and the fact that there is continued growth in employment gives me a little reassurance that we are not in some huge downdraft in the market and that we don’t need to move that aggressively.

speaker: KOHN
text: We do have high headline inflation that we are looking at and some inflation risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think at this point that 25 basis points would send a signal that the Federal Reserve is awake and on the job, and I would stick with language that gives us maximum flexibility, which I think alternative B, section 4, does.

speaker: KOHN
text: President Fisher asked, “What would a decline in the federal funds rate do?” I think it would do quite a bit.

speaker: KOHN
text: It doesn’t address those losses directly, I agree.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think it would offset some of the tightening in financial conditions or would move in that direction.

speaker: KOHN
text: It would help asset prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also asked myself when you asked that question, President Fisher, what would happen if we didn’t lower rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we would have much tighter financial conditions in the market adding to what is already a distressed situation.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I really think that the 25 will be beneficial.

speaker: KOHN
text: A lot of people around the table have said—and President Evans raised the question about whether there are some downside risks—that somehow we could express something more in the statement.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wouldn’t object, Mr. Chairman, if someone found some language to put a little more sense of downside risks about the outlook somewhere in the alternative B statement.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, I think we clearly should be reducing the federal funds rate at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: While I think it is a close call, I guess I would come out with doing a quarter at this meeting.

speaker: STERN
text: Basically, I get there by just trying to weigh the risks.

speaker: STERN
text: I think the principal risk is the dysfunction in financial markets and what that could imply prospectively for the performance of the economy.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that is the basic case for taking action now.

speaker: STERN
text: I think the risks are asymmetric.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t see the same risk to the near or intermediate term in terms of inflation outlook.

speaker: STERN
text: Yes, we may get some high headline numbers, but we hope at least that those will dissipate rather quickly.

speaker: STERN
text: So that is where I come out.

speaker: STERN
text: I would support the language under alternative B.

speaker: STERN
text: Just to add one thought on that: You know, last time we tried to characterize the balance of risk, and I don’t think it turned out to be persuasive.

speaker: STERN
text: We would do well to be very, very cautious at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: Obviously, there is a lot of uncertainty out there, and at this point, discretion is the better part of valor.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the last two meetings, the Committee cut the funds rate 75 basis points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We did so because the outlook for the economy has clearly deteriorated relative to our views in early August.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have argued that we have been acting preemptively to help forestall and to mitigate potential fallout from the deteriorating housing market and financial disruptions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How successful have those rate cuts been?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it is too early to tell.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is still true that the effects of monetary policy on the broader economy— especially on spending, output, and employment—operate with a considerable lag.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is my guess that our previous cuts or anything we do today will not have measurable effects on the broader economy in terms of spending and output until late in the first quarter of next year and more likely in the second and third quarters.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I don’t think anything we do today will have an appreciable effect, if any, on the economy’s first-quarter performance.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, one’s view about the future path of the economy during the second half of ’08 depends critically on what you think the effect of our decisions will be going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, contrary to what some may think, I am not immune to the drum beat of downbeat news that we have heard.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am keenly aware of the concerns expressed around this table and by others who are more concerned and anticipate a much more prolonged period of reduced growth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have marked down my forecast for the first half of ’08, but my view of the second half has not changed very much.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, while I am okay with the 25 basis point cut at this meeting, I would like to highlight that there are risks to that decision.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would oppose a 50 basis point cut.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As suggested in my earlier remarks, I do think that there are increasing underlying inflation pressures, and although we have not seen inflationary expectations change very much in the data, I do think they are fragile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Before I stop, I would just like to give one example of that concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the last Philadelphia Fed Survey of Professional Forecasters, conducted in early November, we asked a special question.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We asked panelists whether they believe that the FOMC has an inflation target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: About half the survey respondents said that they believe the FOMC has an inflation target, and of those, close to 90 percent responded that they thought our target was for core PCE inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They also provided their views on what the target was.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The median estimate of that target was between 1.6 and 1.7 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Among these forecasters, almost all those who thought that we had a target also indicated that their long-term—that is, their ten- year—forecast of PCE core inflation was systematically 50 basis points, ½ percentage point, higher than what they thought our target must be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We asked the forecasters, if their forecast was different from the target, why it was.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Almost all the forecasters presented a variation on a very similar theme.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Many of them said, “Well, the Fed really has goals other than inflation,” or “they wouldn’t stick to it,” or “they would find it painful and, therefore, not commit to the goal,” or “they lacked credibility.” Now, this is a small subsample of people.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nevertheless, I find it interesting that these professional forecasters are really not terribly sure about our commitment to price stability.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The issue is not what they thought the target was per se but what the differential between their forecast and the target was.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Finally, just regarding language, I have been uncomfortable for some time with the practice of summarizing the balance of risks, and I share President Lacker’s concern in that I would like to get rid of it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would support alternative B with the language.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I will also reiterate the point that, while we may be making ourselves feel better, the fact is that we need to be prepared to act quickly if things reverse themselves and we have to reverse the rate cuts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the other hand, I think the history of this institution is such that it is in fact more difficult to do than it is to say, so I think we need to have some caution.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I favor alternative B and the language as expressed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I listened to the first go-round comments, I charted everyone in a quadrant chart with high risk to growth and benign inflation in the upper left-hand corner.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Then, I had of course three other squares or quadrants, and so far I am seven for eight listening to the remarks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So maybe this predictive power has some influence or some spillover into how I come out on this.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I don’t suppose 37½ would fly.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: You know, on balance I find myself in the upper left-hand quadrant, more concerned about downside risk to the economy and viewing, at least for the present, inflation as a relatively benign consideration.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So given my sense of the downside risks and the uncertainty that is associated with the financial markets, my recommendation is 50 basis points at this meeting, and my preference is to remain, as much as possible, agnostic on the January action.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I take note from the advice I get from some of my own staff that Taylor rule projections suggest that the medium- term nominal equilibrium rate is about 4 percent, and 4 percent comes the closest to being the likely neutral rate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is relatively likely that incoming data will suggest that a cumulative cut of at least 50 basis points is warranted by the end of January.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So in my view, moving to that rate now is really the most prudential.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In some respects, that is the most conservative and risk- attentive policy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I continue to adhere to the risk-management perspective in dealing with our challenges, and continuing to take out insurance against extreme downside scenarios seems correct to me.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Notwithstanding the view that the Fed is, and should be, reluctant to take back a rate cut, I prefer facing up to that difficult decision possibly next spring to undershooting the needs of the situation and potentially compounding the problems.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I don’t see a lot to be gained from an incremental approach of 25 basis point cuts.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It has been argued with much validity that overnight liquidity isn’t really the problem and won’t cure the information gaps that beset the market.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But I would argue that, given the profoundly unsettled state of the financial markets, erring on the side of more-aggressive action provides some insurance against continuing liquidity seizures.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: To the extent that psychology and confidence matter—and I think they matter a great deal in these circumstances—it is on its face a stronger message.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding the statement, I actually prefer alternative B. I think the finessing, if you will, of the balance of risks and its mention of increased uncertainty come closest to my views.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I suggest consideration of the thrust of alternative B, possibly with the insertion that Brian mentioned, connected to a 50 basis point policy action.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I don’t think I could have said it better than Governor Kohn said it.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am on his wavelength.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would just add a couple of things that I would suggest we consider.

speaker: FISHER
text: First of all, with regard to the financial situation, which is obviously driving this conversation, I appreciate the medical pathology that the Vice Chairman suggested.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have gone now from cardiology, which is my thing, to this fever and the fever breaking, and so on.

speaker: FISHER
text: I combine it with a bit of the strawman that Governor Warsh raised.

speaker: FISHER
text: No one has suggested a panacea.

speaker: FISHER
text: No one has suggested that the existing pool of ersatz money, outside money, or shadow money is fully sufficient to relieve the stress the system is under.

speaker: FISHER
text: What has changed, however, since the August crisis is the process of price discovery.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are beginning to actually get realistic pricing.

speaker: FISHER
text: I spent twenty-one years buying distressed assets on Wall Street.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think I understand the process.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is a patient process, and it takes time.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I think that is the only difference.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have begun the process; it has a long way to go.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have enormous risks, and I fully agree with Vice Chairman Geithner that there is significant risk that might stem from this.

speaker: FISHER
text: But let’s not also understate the fact that some adjustment has begun and that is good news.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would suggest 25 basis points, Mr. Chairman, because I think we have to be very wary of shooting an entire bolt here.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we do 50 basis points plus the TAF plus the swap lines—this is all very subjective—my opinion is that we would scare the hell out of the markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is a significant risk if we send a signal, as was previously said—I think Brian may have said this— that we have information that other people do not have.

speaker: FISHER
text: President Lockhart referred to delicate psychology.

speaker: FISHER
text: From a risk-management standpoint, I think the psychology is the opposite of what he stated, which is that we are at risk of interfering with the beginning of the adjustment process that I just described.

speaker: FISHER
text: If people feel that we know more than they do, that we have greater fear of the downside, you are going to see a delay in that adjustment.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are wanting to step up and cherry-pick a little before you start going through the whole orchard.

speaker: FISHER
text: So those would be the two factors that I would suggest.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to come back to the last point.

speaker: FISHER
text: Our job is to keep inflation at bay.

speaker: FISHER
text: The nominal anchor you mentioned is critical.

speaker: FISHER
text: I heard more people speak around this table about being worried about inflation than did not so speak.

speaker: FISHER
text: I agree with President Poole and the suggestion of, I think, Charlie Plosser.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would like to be like the Reserve Bank of Australia and raise the rates despite the political election, if we had to.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I think the scrutiny of this institution will be intense, and my preferred mode is just to stay out of the way.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it is politically very brave and possibly foolish to say that, well, if we do too much here, we can always pull it back.

speaker: FISHER
text: There will be a lot different circumstances next year, and I worry that we may do too much.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would be against 50 basis points.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would be in favor of 25 basis points, and I would be in favor of alternative B as stated, if I had a vote.

speaker: EVANS
text: I favor a ¼ point reduction in the fed funds rate today.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I noted earlier, assuming some ease in policy, my forecast is that the economy will experience subpar growth stretching into the middle of 2008 but then recover as we move into 2009 and that inflation will remain contained.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our forecast assumes that the disruptions in financial markets will generate more-restrictive credit conditions for consumers and businesses than we have seen to date, though not to the degree assumed in the Greenbook baseline.

speaker: EVANS
text: In light of my outlook, I think that policy should be somewhat accommodative; and given that I think the long-run neutral nominal funds rate is somewhere around 4½ to 4¾ percent, I support further easing.

speaker: EVANS
text: Given our expectations of coming financial restraint, there is a good chance that we will ultimately want to reduce the funds rate 50 basis points, but I prefer to go slower than that and move down only 25 basis points today.

speaker: EVANS
text: The slowing in consumption that we have recently seen reflects only a couple of months of data that followed quite strong growth during the summer, and much of that softening may reflect the transitory jump in gasoline prices.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I don’t think it is clear that we have seen a real change in the trajectory of consumption.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think the degree of financial spillover built into the Greenbook baseline is a plausible scenario, but we have not seen such spillover yet.

speaker: EVANS
text: The pessimistic view is a very forward-looking one, and I applaud forward-looking thinking.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not quite there yet, but that is definitely a risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: I hesitate to say that we will know more next meeting because it is such an obvious thing to say, but I definitely agree with Governor Kohn that by the end of January we will at least have a better idea of how the TAF funding went and how much of the recent increase in liquidity demand and related disruptions are transitory end- of-year problems as opposed to more-fundamental problems that would impinge dramatically on credit conditions for nonfinancial borrowers.

speaker: EVANS
text: We will also know more about the actual strength of consumption and investment.

speaker: EVANS
text: Another concern I have about a 50 basis point move today is that the public might see it as an indication that we have read the incoming news more negatively than I at least think we should have, so I agree with Presidents Hoenig and Fisher on that.

speaker: EVANS
text: This would have negative implications for the already fragile state of consumer and market sentiment.

speaker: EVANS
text: But from here to a 4 percent fed funds rate, I think that the inflation risks are acceptable.

speaker: EVANS
text: Beyond that, I think it depends importantly on inflation developments and also developments in the economy.

speaker: EVANS
text: In terms of the statement, I prefer alternative B. I like the additional sentence that Brian was suggesting in section 4 for the balance of risks.

speaker: EVANS
text: But however that comes out, in reading section 2, when I was asking the question, it just seemed to me natural that after “incoming information suggests that economic growth is slowing” something like “somewhat more than previously expected” might be helpful, but nobody else has really mentioned that, and I am okay with that.

speaker: EVANS
text: Finally, on the political concerns, my memory is that we raised the funds rate during the 2000 and 2004 elections, so I am not really concerned about that, although people will wonder.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I favor a 25 basis point cut in our fed funds rate target and the language in alternative B.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: More losses at financial companies, in combination with uncertain year-end funding pressures, obviously have unsettled financial markets again.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As I said earlier, sentiment about business conditions next year have become considerably more pessimistic in the past few weeks.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In this environment, leaning toward caution and providing the added short-term liquidity that markets appear to need makes sense to me.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Although I can see the arguments for a 50 basis point adjustment in our policy rate, I am inclined to think that a lesser policy response is called for.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As others have indicated, it may be that a 25 basis point action is going to prove to be insufficient, and another cut might be necessary.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But I am also mindful that efforts to address the problems that are affecting the real economy have the potential to aggravate inflation expectations.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Indeed, by some cuts of the TIPS data and from a few reports that I am receiving from business contacts about rising commodity prices and rising import prices, inflation expectations may be tugging on their anchor just a bit.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given these considerable uncertainties, I think smaller moves are preferable to larger ones.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At this time, I simply can’t assess with any useful precision how to weigh the risks we face, only that the risks we face are very difficult.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Consequently, I favor the language expressed in alternative B as it is currently written.

speaker: WARSH
text: I support alternative B as is.

speaker: WARSH
text: Without monetary policy action, it does strike me that the harm to the real economy could be larger and longer than otherwise.

speaker: WARSH
text: Similarly, I would say that without employing the liquidity tools that we discussed when we met by videoconference, monetary policy may well be insufficient to bring about real improvement over a reasonable period of time.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I like the combination as a very useful, natural experiment to help us figure out what the diagnosis of the patient really is.

speaker: WARSH
text: It does concern me that, if we go with 50 basis points today along with the TAF, the swap, and other actions, it would be harder to disentangle what exactly ails these markets, which is some combination of capital and liquidity.

speaker: WARSH
text: With respect to the question of how much—again, back to the 25 or 50 basis point move—it strikes me at least that this is a very hard time for us to be evaluating what the equilibrium fed funds rate is.

speaker: WARSH
text: If policy is a function of both the fed funds rate target and what is going on and how capital markets are reading and processing that information, these markets are in a period of incredible dysfunction.

speaker: WARSH
text: That suggests to me that we should go slower and be more cautious in trying to get to equilibrium.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is easier to assess that when markets are functioning at levels that are superior to where they are functioning now, and I hope by the time we meet next that the markets will be giving us a clearer read, so we can approach equilibrium or at least understand it better.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, with respect to some of the discussion around alternative B, section 4, I think as written it gives us maximum flexibility, as was referenced earlier.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t happen to think that market expectations would be changed much if we added a sentence about downside risks to growth.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think last time around they took our uncertainty paragraph, learned that it meant that there was a rate cut coming, and I don’t think we need to push farther than that at this point.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we have two fronts on which we have to work—both the macro risks, in particular the housing risks and the liquidity issues, and their interaction, as a lot of people have discussed.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I favor a 25 basis point reduction with the other actions that we will be taking with respect to liquidity—the TAF and the swap.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it is very important, at least in my thinking, to see them as a package, to try to work on both margins, because many people have raised concerns about the liquidity issues perhaps spilling over into being real economy issues—so liquidity issues turning into capital issues that can turn into credit constriction issues.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With respect to the macro risks, most people around the table have said that those are real and that we need to work on those.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Then, of course, there is an interaction between the two.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Part of the reason for the difficulty of reviving the price discovery process is uncertainty about what is going to happen in some markets, particularly housing markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So providing a little more insurance there is valuable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But there is also a concern that, even independent of that, there could be liquidity problems that cause difficulties, so working on these two fronts is certainly very valuable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We will, then, have cut the federal funds rate 100 basis points and will have taken some steps, both with the reduction of the difference between the fed funds rate and the discount rate and these new actions, to try to provide more liquidity.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With respect to the statement, I think the statement as it is in alternative B is probably the most effective.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is important for us to express the uncertainty with respect to the balance of risks rather than try to describe the balance of risks.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t really see what would be added by talking about particular downside risks when we can simply say that there is uncertainty.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I agree with Governor Warsh that the markets would interpret this as that there may be more to come and that we will mindful and watching what is going on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Particularly in the context of the new liquidity actions that we will be taking, it is better to say that we are uncertain than to say that we are uncertain with downside risks and then take these other actions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is more appropriate for us to convey that the combination of actions leaves us uncertain because that, rather than uncertainty with downside risks, may help unlock some of these markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The modal forecast suggests a cut of at least 25 basis points.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, it indicates that we need to have further declines after that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As Governor Kohn pointed out, the 25 basis point cut still leaves us as somewhat restrictive.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So we could just sit at a 25 basis point cut and not move further and keep our options open.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think Governor Kohn made a very good argument for that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, I do really worry about the significant probability that things could go south in a vicious circle.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that context, I think that the issue of macroeconomic risk is really a severe one, and an action of 50 basis points could help deal with that risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I would prefer alternative A.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If the Committee were going that way, which it is not, I would have added a sentence about high uncertainty because I think the balance of risk sentence does create certain problems.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There is a question about whether you should have that at all.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But if you have it in there in situations like this, we definitely should emphasize the uncertainty much more and use a sentence like the one that is in alternative B in that case.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So let me just lay out this argument.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Would a 50 basis point cut matter?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is a question that President Fisher has asked.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think the answer is very much “yes.” It is not the actual cut itself that matters; it is the managing of expectations that really matters.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, whenever we make a 25 basis point cut and you ask, “How big an impact does that have on the economy?” the answer is, “Not a whole lot.” That comes out of our simulations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is really the path of interest rates implied by our actions that is important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, the idea here of a 50 basis point cut is that, by getting ahead of the curve, we provide a signal to the markets that we would be willing to take steps to react to events in the financial markets that might indicate that we are getting into a vicious-circle type of situation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is exactly what I felt we did in the September meeting.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That move was very successful, and the markets really improved very dramatically afterward.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The signal we were sending at that point was that, if things got much worse, we might have to do it again.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Now, as I said, we thought in October that things were looking pretty good.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I thought we had this great game plan; we were on board for the game plan; and, of course, the game plan is unfortunately out the window.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think that taking an action like a 50 basis point cut would have an important impact and would provide the signals and the managing of expectations that can have critical implications for how the economy evolves, particularly how the credit markets evolve.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It also raises the issue that one thing we do need to do, no matter what, is to indicate to the markets that we understand that our job is to prevent bad shocks from propagating in a very bad way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We can’t prevent the shocks—because things happen—but our job is to make sure that they don’t propagate in a very bad way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The same issue comes up in terms of inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have talked about the real side and the justification for a 50 basis point cut in that case.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Normally this Committee acts in a very inertial way, and under normal conditions, there are good reasons for doing so in terms of the way you manage expectations about the term structure and so forth.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But thinking that way about operating in a situation of financial disruption is not the right way to think.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, the word that I really like in this context is Governor Kohn’s “nimble,” which was exactly the right word.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You have to be nimble.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What do I mean by that?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Well, as all of us completely agree, keeping inflation expectations contained is the most critical thing that we do.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We do need to worry about the real side of the economy; but we know that, if you unravel inflation expectations, then the jig is up, and you get very bad monetary policy outcomes, not just for inflation but also for the real side of the economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is one of the key lessons that we have learned in the past fifty years about monetary policy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the question here is, Is this a problem?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Well, I don’t see that there is a problem right now with inflation expectations getting unhinged, but it could happen, and could happen quickly, in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That says that we have to be aware of this and possibly change policy very quickly and that the word is “nimble.” I don’t know if that is what you meant by “nimble,” but I like the word.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This requires that we reverse course very quickly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Now, the problem that President Plosser and others have raised is that the Committee has not acted that way in the past, and that really is a serious concern of mine.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There are ways to operate differently on that, which is to recognize that if you are going to reverse course, you are not going to do it on the basis of what is going on in the real economy or what is going on in terms of actual inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Just as right now our decision is really not so much about the incoming economic data as much as it is about the problems in financial markets and the credit disruption, I think we are operating in a very proactive, forward-looking way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that regard, we would have to act similarly in terms of thinking about inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There are two cases in which there would be signals that we would have to act very differently.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is that credit conditions could improve very quickly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We are hoping that this would happen, and actually sometimes you do see these things just turn around on a dime.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: All of a sudden a virtuous circle occurs.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If that actually started to happen, it would be imperative if we did a 50 basis point cut that we reverse very quickly on that action.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Second, we have information about inflation expectations, and if we saw those numbers starting to go in a bad direction, we should also operate very quickly in a reversing direction.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is extremely important not to be in the Taylor-rule type of framework, where you wait to see actual inflation and output outcomes to drive your policy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It really has to be much more proactive than that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There have been mistakes in the past, at least in my viewpoint, when we could have reacted more quickly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: For example, in ’98, it was very appropriate for us to cut rates the way we did.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we were a bit slow to raise them, and I think part of the reason was that we were reacting more to what was going on.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m not sure—you can correct me in private afterward, Don—but I think that inertia was there, and if we think about doing things differently, it could work out very well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have to say that I do not worry about the political issue of the election.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is a change in the way this Committee operates, but I believe that we can change.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If we just think about it and have a framework with which to think about it, we could be much more nimble than we were in the past.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Although I prefer alternative A, I am going to accept alternative B. I am perfectly happy with the language of alternative B because I think there is a lot of uncertainty in the marketplace right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, I feel that showing that the FOMC has consensus in a very difficult situation like this will be beneficial to the markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If I were not willing to accept alternative B, it could create some problems in terms of the marketplace, and I certainly am not willing to do that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I support the reduction in the fed funds rate of 25 basis points and the language in alternative B for almost all the reasons that were raised around the table.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just want to say two quick things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One is that, if we start acting as though we are constrained by the political calendar of this country and choose to shade our judgments one way or the other because of knowledge of that calendar, I think it would be a dark day for the future of the central bank.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I also think that many of you are being a little unfair to the history of the Committee.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I am not sure you can look at the evidence of monetary policy responses over the last two decades and say that there is systematic evidence of a Committee that is quick to lurch down and slow and reluctant to tighten.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If that were the case, you would have had a level of GDP volatility and a level of inflation expectations and a volatility of inflation expectations that are substantially higher than they have been relative to central banks that operate with a different kind of regime.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I wasn’t here for that period, but I am a little surprised by the strength of the conviction many of you have expressed that we have been systematically vulnerable as a Committee to that basic bias.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But, Mr. Chairman, I like this option and the language in it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the choices ahead of us are going to be harder than this one.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We may have some 50 basis point moves ahead of us, but I think at the moment this is the best of the alternatives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, again, thank you, thank you all.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think we need to move today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Once we take into account the drag from financial conditions, arguably the current rate is neutral or even somewhat restrictive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, the Taylor rules in the Bluebook have the neutral rate between 4 and 4¼ percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Moreover, there has been quite a market change.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Whether you look at markets or look at simulations, the FRB/US equilibrium real funds rate, for example, is down 70 basis points since the last meeting, which of course is just a summary of the revision of the forecast.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, you get similar numbers when you look at actual market indicators.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think there is a sense in which our policies become de facto more restrictive and need to be addressed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On top of that, there is some case for insurance, although the discussion around the table illustrates that that is a complex idea when you, in fact, have a dual mandate and there are risks in both directions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If the choice were between 0 and 50 basis points, I would be very tempted to do 50 basis points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it would move us more toward accommodation, and it would be very pleasant to get the same kind of market response we got after September in terms of improved functioning and credit extension.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That said, I think there are some risks to going with 50 basis points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I acknowledge what others have said, which is that it is not just about the rate but also about what the message is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular the markets already expect us to ease quite a bit more.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are not pushing strongly back against it with 25 basis points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we do 50, we may be saying to the market that we are willing to do even more than you currently expect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that poses some risks to inflation expectations and poses some risks to the dollar, which is a little fragile right now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You can imagine it even having reverse effects with respect to the economy—for example, if it caused oil prices to jump or if it caused nominal interest rates to rise, thereby raising nominal mortgage rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other concern I have is that, for better or worse, given our communications and market expectations, at this point a 50 basis point cut would be viewed as something of a lurch and might signal, as others have suggested, more concern or private information about the economy that we in fact don’t necessarily have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You can tell that I am quite conflicted about it, and I think there is a good chance that we may have to move further at subsequent meetings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In that respect, it is very important that both in our statement and in our intermeeting communications that we signal our flexibility, our nimbleness: We are not locked in, we are responsive to conditions on both sides of the mandate, and we are alert to new developments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With all of that in mind—and although I don’t think the TAF is really a significant substitute for monetary policy, on the margin I think it is helpful—I recommend 25 basis points and alternative B. I did not hear much support for a downside risks sentence, and I agree that adding it would probably not very substantially affect the signal that we are sending today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is my proposal.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, could you please call the roll?

speaker: DANKER
text: The vote today encompasses the directive from the Bluebook and the language of alternative B that was in the Bluebook and in the handout.

speaker: DANKER
text: The directive reads as follows: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: DANKER
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with reducing the federal funds rate to an average of around 4¼ percent.” Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes President Evans Yes President Hoenig Yes Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes Governor Mishkin Yes President Poole Yes President Rosengren No Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to recess briefly here for the discount rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just reiterate what I was saying about the statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I hope as we go through the intermeeting period that we will try to maintain our flexibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As we discuss the outlook in public, we should of course give our honest and full views on the outlook and the risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we should try to maintain, with respect to policy action, flexibility in the ability to respond to new conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That way I hope when we come to January we will be able to respond as the data and the markets best indicate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are no longer doing communications in our two-day meetings, so there is a question of what to do in that time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We would like to suggest several things to the Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, as part of the international processes and the efforts of the President’s Working Group to study the lessons that we have gained so far from financial turmoil, there are numerous work streams going on about different aspects of the turmoil, including a lot of work being done by people in the System.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we would like to propose—and I hope that we would consider it complementary to our policy discussion—a presentation in January by the staff on various policy lessons learned from the experience we have had with the financial turmoil.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, this is material that will be feeding into international discussions about how policy, financial regulation, and so on might respond to these situations in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The subsequent two-day meeting is in April.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The staff is working hard on the issue of interest on reserves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They would like to present to us what they have done and get feedback from us on some parameters of the process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is in fact quite relevant to our current situation because it bears on issues of monetary control.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we have interest on reserves, we would, for example, be better able to manage the overnight funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if there is no objection, we would like to put that on the schedule for April.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Subsequent to that, we would like to go back to our practice of having presentations on topics of interest.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We would like to put special emphasis on research taking place at Reserve Banks, and we will be sending out a memo soliciting ideas from the Committee and from the Reserve Banks in the hope that individual Banks, in collaboration with others, might take the lead in making presentations of relevant research.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is the current plan for two-day meetings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, the next meeting is Tuesday and Wednesday, January 29 and 30.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will adjourn in a moment for lunch, and over lunch Laricke Blanchard will give us a brief presentation of congressional matters.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, may I make one point about January, which, as you are all aware, is that I don’t think any of us—and it is really not the staff—will be in a position in January to provide a definitive set of convictions about really what worked, what didn’t work, what really contributed to it, and what we did to the incentives that financial market participants face.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just to make sure that we don’t raise expectations too much for the Committee, I think that it will be at best an initial, tentative diagnosis with some initial, tentative sense of the things we want to look at and that it will probably be the end of the beginning, not the beginning of the end, of that process.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Is that okay, Mr. Chairman?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it will be very interesting.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I just have a question.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to the implementation of the TAF, could you clarify what we need to ask our boards of directors to do and when?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Can I get some help?

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: I circulated to the general counsels yesterday resolutions that could be presented to the boards of directors that adopt the result of the auction as the recommendation by the Reserve Bank for the discount rate on the TAF.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The Board would then be accepting those and voting on them.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have a meeting on Thursday morning.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The resolutions have all been circulated to all of the general counsels of the Reserve Banks, so they should have them and could be presenting them.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But you are not circulating them to us?

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: I could give them to you.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: It is less for you to carry home.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But general counsels normally don’t participate in this process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: He is not speaking to you?

speaker: YELLEN
text: No, he didn’t speak to me.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: I can send a copy to all the Presidents.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I just want to make sure that I heard you clearly earlier.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have kept this contained, including the swap ranges, which is very impressive.

speaker: FISHER
text: Everybody should pat themselves on the back.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’re broadening the circle tonight or this afternoon, and I’m not quite sure what your message is.

speaker: FISHER
text: I assume that we are announcing it tomorrow morning because of the international complexities.

speaker: FISHER
text: Nobody seems to know about this yet that I am aware of.

speaker: FISHER
text: Do you want us to inform our full boards, or do you want us just to inform our chairmen, or do it late tonight, or is it up to our discretion?

speaker: FISHER
text: I just worry about leakage.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We were asked whether it was okay to inform the boards.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Given that the boards are often privy to confidential information, I didn’t see any reason to prohibit that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think in some cases it might be a useful compromise, instead, just to inform your chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we are not requesting that you inform your board.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is up to you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you think it would be useful, by all means.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Of course, this will all be available first thing in the morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if you prefer to call immediately after and discuss it—any way that is good for you is fine with us.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just wanted to make sure there wasn’t a subtext to the message, but I’ve got it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Just to clarify what our boards have to approve, as I understand, it is the willingness to accept the rate that comes out of the auction at the discount window.

speaker: LACKER
text: For the loans made at the facility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The discount window will still exist.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They will still be making loans at 50 basis points above the fed funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is a new facility, approved by the Board.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What your board has to approve is the willingness to make loans from your discount window at the rate determined by the auction.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is what I understood.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One clarifying thing, and just a question for Scott.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Is it okay from your perspective if the recommendations come from boards of directors after the announcement, so long as they come before the first auction?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So Thursday would be fine?

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: They just have to be here by December 17.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Today is the last meeting for our friend and colleague, Bill Poole.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Bill has been here for 81 meetings, 80 as a Reserve Bank president and one as an adviser to the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I thought I would read to you the transcript from March 31, 1998, when Bill first joined the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I especially want to welcome back an old colleague, Bill Poole.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I didn’t realize the last time he sat in this room was 25 years ago.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I was sitting back there along the wall.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has taken you 25 years to move from there to here?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Baby steps.” We’ll have a chance to honor Bill at our farewell luncheon on March 18, at our next meeting, but let’s take this opportunity to thank you for 10 years of service and collegiality.

speaker: POOLE
text: I came here 10 years ago with a boom.

speaker: POOLE
text: I’m going out with a pause.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll let Bill have the last word on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Today is the first regular meeting of the year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is our organizational meeting, so we have some housekeeping things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Item one, nomination of the Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s an honor and a privilege to nominate Ben Bernanke to be the Chairman of this Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Without objection, thank you very much.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need a nomination for Vice Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: I can do that, too.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s another honor and a privilege to nominate Tim Geithner to be the Vice Chairman of this Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Ms. Danker will read the nominated staff officers for the Committee.

speaker: DANKER
text: Secretary and Economist, Brian Madigan; Deputy Secretary, Deborah Danker; Assistant Secretaries, David Skidmore and Michelle Smith; General Counsel, Scott Alvarez; Deputy General Counsel, Thomas Baxter; Assistant General Counsel, Richard Ashton; Economists, Nathan Sheets and David Stockton; Associate Economists from the Board, Thomas Connors, William English, Steven Kamin, Lawrence Slifman, and David Wilcox; Associate Economists from the Banks, Loretta Mester, Arthur Rolnick, Harvey Rosenblum, Mark Sniderman, and Joseph Tracy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Item two on the agenda: There are some cosmetic changes to the Committee rules.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Scott Alvarez and Debbie Danker circulated a memorandum.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, I’ll need a vote in favor.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Item three: We need to select a Federal Reserve Bank to execute transactions for the System Open Market Account.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have been informed that New York is again willing to serve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to select a manager for the System Open Market Account.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Bill Dudley is the incumbent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, if not, in favor?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We turn now to annual authorizations for Desk operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Bill circulated a memo that had one revision to the authorization for foreign currency operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any questions about that change?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, all in favor?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are no changes proposed for the authorization for domestic open market operations, the foreign currency directive, or the procedural instructions with respect to foreign currency operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We turn now to the business of the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me call on Bill Dudley to give us the Desk report.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’ll be referring to the handout that you should have in front of you.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Over the past month, term funding pressures for banks have generally subsided.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the bigger story remains the continued pressure on bank balance sheets, the tightening of credit availability, and the impact of this tightening on the outlook for economic activity.

speaker: DUDLEY
