text: The travails of the monoline financial guarantors—some of which have already been downgraded by one or more of the rating agencies—have exacerbated the worries about the potential for further bank writedowns and have created risks that some financial instruments that rely on monoline guarantees might no longer be viable.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At this juncture, whether the major monoline guarantors will receive the new capital needed to keep or restore their AAA ratings remains uncertain.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’ll start today by noting that U.S. and global equity and fixed-income markets have behaved in a way consistent with a darker economic outlook.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 1, the major U.S. indexes have fallen sharply since the December 11 FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These declines in the stock markets have been mostly matched abroad, as shown in exhibit 2.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the same time, corporate credit spreads have risen in tandem with the equity markets’ decline.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 3, high-yield corporate bond spreads are up more than 100 basis points since the December FOMC meeting, pulling the interest rates on high-yield debt significantly higher.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Investment-grade spreads have also widened.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But for investment-grade debt, the decline in Treasury yields has been larger than the rise in spreads, lowering somewhat the absolute level of yields.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Global credit default swap spreads have also increased sharply, as shown in 1 The materials used by Mr. Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Market price risk has increased.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is most visible in the rise of most market measures of implied volatility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, the VIX, which measures implied volatility on the S&P 500 index, recently climbed back to the peak level reached in August (exhibit 5) and the MOVE index, which measures volatility in the Treasury coupon market, has climbed to its highest level since 1998.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problems of the financial guarantors have been an important part of the story.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In recent years, the major financial guarantors have diversified into insuring structured-finance products, including collateralized debt obligations (CDOs).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Currently, their exposure to all structured-finance products is about $780 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 6 shows the distribution of exposure across three buckets: U.S. public finance, U.S. ABS and structured finance, and the total non-U.S. exposure for the six major monoline guarantors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because the structured-finance guarantees have typically been issued against the highest rated tranches at the very top of the capital structure, until recently the rating agencies did not think that these guarantees would result in meaningful losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, as the housing outlook has continued to deteriorate and the rating agencies have increased their loss estimates on subprime and other types of residential mortgage loan products, the risk of significant losses has increased sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is particularly the case with respect to these firms’ collateralized debt obligation exposures—a portion of their total structured-finance exposure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As I discussed in an earlier briefing, given the highly nonlinear payoffs built into these products, modest changes in the loss assumptions on the underlying collateral can lead to a sharp rise in expected losses on super senior AAA-rated collateralized debt obligations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Unfortunately, the CDO exposures of several of these financial guarantors are quite large relative to their claims-paying resources.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 7, statutory capital for even the biggest firm is less than $7 billion; the total capital for the entire group is slightly more than $20 billion; and total claims-paying resources for this group from all sources is about $50 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 8 compares these claims-paying resources with the subset of CDO exposures that contain some subprime mortgage-related collateral.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For four of the six major guarantors, these CDO exposures represent more than 200 percent of their total claims-paying resources.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These exposures and the uncertainty about how these exposures will actually translate into losses are the proximate cause for the collapse in the financial guarantor share prices and the widening in their credit default swap spreads.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is why new sources of capital have been either prohibitively expensive or dilutive or both to existing shareholders.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As I noted in last week’s briefing, credit rating downgrades of the financial guarantors would likely lead to significant mark-to-market losses for those financial institutions that had purchased protection.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, in its fourth-quarter earnings release, Merrill Lynch wrote down by $3.1 billion its valuation related to its hedges with the financial guarantors; $2.6 billion of this reflected writedowns related to super senior ABS CDO exposures.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Unfortunately, there is not much transparency as to the counterparty exposures of the guarantors on a firm-by-firm, asset-class-by-asset-class, or security-by-security basis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, major broker-dealers have considerable non- ABS CDO exposures to the financial guarantors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, they are thought to have hedged an even larger amount of the super senior tranches of synthetic corporate CDOs with the financial guarantors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This suggests the potential for significant additional mark-to-market losses for commercial and investment bank counterparties should the financial guarantor credit ratings get further downgraded.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In addition, such downgrades would increase market anxiety about counterparty risk because there would be considerable uncertainty about the magnitude and incidence of the prospective losses such downgrades might trigger.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Financial institutions are also exposed to the monoline guarantors via the wraps these guarantors have issued on certain money market securities, including auction rate securities, tender option bonds, and variable rate demand notes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The amount of these securities outstanding is significant.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The total market size for these three types of securities is estimated to be about $900 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The major risk here is that the loss of the AAA-rated guarantee from the financial guarantor could undercut the demand for these securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the case of tender option bonds and variable rate demand notes, this could trigger the liquidity backstops provided by major commercial banks and dealers, leading to further demands on their balance sheets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the case of the auction rate securities market, the dealers would be faced with a difficult Hobson’s choice.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They could either allow the auction to fail or take the securities onto their books to prevent a failed auction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the case of a failed auction, the investor receives a higher interest rate but has to wait until the next auction to try to redeem the securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If failed auctions were to persist, as would be likely, then the securities would essentially become long-term rather than short-term obligations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Failed auctions would undoubtedly distress clients that had purchased the securities on the assumption that they would be liquid and could be redeemed easily.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Failed auctions would also likely lead to broader distress in the associated municipal and student loan securities markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have already experienced a number of failed auctions for auction rate securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the recent downgrades of Ambac and FSA have led to significant market differentiation among tender option bonds and some upward pressure on municipal bonds wrapped by weaker monoline financial guarantors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If the monoline guarantors are unable to find additional equity or other forms of support, these pressures are likely to intensify in coming weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The travails of the financial guarantors have added to the pressure on major commercial and investment banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 9 and 10, commercial and investment bank equity prices and credit default swap spreads have generally continued to widen.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The cumulative writedowns reported for a selected group of large banks has now reached $100 billion over the past two quarters (exhibit 11).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Coupled with balance sheet growth and other factors, such as acquisitions, these writedowns have put significant downward pressure on bank capital ratios.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, although all of the top five U.S. commercial banks can still be characterized as “well capitalized,” there has been significant erosion of their capital ratios over the past two quarters (exhibit 12).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This balance sheet pressure helps to explain why commercial bank counterparties continue to complain about their access to credit, the tightening in lending standards, and the wider spreads for assets such as jumbo residential mortgages, commercial mortgages, and leveraged loans that can no longer be readily securitized and distributed into the capital markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Shifting now to what market participants expect from us from this meeting: Monetary policy expectations continue to shift in the direction of more cuts that are delivered more quickly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 13, the federal funds rate futures market currently implies that market participants now expect additional rate cuts totaling about 100 basis points by midyear.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Further out, as shown in exhibit 14, the Eurodollar futures curves indicate that about another 25 basis points is anticipated during the second half of the year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But these expectations are volatile and have been shifting considerably day to day.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The primary dealer survey tells a similar story.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The modal forecast of the primary dealers shows a federal funds rate trough slightly below 2.5 percent (exhibit 15).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Compared with the previous dealers’ survey conducted for the December FOMC meeting (exhibit 16), the trough has moved down about 75 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As of last Friday, seventeen of the twenty primary dealers expected a 50 basis point rate cut at this meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This sentiment appears to be generally shared by market participants.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 17, as of last Friday, options on federal funds rate futures implied a rate cut at today’s meeting, with the highest probability on a 50 basis point rate cut to 3 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, it is important to recognize that the probabilities shown in exhibit 17 put a zero weight on the notion of another intermeeting cut in February—so they should not be taken literally as to the outcome at today’s meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The distribution of yields on Eurodollar futures 300 days ahead suggests that there has been a regime shift since the December FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 18, not only have expectations shifted down sharply, but the skew has reversed direction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The mode of the distribution is at 1.75 percent, and the skew of the distribution around that mode is toward less extreme rate outcomes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This could be viewed as market participants now pricing in considerable risk of a severe recession but maintaining some hope that a milder downturn might occur or that a recession could possibly be averted altogether.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 19, the intermeeting rate cut was accompanied by a rise in inflation compensation at the five-year to ten-year time horizon.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, it is unclear that this represents a genuine deterioration in inflation expectations for several reasons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, the rise occurred, in part, because breakeven inflation at the five-year horizon has fallen as nominal five-year Treasury yields have dropped sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is this decline that has lifted the five-year, five-year-forward measure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would agree with the memo by Board staff that was distributed to the FOMC yesterday on this issue: The rise in five-year, five-year-forward inflation compensation likely reflects a greater liquidity premium for nominal Treasuries.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rise in interest rate volatility is also a factor.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: According to TIPS traders, the rise in five-year, five-year-forward inflation reflects technical factors such as a temporary increase in the demand for shorter-dated Treasuries, month-end index extension flows, and a greater liquidity premium for nominal, on-the-run Treasuries.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The general rise in interest rate volatility is probably also a factor.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the rise in five-year, five-year-forward expectations has not been accompanied by a broad set of other signals consistent with deteriorating long-term inflation expectations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, the four- to five-year-forward breakeven inflation measure shows a much smaller rise, the dollar has been relatively stable, and estimates of bond term risk premiums remain low.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the other side, gold prices have increased sharply in the past week.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, in our primary dealers’ survey, there was very little change in long- term inflation expectations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, it is worth noting that following the 50 basis point rate cut in September, which was more aggressive than expected, the five-year, five-year-forward rate also rose, but the rise proved temporary.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would also like to briefly discuss the state of play in bank term funding markets—some good news.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 20, the spreads between the one- month LIBOR and the one-month OIS rate and the three-month LIBOR and the three- month OIS rate have fallen sharply since year-end.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, over the past week, there has been considerable volatility in these spreads.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This could be due to a variety of factors—including a temporary increase in the demand by Societé Générale for term funds and the sharp shift in expectations about the near-term federal funds rate path.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Currently, these spreads are close to the narrowest we have seen since the market turmoil began last August.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the passage of year-end was the predominant factor behind the decline in term funding spreads, the term auction facility (TAF) also appears to have been helpful.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 21 shows the results for the first three U.S. auctions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Completing the exhibit, the results for the fourth auction, which was conducted yesterday, were minimum bid rate, 3.10 percent; stop-out rate, 3.12 percent; propositions, $37.5 billion; bid-to-cover ratio, 1.25; and number of bidders, 52.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In general, the pattern is one of declining bid-to-cover ratios and a declining spread between the stop-out rate and the overnight index swap rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The results for the ECB and Swiss National Bank auctions show a similar pattern.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the latest auction, the ECB had $12.4 billion of bids, a bid-to-cover ratio of 1.24, and their number of bidders fell to 19 from 22 at the previous auction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Board of Governors has said that on February 1 it will announce plans for the TAF in February.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The staff has recommended to the Chairman that the auctions continue on a biweekly basis, that the size be maintained at $30 billion per auction, and that the minimum bid size be cut to $5 million from $10 million to make it easier for smaller institutions to participate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, there was no foreign currency intervention activity during this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I request a vote to ratify the operations conducted by the System Open Market Account since the December 11 FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, as always, I am happy to take any questions.

speaker: POOLE
text: Bill, could you talk about the role of foreign banking organizations?

speaker: POOLE
text: What fraction roughly are they responsible for?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have been very cautious about talking about the role of the foreign banks, but they’re definitely a significant factor.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The best way to look at it is just to look at the New York District, which is taking an overwhelming share of not all but most of these auctions, and most of that is foreign.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Regarding the participation in terms of number of bidders, the split is more even between domestic and foreign; in terms of the actual takedown of dollars, it does skew a bit to the foreign side, but it has been variable.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is not the same in each auction.

speaker: POOLE
text: If I may make a comment about that—I think everyone is aware of my view that the TAF does not change the marginal conditions.

speaker: POOLE
text: It’s entirely an inframarginal operation.

speaker: POOLE
text: What it does is to save banks the spread between what their cost of funds otherwise would be and what they get at the TAF.

speaker: POOLE
text: So it increases bank earnings by that amount.

speaker: POOLE
text: It seems to me that there is potentially some reputational risk to the Federal Reserve in the long run if a significant share of the benefit is going to foreign banking organizations.

speaker: POOLE
text: I guess one question that I would pose is, If we think that this information would be terribly sensitive to release, shouldn’t we be careful about whether we continue if the foreign banking organizations are taking a very large fraction?

speaker: LACKER
text: Yes, I have a couple of questions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to start with the issue about foreign banks, though.

speaker: LACKER
text: Why are we sensitive about talking about foreign banks—I mean, is this a public stance, or is this in the Committee?

speaker: LACKER
text: The information about the identity of the winning bidders was sent to every Reserve Bank.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think we’re particularly sensitive, but I think other central banks would be very sensitive.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, these are confidential proceedings—this is a consequential policy matter.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Mr. Chairman, if I could.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think, President Lacker, just one point is that the detailed information on the bidders was sent only to those Reserve Bank presidents and Board members who specifically asked for it, so it was not distributed unilaterally.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, the spreadsheet of bidders.

speaker: LACKER
text: I thought that every Bank, all the discount officers, received the identity of the winning bidders, and the other information about all the bids went only to those who requested it.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The second point I would make is that I do not think there is particular sensitivity about foreign banks but instead sensitivity about taking any chance of identifying who the bidders are at all because of the great concern about avoiding stigma from the TAF.

speaker: LACKER
text: I wanted to ask a couple of questions about the term auction facility.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, I’d like to hear more from you about what your understanding is of the effects the term auction facility had on the funding market.

speaker: LACKER
text: The first question under that would be, To your knowledge, were these completely sterilized or just partially sterilized?

speaker: LACKER
text: Another question would be, For the recipients, were these additional funds that they wouldn’t have otherwise borrowed, or did they displace some other borrowing?

speaker: LACKER
text: The next question would be, This crowded out something, and if it didn’t change materially the total amount of reserves in the system, some lending ought to be shifted from the recipients to someone else—so what do we know about other spillover effects in the markets?

speaker: LACKER
text: The focus of our attention probably for data reasons was the LIBOR market, but there was also discussion in December of the term fed funds market.

speaker: LACKER
text: What do we know about the behavior of that since then?

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d be interested in your sense of whether bidders were riskier than nonbidders and whether riskier institutions bid more than nonrisky institutions.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve done a bit of empirical analysis—it’s preliminary—but I’d be interested in your folks’ sense of that.

speaker: LACKER
text: About the foreign institutions, I’m interested in learning about what the advantage was of our lending dollar balances via this mechanism to foreign banks versus the alternative of having them borrow dollar balances from their central bank, perhaps funded by a swap or out of the foreign central bank’s own dollar balances.

speaker: LACKER
text: Finally—and this is sort of the most important question—how should we evaluate whether this has been a success or not?

speaker: LACKER
text: To what sort of objective evidence should we look to decide whether we achieved our objectives?

speaker: LACKER
text: Related to that, can a case be made for ending this facility soon in light of the fact that the LIBOR–OIS spread is now half of what it was in September, when we decided that it had come down enough to shelve the plan?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Those are a lot of questions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Okay, I’ll take the easy one first.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The TAF is completely sterilized.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For every dollar that goes into the TAF we drain reserves, and we’ve been doing that mainly by redeeming maturing Treasury bills.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Regarding whether these are additional funds to those entities, it is hard to know what they would have done if the TAF facilities hadn’t been available.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This may have funded some assets on their balance sheets that they otherwise would have decided not to fund.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think it is very difficult to know what that counterfactual is.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is hard to believe that in the system as a whole it led to a lot of additional funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would be surprised by that, especially given that we did sterilize reserves and didn’t allow expansion of the balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of the issue of crowding out, the way I think about the TAF is changing the composition of our balance sheet and changing the composition of the banking system’s balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are basically supplying Treasury securities by redeeming bills, and then the Treasury issues more bills that the markets want, and we are essentially absorbing collateral from the marketplace that’s hard for them to finance elsewhere.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it is a change in the composition of the balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That’s how I would think of the way it works.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of how we should evaluate the success, we don’t know how much was the year- end.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We don’t know how much was monetary policy easing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But market participants view the TAF as very positive.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that, if we were to discontinue it abruptly, they would be unhappy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There’s no evidence to suggest that the TAF has caused any great harm.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It looks as though the benefits, to my mind, are likely to significantly exceed the costs even though we can’t measure those benefits very accurately.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Regarding the foreign institutions issue—the choice between dollar balances from us versus dollar balances from foreign central banks—I think it was a little more complicated than that because, if I remember how we got to the foreign exchange swaps, they were essentially more or less conditional on our doing the TAF.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They were willing to do the swaps if they could get the auctions in tandem with our term auction facilities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So my judgment would be that we probably didn’t really have a choice of getting the dollars to those foreign banks through the ECB if we hadn’t done the term auction facility.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I could just follow up.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, on the last point, that’s a matter of the ECB’s willingness to lend to those institutions.

speaker: LACKER
text: You’re saying that they would be willing to lend themselves to those institutions only if we did this.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s not about the economics of their borrowing from their central bank versus borrowing from us—nothing about the market functioning.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I wouldn’t say it’s about their willingness to lend to their institutions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s their sense of what their responsibility is in terms of providing dollar liquidity to their institutions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To the extent that they could just passively take the dollars and funnel them through this auction process in which their auction was very passive—their auction was essentially a noncompetitive auction that was based off ours—they were willing to do that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They were less willing to do something in which they were taking responsibility for the problem and saying that they were going to get the dollars and supply them to those banks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Do market participants view foreign banking organizations as broadly riskier than comparable-sized institutions based in the United States?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, it’s difficult to say.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If you look at credit default swaps, that would say not.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But as President Rosengren and I were talking before the meeting, those credit default swaps may also contain different appetites to recapitalize banks when they get in trouble in the United States versus abroad.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the one thing that we can probably say with confidence for the period is that there’s more anxiety that things are hidden in certain foreign banks that are probably not as likely to be hidden in U.S. banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There’s better disclosure in the United States on a faster and more real-time basis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The market sense is that there isn’t really the same kind of quarterly disclosure process abroad that happens for U.S. institutions.

speaker: MOSSER
text: May I add one factual comment to that?

speaker: MOSSER
text: During the height of the dislocations in December, the fed funds rate overnight was regularly trading substantially higher early in the morning—this happened also in August for a while—either early in the U.S. trading session or before that.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Our understanding from market participants was that the reason for those higher rates in the morning was excess demand from European-based institutions to borrow in the funds market, and when the U.S. institutions became more active later in the day, the funds rate would then go back down to the target.

speaker: LACKER
text: Going back to the LIBOR–OIS spread—that was what motivated this.

speaker: LACKER
text: It has fallen a lot.

speaker: LACKER
text: The bid-to-cover ratio is falling.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we try to lend $30 billion three more times, we could get to a point at which we satiate the market in term funds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, first of all, continuing that $30 billion is not supplying any additional dollars, so we’re just going to be rolling over maturing auctions.

speaker: LACKER
text: Yes, but the bid-to-cover ratio keeps falling.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But, second, I would caution you that this last auction was right before an FOMC meeting and that may have diminished the appetite.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We don’t know with certainty, but our supposition is that the demand would have been higher if the auction had been a week later, if that’s how the schedule had fallen.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, February might be fine, but March is a quarter-end.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Lastly, the fact is that, while the term funding pressures seem to be better, a lot of other things seem to be worse, and clearly the pressure on bank balance sheets has not diminished at all.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If anything, it has grown more intense.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So to remove this prematurely would be a risk, especially when market participants view this as helpful and it gives them a sense of confidence that the Fed is there.

speaker: FISHER
text: The questions that President Lacker asked covered one of the questions I wanted to ask.

speaker: FISHER
text: But as we go down in terms of the number of bidders as we proceed, is the portion that is foreign increasing, relatively speaking?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t remember any strong sense of that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: What has happened, as the auction has proceeded, is that people have bid more tightly around where they think it’s going to come, except for a few institutions who just say, “I want the money,” and they bid at very high rates because it’s a single price auction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You usually see some behavior like that.

speaker: LACKER
text: Foreign banks were $19 billion out of $20 billion at the first auction; $18 billion out of $20 billion at the second auction; and a declining fraction thereafter, President Fisher.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Bill, in your remarks, you devoted quite a bit of time to the deteriorating situation in the monolines, the implication being that the risks they may have affect the whole system.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the normal course, do we have direct contact with them to get any insight beyond what we get through analysts and rating agencies?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think you said that they are not terribly transparent in terms of asset class and individual securities as to what they really hold.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Have we had any direct dialogue just to inform ourselves as to what the real situation is?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I haven’t had much contact with them.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t know if Tim has.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have not been in touch with them directly to get a sense about their risk profile and so forth.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have had extensive conversations with the New York State Insurance Commissioner, who is the lead supervisor of many of them, but not all of them.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It turns out that office also has very little information, particularly on the stuff that is on the leading edge of concern, which is to whom they sold credit protection and on what.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But it is in the process of trying to remedy that, and we have been giving them a little help in trying to figure out what they need to ask for.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Another thing that is not very well known is what their assets consist of.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have rating buckets, but we don’t know what those ratings actually apply to.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We don’t know who they have reinsurance with.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Some people think that they’re reinsuring each other to an extent or they have reinsurance with subsidiaries that they own so that the insurance is not at arm’s length.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So there’s quite a bit of cloudiness about what their true condition is.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have better information on the protection that banks purchased from the monolines—by monoline and by underlying asset—and it is important, of course, to have that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would just note with the TAF experience, going back just for a minute, that the Boston financial community has been overwhelmingly supportive.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I don’t know whether you have gotten the same sense when you talk to the financial community in New York, but whether people were bidding or not, they actually thought that it was quite a fruitful exercise.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the credit default swaps, just looking at some of the institutions that were involved, it seemed as if the U.S. institutions, if you look at individual organizations, may have had much higher credit default swap rates than many of the foreign institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As you noted, many of the foreign institutions were substantially lower than at least a couple of the U.S. ones that were involved, and we obviously thought the U.S. ones were sound, or we wouldn’t have been willing to have them participate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We should look at the LIBOR rate, but I think we should also look at the Treasury securities market because you don’t have to do as much in open market operations if you’re doing some of it in the TAF, and we’ve had the interest rate on Treasury securities quite low.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I’m wondering whether, when we think about the analysis, we look not only at things like LIBOR but also at the functioning of the Treasury market, and whether that was actually helped out by this process.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I don’t know if you’ve done any work on that, but it would be of interest to know if that had helped with the better functioning of the Treasury market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I think the presumption is very much that it went in the right direction in terms of the Treasury market because basically the Treasury has auctioned off larger weekly one-month, three-month, and six-month bills to replace those that we were redeeming.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the floating public supply of bills went up.

speaker: POOLE
text: Very quickly, we should not be surprised that banks like the TAF.

speaker: POOLE
text: It increases the bank’s profits because of the difference between the funding costs.

speaker: POOLE
text: The issue is whether the TAF improves the way the markets are functioning, not whether it’s feeding profits into the banks and whether they happen to like it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it’s clear in Bill’s presentation that there’s a very strong case that the TAF, the associated measures by other central banks, and, as important, the commitment and the signal that we would continue the TAF longer than was necessary have been very important to the improvement of market functioning and very important to the improvement and confidence in liquidity and markets going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very hard to know how important it has been to that, but I think it has absolutely been very important, and I think it is very important for us to continue it until we can comfortably say it is no longer necessary in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think we are far from the point that we can claim that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It was 24 basis points in October, President Lacker, and there are a lot of reasons that we should be expecting to be living with a long period of fragility in markets going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We all debated the merits of this going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There’s a set of good, principled objections to this kind of stuff, and I didn’t expect that those objections would change on the basis of the experience with this thing, and I don’t think we’ve learned anything new about the merits of those objections, except that there’s a very good basis of evidence for suggesting it has been important to the improvement in confidence and market functioning.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One of our jobs is—and I think we’ve been pretty successful in doing it—trying to give some confidence to people that we as the central bank have provided a quality of liquidity insurance more powerful than we can through our classic instruments.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it has been very successful in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: To take it back prematurely would be damaging to the improvements we’ve achieved.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any other questions for Bill?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, I need a vote to ratify domestic operations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I move that we ratify the operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We turn now to the economic situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We begin with Dave Reifschneider, whenever you’re ready.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: 2 Give me one second.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: On balance, the news we have received since the December Greenbook has been disappointing.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The top panel of your first exhibit sorts some of the main indicators into two categories—those that were surprisingly weak and those that came in to the upside of our expectations.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As you can see, the list to the left is long.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Private payrolls fell in December, and the unemployment rate jumped to 5 percent.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Manufacturing output has declined since the summer.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Single-family housing starts, new permits, and home sales have fallen further.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: New orders and shipments of capital goods were disappointing, although a little less so after today’s release of December data.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Business sentiment deteriorated, joining already unusually low readings on consumer confidence.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Finally, stock prices have tumbled, and credit conditions have tightened.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Not all the news was bad.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Nonresidential construction activity has continued to be surprisingly robust, and defense spending looks to have been higher last quarter than we anticipated.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Moreover, retail sales in November came in stronger than we predicted, and the figures for September and October were revised up.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Overall, we read the incoming 2 The materials used by Mr. Reifschneider, Ms. Liang, and Mr.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Sheets are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: data as implying an increased risk of recession.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The middle left panel provides some evidence for this assessment.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As was discussed at yesterday’s Board briefing, based on the signal provided by 85 nonfinancial indicators (the black line), the estimated probability of being in recession now or over the next six months stood at 45 percent in December, up from 19 percent in June.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: A similar exercise carried out using 20 financial indicators, the red line, yields an even bigger jump in the estimated likelihood of recession, from 14 percent at midyear to 63 percent this month.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As you know, we are not forecasting a recession.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: While the model estimates of the probability of recession have moved up, they are not uniform in their assessment that a recession is at hand.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Another argument against forecasting recession is that, with the notable exception of housing, we see few signs of a significant inventory overhang.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In addition, the recent weakness in the labor market and spending indicators is still limited; for example, initial claims have drifted down in recent weeks rather than surging as they typically do in a major downturn.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Finally, a good deal of monetary and fiscal stimulus is now in process that should help support real activity.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: That said, it was a close call for us.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Even without a recession, our assessment of the underlying strength of aggregate demand has revised down markedly since the summer.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: This is illustrated in the bottom panel by the recent decline in the Greenbook-consistent estimate of short-run r*, the value of the real funds rate that would close the output gap in 12 quarters.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: By our estimate, short-run r* has fallen more than 2 percentage points since the middle of last year and 1¼ percentage points since December.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: A jump in the equity premium accounts for most of the downward revision since the last Greenbook, although a further deterioration in the outlook for residential investment is also a factor.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Your next exhibit summarizes the current forecast.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So, how did we respond to all this bad news?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As shown in the panel at the top, we boosted real GDP growth a little from 2007 through 2009.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In 2008 and 2009, however, this faster growth is not demand driven but instead reflects upward revisions to the supply side of our forecast that I will discuss in a moment.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: For 2007, the upward revision to real GDP in the fourth quarter—noted in the panel to the right—reflects the stronger data on nonresidential construction, defense spending, and retail sales that I just mentioned.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: However, because the incoming data point to a weaker trajectory for real activity in the near term, we have trimmed our forecast of GDP growth for the first half of 2008, and we have marked down final sales growth (not shown) quite a bit.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Beyond the middle of the year, we project real output to expand at a rate close to its potential.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Under these conditions, we project greater labor market slack than in December, with the unemployment rate—shown in the middle left panel—now expected to edge up to 5¼ percent by next year.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: And as shown in the bottom two panels, we continue to expect both core and total PCE prices to decelerate noticeably by 2009, although inflation this year is likely to run a little higher than we previously projected.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Your next exhibit provides an overview of some of the key factors influencing the outlook.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As shown in the upper left panel, we conditioned our forecast on an additional 50 basis point cut in the funds rate at this meeting and then held it flat at 3 percent.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We made this revision in response to the weaker underlying level of demand in this projection but with an eye to keeping inflation on a long-run path to 1¾ percent—the midpoint of the range of 2010 inflation projections that you provided in October.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Another key element in the outlook is our assumption that concerns over financial stability and a possible recession will begin to abate once the economy gets through a rough patch in the first half of this year.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As Nellie will discuss in more detail, this assumption implies that risk premiums on bonds and corporate equity should drift down over time.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As a result, we project that equity prices, shown to the right, will stage a partial recovery over the second half of 2008 and in 2009.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: These and other financial market developments, coupled with an improvement in business and consumer sentiment, should help to support consumption and investment over time.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As regards fiscal policy, odds now seem high for the passage of a fiscal stimulus package, although the details are still up in the air.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As a placeholder, we built a $125 billion package into the baseline, with two components—$75 billion in tax rebates that households will receive in the third quarter and a 30 percent one-year bonus depreciation allowance that should cost the Treasury about $50 billion in 2008.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Our judgment is that the rebate component will provide a significant, albeit temporary, boost to the level of consumer spending during the second half of this year and in early 2009, the period over which we expect most households to spend their checks.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In contrast, we think that bonus depreciation will have only a small effect on equipment and software outlays.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As indicated by the blue bars in the panel to the right, these assumptions imply a large fiscal-driven contribution from PCE and E&S to real GDP growth in the second half of this year, followed by a similar-sized negative contribution in the first half of 2009.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As a result, the long-run contribution to real GDP growth from these two factors is essentially zero.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We have assumed that inventories and imports in the short run will offset a substantial fraction of the swings in domestic demand, thereby muting the overall effect of the fiscal package on real GDP growth (the green bars).

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As I noted earlier, we also have reassessed our supply-side assumptions—shown in the bottom left panel.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Specifically, we have raised our estimate of potential output growth from 2005 to 2009 about ¼ percentage point per year, partly in response to the solid gains in output per hour recorded last year.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: These revised estimates have two important implications.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: First, the upward revision to potential output translates roughly one for one into faster growth in actual output during the projection period because of its implications for permanent income and hence consumption and investment.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Second, the revisions to potential output in history imply that the output gap—shown to the right—currently is lower than we previously thought, and we expect it to remain lower.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Your next exhibit provides some details on the real-side outlook.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As shown in the top left panel, we have once again revised down the projection for new home sales in light of weak incoming data, including those received after we put the Greenbook to bed.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: However, we continue to expect that sales will reach bottom in the first half of this year and then begin to edge up as mortgage credit availability improves.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: This stabilization in demand should allow single-family housing starts (shown to the right) to level out at about 660,000 units by midyear, well below our December projection.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Thereafter, we anticipate a slow pickup in starts.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As shown in the middle left panel, builders still have a long way to go to bring the backlog of unsold homes down to a more comfortable level, and this overhang should restrain construction activity into next year.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We have also revised down the near-term outlook for real business fixed investment—the middle right panel—in response to slowing sales, tighter credit conditions, and some deterioration of business sentiment, but we now expect a greater cyclical rebound starting in the second half of this year as overall conditions start to improve.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The bottom left panel shows our projection for consumption, the blue bars, together with the profile for spending excluding the effects of fiscal stimulus, the green bars.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Absent the stimulus package, we would expect consumer spending to increase only 1 percent this year but then to pick up around 2¼ percent in 2009 as confidence recovers and credit conditions ease.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: However, the tax rebates will likely obscure this cyclical pattern by inducing saw-tooth swings in spending, with actual growth realigning with longer-run fundamentals only in the second half of next year.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As shown to the right, some of these fundamentals are less favorable than before; we estimate that wealth effects will hold down PCE spending growth by ½ percentage point this year and almost ¾ percentage point in 2009.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Your next exhibit reviews the inflation outlook.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As indicated by the blue line in the upper left panel, monthly readings on core PCE inflation have moved up since the summer.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We are inclined to take only a small signal from this movement, much as we did early last year when price increases were unusually subdued.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In part, this is because a portion of the recent pickup was attributable to the erratic nonmarket component and quarter-to-quarter fluctuations in this category tend to fade away quickly.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In addition, while market-based prices also came in higher than expected, we are interpreting some of that surprise as a reversal of some earlier low readings in particular categories.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: That said, we also think that a portion represents somewhat more persistent inflation pressure coming into 2008.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We project both core and total PCE inflation to moderate over time because of several factors.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: To begin with, futures prices for crude oil imply the sharp deceleration in energy prices shown to the right.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We also expect food prices (the middle left panel) to decelerate into 2009, partly as result of the increased production of beef and poultry that is now under way.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In addition, the impetus to inflation from core import prices (the middle right panel) should diminish over time, although by less than projected in December because we now anticipate a faster rate of dollar depreciation.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: These developments, coupled with the additional economic slack built into this projection, should help to keep inflation expectations anchored, allowing actual inflation to fall below 2 percent in the longer run.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Indeed, survey measures of long-run inflation expectations (the blue and red lines of the bottom left panel) remain stable.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: TIPS inflation compensation (the black line) jumped following the intermeeting fed funds rate cut, as Bill pointed out.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But as was discussed in the memo by Jonathan Wright and Jennifer Roush that was circulated to the Committee, we are inclined to attribute most of this increase to changes in inflation risk and liquidity premiums, not to a rise in inflation expectations per se.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Putting all this together, we project core inflation—the first column of the panel to the right—to remain at 2.1 percent this year but then to drop down to 1.9 percent next year, the same as in December.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Similarly, we continue to expect that headline inflation will slow to 2¼ percent this year and slide to 1¾ percent in 2009 as energy prices moderate.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I will now turn the floor over to Nellie.

speaker: LIANG
text: As discussed earlier, Treasury yields and stock prices are down sharply since the December FOMC meeting on news that indicated greater odds of a recession and large writedowns at financial institutions.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the blue line in the top left panel of exhibit 6, the fall in stock prices pushed up the ratio of trend forward earnings to price.

speaker: LIANG
text: The difference between this ratio and the real Treasury perpetuity yield, shown by the shaded area and plotted to the right, is a rough measure of the equity premium.

speaker: LIANG
text: As you can see, this measure jumped in the past few months and is now at the high end of its range of the past twenty years.

speaker: LIANG
text: In the corporate bond market, the spread on high-yield corporates, the black line in the middle panel, widened sharply, and investment-grade spreads, the red and blue lines, also rose.

speaker: LIANG
text: Forward spreads (not shown) rose especially in the near-term, suggesting particular concern about credit risk in the next few years.

speaker: LIANG
text: In the forecast, we assume that the equity premium and bond spreads will recede some from their recent peaks as the risk of recession recedes and activity picks up, but they will remain on the wide side of their historical averages.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the bottom left panel, our most recent indicators suggest that the OFHEO national purchase-only house-price index, the black line, fell 2¾ percent in the fourth quarter; we project further declines of about 3¼ percent in both 2008 and 2009.

speaker: LIANG
text: In some states with many subprime mortgages— such as California, Arizona, Nevada, and Florida—house prices, the red line, began to fall earlier and have declined by more.

speaker: LIANG
text: Reports of spectacular writedowns from some financial firms may also have caused investors to assign greater odds of tighter financial conditions.

speaker: LIANG
text: As noted in the bottom right panel, financial firms took writedowns and loan-loss provisions of more than $80 billion in the fourth quarter.

speaker: LIANG
text: Most of the reported losses were from subprime mortgages and related CDO exposures, but many banks also increased loss provisions for other types of loans.

speaker: LIANG
text: In response, financial firms raised substantial outside capital and cut dividends and share repurchases.

speaker: LIANG
text: Still, the risk remains that writedowns and provisioning will grow larger if house prices or economic activity will slow more than currently anticipated or if financial guarantors are downgraded further.

speaker: LIANG
text: Moreover, many of the largest firms are still at risk of further unplanned asset expansion from previous commitments for leveraged loans and their continued inability to securitize non-agency mortgages.

speaker: LIANG
text: Consequently, these firms are likely to be cautious in managing asset growth.

speaker: LIANG
text: Your next exhibit focuses on business financial conditions.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the black line in the top left panel, top-line operating earnings per share for S&P 500 firms for the fourth quarter are now estimated to be about 23 percent below their year-ago level, dragged down by losses at financial firms.

speaker: LIANG
text: For nonfinancial firms, the green line, earnings per share are estimated to be up 10 percent from a year ago.

speaker: LIANG
text: Analysts’ estimates of Q1 earnings for nonfinancial firms were trimmed a bit last week but suggest continued growth.

speaker: LIANG
text: Robust profits since 2002 have put most businesses in strong financial shape.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the right panel, loss rates on high- yield corporate bonds, the black line, have been near zero for more than a year as very few bonds defaulted and recovery rates were high.

speaker: LIANG
text: However, we project that bond losses will rise gradually in the next two years as the nonfinancial profit share slips from its currently high level.

speaker: LIANG
text: In commercial real estate, the middle left panel, the net charge-off rate at banks, the black line, was low in the third quarter of last year despite a slight tilt up mostly from troubled loans related to residential land acquisition and construction.

speaker: LIANG
text: We project that this rate will rise fairly steeply, reflecting weakness in housing and expected softening in rents for commercial properties.

speaker: LIANG
text: A similar outlook may lie behind the tighter standards for business loans reported in the January Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the orange line in the middle right panel, the net percentage of domestic banks reporting having tightened standards on commercial real estate loans in the past three months reached 80 percent, a notable increase from the October survey.

speaker: LIANG
text: In addition, one-third of domestic banks tightened lending standards on C&I loans in the past three months.

speaker: LIANG
text: Large majorities of the respondents that tightened standards pointed to a less favorable or more uncertain outlook or a reduced tolerance for risk.

speaker: LIANG
text: Despite wider spreads, borrowing rates for investment-grade firms are lower than before the December FOMC meeting.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown by the red line in the lower left panel, yields on ten-year BBB-rated bonds, the red line, fell about 25 basis points, and rates on thirty-day A2/P2 nonfinancial commercial paper, the blue line, have plummeted about 200 basis points since just before year-end.

speaker: LIANG
text: In contrast, yields on ten-year high-yield bonds, the black line, are up and now are close to 10 percent.

speaker: LIANG
text: Net borrowing by nonfinancial businesses, shown in the right panel, is on track in January to stay near the pace of recent months.

speaker: LIANG
text: Net bond issuance, the green bars, has been sizable in recent weeks with most of that issuance by investment-grade firms.

speaker: LIANG
text: Unsecured commercial paper, the yellow bars, rebounded after substantial paydowns ahead of year-end.

speaker: LIANG
text: Your next exhibit focuses on the household sector.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the top left panel, delinquency rates at commercial banks for credit cards, the blue line, and nonrevolving consumer loans, the black line, edged up in the third quarter, as did rates for auto loans at finance companies through November.

speaker: LIANG
text: Some of the recent rise in delinquency rates for credit cards is in states with the largest house-price declines, and could represent spillovers from weak housing markets.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown to the right, delinquency rates on subprime adjustable-rate mortgages, the solid red line, continued to climb and topped 20 percent in November, and delinquency rates on fixed-rate subprime and on prime and near-prime mortgages also rose.

speaker: LIANG
text: Looking ahead, we expect delinquency rates on consumer loans to rise a bit from below-average levels as household resources are strained by higher unemployment and lower house prices.

speaker: LIANG
text: These developments have spurred lenders to tighten standards on consumer loans.

speaker: LIANG
text: As noted in the middle left panel, responses to the January Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey indicate a further increase in the net percentage of banks tightening standards on credit cards and other consumer loans in the past three months.

speaker: LIANG
text: Banks also reported substantial net tightening of standards for subprime and prime mortgages, with the latter up considerably from the October survey.

speaker: LIANG
text: In addition, spreads on lower-rated tranches of consumer auto and credit card ABS jumped in January amid news that lenders were increasing loan-loss provisions.

speaker: LIANG
text: That said, interest rates on auto loans and credit cards, not shown, are not up, and most households still appear to have access to these forms of credit.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown to the right, issuance of securities backed by these loans was robust through January.

speaker: LIANG
text: Securitization of nonconforming mortgages, the grey bars in the lower left panel, was weak in the fourth quarter of last year, and there has been little, if any, this month.

speaker: LIANG
text: But agency-backed securitization, the red bars, was quite strong in the fourth quarter and appears to be again in January.

speaker: LIANG
text: Moreover, as shown to the right, interest rates have fallen appreciably.

speaker: LIANG
text: Rates on conforming thirty-year fixed-rate mortgages, the blue line, and one-year ARMs, the red line, fell, and offer rates on prime fixed-rate jumbo mortgages, the black line, are also down.

speaker: LIANG
text: The six-month LIBOR, the rate to which most subprime ARMs reset, plunged in January, although, even at this level, the first payment reset will still be substantial for many households.

speaker: LIANG
text: The next exhibit presents our outlook for mortgage defaults.

speaker: LIANG
text: The top left panel shows cumulative default rates for subprime 2/28 ARMs by year of origination.

speaker: LIANG
text: A default here is defined as a loan termination that is not from a refinancing or sale.

speaker: LIANG
text: The default rates for mortgages originated in 2006 and 2007, the red and orange lines, respectively, have shot up, and for mortgages originated in 2006, about 18 percent will have defaulted by the loan age of eighteen months.

speaker: LIANG
text: This rate is higher at every comparable age than for mortgages made in 2005, the blue line, and the average rate for loans made in 2001 to 2004, shown by the black line, with the shaded area denoting the range across years.

speaker: LIANG
text: Softer house prices likely played an important role in defaults on 2006 and 2007 loans because borrowers had little home equity to tap when they lost their jobs or became ill, or they walked away when their mortgages turned upside-down.

speaker: LIANG
text: These mortgages have not yet faced their first interest rate reset.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown to the right, we expect a sizable number of borrowers to reset to higher payments, about 375,000 each quarter this year, if these mortgages are not prepaid or rates are not reduced.

speaker: LIANG
text: While many borrowers still have time to refinance or sell before the first rate reset, lower house prices and tighter credit conditions are likely to damp this activity.

speaker: LIANG
text: As noted in the middle left panel, to project defaults on subprime ARMs, we use a loan-level model that jointly estimates prepayments and defaults.

speaker: LIANG
text: The model considers loan and borrower characteristics at origination, subsequent MSA- or state-level house prices and employment fluctuations, interest rates, and “vintage” effects.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown to the right, with data for the first three quarters in hand, we estimate that defaults in 2007 about doubled from 2006 and predict that they will climb further in 2008 and stay elevated in 2009.

speaker: LIANG
text: These estimates imply that 40 percent of the current stock of subprime ARMs will default over the next two years.

speaker: LIANG
text: An important source of uncertainty around our projections is how borrowers will behave if falling house prices push their loan-to-value ratios above 100 percent.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the first line of the bottom left panel, we estimate that 20 percent of subprime borrowers had a combined loan-to-value ratio of more than 100 percent in the third quarter of last year.

speaker: LIANG
text: If we assume that national house prices fall about 7 percent over the forecast period, as in the Greenbook, an estimated 44 percent of subprime mortgages would have combined LTVs above 100 percent.

speaker: LIANG
text: A similar calculation for prime and near-prime mortgages, shown in the second line, indicates that a not-inconsequential share, 15 percent, of these would also be upside-down by the end of 2009.

speaker: LIANG
text: While prime borrowers likely have other financial assets upon which to draw in the case of job loss or sickness, such high LTVs pose an upside risk to our baseline projection of defaults.

speaker: LIANG
text: Another source of uncertainty—this one on the positive side of the ledger—is how loan modifications can reduce defaults or loss of a home.

speaker: LIANG
text: We have limited information, but recent surveys indicate that loan workouts and modifications were modest through the third quarter of last year but likely accelerated in the fourth quarter.

speaker: LIANG
text: Servicers are strained working on the large number of loans that are delinquent before the first reset.

speaker: LIANG
text: One survey indicated that servicers assisted about 150,000 subprime borrowers in the third quarter, which would represent about 15 percent of those with past-due accounts, but were not addressing current accounts with an imminent reset.

speaker: LIANG
text: As highlighted in the top panel of your next exhibit, we summarize our projections for credit losses in the next two years for major categories of business and household debt.

speaker: LIANG
text: These projections rely on the paths for house prices, unemployment, interest rates, and other factors from the Greenbook baseline.

speaker: LIANG
text: We also present projections based on the Greenbook recession alternative with the additional assumption that national house prices fall 20 percent.

speaker: LIANG
text: In this alternative scenario, real GDP growth turns negative in 2008, and the unemployment rate rises above 6 percent in 2009.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the first column of the bottom panel, if we use the loss rates over the past decade or two as a guide to approximate losses under average economic conditions, total losses, line 6, would be projected to be $440 billion over the next two years.

speaker: LIANG
text: Such losses could be considered what might be expected by lenders of risky debt in the normal conduct of business.

speaker: LIANG
text: But conditions over the next two years are not expected to be normal, even under the baseline scenario.

speaker: LIANG
text: As shown in the second column, losses under the Greenbook baseline are expected to be considerably higher than average and total $727 billion, given our outlook for only modest growth.

speaker: LIANG
text: These losses might not greatly exceed the amounts that investors already have come to expect given signs of slowing activity.

speaker: LIANG
text: The above-average losses are especially large for residential mortgages, line 1, including those for nonprime mortgages, line 2.

speaker: LIANG
text: In contrast, losses for consumer credit, line 3, and business debt, line 4, are only a touch higher than normal.

speaker: LIANG
text: In the alternative scenario, in which business and household conditions worsen further, losses are projected to rise even more, not only for mortgages but also for other debt.

speaker: LIANG
text: Losses of this dimension would place considerable strains on both households and financial institutions, creating the potential for more-serious negative feedback on aggregate demand and activity than is captured by our standard macroeconomic models.

speaker: LIANG
text: Nathan will continue our presentation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Your first international exhibits focus on the recent strength of the U.S. external sector.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the top panel of exhibit 11, U.S. exports are now seen to have expanded at a moderate 4½ percent pace in the fourth quarter, following the 19 percent surge in the third quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: With import growth in the fourth quarter stepping down to 2 percent, net exports are estimated—as shown on line 3— to have made a positive arithmetic contribution to real GDP growth of 0.2 percentage point.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Going forward, we see the external sector contributing 0.5 percentage point to GDP growth in 2008 and 0.3 percentage point in 2009.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Exports are expected to expand at a crisp 7¼ percent pace in both years, supported by stimulus from the weaker dollar.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The pace of import growth, after stepping down on average in the first half of this year, should pick up some through the forecast period, broadly mirroring the contour of U.S. growth.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the bottom left panel, some additional impetus to import growth should come from a projected decline in core import price inflation, due to moderation in both exchange-rate-adjusted foreign prices (the red bars) and commodity price increases (the blue bars).

speaker: SHEETS
text: Returning to line 4 of the upper panel, we estimate that the current account deficit increased to 5½ percent of GDP during the fourth quarter, driven up by a surge in the oil import bill.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We see the deficit declining to 4¾ percent of GDP in 2009, as the non-oil trade deficit narrows to just 1½ percent of GDP.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown on the bottom right, the oil import bill—which has increased from around 1 percent of GDP early this decade to about 3 percent of GDP at present—looms as an increasingly important factor influencing the evolution of the current account balance.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Your next exhibit examines U.S. external performance from a longer-term perspective.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the top panel, the arithmetic contribution from net exports was persistently negative from 1997 to 2005, subtracting ¾ percentage point on average from the growth of U.S. real GDP.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The contribution from net exports, however, has swung into positive territory over the past two years, adding about ½ percentage point to growth, and we expect net exports to continue to make a positive contribution over the next two years.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the middle left panel, this upswing in the net export contribution has reflected—in roughly equal measure—an acceleration in exports and a slowing of import growth.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Over the past two years, export growth has stepped up to 8½ percent, more than twice its average 1997-2005 pace, and it is projected to moderate only slightly in 2008 and 2009.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In contrast, import growth over the past couple of years has fallen off to less than half its 1997- 2005 average and is expected to remain soft through the forecast period.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The individual contributions of exports and imports to U.S. GDP growth have both risen about ½ percentage point in recent years.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This swing in U.S. external performance has been driven in large measure by the cumulative effects of the decline in the dollar (shown on the middle right).

speaker: SHEETS
text: Since its peak in early 2002, the dollar is down more than 20 percent in broad real terms, including a 30 percent fall against the major currencies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We project that going forward the broad real dollar will depreciate at a pace of a little less than 3 percent a year, with this decline coming disproportionately against many of the emerging market currencies (including the Chinese renminbi), which have moved less since the dollar’s peak in early 2002.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The bottom panel highlights another factor that has supported the shift in U.S. external performance.

speaker: SHEETS
text: From 1997 to 2005, U.S. growth was on average just ¼ percentage point below that of our trading partners.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In recent years, U.S. growth has slowed relative to foreign growth, and this gap has widened substantially, reaching 1½ percentage points on average in 2006 and 2007.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This has, consequently, restrained imports relative to exports.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our forecast calls for this gap to narrow only slightly through the forecast period.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But this projection depends crucially on the resilience of growth abroad—an issue that is examined in your next exhibit.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Recent data have confirmed our expectation that foreign activity slowed markedly in the fourth quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the top left panel of exhibit 13, economic sentiment in the euro area fell in December for the seventh consecutive month, and the ECB’s survey of bank lending pointed to further tightening of credit standards for both households and firms.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, euro-area retail sales volumes and industrial production (not shown) have moved down in recent months.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the United Kingdom, the preliminary reading on fourth-quarter GDP growth was surprisingly strong, but other indicators seem to point to some softness going forward.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown on the right, the Bank of England’s new survey of credit conditions indicates a further decline in the availability of credit to corporations during the fourth quarter, and the level of new mortgage lending has plunged.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Other indicators, including consumer confidence, have also slid of late.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Japanese economy may be weakening as well.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the middle left panel, the December Tankan survey showed a further retreat in business confidence, including a softening of sentiment among both large manufacturers and large nonmanufacturers.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Housing starts have declined dramatically lately, as the construction sector adjusts to new, tighter building standards.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We also see signs that labor market conditions may be weakening.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the bottom panel, our assessment is that total foreign GDP growth slowed to about 2¾ percent during the fourth quarter, distinctly down from the 4 to 4½ percent pace recorded through 2006 and the first three quarters of 2007.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, the fourth- quarter slowdown was broadly based.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We estimate that growth in Mexico (line 8) declined sharply, in line with a contraction in U.S. manufacturing output.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Chinese GDP data, which were reported after the Greenbook went to press, indicate that growth in the fourth quarter remained below its double-digit pace in the first half of the year, with exports posting a contraction.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The middle right panel summarizes what we see as the key sources of this near- term slowing.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First, a number of countries have experienced headwinds from the ongoing financial turmoil; this is particularly the case for the euro area, the United Kingdom, and Canada.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, sharp recent declines in equity markets have occurred in a much broader set of countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The softening of U.S. growth is a second factor weighing on activity abroad, especially for countries like Canada and Mexico and many in emerging Asia that have sizable trade linkages with the United States.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Third, through 2006 and 2007, many of the foreign economies enjoyed exceptionally rapid cyclical expansions, so some eventual moderation in the pace of growth seemed inevitable, and we have been projecting a deceleration for some time.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Returning to the bottom panel, we see these factors as continuing to weigh on foreign activity through the first half of the year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Thereafter, growth should gradually strengthen, to 3 percent in the second half and to 3.4 percent in 2009, as financial turmoil subsides and as the U.S. economy rebounds.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, we expect that growth will remain well below the heady pace recorded over the past two years.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the top left panel of exhibit 14, our foreign outlook is also supported by projected easing of monetary policy abroad.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given mounting evidence of economic weakness and continued financial stress, we see the ECB and the Bank of Canada cutting policy rates 50 basis points by the middle of the year, and the Bank of England easing 75 basis points.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given the persisting inflation risks, this is admittedly an aggressive call.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But we see the case for monetary action as compelling and believe that these central banks will be persuaded, notwithstanding their recent hawkish rhetoric.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The futures markets also appear to be pricing in some easing, albeit at a more gradual pace than we envision.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Finally, we now expect the BoJ to remain on hold until the end of 2009.

speaker: SHEETS
text: To be sure, there are a number of risks surrounding our forecast, most of which are on the downside.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First, the prevailing financial headwinds or the slowing of U.S. growth may be larger or more protracted than we currently project.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Second, we do not yet have a good sense of the extent to which many foreign financial institutions have been affected by the recent turmoil, and the release of year-end financial statements over the next six weeks or so could bring some bad news.

speaker: SHEETS
text: A third risk is that overly optimistic expectations of decoupling may lead to policy mistakes.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Specifically, to the extent that foreign authorities are convinced that they have decoupled from the United States—or that they are immune from spillovers due to the financial turmoil—they may be too slow to ease policy to address weakening demand.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Policy abroad may also be restrained by too narrow a focus on the recent rise in inflation, a topic to which I will return momentarily.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Finally, housing markets in some countries may be vulnerable.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the bottom left panel, many countries have experienced run-ups in house prices in recent years that are similar to or even exceed those recorded in the United States, and house prices are now decelerating sharply in a number of these countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Further weakening of house prices poses the risk of adverse wealth effects.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, of the major economies shown in the right panel, only the United States has yet seen a marked downward swing in the contributions from residential investment to GDP growth.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Your final international exhibit discusses our projections for foreign inflation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the top panel of exhibit 15, average foreign inflation jumped up to an annual rate of 4½ percent in the fourth quarter, with marked increases in both the advanced foreign economies (line 2) and the emerging markets (line 7).

speaker: SHEETS
text: The sources of this rise in inflation—including rapid increases in the prices of food and oil—have been well documented.

speaker: SHEETS
