text: Going forward, we see average foreign inflation moving back down to an annual rate of 2½ percent in the second half of this year and continuing at that pace in 2009.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Despite the run-up in realized inflation rates, readings on long-term inflation expectations have remained well anchored.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the middle left panel, breakeven inflation rates for the advanced foreign economies have continued to hover around 2.3 percent on average, and long-term inflation forecasts have stayed near 2 percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For the emerging markets, average long-term inflation forecasts (shown on the middle right) have remained between 3 and 3½ percent in recent years.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The bottom panels show four-quarter percent changes for the prices of oil, food, and metals.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given the marked slowing of global activity, the stage seems set for some deceleration in commodity prices; indeed, metals prices are already on a downward trajectory.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Thus, in line with quotes from futures markets, we see the pace of increases in oil prices and food prices as declining significantly over the next few quarters.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, we have been wrong on this score before and freely acknowledge that there are upside risks to this projection.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Brian Madigan will now continue our presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 3 I will be referring to the separate package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Economic Projections.” Table 1 shows the central tendencies and ranges of your current forecasts for 2008, 2009, and 2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Central tendencies and ranges of the projections made by the Committee last October are shown in italics.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As for conditioning assumptions, most of you see the appropriate near-term path of the federal funds rate as at or below that assumed in the Greenbook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Eight policymakers explicitly assumed somewhat more near-term easing than in the Greenbook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, several of you assumed that policy would need to begin firming no later than 2009.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Many of you also projected that the funds rate would exceed the level forecasted in the Greenbook by the end of the forecast period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the first row, first column, of table 1, the central tendency of your forecasts of real growth for 2008 has been marked down about ½ percentage point since last October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you remarked that a range of factors had prompted you to lower your growth expectations for the current year, including the continued turmoil in financial markets and the resulting tightening of credit conditions, the persistent deterioration in the housing market, incoming data suggesting slower consumption expenditures and business investment growth, and higher oil prices.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A few of you suggested that stronger export demand as well as fiscal stimulus would provide some offset to weakness in private domestic demand, particularly beginning later this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your half-yearly projections, not shown, suggest that you all think that, more likely than not, the economy will skirt recession.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On average, you see real GDP growing at an annual rate of about ¾ percentage point over the first half before picking up to a 2½ percent pace in the second half.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the second row, in view of the weak growth forecast for this year, most of you revised up your expectations for the unemployment rate in the fourth quarter about 0.4 percentage point, to around 5¼ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you project slightly brisker growth this year than the Greenbook does—perhaps partly reflecting the assumption that a number of you made that there would be more near-term monetary ease than the staff assumed.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the third and fourth sets of rows, with incoming inflation data a bit higher than previously expected and despite projected weaker real activity, the central tendencies of your projections for total and core PCE inflation this year have increased about 0.3 percentage point.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That upward revision is a bit larger than the 0.2 percentage point upward revision to the Greenbook inflation forecasts but leaves the level of your projections close to those in the Greenbook: Most of you see total and core 3 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: inflation this year at a little above 2 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But as shown in the bottom section, the upper limit of the range of your overall inflation projections for this year has moved up to 2.8 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your forecasts for total PCE inflation this year remain a bit higher than for core inflation, reflecting the expectation of higher energy, food, and in some cases, import price inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Looking ahead to next year, your forecasts indicate that you expect economic growth to pick up as the drag from the housing sector dissipates and credit conditions improve.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The midpoint of the central tendency of your forecasts for real GDP growth is 2.4 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your growth forecasts for next year are mostly above the staff’s forecast of 2.2 percent, perhaps again because a number of you assumed more- aggressive policy easing in the near term and perhaps because at least some of you appear to see potential output growth as a bit brisker than the staff does.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With most of you evidently seeing growth a bit above trend next year, the unemployment rate begins to edge lower, but the central tendency of your unemployment projections still remains distinctly above that in October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although you are generally optimistic about improving conditions next year, your views have become considerably more dispersed: As shown in the lower section, the width of the range of the growth projections for 2009 has nearly doubled, as has the width of the range of the unemployment projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The third and fourth sets of rows in the upper panel indicate that most of you see overall and core inflation as moving below 2 percent next year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Some of you said that those declines reflect less pressure from energy prices and, with the unemployment rate above the NAIRU, the emergence of some slack in the labor market.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is worth noting, however, that despite the easing of pressure on resources during 2008 and 2009, the central tendencies of your inflation projections for next year are essentially unchanged from October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This development presumably reflects your perception of some deterioration in the near-term inflation- output tradeoff, perhaps prompted in part by the publication of surprisingly high inflation data for the fourth quarter of 2007 and an expectation that those effects will linger in 2009.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Turning to 2010, the interpretation of your longer-term projections is a bit less straightforward than it was in October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It was noted during the trial-run phase that a time may come when the economy is seen as unlikely to be in a steady state by the third year of the projection.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To some extent, that time seems to have already arrived.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In particular, a comparison of the central tendencies for unemployment in 2010 from your January and October projections suggests that you now see a bit of slack persisting that year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendencies and ranges of your total and core inflation projections for 2010 have changed just a bit from those in October, but those changes might be viewed by outside analysts as significant.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In particular, the central tendency for total inflation in 2010 has inched up 0.1 percentage point, and the lower limit of the central tendency for core inflation has increased the same amount.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Absent guidance to the contrary, some analysts might now conclude that your “comfort zone” has edged up to 1¾ to 2 percent from 1½ to 2 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To counter this impression, presumably the published “Summary of Economic Projections” should suggest that, because a bit of economic slack is expected to persist at the end of 2010, inflation could continue to edge lower beyond the projection period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This discussion, however, raises not only a presentational point but also a substantive one, and that is, Why should your inflation projections for 2010 have revised up at all?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: True, the inflation-output tradeoff appears to have deteriorated a little recently, but as Dave Reifschneider noted, some of that deterioration is likely to be temporary.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, higher inflation than otherwise might in principle be a consequence of taking out some insurance now against especially weak economic outcomes.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But given the significant negative shock to aggregate demand embedded in your modal forecasts and the associated upward revision to slack across all three years of your projections, as well as the absence of any upward revision to your inflation projections for 2009, even the small upward revision to your inflation projections in 2010 seems somewhat surprising.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Turning to the uncertainties in the outlook, the upper panel of exhibit 2 shows that even more of you than in October judge that uncertainty regarding prospects for economic activity is higher than its historical level.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even with the significant reductions in the target funds rate already in place and, for many of you, an assumption of more easing to come, the lower panel illustrates that most of you still see the risks to growth as tilted to the downside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As reasons, you again cited tighter credit conditions for households and businesses emanating from further disruptions in financial markets as well as the persistently deteriorating housing outlook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the upper panel of exhibit 3, more of you than in October see the uncertainty around your total inflation forecasts as close to that of the past two decades, while a smaller minority viewed uncertainty as greater than in the past.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the lower panel, fewer of you now see the inflation risks as predominantly to the upside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On balance, as in October, downside risks to growth were more frequently cited than upside risks to inflation, which seems broadly consistent with each of the alternative policy statements that were in Bluebook table 1.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s quite a bit of information to digest.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Does anyone have questions for our colleagues?

speaker: EVANS
text: I have a couple of questions that are somewhat different.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the labor front, I’m curious if you could offer some thoughts on how deterioration in the labor market might be coming about—whether or not it would be from the hiring front or the job-destruction front.

speaker: EVANS
text: As the research literature has evolved over a long time, I think it has moved a bit away from job destruction playing the key role and more toward reductions in hiring.

speaker: EVANS
text: I wonder how this informs the way you look at the data.

speaker: EVANS
text: Any insights you have into that would be quite helpful.

speaker: EVANS
text: Then I wonder if you could just talk a bit more about the interesting memo that was distributed on inflation compensation and the implications for expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I read it, it seemed to indicate that inflation expectations, if anything, were coming down from the five-year forward but that inflation compensation was higher.

speaker: EVANS
text: So does that mean that the variance of inflation is higher?

speaker: EVANS
text: Are people talking about the possibility of disinflation during this period?

speaker: EVANS
text: I would expect it to come with that type of compensation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Your thoughts on that would be great.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Do you want me to take that last question, or do you want to?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, I could start if you would like.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think the points we are trying to make in that memo regarding inflation compensation were that, first of all, it’s very difficult to make these judgments about what is going on with inflation expectations, inflation risk premiums, and so on; but our best reading of the evidence was that probably inflation expectations have not moved up significantly recently.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We base that on a variety of indicators.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I won’t go through all of them now, but to me the most compelling evidence to support that point is that inflation compensation over the next five years has actually come down over the intermeeting period, and it is a little hard to rationalize why inflation expectations would have risen so far out, whereas in the near term they seem, if anything, to be declining.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, various factors can affect inflation compensation, including relative liquidity and inflation risk premiums, and we certainly don’t want to exaggerate our ability to decompose these changes into these various factors.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is possible that inflation risk premiums, in particular, have moved up, and some evidence does suggest that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I neglected to say how interesting that memo was.

speaker: EVANS
text: The analysis is really very good.

speaker: EVANS
text: I look forward to seeing more of it.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The only thing I would add to Brian’s statement is that I think uncertainty about inflation in the long run could be moving up noticeably without really bringing into play disinflation or something like that.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In other words, you could be more worried about going down to 1½ or 1¼ than you were before—I don’t know—it could be more just as it was in the forecast.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: May I have a two-hander on this?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When you think about what’s going on, it is plausible that it is both up and down.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s the key point here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Because if you also look at the projections, there is a lot more uncertainty about what’s going on in the real side of the economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That could mean that inflation could drift down and longer-run inflation expectations could drift down if, in fact, there’s some uncertainty about what the objectives of this Committee are.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On the other hand, we actually did take a very sharp interest rate cut, and that could indicate that the Committee might tolerate somewhat higher inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So even though the action that was related to the big jump in inflation compensation was a cut in interest rates, I think there is a plausible argument that it could be symmetric in terms of increasing uncertainty on both sides.

speaker: EVANS
text: That’s what I was focusing on—the mean-preserving nature of that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think it is consistent with your view, but I just wanted to clarify.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: On job destruction versus a slower pace of new job creation, it’s hard to answer that one.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Some of those patterns have changed over time; and in monitoring labor market developments, we’re trying to keep track of those two elements and that sort of thing.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Whether that would materially change the way we would look at, say, just what payroll employment growth was doing, it would still be one of our main reads coming in.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As to exactly how that worked out behind it, I’m not sure it would make too much of a difference.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I don’t know whether Dave might want to add something to that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, we would be monitoring those developments.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are monitoring the gross flows in the labor market, and I think to a large extent the slowing that we have seen thus far in employment growth has come more from a slower pace of hiring than it has from an increase in layoffs.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: More recently, in the JOLTS data as of November, there has been a significant increase in layoffs and discharges, and there has been some further slowing in hiring.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If we were to truly move into a recession, you would still see a lot of layoffs, and there would be a fair amount of job destruction, so the cyclical aspect would still likely show through pretty strongly.

speaker: EVANS
text: I guess I was thinking that, if you talk to people, you hear more about the job destruction aspect, but you don’t hear quite the same information about hiring, except you might hear more nervousness.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Hiring plans have come off a bit in most of the surveys that we follow, but just a bit—not a lot yet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lockhart, did you have an interjection?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My staff is suspicious that the employment numbers have actually been weaker than the data have shown.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: They have been focusing on the birth-death model and the payroll survey is based upon assumptions related to the birth of construction firms, which logically would not be creating jobs in this environment.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Do you have a take on that issue?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Well, if Bill Wascher, who is our expert in this area, wanted to say something, I would certainly let him go ahead and say something.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The birth-death model basically assumes that the cyclical properties of births and deaths are the same as for continuing establishments.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The BLS has only about five years of experience with the birth-death model, so I think it is pretty difficult to judge whether they need to make any additional adjustments in births and deaths, other than the same pattern that occurs in terms of net employment changes in continuing firms.

speaker: WASCHER
text: But without much to go on, they don’t take a very strong stand on whether they do a very good job of picking up the turning points because they don’t have any history on which to base their analysis.

speaker: WASCHER
text: So I think there are reasons to suspect that that is possibly the case, but I don’t think there is any strong evidence that it is, and it is important to note that they do assume some cyclicality in births and deaths in their procedures.

speaker: POOLE
text: Brian, I want to ask you about the projections.

speaker: POOLE
text: Well, it is more than an exercise now—the projections that we are offering are for real.

speaker: POOLE
text: What is the message that comes out of the projections—that is, if I am talking to the press or to others and they say, “What do I make of all of this?” My question to you is, What do you make of all of this?

speaker: POOLE
text: What is the message for the implications for policy or the implications for anything?

speaker: POOLE
text: You know, the data don’t really speak for themselves.

speaker: POOLE
text: We are throwing out a lot of stuff here to the market, and what is the market supposed to make of it?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, that is a hard question, actually.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You know, obviously in some sense the numbers at some level do speak for themselves.

speaker: POOLE
text: What are they telling us?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think they say that the Committee is expecting relatively slow growth in the period immediately ahead but that the economy avoids a recession.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: There is some recovery over the subsequent years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is not extraordinarily brisk.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is a fairly gradual recovery in terms of growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The unemployment rate moves up a little, as you would expect with a period of growth below trend, but does not get extraordinarily high; and inflation, after coming under some upward pressure of late, gradually edges back down to levels below 2 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I am not sure that I am saying anything terribly enlightening here.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, one point that I should emphasize is that the full summary of economic projections, we hope, gives more texture than I was just able to give to the Committee’s views about the modal outcome and to the Committee’s concerns about the risks to both growth and inflation.

speaker: POOLE
text: The reason I raise the question is that it seems to me very important that we have some interpretation as to what we make of all this and what we want the market to make of all this.

speaker: POOLE
text: In particular, let’s say the observation that the projections or the risks are weighted to the downside.

speaker: POOLE
text: You might get some people saying, “Well, if we get some employment reports or others that in fact come in weaker than anticipated, that means that the Committee is on the edge of pulling the trigger to respond to it.” That might be a possible message that people would take from this.

speaker: POOLE
text: If that is not the message that we want to convey, then we had better be very careful how we talk about these.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Poole, I would just point out that when these are released it will be simultaneous with my testimony to the Congress, and so I will have opportunities to put some context on it at that time.

speaker: POOLE
text: I guess my question is directed as much to the Chairman as it is to Brian, which you will answer in the testimony.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will answer in the testimony.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, I, too, wanted to thank you all for the paper on forward inflation compensation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I agree with the conclusion that it is difficult.

speaker: FISHER
text: Especially in times of strained trading conditions, I think that is the conclusion—whether you interpret the outcome the way it was interpreted in the paper or the way I do it more cynically, I think that is the key underlying point.

speaker: FISHER
text: I thought that was a very valuable, useful paper, and I want to thank you, Governor Mishkin, for commissioning it.

speaker: FISHER
text: My question is to Nathan on your inflation projections.

speaker: FISHER
text: Reading through the Greenbook—even though the section on the international side is very thin—with the exception of China, where I think we can sell a lot of “Whip Inflation Now” buttons, and of Argentina, where the numbers are rigged, but even in those countries, what I took home was that everybody was surprised on the upside in every country ranging from the advanced countries, as we call them, to Turkey.

speaker: FISHER
text: Then, if you look at the exhibit 15 that you just presented to us, those numbers are confirmed in the fourth quarter, and then there is a sharp falloff proceeding from there.

speaker: FISHER
text: You gave us a good analysis of the risk to the foreign outlook in growth, and then you concluded your comment on inflation by saying that we have been wrong before, that there is some upside risk.

speaker: FISHER
text: So my question is, What are the risks on the inflation side?

speaker: FISHER
text: Could you elaborate on them, just as you elaborated on the risks to growth in the foreign outlook?

speaker: SHEETS
text: We are happy to hear that there is demand for a bigger international section.

speaker: SHEETS
text: You had better be careful what you wish for.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I am very serious about this.

speaker: FISHER
text: Suddenly there is a falloff.

speaker: FISHER
text: Would you give us a sense of the risk?

speaker: FISHER
text: It can’t be all one-sided.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Just a word of background.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The rationale for the falloff is the expected decline in these commodity prices and the expected slowing of global demand.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now, thinking about the risks, I am reasonably convinced that global demand is going to slow, which I believe will translate into reduced demand for many of these commodities that have driven up inflation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, that says something only about the demand side of these commodity markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There is also a lot going on on the supply side.

speaker: SHEETS
text: At the last FOMC meeting, we talked about ethanol and the fact that many of these emerging-market countries are wealthier, that they want to eat better than they used to, that the relative price of energy has risen, and that it takes a lot of energy to raise these crops.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So there are supply factors as well as demand factors at work in driving up these commodity prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It is very hard for us to forecast the supply side of these markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It is driven by things like weather and geopolitical developments and so on and so forth.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the commodities, my sense is that demand is going to shift in to some extent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As long as the supply doesn’t shift in as well, we should be able to see a decline, or at least a slower rate of increase, in these prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: A very important point here is that, in order to get less of an impetus coming from commodity prices and inflation in these countries, we don’t necessarily need oil prices to come down in level terms.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We just need them to stop going up at such rapid rates.

speaker: SHEETS
text: If we get slower rates of price increases, that will be disinflationary relative to where we have been.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That is how I would characterize the risks around this forecast, mainly on the supply side of these commodity markets.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Nellie, I have two questions for you.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One is on exhibit 9, where you forecast in the middle right panel the rate of increase in defaults on subprime ARMs.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If you compare that with your reset rate estimate and your house-price assumption or the house-price assumption in the market, I wonder whether that looks a little optimistic.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Can you just say a little more about why, under the baseline scenario, given what has happened to house prices already and what is ahead, you wouldn’t think that would be substantially greater?

speaker: LIANG
text: We have revised this forecast up quite a bit since the first time we looked at this maybe in June or August, in part because of lower house prices and tighter credit conditions.

speaker: LIANG
text: The model requires as inputs defaults and prepayments, and the prepayment rates have been fairly slow but not zero.

speaker: LIANG
text: The 2006 vintage, as it approaches its first reset, has been that 20 to 25 percent are able to prepay.

speaker: LIANG
text: They are able to find something.

speaker: LIANG
text: So we don’t want to assume that none of them will be able to.

speaker: LIANG
text: The model would approach both of those, so that is the positive side.

speaker: LIANG
text: The downside is that our forecast, with the national house-price assumption of roughly minus 7 over the forecast period, does imply house-price declines on the order of minus 20 percent a year or more in California, Florida, and some other places.

speaker: LIANG
text: That does leave the loan-to-value ratio, as I mentioned, pretty high for many borrowers.

speaker: LIANG
text: We have never had this kind of episode, so we have to make a judgment about the point at which subprime borrowers walk away from their houses.

speaker: LIANG
text: The current assumption is that at about 140 percent we just say you are out; but it has to be almost an assumption that, if by then you hadn’t defaulted, we would push you out.

speaker: LIANG
text: So there is an upside.

speaker: LIANG
text: On the other hand, saying 40 percent of the outstanding stock will default over two years sounds like a big projection as well.

speaker: LIANG
text: So we tried to balance.

speaker: LIANG
text: There are risks on both sides, for sure.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My second question is about your projected credit loss, and I apologize if you said this in your introduction.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Are these losses across all holders of that credit risk?

speaker: LIANG
text: We have not distinguished between who is holding the securities— banks or investors—so mortgages would include the 20 percent or so that are commercial banks, and it would also include those held by investors in the primary form.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We, being the Fed, know a fair amount about what banks hold.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Do you have a crude estimate of what share of this banks hold, or what share of this would end up being eaten by banks?

speaker: LIANG
text: In mortgages, 20 percent is actually probably a pretty good estimate.

speaker: LIANG
text: They have that much of the business sector and that much of the mortgages, so that pretty much covers it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I am just trying to get at how you interpret this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So 20 percent of the additional $600 billion relative to normal or relative to bank capital cushions now, is what?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Is it a lot or not so much?

speaker: LIANG
text: One issue here is whether you want to do it relative to current capital cushions.

speaker: LIANG
text: If they anticipate that they will need to raise capital, they can cut dividends further.

speaker: LIANG
text: I haven’t done that sort of exercise.

speaker: LIANG
text: One way to think about this is that the average long-run rate is about 60 basis points on debt; in the Greenbook baseline it runs to about 1 percent, and in the alternative, it gets close to about 1½ percent of debt.

speaker: LIANG
text: So, it is not outside the realm of history.

speaker: LIANG
text: It is on the high side.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have had some bad points in history.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I am not trying to force you to give a prediction, but were you reassured by this or troubled by it, fundamentally, in terms of the capacity of the financial system to absorb it?

speaker: LIANG
text: I think the third alternative gets beyond what most are expecting at this point.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Yes, I would agree with that.

speaker: LIANG
text: In that sense, it does represent a risk that you are going to get dynamic feedback between losses and household spending and lending—it is a high risk.

speaker: LIANG
text: So I wouldn’t say “comforted.” I think we were saying that this is beyond probably what our models could respond to in our typical way or it would be another dynamic feedback loop of some sort that we don’t typically adjust for.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Oh, I am sorry—a two-hander.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just a quick followup, this doesn’t include losses from securities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It is only the loans, right?

speaker: LIANG
text: The loans could be packaged in securities.

speaker: LIANG
text: Now, whether it is repackaged into an MBS, it would be there.

speaker: LIANG
text: It wouldn’t be if it got in a CDO or something.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just in corporate bonds, for example.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Let me go to Brian first.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is more of a comment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In your description of the forecast, you referred several times to the notion that there might be slack in the economy in 2010 based on these numbers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess my reaction to that, while I was kind of skeptical, I am not sure exactly how you infer that from what was reported.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Certainly, that seems to be true in the Greenbook forecast, but trend growth seems to be as good as or better than it was in the last projection.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In 2010, inflation—true—is a little higher.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The unemployment rate may be a 0.1 or 0.2 percentage point higher.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But unless you infer something about what people thought the NAIRU might be, I don’t know how you would necessarily infer that the reason inflation went up in these forecasts was that there was slack in the economy in these projections.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I just wanted to caution about the language we use in how we describe what we see here without necessarily inferring something about whether, in any individual person’s forecast, there may or may not have been slack.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In mine, there wasn’t in 2010, but I don’t see that necessarily follows from what these numbers look like.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That was my only observation here.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Maybe I can respond to that.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is very inferential, and it is based partly on the two-tenths’ difference from the October exercise when it was actually clear—I think clearer at that time—from participants’ forecasts that many participants characterized their NAIRU as being in the vicinity of 4¾ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Unfortunately, the writeups this time were not all that explicit on this point, but it is the comparison with October that I was leaning on fairly heavily.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have two other questions that I would like to pose.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One is the change in the Greenbook’s assumption about the increase in potential GDP.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In particular, I am curious because what it essentially does, it seems, is to build in a significant amount of slack or output gap in 2009 and 2010 that didn’t exist in the last Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am inferring that part of the reason the more-aggressive easing in the policy assumption does not have any effect on inflation to speak of is that it is offset by the increased gap that you have built in.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would like a little more explanation about the justification for building in a greater gap or a higher potential.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I am also curious to know, if you hadn’t done that, what your forecast for growth and inflation would look like in, let’s say, 2009 and 2010.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Could you give some guesstimate of how that might have affected it?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In terms of the rationale for increasing potential going back over history, some of that, as I think I mentioned, was just that actual productivity performance has been better than the last time we reviewed this in the summer, and we are taking that on board.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: That is part of the motivation.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Another part of the motivation is what we perceive is a somewhat growing tension between the way we saw labor market slack developing and the way we were looking at slack in terms of the product side through the output gap.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We had arrived at a point this round where those tensions had increased over time, and this revision mitigates some of that tension, so those two things are in better alignment with each other.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We also were taking the opportunity, when we opened up, to look at some other technical factors we used that get involved in going from, say, the nonfarm business sector to GDP, that sort of thing, and those also pushed us in the direction of being a bit more optimistic on growth going back.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So we did view it, if you look at it in terms of product markets, as that there was more slack now than we had previously been thinking and that there was also more slack in the labor market—but that was from the actual data that came in.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Going forward, we have more slack.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We have more slack just in the labor market because we have revised up the unemployment rate.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: With that, and taking on board these assumptions of potential output, we have more slack on the output side.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Now, one question would be, to address your second question, how would things have changed if we hadn’t taken that on board?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Well, going forward, we would have written down a lower GDP forecast because what we are really saying here is that it is not that households and firms have changed their perceptions; this is just us, the poor econometricians, trying to infer what is out there in the real world.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So the poor econometricians have inferred that potential output is growing stronger.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We have to look at it and say, “Well, so the prospects going forward for permanent incomes, corporate earnings, and that sort of thing, will be stronger, and that implies basically a one-for-one ratcheting up.” If we had said, “Well, no, potential output growth going forward won’t be stronger,” we would have revised down the GDP growth rate with it, so there wouldn’t have been any change in the output gap from that.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: That would have been shifting one for one.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: It wouldn’t have changed our sense of what resource utilization would be going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So are you saying that your path of the gap would have been unchanged?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The path of the gap would have been to a first approximation unchanged going forward.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Some of the greater resource utilization now and going forward is a combination of the fact that we haven’t really changed our view on the labor market, aside from once we took on board the new unemployment rate data, but that we did change on the product market.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Going forward, the way it evolves further on, we see the labor market gap opening up a little more and the output gap opening up a little more—that is driven primarily by our sense that the economy in an underlying sense is weaker—and we have made an adjustment for that with the monetary policy assumption.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But it is not quite enough.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We haven’t lowered the funds rate as much as we would have needed to do to totally wipe out that fact and keep resource utilization constant going forward on the product side.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: This is a difficult question.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: It was a difficult one for us, definitely, going through it because we had many moving parts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, it does really change the character of the forecast substantially, I think.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: If you think about the forecast as resource utilization and inflation, then it has an effect on resource utilization that is bigger now going forward in the product market.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We also see a bigger effect in the labor market, and if that were the only thing, it would have put more downward pressure—but not a lot—on inflation.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But as I mentioned, we are coming into this forecast with somewhat worse inflation performance lately, and we think that has some persistence.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So that is helping balance it out.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My last question is also related to some adjustments that struck me in the panel you talked about where you constructed the revised estimates of r*.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The first item on your list that you talk about was that the equity premium had gone up, and that was a big factor.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I have a couple of questions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That was an adjustment factor.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, the way I would think about the stock market declining would be primarily having a wealth effect that works its way through consumption—that would be the normal channel.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yet the Greenbook and this discussion seem to suggest that somehow there was an additional adjustment made because of the rise in the equity premium.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is that correct or not, or is it just the wealth effect that you are talking about?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: No, it is not separate; the equity premium is a large reason that we had the big drop in stock values.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But is the mechanism through a wealth effect on consumption growth?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, what does that mean?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I would say a couple of things.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: One, you can think of the cost of raising capital through equity as having some small influence on business investment.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The big effect would be primarily on consumption, as you mentioned.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Wealth effects to a smaller extent would affect housing as well.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But I think of that as a wealth channel.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But there is a bit of a cost-of-capital effect through raising funds through equity that you might think of as well.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Another thing I would say is that the difficulty here is distinguishing the equity premium from general risk concerns, risk premiums in general, or increased compensation for higher risk or default risk in a number of these credit spreads we are talking about; those are sort of related.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: It is hard to keep these things separate in any kind of an accounting.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Also, these things tend to be correlated with consumer and business sentiment.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Again, that is another thing that is hard to keep separate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So are these “extra channels”— if you want to call them that—typically part of the forecast change and how you evaluate?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is to say, in the fall, when the stock market booms 10 percent, are we going to get another kicker upward in r* due to these same factors?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I mean, you could have a situation in which business sentiment would not take a hit, for example, simultaneously with the stock market tumbling, and you would not see some risk premiums on bonds going up.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: That would be very unusual.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am just reacting to this very large change in your estimate of r* and attributing it to equity premiums, and I was just trying to figure out both.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We just had a really big drop in the stock market, and that is the biggest piece of what is going on.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we have also marked down considerably our housing forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is in an exogenous shift in aggregate demand, the IS curve.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is another chunk of what is going on here.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have had some increase in risk spreads, not just in the equity premium.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Despite the fact that Treasury rates have fallen, corporate bond yields have not as much, and we don’t have as much there, so there is in general a widening of risk premiums.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, I am just trying to sort out how much of this is really due to the stock market moving around.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: A big chunk of this is due to the stock market, so I don’t know what we can do other than to take that on board in our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As Dave noted, there are a few other, small wrinkles, and we didn’t just invent those extra wrinkles this time around.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: They have always been there.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But most of this is working through the wealth effect on the consumer spending side.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So it is a weaker stock market and much weaker consumption.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is the aggregate demand channel.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other piece is housing, which I don’t want to minimize because, in fact, that is another nontrivial factor holding down demand and, we think, depressing our estimate of the equilibrium funds rate here over the intermediate term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I didn’t understand that this was just primarily the wealth effect or whether you were referring to something different.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, the way the stock market and other elements of spending operate is a little more complicated than just a consumer spending channel, but it really is wealth effect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I wonder if I could entice anybody for a cup of coffee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a fifteen-minute break, and then we’ll commence with the go- round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If it is okay with everybody, we can start the economic go- round at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Poole, you are up.

speaker: POOLE
text: I am not sure how I got to be first here, but I guess I was being unusually agreeable when Debbie asked me.

speaker: POOLE
text: The general tenor of comments that I hear from our directors and people around the Eighth Federal Reserve District— these are the community bankers and smaller firms—is that things are slow but not disastrously slow.

speaker: POOLE
text: The comments that I hear from a series of phone calls to much larger national companies are decidedly more pessimistic, with one exception that I will talk about in a moment.

speaker: POOLE
text: My contact at a large national trucking firm says that they are in a 20-month recession in transportation.

speaker: POOLE
text: They are cutting their capacity, cutting the number of trucks, and I think the numbers on their cap-ex illustrate the situation: for 2006, $410 million; for 2007, $336 million; and their plan for 2008 is $200 million.

speaker: POOLE
text: That is down a little more than 50 percent in two years, so they are really cutting back.

speaker: POOLE
text: I also called friends at UPS and FedEx, and generally things are not a whole lot different but a little weaker than they have been.

speaker: POOLE
text: Neither firm has any particular issues with labor supply.

speaker: POOLE
text: Domestic express business is flat, and customers are switching to the lower-priced services instead of overnight delivery at the end of the afternoon, shifting to ground services, and that sort of thing.

speaker: POOLE
text: On international business, U.S.-outbound volume for FedEx is up 6 percent.

speaker: POOLE
text: That would be consistent with the export increases that we have seen.

speaker: POOLE
text: Reports are that Asia is a bit slower but is still growing very rapidly.

speaker: POOLE
text: Asia to the United States is up 80 percent, 20 percent to Europe and Latin America.

speaker: POOLE
text: The freight market is dead—that is the way my contact put it—down 5 percent year over year.

speaker: POOLE
text: That is consistent with my trucking industry contact—and pretty much the same with UPS.

speaker: POOLE
text: My contact with the fast food industry—the quick-serve restaurant, or QSR, business—says the demand there is definitely weak.

speaker: POOLE
text: They are coming in roughly flat, I guess, or actually down so far this year.

speaker: POOLE
text: Prices are up because of the increase in food costs.

speaker: POOLE
text: The casual dining industry is in worse shape than the fast food industry.

speaker: POOLE
text: My contact also follows retail in general pretty closely and finds that retail business in general is weak.

speaker: POOLE
text: That is consistent with a lot of the reports that we have been receiving.

speaker: POOLE
text: A major exception is in the IT area—software.

speaker: POOLE
text: I have contact with a large software company, and the contact noted that, as announced, Microsoft had a fantastic quarter.

speaker: POOLE
text: The earnings were up sharply.

speaker: POOLE
text: PC hardware sales are growing at a rate of 11 to 13 percent expected in the first half of this year, so we see strong growth in the PC market.

speaker: POOLE
text: Consumer demand is stronger than business demand.

speaker: POOLE
text: Both, however, are pretty strong.

speaker: POOLE
text: The international business is doing better, in part because the industry is having some success in reducing the amount of software piracy.

speaker: POOLE
text: The biggest problem is finding software engineers.

speaker: POOLE
text: This particular company is running 8 percent behind its hiring forecast and cannot find software engineers.

speaker: POOLE
text: Positive for us old guys; some of the retirees are coming back to write code.

speaker: POOLE
text: That is all I have.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I broadly agree with the Greenbook forecast for economic growth this year and with the assessment that the downside risks to that forecast are considerable.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The severe and prolonged housing downturn and financial shock have put the economy at, if not beyond, the brink of recession.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My forecast incorporates fiscal stimulus of the same magnitude as the Greenbook and monetary stimulus that is somewhat larger.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have assumed a 50 basis point cut at this meeting and an additional 25 basis point cut during the first half.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My forecast shows growth of 1½ percent in 2008, like the Greenbook, but it has a more pronounced acceleration in 2009 as the monetary and fiscal stimulus kickstarts the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The unemployment rate edges up this year to 5¼ percent before dropping gradually next year toward the natural rate of 4¾.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am especially concerned about the outlook for consumer spending.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The combined hits to equity and housing wealth will extract a considerable toll, and consumer spending will be further depressed by slower growth in disposable income due to weaker employment growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Delinquencies and charge-offs on most forms of consumer debt have already risen, and slower job growth seems likely to exacerbate this trend, prompting financial institutions to further tighten credit standards and terms.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In my forecast, such developments reverberate back negatively onto economic activity.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Like the Greenbook, I downgraded my economic outlook substantially since our last in- person meeting.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The December employment report was probably the single most shocking piece of real side news prompting this revision.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But knowing that it is unwise to put too much weight on any single piece of data, I have been examining the question of whether that report was more signal or noise.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The drop in initial UI claims to relatively low levels in recent weeks makes such an assessment important.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Because the behavior of both series may have been affected by seasonal factors near year-end, it seems worthwhile to examine a broad range of data bearing on the labor market.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My conclusion is that the labor market has indeed been weakening since mid-2007, and the extent of weakening, while relatively modest thus far, is quite typical of patterns seen when the economy is tipping into recession.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Independent evidence of a weakening in the labor market comes from the household survey.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even when adjusted for definitional and measurement differences from the payroll survey, the household survey shows a fairly smooth trend of declining employment growth during 2007.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The drop in payroll employment in December helped bring the establishment data into closer alignment with the household employment data.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In the payroll survey, the slowdown is concentrated in construction and finance.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In the household series, higher unemployment is actually widespread across sectors.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The household survey also contains other signs of a weakening job market: a 25 percent increase in the unemployment rate for job losers, which accounts for the lion’s share of the overall increase in aggregate unemployment; an increase in the number of newly unemployed job losers, which can be thought of as a broader measure than UI claims of inflows into unemployment; and an increase of 5 to 10 percent in the estimated expected completed duration of an unemployment spell, suggesting a reduced pace of outflows from unemployment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The labor force participation rate of men and women of age 16 to 24 years has also fallen notably in recent months.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Labor force participation rates for this group have been edging down since the last recession, but the decline accelerated in 2007, and historically this group is among the first to respond to weakening labor market conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Data from the JOLTS survey, which we discussed in the Q&A round, confirm the weakness revealed elsewhere.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The job openings, or vacancy, rate is down, consistent with the reduced pace of outflows from unemployment, as reflected in continuing UI claims and unemployment durations, and layoffs and discharges are up sharply.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Other data cited in the Greenbook, Part 2, such as net hiring plans for Manpower, and NFIB and survey measures of job availability and unemployment expectations further corroborate a slowdown.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With the aggregate unemployment rate now up only 0.6 percentage point off its low, I would describe the deterioration in the labor market thus far as modest, but it is noteworthy that an increase in unemployment of this magnitude, in the space of 12 months, has occurred only twice since 1948 outside of recessions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: While my modal scenario contains a near-term slowdown rather than a contraction, it is actually pretty rosy compared with what I fear might happen.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My contacts have turned decidedly negative in the past six to eight weeks, and further financial turmoil may still ensue.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On consumer spending, two large retailers report very subdued expectations going forward following the weak holiday season, which involved a lot of discounting.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On hiring and capital spending, my contacts have emphasized restraint in their plans due to fears that the economy will continue to slow.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A serious issue is whether the tightening of credit standards that is under way will deepen into a full-blown credit crunch.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The new Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey shows a noticeable tightening in lending standards, and this is confirmed by my contacts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, senior officers of a large bank in my District recently described a variety of new steps they are taking to protect against credit losses.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They are tightening underwriting practices across the entire consumer lending and small business loan portfolio.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A recent strategy has involved classifying MSAs according to whether their real estate markets are stable, soft, distressed, or severely distressed, using both historical and prospective views of property values.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Based on these designations, the company has reduced permissible combined loan-to-value ratios in their home equity portfolio, and going forward they intend to apply them across the entire consumer portfolio.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the positive side, though, they note that lower interest rates have spurred a surge in applications for mortgage refinancing, and a recent analysis shows that the reduction in the prime rate is having a significant impact on ARM reset expectations, shifting a large number from increases to reductions at reset.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In fact, an analysis conducted before our most recent rate cut that assumed a 7 percent prime rate in February 2008—and it is now at 6½—estimates that two-thirds of the subprime ARM portfolio would now experience a decrease in their monthly payments at reset.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This is a sharp contrast from an analysis in June 2007 with a prime rate of 8 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Now let me turn briefly to inflation and inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I project that inflation will decline over the forecast period to around 1¾ percent, and I see the risks around that forecast as balanced.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Admittedly, though, the recent data on inflation have been worrisome, and they raise the issue of whether or not we can afford to cut rates as much as needed to fight a recession without seriously risking a persistently higher rate of inflation and inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I tend to think this risk is manageable, largely because of the credibility we have built.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It appears to me that this credibility has reduced the response of inflation to all the factors thought to influence it, including energy prices, the exchange rate, and business cycle conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Thus I consider it less likely that rising energy prices are going to push up core inflation very much or that the pass- through that does occur will easily get built into inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I view inflation as less persistent now than it once was, tending to revert fairly quickly to the public’s view of our inflation objective.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I do hope that our long-run inflation forecast will help people identify what that objective is.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But even if inflation expectations turn out to be less well anchored than I think, I still see the inflation risk going forward as roughly balanced.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With less well anchored inflation expectations, there is greater risk that higher energy and import prices will pass through into core inflation and inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: By the same token, there is also a greater likelihood that inflation will decline should a recession occur.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We looked at the behavior of core and total inflation in the first three years following recessions from 1960 to the last one in 2001, and inflation declined in most of these episodes.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The exception is 2001, when core inflation remained essentially unchanged—which seems consistent with my view that inflation has become less responsive to the business cycle over the past decade or so as we have acquired more credibility.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: President Yellen, I think you answered this, but could you say a bit more about your monetary policy assumption in your forecast.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: How did you get to an additional 75?

speaker: YELLEN
text: We assumed 50 at this meeting.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We assumed an additional 25, which would be held in place through 2009:Q1, and then a gradual rise.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I mean the “why,” not the “what.” Sorry.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Why that much rather than—

speaker: YELLEN
text: I wouldn’t attach too much significance to the precise figure—it’s somewhat more.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Fifth District economy has shown additional signs of softness in recent weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: According to our surveys, manufacturing activity drifted lower in the past few months, although we also heard reports of stronger overseas demand for U.S. goods.

speaker: LACKER
text: Revenue growth in the District’s services firms also weakened in January, and our index for that sector dipped into negative territory for only the second time in the past four years.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our retail index, which in December had blipped up to neutral after three negative months, dived again in January.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our retail respondents say that the holiday sale season finished up weaker than expected and that big ticket categories continue to slump, especially furniture and appliances.

speaker: LACKER
text: Business spending seems to have softened as well in recent weeks, as an increasing number of firms reported that they were delaying capital spending projects such as IT upgrades.

speaker: LACKER
text: At our December meeting, I reported on a former director who headed a firm that owned a large portfolio of retail properties and said that he described the sector as in the best shape he had ever seen in his life.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, he is singing a different tune.

speaker: LACKER
text: Although his portfolio is in good shape so far, he is hearing a lot about cancelled projects as a result of financial constraints from lenders or equity interests, and he says that the environment that he is operating in is completely different from what it was when he talked to me sixty days ago.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are hearing very similar comments from a wide range of contacts in commercial real estate and community bankers.

speaker: LACKER
text: Residential real estate markets in the District remain generally weak.

speaker: LACKER
text: Home sales and construction remain dormant in many markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: Several Realtors reported seeing more prospective buyers, but they seem interested only in kicking the tires, in part because of difficulties in selling their current homes.

speaker: LACKER
text: Turning to prices, concerns about rising input costs were more widespread among our contacts in recent weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our survey measure of manufacturing raw material prices was up sharply in January at 4.3 percent, the second highest reading in the fourteen-year history of the survey.

speaker: LACKER
text: The prices-paid measure in manufacturing was a touch lower but still in an elevated range.

speaker: LACKER
text: Expected price trends in manufacturing were off sharply, however, perhaps reflecting the softening in demand that many respondents said they expected.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the service sector, both current and future price trends picked up outside of retail.

speaker: LACKER
text: Labor market conditions in the Fifth District have deteriorated in the last month.

speaker: LACKER
text: In a noticeable shift from previous surveys, numerous contacts told us they had begun to trim payrolls.

speaker: LACKER
text: The job cuts were concentrated in machinery and building material manufacturers, financial services firms, and general contractors.

speaker: LACKER
text: In some regions, however—Northern Virginia, for example—some labor markets remain tight, and we continue to hear of difficulty finding highly skilled workers.

speaker: LACKER
text: I spent a bit more time than usual on our regional picture because right now I am placing a bit more weight than usual on our District reports and what I read in the Beige Book.

speaker: LACKER
text: One can be skeptical about the incremental value of anecdotal reports in typical times, but at times like these, I believe they can and do provide a more timely read on what is going on.

speaker: LACKER
text: These regional reports have shaded my outlook to the downside relative to the picture painted by the national data, which is itself a somewhat discouraging picture.

speaker: LACKER
text: Home construction has continued to decline, and the fall in permits last month suggests that further declines are in store.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consumer spending appears to have slowed somewhat at the end of last year and seems to be carrying less momentum into this quarter, as the Greenbook likes to put it.

speaker: LACKER
text: The December employment report certainly was weak and has added considerably to fears of a recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Greenbook forecast just skirts the border of an outright recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: My own projection is fairly similar but a bit weaker in the first half and with the weakness stretching out a bit longer this year.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am inclined to see the bottom in housing as occurring later than in the Greenbook, which has housing starts flattening out relatively soon, and I am a bit less hopeful about business investment, particularly structures.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree with the Greenbook that the main effect of a stimulus package will be to shift consumption growth from ’09 to late ’08 but that the effects are uncertain.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the risks are on the side of a smaller boost to spending, though.

speaker: LACKER
text: But there is a chance that many rule-of- thumb consumers will find that their rule is telling them to pay down debt.

speaker: LACKER
text: In sum, I expect very weak growth in the first half of this year with only gradual recovery to trend.

speaker: LACKER
text: While I think weak growth is the most likely scenario, similar to President Yellen, I do think that a recession is a quite distinct possibility this year.

speaker: LACKER
text: If that happens, I think it will be due to a more sizable pullback in nonresidential construction than we are expecting right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: Turning to inflation, it is hard to put a good face on the recent numbers.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Greenbook describes the recent upside surprise as transitory and expects inflation to diminish this year.

speaker: LACKER
text: Indeed, we have been getting some relief on retail gasoline prices in recent weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I don’t think our problems with inflation are transitory, and I don’t want to lose sight of them in the midst of the current weakness.

speaker: LACKER
text: If you look back over the past four years, the overall PCE price index has averaged 2¾ percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: On a 12-month basis, the index has been below 2 percent only four months in that span.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, one could interpret this as a regime of 2 percent inflation with a series of misses that happen to be virtually all on the plus side.

speaker: LACKER
text: Alternatively, you could view this as a regime in which inflation fluctuates around a mean of 2¾ percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: Market measures of inflation expectations seem more consistent with the former right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: But the longer that inflation averages well above 2 percent, the more risk we run of seeing expectations rising to match actual inflation rather than the other way around.

speaker: LACKER
text: Another way to see this is that the fragility we need to focus on now is our credibility.

speaker: LACKER
text: I mention all of this because it is why, in my economic projections this round, I wrote down a relatively sluggish recovery after the first half of this year.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am skeptical that we have seen nothing but positive inflation misses around a 2 percent trend for four years because of chance alone, and I am not optimistic about inflation coming down in a sustained way on its own.

speaker: LACKER
text: As a result, I believe that, in order to keep expectations from drifting up and to bring inflation down, we will need to raise rates later this year, even if that means a longer and slower recovery.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You know, listening to the staff discussion I have certainly come to understand why everyone continues to believe that economics is a dismal science.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is quite a dismal picture.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But more seriously, recent economic data have certainly helped feed that view, and the Third District is no exception.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Economic activity has weakened in our District since December, and to double the fun, firms continue to face increasing price pressures—not a very comfortable position for monetary policymakers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Philadelphia staff’s state coincident indicators indicate that overall economic activity has been moderate in New Jersey, flat in Pennsylvania, and declining in Delaware over the past three months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our Business Outlook Survey of manufacturers fell sharply in January.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The index fell to minus 20.9 from minus 1.6 in December.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, some of that we have to remember is sentiment, in the sense that the question has to do with general activity and doesn’t necessarily reflect just their firm.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But it is a sentiment of pessimism that certainly is more prevalent than it once was.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A reading that low, of minus 20, indicates declining manufacturing activity in the region and is usually associated with very low GDP growth or perhaps even negative GDP growth at the national level.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: More related to the firms’ own performance, though, the survey’s indexes of new orders and shipments also declined in January, and both are now in negative territory, although much less so than the general activity index.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the other hand, while expectations of activity six months from now have moved down somewhat this month, they remain firmly in positive territory, and firms’ capital spending plans over the next six months remain relatively strong.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: District bankers are reporting weaker consumer loan demand, but business lending continues to advance at a moderate pace from their perspective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Loan quality has shown slight deterioration, mainly in residential real estate and auto loans, to a lesser extent in credit cards, and to an even lesser extent on the business loan side.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This downtick in quality follows a period of extraordinarily low delinquencies and default rates and thus is well within historical norms, so it has not greatly alarmed our banking community.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus far, our District banks apparently have largely escaped the credit problems plaguing the larger money center banks and investment banks.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While there has been some tightening in credit conditions and standards around the District, most non-real-estate-related firms I spoke with are not finding it difficult to obtain credit for any reasonable project they want to do, and so they have not identified largely with the credit crunch scenario.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite the softness in the activity, firms in our District report higher prices in their inputs and outputs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As President Lacker said, inflation seems to be alive and well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The current prices-paid and prices-received indexes in our Business Outlook Survey accelerated sharply in January and are at very high levels, almost record levels, of the past twenty years.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Firms also expect prices to rise over the next six months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: These forward-looking price indexes, too, are at very elevated levels relative to their twenty-year history.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am hearing from business contacts and from one of my directors, for example, that they are planning to implement price increases to pass along costs they are experiencing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, even though they are pessimistic about growth in the future, they are not pessimistic about price increases.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This adds to my skepticism about arguments that link inflation too closely with resource utilization.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The national near-term economic outlook is also deteriorating, as we have been hearing, and I have revised down my growth forecast for 2008 compared with my October submission.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is hard to find much positive news in the data released since our last meeting, and the Board staff has summarized that quite eloquently, and so I won’t repeat them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nevertheless, in general, my forecast is probably slightly less pessimistic than the Board’s forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, I must add that, at the same time that growth has slowed, inflation has trended up.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Both the core CPI and the core PCE accelerated in the second half of ’07, compared with the first half.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The core CPI advanced at a 2.6 percent rate in the second half of ’07, compared with a 2.3 percent rate in the first half, and the core PCE was up at a 2.4 percent rate in the second half compared with 1.9 in the first half.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As we know, the PCE price index gets revised.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Recent research by Dean Croushore, one of our visiting scholars, has shown that between 1995 and 2005 the average revision from initial release until the August release the following year was positive on average for both the core PCE and the total PCE.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This suggests that inflation is likely to be even higher in the second half of ’07 than the current estimates indicate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am also concerned that, over the past 10 year period, core and headline inflation for both the PCE and the CPI have diverged on average about 50 basis points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Headline rates have exceeded core rates in 8 of the last 10 years for the CPI and 9 out of the last 10 years for the PCE.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While I would like to believe that these two rates should be converging on average, I am concerned that core rates may not be as indicative of underlying trend inflation as we might have thought.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This line of thinking also leads me to question estimates of ex post real funds rates calculated by the staff and presented in the Bluebook, which are based on subtracting core PCE from the nominal funds rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am not convinced that the core PCE is the right measure of inflation in this context.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Even if you thought it was, then the reported real rates are likely to be overstated for recent quarters given the apparent systematic bias in the preliminary estimates of the PCE that I have noted before.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, some measures of inflation expectations are not encouraging: In particular, the Michigan survey one-year-ahead measures and five-year-ahead measures are up.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have already discussed a bit the acceleration in some of the TIPS measures.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I will return to that in a minute.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Livingston survey participants have also raised their forecast for CPI inflation in 2008 from 2.3 percent to 3 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My forecast overall is similar to the Greenbook’s, and I expect a weak first half and a return toward trend growth later this year and into ’09 and inflation at the 1.7 to 2 percent range.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But the policy assumptions that I make to achieve the forecasted outcomes for the intermediate term are different from the Greenbook’s.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The ongoing housing correction and poor credit market conditions are a significant drag in the near term on the economy, and I expect growth in the first half of the year to be quite weak, probably around 1 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As conditions in the housing and financial markets begin to stabilize, I expect economic growth to improve in the second half of the year and move back toward trend, which I estimate to be about 2¾ percent, about 50 basis points higher than the Greenbook, I think, in 2009.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The slowdown in real activity suggests a lower equilibrium real rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How much lower is difficult to measure with any precision.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Ten-year TIPS have fallen about 100 basis points since the beginning of September.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In such an environment, optimal policy calls for the FOMC to allow the funds rate to fall as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And we have; the funds rate is down 175 basis points since September—or more if we cut today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But we also must remain committed to delivering on our goal of price stability in this environment of rising prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To my mind, that means we must continue to communicate that commitment to the markets and to act in a manner that is consistent with that commitment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I want to stress that while many of us, myself included, have argued that inflation expectations remain well anchored, we cannot wait to act until we see contrary evidence to such a claim because by then it will be too late and we will have already lost some credibility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also might add that the staff memo on inflation compensation, which I thought was very good, suggests that one reason for the increase in forward inflation compensation might be a greater inflation risk premium rather than a rise in expected inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That may, in fact, be true, and I think the memo was very well done.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But if that is the case, if the rise is in the inflation risk premium, then I think it might be worth asking ourselves if the increase in inflation uncertainty might be an early warning sign of our waning credibility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This perspective leads me to a different policy assumption from the Greenbook’s.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In particular, once the real economy is stabilized, the FOMC must act aggressively to take back the significant easing it has put in place in order to ensure that inflation is stabilized in 2010.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Employment is a lagging indicator, so we will likely have to act before employment growth returns to trend, should output growth pick up in the second half of the year as forecasted.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, I expect we will need to begin raising rates by the fourth quarter of this year and perhaps aggressively so.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In contrast, the Greenbook assumes a flat funds rate at 3 percent throughout the forecast period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite the real funds rate remaining below 1 percent—and well after the economy has returned to trend growth—inflation expectations remain anchored in the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my view, this seems somewhat implausible or, at best, a very risky bet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It appears that the Greenbook achieves this result through an output gap—related to the question I was asking earlier this afternoon.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think all of us understand the very real concerns that many researchers have with our ability to accurately estimate the level of potential GDP.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Furthermore, in the recent research on inflation dynamics that we have discussed—and President Yellen was referring to this—inflation becomes less persistent and appears to be less related to other macroeconomic variables as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
