text: We do not know whether these changes are an outcome of a more aggressive and credible stance of monetary policy against inflation or are due to some fundamental changes in the world economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If the lower persistence is due to enhanced policy credibility, then it is incumbent upon this Committee to maintain that credibility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Otherwise, we cannot expect inflation persistence to remain low.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, if the economy performs as forecasted on the growth side, with a return toward trend growth in the second half, I would be very uncomfortable leaving a real funds rate below 1 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Bluebook scenarios involving risk management indicate that the inflation outcome is poor when there is a gradual reversal of policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Better outcomes are achieved under a prompt reversal strategy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given that forecast, I believe we must begin thinking now about what our exit strategy from this insurance we have put in place is going to be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How we communicate our monetary policy strategy will also be crucially important because of the effects such communications will have on expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We need to better understand in our own minds, I think, what our reaction function looks like so that we can be more systematic and articulate in our implementation of policy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my view, the decision we took on January 21 reflected a broad consensus that economic fundamentals were weakening at a rapid pace in an environment of continuing, even heightened, concern about financial market stress and fragility.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My contacts over this last week in the business and financial markets may add a little texture to the picture on which we based our January 21 policy action.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Conversations with these contacts in various industries provide information generally consistent with a downward revision of the outlook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Forward-looking sentiment of the directors of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta turned decidedly pessimistic in January.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Retail contacts noted quite disappointing results through mid-January and are taking a conservative approach to 2008 in terms of hiring and inventory.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding the residential construction industry, regional weakness continues and is spreading from coastal markets to interior markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In addition, I had a conversation with the CEO of a large public homebuilder of national scope.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: He cited historically high contract cancellation rates, especially on the West Coast and the D.C. area, because of the buyers’ difficulty selling existing homes and getting financing.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This limits their market to first-time buyers.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: His judgment is that a change in market atmosphere will require inventories falling to around six months.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: He pointed out that the spring is traditionally the key season for sales, so the next several months will be particularly telling.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Weakness in the region’s commercial real estate market appears to be spreading.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The retail segment is continuing to experience declining leasing activity, and weakness is now emerging in the warehouse and office markets as well.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In partial contrast, reports from the manufacturing sector are more mixed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Activity remains very weak in housing-related industries.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One CEO, reflecting the concern of others, predicted business failures in lumberyards and construction supply firms because of excess capacity and the slow response to a lower building environment.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The trucking sector continues to slump.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, industries related to oil and gas production; import-substituting industries, such as steel, aerospace, and defense; and the foreign brand auto sector are all performing quite well.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Atlanta’s national forecast is largely consistent with the Greenbook in direction, and our differences with the Greenbook in magnitude and timing are not material.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Like the Greenbook, we premise our forecast on a lower funds rate at the level of 3 percent.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So the principal risk to the forecast in my view is the fragility of the financial markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Uncertainty and fear continue to loom large.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I made a number of calls to financial market players, and my counterparts cited a variety of concerns relevant to overall financial stability.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: For instance, one of the recent concerns, as Bill Dudley depicted, has been the situation of the monoline credit insurers.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Several of my contacts had comments, but I spoke to the newly appointed interim CEO of one of the two monoline insurance firms most prominent in the news, and he characterized the firm’s solvency and liquidity fundamentals as in question only toward the far end of current independent forecasts of subprime losses.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Perhaps predictably, he contrasted his assessment with what he views as alarmist atmospherics resulting from press coverage, quixotic rating agency actions, and state regulator political positioning.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A regional bank’s CFO cautioned that more data on actual mortgage performance in 2007 will soon be available, and that could force restatements in 2007 bank earnings.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Commenting on market illiquidity, one source said that in some fixed-income markets, where many on the buy side currently depend on moderate leverage to achieve the required rates of return, banks have greatly reduced their lending.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: He also indicated that, even though there are real money investors—as he called them—interested in return to the structured-finance securities markets but currently on the sidelines, they are reluctant to expose themselves to volatility that arises under mark-to-market accounting using prices set in such illiquid markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: These anecdotal inputs simply point to the continuing uncertainty and risk to financial stability with some potential, I think, for self-feeding hysteria.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I share with my colleagues on the Committee worries about the heightened levels of inflation and uncertainties around my working forecast that inflation will moderate in 2008.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The assumptions about energy prices are the most precarious.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Nevertheless, I am prepared to take the position that the economy, with its apparently rapid deceleration compounded by continuing financial volatility, is a greater concern than inflation at this juncture.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Let me talk a bit about the region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The Tenth District is generally moving forward at a fairly steady pace, but there are some mixed data.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The obvious wide variances are in real estate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Housing is weak—not as weak as some parts of the country but still weak.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Also, it is interesting that commercial real estate in each of our major cities right now continues to do well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I recently talked with several developers.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They are all doing well but are very concerned, and they are beginning to cut back on their plans and move away from them.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So you can see the worry carrying forward in terms of what actions they are taking.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In the agricultural area and in the energy area, real estate is a different story.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Land values have gone up in the ag part—non-irrigated land, something like 20 percent over the past year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If you are near an ethanol plant, it has gone up 25 to 30 percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It is also interesting that the ag credit system is helping to fund that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Their increase in lending was about 12 percent this past year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is up from about 9 percent the year before, so they are providing that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They are also now involved in lending to these ethanol plants in a very significant way, helping to carry that boom forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That gives me some pause in terms of what is going on in some of the rural areas.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Related to that, the energy and lease values are also accelerating at a fairly high rate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I found it reminiscent and somewhat disturbing in talking to a couple of individuals when they noted that the land values have about doubled over the past two or three years in some areas, and they said that I should relax because on current ag prices they should have tripled.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Where have I seen that before?

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the other side, actually, manufacturing in our region has held steady.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have a lot of aircraft manufacturing, which is really strong, and some other smaller manufacturers providing support in both ag and energy, and they seem to be doing well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Technology is also doing well in the region, especially in the mountain areas—the Colorado and Denver areas.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Engineering firms are still very strong—the strong demand for engineers and the unfilled positions continue.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They are supplying that service across the globe and see continued demand there.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So it is mixed, but overall probably our region is doing better than average relative to the rest of the nation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the national level, my projections suggest that we are going to grow below our potential growth rate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am not as pessimistic as the Greenbook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I also have inflation coming down, but that is on the assumption that we are able to reverse our monetary policy at a fairly quick pace as we move through this year and into 2009.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I will leave it there.

speaker: STERN
text: Let me talk about the economic outlook.

speaker: STERN
text: My initial comments are organized kind of along the lines of Dave Reifschneider’s exhibit 1.

speaker: STERN
text: There are certainly still some positive things going on: growth in exports, and I think that is likely to continue; strength in the agricultural sector and in natural resources in general, outside of lumber and wood products; state and local construction spending—there seem to be a lot of schools, hospitals, sports stadiums, et cetera, being built now; and the labor market may be a bit better than the December household and payroll surveys depicted, given the low level of initial claims.

speaker: STERN
text: But I think those considerations are really overwhelmed by several factors on the negative side, and let me summarize those quickly.

speaker: STERN
text: First is the breadth of the negative news on the national economy that we have received recently.

speaker: STERN
text: The vast bulk of the news has been negative.

speaker: STERN
text: It doesn’t suggest to me that there is a lot of positive momentum or latent strength left in the economy.

speaker: STERN
text: The second factor I would cite—and this is not new—is the persistence of a large volume of unsold, unoccupied houses, with implications for activity in that sector, for prices, for wealth, and for foreclosures.

speaker: STERN
text: Of course, as somebody already noted, many recessions turn out to be inventory recessions.

speaker: STERN
text: If we have one, this will be an inventory recession, too; and the inventory in question is housing.

speaker: STERN
text: Third, maybe even more important, are the financial conditions themselves—prominently but not exclusively, the impaired capital positions of large banks and likely prospects for growing credit quality problems in auto loans, in credit cards, in commercial real estate, and perhaps in other areas as well.

speaker: STERN
text: Adding up those considerations, I think what we confront resembles the aftermath of the 1990-91 recession, when so-called headwinds restrained growth in real GDP, and my forecast anticipates something similar going forward, something like the persistent weakness scenario in the latest Greenbook.

speaker: STERN
text: So I expect subpar growth both this year and next year before better growth resumes in 2010.

speaker: STERN
text: I further expect lots of inertia in both core and overall measures of inflation this year and next before some diminution below 2 percent in 2010.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, Mr. Chairman, I want to say a good word about President Poole.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have sat next to him since I got here.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would give him hyperbolic praise if he hadn’t handed me the IT Oversight Committee; otherwise, I think he is a wonderful human being.

speaker: FISHER
text: Much of what I was going to say has been said.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think President Plosser, President Lacker, and others have summarized what I would have said about my own District.

speaker: FISHER
text: We continue to grow, but at a decelerated pace, and our current forecast is for employment growth of 2 percent for our District for 2008.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is relatively healthy, and I really am not going to take more time on that subject.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am delighted to hear all this anecdotal evidence.

speaker: FISHER
text: We were talking, Governor Mishkin and I, about Woody Allen earlier.

speaker: FISHER
text: If I remember correctly, he had a wonderful quip—that he cheated on his metaphysics exam by looking into another boy’s soul.

speaker: FISHER
text: Basically, what we are doing at this time of transition is almost cheating on the data by looking at the anecdotal evidence.

speaker: FISHER
text: My broader CEO soundings indicate pretty much the same as what we are seeing in our District and what others have mentioned—shipping, rail, express delivery, manufacturing, and other activities are much slower.

speaker: FISHER
text: As President Poole and others pointed out, truckers are suffering.

speaker: FISHER
text: Receivables are being stretched out.

speaker: FISHER
text: I could bore you with specifics company by company, as I am tempted to do, but I will not unless you wish me to.

speaker: FISHER
text: The point is that, while there are tales of woe, none of the 30 CEOs to whom I talked, outside of housing, see the economy trending into negative territory.

speaker: FISHER
text: Some of them see much slower growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: None of them at this juncture—the cover of Newsweek notwithstanding, a great contra-indicator, which by the way shows “the road to recession” on the issue that is about to come out—see us going into recession.

speaker: FISHER
text: I will just give you two indicators there.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you look at MasterCard and dig into their data, their December retail sales ex-auto, ex-gas, were up 5 percent and in January to date were up 4 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: President Poole mentioned UPS, and President Lockhart has the incoming CEO of UPS on his board.

speaker: FISHER
text: Year over year to January, they are up 2 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: The expectation is not to be negative.

speaker: FISHER
text: My CEO soundings indicate pretty much what we have forecast as a group—much slower growth, not necessarily a recession.

speaker: FISHER
text: Where the difference comes, Mr. Chairman, is on the inflation front.

speaker: FISHER
text: Others have spoken eloquently about inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just want to make a couple of comments here.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is uncanny in the charts that we show in exhibit 5, for example, that we have food PCE prices and energy PCE prices peaking almost as we speak.

speaker: FISHER
text: That may be true in the spot markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is not the way it works in reality.

speaker: FISHER
text: Southwest Airlines has I don’t know how many airplanes.

speaker: FISHER
text: They contract and hedge out forward their energy costs, and the kick-in of any turndown does not occur immediately but rather is stretched out over a time period.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would ask our staff, as we go forward, to try to get a better feeling for that.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are certainly struggling with that in Dallas.

speaker: FISHER
text: As far as food prices are concerned, which again I remind you are twice the weight of energy prices in the headline PCE and the CPI, I heard some very disturbing news.

speaker: FISHER
text: Frito-Lay, for example, which when we last met I reported was going to increase prices 3 percent, has inched them up another 3 percent, to 6 percent, and that is their planning for the year.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is the first time in memory, according to my contacts, that grocery prices are rising faster than restaurant food.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet it is not simply food where we are seeing this kind of pressure, and I want to come back to the lag effect that occurs.

speaker: FISHER
text: This morning the CEO of Burlington Northern told me that the so-called rail adjustment factor, which captures fuel, labor, supply, and other costs from the previous quarter and is contractually input into contracts for the coming quarter, rose at the highest rate in history—11 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: That means that even if you are shipping lumber, even if you are shipping whatever goes into housing, by contract—of course, that can be negotiated, I am sure—for the coming quarter the price rise from the shippers, the railers, will be 11 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: Finally, going back to food and other items bought by consumers—when you drill down deep into Wal-Mart, which has 127 million customers, and you talk about the specifics of their sales, their expansion is not coming from unit sales, it is coming from price inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: A senior official there tells me that they are budgeting a 2 to 3 percent increase for nonfood items for ’08, 6 to 7 percent for food items.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is the first time in his fifteen-year history at the company that they are going to use their price leadership strategy on the plus side of the inflation ledger.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I do worry about inflation expectations, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: FISHER
text: I will summarize with the statement that was in today’s New York Times by the CEO of Tyson Foods, who said, “Because of the unanticipated high corn and soybean meal costs, we have no choice but to raise prices substantially.” That is my major concern besides the additional weakness we are seeing in the economy.

speaker: EVANS
text: My assessment of the national economy is that we are in the midst of a period of very weak growth and that there is a significant chance of a serious downturn.

speaker: EVANS
text: The three-month average of our Chicago Fed National Activity Index in December was minus 0.67.

speaker: EVANS
text: Historically, by my calculation, such a value has been associated with a recession about 70 percent of the time.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, in the Board briefings yesterday and again today, I noticed that Thomas Laubach’s estimate is 45 percent based on the same data, and that is certainly large enough for concern.

speaker: EVANS
text: Reports from my business contacts seem broadly consistent with this slow but positive growth scenario.

speaker: EVANS
text: The most positive news I received was from firms whose international businesses were strong.

speaker: EVANS
text: As one would expect, the most dire reports were from those in residential construction and related industries.

speaker: EVANS
text: While I was surprised to hear from the CEO of a national specialty retail chain that its business over the past 60 days was the worst he has seen in 45 years, much of his business is in housewares and furniture; but he indicated that many other segments of the retail sector were also struggling.

speaker: EVANS
text: I also spoke with the CEO of General Motors.

speaker: EVANS
text: His outlook was a lot like what President Fisher was just mentioning from other CEOs.

speaker: EVANS
text: They are looking for slow economic growth overall, and they are concerned about the risk of a serious downturn.

speaker: EVANS
text: That is not what they are planning on.

speaker: EVANS
text: The industry is clearly facing softer demand, but his expectation for 2008 as a whole is for only a moderate decline in light motor vehicle sales, down to a pace of about 15¾ million units.

speaker: EVANS
text: GM’s current production plans are not premised on recession-level sales, but they are prepared to cut production quickly if they see the economy turning down.

speaker: EVANS
text: He also reported that, while the performance of GMAC’s auto loans currently was okay, the credit quality of prospective buyers—people coming into showrooms— has declined and that lenders have tightened underwriting standards for those loans.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, if auto loans became more difficult to securitize, it would be a big additional problem.

speaker: EVANS
text: Apparently, so far they are robust, though.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning to the forecast details, my modal outlook for 2008 is close to that in the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: I expect that we will eke out positive growth in the first half of 2008.

speaker: EVANS
text: This expectation largely reflects the judgment that businesses have not begun to ratchet down spending plans in the nonlinear fashion that characterizes a recession.

speaker: EVANS
text: My assessment also has been influenced by some positive developments that we have seen.

speaker: EVANS
text: The most notable ones in my mind are that UI claims have moved down, that major banks are having some success raising capital from a variety of sources, and that the orders data today were better.

speaker: EVANS
text: For the second half of 2008, I see growth increasing toward potential by year-end.

speaker: EVANS
text: This assessment depends importantly on accommodative monetary policy and expansionary fiscal policy.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our cumulative actions following this meeting should provide noticeable stimulus to the economy by midyear.

speaker: EVANS
text: Tax rebates should also help somewhat this year.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, the financial system should continue to sort through its difficulties, making further headway in price discovery and repairing capital positions.

speaker: EVANS
text: So in the absence of further negative developments, growth should improve in the second half of this year.

speaker: EVANS
text: I then see real GDP rising at a pace a bit above potential in 2009.

speaker: EVANS
text: Although this seems like a plausible projection, it has the feel of threading the needle, which brings to mind nimbleness, and Governor Kohn is our expert at nimbleness, so I start thinking about how his nimble fingers will be critical for threading this needle.

speaker: EVANS
text: The downside risks are large, and the recession scenarios are quite possible.

speaker: EVANS
text: Any of the factors currently holding back growth could intensify.

speaker: EVANS
text: For example, a reduction in bank lending capacity could make financial conditions much more restrictive.

speaker: EVANS
text: This, along with increased business pessimism and caution, could cause a more pronounced cutback in investment and hiring.

speaker: EVANS
text: Even a moderately weaker job market would add to the factors already weighing on consumer spending.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, unfortunately, even while we are dealing with concerns on the growth front, the inflation picture is difficult and quite uncertain.

speaker: EVANS
text: The inflation outlook will likely be affected by more crosscurrents than usual.

speaker: EVANS
text: Headline inflation has been quite high, driven largely by increasingly high energy, food, and commodity prices.

speaker: EVANS
text: Although our best assessment is that these pressures will come off later this year, these influences have lasted longer than typical and could well continue to do so.

speaker: EVANS
text: I had calculated the same type of statistics that President Plosser calculated, but only since 1999.

speaker: EVANS
text: Headline PCE inflation has been running about 0.4 percentage point higher than core PCE since that time.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is a source of some concern and cautions us against relying too heavily on core inflation measures.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t think that is a big issue today, but we need to be thinking about that in our inflation strategy.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, core inflation has not improved as much as I expected.

speaker: EVANS
text: As the Greenbook discusses, the decline during the second quarter of last year may have reflected technical quirks in the indexes rather than true improvements in underlying inflation as I had hoped.

speaker: EVANS
text: The weakening U.S. economy is likely to diminish inflation pressures somewhat in 2008, but it is unclear how big a factor this will be or, given our projection that growth improves, how long it will last.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I think that inflation risk will be rising next year.

speaker: EVANS
text: Consequently, recalibration of short-term interest rates will be an important element of monetary policy in 2009.

speaker: EVANS
text: Looking at the write-up, it seemed to me as though 10 out of 17 participants had that viewpoint—different timing.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our inflation projection has core PCE running 2.1 percent in 2008 and edging off to 2 percent by 2010.

speaker: EVANS
text: In the context of what Brian was talking about in terms of slack, we have a higher inflation path and inflation coming down with a bit of slack.

speaker: EVANS
text: Much of the Committee’s discussion today has suggested that 2 percent is slightly higher than most participants’ benchmarks.

speaker: EVANS
text: For me, the trajectory of my outlook is satisfactory as long as I see inflation prospects continuing to improve as we move beyond the end of our current forecast period.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In my view, economic conditions have deteriorated significantly since our December meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Taken as a whole, the stories that have been relayed to me by my Fourth District business contacts have been downbeat, and several of the contacts are concerned that we may be slipping into a recession.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I’m hearing that consumer spending has declined appreciably since the soft December retail sales numbers were reported.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The CFO of one of the nation’s major department store chains told me last week that her company’s January sales are shaping up to be the worst that they have seen in the past twenty years.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: She said that they had already cut back some of their buying plans because of the weak holiday sales, but after seeing the numbers for the first three weeks of January, she is concerned that they have not cut back buying plans enough.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In December I had heard some upbeat assessments about the demand for capital goods and exports, but in January the incoming numbers are softer, and expectations for the coming year are less optimistic than they were just a month ago.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I’m also concerned that I’m now detecting the first signals of a credit crunch.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Bankers in my District tell me that they’re finding it much more difficult to issue debt and that they are safeguarding their capital.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I’ve heard several motivations for this, depending on the institution.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Some bankers are simply preparing for further losses.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Some are expecting to have to bring some downgraded assets back onto their balance sheets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Even those bankers who have adequate capital say that they have become much more disciplined about how they’re going to allocate that capital.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Collectively, the concerns that bankers have expressed to me about capital have convinced me that credit will be less available and more expensive than it has been in quite a while.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Deals that bankers would have done for creditworthy borrowers not long ago are simply not being done today.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Of course, it’s possible that nonbank financial companies will step in and fill the gap, but it is not clear to me that they have the capital and the risk appetites to do so.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: These developments have had a significant influence on the economic projection that I submitted for today’s meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like many around the table, I continue to mark down my outlook for residential and nonresidential investment in response to the incoming data and also in response to greater business pessimism about the economic prospects.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In addition, I’ve built in a sharper and more protracted slowing in consumer spending stemming from greater deterioration in the household balance sheet and tighter credit market conditions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: These adjustments have caused me to cut my 2008 GDP growth projection about 1 percentage point since the December meeting, and some of that weakness spills over to the out years.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: If credit conditions deteriorate further than I have expected, then my projection would more closely resemble the persistent weakness alternative scenario described in the Greenbook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But that isn’t my projection for the economy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Rather, my projection is roughly in line with the Greenbook baseline.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My inflation outlook hasn’t changed much from where it was in December—or October, for that matter.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like the Greenbook, I still project inflation to moderate as commodity prices level off and business activity wanes, but the risks to my inflation outlook have shifted to being weighted to the upside.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The December CPI report was not much improved from the troubling November data, and my business contacts continue to report that commodity prices are being passed downstream.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I have less conviction in the inflation moderation than I did a month ago.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: That said, the downside risks to the economy still dominate my thinking about the outlook today.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do believe, however, that our policy response to date combined with an additional rate cut tomorrow will allow the economy to regain some momentum as we move into the second half of 2008.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The contours of our forecast are broadly in line with the Greenbook: Growth well below potential for the first half of this year results in additional slack in labor markets with a consequent reduction in the core rate of inflation over time.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Our forecast returns to full employment by 2010 only if we reduce interest rates more than they are in the Greenbook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Thus, our baseline forecast assumes that we reduce rates 50 basis points at this meeting followed by additional easing in 2008, which eventually results in core inflation below 2 percent and the unemployment rate settling at our estimate of the NAIRU, somewhat below 5 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But even with this easing, there are significant downside risks to this forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Historically, increases in unemployment in excess of 0.6 percent and forecasts of two or more quarters of real GDP growth below 2 percent have almost always been followed by a recession.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In fact, a variety of probit models looking at the probability of recession in 2008 indicate an uncomfortably high probability of recession, in most cases above 50 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Several factors make me concerned that the outlook could be worse than our baseline forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, we have consistently underestimated weakness in residential investment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While our forecast assumes a gradual decline in real estate prices, it does not have a substantial feedback between rising unemployment rates causing further downward pressure on real estate prices and the health of financial institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Were we to reach a tipping point of higher unemployment, higher home foreclosures, increased financial duress, and falling housing prices, we would likely have to ease far more than if we were to act preemptively to insure against this risk.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, our weak consumption is driven by negative wealth effects induced by weakness in equity markets and modest declines in real estate prices.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, the heightened discussion of a potential recession could easily result in a larger pullback by consumers.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This would be consistent with the behavior of rates on credit default swaps of major retailers, which have risen significantly since the middle of December.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Third, banks are seeing increasing problems with credit card debt.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Capital One, one of the few concentrated credit card lenders, has had their credit default swap rate rise from less than 100 basis points to more than 400 basis points as investors have become increasingly concerned about the retail sector.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While liquidity concerns have abated, credit risk for financial institutions has grown.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Rates on credit default swaps for our largest banks have been rising since December, despite the announcement of additional equity investments.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In addition, the greatest concern I hear raised by the financial community in Boston is a risk posed by the monoline guarantors.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The movement in equity prices last week as a result of highly speculative statements on resolving the monoline problem indicates a sensitivity of the markets to significant further deterioration in the financial position of the monolines.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Fourth, our model does not capture potential credit crunch problems, although supplementary empirical analysis conducted by the Boston staff suggests that such problems pose additional downside risks to our outlook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Bank balance sheets continue to expand as banks act in their traditional role of providing liquidity during economic slowdowns.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While the balance sheet constraints are likely to be most acute at our largest institutions, further deterioration in real estate markets is likely to crimp smaller and midsize banks that have significant real estate exposures.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given my concerns that we could soon be or may already be in a recession, I believe the risks around our forecast of core inflation settling below 2 percent are well balanced.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Inflation rates have fallen in previous recessions, and I expect that historical regularity to be maintained if growth is as slow as I expect.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Let me just start by saying it’s not all dark.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I’m going to end dark, but it’s not all dark.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The world still seems likely to be a source of strength.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You know, we have the implausible kind of Goldilocks view of the world, which is it’s going to be a little slower, taking some of the edge off inflation risk, without being so slow that it’s going to amplify downside risks to growth in the United States.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That may be too optimistic, but the world still is looking pretty good.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Central banks in a lot of places are starting to soften their link to the dollar so that they can get more freedom to direct monetary policy to respond to inflation pressure.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: U.S. external imbalances are adjusting at a pace well ahead of expectations.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That’s all good, I think.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As many people pointed out, the fact that we don’t have a lot of imbalances outside of housing coming into this slowdown is helpful.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There’s a little sign of incipient optimism on the productivity outlook or maybe a little less pessimism that we’re in a much slower structural productivity growth outlook than before.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The market is building an expectation for housing prices that is very, very steep.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That could be a source of darkness or strength, but some people are starting to call the bottom ahead, and that’s the first time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It has been a long time since we’ve seen any sense that maybe the turn is ahead.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It seems unlikely, but maybe they’re right.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In the financial markets, I think it is true that there is some sign that the process of repair is starting.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have seen very, very substantial adjustment by the major financial institutions; very, very substantial de-leveraging ahead as the institutions adjust to this much, much greater increase in macroeconomic uncertainty and downside risk; very, very substantial early equity raising by major firms; pretty substantial improvement in market functioning; and easing of liquidity pressure.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Those are useful, encouraging things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is a huge amount of uncertainty about the size and the location of remaining credit losses across the system.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But based on what we know, I think it’s still true that the capital positions of the major U.S. institutions coming into this look pretty good relative to how they did in the early 1990s.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course, as many people have said many times, there’s a fair amount of money in the world willing and able to come in when investors see prices at sufficiently distressed levels.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One more encouraging sign, of course, is that the timing, content, and design of the stimulus package look as though the package will be a modest positive.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It could have been a worse balance of lateness and poor design, but I think it looks to be above expectations on both timing and design, and it will help a little on the downside and take out some of the downside risk.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Having said that, though, I think it is quite dark still out there.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Like everyone else, we have revised down our growth forecast.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We expect very little growth, if any, in the first half of the year before policy starts to bring growth back up to potential.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The main risk, as has been true since August, is the dangerous self-reinforcing cycle, in which tighter financial conditions hurt confidence and raise recession probability, causing people to behave on the expectation that recession probably is higher, reinforcing the financial headwinds, et cetera.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The dominant challenge to policy is still to arrest that dynamic and reduce the probability of the very adverse outcome on the growth side.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course, we have to do that without risking too much damage to our inflation credibility and too much damage to future incentives and future resource allocation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Like many of you, I think the inflation outlook for the reasons laid out in the Greenbook is better than it was.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s not terrific, but it’s better.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The risks are probably balanced around the inflation outlook.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our inflation forecast still has core PCE coming down below 2 percent over the forecast period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There’s obviously a lot of uncertainty around that, but I really think that you can look at inflation expectations in the markets as somewhat reassuring on the credibility front to date.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So again, I think the key question for policy is how low we should get real short-term rates relative to equilibrium, and our best judgment is that we’re going to have to get them lower even with another 50 basis points tomorrow.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We’re still going to need to try to reinforce the signal that we’re going to provide an adequate degree of accommodation or insurance against this very dangerous risk of a self-reinforcing cycle in which financial weakness headwinds reinforce the risk of a much deeper and prolonged decline in economic activity.

speaker: KOHN
text: Thank you, Vice Chairman Geithner, for a little less gloom here.

speaker: KOHN
text: I didn’t expect the bright side from that source.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like everyone else around the table, I have revised down my forecast, which looks very much like the Greenbook: a couple of quarters of very slow growth before a pickup in the second half of the year spurred by monetary and fiscal stimulus.

speaker: KOHN
text: The collapse of the housing market has been at the center of the slowdown, and most recent information was weaker than expected.

speaker: KOHN
text: There is no sign in the data anyhow that a bottoming out is in sight.

speaker: KOHN
text: Sales of new homes have dropped substantially, and that must reflect reduced availability of credit, especially for nonprime and prime nonconforming loans, and perhaps buyers’ expectations of further price declines.

speaker: KOHN
text: As a consequence, a steep drop in housing construction has made only a small dent in inventories, and those will continue to weigh on activity and prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: Indeed, house-price declines in the Case-Shiller index picked up late last year.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we just got November.

speaker: KOHN
text: It looks increasingly as though other sectors are being affected as well, slowing from the earlier pace of expansion and slowing a little more than expected.

speaker: KOHN
text: You can see this in broad measures of activity, as President Stern pointed out: industrial production, purchasing manager surveys, and the employment report.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it is also evident in some measures of demand.

speaker: KOHN
text: Retail sales data suggest a deceleration in consumer spending late in the fourth quarter.

speaker: KOHN
text: Orders and shipments for capital equipment excluding aircraft picked up in December, but that followed a couple of months of flat or declining data.

speaker: KOHN
text: A slowdown in consumption and nonhousing investment probably reflects multiplier-accelerator effects of the drop in housing, a decline in housing wealth, and additional caution by both businesses and households given the highly uncertain and possibly weakening economic outlook.

speaker: KOHN
text: Certainly the anecdotes we’ve heard around the table reinforce the sense of business caution.

speaker: KOHN
text: But like other people, I see the softening outlook and the spread beyond the housing sector as importantly a function of what’s going on in the financial sector and of the potential interaction of that over time with spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have seen improvements in short-term funding markets, in spreads, and in the leveling out of the ABCP (asset-backed commercial paper) outstandings, but investors and lenders seem increasingly concerned about the broader economic weakness and spreading repayment problems, and they are demanding much greater compensation for taking risk in nearly every sector.

speaker: KOHN
text: To me one of the defining characteristics of the period since, say, mid- November is the spreading out from the housing sector of lending caution to other sectors in the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: Nonfinancial corporations have experienced declines in equity prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: Credit spreads on both investment-grade and junk bonds have increased.

speaker: KOHN
text: A substantial portion of banks reported tightening terms and standards for C&I loans.

speaker: KOHN
text: Commercial real estate sector lenders are very concerned about credit.

speaker: KOHN
text: Spreads on CMBS have risen substantially, and most banks—like 80 percent—tightened up on commercial real estate credit, and that has to affect spending in that sector over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: Banks tell us that they are being more cautious about extending consumer credit, as President Yellen noted.

speaker: KOHN
text: A number of large banks noted a pullback in this area and deterioration in actual and expected loan performance when they announced their earnings over the past few weeks.

speaker: KOHN
text: There have also been increasing doubts about how robust foreign economies will remain, and this was evident in equity markets around the globe and in rising risk spreads on emerging- market debt.

speaker: KOHN
text: The staff has marked down its forecast of foreign GDP growth again this round.

speaker: KOHN
text: The total decrease in projected foreign growth in 2008 since last August has been around ½ percentage point, and this is at a time when we are counting on exports to support economic activity.

speaker: KOHN
text: The extraordinary volatility in markets is, I think, indicative of underlying uncertainty, and that underlying uncertainty itself will discourage risk-taking.

speaker: KOHN
text: The uncertainty and the caution are partly feeding off the continued decline in housing, the still-unknown extent of the losses that will need to be absorbed, and the extent to which those losses are eroding the capital of key institutions like the monolines.

speaker: KOHN
text: The monoline issue raises questions about who will bear the losses and provides another channel for problems spreading through the credit markets, through losses being felt or credit being taken back on bank balance sheets, making them more cautious, and even more directly, into the muni market through the monolines.

speaker: KOHN
text: Despite these developments, my forecast for 2008 was revised down only a few tenths from October.

speaker: KOHN
text: But that is because of the considerable easing of monetary policy undertaken and assumed in my forecast.

speaker: KOHN
text: I assumed 50 at this meeting, and unlike that piker, President Yellen, I assumed another 50 over the second quarter.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’ll see you and up you.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This is a bad dynamic.

speaker: KOHN
text: I thought we needed some insurance, and I also assumed some fiscal stimulus as in the Greenbook.

speaker: KOHN
text: I still see, despite these policy responses, risks around my outlook for activity as skewed to the downside, and it’s because of the potential further increases in required compensation for risk and tightening standards for extending credit and the feedback on demand.

speaker: KOHN
text: Although inflation has been running higher than expected of late, and that is troubling, I expect it to ease back even with my more accommodative policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: The combination we’ve seen of slower income growth and higher inflation suggests elements of a supply shock, and that’s obviously coming from the energy sector and its spillover into food.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is true, as President Fisher pointed out, that some of those increases in food and energy prices are coming from demand from emerging-market economies, but to the extent that such demand is putting upward pressure on our prices and it’s not really sucking exports from the United States at any great rate, I think that it acts more like a supply shock on the U.S. economy than a demand shock.

speaker: KOHN
text: Energy and other commodity prices should level off in an environment of slower global growth, and they’ve started to do that.

speaker: KOHN
text: They have at least showed signs of leveling off recently.

speaker: KOHN
text: Greater slack in resource utilization and product markets should discipline increases in costs and prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: At least some of the reports about airlines suggest that they have tried to pass through fuel surcharges and have been unable to do so, and I think that’s an encouraging sign from the inflation perspective.

speaker: KOHN
text: Any easing of inflation pressure does require that inflation expectations not begin to ratchet higher.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with everyone else.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m persuaded that the balance of evidence is that they have not, despite the rise in five-year- forward inflation compensation and despite the persistently higher rate of increases of total headline than of core inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: But this is something we will need to monitor very carefully.

speaker: KOHN
text: I interviewed Paul Volcker yesterday afternoon for our oral history project.

speaker: KOHN
text: The discussion with him reminded me again of the high cost of reversing a rise in inflation once higher inflation expectations become entrenched.

speaker: WARSH
text: I will endeavor to stay out of the growing, creeping pessimism caucus.

speaker: WARSH
text: You can judge for yourselves whether I’ve been successful doing so.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me talk briefly about two economies that are in a tug-of-war, and rather than reference the housing and nonhousing economies, let me try to talk about it in the context of the economy of financial services versus the real economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: On one level, of course, financial services are not so large a share of GDP that they could threaten the macroeconomy.

speaker: WARSH
text: But the transmission mechanism between credit markets and the real economy, whether it be through the credit channel or other channels, while imperfectly understood, is having very negative effects on the cost and availability of credit for real businesses and households, with the risks there to the downside.

speaker: WARSH
text: Financial institutions, as many of you said, are open for business, but I would say somewhat less so than when we met in December.

speaker: WARSH
text: As we approach the credit line renewal season, that is happening amid a period of depleted credit availability and significantly tighter lending standards.

speaker: WARSH
text: In addition, financial institutions as a group are, in my view, undercapitalized, even with the recent capital infusions.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, the dynamism that I would be hoping to see among financial institutions is clearly lacking; and while I think, as President Pianalto referenced, that there are new market entrants like hedge funds that are pretty keen to provide mezzanine financing, it’s a pretty slow process to match providers and users of capital.

speaker: WARSH
text: So at least for the near-term forecast, I wouldn’t expect that to come much to our rescue.

speaker: WARSH
text: If the U.S. financial institutions were an economy all to themselves, they would probably already be in a recession.

speaker: WARSH
text: While that doesn’t necessarily equate to a recession for the broader economy, it sure doesn’t help.

speaker: WARSH
text: The repair process that President Geithner referenced among financial institutions strikes me as very fragile and quite incomplete.

speaker: WARSH
text: Income statement shortfalls due to falling profits, poor visibility, weaker pipelines, and the need to reduce headcounts very meaningfully strike me in some ways as a more urgent and troublesome issue for large financial institutions than their balance sheet weakness.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the balance sheet front, however, I’m also concerned that more impairments are to come for large financial institutions and more dilution is expected for current shareholders.

speaker: WARSH
text: Although the window for foreign investment is open now, I wouldn’t expect that window to stay open throughout 2008.

speaker: WARSH
text: So even though I’d say that income statement concerns should be more pressing for them, these balance sheet issues are very real.

speaker: WARSH
text: In some way these institutions have been built, or I should say rebuilt, over the past six years to prepare themselves for a low volatility, high liquidity world, and what they found is the exact opposite.

speaker: WARSH
text: They are at different levels of understanding the new world, and it will take them quite some time to rebuild their businesses to be profitable in it.

speaker: WARSH
text: Rolling capital calls across financial institutions are continuing.

speaker: WARSH
text: Many are hoping to play for time, but I think there’s a risk that time will run away from them as new events find their way into the front pages.

speaker: WARSH
text: Virtually no financial institution strikes me as immune to these pressures, and while we see that new problems and new acronyms are emerging daily, they strike me as having the same underlying problems affecting different asset classes.

speaker: WARSH
text: Regional banks have begun to fund their balance sheets successfully—certainly a good sign—but I suspect that they are also in the early stages of needing to raise considerably more capital.

speaker: WARSH
text: As Governor Kohn said, there is a hope and an expectation that global institutions would be a source of strength, at least in financial services.

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, in financial services, my sense is that non- U.S. financial institutions, especially those in the United Kingdom and Europe, are in the midst of playing catch-up to their U.S. counterparts.

speaker: WARSH
text: I expect the year-end reporting process for them, which really begins now but will be at full speed by mid-February through early March, will find many of the Landesbanks needing to be recapitalized.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we’re going to find that both large and small institutions are having a hard time getting through the bank reporting season in Europe.

speaker: WARSH
text: Equity prices in Europe and CDS spreads are already giving us some indication of what’s on the horizon.

speaker: WARSH
text: It’s not just about subprime in Europe, contrary to some of the indications we received.

speaker: WARSH
text: Perhaps even more than U.S. institutions, many European financial institutions have incorrectly believed that high credit ratings across asset classes would in and of themselves serve as protection.

speaker: WARSH
text: The overreliance on credit ratings that we see in the United States strikes me as even more pronounced in Europe.

speaker: WARSH
text: The shocks caused by these financial institutions could have a dramatic impact on their economies, probably more so than the effect of U.S. financial institutions here in the United States.

speaker: WARSH
text: That obviously has a consequence in terms of a further shock and also a consequence on the real side in terms of U.S. exports.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn to the other side of that, that is, the real economy itself, excluding financials.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think many of you referred to the labor market data, which strike me as mixed.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m perhaps a touch more optimistic that we’re going to see some improvement at least in the short term there, but I can’t have the conviction that I’d like.

speaker: WARSH
text: The real economy is doing its best to resist these financial shocks.

speaker: WARSH
text: We can see that fight playing out around E&S spending, around business fixed investment, and around cap-ex more generally.

speaker: WARSH
text: You have nonfinancials with strong corporate balance sheets, excess cash, and high profit levels that are debating in corporate boards about the uncertainty posed by the macroeconomy.

speaker: WARSH
text: It’s hard to say which side is going to prevail in that battle.

speaker: WARSH
text: The backdrop, as many of you mentioned, has weakened, with risk premiums widening across the board.

speaker: WARSH
text: Real PCE for January is not showing much of a snapback from a weak December but also, I would say, not much more deterioration from December levels according to the credit card companies that I spoke to.

speaker: WARSH
text: The bottom line on the real economy—the trends in the real economy may be a bit more positive coming into the first quarter from the fourth quarter than the Greenbook projections, but I would say I am a little less optimistic that the fiscal stimulus package is as likely to be as constructive as the Greenbook would have us believe.

speaker: WARSH
text: The forecast, as a result, overall depends on the ability of nonfinancial corporations to hire and invest despite this macroeconomic uncertainty.

speaker: WARSH
text: I have some confidence that the Fortune 500 will be willing to continue to push along this path of moderate growth; but small companies, particularly those that are really the source of job creation, may be more negatively affected while the credit channel is impaired, and this is happening at a critical time.

speaker: WARSH
text: The Greenbook base case or the “faster recovery” pace depends to a degree on improvement in credit intermediation or at least not another shock, and it’s that other shock that worries me.

speaker: WARSH
text: If deterioration among credit intermediaries continues, the real economy will suffer.

speaker: WARSH
text: Of course, the correlation is hard to pin down.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, on the inflation front, I share the concerns expressed by several of you that the persistence of recent inflation information coming into this period is a cause for concern.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m less sanguine than the Greenbook that we’re going to see the power of that inflation fade in the event that the economy softens some.

speaker: WARSH
text: The backdrop of stubbornly high commodity prices, despite lower global demand in recent weeks, and a lower exchange value of the dollar are likely to put pressure on the inflation front.

speaker: WARSH
text: The data, as we have all talked about, on core and total inflation are not promising, so I would consider that also to be an upside risk.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, if that’s the optimistic scenario, I think we had all better pray.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I think it’s a relatively balanced scenario that accurately reflects the risks that are there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The Greenbook has done a very good job of trying to thread the needle, and I think making a close call for contraction but not actually calling it seems to be very reasonable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The kinds of insurance discussions in both the Greenbook and the Bluebook and that we’ve had preliminarily here make a lot of sense.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Our models have never been successful at assessing turning points, and that is true whether they are the typical linear models, nonlinear models, probit models, Markov switching models, or other things like that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We sort of know once we’ve switched, but it’s hard to get that transition.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As many people have suggested, there are an awful lot of indicators that would go into those kinds of models that would flash for contraction being likely.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that is correct, but that makes it very difficult for us to assess what will happen.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I think—as well reflected in the projections—a lot of downside risk is there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I do share some of the optimism about improvements that we’ve seen in the financial markets, but I had that feeling in October and November, and it is hard for me to really understand exactly what drove the subsequent deterioration.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Certainly there were some issues around year-end, but it seems that more issues than just the year-end were driving the fairly significant reversal of improvement that occurred during October through mid-November and the fairly sudden backing up.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I’m concerned that, since I don’t really understand what happened there, I don’t want to take too much comfort from what has happened so far.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I also don’t want to dismiss what has happened so far because it’s certainly conceivable that things will move in a more linear way forward for improvement.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One issue that I raised both at the last FOMC and in our various conference calls related to some discussions I’ve had with the major credit card companies, which in some sense have a very good feeling for real-time consumption.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I’ve talked with two major credit card companies, and they both had very negative views of what had happened in the very sharp transition consistent with a switch into a contractionary state from the discussions before the October FOMC versus before the December FOMC.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But in the most recent discussions, basically it flattened out.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s certainly not recovering, but it is not a continuing downward trend, which at least in my view provides a great deal of comfort because I was very concerned about the nonlinear break to a very low consumption state, and I think there’s less evidence of that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I won’t go through the specifics of what they said, but basically we’re still seeing challenges and increases in personal bankruptcies, slower repayment rates, more people slipping from 30 days overdue to 60 days overdue, et cetera, et cetera.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But it’s not as dramatic a change, and it’s sort of within the range that they have been anticipating given the data from December.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also as someone mentioned, and I have forgotten who, these numbers are still at relatively low levels.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now, the change is in a very bad direction and certainly could move very quickly, and we’ve seen that in other recession scenarios.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But fortunately it seems, at least from this anecdotal evidence, that it isn’t a significant change to the downside, and it’s possible that it could just be re-flattening out.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: My concern is still that sort of “slow burn” scenario that I’ve talked about and that Nellie and others have fleshed out on the pressures on banks’ balance sheets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I liked Nellie’s very politically correct phrase “unplanned asset expansions.” That’s a very nice way of putting like “oh, my goodness, something is suddenly on the balance sheet that we didn’t expect”—SIVs, asset-backed commercial paper, and so forth.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think people are still waiting for the other shoe to drop, and the other shoe certainly could drop.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There may be things that we haven’t fully anticipated, but we know that there are still leveraged loans that they can’t get off their books, a pipeline that’s still coming on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We know that many banks are still making mortgage loans and cannot get those off their books—at least the jumbo ones.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s conceivable that raising the limits at Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae may help in the short run even if there may be costs in the longer run.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A number of other things could suddenly come on the balance sheets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The example of what happened at SocGen is just another uncertainty that could be out there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So even at a major financial institution that was generally quite well respected, something like this could happen.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A lot of finger pointing and a lot of uncertainty can come from that, and that’s broadly reflected in the CDS spreads.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: About the point that Bill Dudley made in conversation with President Rosengren about being careful to say, well, CDS spreads are lower in Europe and that suggests there’s less risk in Europe—you have to take into account the reaction function by the governments, by the regulators, in terms of recapitalization, as Governor Warsh made reference to.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There are very real challenges, but overall we have seen these CDS spreads go up quite a bit.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I think that concern about the negative dynamic scenario that people talked about is real, and that’s why it is very important to be thinking about buying insurance.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With respect to inflation, certainly some of the numbers have been worrisome.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is clear that inflation uncertainty is up.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We can disagree as to exactly what that means either about credibility or whether it is just uncertainty or whether it’s upside or downside scenarios, but I think it is up and that is something we should be concerned about.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We should carefully craft our message to take that into account because uncertainty can lead to unanchoring of inflation expectations, and that is something that we certainly don’t want to see.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t see evidence of unanchoring yet, but I do see a potential first step in that direction, which does concern me.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The simple fact that a memo had to be written about what was going on with respect to some of these sharp movements suggests that it’s not clear.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Although the memo was excellent, I think there are elements in it that suggest we don’t fully understand and we need to be very careful about that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think we’re all trying to be cheery here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It reminds me a little of one of my favorite scenes in a movie, which is Monty Python’s “Life with Brian.” I remember the scene with them there all on the cross, and they start singing “Look on the Bright Side of Life.” So let me talk a bit about my views on this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My personality does do that, but it is really that I’m strapped a bit to the cross.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My view on the economy is that we are going to have quite a weak first part of 2008, in which we’re going to skirt recession.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is my modal forecast.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do think that the economy will be stronger in 2009 and 2010, but that’s because I decided to be even less of a piker than Governor Kohn.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: He accused President Yellen, but I was going to accuse him because I did actually assume a 75 basis point cut at this meeting and then another 50 basis point cut at the meeting following.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Then I hoped that afterward we would be able to reverse.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, this is something to discuss tomorrow, but it has to do with my views on how you deal with financial disruptions and risk management.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I’ll talk about that tomorrow.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Even though I have a scenario that looks okay, I do want to point out that four very significant downside risks really worry me.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We all talked about them.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, the first is housing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I worry about a particular dynamic, which is that the negative price movements that we currently see could be getting worse.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: People could be expecting that they’re getting worse, and therefore, they want to hold off from buying a house because the effective cost of capital is higher.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As somebody who stupidly is just going to contract on a new house because I have to please my wife, I actually thought exactly along these lines and was thinking about pulling out but then decided that my marriage was more important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: By the way, if you know my wife, no it wasn’t close.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second issue is that the potential for weaker house prices, which really is a significant possibility, not only could lead to lower household wealth but, more important, also could reduce the value of collateral for households and as a result mean that the relaxation of credit constraints that collateral affords is no longer there.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That could have major implications in terms of household spending, so it is also a very substantial downside risk to PCE.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The third issue is that we also see that the financial disruption has already gotten worse.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The good news is that there has been improvement on the liquidity front, and I give a lot of credit to the TAF, which was superbly thought out by our staff and has been quite helpful.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, credit conditions have worsened.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Particularly worrisome—and something that hasn’t been discussed much—is that the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey had substantial tightening.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Usually when you see this kind of tightening, it could indicate that we could have serious negative economic consequences.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Again, that actually makes me very nervous.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Finally, to get even more depressed, there really is potential for a negative feedback loop that has not yet set in.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The financial disruption that we’re seeing right now could then mean a more substantial worsening of the aggregate economy, and that could make the financial markets have even more strain, and you have a problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I really worry about the downside risks and think that they are very substantial and that we should be very concerned about them in thinking about what the appropriate policy stance is.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On the issue of inflation, I’m more sanguine.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I see inflation going down to 2 percent by 2009.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The key here is that I think that inflation expectations are grounded—in fact, are grounded at a level that is consistent with my inflation objective, around 2 percent on PCE, which might be different from others’ views, but that’s where I am right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that context, given that inflation expectations plus expectations about future slack in the economy are the primary drivers of inflation dynamics, I actually think that inflation will come down.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is true that the recent inflation numbers have been very bad; but in thinking about the overall risks, I’m a bit different from the average person on this Committee because I think the risks are balanced and actually somewhat to the downside.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The reason I say this is that I think that inflation expectations are grounded.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: At the same time, there is a substantial downside risk in the economy that could really widen slack in the economy, and that would mean that inflation would come down.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t want to be too sanguine on the issue of inflation expectations being grounded.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, one thing that I think we have to monitor very closely is what’s happening in terms of inflation expectations, particularly financial markets’ views of inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In a sense, I think of that as the canary in the coal mine.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We are also going to want to look at expectations spreading to professional forecasters and to households, but I think information would come in first in terms of the financial markets for the reason that they put their money on the table and react quickly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s one reason I think it’s very important to look at things like inflation compensation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we do need to look at this and do the analysis.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My reading of the analysis that the staff gave and my thinking about the issue is that there is just no evidence that inflation expectations have gone up.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The story is extremely hard to tell to go in that direction.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, it is very easy to tell a story that inflation uncertainty has gone up a lot, and this is something that President Evans talked about and we talked about at the very beginning of a long day.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In this context, that does concern me, and it really tells me that we have to think about whether we can better anchor inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think that this is something that we have to be concerned about, but I do not think that what has happened in inflation compensation is that the canary is dropping dead at this stage.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we do have to monitor this very, very closely, and again, it’s part of the risk-management strategy that I think we have to pursue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you, and thank you all for succinct and very insightful comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m going to try as usual to summarize what I’ve heard; but even more so than usual, no warranty is expressed or implied.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, trying to bring together some of the comments, we noted that incoming data since the last meeting have been broadly weaker than expected, and anecdotes generally suggest slower growth, in some cases significantly slower growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing demand, construction, and prices have continued to weaken, and inventories of unsold homes are little changed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing weakness has implications for employment, consumer spending, and credit conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to households, consumption growth has slowed, reflecting falling house and equity prices and other factors, including generally greater pessimism about the labor market and economic prospects.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The labor market has softened by a range of measures, with unemployment jumping in December.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, workers in some occupations remain in short supply.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Together with financial indicators, weaker labor and consumption data suggest that the economy is at a risk of recession; in any case, it is likely to grow slowly for the first half of the year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second half of the year may be better, the result of easier monetary policy, fiscal stimulus, and possible improvement in housing and credit markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, there are significant downside risks to growth, including the possibility of an adverse feedback loop between the economy and credit markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Reports by firms are mixed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Investment may have slowed, reflecting uncertainty and slower growth in demand.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Commercial real estate activity may be constrained by tighter credit conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Manufacturing is slow to mixed, though IT, energy, and some other sectors continue to be strong.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit conditions more generally appear to be worsening, and the problems may be spreading beyond housing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Additional risks are posed by the problems of the monoline insurers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit losses have induced tighter lending standards, and a key question is how severe those may become and how persistent they may be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One offset is the ability of banks to raise capital.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Core inflation and headline inflation have remained stubbornly high and are a concern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One risk is the ability of some firms to pass through higher input costs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inflation compensation has risen at long horizons, reflecting some combination of higher inflation expectations and inflation risk premiums.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Going forward, a slowing economy, anchored inflation expectations, and possibly stabilizing food and energy prices should lead to more moderate core and total inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, some see upside risks, especially the possibility that higher headline inflation might affect inflation expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s my attempt to summarize.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s a great deal more detail and a great deal more color in the conversations around the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me try to add a few points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, much of what I’ll say has been said.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think that there has been a significant deterioration in the outlook for economic growth and an increase in the downside risks to growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It was sufficiently severe as to prompt me to call the January 9 videoconference that we had, and I think that since then we have had further deterioration.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A number of things have happened and are going on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Very important, perhaps most important, is the continued further deterioration in the prospects for the housing market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing, of course, feeds directly into the real economy through employment, income, and wealth, and I think there are some indications that spillover from the housing sector to the rest of the economy is increasing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, the critical aspect of the housing outlook is the relationship to the financial system, which I’ll come back to.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there’s little doubt about that at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are a lot of factors now that are acting as headwinds in the consumer sector.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just point out the basic fact that most households in the United States have very little in the way of liquid financial assets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, when they, on the one hand, are denied access to home equity if they see tighter credit conditions on cards, autos, and so on, and if at the same time they see greater uncertainty in the economy and the labor market, then their natural tendency would be to be much more conservative in their spending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do note that fiscal action may be of some help, particularly for people in that kind of situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Like President Yellen, I think the indicators of a weakening labor market are broader than just the payroll report.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are a number of other things as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We may get a better report this week.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The UI claims are a little encouraging, but I do think that the weakening economy is going to drag down the labor market to some extent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Certainly the financial markets have deteriorated, reflecting greater concern about recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
