text: We see it in the equity markets but also in short-term interest rates and a variety of credit measures as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, just going through this list of items, we continue to see problems—credit issues, banks concerned about additional losses not just in mortgages but perhaps in other areas as well—with the potential implication of a further tightening of credit conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those are some of the developments that we’ve seen since the last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On our January 9 call, I talked about the regime-switch model and those ways of thinking about the business cycle.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Others have talked about that today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think many of those models would suggest that the probability of recession at this point is quite high, at least 50 percent or more.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think any of us would be happy to see a garden variety NBER recession; but if we had that, there would probably be a few benefits, including correction of some imbalances that we’re seeing in the economy and perhaps some reduction at the edge in the inflation picture.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But, like others, I am most concerned about what has been called the adverse feedback loop—the interaction between a slowing economy and the credit markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A phrase you might have heard, which is getting great currency among bankers, is “jingle mail.” Jingle mail is what happens when otherwise prime borrowers decide that the value of their house is worth so much less than the principal of their mortgage that they just mail their keys to the bank.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: (I wonder if that 140 percent is the right loan-to- value number.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Maybe it’s less than that.)

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Even if prime mortgages hold up—and I think in some regions of the country there will be significant problems with prime mortgages—there is a lot of other potential trouble.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re just beginning to enter the period of maximum subprime ARM resets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second lien piggybacks and home equity loans are all questionable at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We haven’t begun to address the option ARM issue, which is about the same size as the subprime ARM category, and of course, we have the issues with the monolines and private mortgage insurers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Outside of mortgages, expectations for credit performance are worsening in a range of areas, including commercial real estate and corporate credit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that even under the relatively benign scenario that the Greenbook foresees, we’re going to see a lot of pressure in the credit markets and perhaps a long period of balance sheet repair, tight credit, and a drag on the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, our experience with financial drag or headwinds has been that it can be quite powerful and deceptively so, and I think that’s a significant concern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, the central issue here, though, ultimately comes back to the housing market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Certainly by this point there must be some pent-up demand for housing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ve had obviously very low sales for a period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What’s keeping people from buying houses is the fact that other people aren’t buying houses.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there were some sense that a bottom was forming in the market or in house prices, we probably could actually see a pretty quick snap-back, an increase in housing demand, and that in turn would feed back into the credit markets, I think, in a very beneficial way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there’s the possibility that, if the housing market can get restarted, we could get a relatively benign outcome.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, there appears to be a law of nature that the turnaround in the housing market is always six months from the present date.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We simply don’t have any evidence whatsoever that the housing market is bottoming out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have guesses and estimates about how far prices will fall and how far demand and construction will fall.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The key issue is prices, and we are far from seeing the worst case scenario that you could imagine in prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So long as we don’t see any stabilization in the housing market or stabilization in house prices, then I don’t think we can say that the downside risks to the economy or to the credit system have been contained.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Until that point, I think we need to be very, very alert to those risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Everyone has talked about inflation, as should be the case.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The pickup in core inflation is disappointing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are some mitigating factors, such as the role of nonmarket prices, which tend not to be serially correlated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We haven’t discussed owners’ equivalent rent in this meeting for the first time in a while, but we know that it can behave in rather odd ways during periods of housing slowdowns.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The hope is that energy and food prices will moderate; in fact, if oil prices do rise by less than the two-thirds increase of last year, it would obviously be helpful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nominal wages don’t seem to be reflecting high inflation expectations at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think there are some reasons for optimism; but as many people pointed out, there are upward pressures, including the point that President Fisher made that the lagged effects of the previous increases in energy, food, and other commodity prices have probably not been fully realized in core inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Furthermore, as we’ll talk about more tomorrow, to the extent that we decide at this meeting to take out some insurance against downside risks, then implicit in that insurance premium might be a greater risk of inflation six months or a year from now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we have to take that into account as we think about policy and about our communications, as President Plosser and others have pointed out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, as Governor Mishkin and others have noted, we need to think about a policy strategy that will involve not only providing adequate insurance against what I consider to be serious downside risks but also a policy strategy that involves removing the accommodation in a timely way when those risks have moderated sufficiently.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So my reading of the situation is that it’s exceptionally fluid and that the financial risks, in particular—as we saw, for example, after the October meeting—can be very hard to predict.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are a lot of interactions between the financial markets and the real economy that are potentially destabilizing, and so we are going to have to be proactive in trying to stabilize the situation, recognizing that we have a confluence of circumstances that is extraordinarily difficult and that no policy approach will deliver the optimal outcome in the short term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re just going to have to try to choose a path that will give us the best that we can get, given the circumstances that we’re facing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any further comments or questions?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will reconvene tomorrow at nine o’clock.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a reception and dinner, optional, available in the Martin Building.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s begin our meeting by calling on Dave Stockton to report on the GDP data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: 4 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: My dictionary defines a miracle as an event so improbable that it appears to defy the laws of nature.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Along those lines, we distributed a GDP report that compares our forecast with the actual number that was published this morning, and they are exceedingly close.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you can see comparing the Greenbook and advance estimate columns, in fact, it wasn’t just close on the top line, but it was really quite close in terms of the various components.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Personal consumption and business fixed investment were very close to our estimate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Residential investment was not quite so weak in the advance release as it was in our forecast; that might reflect either a different estimate by the BEA about cost per start or something they know about additions and alterations that we don’t.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In the opposite direction, federal spending—in particular, defense spending—was weaker in the advance estimate than we have incorporated in the Greenbook estimate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At the bottom of the table are the price indexes.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Both total PCE and core PCE were spot-on with the forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Really, I didn’t see anything in this report that would alter our outlook at all going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I would just note, obviously, that both the advance estimate and our Greenbook estimate are based on partial data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There is still a lot left to be learned about the fourth quarter, and even more about the first quarter going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One other piece of information that became available this morning was the ADP report for private nonfarm payroll employment.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That report showed an increase of 130,000.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Looking at that report and thinking about our forecast of 20,000, we’d probably up our forecast to about 50,000 for the month, following our normal rules of thumb in responding to that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Quite frankly, I don’t think that particular piece of information would alter my view about the state of the labor market going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As we noted yesterday, we have seen a fair number of other indicators suggesting that there has been some softening in the labor markets.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think that is probably still the best bet going forward, so I don’t think at this point we would change too much our employment forecast.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any questions for Dave?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, Brian, would you like to talk now?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 5 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will be referring to the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” Your policy decision today takes place against an unusually complicated and uncertain backdrop.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Over recent months, reverberations from the contraction in the housing sector have 4 The materials used by Mr. Stockton are appended to this transcript (appendix 4).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 5 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 5).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: spread to the subprime mortgage market, to financial markets and institutions more generally, and now evidently to the broader economy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It seems clear, based on the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey and numerous other sources of information, that these factors are interacting, with mortgage-related writedowns and concerns about the economic outlook triggering a broad and substantial tightening of credit to businesses and households and the tightening of credit feeding back onto the housing market and the economy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: At the same time, recent inflation performance has been disappointing, the near-term policy tradeoff appears to have deteriorated somewhat, and inflation compensation has risen.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Meanwhile, investors have been rather skittish and, in the environment of heightened uncertainty, have sought more clarity in your communications and more assurance about policy prospects than you can reasonably provide.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The combination of all these factors has left financial market prices unusually volatile.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In these circumstances, the Committee faces a difficult task in reaching judgments as to the outlook and the balance of risks, gauging the appropriate policy course, and communicating your views to the public.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To provide some assistance in your policy deliberations today, a box in the Bluebook explored the possible implications of addressing pronounced downside risks to growth through monetary policy, and the charts from that box are replicated in exhibit 1.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The panels in the left-hand column consider the possible benefits of risk management under the assumption that a recession does develop.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The recession considered in this exercise is the same as that examined in an alternative scenario in Part 1 of the Greenbook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As you may recall, that scenario was calibrated to match the typical degree of weakness relative to fundamentals in expenditures other than those for housing in six past recessions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The dotted line shows the results, as gauged using the FRB/US model, if the Committee were to respond to emerging evidence of an unfolding recession by adjusting policy in a manner similar to its past behavior, as captured by the staff’s estimated outcome-based policy rule.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In this case, the Committee lowers the federal funds rate gradually to about ¾ percent by mid-2009.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The unemployment rate peaks at about 6.1 percent, and inflation eventually falls below 1½ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The blue line shows the results that would be predicted if, instead, the Committee responded more aggressively.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Here we have arbitrarily assumed that the Committee lowers the federal funds rate to 1½ percent this quarter and holds the rate at that level through the second quarter.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: From that point forward, it follows the outcome-based rule.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If the recessionary conditions do eventuate, the timely policy stimulus moderates the downturn in activity, trimming about ¼ percentage point off the peak unemployment rate, and helps keep inflation from falling toward a region that some of you might find uncomfortably low.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although aggressive policy easing would help mitigate economic weakness, it would also raise the risk that policy could add unduly to inflation pressures should recessionary weakness not develop, a possibility explored in the right-hand column.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The simulations underlying this column are carried out under the baseline Greenbook scenario.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown by the blue line, the cost of an aggressive near-term easing in the absence of a recession could be limited if policymakers were to recognize quickly that the economy was not weakening to the degree feared and boosted the federal funds rate rapidly.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In this simulation, the Committee increases the funds rate about 2½ percentage points in six months—that is, at a pace of more than 50 basis points per meeting—to around 4 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This prompt reversal brings the funds rate 1 percentage point above the baseline, providing an offset to the earlier period of excessively easy policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In this case, core inflation would run slightly higher than baseline for a couple of quarters—as shown in the bottom right-hand panel by the distance between the solid blue line and the dotted black line—but would subsequently return to baseline.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In contrast, as shown in the dashed red line, if policymakers were slow to recognize that no recession was in train and so reversed policy more gradually after the first two quarters—that is, in line with your historical behavior—considerable momentum could be imparted to economic activity, with the unemployment rate, the middle panel, running roughly ¼ percentage point below baseline into 2011.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The cost of responding more aggressively to the risk of a recession in this case could be inflation that remains 0.1 or 0.2 percentage point above the baseline path for several years, the bottom right-hand panel.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Concern about such an outcome could give you some pause as you consider how much insurance you wish to seek at this and coming meetings.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your concerns in this regard may also be exacerbated by the fact that the inflation picture seems to have deteriorated somewhat in recent months.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your current projections reflect some worsening of the inflation–output tradeoff, with more slack apparently required over the next three years to push inflation down toward what would appear to be your preferred outcomes.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, as was discussed yesterday, five- year-forward inflation compensation increased notably over the intermeeting period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: While there are reasons to question whether much of that rise represents an increase in inflation expectations, it might be due in part to a higher inflation risk premium, perhaps signaling that inflation expectations are becoming more loosely moored and are hence more prone to drift in response to various shocks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If you were particularly concerned about a possible unmooring of inflation expectations, you might be inclined toward alternative D, shown in the right-hand column of table 1, which is included as the next page.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under this alternative, you would hold the stance of monetary policy steady at this meeting but would indicate that the risks to growth remain tilted to the downside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, based on the interest rate assumptions provided with your forecast submissions, the recommendations of most Reserve Banks to reduce the discount rate by 50 basis points, and your comments yesterday, it appears that most if not all of you see some easing today as appropriate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Consequently, I will dispense with a detailed discussion of alternative D. Rather, the questions for today’s meeting would seem to be not whether to reduce rates but how much and what to say about the outlook for growth, inflation, and policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative C, the Committee would reduce rates 25 basis points today.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The rationale section of the statement would note that financial markets remain under stress, cite the tightening of credit availability, and mention the deepening of the housing contraction and the softening of labor markets.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With regard to inflation, the Committee would note its expectation that inflation should moderate, but it would also cite a range of factors that could put upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement would conclude by indicating that the policy action, combined with actions taken earlier, should help promote moderate growth over time, but it would also warn that downside risks to growth remain.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee might see alternative C as appropriate if it believes that some further easing of policy is warranted by the deterioration in the economic outlook and the associated risks but feels that a moderate move is preferable today, given the policy steps you have taken to date, the possibility that the fiscal stimulus could still turn out to be larger than currently envisaged, and questions about how firmly inflation expectations are anchored.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Market participants currently put considerably greater odds on a 50 basis point move today than on a 25 basis point action.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, market participants reportedly expect you to issue a statement similar to the January 22 announcement, but the addition of the sentence on inflation risks in the third paragraph would likely suggest to investors that you have significant concerns about inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The combination of a smaller-than-expected policy move and the statement drafted for alternative C would likely suggest to investors that monetary policy had shifted into an incremental mode.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Shorter-term interest rates would likely rise somewhat, and equity prices could decline noticeably.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Should the Committee see an outcome along the lines of the Greenbook forecast as most likely, it might be attracted to the 50 basis point easing of alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative B, the Committee would issue an announcement that closely resembles the January 22 statement.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, the fourth paragraph would include a sentence indicating that the policy actions to date should help to promote moderate growth over time and to mitigate downside risks to growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the second sentence of that paragraph, the word “appreciable,” used in the January 22 statement, would be dropped from the characterization of the risks, presumably in recognition of the significant further adjustment of policy under this alternative.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As discussed yesterday, the Greenbook-consistent measure of r* has declined more than 1¼ percentage points since the December meeting, to about ¾ percentage point.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A 50 basis point move today would leave the real federal funds rate just below 1 percent, gauged on the same basis as our r* measure.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus, by the r* metric, policy would remain slightly restrictive under alternative B, consistent with applying modest downward pressure to inflation going forward.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Policymakers might view such a policy stance as appropriate if they saw the downside risks to growth as roughly balanced by the upside risks to inflation following such a policy action.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, given the views expressed in your economic projections—in particular, the assessment expressed by many that the trajectory for the funds rate would probably need to be a little lower in the near term than assumed in the Greenbook—it seems more likely that you would prefer the approach of alternative B if you believed that further easing will likely be warranted but should be implemented somewhat gradually, perhaps to provide time to assess the effects of the policy easing already put in place.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With investors placing greatest weight on a policy choice at this meeting along the lines of alternative B, this approach would likely prompt relatively little reaction in financial markets this afternoon.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Given recent developments, the Committee may place a larger premium than usual on avoiding policy surprises.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If you have lowered your economic outlook even more sharply than the staff or if you see the downside risks as particularly large, you might not see moderation as a virtue and prefer to ease policy aggressively by 75 basis points at this meeting, as in alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This approach would seem consistent with the concerns and policy assumptions expressed by many of you in your forecast narratives.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, some of you have espoused a risk-management approach to policy in which the federal funds rate is lowered sharply in the near term to provide greater assurance of continued economic expansion and then that policy easing is reversed quickly once it becomes clear that risks are diminishing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As suggested by the risk-management simulations that I discussed earlier, this approach relies heavily on your ability to recognize promptly that the stimulus is not needed and to reverse field rapidly.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Binary options on target fed funds futures suggest that, over the past few days, market participants have essentially priced out the possibility that you will take such aggressive action today.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus, money market rates would likely decline sharply in response to implementation of this alternative, downward pressure on the foreign exchange value of the dollar could increase, and equity prices could rise somewhat, although any rally could be damped by a sense among investors that you were motivated to take this action by concerns about pronounced economic weakness.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Obviously, a significant concern with a step of this magnitude today would be the possible implications for inflation expectations and inflation uncertainty.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although the relative contributions of various factors to the recent increase in inflation compensation can be debated, last week’s policy move seemed to be well understood at the time as a response to incoming evidence of a sharply deteriorating economic outlook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: By contrast, the motivations for a larger-than-expected move today might be less clear to market participants, potentially elevating the risk of loosening the inflation expectations anchor.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Brian?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I would like to ask a question and possibly make a comment about the risk-management strategies.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Am I correct in understanding that the treatment of expectations is basically backward-looking?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That is correct, Governor Mishkin.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So even though you know I am a fan of—well, let’s put it this way, you said moderation, and I am not a fan of moderation in many dimensions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But there is a potential cost here that is not articulated, which is that if there is a very aggressive easing and it has an effect on inflation expectations, then the more benign scenario that we have in terms of cost may not be there.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is one of the reasons that, if we think about a risk-management approach, we have to think about whether we can do it more systematically.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What kind of communications would be attached to it?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also, what kind of information would we have to watch out for to make sure that we don’t unhinge inflation expectations?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So although I think this is a terrific box and it was very, very useful, there is a bit of a qualm here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is also very hard to model the issue of what would happen to expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I am not complaining in any way about the usefulness of this; but we should have another concern, which is how we would manage inflation expectations if we pursued an approach like this.

speaker: EVANS
text: My question is related to what Governor Mishkin just asked about.

speaker: EVANS
text: The risk-management analysis was very helpful; it was a very good addition, and it captures a number of things that we have talked about.

speaker: EVANS
text: One is sort of a quick policy reversal or the potential for that if things go well.

speaker: EVANS
text: My question is, How do you see the path of communications likely to evolve?

speaker: EVANS
text: What is it going to look like?

speaker: EVANS
text: What will it sound like if we are thinking about reversing policy, and we get to the bottom, and then we start taking it back a little more quickly than normal?

speaker: EVANS
text: A lot of times when we have done this before you heard the phrase that markets need to be prepared for this and they have to understand it.

speaker: EVANS
text: Would that somehow get in the way of the stimulus?

speaker: EVANS
text: I think this gets a bit at what Governor Mishkin was talking about in terms of expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: In particular, do you have any thoughts about how the slope of the yield curve might help inform how people are going to be thinking about this?

speaker: EVANS
text: Are we going to move from something that is potentially inverted or flat to a rising yield curve that could inform a better outlook, and then raising rates could maybe in a parallel fashion move the yield curve up?

speaker: EVANS
text: I am just curious whether that could be helpful for the communications strategy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think my response is that it is very difficult to say how your communications should or will evolve going forward at this point because of the very substantial uncertainty in the economic outlook, which shows up very clearly in the Committee participants’ economic forecasts.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Presumably, what you say will depend on evolving circumstances.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In terms of the yield curve, again, I think that is difficult.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That will depend on the interaction of market participants’ perception of incoming economic information with their sense of your own policy reactions.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m just curious if, in the path of this simulation, the yield curve behaves in that fashion or not.

speaker: EVANS
text: This gets at what the mechanism is for the stimulus.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is it to improve market liquidity, market functioning, long rates, or an expectation of short rates?

speaker: EVANS
text: If they start expecting a tightening, is that going to get in the way of something, and so we are going to view that as more difficult to move at that time?

speaker: EVANS
text: I think everybody is quite committed to the idea that we need to do the right type of policy reversal when it is called for, but it is going to be very difficult to identify in the moment.

speaker: EVANS
text: So the yield curve could help.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In these simulations, the standard channels of monetary policy are working through things like the yield curve, asset prices, the foreign exchange value of the dollar, household wealth, et cetera.

speaker: LACKER
text: Brian, I want to compliment you and the staff for presenting these risk-management strategies.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it is really useful for the Committee to see and think about these in terms of strategies rather than sort of one-off policy choices, and thinking through a sequence of actions like this is very, very helpful.

speaker: LACKER
text: Governor Mishkin asked about expectations and noted that they were backward-looking, and I wanted to ask about that.

speaker: LACKER
text: You guys have described to us before that there are firms and wage setters and then there are financial markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is there a forward-looking part in the financial markets, or is that backward-looking as well?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The financial markets are forward-looking in these simulations.

speaker: LACKER
text: As you know, in applied macroeconomics, there is a range of approaches to handling expectations, and the rest of the range is filled out with more forward- looking approaches.

speaker: LACKER
text: In this instance—in the instance of a recession—you hear and read a lot about recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, there was a story in the paper today about businesses preparing for a recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: So you get the sense that market participants might be understanding that this is a special episode of economic dynamics called a recession and look back to past recessions and think of it in sort of a forward-looking way.

speaker: LACKER
text: That to me, more than in the usual circumstances, heightens the value of thinking through or at least exploring the implications of a forward- looking approach to expectations.

speaker: LACKER
text: I say that in particular thinking about these strategies because we get only a few trials on recessions.

speaker: LACKER
text: They are pretty rare, and so the inferences a set of market participants are going to make about recessions is going to be influenced by their past recessions.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is going to be the last chance to influence their perceptions about how we behave in the next recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I am really interested in thinking through our strategy for this recession from the point of view of, well, what if from now on market participants expect us to adopt the strategy that we do adopt in this.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is why I would like to see some analysis that says, “Well, all right, if this is the strategy and it is understood by agents that this is our strategy, how does the economy behave?” So we adopt a strategy, and it is one that we think we can sustain and one that we would like to choose again in the future if it is understood.

speaker: LACKER
text: Related to that, Governor Mishkin mentioned inflation and inflation expectations, and I was a little confused about the discussion yesterday because I always thought of us as wanting to minimize the distortion in the rate of return on money, and that suggests minimizing the raw- return gap between nominal and real securities.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I am not quite sure that we don’t care nearly as much about the variance in inflation or the risk premiums due to inflation as we do about expected inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is that your understanding when you guys think through optimal monetary policy?

speaker: LACKER
text: I know you do scenarios like that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I mean, how do the fluctuations and the variance in inflation fit in?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I don’t think they fit in in a direct way.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We still have a lot of work ahead of us, despite the progress that we have made in modeling in recent years, to consider things like the distribution of different economic outcomes and how skewness in those distributions, both with respect to output and with respect to inflation, would interact with risk- aversion in monetary policymaking.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I don’t think our science has quite gotten to that stage yet, but I agree that these are worthwhile things to study further.

speaker: LACKER
text: One thought I had in that discussion about expected inflation, you noted that the one-to-five-year rise in inflation hadn’t been affected much, but the five-to-ten-year rise had.

speaker: LACKER
text: If it is well understood by agents when going through something like a recession, which comes around only every once in a while, maybe it is ratifying current inflation and not bringing it down.

speaker: LACKER
text: You might expect that the inference would change about how inflation behaves in the next recession, which would come five to ten years from now.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I see the point you are making, and that sounds plausible.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You know, again, our thought was that, if investors were concerned that monetary policy makers were making an inflationary mistake, it would begin to affect inflation in the near term, meaning within several years rather than seven or eight years ahead.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have just a technical question on inflation expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You presented to us at some point a variation of the model in which the policy action itself was fed into the model for inflation expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is that part of the model at this point?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It is not part of the baseline model that we are running off of.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: That is operating here very much.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: It is the same mechanism, but it works differently in the two cases, because in the case where the recession actually shows up, whether you take the gradualist approach or you take the risk-management approach, they see the recession, and the easing in monetary policy doesn’t surprise them very much, although we can take our risk-management approach and respond a bit more than usual.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But then, things behave as they expect, and so not too much happens to inflation expectations.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In the other case, in which recession doesn’t emerge, they say, “Oh, this was an easing that wasn’t expected,” and then it becomes critical how long you hold it.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: If you hold it and you get rid of it only gradually, then inflation expectations start to shift up.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: They think the Fed’s inflation goal has changed.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In the case where you take it away quickly, they say, “Okay, you took it away quickly,” and so not much happens to long-run inflation expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the answer is that the funds rate is affecting inflation expectations in these simulations.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But the question is whether it is viewed in the context of what is happening to output and inflation, whether they say, “Yes, that fits with the historical pattern of stabilization,” or whether, because the recession didn’t emerge, this looks as though it was after the fact an ease in policy that was not warranted.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Then the question is, Do you take it away quickly, or do you take it away slowly?

speaker: LACKER
text: So in the case where we are doing the risk-management approach, do they understand that we are more likely to reverse course, or do they just mark down their whole expected path for policy?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: No, they don’t know that you are more likely to reverse course in that case.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So when you think of a communication strategy, which is not in these simulations, it says, “Oh, we’re going to do this, but in the event that the recession doesn’t occur, we will take it away more quickly than we might have based on historical averages.” But it doesn’t make too much difference in the simulation, because it is taken quickly.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Just because the funds rate is down surprisingly low for a quarter or two, that is not long enough to have much of an effect on long-run inflation expectations in that simulation.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: What it would do in the real world is different.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are trying to model the real world.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is a “castle in the sand” quality in this discussion.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Let me make just three points on what I took from this and see if I got it right.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One is, in the staff’s judgment, at 3 percent—in that view of the world, which is not way off from where the discussion was yesterday—policy is not providing any degree of insurance or accommodation against the adverse outcomes that may be ahead.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The second thing I took away is that this framework seems like a good way of thinking about how you think about moving lower, how you think about what mistake we’re going to make or we want to make.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are going to make a mistake, but it is good to think about what mistake is more costly and what mistake is easier to correct.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It seems to me it tells us almost nothing, frankly, about when we are going to be in a position where we are going to want to start to take it back.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It also probably tells us very little about how quickly we are going to want to take it back.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would have thought that the most remarkable thing in these paths is how little difference the variance is in the outcomes a year out.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I mean, they must be so far within the range of uncertainty in this context, and for us to start thinking now about how to design the optimal exit and communicate it, not just for President Evans’s reasons but many others, just basic humility, it seems to me kind of premature.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I have a lot of sympathy for the fact that we will want to make sure that we are choosing which error we are going to make.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I have a lot of sympathy for thinking through how we correct for that error.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But for us to assert, because we are worried about the implications of that, that we are going to start focusing now on the design of the exit, sounds to me a bit like a statement of the obvious.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course we are going to move with alacrity to take back and make sure those inflation expectations stay anchored at a reasonable level.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: To suggest otherwise and to assert it would look kind of insecure—a lack of confidence in what we are here to do.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The third thing I took away from it is that it seems to say that, if you make policy in a way consistent with the response of this Committee over the past decade and a half or so, you have pretty good outcomes in the strategy in which you take out enough risk against the downside error.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Now, life could be uncertain.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Maybe that is too charitable to the past, but it seems to be kind of reassuring in that way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that it is hard to generalize.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You say there are so few recessions, so the specific communication that is undertaken—for example, in the last episode there was actually communication that leaned against the rapid reversal—you know, “considerable period” and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So rather than trying to generalize from two examples, I think it would much more have to do with how we present the outlook and communicate our intentions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I just want to make a comment about what President Geithner said and follow up on President Evans’s question.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One thing that the simulation doesn’t get at is the adverse feedback loop.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s just not built into the model.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the benefits of pursuing a risk- management approach are not as clear as they would be if they were included in the simulation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, I would like to focus on President Evans’s issue because I think it really is critical.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: He asked about how we might know whether or not we should reverse and talked about things like the yield curve.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But one thing that is important to recognize in this scenario is that I think it is very unusual in terms of this Committee’s past behavior.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Don, you are my man who is the ancient mariner here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Have we ever reversed this quickly in past episodes?

speaker: KOHN
text: By “this quickly,” what do you mean?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What the path of the prompt reversal is.

speaker: KOHN
text: As the Chairman was saying, there hasn’t really been a typical recession.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have had two recessions in the past twenty years, and I think in both cases we stayed down longer because of the circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: So in 1992-93, we had a zero real funds rate while the economy was growing for two years.

speaker: KOHN
text: Then when we started raising, we did raise very quickly.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think that was mixed.

speaker: KOHN
text: I can remember presenting to the Board, as a staff member, charts in 1990 showing how interest rates always reversed with the trough of the recession, a couple of months this way, a couple of months that way.

speaker: KOHN
text: And that was just wrong.

speaker: KOHN
text: I mean, it was just a different circumstance because of the 50 mile an hour headwinds.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it is going to be very hard to set expectations about what we are going to do that will influence people in the future because each episode is so different.

speaker: KOHN
text: As the Chairman was saying, we were very worried in 2003-04 that people would generalize from 1994 and see us reversing rather quickly, so we got into this verbal gymnastics to try to modify their expectations because we thought the rapid reversal in that case would not be consistent with macroeconomic stability.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is a case in which we are just going to have to judge when we get to the circumstances what is necessary without knowing ahead of time what the pattern is going to be.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So let me turn back to President Evans’s question because there is an issue about what kind of information might tell us that we took out insurance and then it wasn’t needed.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think some pieces of information that the staff has been looking at are relevant.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Particularly important in this regard is that there are a lot of indicators of financial stress.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What is different about this episode is that the reason we are so worried about downside risk is the financial strains, and there are a lot of pieces of information that the staff has been producing that could be very important in terms of looking at this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: They have a financial—I don’t know what you call your indicator, but you have something that you have been using in your model, Dave, that takes up spreads and volatility and—

speaker: MISHKIN
text: —principal components of these things.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There are a lot of financial variables.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also an issue that the Chairman raised yesterday was that the housing market is a big component of our downside risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The market’s concerns about future declines in housing prices are causing a very sharp decrease in demand for housing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That could turn around very quickly as well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Even now we should be thinking about these issues, and Governor Kohn’s use of the word “nimble”—I like “flexibility,” but I think “nimble” is probably a better word—is really I think key here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is somewhat of a departure from normal—exactly what the Chairman said.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This episode is different from past episodes.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So we do need to start thinking about this, and the staff will need to think about exactly these issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Poole, you had an interjection?

speaker: POOLE
text: I am older than Governor Kohn, so I can answer.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is how long you have been in the System.

speaker: POOLE
text: 1958 was just about like that.

speaker: POOLE
text: It was very much a sharp V.

speaker: EVANS
text: I just wanted to point out that the reason I asked the question about how you think about the exit strategy is that, since we are putting a lot of discussion weight on the reversal, it is going to color how you think about the next move potentially, if not today then another day.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I think it brings the future into the present very quickly.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I could just continue the dialogue with Governor Kohn.

speaker: LACKER
text: It has been observed by some that the past two recessions differ from previous post-war recessions in some key dimensions, and some have drawn the conclusion that it is the changing nature of the business cycle after the Great Moderation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Both have been characterized as shallow and longer lasting.

speaker: LACKER
text: I take the point that one’s inferences about a third instance are going to be very tenuous, naturally.

speaker: LACKER
text: But it is also natural to look back to those episodes and see what we can draw out of them.

speaker: LACKER
text: You mentioned headwinds in 1990, and we had some special stuff that kept us from raising rates with nimbleness in 2003 and 2004.

speaker: LACKER
text: To what extent do you think that is likely coming out of this episode, that the types of things that kept us from raising rates in the 1990s and in both of these episodes are likely to recur?

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, I asked Governor Kohn, but if he gets to respond.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we are really getting into the policy discussion right now, and the issue, really, will be the headwinds, the financial market restraint.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it is reasonable to think that we are facing at least 25 mile an hour headwinds.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also think that it is going to take a while for the headwinds to abate.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is going to take a while to rechannel these credit flows, to restart many of the secondary markets in mortgages.

speaker: KOHN
text: So my personal view is that I wouldn’t be surprised to see us having to run with a real federal funds rate that is below the historical average for some time.

speaker: KOHN
text: But as everyone has been saying, it is highly uncertain and very dependent on how the financial markets evolve and how the real economy responds to those markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: For follow-up before President Geithner responds, to the extent that we place greater likelihood on that, should these simulations suggest that we should take that into account in how rapidly we cut now?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would just point out that with the 1990-91 episode, inflation after the recession—after the whole episode was over—was significantly lower than in the period before it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if there are headwinds that are bringing the economy below potential and are causing high unemployment, for example, there has to be a mechanism.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Expectations have to be tied to something, and there has to be some way in which excessively low interest rates are stimulating inflation, through either commodity prices or wage pressures or some other mechanism.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If those pressures aren’t there because of headwinds or some other factor, then unusually low interest rates will not by themselves create inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vice Chairman, did you have anything else you wanted to add?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I really couldn’t tell, President Lacker, what inference you were going to draw from that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I would just reinforce the point that, if you are more worried and uncertain now about the magnitude of the headwinds and the duration, I think it has to mean that you err on the side of going lower sooner.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But the main point is that we just don’t know much about it, and I think it is worth a lot of humility.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I mean, think how surprised we have been by so much over this period, even with all our thinking through three years ago about alternative paths for housing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I would just vote for humility.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But the basic point is that we have to err on the side of being worried about reducing the risk that you end up with 75 mile an hour headwinds rather than 25 for a long period of time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Could we start our policy round?

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like the Greenbook, my projection for the real economy incorporates a sharp decline in the equilibrium real fed funds rate.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given the large risks facing the real economy, I think we need to take precautions against having a restrictive fed funds rate target.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think a 50 basis point cut in the target fed funds rate today may be large enough to eliminate that possibility, although there is plenty of uncertainty around that estimate, as we have been discussing.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Based on my analysis, comments from my business contacts, and what I have heard from all of you at this meeting, I feel very comfortable supporting this position today.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The economic environment has been volatile and highly uncertain, and I realize that my outlook could change appreciably in the weeks and months ahead.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I can imagine that my economic projections will evolve in a way that supports even further reductions in the fed funds rate target.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At the same time, as I said yesterday, I am concerned about inflation risks and that they may now be elevated.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I can also imagine scenarios that would lead me to want to pursue a more restrictive policy than would be appropriate based on the downside risk to growth alone.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At some point, on the margin, inflation concerns could become my dominant concern.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We know that inflation expectations play a crucial role in determining the inflation outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We have been talking about that.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But, unfortunately, we don’t really know all that much about what it is going to take to unanchor inflation expectations.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: It is hard to know for certain how far out on the ice we can skate without needing to worry that the ice has become too thin.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I know that we are bringing our best thinking to bear on this issue by developing diagnostic tools such as the decomposition of inflation compensation into its component parts, as we talked about yesterday and this morning.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I hope that we are going to come to learn that these tools are useful guides to policy, but we just don’t have enough experience with them to know how much confidence to place in their estimates.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Yesterday Governor Kohn told us about his conversation with Paul Volcker and that Paul Volcker told him that unfortunately we do have experience of seeing the erosion of public confidence in our ability to meet our price stability objective, and we know from this experience that it makes the attainment of price stability more costly.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But today I support the policy directive expressed in alternative B.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My concerns today are more with the downside risk to economic growth.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given what I know today, I think it is the right course of action.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I have discovered during the past couple of weeks that I can be very nimble when it comes to the reduction in our fed funds rate target.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: If inflation developments require, I want to be just as nimble in the other direction.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Given the discussion I have heard so far, it is apparent to me that we will most likely move to a 3 percent fed funds rate today.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we do so, I think we should be prepared to stop at this point and let the market work through the disturbances that only time and market adjustments will correct.

speaker: HOENIG
text: While I would not pre-commit to no further cuts, I would give no hint of them either.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that is important.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The discussion we just had around this table is that we cannot know the future, there are always headwinds, and we will make a mistake.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Therefore, we should limit ourselves to some extent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As I have expressed in this Committee before, I think we should narrow the range to which we are willing to move the fed funds rate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: My judgment is that to move to levels outside the reasonable range that, yes, I know would be debated, but a reasonable range of neutral, is as likely to introduce disturbances into the economy as it is to moderate the economy’s performance.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I find an approach to policy that focuses on the real equilibrium rate compelling.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think it is good theory, and it is common sense and can be explained to the public.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I understand that we cannot observe the equilibrium rate, but we cannot observe the NAIRU, potential GDP, or most other criteria.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The real rate is at least related to the policy tool that we focus on, which is interest rates.

speaker: HOENIG
text: When you systematically move below or above the neutral rate, you systematically stimulate or restrict the economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: With that in mind, and since monetary policy works with a lag, I would recommend that we follow a policy in which we stop moving rates and let the market work once we are notably below or above the long-run neutral rate based upon a reasonable estimate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: This is a credible approach to policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Today, a nominal 3 percent fed funds rate would provide for an actual inflation-adjusted rate that is less than 1 percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That will serve to support the real economy as the financial sector adjusts, and it has to adjust.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To stimulate the economy further at our current inflation rate is to invite, or at least to increase the probability of, higher inflation or encourage the next asset bubble or both, and it will undermine our credibility in the long run.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to the press statement, I have three brief comments.

speaker: HOENIG
text: First, in paragraph 2, I would begin by putting the economic rationale before the financial market reference, which would most appropriately align our recent actions with our concern for the downside risk to the economy and place our concern for financial market stress in better perspective.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Second, I believe that a detailed discussion of inflation risk may not be helpful at this time, and the less said the better.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Therefore, I prefer the language in paragraph 3 of alternative B rather than any other of the options.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Finally, I believe we should modify the risk assessment to provide more flexibility for future decisions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Most important, it should place less emphasis on the possibility of future rate cuts and better position us to return to a neutral position later this year and early next.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Therefore, I would rewrite paragraph 4 along the lines that President Plosser suggested.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To summarize, I suggest that we act at this meeting, explain our action as I suggested, and hold at that point.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I support alternative B, though I think a case can be made for alternative A.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Boston model indicates that even after a 50 basis point reduction, we still need more easing to return to an economy with both full employment and inflation below 2 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Taking out insurance against more-severe downside risks would imply even more easing than our baseline forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given our recent move and the additional easing in alternative B, I am comfortable waiting to take more aggressive action only if incoming data warrant it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, I will not be surprised if we find further action is indeed needed.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: What would be the arguments against taking an aggressive tack?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Certainly, one argument might be that elevated oil and commodity prices and core inflation currently above 2 percent warrant a more restrained approach.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, I would note that in previous recessions the inflation rate has declined significantly, even in the 1970s, in the midst of historic surges in energy and food prices.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Whether we skirt a recession or experience a recession, I expect core inflation to trend down.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A potential second argument is that we have responded too slowly to the need for tighter policy in the past, so we should be more reluctant to ease in the present.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While it may be true that we raised rates too slowly at the onset of previous expansions, I see no reason for this Committee to behave in a manner that it believes is suboptimal.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As a Committee, we seem to have consensus on the importance of maintaining low inflation rates, and I am confident we have the will to raise rates with the same alacrity that we reduced them, should economic conditions warrant such action.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Since September, this Committee has lowered the federal funds rate 175 basis points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My estimate is that the real funds rate before any action today is 1 percent or slightly below that, and that is very low by historical standards.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The slowdown in growth suggests that the equilibrium real rate really has fallen, and the Committee has appropriately allowed the nominal funds rate to fall as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Do nominal rates need to go lower and, if so, about how much?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Part of this depends on what you think the equilibrium real rate of the economy is now.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Bluebook indicates that estimates of r* vary considerably by the model and the process they use to calculate them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The 70 percent confidence interval around them is 3 percentage points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, the estimates of r*, as we talked a bit about yesterday, can be quite volatile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It troubles me that the estimate of r* consistent with the Greenbook has changed by 140 basis points from December to today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am uncomfortable using an estimate that is so variable and so sensitive to stock markets as a guide to setting policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also want to note that the Bluebook indicates that the appropriate funds rate, based on a range of Taylor rule specifications, is anywhere from 40 to 120 basis points above where we currently are today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That includes forecast-based versions of the rule that rely on the weak forecast found in the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While I don’t want to suggest that such guidelines are definitive, they do suggest that the current level of the fed funds rate is clearly accommodative and that we have taken out insurance against downside risk.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: When do we stop taking out more insurance?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we do cut 50 basis points today, which is the amount the market is expecting, it would bring, to my mind, the real funds rate down to below ½ percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is based on expectations of about 2½ percent inflation, which in fact may be conservative.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To my way of thinking, that is a very accommodative policy by any standard.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, I don’t believe that enough time has elapsed for us to realize the full effect of the cuts that we have already put in place.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I share President Hoenig’s concern that only the market can solve many of the problems that we see out there, and we must give the market time and patience to do so.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The last time real rates were this low was in 2003-04, when the real rate was in fact apparently negative.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation was running around 1 percent or less, and our concern was possible deflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Today, we are not worried about deflation in the near term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We are worried about inflation; inflation has been moving up.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Lowering rates too aggressively in today’s situation would seem to me a risky strategy, fueling inflation; possibly setting up the next boom-bust cycle, which I worry about; and delaying the recognition of losses on bank’s balance sheets but not eliminating them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The main effect of the rate cut will be after the first half of the year, if the economy begins to recover.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we need to be very cautious not to get carried away in our insurance strategies with lowering rates too much.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my view, we are on the verge of overshooting, and I worry about the broad range of consequences for our credibility and the expectations of our future actions such behavior may have.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is closely related to President Lacker’s comments about what people interpret that behavior to mean about what we may do in future episodes.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But two things are even more important, in my mind, about what we may do and what we do today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, we need to be very careful about our communications and not to excessively reinforce the market’s expectation that further rate cuts are coming.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In particular, I would feel much more comfortable with supporting a moderate 25 or 50 basis point cut if the statement language today were more agnostic about the balance of risks, as I suggested in my memo before the meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The market interprets our saying that there are downside risks to growth as that we are planning to cut rates again.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do not think we should encourage those beliefs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I worry that the balance of risks portion of our statements has come to be a code for predicting the path of our federal funds rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that is not a good position for us to be in, nor should we condone it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given the Greenbook forecast, I don’t believe that negative real rates are called for, and signaling further cuts clearly sends the message that negative real rates are on the way, if not already here.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: When our forecasts are released, the public will get our assessments of the risks in our outlook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We don’t need to say anything more about it in the statement.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That, of course, does not preclude us from cutting rates again if our forecast deteriorates further.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But until it does, I am reluctant to encourage the perception that more rate cuts are forthcoming.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Second, as I said in the last go-round, we need to be able to better understand how we are going to unwind these cuts that we have implemented as insurance against the macroeconomic effects and financial disruptions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, this was the theme of the discussion we had before the go-round.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Unwinding those cuts too slowly not only risks our credibility on inflation but also risks setting up the next boom–bust cycle.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Hindsight, of course, is always 20/20, but as we discussed in Monday’s videoconference, the Fed’s being slow to raise rates back up after the deflationary scare was over in 2003 may indeed have contributed to the conditions we are facing today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, it is crucially important, to my mind, that we do have a plan for unwinding the significant cuts we have implemented as insurance against the financial turmoil.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If the market turmoil subsides, I believe this Committee needs to have clear signals as to what we are going to look at and what has to happen before we start to remove the accommodation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe that the Committee must undo the accommodation as aggressively as we put it in play.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We need to determine what indicators we will be looking at to determine when that process should begin.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: When we know ourselves, we want to help the markets and public understand what our process will be as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I strongly believe that we must be both credible and committed policymakers, and our communications must signal not a particular funds rate path but articulate and focus on the contingent nature of that path and help the public understand and appreciate the systematic part of our policies and our policy decisions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think the best course of action today is to lower the fed funds rate by 50 basis points as in alternative B. I’ve heard cogent arguments that 50 basis points would be restrictive and likewise accommodative.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Yesterday I had a chance to look at the disabilities-related display in the elevator lobby on the Concourse Level, and I took some comfort in the fact that many great people are or were bipolar.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So whether it’s restrictive or accommodative, I can be convinced either way.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I can live with the idea that this does not incorporate a great deal of insurance against the downside, provided that the language doesn’t preclude further timely action as we have been using the word “timely.” So regarding paragraph 4, my preference is for language that, first, serves to signal that the Committee is fully aware of the situation and not behind the curve, a signal that’s reassuring and confidence enhancing, and, second, preserves our nimbleness, our flexibility, meaning that it doesn’t preclude any options to respond to developments, including further moves and intermeeting actions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think the straightforward phraseology “downside risks to growth remain” as opposed to what was suggested in alternative A, which included “may well,” is preferable because the alternative A language strikes me as a bit too clever and risks appearing out of touch.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I also think that repetition of the “in a timely manner” language from the January 22 statement preserves the options to move in an intermeeting action if necessary.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I think alternative B language is acceptable because it is spare, straightforward, and familiar, and it’s the least likely to confuse the markets in the near term.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like President Lockhart, I agree with the action and the language of alternative B.

speaker: KOHN
text: As I noted a few minutes ago, I don’t think a real interest rate of around 1 percent, which is where we would be after this action, is really all that aggressively low, given what we’re facing in financial markets and the uncertainty that’s constraining business and household behavior in terms of spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: I guess I wouldn’t obsess so much—a loaded word there—about where we are exactly relative to some estimate of the neutral federal funds rate.

speaker: KOHN
text: As President Plosser pointed out, our band of confidence around that is huge.

speaker: KOHN
text: It moves around a lot when it’s defined in the short-term, three-year window that the staff has been using, but I think we just need to concentrate on the forecast, where we think this path of rates would have us go.

speaker: KOHN
text: The forecast central tendencies that we looked at yesterday look like a pretty good set of tradeoffs between getting back to full employment and damping inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think one message from this longer-term forecast exercise is where the Committee thinks the Taylor curve is and where we would like to end up on it in terms of trading off inflation and output variability.

speaker: KOHN
text: If I heard Brian correctly, these results encompass not only a fairly universal assumption of 50 basis points at this meeting but at least ten of the cases see further rate cuts after that.

speaker: KOHN
text: In my case, I assumed further rate cuts but that they would start to be taken back in 2009.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it seems to me, heading where we’re heading, and maybe even moving a little lower if circumstances permit over future meetings, is perfectly consistent and is consistent in the view of the majority of the Committee with some pretty reasonable outcomes for the economy given the shocks we’re facing and the circumstances we’re in, whatever it implies for where we are relative to some long-run neutral real rate that might pertain over ten or twenty years.

speaker: KOHN
text: Implied by that—and the Vice Chairman said this a few minutes ago—is that it’s not clear that the 1 percent real rate has much, if any, insurance built into it relative to the kinds of headwinds we’re facing.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that a 1 percent real rate is not sustainable indefinitely, but as I pointed out before, we ran with a zero real rate for two years in ’92 and ’93.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think that had any adverse effects on inflation expectations at the time.

speaker: KOHN
text: We explained why we were doing it.

speaker: KOHN
text: We explained the circumstances that were forcing us into that.

speaker: KOHN
text: We kept our eye on inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: You might remember that at the time there was a lot of political pressure that we should lower the rate even further, and we resisted that pressure in part by keeping our eye on inflation expectations and making sure they weren’t moving higher.

speaker: KOHN
text: So if circumstances dictate, I think we could sustain, as the Greenbook has us doing, a 1 percent real federal funds rate for some time without any adverse effects on inflation expectations going forward.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think 50 implies an unacceptable inflation risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it’s consistent with the gradual reduction in inflation that we’ve outlined in our forecast.

speaker: KOHN
text: In these circumstances, we need to concentrate on addressing the economic and financial stability issues that we’re facing.

speaker: KOHN
text: That’s the bigger risk to economic welfare at this time than the risk that inflation might go higher, and the 50 basis points in my mind is just catching up with the deterioration in the economic outlook and the financial situation since the end of October.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are just getting to something that barely takes account of what has happened, with very little insurance.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, I agree that if we got into a situation where we went lower, then these subtle tradeoffs between risk management and the inflation outlook would come into play, but I don’t really see them in play at the level of interest rates that I’m suggesting we be at at the end of this meeting under the current circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do agree with President Plosser.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to think about the circumstances under which we would begin to take back the easing.

speaker: KOHN
text: In the staff forecast we don’t have to think about this for two years, if they’re right.

speaker: KOHN
text: But they may not be right, and if we go further and have insurance, then I think that’s a more important issue.

speaker: KOHN
text: One point that I took from President Evans’s discussion was that there might be a risk in talking about taking it back right now because it would undermine the effects of the ease you put in place.

speaker: KOHN
text: So as a Committee we need to think about the circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s a very subtle and tricky issue.

speaker: KOHN
text: The Chairman can perhaps cover this in his testimony, and obviously we’ve talked about it.

speaker: KOHN
text: It must be reflected in the minutes.

speaker: KOHN
text: But going out front with hammering in public how we’re going to take it back is going to undermine the effects of the ease itself.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we can talk about those circumstances, but I think we need to be careful about overemphasizing the “taking it back” idea, particularly from the current level.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m comfortable with the language of alternative B. I think the first sentence of paragraph 4 does help to say that we think we’ve done something considerable that’s going to be helpful.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is a change from the last thing we put out.

speaker: KOHN
text: Removing “appreciable” in terms of downside risk is also a change, and I agree with that.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I do think there are downside risks even after we move today, and it would be a mistake to avoid that topic.

speaker: KOHN
text: Those risks are still going to be there, even after the funds rate is 3 percent, until the financial markets begin to stabilize and for more than a few weeks.

speaker: KOHN
text: We had a bit of a head fake in October, right?

speaker: KOHN
text: They seemed to be stabilizing.

speaker: KOHN
text: We said the risks were roughly in balance, and then the financial markets collapsed.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we need a period of stable financial developments so that we can gauge the effect on the economy before we go to a balanced risk statement.

speaker: KOHN
text: Right now the risks are still tilted toward the downside on real activity, and that should be our focus.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I support alternative B in the Bluebook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If we cut the federal funds rate a further 50 basis points today, we will have done a lot in just a week and a half, but I think these actions do represent an appropriate response to a substantial deterioration in economic conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I said in my comments on the economic situation, I basically agree with the Greenbook forecast for this year and perceive the risks to be to the downside.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With the fiscal package, a funds rate of 3 percent will likely promote growth in the second half of this year that’s moderate after a brush with recession in the first half.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’m comfortable with this action because I believe our inflation objective is credible, and I do have confidence that we will be able to reverse the accommodation we’re putting in place when it’s appropriate to do so.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But our discussion does highlight the important point that alternative B seems to be appropriate monetary policy in the context of the modal forecast.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It just brings the real funds rate down to the Greenbook estimate of neutral, around 1 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If the economy were to go into a recession, additional easing would be needed and would be appropriate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Also, as Governor Kohn and others have emphasized, alternative B still doesn’t seem to incorporate much of anything for insurance against recession.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So, indeed, there is a case for doing more than B.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There is a case for A, but I wouldn’t go there today.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we can wait, and I think we can watch as developments unfold and monitor data.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to language, the skew in the risks toward a downside surprise and the possible need for insurance against that possibility, especially if we see some further deterioration in financial conditions—that strongly inclines me toward the assessment of risk sentences in alternative B with their asymmetry toward ease.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We need to be absolutely clear, to state clearly today, that we recognize the continued existence of downside risk and communicate that we stand ready to cut further if necessary.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Therefore, I would definitely retain the sentence in alternative B, paragraph 4, that states, “However, downside risks to growth remain.” However, I could see a case, following President Plosser’s suggestion, to substitute the wording from the last sentence of the December 11 statement to the wording in the last line in alternative B.

speaker: YELLEN
