text: This list is dominated by European banks.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Indeed, the only U.S. bank among the top nineteen sponsors is Citigroup.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: However, Citigroup was the largest sponsor of SIVs, which, in addition to issuing ABCP, issue substantial amounts of medium-term notes.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Citigroup, like nearly all SIV sponsors, eventually felt obliged to provide full liquidity support for all the liabilities of its SIVs, which amounted to around $60 billion at year-end.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The memo item shows that some other U.S. banks sponsored securities-related ABCP programs that were relatively small in absolute terms but significant as a share of their total assets.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But losses from leveraged-loan commitments and conduit sponsorship have paled in comparison to the losses some banks and securities firms have incurred from the retention of super senior exposures from ABS CDOs.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: These include exposures that the underwriters never sold, exposures that originally were funded by ABCP issued by the CDOs that was supported by liquidity facilities provided by the underwriters, and relatively small amounts of exposures purchased from affiliated money funds for reputational reasons.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The middle right panel shows the leading underwriters of ABS CDOs in 2006-07.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Merrill Lynch, Citigroup, and UBS head the list.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Each of those firms has suffered very large subprime CDO-related losses, and Citigroup and UBS still reported very significant exposures at year-end.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: As shown in the memo items, among the other very largest U.S. bank holding companies, only Bank of America has suffered significant losses or still has significant exposures from underwriting ABS CDOs.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I should note that the exposures shown in the exhibit are net of hedges purchased from financial guarantors, and most of these firms have hedged a significant portion of their exposure.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: As you know, there are concerns about the ability of the guarantors to honor their obligations under the hedging contracts.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Indeed, some firms have begun to write down the value of their hedges with the most troubled financial guarantors.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The bottom left panel shows total risk-based capital ratios for the four largest U.S. bank holding companies.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: All four remained comfortably above the 10 percent minimum for well- capitalized companies at year-end.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Of course, Citigroup was able to do so only by raising substantial amounts of capital at a relatively high cost, and each of the other companies also announced capital-raising efforts.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Moreover, Citigroup’s year-end ratio of tangible common equity to risk-weighted managed assets was 5.7 percent, well below the 6.5 percent target ratio that several of the rating agencies monitor and that Citigroup seeks to meet.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The bottom right panel shows credit default swap spreads for the three largest U.S. BHCs.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: On balance, spreads for all three have moved up about 60 to 70 basis points since the market turmoil began.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The spread for Citigroup has been elevated since October, when investors began to become aware of its subprime CDO exposures.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The spreads for Bank of America and JPMorgan were in line with a broad index of bank spreads at year-end but jumped in early January on Bank of America’s announcement of its planned acquisition of Countrywide and JPMorgan’s announcement of substantial additions to its loan-loss reserves.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Spreads for all three companies fell back more in line with the index last week.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I will now take your questions on this presentation before you proceed to Mike and Beverly’s presentation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Pat?

speaker: LACKER
text: You characterized underwriting as weak, and I guess the document circulated had some heavy criticism for the credit rating agencies.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to understand more what the nature of that assessment involves.

speaker: LACKER
text: Basically is it ex post regret, or do we have objective evidence about the quality of the decisionmaking ex ante?

speaker: LACKER
text: That evidence, of course, would involve assessments of the probability they should have placed on things we saw.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Mike is going to address that in his briefing.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I guess I’d prefer to delay and just simply say that I think we can point to aspects of their methodology that look fairly weak so that it wasn’t simply an ex post result but one that should have been foreseen at least to a degree if they had had a stronger methodology ex ante.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Obviously that’s Monday morning quarterbacking, but still you can point to specific things that were weaknesses.

speaker: POOLE
text: I have a question on exhibit 2, the top right corner: Are those AAA examples rated as of January 1?

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I think that was the rating at origination.

speaker: POOLE
text: The other question I have is really a comment.

speaker: POOLE
text: On exhibit 1, the middle panel, it seems to me something that needs to be explored here, given that this is not the first time that banks have made a lot of bad bets, is the way in which the management incentives are designed.

speaker: POOLE
text: I just get the impression—and there has been some stuff in the paper recently, the Wall Street Journal or somewhere—that a lot of people are really given incentives to push these products and to make these deals.

speaker: POOLE
text: They walk away with big bonuses, and who in the heck cares what happens some time later.

speaker: POOLE
text: So I think that the management incentives are something very important to investigate in order to have an idea of how that works, and we might be of some assistance in designing something that would be helpful here.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Your exhibit 4 and your risk-based capital ratios, fourth quarter, are those as of December 31?

speaker: HOENIG
text: And do these reflect losses already taken in capital rates?

speaker: PARKINSON
text: They reflect the developments in terms of the changes in their financial statements during the fourth quarter until the year-end.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you have a question, President Yellen?

speaker: YELLEN
text: I wanted to support President Poole’s comment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I remember very well back at Jackson Hole in 2005 that Raghuram Rajan presented a paper in which he emphasized the misalignment of incentives between investors and managers and the fact that almost everyone down the line right up to the investors themselves should have had incentives here.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t know what they were thinking, but everybody was rewarded for the quantity and not the quality of originations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: He warned us before any of this happened that this could come to no good, and I think he did have some suggestions about compensation practices.

speaker: YELLEN
text: These were not popular suggestions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I think this is worth some thought.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t know what the answer is in terms of changing these practices.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Maybe the market will attend to them, but it seems to me that we have had an awful lot of booms and busts in which this type of incentive played a role.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Your presentation and the paper started from the fact that you note the deterioration in underwriting, but we should go one step backward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I suppose another issue here is what we saw in our supervision and whether we acted appropriately given what we saw.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That raises a number of issues that I won’t go into at the moment but that I think we need to be sensitive to.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just a question on exhibit 4, the bottom two panels.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: You have the four banks there, and when you look at the capital ratios, it doesn’t look that discouraging.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But when I look at the credit default swaps, it looks a little less encouraging.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So if I put Wachovia on this, I believe Wachovia’s credit default swaps now are up to 166, which would be much higher than your scale is right now.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So it would be interesting actually to add Wachovia to that list.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The second thing is what you take from the fact that the capital ratios don’t look so bad but the credit default swaps and what the markets are looking at indicate that, in the past month and a half, people— despite the capital infusions—are actually exhibiting more concern about the default experiences that might occur.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Well, particularly with respect to developments in the last month or two, obviously the economic outlook is cloudier.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: As you know, I don’t think we try to reflect that fully in the capital ratios, and there is an element of stress testing and whatnot, but your other important effects are essentially looking through the cycle.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: So that may be part of it.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Also, if you look at the credit default swap spread behavior compared with that for lots of other financial intermediaries out there, these look like very modest changes.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I don’t know—if Mike or someone could help me out—to what extent these would translate into significant increases in actual implied default probabilities, but I wouldn’t think it would be all that large an increase.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I agree with President Poole and President Yellen about the need to focus on compensation structures and incentives, but just two observations.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One is that, if you look at compensation practices among the guys who actually look as though they did pretty well against those who didn’t do so well—I’m not talking about in a mortgage-origination sense but in the major global financial institutions—the structure of compensation doesn’t vary that much.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What varies a lot is how well people control for the inherent problems in the basic compensation structures.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Remember Raghu’s presentation was mostly about hedge fund compensation, and I think he is mostly wrong when you think about that and the incentive structure.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The difference really is how you design your limits to make sure that your traders’ incentives are more aligned with the incentives of the firm as a whole.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The biggest errors and differences are in the design of the process of the checks and balances to compensate for the inherent problems in the compensation structure.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That’s important to know because a lot of these things, if you look at the formal attributes of the risk-management governance structure across these firms, don’t look that different.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What distinguishes how well the guys did is much more subtle around culture, independence, and the quality of judgment exercised at the senior level, and this is important because, when you think about what you can do through supervision and regulation, to affect that stuff is hard.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I have a question for Pat.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Pat, not to overdo this, but where do you put in your diagnosis of contributing factors the constellation of financial conditions that prevailed during the boom and what those did to housing prices?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You know, there’s a tendency for everybody to look at regulation and supervision and the incentives that they have created or failed to mitigate, but there is a reasonable view of the world that you wouldn’t have had the pattern of underwriting standards of mortgages without the trajectory of house prices that occurred.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Sure, maybe what happened in the late stage of the mortgage-origination process contributed to the upside, but if you look at a chart, the rate of house-price appreciation started to decelerate about the time you had the worst erosion in underwriting practices.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Anyway, my basic question is, Where do you put the constellation of financial conditions, not so much just what the Fed was doing but what was happening globally that affected long rates, expectations of future rates, et cetera?

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Well, partly what I would say, in general, about the pricing of risk is that many, many people, including people in the Federal Reserve, were concerned about how narrow spreads were, were concerned about some of the slippage of practices, and were predicting that trouble lay ahead.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But—and I’m certainly speaking for myself—I never expected this magnitude of trouble.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: What I’ve been focusing on are some of the factors that essentially made a bad situation much worse than we expected it to be.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But there is no question that we entered the period with risk being priced very cheaply and a fundamental reassessment of risk.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Again, I think that shouldn’t have surprised anyone, but almost everyone except the most extreme pessimists has been surprised by just how much trouble that repricing of risk has caused.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Some things that we have focused on certainly were not anticipated, and we think they made the situation markedly worse than we expected it to be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there other questions for Pat?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We can continue the presentation.

speaker: GIBSON
text: As noted in the top left panel of exhibit 5, we would like to stress two key points on the rating agency and investor issues.

speaker: GIBSON
text: First, credit rating agencies are one of the weak links that helped a relatively small shock in the subprime mortgage market spread so widely, though certainly not the only one.

speaker: GIBSON
text: This is not just our staff working group’s view—most market participants have also expressed the opinion that rating agencies deserve some of the blame.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Second, the way that some investors use ratings for their own risk management has not kept up with financial innovations, such as the growth of structured finance.

speaker: GIBSON
text: These financial innovations have made a credit rating less reliable as a sufficient statistic for risk.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The top right panel provides a roadmap to our presentation.

speaker: GIBSON
text: To start, I’ll expand on some of the points that Pat made on the role of rating agencies in the financial crisis.

speaker: GIBSON
text: My aim is to show why credit rating agencies were a weak link, which will lead naturally to our recommendations on rating agency practices.

speaker: GIBSON
text: As we go, I’ll point out several places where the rating agency issues link up with the investor practices issues that you’ll hear about next from Bev.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We feel strongly that the ratings and investor issues are really just two angles on the same underlying issue.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The crisis began in the subprime market, the subject of the next panel.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The subprime mess happened—and keeps getting worse—in part because of the issues associated with rating agencies (though as I said earlier, there is plenty of blame to go around).

speaker: GIBSON
text: Our staff working group was asked whether the rating agencies got it wrong when they rated subprime RMBS.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The answer is “yes”—they got it wrong.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Rating agencies badly underestimated the risk of subprime RMBS.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Last year, Moody’s downgraded 35 percent of the first-lien subprime RMBS issued in 2006.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The average size of these subprime RMBS downgrades was two broad rating categories—for example, a downgrade from A to BB—compared with the historical average downgrade of 1⅓ broad rating categories.

speaker: GIBSON
text: As indicated in the exhibit, the rating methodologies for subprime were flawed because the rating agencies relied too much on historical data at several points in their analysis.

speaker: GIBSON
text: First, the rating agencies underestimated how severe a housing downturn could become.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Second, rating agencies underestimated how poorly subprime loans would perform when house prices fell because they relied on historical data that did not contain any periods of falling house prices.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Third, the subprime market had changed over time, making the originator matter more for the performance of subprime loans, but rating agencies did not factor the identity of the originator into their ratings.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Fourth, the rating agencies did not consider the risk that refinancing opportunities would probably dry up in whatever stress event seriously threatened the subprime market.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Of course, the rating agencies were not alone in this.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Many others misjudged these risks as well.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Some have suggested that conflicts of interest were a factor in the poor performance of rating agencies.

speaker: GIBSON
text: While conflicts of interest at rating agencies certainly do exist, because the rating is paid for by the issuer, we didn’t see evidence that conflicts affected ratings.

speaker: GIBSON
text: That said, we also cannot say that conflicts were not a factor.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The SEC currently has examinations under way at the rating agencies to gather the detailed information that is needed to check whether conflicts had a significant effect.

speaker: GIBSON
text: In the next panel, I turn to the ABS CDOs that had invested heavily in subprime.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Rating agencies got it wrong for ABS CDOs.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The downgrade rate of ABS CDOs in 2007 was worse than the previous historical worst case, just as it was for subprime.

speaker: GIBSON
text: AAA tranches of ABS CDOs turned out to be remarkably vulnerable: Last year, twenty-seven AAA tranches were downgraded all the way from AAA to below investment grade.

speaker: GIBSON
text: As indicated in the exhibit, the main reason that rating agencies got it wrong for ABS CDOs was that their rating models were very crude.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Rating agencies used corporate CDO models to rate ABS CDOs.

speaker: GIBSON
text: They had no data to estimate the correlation of defaults across asset-backed securities.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Despite the many flaws of credit ratings as a sufficient statistic for credit risk, the rating agencies used ratings as the main measure of the quality of the subprime RMBS that the ABS CDOs invested in.

speaker: GIBSON
text: And the rating agencies did only limited, ad hoc analysis of how the timing of cash flows affects the risk of ABS CDO tranches.

speaker: GIBSON
text: As a result, the ratings of ABS CDOs should have been viewed as highly uncertain.

speaker: GIBSON
text: As one risk manager put it, ABS CDOs were “model risk squared.” A final point on ABS CDOs is that the market’s reaction to the poor performance of ABS CDOs makes it clear that some investors did not understand the differences between corporate and structured-finance ratings.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Because structured-finance securities are built on diversified portfolios, they have more systematic risk and less idiosyncratic risk than corporate securities.

speaker: GIBSON
text: They will naturally be more sensitive to macroeconomic risk factors like house prices, and by design, downgrades of structured-finance securities will be more correlated and larger than downgrades of corporate bonds.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Turning to the bottom panel, as Pat noted, in August of last year the subprime shock hit the ABCP markets, especially markets for ABCP issued by SIVs.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Rating agencies also got it wrong for the SIVs.

speaker: GIBSON
text: More than two-thirds of the SIVs’ commercial paper has been downgraded or has defaulted.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The problem with the ratings was that the rating agencies’ models for SIVs relied on a rapid liquidation of the SIVs’ assets to shield the SIVs’ senior debt from losses.

speaker: GIBSON
text: While this might have worked if a single SIV got into trouble, the market would not have been able to absorb a rapid liquidation by all SIVs at the same time.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Once investors began to understand the rating model for SIVs, even SIVs with no subprime exposure could not roll over their commercial paper.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Investors who thought they were taking on credit risk became uncomfortable with the market risk and liquidity risk that are inherent in a SIV’s business model.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The next exhibit presents the staff subgroup’s recommendations for addressing the weaknesses in credit ratings for structured-credit products.

speaker: GIBSON
text: A common theme of our recommendations is drawing sharper distinctions between corporate ratings and structured-finance ratings.

speaker: GIBSON
text: First, we recommend that rating agencies should differentiate structured-finance ratings from corporate ratings by providing additional measures of the risk or leverage of structured-finance securities to the market along with the rating.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We don’t make a specific recommendation on exactly what measures of risk or leverage because we believe rating agencies and investors should work out the details together (on this and the recommendations to follow).

speaker: GIBSON
text: Second, rating agencies should convey a rating’s uncertainty in an understandable way.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The ratings of ABS CDOs were highly uncertain because the models were so crude.

speaker: GIBSON
text: This is what I call the Barry Bonds solution—put an asterisk on the rating if you have doubts about the quality.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Third, we recommend more transparency from rating agencies for structured-finance ratings.

speaker: GIBSON
text: What we need is not just a tweak to the existing transparency, but a whole new paradigm that actually helps investors get the information they want and need.

speaker: GIBSON
text: For example, why can’t the rating agency pass on to investors, along with its rating, all the information it got from the issuer that it used to assign the rating?

speaker: GIBSON
text: Fourth, we recommend that rating agencies be conservative when they rate new or evolving asset classes.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Fifth, the rating agencies should enhance their rating frameworks for structured products.

speaker: GIBSON
text: For example, when they rate RMBS, they should consider the originator as well as the servicer as an important risk factor.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Our last recommendation is addressed to regulators, including the Federal Reserve.

speaker: GIBSON
text: When we reference a rating, we should differentiate better between corporate and structured-finance ratings.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Sometimes we do that already, but we could provide some leadership to the market by doing more.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Now Bev will discuss the work on investor practices.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Mike has described how the rating agencies treated structured- credit products; a closely related issue is how investors used these ratings.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Did investors rely too much on ratings in making their investment decisions?

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Did they take false comfort from ratings and not really appreciate the risks they were assuming, leading to excessive growth of the market for subprime structured credit?

speaker: HIRTLE
text: As noted in the top panel of exhibit 7, our approach was to examine these questions through the lens of one representative type of institutional investor: public pension funds.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Public pension funds are an informative example of investor use (and misuse) of credit ratings for several reasons.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: First, public pension boards of directors are composed largely of representatives of the employees and retirees covered by the pension plan and have only limited financial expertise in some cases.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Second, survey evidence suggests that a high portion of these funds use credit ratings in their investment guidelines.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Finally, relative to some other investors, many public pension funds provide significant public information about their activities.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: While we need to be cautious in generalizing, we believe that practices in the pension fund sector reflect the tensions faced by other institutional investors in making risk assessments and investment decisions.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: We examined the investment practices and fund governance of 11 public pension plans.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: These plans ranged from the largest fund—CalPERS, with $250 billion in assets—to six much smaller plans with assets of $6 billion to $11 billion.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: We used the funds’ 2006 comprehensive annual financial reports, which were generally the most recent available, and the funds’ websites to generate our information.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: We focused specifically on the funds’ fixed-income segments, since this is the asset class in which structured-credit products would likely be held and for which credit ratings are used.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: The middle panel lists some key conclusions from this review.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: The first is that these funds have developed workable market solutions to address inexperience or lack of financial sophistication among their managers and board members.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: These include hiring professional investment managers to make investment decisions on their behalf and, perhaps as significantly, hiring investment consultants to structure asset-allocation strategies, to select investment managers and develop mandates guiding their actions, and to monitor and assess fund performance.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: While these funds clearly obtain significant professional advice in managing their investments, our review suggests several ways in which these arrangements could be improved in light of recent financial innovation.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Specifically, the mandates guiding investment managers have not always kept pace with the growth of structured-credit markets.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: These mandates typically require managers to meet or exceed returns on a benchmark index or of a peer group of investment managers, while constraining the risk the managers may assume.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Credit ratings play an important role in these risk constraints—for instance, by imposing a minimum average rating for the portfolio or a minimum rating on individual securities.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: However, few of the funds we profiled made significant distinctions between structured-credit and other securities in these credit-rating-based constraints, although there were sometimes other limits on the aggregate share of asset-backed positions.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: The failure to make this distinction provides scope for investment managers to generate higher returns by moving into structured-credit products, without raising warning signals about the additional risk these positions entail.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: This is not necessarily a “naïve” use of credit ratings by investment managers, as they could well have recognized that higher-yielding structured-credit products embodied significant additional risk relative to similarly rated corporate debt.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Instead, it reflects a previously effective mechanism used by fund boards to convey risk appetite to these managers falling out-of-date with the emergence and rapid growth of a new form of credit instrument.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: As indicated in the bottom panel, our key recommendation is that the pension fund industry and other investors should re-evaluate the use of credit ratings in investment mandates.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: In a narrow sense, these mandates should distinguish between ratings on structured credit and those on more traditional corporate credit.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: However, the more fundamental point is that mandates would do a better job of enforcing desired risk limits on the overall portfolio if they acknowledged differences in risk, return, and correlation across instruments rather than relying on generic credit ratings.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: A second important point is that investors should ensure that their investment consultants have independent views of the quality and adequacy of credit ratings for the types of positions in their portfolios.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: This is particularly important if mandates guiding investment manager behavior feature credit ratings as a key risk constraint.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: That completes our prepared remarks.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: We would be happy to take your questions before we proceed to the final presentation.

speaker: LACKER
text: How much of these weaknesses would have been identified by an impartial observer in January 2006, say, without knowledge of what has happened since then?

speaker: GIBSON
text: Are you talking about the credit rating agency weaknesses?

speaker: GIBSON
text: There are plenty of investors who said, “We are staying out of that ABS CDO market because we don’t trust the ratings and we don’t think we have an ability to model it.” But there are also enough who were willing to take on that risk.

speaker: GIBSON
text: So I think it is a combination.

speaker: FISHER
text: Going back to exhibit 5, the second panel, your point that we have no evidence of conflicts of interest having an effect on ratings, I am thinking about the investor- practices presentation.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is an inherent conflict of interest because the issuers pay the raters.

speaker: FISHER
text: By one account, Moody’s earned 44 percent of their revenue in 2006 from rating structured products.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have always wondered—and by the way, I have been on the side of the table that has worked a rating agency and have gotten what I wanted—what about just a common sense solution, which is that the investors rather than the issuers pay the rating agencies?

speaker: GIBSON
text: That used to be the way it was before 1970—the investors paid.

speaker: GIBSON
text: I think the common explanation for why that model faded was that, once photocopy machines came into existence, there was no way to constrain the information that they were providing just to subscribers.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am well aware of that.

speaker: FISHER
text: But is there an inherent conflict of interest in the process?

speaker: GIBSON
text: We are not denying that there is a conflict of interest.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We looked at some of the mechanisms that rating agencies have put in place to address conflicts of interest, and that is something that every rating agency is aware of.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The only question is whether the mechanisms that are in place to address conflicts of interest were working or whether they need to be enhanced.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Our conclusion was that we don’t really have the detailed information to know whether there were specific conflicts of interest, and we are looking to the SEC to provide that detailed information.

speaker: GIBSON
text: But lots of other things seemed to go wrong with the rating agencies that don’t rely on conflicts of interest as an explanation.

speaker: GIBSON
text: I think people who have looked at the question of the issuer’s paying versus the investor’s paying feel that, given how costly it is to rate these things even in the mediocre way that it has been done, it would be difficult to generate enough revenue through a pure investor-pay model.

speaker: GIBSON
text: That is not to say there couldn’t be more competition between the two kinds, and there are some proposals out there to do that.

speaker: FISHER
text: Again, remember how costly it has proven to investors to have that built- in conflict of interest.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Actually, I wanted to focus on the same issue—conflict of interest.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is something I did a little work on in the past.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When you look at the standard corporate ratings market, the move to have the issuer pay really did not create a problem in the market.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There clearly is an inherent conflict of interest, but there are things that can counter that—in particular, reputation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We could talk about Arthur Andersen, too, because I am going to talk about the more complicated issues of conflicts of interest.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: With plain vanilla conflicts of interest, if there is enough information, the market frequently can solve the problem because if you know that if you do what the issuer wants and you give a good rating, then you lose your reputation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Then, if it has no value, issuers won’t pay for it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What is interesting here is that for the subprime market, you didn’t find any evidence of conflicts of interest, and I am not surprised by that, because those securities are much more straightforward.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Where I really do worry about the conflict of interest is in the structured products because one thing that happened was that it became less plain vanilla.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You actually had consulting practices inside the credit rating agencies; these structures are very complicated, and you need to slice here and dice here, and consultants were providing advice on structuring them and making a lot of money, and then it was much less transparent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What I wondered about here is that you didn’t say this for the first one, subprime RMBS.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You said you didn’t find the evidence.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But what about the CDOs and the SIVs, for which I would expect that this problem would have been more severe?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In the book that I wrote with others on conflicts of interest in the financial services industry, we actually said that there was not a problem with the plain vanilla products because the markets have the information, but we worried about exactly this issue in terms of the structured products.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am just wondering whether or not it was an accident that you said for the plain vanilla that there was less problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Could there have been an issue here?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The reason this gets complicated is that the standard view of conflicts of interest in Arthur Andersen was in the firm’s compensation scheme.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Actually, the conflict of interest was that the Texas unit did not worry about and weakened—not their ethics, but what is it?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The center has rules for its branches so that they don’t screw the overall firm, and that is what got weakened during the fight between the consulting part and the auditing part.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So do you have any information on these very complicated elements, particularly the nontransparent parts?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Was it an accident that you said for subprime that you didn’t find evidence, and for these is there more possibility that there was a problem?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That really does have important implications for the nature of the regulation and accreditation agencies and also their ability to give good ratings for these very complex nontransparent products.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You talked about investor practices later, Bev, when you said that we should differentiate between plain vanilla and this very complex stuff.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t know whether or not you have views on this.

speaker: GIBSON
text: There is certainly a possibility that conflicts of interest were occurring in all these areas.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We are taking a somewhat neutral position because we don’t really have the detailed information to say more.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But this is the typical Federal Reserve cautiousness, and I am pushing you a little harder.

speaker: GIBSON
text: I know, but I am a Federal Reserve economist.

speaker: GIBSON
text: I would agree with your point that separating out these nonrating businesses from the rating businesses is important, and rating agencies have announced some changes along these lines.

speaker: GIBSON
text: When we looked at our recommendations, we didn’t really feel as though, even if they separated out rating businesses from nonrating businesses and even if they did all the things that people who are concerned about conflicts of interest want them to do, it would solve the problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There would still be problems.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We think the real problem is that they didn’t differentiate well enough between structured-finance ratings and corporate ratings, and that is where we would like to put the focus.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Securities regulators are already focused on conflicts of interest, and there are codes of conduct regarding how rating agencies have to behave, and those are monitored.

speaker: GIBSON
text: So, coupled with the SEC’s already doing examinations, that wasn’t an area we chose to focus on, but we really can’t say for sure what was going on.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One quick follow-up on that—is one implication that we might take from this that structured products are just so complicated that they may never get good ratings or sufficiently good ratings, so the market really has to shrink?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Could the rating agencies just fix themselves up so that they actually could do decent ratings?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m trying to get a feel for this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It really relates to the issue that Bev raised, which is you want to differentiate between the two.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But is there something inherently problematic so that maybe people should just realize that these structured products are just not such a great thing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Financial engineering can go too far.

speaker: GIBSON
text: In fact, ABS CDOs are disappearing or have disappeared.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Investors don’t have any appetite for them.

speaker: GIBSON
text: SIVs are disappearing as well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But they could come back.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think subprime lending will come back under a different business model.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Really, the question is, What sort of market forces would produce that outcome?

speaker: GIBSON
text: It certainly seems as though things should move in that direction, and we feel that some of the recommendations we are making on the differentiation between structured-finance securities and corporate securities would encourage the rating agencies to put more scrutiny on the structured-finance side of it.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Yes, those ratings should be lower, especially when you factor in things like the complexity and the uncertainty.

speaker: HOENIG
text: My comment is on the conflicts of interest as well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The only thing I would like to add is that this is not the first time the rating agencies have miscalculated the risk and put that out there.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The incentives are designed to do exactly that, and it will occur again.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think this statement is too generous to the rating agencies.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The incentives are driving them to do this, they did it, and they will do it again in the future.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It is just inherent that, when you are going to make that kind of money and if you can get it down to working with them and pushing this stuff out, it really is a matter, for those who use them, that you get what you pay for.

speaker: POOLE
text: I didn’t know anything about SIVs before last summer, but I must say when I began to learn something about them, I was astonished because it would seem to me that, in Finance 101, you don’t finance long-term, risky assets with short-dated paper.

speaker: POOLE
text: There’s a maturity mismatch, and there’s a rollover risk, and we’ve known about that kind of thing for 100 years, I suppose.

speaker: POOLE
text: So my question is, Could these things have been marketed as standalone entities without the banks’ sponsorship, which was there in, I guess, most cases?

speaker: POOLE
text: Second, if they wouldn’t really fly as standalone entities, it would seem to me that the regulators should have insisted that they be consolidated on the books of the bank.

speaker: GIBSON
text: A lot of the SIVs were standalone entities managed by independent asset- management companies that were set up to do that.

speaker: GIBSON
text: All the SIVs are in the process of winding down now, and in the immediate aftermath of what happened in August, that was when there was a crunch in the ABCP market.

speaker: POOLE
text: But when you say the asset-management companies, are they providing at least in principle some liquidity support or something?

speaker: GIBSON
text: SIVs had partial liquidity backup lines from banks covering one week’s maximum withdrawal or two weeks’ maximum withdrawal.

speaker: GIBSON
text: That was the way to a rating.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The SIVs were operating under the regulation of the rating agencies.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The rating agencies modeled their portfolios, and they modeled the inflows and outflows, so I think it’s fair to blame the rating agencies at least partially for allowing the SIVs to grow to $400 billion or whatever it was.

speaker: PETERS
text: There is a large, independent SIV not affiliated with a bank, named Gordian Knot, that is still in existence.

speaker: PETERS
text: It’s under severe pressure, but it has been weathering the storm.

speaker: PETERS
text: One can argue it might have been more conservative than some of the other SIVs.

speaker: KOHN
text: My question is on exhibit 6, and the question is, Are we making any progress here?

speaker: KOHN
text: In particular, are the rating agencies stepping up to the process of doing different ratings, different nomenclature for the structured finance?

speaker: KOHN
text: My impression is that there is a lot of resistance, at least there was as of a few weeks ago.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Your impression may be more informed than mine, but I would say that the rating agencies are doing a lot of self-examination now.

speaker: GIBSON
text: I haven’t seen them willing, in my opinion, to go far enough in the directions that we’ve outlined.

speaker: GIBSON
text: A lot of their recommendations focus on managing conflicts of interest and doing a better job of separating compensation from the rating and things like that.

speaker: GIBSON
text: I would say that I haven’t seen enough on the sort of recommendations that we are pushing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Did you have any questions?

speaker: WARSH
text: I’d add only that I think where the rating agencies are now is trying to come up with cleaner boxes and better governance—Sarbanes-Oxley types of structures, ombudsmen, liaisons, Chinese walls.

speaker: WARSH
text: The core issues that Mike and his team bring up seem highly resistant to change, but you know, there will be nothing like three months of public hearings, if not hangings.

speaker: WARSH
text: That could change that dynamic, but that’s in the early stages.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One, on the conflict of interest issue, with respect to traditional corporate credits, it seems that credit rating agencies do pretty darn well and certainly have done very well before this.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So it’s clear that it’s not just fundamental to the model that it can’t work.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it’s clear enough to remind people of that and that people trusted those ratings throughout all the turbulence during the summertime.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But that said, it gets back to some of the other points that have been raised.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: What was special about these particular areas that led to a breakdown?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The question is, Well, why did they have bad models?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If they were able to develop good models for these other things, in principle they are capable of developing good models, but they seem to have developed poor models here.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now, that could be succumbing to a conflict of interest, or it could be something specific in this area.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I am reminded that another area in which they are perceived to have done a very poor job was in sovereign ratings back a couple of decades ago.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t know whether it’s worthwhile to drill down into the characteristics of where this model seems to be successful and doesn’t seem to be subject to significant conflicts of interest or where it does, whether it relates to particular information issues.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, one thought that I had with respect to these structured products—and you should tell me whether this is true or not—is that most times when a corporation comes to get a rating they’ve decided to issue a particular security—that is, if GM comes, their CFO has decided to issue ten-year debt.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If you come to a credit rating agency, however, the credit rating agency can say, “Well, why don’t you issue six securities rather than one?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we chop it up in these different ways, I can make more revenues off that, so I have more of an incentive to work with you on this.”

speaker: GIBSON
text: I definitely agree with you that it’s more difficult to rate structured-finance securities than corporate securities because with structured-finance securities you have a lot of quantitative modeling of future cash flows with a lot of uncertainty.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Clearly the ABS CDOs are very complicated structures because it’s a two-layer securitization—a securitization that invests in securitizations—and the rating agencies didn’t drill all the way down to model the ultimate underlying loans.

speaker: GIBSON
text: They relied on simplifying assumptions and aggregations that were very crude.

speaker: GIBSON
text: But because they were branded as CDOs, people usually understood them to be corporate CDOs that invest in 100 corporate bonds, which is a simpler, one-layer structure.

speaker: GIBSON
text: So the rating agencies were willing to rate these much more complicated things and investment banks were willing to market them to investors who were willing to buy them because they all were willing to believe that a CDO is a CDO is a CDO, and, in fact, that wasn’t really true.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Yes, it might just be interesting to drill down and see where the successes are and where they haven’t been successful and whether it has something to do with the model.

speaker: GIBSON
text: Oh, it’s definitely not a random sample of asset classes that we chose to look at.

speaker: GIBSON
text: The rating agencies have done a great job in many other places, I agree.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Right, but just thinking about those differences, I think sometimes the rating agencies may be excessively maligned.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They actually do provide something that’s very useful, and we don’t want to throw the baby out with the bath water.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But also on that, there is a severe lack of competition among rating agencies, and we’ve tried to address that through some legislation, which doesn’t seem to have been very successful at addressing that issue.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This is getting back to Governor Mishkin’s point and some other points about why competition doesn’t get us to a better solution.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It seems that part of it is a regulatory structure that strongly discourages competition.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Did you think about addressing that issue?

speaker: GIBSON
text: The regulatory structure has been changed now as a result of the law that was passed in 2006, at least if you’re talking about getting the regulatory stamp of approval from the SEC to become a nationally recognized statistical rating organization.

speaker: GIBSON
text: That’s now just a notification process by which, if you meet some minimum requirements, the SEC is required to okay you.

speaker: GIBSON
text: So entry is now easy whereas before it used to be restricted by the SEC.

speaker: GIBSON
text: In some sense there’s a bit of a natural monopoly going on because, if you really had a couple of rating agencies that you trusted, it’s not clear why someone would be willing to transfer from an established to a new one.

speaker: GIBSON
text: But if you were to take some of our recommendations to the next level and talk about how you would actually implement this and how you would go about making this have some success, one thing people have suggested is that maybe we should help investors set up their own rating agencies— maybe they don’t want to do that now—and maybe more transparency from the existing rating agencies and from the issuers.

speaker: GIBSON
text: It would then be easier for a new rating agency that’s funded by investors to get going and get some traction if there were more transparency around the whole process.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: For sure, although I think we tried something like that with the Sarbanes-Oxley issues of independent research—because this in some sense is a parallel to independent research—and even required funding of that, and that doesn’t really seem to have taken off.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So it seems as though the model, even with its flaws, is the only one that seems to be sustainable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But drilling down more into where those flaws are, in some sense we’re seeing a privatization—I’m not quite sure what the right word is—with some of the very sophisticated investors effectively building their own internal credit rating agencies.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That’s what hedge funds do, and so you’re getting in some sense a loss of the public rating—a kind of free rider problem or whatever is the right way to characterize it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In some sense there may be a loss because you’re getting this to be just purely private, but maybe that’s a gain because those are the only guys who should be in this game.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It certainly makes it difficult to sustain the credit rating agency or industry.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We have kind of a dual problem in that we want investors to do a better job of evaluating the risks, and maybe better ratings would help on that.

speaker: GIBSON
text: At the same time, the existing rating agencies did a bad job, so we have to criticize them.

speaker: GIBSON
text: We have to find some way to reconcile those.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have President Evans for a two-hander and then President Lockhart and President Lacker.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I also see that President Plosser has a two-hander, and I think at that point we should probably go onto the last presentation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I can pass if it gets too long.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So President Evans, President Lockhart, and President Lacker.

speaker: EVANS
text: I had an elementary question that Governor Kroszner’s question kicked off.

speaker: EVANS
text: The background briefing was very well written and very clear, which made me think that I understood things, and I probably don’t.

speaker: EVANS
text: But you used the term “get a rating,” and at other times you talk about it as if it’s a sufficient statistic and how the agencies were warned that it’s not a sufficient statistic.

speaker: EVANS
text: There are transition matrices to downgrade, and yet they violated that themselves because you said that for the ABS, they thought of it as a sufficient statistic themselves.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is a lot of this inherently a multidimensional risk model that’s required for some of these structured- finance vehicles, whereas for the corporates it’s closer to a single dimensional risk model?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’d like to ask as a practical matter what weighting we should put in our expectations or even our recommendations on reform of the rating system versus the expectation that investors would actually reduce their reliance on ratings.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My impression is that many institutional investors, especially public pension funds, are notoriously understaffed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Then they work for, as you pointed out in your presentation, boards that either represent the beneficiaries or in some respects are quite political in nature and not necessarily financially sophisticated.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That would lead me to the conclusion that, as a practical matter, they’re going to be highly reliant on ratings.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The ratio of professional employees to the volume of investment is so low that they have to choose their restaurants by stars because they don’t have time to do the tasting themselves or they’re not given the budgets to do that now.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I’m curious about this tension between getting the rating system right versus having the investors reduce their reliance on ratings.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Well, I think you’ve identified the key problem that many of these funds face, and the important entities in many ways are these investment consultants.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: At least the funds we looked at all hire one or more of these investment consultants.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: Many of them are from large, globally active firms, and the role that those consultants play is precisely to address the issues that you’ve raised.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: They help them select the asset manager who is doing the investing.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: They help them design the mandates or instructions.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: They help them monitor what the asset managers are doing and assess their performance.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: So to some extent those consultants are a kind of sweet spot for these funds in terms of where the additional layer of sophistication that doesn’t run just off the rating could come from.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But is your impression that those supplemental parties, the consultants and the asset managers themselves, have the credit analysis and valuation capability to address sophisticated structured products?

speaker: HIRTLE
text: We didn’t do an evaluation of them, but some of them are from very, very large firms.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: They are advising funds in the trillions of dollars across all their different clients.

speaker: HIRTLE
text: That is the service they are selling, and so they should be—they had better be—in a position to do that.

speaker: FISHER
text: May I just suggest that you reexamine that proposition?

speaker: FISHER
text: They usually evaluate performance principally after going through initial screening devices.

speaker: FISHER
text: They almost never, that I’m aware of, provide the kind of analysis that you’re assuming.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I would reexamine that proposition.

speaker: LACKER
text: My memory of Finance 101 is that you don’t buy long-term, risky assets funded by short debt without sufficient compensation.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the neglected aspect of the whole episode we went through was how people would have been compensated in other circumstances, but that’s a different discussion.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think these recommendations make sense, and confirmation of that is that the market is moving in that direction anyway.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t know how many of these recommendations were put forward by those market participants you cited who two years ago were not trusting these ratings—I think that’s a key question.

speaker: LACKER
text: But the broader thing here is that the world of finance now is a world of competing econometric analysis, and we’re never going to rate the model risk if you ask the question, What would you expect the behavior of a market like that to display?

speaker: LACKER
text: You’d expect occasional big misses from erring assumptions.

speaker: LACKER
text: You’d expect those misses to be corrected by people reflecting and improving practices going forward.

speaker: LACKER
text: A sort of Schumpeterian process in this is going to generate model risk and big model misses, and so I think it’s being careful to keep track of whether the insights we’ve gleaned are hindsight or should have been known ahead of time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we continue with the final portion?

speaker: GREENLEE
text: To support the Financial Stability Forum’s Working Group on Market and Institutional Resilience, as noted in the top panel of exhibit 8, supervisors from France, Germany, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States formed the “senior supervisors group” in late October.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Participating U.S. supervisors included the OCC and SEC as well as the Federal Reserve.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: The group’s goal was to develop a common understanding, through a series of interviews with selected firms, of how the risk-management systems of core financial institutions performed during the financial market turbulence.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: The top right panel of exhibit 8 shows the 11 banking firms that supervisors interviewed.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: This effort was not a complete review of all firms and events.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: For example, we did not meet with Bear Stearns or Morgan Stanley as part of this effort.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Rather, it was designed to inform supervisory authorities about the general effectiveness of risk management at global financial institutions.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: The supervisors have prepared a paper detailing their findings, which will be conveyed to the FSF and released publicly.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: The bottom panel lists some observations about the firms’ overall performance.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Most large financial services firms, while affected by market developments, generally avoided significant losses.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Although most firms’ risk-management processes worked as intended, there were some definite outliers.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Some firms recognized the emerging additional risks and took deliberate actions to limit or mitigate them.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Others recognized the additional risks but accepted them.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Still other firms did not fully recognize the risks in time to mitigate them adequately.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Moreover, the risk-management practices varied by firm and by strategy, as did the range of outcomes to date.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: I should note that the primary risk-management weaknesses observed here are not new.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: They have been observed in past episodes and are thoroughly discussed in existing risk-management literature and supervisory guidance.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: As noted in the top panel of exhibit 9, the senior supervisors group identified four primary factors that differentiated the organizations that suffered larger losses from those that did not: (1) the effectiveness of senior management oversight of balance sheet, liquidity, and capital positions; (2) the effectiveness of communications among senior management, business lines, and risk-management functions; (3) the sophistication, diversity, and adaptability of risk measures utilized; and (4) the attention devoted to valuation issues.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: With respect to senior management oversight, as indicated in the bottom panel of exhibit 9, the more effective firms were more disciplined in measuring and limiting these risks in advance of the crisis and proved to be more agile in reducing exposures or hedging when the crisis occurred.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: These firms focused on maintaining a strong balance sheet with strong capital and liquidity positions throughout the entire organization.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Senior management of these organizations had established adequate capital and liquidity buffers that could sustain the firm through a period without access to the market for funding.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: They have created and effectively enforced internal pricing mechanisms, capital allocation methodologies, and limits that provided effective incentives for individual business line managers to control activities that might otherwise lead to significant balance sheet growth or contingent liquidity demands.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Conversely, the less effective firms were not as focused on the overall strength of their balance sheet across all legal entities and thus operated with more limited liquidity and capital buffers.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: These organizations had weaker controls over their balance sheets and were more focused on earnings growth or defense of a market leadership position.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: These firms did not have limit structures that were consistently or effectively enforced, which allowed business lines to grow balance sheet exposures rapidly and increase contingent liquidity exposures.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: They did not properly aggregate or monitor off-balance-sheet exposures across the organization, including the exposure to contingency back-up lines of credit to ABCP programs and generally did not have in place effective financial controls, including capital allocation processes, commensurate with the business strategy.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: The top panel of exhibit 10 provides additional detail on the importance of effective communications among senior management, business lines, and risk- management functions.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: The more effective firms emphasized a comprehensive, firmwide, consolidated assessment of risk.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Senior managers of these organizations were actively engaged and had in place a disciplined culture and well-established processes for routine discussion of current and emerging risks across the business lines, risk management, and the corporate treasury function.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Senior managers at these organizations collectively made decisions about the firm’s overall risk appetite, exposures, and risk mitigation strategies rather than relying solely on the judgment of business lines.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: They were able to effectively leverage the assessment of risks from one business line to consider how subprime exposures, for example, might affect other businesses.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: As a result, the more effective firms had a more timely and well- informed perspective on how market developments could unfold.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: In some cases, senior management had almost a year to evaluate the magnitude of the emerging risks from subprime mortgages on its various business lines.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: This, in turn, enabled them to implement plans for reducing their exposures while it was still practical and more cost effective to do so.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Conversely, less effective firms were siloed, did not effectively share information across business lines on emerging risks, and were comparatively slower in taking actions to mitigate exposures as each business line had to assess and consider emerging risks on their own without the benefit of views or actions taken by other business line managers.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: With regard to the risk measures utilized, as shown in the bottom panel, the more effective firms used a wide range of risk measures and analytical tools to discuss and challenge views on credit and market risk broadly across different business lines within the firm in a disciplined fashion.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: These firms have thought more thoroughly about the interplay of their risk measures than the other firms and used a combination of different risk measures and scenario analysis to understand risk exposures.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: It also appears that the more effective firms had committed more resources to risk- management and management information systems.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: As a result, they had more timely and scalable management information systems and in large part did not have to create new management reports to understand risks and exposures.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Conversely, the less effective firms were too dependent on a single quantitative risk measure, and they did not utilize scenario analysis in their decisionmaking and tended to apply a “mechanical” risk-management approach.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Management information systems also were not as scalable, and there was a need to develop a number of ad hoc reports to help senior management understand the risks and exposures of the company.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: The top panel of exhibit 11 elaborates on the fourth factor that proved critical, which is the attention devoted to valuation issues.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: The more effective organizations were more disciplined in how they valued the holdings of complex or potentially illiquid securities.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: They employed more-sophisticated valuation practices and had invested in the development of pricing models and staff with specialized expertise.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: These organizations were skeptical of and less reliant on external ratings and emphasized mark-to-market discipline in their businesses in ways that others did not.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Less effective organizations in some cases did not have key valuation models in place prior to the market disruption, relied heavily on third-party views of risk, and tended to have a narrower view of the risks associated with their CDO business as mainly being credit risk and did not actively seek market valuation information.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: The bottom panel explains how supervisors are planning to address the specific deficiencies.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: As I mentioned earlier in my presentation, the risk-management deficiencies identified during this exercise are not new, and existing supervisory guidance addresses these issues.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Therefore, supervisory efforts will include addressing risk-management deficiencies at each company through the supervisory process and re-emphasizing the importance of strong, independent risk management through a series of speeches, industry outreach, and possible re-issuance of existing guidance.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: In addition, supervisors plan to complete the work already under way within the Basel Committee on Bank Supervision to update liquidity risk management guidance to strengthen industry practices.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: A review of existing Federal Reserve guidance on market and liquidity risk management is under way to ensure that it effectively outlines the need for banks to use a number of tools to include multiple ways of viewing quantitative and qualitative risk analysis, including VAR, stress tests, and scenario analysis.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Finally, supervisors plan to develop, on an interagency basis, guidance related to the management of the originate-to-distribute model to ensure that banking organizations effectively manage the credit, market, and operational risks of this activity.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: I will now turn it over to Art Angulo to discuss related regulatory policies.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The top panel of exhibit 12 sets forth the question we sought to address—namely, to what extent did regulatory incentives contribute to or fail to mitigate weaknesses exposed by the recent turmoil?

speaker: ANGULO
text: In doing so, we defined the term “regulatory incentives” to encompass both regulatory capital and financial reporting requirements.

speaker: ANGULO
text: In addition, we distinguished between policies that may have mattered for the buildup to the market turmoil and those that have made managing the turmoil more challenging.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Our conclusions are summarized in the middle panel.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Not surprisingly, incentives to minimize regulatory capital are a much more important driver of bank behavior than financial reporting incentives.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Moreover, the current regulatory capital framework is not neutral as to how banks structure risk positions.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Both the leverage ratio and the Basel I risk-based capital framework have encouraged banks to securitize low-risk assets and, importantly, to support securitizations of higher-risk assets through instruments with low mandated capital charges, such as 364-day liquidity facilities.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Financial reporting incentives were not critical to banks’ decisions, although certain financial reporting issues—particularly disclosure practices—have been a factor in how the turmoil has been unfolding.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Before I turn to specific recommendations, it is important to emphasize that improvements were already in train even before the market difficulties emerged last summer.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Most significantly, the Basel 2 advanced approaches and related improvements greatly enhance the risk sensitivity of the regulatory capital framework and create incentives for better risk management.

speaker: ANGULO
text: In the bottom panel are three examples relevant to the issues we have been discussing this morning.

speaker: ANGULO
text: First, capital charges for most unused short-term credit and liquidity facilities have been increased to more adequately reflect the risk exposure.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Second, new standards for banks to hold capital against the default risk of complex, less liquid credit products in the trading book are being finalized, as the Basel Committee is currently seeking public comment on principles for calculating a so-called incremental default risk charge against such products.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I should note that the work to develop the incremental default risk principles was done by a joint Basel Committee–IOSCO working group co-chaired by Norah Barger.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Third, the securitization framework in Basel 2, which builds on previous unilateral U.S. enhancements, establishes a more risk-sensitive capital treatment for securitization exposures—it bases capital charges on estimates of underlying risk rather than on an exposure’s legal form.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I will now turn to recommendations in exhibit 13, beginning first in the top panel with those related to regulatory capital.

speaker: ANGULO
text: First, notwithstanding the improvements brought about by Basel 2, there is scope for reassessing the treatment of securitizations involving ABS CDOs.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The risk weights and resulting capital charges for these “re-securitizations” were calibrated under the assumption that loss correlations within a pool of securitized assets would be no greater than those exhibited by CDOs backed by traditional corporate bonds.

speaker: ANGULO
text: It is now apparent that the actual loss correlations within such re-securitizations—especially for the most highly rated tranches—may be much higher.

speaker: ANGULO
text: At its December 2007 meeting, the Basel Committee agreed to take up this issue.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The second recommendation addresses the issue of “reputational” risk.

speaker: ANGULO
text: There have been several occasions over the last 6 months in which banks have elected to purchase assets from, or extend credit to, off-balance-sheet vehicles they had organized and money market and other investment funds they managed, even though they were not contractually obligated to do so.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Whether a bank management will provide support in excess of its contractual obligations is a business decision.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Thus, it is not practical to attempt to design an explicit capital charge for reputational risk.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Instead, supervisors should exercise supervisory oversight to ensure that banks sufficiently consider reputational risk and its implications for capital and liquidity buffers.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The third and fourth recommendations deal with the issue of the procyclicality of capital regulations.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The existence of fixed capital requirements (as well as rating agency expectations for capital ratios) discourages banks from drawing on their capital cushions in times of stress.

speaker: ANGULO
text: It is therefore very difficult to devise changes in capital regulations that would allow capital to function more effectively as a shock absorber without compromising safety and soundness objectives.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Nonetheless, these last two recommendations are aimed at mitigating the potential procyclical effects of a more risk-sensitive capital framework.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The third recommendation is based on elements of the Basel 2 framework that were designed to allow supervisors to address both safety and soundness and procyclicality concerns.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The advanced internal ratings based approach of Basel 2 requires that banks’ loss-given-default estimates reflect economic downturn conditions and that stress tests of their advanced systems include consideration of how economic cycles affect risk-based capital requirements.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Rigorous supervisory evaluation of these two elements can help ensure that (1) regulatory capital embeds forward-looking forecasts of recovery rates and (2) banks manage their regulatory capital positions in a manner that enables them to accommodate variations in the amount of minimum required capital over an economic cycle.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The fourth recommendation is to explore ways to encourage inclusion in the regulatory capital base of debt instruments that mandatorily convert into equity when a banking organization is under stress.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The automatic conversion of debt instruments into equity under such circumstances is appealing from a supervisory perspective as well as from a broader macroeconomic policy perspective.

speaker: ANGULO
text: This concept has not yet been examined in depth by the staff, but we believe it merits further study, including an assessment of the past experiences of banks with such instruments, to determine its feasibility.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Let’s now move to the recommendations in the bottom panel.

speaker: ANGULO
text: These deal with improving disclosure practices, which can help to reduce the uncertainty that has been a key feature of the recent turmoil.

speaker: ANGULO
text: First, financial institutions—especially those in the United States—improved their disclosures about subprime-related exposures as the turmoil wore on.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Nonetheless, supervisors and regulators should continue to push market participants to make timely and detailed disclosures about the size and composition of subprime-related exposures.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The second and third recommendations focus on disclosures related to asset-backed commercial paper programs.

speaker: ANGULO
text: In view of the potential exposure associated with reputational risk, market participants appear to desire additional details about banks’ dealings with ABCP programs.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Disclosing information about the distribution of assets underlying such programs by type, industry, and credit rating would bring the disclosures on par with those provided for on-balance-sheet assets.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Similarly, in view of the extent to which investors in asset- backed commercial paper have retreated from rolling over or purchasing paper that they suspect may be supported by subprime-related assets, banks and asset managers that sponsor ABCP conduits should improve disclosures to investors, particularly for conduits other than the traditional multi-seller programs.

speaker: ANGULO
text: That completes our prepared remarks.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We would be pleased to take your questions at this time.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It is great to see some bank supervision people at this table, and I would just highlight one of the comments that you made about silos.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It is interesting that this morning we have been discussing issues of bank balance sheet constraints and how that would occur, and it might be useful to think structurally within our own organization whether there are ways to do a better job of getting people in bank supervision to understand some of the financial stability issues we think about, and then vice versa.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Maybe having some bank supervision people come to FOMC meetings might be one way to actually promote some of this.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the things that you were talking about, another issue that I think has been important is that we’ve been talking about the effect of dropping housing prices.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I know a horizontal stress review was done about a year ago, and I’m sure Brian or Jon remembers that the large financial institutions did the stress testing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: When they did that stress testing, what was striking was that there were four institutions—I think it was Citigroup, JPMorgan Chase, Wachovia, and Bank of America—in that stress test, and all four concluded that a housing-price reduction of between 10 percent and 20 percent would affect earnings but wouldn’t affect capital.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Obviously, in retrospect that doesn’t seem to have been a good forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: One, since we do think that stress testing is useful, maybe understanding that and going back to those same four institutions and understanding their stress testing might be a useful exercise to do.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Two, if you did that exercise, we’d learn something about how they’re thinking about housing prices and the indirect effects that might occur because one of our concerns around the FOMC table is that there may be unintended consequences if housing prices drop more than they have historically.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just as the banks have to think about those kinds of stress tests and what they have already learned from the fact that they didn’t pick up some of the indirect effects, our own knowledge would be supplemented if we thought about some of those indirect effects as well.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So the horizontal stress testing was interesting in that I think some of those institutions are on the good side and the bad side of your things.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The horizontal stress testing isn’t what generated the decisions—and I do agree with your conclusion that most of the decisions were made by senior management.
