speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Some organizations didn’t do subprime mortgages at all.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I’m not so sure it was generated from the stress testing as much as a gut feeling by senior bank management that they weren’t going to engage in subprime mortgages.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think that’s true for a lot of these activities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It’s interesting who’s at the top of the list and who’s at the bottom of the list for a lot of these activities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Ideally, over time, both bank supervision and bank risk management would get to the point that it’s not just a gut decision by a person at the top but is a little more systematic and that the risk- management process does that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Are you thinking of ways that we could actually encourage that kind of interaction so that it becomes less gut from senior management and more integrated into the risk management?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I know that was kind of a long entry.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Well, I would just comment on the first point that you made in terms of silos.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I guess we would fully agree we’re having a great time here, so we would love to see more interaction between supervision and the FOMC.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Be careful what you wish for.

speaker: ANGULO
text: You know, when people debate whether to have supervision with a central bank or not, one of the key arguments is that only we can bring to bear the resources of the entire central bank and also provide input from the supervision side.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So clearly, that’s something I think we need to do more of.

speaker: ANGULO
text: In terms of the second question, do you want to take a fresh crack at that, Brian?

speaker: PETERS
text: My perception is that the people who were further down on the list made active decisions to get out of the business or reduce their scale of the business, not necessarily just on gut feeling but because they had invested earlier on in the staff and the models to evaluate the product space.

speaker: PETERS
text: So they understood that the economics of the subprime business had deteriorated and that the risk relative to the return was rising, and they made an active decision, usually, to retract a bit from that space.

speaker: PETERS
text: Now, they may have made those decisions gradually and incrementally over the year from mid-2006 forward.

speaker: PETERS
text: It wasn’t one stress test, but it was a thorough understanding of the economics of the actual business that drove their decisionmaking.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I would also agree that your general point about banks being more exacting in their stress testing is a good one because it’s something we and other supervisors, to be honest with you, continually look at, and many times the response that banks get internally from either owners or managers or through supervisors is that, well, if it’s too extreme, it’s not really plausible, and you can’t really act on it.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The other argument you sometimes hear is, well, it costs a lot of money to integrate that across the firm and do it the right way, and that’s a tough sell.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So I agree with your point that we need to do more and then push harder on stress testing.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The way that you suggest is kind of novel: You do a back test and show it to them.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: I might add one thing to that.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: In interviews we did with some firms, one point that they made was that stress testing was informative and important, but a next step they’re trying to take is what it would take to cause that stress event to happen for different types of assets.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: So they are trying to anticipate—not so much that they just assume a 10 percent drop but how they would get to a 10 percent drop.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: What would be the events that would cause that to happen?

speaker: GREENLEE
text: Then they think that through in a more systematic way.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: I know some companies have learned what their highly rated things are that are viewed as stable-value assets elsewhere on their balance sheets and are thinking about how those could start to unwind or to deteriorate.

speaker: PETERS
text: We need to be careful with the nomenclature.

speaker: PETERS
text: Stress testing right now in the industry encompasses a lot of things, and people will tell you that they do stress testing, but they are really doing static shocks.

speaker: PETERS
text: What we are talking about is not a historical analysis but a kind of forward-looking scenario that builds in your view of the world.

speaker: PETERS
text: Those are the firms that, again, made more-active decisions to reduce their exposures.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think this was very interesting, and I have a suggestion and then a question.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The suggestion is that this morning we had the Federal Open Market Committee meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: This afternoon we should have the Federal Market Oversight Committee meeting, and that is what we’re doing right now in looking at some of these institutions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: My question is, As you look at these and you compare the most effective and least effective, are you in the process and shouldn’t we be in the process—because we go back and look at these horizontal reviews—of looking at what lessons we’ve learned about more-effective institutions and less-effective institutions during the horizontal review so that we can be more proactive in terms of the outcomes that we’re now seeing?

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we do that in a systematic fashion over time, we could anticipate not all—we learned a long time ago that you cannot anticipate it all—but some of these differences and put more pressure on some institutions that were not doing good risk analysis to step up to it before it becomes a crisis.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I don’t know if we’re doing lessons learned for ourselves in that regard.

speaker: PETERS
text: I would say we’ve looked at a lot of that.

speaker: PETERS
text: The one place I would highlight most articulately is the degree of international coordination and cooperation we’ve had under way.

speaker: PETERS
text: The core firms in the United States are one portion of this system now, with a number of very significant global competitors.

speaker: PETERS
text: So the coordination between us, the OCC, the SEC, the U.K. FSA, and the other senior supervisor groups has been really necessary for everyone to get a good understanding of practices.

speaker: PETERS
text: It’s perhaps more valuable to some of the foreign supervisors who have only one or two large firms under their jurisdictions.

speaker: PETERS
text: But even from our vantage point of what our direct supervisory responsibility is, the consolidation within the industry has collapsed the number of firms that we view directly.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: I might add that we are trying to look at this.

speaker: GREENLEE
text: It’s not just an issue of guidance, but we are going back through the supervisory process in terms of what we’ve learned through these interviews and challenging our beliefs and prior assessments.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that is good because, if you think about it, we have the Basel capital standards coming forward, which involve the advanced method—relying on those institutions to a great degree in terms of judging their capital and their capital levels.

speaker: HOENIG
text: When they are under pressure, they will tend to work the model.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As we have said before, the incentives are that they will work the model.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So if we are not taking lessons learned from this in terms of anticipating those behaviors, I think we will repeat history in the surprises that we get.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just very quickly, you did a terrific job.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it’s important, though, to recognize that this isn’t done yet, and we’re not going to know fundamentally how we feel about the relative strengths and weaknesses in the system until we see how this plays out.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Don’t let these initial presumptions—either the diagnosis or the prescription, particularly your list of prescriptions—harden too much because there are some judgments that we’re just not going to be able to make until the dust settles and we have a little time for reflection in that context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think a lot of damage has been done to the credibility of our financial system.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s not clear how much damage because we don’t know how this is going to play out.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But damage has been done, and we are going to bear a lot of the burden of figuring out how to craft a compelling policy response, recognizing of course that regulation may be part of the problem and won’t necessarily be part of the solution.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Anyway, mostly I just meant to compliment you.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You did a great job, and I think it’s helpful really to have this much work done early on in getting us to the point where we know what we’re going to do to the system to make it less vulnerable to this in the future.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Even as we manage the crisis, I think it’s good to have made that investment and a good tribute to the strength of the system that we were able to devote these quality resources even though we’ve all been busy managing the storm.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me also thank the staff for an excellent presentation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is just the tip of the iceberg in terms of the work that’s being done on all these different topics, and in turn we’re collaborating with our colleagues here in the United States and abroad, and I guess we’ll keep working and hope to find some valuable lessons out of this experience.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ve been asked to remind people that you have until tomorrow close of business if you wish to revise your projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Brian Madigan raised a few questions about consistency.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you want to think about that, of course, feel free to do so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our next meeting is March 18.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I look forward to seeing you then, and there’s a lunch available for those of you who can stay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me extend a welcome to First Vice President Sapenaro, who is sitting in for St. Louis this morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A quick comment on special topics: I’m sure we’re all disappointed that we won’t have further conversations on the communications strategy, [laughter] but that being the case, we have the opportunity to have special topics again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In April we will be discussing interest on reserves, as we mentioned before.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We asked for suggestions for October, and a number of Banks proposed to look at inflation modeling, which seems obviously a good and policy-relevant topic.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is what we propose to do in October.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We look forward to Reserve Banks taking the lead on presentation and research in this area, and there will be meetings among the research directors and the System Research Advisory Committee to figure out how to go forward, but obviously we have about seven months to get to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We look forward to having special topics.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the first item, Mr. Dudley, if you’re ready.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To start, I just want to update people on what happened overnight in markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Equities rebounded a bit in both Asia and Europe, and bond yields reversed some of the decline that they saw on Monday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The dollar was slightly weaker against the yen and the euro but still in the range that it established.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It did not go back below the lows that it reached early on Monday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would say that generally the markets’ function was okay.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The big issue was bank funding pressures in Europe were evident for dollar funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The funds rate bid as high as 3¾ percent, which is quite surprising on the eve of a meeting in which we are likely to reduce the federal funds rate target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Term funding pressures, if you look at the one- month or three-month LIBOR–OIS spread, are basically unchanged from Monday, when they were up quite sharply from last Friday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Before talking about what markets have been doing over the six weeks since the last FOMC meeting, I’m going to talk a bit about the Bear Stearns situation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In my view, an old-fashioned bank run is what really led to Bear Stearns’s demise.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But in this case it wasn’t depositors lining up to make withdrawals; it was customers moving their business elsewhere and investors’ unwillingness to roll over their collateralized loans to Bear.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rapidity of the Bear Stearns collapse has had significant contagion effects to the other major U.S. broker–dealers for two reasons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, these firms also are dependent on the repo market to finance a significant portion of their balance 1 The materials used by Mr. Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the $2 per share purchase price for Bear Stearns was a shock given the firm’s $70 per share price a week earlier and its stated book value of $84 per share at the end of the last fiscal year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The disparity between book value and the purchase price caused investors to question the accuracy of investment banks’ financial statements more generally.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The contrast in the behavior of investment bank equity prices versus credit default swap (CDS) spreads is revealing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Share prices fell sharply, but the CDS spreads narrowed a bit, indicating a lower risk of default.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, Lehman’s stock price fell 19 percent, but its CDS narrowed by 20 basis points, to 450 basis points, yesterday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This underscores the difference between the $2 per share buyout price for Bear Stearns—less value than people thought—and the introduction of the Primary Dealer Credit Facility (PDCF)—a reduction in the risk that a liquidity problem could drive a firm into insolvency.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I have a few words about the PDCF, before moving to a discussion of market developments since the January FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The PDCF should help to restore confidence among repo investors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It essentially creates a tri-party repo customer of last resort—us.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When investors have concerns about the ability of a dealer to fund itself, they are reluctant to roll over their own repo transactions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The reason is the fear that the clearing bank may not send their cash back the next morning when the overnight repos mature.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This fear may not be misplaced.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If the clearing bank is worried about whether investors will stay put, the clearing bank may decide to keep the cash.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In that case, the investors would be stuck with the securities that collateralize the repo transactions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The PDCF should break that chain of worry by reassuring the clearing bank that the Fed will be there as a lender to fund the repo transactions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The repo investors are reassured that the clearing bank will send back their cash the next day and thus are willing to roll over their repo transactions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At least that’s the theory.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As noted, the PDCF should provide some comfort to the counterparties of these firms that these firms will, in fact, be able to fund their obligations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yesterday, the major money market mutual fund complexes did roll their outstanding repos with the major investment banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, the jury is still out on whether the PDCF will be sufficient to stabilize confidence.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: High use of the PDCF would result in a large increase in the amount of reserves added to the banking system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think it is important to go on record on that because, if that were to occur, over the short run the New York Desk might not be able to drain reserves sufficiently quickly to keep the federal funds rate from trading extremely soft to the target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We will make all efforts to make the “short run” as short as possible.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But realistically, there is a good chance that the federal funds rate could trade soft relative to the target, especially through the end of the current reserve maintenance period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In fact, yesterday we saw that, although it started the day quite firm, the funds rate crashed at the end of the day, and the effective fed funds rate for the day was 2.69 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It depends, in large part, on the volume of use of the PDCF.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Stepping back from developments of the past few days, recent weeks have been marked by rapid and, at times, disorderly deleveraging of financial holdings within the global financial system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As I discussed last week, the most pernicious part of this unwinding has been the dynamic of higher haircuts, missed margin calls, forced selling, lower prices, higher volatility, and still higher haircuts, with this dynamic particularly evident in the mortgage-backed securities market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’ll be referring to the handout from here.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Over the past six weeks, we have surveyed a number of hedge funds and one REIT about the haircuts they face for financing different types of collateral.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 1, the rise in haircuts has been most pronounced in non-agency mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But even agency MBS have seen a significant widening of haircuts in recent weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The collateral funding pressures have been particularly evident for residential-mortgage-backed securities collateral.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is due to several factors including very unfavorable fundamentals for housing, a high level of uncertainty about the ultimate level of losses, and an overhang of product for sale, both currently and prospectively.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In our discussions with market participants, unleveraged players have been unwilling to step in to buy “cheap” assets for several reasons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, there are few signs that housing is close to a bottom.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, a significant amount of product sits in weak hands and, thus, could be dumped on the market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, this particular asset class has characteristics that exacerbate price volatility and, therefore, risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, when spreads widen and yields climb, prepayment speeds slow.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When the yield curve is upward sloping for longer maturities, the rise in duration generates an increase in yields.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rise in yields also reduces housing affordability, which puts further downward pressure on home prices, increasing prospective losses on the mortgage loans that underpin the securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Signs of distress in this market include the following.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, a sharp widening in option-adjusted mortgage spreads—as shown in exhibit 2, option-adjusted spreads for conforming fixed-rate mortgages have widened considerably since the January 30-31 FOMC meeting, though they have come in quite a bit over the past couple of days.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, jumbo mortgage spreads relative to conforming mortgages rates remain very wide.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 3, this spread has averaged more than 100 basis points this year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The current yield on prime jumbo loans is around 7 percent, a margin of about 3½ percentage points over ten-year Treasury note yields.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, mortgage securities prices continue to fall.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, as shown in exhibit 4, the prices for AAA-rated tranches of the ABX 07-01 vintage continue to decline.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fourth, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac reported large fourth-quarter losses, and their stock prices and CDS spreads have performed accordingly (exhibit 5).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The sharp decline in the equity prices has made the companies reluctant to raise new capital, despite the prospects of higher-margin new business, because additional share issuance at the current share prices would lead to massive dilution for existing shareholders.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fifth, the yield levels on many mortgage-backed securities have climbed significantly above the yield on the underlying mortgages that underpin the securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is the opposite of how securitization is supposed to work.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This phenomenon reflects the glut of supply of such securities on the market and the added risk premium attached to assets that are typically held on a mark-to-market basis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the residential mortgage market is the epicenter of the crisis, distress has been evident much more broadly—with the municipal market fully implicated in the period since the January meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The deleveraging process evident among financial intermediaries operating outside the commercial banking system has led to a widespread repricing of financial assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When available leverage drops, risk- adjusted spreads have to rise for leveraged investors to earn the same targeted rate of return as before.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This helps explain why the problems in the residential mortgage market have infected financial markets more generally, leading to wider credit spreads (exhibits 6 and 7) and lower equity prices (exhibit 8) both in the United States and abroad.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As leverage is reduced and spreads widen, financial arbitrage implies that all assets should reprice.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The risk-adjusted returns from holding different asset types should converge—recognizing that the degree of leverage that is available in markets may differ across asset classes in accordance with divergences in price volatility, liquidity, transparency, and other characteristics.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, the notion of convergence to equivalent risk-adjusted returns is an equilibrium concept, and we are not in equilibrium.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The events of the past week underscore that point.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But there are plenty of other examples of disequilibrium at work.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, for mortgage-backed securities, the losses implied by the prices of the AAA-rated ABX index tranches appear to be high even relative to the darkest macroeconomic scenarios.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The municipal bond market is also a good example of how market valuations can become unusually depressed when supply increases rapidly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Then the value inherent in the securities becomes broadly known, this mobilizes new money, and risk-adjusted returns come back down relatively quickly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Term funding spreads also indicate greater stress within the financial system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 9 and 10, the spreads between one-month and three-month LIBOR– OIS spreads have widened sharply in recent weeks, even before Bear Stearns’s demise.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are sitting today at 56 basis points for the one-month LIBOR–OIS spread and 77 basis points for the three-month LIBOR–OIS spread, about the same as yesterday morning.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you are all aware, we have been active in responding to the growing market illiquidity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 11 illustrates the results of the TAF auctions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Note how propositions and the number of bidders have increased recently and the spread between the stop-out rate and the OIS rate has risen over the past few weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Even before the Primary Dealer Credit Facility was implemented this weekend, we were in the middle of a historic transformation in the Federal Reserve System’s balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are increasing the supply of Treasuries held by the public (either outright or borrowed) and reducing the supply of more-illiquid collateral held by the private sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Even excluding the uncertain impact of PDCF borrowing, this shift will speed up noticeably over the next month or two.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Our current plans are to increase the size of the TAF to $100 billion, scale up the single-tranche RP book to $100 billion, renew and increase the size of the foreign currency swaps with the ECB and the SNB to $36 billion outstanding (if fully subscribed), and implement a $200 billion TSLF program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 12 shows how these programs are likely to change the composition of the Federal Reserve’s SOMA portfolio.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, when all the current programs are fully phased in by May, Treasury holdings will have shrunk to about 45 percent of the total portfolio, down from about 97 percent last July.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the same time that financial markets have been under severe stress and the macroeconomic growth outlook has deteriorated, the inflation news has also been disturbing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Several market-based indicators are adding to investors’ concerns about the inflation outlook.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, commodity prices have increased sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 13, the increases have been concentrated in both energy and agricultural prices.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, subsidies to stimulate the production of ethanol from corn have been an important factor.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: By diverting corn production to this purpose, the linkage between energy and grain prices has been significantly strengthened.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the dollar, after a period of stability that lasted from mid-December into February, has begun to weaken anew (exhibit 14).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This has gotten considerable attention in the press and abroad as the dollar has hit new lows against the euro and has fallen below 100 against the yen.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Up to now, the decline has generally been orderly, and the downward slope of the broad real trade-weighted dollar trajectory shown in exhibit 14 has not changed much.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The foreign exchange markets are clearly very skittish.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, there has been considerable focus on China and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries and their willingness to maintain their pegs against the dollar.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For China, investors expect its crawling peg to move faster.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 15, the Chinese yuan is now expected to appreciate about 11 percent against the dollar over the next year, up from an 8 percent pace at the beginning of the year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For the GCC countries, there is speculation that some of these countries might decouple from the dollar.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, on a one-year-forward basis, market participants are currently building in only a couple of percentage points of expected appreciation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Breakeven rates of inflation have continued to widen.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 16, both the Board staff’s and the Barclays measures have broken out above the ranges evident in recent years.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is difficult to differentiate how much this widening reflects a higher risk premium due to greater uncertainty about the inflation outlook versus higher expected inflation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But either way, it is probably fair to say that inflation expectations have become less well anchored over the intermeeting period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I will say, however, that yesterday breakeven rates of inflation came down very sharply—the move was 15 to 20 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Today, we are back in the range we were in, but that is only today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Short-term rate expectations continue to move lower.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 17, federal funds rate futures now anticipate a trough in yields a bit below 1.5 percent.

text: Breakevens came down a lot yesterday, but my understanding is the five-year, five-year forwards did not come down nearly as much.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am concerned about this late-day softening problem with the Primary Dealer Credit Facility.

speaker: LACKER
text: Everything else we have done has been fairly straightforward to sterilize, but because with this the quantity is activated late in the day, the funds are just going to flow into the market.

speaker: LACKER
text: You know, you’re in the position of predicting something with a huge variance, the take-up on that.

speaker: LACKER
text: If late-day softness becomes the norm, because of the arbitrage that’s available to banks within the maintenance period for holding reserves, this could erode our ability to hold the target.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, you people have been really creative about lending money, so I was wondering if maybe you could turn your creative talents toward this problem.

speaker: LACKER
text: The thing that comes to mind is some mechanism for sucking up funds at the end of the day on an automated basis.

speaker: LACKER
text: The natural thing would be for us to do sort of the opposite of repos late in the day for return the next morning.

speaker: LACKER
text: Have you given that some thought?

speaker: LACKER
text: Are you working on that?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have given it some thought, but the press of other business, frankly, has overwhelmed us in the very short run.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think it is a good point.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would say two things about the Primary Dealer Credit Facility and our ability to keep the funds rate at the target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One, if this works the way we hope it works, there are not going to be many people showing up at the Primary Dealer Credit Facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We hope, over time, none—because if we reassure the repo investors that they can roll their repo, we think that will dominate coming to the Primary Dealer Credit Facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So if this works out the way we imagine it could work, the Primary Dealer Credit Facility use will be very nominal, so we won’t have this issue.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second thing I would say is that, if people do come to the Primary Dealer Credit Facility and that leads to softness in the federal funds rate, by definition it will make the Primary Dealer Credit Facility less attractive because, remember, the Primary Dealer Credit Facility cost is tied to the target federal funds rate not to where the federal funds rate actually trades in the market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So that also will obviate some of that issue.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But look, we haven’t done this before.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have now had one day of experience.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We’re going to have to work on the issues that you raised, and we’re going to have to see how it goes, frankly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, could I just add one thing on this?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the delicacy of the whole tri-party repo thing is hard to overstate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: For better or worse, mostly for worse, the full tri-party repo market generally has spread over the last few years well beyond Fed- eligible securities, and until we get to the other side of this, there is a lot of risk in that stuff on repo that goes further out the eligible collateral quality spectrum.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Even in a world where confidence comes back around the primary dealers as counterparties, the thing is there’s just some natural risk that that stuff is going to have to be financed in some other form.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The hardest thing in this balance now is to try to do something that doesn’t increase the incentives so that we become the counterparty to everybody.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We’re trying to make sure that it’s a backstop, but not a backstop that’s so attractive that they come, and that’s going to be a very hard line to walk.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I say that, Bill, because, just to lower expectations, the necessary cost of the choice we’ve made is that we’re going to take the risk that we end up funding a bunch of stuff like that, and the commitment to do that is the only way this helps.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very hard to know.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, even if confidence holds, there is a reasonable probability that some of that stuff is just going to have to move into different forms and other hands, and that could be a delicate transition, particularly if people read into that a broader loss of confidence in this stuff.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The other thing that’s important to point out is that it is just not realistic to expect, even with the force of the things that we announced on Sunday night, that we don’t still have a wave of deleveraging ahead of us.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is still just a huge part of the world that knows they are really long on risk in a fragile environment and have not yet gotten to that point.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: With everything that’s happened in markets, their leverage is going up as the world goes against them, and they’re going to want to keep bringing it down.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That really is going to work against the effect of all the things we’re doing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So just be prepared under the best of circumstances for a sustained period of substantial fragility.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But to underscore your point, Jeff, we agree with your point and had been discussing in what we thought was a slightly calmer world over the past two weeks exactly that mix of things, and we’ll be on it together and consulting.

speaker: LACKER
text: Yes, I just want to emphasize that what we have done so far has had this separability about it, and except for the brief period in late August last year, it has not threatened our ability to manage the federal funds rate in a way we thought appropriate for the whole economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we don’t cure this problem soon, it will become visible; it will become well known; it will get priced in, and to some extent it will overtake this Committee’s deliberations in the sense that it rather than our target rate will run the fed funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that would be a fairly dangerous outcome, and it just strikes me that this is incredibly urgent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You make a good point, President Lacker.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I’d like to commend the New York Fed staff for what I know has been a very difficult time over the past week.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My question is almost the opposite of President Lacker’s.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: He raises some interesting points, but I wonder.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given the stigma issues involved and what’s just happened with Bear Stearns, you would think that borrowing at any kind of penalty rate for an investment bank, which arguably is more susceptible to runs than the typical commercial bank, is something that no one would take advantage of because of concerns about stigma.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Is there any evidence that there’s more stigma?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: How are the primary dealers viewing this, and have they raised concerns about confidentiality and what would be disclosed?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, we have certainly gotten questions about how this will be disclosed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, there will be a disclosure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There will be a line item in the H.4.1 release, but it will just show the total dollar amounts extended through this facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is all bid through the New York District, so the total primary dealer borrowing will be shown in that release.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The stigma issue is a legitimate issue, and that is why we have to be very careful about how we talk about this and take tremendous care not to disclose who or even what type of institution uses it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But at the end of the day, if you can’t fund your repo and your only choice is to come to the PDCF, that is probably what you are going to do.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, to come back to Vice Chairman Geithner’s point, I think that is exactly right, though.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The fact that to the extent that there is stigma, they are not going to want to come, and that is going to reinforce the deleveraging process that is clearly under way, as is the fact that they just saw Bear Stearns go from a troubled but viable firm to a nonviable firm in three days.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The lesson from that for a lot of firms is going to be, oh, I need more liquidity, I need to be less leveraged, and that lesson, from what happened to Bear Stearns, isn’t going to go away.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m under the impression—Bill, you correct me—in the earnings call from the investment banks today and tomorrow, the four remaining are going to do all they can to destigmatize this facility with answers to the effect that “we haven’t tapped the facility yet, but we would be very open to do it in the right circumstances” and to provide some comfort that it is not stigmatizing in their own minds.

speaker: WARSH
text: For the strongest of those firms to say that should provide some halo for the rest.

speaker: WARSH
text: But to Bill’s point, I think we will have to evaluate that as we go.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it is incumbent upon me to point out that the Board staff was also very involved, and I mention Brian Madigan, Pat Parkinson, Scott Alvarez, Deborah Bailey, and others as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it was very much a joint effort.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, we’ll turn to Dave Stockton.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Oh, I am sorry, we need a vote to ratify the open market operations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I move that we ratify the open market operations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, we have made some very large changes to the economic projection in this round—so large, in fact, that we had to adjust the scale on the forecast evolution charts that we put in the back of the Greenbook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, the most notable change has been our adoption of the view that the economy is moving into recession.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I thought it would be helpful to briefly review this morning our reasons for making that call at this time.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In addition, I will lay out the rationale for the depth and duration of the weakness in real activity that we are now projecting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Finally, I will explain why, with so much more projected slack in resource utilization, inflation has, on average, been revised up from our January projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have noted on several occasions in the past few months that our decision to stick with a forecast in which the economy muddles through its current difficulties without falling into recession was a close call.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Well, over the intermeeting period, we continued to accumulate a bleak array of economic indicators.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Consumer confidence moved still lower and, in the case of the Reuters/Michigan measure, dropped to levels last registered in the early 1990s.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Regional indexes of business sentiment continued to deteriorate noticeably, with steep drops in the measures reported for New York, Chicago, and Philadelphia.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Although the weakness was less pronounced in the national ISM surveys, the composite indexes for both manufacturing and nonmanufacturing were below 50 in February.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Small businesses—as reported in the survey conducted by the National Federation of Independent Businesses—and larger businesses—as captured by the Duke University Survey of Chief Financial Officers— have turned very pessimistic.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: These indicators taken alone, or even in limited combination, might not be that troubling.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But when viewed as a whole and especially when taken in conjunction with the many financial indicators that have been flashing recession signals for some time, the pattern of recent readings is disturbing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Furthermore, recession signals are no longer limited to surveys and financial indicators.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Private payroll employment is estimated to have dropped 101,000 in February, and there were sizable downward revisions to earlier months that left employment showing declines in both December and January.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Industrial production dropped 0.5 percent in February, and manufacturing IP fell 0.2 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The weakness in industrial production occurred not only in the series in which we use production worker hours to estimate output but also in series where we have measures of physical product.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For both payroll employment and industrial production, diffusion indexes indicate that the weakness has been spread widely across industries.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This morning’s data on housing starts also suggest little end in sight to the ongoing recession in housing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Single-family starts fell more than 6½ percent, to 707,000 units, in February, and permits dropped a similar amount.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Both figures were very close to our expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Multifamily starts moved up to 360,000 units, but that figure follows some low figures late last year, and we wouldn’t attach much signal to that reading.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, while I certainly am not going to try to predict what the NBER will ultimately do, a number of the series consulted by the dating committee appear to have peaked late last year or early this year—at least on the currently published data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Real personal income, industrial production, payroll employment, and real manufacturing and trade sales all have local peaks sometime between October and January.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: All told, the evidence of a serious weakening of the economy appears to us more palpable now than it did in January.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If one grants that the economy, from time to time, exhibits nonlinear behavior, then our forecast will need nonlinear changes to avoid making outsized errors.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At this point, we’ve seen enough to make us think that recession is now more likely than a period of weak growth, and that is what we are forecasting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But having made that discontinuous change to our projection, I want to impress upon the Committee just how much this remains a forecast of recession; a lot has to happen that we haven’t seen yet to be confident of this call.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, there are several reasons to be skeptical that we have transitioned into recession.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One striking feature of several surveys of business sentiment is that businesses appear more pessimistic about the overall economic picture than they do about the prospects for their own firms.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Another cautionary reading comes from the motor vehicle sector.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Sales have softened noticeably over the past couple of months, but they haven’t tumbled as they might have if the economy had already moved into recession.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In labor markets, initial claims for unemployment insurance, which had risen earlier in the year, have leveled off of late, with the four-week average running about 360,000 in recent weeks.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That level of claims is not yet high enough to clearly signal the declines in private payrolls of between 150,000 and 175,000 that we expect will be occurring this spring.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Finally, orders and shipments for nondefense capital goods flattened out late last year but as yet have not shown any signs of serious deterioration, which will be necessary shortly if our projected downturn in capital spending is to come to pass.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For now, we are willing to treat these readings as suggesting that there is some upside risk to our forecast of a modest recession.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One of the key features of past recessions, as viewed through the lens of our models, is a tendency to observe large negative residuals that are correlated across the major spending equations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have built that feature into this projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But this also remains a forecast because a pattern of correlated negative residuals is not yet clearly evident in the data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: To gain some perspective on how the forecast would have looked had we not built in these recession effects, we showed an alternative scenario in the Greenbook that effectively removed these residuals.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The result is a forecast that is similar to, though in the near term a bit weaker than, the one we showed in the January Greenbook largely because of higher oil prices and weaker housing prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we have marked down the baseline forecast considerably more than would be suggested by these factors alone.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: To be sure, we may have overreacted by moving to a recession call.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But that possibility is counterbalanced by some clear downside risks even relative to this more pessimistic forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The recession that we are forecasting is relatively shallow.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In our forecast, the depth of the downturn is limited in the near term by tax rebates, which provide a substantial boost to disposable income starting in May.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This should help to buffer some of the drag on spending that is anticipated to result from declining employment, higher oil prices, and weaker household net worth.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, domestic production benefits appreciably from the past and prospective decline in the exchange value of the dollar and the continued growth in the economies of our major trading partners—factors that help to provide a sizable boost to net exports this year and next.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: These influences result in a small upturn in real GDP in the second half, and the unemployment rate rises only 1¼ percentage points, to 5¾ percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is a small increase in unemployment even by the standards of the past two mild recessions.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As I’ve noted, well-timed macro policies and substantial support from the external sector lead us to expect that this time will be different and that the unemployment rate will rise less than usual.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But you should always be wary of forecasts that expect this time to be different.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Another notable feature of our forecast is that, although the projected downturn in activity is shallow, the period of weak aggregate demand is lengthy, especially given the assumed low level of the real funds rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For those of you so inclined, this might be a good time to check your Blackberries for e-mail or to get in a couple of games of BrickBreaker because I can assure you that I will not be offering much in the way of scientific insight on this issue.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In our forecast, the growth of real GDP picks up next year for several reasons.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Housing demand finally bottoms out, and accordingly, construction activity begins to arrest its steep decline.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In addition, given our forecast of a flattening of crude prices, the drag from higher oil prices on consumer spending is expected to wane next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Importantly, we also assume that there will be a gradual lifting of the restraint on spending as financial stress abates.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The last influence is now assumed to lift more gradually than in our previous forecast and, along with an intensifying drag from lower house prices, accounts for much of the lingering weakness in this projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Correspondingly, the unemployment rate falls to only 5½ percent at the end of 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In our previous forecast, we had the effects of financial stress fading over this year, on the thought that, as it became apparent that the economy would avoid recession and that housing was bottoming out, risk spreads would narrow, credit conditions would loosen up, and spending restraint would ease.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, in our current forecast, the economy experiences recession this year, and housing doesn’t show much sign of stabilizing until next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As a consequence, we don’t begin to phase out the unusual restraint on spending resulting from financial stress until next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This aspect of our forecast, even more than others, is largely guesswork.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We just don’t have much in the way of historical experience on which to calibrate the projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In recognition of that uncertainty, we included in the Greenbook two alternative simulations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In the “faster recovery” alt sim, we assume a stabilization of housing later this year and a reversal of most risk spreads by the middle of next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Under these assumptions, growth picks up more noticeably, and a tightening of monetary policy is required next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Alternatively, one cannot rule out some further deterioration in financial conditions and an even longer period of subpar economic performance.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In the “greater housing correction with more financial fallout” scenario, a steeper decline in home prices results in a deeper contraction in construction activity, a further widening of risk spreads, tighter lending conditions, and an additional deterioration in household and business sentiment.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Although this scenario might sound extreme, it only pushes the outer edge of the 70 percent confidence interval for real GDP and unemployment.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It is also sobering to recognize that this simulation results in a nominal funds rate path that skirts the zero bound.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The bottom line: We know with probability 1 that the baseline forecast will be wrong.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But with the downward adjustments that we have made to this forecast, we feel that there is significant probability mass on both sides of our projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Despite marking down our forecast of real activity substantially this round, our projection of consumer price inflation, both headline and core, has been revised up in 2008 and is largely unchanged in 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Those revisions reflect marginally worse news on the incoming price data as well as further deterioration in some of the key determinants of price inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As for the news, our reading of the recent price figures is that core PCE prices probably did not rise as rapidly in January as is currently published but that they likely rose faster in February than might be suggested by a cursory examination of last Friday’s CPI report.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As we noted in the Greenbook, barring offsetting influences, we believe that the currently reported increase in core PCE prices of 0.3 percent in January will be revised down to 0.2 percent after the BEA incorporates the low reading on medical care services that was shown in the January PPI.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As for February, the core CPI being unchanged was a favorable development.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But a sizable fraction of the good news was in rents and medical care; rents receive a much smaller weight in PCE prices than in the CPI and, as I just noted, the PCE price index uses the PPI, not the CPI, for measuring medical costs.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Incorporating medical care prices from this morning’s PPI release suggests to us that core PCE prices rose about 0.15 in February.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: All told, we are projecting an increase in core PCE prices of 2.5 percent at an annual rate in the first quarter, 0.1 percentage point more than in January.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have also incorporated into this forecast a further jump in the cost of crude oil and higher import prices associated with the weaker dollar and more-rapid gains in commodity prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, we have read the survey measures and TIPS spreads as suggesting that there may have been some deterioration in inflation expectations of late.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Taken together, these less favorable developments more than offset the projected emergence of some slack in resource utilization.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As a consequence, we are now projecting core PCE prices to rise 2.3 percent this year, up ¼ percentage point from our January projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Despite an unemployment rate that runs nearly ½ percentage point above our previous forecast, we have left unrevised our projection of core PCE prices in 2009 at 1.9 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Higher food and energy prices have resulted in a further upward revision to total PCE price inflation of nearly ¾ percentage point, to 2.9 percent, in 2008.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Total PCE price inflation for 2009 is unrevised at 1.7 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Before turning the floor over to Nathan, I want to let the Committee know that the three research divisions are undertaking a review of the structure of our policy documents.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The Greenbook and Bluebook have grown in length and complexity over the past decade.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Our objective in this review will be to improve the focus and flow of the documents and to eliminate the redundancy that has crept in over time so as to reduce the burden on you in reading the documents and the burden on the staff of producing them.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We will, of course, consult with the Committee before implementing any substantive changes.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan will now continue our presentation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The global economy has likewise seen some extraordinary developments during the intermeeting period.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, the spot price of WTI has surged more than 15 percent, briefly reaching $110 per barrel, and many nonfuel commodities prices have moved up by similar magnitudes.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The exchange value of the dollar, which had been relatively stable since November, has returned to a depreciating path, falling more than 5 percent against the major currencies since mid- February and reaching a post–Bretton Woods low.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The global financial stresses that began last summer have further intensified.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Also, as Dave has outlined, recent data suggest that the U.S. economy has continued to weaken.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, not all the news from the foreign sector has been grim.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indeed, given the shocks that have materialized, the foreign economies appear to be showing somewhat more resilience than we would have expected.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Total foreign real GDP growth in the fourth quarter of last year stepped down to 3.2 percent from the rapid 4.5 percent rate that had prevailed through the previous three quarters, as the pace of activity slowed in both the advanced economies and the emerging market economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This fourth-quarter out-turn, however, was about ½ percentage point stronger than we had expected, reflecting an upside surprise in the emerging markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Available indicators of first-quarter activity paint a mixed picture.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the euro area, economic sentiment fell in February for the ninth consecutive month, but the purchasing managers index for the services sector and the German IFO index of business conditions picked up.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, industrial production and retail sales posted stronger readings in January.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The ECB’s bank-lending survey indicates a tightening of lending standards, but measures of bank credit to the corporate sector have continued to expand.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indicators of activity in the United Kingdom have also been mixed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Consumer confidence in February slid to a five-year low, but business confidence and conditions in the services sector have been more upbeat.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In emerging Asia, while the impetus from external demand is clearly diminishing, Chinese retail sales have continued to grow robustly; industrial production in Korea, Singapore, and Taiwan moved up in January; and domestic consumption in the ASEAN countries has remained solid.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Taken together, these data seem to indicate that growth abroad has cooled but has not stalled.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our forecast thus seeks to balance several offsetting considerations.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the one hand, the projection for U.S. growth this year has been cut by a sizable 1½ percentage points; this has particularly stark implications for countries like Canada, Mexico, and some in emerging Asia that have close trade ties with the United States.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The further deterioration in global financial conditions should also weigh on activity abroad.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the other hand, the incoming data suggest that the foreign economies are not yet following the United States into recession, and the red-hot commodities markets also lead us to believe that activity is holding up in some corners of the world.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Weighing these factors, we have cut our forecast for total foreign growth in 2008 to 2.3 percent, down from 2.9 percent in the last Greenbook, with much of this markdown reflecting softer growth in Canada and Mexico.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our projections for emerging Asia have also been reduced, but we see these economies still expanding at a moderate pace.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Clearly, there are both upside and downside risks around this forecast.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the downside, the adverse spillovers from the U.S. slowdown and continued financial stresses may be more severe and more broadly felt than we envision.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the upside, the apparent resilience in foreign demand to date suggests the possibility that growth abroad may hold up better than we now expect.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In 2009, foreign growth is projected to rebound to 3½ percent, in line with the expected easing of global financial stresses and economic recovery in the United States.

speaker: SHEETS
text: With commodities prices increasing sharply, foreign inflation has continued to rise.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, in the euro area, 12-month headline consumer price inflation climbed to 3.3 percent in February, well above the ECB’s 2 percent ceiling, driven up by food and energy prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In China, 12-month inflation in February surged to 8.7 percent, at least in part reflecting sharp increases in food prices due to severe winter weather.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In an effort to temper these pressures, the Chinese authorities have introduced temporary price controls for some basic necessities and this morning announced plans to raise reserve requirements another 50 basis points.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We now see average foreign inflation in 2008 as coming in at around 3¼ percent, up ¾ percentage point from the last Greenbook.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Central banks have responded to this cocktail of slowing growth and higher- than-desired inflation in divergent ways.

speaker: SHEETS
text: To date, the ECB has held its policy rate firm at 4 percent, citing the level of headline inflation, possible second-round effects from commodity price increases, and risks from ongoing wage negotiations.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given these concerns, we now expect the ECB to remain on hold a while longer but, in response to a projected further slowing of activity, to cut rates 50 basis points later this year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Bank of England, in contrast, has reduced its policy rate 50 basis points since the fall—and we expect another 75 basis points by year-end—in an effort to cushion the economy against financial headwinds and slowing in the housing and commercial real estate sectors.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Finally, the Bank of Canada has reduced rates 100 basis points since the autumn, in response to downdrafts from the United States and the strong Canadian dollar, and the Bank has indicated that “further monetary stimulus is likely to be required.” Thus we see another 50 basis points of easing in the second quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As noted earlier, the dollar has depreciated more than 5 percent against the major currencies since mid-February as the widening divergence between the path of policy rates in the United States and other industrial countries, particularly the euro area, has weighed on the dollar.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As a related factor, the tone of the recent U.S. economic data has been much softer than for most other advanced economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In broad real terms, the path of the dollar in our current forecast is about 2½ percent weaker than in the January Greenbook.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Going forward, our forecast calls for the broad real dollar to decline at a 3 percent annual rate, with this depreciation expected to come disproportionately against the currencies of the emerging market economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I conclude with a few words regarding the performance of the U.S. external sector.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The January trade data showed exports continuing to rise at a healthy pace while nonpetroleum imports contracted.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Imports of consumer goods were particularly soft.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For 2008 as whole, we now expect the external sector to contribute a substantial 1.2 percentage points to growth, about twice as much as in our previous forecast.

speaker: SHEETS
text: To be sure, much of this larger arithmetic contribution from net exports reflects a contraction in imports caused by the slowdown in U.S. demand.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, part of the reduction in imports is also due to the decline in the dollar.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Exports this year are seen to grow at a pace of nearly 7 percent, just a touch less than in the last Greenbook, as the effects of the weaker dollar almost offset the markdown in foreign growth.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In 2009, imports rebound as the U.S. economy recovers, and the positive contribution from net exports accordingly shrinks to about ⅓ percentage point.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Finally, yesterday the BEA reported that the current account deficit narrowed to 4.9 percent of GDP in the fourth quarter, its smallest share of GDP since 2004.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We had expected the rise in oil prices to drive up the deficit, but this was more than offset by a marked improvement in net investment income, partly as earnings received by foreigners on their investments in the U.S. financial sector declined, reflecting the effects of the ongoing financial turmoil.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We will now be happy to take your questions.

speaker: FISHER
text: If I put the two comments together, one of the messages I receive is that we are less confident in the linkage between U.S. slowing growth and rest-of-world slowing growth than we or conventional wisdom was before.

speaker: FISHER
text: You mentioned, in the discussion of the international side, the downside and upside on growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is also a downside and an upside on inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just want to ask about our thoughts on this from a staff standpoint.

speaker: FISHER
text: Clearly, the downside price pressures come from our housing crisis and all of the other related issues and, I presume, from the building of slack and rising unemployment and, therefore, restrained wage demands.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is the domestic side.

speaker: FISHER
text: At the same time, I think I hear you saying that on the global side it is not happening in that fashion elsewhere.

speaker: FISHER
text: The emerging countries, particularly China, are still growing at a rapid pace.

speaker: FISHER
text: However, it may become somewhat slower.

speaker: FISHER
text: My question is, Do we feel that there is as much an offset to our domestic disinflationary/ deflationary forces as we thought before?

speaker: FISHER
text: Are these global demand-pull inflationary forces basically mitigating our expectations of the contractionary domestic forces?

speaker: FISHER
text: How has your opinion—the two of you—changed in the intermeeting period?

speaker: FISHER
text: I hope that is a clear question, but I think you get the point that I am making.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Over the intermeeting period we have lived through an experience that manifests the upside risk to our inflation forecast; and I would indicate that, with the ¾ percentage point markup to headline foreign inflation in 2008 in our forecast, the vast majority of that is a reflection of these red-hot commodity markets, which then presses the question to us, Well, what is going on there?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Certainly, in the case of the demand in these markets, by now I would have expected to have seen some attenuation or a bit of softening.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Really, it seems to be quite the opposite.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The demand since the first of the year has accelerated.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Some other factors are at work as well—idiosyncratic supply stories, electrical outages that made it harder to smelt aluminum and copper, and so on.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So there are some supply factors as well.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The demand side seems to be important, and to the extent that demand remains strong, I am not sure where these commodity prices are going to top out.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The futures path is a reasonable guess at sort of the balance of supply and demand.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There is also some upward pressure on these prices from the depreciation of the dollar.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But to the extent that commodity prices move up, I would say that we will probably be marking up our forecast of foreign inflation next time.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Just a broader comment on the linkages between the U.S. and the foreign economies— again, I was surprised at the strength of demand in these commodity markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I would have expected by this point to have seen more marked evidence of slowing in the foreign economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So we have marked down our forecast for 2008 in line with these prospective developments, the further slowing in the United States, and the financial stresses.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But we didn’t mark down our forecast very much, just a tenth or two, and mainly in Canada in Q1; and the data that we have in hand are not pointing to a dramatic slowing.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We are expecting more of that to come through in the second and the third quarters.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: President Fisher, I will just basically reiterate what I said earlier and amplify many of the same things that Nathan just said in terms of the influences on our headline forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We revised up ¾ percentage point as well, and that really is coming from higher energy prices, higher food prices, and higher commodity prices, all of which we think are already showing through to some extent and we expect to continue to show through to headline inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Despite the fact that we run with a much larger output gap in this forecast, we haven’t revised down our forecast for 2009 because of the lingering effects of the run-up in commodity prices that we are expecting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As I indicated, we think there has probably been some small deterioration in inflation expectations as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: Dave, my question is basically about the influence of the financial stress on the outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: I was talking to an official at the Bank of Canada last week, and she had an intriguing calibration by which she said that, since last August, they thought that financial stress for Canada was worth about 25 basis points of restraint at the outset and now they thought it was more like 50 basis points for their economy, which is doing quite well.

speaker: EVANS
text: I guess the impossible question is, Have you thought about that type of calculation and how it influences the way we think about interest rates for your forecast?

speaker: EVANS
text: The way that I am thinking about this and that President Lacker and others have thought about this is that we are trying to separate the effects of standard monetary policy and of the innovative policies.

speaker: EVANS
text: Any separation that affects financial markets directly helps us think about the more normal calibration of policy.

speaker: EVANS
text: But, of course, with financial stress we have these add-on effects.

speaker: EVANS
text: So that is why I think that would be interesting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have thought about that, and the difficulty at this point is trying to identify the truly exogenous features of the current financial stress that is operating over and beyond the channels that are normally incorporated in our models.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Our models, obviously, have asset prices, such as house prices and stock prices, and have interest rates and interest rate spreads, and as those things have changed, we have been able to incorporate them into our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But then, over and above that, we think that the model doesn’t really capture a lot of the credit-availability channels.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There is a lot more stress in the market beyond that captured by the interest rates in our models.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So taking this with more than a grain of salt, we think roughly ¾ percentage point on the level of GDP this year—over and beyond the effects of lower house prices, the weaker stock market, and the higher interest rate spreads—that basically lingers on into next year and only then begins to gradually phase out.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is an important factor as to why this forecast is based on such a low real federal funds rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, if you came to a different conclusion either about the depth of what is likely to be occurring in the next few months in terms of the restraint—not just from these financial stress conditions but also from our call that we are moving into a recession—or about the way that restraint fades out over the forecast, that would have a huge influence on the projected path for the funds rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So it is important to recognize that this forecast is conditioned on one in which those effects linger quite significantly into next year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, we will begin our economic go- round.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I thought I would talk a bit about some events in our region that I think have global implications—that is to say, I will talk a bit about agriculture.

speaker: HOENIG
text: You have heard others here this morning talk about some of the price movements, and I think it is worth perhaps spending a few minutes on their effects.

speaker: HOENIG
text: First of all, agricultural commodity prices have surged to record highs, driven by obviously strong demand, lean supplies, and a weak dollar.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Since the fall of 2007, winter wheat prices have doubled, and corn and soybean prices have risen about 70 percent, to record highs.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Rising crop prices are boosting farm income.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In real terms, U.S. net farm income is expected to climb to the second highest level on record, trailing only 1972, when abrupt sales of U.S. wheat to Russia pushed up farm income.

speaker: HOENIG
text: An emerging concern is the growing disarray in futures markets for agricultural commodities caused by a surge in investment by index and hedge funds going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Recent reports indicate that hedge and index fund investment in futures markets for corn, soybeans, and wheat rose from $10 billion in January 2006 to $45 billion this past January.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Early this month, index funds held more than 40 percent of the long positions on wheat contracts on the Chicago Board of Trade.

speaker: HOENIG
text: At this rapid pace of investment—since the beginning of this year averaging $1 billion per week—the funds would own the nation’s entire 2008 corn, wheat, and soybean crops by early 2009.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Now, that is obviously theoretical, but that is how much money is going into this market.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The resulting market disarray is constraining the traditional use of commodity futures to hedge market risk.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Grain elevators, which use futures to hedge their contracts to purchase crops from producers for future delivery, are facing much larger than normal margin calls on their futures positions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Some reports indicate that lenders are beginning to restrict their funding of elevator hedges.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As a result, an increasing number of elevators are limiting their contracts for crop purchases to no more than sixty days in advance of the delivery instead of the normal one to two years.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Now, this surge in crop prices and farm income is pushing up farmland values.

speaker: HOENIG
text: According to our bank’s agricultural credit survey in the fourth quarter of 2007, non-irrigated cropland values jumped 20 percent over 2006 levels, with strong gains also reported in irrigated cropland and ranchland.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our directors and other contacts report a further strong gain since the beginning of the year, and some have reported as much as a 20 percent increase in the first quarter alone.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Adjusted for inflation, the average price of farmland across the nation now tops the early 1980s peak, which immediately preceded the plunge in the early to mid 1980s.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To date, crop production budgets suggest that the recent run-up in farmland values is supported by current revenues from crop production.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, farm input costs have also risen sharply, driven by higher energy costs, suggesting that a drop in crop prices could quickly erode farm cash flow and undermine these values.

speaker: HOENIG
text: District bankers report a surge in farm capital spending.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In February, sales of four-wheeled major equipment rose 45 percent above 2007 levels, and combine harvester sales were up 13 percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Farm equipment prices have risen sharply, and our directors and other contacts report that some equipment dealers are rationing purchases among their customers.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In the past month, anecdotal reports from District contacts indicate that nonfarm investors have boosted their farmland purchases.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our contacts at a national farm management company based in Omaha stated that the number of inquiries for farmland purchases by corporate interests has jumped significantly recently.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Similarly, one of our directors reported that a hedge fund with assets of more than $7 billion is expected to invest $500 million in cropland from Texas and Nebraska.

speaker: HOENIG
text: This fund recently purchased nearly 25 square miles of corn acreage in western Nebraska.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Now, we continue to watch for signs of rising leverage, but to date farm debt levels have risen modestly only, and agricultural banks seem to remain healthy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Bankers report continued use of cash to finance farmland purchases, but I would note that leverage is being brought into the picture, and I think that will accelerate as opportunism and greed have their way.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Total farm lending in the District banks has increased a modest 14 percent over the past four years, with most of that growth being in farm real estate lending.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But District bank examiners and respondents to our surveys reported that the Farm Credit System was being more aggressive in funding farm real estate transactions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Real estate mortgage loans held by the Farm Credit System rose about 12 percent in 2007.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Asset quality at our ag banks remains, at this point, solid.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Noncurrent assets—all assets, not just farm loans—at ag banks are up only slightly from a year ago and remain well below historical averages.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Net loan losses are still very low.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Earnings have remained solid primarily because of cost control and very low loss provisions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am very pleased, but I will tell you that, going forward, in terms of the surveys with the kinds of pressure and price appreciation going on, I think the push for leverage is just beginning.

speaker: HOENIG
text: At the national level, in terms of the Greenbook, every indication is that the economy is slowing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Whether it is recession or very slow growth is a matter of degree, but I think our projections are in the same direction as the Greenbook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to the inflation outlook, I am concerned, as I have said before, about the upside risk to inflation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Though I certainly agree with others around the table that weaker economic activity may put some downward pressure on goods price inflation, I think we can also agree that a number of factors could push inflation higher, including rapidly rising commodity prices worldwide and a weaker dollar.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As discussed in the Bluebook, there is some indication that inflation expectations may be moving higher as well.

speaker: HOENIG
