text: As I have indicated before, I am increasingly concerned that, in our need to respond to signs of economic weakness, we risk losing our hard-won credibility on inflation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: For the past four years, core PCE inflation has averaged about 2.1 percent, considerably above the numbers that this Committee has put forward in its long-term projections.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Frankly, I do not think that many people outside this room think that this Committee can deliver the longer-run projections that we have put forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I don’t think that we can keep inflation expectations anchored only by talk if actual inflation rises further in the months ahead and we continue to ease policy in a rising inflationary environment.

speaker: HOENIG
text: This is something that we need to keep in mind as we discuss our policy options today.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Since our last meeting, the economic data have continued to indicate a very weak economy and that, in all likelihood, we have entered a recession.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Like the Greenbook, my outlook is particularly influenced by indications of significantly weaker labor markets and a housing market that is as yet showing no signs of reaching bottom.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Private payroll employment fell 101,000 in February, and the sum of the downward revisions in December and January was about the same magnitude.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Not only have we had three months of declining private payroll employment, but also the decline has been widespread across most industries.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Blue Chip economic forecast, the Greenbook forecast, and our own forecast have the unemployment rate peaking somewhere between 5½ and 6 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While most analysts are in the process of downgrading their forecasts from skirting to actually having a mild recession, the risk of a more severe downturn is uncomfortably high.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A major determinant of the severity of a downturn will be the housing market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Because recent developments in the housing market are so different from most postwar history, I remain very concerned that the effects of substantial declines in housing prices will be difficult to capture in statistical models based on historical data.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Case-Shiller index indicates that housing prices fell approximately 10 percent in 2007, and a decline of similar magnitude this year would mean that many homes purchased in the past several years are in a negative equity position.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Elevated foreclosures and large inventories of unsold properties are providing abundant opportunities to purchase homes at heavily discounted prices financed at low interest rates by historical standards.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But widespread concerns that prices will continue to fall have resulted in many prospective buyers deferring purchase decisions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: To date, the housing market has been quite weak, despite relatively low unemployment rates.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But if our forecasts are right, job losses this year are likely to exert a significant further drag on housing prices as rising unemployment rates force additional home sales or foreclosures.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Falling housing prices are likely to have a collateral impact on consumption.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Perhaps reflecting this risk, the credit default swap rates on retailers have been rising, and we are increasingly hearing of retailers that are closing stores or postponing expansions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Retailers, like consumers, are aware that high oil prices, increasing job losses, and losses of wealth in the stock and housing markets are not likely to be conducive to robust consumption.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Exacerbating the negative economic news is the continued deterioration in financial markets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Credit spreads have widened significantly over the past six weeks, with many spreads more than 50 basis points higher than at the last meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Hedge fund and money managers that I talk to are acutely aware of the counterparty risk and are very carefully managing their collateral.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Most firms with excess collateral are in the process of managing that position down.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The deleveraging that is going on has reduced the willingness of banks and other financial intermediaries to finance their positions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In addition, as concerns with liquidity rise, we are once again seeing renewed pressure on the asset-backed commercial paper market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The rise in credit default swaps for companies like Washington Mutual and Lehman Brothers indicates increased concerns for the solvency of other large financial institutions with large exposures to mortgages.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The potential for a further episode of financial market dysfunction and for runs on additional financial firms is significant.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My primary concern at this time is that we could suffer a severe recession.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Falling collateral values and impaired financial institutions can significantly exacerbate economic downturns.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Some indicators of inflation are higher than we want, but during previous recessions, commodity prices and inflation rates fell.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given my forecast for the economic outlook, I expect substantial excess capacity to significantly reduce inflationary pressures going forward, and I see little evidence that higher commodity prices are causing upward pressures on wages and salaries.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Since we met at the end of January, there has been an utter dearth of good news concerning both the real and the financial sides of the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the real side, I just can’t recall any intermeeting period in which nearly every single data point was dismal.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the financial side, there have been occasional good days, but the net changes over the intermeeting period have been negative across the board in both the equity and the credit markets, so financial conditions have unambiguously tightened.

speaker: YELLEN
text: These developments are familiar to all of us, and I won’t take up time to review the specifics.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My overall sense at this point is that the effects of the severe and prolonged housing downturn, the financial market implosion, and the price increases for oil and other commodities have now spread to most corners of the economy, including the major segments of consumption and business fixed investment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Exports represent about the only source of strength, and while that is welcome, I must say that the economy is pretty clearly in trouble when the contribution to real GDP growth from exports exceeds overall real GDP growth, as may well happen this year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The bottom line is that, like nearly everyone else, I have downgraded my economic outlook substantially.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Assuming that the stance of policy is eased substantially at this meeting and additionally by midyear, I see the economy as essentially in recession during the first half before picking up somewhat in the second because of the effects of monetary and fiscal policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, I certainly see large downside risks to my forecast, and I think the Greenbook’s view that recessionary nonlinearities have already set in seems to me to be within a reasonable range of outcomes.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In fact, we have also been looking at monthly data on coincident business cycle indicators, and that examination suggests to us that the NBER may well date the beginning of the recession to last November.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The prospect of this outcome has been made more palpable for me by the rather sudden increase in the frequency and intensity of pretty dire comments I am hearing from my contacts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, I have heard widespread reports of reductions in capital spending plans due to caution or pessimism regarding economic growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, a large manufacturer and retailer of outdoor sports equipment reported that technology and infrastructure spending has been cut by at least a third in 2008.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In another example, a large player in commercial real estate in the San Francisco Bay area described how projects are being canceled because the financing spigot has been shut.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, nonresidential construction is one sector where I think the Greenbook may be too optimistic.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I envision growing weakness there.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Second, my retail contacts suggest that spending has softened further in the wake of a weak holiday season, and expectations are for continued weakness at least through spring.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, the CEO of a large high-end national retail operation reports that for January and February he has seen declines in sales that haven’t been experienced for almost fifteen years.

speaker: YELLEN
text: These declines have created tremendous pressure on inventory levels requiring large markdowns with negative effects on profits.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Vendors are reeling from the cancellation of orders, the return of goods, and sharp reductions in new orders.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Third, a number of contacts have provided comments reinforcing the view that a significant credit crunch is under way.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Slightly more than half of the comments received on this topic indicate that credit standards have tightened significantly in recent months.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In one example, the CEO of a bank in my District reports that several of the nation’s largest mortgage lenders have suspended withdrawals from open home equity lines out of concern that borrowers could now owe more than their homes are worth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As a final anecdote, a banker in my District who lends to wineries noted that high-end boutique producers face a distinctly softening market for their products, although sales of cheap wine are soaring.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Now let me turn to inflation and inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, much of the recent data have been disappointing, having been pushed up by rising energy and other commodity prices.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Though I was heartened by Friday’s CPI report, this one observation hasn’t changed my overall impression that prospects for core inflation this year have worsened a bit since we met in January, and I have raised my projection for core PCE inflation about ¼ percent in 2008, to 2¼ percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: These data raise the issue of whether cutting rates as much as needed to fight a recession may risk persistently higher inflation and inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I tend to think this risk is manageable.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, as I have said before, I view inflation as less persistent now than it once was, tending to revert fairly quickly to its longer-run trend.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have recently reviewed and updated our econometric evidence for this and found it to be even more convincing now than it was a couple of years ago.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, it is important to remember that the current lack of persistence presumably is due to our enhanced credibility, so we do have to be careful to maintain it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Recent increases in inflation compensation in Treasury markets highlight the risk that our attempts to deal with problems in the real economy possibly could lead to higher inflation expectations and an erosion of our inflation credibility.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But inflation compensation is just one indicator of inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I very much like the Board staff’s approach, which is in the current Bluebook, of combining the information from a wide variety of indicators into a principal- component-type model.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I found it reassuring that the resulting index of inflation expectations and uncertainty is still within the range of variation that we have seen over the past decade or so.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Second, I tend to think that developments in labor compensation are an important part of the transmission process for monetary policy to inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Before we get into too much trouble with inflation and inflation expectations, I would expect to see labor compensation begin to rise more rapidly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I find it reassuring that both our broad measures of compensation have expanded quite moderately over the past year, and productivity growth has been fairly robust.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So after incorporating its effects, unit labor costs are up less than 1 percent over the past four quarters.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Finally, the more pronounced slowdown that I expect for economic activity is likely to put somewhat greater downward pressure on inflation going forward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Overall, I expect core PCE inflation to fall below 2 percent next year under an assumed leveling out of energy and other commodity prices and the projected weakening of labor and product markets.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, the baseline forecast in the Greenbook looked to me a lot like the 2001 recession experience—very brief and very mild.

speaker: STERN
text: If things turn out that way, we will have been very fortunate, frankly.

speaker: STERN
text: The forecast I submitted at the last meeting was lower than most around the table, and now my bottom line is that I think the recession that, if we are not in, we are confronting is more likely to resemble that of 1990-91, which, while brief, wasn’t that mild.

speaker: STERN
text: There were a couple of quarters, as I recall, where the economy contracted by at least 3 percent in real terms.

speaker: STERN
text: I am not sure that this recession is likely to be as brief as the previous two either.

speaker: STERN
text: I have tried to use the 1990-91 experience and its aftermath as sort of a guide to thinking about where we are today and how things might unfold and evolve because there are some significant similarities as well as some significant differences between the periods.

speaker: STERN
text: But it is also a way for me to start to organize things and think about this.

speaker: STERN
text: So let me just describe a few of what I think are relevant features from that experience and how today’s circumstances are either similar or different.

speaker: STERN
text: If you compare our circumstances today with what we were confronting back in 1991, on the positive side inflation and inflation expectations are both lower today.

speaker: STERN
text: The unemployment rate is lower than it was going into that recession.

speaker: STERN
text: Nominal and real interest rates appear to be lower today than they were back then.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that nonfinancial business balance sheets are in better shape today on average than they were going into the 1990-91 experience, and depository institutions overall are in better shape today than they were back then, although of course they are having some very high profile problems.

speaker: STERN
text: Of course, that was the period when we saw more or less the virtual demise of the thrift industry and problems of major banks.

speaker: STERN
text: There was also a significant correction in housing activity, which commenced in 1987 and ran through into 1990.

speaker: STERN
text: It wasn’t as sharp as the one we are experiencing, but it was significant nevertheless.

speaker: STERN
text: There was also a credit crunch back then, and that was given a lot of responsibility not only for the recession but for its aftermath—that is, the relatively sluggish recovery that occurred once the recession ended—because it was alleged that financial institutions, nonfinancial businesses, and households were all trying to strengthen their balance sheets simultaneously, and so there was a good deal of caution throughout the financial sector.

speaker: STERN
text: So there are a number of similarities as well as a number of differences.

speaker: STERN
text: When I think about today’s circumstances, a couple of things come to mind.

speaker: STERN
text: One is, as President Yellen summarized, that the breadth of negative news about the economy is striking to me.

speaker: STERN
text: On top of that, I think today’s financial problems are, without question, more severe and more intense than they were back then.

speaker: STERN
text: They have engulfed many financial markets, as we are well aware.

speaker: STERN
text: While there were declines in housing prices and housing values in some markets back then, the decline we are experiencing today is both more widespread and is likely, before it is done, to be a good deal deeper.

speaker: STERN
text: So I think that at least a reasonable parallel is the kind of thing we experienced back in 1990-91.

speaker: STERN
text: Now, on the inflation side, let me start with policy.

speaker: STERN
text: We weren’t targeting the federal funds rate back then.

speaker: STERN
text: We were still wedded to the monetary aggregates, more or less.

speaker: STERN
text: But the funds rate, nevertheless, provides some useful information.

speaker: STERN
text: The funds rate, in early 1989, was around 9¾ percent.

speaker: STERN
text: It got to 3 percent by September 1992, where it stayed until early 1994.

speaker: STERN
text: I cite that because inflation, whether you look at core or at headline, actually diminished through that period.

speaker: STERN
text: So while some people have been worried, and perhaps justifiably, that this is going to shape up like the late 1960s or much of the 1970s as far as inflation is concerned, all I would say about that is it is not a foregone conclusion if you look at history.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t know that it is easy to distinguish how this is likely to play out, but that was a very significant series of policy moves undertaken back then, and inflation, nevertheless, diminished.

speaker: STERN
text: The only other comment I would add to this—and it is not going to lift the gloom right away, certainly—is that these financial problems are going to persist.

speaker: STERN
text: Even if they bottom out and conditions start to improve, I would expect that they will exert headwinds on the shape of the recovery.

speaker: STERN
text: My view is that 2009 is not likely to be as healthy as the Greenbook envisions, largely as a consequence of the hangover of financial problems.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Reports from my directors and business contacts are consistent with what others have said this morning—that overall economic growth has slowed appreciably since the beginning of the year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Pessimism about the near-term outlook has increased.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: At the same time, many are troubled by the continued elevation of prices and price level increases and are apparently becoming less convinced that inflation will moderate any time soon.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my view, the deliberations this morning and the decision we make must be about, first, financial system stability—the threat to the broad economy of severe financial instability— and, second, inflation risk and the role of rate policy in response to immediate problems.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One addition to the list of concerns is the continuing dollar depreciation since we met last and its role in price pressures and overall uncertainty.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the run-up to this meeting, I heard little that casts doubt on where the economy is trending.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My assessment is that we have entered recession territory.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Previous forecasts premised improvement in the second half on the stabilization of house prices and financial markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Neither has materialized, nor are there early encouraging signs.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the current circumstances, financial stability must be priority one.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That said, the inflation picture has become quite troubling.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Headline inflation, perhaps excluding last month, has been elevated since late summer, as have measures of core inflation, though less so.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The expected easing of pressures hasn’t yet convincingly set in.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A longer view leads to the conclusion that inflation has been relatively high, on average, since 2005.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We must be mindful of this as we address financial stability concerns.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I mentioned the dollar’s trajectory when I listed what in my view are the relevant considerations today.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am concerned about what I perceive as growing mention of the possibility of a dollar currency crisis.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Although only one conversation, I also heard mention of a developing dollar carry trade fueled by interest differentials, expected rate cuts, and possibly the view that recessionary conditions will persist for some time.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Policy is often a balancing act, but I see our current constraints as tightening.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The real side has entered recession in all probability.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There is increasing risk to the inflation objective.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Financial stability is profoundly in play, exacerbated by the trajectory of the dollar, although to be measured about this, I think the current round of financial market problems has not yet thrown the economy irreparably off balance.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I intend to support a downward rate move today, but with reservations about the utility of continuing cuts in addressing financial stability problems.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Discussion in the policy round may address this, but I will comment now that balancing our policy objectives in such a risk-laden environment may require decoupling rate policy from liquidity measures.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Through my conversations with people in the Fourth District financial community, I get the clear impression that some credit channels are closing down.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given the uncertainties in financial markets, some of the large banks in my District are finding it challenging to ascertain potential loss exposures in certain asset categories, especially to residential real estate developers.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Two large banks in the District have seen their asset quality deteriorate more quickly than they had projected in January.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Clearly, banks and other financial institutions are getting squeezed from both sides of their balance sheets, and the most highly leveraged institutions are getting squeezed the hardest.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Many of the large banks in my District are going to considerable lengths to stay liquid and to conserve capital.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The largest and most complex institutions are attempting to raise more capital.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The deteriorating environment in the financial markets is clearly affecting business conditions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Most manufacturers in the District have seen a slowing in business activity.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Those that are doing better are doing so because they are being helped some by stronger export demand.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Pessimism over economic prospects is now prevalent among the CEOs that I talked with, and many are scaling back their business plans for 2008 by a considerable amount.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The faltering business prospects are making the financial environment even more uncertain—a pattern that conforms to the adverse feedback loop that Governor Mishkin and others have been warning about.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like others, I have once more cut my growth projections for 2008 and, again, by a relatively large margin.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As in the Greenbook, I have factored into my projection the weaker than previously expected estimates of spending and employment as well as the sharp run-up in energy costs.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: An especially important element in my current thinking is the future path of housing values.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Many of my contacts have told me that they don’t see how financial market conditions can stabilize without more confidence about where the bottom of the housing market lies and, as a corollary, where the bottom of the residential-mortgage-backed security prices might lie.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Unfortunately, I haven’t seen evidence that we are seeing a leveling out in housing prices.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The Greenbook baseline projection carries with it nominal house-price declines of about 5 percent this year and next.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: A month ago that may have seemed like a reasonably good assumption to me, but today I fear that projection may be too optimistic.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Certainly, the decline in house values that one sees in futures markets for the markets that are covered by the Case-Shiller index indicates a decline of twice that magnitude.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My own baseline projection is closer to the “greater housing correction” alternative than the Greenbook’s baseline projection.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Even the “greater housing correction with more financial fallout” alternative seems somewhat plausible to me.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Turning to the inflation outlook, at our January meeting my modal outlook was one in which the inflation trend declined to just below 2 percent in 2010.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At the same time, I was one of the few participants who said that the inflation risk had shifted to the upside.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I still hold to those views—that is, I still expect the trend of inflation to fall below 2 percent by 2010, but I still worry that we are going to continue to experience upside surprises to that inflation outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Indeed, I can’t recall a single conversation that I have had with my business contacts recently that hasn’t touched on the increasing cost pressures that they are facing.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In most cases, they are now successfully passing along price increases to their customers.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Nevertheless, as I assess the economic environment this morning relative to where I was in January, particularly given the prospects of yet larger wealth losses stemming from the real estate market and certainly the chance for even greater impairment to the functioning of our credit markets, I think the downside risks to economic growth continue to outweigh the upside risks to inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Clearly, the incoming data on activity have been weaker than we expected.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think they point to a downturn in GDP in the first half of the year similar to that in the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: While the February CPI report was welcome news, on balance I think the inflation picture continues to be troubling.

speaker: EVANS
text: I noticed a marked change in the sentiment of my business contacts this round.

speaker: EVANS
text: Many more are now telling me that the problems on Wall Street are affecting their financing.

speaker: EVANS
text: Credit availability is now an issue.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to borrowing from banks, these reports seem consistent with the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey.

speaker: EVANS
text: Credit is an issue for those tapping nonbank sources as well, as in the comments that President Yellen made.

speaker: EVANS
text: As an example, back in December a major shopping center developer indicated that, even though the commercial-mortgage-backed security market had dried up, he was still able to obtain financing on reasonable terms from other sources, such as life insurance companies.

speaker: EVANS
text: Last week he told me that these sources had dried up, too.

speaker: EVANS
text: He’s now trying to raise equity funding, which he considers very costly and an unappealing alternative.

speaker: EVANS
text: Many contacts also expressed increased nervousness over the economic situation and its likely impact on demand for their products.

speaker: EVANS
text: Manpower’s CEO told me that their business had deteriorated in recent weeks.

speaker: EVANS
text: Some of his clients were trimming staff because of a lower current demand, and many others were being cautious and cutting back in expectation of future weakening.

speaker: EVANS
text: Still, even though restrictive financing and heightened caution are weighing on households and businesses, there is a sense from my contacts that spending is not collapsing at this point, and exports of capital equipment in the agricultural sector continue to do well, similar to President Hoenig’s comments.

speaker: EVANS
text: Another common theme I heard from my contacts is that, while the Fed’s innovative response has helped, they do not expect that these measures will do a lot to solve the financial sector’s fundamental problems.

speaker: EVANS
text: I doubt that any of us disagree with that.

speaker: EVANS
text: As one of my directors put it, “Monetary policy is not enough.

speaker: EVANS
text: We need a solution to the subprime mess.

speaker: EVANS
text: Once that happens, the contagion will run in reverse.” I believe our innovative policies are helpful for facilitating market functioning, but they don’t address the root problem.

speaker: EVANS
text: Markets want a firmer sense of where prices for stressed assets will bottom out and of the magnitude of the portfolio losses that will be taken by major financial players.

speaker: EVANS
text: Unfortunately, it will take a good deal of time before these uncertainties will be resolved, and I’m not sure what we can do to speed the process.

speaker: EVANS
text: After all, a number of these losses are going to stem from mortgage delinquencies that have not yet occurred and perhaps from homeowners who have not even contemplated that outcome.

speaker: EVANS
text: This means that financial headwinds likely will be weighing on the real economy for some time, as President Stern said.

speaker: EVANS
text: I agree with his comments there.

speaker: EVANS
text: The substantial uncertainty over the length and breadth of this process adds uncertainty to the medium-term outlook for growth.

speaker: EVANS
text: So while I am hopeful that the economy will begin to recover in the second half of the year, I’m a lot less confident of that outcome than I’d like to be.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning to inflation, Friday’s CPI report was about the only good news I heard during the intermeeting period (I think last time the reports weren’t very good either, President Yellen), although as the Greenbook Supplement points out, the less favorable translation to PCE prices takes out some of the luster.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s no surprise that many of my contacts pointed to increasing pressures from higher costs for food, energy, and other commodity inputs.

speaker: EVANS
text: I also heard numerous reports of higher costs being passed downstream.

speaker: EVANS
text: One notable case was for wallboard.

speaker: EVANS
text: Even though demand is weak and the industry had plenty of excess capacity, higher costs for energy inputs were resulting in the first increase in wallboard prices in 20 months.

speaker: EVANS
text: The director who reported this was concerned that pricing behavior is moving toward a cost-plus mentality.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is, after all, his industry.

speaker: EVANS
text: If so, this would have negative implications for inflation expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: However, I see this as a risk and not a base case scenario because the resource gaps opening up in the economy should bring inflation down.

speaker: EVANS
text: Firms will find it difficult to pass through cost increases in an environment of weak demand.

speaker: EVANS
text: Businesses and financial market participants will be aware of this difficulty in passing through costs, which should help keep down their inflation expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: That said, even in a weak economy, firms will have only so much room to absorb costs, and pressures from higher prices for energy and other commodities and for imported goods pose a risk to the outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, while I expect inflation expectations to be contained, there are risks on this front, too.

speaker: EVANS
text: Some can see a low fed funds rate path, such as that assumed by the Greenbook, as an indication of a lack of resolve on inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t agree with that assessment, but it’s an increasing risk that we will be running, particularly if the inflation news breaks in the wrong way.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve seen two striking macroeconomic developments since our last meeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: We now have compelling evidence that a recession is in train.

speaker: LACKER
text: We now have compelling evidence of erosion in our inflation credibility.

speaker: LACKER
text: Information from our District corroborates a recession call.

speaker: LACKER
text: Various survey indicators and reports from contacts point to weakness in manufacturing, commercial real estate, and consumer spending.

speaker: LACKER
text: No signs have yet emerged of a bottom in housing.

speaker: LACKER
text: The national reports on employment and retail sales for February have sealed the case for recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: It now appears that payroll employment peaked at the end of ’07 along with real income and household spending, and to make matters worse, anecdotal reports suggest that the January fall in nonresidential construction is only the beginning of a sustained deterioration.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m now expecting a period of declining employment, declining nonresidential construction, and flat-to-sluggish consumption.

speaker: LACKER
text: Equipment and software spending may decline as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: Past contractions suggest a trough later this year.

speaker: LACKER
text: More severe scenarios seem unlikely to me, however.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Great Depression, for example, involved us keeping real rates well above 5 percent for several years as activity slowed and the price level declined 30 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: It will take some time before the ultimate size of mortgage foreclosure losses is known well enough to substantially reduce the uncertainty attached to mortgage-backed security returns, and it is not clear that interest rate changes will affect that timetable much.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the meantime, I would expect to see repeated bouts of financial turmoil.

speaker: LACKER
text: When particular markets or entities come under stress, I would also expect to see even wider speculation about and calls for new Fed lending.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s even possible that fluctuations in the perceived prospects for such intervention add to financial market volatility, much the way conjectures about IMF programs seemed to add to market volatility in the 1990s.

speaker: LACKER
text: After a string of adverse inflation reports, the CPI came in virtually flat for February.

speaker: LACKER
text: While this certainly helps for many reasons, including those Mr. Stockton cited, I’m not inclined to make much of one month’s report.

speaker: LACKER
text: The overall CPI is still up over 4 percent year over year, and given the recent behavior of oil and gasoline prices, inflation is likely to be high again in the March report.

speaker: LACKER
text: In any event, I think there is no comforting way to rationalize the substantial rise in the five-year, five- year-ahead inflation compensation we’ve seen since the beginning of the year.

speaker: LACKER
text: This measure of inflation was previously ratcheted upward by similar amounts in early 1999, early 2001, mid-2003, and early 2004.

speaker: LACKER
text: In each of these episodes, our actions and statements communicated an increase in our concern about growth prospects, and market participants seem to have inferred a corresponding reduction in our commitment to price stability.

speaker: LACKER
text: The net result over that period is that five-year, five- year-ahead inflation compensation has drifted up significantly over the past ten years, from below 2 percent to now above 3 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: This expectational drift is likely to overwhelm, in my view, any transitory effect of increasing slack.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe inflation expectations no longer qualify as well anchored.

speaker: LACKER
text: Moreover, they no longer seem consistent with the credibility of even a 2 percent inflation objective.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe that this substantial erosion in our credibility is occurring because of our aggressive policy moves and the perception that the hierarchy of our macroeconomic priorities has changed.

speaker: LACKER
text: It wouldn’t surprise me if our recent credit market interventions are bleeding over into a skepticism about our general approach to time-consistency problems.

speaker: LACKER
text: It cannot help to allow our credibility to drift around.

speaker: LACKER
text: I do not think we want a regime in which long-run inflation expectations ratchet up whenever growth slows significantly.

speaker: LACKER
text: Ultimately we will be forced to act to restore credibility.

speaker: LACKER
text: This just adds needless volatility to financial markets and the economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe we need to adopt a strategy of easing much less aggressively going forward than we have to date and than markets expect.

speaker: LACKER
text: President Stern cited the 1990-91 recession and the fact that both the federal funds rate and inflation came down during that recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: But surely the pace of easing then had something to do with the fact that inflation came down.

speaker: LACKER
text: Unless we’re willing to let inflation expectations continue to drift, we have to disappoint markets sometimes.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Eighth District economic conditions have softened, but with considerable variability across industries and local areas.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: The outlook for District agriculture is very strong in the context of high commodity prices.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: This prospect is reflected in prices of agricultural land, which in areas within the District have risen at a rate of 20 to 25 percent over the past year in active markets.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Production of agricultural equipment for the 2008 crop season is fully booked, and prices of used equipment are at or very close to prices of new equipment.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: There was major activity in the District energy industry, with significant construction projects of coal-fired generation facilities and rapidly developing exploration and production in the Fayetteville Shale play in Arkansas.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Total natural gas production from this source roughly quadrupled during 2007.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: In a recently published study, it is estimated that the direct impact on Arkansas output from exploration and production will average about $2.5 billion per year for the next five years.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: For perspective, this is about 2.8 percent of the 2006 Arkansas gross state product.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Overall activity in the Evansville, Indiana, metropolitan area is particularly strong.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: The unemployment rate there has declined year over year from 4.6 to 4.2 percent, and nonfarm employment has grown 1.4 percent from January ’07 to January ’08.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: A major investment in the auto parts industry is in the works for this area.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Activity in housing markets in the District is soft, with building permits in the four largest metro areas down on average 16.8 percent during 2007.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Nevertheless, house prices in the District have held up much better than the national experience.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: In 21 District metropolitan areas, house prices increased an average of 2.5 percent in 2007, with decreases in house prices reported in only 3 metro areas.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: However, in contrast to other parts of the nation, these areas did not experience major house-price inflation before 2007.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: From 2000:Q4 through 2006:Q4, the average annual price inflation in these areas was only 5.3 percent.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Foreclosures have increased in 2007 in three of the four largest District metro areas but at much lower rates than nationally, and 2007 foreclosure rates are at or below national averages in three of these four areas.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: I solicited information on the national economy from a number of sources.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Contacts in the air and ground cargo industry report significant cost pressures from higher energy prices.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: These affect everything from fuel costs to the cost of snow removal.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Respondents indicate that these cost increases are significantly but not completely passed through to their prices.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: International cargo traffic is reported to show strong growth, but with some customers substituting sea for air shipment and choosing less rapid delivery service to reduce cost.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Year-over-year traffic out of Asia to both Europe and North America has grown at double-digit rates.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: One contact indicated that volume appears to have bottomed out in the first half of 2007 and has slowly but steadily improved since.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: In contrast, a contact in the over-the-road trucking industry reported that there was not much change in the past two months.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: In his view, the industry has been in recession since December 2006.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: He sees improvement for his firm going forward not because of increased demand but because of small competitors exiting the industry through bankruptcy.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Excluding fuel surcharges, freight prices are flat to down.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: A contact at a major credit card bank reported that their credit card activity indicates that retail sales, excluding autos, were flat in February and are likely to be flat to down in March.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: These February data were confirmed by the advance retail sales report last week.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: He also reported that a smaller percentage of customers are making full payment on their credit cards and that a larger percentage are making only the minimum required payment.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: He sees delinquencies spreading to credit cards.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: A contact at a major software producer indicates that revenue growth was robust prior to the first quarter of 2008 and, while remaining strong, has slackened since the beginning of the year.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: He reports strong retail sales, but that was possibly influenced by reductions in prices.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: He sees business IT spending in the United States remaining strong and no deterioration in the collection of receivables.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Nevertheless, he is less optimistic about the industry outlook now than in January.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Finally, a contact in the quick service restaurant industry, or fast food, sees business as stable at the moment, not getting worse but not getting better.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: He notes that while historically this industry is affected least when the economy slows down, this particular time he sees gasoline prices as a significant factor, with many consumers making fewer trips to purchase low-ticket items.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: He also views financial markets as closed to all but the largest and most highly rated nonfinancial corporations.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: In his words, there is no market for deals.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: The national economy certainly appears headed for a weaker first half of 2008 than seemed likely at the January meeting.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: A model estimated by our staff economists for forecasting recessions suggests a probability in the neighborhood of 60 percent that the NBER dating committee will label the current experience an official recession.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Unlike some, I am not an optimist on the effect of the fiscal stimulus program on consumer demand.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Economic theory and past experience with such one- off stimulus programs do not provide a basis for assuming a strong response.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: In the current situation, with many consumers heavily leveraged, it is likely that the stimulus to consumption will be less than historical averages.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Notwithstanding the February CPI report, the inflation situation is deteriorating and appears likely to continue deteriorating.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Beyond the immediate issue of containing systemic risk, the most important issue is the subsequent economic recovery.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: We have eased aggressively already.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: We must not lose focus on the lagged effect of current policy actions on that recovery.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: We must preserve the credibility of our commitment to low and stable inflation.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: The greatest danger is a relapse into a period of higher inflation, which then promotes a policy response that could generate a future recession and start a vicious cycle of increasing inflation and increasing unemployment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As anticipated, Third District business activity showed continued weakness in February and March.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Reports from retailers, manufacturers, bankers, and other business contacts remain somewhat downbeat.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the same time, there has been little moderation in price pressures facing our firms and consumers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There is little new in the regional housing markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So rather than dwell on housing, let me talk about some of the information that we have received since our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Banks in the Third District have generally been relatively unscathed by the toll on the financial markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Many had not been in the subprime market and did not have instruments based on subprime.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They do, however, hold a high proportion of commercial real estate and residential mortgage loans in their portfolios.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So to the extent that the commercial real estate market slows as we expect, our banks are likely to be feeling the effects.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Bankers, thus, have become somewhat more pessimistic over the past six weeks or so.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They don’t expect financial conditions to improve any time soon, and several noted signs of declining business loan demand, which they had not been seeing earlier.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Bankers also report some deterioration in personal-loan credit quality and are expecting increases in credit card delinquencies.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite these increases, these delinquencies and default rates so far remain well within historical norms.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Manufacturing outlook activity in the District remains weak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our March business outlook survey is confidential until we release it this coming Thursday.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It will show a little improvement in February’s dismal readings.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Since the beginning of the year, the general activity index has been at a level typically associated with either a national recession or a substantial slowdown in economic growth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So despite the modest improvement, it doesn’t move us out of negative territory.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Responses to a special survey question in February indicate that the majority of our firms considers their inventories to be at an appropriate level, and firms are unlikely to substantially replenish these inventories until midyear or later.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But it doesn’t seem as though there will be more-dramatic reductions in inventories—as, for example, in the Greenbook’s basic story, where there’s a very large inventory correction, it appears.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite the weakness in activity, there has been little moderation in price pressures in the District.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The current prices-paid index in our business outlook survey continues to accelerate, and both the prices-paid and prices-received indexes over the past three months are at very high levels relative to the last twenty years.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Firms in various sectors, not just manufacturing, were reporting significant increases in prices, particularly of imported inputs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although our firms are expecting continued weak real activity, they expect prices to rise over the next six months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, the forward-looking price indexes in the survey are at very elevated levels, and the future-prices-paid index is at its highest level since the early 1980s.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our firms seem to be as skeptical as I am of the arguments of the critical link between inflation and resource utilization.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Turning to the national outlook, I struggled coming into this meeting with a growing level of discomfort.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There are four dimensions to my concerns: first, the outlook for growth; second, the outlook for inflation; third, the calibration of monetary policy given that outlook; and fourth, the turmoil in the financial markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, in terms of near-term economic growth, the outlook has deteriorated somewhat since our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I expected weak growth in the first half of the year, but the incoming data suggest that growth will probably be somewhat weaker than I anticipated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I and many private-sector forecasters, like the MA or the Blue Chip survey summaries, have responded to the incoming data with downward revisions to our forecast for certainly the first half of 2008.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But our changes are considerably smaller than the revisions in the Greenbook’s forecast, which have revised down personal consumption in 2008 from 2.3 percent in the January forecast to zero in the current forecast while incorporating significantly more monetary policy stimulus.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I realize that the Board’s staff has a good track record, but I am not wholly comfortable with the Greenbook’s forecast, which I think incorporates a number of judgmental adjustments that are responsible for taking it pretty far away from where private-sector forecasts now are.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Second, I’m just less comfortable with the inflation outlook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’ve said before that, if inflation expectations become unhinged, we will face an even more difficult problem as monetary policy will feed more quickly and directly into higher inflation outcomes.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The ensuing loss of credibility will be costly to regain.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wish we had the luxury of waiting for unambiguous evidence that expectations have lost their anchor.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But if we wait until then, it will be too late.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This means that we have to look for early warning signs so we can take appropriate action to ensure that expectations remain anchored, and I am concerned that we are seeing those warning signs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite last Friday’s CPI numbers, headline and core inflation have been trending up.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Oil prices are at record highs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Commodity prices continue to trend up, and the dollar has fallen sharply.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our business and consumer contacts are consistently stressing price pressures as a concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: These developments concern me partly because research indicates that inflation actually may have become less persistent since the 1990s, and I think we have to be careful not to interpret the lack of persistence independent of what monetary policy actions are taken.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, inflation expectations measured by surveys and market-based measures have all risen over the last couple of months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation risk premiums have risen, which could be an early warning signal of a waning credibility or commitment on the part of the Fed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The National Association for Business Economics survey in early March shows that a third of the respondents think that monetary policy is now too stimulative, and that is up from less than 10 percent just a few months ago.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: According to a special question on our November Survey of Professional Forecasters—I reported on this several meetings ago—half of those forecasters, 23 out of the 45, believe that the FOMC has an inflation target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of those 23 forecasters, 20 believe that long-run inflation over the next ten years will be 50 basis points or more above what they view our inflation target is.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I might be able to shrug off one or two of these, but the predominance of these signals has me concerned about the risk to our credibility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m also concerned that the public seems to perceive that the Fed has effectively set aside one part of its mandate, price stability, in our all-out efforts to promote economic growth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Said differently, it seems to suggest that not only are we incorporating new data into our loss function as our forecasts change but we are changing the coefficients on that loss function.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t believe that we are necessarily doing that, and I don’t believe that’s the right way to make policy, but I do believe that ultimately it’s up to us to make that clear to the public as best we can.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Third, we have to calibrate the appropriate level of the funds rate and not just its rate of change.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is not an easy task, especially in the current circumstances.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have reduced the targeted funds rate by 225 basis points since August and 125 basis points in just the last six weeks.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is simply too soon for the economy to have felt the full effects of these rate cuts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While the recent deterioration in the outlook might suggest that we need easier policy, I believe that the recent increases in inflation expectations mean that the real funds rate has already fallen either below zero or close to zero depending on how we measure it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: For example, the real funds rate is now minus 1 percent, which is below the more pessimistic Greenbook-consistent r* of minus 0.5 percent given in the Bluebook, if you measure the real rate as the nominal funds rate minus the Greenbook’s one- quarter-ahead forecasted headline PCE.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Greenbook suggests that the real funds rate can be negative over the next two years and inflation will continue to decelerate as upside inflation pressure is offset by greater slack in product and labor markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This outcome is predicated on inflation expectations remaining well anchored despite aggressive and persistent easing for a sustained period of time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given the current fragility of inflation expectations, this seems very unlikely to me.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The alternative Greenbook scenario with more inflation pressure from oil and imported goods suggests a steeper policy path and higher inflation by 2010-12.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Fourth and finally, like everyone else, I am very concerned about the developments in the financial markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’ve been supportive of the steps we’ve taken to enhance liquidity in the markets through the TAF, the TSLF, the PDCF, or whatever.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, I’ve been supportive of those, and I want to compliment the New York Desk and the people who have worked on this because I think they are very innovative.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not clear how successful these instruments will be, and they are not without their own set of risks of creating some potentially dangerous expectations regarding future Fed behavior, which eventually we must deal with.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I think they are worth trying as long as they are removed in due course.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I can also support a further narrowing of the spread between the funds rate and the primary credit rate, although I would eventually like to see a review of what we think that spread ought to be in more normal times and what our exit strategy might be like as we move toward that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Giving some thought down the road to that I think would be helpful.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So while I believe that we have appropriately reduced the funds rate in response to the worsening economic outlook for the real economy, I am less convinced that reducing the funds rate further will do much to stem the liquidity problems in the market or to lower risk premiums.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Uncertainty about valuations seems to be the root cause of liquidity problems.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The price discovery process needs to continue, and it may take a while.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In this case, I think the Fed needs to continue to do its job to reassure markets that it will act as an appropriate lender of last resort, but we must be careful that a lower funds rate, if that is the path we take, doesn’t become just a form of forbearance that contributes to delaying the necessary writedowns and the price discovery process itself.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yes, the financial markets can have spillovers to the real economy to which the Fed needs to react with monetary policy, and I believe we have.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the same time, we need to keep focused on both parts of our mandate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We put our credibility at risk if we do not do so, and this would be a cause for severe problems later when we may need to act to regain it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We will have to face the fact at some point that we will disappoint the markets with their ever-increasing forecast of a lower funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take twenty minutes for coffee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s start with President Fisher.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, today is my 59th birthday, and I can’t think of a better group of people to spend it with—or a less happy time to do it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We sure know how to take the punch bowl away from this party.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, listen, I know we are suffering because our Deputy Secretary here sitting to your right, Mr. Chairman, just gave me a candle and had me blow it out with no cake attached.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to use very quickly just four examples of what I think is going on with the economy.

speaker: FISHER
text: The first is that 21 miles of boxcars that are 89 feet in measurement each and usually carry lumber are laid up on railroads.

speaker: FISHER
text: The second is that there’s a labor shortage in the Yangtze River Basin, according to one of my interlocutors.

speaker: FISHER
text: The third is that Exxon is rolling $39 billion in cash in overnight deposits.

speaker: FISHER
text: The fourth is, just to keep you listening, that I am going to come back to my ninth birthday in conclusion.

speaker: FISHER
text: As to the 21 miles of boxcars, the average length of a flatbed car that carries lumber is 89 feet.

speaker: FISHER
text: Burlington Northern has 21 miles of it laid up.

speaker: FISHER
text: I mention that because, according to my contacts at the happy housing group that I talk to that builds a significant portion of homes in this country, this housing setback, as they put it, is worse than ’75, ’81, and ’91 combined.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have been a bear on housing from the first time I came to this table, and I agree with everything that has been said about the downside pressure that is being exerted by housing.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would add a couple of points just to underscore that.

speaker: FISHER
text: One is the 21 miles of flatbed cars that are laid end to end.

speaker: FISHER
text: The other is a concern I have from my interlocutors at UPS in that the past six weeks they have seen a downturn in their volume of 2 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: The CEO describes that as a very unusual swing from an up 3 percent in January and something that he has not seen before, and I want to remind you that he was a CFO for many years.

speaker: FISHER
text: The third point is on the growth side, something that perhaps we can monitor going forward: Wal-Mart now polls one million customers.

speaker: FISHER
text: They started doing so last April.

speaker: FISHER
text: There are some imperfections in their polling.

speaker: FISHER
text: They find that 67 percent are concerned about the economic situation, particularly about their financial matters, driven largely by perceptions of their decreasing wealth in their homes but also, more importantly, by cost-of-living factors such as gas prices and the cost of money.

speaker: FISHER
text: With regard to the comment on China, at a conference in Paris recently, Governor Kohn, Presidents Evans and Yellen, and I had the pleasure of listening to Mr. Yi, who is the Deputy Governor of the People’s Bank of China.

speaker: FISHER
text: He made the comment that there is a shortage of labor in the Yangtze River Basin, which I found quite startling.

speaker: FISHER
text: I followed up with him on that conversation more in depth, and because of that, I am not surprised to hear about the inflationary forces that were spoken about at this table.

speaker: FISHER
text: It goes beyond energy, Mr. Chairman, and it goes beyond food, although I want to make some comments on food.

speaker: FISHER
text: I talked to several food producers, and they are all intending to pass through price increases of somewhere between 5 and 15 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: Most distressing to me was Anheuser-Busch, since I am a beer lover.

speaker: FISHER
text: The cost of input of hops and barley has gone up 3½ percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: When you add aluminum, transportation charges, and other things, it totals almost 15 percent, and they expect at the retail level for the price of beer to be passed through at about 5.7 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: So, say, 5 to 6 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: Combine that with the largest producer of pizza crusts, who is expecting a 20 percent increase in the price sought for their product, then you get a sense of a broader issue at hand on food.

speaker: FISHER
text: Let me summarize that broader issue.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to come back to Wal-Mart.

speaker: FISHER
text: They sell 10,000 food items.

speaker: FISHER
text: They expect an average price increase across those 10,000 items that they are budgeting for this year of a little over 5 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: According to a senior official, “We will be aggressive about pricing.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are lagging in terms of our price increases as price leader, and now we are working aggressively to catch up.” That leads to concern on my part.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am well aware of the fact that we have not seen increasing demands from labor, but I don’t consider labor to be a domestic phenomenon.

speaker: FISHER
text: I consider it to be a global phenomenon, and I am concerned that you are hearing such reports in areas where our producers have offlaid certain manufacturing processes and sourcing of inventory, including in China.

speaker: FISHER
text: I, therefore, would suggest that they bear watching.

speaker: FISHER
text: With regard to the comment about Exxon’s rolling cash, to me this gets to the heart of the issue, and that is that I don’t believe, as Mr. Evans said, that monetary policy is addressing the root problem.

speaker: FISHER
text: The root problem is a problem of liquidity, solvency, and trust.

speaker: FISHER
text: When you have a sophisticated operation like that rolling cash in overnight bank deposits, it raises significant alarms to me because it indicates a lack of trust in the system through which you might otherwise conduct your cash and liquidity operations.

speaker: FISHER
text: I liken the situation, Mr. Chairman, to the following—and forgive my simplicity.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’ll use a hydraulic rather than a medical example, which I am often wont to do.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are the water main, and yet the grass is turning brown.

speaker: FISHER
text: The water is not getting to the grass because the piping is clogged with all the hair and residue and all of the ugly stuff that has been building up in this Rube Goldberg piping device that we allowed to happen over a long period of time.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t believe that cutting the fed funds rate addresses the issue.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do believe that the measures we have undertaken recently to enhance liquidity, to improve the functioning of the system, and to address the solvency issues are of significant import.

speaker: FISHER
text: Earlier you mentioned the Duke survey of CFOs.

speaker: FISHER
text: Seventy-five percent of those CFOs said fed funds rate cuts were not helping their business operations.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would have expected otherwise.

speaker: FISHER
text: After the last meeting, praying against my own vote, I hoped that everything that we had hoped would go up would go up and everything we had hoped would go down would go down—spreads et cetera.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet if you look to the chart book—the Bluebook, for example, or the presentation earlier this morning—almost every single graph of what we had hoped would go down went up and vice versa; and I think that indicates that there are limits to the efficacy of cutting the fed funds rate.

speaker: FISHER
text: I said I would conclude with my ninth birthday.

speaker: FISHER
text: When I was nine years old, three-month Treasury bills were trading where they are today.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, may I ask one clarifying question?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: President Fisher, did you just say the efficacy of “any” cut in the fed funds rate?

speaker: FISHER
text: I believe that the efficacy of the cuts that we have undertaken has been diminished by virtue of the liquidity–solvency crisis.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I completely agree with that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But just to make sure that I didn’t misinterpret you, did you say the efficacy of “any” further cut?

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it is pretty clear that I am not going to vote for further cuts.

speaker: FISHER
text: Look, Tim, we cut rates 50 basis points last time.

speaker: FISHER
text: I was in a minority of one, and I respect the group around this table more than I respect myself.

speaker: FISHER
text: Here is the point: Everything that we wanted to go down went up, and everything that we wanted to go up went down.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I just wonder about the efficacy of the cuts as opposed to the measures that we have undertaken.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It was just a clarifying question.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with the others around the table who have said that the prospects for economic activity have taken another sizable leg down over the intermeeting period.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we have been, for a time, in that adverse feedback loop between financial markets and spending that everybody—Governor Mishkin and others—has been talking about.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is not an unusual kind of loop to be in during a soft economic period.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it is probably characteristic of a lot of slow growth and recessionary periods.

speaker: KOHN
text: But certainly it has been more intense this time because the financial turmoil has spread well beyond housing and has intensified significantly over the intermeeting period.

speaker: KOHN
text: The incoming data on spending, employment, and production were weaker than expected.

speaker: KOHN
text: House prices are moving lower by more than we or the markets expected.

speaker: KOHN
text: All of these data have accentuated concerns about the creditworthiness of households and businesses and, hence, about the creditworthiness of the people who lend to them, especially those who lend in the mortgage market.

speaker: KOHN
text: As perceptions of risk and risk aversion rose, there was a flight to safety and liquidity.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we see that a little in the growth of M2 over the past couple of months, which has been very, very strong and suggests that households are retreating to money market funds, probably the ones that hold government securities, and to insured deposits.

speaker: KOHN
text: In wholesale markets there has been unwillingness to take positions and rising concerns about an array of intermediaries.

speaker: KOHN
text: Bill described this process much better than I could—illiquid markets, extreme volatility, deleveraging, margin calls, forced sales, especially in mortgage-backed securities, wider spreads, equity prices falling, and lending and funding tenors collapsing toward the overnight, again.

speaker: KOHN
text: So financial conditions have tightened for everybody but the government—and some of the European governments have seen them tighten, I guess.

speaker: KOHN
text: Mortgage rates have risen, and business bond yields have risen as well, even with Treasury rates going down.

speaker: KOHN
text: Tighter credit and declining equity and house prices are reducing wealth, and all of this weakens spending further.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, to this process, the staff has judged that the economy has entered a recessionary state in which we can expect household and business spending to fall short of normal levels, given income and interest rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am not sure how much weight to put on this.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am a bit uncomfortable with constructs that don’t have a clear story behind them.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I must say that, looking at the sentiment indicators and listening to what I have heard around the table today from almost every Federal Reserve District reporting, I now put more credence in Dave’s recessionary state than I did before the meeting started.

speaker: KOHN
text: Obviously, something is going on that is undermining confidence and making people much more cautious than you would think, given the exogenous variables.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think talking about the recessionary state underlines the extraordinary uncertainty we are dealing with.

speaker: KOHN
text: President Stern pointed out the 1990-91 precedent.

speaker: KOHN
text: There are some precedents for some aspects of this, but we don’t have many; and I think it is really difficult to know how financial markets will evolve and how that will feed through to the variables that affect household and business spending—the reaction of households, businesses, and state and local governments to tighter credit conditions.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with President Stern, President Evans, and others who said they thought that the financial stresses are deeper and will last longer than we thought and will, therefore, put more restraint on spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: Until markets stabilize on a sustained basis, the risk to satisfactory economic performance by the U.S. economy will remain skewed very much to the downside.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, Federal Reserve liquidity tools that we have used are necessary to reduce the odds on even more-intense, downward-spiral crises and market liquidity feeding back onto spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think our innovations here have been useful to reduce the downside risks a little and thereby to promote spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I agree with the others who say that they don’t directly deal with the underlying macro risk, which is really a story about capital, solvency, wealth, and prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think monetary policy easing is a necessary aspect of addressing these macroeconomic risks.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with President Fisher, President Plosser, and others that there is more going on and that monetary policy easing may not be a sufficient way of addressing these risks.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I do think, as long as the economy is weakening the way it is and we have these risks, that easing monetary policy will be helpful.

speaker: KOHN
text: It will help bolster asset prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: It will make the cost of capital lower than it otherwise would be.

speaker: KOHN
text: It may not be sufficient to turn the thing around, but I do think that without the easing that we have done— and that I hope that we do today—the situation would be far worse than it otherwise would be.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to ease to compensate for the substantial headwinds that we are facing.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, the forecast for inflation has not been marked down despite the greater output gap.

speaker: KOHN
text: As others have remarked, this output gap is offset, to a considerable extent, by the upward pressure on prices from oil and commodities and import prices as the dollar has fallen and prices have risen in our exporting partners—China, for example.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have to confess that I don’t really understand what has been happening to commodity prices in recent months.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think the rise has been justified by the news on the underlying conditions of supply and demand.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is much larger than the dollar weakness has been, and the dollar–commodity price has always been a weak relationship.

speaker: KOHN
text: So, in fact, commodity prices are rising in a bunch of currencies.

speaker: KOHN
text: This isn’t just a dollar weakness problem.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have to believe that there is a speculative element here.

speaker: KOHN
text: Partly as a consequence, I am comfortable with the forecast of a flattening commodity price picture in the future—it might even decline, but at least a flattening out.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think a shift from financial assets, especially dollar assets, into commodities is going on, and mostly this has been triggered by concerns about the U.S. economy and financial markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: In some sense, that shift is okay.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is driving down the dollar, and that is helping to stabilize the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: The decline that we saw in oil prices yesterday suggests that, when people get more confidence about where those financial markets are going, some of those commodity prices will actually fall as the concerns about the U.S. economy are alleviated.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is sort of an upside-down relationship, but I do think we saw a bit of it that way.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I also sense that some of the rise in commodity prices and the fall in the dollar reflects concerns about the inflation outlook here.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is not surprising to me, in a very volatile and uncertain environment, that inflation expectations are not as well anchored and that they fluctuate a lot in response to new information.

speaker: KOHN
text: I expect that inflation will come down as commodity prices level off; then the output gap will increase, and that in turn will keep inflation expectations down.

speaker: KOHN
text: Still, navigating this appreciably weaker economic outlook for the real economy and the threats to financial stability, on the one hand, and the tenderness of inflation expectations, on the other, will require some discussion in the next section of our meeting, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: WARSH
text: To join the growing chorus in the discussion today, I would say that there are very significant policy challenges across five areas on both sides of our mandate.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, the real economy is materially weaker.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, inflation risks are quite discomforting.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, we have genuine issues with respect to financial stability.

speaker: WARSH
text: Fourth, we have very real problems with respect to the credit channel and credit availability.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, as I think a couple of others have said, we have risks in terms of possible disorderly moves on the dollar.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of what markets believe that we believe are the big concerns, I think they rightly understand that we are very worried about downside risks to the economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: They believe that we are very focused on financial stability risks; and with the three new facilities announced in recent periods, they are coming to believe that we are finding an effective means to deal with a credit intermediation system that is, to perhaps overstate only a little, broken.

speaker: WARSH
text: But market participants may not yet believe that we are as concerned as we ought to be about inflation risks and about risks with respect to the path of the exchange value of the dollar.

speaker: WARSH
text: With that summary having been made, let me talk, first, about financial market conditions.

speaker: WARSH
text: About the deterioration in market functioning since the last FOMC meeting, Bill spoke in great detail.

speaker: WARSH
text: Over the past couple of weeks, not just in the episode with Bear Stearns, counterparty risk has become the dominant concern in markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: As has been pointed out around this table, it is increasingly difficult to separate liquidity issues from solvency issues.

speaker: WARSH
text: So what should we take from this deterioration in counterparty risks?

speaker: WARSH
text: If we look at a range of financial institutions that have different degrees of implied backstops by the government based on their size and their regulatory structure, we think about the GSEs that have an implied government guarantee and even Ginnie Maes, which have the full faith and credit backing of the U.S. government and about which the Board staff shared some data yesterday with us.

speaker: WARSH
text: The spreads on all of these look as though they have widened substantially.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have seen very real deterioration.

speaker: WARSH
