text: But when you see that it is happening for the Ginnie Maes, just as with many of these other securities, it suggests that this is substantially, but not completely, about liquidity risk because the credit risk of Ginnies ostensibly can’t be called into question.

speaker: WARSH
text: Financial institutions, more broadly than financial markets, are having a hard time finding their way.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have talked around this table before about their balance sheet problems, and most recently we have talked about their income statement problems in figuring out what their core business is.

speaker: WARSH
text: In the markets in the last couple of days, we have had the broker–dealers with widening CDS spreads and falling share prices, and of course, that is about their mortgage exposure and liquidity concerns.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I think, most fundamentally, that the business model of investment banks has been threatened, and I suspect the existing business model will not endure through this period.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a result, the current architecture of the regulation of financial institutions and of the business model across ranges of financial institutions—commercial banks, investment banks, and hedge funds—will change through this period.

speaker: WARSH
text: The old model, at least in investment banking, of high imputed leverage works incredibly well in a world of high liquidity and doesn’t work as well when liquidity is in short supply.

speaker: WARSH
text: Why do I think this matters?

speaker: WARSH
text: It matters because it suggests that any catalyst for improvement from financial institutions feeding into the real economy for the rest of 2008 or even for the first half of 2009 is quite suspect.

speaker: WARSH
text: These institutions are spending all their time and attention on their own business models, figuring out how they can survive this period, not on providing credit to the real economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I don’t look to financial institutions to be very good shock absorbers or very good catalysts going forward.

speaker: WARSH
text: My concern, broadly, about financial institutions is highlighted when I think about the need, across all these institutions, to raise significant capital for safety and soundness purposes and, in addition, for credit availability purposes.

speaker: WARSH
text: It strikes me that this broad class is systematically undercapitalized, and we need to use all our tools to persuade them that it is in their interest and in the interest of the broad economy for them to raise capital.

speaker: WARSH
text: But finding capital, certainly over the next six months, will be a very real challenge.

speaker: WARSH
text: The capital markets are not in a very strong position to satisfy issuer needs at present.

speaker: WARSH
text: That obviously can improve over the next couple of months, but there is no certainty.

speaker: WARSH
text: Sovereign wealth funds and other sources of investment that we have been talking about for some time—and we saw their real interest in investing in financial institutions at the end of last year or early this year— are quite beaten down.

speaker: WARSH
text: Those that I talked to, who are very sophisticated investors from places in Asia and the Middle East, do not want to appear as though they are doormats for these financial institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: Their own political structures make the losses they have had to endure front page news.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the expectation that sovereign wealth funds are going to continue to be a source of funding in this period is well overstated.

speaker: WARSH
text: Moreover, private equity—the case for opportunistic capital—has little ability to get leverage in this environment, and so if they don’t reduce their target hurdle rates, I don’t expect them to be able to come to the rescue.

speaker: WARSH
text: All of that, again, suggests to me that the real economy will have to wait awhile for improvement as this repair is slow and not at all certain over the next six to nine months.

speaker: WARSH
text: Obviously, the implication for the real economy is hard to speculate about, but I think, looking at some rough measures, maybe a third of the credit availability of the real economy has been taken out during this period—maybe more than that.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say that the last week makes it hard for us to judge how much more credit channel capability and balance sheet capacity have left the real economy, but it suggests a picture for the real economy that is worthy of real concern.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now, when I look to the real economy, I would just underscore the comments I have heard from others.

speaker: WARSH
text: A couple of CEOs who have been incredibly optimistic, at least in my discussions with them in the past couple of years—these are CEOs of leading consumer product companies—have thrown in the towel.

speaker: WARSH
text: They have given up trying to justify and explain away weakness.

speaker: WARSH
text: Across the auto sector, a couple of the new owners of the auto companies are now focused on a scenario in which units are in the 14.5 million range rather than the 15 million or 15.5 million range, largely because of weakness of consumption in terms of consumer purchases.

speaker: WARSH
text: But that really goes back to credit, and in some ways the credit availability to fund those auto purchases is a chance for another stepdown in the next month.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that business cap-ex is as threatened as has been represented today.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is the only area for which my own sense is probably more negative than the Greenbook’s in terms of weakness to expect out of Europe and the United Kingdom.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is hard for me to think, as we go through this period, that Europe and the United Kingdom would stay as decoupled as recent data suggest.

speaker: WARSH
text: Their economies are tied to their banking system more concretely than we are tied to ours, and I suspect that their large financial institutions are going to suffer real problems during this upcoming period.

speaker: WARSH
text: If not, it is certainly a risk factor.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn to the last two issues—inflation and currency.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the inflation front, there is little reason to be confident that inflation will decline.

speaker: WARSH
text: There are reasons to believe that our inflation problems will become more pronounced and, I fear, more persistent.

speaker: WARSH
text: The recent run-up in energy prices and commodity prices in the context of weaker global demand is troubling.

speaker: WARSH
text: No doubt partly it is a move to real assets by the financial community—that is, a hedge against all of this is certainly, to the Governor Kohn’s point, raising commodity prices.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I am not sure what catalyst will change that over at least the next six months.

speaker: WARSH
text: As the Board staff has noted, there has been some rise in inflation compensation and inflation expectations.

speaker: WARSH
text: There is acceleration in the fall of the exchange rate of the dollar, suggestive of increasing import inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: Moreover, it is not obvious to me that a slowing economy in this cycle, in the short term at least, will do our work for us on the inflation front.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, let me turn to currency.

speaker: WARSH
text: Given this particular confluence of events, the accelerated depreciation of the dollar is troubling, and I think the risks of a disorderly move on the dollar in the upcoming six weeks are hard to discount.

speaker: WARSH
text: The catalyst of that could be a sudden de-pegging by certain countries in the Middle East.

speaker: WARSH
text: But even if that does not come to pass, there is an expectation in the market, where traders are looking for bets where they believe they can make money with certitude, that there is still a free one-way bet on the dollar.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is not healthy for currency movements, regardless of one’s view of where the dollar should ultimately be trading against the currencies of our trading partners.

speaker: WARSH
text: At this time, particularly, given our concerns about making sure that the U.S. economy remains open for foreign direct investment— that this is where others want to invest their capital—it strikes me as a reasonably dangerous prospect if the view is that the dollar will continue its accelerated path.

speaker: WARSH
text: Obviously, this suggests very difficult judgments for the next round of our discussion, and I will take up monetary policy in that context.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I’ve talked many times before about the slow burn from the financial markets that is spreading out elsewhere.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Unfortunately, I think the fire is a bit hotter than I had expected in my earlier discussions, and it comes particularly through capital pressures in the financial institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: What we’re seeing now is the simultaneity of stress in the housing market and stress in the financial markets, and they will be cured together.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think they are joined at the hip.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Whether we have tools to address those directly is something we continue to discuss, but I think it is this direct connection that potentially leads to the negative feedback loop that we have discussed quite a bit.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: For housing, of course, there are the direct negative wealth effects but also the lingering uncertainty of what’s going to happen, as many people have mentioned.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Part of this comes from just a change in behavior.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: People are acting very differently during this housing cycle from in the past, so it is very difficult to predict the evolution of foreclosures even given a particular macroeconomic outcome.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There’s still the uncertainty of the macroeconomic outcome, but people are going delinquent much earlier—they are going delinquent on their houses before they go delinquent on their credit cards—and so it is really a different model of consumer behavior, which makes valuing the securities particularly problematic.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This is, of course, in addition to uncharted territory in terms of real and nominal price declines.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’ll see exactly how people will respond to these things.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously the markets are closed, and the banks have to keep these on their books, with higher cost and more difficulty financing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some of the changes that came in with the stimulus package to raise the conforming limits for Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae have done little to bring down the spreads because they have significantly increased the cost of the guarantees given this new environment.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s not unreasonable to do that, but the potential benefit from the changes is lower than we might otherwise have hoped for.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This is all having consequences for credit cards.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Even though at first it was the mortgages, now we’re starting to see a significant uptick in delinquencies on credit cards and spending, and a number of people—President Rosengren, President Yellen, and First Vice President Sapenaro— have mentioned some of these things.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I just want to report a bit from my conversations with some of the major credit card companies, which have kind of a window into real-time consumer spending.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They are seeing a continuing flattening but not a falloff of growth.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There’s no collapse but certainly a continued downtrend, as I’ve been reporting over the past few months—a continuing slowing of payments and a continuing increase in delinquencies.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Their so-called roll rates of people moving from 30 days behind to 60 days behind to 90 days behind continue to go up.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They are still going up, although not significantly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They are concerned about that, but it is not spiking up.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They are mainly concerned about when the roll rate gets into 90 to 180 days.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They’re not getting their money back.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Personal bankruptcies are going up.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The cure rates are much lower, and the recovery rates are much lower.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So there seems to be a group of people who are getting into extreme financial difficulty.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: All the series that I’ve quoted are general averages.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The contacts said that in areas of particular housing stress basically all of the numbers are three times as high.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is significantly more stressful there, showing a very clear link between stress in the housing market and these other stresses.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, because of very strong pressures that may be coming directly from us and certainly from Capitol Hill, the credit card companies don’t respond by changing interest rates.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They respond by reducing the amount of credit available, and that’s exactly what they’ve been doing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So they’ve been cutting credit lines of a lot of people.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, as I think President Yellen or a number of people mentioned, they’re also cutting back on the HELOCs because they have been concerned that people are taking money out when no equity is there, and so they really want to pull back on that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: These overall tightening credit conditions are reflecting the continued stress on the balance sheets of banks and financial institutions more generally; as you see with the Bear Stearns example, it’s not just the depository institutions but a broader set of institutions that are creating pressures both on the asset side and on the funding side.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have had a lot of the SIVs and a lot of the other assets coming on board.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Unplanned asset expansions may continue, particularly if the economy does go down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: What now seem to be very good credits in the leveraged lending market may no longer be good credits.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So the anecdotal evidence that you’ve been mentioning around the table could turn into further unplanned asset expansions if these things start to go south.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Consumer write-offs, obviously, are another thing that is putting on funding pressure.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also as I think President Evans mentioned, interestingly there have been few actual losses that have occurred on many of these securities in terms of the inability to make the payments, although the losses in the value in the markets have been quite spectacular in some cases.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some of this has to do with the broad evaluation uncertainty.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some of it has to do with liquidity.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think this is where we have the direct link between liquidity and macro stability because the uncertainties in part are coming from the macro uncertainty about how housing markets will evolve.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously I have said this before.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There are other factors that come in, but that’s a big one.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So doing something to provide some insurance against that or to help provide comfort that these markets can come back is important because there’s a very close link between liquidity issues that we have been seeing, the unwillingness to finance, and the capital issues that have been coming from an incompleteness of markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The markets just aren’t there for people to be trading in.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They are valuing things off an index.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The index can’t be arbitraged against the underlying markets because the underlying markets aren’t there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So the index is doing something else.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s the only somewhat liquid market that’s providing some hedging.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s driving that down, and people don’t want to buy the underlying security because they’ll have to take the mark against this index rather than the true value.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If they have to take the mark against something that they think is going to be pushed down artificially, they’re not going to buy the security in the first place.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: These kinds of continuing stress make me feel a little less optimistic about the bounce-back in ’09 that’s in the Greenbook, although I don’t think it’s ruled out.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Just turning quickly to inflation, we have a bit of a paradox in what has gone on recently as everyone has said—significantly slowing growth over the past four to five months but no evidence of slowing in the pressure on commodity, energy, and agriculture prices.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That’s despite some slowing elsewhere in the world and expectations of slower growth.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The PPI numbers that came out today raised some concerns that some of the good parts of the CPI will not be flowing through to PCE.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, over the last year or two, when we’ve had the unemployment rate below 5 percent or 4¾ percent, whatever your favorite number is, where there would be pressure on wages, we haven’t seen much pressure on wages.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I’m not sure that, if the unemployment rate goes significantly above 5 percent, we’ll see much on the other side that will take pressure off wages to bring things down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I do remain concerned there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I think there’s a final risk that, if commodity, energy, and agriculture prices do significantly move down, it could have a major effect on some of the emerging markets and some of our other trading partners.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So there’s a bit of a paradox here that, if there are some potential benefits of the slowdown to reduce these prices, that could actually also reduce export demand, which—as a number of people pointed out—is very important in the forecast for keeping this a shallow recession.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I remain concerned on both the growth front and the inflation front, but I do think that macro stability is probably the primary thing that we need to be thinking about right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s not my usual personality trait, but the reality is that we’ve had as bad a set of shocks as I could have imagined, and I want to talk about this set of shocks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have been hit with things that are making our policy environment as complicated as I possibly could have imagined.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The reality is that we are in the worst financial crisis that we’ve experienced in the post–World War II era.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t think we should be shy about saying it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We are in a financial crisis, and it is worse than we have experienced in any other episode of financial “disruption,” which is the word I use.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I will not use “financial crisis” in public.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: “Financial disruption” is still a good phrase to use in public, but I really do think that this is a financial crisis.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is surely going to be called that in the next edition of my textbook.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When is it coming out?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Wouldn’t you like to know!

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I believe that actually the Greenbook forecast of a mild recession is reasonable, but the possibility that we could have a severe recession is uncomfortably high, and I find the prospect pretty scary.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The reality is that we are in this adverse feedback loop that I and others talked about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think we’re deep into it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The credit markets have been deteriorating.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s led to a sharp weakening of the economy’s prospects.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is reflected in the very large change in the Greenbook forecast, with which I do strongly concur, so I don’t think that it was out of line to put those in.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, that weakening has been feeding back to deteriorating financial conditions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think we’re really in a tough pickle, and there are costs not just in terms of the economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One result is that we’ve just expanded the safety net to a much wider set of institutions, and we are in a brave new world here, and it is very disturbing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the ramifications in terms of the economy weakening and the adverse feedback loop go beyond just the fact that we might have unemployment.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It may have major effects on the way markets work in the future, and that, I think, is something that we should be worried about and should be a consideration as well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The bottom line on real activity for me is that the prospects are very poor, and I find the downside risk just plain scary.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s the first part of my depression.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second part of the depression is that it’s bad enough that we had these contractionary aggregate demand shocks from the financial sector, but we also have had very negative supply shocks that are both contractionary and inflationary.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So we are getting hit by the double whammy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The news on inflation has generally not been good, even with the recent CPI numbers.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But then, of course, they are reversed by the PPI numbers today.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t put that much weight on the actual current numbers because, as you know, I take a view that the primary drivers of inflation and inflation dynamics are inflation expectations and expectations about future output gaps.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So that’s the framework in which I’d like to discuss what will happen on the inflation front.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have two problems in terms of inflation expectations right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is the supply shock, which I think is having some effects on inflation expectations, and also the view—although I believe it’s incorrect, I do think that there’s a problem that this view is widely held outside, and President Plosser mentioned this—that we on the FOMC are focused only on growth and are not at all worried about inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is a communication issue that is hard to deal with because, even though I’ve been advocating being more aggressive in terms of easing, I do worry very much about the issue that we also have to indicate that, if necessary, we’ll get out the baseball bat to keep inflation under control.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is not an easy thing to do.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So when I look at inflation expectations, which I consider to be a key driver of inflation, I think that the evidence in the data is that we have had not a big increase but a slight increase in inflation expectations, on the order of about 10 basis points.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There’s a lot of uncertainty about that; it could be a little more than that, but I don’t think a whole lot more.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also disturbing is that we certainly have had a big increase in long-run inflation uncertainty.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s reflected not only in terms of inflation compensation but also in the fact that people are buying inflation caps, TIPS are becoming very popular, and so forth and so on.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, one of the negative things that happened to me as a result of taking this job is that I had my entire TIAA-CREF in TIPS and unfortunately I had to divest all of it because they are government securities, and that turned out to be bad.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But that’s only one of the minor costs of being in this position.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The issue here is that, although I don’t think that inflation expectations have gotten unhinged at this point—and I think that we can say that the phrase “reasonably well contained” is okay—there is a greater risk that they could get unhinged.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Now, I want to be clear.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m not talking about the 1970s.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s not “That ’70s Show.” I have not been particularly happy with Allan Meltzer’s comments about a bunch of things.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The issue here is not that inflation expectations would go to that kind of level, but it could be that inflation expectations go up to 2½ or maybe even a little higher and it would be costly to get that down.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s the concern we have to worry about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But let me talk about the other side because, when I think about the inflation dynamics, it’s not just inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do not believe in the deus ex machina view of the inflation process.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Something has to tie things down, and what ties it down is not current output gaps—which is why I think the standard Phillips curves don’t predict very well—but expectations about future output gaps.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On that score, I worry that there could be a lot of downside risk to inflation from that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If really bad things happen, which I think unfortunately is a seriously possibility, inflation could fall.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: A key fact, by the way, is that if you look at past recessions, you do find that inflation falls in the 12 months after recessions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In a couple of cases with supply shocks, there was a rise in inflation at the beginning of the recessions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Seven out of eight are in that category.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Particularly if it’s a severe recession, it’s much more likely for inflation to fall.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So it’s not true that there’s just upside risk; there is downside risk as well, and that’s one reason that inflation uncertainty is not an issue just of potential upside.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, in the 2003 episode that President Lacker mentioned, the reason there was such a sharp rise in inflation compensation was not that people worried about inflation going up but that they worried that inflation would go down.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Nonetheless, there’s still a cost to the fact that long- run inflation expectations are not as solidly grounded as they were before.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So my view in general is that we are facing an incredibly unpleasant tradeoff.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We basically have the risk of the economy turning very sharply and the risk of inflation getting somewhat unhinged.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I want to discuss that later.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I wasn’t going to discuss this, but I just really can’t not react to the comments that you made, President Fisher.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There’s a view out there in the media that monetary policy has been ineffective.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This was the statement that I think you made, and I think it is just plain wrong.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I want to discuss it because it’s actually really important in thinking about a policy stance right now, and it’s important to think about the economics of this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have had a very nasty set of contractionary shocks from the financial sector, particularly the widening of credit spreads and the restriction of credit.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I want us to think about a counterfactual.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Let’s think about a situation in which we had what’s happened and we did not lower interest rates.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What would have been the outcome?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Do you think that credit spreads would have lowered?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think credit spreads would have risen.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, when you think about what credit spreads are being driven by—I’ve argued this before—there’s a valuation risk—the fact that we can’t value assets, and that’s this price discovery problem that we really can’t do that much about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But there is also a macroeconomic risk, which is a lot of what’s going on right now, particularly in terms of the housing market where people don’t know where housing prices are going to bottom out.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The view that they may keep on going down—and we had a very negative number on housing prices recently—means that even the AAA tranches now look as though they’re very vulnerable, and therefore, the credit spreads on them go up a whole lot.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My view is that monetary policy has been very effective because things would be much, much worse if we hadn’t eased.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On the other hand, we just had an incredibly nasty set of shocks as a result of what you described were the problems in these sectors.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I really think that this is very important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: To finish up on this, the example of Japan is constructive because the Bank of Japan had a view very similar to the one that you’ve expressed, which is that they had all these problems in the banking sector, and the problems were not their fault.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But they then took the view that they couldn’t do anything about it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Monetary policy was not the source of the weak economy, so they were very slow to lower interest rates.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The Chairman has talked about this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Every monetary economist who went to the Bank of Japan during this period—I did it when I was with the New York Fed in the mid-1990s—told them that their monetary policy was too tight.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: They basically said, “Well, you know, it’s not too tight, and it’s not our fault that the banks are all screwed up because of poor regulation.” Well, the result was they ended up with deflation, and they lost ten years of growth.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m being a little more blunt than usual, but I think that the economic arguments here are actually central in our discussion.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, may I answer?

speaker: FISHER
text: Just very quickly, I said that the liquidity situation we’re in diminishes the efficacy of fed funds policy; I’m not saying it’s not a worthwhile tool.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, I was fully supportive until we got to 3.5.

speaker: FISHER
text: Then we went from 3.5 to 3 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: Everything we wanted to go one way then went the opposite way.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I just made the observation that it didn’t seem to be effective.

speaker: FISHER
text: Third, I think I spent even more time in Japan than President Geithner, who is an expert on Japan, and you cannot compare the two economies.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are geared totally differently, with totally different efficiency.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’d be happy to debate that at a later point.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it’s a very poor analogy.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, having said that, I respect the enormous macroeconomic downside risk that we have—and I have one of the most pessimistic forecasts—but there’s a price to be paid for what we’re doing unless it is efficient, and that price is reflected in inflation expectations.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s my point, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, I’m going to cede all of my time to you, except to acknowledge and to point out that there’s much I agree with that has been said around the table, particularly with how people characterize the growth outlook and the risks and what’s happening in financial markets and to the outlook.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I can’t say that stuff better than it has been said.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But there’s much I disagree with in what’s been said, particularly on the inflation side, about the lack of credibility.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just want very quickly to say a couple of things about how we talk about this stuff based on what’s been said.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: First, some of you at this table may believe that we are losing credibility, and you may be losing confidence in the capacity of this Committee to mitigate the risk to our long-term inflation objectives.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If you say that in public, you will magnify that problem, and just because you believe it does not make it true.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I believe that you should have more confidence in the commitment of this Committee to do what is necessary to keep those expectations stable over time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Second, the stuff about capital and the financial system is very, very important.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very hard to make the judgment now that the financial system as a whole or the banking system as a whole is undercapitalized.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Some people out there are saying that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In some states of the world, particularly if there is no liquidity, then any financial system will be systematically insolvent.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But based on everything we know today, if you look at very pessimistic estimates of the scale of losses across the financial system, on average relative to capital, they do not justify that concern.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very important to make distinctions in what we say about that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very different to say that their distribution is uneven and to say that for some institutions those losses may be large relative to capital.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That is obviously the case; we have already seen that to be the case.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is important to make the distinction between the average and the distribution.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Although the average losses look relatively manageable relative to capital, the system is short of capital relative to what would be ideal, given that we’ve had the collapse of a very large part of the nonbank financial system.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Banks as a whole are not large enough now, even with their capital cushions, to compensate for the scale of disintermediation of that type of nonbank finance.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Those are very important distinctions to make in this case.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is nothing more dangerous in what we’re facing now than for people who are knowledgeable about this stuff to feed these broad concerns about our credibility and about the basic core strength of the financial system.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I just want to underscore the importance of exceptional care in how we talk about those things, even in private.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: A lot of people out there who should know better—none of us is guilty of this—are casting broad aspersions about solvency that are very dangerous in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: May we get to the point where those concerns are justified?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course we may get to that point.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we systematically mismanage policy, we may get to that point.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But please be careful in that context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I meant to cede all my time to you.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Finally, I have to state for the record that I did submit our forecast.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: To state the obvious, it’s close enough to the Greenbook on most things, and, given the range of uncertainty, there’s no material between our view and the Greenbook’s.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you for all of your comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just briefly summarize and add a few points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To summarize the discussion, incoming data have been weak, and some view the economy as having entered recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing demand and construction have continued to decline sharply, and house-price declines have been somewhat greater than expected.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing weakness has implications for employment, for consumer spending, and for credit conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It also leads to 21 miles of empty boxcars.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial conditions have worsened considerably, reflecting weakness in housing prices, and credit markets in particular are highly stressed and illiquid.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Wider spreads have offset some or all of the decline in safe rates for many credit products, and credit conditions are tighter for most borrowers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial conditions are likely to be a significant drag on economic growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some noted the risk that continued financial turmoil could lead to a more serious and prolonged recession, implying possibly large downside risk to growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to households, consumption growth has flattened out, and there was generally greater pessimism about the labor market and economic prospects.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumer credit quality may be worsening.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Payroll employment growth has turned negative.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was little expectation expressed of strong help from the fiscal stimulus package.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Firms are generally more pessimistic and cautious but also remain concerned about cost pressures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inventories look to be in balance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Exports continue to be an important source of final demand and will continue to contribute significantly to growth, although it’s possible that growth abroad may slow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Readings on core inflation have been mixed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Increases in energy and commodity prices are important sources of increased headline inflation, and some producers have adopted a cost-plus mentality.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Agricultural prices, in particular, are up a good bit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inflation breakevens are up somewhat, especially at the five-by-five horizon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The dollar has depreciated, potentially adding to longer-term inflation pressures and adding some risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, nominal wage increases are moderate, as are unit labor costs, and U.S. and global economic weakness could moderate gains in commodity prices and create domestic economic slack.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Several members warned about the risk of losing inflation credibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me make just a few comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I’m very sympathetic to what almost everyone has said around the table, in particular the fact that we’re facing a three-front war, if you will, which makes this extraordinarily difficult and delicate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I thought in January that we were in recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was my view at that time, and I certainly believe it now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Greenbook has done a good job of trying to factor in the data and the other types of evidence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I’m actually slightly darker on growth than the Greenbook is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The reason is that I don’t see where the recovery is coming from in the beginning of next year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, we won’t have a recovery until financial markets stabilize, and the financial markets won’t stabilize until house prices stabilize, and there is simply no particular reason to choose a time for that to happen.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I do think that the downside risks are quite significant and that this so-called adverse feedback loop is currently in full play.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At some point, of course, either things will stabilize or there will be some kind of massive governmental intervention, but I just don’t have much confidence about the timing of that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to say a word.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would just agree with Governor Mishkin about the efficacy of our policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that it has had an effect and it has been beneficial.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We obviously affect short- term rates, including commercial paper rates and the like, which have implications for financing and for borrowing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We affect the dollar, which has mixed effects, but on the growth side has some positive effects.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s true, as President Fisher pointed out, that medium-term and long-term rates have not fallen because lower Treasury rates have been offset by higher spreads, but again, the question is the counterfactual.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Where would we be if we had not lowered rates?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that lower rates have both lowered safe rates and offset to some extent the rising concerns about solvency, which have caused the credit spreads to widen.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think this argument can go either way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You can say that our policy is less effective and, therefore, we should do more of it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there are two ways of looking at that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, there may be some benefits for capital formation of low financing rates and a steep yield curve in keeping bank share prices from entirely collapsing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On inflation, I agree with much of what’s been said, and I’m very concerned about it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me make one simple point, though, which I don’t think has been adequately discussed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Ninety-five percent of the inflation that we’re seeing is either the direct or the indirect effect of globally traded commodity prices—food, energy, and other commodities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What is happening is that there is a change in the relative price of, say, oil and the wage of an Ohio manufacturing worker.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s a relative price change going on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That has to happen one way or the other.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It can happen either by overall increases in the nominal price of oil, which are reflected in overall increases in headline CPI inflation, or by lower or negative growth in nominal wages.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, if we have temporary movements in these relative prices, I think all the theory tells us that the best way to let that relative price change happen is to let the shock feed through; let the prices of energy, commodities, and so on rise; accept a temporary increase in headline inflation; and focus on making sure that the increase in headline inflation doesn’t feed through into domestic core inflation, say, through wages or domestic prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A good response to that is, well, we’ve had a lot of “temporary” shocks here and they have gone on for a long time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But again, it was very difficult to anticipate how these prices have moved.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Looking forward, the futures markets have been wrong and wrong, but they are the best we have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In my view, if we think about the likely slowdown in the U.S. economy and the global economy, there are going to be some forces that will prevent commodity prices from continuing to rise the way they have been rising, which ought to take the pressure off the inflation process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That being said, I fully recognize that there has been a bit of movement in some of the indicators.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I like the use of the index measure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It uses lots of different indicators.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think we should overemphasize inflation compensation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, the one-year inflation compensation three and four years out has moved up less than the five-by-five, and I think for good reasons.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The five-by- five could reflect, again, general uncertainty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It could also reflect more volatility in the relative price changes of oil, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we think there’s more volatility in that, if it’s up or down, that would create more uncertainty about headline inflation and would feed through into that spread.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Frankly, in thinking about inflation, I am concerned about inflation expectations and the general psychology.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m hopeful at least that it will moderate as commodity prices moderate although, of course, no one can know for sure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with Governor Warsh that, from a financial perspective on the inflation side, the greater dangers are in the currency area.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Exchange rates are very poorly tied down by fundamentals, except over very long periods of time—I think Ken Rogoff had a paper in which he said that over maybe 600 years or so the PPP finally works.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So a lot of psychology is there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that it is an important issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to think about what the Treasury will say and those sorts of things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is a concern, and I consider that in some sense a greater risk at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there are risks on both sides.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the downside risks, including the financial risks, at this point are greater—not to belittle inflation risks, which I think are quite significant.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are obviously going to have to make tradeoffs about how to deal with these.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Using both our policy tools and our communication is very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with Vice Chairman Geithner that we need and I need—and I have a very important role here—to maintain clarity in communication about our attention to inflation, that we are not ignoring that side of the mandate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, let me just say, as I said last night at the dinner with the presidents, that I think we are getting to the point where the Federal Reserve’s tools, both its liquidity tools and its interest rate tools, are not by themselves sufficient to resolve our troubles.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: More help, more activity, from the Congress and the Administration to address housing issues, for example, would be desirable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are certainly working on those issues here at the Board, and I will be talking to people in Washington about what might be done to try to address more fundamentally these issues of the housing market and the financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So those are my comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we turn now to Brian for an introduction to the policy round.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will be referring to the revised version of table 1 distributed earlier today in the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” The revised table presents the same basic set of alternatives that was discussed in the Bluebook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, we have proposed some changes in language that affect the statements for alternatives A and B. I will discuss those changes, shown in blue, shortly.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative D, presented in the right-hand column, would leave the federal funds rate unchanged at this meeting at 3 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Committee members might be inclined to favor this alternative if they were particularly concerned about prospects for inflation and if they believed that, with due allowance for lags, the monetary and fiscal stimulus in train would likely be sufficient to lead to a resumption of moderate growth over time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The wording of this alternative would acknowledge the downside risks to growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But as shown in paragraph 3, the statement would indicate that inflation has been elevated, cite several factors that could put additional upward pressure on inflation, and state that the upside risks to inflation have increased.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: No net assessment of the balance of risks would be included.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative C, the stance of policy would be eased by 25 basis points today.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A modest easing of policy might be motivated by judgments that the economic outlook has weakened, but by appreciably less than in the Greenbook, and that the inflation outlook is troubling.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Members might see financial strains as concerning but likely to exert less restraint on growth than in the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In these circumstances, the Committee might want to be cautious about policy adjustments that could add impetus to inflation, particularly given the substantial easing of monetary policy to date and the lags in the effects of policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The language proposed for alternative C would note that the tightening of credit conditions and the deepening of the housing correction are likely to continue to weigh on economic growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The inflation paragraph for this alternative is the same as that for alternative D. As shown in paragraph 4, the Committee would make an explicit judgment that the downside risks to growth outweigh the upside risks to inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative B, the Committee would reduce the federal funds rate 50 basis points today, to 2½ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Such an approach could be seen as consistent with the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, under that forecast, the Committee is assumed to ease policy 50 basis points at this meeting and another 75 basis points over the next three months.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The motivation for such a trajectory is provided partly by the 1¼ percentage point downward revision to the Greenbook-consistent measure of short-run r*.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee might concur with the staff’s assumption regarding the amount of cumulative easing that will eventually prove necessary and find a gradual shift in policy attractive, particularly in view of what seems to be some upward drift of late in inflation expectations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Such a path would also be qualitatively consistent with the optimal control simulations shown in the Bluebook for a 2 percent inflation target, in which the federal funds rate is eventually eased to around 1¼ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in paragraph 2, the statement issued under this alternative would indicate that the outlook had weakened.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We have suggested striking the reference to risks as that thought is picked up in the risk assessment.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement would go on to mention several factors that could weigh on economic growth, and we have suggested adding “over the next few quarters.” With regard to inflation, the Committee would note that inflation has been elevated.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would also indicate an expectation that inflation will moderate in coming months and cite several factors that could contribute to that moderation but note that uncertainty about the inflation outlook has increased.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Notably, the list does not mention “reasonably well anchored inflation expectations” or some variant of that phrase, which has been used recently in the minutes and other policy communications.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, the first sentence of the paragraph notes that some indicators of inflation expectations have risen.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Partly because inflation compensation includes a premium for inflation risk as well as inflation expectations, we thought that “indicators” of inflation expectations might be a better word than “measures” and have suggested that substitution.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Over the past few days, inflation compensation as read from TIPS has plunged; however, we are skeptical that the decline represents primarily a drop in inflation expectations or inflation risk.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Rather, we suspect that it is importantly a result of shifting liquidity premiums, as yields on nominal Treasury securities have fallen sharply partly because of increased demands for safety and liquidity.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The final paragraph of alternative B would repeat the risk assessment issued after the January meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would again indicate that downside risks remain and emphasize that the Committee will act in a timely manner to address those risks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, under alternative A the Committee would lower the funds rate 75 basis points today.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Given the extent of policy easing assumed in the staff forecast, this alternative could easily be consistent with an outlook along the lines of the Greenbook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This policy approach could also be motivated by concern about the possible implications for the economic outlook of the worsening in financial market conditions in the five days since the staff forecast was finalized or by a risk- management approach that gave particular weight to the downside risks around the outlook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The language proposed for the rationale section, paragraphs 2 and 3, of alternative A is identical to that proposed for alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As with alternative B, the risk assessment paragraph says that policy actions should promote moderate growth over time and mitigate downside risks, but this version also alludes to the measures that the Federal Reserve has implemented to promote market liquidity.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This language could also be used in alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Rather than providing an assessment of the balance of risks, as we did in the Bluebook version, here in alterative A we have suggested simply indicating that downside risks to growth remain.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Given the high degree of uncertainty, you might again prefer not to make an overall risk assessment.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This paragraph differs from the corresponding part of the January statement also by indicating that the Committee will act in a timely manner as needed to promote sustainable economic growth and price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus, while the Committee eases 75 basis points, this language of alternative A would signal some increase in the Committee’s concern about inflation in several ways: by indicating that inflation has been elevated; by noting that some indicators of inflation expectations have risen; and by incorporating a traditional formulation of the dual objectives, including price stability, in the final sentence.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As Bill noted this morning, market participants appear to place substantial odds on a 100 basis point policy move at this meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus, implementation of any of these alternatives would involve at least somewhat less easing than expected.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Given what would appear to be very fragile market conditions and highly skittish investor sentiment, you might see somewhat greater risks than usual in diverging from market expectations, and obviously the risks would be larger the greater the gap between anticipation and your actions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: At the same time, you might see good reasons for some divergence.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: First and most obviously, you might see a smaller move as appropriately calibrated given your outlook and sense of the risks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, some indicators do seem to suggest that inflation expectations have become a bit less firmly moored.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even if you see gradual dollar depreciation as likely to be appropriate given the weakness of the U.S. economy and quite possibly a necessary factor in fostering an improved current account balance over time, you may be concerned about the downward lurch in the dollar over recent days and the potential for disorderly conditions to develop.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You may judge that a policy decision today to implement somewhat less easing than markets expect and a statement that implies somewhat greater concern about inflation could be helpful in leaning against inflation expectations and any sense in markets that you are indifferent to downward pressure on the dollar.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative A would likely prompt some increase in shorter-term interest rates; but given that the risk assessment would point to continued downside risks, market participants would infer that further easing is a likely prospect, and the effects on other financial asset prices and financial conditions more generally could be reasonably limited.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The 50 basis point easing of alternative B, in contrast, would suggest to market participants that you are inclined to be considerably more cautious in easing policy further, even with the downside risk assessment, and short- and intermediate-term interest rates could ratchet considerably higher, equity prices decline, and credit conditions tighten—responses that presumably would be amplified, perhaps nonlinearly, under alternatives C and D.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I just want to update the dealer survey.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We got two more responses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Two people moved from 75 to 100.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So right now as we speak, it is ten in the 100 camp, eight in the 75 camp, and two in the 50 camp.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, it is kind of awkward to ask this in the midst of a meeting, but I think it is important.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think there was a pretty big change this morning at least in risk perceptions today across a bunch of markets.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Can you tell what the fed funds curve has done this morning?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that the April fed funds futures contract earlier this morning was priced at 1.99, and it was up by 4 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t know if it moved subsequently.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Vice Chairman, it has moved up somewhat further at least as of maybe an hour ago.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It looked as though, at least for this meeting, the odds were roughly evenly balanced between 75 and 100, in terms of what was priced in.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Stocks are up about 2 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Both Lehman’s and Goldman’s earnings showed declines, but they were less significant than expected.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So share prices for both of them have rallied a lot.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Lehman’s stock was up 19 percent when I last looked—I don’t know where it is today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So a lot of reversals occurred yesterday in terms of the investment banks.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Financial credit default swaps this morning are much, much narrower.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: May I raise a conceptual question around this, though?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Maybe this is really for you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: How should we think about the tradeoff between what we do with the fed funds rate and whatever effect we have on liquidity and credit spreads, which are obviously in some ways working against the reduction of the fed funds rate?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It doesn’t seem to me quite right to say that they are perfect tradeoffs.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I guess my question is, Don’t they have independent effects?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I mean, they are separate and somewhat different in terms of how we think about mitigating the risk to the overall economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would think of them as complementary—they are not strong substitutes, obviously—in the sense that, as is often pointed out, the liquidity measures can affect credit and solvency concerns.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So maybe to echo the dialogue that you had with Governor Mishkin, if we were to be successful through taking out some of the liquidity risk of markets more generally and we got those spreads maybe back down to—I don’t know—50, in a crude proxy sense, that would be good and powerful but we would still be left with exceptionally tight financial conditions relative to the given target fed funds rate.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m not arguing that lowering the federal funds rate narrows these spreads a whole lot.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It certainly works in that direction, but there is a big independent movement because of both fear in the markets and some liquidity concerns, which is why I think it is very important for us to have both sets of tools.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have tools that can work on the issue of expectations about monetary policy and stance, but to the extent that we can use other tools, that’s also extremely helpful.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is not that we think we can solve all the problems, particularly because these shocks are so large.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is one problem that we are facing, which is that this disruption is really big, big time.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So then the question is whether we want to use all the tools at our disposal that we can.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I just want to make one point to the Vice Chairman’s question.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The way I think about this is that monetary policy tends to move continuously.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, the federal funds rate is essentially continuous, but what we are doing with liquidity measures is designed to combat nonlinearities to the extent that they’re discontinuities, and so I think they have a different qualitative feel.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We’re attempting to prevent a breakdown in markets and allow monetary policy thereby to operate more normally in a more continuous way.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I guess another way to frame the question is, If we are reasonably successful in mitigating this adverse feedback dynamic in markets and the effects that has on financial conditions, would we still need to lower the nominal fed funds rate further to achieve the forecast laid out in the Board staff’s Greenbook?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The answer to that would be “yes.” When we layered on significant additional negative add-factors for this recession scenario, they really weren’t directly tied to our reading of liquidity in financial markets but a reading of the real economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think the issue here relates to the whole question about nongradualism that we’ve been talking about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly, if we got lucky and financial markets turned around in a major way, then the stance of monetary policy would need to change, actually very rapidly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is one of the issues facing us—a communication issue, which is how we indicate to the markets and the public in a serious way that we really care about keeping inflation under control.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m not sure what the answer to that is.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is one of the great challenges that we’re facing at this particular juncture.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly, part of it is that we don’t want interest rates to be particularly low.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, the higher interest rates could be for us, the happier we would be because that would be an indication that financial conditions had turned around a lot.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, the problem, of course, is that inflation expectations get unhinged.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, Vice Chairman Geithner is asking in an elegant way about the issue of efficacy, which I was trying to touch on and did so in a less sophisticated way.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just want to make sure that I understand your answer.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we were to achieve the degree of success that Tim roughly estimated, we would lessen that pressure.

speaker: FISHER
text: From a staff standpoint, what degree of easing would you advocate?

speaker: FISHER
text: Would it be a lesser degree than what is imputed into the—

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I can’t really answer that question.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Over this intermeeting period, we were coping with two important developments.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One was that we saw some increase in overall measures of financial stress.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, we went to a forecast back in September when they first emerged and started marking down the level of GDP to account for that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We did a little more in this forecast to account for what we perceived to be an increase in financial stress.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the bigger factor in marking down our forecasts significantly this year was a reading that we were switching from a sense of a slow-growth scenario and moving into something like a more nonlinear downturn of the economy.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That motivated the more significant portion of the downward movement that we had in the equilibrium real interest rate here.

speaker: EVANS
text: Well, I just want to clarify this because I didn’t get the answer I was expecting.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t think I understood exactly the question about financial stress because I thought the question was whether we would have to do more with the funds rate to achieve what was in the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: Did you mark down your outlook from the Greenbook?

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t think I understood.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I guess I was thinking more along the marginal change that we would make should the factors be more successful than we’re currently anticipating them to be.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That would probably cause us to edge up our path of the fed funds rate to account for that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any other questions for Brian?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With your indulgence, it has been a very volatile period with a lot of changes in views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re also a little short of time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it might be more focused if I gave a proposal and had people react to it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser made the correct point that we need to think about the level of the funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it needs to be lower, frankly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In our last meeting, at 3 percent, many of us viewed that as about neutral without much insurance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Since then we’ve seen, I believe, a much stronger indication of recession, an increase in downside risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When I spoke about the downside risks in the Congress and in speeches, I cited three categories of risks: housing, finance, and labor markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All of those have transpired in that direction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I do think we have to respond effectively against that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For that reason I would recommend the 75 basis point reduction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I recognize the concerns people have, and I have them myself, about both inflation and the dollar.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I would make two comments regarding that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, we will be even now disappointing the market somewhat.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A more aggressive ease is built in.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, as Brian already indicated, in a number of places in alternative A, which I am proposing, we have ratcheted up the language about inflation, notably in paragraph 3, where we talk about it being elevated and inflation expectations, and in the last sentence, where we reinstitute price stability and clarify what our dual mandate is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Minor comments: I’m open to anything, but I point out that in paragraph 3 we added the list of explanations for why inflation may moderate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We didn’t have that last time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If people are uncomfortable with that, we can take that out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other thing we added in paragraph 4 was the comment about market liquidity measures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It shows that we’re doing other things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It creates a sense that there’s more going on besides monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But again, if people have strong objections, I have no strong feelings about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, my recommendation would include maintaining the discount rate difference of ¼ percentage point that we established on Sunday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s where I would be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we now have a rapid go-round?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, I think this is a mistake.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I want to take just a second.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I understand why we’ve been lowering the rate, trying to keep the problems from spreading over to the real economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I’ve been reluctant because our practice has been to go too low and to create a new set of circumstances that we have to deal with although I’ve understood, given the seriousness of this financial crisis, that we’ve had to go down.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I have been and continue to be very supportive of the use of our TAF and our other vehicles to provide liquidity to the market to help address and stanch the panic.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The fact of the matter is, though, that there is an enormous amount of loss.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Whether there is enough capital in the banking industry, we know that there is a solvency issue out there, and these actions, while they provide liquidity, cannot solve that problem.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That’s where fiscal policy goes.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But I’m not sure that our continuing to lower rates isn’t allowing others who should be addressing this to look to us to solve the problem that is not ours to solve, and that concerns me about where we are.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The fed funds rate at 3 percent nominal, I think, is a stimulative rate in terms of where the real fed funds rate is.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In an environment where we now move down even lower than that, we are inviting other speculative activities.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Liquidity has to go somewhere, and it is going there fast.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think there’s a danger in doing that, and this 3 percent will stimulate the economy forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Two and a quarter will stimulate the economy forward and introduce other significant risks both to speculative activity and to inflation, and that’s why I think we should be more careful in going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Now, doing nothing will shock the market, but I’ll tell you that the market has been shocked as much by some of the new actions we have taken as if we said, “Here it is at 3 percent.” There are a lot of people on the sidelines waiting for us to stop so that they can come in and take advantage of the situation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So there are lots of reasons that I would much prefer to hold at this period, and I felt compelled to express that view.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: News of the problems at Bear Stearns and the very fragile situation in financial markets complicate our decision today.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Federal funds futures indicate that the market is anticipating a reduction of at least 75 basis points and probably more than that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Normally the expectations of financial market participants would not factor heavily in my decisionmaking.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, given the fragility in the market and my own expectation that, even with this move, further easing will be necessary, I strongly prefer alternative A.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While I view alternative B as a significant action, I would have concerns about likely market reaction given the gravity of the situation in financial markets and the possibility that a recession may not be mild, given falling collateral values and financial difficulties at many of our major financial institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A 50 basis point move would merely offset the increase in credit spreads that we have seen since the past meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In addition, the Boston forecast and the Greenbook forecast with a 50 basis point ease leave the unemployment rate well above the NAIRU but with inflation rates below 2 percent by the end of 2009.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Easing less than 50 basis points at this meeting would seem entirely inconsistent with the economic and financial deterioration we have seen since the last meeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve spoken a lot about inflation expectations here today.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me at the outset emphasize that what I’m referring to in the measures we have are the expectations of the public.

speaker: LACKER
text: They’re not necessarily my expectations or Governor Mishkin’s, Vice Chairman Geithner’s, or the Committee’s, and they don’t necessarily correspond to the reality of the distribution of inflation realized five years, five years hence, if each of us had our druthers or if the Committee as a whole lasted that long together and conducted policy the way it best saw fit.

speaker: LACKER
text: I trust that no member would deliberately encourage continued discrepancy between what they viewed as objective reality and the public’s expectations.

speaker: LACKER
text: But that said, that discrepancy is not the same as less commitment on our part.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s certainly the same as less credibility about commitment on our part.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think and trust that most members when speaking in public about inflation expectations would endeavor to reduce that discrepancy.

speaker: LACKER
text: Presumably, each of us has a threshold for acceptable inflation expectations that, if it were crossed, would induce us to be willing to disappoint market expectations.

speaker: LACKER
text: Personally, my threshold has been crossed, so I think that, if we ease, we should ease much less aggressively than markets expect.

speaker: LACKER
text: More broadly, I think of this in terms of the following question: What strategy would we want people to believe we will follow in future episodes like this?

speaker: LACKER
text: As I pointed out in my letter to the Committee last week, thinking in terms of our strategy is different from a meeting-by-meeting approach that takes the public’s current expectations, wherever they are, as given.

speaker: LACKER
text: We should ask, I believe, what expectations we would have wanted them to have had about our behavior during episodes like this.

speaker: LACKER
text: Do we want people to believe that we will follow a policy that allows inflation and inflation expectations to ratchet up permanently whenever growth slows?

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think so, but that seems to be what the market believes we’re doing.

speaker: LACKER
text: Conceivably, we could try to use our statements and minutes to communicate our intention to bring inflation down, but at this point, my sense is that our statements about inflation appear to be taken as much less revealing than our actions.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is a uniquely challenging episode in the history of our economy and our institution.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have found it useful to remind myself from time to time about the limits of central banking.

speaker: LACKER
text: We cannot prevent this recession, and it’s doubtful to me that we could have or should have even if we had had perfect foresight.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are unlikely, as I said, to have much effect on the ultimate magnitude of mortgage losses at this point, and I don’t think we can do much to accelerate the resolution of uncertainty about those losses.

speaker: LACKER
text: We cannot resolve uncertainty about the fundamentals underlying the creditworthiness of financial market counterparties, and we cannot enhance the liquidity of any financial instrument without altering its relative price.

speaker: LACKER
text: We can control inflation, and we can limit the extent to which uncertainty about our inflation intentions adds to market volatility.

speaker: LACKER
text: To do this, I like the idea of being clear about our strategy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I take that as consistent with what President Plosser was advocating, that we concern ourselves with what level we see as appropriate now and see as likely to be appropriate later this year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I support your proposal for a 75 basis point cut and the language that’s proposed for alternative A.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I said in my comments, I’m very concerned about economic growth and agree basically with the Greenbook perspective.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we are into an adverse feedback loop, and I agree with the Bluebook assessment that the equilibrium real funds rate has dropped substantially, maybe into negative territory.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t believe in gradualism in circumstances like these.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the argument for more-aggressive action now is similar to when inflation is very low and we face the zero bound for nominal interest rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I agree with Governor Mishkin’s comments about the lessons of Japan.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think that the sooner appropriate stimulus is put in place, the less likely it is that policy will end up facing very unpleasant consequences of essentially reaching the zero bound in this case because of a prolonged and severe recession.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I’d like to see the funds rate moved down to where it needs to go sooner rather than later.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the appropriate level of the funds rate is one that would provide some insurance against really bad outcomes for the economy, and I don’t see this move as taking us into insurance territory yet.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I understand the constraints that you have weighed into this decision having to do with the psychology of inflation expectations and the dollar, and probably this is as far as we can go sensibly today, but I think it is important to move as much as we can.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If the moves prove unnecessary, I think we can reverse the stance of policy quickly, with a good chance of avoiding inflationary problems.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I agree with Governor Mishkin’s views on risk- management policy in the face of financial shocks.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We had an interesting discussion last time about the possibility that a quick reversal might mean that we don’t have much stimulative effect on spending now because we may not lower long-term interest rates enough, and I think that was good food for thought.

speaker: YELLEN
