text: But having spent some time thinking about it, I think that a lower funds rate will actually lower long-term rates, in part because, by reducing the probability of a financial crisis, we will bring risk premiums down, which will lower long-term rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A lower funds rate will also be stimulative because a good deal depends on short- and intermediate-term rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think there are also a number of other ways in which short rates matter to spending through channels like raising firms’ profitability and cash flow and lowering the stress from ARM resets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I strongly support the action that you recommend.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also support your proposal, both the action and the language of alternative A. I think it’s an appropriate response to the developing situation, and I do think that the language will help us on the inflation front.

speaker: KOHN
text: Let me elaborate a bit.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’ve had a marked deterioration in the outlook, as everybody around the table has seen and has agreed with.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think, as President Yellen and others have said, that a decline in the federal funds rate will be helpful in mitigating the recessionary tendencies in the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: The decline of 75 basis points is not as much as the Greenbook r* decline, but I think it’s appropriate and reasonable to await more evidence about whether at some point we need to go further.

speaker: KOHN
text: The resulting real federal funds rate would be approximately zero using core inflation, and I think that’s a reasonable place to be, given the weight of the constraining factors in the economic outlook, particularly from the credit markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: I use core in thinking about the real funds rate because I do think that even a zero real funds rate under these circumstances, at least for a time, will be consistent with inflation coming down as commodity prices level out and as resource utilization goes down.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with Brian that there could be a bit of an adverse reaction in financial markets because it’s not quite as much as they’re expecting, but with that risk sentence in paragraph 4, it shouldn’t be too bad.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think it’s consistent with heightened attention by the Committee to inflation and inflation expectations for the reasons you gave, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s less than the market expects, and both paragraph 3 and paragraph 4 increase the attention to inflation and inflation risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: I came in here thinking that I preferred 50 basis points, but I also recognize that I expected that we would have to go beyond that after this meeting.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I fully support 75 and the language that you discussed.

speaker: EVANS
text: I just want to take a minute to give my perspective on the discussion earlier about the 1970s and inflation expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: I certainly didn’t expect when I came onto the Committee that we would be lowering rates as much as we have done, and I thought we would be more concerned about inflation, but this is where we are, and I think it is the appropriate response.

speaker: EVANS
text: Inflation expectations risk reminds me of Paul Volcker, hero of the Federal Reserve System.

speaker: EVANS
text: How did he do that?

speaker: EVANS
text: Well, when I talked with my colleague, Larry Christiano, he reminded me that it wasn’t really by reducing money growth.

speaker: EVANS
text: M1 growth increased during that period, and yet financial conditions were restrictive.

speaker: EVANS
text: There was a big recession.

speaker: EVANS
text: There was a lot of resource slack, and that was really important for bringing inflation down.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think we’re in a situation where this is most likely a recession.

speaker: EVANS
text: I expect that it will reduce pressures on inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think it’s consistent with the earlier period, and it’s hard to know exactly how much it will bring inflation down, but I think that it will lower inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: The Greenbook is calling for a recession.

speaker: EVANS
text: They could be wrong, but we’ve been chasing them down the whole time, and I’d be very surprised if they were wrong.

speaker: EVANS
text: I would like to know where the bottom of the funds rate cycle is.

speaker: EVANS
text: Like financial market participants who want to know what the value of their mortgage securities is, I’d like to know where the bottom of the funds rate is.

speaker: EVANS
text: But that is wholly unrealistic at this point.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I would be hopeful for eventually something like the Greenbook path assumption.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I support the recommendation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Combined with our separate attempts to relieve financial market stress, we have two prongs going, and that is very helpful.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, as somebody said recently, there are no altogether good choices.

speaker: STERN
text: I strongly support the recommendation and the language that goes with it.

speaker: STERN
text: A couple of weeks ago I thought the funds rate probably should go to 2½ percent.

speaker: STERN
text: I got there basically by saying, well, given what I know about current conditions, the outlook, and everything, 3 percent is not a bad level.

speaker: STERN
text: But there are a lot of things I don’t know, and it’s likely that some events are going to occur in the next couple of weeks or sometime in the future that may disturb things, and as a little insurance for that, 2½ would be a good idea.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, those events—I’m talking about Bear Stearns and other disruptions—occurred sooner rather than later, so it seems to me that we need to go to 2½ and then ask ourselves whether we want some additional insurance.

speaker: STERN
text: My answer to that is “yes.” So I’m perfectly comfortable with taking the funds rate down ¾ percentage point now.

speaker: STERN
text: Does it strike the appropriate balance between our concerns about financial conditions and the outlook, and inflation and inflation expectations on the other side?

speaker: STERN
text: But as I said at the outset of this, I don’t know that there are any altogether good choices.

speaker: STERN
text: I think this is about as good as we can do under these circumstances.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, Mr. Chairman, I don’t like being obtuse and, being a people person, I don’t like being unpopular.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We’re always going to love you, come on.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We don’t like being unpopular either.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just can’t bring myself to go that far, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: FISHER
text: I listened very carefully to what was said at the table, and implicit in Tim’s question to me was, Would you be willing to do something?

speaker: FISHER
text: The answer is “yes,” but not as much as you’re suggesting.

speaker: FISHER
text: I try as hard as possible, even though I’ve made my living in financial markets, to ignore the reports that we were just given as we started this conversation because what we’re paid to do and what I believe is our duty and obligation to do is what’s right for the long-term interests of the economy.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am more bearish now than before, and I was an outlier on the bearish side of economic growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’ve been at the lower end of the range, but I also believe that we have significant inflationary concerns.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have a further point to add to President Hoenig’s—I agree with his intervention.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that, by being accommodative, we are encouraging others who have a role to play here—you mentioned them yourself, Mr. Chairman—to sit back and let us do the job.

speaker: FISHER
text: To me the combination of inflationary pressures, which I consider to be real, imputing into a much weaker economic growth scenario, which I have thought for a long time, means that we cannot do this job alone.

speaker: FISHER
text: The fact of the matter is that we have undertaken significant liquidity enhancement initiatives, and I think we’re going to have to do more, and I’ve been fully supportive of them, but I think 75 basis points, Mr. Chairman, is way too much.

speaker: FISHER
text: My thought is that it encourages the financial markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: They’re not going to be satisfied.

speaker: FISHER
text: I said this last time.

speaker: FISHER
text: They will keep asking for more and more.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have to quit feeding them.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m in a pizza mode, by the way, in this conversation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do have a suggestion, however.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You mean Pizza the Hutt, not Jabba the Hutt.

speaker: FISHER
text: Pizza the Hutt, that’s right.

speaker: FISHER
text: Vice Chairman Geithner made a very interesting point, and that was that we have to be very careful about how we talk about inflation and even saying what we think.

speaker: FISHER
text: What worries me about going down alternative A’s path, if that’s the wisdom of the Committee, is that the second paragraph says a little too much of what we think.

speaker: FISHER
text: It really says that we’re not done.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you want to say that, that’s fine; but it keeps hammering on, even after 75 basis points, that things are soft, things are soft, things are soft.

speaker: FISHER
text: You may disagree with me on that, but I would suggest that we take out the justification reflecting, in paragraph 3, “a projected leveling out of energy and other commodities.” To me that’s a wing and a prayer, and you suggested that you might be willing to take it out.

speaker: FISHER
text: Were I you, advocating 75 basis points, acting as I think you are about to act, with one dissent, I would take that wing and a prayer language out of there.

speaker: FISHER
text: Then I would suggest one other thing—in fact, I would ask for one other thing.

speaker: FISHER
text: In the very last sentence—“The Committee will act in a timely matter as needed to promote sustainable economic growth without sacrificing long-term price stability”—that’s really what we’re talking about on the upside and on the downside.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I would ask for that change because that’s really what we’re saying.

speaker: FISHER
text: You’re saying that we’re worried about the downside.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’re all worried about that, but we’re going to promote sustainable economic growth without sacrificing long-term price stability.

speaker: FISHER
text: Those are my suggestions, Mr. Chairman, and thank you for putting up with me.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I came to the meeting preferring alternative B—50 basis points.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I certainly can bring myself to support your proposal—75 basis points.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I don’t view it as a fist pounder, but let me make the case for 50 basis points, at least as I think about it.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: First, I do think it is a movement that acknowledges financial instability and the growing real weakness.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I argued in my earlier remarks, it may set the scene for decoupling rate policy from liquidity actions if conditions allow.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think the action makes a minimal acknowledgement of inflation risk, and it may signal the view that lower rates can do only so much and that, best case, the market will have to proceed to sort out the market problems and, worst case, the fiscal authorities will have to deal with them.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Although I am not a trained psychologist, let me just propose that, in dealing with market psychology, there may be some value in appearing to firm up our rate-movement policy and to set one element in the fluid situation with greater fixity than it has been in recent weeks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That might generate the kind of firming dynamic and even help produce a turn in psychology.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That’s a lot to ask for simply 50 basis points, but I also prefer the language of alternative A to that of alternative B, and I think Brian said that you could conceivably apply alternative A language substantially to a 50 basis point cut.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So in general I like that approach.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As I said earlier, I do see the risks to the Greenbook baseline as being skewed to the downside because of the absence of any signs of a bottoming out in the housing market.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As others have mentioned, I am concerned about the risk that we will have a more protracted recession.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At the same time, the short-term inflation environment has deteriorated.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am also concerned about inflation expectations becoming unanchored.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As Governor Mishkin and others have said today, we face some very unpleasant tradeoffs; but in the end, I support being more aggressive in our policy actions today.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am hopeful that, as others have said, the language that we have added in paragraph 3 about inflation risks and a reminder in the assessment-of-risk paragraph about our dual mandate will be helpful in keeping inflation expectations from rising further.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Mr. Chairman, excluding for the moment the market’s expectations of a significant downward policy move at this meeting, I have a strong preference for alternative D, like President Hoenig.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: I see widespread evidence that the upside risk to inflation has increased appreciably, as evidenced by rapid money growth, a depreciating dollar, rising prices of energy and commodities traded on the world markets, and higher inflation compensation in bond markets.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: However, as we all know, the market does expect a significant reduction in the funds rate from this meeting, partly because of the state of the economy, partly because of the turbulence in the financial markets, and partly because of past statements and communications from Committee members.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Consequently, under these conditions, I believe that a failure to accommodate much of this expectation would produce additional, major market turmoil.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: Hence, I was prepared to accept a 50 basis point reduction coming into the meeting and, with some trepidation, can accept a 75 basis point reduction.

speaker: SAPENARO
text: In my view, however, it would be desirable for the Committee’s communications going forward to emphasize that we have not lost our zeal to fight inflation and that further rate cuts cannot solve solvency problems without unacceptable future inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I mentioned in my first go-round, and like Rick, I have been terribly depressed on multiple dimensions about what is going on and have struggled mightily in trying to think about what appropriate policy is going forward and, as President Lacker suggested, about what our strategy is as we move forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I certainly believe that easing of policy is appropriate in a weaker economy, and I have supported that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But as I alluded to earlier—and, Mr. Chairman, as you said—I do believe that a weaker economy does not mean that we continue to cut rates as long as the economy is weak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We need to calibrate the level of the funds rate; I think it is very important.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think the markets seem to have the expectation that it is the rate of change, not the level, that matters.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That concerns me and feeds into some of the problems that we are facing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I won’t elaborate any more about expectations, which I mentioned before.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I would prefer actions as well as language that reinforced our commitment to price stability and a pause today in our rate cuts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that the language of alternative D would accomplish that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I also believe that a more modest cut, combined with language such as that in alternative D, might accomplish the same thing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am afraid that an aggressive move combined with the language that we have in A or B feeds the belief that we have placed aside our commitment to price stability and the expectation that we will continue to cut rates for the foreseeable future and that there is no bottom in sight.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have talked a lot about taking out insurance around this table.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe the time has come to buy some insurance against our waning credibility about restraining inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That does not mean that we couldn’t choose to continue to make rate cuts at some future date, should that be called for.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Ultimately, if we wish inflation expectations to be well anchored, we must act in a way that is consistent with such an outcome.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Words are simply not enough.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Reputational capital, whether it be for a central bank, an academic institution, or the brand capital of a firm, is very hard to build.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But most of us know, in the private sector and in other sectors, that capital can be easily squandered.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We must not let that happen.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I appreciate, Mr. Chairman, your comments regarding the idea that we may be reaching the limits of what monetary policy and the central bank can do.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I very much agree with that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the risk of maybe sounding a bit trite to some of my colleagues who are familiar with this—I don’t mean it that way because this expresses some of my concerns—I would like to remind my colleagues of a quotation of Milton Friedman, which he made in 1968, that “we are in danger of assigning to monetary policy a larger role than it can perform, in danger of asking it to accomplish tasks that it cannot achieve, and, as a result, in danger of preventing it from making the contribution that it is capable of making.” Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: WARSH
text: A couple of quick introductory points.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, I have total confidence in the Fed and the FOMC, certainly over the course of my couple of years here, in effectively handling these challenges, which is key to highlight at the outset of my remarks.

speaker: WARSH
text: I have total confidence in this institution’s ability, in particular, to handle both sides of the dual mandate.

speaker: WARSH
text: Moreover, I would say that I have total confidence in our ability to have a really robust discussion here and recognize, as President Geithner pointed out, the fragility in these financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: A lot of our strength comes from being able to have very open, tough discussions with each other and recognize that, if they were in the public square, they could be misinterpreted and destabilizing.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think he is right that we all need to take that into account, particularly over this next intermeeting period, which we all hope lasts six weeks.

speaker: WARSH
text: Moreover, I think that the power of our tools, our creativity, and our innovative abilities over November, December, and these recent weeks has been incredibly impressive.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that those will work in concert with monetary policy.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would underscore a point that the Chairman made, which is that we have taken a huge burden on ourselves and that the burden will have to be matched by others here in Washington—and I suspect before we get too much into the second and third quarter by others around the world—which will go a long way toward helping us accomplish our objectives.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, I have total confidence in U.S. financial institutions over the medium term to deal with these issues.

speaker: WARSH
text: They will come out of this thing stronger, smarter, and faster and will be huge net exporters of services, but that is going to take a while.

speaker: WARSH
text: My own view is that the capital- raising is good and very important.

speaker: WARSH
text: If the tail is as fat as we have discussed, capital-raising by these institutions should help them stave off safety and soundness issues that could arise.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think that it is good prudential management by them and us alike.

speaker: WARSH
text: To the task at hand on monetary policy, I will support alternative A, as the Chairman recommends, and I take particular comfort in the narrative and language in A as being a very important next step for us to guard against risks on the currency front and on the inflation front.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now, these words themselves won’t do a ton in the short term, and they won’t have an immediate effect, but I do think it is important for us to take these and build on them in our private and public statements.

speaker: WARSH
text: So that gives me some comfort.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the decision of 50 points versus 75 points, I would be kidding myself if I thought that those 25 basis points were completely consequential.

speaker: WARSH
text: I wouldn’t ascribe virtue or vice to that sort of bid-asked spread.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say that it is a hard call.

speaker: WARSH
text: I share the view expressed by some that these markets are going to need to be disappointed at some point here.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is the only way the words that we express will be properly understood and taken into account in the markets’ judgments, and I worry that we are not going to have any great opportunities to disappoint them over the course of the upcoming meetings.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, let me say this.

speaker: WARSH
text: I will end where I started in this discussion, which is, at the end of the day, it is this institution’s credibility that is paramount and that is increasingly the case at this point in the cycle.

speaker: WARSH
text: It strikes me that we have to continue to make the case in the upcoming months that we have the will, the wisdom, and the tools to tackle these issues.

speaker: WARSH
text: To the extent that monetary policy is perceived by pundits and Fed watchers as not working, it is important that we rebut those arguments and explain that our tools will work over time and that we are looking for assistance both in Washington and in other nations’ capitals.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, as I said before, we are in a very uncertain situation with respect to inflation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have slowing economic growth, but we have also had very elevated prices.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We had a very low unemployment rate and a very low rate of wage inflation, so we have to worry a little about whether we will get the benefits of lower resource utilization in terms of lower inflation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But when we look back historically at previous slowdowns, as President Stern mentioned about 1990-91 and as we have discussed about 1998-99, when we didn’t actually have a formal slowdown, the Committee cut rates, and we didn’t have a burst of inflation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, after the slowdown in 2001, the main challenge was concern about inflation getting too low rather than getting too high at that point.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we look over the past few cycles—and I think markets are aware of those—we see that you can have cuts in the federal funds rate that don’t lead to inflation getting out of control, both when the economy is growing strongly and when the economy is quite weak.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So although I do think that the situation is uncertain, I don’t think that the markets would read a cut of 75 basis points today as a lack of commitment to inflation control.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think there is a lot of historical evidence that suggests that it is not necessarily inconsistent with that in any way.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The slight uptick that we have seen in some but not all of the surveys doesn’t suggest that our inflation credibility has been lost.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it is very difficult to read what the markets are saying because just look at the volatility over the past few days.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Are those TIPS spreads really telling us about dramatic changes in the market’s views of our credibility regarding what we are going to do in fighting inflation?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t find that credible.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There are a lot of other things that are going on that make it very difficult for us to read something out of that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I support alternative A.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: My thinking is actually very much along the lines of President Stern’s—that we need to take out at least a little insurance going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The statement in alternative A does a very good job of talking about some of the concerns about inflation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: With respect to whether or not we include the explanation of why we expect inflation to come down in coming quarters, one of the things that changed in this version relative to the earlier ones is that there is no explicit mention of inflation expectations, which I think is right because there is such uncertainty about how to measure those.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That the uncertainty about the inflation outlook has increased is the thing that we can read from what the markets are telling us.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The assessment of risk in paragraph 4, where it mentions not only the policy actions but also the measures to foster the liquidity, is valuable so that people see that these are complementary tools and that we understand how they can work together.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The mention of price stability at the end and how that differs from our statement from last time is a good way to signal that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I really don’t see evidence yet that we have lost credibility.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we look back historically at when we’ve done rate-cutting in either financially stressed times or actual economic downturns, at least over the past twenty-five years, it has not turned into inflationary challenges, and I don’t see any evidence that the markets think otherwise.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I support alternative A, as is.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Obviously, we are facing a very difficult policy problem, and that is why, Charlie, we will go have a beer later, so that we can deal with our depression.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly, we are challenged by the fact that we have to balance the risks of both underlying inflation and inflation expectations going up.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Against that, we have to worry about the downside risks to the economy, and the financial sector could really go south.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So that is really the policy problem that we face.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do support alternative A, but I would like to give some perspective on that because I may have a different take than others on this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If you are thinking about the risk-management viewpoint that I and some others have talked about, I want to emphasize that lowering the federal funds rate 75 basis points is not—and I want to repeat, is not—taking out insurance.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If you look at the Greenbook projections, they have 75 basis points, and they have a further decline after that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The r* has dropped 125 to 150—well, it depends on which model, but quite a bit more than 75.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So from an insurance perspective, we should actually be doing more than 75 basis points.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I am not going to argue for that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, I would argue for that if some of the other things, such as negative supply shocks, hadn’t been happening.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I also have a concern about a phenomenon that has occurred, which I don’t fully understand.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Normally I would not worry about dollar depreciation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I gave a speech recently on pass-through—it was an opportunity for me to interact with Nathan’s staff and to read the literature—and the evidence is that there is just not a whole lot in terms of pass-through.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But lately we have seen something that is very peculiar, which is that, every time we have had depreciation in the dollar, the oil price has gone up.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That makes me much more nervous about dollar depreciation than I would usually be.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I hope that it may be just coincidence, but it makes me a little more nervous.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Another problem that we face is that we have not convinced the markets that we will be willing to bring out the baseball bat if inflation starts to get out of control.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is really a key part of the risk-management approach, and a key part of—I think Vince Reinhart called it post- gradualism in his speech.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: He gave a very interesting speech the other day and called it post- gradualism.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we have not yet convinced people about it, and part of the problem is that we really haven’t operated in that way in the past.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is one reason that it is worthwhile talking about this and saying that we need to think about operating in a different way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But it suggests to me that, if we actually were more aggressive than 75 basis points, it could have very negative reactions in the markets about our commitment to controlling inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So, that is one of the reasons that I strongly support the Chairman’s proposal.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I should say, by the way, that even so, the 75 basis point cut, which I don’t think takes out enough insurance, does pose some risk that long-run inflation expectations will rise.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we have to realize that there is a lot of risk of really bad things happening that could mean that things really get out of control.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The discomfort is that we now have a tough tradeoff.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But then, when I think about the tradeoff, I am willing to say that we have to take the risk because otherwise the consequences could be very problematic.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I should mention that I have one concern about the wording in the statement.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I usually don’t make comments about the wording because I am just not subtle enough to get that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I did worry a bit, for exactly the reason that Vice Chairman Geithner mentioned, about the issue that talking about inflation expectations getting unhinged could be actually very dangerous.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The first sentence in alternative A says, “Inflation has been elevated, and some indicators of inflation expectations have risen.” Well, I worry about that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: First of all, the evidence is not completely clear on that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is true that there has been an increase, and I have said it is about 10 basis points.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But there is other research, and there is a lot of uncertainty about these measures.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am wondering, if we put that in, whether it will actually cause a problem in terms of market reaction.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So it worries me a little.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I would probably be more comfortable with what we have in alternative C, which is that inflation has been elevated and then the reasons for upward pressure.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am not sure that this would be helpful.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t feel super strongly about it, but the comments of Vice Chairman Geithner made me a bit more worried about it than I otherwise would have been.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Let me just begin with a question because I think it is really central.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It goes to the issue of how accommodative policy is now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Fundamentally that must be critical to the magnitude of the risks we are taking that we are going to get it wrong and inflation in the future is going to be too high.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Now, I am not really part of your profession, but I have always found this chart to be the most discouraging prism on the choices we face.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is the Bluebook equilibrium real funds rate chart.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But any way you look at it, the real fed funds rate is closer to best estimates of equilibrium than during any downturn of the past two decades or similar periods of time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is no gap between the estimated real rate today and the center of the estimate of where equilibrium is.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If you look back to what that gap was in 1992, in 2001-02, or in 2003, there was a substantial gap, as most judgments about policy would suggest was necessary.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I understand that there is a huge amount of uncertainty about estimates of equilibrium, but we can’t be facing both the most serious risk of a financial crisis and of a deep, prolonged recession in 50, 30, or 20 years and at the same time the risk of having a very substantial rise in underlying inflation over the medium term.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It seems to me that we are going to have one or the other.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The choice we face, of course, is which risk we are prepared to take.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Which mistake is the easier to correct for?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is a very hard judgment to make.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think we have to be confident that, if we end up being successful in averting the risk of a very, very dangerous, damaging spiral in the financial markets with the consequences of a very deep recession or a deeper recession than in the early 1990s, then we will be able to deal with the likely consequences that we will have more inflation and less moderation than we now anticipate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I guess I don’t understand why we would not be confident in that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So let me just say that I don’t think this is easy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Like many of you, I think that it would be great if we got away with 50, but I think that is not tenable—not even close in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Even though it would be nice if we had a consensus in the United States about a set of fiscal measures that we think would be good on the merits, we can’t make monetary policy in a framework where we condition our actions on actions by the Congress.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In an environment like this, it is not possible.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we do the right thing, does that mean it takes the pressure off them?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Maybe, but probably not so much.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But it can’t constrain us from doing what is appropriate now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just one final thing: People who know this stuff quite well, who are reasonably calm people, say, “This is possibly the worst financial crisis in 50 years, and the most challenging set of pressures facing the central bank in 20 or 30 years.” Think about that in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is no surprise that we disagree; it is no surprise that the range of agreement about what we see and what we should do is going to be wide in that context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But just think very carefully about the signal it sends to the world at this moment to be explicit in public about the degree of dispersion about our views.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just think carefully about it because this is a special moment.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I fully support the language and the action in alternative A.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: President Fisher, I would not amend the last sentence to say “without sacrificing” partly because I think we need to project confidence in our capacity to manage long-term inflation outcomes.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I am ambivalent, as you know, Mr. Chairman, about that clause that President Fisher suggested we delete about reflecting a projected leveling out.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The virtue is that it explains and underpins, therefore, the basis for a medium-term forecast.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The vice in it is that, as the Chairman himself said, the first part may seem like a thin reed on which to base our forecast, given what has been happening.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I actually think, Governor Mishkin, that acknowledging some indicators of inflation expectations—it is really about uncertainty having increased—is helpful to our credibility.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: At the margin, it helps, even though, sure, you can say that we really can’t know what they are telling us about the market.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: May I just ask a question back?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do think that inflation expectations are a concern.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is just a question of how the markets—and I am not as good at this as the people who really follow the markets—and the press will react to this phrase because I think that the amount of movement here is still very small.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You know, the kinds of numbers we are talking about for inflation expectations are on the order of 10 to 20 basis points.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Will this mention, because it is new, raise a flag that will get more attention and more concern than, in fact, is justified?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is the tricky problem here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We should acknowledge it, but again, I am not good enough at wordsmithing to figure out how to do that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is a bit of my concern here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t know if anybody has any thoughts about how to handle it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Fisher, I think I agree on the last sentence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to keep it something that we have used frequently before and that emphasizes, in fact, the symmetry of the dual mandate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there other thoughts on either the indicators of inflation expectations or the list of reasons that anyone would prefer to change from where we are?

speaker: KOHN
text: On inflation expectations, because they haven’t risen very much, I agree with President Geithner.

speaker: KOHN
text: I like the fact that we tell people we are aware, but we could say “have edged higher” or something like that instead of “risen.”

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We could use my “smidgen” word, but “edged higher” is better.

speaker: EVANS
text: “Edged higher” is an unusual phrase.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think an issue with “edged higher” is that it really does sound as though you have some very specific measures in mind.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Brian, do you have a thought on “risen” versus “risen somewhat” versus taking it out?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think if you take it out that very much raises the question of what to do with that language in red about the factors that would push inflation down.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would be tough to drop the inflation expectations thought and not have inflation expectations mentioned anywhere in the paragraph.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: There would just be vacant space where you had, at least in previous minutes, referred to it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Adding just the word “slightly”—“risen slightly”—gets to your point.

speaker: WARSH
text: Brian, does “somewhat” mitigate it a little, or does that highlight it?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I mean, in my mind it mitigates it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Is “slightly” better than “somewhat”?

speaker: KOHN
text: “Somewhat” is bigger than “slightly.”

speaker: EVANS
text: That is 50 versus 25 in the old days.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Mr. Chairman, if I understand the discussion about this, when you say “some indicators have risen somewhat,” you are getting into territory that seems sort of mealy-mouthed.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: What is wrong with “slightly”?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, I don’t want to prolong this too much, but in response to the Vice Chairman’s comments, I am not sure I follow what you are saying.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think the model that you showed us, in terms of where the equilibrium rate is, is a short-term model.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It is based upon a variety of estimates and output gaps, and I think there is plenty of room for disagreement around that model.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So the fact that we have different views on this Committee is very healthy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Even to the world it can be very healthy because a lot of people out there have a different view of this and are wondering if there is any variance of views within this Committee.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that can serve as useful a purpose as uniformity without objection.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Let me say for the record that I agree with everything you just said.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My only point is that there is no surprise that we disagree or that it is complicated and we have a different view of the balance.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If anything, what this chart shows is how broad the range of uncertainty is around this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That was part of my point in saying it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I do think that the value of the public display of dispersion is different when you have this degree of a confidence problem in markets generally.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That is the only thing I was suggesting.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I completely agree about the value of diversity of view in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is no surprise that we disagree in this period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My only suggestion is in terms of how we think about talking about it publicly, given that we are at such a delicate moment.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Vice Chairman, we have a bubble developing in some parts of our area.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think they are aware of that, and so I think we have to be mindful of that in our discussion more broadly.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is why I think there are important differences that we should necessarily be able to—and should in fact—acknowledge publicly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Having thought about this, I think that “some indicators” does tone it down a bit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Perhaps we could just leave it where it is?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Who knows what reaction this will get.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, there is some sense here of trying to ratchet up at least our verbal attention to inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me say to everyone that I went through each of these alternatives and tried to find one that didn’t make me intensely uncomfortable—and I am still going through them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: These are very, very difficult decisions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are all people working in good faith, and we are all doing the best we can.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I appreciate the candor and the honest comments, and we will continue to work together and to address these very, very difficult issues that we have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you are ready, then perhaps we could take a vote.

speaker: DANKER
text: The vote will encompass the directive I’ll read from the Bluebook and the statement for alternative A in the chart that you have in front of you.

speaker: DANKER
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: DANKER
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with reducing the federal funds rate to an average of around 2¼ percent.” Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes President Fisher No Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes Governor Mishkin Yes President Pianalto Yes President Plosser No President Stern Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are going to recess for the discount rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unless there are objections, we are going to maintain the ¼ percentage point difference.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next meeting is April 29 and 30, Tuesday and Wednesday, a two-day meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will talk about interest on reserves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And we will meet you shortly upstairs for a lunch in honor of Bill Poole.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s formally begin the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me start by welcoming our new colleague, Jim Bullard from St. Louis, over there in the heartland section of the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We welcome you, and we look forward to your contribution and to working with you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want just to note that there has been some interest in doing more work collectively— Board members and Presidents—on various issues relating to bank supervision and regulation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have some work streams planned, Governor Kohn will talk about this a bit tomorrow during our lunch, and we will discuss some of those things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me now turn to Bill Dudley to discuss Desk operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Bill, if you would, also talk about some of the proposals for expanding liquidity support.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The financial market environment has improved markedly since mid-March.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, concern about the circumstances that led to the demise of Bear Stearns may have provided added impetus to the ongoing deleveraging process.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The result has been improvement in the broader equity and fixed-income markets but heightened term funding pressure within the financial system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Turning first to the broader markets, improvement is evident across most broad asset classes both in the United States and abroad.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 1 of the handout in front of you, the broad U.S. equity indexes have recovered much of their earlier losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the financial sector still lags behind, financial share prices have, in the aggregate, recovered more than 10 percent off their mid-March trough.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Credit markets have also improved.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 2, corporate credit spreads in both the investment-grade and the high-yield sectors have narrowed somewhat.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, global credit default swap spreads—as shown in exhibit 3—have fallen significantly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 4, measures of implied volatility in the Treasury, equity, and foreign exchange markets have declined.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Signs of a recovery in risk appetite can be seen very clearly in the subprime mortgage-backed securities market and the municipal securities market, both which 1 The materials used by Mr. Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: had earlier experienced significant distress.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 5 shows the price performance of the AAA-rated tranches of the last four ABX subprime vintages.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, the AAA-rated tranches have recovered even though housing activity and home prices have continued to decline at least as fast as anticipated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the municipal market, crossover buyers have entered, attracted by municipal bond yields that exceed those available on Treasuries of comparable maturities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As seen in exhibit 6, although the ratios of tax-exempt to Treasury yields of comparable maturities remain elevated, there has been considerable improvement during the past two months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This improvement has occurred even though the outlook for the monoline financial guarantors remains poor.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Ambac’s announcement last week of a $1.7 billion loss in the first quarter made—thus far—barely a ripple in the broader market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The introduction of the primary dealer credit facility (PDCF) seems to have helped to stabilize the repo markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That improvement, in turn, has caused the equity prices of the four remaining large investment banks to recover somewhat and their credit default swap spreads to fall sharply (exhibits 7 and 8).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The PDCF backstop facility also appears to have helped break the negative dynamic of higher haircuts, forced asset sales, lower prices, higher volatility, and still higher haircuts that was in place in the weeks leading up to the Bear Stearns liquidity crisis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the collateral haircuts set by the major dealers for their hedge fund clients in our April 9 survey—shown in exhibit 9—are considerably higher than in the previous month, our contacts indicate that this rise occurred mostly around the time of Bear Stearns’s demise.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Over the past few weeks, haircuts have stabilized.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Despite the improvement in the broad market indexes and in the equity prices and credit default swap spreads of most major financial firms, term funding pressures have intensified rather than subsided.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 10 and 11, the pressures have been evident at both the one-month and the three-month tenures in the United States, the euro area, and the United Kingdom.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The additional deleveraging by the investment banks following the demise of Bear Stearns may have intensified the pressure on commercial bank balance sheets or the urge for banks to delever.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The LIBOR indexes took a jump upward following a Wall Street Journal article that alleged that some of the 16 LIBOR panelists were understating the rates at which they could obtain funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The British Bankers Association reacted by threatening to throw out any panelist that was not wholly honest in its daily posting of its costs of obtaining funds at different maturity horizons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The BBA announcement appears to have provoked an outbreak of veracity among at least some of the panelists.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 12, the LIBOR fixing rose nearly 20 basis points in the few days immediately after the article.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The dispersion in offered rates between the highest and lowest posting banks also increased.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There is considerable evidence that the official LIBOR fixing understates the rates paid by many banks for funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, as shown in exhibit 13, the all-in cost of FX swap financing into dollars out of euros has recently climbed to more than 30 basis points above the cost of LIBOR funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The term funding pressures appear to be mainly the consequence of the deleveraging process that is still firmly under way.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Balance sheet capacity has become strained in three ways.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, pressures to carry more assets on the balance sheet have increased in a number of ways.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, some types of assets can no longer be securitized, and balance sheet assets are created when lines of credit are drawn upon.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, loan-loss provisions and mark-to-market losses have cut into capital, at least until recently, faster than banks have been able to raise new capital.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, desired capital ratios have undoubtedly risen as financial markets have become more volatile and the macroeconomic outlook has worsened.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These pressures have sharply pushed up the shadow price of balance sheet capacity, and term funding spreads undoubtedly reflect that pressure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As evidence, note how the spread between jumbo and conforming fixed-rate mortgage yields in exhibit 14 has mostly tracked the trajectory of term funding spreads shown in exhibit 13.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because banks can securitize conforming mortgages but not jumbo mortgages, this widening spread likely reflects the rise in the shadow price of balance sheet capacity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The term funding pressures have also been evident in the strong demand exhibited in our biweekly TAF auctions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 15, the spread between the stop-out rate and the minimum bid rate has risen sharply since late January, despite the large rise in the size of the TAF auctions over this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, the demand by primary dealers to borrow Treasury securities in our term securities lending facility (TSLF) has been less intense.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is unclear whether this reflects the large and immediate scale of these auctions ($175 billion offered over four weeks) or less need by primary dealers, who rely heavily on secured repo borrowing for their short-term funding needs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 16, two of the five auctions have not been fully covered.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Besides providing liquidity to the primary dealers, the TSLF auctions have helped to generate a dramatic improvement in Treasury market function.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 17, before the first TSLF auction, overnight Treasury repo rates were unusually low, and the Treasury market was distorted by a growing number of security failures (that is, dealers were unable to deliver promised securities) and a large number of securities trading special (that is, with a repo rate below the rate on general Treasury collateral).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So have the TAF and TSLF auctions been helpful in improving market function?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although it is impossible to know what the counterfactual would have been without the auctions, most evidence suggests that these auctions have improved market function.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although a recent study by John Taylor and John Williams found no statistical evidence that the TAF auctions have had an effect on term funding, the choices in terms of econometric design made it very difficult for this study to have found an effect.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Interestingly, minor changes in the specification used by Taylor and Williams produce statistically significant results with the expected sign—in other words, the TAF auctions reduced the spread.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They say that a picture is worth a thousand words.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 18 documents the Federal Reserve’s major initiatives over the past eight months relative to the LIBOR– OIS spread.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Note that virtually all the Federal Reserve initiatives aimed at improving market function have been associated with a decline in the LIBOR–OIS spread.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Perhaps this just represents an announcement or placebo effect.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: More study is obviously needed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, it is interesting that those market participants who are the patients have been clamoring for more medicine in the form of both an increase in the size of the TAF auctions and auctions with longer maturities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As the equity and credit markets have improved, market participants have reduced their expectations of the magnitude of further monetary policy easing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 19, the federal funds rate futures curve has shifted upward and is virtually flat around 2 percent from May though September—implying that market participants expect that tomorrow will likely be the last easing in this cycle.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Eurodollar futures curve, which is shown in exhibit 20, has shifted up even more sharply since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In part, this reflects the rise in term funding spreads and, most important, the view that these spreads are likely to remain elevated relative to the target federal funds rate for the foreseeable future.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Our Survey of Primary Dealers undertaken about ten days before each FOMC meeting shows more stability in dealer expectations (exhibits 21 and 22).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Note that the dealer forecasts now anticipate somewhat greater easing than implied by the federal funds rate futures market and the Eurodollar futures market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is quite different from the pattern in previous months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The average of the dealer modal forecasts has a trough in yields of about 1.50 percent, about ½ percentage point below the market forecast.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of this week’s meeting, there is little disagreement between the dealer survey and market participants.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: All 18 of the primary dealers that responded to our survey anticipate a rate cut at this meeting, with nearly all in the 25 basis point rate cut camp.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 23, this is slightly more aggressive than the expectations embodied in federal funds rate options, which are pricing in a probability of a 25 basis point easing of almost 80 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The shift in interest rate expectations cannot be explained easily by developments on the inflation front.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the continued surge in crude oil prices has pushed aggregate commodity indexes, such as the GSCI, higher, agricultural and industrial metal prices have been much more stable in recent weeks (exhibit 24).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Despite the rise in energy prices, market-based measures of long-term inflation compensation have fallen in recent weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, as shown in exhibit 25, both the Board’s and Barclays’ five- year, five-year-forward measures have declined about 40 basis points from the peak reached in early March.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Turning to the Desk’s operations, we get mixed grades over the intermeeting period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the one hand, we have done a pretty good job of hitting the target on average (through yesterday, the daily effective rate since the last FOMC meeting was a miraculous 2.25 percent).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the other hand, this average conceals considerable intraday and day-to-day volatility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This can be seen in exhibit 26, which charts the daily federal funds rate range and the daily average effective rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Notice how wide the daily range of trading has been.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This reflects three factors: (1) the demand by European banks for federal funds, which has often caused the federal funds rate to be elevated early in the day before Europe closes; (2) stigma associated with primary credit facility (PCF) borrowing—the PCF rate is not a firm cap on federal funds rate trading; and (3) large unanticipated shifts in the autonomous factors that affect the level of reserves in the banking system—especially shifts in the level of PCF and PDCF borrowing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Note the big rise in PCF and PDCF borrowing since mid-March and the large daily shifts in the level of this borrowing shown in exhibit 27.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have little ability to forecast these daily shifts in borrowing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Thus, these shifts are mostly unexpected and do increase the volatility of the federal funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, let me briefly outline a number of policy recommendations for which we seek your approval.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, I will need approval for domestic operations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There were no foreign operations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, as noted in the memo that was circulated to you last week, we are recommending that the outstanding swap lines with Canada and Mexico be renewed for another year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, the staff is recommending approval of an increase in the size of the foreign exchange swap facilities with the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This recommendation is discussed in more detail in a memo that was distributed to the FOMC last Friday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For the ECB, the recommendation is to increase the size of the swap line to $50 billion from $30 billion, and for the SNB, to $12 billion from $6 billion, with maximum draws on these facilities of $25 billion and $6 billion, respectively.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We also recommend extending the term of these swap facilities to January 30, 2009, from September 30, 2008.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As before, these swap lines will be used in conjunction with our TAF auctions to increase the amount of 28-day term dollar funding available to banks with operations in the euro area and in Switzerland.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the same time, we understand that Chairman Bernanke intends to use his delegated authority from the Board to increase the size of the TAF to $150 billion from $100 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fourth, we recommend that eligible collateral for the TSLF be broadened to include AAA-rated asset-backed securities (ABS).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Currently, as you know, this facility accepts only AAA-rated residential-mortgage-backed securities and commercial-mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We believe that broadening the eligibility to AAA-rated ABS will help support the availability of consumer credit, including credit card, auto, and student loan credit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Spreads in AAA-rated ABS backed by auto loans and credit card receivables have risen sharply over the past six months even though the deterioration in the underlying performance of the assets in terms of delinquency and loss has been well within the bounds of past cycles.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We do not recommend increasing the collateral eligibility by greater breadth than this.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As we noted in last Friday’s memo, including additional classes of securities could increase operational costs to an extent that is not likely to be warranted by the marginal benefits.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It could also expose the System to the risks associated with a range of complex structured finance products and, in the case of AAA-rated corporate securities, would not provide much benefit because the amounts of such securities outstanding are relatively small.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Under this proposal, the maximum size of the TSLF would remain unchanged—at $200 billion—as would the other terms of the facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I also want to inform the Committee of a small technical change that the staff plans to make in the TSLF program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We plan to eliminate the requirement that eligible AAA-rated securities not be on watch for downgrade.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We plan to make this change because we have found that enforcing this rule has been very difficult operationally because the two clearing banks that manage the triparty repo system have a limited ability to perform this monitoring function on our behalf.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In addition, I would point out that the added risks from this change are very small.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If securities were downgraded, the primary dealer would have to substitute new eligible collateral.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, it should be pointed out that the PDCF accepts most investment-grade securities—thus, we already have a broader collateral regime in place for our other primary dealer facility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s have questions for Bill on financial markets, and then we will come back to a full discussion of the proposed actions.

speaker: LACKER
text: About consumer-loan-backed securities, spreads have widened and delinquencies and defaults have increased, but not out of line with past experience.

speaker: LACKER
text: You seem to have inferred that spreads have widened more than is warranted by the return on those securities.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would be interested in what computational exercises or what other analytics you and your staff have undertaken to document the hypothesis that these spreads are not warranted by the fundamentals.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am not so much saying that they are not warranted.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am saying that the spreads have widened a lot relative to the actual experience, given that we are in a period of weaker economic growth.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The stress seems to be more on the spreads that the market is demanding for these assets as opposed to a deterioration in the underlying credit card loans or auto loans that back those assets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let me just say a word or two about the proposed liquidity measures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, as Bill noted, the interbank and short-term funding markets remain under some stress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, as you know from the picture, the spreads in the dollar interbank market have gone above the U.K. and ECB markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although it is certainly difficult to identify precisely the size and the significance of the effect of our liquidity facilities, not just the banks and the market participants have been in favor of them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have received very good reviews from international agencies such as the IMF, the OECD, and others, and I do think that it is worth continuing these efforts to try to strengthen liquidity availability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, with respect to interbank markets, first, as mentioned, I propose to use my delegated authority to increase the size of the term auction facility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, I would like to ask the FOMC to approve increases in our swap lines and an extension of the duration of the swap lines with the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As now, they would be auctioning money at the same time that we do in our TAF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The swaps with Canada and Mexico are routine.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have done these for a number of years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I promised you at an earlier meeting, I checked with the Treasury, and they are all in favor of maintaining these facilities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it would be rather odd to end them at this particular juncture, so I ask for renewal of those swap lines as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the TSLF, the auctions that we have had have been undersubscribed, which may be good news.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, it may have something to do with narrowness of the collateral that is accepted.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The TSLF is intended to help the functioning of the Treasury market because it puts more Treasuries into circulation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We do have some evidence that Treasuries are trading at lower spreads and with less volatility since we began these activities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, there is some support for the collateral that is taken and general liquidity support for the market, although, again, it is really both sides of this equation that we are looking at.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The current collateral that is accepted at the TSLF is basically RMBS and CMBS.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The proposal is to increase the range of collateral to include AAA asset-backed securities, which include credit cards, auto loans, and student loans—basically mostly consumer-oriented credit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it makes a lot of sense in the context of what we have been doing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It would make the range of collateral more similar to that in our other facilities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It also would reduce the credit allocation aspects by broadening the range of collateral that we accept.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, as Bill mentioned, unless the situation becomes radically different, we probably don’t want to extend beyond this because of difficulties in assessing the credit quality of other assets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I put this item on the meeting agenda for your discussion because there are some political and public relations complications, and I wanted just to be up front and let you know what they are and get your response and your views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As you know, the student loan market has been dysfunctional, and we have received requests—perhaps you have as well—to do “something” about this problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We received letters, probably about a month ago, from some House members, including Congressman Kanjorski, who asked us to extend our lending authority beyond the current institutions to others.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I assume Sallie Mae, for example, would have been a possibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We wrote back a very clear letter saying that we could not do that; that our 13(3) authority was reserved for unusual and exigent circumstances, which we interpreted as being systemically relevant circumstances; that the bar was very high for the use of that authority; and that, although we certainly want to strengthen the liquidity in the general markets, we didn’t see this as being a possibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We received a second set of letters a couple of weeks ago, really one letter signed by a number of senators, mostly from the Senate Banking Committee, asking specifically that we expand the collateral in the TSLF to include student loans.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now we have the problem that this would do that, along with other much more significant, in terms of size, consumer loans.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We wrote back to Senator Dodd and his colleagues last week and told them that, although we of course are always looking to improve the liquidity of markets and, in particular, we think student loans are a very worthy type of credit, we didn’t see the argument.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, student loans are already accepted as collateral in our other three facilities—the TAF, the window, and the PDCF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, we argued that the real problem with the student loan situation is on the legislative side.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, recent legislative changes have reduced the spreads that private-sector lenders can get from student loans.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Given the increase in funding costs, they have become unprofitable, and so many lenders have withdrawn from that market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we didn’t give any encouragement in that letter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That being said, if we take this action—which was suggested by the staff and which is, I believe, fully justified on its own merits—it would be part of a broader package, and I think we would get two different reactions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the one hand, we would get, I would call it for short, a Wall Street Journal editorial that the Federal Reserve is once again the craven cur and the spineless—boy, I am getting good at this—[laughter] lackey of the Congress by accommodating this request.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m sure we all take seriously even the perception that we are catering to this request.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other side, I suppose that there would be what I could call the USA Today editorial, which is, “Why won’t the Fed, which is bailing out Wall Street left and right, include asset-backed paper in their facilities, even though it is consistent with all of their other practices and they take it in all of their other facilities?” and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think there are PR and political risks on both sides of this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am not going to try to downplay those, but I do think that on the substance this is a good move, and I will just put this on the table for your questions or comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If a significant number of members of the Committee are uncomfortable with proceeding—and what we would do if we proceed is to put this all together in a package to be announced with the Europeans and the Swiss on Friday morning—then I would certainly be willing to table this last item.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me open the floor for any comments.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the political concern you raised and described is a very, very serious one for this institution.

speaker: LACKER
text: Even if we thought of this ourselves before Senator Dodd and others wrote to us—and apparently it is true that we did—we are never going to be able to convince a broad array of observers that this was not a direct response to a senatorial request.

speaker: LACKER
text: Given that, I think the perception that we included this and maybe added some other securities as a fig leaf sets just a disastrous precedent.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would be the use of our balance sheet to circumvent the checks and balances of the constitutional process for legislating about fiscal matters.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that the integrity of our independence as an institution relies, to a substantial degree, on our lack of entanglement or our distance from the political fray.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would also question the value of this on the substance.

speaker: LACKER
text: What we are doing with the TSLF, as Bill’s chart showed, looks as though it has had a big effect on the GC repo rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is hard to see how some additional amount of Treasuries in the market, given the size of the Treasury market, is going to have a gigantic effect.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is also hard to see that there is much strain or dislocation caused by the most recent observation in his graph on the gap between the funds rate and the GC repo rate—which is actually, what, like 10 or 20 basis points or about what it has historically been.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I would question whether we really need this on the substance as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the other measures, the TAF is dominated by European institutions.

speaker: LACKER
text: Term funding spreads seem dominated by the term funding demands of European institutions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t see why we don’t try to shift to European institutions the public policy responsibility for managing those situations.

speaker: LACKER
text: We already have an apparently well-functioning mechanism for supplying dollar balances to foreign official institutions to allow them to do that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t see why we don’t limit our expansion of funding in that direction—to the swap lines—rather than expanding the TAF.

speaker: HOENIG
text: A question—and just remind me—if we bring the student loans and these other assets in under this facility, do we have the right to swap out if the rating changes or questions come up?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They are priced every day; and if they are downgraded, there will be an automatic substitution.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So you are protected both on price and on the ability to substitute.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That was my first question.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The second is that we have been entangled before in appearance issues.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we feel that we are doing the right thing, that doesn’t give me much concern.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the substance, do you judge that the tightness in the market is such that this action is necessary to facilitate liquidity, or will this only marginally improve things?

speaker: HOENIG
text: If it is marginal, the appearance issue becomes more entangled, I think.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If it is pretty clear that we have some liquidity issues and that this will address them, then I would feel much more comfortable with it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I think the honest answer is that we don’t really know exactly where it is on the continuum of very modest to substantive.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One thing we can say is that this should increase the demand at the TSLF auction, so it should increase the likelihood that more of the Treasuries are actually put into the market in exchange for such collateral because we are broadening the eligible collateral.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I don’t think the notion that this is a panacea is true.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I want to say just one thing in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The Chairman alluded to this, too.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think there is some value in taking this opportunity now to try to get a better balance in the relative attractiveness across these facilities.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So in the scheme of things, it is better for us for the auction type of facilities to be relatively attractive compared with the open facilities for which demand is unknown and we can’t calibrate it—those are much bigger reserve-management things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think our exit strategy from these things is easier if we evolve in that direction.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One virtue of the package that the Chairman presented is that it is worth taking another shot at trying to get those interbank term premiums down in dollars because—to use a technical term—they are screwing up the transmission mechanism of U.S. monetary policy now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are not quite sure how much effect we can have.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is a plausible case that increasing the size of the swaps will help on that front.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is worth doing now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Second, the broader package will buy a little more insurance against the risk that these liquidity pressures reignite and we have another wave of the adverse dynamic margin-spiral-downward-self-feeding thing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is better to do that when other things are improving rather than wait until we are again at the edge of the abyss, although that is a tactical judgment.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is hard to know for sure.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that Bill is absolutely right.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is not clear how much incremental benefit the expanded collateral in the TSLF will offer.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But, Jeff, it won’t come because we are increasing the size of the TSLF.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That would increase the amount of Treasuries we are putting in, and we are not increasing the size.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It would come only through what effect it might have on the broader range of asset-backed securities we have there.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Remember, at the beginning we framed this as an effort to address some unique constraints operating on securitization markets, particularly in ABS.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So there is a possibility of some additional benefit in those markets—some greater insurance against another downward spiral in that case—but not that high.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is hard to judge the merits of that against the appearance risk you presented, but I think this is designed pretty carefully to be robust to that perception problem.

speaker: GEITHNER
