text: Our job is to do what makes sense and what we can defend as sensible in this context, and we have to be prepared to do that even if people have made it awkward for us to do the right thing because of the perception problem.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Well, I certainly agree with the last statement that we should do what makes sense, and in this case, differentiating between kinds of collateral that are all AAA doesn’t make sense to me.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We should broaden it out.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would say that in your presentation you didn’t have the asset-backed commercial paper market, but those rates actually have been quite elevated.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Some rollovers for some of the large banks have not been working all that well, and the assets that tend to be in those conduits are the very assets we are talking about expanding.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: They are the student loans, the auto loans, and the various other things that go into these conduits.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I don’t know how big an effect it would be, but if you look at the asset-backed commercial paper rates, they would look a lot like the LIBOR rates.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think that there might be some net benefit, and it certainly does make sense to me that we would expand.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There is no reason to differentiate among AAA collateral that has many similar attributes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, a two-handed comment?

speaker: LACKER
text: Mr. Chairman, you motivated the expansion of the term securities lending facility by the effect it would have by increasing the amount of Treasuries in the market.

speaker: LACKER
text: Vice Chairman Geithner, you appealed to the effect it would have on the asset-backed securities that would be offered on the market.

speaker: LACKER
text: We didn’t discuss the asset-backed securities market, except that I had this exchange with our Manager.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am not aware of any evidence that there is something wrong with the fundamentals of those markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, admittedly, it is not clear that many of our arguments for some of these facilities have been based on some careful diagnosis of fundamentals.

speaker: LACKER
text: If this is about those asset-backed securities markets, that is another thing entirely.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was a little confused about that and wondered about the rationale.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I may have misspoken, but I think I had in mind both sides of the equation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Treasuries have certainly responded.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s harder to judge on the asset side, but I guess that the premise is the same—that all of these markets are suffering from withdrawal of the normal liquidity provision of money market mutual funds and other, less sophisticated investors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Banks and others are finding it hard to finance those assets, and that’s the liquidity backstop that we provide.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think on both sides.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If I may come back to the issue of the AAA securities and the spreads, those are AAA-rated securities for which the spread has widened hundreds of basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If the loss experienced is not unusual relative to the cycle, then it’s hard to understand why AAA-rated securities would be selling at several hundred basis points over Treasuries.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is impossible to square that circle.

speaker: LACKER
text: If the payoff for those securities is unexpectedly low, it is likely to happen in a circumstance in which the economy is doing awfully poorly.

speaker: LACKER
text: Risk premiums are about variances and risk aversion, but they are also about correlation with aggregate states.

speaker: LACKER
text: Arguably, that would rationalize a widening of the risk premiums attached to a wide range of securities, mortgage-backed included.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have yet to see any evidence from our staff refuting that interpretation of the widening spreads we have seen.

speaker: LACKER
text: Mr. Chairman, with all due respect, what you describe is a lack of demand.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am not sure how that squares with viewing the market as somehow malfunctioning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we have seen the breakdown of a particular structure of lending that was based on the credit ratings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The credit ratings have proven to be false.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, there is an informational deficit—an asymmetric information problem, would be my interpretation—which has, in turn, triggered a massive change in preferences.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I don’t think we are going to settle this at the table here.

speaker: EVANS
text: The question that I have gets to the appearance issue, and it is not really about the immediate concerns.

speaker: EVANS
text: To the extent that the markets are not functioning that well, this could be useful, and so I don’t really have any disagreement with that.

speaker: EVANS
text: But the facilities that we are talking about currently have a temporary nature to them.

speaker: EVANS
text: The term auction facility is temporary, although of course the Board could make it permanent.

speaker: EVANS
text: The term securities lending facility is an expansion of a program.

speaker: EVANS
text: What’s the permanence of that and the primary dealer credit facility as well?

speaker: EVANS
text: As we allow other forms of collateral to be taken, what implications might that have for the future if we try to make these more permanent?

speaker: EVANS
text: This is simply a question; I don’t know what the answer is.

speaker: EVANS
text: Do we feel comfortable with these forms of additional collateral on a permanent, ongoing basis, if we were to do that; or do we think it would be possible to turn that off?

speaker: EVANS
text: How costly would it be?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The TSLF and the PDCF are emergency measures, and barring congressional action, we cannot maintain them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Presumably, they will be phased out as markets improve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we are doing these things, I don’t see the argument for one set of collateral versus another.

speaker: FISHER
text: Along those lines, Mr. Chairman, I viewed these facilities as a liquidity bridge, an aqueduct, to getting over this credit crunch that we have had.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am not as concerned about having this facility accept the same collateral as the other facilities.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do have a question about the permanence, and it is a different kind of question, which is whether or not the Congress will encourage us to make these permanent.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that is a risk, and we need to think about it.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t have an answer.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have been on the receiving end, as you may know, of enormous pressure from the Texas delegation on the student loan business, and we have talked about it with the staff quite a bit.

speaker: FISHER
text: I quoted you in my response, by the way, in your first series of letters.

speaker: FISHER
text: It doesn’t bother me to have egg on my face if we are doing the right thing—again, having the same collateral regime as we have for our other facilities.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am more worried, however, about whether it encourages them in interfering with the temporary nature of these facilities.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is just one point to think about.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have a question about the TAF—just to make sure that I understand.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are talking about taking it to $150 billion in outstandings—is that correct?

speaker: FISHER
text: The third point, which is about optics, is a little different.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t know what we’re going to come out with in terms of policy.

speaker: FISHER
text: I know what my preferences are, and I sense what some other people’s preferences are.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m a little concerned that we have to be able to express this in a way that doesn’t look as though we see something that no one else sees.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we need to think about that and the way we articulate it.

speaker: FISHER
text: The last time we had a disconnect between an action on the fed funds rate and agreeing to something and announcing it internationally, it didn’t really work well.

speaker: FISHER
text: They read more into it than was there.

speaker: FISHER
text: We all understood why we were having that time disconnect—it was because we needed to line up our ducks with our foreign counterparts.

speaker: FISHER
text: Maybe we should think about that as well—whether we should move it up to the same time that we announce the action of this Committee on the fed funds rate.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t know if that is physically possible.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I wouldn’t want in any way to convey that we see something that other people don’t see, that there is a problem in these particular markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: Everybody knows that GE is trying to sell a $40 billion credit card portfolio and they are not getting any bidders.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I can see the devious minds, or the minds of those who don’t necessarily think well of us, linking all these little pieces together and saying that we’re reacting or overreacting to something that may not be there.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just wanted to put that on the table for you to think about.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am not against the concept, since we have already gone down this path, of making this subject to the same collateral regime.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I do think—and I am glad you raised the subject—that, though I have interpreted it differently, we have to be concerned about the optics here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Fisher, the timing is dictated by the preference of the Europeans not to be tied into our monetary policy decision and the fact that Thursday is a European holiday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The problem you were alluding to earlier had to do with the very strong market expectation that we were going to act on liquidity measures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We disappointed both on that and on the rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was why we got the strong reaction, and there’s no such expectation to my knowledge here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At the same time, our press release, which we have already looked at in draft, and market expectations are very focused on the LIBOR issue and the interbank issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Given that we have done so many steps in this direction, I don’t think that this would be misinterpreted as anything particularly overdramatic.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, may I just raise one other point?

speaker: FISHER
text: I think President Lacker touched on this.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am concerned, in terms of the eventual optics, about the fact that the TAF is being drawn on predominately by foreign banks.

speaker: FISHER
text: My numbers here are that the last one was 78 percent foreign bank participation and the previous one was 91 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think there we may have some political vulnerability.

speaker: FISHER
text: Again, I just put it on the table for us to consider.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am almost more worried about a backlash on that eventually than what we are talking about currently.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The problem is that European banks are structurally deficient in dollars and they have a time zone shift.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is a dollar market.

speaker: FISHER
text: It has been well presented.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s hard to explain to a politician.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the last point, I think it is helpful to expand both the swaps and the TAF at the same time.

speaker: KOHN
text: People understand that there are pressures in these funding markets, and we can address them both at home and abroad.

speaker: KOHN
text: They do feed back on our market, so I guess I am not too worried about that one.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also, it is quite logical to do the swaps and the TAF.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t see any issue.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the TSLF, I have been thinking about it less on the Treasury side than on the other side.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think the TSLF will increase the demand for holding these securities in any major, direct way.

speaker: KOHN
text: My hope is that, sort of around the margin, it would make dealers more willing to make markets in them and to be on both sides of the market, including the buy side from time to time, because then they would see that they had a place to finance those securities if, at the end of the day, they had more.

speaker: KOHN
text: So if it helps, it will help the liquidity of those markets rather than increasing the ultimate demand for the securities.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it is an indirect thing.

speaker: KOHN
text: My guess is that it might help at most around the margins.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t see how it can hurt.

speaker: KOHN
text: There is a certain logic to it.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think it will help the student loans at all.

speaker: KOHN
text: The structural issues are just overwhelming any of the other issues in that line.

speaker: KOHN
text: If somebody asked you, Mr. Chairman, whether this was aimed at student loans, I think you could say that they just were along for the ride in the sense that they were part of the AAA ABS market and that we didn’t have any expectation that expanding that market would help them.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am the new guy, but I will just put in my two cents here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Everyone seems to agree that there is no quantitative impact.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I can’t see any quantitative impact.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t see why we are doing it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To repeat what Bill said, I think it is hard to measure the quantitative impact, but my guess is that there is some.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the point is well taken.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I would like to do is go through the first votes, and then we will take a straw vote on the TSLF, and then decide what to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, we have to ratify domestic open market operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now the swap agreements with Canada and Mexico.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is there anyone who wants a roll call on this?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, then no objection.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Extend and expand the swap agreement with the ECB.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is there anyone who wants a roll call on this?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Expand and extend the swap agreement with the Swiss National Bank.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, on the TSLF, the proposal is to include this as part of the package.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be no change to the facility except for the increase in the collateral range, to include AAA asset-backed securities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any further comments on this?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am going to ask for a straw vote, just to get a sense.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no further comments, how many people are in favor of this?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I see 10, I think.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Are you asking voters only?

speaker: FISHER
text: Are you asking voters only or the entire table?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to get a sense of all participants, if that is okay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thirteen participants are in favor.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s go ahead and take a vote on this, then.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is there anyone who wants a roll call vote?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, then no objection.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s turn now to the economic situation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan and I thought that we would alter slightly the structure of our briefing today so as to focus a bit more closely than usual on the global and domestic outlooks for inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I’ll start with a brief review of recent economic developments and our outlook for economic activity in the United States.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan will then discuss trade and foreign activity before turning to global commodity markets and our forecast for import prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I will then explain how both foreign and domestic influences are shaping our outlook for U.S. inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Brian will conclude by presenting your forecasts.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Let me turn first to the domestic economy.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: From a forecasting perspective, this intermeeting period turned out to be reasonably tranquil, at least by the standards of the past nine months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The incoming data were very close to our expectations and required few adjustments to either top-line GDP or to the individual components of spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As we noted in the Greenbook, we continue to think it likely that the economy is in recession; and, with the data evolving pretty much as we had expected, we have seen little reason to back away from that call.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Readings from the labor market support the view that, at the very least, a pronounced deceleration in aggregate activity is under way.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Private payrolls fell about 100,000 in March, the third consecutive month with a drop of that magnitude, and the unemployment rate moved above 5 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, a notable weakening of labor markets is signaled by most of the indicators that we monitor.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Surveys of hiring plans have continued to move lower; there are fewer job vacancies; businesses report that jobs are easier to fill; and household attitudes have continued to sour, including their views of the labor market.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In the past, such a configuration of readings has been a reasonably reliable indicator of cyclical downturn.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The spending data also have been consistent with our forecast of a marked weakening in aggregate demand and activity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: After posting modest gains last year, consumer outlays and business equipment spending appear to have been at a near standstill since the turn of the year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Meanwhile, housing continues its steep descent and looks to be on track to subtract about 1½ percentage points from the growth of real GDP in the first half of the year—close to our March projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, while we had anticipated a sharp deceleration in nonresidential construction in response to more-difficult financing conditions, that sector now appears to be turning down earlier and more sharply than we had projected.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Finally, much as we had been expecting, weak domestic demand is receiving some offset from ongoing solid gains in exports.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: All told, we estimate that real GDP rose at an annual rate of ½ percent in the first quarter, just a few tenths above our March forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, tomorrow morning, the BEA will release its advance GDP estimate for the first quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For the second quarter, we are projecting real output to decline at a 1½ percent annual rate, a few tenths weaker than our March forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On net, the outlook for activity in the first half is basically unchanged from the time of the last meeting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Looking further ahead, our medium-term forecast also hasn’t changed much over the past six weeks.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The stock market is more than 5 percent higher than we had anticipated.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the favorable effects of that development on activity are nearly offset by the adverse effects of lower house prices and higher oil prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Consequently, the GDP gap at the end of next year is unchanged from the March forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Our basic story remains the same.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The contraction in activity that we are projecting over the first half of the year is expected to be relatively mild because of the boost to spending and activity from the tax rebates and because export demand remains solid.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In the second half, real GDP turns up, but I wouldn’t really term this a recovery.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: After all, real GDP is projected to grow less than 1 percent at an annual rate, employment continues to decline, and the unemployment rate runs up to 5¾ percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we see a number of factors fostering a more noticeable acceleration of activity to a pace above its potential by 2009.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: First, the contraction in residential investment abates.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Second, the drag on consumption growth from the rise in oil prices wanes.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Third, financial conditions stabilize and then begin to improve, gradually reducing restraint on household and business spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Finally, we assume that monetary policy remains accommodative.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: With the growth in real GDP running 2¾ percent next year, about ½ percentage point above the pace of potential, the unemployment rate drops slowly to 5½ percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, there are large risks on both sides of our projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the upside, we could just be flat-out wrong about an imminent contraction in aggregate activity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Claims were running about 360,000 at the time of the March FOMC and are now averaging about 370,000.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: While that increase suggests some further softening in the labor market, the level of claims seems lower than would comfortably fit our forecast of payroll employment declines averaging about 160,000 over the next few months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Likewise, industrial production has weakened but hasn’t dropped off much.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Because we don’t expect manufacturing to be at the epicenter of this business cycle, we aren’t looking for a plunge, but we are forecasting more noticeable declines than we’ve seen to date.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In addition, although last week’s numbers for shipments of nondefense capital goods in March were close to our forecast, the orders figures were firmer than we had expected.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In sum, while the data have not pushed us away from our recession forecast, they haven’t convincingly confirmed it yet either.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: More broadly, with bond spreads down, the stock market up, and market expectations for the path of policy revised higher, the situation certainly looks less menacing than at the time of the March meeting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But while we would agree that the risk of a very bad tail event seems to have declined, we are not ready to join others in heaving a sigh of relief just yet about the modal outlook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For one, we still see no signs of a bottom in housing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: New homes sales—we received the numbers after the projection was completed—declined more than 8 percent last month to a level that we thought would be the bottom in the second half of this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: A second concern centers on consumption.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: With oil prices running around $115 per barrel, consumers will be facing sizable further increases in gasoline prices over the next few months from already elevated levels.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Also, given the steep declines in employment that we are projecting, incomes and income uncertainty will be taking a hit.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’ve taken those factors on board as best we can, and we are counting on the tax rebates to provide a powerful offset, but we can’t rule out a more adverse reaction to what will be an accumulation of bad news.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Furthermore, while there has been improvement in the general tenor of financial markets, I suspect that we’ve only begun to see the effects of tighter credit conditions on borrowing and spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That restraint could prove larger and more persistent than is implicit in our baseline forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Finally, the mild downturn in activity that we are projecting also suggests some downside risk.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Our projected rise in the unemployment rate of 1¼ percentage points from its low point last year to its high point at the end of this year is small—smaller than occurred in either the 1990–91 recession or the 2001 recession.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This time could be different, but as I noted in March, that argument should always give you pause.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan will now continue our presentation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Much as Dave just described for the domestic economy, our forecast for economic activity abroad also is little changed from the last Greenbook.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Recent data have come in consistent with our view that the slowdown in U.S. activity and the ongoing financial turbulence will leave an unmistakable imprint on economic growth abroad.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But the extent of this imprint appears to be somewhat less pronounced than was the case in the high-tech-led recession earlier this decade, particularly for the emerging market economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Thus we continue to see foreign growth stepping down from last year’s 4 percent pace to near 2 percent during the second and third quarters of this year, as foreign activity is constrained by the weakening U.S. economy and headwinds from the ongoing financial turmoil.

speaker: SHEETS
text: With these factors projected to abate, we see growth abroad rising back to near its trend rate of around 3½ percent in 2009.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Suffice it to say, the risks around this forecast remain significant.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the upside, China’s surprisingly strong first-quarter GDP growth—which we estimate was nearly 11 percent at an annual rate—highlights the possibility that growth in emerging Asia, and perhaps elsewhere as well, may remain more resilient than we anticipate.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the downside, the softer-than-expected German IFO data last week and the negative tone of the Bank of England’s recent credit conditions survey suggest that growth in Europe may slow more than we now project.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The exchange value of the dollar, after falling sharply in the month before the March FOMC meeting, has rebounded somewhat during the intermeeting period.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Against the major currencies, the dollar is up almost 2½ percent, with a particularly sizable gain against the yen.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Going forward, we continue to see the broad real dollar depreciating at a 3 percent pace, reflecting downward pressures associated with the large (albeit narrowing) current account deficit.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This depreciation is expected to come largely against emerging market currencies (including the Chinese renminbi), which have moved less since the dollar’s peak in early 2002.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Turning to the U.S. external sector, we now see the arithmetic contribution from net exports to first-quarter U.S. real GDP growth as likely to be around 0.3 percentage point, down a few tenths from the last Greenbook.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Recent readings on exports have continued to point to strength, but imports in February bounced back from their December and January weakness more vigorously than we had expected.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For 2008 as a whole, we continue to believe that the demand for imports will be significantly restrained by the weak pace of U.S. activity and, to a lesser extent, by the depreciation of the dollar and rising prices for imported commodities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We thus see imports contracting nearly 2 percent this year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In contrast, exports are expected to post 7 percent growth this year, supported by the weaker dollar.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The projected contraction of imports, coupled with still-strong export growth, suggests that net exports will contribute nearly 1¼ percentage points to U.S. GDP growth this year— the largest positive contribution from net exports to annual growth in more than 25 years.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In 2009, import growth is expected to bounce back to around 4 percent as the U.S. economy recovers, and the positive contribution from net exports should accordingly decline to just under ½ percentage point.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Oil prices have continued their apparently relentless march upward, with spot WTI now trading at $115 per barrel.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Since your last meeting, the spot price of WTI has increased $6 per barrel, and the far-futures price has moved up almost $5 per barrel.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Over the past year, spot oil prices have risen a staggering 80 percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: While the high level of oil prices appears to be taking a bite out of oil demand in the United States and other industrial countries, the demand for oil in the emerging market economies—particularly in China and India—has been supported by the resilience of GDP growth there.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, fuel subsidies in some countries (including India) have sheltered consumers from the effects of higher oil prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In line with these observations, India’s state-owned oil company recently released projections indicating that oil demand in the country will increase 8 to 10 percent this year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The supply-side response to the rising demand for oil has been only tepid.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Stated bluntly, OPEC remains unwilling—or unable—to increase its supply to the market.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indeed, OPEC has actually cut its production over the past two years.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, oil production in the OECD countries has been on a downward trajectory, primarily reflecting the decline in the North Sea fields and in Mexico’s giant Cantarell field.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Mexico’s state-owned oil company recently indicated that, for the sixth consecutive year, additions to its reserves had failed to keep pace with production.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The grim outlook for Mexico’s oil industry has prompted the government to consider allowing foreign investment in the country’s energy sector, a move that would require constitutional reform.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Finally, although the potential supply from non-OECD non- OPEC countries is substantial, production continues to be hampered by inadequate infrastructure and by uncertainties about property rights and the stability of tax regimes.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the absence of any better approach, we continue to base our forecast on quotes from futures markets, which see oil prices as likely to remain high—at or above $110 per barrel—through the end of the forecast period.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But the confidence bands around this forecast are exceptionally wide given uncertainties surrounding the outlook for oil supply and demand.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nonfuel commodity prices have also been on a wild ride of late.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The prices of many of these commodities increased particularly sharply in January and February, before peaking in early March.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On balance, our index of nonfuel commodity prices rose at a hefty annual rate of 50 percent during the first quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We project a further 13 percent rise in the second quarter, but—again in line with quotes from futures markets—we see these prices flattening out thereafter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The underlying drivers of the sustained run-up in the prices of nonfuel commodities have been broadly similar to those for oil—sharp increases in demand (particularly from emerging-market economies) coupled with typically lagging and often muted supply responses.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, however, moves in nonfuel commodity prices since the March FOMC meeting have been quite varied.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For example, copper and aluminum prices are up whereas nickel and zinc prices are down.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For foods, corn, rice, and soybean prices have risen while wheat prices have declined substantially.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The overall strength of commodity prices continues to put upward pressure on inflation in many countries and to complicate life for central banks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, in the euro area, 12-month headline inflation in March rose further, to 3.6 percent, well above the ECB’s 2 percent ceiling.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the United Kingdom, inflation pressures stemming from rising utility, gasoline, and food prices are likely to push inflation toward 3 percent during the summer, raising the risk that Mervyn King will be required to write another letter to the Chancellor of the Exchequer explaining why inflation has deviated from the 2 percent target.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Concerns about the inflation outlook have limited the willingness of both the ECB and the Bank of England to cut policy rates to address slowing growth.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Perhaps even more striking, faced with upward pressures on inflation from rising food and energy prices coupled with still-solid economic growth, central banks in a broad array of emerging market economies tightened policy over the intermeeting period.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This group included China, Singapore, India, Brazil, Russia, Poland, Hungary, and South Africa.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, some countries have recently responded to social unrest and other strains brought on by higher food prices by restricting exports of foodstuffs, particularly rice, and this has exacerbated upward pressure on the global prices of these commodities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The run-up in commodity prices, coupled with the weaker dollar, has pushed up U.S. core import price inflation of late.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Core import prices are now estimated to have increased at a 7½ percent annual rate in the first quarter, more than twice the pace of increase in the second half of last year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Prices of material-intensive imports (including industrial supplies and foods) are seen to have surged at a surprisingly rapid pace of 20 percent in the first quarter, on the back of the rapid rise in commodity prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Prices of imported finished goods (including consumer goods, capital goods, and autos) are estimated to have risen at a comparatively muted rate of 3¾ percent, but this also was up sharply compared with recent quarters.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The acceleration in finished goods prices seems well explained by recent moves in the dollar, however, and does not suggest any notable increase in the extent of exchange rate pass-through.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Going forward, we see core import price inflation remaining elevated in the second quarter, at around 6 percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Thereafter, core import price inflation should abate, given the projected flattening out of commodity prices and the slower pace of dollar depreciation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Before explaining how the global developments that Nathan just described intersect with our domestic inflation forecast, I should briefly review some of the incoming information on prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For the most part, the recent consumer price data have been running below our expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At the time of the March Greenbook, we were estimating that core PCE prices had increased at an annual rate of 2¾ percent in both the fourth quarter of last year and the first quarter of this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We now are projecting increases of 2½ percent and 2 percent in the fourth and first quarters, respectively.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Although we are estimating that core PCE prices rose 0.2 percent in March—just a couple of basis points below our previous forecast—there were noticeable downward revisions to the data stretching back to late last year, principally for medical services and nonmarket prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Just as we had discounted some of the earlier elevated increases in core PCE prices, we are now inclined to discount the recent more favorable readings.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The small increases in medical service prices are not likely to persist.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, some of the recent slowdown is attributable to nonmarket prices, which we view as both noisy and mean-reverting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Still, we don’t think all of the good news on core PCE prices of late should be written off; and all else being equal, we would have taken down our forecast for the year as a whole in response to the incoming data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But, of course, all else was not equal.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As Nathan has noted, there has been another sizable increase in crude oil prices; the prices of non-oil imports have increased more rapidly than we had expected; and more broadly, both imported and domestically produced materials prices have risen sharply thus far this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In reaction, we have marked up our forecast for core PCE inflation for the remainder of the year, and that upward revision basically offsets the effects of the recent good news.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For now, inflation this year looks likely to repeat the pattern of the past four years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Since 2004, headline PCE prices have risen at about 3 percent per year, and core prices have been up at a rate of about 2¼ percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Due to a further steep rise in energy prices, large gains in import prices, and another above-trend increase in food prices, we are projecting headline PCE prices to rise 3¼ percent this year and core prices to increase 2¼ percent—similar to the averages over the preceding four years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, our forecast for 2009 bears a striking resemblance to the out-year forecasts that we have continued to make over the past four years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: By now, in answer to the question of why inflation is expected to slow in the forecast, most of you could easily recite the staff’s catechism of disinflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Based on readings from the futures markets, we expect consumer energy prices to flatten out next year and food prices to slow to a rate close to core inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: With the dollar not expected to fall as much as it has over the past year and other commodity prices expected to move sideways, import prices are projected to slow.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Those more favorable developments in combination with a noticeable increase in projected slack cause headline inflation in 2009 to slow to 1¾ percent and core PCE inflation to edge back to 2 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Both of those figures are 0.1 percentage point higher than our March forecasts, reflecting the indirect effects of higher prices for energy and other imports.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As we have noted many times, a key element in our projection is the assumption that oil and non-oil commodity prices will flatten out as suggested by the futures markets.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: To put it mildly, that has not been a winning forecast strategy in recent years, but I’m not sure that we have a superior one to offer you.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, there are some big upside and downside risks to our forecast of domestic inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan has already covered some of those related to prices for oil and other imports, so let me say a few words about the outlook for retail food prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Our outlook for food prices remains relatively sanguine, but there would appear to be more pronounced risks to the upside than the downside.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Although most of the value of what’s in your morning cereal bowl is advertising, packaging, and transportation, some corn and wheat are in there also, [laughter] and those prices have been rising rapidly.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Futures markets are predicting a leveling-out in crop prices, and that expectation is built into our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But worldwide stocks of grains remain tight, and any serious shortfall in production could result in sharply higher prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In that regard, while the growing season here is just getting under way, corn production is off to a slow start because unusually wet conditions have hampered plantings.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Elsewhere, increasing supplies of livestock products and poultry have been a moderating influence on retail food prices in recent months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, while futures markets suggest relatively subdued prices going forward, there are a few worrying signs.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Although cattle on feedlots have remained near record levels, new placements have fallen off of late, reportedly because of the higher cost of feed.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In addition, the portion of feedlot placements composed of females was high last fall and through the winter, which points to a reduction in the size of the breeding herd this year and thus suggests some potential supply risks ahead.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In recognition of the upside risks posed by both food and energy prices, we included in the Greenbook an alternative simulation in which oil prices climb to $150 per barrel next year and food prices continue to run at the elevated pace of the past three years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In this scenario, we also assume that another year of elevated headline inflation results in a further erosion of inflation expectations of about ¼ percentage point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Under these conditions, headline PCE price inflation posts another year north of 3 percent, and core inflation moves a bit higher to 2½ percent this year and next.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It strikes me that this type of persistent upward creep to inflation, which would be difficult to positively identify in real time, is a more likely risk than a sudden upward surge in price inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There are, however, some downside risks to the inflation outlook as well.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, we upped our price forecast a bit in the last round because we saw the incoming readings on inflation expectations as suggesting that there had been some modest upward movement over the preceding few months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Some of that increase may have resulted from your aggressive easing of policy early this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But going forward, the situation may be turned around.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If our forecast over the next few quarters is in the right ballpark, and on our assumption that the easing of policy is coming to an end, you will be standing pat on policy even as payroll employment falls throughout the remainder of the year, the unemployment rate trends higher, and headline inflation begins to back down.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It doesn’t seem a stretch to me that in that environment, inflation expectations could come down somewhat, a development not embodied in the baseline forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: More broadly, one place that inflation expectations might be expected to manifest themselves in a way that would be most damaging to inflation would be in labor compensation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Despite the elevated headline inflation of the past four years, there is little evidence of any noticeable step-up in wage inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If that was the case when the unemployment rate was 4½ percent, it seems less likely that larger nominal wage gains will be secured when the unemployment rate rises to 5¾ percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, increases in hourly labor compensation have been running well below our models for some time, pointing to some additional downside risks to our inflation outlook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For now, we see substantial risks to the inflation outlook, but those risks still seem two- sided to us.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Brian will complete our presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2 I will be referring to the package labeled “Material for Briefing on FOMC Participants’ Economic Projections.” Table 1 shows the central tendencies and ranges of your current forecasts for 2008, 2009, and 2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Central tendencies and ranges of the projections published by the Committee last February are shown in italics.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Regarding your monetary policy assumptions (not shown) about three-fourths of the participants envisage a moderately to substantially higher federal funds rate by late next year than assumed in the Greenbook, a path perhaps similar to the one incorporated in financial market quotes.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you conditioned your projections on a path for the federal funds rate that begins to rise either in late 2008 or sometime in 2009, in contrast to the Greenbook path, which remains flat through 2009.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Many of you were less clear whether you differed from the Greenbook path 2 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: over the near term; but with a little reading between the lines, it seems fair to say that most of you assumed a slightly higher funds rate over the near term.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the first set of rows and first column of table 1, the central tendency of your real economic growth forecasts for 2008 has been marked down nearly 1 percentage point since January.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you pointed to weak incoming data, tight credit conditions, falling house prices, and rising energy prices as factors that prompted you to lower your growth expectations for this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: About half of you forecast a decline in economic activity over the first half of the year (not shown), with another quarter of you seeing a flat trajectory over that period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, only four of you used the word “recession” to describe the current state of the economy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: None of you has a more negative first-half outlook than the Greenbook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The downward revisions to your growth forecasts are roughly equal across both halves of 2008, and so the contour remains one of a rising growth rate over the year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Members’ projections for the speed of the recovery in late 2008 exhibit considerable dispersion, with some calling for a quick return to near-potential growth supported by monetary and fiscal stimulus, and others seeing a prolonged period of weakness owing partly to persisting financial headwinds.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you appear to expect growth to return to near its trend rate in 2009 (column 2) and to move slightly above trend in 2010 (column 3).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Greenbook forecast for real growth in 2008 is near the low end of the central tendency of FOMC members’ projections, but it is at the high end in 2009 and 2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The second set of rows indicates that you have revised up your projections for the unemployment rate throughout the forecast period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of those of you who provided estimates of the natural rate of unemployment, most expect unemployment to remain above the natural rate in 2010 with the others seeing a return to the natural rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the third set of rows, your projections for headline PCE inflation in 2008 have been revised up a full percentage point, largely due to the surge in the prices of energy and other commodities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Incoming information has also prompted a small upward revision to your projections of core PCE inflation this year (the fourth set of rows).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The rate of decline of core inflation in 2009 is essentially unchanged from that in the January projections, presumably reflecting the offsetting effects of the higher unemployment rates in the April projections, on the one hand, and the lagged pass-through of this year’s higher food and energy prices, on the other.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: By 2010 the prolonged period of economic slack pushes down core inflation to around the same rates that were projected in January.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although the central tendencies for headline inflation, the third set of rows, also decline markedly over the forecast period, overall inflation is projected to be about ¼ percentage point higher next year than you anticipated in January.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Nonetheless, by 2010, headline inflation is expected to be in essentially the same range of around 1¾ to 2 percent that you forecasted in January.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your inflation projections for 2010 are close to their values in January, but more than half of you raised your projections for the unemployment rate in 2010 significantly more than 0.1 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To the extent that the higher unemployment rate projections are viewed as implying an economy operating below its potential in 2010, outside analysts may infer that you expect inflation to edge down further beyond 2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Turning to the risks to the outlook, as shown in the upper left-hand panel of exhibit 2, a large majority of you regard uncertainty about GDP growth as greater than normal.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The upper right-hand panel shows that most of you perceive the risks to GDP growth as weighted to the downside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Correspondingly, the risks to unemployment, not shown, are seen as weighted to the upside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You typically attributed the downside growth risks to the potential for sharper declines in house prices and persisting financial strains.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Overall, the distributions of your views on the uncertainties and skews regarding growth are little changed from January.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, as shown in the lower panels, your perceptions of the risks regarding inflation have changed noticeably since January.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the lower left panel, only half as many participants now see the degree of uncertainty regarding the inflation outlook as historically normal, and twice as many see the uncertainties as larger than usual.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As indicated to the right, fewer see the risks to their outlook for overall inflation as balanced, and more see the risks as skewed to the upside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your narratives indicate that you see the upside risks to inflation as deriving from the potential for continued increases in commodity prices, further depreciation of the dollar, and an upward drift in inflation expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for our colleagues?

speaker: EVANS
text: The Greenbook is aggressive and effective at portraying the U.S. economy as being in a mild recession.

speaker: EVANS
text: They’ve overcome the statistical evidence, which often prevents us from forecasting a recession since they are mostly surprises.

speaker: EVANS
text: There’s a nonlinear step-down in the second quarter that begins this recession.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I’m a little curious as to why you didn’t follow this up by forecasting a jobless recovery.

speaker: EVANS
text: In the last two recessions, that has been an important element of what followed.

speaker: EVANS
text: I wonder if it is now a feature of the Great Moderation business cycle.

speaker: EVANS
text: If you look at equilibrium real funds rates, they tend to bottom out during the period of most troubling joblessness in the aftermath of the recession.

speaker: EVANS
text: So if we’re going to be relying on a period in which we’re doing something we haven’t done before, like buying a bit of additional inflation credibility, it will be unusual.

speaker: EVANS
text: I guess my question is why you made that choice.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This year certainly is pretty close to a jobless year in terms of a full year of nothing but employment declines and then fairly modest employment gains next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the principal reason we didn’t predict a pattern like the one we saw in the earlier part of this decade is that we don’t think we’re going to get the kind of productivity surprises that were such an important feature of that recovery.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you may recall, we were stunned by the extent to which, even in a period of cyclical weakening, we kept getting much stronger productivity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think it will be years before research is actually able to shed a lot of light on why that occurred.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The part of the story that we still think was probably in play was that there had been an accumulation of technological advances that businesses were able to draw on over this period and that led to a period in which, even as growth was picking up, employment wasn’t.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We don’t see that happening again—although we didn’t see it happening the last time either, so it’s possible.

speaker: STERN
text: Dave, I have a couple of questions.

speaker: STERN
text: One is technical, and one is a little more substantive.

speaker: STERN
text: The technical one is that you have a very sharp decline in consumer spending on services in the fourth quarter of this year and then not much of a recovery in the first quarter of next year.

speaker: STERN
text: I assume something special is going on there, but I don’t know what it is.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: What was going on there was probably—I don’t know if it was rational or irrational—inattention.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But in looking at that over the weekend, it seemed like something that should not be considered as an analytical feature of the forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Just in terms of the falloff in consumption that we expect to follow from the end of the tax rebates, my guess is that the consumption folks were trying just to put it somewhere and some of it showed up in services.

speaker: STERN
text: “Services” seems like the least likely spot actually.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think I’m raising the white flag here.

speaker: STERN
text: The more fundamental question is that I have been trying to get comfortable with an outlook that would have core inflation leveling off and maybe declining a bit, and that’s the forecast I have.

speaker: STERN
text: But I took your presentation, which I think was certainly on the right topic, to say that the risks around the core inflation forecast seem to be symmetric at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: Is that a fair characterization?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think that is a fair characterization.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: You know, one thing that we’re struggling with—and I assume you are as well in giving your own views about the uncertainty and the skewness around your forecast—is whether things have changed.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Is the skew large enough for us to argue that, in fact, the risks look unbalanced?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We thought about that and about the potential upside and downside risks.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Clearly, as I indicated, upside risks would be associated with ongoing increases in underlying prices for oil and other commodities that would probably feed through indirectly into core inflation over time.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the downside, we have been struck with how little upward pressure there has been on labor compensation and labor costs.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, if you pinned me down and said draw a fine line on this, I’d probably say that, given the pattern of the past few years, it would look to me as though there’s probably a little more upside risk than downside risk, but I don’t see that skewness as being material in the forecast.

speaker: FISHER
text: Nathan, both you and Dave expressed the frustration that I think all of us have about relying on futures markets in terms of our forecast of lower prices.

speaker: FISHER
text: It just hasn’t been very helpful.

speaker: FISHER
text: Do we know or have a sense of how OPEC itself forecasts?

speaker: FISHER
text: Do they just look at futures markets?

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, to what degree do you impute into your own calculations the income elasticity of demand for the rapidly growing countries such as China?

speaker: FISHER
text: We know it is above 1 on oil.

speaker: FISHER
text: Third, linking the two, to what degree would, say, the Saudi royal family or the al-Sabahs of Kuwait be thinking about those high income elasticities of demand with those high growth rates offsetting what used to be their fear of a slowdown in their markets?

speaker: FISHER
text: In 1978, for example, they had only three markets to sell into really: the United States, Japan, and what we used to call Western Europe.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now they have hedges against the weaknesses in those markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I’m wondering as we think about alternative ways to wrap our arms around this—and it is a very difficult thing as the current indicator we have has been shifting all over the place and has not been very useful—have we tried to learn how the swing producers look at this and how they calculate and think about where prices are likely to go or whether they just look at the futures markets as well?

speaker: SHEETS
text: It is, quite frankly, pretty tough to get a straight and compelling answer out of the OPEC folks about how they think about the oil markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: A number of us have sat in international meetings and listened to various explanations.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In fact, at one recent meeting in Basel, the representative from Saudi Arabia indicated that OPEC was not prepared to supply any more oil to the market because the market was already well supplied at the equilibrium price.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It is really quite frustrating.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now, what they say in these meetings is that their analysis of supply-and-demand fundamentals would suggest a price of $70 a barrel, $80 a barrel, or something like that.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Then they blame the residual on speculators and so on, and we spend a fair amount of time looking for such speculative effects in these oil prices, and we wouldn’t want to rule anything out.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I mean, from what we’ve seen, there may be an explanation out there that eludes us, but there are a number of things that we would expect to see if it were speculation—for instance, run-ups in inventories—that we don’t see.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We have also looked at the behavior of noncommercial traders, and it does not seem as though the noncommercial traders are actually predicting prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Quite the opposite—they seem to be chasing the price, which is quite different from what we would have expected.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Most recently, in a statement just this week, OPEC’s president linked the run-up in oil prices to the depreciation of the dollar and indicated that, for every 1 percent decline in the dollar, oil prices would rise $4.00 a barrel, which strikes us as being just absolutely extraordinary.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We can see 1 percent on the dollar moving oil prices 1 percent, but to get a coefficient beyond that just seems—I don’t want to say “economically impossible,” but I’d like to see the model that generates it.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now, about how they actually talk about oil prices behind closed doors, I don’t have any additional insight to provide other than what I’ve heard them say in some of these international meetings.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Certainly in our analysis we try to think through the outlook for demand from countries like China and India.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In fact, quite regularly we do a full-blown supply-and-demand balance exercise in which we say, “Here is the price.

speaker: SHEETS
text: What kind of supply-and-demand fundamentals would be necessary to deliver that price?” We use the IEA, the EIA, and others as input, but we actually do our own separate analyses.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We try to think very granularly about the demand from these emerging market countries and the implications that that has on the price.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As to the last part of your question, I think certainly it’s true, at least until recently, that there was a sense on the part of OPEC that, if they allowed the price to stay too high for too long, there would be a significant supply response that would end up driving the price back down.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now, the fact that they seem quite comfortable to live with the price of $115 or $120 a barrel suggests to me that maybe they have come to the conclusion that there is just more demand out there and, in some sense, they are going to ride the wave of this increasing demand in some of these emerging market economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That said, the prices have risen a lot.

speaker: SHEETS
text: They’re up 75 percent or 80 percent over the past year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: A year ago I’m sure that that’s not what my predecessor was forecasting, and it’s hard for me to imagine that we’re going to see oil at $200 a barrel.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, given the income and price elasticities of this thing, our view is that 1 percent greater global demand that’s not met by supply could very well push prices up at least 10 percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It isn’t going to take a whole lot of surprise on global demand to have a significant impact on prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As I said, I think that OPEC is aware of that and is willing to run the risk that there may be at some point a large supply response that could put significant downward pressure on the price of oil.

speaker: FISHER
text: Thank you for that long and thoughtful answer.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One, in comparing the staff’s forecast with a lot of the private-sector forecasts—what it looks like and its shape—one thing that is striking about the forecast is the very large adjustment swing that occurs in inventories.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My interpretation is that one thing that is occurring in the way you’ve made adjustments to your forecast—or maybe this is more of a question—is that the spending of the tax rebates appears to be occurring out of inventories.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Therefore, there is no production response, or less production response, to the presumably increasing demand that may materialize.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Can you give me some feeling about why you chose that way of treating this?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The second question goes back to inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I thought your discussion of the uncertainties around inflation was excellent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Part of what you talked about in the Greenbook was the uncertainty about pass-throughs of commodity price increases and oil price increases into various measures of consumer price inflation, which you indicated were imprecise and which we don’t really know much about.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was struck that, if there is more pass-through than the baseline says, we’re going to get more inflation in the near term, and then disinflation will be more rapid when you assume that commodity prices are going to come down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But if commodity prices only stabilize and don’t come down, then it’s going to be a more complicated picture.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You do have an alternative scenario that says that commodity prices keep rising, but you allow expectations to move up only fairly modestly in the model.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It seems to me that, particularly if expectations become more unanchored than that, the time paths of the funds rate that are implicit in the simulations become much more aggressive on the other side.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just want to make sure that my intuition is correct here.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Your intuition on that last point is correct.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, in that simulation we have inflation expectations deteriorate a little more from where we think they have deteriorated already over the past year or so.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, this is really hard to pin down, but we think there has probably been an increase of maybe ¼ percentage point in longer-term inflation expectations over the last couple of years in the context of this step-up in headline inflation and the higher commodity prices that are associated with that increase.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So in the simulation, we’re basically assuming that the process continues: If you have another year or two of high headline inflation, you may get additional deterioration of inflation expectations on the order of ¼ percentage point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: You’re right that, if expectations truly became unhinged and people began to view the entire inflation process as generating some greater upward momentum, it would have implications both for inflation and—

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A lot bigger than just the rise in expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: A lot bigger than just the rise in expectations, and the fed funds rate, of course, would have to rise considerably.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the inventory side of the forecast—again, you put your finger on the principal reason that inventories are as weak as they are in the near term, which is that we think there will be a pretty sizable spending response to the tax rebates but we don’t see that as showing up fully in activity in large measure because we think firms are going to understand that this will be a one-time increase in demand.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So they will be somewhat cautious about responding with higher production to that demand and will, especially in the context of a relatively weak economy, be more content with having that run down inventories than actually with ramping up production immediately.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, that’s guesswork on our part.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, I feel pretty comfortable with that basic story, but it is going to require some fairly negative inventory figures shortly.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There is a technical factor here as well.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have occasionally cited a residual seasonality in imports, and in the second quarter that residual seasonality pushes down imports a lot.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we see no residual seasonality in GDP, so we take it out of inventories.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That has been a standard feature of our forecast for the past few years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan and his crew have communicated quite frequently with the BEA complaining about the fact that they have a seasonal adjustment process that takes a relatively flat series and creates lots of noise.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It does not seem as though it is probably the best thing, but it exaggerates the downward movement in inventories.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If I had to cite something that would make me nervous about the weakness in our near-term outlook, I do worry that the inventory liquidation in our forecast is large.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The decline in the inventory–sales ratio in our forecast looks a lot like the decline in the inventory– sales ratio that we saw in 2001 and 2002.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So it’s not out of line with past cyclical behavior, but it’s an aggressive drop.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the theoretical literature there is a lot of discussion about inventory modeling now and what the appropriate way is to think about it.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think I can assure you that our models of inventory investment are not very good.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But they don’t take information and convert it into noise.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other questions for our colleagues?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Just to follow that up, Dave, how do you build your assumption on the spending response to the fiscal stimulus?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That was based on our reading of the literature, especially of the last episode of fiscal stimulus, which was associated with the rebate package in the earlier part of the decade.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’re assuming a marginal propensity to consume out of those rebates of about ½—that seems reasonably in line with what the literature suggests—and that they will be spent out over the next few quarters.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But, again, that’s based on one or two data points.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’re trying to draw some strong inferences from those data points, and it’s our best guess at this point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Another way to ask my question is, Given your assumptions about the fiscal policy stimulus and tax rebates, if I took the view that your estimate of spending was not really 50 cents, 40 cents, or 60 cents but really 10 cents—most of it will get saved and not spent—how would that affect your inventory assumptions and, therefore, the path over the next several quarters?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Roughly, we’re offsetting about half the spending through the inventory drawdown, so you could basically take that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If you took away a significant fraction of the spending, we’d take away a significant fraction of the inventory liquidation, and the GDP effects would be moderated considerably.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let’s start our go-round.

speaker: EVANS
text: I was pleasantly surprised that we have not had any major downside surprises since our March 18 meeting.

speaker: EVANS
text: So while I still recognize the economy’s downside risks, I’ve become less comfortable about signing onto the Greenbook’s judgment that a nonlinear step-down in activity currently is in train.

speaker: EVANS
text: On balance, our projection still looks for weakness in the near term and then has growth picking up as we move through 2008 and into 2009.

speaker: EVANS
text: We see a noticeable output gap opening this year but not one as large as in the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: Under this forecast, it is possible that some portion of 2008 might eventually be labeled a recession, but it is not yet conclusive that it will be.

speaker: EVANS
text: Indeed, given the highly unexpected development that events have proceeded as expected, I think the downside risks to growth have abated some.

speaker: EVANS
text: Some of the stress in financial markets has been mitigated by our new lending policies as well as actions by banks in recognizing losses and raising capital.

speaker: EVANS
text: Neither the incoming data nor the reports from my business contacts seem to be consistent with the bleak downside scenarios that I feared might transpire after we saw the December employment report early this year.

speaker: EVANS
text: In this regard, I will simply note a couple of observations from my contacts.

speaker: EVANS
text: A national shopping mall developer reported that his tenants experienced a small improvement in April retail sales compared with March.

speaker: EVANS
text: He was not expecting that.

speaker: EVANS
text: Similarly, Manpower indicated a small improvement in billable hours for temporary workers over the past month and a half, also unexpected.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, I am not saying that I will be surprised if the outlook deteriorates further.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am saying that the likelihood of that event seems to be smaller today than I expected at our last two meetings.

speaker: EVANS
text: Accordingly, I think that current real interest rates are appropriately accommodative relative to the baseline forecast for economic growth and the risk to that outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: As seen in chart 6 of the Bluebook, the real funds rate is essentially zero.

speaker: EVANS
text: Of course, this uses a core PCE measure of inflation and thus may overstate the true real rate since headline inflation has been consistently running above this core measure.

speaker: EVANS
text: There is the additional accommodation that is being provided by the range of new lending facilities we had put in place.

speaker: EVANS
text: The extra accommodation is appropriate to offset the large degree of restraint still being exerted from financial markets, and our expansion of the swap lines and the TAF adds to this accommodation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Furthermore, in the event of a nonlinear step-down in economic activity, as in the Greenbook forecast, our policy responses can be adjusted appropriately because we’re well positioned now for that.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the price side, on balance, the recent news has been good.

speaker: EVANS
text: My forecast has core PCE inflation falling to just under 2 percent in 2010 largely because of the increasing resource slack in the economy.

speaker: EVANS
text: However, I think there are substantial upside risks to this outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: All of my business contacts have noted how high and rising energy and commodity prices are creating cost pressures that many are passing on to their customers.

speaker: EVANS
text: As Dave Stockton mentioned, with his inflation catechism, without reviewing the past transcripts I will speculate that we have been projecting a leveling-out of energy prices since the price of oil was $70 a barrel.

speaker: EVANS
text: Weak domestic demand may limit the degree to which producers can pass through these higher costs, but it is unlikely to prevent noticeable increases in some downstream prices.

speaker: EVANS
text: The depreciation of the dollar also imposes risks even beyond the effects operating through the commodity price channel.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, I do agree that labor costs have not been cited as a problem for inflationary pressures, and so that does add somewhat to trimming out the risks there.

speaker: EVANS
text: Inflation expectations were also an issue.

speaker: EVANS
text: No matter how often we say that core inflation is a more reliable measure of underlying inflationary tendencies, I find it difficult to believe that the public’s inflationary expectations will not be affected by large and persistent increases in food and energy prices.

speaker: EVANS
text: The past five years have been unkind on this score.

speaker: EVANS
text: On average over this time, higher food and energy prices have pushed total inflation above core about ½ percentage point, and it is also sizable over the past ten years.

speaker: EVANS
text: Another challenge for inflationary expectations comes from our policy focus on the downside risks to growth during a time of rising headline inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Rightly or not, this could make the public question our attitudes toward inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: We are accepting considerable inflationary risks when we hope that these concerns will disappear quickly with future adjustments to policy that have not yet been signaled.

speaker: EVANS
text: How we balance these conflicting risks should be an important component of our discussion tomorrow.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the Third District, there has been little change in economic activity since I reported in March.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Business activity remained weak over the intermeeting period but no more or less than anticipated and than we reported in our March meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Manufacturing activity, residential construction, and employment remained modestly weak in the District.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Retail sales were also sluggish.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our staff’s coincident indicators of economic activity, which summarize our regional data, show a decline in activity in Pennsylvania and Delaware but moderate growth in New Jersey in March and, on average, for the last three months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Overall, our firms are not very upbeat about near- term growth; and like many forecasters, they have revised downward their expectations since the start of the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: For example, in response to a special question in our business outlook survey, the number of manufacturers saying that current demand for their products fell short of what they had expected at the start of the year exceeded those who had underestimated demand.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: More firms have decreased their capital spending plans, with 10 percent indicating that they either delayed capital spending or postponed it indefinitely.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While growth in the District has been weak, price pressures facing our firms and consumers have intensified.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Area manufacturers continue to report higher production costs, and the percentage of firms raising prices on finished goods is larger than earlier in the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The indexes of prices paid and prices received are near 20-year highs for our firms, and firms expect to see prices move higher over the next six months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: These firms have a very pessimistic outlook for inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Turning to the national outlook, I have revised down my growth forecast from what I submitted in January, as almost all of us have, but that revision occurred largely between January and March.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There has been little or no change in my outlook since our March meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Compared with my January forecast, I now see real GDP growth coming in around 1.5 percent for 2008 and close to 2.6 to 2.8 percent in 2009–10.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Overall, this is about ½ percentage point weaker for ’08 than my January forecast, but there is little difference in my forecast for ’09 and ’10.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The indicators that have come in since our last meeting have generally been in line with my March outlook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Certainly they have pointed to continued weakness, but not worse than I had expected.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although some strains in the interbank markets remain, they do not appear to have intensified, and our alphabet soup of targeted tools seems to be having at least modest beneficial effect, even if only psychologically.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I remain concerned, however, about inflation and our calibration of the appropriate level of the fed funds rate consistent with our goals.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation readings have abated marginally since our last meeting; but as the Greenbook suggests, there is reason to believe that this is a temporary reprieve and that the levels remained elevated—year-over-year CPI inflation was 4 percent in March, and year-over-year PCE inflation was 3.4 percent—well above their 2007 levels.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As we have been noting, oil and other commodity prices continue to move up, and businesses and consumers continue to stress inflation as a concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Near-term measures of inflation expectations have risen sharply.

speaker: PLOSSER
