text: In the Michigan survey, one-year inflation expectations rose to 4.8 percent in April, up from 4.3 percent in March and 3.4 percent in December.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Clearly, the greater media attention on inflation and the discussion among the public are bound to have some effect on expectations as time goes on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have some concerns and difficulty interpreting the measure in TIPS given the disruptions in financial markets right now.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I take those with a little grain of salt.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nevertheless, five-year, five-year-ahead inflation compensation is 2.8 percent using the Board’s measure.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is down a little from early March but is still higher than it was at the end of 2007.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, the instability of these measures of inflation expectations itself is a cause of concern for me.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It may suggest that markets question our willingness to take actions consistent with sustained and credible price stability.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, we have often alluded to the idea that near-term weakness will help mitigate some of the inflation pressures.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, I would just like to remind us that this critically depends on inflation expectations remaining well anchored.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I hope that going forward we can reinforce that conditionality of the statement about weakness helping us on the inflation side so that we do not perpetuate the notion that a stable Phillips curve is at work here and that a slowing economy will always lower inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe that the FOMC’s commitment to price stability remains credible at this time, but just barely.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I worry that we may be resting too much on our laurels, trying to talk a good game, but unwilling to take the actions necessary to support and sustain that credibility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I have said before in this group, we must not wait until expectations have broken out because by then it will be too late.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation has been well above at least our implicit goal for a sustained period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As the Bluebook points out, core PCE inflation has been above 2 percent since 2004 every year, and is projected to be so again this year, and the projections are even worse for headline numbers, either CPI or PCE.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we continue easing or maintaining a real funds rate well below zero for a sustained period despite inflation well above our goal, can we really expect inflation expectations to remain anchored?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Greenbook seems to think that we can.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It assumes that the fed funds rate falls to 1.75 percent in June and remains there through the end of 2009.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given the inflation forecast, this means a negative or close to negative real funds rate for almost two years.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite this, Greenbook baseline inflation expectations remain reasonably contained, and inflation is projected to decline over the forecast period even as growth picks up toward trend.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To put it kindly, I have serious reservations about that scenario.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Greenbook discusses an alternative simulation in which there is greater inflationary pressure.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The estimated Taylor rule funds path in that is somewhat steeper than in the baseline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation ends up higher at the end of the forecast period—the end of 2011 and 2012—than in the baseline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: More progress on inflation will require obviously a steeper path, but even in this alternative simulation, inflation expectations only drift up.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They do not become unhinged.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If they did, I would expect the policy path to have to be considerably tighter in 2009.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, I know that talking about money in the context of monetary policy is not very fashionable these days.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I would like to note that the monetary aggregates as measured by M2 and MZM have exploded.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite the flight to quality and the associated increase in the demand for money associated with that, M2 grew less than 5 percent during the fourth quarter of 2007.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Since then, however, its growth rate has nearly tripled.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In January it grew 8 percent on an annualized basis.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In February after our rate cuts, it grew 18 percent, and in March it grew 13 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Growth rates of MZM are even worse over this interval—for the three months the annual rates were 14, 42, and 26 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Such rates suggest to me that there is substantial liquidity in the economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While I don’t really like the old P* model and have had a lot of problems with it, at the back of the Greenbook the story it is telling is one of considerable inflation over the next couple of years.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Combined, the growth in the aggregates, the substantially negative real interest rates, and the fact that most versions of the Taylor rule call for a higher fed funds rate than we have currently heighten my angst about the outlook for inflation and our credibility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Market participants reacted to the incoming data by appreciably tightening their policy expectations—at least as implied by the futures markets, as Bill Dudley pointed out—and that has had a negligible effect, certainly no negative effect, on markets or the economy more broadly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One interpretation is that the market participants have also become uncomfortable, as I have, with a fed funds rate that remains too low for too long.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I take this as a healthy sign actually and one that we shouldn’t ignore.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, we may just wish to use it to our advantage.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I will stop there, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In looking at the latest Blue Chip forecasts for GDP growth, I noted that the range between the highest and lowest is among the largest on record.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The 10 most optimistic forecasters are predicting over 2½ percentage points faster Q4-over-Q4 growth than the 10 most pessimistic ones.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Such forecast dispersion is indicative of the unusually high degree of uncertainty that we are facing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The Greenbook presents one of the most pessimistic economic forecasts; yet I find its recessionary projection quite plausible and see downside risks that could take the economy well below that forecast.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although I found it especially difficult this time to decide on the most likely outcome for the economy, I ended up submitting a forecast that shows somewhat more growth in 2008 than the Greenbook, even though we shared the same assumption concerning monetary policy this year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My forecast projects 2008 growth of ¾ percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This averages no growth in the first half and 1½ percent growth in the second.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The unemployment rate increases to just over 5½ percent by the end of this year, a bit lower than the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In one critical area—namely, the adverse effects of financial sector developments on the real economy—I remain just as pessimistic as the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although the likelihood of a severe financial panic has diminished, the risks are by no means behind us.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Moreover, credit conditions have turned quite restrictive.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This credit crunch reflects the drying up of financing both for markets that were important sources of business and consumer credit and from banks that are contending with capital-depleting losses and illiquid assets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Among banks, the latest Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey noted a clear tightening of lending standards, and my own discussions with bankers confirmed this point.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They say they are carefully reassessing and significantly curtailing existing home equity lines of credit as well as unsecured consumer loans of all sorts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Banks are also clamping down on the provision of revolving business credit, even to very creditworthy customers.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, the treasurer of Chevron, a highly rated oil company that, as you can guess given energy prices, has a very strong profit outlook, recently complained to me that banks were reluctant to extend even its credit line.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Such reluctance is also evident for lending to students, consumers, and other businesses.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The risk of a deepening credit crunch remains as a weak economy—especially with further sharp declines in housing prices—escalates credit losses, harms financial institution balance sheets, and causes them to scale back lending even further.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My sense from our business contacts is that their perception of reduced access to credit is causing them to manage their firm’s liquidity more carefully and is leading to some deferrals in capital spending projects as a precautionary measure.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Certainly the mood is decidedly more pessimistic and cautious.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Amid the gloom of the credit crunch, I do see a possible silver lining in that it may amplify the effects of the fiscal stimulus package, and this is part of the reason that my forecasted downturn is a little milder than the Greenbook’s.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In particular, because of the credit and liquidity considerations, the latest fiscal package could well provide a bigger bang for the buck than the tax rebates in 2001.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, the current tax rebates are more directly targeted at lower-income households, which are more likely to be credit constrained and to spend the cash once it’s in hand.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Second, given the current tightening of credit availability, households will likely spend an even greater fraction of the tax rebates than they did in 2001.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, there is considerable uncertainty about assessing the potential size of these effects.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But over the next few months as the checks go out and the retail sales reports come in, we should get a pretty quick preliminary read on how things are shaping up.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Regarding inflation, the most worrying developments since we met in March have been the price surges for a wide variety of raw materials and commodities, especially the jump in the price of crude oil.

speaker: YELLEN
text: From the U.S. perspective, this run-up in prices represents mainly a classic supply shock, which could threaten both parts of our dual mandate, although the decline in the dollar has slightly exacerbated the severity of the impact.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Like the Greenbook, my forecast for inflation does take commodity price futures at face value and foresees a leveling-out of prices going forward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although I must say, after four years of being wrong, I am beginning to feel like Charlie Brown trying to kick that football.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The most recent core consumer price data have shown some improvement, and like the Greenbook, I’m optimistic that core inflation will subside to around 1¾ percent over the forecast period, assuming that the commodity prices do finally level off and compensation remains well behaved.

speaker: YELLEN
text: An interesting analysis by Bart Hobijn of the New York Fed as well as my own staff implies that, in an accounting sense, pass-through from the run-up in oil and crop prices may have boosted core inflation as much as 0.3 percentage point over the past two years.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So a leveling-off of these prices could lower not only headline but also core inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My core PCE inflation forecast is a tenth or two lower than the Greenbook this year and next also because we assume lower pass- through of the dollar depreciation to non-oil import prices.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have been reexamining the data on this issue and find the evidence quite convincing that pass-through has been quite low recently— lower, for example, than embodied in the FRB/US model.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to inflation expectations, market-based measures have now edged down.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We took little comfort from this fact, however, because we had viewed the uptick in inflation compensation in recent months mainly as a reflection of a higher inflation risk premium and not a reflection of higher inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am also somewhat concerned that the median expectation for inflation over the next five to ten years in the Michigan survey has ticked up.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I want to focus my comments today on what I have heard from my CEO contacts.

speaker: FISHER
text: With regard to my District, it continues to do well relative to the rest of the country, but it is not immune to the pathology that is afflicting the overall economy.

speaker: FISHER
text: Although still positive, economic growth and employment creation are slowing, and our manufacturers in the survey we just took are experiencing substantial price pressures.

speaker: FISHER
text: Seventy-one percent of our manufacturers in the survey report higher prices, and 65 percent are expecting input prices to be even higher six months from now.

speaker: FISHER
text: Setting aside the 11th District, I spoke in depth to 31 CEOs nationwide.

speaker: FISHER
text: You have that list, Mr. Chairman, and I would like to speak to what I deduced from triangulating those conversations with what I read in the Bluebook and the Greenbook.

speaker: FISHER
text: Let me note that the focus of my conversations with these CEOs and CFOs was not what they have seen or what they are seeing now but how their behavior is likely to be affected going forward and how they are budgeting going forward.

speaker: FISHER
text: Distilling the inputs to their essence, it’s clear that activity is likely to weaken further.

speaker: FISHER
text: Those 21 miles of 89-foot flat cars that haul lumber, Mr. Chairman, are now up to 22.6 miles.

speaker: FISHER
text: Inventories of unsold homes are clearly building, and that is important against the background that March is almost always a good month in the housing or home sales business.

speaker: FISHER
text: The CEO of Centex reports that this is the first down March he has seen, and he has been in the business since 1974.

speaker: FISHER
text: It came down hard—20 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: Companies are tightening their head counts.

speaker: FISHER
text: Banks are tightening credit standards, as we have discussed.

speaker: FISHER
text: According to the CEO of MasterCard, year-over-year retail sales to date in April—that is, ex-autos and ex-gas—were 2.2 percent, the lowest he has ever seen.

speaker: FISHER
text: Citibank, Chase, Bank of America, and the other credit card purveyors are experiencing high delinquency rates and a significant slowdown in their revenues from credit cards, and Wal-Mart reports the “cascading” use of credit as a form of payment, as their CEO for U.S. operations put it.

speaker: FISHER
text: In short, the consumer-driven corrective credit cycle is prolonging the economic slowdown and vice versa.

speaker: FISHER
text: Consistent with this sustained headwind, we have revised downward the Dallas forecast and continued for longer our projection of economic “anemia” (we are not among the four that included the word “recession”) not only for ’08 but also for ’09, and we have revised upward, to the upper end, our sense of projected unemployment.

speaker: FISHER
text: Thus, from what I am hearing, from what I am reading, and from what we are getting from our analysis, I acknowledge the thesis of the presence of a negative feedback loop among GDP growth, employment growth, and credit market conditions.

speaker: FISHER
text: I find more worrisome the reports I am receiving on expected price developments and behavior, and I see a feedback loop of another kind at work.

speaker: FISHER
text: Page 30 of the Bluebook notes, as I think President Plosser pointed out and President Evans referred to, that core PCE inflation has averaged more than 2 percent in every year since 2004 and is forecasted, as per David’s earlier comments, as doing so again in 2008.

speaker: FISHER
text: What concerns me more is the left-hand panel in chart 1 on page 4 of the Bluebook that indicates that the staff’s index of inflation expectations and uncertainty is now at the top of its range over the last decade.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is confirmed by my corporate contacts.

speaker: FISHER
text: Something persistent and pernicious, Mr. Chairman, has been occurring on the inflation front and calling into question the credibility of our continued reliance on core measures.

speaker: FISHER
text: Here is what I am hearing from my corporate contacts.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m going to just mention a few because it is fairly consistent across the board.

speaker: FISHER
text: From the CEO of the largest retailer in the country, not to be named but located in Arkansas, [laughter] I reported last time that they are budgeting price increases on 10,000 items of a little over 5 percent in 2008.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet his comment to me was, “Inflation is our number 1 concern, and it’s escalating significantly.” He added, “All the information we have points to an intermediate- and longer-term supply–demand problem, especially for food and any energy-dependent articles.” By the way, that was verified by the CEO of Frito-Lay, who tells me that they are offsetting their input price escalation of 11 percent in 2008 by raising prices 9 percent effective last Sunday.

speaker: FISHER
text: He added that—and this is interesting in terms of the mindset—“We have to—otherwise we’ll disappoint the Street, and in these markets no one can afford at this fragile time to do so.” The price pressures are less for clothing and nonfood items, but they are still there.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would like to use the example of JCPenney.

speaker: FISHER
text: JCPenney sells clothing to one-half of all the families in America, and 60 percent of their sales are apparel.

speaker: FISHER
text: The average price point for an apparel sale at that retailer is $15.

speaker: FISHER
text: The leading source of apparel is China.

speaker: FISHER
text: According to Penney’s CEO, increases in China’s labor costs, changes in their labor rules, and the cost of fuel and of cotton fibers have led to significantly escalating price pressures.

speaker: FISHER
text: He says that they can eat some of those costs and drive them down through other offsets and tighter controls, but they are planning a 4 percent increase in apparel costs in 2009.

speaker: FISHER
text: Here is his punch line, and it is not funny—this is a first-rate CEO, one of the best in the country: “We think the customer can take a little more price.

speaker: FISHER
text: After all, what’s 40 to 60 cents on $15?

speaker: FISHER
text: It won’t even be noticed.” This is the essence of the accommodation of inflationary expectations, and you are beginning to see this mentality set in in several industries.

speaker: FISHER
text: We talked about the increase in the price of crude.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you take what is called the crack spread and figure out what has happened in terms of jet fuel, year over year through mid-April jet fuel was up 70 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s an industry average, mitigated somewhat by the hedging of Southwest Airlines, which has been successful.

speaker: FISHER
text: According to the CEO of American Airlines, “This oil is a tsunami.

speaker: FISHER
text: We will have to get some pricing power, or we’ll be left with only one airline, Southwest.” Kimberly-Clark, a paper producer, notices that the weaker dollar and oil are driving realized costs increasingly up from, in their case, $250 million in ’07 to an estimated $600 million in ’08.

speaker: FISHER
text: They have raised prices, as I have previously mentioned, but the CEO feels that—and this is a winner—“We are having to learn how to run a business in an inflationary environment.

speaker: FISHER
text: We got used to productivity as the driver, but we can’t drive productivity any harder than we can.

speaker: FISHER
text: We will need more pricing.” It even affects semiconductor producers.

speaker: FISHER
text: Texas Instruments reports that the weakness of the dollar and the prices of energy, gold, and copper offset by their hedges added 2½ percent non- annualized to their costs in the first quarter.

speaker: FISHER
text: Asked what he envisions going forward, the CFO said, “Well, that just means we can’t spend it elsewhere.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have to take it out of our employees’ backs or out of cap-ex.” One CEO of a company that is expecting soon to lay off between 12,000 and 15,000 people and is, therefore, carefully surveying the attitudes of their employees because they have a morale problem, is finding out that employees are tapping into their 401(k) plans or not funding them.

speaker: FISHER
text: In their surveys they find the leading complaint is that “the price of gasoline and food is eating into my living standards.

speaker: FISHER
text: I can’t afford them.” Last but not least, just to bring this home, the Eagle Scout who mows my lawn in Dallas sent me a very nice, beautiful letter.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is clear that he and his mother had prepared it on a printer and put a fancy title on it, but the rest of the letter was, “Dear Mr. Fisher, I have to levy a 7 percent fuel surcharge.” We gave into it—he is a nice boy.

speaker: FISHER
text: In summary, Mr. Chairman, while there are many who have voiced concern with the adverse feedback loop that runs from the economy to tighter credit conditions and back to the economy, I am very troubled by a different adverse feedback loop—namely, the inflation dynamic whereby reductions in fed funds rates lead to a weaker dollar and upward pressures on global commodity prices, which feed through to higher U.S. inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: That higher U.S. inflation not only has a price impact but also leads to cutbacks by consumers and by employers so as to offset the effects of inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am worried that, if we do not respond to higher inflation, the whole cycle will intensify.

speaker: FISHER
text: When economic growth and activity return to normal, inflation is likely to have notched up considerably, according to our sense.

speaker: FISHER
text: I know my respected colleagues say that we are willing to be equally aggressive in raising rates once the outlook for real activity improves, but the practicability of that notion I find in talking to my interlocutors is met with some skepticism and doubt.

speaker: FISHER
text: With that, Mr. Chairman, I see a tail risk on the downside of growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: I acknowledge the argument of President Yellen and others.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think I’m sympathetic, but I see a fatter tail, perhaps an otter’s tail, on inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am hearing this loud and clear from my corporate contacts.

speaker: FISHER
text: I believe that the risk posed by inflation is more significant than the extension of further anemia in the economy, especially now that we have put in place innovative liquidity bridging mechanisms, which we are amplifying upon today.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, the other day Governor Kohn reminded me that reasonable people can disagree, and he quipped that he hoped that we could agree on the following—that we are at least reasonable people.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m doing my very best, I hope, to provide reasonable alternative perspectives, and I hope you will judge me on that basis.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Without judgmental adjustments, the Boston Fed forecast is somewhat more optimistic than the Greenbook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As in the Greenbook, our GDP is weak in the first half of this year, though neither of the first two quarters actually turns negative.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Our slightly more optimistic forecast assumes that consumption and business fixed investment are weak, but not as weak as in the Greenbook, and then the fiscal and monetary stimuli are sufficient for the economy to pick up in the second half of this year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In a sense, the Greenbook represents another mode in the forecast distribution with probability roughly equal to our forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The big risk to our forecast is that the financial turmoil and housing price declines, which are not fully reflected in the Boston model, result in a greater drag on the economy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Such an outcome would largely close the gap between the Greenbook and our forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In short, the downside risks to our forecast are appreciable.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With a monetary policy assumption similar to the Greenbook’s, we have core PCE below 2 percent in 2009, but the unemployment rate remains well above the NAIRU even at the end of 2010.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we sought to keep inflation below 2 percent but did not want an extended period in which the unemployment rate was above the NAIRU, our model would require more easing than currently assumed in the Greenbook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Since the last meeting, the economic data have remained weak.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Private payroll employment declined by approximately 100,000 jobs on average over the past three months, and the unemployment rate increased 0.3 percentage point.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In addition, the labor market weakness was widespread across industries.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Such labor market weakness is likely to aggravate an already troubling housing story.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: To date, falling housing prices have disproportionately affected subprime borrowers and those who purchased securitized products.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, if housing prices continue to decline rapidly, that will begin to affect more prime borrowers and a wide array of financial institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Smaller financial institutions that were largely unaffected by the financial turmoil last August are beginning to see increases in delinquencies, and those with outsized exposures in construction loans are now experiencing significant duress.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Commercial real estate loans are also now experiencing increased delinquencies.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Like the Greenbook, I am concerned that commercial real estate may be the next sector to experience problems.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, the biggest concern remains that rising delinquencies and falling housing prices cause a much higher rate of mortgage defaults than we have experienced historically.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Should these mounting problems become more pronounced, we are likely to see credit availability for small- and medium-sized businesses affected.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That sector has not to date been significantly affected by the financial turmoil.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Many financial indicators have improved since the last meeting, as was highlighted in Bill’s report.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The stock market has moved up.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Many credit spreads have narrowed.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Treasury securities and repurchase agreements are trading in more-normal ranges, and credit default swaps for many financial firms have improved.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Nonetheless, several ominous trends remain in financial markets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The LIBOR–OIS spread has widened, so borrowers tied to LIBOR rates have seen those rates rise more than 25 basis points since the last meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Similarly, the TAF stop-out rate in the last three auctions was higher than the primary credit rate, providing another indicator that banks remain in need of dollar term funds.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Finally, the asset-backed commercial paper market is once again experiencing difficulties.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Rates on asset-backed commercial paper have been rising, and there is a risk that more of the paper will end up on bank balance sheets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Higher food and energy prices are both a drag on the economy and a cause for concern with inflation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But despite the extended sequence of supply shocks, I do not see evidence that inflation expectations are no longer anchored.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Labor markets do not indicate that the commodity price increases are causing wage pressures, and such pressures are even less likely if the unemployment rate continues to increase.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Many of the financial indicators of inflation, such as the five-year-forward rate, have fallen significantly from their peaks earlier this year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Finally, core PCE over the past year has been 2 percent, and most econometric-based forecasts expect that the weakness we are experiencing should result in core and total PCE inflation at or below 2 percent next year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Overall, the downside risks to demand that I listed in the outset seem the more compelling cause for concern.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Our high-level view of current circumstances is that the real economy is quite weak, with weakness widespread.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The financial markets are turning optimistic, and elevated prices and inflation remain a serious concern.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Reports from our directors and District business contacts were broadly similar to the incoming national data and information from other Districts reported in the Beige Book.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Observations from such District input support themes in the national data—for example, employment growth is quite weak.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In this round of director reports and conversations, I heard an increasing number of reports of holds on hiring and expansion plans.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One representative of a major retailer of home improvement goods reported that hiring for seasonal employees will be down 40 percent this spring.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This translates to approximately 45,000 jobs.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Nonresidential real estate development continues to slow in the District, especially in Florida and Georgia.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Of the 18 commercial contractors contacted in April, 15 expect that commercial construction will be weaker for the rest of 2008 than for the same period in 2007, with several predicting even more pronounced weakness in 2009.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On the brighter side, Florida Realtors are anticipating that sales over the next few months will exceed year-ago levels, and builders are signaling less weakness than in recent reports.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This is a level of optimism we have not heard from Florida for some time.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, housing markets in the rest of the District continue to weaken.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We heard several complaints that obtaining financing is a serious problem for commercial and residential developers and consumer homebuyers.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In sum, the information from the Sixth District seems to confirm what I believe is the continuing story of the national real economy captured in the Greenbook—that is, shrinking net job creation, developing weakness in nonresidential construction, and a bottom in the housing market still not in sight.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In contrast, conditions in the financial markets appear to have improved substantially.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As has been my practice, I had several conversations with contacts in a variety of financial firms.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There was a consistent tone suggesting that financial markets are likely to have seen the worst.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This does not mean that no concerns were expressed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Some contacts had concerns about European banks and credit markets, and concern about the value of the dollar, notwithstanding the recent rally, is coming up in more contexts.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Concern was expressed about the dollar’s disruptive effect on commodity markets, in turn affecting the general price level—in particular, the effect of high energy prices on a wide spectrum of businesses’ consumer products and even on crime rates in rural and far suburban areas related to the theft of copper wiring and piping from vacant homes and air conditioning units.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I worry that a narrative is developing along the lines that the ECB is concerned about inflation and the Fed not so much.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This narrative encourages a dollar carry trade mentioned, again, by some financial contacts that puts downside pressure on the dollar that potentially undermines both growth and inflation objectives.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I remain concerned about the vulnerability of financial markets to a shock or surprise, but overall, my contacts express the belief that conditions are improving.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The Atlanta forecast submission sees flat real GDP growth in the first half of 2008, with gradual improvement in the second half.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We continue to believe that the drag on economic activity from the problems in the housing and credit markets will persist into 2009.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On the inflation front, I am still projecting a decline in the rate of inflation over this year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’ve submitted forecasts of declining headline inflation in 2009 and 2010, but I should note that my staff’s current projections suggest that improvement to the degree I would like to see may require some rises in the federal funds rate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is my current judgment that, with an additional 25 basis point reduction in the fed funds rate target, policy will be appropriately calibrated to the gradual recovery of growth and the lowering of the inflation level envisioned in our forecast.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This judgment is based on the view that, with a negative real funds rate by some measures, policy is in stimulative territory; that a lower cost of borrowing in support of growth depends more on market-driven tightening of credit spreads than a lower policy rate; that further cuts may contribute to unhelpful movements in the dollar exchange rate; and that extension of the four liquidity facilities may allow us to decouple liquidity actions from the fed funds rate target.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my view, we are in a zone of diminishing returns from further funds rate cuts beyond a possible quarter in this meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That said, as stated in the Greenbook, uncertainty surrounding the outlook for the real economy is very high, and the Committee needs, in my view, to preserve flexibility to deal with unanticipated developments.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The economy of the Eighth District continues to show signs of weakness.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The services sector has continued to soften, and sales of both general and big box retailers are down from the same period last year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The residential real estate sector has continued to decline throughout the District.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Across major metro areas, sales were about 15 percent below the level from last year, and single-family permits were down about 30 percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Employment growth has slowed and is estimated to have turned negative in March for many areas.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Typically, however, employment growth in the District has been stronger than that for the United States as a whole.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Manufacturing has remained roughly flat, despite temporary shutdowns that have affected domestic automobile production.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, commercial real estate construction remains strong, and vacancy rates are low; however, there are increases in the number of delayed projects.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Banks in the District are still in good shape, generally speaking.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There have been modest increases in total loans in all categories, including real estate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Contacts in the shipping and trucking industries reported a mixed bag.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In some instances, business seems to be holding up, whereas in others it is down substantially.

speaker: BULLARD
text: These businesses are being critically affected by increases in energy prices.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Similarly, a contact in the fast food industry painted a picture of a business struggling with substantial increases in commodity prices.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the other hand, a contact in a large technology firm indicated that business is holding up quite well, in part because a large fraction of this firm’s business is overseas.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Contacts in the energy sector reported robust business prospects, as expected.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A contact at a large financial firm suggested that the discovery process concerning asset-backed securities, which has been ongoing for many months, has effectively come to a close.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The idea that the discovery process—and the considerable macroeconomic uncertainty that attended that process—is over is an important consideration at this juncture.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My sense is that expectations of future economic performance are changing rapidly.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The probability that the U.S. economy will enter into a debilitating depression-like state has fallen dramatically.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In the meantime, other risks have increased markedly—in particular, that the FOMC will lose credibility with respect to its inflation goals.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The U.S. economy has certainly encountered a large shock.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Monetary policy can mitigate the effects of a large shock but cannot be expected to completely offset exceptional disturbances.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Attempts to do too much may create more and more- dangerous problems in the future.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Best-practice monetary policy would do well, it seems to me, to avoid setting the stage for future problems.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The problems with the rate structure, which is too low, are threefold.

speaker: BULLARD
text: First, there is the risk of setting up a new bubble.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The exceptionally low rates of a few years ago are sometimes cited as providing fuel for today’s problems.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Some have argued that today’s commodity price increases are exactly that new bubble.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Second, continued unabated reductions in interest rates will bring the zero bound issue into play with unknown consequences.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Third, still lower rates will push the envelope further on inflationary expectations.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Those expectations may appear to be reasonably well anchored today, but that is because the private sector expects us to take actions to keep inflation low and stable.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Should those expectations become unmoored, it will be too late, and an era of higher and more volatile inflation would be very costly for American households.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Much has been done already.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A low rate environment has been created and has been in place only for a short time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Marginal moves at this juncture are minor compared with the general thrust of policy over the last nine months.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The Committee would do much better at this meeting by taking steps to address eroding credibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a break for coffee and return at 4:45.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Pianalto, whenever you are ready.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Regardless to whom I talk with these days, the conversation quickly turns to both the fragile condition of financial markets and the spectacular rise in energy and commodity prices.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I had hoped that one of these problems would have gone away by now, but clearly that is not how conditions have unfolded since our last meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The bankers with whom I talked are paying close attention to their capital and liquidity positions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: They remain concerned about wide bid–asked spreads and low trading volumes in a broad array of securities markets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Indeed, the repercussions of financial turmoil appear to have touched every channel of credit intermediation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: It appears that a rewiring of credit channels is simply going to take some time to work out.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The most significant financial news coming out of the Fourth District is the $7 billion investment of new capital into National City Bank.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: National City is the country’s tenth largest commercial bank, and its problems with mortgage-related credits are now well known.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: National City still has much work to do to clean up its balance sheet, just as many other financial institutions with impaired capital positions must do before they can stand on solid ground again.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Although the fragile state of the financial sector represents a pretty sizable risk to my economic outlook, the National City situation, along with other stories I’m hearing, suggests that modest progress is being made.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: With regard to District business conditions, the stories I hear remain downbeat.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Commercial builders are reporting mixed though generally positive first-quarter numbers.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But their expectations for retail sales in the stores that they lease out across the country have deteriorated, and they are fairly pessimistic about 2008 growth prospects.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: One large national commercial developer whom I talked with told me that, for the first time in his 45-year career, his company has seen sales declines in March in every retail center that they own across the country.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The manufacturers I talked with indicated moderate first-quarter revenue growth as export markets, especially in Asia and Eastern Europe, are still helping to sustain production despite weak domestic demand.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At the same time, manufacturers report intense commodity price pressures, and they report little resistance as they attempt to pass along the rising cost of commodities to their customers.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The projection I submitted for this meeting shows real GDP growth under 1 percent in 2008, with virtually all of that growth coming in the second half of the year.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This is a decidedly more pessimistic projection than the one I submitted in January but not materially different from the outlook when we met just six weeks ago.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I have, however, boosted my headline inflation projection for 2008 compared with what I submitted in January, and it is somewhat higher than what I was estimating when we met in mid-March.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Although I am still projecting that the slack in the economy will be sufficient to bring the core inflation number under the 2 percent threshold sometime next year, I am now anticipating a little more pass-through of commodity prices into core measures than I thought probable six weeks ago.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Indeed, every time I see commodity prices ratcheting up, I become less confident that slack alone will be able to prevent an upward drift in the inflation trend.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: To be clear, I think the downside risks that we face in the real economy remain substantial, and I am inclined to believe that some insurance against those risks is probably warranted.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But in taking such a step, I am inclined to judge that the downside risks we face in the real economy will be roughly in balance with the upside risks that we face from a rising inflation trend.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Economic activity continues to be slow in the Tenth District with a soft tone in our residential and nonresidential construction and certainly in our retail sales.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mitigating this weakness, however, to some extent is continued strength in energy and agriculture exports and, to a lesser degree, manufacturing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: With regard to exports, one interesting development is a shortage of shipping containers domestically and internationally that is limiting the volume of exports of both our agricultural and some of our manufacturing products.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On balance though, the District activity continues to be stronger than the national economy, and this is reflected in better employment growth and firm labor markets in many parts of our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In my recent discussions with directors at our Bank and in our Branches and the Economic Advisory Council members, several themes have been prominent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Concern about inflation has escalated to the highest level I’ve been involved with in the last decade.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Businesses across the board are experiencing the largest input cost pressures in recent memory for them.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Many businesses have not been able to absorb these cost pressures and have raised prices to both retail and business customers, and generally speaking, businesses are finding much less resistance to price increases than in the past.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Businesses also report that suppliers are increasingly reluctant to make contractual price quotes very far in the future.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have also been monitoring the effects of credit availability on business capital spending in our area.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Although businesses report some tightening of credit conditions, credit costs and availability are not the primary factors behind reduced capital spending plans.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Bank loans have actually continued to grow.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Instead, businesses cite uncertainty about the economic outlook as the main impediment to investment.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They are in a wait-and-see mode.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So spending is being held back not for financial reasons but just caution.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Indeed, they suggest that uncertainty about whether monetary policy will be eased further is a factor currently inhibiting their capital spending plans.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They want to see when we’re done.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to the broader economic output and the national economy, I have revised down my growth estimate for the first half of 2008 but have had few changes to my longer-term outlook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Compared with the Greenbook, I see somewhat stronger growth this year and somewhat weaker growth next year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Weaker growth in the first half of this year is coming largely from the effects of higher energy prices on consumer and business spending coupled with the continued weakness in residential construction.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would say that the effect of high energy prices is now about as large as or even larger than the contraction in residential construction, and I think that the energy outlook constitutes a main downside risk to growth in the period ahead.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In contrast—and contrary to the Greenbook and the views of some—I think that energy and housing perhaps now more than credit problems are holding back economic growth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Certainly credit conditions have continued to tighten as reflected in the April Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey, and markets for many asset-backed securities, of course, have shut down.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But the availability of credit for good business and household borrowers does not appear to have really been restricted that much.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They are pricing more wisely for risk, and that is probably a positive.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Consequently, the downside economic risks from a pronounced credit contraction appear to have diminished considerably over the past few months.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I want to turn to inflation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In my view, the inflation outlook has worsened considerably.

speaker: HOENIG
text: For the first time in many years, we are seeing significant inflation pressure from goods prices, especially imported goods prices.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Moreover, the recent moderation in monthly inflation numbers is coming mainly from some softness in service prices, which in my opinion, is unlikely to continue.

speaker: HOENIG
text: More optimistic views of inflation, including those in the Greenbook, rely heavily on economic slack and a turnaround in food and energy prices to improve the outlook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am skeptical on both counts.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I do not think that there will be as much slack generated in the current slowdown as does the Greenbook, and there is evidence that the effects of output and employment gaps on inflation have fallen, well, actually more than a little over the past two decades.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Furthermore, I have not seen any indication that elevated energy and food price inflation is likely to dissipate soon, as many of these pressures are reflective of international economic developments that we have talked about here, including the weakness in the dollar.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I believe that we are entering a dangerous period, if I can use that word, in which inflation expectations are beginning to move higher and inflation psychology is becoming more prominent in business decisions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In this regard, I also do not take much comfort from favorable readings of labor costs as wages tend to follow prices in my experience.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In these circumstances, I am concerned that maintaining a highly accommodative policy stance for an extended period would greatly increase the likelihood that inflation exceeds our long-run objectives.

speaker: LACKER
text: Fifth District economic conditions softened further in recent weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Following a pop-up in March, our manufacturing contacts said that factory activity lost momentum in April.

speaker: LACKER
text: Services firms that we surveyed again reported tepid growth in their revenues, and retail sales continued to be very weak.

speaker: LACKER
text: In real estate, the story is mixed.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our housing markets continue to post generally slow sales, but recent anecdotes suggest some scattered firming.

speaker: LACKER
text: Realtors and others indicate that Northern Virginia and Maryland have seen a spring bounce in sales in recent weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: One Realtor said that a factor supporting sales is that sellers now seem more willing to come off 2006 prices.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Charlotte market has also seen a spring bounce.

speaker: LACKER
text: Coastal areas in the Carolinas, hard hit until recently, are said to be more active lately.

speaker: LACKER
text: Of course, it is hard to know what these anecdotes mean on a seasonally adjusted basis, and contacts caution that it is too soon to call the bottom.

speaker: LACKER
text: In contrast, home sales are weakening in many other areas of the Carolinas, where markets had posted sales and price gains well after the national market had turned down.

speaker: LACKER
text: Residential construction in nearly all areas continues to weaken.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the commercial real estate front, conditions have softened somewhat, although in D.C. proper, commercial rents are firm and vacancies are low.

speaker: LACKER
text: Commercial construction activity is broadly softening.

speaker: LACKER
text: My reading of the national report since the last FOMC meeting is that the real outlook has not changed much.

speaker: LACKER
text: In particular, we still appear to be in a recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: Payroll employment has continued to decline, falling an average of 77,000 per month in the first quarter.

speaker: LACKER
text: Unemployment is rising, although it is still relatively low.

speaker: LACKER
text: Nonresidential construction is weakening, and the falloff in architectural billings is particularly discouraging.

speaker: LACKER
text: Other business investment has been soft as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consumer spending, like business spending, appears to have slowed to a crawl.

speaker: LACKER
text: The length and depth of the recession are likely to depend on stabilization in the housing market.

speaker: LACKER
text: The sharp decline in home construction has continued unabated, and outside of the one-month tick-up in the brand new, as yet untested, monthly home-price index from OFHEO, there’s no sign of any bottoming in any of the national data on housing.

speaker: LACKER
text: Having said that, I noted earlier some scattered reports of a seasonable pickup in home sales.

speaker: LACKER
text: So there’s a chance, perhaps only a slim one, that we’ll see some stability in markets this summer.

speaker: LACKER
text: Concerns are often voiced about the possibility of broad spillovers from financial market conditions in the form of sharply tightening credit conditions for households and businesses.

speaker: LACKER
text: But if we look past the drama in wholesale markets and the end-user credit markets that gave rise to it (in housing and buyout financing), evidence of such spillover is hard to come by, at least so far.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is true that delinquencies have risen across a broad class of credits—commercial real estate, C&I loans, and auto and credit card portfolios, for example—and lenders are reporting tightening terms across many of these borrower classes.

speaker: LACKER
text: But that is generally what happens in recessions: Spreads widen and credit flows fall because many consumers and firms become genuinely riskier.

speaker: LACKER
text: So far, delinquency rates and credit spreads faced by consumers and firms appear to be well within the bounds of what happened in past credit cycles.

speaker: LACKER
text: More broadly, recent experiences have revealed important new information about the efficacy of some prominent financial market mechanisms—information that is, in turn, affecting the current behavior of financial market participants.

speaker: LACKER
text: Auction-rate securities, for example, seem to have worked well for decades because investors attached relatively low probability to contractual clauses that reset their rates and prevented their exit.

speaker: LACKER
text: Reaching those clauses has naturally caused investors to update their estimates of the probability of reaching those clauses, and the result has been much less—in fact, virtually nil—demand for those securities.

speaker: LACKER
text: Similarly, recent experience has brought dramatic revelations about the informativeness or lack thereof of credit agencies’ ratings of asset- backed securities.

speaker: LACKER
text: Its revelations would seem to warrant fairly dramatic shifts in investor portfolios, just as a matter of Bayesian updating.

speaker: LACKER
text: These changing expectations in light of recent information revelation are just as much a change in fundamentals as the invention of the light bulb.

speaker: LACKER
text: Spreads in interbank markets certainly are elevated, of course, but one fundamental factor here is the continuing uncertainty about the severity of looming losses on mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: LACKER
text: Another fundamental factor is the demand for term funding by European banks about which uncertainty remains regarding mortgage-related losses that may be imminent.

speaker: LACKER
text: Those sources of uncertainty will persist as long as uncertainty about the bottom of the housing cycle persists.

speaker: LACKER
text: At our March meeting I had strong concerns about inflation, particularly the increase in five- year, five-year-ahead inflation compensation and the rising trend in overall inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Since then we received more-moderate inflation numbers for February, and five-year, five-year-ahead inflation compensation has backed off as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: Although I still believe that these TIPS spreads are too high to be consistent with stable, long-run inflation below 2 percent, it’s heartening to see them come down following our March meeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: It seems reasonable to infer that the improvement in inflation expectations occurred because of the unanticipated emphasis on inflation risks in our statement and the 25 basis point surprise on the funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: That response, however, confirms for me the hypothesis that the previous erosion in expectations was caused largely by the aggressiveness of our January policy actions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe that substantial risks for inflation and our credibility remain.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Michigan survey number for 12-month-ahead inflation expectations popped up to 4.8 percent, a relatively large number.

speaker: LACKER
text: The March CPI was again too high, and further increases in food and energy prices in recent weeks will continue to press headline inflation upward.

speaker: LACKER
text: Persistently high headline numbers could become ingrained in household and business decisionmaking.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe the risk remains that cutting the funds rate again will have undesirable effects on inflation expectations.

speaker: LACKER
text: The real federal funds rate using the Greenbook’s forecast of overall PCE inflation is now between minus ½ and minus ¾ percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: That seems like plenty of stimulus for now.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, for some time I have been using the headwinds period of the early 1990s as a frame of reference for thinking about credit conditions, economic growth, and inflation prospects for the next several years.

speaker: STERN
text: I won’t belabor that comparison much this afternoon, except to say that I continue to find it helpful.

speaker: STERN
text: With that, and given that the information we have received since our March meeting hasn’t caused me to change my views about financial conditions or about growth, let me just say that I continue to expect financial headwinds of some intensity to persist well into next year.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that the economy will decline—contract in this quarter and in the next quarter—before growth resumes, and that the resumption will initially be fairly mild.

speaker: STERN
text: So my outlook for economic growth next year is below that of the Greenbook.

speaker: STERN
text: It is a pretty modest outlook.

speaker: STERN
text: Recent anecdotes from business contacts and from people in financial services firms have not been what I would call overly negative.

speaker: STERN
text: If I were to give those anecdotes more weight, I would probably be somewhat more optimistic about the economic outlook than I am.

speaker: STERN
text: But I am guessing that those anecdotes are underestimating the weight of the credit constraints that are in train, and people—at least people that I have talked to—don’t fully appreciate that yet.

speaker: STERN
text: Turning to inflation, on average it seems to me that the inflation situation and its prospects are no better, and possibly worse, than I had been anticipating.

speaker: STERN
text: To be sure, the core measures of inflation have not accelerated recently and look to be what I might call close to acceptable, looking at their recent performance.

speaker: STERN
text: But we have been warned that some of that better performance is likely to prove transitory.

speaker: STERN
text: Meanwhile, headline inflation has been elevated and has tended to surprise on the upside.

speaker: STERN
text: Moreover, I worry that the persistence of sizable increases in energy and general commodity prices will have a more pronounced effect on core inflation going forward than they have in the recent past.

speaker: STERN
text: Further, I have the sense, both from some estimates of inflation expectations and from the comments and questions I have been getting about inflation and the foreign exchange value of the dollar, that the public’s conviction about monetary policy’s willingness and ability to maintain low inflation is starting to waver.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In terms of markets, Fed credibility, and negative surprises on the data relative to our forecasts, I think this has been the best intermeeting period in a long time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The markets reflect increased confidence that policy will be effective in mitigating the risks both of a systemic financial crisis and of a very deep, protracted recession.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have seen a substantial upward movement in the expected path of the fed funds rate and in real forward rates, significant diminution in the negative skewness in fed funds rate expectations, and a significant move down in a range of different measures of credit risk premiums, and markets have been pretty robust despite bad news over the past few weeks or so.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Medium- and long-term expectations in TIPS have moved down, and we have had a very important and substantial additional wave of inflow of equity into the financial system.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our forecast, though, is roughly the same as it was in March, and it is broadly similar to the path outlined in the Greenbook.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We expect economic activity to follow a path somewhere between the last downturn—a relatively mild downturn—and that of 1990.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We expect underlying inflation to moderate somewhat over the forecast period to something below 2 percent.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We see the risks to the growth forecast still skewed to the downside, though somewhat less so than in March, and we see the risks to the inflation outlook as broadly balanced.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Uncertainty around both paths, though, is unusually high.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I want to make four points.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: First, on economic growth, again, I still think we face substantial risk in this adverse self-reinforcing interaction among falling house prices, slower spending, and financial headwinds.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Even with the very substantial adjustment in housing construction that has already occurred and even if demand for housing stays stable at these levels, we still have several quarters ahead of us before the decline in housing prices starts to moderate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: A further falloff in aggregate demand during this period would raise the prospect of a much larger peak-to-trough decline in housing prices, with higher risk of larger collateral damage to confidence, spending, credit supply, et cetera.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Weakness, as the Chairman has reminded us several times over the past few years, tends to cumulate and spread in these conditions, and weakness may only just be beginning outside of housing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The saving rate here may have to rise substantially further.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The world is behind us in this cycle, and it is likely to slow further, diminishing potential help from net exports going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Second, financial conditions are, I think, still very fragile.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The financial system as a whole still looks as though it is short of the capital necessary to support growth in lending to creditworthy households and borrowers.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Parts of the system still need to bring leverage down significantly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Liquidity conditions in some markets are still impaired; securitization markets are still essentially shut.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the markets now reflect too much confidence in our willingness and ability to prevent large and small financial failures.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are going to disappoint them on the small ones, which may increase the probability they attach to the large.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: At least I hope we disappoint them on the small ones.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Third, I think the inflation outlook, as many of you have said, still has this very uncomfortable feel to it—very high headline inflation, very high readings on the Michigan survey, and the dollar occasionally showing the spiral of feeding energy and commodity prices and vice versa.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I sat next to Paul Volcker when he gave his speech in New York the other day, and he said that the world today feels as it did in the 1970s.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I was alive in the 1970s, but only just.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think it is better than that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It has to be better than that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Core has come in below expectations.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: David is not going to explain all of that away by these temporary, reversible factors.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You have all acknowledged that there is somewhat of an improvement in inflation expectations at medium-term horizon.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very important that you have not seen any material pressure in broad measures of labor compensation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Profit margins are coming down, but they are still unusually high.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The path of output relative to potential, both here and around the rest of the world, is going to significantly diminish pressure on resource utilization going forward even if you have other forces that push up demand for energy and food secularly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it is worth remembering that we had a very, very large sustained relative price shock in the years preceding this downturn, with very little pass-through to core inflation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In fact, in many ways, core inflation moderated over that period with output to potential much tighter.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Fourth, on monetary policy, it seems to me that we are very close to a level that should put us in a good position to navigate these conflicting pressures ahead.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What matters for the outlook is the relationship between the real fed funds rate and our estimates of equilibrium.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Although we can’t measure the latter with any precision, those estimates of equilibrium have to be substantially lower than normal because of what is happening in financial markets.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The Greenbook and Bluebook presentations suggest that the real fed funds rate now is about at equilibrium.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You can look at it through a number of prisms and see some accommodation—see the real fed funds rate somewhat below equilibrium now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We won’t know the answer until this is long over.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that we are probably now within the zone where we are providing some insurance against the risk of a very bad macroeconomic financial outcome without creating too much risk of an inflation spiral.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We should try for an outcome tomorrow in our action and in our statement that is pretty close to market neutral.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One final point about the future.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What strikes me as most implausible in our forecast in New York, and I think in the average of our submissions, is the speed with which we expect to return to growth rates that are close to estimates of long-term potential.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: A more prudent assumption might be for a more protracted period of below-trend growth for a bunch of familiar reasons.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t know if that is the most likely outcome, but it is a plausible and realistic outcome.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think we should be directing policy at trying to induce an unrealistically quick return to what might be considered more-normal growth rates over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: My forecasts of output and inflation for this and the next two years are in the central tendencies of the Committee forecasts.

speaker: KOHN
text: My Okun’s law machine went haywire under the pressure of Debbie’s deadline, [laughter] so my unemployment forecasts need to be revised.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I hit the 5:00 deadline, I think.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have stronger growth in 2008 than the Greenbook because I was hesitant to adopt the staff’s assumption about persistent, serially correlated downside misses relative to fundamentals in consumption and investment implied by entering a recessionary period when we haven’t seen those misses yet.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I didn’t discount this possibility entirely, reasoning that the extraordinarily depressed business and household sentiment was significant.

speaker: KOHN
text: I came out between the Greenbook baseline and the “near- term upside risk” alternative scenario.

speaker: KOHN
text: Despite slightly stronger growth than in the Greenbook, I have roughly the same headline and core inflation paths that are declining gradually through the next few years.

speaker: KOHN
text: I took some slight encouragement from recent better readings on core.

speaker: KOHN
text: I reasoned that flat commodity prices would reverse any recent tendency for inflation expectations to rise, and I anticipate that vacant housing units will continue to put downward pressure on rent increases.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have a couple of observations on the outlook.

speaker: KOHN
text: First, I think the expectation of improving financial conditions is critical to the favorable medium-term outcome for the economy that President Geithner was just talking about.

speaker: KOHN
text: We don’t really know what the current state of overall financial conditions is and how spending is likely to respond to them.

speaker: KOHN
text: Directionally, I think we can say that the severe deterioration that was much in evidence around the time of the last meeting has stopped, as concerns about an even more generalized set of failures—the seizing up of markets and lending—have abated with our actions and with successful capital-raising by intermediaries.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have seen improvements in many segments of the markets, but continued deterioration in term funding suggests to me that there are continued worries about and pressures on credit availability, and credit availability and the cost of credit will be under some pressure as credit is re-intermediated through the banks.

speaker: KOHN
text: Even with some of the recent gains, markets are still fragile and impaired.

speaker: KOHN
text: Spreads have retraced only a small portion of the run-up since last summer.

speaker: KOHN
text: I noticed in Bill’s charts that most of those spreads are back down to, say, those in January; and in January, we thought the markets were pretty impaired.

speaker: KOHN
text: So they are still very, very high by historical standards.

speaker: KOHN
text: Mortgage securitization markets away from GSEs remain broken.

speaker: KOHN
text: There are problems in some other securitization markets, including CMBS.

speaker: KOHN
text: A number of intermediate- and longer-term interest rates are still higher than they were before the crisis hit in August.

speaker: KOHN
text: Baa corporate bonds, which is about the median borrower rating for a corporation, long-term muni bonds, and prime jumbo mortgages are all higher than before we did any easing.

speaker: KOHN
text: Nonprice terms and standards are being tightened considerably, judging in part from the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey, and I think that process is likely to continue for a while.

speaker: KOHN
text: To be sure, short-term interest rates are a lot lower than they were in August.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I suspect that a continuation of current conditions would not be consistent with much of a pickup in growth and an eventual return toward full employment.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is a circumstance in which relationships between the federal funds rate and other measures of financial conditions have changed very, very substantially, and characterizing the stance of policy and financial conditions by looking at some measure of the real federal funds rate can be quite misleading in these circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we need to be careful about how we characterize and think about the stance of policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: The sense that it is neutral right now, much less accommodative, depends very much on our expectations of substantial increases in risk-taking in financial markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, I do think that the most likely path is improving financial market conditions, lower spreads, reopened securitization markets, and stabilization and maybe partial reversal of some of the tighter terms that have evolved.

speaker: KOHN
text: But this process is going to be slow.

speaker: KOHN
text: Until the housing market shows more signs of stabilizing, it is more likely to be subject to backsliding than to sudden unexpected improvements.

speaker: KOHN
text: A corollary to this line of thinking is that there isn’t a lot of ease in the pipeline in the conventional sense.

speaker: KOHN
text: Our reductions in the fed funds rate have not eased financial conditions.

speaker: KOHN
text: They have kept them from tightening even more than they would have done otherwise.

speaker: KOHN
text: The lagged effects of policy easing come from improvements in financial markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is, as we look forward, the lagged effects of policy easing come from the improvements in financial markets that allow the reductions in the actual and expected paths of short-term rates to show through to the cost of capital more broadly defined.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is a longer and more nuanced process than the usual rules of thumb about seeing the effects of ease on output after X quarters and inflation after Y quarters.

speaker: KOHN
text: My second point about the outlook is that the risks around my forecast for growth are still to the downside.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are sailing in a fog in uncharted waters, and the depth finder is on the fritz.

speaker: KOHN
text: So much for sailing analogies.

speaker: KOHN
text: Too bad Bill Poole is not here, though I am glad Jim is here.

speaker: KOHN
text: Let me note that for the record.

speaker: KOHN
text: Downside risks from financial market meltdown have been reduced, though not eliminated.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think an important source of downside risk now is the economy itself—the threat of recessionary tendencies taking hold.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am told we have never had three months of substantial employment declines and business and household sentiment as depressed as they are right now without sliding into a recession.

speaker: KOHN
text: Businesses and households have been unusually cautious in how they invest their savings, moving into government-only money funds and bank deposits, boosting M2, and demanding much larger compensation for taking risks.

speaker: KOHN
text: They are facing much tighter terms for their credit and uncertainty about its availability.

speaker: KOHN
text: It seems to me there is a reasonable possibility that this extraordinary caution in managing their financial portfolios and uncertainty about credit availability will carry over into their spending decisions.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is not my projection or apparently the central tendency of the Committee, but it must be a significant downside risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: In contrast, the risk to total inflation seems skewed to the upside by the potential behavior of commodity prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t understand why these prices have risen so much over the last six months or so.

speaker: KOHN
text: To be sure, over the last several years the rise in prices must have reflected increasing demand in emerging-market economies, but over the past half-year the prospects for global growth have weakened.

speaker: KOHN
text: In those circumstances, I would expect the effects of lower interest rates—say, in the United States—to be offset by weaker demand.

speaker: KOHN
text: The possibility that those types of surprises will continue poses an upside risk to headline inflation and, along with that, a risk to inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: Nonetheless, I saw the risk around a gradual downtrend in core inflation as about balanced, with the possibility of greater slack offsetting the possibility of higher commodity prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: I take some comfort in my projection for core inflation and implicitly for the more persistent aspects of overall inflation from the continued moderate increases in labor compensation.

speaker: KOHN
text: Those increases have been moderate for some time despite very high headline inflation for several years along with still-elevated markups for nonfinancial businesses.

speaker: KOHN
text: Outside of commodities, cost pressures appear to be muted, and businesses are able to absorb increases.

speaker: KOHN
text: Still, I agree that commodity price increases, like any supply shock, have complicated our choices.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are facing a sluggish economy with downside risks as well as uncomfortably high total inflation that is feeding through to some limited extent into core inflation and, by some measures, into inflation expectations, especially near-term expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think, however, that we need to keep in mind that the higher inflation is largely a function of these commodity prices rather than a broad acceleration in overall prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: Core inflation has come in less than we anticipated it would.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also take some comfort, relative to some of the tone I have heard around the table, in what has happened in markets over the intermeeting period.

speaker: KOHN
text: Markets have built in another ¼ point decline in the fed funds rate but then an increase further out.

speaker: KOHN
text: So somehow they are taking this promise of an increase seriously.

speaker: KOHN
text: At the same time they did that, the dollar rose—it didn’t fall—and the long-term inflation compensation built into markets came down.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I don’t see the evidence in financial markets that we are on the cusp of the broad decline in our credibility that I have sensed that some others see around the table.

speaker: WARSH
