text: As has been described by most around the table, official data on the real economy suggest weakness but haven’t materially changed since we met in mid-March.

speaker: WARSH
text: Others have talked in more detail about weakening labor markets, poor consumer sentiment, and worrying trends in consumer spending.

speaker: WARSH
text: Certainly the reports through March that I have received are that consumer spending in March was as bad as anyone who was in the business of retail or credit card spending could have envisioned.

speaker: WARSH
text: Oddly, there are at least some preliminary data through the first few weeks of April of some improvement, but I don’t take much signal from them.

speaker: WARSH
text: Also, obviously, as others around the table have said, the tone, trading, and expectations of financial market participants have improved markedly.

speaker: WARSH
text: If only I were as confident.

speaker: WARSH
text: Whereas market participants only some weeks ago saw fear, they now perceive promise.

speaker: WARSH
text: Whether that is the triumph of hope over experience only time will tell, but I am skeptical.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me talk for a few moments about a couple of positive factors that should be helping and four or so negative factors.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, on the positive side, I want to give voice to the capital- raising that a couple of others around the table have referred to.

speaker: WARSH
text: We and the Treasury have been calling for some months for capital-raising across all types of financial institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: The questions then were whether financial institutions were willing to take the dilution and go raise capital.

speaker: WARSH
text: At least equally as important was whether there would be sufficient investor demand.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the answer to both of those questions appears to be “yes.” Investor demand from nearly all sources—including sovereign wealth funds, hedge funds, and traditional long-only managers— has funded virtually all classes of financial institutions—that is, investment banks, money center banks, regional banks, and community banks—across the capital structure—equities, convertibles, and preferred debt—in a huge range of distressed and more-stable situations.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that is invariably a very encouraging sign, and we should only be so lucky that those markets remain wide open.

speaker: WARSH
text: Is this improvement likely to be enduring?

speaker: WARSH
text: This strikes me as pretty consequential as to whether or not we see the economy respond as favorably in the second half of this year as the Greenbook suggests.

speaker: WARSH
text: Is the improvement in equity markets, in leveraged loans, and in high-yield markets and the narrowing of CDS spreads sustainable, or is there more bad news to come that is not priced into the market?

speaker: WARSH
text: My own view is that balance sheets are on the road to repair but that income statements for these financial institutions remain highly challenged.

speaker: WARSH
text: March was a terrible month for financial institutions’ profitability, which should make it harder for credit to expand, as would be hoped for with any sort of V-shaped or U- shaped recovery.

speaker: WARSH
text: The second positive factor, building on the increase in capital, is really what is going on among the Fortune 2000, particularly the nonfinancial Fortune 2000.

speaker: WARSH
text: Earnings look pretty stubborn and solid.

speaker: WARSH
text: Though they have come off their peaks, corporate profit levels are quite remarkable for all of the things that are wrong in this economy, and they look to me to be anachronistic with previous periods of recession.

speaker: WARSH
text: The balance sheets of those Fortune 2000 companies look excellent.

speaker: WARSH
text: The investment-grade markets remain wide open.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the question is whether those Fortune 2000 will be hiring workers during the next two or three years in the United States, and on that front, I am probably reasonably skeptical.

speaker: WARSH
text: So if those are the positive factors, let me turn to the negative.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, consumer weakness seems to be spreading.

speaker: WARSH
text: The largest credit card providers report that credit card spend is deteriorating—again, absent a couple of odd noises in April—and that the strains showing up as delinquency, which were once only in states where housing issues were predominant, now seem to be in other states as well.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, credit availability for small business seems under remarkable pressure.

speaker: WARSH
text: Not only has the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey continued to be disappointing, large money center banks appear to be pulling back from some segments of the small business markets entirely.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, interbank funding market problems, as others have discussed, seem inconsistent with the broader improvement in credit markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is a troubling sign that all might not be as well as it appears in this curative process.

speaker: WARSH
text: A fourth and final negative factor is inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: The Greenbook, which has a much more benign forecast for inflation than I do, revised up the forecast for core and headline inflation in the second half of 2008, as David said.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am still more worried about inflation prospects.

speaker: WARSH
text: As for inflation expectations and possible second- and third-order effects of these changes in prices, trading and anecdotes over the last several weeks and months continued to be troubling.

speaker: WARSH
text: I have spent less time in my remarks on inflation than on growth but only because I suppose there is less to say.

speaker: WARSH
text: The relationships among our policy actions, the foreign exchange value of the dollar, and commodity prices are worth further scrutiny.

speaker: WARSH
text: In summary, although we should be pleased with the official data on the economy as not deteriorating in the intermeeting period and with financial markets that have certainly exceeded my own expectations for improvement, I remain quite concerned about pressures on both sides of the dual mandate—a discussion that we will take up more in the next round.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I have talked about many times before, I see what is happening as a continuing slow burn after the fires really heated up for a little while back in March.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Things have cooled off again.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But exactly as Governor Kohn said, we now seem to be comforted at levels that caused us extreme distress last fall and in January.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I think it is important to put it into that context.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There certainly has been improvement, but it is a little early to declare victory—not that anyone has, but I think we just have to be very mindful of that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some of the discussion reminds me a little of the discussions that we had at the end of October, when we thought that things were improving and then they deteriorated in a way that had us very concerned.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But my central tendency scenario has always been not for a financial cataclysm, although that is certainly a real downside risk, but for a sort of slow burn that is just going to continue to weigh heavily on consumption.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it is negative feedback between housing and finance, but not necessarily a broader cataclysm.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I very much agree with President Evans that the chance of a significant nonlinear break to the downside is not gone but lower than it has been.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But the tightening credit conditions are going to make it very difficult for the markets to repair and recover as rapidly as perhaps they do in the Greenbook.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On housing, we know there are direct and indirect effects.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have all the signs that the contraction is continuing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Even after housing starts have fallen more than 60 percent, we are still seeing them in near free fall.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But that hasn’t helped to alleviate the inventories of unsold homes, which remain at extremely elevated levels—although not moving up dramatically.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Part of the concern is that some of the sales may be due to forced sales related to foreclosures because we know that foreclosures are up quite a bit.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So we have to be a bit cautious there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Almost all the measures suggest that expectations of future housing prices are lower, which is causing people to be very cautious about buying.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The anecdotal evidence that I have is that walk-throughs are fine but that actually closing the deal is much more difficult, both because of difficulty in finding credit and because people are unwilling to make a commitment now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They think that prices may be 10 percent lower in 6, 9, or 12 months.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: For many people, this is the largest investment that they will make, and trying to explain to a loved one that they just lost 10 percent of their nest egg is not an easy thing to do.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So people are being more cautious.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We also see some of this in the ABX measures that Bill put forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Those numbers have come off their extreme lows, but they are still much lower than they were before.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is hard to believe that the actual default and delinquency performance will be as bad as those measures are suggesting, but they are still suggesting that things are going to be pretty tough, and so we still need to be very wary there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We are still seeing a difference in consumer behavior—people being willing to walk away from their houses before they walk away from their credit cards or from their cars.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That is suggesting that people are just operating somewhat differently from the way they did before.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The jumbo spreads are still extremely wide, as the charts showed.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We may be getting some offset from the new FHA programs and from Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae, but I am still not optimistic that much of this can come in before the end of the year.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That suggests that we have tightness on that part.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We also have tightness in the credit card market, exactly as Governor Warsh said.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The credit card companies I have spoken to see continuing deterioration.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We didn’t see any sort of nonlinear changes but just a continuing downward trend of real challenges and increasing roll rates of people going 30, 60, 90, and more days delinquent.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Spending is up a bit, but they usually say that’s mostly because of increases for gasoline and groceries due to the high commodity prices.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, as President Yellen mentioned, there is more tightening in the HELOC market.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: More challenges are there, so the banks are pulling back, and more people are getting into trouble.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I have an anecdote from one of the large companies.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A number of large investment-grade firms have drawn down significant parts of their revolvers, not because they actually needed them but because they thought that they better do it now before they are pulled back.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Even these large institutions seem to be hoarding liquidity, much as the banks are doing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think the banks are doing that because we still see CDS spreads that are very high even though they are lower than their peaks.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The LIBOR–OIS spread that a number of people have mentioned still is high and is continuing to increase.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That is the most troubling for me—that we are moving back to the extreme highs we saw when we had the end-of-the-year problem.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But then we had an explanation for its going away.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now we don’t have an end-of-the-year problem, so unfortunately, it is difficult for me to understand what is going to make this go away.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we can provide more liquidity through some of our various facilities, but I am not sure that that, in and of itself, will be the cure.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have seen more capital come in and help out some of the institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But a lot of fragility is still there, as President Pianalto well knows.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The issues with respect to National City were liquidity issues, not necessarily short-term concerns about solvency, although I think there are longer-term concerns about solvency.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Liquidity and solvency issues are ultimately related, but there is a real concern that many of the money market mutual funds that hold between $3 trillion and $4 trillion will just walk away.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We saw this with Bear Stearns.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We can see this with other institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that it’s fragility that accounts for some of these very high levels.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We used to worry primarily about deposit runs, but deposit runs are extremely slow.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Deposit runs are leisurely strolls compared with what could happen in these liquidity markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I do think that issues are there precisely because still more challenges are coming with commercial real estate construction, as a number of other people have mentioned.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There will still be a lot of provisioning that will have to come up, putting more pressure on the balance sheets and making it more difficult for people to borrow.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I also very much agree with Vice Chairman Geithner that the rest of the world is a little behind us and that the boost that we are getting right now from exports isn’t going to persist.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Turning to inflation, as I think a number of people have mentioned, we haven’t seen a lot of pressure on the labor side.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As labor markets soften, it is unlikely that we are going to see more pressure there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So that seems to be a positive.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we do see these very elevated commodity price levels, which don’t seem to have fed through to core.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But exactly as Governor Kohn said, it is a bit of a puzzle how they continue to increase, and that certainly puts some risks ahead of us.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is a particularly difficult time to get a good reading on inflation expectations because there have been lots of changes in liquidity issues and in other particular factors.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some of the survey-based measures are up, but they tend to be very closely related to gasoline prices, and we know that those are at extremely high levels.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I think it is extremely difficult for us now to make a solid determination about where inflation expectations are.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Certainly that raises a caution because we don’t want to have inflation expectations become unmoored.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I think it is more difficult for us to identify right now exactly how they are evolving, and obviously, this will be important for us in our decisions tomorrow.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My modal forecast is for a mild recession in the first half of 2008 and is very much in line with the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am more pessimistic, however, than the Greenbook on the issue of recovery.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Again, the issue is that we have had a major disruption to our financial markets and there is a mess, and I think it is going to take a long time to clean up the mess.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The parallel that President Stern made to the episode in the early ’90s is very apt.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I suspect that there will be substantial headwinds coming from the problems in the financial sector for quite a while, and that means that the recovery we would see would be more L-shaped than V-shaped.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When I look at where I was at the last FOMC meeting, there has really been a big change for me.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I re-read the transcripts, because you always want to see what things sounded like, and I sounded so depressed then, as though I might take out a gun and blow my head off.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is the way it read.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But my sunny, optimistic disposition is coming back.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think it is very possible that we will look back and say, particularly after the Bear Stearns episode, that we have turned the corner in terms of the financial disruption that we have just experienced.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I should mention, however, that it doesn’t mean that we should be complacent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am not sure that is the case.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have been disappointed before.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I think there is a very strong possibility that the worst is over.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You can see this in that there is less concern about credit risks in financial institutions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is because we had a major institution get into trouble, but because of our actions, it didn’t blow up the world.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There is an issue, of course, of potential cost and moral hazard going forward, but I think it has had the effect of calming down the markets in a very substantial way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Very important in this regard is that we are seeing that our large financial institutions are able to raise capital now at not too high a cost.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, they are doing so in a major way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When we think about the long-term solution to the problems in the financial markets, cleaning up the mess and raising capital is going to be absolutely critical, particularly because in the long run the securitization market will come back.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But it is going to very much involve the large financial institutions, which will have to solve the agency problems that were not solved in this recent bout of securitization, which created all of the problems.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So their having enough capital is critical.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think it is very possible that we are on the path to their sorting out their problems, which in the long run will help sort out the problems in the credit markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I should mention, by the way, that I still don’t want us to be complacent about this because things could go in the other direction.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There is still the puzzle about what is going on in the money markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, we see these very large and actually widening spreads between LIBOR and OIS.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So even though I am starting to become optimistic, I don’t want to be Panglossian in my view.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: From my perspective the key issue is that, although my modal forecast hasn’t changed much from March, I see that the tail risks have decreased substantially, and I think that the probability that we will have a severe adverse feedback loop, which really scared me just a little while ago, is going to be much lower.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I still see some downside risks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Particularly, I am concerned about the issue of housing prices.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: They could fall more than we and the Greenbook expect, and that could trigger some problems.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I do think that the downside risk is much, much lower.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Another thing I should mention is that I think there is very high uncertainty right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I could get depressed again, but we will have to see.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On the inflation front, I see that long-run inflation expectations are still reasonably well anchored around 2 percent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The information in the financial markets on this score is that there has not been a big blowout in that case.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There have been problems regarding some of the surveys, but I am a little less worried about the surveys in terms of households.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am very skeptical of them because they tend to react very much to current conditions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also, if you ask people what TV shows they are watching, they will tell you that they are watching PBS and something classy, but you know they are watching “Desperate Housewives.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What is wrong with “Desperate Housewives”?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I do have a concern about the risk to inflation expectations because of the high commodity prices that we see.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is coming from the very adverse supply shock and the fact that we have had headline inflation so high for so long.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The good news, by the way, is that it is actually quite remarkable, given how high headline inflation has been, how anchored inflation expectations have been.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that has to do with confidence in this institution’s doing the right thing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is very important that we retain that confidence.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have to think about that when we decide what we are going to do regarding policy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: About where I think inflation is going to be—I have been a 2 percent guy for a long time.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am not changing that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that inflation expectations are around 2 percent and that there is no expectation that we will have excess demand in the economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If anything, it is the opposite of that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I see the risks as balanced—there are some risks on the upside, particularly because of what is happening with commodity prices.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On the other hand, there are risks on the downside because of the expected slack and because there is some downside risk in the economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So on that ground, I basically have the same story that I had before.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you, and thank you all for very helpful comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As usual, let me briefly summarize what I heard today and then make a few comments of my own.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, in summary, data since the March meeting have been soft, and economic activity is weak.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the recent news has not generally been worse than expected.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was disagreement over whether we are technically in a recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most saw improved economic growth in the second half of 2008 with further improvement in 2009, although some saw more-protracted weakness.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The housing sector remains weak, though there were reports of improvement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Starts and the demand for new houses continue to decline.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inventories of unsold homes remain very high.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing demand is affected by restrictive conditions in mortgage markets, fears that house prices have much further to fall, and weakening economic conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Retail sales, sentiment, and consumer spending have generally been soft, reflecting a long list of headwinds, including tightening credit, weaker house prices, and higher energy prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Payrolls are falling, although there are some pockets of strength.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unemployment is likely to keep rising.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It may remain somewhat high into 2010.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will soon see whether the fiscal stimulus package affects either the consumer or business investment plans.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Possibly, liquidity-constrained consumers may respond more strongly than normally.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Business sentiment is also relatively weak, reflecting in part credit conditions but also the uncertain prospects for the economy and continued cost pressures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Investment has softened somewhat, including declines in commercial real estate investment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Strength in foreign markets is helping support U.S. production and profits, especially manufacturing, although foreign economies may slow in the coming quarters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The energy and agricultural sectors are strong.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial conditions have improved in the past month, with financing conditions better, credit risk spreads coming in a bit, and both equities and real interest rates up since the last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Decent earnings, a sense on the part of some that the bulk of the write-downs in the banking sector have been taken, the ability of financial institutions to raise capital, and possibly Fed actions, including liquidity provision and the actions regarding Bear Stearns, have contributed to the improvement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, many markets remain fragile, including the key interbank market and other short-term funding markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some expressed the view that more- significant write-downs and financial stress lie ahead, as house prices continue to fall and the slowing economy weakens credit quality, and that the full impact of tighter credit has not yet been felt in the nonfinancial economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Others, however, were less concerned about the real effects of the financial conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial conditions and the housing market probably remained the most important downside risks to growth, although energy prices were also cited.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Readings on core inflation were moderate in the intermeeting period, although some of the reasons for improvement may be transitory.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Oil prices have continued to move up, contributing to higher headline inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other commodity prices have also begun to rise again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Many firms noted these strong cost pressures and indicated some ability to pass those costs along to consumers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inflation breakevens showed improvement at some horizons since the March meeting, possibly reflecting lower risk premiums, though survey inflation expectations were higher.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The dollar appreciated during the intermeeting period, but longer-term depreciation and rising import prices remain another source of pressure on inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nominal wage gains remain moderate, however, and markups are high.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Uncertainty about the course of oil and other commodity prices adds to overall inflation uncertainty and perhaps to inflation risks that are now somewhat more to the upside.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Many participants expressed concerns about these upside risks, about inflation expectations, and about the maintenance of the Fed’s inflation-fighting credibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just add a few thoughts to what has already been said.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the real side, I think that I am probably somewhat more pessimistic than the median view that I heard around the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First of all, I am reasonably confident that we are in a recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t see these dynamic patterns of employment, sentiment, and so on without a recession being eventually called by the NBER.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That fact, I believe, raises the risks of more-rapid declines in employment and consumer spending in the months ahead because there seem to be somewhat more-adverse dynamics in a recession scenario.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, I remain concerned about housing, which is not showing really any significant signs of stabilization.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Mortgage markets are still dysfunctional, and the only source of mortgage credit essentially is the GSEs, which are doing their best to raise fees and profit from the situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Sales of new homes remain weak.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inventories of unsold homes are down in absolute terms, but they still are very high relative to sales.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We heard this morning of yet even faster price declines for housing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I’ve said several times at this table, until there is some sense of a bottoming in the housing market and in housing prices, I think that we are not going to see really broad stabilization, either in the economy or in financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, there are some positives—exports, for example—which have kept manufacturing and other industries from declining as much as usual during a recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Interestingly, this could be a mirror image of the 2001 recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In 2001, the business sector was weak, and consumption and housing were strong.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We could have the mirror image this time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In financial markets, there certainly have been improvements, and that is certainly encouraging.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with people about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we have heard a few people in the market say that credit losses and write-downs are in the ninth inning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As a baseball fan, I think we are probably closer to the third inning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me explain why I think that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The IMF recently projected aggregate credit losses on U.S.-based assets of about $945 billion worldwide, with about a quarter of those coming in the U.S. banks and thrifts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Board staff has a somewhat lower number, around $700 billion to $800 billion, but they have a higher fraction in U.S. banks and thrifts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the basic numbers are pretty similar in that respect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The staff projection for credit losses for U.S. commercial banks and thrifts, excluding investment banks, is about $215 billion for this year and next year and $300 billion if the recession is more severe.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, the staff projects about $60 billion in write-downs of CDOs and other types of traded assets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, most of those $60 billion write-downs have been taken.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They are mostly held by the top banks, and they have mostly been already written off.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, of the $215 billion to $300 billion in projected credit losses, so far U.S. banks and thrifts have acknowledged only about $60 billion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if you put together those numbers, you find that we are about one-third of the way through total losses.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, there are, in fact, obviously some countervailing factors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Banks and thrifts have already raised about $115 billion in capital since the middle of last year, which essentially covers the losses announced so far.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But that said, there is still a lot of deleveraging to go.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is going to be a long process of selling assets, reducing extensions of credit, and building capital ratios.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This may not yet be fully felt in the real economy, but it will eventually be there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I do think that we are going to see continued pressure from financial markets and credit markets, even if we don’t have any serious relapses into financial stress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, again, I am somewhat more skeptical about a near-term improvement in economic growth, although I do acknowledge that the fiscal package and other factors that the Greenbook mentions will be helpful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The question has been raised about whether monetary policy is helpful and what the stance of monetary policy is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with the comment that the real federal funds rate is not necessarily the best measure of the stance of monetary policy right now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me take an example that was given in the New York Fed’s daily financial report a couple of days ago, which was about the all-in cost of asset-backed securities backed by auto loans.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: According to this report, in February of ’07, the three-year swap rate was about 5 percent, and the spread on AAA tranches of auto-backed ABS was about 10 basis points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The all-in cost was 5.07 percent for this particular asset.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In February of ’08, the three-year swap rate was 3.15 percent, almost 2 percentage points lower, but the spread on AAA tranches was 195 basis points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, the overall all-in cost of auto loan ABS was 5.36 percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the net effect is—well, is monetary policy doing anything?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have reduced the safe rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have brought down the cost of funds.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the spreads have obviously offset that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So what we have really done is essentially offset the effects of the credit crisis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, if we had not responded to the situation, those costs would be much higher, and the extent of restriction would be a lot greater.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For these reasons, I really do believe that we need to take a much more sophisticated look at what the appropriate interest rate is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Taylor rules, in particular, are just not appropriate for the current situation because the equilibrium real interest rate of 2 percent that is built into them is not necessarily appropriate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me turn to inflation, which a lot of people talked about today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, let me just say that I certainly have significant concerns on the nominal side.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, I have a lot of anxiety about the dollar.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Foreign exchange rates in general are not well tied down, and they are very subject to sentiment and swings in views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, although I think that the depreciation of the dollar so far is a mixed bag—obviously, it has effects on different parts of the economy—I do think that there is a risk of a sharper fall with possibly adverse implications, in the short run, for U.S. assets and, in the long run, perhaps implications for our position as a reserve currency and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that is an issue to be concerned about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For that reason and for other reasons as well, I am very sympathetic to the view I hear around the table that we are now very, very close to where we ought to be, that it is time to take a rest, to see the effects of our work, and to pay equal attention to the nominal side of our mandate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with all of that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I am hopeful that in our policy discussion tomorrow we will be fairly close around the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That being said, I do want to take a little exception to some of the discussion about inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is an obvious and very elementary distinction between relative price changes and overall inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me ask you to do the following thought experiment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Imagine you are speaking to your board.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Last year, as a first approximation, headline inflation was 4 percent, labor compensation grew at 4 percent, and oil prices rose 60 percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s imagine that we had been so farsighted and so effective that we managed to keep headline inflation last year at 2 percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The implications would have been, assuming that relative price changes were the same, that wages would have grown at 2 percent and that oil prices would have risen at 57 percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the conversation with your board, your board would say, “This inflation is killing us.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: These costs are killing us.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have to pass them through.” They would, and they would be right.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When there are big changes in relative prices, that is a real phenomenon, and it has to be accommodated somehow by nominal price shifts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So to the extent that the changes in food and oil prices reflect real supply-and-demand conditions, obviously they are very distressing and bad for the economy and create a lot of pain, but they are not in themselves necessarily under the control of monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we give the impression that gasoline prices are the Fed’s responsibility, we are looking for trouble because we cannot control gasoline prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That said, of course we need to address the overall inflation rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to address inflation expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All of that is very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But, again, we need to make a distinction between relative price changes and overall inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, a more sophisticated response to that is, “Well, maybe monetary policy is contributing to these relative price changes as well”; and I think that is a very serious issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Certainly the dollar has some effects on oil prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But keep in mind that a lot of the depreciation of the dollar is a decline in real exchange rates, which is essential in any case for balancing our external accounts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, yes, the depreciation of the dollar, through our policies, has contributed somewhat to commodity prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But compared with the overall shifts in relative prices that we have seen, I think it is not that large.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are other hypotheses suggesting that we have been stimulating speculation in a bubble, suggesting that low real interest rates contribute to commodity price booms.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t want to take more time, but the evidence for those things is very limited.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, the fact that we have not seen any buildups in hoarding or inventories is a very strong argument against the idea that inflation expectations, hoarding, or speculation is a major factor in energy price increases.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, yes, the nominal side is very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to address that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we should try to help our audiences understand the very important distinction between real and nominal changes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I will stop there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If I can ask for your patience, we could do the briefing on the alternatives today and give ourselves more time tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Around the table, does that seem okay?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll call on Bill English.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, I was wondering if Brian or Bill wanted to talk President Plosser out of his concern about MZM at some point.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If you like, I could try to address that tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll have a special session on MZM.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: 3 I will be referring to the revised version of table 1, which is included in the package labeled “Material for the FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” The revised table presents the same range of options regarding the target federal funds rate as the version discussed in the Bluebook, but we have proposed some changes to the statement language for alternatives B and C. New language introduced in the draft distributed on Monday is shown in blue, with language reintroduced from the March 18 statement shown in black and underlined.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: An additional adjustment made since Monday is shown in purple.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: We have about used up the color palette in Word.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: I will discuss these changes as I go along.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Your policy decision at this meeting would seem to depend on three judgments: Where do you think you are; where do you want to be; and what path do you want to follow to get there?

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The staff’s assessment of where you are—at least in terms of the stance of monetary policy—is summarized in the r* chart that was included in the Bluebook.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: That chart showed that the current real federal funds rate is about 50 basis points above the Greenbook-consistent measure of r*, suggesting that the rapid easing of policy this year has left the real funds rate fairly close to the level required to bring the economy back to its potential over the medium term.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The low level of the 3 The materials used by Mr. English are appended to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: ENGLISH
text: equilibrium funds rate reflects the staff’s judgment that the housing correction and financial market stresses—with their associated effects on consumer and business confidence—have been sufficient to shift the economy into a recession regime in which spending by both households and businesses is likely to be weak.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: As for where you want to be, the Greenbook projection assumes that the real funds rate is moved down to its equilibrium level—that is, the federal funds rate is trimmed 50 basis points further—and then remains unchanged over the rest of the projection period.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Finally, as for the path you want to follow to get there, the staff projection assumes that you move the federal funds rate to the staff’s estimate of the rate’s equilibrium level relatively quickly by trimming the fed funds target 25 basis points at this meeting and another 25 basis points at the June meeting.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: However, there is no overshoot below the equilibrium level in order to provide insurance against a further unexpected slide in spending.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: If you agree with the staff that about 50 basis points of additional easing is needed to bring the real federal funds rate into alignment with its equilibrium level and you are at least moderately confident of that assessment, then you might be inclined to ease policy by 50 basis points at this meeting and issue a statement suggesting fairly balanced risks to the outlook, as in alternative A.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: A relatively large adjustment to policy at this meeting would be particularly attractive if the Committee wanted a somewhat faster recovery in output or was concerned about downside risks to growth and wished to move the funds rate back to its equilibrium value quickly in order to help head them off.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Members might also select a larger rate cut if they were willing to live with somewhat higher inflation over time, as in the optimal control simulation in the Bluebook with an inflation goal of 2 percent.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The rationale language proposed for alternative A sticks fairly closely to the language used in March, making modest adjustments that are intended to avoid leaving the impression that the weakness in economic activity or the concerns about inflation had worsened appreciably over the intermeeting period.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The assessment-of- risk language would continue to indicate that the easier stance of policy should “foster moderate growth over time and .

speaker: ENGLISH
text: mitigate the risks to economic activity,” but it would move toward balance by dropping the explicit reference to downside risks.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: As in March, it would end by promising timely action to “promote sustainable economic growth and price stability.” Investors would be surprised by the adoption of alternative A.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Market participants generally expect a 25 basis point rate cut at this meeting and put very low odds on a 50 basis point cut.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: However, the effect of the relatively large easing would be damped somewhat by the shift to a more balanced risk assessment.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The result would likely be lower short- and intermediate-term interest rates, a rise in equity prices, and a softening of the dollar.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: If the Committee viewed the target federal funds rate as probably close to the level that would appropriately balance the risks to its dual objectives but saw considerable uncertainty regarding that level, then it might be inclined to reduce the funds rate another 25 basis points at this meeting and suggest a more gradual pace of policy easing, or even a pause, after this meeting, as in alternative B.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Policy has been eased very rapidly, and it is difficult at this point to assess the extent to which that easing has been transmitted to households and firms and so to spending.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: That assessment is complicated by the ongoing turbulence in financial markets as well as the usual difficulty in extracting signals from noisy data on economic activity.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Against this backdrop, the Committee may be inclined to take a relatively small policy step at this meeting and then move to a more incremental policy approach under which policy will be guided by incoming information on economic and financial developments.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Moreover, with some measures of long-term inflation expectations having moved higher in recent months, members may be concerned that a larger policy move at this meeting would encourage the view that the Committee is more willing to tolerate inflation than had been thought.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: By taking a smaller policy step at this meeting and suggesting reduced odds of additional near-term policy action, the Committee could limit the extent to which investors extrapolate the recent large policy moves and so build into asset prices more easing than is warranted.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Such a brake on expectations may be seen as particularly useful since the incoming data on employment and economic activity are likely to be pretty soft in the near term, and the data releases could well spur expectations of further rate cuts even though the Committee anticipated the weakness when setting policy.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Communication on this point will presumably be enhanced by the release of the “Summary of Economic Projections” in three weeks, which should clarify the Committee’s views on the appropriate path for policy and the expected trajectory for economic growth over coming quarters.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: In the Bluebook, the rationale portion of the statement associated with alternative B was identical to that under alternative A.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: However, in the revised version of table 1, the first sentence on inflation has been changed to acknowledge the recent improvement in readings on core inflation but point to the continued run-up in energy and other commodity prices.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Rather than simply noting the Committee’s judgment that a further easing move is appropriate, as in alternative A, the assessment-of-risk paragraph begins by stating that “[t]he substantial easing of monetary policy to date, combined with ongoing measures to foster market liquidity, should help to promote moderate growth over time and to mitigate risks to economic activity.” The explicit, time-dependent pause that was suggested in the Bluebook formulation for this alternative has been replaced by wording that is intended to suggest that policy will be more data-dependent, with the final sentence now reading, “The Committee will continue to monitor economic and financial developments and will act as needed to promote sustainable economic growth and price stability.” The addition of the phrase on monitoring developments coupled with the deletion of the indication in the March statement that the Committee will act “in a timely manner” will likely be read by investors as suggesting a slowing in the pace of easing and possibly a pause after this meeting if the economy develops as the Committee anticipates.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Investors appear to expect that the Committee will trim the federal funds rate 25 basis points at this meeting and then leave the federal funds target at 2 percent for some time.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The 25 basis point policy easing and the associated statement under alternative B would seem to be about in line with these expectations, implying little response in financial markets.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: If the Committee thinks that the substantial easing of policy already put in place, along with the coming fiscal stimulus, is likely to foster outcomes that appropriately balance its inflation and growth objectives, then it may want to stay its hand at this meeting and issue a statement suggesting that policy is likely to change gradually going forward and could even be on hold for a time, as in alternative C. The Committee may expect the ongoing weakness in spending to be relatively mild and brief.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The real federal funds rate is already very low, and the incoming data may not be seen as sufficiently weak to confirm the staff’s view that the economy has shifted to a recessionary footing and therefore that spending is likely to come in weaker than one would otherwise expect.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: With financial markets most recently improving, on balance, and investors apparently less concerned about tail events, the Committee may see smaller downside risks to the outlook for growth.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: At the same time, members may think that the inflation outlook remains worrisome.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Prices of oil and some other commodities touched new highs over the intermeeting period, and members may anticipate that firms will be able to pass a larger share of the increase in these costs through to their customers than the staff anticipates.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Longer-term inflation expectations may have increased in recent months, and the Committee might be concerned that failing to push back, at least modestly, against that rise could allow for a more significant increase in expectations that could be very costly to reverse.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Moreover, some members may worry that additional policy easing could trigger declines in the foreign exchange value of the dollar and increases in commodity prices that would give a further boost to inflationary pressures.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Taken together, these arguments might suggest that, if a further easing step were taken at this meeting, it might have to be reversed fairly soon—an outcome that some members may wish to avoid.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The discussion of economic activity in the statement under alternative C is identical to that under the other two alternatives.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The inflation paragraph is similar to that under alternative A, but it does not list the reasons for the anticipated moderation in inflation.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The exclusion of this list is intended to suggest less confidence in the judgment that inflation will moderate as expected.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Some members may also be uncomfortable repeating the reference to “a projected leveling-out of energy and other commodity prices” when those prices have surprised to the upside yet again.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The assessment-of-risk portion of the statement starts by pointing to downside risks, but then proceeds as in alternative B.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The reference to downside risks might counter to some degree the suggestion of a possible pause in the easing process, but the lack of policy action combined with this statement language would presumably limit expectations for easing at coming meetings.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Market participants put only about one-quarter odds on unchanged policy at this meeting, and so the combination of unchanged policy and a statement suggesting that the Committee could remain on hold for a time would surprise investors, even with the retention of downside risks to growth.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Short- and intermediate-term rates would rise, stock prices would likely fall, and the dollar could rally.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: Effects on longer-term rates, and also on inflation compensation, would depend on whether investors interpreted the statement as indicating that the Committee desired a lower level of inflation than had been thought.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: The unexpectedly firm policy decision could boost pressures in short-term funding markets, either immediately, as a result of higher funding costs for leveraged firms and a weaker outlook for the real economy, or over time, in the event that economic data came in weaker than anticipated and the FOMC was seen as less likely to ease policy in response.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: That concludes my prepared remarks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Bill?

speaker: FISHER
text: You emphasized the phrase “reflecting a projected leveling-out of energy and other commodity prices and an easing of pressures on resource utilization.” Can you just refresh my memory?

speaker: FISHER
text: For how long have we been using that phrase—just in the March statement, or have we used it before?

speaker: ENGLISH
text: I’m afraid I’m not sure.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We must have used that just in March.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It was not here in January.

speaker: FISHER
text: So not in January—it was just in March that we used that.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, let’s say we were to have a rally in the dollar.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we voted for no change, might that positively affect equity prices or the credit markets in the United States?

speaker: ENGLISH
text: I suppose it’s possible, but I guess I would expect that, if monetary policy came out tighter than people had expected, it would lead to at least a modest marking- down of the outlook for the economy.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is a personal view, but it’s not clear to me that things are that clear-cut on a sustainable basis.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of the things that seems to be undercutting confidence is the weakness in the dollar, even though in the past few days the dollar has rallied.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m just wondering if it’s clear-cut that we would necessarily have a sustained selloff.

speaker: FISHER
text: I can see an immediate reaction, particularly on the announcement.

speaker: FISHER
text: But it’s conceivable, is it not, that if we had a dollar rally that we could have a positive effect on equity prices or on the credit markets?

speaker: ENGLISH
text: I think it’s hard to know how people would read the news.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: But as was emphasized earlier, a weaker dollar supports exports and supports the outlook for the real economy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think you could get your result if people took the action as that the Federal Reserve’s view was that the economy wasn’t as great a risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So risk premiums would come down, the dollar would rally, and the stock market would do better.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just wanted to ask a question.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think it goes exactly to what both Bills just said, in that it depends fundamentally on whether the disappointment is reassuring or troubling.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have had two examples of disappointment that have been troubling, and we have had one example of disappointment being reassuring—the most recent one being the latter.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I think what matters most is what happens to the expected path of the fed funds rate going forward, and that is how you would know.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If you disappoint significantly and the markets lower the expected path going forward, as they did in October and December, you could have the dollar weaken as a result just as easily as strengthen.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are not very good at speculating about the effect on the fed funds rate expectations of our statements, and it is much harder to speculate about the effect on the dollar in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You can tell a compelling story on both sides.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It sort of depends how plausible it is, particularly if you have language saying that downside risks to growth remain even without moving, that we are signaling greater confidence in the strength of the economy going forward with an action that implies not moving.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is also being significantly driven by the subsequent data.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, this just illustrates the point.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s not as clear-cut as one might guess.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have a couple of questions, unfortunately.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am very sympathetic to your point about how difficult it is to understand what the relationship is between the equilibrium fed funds rate and where we are with respect to financial stress.

speaker: EVANS
text: Actually, my question is for the Greenbook team—if you could remind me again, within the Greenbook-consistent measure, how do you deal with these?

speaker: EVANS
text: You have add factors in your forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: Presumably, they’re related to the financial stress.

speaker: EVANS
text: I know that they are acting as if there is a higher interest rate at work.

speaker: EVANS
text: We also have the role of the lending facilities, which perhaps have relieved a bit of that stress.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not quite sure how that plays out here, so if you could, please clarify that as best you can.

speaker: EVANS
text: Again, in chart 6 there is no role for the inflation preference, right?

speaker: EVANS
text: This is all about how long it takes to get back to potential over three years with this interest rate.

speaker: EVANS
text: The Board staff was very helpful over the weekend, when I asked a question about chart 7 and the fact that the funds rate took off from a higher level.

speaker: EVANS
text: If you add that type of analysis in there, it seems as if it comes down a little to what your inflation preference is.

speaker: EVANS
text: For the 1½ percent inflation rate, you might want to stick where you are; if it’s 2 percent, you would move down a bit.

speaker: EVANS
text: Again, that is taking it as given that you can interpret these at face value, if you will.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have another question about the fed funds futures market and Bill Dudley’s chart about how the dealers seem to have slightly different expectations and whether or not that teases out anything about what Governor Kohn was talking about, because that’s a very interesting observation.

speaker: EVANS
text: You know, there is much more weight below the market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, it’s hard to know what to read into that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It could be that the forecasts have more inertia to them.

speaker: EVANS
text: I thought these were the smart guys who really were on top of it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But forecasts don’t change that fast, so it is hard to know; but that could be one factor.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Dave, did you want to respond?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: First, you are absolutely right.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The equilibrium funds rate calculation has no reference to inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It shouldn’t be viewed as a policy recommendation or where the fed funds rate should be.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In essence, it is one transformation of the IS curve interacting with the supply side of the economy—set the real funds rate at that level, and it is designed to deliver the return of the economy to potential in 12 quarters.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, as for the way that we have treated financial stress and its effect on the equilibrium funds rate, we have marked down our estimate of the equilibrium funds rate a huge amount since last August.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: A couple of those big steps really were putting in add factors for our sense of the extent to which financial turbulence and stress were going to depress aggregate spending going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: How do we get that?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have taken some of these principal component measures of financial stress—in some cases, principal components of the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey—and regressed those on the errors in the spending equations, and observed that there is a pretty high correlation between those measures and our spending errors.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’ve tried, as best we could, to build that correlation into our spending forecast, so that when we calculate the equilibrium funds rate, it reflects a much weaker level of spending for any given funds rate than you otherwise would have observed.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The adjustments show up as a lower equilibrium funds rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The second factor that is currently depressing our estimate of the equilibrium funds rate is indirectly related to financial stress.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But in the last forecast, when we shifted to this recession- like scenario, we incorporated additional negative add factors on spending to reflect the observation that, when we are in a cyclical downturn, there tend to be correlated errors across these equations that are related to the cyclical event.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That was a second factor that was leading to the very low estimate of the funds rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So those are, as best as we could, incorporated in those measures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Mishkin first, and then President Bullard.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Is yours on this point?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Then why don’t you take my slot, and I’ll come in after.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is it a regime-switching kind of model in which you enter the recession state—you call it the recession state—and then add-factor down further?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Yes, though that may be putting it too scientifically.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In essence, we were looking at a configuration of data that, at the time of the March meeting, appeared to indicate recession.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Even though we did not have the spending data in hand—and, as Governor Kohn indicated, we still haven’t seen these correlated negative errors on spending yet—we had seen enough other signals in terms of the business and consumer sentiment surveys, the rise in the initial claims for unemployment insurance, and the jump in the unemployment rate that, taken together, suggested to us that there was a likelihood that we were or would be in a recession scenario.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We then added in more negative add factors to account for that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Then, is that calibrated against the 1990–91 recession or the 2001 recession?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Basically, we did an average of the residuals in recessions since 1970.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Oh, is 1980–82 in there?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Yes, 1980–82 is in there.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, the composition of where these residuals are is obviously heavily tilted in this case to housing, some of which is already behind us.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So it isn’t quite as though all of this weakness is prospective.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Some of this weakness we have already had, and so there are very big negative residuals now on housing relative to where you would otherwise have been.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Just to ask Bill a question—first the tall Bill, but the shorter Bill can answer afterward.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On alternative B, you indicated that this would be very much in line with market expectations and, therefore, shouldn’t have much impact.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I was wondering about the statement aspect, in particular the assessment-of-risk part, because this is not just saying that we are doing 25 basis points; it is also saying that we are now in a different mode of operation regarding the cycle.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So where do you think the markets are concerning where the statement would be in this regard?

speaker: ENGLISH
text: In recent days the stories we have been hearing from market participants and observers are that they think there may well be something—maybe not signaling strongly that we’re done but talking about slowing down or possibly a pause.

speaker: ENGLISH
text: So I think this really is pretty close to what is built in.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, a soft pause rather than a hard pause is the way I would think about what the market is looking for.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we have overnight to reflect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will also have the GDP data in the morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m sure that they will be informative.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will reconvene tomorrow at 9:00 a.m.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a dinner and reception, for those of you who would like to attend, and we’ll see you there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we start with the report from Dave Stockton on the data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: 4 We left at your place, and I hope you have found, a GDP advance release for the first quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It came in at plus 0.6 percent versus our Greenbook forecast of 0.4.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It was really very close to our expectations, both for the total and for the individual components.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There were a few small differences.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nonresidential structures, as you can see about halfway down that sheet, are estimated to have been weaker than we were forecasting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think that additional weakness certainly reinforces the story I was telling yesterday about this being an area in which we are now seeing more convincing signs of softness.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Residential investment was not quite as weak as we thought, but I don’t think the difference between a minus 27 and a minus 31 changes the basic tenor of that particular story.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Two small areas for which we had some upside surprises were federal spending and inventory investment, but those surprises were really quite small.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t see anything in this report, quite frankly, on the real GDP side that would cause us to change our basic outlook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, when we get the detail, we might make some minor adjustments to the second-quarter forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As for prices, the final two lines of that table, total PCE came in right as we had expected.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Core PCE was estimated by the BEA to be a tenth higher than we had projected, but that is still ½ percentage point below what we were projecting back in the March Greenbook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So, again, I don’t think that the report that I gave yesterday would be altered by this release.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We also received the employment cost index.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In the release, we get those figures only to one decimal place.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: To one decimal place, we are right on for total compensation—wages and salaries and benefits; in terms of the 12-month change, it was 3.2 percent, and that was what we 4 The materials used by Mr. Stockton are appended to this transcript (appendix 4).

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Wages were a bit higher than we thought—3.2 versus the 3.1 we projected— but benefits came in a little lower than we were projecting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There again, I think the data just basically confirm the story that we are not really yet seeing any signs of pressure on the labor cost side.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, yesterday we had an introductory presentation by Bill English on the alternatives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You will be pleased to know that there have been no further changes in the proposed statements.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So why don’t we take comments now from the participants.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What I would like to do—it will probably come as no surprise—is to make the case for why we should stand pat today and make no change.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My case is built on a number of points, and I’d like to articulate those as best I can.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, as we all know, the economic outlook has weakened since the start of the year, but that deterioration occurred largely between January and March.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Since the March meeting, there has been little change in the Greenbook forecast or in my own outlook for the economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Incoming data over the intermeeting period are consistent with a weak first half but not appreciably weaker than we earlier anticipated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe that easing policy is appropriate in a weaker economy, but continuing to cut rates for as long as the economy remains weak is not appropriate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although it is a difficult task, we must try to calibrate the appropriate level of the fed funds rate with the economic prospects and our policy goals.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I will just note that, since last September, we have lowered the funds rate 300 basis points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This year alone, in a period of less than 60 days, we have cut 200 basis points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is a very aggressive policy of easing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Not enough time has passed, in my view, to see the full effect on the economy of those cuts, and a further 25 basis point cut in the funds rate at this point will do nothing to change the near-term outlook of the economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Second, we are currently running a very accommodative monetary policy, no matter how you look at it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The real funds rate is negative or very negative, depending on which measures of inflation you use to construct it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The nominal funds rate is below the level of most versions of the Taylor rule, even when adjusting for some interest rate and real rate effects, given our objectives.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I noted yesterday, monetary aggregates as measured by M2 and, to some extent, MZM have expanded very rapidly, especially since our rate cuts in late January.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, although none of these measures of monetary accommodation or monetary ease is perfect—each has its drawbacks—I am concerned that all the measures of monetary accommodation suggest that we are very accommodative at the current time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Third, inflation is high, unacceptably high in my view, and has been that way for a sustained period, as I talked about yesterday.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some would argue that the weakened economy will bring the inflation rate down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But theory and experience both say that such will occur only if expectations of inflation remain anchored.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But since the end of last year, most measures of expected inflation have moved up.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The instability in the measures of expected inflation is a cause for concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It suggests to me that markets may be less convinced of our willingness to take the necessary actions that are consistent with sustaining a credible commitment to price stability.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I certainly understand the difference between a relative price shock and inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Clearly, oil prices and other commodity prices are in part a relative price shock.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There is no question about that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But it is also true that in the 1970s one of our mistakes was that we accommodated relative price shocks with very accommodative monetary policy, and in so doing helped convert a relative price shock into sustained inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we should be careful not to fall into the same trap.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Besides, I think that in most monetary models today we worry particularly about stabilizing core inflation because it represents the sticky prices in our sticky- price models.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So if relative price shocks begin to seep into the core, or into the sticky-price elements, monetary theory would suggest that we need to respond to those.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we are going to achieve something close to optimal monetary policy, we should be concerned about that seepage because it may affect expectations and it is part of what monetary policy should be doing, at least in that class of models.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although it is true that we have not seen much in the way of wage inflation to date and that is encouraging, I would also reiterate, as some people noted yesterday, that wage inflation tends to be a lagging, not a leading, indicator of overall inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Contrary to the Greenbook forecast, which has us maintaining a negative real funds rate for two years and inflation coming down, I think that, if we continue easing or maintain the real funds rate well below zero for a period of time despite inflation well above our goal, it is reasonable to assume that expectations will not remain anchored.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The FOMC’s stated goal of price stability cannot remain credible independent of our actions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we want expectations to remain well anchored, we have to act in a way that is consistent with that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Fourth, I believe that we are in the fortunate position today of being able to pause.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Market participants have reacted to the incoming data by appreciably tightening their expectations of future funds rate moves—at least as measured by the futures markets, as we have seen.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Participants seem to be getting less comfortable with the idea of very easy monetary policy over a sustained period, given the outlook for inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I note that the markets’ reassessment of their policy expectations over the intermeeting period doesn’t appear to have had any significant negative effect on the markets, or the economy more broadly, during this period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think this reassessment by the markets presents us with an opportunity to reinforce our stated commitment to price stability, not just with words but with action or, in this case, inaction.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think a pause today would send a strong signal of our commitment to price stability, which could further help anchor inflation expectations, which I consider to be very fragile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A pause, it seems to me, balances the risks of the two parts of our mandate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some might argue that, in the midst of the financial market disruptions that we have seen this year, it is important for the Fed not to add to market turmoil by taking policy actions not anticipated by the markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The mean expectation for the markets is for 25 basis points of easing today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But market participants are placing odds of somewhere between 25 percent and 30 percent on our pausing, so I don’t think a pause would be very disruptive to the markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The magnitude of the surprise would be about the same as the surprise we had last time when we cut 75 basis points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That surprise, in my view, did not really cause much turmoil in the marketplace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Finally, when I say that cutting 25 basis points won’t help the outlook for the economy very much, others might respond that cutting 25 basis points won’t hurt it very much either, so why not.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think a cut today will not be a disaster but will contribute to a further eroding of our credibility in the eyes of the public.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At past meetings this Committee has spoken a lot about the need for rapid reversals of our rate cuts that we took out for insurance.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we should not be overly confident of our ability to implement such rapid reversals.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, the lower the rates go, the further we will need to come back when we start taking the accommodation back.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am dubious of our ability because we will be so much further from what might be a more neutral rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In summary, to my mind the gain in credibility from pausing today substantially outweighs any negative effects from slightly disappointing the markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It doesn’t preclude us from choosing to resume cuts at a later date should economic conditions warrant them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: After all, I think this Committee has demonstrated its ability to act aggressively in response to economic conditions, and we can do so again.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But that is the future.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: For today, I think we should take the opportunity that the economy and the markets have afforded us to pause.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As the old Latin expression says, “Carpe diem.” With regard to language, I am happy with alternative C. Rather than the language in paragraph 4 of alternative C, I would prefer the language of paragraph 4 of alternative B. I would just make that the language for paragraph 4 in alternative C—that is the only change that I think would be necessary.

speaker: EVANS
text: I, too, favor maintaining the federal funds rate at 2¼ percent today.

speaker: EVANS
text: The current real interest rate provides accommodative monetary conditions for an economy that is struggling near recession or is in mild recession.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our lending facilities are probably doing as much as can be expected to mitigate the serious and necessary financial adjustments that must be accomplished by the private markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: If the economy takes another serious leg down, our current funds rate setting is well positioned for us to respond promptly, appropriately, and aggressively, if circumstances warrant.

speaker: EVANS
text: A pause today affords us a unique opportunity to wait and see how our recent aggressive actions are influencing the trajectory of real activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: Since markets are putting substantial weight on a 25 basis point easing today, a pause will be a relatively small disappointment.

speaker: EVANS
text: As President Plosser pointed out, that was similar to our March disappointment, which seemed to be all right.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think it is important for us to understand how the economy will respond to a pause in rate-cutting when it does occur.
