speaker: EVANS
text: With high food, energy, and commodity prices, the extended positive differential of headline inflation over core measures risks an increase in the public’s inflation expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: I agree with President Plosser’s discussion of relative prices on that front.

speaker: EVANS
text: From a longer-term perspective, which we don’t really talk about very often, I worry about the asymmetric response of policy to high inflation as opposed to when it is low.

speaker: EVANS
text: When headline inflation is above core inflation, we take on board the relative price adjustment, and then we are content, I would guess, to bring inflation down to our perceived inflation targets.

speaker: EVANS
text: But on the downside, when inflation gets low, we become uncomfortable with certain low inflation settings, and so I fear that we would respond more aggressively, as we did in 2003, which really was a positive productivity environment.

speaker: EVANS
text: If you have an asymmetric type of response, you are going to take on board increases in the price level because of that asymmetry.

speaker: EVANS
text: That’s one reason that I am concerned about these types of behaviors.

speaker: EVANS
text: Although I expect emerging resource slack to temper any adverse inflation developments, the risk is simply growing in importance with every additional policy easing, compared with the economic risks, which presumably are abating as we respond to them with such easings.

speaker: EVANS
text: Calibrating the current policy stance against these divergent economic and inflation risks is important and challenging, as you pointed out yesterday, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that comparisons to the rate troughs in the previous cycles of recession policy are instructive.

speaker: EVANS
text: The current real fed funds rate is somewhere in the neighborhood of zero, or it could be lower if you choose a different way to deflate the funds rate by total inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: I was very impressed with Dave Stockton’s response to my question about what types of factors from financial market stress are embodied in the Greenbook-consistent real interest rate.

speaker: EVANS
text: It seems as though a tremendous amount of care has been taken to introduce some of these special factors in innovative ways, and while they may not capture all facets of that, I thought that they did quite a good job.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I feel a bit more comfortable in making those comparisons, but I do recognize that it is a treacherous period.

speaker: EVANS
text: That said, this is about the same place the real funds rate bottomed out during the jobless recovery with financial headwinds in the 1990–91 recession, and with the data we had in hand at the time during the disinflation concerns in 2003.

speaker: EVANS
text: Both periods were unique in suggesting a high degree of accommodation, and the factors that were at work in each of those episodes were unique.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our attempt to incorporate these factors has been quite useful, and so it’s a reasonable, if not definitive, comparison.

speaker: EVANS
text: With our current lending facilities addressing financial stress, I think our current policy accommodation, now at 2¼ percent, is appropriately similar to those episodes.

speaker: EVANS
text: My final observation has to do with these end-of-cycle expectations and what they might mean for long-term interest rates.

speaker: EVANS
text: If 25 basis points is viewed as additional insurance against downside risks, I just don’t think this action is significant enough to have much of an effect.

speaker: EVANS
text: We expect to take back some portion of the aggressive cuts, especially the ones that have been an attempt to respond to the financial stress.

speaker: EVANS
text: If the financial stress is mitigated to some extent, we should be expected to take that back.

speaker: EVANS
text: Expectations, as in the fed funds futures market, should limit the effect of those actions on long-term interest rates.

speaker: EVANS
text: After all, by the expectations hypothesis, you are going to be averaging these short-term paths into long-term rates.

speaker: EVANS
text: That is one reason that the Committee injected the language “considerable period” back in 2003, to try to convince people that we would do this for a longer period of time and affect long-term rates.

speaker: EVANS
text: So if there is an expectation of some type of rebound, these last insurance cuts might not have that large an effect.

speaker: EVANS
text: Again, I think our lending facilities are better geared for the financial stress.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think we have clearly demonstrated our willingness to provide appropriately accommodative policies in a timely fashion when the economic situation demanded it.

speaker: EVANS
text: For me, the public’s expectation of these actions in that event argues against one further small insurance move.

speaker: EVANS
text: Because we are concerned about inflation risks and have indicated that we must flexibly move toward more-neutral policy stances once the economy and financial markets improve, a pause today is a small down payment on those difficult future actions.

speaker: EVANS
text: In terms of language, if it came to that, I would be comfortable with the language of alternative B with this particular rate action.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I must say that I am sympathetic to the “hold” advocates and the view that we are already accommodative.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think an apt anecdote is a conversation I had in the past six weeks with a cruise line CEO who doesn’t know how to drive his ships but who has in fact been at the helm a couple of times.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: He said, “When you turn the wheel and nothing happens for several miles, the temptation to keep turning the wheel is overwhelming.” So I do have some sympathy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That said, I am going to support a reduction in the target rate of ¼ percent, effectively alternative B, as I indicated yesterday.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think it is pretty clear that we have a tradeoff between “a little more help to the economy” and “enough for now” and really some shift in our focus to combating inflation.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So let me lay out my rationale for not holding.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think there is still substantial downside risk to the general economy, and it may take quite some time for recovery to materialize.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A quarter would help slightly to effect a lower cost of borrowing and, therefore, would stimulate activity, although much of that is really beyond our control.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It will be dictated by market forces.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think that halting today versus conceivably halting at the next meeting risks some interpretation as a lack of recognition of the real state of weakness in the economy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding inflation, I think the core numbers in the first quarter were not overly discouraging, and I have to believe my own forecasts—in many respects, the forecasts I heard— that inflation will soften in the coming months and be consistent with our working view of expectations.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I would say, however, that I am concerned that, in the minds of the general public, high prices actually translate into inflation, whether or not the rate of inflation has flattened.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I have suggested, I am inclined to pause after this move, provided that the incoming data are not too adverse and too divergent from expectations, but with the caveat that I think a lot of shock risk is still out there and we have to remain flexible to deal with surprises.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Holding or signaling a pause may help the housing market a bit by starting to construct a bottom, as borrowers or buyers begin to perceive that they shouldn’t expect any further rate cuts from us.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding the statement, I think the rationale section in alternative B is appropriate to the situation that we face.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Section 3 is a realistic acknowledgement of inflation trends and risk.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I gather that, with the changes in section 4, the question was whether or not to signal a pause or an inclination to pause, and I tend to agree with a more cautious, less committal approach of the proposed language—what yesterday was called a “soft” pause.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I am, on balance, quite happy with the language in alternative B.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, I have given serious consideration to both alternatives B and C, and I think a credible case can be made for either one.

speaker: STERN
text: There are, of course, risks associated with adopting either one as well.

speaker: STERN
text: On balance, I come out in favor of alternative B, for the following reasons.

speaker: STERN
text: First, we are certainly not yet out of the economic woods.

speaker: STERN
text: Although my forecast is for a relatively mild recession, I would not be particularly surprised if it turned out to be both deeper and more prolonged, given, among other things, the persistent overhang of unoccupied, unsold homes and the severity of the financial dislocations of the past nine months.

speaker: STERN
text: As I have tried to emphasize, I think it could be dangerous to underestimate the effects of the financial headwinds now in train and likely, in my judgment, to get more severe.

speaker: STERN
text: Second, and closely related to those observations, financial conditions remain quite sensitive.

speaker: STERN
text: Even if improvement is now under way in some markets, I think it will be some time, as I said yesterday, before credit conditions are fully supportive of economic growth.

speaker: STERN
text: To amplify a bit, I think we need to be a bit careful about the weight we put on the low level of the real federal funds rate per se for, as Governor Kohn pointed out yesterday, the credit situation is a good deal more complicated than that.

speaker: STERN
text: My principal reservation about supporting alternative B has to do with the inflation outlook.

speaker: STERN
text: The news here has not been uniformly bad, especially with regard to core inflation, but I am not convinced that inflation will abate in a timely way without policy action.

speaker: STERN
text: On the other hand, I take some comfort from the fact that apparently financial market participants do not anticipate further reductions in the federal funds rate target beyond this meeting.

speaker: STERN
text: I think the language associated with alternative B should help to reinforce the view that, at a minimum, a pause in the reductions in the target is not that far off, given what we know today.

speaker: STERN
text: I think it important that we find opportunities to bolster that view when we can.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There seems to be a groundswell of opinion in financial markets, and perhaps around this table, that given the easing to date we are at or close to a point where we should pause and assess the impact of both fiscal and monetary stimulus already provided.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Should we pause at a fed funds rate below 2 percent, at 2 percent, or over 2 percent?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Greenbook forecast assumes that we pause at 1¾ percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With this degree of stimulus, core and total PCE inflation is at or below 2 percent in 2009, but the unemployment rate remains well above the NAIRU, even at the end of 2010.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Boston forecast generates similar outcomes.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Greenbook and the Boston forecasts suggest that 25 basis points at this meeting may not be enough.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Both forecasts imply that a significant degree of slack remains in the economy, even with a 25 basis point reduction at both this and the following meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In addition, there are significant downside risks to the outlook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Falling asset prices in other countries have frequently been accompanied by prolonged periods of weakness.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Finally, given the rise we have seen in the LIBOR rate, for many borrowers a 25 basis point decrease leaves policy no more accommodative than at our last meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The consensus seems to be that we should be moving in smaller increments.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But if we choose option B, it is not at all clear to me that we should pause after this meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In that regard, I was happy to see the revised language in the Bluebook table 1, which does not imply that our easing cycle has definitely ended.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While I hope that the economy recovers sufficiently that further easing is not necessary, we need to remain flexible, particularly given that our models indicate that even with further easing we are likely to experience several years of elevated unemployment rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think I can be brief by just associating myself with the comments of President Stern.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is a difficult decision.

speaker: KOHN
text: You could make a case for either of these.

speaker: KOHN
text: But on balance, I think we should be lowering interest rates 25 basis points, as under alternative B.

speaker: KOHN
text: As President Stern said, I don’t think just subtracting past inflation from the nominal federal funds rate is a good metric for where the stance of policy is today.

speaker: KOHN
text: It would be if financial conditions were consistent with historical relationships, but they’re not.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have very tight credit conditions in many sectors of the market, and a zero or negative federal funds rate means a very different thing today than it did even in the early 1990s, Gary, because then you had the banking system broken but the securities markets working.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now you have the banking system broken and the securities markets not working very well.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think we have stronger—I guess Greenspan called them “50 mile an hour”—headwinds.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would say they are 60 or 70 today, at least for now.

speaker: KOHN
text: We expect the headwinds to abate; and as they abate, policy will look a lot more accommodative.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I don’t think we really have insurance right now against the contingency that the headwinds don’t abate very quickly or even get worse, or against the contingency that the staff is right and we are entering a recessionary period in which consumption and investment fall short of what the fundamentals would suggest.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that 25 basis points probably won’t buy us much, if any, insurance, but it will get policy calibrated a little better to the situation that we are facing today.

speaker: KOHN
text: I expect a small decrease in the funds rate to be consistent with further increases in the unemployment rate—and everybody does, I think, judging from the central tendencies of the forecast—which will put downward pressure and help to contain inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that there is an upside risk from continued increases in commodity prices that feed through, as President Plosser noted, into core inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that this is a very different situation from the 1970s.

speaker: KOHN
text: I looked this morning at the Economic Report of the President, at those tables in the back.

speaker: KOHN
text: The stage for the 1970s was set in the 1960s.

speaker: KOHN
text: Core inflation rose from 1½ percent in the mid-1960s to 6¼ percent in 1969.

speaker: KOHN
text: That’s a situation, obviously, in which inflation expectations can become unanchored, and then these relative price shocks feed through much more into inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: Looking in the Greenbook, Part 2, page II-32, every measure of core inflation for 2007 was lower than the measure of core inflation for 2006, and half of them—these are Q4-to-Q4 measures of core inflation—are lower than for 2005.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we are not in a situation of a gradual upcreep in core inflation, which I think was what set the stage for the 1970s.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t expect a small decrease in interest rates to result in higher inflation through this dollar–commodity price–inflation expectations channel either.

speaker: KOHN
text: The decrease in interest rates is already in the markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: If anything, a statement like alternative B might firm rates a bit; and taking out “downside risks” and “act in a timely manner” reinforces the notion that the Federal Reserve is not poised to ease any more.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wouldn’t expect interest rates to go down; therefore, I wouldn’t expect the dollar to go down, and I wouldn’t expect commodity prices to go up from this.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the markets reacted very well over the intermeeting period to incoming data.

speaker: KOHN
text: They saw the tail risk decrease.

speaker: KOHN
text: They put a U shape in our interest rate path.

speaker: KOHN
text: It seems to me that path is very close to what many of us said we expected and thought was appropriate, give or take ¼ point, for the federal funds rate over the coming couple of years.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t see any reason to act in a way that changes those expectations; I think the market expectations are fine.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wouldn’t lower interest rates ¼ point just to confirm market expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it is the right thing to do, and I don’t see any reason to lean against it to change expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that expectations are lined up pretty well with our objectives.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, Mr. Chairman, I was listening very carefully to Governor Kohn, as I do the rest of my colleagues.

speaker: FISHER
text: I noted your comment that it doesn’t buy us much.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m worried that it may cost us much.

speaker: FISHER
text: Had I gone first, I would have made arguments similar to those of President Plosser and President Evans.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am in favor of a pause.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that is pretty clear.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to stress a couple of things I mentioned yesterday because I think they’re important.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am concerned about our costs regarding what I call a different kind of adverse feedback loop, which is the inflation dynamic whereby reductions in the fed funds rate lead to a weaker dollar and upward pressure on global commodity prices, which feed through to higher U.S. inflation and to cutbacks in consumption by consumers and actions by employers to offset the effects of inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I quoted a CEO, whom I consider to be very highly regarded, regarding his company’s behavioral patterns.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is someone, by the way, who was in the business in the 1970s.

speaker: FISHER
text: He said, “We’re learning to run a business, once again, in an inflationary environment.” That quote bothers me because it shows a behavioral response.

speaker: FISHER
text: This goes beyond the issue, but I thought that comment you made yesterday about relative prices, Mr. Chairman, was very interesting.

speaker: FISHER
text: But it shows a behavioral response, and behaviors eventually become habits, and habits become trends, and I’m worried about that.

speaker: FISHER
text: There was a period when I felt that we were at risk of a repetition of the 1930s.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think the liquidity measures that we have taken—which I have fully supported, and I applaud you, Mr. Chairman, and the New York group for thinking these through with the staff—have provided the bridge that we spoke of yesterday.

speaker: FISHER
text: Don, you mentioned the 1970s.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am no longer worried about the 1930s, although I think there are tripwires out there that are very, very serious.

speaker: FISHER
text: You pointed to them in your intervention.

speaker: FISHER
text: You are right; under Bill Martin these pressures were put in place.

speaker: FISHER
text: But somebody mentioned yesterday—it may have been Vice Chairman Geithner—that he wasn’t around in the 1970s.

speaker: FISHER
text: I actually sat by President Carter’s side when he got lectures from a left- wing socialist named Helmut Schmidt and by a right winger named Margaret Thatcher.

speaker: FISHER
text: Their points were that you cannot risk appearing to be complacent about inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I worry that we risk appearing to be complacent about inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am speaking within the family here, but I sense that we are giving that appearance on the outside.

speaker: FISHER
text: The question really is, Is it worth ¼ point?

speaker: FISHER
text: What is the risk–return tradeoff here?

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t think it’s worth cutting ¼ point.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it is worth staying where we are.

speaker: FISHER
text: I know that the markets anticipate X or Y.

speaker: FISHER
text: We had a conversation about that yesterday.

speaker: FISHER
text: I made my living in the markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: The markets come and go, and I am happy to hear Governor Kohn say that we are not influenced by the markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t think we should be.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I just don’t feel the risk–return tradeoff makes it worthwhile for a ¼ point cut here unless we saw evidence of substantial downside slippage beyond what we are all discounting for housing, which is very negative.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have spoken about a price correction of 35 percent from peak to trough, and we’re not there yet.

speaker: FISHER
text: It would have to be more negative than that to convince me to cut rates further.

speaker: FISHER
text: So, Mr. Chairman, I respectfully submit that we should pause, and that’s how I plan to vote.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I favor alternative B with the wording that has been proposed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I do appreciate that there is a case for alternative C as well, and I understand and appreciate the arguments that have been made in favor of it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the pure economic merits, I definitely support a 25 basis point cut.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I noted in my comments on the economic situation, it appears that the economy has stalled and may have fallen into a recession.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I share the same concerns as Governor Kohn and President Stern.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My forecast is close to the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think a further easing in financial conditions is needed to counter the credit crunch, and I believe that a cut in the federal funds rate will be efficacious in easing financial conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although the real federal funds rate is accommodative by any usual measure of it, I completely agree with Governor Kohn’s discussion of this topic.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This is a situation in which spreads have increased so much and credit availability has diminished so much that looking at the real federal funds rate is just a very misleading way of assessing the overall tightness of financial conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I consider them, on balance, to be notably tighter than they were in the beginning of August.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t agree that further cuts in the federal funds rate will be ineffective in helping us achieve our employment goal or counterproductive to the attainment of price stability over the medium term.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given that a 25 basis point cut is what the markets are now anticipating—it is built in—I would not expect this action, coupled with the language in alternative B, to touch off further declines in the dollar or to exacerbate inflationary expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That said, I did see arguments in favor of alternative C as well.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I can see some advantage in doing a little less today than markets are expecting as long as we reaffirm that we do retain the flexibility to respond quickly to further negative news with additional cuts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A case that could be made for pausing is that we will soon get information relating to GDP in the second quarter and get a better read on just how serious the downturn is.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to market and inflationary psychology, I also can see a case for doing less than markets expect.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is true that some measures of inflation expectations have edged up a bit, and I would agree with President Fisher that perhaps a pause would counter any impression that we have become more tolerant of inflation in the long run.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I don’t think we have become more tolerant of inflation in the long run, and I did see today’s reading on the employment cost index as further confirmation that at this point nothing is built into labor markets that suggests that we are developing a wage–price spiral of the type that was of such concern and really propelling the problems in the 1970s.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the other hand, I agree with President Plosser, too.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Wages aren’t a leading indicator.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have to watch inflationary expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I don’t think that is definitive.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Nevertheless, I do find it quite reassuring that nothing is going on there at this point.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think doing nothing today might mitigate the risk of a flight from dollar assets, which could exacerbate financial turmoil.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So there are arguments in favor of alternative C, and I recognize them.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But, on balance, I believe that the stronger case is for B.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The FOMC is badly in need of a stopping rule on the federal funds rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Continued reaction to bad economic news—and there is likely to be bad news in the coming months—is going to set up serious future problems for this Committee.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The fragile credibility of the Committee is being eroded as we speak, and we will do well to take steps to reassert inflation-fighting resolve at this meeting.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The intuition in dealing with the current crisis is that we can use new lending facilities to help return financial markets to more normal operation and that interest rate policy is not that likely to help on this dimension.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But exceptionally low rates can create new problems.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Since lower rates are not really helping directly with the smooth operation of financial markets, I suggest that we put that on hold for the time being and let our past, stunningly aggressive, interest rate moves have an effect through the summer and into the second half of the year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This would be consistent with alternative C in the policy alternatives.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Many participants have emphasized that there will be a long unwinding process.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The Chairman described us as being in the third inning on this, similar to the late 1980s and early 1990s.

speaker: BULLARD
text: During that episode, the Fed went on hold at 3 percent, considered an exceptionally low rate at the time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That gave financial markets a chance to heal following the S&L problems without creating other problems for the mid to late 1990s.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In retrospect, this policy worked quite well during that era, and it seems to me that something similar could be done today at the current level of the federal funds rate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, I’m glad that reasonable people can differ.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I do continue to hold the view that easing policy today is a mistake.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If I were voting on it, I would vote to hold where we are.

speaker: HOENIG
text: With the fed funds rate at the level it currently is, I think that continuing to ease policy in an environment of rising inflationary pressures gives serious erosion to our long-run credibility.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We are seeing increasing signs that inflation expectations are rising.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I see it constantly, as the public’s inflation psychology is changing as well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: This change reflects the large, sustained now, increases in food, energy, and other commodities and accelerating import prices.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am concerned that maintaining at this highly accommodative policy level for an extended period, while it may bring some short-run stimulus into the economy, increases inflationary risk to an unacceptable level, which will, over the not-too-distant future, begin to distort long-run investment decisions and continue to increase the risk of financial instability and imbalances in the longer-run.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Finally, on the psychology of the markets, holding rates constant, although it might disappoint some on Wall Street, will please many, many on Main Street.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I judge that it will confirm to the world that we are turning our attention to these longer-run issues, and I’m disappointed that we’re not seizing the opportunity to make that statement.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My concerns about the real economy are similar to those that I had in March.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I continue to believe that residential real estate markets could deteriorate even further than what I have in my baseline projection and could exert even greater downward pressure on business activity.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Financial markets in my view are still fragile, and larger or more-widespread liquidity pressures could quickly present us with an even weaker set of economic fundamentals.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At the same time, I can’t easily dismiss the ongoing escalation of energy and commodity prices.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Although many of us, as we talked about yesterday, have expected these price pressures to abate for some time, they have not; and as I indicated yesterday, I do believe there is a risk that core inflation will not follow the downward path that I submitted as my projection for this meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So like others, I can see a case being made for alternative C. However, I think a modest reduction to our policy rate today as a precaution against further slippage in the real economy is prudent.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But I also strongly support the language that indicates we’re very close to, if not at, a pausing point in our easing cycle.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I support the policy recommendation and the language in alternative B.

speaker: LACKER
text: I find myself agreeing with my colleagues who have advocated alternative C. One way to think about our approach to the policy decision today is to look ahead and think about the probabilities associated with two bad outcomes.

speaker: LACKER
text: Will the economy go into a substantially deeper recession than we expect?

speaker: LACKER
text: Or coming out of this recession, will the trailing inflation rate be higher than it was when we went in?

speaker: LACKER
text: Although I hope neither of these occurs, my sense right now is that the chance of an increase in trend inflation is more likely than a much deeper recession, and I think we should alter our policy path accordingly.

speaker: LACKER
text: The incoming data since the beginning of the year have resulted in a more adverse outlook, and that change in the outlook is already, in my view, reflected in the current stance of policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I noted yesterday that the real federal funds rate using the Greenbook’s inflation forecast rather than four-quarter lagged core inflation is now between minus ½ and minus ¾ percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it makes sense to take advantage of information about foreseeable gaps between overall inflation and core, and the stance of policy strikes me as very stimulative, certainly plenty for the recession we now expect, when we look at back historical recessions.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I noted yesterday, at the retail level for firms and consumers, spreads aren’t out of line with where they’ve been in past recessions.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is true that jumbo mortgage rates and some other rates have not come down as much as they’ve come down in past recessions, but I just remind people of the secular technology shift.

speaker: LACKER
text: There’s a sort of level shift in intermediation technology that we’re going through right now that really constitutes a change in the relative prices of different financial assets.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, I can’t think clearly about the stance of policy without talking first about the risk-free rate and then thinking about various spreads as really having to do with the relative prices of different financial claims.

speaker: LACKER
text: So in looking at and through retail rates, that’s informative.

speaker: LACKER
text: But the risk- free rate is the risk-free rate, and an array of factors affects how those relative financial prices evolve.

speaker: LACKER
text: The securitization channel that seemed to work very well for a while is now exposed as more costly and less efficacious than once was thought.

speaker: LACKER
text: Some of these securitization vehicles didn’t exist in past recessions or expansions, and only a couple of decades ago these spreads were as high as or higher than they are now.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I stick to thinking about the stance of monetary policy in terms of the real risk-free rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think our experience between the January and the March meetings with inflation expectations is pretty good evidence of their fragility in the current environment without our having articulated what our long-run objective is for inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think that the level of inflation expectations is aligned with our objectives; I think it is too high relative to our objectives.

speaker: LACKER
text: Market participants see a good chance of our dropping the rate ¼ point today and reversing field later in this year and raising rates again.

speaker: LACKER
text: I suspect they don’t fully grasp how difficult it’s going to be to reverse course while we negotiate the murky waters of the recovering economy later this year.

speaker: LACKER
text: Indeed, I think that the fiscal stimulus that we’re going to get will make those waters even murkier.

speaker: LACKER
text: It will be even harder to divine the underlying, ex-fiscal-policy strength of the economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: So for these reasons, I believe that we should leave the fed funds rate alone today.

speaker: LACKER
text: The upward surprise at our last meeting did not appear to affect financial markets adversely.

speaker: LACKER
text: Coupled with that statement’s emphasis on inflation risks, it did seem to have the beneficial effect of reversing the run-up in inflation expectations.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would expect that leaving the funds rate alone today would have a similar beneficial effect in stabilizing inflation expectations.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I favor alternative C, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: WARSH
text: I can support alternative B, but I must admit I can’t do it with the conviction that I would prefer to have.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think market participants will look at our decision today and at the data over the next few weeks and try to measure whether we can hold up to the pause language that accompanies alternative B.

speaker: WARSH
text: Taking action with a 25 basis point move today, we have to then be prepared to stomach the continued weakness in the real economy that is in many of our projections.

speaker: WARSH
text: Speaking for myself, I’d say we also have to be prepared when we next meet to hold the line even if we see a retracing of some of the improvements in financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: So in my own base case, the judgment when we next meet will be a harder one.

speaker: WARSH
text: The economy might look weak; financial markets might look weaker than they are; and trying to signal to the markets in alternative B that we are serious about holding the line at what would then be 2 percent is putting a pretty hard task on us.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we’re capable of holding the line there, but we have to hold ourselves to that standard.

speaker: WARSH
text: The 25 basis point move, in and of itself, doesn’t strike me as that consequential.

speaker: WARSH
text: What strikes me as consequential is the symbolism.

speaker: WARSH
text: Given the uncertainties that Dave and the team have spoken about, it strikes me that the 25 basis points is not nearly as consequential in effect as what might well happen to the transmission mechanism and the efficacy of this change in federal funds rates on the real economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: Put differently, if the financial markets can get back to business, they will be helping the real economy, in effect lowering the cost of capital far more than our actions would today.

speaker: WARSH
text: As I said, I think the symbolism here does matter.

speaker: WARSH
text: By moving 25 basis points today, we’re taking some risks with the dollar.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that the dollar improvement we have seen over the past several days and weeks has occurred because there’s an expectation that we are closer to a pause and that this Committee is going to have a tougher decision about whether or not to move than they had anticipated some weeks ago.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even though the language in alternative B is useful in trying to lay the factual predicate for a pause when we next meet, there will be a lot of folks who will be wondering about our convictions there, and when they do, I think we are assuming some dollar risks.

speaker: WARSH
text: We are also assuming incremental risks on the inflation front.

speaker: WARSH
text: Continued easing could well encourage the perception that the FOMC has a greater tolerance for inflation than is prudent, with potential adverse effects on inflation expectations, a further run-up in commodity prices, and a continued decline in the foreign exchange value of the dollar.

speaker: WARSH
text: So this is a tough judgment that we’re making, with significant uncertainty.

speaker: WARSH
text: I take comfort in believing that the language in the minutes and the remarks that we all offer between now and the next time we meet will suggest not that this is a cut with a dovish pause but that this is a cut with an expectation of holding after our actions today.

speaker: WARSH
text: We are not barring all events because we can certainly imagine the world turning yet again and we can certainly imagine another let-down, particularly in the global economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: But this is a statement that we want to hold after our action today and that we are prepared to stomach some additional bad news with respect both to the economy and to financial markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As many speakers before me have said, this is a pretty close call, and reasonable cases can be made for both alternative B and alternative C. If you look at financial market conditions, you can see your favorite indicator and say whether things have eased or not eased.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One indicator that I look at when thinking about the transmission of monetary policy is the LIBOR–OIS spread, which has gone up very significantly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A lot of short- term borrowing is priced off of that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we wanted just to keep policy where it was six weeks ago, we would actually have to cut more—not that I’m suggesting that we should.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But if you use that spread as the relevant indicator, it would suggest that, if one were to keep the same stance, or potentially the same stance, of monetary policy, you’d have to cut a lot.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It doesn’t seem as though our liquidity facilities have been effective on this particular dimension.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We had been hopeful that they would be, but they don’t seem to be.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Even with some of the things that we voted on yesterday, we’re still going to see very elevated spreads in some of these markets, still making borrowing costs relatively high and so disrupting the traditional monetary transmission mechanism.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So that’s where I would argue for alternative B.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Another argument for alternative B is the potentially protracted slowdown.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I agree very much with President Stern.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I’ve talked about a lot before, this sort of slow burn is related to the housing market.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The repair and recovery of those markets is going to take a long time.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The spreads are still quite elevated in a number of these markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So providing more cushion against the downside risk there for those markets and then thinking about how that risk affects the potential for broader downside risks, in which the housing market seems to be a potential trigger point for negative nonlinear dynamics, again suggests that moving down 25 basis points now is prudent.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The key, of course, that people have been talking about is inflation pressures going forward—inflation expectations.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Here a case can be made on either side with some cogency.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One challenge we have right now is that we have a lot of differences in the way to read inflation expectations.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Looking at the five-year-ahead versus the five-to-ten-year-ahead, we’ve seen them spread apart quite a bit and now start to come back together, with the next five years starting to move up but the five-to-ten-year-ahead moving down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have a number of other measures of expectations, some of which have moved up quite significantly but maybe primarily because of some relative price movements rather than underlying inflation trends.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One thing that is comforting for me on the alternative B side is that during the last year to 18 months, when we have had very low—below 5 percent—unemployment rates, we have seen very little evidence of high wage pressure.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I find it unlikely that it is going to increase as the unemployment rate goes above 5 percent, and I think, as many people around the table do, that unemployment may sustain itself above 5 percent for quite some time.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We also haven’t seen some of the real shocks to energy and commodity prices feed through to core.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now, that still could be coming.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we’ve seen very elevated prices in these areas for quite some time—six to nine months—and the most recent readings from the PCE index suggest that they haven’t fed through.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Maybe that is still to come, and I think to be worried about that is reasonable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is also reasonable to be worried about implications for the dollar if we were to go for alternative B rather than alternative C. But the language in alternative B can provide some comfort to the markets that we are unlikely to be pushing much further, given what we see and what we expect, but that we are open to that possibility.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We certainly have a very long time between this meeting and the next meeting.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’re going to be getting two employment reports, GDP, and a lot of other information, so we may need to revisit some of these issues.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But at this point I would come down for alternative B with the language that we have.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it gives us the appropriate flexibility, and I don’t see sufficient evidence of an unhinging of inflation expectations or actual inflationary pressures, at least with respect to core, to say that we need to take a pause now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Well, I’m in a very uncomfortable position here because I usually like to be very decisive, and I think in all past cases I’ve had a strong view before going into the meeting in terms of what is the appropriate alternative that the Committee should take, at least that I should take.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m in a very uncomfortable position because I’m actually sitting exactly on the fence between alternative B and alternative C. As you know, sitting on the fence and having a fence right in that anatomically uncomfortable position is not a good place to be.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So let me go through the current situation and argue why I’m in this uncomfortable position.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The first point to make is that inflation expectations are actually reasonably well contained.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is true that I have a concern that high headline inflation could make containing inflation expectations and preserving the nominal anchor more difficult.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But it is important to note that we have been in a situation in which we’ve had very high headline inflation and, in fact, core inflation and inflation expectations have behaved very well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So it’s very important to emphasize that this is not the 1970s, and I really get disturbed when people point to that as a problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We do have to worry about inflation expectations possibly going up, but it’s not a situation that, if we make a mistake, they go up a whole lot.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: They could go up, and it might be costly to get them down, but it would not be a disaster.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second issue is that, although we may have turned the corner, we are still in a situation of very fragile financial markets, and we have been disappointed before.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am getting more optimistic.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m hopeful and think it’s very possible that we’ll look back at the middle of March and say that was the worst of it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But there is a possibility, and it’s not a small possibility, that things could go south again, and that would argue for the need for aggressive cuts in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The third thing that I point out about the situation is that the modal forecast given by the Greenbook—and consistent with my modal forecast and with the modal forecasts of most of the participants—suggests that we may have to cut a bit further in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the problem is that, given the conditions that we face, we need a lot of flexibility to deal with potential downside risks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think the downside risks have diminished, but they could go back up again.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So there could be a situation in which we need to ease aggressively in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, we’ve convinced the markets that we are non-gradualists, but so far we’ve been non-gradualists in only one direction, which is to ease.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, we’d like to be in a situation where we could aggressively ease in the future if we had to but not risk having inflation expectations go up.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s a very serious problem that many participants have pointed out.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So how would I like the markets to perceive us?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Well, I’d like the markets to perceive us as being willing to be very aggressive in terms of easing, if necessary; but I’d also like them to perceive us as having the Volcker characteristics of being six feet, six inches, tall and having a big baseball bat and, if inflation and inflation expectations are starting to unhinge, being willing to take out the baseball bat and do whatever is necessary.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You really would like to position yourself to have those characteristics.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So let me first talk about the case for alternative C of not changing and then go to the case for alternative B.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In the case for C, the advantage of pausing at this point is that it would actually indicate to the markets by our actions that we’re serious about keeping inflation under control and that it’s more likely that we would bring out the baseball bat.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that sense, it could enhance credibility, and a very important, positive element of that is that it would be easier for us to be flexibly aggressive if we needed to be so in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is one reason that I think there is a strong case for alternative C. But I also think there is a strong case for B.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: First, the evidence that inflation expectations are unhinged or are likely to get unhinged is not very strong.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do not put a lot of stock in consumer surveys.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I tend to look at financial markets as being the canary in the coal mine.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Though being a New Yorker, I actually have been in a coal mine [laughter] – at the Museum of Science and Industry in Chicago.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: All of you should go there someday when you go visit Charlie.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But he has never seen a canary.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have seen a canary.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But the key is that the canary has not keeled over.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, if you look at what’s going on in the financial markets, the concerns in terms of inflation compensation have dissipated somewhat.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think the fact that they were moving up is an indication of greater inflation risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: They’ve come back down again.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t think that should make us complacent, but I do think it tells us that we haven’t seen anything really bad happen at this stage.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the question is why we should cut now and go with alternative B rather than C. Well, first, I think the modal forecast suggested that a cut is in line with optimal monetary policy, and I think that’s an important argument.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is particularly so because there is a very strong likelihood that, even though I’m a little more confident that the recession that we’re probably in now will be very mild, if it’s even a recession at all—I think it is likely that we’re in a recession but a mild one—the recovery actually is going to have a lot of the characteristics of the recovery that we had in the 1990s because it’s just going to take a long time to clean up this mess.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That again argues for a cut.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The other issue that I think is important is that there is a very long period between now and the next FOMC meeting.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Given that the modal forecasts indicate that things are likely to get worse in the economy in this quarter, there is an issue that, if we get bad news, then we might regret not having cut now, and I’m not a big fan of intermeeting cuts.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That would be another argument for cutting now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I guess the bottom line is that I’m just in a very uncomfortable position in that I dislike being not very decisive here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One thing that has helped me a lot in being comfortable with alternative B is that the language has changed quite significantly from the initial wording.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I was not happy with the idea that, if we suggest that there will be a pause in the future, it would be time dependent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It should be clearly data-dependent.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If it were time-dependent, we would get into exactly the problem that Charlie Evans talked about: We want the flexibility of saying that what we’re doing is dependent on data, not time, because if people know that you’re going to reverse things later on, it doesn’t have the impact.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that is an important change here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I’m quite comfortable with the language of alternative B. I’m willing to support B.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It looks as though that is the consensus, and my view today is that I’m going to go with whatever the consensus is.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The transcript says, “Mishkin says canary wheezing but hasn’t keeled over.” I support alternative B. I think you could frame this as a modest recalibration of policy with a hawkish soft pause.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think the canary is wheezing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Look, I think there are lots of good arguments on both sides of this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think all the good ones have been made.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The markets have been giving us a pretty good test against the concern, which I think we all share, that if we move today we risk some significant erosion of our inflation credibility or inflation expectations feeding through the dollar into a commodity price spiral.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have had a pretty good test of it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Over the past several weeks, there has been a very substantial shift in expectations for the path of the fed funds rate, which embody substantial expectations around a near-term cut and very little beyond that and some modest retracing as we go forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Expectations have come down despite what has happened to oil prices.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The dollar is stronger on net over that period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is pretty good validation that the path that is represented in alternative B does not come with excessive risk that we will be eroding our credibility.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We can’t know for sure.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s good to be worried about that risk, but the protection against that risk is fairly good.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What strikes me about this discussion is the extent of the gap in this Committee in how we think about the way to measure the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What we could do is use a seminar and a bit of history on this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It would be nice to run monetary policy back over the past four decades to see, if it had been set with a basic policy regime in which we looked only at the real fed funds rate deflated by headline inflation today, what the outcomes would have been for the economy at that time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That’s essentially what you guys are saying.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It seems to me that you are basically saying that equilibrium doesn’t vary and that deflating the nominal fed funds rate with some mix of headline and core today is the best way to judge the stance of policy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think it’s worth having a little exercise in it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is hard to look back.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Make sure that you say you’re speaking for yourself, not for me, in terms of how I think about policy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Okay, but it is a surprising gap.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I think it would be worth some time to think through that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Obviously we also disagree about how inflation works in the United States, how relative price shocks take effect, and what we should respond to in that sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That would be worth a little time, too.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, it is a surprise to me.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We sit here to make monetary policy, and we haven’t talked much about this basic core question: How should we judge the stance of policy?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It would be worth some attention.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just want to end by saying something about the dollar.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My basic sense about the dollar— and I’m very worried about this dynamic now—is that it has been trading more on concern about tail risk in the economy and in the financial system than anything else.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As I said yesterday, if you look back to when there has been an increase in perceived tail risk, however you want to measure it—credit default swaps on financials or something like that—and the two-year has fallen sharply or we have had a big flight to quality, those have been the periods that have been most adverse to the dollar.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Now, it is not a consistent pattern, but I think it’s basically right; and I think it gives an important illustration that what goes into a judgment about whether people hold dollars and U.S. financial assets has to do with a lot of things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It has a lot to do with confidence that this Committee will reduce the tail risk in the financial system and the economy to tolerable levels.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It also has a lot to do with confidence in our willingness to keep inflation stable over a long period, but it’s not only that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, we have had a pretty good experiment in that proposition over the past year or so.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My sense is that the biggest risk to the dollar, since I’m pretty confident that this Committee is going to make good judgments about inflation going forward, is in the monetary policy of other countries.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The real problem for us now is that we have a large part of the world economy—in non- China, non-Japan Asia and the major energy exporters—still running a monetary policy that is based on the dollar as nominal anchor.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That has left them with remarkably easy monetary policy and a pretty significant rise in asset-price inflation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The transition ahead for them as they try to get more independence for monetary policy and soften the link to the dollar is going to carry a lot of risk for us because the market is going to infer from that a big shift in preferences for the currencies that both governments and private actors in those countries hold.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As that evolution takes place in their exchange rate and monetary policy regimes the risk for us is that the market expects a destabilizing shift in portfolio preferences, which people might infer is also a loss of confidence in U.S. financial assets.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that’s a big problem for us.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s not clear to me that it means that we should run a tighter monetary policy against that risk than would otherwise be appropriate because I don’t think it buys much protection against that risk.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just want to associate myself with all the concerns said about the dollar in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The judgment that goes into confidence and people’s willingness to hold U.S. financial assets is deeply textured and complex, and it has a lot to do with confidence in this Committee’s capacity to navigate the perilous path between getting and keeping down that tail risk and preserving the confidence that inflation expectations over time will stay stable.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I support alternative B and its language.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The discussion was very good as usual, and let me just assure you that I listened very, very carefully.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I’m certainly hearing what you’re saying, and I understand the concerns that people have expressed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I play Jekyll and Hyde quite a bit and argue with myself in the shower and other places.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me first say that I think we ought to at least modestly congratulate ourselves that we have made some progress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our policy actions, including both rate cuts and the liquidity measures, have seemed to have had some benefit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the fear has moderated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The markets have improved somewhat.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I said yesterday, I am cautious about this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s a good chance that we will see further problems and further relapses, but we have made progress in reducing some of the uncertainties in the current environment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I also think that there’s a lot of agreement around the table—and I certainly agree—that we have reached the point where further aggressive rate-cutting is not going to be productive and that we should now be signaling a willingness to sit, watch, and listen for a time, for two reasons.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, risks are now more balanced.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is, there is more attention to inflation risks and dollar risks, and although our output risks remain quite significant, the balance is closer than it has been for some time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, given that we have done a lot in a short time and moved aggressively and that we’re seeing fiscal actions coming in and perhaps other policy effects as well—lagged effects of our own actions— it seems to be a reasonable time for us to pause, to watch carefully, and to presume that we’re not going to move unless conditions strongly warrant it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that, at least in that broad respect, there’s a lot of agreement around the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The two alternatives that have been discussed by most people are B, which is to move 25 basis points today but to send a fairly strong signal of a preference to pause after this meeting, and C, which is not to move but to keep some elements of the downside risk alive in our risk assessment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Like a number of people, I think both are plausible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Alternative C, in particular, has the appeal of pushing back against some critics on the inflation side who have criticized us for not being sufficiently attentive to the dollar, to commodity prices, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I said yesterday, I think that inflation is an important problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s a tremendous complication, given what is happening now in the other parts of the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In no way do I disagree with the points made by many participants that inflation is a critical issue for us and that we have to pay very close attention to it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I said yesterday, I do think that some of the criticism that we are getting is just simply misinformed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think there’s any plausible interest rate policy that we can follow that would eliminate the bulk of the changes in commodity prices that we’re seeing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think they are due mostly to global supply-and-demand conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A small piece of evidence for that is that yesterday the ECB was mentioned favorably as having the appropriate inflation attitudes compared with our attitudes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would just note that headline inflation in the euro zone is about the same as it is here, despite their stronger currency, because they are being driven by the same global commodity prices that we are.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would also say that, although the inflation situation is a very important concern, I don’t see any particular deterioration in the near term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Since the last meeting, oil prices have gone up, which is very high profile, but gold, for example, has dropped about 12 or 13 percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other precious metals are down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some other commodities are down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: TIPS breakevens have moved in the right direction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Wages, as we saw this morning, are stable, and I would urge you to compare wage behavior over the past five years with wage behavior during the 1970s.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Wage growth then was not only high but also very unstable and responsive to short-term movements in headline inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think the canary is still getting decent breath here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want us to be careful not to overpromise.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We cannot do anything about the relative price of gasoline, and I don’t think that we’re on the edge of an abyss of the 1970s type.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think it’s an important issue, and I do think that there is benefit to pushing against the perceptions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In this business, perceptions have an element of reality to them, and we understand that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s an important part of central banking, and I fully appreciate that point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So again, I see a lot of merit in the alternative C approach.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I think you can conjecture, I’m going to recommend alternative B—25 basis points but with a stronger indication of a pause.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me discuss why in the end I come down on that side.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First is the substance, the fundamentals.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think that 25 basis points is irrelevant.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, one-month LIBOR is up about 35 basis points since our last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: These short-run financing costs do matter, particularly in a situation of financial fragility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is not just an issue, as President Evans mentioned, of long-term interest rate expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Overnight and short-term financing costs do matter for the financial markets, and a lower rate will help the markets to heal.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It will affect other rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To take an obvious example, it affects the adjustable rate that mortgages move to in the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think there’s a case to be made on the substance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will not add much to the discussion about how we define “accommodative.” But one way to do it, I guess, is to look at the Greenbook’s very thorough analysis, which rather than using rules of thumb attempts to look at a broad forecast conditional on what the staff can ascertain about the financial drags that we’re seeing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Their analysis suggests that something around where we are or a little lower is consistent with slow economic growth but also price stability within a relatively short time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is one way of trying to calibrate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, there are other ways as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second point I’d make, besides just the substance, is the consistency with our own projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Virtually everybody around the table still thinks that the downside risks to growth are significant, and we’ve mentioned the same factors—financial conditions, housing, and a few other things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those remain very serious downside risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think anybody thinks they are under control at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yes, we also see an increased number of people with upside risks to inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But again, in terms of the numbers we’ll publish, I think the downside risks are still held by more people than the inflation assessment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That, by the way, suggests why we can’t really do what President Plosser suggests—hold and move to the alternative B, paragraph 4, language.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Not to move and to say that the risks are balanced would, I think, be clearly inconsistent with the risk assessments that are in the projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other issues have to do with communications.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are at an important transition point in our communication strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One of the risks that we took when we made the very rapid cuts in interest rates earlier this year was the problem of coming to this exact point, when we would have to communicate to the markets that we were done, that we were going to flatten out, and that we were going to a mode of waiting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It was always difficult to figure out how that was going to work in a smooth way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Whether through luck or design, market expectations have set up perfectly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I mean, basically they’re now assuming a flat path going forward, with some increase later; and that appears to be consistent, as Vice Chairman Geithner noted, in the last few days with significant dollar appreciation, declines in commodity prices, and declines in inflation expectations—all the things that we want to see.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It appears that we’re in a position that had seemed really problematic some time ago, so we are now able to make the transition in a way that will be relatively clear and, I hope, not too disruptive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, I want to come back to the issue of disappointing markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with President Fisher and many others that disappointing markets can be a good thing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is certainly not always a bad thing, by any means.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the issue is a little more subtle than that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The issue here is the clarity of what we’re trying to say and the way our message is going to be read.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me make two points about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we were to do alternative C, I think there would be essentially two issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that, although we would not be moving, which would be a surprise, we would also not be declaring a pause because of downside risk, which would be another surprise.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’d have a surprise both in the action and in the statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The risk there is that we confuse the markets about what our intentions are and what would cause us to respond.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, the Greenbook’s projections of Friday’s employment numbers are somewhat more pessimistic than those being held in the market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we took action C today and Friday’s numbers were consistent with the Greenbook forecast and with our own projections but worse, significantly worse, than the market expectation, would statement C then lead to the building in of additional ease?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there would be a lot of confusion there—a lot of uncertainty about what exactly we are saying about when we’d be willing to respond.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other communication issue that I have with alternative C—and this, again, is something President Fisher said yesterday—is that if we don’t move and we put C out there, the stock market could go up because it might be read as saying that the Fed has increased confidence, is seeing things looking better, and is feeling stronger about the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m not sure that really is the assessment we have, and if we then have bad data on the labor markets and the financial markets weaken somewhat, will we be seen as having made a wrong call, as being blindsided by circumstances?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is more discussion than it’s worth, but what I’m trying to convey is that it’s not just a question of disappointing or not disappointing markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s a question of whether or not we’re sending a clear message.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think alternative B, while it’s consistent with our risk assessments, is also a pretty strong statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me, just for what it is worth, assure you now that data that come in within the general, broad ranges of what we’re expecting, even though they will be weak, should not cause us to ease further, given this statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I believe that this statement will provide us with plenty of cover.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: No matter what the markets expect, we have said that we have come to a point at which we need to take a pause, we need to see what’s happening, and we are going to be watchful and waiting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to the language, I just want to point out how much the language in alternative B has moved from March.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It really is a very significant change.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First of all, we are acknowledging explicitly how much we have already done—the substantial easing of monetary policy to date plus the measures to foster market liquidity—and expressing a general confidence implicit in that first sentence that we have done a lot; that it is likely to help; and therefore, that we should wait and see what happens.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, we removed any reference to downside risk to growth, which has been in there for a long time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s a very strong statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That says a lot about our inclinations going further.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Third, we’ve added the phrase “continue to monitor,” which to me suggests very much a watchful waiting rather than an active approach to developments in the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, we have made it clear that we are going to be data dependent and, in particular, though we have done a lot, we are expecting continued weakness, and we’ll act as needed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we have taken out the “timely manner,” so the presumption that we’ll be responding in a very rapid and aggressive way, I think, has been moderated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think of alternative B as being a compromise in the sense that it takes a step that is consistent with the fundamentals in terms of the underlying tightness of the financial system and the risks that most of us see to economic growth as well as inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At the same time, I think it is a rather strong step in expressing a shift in our strategy—that we are moving from the phase of rapid declines and aggressiveness to a phase of waiting and observing how this economy is going to evolve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, with full respect to everyone’s comments, I understand.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unlike Governor Mishkin, I wasn’t sitting on the fence; I thought that was a little uncomfortable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I understand the concerns and the arguments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The communication issues did concern me, and largely on that basis, I would advocate B today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, could you please take a roll call?

speaker: DANKER
text: This vote encompasses the language of alternative B in the table that was handed out as part of Bill’s briefing yesterday, as well as the directive from the Bluebook.

speaker: DANKER
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: DANKER
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with reducing the federal funds rate to an average of around 2 percent.” Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes President Fisher No Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes Governor Mishkin Yes President Pianalto Yes President Plosser No President Stern Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will ask the Governors to join me in the office for the discount rate decision.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Everyone else, why don’t you take a 20-minute coffee break.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The meeting that we are about to begin is a joint meeting of the FOMC and the Board, so I need a motion to close the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The discussion is about interest on reserves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me turn to Brian.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 5 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We will be referring to the package of material labeled “Implications of Interest on Reserves for Monetary Policy Implementation.” Today, the staff will report on work prompted by two changes the Congress made to the Federal Reserve Act in October 2006 and will seek your guidance on further work.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Both changes become effective in October 2011.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown on page 2, the first change allows the Board to authorize the Reserve Banks to pay interest on balances maintained by depository institutions at an interest rate or rates not to exceed the general level of short-term interest rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The second allows the Board to set required reserve ratios on transaction deposits within a range of 0 to 14 percent rather than the currently mandated range of 8 to 14 percent, permitting the Fed effectively to eliminate reserve requirements if it chooses.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: These two changes will allow the Federal Reserve to make significant improvements in its approach to monetary policy implementation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: They give us an opportunity to reduce distortions and deadweight losses resulting from our current complex system of reserve requirements.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: They also give us an opportunity to improve the effectiveness of monetary policy implementation in routine circumstances as well as in conditions of financial stress.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 5 The materials used by Messrs. Madigan, Meyer, Clouse, Hilton, and Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 5).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: While the Congress made important changes in the law, it also left some key statutory constraints in place.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As discussed on page 3, if the Board chooses to retain reserve requirements, the law continues to allow them to be imposed only on transaction deposits, nonpersonal time deposits, and Eurodollar liabilities and only on depository institutions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In effect, the law continues to enshrine a system of reserve requirements that was designed to facilitate control of M1—an objective that has had little relevance to the conduct of U.S. monetary policy for a quarter-century.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Second, the prohibition against paying interest on demand deposits remains in force and is a significant continuing distortion in the U.S financial system.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We continue to work with congressional committees and staff to seek opportunities for the repeal of this prohibition.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Third, the law retains significant constraints on the assets that the Federal Reserve can purchase in the open market.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Fourth, interest on reserves has potential implications for priced services and for Reserve Bank operations more generally.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, the Federal Reserve remains unable to pay explicit interest on balances held at the Federal Reserve by the Treasury and by foreign central banks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Page 4 summarizes the steps we have taken to date in our work on interest on reserves.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Shortly after the legislation was passed, the Chairman asked the staff to begin background work.

speaker: MADIGAN
