text: Last year, a System workgroup undertook a preliminary study of a range of options for implementing monetary policy given the new authorities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I’d like to recognize the participants in that workgroup, who made remarkable progress during a period in which some of these individuals were experiencing considerable pressures relating to the implementation of monetary policy that day, not just in five years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: These individuals included Jim Clouse, Seth Carpenter, John Driscoll, Sherry Edwards, David Mills, and Travis Nesmith from the Board; Spence Hilton, Leo Bartolini, Chris Burke, Todd Keister, Antoine Martin, and Jamie McAndrews from the New York Fed; Ron Feldman from Minneapolis; Steve Meyer from the Philadelphia Fed; and Huberto Ennis and John Weinberg from Richmond.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Separately, a System workgroup co-headed by Don Hammond here at the Board and Ron Mitchell at the Boston Fed has begun work on the implications for priced services of paying explicit interest on balances.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In February, the Board hosted a workshop on monetary policy implementation; five foreign central banks and the Federal Reserve participated.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown on page 5, our briefing today is in four parts.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: After this introduction, Steve Meyer will present a summary of the Federal Reserve’s current approach to implementing monetary policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Next, Jim Clouse and Spence Hilton will discuss five options for implementing the new legislative authorities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, Bill Dudley will make a number of concluding comments and present our recommendations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown on page 6, we will be seeking your comments on the criteria that we have tentatively adopted for evaluating the options; on the options themselves; and on the process and timeline that we are tentatively proposing for this project.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One of the key issues is whether you would be prepared to see reserve requirements reduced to zero.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Steve will now continue our presentation.

speaker: MEYER
text: As Brian noted, I will summarize our current approach.

speaker: MEYER
text: As indicated on page 7, I will discuss depository institutions’ demand for central bank balances, how the Desk manages the supply of balances, and outcomes in the federal funds market.

speaker: MEYER
text: There are three components of demand.

speaker: MEYER
text: Some depository institutions (DIs) hold balances to satisfy the reserve requirements shown on page 8.

speaker: MEYER
text: Many more hold contractual clearing balances, and some routinely hold excess reserves.

speaker: MEYER
text: Page 9 notes that DIs can meet their reserve requirements by holding currency, by holding balances at a Reserve Bank, and by holding deposits at a correspondent that holds an equal amount at a Reserve Bank.

speaker: MEYER
text: These assets earn no interest, so DIs have an incentive to reduce their required reserves to the level of vault cash and reserve balances they would choose to hold if there were no requirements.

speaker: MEYER
text: In practice, DIs cut required reserves by using sweep programs that shift deposits out of transaction accounts into linked nonreservable accounts.

speaker: MEYER
text: This stratagem works because the Fed applies reserve requirements to end-of-day, post-sweep, deposits.

speaker: MEYER
text: About half of the DIs have no reserve requirement.

speaker: MEYER
text: A large majority of the remainder meet their requirements entirely with vault cash.

speaker: MEYER
text: Only 1,500 DIs hold balances to meet reserve requirements, so last year required reserve balances averaged less than $7 billion, an amount equal to 0.1 percent of total deposits in the U.S. banking system.

speaker: MEYER
text: Economists claim that central banks impose reserve requirements to ensure a sizable demand for central bank balances.

speaker: MEYER
text: Imposing a high required reserve ratio on a narrow deposit base and then allowing DIs to run sweep programs and use vault cash to meet reserve requirements does not achieve that goal.

speaker: MEYER
text: More than 7,000 DIs have accounts at Reserve Banks.

speaker: MEYER
text: On an average day, they use their accounts to make and receive more than 0.5 million interbank payments with a value of roughly $2.5 trillion.

speaker: MEYER
text: As noted on page 10, many of those DIs need a larger balance to avoid frequent overnight overdrafts than to satisfy reserve requirements.

speaker: MEYER
text: About 5,700 choose to hold a contractual clearing balance.

speaker: MEYER
text: The incentive to maintain a contractual balance is that such balances earn implicit interest that offsets the fees a DI incurs when it uses our priced services.

speaker: MEYER
text: But these “earnings credits” cannot be paid in cash, so DIs that do not use our services have no incentive to hold a contractual balance.

speaker: MEYER
text: Page 11 shows that DIs hold a bit less than $7 billion of contractual clearing balances.

speaker: MEYER
text: The rough equality with required reserve balances is coincidence.

speaker: MEYER
text: Required and contractual balances, though small, facilitate the implementation of U.S. monetary policy in two ways, as indicated on page 12.

speaker: MEYER
text: First, required and contractual balances are set before the start of each reserve maintenance period, so they establish a predictable lower bound on the period-average demand for balances.

speaker: MEYER
text: Second, DIs are allowed to meet reserve requirements and contractual balance commitments on average over multi-day reserve maintenance periods.

speaker: MEYER
text: This averaging feature helps make the demand for balances interest elastic.

speaker: MEYER
text: DIs reduce the opportunity cost of meeting requirements by holding smaller balances on days when the fed funds rate is above target and larger balances on days when the funds rate is below target.

speaker: MEYER
text: Carryover provisions and clearing bands, which give DIs some flexibility to hold too many or too few balances in one maintenance period and the opposite in the next period, also help make the demand for balances interest elastic.

speaker: MEYER
text: Page 13 summarizes the third component of demand for balances: desired excess reserves.

speaker: MEYER
text: Large DIs usually aim to hold zero excess reserves on average.

speaker: MEYER
text: Small DIs as a group generally hold positive excess reserves.

speaker: MEYER
text: The left half of the graph on page 14 illustrates that the daily sum of required, contractual, and excess reserve balances averaged about $15 billion from January through July of last year but varied between $10 billion and $25 billion.

speaker: MEYER
text: The day-to-day variation largely reflects big banks’ behavior: Big banks want much larger balances on days when an unusually large volume of payments flows through their Federal Reserve accounts than on other days.

speaker: MEYER
text: This strategy lowers their risk of incurring overnight overdrafts on high-payment- flow days while reducing their opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing balances on other days.

speaker: MEYER
text: The right half of the graph shows that demand for balances has oscillated even more widely since August.

speaker: MEYER
text: Even at $25 billion or more, DIs’ balances are not big enough to clear $2.5 trillion of Fedwire payments per day without incurring overdrafts.

speaker: MEYER
text: Indeed, DIs make heavy use of daylight credit.

speaker: MEYER
text: At least in theory, ready availability of inexpensive daylight credit reduces DIs’ demand for central bank balances.

speaker: MEYER
text: A proposed reduction in the cost of collateralized daylight credit—the proposal is now out for public comment—may further reduce demand for balances.

speaker: MEYER
text: We turn next to the supply of balances, beginning on page 16.

speaker: MEYER
text: You’ve told the Desk to keep the federal funds rate close to target on average.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Desk does so by trying to make each day’s supply of balances equal to the quantity that DIs would demand that day if the funds rate were at target.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Desk’s strategy is to use outright purchases or sales of Treasury securities, plus 14-day and 28-day repurchase agreements, to supply a level of balances somewhat lower than the minimum amount the banking system is likely to demand going forward.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Desk then uses one- to seven-day repo to supply the remainder.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Desk structures its operations so that maturing repo almost always leave the supply of balances short of the quantity demanded and then undertakes a new repo to fill in the gap.

speaker: MEYER
text: But as indicated on page 17, the Desk does not completely control the supply.

speaker: MEYER
text: Unanticipated changes in autonomous factors can make the supply of balances larger or smaller than projected.

speaker: MEYER
text: The staffs at the Board and in New York do a very good job, but not a perfect job, of predicting changes in these factors.

speaker: MEYER
text: Variations in borrowing from the primary dealer credit facility also affect the supply of balances.

speaker: MEYER
text: For example, Citigroup Global Markets borrowed on 20 of the first 25 business days that the PDCF was in operation, in amounts that varied from $0.5 billion to $2.7 billion.

speaker: MEYER
text: Barclays Capital borrowed on 21 days, in amounts that ranged from $1 billion to $7 billion.

speaker: MEYER
text: Four other primary dealers were frequent borrowers; another six borrowed less often.

speaker: MEYER
text: Changes in PDCF credit are not always captured in the staff’s daily projections, so they can, and do, cause the supply of balances to deviate from the intended level.

speaker: MEYER
text: In any case, if the day’s projected supply is not close to the forecast of quantity demanded, the Desk conducts an open market operation to make the two roughly equal.

speaker: MEYER
text: As noted on page 18, the Desk was in the market almost every business day—indeed, all but six business days—from January 2006 through July 2007, replacing maturing repo with larger or smaller repo as projections showed a need to add or to drain balances.

speaker: MEYER
text: How well does this approach to implementing monetary policy work?

speaker: MEYER
text: If the key criterion is keeping the funds rate close to target, our current approach works well in normal times and not so well when interbank markets are under stress.

speaker: MEYER
text: But our current approach imposes substantial and unnecessary burdens.

speaker: MEYER
text: As the graph on page 20 indicates, the effective fed funds rate is almost always within a few basis points of target during normal times, as it was from January through July of last year.

speaker: MEYER
text: But there have been many larger-than-usual deviations from target since last August, for two primary reasons.

speaker: MEYER
text: First, daily variations in demand for balances have become larger and more difficult to forecast.

speaker: MEYER
text: Second, demand apparently has become less responsive to temporary deviations of the funds rate from target—that is, demand has become less elastic.

speaker: MEYER
text: Even so, the average of daily deviations from target has been close to zero since mid-September.

speaker: MEYER
text: Pages 21 and 22 summarize equilibrium in the federal funds market and the reasons for large deviations from target.

speaker: MEYER
text: Fed funds typically trade near the target early in the morning because buyers and sellers usually expect the Desk to supply enough balances to get the funds rate to target in the afternoon.

speaker: MEYER
text: But the funds rate sometimes is firm or soft in early trading, signaling a likely shortage or surplus of balances and leading the Desk to aim for a somewhat larger or smaller supply than otherwise.

speaker: MEYER
text: After the Desk conducts the day’s operation, three things happen concurrently: The supply of balances responds to changes in autonomous factors and PDCF credit; the demand for balances is realized as DIs make and receive payments; and DIs trade federal funds, determining the day’s average or “effective” funds rate.

speaker: MEYER
text: If the supply of balances is close to the actual quantity demanded and if the payment system and the federal funds market work normally, the funds rate will be close to target.

speaker: MEYER
text: Any excess demand or supply generally does not become apparent until late in the day, when the Desk is unable to adjust the supply of balances because primary dealers no longer have uncommitted collateral.

speaker: MEYER
text: DIs that end up with larger balances than they want late in the afternoon seek to sell fed funds.

speaker: MEYER
text: When the banking system as a whole has sizable excess balances, DIs that try to sell fed funds late in the day find few buyers.

speaker: MEYER
text: Because balances earn no interest, the funds rate can fall to zero in that situation.

speaker: MEYER
text: On the other hand, an excess demand for balances makes the funds rate rise relative to target.

speaker: MEYER
text: If the funds rate climbs sufficiently above the primary credit rate, some DIs overcome their reluctance to borrow, raising the supply of balances and helping limit the increase in the funds rate.

speaker: MEYER
text: Last August provides an interesting case study.

speaker: MEYER
text: The demand for balances rose as DIs sought greater liquidity.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Desk increased the supply.

speaker: MEYER
text: Even so, the funds rate traded firm relative to target almost every morning as European banks bid aggressively for fed funds to lock in dollar funding before the end of their business day in Europe.

speaker: MEYER
text: The firm morning rate suggested a shortage of balances.

speaker: MEYER
text: But late in the day in New York, the funds rate often fell well below target as domestic banks that held larger-than-normal balances during the day tried to sell fed funds rather than hold big non-interest-bearing balances overnight.

speaker: MEYER
text: While our current regime keeps the funds rate close to target on average, it imposes sizable and unnecessary burdens.

speaker: MEYER
text: As noted on page 23, DIs use real resources to run sweep programs and to carefully manage each day’s balance in their Federal Reserve accounts.

speaker: MEYER
text: While those efforts generate private gains, they are a waste from a social perspective.

speaker: MEYER
text: Even with sweep programs, the opportunity cost of holding unremunerated reserve balances averaged about $360 million per year during the past two years.

speaker: MEYER
text: In addition, the banking system and the Federal Reserve spend many millions of dollars each year to ensure and monitor compliance with complex reserve requirement rules.

speaker: MEYER
text: As indicated on page 24, our current approach to implementing monetary policy has strengths: It usually keeps the funds rate close to target, and it supports an active interbank market.

speaker: MEYER
text: But our current approach also has shortcomings: It allows occasional large deviations of the funds rate from target even in normal times and more-frequent large deviations when interbank markets are disrupted.

speaker: MEYER
text: Our approach is less than transparent; even well-informed market participants sometimes are surprised by the Desk’s daily operations, and there was widespread misunderstanding of the Desk’s actions last August.

speaker: MEYER
text: Finally, our current approach imposes burdens that simply are not necessary to enable the Desk to keep the funds rate close to target.

speaker: MEYER
text: Theory and foreign experience suggest that it is possible to reduce the shortcomings of the current U.S. approach to implementing monetary policy without sacrificing its strengths.

speaker: MEYER
text: Jim Clouse and Spence Hilton will now discuss a range of options for improving the U.S. approach.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted on page 25, the Interest on Reserves Workgroup developed a set of options for monetary policy implementation in the United States based on alternative settings for a small set of core structural elements.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The first core element—so-called balance targets—is a central feature of many systems.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: In the United States, Japan, Switzerland, and the euro area, balance targets are established through mandatory reserve requirements.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: In the United Kingdom, balance targets are established through voluntary contractual arrangements.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Other countries, such as Canada and Australia, operate with no formal balance targets.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Target bands are a second structural element incorporated in many systems to afford banks some flexibility in meeting their targets.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The carryover provisions for required reserves and the clearing band for required clearing balances play this role in the United States.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The structure of the maintenance period is another core structural element.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As Steve noted, the U.S. system operates with a mixture of one-week and two-week maintenance periods.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The United Kingdom and the euro area operate with maintenance periods that correspond to the interval between monetary policy meetings.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Central banks like the Bank of Canada and Reserve Bank of Australia that operate without balance targets implicitly operate with a one-day maintenance period.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Finally, most systems involve some form of interest rate corridor with the upper bound of the corridor established by a standing lending facility and the lower bound set by the rate of remuneration on excess reserves or a redeposit facility.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted on page 26, market developments may, at times, impair the efficacy of one or more of these core structural elements.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: For example, the standing lending facility should, in theory, establish a cap on interbank rates.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: However, the presence of stigma in using the standing lending facility can impair the effectiveness of the cap.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: That certainly seems to have been the case in the United States over recent months.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: We have observed depository institutions regularly bidding for funds in the market at rates above the primary credit rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The table at the bottom reports some evidence on this score culled from data on Fedwire transactions.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Over recent weeks, many of the largest banks in the country have executed numerous trades for sizable amounts at rates well above the primary credit rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: It may be possible to redesign the discount window to mitigate stigma to some extent, but it appears likely that stigma will continue to be an issue for the discount window, especially during periods of financial distress.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As a result, systems that rely heavily on a standing lending facility to establish an upper bound on the federal funds rate implicitly disadvantage those institutions that are most wary about using the discount window.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As you can see in the table, that set of institutions in the United States includes many that are critical providers of liquidity across a range of markets.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: It is noteworthy in this regard that Citibank in the past has been willing to provide liquidity in the funds market by borrowing primary credit and relending the proceeds in the funds market.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: However, in recent weeks, Citi has seemed reluctant to pursue this strategy and has, in fact, executed more than 100 trades from late March through last week in sizable amounts at rates above the primary credit rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Indeed, the three largest banks in the country— shown in the first three rows—all appear to be quite wary about using the discount window.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted on page 27, it is helpful, broadly speaking, to think about the five options discussed in the paper as falling into two basic categories—systems that incorporate a multiple-day maintenance period and systems in which depositories manage their reserves to meet a daily reserve objective.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The multiple-day systems— options 1 and 2 in the paper—rely on arbitrage across days of a maintenance period as an important factor contributing to day-to-day funds rate stability.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Single-day systems tend to rely more heavily on standing facilities and the structure of remuneration rate(s) on reserves to stabilize the funds rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The next few slides focus on multiple-day systems.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted on page 28, option 1 considers a straightforward modification of our current system of monetary policy implementation.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Required reserve balances would be remunerated at a rate close to the target funds rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The primary credit facility, in theory anyway, would establish the upper bound of an interest rate corridor.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The lower bound of the corridor would be established by paying interest on excess reserves at a rate appreciably below the target funds rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The solid line in the picture displays what the demand for reserves might look like on the last day of the reserve maintenance period.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The curve would be downward sloping and might entail some precautionary demand for excess reserves.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The reserve demand curve on previous days in the maintenance period—the dotted line—would be much flatter at the target rate over a wide range, reflecting the ability of banks to substitute balances across days of the maintenance period in meeting reserve requirements.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Eventually, though, at very low levels of balances, the increased risk of an overnight overdraft would push the intraperiod demand curve up to the primary credit rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: At high levels of balances, the intraperiod demand curve would eventually fall to the remuneration rate on excess reserves as banks recognized that they held excess balances that could not be worked off by the end of the maintenance period.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The width of the “flat portion” of the intraperiod demand curve tends to narrow over the maintenance period as the scope for substitution diminishes across the remaining days of the period.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: In this structure, the Desk would operate much as it does today, supplying an aggregate quantity of reserve balances each day to address both daily demands and maintenance-period average needs.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted on page 29, option 2 in the paper is a multiple-day system based on voluntary balance targets rather than mandatory reserve requirements.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: This system would share many of the key structural elements of the system for monetary policy implementation employed in the United Kingdom.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Depository institutions would establish a voluntary balance target that they would agree to meet, on average, over a maintenance period.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The maintenance period could be set equal to the interval between FOMC meetings.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The system could include a target balance “band” to afford banks some flexibility in meeting their voluntary target balance.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As shown on the right, the demand for reserves on the last day of the period would again be downward sloping, and the Desk would supply an aggregate quantity of reserves equal to the quantity demanded at the target funds rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Reserve management and the funds market under this option probably would be similar to that for option 1.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The longer maintenance period might allow depository institutions more scope for substitution of balances across days of the maintenance period.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: That could imply less need for daily fine-tuning of balances and greater funds rate stability.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: A key issue, however, is whether the aggregate quantity of voluntary balance targets would be large enough to provide adequate leeway for effective arbitrage across days of the maintenance period.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Many banks might choose not to establish a voluntary balance target in this system, and those that do may not choose to establish a large balance target.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: In this case, the funds rate could be fairly volatile within the interest rate corridor.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted on page 30, option 3 in the paper—the simple corridor—is similar to the systems employed by the Bank of Canada and the Reserve Bank of Australia.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Banks would not need to establish a balance target of any sort and would simply manage their accounts each day to balance the opportunity cost of holding reserves against the risk of overnight overdrafts.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The system would involve a fairly narrow symmetric funds rate corridor.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted in the figure, the Desk would supply reserves each day equal to the quantity demanded along the downward sloping portion of the demand curve.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Because the demand curve is likely to be fairly steep, shocks to reserve supply are likely to result in significant volatility in the funds rate within the corridor.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted earlier, the heavy reliance on the primary credit facility to establish an upper bound on the funds rate may be suspect, especially during periods of financial distress.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted on page 31, option 4 in the paper is a system similar in many respects to that employed by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Key structural features of this system include an asymmetric interest rate corridor and a relatively high level of balances to ensure that the funds rate trades near the floor of the interest rate corridor.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As in option 3, depositories would not need to establish a balance target of any sort.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The reserve demand curve for this system might look like that shown to the right.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: At low levels of balances, the demand curve would be downward sloping reflecting precautionary demands for balances to avoid overnight overdrafts.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: But at sufficiently high levels of balances, the risk of overnight overdrafts should become very low, and the demand curve would asymptote near the floor of the funds rate corridor.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: It is difficult to estimate the level of balances that would be necessary to reach this point, but an aggregate level of balances on the order of $50 billion would probably be sufficient in most cases.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: In principle, fluctuations in various factors affecting reserves would not have much effect on the funds rate, and the generally high level of balances could reduce daylight overdrafts.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Partly because of the experience in New Zealand, there are questions about incentives for strategic behavior in this structure.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted on page 32, option 5 is a hybrid single-day system that would involve a voluntary daily balance target and a relatively wide target band.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Depositories would receive full remuneration on balances maintained up to the upper bound of the target band and would be penalized for any shortfall in balances below the lower bound of the target band.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: With these structural elements, the reserve demand curve should be fairly flat at the target rate over a wide range, but the curve would be downward sloping near the upper and lower bounds of the target balance band.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The Desk would presumably operate by targeting a quantity of balances each day near the middle of the target band.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As with option 2, a significant issue with option 5 would be whether depositories would choose a high enough level of voluntary balance targets to allow the target band to play the desired role in stabilizing the federal funds rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As noted on page 33, the paper also identifies a number of general issues that cut across all the options.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: First, depository institutions will still be subject to statutory limitations on their ability to pay interest on demand deposits.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As a result, the Federal Reserve’s initiative to pay interest on reserves may be seen by correspondent banks as unfair competition.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: There are also technical issues associated with the setting of the remuneration rates on reserve balances that appropriately account for the essentially risk-free nature of balances held with the central bank.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The Federal Reserve would need to work through governance issues associated with all the options.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: In particular, the Board is responsible for setting all remuneration rates on balances, and this would need to be closely coordinated with the FOMC’s determination of the target federal funds rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Finally, many if not all the options discussed would likely require some transition period that would need to be carefully managed.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Spence will now discuss some of the pros and cons of each option in more detail and how they stack up relative to key objectives.

speaker: HILTON
text: We have identified four critical objectives for a new operating framework, which are listed on page 34 of your handout.

speaker: HILTON
text: These are (1) to reduce burdens and deadweight loss associated with the current regime, (2) to enhance monetary policy implementation, (3) to promote efficient and resilient money markets, and (4) to promote an efficient payment system.

speaker: HILTON
text: For each of the five options that Jim has just presented, I am going to describe what we see as the major advantages and disadvantages of each vis à vis these objectives.

speaker: HILTON
text: I will also highlight some important sources of uncertainty that we have about how some of these options might function in practice.

speaker: HILTON
text: Then I will close with a broad assessment of how the five options measure up against each of these four objectives.

speaker: HILTON
text: The key advantages and disadvantages of option 1—remunerate required and excess reserve balances—are listed on page 35.

speaker: HILTON
text: This option would have the advantage of being relatively easy to implement given that it would build largely on elements of the current operating framework and would simply pay interest on reserve requirements and, at a lower rate, on excess reserves.

speaker: HILTON
text: The basic framework, which consists of an interest rate corridor with reserve requirements and maintenance periods, is widely used by other central banks, and we’re pretty certain how it would function in practice.

speaker: HILTON
text: For central banks that have adopted this basic framework, it has proven to be reasonably effective for controlling short-term interbank rates under a variety of circumstances.

speaker: HILTON
text: However, this option would do little to reduce the administrative burdens associated with our current regime.

speaker: HILTON
text: This framework is also somewhat rigid, particularly in the flexibility it would provide to us and to banks themselves to adjust the level of requirements in ways that would facilitate monetary policy implementation.

speaker: HILTON
text: A particular shortcoming is that many depositories active in the interbank market have a very small base of deposits against which requirements of any level could be assessed.

speaker: HILTON
text: An important source of uncertainty with this option is whether it would lead to a significant increase in total required operating balances, which would be helpful for damping interest rate fluctuations that can arise when requirements are very low.

speaker: HILTON
text: However, the Fed would have some power to influence the aggregate level of requirements by raising requirement ratios.

speaker: HILTON
text: Option 2—voluntary balance targets—(shown on page 36) would lead to some reduction of administrative costs and burdens compared with the current framework (option 1), as relative simplicity would be one of the principal design objectives for a new system of voluntary reserve targets.

speaker: HILTON
text: The basic framework is similar to that of option 1.

speaker: HILTON
text: It consists of an interest rate corridor with maintenance periods but substitutes voluntary targets for reserve requirements.

speaker: HILTON
text: As already noted, this basic framework has proven to be reasonably effective for controlling overnight interbank rates where it has been adopted.

speaker: HILTON
text: Furthermore, a new system of voluntary targets could provide all DIs with considerable flexibility for setting their own level of targets and for adjusting the size of these targets, a feature that banks might find useful during periods of heightened uncertainty or stress.

speaker: HILTON
text: With this option, there would also be the opportunity to review and totally revamp the length and mechanics of the maintenance period to make them more supportive of monetary policy implementation.

speaker: HILTON
text: However, almost any system of voluntary targets for reserves is bound to impose some administrative costs on both depositories and the Fed, and there may be some tradeoff between administrative simplicity and design flexibility.

speaker: HILTON
text: An important source of uncertainty with this option is that we have yet to identify with precision a system of voluntary reserve targets that would be workable, in the sense of being easy to administer across a large number of DIs with disparate structures, and that would be effective in yielding a total level and distribution of voluntary targets across DIs that would enhance our ability to achieve our operating objectives.

speaker: HILTON
text: Unfortunately, experiences of other central banks offer little guidance in how to design voluntary targets.

speaker: HILTON
text: A particular risk that concerned the Bank of England when it designed its voluntary target scheme was the potential for market manipulation that a new system might offer individual banks if they were entirely free to choose their level.

speaker: HILTON
text: Option 3—simple corridor—(on page 37) would go about as far as possible toward eliminating administrative burdens by doing away with all requirements and maintenance period accounting rules.

speaker: HILTON
text: This option should also keep the overnight interbank rate within a narrower range than the other options, assuming that we adopt a narrower spread between the discount rate and the interest rate paid on excess reserves.

speaker: HILTON
text: Experiences of other central banks that have adopted this kind of operating system support that belief.

speaker: HILTON
text: However, there is also reason to believe that, with removal of the ability of banks to average reserve holdings over a maintenance period, interest rate volatility within the interest rate corridor could be high.

speaker: HILTON
text: We could respond to high volatility within a corridor by further narrowing that corridor.

speaker: HILTON
text: But there is the risk that, at some point as you go in that direction, market participants could use our discount window or interest on excess reserves as a first recourse rather than as a last resort and thus affect the Fed’s role as intermediary and impair normal market functioning.

speaker: HILTON
text: There are some important questions about how effectively a simple corridor system would function in our particular environment.

speaker: HILTON
text: All the options we are considering propose to use the primary credit facility to limit upward movements in market rates.

speaker: HILTON
text: To the extent that this facility might not serve as an effective brake on upward rate movements, the consequences would be greatest for this option because there are no other mechanisms for smoothing interest rates.

speaker: HILTON
text: Some central banks that have a simple corridor framework have also developed arrangements to adjust reserve levels late in the day to prevent exogenous reserve shocks from pushing market rates to either the upper or the lower end of the corridor.

speaker: HILTON
text: Option 4—floor with high balances—is shown on page 38.

speaker: HILTON
text: It would also do away with all requirements and maintenance period accounting rules and, like option 3, would go a long way toward eliminating administrative burdens.

speaker: HILTON
text: Moreover, because the rate effects of even a large aggregate reserve shock or a payment shock at an individual DI are likely to be relatively small, the need for depositories or for the Desk to manage daily reserve positions intensively is likely to be reduced, which should translate to further resource savings.

speaker: HILTON
text: Better insulation of market rates from exogeneous reserve shocks is a design objective, and it is a particularly distinctive feature of this framework.

speaker: HILTON
text: However, completely severing the link between daily reserve levels and interest rate movements can be a double-edged sword.

speaker: HILTON
text: While we may wish to better insulate market rates from reserve shocks, we may also wish to preserve some ability to influence market rates by manipulating reserve supply when other factors are distorting rates.

speaker: HILTON
text: One risk associated with this option is that it would represent a radical departure from the basic elements of our own current framework and from those of almost every other central bank, preventing us from learning from the experiences of other central banks.

speaker: HILTON
text: A particular unknown with this option is the possible implication for the functioning of the interbank market.

speaker: HILTON
text: Offering to compensate DIs for all the reserves they might choose to hold at a rate that is in line with market rates could have profound effects on their willingness to lend in the market, under both normal circumstances and during periods of market stress.

speaker: HILTON
text: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand, one central bank that has experimented with a system similar to option 4, did run into some difficulties with the hoarding of reserves by individual banks to the detriment of the interbank market.

speaker: HILTON
text: As a result, they adjusted their framework to cap holdings of excess reserves by individual banks.

speaker: HILTON
text: Option 5—voluntary daily target with clearing band—is on page 39.

speaker: HILTON
text: It has many of the same advantages and disadvantages as option 2, stemming from the fact that both feature voluntary reserve targets.

speaker: HILTON
text: Because simplicity would be one of the design principles, it should reduce current administrative burdens.

speaker: HILTON
text: It would also provide DIs with the same kind of flexibility that option 2 does for setting and adjusting their own reserve targets.

speaker: HILTON
text: On the other hand, a system of voluntary targets for reserves would still leave some administrative costs, and we have yet to specify a system of voluntary reserve targets that would be workable and effective.

speaker: HILTON
text: An additional advantage of this option is that it could allow the Fed to adjust the width of the daily clearing band around the reserve target.

speaker: HILTON
text: The final choice of clearing band width could be made after some experimentation based on what works best.

speaker: HILTON
text: Moreover, being able to make temporary adjustments to the width of this daily clearing band could be a powerful tool for dealing with exigent circumstances.

speaker: HILTON
text: Experiences of other central banks provide little guidance about how this flexibility might be best employed.

speaker: HILTON
text: But the Bank of England did widen its maintenance period clearing band during the recent financial market turmoil, and they have been happy with the results.

speaker: HILTON
text: Interestingly, the ECB, quite independently, has been examining the possibility of a new system centered on a one-day clearing band rather than a multi-day maintenance period.

speaker: HILTON
text: Let me sum up by outlining how these five options stack up against the four objectives that we have established for a new operating framework, which are summarized on pages 40 and 41.

speaker: HILTON
text: First, all the options would eliminate most of the current “reserve tax” associated with the nonpayment of interest on reserves, and perhaps with the exception of option 1, they would reduce the administrative burdens associated with our current framework.

speaker: HILTON
text: Option 3 (simple corridor) and option 4 (floor with high balances) would do the most to eliminate these administrative costs.

speaker: HILTON
text: Second, all the options would improve monetary policy implementation by helping set a floor on the fed funds rate.

speaker: HILTON
text: Most have additional features that could help control rate volatility, although these differ from one another in terms of their mechanics.

speaker: HILTON
text: But some of the options offer greater potential to adjust parameters in ways that could be helpful amid changing circumstances—say, during periods of market stress or heightened uncertainty about developments that could affect our balance sheet.

speaker: HILTON
text: An adjustable clearing band in option 5 could offer considerable flexibility.

speaker: HILTON
text: Adjustable reserve targets, a feature of both options 2 and 5, are another possibility.

speaker: HILTON
text: Third, all the options would rely on efficient money markets for distributing reserves between DIs.

speaker: HILTON
text: There is more uncertainty, however, about how some of the options might influence the incentive structure for trading and the allocation of liquidity in short-term financing markets and the role of the central bank in that process.

speaker: HILTON
text: This is the case with option 3 (simple corridor), should that corridor be too narrow, and with option 4 (floor with high balances), where the choices of lending excess liquidity in the market versus holding excess reserves would be nearly equivalent.

speaker: HILTON
text: Fourth, all the options are compatible with the proposed changes in payment system policies.

speaker: HILTON
text: However, there are differences among the options in the levels of reserves that would likely be in place and that could serve as a substitute for the provision of central bank daylight credit.

speaker: HILTON
text: Option 4 (floor with high balances) would provide the most reserves in the system, and option 3 (simple corridor) would provide the fewest, perhaps even lower than current levels.

speaker: HILTON
text: A system of voluntary reserve targets, a feature of both options 2 and 5, could be deliberately designed to encourage a relatively high level of reserves.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Building on the earlier presentations, I am going to focus briefly on four areas.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, I’d like to put the interest on reserves project in the broader context of monetary policy implementation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, I will discuss briefly the implications of our experience during the recent market turmoil in terms of how it might influence our choices in this project.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, I’ll suggest some next steps and a potential timeline.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fourth, I’ll focus on the criteria for evaluating the different options and those areas where your guidance will likely be particularly important.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Turning to page 42 of the handout, the issue of paying interest on reserves should be placed in a broader context.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, this project should be considered as part of the process of improving the overall monetary policy framework.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Put bluntly, although the current system works very well during normal times, we have found it recently to be less robust during times of stress.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, we should use this opportunity to strengthen the robustness of the framework.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So what are the weaknesses of the current monetary policy framework?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown on page 43 of the handout, four come immediately to mind.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: (1) In times of stress, the federal funds rate can be very volatile—both day-to-day and intraday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: (2) On the upside, the primary credit facility rate is not a binding ceiling on rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: (3) When there is a large reserve adding miss, the Desk can temporarily lose control of the federal funds rate target to the downside.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: (4) Stability in the federal funds rate may not limit upward pressure in term funding rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Today I’ll focus on the volatility issue and the failure of the PCF rate to be a binding cap.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Two issues are worth noting regarding volatility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, the federal funds rate has become more volatile on a day-to-day basis since last August.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This can be seen on page 44.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the federal funds rate has become very volatile intraday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The exhibit on page 45 shows how wide the range of federal funds rate trading has been recently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The vertical dashed lines indicate the daily range.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Note that the primary credit facility rate has not acted as a firm cap on the upper end of the daily range.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown on page 46, these shortcomings suggest that paying interest on reserves should be considered in tandem with other changes to the overall monetary policy framework.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We should be willing to make significant adjustments to our monetary policy framework so that it is more robust during times of stress.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In this context, although option 1 (paying interest on required and excess reserves) and option 2 (eliminating reserve requirements) are attractive because both would eliminate the reserve tax distortion, they do not do much in terms of making the monetary policy framework more robust.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That said, option 2 has a number of favorable features.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is voluntary and would lessen the regulatory burden.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have considerable experience with this type of framework, so the risks of unintended consequences might be lower than for some of the other options.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Bank of England has been using this framework successfully, and it has proven to be reasonably robust through this period of market turmoil.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Nevertheless, we may wish to be more ambitious.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Turning to page 47, option 5 (voluntary daily target with clearing band) is potentially more robust than option 3 or option 4.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In part, this is because it is very flexible.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This proposal has a number of parameters that can be adjusted—for example, the width of the corridor and the size of the voluntary reserve band.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Thus, this option has the advantage that it could be modified relatively easily in light of experience or in response to changing market conditions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The biggest shortcoming of option 5 is that no other central bank has adopted such a model.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Thus, experience and empirical evidence are lacking compared with the other proposals.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So what is our recommendation in terms of pushing this forward (see page 48)?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As Jim noted in his presentation, the five options can be broken down into two classes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Options 1 and 2 operate in a framework of a multiple-day reserve maintenance period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Options 3, 4, and 5 are single-day systems.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Reserve maintenance periods have both advantages and disadvantages.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Reserve maintenance periods reduce volatility by averaging—which can be a good thing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But there is a cost.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, in single-day systems, each day is a new start, so one avoids the problem of a large shock contaminating an entire reserve maintenance period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This suggests that a reasonable next step might be to develop the best proposal within each of these two broad classes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We recommend focusing on option 2 as the best proposal within a reserve maintenance framework and option 5 as the best proposal in a single-day system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: What would be the next steps (see page 49)?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, we would need to identify workable systems of voluntary targets for reserves needed for either option 2 or option 5.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This would include setting clear objectives for the aggregate size and the distribution across depository institutions and how such a system would be applied to a heterogeneous banking system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, we would need to critically assess the relative merits of maintenance periods versus daily clearing bands.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In this context, we would need to determine the optimal length of a reserve maintenance period and the width of a clearing band.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, we would have to define the optimal width of a rate corridor under both options.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Here we would have to understand the implications for rate dynamics and the functioning of the market during normal conditions and during times of stress.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, we would need to assess whether the options were compatible or could be made compatible with other changes that we might implement, such as changes in our counterparties or in the types of collateral we accept as part of our central bank operations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So what would be a possible timeline between now and implementation in October 2011?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The timeline that I will discuss should be viewed as tentative and subject to revision in light of your comments and further discussion within the Federal Reserve System.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Turning to page 50, we would propose that most of the remainder of 2008 be used for an extensive study of the options.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In May 2008, the staff would publish a white paper on possible approaches for public comment.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In December, the staff would propose a specific approach to the Board and to the FOMC.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Continuing on page 51, the first half of 2009 would be spent filling in the details, with the final proposal published for public comment in August 2009.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rules implementing the proposal would be published by the Board in October 2009.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The final two years would be spent preparing for October 2011 implementation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the last page, we outline areas in which we particularly seek your guidance.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These include the following questions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Do you agree with our metrics for evaluation of the policy options?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, what are the appropriate weights to place on the reduction in burden and distortions versus the other criteria?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Which options should be studied further?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Are you comfortable with our proposed timeline?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, how do you view the interaction of the interest on reserves project with other issues—for example, collateralized daylight overdrafts?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We would now like to open the floor for questions and comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, let me first congratulate and compliment the staff for a really thorough piece of work, both the presenters and all the other people whom Brian mentioned.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is excellent work, particularly under very trying circumstances.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I mentioned that in February a workshop was held here at the Board on monetary policy implementation, which brought together people from major central banks around the world.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there has been a very, very serious attempt to evaluate others’ experience.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you very much for all of that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take some questions first, if there are any.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then anyone who would like to make comments can do so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Hoenig, do you have a question, sir?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Option 1 doesn’t seem to be one of your recommendations, and yet it is something that basically people know how to do.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The idea is to eliminate the pack so that you have the system already in place.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It’s simple; you can learn from it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Why wouldn’t that be one of the options you’d pursue?

speaker: HOENIG
text: I don’t have any real opposition to option 2, but I was just curious because the transition seemed so simple with option 1.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: President Hoenig, I would say that we believe we already have a fairly good sense as to how paying interest on the required reserve balances and on excess reserves would work, at least qualitatively.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We do think it would be an acceptable means of implementing monetary policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As Jim noted, it probably wouldn’t be all that different in terms of monetary policy effectiveness from the way things work now.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, as we also emphasized, the current system of reserve requirements has a lot of problems.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Admittedly, paying interest on required reserve balances in some sense solves the first-order problem, but there are lots of costs associated with the system of reserve requirements that we’ve discussed, and we think that those may warrant serious consideration of eliminating reserve requirements.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But to be clear, we’re not suggesting that we rule out option 1 at this stage.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We could certainly view it as a fallback position, for instance.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’d like to understand this issue in terms of the voluntary targets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: How are they deciding on these?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly a big part of the issue is whether or not they choose you.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I was just completely confused about what their considerations in choosing these numbers would be and what implications that would have.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Now, there is experience for that one case.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m sure you have views on this, but it’s sort of the black box in this proposal, and it’s a really important part of it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second question regards the corridor approach.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do not think it is a good model for us because the countries that use it have very few banks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The issue of using the central bank as a financial intermediary is less of a problem for them because there are fewer guys that they have to look at, and we have to look at a zillion people.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But is it true that they have high volatility?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I just would like to know the facts, but as I say, I don’t think it’s critical.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t think the experience there, even if it worked well, really does tell us that we should do something here.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Maybe I could just take the second question, and Spence or Jim may want to take the first.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On the corridor approach, for other countries that are using it—I’m thinking of the Bank of Canada in particular here—their institutional set-up allows them extremely precise control over the supply of reserves.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also the demand for reserves—I’m talking about reserve balances—is considerably less uncertain than in the United States.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Part of it comes from the fact that they have only a handful of large banks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is five or six banks, right.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So the communication with banks regarding their reserve management is extremely simple compared with what we could expect here in the United States.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The determination of voluntary targets, as Spence mentioned, is a really big issue that we’d have to study much further.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: At least in the context of the simple models, banks will face some probability of an overdraft charge if they are operating with very low balances, so they might have an incentive to set up a voluntary requirement on which they receive remuneration.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: On the other hand, they may not view even fully remunerated balances as an especially attractive asset, so there might be some balancing between the desire to hold large enough requirements to stay away from overdrafts and the idea of having balances or assets booked that aren’t particularly high earning.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: But this is a major uncertainty for these types of models.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The Bank of England has used a procedure like this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What has been their experience?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Again, it may not be completely comparable.

speaker: HILTON
text: Well, for the Bank of England, the way the voluntary target rules are set is really very simple.

speaker: HILTON
text: The bank chooses its own voluntary target.

speaker: HILTON
text: It can’t be below zero, of course, but they have a cap.

speaker: HILTON
text: It can’t be any higher than a certain amount, and I think it’s 2 percent of some measure of their liabilities on their balance sheet.

speaker: HILTON
text: They had no idea what they were going to get.

speaker: HILTON
text: Their experience was encouraging in that they got an aggregate level and a distribution that have brilliantly facilitated their control over their interbank market.

speaker: HILTON
text: But it is sort of taking a leap to go into that system, although we have some experience with our clearing balance program.

speaker: HILTON
text: We do see how banks adjust their participation with reserve-management objectives in mind.

speaker: HILTON
text: In our case, because there are practical limits—ceilings on the size of a clearing balance that makes sense for any bank to have—we don’t really have a direct observation of what we would get if it were entirely voluntary.

speaker: HILTON
text: The evidence that I see from our experience of clearing balances and from the Bank of England is encouraging that we would get, even with a very simply designed set of voluntary targets, a good aggregate level and distribution of voluntary targets.

speaker: HILTON
text: But right now, based on what we know, it is an uncertainty.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The big risk would be if the voluntary balances were really low.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So let’s say that actually happened, that they were zero.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Let’s say we implemented this and they came out at zero.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You’d have to change the incentives somehow.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Right, and that would be the answer.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You could raise the cost of daylight overdrafts.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You could raise the cost of daylight overdrafts, or you could adjust the interest rate that you pay on reserves to get it right.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That could solve the problem.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As long as you have enough parameters that you can adjust to change the incentives, you’re probably going to be okay in that environment.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But if you have a system in which there aren’t any parameters that you can actually move, then you have a real problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But in the context of the law, we would have the ability to adjust these parameters.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Governor Mishkin, to state the obvious, we’d want to avoid that situation completely.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We want preparation and consultation with banks ex ante as to how they would react under various subparameterizations.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: As Steve noted, we already have $7 billion in required clearing balances with a rate of remuneration that’s only 80 percent of the T-bill rate.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: So in all likelihood, we would have a positive number.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: How large that number would be is the question mark.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have a comment, not a question.

speaker: LACKER
text: This represents a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reengineer our monetary policy operational framework, and I think it’s important that we do our best to get it right.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to start by applauding the staff for taking a very deliberate, very thoughtful approach to this project.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was able to attend the workshop on foreign central banks’ operations.

speaker: LACKER
text: I found it very illuminating, instructive, well organized, and well thought out.

speaker: LACKER
text: So far the work has been well organized, and the broad-based involvement has been very good.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to compliment you on sifting down.

speaker: LACKER
text: The combinatorics must have been mind-boggling given the number of free parameters in the design of one of these schemes.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to applaud you for boiling it down to a good, representative set that spans everything that I think we’d want to consider.

speaker: LACKER
text: What you produced—with one slight exception that I’ll talk about in a bit—is a very thorough and careful analysis.

speaker: LACKER
text: In Richmond, we have thought about the issue of interest on reserves for many, many years—even before the Congress considered it.

speaker: LACKER
text: Toward the end, I’m going to argue that option 4 deserves serious consideration, and I’d like to see you focus on that as well as the other options going forward.

speaker: LACKER
text: Before I do, though, I want to comment briefly on the objectives.

speaker: LACKER
text: You asked for feedback on this.

speaker: LACKER
text: In particular, I think objective 3 needs to be interpreted very carefully.

speaker: LACKER
text: The report often seems to interpret objective 3 as implying that anything that reduces the amount of lending in the fed funds market must reduce financial market efficiency.

speaker: LACKER
text: I just don’t think that’s right.

speaker: LACKER
text: The prohibition of interest on reserves is obviously a tax on reserve holdings.

speaker: LACKER
text: You have focused on the tax that it implies on reservable liabilities, but the fact that we also don’t pay interest on excess reserves is a tax on excess reserve holdings.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we eliminate reserve requirements and we still don’t pay interest on reserves, we’ll still be taxing reserve holdings.

speaker: LACKER
text: That gives rise to inefficiencies for the same reason that the lack of interest on currency gives rise to inefficiencies, and so in this setting, obviously banks do a lot of things to avoid the reserve tax.

speaker: LACKER
text: Some of the measures involve a lot of monitoring of the reserve account, monitoring of the prospective payment flow, and making sure that they can predict where they’re going to be at the end of the day.

speaker: LACKER
text: But some of the measures undoubtedly involve some transactions—such as fed funds loans, purchases of Treasury securities, repo lending, and the like—that are aimed at minimizing their non- interest-earning balances.

speaker: LACKER
text: Such transactions are exactly analogous to the classic shoe-leather costs of inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Additional transactions that are induced by the tax on currency are a waste.

speaker: LACKER
text: Reducing the inflation tax results in fewer trips to the bank or to the ATM to get money out, and that reduction is a good thing, not a bad thing.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would be a benefit, and that is exactly what it means to reduce the dead weight burden of inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Similarly, I think that paying interest on excess reserves will reduce transaction volumes in the fed funds market, but we should count that as a benefit, not a cost.

speaker: LACKER
text: Put more generally, the effectiveness of a market isn’t the same as the quantity of transactions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I bring this up because one of the main objections to option 4, at least in the report—it didn’t appear in the slides—is that it could reduce fed funds market lending.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it should be obvious at this point why that wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s sort of like saying that reducing inflation would be a bad thing because people would make fewer trips to the bank.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think you’d say that.

speaker: LACKER
text: Even if we believed that fed funds volume is important, I think a quick look at the numbers would suggest that it’s not likely to be that big a problem.

speaker: LACKER
text: The staff estimates that the fed funds market is about $225 billion, on average.

speaker: LACKER
text: So how much by way of reserves will we need to add to ensure a negligible chance that our autonomous reserve factor drains reserves enough to drive the funds rate up?

speaker: LACKER
text: You showed a graph, and there was a flat spot, and you had supply way, way, way out on the curve.

speaker: LACKER
text: But it doesn’t need to go out that far.

speaker: LACKER
text: It just needs to go out so that you’d know that you’re not going to accidentally go in on the upward part.

speaker: LACKER
text: My reading of your intermeeting report is that reserve misses are typically on the order of $1 billion or $2 billion.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the average absolute value is about $990 million.

speaker: LACKER
text: It happens every now and then.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it seems as though $5 billion would do plenty.

speaker: LACKER
text: The report says that $35 billion would be how much reserves you’d need to add.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m a little curious about where that number came from.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s hard for me to believe we’d need that much.

speaker: LACKER
text: But certainly more broadly than that, if you think about the market, is that right now $225 billion in lending is going on.

speaker: LACKER
text: If you do the thought experiments about current equilibriums and you are a bank that just walks into the market and needs some reserves, will it be hard to get reserves?

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, you’re going to run into $225 billion worth from banks that are already lending their reserves with interest.

speaker: LACKER
text: So if you’re going to get your loan, you’re going to have to pay a competitive rate and shake loose some money from one of them.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we are paying interest on $35 billion in reserves, will that change that calculus much?

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that your markets are still going to work the same way.

speaker: LACKER
text: If you want reserves, you’re going to have to pay a competitive rate for them.

speaker: LACKER
text: If you’re not getting reserves at that rate, you’re going to bid up until you get them.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I just don’t quite get this concern about the volume of transactions in the funds market.

speaker: LACKER
text: A related objection is the issue of hoarding—the idea that one bank might decide to hold a whole bunch of reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: The staff cited the example of New Zealand.

speaker: LACKER
text: I thought that was a really interesting discussion at the workshop.

speaker: LACKER
text: One bank accumulated $8 billion or $9 billion in reserves, I think it was, which was large for them, and they had to add a large amount of reserves to accommodate that demand plus the demand of other banks in the system.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, the problem for the Bank of New Zealand is, as I understand it, that the government doesn’t issue debt.

speaker: LACKER
text: When they have to issue deposits, they have to acquire foreign exchange reserves, and that involves a fiscal risk that they’re reluctant to take on.

speaker: LACKER
text: My sense of the conversation is that they don’t like to accumulate foreign exchange reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: We seem to be quite willing to expand our balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: Plus, there are plenty of government securities around.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I just don’t see why it would be a problem for us if reserve demand was unexpectedly high or some bank decided to hold $50 billion in reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to talk about one more thing, which is the issue of the rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: The way you have written it up is that what we target now is the average rate of brokered deposits.

speaker: LACKER
text: You said it was $80 billion to $100 billion out of $225 billion, on average—so less than half the market—just the weighted average of trades during the day that go through brokered channels.

speaker: LACKER
text: That doesn’t include direct credit funds.

speaker: LACKER
text: The approach you envisioned is that we try to set a remuneration rate so that the effective rate, that average, comes out at the target rate that the Committee sets.

speaker: LACKER
text: A very natural alternative, it seems to me—and I think this is the way the Bank of England does it—is that our policy rate is now the deposit rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: When we issue a press release, we say we’re changing the policy rate—I don’t know whether or not we would rename it.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, you folks estimate that the risk premium that would, on average, be the gap between this deposit rate and this effective fed funds rate you measure might be 10 basis points.

speaker: LACKER
text: We now set the funds rate target in ¼ point increments.

speaker: LACKER
text: In theory, we could set our policy rate 10 basis points below ¼ point increments.

speaker: LACKER
text: That seems a little bizarre.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not sure that we have such precise confidence in the optimal funds rate that we’d know that it should be on the ¼ point and not 10 basis points below or above.

speaker: LACKER
text: It strikes me that a natural version of option 4 or any of these options would be to set the remuneration rate at ¼ point increments and have that be the policy rate, and just make that the reference point for how we do.

speaker: LACKER
text: Admittedly, econometricians would have to do a lot of work in the future to splice these series together, but I think that’s a workable alternative we ought to think about.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that option 4 has some obvious benefits over the other options.

speaker: LACKER
text: Intuitively, if you were given a limited budget and were asked to peg the price of a commodity—minimize the variance of a commodity price around a given target—your natural inclination would be to stand ready to buy and sell that commodity at the target price.

speaker: LACKER
text: That would be, right out of the box, the first thing every economist would say.

speaker: LACKER
text: Option 4 is the closest practical analogue to that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it’s eminently workable.

speaker: LACKER
text: I just don’t see the force of the objections.

speaker: LACKER
text: In comparison, option 5, which is the one that comes closest to option 4, involves the monitoring of voluntary targets.

speaker: LACKER
text: You have to monitor these bands.

speaker: LACKER
text: You have to check the balances every night against the bands.

speaker: LACKER
text: It just seems like a lot of superfluous machinery.

speaker: LACKER
text: Option 4 would go furthest toward reducing our dependence on forecasting uncertain autonomous factors.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would also go furthest toward solving the problem that the primary dealer credit facility has given rise to, which has been particularly acute in the last intermeeting period, which is that rates are firm.

speaker: LACKER
text: You’ve done a pretty good job with the average daily rate, but it crashes at the end of every day.

speaker: LACKER
text: More than half the time you look at the low for the day and it’s under 1 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: So we have a chronic intraday problem of rates being firm and then crashing because you don’t know.

speaker: LACKER
text: Primary dealers come in, that stuff goes on the market, and the rate crashes.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think option 4 would also be the most transparent approach.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would be the easiest to explain to people.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would go furthest toward eliminating the risk of the downside target misses and concerns about stealth easing.

speaker: LACKER
text: Option 4 would also facilitate long-run moves toward lesser lines of daylight central bank credit, and I think that’s an important consideration.

speaker: LACKER
text: It shouldn’t be the deciding consideration, but it is important.

speaker: LACKER
text: In terms of the timeline, you have yourselves focusing on two options before the results of the public comment come in.

speaker: LACKER
text: To some extent that’s prejudging where the public comment is going to come in.

speaker: LACKER
text: So, in short, option 4 strikes me as the most straightforward and practical way to do it, and I’d urge that we direct the group, which has done great work so far, to focus on option 4 and to keep it as a live option.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You kind of segued into the positions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Does anyone have a short question of fact?

speaker: KOHN
text: I actually have a couple of questions rather than positions.

speaker: KOHN
text: One is a bit more about what we’ve learned in this period of stress.

speaker: KOHN
text: For example, on page 26, you list a bunch of banks that don’t seem to have taken advantage of primary credit.

speaker: KOHN
text: I assume that you have talked to them, and I wonder how they had rationalized their concerns about stigma and what they said about that.

speaker: KOHN
text: Along similar lines about stress, and following up on Governor Mishkin’s question, how did the U.K. system work in this period of stress?

speaker: KOHN
text: My impression is that they had problems.

speaker: KOHN
text: Initially the banks wanted to increase their voluntary targets and that required the Bank of England to be a little more flexible than it started out to be.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’d be interested in how option 2 behaved under stress and then any new insights you have about bank behavior in this period that produced the oscillations that we saw.

speaker: KOHN
text: A second point is that Brian, Scott, and I have been talking about asking the Congress to allow us to pay interest on reserves sooner rather than later.

speaker: KOHN
text: If we got that authority, I assume that it would not involve implementing this over four years but that we could implement something in one or two weeks, in the maintenance period after we got that authority.

speaker: KOHN
text: How would you go about that?

speaker: KOHN
text: What are you thinking in that regard?

speaker: KOHN
text: I think I’ll stop there.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If I may start with the last question, we can work our way up or around the list.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On pursuing legislative authority, the Federal Reserve is interested in accelerating that authority.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We have had some conversations with congressional staff about this.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For instance, the staff of Senate Minority Leader McConnell has asked us recently whether we’d be interested in legislation to accelerate the authority.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, we responded enthusiastically.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We did say to them that it would be helpful if it were clear that we could use that authority in such a way as to be able to pay interest on excess reserves or, rather, to buy federal funds as a way of paying interest on excess reserves, in effect.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Buying federal funds when the rate is falling would help us put a floor under the funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So we would want to be sure—perhaps Scott wants to comment on this—that the legislation clearly permitted that.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Presumably we would be able to use that authority fairly quickly at an operational level—Bill or Spence may want to comment on this.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Paying interest on required reserve balances is, of course, a whole other matter.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That involves complicated systems, and we would simply want to be sure that we made this clear to the congressional staffs, that it would take a longer time before we could implement that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We think we could implement it pretty quickly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Another benefit would be not just addressing the crashes of the funds rate late in the day but also enabling us to actually expand our balance sheet if needed.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just to clarify, what are the implications for scoring?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s pretty small if you just confine it to excess.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: My impression is, as Bill said, that it is small and there may not even be positive costs if you confine it to excess.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The issues of paying interest on required reserves are possibly a little more troublesome, but that may be viewed as a worthwhile cost to undertake at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there’s a sense of the Committee that this is something we should escalate, let’s move it up the ladder and do that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But anyone who wants to comment on that during the go-around, please feel free.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was a second part about the United Kingdom, I believe.

speaker: MEYER
text: With respect to the U.K. system during the period of turmoil, banks’ initial reaction was to lower their reserve deposits, their contractual commitments.

speaker: MEYER
