text: But they came to their senses and realized that holding more rather than less was a more sensible approach, and the Bank of England accommodated the banks’ desire both to increase their targets and to widen the bands.

speaker: MEYER
text: Quite dramatically, to avoid the end-of-period spike in rates.

speaker: MEYER
text: In terms of rate volatility, the Bank of England, the ECB, and the Fed all achieved about the same rate volatility during the period of market turmoil.

speaker: MEYER
text: For the Bank of England, the spikes just tended to be more on the upside than the downside, but that had to do with their implementation procedures and not getting to the end of the period and being willing to accommodate.

speaker: KOHN
text: I assume it was the stigma problem as well.

speaker: MEYER
text: Though they had a few trades above their lending rate, in fact that was not much of a problem.

speaker: MEYER
text: Their system worked quite well.

speaker: MEYER
text: Interestingly, the country with the smallest rate volatility during the whole period of market turmoil was Canada, and that’s because they knew the demand for balances at the end of every day and could adjust the supply by adjusting the government balance at the end of every day.

speaker: MEYER
text: So they hit it basically every day.

speaker: FISHER
text: A very short question having nothing to do with what everybody else has asked about—but going back to page 33, what are the governance issues, and how do you resolve them, in 30 seconds or less?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, the governance issues are that the FOMC is in charge of open market operations and setting the target for the federal funds rate, at least under current approaches to policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The legislation specifies that the Board is in charge of setting the rates paid on balances to institutions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For instance, there may be differential rates as in option 1 on required reserve balances and excess reserve balances.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Presumably, if we went with option 1, for instance, one approach would be to simply set them by formula relative to the target federal funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We don’t mean to say that this is likely to be an enormously large issue, at least in some of the options, but it ought to be handled carefully.

speaker: STERN
text: My question is about intraday and day-to-day volatility in the funds rate.

speaker: STERN
text: I would think that as long as we hit the target on average, that kind of volatility wouldn’t have any significant macroeconomic consequences.

speaker: STERN
text: So why would we care?

speaker: HILTON
text: That’s our impression, that it doesn’t have macro consequences.

speaker: HILTON
text: Maybe it’s a tempest in a teapot, but for the participants in that market, the uncertainty and the costs that are borne by borrowers and lenders are an important issue.

speaker: HILTON
text: But the macro fallout, the effect on longer- term rates, doesn’t seem to be significant.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: What we don’t know is whether that volatility somehow has consequences for term funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: How do you know the linkage between the two because they’re happening sort of simultaneously?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I agree with Spence that we don’t think there’s any significant macro effect.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There may be some marginal effect of volatility creating a greater risk premium in the market, but it’s hard to say.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is an effect on swaps, like foreign exchange swaps, right?

speaker: HILTON
text: Well, for a lot of what we seem to get—like the Eurodollar rates and LIBOR and foreign exchange swaps and the way they relate to what goes on in our overnight funds market—the typical intraday pattern is firm in the morning and coming off late in the day.

speaker: HILTON
text: Those higher morning rates are the ones that are linked to the other rates—Eurodollars, swaps—and so it’s not the average rate over time that seems to get priced into these other vehicles.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The high morning rate could conceivably affect other rates in a way that’s—

speaker: STERN
text: It sounds like an obvious arbitrage opportunity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, we’re not seeing much arbitrage.

speaker: HILTON
text: We are finding a great reluctance to do intraday arbitrage.

speaker: HILTON
text: We’re hearing this from the banks that in the past would do that from time to time.

speaker: HILTON
text: Coming back to one of the other questions that Don had about what we are hearing about stigma from some of the banks, one of our better contacts, Citibank, as Jim mentioned, used to do a lot of arbitraging and using the discount window, the primary credit facility.

speaker: HILTON
text: On occasion, after they borrowed to re-lend in the market at a higher rate last year or so ago, they would call us in the morning to let us know how it was that they were helping us out with the funds rate.

speaker: HILTON
text: That has pretty much stopped cold, and they have decided on sort of classic stigma.

speaker: HILTON
text: They routinely point to the publication of borrowing data in the H.4.1 release, and they are just not interested in the small gain from that kind of activity while taking the risk in the market of being seen as in dire need of liquidity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The TAF auction results underscored the idea of stigma at the primary credit facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s possible that we have actually a bit more stigma now than we did before because you can just see very clearly that there would have to be stigma for people to be bidding that much in the TAF auction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Evans had a two-hander.

speaker: EVANS
text: My primary comment in all of this is related to what President Stern, I think, said.

speaker: EVANS
text: The way the objectives are worded here is “enhanced monetary policy implementation,” and the memo is worded more like, “How do we get our federal funds rate target effectively?” or something like that.

speaker: EVANS
text: But there is really no discussion that I could find about the transmission of our policy actions to the economy and to inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Under our current regime, we think, quite confidently, that the short-term federal funds rate prices short-term risk-free assets along the yield curve all the way up to the Treasuries and then corporates are priced off all of that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I associate that with Marvin Goodfriend, who taught me that quite some time ago.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s not money; it’s not liquidity; it’s not the reserves per se.

speaker: EVANS
text: It would be nice if, for each alternative, there were some discussion that we are preserving our understanding of the policy transmission mechanism or that we are enhancing it or whatever.

speaker: EVANS
text: President Lacker mentioned the Bank of England—maybe we could set the policy rate as they do.

speaker: EVANS
text: The question is, What will the markets do in terms of actively arbitraging something that helps price these securities?

speaker: EVANS
text: This may not be an issue for many of these systems, but until there’s some kind of analysis, I’m not so sure.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s not just averaging over the maintenance period, and I think that analysis would be useful.

speaker: WARSH
text: Governor Kohn shamelessly stole my question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Kroszner, do you have a question?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In a lot of the discussion you just take as given the stigma associated with the primary credit facility, and you were just discussing that related to the publication of information about the facility.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Is that something that could also be on the table?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That seems to be potentially an instrument for which we might have to consider how much information to provide or about making it less or more attractive, which then would affect which options are more or less attractive.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Is there some reason not to do that?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think that’s worth some further thought, Governor Kroszner.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One issue though, as I’m sure you know, is that the Board is required by law to publish weekly information on the individual Banks’ balance sheets as well as the consolidated balance sheet with a certain amount of detail.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I don’t remember the exact legal wording, but at least within the current law, to back away from that might be difficult.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, you could conceivably pursue a change in the law, but I think we would want to think about the pros and cons of that before you went in that direction.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: For sure, but just thinking about whether there are other things that we could do related to stigma might be worthwhile in this context.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, when the Board adopted the primary credit program in 2003, we gave a lot of thought before that and did considerable work after that to try to minimize the amount of stigma by trying to make very clear to banks that in our view use of the window didn’t entail stigma.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But the fundamental problem still is that banks are concerned that their use of the window may be detected in the market one way or another, especially in a period of financial stress, and that is just not a cost worth incurring.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser, did you have a question?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yes, just an implementation question.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One thing you talked about was in periods of stress, the way we’ve conducted policy intraday, you have had firmness in the funds rate in the morning and then weakness in the afternoon causing some intraday volatility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The difficulty of hitting the target was partly the fact that we were entering the market only once a day, in the morning, and you had to see through that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: With all these other strategies, as they are implemented in other countries, are the central banks doing the same thing?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are they entering the market only once a day, or do they come in several times a day?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just wondered if there are differences in their approaches as to how often they interact in the marketplace.

speaker: HILTON
text: I would say, as a general characterization, that the common practice is to intervene only once a day, in the morning—not unlike what we do.

speaker: HILTON
text: Where there’s an exception, it’s like with the Bank of Canada.

speaker: HILTON
text: They have access to information that would allow them to know with precision late in the day what the supply of reserves is in the absence of any further open market operations, and then they make an adjustment accordingly.

speaker: HILTON
text: The fact is that, even if we were to operate late in the day but still before the close—let’s say, 5:30 or 6:00—we really have no more information than we had at 9:30 in the morning upon which to make an estimate of that day’s reserve supply.

speaker: HILTON
text: We can observe rates, but we don’t know what amount of a reserve adjustment would be needed to bring supply in line with demand.

speaker: HILTON
text: The risk of just opening up and offering to be one side or the other of the market in that situation late in the day is that we could get the entirety of one side of the market and actually create a reserve imbalance in the other direction between that time and the close of the day.

speaker: HILTON
text: So simply being willing to operate late in the day isn’t really enough.

speaker: HILTON
text: You do need reserve information as well upon which to size those operations.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just to make this clear, Spence, is it the number of banks that make that information more accessible in Canada, or is it something else?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Is it fundamentally that they have just five banks?

speaker: HILTON
text: No, it is that they know the balance sheet.

speaker: HILTON
text: They know it by late in the day with certainty.

speaker: HILTON
text: They have few sources of uncertainty to begin with, and their major source of uncertainty, government balances, is something that perhaps the small number of banks they’re dealing with facilitates.

speaker: HILTON
text: But it is that they know by late in the day what the supply of reserves will be with real precision.

speaker: MEYER
text: Basically everything clears through their equivalent of Fedwire, so they know in real time what the balances are.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Did you have a question?

speaker: LACKER
text: Every financial transaction that a substantive firm engages in that becomes known is relied upon by market participants to make inferences.

speaker: LACKER
text: There’s a huge literature on the effect on equity values of the announcement of a bank line of credit; and like through this last crisis, if you talk to funding-desk guys, they’re very aware at the tactical level about what counterparties are revealing by their actions in funding markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: They take that on board, and they’re very strategic about what they reveal with their market transactions.

speaker: LACKER
text: We can try to keep it secret, but there’s a broad ability in the market to infer when somebody goes to the window by their behavior before that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m saying that I don’t think we should get our hopes up about ever eliminating stigma.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s take positions and comments, keeping in mind that lunch is being held hostage.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just a quick question, which doesn’t have to be answered now—given all of the financial turmoil, it would be interesting to see whether in other countries that have these different arrangements there was a decrease in either overnight or term lending with counterparties.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given the extent to which you can just work with a central bank rather than counterparties, is there any evidence in these other regimes that interbank lending transaction volume disappeared in some of these countries?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would be interested in seeing that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Regarding Governor Kroszner’s comment on the H.4.1 release, it does seem that we could probably have a materiality requirement in our balance sheet.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Under most circumstances, what we are doing at the discount window would seem not to hit that materiality criterion.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think we could be a little more innovative—I agree with President Lacker’s point—but I think that the H.4.1 does seem to have an effect; and if we will be doing all these other things, taking another look at the H.4.1 and making sure that we don’t have more untapped flexibilities probably makes a lot of sense.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would like a little more discussion of “promote efficient and resilient money markets and government securities markets” as a criterion.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I’m not sure I would weight those criteria equally.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It seems that all these criteria, for the most part, take care of most of the dead weight loss; and given that the banks still have to administrate for daylight credit, I am not sure that the burden is all that different across these various regimes.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But I can imagine that that one might be different, and given we just had financial turmoil—I know this is a bit different from what President Lacker said—I would put a little more attention to that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Overall, I like option 2 and option 5.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I’m comfortable with those two.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I’m attracted to the voluntary balance program.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: On net, I would probably prefer a longer maintenance period to a one-day maintenance period, but I don’t have a strong preference and could easily be convinced otherwise.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I mentioned earlier, I would find some discussion about the transmission mechanism useful—at what rate we think the markets would be picking up the price of risk-free yield curves.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that would help.

speaker: EVANS
text: To the extent that we can align this with other foreign central bank experiences, we might be able to draw on how they view that and what the financial market data look like.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I am comfortable with focusing primarily on options 2 and 5.

speaker: EVANS
text: I was thinking along the lines of President Hoenig, which is that the Federal Reserve tends to go slowly.

speaker: EVANS
text: Vince isn’t here, but he often reminded us of that.

speaker: EVANS
text: Option 1 is the easiest one.

speaker: EVANS
text: If we have enough information about it, then that’s fine.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that’s all I have.

speaker: STERN
text: I have only two comments.

speaker: STERN
text: I would drop option 1.

speaker: STERN
text: I just think it doesn’t do enough to reduce the burdens and dead weight losses.

speaker: STERN
text: As long as it’s there, there will be a tendency to fall back to it for all sorts of reasons, given bureaucratic tendencies.

speaker: STERN
text: So I would just discard it.

speaker: STERN
text: I would not discard option 4, so I would include options 2, 4, and 5.

speaker: STERN
text: I was originally attracted to 4.

speaker: STERN
text: I read the reservations in the report and thought, okay, it’s not worth pursuing.

speaker: STERN
text: But I listened to President Lacker, and he reconvinced me that there are some significant merits there.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, I do really appreciate all the excellent work the staff has done on this topic.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I really learned a lot from these papers.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I thought they were very clear and very comprehensive.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have just a couple of comments on the questions that Bill and Brian raised in the memo.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The first one has to do with whether or not we agree with the objectives, and I do have a couple of issues.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, I think that the stated objective of reducing the burdens and dead weight losses associated with the current reserve tax is too narrowly framed in the paper.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My starting point is, about burden, that to cover a given program of government spending, the Treasury has to obtain revenue from some source, and nondistortionary lump-sum taxes are not one of the available options.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So the real question from the public finance standpoint is what to tax and how much.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That means, to my mind, that the issue here is how the magnitude of the welfare gains that would come from lowering the dead weight loss due to the implicit tax on reserves compares with additional dead weight losses that would result from the alternative taxes that would have to be raised to make up for this lost revenue.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Now the answer depends in part on the interest elasticity of demand for reserves, I believe.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it is the case that, if the interest elasticity is relatively small, the dead weight loss from the reserve tax is relatively small, and the net welfare gain, taking into account the burdens of raising other taxes to make up for the lost seigniorage, in effect, could easily turn out to be negative.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Let me give you an example of where this comes into play.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There is a well-known paper by Martin Feldstein in which he looks at the benefits of moving to price stability, zero inflation, which he favors.

speaker: YELLEN
text: He looks at this issue in that context, and he concludes that there would be net social losses, not gains, from the reduction in seigniorage that would be associated with a move to zero inflation from positive inflation because the dead weight loss due to the shoe-leather cost, also known as the Bailey effect, is smaller than the dead weight losses that would be associated with alternative taxes.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In his analysis they are taxes on labor supply and saving.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I actually think that this is a serious problem with the framing of the objectives in this paper.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is, in effect, saying, “We think we should give a tax cut.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We think we should give it to banks, and we think that, because there is a welfare loss—a Harberger triangle—associated with that, this is clear welfare gain.” Now, I am not pretending to know exactly how this would come out, but I do think that’s the issue.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If it were to come out that this is a net loss, not a gain, a possible implication is that if there were a fallback to option 1—I’m not saying that I favor option 1— there could be a case for paying no interest on required reserves rather than paying interest at the federal funds rate but paying interest on excess reserves at some rate that we would determine.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There are administrative costs with having voluntary target balances, and it seems to me that the paper, as we come out with it, ought to try to at least estimate what the administrative burdens associated with options 2 and 5 would be.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Another comment on the issue of objectives: If we are coming out with a white paper, it seems to me that the objective that everybody is now discussing and that was just discussed— namely, that paying interest on reserves would enable us to expand the size of our balance sheet in times of financial crisis, like now, and perhaps greatly enhance the scope for liquidity-altering interventions that would be possible without having to push the federal funds rate to zero—is a real improvement in the tool kit that is available to us to address market disruptions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would see it as an advantage of paying interest on reserves.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If you are discussing this right now with the Congress and it is much discussed in the press, I think it is kind of odd to come out with a paper that doesn’t even mention it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Maybe there are disadvantages and not just advantages.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But it seems to me it should be there.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Also, I would just say on the question of options 2 and 5 versus options 3 and 4, an advantage that the paper attaches to having voluntary targets is the ability to moderate the volatility in the federal funds rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So it does seem to me that—I understand it may be difficult—the possibility of intervening multiple times during the day as an alternative, if it were possible to change the procedures so that there could be multiple interventions to reduce volatility, would mean that 3 and 4 could be on the table, and there might be less burden associated with those.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I think that possibility deserves at least careful consideration.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is a proposal for study.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The timeline seems fine to me.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The study period is pretty important in this case because it is not clear to me which option is best, and so I think maybe we should keep more of the options on the table.

speaker: BULLARD
text: One question that I have is, To what extent are current reserve requirements actually binding for depository institutions?

speaker: BULLARD
text: There is a past study by the St. Louis staff—Dick Anderson and Bob Rasche—suggesting that, by and large, existing reserve requirements are not binding.

speaker: BULLARD
text: To me that calls into question whether objective 1 for this study group is really appropriate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Dead weight losses make sense to me only if there is a binding reserve requirement.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In that regard, I’d like to endorse President Yellen’s comment, which I thought was right on target, about whether you are going to make up for lost revenue from somewhere else and how distortionary that would be.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There is a bit of political risk here that, if this starts to get painted as a handout to banks, maybe it wouldn’t serve us well.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would like to see more emphasis on option 3, which based on the discussion seems to be not too bad a system.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is the Canadian system.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is a tested system in an economy that is not too different from our own—certainly, an economy that is closely integrated with this one.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The corridor would be narrow.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There might be more volatility within that corridor, but you still seem to get pretty good results.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I know they have a small number of banks, but it seems to me with today’s technology you might be able to get a good read even for a large economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would like to see it kept in the mix here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They have had lots of success and very low administrative burden, if that is what you are worried about.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am perhaps not so familiar with options 2 and 5, which are the favored options in this discussion.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But I am concerned about the language of voluntary balance targets, which seem to be maybe not that voluntary.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It seems to me to create a risk that the systems are really not as market-oriented as I would like to see or that they could be manipulated by market participants, particularly in a time of stress.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Those are some of the concerns I had about this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the public finance question, of course, the Congress has acted and they score it to cost.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in some sense that is moot from our perspective.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Let me also start by commending the authors of the papers that were prepared on this topic.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I found the material very informative and helpful.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I agree with the objectives established by the staff to evaluate the set of proposals, and I also support the process and the proposed timeline for moving the proposals forward.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think it is good that the timeline provides for comments from banks so early in the process.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: It will be important for us to receive their input at an early stage.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I found option 2 to be preferable to option 1 because option 2, as we have discussed, clearly reduces the administrative burdens relative to option 1.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think that option 3 leaves too much potential for fed funds rate volatility in its corridor.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I was also intrigued by option 4 with caps.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, I ultimately rejected option 4 out of the concern that it might lead to a less robust interbank lending market.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But given the comments of President Lacker and others, perhaps it makes sense to keep option 4 on the table.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In the end, however, I am comfortable with moving forward with our focus on options 2 and 5.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Just to answer the questions that were posed, I am comfortable with options 2 and 5, but I thought President Lacker’s presentation made the case that option 4 deserves to remain in the mix.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think the objectives are appropriate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The only comment I have—and this is a bit vague, I realize—is to ensure that we are thinking far enough ahead to ensure that we have a durable system that can operate in different mixes of private and public in the payment system.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Certainly, I think it is conceivable that in some years we will be out of the business of retail payments, so I think we have to address different mixes of private and public payment systems.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding the timeline, Governor Kohn already asked the question about approaching the Congress to accelerate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Assuming that we do not approach the Congress to accelerate this, then this timeline seems to me quite comfortable and gives plenty of time for very careful consideration.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the room here is Will Roberds from our research staff, who by chance was at the Bank of England talking about their experiences recently.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I thought I would share a couple of things that are apropos.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: They tried maintenance periods other than the intermeeting period, and they found them to be not so effective, apparently because of ambiguity around the target rate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That is a useful way of thinking—that the maintenance periods would be designed around the intermeeting period.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: They apparently tried option 3, and it didn’t work because of too much volatility within the corridor.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Those two tidbits are feedback from the visit of a member of my staff to the Bank of England.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would look at this meeting as an introduction to this topic, given the breadth of the discussion here, which I found extremely interesting and useful.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think we will need to come back to another discussion of it—not necessarily with another 100-page study.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I wouldn’t want to put that burden on you—it might negate any savings we get from this project.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To the point of the options, the one that was most attractive to me was option 2.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It is a good transition.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have some familiarity with it, given the way we do clearing balances now, and I think we can work on it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The reason that I was a little questioning about option 1 is that in option 2 you are not quite sure what you are going to end up with, given how the banks may choose to target the amount of reserves and so forth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But with any choice we make, we are going to have to go up that learning curve.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So of those, I prefer option 2.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am fascinated, though, with President Lacker’s comments on option 4 and will look at it again with that in mind because I thought he made some good points.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But at the moment, I think option 2 is a pretty good path to go down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This will be very brief.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Option 2 looks very attractive to me.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think option 1 may be a fallback position, but like President Stern, given our tendency to move slow too quickly, if that makes sense, I would rather take the opportunity to make a larger step.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think option 2 is fine.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Option 5 is interesting, but its distinction is that nobody else is really doing that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So it would be a little more of a wild card in terms of how we might implement it and how it might work.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I think it has some merit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I had asked Bill Dudley back in the fall, when we were having trouble meeting the end- of-day targets, about why we didn’t set the price.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The answer I got was, “Well, this was a good time to think about that option in the context of paying interest on reserves.” I was probably a little disappointed that we didn’t see more of what such a strategy might look like and how it would behave.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thanks to President Lacker, his interpretation of option 4 is pushing us more in that direction.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I hadn’t really thought of option 4 in that context that way, but I like it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I still have the view that essentially looking at everything as a quantity-based view of how we go about doing this restricts the way we think about what our options might be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would like to see a little more explanation of what a price target, where we buy and sell, might actually do.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How that might interact with option 4 would be an interesting way to enrich the set of options.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Another question I had—and I don’t know the answer to this—is that we have instituted a number of new facilities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There is the TAF, there is the TSLF, and so forth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wasn’t quite clear how those facilities would interact or be appropriate or inappropriate within the context of these things, or whether this would substitute for all of those in some sense.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we wanted to pull those off the shelf again at some future time, how would they interact with these systems?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it would be useful to have a little discussion about what those interactions might be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The last observation is related to President Lockhart’s comment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How we go about paying interest on reserves has implications for other parts of what the Federal Reserve System does—in particular the retail payment system and the way we calculate cost recoveries and our revenues under the Monetary Control Act.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There are some separate study groups that are thinking about this, but we ought to make sure that we tie these pieces together as we go forward so that we know what the domino effects of going this direction might be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Maybe there will not be a concern, if we get out of retail payments, how it affects the Monetary Control Act requirements on fees for services and things like that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would like to see that loop closed somehow before the end of the discussion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Otherwise, I want to congratulate the staff on a very thorough report.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was at the conference as well in February.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I thought it was very interesting, and I applaud the staff on some good work.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, we have been in favor of paying interest on reserves for some time.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is an excellent paper.

speaker: FISHER
text: Like everybody else, I learned a great deal from all the papers that were sent and this superb summary that was just presented.

speaker: FISHER
text: I personally tend toward option 2, but I think it is worthwhile considering options 4 and 5 as well in terms of vetting this under the timetable.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that Charlie asked a good question about how this relates to the other facilities, but generally, the optics on this are favorable.

speaker: FISHER
text: Again, we are moving forward.

speaker: FISHER
text: The public doesn’t really understand the background of this—where the Congress has stood and what we have achieved so far.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it would be just one other good thing for us to be modernizing the Federal Reserve.

speaker: FISHER
text: I asked the question on governance just because I understand that the current plan calls for rates to adjust automatically to changes in target set by the FOMC.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would want to make sure that was the case.

speaker: FISHER
text: In other words, I don’t like the potential for vesting all the power in the Board; and, of course, that potential is there.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it is worth preserving the federal system of the Federal Reserve.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is the only reservation I have.

speaker: KOHN
text: I thought this was a great piece of work by the staff, and I thank them all.

speaker: KOHN
text: You did a good job of organizing it and laying out the general principles in a way that people can understand.

speaker: KOHN
text: Despite President Yellen’s comments, I have no regrets about my testimony in favor of paying interest, perhaps because I bore so much of the administrative costs over the years [laughter]—along with Stephanie Martin and her predecessors in the Legal Division.

speaker: KOHN
text: Those costs that were borne were considerable, in addition to the dead weight losses.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we should consider options 2 and 5 for sure.

speaker: KOHN
text: On option 4, I think we need to understand a bit—other people have said this—what the third objective, “promoting efficient and resilient money markets,” means exactly, what is entailed, and how that would intersect with option 4.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think that needs to be fleshed out a little more.

speaker: KOHN
text: Because you have planned to get a white paper out soon, I think perhaps including option 4 would be easier than not including it, just to get people’s comments.

speaker: KOHN
text: Perhaps because of my administrative burden experience, I would like to see reserve requirements at zero, ruling out option 1.

speaker: KOHN
text: On option 3, I just don’t think, at least with our system and in periods of crisis, that the top of the band would hold, so I don’t think that option would really work very well.

speaker: KOHN
text: Thank you all for your work.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me add my plaudits to those already expressed on the quality of this work, and then let me confine my comments to the timing and sequencing.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, with respect to the rollout of the white paper, it strikes me that, given that questions have been raised about what our flexibility is around our balance sheet and tools in the event of continued problems in the financial markets, we just need to be cognizant in that paper of how this discussion might be read, not in the context of a long Fed effort to get interest on reserves but perhaps as being solely responsive to what are perceived to be burdens on our balance sheet flexibility.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am just sensitive to how that white paper will be read and rolled out.

speaker: WARSH
text: More broadly, on timing—come fall, in the event that we decide collectively to go to the Congress seeking other authority with respect to the PDCF, investment banks, and other things that might or might not be concluded, even though this timeline makes a lot of sense, we might be in good stead to have a fairly good sense of the conclusions to which we will ultimately come, even if our exhaustive Fed rigor isn’t complete by that time.

speaker: WARSH
text: If there is real benefit to accelerating our new authority from late 2011 to some earlier period, we could put that in the context of some of broader asks from us with an expectation that we might get some traction there.

speaker: WARSH
text: So as a sort of secondary timeline, having that option value come fall strikes me as useful.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is impressive to get through fifty-two pages in less than fifty-two minutes, and so I applaud you on that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Basically I agree with a lot of the stuff that has been said before.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The trick may be thinking a bit creatively about stigma issues, if there is any way to deal with those.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I am not quite sure what you are suggesting putting out in a white paper for comment—options 2, 5, and possibly 4?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Or were you thinking of putting all five out?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, I certainly think at this point the three that you mentioned first.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: At this stage, if we are going to go to with three, we might want to think about putting all five out, just to flesh out all parts of the spectrum and acknowledge that option 1 could be a fallback.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We have to think about the pros and cons of that, but certainly the three at this point is where the consensus seems to be.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Doing three of them seems perfectly reasonable.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am very comfortable with the analysis and the approach, so I don’t have any major comments there.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Although in the white paper you might mention them, I would like to take options 1 and 3 off the table.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Option 1 has just too much administrative burden.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have enough tsuris already.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Although option 3 may work well in countries with very different structures of the banking system, I don’t think it is a feasible alternative for us.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think that we should look at options 2 and 5, and I am certainly comfortable with another look at option 4.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One issue that I worry about a bit is that these markets do sort out some interbank credit risk issues.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We don’t want to lose that, so we have to be very aware of it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I also worry a bit about setting a price when there is a credit risk element to it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When there is no credit risk element—if you want to set the Treasury bill rate—it is no big deal.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But there may be an issue there, I am not sure, and it should be one of the considerations in this context.

speaker: LACKER
text: Presumably, the rate we pay would be viewed as a risk-free rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Presumably, any market rate would be priced relative to that to include a credit premium in the usual way.

speaker: LACKER
text: If any other dynamics are anticipated by the staff, it would be useful to know that.

speaker: LACKER
text: But the usual presumption we have is that observed market rates would have our rate plus a credit premium booked into it, or transaction costs, or whatever.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d just make that comment.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t have a conviction yet on the options, but I agree that we should narrow our focus to options 2 and 4-5.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think we should design a process that tries to force us to get conviction more quickly on which option we would prefer.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it is possible.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You have made a huge investment already.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it is worth, again, a goal that gets us conviction more quickly, in part because we do have a brief window now in which we might be able to get the Congress to accelerate and we could implement more quickly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would get the Congress to accelerate if I could be totally confident that it would be free, that we would pay no price, and that there would be no risk that anything else would be on the table or that it would compromise any other objective.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very hard to have confidence on that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But if you get confidence on that, then I would go do it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I would certainly run a process by which we get conviction early.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would want us to have conviction before we go out for public comment.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The general rule is to figure out what you want to do and design a process that maximizes the chance that you get there quickly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It also strikes me that a process this drawn out will take much more staff time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We don’t have a lot of time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We don’t have a lot of excess capital in the Federal Reserve System now relative to the challenges we face.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The longer it is drawn out, maybe the smaller the tax day by day, week by week, but it is just a huge tax.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would not want to go out for public comment on a white paper in this time frame until I knew two things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One is, Are we going to get the Congress to accelerate?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Are we going to ask for it?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The other is I wouldn’t do it until I knew that we were closer to saying, “If we got it, we would do this in this time frame.” Finally, I think it is hard to have this discussion in public with the Congress now without an answer to what they will perceive to be the larger questions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What are the larger questions?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that you can reduce some of the larger questions simply to, What are we going to do with our role as lender of last resort going forward?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is a version of President Plosser’s and Governor Warsh’s questions—what the future of our facilities is, in some sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The staff has assured me that these options all preserve optionality on any future facility framework.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: They don’t prejudice those options, which is very important.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think there is a demand now and interest in what our answer is to those broader questions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is hard to see the architecture of our role as lender of last resort without having the answer to what the framework will be for restraints on risk-taking by institutions that have access in normal times and in extremis to those lender of last resort facilities.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We can’t get conviction on that in the same time frame that we need to accelerate legislation on this stuff, but—and probably because—I think those things are fundamentally more important than whether we end up with 2 or 4.5 or 5 on the way to 4.5.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would try to shorten the amount of time and effort we put into this, and I would increase the amount of time and effort we put into that broader set of policy questions, which are going to be essentially about the intersection among the lender of last resort role, our monetary policy regime, the moral hazard consequences of all the stuff we have done, and how we deal with those in the future.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that is going to take a lot of time, effort, and care.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t know how to reconcile all of what I just said in the context of a practical path forward, except just to repeat it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Why not try to run a process in which you get conviction more quickly on this relatively small set of adjustments as to how we operate?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Try to get a judgment quickly about whether we can get the Congress to accelerate without any meaningful political cost, then design a process whereby we put ourselves in the position to implement early next year, if the Congress were to accelerate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: And try to have the resources saved by attenuating that process devoted to these deeper questions about our future facilities and the associated constraints we are going to have to put on a broader set of institutions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On those broader questions, Vice Chairman, we are going to talk at lunch about some initiatives by which we will address some of the broader regulatory and bank supervision issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That process will be parallel to this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I would say about this issue is that, as you go forward, you should keep in mind the possibility we might want to go to the Congress for some kind of interim power.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, there are things that we can do that are not the full panoply of things you described today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They would be interim steps, and I think that the most important thing is to make sure that whatever we ask for would not be inconsistent with or contradictory to some of the longer-term plans.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We obviously don’t anticipate implementing option 5 next year, but we could take some interim steps that potentially might be useful in the current circumstances.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Very briefly, I agree with President Fisher and President Lacker.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is a once-in-a- generation chance to modernize our system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is a relic that we use a quantity-based management of the federal funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think option 1 should be a fallback if we can’t make something else work, but we should try very hard to see if we can find a system that will let us manage the funds rate tightly, even as our balance sheet expands and contracts, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have the same concerns about option 3, that it might not tie down the fed funds rate very much.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Options 2 and 5 are interesting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with President Lacker that option 4 is worth exploring.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I broached this with the staff before the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Option 4 seems a lot like Friedman’s optimum quantity of money: You just throw out money until the transaction cost on margin is zero.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s basically what it is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t, frankly, fully understand what the implications would be for the federal funds market—whether the federal funds market is just a shoe-leather cost or whether it actually has some useful functions, including price discovery, credit risk management, and counterparty discipline.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There may be some functions of that market that are important, and even if it still existed, if its liquidity were greatly reduced so that it wasn’t functioning in a normal way, it could be a question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To my mind, that is the main question we have to understand as we think about option 4.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Once again, terrific work, and this is really exciting, interesting stuff.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So thank you all very much.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any other comments on interest on reserves?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, again, the projections are due Thursday at 5:00 p.m.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If anyone has changes, please make the effort to do that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will be circulating information on the 2009 FOMC schedule to try to come to closure on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next meeting is Tuesday and Wednesday, June 24 and 25.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In a moment, we will adjourn and get lunch, but please come back to the table so that we can have some discussion about some of our longer-term issues on supervision and regulation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we begin, as usual, with the Desk report and Bill Dudley.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’m going to be referring to the handout that you should have in front of you.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Financial markets have become more resilient to bad news in recent weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the news associated with several important groups of financial intermediaries—including investment banks, commercial banks, and the monoline insurers—has not been favorable, contagion has been limited compared with some of our earlier experiences during the past year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the types of vicious feedback loops that were evident, for example, in early March have been largely absent more recently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Despite this, much of the news has not been good.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Looking first at the U.S. equity and credit markets, a good portion of the improvement that occurred in the run-up to the April FOMC meeting has been unwound recently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The broad U.S. equity indexes are only marginally above their low points reached in mid-March and the price of the Standard & Poor’s 500 financial sub-index has fallen to a new trough (exhibit 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, corporate credit spreads have held on to much of the gains achieved after mid-March.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 2, the spreads on both investment- grade and high-yield corporate debt have been quite stable recently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, as shown in exhibit 3, corporate credit default swap spreads have widened over the past few weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Most of the major investment banks have continued to struggle.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 4, the share prices of the four remaining independent U.S. investment banks remain depressed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Further write-offs, capital-raising (which is increasing the number of common share equivalents outstanding), and investors’ concerns about the consequences of deleveraging on long-term profitability have all been important factors weighing on share prices.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast to this poor equity-price performance, credit default swap (CDS) spreads remain much narrower than at the time of Bear Stearns’s demise in mid-March (exhibit 5).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The establishment of the Primary Dealer Credit Facility and the Federal Reserve’s role in the acquisition of Bear Stearns by JPMorgan Chase are undoubtedly both important factors behind the divergence of equity prices and credit default swap spreads.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Lehman Brothers, which reported a second-quarter loss that was considerably larger than expected, has been under the most stress.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, in contrast to Bear Stearns’s experience in mid-March, Lehman’s short-term financing counterparties have generally proved to be patient.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The financing backstop provided by the Primary Dealer Credit Facility has been cited by many counterparties as a critical element that has encouraged them to keep their 1 The materials used by Mr. Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: financing lines to Lehman in place.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The investment banks have begun to rapidly deleverage their balance sheets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 6, the gross leverage ratios for Lehman Brothers, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley all fell sharply in the second quarter.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This stands in marked contrast to the rise in leverage ratios that persisted through the first quarter of this year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Regional banks have also come under considerable strain recently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Deterioration in their construction lending, commercial real estate, and residential mortgage books has caused many banks to raise their loan-loss provisions sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Potential acquirers of troubled regional banks have been discouraged by the accounting requirement that these banks must mark down the assets of the bank that they’re acquiring to the current market value at the time of the acquisition.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The financial guarantors have also been under stress.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Both Standard & Poor’s and Moody’s recently downgraded Ambac and MBIA.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Moody’s downgrade of MBIA was particularly sharp—five notches to A2 from AAA.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These downgrades of the monoline guarantors have a number of important implications.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, the firms that have purchased protection from Ambac and MBIA will have to take significant write-downs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Citigroup, Merrill Lynch, and UBS appear to have the largest exposures to these two firms.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the ability of Ambac and MBIA to establish new AAA-rated subsidiaries that would enable them to write new municipal bond insurance is increasingly in doubt.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Most likely, these firms will be forced to go into runoff mode in which they can no longer write new business.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, the financial resources of these firms will be strained by the downgrades.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, MBIA said that, as a result of the downgrades, it may have to pay out $2.9 billion to satisfy certain contracts and post up to $4.5 billion of additional collateral.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fourth, the risk of a default or a restructuring event by a major monoline guarantor could potentially unsettle the CDS market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 7 and 8, the share prices of the monolines have continued to slide, and their credit default swap spreads have risen further.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As has been the case for some time, there remains—even after the credit rating downgrades—a big disconnect between the CDS spreads of these firms and their credit ratings.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Despite these rating downgrades, the effect on the municipal securities market has been muted compared with the turmoil evident in the first quarter.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Put simply, much of the adjustment in the short-term municipal market—for example, the demise of the muni auction rate securities market and the restructuring of many variable rate demand notes (VRDN) and tender option bond (TOB) securities, has already taken place.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the yields on the VRDNs wrapped by Ambac and MBIA have increased sharply, up to now much of this paper has been remarketed rather than put back to the liquidity providers.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The effect on the municipal bond market has been even more subdued.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 9, the ratios of 10-year and 30-year municipal yields to comparable Treasury yields have risen only slightly recently and remain well below the peaks reached in mid-March.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Investors have already been looking through the credit ratings of the monoline insurers to the quality of the underlying tax-exempt issuer.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The performance of term funding markets also suggests a greater resilience to bad news.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Subsequent to the May expansion of the TAF auction sizes and the increase in the foreign exchange swap lines with the European Central Bank and the Swiss National Bank, one-month and three-month LIBOR–OIS spreads have narrowed significantly (exhibits 10 and 11).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The decline in term funding spreads is particularly noteworthy because it stands in contrast to the widening that occurred in the last month of the three preceding quarters—September, December, and March.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The increase in the size of the TAF auctions has also been associated with a decline in bid-to-cover ratios.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, as shown in exhibit 12, the spread between the stop-out rate and the minimum bid rate has been relatively low.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast to the U.S. auctions, the bid-to-cover ratios in the ECB and SNB auctions have risen sharply over the last three auctions (exhibit 13).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This likely reflects several factors including (1) a reduction in the willingness of U.S. banks to lend at term to European banks—due mostly to balance sheet constraints and (2) strategic bidding behavior.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you recall, the ECB auction is a noncompetitive auction with the stop-out rate determined by the TAF auction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a consequence, increasing the bid size in the ECB auction will not raise the price that the banks will have to pay, and that encourages more bidding in the ECB auctions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This strategic bidding explanation, however, is undercut by the fact that European banks have also been strong bidders in both the TAF and the SNB auctions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The introduction by ICAP of a competing measure of bank funding costs— the New York Funding Rate (NYFR)—has mostly bolstered the credibility of LIBOR.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The NYFR rates have consistently been within 1 or 2 basis points of LIBOR.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, it is unclear how much this conformity reflects the accuracy of LIBOR.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is possible that the NYFR respondents use LIBOR as a benchmark for their own responses, since LIBOR comes out earlier in the day than when they have to respond.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Demand for the term securities lending facility (TSLF) auctions has also generally been subdued.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Only one of the last nine auctions has been fully subscribed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This mainly reflects the convergence in Treasury and non-Treasury repo financing rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Following the first TSLF auction, Treasury repo rates rose sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Given the minimum bid rates for the schedule 1 and schedule 2 auctions of 10 and 25 basis points respectively, the convergence in repo rates has eroded the economic appeal of the TSLF auctions as a funding vehicle.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The $80 billion of the single-tranche repo program has been more attractive as a source of funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the PDCF backstop has made investors more willing to finance the non-Treasury collateral held by the investment banks and other primary dealers, and this has also reduced the demand for TSLF borrowing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The continued rise in commodity prices has been another important market development.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 14, both energy and agricultural prices have been rising sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the weakness of the dollar has often been cited by analysts as a causal factor behind the surge in commodity prices, the recent rise in energy and food prices has been accompanied by a slightly stronger, rather than weaker, dollar (exhibit 15).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Nevertheless, short-term movements in the dollar and oil prices do appear to have become more closely linked over the past few years.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 16 plots the six-month rolling correlation between the weekly change in the spot price of West Texas intermediate crude oil and the weekly change in the value of the trade- weighted dollar.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, these price changes have become increasingly negatively correlated in recent years.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, correlation does not imply causality.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Even if there is causality, it is unclear in what direction the causality runs—from commodities to the dollar or from the dollar to commodities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although many factors are undoubtedly at play, a couple of possible explanations that have made the rounds may be worth considering.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, higher oil prices swell the dollar reserves held by the oil-producing countries.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because these countries may respond to this dollar influx by selling dollars to diversify their foreign exchange reserve holdings, traders may sell dollars in anticipation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, trade data suggest that the composition of import demand from the oil-exporting nations is skewed away from the United States, and this may also weigh on the dollar.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rise in commodity prices has fanned anxieties about inflation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 17, the University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey measures of one- year and five-to-ten-year inflation expectations have increased recently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, both Barclays’ and the Board’s five-year, five-year-forward measures of breakeven inflation have moderated a bit since the last meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These measures remain well inside the ranges evident over the past year (exhibit 18).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The anxiety about higher commodity prices and inflation has been an important factor behind the sharp shift in monetary policy expectations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 19 and 20, the federal funds rate and Eurodollar futures curves have continued to shift upward since the April FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 21 and 22, our survey of primary dealer expectations also shows an upward shift in the expected path of the federal funds rate target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, compared with the expectations embodied in futures prices, the rise has been more modest.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, the gap between the average of the dealers’ forecasts and the market’s forecast has continued to increase and is now unusually wide.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The divergence between the dealers’ forecasts and market expectations and the wide range of the dealers’ forecasts one year ahead indicate that there is considerable uncertainty about the future path of short-term rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This uncertainty is also evident in the fact that the implied volatility of short-term interest rates is unusually high currently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The tightening expected over the next year is not anticipated to begin soon.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 23 and 24, options on federal funds rate futures contracts currently imply that market participants expect that the FOMC will stand pat at both this and the August FOMC meetings.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although considerable tightening is priced in over the next year, this is not unusual at this stage of the monetary policy cycle.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Assuming that we are at the trough of the current rate cycle, the magnitude of tightening expected over the next year is not significantly greater than what has been priced in following other troughs in the federal funds rate target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Tomorrow we will be eight weeks beyond what may turn out to be the onset of the trough in the target rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 25, the roughly 125 basis points of tightening that is currently priced in over the next year is comparable to what was anticipated at the same point after the federal funds rate trough in 1992.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, a few words about the Primary Dealer Credit Facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: (Art Angulo will talk about this in more detail tomorrow.)

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have been actively managing our counterparty risk in this facility and have made it clear to market participants that this should be viewed as a backstop facility rather than as a core source of funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: By the end of next week, borrowing from this facility is likely to drop sharply because of two events.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The first is this week’s closing of the Bear Stearns–JPMorgan Chase transaction, which will result in the elimination of Bear Stearns’s PDCF borrowing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second is the anticipated closing next week of the Bank of America acquisition of Countrywide, which is expected to eliminate Countrywide’s PDCF borrowing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the absence of new financial shocks that could provoke renewed funding difficulties, we would anticipate little persistent PDCF borrowing after these mergers are completed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Last week I sent you a memo informing you of our plans to initiate a euro time deposit with the Netherlands Central Bank, subject to Regulation N approval by the Board.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There were no foreign operations during this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I request a vote to ratify the operations conducted by the System Open Market Account since the April FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As always, I am very happy to take any questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The quarter-end premium seems less this time, but am I correct that the dollar premium is higher than the euro and pound premiums?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is a bit higher, yes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is there anything to be inferred from that?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: About 225 basis points are priced in for our dollar turn—maybe 150 basis points or 175 basis points elsewhere—but those are pretty small differences measured over just a couple of days.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I wouldn’t read too much into it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The reality is that the European banks are structurally short of dollar funding, and so that may be why there is a little more upward pressure on dollar rates over the quarter-end.

speaker: LACKER
text: I notice that in chart 18, in your TIPS-implied average inflationary plot to the ten-year horizon, you omit the Markets Group’s estimate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is that because of skepticism on your part that leads you to judge it as inferior or an overabundance of humility?

speaker: LACKER
text: It does, of course, show a slightly different trend, right?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It actually has increased a bit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I have consistently shown just the Barclays and Board measures over the past few months, so this is not “pick and choose.”

speaker: FISHER
text: Bill, by inference, talking about the Primary Dealer Credit Facility, two of the limited number of borrowers have been the two institutions you mentioned.

speaker: FISHER
text: Have there been many more or just one or two?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There have been more borrowers than just them.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Some have done it because they wanted to test the facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Some have done it because they viewed it as a fairly advantageous cost of funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You know, there have been quite a few different borrowers, but those two borrowers mentioned are the ones that I would view as more persistent than desired.

speaker: FISHER
text: Thank you for discreetly answering the question.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Just to follow up on that question, I was at a meeting in New York not too long ago and was talking with some people on Wall Street.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They suggested that for the primary dealers there was stigma attached to borrowing from the PDCF.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wasn’t quite sure what to make of that, and I just wondered if you had any observations or comments about whether you thought that was real or perceived, or is there an interpretation I should give to that?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think there is some stigma attached to the Primary Dealer Credit Facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is hard to know exactly how much.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One thing I thought was interesting: The first week the facility was outstanding, a number of institutions went to the Primary Dealer Credit Facility and then announced that they were doing it as a test.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, presumably you wouldn’t announce that you were doing it as a test if there were no stigma associated with the facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I would judge that it is clearly less stigmatized than the Primary Credit Facility, probably because it doesn’t have the history that the Primary Credit Facility has.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The fact is that it is an advantageous rate or was an advantageous rate several weeks ago, and there were some institutions that were borrowing from the facility just on the basis of rate—so that suggests less stigma than the discount window.

speaker: STERN
text: Bill, on chart 6, just a quick question on the leverage ratio: Do we know how good those data are?

speaker: STERN
text: I mean, to the best of our knowledge, is that reliable stuff?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is just assets divided by equity, so I think it is pretty good.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When the investment banks start proposing their adjusted leverage ratios, then I think you have a problem—you know, apples and oranges—because the different investment banks calculate those kinds of adjusted leverage ratios a bit differently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Usually you see two leverage ratios— one that is gross and another one that excludes the matched book—and the leverage ratio falls pretty significantly when you exclude the matched book.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: President Stern, I have just one thing to add.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: For the first time with the three investment banks that reported for the quarter that ended in May, the SEC allowed them to disclose their risk-weighted ratio on the SEC’s version of Basel II.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That’s the ratio for which your question is more germane in some sense because it shows a pretty significant cushion of capital against risk-weighted assets.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The question is, How good are those measures of risk-weighted assets?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is a subject for discussion tomorrow, but part of our problem is that we have much less confidence in judging the integrity of what goes into those measures of risk—not to mention whether the risk weights are any good, which is a harder thing for the market to judge.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But for the first time the market can see what their risk- weighted measures are, at least on an SEC basis, which is pretty close to Basel II, and those ratios were, if I recall correctly, north of 10, tier 1, for the three that reported—significantly higher than they were on March 1, by their own measures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, would someone move the ratification.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s turn now to the economic situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nathan, I’ll start with you.

speaker: SHEETS
text: 2 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given that developments in global commodities markets have continued to have influential effects on our forecast for domestic activity and prices, we felt that it would be useful for me to lead off with the international portion of the chart show, which will include a discussion of these markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Following my remarks, Larry and Bill will present our outlook for the U.S. economy.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the top panel of your first exhibit, total foreign real GDP growth (line 1) stepped down from an average pace of 4½ percent in the first three quarters of 2007 to around 3 percent in the fourth quarter of last year and the first quarter of this year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We see growth abroad as likely to decline to 2.2 percent in the current quarter and to pick up only slightly in the second half of the year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Next year, with the expected firming of U.S. activity and diminishing headwinds from the financial turmoil, foreign growth should rise back to a 3½ percent pace.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Growth abroad was just a bit stronger in the first quarter than we had anticipated, but the composition of that growth came as more of a surprise.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Canadian GDP (line 3) posted a slight contraction, reflecting a continuing downturn in exports and stagnant investment.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In contrast, the pace of activity in Japan (line 4) and the euro area (line 5) was much more vigorous than we had expected, including a 6¼ percent surge in Germany.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, recent data for these economies point to much weaker growth in the second quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the middle left panel, Japanese manufacturing output 2 The materials used by Messrs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Sheets, Slifman, and Wascher are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: SHEETS
text: has declined recently, and labor market conditions have softened.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For the euro area (the middle right), various indicators are showing weakness, including retail sales and the purchasing managers’ index.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As highlighted in the bottom panel, growth in the emerging market economies is expected to step down over the next few quarters but should remain relatively resilient, especially compared with the weak performance of these economies during the U.S. recession earlier this decade.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Many of the EMEs were particularly vulnerable to the high-tech- and manufacturing-led downturn that occurred at that time, and fundamentals in the EMEs are now stronger than was then the case.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, Chinese domestic demand has remained quite robust of late, and this has likely helped to support growth in emerging Asia.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the top left panel of exhibit 2, oil prices have continued to soar with the spot price of WTI closing yesterday at $136 per barrel.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The far-dated futures price has climbed to about the same level.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our forecast for the path of oil prices is now roughly $50 a barrel higher than at the time of the January chart show.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Divining the causes of this staggering rise in oil prices is no doubt ground on which angels fear to tread, but we continue to assert bravely that the primary driver of higher oil prices is constrained (and price inelastic) oil supply coupled with relatively strong (and price inelastic) oil demand.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These deep features of the oil market—along with stressed geopolitical conditions in many oil-producing countries, rising production costs, and concern about the reliability of medium- to long-run supply—have sent oil prices spiraling upward.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the last column of the middle table, the increase in oil prices appears to have contributed to modest declines in oil consumption in the advanced economies, including the United States (line 3).

speaker: SHEETS
text: But oil consumption has continued to move up in the emerging market economies, especially in China (line 5) and the Middle East (line 6).

speaker: SHEETS
text: Consumers in many EMEs have been shielded from rising prices by government fuel subsidies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The economic and fiscal costs of such subsidies are becoming increasingly burdensome, however, prompting some countries (including China late last week) to allow domestic fuel prices to move toward world levels.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As seen on the top right, oil inventories in OECD countries have declined over the past year and a half.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Unfortunately, little information is available about the behavior of inventories outside of OECD countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The bottom left panel shows that the rise in global oil production since 2004 has significantly lagged the expansion of world GDP (weighted by oil consumption); indeed, production has remained relatively flat during most of that period.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, however, the lack of oil production is not due to geological constraints.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Data on years of proved reserves (shown on the bottom right) are at roughly the same level as a decade ago.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But those reserves are now concentrated in areas where production is constrained by acute geopolitical risks, uncertainty about property rights, inadequate investment, and high production costs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Turning to your next exhibit, nonfuel commodity prices have also risen significantly on average since your last chart show, with most of the increase coming in the first few months of the year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Here, too, we believe that the elevated level of prices is a result mainly of strong and sustained global demand, lagging supply responses, and rising production costs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Consistent with this observation, inventories of key commodities, shown in the middle left panel, have trended down in recent years.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It bears emphasizing, however, that nonfuel commodity prices certainly have not moved in lockstep with each other.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As seen in the bottom left panel, the price of corn has surged to new highs, supported by ethanol demand and, more recently, as adverse weather in the Midwest has endangered a substantial fraction of this year’s crop.
