speaker: SHEETS
text: In contrast, the price of wheat has fallen back from its recent peak, as improved growing conditions in Australia seem likely to boost supply.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For metals, the price of zinc has moved down significantly since its peak in late 2006, as new smelters have come on line.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The price of copper has moved sideways—but at a high level—over the past two years, as prospective increases in supply have not yet materialized.

speaker: SHEETS
text: A number of other explanations for the recent run-up in oil and other commodity prices have also been advanced, including the possibility that increased purchases by “speculators” in commodity futures markets may be playing an important role.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given the magnitude of the financial flows into these markets, we are hesitant to slam the door completely on this explanation, but our work finds little supporting evidence.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As noted on the top right, prices of a number of commodities that are not traded in futures markets have also risen substantially.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Second, a sustained increase in demand by investors would suggest that inventories should be rising; instead, as I have noted, inventories are now relatively tight.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Finally, we see no evidence that the positions taken by noncommercial traders in futures markets actually predict commodity prices; for example, such positions for light sweet crude oil on the New York Mercantile Exchange have been roughly flat since mid-2007.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Two other frequently cited explanations for the rise in commodity prices are the depreciation of the dollar and declines in interest rates.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The middle-right panel shows the correlation of the broad nominal dollar with oil prices and with an index of nonfuel commodity prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Both correlations are negative over most of the sample, implying that depreciations of the dollar have tended to happen at the same time as rises in commodity prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: While these correlations have become more negative since mid-2007, they remain within the ranges seen in recent years, and interpreting the direction of causality for this relationship is difficult.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Also, as Bill noted, the dollar has been relatively stable over the past several months, but oil prices have continued their upward climb.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Similar plots of correlations of interest rates with commodity prices (shown on the bottom right) are quite noisy and fail to point to any clear conclusions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in exhibit 4, the run-up in commodity prices has continued to lift headline consumer price inflation in both the advanced foreign economies and the emerging markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We expect that inflation abroad will remain elevated in the near term but eventually move back down as slower global growth reduces pressures on resources and as commodity prices flatten out (consistent with quotes from futures markets).

speaker: SHEETS
text: Of course, one clear risk to these projections is that commodity prices may, yet again, confound our expectations and continue rising.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Another risk is that the high rates of inflation now being recorded may become embedded in inflation expectations.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the top right panels, measures of long-term inflation compensation have recently edged up in the euro area and increased more markedly in Canada.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In recent weeks, major foreign central banks have intensified their inflation-fighting rhetoric.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, the ECB has warned that it may raise rates at its next meeting; and in the United Kingdom, Mervyn King—in his letter to the Chancellor—underscored his determination to ensure that inflation remains contained.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown on the bottom left, we now assume that both the ECB and the Bank of England will raise rates in the second half of this year, compared with the near-term cuts we had anticipated in the April Greenbook.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, we now see the Bank of Canada keeping policy on hold.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the emerging market economies, including Mexico and China (the bottom right panel), increases in inflation have largely been driven by rising food prices, which account for a substantial share of consumer expenditures.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Policymakers in the EMEs have taken steps to slow the rise in food prices, with some countries introducing price controls and export bans on agricultural goods.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But officials have also relied on more-orthodox policies to combat inflation, including raising policy rates and hiking reserve requirements.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indeed, over the intermeeting period, monetary policy was tightened in a range of emerging market economies, including Mexico, Brazil, China, India, Russia, and Hungary.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the top left panel of exhibit 5, the path of the broad real dollar is now just a little weaker than we anticipated at the time of the January chart show.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We continue to expect the dollar to depreciate at an annual rate of 3 percent through the forecast period, reflecting persisting downward pressures associated with the current account deficit.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This depreciation is projected to come largely against emerging market currencies (including the Chinese renminbi), which have moved less since the dollar’s peak in early 2002.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It’s safe to say that core import price inflation (on the right) has come in substantially higher than we projected in January.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Incorporating the BLS monthly data for April and May, we now see core import prices in the second quarter surging at an annual rate of 10½ percent, the fastest rise in two decades.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This increase, which comes on the heels of an 8 percent jump in the first quarter, was heavily concentrated in material-intensive goods and suggests a much more rapid and, perhaps, stronger effect from the run-up in commodity prices than we saw in the past.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Conditional on nonfuel commodity prices flattening out, core import price inflation should decline to less than 2 percent next year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Finally, summing up what these developments mean for U.S. activity, we now see the contribution from net exports to U.S. real GDP growth (line 3 in the table) as likely to exceed 2 percentage points in the second quarter, as exports expand at a smart pace (supported by the lower dollar) and imports contract sharply.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This marked weakness in imports reflects both a steep drop in real oil imports and a continued decline in imports of core goods (reflecting sluggish U.S. GDP growth and rising prices of imported commodities).

speaker: SHEETS
text: The positive contribution from net exports moderates to ¾ percentage point in the second half of this year and to ½ percentage point in 2009.

speaker: SHEETS
text: While the pace of export growth is projected to remain strong, at above 7 percent, imports should gradually accelerate as the U.S. economy recovers.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Larry will now continue our presentation.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Last week, the Washington Post ran a front page story with the headline, “Why We’re Gloomier than the Economy.” Like the author of the Post article, we too have noticed the difference between what people are saying about the economy in surveys and what they apparently are producing and spending.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Starting first with the survey indicators, the top left panel of exhibit 6 plots the plunge in the Michigan index of consumer sentiment, which is far deeper than can be explained by its usual predictors such as labor market conditions, inflation, and the stock market.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: The panel to the right plots two of the most timely surveys of business attitudes, which continue to suggest that the respondents are pessimistic about overall business conditions.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Meanwhile, as shown in the middle left panel, although private payrolls continue to shrink, the declines have been much smaller than we were expecting and, as you can see from the shaded area (if you look very closely), [laughter] much smaller than the ones that occurred during the last recession.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: In terms of spending data, the most striking piece of news was the upward revision to earlier retail sales figures.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: At the time of the April Greenbook, real outlays for consumer goods other than motor vehicles appeared to be moving sideways (the red line in the middle right panel).

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: However, the black line shows that according to the latest estimates—which, of course, are still subject to additional revisions—spending rose rapidly in March and April and climbed further in May.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: With these numbers, we revised up appreciably our near-term estimates of the growth rate of real PCE goods other than motor vehicles (the inset box).

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: On the business side, the bottom left table, shipments of nondefense capital goods, excluding transportation, rose further in April, and new orders jumped.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: In addition, outlays for construction of nonresidential buildings, the bottom line of the table, continued to climb in April.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: All told, these indicators suggest stronger business spending than we had anticipated in our April forecast.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: A potentially important downside development may be emerging in the motor vehicles sector—the bottom right panel—where, according to our industry contacts, sales of light vehicles appear to be plummeting in June.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Whether this is just a reaction to the surge in oil prices that will be contained within the auto sector or whether it’s a canary in the coal mine pointing to something far more serious for the entire economy remains to be seen.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: But it certainly has grabbed our attention and highlights a downside risk to our projection.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Exhibit 7 focuses on the overall GDP forecast through 2009 and some of the key factors that informed our thinking about the outlook.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: We had a lot of moving parts to deal with this round, and the upper panel summarizes how we put them together.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: First, in light of the incoming information, we revised up our forecast for the first two quarters of this year, especially the second quarter.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: We now think that real GDP growth came in at an annual rate of 1.1 percent in the first quarter and picked up to a 1.7 percent pace in the second quarter.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: As you know, earlier this year we put in some judgmental adjustments to the forecast, which reflected a combination of the tendency for negative model residuals to be correlated during cyclical downturns as well as the macro effects of financial turmoil and uncertainty that are not well captured by our models.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: We have interpreted some of the recent spending surprise as suggesting that we went too heavy on such effects in the April Greenbook, and so we have tempered them in this projection.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: That said, we still anticipate that some of these influences will show through to spending, especially in the household sector, and we expect the economy to be on a very subdued growth path for the next few quarters.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: As I will discuss shortly, residential investment is still projected to be a drag on economic growth well into next year.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Moreover, with house prices expected to fall through the end of next year, the ratio of household net worth to income remains on a downward trajectory, reducing some of the wherewithal for consumer spending.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Household purchasing power also is being held down by the surge in oil prices that Nathan discussed (the middle left panel).

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: As shown in the inset box, by our reckoning the increases in the spot and futures prices of WTI since the April Greenbook subtract about ¼ percentage point from real GDP growth in both 2008 and 2009, with much of the effect working through PCE.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Despite these negative influences, if the story ended here, the economy still would be operating with a somewhat higher utilization rate—that is, a smaller GDP gap—than in the April Greenbook.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: In light of this consideration, as well as the less favorable outlook for inflation that Bill will discuss, we have conditioned this forecast on a tighter path for monetary policy than the one in the previous Greenbook.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: As you can see in the middle right panel, by the end of next year the federal funds rate is 100 basis points higher than in the April Greenbook.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: I should note here that we also have raised our estimate of the growth rate of potential GDP, which Bill will discuss shortly.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Because we view our revised estimate of potential as merely the staff’s catching up with what individuals and firms were already expecting, these revisions result in corresponding adjustments to the growth rate of real GDP going forward.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: All told, as illustrated in the bottom left panel, after increasing substantially faster in the first half of the year, real GDP is now projected to grow at an annual rate of ¾ percent in the second half of 2008, a bit less than in our previous projection.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: In 2009, real GDP is expected to increase 2.4 percent, about ½ percentage point less than in the April Greenbook.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: The bottom line of the forecast is perhaps most easily seen by the path of the GDP gap.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: As shown in the bottom right panel, the gap starts out the projection period being much narrower than in the April forecast.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: By the fourth quarter of 2009, however, the gap is essentially the same as in the April Greenbook.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: After that high-altitude flyover of the projection, the next two exhibits swoop down for a closer look at some of the details.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Exhibit 8 focuses on the housing sector.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: With demand weak, the overhang of unsold new and existing single-family homes— the vacancy rate—has soared, putting downward pressure on prices.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: As shown to the right, the OFHEO purchase-only index of house prices fell at an annual of 6.7 percent in the first quarter of 2008, and we expect home prices to continue declining around this pace into next year.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Anecdotes and common sense suggest that many prospective homebuyers, leery of purchasing an asset whose value is falling, are waiting for house prices to bottom out before entering the market.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: This behavior further saps already sagging housing demand.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: We don’t have direct survey evidence for this supposition; however, the middle panels present some suggestive numbers taken from the Michigan survey.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: First, as shown by the black line in the panel to the left, the share of current homeowners who think the price of their home fell over the past 12 months jumped dramatically through early this year and remains elevated.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: In addition, the share that thinks the price will fall over the next 12 months also has drifted up.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: The panel on the right, which is based on work by my colleague Claudia Sahm, looks at the views of renters.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Here the blue bars show the percentage of renters in the Michigan survey who say that now is a bad time to buy a house.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: The red line plots an estimate of house price overvaluation derived from a price–rent model that we follow.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: As you can see, as houses became increasingly overvalued, more and more renters became pessimistic about homebuying—apparently for affordability reasons.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Of course, relative prices are not the only influence on affordability.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: General macroeconomic and credit market conditions also are important.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Thus, even though the extent of overvaluation has diminished so far this year, renters, at least thus far, remain quite pessimistic about homebuying conditions.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: So what brings us out of this seeming death spiral?

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: If house prices follow the expected trajectory, we estimate that they will move into rough alignment with their long-run relationship with rents early next year and then, as typically happens, overshoot somewhat.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: As the market returns to something closer to equilibrium, prospective homebuyers who had been waiting out the price bubble in rental quarters should begin to see housing as more affordable and be more willing to buy into owner-occupied housing.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: As that happens, the rate of decline in house prices should slow, and sales of single-family homes (the bottom left panel) should start to improve.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: With demand improving and the inventory overhang being worked off, we expect housing starts to level out and then begin to gain altitude slowly in 2009.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Exhibit 9 presents the medium-term outlook for consumer spending and business investment.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Starting with PCE, real spending is projected to fall, on balance, in the second half of this year.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Tax rebates push up the third quarter and create a pothole in the fourth quarter as rebate-related spending drops off.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: More fundamentally, spending is held back by the effects of higher oil prices on household purchasing power, the ongoing hit to household wealth from falling home prices and earlier declines in equity prices, and the restraining effects of financial turmoil and unusually pessimistic consumer sentiment.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: In 2009, spending picks up as many of these factors begin to improve; but at 1½ percent, the increase is still rather tepid.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: The middle panels focus on business outlays for equipment and software.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Real spending on the high-tech component (the green bars) has slowed sharply this year and is expected to remain relatively soft throughout the projection period.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: The major U.S. computer manufacturers—such as HP, Dell, and Sun—have expressed caution about the outlook for sales.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Meanwhile, capital spending guidance from telecommunications service providers points to a slowing in their outlays for communications equipment.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: As shown by the blue bars, investment outside the high- tech segment has been declining at a modest pace since late last year, and we expect it to contract further over the next year and a half.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Spending is held back by normal accelerator effects, tight lending standards, and gloomy business sentiment.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: For nonresidential structures, the lower panels, the BEA reported that outlays in the drilling and mining component (the green bars) dipped in the first quarter.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Anecdotal reports suggest that this may have reflected bottlenecks stemming from shortages of skilled labor and supplies.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: However, recent data on footage drilled and the number of drilling rigs in operation have picked up, signaling a near-term rise in spending.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Looking forward, escalating energy prices are likely to spur continued increases in investment.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: In contrast, as shown by the blue bars, real construction spending for buildings is projected to be very weak following sizable increases in 2006 and 2007.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: The evolving supply-and-demand factors for this sector are almost uniformly downbeat: Vacancy rates are moving up; sales and prices of existing properties are sagging; and financing conditions are tight for new projects.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Because of these developments, we expect outlays in this category to fall throughout the projection period.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Bill will now continue our presentation.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Exhibit 10 reviews our assumptions about aggregate supply.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As you can see from the first two rows of the table at the top, we now assume that potential output growth will hold steady at about 2½ percent per year over the forecast period, about ¼ percentage point per year higher from 2007 to 2009 than we had assumed in the April Greenbook.

speaker: WASCHER
text: This upward revision is split roughly equally between structural productivity growth (lines 3 and 4) and trend hours (lines 5 and 6).

speaker: WASCHER
text: The middle two panels provide the reasoning for our change.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The left panel shows the difference between actual productivity growth (the black line) and a simulation from our standard model (the green line) using the pace of structural productivity growth that we had assumed in April.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As you can see, labor productivity growth in recent quarters has been stronger than the model would have expected given the deceleration in economic activity.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As shown in the inset box, a purely statistical model based on a Kalman filter would have responded to the recent data by raising its estimate of structural productivity growth 0.2 percentage point.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Because we place less weight on data that have not yet been through an annual revision, we generally tend to revise our own estimate by less than the amount suggested by such models; moreover, the Kalman filter model does not take into account the steep rise in energy prices, which we think might subtract a bit from structural productivity growth in coming years.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Nevertheless, we did think it appropriate to nudge up our productivity growth trend a little.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The green line in the middle right panel shows a similar model simulation for the labor force participation rate, again using our previously estimated trend.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Here, too, the incoming data have been a little higher than the model would have expected.

speaker: WASCHER
text: One can think of potential explanations for this—for example, it may be that strains on household budgets associated with rising costs of food and energy have increased labor force participation among secondary earners, an influence not captured by the model.

speaker: WASCHER
text: We are not ready to back away from our basic story that demographics will continue to put downward pressure on the participation rate over time, but we did slightly raise our assumed trend in response to the recent data.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The key elements of the labor market forecast are shown in the bottom panels.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As indicated to the left, nonfarm payroll employment (the black line) is projected to decline about 40,000 per month through the rest of this year.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As the economy improves in 2009, we expect payrolls to start rising again, although at a pace below our estimate of trend employment growth (the green line) for most of the year.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As shown in the inset box in the bottom right panel, we expect the unemployment rate to drop back in June from its suspiciously high May reading, which would leave the average jobless rate in the second quarter at 5.3 percent.

speaker: WASCHER
text: However, with employment declines projected to continue for a while longer, we expect the unemployment rate to drift up to 5.7 percent by early next year and remain near that level through the end of 2009.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Exhibit 11 presents the near-term inflation outlook.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As you can see in the top left panel, the recent data on consumer prices have come in a little lower than we had expected at the time of the April Greenbook.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As shown on line 3, core PCE prices rose only 0.1 percent in April, and based on the latest CPI and PPI readings, we expect an increase of 0.2 percent in May.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As a result, we have marked down our estimate of core PCE inflation in the second quarter by 0.3 percentage point, to an annual rate of 2 percent.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Total PCE prices (line 1) have risen at a substantially faster pace than core prices; but here, too, the current-quarter forecast is a little lower than in our previous projection, both because of the lower core inflation and because the sharp increases in oil prices have been slow to feed through to finished energy prices.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Despite this recent news, we expect inflation to rise sharply over the next few months.

speaker: WASCHER
text: In part, this reflects our judgment that core prices were held down in the first half by some factors that will not persist into the second half.

speaker: WASCHER
text: In addition, as shown to the right, we expect increases in food and energy prices to push up the twelve-month change in the total PCE price index more than 1 percentage point over the next several months, to about 4½ percent.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The remaining panels of the exhibit focus on the projection for energy and food prices.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As shown by the black line in the middle left panel, rising crude oil prices have pushed up retail gasoline prices sharply so far this year.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Even so, margins are still relatively low, and we expect further sizable increases in pump prices in coming months.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Spot prices for natural gas (the red line) have also risen noticeably, reflecting its substitutability with crude oil.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Meanwhile, prices for crops, plotted in black at the right, have moved well above the levels at the time of the April Greenbook, mainly in response to the severe flooding in the Midwest.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The higher prices for grains have also pushed up livestock prices (the blue line), although recent increases in supply have tempered this rise somewhat.

speaker: WASCHER
text: In both cases, futures prices indicate that market participants expect these prices to flatten out at about their current levels.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The bottom two panels show our forecast for overall consumer food and energy prices.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Based on current futures prices, we expect energy price inflation to move yet higher next quarter before slowing to a pace close to zero in 2009.

speaker: WASCHER
text: We expect food prices to show a similar—albeit less pronounced—pattern, with the four- quarter change peaking at about 5 percent this quarter and then decelerating to a pace of 2½ percent next year.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The upper panels of your next exhibit examine the implications of the recent increases in energy and other commodity prices for core inflation.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The first thing to note is that these increases are showing through to producers’ costs.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As indicated in the top left panel, the producer price index for core intermediate materials (the black line) has accelerated yet again and was up more than 7 percent over the past twelve months, with especially large increases for metal products and energy-intensive materials.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Likewise, the diffusion index for prices paid from the Institute for Supply Management’s manufacturing survey (the red line) has climbed steadily since late last year.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As Nathan noted, rising commodity prices have been an important source of the sizable increases in import prices shown to the right.

speaker: WASCHER
text: In addition, higher energy prices have boosted the costs of shipping goods from manufacturers to wholesalers and retailers.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As you can see in the middle left panel, the PPIs for both trucking and rail transport have accelerated sharply over the past year or so.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Obviously, a key question is the extent to which these higher costs will be passed through to core consumer prices.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The panel to the right provides rough estimates of the size of these pass-throughs from our suite of econometric models, with the effect of energy prices on core PCE inflation shown by the blue bars and the combined effects of import prices and other commodity prices indicated by the red bars.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As you can see, these effects add more than 0.6 percentage point to our forecast of core inflation this year.

speaker: WASCHER
text: With energy and import prices expected to decelerate, the contribution of these factors to core inflation steps down to ¼ percentage point next year.

speaker: WASCHER
text: In contrast to the evidence of greater cost pressures from commodity prices, we’ve seen no signs of acceleration in labor costs.

speaker: WASCHER
text: The bottom left panel plots the three main measures of labor compensation that we follow.

speaker: WASCHER
text: None of them suggests that employers have experienced a step-up in the pace of compensation growth; and given the weaker labor market in our projection, we don’t think that workers will do much better over the next year and a half either.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Accordingly, we expect the rise in trend unit labor costs, shown in the table to the right, to hold steady at about 2 percent per year over the projection period.

speaker: WASCHER
text: In putting together our forecast, we’ve also had to make some decisions about how to interpret the recent data on inflation expectations—the subject of your final exhibit.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As shown in the top left panel, some measures of short-run inflation expectations have jumped sharply in response to the run-up in energy and food prices this year.

speaker: WASCHER
text: In particular, the Reuters-Michigan measure of one-year-ahead expectations (the blue line) rose above 5 percent in May and remained high in the preliminary June survey.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Meanwhile, as shown to the right, indicators of long-run inflation expectations have ranged from roughly unchanged to higher since late April.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As I already noted, the recent compensation data do not suggest that higher inflation expectations have started to push up wage increases.

speaker: WASCHER
text: However, on balance, we view the data as consistent with a slight updrift in the underlying long-run inflation expectations that drive actual inflation, and we have carried this updrift into the projection period.

speaker: WASCHER
text: All told, we expect core PCE inflation (line 3 of the middle left table) to step up to a 2½ percent annual rate in the second half of this year, pushed up by the effects of higher input costs and the increase in inflation expectations.

speaker: WASCHER
text: In 2009, core inflation is projected to step back down to 2¼ percent, as the effects of decelerating energy and import prices and a wider unemployment gap offset a small further updrift in expected inflation.

speaker: WASCHER
text: We have taken only a small signal from the apparent deterioration in expected inflation, but we view the possibility that inflation expectations will become unmoored in response to the persistently high rate of headline inflation as a risk to our forecast.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Accordingly, as indicated in the box to the right, we included in the Greenbook an alternative simulation that assumes that long-run inflation expectations move up ¾ percentage point relative to baseline in the third quarter.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Consistent with our usual practice, monetary policy in this simulation is assumed to respond according to the estimated Taylor rule.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Both wages and prices are affected by these higher inflation expectations, and as you can see by the green line in the middle panel at the bottom, core inflation rises to 2.6 percent in 2009, almost ½ percentage point higher than baseline.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Monetary policy responds in this simulation by raising the federal funds rate more than in the baseline forecast.

speaker: WASCHER
text: As a result of this additional tightening, the unemployment rate declines a bit more slowly, and core inflation moderates to about 2¼ percent in 2012.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Brian will now continue the presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 3 I will be referring to the separate package labeled “Material for Briefing on FOMC Participants’ Economic Projections.” The top two sections of table 1 show the central tendencies and ranges of your current forecasts for the first and second halves of 2008; central tendencies and ranges of the projections published by the Committee this past April are shown in italics.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To facilitate comparisons, the Greenbook projections are shown in the bottom section.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In your forecast submissions, most of you indicated that you saw appropriate monetary policy as entailing a path for the federal funds rate that lies above that assumed in the Greenbook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the first row, first column, of table 1, the central tendency of your real growth forecasts for the first half of 2008 has been marked up substantially since April.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, a number of you noted that recent upside surprises to consumer and business spending are likely to prove transitory and that falling house prices, tight credit conditions, and elevated energy prices will probably restrain growth over the remainder of 2008.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Accordingly, some of you revised down a touch your growth expectations for the second half of this year (the second column) especially those of you who had previously anticipated the briskest 3 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: growth rates, as indicated by the downward revision to the upper end of the range shown in the middle section.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you think the economy will skirt recession.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Nonetheless, your projections for the speed of recovery over the second half exhibit considerable dispersion: Four participants are projecting growth rates of real GDP between 2 and 2¼ percent, whereas an equal number are calling for growth at an annual rate of only around ½ percent, a pace similar to the one projected in the Greenbook, with many of you attributing the tepid growth partly to financial headwinds.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The tendency for some clustering of your second-half growth forecasts at the extremes can be seen by noting the similarity between the central tendency and the range.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the second set of rows in the top panel, your projections for headline PCE inflation in the second half of 2008 have been revised up more than 1 percentage point, to around 3½ to 4¾ percent, largely as a result of the surge in prices of energy and agricultural commodities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, in view of better-than- expected news on core PCE inflation, the central tendency of your projections for core inflation during the second half (shown in the third set of rows) revised up only 0.1 percentage point.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Looking ahead to 2009 (table 2, the middle column), you continue to expect growth to pick up as the drag from the housing sector dissipates and credit conditions ease.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The midpoint of the central tendency of your forecast for real GDP growth next year is 2.4 percent, the same as in April and the same as the staff’s current forecast.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your growth forecasts for 2010 (the third column) are a shade lower than in April, and the central tendency of your forecasts for the unemployment rate is a touch higher, perhaps because a number of you assumed more policy tightening over the forecast period in order to counter heightened inflation pressures.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The midpoint of the central tendency of your projections for the unemployment rate edges down from about 5½ percent in 2009 to about 5¼ percent in 2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your commentaries suggest that many, albeit not all, of you view those rates as a quarter-point to a half-point above your estimates of the NAIRU.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The third and fourth sets of rows indicate that most of you see overall and core inflation staying above 2 percent next year; but by 2010, the extended period of economic slack and the assumed leveling-out of energy prices push down overall and core inflation to around 1¾ to 2 percent; for core inflation, the central tendency and range are a touch higher than you forecasted in April.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For the first time since you started these projections last October, the upper end of the range of your projection of total inflation in 2010 exceeds 2 percent, albeit marginally.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus, many of you project that, at the end of the forecast period, the economy will still be operating with some slack and real output growth will be slightly above the growth rate of potential.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The continued presence of slack suggests that you anticipate that inflation will continue to edge lower in 2011 and, given the assumption of appropriate monetary policy, implies that you typically anticipate that inflation will still be a bit higher in 2010 than you see as consistent with price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Exhibit 3 presents your views on the risks and uncertainties in the outlook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown by the green bars in the top two panels, a large majority of you continue to perceive the risks to growth as weighted to the downside (the left panel), and many judge that the degree of uncertainty regarding prospects for economic activity is unusually high (the right panel), although the number of you seeing uncertainty about growth as elevated has declined slightly over the first half of the year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In your narratives, you attributed the downside risks primarily to the potential for steeper declines in house prices and persisting financial strains, which through a further tightening of credit conditions could exert an unexpectedly large restraint on household and business spending.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although your views of the risks regarding growth have shifted only modestly, the distribution of your perceptions of the risks regarding inflation (shown in the bottom two panels) has changed significantly so far this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the lower left panel, about three-quarters of you now see the risks to the outlook for overall inflation as skewed to the upside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In your commentaries, you typically pointed to continued increases in energy and food prices and an upward drift in inflation expectations as the main reasons for the upside risks to inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In addition, as shown to the right, the number of participants who perceive the degree of uncertainty regarding the inflation outlook as larger than usual has risen considerably.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Turning to exhibit 4, as I noted, your projections suggest that you do not see the economy as having fully settled into a steady state by 2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The dynamics of the economy evidently are such that, following moderately large shocks, it can take quite a few years to converge back to steady state, a view that is captured by many econometric models such as FRB/US and is also reflected in the current Greenbook forecast.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus, the three-year forecast horizon currently used by the Committee does not necessarily allow your forecasts to reveal fully your views of the steady-state characteristics of the economy and your views of the rate of inflation consistent with the dual mandate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Recognizing this, the Subcommittee on Communications recently sent the Committee a memo outlining several possible approaches to providing longer-term projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The approaches are summarized in the lower panel.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One option would be for participants to extend their entire set of projections out to, say, five years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under this option, participants would be asked to submit projections for economic variables in year 4 as well as in year 5.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You would also expand your individual forecast narratives to explain the trajectory of the economy and inflation over the five-year projection period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This approach would have the advantage of providing the basis for a complete presentation of the Committee’s medium-term and long-term views.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The principal disadvantage of this option is the relatively heavy burden it places on Committee participants to make projections covering five years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Another disadvantage is that in some circumstances—that is, following a very large shock—the economy still may not be in a steady state after five years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A second option is for participants to continue to submit economic projections and narratives out to three years as now but also to provide estimates of the values of output growth, unemployment, and inflation in year 5 under the assumption of appropriate monetary policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under this approach, you might wish to collect and publish long-term projections only for output growth, unemployment, and total inflation, and not for core inflation, in order to emphasize that total inflation rather than core inflation is the appropriate metric for the longer-run goal of price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This second approach presumably places less demand on your time than the first but it would make for a less integrated presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would also suffer from the same defect as the first approach, in that the figures you submit might not reveal the steady- state characteristics of the economy after a large shock.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In a third approach, you would augment your three-year projections with projections of the average values for output growth, unemployment, and total inflation over the period five to ten years ahead.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This approach would have the advantage of more directly revealing your estimates of the key operating characteristics of the economy—that is, the parameters related to productive capacity and your inflation objective.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It might also be less demanding of your time in the sense that you would need to project fewer time periods than in the first option.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On the other hand, it might be more difficult in that you would need to consider likely trends in demographic variables and productivity further ahead than is ordinarily necessary for monetary policy making.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, it is possible that some of the parameters you would be supplying for the period five to ten years ahead might take on different values than would apply to the medium term that is relevant for monetary policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In your comments in the upcoming economic go-round, you may wish to express your views on whether you support publication of longer-run projections and, if so, which of the approaches you prefer.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You might also wish to comment on the desirability of conducting a trial run with long-term projections—say, in October— before going live with long-term projections, perhaps in January.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That concludes our prepared remarks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for our colleagues?

speaker: FISHER
text: If I may, I would like to ask Nathan, Mr. Chairman, about exhibit 4 and exhibit 5.

speaker: FISHER
text: Particularly noteworthy is that exhibit 4 is the forecast period showing a significant decline in inflation in the emerging market economies.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am wondering what that is based on.

speaker: FISHER
text: Do we have a sense of capacity utilization or slack, if it is all reliable, or is it based on a sense of commodity prices?

speaker: FISHER
text: What is that noticeable down-swoop?

speaker: SHEETS
text: You are asking particularly with respect to the emerging market economies?

speaker: FISHER
text: In the top left-hand panel.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the process of preparing our forecast, we do come up with estimates of slack for the emerging market economies, but we are not inclined to put a whole lot of weight on them.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The concept of an output gap is not really a well-defined construct for, say, China.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, these economies will be growing a little more slowly than they have in the past, and some of the pressures on resources associated with that growth may abate a bit.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think that is at least a piece of the story of what you see here as the decline.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But at the end of the day, it has to be a story about commodity prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Food prices and energy prices have pushed this up.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Depending on exactly which emerging market economy you’re in, food prices will range anywhere from 25 percent to 33 percent of their basket.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As long as those food prices and energy prices are moving up dramatically, you are going to see rapid increases in inflation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So the decline that you are seeing in this chart really is conditioned first and foremost on commodity prices flattening out.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I wish I had a better story.

speaker: FISHER
text: You don’t know how happy I am to see global things come first.

speaker: FISHER
text: But are you saying that a great deal of uncertainty is attached to that forecast?

speaker: FISHER
text: Then, in exhibit 5 on core import prices, I guess it is pretty much the same answer.

speaker: FISHER
text: One would expect that these would fall of their own weight after a while.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The spike that we have seen is driven particularly by commodity prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The depreciation of the dollar has played a secondary role, so the decline in core import price inflation to below 2 percent next year is conditioned crucially on commodity prices flattening out and the dollar not depreciating as rapidly as it has over the past few years.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, if I could ask just one other question—of Larry, I think it was—on the housing exhibits.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am wondering if we are not in the eye of the storm here.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have had the first wave of buckling at the knees—or worse, cascading.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you talk to the homebuilders, they are, of course, the most depressed group imaginable.

speaker: FISHER
text: But they are waiting for another shoe to drop, which is the foreclosures on alt-As.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m wondering what our opinion is on that.

speaker: FISHER
text: Things have calmed down a bit, but we still have another phase of the storm coming through, which is what I just described.

speaker: FISHER
text: What are our assumptions about that?

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: We expect foreclosures to rise—and to rise appreciably.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: One thing we have done in thinking about house prices is, in effect, to build in some extra house-price depreciation, above and beyond what our price–rent model would want to say, to reflect the kinds of factors that you are talking about—the foreclosures, what that means then for the vacancy rate, and what that does to house prices, particularly in certain parts of the country.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: I see President Yellen nodding her head because California, for sure, is one place where that could clearly be an important factor.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’d like to ask a question about inflation and labor compensation.

speaker: EVANS
text: At the last meeting, many of us, myself included, mentioned that labor compensation had not been growing very strongly, and we took that as a possible comforting comment about inflationary pressures not being too strong.

speaker: EVANS
text: That comment was in this presentation and yesterday’s, too.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, statistically, isn’t it the case that labor compensation is not really a good predictor of inflation?

speaker: EVANS
text: It really tends to lag more.

speaker: EVANS
text: So how should we think about interpreting that lack of acceleration for inflation expectations and pressures?

speaker: EVANS
text: Feel free to dispute that.

speaker: WASCHER
text: No, I agree with you.

speaker: WASCHER
text: I think our models have been surprised by the low rates of compensation growth.

speaker: WASCHER
text: One way to think about it is that in the past we might have seen higher headline inflation passed through more quickly to compensation growth—as in the ’70s, when those wage–price spirals were really led by prices, but then wages contributed by following.

speaker: WASCHER
text: So far we haven’t seen any sign that higher headline inflation has been putting upward pressure on compensation costs.

speaker: WASCHER
text: I think there’s a risk.

speaker: WASCHER
text: We obviously included the simulation because we think there’s a risk that could happen in the future, but to date we have not seen evidence that that’s been the case.

speaker: WASCHER
text: There are a number of reasons to think that things now might be different than they used to be.

speaker: WASCHER
text: For example, just a structural reason, unions are less powerful than they used to be; a much smaller share of the work force is unionized.

speaker: WASCHER
text: In the 1970s there were all sorts of automatic cost-of- living adjustment clauses.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Even when there weren’t, there were big catch-ups for past inflation.

speaker: WASCHER
text: Another structural reason might be that the minimum wage was higher in the 1970s, and it is lower in real terms now.

speaker: WASCHER
text: I think more generally this fits in with the general notion that inflation expectations are less responsive to immediate shocks in headline inflation than perhaps they used to be.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: From a forecasting perspective, President Evans, I think you’re right.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t think models that rely simply on labor costs to predict prices are very sound in terms of their forecasting ability versus just a plain old price–price type of Phillips curve or a price type of Phillips curve augmented with price expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Part of the reason may be that the compensation data themselves are just so poor that, in fact, it’s really a measurement problem.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It’s not that you would argue that labor costs, which are a very significant chunk of overall business costs, don’t matter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I do think you can probably take, and we certainly have taken, some limited comfort from the fact that we have not yet seen an acceleration of labor costs.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That likely indicates that you are not seriously behind the curve already or that something is baked in the cake.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t think you can necessarily take comfort from the well-behaved compensation thus far that you are not going to confront some inflation problems going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It’s more that the compensation data don’t suggest that you’ve fallen seriously behind the curve.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In some sense we see the higher inflation expectations readings themselves, or at least some of the mixed-to-slightly-higher inflation expectations data, as suggesting that you’re facing a bit more of an inflationary difficulty over the next two years than we thought two months ago would be the case.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just a quick follow-up, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: FISHER
text: To what extent do you impute the kind of insecurity that comes from competition and broader outsourcing?

speaker: FISHER
text: If you impute anything there in terms of wage behavior here, to what extent are you assuming going forward that the increase in wages being paid elsewhere might bleed into our wage behavior here?

speaker: WASCHER
text: Well, we don’t account for that in our compensation model.

speaker: WASCHER
text: That said, as I mentioned, the models have been surprised about how low compensation has been.

speaker: WASCHER
text: That would be one possible explanation for that residual.

speaker: WASCHER
text: If that factor were to diminish, it would imply that that residual would diminish, but we haven’t built such an effect into our forecast.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I want to ask a question about exhibit 7, which talks about factors affecting the GDP forecast.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The second bullet point mentions judgmental adjustments, which were tempered this time relative to last time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Last time I described this as a regime-switching model, and you said that was perhaps too much.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The economy sort of switches into this recession-like behavior, and we know that the economy might behave differently in that environment.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But do we now think the probability of switching into that behavior is smaller?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is the forecast some kind of average between this high state and this low state?

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s what you said here—it has tempered our judgmental adjustments.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It sounds as though there is less probability of switching into that state.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: It’s hard for me to think of it in these probabilistic terms.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: I would say that we still think that the economy is going to have these negative effects that are associated with periods of low growth.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Now, whether that is precisely a recession or simply just a low-growth period, it’s hard for me to distinguish.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But the rationale is that you switch into the recession and you get the correlations from—

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: The way to think about it is that we switched into a low-growth period.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Whether it is precisely a recession or just simply a low-growth period shouldn’t be the demarcation point.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: We still think that the economy is operating in a low-growth period.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: There is probably not as much severity to that low-growth period, but we still think that is where it’s operating.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But then you’re switching into the low-growth period, and then we take the correlations for low-growth periods, which I guess are maybe not as severe as in recession periods.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Just as a factoid to throw out here, one of my colleagues on the Board staff, Jeremy Nalewaik, has estimated some of these models looking at switching between high- growth periods and low-growth periods, where a low-growth period does not necessarily have to be a recession.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: Using the GDP data through the first quarter plus our forecast for second-quarter GDP, which is now at an annual rate of 1.7 percent, his model still would suggest that there’s an 84 percent probability that the economy is operating in a low-growth state.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: So I think that it was a fair thing for us to continue to have the judgmental adjustments, which by the way aren’t just recession-like effects.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: They also include financial turmoil effects and some uncertainty things.

speaker: SLIFMAN
text: I think it’s a fair thing for us to have included those, but as I say, we’ve tempered them.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to make sure I understand what you just said.

speaker: LACKER
text: Your response suggests that there’s a third state that’s even worse than we are in now, that one could possibly go into, and that what you’ve tempered is the probability that we’re in that worst state?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Again, we want to step back a bit from taking this regime-switching too seriously as implying that there are just two states of the world or maybe three states of the world.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There are lots of different states of the world.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: What we are trying to do is look at the residuals in our spending equations and ask how they behave in various kinds of periods.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In periods with substantial increases in the unemployment rate, weak payroll employment, and big declines in consumer sentiment, there also are substantial negative residuals in our spending equations, particularly on the consumer spending side.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is still built into this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So we have not interpreted the last six weeks of data as suggesting that recession concerns are all behind us, that we were just completely wrong, and that we are now on a much stronger growth path than we previously thought.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If, in fact, you’re worried that the incoming data might be signaling a stronger growth path, then I would take a look at the “upside risk” scenario that we show in the Greenbook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There we take out all of our spending residuals—those that are incorporated because we thought we might be in this low-growth or recessionary-like state and the ones that are associated with financial turmoil—and you get growth in that case that is a little above potential growth and a path for the fed funds rate that is even steeper than the current market expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, although we kept these negative residuals in our forecast, we did have to acknowledge the fact that underlying aggregate demand appeared stronger than we thought it was going to be at the time of the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There is an underlying strengthening of aggregate demand in this forecast that shows up as an increase in the equilibrium funds rate of roughly ½ percentage point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So we’re trying to acknowledge the strength of the incoming data, but we want to be clear that this forecast still embeds some significant negative add-factors on spending going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Maybe the incoming data are signaling that we are just fundamentally wrong about that aspect of the forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As Larry showed, given the stunning decline in consumer sentiment, the continued weak business sentiment, and the fact that the unemployment rate has risen as much as it has and has done this in the past only in periods of recession, we felt comfortable still presenting you with a forecast that anticipates that aggregate demand is going to be very weak over the next several quarters.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t want to belabor this too much.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was curious about what you tempered.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think President Bullard was looking for whether you tempered the probability on state 2.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m with you in not wanting to place a lot of probability on n states, but it sounds as though the growth trajectory—you know, the magnitude of the add-factors you were thinking of—has been drawn back a little.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is that a fair characterization?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So there are two aspects.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One is that we have interpreted some of the surprise as a persistent strengthening in aggregate demand that we had not anticipated.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other is that the economy is not as weak now, and therefore the bounceback in activity next year won’t be as strong.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As Larry said, there are a lot of moving parts, but both of those considerations are built into this forecast.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are about ready for our go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me remind you about the proposal to add a long-term line to our projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The rationale for doing so is that the current system doesn’t necessarily let the public know what our views on the steady state of the economy are.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To show my own hand, I think it would be helpful to add maybe one line that said in five to seven years out what we think the economy would do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I think it is important for those of us who want to express an opinion to do so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there is interest, as Brian mentioned, we can do a trial run in October, and we won’t have to make a final decision about whether to go forward until October or December or perhaps later depending on how things go.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But if you have a view on that, please add that to your commentary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let’s begin with the economic go-round, and we’ll start with President Hoenig.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, I will begin my remarks this afternoon with a brief update on the conditions in our District.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Overall, District economic activity continues to expand moderately, with strengthened energy, agriculture, and export manufacturing more than offsetting the softness in our housing, retail sales, and other types of manufacturing activity.

speaker: HOENIG
text: District labor markets continue to perform reasonably well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: While job growth has slowed over the past few months, unemployment remains very low, and many sectors continue to have difficulty finding workers, especially skilled ones.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Evidence on wage pressures is mixed.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Although wage pressures have moderated somewhat in our Beige Book survey, some recent labor union contracts have built in rising profiles for hourly wage increases over the term of the contract.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Rising energy and commodity input prices are continuing to negatively affect our District economic activity.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Reports from businesses suggest that higher energy and food prices are being quickly passed on to the customer now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, businesses are having mixed success in passing on other cost increases, resulting in some severe erosion in margins and profitability in some of the firms.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To illustrate some of the cost–price dynamics, I would like to take just a minute and relate the recent experience of one of our Branch directors, who operates a multi-line manufacturing firm.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I mention this because I am hearing it more and more.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition to rising fuel prices, his business has seen a doubling in steel costs since January, with July quotes on steel tubing up an additional 25 percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In response, his company recently announced a price increase of 16 to 18 percent across a range of products.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Competitors immediately matched or exceeded his price increases.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Notably, he made these price increases despite a decline in new orders in May.

speaker: HOENIG
text: He also noted that import prices from China that he has seen have risen 28 percent this year and that ocean freight prices have risen about 20 percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As a result, customers who previously bought Chinese products are now purchasing U.S.-manufactured goods.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It is interesting—I talked with some of the folks at Union Pacific, and their shipments into the Midwest have dropped slightly, but their shipments out have increased about 3 to 4 percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So that is what is going on in the region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: More broadly, turning to the national economy, I have revised up my growth estimate for the first half of 2008, but it has made little change in my longer-run outlook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Compared with the Greenbook, I see somewhat stronger growth in the second half of this year and somewhat weaker growth next year and in 2010.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Most of the difference from the Greenbook in 2009 and 2010 comes from the policy path assumptions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I assume that policy accommodation is removed at a more rapid pace than does the Greenbook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Recent economic data suggest that, although downside risks to growth remain, they have diminished.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I continue to judge that the potential spillover effects from the financial distress have understandably been overestimated in this Committee’s recent decisions and in Greenbook forecasts in recent months.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In my view, the greater risks to the outlook come from rising energy and commodity prices and less from the financial distress as we go forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In my view, current policy accommodation is greater than needed to address these risks.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As I indicated at the last meeting, I believe that the upside risks to inflation have increased considerably over the past several months.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Like the Greenbook, I expect both overall and core PCE inflation to move higher in the second half of this year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If this happens and we maintain the current level of the funds rate, I believe we are likely to see further erosion in inflation expectations, which will undermine our credibility with financial markets and the public.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In this event, I judge we will greatly increase the likelihood that we will need to raise rates more aggressively, taking rates above neutral, in order to achieve our longer-run inflation objectives; and that is of significant concern to me, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to the issue of long-term projections, let me comment that I have felt somewhat constrained by the current three-year horizon for our quarterly projections.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Of the options presented by the subcommittee, I am most comfortable with providing estimates of the values for total inflation, output growth, and unemployment at which the economy is likely to converge.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am not sure, however, how we want to label these estimates, if they are included in the table.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I understand that putting these estimates out might be interpreted as a move closer to inflation targeting, but I think that this is a bridge we are ready to cross since we adopted the enhanced projections process.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The other options seem less desirable.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Given the resources required, by my staff at least, I doubt that we could provide a meaningful forecast at a four-year or five-year horizon, and I am not sure how projections for average values over a period of five to ten years ahead would be interpreted by the public.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In my view, appropriate policy should be expected to return the economy to its long-run equilibrium over a three-to-five-year period, with the length of the period depending on the nature of the shock.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Setting out a five-to-ten-year horizon could be construed as a weakening in our commitment to achieve our mandate in a timely manner.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The intermeeting period has been full of surprises.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Real-side data came in considerably stronger than I anticipated, so like the Greenbook I have adjusted up my forecast for growth in the current quarter.

speaker: YELLEN
text: At the same time, the adverse fundamentals that will weigh on household and business spending going forward have grown somewhat heavier overall, and that has prompted me to revise down my growth forecast for the second half.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the inflation front, readings on core inflation surprised to the downside.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Nonetheless, given that the prices of many commodities have continued to rise more rapidly than I anticipated and that some measures of inflation expectations have turned up, I have adjusted up my inflation forecast for 2008, considerably up for headline inflation and modestly up for core inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The strong incoming data on spending eased my fears that we are in or are approaching a recession regime of the sort embedded in the last two Greenbooks.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, given the numerous large and worsening drags on spending, a couple of months of data aren’t enough to convince me that we are on a solid trajectory.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Moreover, the spending data may well fail to reflect the real underlying strength of consumer demand because of the effects of the tax rebates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Spending patterns could easily be distorted by small differences between what we projected that households would spend each month out of rebate checks and what they actually spent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In monthly spending data, a swing of just a few billion dollars looks enormous.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Perhaps households who were already paying through the nose for food and gas and are increasingly credit constrained have put their rebate checks to work a bit early this time.

speaker: YELLEN
text: After all, households knew in advance that the checks were going out.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, Google searches related to tax rebates peaked in April.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We actually kept track of the data on that.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I will be closely watching the data over the next few months, hoping to get a cleaner read on the underlying state of consumer demand.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I said, the adverse fundamentals are still with us and in some part are worsening.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Evidence that the credit crunch is ongoing is all too clear.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Bank asset quality continues to deteriorate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Banks continue to deleverage, and they are tightening lending standards as they do so.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The market for private-label securitized mortgages of even the highest quality remains moribund.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Spreads on agency-backed mortgage-backed securities have risen during the intermeeting period, which are likely to spill over to the primary mortgage market with a lag.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Anecdotal reports suggest that the constraints on household borrowing continue to tighten.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, two of my most senior bank supervisors—both with FICO scores in the stratosphere— have had their home equity lines slashed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One has deferred a planned home renovation project as a consequence.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If that is happening to them, I can only imagine how hard it must be to get a loan if you have a merely average credit rating.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Housing prices have also fallen at a somewhat faster rate than the Greenbook previously anticipated.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the overhang of homes for sale, the recent rise in mortgage rates, and the fact that the homeownership rate is likely to continue trending lower, I think the downward pressure on home prices and construction will persist, as the Greenbook suggests.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The Greenbook is actually at the conservative end in its estimates of the wealth effect.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It assumes a marginal propensity to consume out of housing wealth of about 3½ cents on the dollar.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In contrast, a number of recent estimates in the literature are in the 6 cent to 9 cent range.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There is a clear risk, then, that the combination of declining housing wealth and tightening credit could lead households to restrict spending more, and more persistently, than anticipated.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But the big adverse shock since the last meeting is oil prices, which are up $25 a barrel from the already elevated April levels.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Empirically, since the mid-1980s, the estimated responses to relatively exogenous increases in the relative price of oil have tended to look qualitatively like the simulations in the Bluebook and the Board staff’s special memo on oil prices, in which we are credible in our commitment to long-term price stability.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Most notably, the empirical estimates suggest at most a modest effect on core inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Nominal wages barely respond; by some estimates they even fall slightly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The model results suggest that the outcomes we have seen in the actual data are crucially dependent on our having credibility.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With substantial target drift, workers demand higher wages, which firms pay and then pass on.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Fortunately, the anecdotes I hear are more consistent with credibility than with an upward wage–price spiral.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In particular, my contacts uniformly report that they see no signs of wage pressure.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There also is no evidence of real wage rigidity in response to energy prices.

speaker: YELLEN
text: When energy prices have risen, real wages—in product as well as consumption terms—have generally fallen.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In other words, real wages have been depressed in the 2000s, at least in part reflecting rising energy prices.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But there is no sign that workers have over a number of years tried to recoup these losses at the bargaining table.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the importance of credibility, the substantial increase in expected inflation in the Michigan survey is concerning but not yet alarming.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I discount these readings somewhat because of analysis by my staff that suggests that, at either the one-year or the five-to-ten-year horizon, consumers have always tended to react strongly to contemporaneous inflation data.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Changes in credibility are fundamentally about changes in the process by which people form expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But as far as consumer expectations are concerned, that process appears remarkably stable.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, if you use data through the early 2000s to estimate equations that link inflation expectations to contemporaneous inflation, you will find that those relationships fit remarkably well out of sample.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They don’t show the systematic underprediction of inflation expectations one might expect if the Fed had suffered a significant loss of credibility at this point.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The dependence of consumer inflation expectations on recent data also leads me to believe that they will fall if, in fact, headline inflation comes down as we are predicting as commodity prices level off.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Furthermore, I don’t think that households’ elevated expectations will make it harder to achieve our projections.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Earlier research suggested that surveys did, in fact, provide useful information about future inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But during the past 15 or 20 years, the actual inflation process has become much less persistent even though households appear to assume otherwise.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There is, thus, a notable divergence between the actual inflation process and the one that is embodied in consumers’ inflation forecasts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As a result, inflation forecasts incorporating consumer expectations have been a lot less than stellar over this recent period.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So it does not appear unreasonable to believe that the effects of recent commodity price shocks will wear off faster than consumers are expecting.

speaker: YELLEN
text: An unresolved question is, Whose expectations matter for the dynamics of inflation?

speaker: YELLEN
text: I take some solace from the fact that 10-year inflation expectations in the Survey of Professional Forecasters have been relatively stable since the late 1990s and from the fact that five-to-ten-year breakeven rates on TIPS are below their peaks from earlier in the year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Taken all together, I think inflation expectations remain reasonably well anchored.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The oil price increases have led me to raise my projections for overall PCE inflation sharply.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Cost pressures are likely to push core inflation up a bit, though I see less pass-through than the Greenbook does.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Higher oil prices and interest rates and lower housing prices have led me to modestly reduce my forecast of growth in the second half of this year and next year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My forecast is predicated on fed funds rate increases that begin in December of this year, gradually bringing the funds rate to 4¼ percent in 2010.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Briefly, on the issue of long-term economic projections, I welcome greater transparency about our long-term objectives.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think that would be beneficial, and there is a good reason, as you have articulated, to try to do that now, given that for many of us—certainly for me—2010 is not long enough for me to project that the economy will have converged to a steady state.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My preference is to provide projections of the average values for output growth, unemployment, and total inflation that are expected, say, five to ten years out.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think that these values can communicate the necessary steady-state information without burdening us with forecasting every year of the transition to the steady state.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Also, I would favor conducting a trial in October.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, you are going to get a contrapuntal tune here.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is the beauty of this table and the different perspectives around it.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am going to take a different approach today than I have in the past.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am going to talk a bit about the Eleventh District first, which I don’t often do.

speaker: FISHER
text: The reason for that is, because of its nature and size, because of its being the leading exporting state in the country now, and because of its job creation, it is in a slightly different position—or significantly different position, depending on which District it is compared with—from the rest of the country.

speaker: FISHER
text: Our job growth through March is running about 3.8 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: Unemployment in April was 4.1 percent, despite a sizable influx of immigrants, which we see from new license plate registrations from California and particularly from Florida as well as from people still coming across the border.

speaker: FISHER
text: Sales of existing homes rose in May, while inventories and prices held steady.
