speaker: FISHER
text: Apartment demand is robust, and rents in the major cities, such as Dallas and Houston, are rising.

speaker: FISHER
text: The real export growth of Texas was 7.2 percent in April after 3.9 percent in the first quarter.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is telling you that our chemicals are now being priced aggressively but also that everything else is being priced aggressively worldwide.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s a significant export sector for us.

speaker: FISHER
text: Importantly, on the price front, the Dallas Fed’s own Texas manufacturing outlook survey and the regional CPI data indicate continuing price increases and substantial evidence of pass- through to higher final goods prices.

speaker: FISHER
text: Thirty-nine percent of the respondents report the ability to realize higher prices of finished goods currently; another 45 percent expect to be able to realize higher prices in the next six months.

speaker: FISHER
text: Despite these strong numbers, our soundings and our instinct project a slowdown in the future.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have been projecting a slowdown—we haven’t seen it.

speaker: FISHER
text: Discretionary income has been bolstered by employment, but squeezed by rising food and energy prices and credit constriction.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we are looking for the District to slow and yet to continue to outperform relatively speaking.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would like to devote the rest of my comments to the U.S. economy and to the global economy, particularly to the contrapuntal insights I have gained from my soundings.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, on the global economy, Nathan, our own research at our little globalization institute in Dallas indicates that the projections of real economic growth of most of the advanced countries are being revised downward whereas expected inflation is being revised upward.

speaker: FISHER
text: For the major emerging market economies, growth realization, at least as it appears in their forecasts, for the most part holds up, but inflation expectations are being steadily revised upward.

speaker: FISHER
text: In other words, the two types of economies share on the inflation front, whereas there is disparity and a little cacophony as far as growth is concerned.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are working on it, but we have yet to develop a reliable measure of global slack.

speaker: FISHER
text: JPMorgan, with whom we have been working, has a slack index that purports to be global.

speaker: FISHER
text: But as you pointed out, Nathan, it excludes China.

speaker: FISHER
text: One would think that the growing slack in the advanced countries would be mitigating price pressures.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet those countries with numerical price objectives or inflation targets—from Mexico to Turkey to New Zealand to the European Central Bank to the Brits—are now contending with inflation in excess of their target or comfort range.

speaker: FISHER
text: I was thinking the other day of Mervyn King’s comment that, once they had to write to the Chancellor of the Exchequer, it would lead to a lot of letter-writing.

speaker: FISHER
text: It took 15 years for the first letter to be written after inflation targeting was embraced.

speaker: FISHER
text: Of course, two years ago this was resurrected, and now they seem to be doing so with a great deal more frequency.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now there is a risk of acquiring writer’s cramp.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would say that, if we were under the same strictures as the Bank of England, we might be subject to the same concerns.

speaker: FISHER
text: In our last meeting, I posited that something persistent and pernicious was occurring on the inflation front.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, the one thing that is even clearer now—particularly after my soundings, which I’ll report in just a second—than it was in May is that inflationary pressures, inflation expectations, and anticipatory behavioral responses among consumers and businesses have intensified, whereas our confidence about economic growth has improved.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t believe that we are out of the woods yet on the risk of a credit-induced slowdown, though I believe our liquidity initiatives are a proper and good palliative, as you know.

speaker: FISHER
text: But if Robert Frost will forgive me, the woods are not lovely, and they are indeed deep and dark on the price front.

speaker: FISHER
text: Although the tail risk of economic recession has diminished, I think it still exists; certainly the anemia—just to use another word that you referred to—does.

speaker: FISHER
text: But the risk of inflation, in my view, has assumed greater depth and breadth since we last met.

speaker: FISHER
text: Stated differently, I don’t believe that inflation expectations are presently well anchored, here or elsewhere.

speaker: FISHER
text: I believe they are being—just to kill the sea analogy, Don—torn from their moorings and are at risk of going adrift.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, I took a different approach this time with the 30-odd interlocutors with whom I discussed the outlook.

speaker: FISHER
text: I simply asked them one question: What is different in this cycle from what you have seen before?

speaker: FISHER
text: Most of these people have been in business for 30 years plus.

speaker: FISHER
text: Here are some sample testimonials as to what they are seeing.

speaker: FISHER
text: The CEO of Fluor, which has a $38 billion backlog currently, said, “When I started here in 1974, we put inflation contingencies into every contract.

speaker: FISHER
text: In the 1990s, that had not only gone away, but we were confident we could negotiate cost down to below what we were bidding.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now it is just the opposite.” The CFO of Frito-Lay, which just pushed through a 9 percent price increase (which, parenthetically, Wal- Mart accommodated at 7 percent), said, “Most of our executives are in their late 30s or early-to- mid 40s.

speaker: FISHER
text: They have never seen these kinds of numbers.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is reminiscent of the aftershock to Nixon’s wage and price controls, and we are currently having to hold seminars to teach management how to manage inflation.” From the CEO of Wal-Mart USA: “We see increased”—and this is his word—“pervasive price pressures.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am telling you that we have an economy where the real people are being trampled by inflation, and for the first time in memory, we are getting noise from employees about the cost of living.” Wal-Mart raised the pay of 60 percent of their associates between single and double digits in the last quarter, and my contact said, “We are now contemplating a series of measures such as providing discounts to employees to counter considerable employee angst about the cost of living.” From the CEO of Kimberly- Clarke, who just notified the retailers of a 7 percent price increase to come in August after the 7 percent they pushed through in February, in addition to which they are going to add a shipping surcharge: “Customers are no longer asking if, but when, we will increase prices, so they can move in anticipation.” I can give you other testimonials, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of my favorites, by the way, has to do with a very small operation, a three-store dry cleaning operation, Faulkner’s Fine Dry Cleaning in Dallas.

speaker: FISHER
text: They approached me the other day to say that they would have to increase the price of cleaning our shirts because the price of 18-inch white hangers, which are steel-based, has increased 65 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: They showed me the circular that had been sent around by the fabric cleaning supply company that is the last remaining manufacturer of hangers in the United States.

speaker: FISHER
text: All of that manufacturing has gone to China.

speaker: FISHER
text: The circular that they are sending their customers, the cleaners, says “What should cleaners do?

speaker: FISHER
text: You’re worth it.” Then—and this strikes at the heart of every son of every Australian—Budweiser, which raised its prices 3½ percent in February, according to our local distributor, plans to raise 3½ percent again in September.

speaker: FISHER
text: And the Bud distributor in North Texas, who has had that distributorship for 43 years, said that never before in his lifetime had he seen two price increases in one year.

speaker: FISHER
text: Finally, the CEO of JCPenney’s just returned from an around-the-world buying trip.

speaker: FISHER
text: After 11 years of apparel price deflation, Chinese manufacturers are seeking 8 to 9 percent price increases in ’09, 11 to 12 percent for footwear, and for small kitchen appliances in the mid-20s.

speaker: FISHER
text: The CFO of the company told me that they are running at minimum staffing levels.

speaker: FISHER
text: If anybody begins to break the wage barrier, then, “Katie, bar the door!” So, Mr. Chairman, I would say that currently our patient—the economy—is indeed a sick puppy.

speaker: FISHER
text: Some of its vital organs—geographic regions such as the one I am fortunate to live in, or a strong export sector of the United States, or entrepreneurs and business leaders who have learned to wring unanticipated efficiency and profits out of globalization or from within cyberspace—are very strong.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet others—states like California and Florida, the housing sector, and overall consumer confidence—are bleeding, if not hemorrhaging.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is not to mention the still precarious state, despite the very good report that Bill gave, of our financial system as it recovers, I hope with our help, from years of its recklessness and excess.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we have, like loyal practitioners and with the equivalent of the Hippocratic oath, done the job that we are expected to do in terms of resuscitating the victim.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is the good news.

speaker: FISHER
text: The real bad news is that our patient appears to be acquiring a staph infection in this hospital that we have created, and that staph infection is inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I believe inflation is upon us.

speaker: FISHER
text: I believe expectations are discounting more inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: Very importantly—and this is tough to get from the models—I believe that behavioral changes are beginning to manifest themselves.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, some would argue that this infection is temporary and may well go away.

speaker: FISHER
text: Others will argue that it will be stayed by strong rhetoric.

speaker: FISHER
text: Still others say that it will require—I don’t know if it’s an antibiotic or an antidote—further tightening, lest the infection spread and counteract the good that we have done with our liquidity facilities and by previous policy decisions.

speaker: FISHER
text: That seems to me to be the problem that we will have to deal with at this meeting, and I look forward to hearing my other colleagues’ opinions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I would like to start with some anecdotal feedback from the region.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As you know, we have a lot of Branches, so we have a lot of directors, and we ask our directors a lot of questions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The anecdotal feedback from our 44 directors about the second half can be characterized as subdued.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Almost all reported that they expect economic activity to be flat or slower, and I took special note that these expectations deteriorated in June after having actually improved a bit in May.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The residential housing situation in the District resembles the national picture.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Both sales and new construction are weak.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: High levels of inventories are being exacerbated by foreclosures, which are adding to downward pressure on prices.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, there are tentative signs of a bottom forming.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Our survey of Realtors across the District indicates that the pace of decline of single-family home sales may be abating.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Industry contacts tell us that foot traffic and buyer interest are picking up, particularly in Florida, although I would say that what constitutes progress in Florida would not be considered very encouraging elsewhere.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Nevertheless, our view is that the beginning of an adjustment process is under way, but the end of the process looks to be a long way off.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Some further home-price deterioration is likely to accompany this bottoming process.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Credit conditions in the District continue to tighten because of perceived risk and also liquidity pressure on our banks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Our banks indicate that the process of deleveraging continues, which is affecting lending for residential real estate and, to some extent, commercial real estate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We are also hearing from several sources that funding of community banks is becoming an increasing problem because of their previous dependence on wholesale and correspondent bank sources.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Higher energy prices are, not surprisingly, affecting our outlook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Hospitality industry contacts, for instance, expressed concern about low summer bookings.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Although most tourist destinations have reported solid activity to date, few expect this to continue.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The reacceleration of energy and commodity price inflation has businesses focused on cost pressures.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Several business contacts indicated that price increases had been relatively easy to pass through and make stick in this environment.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I wouldn’t say that it’s widespread yet, but I do hear some reports that businesses are expecting wage increases to eventually reflect the recent increases in the cost of living.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This could be a significant factor, particularly in service price inflation.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This and other anecdotal input has colored my outlook for the national economy for the balance of the year and into 2009.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I have revised up my forecast for headline inflation in 2008 and 2009 by 50 and 25 basis points, respectively.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am also assuming that the recent inflationary pressures from elevated energy and food prices will unwind more slowly than I previously projected—a view reinforced by expectations expressed by my District contacts.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Like everyone else, I am deeply concerned that inflation expectations seem to be rising and that expectations of general price inflation, reflecting second-, third-, and fourth-order effects of recent oil and commodity price rises, risk becoming institutionalized.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am prepared in the near term to think tactically regarding the conflict between growth and employment policy objectives and inflation objectives; but sustained inflationary pressures that extend well into the fourth quarter and rising expectation readings may force, at least on my part, a more strategic look at the tradeoff.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I would like to talk for a moment about financial markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I made a number of calls during the intermeeting period, and the growth-versus-inflation tactical dilemma is complicated further by a very mixed picture in financial markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My contacts all acknowledge improved conditions since mid-March, but discussion of the current market circumstances and the outlook had a sort of half-full/half-empty quality.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My contacts, taken together, pointed to several positives, including the health of the corporate loan market, improved CDO pricing, the readiness of forming distressed funds to buy asset-backed securities, alt-A mortgage demand, the growing perception that subprime loss estimates have been overstated, and some comment on Goldman’s Cheyne deal, which they believe will help create price determination for certain securities.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: At the same time, these contacts cited areas of continuing or worsening weakness, including: HELOCs and second mortgages; option ARMs and alt-A hybrids; indirect auto, given the collateral value of SUVs in current circumstances; in contrast to CDO pricing, CDO squared pricing is very weak and deteriorating; the obvious concern about the growing liquidity issues of regional banks; and the view that the auction rate securities market valuations, given illiquidity, are suggesting that this market has little probability of returning to normalcy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Overall, my contacts in financial markets were encouraged but expressed worries over still-substantial downside potential.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Let me turn now to my national forecast compared with the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The Atlanta projections for the national economy are broadly similar to those of the Greenbook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We have the same general narrative of slow growth for the balance of the year followed by a gradual pickup through 2009 and 2010.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My projections for headline and core inflation are virtually identical to the baseline Greenbook projections.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, I believe that there may be less disinflationary pressure than seems implicit in the Board staff’s forecast.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As a consequence, the fed funds rate path that supports my inflation outlook is well above the Greenbook’s at the end of 2009 and 2010.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We are 75 basis points higher at year-end 2009 and 100 basis points higher at year-end 2010.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Notwithstanding the upward revision of the first-quarter GDP number and the better expectations for this quarter, I still believe the near-term risks to growth are weighted to the downside.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: At the same time, as suggested by my revised forecast, I see the risks to our inflation objective as weighted to the upside.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On the subject of the long-term projections, I favor the third approach, which is three years plus long-term averages, and certainly would be comfortable with approach number 2.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’m generally dubious about the ability to do actual forecasting for the outyears, even as near-term as the third year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I really don’t favor approach number 1.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My experience, in the brief time I have been with the Fed, has at least personally been, shall I say, challenging from the point of view of forecasting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I tend to think of the long-term projections as being roughly equivalent to our targets or policy goals.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In fact, the approach we have generally taken with our three-year forecasts is making the outyear approaching at least what we would consider to be the trend rate for growth and the employment and inflation objective.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I think long-term projections really do amount to more-explicit targeting, and very likely the first question we get when we come out of the blocks—if we have this kind of approach—will be, Is this your target?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am comfortable saying “yes” to that question and, therefore, would support the third approach.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Despite some encouraging data recently, the Boston Fed economic outlook continues to see the economy growing below potential over the next several quarters, further weakening in labor markets, and core PCE trending down in response to excess capacity.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Overall, our forecast has not changed significantly since our April meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I view recent strength in consumer spending indicators as largely borrowing from the second half of this year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This view is supported by the assessment that, apart from the fiscal stimulus, consumption fundamentals—income, wealth, and employment—remain on the weak side.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Taking on board some of the increase in the May unemployment rate, our forecast has the unemployment rate peaking at a slightly higher rate than at the last meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In this respect, we are similar to many other forecasters.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The May Blue Chip forecast had unemployment peaking at 5.6 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The June Blue Chip forecast for unemployment peaks at 5.7 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While the Greenbook has the unemployment rate peaking at 5.7 percent, as it did in April, it has the unemployment rate at 5.6 percent at the end of 2009—0.1 percent higher than the April Greenbook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So at least as measured by the unemployment rate, there seems little improvement in the outlook since the April meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As in the Greenbook, residential investment in our forecast continues to be a drag on the economy in 2009, and consumption holds up primarily as a result of the fiscal stimulus package, which is in part offsetting the negative impact of significantly higher oil prices on consumption.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A major uncertainty remains whether further home-price declines will have a more negative effect on residential investment and consumption than we currently have in our forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Similarly, I would view financial market conditions as not having changed significantly since our April meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The three-month LIBOR–OIS spread remains quite high by historical standards at roughly 70 basis points, where it has been trading since the April FOMC.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Dow Jones, S&P 500, and Nasdaq indexes have all declined since our April meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Investment banks, such as Merrill Lynch and Lehman Brothers, are now trading substantially below where they were trading at our April meeting and below where they traded during the middle of March when Bear Stearns experienced difficulties.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Stock prices for large regional banks have declined as they have needed to increase loan-loss reserves, raise new capital, and reduce dividend payments.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I continue to be concerned that we have more, significant difficulties ahead for many financial institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First and second mortgages and home equity lines of credit are deteriorating at many banks as falling home prices and job losses create problems that have now spread to some prime residential products.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would characterize financial markets as remaining fragile.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The past two TAF auctions still produced stop-out rates above the primary credit rate, and financial markets remain susceptible to event risk.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The recent flurry of articles on Lehman before their announcement of their capital infusion highlights continued concerns about investment banks, despite our new liquidity facilities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As a result, I continue to view the downside risk of further financial shocks as being significant.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Core PCE inflation has trended lower during this quarter, bringing the four-quarter change for the past year to 2.1 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given that the Boston Fed forecast expects significant excess capacity over this year, we forecast that core PCE inflation will be slightly below 2 percent in 2009.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If food and energy prices stabilize, we expect total PCE to converge to core PCE.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We have experienced significant food and energy shocks, and oil prices continue to be higher than our expectations.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would be quite concerned should the serially correlated surprises in food and energy become embedded in inflation expectations and wages and salaries.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But a critical element to my forecast is that total PCE inflation converges to core PCE as wage and salary increases remain largely unaffected by the supply shocks.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In the data to date, wage and salary increases have not trended up in response to the supply shocks, and my expectation is that excess capacity in labor markets and continued competition from abroad make it unlikely that the relative change in food and energy prices will become embedded in labor contracts.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: For the intermediate term, I remain focused on core PCE rather than total PCE for several reasons.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, monetary policy is unlikely to have much effect on food and energy prices, which are responding, among other developments, to the impact of natural disasters such as flooding in the Midwest and manmade disasters such as ongoing political difficulties in Nigeria and the Middle East.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, statistical evidence provided by our research department seems to indicate that over the past 20 years, when total and core inflation diverge, total has tended to converge to core and not the opposite.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Third, while inflation expectations are difficult to model, the lack of an upward trend in wages and salaries seems consistent with worker expectations being driven by core rather than total inflation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While the supply shocks may have increased the upside inflation risks, the downside risks to the economy and financial markets remain quite elevated.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In my view, we need more time and data to determine with greater confidence which of these risks poses the greatest danger to the economy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the options, I am comfortable with either 1 or 3.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I have a slight preference for option 1.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It is not that difficult for us to extend our forecast out five years.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I actually think it would be easier to explain to the public than option 3, and I think explaining to the public is one of the main goals of expanding the forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But I could be happy with either option.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the Third District, as anticipated, manufacturing activity, residential construction, and employment have remained weak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nonresidential construction has now softened, although vacancy rates in Philadelphia and around the District remain relatively low.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Bank lending has been restrained.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The outlook among our business contacts, however, varies significantly by sector.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Manufacturers expect a rebound in activity over the coming six months, and residential real estate contacts report that they believe market conditions may be near bottom, although they expect any recovery to be slow.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Interestingly enough, it is the same sort of anecdotal evidence that President Lockhart referred to.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, it is hard to know whether it is just mostly wishful thinking or whether there is something real there—although his saying it and my saying it sort of reinforces it a little.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But it is the first time that I have heard such news in a very, very long time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Retailers are quite pessimistic, however, because they are expecting the increase in energy prices to limit sales, especially among lower-income customers, despite the tax rebates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite the soft economic conditions, the most prominent concern that we have heard from our business contacts across a variety of industries is the run-up in commodity prices and other prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus far, firms have resisted passing along their rising costs to customers, to the extent that they could, but many firms tell us that they have gone as far as they can on holding the line on their own prices and plan to raise prices further in the next few months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some firms are including general cost-increase clauses in their new contracts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Earlier we saw various sorts of fuel surcharges added onto prices, but now contracts are being written in a way that includes broad cost-adjustment increases.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is still only anecdotal evidence although it has been referred to—I think President Fisher made a couple of comments in this regard.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But it may be yet another early warning sign that inflation expectations cannot remain in check indefinitely in this current environment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In June, the prices-paid index in our business outlook survey of manufacturers rose to the highest level it has been since 1980.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Manufacturers and firm contacts across a wide range of industries say that they expect their input prices and the prices of their own goods to increase further over the next six months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They see no abatement of price pressures in the near term or medium term and are very pessimistic about inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The national economic situation is similar to what I see in my own District, and it is an uncomfortable situation for all of us.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The data we have received on economic activity over the intermeeting period have come in slightly better than I expected, but the continued price increases, particularly in oil and commodities, have been a very unpleasant development.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Certainly, economic conditions remain weak, and the recent positive news may prove to be transitory.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: From the financial side, credit spreads have fallen, bond issuance has risen, and it appears that financial market functioning has at least improved.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my view, although downside risks to growth remain, the tail risk of a very bad outcome has clearly been diminished.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I expect GDP growth to come in around 1.7 percent this year—only marginally higher than my April projection—before picking back up to trend of around 2.7 percent in 2009-10.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite the upward revisions in the Greenbook baseline, my forecast remains somewhat more optimistic for growth in 2008 and 2009 than the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, my forecast is similar to the Board staff’s “upside risk” alternative scenario, which essentially removed the downward adjustment factors the staff added to build in more recession-like features caused by the financial turmoil and other factors not captured in their baseline model, which is what Dave was mentioning earlier.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My concerns about the inflation outlook have increased since our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation has become a predominant concern for many businesses and consumers, and you only have to read the newspapers to see that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Obviously, monetary policy cannot control the price of energy, but we do have a responsibility to act to keep broad-based inflation under control.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Contributing to the increase in inflation risk is not only the surge in energy and other commodity prices; it is supported also by our own accommodative stance of monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Short-term inflation expectations and headline inflation measures are up significantly since our last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So far, core inflation increases have been modest, and long-term inflation expectations remain, although volatile, within a tolerable range.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But if we continue to maintain the real funds rate well below zero, despite inflation that is well above acceptable levels, can we really expect inflation expectations to remain anchored?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We must remember that longer-term inflation expectations tend to lag inflation not to lead it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we wait until these measures rise, we will be too late.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Apropos of President Evans’s question about wages, I have been troubled by stories in the press suggesting that we can be less concerned about inflation than we were in the 1970s because wages haven’t risen and labor unions are less prominent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: These stories suggest that the wage–price spiral caused the unanchoring of inflation expectations in the ’70s.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I think this gets the direction of causation backwards.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my view, the story of the ’70s was that the public lacked confidence in the central bank’s commitment to price stability—it didn’t believe the central bank would take the necessary steps to bring inflation under control.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As a consequence, inflation expectations rose and wages rose.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It was the higher inflation and the lack of credibility that led to higher wage demands.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The key to avoiding such a situation, in my view, is maintaining the credibility that the Fed has worked so hard to achieve.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Board staff memo on optimal monetary policy in the context of higher oil prices illustrates the importance of maintaining credibility, and I want to thank the staff for their efforts in this regard.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it was an excellent piece of work.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As they clearly say, the critical factor in containing inflation through an expectations channel is the belief that policymakers will always adhere to a full-commitment rule.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: When the central bank is unable or unwilling to commit in a credible manner to future policy actions or to a long-run inflation goal, the result is both higher inflation and lower output.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the real world, of course, full commitment can never absolutely be achieved.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But beliefs about which regime better approximates reality are informed by the actions taken by the central bank to maintain its commitment to price stability.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe that the FOMC has done a good job with our words—including FOMC statements, minutes, and speeches—in helping to anchor longer-term expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe the Chairman’s speech at the Boston Fed conference earlier this month delivered a well-articulated and important message about the importance of keeping longer-term inflation expectations anchored.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But our credibility rests on more than just words.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We must act in a way that is consistent with our hard-earned reputation, or our credibility could soon vanish.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To underscore our words, we should take actions and take back some of the insurance we have put on in the context of elevated downside tail risks.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given recent economic developments and the improvement in financial market functioning, coupled with our accommodative stance of policy, it seems pretty clear to me that, if the economy continues to evolve as it has over the past couple of months, we should move to raise the funds rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is also the view of market participants, whose expectations for policy have steepened considerably over the intermeeting period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My forecast, therefore, incorporates a monetary policy path that is steeper than the one in the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I assume that the funds rate will reach 2.75 percent by the end of 2008 and move up to 4.5 percent by the end of 2009.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This steeper funds rate path is necessary, in my view, to deliver inflation that is declining back toward our goal.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Regarding the suggestion by the Subcommittee on Communications on lengthening the forecast period, I think it can be a very useful device, and I support it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My preference, however, is for option 2, although I think option 1 could work just as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m for option 2 partly because I, too, am less confident about forecasting whatever the dynamic adjustment process happens to be, and so just going to year 5 I think would be useful.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Omitting year 4 is not omitting any information that is terribly informative, as far as I am concerned.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am a little reluctant to go to some longer-term average like five-to-ten years because I think that muddles the communication picture and may signal a weakening of our commitment about the timeframe over which we think we can really achieve some objective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I am most comfortable with option 2, or I could be happy with option 1 as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: Economic activity in the Fifth District has remained soft in recent weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our retailers report declining activity in June, especially in autos.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are still hearing scattered reports of delayed or canceled new construction projects, either because of a lack of financing or because demand is expected to decline.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our survey measure of manufacturing activity, which by the way covers a manufacturing sector bigger than the Philadelphia and the Empire indexes combined, [laughter] has edged lower in the last two months; but exports continue to be a bright spot with reports of robust outbound activity at area ports.

speaker: LACKER
text: Manufacturing contacts report some success in passing on rising energy and transportation costs to their customers, and their indexes of expected six-month-ahead manufacturing price trends, both for prices paid and prices received, reached new record highs for the 14-year history of those series.

speaker: LACKER
text: I, too, have heard scattered reports in the last couple of weeks of employers contemplating providing extra compensation boosts to their employees to make up for rising energy costs.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the whole, I think the risk of the national economy sinking into a serious recession has receded, and the growth outlook has edged up a bit.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was relieved by the strength in retail sales in May as well as the upward revisions for April and March.

speaker: LACKER
text: The ISM indexes have steadied at right around 50 over the past four months; and although the labor market has been weak, it has not yet shown the accelerating declines that I feared.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Greenbook projection for Q2 real GDP has been revised from minus 1.4 to plus 1.7, and we have made a similar adjustment in our own projection.

speaker: LACKER
text: There remain plenty of reasons for concern on the real side of the economy, of course.

speaker: LACKER
text: Real disposable income has suffered with the fall in employment over the last half-year, and the rising cost of gasoline is taking its toll as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: The continued fall in housing prices has cut into household net worth and could contribute to a rise in consumer saving.

speaker: LACKER
text: Stimulus checks might be playing an important role in supporting consumer spending right now; it is not clear how much.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I am concerned that, when the stimulus effects wear off later this year, we may find that the underlying trend in consumer spending is fairly soft.

speaker: LACKER
text: Commercial construction also remains a potential risk, I believe.

speaker: LACKER
text: There is a bit of a disconnect between the surprisingly strong data on nonresidential construction and the reports of slowing that we keep hearing from regional contacts.

speaker: LACKER
text: This suggests that the numbers reflect projects initiated before the beginning of the year and that commercial construction is likely to soften later this year and to be a drag next year.

speaker: LACKER
text: Despite all of these elements that could depress growth, I think the economic situation has undoubtedly turned out better than we expected at the April meeting because of the better-than- expected consumer and business-investment numbers.

speaker: LACKER
text: Greenbook now forecasts a period of low but positive real growth, significantly better than the experiences of the last two fairly mild recessions, and I think that is about right.

speaker: LACKER
text: Inflation is a growing problem, though.

speaker: LACKER
text: CPI came in at an annual rate of 8 percent in May and has averaged 4.9 percent over the last three months.

speaker: LACKER
text: The core intermediate goods PPI is increasing at double-digit rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: Oil prices have risen 16 percent by my calculation since the last meeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: Retail gas prices are up 13 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: Changes in inflation expectations since the last meeting vary with the measure that you choose.

speaker: LACKER
text: But my reading is that they continue to deteriorate.

speaker: LACKER
text: In any event, they are above levels consistent with price stability.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Michigan survey numbers for inflation expectations have risen notably, especially for the one-year horizon.

speaker: LACKER
text: The TIPS-based measure of expected one-year inflation five years forward has increased 30 basis points since the April meeting, and although the five-year, five-year-forward figure has been stable since then, it is still quite close to the highest value it reached at any point last year.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is popular, as many have noted around the table, to cite the stability of compensation gains as evidence that we are not seeing a wage–price spiral.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have done it myself recently.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I share the concerns expressed by President Evans and others around the table about that being a lagging indicator.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am concerned that, if we wait until we see rising inflation expectations showing up as wage pressures, we will have waited too long.

speaker: LACKER
text: I noted in just a casual glance at the data from the 1970s that, although wage acceleration was a prominent component of the acceleration of inflation in the late 1960s, it was largely absent in the accelerations that occurred in ’74 and ’79.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think monetary policy is quite stimulative right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: Using the Bluebook’s standard approach of subtracting four-quarter lagged core inflation, the real funds rate now stands just below zero, about where it bottomed out in the ’91 recession and a good deal above its trough in 2004.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I don’t think lagged core inflation is the best estimate of overall inflation now.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am drawn to the Bluebook’s real rate estimate, new in this edition, that uses the Greenbook’s projection for headline inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Using that measure and going back and reconstructing it for the past, the real funds rate is now minus 1.3 percent, and that is substantially lower than its troughs in the last two recessions, which were right around zero.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is a lot of stimulus, arguably way too much given the improvement in the growth outlook, the reduction in downside risks, and the continuation of inflation pressures.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think withdrawing the stimulus is going to be challenging, however.

speaker: LACKER
text: About the extended projections, I am not convinced that the benefits exceed the cost.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think it is going to provide much help on communicating an inflation objective.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it will show about as much dispersion as our third-year forecasts show now.

speaker: LACKER
text: In any event, I haven’t noticed much of a decline in the volatility of inflation expectations since we began releasing projections on an accelerated calendar late last year.

speaker: LACKER
text: Moreover, I think those steady- state or longer-run projections are just going to tempt people to think that we have an unemployment rate target and a growth target.

speaker: LACKER
text: That some politicians have suggested that we actually adopt such makes it dangerous to engage in any exercise that seems to comply with that suggestion.

speaker: LACKER
text: Besides, I am not sure who cares about our steady-state growth forecasts besides maybe some business-cycle-model calibrators.

speaker: LACKER
text: But we are likely to get our steady-state growth forecasts from those people in any event, so I am not sure that is going to be very helpful.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think we should bother with these extended forecasts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a break until 4:45 and have some coffee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Bullard, whenever you are ready.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The District economy continues to be sluggish.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Severe weather, combined with a very wet spring, is hampering agriculture in some areas.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Major flooding has caused significant damage already, and the situation continues to develop.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Many business contacts in the District emphasize energy costs along with some other high commodity prices as an overriding concern.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Most of the descriptions I have encountered concern businesses and consumers scrambling to adjust to new pricing realities.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Many contacts are reporting skittishness over the inflation outlook, fueled by dramatic increases in key commodity prices.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Many contacts with deep experience in the commodities markets remain convinced that market manipulation or speculation is behind the run-up in commodity prices across the board over the past several years.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This belief is widespread and deeply held.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Many predict a crash in market prices of these commodities once the bubble bursts.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My assessment is that this very strong belief may, by itself, have important macroeconomic implications.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Businesses and households may be reacting very differently to price increases that they see as temporary, as opposed to their reaction if they view price increases as permanent and unlikely to reverse.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Reports on the level of economic activity are decidedly mixed.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The housing sector remains in a deep slump and subject to a widespread shakeup.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Business in the energy sector continues to boom.

speaker: BULLARD
text: High energy prices are affecting the logistics business, which has to try to be profitable at higher prices with reduced demand.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Still, a very large retailer reports brisk activity, and a large technology firm is essentially unaffected by the macroeconomic slowdown.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Recent data on the U.S. economy have been stronger than forecast, keeping economic performance weak but avoiding a particularly sharp contraction.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The worst outcomes stemming from financial market turmoil have failed to materialize thus far.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There is, to be sure, still some potential for additional upheaval, depending in part on the managerial agility among key financial firms.

speaker: BULLARD
text: However, the U.S. economy is now much better positioned to handle financial market turmoil than it was six months ago.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is due to the lending facilities now in place and to the environment of low interest rates that has been created.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Renewed financial market turmoil, should it occur during the summer or fall, would not now be as worrisome from a systemic risk perspective.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In addition to this lessened risk from financial markets, I see the drag from housing dissipating during the second half of the year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Most likely we will also see a moderation in energy price increases.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Output growth is, therefore, likely to be moderately stronger going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Policy was very aggressive during January and March of this year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This was, in part, a preemptive action, insurance against a particularly severe downturn brought on by financial contagion.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This was a very real possibility, but it did not materialize.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This has created a situation with more stimulus in train than would have been intended had we known the outcome in advance.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is putting upward pressure on inflation and inflation expectations in the second half of this year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Policy has to turn now to face this situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the long-term projections, I think it is a good idea to put down long-term projections.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am happy with any of the options.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I have a slight preference for option 3.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think a trial run would be good.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If the objective is to name these numbers, such as an inflation target or the potential growth of the economy, another way to do it would just be to name those numbers and not have it tied to any projection or any particular year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We could just say, “This is what I think the inflation objectives should be.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is how fast I think the economy could grow in the absence of shocks.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And this is what I think the unemployment rate would be if output were growing at potential and inflation were at target.” You could just name those numbers.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You wouldn’t have to say five years away or ten years away, which kind of brings in new long-run factors that you might not want to get into.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The last two months have brought an interesting shift in my conversations with my business contacts.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Their concerns have shifted from problems in financial markets to the rapid increase in input prices.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Energy prices are the focus nationwide, but steel prices are also capturing the attention of the business people in my District.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Several manufacturers and builders noted that the price they pay for steel has almost doubled since the beginning of this year.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Clearly, businesses are worried about signs of growing price pressures, but their reactions to these price shocks tell a more complicated story.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Many manufacturers have not been able to pass on price increases, resulting in a clear loss to profit margins.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: These businesses often report cost-containment or efficiency programs that will affect their hiring and capital decisions for months to come.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Interestingly, the consumer price data show a similar dichotomy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My staff noted that our primary measures of core inflation are not providing a consistent story about the path of underlying inflation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In the May CPI report, roughly one-third of the weighted price changes increased at rates above 5 percent, and roughly one-third of prices changed by rates less than 1 percent.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: For example, while energy costs were up strongly and prices for a number of general service components have been drifting higher, large declines in apparel and vehicle expenses are imparting significant offsets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The 16 percent trimmed mean indicator showed an alarming 4 percent rise in prices, while the median rose just at 2.2 percent.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The weight of price changes in the 1 percent to 5 percent range was unusually small, making it difficult to estimate the central tendency of the price change distribution with much confidence.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So this makes it difficult to get a good read on where future prices are headed.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My District business contacts remain pessimistic about growth prospects.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: District retail reports focused extensively on the likely effects of gasoline and food prices on the purchasing decisions of consumers.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Many manufacturers, builders, and distributors are facing complicated output and investment decisions in the context of input price growth and weaker markets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Overall, most of the business people that I talk with are still quite cautious about their business plans, despite the fact that most of them have found sources of credit and terms that are not too elevated from what they have seen in previous years.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In the economic projections that I submitted for this meeting, I raised my near-term forecast for output growth slightly and for headline inflation slightly more.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Over the medium term, my outlook continues to be for modest growth because the housing market, in my forecast, recovers slowly, actually more slowly than in the Greenbook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My staff estimated a model for national housing starts that takes into account what has happened in the past in states that have seen major increases in foreclosures.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The real estate difficulties that these states faced were much more persistent than anything that we have yet seen in the national data.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The bottom line of this analysis is that, if the patterns of past housing cycles from the states that experienced the boom–bust cycles are repeated at the national level, then housing starts should remain relatively weak over the next couple of years.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Supporting this analysis, three of the large regional banking organizations in my District are increasing their loan-loss provisions significantly in the second quarter based on the continued deterioration in the housing sector.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Based on current projections, these institutions are projecting housing sector credit losses to accelerate in the second half of 2008 and to continue into 2009.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Currently, the weak output growth contributes to my forecast of declining inflation rates, especially the core rate, but I also see evidence supporting that view in the “less worker bargaining power” scenario that is in the Greenbook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My contacts see very little price pressures coming from labor costs now or in the near future.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Finally, implicit in my forecast for output growth and inflation is a fed funds rate path that includes increases later this year and into next year.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Although additional risks to growth remain, the primary risk to my forecast concerns input prices and inflation expectations.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: If commodity prices continue to accelerate, they are going to put upward pressure on both headline and core inflation and downward pressure on output.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: That environment could lead to a highly undesirable increase in inflation expectations.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: On the positive side of risk to the outlook, I think that the fed funds rate actions that we have taken, in conjunction with the actions that we took in August to bolster market liquidity, have improved confidence, and I have substantially lowered the odds I had placed on financial market meltdown and on a severe recession.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In that sense, since our meeting in April the downside risks to my outlook for economic growth have lessened somewhat, and the risks to my inflation outlook have moved up somewhat.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Regarding the issue of providing longer-term forecasts, I have long supported efforts to clarify the underlying objectives of FOMC participants by providing our longer-term economic projections.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Of the proposals that were offered by the Subcommittee on Communications, I favor reporting the average values for output growth, unemployment, and total inflation expected over a five-to-ten-year period—option 3.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The features of these five-to-ten-year projections that I find attractive are that they indicate where the economy might converge and don’t imply too much knowledge of the path to the long run.

speaker: EVANS
text: Most of my contacts continued to report sluggish domestic demand, and they are not currently seeing any improvement in activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, their comments often focused on the substantially higher costs that they are facing for a wide range of nonlabor inputs.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to business activity, much of what we heard about the District and the national economy was a rehashing of preexisting developments.

speaker: EVANS
text: At our last meeting, we felt that there was substantial risk of a further softening in second-quarter growth, so the absence of new news is a positive development.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to specific sectors, exporters I have talked with continue to thrive, and steel producers are doing quite well.

speaker: EVANS
text: But any business associated with housing markets is very weak, and the motor vehicle outlook continues to worsen.

speaker: EVANS
text: All Detroit Three CEOs are expecting light vehicle sales to be less than 15 million units in 2008.

speaker: EVANS
text: The Seventh District has experienced substantial flooding in recent weeks, particularly in Iowa.

speaker: EVANS
text: We have been in contact with state officials and numerous businesses.

speaker: EVANS
text: The corn and soybean crops have experienced significant losses, though the range of estimates is wide.

speaker: EVANS
text: Higher estimates for lost corn output in Iowa are about 10 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: That substantial loss would represent a national crop loss of just about 2 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, although there have been transportation disruptions, especially on the Mississippi, our contacts expect these to be short-lived.

speaker: EVANS
text: So overall, our sense is that the economic damage seems to be relatively contained, especially in comparison with the floods in 1993, which hit a much wider geographic area and affected activity for a longer period of time.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning to the national picture, the incoming data regarding growth generally have been positive.

speaker: EVANS
text: Indeed, the string of upward quarterly forecast revisions continues.

speaker: EVANS
text: In particular, I have been impressed by how much second-quarter GDP growth forecasts have moved up.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is not to say that we are out of the woods.

speaker: EVANS
text: Clearly, the continued difficulties in the housing and credit markets as well as the unrelenting increases in energy prices pose important downside risks to activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our Chicago Fed national activity index continues to be in territory I would characterize as a recession—the three-month moving average is minus 1.08 this past month.

speaker: EVANS
text: Still, the risk of the adverse feedback loop that concerned us so much clearly seems less likely today.

speaker: EVANS
text: Importantly, the financial situation seems better.

speaker: EVANS
text: Though conditions are still far from normal, institutions have had time to cope with bad portfolios, much as President Bullard mentioned.

speaker: EVANS
text: They have made significant progress in raising capital and have increased provisions against losses.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think our lending facilities have helped financial institutions gain time to facilitate the adjustment process.

speaker: EVANS
text: It seems well beyond our abilities, however, to engineer a return to “normal financial conditions,” given the extent of financial losses and overbuilding in housing.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to our economic projections, we expect growth this quarter to be similar to the Greenbook; but unlike the Greenbook, we are looking for the momentum to carry forward to a better second half of the year.

speaker: EVANS
text: Beyond this year, we think growth will run near potential.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is based on a fed funds rate path close to that in the futures markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: We are assuming a fed funds rate of 2½ percent by the fourth quarter and 3¾ percent by the end of 2009.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning to inflation, a number of factors present a concern for inflation expectations and our ability to bring inflation down.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I mentioned, my contacts spent a good deal of time talking about materials cost pressures, and many around the table have talked about those as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: Many manufacturers were citing large increases in energy and most commodity prices, and everyone was passing along some portion of these cost increases.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have one anecdote on this: In retail, Crate&Barrel reported on recent buyers’ trips to Asia, saying that prices for items purchased there would be 15 to 20 percent higher for next year.

speaker: EVANS
text: Finally, wage pressures have been subdued thus far.

speaker: EVANS
text: Still, econometric analysis by my staff reminded me that wage inflation tends to follow price inflation not the other way around.

speaker: EVANS
text: So by the time we see wage pressures, either we are not behind the curve now, or it is “Katie, bar the door!” It is probably one or the other.

speaker: EVANS
text: Indeed, I am concerned that large and persistent changes in costs and in relative prices of high-profile items, such as energy, could change the inflationary mindset of businesses and households.

speaker: EVANS
text: The resulting increase in inflation expectations would pose a difficult challenge for monetary policy.

speaker: EVANS
text: Maybe it will end up being okay; maybe surveys will be right.

speaker: EVANS
text: But it is a big risk, and that risk is a bit large for my comfort.

speaker: EVANS
text: Looking ahead, we all see the substantial upside risk to price stability posed by the pass- through of higher costs and any possible increase in inflation expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: While I hope I am wrong, I feel that we may need to accept a somewhat longer period of resource slack than we would like in order to address these risks and put inflation more firmly on a downward trajectory.

speaker: EVANS
text: Under our projection for GDP growth, the economy does not close the modest resource gaps we project will be in place at the end of 2008 until beyond the forecast horizon.

speaker: EVANS
text: Along with a flattening in energy and other commodity prices, such gaps should be sufficient to contain inflation expectations and bring overall PCE inflation near 2 percent in 2009 and 2010.

speaker: EVANS
text: But my base case does not have inflation moving below 2 percent until after 2010, and that is even with more aggressive policy tightening than the Greenbook path.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, turning to the long-term projections, I think that our forecasts for 2010—or at least the way that I think about it—do suffer from some difficulties.

speaker: EVANS
text: We would like to mention in the write-up that, at the end of the period, the range is between 1½ percent and 2 percent, and we can infer policymakers’ preferences from that.

speaker: EVANS
text: Given the inflationary pressures, that is harder and harder for many people to come up with.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think in some cases it requires a monetary policy response that is beyond what most people would expect that we could actually do.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I don’t try to force my inflation forecast into my preferred range if it is too hard.

speaker: EVANS
text: Based upon monetary policy, it is more medium term.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I do tend to favor a longer period.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am somewhat indifferent between the first and the second options.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t really see a lot of difference, but something that has a five-year forecast I think is useful.

speaker: EVANS
text: Whether or not it has the fourth year and whether or not it is core PCE or total are less important issues.

speaker: EVANS
text: One argument for this is an interesting body of research, which I have been exposed to only at conferences—and Jim probably knows it better than most—on learning and whether individuals in the economy can learn these rules without a variety of information.

speaker: EVANS
text: Some of the better papers that I have seen on that remind us that you need more pieces of information than just what the target is, whether it be 1½ percent or 2 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: You need some type of contour when people are learning with simplistic learning rules, like least squares learning.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I think a bit more contour on the forecast would be helpful.

speaker: EVANS
text: In my mind, that pushes you toward the five years of forecasting as opposed to a steady state or a five-to-ten-year forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that’s an important element.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the trial run, I think we could do it sooner than that, but I know a lot of staff resources are involved.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I favor sooner rather than later.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, like some others—maybe many others—I, too, have raised my forecast for growth for this year, basically just extending what’s happening in the first half of the year, and I’ve raised my projection for growth next year marginally as well.

speaker: STERN
text: Still, I must admit to some significant reservations about doing that.

speaker: STERN
text: As I look at the outlook and as Larry Slifman pointed out, there are a number of weaknesses, concerns, or downsides that you can pretty readily identify—tight or tightening credit conditions, a still significant decline in housing activity, a decline in housing values and the negative wealth effects associated with that, the run-up in energy prices, and so forth.

speaker: STERN
text: Many of those will adversely affect the consumer, it seems to me.

speaker: STERN
text: When we have that high a number of what I would call identifiable negatives, I wouldn’t be surprised if we had one or more quarters of significant economic contraction still ahead of us despite the recent relatively good news on the growth side.

speaker: STERN
text: At the same time, the news on inflation hasn’t been particularly positive from my perspective, and that’s particularly true if the Greenbook is right and some of the relatively favorable recent readings on core inflation are likely to prove transitory.

speaker: STERN
text: I’m struck by the volume of questions I get and concerns expressed about inflation when I’m out talking with business groups or giving a speech to a more general audience.

speaker: STERN
text: Now, a lot of this, of course, is focused on or stems from what’s happening to energy prices and food prices, which are highly visible and which people experience directly and frequently.

speaker: STERN
text: Nevertheless, I’m concerned that all of that makes inflation expectations a bit more vulnerable, maybe more than a bit more vulnerable, than they have been to this point.

speaker: STERN
text: My reading of inflation expectations per se is that they, at least the longer-term expectations—and I’m relying mostly on the TIPS data here—have been remarkably well anchored so far.

speaker: STERN
text: Perhaps a partial explanation for that is that core inflation really hasn’t moved much since 2003–04.

speaker: STERN
text: That’s a bit of a double-edged sword because it has locked in a bit higher than I might have preferred.

speaker: STERN
text: Nevertheless, stability that has been maintained is there.

speaker: STERN
text: Perhaps it goes some distance to explain our continuing, or what appears to be our continuing, credibility on that issue.

speaker: STERN
text: Now, the Greenbook does have some inching up of core inflation from here.

speaker: STERN
text: If they’re right and that’s all we get, then I would be surprised if that led to a real deterioration in inflation expectations.

speaker: STERN
text: But that may prove to be a big “if.” As far as extending the projections goes, I’m in favor of doing that.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t think there will be a huge payoff, but I think it will provide some additional information to us internally and to the public.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t have a strong preference about which alternative we go with.

speaker: STERN
text: Maybe the trial run will point out some advantages or disadvantages that we didn’t anticipate.

speaker: STERN
text: At the moment, if I had to vote, I’d probably vote for the second alternative, which would be to split the difference, put down the fifth year, and let it go at that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think we face an extended period of relatively weak economic growth, quite weak domestic demand growth, and overall growth significantly below trend.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think this is both likely and necessary.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s likely because we have more weakness ahead as the housing drag continues, financial headwinds remain acute, the economy adjusts to the very large and sustained energy price shock, the saving rate increases, and global demand moderates.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s necessary to achieve a reasonable inflation outcome over the forecast period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our central projection has the U.S. economy growing, though at a rate significantly below potential, and then recovering gradually toward trend over the next year.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is our modal forecast; and in this forecast, the economy just skirts a recession.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The output gap begins to narrow over the forecast period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Housing prices begin to stabilize only late in ’09, after a cumulative peak-to-trough drop of roughly 12 percent, using the OFHEO repeat sales purchase-only index.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Net exports provide a significant, though fading, boost to GDP growth this year and next.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We project a very gradual, very modest moderation in core inflation over the forecast period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course, this forecast depends on a lot of things happening.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It depends on expectations remaining reasonably well contained, energy and commodity prices following the futures curve, the dollar only modestly weaker, somewhat diminished pressure on resource utilization here and around the world, and continued moderate growth in compensation and unit labor costs.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our policy assumption builds in significant tightening—a significant move up in the fed funds rate over the forecast period—though not as soon as the market now expects.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The uncertainty around and risks to this central projection are substantial.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the growth front, although we believe the risks of a very deep, prolonged economic downturn have diminished—not on their own but because of the force of the policy response so far—we still think the risks are weighted significantly to the downside.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The main risks remain: the ongoing stress on financial markets; the risk that this further restricts the supply of credit, exacerbates financial conditions, pushes home prices and other equity prices down more further tightening credit conditions, et cetera; a steeper-than-expected rise in the saving rate; and the adjustment to the ongoing drag from energy prices.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the inflation front, we—I think like the rest of you—see the risks ahead tilted somewhat to the upside for many obvious reasons.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it’s true that, looked at together, the mix of measures of inflation expectations suggests that private agents may have less confidence in the FOMC’s commitment to price stability than they did in previous periods when total inflation was running significantly above core.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So this is going to be a very challenging period for policy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Productivity growth is a little higher than we thought.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Underlying inflation and long-term inflation expectations certainly could already have been showing signs of a more compelling, immediate danger.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Spending has been somewhat stronger than confidence measures would have suggested.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The current account balance has narrowed significantly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are seeing very substantial changes in behavior across the U.S. economy in the consumption of energy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So there are good things to point to.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But in the two dangerous areas—in the financial sector and in the global inflation environment—I think things are materially worse than at our last meeting.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, the risk of inflation is readily apparent.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Apart from the numbers, I agree with many of you who said that the alarm and concern is materially higher and materially different today across a broad range of firms in different industries than it was even as recently as two months ago.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have to be worried about intensified pressure on compensation growth even with the degree of slack that we now see in the labor market.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Although firms are absorbing in margins a significant part of the increase in unit costs—and a lot of the complaining that we hear is about margins that are coming down and those that are expected to come down—I do think that firms are demonstrably able to pass on more than they would have been before.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course, what makes it very hard for us is that the pressure on resources is coming largely from outside the United States and the other major economies, from countries that are growing significantly above trend with central banks that are not independent and are running very expansionary monetary policies.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think we are really seeing an alarming acceleration in inflation rates in large parts of the world for the first time in a couple of decades.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If these countries do not tighten monetary policy sufficiently and reduce energy price subsidies materially, then we will have to be tighter than we otherwise would have to be.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In the financial world, although I think it’s true that the market believes there has been some significant reduction in the risk of an acute systemic financial crisis, I think we have a long period of acute fragility ahead.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We’re in the midst right now of more material erosion in sentiment, spreads, asset prices, balance sheet pressures, and liquidity in some markets.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Overall financial conditions are probably somewhat tighter than when we last met.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The financial headwinds have intensified again, and they are likely to remain intense for some time.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, I think this is going to be a very challenging road ahead.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is important to recognize that the current stance of policy embodies not just the fed funds rate today, relative to our best measure of equilibrium, but also the expectations about policy that are now built into the Treasury curve.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That policy today does not look that accommodative.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If you look at the Bluebook charts and at a range of measures of real fed funds rates today relative to different measures of equilibrium, policy is less accommodative just on that simple measure than it was at the most accommodative point of the last two downturns.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That said, we’re going to have to tighten monetary policy, and the question is when.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My sense is soon but not yet.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Right now we still face a very delicate, very fine balance and have to be careful not to declare victory prematurely on the growth front or on the financial front.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it’s going to be hard for us to do that until we see that we are closer to the point at which we can confidently say that we start to see the bottom in housing prices.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Also, we have to be careful not to raise expectations too much that we’re on the verge of an imminent, significant tightening in policy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is a difficult balance.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We should take some comfort from the fact that the market believes we will do enough soon enough to keep those expectations down.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the projections front, I have a complicated view, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we are going to change, we should focus on stuff that will change things significantly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t see huge gains from the changes in these options to our current communication regime.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we’re going to change, a trial run in the fall is fine.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think the fall is too soon to change.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We need to get through this thing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have a very challenging period with a lot of stuff going on, and I think we need to use every molecule of oxygen in the System to get through this mess.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t think this projections change materially helps the communication challenge in getting through this mess and may complicate it in some ways.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we are going to do something beyond our current regime, I would favor doing something slightly different from this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would favor at least considering publishing the average of our individual views on what the desirable long-run rate of inflation is, an average of our judgments of what trend growth is today, and maybe what the natural rate of unemployment is today.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We know very little about what those latter variables—trend growth and the natural rate of unemployment— are five to ten years ahead.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very hard for us individually to put much confidence on whatever the path is toward that point.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Our current regime for aggregating our forecasts the way we do, tossing out the individuals, makes our basic forecast not particularly useful as a prism.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I would focus on doing something slightly different to change the regime, and I wouldn’t do it this soon.

speaker: GEITHNER
