text: If we’re going to change, let’s debate the big things and not spend too much time on things at the margin, which fundamentally aren’t going to offer too much promise relative to the level of ignorance we have or relative to the complexity that people face in reading any particular meaningful value in the aggregation of our forecasts the way we now do them.

speaker: KOHN
text: My forecasts for both economic growth and inflation are within the central tendency of the rest of you and a little stronger than the staff’s outlook.

speaker: KOHN
text: In fact, my 2008 projections for economic activity for the second half of the year were revised very little from two months ago.

speaker: KOHN
text: Growth turned out to be stronger than I expected in the first half, and that carries some weight going forward; but financial conditions are tighter with higher bond rates and lower equity prices, and of course oil prices are a lot higher and that will damp demand going forward.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I expect slow growth in the second half followed by expansion around, maybe a little above, the rate of growth of potential in ’09 and ’10, with the same basic story that everybody else has: drags on activity from declining housing activity, decreasing wealth, tight credit conditions, and higher petroleum prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: All of those drags will abate over time, allowing the natural resilience, with slightly accommodative financial conditions, to show through, and I assume a gradual tightening of monetary policy beginning next year.

speaker: KOHN
text: Incoming information on prices and costs has been mixed.

speaker: KOHN
text: Oil and food price increases will raise headline inflation, but core has been stable and has come in a little to the soft side of expectations, and labor costs as yet show no signs of accelerating.

speaker: KOHN
text: Going forward, I see a sharp decline in headline inflation later this year with the assumed leveling-out in oil prices and a gradual decrease in core as economic slack inhibits wage and price increases, offsetting the pass-through from oil prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, that’s my central tendency.

speaker: KOHN
text: I consider the odds on that being realized to be even lower than usual, and the usual odds are disappearingly small.

speaker: KOHN
text: It seems to me that the defining characteristics of the current situation are uncertainty and risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’re facing multiple shocks, many of them unprecedented in size and persistence, in the housing market, financial markets, and commodities.

speaker: KOHN
text: The outlook is full of puzzles, and in my mind anyone who thinks he or she understands what’s going on is either a lot smarter than I am or delusional—or both.

speaker: KOHN
text: I class the risks for both output and headline inflation as greater than usual, and let me tell you about some of the things I wrestled with.

speaker: KOHN
text: Financial conditions, are they accommodative?

speaker: KOHN
text: I continue to believe that the 2 percent nominal funds rate is not indicative of a highly accommodative financial condition, given the current state of financial markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is, in my view we have limited insurance.

speaker: KOHN
text: Spreads have widened sufficiently over the past 10 months both for long-term and short-term credit, and bank terms and conditions for loans and lines of credit have tightened enough that only a small part of the drop in the fed funds rate is showing through to the cost of capital for median households and firms.

speaker: KOHN
text: The staff’s flow of funds estimates show a marked deceleration in the growth of both household and business debt in the first half of this year, from 10 percent for households last year to 3 percent in the first half of the year and from 12 percent for businesses to 7 percent in the first half of the year.

speaker: KOHN
text: A 2 percent fed funds rate will become accommodative as spreads narrow and financial functioning returns more toward normal, and that’s one reason I assumed a gradually rising federal funds rate over 2009 and forward.

speaker: KOHN
text: The evidence about improving financial markets over the intermeeting period was decidedly mixed.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some spreads did come in from late April.

speaker: KOHN
text: Investment-grade businesses tapped bond markets in size, but almost all spreads remain unusually wide.

speaker: KOHN
text: We were reminded of the fragility of the evolving situation, especially in the financial sector, with the worries about continuing credit problems resulting in sharp declines in equity prices on financials and an uptick in their CDS spreads, which had narrowed the previous month or two; the downgrading of monolines and investment banks; and the increasing attention to the problems of regional banks.

speaker: KOHN
text: It would be surprising if these were not reflected in even greater caution by banks and other lenders in their lending practices.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also the securitization markets, especially for non-agency mortgages, are not functioning in a way to replace bank intermediation.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is going to be a prolonged process of re- intermediation, deleveraging, and building liquidity with an uncertain endpoint.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like the staff, I assume that the conditions return to something approaching normal over the next 18 months, but the risks are skewed toward an even longer recovery period.

speaker: KOHN
text: The second topic is household spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: Households are facing a huge number of adverse shocks: higher oil prices, tighter credit, declining house prices, and rising unemployment.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s not surprising that confidence is at recessionary levels.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is surprising that spending is so resilient.

speaker: KOHN
text: I assumed that the saving rate would rise very gradually once the tax rebate effects wore off, but I think a more abrupt and sizable increase in household saving is a distinct downside risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some sales measures have shown a few tentative indications of leveling off.

speaker: KOHN
text: I was encouraged by President Lockhart’s report from Florida, but I’m also struck by renewed pessimism about housing in the financial markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: Equities of construction firms and builders have declined after stabilizing, actually rising, earlier this year.

speaker: KOHN
text: ABX indexes have turned down, reversing earlier improvements; and perhaps underlying the previous two developments, the Case-Shiller futures indexes remain in steep decline, though today’s information was less weak than expected.

speaker: KOHN
text: The view of the financial markets, anyhow, is that the light at the end of the housing tunnel is receding, and declines in expected house prices must be an important reason for the erosion in market confidence in financial intermediaries.

speaker: KOHN
text: In sum, although the incoming data may have reduced the threat of a sharp drop in spending, in my view there remains a very pronounced downward skew around my outlook for modest growth in H2 and a strengthening next year.

speaker: KOHN
text: However, that downward skew around output did not translate into a downward skew around my forecast for headline inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: In fact, I saw the risks on headline inflation as tilted to the upside, though roughly balanced around the gradual decrease in core.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the upside risks result from two additional areas of uncertainty.

speaker: KOHN
text: One area is commodity prices, though the trend increases in commodity prices over the past few years can be attributed to rising demands from emerging market economies relative to sluggishly responding supplies.

speaker: KOHN
text: Despite Nathan’s best efforts, I really don’t think we have much of a clue about the cause of the spike in oil prices this year.

speaker: KOHN
text: It has been especially striking to me over the intermeeting period, when the prices of industrial commodities have been falling on balance.

speaker: KOHN
text: Presumably prices in these markets already incorporate expectations of reasonably strong global growth outside the United States as in the Greenbook.

speaker: KOHN
text: Absent any surprises, futures market quotes ought to be the best guide, but what we don’t understand can fool us, especially when so much of the relevant information involves emerging market economies, where data are sparse and of questionable value.

speaker: KOHN
text: Given our experience over the past few years, I think continued increases in commodity prices would seem to be an upside risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: The other area is inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I assume that as headline inflation comes down, both short- and long-term inflation expectations, especially in the survey data, will reverse their recent increases based a lot on the kind of information that President Yellen was observing about how the household survey has tended to follow contemporaneous inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m encouraged by the relatively flat readings on core inflation and labor compensation increases.

speaker: KOHN
text: Higher expectations have not so far become embedded in prices and costs, despite all the talk of passing along cost increases.

speaker: KOHN
text: But headline inflation is going to rise before it falls.

speaker: KOHN
text: Real wages will be further eroded by higher energy costs.

speaker: KOHN
text: Although this is a necessary part of an adjustment to an adverse terms-of- trade shock, it will be resisted.

speaker: KOHN
text: Hence, a further rise in inflation expectations and a stronger determination by households and businesses to act on those expectations will be a risk over coming months.

speaker: KOHN
text: With that further rise in oil prices, it’s a bigger risk than it was a couple of months ago.

speaker: KOHN
text: In terms of the long-term projections, Mr. Chairman, I think I’m fine with something like your proposal.

speaker: KOHN
text: Our objective for adding a year was to give the public a better sense of where we’re going over the long term.

speaker: KOHN
text: Given the shock to the economy, that’s not as informative as it was before.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we’re close to where most people would say their inflation objective was, but not for the growth rate of potential or the NAIRU.

speaker: KOHN
text: I could live with option 3 or President Bullard’s alternative to that—to state exactly what our long-term expectations are instead of talking about five to seven years or five to ten years.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think we’ll gain a lot.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think the costs or benefits are very large on either side of this.

speaker: KOHN
text: Our problems now are not that people don’t understand where we’re going in the end.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think they have a pretty good idea that we want inflation to be a lot lower than it has been.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think they don’t really understand how we’re going to get either to full employment or to price stability, given where we’re starting.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think the uncertainty about our objectives is a very small problem relative to the other problems now.

speaker: KOHN
text: But if we can reinforce what those objectives are, it might help a little around the edges.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do worry, as President Lacker said, that what we say about output and employment not be interpreted as goals but rather as a judgment about the state and the structure of the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am hopeful that we could take care of that in what we say about what we’re publishing.

speaker: WARSH
text: At this point everything has been said, but everybody hasn’t said it.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me make three summary points, and then I will talk about three issues that I think are harder.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, on the economy, through late May, as the Greenbook suggests, the real economy proved more resilient and more dynamic than the consensus had anticipated.

speaker: WARSH
text: Consumer spending was moderate but positive, and the labor markets were soft, but neither was necessarily indicative of a recession through late May.

speaker: WARSH
text: Business fixed investment and corporate profits ex financials look all right.

speaker: WARSH
text: Productivity growth looks, frankly, impressive, and corporations, unlike consumers, still appear okay through the month of June—but I’m going to return to June in just a short while.

speaker: WARSH
text: In sum, my assessment of the economy reasonably approximates the average GDP from the Greenbook for 2008, but I remain considerably more cautious on the catalyst for return-to-trend growth in the forecast period of 2009 and beyond.

speaker: WARSH
text: I suspect that this is a long, slow climb with the credit channels needing to be rebuilt and that the process is still in its very early stages.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, let me talk about the financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: Financial markets continue to show tenuous but real improvements in market functioning—which, as Bill Dudley suggested, is remarkable given the weakness among financial institutions themselves.

speaker: WARSH
text: Leveraged loans and high-yield markets continue to trend toward improved market functioning.

speaker: WARSH
text: Credit spreads are well off their March highs.

speaker: WARSH
text: Credit markets, in particular, are holding up well, despite the broad weakness across equities.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, let me turn to inflation risks.

speaker: WARSH
text: Inflation risks, in my view, continue to predominate as the greater risk to the economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: There is more evidence of a global secular reversal of inflation trends, making the jobs of central bankers worldwide considerably more difficult.

speaker: WARSH
text: I remain worried about energy and food pass-through and the effect of a weakening dollar if our policy rates and those of our major trading partners are perceived to diverge.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would expect import prices, core inflation, and expectations to move up in the coming months even more than in the Greenbook, likely causing a policy response by our foreign peers.

speaker: WARSH
text: Commodity prices, again, with the exception of metals, have been moving up while global demand is falling, and markets have come to see this rise of some, if not most, commodities as essentially permanent.

speaker: WARSH
text: So at the end of the day, we have to be concerned about this period of above-acceptable inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: It’s crucial that broader prices do not start to rise at still-faster rates, and that could well happen if those making decisions about prices and pay expect higher inflation in the future.

speaker: WARSH
text: Anecdotes are not comforting, particularly on the price front.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a result, I think the trajectory of inflation is less favorable than in the Greenbook, thereby necessitating a policy response more significant than the Greenbook would suggest.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn to three even harder issues.

speaker: WARSH
text: We’re not done with the second quarter, and my sense of what’s happened in the first three weeks of June is pretty miserable.

speaker: WARSH
text: I hate to extrapolate based on three weeks of data to the trajectory of the economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: But from a discussion with contacts from three credit card companies that constitute a little more than half of the credit card spend, I would say that the views from these guys were shocking in how bad things looked in the past three to four weeks, particularly in comparison to reasonably positive news from the previous two months.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is suggestive that June will be much weaker than May, and if I add that to the figures on autos that are coming out of the Detroit Three, those are a couple of anecdotes that make me a little hesitant to declare with an exclamation mark what an enviable second quarter we’ve had.

speaker: WARSH
text: I also look at equity market prices sometimes as maybe telling us something.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say that consumer companies and retailers over the last three weeks have gotten killed.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I’m a little hesitant to suggest that the second quarter is going to be strong.

speaker: WARSH
text: Delinquencies and charge-offs have also moved meaningfully to the downside in the last three or four weeks among these credit card companies, and this weakness appears to be much more focused on the coasts than it is in the center of the country.

speaker: WARSH
text: I heard that from three of three.

speaker: WARSH
text: My own view may be influenced by my take on the fiscal stimulus—it sure doesn’t appear to be helping very much.

speaker: WARSH
text: The second issue that I continue to struggle with is financial institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: Financial institution equity prices showed significant underperformance, and some people say that is the Federal Reserve’s fault.

speaker: WARSH
text: We’re talking up our concerns about inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: We’re changing the Treasury curve going forward.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that is a total red herring.

speaker: WARSH
text: The reason that financials are getting killed is an equity story.

speaker: WARSH
text: They have business models that are having a hard time delivering profits in this environment.

speaker: WARSH
text: They have had to show a very tough quarterly set of losses.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the problems on financials have to do with financials and not with the Fed, though there is a disturbing amount of chatter in the markets that somehow we’re the cause of that.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am comforted, again as Bill Dudley reminded us, that the broader market functioning has been able to withstand this dramatic financial institution weakness.

speaker: WARSH
text: Whether at some point that will give out I don’t know, but I’d say that’s extremely encouraging.

speaker: WARSH
text: In addition, we have to recognize that massive amounts of new capital are going to be needed for financial institutions of all sizes.

speaker: WARSH
text: Given the weak performance of virtually every financial investment from November till now, I think it is very easy to see a supply–demand problem.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is very easy to see that, with the number of banks that come to these markets, some of them at some point might not be able to find capital even at dramatically lower prices than their expectations.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is prudent for us at the Fed to think about alternative sources of more-patient institutional funding during this period.

speaker: WARSH
text: The third issue for discussion is credit availability, especially for small businesses.

speaker: WARSH
text: This strikes me as being key to the labor market situation.

speaker: WARSH
text: Credit availability for small businesses has held up better than I would have expected four or five months ago, but pockets of weakness remain, particularly among the regional banks, which are a source of concern.

speaker: WARSH
text: I guess I’ve become convinced that credit lines have not been tapped out.

speaker: WARSH
text: There was a theory, one that I even had some sympathy toward, that increases in C&I lending in the last few quarters were involuntary, reflecting existing credit lines that were called upon.

speaker: WARSH
text: That strikes me as being somewhat overstated.

speaker: WARSH
text: According to anecdotes and our own survey of the terms of business lending, it does suggest that capital is still available for these small businesses to provide some strength to the economy; but again, continued weakness among the regionals could call that into question.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn finally, Mr. Chairman, to the projections.

speaker: WARSH
text: I have some sympathy for the view that Vice Chairman Geithner put forth.

speaker: WARSH
text: It strikes me that at this time the markets will see the benefits of changing our communication strategy as, yet again, pretty small.

speaker: WARSH
text: The costs are harder for me to be certain about.

speaker: WARSH
text: So if anyone is proposing to do this during the next six months, I would have real hesitancy about introducing this variable into our communication strategy amid our assessment of all the other challenges that we have.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I favor having a trial run come October, but I think we should revisit where we stand on the inflation front, the financial institution front, and the growth front before adding this to the mix.

speaker: WARSH
text: To the extent that we find the appropriate time to go down this path, I would favor option 3.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, as I’ve mentioned many times before, I have thought about this as sort of a long, slow burn scenario; and as we well know, the embers are still smoldering.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It seems to be less of a risk that they could re-ignite, causing a major conflagration; but there is still some chance of re-ignition, and I think there’s still a fair amount of heat.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Consistent with that, my central tendency view is probably closer to the Greenbook’s “delayed credit recovery” alternative scenario than to the main Greenbook forecast.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In looking at the alternative scenario, there’s not much of a real effect on growth, but that response is due to a lower fed funds path.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Given the discussions that we’ve had, I think it may be very difficult to pursue something like that in this environment, particularly given higher uncertainty about inflation and inflation expectations, even if, as a number of people have mentioned, inflation expectations haven’t moved up that much or you pick your favorite measure and some have moved up more than others.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Given that it’s likely that we had some transitory factors keeping core and headline inflation down a little lower than they otherwise might have been and they probably are going to go up, I think that dealing with the “delayed credit recovery” alternative scenario in the way that’s discussed in the Greenbook makes our policy choices particularly difficult.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So let me focus briefly on why I think the delayed credit recovery or slow burn scenario is a reasonable central tendency one.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it relates largely to our continuing challenges on banks’ balance sheets, liquidity, and capital.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Banks are facing very high short-term financing costs.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Those LIBOR–OIS spreads are still at extremely elevated levels compared with what they’re used to in funding themselves, and this is true whether they are commercial banks or investment banks.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The forwards suggest that this ain’t going away anytime soon.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So one thing that this does is simply to cut into profitability and the ability to earn your way out of the challenges.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: An easy way to do it— of just allowing the machine to go forward—is going to produce less than it otherwise would.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A lot of institutions rely on the Federal Home Loan Banks, but those are largely tapped out as another source of financing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We know that the monoline issue has sort of come back, and the challenges there are great.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is undoubtedly going to be leading to a lot more write-downs over the next couple of quarters.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On the other hand, as President Lockhart, Governor Warsh, and some others have mentioned, there have been a few areas that seem to have opened up.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The leveraged-loan market seems to have opened up a bit.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: People seem to be getting those leveraged loans off their books— and not even at effectively subsidized financing rates.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They were proud of getting these off their books before, but they were doing it by basically just making another loan, which effectively doesn’t get them off the books.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now it seems as though they are legitimately able to move this, and obviously that book is not growing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Of course, one of the biggest challenges is in housing, and I see the shocks of some of the resets from the nontraditional mortgages continuing through ’09.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’re seeing very significant increases in delinquencies and foreclosures, not only in the subprime space but also in the adjustable rate space generally—that’s both subprime and prime, although the levels for prime are dramatically lower.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The increases are quite significant for prime ARMs, and that starts to raise some challenges for the institutions that didn’t do subprime but may still have a reasonable amount of prime ARMs on their books.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: HELOCs have been mentioned and the inability to securitize anything that’s nonconforming.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’ve seen very little benefit yet from the changes that allow Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae to raise those limits.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, as many of you know, from my visits around the country to your Districts, I see that conditions in different areas are dramatically different, but in general a lot of markets remain in very difficult circumstances.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One of the largest mortgage lenders in the country said that, over the last couple of months, their average FICO score on what they’ve been originating outside the conforming market has been 800.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That’s astonishingly high—so that gets back to President Yellen’s comment about even with FICO scores in the stratosphere—and they claim that’s an average FICO score, and they have been pulling back on the HELOCs et cetera.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On rising delinquency rates for credit cards, I didn’t hear quite as bleak a view as Governor Warsh described.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I wouldn’t want to say a positive view.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They seemed to say that it is where they would have expected it to be in this part of a cycle with increasing delinquencies.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One thing that they were seeing was a little increase in payments, and so that may be one of the consequences of the stimulus check coming—that people are using it to pay down some of their credit card debt.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But a big challenge that they have been seeing is the so-called roll rates—that once someone begins to go delinquent, they tend to roll right to full loss rather than getting some recovery.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It suggests that, when people get into trouble, they are in fairly deep trouble.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: All of this means that the demand for capital is going to be very high going forward at these institutions as provisioning has to go up.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: You know, we’ve tapped sovereign wealth funds, institutional investors, and a lot of others.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As Governor Warsh said, tapping other sources, encouraging perhaps private equity to come in, is something that’s important.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But how long are these guys willing to invest when over the past nine months every single investment has seen a reduction rather than an increase in value?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I’m borrowing a prop from President Fisher—we have been going around and saying, “Raise capital.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: You’re worth it.” I hope the investment banks are going around to their shareholders and saying that also.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So far there’s not a lot of evidence that they have been.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think in the long run they will, but we have to worry about that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This slow burn scenario is even more problematic in the context of what Vice Chairman Geithner mentioned about some slowing of foreign demand that I think may be coming and in the context of a fair amount of increases in interest rates that may be coming in a lot of these countries.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: You’re going to be seeing some credit tightening globally, as I think a number of people have mentioned.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is more likely, unless there’s a major shock, to be more on the tightening side going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This makes it more difficult to deal with some of the issues in the “higher inflation expectations” alternative scenario that was in the Greenbook because, when you have this financial fragility, it’s harder perhaps to raise interest rates as quickly or as much as you would like because of the concerns about what might happen in the financial markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On inflation, I think much like President Stern and a number of others—it depends on which particular series you look at.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is hard to say that things have really become unmoored, but I think there’s a lot more uncertainty in the minds of both the public and the market participants about where inflation may go.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That’s particularly problematic when you have the likely increase in the actual numbers coming that the Greenbook is forecasting for the next quarter or so; and in that context, dealing with some of the challenges is more difficult.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we’ll talk about that more tomorrow.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On the projections, I think it is important that we continue to increase transparency over time.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We structured what we did last time to make it part of a process, and I think it makes sense to periodically revisit whether we want to continue on that road.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I very much prefer a gradualist approach, in principle, to add year 5 or so—as the Chairman said—but I think there’s a bit of a problem in doing that because too much meaning may be attributed to it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It may be too difficult to avoid saying, “Well, we’re just doing a target.” If we add year 4 and year 5, even though there’s not a lot of information content in year 4, I think it helps to reduce the kind of shock value of seeing that fifth year out there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now, that’s potentially a negative because, in some sense, we want to provide more information that way.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But given the fragile conditions, as Vice Chairman Geithner mentioned, I don’t think that we want to generate a debate on inflation targets, employment targets, and other things like that particularly right now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So maybe having a gradualist approach, by which we just extend things to year 4 and year 5, which is seen as a natural outgrowth, wouldn’t be as much of a shock.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Not that I think it would be shocking, but I think it might raise as many concerns and as much of a debate and distract us from the key issues that we have before us.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Well, we have seen recent data that actually have been stronger than expected.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also as time goes on, there seems to be a lower probability of financial meltdown and these adverse feedback loops that we’ve all been discussing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I don’t think we want to become too sanguine about the current data because some very negative things are going on that might tell us that this is just very temporary stuff.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, it’s really remarkable how weak consumer sentiment is.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There is also a huge hit from energy prices, and it’s going to get worse.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One thing in the Greenbook is that the very low margins that we’ve had in refining are going to increase, so we’re going to see gasoline prices that are well over $5.00 a gallon, according to the kind of numbers you’re coming out with, and that is going to be a major contractionary hit to household spending.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Luckily I don’t drive much anymore—I’m down to less than 600 miles a year right now—so maybe that is okay, but unfortunately I’ll get back to driving more in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In any case, I do think that what the Greenbook has done is reasonable in terms of changing the forecast.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: They have a stronger first half, but the longer-run forecast, particularly regarding the output gap, is really not very different, and I think that’s a reasonable forecast.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My baseline is somewhat less optimistic because I feel that the “delayed credit recovery” alternative scenario was actually a nice one to put in this Greenbook, and I was glad to see it because it is very close to the way I am thinking about the situation right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think there’s going to be a much slower recovery of financial markets than was in the Greenbook baseline because two things have to occur for us to get back to normal underwriting.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This, of course, doesn’t mean what we had before, which did not have serious enough underwriting standards, but something we think is realistic given the kinds of risks in the economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Financial institutions have to have enough capital just to make loans—so there’s the direct effect that we think about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But also the securitization market is clearly very impaired.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Eventually it will come back, but it will need new business models to solve the agency issues that have led to all of the heartache that we’ve seen recently.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When I think about how that is going to happen, I think the large financial institutions have to play a key role because you need somebody who will originate these loans and then will have the incentives to make sure that the agency problems are not severe.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Only when that’s done can they be sold off, and that requires that there is recourse, which requires that they have plenty of capital.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, it is a very slow process for them to build up capital in the current environment.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So given that situation, I think the idea that the financial markets will be back to normal over the next year or two is a little optimistic.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s going to take a long time for this to get worked out.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So the bottom-line scenario is one in which we’re going to have strong headwinds for quite a time, and that’s going to be important in terms of our monetary policy stance.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When I think about inflation, as you know, I put a lot of emphasis on long-run inflation expectations and on expectations about future economic slack in the economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: At this point, I do not see a major change and deterioration in long-run inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’ll explain that in a second.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I should emphasize that I say that is true so far.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But an issue is whether that will change, and that’s going to be very important in terms of how we manage monetary policy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The first things I look at when I think about long-run inflation expectations are, of course, the surveys of consumers.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As you know, I’ve always been a little skeptical of them, but I think that my views are very similar to the ones that President Yellen mentioned.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have a slightly different explanation using behavioral economics.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Behavioral economics tells you that surveys will rise a lot with what happens currently and overreact and that’s exactly what should happen because it’s a framing issue.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You see very high headline inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You’re going to raise expectations of inflation one year out.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But it’s very natural that you’re going to raise them for the longer term, and they’ll come back down when headline inflation comes down.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I really am not as concerned about the survey expectations being a long-run problem as long as inflation comes back down.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think there are good indications that it will, given that headline is so much higher than core and that core has actually stayed very stable.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The other things that I look at, and look at much more seriously, are the Surveys of Professional Forecasters (which have basically moved up a bit but not very much and have not gotten much out of the range in which they have been in the past) and then information from financial markets, that is, inflation compensation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Again, that has not risen recently, and actually it’s better than it was at its peak.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I don’t see a huge problem there.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What this tells me about the inflation forecast is—you know, I’m a 2 percent kind of guy on PCE, and I’m still a 2 percent guy—that even though headline inflation is very elevated, we’re going to see over the forecast period that inflation will come back down to around the 2 percent level both on the headline and on the core.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, though my baseline on this is that inflation will return to a level that, by the way, I am comfortable with as an inflation objective, I do very much worry that inflation expectations could be more fragile in the current environment.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So it’s not that I think we have to do something now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we do have to be extremely vigilant to see whether inflation expectations are actually starting to move in an undesirable direction, and if so, we will have to take action.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The challenge may be that we have to take action when unemployment is still rising, but what is key is that we have to be aware of that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My modal forecast is that it isn’t going to happen, but I think we have to be ready to deal with it and deal with it quickly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As you know, I’m not a believer in gradualism in circumstances such as we are in currently, and I think this applies to dealing not only with financial disruptions but also currently with inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have to be willing to move very quickly in that context.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Let me turn to the issue of long-term projections.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You will not be very surprised to know that, in fact, I’m a supporter of this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This Committee has actually been well served.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Even though it is not my normal personality—as you know, I like to move fast on things—we have moved in an evolutionary process in terms of communications, and I think that has worked quite well for us.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is just an obvious next step.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Our communication strategy in terms of the long-run projections now has an important flaw in that we are not providing the information that we intended to provide, and it needs a fix.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We now realize that that’s the case.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s particularly relevant concerning information about potential output growth and the NAIRU.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do share the concerns that President Lacker mentioned on these, and I have talked about this in many speeches.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think this can be handled by speeches—in particular, by the Chairman emphasizing these issues going forward.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I don’t see it as a huge problem, but it is something that we have to deal with.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In any case, we need to clarify what our projections mean.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We’re not providing information that we should.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have to fix it, and there’s no reason not to.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think it’s a minor change.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do not think that there will be much reaction by the markets or in the political sphere on this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I agree completely with Governor Kohn that, relative to the other problems that we are dealing with, this is very small potatoes; but I think it is good to show that we’re still sticking to the basic things that we need to stick to and that, in this very complex environment, we can do the things that need to be done on communication strategy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That argues that we should be doing this and even doing it right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Regarding the issues that you raised about going more to the full Monty on this kind of stuff, I do agree with Vice Chairman Geithner that now is not the time to do that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I should mention that I will be giving a speech in which I will be advocating going to an explicit inflation objective, but that’s because I’m leaving the Board, and I have to say what I think.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But there’s an issue in terms of what this Committee should be doing, and I am sympathetic to Vice Chairman Geithner’s view that this is not what we should be doing for the Committee right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On the other hand, I’m a free individual now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In going back to be a civilian, I can say what I want.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In terms of my preferences, I really don’t feel strongly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There are a lot of issues here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When I first thought about it, I preferred an option like 3 because I didn’t want to give the impression that we’re great at forecasting five years out, and I think that’s really the strongest argument for it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I do understand how we articulate that is a little tricky, and I think that’s something that we have to think about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It might be clearer to do something along the lines that President Bullard discussed, as arguing it that way, but maybe we can do it in some other way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that’s exactly why the staff can have some extra work for themselves to think about the best way to describe this, but I think something along the lines of providing information that we actually are putting in our projections right now, where we have a little section that says, “What are your long-term assumptions?” and we put them down.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Somehow we need to convey that information to the public.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Then the question is, What’s the best way to do that?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You can have all the wonderful arguments that we have over the statement each period.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We’ll get something like that going, and I think we’ll figure it out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you, and thank you all.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, on the long-term projections, I think there’s consensus that we should just go ahead and have a trial run.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The staff should review the transcript and make gold out of straw there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should consult with the subcommittee, and we should think about maybe even a couple of alternatives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Maybe we could try a couple of alternative ways of doing it in October.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let’s go ahead and do something along those lines and keep thinking about how best to do it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me first, as I usually do, try to summarize the discussion around the table, and I’ll add some comments of my own.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Beginning with the summary, the incoming data were stronger than expected, notably for consumer spending but for some other components as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As a result, economic growth in the second quarter, though not robust, was likely positive, continuing the pattern of weak but positive growth since the fourth quarter of 2007.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, to the extent that strength in consumption was transitory or due primarily to fiscal stimulus, some of the growth in the second quarter may have been borrowed from the second half.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Participants generally saw growth continuing at a slow pace the rest of the year and improving in 2009.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was, however, some divergence of views, with some expecting a longer period of slow growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Recent numbers on retail sales suggest that the consumer is holding up better than expected.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumer finances may be better than feared, and the fiscal stimulus may already be having an effect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, as many have noted, there are substantial drags on consumption going forward, including falling wealth and income, credit constraints, and the recent rise in energy prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Sentiment has also fallen noticeably further.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Weaker consumption may, thus, restrain growth later this year, particularly after the effect of the stimulus wanes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Labor markets continue to soften but at a relatively moderate pace.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The peak in unemployment is projected to be between 5½ percent and 6 percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s what I generally heard around the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Prospects for housing continue weak, with falling prices, high inventories, and weak demand.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some saw a possible bottom forming but noted that the recovery of this sector is still some way off.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As has been the case for a while, businesses are quite cautious, noting economic uncertainties and surging input costs, with one or two mentions of tighter credit, although that was not a dominant theme today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Real exports continue to grow and are partially offsetting weaker domestic demand, especially in the case of manufacturing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial conditions have been mixed since the last meeting, although the improvements from March have largely been maintained and the risk of systemic crisis may have receded to some degree.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Funding markets are generally doing better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The concerns about credit losses have led the stock prices of banks, including regional banks and investment banks, to fall sharply.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Capital raising continues, though at less favorable terms and with perhaps declining availability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As the economy continues weak and housing contracts further, more credit losses for banks may well be in store, adding to financial market stress and reducing the availability of new credit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Progress in the financial markets is likely to be slow as the deleveraging process will take a while.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Stock prices in general are also lower.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial conditions in the housing market remain important downside risks to growth, with the spurt in oil prices adding to those risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Uncertainties about the growth prospects are great.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, tail risks may have moderated somewhat.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Readings on core inflation have remained relatively moderate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, the sharp rise in oil prices and some other commodity prices, in part reflecting flooding in the Midwest, is likely to lead to very high levels of headline inflation over the next few months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Gas and food prices have become perhaps the most important economic issue for consumers, and firms are feeling ever- increasing cost pressures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Moreover, inflation pressures are global.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are increasing reports of firms being able to pass through these costs, which could lead to an increase in core inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, slack may restrain core inflation increases.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Measures of longer-term inflation expectations have been up a bit on net since April, depending to some extent on the measure chosen.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nominal wage growth is still slowing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Participants debated how much comfort to take from slow wage growth, some arguing that, by the time wages reflected higher inflation expectations, it would be too late.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most saw inflation risks as now to the upside, with the primary concern being the possibility that inflation expectations could rise further as headline inflation rises and more costs are passed through.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s my very, very quick summary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If anyone has any comments, I’d be happy to hear them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let me just say a couple of words on my own views here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This may come as a surprise to some of you, but I am not a fine-tuner.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the objective of the Federal Reserve ought to be to avoid a very bad outcome, and so my concerns are primarily with tail risks on both sides of our mandate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the evidence of the last month or so provides a bit of reassurance, on both the real side and the financial side, that the tail risks on the growth side of the mandate have moderated somewhat.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That being said, I think they remain and are still significant.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, as I mentioned in the summary, I am at this point still suspicious of the strength that we saw in the second quarter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we look at the fundamentals for consumption—including wealth, income, employment, and energy prices—and look at the plunge in sentiment, which is at remarkably low levels, I think there’s a very good chance that consumers will weaken going forward and bring the rest of the economy along with them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, of course, housing remains extremely uncertain.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are at best some distance from stabilization in that market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Even when residential construction begins to stabilize, we’ll still see continuing declines in house prices, which will affect consumer spending and, importantly, will affect financial markets as well as the value of mortgages.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to financial markets, I agree certainly that the crisis atmosphere that we saw in March has receded markedly, but I do not yet rule out the possibility of a systemic event.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We saw in the intermeeting period that we have considerable concerns about Lehman Brothers, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We watched with some concern the consummation of the Bank of America–Countrywide merger.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We worried about a bank in the Midwest.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other regional banks are under various kinds of stress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re seeing problems with the financial guarantors, with the mortgage insurers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that those kinds of risk are still there, and we need to be very careful in observing them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Moreover, even if systemic risks have faded, we still have the eye-of-the-storm phenomenon—we may now be between the period of the write-downs of the subprime loans and the period in which the credit loss associated with the slowdown in the economy begins to hit in a big way and we see severe problems at banks, particularly contractions in credit extension.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I’m not yet persuaded that the tail risks are gone.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it would be very valuable to have some more data, some more observations, to see how the financial markets and the economy are proceeding.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I want to say that I do agree that the developments in financial markets and the surprisingly strong data in the second quarter should lead us to feel somewhat better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we should take a little credit for our various efforts to support both the financial system and the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, what about tail risks on the other side—on inflation?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The increase in oil prices that we’ve seen in the past six weeks is obviously very, very bad news.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the combination of the commodity price increases and what we’re going to see as very ugly headline inflation numbers is beginning to generate a tail risk on that side of the mandate as well, and I am becoming concerned about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Indeed, I think that it’s now appropriate that we begin, as some of us already have, to move rhetorically toward acknowledging that risk and agreeing that it may be at the point where it even exceeds the risk that we see on the growth side, although I think we’re very uncertain about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, the concern I have is the following, which is that there has been a lot of talk about policy action.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think that a 25 basis point or even a 50 basis point move, if it’s not viewed as being the start of a continued increase, is going to do very much on the inflation side, frankly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We had a good test of that over the intermeeting period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Partly because of our rhetoric and for other reasons, the dollar strengthened.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The two-year rate rose 50 or 60 basis points, and oil prices went up $25.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do not think that with a small change in our stance we can do anything about commodity prices, and frankly, it’s commodity prices that you’re hearing about from your Board members and from people you talk to.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s the real change in the relative price of those commodities that is painful and the real change in the terms of trade coming through the dollar which is painful, and I don’t think we can do very much about those in the short term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our objective, of course, as everyone has noted, is to prevent that from becoming a sustained and persistent source of inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the problem then is that a small amount of movement will not solve the problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A small to moderate movement, however, might create some serious financial strains given the fragility of the system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think what we need to do is to decide when we reach that tipping point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be a tipping point at which we’re sufficiently confident that the system is stabilizing and that we can begin to turn in a serious way to the inflation concern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A partial one step, unless it signals a longer-term tightening program, could give us the worst of both worlds.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will just have to make the judgment about when we have reached the point of having to switch from our previous approach of supporting the economy and financial system to an approach that is aimed more at containing inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s going to be a very difficult and delicate situation, but I want to express again my agreement with those of you who are worried about inflation and my belief that the time might be relatively soon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it’s going to be a very, very delicate decision and one that we have to make with great concern and consideration.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A little anticlimactically, I would like to say just a couple of words about the 1970s because they keep coming up and I do think that these comparisons are a bit misleading.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, in the current episode, commodity prices—particularly oil prices—are basically most or almost all the inflation that we’re seeing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was not the case in the ’70s.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, inflation rose considerably before the first oil price shock in 1973.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: PCE inflation was 5 percent in 1970, which prompted the wage– price controls, of course, which is an episode we’re all familiar with; and in 1972, before the oil shock, average hourly earnings were growing between 7 and 8 percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was already a serious inflation problem before the oil price shocks came.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Hence, credibility was already damaged at the time of the oil price shocks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is not the case here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, the movement in wages and core inflation following the oil price shocks in the 1970s was very striking.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: From the time of the oil price shock right before the second quarter of 1973 until the first quarter of 1975, total inflation rose a little over 5 percentage points, reflecting the quadrupling of oil prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: During the same period, core inflation rose more than 6 percentage points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In other words, core inflation responded almost one for one to total inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Moreover, average hourly earnings rose more than 2 percentage points, and productivity and cost compensation rose 3½ percentage points in that year and a half.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there was a very strong sensitivity of expectations and pass-through to these commodity price shocks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, we’ve been seeing oil price increases since 2003, and they have not yet shown anything like that effect on core inflation or on wages.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The final observation I’d make about the 1970s is that we shouldn’t forget that, even in that very bad situation with very poorly anchored inflation expectations, the slowing of the economy did do something to reduce inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, core inflation fell 3½ percentage points during 1975 following the 1973–75 recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So while we cannot do much about oil prices, I do think that there is some hope that weakness in the economy is going to provide some restraint on core inflation, which of course will generate a more stable total inflation rate if and when commodity prices stabilize.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I’ve been very all over the map here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I tried to organize my thoughts in the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My bottom line is that I think the tail risks on the growth and financial side have moderated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think, however, that they remain significant.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m also becoming concerned about the inflation side, and I think our rhetoric, our statement, and our body language at this point need to reflect that concern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to begin to prepare ourselves to respond through policy to the inflation risk; but we need to pick our moment, and we cannot be halfhearted.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When the time comes, we need to make that decision and move that way because a halfhearted approach is going to give us the worst of both worlds.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s going to give us financial stress without any benefits on inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we have a very difficult problem here, and we are going to have to work together cooperatively to achieve what we want to achieve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The last thing I’d like to say is on communications.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just talking about communications following this meeting, I’d like to advise everyone, including myself, to lean, not to lurch.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is, we are moving toward more concern about inflation, but we still have concerns about economic growth and financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should show that shift in emphasis as we talk to the public, but we should not give the impression that inflation is the entire story or that we have somehow decided that growth and financial problems are behind us, because they are not.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if we can convey that in a sufficiently subtle way, I think we will prepare the markets for the ultimate movements that we’re going to have to make.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I very much appreciate your insights and your attention today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have a dinner at 7:30, and for that reason I think we should probably bring this to a close.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll start tomorrow morning with Brian’s presentation of the policy options.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The statement is essentially the same as the Bluebook’s.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There won’t be any surprises there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we’ll begin with that first thing in the morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have two major items this morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll first complete the discussion of policy action and the statement; and in the second part of the meeting, we’ll discuss supervision of investment banks and some related policy issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Over lunch, if time permits, we’d like to hear Laricke Blanchard talk about congressional developments, and we’ll have a chance to ask questions there as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So without further ado, let me turn to Brian to introduce the policy discussion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 4 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will begin by referring to the draft announcement language in table 1, included in the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” As Chairman Bernanke noted yesterday, this version is only slightly revised from the version discussed in the Bluebook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Rather than keep you in suspense, I will note now that the revision is simply to strike the phrase “near-term” from alternative B, paragraph 4.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Turning first to alternative A, the Committee would ease policy 25 basis points at this meeting and would issue a statement similar to the one published after the April FOMC meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The second paragraph would indicate that economic activity has remained weak in recent months.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would recognize that consumer spending appears to have firmed but would go on to mention other aspects of economic performance that remain weak.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The paragraph on inflation would cite the recent further increase in energy prices but would also note the stability of core inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would again express the Committee’s expectation for inflation to moderate, partly reflecting a leveling-off of energy prices, but would acknowledge that uncertainty about the inflation outlook remains high.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As in April, the final paragraph would be silent on the balance of risks and on the likely path of policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For most of you, your baseline outlook would seem to provide little support for selection of alternative A at this meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As was noted yesterday, most of you conditioned your projections on a path for policy that begins to tilt up either immediately or sometime in the next few quarters.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With such a policy path, the central tendency of your projections points to a gradual pickup in economic growth and a fairly prompt drop in total inflation as energy and other commodity prices level out but only a gradual decline in core inflation, which reflects the moderate amount of economic slack that you foresee over the next few years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As was illustrated in one of 4 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 4).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: the optimal control simulations presented in the Bluebook, a case can be made for alternative A if you agree with the staff baseline outlook and favor aiming for 2 percent inflation over the longer term.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One of the estimated policy rules presented in the Bluebook also suggests modest further easing, but again that prescription relies on the staff’s forecast rather than on your generally stronger near-term outlook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But given the modal outlooks of most members of the Committee, any case for easing at this meeting would seem to be best motivated by persisting concern about the downside risks to growth that many of you again cited in your forecast submissions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The “recession” simulation in the Greenbook provided one plausible scenario for the realization of such risks and suggested that the funds rate might need to be lowered to 1½ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative B, the Committee would leave the stance of policy unchanged at this meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement would note that economic activity continues to expand and, as in alternative A, would mention the firming of consumer spending.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would cite the same factors that could restrain economic growth that were referenced in April and would add the rise in energy prices to the list.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The inflation paragraph would again convey the Committee’s anticipation that inflation will moderate but would elide the explanation for that expectation and would reference high uncertainty about inflation prospects.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The final paragraph would indicate that the downside risks to growth appear to have diminished somewhat and that the upside risks to inflation and inflation expectations have increased.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As I noted previously, we have suggested that the phrase “near-term” be struck as the Committee’s focus presumably is on longer-term inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The references to risks to both growth and inflation would be consistent with the concerns that you expressed in your forecast submissions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement proposed for alternative B seems generally in line with market expectations, and an announcement along these lines is unlikely to provoke much market reaction.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: By pointing to reduced risks to growth and increased risks to inflation while not explicitly stating that the inflation risks predominate, the Committee would likely be seen as suggesting that its next policy move could be toward firming but also that such a move probably was not imminent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A policy approach along the lines of alternative B seems generally consistent with the projections that many of you provided for this round.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although most participants conditioned their projections on a steeper policy path than the one in the Greenbook, many also appeared to assume that the firming process would not commence until later this year or in 2009.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A decision to stand pat at this meeting might be motivated importantly by your sense that the risks in both directions around your baseline projections are substantial.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: While staying your hand today might risk a further upcreep in inflation expectations, you might also be concerned that a policy firming now, given that financial markets are still fragile, would risk having outsized market effects with adverse implications for an economy that remains weak.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As a result, you may see benefits to allowing more time for financial markets to recuperate and more time for information on the outlook to accumulate before taking policy action.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Holding the funds rate at 2 percent at this meeting would be consistent with the Committee’s past behavior as captured by the estimated outcome-based rule presented in the Bluebook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative C, the final column, the Committee would firm policy 25 basis points at this meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the statement, the paragraph on real activity would be identical to that for alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, the third paragraph would provide the motivation for the action by emphasizing that overall inflation has been elevated, that energy prices have risen further, and that inflation expectations have risen further.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: No assessment of the balance of risks would be provided in the final paragraph, thus avoiding a suggestion that the firming signaled a sequence of further rate increases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Nonetheless, with market participants currently seeing only a small chance of a rate increase at this meeting, an announcement along the lines of alternative C would likely prompt a considerable jump in short- and intermediate-term market interest rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although most of your forecasts appeared to assume that policy firming would begin later this year or early next year, some of you explicitly assumed an earlier start to policy tightening.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Members might believe that firming at this meeting is warranted partly by evidence of some reduction in downside risks to growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Recent spending data suggest that economic activity has a bit more forward momentum than previously perceived, reducing the odds on recession; the modest improvement in financial market conditions points to some reduction in downside risks; and the Federal Reserve’s special liquidity facilities appear to have been successful in reducing the odds of negative tail events and severe adverse feedback loops.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus members might see it as appropriate now to begin to reverse some of the Committee’s past policy actions to the extent that those actions were seen as motivated by downside risks that have now diminished.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, near-term firming might be motivated by the further increases in inflation pressures and risks resulting from the continued upward march of energy and some other commodity prices.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, with inflation expectations continuing to show some signs of moving up, a firming of policy at this time might be viewed as a timely shot across the bow that could be helpful in restraining such expectations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I thought that it might be helpful to conclude by reviewing two exhibits from the medium-term strategies section of the Bluebook, starting with the optimal policy simulations that are reproduced in exhibit 2.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The simulations underlying these exhibits are based on the FRB/US model after adjusting it to line up with the Greenbook forecast and extension.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As usual, these simulations assume that you aim to minimize the sum of squared deviations of inflation from target, squared deviations of the unemployment rate from the NAIRU, and squared changes in the nominal funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Two key points can be drawn from these simulations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: First, whether policy firming should begin sooner or later may depend partly on your longer-run inflation objective.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown by the black line in the top right-hand panel, if your objective for the longer run is to get back to a 2 percent inflation rate, these simulations suggest that you can hold the funds rate steady or even ease slightly further before beginning to firm in 2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This policy path produces a somewhat faster decline in the output gap and thus somewhat slower disinflation than in the Greenbook and extension.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In contrast, the simulations shown in the left-hand column suggest that pursuit of a 1½ percent inflation objective would involve policy firming beginning quite soon.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In general, the policy paths described by many of you in your forecast submissions seem to fall between these two scenarios, apparently reflecting your sense that aggregate demand growth could be a bit stronger and inflation pressures a bit more intense than projected by the staff as well as your dissatisfaction with a path for inflation that is as shallow as that for the scenario with a 2 percent inflation objective.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The second point underscored by these simulations is that, even though the near- term path for the unemployment rate is a bit lower than in April, reflecting the recent indications of somewhat greater strength in aggregate demand, the medium-term outlook involves larger and more persistent slack than foreseen in April under either inflation goal.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Despite that greater slack, as shown in the bottom two panels, core inflation under both inflation objectives runs 0.1 to 0.3 percentage point higher over the next four years than in the April simulations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That, of course, is the fundamental nature of a negative supply shock: Policymakers are forced to accept some combination of greater economic slack and higher inflation during a period of transition to a lower output path and, presumably, to an unchanged long-run inflation rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That same point was made in a Bluebook box and in a staff paper on this subject.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Turning to your final exhibit, I would like to note that, in response to the comments of some members at recent FOMC meetings, the r* exhibit in the Bluebook has been augmented to include two additional measures of the real federal funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Line 11 in the table at the bottom shows a measure of the real federal funds rate that uses lagged headline inflation as a proxy for expected inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: By contrast, our standard measure, shown on line 10, employs lagged core inflation as the proxy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Line 12 shows a measure based on the staff’s projection of headline inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Both of these new measures, at minus 1.3 percent, are considerably lower than the current value of the standard measure, minus 0.2 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I want to emphasize, first, that these additional measures should not be compared directly with the r* measures shown in lines 1 through 9 of the table because the values of those measures are in part a function of the proxy used for expected inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, the r* value that would be consistent with the Greenbook projection and the actual real funds rate based on the lagged four-quarter average of headline inflation is minus 0.7 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, even if we redefined the Greenbook-consistent measure of r* to use lagged headline inflation, the implied 0.6 percentage point gap between the actual and the estimated equilibrium real rates would not necessarily imply that you should quickly raise the nominal funds rate by more than ½ percentage point.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If, like the staff, you think it likely that headline inflation will moderate substantially later this year, then it follows that a gradual firming of policy in nominal terms would be consistent with a substantial rise in the real funds rate on this measure over time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, in the staff’s view, the average value of the real federal funds rate over the next few years on any measure is a bit above the corresponding value of r*, and consequently the trajectory of the real funds rate on any measure would be consistent with protracted slack and declining inflation over the next several years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, you may not agree with the staff about underlying trends for prices and real activity and, hence, about the value of r*.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even if you do agree, you may be dissatisfied with the projected trajectories for key variables such as output, employment, and inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Such considerations illustrate why no estimate of r* can be a complete guide to policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That completes my prepared remarks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Brian?

speaker: LACKER
text: Thanks, Brian, for including these two new lines of the real federal funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I remarked yesterday, one use of the figures is to look back and judge the degree of accommodation relative to other historical episodes.

speaker: LACKER
text: My understanding is that the Greenbook forecast of headline inflation four quarters ahead is higher now than it was in 2004, when the black line in your exhibit 3 last hit its lowest point.

speaker: LACKER
text: My understanding is that, if you drew that black line using the equivalent of line 12, the Greenbook’s forecast for overall inflation, the trough in 2004 would lie around zero, and we would now be at minus 1.3.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Unfortunately, President Lacker, I haven’t made that computation, so I can’t confirm that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Just a quick question: When you do this based on the Greenbook projection for headline inflation, how far forward are you going with headline inflation?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, in any given quarter, it’s four quarters ahead.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Brian, it might be helpful if you would circulate your remarks about the new exhibit 3 and its implications after the meeting.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I just want to clarify one thing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Could you just repeat what you said—looking forward under any of these basic measures, where do you expect the real fed funds rate to be in relation to r*?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The actual real federal funds rate is above r* under any measures—so in other words, our outlook is the same.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: These are just different yardsticks for assessing our basic view of the stance of policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no further questions, why don’t we begin our go- round?

speaker: EVANS
text: I’d like to start by saying that I agree with your comments yesterday about how we should proceed with the Committee approach and think very collaboratively about the policies and delicate strategies that we’re facing.

speaker: EVANS
text: Although we disagree on a number of the elements of the outlook, I think that bringing everything together is a very important part of this.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have fully endorsed funds rate cuts that we have taken so far in large part as insurance against tail risks to growth.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that policy last summer was much too restrictive given what we were facing and that, along the way, a lot of these cuts have been motivated by tail risks to growth.

speaker: EVANS
text: The funds rate at 2 percent is pretty ample insurance to my mind—more so given the improvement in the outlook for growth that we’ve seen as second-quarter growth has been marked up so much and even more so given the inflation risks that we’re facing, the risks to inflation expectations, and the potentially very low real interest rates that we might be looking at, depending on the measure.

speaker: EVANS
