text: If we had the opportunity to recalibrate things a bit, I probably would prefer something more like a 2½ percent fed funds rate to be positioned against the different risks that we’re facing, but I understand that we’re at 2 percent, and no change seems like the right move for today.

speaker: EVANS
text: I do have a few concerns about the way we’re thinking about this, more in the line of risks.

speaker: EVANS
text: One is that, as we take insurance against tail risk, we’re positioning the funds rate against an event that we think is not the most likely and is negative compared with where we are.

speaker: EVANS
text: Unless and until that event happens, policy is somewhat accommodative because it hasn’t happened, and we’re thinking that it is closer to where it ought to be if that should happen.

speaker: EVANS
text: Unless you think that we haven’t taken out insurance, then I think that we have more accommodation than we might like.

speaker: EVANS
text: The second concern is whether it is possible to be more precise about what we mean by this tail risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: I mean, it’s really a catch-all.

speaker: EVANS
text: Nobody is very comfortable with all of this.

speaker: EVANS
text: What are the markers that we could look at for improvement if we could quantify this somehow?

speaker: EVANS
text: Is it that financial markets should be functioning better?

speaker: EVANS
text: I think surely that is the case.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is there a way that we could describe that?

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m sure we’ll disagree on many elements of this.

speaker: EVANS
text: Labor market improvement—we should expect that, if the labor market does better than we were thinking, then that would tend to bolster consumption spending a bit better in the face of all the shocks that we’re looking at.

speaker: EVANS
text: So the extent to which the labor market doesn’t continue to deteriorate, at least in line with some of the recession scenarios and the tail risk scenarios that we were thinking about, is a potential marker.

speaker: EVANS
text: As we keep pushing out our expectation that the economy is going to weaken—and we’ve done this a number of times—and if we’re looking at the third quarter being revised up—and I agree that we’re facing a lot of risks there—but if we start marking that one up, I think that’s a marker that we have to be concerned about.

speaker: EVANS
text: Obviously, if oil prices and commodity prices were to decline and free up purchasing power for consumers, that would help out, too.

speaker: EVANS
text: So these are just some of the things that come to mind.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is there a way to think about the details a little better, with a bit less of a SWAG?

speaker: EVANS
text: Another risk relates to financial markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: Here I’m thinking about the really influential work of yours, in 1983, on nonmonetary influences on the Great Depression.

speaker: EVANS
text: A lot of the actions that we have taken are defenses against those types of issues, right?

speaker: EVANS
text: In the 1930s, when the economy was doing very badly and banks were failing—I’m telling this to you, and you’ve described it to everyone—then the knock-on effect was that the banks weren’t there anymore and important resources for evaluating credit were lost, and so it was more expensive and very difficult to do.

speaker: EVANS
text: We have some of that going on now, right?

speaker: EVANS
text: We’ve moved from the banks making mortgages and holding them to the “originate to distribute” model.

speaker: EVANS
text: Those resources have been dispersed, and now that securitization market is closed.

speaker: EVANS
text: I heard that very clearly yesterday.

speaker: EVANS
text: Those important resources aren’t there to originate mortgages, so if we get to the point that buyers are willing to purchase these houses, that could be a concern.

speaker: EVANS
text: What happens if there’s a true impairment to the financial capital stock, and real resources aren’t there anymore to help out with this?

speaker: EVANS
text: We’re probably looking at a reallocation of resources from that sector of the financial market either back to banks or to somewhere else.

speaker: EVANS
text: But as we see those resources reallocated and as we think about unemployment being higher, we can talk ourselves into thinking that a lot of slack is in the economy when, in fact, there may not be so much slack.

speaker: EVANS
text: At some point it may be slack, and at other times it won’t be, until those resources are reallocated most efficiently.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think this could reduce potential growth rates and have structural elements to it, not just cyclical elements.

speaker: EVANS
text: So there’s not a slam-dunk for this.

speaker: EVANS
text: There is just a risk that an element of that is playing out throughout this, and other factors are superimposed on that.

speaker: EVANS
text: But it’s something that I worry about.

speaker: EVANS
text: In a robust type of policy development, I think we should be considering things like that.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s just the case that, in the current situation that we’re looking at, there might be a limited role for monetary policy to repair real capital stocks.

speaker: EVANS
text: Another concern is that anytime we’ve engaged in substantial risk-management policies, there has always been difficulty in taking them back.

speaker: EVANS
text: That’s part of the delicate strategy that you are referring to, I think.

speaker: EVANS
text: That’s how I heard it.

speaker: EVANS
text: So we have to be very careful.

speaker: EVANS
text: There’s a lot of art to this clearly, but it would be good if we could offer a few more bright lines about how we’ll approach that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think we need to seek consensus.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s our role to raise these issues and then come to the best judgment.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I’m quite comfortable with no change today.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m quite comfortable with the language in alternative B, although in the third paragraph we say, “However, in light of the continued increases in the prices of energy,” and I think it would be better if we didn’t say “continued.” I think it’s enough to say “the increases.” In part, I don’t know if this is a marker that, if prices level out, we’d still be comfortable with the inflation risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that there will be a lagged effect of all the very large increases that we’ve seen for oil as they work their way through.

speaker: EVANS
text: If prices just level out, we still have risks to inflation expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I prefer taking that out.

speaker: KOHN
text: President Evans, so you are arguing that the re-intermediation process is going to raise the NAIRU.

speaker: KOHN
text: I thought that the NAIRU depended on the structure of the labor markets, job matching, and stuff like that, so I didn’t quite understand the connection.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m alluding, without understanding or working out, to a sectoral-shifts model of unemployment and how that search process could be more difficult.

speaker: EVANS
text: You’re just taking resources that over some period took a while to allocate to the financial sector and now they have to be reallocated somewhere else.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Recognizing, as I do, where we’re coming from and its dangers, I think more-recent data suggest that the downside risks to growth have diminished, and in my judgment the current stance of policy is much more accommodative than necessary to address these risks.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I continue to believe that the two most recent policy actions of this Committee were more than sufficient, and we really need to think about reversing them sooner rather than later.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Inflation risks have risen, and we have seen erosion in longer-term inflation expectations.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As I noted in my previous remarks on the outlook, if we do not begin to remove policy accommodation soon, I think we risk having to tighten policy more aggressively in the future to reestablish our credibility.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It struck me in looking at some of the major economies besides the United States—the European Union, Japan, and China—if you look at the real interest rates, they’re low.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I mean, they are 1 percent or less or negative.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So this is a lot of stimulus coming into the world economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: And to make my point again, I don’t think you can have a sustained recovery with a sustained inflationary environment, which we’re in danger of encountering if we continue on this path.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Over the past several weeks, markets have significantly altered their expected funds rate path to remove policy accommodation, and therefore, I don’t know that doing something today would be that big a surprise.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The current funds rate path built into the market rates is closer to what I believe is desirable to maintain price stability over the long run, but I would prefer moving somewhat faster—3 percent by the end of this year and perhaps 4¼ percent by the end of ’09.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Thus, in my view, we should begin the process of removing monetary policy accommodation by increasing the fed funds rate target by 25 basis points at this meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think this action would perhaps be somewhat unexpected, and I recognize that there is some risk that markets would react by moving the funds rate path up more dramatically than some might desire.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, taking this action would move us beyond merely talking about inflationary risk and would help us contain inflation expectations by reaffirming our commitment to maintaining price stability.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think it would quickly have a positive effect on the economy as these expectations begin to shift.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Now, assuming that’s not the majority view today, I would then encourage us to set the stage in our language for stronger actions coming in the future.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is an important issue especially, as you mentioned yesterday, in terms of remarks that we might make following this meeting, in speeches and so forth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Finally, let me just say that I think policy is currently accommodative, perhaps very accommodative.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The insurance policy taken out earlier this year to guard against the tail risk of spillovers of the financial distress to activity is less necessary, perhaps far less necessary, and it is potentially even harmful to the efforts of maintaining price stability.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Therefore, I encourage action sooner rather than later.

speaker: LACKER
text: The growth outlook has improved over the last two months, but the inflation picture has not.

speaker: LACKER
text: If anything, it has deteriorated.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it’s clear, as President Hoenig argued, that we should be tightening policy soon.

speaker: LACKER
text: The extent to which we brought the funds rate down was predicated on downside risks and the notion that we could reverse course rapidly.

speaker: LACKER
text: As downside risks now look much less likely, I just don’t see how an argument that 2 percent was the appropriate funds rate in April does not also imply that a higher funds rate would be appropriate now.

speaker: LACKER
text: Taking back some of that stimulus at this meeting, however, is probably inconsistent with the commitment implied by the Committee’s traditional interest rate smoothing behavior.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’m willing to stand pat today with the funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: The timing of such moves is going to present us with some trouble going forward, though.

speaker: LACKER
text: Even if we avoid outright recession, as now seems probable, the unemployment rate is likely to keep rising for a time.

speaker: LACKER
text: But waiting isn’t going to make it easier for us, in any event, because there’s a likelihood of the fourth quarter’s showing a slowdown when the stimulus wears off.

speaker: LACKER
text: But inflation is going to increase in the near term as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: At least that seems likely, and holding rates down while that happens and while inflation expectations are already fairly elevated seems awfully risky to me.

speaker: LACKER
text: I can understand the need for some conviction when we raise rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: When we began cutting rates aggressively in January, there were some significant uncertainties in the inflation outlook, though.

speaker: LACKER
text: I hope we don’t set any higher a threshold of conviction for rate increases than we set for rate cuts.

speaker: LACKER
text: Looking back at 2003-04, and this is strictly in hindsight, one can argue that we erred by waiting too long to reverse course, and I’ve heard you yourself make that argument, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the logic of risk management works in both directions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we need to keep that in mind.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I favor alternative B with the proposed wording.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the forecast and the risks around it, our next move on the funds rate is likely to be up, and the question is when.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Assuming that the data on growth and inflation come in roughly as I and the Greenbook expect, I would envision beginning to remove policy accommodation toward the end of this year, similar to the assumption in the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I mentioned, I’m not very confident that the outlook for growth and employment has improved as much as the Greenbook assumes.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’m concerned that households and firms are in a python squeeze of an intensifying credit crunch and a continuing decline in housing wealth as well as pressures from surging food and energy prices.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the economy has shown resilience so far, and that’s reassuring, but I don’t think it’s assured for the future.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The aggressive policy actions that we have put in place since January are actually working to cushion the blow, and that’s part of the reason that we haven’t seen a greater unraveling so far.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I mentioned yesterday that, with respect to inflation, the behavior of both core inflation and wages thus far makes me optimistic that headline inflation will come down if commodity prices finally level off.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I think there’s no doubt that the risks with respect to inflation are not symmetrical at this point, and they have definitely increased.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I still see inflation expectations as reasonably well anchored, but there’s no doubt that a wage–price spiral could develop, and dealing with it would be a very difficult and very painful problem for the Committee.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So while I feel that we are essentially credible now, I wouldn’t want to take absolutely for granted that this is something that we can count on going forward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: At this point, the federal funds rate remains well below the recommendations of most versions of the Taylor rule.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have viewed this as appropriate, not largely as insurance against downside risk but simply in refection of the unusually severe pressures from collapsing wealth and tight credit and financial constraints.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But it does seem to me to be appropriate going forward to at least take out some insurance against the development of a wage–price spiral mentality, and that could take the form of gradually removing that discrepancy from what, for example, a Taylor rule recommends.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But before we begin to do that, it does seem to me that we should wait to get a somewhat clearer picture of where the real side is going.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my view the economy is evolving in a way that suggests that we need to take back sooner rather than later some of the insurance we put in place against downside tail risk.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I base this view on several points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, economic activity remains weak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The data since our last meeting have been better than expected.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Greenbook forecasts as well as most private-sector forecasts have been revised up.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So although downside risks remain, the tail risk of a significant recession-like outcome for the economy, though it has not vanished, has certainly diminished.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Second, financial market indicators suggest that market functioning, though not back to normal, has certainly improved somewhat in recent months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Demand for Fed liquidity from the primary dealers has fallen.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Primary credit borrowing generally is down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, although we may wish to keep our liquidity facilities for now as a backstop, the extra accommodation that we have built into monetary policy may no longer be needed or even appropriate at this point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The real economy and financial functioning have improved since our last meeting, but the inflation outlook has worsened, as we have been hearing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Expectations of various kinds are elevated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Upside risk to core inflation has increased, as the Greenbook has said.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I said yesterday, these upside risks stem not only from the potential pass- through of energy prices but also, in my view, from the fact that we’re running a very accommodative policy despite rising inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, I believe that policy has actually become more accommodative since the meeting at the end of April.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, the nominal funds rate has been at a constant level, but expectations of inflation have risen.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So, in fact, the real funds rate has actually declined since our last meeting as inflation has risen.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Second, real rates of interest more broadly have been gradually drifting up since late March or early April.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The TIPS rates, the real interest rates, have been drifting up by, depending on which term you look at, anywhere from 25 basis points to 35 basis points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So as the real rates on risk-free securities have risen, which may be appropriate given the fact that prospects for the real economy have improved modestly, the real funds rate has been declining.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As a consequence, whatever you think about the level of the fed funds rate, we have become more accommodative since the last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I’ve argued before in this Committee, optimal monetary policy in a broad class of models suggests that you get Taylor-rule-like rules but that the funds rate follows the real interest rate as it moves around.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Optimal policy calls for following the real rates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I argued that was the case and appropriate as real rates fell in the context of a weakening economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It was important that policy match those declines in the real rates, which I think it did.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s a coherent policy, but it also means that as real rates begin to rise, as we have been seeing, policy needs to adjust to those real rates rising.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, of course, a lot of judgment is required in this type of policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Real rates could be quite volatile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There’s debate about which real rate you want to be looking at.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I don’t think there’s any question that the objective should be to match those movements in the real rates, and we should be thinking about it in those terms.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Long-term inflation expectations have been volatile but have moved within a reasonably defined range over the last period, and I’m comforted somewhat by that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But as I have said, I believe that inflation expectations are fragile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the very least, the anchor is dragging, and if we continue to maintain a real funds rate well below zero with rising inflation well above our goal, I do not think we can continue to assume and trust that expectations will remain well anchored.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We’ve done a good job with our words so far, but with the shift from downside risk to growth to upside risk to inflation, we need to take action to ensure that price stability remains a credible objective of this Committee.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If the economy and financial markets continue to evolve as they have over the last couple of months, that time may be soon.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We must take back some of the insurance we put on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Not doing so soon risks having to respond more aggressively later on, which I believe will be much more difficult for the Committee to do.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, smaller moves sooner will help with our credibility in the marketplace and will help anchor those expectations as we wait for more data and for the economy to strengthen.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In this regard, I think we are fortunate that market participants reacted to the incoming data by appreciably tightening their policy expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, a move to raise rates is unlikely to catch them off guard.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, I don’t think that we should disabuse them of such policy expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some might argue that an increase in policy expectations is a negative development.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that it reflects rising expectations of a somewhat stronger economy and concerns about inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As the Chairman said, we should resist any erosion, any rise in longer-term inflation expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, as I said, the timing of such a move is a judgment call, and I expect that my views will differ from those of some of my colleagues, particularly since I had my fed funds rate path rising to 2¾ percent by the end of ’08.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So let me turn to language.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the rationale in paragraph 2, I have only one suggestion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that we should acknowledge that the functioning of financial markets, while not back to normal, has improved.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So instead of saying “financial markets remain under considerable stress,” which we have said for some time, perhaps it might be easy to say just that the financial markets remain under stress, leaving out “considerable.” That acknowledges the fact that there’s some improvement but that stress is still there.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Finally, in paragraph 4, I am pleased that the revisions make more explicit that the upside risks to inflation and inflation expectations have increased and that the downside risks to growth remain but are diminished.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was going to suggest that we strike “near-term,” but Brian beat me to the punch there.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I approve of that change.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that’s very good.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In alternative B, I would prefer that we add some of the language from the Chairman’s recent speech to paragraph 4.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it would be a stronger message that the Committee will take actions to ensure that inflation expectations do not become unhinged, and it would also convey that both parts of our dual mandate, price stability and economic growth, are at risk should inflation expectations become unhinged.

speaker: KOHN
text: I support the action and language of alternative B; Brian’s striking of “near-term” is fine with me.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is a tough situation, as we all remarked yesterday.

speaker: KOHN
text: Commodity prices are at the center of the problem that we find ourselves in.

speaker: KOHN
text: In my view, we didn’t cause the rise in commodity prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: We may have contributed a little around the edges, but whatever we contributed was a necessary byproduct of what we needed to do to cope with what was happening to the U.S. economy, and we can’t reverse the rise in relative prices without tremendous cost to the U.S. economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: Or even the rise in headline inflation, we couldn’t undo that without putting a huge amount of slack in the economy to force down wages, sticky prices, et cetera, and that would not be appropriate.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the classic response that we’ve all been talking about is to take a temporary increase in inflation and in unemployment that facilitates the relative price changes that need to happen, concentrate on second-round effects, and make sure those increases are temporary.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that’s inadvertently what we’ve fallen into here.

speaker: KOHN
text: Given the housing and financial shocks, the 2 percent fed funds rate of alternative B is consistent for now with continuing along the path of the temporary increases in inflation and unemployment.

speaker: KOHN
text: Unlike many of you, I don’t see the current rate as extraordinarily accommodative, given what else has happened in financial markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: There is no insurance in the staff forecast, right?

speaker: KOHN
text: The Greenbook forecast has zero insurance in it.

speaker: KOHN
text: My own forecast was a little stronger than the Greenbook’s.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think all of ours were a little stronger than the Greenbook’s, but even if I marked up r* by ½ point or 1 point, that’s not a huge amount of insurance in the circumstances that we’re facing.

speaker: KOHN
text: I note that no one sitting around this table predicted a decline in the unemployment rate over the balance of the year; so everybody has 5½ percent or higher unemployment rates predicted by the end of the year.

speaker: KOHN
text: The staff thinks that the current 5½ percent is a little too high.

speaker: KOHN
text: So they are expecting the unemployment rate to come down in the next month or two.

speaker: KOHN
text: Given this, we’re all expecting the unemployment rate to rise over the balance of the year.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would think, given the lags in policy, that if you thought policy was hugely accommodative, you’d see some decline in the unemployment rate over the next six, seven, or eight months.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think our own forecasts suggest that some insurance might be here, but not the amount that I’m hearing some of you talk about.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t see the consistency there.

speaker: KOHN
text: My own view is that there’s probably a little insurance in it, and it’s appropriate for now.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that the next move in interest rates is more likely to be up than down.

speaker: KOHN
text: I assumed, like President Yellen, that it would be at the end of this year or at the beginning of next year.

speaker: KOHN
text: The rising unemployment that we all expect should help damp inflation and inflation expectations and make it very hard to pass through all these cost increases that we’re hearing from businesses that they want to pass through and certainly make it hard for wages and cost pressures to rise.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I agree with everyone else that the weight in the two tails has shifted.

speaker: KOHN
text: There’s less weight in the downside risk tail for output and more weight in the upside risk tail for inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: The statement does a very nice job of saying that explicitly, and I think that we just need to await incoming data and information about inflation expectations, costs, and whatnot to see when the appropriate time to move will be.

speaker: KOHN
text: Because I don’t think there’s a tremendous amount of insurance in there, I think we can afford to be a little patient and data dependent here.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Governor Kohn, a question, or a comment, about interest rates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A lot of our discussion has been centered on how accommodative we think policy is and how we interpret it in the current environment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If I want to quantify the magnitude a bit, at least the way I think about it, even if I believe that the economy is weak enough so that the appropriate equilibrium real rate of interest is zero, we have inflation running somewhere north of 3 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That would suggest a nominal funds rate of about 3 percent as opposed to 2 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So roughly speaking, I would interpret that to say that we have roughly 100 basis points of extra accommodation built into our fed funds rate relative to what—and that’s assuming an equilibrium real rate of zero, which might even be low.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So if I’m thinking about it that way, could you clarify how we should quantify it in some way?

speaker: KOHN
text: We don’t know what inflation expectations are.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’re all using proxies, as came forth very strongly at the Cape Cod conference where we both were, President Plosser.

speaker: KOHN
text: We don’t even understand very well how expectations are formed, and I think what we’re looking for is how people perceive the cost of capital to finance purchases.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we’re wondering whether this low interest rate is causing them to bring purchases forward from the future to the present to induce them to buy things, capital goods, right?

speaker: KOHN
text: That’s the interest rate we’re really looking at—the perceived cost of credit to folks—and I’m not sure that subtracting any rate of inflation is the way to get that.

speaker: KOHN
text: Obviously, the cost of credit for housing is perceived as hugely high right now.

speaker: KOHN
text: The cost of credit for automobiles is perceived as hugely high for reasons that perhaps aren’t related to monetary policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think we see a surge in purchases of capital equipment that would suggest that businesses perceive the cost of credit to be very negative.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think, because we don’t understand inflation expectations and can’t measure them, you have to look for a lot of different things around the edges to confirm what people perceive the real rate to be.

speaker: KOHN
text: I just don’t see a lot of information that suggests that people perceive the real rate to be very negative and that it is influencing how they manage their purchases of goods and services over time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess just to say it more simply, all the rates that have determined behavior—for example, mortgage rates, auto rates, or corporate bond rates—are higher than a year ago.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, unless there has been a major change in long-term inflation expectations, which the TIPS data don’t suggest, there don’t seem to be indications, as far as interest rates that are relevant to people’s spending decisions, that there has been a significant reduction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Someone else had a comment.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s directly on this point.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It seems that in the situation we’re in, with very elevated spreads in LIBOR, there are almost no contracts in the real markets that are related directly to fed funds.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s usually through three-month LIBOR, and we know that the spread is now roughly 70 or 75 basis points higher than it used to be.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It used to be about 10 basis points, and now it’s around 80.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: For me that’s one rough proxy in how I think about this—that the way in which our actions are being translated into market prices is somewhat different from the way it was when the spreads were lower.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker will back President Plosser up though.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is like pro wrestling.

speaker: LACKER
text: Spreads always rise in recessions.

speaker: LACKER
text: We always lower real rates in recessions.

speaker: LACKER
text: So to say that the fact that spreads have risen by itself doesn’t make this an exceptional circumstance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The magnitude is somewhat greater, though.

speaker: LACKER
text: For some; not for others.

speaker: LACKER
text: Corporate bond spreads aren’t as high.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I support keeping the fed funds rate target at its current level and the language in alternative B. I see some hopeful signs that stress in financial markets has diminished as has the threat of a sharp recession.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Despite these recent signs, I expect that the growth momentum in the economy will build only slowly.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Moreover, I continue to worry that the residential real estate market could deteriorate even more than I had put in my baseline projection.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Nevertheless, I am somewhat more comfortable with the prospects for economic activity than I was in April.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At the same time, I can’t easily dismiss the recent behavior of energy and some other commodity prices.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I found the Bluebook’s supplemental analysis on oil prices, inflation expectations, and monetary policy to be very useful in thinking about the dilemma that we face.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The fact that oil prices have risen so sharply and have been so persistent highlights the risks surrounding the downward projection that I have for core inflation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Without some evidence of less inflationary pressure I don’t believe that the fed funds rate can be kept at its current level for very long.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But while I do believe that the next policy action will be a rate hike, the potential for the recovery to sputter makes me cautious about embarking on an upward trajectory for the fed funds rate just yet.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I believe that the language in alternative B conveys the right sense of direction for the fed funds rate path, with the right amount of caution.

speaker: BULLARD
text: U.S. economic data have been stronger than expected during the intermeeting period.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The earlier, very aggressive moves in January and March taken by the FOMC were viewed in part as insurance against the possibility of a very serious downturn brought on by financial market turmoil.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That very serious downturn has not materialized.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Tail risk has diminished significantly.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This means that this Committee has put too much economic stimulus on the table and must think about ways to remove it going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Failure to do so will create a significant inflation problem on top of problems in housing and financial markets.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Slack might be helpful, as mentioned by Governor Kohn, but those effects are small compared with expectations effects.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it is too early to tighten at this meeting.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Therefore, I am supporting alternative B with the language proposed by President Plosser.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But the Committee has to think carefully about how and when to embark on a path for interest rates that will set us up to achieve price stability in a reasonable time frame.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My sense is that this will require more-aggressive tightening of policy than currently envisioned in staff simulations.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Financial market problems have been described here as a slow burn, and I think that may well be an apt description.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Many firms in this sector took on too much risk and, in retrospect, had poor business models.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I expect that this will take a long time to unwind.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Despite this, the systemic risk component of the situation has diminished considerably.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Systemic risk is in part a function of the degree of surprise in the failure of a financial institution that was perceived to be in good health.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Surely by now few market participants would be surprised to encounter the failure of certain institutions.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Failures, should they occur, can be handled in an orderly way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Certain investors would lose out in such an event, to be sure, but my sense is that the panic element that would be associated with systemic risk would not be present.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I believe that we should start to downweight systemic risk concerns substantially going forward because it is no longer credible to say that market participants are surprised to learn of problems at certain financial institutions.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, first of all, I believe that policy is well positioned for now from a couple of perspectives.

speaker: STERN
text: For the next quarter or two, I think there is still some potential for significant disappointment in terms of economic growth—but only for a quarter or two.

speaker: STERN
text: Beyond that, a pickup in real activity appears pretty likely.

speaker: STERN
text: That is, based on what I know now, further reductions in the federal funds rate shouldn’t be required for the economy to improve next year and beyond, and we do have the liquidity facilities available should strains in financial markets threaten to intensify.

speaker: STERN
text: Policy is also well positioned for now from a second perspective—namely, that the fed funds futures curves have priced in an increase in the funds rate beginning in the late summer or the fall.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that this is appropriate because I think we are going to find that we will want to and have to start moving to contain inflation expectations.

speaker: STERN
text: Precisely when to move may turn out to be a difficult call, but I would like to see futures priced to anticipate such action on our part—as indeed they are at the moment.

speaker: STERN
text: That brings me to the recommendation and the language.

speaker: STERN
text: I think the strategy expressed in the Bluebook associated with alternative B is fine for now, and so I favor alternative B.

speaker: STERN
text: The language in alternative B is okay as well, although I would endorse President Plosser’s recommendation to drop “considerable” from the description of financial strains.

speaker: STERN
text: The other thing I would point out is that the Bluebook says that, at least in the staff’s judgment, the language associated with B might push back expectations for the onset of policy tightening.

speaker: STERN
text: I am reading from page 33.

speaker: STERN
text: It is not that I am anxious to tighten necessarily as early as possible, but I would rather not push those expectations back at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: So if that assessment is correct, it might be advisable to find a way to address that issue.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t feel all that strongly about it, but I think we could, if we wanted, take the sentence in paragraph 4 that’s in red, drop three words—the first word “although,” a word at the end of the phrase “remain,” and then “they.” So you would just say, “Downside risks to growth appear to have diminished somewhat,” which I think is true.

speaker: STERN
text: It doesn’t suggest that we are sanguine about growth, although I suppose it could be read that way.

speaker: STERN
text: But I am a little concerned about the way we might change expectations based on the Bluebook commentary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You have your Strunk and White style manual with you, I can see.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: At this time, there are significant downside risks to the economy and financial markets, as the collateral damage from the housing problems works through the economy and financial institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: At the same time, continued increases in oil and food prices raise the risk that some part of these supply shocks will be incorporated into inflation expectations.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In the absence of more-compelling evidence about which of these two risks will dominate, I would favor remaining on hold at this meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I hope that the economy picks up in the second half of this year and that the financial markets stabilize so policy can become less accommodative, but it is not clear that this will be the outcome.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While the inflation outlook has been affected by continued energy shocks, the future path of oil prices remains uncertain, and recent history has many instances in which oil shocks are short-lived and have little effect on longer-run inflation expectations.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Until we have more clarity on the path of the economy and inflation, policy should remain on hold, and our language should be consistent with that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I also prefer the fed funds rate recommendation and language of alternative B.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It captures the delicacy—I think that word was used yesterday—of the current tradeoffs and leans fairly heavily rhetorically against inflation and inflation expectations.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I note that inflation and inflation expectations are mentioned in both paragraphs 3 and 4 using the language, “Uncertainty .

speaker: LOCKHART
text: remains high” and “risks .

speaker: LOCKHART
text: have increased.” I think this constitutes considerable stress on the seriousness of our commitment to address inflation and expectations, and it is a complete statement and will serve to condition the market.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As Brian said, it suggests that firming later in the year could occur, and I believe that is appropriate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I would like to give the medicine that we have applied to resolve the situation and the financial markets a little more time to work.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am in accord with Governor Kohn’s thinking of stimulus or accommodation in terms of the cost of borrowing to real borrowers—individuals and businesses—and, therefore, we really have not seen a proportionate improvement in the cost of capital, notwithstanding such a strong reduction in the fed funds rate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So as of now, I would expect to support a reversal a little later in the year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I also think there is enough ambiguity currently that giving the situation a little more time to clarify would be helpful.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Core inflation has not risen dramatically, whereas headline has, and it is headline that the public is reacting to.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Measures of expectations, such as they are, seem to suggest that short- term expectations have risen more than long-term, so there really hasn’t been a clear breakout of long term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It may be true that it would be too late if we saw that breakout, but I think we can afford to wait for a greater preponderance of evidence to accumulate over the next few weeks before considering a reversal.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I support, as I said, alternative B and the language of alternative B.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I listened very carefully to what was said around the table yesterday, and I especially listened very carefully to you.

speaker: FISHER
text: You made a very good and interesting point about the differences from the 1970s.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would add that there are significant differences from the 1970s.

speaker: FISHER
text: We didn’t have the Internet in the 1970s.

speaker: FISHER
text: We were not globalized in the 1970s.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you were selling oil into the market, you sold to three buyers—the ten countries known as Western Europe, the United States, and Japan—whereas now you have several billion people more to sell to.

speaker: FISHER
text: Another difference is that the transmission mechanisms were not as fluid, which gets me to a question, really, with which I am wrestling constantly.

speaker: FISHER
text: Before, a cyclical slowdown would lead to a lessening in price pressures.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am not so sure that’s correct if we are talking about a cyclical slowdown in the United States.

speaker: FISHER
text: We already have wages going up significantly in the largest factory in the world, which is China, where we source a great deal.

speaker: FISHER
text: So there is wage–price inflation, but there are enormous demand-pull forces that are quite different from what we had before.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am a little concerned—and I say this with not only respect but humility at having less training—Governor Kohn, when you say that we might tolerate a “temporary increase in inflation.” If you opened the New York Times this morning, you would have seen that Dow Chemical raised prices 25 percent after just raising them 20 percent—in one month.

speaker: FISHER
text: By the way, I notice that these little bottles of water have gotten smaller—this will be a Visine bottle at the next meeting.

speaker: FISHER
text: What goes into this—the plastic?

speaker: FISHER
text: Many micros make a macro.

speaker: FISHER
text: Micro business operators are not going to tolerate temporary increases in inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are going to act on them.

speaker: FISHER
text: I worry about that enormously, particularly given the fact that they are globalized and they sell to a globalized market.

speaker: FISHER
text: We can be victimized by that.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, I may have over-analogized yesterday.

speaker: FISHER
text: You teased me after the meeting.

speaker: FISHER
text: Although I like Janet’s analogy of the python—one of my tutors at St. John’s had a python named Julius Squeezer, by the way.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just to kill that reference, I feel a bit squeezed here at the table.

speaker: FISHER
text: You mentioned yesterday, Mr. Chairman, three things that caught my ear.

speaker: FISHER
text: Obviously, we need to strive to avoid bad outcomes.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, we need to decide when we’re at the tipping point.

speaker: FISHER
text: We need to pick our moment, as you said.

speaker: FISHER
text: Third, you also said that we need to lean and not lurch.

speaker: FISHER
text: I listened very carefully just now to President Evans, who was most eloquent in his presentation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I happen to agree with him in terms of where I think we should be.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yesterday I said I thought there were three ways to deal with our current predicament now that the tail risks have shifted.

speaker: FISHER
text: One is to hope it will cure itself.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t believe that is going to happen because of the way micro operators operate.

speaker: FISHER
text: The second is to treat it rhetorically, and I think that the language in alternative B is quite good, if that is the way you wish to go.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I don’t think it is going to get any easier, as was mentioned earlier at this table.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am not sure that things will get easier by August.

speaker: FISHER
text: We then get into an election season, which I think still conditions somewhat our thinking.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it is important to take a shot across the bow.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we have to put some substance behind our words.

speaker: FISHER
text: As I said before, and I know you know, I like to be liked.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t like to be alone.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I am going to vote for alternative C. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me say just a few things.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, to state the obvious—there are risks on all sides of these decisions.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, I will try to wade into the debate briefly on this accommodation point.

speaker: WARSH
text: My own view is that policy is accommodative—the degree of that is why we are having this debate.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think about our degree of accommodation as a function both of our target fed funds rate and what the financial markets do with it, by which I don’t mean just what the expected fed funds targets are out in the future but the transmission mechanism.

speaker: WARSH
text: The degree of accommodation, as we think about our decision now and in the next several months, will depend more on financial market developments than, frankly, the decisions that we end up making on the target; and it is very hard for us to judge the direction of these markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: As much as we have talked about tail risks on the financial market side and the real economy side being diminished, I think all of us would say that there is a real chance that this will be a long, hot summer.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is hard to know what the credit channels are going to do with our target federal funds rate.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is not obvious to me that we should try to perfectly offset the changes in financial market developments by contemplating changes in the federal funds rate now.

speaker: WARSH
text: What I think most likely is that we won’t be as certain as we would like to be regarding growth risks and we won’t be as certain as we would like to be regarding financial market developments before we have to begin a posture of removing policy accommodation.

speaker: WARSH
text: So with all those caveats and a view that policy remains more accommodative than we can allow it to be for too long, I will support alternative B and think that we have to remain very open-minded, very nimble, in our task of removing policy accommodation.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of President Plosser’s suggestion on “considerable,” I think the reason for the debate over using that word is in my own view that these markets are still under considerable stress, but the trend from the last statement to this statement is that they are under less considerable stress.

speaker: WARSH
text: Therein lies the difficulty in wording this in the statement.

speaker: WARSH
text: If we do remove “considerable,” it wouldn’t surprise me that when we next meet we will say, “Boy, it seems as though stress is up.

speaker: WARSH
text: Wonder if we should put it back in?” I don’t feel strongly, other than I don’t like the idea of removing it now if we think that there’s a chance that the trends, which are very tenuous, turn around.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think I would favor the language that you have written.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, as we have all discussed, we are facing enormous challenges from the continuing strength in prices and price changes in energy and raw materials.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now, some of those are relative price changes that we don’t have the tools to address directly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Recently, we have seen wheat come down as Australia has been able to replant, and it seems that things are going to come back.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Corn has gone up, as we heard from a number of people around the table, because of the challenges there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We don’t have the tools to address that directly, but obviously, when so many of these commodity prices and energy prices are going up, that leads to concerns about where both headline inflation and core inflation are going.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So we definitely do have to be very mindful of that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think the type of approach that we are taking in alternative B is a reasonable one.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Given the challenges that we are facing right now with the fragility in the financial markets—the continuing smoldering of those embers, with still chances that they could reignite and cause us a great deal of difficulty—it seems sensible to me to be roughly where we are now in terms of policy but to be signaling that we understand that challenges are coming from various sources that could lead to inflation pressures and that we need to be ready to offset those.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In terms of how accommodative monetary policy is, I think actually it would be worthwhile—and maybe at the end of this I might pose a question to Brian—to look at LIBOR– OIS spreads and how much they typically go up during recessionary periods.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I know that other risk spreads typically go up, but my understanding is that those typically don’t go up as much.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Since so many contracts are based off the one-month and three-month LIBOR, that 75 basis points suggests that at least now we might want to take that into account in thinking about where monetary policy stands relative to other times when we would have had a funds rate at roughly this level.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In terms of the language, I share Governor Warsh’s view on the use or lack of use of the word “considerable.” I think President Stern’s suggestion—this is always a very dangerous and difficult game—would actually push the markets further than they are because I agree that broadly the path that they are seeing in the future is a reasonable one for them to see.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This language would roughly keep it there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Taking out the acknowledgement of downside risks to growth remaining would make me concerned because (1) I certainly see those as still being there and (2) I think that would push the markets further to think that this is a signal that next time we are going to do it, and I don’t think we are quite there yet.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do support alternative B and the current language in the statement.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have no problem with that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think it conveys what we need to convey.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Although I think that the next move is very likely to be up and it maybe should be done quite soon, I would argue that we still need to have a lot of flexibility and to think in terms of having a lot of flexibility in where we may have to head in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I want to argue along those lines and outline why I think that is the case.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The first issue is something that the Chairman mentioned yesterday, about which I felt very strongly—in fact, I meant to say it, but as always the Chairman says things better than I could in this context—that there really is still a very serious possibility that the shoe could drop in the financial markets.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The Chairman mentioned a set of institutions that we have to be concerned about, and although there has been some improvement in terms of the stress that the financial markets are under, I don’t think we are out of the woods yet.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We are likely to be, but we have to be ready to recognize that things could go south.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second issue is that the recent positive data we have seen are, again, very tenuous to me.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m hoping that they indicate that things are going in the right direction.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But a bunch of things make me very nervous, which I mentioned yesterday—how consumers react in housing crises, consumer sentiment, and the big problem that is going to occur when people have to face very high prices of food and energy, which hit their pocketbook very directly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So, again, that could be quite contractionary.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The good news that we have seen recently might reverse very quickly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The third issue is that I think the headwinds could be very substantial in the future, that this cleanup will take a long time, and in that case we could have very slow and subpar growth that could widen output gaps more than the Greenbook and most participants here are expecting.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I do not consider the current stance of monetary policy to be overly stimulative.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: For me it is just about right and very much along the lines of what I think would be optimal policy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Of course, my view relates not only to the real economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I also think that inflation expectations, as far as I can tell so far, are reasonably well contained.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There is very little movement in the measures of inflation expectations that I pay most attention to.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That argues that our stance is about right.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I would also very strongly argue that I do not think that we have taken out a lot of insurance.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have argued that before.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have moved less gradually, which I think is very beneficial, and I would commend the Committee in that regard.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But we moved in line with what the forecasts have been telling us optimal policy would be, and I think that is quite important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, here is why I think we need to have flexibility in the other direction.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If you think about a risk-management approach, it should not be focused just on tail risk to economic growth, which has been our most major concern because of the financial disruption.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It equally implies that, symmetrically, we should be just as worried about tail risk to inflation, particularly to long-run inflation expectations, which I think are the key driver of underlying inflation, which is what monetary policy can particularly deal with.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Here we have a situation in which we have hit the perfect storm of shocks because of the huge supply shock and there are much more serious upside risks and tail risks in terms of long-run inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I really do worry that with long-run inflation expectations and, therefore, underlying inflation we are in a more fragile situation and that we have to be very cognizant of that in terms of what we do in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The bottom line is that we may have to move very quickly to raise rates if any of several things happens.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is that headwinds are not as serious as I think they are likely to be.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There is certainly a very serious possibility that things could be better than I expect.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I would not be unhappy, so I would not get depressed, about that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Really more depressing would be if inflation expectations started to look as though they were getting more unanchored.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Particularly, I would worry much more about what happens in terms of inflation compensation and the Survey of Professional Forecasters, paying some attention to consumer surveys but putting a lot less weight on them.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If the canary starts to look as though it is keeling over, we have to move very quickly, and so I am going to watch that canary very, very carefully.

speaker: FISHER
text: Before the python gets it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Before the python gets it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think another consideration is very important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have to commend you on the Bluebook this time—it just had some great boxes.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It would be nicer if they had a little color to them.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As a textbook author, I think they could have been a little ritzier and have had a little color, but they were great boxes.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, a very important box was the one on the optimal reaction to oil price shocks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One thing that comes out very strongly from that box is that if your credibility is weak on commitment to price stability and containing inflation expectations, you would have to tighten more to restore that credibility and get to a policy that would produce better outcomes.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So here is an issue that, with these supply shocks potentially causing a problem for long-run inflation expectations, we actually may have to react more quickly and more aggressively than we otherwise would.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is an issue that I have been concerned about in terms of communication strategy—about how we better anchor long-run inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So my bottom line is that I support alternative B. I would like to keep the language the way it is currently, which I think works quite well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I do think that, going forward, we should not lock ourselves into what our policy is going to be, in either direction.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We need to preserve flexibility because we could be very surprised, although I think that the signal we have made that we are more concerned about inflation risks is absolutely appropriate.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have to make clear that we will do whatever it takes, including raising interest rates when unemployment is rising, if we feel that long-run inflation expectations and inflation are not remaining under control.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just want to say at the beginning that I think the way you framed your remarks yesterday had perfect pitch and balance, and it is really important that we not get ahead of ourselves in taking too much comfort from the fact that the first half was not as bad as we thought and think that the risks on the growth front are definitively behind us.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The improvement in financial markets that many of you spoke of is not as significant as we think or hope; we have had a lot of false dawns over this period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: A lot of what you see as improvement is the simple result of the existence of our facilities in the implied sense that people infer from our actions that we are going to protect people from a level of distress that we probably have no desire, will, or ability to actually do.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is sort of like waking up in the hospital and having them say, “You are not dead yet, but we are not sure you’re going to live.” It is not as good an improvement, and there has been a material erosion over the past four weeks.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very unlikely that you will have a substantial improvement in overall confidence in markets, a durable improvement in market functioning, and a substantial reduction in those spreads until there is more clarity about the likely path of the economy going forward, house prices in particular, and therefore the cash flows associated with the huge amount of credit that was extended over the past five years.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, it is going to be very hard for us to have a better feel for the balance of risks on growth front and the financial sector until we think we see signs ahead of some significant deceleration in the rate of decline of housing prices, if not some actual bottom.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the basis of everything we know, that is still several quarters ahead.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Maybe it is going to surprise us on the upside and maybe we are going to see a big improvement in housing demand, but I think that the sense of a bottom looks to be several quarters ahead of us still.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would say that the risks are still acute.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Sure, the markets are a little more confident that we are going to successfully avoid a systemic financial crisis, but I wouldn’t take too much comfort from that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it is also plausible that oil will be at $150 or $200 over the next six months or so.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is some material probability that the set of challenges on that front is going to get worse.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So all that is just in favor of a fair amount of care and caution now, given the scale of the uncertainty out there and how fat the tail risks are on both sides of our mandate going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I like, and fully support, the language in alternative B. I would not—as you might sense from my comments—take out the word “considerable” from the characterization of stress.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I am pretty comfortable with the framework laid out here, and, more important, Mr. Chairman, with the broad balance and strategy that you outlined yesterday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In April, we signaled that, following our aggressive rate actions and our other efforts to support financial markets, it was going to be a time to pause and to assess the effects of our actions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was not that long ago, and I think it is appropriate to continue our watchful waiting for just a bit longer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I talked yesterday about the balance of tail risks as opposed to the balance of risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that, although the tail risks on the growth and financial side have moderated somewhat, they are still quite substantial.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with the Vice Chairman on that point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They arise from two separate but related sources.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first is that, notwithstanding the stronger-than-expected performance in the second quarter, I think there is an excellent chance that we will still see a recessionary dynamic with the associated strong movements in employment and production.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second—again as the Vice Chairman mentioned—I do not agree that systemic risk has gone away.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it is in abeyance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is perhaps, if anything, excessive confidence in the ability of the Fed to prevent a crisis situation from metastasizing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Even if we don’t have a failure of a major firm, we still have the possibility of a significant adverse feedback loop as credit conditions worsen and banks come under additional pressure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if I could try to think about this—I don’t want to say “mathematically”—a lot of our discussion has implicitly suggested that there has been a linear model, which is that we are just trying to balance on the scales this risk against that risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, if you are worried about preventing bad outcomes, you have to worry more about nonlinear or discontinuous changes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that, at this point, we still have significant risk of a nonlinear, discontinuous change in the financial markets or in the real economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Tail risks have risen for inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is no question about it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I take what has been said around the table extremely seriously, and I am quite anxious about it, I have to concede.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If I were making a comparison of tail risks to tail risks, I still think that the inflation tail risks have not yet reached the level of the concerns I have about the financial crisis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, some important indicators—such as wages, inflation expectations, and core inflation—have not yet signaled a major shift.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That being said, I do think we need to acknowledge the relative change in those risks, and we need to begin to prepare the market for the normalization that is going to have to come.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Both President Fisher and President Stern talked about the rhetorical aspects of our policy and the effects on policy expectations, and I think we are all in agreement that words mean nothing unless they are eventually backed up by actions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, actions may be better if they are preceded by words, if you will.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We do need to begin to prepare the markets and to communicate clearly so that people will know what’s coming and that the system will be better able to deal with that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If I thought for sure that we were going to begin renormalizing very soon, I would propose doing it today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I think enough uncertainty and enough risks are on both sides that there is some benefit from waiting just a bit longer to see, first, how the financial markets evolve and, second, whether we continue this stronger-than-expected growth pattern or whether we begin to see a more recessionary-type of pattern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, between now and the next meeting, we have two employment reports, a lot of other relevant information, and a lot of insight from the financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At the same time, on the inflation side, we will see how commodity prices evolve, whether we have any kind of relief from what we saw in the last intermeeting period, how the dollar behaves, and how inflation expectations behave.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All those things will give us a better sense of where we are and how we should proceed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think we should try to be nimble.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should try to respond to the information as it comes in.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should be focused particularly on tail risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we should begin to move, or should maintain, market expectations toward tightening.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Fisher, I think I have to note for the record that I don’t think we should let political considerations affect our decisions in any way, and I am not concerned about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we are all prepared to do what is necessary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know what we are going to do in the next meeting or the meeting after that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But my expectation now is that, as others have mentioned, we will begin normalizing interest rates relatively soon, and we should, if possible, begin to prepare the markets for that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For today, as I have indicated, I recommend no change in the federal funds rate target and alternative B for the statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think alternative B captures the facts pretty well on the whole.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I won’t go into it, but I think the inflation paragraph is a little more hawkish.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It drops the discussion of a leveling-out of commodity prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It doesn’t refer to core inflation, which we have taken before as sort of a reassuring element.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m disappointed that President Fisher is going to vote against his own language in alternative B, paragraph 4, which we have adopted and which I think is a very good expression of the risks.

speaker: FISHER
text: I appreciate the adoption of the language.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it is much better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think President Stern’s suggestion is interesting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am a little worried that it might go just a bit too far in suggesting that we have discounted the downside risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am struggling with the “considerable” in alternative B, paragraph 2.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have sort of heard two for and two against.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know if others have a view.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is a bit risky to change, given how quickly things can move.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But if others would like to express a view, I think yet a third thing that we could do would be to say, “Financial markets, though somewhat improved recently, remain under considerable stress.” That might be a way to address it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Does anyone have any thoughts on that word?

speaker: LACKER
text: I thought Vice Chairman Geithner’s characterization of markets was pretty good, but it is compatible with your suggestion.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we look back and try to recalibrate at each meeting whether things are getting better or things are getting worse, we would regret each zig and each zag.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I would just say that we have a suite of facilities in place.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: They are in place today.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: They are exceptionally significant in terms of a change in policy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: They are there because we think they are playing an important role in helping facilitate the necessary process of repairing markets et cetera.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we were going to take them back tomorrow or dial them back substantially, then I would be willing to rationalize and explain that part of the judgment is that we think things are improving materially.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just feel as though the risk is too high.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the Vice Chairman raises an interaction that I hadn’t thought of, which is that our facilities are existing under the premise of unusual and exigent circumstances, and we don’t really want to undercut that.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would support what Vice Chairman Geithner mentioned because I think we may be faced with a situation of having to raise rates even though there is considerable risk in the financial market.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I think showing sensitivity to that is very, very important.

speaker: FISHER
text: On a second point, Mr. Chairman, I do appreciate the change in the language.

speaker: FISHER
text: I also suggested some changes to alternative C, but I won’t go into them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given that I suggested removing the word “considerable,” my purpose there was merely to indicate, as many people around the table have said, that things are somewhat better.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t think that we should suggest that problems are solved, because things are still under stress.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I agree with Vice Chairman Geithner in that regard.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am willing to withdraw that suggestion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t feel that strongly about it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I thought it would have been useful to convey a direction that we saw.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I don’t disagree with Vice Chairman Geithner’s suggestion that these things can reverse themselves and maybe a little more stability might save us some zigging and zagging down the road.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I withdraw that suggestion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I can live with the language as it is, if that simplifies things.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: And it will come out in the minutes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Of course, all of these subtleties will.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to propose no change in alternative B as given in exhibit 1.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, could you please take the roll?

speaker: DANKER
text: This vote applies to the directive as well as the language of the statement in alternative B of exhibit 1.

speaker: DANKER
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: DANKER
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with maintaining the federal funds rate at an average of around 2 percent.” Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes President Fisher No Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes Governor Mishkin Yes President Pianalto Yes President Plosser Yes President Stern Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a fifteen-minute coffee break, and we will come back and discuss investment banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we commence, then.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is a joint FOMC and Board meeting, and so I need a motion to close the Board meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our topic for this morning is investment banks, their supervision, and related policy issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me turn it over to Art Angulo of the New York Fed, who will introduce the topic.

speaker: ANGULO
text: 5 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We’re now in the handout.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Why don’t we start on page 2, and I’ll give you an overview of where we are headed this morning, at least from my section.

speaker: ANGULO
text: First I’ll talk a bit about the objectives and the approach of our monitoring program.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Then I’ll talk about how we’re focusing primarily, but not exclusively, on four investment banks and where our focus is there.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I’ll say a few words about the extent of usage of our section 13 facilities.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Again, the PDCF is primarily our focus, but for the sake of completeness, I’ll also discuss and provide some highlights on TSLF usage by the primary dealers.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Then I’ll close by just highlighting near-term issues that we’re addressing or dealing with.

speaker: ANGULO
text: 5 The materials used by Messrs. Angulo, Alvarez, and Parkinson are appended to this transcript (appendix 5).

speaker: ANGULO
text: On page 3, in terms of the objectives of our monitoring program, we’re very cognizant that our efforts are tied closely to our section 13(3) authority in the establishment of the Primary Dealer Credit Facility.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Our effort does not stem from our general supervisory examination authority.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We’re very clear on that.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We have two key objectives.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The first is the ability to exercise informed judgment about the capital and liquidity positions of the primary dealers that have access to the PDCF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Second and just as important, we’re aiming to, in shorthand, mitigate the moral hazard that accompanies the creation of the PDCF in particular.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So we will make sure that the PDCF does not undermine the incentives for the primary dealers and the firms that own them to manage capital and liquidity more conservatively.

speaker: ANGULO
text: On page 4, in terms of our approach, our focus is on the firms that own primary dealers that are not affiliated with financial holding companies.

speaker: ANGULO
text: That’s primarily, but not exclusively, the four largest investment banks.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I’ll touch at the end of my presentation on several other primary dealers with which we’ve had interactions of late.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Our effort does include an on-site presence, but that is limited to examiners at each of the four largest investment banks.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We also have a small off-site staff, which includes staff members from our Research Group, our Markets Group, our Legal Group, and Bank Supervision.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We are in direct contact with the management of these firms.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We are obtaining information directly from the firms as well as from the SEC, and of course, we are communicating and coordinating closely with the SEC.

speaker: ANGULO
text: It’s important to point out, however, that we’re not engaged in traditional bank supervision.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Our scope is fairly narrow.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We’re not conducting examinations, and we’re not providing or issuing examination reports back to the firms.

speaker: ANGULO
