text: Therefore, we are making assessments, I would say, without the normal range or normal complement of supervisory protections that we’re accustomed to.

speaker: ANGULO
text: To be frank, that carries with it some risk and some vulnerability for us.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I’ll touch on that at the end of my presentation as well.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Our current focus is limited or narrowly focused on capital, as well as liquidity, which I’ll get into in a moment.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So let’s turn to page 5.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Page 5 gives us a view of the leverage of the four investment banks.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I should note that it may be a bit confusing at first glance.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Leverage is typically expressed as a multiple.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We’ve converted that into ratios because bank supervisors tend to look at ratios.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So bear that in mind.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Investment bank leverage does tend to be cyclical.

speaker: ANGULO
text: This graph picks up really the latter half of the last cycle, so I can orally give you some perspective.

speaker: ANGULO
text: If this graph had moved back to the left, in approximately 1999 to 2001 you would have seen the investment banks deleveraging in response to the Russian default and the LTCM crisis in the third quarter of 1998.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So we would see leverage coming down between then and 2001.

speaker: ANGULO
text: In 2001-02, leverage was essentially flat, and then this graph picks up the increasing leverage from 2004 to the end of 2007.

speaker: ANGULO
text: As you can see, 2007 marked the cyclical low point in the ratio, or high point in leverage as a multiple.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Since then, the firms have been deleveraging.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Right now they are clustering around 4 percent, with the trajectory, I hope, still up, and we may have something to say about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Art, could you define “leverage” in this picture.

speaker: ANGULO
text: This is gross leverage, so it is just equity—in this case, a ratio of equity over total assets—a very blunt measure.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Page 6 gives us a more current view.

speaker: ANGULO
text: In the left-hand panel is the tier 1 capital ratio for the four largest securities firms.

speaker: ANGULO
text: As I think you know, the SEC has made a decision to use and hold investment banks to a Basel II ratio that’s consistent with how the bank supervisors apply it.

speaker: ANGULO
text: To date, the firms have not disclosed those ratios.

speaker: ANGULO
text: That begins this quarter, the second quarter.

speaker: ANGULO
text: For Goldman, Lehman, and Morgan Stanley, that quarter ended May 31, 2008, so we show the estimated ratios there.

speaker: ANGULO
text: These were not in their earnings releases, although they were picked up by some of the analysts in their conference calls—so these numbers are seeping out there.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Merrill reports on a bank cycle, June 30, so they have not yet released their tier 1 capital ratio.

speaker: ANGULO
text: A couple of takeaways from the left side of this page: First, the quarter has not ended, but Merrill was obviously low compared with its peers.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They do have the benefit of seeing and being aware of where their peers have come out, so we shall see if Merrill takes some action in the near term to bolster capital.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The second point is that the investment bank ratios look fairly high compared with where the commercial bank tier 1 capital ratio would be.

speaker: ANGULO
text: There are a couple of reasons for that.

speaker: ANGULO
text: First, the assets of the investment banks are concentrated in the trading book, so there are two issues there.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Those assets tend to have a lower credit charge.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The other issue, which we have to do more work on, is that we need to understand better the modeling methodologies and the model approvals that the SEC has given these firms to compute tier 1 capital.

speaker: ANGULO
text: That could be a significant factor as well.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So at first blush they look very healthy, very high; but I think it will take more analysis to get beneath those.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The right-hand side of page 6 gives another way of looking at capital—what we call an “FRBNY-adjusted leverage ratio.” What we’re trying to do here is to have another way of putting investment banks and commercial banks on a somewhat similar footing.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So in terms of the numerator, we use tangible equity for two reasons.

speaker: ANGULO
text: First, it’s a higher form of equity capital, perhaps the highest form.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Second and just as important, it avoids current differences between how investment banks and commercial banks calculate tier 1 capital.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Right now there’s a grandfathering period in which the securities firms are allowed to carry a higher portion of subordinated debt in tier 1 capital.

speaker: ANGULO
text: It does not apply to bank holding companies.

speaker: ANGULO
text: This puts them on more of an equivalent basis in terms of the numerator.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The deal is the same with the denominator.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Again, we’re trying to make allowances for the differences in business models.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So here we subtract from the denominator secured financing assets.

speaker: ANGULO
text: These are reverse repos and securities borrowings.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Of course, these are collateralized by cash and thus are relatively low-risk assets.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So by making those two adjustments, we have a somewhat comparable view.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The takeaway here is that they don’t look too far apart—they are not dissimilar—at least at this point in the cycle.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Why don’t we move now to page 7, to liquidity?

speaker: ANGULO
text: I have a picture of liquidity, but not a full picture.

speaker: ANGULO
text: This shows the trend in parent company liquidity pools.

speaker: ANGULO
text: This is unencumbered cash or high-quality securities at the parent company of the four investment banks.

speaker: ANGULO
text: As you can see, the trend has been increasing since the middle of March.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The general trend has been to increase.

speaker: ANGULO
text: This, of course, tells us only half the story because one wants to know what that pool is held against.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So, let’s turn to page 8, and I can talk a bit about how we’re trying to look at and assess this.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We’ve been engaged with the SEC and have entered into an approach in trying to assess liquidity at the four investment banks.

speaker: ANGULO
text: When we first started this endeavor back in late March, the first thing we did was to go back to the firms and to say, “Show us what would happen to liquidity if you experienced a Bear Stearns, full-run kind of scenario?

speaker: ANGULO
text: For that exercise we want to know what assets you have eligible for the PDCF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We want to know how bad and how dark it would get.” That exercise was pretty demanding.

speaker: ANGULO
text: No one would have passed the test.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We looked at that and asked whether a full run on the institution was an appropriate way to look at it or an appropriate standard to hold them to.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So we came up with another scenario that we put back to the firms.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We basically said, “Listen, we want you to do a stress analysis for us.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Look at something that’s pretty severe but short of a full Bear Stearns scenario.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Look out over thirty days.

speaker: ANGULO
text: By the way, you have no access to the PDCF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Let’s see how that looks.” We’re in the process of doing that right now.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The table on the left gives you an idea of some of the things that we’re looking at and how we’ve asked the firms to provide the information to us.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Basically there are several buckets: (1) their unsecured and secured funding; (2) what comes on the balance sheet under stress, either general market stress or firm-specific stress; and (3) the impact from operating cash flows toward the bottom.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Those are the combination of liquidity claims that they would face under stress.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The last piece is the additional funding from affiliated or unaffiliated bank lines along with, obviously, the liquidity pool, which we have separately.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Basically, we’re engaged in an exercise in which we compare and converge assumptions.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We’ve had multiple discussions with each of the four firms, trying to understand where their assumption differed and trying to converge those.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We then constructed, or are in the process of constructing, a cash flow analysis.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Again, we are relating their cash needs under stress, given these assumptions, to their available liquidity pool plus the unaffiliated or affiliated bank lines that can be drawn.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The drivers here, obviously, are going to be the mix and term of secured funding, which is going to be a big driver in terms of the liquidity needs, as well as some of the operating cash flow assumptions that firms make in looking at a stress scenario.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We are fairly close to pulling together information with which we can construct an analysis, go back to the firms, share with them our assessments of where they are, and give them a chance to explain to us how we were spot on or where we may have missed certain things.

speaker: ANGULO
text: But those conversations will happen in the near future.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So that’s basically what we’re doing in terms of liquidity.

speaker: ANGULO
text: It has been an interesting exercise.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I think that there is no simple way to look at liquidity but that this is the best way to do so.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Let’s turn to page 9.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I have just a few words about the use of both the PDCF and the TSLF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I have graphs later on the TSLF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: A graph of the PDCF usage would be kind of boring.

speaker: ANGULO
text: It would show Bear Stearns as far and away the dominant borrower.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Actually I think Bill Dudley conveyed to you yesterday that Monday was their last night of borrowing under the PDCF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So Bear Stearns is now out.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Until very recently there were three others that I’ll call chronic users of the PDCF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I’ll say a few words about that.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They started borrowing in late March, initially $600 million to $700 million.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They stabilized in mid-April at about $500 million.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We saw that borrowing coming in every night.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Members of the team here spent one afternoon at Cantor at the end of April.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We asked them for some information in advance.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We spent a good chunk of time with them.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We came away not being comfortable with the number or the size of their borrowings in relation to the firm’s capital.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We then consulted with our colleagues in both the Legal and Markets Groups.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We asked Cantor to submit a plan to wean itself from the PDCF and to submit that to us in writing.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We then followed up with a friendly letter from Mr. Dudley and Mr. Baxter asking for a little more information and a little more specificity.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They started to bring that down in accordance with the schedule they gave to us.

speaker: ANGULO
text: In fact, they ended up winding down to zero in their borrowing last week, ahead of schedule, and they obtained third-party financing.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So that was the Cantor story.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Countrywide was a somewhat similar situation.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They had been borrowing from day 1 of the PDCF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Initially they would ask us for $1 billion.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They had borrowed and stabilized at about $900 million.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Our Markets Group initiated a conversation with Countrywide Securities at the end of May.

speaker: ANGULO
text: In short, we were uncomfortable with, in essence, providing bridge financing to the close of the acquisition by Bank of America.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We felt some vulnerability there.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So our initial salvo or proposal back to Countrywide Securities was that they needed to wind down the use of section 13(3) facilities by the end of June—both the PDCF and the TSLF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They came back to us and in essence said, “Well, couldn’t you just let us go into July a bit because our merger is supposed to be approved today actually by the Bank of America board?

speaker: ANGULO
text: Our legal Day 1, our closing is July 1.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We can transfer positions July 2.

speaker: ANGULO
text: What’s a couple of days among friends?” We had a little negotiation back and forth.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We reached, I think, an agreement that was amenable to all.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They agreed to wind down their use of the TSLF—no new borrowings.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They could swing some of that into the PDCF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We would allow them to go until the closing, July 2, when they could transfer those positions.

speaker: ANGULO
text: In return we got a little extra margin.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So, in effect, those borrowings were being collateralized at a margin of roughly 7 percent.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We got an additional 13 percent, bringing us to 20 percent, which will bring us through until July 2.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So I think all sides are reasonably comfortable there, and with friendly persuasion, Dudley and Baxter sealed the deal there.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Let me say a few words about Barclays Capital.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We handled this a bit more informally.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They started using the PDCF more in late March, at around $5 billion.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They got to a peak of about $7 billion.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Both Bank Supervision and Markets had conversations with Barclays, asking them to tell us a little more about why they were using this.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They had a consistent story.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They would tell us that it was economically advantageous for them to use that.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They thought it was good.

speaker: ANGULO
text: In one conversation with our colleagues in the Markets Group, one of the traders conveyed that Barclays thought they needed to support the TSLF in much the same way that they supported open market operations.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Our colleagues in Markets very quickly disabused them of that notion.

speaker: ANGULO
text: After a couple of conversations, they got the message.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They eventually ceased borrowing from the PDCF around the beginning of June.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So as of now, the only outstanding we have is with Countrywide Securities, and that should come to a close next week, knock on wood.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Again just for the sake of completeness, on page 10 I’ll talk about the TSLF usage.

speaker: ANGULO
text: First, schedule 1, which is OMO-eligible collateral—as you can see among the primary dealers, Merrill has had the highest amount outstanding.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Merrill is, I guess, the tan line.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The biggest users have been the commercial banks—Deutsche Bank is up top, a pretty consistent user.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Then Citigroup (the green line), which has also been a fairly consistent and heavy user.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Let’s turn to schedule 2 (page 11), which is the less liquid collateral.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Here among the primary dealers, Lehman (the blue line) has been the most consistent user, followed by Merrill Lynch.

speaker: ANGULO
text: As you can see, UBS among the banks was clearly far and away the biggest user, although within the past two weeks they have reduced their TSLF borrowings.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So that’s, very briefly, the top five.

speaker: ANGULO
text: There’s again a bit of a mix here.

speaker: ANGULO
text: But as you can see, the investment banks are not the biggest users of the TSLF.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Let’s turn to page 12, and I’ll finish up here.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I’ll just highlight a very near-term challenge that we face, and I think it will provide a nice transition to Scott’s and Pat’s portions of the briefing.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I don’t want to get too much into their sections.

speaker: ANGULO
text: But I think generally we have an issue.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I think that, the longer we stay on site with this effort, the reputational risk to the Federal Reserve increases.

speaker: ANGULO
text: As Governor Kohn testified last week, we’re not examining; we are just very narrowly focused.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I think that message was well received.

speaker: ANGULO
text: At this time, it’s not too problematic.

speaker: ANGULO
text: But if someone is up on the Hill six months or a year from now, I think it’s going to be very difficult to say that we’re just doing this liquidity and capital thing.

speaker: ANGULO
text: People are going to want to know a little more about our judgments and how we made those judgments.

speaker: ANGULO
text: As I said early on, I think there’s some risk to making those judgments without having a little more information.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So I think the trick for us is, if we have our traditional bank supervision model on the left and what we’re doing right now on the right, we have to move this way, more to the left.

speaker: ANGULO
text: By no means should we be way over here.

speaker: ANGULO
text: But I think we have to figure out how to get this way a little more.

speaker: ANGULO
text: With that, I will end my remarks and pass to Scott and then to Pat.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Well, as you can tell from Art’s presentation, there’s been a significant amount of information-sharing and collaboration already between the Federal Reserve and the SEC.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: So we’ve taken this opportunity simultaneously with what’s going on with the primary dealers to fashion a document that will lay out a framework for how this information-sharing and collaboration will go forward.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We’ve made some pretty good progress on a document, but we’re still negotiating.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: In fact, the Chairman is negotiating this afternoon with Chairman Cox.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: This is one in which the principals have been intimately involved.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The agreement as it is currently structured really has two parts.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The first part outlines plans for sharing information between the two agencies.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Here I would divide the world into two pieces.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: There are the consolidated supervised entities (CSEs), which are the four large investment banks—Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Lehman Brothers, and Merrill Lynch.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We have agreed to share information and analysis of the financial condition, risk management, internal controls, capital, liquidity, and funding resources of those firms.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The agreement is focused primarily on those areas—so the financial condition, liquidity, and risk management of the firms.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: As you know, we have accessed information from these companies in connection with our providing liquidity through the PDCF and the TSLF, so we’ll share that with the SEC.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Similarly, the SEC, which is the primary regulator for those and has access to much more information, will share their information with us.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We’ve also agreed to share information and analysis on various financial markets that these companies are intimately involved in—in particular, the tri-party repo market and the interbank lending market.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Now, two bank holding companies participate in the SEC’s CSE program— Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We have agreed to share with the SEC the same type of financial and risk-management information regarding those two firms but only to the extent that that information affects the broker-dealers that are controlled by those two firms.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: So we are not expecting, nor is the SEC expecting us, to share information that relates to the condition of the bank or the condition of the other nonbank portions of either of those two firms—just the part related to their broker-dealer.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We have an interest here in the Federal Reserve in the financial condition of broker-dealers that are not in the CSE program.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: That would be any broker-dealer that’s in a bank holding company regulated by the Federal Reserve.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Our plan is to include an information-sharing arrangement regarding those institutions as well.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: More broadly, the SEC would provide us with information on an ongoing basis about the financial condition and risk management, internal controls, capital, liquidity, and funding resources of all broker-dealers that are controlled by a bank holding company.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: This would allow us access beyond what we’re currently getting.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Right now we’re getting primarily FOCUS reports on the broker-dealers, which are not always the most informative documents.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: So we’ll get more access.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We also are expecting to agree to provide similar kinds of financial and risk-management information to the SEC, again to the extent that the information affects the broker- dealer.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: So we would not be routinely providing information about bank holding companies related to the bank or related to the nonbanking operations that are not broker-dealers.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We also are expecting to include a provision that outlines several existing agreements that we have for sharing information regarding some of the clearing companies—DTC in particular—transfer agents, municipal securities dealers, and investment advisers.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: This would simply incorporate, without changing, the arrangements we already have.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: An essential part of all this sharing of information is that both agencies would agree to keep the information confidential.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: In addition, the SEC is agreeing not to use our exam or supervisory information, in particular any opinions that we might have, in their enforcement actions or investigations without the permission of the Federal Reserve.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The second part of the agreement, as we’re working through it, relates to supervisory expectations for the four large investment banks and for the primary dealers that have access to the PDCF and the TSLF.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: There the current proposal is that the two agencies would agree to collaborate and coordinate with each other in obtaining access to the information on the financial condition of these organizations and in setting supervisory expectations concerning the capital, liquidity, risk management, and funding for the CSEs and the primary dealers.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We’d also collaborate and coordinate our communications to those entities about supervisory expectations, something that’s already begun with Art and his group.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The memorandum of understanding (MOU) is intended to serve as a bridge from the existing world to whatever brave new world the Congress may put together.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: But it is not tied specifically to the PDCF or the TSLF and is intended to last beyond access to those facilities.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: It also does not change the legal authority that either of the two agencies has.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We continue to have full, unfettered legal authority over bank holding companies.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: They continue to have full, unfettered authority over the broker- dealers.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: But we do agree to talk more, collaborate more, and coordinate more.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: As I mentioned, the MOU is substantially worked out.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We are still, though, in negotiation over a couple of key points.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Our goal is to have it done this week, we hope with an announcement at the end of the week or sometime next week.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We expect that the terms of the MOU will be made public.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: As soon as we have something that’s concrete enough, we’ll also send that around to you.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I’m just going to go over the last few pages of the handout you have, pages 13 through 15.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Page 13 is just a table reminding you who the primary dealers are and providing some basic information about their size, borrowing activity, and regulatory status.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: As you probably know, there are currently 20 primary dealers, although as Art mentioned we’re about to lose two of them—Bear Stearns and Countrywide.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: An important point to note, which ran through Scott’s presentation, is that although the investment banks—the four firms that are subject to consolidated supervision by the SEC under their CSE program—are among the largest primary dealers, there are some very large bank-affiliated dealers, including not only affiliates of U.S. banks but also affiliates of German, Swiss, British, and French banks.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Also, if you look at column 3, you’ll see—and these are data that we get from the two government securities clearing banks that facilitate tri-party repo, JPMorgan Chase and Bank of New York—that it shows that the investment banks are not, in fact, the largest borrowers in the tri-party repo markets.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Rather that distinction belongs to Deutsche Bank, Banc of America, and Barclays.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I think that’s significant because arguably the biggest threat from Bear’s bankruptcy was the impact on the availability of secured financing, especially from money funds and other highly risk- adverse investors that provide tri-party financing to the dealers.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: So we have some very large borrowings by those non–investment bank firms.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Columns 4 and 5 provide some information about how these firms are regulated.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Essentially the legal entity itself in every case but one is a broker-dealer regulated by the SEC, and in that case it’s a government securities dealer regulated by the Treasury but the SEC really does the enforcement of those Treasury regulations.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Finally, all of these firms except one, Cantor Fitzgerald, which is an inter-dealer broker, are subject to some form of consolidated supervision by one or another consolidated regulator, although the regimes can differ appreciably.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The OTS has a regime for Countrywide, I guess being a notable example itself, quite different from the one that we would apply.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: So with those facts in mind, turn to the next two pages.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I don’t intend to go through all these questions, but what we’ve done here is set out some issues for discussion.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Basically there are two sets, one relating to the future of our liquidity facilities for the primary dealers and the other relating to the supervisory arrangements through which we’re seeking to mitigate the moral hazard that those liquidity facilities create.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: In each case, there are questions about what to do under current laws, until such time as the Congress may change those laws.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Then there are questions about what legislative changes we might seek, particularly if the Congress shows an inclination to legislate in this area.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Our purpose for this list of questions is to stimulate a discussion among you about these important issues and to provide you with an opportunity to express any preliminary views you may have.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: With that, I think we’d be pleased to answer questions on any of the three staff presentations.

speaker: LACKER
text: Thank you, Art, Scott, and Patrick, for a very forthcoming presentation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Two things for you, Art: First, on page 8 you presented some information about the details of the stress test that you’re applying, and the table lists various unsecured funding and secured funding from other sources, and you have numerical assumptions for the severity of stress.

speaker: LACKER
text: I take it that you apply those to the balance sheet numbers and do some calculations to calculate the stress test.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We went back to the firms and asked them to give us the information cut this way because it’s not readily available from any public information that we have.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We also asked them to give us, under a severe test scenario, what their assumption was.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Based on the submissions that we got from the four, which we converged and massaged, we came out pretty close to these assumptions.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We didn’t make these up.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was going to say that you essentially asked the question, What does “severe” mean in your stress system?

speaker: ANGULO
text: We left it somewhat in their hands, saying that it’s going to be short of a full run.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then you had some iteration to get to an agreed-upon set of numbers for these.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, you also said that you started your first iteration by asking them to give you the results of a Bear Stearns failure scenario.

speaker: LACKER
text: What numbers does that correspond to on this table?

speaker: ANGULO
text: You would have a lot higher numbers on secured funding.

speaker: ANGULO
text: You would have the numbers coming much closer to the illiquid, 100 percent, and you would have a—

speaker: ANGULO
text: Under fixed-income finance, for example, under the secured funding, there’s liquid and less liquid.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Those are 20 percent and 50 percent.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Those would have been approaching 100 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the severity, that’s how much of the money goes away.

speaker: LACKER
text: So do you have those numbers for Bear—what they actually experienced?

speaker: ANGULO
text: The SEC is working on a post mortem.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They have promised to share it with us when they’re done.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They have folks—I wouldn’t say forensic accountants—in there looking at that, trying to piece together what happened.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So we did not have the exact numbers.

speaker: LACKER
text: You didn’t have the exact numbers.

speaker: LACKER
text: But you knew roughly what they were.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Things moved pretty quickly at the end.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, I was just interested in information on exactly how that transpired.

speaker: LACKER
text: If there’s a chance that you could share with us that information when you get it, that would be very useful.

speaker: LACKER
text: A second question for you: You noted reputational risk from being in on the supervisory basis, and I want just to probe as to how you think about that.

speaker: LACKER
text: What eventualities would be risky for us?

speaker: ANGULO
text: We’re saying that we’re looking at the capital position.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I think Governor Kohn was careful to say in his testimony that we’re looking at capital in relation to near-term earnings prospects.

speaker: ANGULO
text: That gives us kind of a short window, but we know from examining banks that a capital number that’s reported to you depends on how you’re carrying your assets.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We have not done any work in trying to get behind, for example, the evaluations on Lehman’s commercial real estate portfolio.

speaker: ANGULO
text: That’s a potential vulnerability there.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Also, we have not really looked to a consolidated assessment of risk management at these firms, something we do in the bank supervision process.

speaker: ANGULO
text: So we’re basically taking the inputs, for lack of a better word, at face value and not doing our own work to try to validate those.

speaker: ANGULO
text: That’s what I was referring to in terms of the risk to us.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I think as long as we’re there, people expect us to be doing a little more than what we’ve been doing to date.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it’s essentially the risk that, after the fact, marks are questioned, and they ask, “You guys were in there—why didn’t you .

speaker: LACKER
text: The third question is for Pat.

speaker: LACKER
text: You talked about the repo market.

speaker: LACKER
text: My understanding is that some supervisory work under the LFI (large financial institution) umbrella is aimed at conditions in the repo market and mitigating some risk there.

speaker: LACKER
text: You mentioned that it was obviously an important factor in Bear.

speaker: LACKER
text: To what extent do you think paying interest on demand deposits would obviate the need for the huge volume of transactions in the repo market and the extent to which that legislative prohibition could have contributed to the market structures and fragility that gave rise to what happened in Bear.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I can’t answer that, but that’s a good question.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I mean, the basic problem here is that you have a tremendous demand for investments that have essentially the characteristics of Treasury bills, but the supply of Treasury bills isn’t nearly as large as that demand coming from money market mutual funds and from investment of cash collateral on securities lending and other kinds of secured financing.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Over time, the marketplace has come up with synthetic Treasury bills of various sorts, but those short-term investments have been created outside the banking system by and large because the inability to pay interest on demand deposits doesn’t allow them to be provided by the banking system.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Now, if that prohibition were removed, I think you would see banks offering things that would be competing with overnight repos, overnight commercial paper, and other sorts of things that are outside the banking system that are meeting these needs.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: In terms of the effects on stability, whether that leaves us in a better place obviously would depend on how good a job we do of regulating maturity transformation by the commercial banking system.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: An interesting question there is—whenever I hear Art give his presentation and look at these stress tests we’re applying to the investment banks, even under current conditions, when they’re not offering overnight interest-bearing deposits—how well our banks would fare if we tested them against these standards.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But I think your observation and your question are good ones.

speaker: LACKER
text: I mention that because it sounds as though it would be worthwhile knowing if it’s important.

speaker: LACKER
text: Since we’ve asked the Congress twice now for permission to pay interest and they’ve declined, and if this was a factor in the recent crisis, we might want to point that out to them as part of our legislative dialogue with them over the next couple of months to try to get them to do something.

speaker: KOHN
text: Just a comment on President Lacker’s question: I guess in the end it would depend on how big Bear Stearns’s balance sheet would have been and whether paying interest on demand deposits at commercial banks would have somehow shrunk Bear Stearns’s balance sheet and the secured funding that could then run.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s not obvious to me whether it would have made Bear Stearns a smaller player and a less significant part of the market, but it’s interesting.

speaker: KOHN
text: Tim looks as though he wants to say, “Yes, it would.”

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You know, we think that the money funds finance about a quarter or a third of the stuff in tri-party.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Money funds have a unique type of liquidity risk.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So it is possible, if the same set of assets were financed by banks, that because banks have a different liquidity risk the system would be more stable.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So you can maybe say, even with the same balance sheets as investment banks and the same mix of illiquid stuff financed through that mechanism, if the banks were the dominant providers of liquidity or it was provided through banks, that the system would be more stable, and the broader protections that we designed over the last century to limit the risk of runs on banks because of the risk to the system might have more power, insulating us from a system where nonbanks are large.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that’s the argument.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It would be interesting to know a bit about the politics on the Hill of thinking about that legislative change.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It would probably look a little like the Middle East, I suspect.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That would be a huge change in the relative return on different types of financial businesses that now would come with that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But it would be worth knowing a bit about the history of that debate in the past and what the probability is that we could get something like that through.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also had a question, Mr. Chairman, and it’s on the PDCF.

speaker: KOHN
text: I find some tension in my own attitudes here.

speaker: KOHN
text: Your leaning all over these people not to borrow helps protect the Board’s decision that this is unusual and exigent, credit couldn’t otherwise be available, and all of that.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it’s supportive of that.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the other hand, it sounds really like what we used to do with commercial banks all the time and thought it created stigma in the process.

speaker: KOHN
text: We don’t want you to borrow.

speaker: KOHN
text: If you come in and borrow, given that we don’t want you to borrow, you must really be hurting to overcome Art Angulo’s or Bill Dudley’s frown.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think the more we do this, the less useful this thing is as a backstop in some sense.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t have an easy answer as to how to resolve this tension.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, may I—not to preempt Art and Scott—in this case?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very important not to undermine the value of these liquidity backstops by introducing stigma in their use until we get to the point at which we want to dial people back.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But the decisions or the actions we took in the context of Cantor and Countrywide had a very compelling rationale.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It would have been irresponsible for us, given the facts that over Cantor we have no comparable framework of supervision and that their exposure was very large relative to capital.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In that context, we could do it without any risk that we were going to stigmatize the use of the PDCF because it’s a unique thing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Countrywide, as you know, had a slightly different but similar rationale.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It would have been imprudent for us to have had a substantial amount of securities outstanding, insufficiently collateralized, in the event that the deal didn’t go through, because they were not viable on their own without Bank of America’s buying them.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That was a necessary and prudent thing to do.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think also that the risk was very limited that we introduced stigma to the facilities.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The Barclays thing was more delicate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We would not say to them, “You can’t use the facility.” We just asked some careful questions about what they were doing and why, because their pattern of use was so different from everybody else’s in that context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I completely agree with your concern about that stuff.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think we must be very careful going forward that we don’t do things that will alter this balance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, you had something?

speaker: LACKER
text: About the general topic of stigma and lending at our facilities, I think it would be a useful agenda item for future research, and it would be useful for us to work at thinking carefully about this.

speaker: LACKER
text: Stigma represents some information revelation to market participants attending on some act, whether it’s borrowing from us or from someone else.

speaker: LACKER
text: The usual presumption is that more information is better.

speaker: LACKER
text: We talk as if stigma is a bad thing.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’d want to see a model that lays out how the sense in which it’s a bad thing counteracts the sense in which information is usually a good thing.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m really curious about that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it’s something we ought to think more carefully about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser, did you have a comment?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I asked Bill Dudley yesterday a question about what I had heard from the Street—that they perceived that stigma was attached to it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: With this conversation, it certainly appears to me that I was hearing them say that, at least from the investment banks’ point of view, they do feel that some stigma is already attached to it, good or bad.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now that I’ve heard this discussion, it is consistent with what I was hearing from those Wall Street firms.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: May I just interject one thing on this?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Vice Chairman Geithner makes the important point that one issue is counterparty risk for Cantor and Countrywide, which was sort of separate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The other issue is, since this is permissible only under section 13(3), that it can’t be a chronic source of funding and it can’t be part of their core funding plan.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We want to make it clear to them that this is going to go away, and we want to be confident that they’re not dependent on the PDCF as a source of funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I would distinguish between Barclays coming in occasionally with Barclays coming in every day, and that’s really the point we were trying to make to them.

speaker: ANGULO
text: It may be too fine a distinction, but we didn’t say “no” to anyone when they came in.

speaker: ANGULO
text: When they came in and stayed for a month and a half or two months, then we started to say “no.”

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But these are very different.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I was just going to say that it’s a very delicate balance.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We want this set of firms to get themselves to the point where, in the eyes of the market, they have a more conservative mix of leverage (appropriately measured) and funding risk so that they are less likely, even in a pretty adverse shock, to need to finance illiquid stuff with their central bank as a defense against that liquidity pressure.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We’re trying to do that without forcing a level of deleveraging that would be adverse to our broader objectives of trying to get markets back to some point where they’re functioning more normally.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We’re not going to get that perfect.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: By definition, our facilities by design should allow them to run with a mix of leverage and liquidity risk that is above what the market probably now would permit.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In the absence of our facilities, leverage and liquidity risk, if you measured it on a scale, would have to be lower in some sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But that’s the purpose and the necessary complement of the facility, and it is a delicate balance.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But just to come back to President Plosser’s point, I don’t think that the stigma is the result of how we’re applying the discretion we preserved for ourselves around use.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is really the result of the fact that, particularly if you’re at a point when you perceive escalating concern about your viability, people don’t want to risk that their pattern of use, if disclosed, would magnify the concern.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That’s really what accounts for the care in use, particularly as concern about viability has been intensified these last few weeks or so.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If I could add just one more thing, I also think that the stigma doesn’t really undercut the benefit of the PDCF as a backstop to these firms’ financing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If the stigma really undercut the benefit, then the stigma would be quite important.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think that the PDCF is still a very viable backstop even with some stigma associated with it in the current environment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Hoenig, did you have an intervention?

speaker: HOENIG
text: To follow up on Governor Kohn’s point, I think it’s important to our discussion going forward in terms of how we view these firms, from commercial banks to investment banks and primary dealers, because we are lending under exigent circumstances to these institutions under the primary dealer facility.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Therefore, they almost by necessity should be concerned about stigma if they were to continue to borrow through there.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the other hand, it’s important because the TAF is a different instrument and has different implications going forward in how we think about it and whether we want stigma with that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think about how and how broadly we view different financial institutions, that is, investment banks.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Are they blending into commercial banks?

speaker: HOENIG
text: We are going to have discussions about other types of financial institutions—should they not continue to be lent to only under exigent circumstances versus an ongoing TAF type of arrangement?

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I think there is stigma and probably should be unless we are concluding that they’re more like banks than not like banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re going to have a chance, of course, for everybody to give their views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Fisher, did you have a question?

speaker: FISHER
text: I just wanted to get in on this point that Governor Kohn raised.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m not uncomfortable with our being parsimonious with the Primary Dealer Credit Facility.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is under unusual and exigent circumstances, and I think we need to be sure that they are unusual and exigent circumstances.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s the reason it was created, and I think we have to respect that.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m just wondering, judging from the decline in the extent of the outstandings and given what you described, can we assume that there’s a lessening of unusual and exigent circumstances?

speaker: ANGULO
text: I would defer to my colleagues in Markets, but I would just give one anecdote.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Over the past few weeks, in particular, when Lehman announced its second-quarter results, some observers in the market stated that Lehman might not have come through this period if the PDCF had not been there.

speaker: ANGULO
text: They never drew on it.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I think it’s an interesting point.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I think there may be some relevance, some truth, to that.

speaker: ANGULO
text: Bill, you would have a better sense as to whether the markets are back to normal or not.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think they’re back to normal, and I also think very strongly that the amount of use of the Primary Dealer Credit Facility is not a guide to how important it is as a backstop for financial firms.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There were a number of people to whom we talked who said that the reason they stayed with Lehman during this period of stress was that they knew that the Primary Dealer Credit Facility was there as a backstop.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I have a high degree of confidence that Lehman would have been in great difficulty without it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just to make sure—it isn’t quite as awkward as it sounds.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I mean, it’s not clear.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The test for us about whether or not these make sense is not fundamentally about whether the PDCF would save Lehman from itself.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would just make the observation that we thought originally that you could look at the bid to cover and at the clearing price in the auction facilities as a measure of stress in markets, and they would be a test by which you could see conditions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it’s important to recognize that that’s not itself a particularly useful prism on stress today.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Independent of the specific circumstance around Lehman, the people who are funding tri-party balance sheets, for better or worse, tell anybody who listens that they’re doing so significantly because of the existence of this facility as a backstop.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So the use is not a very good measure of stress probably because of the stigma around it and because we’re affecting prices anyway by the existence of these facilities.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We’re doing as much as we can to improve the odds that these firms get to the point at which, in the eyes of their short-term secured or unsecured creditors, they look as though they can withstand a pretty large shock in the future without recourse to our facilities.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I don’t think we’re at the point yet where we can say that confidently, not because they haven’t deleveraged sufficiently or bought enough liquidity—though there’s a bit of that still left—but because there’s so much uncertainty left still about the scale of pressure on balance sheets, what that might do to the losses, what that might do to asset prices going forward or to behavior.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So this is just one man’s view, but I think a very good, substantive case based on what you can observe and what people say about behavior suggests that circumstances are still so fragile that we could justify the provision of these facilities as a responsible, sensible act given our broader objectives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Did you complete your questions?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I just have a couple of questions of fact.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: How big was Bear Stearns’s tri-party repo on the Thursday that they started getting into trouble—just to give a rough sense of scale?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I know it’s not exact.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It was a little over $100 billion.

speaker: LACKER
text: It hadn’t run off that week?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It was starting to run off.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The numbers seemed to be in that range.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Now, one of the reasons that we’re worried about the tri-party repo was that the securities in that tri-party repo were very illiquid.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Was Bear Stearns unusual in the amount of illiquid securities that were being financed?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As we look down this list, is the nature of the tri-party repo across these different parties similar or different?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: You could have a tri-party repo with collateral that would be easy to liquidate, or you could have a tri-party repo with something very difficult so that the counterparty would have a difficult time actually selling it into a distressed market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: From the work you all have been doing, are there big differences or not?

speaker: ANGULO
text: There are definite differences among dealers.

speaker: ANGULO
text: I don’t have the Bear Stearns cut, but we did a cut recently, and there are very clearly differences among dealers.

speaker: ANGULO
text: As we know, the share of less liquid assets being financed by tri-party has been growing over the last— pick a number—five, seven years.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The trend line is going like that, clearly at a steeper or more pronounced rate than the growth in more liquid or more eligible collateral.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So—I’m sorry—what percentage would that be?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: When you say it’s growing, is it now 10, 20, 50, or 80 percent?

speaker: ANGULO
text: Pat, do you have that?

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I have in front of me data from Bank of New York, which facilitates about two-thirds of the repos.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: At Bank of New York, 18 percent of the collateral is debt that’s settled through DTC—so that would be non-government, non-agency debt—and another 6 percent is equity.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: So about 25 percent is non-OMO things.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The biggest chunk by far is agency MBS.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Of course, I think in extremis Bear was having trouble financing even agency debt, importantly given the illiquidity that had developed in even the agency debt markets at that time, which was the critical thing that made investors no longer willing to provide financing for that kind of collateral with a shaky counterparty.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: For Bear Stearns, we have one side of the transaction looking at the investment banks.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: On the other side of that transaction, you have companies like Fidelity, Schwab, and Federated.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So as we think about who poses systemic risk, we probably want to think about both sides.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of a distress scenario, you have tri-party repos that are very illiquid.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The clearing bank does not want to provide the cash.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As a result they have to liquidate, and you have companies like Fidelity, Schwab, and Federated having to break the buck, and they don’t have much capital to infuse.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So just as we think about systemic risk, as you’re looking at these other organizations, are there other people that you would add to that?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I know for Bear Stearns that Fidelity, Schwab, and Federated played a very large role.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Were there other organizations that we ought to be thinking about that would have the same kind of nature?

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Well, the other big category that we have been able to identify of entities that are providing tri-party financing is the custodian banks that act as agents for securities lenders.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: When someone lends out securities, they often take in cash collateral.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Then they want to reinvest that collateral, and the big bank custodians do that on their behalf and invest a portion of that cash in tri-party.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Interestingly, JPMorgan Chase and Bank of New York Mellon are two of the big banks involved in that particular business.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I think maybe what you’re getting at is about dealing with the issues of the tri-party market per se.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: We have to be very careful in our approach to these issues because the situation is still very fragile, and until we get out of this period of turmoil, we first want to do no harm there.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But any solution can’t be focused solely or even primarily on the clearing banks and the way they process these transactions, although that’s part of it.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: It also has to focus on the behavior of the borrowers and the lenders, and the borrowers are basically all of these primary dealers and certain other big broker-dealers.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The lenders are more diverse, which makes them more difficult to deal with.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But I think there are certainly questions about whether they’re managing their risks effectively.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: If you’re a money fund and you’re treating an overnight repo secured by illiquid collateral as the equivalent of an overnight Treasury bill, there’s something problematic about that in terms of your own thinking about the situation you’d be in if, in fact, the borrower were unable to repay.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Sorry for so many questions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The situation of Lehman was kind of interesting because you saw their stock price go down.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Talking to financial institutions, both regulated and unregulated, in Boston, a lot of people were evaluating counterparty risk and deciding whether or not they were going to start running before the capital issue.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Did your measures of liquidity pick up the amount of stress that was going on in the counterparty analysis being done, I assume, all over the country?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: One of the conditions for an institution’s access to the discount window at a primary credit rate is that it not be rated a 4 or a 5.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I know we’re not doing bank exams, and I know we’re not looking at all the elements of the bank exam.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: How confident are we, if we were to do something like that for Lehman or for Merrill Lynch, that we wouldn’t rate them a 4 or a 5?

speaker: ANGULO
text: On the first question, yes, we were picking up the pressures on liquidity.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We saw some cracking, but it never broke.

speaker: ANGULO
text: There were some counterparties that were skittish, but we never saw the type of accelerated withdrawals or running that came to mark Bear Stearns.

speaker: ANGULO
text: We were watching it very closely, and so were they.

speaker: ANGULO
text: But basically it hung together.

speaker: ANGULO
text: The second question is a very difficult one.

speaker: ANGULO
text: It goes back to the point I finished on, that we are somewhat vulnerable in making these assessments without having a more robust process.

speaker: ANGULO
text: One way to look at it in the near term, though—again, as best we can, looking at capital—is the chart on page 6.

speaker: ANGULO
text: If you look at Lehman—with its capital raise, their tier 1 risk-based capital would be 12.5 percent.

speaker: ANGULO
text: There may be some range around that.

speaker: ANGULO
text: There are certainly questions about how accurately Bear’s capital was stated.

speaker: ANGULO
text: But as a rough measure, I think it would be difficult to say that Lehman would be a 4 or a 5, looking at it from a solvency perspective.

speaker: ANGULO
text: As I said, it started to crack, but it never really shattered.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Warsh, did you have a question?

speaker: WARSH
text: Not a question, just for the go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we then have an opportunity for general comments on these issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just give a bit of context.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When we instituted the PDCF and the TSLF in March, about the time of the Bear Stearns event, we stipulated that they would be available for up to six months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That date, mid-September, is coming closer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s my view, and I think others share it, that markets remain fragile, and in the case of Lehman, for example, the existence of the backup was an important support in maintaining the stability of that institution.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, given the state of the markets and given that I think we still face some systemic risks, I am quite inclined at this point to ask the Board to extend the PDCF and the FOMC to extend the TSLF over year-end, which is a difficult period—subject, of course, to the continued finding of unusual and exigent circumstances.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we do that, I would ask the Board to consider that in a Board meeting, and depending on the comments today, if there’s sufficient support, I would ask the FOMC to do that in a notation vote later this month.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, if we make the announcements that we’re going to at least provisionally extend these facilities, I think it’s important that we do so in the context of explaining that we have an exit strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, we are working to strengthen supervisory oversight, market resilience, and the overall regulatory structure so that there is understanding and confidence that we’re moving forward in a way that will over time make this unnecessary not only in the short term but in the long term as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are several parts to the plan here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One, as Scott already described, is the memorandum of understanding with the SEC, which will provide the basis for cooperation and collaboration in the medium term for our oversight of the investment banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Two, working with the SEC, we’d like to push forward along the lines that Art was describing, go beyond where we are now, and begin to establish a set of supervisory expectations regarding what we expect to see for the investment banks and to make sure that we have greater confidence in what we’re doing and what they’re doing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A third element that I think is important as we go forward is to try to improve the financial infrastructure in a number of dimensions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A lot of this work is already taking place at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, working with other regulators and with the private sector.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It includes things like improving the clearing and settlement process for various kinds of derivatives and improving risk management of derivative positions and counterparty positions, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It would be important for us going forward to make sure that major institutions can identify their exposure to a given counterparty through derivatives and other instruments and be able to close out that counterparty in an efficient and effective way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, work is going on here at the Board and in conjunction with New York on the tri-party repo market, trying to think of ways that we can strengthen that—perhaps, for example, by narrowing the range of collateral that is normally accepted and through other steps.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the way I would envision this proceeding would be—again, with your assent and subject to your comments—that we will announce within the next few days the MOU agreement with the SEC, which I would reemphasize is not tied to the PDCF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is, we would anticipate that this relationship would continue even should we close those facilities, on the grounds that the moral hazard issue is still there, until such time that there is further resolution by the Congress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, I’ll be giving a speech at the FDIC on July 8, followed by testimony on regulatory reform on July 10, when Secretary Paulson and I and others will be laying out some broad principles, including some of the issues of infrastructure, and will be discussing some of the longer-term legislative issues—for example, the issue of how we should perhaps normalize or regularize the resolution of a failing systemically important firm and, in so doing, maybe define more strictly what the parameters are for Fed lending and what our responsibility is in this kind of situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So to summarize, the MOU is this week.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be testimony coming up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Presumably after the monetary policy testimony later this month, we would like, conditional on your approval, to announce the extension of these facilities conditional on continuing unusual and exigent circumstances.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We would like to package that with a series of announcements concerning investment bank expectations, infrastructure, and as part of this environment as we talk about this in testimony and so on, some of our thoughts about how we might go forward in terms of statutory change in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I’m trying to convey is that, although I think we need to extend these facilities, we should do it in a context of increasing clarity about how we are working to make them less and less necessary in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So with that as context, let me just open the floor for any comments that people might have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have first President Lacker.

speaker: LACKER
text: The issues around the liquidity facility and what supervisory apparatus we have wrapped around primary dealers have to do with our having extended our lending reach.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think there’s now a substantial gap between our implied lending commitment and the scope of our supervisory authority.

speaker: LACKER
text: Vice Chairman Geithner spoke very eloquently about that earlier this month.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it’s paramount that we close that gap in order to keep borrowers from exploiting the obvious lending commitment and choosing to leave themselves vulnerable to runs and run-like behavior.

speaker: LACKER
text: But this leaves open the question of the extent of our lending reach and how we close that gap, and I think that that’s the most critical challenge for us in the year ahead, particularly as we approach negotiations with the Congress.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d like to share a couple of thoughts on that broader question because the questions posed to us sort of get at those.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s important to start this from a peacetime perspective, sort of a timeless perspective, and ask the question as if you were choosing afresh a lending and regulatory policy that was going to last a long time.

speaker: LACKER
text: If you imagine for the moment that whatever we announce and adopt would be perfectly credible and immediately viewed as credible, I think you’d obviously choose to not have this gap.

speaker: LACKER
text: You’d obviously choose to have lending and regulatory policies that are mutually incentive compatible.

speaker: LACKER
text: So you’d want an adequate supervisory regime in place for any institution that market participants believe we’ll lend to.

speaker: LACKER
text: Conversely, it means that you would want market participants to believe that we will constrain our lending to those institutions for which we have an adequate supervisory regime in place.

speaker: LACKER
text: So then the question comes up: How do you choose the boundaries of our lending commitment?

speaker: LACKER
text: I take it as self-evident that our lending commitment shouldn’t be open-ended and unlimited.

speaker: LACKER
text: We don’t want to supervise every financial intermediary in the world or in the United States, much less all individuals, partnerships, and corporations.

speaker: LACKER
text: But even limiting ourselves to what’s called systemically important financial institutions is going to be problematic as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: I take that phrase to mean any institution whose failure could be costly or disruptive to many other market participants.

speaker: LACKER
text: Any institution that chooses to engage in maturity transformation to some extent faces the potential for run-like behavior by the creditors.

speaker: LACKER
text: Unless we impose draconian regulations, market participants will always have a virtually unlimited capacity for creating financial arrangements that run the risk of disruptive failures.

speaker: LACKER
text: So extending our lending reach to whatever institution that makes itself systemically important just leads us down a path of ever more financial regulation of an ever larger portion of the financial system.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we’re going to have to set some boundaries.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d like to see them tighter rather than looser, and making them credible is going to be the hard problem for us going forward.

speaker: LACKER
text: In doing that, we’re going to face a classic time-consistency problem.

speaker: LACKER
text: I take that as given.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not sure everyone else shares that view, but I take it as obvious.

speaker: LACKER
text: Inevitably the exigencies of crisis management are excruciating, but I think there are times when they conflict with our long-run interest in the type of financial system that we would design from a peacetime, timeless perspective, just the way short-run concerns about growth sometimes conflict with our long-run interest in price stability.

speaker: LACKER
text: But just as sustaining monetary policy credibility sometimes requires resisting the temptation to ease policy to stimulate growth, sustaining credible lending limits is going to sometimes require not preventing a disruptive failure of an institution and not ameliorating the cost of financial distress.

speaker: LACKER
text: To put it another way, I think it would be a mistake to adapt our supervisory reach to a purely discretionary lending policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’re going to have to choose a policy and commit to it and then take hard actions to make that credible.

speaker: LACKER
text: From this point of view, I have a deep question about the questions posed by the staff.

speaker: LACKER
text: They focus entirely on primary dealers, and it doesn’t strike me that the fact that Bear Stearns was a primary dealer was what made us lend.

speaker: LACKER
text: It was the fact that it was more disruptive.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it’s likely that any other institution that presents the same threat of a disorderly resolution is going to be perceived as benefiting from our implicit lending support, whether or not they’re a primary dealer, unless we say something otherwise, unless we draw a boundary, and unless we make that credible.

speaker: LACKER
text: So, for example, other large broker-dealers, hedge funds, private equity firms, or insurance companies could easily fail in a disruptive way.

speaker: LACKER
text: We need to think through whether we’re going to let that happen or whether we’re going to be forced to step in.

speaker: LACKER
text: At some point we’re going to have to choose to let something disruptive happen.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that ambiguity about our lending limits would be a bad choice.

speaker: LACKER
text: Market participants are going to form their own views about the likelihood of us lending.

speaker: LACKER
text: Any lack of clarity about the boundaries is just going to lead some firms to test the boundaries, and it’s not going to help us resist the temptation to lend beyond the boundaries we want to establish.

speaker: LACKER
text: Besides, Mr. Chairman, you’ve emphasized the value of de-personalizing and institutionalizing the conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s important that we strive for lending policy that isn’t critically dependent on particular officeholders.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I said, I’d favor fairly tight limits on our lending commitments, and you are probably not surprised about that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we really ought to maintain this section 13(3) hurdle at a fairly high level, but the exit strategy makes me nervous.

speaker: LACKER
text: Crafting this MOU, a permanent shift in our visibility into and in our ability to protect the system from primary dealers, is just going to sustain the expectations that have arisen since Bear—which have been described and referenced a couple of times and which you see in the fall in CDS spreads for those institutions—and it is just really hard to see how to put that genie back in the bottle and limit the extent to which we’re viewed as backstopping them.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I think we ought to strive to make that somehow be viewed as unusual as possible.

speaker: LACKER
text: More broadly, my reading of the history of economics and financial intermediation is just my reading.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I’m motivated broadly by the sense that we’d be better served in the long run with as small an extent of central bank lending commitment as possible.

speaker: LACKER
text: Central bank credit is fiscal policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: It entangles us in politics.

speaker: LACKER
text: It risks compromising the independence of our monetary policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: You’ve heard me say this before.

speaker: LACKER
text: Expanding our lending forces us to extend our regulatory reach, and that can’t be good for the financial system even though I trust our staff to do a very good job of being as efficient and effective as they can be.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s not obvious on the evidence that our financial system is terribly fragile apart from the volatility induced by uncertainties about government and central bank policies.

speaker: LACKER
text: Besides, I think that we should take seriously the notion that some amount of financial instability is undoubtedly optimal, as work by economists such as Allen and Gale has demonstrated.

speaker: LACKER
text: Those are the kinds of considerations that I think ought to guide our policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: Finally, Mr. Chairman, a word about process.

speaker: LACKER
text: At our last meeting we discussed interest on reserves, a historic and consequential decision for us.

speaker: LACKER
text: We had a briefing package of 100-plus pages reflecting substantial staff work.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Committee very much benefited from that.

speaker: LACKER
text: At an upcoming meeting we’re going to talk about inflation dynamics, another consequential topic.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve received somewhat less material, even going back several months, about financial markets, their character, and the welfare economics of our interventions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d urge you to consider a special topic at some future meeting at which we explore the economics of financial stability, since it is becoming such a consequential part of what we do.

speaker: LACKER
text: Related to that, I was happy to learn from Art that an after-action review by the SEC was under way.

speaker: LACKER
text: Because our role is different from the SEC’s, I’d like to suggest that maybe building on that or maybe in parallel to that we conduct our own after-action review of the factors that went into how that event played out.

speaker: LACKER
text: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with you that we need to define limits, but I think we have stronger tools than just our declarations of piety.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would just note that there are models.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One good model is the FDICIA model, for example, which lays out a whole set of criteria under which intervention can be taken and, if intervention is taken, has a set of rules.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are ways through the legal structure to solve some of these problems without our necessarily having to make time-inconsistent promises.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree, and those are mechanisms for legislatively tying our hands, and that ought to be high on the agenda.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On that point, I have been reading a bit recently.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It might be useful in thinking about some of these issues about how we tie our hands and the mechanism for doing that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The IMF went through an extraordinary study effort during the sovereign debt crisis and came up with some very important mechanisms for how to change the contracts that were being written by sovereign countries so as to avoid the IMF’s having to step in and look for other solutions, which is, I think, along the same lines.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t know whether or not there are things from which to learn in parallel with that to think about how we approach that issue.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I have three comments for the long term and three comments for the short term.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: For the long term, in the tradeoff between focusing on markets versus institutions, to the extent that we can have standardized products traded on exchanges, we don’t need to spend as much time with institutions, and that takes care of a lot of the counterparty risk.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: To the extent that the products have to be customized and done in dealer markets, then we have counterparty risk and that becomes an issue.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I applaud what the New York Fed is doing with the credit default swap market in thinking about a way to more systematically reduce counterparty risk.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I wonder if we should more forcefully be trying to push it not only to a clearinghouse but also maybe to exchange traded.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I know there is a tradeoff between standardized products and nonstandardized products.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But if we can get things to be more standard so that they can trade on an exchange, we won’t have to spend as much time talking about some of the issues that we’ve been talking about.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Not just a credit default swap market has that characteristic.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So if we can push a number of areas in which there’s counterparty risk into an exchange, then we can get out of the business of focusing on all the institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The second point is that there’s a broader role for us as a holding company supervisor.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: When I look at this list and look at Countrywide, it’s not because they’re a primary dealer that I would be focused on them.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It’s because they were 20 to 25 percent of the residential mortgage market; they were a very large player.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The OTS has holding company supervision over them.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We ought to ask ourselves whether now is the time to think about what organizations we ought to have holding company responsibility for.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The OTS has WaMu and had Countrywide.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We ought to give some thought to that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Now is the time to think about whether or not that’s appropriate and push for it if there are going to be legislative recommendations.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of broker-dealers, I think the same thing applies.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I don’t think that we should be the primary regulator for these organizations.
