speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But if we’re going to be lending to them in exigent circumstances, having holding company regulatory authority does become important.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The third point is that, when you look at this list, there are a lot of foreign institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: One insight that we’ve gotten is that an organization as big as UBS could potentially fail.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That may not be something that we thought was very likely nine months ago, but it is obviously more likely now than we would have anticipated.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Foreign organizations can either establish themselves as a branch or have a domestic holding company.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: To the extent that foreign supervisors decide to wall off their organizations around their geographic borders and say that, if there is a problem, we’re not going to support institutions that are in the United States and you’re on your own, I think we need to revisit some of our rules on how much capital we expect foreign holding companies that are intermediary holding companies to hold.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We might also want to think about, if there’s a lot of activity being done through a branch that has no capital supporting it, how concerned we should be about that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Should we be taking actions to make sure that, if the foreign parent decides that they are going to abandon the branch, we feel very comfortable with that outcome?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given the list of the primary dealers, I think the numbers are fairly large, larger than they were for Bear Stearns, and that’s something that we probably should give a bit more thought to.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: On the short-term issues, I certainly think that we should extend the facilities past the end of the year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A number of us have made the point that the markets are still fragile.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just the announcements about Lehman Brothers over the last month highlight that we’re not yet safe, and I think that it makes perfect sense to extend through the end of the year because there could be an end-of-the-year financing problem this year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, narrowing tri-party repo collateral also makes sense.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But it has implications for what securities people hold, and some of those markets may become much more distressed if we announce that they no longer can be part of a tri- party repo.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So we need to give some thought to whether there will be collateral damage and to the unintended consequences from that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Third, I agree with President Lacker that primary dealers wouldn’t be where I’d focus.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I’d focus on systemically important.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That would be key players and key markets whose failure might cause a cascading of counterparty failures.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think we ought to start with that premise and which organizations fit into that category.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Some of them will be on the primary dealer list, but they are on the primary dealer list for a reason very different from the reason they are systemically important.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So maybe distinguishing between those two would be useful.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, on the short term, I think extending through the end of the year is prudent and would support that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would say that the possibility of its naturally dying off would be ideal.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would support that because it is “exigent circumstances.” We should make that clear and work these people out of it as quickly as possible.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the longer-term issues, I share the view of a lot of what President Lacker said.

speaker: HOENIG
text: A couple of things: I’m very uneasy about extending our lending and supervisory authority to these institutions on the basis of systemic risk.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The banking industry has been under our umbrella, importantly around transactions activities—that is, payments—and how important they are systemically.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It’s clear, and a line is there.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Beyond that, it is size that’s systemically important.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we extend this and institutionalize it because we’ve had this emergency and we’ve used section 13(3), then I have to ask what will happen when the next Long-Term Capital occurs that’s larger, more complicated, with a lot more interaction that will affect the markets globally.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To what then will we extend ourselves in terms of supervisory oversight, memos of understanding, agreements for the group of hedge funds that aren’t regulated, and so forth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I think it’s important that we focus on the fact that this is an emergency and that we go back to “exigent circumstances” in the future for these institutions so that we have clear boundaries on that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think it has served us well and will continue to serve us well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Then we use our best judgment in exigent circumstances and very sparingly.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that’s a lot of what President Lacker said, so I won’t repeat everything else, but those are the concerns that I really do have going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: May I make a suggestion?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You know, these are deep, consequential questions we face.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is a question on the economy, and we’re not going to resolve it today.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it’s important that we recognize that we’re going to have to build some time into our agenda—later this year probably, certainly early next year—and get deeper into the basic question about what we are for in the future.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What amendments to the Federal Reserve Act, if any, would we support?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What mix of these things?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That’s important because we’re not going to do an adequate job of getting ourselves on the table on those actions today.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are going to need to be very careful that the stuff we’re doing in the here and now doesn’t prejudice those decisions long term.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, I think the package that the Chairman laid out and the strategy we have are pretty carefully designed to mitigate that risk.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We’re trying to be very careful that we’re preserving full optionality, once we get through this particular period, to go on any of the paths that are ahead in this context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course, this short-term stuff is vulnerable to the risk.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It looks as though we’re prejudicing some of those choices, but I think we’re trying to be careful not to do that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just wanted to make the point that we’re all going to need a little time to think through this stuff, and we’re going to need some time to come back and talk about the deeper policy questions that we face in this because they are very consequential.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I have a lot of sympathy for all the concerns that are on the other side of where we are today.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would very much like to see us make that happen sooner rather than later just because of the force of events taking us forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Because of testimonies and so on, we are going to have to at least enunciate some broad principles, and that is why this discussion is very useful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, details will be worked out over a longer period.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Yes, I just have a few comments.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In reading through this memo and hearing the presentation this morning, I think that these are fantastic questions.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They deserve a lot of research and analysis.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Just to echo Vice Chairman Geithner, they cannot easily be answered in a forum like this one.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What is happening is that we start out looking at these questions, which just spawn more and more questions; so we end up with an even longer list of questions.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The short-term strategy seems perfectly reasonable, somehow tied to an exit strategy maybe next year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I didn’t have any problems with that as outlined by the Chairman.

speaker: BULLARD
text: When we get down to approaching a more detailed analysis of what we want to do overall, it brings up very difficult questions of what the optimal regulatory environment is.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that we all think the regulatory environment in the United States is not optimal right now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, in a world of increasing globalization, it is not so clear how you should set up your regulatory structure.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is a once-in-a-generation chance to possibly reformulate the regulatory structure.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I wouldn’t hold my breath on that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think the Congress does not have a great record of dealing with issues like this.

speaker: BULLARD
text: These issues are complicated, and it is very hard to get agreement on them.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But you would like to have a benchmark.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that one is out there in the economics literature about what that environment should look like.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is what we could possibly work on over the next nine months or so.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Then I have another comment.

speaker: BULLARD
text: When we are evaluating these programs, we have to think about whether these programs have been effective and to what extent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: How do we measure success?

speaker: BULLARD
text: One of the comments earlier was that the mere existence of the programs might be success in some sense.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In a model, that is going to work.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Even if you take it out of existence, because the market knows it’s there and you can put it back into existence in the future, it will have exactly the same effect.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Whether or not you have the program in place, the equilibrium is going to be the same in a lot of models, so the effects would still be there.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If it is just the potential of putting the program in place that is considered successful, then maybe it is not critical whether it is in place but priced not to be used or whether it is actually taken out of existence temporarily.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I am in favor of keeping these facilities open through year- end as you have suggested.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that just the existence of the PDCF is important, which we talked about earlier, and your overall outline of an approach, the topography of that approach, is attractive.

speaker: FISHER
text: The question I have is about—and you used the term—“supervisory expectations.” I have a question for Scott, and then a thought to follow up on.

speaker: FISHER
text: Since, Scott, no one asked you a question, I want to ask you a question.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: I was perfectly content to get through this without any questions.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: But I am happy to answer anything.

speaker: FISHER
text: In working up this MOU, have you had any interaction with Chairman Frank or any of his staff, getting a sense of how they might react or what it does in terms of their own expectations?

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Well, we have had a bit of interaction on the Senate side.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: The Senate folks are very interested in what we are doing and whether this would preempt a congressional action.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: Chairman Frank has been more sanguine about our doing what is appropriate to deal with the situation now—Laricke may speak to this more at the lunchtime conversation.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: But we are building on existing authority.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We are not expanding beyond the existing framework.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We are agreeing to collaborate more, work together more, but we don’t gain any legal or statutory authority through this MOU.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We gain some admission because we are standing next to the SEC.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: We expect that the primary dealers and CSEs will be more willing to talk with us because we are with the SEC.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: But in the end, it depends on voluntary cooperation by all.

speaker: FISHER
text: Are you picking up any signals in return, in this interaction with the Senate or elsewhere, about what they might be thinking?

speaker: FISHER
text: Are we picking up any other signals that might be of concern?

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: On the House side, Chairman Frank is thinking of a model that is similar to what the Treasury blueprint outlined, where the Federal Reserve would be a systemic regulator and have some authorities that go along with that.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: I think that on the Senate side they are very much in disarray.

speaker: ALVAREZ
text: They want to visit this issue, but they haven’t figured out exactly what point of view they want to have.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am a little confused.

speaker: FISHER
text: You testify in July and then have a speech.

speaker: FISHER
text: You said that you and Paulson will be speaking.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that is a very important point.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is going to be a tough act because you don’t want to take anything off the table, but you want to keep a lot open and not show your hand.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, we don’t know what our hand is yet.

speaker: FISHER
text: You may, but I don’t think we have it as a group.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we can’t really show our hand.

speaker: FISHER
text: Anyway, I don’t know how this is going to be prepared, but I’m sure there are lots of feelings around this table.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is the substance that Vice Chairman Geithner referred to earlier—these very, very important questions.

speaker: FISHER
text: But you are going to have to show some leg during that speech.

speaker: FISHER
text: Obviously, this is a Board issue, but with regard to the FOMC, I would just ask that it be fairly carefully vetted.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I was planning to do that.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just for some suggestions, for whatever they’re worth.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to the short- term plan of extending the facilities over the turn of the year and so forth—that is, the MOU and the testimony that goes with it—that is all fine with me.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t have any problem with that.

speaker: STERN
text: That sounds sensible under the circumstances.

speaker: STERN
text: A number of important points have already been raised.

speaker: STERN
text: I won’t reiterate all of them.

speaker: STERN
text: Maybe the one that caught my attention most completely was President Lacker’s point about credibility.

speaker: STERN
text: Whatever we go forward with obviously has to be seen as credible, and as he pointed out, it is important that at some point, to limit our involvement in supporting institutions and markets going forward, we may have to be prepared to let one large institution fail.

speaker: STERN
text: The reason, of course, that we are very concerned about protecting them over time is the spillover effect.

speaker: STERN
text: As I have said many times before, where we need to concentrate our efforts—not necessarily exclusively, but certainly in part—is in devising ways to limit spillovers.

speaker: STERN
text: That is all about preparation—the analysis and so forth that goes with it—and it is all about communication—that is, putting uninsured creditors on notice that the regime is in fact in the process of changing.

speaker: STERN
text: Now, having said that, I don’t mean to suggest that it is easy.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t mean to suggest that we will get it 100 percent correct.

speaker: STERN
text: But if we don’t do those kinds of things, then statements about boundaries aren’t likely to be credible.

speaker: STERN
text: They are just going to be, well, you guys wish it were this way, but you have section 13(3), and we know it’s there, and we are going to act accordingly.

speaker: STERN
text: So I think it is very important, as we go forward with this, that we focus some attention exactly on those areas.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I will be very brief, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I do want to say, with respect to the short-term issues, that I fully support the plan that you laid out.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I certainly favor keeping these facilities in place beyond September.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even if their use diminishes, I agree with the point that it doesn’t necessarily indicate that they are not playing a tremendously important role.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The ramping up of our oversight of these institutions in the agreement with the SEC is a very important part of continuing these facilities.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the long-run issues, it is a wonderful list of questions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t know the answers to the questions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we really need to dig in very rapidly and do serious work on them.

speaker: YELLEN
text: President Rosengren raised a list of issues about this, the same ones that have been very much in my mind.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is not obvious to me that the right list of systemically important institutions is the primary dealers.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think someone—maybe President Rosengren—raised the issue of Countrywide, a huge mortgage company.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I certainly worried last summer that it had created systemic risk, and it is not just the primary dealer there.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I also think there is an issue with respect to hedge funds, similar to those that arose with Long-Term Capital Management.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This raises very troubling issues to me about our trying to identify and take on supervision of all systemically important institutions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This is a very tough issue that I don’t know the answer to.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But also, what is going on raises fundamental issues about how we conduct consolidated supervision.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even if all the systemically important institutions were primary dealers or mortgage companies within bank holding companies that currently we do have umbrella supervision over, I am not at all convinced that the way we are carrying out supervision now would have prevented a Bear Stearns-type of episode within an institution that is currently solidly under our supervision.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Last summer I was pleased in some ways that we had lost direct supervision of Countrywide to the OTS.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But it might well have been in our domain—six months earlier it would have been—and it could have created a systemically important problem if it had failed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So just the nature of how we carry out this Fed-lite approach, is that really the right way?

speaker: YELLEN
text: I see us as very focused on process in our supervision of holding companies.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We don’t do a lot of transaction testing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Obviously, this raises very fundamental issues, even within our existing domain, about how we carry out comprehensive umbrella supervision.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t have any answers, but we clearly need to get on it quickly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I will be very brief.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A lot of my views have been shared already.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Just to expand on President Rosengren’s comment—how we define the right institutions, the scope of this, I think that some of the questions here are really hard.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is my understanding that the workgroups we talked about last time are going to be working on some of these things, and we need to get those well under way to help us define these problems.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the longer-term problem—Vice Chairman Geithner made this point, and I just want to reiterate it—it is really important in the short run that we not do things that constrain our longer- term options.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is a very slippery slope that the long run ends up being transformed into a series of short-term steps, and by that almost inevitably you end up in places you don’t want to be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I just want to make sure that we stay abreast of that and not let that happen to us—that we find ourselves six months from now in a position where, gee, we wish we hadn’t done that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I just wanted to stress that again.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m fine with extending the facilities through the end of the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t have any tremendous problem with that, although I have always been a little puzzled by “unusual and exigent circumstances.” What does that really mean?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How do we define that?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It would be a lot easier for me to think about when to take it off if I knew what the criteria were for putting it on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It would be helpful to me, anyway, if we could work on defining those criteria a little more rigorously.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I know there will be judgment involved in that at the end of the day.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t disagree with that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But it would help us to define what we mean by that because it is going to be really hard to define what we mean by a “systemically important institution.” I am not sure I know the answer to that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it is a very difficult question.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I am okay on the short run.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I will just reiterate the other point that President Stern made about the issue of credibility and commitment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You know, I have talked a lot about this over the last couple of years regarding monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It applies equally well in this framework.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Figuring out ways to implement our policies, whatever they may be, in both a time-consistent and committed way, and defining those boundaries and how we live up to them, is a really hard problem.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I don’t think we can avoid dealing with it, and it is going to be a critical piece of how we think about the longer term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I will just leave it at that.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also support extending our lending facilities to get through the year-end funding problems.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As many others have already said, I agree that we should undertake an evaluation of the changes to our emergency liquidity facilities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think it is important that we do it more broadly and that we don’t do it in a piecemeal fashion.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: How the pieces fit together matters greatly.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Any extension of Fed authority to provide routine liquidity support beyond insured banks should be something that we consider as part of a comprehensive regulatory and financial safety net reform.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My own view may be that I prefer a narrower lending facility than I think was envisioned in some of the documents that we received, but I do think that the top priority is to have a well-thought-out, documented plan for how we move forward.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: That will help us address some of the moral hazard issues that we have been concerned about.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think it will avoid our having to create any new institutions or new facilities to respond to future crises.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also think it will help better define some of the boundaries.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I have maybe a variation on Governor Warsh’s comment of yesterday: Much has been said by many, so I will try not to take too much time here.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think Vice Chairman Geithner’s admonitions are correct, and I certainly support them.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am quite supportive of extending through the year-end, and the short-term plan that the Chairman laid out seems quite sensible to me.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I don’t have well-informed or well-thought-out answers to the more detailed questions that were posed in advance of the meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I didn’t devote the time to study them in any depth.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So let me take refuge in some sort of high-level comments.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A number of people around the table have been expressing overview types of comments.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I see the touchstone of all of this to be our perceived accountability for systemic risk and financial stability.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There may be, in the context of legislation, regulation, and so forth, limits to that; but I think that we are largely perceived as the most accountable party.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I have to ask myself, Do we have a system today that is aligned with the reality of the financial markets?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Or, put in more vernacular terms, do we have the right stuff to do what we need to do to take responsibility as best we can for financial stability?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My answer to that is “no.” I don’t think we have the right stuff.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think the answer to that lies in working out the details of what the right stuff is.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But the reality is that financial markets are not bank-centric any longer, with the widely discussed shadow banking system, including hedge funds, a complexity that is not going to go away; international integration that is not going to go away; very, let’s just say, compelling economic and financial reasons for off-balance-sheet treatment of various kinds of things; and on and on.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We could make a long list of what that reality is.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: To me, and I have been kind of dwelling on this for some time, that is a reality that is likely to continue.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It may take a couple of steps back, but it will continue to develop along certain lines.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Do we have a system that is aligned with it?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The answer to that is “no.” So if we can take care of the short-term plan and then buy the time over the next several months to hammer out what we think is the best possible thinking opposite that reality, then that is what I believe we need to be doing.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: EVANS
text: I will also try to be brief, in spite of the large number of questions that were handed out.

speaker: EVANS
text: The short term should be quite easy.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the tactical issues, I agree with the suggestion of extending the facilities through year-end.

speaker: EVANS
text: They seem to have worked well.

speaker: EVANS
text: Also, a number of very interesting and important initiatives are ongoing as well on the CDS over-the-counter market and tri-party repo, and those should help out as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the longer-term issues, I am very happy to hear that you will be giving a speech and testimony on this, and I will be looking forward to how you lay out those issues.

speaker: EVANS
text: Obviously, there are large-scale changes in our regulatory environment that are being contemplated.

speaker: EVANS
text: These happen only every now and then.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is an opportunity to improve or to make a tremendous mistake if we are not very careful.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I think it, obviously, requires a tremendous amount of time.

speaker: EVANS
text: People have talked about the various issues, so I won’t dwell on them.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think there have been a lot of very good comments around the table and speeches that have laid out the important issues that we are facing.

speaker: EVANS
text: One that I am sure we will have to talk a bit more about is that we can’t think about this in a static environment.

speaker: EVANS
text: Obviously, the markets are very dynamic.

speaker: EVANS
text: As soon as we lay out a structure that will help out certain types of institutions, then there is going to be an opportunity to arbitrage that.

speaker: EVANS
text: We are presumably talking about reducing earnings of a number of institutions, and so they will be seeking those out.

speaker: EVANS
text: Another way to characterize the big question—it is nothing new—is how we maintain the incentives for market discipline.

speaker: EVANS
text: Many of the comments that President Stern and others made about how we think about preparing for possible resolutions will be very important.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I am looking forward to many more discussions about this.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think I would just like to dig into some of the comments that President Lockhart and President Evans just made, just for a second, take a step back, and ask why we are here having this conversation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I know the timing is because we have this PDCF, but what happened was that the financial markets evolved in such a way that simply having a liquidity backstop for commercial banks was not sufficient to protect the economy from systemic risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: I myself have been very surprised—I will be very open about this—at the persistence, the extent, the depth, and the spread of this crisis and how long it went and what it covered.

speaker: KOHN
text: Every couple of months, I thought it was about to be over, and then another wave would come.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that we have learned something about the financial system in the process, and we have learned that the regulatory structure and the liquidity provision structure were not sufficient to give the economy the protection it needed from the new style of financial system.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is really the background of why we are here, not just because we made the loan or we set up the facilities because we thought we needed to do so to protect the system under the circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: I completely support, Mr. Chairman, your suggested path forward for the near-to- intermediate term.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that is the right way to go.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would say, relative to the two senators that I testified in front of last week, that they were very supportive of the memorandum of understanding between the Fed and the SEC and particularly supportive of the efforts that the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the other regulators are leading to strengthen the infrastructure of the OTC derivatives markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: We didn’t get into tri-party repos, fortunately.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I’m sure they would have been supportive of that, too.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think everybody has raised very good questions about where, in this new financial system, you draw the boundaries.

speaker: KOHN
text: What do you need to do?

speaker: KOHN
text: There are no easy answers here, and I look forward to coming back to this.

speaker: KOHN
text: My going-in position is that our liquidity facilities outside of commercial banks ought to be available in systemic circumstances, not in just any circumstances, and they ought to be available at this point to just broker-dealers or investment banks.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would hesitate to get outside that realm.

speaker: KOHN
text: Those guys are already regulated, and so what we’re talking about is strengthening the regulation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that we can strengthen the core of the system to make it resilient to things happening outside, but I am not totally dug in on that.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I look forward to more discussion.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is going to be very hard to draw the line and make it credible.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree, partly this will be defining what we mean by “systemic,” but I don’t think we will ever really get to the point of having a bright line around that.

speaker: KOHN
text: It will always need a great amount of judgment, combined with—as you said, Mr. Chairman—a process by which you make that decision, to help limit the moral hazard.

speaker: KOHN
text: You get into a crisis, and the near-term costs are much more palpable than the long-term costs that might be there.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it is always hard to say “no.” We have said “no” in the past on certain circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: Drexel is the obvious example.

speaker: KOHN
text: Markets were a little stressed.

speaker: KOHN
text: There was a little disorder.

speaker: KOHN
text: It was fine, but it was a very different circumstance.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that completes my remarks.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me make a few prefatory comments, and then try to answer a couple of the key questions in the memo.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, a crisis is a terrible thing to waste.

speaker: WARSH
text: My sense is that we have an opportunity here to do the right thing over the period to try to get market discipline—to Charlie’s point—back and vibrant and working countercyclically with regulatory discipline and capital standards.

speaker: WARSH
text: So this is an opportunity.

speaker: WARSH
text: As we contemplate our six-months-and-a-day problem, what do we do between September and year-end?

speaker: WARSH
text: I agree with Vice Chairman Geithner’s comment that we need to keep options open, and I will make a proposal in a moment for how to do that.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, the memo from the staff said that improvements in financial markets have resulted, importantly, from the availability of the special liquidity facilities, and I agree with that.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I wouldn’t give short shrift to the other things that have been going on in the markets that have improved market functioning.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t think it is fair to say that we deserve a disproportionate amount of credit for what has happened.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have seen a ton of capital-raising.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have seen a lot of diversification of funding sources.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have seen changes in duration by financial institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have seen improved disclosure and transparency.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have seen big write-downs.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have seen brutal changes in management teams.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have seen pairing of business lines and improved risk management.

speaker: WARSH
text: So it strikes me that market discipline is alive and well.

speaker: WARSH
text: It was necessary for us to do what we did, but I think it hangs way too much on our facilities if we suggest that we are the only thing that is keeping the system together.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a final prefatory comment, the memo says that some investors have indicated their willingness to lend to primary dealers in recent months, and that has been conditioned on dealers’ access to the PDCF.

speaker: WARSH
text: It strikes me that proves too much.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am not sure that is a good thing.

speaker: WARSH
text: The concerns we have late in the cycle, when we look back, include that market discipline broke down.

speaker: WARSH
text: In the short term, obviously, we want to see some of the money market mutual funds from President Rosengren’s neck of the woods hang in there with these institutions so we don’t have a sort of panic coming.

speaker: WARSH
text: But over the short to medium term, we want the guys in money market mutual funds to recognize that, when they are providing funding overnight, they are making an investment decision that has a risk.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I hesitate to suggest that we want to do things over the period that let them be complacent.

speaker: WARSH
text: We want to do things that make them very focused on the decisions they are making.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now a bit to the key questions that were asked in the memo.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, on liquidity facilities, on the question of the PDCF and its symmetry with the TSLF, I like that notion of the balance of having an auction and having one that is available more regularly.

speaker: WARSH
text: But we have to recognize that the PDCF, whether intended or not, has been stigmatized.

speaker: WARSH
text: If Lehman Brothers, when they were on their darkest day, had answered the question differently, I dare say they might not be in existence.

speaker: WARSH
text: They were asked, “Have you accessed the PDCF?” The answer was, “Absolutely not.” If their answer to that had been “yes,” I suspect that they and we could have been in a very different circumstance.

speaker: WARSH
text: So what does that prove?

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that proves that the existence of these facilities matters.

speaker: WARSH
text: It keeps institutions in the game.

speaker: WARSH
text: The particular terms matter less.

speaker: WARSH
text: But also, in extremis, accessing that facility, unlike the securities lending facility, causes losing a considerable amount of control over one’s own fate.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think we have to take that into consideration.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have considerable leverage over these institutions at this time.

speaker: WARSH
text: No matter what they and their lobbyists say, they want us to be their regulator more than they can possibly contain themselves—mostly for our credibility and mostly for our balance sheet.

speaker: WARSH
text: I worry that if we extend the PDCF as is by just punting it down the road some months, we will lose some of that leverage.

speaker: WARSH
text: So one idea, which I must say I haven’t explored as much as I probably should, is extending the PDCF, not as is but by modifying it in a way that would make Bagehot proud—by making it more expensive, by widening the spread.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now, there are other things we could do in this short-term extension that modify its terms—changing collateral or changing haircuts.

speaker: WARSH
text: But it strikes me that price might be an interesting way to say, “Listen, we aren’t pre-judging outcomes, but you can see from this move that we aren’t comfortable with the status quo, and we are asking ourselves these very hard questions that we brought to bear.” That could send an important signal, which I don’t think would be overly disruptive to the markets if we explained some of the rationale for doing it.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn, finally, to the prudential supervision questions.

speaker: WARSH
text: I have a note here in answer to the first question, “How do we limit moral hazard if we continue the facilities?” My bold answer is “carefully,” so I guess not much is there.

speaker: WARSH
text: On what principles should supervisory expectations be based?

speaker: WARSH
text: I think Art talked rightly about these different regulatory frameworks for the big money center commercial banks and the investment banks.

speaker: WARSH
text: We’d be doing ourselves a disservice over the period, Mr. Chairman, to take the regulatory regime that we have now had for a long time for these big complex commercial banks and try to put it on the investment banks.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’ll answer this the way I began.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have an opportunity to start with a blank sheet of paper, with four institutions over the period, and figure out how to be really, really good regulators, building on the lessons that we have learned from our traditional supervision and regulation function.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that we would be making a mistake by saying, “We have a model, and let’s throw it on these guys.” If we regulate these four institutions the way we have long been regulating commercial banks with the OCC and others, I think we won’t have maximized the best of regulation.

speaker: WARSH
text: The goal would be to figure out how to regulate these four right and then, frankly, to export those lessons to what we have long been doing to make regulation better and stronger across this group.

speaker: WARSH
text: If it turns out that we do to Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley what we have been doing to Citi and JPMorgan, as was suggested, we will find other people will be in the business of investment banking, so we won’t have done terribly much to mitigate systemic risk.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, on the question about the role for the Congress.

speaker: WARSH
text: Both in the medium term, Mr. Chairman, in the context of your speeches and as we get toward the end of July, when you announce some modification—if the FOMC agrees—about these facilities and the PDCF, it is very important that the Congress be given serious responsibility for this.

speaker: WARSH
text: It has been very easy for them to criticize, on the one hand, and to whisper to us all their support, on the other.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think they need to be given very important homework assignments in terms of what they can do.

speaker: WARSH
text: Some form of FDICIA with investment banks might be one example.

speaker: WARSH
text: Wrestling about these issues in terms of regulatory organizations strikes me as very consequential.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even if we could convince ourselves that we have all the regulatory authority to figure this out with our regulators, we would be better off, when we are ready and we have the right answer in our own view, to bring it to the Congress for final clarity and to get their imprimatur.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I agree with a lot of what Governor Warsh said and a lot of what has been said before.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Let me just take a slightly different tack answering the question that Governor Kohn raised: Why are we here?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Part of that is, because of the Glass- Steagall Act, we have this unusual structure in the United States.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Other central banks can provide credit much more easily to a wide variety of institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have a legacy that created this separation, which isn’t as strong in most other countries.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In continental Europe, for example, you just don’t really see this.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Then, we have built a regulatory regime that helped to promote that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Remember, the discussions have been about markets and the challenges in the markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, I think our regulatory regime, not just in the United States but throughout the world, helped promote the disintermediation to promote greater reliance on the markets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In certain ways this is a very good thing, but it creates exactly the kinds of problems and challenges that we are facing now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we need to be mindful of that and take that into account when we are thinking about what to do next in dealing with these issues.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Thinking about market resiliency and market infrastructure is crucial, but we also have to be mindful that, if we try to get things to migrate to the exchanges, to clearinghouses, et cetera, it is great for us as regulators, and it is also useful because the information is much more centralized.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But it also could create market dynamics, as President Evans said, that could lead to trying to get around that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Then the risky stuff goes OTC.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The risky stuff is in new institutions that we haven’t thought of yet.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: President Yellen mentioned some other institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We can mention hedge funds and money market mutual funds, but in five years there may be institutions that we haven’t even thought about.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: No matter what structure we set up, there would be ways to try to get around it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So we need to think about a regulatory regime that gets the costs and benefits right to make the different relevant institutions not bridle too much at being part of it and so to rethink the financial holding company structure.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If the investment banks had found the financial holding company structure an amenable one, then we wouldn’t be here either because we would have solved the Glass-Steagall legacy problem.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we haven’t quite done that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So actually exactly as Governor Warsh was saying—and believe it or not, we didn’t coordinate beforehand—I think that we should think about how to revise our general regulatory structure to get more institutions under this umbrella, not have them find it scary, upsetting, or disturbing but to see that we are doing it in a reasonable cost–benefit way.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I can see just in all the issues that we have been facing regarding some capital relief in particular circumstances— so-called 23.80 relief on particular types of transactions, issues of what’s included in the definition of a leverage ratio.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it gives us an opportunity to rethink why so many institutions find it onerous and are so lacking in desire to be part of this regime.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, there is some regulatory competition—President Rosengren, I think, brought that up—so we need to think of that as a whole.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This is part of the homework assignment that the Congress needs to think about—setting up a reasonable FDICIA-like regime for a broader set of institutions that would choose to come and be regulated by the Fed.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have been talking about where the bright lines are.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But if we okay someone to be a financial holding company, then they become part of our regime in the existing structure.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So the lines aren’t completely carefully drawn.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It really is sort of a cost–benefit analysis if someone chooses to apply.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So we need to think about that carefully and about the costs and benefits of getting people in because the long-term dynamics will be that people always try to get away from regulation unless they see that there is some sufficient benefit.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Being very mindful of that, both from the institution context and the broader context of the markets, is very important.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Oh, and I apologize—I fully support going ahead with extending the facility past the year-end.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I would make sure that it’s a bit more than just immediately past year- end and go some time into February so there are no questions about year-end.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I also strongly support the short-term strategy that was laid out by the Chairman.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t see that we really have an alternative in that context.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There are a lot of issues here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The reality is that this is super complex, and we have a lot of work over the next year to be ready for the next Administration, when all these issues are going to become extremely relevant.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In general terms, regarding the long-term issues, although we got here under exigent circumstances, in a financial disruption, we might have gotten here anyway.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The reality is that there was a fundamental change in the way the financial system works.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When banks are not so dominant, the distinction between investment banks and commercial banks in terms of the way the financial system works is really much less.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It would be nice to think that we could limit the kinds of lending facilities that we have so that we didn’t have to worry about regulating or supervising other institutions, but I don’t think that is realistic.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The nature of the changes in the financial system means that we extended the government safety net but it probably would have been extended anyway.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It was just unfortunate that it had to happen in such a crisis atmosphere.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I think we have to think very hard about the issue of limiting moral hazard in terms of a much wider range of institutions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am very sympathetic to the issues that President Stern raised, which is that we have to think about the kind of things that we have thought about more in terms of the banking industry: How do we actually set things up so that it is easier for firms to fail and not be systemic?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There are a smaller number of firms that we actually have to supervise and regulate, and the reality is that we have to think very hard about how we’re going to extend regulation and supervision to a wider range of firms.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We just can’t escape that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It would be nice to say that we could limit it, but we are not going to be able to limit it except to the extent that we can think about some of these issues.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But it is going to be a huge issue going forward, and we really have to be ready to deal with the political process.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The way we are proceeding makes a lot of sense.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is not committing us in a way that creates a problem, but we have to be ready when this issue is dealt with.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It will be one of the hottest issues that the next Administration and the next Congress will have to deal with.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have to be really on point and to have positions very carefully thought out, not just by the Board but by the entire FOMC and the entire System, so that we can have a unified position to make sure that crazy stuff doesn’t happen and that sensible stuff does.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I obviously support the strategy laid out.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just want to underscore, particularly in response to Governor Warsh’s comments, that this is in effect a conditional extension, in the sense that we are being careful to get ourselves more comfortable with where these four firms in particular are on capital and liquidity before we announce an extension.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are trying to get clarity on the ongoing supervisory relationship with the SEC before we announce an extension.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have already gotten the 18 major dealers in the world to commit themselves to a path to improve the capacity of the OTC derivatives infrastructure to withstand failure before announcing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have already begun to get the resources held against default risk in the existing central counterparties higher, in satisfaction of President Stern’s general admonition that we want the system better able to withstand failure.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think we are just beginning the delicate process of taking some of the air out of the vulnerable tri-party repos before the extension is announced.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So, in that sense, we have left ourselves in this strategy that the Chairman laid out with a little less vulnerability to the possible impression that we would just willy-nilly extend with no effort to make the system safer.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are not going to get far enough.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We are not going to know what’s far enough.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think we have a credible plan to say, “We took the initiative, even in a moment of incredible delicacy for dealing with the system, to try to get these institutions and the system in a better capacity to withstand the possibility of failure.” In that sense it’s a defensible and sensible strategy.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I really don’t know what the right mix of boundaries is on access to liquidity in normal times and in extremis and what mix of supervisory authority conditions with what type of resolution regime is optimal.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just don’t have a sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I feel as though I know the broad tradeoffs in it, but I don’t know what really looks ideal in terms of the mix of those things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You can make a pretty reasonable case for a whole bunch of variance in that mix of things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The complication for us is that we won’t be able to fully control the outcome because it is going to require legislation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Part of the consequence of the system that we live with and part of the reason that we live with the system we have today is that policymakers and regulators don’t fully control the outcome in terms of the incentives created in the legislation for these kinds of things.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So it will be difficult for us, but all we can do is focus on the merits, think through those ahead of everybody else, and try to have the best package of suggestions that we can.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But just to come back to what we spent most of the last two days talking about, let’s not lose sight of the fact that we are in the middle of this still.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It likely has a long way to go.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very hard for us to know now what we are going to decide at the end was the most critical source of vulnerability and, therefore, what to do to fix it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We don’t know what the market is going to think the new equilibrium should be in terms of the return on equity across different types of financial institutions and models.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Another reason to be careful as we try to contain the risks in this crisis and make the system stronger in the near term is so that we don’t prejudge some of those longer-term questions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I want to come back to one of Governor Warsh’s comments, just probe it a little further, because I was intrigued by his notion that in some way trying to wean ourselves from this he suggested that we raise the price.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It occurred to me in that same context, if we thought that had value in some sense, another way we could do the transition is to cut back either the frequency or the size of the TSLF, as we sort of wean the markets off access.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Announcing both those things in advance might have some value to us moving forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts and reactions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: First, I completely agree that, once we get to the point at which we believe the best policy is to dial this stuff back and transition to a world in which they don’t exist, we are going to want to look at a whole bunch of things—changing terms, changing the relative attractiveness across the auction facilities, thinking about size, and thinking about price.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that will be very important to do.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is very unlikely that the optimal path is going to be that there is a cliff—one day they are there, and the next day they aren’t.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I completely agree with that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My own judgment is—but it may not be right, and it could change over time—that for the moment we want to have a clean, crisp signal.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Better to say that we are going to extend in the context of these broader initiatives to strengthen the system and not at the same moment alter their terms and relative attractiveness.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But we are going to have to think very carefully over the fall, conditions permitting, and well ahead of whatever the new date is, what the desirable exit strategy is in changing incentives around use.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: However, my basic sense is not now, not yet, partly because of the complexity of the signal you are sending and the difficulty of how it will be interpreted.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have done all this stuff in part because we are trying to address a complicated mix of things around incentives, stigma, and that kind of thing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is hard for us to predict what the effect would be.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Its purpose is to wean, but to do it now would make the message a bit more complicated.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If the world is strong enough that you can wean them now, why are you extending?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So my basic sense is, absolutely, we are going to have to figure it out by the transition, not quite yet but well ahead of February 15 or whenever it is going to be.

speaker: LACKER
text: I support Governor Warsh’s suggestion for raising the price.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is hard for me to believe that confidence in any of these institutions depends materially on 100 basis points of the price.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is the access, the funding, that they would be able to use to fund withdrawal or flight by somebody.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it sends the right signal that we view this as exceptional.

speaker: LACKER
text: Conditions are certainly different than they were in March, when we designed and implemented it, and I think they are unlikely in the fall to be anywhere close to where they were on March 16.

speaker: LACKER
text: You might disagree, and we could always change things between now and then.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I like the signal of withdrawing the generosity just a tad.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Remember that we are doing moral suasion as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I mean, we are not really allowing investment banks to use this as a profit center.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I’m not quite sure what the marginal effect would be on incentives.

speaker: LACKER
text: But this would also place less weight on moral suasion to discourage and would use the price system a bit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It also might increase the stigma.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is a very complicated calculation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There are many things that I would love to do.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would like to make them pay for it and say that we are not going to extend it unless they pay for it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would like to say that we are not going to extend it unless they pre-fund some liquidation facility for one of their little counterparties.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There are a million things that I think would be good to do from an incentive angle—but not at the same time that we are trying to maximize the chance that we get through this and have the flexibility to let monetary policy adjust to the changing amounts of risk on the other side of the tail.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So there are a million things I think it would be cool to do, and we will have to do them.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We will design them really in a clever way once we are at the point where that is optimal, but I just don’t think that’s now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The risk is that it will undermine what we are trying to achieve with a fleeting “make us feel better” benefit.

speaker: WARSH
text: So just on behalf of the troublemaker caucus, [laughter] let me make a suggestion.

speaker: WARSH
text: It doesn’t strike me as though the deltas between Vice Chairman Geithner’s formulation and what I proffered are that large.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is, I think we collectively agree that we need, as part of an extension of the facility, to ensure that there is a suite of facilities and self-help efforts—tri-party repos, OTC derivatives, principles by you, and clarity on what the horizon looks like.

speaker: WARSH
text: I guess the only question is, At the time that you solicit the notation vote and announce this—let’s say that is the second half of July—how comfortable are we at how that package looks to suggest that we are keeping options open and that the signal we are sending is not that this is a business that we want to stay in forever?

speaker: WARSH
text: Maybe in that context we will see what kind of progress we are making in truth on some of those infrastructure improvements and in the narrative, so that we can revisit—I think maybe with some guidance from Brian, Bill, and the staff—what the incremental benefits are of a modest change to the PDCF in that context.

speaker: WARSH
text: By the second half of July, we might find that we are much more informed so as to weigh the benefits and costs of it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Bill Dudley, did you have a comment?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The real issue may be that the PDCF borrowing may be de minimis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In that environment, it’s not really clear what raising the price really means.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It might even be confusing to people if you raise the price at the time the borrowing was de minimis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think that is just one consideration.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no other pressing comments, thank you very much for this discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I heard general support for the short-term strategy, which means, I hope, that if we do come to ask you for an extension of the TSLF we can do it by notation vote without a videoconference meeting, unless things change.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There clearly is a lot of dissatisfaction among all of us about the ad hoc nature of the way we had to deal with the crisis in March.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We would all like much more clarity about our authorities, the limit of those authorities, and the match between our responsibilities and our authorities; and, as we go forward, we will try to get clarification on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At the same time, we also want to take steps to try to increase the resilience of the system and reduce the risk that we will be in the same situation again in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will try to vet my speech.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t want to overpromise.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has to be done over the Fourth of July weekend, so I expect everyone to be available 24/7 for commentary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I will generally be talking about things that we are doing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will talk only in general terms about some of the principles that we have discussed today about the need for clarification about how to resolve a troubled institution, how to set those limits, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I will try to circulate that, to the extent that it is feasible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s see, our next meeting is Tuesday, August 5.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You are invited to get lunch and come back to the table to hear Laricke Blanchard’s update on congressional matters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you have any revisions to your economic projections, you have until 5:00 p.m. tomorrow to send those in.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I want to thank—I haven’t done this—Art, Scott, Pat, and all of their colleagues, who have been working very hard on these issues, for their presentation and their hard work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Today is the last meeting for our colleague, Governor Mishkin.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Rick has attended 16 FOMC meetings as a Committee member and 23 additional meetings, I assume mostly as the research director for New York.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are certainly going to miss your singular interventions—[laughter] as well as your insights and your collegiality.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be a lunch today in honor of Rick, and we will have a chance then to express our appreciation for your time here and for your contributions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are comings and goings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Today is also the first meeting for Governor Duke, whom I was pleased to swear in about 15 minutes ago in my office.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It took an unconscionably long time for this qualified person to be confirmed by the U.S. Senate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are very glad that she had the patience to stick it out and that she is finally here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: She brings a great deal to the table, including a lot of experience in banking, which obviously is something of great interest to us these days.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We look forward to a long and productive association.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Turning to Desk operations, before Bill begins, a couple of issues were raised in our last videoconference.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One had to do with the concern about whether we have a sufficient balance sheet to address liquidity needs going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Bill, I believe you are going to talk a bit about that—give an interim report on where we are on balance sheet issues and what we might do in case those constraints start to bind.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second concern that was raised had to do with what we mean by “unusual and exigent” and how we determine whether those conditions are still prevailing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have asked Brian and the staff to put together a memo giving us some thoughts on that issue, and that will come to you before the next meeting and give us a chance to think about it and, as time permits, discuss it at the next meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am going to be referring to the handout in front of you.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It seems to be getting thicker at every meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Since the June FOMC meeting, financial markets have been characterized by two distinct phases.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Until the middle of July, share prices weakened substantially, and credit spreads widened.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The financial sector’s difficulties were at the forefront as housing- price declines continued to pressure this sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The IndyMac failure led to uninsured depositors taking losses, and this roiled the regional banking sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The equity prices of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac plummeted, and their ongoing viability was called into question.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The passage of housing legislation that provided support to the GSEs then led to an improvement in investor sentiment and a modest recovery in share prices.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 1, financial sector shares led the recovery.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, the overall improvement in the broad market indexes was very modest, both in the United States and abroad (exhibit 2).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, no meaningful improvement was evident in the corporate debt or CDS markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: CDS spreads have not changed much, and spreads of asset-backed securities have begun to widen again (exhibits 3 and 4).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Despite intermeeting news that I would characterize on balance as more bad than good, this news did not trigger the type of risk-reduction spasms by investors that have sporadically plagued financial markets over the past year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibits 5 and 6 compare the correlation of daily asset price changes across a broad array of asset classes in July to the corresponding period in March.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The blue boxes denote correlations with absolute values of more than 0.5.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As can be seen, asset price movements have become much less correlated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the mood is slightly improved today compared with a few weeks ago, the underlying news, especially from the financial sector, remains quite bleak in most respects.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, there is little conviction that financial shares have reached a bottom.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This can be seen in the unusually high volatility of financial share prices (exhibit 7) and the positive skew in options prices for financial firms, in which the price of a put has been much higher than an equivalent out-of-the money call (exhibit 8).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Financial market participants are paying more to protect the downside than to participate on the upside.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Merrill Lynch’s recent experience is reflective of the challenging environment faced by financial firms.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Merrill Lynch raised new equity capital and announced that it had sharply reduced its net ABS CDO exposure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Investors were initially pleased that the company had bitten the bullet, and the share price rallied in response.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But further consideration tempered the initial enthusiasm—and there are more articles on this in the Wall Street Journal today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A closer look revealed some troubling aspects of the transactions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, Merrill Lynch took an additional $4.4 billion of CDO write- downs from the June quarter-end valuation date.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Merrill Lynch sold CDO exposures with a par value of $30.6 billion to Lone Star for $6.7 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At quarter-end, these positions had been carried on the books for $11.1 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, this transaction resulted in a drop in net CDO exposure of only $1.7 billion because Merrill Lynch 1 The materials used by Mr. Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: provided 75 percent nonrecourse financing to Lone Star.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Merrill Lynch gave away all the upside on these assets in exchange for a payment equal to 6 percent of their par value.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, Merrill Lynch’s equity issuance reportedly resulted in 38 percent dilution to existing shareholders.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The dilution was exacerbated by the terms of an earlier share issuance agreement with Temasek, a Singapore sovereign wealth fund.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This agreement granted Temasek a “make whole” provision if, within 12 months, common stock was issued at a price below Temasek’s $48 per share investment.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This resulted in Merrill Lynch’s paying $2.5 billion to Temasek, which Temasek then rolled into a new $3.4 billion share investment.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Over the past month, the troubles of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have taken center stage.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Rising loan delinquencies for prime single-family mortgages caused share prices to plunge.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This eroded confidence that the firms would be able to raise new equity capital and raised concerns about the viability of these firms.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This, in turn, intensified the downward pressure on share prices.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, investors began to lose their enthusiasm for the firms’ debt.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Investors in short-term discount notes were uninterested in taking on any potential credit risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, issuance volumes fell, and discount note rates climbed (exhibits 9 and 10).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Some investors in the firms’ longer-term debt obligations—including some major foreign central banks—became unwilling to add to their long-term agency debt and agency MBS positions, and one or two of the central banks actually cut their positions somewhat.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, longer- term debt spreads did not change much because the loss of central bank demand was offset by buying from U.S. fixed-income asset managers, who believed that the implicit Treasury support of GSE debt was likely to be hardened (exhibit 11).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fannie and Freddie responded by issuing less debt.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To husband their liquidity, the two firms have backed away from purchasing agency mortgage-backed securities for their own portfolios.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The removal of this bid was one factor that caused the mortgage basis— the spreads between the option-adjusted yield on agency MBS and other benchmark yields, such as Treasuries and interest rate swaps—to widen significantly (exhibit 12).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Congress responded by enacting housing legislation that included provisions that hardened the implicit government guarantee and, thus, reduced debt rollover risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Treasury now has authority to lend the GSEs an unlimited amount of funds, the magnitude being constrained only by the debt-limit ceiling.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In response, discount note issuance costs have fallen in the most recent auctions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, enactment of the legislation has not generated any comparable narrowing in the mortgage basis or resolved the longer-term outlook for the GSEs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The mortgage basis remains wide in part because Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have few incentives to expand their balance sheets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although their regulatory capital is still well above minimum levels, these capital standards are under review.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, because further losses are likely in coming quarters, it is unclear how long this excess capital will be available to support portfolio growth.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, the two firms could respond by issuing new equity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, the low level of these companies’ share prices makes this option unattractive.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To raise sufficient funds to ensure long-term viability would cause massive dilution for existing shareholders.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To put this in perspective, the current market capitalization of Freddie Mac is only about $5 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This compares with a book of business in terms of its portfolio and guaranteed book of $2.2 trillion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because the GSEs will likely remain reluctant to expand their balance sheets in the near term, the mortgage basis will probably remain elevated, keeping mortgage rates high.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This will intensify the downward pressure on housing activity and prices, which in turn will lead to greater loan delinquencies and losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The consequence will likely put further pressure on Fannie’s and Freddie’s capital positions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So what’s the bottom line?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In my view, the legislation has helped to avert—at least for now—a meltdown in the agency debt and agency MBS markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the passage is no panacea for ensuring the viability of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac or in enabling the two firms to provide significant support to the U.S. housing market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One consequence of the GSE-related turbulence was a temporary pickup in demand in the most recent schedule 1 TSLF auction, on July 25 (exhibit 13).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As term mortgage agency repo spreads widened relative to term Treasury repo rates, the cost of borrowing via the TSLF became more attractive.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This illustrates how the TSLF program can act as a shock absorber and reduce volatility in term repo rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: With the exception of the July 25 auction, the TSLF auctions continue to be undersubscribed with relatively stable bid-to-cover ratios.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast to the turbulence evident in the financial sector, the bank term funding markets have been relatively stable since the June FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 14 and 15, the spreads of one-month LIBOR and three-month LIBOR to OIS remain elevated in the United States, Europe, and the United Kingdom.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, this masks the fact that forward funding rates appear to have risen significantly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 16, the forward three-month LIBOR–OIS spread has risen about 20 basis points over the past three months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This spread is now anticipated to remain elevated at around 50 basis points on a one-to-two-year time horizon, indicating that market participants expect term funding pressures to persist for the foreseeable future.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Before the crisis, the spread was about 10 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The U.S. TAF auctions also show a stable trend.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 17, the bid- to-cover ratio remains around 1.2 to 1, and the stop-out rate has been quite steady over the past five auctions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, as shown in exhibit 18, the bid-to-cover ratio for the ECB dollar auction continues to climb.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As I noted in an earlier briefing, part of this rise reflects the fact that the ECB auction is noncompetitive.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The bids are prorated, and the banks pay the U.S stop-out rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Larger bids by European banks in the ECB auction do not affect the interest rate they pay for such funding, and that encourages more-aggressive bidding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Conversations with the ECB staff indicate that they are concerned that the outcome could be a bidding spiral.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Individual banks could keep raising the size of their bid submissions to ensure a stable amount of dollar funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is possible that these pressures could eventually encourage the ECB to switch to a Swiss National Bank type of multiple-price auction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This would eliminate the incentives to bid more and more aggressively on the part of the European banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, such a change probably would result in a higher stop-out rate in the ECB auctions compared with the United States or Switzerland.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: ECB officials might not be fully comfortable with such an outcome.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Early reactions by primary dealers and depository institutions to the two refinements to our liquidity facilities—the $50 billion program of options on the TSLF and the introduction of the longer, 84-day, maturity TAF auctions—have been favorable.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We recently—last Friday and this Monday—completed an extensive set of interviews with the primary dealer community about the TSLF options program and will be proposing final terms, within the set of parameters approved by the FOMC on July 24, by the end of this week.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, we will keep you fully apprised as we go forward on this.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you know, our liquidity facilities have placed significant demands on the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet, as the Chairman mentioned.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As the liquidity facilities have been expanded, we have reduced the size of our Treasury portfolio.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We do this to drain the reserves added by our liquidity programs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The use of our balance sheet to sterilize these reserve additions has raised questions about whether sufficient capacity is still available to meet prospective demand—especially a large unanticipated rise in PDCF or PCF borrowing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 19 illustrates the transformation of the Federal Reserve System’s balance sheet over the past year, out of Treasuries into non-Treasury lending.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 20, the non-Treasury portion consists mainly of $150 billion of TAF loans, the $62 billion (in steady state) of foreign exchange swaps executed with the ECB and the SNB, and our $80 billion 28-day maturity, single-tranche repo program.

speaker: DUDLEY
