text: Although the amount of Treasuries held in the SOMA portfolio still totals $479 billion, a majority of these securities are encumbered in one way or another.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 21, from that $479 billion we need to allocate $45 billion of Treasuries to collateralize the foreign central bank repo pool, retain $35 billion of on-the-run Treasury securities to keep available for our traditional Treasury securities lending program, and set aside $175 billion for the TSLF program and now an additional $50 billion for the TSLF options program (TOP).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When the options program is included, we have about $174 billion of unencumbered Treasuries available to offset additional PCF and PDCF borrowing or to fund further expansion of our liquidity programs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, further expansion of our TAF or TSLF auctions or single-tranche repo operations would be at our discretion and, thus, does not pose a meaningful problem in terms of reserve management.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We wouldn’t expand these programs if we didn’t have the ability to conduct offsetting reserve draining operations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, what would we do if faced with a huge rise in PCF or PDCF borrowing?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: An inability to drain the reserves added by such lending would cause the federal funds rate to collapse below the target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fortunately, we have a number of alternatives that would enable us to offset very large demands for PCF or PDCF borrowing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, we could sell our remaining unencumbered Treasury holdings or use them to engage in reverse repo operations with the primary dealer community.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This could be augmented by the $35 billion of on-the-run Treasury securities currently set aside for securities lending.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Together, these two sources could be used to drain more than $200 billion of reserves.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, we have made arrangements with the Treasury so that, if the need arises, the Treasury would issue special Treasury bills into the market on our behalf and take the proceeds and deposit them at the Federal Reserve.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Putting the proceeds of such T-bill sales on the Fed’s balance sheet would drain reserves from the banking system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The potential scope here is large.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The housing legislation raised the debt limit substantially.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There is now about $1.2 trillion of headroom under the debt limit compared with only about $400 billion previously.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, we continue to press for legislation that would accelerate the timing of the Federal Reserve’s authority to pay interest on reserves.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Being able to pay interest on reserves would put a floor under the federal funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In this case, an inability to drain additional reserves from the banking system would not result in the federal funds rate collapsing toward zero.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, we continue to explore the legal and operational feasibility of expanding our balance sheet in other ways.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, could we engage in reverse repurchase transactions using the collateral obtained from our single-tranche repo and from our TSLF operations?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I wouldn’t say I am confident that we can handle any eventuality—after all, the triparty repo system provides trillions of dollars of funding to the primary dealers.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the unlikely event that it all came to us, we wouldn’t have the capacity to fully offset it at present.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But we could accommodate hundreds of billions of dollars of demand if that proved to be necessary.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That said, I want to go on record that any very large unanticipated demand for funding from the Federal Reserve by dealers or depository institutions might take a few days or more to offset by reserve-draining operations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Thus, in such a circumstance, the federal funds rate could temporarily trade below its target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Turning now to interest rate expectations, monetary policy expectations have reverted back to the very slow path toward tightening that was evident before the April FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 22 and 23, the federal funds rate and Eurodollar futures curves have shifted down sharply since the June FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Our current survey of the primary dealers shows an even slower anticipated pace of tightening.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 24, the average of the dealer forecasts in our most recent survey anticipates no tightening until the second quarter of 2009.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the change in the dealers’ forecasts since the June FOMC meeting is more modest than the shift in market expectations (compare exhibits 24 and 25).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Looking at the probabilities of different rate outcomes implied by options on federal funds rate futures in exhibits 26 and 27, one sees that there has been a steady trend upward in the probability that the FOMC will keep its policy target rate unchanged at both the August and the September FOMC meetings.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Note also that the probability assigned by market participants to further easing is lower than the probability assigned to tightening.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The past month has been marked by a significant decline in commodity prices.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 28, although the energy complex has led the way down, agriculture and industrial metals prices have also declined significantly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These declines have spurred a large decline in breakeven rates of inflation measured by the spread of nominal Treasury and TIPS yields (exhibit 29).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 30, longer-term market-based indicators of inflation expectations have increased a bit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Both the Barclays’ and the Board staff’s measures of five-year, five-year-forward inflation implied by nominal Treasury versus TIPS yields have drifted upward since the June FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, both measures remain well below the peaks reached in early March.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There were no foreign operations during this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I request a vote to ratify the operations conducted by the System Open Market Account since the June FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As always, I am very happy to take any questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you very much, Bill.

speaker: EVANS
text: Bill, at our recent intermeeting call, I wasn’t expecting the characterization of the financial stresses to sort of backtrack to the point that it feels like March.

speaker: EVANS
text: Maybe somebody said it was as scary as March.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have noticed in a lot of our speeches that many have noted that financial conditions have not returned to normal, and I have always kind of wondered what “normal” would be.

speaker: EVANS
text: With hundreds of billions of dollars of losses at major financial institutions, I guess I am wondering whether we can reasonably expect that this distress and adjustment will be alleviated over some reasonably short period of time.

speaker: EVANS
text: We are 12 months in.

speaker: EVANS
text: Isn’t this likely to take 12 more months or longer?

speaker: EVANS
text: Financial institutions have a lot to digest.

speaker: EVANS
text: What do you think financial institutions and markets have to do to signal a return to acceptable functionality?

speaker: EVANS
text: What are we looking for, and what changes in fundamentals are likely to occur that would deliver sustainable liquidity improvements?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is a big question.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think this is a good time to revisit our strategy and what we are thinking about accomplishing here.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is my understanding that the Chairman has asked you to look at unusual and exigent circumstances.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the first thing we can say is that market participants expect this to last a long time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The fact that the forward LIBOR–OIS spreads are elevated, looking out a year or two years, suggests that the market views the balance sheet adjustment process as taking quite a long time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, I would say that how long is really going to depend in part on how the macroeconomy evolves.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If the macroeconomy evolves in a favorable way, then the losses that will be borne by the financial sector will be discretely smaller, and so you can get through this process sooner.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, if the economy has a bad macroeconomic outcome, then obviously this is going to be a lot worse.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We don’t really know the answer to that yet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Part of that is also going to be very sensitive to what happens in terms of individual institutions over the next 6 to 12 months because we are putting a tremendous amount of strain on the financial sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If there is little breakage, then the chance of our getting through relatively quickly, say in 12 months, is pretty high.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But if that stress creates failures and systemic contagion because of those failures, then this could last quite a long time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the answer is that we don’t really know yet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think there is a long way to go.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are about one year in, by my measure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I date this back to August 9, when the ECB did their massive reserve intervention.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I wouldn’t want to make a bet on what inning this is, but it is definitely not the ninth inning.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I want to follow up on that a little because it seems to me that, over a year ago now, there was a lot of discussion by various parties that had to do with risk premiums being very low.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: People were worried that the economy and the financial markets were underpricing risk.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, all of a sudden, these spreads have increased.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If you look at the OIS spread that you referred to, the one-to-two years out, is there a possibility that this is permanent—that in some sense the level of spreads in the pricing of the risk is just now higher and it is going to stay higher, maybe not as high as the peak but at some higher level?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If that is true, then using those spreads as a measure of how distressed the market is could be very misleading.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As a consequence, it would seem as though you would want to be asking questions not just about the prices and the spreads but also about volumes in these markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Maybe, Bill, you can elaborate on what volumes are doing—certainly in the near-term, the overnight, and the one-month interbank funding markets?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are volumes back to their levels even though the spreads are higher?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we have to be a little careful that, if this really is a permanent shift in risk premiums, looking at these things may be the wrong metric for assessing what is going on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If you have any observations about that, I would like to hear them.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think it is a fair point that we shouldn’t assume that “normal” is returning to the LIBOR–OIS spreads that applied before August 2007, so we have to look at a broader set of indicators.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, I think that it would be worthwhile looking at the spread between jumbo mortgage rates and conforming mortgage rates as evidence of the degree of the shadow price of balance sheet capacity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that, once financial institutions either raise sufficient capital or stop taking loan-loss provisions or writing down assets so that they have enough capacity to expand their balance sheets, we will be getting to the end of this process.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Another thing I would say to add to the answer I gave earlier to President Evans is that the trajectory of housing in all of this is going to be hugely important.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One thing that may signal the next phase, maybe the beginning of the end, is when people really do get a sign that the housing sector is starting to bottom, probably first in activity and then in price.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Once that happens, the huge risk premium embedded in some of these mortgage-related assets will then collapse.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That means that the mark-to-market losses in a lot of institutions will start to fall.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think that is going to be a very, very important metric once housing starts to really bottom and people get some visibility about how much home prices will go down.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You know, when the argument is about whether home prices are going to go down 15 percent or 20 percent, that will be a very different argument from the argument now, which is whether home prices are going to go down 15 percent or 30 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that the market function has varied, frankly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the middle of the GSE turmoil, the agency market was basically shut down.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: With the passage of the legislation, it has improved.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Haircuts are still quite elevated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Liquidity is certainly not as good as it was back before this crisis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The cost of funding through the FX swap market is still very elevated relative to LIBOR.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think things are improving, though, in the sense that shocks are not as broadly contagious as they were before.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The reason is that people now are pretty cognizant of what the problems are; and so when there are new, bad pieces of information, people aren’t quite as shocked, and they don’t revise their outlook to the same degree about a whole variety of asset classes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think that is why the correlation slide that I showed you in the exhibits showed less of a correlation between different asset classes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are still getting tremendous amounts of movement in asset prices, but it doesn’t seem as though, if something happens in one sector, it necessarily ripples through to other sectors.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’m just following up here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I mean, as much as I love exhibits 14, 15, and 16—and I have used a lot of them myself when I talk about the economy—it is not really appropriate to look at these as measures of stress.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You could just say that these are the equilibrium prices in an economy that is adjusting to a big shock.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You could have a completely flat line here that would indicate stress in markets because these prices aren’t moving around appropriately to the risks that have developed and opened up.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So a lot of the concern around the table has been exactly that, when markets freeze up, you can’t do any trade at any price; and for that the volume data would seem to be a much better indicator of the kinds of things that we are worried about.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that this is conditioning a lot of our thinking about the economy—you look at this picture, and you naturally think it has to go back to 10 basis points before the crisis is over.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That probably is not going to happen anytime soon and maybe never.

speaker: LACKER
text: I thought that part of President Evans’s question was whether markets are back to normal for a period in which they are adjusting to hundreds of billions of dollars of losses on mortgage loans.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I would be interested in your characterization of how markets are working relative to how well they ought to work in that circumstance.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I guess we don’t have a lot of observations to know what normal is in that environment.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that the markets are generally doing somewhat better, as I said, relative to the flow of new information.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think the information flow has improved, but I think the markets are responding a little better to the bad information.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is how I would characterize it.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I could follow up, the reactions you described sound warranted by the information coming in.

speaker: LACKER
text: The market is digesting information about the location and magnitude of losses and the extent to which housing is going to recover.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the market is reacting pretty appropriately to the information it is seeing, although I would say that the risk premiums are still high in a pretty broad array of assets relative to what one would think would be normal.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Haircuts are high, and market liquidity is still impaired.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are definitely not back to normal market function in a pretty broad array of asset classes.

speaker: LACKER
text: But when you use “normal” in that sentence, you mean a time period without hundreds of millions of dollars of losses that we don’t know quite the magnitude of, right?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is hard to benchmark how markets are supposed to behave in a period with hundreds of billions of dollars of losses—because how many times have we actually gone through this experience?

speaker: LACKER
text: So if I could just follow up—in these graphs, what would you point to as the effects of our actions or our lending?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The effects of our actions have been to mitigate the rise in term funding pressures and to somewhat mitigate the forced liquidation of collateral because of the inability to obtain funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because of that, our actions have helped prevent the kind of pernicious margin spiral that we saw in March, when volatility was going up and haircuts were going up, which was then causing mark-to-market losses, which were causing forced selling.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think our actions have mitigated those to some degree.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, obviously, we don’t know what the counterfactual would have been in the absence of our actions, but I believe—and most market participants believe—that our actions have been helpful in those respects.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess I would comment that there is an asymmetry here, which is the possibility of systemic risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are situations in which failures—major collapses of certain markets—can have discontinuous and large effects on the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have seen that in many contexts across a large number of countries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: These stresses do reflect the working out of equilibriums given fundamental losses, which we can’t do very much or anything about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But they do create machinery that is less flexible and less able to respond to new shocks, and that raises systemic risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is the risk that we want to try to minimize, even as we allow the markets to work their way through and to price the changes we have seen.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have never argued that the role of our facilities is to prevent the adjustment.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have always argued that the role of the facilities is to allow the adjustment to be orderly rather than disorderly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is what we have been going for.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would be interested in seeing a model, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any other questions for Bill?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let me turn to David Wilcox for the economic situation.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In putting together the economic outlook for the current Greenbook, we confronted three main changes in circumstances relative to the situation as it stood in June.

speaker: WILCOX
text: First, the labor market looked distinctly weaker than we had anticipated.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In the employment report that was released in early July, payroll employment declined by more in June than we had been expecting, and the unemployment rate held at 5½ percent rather than dropping back as we had anticipated, following the increase of 0.5 percentage point in the previous month.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The fraction of the labor force working part time for economic reasons had moved up sharply, and claims for unemployment insurance were trending up.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The second major change in circumstance that we confronted was a second- quarter increase in real GDP that apparently continued to outpace our expectations.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In last Wednesday’s Greenbook, we projected growth at an annual rate of 2.7 percent in the second quarter, 1 percentage point stronger than in the June Greenbook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: At that pace, GDP growth would have slightly exceeded our estimate of the rate of growth of potential output.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The third major change was a financial sector that looked more hostile to economic activity, on balance, than at the time of the last meeting despite the improvement during the second half of the intermeeting period that Bill Dudley has just described.

speaker: WILCOX
text: When we put the Greenbook to bed, the stock market was about 7 percent lower than we had expected as of June, a variety of spreads remained wide or had widened further since the previous Greenbook, and concerns had been heightened about some key institutions.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In addition, the latest reading from the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey pointed to a remarkably widespread continued tightening of terms and standards for both households and businesses.

speaker: WILCOX
text: These three factors—a weaker labor market, apparently stronger aggregate demand, and a more hostile financial environment—did not easily fit together.

speaker: WILCOX
text: To resolve the situation, we began by ruling in favor of the profile presented by the labor market and heavily discounting the greater vigor being signaled by the spending indicators.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In our judgment, the story being told by the labor market seemed by far the more credible one, what with housing prices continuing to decline at a rapid pace, consumer sentiment dropping into sub-basement levels, energy prices remaining high even after their recent partial reversal, loan officers reporting a pervasive tightening of credit terms and standards, and other measures of financial stress flashing at least amber.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Moreover, while quarter-to-quarter discrepancies between GDP and IP are commonplace, the nearly 4 percent drop in manufacturing IP during the second quarter fueled our skepticism that the economy was on a fundamentally sound footing.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As you know, for several Greenbooks our GDP projection has been substantially weaker than it would have been if we had kept in line with the advice from our forecasting models.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We were motivated to impose this judgmental weakness partly in recognition of the possibility that we might be entering a recession, and recessions are times when spending tends to fall short of the level that would be indicated by the fundamentals.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We also were motivated by the restraint that we think financial markets are imposing on real activity and which our models are ill-equipped to capture.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In the current projection, we had to modify these assumptions in light of the changed circumstances.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In effect, we interpreted the greater-than-expected strength of real GDP during the second quarter as reflecting an error of timing with respect to the judgmental weakness that we had built into the forecast but not a misjudgment about the overall magnitude of that weakness.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Implementing that interpretation involved three steps.

speaker: WILCOX
text: First, we responded to the unexpected strength in first-half GDP growth by shifting some judgmental weakness into the second half.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Second, we deepened the overall amount of restraint that we imposed in light of the less favorable financial climate.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Third, we stretched out the period of financial recuperation: Whereas previously we had financial market conditions essentially returning to normal by the middle of next year, in this projection we have the period of recuperation extending into 2010.

speaker: WILCOX
text: These adjustments left our projection for real GDP growth 0.1 percentage point lower over the second half of this year and 0.2 lower next year, despite the offsets from lower oil prices and a slightly greater dose of fiscal stimulus, reflecting the introduction of extended unemployment insurance benefits.

speaker: WILCOX
text: For the most part, the avalanche of information that we received since putting out the Greenbook last Wednesday has corroborated our projection.

speaker: WILCOX
text: This year’s revision of the national income and product accounts threw us no real curve balls.

speaker: WILCOX
text: (Sorry for the baseball analogy.)

speaker: WILCOX
text: The growth of real GDP was revised down by an average of 0.2 percentage point per year.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The revisions to the PCE price indexes, both core and total, were very slight.

speaker: WILCOX
text: While the BEA has given us some homework to do between now and the September meeting in folding these data into our thinking, any adjustments that we might be prompted to make, including to the supply side of our forecast, are likely to be slight.

speaker: WILCOX
text: On the face of it, the advance estimate of real GDP growth in the second quarter of this year seemed to hold a bigger surprise.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The BEA’s estimate, at 1.9 percent, came in ¾ percentage point below our estimate in the Greenbook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: However, as best as we can tell—based on still-incomplete information—the miss was attributable to lower estimates by the BEA of farm inventory investment and of value added in the trading of used motor vehicles.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Our preliminary reading is that neither of these errors carries any signal for the forward momentum of the economy moving into the second half of the year.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Friday’s employment report was likewise mercifully well behaved— at least in the narrow sense of conforming to our expectation.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Private payroll employment declined an estimated 76,000 in July; together with small downward revisions to May and June, that left the level of employment in July very close to our forecast.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In addition, the unemployment rate came in only a few basis points higher than we had expected.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The only real news since Greenbook publication came from the motor vehicle manufacturers.

speaker: WILCOX
text: On Friday, they reported that sales of light vehicles in July were at an annual pace of 12.5 million units, much weaker than our already weak forecast of 13.3 million units.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Moreover, they knocked their assembly schedules for the third quarter down from 9.4 million units to 8.9 million units.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Taking their schedules on board would slice another ½ percentage point from our estimate of GDP growth in the third quarter.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The manufacturers have already announced increases in incentives, but it remains to be seen how vigorously consumers will respond in the current environment and how great the financial wherewithal of the manufacturers will prove to be to sustain such moves.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In any event, the drop in sales and production is certainly large enough to give renewed urgency to the question as to whether a broader retrenchment in spending might be in train.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Turning to the inflation side of the projection, our forecast for core PCE prices over the remainder of this year is nearly unchanged from the June Greenbook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We still have core inflation stepping up from a little more than 2 percent during the first half of this year to a little more than 2½ percent in the second half, as the surge in prices for imports, energy, and other commodities passes through to retail prices and as some components that saw unusually low readings earlier in the year accelerate to a more normal rate of increase.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Next year, with the pressures from import, energy, and commodity prices diminishing and with slack in resource utilization becoming a little greater, we have core inflation dropping back to 2¼ percent.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The projection for next year is also the same as in the June Greenbook, as the influences from lower energy prices and slightly greater economic slack are roughly offset by the pass- through of higher import prices.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The more dramatic changes in our inflation outlook came in the noncore pieces.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Not surprisingly, the plunge in oil prices since the June meeting caused us to whack our forecast for retail energy price inflation over the second half of this year.

speaker: WILCOX
text: For next year, however, we marked up PCE energy price inflation a little, partly because natural gas futures prices have a more positive tilt than they did before and partly because gasoline margins will still have some recovering to do.

speaker: WILCOX
text: At the same time, we have become more pessimistic about the outlook for food price inflation.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The CPI for food in June came in at 0.8 percent, much higher than our forecast of 0.3 percent.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Because we have mostly been surprised to the upside thus far this year, we decided to move closer to our food price model, which has been calling for larger increases than we were previously willing to write down.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The net result, as you saw in the Greenbook, is an outlook with faster food price inflation despite the fact that futures curves for both livestock and crops have moved down since the last meeting.

speaker: WILCOX
text: All told, we now have headline PCE inflation running at an average annual pace of 3½ percent over the second half of this year, nearly 1 percentage point slower than in the June Greenbook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: For next year, we have marked up total PCE inflation by a few tenths in light of our reassessment of the food price situation and the slightly greater rise in energy prices that we now see next year.

speaker: WILCOX
text: With regard to the risks in the outlook, my sense is that the downside risks to economic activity have increased since the time of the June Greenbook.

speaker: WILCOX
text: That view is informed by two main factors: First, while we have factored the more unsettled nature of the financial environment into our baseline outlook, the situation seems more fragile than before, and the implications for real activity of a sharp deterioration in financial conditions could be quite large.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The first alternative scenario that we presented in the Greenbook—entitled “severe financial stress”—updates our periodic attempt to assemble an integrated macroeconomic and financial scenario.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Second, the deterioration in the motor vehicles sector now, to my eye, more convincingly takes on the profile of what we usually see in the course of a typical recession.

speaker: WILCOX
text: During the intermeeting period, we will be on high alert for evidence suggesting that the weakness in vehicle sales is a harbinger of a broader shortfall in consumer spending.

speaker: WILCOX
text: As for inflation, the upside risks have, in my view, diminished somewhat.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Again, two factors inform this assessment.

speaker: WILCOX
text: First, the downtick in the long-term inflation expectations measured in the Reuters/Michigan survey is somewhat reassuring.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Second, the drop in oil prices is a welcome relief from the steady drumbeat of bad news from that sector and suggests a somewhat diminished probability that persistently high topline inflation will be reflected in a more serious erosion of household expectations, with all the adverse implications for monetary policy that would entail.

speaker: WILCOX
text: To be sure, even with those favorable developments, upside risks remain.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We illustrated one such risk in the scenario entitled “inflationary spiral,” in which we posited an initial shock to inflation expectations of 50 basis points followed by an adverse feedback loop that causes actual and expected inflation to chase each other up nearly 1 percentage point above baseline.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Monetary policy eventually brings the process under control but only over a lengthy period of time, partly because the rule that we use in the simulations has policy responding to actual but not to expected inflation.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Steve Kamin will now continue our presentation.

speaker: KAMIN
text: For the next couple of weeks, millions of people around the world will be watching the Olympic games in Beijing.

speaker: KAMIN
text: For those of us charged with forecasting the global economy, of course, China-watching is a year-round task.

speaker: KAMIN
text: But notably, the most salient developments since your last meeting have arisen outside of China.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Chief among them, of course, have been the precipitous fluctuations in the price of oil.

speaker: KAMIN
text: When the last FOMC meeting concluded on June 25, the spot price of WTI crude oil was running at $134 per barrel.

speaker: KAMIN
text: It soared to over $145 by mid-July before plunging to about $119 as of this morning.

speaker: KAMIN
text: The $26 per barrel drop over a three-week period was the largest on record in nominal dollar terms, although in percent terms, the 18 percent decline we’ve seen has been exceeded on a couple of occasions in recent years.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Notably, many other commodity prices, especially those for natural gas and many food crops, also declined sharply.

speaker: KAMIN
text: It has been heartening, and a welcome change, to see oil prices undershoot rather than overshoot our previous forecast.

speaker: KAMIN
text: But it would be premature to pop open the champagne.

speaker: KAMIN
text: We’ve seen several other steep declines in oil prices in recent years that gave way to renewed upward surges, and it remains to be seen whether an important shift in the supply–demand balance has occurred.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Saudi Arabia added a total of 400,000 barrels a day to its production of oil in May and June, and there are indications that its production rose in July, too.

speaker: KAMIN
text: However, these increases bring total OPEC production up only to their level in early 2006, and the world economy has grown considerably larger since then.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Analysts have cited gloomier forecasts of global economic growth, and thus global oil demand, as contributing to the weaker oil prices; but those forecasts have been coming down for the past year with little apparent effect.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Although oil consumption in the industrial economies clearly has slowed over the past year, we have yet to see either a concerted buildup in U.S. oil inventories or any indications that oil demand among developing countries is slowing.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Therefore, a further lurch upward in oil prices is a distinct possibility.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Moreover, with spot and futures prices having first soared and then plunged since your last meeting, the relatively flat path of oil prices that we are projecting is only about $12 per barrel lower, on balance, than in the previous forecast.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In the meantime, indicators of foreign growth have come in a bit weaker than we expected, and inflation readings have been on the high side.

speaker: KAMIN
text: These gloomier aspects of the international outlook counterbalance, to some extent, the improved tone of oil and other commodity markets.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Clearly, prospects appear weakest in the advanced economies.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Consistent with our earlier forecasts of a sharp deceleration in activity, we estimate that growth in all four of our largest industrial country trading partners—Canada, the euro area, the United Kingdom, and Japan—came in below 1 percent in the second quarter.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In the United Kingdom, a sharp contraction in the housing sector appears set to drag the economy into a mild recession in the second half of this year.

speaker: KAMIN
text: The remaining major economies should skirt recession but remain quite weak in the near term amid slackening export performance, continued stresses in financial markets, tightening credit standards, and very sharp erosions in business and consumer confidence.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Why are the foreign industrial economies slowing about as much as in the United States, when the subprime crisis originated in this country and the major drag on the U.S. economy is the slump in a nontradables sector, housing?

speaker: KAMIN
text: Clearly, part of the story involves the international financial linkages that have led foreign markets and institutions to share in the stresses and losses induced by the U.S. subprime crisis.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Another part of the story involves a common shock—the global boom in oil and food prices—that has cut into real household income and spending around the globe.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Third, even as the persistent decline in the dollar since 2002 has buoyed U.S. exports and growth, this has come at the cost of trade performance and economic activity in our trading partners.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Finally, the foreign industrial countries have enjoyed little or none of the substantial monetary and fiscal stimulus we’ve seen in the United States over the past year.

speaker: KAMIN
text: We estimate that growth in the emerging market economies also slowed further in the second quarter, to a pace of roughly 4 percent, where we have it staying for the remainder of the year.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Obviously, this is well above the growth rate of roughly 1 percent that we’ve penciled in for the industrial economies, but it is still below their likely potential rate as many developing countries struggle with softening export demand and rising food and energy prices.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Notably, however, even after slowing in the second quarter, estimated Chinese growth powered on at about 10 percent.

speaker: KAMIN
text: By 2009, we see both foreign advanced and emerging market economies accelerating as financial stresses ease, the U.S. economy picks up, and commodity prices stop restraining the growth of real household incomes.

speaker: KAMIN
text: This recovery scenario depends crucially on our projection that headline inflation starts moving down within the next quarter or two, so that substantial monetary tightening is not needed.

speaker: KAMIN
text: The recent decline in oil and other commodities prices provides some comfort that this scenario will materialize.

speaker: KAMIN
text: However, we saw some surprisingly sharp increases in consumer prices in June, bringing 12-month headline inflation to around 4 percent in the euro area and the United Kingdom, 5¼ percent in Mexico, and 6 percent in Brazil.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In most of our major trading partners, inflation excluding energy and food prices has remained better contained; and in China, headline inflation has actually moved down from its February peak of 8.7 percent, registering 7.1 percent in June.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Even so, until we see several quarters in a row of declines in aggregate measures of inflation, we will not be out of the woods.

speaker: KAMIN
text: So far, the imprint of slowing foreign growth and rising foreign inflation on the U.S. external sector has been limited but not negligible.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Turning first to prices, core import price inflation has moved up sharply, from about 3 percent last year to 11 percent in the second quarter; this was the fastest quarterly increase since 1987.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Most of this acceleration was concentrated in material-intensive goods, such as food and industrial supplies, and was likely due to rising commodity prices rather than to more-generalized pricing pressures abroad.

speaker: KAMIN
text: However, inflation in imported finished goods also increased this year.

speaker: KAMIN
text: As we noted in a special box in the Greenbook, prices of imports from China have been moving up briskly as a result of increases in domestic costs and in the value of the renminbi.

speaker: KAMIN
text: This step-up in the so-called China price explains less than one-fifth of the overall acceleration of core import prices but about one-third of the run-up in inflation for finished goods imports.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Even so, assuming commodity prices stabilize going forward, we expect changes in overall core import prices to slow quite substantially in coming quarters.

speaker: KAMIN
text: So far, U.S. external sector performance has held up well in spite of the slowing global economy.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Net exports added 2¼ percentage points to real GDP growth in the second quarter, the largest quarterly positive contribution since 1980.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Admittedly, much of this reflected a 6 percent decline in imports, which were dragged down both by weak U.S. demand and the quirky seasonal pattern in the data on oil imports.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Even so, exports expanded at a very healthy 9½ percent, supported both by the depreciation of the dollar and by continued robust demand for commodities.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Going forward, we anticipate export growth holding up at a still healthy 7 percent or so, as foreign economic growth picks up right around the time that the boost from previous dollar depreciation starts wearing off.

speaker: KAMIN
text: The contribution of net exports to U.S. GDP growth should move down, but this will chiefly reflect a recovery in imports as the U.S. economy picks up.

speaker: KAMIN
text: David and I will now be happy to address your questions.

speaker: FISHER
text: David, in terms of the relatively benign outlook for core inflation now and for headline inflation, I’m wondering what your assumptions are about margin compression and for the ability of corporations to pass through price increases.

speaker: FISHER
text: By the way, I found the core revisions somewhat alarming because they’re well above 2 percent, but less alarming than what I think I heard you say about headline inflation projections.

speaker: FISHER
text: If my memory is correct, over the past two years there has been a wider spread between core and headline, and part of that has been due to the ability of firms at least to restrain or not to exploit any perceived pricing power.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you’re assuming that core will be relatively well behaved over time, some assumptions must be in there about margins and margin management, and I wonder what they are.

speaker: FISHER
text: Then I have a question for Steve on the international side to follow up on that.

speaker: WILCOX
text: By our highly imperfect measure of margins, which we see through the filter of the national income and product accounts, margins at this point are somewhat above the average over the past 30 years, and we have them coming down for the nonfarm business sector.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We have them coming down a little, but not very much.

speaker: WILCOX
text: So we have some slight erosion in margins, but they remain above average.

speaker: WILCOX
text: In the corporate sector, which is measured a little differently from the overall nonfarm business sector, margins are about average at the moment.

speaker: WILCOX
text: So I would not say that a big move in the markup of price over cost is a material driving factor in our inflation outlook.

speaker: FISHER
text: Obviously the implication of this more dire outlook for economic growth is that movement of the top line will be very, very difficult, so again, more pressure comes into the margin side to see that one can satisfy shareholders that things aren’t as bad as they might be.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s really the nature of my concern.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t know if we’re surveying or getting a sense as to the pressures that people feel.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m going to talk about some of that, but you may be doing this more formally than I’m able to do to get a sense of what kinds of pressures are occurring on margins.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the international side, Mr. Chairman, if I may—Steve, I’m curious about these Chinese inflation numbers.

speaker: FISHER
text: As I understand from the Chinese Ministry of Human Resources, the average wage of urban workers rose 18 percent year over year in the first half of ’08, and yet they report an official inflation number that I believe you say is 4 or 5 percent of something.

speaker: FISHER
text: How do you square that corner?

speaker: KAMIN
text: Well, the short answer is that we don’t have enough consistent sources of data to square it.

speaker: KAMIN
text: But you certainly point to a factor that many people have talked about—the rapidly increasing wages, particularly in those industrial areas on the seaboard that are responsible for most of the manufacturing.

speaker: KAMIN
text: It’s hard to square the relatively limited data that we have on those wages with movements in overall CPI.

speaker: KAMIN
text: But there, too, is a limitation—those CPI numbers that are cited from China are mainly for urban areas, so it’s hard to know how comparable those are with the others.

speaker: KAMIN
text: As you know, there’s also an extremely large food component in the Chinese CPI.

speaker: KAMIN
text: So because basically food is probably less labor-intensive than the types of manufacturing in which most of the workers are working, that’s part of the way to square that.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In some sense, the food prices aren’t reflecting those high wages as much.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Then a final wild card is that there are different views on what’s happening on both the level of profit margins in China and what they’ve been doing.

speaker: KAMIN
text: A lot of anecdotal reports suggest that profit margins are razor thin and that they are being squeezed.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Other analyses, including some of the World Bank’s, suggest that those profit margins are still pretty ample.

speaker: KAMIN
text: So I think you correctly allude to an important phenomenon—the rising wages because of high demand for workers—but we’re still busy sorting out the data to figure out exactly how that maps into prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, on the Greenbook forecast, one thing that struck me is that there was a fairly large revision in your forecast for nonresidential structures going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, after a pretty good showing in the first half of this year, you marked down the second half of this year for that and marked down substantially 2009.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the last Greenbook, you had structures actually growing positively in 2009; now it’s minus 4 percent, something like that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is that driven by something in the model, or is that some adjustment factor that was added in?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If so, what was the rationale for that, or why might it be coming out?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Why do we have that change?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Then I’ll follow up with another question.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We don’t quite understand why this sector seems to have resembled the cartoon character that keeps running along when we think there shouldn’t be any support underneath it.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We are staunchly negative about the second half for this sector, and that view is informed by the precipitous drop in the architectural billings index.

speaker: WILCOX
text: That’s one of the relatively few indicators that gives us any purchase on what’s going to happen in this sector.

speaker: WILCOX
text: It’s a helpful indicator of spending about six months ahead.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We think that financial conditions are pretty tough in this area.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We’re getting a lot of anecdotal evidence that people are having greater difficulty financing projects than was the case before, and we’ve seen some uptick in vacancy rates as well.

speaker: WILCOX
text: So we think all of those are factors.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I guess I would say that we’ve heard very persistently negative reports from our supervision colleagues as well about what’s going on in that area.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But the change is not just in the second half of this year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You’ve got a big change for ’09, too.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we think about the phrase that people use—“financial headwinds”—and the credit problems that we see, my interpretation of how the staff has modeled that is on the demand side—of restrained credit limiting demand.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I can also think of the financial sector as having been hit by a very significant productivity shock, if you will, where the production function for intermediation has taken a huge productivity shock to it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So in thinking about a model in which that has happened, you might find yourself thinking about the consequences of that, particularly how that affects the path of potential output over the near term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If you think that type of shock is driving potential output down over the near term, depending on the magnitude of that, it is going to affect your estimates of the gaps and therefore your estimates of inflation and what the economy looks like going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I guess my second question is, Have you thought much about this, or is much of this incorporated in the evolution of your output gaps or your potential output measures, working through that channel?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If so, what might be the ramifications for inflation and policy going forward?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I’ll take that because we did have a bit of an internal debate on that issue awhile back.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In particular, Spencer Dale, who was visiting us from the Bank of England, was basically making exactly the same point you’re making and raising that issue.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So maybe I’m not so kooky after all.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we sent him out of the country.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: One test is whether in previous periods of financial stress like this, we saw what might be more upward inflation pressure than we otherwise could explain or productivity performance that we had trouble explaining.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: After looking at the experience during the early 1990s in the headwinds period and trying to think about the likely magnitude of the effects of such a productivity shock coming out of the financial system, we decided that you could see a negative productivity shock of that sort going on but that its effects are overwhelmed by the fallout from its effect on demand.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So although there might be some negative productivity shock, on net it turns out to be more of a disinflationary effect.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But we also had difficulty seeing it show up in productivity data.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: That said, that would be extremely hard for us to find.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: You know, it could be there, and we just couldn’t find it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So in the way you’ve modeled this in your forecast, are you thinking of yourselves as modeling that net effect, or do you think of yourselves as modeling and forecasting just one side?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Have you made any effort to incorporate both sides of this potential effect?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Even though it may be small, the question is how small it is.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We’ve made no explicit adjustment for that in the potential output assumptions we have going in.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Looking back, it was hard to see that there was much, if any, effect, but that’s a risk knowing that there could be some productivity effect and it’s just hard to find.

speaker: WILCOX
text: May I just augment my earlier answer?

speaker: WILCOX
text: I spoke about the nonresidential building sector.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Another factor taking down overall nonresidential spending is that the lower energy price trajectory reduces our expectation for drilling and mining expenditures, which have also fallen.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Could you review your thought process on core import prices and comment on how sensitive our inflation projections are to the assumption of, I believe, moderation in core import prices in 2009?

speaker: KAMIN
text: As I mentioned, core import price inflation shot up very rapidly to over 10 percent in the second quarter, and our approach toward modeling and predicting core import price inflation focuses on three main sources of increase.

speaker: KAMIN
text: First are increases in foreign cost pressures, which we proxy by CPIs, which have not been a particularly important driver of core import prices as of late, though they are not negligible.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Then the other two, which are more important, are declines in the dollar, which push up our prices, and finally increases in commodity prices because a lot of our imports, even core imports, which exclude oil and high-tech products, still have a lot of commodity input into them.

speaker: KAMIN
text: For the past few years, our experience has been that the pass-through of declines in the dollar into core import prices has been relatively moderate.

speaker: KAMIN
text: It has definitely contributed materially to the increase in core import prices but not as much, we feel, as the run-up in commodity prices, which has had a pretty substantial effect.

speaker: KAMIN
text: One way that we can sort of confirm that impression is that we know that the prices of imported material-intensive products that have the most commodity input have gone up much more rapidly than prices of finished goods, and that has been true over the past year as well.

speaker: KAMIN
text: So for all of those reasons, we feel that commodity prices have been the prime impetus for the run-up in core import price inflation.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Going forward, we take our guidance from the futures markets, which indicate that oil prices and other commodity prices will flatten out.

speaker: KAMIN
text: As a result, we anticipate that, relatively shortly, core import price inflation also should start to decline.

speaker: KAMIN
text: At the same time, our anticipation is that, compared with the past few years, the dollar will fall less rapidly going forward than in the past, and that should be another factor supporting our view that core import price inflation should diminish.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Steve, you might want to define “core import price inflation.” It’s not analogous to the other core.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In the case of core imports, we exclude oil, which is very important, as well as computers and semiconductors.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I have a question similar to President Plosser’s.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Both the financial shock—the housing adjustment—and the big relative price shock you could say all in different forms could hurt the rate of growth of the economy’s productive potential.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You could say that they all might, in some dimension, reduce the near-term expected path of potential growth.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I guess my question is that you have this “costly sectoral reallocation” alternative scenario—do you attribute any effect on potential growth over the forecast period in your baseline to the combined effect of the housing adjustment and the big relative price shock from energy?

speaker: WILCOX
text: One of the facts that we learn from microeconomic data about, for example, job flows is that there is always a huge, astonishing amount of churn—job destruction and job creation—just astonishing; and that’s true even in normal macroeconomic times.

speaker: WILCOX
text: So the background radiation level is not zero.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But we haven’t incorporated in our baseline any allowance for greater cost, and that’s what this alternative scenario was intended to illustrate, making a pretty generous allowance for the potential effect of that sectoral reallocation on the productive capacity of the economy.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But it’s a serious question.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: There’s one minor qualification to what David just said.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We do keep track of rough estimates of what we think that the rise in energy prices over the past few years is possibly doing to trend productivity, and we’ve come up with estimates that maybe it’s 0.1.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We think that effect has been ongoing, and it is built into the data.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In some sense it’s occurring, and so in some sense it’s in our trend estimates.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: It is not as though our trends aren’t implicitly taking in the fact that there’s an ongoing loss in productivity associated with rising energy prices.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I was just going to say that I thought the interesting thing about that scenario was that it doesn’t really change your view about the appropriate path of monetary policy going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s basically at the baseline.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So even if you were to build in a material change in potential growth, because of the effects on demand going forward it doesn’t affect your view about the appropriate path of policy.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The reason is that it operates like a classic supply shock, which presents monetary policy with just simply a less pleasant policy menu to choose from; and in the context of that costly sectoral reallocation, the economy is running closer to its productive capacity.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I lost my train of thought here.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Well, basically you can just stop there.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: It’s the tradeoff between the two.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Obviously, if you were more concerned about inflation outcomes than real activity outcomes, you might tilt it a different way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Isn’t it true, though, that changes in potential growth also have demand effects as well—to some extent offsetting?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It means that it’s another way of saying that you wouldn’t expect the estimates of the now-prevailing equilibrium real fed funds rate to be higher.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Not to stretch this too far, but another way of saying why the likely expected path or the appropriate path of policy doesn’t change in terms of the nominal fed funds rate is that we have these offsetting effects on demand.

speaker: EVANS
text: Regarding a comment that Bill Dudley made about housing prices, for financial institutions, it’s going to matter a lot whether we’re looking at a decline from 15 percent to 20 percent or from 15 percent to 30 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: Housing inventories, unsold homes, are very high, and I guess I’m wondering again—we have gone over this a few times—what factors are likely to get housing advancing if it’s not a sharp decline in housing prices?

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m having a hard time understanding why the expectation would not be for a relatively sharp decline.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m translating the Greenbook/OFHEO numbers to Bill’s numbers, and I’m not sure, but it seems to me that financial institutions ought to be thinking that a significant adjustment must still be in train if we’re not expecting demand to pick up all of a sudden.

speaker: EVANS
text: The mortgage origination challenges are there.

speaker: EVANS
text: Or is this disequilibrium just going to sit there for an extended period of time?

speaker: WILCOX
text: I guess I would push back on the premise that we don’t have a pretty significant adjustment in house prices built into our baseline.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We have house prices as measured by OFHEO declining 7 percent this year and another 5 percent in 2009, and I wouldn’t anticipate any rebound in 2010.

speaker: WILCOX
text: You know, our ability to measure where that would leave house prices relative to some notion of fair valuation is incredibly imprecise.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But one regression-based indicator that we follow suggests that it would have house prices relative to rents swinging from a relatively high valuation to a noticeably low valuation.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Charles Fleischman illustrated this yesterday in his pre- FOMC briefing.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The major factor that provides some reason for optimism is that construction starts are now low enough that builders are making progress in chipping away their inventory of unsold homes.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The months’ supply figures remain extraordinarily high because the denominator is very low; but in terms of units of unsold homes, my recollection is that we’ve chipped away about half the run-up in terms of absolute number of units in inventory.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We also have starts continuing to come down materially from their current level.

speaker: WILCOX
text: So we think that the process will begin to get inventories into a more normal alignment.

speaker: EVANS
text: The staff has been way out front in projecting the housing decline, and that has been very helpful.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is there any dissonance between what Bill said and your pretty substantial expectation of housing-price declines?

speaker: EVANS
text: Was it 15 to 20 or 15 to 30?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think what makes it complicated, though, is that there’s a nonlinearity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If the housing-price declines do turn out to be on the higher side, it then puts more stress on the financial system and on credit availability, which then leads to a weaker economy, which then puts more stress on the housing sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So small differences in the path get amplified.

speaker: EVANS
text: I agree with that chain and those risks, but what I thought I was hearing from David was that the staff estimate has in it quite a substantial adjustment process in housing, and then I would expect financial players to share that assessment.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I wasn’t really addressing the point estimate of where housing was going as opposed to the uncertainty around that estimate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would argue that the uncertainty around that estimate is still quite wide.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At some point it will be resolved.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When it is resolved, that will be a favorable development, but I don’t think we’re there yet.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I would just augment Bill’s comment with two other observations.

speaker: WILCOX
text: There’s plenty of probability mass out in the tail.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I think it actually is two-sided risk.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We illustrated one side of that risk in our “severe financial stress” scenario.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The other point I would make is that our projection for national house-price declines of 12 percent cumulative in 2008 and 2009 makes plenty of room for a very much more severe decline in Florida, California, and other highly stressed areas, and we have attempted to take that regional diversity into account.

speaker: WILCOX
text: It’s a rough exercise, to be sure, but we’re not oblivious to the fact that some areas are doing much worse than the average.

speaker: WILCOX
text: That is the nature of averages.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vice Chairman, did you have an intervention?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I was just going to say this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that you can do crude estimates of likely total losses across the U.S. economy and credit markets in a scenario like the baseline scenario in the Greenbook, and if you use Nellie Liang’s study or the stuff done in New York, there’s a huge amount ahead still.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Even though financial market prices now reflect an expectation for house-price declines that are not significantly more optimistic than David’s baseline scenario, I don’t think you can say with confidence now that financial institutions have already provisioned for or written down losses to accommodate that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Because the trajectory of house prices will depend in part on financial behavior—the availability of credit—as financial institutions catch up and adjust to that and adjust capital and asset growth, et cetera, there is some risk that you’ll push that expected path of house prices down further from where it is.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So if institutions have to prepare for the possibility that you’re going to have a much weaker economic outcome because there’s some probability around that, then there’s a risk that they will produce that outcome through the combined effects of their behavior, which is why we’re living with such a delicate balance.

speaker: EVANS
text: They do seem to be taking out a lot of insurance on the downside, right— like your Merrill Lynch put option?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They’ve had to pay a lot for not very much insurance in the case of Merrill Lynch.

speaker: LACKER
text: Just to point out that it must be the case that lower house prices have a positive effect on the homeownership rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: So there must be some mitigation, some good effect.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’re obviously getting to where we need to get eventually.

speaker: LACKER
text: The question I have for the staff about this is, Have you thought about the sequence?

speaker: LACKER
text: I mean, it strikes me that we’re likely to get to a point of stability in prices and construction activity before we get months’ supply back down to some historical norm.

speaker: LACKER
text: Because it’s sort of a stop variable, are you guys expecting it to converge smoothly, and have you thought about what measures of activity you expect to see stabilize first?

speaker: WILCOX
text: We expect starts to stabilize next year, and that will be followed by a pretty considerable period of several quarters with house prices finally stabilizing.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But we think that builders will look ahead and see that they’ve cut their additions to supply by enough to make even more rapid progress against their inventory of unsold homes.

speaker: WILCOX
text: The question of the dynamics of house prices is a tricky one because it depends on what model of expectations one assumes that homebuyers will have.

speaker: WILCOX
text: If every homeowner were a rational economic being, then it’s pretty unambiguous that a lower level of home prices would elicit greater optimism on the part of home shoppers that, gee, the valuation is better compared with yesterday; I should be more enthusiastic about getting into the housing market; I should be happier today than I was yesterday.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I think it’s at least an open question as to whether expectations aren’t more extrapolative than that.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We haven’t seen any diminution in, for example, the Michigan survey in response to what homeowners expect to happen over the coming 12 months, and I think it’s a serious possibility that they look at their recent experience and extrapolate that forward and conclude that over the next 12 months the user cost of owning a home is going to be really high.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We just don’t have a very good grip on exactly what the dynamics of prices and housing demand will be.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I just want to point out that we hear a fair amount of anecdotal feedback suggesting that just determining what is the net real price for a house is not so easy because of incentives, particularly in multifamily but also new homes in general.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: You pay list, but you get a Mercedes and a year’s worth of gasoline and your lawn mowed and a lot of things thrown in for the seller to hold the price close to what the list is.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I don’t know how these things are actually measured to take into account those kinds of incentives.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I don’t know what the OFHEO does to capture the quality of automobile that comes in the driveway.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I suspect that there’s no adjustment for that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the inventories and the sequencing, which I think is very interesting because of how it plays out, I learned recently—and you can correct me if this is wrong—that, in the inventory of new homes for sale, the way that’s counted includes permits that have been issued even though there’s no home that’s been built.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So a developer may get permits but may not have started the home yet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It may just be sitting on a pile of permits.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So if that’s correct, and I think it is, it means that, if you think about the sequencing of what’s going to happen as demand begins to turn around, those permits don’t have to get bought, but they may start building on permits that they’ve already been issued and they haven’t started building yet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is that a correct way of looking at the data?

speaker: WILCOX
text: I don’t know what the story is with regard to permits that you’re mentioning.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I do know that the cancellation rate of new home sales has declined a bit.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Previously we were emphasizing that the high level of cancellations that the builders were experiencing was actually causing the supply situation to be even worse than one would infer from the Census Bureau data.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Now the cancellation rates have come down, and so that situation is not as severe as it was six or nine months ago, I believe.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Rosengren, you have been patient.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My question is for Steve.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There have been judgmental adjustments to the domestic forecast reflecting financial headwinds in the United States.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I’m wondering if we made the same adjustments for financial headwinds in Europe.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: You highlighted that residential investment looks a bit different in Europe, but they do have a lot of capital losses in their banking system.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Their LIBOR–OIS spread is quite elevated, and at least in some European countries— Ireland and Spain as well as the United Kingdom, which you mentioned—housing has been quite soft.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Are you doing judgmental forecasts to reflect those headwinds, or do we do it on the domestic side but not for the European outlook?

speaker: KAMIN
text: As you correctly point out, Europe, in particular, does indeed have a lot of financial stresses; and some parts of Europe, particularly the United Kingdom as well as Ireland and Spain, are looking at some very serious weaknesses on the housing side.

speaker: KAMIN
text: So we are, indeed, kind of in parallel but not exactly the same as our domestic colleagues building financial stresses into our outlook.

speaker: KAMIN
text: We don’t necessarily increase or decrease the amount of financial stress in our forecast in lockstep with the domestic side.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In particular, the European financial situation has probably gotten a bit worse over the intermeeting period, but some indicators haven’t deteriorated to quite the extent that they have in the United States.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Nonetheless, we have built in a fair amount of financial stress.

speaker: KAMIN
text: One factor that’s worth keeping in mind is that we built it into our outlook fairly early on.

speaker: KAMIN
text: So we haven’t adjusted downward the outlook for Europe by that much compared with the last couple of Greenbooks, but we had already built in quite a bit of weakening of activity, and a lot of that does reflect both the direct effects of financial stresses as well as their knock-on effects on tightening credit standards for banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have President Fisher, and then if it’s okay with everybody, we should probably start our go-round.

speaker: FISHER
text: Very quickly, I want to come back to the housing issue.

speaker: FISHER
text: You know, I’ve been more pessimistic than I think anybody around the table from the standpoint of peak-to-trough correction, and I find the numbers you mentioned very benign relative to my expectations.

speaker: FISHER
text: One issue that I’m trying to understand a little better in terms of its likely effect is that the real bulge in resets comes in 2009 to 2012 because that’s when the alt-A resets kick in.

speaker: FISHER
text: We talked about this many, many moons ago, the ultra-poor documentation on those types of loans, in particular, and I’m wondering to what degree you’re factoring this into your outlook going forward, particularly for those out-years.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We’re certainly aware of that.

speaker: WILCOX
text: To my eye the numbers look astonishingly negative.

speaker: WILCOX
text: For foreclosures, we have 2.5 million foreclosures this year and another 2 million foreclosures next year.

speaker: WILCOX
text: We have a very bleak landscape built into the projection.

speaker: FISHER
text: On that happy note, Mr. Chairman, thank you.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The contours and basic outcomes of Atlanta’s forecast are similar to the baseline of the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I want to focus my remarks this morning on the underlying assumptions in both forecasts—assumptions that I view as pivotal and if we miscalculate could result in a longer-term policy error.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It seems that at every meeting there’s great uncertainty around the outlook, and this juncture is no different.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I perceive considerable uncertainty and debatable assumptions in the base-case scenario.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I see it, the key assumptions broadly are that housing stabilizes, perhaps as indicated by housing prices, in the second half of ’09.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Inflation pressures intensify in the near term but then abate because of economic slack and lower commodity prices and, as discussed, core import prices.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Recent declines in oil prices stick, and prices remain more or less flat.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Certainly since the Greenbook was published, we note the fluctuations just in the past few days that were referred to earlier, and I also can’t dismiss geopolitical risks and the potential of a severe shock.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Finally, financial market stress will persist for some months but diminish next year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: These assumptions, using the respectable term “assumptions,” have the feeling to me of “bets,” not so respectable a term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The policy assumption integral to both the Greenbook and the Atlanta forecasts could be added to this, and that is that rate rises starting in 2009 won’t choke off improving growth and will be enough to blunt remaining inflation pressures.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I’ll devote my comments to input from regional and other contacts that either serve to confirm or cast doubt on these assumptions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We oriented this cycle’s questions to our Atlanta and Branch directors to, first, evidence of wage pressures and pass-through of higher costs.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In interpreting the feedback, we noted some confusion between a business’s management of its labor costs versus general wage pressures.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We heard that businesses are working to keep their total wage bills in check by raising wages for key talent but letting less critical employees go or cutting their work hours as an offset.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The reduction in hours is attributed to some combination of weaker product demand and increased average productivity.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Rising unemployment appears to be keeping wage demands in check.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There are exceptions, such as the oil field services industry, for which qualified staff are in short supply, and certain skilled industrial and business trades in which local bottlenecks exist.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In businesses enjoying strong export demand, some employers are utilizing bonuses rather than commitment to permanent wage increases.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So our regional contacts did not indicate the development of broad-based underlying pressures on labor costs reflecting wage demands.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As for inflation pass-through, our contacts reported widespread and growing efforts to pass through higher input costs.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Pass-through efforts appear to be the rule rather than the exception.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As one Branch director put it, people are passing through costs like crazy using high energy costs as cover.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The reports of my supervision staff regarding banking conditions indicate a continuing decline in asset quality and a very nervous interbank funding market.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Foreclosed properties, both single-family and condo, are making up the majority of house sales and slowing the absorption of the oversupply of new homes.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Some contacts are very concerned about the prospect of a second wave of foreclosures as option ARM mortgage borrowers, mostly concentrated in large states like Florida and California—these are borrowers who are currently paying less than the accrued interest—run up against maximum loan-to-value ceilings.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: New, higher GSE standards are resulting in fewer borrowers being qualified, putting downward pressure on house prices and bringing more foreclosures.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Virtually all comparables for Florida residential valuation are based on forced sales and foreclosures, we are told.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Beyond the deterioration in real estate portfolios, banks are reporting growing problems in credits to food distributors, restaurants, trucking, and other petroleum fuel or input-intensive industries.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Based on my calls with financial market contacts, it seems that—no surprise—much of the attention in financial markets has shifted from private fixed-income markets to Fannie and Freddie.

speaker: LOCKHART
