text: Fixed-income markets for private securities appeared to have improved relative to their lows since the current financial turmoil began.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Although significant concerns remain, it appears that leveraged-loan deals are getting done.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Volume is down, spreads are up, and the deals are very conservative, but deals are getting done.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That said, one of the patterns in my calls over the past year has been that, every time one concern abates, another seems to jump up and take its place.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Although the recent legislation appears to have alleviated concerns about the Fannie and Freddie senior debt, my contacts indicate that there is widespread uncertainty about what will happen to junior securities if the Treasury injects funds.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Furthermore, more than once I heard the view that foreign holders of GSE debt are concerned that their positions are not as safe as they believed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One contact mentioned that the 18-month term of the guarantee is reportedly affecting some holders’ maturity choices.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In response to my question about the relative weakness of European banks, one contact suggested that they have booked much of their troubled assets in the “hold to maturity” account, suggesting slower recognition of losses and difficulties ahead.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We confirmed with one large regional bank CFO significant deterioration of HELOCs in their portfolio and, by implication, broadly among regional banks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The option ARM problem, by contrast, is perceived to be possibly the next shoe to drop but, as I said earlier, not uniformly distributed across the country.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Finally, we heard the view that markets perceive banks as facing protracted difficulty raising capital.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: To conclude, the downside risks to growth have not diminished in my opinion.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On the flip side, I agree that the upside risks to inflation are obviously a serious concern.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In particular, I put a fair amount of weight on the possibility that inflation will not moderate sufficiently without a more substantial tightening of monetary policy than that projected in the Greenbook baseline.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My intermeeting internal and external discussions make it difficult for me to dismiss some of the alternative scenarios in the Greenbook, specifically the “severe financial stress” scenario, the “typical recession” scenario, and the “inflationary spiral” scenario; and in a high-uncertainty environment, I don’t view any of these scenarios as exclusive of another.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That said, I see the risks to both the inflation and the growth objectives as very roughly in balance at this time.

speaker: EVANS
text: Overall there has been little change in the sentiment of my business contacts since our last meeting.

speaker: EVANS
text: Most are still reporting sluggish domestic demand with little evidence of any improvement over the near term.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the price front, everyone continued to cite cost pressures.

speaker: EVANS
text: Manufacturers have long lists of materials cost increases, while retailers note large increases in wholesale prices of imported consumer goods.

speaker: EVANS
text: Everyone discusses how they are planning to continue passing these costs along to customers in second-round effects.

speaker: EVANS
text: Undoubtedly weak market conditions will limit their efforts, but I suspect that many will be successful in raising prices significantly.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning to the financial situation, to start I should note that I did hear some good reports with regard to liquidity in Chicago financial markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: A contact at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange told us that they conducted extensive liquidity reviews for their largest clearing members, with special scrutiny of firms that had substantial volumes of hard-to-value assets on their books.

speaker: EVANS
text: The clearinghouse was very pleased with the results, finding that these firms had good access to liquidity.

speaker: EVANS
text: Overall, however, my financial conversations this round were relatively downbeat.

speaker: EVANS
text: I did hear some interesting details, though, about the dynamics of the restructuring of credit intermediation.

speaker: EVANS
text: With commercial-mortgage-backed securities markets effectively shut down, a highly rated owner-developer of high-end shopping malls described his increasingly difficult attempts to find funding for his regular flow of balloon payments on mortgage properties.

speaker: EVANS
text: He has gone from restrictive loans from life insurance companies to attempting to put together his own structured-debt securitization.

speaker: EVANS
text: They want to issue bonds backed by the revenues generated from a pool of their high-quality properties and sell them to major fixed-income investment funds.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is one example of what economists like Kashyap and Shin estimate will be a reduction of at least $1 trillion in lending to nonfinancial institutions due to mortgage-related losses at U.S. financial institutions.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is also an example of how firms are trying to find workarounds for the functions that intermediaries used to do for them.

speaker: EVANS
text: But such restructuring must be raising the cost of financing in ways that are not obviously amenable to mitigation through liquidity policies.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning to the national outlook, the information we have received over the past several weeks has contained many crosscurrents, but overall our forecast for output growth is little changed from our June projections.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to prices, I am concerned that inflation risks continue to grow.

speaker: EVANS
text: The most recent news on core prices has not been good.

speaker: EVANS
text: Oil prices may be coming off the boil, but they are still scalding.

speaker: EVANS
text: Prices are still down only to where they were in May.

speaker: EVANS
text: My impression from my contact calls is that the ultimate pass-through to final product prices of earlier increases could take a disconcertingly long period of time.

speaker: EVANS
text: Furthermore, I continue to think that the current funds rate in conjunction with our enhanced lending facilities represents a quite accommodative monetary policy stance, even given the disruptions in financial markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: If the policy path remains as accommodative as futures markets expect, then improvement in inflation will most likely require fortuitous favorable developments in inflation expectations and more restraint from resource slack than we might have otherwise expected.

speaker: EVANS
text: This brings me to three considerations that I would like to highlight as we evaluate the risk- management positions underlying our views on appropriate policy and our economic projections.

speaker: EVANS
text: The first factor is that, according to many econometric estimates, the 5¾ to 6 percent unemployment rate envisioned in the projections would provide only very modest restraint on inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, costly reallocation could lead to less resource slack, perhaps temporarily driving the NAIRU above 5 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: You know, when I talk to my staff, they assure me that there are very good reasons, demographically based, to believe a NAIRU under 5 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I tend to think I’ve read a few too many papers on policy and policy mistakes where that’s exactly the issue—when you think the sustainable unemployment rate is lower than it actually is.

speaker: EVANS
text: So that’s a risk, I think.

speaker: EVANS
text: The second factor is that many individuals and businesses see the large relative price changes in oil, food, and commodities as precursors to more-persistent inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Whether or not their assessments are analytically correct depends on their expectations of our policy response.

speaker: EVANS
text: A substantive response may be necessary to prevent self-fulfilling price increases and keep inflation under control.

speaker: EVANS
text: Words can take us only so far.

speaker: EVANS
text: The third consideration is the potential diminishing returns through our efforts to mitigate distressed financial market conditions.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is my interpretation that our current accommodative monetary policy and suite of lending facilities are set to mitigate severe downside risks and the systemic risks that you mentioned earlier, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is helpful under the assumption that reducing liquidity strains will assist financial markets to return to normal operations and prevent a permanent impairment of our financial infrastructure.

speaker: EVANS
text: But financial conditions seem unlikely to return to our previous perceptions of normal, at least for some time.

speaker: EVANS
text: Thus, I see a risk that extra accommodation intended to grease the financial wheels could be left in place too long and prove counterproductive for price stability.

speaker: EVANS
text: Indeed, the old perception of “normal” likely is not the correct benchmark for us to use in looking for whether we are experiencing structural changes in the intermediation process in which new liquidity providers are playing enhanced roles in the lending process and in which risk standards are changing.

speaker: EVANS
text: So when thinking about market functioning, it would be useful to discuss this within a longer-term framework of what we can feasibly expect from market functioning and what central bank liquidity has the ability to usefully and appropriately influence.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I may have to leave the lunch early.

speaker: FISHER
text: So before I start, I do want to bid Rick adieu.

speaker: FISHER
text: Rick, I remember describing you as charming in one of our early meetings.

speaker: FISHER
text: You have charmed me by your intellect and devotion.

speaker: FISHER
text: Anyway, I’m going to miss you.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I wanted to say that in case I do have to leave early.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, in the intermeeting period, I spent almost as much time in President Rosengren’s District as I did in my own—part as vacation but the rest consulting with some advisers and mentors in the People’s Republic of Cambridge at my alma mater.

speaker: FISHER
text: I mention this because I want to underscore that, in arguing a perspective, I tend to move away from the rather felicitous circumstances that prevail in my District.

speaker: FISHER
text: Even though things are slowing, we still expect employment growth to come in a little short of 2 percent a year, and our banking situation thus far is holding up rather well.

speaker: FISHER
text: In terms of my national soundings, and you know the list and the group is familiar with it, the anecdotal evidence from everyone—from the bankers to the credit card companies to retailers to fuel producers, food producers, energy companies, shippers, equipment manufacturers, homebuilders, and entertainment companies—confirms reports of progressively higher obstacles to growing their top lines and continued efforts to drive down their cost of goods sold through reducing their head counts, running very tight inventory cycles, tightening their operating expenses, and reexamining and in many cases cutting back significantly on cap-ex.

speaker: FISHER
text: Nationally I expect continued anemia on the growth side.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are, as you know, not at the extreme but at the low end of expectations for economic growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would expect zero growth as we approach year-end.

speaker: FISHER
text: As I said earlier, from our perspective we’re only about two-thirds through the peak-to-trough correction on housing, and I view that as a continued weak influence.

speaker: FISHER
text: So the summary is that most of my contacts are planning around expectations of a prolonged U.S. and advanced-country slowdown and have a rather woeful outlook as to the growth side.

speaker: FISHER
text: At the same time, there is also a woeful concern with regard to price pressures—intensifying cost pressures affecting their margins at a time when the stock market is most unforgiving of people who miss their mark.

speaker: FISHER
text: Even in the First District, I might note.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to quote the Beige Book report from Boston: “Almost all contacted manufacturers voiced concerns about elevated .

speaker: FISHER
text: Respondents generally have raised their selling prices in recent months.

speaker: FISHER
text: Over one-half of contacts expect to increase their selling prices further in the second half of 2008 and/or early 2009.” It went on to say that, while some contacts express worry that price increases have led or will lead to loss of market shares, others indicate that—and these are the key operative words—“customers have become more receptive to price increases because they see them as a consequence of generalized cost pressures.” Mr. Chairman, that passage captures the message that I’m receiving from my CEO and CFO contacts around the country.

speaker: FISHER
text: By and large, we appear to be transitioning from vigilance on the price front to acquiescence.

speaker: FISHER
text: Inflation expectations are, I think, becoming unmoored, and I believe they are, if not already adrift, at risk of drifting.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the small business front, I do like to look at Bill Dunkelberg’s recent reports from the National Federation of Independent Business.

speaker: FISHER
text: His most recent report indicates that the percentage of small business owners citing inflation as “the number one problem they face,” rose to 20 percent in June, the highest rating since 1982, and that 41 percent of his respondents report raising selling prices.

speaker: FISHER
text: At the other extreme of size, to put this in perspective, Wal-Mart’s CEO for the United States reported last week—and I quote this: “My biggest concern is inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: This month we had an experience that Wal-Mart has never ever”—that’s literally what he said—“had before, which is that a major supplier told us we need a 9 percent increase or we will not supply you at all.” Now, he did not mention the name of that supplier.

speaker: FISHER
text: It could have been Unilever, which saw the volume of goods it ships slip 0.5 percent year over year in the second quarter.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yet according to our conversations but also quoted in the Wall Street Journal on August 1, Unilever’s CEO reported that he “raised average prices on his thousands of products 7.4 percent,” and then added that he “doesn’t plan to reverse any price increases.” Or it could have been one of the largest snack food companies, whose CFO has informed us that, after taking and having stick a 9 percent increase in price in March—I reported this at our last meeting—they will effect another 9½ percent increase in October.

speaker: FISHER
text: Here’s the pithy quote he gave me: “Thus far we’ve been bleeding out price increases to our customers.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now our strategy is to bludgeon them—to broadcast our increases in the expectation that competitors will do the same.” I doubt the supplier to Wal-Mart was Kodak.

speaker: FISHER
text: Last week the New York Times reported that “hurt by higher manufacturing and materials costs, the company said it will combat these cost pressures by passing on to consumers and raising prices on some products by as much as 20 percent.” I have lots of examples of similar responses.

speaker: FISHER
text: President Evans indicated similar pressures.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m not going to go through them.

speaker: FISHER
text: I will add, by the way, the one thing that surprised me.

speaker: FISHER
text: Despite Disney’s brilliant annual report of record earnings, they, too, plan to raise their single day prices by 5 percent, to $60, in the next quarter.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is also a growing feeling, which I haven’t heard before, among semiconductor manufacturers that, after years and years of constant price deflation, they expect that there may—and the operative word is “may”—be a bottoming out because of the raw materials prices they face and the wage prices and pressures they are receiving in China, which has become a major semiconductor manufacturer.

speaker: FISHER
text: One might take heart from the recent correction in commodity prices.

speaker: FISHER
text: I agree with Steve that we have to be very careful about that.

speaker: FISHER
text: My smartest energy contacts have been expecting a correction in prices.

speaker: FISHER
text: Natural gas prices have reacted to recent developments like the Barnett Shale and, even more important, the so-called Haynesville Play in Louisiana.

speaker: FISHER
text: The “oilies” note that increased Saudi supply hit our shores with the normal six-week lag.

speaker: FISHER
text: They were talking about production increases in May and June, and those have just hit our shores recently.

speaker: FISHER
text: So they’re not surprised at the price reaction at the pump.

speaker: FISHER
text: But none feels that the basic demand–supply situation has been dramatically altered—much as you argued, Steve—and most expect structural prices to obtain at or near current levels.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, what does “at or near current levels” mean in terms of price impact?

speaker: FISHER
text: I had a long conversation with the CEO of Burlington Northern, and just for data purposes, in terms of what they call their RCAF—an automatic cost- adjustment contract that covers 25 percent of the goods shipped by their rail—their third-quarter RCAF is 17 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: The 75 percent of products that are not covered by that automatic contract are subject to a fuel surcharge.

speaker: FISHER
text: That fuel surcharge at $120 a barrel is a 30 percent increase for the third quarter.

speaker: FISHER
text: One might also take comfort in the purported calmness in compensation growth seen so far, along the lines of what I read in the Financial Times by Mark Gertler on July 29.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t hear confirmation of that benign argument among business operators.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, as President Evans and Mr. Stockton pointed out in our last meeting, labor compensation is not a good predictor of inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I remember Dave said that it’s not that labor costs, which are a significant chunk of business costs, don’t matter but that you can’t necessarily take comfort from the well-behaved compensation thus far that you are not going to confront some inflation problems going forward.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, the last anecdote I want to give you illustrates that point.

speaker: FISHER
text: Yesterday I had a lengthy visit with the CFO of General Mills.

speaker: FISHER
text: Until their fiscal year ’08, which ended in May, they priced over many years an average increase of 0 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: They took 2½ percent as the year ended, and they’re taking another 5 percent this year.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are having to reexamine their elasticity models, he said.

speaker: FISHER
text: Here is what he said that worried me the most: They are finding those models less predictive because (a) “everybody is raising prices,” and (b) consumer perception is that inflation is back.

speaker: FISHER
text: So, again, vigilance is giving way to acquiescence.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I do want to comment very briefly on something I mentioned last time, which regards calculating the cost of goods sold.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am hearing more and more from companies that have shifted production to China a verification of the 18 percent number that the ministry gave us.

speaker: FISHER
text: Whether it’s a hospital producer whom I talked to in California or a Black & Decker tool assembler in China, they’re complaining not only about cost increases of 15 to 20 percent, depending on whether you’re operating in the north or south, but also about the employee contract law that was just put into place, which in essence allows for almost an old-fashioned scala mobile Italian/French model, which feeds a wage–price spiral, and it is beginning to infect their wage cost and inject rigidities into their ability to operate in China.

speaker: FISHER
text: So overall, Mr. Chairman, I am concerned, obviously, about economic growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we, as President Lockhart mentioned, are in a very difficult spot.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have three enormously worrisome scenarios facing us.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we have to be very careful how we word ourselves on inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: Last night at 6:00 National Public Radio opened their Marketplace report with this headline: “The Fed Fuels Your Pain.” We have a perception issue that we must address, and there are two ways to do it.

speaker: FISHER
text: One is by being strong in terms of how we argue the case of inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: The other is to act by raising rates.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m going to listen very, very carefully because, frankly, I’m undecided here as to what the right approach is.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I think we have to be careful when we state a balance of risks, which are enormous, that we don’t understate the fact that inflation is now being accommodated in the minds of the marketplace.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Fisher, I’m going to ask you a very innocent question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You’ve given many chilling anecdotes over the last few meetings about increases in prices, but the official statistics just don’t show anything like that outside of oil, gas, gasoline, and the direct commodity price increases.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you believe that the CPI is not an accurate measure?

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, I do see the CPI rising.

speaker: FISHER
text: The monthly report was not encouraging.

speaker: FISHER
text: The last 12 months have not been encouraging, and I think what worries me is the spread between core and headline.

speaker: FISHER
text: Core is rising as well, by the way.

speaker: FISHER
text: Even our own estimates indicate that.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do see it in headline numbers.

speaker: FISHER
text: The numbers I saw that were just reported I thought were quite alarming.

speaker: FISHER
text: You are seeing the pass-through.

speaker: FISHER
text: You’re hearing evidence of this in the anecdotal reports.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do believe, Mr. Chairman, that it’s visible in the data.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m just trying to report what I’m hearing from the field against the background of much more sophisticated analysis, which I respect enormously.

speaker: FISHER
text: What I’m worried about is the perception.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do believe that the data are very imperfect on inflation expectations—I noticed that David said that about the further-out expectations in the Michigan survey.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you look at the reliability of the data, the one-year survey, which has risen significantly, has been quite reliable over time.

speaker: FISHER
text: The five-to-ten-year—I don’t know if they’re talking about ten years, five years, or somewhere between the two, and I don’t think statistically that’s been a very accurate indicator historically, but I’m not sure about that.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we have very imperfect hard data on inflation expectations, and I think that’s when anecdotal evidence may be helpful.

speaker: FISHER
text: All I’m trying to do, Mr. Chairman, is report to you what I’m hearing from the field, and not from my District, and I hope it is useful in the deliberations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think there’s no question that headline inflation is very high right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly, when you get these kinds of increases in energy prices and food costs, you’re going to have to reflect them in current prices.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, that’s exactly what you need to have happen so that relative prices shift.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The reality is that high oil prices have to mean that real wages fall.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: People have to conserve and not drive as much and so forth.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So this is a normal process, and monetary policy does not control these relative price shifts.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What I think is more critical is that, although there are some problems in terms of core, the effect has actually been quite limited given the incredible rise in energy prices.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: While it’s important to think about headline in the long run, the information from core is very useful in terms of thinking about policy because it tells you whether this is spilling over into underlying inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One of my concerns about going to anecdotal information and why I think we need to use an analytic framework in thinking about what is really driving the inflation process is that we do need to focus on the longer-run because that’s what monetary policy can control.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I get a bit nervous about these anecdotal concerns, which I think can tell us something about headline.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Then we have to ask what they tell us about the longer-run context but not put too much weight on them.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s one reason that I think some of the analytic frameworks that we’ve developed here are very useful for thinking about these things.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, in terms of the weight, again, I’m just one of 17 or 18, and I would weigh it accordingly.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I am worried that we’ve had a spread between headline and core for a long period now.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am worried that we’re seeing core expectations pick up—modestly but they are beginning to pick up.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am worried that core expectations are above 2 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: And I am particularly worried about developments on the global wage front in terms of how it affects the cost of goods sold here in the United States.

speaker: FISHER
text: One last thing that I just started to detect—and again, it’s all just hearsay—but I’m increasingly hearing reports of concerns of people who operate companies about the welfare of their employees and about their ability to pay transportation costs, pay food costs, and maintain the value of their 401(k) plans and, as President Lockhart reported, some way to try to manage, if not through formal demands on wages, at least to try to cushion their welfare.

speaker: FISHER
text: These are marginal influences, and I don’t disrespect the analytical side.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do worry that data capture history, and I’m trying to give myself a sense for what is happening at the margin in terms of microeconomic behavior, and the report is only what it’s worth.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s just one input in the many.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Economic activity in the Eighth District has remained roughly stable during the summer.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Activity in the services sector has increased slightly, and except for the auto industry, manufacturing activity is also stable to slightly higher.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Automotive contacts reported a variety of plans to lay off workers or to idle production, and at least three automotive parts suppliers will close plants in the District.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Contacts in the auto industry are not optimistic that production will increase in the short term.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Retail and auto sales have softened in recent weeks, and some District retail contacts have expressed concerns about summer sales.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Many contacts continue to emphasize commodity price levels as a key factor in business decisions.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They are concerned both about the necessary business adjustments, given the new pricing structure, and about the implications for the overall level of inflation going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The residential real estate sector continues to decline.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Across four of the main metropolitan areas in the District, home sales through May declined about 18 percent compared with 2007, whereas single-family construction permits declined about 40 percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The number of foreclosures in the St. Louis area in the second quarter increased to about 6,300 filings, up about 77 percent from last year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am impressed, however, with the regionalism in the foreclosure situation, as some areas of the nation continue to have far higher foreclosure rates than others.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In contrast with the generally positive reports in commercial real estate activity for the earlier part of 2008, recent reports have indicated more uneven conditions in the nonresidential real estate sector across the District.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Turning to the national outlook, I was encouraged by the recent GDP report for the second quarter, which showed growth at an annual rate of 1.9 percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Real final sales increased at an annual rate of 3.9 percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It now appears that the worst quarter associated with the current episode of financial turmoil was probably the fourth quarter of 2007, when the economy abruptly stalled.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The slow- or no-growth period was through the winter, with the economy gradually regaining footing through the spring and summer.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If there were no further shocks, I would expect the economy to grow at a more rapid rate in the second half of this year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But there has been another shock—namely, substantial increases in commodity and energy prices.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it’s important to be careful not to confuse the effects of this latter shock with the effects of the housing-sector shock.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My sense is that the level of systemic risk associated with financial turmoil has fallen dramatically.

speaker: BULLARD
text: For this reason, I think the FOMC should begin to de-emphasize systemic risk worries.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My reasoning is as follows.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Systemic risk means that the sudden failure of a particular financial firm would so shock other ostensibly healthy firms in the industry that it would put them out of business at the same time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The simultaneous departure of many firms would badly damage the financial services industry, causing a substantial decline in economic activity for the entire economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This story depends critically on the idea that the initial failure is sudden and unexpected by the healthy firms in the industry.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But why should this be, once the crisis has been ongoing for some time?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Did they not realize that they may be doing business with a firm that may be about to default on its obligations?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Are they not demanding risk premiums to compensate them for exactly this possibility?

speaker: BULLARD
text: My sense is that, because the turmoil has been ongoing for some time, all of the major players have made adjustments as best they can to contain the fallout from the failure of another firm in the industry.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They have done this not out of benevolence but out of their own instincts for self-preservation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As one of my contacts at a large bank described it, the discovery process is clearly over.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I say that the level of systemic risk has dropped dramatically and possibly to zero.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Let me stress that, to be sure, there are some financial firms that are in trouble and that may fail in the coming months or weeks depending on how nimble their managements are at keeping them afloat.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is why many interest rate spreads remain elevated and may be expected to remain elevated for some time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: These spreads are entirely appropriate for a financial system reacting to a large shock.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But at this point, failures of certain financial firms should not be regarded as so surprising that they will cause ostensibly healthy firms to fail along with them.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The period of substantial systemic risk has passed.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Of course, we have also endured a bout of systemic risk worries stemming from the operations of the GSEs.

speaker: BULLARD
text: However, my view is that the recent legislation has addressed the systemic risk component of that situation as well.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Because of these considerations, my assessment is that the chances of unchecked systemic risk pushing the U.S. economy into a severe downturn at this point are small, no larger than in ordinary times.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Unfortunately, while the threat from this source is retreating, another threat is upon us— namely, a substantial shock from increased energy and certain commodities prices, which is leading many to forecast slower growth during the fall.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Real automotive output subtracted 1.1 percentage points from real GDP growth in the second quarter.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Many contacts seem to attribute this largely to consumer reaction to increased gasoline prices.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If this is true, then it seems to me that some of the most visible reaction to this shock may have already occurred, being pulled forward into the second quarter.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Labor markets have been weak, but I am not as pessimistic as most on this dimension.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So far this year, the U.S. economy has shed about 387,000 nonfarm payroll jobs as compared with a drop in employment of 402,000 jobs during the first seven months of 2003 or 315,000 during the first seven months of 2002.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Neither of these latter two episodes is associated with the recession label.

speaker: BULLARD
text: These two years might provide better historical guides to the behavior of today’s economy than those associated with the recession label, such as 2001, 1990–91 or 1980–82.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is one reason that I think the labeling game can mislead us in our thinking about the economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The main contribution that the FOMC can make to the economy is to keep inflation low and stable.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The headline CPI inflation rate is running close to 5 percent measured from one year earlier.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The University of Michigan survey of inflation expectations one year ahead reflects this reality with the most recent reading at 5¼ percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The June CPI annualized inflation rate was a 1970s- sounding 13.4 percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Of course, much of this is due to energy prices.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Still, with these kinds of numbers we’re going to have to do more than talk about inflation risks.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Developments during the intermeeting period have heightened my concern about downside risks to economic growth and slightly allayed my concern about upside risks to inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Let me begin with growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The moderate growth rate registered in the second quarter was disappointing, especially because it benefited from the temporary effects of the fiscal stimulus package.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Moreover, the pattern of consumer spending during the quarter, with weakness in June, is worrisome.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With all the publicity surrounding the rebate checks, households may have put them to work earlier than usual, especially since they were facing significantly higher prices for food and gasoline.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This interpretation does not bode well for activity in the current quarter.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Assuming no change in the funds rate this year, we have lowered our forecast for real GDP growth for the second half of the year about ⅓ percentage point, to just ¾ percent, and project a correspondingly higher unemployment rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Our forecast for weak second-half growth reflects not only the unwinding of fiscal stimulus but also adverse financial sector developments.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The credit crunch appears to have intensified since we last met.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Evidence of tighter financial conditions abound.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Risk spreads and the interest rates charged on a variety of private loans, including mortgages, are up noticeably, and lending standards have tightened further.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Credit losses have risen not only on mortgages but also on auto loans, credit cards, and home equity lines of credit.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As a consequence, the list of troubled depository institutions is growing longer.

speaker: YELLEN
text: IndyMac and First National will not be the last banks in our region to fail.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, the decline in broad stock market indexes is partly a reflection of the market’s concerns about the health of the financial sector.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Many financial institutions are deleveraging their balance sheets and reducing loan originations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, a large bank in my District has begun now in earnest to cancel or cap outstanding home equity loans and lines of credit, despite an ongoing concern about alienating consumers.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Tighter credit is affecting demand.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Anecdotal reports suggest that the plunge in July car sales partly reflects a tightening of credit standards for auto loans and leases.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A large bank reports a substantial drop in demand for mortgage credit in response to the recent rise in mortgage interest rates, and the anecdotal reports that we hear support the Greenbook’s negative view of the effect of credit conditions on investment in nonresidential structures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The housing sector is of considerable concern.

speaker: YELLEN
text: House prices have continued to fall at a rapid rate, and futures prices suggest a further decline of around 10 percent over the next 12 months.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This forecast seems reasonable given the overhang of homes for sale, the recent rise in mortgage rates, and the tightening of credit.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Unfortunately, the risk of an adverse feedback loop from tighter credit to higher unemployment, to rising foreclosures, to escalating financial sector losses, to yet tighter credit remains alive and well, in my opinion.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, stress tests conducted by some of the large financial institutions in our District reveal an exceptionally high sensitivity of credit losses to both home-price movements and unemployment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The “severe financial stress” simulation in the Greenbook illustrates my concern.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is not my modal forecast, but it certainly seems well within a reasonable range of outcomes.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The probability of such a scenario has risen, in my view, since we met in June.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One partially mitigating factor that should help to support consumer spending is the drop in the price of oil since our last meeting.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But to the extent that the decline in oil prices partly reflects reduced expectations for global growth, the net impetus from stronger domestic spending will be offset by weaker export growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Continued declines or even stabilization in oil prices will, however, be good for inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have revised down slightly our forecast for core inflation as a consequence.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Moreover, the fact that we were not once again surprised on the upside by oil prices has had a small favorable effect on my perception of inflation risks going forward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That said, inflation risks obviously remain.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even with the recent decline, energy prices are well above year-ago levels and are not only pushing up headline inflation but also spilling, to some extent, into core.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Higher headline inflation could undermine our credibility and raise inflation expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If the public concludes that our implicit inflation objective has drifted up, workers may demand higher compensation, setting off a wage–price dynamic that would be costly to unwind.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Fortunately, the reports I hear are consistent with the view that no such dynamic has taken hold.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My contacts uniformly report that they see no signs of wage pressures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They note that high unemployment is suppressing wage gains.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Growth in our two broad measures of labor compensation are low and stable; and taking productivity growth into account, unit labor costs have risen only modestly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I tend to think of the chain of causation in a wage–price spiral running from wages to prices, but it is certainly possible that the causation also, or instead, runs in the opposite direction.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Either way, though, faster wage growth is an inherent part of the process by which underlying inflation drifts up, and at present we see not the slightest inkling of emerging wage pressures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Growth in unit labor costs also remains at exceptionally low levels.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would also note that I have looked for evidence of some increase in the NAIRU due to sectoral reallocation by examining the Beveridge curve, thinking that if there were sectoral reallocation we might see an outward shift in the Beveridge curve.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have detected no evidence of such an outward shift.

speaker: YELLEN
text: These facts provide me with some comfort.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Moreover, various measures of longer-term inflation expectations suggest that they remain relatively well contained.

speaker: YELLEN
text: When we met in June, the Michigan survey of inflation expectations five to ten years ahead had recently jumped a couple tenths of a percentage point.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I argued then that the respondents to that survey typically overrespond to contemporaneous headline inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Since that meeting, oil prices have come down a bit, and so have the Michigan survey measures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Assuming that the funds rate is raised from 2 percent to 3 percent in 2009, my forecast shows both headline and core PCE inflation falling to about 2 percent in that year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So, in summary, during the intermeeting period, my forecast for economic growth has weakened, and that for inflation has edged down slightly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I consider the risks to our two policy objectives pretty evenly balanced at the present time.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My outlook for economic growth and inflation over the next few years is broadly similar to the one that I held last meeting, although I think that the prospects for both inflation and economic growth in the near term have deteriorated since June.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: To a close approximation, my outlook ends up looking very similar to the Greenbook’s baseline scenario.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The most significant change I am making to my outlook is to mark down the prospects for business fixed investment this year and next, based on the reports that I am hearing from the manufacturers in my District.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: There is an interesting short-term/long-term dynamic taking place in the manufacturing sector.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The manufacturing CEOs with whom I have spoken say that over the long term they are very bullish on America.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The dollar depreciation, increased transport costs, and rising wages in China all favor more U.S.-based production.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: A senior executive from Alcoa told me that, in his 35 years of working in the manufacturing sector, he has never seen the fundamentals point so strongly toward the United States as a profitable location for manufacturing.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The short term, however, presents a more mixed picture for manufacturers.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Although some industries, such as power generation equipment and aerospace, are running flat out and expect to continue doing so, companies in other manufacturing industries have received or expect to receive order cancellations.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In particular, the manufacturers that supply the automotive and commercial construction sectors are reporting a worsening outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Perhaps the best way to summarize the sentiments that I am hearing from manufacturers is to say that they see a bright future but they see challenging conditions over the next 12 months.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We all know that housing markets are extremely weak.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Housing prices began their decline earlier in Cleveland than in the rest of the country, and we are now seeing some stability in housing prices.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Despite that hopeful glimmer, we have not seen any pickup in home sales.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Based on this experience, it seems that we still have a long way to go nationally before we see any pickup in residential construction.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In regard to financial markets, my chief concern is that lending is going to be constrained by lenders needing to maintain sound capital ratios in the face of asset write-downs and loan charge-offs.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Balance sheet constraints and a declining risk appetite on the part of bankers mean that some worthy borrowers are going to be rationed out of credit markets, further restraining economic activity.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Turning to inflation, I anticipate that price pressures will intensify further before we see some relief, just as the Greenbook baseline scenario depicts.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Manufacturers are still raising their prices in response to rising prices for raw materials that they purchase.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Some companies have had fixed-price contracts in place for five and ten years, and as these contracts mature, the companies are passing on huge price increases to their customers.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Consequently, I think that even after a point at which energy and commodity prices flatten out, prices at the wholesale and retail levels are likely to adjust upward for a while longer.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I just said that manufacturers are expecting some challenging times ahead.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: One reason is that many of them are caught between weakening demand conditions and soaring input costs.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Sherwin-Williams represents an extreme case, but I think it illustrates the situation pretty starkly.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The CEO of Sherwin-Williams told me last week that their business is down more than 20 percent in sales channels both to new construction and to existing homes.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: They have been in business for 126 years, and the last time this occurred was during the Great Depression.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Despite these dismal sales, they are having to raise prices.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The CEO told me that the company typically raises prices once a year, but in July they announced their third price increase this year.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In the entire history of the company, they have never before had three price increases in one year.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I continue to see the risk to my projection for output as being to the downside for the reasons that we have been discussing for some time—high energy prices, severe financial stress, and a depression in the housing markets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The risk to my inflation outlook is weighted to the upside because I am concerned that inflation could remain elevated for too long, potentially destabilizing inflation expectations.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The Greenbook baseline scenario expects the near-term inflation picture to worsen in the second half of this year before improving gradually over the entire forecast period.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This pattern is a concern to me.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In that environment, I worry that inaction on our part before next year could be seen as complacency on our part.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So when I stack up the two risks against one another, I regard them as fairly equal right now.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But my outlook is conditioned on a federal funds rate path that begins to increase about a quarter earlier than called for in the Greenbook baseline.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I will speak to the relevance of this factor when we discuss monetary policy in the next go-round.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Economic conditions in the Third District remain relatively weak, but they are not materially different from what we and our business contacts have been expecting for the past several months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Manufacturing and residential construction sectors continue to show a slow decline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Payroll employment in our three states fell in June, but it is still above the levels of where it was three months ago and so has been performing somewhat better than in the nation as a whole.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The pace of retail sales seems to have been softening, and commercial real estate firms indicate that most office and industrial markets have weakened slightly since the spring.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My business contacts generally expect weak growth for a while.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Manufacturers do expect a rebound during the next six months; but most other sectors, particularly retail sales, anticipate only soft or slightly improving conditions in the near term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Residential real estate is not expected to strengthen appreciably in the second half of the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Banks expect somewhat sluggish growth in overall lending for the rest of the year, although compared with some regions, banks in our District are in pretty good shape.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There are stresses, but they seem to be manageable.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Credit, however, is generally available to businesses, and we hear only sporadic information from businesses that they are unable to obtain needed loans.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: For some time my business contacts have expressed concern about rising energy and commodity and transport prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our business outlook survey’s prices-paid index rose yet again in July, and it is now at its highest level since March 1980.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although the prices-received index edged down slightly, it remains at a very, very high level relative to historical standards.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The BOS’s future prices-received index rose to 49.6 percent, which is the highest level it has been since January 1989.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This indicates that roughly half the manufacturing firms that responded to our survey expect the prices they receive for their products to be increased over the next six months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To gauge the extent to which manufacturing firms have been able to pass on rising costs to their customers, we asked several special questions about product pricing in our July survey.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: More than 60 percent of our respondents indicated that, since the beginning of the year, they have been able to raise prices and pass along increased costs to their customers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: About 26 percent said this took the form of increases in base prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Almost half of them had increased base prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The rest said they have used either surcharges or escalator clauses and, in some cases, combined those with base price increases as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Surcharges and escalation clauses are not likely to go away anytime soon and may even become more widespread.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: About 56 percent of our respondents indicated that price escalation clauses and surcharges are likely to be a part of their pricing in the future.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Further, since a large number of firms have already built cost increases into their base prices, it is not clear at all that prices will come down quickly, even if oil prices stabilize at a lower level.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the national level, the incoming data since our June meeting have been mixed but largely in line with my expectations for the near-term path of the economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Real GDP growth for the second quarter came in somewhat weaker than many expected, although I will note that as recently as April many people were expecting negative growth in the second quarter and it is now almost 2 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I think that the strength is a remarkable testament to the ability of this economy to weather shocks from financial market disruptions, a severe housing correction, and surges in energy and commodity prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nonfarm payroll employment has fallen an average of 66,000 jobs per month over the last seven months—a weak number to be sure but not nearly as severe as the job losses over the last three recessions, which averaged nearly 180,000 jobs a month.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Since our June meeting, we have taken further steps to address fragile financial markets that were manifested by the difficulties surrounding the GSEs and the IndyMac takeover.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On balance, my outlook for the economy is little changed, although the financial market developments since our last meeting have marginally increased the uncertainty surrounding my forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do see near-term weak growth for the economy, but I continue to expect an improvement in output and employment growth next year as the economy rebounds closer to trend.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Unfortunately, there has been a resurgence in financial market volatility, especially on the part of the banking sector and mortgage markets related to the problems of the GSEs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The liquidity in the interbank and primary dealer markets appears to have improved somewhat relative to the first quarter of this year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I read the conditions in the financial markets and the wide spreads on selected assets as having improved somewhat on net and the spreads we are seeing increasingly reflecting real credit risk as opposed to dysfunctional markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I indicated in my questions earlier, we should not use such spreads as the primary criteria for assessing the fragility of the financial markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, we must be cautious in using monetary policy or other tools at our disposal as a form of forbearance that delays the necessary adjustments in the pricing of various financial claims.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we need a high hurdle—that there are real market failures—before we intervene to stem liquidity desires on the part of traders or attempt to influence the price of specific asset classes.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To agree with President Bullard’s comments, we should begin to deemphasize and de- stress the importance of systemic risk because I think it is gradually dissipating as firms adjust to the more volatile and risky environment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The current state of the financial markets seems to me to bear some resemblance to the financial headwinds analogy that many people referred to during the early 1990s.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, spreads on many forms of business and consumer loans are behaving now much in the way as they typically behave during recessionary times as credit risks rise.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the early ’90s, monetary policy was less accommodative than it is now—at least the funds rate reached a low point of 3 percent from October 1992 to February 1994—and during that time headline PCE inflation ran about 2 to 3 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The real funds rate, measured by a one-quarter-ahead forecast of the CPI from the professional forecasters, was minus 0.1 percent over the six quarters from 1993:Q3 to 1994:Q4.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Currently, the real funds rate using the same measure of one-quarter-ahead professional forecasters’ CPI stands at minus 1.1 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The inflation outlook remains a cause of concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Headline inflation is higher, and there is evidence of modest pass-through to core inflation measures.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation compensation on the six-to-ten-year horizon has risen modestly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation compensation at the near term has fallen with recent declines in oil prices, but it remains volatile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The staff has suggested that a portion of the increase in the longer-dated inflation compensation measures may reflect an increase in inflation risk premiums.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is, markets are uncertain about the long-run path of inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is not terribly comforting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It suggests that our credibility may be waning.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite the recent drop in oil prices, I remain uncomfortable with the longer-term inflation outlook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, the focus of monetary policy must be on the intermediate to longer term, and we must resist the temptation to act as if our funds rate decisions can manage the outcomes over the very near term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Year-over-year inflation, headline CPI and PCE inflation, have now been consistently above 3 percent since October 1987.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Year-over-year core PCE inflation has exceeded 2 percent every month but one since April 2004.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Businesses are reporting an increased willingness to pass on cost increases.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Near term, we might get some moderation in headline inflation, if the recent drop in oil prices holds.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This might result in less upward pressure on inflation expectations, at least in the near term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, as has been pointed out, oil prices are notoriously hard to predict, and we may well see a resurgence in oil prices before the year’s end; but we don’t know.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: More important, a drop in oil prices will only temporarily mask what I view as the underlying inflationary pressures.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Oil prices have clearly exacerbated the recent numbers and may mitigate them in the near term going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But my concern is that the real source of intermediate-term to longer-term inflationary pressures comes from our own accommodative policy, whose consequences for inflation will be felt only over time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We are unable to control the rise in oil prices and its consequences for inflation in the short term, but we must hold ourselves accountable for the longer-term consequences of our choices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Should we maintain our accommodative stance for too much longer, my view is that we are likely to see higher trend inflation in the intermediate term and a ratcheting up of inflation expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If that scenario unfolds, it will take a much more costly policy action to re-anchor those expectations than the cost of a preemptive move to raise the funds rate in the near term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To be sure, shifting policy to a less accommodative stance will be a difficult decision to make, given the continued volatility in financial markets and the projected near-term weakness in employment and output growth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, what has been referred to as the tail risk of a very negative growth outcome has decreased since the start of the year, whereas inflation risks have increased.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think the enhancements we have made to our liquidity facilities should be sufficient to address any remaining dysfunctions in the financial markets, but they will not address the credit or solvency issues, nor should we expect them or desire them to do so.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The markets will have to do that admittedly heavy lifting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do not believe that we can wait until employment growth and the financial markets have completely turned around to begin to reverse course.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But by our aggressive attention to short-term risk to growth and financial turmoil, we do put at some risk our ability to deliver on our intermediate- and longer-term goals of both price stability and sustainable growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a coffee break until 11:20.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Boston forecast used for the June meeting expected that the unemployment rate would peak at approximately 5.7 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Unfortunately, with the July employment report, the unemployment rate has already reached 5.7 percent, and we expect the economy is likely to grow less than potential for the next several quarters.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With the unemployment rate rising in the past three months by 0.7 percentage point and payroll employment declining for the past six months, I am concerned that there remains a significant risk that the second half of this year would look a lot like the “severe financial stress” or “typical recession” scenarios.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My concern reflects the potential impact of further deterioration among financial institutions and financial markets that may create a significant headwind for the economy and the likelihood that economic problems are growing in other countries, which would slow one of the few bright spots in the economy—exports.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Since our last meeting, much has been written about the problems at the GSEs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Concern with the viability of the GSEs and potential future losses has contributed to mortgage rates rising despite our past easing, the weak economy, and diminished demand for mortgages.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With financial institutions showing little interest in lending to subprime or jumbo borrowers, the increased cost for individuals that qualify for conforming loans is likely to weaken the one part of the housing market that had been relatively resilient to financial problems to date.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: For potential buyers, higher interest rates and the likelihood that housing prices will continue to fall provide little current incentive to purchase a home, while the job losses are providing an immediate need for some owners to sell their homes.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We need the housing market and housing prices to stabilize, which I had hoped would occur in the second half of this year, but now it looks as though it will be deferred until next year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Falling housing prices have created significant collateral damage.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Liquidity problems that began one year ago remain in play.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The capital-constrained financial institutions that are forced to shrink their balance sheets may pose a significant additional problem in the second half of this year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While many of the largest banks that suffered significant losses last year were able to raise additional capital fairly readily, the capital losses on newly issued bank equity may have reduced many investors’ appetite for providing new capital for banks until it is clear that the economy is recovering.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The falling national housing prices and problems in commercial real estate in some sectors of the economy are now affecting regional and community banking institutions, many of which are unlikely to get equity infusions and thus will be forced to shrink.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A reduction in the willingness to lend, as represented by the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey, has often portended a reduction in credit to bank-dependent borrowers.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As we get a more traditional credit crunch compounding the liquidity problems, I am concerned that credit will be less available to consumers and businesses and further slow consumption and business investment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Since the June meeting, the stock market has fallen 7 percent; and with the number of large financial institutions experiencing very elevated CDS spreads and stock prices in the single digits, the failure of one or more relatively large domestic or foreign financial institutions is a real possibility.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In such an environment, the assumption of annual equity prices rising 7 percent in the rest of this year and 12 percent in 2009 as assumed in the Greenbook would seem to have some significant downside risk.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Elevated unemployment rates and a flat or slightly falling trend in wage and salary inflation suggest an absence of the inflationary pressures in labor markets that would lead to rising inflation once energy and food prices stabilize.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: These factors give me some confidence that we will see core and total inflation in 2009 close to 2 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Since our last meeting, labor markets have been weaker than expected, and oil prices and many other commodity prices have fallen, in part as a result of the concern with a slowing global economy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Although total inflation measures are clearly higher than any of us would want, these readings appear to be transitory responses to supply shocks that are not flowing through to labor markets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In fact, evidence from the labor market would seem to indicate that the downside risks to the economy are affecting labor markets through job losses but are not creating an environment in which labor tries to offset supply shocks with higher wage demands.

speaker: LACKER
text: Before I begin, let me add my words of welcome to Betsy Duke, welcoming Governor Duke back to the Federal Reserve System.

speaker: LACKER
text: I say “back” because she has served excellently on our board of directors beginning almost 1 years ago.

speaker: LACKER
text: She’s a fast friend and strong supporter of the Federal Reserve System.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m delighted that the long wait for her installation is over, and I look forward to working with her; but I don’t want any of my compliments to her to be detrimental to her effectiveness.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Fifth District economy has remained weak in recent weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Manufacturing and service sector activity fell.

speaker: LACKER
text: Real estate conditions remain sluggish.

speaker: LACKER
text: Export activity remains the bright spot, with reports of sustained growth in outbound cargo at District ports.

speaker: LACKER
text: In a new development, however, manufacturers’ expectations for the very near future turned negative in our most recent survey.

speaker: LACKER
text: Respondents are typically relatively optimistic about things six months from now.

speaker: LACKER
text: Retail contacts indicate that the decline in sales broadened in July in our survey, and there aren’t many reports mentioning the effect of tax stimulus checks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Price expectations for both raw materials and final goods rose in our July survey, and some of those measures are at record highs.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the national level, my outlook for real growth is broadly consistent with the Greenbook’s this time.

speaker: LACKER
text: I expect sluggish growth to continue through the remainder of the year, with a pickup beginning sometime next year.

speaker: LACKER
text: Housing is likely to continue to be a drag, though a diminishing one, until then.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consumer spending is likely to remain subdued, and business investment is likely to moderate somewhat.

speaker: LACKER
text: I expect payroll employment to continue to decline for a while at about the current pace—a pace that, as others have noted, is quite modest relative to what we typically see in a recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the most likely outcome is for us to continue to skirt an outright recession.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think there is some risk of a broader and sharper contraction.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe the magnitude of that risk is modest, but it’s not negligible to me.

speaker: LACKER
text: Business investment could deteriorate, a risk that’s most prominent in the nonresidential construction sector that we discussed earlier.

speaker: LACKER
text: But this is a small component of aggregate demand, smaller than housing; and given the nature of gestation lags in this sector, I think a downturn is likely to be gradual rather than abrupt.

speaker: LACKER
text: Household spending probably poses the greatest risk to growth at this point.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consumer spending has flattened out in real terms, although that’s what one would expect given the increase in food and energy prices that we’ve seen.

speaker: LACKER
text: Given the difficulty of assessing the extent to which tax rebates are propping up consumer spending right now, we do not know how much Q4 consumption is going to be affected by the stimulus rolling off.

speaker: LACKER
text: Potential growth effects of credit constraints or financial headwinds have gotten a lot of attention these days.

speaker: LACKER
text: I remain skeptical about the magnitude of the drag on consumption and investment spending that credit market conditions are likely to create.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have, of course, seen reports in the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey of tightened credit terms, but through June both C&I and consumer loans have continued to grow.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would note that we are hearing in the Fifth District concerns from some of our smaller institutions that some large banks are bidding aggressively for deposits—this has been going on for several months now, of course—and as a result, the smaller banks are paying more to fund their loans.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’re also hearing now—and this is a new report—of larger banks cutting back on fed funds lending to smaller institutions, no doubt out of a concern about possible bank failures.

speaker: LACKER
text: What I think we’re seeing in banking markets is more of a reallocation of activity among banks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Different institutions have been affected very differently by recent events depending on the strategies they chose to pursue in the years preceding this episode.

speaker: LACKER
text: As a consequence, intermediation is just shifting from some institutions to others.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, we’ve heard of banks picking up business that other banks are shedding.

speaker: LACKER
text: Anecdotes about particular banks cutting back on lending thus need to be taken with a grain of salt, and I don’t think they’re necessarily representative of the banking sector as a whole.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, there was a really egregious case in the New York Times of people not getting credit from banks because of this credit crunch.

speaker: LACKER
text: In paragraph 6, one is introduced to their lead anecdote: a borrower at Wachovia who was denied credit.

speaker: LACKER
text: In paragraph 22, we find out that he actually got credit two weeks later at this same institution.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’m a little skeptical about all of this anecdotal evidence about credit constraints.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s undoubtedly the case that credit standards have tightened, but the environment is such that a lot of borrowers have gotten genuinely weaker.

speaker: LACKER
text: I mention all of this just because it influences how I feel about arguments that credit market conditions make the current level of the real funds rate any less meaningful as an indicator of the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I just don’t find those arguments convincing right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: The real funds rate using the Greenbook’s forecast of overall inflation four quarters ahead is lower than it has been at any time since the 1970s.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, this measure is about 1½ percentage points lower than the lows it reached in 2003 or 1994, and I think this is to my mind a better way to measure the actual real federal funds rate than what’s plotted in the Bluebook.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Greenbook forecast is that core PCE inflation will rise to 2.6 percent for the second half of this year and then gradually subside to 1¾ percent a year or so after that.

speaker: LACKER
text: This forecast is a very risky path, I believe, because at any point along that hump, higher inflation could well become embedded in expectations.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think getting back to price stability after this episode is going to depend critically on the stability of inflation expectations, as many of you have noted.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is true that TIPS compensation measures have been reasonably steady for a few months and that wage rates show no sign of accelerating as yet.

speaker: LACKER
text: But if we wait to raise rates until wage rates accelerate or TIPS measures spike, we will have waited too long.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that’s very clear, and it will cost us too much to recover our credibility.

speaker: LACKER
text: Accordingly, I believe that the biggest policy risk we’re going to be facing in the months ahead is the risk of waiting too long.

speaker: LACKER
text: In past episodes of economic or financial weakness, we’ve been unwilling at times to raise the funds rate until we were almost completely certain that economic recovery would be sustained.

speaker: LACKER
text: I do not think that we can afford that luxury at the present time.

speaker: LACKER
text: The risk is too great that inflation expectations will ratchet up again.

speaker: LACKER
text: We need to be prepared to raise rates even if growth is not back to potential and even if financial markets are not yet tranquil, and we need to be prepared to raise rates even if we think that we might have to reverse course.

speaker: LACKER
text: After all, we cut rates aggressively even though we were not certain that a recession was in store for us and, in part, on the grounds that we could reverse course if it proved that we cut too far.

speaker: LACKER
text: To insist on more certainty to raise rates than to reduce them would introduce a fatal asymmetry in our reaction function.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me add a comment or two inspired by some of the discussion around the table.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to commend President Bullard’s discussion of systemic risk.

speaker: LACKER
text: You mentioned this earlier in your Q&A session, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is a notoriously slippery concept.

speaker: LACKER
text: In popular usage, it seems to mean an episode in which one bad thing happens followed by a lot of other seemingly related bad things happening, and as such, it’s a purely empirical notion without any content or usefulness by itself as a guide to policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: It doesn’t say whether those other bad things are efficient—things that ought to happen—or inefficient and preventable by suitable policy intervention.

speaker: LACKER
text: To invoke the notion of systemic risk to support a particular policy course requires theory.

speaker: LACKER
text: I spoke about theory last night, but it requires some theory, some coherent understanding of the way you think the world works.

speaker: LACKER
text: The theoretical literature related to systemic risk is relatively young, and this isn’t the place to go into it.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’ve said before that I think it would be useful for this Committee to learn more about this.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Committee might be surprised that the literature provides only relatively tenuous rationales—I think is a fair judgment—for policy intervention.

speaker: LACKER
text: I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the group you’ve commissioned to study the meaning of unusual and exigent circumstances can explore this terrain in a little more depth.

speaker: LACKER
text: Going forward, I think our deliberations would be aided if we were to strive to put our theoretical frameworks on the table when discussing how financial markets work and what we ought to do about them.

speaker: LACKER
text: In case there’s any suspense, for my own money—and this is just one man’s view—I haven’t seen a convincing case for the existence of policy-relevant market failures in the financial markets in which we’ve intervened, apart from the usual distortions owing to the federal financial safety net.

speaker: LACKER
text: We systematically expanded that safety net.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe what we’ve done has been to subsidize selected borrower classes and prop up prices of various financial assets, and I think the problem we face now is the tremendous dependency of financial institutions and markets on our credit.

speaker: STERN
text: Let me make just a few comments about the Greenbook forecast at this point, which I found quite useful for thinking about policy going forward only in part because it is quite close, at least in broad overview, to the forecast I submitted before the June meeting on the economic outlook, inflation, and so forth.

speaker: STERN
text: In any event, given the alignment in these forecasts, I think there are several characteristics worth emphasizing.

speaker: STERN
text: First, financial headwinds persist—we have talked about this for quite a while—and the Greenbook now assumes more stress and more persistence than it assumed earlier.

speaker: STERN
text: Second, the inventory overhang in housing persists with negative implications for activity and for prices in that sector.

speaker: STERN
text: Third, real growth is subdued over the next several quarters at least.

speaker: STERN
text: Against the background of the Greenbook forecast, growth over the balance of this year in excess of 1 percent in real terms would have to be considered a positive surprise.

speaker: STERN
text: Growth in excess of trend next year would have to be considered a positive surprise.

speaker: STERN
text: Finally, with regard to inflation, headline inflation abates after the current quarter, although overall both headline inflation and core inflation remain above 2 percent through 2009.

speaker: STERN
