text: I realize that there’s considerable uncertainty surrounding all of that and that not everybody shares that assessment, but I think it’s worth emphasizing those features because we need to try to think several months and several quarters ahead in terms of the environment in which we will be making policy decisions.

speaker: STERN
text: If these forecasts are at least in the ballpark—at the risk of perhaps belaboring the obvious—it seems to me that a major message of those forecasts is that the policy environment is likely to remain significantly challenging for several more quarters at least.

speaker: STERN
text: I could put that another way.

speaker: STERN
text: It seems that evolving readings on the economy and inflation are not likely to line up appreciably at all with either aspect of the dual mandate over the next several quarters.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, let me say that the Tenth District probably, on the whole, performed a little better than the national average in the industries that we have; but in terms of job growth, it has slowed.

speaker: HOENIG
text: At the same time, we’re still adding jobs in the region, and our unemployment rate remains relatively low compared with national measures.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Although wage pressures actually do show some elevation relative to our Beige Book survey, they have obviously eased a bit in recent months.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But it’s interesting that, as we talk and monitor the labor conditions and we talk to some of the labor unions, there is a great understanding that they’re losing ground.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They are going to begin entering contracts at the end of this year and in the next year, and how they approach that is extremely important because, again, they are looking and talking now about cost- of-living adjustments and those sorts of things, which gives me some pause.

speaker: HOENIG
text: According to our manufacturing survey, our activity actually strengthened in July, although the expectations for future activity have diminished somewhat.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Not surprisingly, manufacturers producing energy and agriculture and in export-related markets continue to operate at relatively high levels whereas the other areas within the District are showing some slowdown.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Let me talk just a second about oil.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Although oil prices have declined, as was noted, they are still high enough that capital spending and production remain elevated and look to remain so in the foreseeable future.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In fact, some of our industry contacts suggest that, as long as expected prices for oil remain in the $70 to $80 range, there should continue to be a fair amount of investment in that particular sector.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As you well know from reading the Wall Street Journal, we did have the SemGroup go bankrupt in the Tulsa area.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It has had, I think, fairly confined effects.

speaker: HOENIG
text: One of our regional banks took some pretty heavy losses.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They’re very well capitalized and did recapitalize some of it, so they’ve not been dramatically affected by it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Local producers are in the worst bind because they haven’t been paid for some of the oil delivered and there’s no other party to contract with for future deliveries.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So that has brought a lot of uncertainty in the local area about where to provide some of this oil that they’re producing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In my discussions with businesses around the District, it’s interesting that there’s a lot more conversation about and focus on managing your price strategy in this environment.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As has been true for a while, fuel surcharges are prevalent, and firms are able to pass those along with a fair amount of ease.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, businesses are reporting that materials suppliers are placing 10-day to 30-day time limits on their price quotes.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Finally, most price indexes in our manufacturing survey remain near historically high levels, and plans for future pass-throughs have actually intensified.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to the national outlook, my outlook for growth has not changed materially since the last meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I expect that growth will slow in the second half because of these higher energy prices, some weakness in the labor market, and sluggish activity in some of the manufacturing sectors.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The fact is that the uncertainty regarding the economic outlook is considerable, and downside risk to growth in the near-term future is there.

speaker: HOENIG
text: These risks are being addressed, from our perspective, by our current stance of accommodative monetary policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So we are addressing that uncertainty.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The point I would like to make is that I’m less uncertain about the outlook for core inflation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have seen erosion in longer-term inflation expectations, and I believe inflation risks have actually risen.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If core inflation rises in the second half as expected, there is a real possibility that inflation expectations will become unanchored, especially if we maintain our current accommodative stance of policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: An expected leveling-off of food and energy prices and slack in the economy could help moderate upward pressure on inflation, but I do not think they will be enough to actually bring inflation down to an acceptable level.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In fact, if we maintain the funds rate at 2 percent, I think inflation is more likely to move higher than lower over the medium term, and that concerns me.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Like the Greenbook, our modal forecast shows weaker real activity and slightly higher core inflation over the forecast period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Downside risks to growth remain substantial, in my view, and have probably increased relative to what we thought in June.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Risks on the inflation front remain weighted to the upside, perhaps somewhat less than in June, but this is hard to know with confidence.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The adverse growth risks are worse for several reasons.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The labor market and labor income are weakening more quickly than expected.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Although there were some tentative signs of stabilization of housing demand in the spring, demand seems to have fallen further since.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Credit conditions are tighter and are expected to be tighter longer, and this seems likely to produce a further deterioration in overall demand—note, of course, the reduction in credit for autos, the rise in mortgage rates, and the more conservative lending standards for consumer and corporate credit.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Growth outside the United States seems likely to slow further.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course, fundamental to this dynamic, as has been true for 12 months, each shift in perceptions that the bottom in overall economic growth is further away produces additional stress for financial institutions and markets, adding to the intensity of prospective financial headwinds and to concerns about downside risks to growth.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Now, the adverse tail on the inflation front remains significant.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Many measures of underlying inflation suggest a broad-based, if limited to date, acceleration in the rate of underlying inflation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Market- and survey-based measures of long-term expectations are high.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Surveys suggest that firms are able to pass on some part of the acceleration in energy and materials costs.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the more positive side, energy, commodity, and materials prices have declined significantly, principally it seems because of expectations of slower growth in global demand.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Growth is moderating significantly around the world, and it’s going to have to moderate further in the most populous parts of the world as central banks there get monetary policy tighter.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The growth of unit labor costs has been and is expected to be very moderate here.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Profit margins still show plenty of room to absorb cost increases, and as David reminded us, you can have a relatively benign outlook for the path of core inflation without margins narrowing very dramatically.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Inflation expectations have not deteriorated meaningfully here, even with the flatter expected path of monetary policy in the United States.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Of course, it’s very important that inflation expectations and pricing power moderate from current levels.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If some of the downside risks to growth materialize, this will happen, and inflation risks will moderate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If, however, the economy continues to prove to be resilient to these downside risks, then we will face higher inflation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On balance, the rate of growth in underlying inflation suggests that growth in demand in the United States will have to be below potential for a longer period of time if inflation expectations are to come down sufficiently.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This means that we will have to tighten monetary policy relatively soon compared with our previous behavior in recoveries—perhaps before we see the actual bottom in house prices and the actual peak in unemployment.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: However, at this point, the risks to real growth remain critical.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In my view, we need to have more confidence that we have substantially reduced the risks of a much sharper, more protracted decline in growth before we begin to tighten.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think it is unlikely that we will be able or will need to move before early next year.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Short-term market expectations for monetary policy in the United States seem about right at present.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t see a strong case for trying to alter those expectations in either direction at this point.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: To try to pull forward the expected tightening would risk adding to the downside risk to growth and magnifying the risk of a much more severe financial crisis.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the other hand, if we avoid some of these downside risks to growth, then policy will need to tighten more quickly, perhaps, than the expected path now priced in the markets.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The evolution of monetary policy expectations and of inflation expectations since May illustrates how uncertain the markets are about what path of policy will be appropriate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But the pattern of changes in both of these measures of expectations suggests that the markets believe we will get this balance right—that we will do enough soon enough to keep underlying inflation expectations from eroding materially.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like others around the table, I made only small revisions to the central tendency of my forecast going forward as a result of the developments of the intermeeting period, maybe a slight reduction in the path of output and a quicker decline in headline inflation owing to the oil prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think more important than any shift in central tendencies is the sense that the information tends to reinforce—to reduce the uncertainties around—the basic contours of a projection in which the economy operates with a wider output gap and a lower inflation rate on balance over the next 18 months or so than it has over recent quarters.

speaker: KOHN
text: About the output gap, the incoming information strongly suggests that we are on a trajectory that at least for some time will have the economy growing appreciably below the growth rate of its potential.

speaker: KOHN
text: The most obvious evidence is the persistence of a soft labor market—continuing declines in employment and no sign of near-term strengthening in the initial claims data.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that the declines in employment, as several of you have pointed out, are not consistent with a recession, but they’re certainly not consistent with the economy growing close to its potential.

speaker: KOHN
text: You need another 150,000 or 200,000 jobs rather than minus 60,000, which is where we are now.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think the economy is likely to grow below potential for some time.

speaker: KOHN
text: Even on the spending side, the decline in consumption in June, when rebate checks were continuing to hit bank accounts, and a further sharp drop in auto sales in July might be early signs that households are beginning to pull back under pressure from higher energy prices, job worries, declining house values, and reduced credit availability.

speaker: KOHN
text: To be sure, one month’s consumption data along with auto sales, which are subject to all kinds of idiosyncratic influences, are not enough to justify a major change in outlook.

speaker: KOHN
text: But as President Lacker noted, household spending has for some time been a source of downside risk to the forecast.

speaker: KOHN
text: At some point, household spending could begin to reflect attitudes, and this information at a minimum seems to underline those risks as well as to point to sluggish growth of spending in the third quarter.

speaker: KOHN
text: Soggy economic news has extended to our trading partners, where actual activity and expected activity also have been marked down.

speaker: KOHN
text: The tone of news from abroad has been decidedly downbeat, as those economies feel the effect of weaker purchases from the United States, continuing financial strain, softening housing markets, and higher energy prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: Much as in the United States, attitudes abroad seem weaker than the data; but the euro area did report a record decline in retail sales in June this morning, and my sense is that our trading partners are facing larger downside risks to growth as well as a markdown of central tendencies.

speaker: KOHN
text: The dollar hasn’t changed much on balance for four or five months now.

speaker: KOHN
text: With a stable dollar and weaker demand abroad, production in the United States will be getting a lot less cushion from net exports over the next few quarters than it did in the first half of the year.

speaker: KOHN
text: Finally, despite the downward movement in Treasury interest rates and in the expected federal funds rate path, financial conditions for households and businesses have tightened since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: Savers and intermediaries have become even more cautious amid concerns about deepening losses spreading beyond subprime mortgages, about the safety of uninsured deposits at regional banks, high volatility in markets, and the possible weakening of the underlying macro situation.

speaker: KOHN
text: Lenders are hunkering down to endure a long period of rising credit problems and great uncertainty.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think we need to rely on anecdotes here.

speaker: KOHN
text: Mortgage interest rates have actually risen on balance, as have corporate bond yields across many risk categories; and in many of these cases, the nominal interest rates are at least as high as or in some cases much higher than they were last August when the federal funds rate was at 5¼.

speaker: KOHN
text: Banks continue to tighten terms and standards for nearly all categories of loans.

speaker: KOHN
text: Equity prices have fallen, adding to the downward pressure on wealth from declining house prices, and I think these developments underscore the very slow recovery likely in financial markets and the possible downside risks relative to even that very gradual improvement that many of us were expecting.

speaker: KOHN
text: The tightening of conditions is damping credit growth broadly defined and will constrain, at least to some extent, spending going forward, delaying the return to trend or above-trend growth.

speaker: KOHN
text: Thus although uncertainties remain quite elevated, I think we can be a little more confident that the economy will be subject to further quarters of below-trend growth and declining resource utilization.

speaker: KOHN
text: Furthermore, with housing prices still falling fast, inventories of homes still high, and financial markets quite skittish, the downside risks even to a slightly lower central tendency forecast remain high.

speaker: KOHN
text: Greater confidence that output will grow below potential for a time contributes to a little more optimism on my part that inflation will, indeed, come down substantially over the coming quarters.

speaker: KOHN
text: An environment of rising unemployment and declining capacity utilization is not one in which businesses or labor will find it easy to restore real incomes or raise profit margins after the increase in energy prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: With regard to that increase in energy and other commodity prices and how it affects headline inflation, I like to differentiate pass-through from spillover.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we can expect pass- through.

speaker: KOHN
text: Pass-through to consumer prices of the higher energy and commodity prices is part of the adjustment process by which demand gets damped and by which consumers realize, unfortunately, the lower real income that they get from the adverse terms of trade.

speaker: KOHN
text: So the fact that businesses are able to pass through higher commodity prices and higher petroleum prices I don’t find all that worrisome, provided that they’re passing through a one-time increase in prices rather than a continuing rise.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we have some further evidence that at least to date—things could change, I admit—what we are seeing is a pass-through of a one-time rise rather than some continuing increases.

speaker: KOHN
text: For one thing, commodity prices, as shown in Bill’s chart, have flattened out or actually declined in the past few months.

speaker: KOHN
text: So presumably that pass-through is a one-time jump, if that’s what they’re doing, passing through those prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: Second, I think we saw in the GDP chain-type price indexes that the price of domestic value added increased at an annual rate of only 1.1 percent in the second quarter—which suggests to me that, at least through the second quarter, there was very little spillover from these higher commodity and energy prices to the stuff we produce here at home.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also, labor compensation growth, which could be a lagging indicator, at least to date hasn’t increased.

speaker: KOHN
text: If anything, it has slowed a little further, which along with relatively robust productivity growth is holding down unit labor costs.

speaker: KOHN
text: Headline inflation—the goods and services that people purchase—has been high.

speaker: KOHN
text: Energy prices are being passed through, but I think to date there’s no evidence or very little evidence that it’s spilling over into other prices in the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: So this is about the adjustment to relative prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: Obviously the decline in oil prices, if it holds, will be helpful on the inflation front, both in its direct effect on headline inflation and its indirect effect on inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: We finally have evidence of two-way risk in oil prices, and that should make us more comfortable with an assumption of stable prices as a reasonable basis for forecasting.

speaker: KOHN
text: Other recent contributors to higher price levels have also become less averse.

speaker: KOHN
text: As I mentioned, other industrial commodity prices have leveled out or declined, and the dollar has been relatively stable in recent months.

speaker: KOHN
text: Although I feel a little more confident about the expectation of lower inflation going forward, I agree that upside risks still prevail.

speaker: KOHN
text: Core inflation has ticked up.

speaker: KOHN
text: Headline inflation will be high for some time and could threaten to spill over through increases in inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: Oil and commodity price declines are largely an endogenous response to perceptions of weak growth, and if those perceptions turn around, so will those prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: Longer-term inflation expectations remain elevated by some measures and are probably less well anchored than they were a couple of years ago, before oil and commodity prices rose so much.

speaker: KOHN
text: In sum, I see upside risks to both the inflation gaps and the output gaps as having diminished over the intermeeting period, and we’ll get to the implications of that for policy in the next part of the meeting.

speaker: WARSH
text: I have no material changes to report in my view on the overall state of financial stability, growth, or inflation; but as I talked about at the last meeting, it still is likely to be a long, hot summer, and we’re only about half over with it.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’ll talk first about financial institutions—make maybe four or five points—and then turn quickly to the economy and inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, on financial institutions, I think the body blow that the financial markets and the real economy have taken because of the turmoil at the GSEs is not complete.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is easy for those of us in Washington to forget that bill signings don’t always solve problems.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’d say, if the last thing that happens on GSEs is that the bill was signed two weeks ago and action isn’t taken in the coming weeks and months, then I would be surprised if we could get through this period without more GSE turmoil finding its way onto the front pages.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, in terms of financial market conditions, the fall in oil prices and the rest of the energy complex is, indeed, good news, but it strikes me that it has camouflaged an even tougher period for financial institutions than would otherwise be the case.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is, financial institutions somehow look a little more resilient, but I think part of that is only because of the negative correlation that’s developed in recent times between equity prices of financials and oil prices.

speaker: WARSH
text: The financial institutions themselves strike me as being in worse condition than market prices would suggest.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, capital raising, as we have long talked about, is essential to the fix among financial institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: The way I best describe capital raising over maybe the last nine months is that the first round of capital raising, which was in November and December, was really the vanity round.

speaker: WARSH
text: This consisted of very limited due diligence, sovereign wealth funds signing up, issuers relying upon their vaunted global brands, and capital being raised in a matter of days.

speaker: WARSH
text: The second round probably took us to the spring, a round that I’d call the confessional round.

speaker: WARSH
text: In this round, financial institutions said, “Oh my, look at these real write-downs that I have.

speaker: WARSH
text: Look at the need for this real capital raising, and here I’m telling you, the investors, all that I know.” But the second and third confessions usually have less credibility than the first.

speaker: WARSH
text: The third round is the round that we’re in the middle of, which I think of as the liquidation and recap round, likely to be the hardest round to pull off.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is likely to force issuers of new shares or of new forms of preferred stock to be asking of themselves and their investors the toughest choices.

speaker: WARSH
text: They have to assess the strength and durability of their core franchises.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that this will be happening in very real time.

speaker: WARSH
text: So the circumstance of an investment bank that Bill mentioned at the outset I don’t think will be the sole case of this.

speaker: WARSH
text: This liquidation and recap round is later than would be ideal from the perspective of the broader economy, but it is absolutely needed.

speaker: WARSH
text: Until we see how it occurs, it’s hard for me to be much more sanguine that the capital markets or the credit markets will be returning to anything like normal anytime soon.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me make a fourth broad point about financial institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: Because of these different phases of capital raise, I think management credibility among financial institutions is at least as suspect as it has ever been during this period.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even new management teams that have come in have in some ways used up a lot of their credibility.

speaker: WARSH
text: It would be nice to believe that they have taken all actions necessary to protect their franchises and their businesses, but most stakeholders are skeptical that they’ve taken significant or sufficient action.

speaker: WARSH
text: At the end of the day, no matter where policy comes out in terms of regulatory policy from the Fed and other bank regulators or accounting policy from the SEC or FASB, it strikes me that those changes in policy are less determinative of how things shake out.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is, management credibility is so in question that the cure is not likely to come from accounting rules or regulators but from the markets’ believing that what management says is what management believes and will act on it.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a result, I think that many of these financial institutions are operating in a zero-defect world, which is posing risks to the real economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: Fifth, let me make a final point about financials.

speaker: WARSH
text: We’ve all talked a lot about the effect of different curves for housing prices on the financial institutions themselves.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t mean to give short shrift to any of that, but I would say that the level of uncertainty and associated risks of their non-housing-related assets are now very much a focus.

speaker: WARSH
text: According to July 2008 data, of credit currently being extended by banks, only about 20 percent is for residential real estate.

speaker: WARSH
text: Only about 9 percent is for consumer credit.

speaker: WARSH
text: So that leaves the balance in areas where these financial institutions and their management teams have to be asking themselves whether the weaknesses that are emerging in the real economy will place uncertainty over assets that have nothing to do with housing.

speaker: WARSH
text: That’s a major downside risk for financial institutions and has not been much of a focus of shareholder and stakeholder concerns.

speaker: WARSH
text: There are two open issues that will guide some of our thinking, at least with respect to these credit markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, as we talked about a little last night with the presidents, are the embedded losses so great at such a critical mass of institutions with management credibility so low that many more than currently expected might be unable to survive?

speaker: WARSH
text: This is a question that I’m not sure I know the answer to.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, despite the concerns about the effect of the credit markets on the broader economy that I talked about, our monetary policy may not be terribly well suited to be fixing those problems, and financial institutions may not be terribly sensitive to the extent we decide that we should change the stance of policy.

speaker: WARSH
text: Taking all that into account, let me say a couple of words about growth and inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, on the economic growth front, given my views of what’s happening in the credit markets, it’s very hard for me to believe that the economy will get back to potential anytime soon.

speaker: WARSH
text: There are continued financial stresses that could last through year-end, and in there could be an upside surprise.

speaker: WARSH
text: Still, all things considered, my base case has second-half growth still above staff estimates owing in part to the productivity we’ve seen in recent months and the remarkable resiliency of this economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: If we look beyond that horizon, though, toward the Greenbook forecast in 2009 and beyond, I must say I don’t really see the inflection point to take us back to economic growth of 2.2 percent or whatever the Greenbook suggests.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we’re going to be in this period of below- trend growth for quite some time.

speaker: WARSH
text: My own view is that, when the Congress comes back after its August recess, we will be in the middle of a big debate on “Son of Stimulus” and that the stimulus probabilities have moved up quite materially.

speaker: WARSH
text: However, it is not at all obvious to me that it will do much in terms of helping the real economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: Outside the United States, I share the view of Governor Kohn, which is that I’d expect global GDP, particularly GDP among advanced foreign economies, our major trading partners, to continue to disappoint, making the remarkable addition of net export growth to our own GDP likely to dissipate.

speaker: WARSH
text: Turning finally to inflation, my view is that inflation risks are very real, and I believe that these risks are higher than growth risks.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t take that much comfort from the move in commodity prices since we last met.

speaker: WARSH
text: If that trend continues, then that would certainly be good news; but I must say I don’t feel as though inflation risks have moved down noticeably since we last had this discussion.

speaker: WARSH
text: The staff expects food prices to continue to be challenging; that is certainly my view.

speaker: WARSH
text: The staff also expects core import prices to fall rather precipitously.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m a little skeptical of that view.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think it’s possible, but I don’t really see the catalyst for that given what we see about changes in input prices overseas and given expectations of the dollar in foreign exchange markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: So with that, I think that the inflation risks are real, and I’ll save the balance of my remarks for the next round.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have now had the first anniversary of all the financial turmoil, and how have the markets celebrated?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, we have had Freddie and Fannie go down and need one of the largest bailouts.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have had IndyMac go down—the second largest bank failure in U.S. history and perhaps the most costly bank failure in U.S. history.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I am talking just in nominal terms; I haven’t actually done the real adjustments.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, we’ve seen a variety of widening risk spreads.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: At the last meeting I went on with my standard metaphor of the slow burn and said that things could reignite, and I think we certainly have seen a few things reignite.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I very much agree with Governor Warsh with respect to Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae that, although legislation has been passed, the devil will be in the implementation details.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Simply because the Treasury has the capacity to do something, it is not quite clear what it will do or be able to do or how the markets will respond to that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, Freddie and Fannie have been really the only game in town for mortgage securitization.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The jumbo markets have not been working.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The subprime market is not there right now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So until and unless we can be assured that they will operate properly, they still have a lot of potential for more flames coming out.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There are also a number of other reasons that I am still concerned about financial markets being very far from normal.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One, reference was made to a study that we have done here at the Board that Nellie Liang is taking the lead on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: New York has also done a study; I think they used very different methods but came out with similar numbers.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The studies say that large losses are still to come and that total losses associated with the challenges that we have been seeing will be on the order of $900 billion.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: U.S. and European financial institutions have taken about $400 billion of write-downs.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Not all of those losses will be on financial institutions’ balance sheets, but there certainly are potentially more losses to come—not only in mortgages, in leveraged loans, and in commercial real estate but also in the consumer parts of the portfolio and potentially other parts of the portfolio.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A fragility is there, which has to be taken into account when we look at capital ratios.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If you simply look at reported capital ratios, they are off their peaks of a few years ago.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: However, if you were to do a more-thorough mark-to-market on a lot of different pieces of the portfolio or if you did have to liquidate—even assuming it wasn’t a broad fire sale but just one institution that had to liquidate now and it had no further consequences for anyone else’s expectations, which I don’t think is accurate—you would see those capital ratios be in fact much, much thinner than they appear in an accounting sense.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A number of people talked about the OIS spreads and said that things seem to be at 50 basis points rather than at 10 basis points.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, that is true not only in the U.S. dollar but also in the euro and in sterling.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If you look to the forward market, that number is increasing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is not staying the same.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is going up quite a bit, to about 75 basis points over a year period for the dollar to 130 to 150 basis points in sterling and in euro.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That suggests a lot more challenges to come.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So even if 50 is the new 10, it is still a major challenge going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That puts a lot of pressure on banks to generate earnings to make up for the write-downs and other challenges.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In the old days, when you could finance yourself at 10 basis points, the institutions were undertaking a lot of activities that would allow them to generate a lot of revenue, even if they kept taking hits in certain parts of their portfolio.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But when funding is at 5 times that, or 10 times that, or 15 times that, a lot of activities that once were profitable are not profitable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The margins are much lower, and their ability to earn their way out of this is much, much more of a challenge.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that is going to be even truer for the European institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That is actually one area in which I see it as more likely that an important shoe might drop, not just in the United States but in a major European institution.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: European institutions haven’t been as active in raising capital, and there are more constraints on their ability to raise capital, given the way rights issues work.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that greater challenges are going to come in the European economies and that the ECB faces greater challenges in dealing with the increasing inflation threat that they have there and worldwide, while being able to provide some policy accommodation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Third, securitization markets have certainly not recovered.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have talked about that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The infrastructure investment that will be needed for these to come back in terms of data, contract certainty, et cetera is going to take a long, long time.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is not clear exactly how long, but it is clear that recovery will not be right around the corner.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That means continuing pressure on banks’ balance sheets independent of all the other capital issues.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If they just want to continue on, they have to keep a lot of things on their balance sheets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One bright light, just in case you see nothing positive, is that we were able to put off some very significant changes in accounting— FAS 140 and FIN 46(R).

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They were on a very fast track to make changes that could have brought literally trillions of dollars of assets back onto balance sheets and would have made it extremely difficult for securitization markets to work.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That has been significantly delayed, and I think they will take a more balanced and measured approach.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Not only has that been put off, but also the institutions will have more time to deal with it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But this pressure is real.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey couldn’t be more crystal clear on the challenges that are there and that are likely to continue to be there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, as a number of people have mentioned, it is because of challenges on the HELOC portfolios and on the option ARM portfolios and uncertainty about a lot of other pieces of the portfolios.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So given my views, I am really glad that the Greenbook baseline has taken on board much more of what was previously a “delayed recovery” alternative simulation scenario, much in line with what President Stern mentioned.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I continue to see that the situation is quite brittle and that small pressures potentially can lead to large and rapid responses.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The “severe financial stress” alternative simulation in the Greenbook is certainly not my central tendency one, but I think that we can’t dismiss it too easily because there still could be another—what I have now taken to calling, since I chair the supervision and regulation committee—flare-up with one of my problem children.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Many of you know the problems in your Districts, but there are a lot of problems, unfortunately, in all the Districts and around the world.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I hope no one will ever hear about the problems that my children are having, but sometimes they do come out.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As Governor Warsh said, one way to try to deal with those is through capital.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is becoming increasingly difficult to do that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In the old days the accounting rules were such that you could take over an institution through so-called pooling accounting methods, so you would not face an immediate write-down of everything to current market values.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One challenge we have with the institutions that are likely to be failing over time is that these accounting standards are no longer available, so it is very, very difficult to use the kinds of methods that have been used in the past by the FDIC and other regulators to avoid the IndyMac type of problems.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is quite possible that we will be seeing more people queuing up, and more people pulling money out of accounts, even though they are insured accounts.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There has certainly not been a generalized drain from the banking system.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There has been a recent shuffling, as President Lacker said.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But it also makes a lot of institutions much, much more vulnerable than they have been in the past.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If you look at the “severe financial stress” scenario in the Greenbook, what is interesting about it is that it is relatively benign.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: For something that is severe stress, the macroeconomic outcomes in terms of GDP and unemployment aren’t that severe because of the policy response—taking the federal funds rate down to ¾ percent.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t think we can possibly do that in the current environment.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is not that I think that inflation expectations have become unanchored or are not contained, but I do think that our policy responses are contained precisely because we can’t quite go there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If you look at the “inflationary spiral” scenario, it says that by 2009 the fed funds rate would have to go up to 3½ percent.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t think we are in that or anywhere close to that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But if we had to respond as the Greenbook said to bring the fed funds rate down below 1 percent, I think we would get close to that, and we would be in a very, very difficult position.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have to be very careful about inflation expectations.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we have mixed evidence on inflation expectations and inflation, although I am heartened that things do not seem to have become unanchored.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some of both the market-based measures and the survey-based measures have come down a bit, although I think, as Governor Kohn said, that the situation is much more fragile.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t want to take on board too much comfort from the change in commodity prices because we have seen temporary movements up and we have seen temporary movements down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is heartening, but I think we have to still be very, very careful on this issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Mishkin, your swan song.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Well, I get one more chance in the policy round.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is the one I am going to really go for.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am sure that people are waiting for it.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: My modal forecast has not changed appreciably.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly, I am very concerned about the headwinds as a result of the difficulty in recapitalizing financial institutions, which Governor Warsh talked a lot about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As a result, I think that we are going to have subpotential growth for quite a period of time.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: However, the bigger concern is that I see downside risks as having risen substantially.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So let me first talk about the things that are the less worrisome downside risks.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think there are increased downside risks just on the real side of the economy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, the consumer has been very resilient, but I am not as sure that that will be true in the future.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We just saw terrible auto sales.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It could be just one month, and it could bounce back up.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But it could be a precursor to much bigger problems, which would not be completely surprising given some of the other things going on with housing prices and credit restrictions.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is one downside risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second is that European growth may have shifted down, and so the kind of problems that we are experiencing here perhaps are being experienced there, particularly in terms of lower housing prices in some parts of the euro zone.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That could mean less demand for our exports, and it would be another negative for economic activity.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The third is that we have actually seen a backup in mortgage rates, and that can have a direct effect on housing demand.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is pretty grim when you look at what is going on in terms of housing starts, but it could get worse.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It can’t go below zero, but it could get worse.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So if that were all there was, I would say that there may be a little increase in downside risk, but it wouldn’t frighten me.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I really am very worried about the potential downside risks in the financial sector.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have to disagree very strenuously with the view that, because you have been in a “financial stress” situation for a period of time, there is no potential for systemic risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, I would argue that the opposite can be the case.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Just as a reminder, remember that in the Great Depression, when—I can’t use the expression because it would be in the transcripts, but you know what I’m thinking—something hit the fan, [laughter] it actually occurred close to a year after the initial negative shock.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In this particular environment, we have to think about where we started.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We were very lucky that this financial disruption occurred when bank balance sheets actually were in very good shape initially.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You know, thank our lucky stars that it happened at that point.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We are now a year into this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Bank balance sheets do not look very good, for all the reasons that we have been discussing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In fact, they look pretty grim.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have had some failures, and we are concerned about other failures.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So we have a very different environment.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that situation, if a shoe drops—and we have had big shoes dropping; we had Bear Stearns, we had the GSEs, and we had smaller cases like IndyMac—and if financial systems are in a very weakened state, really bad things could happen.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that there really is a serious danger here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, we could have a dynamic through a decline in demand for housing because of the backup in mortgage rates or other reasons lowering housing prices and that spilling over into the financial system in terms of raising credit spreads, which then lowers demand, and we could get a nasty, vicious spiral.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is exactly one of these adverse feedback loops that we are all concerned about.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So this is not off the table, and it very much worries me.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I will talk about the implications of that for policy later.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: On the inflation front, although I definitely see upside risks, I think they may have diminished just a smidgen.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There is a question about how large those upside risks are.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In terms of my thinking about what drives the inflation process, it is expectations about future output gaps and expectations about inflation over a long period, not a short-term period.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I see absolutely no evidence that, in the last couple of months, we have had deterioration in long-term inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If anything, they have gotten a little better since March.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If you look at the numbers—and Bill had it in his picture—basically there was some ratcheting up when the crisis first hit.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I would argue a lot of that had to do with inflation risk, because there really was increasing inflation risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There has been a slight movement up—maybe a tenth, maybe you could say two-tenths—in expectations when you look at forecasters.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I am very skeptical of consumer surveys because, exactly what behavioral economics tells us, there is framing.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If headline inflation is high, short-term inflation expectations go up, which should happen, but long-term inflation expectations also go up.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: When headline goes down, then they will come down.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There was a nice little article from the San Francisco Fed in one of those little letter deals on exactly this issue, which came up with exactly this conclusion.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I recommend that you read it; and the good news is that it takes only four minutes to read because the articles are meant to be very short.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I really do not see that there has been deterioration, and—I think that this is very important—it is why I stressed the issue of the analytic framework for thinking about the inflation process and what monetary policy can do.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We can’t control relative prices, but we can do something about long-run inflation expectations and expectations about future output gaps.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I haven’t seen a problem lately that there has been deterioration in long-run expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Well, if anything, they look as though they are expected to widen maybe a smidgen, not that much.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We don’t have any indication to expect that we will be overshooting in terms of having output greater than potential.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Again, that should not be raising inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It should, if anything, maybe lower it a bit.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Finally, of course, oil prices are lower.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I don’t think that means that they will stay low because the volatility is huge; but at least the fear that they are going to keep on going up and up and up—so it would not be a one-shot change but would be put into long-run inflation—has, I think, diminished somewhat.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So where do I stand in terms of the upside risk?

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There still is upside risk because having high headline inflation does have the potential to spill over into inflation expectations.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: All of us have that concern.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I want to emphasize very strongly that it has not happened yet; I think that is very important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I also think it is very important to monitor this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One concern that members of the Committee have is that we wouldn’t react fast enough because we have sometimes been inertial in the past.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That is a serious concern.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But I think there is a strong argument that, when you have very big downside risks to economic activity, you want to deal with inflation expectations when they actually indicate that there is some problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: And I just do not see that at this juncture.

speaker: DUKE
text: I was advised to speak of things I know, so all of my comments will have to do with commercial banks and the traditional banking operations within those banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: Also, they are limited to the market area that I operated in.

speaker: DUKE
text: I was in a large community bank.

speaker: DUKE
text: The primary competitors were 2 of the top 5 banks and 4 of the top 20 banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: I hope to expand that on the supervision committee.

speaker: DUKE
text: I guess the major observation I would have is that I can’t see lending growth ever resuming until the market for financial stocks improves.

speaker: DUKE
text: That market is not going to improve until it is clear that the credit risk is manageable.

speaker: DUKE
text: I haven’t seen the confidence in banking and banking institutions this low since we were well into the S&L crisis back in the early 1990s.

speaker: DUKE
text: At the same time, the credit numbers—or at least the commercial banks’ part of the credit numbers—don’t look all that bad.

speaker: DUKE
text: At this point, we are sharing those credit losses with a number of other types of institutions, and I think the banks got the better slice of that pie.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I do believe that the banks will be able to manage through this.

speaker: DUKE
text: On the equity side of things, you have had equity destroyed through credit losses, and so those banks are certainly reducing their lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: I don’t think there is enough capital in the system.

speaker: DUKE
text: I don’t think earnings are strong enough.

speaker: DUKE
text: There is certainly no external capital available to pick up that slack.

speaker: DUKE
text: So while you hear smaller banks say, “We are getting great business now because the larger banks have cut back on their lending,” they just don’t have the capacity to take in that business.

speaker: DUKE
text: No matter why they are trying to raise capital, capital issuance is viewed as a sign of weakness.

speaker: DUKE
text: The short selling has been just amazing.

speaker: DUKE
text: It has really driven down the prices.

speaker: DUKE
text: For some of the larger banks, it is running anywhere from 10 to 15 percent of total float.

speaker: DUKE
text: It has even gotten down into banks smaller than $5 billion.

speaker: DUKE
text: I was looking at one, and the short interest on July 15 was 10 times that of April 15.

speaker: DUKE
text: It was running about 7 percent of float on a very thinly traded stock.

speaker: DUKE
text: I can’t believe that it has anything to do with the fundamentals of the institution.

speaker: DUKE
text: It is just all being painted with the same brush.

speaker: DUKE
text: For institutions that must raise capital or fail, my concern is that the capital that is being raised or being offered comes with an exit strategy.

speaker: DUKE
text: I don’t think that the capital is going to have the patience to wait for a longer-term resumption of lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: Those that do have capital cushions seem to be spending them on small buybacks or dividend increases in an effort to demonstrate some confidence in the future.

speaker: DUKE
text: On the liquidity side, central core funding is very tight and incredibly uncertain.

speaker: DUKE
text: CD rates do remain high, and as one institution after another desperately needs money, they raise the rates.

speaker: DUKE
text: As one falls out of that situation, somebody else picks it up again.

speaker: DUKE
text: After the full weekend of IndyMac coverage in the press, the phones just lit up everywhere asking about FDIC insurance.

speaker: DUKE
text: Now there is a renewed interest in the CDARS program.

speaker: DUKE
text: I didn’t realize that these deposits are classified as brokered deposits.

speaker: DUKE
text: It will be interesting to see if we have a big jump in brokered deposits in the next couple of quarters.

speaker: DUKE
text: The Home Loan Banks are tightening their collateral requirements.

speaker: DUKE
text: They are introducing risk rating systems, so that source of funding is not as available as it was.

speaker: DUKE
text: Nonconforming mortgages are impossible to place.

speaker: DUKE
text: On the asset side, I talked to several correspondent bankers, and they have been told to cut their overall fed funds lines sometimes in half.

speaker: DUKE
text: It doesn’t matter who it is, just cut them in half.

speaker: DUKE
text: A number of the banks are cutting home equity lines across the board and freezing those lines.

speaker: DUKE
text: The full-relationship lending is prized, but even in that it is only to the extent that lending is in some ways self funding.

speaker: DUKE
text: Transaction deals are like hot potatoes; nobody wants to touch them.

speaker: DUKE
text: We had some calls from other bankers who were asking what liquidity premium we were adding to our pricing, so there is clearly a change in the pricing, which may actually improve profitability.

speaker: DUKE
text: However, I think a lot of it is in order not to turn down the credit but simply to price out the credit, so that the borrower makes the decision not to borrow rather than the bank making the decision not to lend.

speaker: DUKE
text: On the credit side, the reserve additions have been incredibly dramatic, but a lot of that is because reserve levels were so low going into this.

speaker: DUKE
text: Capital was strong, earnings were strong, but reserve levels were down at 70 or 80 basis points.

speaker: DUKE
text: I had not ever seen them below 1 percent until two or three years ago.

speaker: DUKE
text: That is because of the change in the accounting for reserves as well as 10 years of no demonstrable losses.

speaker: DUKE
text: Oddly enough, the charge-off and delinquency rates really don’t look all that bad.

speaker: DUKE
text: When I looked at first-quarter rates, they didn’t look a whole lot different from what used to be the norm, at least in terms of commercial loans.

speaker: DUKE
text: Then, on the consumer side, in this case it was mortgage loans versus consumer loans, but still a 75 basis point loss on consumer loans historically was actually normal.

speaker: DUKE
text: It is really difficult to follow any discussion of what is going on in terms of credit losses because you get confused between what is mark-to-market loss, what is actual credit loss, what are charge-offs, what are reserves, and then who owns those losses.

speaker: DUKE
text: I am not quite sure what the rate of deterioration or the rate of resolution is.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of collection, it takes an awful lot of time to ramp up collection and recovery efforts, and I don’t know where we are in that cycle, but I think we have a long way to go.

speaker: DUKE
text: The last cycle was all about commercial real estate, and nobody could work up much sympathy for commercial real estate developers.

speaker: DUKE
text: In this situation, there is so much political sensitivity around foreclosures that I think it is going to be much elongated.

speaker: DUKE
text: When a borrower cannot or will not pay and you can’t restructure it to create capacity or willingness to pay, then some form of forced sale is the only thing that gets you off go.

speaker: DUKE
text: I think that has been pushed out and pushed out.

speaker: DUKE
text: It is also the only way to clear any junior liens.

speaker: DUKE
text: This process is expensive and time-consuming, and owning the property is even more expensive.

speaker: DUKE
text: So as the lender-owned properties become a larger and larger segment of the properties for sale, I do think price declines are going to accelerate significantly.

speaker: DUKE
text: I will be watching the IndyMac resolution particularly closely.

speaker: DUKE
text: In the last cycle, if you will remember, the properties that were sold by the RTC brought the biggest discounts of all.

speaker: DUKE
text: So it will be interesting to see what this theory of holding off on foreclosures and then at some later point having to move the assets actually does to prices.

speaker: DUKE
text: The good news is that once lenders start selling, they do tend to move units at whatever price it takes.

speaker: DUKE
text: Lenders are going to have to do that.

speaker: DUKE
text: There is no justification for wasting precious capital or liquidity on dead assets.

speaker: DUKE
text: But there is also no justification for selling the portfolios at fire sale prices if the net realizable value of collecting them is higher, and I think it definitely is for the banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: Finally, if I could take one more minute, I did do some very in-depth personal research on the housing decisions of a relocating worker.

speaker: DUKE
text: I purchased a residence in January ’06 for a May ’06 closing and hit the peak.

speaker: DUKE
text: The current value, I am told, is 80 to 85 percent of the purchase price, marketing time 6 to 12 months.

speaker: DUKE
text: The purchase in the new location—I did do the calculation—it was 15 to 20 times annual rent, but that didn’t matter.

speaker: DUKE
text: I had already had all the thrill of ownership that I could stand and will be renting.

speaker: DUKE
text: The second thing is that, if I had financed this property at 80 percent, I would have had no equity to roll into a new purchase anyway, so there would have been no decision involved.

speaker: DUKE
text: The good news is that as long as there is no need to sell, the price doesn’t matter, and I could have waited it out very easily.

speaker: DUKE
text: So the conclusion that I came to is that this current elevated inventory we have of housing includes only those who absolutely have to sell because nobody in this market would choose to sell.

speaker: DUKE
text: So once that begins to turn around, again, there just have to be a whole lot of pent-up houses for sale.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Michelle, what time is our hard cutoff here?

speaker: SMITH
text: We can be pretty flexible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You want it before 2:15, though.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, I spent a lot of time through the meeting and during the break working up a crystalline summary of the discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I am a bit concerned about getting to lunch and avoiding the 2:15 hard deadline; so if you would excuse me, this time I will just go directly to a few comments of my own, and then we can go to the policy round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We saw growth of about 2 percent in the second quarter, which suggests a campaign slogan for the Republicans, “The Economy: It Could Be Worse.” The question, though, is whether this higher-than-expected growth rate in the second quarter implies that we are actually looking forward to a better-than-expected remainder of the year or whether this was in some sense a last hurrah of borrowing from the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I feel that I am very strongly in the latter camp, unfortunately.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think that, for reasons people have talked about, the remainder of the year and into next year are likely to be quite weak.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know how weak, but if you look at each component of spending or component of production, you see mostly very negative indicators.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have talked about consumption.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We know about all the fundamental issues that are affecting consumers, and we have seen recently, I think both anecdotally and in terms of the data, some softness, particularly in the auto area.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the labor market, several people have noted that the loss of payroll jobs has not been as rapid as, for example, in 2001.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The unemployment rate, though, has risen as quickly as in previous episodes, and any look at the unemployment rate would suggest that this is something close to a normal recession dynamic.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing, of course, remains very uncertain.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t really know when the bottom will be, although I would add, a point that I think Bill Dudley made, that there seems to be a growing confidence that when we have reached the bottom in housing, whenever that may be, we will see a very quick improvement, both in the financial markets and then, presumably, in the economy as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In other areas, such as nonresidential construction, architectural billings and other factors suggest slowing there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We see slowing in the other industrial countries, although some strength is still in the emerging markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So just looking at the traditional indicators of growth and production, I think the best guess is for a slow second half, a slow beginning of 2009, and an unemployment rate that continues to rise from here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do believe that the financial stress and its implications for credit availability are important in this whole dynamic.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess President Lacker and I keep talking past each other, but I don’t think that the federal funds rate is an adequate description of the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To give another example, in the past we have used money growth as an indicator of monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we used that indicator, it would look quite different.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the appropriate indicators are the rates and terms that are being faced by the people making decisions to spend in the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You can go through the entire list, and in every case, as Governor Kohn suggested, the actual rates being faced in the data by borrowers are as high as or higher than they were last summer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Mortgages, which are a particularly sensitive area, are of course critical here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Despite the decline in the federal funds rate, the spread between mortgage-backed securities and duration-matched Treasuries is now about 260 basis points compared with 120 basis points last summer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, for the spread between jumbo loans and conforming loans, which in the past has normally been between 25 and 50 basis points, the offer rate is about 120 basis points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there seems little doubt—and we can check with Governor Duke about this—that, despite the lower rate on overnight bank lending, the rates that matter for economic activity are largely higher than they were a year ago.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, I don’t think it is evident at all that we are in a financial situation that is conducive to rapid, excessive growth and inflationary increases a priori.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, going forward, of course, a lot of what happens in the economy is going to depend on bank balance sheets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I won’t spend much time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In April, I talked about the staff’s estimates of losses going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nellie Liang is working with people in New York.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The numbers are not too encouraging under the baseline scenario, forgetting about the more severe scenarios.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The staff now projects about $228 billion in losses for U.S. banks and thrifts in ’08 and ’09.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If that occurs, it would be about a 2 percent loss rate over the next two years, which would be above the peak of 1991 and 1992.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Of course, if the economy does worse, it would be even higher.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Relative to that $228 billion in losses, there are so far loan-loss provisions of about $68 billion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it looks as though we still have a long way to go in terms of bank losses and write-downs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, some of the biggest banks will take very significant hits.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is very preliminary, and I don’t want to make too much of it, but the preliminary analysis shows that for five of the very biggest banks, under a baseline scenario and looking at the composition of their asset holdings, their current tier 1 capital ratios will be reduced between 30 percent and 50 percent over the next two years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there is a real concern about the availability of credit and about the cost of credit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I could go on and talk about a variety of other areas, including the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey, which suggests that credit will be a concern going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker and I have, I hope, respect—I respect him, and I hope he respects me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we disagree also about President Bullard on systemic risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I take his criticism to be that it works in practice, but can it work in theory?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Systemic risk is an old phenomenon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are literally dozens and dozens of historical episodes that are suggestive of that phenomenon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is also an enormous theoretical literature.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Maybe it is not entirely satisfactory, but certainly many people have thought about that issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I, myself, have obviously worked in this area.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Clearly, it is not something that we can tightly explain in all aspects, but I do think it is a concern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to remain concerned about it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although it is true, as President Bullard points out, that there is an accommodation and a basis for anticipating crises as we go forward, it is also the case, as I think Governor Mishkin noted, that after a year we are also facing a situation of greater fragility, of much lower capital, and fewer shock absorbers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those things will make any crisis that much more severe, should it occur.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So overall I think there is still significant downside risk to growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the baseline of slow growth is right.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am hopeful that we will see growth restored early next year, but I think it is very uncertain at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On inflation, I do have concerns, as everyone else does.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the commodity price movements we have seen are good news.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They have been quite significant.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Besides oil prices down about 10 percent and natural gas prices down about 32 percent, since the last meeting corn is off 27 percent; soybeans, 17 percent; and wheat, 16 percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those are not small changes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, obviously, the level of prices is still very high.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has risen considerably over the past year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will continue to see that high level of prices being passed through into the core, as Governor Kohn noted, but I would argue that if—and this is a very big “if”—commodity prices do begin to stabilize within the general range of what we see now, I think that the inflation concerns will moderate over time because they will have lost essentially their driving force.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t really have the conditions to turn the commodity price increases into persistent inflation, absent continued pressure on that front and absent changes in inflation expectations, of which there is only limited evidence at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I want to be very clear: I think that containing inflation is enormously important, and I think it is our first responsibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to watch this very carefully.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there will be continued pressures even if commodity prices don’t rise, but I do think there is also a chance that we will see a moderation of this problem going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess there has been a lot of discussion about the appropriate withdrawal of stimulus.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I don’t think I accept the idea that we are currently in an extremely stimulative situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, if financial markets were to normalize, for example, that would lead to a more stimulative situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to say just a word about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is to say that the speed at which we remove the accommodation—and I think it is clear we do have to do that relatively soon—should depend to some extent on how inflation evolves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Under the more benign scenario that I have just described—if inflation does decline significantly because of commodity prices—I think that we obviously have more time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would just note for comparison past episodes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In 1994, for example, the pause lasted 17 months, and the first increase in rates came two years after payrolls began growing again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In 2001, again, it was more than a year after unemployment rates started coming down, and payrolls began growing before the rates started going up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, I think there is a view, which is a reasonable one, that maybe in at least the second of those two episodes we waited too long to begin to normalize.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But, again, it would be extraordinary if we were to begin raising rates without an immediate inflation problem with the economy still in a declining or extremely weakened situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If inflation does in fact become the problem that many around the table think it is, particularly if commodity prices begin to go up again or if the dollar begins to weaken, then I will be the first here to support responding to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think it is incredibly important to keep inflation expectations well anchored, particularly to the extent that movements of commodity prices and the dollar seem to be derived from monetary policy as opposed to things like geopolitical risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then, I think we can’t treat them as truly exogenous.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We would have to respond to those things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I welcome the ongoing discussion we should have about the pace of withdrawal of accommodation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think it depends very much on how things evolve, and I do think that our strategy should be to watch carefully and to make the right decisions as we see the data come in.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me stop there and turn to the last round and ask Brian, please, to introduce the policy discussion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If you prefer, in the interest of time, I can cut back my remarks to focus just on the policy statement and not the general background.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will be referring to the version of table 1 included in the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” This version incorporates some small revisions from the draft that was included in the August Bluebook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The table presents two policy alternatives.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative B, the Committee would maintain its current policy stance at this meeting but in its statement would underscore its concerns about inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative C, the Committee would firm policy 25 basis points today and issue a statement indicating that the action was taken to better balance the risks to growth and inflation; the statement would be noncommittal about whether further rate increases were imminent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The language proposed for paragraph 2 of alternative B has been modified a little from that proposed in the Bluebook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most important, the first clause is now in the past tense, referring to economic growth in the second quarter, thus avoiding an implication that the economy is continuing to expand in the current quarter.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In a change relative to the June statement, exports as well as consumer spending are cited as factors that supported growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, the sentence beginning with “over time” has been moved up from the risk assessment paragraph.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That shift is likely to be seen as underscoring a view that policy is currently positioned to foster a gradual resumption of moderate economic growth, suggesting that further easing is not likely to be forthcoming.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That sense may also be reinforced by the omission of the phrase “to date” after “easing of monetary policy.” In paragraph 3, the inflation discussion for alternative B gives slightly greater emphasis than in June to the Committee’s inflation 2 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: concerns, partly by starting with the flat statement that “inflation has been high” and by giving less prominence to the expectation that inflation will moderate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The slight change to the final clause in paragraph 3 is proposed for purely stylistic reasons.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In paragraph 4, the first sentence of the risk assessment states that “although downside risks to growth remain, the upside risks to inflation are also of significant concern to the Committee.” While this sentence does not provide any explicit weighting of the two risks and does not suggest that policy firming is imminent, the statement as a whole probably would be read as giving a bit more emphasis to inflation concerns and a bit less to growth concerns than market participants now expect.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus, even though the absence of a rate action today would be consistent with market expectations, the statement would likely be viewed by market participants as a bit more hawkish than they anticipated, and market rates could rise modestly in response.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Turning to alternative C, concerns about upside risks to inflation could motivate the Committee to begin firming the stance of monetary policy at this meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The first three sentences of alternative C, paragraph 2, are identical to those of alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, the final sentence differs, partly by indicating explicitly that the Committee sees the current stance of monetary policy as accommodative.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, by dropping the phrase “over time,” which appeared in paragraph 4 of the June version, the Committee would suggest that it sees moderate economic growth as resuming sooner rather than later.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In paragraph 3, the Committee would still note that inflation is expected to moderate but, in the last sentence of the paragraph, it would explicitly cite the risk—and note its concern—that inflation might not fall as expected.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, the risk assessment, paragraph 4, would indicate that the Committee firmed policy today in order to better balance the upside risks to inflation and the downside risks to growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, the statement would avoid an explicit judgment about whether the risks were now balanced and would provide little information about whether further tightening was imminent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even though the wording of the statement for alternative C would not indicate that policy was now on a steady firming march, market participants would likely conclude that the firming process had been accelerated considerably relative to their expectations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With the Committee having tightened amid bad news about financial institutions and in the immediate wake of the implementation of a number of additional Federal Reserve liquidity initiatives, investors would likely conclude that the Committee did not see financial stability considerations as raising a barrier to further policy tightening.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: They would view the Committee as adopting a more aggressive posture toward inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Because it has been historically rare for the Federal Reserve to implement a one-off tightening, investors would likely see fairly steady rate hikes over the course of future meetings, and thus short- and intermediate- term interest rates would, in all likelihood, move up sharply after this action.

speaker: MADIGAN
