text: Yields on longer-term fixed-rate mortgages might rise particularly substantially, as premiums for interest rate and prepayment uncertainty increased and as mortgage investors hedged the increase in mortgage durations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Such a development could adversely affect the prices of financial assets that are closely tied to housing markets and mortgage performance.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, yields on long-term Treasuries could decline, particularly if market participants marked down their expectations for economic growth and inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: In terms of the wording in paragraph 3, if we do not raise rates, I am wondering why the second sentence that is now in alternative C wouldn’t be more appropriate for alternative B, and I am wondering what your thinking is about that.

speaker: FISHER
text: In other words, if we don’t take action, that seems to be a more emphatic statement than what you have currently, assuming no change in rate—“The Committee expects inflation to moderate later this year and next year,” et cetera—whereas if we are trying to send a signal that we are really concerned and we do not change rates, why wouldn’t we have used, “Although the Committee expects inflation to moderate .

speaker: FISHER
text: the possibility that inflation may fail to decline as anticipated is of significant concern”?

speaker: FISHER
text: Then, maybe take the word “also” out of the fourth paragraph.

speaker: FISHER
text: It just seems to me odd that if we act and describe the risk after acting, the language is even stronger.

speaker: FISHER
text: Whereas if we don’t act and we want to emphasize that we are remaining vigilant, why wouldn’t we use that stronger language?

speaker: FISHER
text: I am curious as to why you chose the two or what you feel the tradeoff is there.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I would say, President Fisher, that the substitution that you are suggesting seems plausible to me, but I would also say that the first sentence of alternative B already does suggest some pretty significant concerns about inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me start, then, with President Yellen.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I favor alternative A—no change in the funds rate and a balanced assessment of risks designed to leave market expectations concerning the path of the funds rate roughly unchanged.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Oops, I made a mistake, there is no A.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I propose to create it by changing the wording of the first sentence of alternative B, paragraph 4, to read, “Both downside risks to growth and upside risks to inflation are of significant concern to the Committee.” As it is currently worded, B(4) downplays the downside risks to growth, which have intensified since our last meeting as the credit crunch has worsened and emphasizes inflation risks, which have moderated slightly as oil prices have fallen.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The assessment of risks in alternative B, as it stands, is unbalanced and—as Brian just pointed out and the Bluebook does also—is more hawkish than the primary dealers and most market participants generally expect.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So it is likely to shift the fed funds futures path and other interest rates upward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I see no case, at this juncture, for signaling that we are likely to adjust policy upward before the end of the year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, there is a non-negligible probability, to my mind, that the next move will be down and not up.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There is already significant slack in the labor market, and with the economy expected to grow at a near-recessionary pace in the latter half of this year, the unemployment rate is poised to rise further.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This growing slack is working to contain inflationary pressures as evidenced by the stability and low level of wage growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I expect that growing slack will continue holding down wage inflation going forward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Long-term inflation expectations seem relatively well contained, and core inflation has been stable for the past several years.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Finally, a major component of the surge in headline inflation—oil price increases—has finally started to show some sign of reversing direction.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although the real funds rate remains quite accommodative by the usual metrics, we are clearly not in a business-as-usual situation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We are in the midst of a serious credit crunch that has, again, worsened during the intermeeting period, as exemplified by the developments at Freddie and Fannie and the other things that many of you have pointed to in our last round.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We are likely seeing only the start of what will be a series of bank failures that could make matters much worse.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given these financial headwinds, it is not clear to me that we are accommodative at all; I agree, Mr. Chairman, with the comments you just made on this matter.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given my preference for an inflation target of around 1¾ percent and equal welfare weights on the inflation and unemployment gaps, I view the Greenbook policy path and forecast as a roughly optimal trajectory to the attainment of our goals.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although core inflation exceeds the level I consider consistent with price stability, unemployment also exceeds the level consistent with full employment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given our dual mandate and a forecast that envisions a growing unemployment gap, coupled with declining inflation under the Greenbook funds rate path, I see no case for jolting expectations in such a way as to, in effect, tighten policy now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I feel especially strongly about this in view of the major downside risks to the economy from an intensifying credit crunch.

speaker: EVANS
text: A funny thing happened at my board meeting the other week.

speaker: EVANS
text: I was all set to prepare them not for a rate change recommendation this time but for one in the not-too-distant future.

speaker: EVANS
text: By the time I was done, they were asking what the procedure was for dissenting from my recommendation.

speaker: EVANS
text: So, in fact, they forwarded a recommendation for an increase this time around.

speaker: EVANS
text: You know, we can disagree over the inflationary consequences of a lot of this, but I think there is a message from around the table and the public, our directors, and whatnot, that they do feel that there is a concern about inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I favor alternative C, although I recognize the reality of today.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am struggling with the fact that we lowered the funds rate rather aggressively, and things have worked out much better than we expected against the risks that we thought that we were facing.

speaker: EVANS
text: We could disagree over that as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: I do take the point that uncertainty is very high at the moment.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I think that we will need to increase rates sooner than currently expected by markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: We are counting on a modest degree of slack and our credibility with the public to keep inflation and inflation expectations contained while we leave rates on hold.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I am concerned that there will be only modest inflationary restraint from the slack that we see and that we may not be able to convince the public that they shouldn’t worry about high headline inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: I certainly agree that bank balance sheets were pretty good in 2007, but I am concerned that headline inflation has been above core inflation for quite a long time.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not sure our own balance sheets would reflect that.

speaker: EVANS
text: So by following a wait-and-see strategy, we are accepting a large baseline inflation risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, there is an enormous tail risk—that is, a return to much higher underlying inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Also, I was a little concerned to see in the dealer feedback to the TAF extensions that some market participants think that we will not increase the policy rate as long as we keep the “unusual and exigent” determination in place.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not sure that is a good expectation for them to have.

speaker: EVANS
text: Fundamentally, it is my opinion that there has been a change in the balance of the economic rationale and risk-management calculus that we used to lower the funds rate to 2 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is not a huge change, but I think there has been a change.

speaker: EVANS
text: One year on, the economy has withstood the financial shock in a resilient fashion, especially given the add-on shock from oil.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t know what more we could have hoped for from the vantage point of the fall of 2007 and the losses that have been taken.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think the odds of preventable negative feedback loops that we took out the last 75 basis points of insurance against are somewhat smaller than they were five to six months ago.

speaker: EVANS
text: Part of our earlier logic to appropriately lower rates to a decidedly accommodative policy stance was to guard against disorderly market conditions that might permanently damage our financial market infrastructure and destroy the financial capital stock in a real, productive sense the way that I think President Plosser was alluding to.

speaker: EVANS
text: But real forces have unmasked dramatic weaknesses and faults in our financial system, and markets will be evolving to a new intermediation structure.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our policy can ease transitions only to a degree, but it cannot restore the previous financial status quo, nor should it be aimed at doing so.

speaker: EVANS
text: During the transition, I would not be surprised if we revisit periods of market volatility as the disadvantaged players are repeatedly challenged to restructure to the new environment.

speaker: EVANS
text: Counterparties are shying away from previous financial partners, in part because of uncertainty over the risk–return profiles and the transitioning industry structure.

speaker: EVANS
text: These profiles involve both liquidity risk and credit risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think our lending facilities allow a modest decoupling of the fed funds rate setting to deal with this.

speaker: EVANS
text: In my view, the balancing of current risks calls for increasing the funds rate in the range of 50, maybe 75, basis points within some reasonably short period of time.

speaker: EVANS
text: If events change importantly, I would certainly advocate further adjustments in either direction, depending on how those risks adjust.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would just note on the “unusual and exigent” issue that there are two schools of thought.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other school is the one you said, which is that having done this, we would have the freedom to raise rates; so I think it sort of cuts both directions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the interest of time, I will be very brief.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I support alternative B in substance and concur with its wording.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think we are in a delicate rhetorical balancing act at this stage, and as Brian described, the slightly greater emphasis on inflation is appropriate at this time.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think alternative B has substantially captured the current situations and concerns of the majority of the Committee, so I support alternative B.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I appreciate the fact that reasonable people may differ, and I do differ.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In saying that, I am not advocating a tight monetary policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am advocating a less accommodative monetary policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I recognize Governor Kohn’s point that relative prices are adjusting, and others have made that point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think around that context is the fact that we are seeing a systematic increase in the price indexes, both total and core, and I don’t think we should ignore that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Now, the core is creeping up, but up nevertheless, and it is systematic in my view.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would feel more comfortable that it was transitory if policy were not so accommodative, which affirms the likelihood of further increases in inflation going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is really where I am focused, I guess is the way to say it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We introduced the policy that we have, as I think others mentioned, as an insurance policy early on, when we were more in an immediate crisis.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I don’t negate or minimize the tension that we are under, but I do think we have become very accommodative in our policy with negative real rates.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So here we are with this insurance.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have this subpar growth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The subpar growth is not going to go away soon, so we are delaying removing the insurance policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think in the long run that does increase the risk of an inflationary problem of a sizable magnitude later on.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I know we have this immediate problem, but our role also is to take a long-run view, and I think we would be wise to raise the rate now modestly.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It would still be an easy policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The effects of that increase might be disturbing to the markets.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the other hand, it might actually give more confidence to the markets that inflation is going to come down because we are going to insist that it does.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think there would be some good effects from that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So that is where I am coming from on preferring that we move rates up slightly at this point.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am going to make my remarks a little shorter here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My judgment is that the current situation is a difficult one for the Committee.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Because of the very appropriate focus on financial market turmoil over the past year, our attention has naturally turned away from keeping the level of interest rates consistent with longer-term inflation objectives.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This was done to avert particularly extreme, but low probability, outcomes in which the economy would experience an especially severe downturn.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As it turned out, the bad state did not materialize, which I think will go down in history as a successful element of the Committee’s policy over the past year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The ability to take on financial market turmoil of this magnitude and prevent it from doing substantial damage to the economy— a recession of the magnitude of 1980-82, let’s say—has been a real achievement.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In that sense, all has gone according to plan.

speaker: BULLARD
text: At the same time, we have moved interest rates to a very low level in the context of rising inflation and rising inflation expectations.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A severe downturn was unwelcome, to be sure, but it was also projected to keep inflation in check.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Since that did not materialize, we are left with low rates and an environment of CPI inflation running at 5 percent headline, measured from one year earlier, and long-term inflation expectations creeping higher.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We face more risk now of creating a serious inflation problem than we have in a generation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: To make progress, I think we should keep rates steady today but with the plan of preparing markets for an increase in rates at the September meeting, conditional of course on incoming data.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This would be consistent with alternative B today; and with intermeeting statements, it would move probability mass toward higher rates through the fall and through the first half of 2009.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I have several remarks on a fall tightening campaign.

speaker: BULLARD
text: First of all, moving 25 basis points is by itself not likely to have a large effect on economic activity, nor does it bring the level of the federal funds rate high enough to have a meaningful effect on inflation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The FOMC started tightening in mid-2004 but achieved a core CPI inflation rate below 2 percent in only one month during the entire three-year period of 2005, 2006, and 2007.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What the move would do is get the Committee started on returning interest rates to a more normal level, a level more consistent with our inflation objectives.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The Committee could pause or even reverse course should particularly adverse data suggest that economic activity was weakening substantially.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Preparing for an increase in rates means that we would be signaling that financial market turmoil is no longer the paramount concern.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On that, I think we can reasonably stress that we have provided accommodation over the past year in the form of lower interest rates and innovative liquidity facilities.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We have bought time for financial firms to repair and adjust.

speaker: BULLARD
text: While all is not as it was, we do not want to create an inflation problem in the aftermath of a shock of this magnitude, which may actually compound the situation and make it worse.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Longer-term inflation expectations have been creeping higher, a fact that has been widely cited in commentary on monetary policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would like to stress that, in my view of a well- functioning inflation-targeting regime, these inflation expectations would not be moving at all.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Short-term interest rates would be moving higher and lower in response to shocks to the economy, and inflation expectations would never move.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This would reflect the confidence that the central bank’s short-term interest rate adjustments were being accomplished in just the right way to offset disturbances buffeting the economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Because of this, I prefer not to interpret observed movements in inflation expectations as evidence of what we should or should not do with respect to interest rates.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The short-term interest rate would have to move to offset the shocks to the economy even if longer-term inflation expectations never moved.

speaker: KOHN
text: I support keeping the federal funds rate at 2 percent for now.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that is consistent with bringing inflation down over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that we’re going to have to tighten at some point.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with your analysis, Mr. Chairman—I don’t think we have a highly accommodative policy right now.

speaker: KOHN
text: Not only would I cite the interest rates that you cited, but I would cite the behavior of households and businesses, which aren’t acting as if they’re looking at very low real interest rates by making purchases of durable goods, capital equipment, et cetera.

speaker: KOHN
text: The cost of capital is not perceived to be low right now, and I think it’s for the reasons you cited.

speaker: KOHN
text: In my view, over the intermeeting period the inflation risks have narrowed just a bit.

speaker: KOHN
text: The damper on inflation risk comes from the decline in oil and commodity prices, the steadiness of the dollar, and my perception that we can count on a more negative output gap going forward, which will provide some discipline on prices and wages.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is a difficult situation.

speaker: KOHN
text: There are no ideal outcomes when you have this change in relative prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: We will have to live with higher inflation and higher unemployment temporarily.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have to keep our eye on the second-round effects, not just the pass-throughs but the spillovers, and I think so far so good.

speaker: KOHN
text: That’s a tenuous situation, I agree, but my read of the incoming information is that we can be a little more patient than we thought we could be six or seven weeks ago.

speaker: KOHN
text: As for the wording of the statement, I could live with President Yellen’s rewording, but I think that this language Brian suggested is okay as well.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m actually not sure how the markets will react to this.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some of the commentary I read over the last couple of weeks thought that we were tilted toward inflation last time because of the way we worded things.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think that the market reaction will be large to this, and I agree that the first choice would be not to change market expectations substantially.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think they’re aligned pretty well right now, but I think the reactions will be small, and I can live with the alternative B wording.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As I indicated in the earlier go-round, I found the balance of risks to economic growth and inflation to be essentially the same.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So other things being equal, I might prefer to have risk assessment language that is even more balanced than the risk assessment language that is presented in alternative B.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But I have a tactical reason for wanting to see words that express a stronger concern about inflation risk.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do, as I said earlier, expect inflation to worsen before it improves.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In particular, as we have been discussing, the core statistics are likely to worsen notably during the next several months, and I could just shrug those worse numbers off because I have a projection that calls for those numbers to improve by early next year.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But I’m not confident that the public will shrug them off.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As we have been talking about, the cost of longer-term inflation expectations drifting up is large.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I believe that we can influence those expectations, and I think it is important that we do let the public know that we are serious about opening the doors to a rate increase if that becomes necessary.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We need the flexibility to move nimbly, and I think the language that is contained in alternative B puts the markets on notice.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think alternative B enables us to hold our present strategy of watchful waiting, but it does call somewhat greater attention to inflation risks than we expressed at the conclusion of our last meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I find both the strategy and the language of alternative B to be quite appropriate for the circumstances we face today.

speaker: STERN
text: I favor alternative B and the language as displayed here.

speaker: STERN
text: Let me say a few words about the issue of withdrawal of accommodation, which I’ve been giving thought to and will want to give more thought to over time.

speaker: STERN
text: Earlier today I talked about the Greenbook forecast and indicated that I found it credible.

speaker: STERN
text: But another virtue of it, even if you don’t find it that credible, is that the cards are on the table.

speaker: STERN
text: I mean, it has a path for the federal funds rate.

speaker: STERN
text: It has a path for the foreign exchange value of the dollar and so on and so forth.

speaker: STERN
text: Two of the key elements, as I indicated earlier, are, at least over the near-term to intermediate-term, that real growth is subdued and that headline inflation abates after the current quarter, and I think that’s relevant.

speaker: STERN
text: Given the current stance of policy, I think we are well positioned for that subdued pace of real growth.

speaker: STERN
text: Indeed, even if we get contraction for a quarter or two, I would argue that we have maybe not entirely but largely already addressed that.

speaker: STERN
text: On the inflation side, it seems to me that the key part of that forecast is the diminution of headline inflation starting in the fourth quarter.

speaker: STERN
text: What that means as a practical matter is that in November, December, and January, when we get those data, we’ll get confirmation that it is either happening or it’s not.

speaker: STERN
text: Now, assuming that there are no major, decisive surprises between now and then—and that may be heroic—we’ll get confirmation of whether that inflation outlook was the accurate one.

speaker: STERN
text: If we do, then it seems that the path of the funds rate inherent in the Greenbook looks as though it could be acceptable.

speaker: STERN
text: If we get disappointments on headline inflation for whatever combination of reasons, it calls into question, at least in my mind, that path for the funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: For my part, our exchanges have in the past been predicated on nothing but the utmost respect.

speaker: LACKER
text: I expect that to continue.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I have done anything or said anything to contribute to any other impression, I regret it, and I apologize.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That wasn’t my intention, President Lacker.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the interest of avoiding talking past each other, let me say a bit about why I view real rates as low.

speaker: LACKER
text: I recognize what you and Governor Kohn said about other interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: But when I look at the low real rate now and at times in the past when it has been low and I look at things like corporate borrowing rates then, they didn’t fall nearly as much as the fed funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: If you plot them by lining up the NBER dates, it doesn’t look as though what’s happened now with those borrowing rates is out of line with past experiences.

speaker: LACKER
text: So if we think now that real rates were low in ’03, I’m led to conclude that I ought to think that they are low currently.

speaker: LACKER
text: Another way of saying this is that spreads always go up in recessions.

speaker: LACKER
text: We drive real rates down in recessions.

speaker: LACKER
text: If consumers and businesses were spending with frenzy now because of low rates, to me that would be a reason that we have to raise them, get them up right away.

speaker: LACKER
text: You know, my sense of the economics of why we push real rates low in recessions is that the state of aggregate demand needs it.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s exactly when consumer and business spending is sort of moribund that we have real rates low.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not sure that the fact that it’s moribund tells me whether they’re low or not relative to where they ought to be.

speaker: LACKER
text: That’s how I think about that evidence, but I look forward to being enlightened further in the future on this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You raise a good point—that we ought to look empirically at the relationship between borrowing rates and the federal funds rate in this episode and other episodes, which we really haven’t done.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we need to do that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’ll dispense with the rest of my prepared remarks and just say that I recognize the real risks ahead of us.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve experienced sluggish growth, and all the downside risks to growth that have been enumerated are very tangible and very plausible right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we should hold off raising rates at this meeting, but I’m very concerned about the inflation risks.

speaker: LACKER
text: I find myself leaning toward a tightening campaign earlier rather than later, and I’d like to see the statement do what it can to prepare markets for that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I liked the first version of alternative B, the one without the word “also.” I think “also” damps the concern about inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: It kind of makes it a little too balanced for my taste.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m also concerned—I should say “broadly”— that we seem to have left the impression over the past several months, since the beginning of the year, that our concerns about inflation fluctuate.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree with President Bullard.

speaker: LACKER
text: What we ought to view as ideal is an equilibrium where inflation expectations are rock solid and don’t change and, moreover, that people don’t perceive our concerns and worry about inflation or the weight we’re giving in policy deliberations as shifting from time to time.

speaker: LACKER
text: So that’s an aspect of our communications that concerns me.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I support alternative B. I would actually prefer President Yellen’s language but definitely believe that we should have the word “also” in there.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Tightening at this time would sap more strength from an already weak economy, and should the forecast look like the “severe financial stress” scenario or the “typical recession” scenario, it would be extremely poorly timed.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If the data indicate that inflation is not ebbing as I expect and the economy is on a surer footing than I fear, then it would be appropriate to begin what is likely to be a series of increases in the federal funds target.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But the data to date don’t indicate that, so I support alternative B.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, Mr. Chairman, I’m already out of the closet in terms of my economic proclivities.

speaker: FISHER
text: I realize it’s awkward for some folks, but I haven’t heard enough today that would change my view that we are running an over-accommodative monetary policy.

speaker: FISHER
text: I agree with your point very much that the rates and the terms being faced by those who drive the economy count.

speaker: FISHER
text: As to Governor Kohn’s point that some of these key rates have not come down, I think that has more to do with risk premiums, and I hate to see it migrate toward inflation premiums, which I believe is a significant risk.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m obviously driven by what I hear from my contacts, although I respect the analytics you mentioned, Governor Mishkin.

speaker: FISHER
text: My long-run thinking is as conditioned by globalization as it is by domestic policy, and I just still have a great concern about the wage–price spiral that’s taking place in some of our manufacturing centers in the developing countries.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it would be wise, just to shift my analogy here and think in canine terms, to take a newspaper across the snout and call for a 25 basis point increase.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’re always talking about tightening at some point.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it just becomes increasingly difficult to take that first step.

speaker: FISHER
text: I grant you that the economy is weak.

speaker: FISHER
text: The financial situation is brittle.

speaker: FISHER
text: That hasn’t changed in my view, but the inflationary behavioral patterns that I’m beginning to hear about reinforce my concern about an updrift in the core and the headline data.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I apologize, it perhaps is being a little too strong to say that we’ve become unmoored or that maybe we are no longer anchored.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that is nonetheless a real perception.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m going to vote against alternative B and for alternative C. I may be a minority of one, but perhaps I’ll be a sea anchor, if you understand the sailing analogy here, and assist the process of our commitment to be focused on inflation as a risk just as we focused on downside risk to growth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As you can imagine, as we’ve discussed, this meeting presents a difficult policy position for us—and for me in particular.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we must pay careful attention to the financial market volatility; and to the extent that it has consequences for the real economy, I’m certainly sensitive to that concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I had a similar experience with my board of directors that President Evans did.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I went into my board recommending no change and got considerable push-back in discussion about how we dissent and what the consequences of doing that are.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They are concerned about inflation, and I’m concerned about our mandate to keep longer- term and intermediate-term inflation in check.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We’re unlikely, in my view, to get confirming or convincing evidence about whether expectations have become unanchored until well after the fact.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I agree there has been very little wage–price pressure to date.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But that will be the last shoe to drop in this sequence of raising expectations, and by the time we get to that, I’m afraid it will be too late.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think in the near term we might see some relief in headline inflation; but as has been discussed, whether that will persist is highly dubious.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My real concern is that I believe that monetary policy is accommodative, and with all due respect, Mr. Chairman, when I look at the data comparing the levels of borrowing rates of consumers and businesses, both the levels in real and nominal terms and the spreads, what we see in this period looks remarkably similar to what we’ve seen in lots of other recessionary, slow growth periods.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So, again, following the analogy that President Lacker was using, I see this period as less atypical and more typical of what we see in slow-growth periods.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it’s important that we begin to prepare the markets for an impending shift to a tighter policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I agree with President Hoenig.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The request here is not for tight policy but somewhat less accommodative policy; and if we choose to go with no funds rate increase today, I think the language must help prepare the markets going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m pleased with a lot of the discussion around the table.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We are actually beginning to talk, I think, about what our exit strategy is going to be from this.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it’s very important to have those conversations, and I appreciate them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I, too, share the observations that President Evans had about talking with people who say, “Well, we can’t possibly remove accommodation until we get rid of the facilities.” I think that is wrong.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As you said, Mr. Chairman, actually having the facilities might make it easier for us to correct monetary policy, and I think that’s very, very important.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess my bottom line is that I can accept leaving the funds rate unchanged today as long as our language is sufficiently strong about inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To that end, I was actually a little more comfortable with the draft table 1.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I didn’t like the addition of the word “also.” I thought that weakened the statement.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would prefer paragraph 4 without the “also.” I also have one other, minor observation about paragraph 3, and that’s the first sentence, which says that “inflation has been high, spurred by the earlier increases in the prices of energy and some other commodities.” Well, I think that’s partly true, but I’m concerned that somehow it conveys the impression that the problem with inflation is oil and commodities, when in fact more correctly my concern about inflation is not just oil.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My concern is about the stance of policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would put on the table the possibility of saying that “inflation has been high, partly spurred by high oil and commodity prices” to say that it’s more than just the short-term behavior of commodity prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think the word “also” means that inflation concerns there are added as an afterthought, which is my reading of the change from the draft table 1 to paragraph 4.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I prefer that “also” be eliminated.

speaker: WARSH
text: I favor alternative B as written and presented.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think it strikes the right balance by highlighting the risks that we see on the inflation front, and I agree with Brian’s characterization that the capital markets’ reaction might be a little surprise.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is hard for us in a time like this to predict exactly how the capital markets are going to interpret this, but it wouldn’t surprise me to see some initial market reaction that is ostensibly negative.

speaker: WARSH
text: That doesn’t trouble me too much.

speaker: WARSH
text: Ideally, the removal of policy accommodation, which we talked about today, would be from a position of strength not weakness, but we may or may not have the luxury of waiting for that opportunity.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, I think it’s important over this period that we not be perceived to be lurching.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think alternative B strikes the right balance of explaining our concerns and provides us reasonable optionality—that is, as you’ve described previously, state- determined rather than time-determined.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I support no change, alternative B.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I mentioned before, I don’t want to put the commodity price decreases and energy price decreases in the bank and say we don’t have any problems going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we also can’t ignore them, and I think that does take off a bit of the pressure.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It also manifests itself in some of the survey numbers and some of the market-based numbers in terms of expectations.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I think it allows a little more time, as someone said earlier, to be patient, to make the determination, given that I still think there are some very real downside risks, as I’ve mentioned.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think this type of statement will be largely consistent with market expectations, although I do think, and Brian can correct me, that this is one of the first times that we have made a very clear statement such as “inflation has been high.” I think that’s a bit of a change from where we have been.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That’s a much stronger acknowledgement of the inflation situation, which I think is appropriate to be acknowledging.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I do think that it may send a relatively strong signal to the market, and it makes me feel more comfortable about no change today with the statement because it shows a lot of concern about the level of inflation in actually characterizing it as high.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Just let me talk a little about monetary policy, and I’ll be brief there.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But then I have to use my opportunity to raise some issues for the Committee when I’m not here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do support alternative B.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: As is obvious from my earlier discussion, I believe that the risks are balanced.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have one modification to Janet’s language because I think it is just simpler to say that “the downside risks to growth and upside risks to inflation are of concern to the Committee.” I don’t see the need for “both,” but we’re actually on the same wavelength in terms of this issue.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What I’d like to spend some time on—because I feel this is sort of my swan song, but maybe because I’m a classy guy, I’ll call this my “valedictory remarks”—are three concerns that I have for this Committee going forward.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m not going to be able to participate, but I have a chance now to lay them out.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The first is the real danger of focusing too much on the federal funds rate as reflecting the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I want to talk about that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Second is that I think it’s absolutely critical that we keep our options open in the current circumstances, and so I want to talk about that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The third is on the communication issue, but it’s not going to be on inflation objectives.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’ve already talked about that enough in public, so it’s clear to you one way or the other.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I hope you consider it, but that’s something that I don’t need to go into here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: First of all, let me talk about the issue of focusing too much on the federal funds rate as indicating the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This is something that’s very dear to my heart.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have a chapter in my textbook that deals with this whole issue and talks about the very deep mistakes that have been made in monetary policy because of exactly that focus on the short-term interest rate as indicating the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In particular, when you think about the stance of monetary policy, you should look at all asset prices, which means look at all interest rates.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: All asset prices have a very important effect on aggregate demand.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Also you should look at credit market conditions because some things are actually not reflected in market prices but are still very important.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If you don’t do that, you can make horrendous mistakes.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The Great Depression is a classic example of when they made two mistakes in looking at the policy interest rate.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is that they didn’t understand the difference between real and nominal interest rates.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That mistake I’m not worried about here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But it is an example when nominal rates went down, but only on default-free Treasury securities; in fact, they skyrocketed on other ones.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The stance of monetary policy was incredibly tight during the Great Depression, and we had a disaster.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The Japanese made the same mistake, and I just very much hope that this Committee does not make this mistake because I have to tell you that the situation is scary to me.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’m holding two houses right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second issue is that it’s absolutely critical that we keep our options open.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: This relates to the points that I already made in my discussion—I argued that we don’t know where this situation of financial stress is actually going to head and that the potential for shoes dropping and bad things happening out there is real.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think it’s likely that it won’t happen, but it’s a significant probability with very serious negative consequences.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that situation, we don’t know exactly the direction of where we have to go.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I was actually very pleased with President Evans’s comments.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Charlie has been a good friend for a long time, and he is one of the people I have tremendous respect for as an economist.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Although we had a disagreement in our view of monetary policy today, on the issue going forward I was pleased to see that you actually indicated that there is a possibility—we hope it doesn’t happen, by the way—that things go south and that we actually have to be much more aggressive on monetary policy and on liquidity issues.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I know that there have been some concerns on the Committee about that as well, but no option should be taken off the table if bad things happen, and we cannot get boxed in.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I feel very, very strongly about that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I would also say that the same issue comes up in terms of inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have argued very strenuously for nongradualism in a situation like the one we’re in.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We are in a different world when we are in a situation of financial stress, and it’s very possible that we might have to raise rates very quickly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There’s a good news case and a bad news case.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The good news case is that housing prices stabilize.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That could actually turn things around very quickly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think, Bill, if I’m not incorrect, you mentioned that possibility, and I think you’re absolutely right.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: In that kind of situation, our policy would become very accommodative.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I do not think it’s too accommodative at all right now.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think it’s balanced; it’s appropriate.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But if the financial markets improve, it will become much too accommodative very quickly, and we then have to respond very quickly in order not to have inflationary consequences.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’d like to see that happen, by the way.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The other case, which I would not like to see happen, is that inflation expectations get unhinged.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have seen no evidence that long-run inflation expectations have gotten unhinged, but there is substantial risk.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If that happened, we would also have to move up very quickly.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I really implore this Committee to keep your options open.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Do not get boxed in.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Let’s hope and pray— let’s all get around in a circle and hold hands—that oil prices fall, which will also help us not get boxed in.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Don, I told you I was going to be a little colorful.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: He was waiting for this one.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I should mention that Don was actually at a conference where he talked about constraints on people’s behavior as a result of the transcripts being recorded, and he said, “But not Rick.” The third issue is something about which I am less constrained, which is communications.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I would not have talked about this earlier, but it really does worry me.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have a complicated governance structure in this Committee, which I actually think is the right governance structure.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have two types of groups that vote on this Committee.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We have the people who are Presidential appointees and then confirmed by the Senate, who are Board members, and I will soon not be one of them.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’ll be a civilian again.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Then we have Bank presidents, who are much more tied into the private sector because your boards of directors, which are composed of private-sector people, recommend you.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Then we do have some role, but they’re the primary people who decide who becomes a Bank president.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think that’s a very good framework.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It actually serves us very well.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’ve been on both sides.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I’ve been on the other side of the fence, not as a president but as an executive vice president.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It serves us very well because we have a link to the private sector that we normally would not have; importantly, it keeps us real in terms of information; and there’s a group of people out there who are not in Washington or New York (because people also have a hard time about New York) but who tend to be very important supporters for us politically.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So this is a system that I would very much like to see preserved.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It does have a problem because of the different roles here.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What I have been very concerned about—and I have had people in the markets speak to me about this—is that recently I had a very prominent central bank governor say to me, “What in the hell are you guys doing?” The issue here is that we need to have a situation where Bank presidents and also members of the Board can speak their views.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: They may have different views, and I very much encourage that in terms of discussion, of where they think the economy is going, which is what we do inside; and I think that does need to be done outside the Committee because it shows that there are different views, that we’re thinking about it, that we’re trying to learn from each other, and so forth and so on.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: What is very problematic from my viewpoint are the speeches, discussions, and interviews outside, when people talk about where they think interest rates should head and where the policy rate should head.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That’s where the criticism has been coming from.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I have to tell you that a lot of people whom I respect tremendously are saying to me that it’s making us look like the gang that can’t shoot straight.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think it’s a really serious problem.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I understand that we want to keep the priority of speaking our minds, but we have to work as a team, and I think that we’re having a problem in this regard.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Let me talk about why I think this is dangerous.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s dangerous in terms of policy setting.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: You can see this is very blunt.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Clearly, if you were in a multi-period game, you wouldn’t be this blunt.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But now I’m not going to be here anymore, so you can hate me—I don’t care.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: But this kind of cacophony on this issue has the potential to damage us in two very serious ways.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is that it weakens the confidence in our institution, and I have to tell you that I love this institution.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It’s very hard for me to leave this place, but it’s something I have to do.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: If the institution is damaged in terms of the confidence that the public and the politicians have in us, it will hurt us deeply.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It will hurt us in terms of policy because it will weaken our credibility, which actually will make it harder to control inflation.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I consider this a very serious cost.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The second issue is on the political front.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: It is very possible that we’re going to have a reopening of the Federal Reserve Act with the next Administration and the next Congress.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The reason I think it is possible is that we have to restructure our regulatory structure.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: There’s no way to get around it—we are in a brave new world on this.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: That could lead to an opening of this issue.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The problem here is, in that opening, there are a lot of people in the Congress who are very uncomfortable having policymakers who are not Presidential appointees and confirmed by the Senate.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Two outcomes could come out of that.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: One is that they could take the vote away from the presidents, which I think would be a disaster because then you’re not going to have good people going into the System.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We won’t have boards of directors that will be good.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: We won’t have all of the benefits that we think we have from the current system.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: The other alternative is that we then have presidents who are actually appointed by the President and then confirmed by the Senate.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: I think, again, that hurts the private linkage.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I feel very strongly about all three of these issues, but I think that you’re going to come up with serious challenges in the future that could be very damaging to the System.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: So I hope you think about this and still like me for being blunt, and also miss me because there will be a little less amusement.

speaker: MISHKIN
text: Who else would have brought Monty Python into the FOMC?

speaker: DUKE
text: I support alternative B. I don’t think that the “severe financial stress” scenario is out of the question right now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I support alternative B for the reasons that you and many others have already stated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to thank everyone for your comments today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I know we don’t have agreement around the table, but as somebody once said, if everybody agrees, then everybody except one is redundant.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I listened very carefully to what has been said.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think hard about them—I do every day.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As we go forward, we will obviously continue to have these fruitful discussions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think that we need to continue to clarify this exit strategy issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One point I would make, and Governor Warsh alluded to it, is that we need to think of this as a state-dependent rather than a time-dependent strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to be clear not so much as to whether we are or are not going to raise rates but under what circumstances and why and what our objectives are.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On that basis, I reiterate that my greater attention recently to financial and real conditions has to do with my view of the risks rather than my objective function.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I recommend no action today and alternative B.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There were a number of suggestions for changes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I will avoid them just to avoid further controversy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My reasons for suggesting alternative B were well stated by President Pianalto.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know what the markets will make of this, but my intention is for it to be slightly hawkish—to indicate a slight upward tilt in policy—which has several functions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, if we don’t move, it emphasizes our ongoing concern with inflation and perhaps provides some prophylactic protection with respect to expectations and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, if conditions do warrant action, and it could be quick action, at least we will have provided the markets with some warning and some indication of our concern about this issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would you call the roll?

speaker: DANKER
text: This vote includes the alternative B language from the table distributed this morning and the directive from the Bluebook.

speaker: DANKER
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: DANKER
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with maintaining the federal funds rate at an average of around 2 percent.” Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes Governor Duke Yes President Fisher No Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes Governor Mishkin Yes President Pianalto Yes President Plosser Yes President Stern Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next meeting is September 16, and we will adjourn now to the Terrace Level of the Martin Building to pay honor to Governor Mishkin.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Sorry for the late beginning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The markets are continuing to experience very significant stresses this morning, and there are increasing concerns about the insurance company AIG.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is the reason that Vice Chairman Geithner is not attending, and Chris Cumming will sit in his place.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to turn in a minute to Bill Dudley for his usual report, and he will be able to give you more information about the situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is another action item I would like to add, given what is happening, which is that there are very significant problems with dollar funding in other jurisdictions—in Europe and elsewhere.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: After Bill makes his presentation and we have our discussion, I would like to put on the table a request for authorization for swap lines.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I prefer not to put a limit on it, so I know I’ve got my own bazooka here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a Foreign Currency Subcommittee that consists of myself, the Vice Chairman of the FOMC, and the Vice Chairman of the Board.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, after Bill’s discussion, I would like to discuss the possibility of giving us a temporary authority to use swap lines as needed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Before I turn to Bill, let me say one other thing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have a lot to talk about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like—just for today, if you would indulge me—to condense our discussion to one round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In your discussion, please include your tentative views on the policy decision.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, that is not ideal because you will not have heard everyone else’s views, but we will have an opportunity afterward for people to amend, revise, and give additional thoughts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But in the interest of time, I think it would be more efficient at this time just to do it that way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Without further ado, let me turn to Bill and ask for a report.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am not going to go through this in great detail.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You can look at these charts at your leisure.1 I am going to focus on 1 The materials to which Mr. Dudley refers are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: what is going on right now, how we have responded to it, and what I think the issues are.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Just to give you a snapshot of what has happened since Sunday evening, stocks are down worldwide—4 percent plus everywhere.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yesterday, the U.S. stock market was down about 4½ percent, and S&P futures indicate a lower opening today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you might expect, there has been a big flight to quality, especially into the Treasury bill market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Ten-year Treasury note yields fell about 30 basis points yesterday, and there has been a big rally throughout the Treasury curve.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The big thing, where there has probably been the most severe stress in the market, is in dollar liquidity for foreign banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you remember, foreign banks, especially in Europe, have a structural dollar funding shortfall, and they look to execute foreign exchange swaps or borrow in the dollar LIBOR market to fund that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There was significant upward pressure in that market—overnight LIBOR rates today were 6.44 percent—and that pressure in Europe is leaking over into our market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yesterday the federal funds rate opened at 3 to 3½ percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Despite our doing a $20 billion repo at our normal 9:30 a.m. time, the upward pressure on the funds rate yesterday continued.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It rose to as high as 6 percent in the late morning, and that is why we came in with a second operation of $50 billion around noon yesterday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To try to have more effect on this issue, this morning we came in much earlier than we normally do—around 8:00 a.m. We did a $50 billion overnight repo.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The funds rate at the time was trading at 3¼ percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think this means that we are obviously adding way too many reserves for the current maintenance period; but the good news is that, when this maintenance period is over a week from tomorrow, we get a fresh start.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So at the current time I think we will see essentially a lot of firmness in the funds rate in the morning and then the funds rate trading down to zero late in the day.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Where the funds rate averages relative to the target is going to be somewhat difficult to say.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yesterday, despite the collapse in the funds rate to essentially zero at the end of the day, the funds rate was quite firm relative to the target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t remember the numbers, but it was in the 2½ percent range.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are going to try to hit the target on average, but it is going to be very difficult.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the current circumstances, it probably is more sensible—at least my advice would be—to err on the side of providing enough liquidity to the market rather than trying to be cute and worrying just about the target federal funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, the Lehman filing has also intensified the pressure on Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs in a number of respects.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Lehman failure means that investors now view the debt of Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs as having much more risk than it did on Sunday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This means that these firms need bigger liquidity buffers than they had before, and it does have implications for long-term profitability.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a consequence, their share prices fell very sharply yesterday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Morgan Stanley was down about $5 a share, to $32, and Goldman Sachs’s stock was off 18 points, to $135.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Morgan Stanley experienced a modest, but not insignificant, pulling back of their counterparties and ate into their liquidity buffer by a measurable degree.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Lehman problems also were evident in some other areas.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is very incomplete, but the ones that came to my attention were money market funds—especially, the Reserve Fund that had large withdrawals, and they encountered a significant liquidity problem.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am actually not sure how that was resolved, but I think that State Street was in the situation of having to cover a very large shortfall of the Reserve Fund last night.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The risk here, of course, is that, if AIG were to fail, money funds have even a broader exposure to them than to Lehman, and so breaking the buck on the money market funds is a real risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The capital resources of the entities that are associated with the money market funds often are quite modest, so their ability to top up the money funds and keep them whole is quite limited.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Thus the money market funds are definitely one important issue in how this contagion could be broader.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second issue is the people who are dealing with Lehman and who have positions with Lehman as their counterparty and how they wind up those positions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you know, the parent filed for bankruptcy, but the U.S. broker-dealer is still in operation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But being in operation doesn’t mean that they are necessarily conducting business in a normal way.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One issue that has received a lot of attention is from some of the asset managers on their mortgage TBA positions with Lehman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Apparently, the sell side can net these up pretty easily through the FICC (Fixed Income Clearing Corporation), but the asset managers have positions with Lehman to either take on mortgage-backed securities or to sell mortgage-backed securities on a forward basis, and they are not really sure what those positions are going to be when we get to that date.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Lehman was not executing those trades yesterday, and so these asset managers are in the very unfortunate position of not knowing what to do.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Do they offset their Lehman position with a trade elsewhere or not?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So that has been another very open- ended issue for the market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of market function yesterday, it was manageable in the sense that markets did trade.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think it is much too soon to think that we are going to make it through just based on yesterday’s move because that move, even though it wasn’t particularly severe in terms of, for example, the share price movement, did cause quite a bit of damage, and people are still pulling away.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, we also have the issue of AIG.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The AIG problem is at least starting as a liquidity crisis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problem with AIG is that the parent company doesn’t have a lot of liquidity resources and doesn’t have easy ability to funnel liquidity up from their subsidiaries because most of the subsidiaries are regulated entities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So AIG is running into two problems: One, they are unable to roll their commercial paper and, two, as their ratings are downgraded—they were downgraded by Moody’s yesterday, I think from AA minus to A minus, but don’t quote me on that—they have to post a lot more collateral against their derivatives exposures and also with respect to their GIC (guaranteed investment contract) business.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So AIG is in a situation in which the parent is basically going to run out of money—today, tomorrow, Thursday, or very, very soon.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now we say it’s a liquidity thing, but a lot of times when people look closer at the books they find out that the liquidity crisis may also be a solvency issue.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think it is still a little unclear whether AIG’s problems are confined just to liquidity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It also may be an issue of how much this company is really worth.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, let me talk a bit about the facilities that we introduced over the weekend.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Basically, we did two things.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We broadened the Primary Dealer Credit Facility (PDCF) significantly in terms of collateral eligibility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Whereas, before, the PDCF took investment-grade securities only, we broadened it to include basically everything that is in the tri-party repo system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We felt that, by backstopping the tri-party repo system completely, we would reassure tri-party investors that they didn’t face rollover risk, and so we would keep tri-party investors investing with the banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That seems to be mostly what happened, at least yesterday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We did get quite a bit of PDCF borrowing yesterday evening, but it was predominantly Lehman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It was about $28 billion of Lehman borrowing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the total borrowing was something on the order of $42 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is telling you that most of the borrowing we had was associated with Lehman’s not being able to roll over their tri-party repo positions with their investors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We don’t really know the reasons for the other borrowing, but it probably was mostly to test the facility as opposed to actual need.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So broadening the PDCF collateral eligibility does seem to be working, so far at least, in keeping tri-party investors in the game and continuing to provide funds to the other primary dealers.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second thing we did was to the Term Securities Lending Facility (TSLF).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of the collateral requirements, that had been AAA-rated RMBS, CMBS, and asset-backed securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We broadened that collateral, so the terms are now the same as the old Primary Dealer Credit Facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We think that there is quite a bit of collateral that the primary dealers have in those AA, A, and BBB classes of asset- backed securities, CMBS, and RMBS.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So we think that is going to provide more support to the primary dealers in terms of funding their liquid collateral in this environment.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We also increased the size.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The original authorization was for $200 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Our auction schedule had been $175 billion, and we put that $25 billion increase into schedule 2.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Remember, there are schedules 1 and 2.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Schedule 1 is Treasuries and agencies.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Schedule 2 is Treasuries, agencies, and this other stuff.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the schedule 2 auctions are going to go up in size, and we frontloaded that increase because the TSLF has not been fully subscribed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are actually going to be able to do two TSLF schedule 2 auctions this week of $35 billion, so we are going to get quite a bit of TSLF liquidity into the market this week, which we think will also be helpful.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So that is where things stand.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Otherwise, I think things in the market are doing what you would expect.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There is a flight to quality.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Japanese yen and the Swiss franc are outperforming.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The dollar is sort of in the middle, and the high-yielding currencies continue to be under pressure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But that is just what we have seen for the last year underlying these risk trades.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I have a lot more material, so if you ask questions I can get into that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think I will just leave it there.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just an amplification on the State Street situation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My understanding is that no money actually went out.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There was $20 billion in withdrawals that came in late in the day.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: They had a $7½ billion credit line.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: State Street had enough collateral to do $7½ billion.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: They were unwilling to do $20 billion.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: They asked us what our position was, and we told them that they needed to make their own business decision in this case.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I haven’t heard what has happened this morning.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I assume that they are scrambling for funds.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But I would emphasize that a real concern is that there will be a run this week on money market funds because they may have to freeze the funds.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It is possible that they will break the buck, and this will be at organizations that don’t have sufficient capital to make people whole.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I think that is a real concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Just a question on the PDCF, about the expansion of the collateral base.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You said there was $42 billion, $28 billion of it was Lehman.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Do we know what kind of collateral Lehman posted?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Did they actually make use of the expanded options or not?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What was the nature of it, do you know?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That was not actually even known until late yesterday evening.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It takes a while for us to get the reports from the clearing bank to be able to go through and tell you what the collateral is.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of the Lehman collateral, they are not allowed to broaden the PDCF— they are basically bringing us the stuff they had on Friday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is also important to recognize that for Lehman we are demanding a lot higher collateral requirements on the non-Treasury and non- agency securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Their collateral haircut for those is 20 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the Fed is taking some credit exposure there, but we put in place on Friday—and we are continuing that—a 20 percent collateral haircut on the non-Treasury and non-agency stuff that is in the PDCF for that exposure to Lehman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We think that’s about roughly three times the market level that investors had been charging previously, so I think that gives us a fair degree of protection.

speaker: LACKER
text: The higher collateral requirement, is that just Lehman?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At this time, I believe that is right.

speaker: LACKER
text: I know there was a lot of concern going in yesterday about the tri-party repo market, and I envisioned two scenarios and anything in between them.

speaker: LACKER
text: One is tri- party lenders pulling away from particular names and moving their funds to other names.

speaker: LACKER
text: Another, at the other extreme, would be tri-party repo lenders pulling away from the market as a whole.

speaker: LACKER
text: If you look at the tri-party repo market from the point of view of the borrowers, that is a frightening scenario.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then the lenders are going to do something with that money.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have been curious about what they would do.

speaker: LACKER
text: My understanding is that cash balances, in essentially deposit accounts, piled up at State Street and BONY yesterday and that they were able to do tri-party repos with some institutions that had been pulled away from.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is that a valid observation?

speaker: LACKER
text: What are the prospects for that providing some kind of resilience for the tri-party market?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I guess the first thing I would say is that you are absolutely right.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If investors pull away, they have to take their money somewhere.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that the Primary Dealer Credit Facility has been shown to be pretty significant in providing support to this market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If you look at what happened to Lehman, for example, even though Lehman was under extreme pressure on Friday, the tri-party repo investors stayed with Lehman on Friday night, which actually surprised me.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the reason that they stayed is that they knew they didn’t really have a lot of rollover risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As long as the broker-dealer didn’t file for bankruptcy over the weekend—and that was the risk they really were taking—the Federal Reserve and the PDCF would be there as the tri-party repo investor of last resort.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Lehman’s experience suggests to me that, if we can contain the broad parameters of this crisis so that it doesn’t spread much further, then we can keep the tri-party repo investors from bolting because they don’t really have a huge amount of risk as long as we are there behind them to take them out when their overnight obligation comes due the next day.

speaker: LACKER
text: So, if I can just follow up, my understanding is that tri-party repos are exempt from the automatic stay, so it is not filing per se that is the risk.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s the risk that they don’t have the cash, right?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I’m not sure about that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I thought that there was an issue about broker-dealer filing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I know that the clearing banks are certainly quite nervous about that eventuality, but I’m not a lawyer.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The repos are exempt from the automatic stay provisions of the bankruptcy code.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But if Lehman had gone into SIPA liquidation, they could have been subject to a SIPA stay.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then a question about the TSLF.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is it this program in which we provide Treasuries?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We give them Treasuries, and they give us other stuff.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You know, this will also probably be helpful this week in providing more Treasuries to the market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There was a tremendous amount of Treasury fails yesterday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So this mechanism does two things.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It takes illiquid collateral from the dealers, and it also supplies a lot of Treasuries to the market, which should help improve the market function in Treasuries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Bill, would you be able to talk a bit about the need for swaps?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I have just sketchy details based on a phone call, so this may not be quite right.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But my understanding is that this morning Norway put in place a facility by which they are going to offer their banks dollars, up to $5 billion, on a one-week term—sort of an open facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The fact that Norway is doing this suggests that the situation has broadened quite a bit further because this is the first time that we have heard about Norway in this story, except for maybe some exposures to the Icelandic banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I have had some conversations with my counterparts at the ECB this morning—this is at a staff level, so I can’t really say what would happen if you were to take this up the chain of command.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But certainly, at least on a preliminary basis, there is quite a bit of interest in having a similar facility for the ECB, which would not be a TAF loan type of facility but more of an open facility where European banks could come and get dollars.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This would reassure people that dollar liquidity was available in Europe throughout the European day.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: My advice to you is that this is probably a good idea in this environment because we are seeing that the lack of dollar liquidity in Europe is really having a feedback effect on people’s willingness to do business with one other in the broader markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we should be open to doing this with the ECB and perhaps with the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan as well—at least have the ability to do it should it prove necessary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You had a two-hander, Governor Kohn?

speaker: KOHN
text: Just to note that we did have a discussion of foreign exchange swaps in the Committee on the Global Financial System a week and a half ago, and the general consensus was that these had been very handy in damping pressures in money markets—dollar funding markets in particular—when the foreign exchange swap market isn’t working very well in Europe and in Switzerland.

speaker: KOHN
text: The central banks around the table, which are all the major central banks, are quite supportive of expanding the facility.

speaker: KOHN
text: We were talking about putting something on a standby basis for use in situations just like this.

speaker: KOHN
text: So the other central banks view this as very helpful to them in containing pressures in their own markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Bank of Japan has requested at the staff level to set up a facility that would be on the shelf for year-end because the Japanese are quite worried that their banks are going to face a dollar funding problem at year-end.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, this preceded the recent crisis, so even before this last week they were concerned that the Japanese banks could potentially have problems, and they were interested in exploring with us having a facility in place.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We were actually going to pursue this, and I hope we will have more at the October FOMC meeting if not sooner.

speaker: BERNANKE
