text: Bill, if we were going to take action today, what would you recommend in terms of counterparties?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Should we say an unlimited amount?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Should we specify an amount?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Can we leave the time open?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What are your recommendations on all those dimensions?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Certainly you want to make it pretty broad.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You want to make it to the Bank of England, Switzerland, the ECB, the Bank of Japan, potentially Canada.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would leave it to their discretion if they would like to participate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would make the offer to them; and if they want to participate, then we should be willing to do that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of size, I think it is really important that you don’t create notions of capacity limits because the market then can always try to test those.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Either the numbers have to be very, very large, or it should be open ended.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would suggest that open ended is better because then you really do provide a backstop for the entire market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As we’ve seen with the PDCF, if you provide a suitably broad backstop, oftentimes you don’t even actually need to use it to any great degree.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think that should be the strategy here.

speaker: LACKER
text: Remind me again how big the European system of central banks’ own outright holdings of dollar balances are.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Do you mean in terms of their dollar foreign exchange reserves?

speaker: LACKER
text: The ECB—they all have their own dollar reserves.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t have the numbers.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I believe that number is about $180 billion of dollar reserves in the euro system.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The ECB itself has control of only a fraction of that.

speaker: LACKER
text: These are held at individual national central banks, so our swap lines to them aren’t approaching that level yet, right?

speaker: LACKER
text: Note here a sense of discomfort with our lending them dollars that they already have and so our serving as a substitute for their mobilizing their own dollar reserves for this purpose.

speaker: LACKER
text: Obviously, the demand could swamp their own reserves, and at that point I would feel differently about this.

speaker: LACKER
text: But my understanding is that the distribution within the European system of central banks is uneven, and in some sense this just provides them with a way to circumvent negotiating how those dollars would be distributed from different central banks to different private-sector banks within their own system.

speaker: LACKER
text: Broadly, I’m uncomfortable with our playing that role.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Whether it’s sensible or not, the ECB has made a pretty strong distinction with us between their foreign exchange reserves and their dollars that they use in these operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They really want to keep those segregated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They want, to some extent, to represent this as being a collaborative effort with the United States as opposed to something they are taking on their own behalf.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: From their perspective—actually President Poole raised the same issue earlier on, and we had this discussion—they seem to put a lot of value on having a distinct swap line, which symbolizes the cooperation and coordination of the two central banks as opposed simply to using their own reserves.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I was going to say that we had this discussion before.

speaker: FISHER
text: We did approve the swap lines.

speaker: FISHER
text: I wonder if you could just summarize for us what you view as the downside risk to our doing this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, I don’t think there are any significant downside risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are operational issues that Bill Dudley and his team have to worry about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we extend funds to the Europeans, which they then relay to their banks, it affects our reserve positions and affects the management of the federal funds rate and requires sterilization.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I suppose, if there were really very large draws, it would begin to affect some of these balance sheet constraint concerns that we have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that is not an entirely separate issue, but it is certainly one that we are looking at in terms of trying to get interest on reserves and those other kinds of measures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, my expectation is that having the facility would in part provide some confidence over and above how much we actually extend.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I guess the operational issues and the further draw on the balance sheet would be the downside, but to me, it seems to be a relatively straightforward step—one we’ve done in the past and one that has the additional benefit of indicating global cooperation on these issues.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In principle, we could talk to the ECB and other central banks about having the rate on these swap lines be at a slight penalty relative to normal times to try to mitigate the potential reserve impact.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I mean, it doesn’t have to be at 2 percent or 2¼ percent for overnight funds—it could be somewhat north of that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But if we have a credible backstop, then it should calm the markets, and then the backstop should not be used.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If we have a backstop and it actually is used, that is presumably because market conditions are horrific.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So in that environment, you could argue that the reserve-management things are very second order concerns in some sense.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then I’d like to propose that the FOMC delegate to the Foreign Currency Subcommittee an unspecified authority, in terms of amount, to offer swaps to foreign central banks as needed to address liquidity pressures in those other jurisdictions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those decisions will be made, again, by the Foreign Currency Subcommittee in consultation with the Open Market Desk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We would keep the FOMC closely informed, and we would revisit and discuss this issue again in October.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is that an acceptable resolution?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Further discussion, comments, or concerns?

speaker: STERN
text: I am in favor of this.

speaker: STERN
text: I just wonder how the marketplace will look at the open-ended nature of this because typically we have dollar magnitudes associated with swaps.

speaker: STERN
text: It may all go relatively smoothly; on the other hand, it may raise questions about exactly what we think the issues are here.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I think we are going to have discussions with our foreign counterparts to decide what the right strategy is.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think right now it is better to have it open ended.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we have discussions with our counterparties— we won’t announce anything today, I would assume?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: No, I think they have to take it up the chain of command, just as we do here.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it’s going to take probably a day.

speaker: KOHN
text: This would come out in the minutes for this meeting.

speaker: STERN
text: But I assume there will be an announcement at some point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When would we announce this measure?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think it would be after we’ve had a chance—I mean, I think we have a lot of work to do with our foreign counterparties.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This was basically raised to me this morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So this is all conditional on agreements and discussions with other counterparties.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will come up with a joint communication announcement strategy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just have one clarification.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have no basic objection to this.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wonder whether or not, if the FOMC is going to delegate the decision to this group, it is sort of an open- ended delegation to do this on an ongoing basis.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Does it make sense to define a period of time for which this open-ended delegation is appropriate—that it would expire and would have to be renewed?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have authorities extending right now to January 30 for a lot of these facilities, so that would certainly be a reasonable time frame, I think.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Existing facilities go to January 31, is that right?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it ought to have a termination point so that, if we wanted to renew it, we would be free to do so, but it wouldn’t last forever.

speaker: KOHN
text: One more clarification, Mr. Chairman—this is intended for G-10 central banks, to include the ECB.

speaker: KOHN
text: Just to be clear, if somebody asks, this is not to give to central banks of emerging-market economies.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we should presume so.

speaker: KOHN
text: If the other were to happen, we would come back to the Committee.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, this is about the major financial centers and the ability of large banks that operate globally to obtain dollar funding.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I amend the proposal to terminate on January 30.

speaker: LACKER
text: Could I hear a little more about the benefits of an open-ended commitment?

speaker: LACKER
text: All of our programs have been capped at a certain size.

speaker: LACKER
text: You said something about “test the limits,” and it makes me think of foreign exchange regimes.

speaker: LACKER
text: What kind of scenario do you have in mind?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think a lot of the programs that we have are actually open ended.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The discount window is open ended in the sense that it’s limited only by the amount of collateral that the banks post there.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Primary Dealer Credit Facility is open ended in that it is limited only by the size of the tri-party repo system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: My point here is that, if foreign banks worry about capacity limits, even having a large program could in principle not be sufficient in extremis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But if the program is open ended, the rollover risk problem goes away.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If I lend you more dollars today, I don’t have to worry about getting those dollars back because I always know that the facility is there.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it’s really the elimination of the ability to flatten out your position if you need to in terms of your dollar exposures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not open ended in the sense that it is not an open window that anybody can come to and take.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It just gives us the authority to adjust the amount.

speaker: LACKER
text: So you will set a definite amount?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will certainly negotiate with the other central banks and tell them what we’re doing now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we want to have the flexibility in case of an emergency to respond, and we also don’t want to communicate to the markets somehow that we have a hard limit that is not going to be changed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would be potentially bad for confidence.

speaker: LACKER
text: But we will communicate a program size?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that remains to be discussed with our counterparties.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we need to have discussions about what would be most effective.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Would a big size that’s fixed in quantity be most effective?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Would an open limit be most effective?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we have to have those discussions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the important thing here—and what we’re going for—is credibility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In a crisis you need enough force—more force than the market thinks is necessary to solve the problem—and we’re going to have to have discussions to determine how much is enough force.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it is mostly a communication issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you want to call the roll on this one?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Can we read the resolution?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The resolution is to provide to the Foreign Currency Subcommittee the authority to enter into swap agreements with the foreign central banks as needed to address strains in money markets in other jurisdictions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This will be done in cooperation with the Open Market Desk and in consultation with those other central banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The amounts are unlimited in principle, but the decisions will be made by the Foreign Currency Subcommittee as needed and as appropriate for the particular circumstances.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The FOMC is providing this authority through January 30.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It will, of course, be open to discussion at any meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As actions are taken, presumably you’ll circulate the outcomes of these decisions to this Committee in advance of any announcements?.

speaker: DANKER
text: Chairman Bernanke Yes First Vice President Cumming Yes Governor Duke Yes President Fisher Yes Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes President Pianalto Yes President Plosser Yes President Stern Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Brian, have you circulated the statement?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Has everyone a copy of that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Before we get started on that, I just want to comment that we may want to say something in the statement about financial conditions, but we’ll come back to that later.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need also now a vote to ratify the domestic open market operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s turn now to the economic situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Dave Stockton and Nathan Sheets.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In response to your request for some economy in our remarks this morning, I’m going to set aside my prepared remarks and just hit some of the highlights here.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We did receive a great deal of macroeconomic data since we closed the Greenbook last Wednesday.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We didn’t seem to get any of it right, but it all netted out to just about nothing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Retail sales came in considerably weaker than we had anticipated, enough by themselves to have knocked about ½ percentage point off third-quarter GDP growth.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But some of that was offset in higher retail inventories, and the rest was offset by a stronger-than-expected merchandise trade report for July.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It all left us still feeling very comfortable with our forecast because it looks to us as though economic growth is going to drop below 1 percent on average in the second half of the year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In terms of the things that really have stood out over the intermeeting period, at least to my mind, one has been the weakness in consumption.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As I indicated, the retail sales report was weak; and now with that report in hand, we’d probably mark down our current-quarter consumption forecast to a decline of 1½ percent at an annual rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: What I think is really remarkable about that is that this weakness is occurring even though we still think spending is probably receiving some boost from the rebates.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So excluding that effect, we’d be looking at something even weaker.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, as you know, we’ve been head-faked a number of times by the retail sales data, which are subject to some pretty substantial revisions.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I wouldn’t necessarily take that report at face value.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the drop we’ve seen in motor vehicle purchases pretty much mirrors in size and timing the kind of falloff that we’ve seen in overall consumption spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So it looks like a very weak picture for consumption.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other notable development over the intermeeting period has been the weakness in the labor markets—now not principally in the payroll employment figures.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Private payroll employment has been falling pretty sharply but not any faster than we would have thought.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the rise in the unemployment rate is remarkable.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, some of the 0.4 percentage point increase in the unemployment rate last month could be statistical noise.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It wouldn’t be entirely surprising to see it fall back some.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the more than 1 percentage point rise that we’ve had since April is not going to be statistical noise.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Some of that increase probably reflects a bigger response to the emergency unemployment compensation program than we previously thought, and we’ve upped our estimates for that to a little less than 0.3 percentage point on the level of the unemployment rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But even putting that aside, we have experienced a more significant rise in the unemployment rate, and I think that’s consistent with other things that we’re seeing in terms of the labor market data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’ve seen another appreciable jump in initial claims.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Announced job cuts are up.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Survey hiring plans have softened.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, this sharp rise in the unemployment rate is a bit difficult to square with a GDP figure that looks as though it was running above 3 percent in the second quarter and even 2 percent if you want to average the first and second quarters together.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There are occasionally large errors in Okun’s law, as I think I’ve noted in the past.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It seems as though Okun’s law gets obeyed about as frequently as the 55 mile an hour speed limit on I-95.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But still, one of the things that we should probably be considering is that perhaps the economy has not been as strong as suggested by the real GDP figures.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Real gross domestic income, which is output measured on the income side of the accounts, has risen about 2 percentage points less than GDP over the past year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: And if we look at industrial production and compare that with the components of GDP that are, in essence, goods production, there’s about a 1 percentage point discrepancy there, with industrial production suggesting weaker figures than GDP.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We see no reason to discount the rise in the unemployment rate as suggesting that we’re entering the second half with more labor market slack than we had previously thought.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Furthermore, on net, we’ve revised down our projected growth in GDP over the next two years—admittedly just a bit—and that was in response to two pretty strong crosscurrents.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One was the significantly lower oil prices that we have in this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We do think they’re going to provide some support to underlying disposable income and spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the positive effect of that on our forecast going forward was more than offset by a significant marking down in our forecast for net exports—which Nathan will be discussing—in response to an appreciation of the dollar and a further downward revision to our outlook for foreign activity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On net, that left us with a little lower growth rate and carrying forward a noticeably higher unemployment rate over the forecast period.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, those were pretty small adjustments.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t think we’ve seen a significant change in the basic outlook, and certainly the story behind our forecast is very similar to the one that we had last time, which is that we’re still expecting a very gradual pickup in GDP growth over the next year and a little more rapid pickup in 2010.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The three things that are absolutely central to producing that outcome are our projection that we’re going to get a stabilization in housing in 2009—and early in 2009; that there will be some diminishment of the drag on growth from the financial turbulence; and that oil prices flatten out.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Of those three, to my mind, the component that probably is most central and most important would be seeing some stabilization in the housing market, not only because this has been a big drag on growth and will also have consequences for household wealth but also because if there’s going to be some clarity and reassurance to financial market participants, it seems as though some end to the housing debacle has to be in sight.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We think we are seeing a few glimmers of hope there—however, we thought that on occasion in the past and have been proven wrong.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But sales of existing homes have been flat since the turn of the year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Sales of new homes have been flat for several months now.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’ve had a drop in mortgage interest rates that followed the takeover of Fannie and Freddie.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Starts have fallen so much now that, in fact, builders are making significant progress in working down the inventory of unsold new homes and even months’ supply has tipped down of late.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So we think that some things are looking a little better for us there.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As a consequence, we’re expecting to see some bottoming-out near the end of this year or the beginning of next year—but not a sharp recovery.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Overall residential investment actually is still a negative for 2009 but less of a negative than it has been this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know from the Greenbook, our estimates suggest that the financial restraints on overall activity—actually on the level of GDP—will increase between 2008 and 2009, but their effects on the growth rate of GDP are diminishing somewhat.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Finally, with regard to oil prices, by our assessment the rise in crude oil prices since the beginning of 2006 is probably knocking about ½ percentage point off growth in 2008; and with a flattening out of oil prices, we expect that to be more of a neutral factor over the next two years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: A lot of what’s going on in our forecast is bad things not worsening any more quickly next year than they did this year, rather than things actually getting better.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I guess it’s a sad comment that we’re relying on second derivatives turning positive to be the main force generating some upward impetus to economic growth.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we are projecting a gradual pickup.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, on the inflation side, this morning’s CPI report for August actually came in a little better than we were expecting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The CPI in August fell 0.1 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We had been expecting an increase of 0.1 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That surprise was all in the energy component, but we at least did see some moderation in the retail food price side that we were looking for, and the change in core CPI fell back to 0.2 percent after a string of 0.3 percent increases.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t think these data will do much to change our basic forecast, which is for total PCE prices to be up somewhere in the neighborhood of a 5 percent rate in the third quarter, and core prices up 3 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Still, if one looks back at the last few CPIs and PCEs, things have come in a little higher on the core side.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The projected 3 percent increase is up about ¼ percentage point from where we were in our August forecast, and our interpretation of this is that we’re probably seeing more upward impetus and pass- through from the higher energy prices, other commodity prices, and imports than we had previously expected.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That certainly squares with what we’re hearing from our business contacts.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It also squares with what we saw last week in the PPI, which was another very sharp increase in prices of intermediate materials.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At least going forward, for the first time since this process got under way, we are seeing more than just a futures price forecast flattening out.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Some easing in the prices of both oil and other commodities and the appreciation of the dollar are giving us at least a little more confidence that some of these cost pressures are going to abate going forward and that we will get the disinflation that we have been forecasting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We continue to see reasonably encouraging signs on inflation expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The medium-term and long-term inflation expectations in the preliminary Michigan report last week dropped 0.3 percentage point, to 2.9 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: TIPS haven’t really done very much, and hourly labor compensation continues to come in below our expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So based on our assessment, once these cost pressures work their way through the system—and we still think that the process will take place over the second half—we think that we’ll get some receding of core inflation from the 2.4 percent that we’re projecting for this year to 2.1 percent next year and 1.9 percent in 2010.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Just a couple of final remarks on current events.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Hurricanes Gustav and Ike obviously created an enormous amount of devastation for a whole lot of people, but they don’t really appear to us to have significant macroeconomic consequences.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There will be some temporary disruption to oil and gas extraction and refining, but it looks as though the basic infrastructure has largely been spared.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I’ll be interested to hear President Fisher’s report.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Retail gasoline prices have jumped in the last few days, but wholesale prices for delivery in October are actually lower than they were before the storms were on the horizon.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think that suggests that this is not going to be a major negative event.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Undoubtedly, industrial production is going to fall like a stone in September, reflecting these two hurricanes as well as the Boeing strike, but we’re expecting that to bounce right back again.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t really have anything useful to say about the economic consequences of the financial developments of the past few days.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I must say I’m not feeling very well about it at the present, but I’m not sure whether that reflects rational economic analysis or the fact that I’ve had too many meals out of the vending machines downstairs in the last few days.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But in any event, we’re obviously going to need to wait a bit to see how the dust settles here, but I think the sign would be obviously in a bad direction.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I’ll turn over the floor to Nathan.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I also will be very brief in summarizing economic developments abroad.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indeed, I would just like to make six very brief points.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The first one is that the incoming data we’ve received since the last Greenbook for the foreign economies have been extraordinarily soft.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indeed, we’ve marked down our forecast or projection of the second quarter by a full percentage point.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The data also suggest that we should carry forward a fair amount of that softness at least through the next year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So our foreign outlook is much softer than it was before.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The second point is that this softening outlook in our view has been a key factor that has contributed to further sizable declines in oil and commodity prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This morning, oil prices were trading around $92 a barrel, which was down another $25 a barrel from where we were at the time of the last meeting.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The third point is that this deteriorating foreign outlook also seems to have triggered something of a reassessment in currency markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Since your last meeting, the dollar has strengthened nearly 5 percent in broad nominal terms.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In our view, what happened in currency markets was that the markets had priced in the expectation that the foreign economies would remain quite resilient in the face of a slowing in the United States.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now with the incoming data over the past couple of months, it is becoming clearer and clearer that the U.S. slowing is going to have a marked effect on these foreign economies, and this has shifted the relative attractiveness of the dollar and supported the appreciation that we’ve seen over the last couple of months.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The fourth point is that, in a number of emerging market economies, we’ve seen a resurgence of certain sorts of financial vulnerabilities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We’ve seen across really a broad array of these economies rising external debt spreads and rising CDS spreads.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We’ve seen falling equity prices and, for a number of these economies, downward pressures on their currencies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On that last point, a number of the Asians have been intervening in the foreign exchange market over the intermeeting period but have actually been intervening to try to prevent their currencies from depreciating, which is a marked change from what we’ve seen in the last couple of years.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The fifth point is that the surprisingly strong performance of U.S. exports that we’ve seen appears to have continued through July.

speaker: SHEETS
text: After the Greenbook went to bed, we got the July trade data, and they continue to point to a fair amount of strength in the export sector.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It was particularly strong in the auto sector, but it was a broad-based strength through July.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, our view is that, given the rise in the dollar and the softening outlook for foreign growth, we’re very likely to see some slowing in export growth going forward.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The final point I’d like to mention is that, also late last week after the Greenbook went to bed, we received data on import prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These data, really for the first time in a long time, showed a marked deceleration in both material-intensive goods import prices and finished goods import prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our forecast for a long time has called for a deceleration in import prices in line with the projected flattening out of commodity prices and a projected flattening out of the dollar.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now it seems that we’re at a point at which all those things that have been incorporated into our forecast but we haven’t had a lot of evidence for are starting to materialize.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We have the dollar flattened out and, indeed, somewhat stronger than in the last Greenbook.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We have lower paths for commodity prices, and then the data that we recently received showed an actual deceleration in core import prices, which gives us some confidence that perhaps the rise in those import prices has peaked.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Dave and Nathan?

speaker: FISHER
text: Could I ask just one question, Mr. Chairman?

speaker: FISHER
text: Could you interpret for us the Bank of China’s cut in the bank lending rate?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Yesterday the PBOC cut its main policy rate 27 basis points.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I guess they felt that 26 would not have been enough and 28 would have been too much.

speaker: SHEETS
text: And 27 was just the right number.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I’d say a couple of thoughts were there.

speaker: SHEETS
text: One important point is that inflation in China has decelerated significantly.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the spring they were looking at twelve-month inflation rates of around 8.3 percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The latest reading for August was 4.9 percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So it’s clearly on a decelerating trajectory.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That has been driven by a marked decline in food prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Earlier this year, food prices were moving up at over a 20 percent rate, and now it is about 10 percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So the deceleration in prices; some concerns about where activity is going, particularly in the aftermath of the Olympics; and signs of slowing external demand have given them the scope they need to cut policy rates.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Besides the cut in monetary policy, we’re also hearing reports that the authorities are poised to implement fiscal stimulus if that’s necessary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Three is a lucky number in China.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Don was going to tell you that 3 cubed is 27. .

speaker: KOHN
text: He was also going to wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether we needed to harness the mystical powers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we have good feng shui here.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The science of monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any other deep questions for our colleagues?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We’re all trying to be brief, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Everyone has been very brief.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My proposal, which I can be argued out of, is to do one round, if that’s acceptable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Please indicate your preliminary view on policy, and you will have another opportunity to refine and extend your views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is that acceptable with everybody?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Should we have Brian’s presentation?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I was about to turn to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If that’s acceptable, let’s turn to Brian and have your discussion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2 I will be referring to the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives and Trial Run Survey Results.” The results of the survey are shown in exhibit 2.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the interest of time, I will not cover them this morning.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Subcommittee on Communications plans to be in touch with the Committee on this issue over the upcoming intermeeting period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The first page of the package reproduces the version of table 1 that you received yesterday afternoon.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This version includes three policy alternatives.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As in the Bluebook, alternative B would leave the stance of policy unchanged at this meeting, and alternative C would involve a 25 basis point firming today.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, alternative A now entails a 25 basis point policy easing rather than the unchanged funds rate that was specified in the Bluebook version of this alternative.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will begin by discussing alternative C. The discussion at your last meeting suggested that you generally saw the next move in policy as likely to be a firming, a point that was explicit in the minutes of the meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even though market volatility and financial strains have increased notably in recent weeks, you might view those developments as having only limited implications for the economic outlook and hence see economic fundamentals as continuing to suggest that policy should soon be firmed.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Inflation has been well above the rates that Committee members judge as appropriate for the longer run, and despite lower oil prices and greater slack in labor markets, there remains considerable uncertainty about how soon and how much core inflation will slow.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In these circumstances, you may believe that a firming of policy is appropriate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under the version of alternative B distributed yesterday evening, the Committee would hold the target funds rate constant at this meeting, and the statement would suggest that the Committee sees the risks to growth and inflation as roughly balanced.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You may believe that this combination is appropriate for this meeting if your modal outlook for the economy has not changed much since the last meeting and if you judge that the upside risks to inflation have diminished, given the sharp drop in energy prices, the decline in indicators of inflation expectations, and the greater economic slack implied by the recent unexpectedly sharp jump in the unemployment rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You might also believe that the downside risks to growth have increased as a result of the recent increase in financial strains.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But at the same time, you may want 2 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: to let the dust settle a bit before concluding that these developments warrant an adjustment in your policy stance.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In particular, you may think there is a good chance that the latest enhancements to the Federal Reserve’s special liquidity facilities will help keep markets functioning and mitigate the risks to growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Relative to the Bluebook version, the language of alternative B has been revised in three material ways.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: First, B2 now notes that “strains in financial markets have intensified.” Second, the clause “some indicators of inflation expectations have been elevated” has been dropped from B3 in view of the recent declines in inflation compensation and survey measures of inflation expectations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, the first sentence of B4 has been revised to suggest that the Committee now sees the significant risks to growth and inflation as roughly balanced.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Given market participants’ expectation that the funds rate could trade soft to the target for a time in light of recent developments, gauging exactly what is built into markets for the outcome of today’s meeting is difficult.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But earlier this morning, market prices appeared to incorporate high odds of at least a 25 basis point easing today or possibly more.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus markets might well see a decision to keep the funds rate constant and to make no appreciable change to the language of the statement as signaling less concern about financial developments than they anticipated.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If you saw recent developments as significantly boosting the downside risks to growth or noticeably lowering the modal outlook, you might consider easing the federal funds rate 25 basis points at this meeting, as in alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The rationale language for this action would begin by noting that strains in financial markets have increased significantly and would go on to indicate that the policy action should help to promote moderate growth over time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee would cite the recent decline in energy and other commodity prices and the increased slack in resource utilization as factors that are expected to foster a moderation of inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The risk assessment would indicate that “the downside risks to growth have intensified, but the upside risks to inflation remain a concern to the Committee.” With a policy easing largely built into markets, shorter-term interest rates would likely decline modestly in response to such an action, depending on how much is built in, or they might be little changed.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As the Chairman indicated earlier in the meeting, adjustments to the statement could be considered in light of the further volatility in markets over the past day.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If I could add a few thoughts on market expectations about this meeting—I think it looks as though easing is priced in for two reasons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One, dealers do expect the federal funds rate to trade soft as we add excess reserves, so I would not take the softness in the September federal funds futures contract as indicative of necessarily expecting an easing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Two, I think it is important to recognize that the rates embodied in those fed fund futures contracts are means not modes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I would characterize the market expectation as either that things get very, very bad and the FOMC cuts rates significantly or that the FOMC does nothing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that actually a 25 basis point cut is probably the least likely outcome that the market anticipates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As evidence of this, a couple of dealers yesterday did change their forecast to a 50 basis point rate cut.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’m not aware of anybody who has changed to 25.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Probably people like that are out there.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I know that my colleagues at Goldman Sachs, where I used to work, are saying that they think the FOMC is going to keep rates unchanged today but, if they were to move, it would be 50.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That gives you a sense that it’s really a bimodal kind of view and that putting different probabilities on 50 and zero gives you some easing priced into the federal funds rate futures market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think the consensus view still in the marketplace is that the Fed probably will not cut rates today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That would be a disappointment to a degree because there’s some probability placed on the idea that the Fed might do 50, but that’s how I would interpret what’s priced into the markets today.

speaker: FISHER
text: Could I ask for a little clarification here?

speaker: FISHER
text: The indication of sentiment is important, is it not, in terms of expectations from the population that you’re talking about?

speaker: FISHER
text: The signaling of our direction would be important here?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I think the market participants would gain some comfort to the extent that the Federal Reserve as an institution indicates concern about what’s going on in the financial markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But in some ways the Desk has already signaled that concern by its intervention, so I’m not sure that additional indications are needed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But in the language you might want to indicate to market participants that, if things were to materially worsen in the financial markets, the Committee might revisit the issue of where the federal funds rate should be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just on the issue of trading soft, though, the October- December has also come down, and there is certainly some shift in the actual policy expectation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think on Friday the mood was basically that the funds rate was going to be flat for a long time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Probabilities placed on either easing or tightening were quite low, and since then the probability of easing has gone up fairly significantly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think it’s hard to interpret because it’s really not about 25 versus zero.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s really about zero versus 50 or maybe even 100 as you look out longer term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Either the financial system is going to implode in a major way, which will lead to a significant further easing, or it is not.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let’s begin with President Lockhart.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I finalized the thinking that went into my prepared remarks late last week, which seemed like a good idea at the time.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But I should follow the philosophy of Charlie Brown, who I think said, “Never do today what you can put off until tomorrow.” Obviously, we can’t ignore the events of the weekend and yesterday’s financial markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So late yesterday I reviewed the views that I shaped last week and tried to ground them in an assessment of whether the outlook for the real economy has changed materially, whether the balance of risks has been altered, and whether, in my opinion, we must reintroduce a risk-management approach and consider taking out more insurance.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: With that as prologue, let me make just a couple of comments on regional soundings from the last couple of weeks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Anecdotal reports from the Sixth District support the view that the economy is quite weak but not deteriorating markedly.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The CFO of a large retailer of housing-related goods said that they think they see a bottom forming.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am also starting to hear some reports that housing markets feel as though they are beginning to stabilize; but, really, it is a little too early to say that a bottom has formed in any of our housing markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My overall sense from District contacts and our surveys is of an economy that is quite weak, with no clear trend evident.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Turning to the national outlook, like most forecasts, my view on the likely path for the economy has not changed materially since our August meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I see nothing in the data and hear nothing from District reports that alters my views that the second half will be very weak.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I expect this weak period to be followed by a slow recovery gathering in 2009, but the foundation of a recovery starting around year-end or early 2009 may be far from solid.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The contraction of credit availability that is confirmed by both surveys and anecdotal evidence could deepen as financial institutions face tight liquidity and difficulty recapitalizing.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A protracted credit crunch would likely operate as a substantial drag on the economy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Consistent with the Greenbook, I expect some near-term improvement in headline inflation, as we saw this morning, some near-term deterioration of core inflation measures, and inflation moving in the right direction later this year and into next year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That said, one director said that he and his particular industry had seen no moderation of price increases up to this date.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am comforted somewhat that the upward drift in some inflation expectation measures appears to have been reversed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In addition, my staff has been monitoring revisions to inflation forecasts of professional forecasters, which also seem to suggest that concerns about accelerating inflation have abated somewhat.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding the balance of risks in the economy, I am concerned that the downside risks to growth may be gathering force, as evidenced by the weakening personal consumption and retail sales data, the weakening economies of export partners, and the delicate state of the financial markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: At the same time, I perceive that there is significant risk that the current disinflationary environment may fail to bring core inflation down to anything resembling acceptable levels for the longer term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Adding up all of this, I perceive a very rough balance of risks that could break either way in coming months.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My view of the appropriate policy path is consistent with the Greenbook—that the fed funds rate target will remain stable at or close to the current level for several months going into 2009.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My preference is to hold the fed funds rate at the current level of 2 percent.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Among the reasons is that a ¼ percentage point drop, as suggested by alternative A, is really not clearly called for by a changed outlook for the real economy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Inflation risks are still in play, and I think we should give credit markets more time to digest events and sort out rate relationships.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As regards the statement, my preference is alternative B.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, I am concerned that the reference to the recent financial turbulence is not quite strong enough, so I took a shot at rephrasing just the beginning of the rationale section to read as such: “Economic growth appears to have slowed recently, and labor markets have weakened further.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In addition, strains in financial markets have increased significantly”—basically taking the slightly stronger expression in the alternative A rationale and putting it in alternative B.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So my position, Mr. Chairman, is to hold at this meeting.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This is already a historic week, and the week has just begun.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The labor market is weak and getting weaker.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The unemployment rate has risen 1.1 percentage points since April and is likely to rise further.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I am not convinced that the unemployment rate will level off where the Greenbook is assuming currently.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The failure of a major investment bank, the forced merger of another, the largest thrift and insurer teetering, and the failure of Freddie and Fannie are likely to have a significant impact on the real economy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Individuals and firms will become risk averse, with reluctance to consume or to invest.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Even if firms were inclined to invest, credit spreads are rising, and the cost and availability of financing is becoming more difficult.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Many securitization vehicles are frozen.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The degree of financial distress has risen markedly.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Deleveraging is likely to occur with a vengeance as firms seek to survive this period of significant upheaval.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given that many borrowers will face higher interest rates as a result of financial problems, we can help offset this additional drag by reducing the federal funds rate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I support alternative A to reduce the fed funds rate 25 basis points.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, I see no reason to focus on the details of the forecast.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Clearly, the economy is under stress, both as we look at the economic growth forecast and as we look at the inflation forecast.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I recognize the amount of stress we are under here.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would say to you, in dealing with that stress, I am fully supportive of the actions that we take in terms of liquidity—the TAF and the other efforts to provide liquidity into the market.

speaker: HOENIG
text: These are tools that we can and should use for these kinds of shocks in a short-term context.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the other hand, I would encourage the Committee to resist the impulse to ease policy in a sense of doing something.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The issue is not the level of our policy rate at this time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It is the dysfunctioning of the markets that we hope our liquidity efforts will help address.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To begin to talk about easing or even to put language in there that suggests easing is to cause people, on the expectation that we might ease at some point even if we hold off now, to delay decisions that they would otherwise make that would benefit the economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I also encourage us to look beyond the immediate crisis, which I recognize is serious.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But as pointed out here, we also have an inflation issue.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our core inflation is still above where it should be.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Headline inflation has been up, even though there are some signs that commodities and energy are backing off.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But the businesses themselves are saying, “How do I recover my margin?” So there is no impulse to pass along those reductions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We talk about wages and labor backing off.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But they are holding off, they are not backing off, and in negotiations they are much more antagonistic.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Those kinds of pressures will emerge at some point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Those are the longer-run issues that I think we need to keep in mind as we deal with this immediate crisis.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I would strongly encourage us to leave rates where they are, to be very careful with our language, not to encourage the expectation of further rate decreases, and to continue to be aggressive in our liquidity provisions as we have been the last several weeks and months.

speaker: YELLEN
text: During the past several weeks, my head office and Branch directors have become decidedly more pessimistic about the economic outlook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My own assessment of incoming data coincides with theirs.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My contacts also report that their businesses are still raising prices in response to past increases in commodity and import prices that boosted their costs.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I expect as a consequence that core inflation will remain uncomfortably high for a while longer, but the marked decline in commodity prices since June reinforces my conviction that there is light at the end of this inflation tunnel.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to growth, our forecast is similar to the Greenbook’s, with a little more weakness in the second half of this year and a little more strength in 2009.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the risks to this forecast are decidedly skewed to the downside.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I agree with the Greenbook’s assessment that the strength we saw in the upwardly revised real GDP growth in the second quarter will not hold up.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Despite the tax rebates, real personal consumption expenditures declined in both June and July, and retail sales were down in August.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My contacts report that cutbacks in spending are widespread, especially for discretionary items.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, East Bay plastic surgeons and dentists note that patients are deferring elective procedures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Reservations are no longer necessary at many high-end restaurants.

speaker: YELLEN
text: And the Silicon Valley Country Club, with a $250,000 entrance fee and seven-to-eight-year waiting list, has seen the number of would-be new members shrink to a mere thirteen.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Exports were a huge source of strength in the second quarter, but I am concerned that we cannot count on very large contributions to growth from exports going forward, now that the dollar has begun to rise and economic growth abroad has slowed, even turning negative in some important trade partners.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, the growing weakness of the global outlook appears to be an important explanation for the reversion in commodity prices, and this adds a dimension of gloom to what would otherwise be a decided plus for both inflation and demand.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Recent data also suggest that labor markets are weakening across the board—a development that will cast a pall on household income and spending.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The interaction of higher unemployment with the housing and financial markets raises the potential for even worse news—namely, an intensification of the adverse feedback loop we have long worried about and are now experiencing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, delinquencies have risen substantially across the spectrum of consumer loans, and credit availability continues to decline.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One ray of hope is that the changes at Fannie and Freddie have caused a notable drop in mortgage rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Another is that the decline in home prices has become somewhat less steep, and we have seen an outright improvement in home inventories relative to sales.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But my contacts are very pessimistic about the prospects for nonresidential construction.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They note that construction is continuing on projects in the pipeline with committed funding, but new projects are all but impossible to finance.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Turning to inflation, I have long anticipated and still expect that inflation will fall to more-reasonable levels in 2009.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, developments since our August meeting diminish the upside risks to this projection.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The drop in oil and other commodity prices, along with the appreciation of the dollar, should work to moderate the current inflation bulge and diminish the potential for a wage–price spiral to develop.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Import inflation has already begun to ease.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Furthermore, we have seen a remarkable decline in inflation compensation for the next five years in the TIPS market.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would not rely heavily on this decline to support my view, but I do have to say that the decline is a lot more reassuring than the alternative.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I was also encouraged by the 30 basis point drop in long-term inflation expectations in the most recent Michigan survey.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I anticipate that the recent jump in the unemployment rate will place some additional downward pressure on growth in labor compensation, which has been quite low, and in core inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although the jump in the unemployment rate probably partly reflects the extension of unemployment insurance coverage, a back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that the upper bound on this effect is just a few tenths of a percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would agree with the Greenbook estimates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have also examined the possibility that the increase in unemployment reflects a rise in the NAIRU due to sectoral employment shifts out of construction and finance and into other industries.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Ned Phelps has argued that the sectoral shift story implies a sizable dispersion of employment growth across industries and states.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But we looked at these data and found no significant increase, so I don’t find this Phelps argument particularly convincing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Considering all of these factors, I expect both headline and core PCE price inflation to fall to about 2 percent for 2009 as a whole, and I see the risks to this projection as roughly balanced.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to policy, I would be inclined to keep the funds rate target at 2 percent today.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For now, it seems to me that the additional liquidity measures that have been put in place are an appropriate response to the turmoil.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am fine with the wording of alternative B and would support President Lockhart’s suggestion for change.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That would seem fine to me, too.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In view of the intensified financial stress and the potential for more turmoil, obviously I think we will need to be flexible in setting policy going forward, and I am very concerned about downside risks to the real economy and think that inflation risk is diminished.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am going to start with the national economy in the interest of brevity here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Concerning the national outlook, it is difficult and probably unwise to try to assess growth and inflation prospects in the immediate aftermath of an event like the Lehman bankruptcy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I expect to see more failures among financial firms, and I expect those failures to continue to contribute to market volatility.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is part of an ongoing shakeout among financial market firms, following some of the worst risk management in a generation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I expect sluggish growth in the second half of 2008, in part due to labor markets that are somewhat weaker than expected.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Financial market turmoil is certainly a key concern, but the U.S. economy still outperformed expectations in the first half of 2008, despite the demise of Bear Stearns—an event not too different in some respects from the current episode.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My sense is that three large uncertainties looming over the economy have now been resolved—the GSEs and the fates of Lehman and Merrill Lynch.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Of these, the resolution of GSE uncertainty seems to be the most pivotal, even though it is not the one leading the news today.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Normally, the elimination of key uncertainties is a plus for the economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As is typical in this type of situation, safe interest rates have fallen dramatically across the board.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A second macroeconomic shock stemming from the dramatic rise in oil and other commodities prices has been an unwelcome development during the past six months.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The retreat of West Texas intermediate prices to $94 a barrel, and today down to $92 a barrel, should improve second-half growth prospects.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Meanwhile, an inflation problem is brewing.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The headline CPI inflation rate, the one consumers actually face, is about 6¼ percent year-to-date.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That does not include today’s report.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is against the federal funds target of 2 percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: While it makes sense to focus on financial markets for the time being, it is essential that we keep in position to put downward pressure on inflation going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The financial crisis threatens to roll on for such a long time and to demand so much attention that the private sector may rationally conclude that we have lost all sight of our inflation objective.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In such a case of unmoored expectations, outcomes could be far more severe than those envisioned in the Greenbook.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My policy preference is to maintain the federal funds rate target at the current level and to wait for some time to assess the impact of the Lehman bankruptcy filing, if any, on the national economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In uncertain circumstances like these, I think it would be unwise to react too hastily to a fluid situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Any immediate effects may not be the ones that are intended, and further down the line—that is, once more data have accumulated—a hasty action may leave the Committee out of position relative to the incoming data.

speaker: BULLARD
text: By denying funding to Lehman suitors, the Fed has begun to reestablish the idea that markets should not expect help at each difficult juncture.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Changing rates today would confuse that important signal and take out much of the positive part out of the previous decision.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In addition, a rate move would be poorly targeted toward mitigation of difficulties at particular financial firms.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The FOMC has already done a great deal to create a low interest rate environment in order to shepherd the economy through a substantial shock to the financial and housing sectors.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The Committee now needs to allow the financial sector shakeout to occur using liquidity facilities to the extent possible to help navigate the resulting turbulence.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: New data and survey and anecdotal information in the Third District suggest that the economy in our District continues to be weak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There have been further declines in some industries and deceleration of growth in others, but generally data are coming in as expected.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Employment growth was flat over the three-month period ending in July, and I expect that unemployment rates in our three states will tick up in August, when the regional data come out, much as it did in the national data.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Overall, the activity in our region, as I said, has remained weak since the last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Housing construction continues to be weak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Sales of existing homes remain sluggish, and inventories remain high.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One builder said, “Things don’t feel very good.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I feel as though I am in a tar pit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My feet are maybe now on the bottom; my nose is still above the level of the tar; and while I may feel the bottom, it still doesn’t feel very good.” On the commercial real estate side, we saw a slight uptick in the value of July contracts, but they are not very high.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, they really remained at the average level of the last seven years.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Retailers remain pessimistic in the latest Beige Book.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: District banks saw loans rise slowly but steadily in August.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Beige Book reports from them see slight gains in consumer and real estate lending and C&I loans essentially flat.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The good news is from our business outlook survey for September, which will be released to the public on Thursday at 10:00 a.m., but the results are in.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The survey is from the first two weeks of September.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The general activity index has been negative, if you recall, for the last nine months—since December 2007.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The last value was minus 12.7.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The September number, not to be released until Thursday, is a positive 3.4, so that’s a swing of 15 points to the good.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is clearly somewhat encouraging, although we don’t want to get too excited about one month—but it is good news.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Furthermore, both the new orders and shipment indexes in the survey improved in September.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Price pressures have abated somewhat with the fall in commodities and oil, but they remain.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The six-month-ahead outlook indexes also improved substantially in the new survey.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is the best picture that the survey has painted in certainly quite a while—about the last six or eight months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In summary, the economic conditions of the Third District remain weak and sluggish but are not materially different from what we and our business contacts had been expecting over the near term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While a lot of attention in the short run is being paid to financial markets’ turmoil, our decision today must look beyond today’s financial markets to the real economy and its prospects in the future.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In this regard, things have not changed very much, at least not yet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, the Greenbook forecast has changed only modestly since the last Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The economy remains weak but not appreciably different from what I anticipated or even what the Greenbook anticipated at the last meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I agree that the recent financial turmoil may ultimately affect the outlook in a significant way, but that is far from obvious at this point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We also need to acknowledge the long lag times associated with the effect of monetary policy actions on the real economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Actions today will not help us very much in the very, very near term where the real economy is concerned.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the inflation front, there has been some good news.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The decline in the retail price of gas has contributed to a decline in headline inflation in August.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my view, the price declines in commodities and oil have mitigated somewhat the upward pressure on expectations and have reduced the likelihood that inflation expectations will become unanchored, at least in the near term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nevertheless, I remain concerned about the inflation outlook going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In part, my concern stems from the fact that I do not see that the ongoing expected slowdown in economic activity is entirely demand driven.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I noted before, the impact of financial shocks and high commodity prices can plausibly lead to a decline in the growth rate of potential output.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If so, there will be less offset to inflation going forward than incorporated in the baseline Greenbook forecast, which relies heavily on slack variables to control inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Greenbook simulation entitled “costly reallocation” provides some welcome effort from the staff in this regard, and I appreciate that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yet the details of that experiment were a bit sketchy for me, and at some point I would be interested in a little more detail as to how that actually plays out.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my view, the main driver for the outlook of future inflation over the next two years is not, nor has it been, oil prices per se, but the path of monetary policy that the Committee will adopt over the next several months and quarters.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I appreciate the memo that the staff produced regarding the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: According to the memo, the current stance of policy is not unusually accommodative.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, I would like to note that that conclusion depends critically on the specific forecast and the nature of the FRB/US model.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A different model, one that says that inflation expectations are more forward looking, may well lead to a very different conclusion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I take the message of the memo to be that the assessment of the stance of monetary policy is dependent, at a point in time, on a model, and I very much agree with that assessment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given that my model is somewhat different from the staff’s model, I continue to believe that monetary policy at its current level is accommodative and that, if this current stance is sustained, the economy will experience faster inflation in the medium term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Clearly, we must pay attention to the adverse effects of the financial disruptions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But we also must recognize that our policy actions today and over the next several months will affect the outcomes of inflation over the medium term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I said, it is my view that the current stance of policy is inconsistent with price stability in the intermediate term and so rates ultimately will have to rise.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, I acknowledge that there are risks to economic growth going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The slowdown and the financial market turmoil could turn out to be worse than I expect.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also recognize that, given the events over the weekend, now is probably not the time to shock markets by raising rates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But neither is it a time to panic and lower rates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A cut today may be reassuring to some in the financial markets, but it also may serve to scare markets by sending a signal that we are much more worried than perhaps they are.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There is just way too much volatility and dust blowing around to make such snap judgments on monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have been aggressive with our liquidity provisions, and we will continue to be so, and I support that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Stability coming from monetary policy is an important attribute, and I think we have an opportunity to provide some stability here.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, I am uncomfortable with the current Greenbook baseline path that has the funds rate remaining unchanged well into the second half of next year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my view, that will not deliver an acceptable path of inflation outcome over the medium term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the same time, I do not perceive an immediate threat to the unanchoring of expectations, so I can accept keeping the funds rate at an unchanged level at this meeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But at some point, before the unemployment rate begins to improve substantially, I believe this Committee will need to raise rates in order to deliver on our inflation objectives.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Regarding language, I can live with the language in alternative B.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, even before the events of the last several days, I thought that this was the most severe financial crisis, certainly, that I have seen in my career.

speaker: STERN
text: And the last several days—as well as some of Bill’s comments about possible contagion spreading from breaking the buck and so on and so forth—have only heightened that conviction and my concern about where we are.

speaker: STERN
text: So I think it is fair to say that the headwinds confronting the economy have intensified even further.

speaker: STERN
text: It is difficult to comment on the degree or the duration, but I think we know the direction.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as the near-term economic outlook is concerned, I wasn’t terribly optimistic about the next two or three quarters to begin with.

speaker: STERN
text: If I were going to prepare a new forecast at this point—or even had I prepared one last week—I probably would mark it down a bit.

speaker: STERN
text: But, of course, there is not much we can do about that at this stage.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as the inflation outlook is concerned, I have thought that, late in this year and into next year, inflation would start to abate, and recent developments perhaps heighten my conviction about that.

speaker: STERN
text: But I will agree that it is still an open issue.

speaker: STERN
text: So it seems to me that all of this suggests that the outlook, at least in terms of financial conditions and the economy in the near term, has clearly deteriorated.

speaker: STERN
text: The inflation outlook, if anything, has perhaps improved a notch, or at least the outlook that I had earlier is a little more solid.

speaker: STERN
text: Given the lags in policy, it doesn’t seem that there is a heck of a lot we can do about current circumstances, and we have already tried to address the financial turmoil.

speaker: STERN
text: So I would favor alternative B as a policy matter.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as language is concerned with regard to B, I would be inclined to give more prominence to financial issues.

speaker: STERN
text: I think you could do that maybe by reversing the first two sentences in paragraph 2.

speaker: STERN
text: You would have to change the transitions, of course.

speaker: STERN
text: I would say that if we wanted to change policy at this meeting—and that is not my preference—I would do it by ½ percentage point, and I would think that the rationale would be psychological reasons.

speaker: STERN
text: Again, I don’t think we are going to have a big effect on the near-term performance of the economy.

speaker: STERN
text: But if we think psychology in the marketplace is sufficiently bad or that there is sufficient concern that the Federal Reserve somehow doesn’t quite get it—I would think that all our actions cumulatively, including the actions over the weekend, should not make that a grave concern—then I think we would want to do more than ¼ percentage point.

speaker: EVANS
text: The unfolding financial situation is injecting enormous uncertainty into the economic outlook and policy picture.

speaker: EVANS
text: Although this analogy is imperfect, today’s uncertainty reminds me of March 2003.

speaker: EVANS
text: Then, on the eve of the invasion of Iraq, the FOMC decided that geopolitical uncertainty was so great that the Committee could not characterize the balance of risks at all in the policy statement.

speaker: EVANS
text: Today, the downside risks to output are almost too dispersed to characterize.

speaker: EVANS
text: In one or two weeks, we may know better that either the economy will somehow muddle through or we’re likely to be facing the mother of all credit crunches.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that the first outcome would be quite an accomplishment under the circumstances, but at the moment it’s very hard to say how this will turn out.

speaker: EVANS
text: Nevertheless, we have to offer an opinion.

speaker: EVANS
text: With respect to the economic landscape before the developments of last weekend, one thing that I kept hearing was that uncertainty and caution in the business community had increased in recent weeks and that they were causing many firms to hold back on spending and committing to financial investments.

speaker: EVANS
text: But a number of my contacts indicated that the weakness was not out of line with their earlier expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the plus side, I got the impression that, with the exception of housing, there are not many excesses on the real side of the economy that needed to be worked off.

speaker: EVANS
text: Notably, I did not hear of inventory overhangs or unused capacity, and Manpower even indicated that their clients had been careful not to go overboard earlier in the hiring cycle, and so we’re not left with bloated workforces.

speaker: EVANS
text: Still, this sentiment and the incoming data did not paint a pleasant picture with regard to the national outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: As one of my directors said, turning the common phrase against me, the economic problems that we are facing appear to be remarkably resilient.

speaker: EVANS
text: Even before last weekend’s events, the economic risks had increased somewhat.

speaker: EVANS
text: We had the large rise in the unemployment rate, the recent weak consumption data, and heightened caution by firms.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, of course, the financial risks have increased substantially and further threaten the growth outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: At a minimum, credit standards are likely to tighten further and crimp spending.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m not looking forward to putting a forecast together in October.

speaker: EVANS
text: Dave and the Board staff have my sympathy and respect for doing this each meeting.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s unfortunate, Dave, that we haven’t had the time to spend talking about the excellent special memo that you and your staff put together on gauging the effective stance of policy.

speaker: EVANS
text: I thought that was very helpful.

speaker: EVANS
text: I had on previous occasions mentioned that it would be nice to have some markers that we could look at, and at least for me, that was quite helpful.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, it’s not a large stretch to expect that inflationary pressures will recede, given what we’re facing.

speaker: EVANS
text: We could see enough weakening in the economic outlook that the projected slack in the economy will point inflation more clearly down and below 2 percent over the medium term.

speaker: EVANS
