text: Just last week I was still a bit skeptical that these forces would be large enough to achieve this disinflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: But we need to be forward looking, and that would be how I would mark my inflation forecast down today.

speaker: EVANS
text: So what does this mean for policy today?

speaker: EVANS
text: In my view, we’ve kept the policy rate low so that we would not be far from appropriate policies if and when the risks to growth intensified enough relative to the risks to inflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: So we are well positioned to act if we need to.

speaker: EVANS
text: I agree with President Stern that, if we were to act, we should do something significant on the order of 50 basis points.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I think we should be seen as making well-calculated moves with the funds rate, and the current uncertainty is so large that I don’t feel as though we have enough information to make such calculations today.

speaker: EVANS
text: We will know much more in a couple of weeks, I hope at least about the changes in underlying financial conditions, and will thus have a better sense of the risks to both elements of the dual mandate and the associated policy actions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The recent financial market news is shaking people’s confidence dramatically.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But even before recent events, the evidence was already pointing to more effects of the financial crisis on the real economy than I had built into my projection at our last meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The reports from my District contacts and the incoming data caused me to revise down my near-term output projection even before the latest round of financial market troubles.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The improvement in net exports that was reflected in the second-quarter GDP growth has not encouraged manufacturers in my District to revise up their export projections.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: They are still holding firmly to the opinion that the global economy is slowing and that export growth will slow with it for several quarters.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Of course, manufacturers are concerned about weakness spreading further within their domestic customer base.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The ongoing turmoil in financial markets continues to affect businesses in my District.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Some of the banks in my District are finding it very, very difficult to attract new capital and to manage their way out of trouble.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am hearing that credit is harder to come by for many borrowers who in the recent past would not have thought twice about their creditworthiness.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Last week I met with a business contact with a very long and successful track record of buying and operating private companies.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: He reported that he had reached a deal with a bank to finance a project at a 7 percent interest rate with the loan amortized over a fifteen-year term.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: On the morning of the close just three days later, the bank faxed him the paperwork, which reflected a 12 percent interest rate on a non- amortizing loan with a 10-year term.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So the deal obviously is not going forward.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: One of my directors, who heads a very large regional banking organization, reported at our board meeting last week that many banks are shedding assets and that in some cases they are walking away from longstanding customer relationships in order to do so.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: He said that investors are very skeptical about putting new equity into banking deals and that those who have done so in the past vow not to be burned twice, let alone a third time.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Of course, inflation remains an important issue as well.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My contacts, as Dave mentioned in his report, are not so confident that a broad array of intermediate and retail prices are actually going to move back down as a result of the recent decline in energy and other commodity prices.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Several of my contacts report that major suppliers are trying to maintain their prices despite the decline in raw material costs just to make up for a long period of absorbing price increases.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Nevertheless, most of my contacts agree that the commodity price environment has stabilized considerably, making me more confident that core inflation will gradually slow over the next couple of years.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At our last meeting, my forecast was broadly consistent with the Greenbook baseline.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Today my forecasts for output and prices are broadly similar to the Greenbook’s for 2009 and 2010, although I am expecting more weakness in economic activity in the second half of this year than the Greenbook is forecasting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My contacts in the manufacturing sector have persuaded me that exports are going to be weaker in the short term than I had previously thought, and I have also revised down my consumption path on the basis of the credit constraints on households.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Although I am more encouraged about the recent decline in energy and commodity prices, I would like to see further evidence of price stability in these markets and also continued stability in inflation expectations for a while longer before I reduce the upside risk that I place on my inflation outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, a growing risk to my outlook is that the short-term weakness that I have now built into my outlook extends further out into the forecast period.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I worry that my outlook doesn’t fully capture all of the many ways in which financial forces at work in the economy are actually going to restrain spending.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: On Friday, I was convinced that the best course of action was to keep an even keel in these rough seas—to be flexible, of course, but to look beyond the latest wave crashing over the bow.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Only six weeks ago, inflation risks were on the verge of being unacceptable, and today the troubles of Wall Street are the focus.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I was sure that we were going to be in for many more surprises; I just didn’t know when and from where they would be coming.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I supported not only keeping our policy unchanged but also keeping our language changes to a minimum even if that language missed some nuances of the outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given the events of the weekend, I still think it is appropriate for us to keep our policy rate unchanged.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I would like more time to assess how the recent events are going to affect the real economy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I have a small preference for the assessment-of-risk language under alternative A. I think it captures my concern that the downside risks have intensified.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, I can support some of the comments and changes to highlight the financial market strains that were made by President Lockhart and President Stern.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I can support the language under alternative B with some additional comments about the financial strains that we are facing.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Fifth District hasn’t changed much; it pretty well aligns with the national outlook.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the national outlook, I find myself, all except for the policy path, aligned well with the staff.

speaker: LACKER
text: There have been a lot of economic reports since the last meeting about particular categories of spending or particular sectors of the economy, but they net out to only a small change, if any, in the broad contour of the outlook for me for overall growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: I expect it to be sluggish for the remainder of the year with recovery beginning at some point in the first half of next year.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’ll commit the sin of saying that uncertainty is especially high now.

speaker: LACKER
text: There seem to be reasonably plausible risks in the outlook in virtually every spending category and, in many cases, on both sides of the outlook.

speaker: LACKER
text: About inflation, so far our credibility has helped to prevent a pickup in compensation growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, it’s heartening that compensation growth is coming in a little below expected in response to the energy price shock this year.

speaker: LACKER
text: This has allowed us to accomplish the inevitable decline in real wages without setting off an inflationary acceleration in wage rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: But we’re still in the midst of an upsurge in core inflation, which the Greenbook expects is going to tick up near 3 percent this quarter.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I said before, I think it’s critically important for us to emerge from this episode without trend inflation ratcheting upward, and I’m not sure we can take the forecasted moderation for granted.

speaker: LACKER
text: Inflation compensation has been well contained, and that has been heartening.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I have also said this before—I think the current level of five-year, five-year- forward inflation compensation seems more consistent with a trend above 2½ percent than it does with a 2 percent trend.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’m not convinced that there’s going to be much gravitational pull down from an elevated rate once core rises.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the very least, I think there’s some uncertainty about that.

speaker: LACKER
text: For financial markets, this is yet another historic week, as President Rosengren remarked.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the questions facing financial market participants, the uncertainty they face, can be usefully partitioned into three broad categories.

speaker: LACKER
text: One is the aggregate magnitude of fundamental losses that the financial sector faces.

speaker: LACKER
text: Another is the location of those losses—where they are going to pop up within financial intermediary sectors.

speaker: LACKER
text: The third is the likelihood and the magnitude of fiscal transfers in the form of governmental support for particular firms.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the weekend’s events have caused financial market participants to revise their assessments of the future.

speaker: LACKER
text: It seems to me at this early date in the process that the revision in the outlook has had more to do with the latter two categories than with the aggregate size of fundamental losses we have coming down the pipeline.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is to say, it’s about where they’re popping up, which firms are affected and are going to be hit, and about the likelihood of government support.

speaker: LACKER
text: What we did with Lehman I obviously think is good.

speaker: LACKER
text: It has had an effect on market participants’ assessment of the likelihood of other firms getting support, and I think you would have to attribute at least some of changes in equity prices to that.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’re likely to see a lot more disruption this week and in the days going forward than we’ve seen so far.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t want to be sanguine about it, but the silver lining to all the disruption that’s ahead of us is that it will enhance the credibility of any commitment that we make in the future to be willing to let an institution fail and to risk such disruption again.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the other hand, if the disruption proves less severe than we expect, the silver lining is that that will strengthen our hand in the future as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: However, I would note that I don’t think that what we did with Lehman has set a clear and firm boundary on the circumstances under which government support is likely to be forthcoming.

speaker: LACKER
text: All the language around not supporting Lehman was of a one-off nature.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’m not sure about the extent to which we’ve diminished uncertainty about the likelihood of support going forward, and I think that such uncertainty is likely to exacerbate financial volatility in the months ahead until we can make more progress on articulating a reasonably principled policy on when we’re going to intervene and when we’re not, or at least enhancing clarity about that.

speaker: LACKER
text: Overall, I don’t take what’s happened in the last few days as changing much.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s not obvious to me what the implications are for the outlook for inflation and growth, at least at this point.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I don’t see a reason to deflect from our policy path at this point.

speaker: LACKER
text: I can support standing pat with the funds rate today.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that’s a good idea.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think, looking forward, that we will want to raise rates sooner rather than later if core inflation doesn’t moderate.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we’re more likely to require a path more like the August Greenbook than the current one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, I have a question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I really would like your advice on this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Historically, if we look at situations like Japan and Scandinavia, ultimately there comes a point at which the banking system is decapitalized and dysfunctional and the government intervenes on a large scale.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those interventions have been very expensive, but in those cases I mentioned, they have generally restored the banking system to health and have helped the economy recover.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What’s your view on the right sequencing?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you think that we should remain very tough until such time as it becomes inevitable that fiscal intervention is needed?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you think that we should avoid fiscal intervention at all stages?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m seriously interested in knowing what you, or anyone else who would like to comment, think is the appropriate stage, if any, at which fiscal intervention becomes necessary.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have a legislated program of fiscal intervention—deposit insurance— and the boundaries around that are very clear.

speaker: LACKER
text: Which liabilities are insured and which ones are not are very clear.

speaker: LACKER
text: Around the edges there’s some lack of clarity about what least-cost resolution means and the extent to which deviations from that can be verified, and that provides some room for the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to deviate from that and implicitly to forbear to some extent.

speaker: LACKER
text: But even that is sort of a well-contained and well-defined government support.

speaker: LACKER
text: That’s what the Congress has enacted, and it’s not clear to me whether we should go beyond that.

speaker: LACKER
text: Japan got down to deposit insurance.

speaker: LACKER
text: That seems like a natural benchmark.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I think this is a historical fact—that, once the banks became decapitalized, there were also capital injections into the banks in both of those cases.

speaker: LACKER
text: And the FDIC does exactly that when it resolves a failed institution.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, I have thought about this considerably because I think we have come to a time in our history when we have institutions that clearly ought to be and may in fact be too big to fail.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think we tend to react ad hoc during the crisis, and we have no choice at this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But as you look at the situation, we ought, instead of having a decade of denying too big to fail, to acknowledge it and have a receivership and intervention program that extends some of the concepts of the FDIC but goes beyond that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is, if you are insolvent, it is not a central bank issue—we are a liquidity provider—and therefore the government comes in.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But unlike the GSEs, everyone has to take some hit—the equity holders, certainly the preferred stockholders, also the subordinated-debt holders, and perhaps the senior ones—by assuming a certain amount of loss.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They would have immediate access to—pick a number—80 percent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The research would help us pick that number, and they can have access, but the rest becomes a subordinate-subordinate position after the liquidation so that you have still a sense of market discipline in play and you don’t get the system gaming it in that, if you know there’s a bailout coming, you buy the debt and sell the equity short to make a bundle.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think therein lie the distortions that are absolutely detrimental to the long- run health of the economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Regarding how we go forward, I think we are going to have many lessons from this.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Part of the problem has been very lax lending and, obviously now, weaknesses in some of the oversight.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Also a history of our reacting from a monetary policy point of view to ease quickly to try to take care of the problem and, therefore, to create a sense in the market of our support has raised some real moral hazard issues that we now need to begin to remedy as we look forward in dealing with future receiverships.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We are in a world of too big to fail, and as things have become more concentrated in this episode, it will become even more so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I certainly agree—and the Treasury Secretary and I have said publicly—that we need a strong, well-defined, ex ante, clear regime.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we have the problem now that we don’t have such a regime, and we’re dealing on a daily basis with these very severe consequences.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is a difficult problem.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think what we did with Lehman was the right thing because we did have a market beginning to play the Treasury and us, and that has some pretty negative consequences as well, which we are now coming to grips with.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think it’s too soon to know whether what we did with Lehman is right.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given that the Treasury didn’t want to put money in, what happened was that we had no choice.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But we took a calculated bet.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we have a run on the money market funds or if the nongovernment tri-party repo market shuts down, that bet may not look nearly so good.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think we did the right thing given the constraints that we had.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I hope we get through this week.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But I think it’s far from clear, and we were taking a bet, and I hope in the future we don’t have to be in situations where we’re taking bets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It does highlight the need to look at the tri-party repo market, look at the money market fund industry, and look at how they’re financing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There are a lot of lessons learned, but we shouldn’t be in a position where we’re betting the economy on one or two institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That is the situation we were in last weekend.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We did what we had to do, but I hope we will find a way to not get into this position again.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, it may surprise you that President Yellen and I agree, [laughter] at least with the recommendation, as I do with the majority.

speaker: FISHER
text: I also agree firmly with President Hoenig.

speaker: FISHER
text: David wanted to know a little more about Houston, so I will start out with that, and then I’ll quickly go to the policy matter.

speaker: FISHER
text: The storm devastated Galveston and Beaumont.

speaker: FISHER
text: Their combined population is 650,000.

speaker: FISHER
text: The population of the greater Houston area is 6.5 million.

speaker: FISHER
text: The damage to Houston was moderate.

speaker: FISHER
text: The overall effect on the Texas economy should be relatively mild.

speaker: FISHER
text: We still expect employment growth this year of 1½ percent or so, plus or minus, even though the storm really hit hard an area that accounts for 26 percent of our employment and 30 percent of our output.

speaker: FISHER
text: In terms of the national impact, I think it’s important to understand that the energy infrastructure took minor losses.

speaker: FISHER
text: The short-term functioning of that infrastructure is hampered by power losses and water problems.

speaker: FISHER
text: Gasoline prices have gone up because 3.9 million barrels a day, or roughly 22 percent of the U.S. refining capacity, has been shut down.

speaker: FISHER
text: By the way, that affects the spot market—I think that’s some of the reason you’ve seen this weakness recently—and maybe the near-term futures market.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you look at the gasoline price market, the gasoline price went up another 13 cents yesterday, but the near futures market is down 19 cents.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it reflects expectations that, once power is restored, the refineries will come back on line about a week later.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we will likely have a temporary bump-up in inflation due to the gas prices.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I think it is important to realize that this, unlike Katrina, didn’t shut down the Mississippi, and the effect on other commodity prices is likely not to be significant, with one exception.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you look, you’ll see that prices of soybeans and soybean oil have spiked recently.

speaker: FISHER
text: Clearly, the weather has an impact, but I think that’s more supply–demand imbalance— something that I’m watching carefully.

speaker: FISHER
text: The silver lining, if there is a silver lining to human tragedy, is probably twofold.

speaker: FISHER
text: One is, if you notice, that lumber prices are actually up this year, which is kind of odd in terms of lumber trading.

speaker: FISHER
text: Of course, lumber producers are probably pretty happy with the devastation in our state.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, Mexican laborers will be very happy if we let them into the country because the Hispanics build most of our buildings in the United States.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I would say that the storm should not have any effect on nor should it alter our preferred policy direction, and I would like to talk about that very quickly.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have been affected in my thinking about economic growth and inflation by what I’m seeing overseas.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do expect that we’re going to have less impetus from exports, which were significant in carrying our growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: Our numbers show that, and your numbers, David, show that, and all of our conversations have revolved around that.

speaker: FISHER
text: We were surprised on the upside by it.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now I think weakening economic growth elsewhere is likely to subdue that effect.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have also had an appreciation of the dollar.

speaker: FISHER
text: I dove deep in my anecdotal explorations with the majors and also with all supply companies.

speaker: FISHER
text: For whatever it’s worth, they are convinced that OPEC now has $100 rather than $70 as their benchmark.

speaker: FISHER
text: Most of them expect prices to slide down to somewhere in the $80 range.

speaker: FISHER
text: But over the longer term, whatever that term may be, we’re going to talk about $100-plus oil.

speaker: FISHER
text: Then, of course, many commodity prices are off their peaks.

speaker: FISHER
text: They have retraced significantly—some entirely.

speaker: FISHER
text: That said, in my anecdotal interchanges, I am still hearing about the likelihood, as I think President Pianalto mentioned, that people are seeking to preserve their margins.

speaker: FISHER
text: They’ve been stung for many years, and I’ll just give you one case because I think it tells us something.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you talk to the CEO of Wal-Mart USA, what they are pricing to be on their shelf six to eight months from now has an average price increase of 10 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, of course, you might have this reversed as we go through time.

speaker: FISHER
text: My biggest disappointment, incidentally, was that the one bakery that I’ve gone to for thirty years, Stein’s Bakery in Dallas, Texas, the best maker of not only bagels but also anything that has Crisco in it, [laughter] has just announced a price increase due to cost pressures.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I do think we have a mitigation of inflation, and we also have a mitigation of the impetus to economic growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: As to the current financial predicament, I want to go back to a comment I made a long time ago.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is not the first for me.

speaker: FISHER
text: I like to tease President Stern about his maturity—I don’t go back to the Panic of 1890, but to Herstatt, 1974; New York City’s failure, 1975; 1987; and what happened in Japan.

speaker: FISHER
text: Incidentally, you see the same pictures repeated in every newspaper.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s always the trader holding his head or looking up at the board.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now it’s in color; it used to be black and white.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it comes from the same archive, and it is repeated throughout time.

speaker: FISHER
text: All of that reminds me—forgive me for quoting Bob Dylan—but money doesn’t talk; it swears.

speaker: FISHER
text: When you swear, you get emotional.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you blaspheme, you lose control.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think the main thing we must do in this policy decision today is not to lose control, to show a steady hand.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would recommend, Mr. Chairman, that we embrace unanimously—and I think it’s important for us to be unanimous at this moment—alternative B.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take about thirty minutes?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a couple of calls to make.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: See you at about 11:20.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we’re ready, we can reconvene.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In our forecast, we do show a downgrade in real activity in the near term since the August meeting.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Downside risks to the economy we see as still very considerable, and I would probably say that they really have increased quite a bit.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I’ll say a few more words about that.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I’ll also talk about the inflation front.

speaker: CUMMING
text: We have long thought that inflation in the medium term will moderate, and we’ve been taking some comfort from recent developments that have been cited already.

speaker: CUMMING
text: On the weaker economic outlook, we see the intensification of adverse growth coming from many things mentioned already: the unemployment rate increase and the likelihood that consumer spending is going to be negative.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I would put great stress also on indications that world demand is slowing abruptly, as Nathan mentioned.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I think that all three of these things are occurring in an environment in which we have massive correction, adjustment, structural change in autos, housing, and financial intermediation.

speaker: CUMMING
text: That adjustment is really interconnected—one has effects on the others.

speaker: CUMMING
text: As part of this—particularly in the financial sector, I would say—in our senior loan officer survey we’ve seen indications that, even as rates in, say, the mortgage markets start to ease a bit, nonprice terms may still be tightening.

speaker: CUMMING
text: President Pianalto talked about other areas in which borrowers are facing much tougher terms.

speaker: CUMMING
text: As financial institutions feel their capital is constrained—and there’s plenty of evidence that balance sheets are constrained across much of the financial sector—those kinds of nonprice rationing measures probably will become more evident.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Second, as we discussed earlier, we’ve seen that credit losses, which thus far have been largely confined to the financial sector and increasingly their shareholders, run some risk of spilling over to other kinds of investors, who to date really have not felt that impact, such as money market fund investors, as mentioned earlier.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In addition, the three big corrections that we have seen in autos, housing, and financial intermediation are not limited to the United States.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In particular, as you know, several G-10 countries are facing very difficult situations in their housing markets, not much different from us; and the financial intermediation adjustment is truly a global correction.

speaker: CUMMING
text: On the inflation side, as I mentioned, we have acknowledged that we’ve seen elevated rates of inflation.

speaker: CUMMING
text: But the recent developments—as we’ve seen in inflation expectations discussed earlier, in energy and other commodity prices, the unit labor cost developments that President Yellen discussed, and the year-over-year changes in import prices—are all pointing in the direction of some moderation of inflation and moderation of inflation expectations.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In particular, we have looked at inflation expectations as measured by financial markets and feel that the decline that we see in those expectations cannot be explained simply by the drop in energy prices and technical factors but look larger than that.

speaker: CUMMING
text: We would attribute that to indications, again, that global demand is slowing.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Coming into this meeting today, we favor alternative B. I would associate myself with the comments of President Stern and President Evans, that if we were, in fact, going to make a move today, it would be better to make a large move of 50 basis points.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that, even before the recent intensification of financial market turmoil, there were trends becoming increasingly evident over the summer, since late June, that suggested that the economy was on a substantially slower path than it had been before.

speaker: KOHN
text: Resource utilization was falling appreciably, and the expected downward path of inflation in the future had much better odds of occurring.

speaker: KOHN
text: Indeed, I think that the expected weakness in the economy and the financial markets are interacting.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have one of these feedback loops in play.

speaker: KOHN
text: There has been a lot of concern not only in the United States but in other countries as well, as I heard in Basel last weekend, about a spillover—that the problems were not confined to the mortgage markets but were spilling into the loan books of the banks.

speaker: KOHN
text: That was related to the weakening in economic activity and was tightening up credit conditions, which would, in turn, further weaken economic activity.

speaker: KOHN
text: So this feedback loop was at work certainly in the United States and was beginning to be felt a little more in other countries as well.

speaker: KOHN
text: Since late June we have come to know a couple of things a little better.

speaker: KOHN
text: One is that consumption is not immune to soft labor markets, increases in energy prices, declining housing wealth, and tighter borrowing conditions.

speaker: KOHN
text: Even if we can’t parse out the effects of each of these factors, consumption has weakened substantially.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have had three months in a row of declines in the retail control component and very weak auto sales.

speaker: KOHN
text: Although recent declines in oil prices will support disposable incomes and consumption, I think the other sources of restraint on households— declining house prices and tighter credit conditions—are more likely to intensify than to abate in coming quarters.

speaker: KOHN
text: Another thing we know is that businesses have not gotten ahead of their need to shed labor, and they continue to trim staff in response to actual and expected weakness in demand.

speaker: KOHN
text: The decline in employment shows no signs of abating.

speaker: KOHN
text: Initial claims are running more than 50,000 higher than they were at the end of June, and they have remained elevated past the time that the introduction of the temporary extended benefits should have been felt.

speaker: KOHN
text: The unemployment rate is already ¼ percentage point higher than anyone around this table predicted for the end of the year.

speaker: KOHN
text: The household survey, along with national income statistics, could be signaling greater softness in activity and higher output gaps than is evident in the GDP and spending data.

speaker: KOHN
text: Another thing we have learned, as Nathan emphasized, is that foreign economies have not decoupled from the United States, and their prospects have been revised down substantially.

speaker: KOHN
text: They’re absorbing the effects of weaker U.S. domestic demand on their exports, and growing risk aversion in financial markets is spreading abroad.

speaker: KOHN
text: The latter, the growing risk aversion, is beginning to have, as Chris Cumming was noting, effects on a number of emerging-market economies, where capital inflows show signs of abating or even reversing; and indicators of financial stress have risen as a consequence of all this.

speaker: KOHN
text: Because of the stronger dollar, we will be able to rely less on exports going forward than we did before.

speaker: KOHN
text: We never expected a rapid return to more normal financial market functioning, but the adjustment in the financial sector now looks to be more severe and to take longer than we thought before.

speaker: KOHN
text: Financial firms need to bolster profits to offset losses and track capital.

speaker: KOHN
text: They need to de- lever by reducing debt relative to equity.

speaker: KOHN
text: They need to consolidate, and above all, they need to protect themselves against the possibility of a run.

speaker: KOHN
text: All of this implies a prolonged period of very cautious lending and a high cost of capital for borrowers relative to benchmark interest rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: If the current severe financial situation persists, I think the flight to safety and liquidity could dry up credit to a broad array of all but the very safest borrowers and reduce asset prices with feedbacks on spending, and that feedback loop could intensify if these market conditions pertain.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that’s a substantial downside risk to the growth outlook.

speaker: KOHN
text: Not all news affecting spending has been negative.

speaker: KOHN
text: Capital goods orders have held up.

speaker: KOHN
text: The decline in interest rates and commodity prices that respond to the markdown in global growth will help support domestic demand, and actions to stabilize the GSEs are helping the mortgage market.

speaker: KOHN
text: Activity is more likely to stagnate than to decline.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think that we can be more certain than we were, say, at the end of June that the economy will move substantially away from our high employment objective over the next several quarters and that the downside risks to that are larger.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the inflation side, incoming data have been disappointing, a little worse than anticipated, perhaps suggesting greater pass-through.

speaker: KOHN
text: The rise in import prices at the beginning of the third quarter was higher than anticipated.

speaker: KOHN
text: But we’ve also learned over the last couple of months that oil and other commodity prices can go down as well as up.

speaker: KOHN
text: The drop in retail energy prices helped to reverse much of the run-up in inflation expectations at the household level and reduced inflation compensation in financial markets at least over the next five years.

speaker: KOHN
text: Weaker economies, along with lower commodity prices, are expected to reduce inflation in our trading partners, and that along with the dollar should lower import price inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: The broadest measures of labor compensation available through the second quarter continue to suggest no upward pressure on the pace of increases in nominal labor costs.

speaker: KOHN
text: Despite elevated headline inflation, surprisingly good growth of productivity is holding down unit labor costs.

speaker: KOHN
text: Taking all of this together, I think that, despite the incoming inflation data, we can have greater confidence in our forecast that inflation will decline late this year and run much lower in the next few years than in the past year or so, though the risks to that still lie on the upside until we actually see the decline in headline inflation persist.

speaker: KOHN
text: On policy, Mr. Chairman, I support alternative B, keeping the funds rate at 2 percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that, at least for now, is consistent with lower inflation and a slow return to full employment in the future over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to assess the effects of the financial turmoil.

speaker: KOHN
text: If asset price declines accelerate and the tightening of financial conditions is large and likely to be sustained, I would be open at some point in the future to a lowering of interest rates.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me do three things.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’ll talk first about a modal forecast but probably give it short shrift; second, about financial market conditions; and third, about policy.

speaker: WARSH
text: Working under the assumption that our modal forecast doesn’t look quaint a week from now, if the world were somehow to hew to a reasonably moderate view of how financial market conditions work going forward, personally I’d be a bit more optimistic than the Greenbook for the second half of ’08.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that the net export growth is likely to prove stickier than embedded in that forecast in spite of a stronger dollar and weaker global demand.

speaker: WARSH
text: But as we get to 2009 and 2010, I would actually be less rosy than the Greenbook.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t see real catalysts for the economy to normalize and to approach trendlike growth.

speaker: WARSH
text: Key uncertainties around financial markets, labor markets, and housing and, I think, broader macroeconomic uncertainties that I’ve discussed before in terms of trade policy, tax policy, and regulatory policy, would make the creep- back to potential slower than embedded in those forecasts.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the inflation front, I continue to be encouraged by the strength in the exchange value of the dollar and the work that is doing for us on import price inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m encouraged by the move down across a breadth of commodities—not just energy, metals, and food but really across the entire basket—but I’m still not ready to relinquish my concerns on the inflation front.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn now to financial market conditions.

speaker: WARSH
text: I have talked before about the financial architecture.

speaker: WARSH
text: I guess what we can say today with more confidence than I’ve been able to say before is that the dismemberment of the existing financial architecture has accelerated in the last few days and weeks, and we will very quickly look at business models, and industry will find new business models, we hope, to provide credit to the real economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: Financial markets have been testing financial institutions with weaker capital structures, uncertain management teams, and unsustainable business models.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the question before us today that’s hard to judge is whether financial markets are now to the point at which they are acting indiscriminately, testing all financial institutions regardless of capital structure or business model.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’d say that the evidence of the past twenty-four or forty-eight hours is still unclear.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we’ll have a greater clarity several days from now about whether markets are able to make the distinguishing judgments that we would count on.

speaker: WARSH
text: Look at the CDS spreads for the two remaining independent broker-dealers, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, which Bill referenced.

speaker: WARSH
text: Goldman Sachs’s CDS moved up another 190 or so this morning.

speaker: WARSH
text: They are up 340 in the last two days.

speaker: WARSH
text: Morgan Stanley’s are up 690.

speaker: WARSH
text: I wouldn’t want to say whether those numbers are right or wrong.

speaker: WARSH
text: It may be that the business model is a failing one—that is, wholesale funding is no longer practicable in the world that we’re now in.

speaker: WARSH
text: If the problems were confined to that part of the financial services industry, it would be tough and it would be ugly and, if you were a resident of New York, particularly painful.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I don’t think it would rise to the level that would force us to recalibrate monetary policy.

speaker: WARSH
text: But if, in fact, those losses end up being endemic to all financial institutions, even those with strong deposit bases and higher capital ratios, then we certainly would have to take that into consideration.

speaker: WARSH
text: The few that are trying to swim against this tide are flailing; and without extraordinary actions either by a consortium of their competitors or by the official sector, they’re likely to continue to fail.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think our efforts to date to protect the broader financial markets and the economy from knock-on effects in particular financial services sectors do seem to be helping to cushion the blow.

speaker: WARSH
text: But the prospect of some meaningful discontinuity and of some systemic risk remains real, and it’s hard for me to judge today whether that prospect is as low as we might have thought even some weeks ago.

speaker: WARSH
text: Ultimately, the question for the real economy is whether the emergence of this new financial architecture can come quickly enough to get credit markets to normalize.

speaker: WARSH
text: Is the suddenness of events in the last week going to accelerate the move toward a new financial architecture?

speaker: WARSH
text: Will the forces of creative destruction make that faster but ultimately bring credit back to these markets sooner?

speaker: WARSH
text: Are these forces so strong and overwhelming that all financial institutions will be hunkering down, clinging to an architecture that no longer works?

speaker: WARSH
text: That’s a question to which I don’t know the answer.

speaker: WARSH
text: A couple of more points on markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the work that was done over the past few days on Lehman Brothers should make us feel good in one respect.

speaker: WARSH
text: Market functioning seems to be working okay—by which I mean that the plumbing around their role in the tri-party repo business, due in part to the Fed’s actions, seems to be working.

speaker: WARSH
text: The backroom offices of these places are going crazy.

speaker: WARSH
text: There’s a lot of manual work being done.

speaker: WARSH
text: So they wouldn’t give it high marks.

speaker: WARSH
text: But it looks as though positions are being sorted out in a tough workmanlike way, and so that’s encouraging.

speaker: WARSH
text: Other than the CDS moves and the equity moves on the other broker-dealers, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, I don’t think that that is the real specter that’s casting some question over broader financial institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the Lehman situation, no matter what judgment we made this past weekend about whether or not to provide official-sector money, is not what is driving markets broadly outside of the investment banks.

speaker: WARSH
text: What’s driving the broader uncertainty are questions about institutions like AIG that were rated AAA, that were so strong that counterparties didn’t need collateral, and that were a certain bet to be a guarantor around stable value funds and all sorts of other products.

speaker: WARSH
text: If in a matter of weeks that AAA rating and that security could turn out to be worthless, then that would force institutions to evaluate two things.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, narrowly, how much AIG exposure do I have?

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, more broadly, if that’s AIG, what about the rest of the insurance companies?

speaker: WARSH
text: What about the rest of the financial institutions, which aren’t investment banks but are really representing the foundations of the U.S. financial system?

speaker: WARSH
text: So it is both those direct and indirect aspects that we have to try to understand as best we can.

speaker: WARSH
text: My own view is that the AIG question would be more financial devastation if these institutions turn out to be meaningfully insolvent but actually, in some ways, less market dislocation among intermediaries.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is, Lehman Brothers, Merrill Lynch, and Bear Stearns are touching and are in the middle of many more flows of data, and there are real losses being felt.

speaker: WARSH
text: But if an AAA company like AIG were really fundamentally insolvent, the direct losses to a range of institutions, particularly those that are not just wholesale institutions but are retail institutions, could be very significant.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t think we know the answer yet to the question of whether AIG speaks to a broader loss of confidence that could affect the foundations of the U.S. financial system.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn finally to policy, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: WARSH
text: I support alternative B and, based on some of the discussion from Presidents Lockhart and Stern, I’d make some simple suggestions that may strike a balance that acknowledges the concerns we have about financial markets but doesn’t put us in the position where we are inclined to lurch in one direction, which as some people suggested could create more uncertainty than we intend.

speaker: WARSH
text: My suggestion, Mr. Chairman, would be to take the first sentence from alternative A, paragraph 2—“strains in financial markets have increased significantly and labor markets have weakened further”—and make that the first sentence of alternative B.

speaker: WARSH
text: Then strike the second sentence of alternative B, because I think we’ve largely covered that.

speaker: WARSH
text: That order gives proper attention, it strikes me, to the financial market developments.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, in the assessment of risk, Mr. Chairman, if you look at the last sentence, I would suggest modifying that ever so slightly by inserting the word “closely” and making one other modification.

speaker: WARSH
text: So that last sentence would read, “The Committee will continue to monitor economic and financial developments closely and will act as needed to promote sustainable economic growth and price stability.” Also, if you think it’s acceptable, rather than saying “financial developments” maybe there we would say, “The Committee will continue to monitor economic and financial market developments closely.” Those would be my suggestions to try to strike that balance—that we are keenly focused on what’s going on, but until we have a better view of its implications, we are not going to act.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Since the last meeting, there have obviously been a number of flare-ups in the fires that have been burning in the financial markets—the GSEs and then certainly what’s come this past weekend and what’s likely to come over this week and into the future.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A number of people have mentioned things ranging from AIG to pressures on money market funds to some large financial institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There are some very large regional banks and a very large thrift that will be facing a lot of challenges as the uncertainties in the markets continue.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I won’t repeat what Governor Kohn said about the continuing pressures on the bank balance sheets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it is important to take into account that those pressures will be there going forward not only on U.S. institutions but also increasingly on international institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: No one has mentioned UBS yet, but that’s another institution about which there’s a lot of concern, and if you look at CDS quotes there, they are skyrocketing also.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Much as Governor Warsh said, I think that people are worried about what the next shoe to drop will be and whom we have to challenge.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Whom do we have to get more information about to make us feel comfortable?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If that suddenly becomes everyone, then of course the markets don’t function.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I just want to focus quickly on consumption and consumer credit markets and then on inflation, and then I’ll conclude.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have made some references to how consumers have acted in the past and whether they will continue to act this way.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In some sense the consumer has been on a marathon since the early 2000s, facing an incredible amount of shocks—a lot of contraction in 2001, significant declines in stock market wealth, September 11, corporate governance scandals, sustained job losses, and low real income growth.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Nonetheless, the consumer continued to consume.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But now the consumer seems to be flagging.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have perhaps a very modest effect of the stimulus, which obviously can lead to negative payback for the rest of the year—so a drag going forward as well as drags from housing and stock market wealth, continuing job losses, rising unemployment, and pressures on income.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Although many of these shocks were similar to ones that happened earlier in the decade, it seems that consumers do not have the same resilience now that they did at one point.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s not surprising that, after having run this marathon, they’re going to be a bit tired.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Part of it could also be the credit conditions that are putting much more pressure on them.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Just to give you an anecdotal report, but it’s from one of the largest providers of consumer credit in the economy.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: After stabilization basically through our FOMC meeting in August, we’ve seen some significant deterioration in delinquencies and in the performance of those who get into delinquencies—they roll right to full chargeoff much more rapidly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So we have seen not exactly a qualitative change but a significant deterioration.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, the ability to securitize credit cards has changed dramatically.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: After our having opened the window and the markets having opened up in the second quarter, they basically haven’t been able to do anything in the third quarter, and that’s before this weekend.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously that’s not going to be helping them.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Of course, there are some offsetting factors that can help the consumer.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The very significant decline in mortgage rates has led to quite a response, according to this very large provider of consumer credit in the United States.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The number of applications for mortgages, particularly for refis, has doubled over the last couple of weeks.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So people do respond to prices, and that can help to ease some of their income burdens.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, the reduction in energy prices and many food prices is helpful on that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But of course, what has been good news for U.S. consumers may not be good news for international consumers.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As a lot of people have mentioned, the rest of the world is seeing a very significant slowdown.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think the elevated commodity prices had helped to mask a lot of the underlying fiscal and structural problems in these economies, actually much like rising housing prices in the United States had masked the problems in underwriting standards and what was going on in the mortgage market.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I think there are going to be significant challenges in a lot of countries around the world.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The boost that we had earlier this year from the international sector is something we can’t rely on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On inflation, we’re heartened by some of the lower energy prices.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I want to relate one anecdote.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In a meeting at the OECD, the CEO of one of the largest private oil producers in the world was asked what reference price he used because obviously he has to make tens of billions of dollars of decisions on investment and so they thought here’s someone who would really have a good notion of what the price of oil would be going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Without hesitation the person responded, “$100, plus or minus $50.” That kind of uncertainty from someone who is really in the markets and making those kinds of decisions shows us that we have a reasonable degree of uncertainty in inflation pressures going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That said, I think the Greenbook forecast is where I would be also, although we’re at uncomfortably elevated levels now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There are a lot of reasons to believe that, although they may be even a bit more elevated in the coming quarter, there are likely forces to bring things back down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This is particularly credible in the context of both survey-based and market-based expectations being quite contained, the market-based expectations being at the low of the year or even over the last couple of years.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So this brings me to support alternative B for no change today.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On the statement, I do believe that some greater recognition of the stress would be valuable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it would be valuable to have something in the first sentence of paragraph 2 that focuses on the strains—perhaps just a single sentence about the strains—and then we can put the other pieces on consumption and housing into the next sentence.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is important in the final paragraph to leave our options open if we do see significant negative feedback effects so that we can make a move that wouldn’t be a shock to the markets but it also wouldn’t be something that the markets could bank on.

speaker: DUKE
text: I continue to focus on the traditional commercial bank structure.

speaker: DUKE
text: I looked at two large retail banks, three regional banks, and three community banks, and two things came out of this.

speaker: DUKE
text: First, capital is driving everything, and the amount of capital that the banks need is now being driven more by the analysts and the rating agencies than it is anything that the regulators are doing.

speaker: DUKE
text: The banks feel as though they have done everything they can do in terms of capital management.

speaker: DUKE
text: They’ve quit buying back stock.

speaker: DUKE
text: There is no more capital available in external markets—not common stock, not preferred, not anything.

speaker: DUKE
text: One bank did issue some preferred stock through its own networks and a common stock issue—interestingly sort of snuck it into the market.

speaker: DUKE
text: They dribbled it out in small amounts because they found that, as soon as the markets determined that they were going to need to issue capital, they started to short the stock, figuring they could buy it back.

speaker: DUKE
text: So they did almost a reverse stock buyback.

speaker: DUKE
text: The markets are fragile to dead.

speaker: DUKE
text: So what are they going to do?

speaker: DUKE
text: The only thing they can do is contract the balance sheet and not lend.

speaker: DUKE
text: Before I get to that, there was again discussion in several of the conversations about naked short selling.

speaker: DUKE
text: One bank reportedly had 103 percent of total outstandings in short interest, and that seemed odd to me.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I went and checked it this morning, and it turns out that it was not 103 percent.

speaker: DUKE
text: It was only 93 percent.

speaker: DUKE
text: But if you subtract out the stock that was owned by the officers and the directors, then it was over 100 percent.

speaker: DUKE
text: Another bank said that the rules in the disclosure that surround long positions have to be replicated somehow in short positions because they’re having just as much control over what happens in the fate and the management of the firm.

speaker: DUKE
text: So what are they doing in terms of credit?

speaker: DUKE
text: Any heavy uses of credit or predominant uses of credit are just not being done.

speaker: DUKE
text: This eliminates all commercial real estate.

speaker: DUKE
text: They’re actively trying to move that off their books.

speaker: DUKE
text: Participation loans, in which the participants get only the credit piece, are drying up.

speaker: DUKE
text: No bank has any interest in going back into residential construction lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: One large bank said they were approving only one-third of the consumer credit that they would have approved a year ago.

speaker: DUKE
text: The secondary market for jumbos for takeouts on commercial are nonexistent, and one bank told me that, with the current cost of capital and cost of funding, the breakeven spread for a loan was 400 basis points over LIBOR.

speaker: DUKE
text: That’s the new lending market, and I don’t see it getting any better until some capital is available.

speaker: DUKE
text: The credit quality side is actually a better story.

speaker: DUKE
text: First, except for residential real estate, it’s really still pretty good.

speaker: DUKE
text: C&I lending is holding up extremely well.

speaker: DUKE
text: In commercial real estate, again, outside of residential development, things are really looking pretty good.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some small retail centers are showing softness with the small storefronts; and in areas like Michigan, they’re worried about losing the anchor tenants.

speaker: DUKE
text: Other than that, everything is okay.

speaker: DUKE
text: The other consumer credit feels like a mild recession but, again, is normally cyclical.

speaker: DUKE
text: The bank-originated loans range from good—one institution had 39,000 loans with 44 past due—to performing similar to unsecured credit.

speaker: DUKE
text: The broker-originated loans, especially the later vintages, are 100 percent loss.

speaker: DUKE
text: Within the mortgages, the rate of acceleration in new past-dues has slowed down.

speaker: DUKE
text: About rejections, I asked them to project when the new delinquencies would be offset by the resolution of existing delinquencies, and they said somewhere between year-end 2008 and mid-2009.

speaker: DUKE
text: So we are moving through that process.

speaker: DUKE
text: The severity, however, continues to grow as housing prices decline.

speaker: DUKE
text: It does appear that the portfolio lenders are getting their arms around the collection and the loss-mitigation effort.

speaker: DUKE
text: They’re assigning resources, accountability, and priority.

speaker: DUKE
text: It looks as though they are finally set up to do a pretty good job on that, managing it on several fronts—the analysis of the issue, the early stage collection, contact, and loss mitigation—and actually assigning a permitted spend, if you will, to resolve the loan.

speaker: DUKE
text: Foreclosures are going to take a lot longer and are particularly affected by state law.

speaker: DUKE
text: Apparently in Florida it takes a year to get a property in foreclosure.

speaker: DUKE
text: So those foreclosures are going to happen over a fairly long period of time.

speaker: DUKE
text: I asked about a bottom, and they said they do feel as though they’re seeing bottoms in some markets—Ohio and coastal areas in California, although not inland.

speaker: DUKE
text: Las Vegas and Atlanta are overbuilding, but the in-migration will absorb it.

speaker: DUKE
text: Florida is a bottomless hole—speculation combined with insurance problems.

speaker: DUKE
text: In Arizona so much land was available that they can’t find a bottom there.

speaker: DUKE
text: Regarding lot inventory, a community banker in Omaha said they had seven years of inventory in terms of lots, which I thought was pretty startling until I read in the American Banker the same story in Atlanta and the same story in Orlando.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I think when residential development does resume, it will be to work out the lot inventory.

speaker: DUKE
text: Also, the phantom inventory is at least as large as the current inventory—phantom inventory being defined as people who want to sell but don’t want to sell in the current market.

speaker: DUKE
text: Asked to compare current credit metrics with those in the 1980s and 1990s, one contact said they peaked in 1988 at 5.8 percent nonperforming.

speaker: DUKE
text: Now they are at 1.66.

speaker: DUKE
text: I found a chart, and for the entire industry, nonperformers were 4 percent in 1991.

speaker: DUKE
text: They’re 1.2 percent right now.

speaker: DUKE
text: So the credit metrics are just nowhere near what they were in the S&L crisis for the industry.

speaker: DUKE
text: I came out of that really believing that, if we are going to do something, we need to address the availability of capital to commercial banks but we should leave the bad loans in the banks because they’re getting to the point where the portfolio lenders are doing a good job of working through these loans.

speaker: DUKE
text: To try to take them out and put them into another structure, we would just have to replicate that whole gearing-up process.

speaker: DUKE
text: I don’t necessarily think that’s the case with the servicers, particularly the servicers of private-label mortgages.

speaker: DUKE
text: That’s something on which I know we’ve done some research here, and I want to investigate that a bit more to see if there’s something to be known there.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of the policy, I, too, would favor alternative B with some change in the language to paragraph 2.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you very much, and thanks, everyone, for very helpful comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me try to summarize, and I will just make some comments, and then we can turn to the statement and policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The group indicated, of course, that economic growth has slowed and looks to be quite sluggish in the second half.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I didn’t hear a great deal of change in the general profile, with most people still viewing growth as being slow in the near term but perhaps recovering somewhat in 2009.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But obviously there is a lot of uncertainty surrounding that judgment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The ongoing problems in housing and the financial system are, of course, the downside risks to growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Another factor, which is becoming more relevant, is the slowing global economy, which together with the stronger dollar may mean that U.S. export growth will be somewhat less.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Despite the tax rebate, consumer spending seems likely to be weak in the near term, reflecting a variety of factors that we noted before, including housing and equity wealth, credit conditions, and particularly perhaps the ongoing weakness in the labor market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The labor market is deteriorating, with unemployment up, although UI programs may play some role in the unemployment rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is somewhat difficult to predict the peak of the unemployment rate, given the upward momentum we are seeing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Declines in energy prices, however, will improve real incomes and help consumer sentiment—so that is a potentially positive factor.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The housing sector continues to be the central concern in the economy, in both the real and the financial sides.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are no clear signs of stabilization, although obviously regional conditions vary considerably.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The government action regarding the GSEs has lowered mortgage rates and may be of some assistance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit conditions have tightened, though, in other areas as well, including nonresidential construction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Firms are continuing to struggle with weaker demand, higher uncertainty, and high costs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Manufacturing has been relatively stable to weaker, but we had at least one report of a survey that in the medium term the outlook is looking a little better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inventories appear to be relatively well managed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit conditions for business vary, but there are indications that some firms are finding it very difficult to attract capital.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial markets received a lot of attention around the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Conditions clearly have worsened recently, despite the rescue of the GSEs, the latest stressor being the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers and other factors such as AIG.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Almost all major financial institutions are facing significant stress, particularly difficulties in raising capital, and credit quality is problematic, particularly in residential-related areas.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One member noted that it is not evident that markets are clearly differentiating between weaker and stronger firms at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Deleveraging is continuing, and securitization markets are moribund.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit terms and conditions are quite tight and may be a significant drag on the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, the medium- term implications of the recent increases in financial stress for the economy are difficult to assess.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We may have to wait for some time to get greater clarity on the implications of the last week or so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the inflation front, recent core and headline numbers have been high, reflecting earlier increases in the prices of energy and raw materials.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are positive factors, including the significant intermeeting declines in the prices of oil and other commodities, which, if maintained, would bring headline inflation down rather notably by the end of the year or next year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The dollar has also strengthened.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Generally speaking, inflation expectations, though noisy, have improved.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have seen a decline in TIPS breakevens and some decline in survey expectations as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it was noted that the five-by-five TIPS breakeven remains above a level consistent with long-term price stability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nominal wage growth has remained subdued so far, slack is increasing, productivity has been strong, and therefore, unit labor costs are well controlled.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, all of these factors are positive in terms of a better inflation picture going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, recent declines notwithstanding, the cumulative increases in commodity prices over the past year or so do remain large, and there is some evidence that these cost increases are being passed through into core prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Commodity prices are extremely volatile, which makes inflation very difficult to forecast and makes the inflation outlook, therefore, quite uncertain.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Wages could also begin to rise more quickly as the economy strengthens.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For all these reasons, inflation risks are still in play and remain a concern for the Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some participants reiterated their concern that maintaining rates too low for too long risks compromising our credibility and stimulating inflation over the medium run.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is a very quick survey of the comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any comments or questions?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let me just make a few comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Personally, I see the prospects for economic growth in the foreseeable future as quite weak, notwithstanding the second quarter’s strength.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think what we saw in the recent labor reports removes any real doubt that we are in a period that will be designated as an official NBER recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unemployment rose 1.1 percentage points in four months, which is a relatively rapid rate of increase.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The significance of that for our deliberations is, again, that there does seem to be some evidence that, in recession regimes, the dynamics are somewhat more powerful and we tend to see more negative and correlated innovations in spending equations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that we are in for a period of quite slow growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is confirmed by what we are seeing in consumption, which probably would be quite negative if it weren’t for the remainder of the fiscal stimulus package.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other components of demand are, likewise, quite weak.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are all familiar with the housing situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some other factors that were supportive in Q2 are weakening—a number of people have noted the export growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Actually, it is net exports—which is important—not just exports, and we are seeing both slowing growth in exports and some forecast of increased growth in imports.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A factor that we haven’t talked about much is the fiscal side.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That has been supportive and may be less supportive going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Generally speaking, though, I do think—and I have said this for a long time—that the credit effects will be important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They operate with a lag.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is very difficult to judge the lag.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But my strong sense is that they are still some distance from their peak; that they will begin to be felt outside of housing, in nonresidential construction, for example, in consumer spending, and in investment; and that this is going to be independent of last week’s financial developments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that is going to be a major drag, probably well into next year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are a few positives, which give some hope of some improvement next year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have talked about energy and commodity prices as they relate to inflation, but of course, the decline in energy and commodity prices is also a plus for consumers and raises real incomes and would be supportive of sentiment, as we have already seen.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are a few positive indications here and there on the housing market, a few glimmers of stability, particularly in some regions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the GSE stabilization is going to be very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has already lowered mortgage rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It suggests that there will be a market for securitized mortgages, and I think that is positive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if I wanted to outline an optimistic scenario, it would involve stronger indications of stabilization in housing, which in turn would feed into more confidence in the financial sector and would lead over time to improvement in the broader economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think that financial conditions are a major concern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The situation right now is very uncertain, and we are not by any means away from significant systemic risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Even if we avoid a major systemic event, the increase in risk aversion, the pullback from all counterparties, the deleveraging, the sale of assets—all of these things are going to continue for some time and are going to make the financial sector very stressed, which obviously will have effects on the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have been grappling with the question I raised for President Lacker, and I would be very interested in hearing other views either now or some other time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The ideal way to deal with moral hazard is to have in place before the crisis begins a well-developed structure that gives clear indications in what circumstances and on what terms the government will intervene with respect to a systemically important institution.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have found ourselves, though, in this episode in a situation in which events are happening quickly, and we don’t have those things in place.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t have a set of criteria, we don’t have fiscal backstops, and we don’t have clear congressional intent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in each event, in each instance, even though there is this sort of unavoidable ad hoc character to it, we are trying to make a judgment about the costs—from a fiscal perspective, from a moral hazard perspective, and so on—of taking action versus the real possibility in some cases that you might have very severe consequences for the financial system and, therefore, for the economy of not taking action.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Frankly, I am decidedly confused and very muddled about this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it is very difficult to make strong, bright lines given that we don’t have a structure that has been well communicated and well established for how to deal with these conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think there is some chance—it is not yet large, but still some chance—that we will in fact see a much bigger intervention at the fiscal level.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is tempted to argue that by doing more earlier you can avoid even more later, but of course that is all contingent and uncertain.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we will collectively do our best to deal with these very stressful financial conditions, which I don’t think will be calm for some time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to inflation, I accept the many caveats around the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have to say that I think, on net, inflation pressures are less worrisome now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The last two meetings have been very positive in that respect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The declines in energy and commodity prices are quite substantial.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Natural gas, for example, has reversed all of its gains of the year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Steel scrap is down 40 percent in two months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are seeing many other indications that commodity prices really have come down quite a bit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The dollar’s increase is also quite striking, and we have talked about wages, TIPS, and other factors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think overall I see at least the near-term inflation risk as considerably reduced.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do agree, though, with the points that were made that we may well see pressure on core inflation for a while longer, despite this morning’s reasonably benign number.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The increases in commodity costs, although they have been partially reversed, have not been entirely reversed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Certainly over the last year to year and a half there is still a net substantial increase, which will show up as firms begin to pass through those costs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is also the case, of course, that we have seen a very, very sharp movement in commodity prices and the dollar.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, there is no logical reason why that couldn’t be reversed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Clearly, one problem we face is that the uncertainty about forecasting commodity prices is so large that it makes our forecasting exercises extraordinarily uncertain and means that we need to be somewhat more careful than we otherwise would be if we were back in the days of the Texas Railroad Commission, when we knew the price of oil six months in advance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t have that privilege anymore.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think core inflation may be elevated for a while.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It may take a while for inflation to moderate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Everything I say is contingent on the dollar and commodity trends not being strongly reversed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But if those things are not reversed, I think we will see some improvement in inflation in the near term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I also agree with those who say that, when the time comes, we do need to be prompt at removing accommodation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is just as much a mistake to move too late and allow inflation, and perhaps even financial imbalances, to grow as it is to move too early and be premature in terms of assuming a recovery.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that is a very difficult challenge for us going forward, and I acknowledge the importance of that, which a number of people have noted.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is a quick summary of my views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just turn briefly, then, to policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do we have the statement?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I talked with Governor Warsh, and he gave me now during the break some of those suggestions he made.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As they fit closely with other things that people said around the table, we have made a version here that incorporates them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll discuss that in just a minute.3 First, as a number of people have said, let me just say that I thought the memo that the staff prepared over the intermeeting period was extraordinarily helpful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have been debating around the table for quite a while what the right indicator of monetary policy is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is it the federal funds rate?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is it some measure of financial stress?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the only answer is that the right measure is contingent on a model.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As President Lacker and President Plosser pointed out, you have to have a model and a forecasting mechanism to think about where the interest rate is that best achieves your objectives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It was a very useful exercise to find out, at least to some 3 The statement referred to here is appended to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: BERNANKE
text: extent, how the decline in the funds rate that we have put into place is motivated.

speaker: BERNANKE
