text: In particular, the financial conditions do appear to be important both directly and indirectly—directly via the spreads and other observables that were put into the model and indirectly in terms of negative residuals in spending equations and the like.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The recession dynamics were also a big part of the story.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I hope that what this memo does for us—again, I think it’s extraordinarily helpful—is to focus our debate better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As President Plosser pointed out, we really shouldn’t argue about the level of the funds rate or the level of the spreads.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should think about the forecast and whether our policy path is consistent with achieving our objectives over the forecast period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am sympathetic to the general view taken by the staff, which argues that those recession dynamics and financial restraints are important, that we are looking at slow growth going forward, and that inflation is likely to moderate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Based on those assumptions, I think that our policy is looking actually pretty good.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To my mind, our quick move early this year, which was obviously very controversial and uncertain, was appropriate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Their analysis also suggests that the amount of insurance that we have is perhaps limited, given that they take a risk-neutral kind of modeling approach.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Having said that, I think they have also clearly set out the conditions and the framework in which we can debate going forward exactly where we should be going.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To the extent that those around the table disagree with the model or with the projection, then that is the appropriate way, it seems to me, to address our policy situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, again, I do very much appreciate that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It helped me think about the policy situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I said, I think our aggressive approach earlier in the year is looking pretty good, particularly as inflation pressures have seemed to moderate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Overall I believe that our current funds rate setting is appropriate, and I don’t really see any reason to change.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the one hand, I think it would be inappropriate to increase rates at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t have enough information.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is not enough pressure on inflation at this juncture to do that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, cutting rates would be a very big step that would send a very strong signal about our views on the economy and about our intentions going forward, and I think we should view that step as a very discrete thing rather than as a 25 basis point kind of thing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should be very certain about that change before we undertake it because I would be concerned, for example, about the implications for the dollar, commodity prices, and the like.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is a step we should take only if we are very confident that that is the direction in which we want to go.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore my recommendation to the Committee—and I will open it up for comment in a moment—is to keep the funds rate at its current level.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I listened very carefully to the conversation around the table in terms of the statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it was President Lockhart, President Stern, and Governor Warsh, among others, who talked about strengthening the language on financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the draft statement that you have in front of you is an attempt to make that change.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has two changes relative to existing alternative B.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, as Governor Warsh suggested, it reverses the first two sentences and so focuses in the first sentence on “Strains in financial markets have increased significantly and labor markets have weakened further,” and then the rest of it is basically the same as it was.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other change, which is in the last paragraph in the risk assessment, is pretty small, but it is probably worth considering.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The word “closely” has been added to suggest, obviously, that we understand that the situation is changing rapidly and that we are carefully following conditions as they evolve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Kevin, we took your word “market” there—what was the rationale for it?

speaker: WARSH
text: My sense is—and this is certainly open for discussion—that we want the focus to be that we are really watching market developments closely.

speaker: WARSH
text: We are not trying to monitor the broader economy, which we might not be able to measure too much.

speaker: WARSH
text: I will admit that we have “economic and financial markets,” with “closely” modifying both of them, but the idea was to put the focus on the market side to a slightly greater extent than we normally do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that’s useful, although I do note that, all else being equal, there’s a slight barrier for making any change, and that one word is a change.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am sort of indifferent about this, but I don’t want to forget what Governor Duke was talking about.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s not just financial markets; it’s financial developments.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are also talking about the internal dynamics of what is happening in the banking system and the credit contraction you spoke of.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we lead off with financial markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t want people to think we are focusing only on markets—Governor Warsh, I would disagree on that point.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s a minor disagreement, but I think it is overkill.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me open it up for any other comments on the statement or the policy action.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is really just a question.

speaker: EVANS
text: What type of reaction do we think will be engendered by inserting “closely”?

speaker: EVANS
text: Everybody understands that we monitor financial developments very carefully.

speaker: EVANS
text: So we are bringing attention to this.

speaker: EVANS
text: Will there be a presumption that we are likely to do something intermeeting or something like that?

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not saying that is wrong, but it is a question.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would say that the markets will take it as a statement that is conditional on what happens in markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If markets get sufficiently bad, if there is some threshold of deterioration, that can potentially provoke an intermeeting move is the way I think they would take it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Brian, would you agree with that?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The fact that the first sentence of the risk assessment has a parallel treatment of the upside and downside risks may communicate a bit the sense that you are not ready to ease immediately.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will take a vote on it, if necessary.

speaker: LACKER
text: I echo President Evans’s concern.

speaker: LACKER
text: My recollection is—and I haven’t consulted the record recently—under your predecessor there was some phrasing like “watch market developments closely” that came to be widely understood as a signal of an intermeeting move.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it was “monitor closely.” Is that what it was?

speaker: LACKER
text: “Monitor closely” or some language like that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yes, “monitor closely.” Maybe you’re right.

speaker: LACKER
text: Yes, and that gives me pause.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then, about “market”—like a lot of economists, I am willing to construe the word “market” very broadly to include intermediation mechanisms of all types and the market for commercial credit in, you know, Dillon, South Carolina.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I am not sure that market participants are going to take it that broadly.

speaker: LACKER
text: They are going to take it in the sense of markets in traded financial instruments and organized exchanges and such.

speaker: LACKER
text: I just wonder if they are going to interpret it too closely as Wall Street.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the sentiment over here on this side is that nobody thinks “market” is important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s get rid of “market.” We’ll discuss “closely.” President Plosser.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think “market” may be construed too narrowly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We don’t really mean it that way, I don’t think.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other comments, suggestions, or thoughts?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I do think it is the delta, so it is the change.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: By including “closely,” I think the markets are going to look very closely at that change, and they are going to think that we are clearly trying to convey something with that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I just think we have to make sure that we feel comfortable in doing so.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Certainly some people have suggested that they would be happy to move 50 basis points if they saw the markets moving, but I do think that that one particular word will get a lot of attention.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Not that it should, but I think it is going to be focused on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Just as at one point we used the word “yet,” and that got an enormous amount of attention.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: And this has two syllables.

speaker: FISHER
text: Unless you are from the south.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The sad thing is that Governor Kroszner is right.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have seventeen people debating over this word, and it actually does matter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Does anyone else want to weigh in?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think my sense is that there should be a barrier, a bit of a hurdle, to changing; so I am leaning toward sticking with what we have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would that be okay, Governor Warsh, do you think?

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me ask Brian and Bill.

speaker: WARSH
text: Brian, without “closely,” how do you think the markets will react to that?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That you are not particularly ready to change your stance of policy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the expectation going in is, for most people, that you are not prepared to ease today, but if things got really dark from here you would.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the question is, How do you convey that with the right word?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You need something in between “closely” and—

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the sentiment we are trying to suggest is watchful waiting.

speaker: WARSH
text: We are not indifferent, we are not clueless, we are paying attention, but we are not predisposed.

speaker: KOHN
text: My suggestion was to substitute “carefully” for “closely.” I agree that “monitor closely” had this other connotation, but I think we should be seen as paying more attention than usual.

speaker: KOHN
text: There might be another alternative.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: “The Committee will carefully evaluate economic and financial market developments.” That means you are on the case.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, it is not an analytical thing we are doing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are just watching closely.

speaker: LACKER
text: Including “closely,” what does that imply about the opposite?

speaker: LACKER
text: I mean, are we going to be able to take that out?

speaker: WARSH
text: Well, we have done things like “in a timely manner” and other kinds of phraseology.

speaker: LACKER
text: Yes, but this is an adjective.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we take it out, can we use the phrase without it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What we have done in the past is basically just use a new phrase.

speaker: LACKER
text: So that means we have to throw this phrase out.

speaker: WARSH
text: Mr. Chairman, I would support “carefully.”

speaker: EVANS
text: Just to be clear, we have gone a long way just now from its being a semantic discussion to whether or not the Committee wants to hint at the possibility of a near- term action.

speaker: EVANS
text: I do not have a problem with that.

speaker: EVANS
text: In fact, in my comments I suggested that the resolution of uncertainty might improve in the next couple of weeks, but that seems to be the principal issue here, which I don’t really recall us discussing in as much detail as we just have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But there is another issue, which I think is the thing we’re concerned about and which motivates the change in alternative B, paragraph 2.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t want the world to feel that we are not awake, that we are not paying attention.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We know that very unusual things are going on in the financial markets; and we are prepared, maybe not through monetary policy but through whatever mechanism is necessary, to address that.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I fully support that sentiment, and if you find the right wording that captures it, that’s fine with me.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As long as we are throwing monkey wrenches into the language, I think we do signal our concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In paragraph 2, we put the very first sentence, which says, “Strains in financial markets have increased significantly.” So we have acknowledged that at the very top of this statement.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So there is no going back on that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am a little concerned about what moving back “closely” means.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Another alternative that I’ll throw out would be, rather than use “closely,” to say that “the Committee will continue to monitor economic and financial developments.” SEVERAL.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That’s what it said last time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We are monitoring these things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is this the FOMC statement dictionary we are going to?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is this the code book?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just ask for a straw vote: “closely,” no “closely,” or “carefully.” Do we want “carefully”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is “carefully” more acceptable to those who are concerned?

speaker: MR.KOHN
text: It’s less of a code word.

speaker: MR.KOHN
text: The intention was to loosen it up a bit but not revert to those code words that nearly promise intermeeting action.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We make note of this in the lexicon of FOMC terminology.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The semiotics class will begin as soon as the— All right.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we are changing the last part of that sentence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are striking the word “market” and changing “closely” to “carefully.” Any other comments or thoughts on the substance, sizzle, or marketing?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Or as Rick would say, “moychandising”— but he’s not here.

speaker: DANKER
text: I will be reading the directive from the Bluebook and the statement that was just circulated.

speaker: DANKER
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: DANKER
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with maintaining the federal funds rate at an average of around 2 percent.” Then the statement is as it was handed out, except the last sentence reads, “The Committee will monitor economic and financial developments carefully and will act as needed to promote sustainable economic growth and price stability.” Chairman Bernanke Yes First Vice President Cumming Yes Governor Duke Yes President Fisher Yes Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes President Pianalto Yes President Plosser Yes President Stern Yes Governor Warsh Yes

text: The next meeting is October 28 and 29.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Lunch will be available in the anteroom.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: While we have lunch, Laricke Blanchard will provide us with an update on congressional developments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you all very much.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We received requests from members for more time at this meeting to discuss the economic situation and our policy response.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So as you know, we postponed the special presentations on inflation—my apologies to the presenters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will come back to that at the appropriate time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What we are going to do instead is to have three rounds of briefings today and tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are going to start in the first round with Bill Dudley and his usual presentation on open market operations, followed by Nathan Sheets on the swaps proposals that you have been informed about, and then Bill Bassett will give a supplementary briefing on financial markets to complete that round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then we’ll have Q&A at that point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will then turn to the economic situation and hear from Norm Morin on the nonfinancial economy and Linda Kole on the international economy and from Brian Madigan on our projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then we will have another round of questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Tomorrow at lunch, after the close of the formal meeting, we will have some additional briefings on the TARP (troubled asset relief program), on the FDIC program, and on the supervisory and regulatory implications of that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we hope to make this a very informative two days, and we hope to have plenty of interaction and conversation about our broad policy response to these very difficult times.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me start, then, by turning to Bill Dudley.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Today my attention will be narrower than usual, given the briefings by Bill Bassett and Linda Kole that will follow covering the broader developments in the equity, fixed income, and foreign exchange markets in the United States and abroad, which have been considerable over the past six weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I will focus on three topics: (1) the impact of our new facilities and other government initiatives on market function, (2) the consequences of the expansion of these facilities on our balance sheet and our ability to hit the federal funds rate target over time, and (3) the travails of the hedge fund community and how 1 The materials used by Mr. Dudley are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: this could potentially add to market dysfunction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I will be referring to the chart package that should be in front of you.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you all know, the Lehman bankruptcy led to sharp outflows from prime money market mutual funds into Treasury-only funds (exhibit 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The result was a collapse in Treasury bill yields (exhibit 2).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the same time, the cost of financing Treasury securities via repo fell sharply—this is illustrated in exhibit 3 by the drop in the overnight general collateral (GC) repo rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This increased the incentive for Treasury traders to short Treasury securities that were already hard to obtain because the effective cost of borrowing such securities is determined by the level of the GC repo rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, Treasury fails, which represent Treasury securities that are not delivered as promised to their buyers, soared.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Treasury fails were also exacerbated by the withdrawal from the securities lending market of some large holders of Treasuries, including some major foreign central banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although Treasury yields fell sharply and Treasury bills were in great demand, the rise in fails resulted in a sharp diminution of trading and liquidity in the Treasury securities market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The fact that there are severe market-functioning problems in the asset class that is in greatest demand—Treasuries—underscores the scope and severity of the markets’ broader dysfunction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the same time, the outflows from prime money market funds led to a sharp drop in the demand for commercial paper, a significant rise in commercial paper rates, and a shortening of commercial paper maturities (exhibits 4 and 5).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Term bank funding spreads rose sharply, with the one-month and three-month LIBOR–OIS spreads increasing to levels that make the earlier peaks look like modest speed bumps (exhibits 6 and 7).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Lehman bankruptcy caused counterparty risk concerns to intensify.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the Lehman bankruptcy disrupted a number of markets because participants in these markets were uncertain how to adjust their long- and short- position exposures that offset their open positions with Lehman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The result was a sharp drop in the willingness of counterparties to engage with one another, especially at term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Essentially, the result was a massive coordination problem that has led to a very unattractive equilibrium.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would put it this way: “I won’t lend to you even though I think you’re okay because I am not sure others will lend to you either.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I need some assurance that others will lend to you in order to have some assurance I can get my money back if I need it.” Even though it has been in the interest of all parties to engage, no party has been willing to go first.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In response, the Federal Reserve dramatically expanded its programs of liquidity support.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The size of each TAF auction has been raised to $150 billion—the same size as the entire TAF program just six weeks ago.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fixed-rate tender dollar auctions were implemented by the BoE, the BoJ, the ECB, and the SNB.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The asset-backed commercial paper money market mutual fund liquidity facility (AMLF) and the commercial paper funding facility (CPFF) were implemented, and plans for a money market investor funding facility (MMIFF) were announced.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Federal Reserve and other central banks stepped forward to engage in transactions with a broad range of bank and, in the case of the Fed, nonbank counterparties.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The hope, of course, is that this willingness to engage will reduce rollover risk and therefore encourage others to re-engage with their counterparties.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At least for now, the escalation in the size of the TAF auctions appears to have been sufficient to satisfy the demand for dollar funds in the United States.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 8, the first two auctions of $150 billion have been slightly undersubscribed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Currently, about $300 billion of TAF credit is outstanding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Demand for dollar funding in Europe has increased sharply even though the cost is much higher than in our TAF auctions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Whereas the two most recent TAF auctions were stopped out at the OIS rate, which is the minimum bid rate, the foreign fixed-rate tender operations have been conducted at a rate of OIS plus 100 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 9 and 10, swap outstandings have grown to nearly $500 billion currently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The ECB swap size is currently about $280 billion, more than half the total amount of swaps outstanding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The amount of outstanding swaps is likely to climb sharply when the first 84-day fixed-rate tender operations are conducted in Europe next week.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The CPFF facility is another important element in the Fed’s program of liquidity escalation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you know, this facility provides a backstop for domestic issuers of A1/P1-rated commercial paper.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Issuers can sell commercial paper to the facility at three-month term for an effective cost of OIS plus 200 basis points for nonfinancial and financial issuers and OIS plus 300 basis points for asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This facility complements the AMLF, which lends funds to banks at the primary credit facility rate against the ABCP purchased from money market mutual funds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yesterday was the first day that the CPFF was open for business, and a number of borrowers issued commercial paper to the facility totaling more than $50 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the close of business last week, 79 issuers had registered to use the facility, paying 10 basis points, or $580 million, to cover the potential issuance of commercial paper.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The 10 basis point fee provides a little equity to get the program off and running.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, the most recent facility, the money market investor funding facility, was announced last week.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This facility will provide liquidity to five conduits that will purchase commercial paper and certificates of deposit of designated issuers from 2a-7 money market mutual funds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It will likely be several more weeks before this facility is operational.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The escalation in the provision of liquidity and some of the other initiatives I will discuss shortly have led to a grudging improvement in the interbank funding markets and in the commercial paper market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Reviewing the earlier exhibits, most term funding spreads have narrowed, but the improvement is modest relative to the earlier deterioration.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is unclear at this stage whether the modest extent of improvement reflects the limited ability of additional capacity and breadth in terms of liquidity provision to restore confidence, especially at a time that the macroeconomic outlook has deteriorated globally, or whether it will just take time for these liquidity facilities to restore confidence and some semblance of normality to the money markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The expansion of the Fed’s liquidity provisions has been accompanied by escalations on two other fronts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, the FDIC announced a bank funding guarantee program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the terms and conditions of this program have not yet been finalized, the program is likely to guarantee most of the new senior debt obligations of participating depository institutions and their associated holding companies up to a cap of 125 percent of the maturing obligations through June 30, 2009.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Importantly, new interbank funding will be covered.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: How this affects the federal funds market remains to be seen.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the Treasury has committed $250 billion of funds from the TARP program to inject as preferred stock into the banking system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Nine large banks announced two weeks ago that they will accept $125 billion of preferred stock investment from the Treasury.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Over the past few days, the Treasury announced that an additional $35 billion of capital has been committed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The FDIC guarantee announcement and the TARP capital infusion have been effective in shoring up confidence in the major U.S. banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 11 and 12, credit default swap spreads for most major U.S. financial institutions have narrowed sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the guarantee of the senior debt of depository institutions and their associated holding companies has generated some unintended consequences for those firms not covered by these guarantees.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, the credit default swap spreads for major nonbank financials have narrowed less than those for the banks (exhibit 13).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the funding costs for the GSEs have climbed, especially for short-term discount note issuance.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The funding costs for Fannie and Freddie for both long-term and short-term debt are shown in exhibits 14, 15, and 16.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, the fear that funds would flow out of prime money market funds back into bank assets guaranteed by the FDIC has not been realized—at least not yet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The expansion of the Fed’s facilities and the open-ended nature of the fixed-rate tender dollar operations by the foreign central banks that we are funding by swaps have led to rapid expansion of our balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 17 provides a snapshot of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet at different times before and during the crisis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: During the first 13 months, the size of our balance sheet was little changed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We accommodated our liquidity programs mainly by selling Treasury securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: During the next stage, which began around the time of the Lehman bankruptcy filing, we expanded our balance sheet but drained the reserve additions primarily by having the Treasury issue supplemental financing program bills and placing the proceeds on our balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, the capacity to continue to drain reserves via SFP bills was unlikely to be a long-term solution because the Treasury would ultimately be constrained by the debt limit ceiling.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The passage of the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008 granted the Federal Reserve the authority to pay interest on reserves immediately.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This was very important because it meant that we could expand our balance sheet size by unsterilized reserve additions but at the same time keep the federal funds rate from crashing to zero by paying a positive interest rate on holdings of excess reserves.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Further rapid balance sheet expansion appears inevitable as the takedown from the TAF auctions and the fixed-rate tenders expands further and as our new facilities, such as the CPFF and MMIFF, begin operation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the estimates shown for year-end in exhibit 17 are indicative—the actual size will be driven by the use of our various liquidity facilities—it does seem likely that the Federal Reserve System’s balance sheet will grow very rapidly through year-end.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are now nearly three weeks into the new interest-on-reserves regime, which was implemented on October 9.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you know, the Board of Governors initially set the spread between the target federal funds rate and the rate paid on excess reserves at 75 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Policymakers erred on the size of a wide margin given unsettled market conditions and the lack of experience with the new regime, recognizing that the spread could be reduced if the federal funds rate traded soft relative to the target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 18, despite the payment of interest on reserves, the federal funds rate has continued to trade soft relative to the target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, the Board narrowed the spread to 35 basis points with the start last Thursday of the second reserve maintenance period under the interest-on-reserves regime.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is too soon to assess the effect of the narrower spread on our ability to push the federal funds rate back up to the target because the interest rate paid on reserves is based upon the lowest target federal funds rate during the reserve maintenance period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So currently it is hard to separate the impact of the narrower spread on the effective federal funds rate from the expectations for further cuts in the target federal funds rate that might occur at this meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There are two complications in fixing the interest-on-reserves spread at a level consistent with the target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, some of the GSEs, which hold balances at the Fed, are not allowed to earn interest on their balances.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Thus they have to sell federal funds to banks that, in turn, hold the funds and are paid the interest-on- reserves rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, some banks have also been selling federal funds below the interest-on-reserves rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We expect this to diminish over time as they gain more experience with the new regime.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, other factors, such as concern with their overall leverage ratios, could cause this phenomenon to persist.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, there has been a significant amount of federal funds rate trading below the interest-on-reserves rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is illustrated in exhibit 19, in which the circles are sized to reflect the amount of trading at a particular rate level.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This trading of fed funds below the interest-on-reserves rate has two consequences.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, it blurs the meaning of the effective federal funds rate with respect to its relationship to the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Conceptually, the interest- on-reserves rate, rather than the effective federal funds rate, could be viewed as representing the default risk-free investment rate for banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, it implies that we may have to narrow considerably further the spread between the target federal funds rate and the interest rate paid on excess reserves in order to push the effective federal funds rate up to the target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In principle, if fed funds sales were to continue in large volume below the interest-on-reserves rate, the interest-on-reserves rate might need to be set right at the federal funds rate target in order to support the federal funds rate close to that level.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Before turning to a discussion of monetary policy and inflation expectations, I want to make a few comments about the hedge fund industry.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Before this crisis began, most of the fears about a market meltdown were focused on hedge funds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Until now, these fears have been mostly misplaced.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, the risks that hedge fund problems will now exacerbate the crisis have increased substantially recently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The underlying problem is that the recent performance of the hedge fund industry has been very poor and hedge fund viability is not very robust when net asset values slip considerably below their high-water marks in individual funds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: September was the poorest month in the past 10 years, and so far October returns are on pace to be even worse.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Net asset value for the entire hedge fund industry is down more than 10 percent year-to-date.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The average performance, shown in exhibit 20, masks substantial dispersion in returns and particularly poor performance for certain strategies.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, convertible arbitrage, emerging market arbitrage, and fixed- income arbitrage strategies suffered double-digit losses in the month of September, and further losses are likely in October.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Poor hedge fund performance has been exacerbated by several factors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, policy shifts such as the short sales ban have caused big problems for convertible arbitrage, statistical arbitrage, and long/short equity strategies.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This has been an important factor behind Citadel’s travails.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, prime brokers continue to pull back in their willingness to provide financing by raising their haircuts assessed against hedge fund assets as market volatility rises (exhibit 21).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, investors are pulling funds out of hedge funds because of their poor performance and a generalized increase in risk aversion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, hedge funds are raising cash to meet actual and potential redemptions, and many hedge funds are either hitting or approaching their net asset value trigger points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Let me say a few words about net asset value triggers.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Hedge funds often negotiate agreements with each of their prime brokers that set the terms for their access to financing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These contracts give the prime brokers the option to seize and liquidate collateral if the hedge fund net asset value falls by more than a certain magnitude—say, a 30 percent decline in assets under management over a three-month period; that’s a very common trigger.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, if only a few hedge funds are close to these triggers, there is little problem as there is no potential flood of asset sales into the market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But when so many hedge funds are under pressure at the same time, the risk of broader asset liquidation increases.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The prime broker may have a lessened incentive to waive its right to liquidate collateral when a greater proportion of the industry is troubled because the first-mover advantage of selling collateral likely becomes more important under such circumstances.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I anticipate that the pressure from the liquidation of hedge fund assets will continue to weigh on financial markets over the next few months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Some major fund of fund managers anticipate redemptions between now and early 2009 of at least 25 percent of the total industry, or about $500 billion based upon the estimated $2 trillion size of the global hedge fund business.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Market participants continue to price in additional cuts in the federal funds rate target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, it is a little harder than usual to tell what they are expecting based on futures prices because the federal funds rate has traded soft relative to the target and those expectations are also embedded in the near-term rates for fed funds futures contracts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Regardless of the cause, if you look at exhibits 22 and 23, there has been a fairly sharp downward shift in the federal funds rate curve and the Eurodollar futures curve—they have shifted downward about 100 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the curves are considerably flatter than they were a few months ago, indicating that market participants expect that the FOMC will be slow to raise the federal funds target in 2009.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Our primary dealer survey indicates that most survey respondents expect the Committee to lower the target federal funds rate over the next two meetings to around 1 percent and keep it there through most of 2009.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This also represents a downward shift of about 100 basis points from the survey conducted before the September 16 meeting (exhibits 24 and 25).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When the survey was conducted more than a week ago, the majority of respondents anticipated a 25 basis point cut.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Since then, the consensus has flipped, with most now anticipating a 50 basis point rate cut at this meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the inflation expectations front, normal relationships between TIPS and nominal Treasuries have been distorted by the illiquidity of TIPS relative to nominal Treasuries and the high level of chronic fails in the five-year sector of the nominal Treasury market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, TIPS yields have climbed sharply relatively to nominal Treasuries, leading to a sharp fall in breakeven inflation measures (exhibit 26).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The fact that breakeven inflation rates have fallen more sharply in the five-year sector than in the ten-year sector has generated a rise in five-year, five-year-forward measures of inflation (exhibit 27).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The distortions in the U.S. Treasury market suggest considerable caution in interpreting the rise in these measures.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Interestingly, our Desk survey of primary dealers shows a slight drop in long-term inflation expectations since the September survey (exhibit 28).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Before concluding, let me note that the staff recommends approval of a $15 billion foreign exchange swap line with the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to help satisfy the dollar funding needs of banks that operate in New Zealand.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As noted in the memo to the Committee from Nathan Sheets and myself that was distributed on Friday, this would complement the swap agreements that we have already enacted with other advanced economies and would have the same technical features as those with the smaller advanced countries (that is, Australia, Denmark, Norway, and Sweden) with fixed swap line limits.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Nathan will be discussing the potential for additional swap line authorizations for four emerging market countries recommended by the staff that were discussed in a second memo to the Committee on Friday.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There were no foreign operations during this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I request a vote to ratify the operations of the System Open Market Account that have been undertaken since the September 16 FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Nathan will continue our presentation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In response to intensified global financial stresses, the central banks of four major emerging market economies—Mexico, Brazil, Korea, and Singapore—have recently expressed interest in temporary liquidity swap lines with the Federal Reserve.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For the reasons outlined in our background memo, which was circulated on Friday, the staff recommends that the Committee approve these requests.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We propose that the lines be sized at $30 billion for each of these four countries, similar to our existing lines with Canada, Sweden, and Australia.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We envision that these lines would expire on April 30, 2009, as is the case with our other swap lines.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We also recommend that these lines have several safeguards relative to our lines with central banks in the advanced economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, even following initial FOMC approval, the proposed lines could not be drawn on without further authorization, and individual drawings would be limited to $5 billion.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We recommend that the FOMC delegate to its Foreign Currency Subcommittee the authority to approve these drawings.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The subcommittee would ensure that the dollars drawn would be used in a manner consistent with the purposes of the swap agreement.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The central banks in these countries would also agree to publicly announce the fact that they had drawn on their lines and the mechanisms that they had used to allocate the dollar liquidity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These safeguards are designed to provide protections for Federal Reserve resources and to ensure that the swap lines are used in a manner consistent with our envisioned objectives.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These safeguards, however, are not intended to be so onerous as to discourage the use of the lines if the situation warrants.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We see the case for these swap lines as resting on three important observations.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First, each of these economies has significant economic and financial mass.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Mexico, Brazil, and Korea are all large economies with GDP of around $1 trillion, and Singapore is a major financial center.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given the structural interconnectedness of the global economy and the financial fragilities that now prevail, a further intensification of stresses in one or more of these countries could trigger unwelcome spillovers for both the U.S. economy and the international economy more generally.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our interdependencies with Mexico are particularly pronounced.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Second, these economies have generally pursued prudent policies in recent years, resulting in low inflation and roughly balanced current account and fiscal positions or, in the case of Singapore, sizable surpluses.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Accordingly, the stresses that these countries are feeling seem largely to reflect financial contagion effects from the advanced economies, including sharp reductions in risk appetite, rapid deleveraging by global investors, and a drying up of liquidity in dollar funding markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Third, there is good reason to believe that swap lines with the Federal Reserve would be helpful in defusing the economic and financial pressures that they now face.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These lines would promote financial stability by helping to ensure that financial institutions and corporations in these countries have access to dollar liquidity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Dollar funding pressures in Brazil and Korea appear to have intensified significantly.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Such pressures remain less acute in Mexico and Singapore, but the authorities there view these lines as valuable protection should such pressures intensify, particularly over year-end.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, the authorities in these countries have expressed the view that these lines could provide a significant boost to confidence, although such outcomes are admittedly hard to predict.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I turn now to two questions that have been the focus of energetic deliberations among the staff as we have formulated these proposals.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First, is there some better approach that we could recommend?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Second, what are the risks associated with initiating swap facilities with these emerging market economies, or EMEs?

speaker: SHEETS
text: As for the first question, we could ask these countries to rely on their sizable stocks of foreign exchange reserves.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Across many contingencies, we believe that these countries do have sufficient resources to address financial pressures on their own.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Consistent with this observation, they don’t have any immediate plans to draw on their swap lines.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In this sense, the lines serve as a backstop.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, in the event of intensified stresses, we believe that it would be desirable for these countries to able to meet the dollar funding needs of their institutions by drawing on the swaps rather than by going into the Treasury or agency markets to liquefy their foreign exchange reserves.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Alternatively, we could ask these countries to go to the IMF.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Tomorrow, the Fund is likely to approve a large, rapidly disbursing facility that might be appropriate.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That said, we see the IMF’s efforts in this area as broadly complementary to those of the Federal Reserve.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Meeting the potential liquidity needs of these large countries would strain the available resources of the Fund.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Conversely, the Fund is much better placed than we are to judge the liquidity needs of smaller, less systemically important countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As an additional consideration, these top-tier EMEs that we are recommending for swap lines are very reluctant to return to the IMF.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given the strength of their policies, they no longer view themselves as clients of the Fund and would prefer to go it alone rather than seek IMF financial support.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We note that there are indeed risks associated with our recommendation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: One obvious concern is that the swaps might not be repaid.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, given the large reserve holdings of these countries, their prudent policies, the weight they place on good relations with us, and the safeguards built into the swap agreements, we judge the risk to Federal Reserve resources to be very low.

speaker: SHEETS
text: More notable is the risk that approving these lines might cause us to be flooded with requests from many additional EMEs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, in proposing lines with these four countries, we feel that we have set the bar quite high.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Their importance to the global economy and the quality of their policies set a standard that few, if any, other EMEs can match.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, the potential IMF liquidity swap facility might be helpful to us in limiting the risk of a slippery slope, as additional countries that request lines with us could be asked to go to the IMF.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Similarly, European EMEs seeking swap lines could be encouraged to approach the ECB.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In assessing these issues, the staff has conferred with senior officials at the U.S. Treasury and the State Department.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In both instances, these agencies emphasized the global economic significance of Brazil, Mexico, Korea, and Singapore.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, they also cautioned that expanding the swap lines beyond this group could leave us increasingly vulnerable to a “pile on” effect, which might manifest itself either in a large number of additional swap line requests or in political pressure.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given these considerations, the staff would benefit from some signal from the FOMC regarding its willingness to consider swap lines with other emerging market economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We see two broad options in this regard.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First, the FOMC could indicate that it is not inclined to establish swap lines with other EMEs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Inquiries from additional countries could be forwarded to the IMF.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Alternatively, the FOMC could emphasize that the bar for any additional EME facilities is high and that swap lines would be extended only if the case is seen as being comparable to that of the four countries that are being voted on today.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Under this second approach, the FOMC might consider granting the Foreign Currency Subcommittee the authority to establish swap lines with the central banks of other large and systemically important EMEs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Bill Bassett will now continue our presentation.

speaker: BASSETT
text: I will be referring to the exhibits labeled in red, “Staff Presentation on Financial Developments.” The intermeeting period was characterized by persistent strains in financial markets and a sharp drop in asset prices.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Although some markets have improved in recent days, the ongoing disruptions have generated intense pressures on financial institutions and have contributed to a significant further tightening of credit conditions for households and businesses.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As Bill Dudley noted, spreads on credit default swaps (CDS) for financial institutions have been quite volatile.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown by the top left panel of your first exhibit, median spreads for large bank holding companies (the black line) and regional commercial banks (the red line) declined substantially after the announcement of the Treasury’s capital purchase program and the FDIC’s temporary liquidity guarantee program on October 14; they ended the period almost 70 basis points lower, on balance.

speaker: BASSETT
text: The median CDS spread for insurance companies (the blue line) increased substantially over the latter part of the intermeeting period amid concerns about the financial condition of these firms.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Judging from the wide range of dealers’ price quotes on CDS for the same firms (shown in the top right panel), liquidity and price discovery in the CDS market remain strained.

speaker: BASSETT
text: The functioning of markets for corporate debt is also impaired.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown by the blue line in the middle left panel, the staff’s proxy for the bid-asked spread on high- yield bonds spiked to more than 4 percent before partially reversing course over the past week.

speaker: BASSETT
text: This spread is also unusually elevated for investment-grade bonds (the black line).

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown to the right, the average bid-asked spread on syndicated loans traded in the secondary market (the black line) jumped up over the intermeeting period.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Secondary market prices for syndicated loans (the blue line) dropped to unprecedented levels, reportedly reflecting heavy sales by hedge funds that were forced to meet investor redemptions as well as the unwinding of some types of structured investments.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Municipal finance, the subject of the bottom two panels, was significantly disrupted by dislocations in money market mutual funds in September and record 2 The materials used by Mr. Bassett are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: BASSETT
text: withdrawals from long-term municipal bond funds in early October.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Markets for structured products, such as tender-option bonds, that issued short-term variable-rate debt backed by longer-term municipal bonds were particularly affected.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Yields on those short-term instruments (shown by the black line in the bottom left panel) jumped for a time, and the sales of the underlying long-term bonds as the structures unwound boosted long-term municipal bond yields (the blue line).

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown to the right, issuance slowed substantially until mid-October, when a few states—notably California—placed a sizable amount of new debt, though they paid fairly elevated interest rates to do so.

speaker: BASSETT
text: In recent days, however, liquidity conditions have shown signs of improvement, yields have decreased somewhat, and issuance has moved back up from the extremely slow pace seen in the second half of September and the first half of this month.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Please turn to exhibit 2.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As noted by Bill Dudley, prime money market funds suffered a wave of redemptions in mid-September, shown by the red bars in the top left panel.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Although the flows diminished after the Federal Reserve and the Treasury announced steps to support money funds on September 19, prime funds lost about one-fifth of their assets, on net, over the intermeeting period.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As a result, prime funds have dramatically reduced their holdings of commercial paper, generating significant disruptions in that market.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown by the black line in the top right panel, unsecured financial commercial paper outstanding has declined sharply since mid- September, and the ongoing contraction in ABCP (the blue line) has continued.

speaker: BASSETT
text: In contrast, the amount of unsecured commercial paper placed by nonfinancial firms (the yellow line) was little changed, on net, over the period.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown in the middle left panel, broad equity prices (the black line) dropped about 30 percent over the intermeeting period as the outlook for both economic growth and earnings dimmed, and implied volatility increased to record levels.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As depicted by the red bars to the right, those developments were accompanied by record outflows of about $60 billion from equity mutual funds in September.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Weekly data indicate that, over the first half of October, investors withdrew more than $100 billion from long-term mutual funds, including about $70 billion from equity funds, but outflows have slowed in recent days.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown in line 1 in the bottom left panel, M2 expanded rapidly in September and early October as some firms and households shifted toward safer assets.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Liquid deposits (line 2) increased significantly in September and stayed about flat in October.

speaker: BASSETT
text: In contrast, retail money funds (line 3) were little changed in September but have grown briskly this month.

speaker: BASSETT
text: The sizable increases in small time deposits in both months (line 4) were widespread, in contrast to the more concentrated gains seen over the summer in response to elevated yields at a few financial institutions.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Currency (line 5) began increasing rapidly in recent weeks, apparently supported by higher demand from both foreign and domestic holders.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As a result of the disruptions in short-term funding markets, a range of borrowers turned to banks for funding.

speaker: BASSETT
text: The “other loans” category (the blue line in the bottom right panel) rose sharply beginning in mid-September as a result of both unplanned overdrafts and draws on existing credit lines by nonfinancial businesses, money market mutual fund complexes, foreign banks, nonbank financial institutions, and municipalities.

speaker: BASSETT
text: C&I loans at banks (the black line) have also increased significantly in recent weeks, as a broad spectrum of nonfinancial firms tapped existing credit lines.

speaker: BASSETT
text: According to the October Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey, however, about 25 percent of the largest banks and 35 percent of other banks surveyed indicated that C&I loans not made under previous commitment accounted for some of the recent increase.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Additional results from the survey are the subject of your next exhibit.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Large net fractions of institutions reported having continued to tighten their lending standards and terms on all major loan categories over the previous three months, with some banks reporting that they had tightened lending policies considerably.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown by the black line in the top left panel, about 80 percent of domestic respondents tightened their lending standards on C&I loans since July, and all but one of the 54 banks surveyed reported charging higher spreads over their cost of funds on such loans (the red line).

speaker: BASSETT
text: As noted to the right, nearly all the banks that tightened standards or terms did so in response to a more uncertain or less favorable economic outlook and a reduced tolerance for risk.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Almost 40 percent of domestic banks tightened in part because of concerns about their capital or liquidity position, somewhat more than had cited those pressures in July.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As indicated in the middle left panel, a large fraction of domestic banks again reported tightening standards on commercial real estate loans over the past three months.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Moving to loans to households, almost 70 percent of respondents tightened standards on residential mortgages to prime borrowers (the red line in the middle right panel).

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown by the blue line, nearly 90 percent of the institutions that originated nontraditional mortgages tightened standards on such loans.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown by the short black line in the bottom left panel, about 75 percent of the respondents tightened lending standards on home equity lines of credit, and about 60 percent tightened standards on both credit cards (the blue line) and other consumer loans (the red line).

speaker: BASSETT
text: As noted to the right, almost 25 percent of banks, on net, reported reducing the credit limits on existing credit card accounts of some prime customers over the past three months, and about 60 percent of banks reported cutting existing lines of some of their nonprime borrowers.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Banks that had trimmed the limits on existing credit card accounts most often cited the more uncertain economic outlook as a very important reason followed, in turn, by a reduced tolerance for risk and deterioration in the credit quality of individual customers.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Business finance is the subject of your next exhibit.

speaker: BASSETT
text: The spread on BBB-rated bonds issued by nonfinancial corporations (the blue line in the top left panel) rose about 275 basis points over the intermeeting period, to more than 600 basis points, whereas that on bonds of financial firms (the black line) reached nearly 1,000 basis points before easing some in recent days.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As spreads spiked and volatility increased, bond issuance by both nonfinancial and financial corporations (shown in the table to the right) dropped appreciably in the third quarter (row 3) relative to the pace seen in the first half of the year (row 2).

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown in the last row, there has been no high- yield issuance by nonfinancial firms so far this month, and bond issuance by financial firms has come to a near halt.

speaker: BASSETT
text: In commercial mortgage markets, secondary market spreads on AAA-rated commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS), shown in the middle left panel, continued to increase on net, and no new CMBS have been issued for several months.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As noted to the right, using announced earnings for about 200 firms and analysts’ estimates for the rest, the staff expects third-quarter S&P 500 earnings to come in about 10 percent below the level posted in the third quarter of last year.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Losses at financial companies account for the drop.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Bank holding companies reported further substantial write-downs on mortgage-related and other securities as well as higher loan-loss provisions necessitated by widespread deterioration in credit quality.

speaker: BASSETT
text: In contrast, earnings of nonfinancial companies are projected to have risen about 12 percent from a year earlier, but increased profits of energy companies account for virtually all of those gains.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As indicated in the bottom left panel, analysts have revised down significantly their expectations for earnings of nonfinancial firms (the red line) over the next year, likely in response to the worsening economic outlook.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Expected earnings for financial firms (the black line) also have been cut further this month.

speaker: BASSETT
text: A rough estimate of the equity premium (shown in the bottom right panel) stands at an extremely high level.

speaker: BASSETT
text: The household sector is the subject of your last exhibit.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown by the top left panel, interest rates on conforming residential mortgages have been volatile—partly in response to the renewed pressures on GSE debt noted by Bill Dudley—but ended the period only slightly higher at around 6 percent.

speaker: BASSETT
text: The staff expects home prices (the black line to the right) to decline significantly further through the end of 2010 and mortgage debt (the red line) to be about flat over that period.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Both paths have been marked down from the September forecast to reflect a weaker economic outlook and tighter credit conditions.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Spreads on asset-backed securities backed by credit card loans (the black line in the middle left panel) and auto loans (the red line) have risen more than 150 basis points since mid-September, moving well above their spring peaks.

speaker: BASSETT
text: The cumulative increase in spreads since midyear has hindered issuance of such securities, and the volume of new deals, shown to the right, dropped more than 50 percent in the third quarter.

speaker: BASSETT
text: The latest data, available through October 17, suggest that very little issuance has occurred this month.

speaker: BASSETT
text: As shown in the bottom left panel, consumer credit has decelerated recently.

speaker: BASSETT
text: With lending conditions likely to remain tight and with spending on durables expected to be soft, the staff sees significant further weakness in consumer credit in coming quarters.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Summing up, although there has been modest improvement in several financial markets recently, the worsening of the global financial crisis sharply increased pressures on financial firms and markets over the intermeeting period as a whole.

speaker: BASSETT
text: Those pressures have led to further deleveraging, diminished liquidity, increased concerns among investors about the economic outlook, and a reduced tolerance for risk-taking.

speaker: BASSETT
text: The resulting sharp fall in asset prices and the further tightening of credit conditions have had substantial adverse effects on nonfinancial businesses and households.

speaker: BASSETT
text: That concludes my prepared remarks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m going to open up in a minute to questions for Bill, Nathan, and Bill.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to say just three brief things about the emerging market swaps.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, we have been talking with these countries for some time, and I think when the conversations began it was more of a preventive measure than a response to conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the EMEs are now at a flashpoint in the financial crisis, and as I think Linda Kole will probably discuss, the urgency has increased, and the risks to the broader global economy are probably higher than they were a few weeks ago.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, with respect to the choice of four countries that Nathan proposed—as he mentioned, we have talked to the Treasury and the State Department.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I spoke to Secretaries Paulson and Rice about this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was an interesting confluence of agreement that, if you are going to do this, these are the right four countries and we probably shouldn’t do more, both from an economic perspective and a diplomatic perspective in the sense that these are the countries that among the emerging markets are the most important from a financial and economic point of view.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Third, as I think Nathan also mentioned, the IMF is planning to create a liquidity facility, which will be a low-conditionality facility available to a broad range of countries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there has been some discussion back and forth about the relationship between this, if we do it, and the IMF facility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I had a conversation this morning with Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the head of the IMF, and we agreed that the two facilities are complementary—that ours would provide important additional resources to the total availability of liquid resources for these countries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we decide to take this step, we have agreed that tomorrow, after the IMF board approves their facility, we would jointly announce these two actions so that it would create an impression of cooperation and coordination between the Federal Reserve and the IMF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So those are just a few additional pieces of information.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m sure that you have plenty of questions.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just to follow up on your note, Mr. Chairman, I spent four years as the senior trade negotiator with all four of these countries, and I’d just like to comment on their importance to us.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s a national security risk.

speaker: FISHER
text: They have a sophisticated central bank and a very good central bank governor, and I think that would be number one on the list.

speaker: FISHER
text: I doubt that Singapore would ever go to the IMF.

speaker: FISHER
text: It would be beneath Lee Kuan Yew’s dignity.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is a vital link in terms of that sphere of the world.

speaker: FISHER
text: You made the case earlier, or at least Nathan made a case, as to the uniqueness of Singapore.

speaker: FISHER
text: In terms of Brazil, I’d say that is the dodgiest of the lot.

speaker: FISHER
text: However, we should remember that 40 percent of the GDP of Latin America south of the Yucatan is produced by that one country and roughly 60 percent of the population is represented by that one country.

speaker: FISHER
text: It has made significant progress since Cardoso was president, and it is a robust economy relatively speaking.

speaker: FISHER
text: Every economy in Latin America borders upon it.

speaker: FISHER
text: It does have a unique negotiating history—and Tim knows this as well as I do, having spent a lot of time negotiating with them—but I would say that it is a critical part of our hemisphere and that is the justification for including them in the package.

speaker: FISHER
text: Finally, we have been trying to negotiate a free trade agreement with Korea for some time.

speaker: FISHER
text: Korea is an underrepresented country in terms of discussions about developments in that part of the globe, and yet it is inordinately successful.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would argue that it is also a strong case to make.

speaker: FISHER
text: The only other country that I would include under the rubric that we might ever consider is Chile.

speaker: FISHER
text: Even though it is tiny, its representation is important and its nature unique.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think you could justify doing this by virtue of their immediate impact on our economy, their unique role in our hemisphere, and the fact that I doubt that they would want to go to the IMF in the first place.

speaker: FISHER
text: Therefore, it is complementary to the package you announced earlier.

speaker: FISHER
text: My only discomfort in the discussion would be the idea of allocating to the Foreign Currency Subcommittee the authority to approve additional countries.

speaker: FISHER
text: As to the supplement for these four countries that has been proposed, I would be in favor of that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I thought there was some pretty good risk management described in the memo, but I didn’t really follow or don’t understand exactly the process by which we would generate a loss through these swap lines.

speaker: EVANS
text: Could you take us through the state of the world in which we would actually generate a loss?

speaker: EVANS
text: I raised this question before with the industrialized countries, and the answer was that because those are very high quality countries, we don’t really have to worry about that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I understand that they follow pretty reasonable economic policies during normal times.

speaker: EVANS
text: But what are the safeguards, and what would be the process by which we would generate a loss?

speaker: SHEETS
text: I very much agree with the thrust of the question—it would take a very severe state of nature for us to sustain losses on these.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We are protected by the full faith and credit of our central bank counterparty.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition to that, when we give them dollars, we take their domestic currency.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So I suppose, in some very extreme state of the world, one could imagine that the loan that was made in dollars defaulted on the central banks, the central bank chose not to make us whole, and the currency that was escrowed for us had depreciated significantly in value.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But I’d say that you are multiplying three very small possibilities, particularly the last two, that the central bank would choose to default on us, and there would have to be such a substantial fall in their currency that it would reduce the value of that effective assurance or collateral or whatever you want to call it.

speaker: EVANS
text: But it would be that we have their currency and presumably that would be a state in which it had depreciated.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These would function very similarly to the swap lines that we have with the advanced economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, we are going to allow them to draw only $5 billion at a time at the discretion of the Foreign Currency Subcommittee.

speaker: SHEETS
text: When the Foreign Currency Subcommittee makes the determination as to whether or not a drawing should occur, it has the scope and the mandate to look broadly at what is happening in the economy and make sure that the resources are going to be used in a manner that is consistent with the terms and the expectations of the swap agreement.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: A clarifying question, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Nathan, on page 4 of the memo, at the last bullet, you say, “FRBNY would have broad ‘set-off rights.’”

speaker: SHEETS
text: Maybe Trish and Bill want to jump in here as well.

speaker: SHEETS
text: What this means is that, in extinguishing any obligation that arises from the swap agreement, if the central bank for some reason doesn’t pay us, we can take other assets on the books that are being held by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to extinguish those liabilities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So if the Brazilians are holding some additional assets at the New York Fed that are unrelated to the swap and they are not making good on the swap, we can draw on those other assets to extinguish the obligations from the swap.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But there is nothing that prevents them from withdrawing those assets before that, right?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Presumably, if they’re in a situation of default, they would withdraw any Treasury securities held here first.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But any drawing under the swap agreement would be no longer than three months, and some drawings would be much shorter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So they would have to move very quickly, given the short nature of these transactions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But there are certain states of nature that are so severe that we couldn’t rule it out.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Let me just state my understanding of this so that I can be corrected by Nathan or by Bill.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: These countries hold substantial amounts of their reserves in dollars.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: They hold a substantial fraction of those dollars in accounts at the New York Fed.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If they defaulted on their piece of the swap and the falling value of their currency left us with some exposure, we would have the ability to take assets from their accounts to cover any loss.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So it’s better than the fact that this is a sovereign credit and it is better than the fact that we have an asset on the other side of the swap, because they hold substantial foreign exchange reserves with us.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The way to think about this is just as a mechanism to help them transform the composition of their dollar reserves in a way that might be more effective in responding to lender-of-last-resort needs in dollars, rather than having to sell Treasuries or agencies into the market in a period of panic or distress to meet that cash need.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I meant it as a confirming question.

speaker: STERN
text: But I thought we were concerned about a shortage of Treasury collateral in the market.

speaker: STERN
text: So why wouldn’t we want them to sell, and in fact, what are reserves for if they don’t use them in these circumstances?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I have never stood in their shoes, so I’m not sure I fully understand it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You are right that the world is a little short of the risk-free asset now, and so a greater supply would be terrific in some sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But they have a general view, which I think our people share, that to meet the kind of lumpy, unpredictable, potentially large needs for lender-of- last-resort purposes you may face in our currency, you have to manage reserves in a way that you can meet those needs without selling Treasuries or agencies.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It would not be so terrific for the world.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I have never stood on the other side, but that’s my basic sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Another way to think about this is that the privilege of being the reserve currency of the world comes with some burdens.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Not that we have an obligation in this sense, but we have an interest in helping these guys mitigate the problems they face in dealing with currency mismatches in their financial systems.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have an interest in helping them meet that in some sense.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have the same basic interest that led us to be responsive to the European need in some cases.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: These guys are different in that they actually have managed the countries’ balance sheets better because they at least have a huge amount of their assets in dollars.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That should make us in some ways as comfortable as—maybe more comfortable than—doing it with the Europeans because they ran a banking system that was allowed to get very, very big relative to GDP with huge currency mismatches and with no plans to meet the liquidity needs of their banks in dollars in the event that we face a storm like this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, you had a two-hander?

speaker: LACKER
text: President Geithner, you described the EMEs as motivated by a desire to transform their reserves from illiquid Treasuries or from Treasuries to some more fungible and more convenient form of dollars.

speaker: LACKER
text: That strongly suggests collateralizing their swap line with the Treasuries rather than their own currency.

speaker: LACKER
text: What would be the disadvantage of doing that?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think effectively we have done that by the way in which the thing is structured.

speaker: LACKER
text: But the point that President Evans made is that we’re not constraining them to not withdraw the reserves.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Do you mean that you want to put a reserve floor on them, too?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The question is whether, in an unlikely but possible state of the world in which they don’t want to pay us back, they could withdraw their Treasuries in advance of defaulting.

speaker: LACKER
text: Or we could lend to them, collateralized by the Treasuries rather than by their own currency.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Well, lots of things are possible.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think this is a pretty good conservative balance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would basically be a repo agreement, I guess.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For what it’s worth, the ECB has entered into something similar to that with the Hungarians, in which the Hungarians are able to repo to them long-term euro- denominated stuff and get euros back.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think I’d be a little concerned about stigmatizing the swaps by saying that we have enough doubts about these other countries that we need to take collateral— we don’t have confidence that their central banks will meet the obligations that they have taken on.

speaker: KOHN
text: So my preference would be to stick with the extension of our current swap agreements to these countries.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think they all are using their reserves to some extent already, so this is not a case of them not touching their reserves and instead taking the swaps.

speaker: KOHN
text: They say they don’t intend to use them, but they could very well use them.

speaker: KOHN
