text: The other market that the Treasury has expressed some concern about is the agency market.

speaker: KOHN
text: If they were just meeting a huge demand for Treasuries by selling Treasuries, that might be one thing—although intermediate- and longer-term Treasury yields themselves have moved up presumably because of supply pressures there.

speaker: KOHN
text: But the agency spreads have widened quite a bit, and I think forcing them to sell agencies in a kind of lumpy way would feed back on our mortgage markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: It would not be in our interest.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just responding to President Lacker.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it would be an insult to these four parties, particularly given the fact that we appear to have negotiated, again, the ability to attach other assets.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am, frankly, surprised that Singaporeans would go along with that.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we got that, I’d use it and pocket it.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I would argue, especially for the case of Mexico, that I don’t see any reason that we should differentiate between them and Canada, for example.

speaker: FISHER
text: It would stigmatize them in a way, and it would be an insult to these people.

speaker: FISHER
text: At the same time, as I think I understand the explanation from Vice Chairman Geithner and from Nathan, we do have some ramped-up security here—so it’s a special arrangement.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think going further than that would not be appropriate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me say just a couple of quick things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that this would require renegotiating the whole thing from the beginning, and we would like, if possible, to do this tomorrow with the IMF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second point I would make is that we do have considerable security, and we will be dispensing this—under strict conditions—in limited tranches.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we could monitor pretty well what was going on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the point is well taken.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have just a clarification.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Don’t we already have a swap line, a standing facility, with Mexico as a part of NAFTA?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So we don’t have to add it.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We do have a swap line with Mexico.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It’s a standing swap line.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It’s $3 billion under the North American Framework Agreement.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It’s the counterpart to NAFTA.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Under that agreement, we also have a $2 billion swap line with Canada.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Here we would be adding a new temporary liquidity swap line, so it would be a new legal construct.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess my question is why we can’t use the swap line that is already in existence.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In principle, if you were so inclined, you could probably just raise the size of the existing swap line to $30 billion.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, we built in a variety of mechanisms and safeguards in this proposal.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, the structure of what we’re putting forward is tailored particularly to meet the kinds of challenges and liquidity pressures that exist right now.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So in some sense this one is structured to meet the challenges that the Mexicans are most likely to face in the current episode rather than the more generic one that already exists on the books.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me go to President Rosengren, who has been waiting patiently.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I have two unrelated questions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: One follows up on this, but the other one is on the term auction facility.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, given how much we have expanded the term auction facility, is there any consideration to having a minimum stop-out rate, given that the last two have had fairly low stop-out rates?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I wonder if that was being considered at all, given how much we expanded the size.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Then the second question gets to the stigma issue related to the swap lines.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There was quite a lot of discussion about how to differentiate the countries.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I had the same thought that President Lacker had—if we could have set-off rights that enable them to collateralize the swaps.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I do think going to the IMF will attach a fair amount of stigma to the organization.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I am worried that the spillover benefits to other countries will be negative, not positive, because of that stigma.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: One option would be to say that either you could go to the IMF or we would provide collateralized loans for other than these four, since it sounds as though these four are a done deal.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But rather than trying to draw the line and figure out whether Chile or some other country is appropriate, we could collateralize it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If they held enough Treasury securities at the New York Fed, then it would seem that we would have no reason not to do it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If they didn’t have Treasury securities, which would probably partly reflect some of their own mismanagement in their countries, then they wouldn’t be able to use the facility and would have to use the IMF.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But it would seem to be a way to get around some of the stigma issues, if someone chose to come to us and fully collateralize it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That might be an alternative way to draw the line rather than trying to come up with criteria that seemed a little difficult to understand, as I went through the memo.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Under the term auction facility, there is a minimum bid rate, the OIS rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So when we have a $150 billion auction and let’s say there are propositions of $120 billion, the winning bid rate is the OIS rate for everybody.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But I’m just wondering, as the OIS rate has come down, when you think of the band that we have for excess reserves, it does seem that the OIS provides a much bigger band, for example, than what we have even for excess reserves.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I wonder whether, during periods in which people are considering a reduction of as much as 50 or more basis points, the OIS ends up being a very low lower bound.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, right now it is a very low rate because the market is building in future rate cuts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think the OIS rate is now below 1 percent on a three-month basis.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But as we narrow the target for excess reserves and have a narrow band there, you wonder whether the stop-out rate, having a lower band that is a little higher than the OIS, might be an alternative way to think about it, now that we have the excess reserves option as to the lower bound.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that is something worth considering.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The emphasis right now has been getting term funding out in as much size as possible and not worrying so much about whether the cost of the funds is or is not at a penalty.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think the emphasis of the program did shift a bit over the past six weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, if things settle down and the demand at the TAF auctions subsides, then you can have the option of cutting the size of the auctions or increasing the minimum bid rate or some combination of the two.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, may I make an amendment to Eric’s question or suggestion?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that, when we have a chance to breathe and we feel as though we have achieved some durable stability in the panic, then we will want to reassess not just the basic complement of our facilities and how we think about the future but the relative economics of what we’ve done with the dollar swaps and our existing open-end auction facilities for institutions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Ideally, we want a situation in which it is more attractive for them to borrow from their foreign central banks—the dollars we provided through the swaps—than to come to us in our auctions and other areas through their U.S. affiliates.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I am a bit less troubled by the point you made than I am by the fact that we have set up a regime in which the incentives for them to come to our facilities are still substantial when they have now the ability they didn’t have before to go to their foreign central banks for dollars in large scale.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As we think about consolidation and not just exit—about how we prepare the ground for a shift over time—I think we want to come back to looking at the relative economics between our dollar facilities for U.S. banks and U.S. affiliates of foreign banks and what is open to them from their home country central banks now.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: As part of that, we could think about size, reserve price, and price in our auction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The awkward thing right now is that we are trying to add liquidity as powerfully as we can.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So to raise the minimum bid rate or do anything that somehow suggests a pulling back would be a bit inconsistent with the LIBOR–OIS spread widening that we have seen and the fact that it still remains very, very elevated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You might want to do exactly what you suggested, President Rosengren, at some future date, but I think that doing it now would send a very mixed message to the market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think people would be confused about what we are doing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m sorry, Nathan had an answer.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Could I just respond to President Rosengren’s second question?

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think you put your finger on two very difficult judgments that we made when structuring this facility.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I don’t see the risk of creating stigma for emerging market economies that are not in our swap network as being a first-order concern.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It is broadly recognized that the folks that we are recommending are larger, more systemically important, and as well managed as anybody else.

speaker: SHEETS
text: If you were sitting down to make a list—and the Fund has recently done this—the economies that we’re recommending would be at the top of the list, and I think that is recognized by essentially all observers.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So I see what we’re doing here as really ratifying perceptions rather than creating new ones.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the second point, the choice between the swaps versus the repos, that one is particularly tricky.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I very much agree that the repos would give us a little more security.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the other hand, the swap framework gives the emerging market economies a little more flexibility.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As to how they are going to proceed, as President Fisher mentioned, it also creates symmetry between the industrial countries and the way we’re treating them and the emerging markets and the way we’re treating them.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given the successes of many of these economies over the past ten years, I see this as being an appropriate step.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, I admit that the choice between the swaps and the repos is a difficult one.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Another thought is that the repo structure might provide a bit more security, but we have tried to get that security through other ways—through tranching, careful reviews, and so on.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In fact, it follows right on with what Nathan was just answering.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is, for the moment we are creating kind of a broader in-list for these four countries and stigma with the non-accepted group at this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: What will happen, then, if we do have an issue that involves—pick a country—Chile?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Are we going to send them to the IMF?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Are we going to have our subcommittee make a decision as to whether to give them a swap?

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we do that, will that then create uncertainties about others?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Are you really not concerned about the stigma and the implications of this, especially—I guess they are asking this in anticipation of the possibility, even though they think it’s fairly remote—would we not be increasing the probabilities of a problem by doing this now?

speaker: HOENIG
text: I know these are tough questions; but in this environment, I am anticipating a bad event.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So what do we do in the case of that bad event?

speaker: SHEETS
text: I would hope that initiating these swaps would reduce the probability of bad outcomes in the emerging market economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Certainly, if Brazil, Mexico, and Korea are up against the ropes and experiencing significant financial stresses, my sense is that it would be an environment in which many other EMEs would be experiencing negative spillovers.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So to the extent that we can backstop these major linchpins in the emerging market world, I see that as having very positive effects for others.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That would be one point.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Second, the decision as to how to handle Chile, if Chile comes to us for a swap line, I think is very much a policy decision for the Committee to determine.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As I said in the remarks, we as staff members would very much appreciate some sort of signal from you as to whether you want to say four and that’s all we’re willing to do, and everyone else—Chile, India, and South Africa—goes to the Fund?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Or is the Committee open to having potentially a few other large, important emerging market economies have swap lines with the Federal Reserve?

speaker: SHEETS
text: I see that as being a policy decision.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But it’s something that we ought to think about sooner rather than later because the likelihood is that, if you take care of these four and you get another request, you are going to get three others and not one other.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Wherever you draw the line, there is going to be somebody who is just a bit away from the line that says, “I am very similar to those folks.” I am reasonably comfortable with where we draw the line.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Here there is as much gap as you’re going to find.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In my mind, the next one for which you could make a case would be India.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, India’s financial system isn’t as developed as is the case with these folks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: They are not as integrated into the global financial system as is the case with these, so there is a bit of space there.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But these are admittedly hard judgments, which we tried to flesh out regarding some of these issues in our memo.

speaker: FISHER
text: Have we been approached by any other countries?

speaker: SHEETS
text: We have been approached by 552 U.S.C.

speaker: SHEETS
text: (b)(4) , and we have had very informal inquiries from a couple of other countries, including 552 U.S.C.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we have not encouraged that.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We have done everything we possibly can to discourage it.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Another question for Nathan on swap lines is how this works exactly.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: If the pattern holds and Mexico, for example, supports its banking system—in the case of Mexico it is a little different from others, in that all of the large banks are foreign-owned (Citibank owns Banamex, and the Spanish banks own the other two or three large banks)— where does our responsibility stop and theirs begin?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Is it possible for the subsidiary of a U.S. bank or a Spanish bank to draw dollar liquidity in Mexico and with fungible dollars move that around the world?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Or does it in one manner or another stay in Mexico?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Certainly these home-versus-host issues bedevil many, many discussions of banking issues right now.

speaker: SHEETS
text: They are true in Mexico, as you suggested, and they are true in spades in Central and Eastern Europe, where instead of U.S. banks there are European banks in the tension between the home and host.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So these considerations are very relevant and also exceedingly complicated.

speaker: SHEETS
text: If the Bank of Mexico or the Mexican authorities move to address tensions in their financial system, the standard that has been set by several Federal Reserve actions, the Brits in the things they have done, and I believe a number of the other countries is to include subsidiaries of foreign firms that are operating in that country.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So, for instance, for the United States, Deutsche Bank’s U.S. subsidiary has had access to our various facilities, and that has been the coin of the realm in the announcements today.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So my feeling is that Banamex, which is owned by Citi, would have the same access to these kinds of facilities as other Mexican institutions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now, there is no guarantee of that, but that would be my feeling.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Regarding the question of, once a Mexican institution gets its hands on dollars, what happens to those dollars, my understanding is that they can move around.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In fact, in a discussion, Guillermo Ortiz indicated that to date Mexican institutions were net suppliers of dollars to the United States rather than the other way around.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So in the case of a foreign bank—they lend to a foreign bank in their country, in Mexico in this case—defaulting, whose problem is it?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Is it the home country supervisor’s problem, or is it Mexico’s problem vis-à-vis us?

speaker: SHEETS
text: I would guess that it is a joint problem.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I’m not sure that this is helpful, but maybe I can give a slightly different example from another perspective.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have a bunch of U.S. affiliates of some of the weakest European institutions that have faced very substantial dollar funding needs and have come to us and asked for substantial ongoing access to liquidity.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: When they have a substantial amount of lendable collateral, collateral with substantial market value relative to the needs, we have been comfortable meeting those needs.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: When their needs have substantially exceeded or might potentially exceed the market value of their eligible collateral, then we have talked to the home central bank.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have said that, in effect, if you want us to be able to meet those needs and they have collateral in your market that is substantial relative to those needs, then the better way for us to do this is for the home country central bank to meet their dollar liquidity needs against the collateral there or meet the liquidity needs and we provide the dollar’s worth of guarantees from the central bank.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So this home–host thing is a delicate balance, and as Nathan said, it shouldn’t all fall on the host central bank.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The best thing possible is for the home country central bank to take most of the responsibility for meeting the liquidity needs and for us to help them facilitate that where necessary.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But when those needs exceed what we would normally give in terms of access, then you have to have a conversation with the foreign central bank.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So, for example, if a weak U.S. institution in Mexico faces substantial needs in Mexico well in excess of their eligible collateral in Mexico, I suspect they would call us and say, “We want you to meet those needs.” We would have to consider at that point where they are in the liquidity-solvency spectrum and how comfortable we are in meeting those needs.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have a question for the staff.

speaker: LACKER
text: You noted that the countries believed that this would help market confidence.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the choice of extending a line is potentially consequential here.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have a two-part question.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, what do you think the risk is of the uncertainty surrounding whether particular other countries will or will not in the future be able to obtain a swap line from the Federal Reserve?

speaker: LACKER
text: Second, what would you suggest that we say if asked by the public or if the Chairman is asked in the Congress about what criteria or principles we used to draw the line between the countries that have swap lines and those that don’t?

speaker: LACKER
text: I know that you posed the question to us, but what would you suggest that we say?

speaker: SHEETS
text: As outlined in the memo and then also my remarks, the first is that we are looking for economies that are large and systemically important.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The second is that we are looking for economies in which their policies have been strong and it appears that they are largely being influenced by contagion.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The third piece is countries for which we believe that the swap line might actually make a difference.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now, let me just give you a concrete case of the third criterion because that’s a little more abstract than the first two.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Iceland came to us and requested a swap line of approximately $1 billion to $2 billion, which would have been 5 to 10 percent of Iceland’s GDP—so it was fairly large relative to the size of the country.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But the liabilities of the banking system were on the order of $170 billion, and the underlying problem was really that there was a loss of confidence in its banks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We came to the conclusion that a $1 billion to $2 billion swap line was very little ammunition to use against a potential loss in confidence in this $170 billion financial system.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For that reason, we as the staff recommended against a swap line for Iceland.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Those are the three conditions that we’d emphasize.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Sort of subsidiary to that is that I think it is very appropriate for all the European EMEs to report to the ECB for their liquidity needs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That would further constrain the list of countries that we’d look at.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As we work down the list of countries, I think it gets easier to say “no” in that fewer and fewer of the countries can make a case that they are large and systemically important.

speaker: SHEETS
text: With the risk of creating stigma, some countries are big, and some aren’t, and that’s pretty darn objective.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now, you can debate about, well, what’s big and what isn’t and where you draw the line, but it just so happens that these three major economies that we’re putting forward all have GDP of around $1 trillion.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That seems like a reasonable line to draw.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Again, there’s an element of arbitrariness here, but any line you draw will have an element of arbitrariness to it.

speaker: LACKER
text: And the first part of my question?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Oh, I thought I got it.

speaker: SHEETS
text: What was the first part?

speaker: LACKER
text: What sort of uncertainty might this engender about the likelihood of other countries qualifying?

speaker: LACKER
text: My recollection is that many economists have claimed that the IMF had this trouble in the 1990s, when interventions would give rise to uncertainty about subsequent interventions in other cases.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Well, I guess I’m not sure I know exactly what you’re driving at.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Are you concerned that, by moving on these, we’re sending a negative message about the ones we’re not moving on?

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m just wondering about the uncertainty that might be created about the lack of clarity about who’s in, whether this is the final list, and so on.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our press release that we are negotiating lists, as clearly as one can in a press release, the criteria that we were looking at—that they are large, well-managed, fundamentally sound, systemically important countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So we are trying to communicate that.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, in conversations when these folks come to us—and especially if we get some direction from the FOMC as to how you’d like to proceed on this issue—we can be very, very blunt with them in telling them why the answer is “no” or “yes,” depending on which way the FOMC goes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vice Chair, did you have a two-hander?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Well, I just want to point out that I think these are absolutely the right kinds of questions about this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think these concerns are substantially mitigated by the fact that the IMF is putting in place a facility at basically the same time, which will be there with relatively little stigma for a range of other countries that need it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There will be a universe of other countries that would not meet the test for eligibility for this swap type of facility, for the IMF or us, that will have to go through a program with conditionality and a bunch of adjustments such as Iceland is going through or Hungary will go through.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So it is right to raise these questions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But the boundary problems around our swap lines are substantially mitigated by the fact that there is a new facility coming out that’s going to the same place.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Raising the question of why we need to do our swaps is good, too, but you’ve heard lots of good arguments for that, and I think that realistically there’s a natural division of labor between what central banks have classically done with each other in the swap context and what the IMF does.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What we’re doing is a natural extension of what central banks do.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The IMF is moving a little further in from where they are in this case, and I think that will mitigate some of the signaling problems and uncertainty created by having this evolution in the scope of swap lines.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess I’m worried about this for all of the considerations that President Hoenig and President Lacker have just been talking about.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t know where we draw the lines, and when we have to go to the State Department and start asking what countries we can or can’t develop swap lines with, I’m not sure those are the criteria we want to be using.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We mentioned the countries already.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What happens when 552 U.S.C.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You can just go down the list.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We have already said “no” to some of those.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I understand, but if you really follow the logic of the argument about being large and systemically important, if we draw a line somewhere, we start expanding this now bit by bit and we draw a line somewhere, and the question then becomes, Will markets begin to question other countries on the periphery and create problems?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s not that any one of them—552 U.S.C.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: (b)(4) , I don’t know, pick one—is large and systemically important, but by doing what we’re doing and creating the uncertainty that President Lacker was referring to, maybe we are forced to go and do it collectively because they all band together and as a group say, “We’re all facing this problem.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Why can’t we have the same access?” Partly I like President Rosengren’s suggestion about using repos with securities, which we have here as a mechanism.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Alternatively, if the IMF is creating a largely unconditional or low conditionality type of program, why not just say that everybody else goes to them first?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If they tap out of the IMF access, maybe then we might consider being a backstop rather than their coming to us in the first place.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just don’t know where this ends.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that, with all of the questions you raised and tried to answer, you hit it right on the head.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On all of them that you said were kind of marginal, you went one way, and I’m leaning the other way on the same criteria.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser, a couple of things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The IMF has very limited resources.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They’re not remotely able to meet the needs of—

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We don’t know what the needs are yet, do we?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, the resources are very limited.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other thing is that the staff asked for guidance on the limits here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d like to propose that, when we get to that point, to ask the voters to suggest how they stand and what qualifications they might have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One thing that you could do, for example, would be to say, “I do or do not support this, but if I do, I think a very sharp line should be drawn at this point and be communicated that way.” The legislative history can be part of this, and we can communicate to the staff how we feel about potential extensions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Just to put some numbers on IMF lending capacity—total IMF lending capacity is about $250 billion.

speaker: SHEETS
text: To get even that high they have to call in some special arrangements that they have with a variety of countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The maximum capacity is $250 billion.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So the $120 billion that we’re proposing today would be essentially half of what the IMF could do.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In that sense I really see what we’re proposing as our taking off the IMF’s hands some of the largest potential liquidity needs, which then allows them to focus on a whole range of additional countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: A related point is that I understand that, in an IMF executive board meeting today, the managing director indicated that they are getting a fair amount of interest in this new facility.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It really is a different kind of facility, and frankly, even a week ago if you told me that the IMF was going to be able to put this facility together in this quick a time, I would have said, “No way.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There’s no way that the IMF can move this quickly.” So it is about as good as we could expect and maybe even better than what we could have expected from the Fund.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think that they are doing what they can to minimize stigma.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the other hand, they don’t have enough lending capacity to really handle these folks that we’re talking about today.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In the Bluebook here, it says, “Additionally, the Swiss National Bank announced plans to draw on its swap line to help finance up to $60 billion in purchases of assets from a major Swiss bank.” So is that really what you have in mind here for a country like Brazil—that they’ll draw on their swap line to purchase assets from banks?

speaker: SHEETS
text: No, and maybe the folks in New York want to talk a bit more about this.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The transaction with the Swiss National Bank was a very special transaction that occurred outside the typical constraints of the swap lines that we’d be agreeing to with these folks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the swap lines with these folks, they would have to tell us up front how they’re going to allocate the resources.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We would envision that it would be done in something similar to an auction, in a very transparent, on-market sort of way.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But it would not be that kind of a transaction, which was a special case in order to help a particular financial institution.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Well, if you think that there are systemically important institutions in these countries, why not?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Again, we’re drawing lines here.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I am not prepared to give these folks carte blanche.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That’s why we’ve added additional safeguards and additional governance structures to these facilities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Maybe the Committee has a different view on that, but I wouldn’t be prepared to let them do whatever they wanted with these resources.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: To continue to grill you, Nathan—

speaker: SHEETS
text: I’m earning my pay today.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: You know, the atmosphere right now is largely precautionary on their part—they are well capitalized with foreign currency reserves.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But if we want to deal with hypotheticals, let’s assume that some of these recipients of the swap lines get into a liquidity crisis.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Is the European Central Bank being approached for swap lines?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I recognize that they need dollar liquidity, but in a general liquidity crisis, the euro would do as well to help.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Do we have any sense of whether the ECB is considering swap lines for some of these emerging markets?

speaker: SHEETS
text: I don’t have details on that.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As I’ve mentioned, I know that they have created a facility with the Hungarians, a €5 billion facility.

speaker: SHEETS
text: They were also approached by Iceland at the same time that we were.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I would speculate, but I don’t have any basis for that speculation, that given the emerging tensions in Central and Eastern Europe and Northern Europe that they probably are being approached, but I don’t have any details on that.

speaker: MOSSER
text: My understanding is that they have been approached.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t know what decisions have been made other than the ones that may have been mentioned.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In addition, they have opened a swap line with the Danish Central Bank in euros, which was virtually identical to the dollar arrangement that we have with the Danish Central Bank.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So they definitely have been approached for swap lines.

speaker: MOSSER
text: On how many of them they’ll put into place, we don’t have any particular information at this point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just want to clear up the question.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think Tim and Nathan may have both answered this, but it’s a question that President Lockhart raised earlier.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In Mexico’s case, for example, where almost all the major banks are foreign owned—EU banks, Spanish banks—those banks clearly have access to dollars through the ECB swap line.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There’s no reason that the dollar funding needs of those banks, to the extent that they can move these things around, can’t be satisfied by access to dollars from the ECB.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is that a correct or an incorrect assumption?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The collateral isn’t always in the right place.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You are absolutely right if the collateral could be easily moved; but the collateral oftentimes isn’t in the right place.

speaker: FISHER
text: Let me ask Nathan a question to follow up, if I may.

speaker: FISHER
text: Obviously you’ve been approached by the governor of the Central Bank of Mexico—Ortiz has been here to visit.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would assume that you asked these questions.

speaker: FISHER
text: So inform us as to what his justification is.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Mexico is experiencing increased financial stresses, particularly in its corporate sector, where recently some bad bets on structured finance products have emerged, and Ortiz was very concerned about continued confidence in the Mexican economy.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now, that said, from what he had to say, dollar funding pressures had not yet emerged, and he was emphatic that they would not draw on these until the time that those funding pressures emerged or until the time that they saw a significant further deterioration in conditions in their economy.

speaker: SHEETS
text: He was very specific about the fact that they would use their own reserves as their first, second, and third lines of defense.

speaker: KOHN
text: Just to add to that, he said that, to deal with the issue that Nathan raised about the problem with their businesses and the kind of dollar needs they had, they were meeting those needs out of their own foreign exchange reserves.

speaker: KOHN
text: So they were not going to engage in a swap with us in order to meet that particular problem, but they were concerned about the dollar pressures more generally on their financial segment, particularly as year-end approaches.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If it’s okay, maybe we could just go ahead with the votes on this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d like first to do the open market operations, which I hope are not too controversial.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was no discussion of the New Zealand swap line.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll ask to see if there is any comment on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then on this issue, I’ll take a set of positions from the voters, if that’s okay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let’s go back to domestic open market operations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I move that we approve.

speaker: KOHN
text: I move we approve that, too.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is there any discussion or concern?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, turning to the resolution on the EME swaps, in the interest of time I propose—and I hope it is okay—to go through the voters and ask each one to state whether you are in favor or opposed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You can say what you want and, if you want, whether you have some argument to make or if you’re conditionally in favor—for example, I’m in favor if X or if we do Y—but just to get a sense of where everybody is, and then we’ll decide what to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let’s go down the roll here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we should be fairly tough at this point.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: On the basic question of how you would deal with other requests beyond the four, Nathan gave two options.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One is that you delegate to the subcommittee discretion to make those judgments.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The second option was to say, “No, not without coming back to the Committee.” I do think it makes sense to see how the IMF thing works and how it is received, how much participation they get, and how these boundary problems and the signaling problem play out, and it is probably a good idea for the Committee to have at least a briefing about how that is playing out so that there is some context going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I would be in favor of your delegating that authority to the subcommittee, as you would expect me to be, just because sometimes these judgments need to be made quickly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I certainly understand why people would want to have a better sense of how this is unfolding and how we deal with it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The boundary problems are going to get worse if we have to go broader than this.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m in favor Mr. Chairman, and I would also favor, in terms of the screening device for future requests, that you come back to the full Committee.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m in favor, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think these boundary problems are difficult.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with the Vice Chairman that our having the IMF there mitigates them.

speaker: KOHN
text: I was encouraged by Nathan’s sense that there are some people interested in the IMF, so there might not be much stigma there.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would be in favor of very strongly encouraging other countries to go to the IMF.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I, too, favor the facility.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it’s very important that we are tranching this and using somewhat different ways of providing the money to these countries than we have with other countries because, as President Bullard and others mentioned, if we’re not careful, this could be used for purposes with which we are not comfortable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It could be used for supporting a currency, and I don’t think we’d be particularly comfortable with that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously, we have to be realistic.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They have very large reserves.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They could be using the reserves for these other purposes and using the swaps for purposes that we find acceptable.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I think, given the circumstances, it makes sense to be coming up with something that’s complementary to the IMF facility and make sure that the IMF facility and our facility together are sufficient to deal with the pressures in this environment.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I would be satisfied to delegate the authority to the subcommittee.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I’m also in favor of the program, and I agree with Vice Chairman Geithner’s comments that this announcement along with the IMF program should be sufficient.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But if there are other requests, I think it is important to bring them back to the Committee.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess I’ll approve, but with reluctance.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think this is a very slippery slope.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m worried about other central banks ganging up on us as a group, saying that they have to have this.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would prefer that even these large countries use some combination of the IMF facility plus their own reserves to meet these needs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that would be a better outcome and better for us in that regard.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So that’s a very reluctant “yea” vote.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’d also insist that any further expansion come back before this Committee.

speaker: STERN
text: I’m reluctantly in favor of this.

speaker: STERN
text: I won’t elaborate very much.

speaker: STERN
text: I’m just not persuaded that this is a very valuable contribution, as best as I can judge it.

speaker: STERN
text: I would be in favor of limiting it to these four countries.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t know if that’s credible, though.

speaker: STERN
text: Certainly I would be in favor of any additional considerations coming back to the full Committee.

speaker: WARSH
text: Mr. Chairman, I support the proposal on the floor.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the safeguards are meaningful and real and should help.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the bar for further consideration, as Nathan described, should be high, but we shouldn’t overstate what that bar is, given how circumstances can change quickly.

speaker: WARSH
text: I wouldn’t want to have to change that rule in the middle of the game, but I think the high- bar language works.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the question of delegating to the subcommittee, I think in the interest of speed it would be appropriate; but given the sense around the table, certainly making sure that the folks around the table were at the very least briefed as to the thought process might be a prudent path forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the sense I hear is that people are willing to accept it, but the bar for additional countries should be high.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should bring any country that we propose to add back to the FOMC for approval, and we will keep you well briefed on the conditionality, the draws, and anything else that happens.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: May I have a motion?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am going to say without objection because we had a unanimous view.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me go on next to the economic situation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Do we have time for a brief question for the Manager about the funds market?

speaker: LACKER
text: It has behaved a little unusually in the last period.

speaker: LACKER
text: Thank you, Mr. Chairman—I appreciate this.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have a three-part question.

speaker: LACKER
text: As you said in your presentation, the effective funds rate (the average of brokered transactions) has been below the interest rate on reserves, and there are all of these institutions that apparently aren’t eligible to earn interest on reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: One, what’s the policy reason for excluding them from eligibility for interest on reserves?

speaker: LACKER
text: I understand the policy reason for excluding them from credit, but this is the opposite, and so I’m not quite sure why we screen them out.

speaker: LACKER
text: Second, as I read the data on your operations, it seems to me as though we have added enough reserves to drive the funds rate virtually down to the interest rate on reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to know if that’s a fair characterization of the state of open market operations and the funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Third, I’m interested in knowing, especially if that’s true, why don’t we just give up and say that the interest rate on reserves is our target rate?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Let me take them in reverse order.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t like to give up, but if I could just exclude that portion of it, it’s possible that you might want to consider the interest rate on reserves or some reasonable facsimile thereof as your target because that is essentially the risk-free rate that banks face.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That may be the purer measure of what you’re really trying to accomplish in terms of its link to monetary policy than the federal funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There are obviously important governance issues that surround that choice, though, in terms of what’s the Board’s prerogative and what’s the FOMC’s prerogative.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But that’s a completely reasonable thing to think about, just as long as we don’t characterize that as giving up.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Have we added enough reserves to drive the federal funds rate down to the interest on reserves?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I wouldn’t look at it quite that way because the gap in principle, if other things are not going on, should be the difference between us as a counterparty and a bank as a counterparty.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One is an unsecured loan between one bank and another bank, and the other is us as the counterparty.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So normally there should be a spread between the interest on reserves and the federal funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, obviously what complicates that in the current environment is the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation’s guarantee on interbank funds going forward.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So federal funds may be covered—in fact, they look as though they could be covered by that guarantee.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In that circumstance, one might argue that the federal funds rate and interest on reserves should probably be the same rate because there’s no difference in credit risk.

speaker: LACKER
text: Without interest rates on reserves, there’s that spread plus a scarcity factor, and we’ve essentially driven that scarcity factor down to zero—that’s how I meant the question.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Right, but I still think that generally a bank faced with a choice of having risk with the Fed or selling fed funds to another bank would want to be compensated for that risk of selling, so they are going to get some positive spread.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I would say that we may well be in a situation where the interest rate on excess reserves is the effective tool for controlling the federal funds rate, and there may be a spread.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As Bill said, we are in the process of learning how this works, and it may well be the case that we need to push that interest rate on excess reserves very close to the federal funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It would not surprise me at all if, when we are finished with this process—I hope over the next six weeks as we go through a couple more reserve maintenance period rounds— that that margin might be zero and we might see the federal funds rate trading right on top of the interest rate on reserves.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But we are going to have to see.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think our presumption at the current time would be to recommend to the Board next round to narrow that spread further—it is 35 basis points today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Another thing that we don’t know is how much learning is going to go on by banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the selling of fed funds below the interest rate on reserves is not just the GSEs; it is also banks, and so it’s a little hard to understand exactly why they’re doing that unless the leverage ratio is what’s driving that behavior.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Maybe they are just not very well informed or they haven’t gotten their first check for the interest rate compensation, so I think it’s a little too soon to be certain about how they’re going to behave going forward.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You had one other question about the policy reason for excluding the GSEs.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: There’s not really a policy reason.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I would say there’s a legal reason.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statute allows us to pay interest only on balances held by depository institutions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: My own view is that it would be a good thing if we were able to pay interest to the GSEs exactly for the reasons that we’ve been discussing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It might be something we could seek authority for at some point in the future.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we were to take that step, are there any other institutions that participate, other than the GSEs?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We would have to look at that.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think there are more than just the three GSEs that we usually think of.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But they’re the biggest institutions that participate in the federal funds market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is not at all clear that their behavior is going to persist necessarily, because they may decide to manage their short-term liquidity in a different way than selling at a very low federal funds rate to banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: Mr. Chairman, if I could.

speaker: DUKE
text: As part of my preparation when I talked to the banks, I asked them specifically this question about interest on reserves, and every single one of them said, “We haven’t had time to even focus on it.

speaker: DUKE
text: We don’t even know what’s going on with that.

speaker: DUKE
text: We’re not changing anything.” There’s so much going on right now.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I think we’re really going to have to wait until some of the other decisionmaking has worked through before we can draw any conclusions as to what behavior this might drive.

speaker: MORIN
text: 3 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MORIN
text: I’ll be using the packet with the green lettering on the cover entitled “Staff Presentation on Nonfinancial Developments.” Over the intermeeting period, the data we received on real activity were considerably weaker than we had been expecting.

speaker: MORIN
text: That, combined with the intensification of financial turmoil since mid-September, led us to significantly mark down our near- term and medium-term projections for economic activity.

speaker: MORIN
text: Your first exhibit focuses on the near-term outlook.

speaker: MORIN
text: As shown by the blue bars in the top left panel, we currently expect real GDP to fall at an annual rate of slightly more than 1 percent, on average, in the second half of 2008—a reduction of about 2 percentage points from our projection in the September Greenbook (the red bars).

speaker: MORIN
text: One factor that has informed our thinking about the near-term forecast is the labor market, which looks weaker than at the time of the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: MORIN
text: As you 3 The materials used by Mr. Morin are appended to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: MORIN
text: know, payrolls fell steeply in September.

speaker: MORIN
text: Since then, initial claims for unemployment insurance (the black line in the top right panel) have been quite elevated, even after adjusting for factors that are temporarily boosting claims (the red line).

speaker: MORIN
text: As shown in the inset box, the latest claims data point to another sizable drop in employment this month.

speaker: MORIN
text: Turning to spending, sales of light motor vehicles (plotted in the middle left panel) have been dismal of late and are expected to stay that way at least through the end of the year.

speaker: MORIN
text: Motor vehicle sales have been depressed, in part, by financing constraints, limited sales incentives, a retreat by the automakers from leasing, and worsening consumer assessments of car-buying conditions.

speaker: MORIN
text: More broadly, as you can see by comparing the black and red lines in the panel to the right, consumer spending excluding motor vehicles has been significantly softer in recent months than we were expecting.

speaker: MORIN
text: In addition, the conditions influencing consumer outlays have worsened considerably, including a sharp drop in household wealth, tepid real income gains, a weakening labor market picture, historically low levels of sentiment, and reduced credit availability.

speaker: MORIN
text: Consequently, as reported in the inset box, we substantially revised down the projection for overall real PCE in the second half of the year.

speaker: MORIN
text: In the housing sector, single-family starts, shown in the bottom left panel, fell to about 550,000 units in September—6 percent below our expectation.

speaker: MORIN
text: Even with the ongoing cutbacks in production, the weak demand has left the months’ supply of unsold new homes (not plotted) very elevated, and we expect starts to decline well into next year.

speaker: MORIN
text: In the business sector, the spending data in hand are somewhat stale— tomorrow morning we receive the advance reading on durable goods shipments and orders in September—but the information we do have points to softening business investment in the third quarter.

speaker: MORIN
text: Moreover, as shown on the right, the first available surveys on business activity in October plunged to very low levels.

speaker: MORIN
text: Exhibit 2 summarizes the enormous changes to the key conditioning factors that we confronted in putting together the staff forecast.

speaker: MORIN
text: As shown in the top left panel, reflecting the recent plunge in equity prices, the stock market path in this projection is markedly below the path anticipated in our September forecast.

speaker: MORIN
text: This downward revision, together with the projected declines in house prices that Bill Bassett presented in his briefing, leaves the level of the wealth-to-income ratio, plotted to the right, substantially lower than in the September Greenbook.

speaker: MORIN
text: As a result, over the next two years, household wealth exerts a much greater drag on consumer spending than we assumed earlier.

speaker: MORIN
text: Yields and spreads on corporate bonds, illustrated by the Baa rate in the middle left panel, soared over the intermeeting period.

speaker: MORIN
text: We expect the higher cost of capital in this forecast to weigh on business capital spending over the projection period.

speaker: MORIN
text: A further drag on economic activity in the medium term is the recent jump in the exchange value of the dollar, shown to the right.

speaker: MORIN
text: While we expect the dollar to decline a touch more quickly than in the September Greenbook, by the end of 2010 it remains more than 4 percent above the level assumed in our previous forecast.

speaker: MORIN
text: In addition, as Linda Kole will discuss shortly, the outlook for foreign activity has deteriorated.

speaker: MORIN
text: A partial cushion to these factors depressing activity is the plunge in oil prices over the past few weeks; the bottom left panel shows the spot price of West Texas intermediate crude oil.

speaker: MORIN
text: The path for oil prices over the projection period, based on futures quotes, averages nearly $30 per barrel below the September Greenbook path and should provide some countervailing support to household purchasing power and consumer spending.

speaker: MORIN
text: As noted to the right, according to our standard forecasting models, the lower level of equity prices, the higher bond rates, and the higher exchange value of the dollar—all of which are intertwined with the intensification of financial turmoil—exert a considerable drag on real activity over the next two years.

speaker: MORIN
text: Through conventional wealth, cost-of-capital, and terms-of-trade channels alone, these developments would lead us to revise down real GDP growth about 1¼ percentage points, on average, in 2009 and 2010.

speaker: MORIN
text: But these effects likely understate the full extent of the fallout on real activity from financial turmoil.

speaker: MORIN
text: This is because our standard models do not explicitly account for the additional effects of such factors as tighter lending standards and heightened uncertainty.

speaker: MORIN
text: Consequently, for some time we have been using supplementary analyses to try to account for these credit-channel effects in our judgmental projection.

speaker: MORIN
text: Your next exhibit provides some detail on how we updated these adjustments in light of the intensification of financial stress during the intermeeting period.

speaker: MORIN
text: Two measures that we have found useful for measuring the extent of financial turmoil are plotted in the top row of your third exhibit.

speaker: MORIN
text: On the left is an index of financial market stress, and on the right is an index of bank credit standards derived from the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey.

speaker: MORIN
text: Both indexes have skyrocketed lately, reflecting the sharp deterioration of financial conditions.

speaker: MORIN
text: As discussed in the past two Greenbooks, we use two basic empirical approaches to try to quantify the effects of financial turmoil on real activity that are not captured by our standard models: One is based on the historical correlations between these financial turmoil measures and errors in FRB/US spending equations, and the second method incorporates these indicators of turmoil into small-scale vector autoregressions.

speaker: MORIN
text: The middle left panel shows estimates of the cumulative effect of our judgmental adjustments for financial turmoil, outside the conventional channels noted earlier.

speaker: MORIN
text: The effects are shown relative to the level of real GDP in the fourth quarter of each year.

speaker: MORIN
text: The solid black line is the judgmental estimate built into the current Greenbook forecast, whereas the red dashed line plots the estimates used in the September projection.

speaker: MORIN
text: The shaded area shows the range of results from the model-based estimates detailed in Part 1 of the October Greenbook.

speaker: MORIN
text: As you can see by comparing the black and red lines, we now expect that financial turmoil, outside the usual channels, will impose a markedly greater drag on real activity than we projected in the last Greenbook.

speaker: MORIN
text: For 2008, we think that much of the unexpected weakness observed recently in the spending data reflects financial turmoil effects, which puts our judgmental adjustment near the bottom of the model-based range.

speaker: MORIN
text: In contrast, our adjustment for 2009 is in the middle of the range of model-based results, whereas for 2010 our adjustment is near the top end of the range.

speaker: MORIN
text: We are more optimistic than the models for 2010 in part because none of the model-based estimates fully accounts for what we assume will be the likely restorative effects over time of the actions taken by governments to mitigate the problems afflicting the financial system.

speaker: MORIN
text: As shown in the middle right panel, these restraining influences, taken together, led us to mark down our assumed path for the federal funds rate.

speaker: MORIN
text: We now assume that the funds rate is lowered to ½ percent by early next year and is held at that level until mid-2010.

speaker: MORIN
text: Although the path for the funds rate is appreciably lower than we had assumed in the September Greenbook, the additional monetary easing only partially offsets the greater restraint on activity from the other factors shaping the projection.

speaker: MORIN
text: All told, as shown in the first line of the table at the bottom of the page, we project that real GDP will fall at an annual rate of nearly 1 percent in the first half of 2009 and then turn up modestly in the second half.

speaker: MORIN
text: In 2010—with the drag on activity from the strains in financial markets beginning to ease, housing market conditions stabilizing, and an accommodative monetary policy in place—activity accelerates further, and real GDP increases 2.3 percent over the four quarters of the year.

speaker: MORIN
text: The contributions of selected domestic spending categories to changes in real GDP are shown in lines 3 to 5.

speaker: MORIN
text: As you can see, we think that consumption will begin to recover next year and that the drag from housing will diminish over time.

speaker: MORIN
text: In contrast, we expect business fixed investment to remain quite weak next year, reflecting in part the lagged effects on investment of declining business output, the high cost of capital, and heightened uncertainty.

speaker: MORIN
text: Although each of the major components of private domestic demand contributes to the acceleration in economic activity in 2010, the contribution to growth from net exports (line 6) is expected to turn slightly negative late next year.

speaker: MORIN
text: As shown in the top panels of exhibit 4, the margin of slack both in labor markets (the panel to the left) and in the industrial sector (the panel to the right) is expected to remain substantial through the end of the projection period.

speaker: MORIN
text: We expect this persistent slack to be a source of downward pressure on inflation.

speaker: MORIN
text: Other influences are also likely to hold down inflation over the projection period.

speaker: MORIN
text: As shown in the middle panels, energy prices and core goods import prices decelerate sharply from their recent elevated paces.

speaker: MORIN
text: The projected path for consumer energy prices (the left panel) largely reflects the effect of the intermeeting plunge in oil prices, and the forecast for core import prices (the right panel) reflects both the sharp drop in commodity prices and the stronger dollar.

speaker: MORIN
text: As shown in the bottom left panel, while the Michigan survey readings on near-term inflation expectations have remained elevated (the black line), those on longer-term inflation (the red line) have more than retraced the run-up observed earlier this year.

speaker: MORIN
text: Taken together, as shown in line 7 of the bottom right panel, we now expect core PCE inflation to move down to 1½ percent in 2009 and to slow further to 1¼ percent in 2010, roughly ½ percentage point less in each year than projected previously.

speaker: MORIN
text: Total PCE inflation (line 1) is projected to run at about the same rate as core PCE inflation in both years.

speaker: MORIN
text: Turning to exhibit 5, a critical feature of the staff forecast is our assumption that the strains in financial markets will ease gradually over the next two years.

speaker: MORIN
text: However, the current situation is so extraordinary, in terms of both the financial disruptions and the policy responses to those disruptions, that an extremely wide band of uncertainty surrounds this assumption: Matters could easily turn out much worse or much better.

speaker: MORIN
text: To give some sense of possible magnitudes, this exhibit reviews two alternative scenarios from the Greenbook.

speaker: MORIN
text: In the first scenario, outlined in the top left panel, financial turmoil intensifies further over the projection period rather than gradually abating, and the accompanying economic fallout turns out to be more severe than in the baseline projection.

speaker: MORIN
text: Specifically, risk premiums on loans, corporate bonds, and equity jump a further 50 basis points and are slower to fall back over time; in addition, the level of house prices falls an additional 10 percent relative to the baseline.

speaker: MORIN
text: We also assume that credit-channel and other nonconventional effects are even more restrictive in 2009 and 2010 than those built into the staff forecast—to a degree more in line with the bottom end of the range of empirical estimates I presented earlier.

speaker: MORIN
text: As shown by the red line in the middle left panel, with the intensification of the financial turmoil and the larger judgmental adjustments for the impact of financial stress on economic activity, real GDP is significantly weaker than in the baseline (the black line).

speaker: MORIN
text: As a result, the unemployment rate (plotted to the right) rises faster and farther, peaking at nearly 8½ percent at the end of 2010, more than 1 percentage point above the baseline.

speaker: MORIN
text: Reflecting the greater accompanying slack, core PCE inflation (shown in the bottom left panel) moves down appreciably faster than in the baseline, reaching just ¾ percent at the end of 2010.

speaker: MORIN
text: With substantial slack and a low and falling inflation rate, the funds rate remains pinned through 2010 at ½ percent and continues at that level through 2012 in the extended simulation presented in the Greenbook.

speaker: MORIN
text: In the second scenario, outlined in the top right panel, the stress weighing on financial institutions and markets lifts much more quickly than in the baseline, perhaps in response to the extraordinary recent government actions.

speaker: MORIN
text: Here, we assume that risk spreads recede by early next year to the levels that were projected in the September Greenbook, and as a result, equities reverse most of their recent losses by the middle of next year.

speaker: MORIN
text: In addition, we cut back the size of the judgmental adjustments for financial turmoil to their September Greenbook levels.

speaker: MORIN
text: As shown by the blue lines in the middle panels, economic activity responds fairly vigorously to the improvement in financial conditions, with GDP growth reaching about 4½ percent by the end of 2010 and the unemployment rate moving down to 5¾ percent.

speaker: MORIN
text: As shown in the bottom left panel, the narrower margin of slack in the alternative scenario tempers the decline in core PCE inflation relative to baseline.

speaker: MORIN
text: Finally, as shown to the right, the federal funds rate, under an optimal control monetary policy, declines briefly to 1 percent early next year but then moves up steadily as it becomes clear that the financial strains are lifting rapidly.

speaker: MORIN
text: Linda Kole will now continue our presentation.

speaker: KOLE
text: 4 I’m referring to the next exhibits that are attached to the material you are already looking at.

speaker: KOLE
text: Since the September FOMC meeting, financial market distress has intensified and has spread around the world, threatening many emerging market economies that previously had been less affected by the U.S. and European credit crisis.

speaker: KOLE
text: As shown in the top left panel, equity prices have fallen sharply in Europe, 4 The materials used by Ms. Kole are appended to this transcript (appendix 4).

speaker: KOLE
text: Japan, and the United Kingdom.

speaker: KOLE
text: Indeed, the Nikkei is at a 26-year low today.

speaker: KOLE
text: The carnage has been just as pronounced in emerging markets, shown on the right.

speaker: KOLE
text: Credit spreads between industrial countries’ risky corporates and government bonds (plotted in the middle left panel) soared, especially in the euro area; and as shown in the right panel, credit default swap premiums on sovereign debt in many emerging market economies have skyrocketed.

speaker: KOLE
text: The widespread pullback from risk led to safe-haven flows into dollar assets; as shown in the bottom left panel, the dollar appreciated nearly 11 percent against the major currencies (the black line) despite a 9 percent depreciation against the yen (the red line) as carry trades were unwound.

speaker: KOLE
text: The dollar strengthened 9 percent against the currencies of our other important trading partners.

speaker: KOLE
text: As shown on the right, effective exchange values of the currencies of Brazil, Mexico, and Korea were particularly hard hit.

speaker: KOLE
text: In your next exhibit, the top left panel shows the extent to which investors fleeing risk have been liquidating emerging market equity funds.

speaker: KOLE
text: Several foreign governments, notably Russia’s, have fought related currency pressures by drawing down their reserves (the top right panel).

speaker: KOLE
text: For instance, since the peso fell sharply against the dollar in early October, the Bank of Mexico has deployed 15 percent of its reserves to shore up its value.

speaker: KOLE
text: China and Russia have even intervened to stem the fall in their equity prices.

speaker: KOLE
text: Following the collapse of Lehman Brothers, credit markets seized up, and dollar funding needs intensified.

speaker: KOLE
text: Since then, governments around the world have taken several steps to support their banking systems (the middle panel).

speaker: KOLE
text: Some central banks have injected massive amounts of liquidity, and many have cut policy rates or reserve requirements or both.

speaker: KOLE
text: In addition to the countries joining the Fed in a coordinated 50 basis point rate cut on October 8, a wide range of other economies have eased policy lately.

speaker: KOLE
text: Note that there have been a few exceptions: Hungary, Iceland, and Denmark increased rates to counter currency pressures.

speaker: KOLE
text: Governments have also expanded bank deposit insurance and guaranteed new bank lending in order to improve confidence and liquidity.

speaker: KOLE
text: Following a similar initiative in the United Kingdom, euro-area governments announced plans to guarantee the issuance of new medium-term senior debt by banks and to directly assist their recapitalization if necessary.

speaker: KOLE
text: In recent weeks, authorities have announced capital injections into a number of banks whose financial soundness was in question.

speaker: KOLE
text: The swap lines extended by the Federal Reserve to foreign central banks have been expanded.

speaker: KOLE
text: The ECB approved a €5 billion swap line for Hungary and a €12 billion one for Denmark, and several Asian countries are currently negotiating swap lines with each other as well.

speaker: KOLE
text: Private firms in several emerging market economies have confronted pressures in rolling over foreign currency funding, and authorities there have also raised deposit guarantees, guaranteed bank lending, and injected capital into vulnerable banks.

speaker: KOLE
text: Finally, several countries have applied to the IMF for assistance.

speaker: KOLE
text: The bottom left panel shows median credit default swap premiums for banks in Europe, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

speaker: KOLE
text: The declines since the beginning of this month suggest that the announcement of these plans has improved confidence in banks’ safety, even if they have not restored confidence in broader economic prospects.

speaker: KOLE
text: As shown by the implied OIS forward rates in the bottom middle panel, market participants expect considerably more monetary policy easing in Europe than they did at the time of the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: KOLE
text: We assume that further cuts in official rates (shown on the right) will be forthcoming as output falls short of potential and inflation recedes.

speaker: KOLE
text: As can be seen in exhibit 3, highly stressed global financial conditions and the weaker U.S. outlook have led us to take a whack out of our outlook for foreign growth.

speaker: KOLE
text: Comparing lines 1 and 2, we have marked down our estimate of total foreign growth for the third quarter more than 1 percentage point, and we have slashed our forecast even more for Q4 and 2009.

speaker: KOLE
text: We project outright recessions in the advanced foreign economies (lines 3 through 7) and in Mexico (line 12).

speaker: KOLE
text: In other emerging economies, we foresee growth rates well below potential.

speaker: KOLE
text: Chinese real GDP growth (line 10) is estimated to have slowed considerably in the third quarter.

speaker: KOLE
text: We expect some payback in Q4, but beyond that we have revised down our outlook.

speaker: KOLE
text: As can be seen in the middle left panel, exports fell in August in many of our largest trading partners, though they still chugged along in China through September.

speaker: KOLE
text: The black line in the middle panel shows that the volume of exports from Canada has been falling for some time, but exports had held up in Japan and Germany until the third quarter, when they fell.

speaker: KOLE
text: Industrial production in Japan (the red line in the middle right panel) has fallen nearly 5 percent below its year-ago level, and IP has also fallen over the past year in the United Kingdom and the euro area.

speaker: KOLE
text: As global demand has slumped, oil prices (the black line in the bottom left panel) have plummeted, and nonfuel commodity prices have fallen as well.

speaker: KOLE
text: The decline in commodity prices along with slackening economic activity is projected to help bring down inflation in all of the regions shown (on the right).

speaker: KOLE
text: Exhibit 4 focuses on the outlook for Europe.

speaker: KOLE
text: Banks remain leery of lending to each other, as evidenced by the growing amount of funds parked at the ECB’s deposit facility.

speaker: KOLE
text: The latest BoE bank lending survey (the top right panel) pointed to further tightening of U.K. lending standards in the third quarter and suggested that banks expected to tighten them somewhat further in the fourth quarter (the striped bars).

speaker: KOLE
text: Notably, this survey was taken before Lehman failed.

speaker: KOLE
text: A confidential conversation with a contact at the BoE who had talked with a few bankers more recently suggested that the latest survey considerably underestimated the recent tightening of standards.

speaker: KOLE
text: The quarterly growth of U.K. loans to nonfinancial corporations (the red line in the middle left panel) fell from double-digit paces for the past two years to 5 percent in the third quarter.

speaker: KOLE
text: Credit expansion to households (the dashed line) declined as well.

speaker: KOLE
text: Loan growth in the euro area (the middle panel) also slowed.

speaker: KOLE
text: Europe has clearly moved into recession.

speaker: KOLE
text: The middle right panel shows that house prices have fallen over the past year in the United Kingdom and Ireland and have also slowed in other European locales.

speaker: KOLE
text: But it is not just the property sector that has slumped.

speaker: KOLE
text: Business confidence (the bottom left) has disintegrated.

speaker: KOLE
text: Total economy purchasing managers’ indexes (the middle panel) are in the downturn range in both the United Kingdom and the euro area.

speaker: KOLE
text: Unemployment rates have increased, especially in France and Spain, where construction activity has slowed sharply.

speaker: KOLE
text: Your next exhibit takes a quick tour through the rest of the world.

speaker: KOLE
text: In Japan, business confidence (the red line) has plunged, partly because lending terms faced by firms, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, have become more restrictive.

speaker: KOLE
text: Investment intentions (not shown) have deteriorated as shipments (the black line) and exports have declined.

speaker: KOLE
text: The labor market has deteriorated, with the ratio of job offers to applicants (in blue) falling to its lowest level in the past four years.

speaker: KOLE
text: The Bank of Japan recently downgraded its outlook and stepped up measures to deal with financial market stresses.

speaker: KOLE
text: In China, investment spending (the black dashed line in the top right panel) continued to be strong through September, and retail sales accelerated.

speaker: KOLE
text: However, industrial production (middle left panel) slowed this summer partly because of efforts to reduce pollution in Beijing during the August Olympics but also because of declining steel production, suggesting further slowing.

speaker: KOLE
text: Industrial production has also slowed in Korea and Taiwan, and export orders (shown on the right) are falling in China, Brazil, and Singapore.

speaker: KOLE
text: As shown in the bottom left panel, Mexico has suffered a steep fall in remittances, flattening industrial production, and declining auto exports.

speaker: KOLE
text: Oil revenues (not shown) are down as well.

speaker: KOLE
text: Finally, global PMI and new orders indexes, which aggregate data for 26 major countries, are both in contractionary territory but have not yet reached their depths at the trough of the 2001 recession.

speaker: KOLE
text: Exhibit 6 reviews the main elements of the U.S. external outlook.

speaker: KOLE
text: As shown in line 1 of the top panel, net exports contributed 1.8 percentage points to growth in the first half of this year, but we expect this contribution to drop off considerably in coming quarters as exports (line 3) slow with foreign growth and imports (line 5) remain flat.

speaker: KOLE
text: Total foreign growth (the black line in the middle left panel) is now projected to dip down about as much as U.S. growth, while the dollar (shown on the right) is well above the level we projected in the September Greenbook.

speaker: KOLE
text: As shown in line 3 of the table, we now expect export growth to move down sharply starting in the current quarter and to remain well below what we’d written down in our last forecast.

speaker: KOLE
text: Although lower U.S. demand caused us to lower import growth (line 5), the projected contribution of net exports to GDP growth has, on net, been revised down a bit over the forecast period.

speaker: KOLE
text: The bottom panel gives a longer perspective on U.S. external deficits.

speaker: KOLE
text: The non-oil trade deficit (the dashed orange line) and current account deficit (the red line) have continued to narrow over the past year and a half although oil imports have remained large.

speaker: KOLE
text: The current account deficit to GDP ratio is forecast to fall below 3 percent in 2010, a level last reached in 1998.

speaker: KOLE
