text: Brian Madigan will continue with our presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 5 I will be referring to the separate package labeled “Material for Briefing on FOMC Participants’ Economic Projections.” Exhibit 1 shows the central tendencies and ranges of your current forecasts for 2008; corresponding information about the Committee’s most recent projections, those from June, is shown in italics, and Greenbook projections are included as a memo item.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your June projections regarding GDP growth and inflation for the first half of 2008 turned out to be quite close to subsequent BEA data releases; therefore, the revisions in your 5 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 5).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: projections for the year as a whole are almost entirely due to the changes in your implicit projections for the second half of 2008.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the right column of the top panel, your GDP growth forecasts for 2008:H2 now range from minus 2½ percent to minus ¾ percent; compared with June, each of you has marked down your projection for second-half growth by at least 2 percentage points.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the second panel, your forecasts of the fourth- quarter average unemployment rate fall in a range of 6.3 to 6.6 percent, more than ½ percentage point higher than in June.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In accounting for the sharp deterioration in the near-term outlook for activity, your narratives point to the intensification of the financial crisis and its impact on credit conditions and stock market wealth as well as the weakness of incoming data on consumer spending and labor market conditions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your assessments of inflation in 2008 have also shifted significantly since June.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendency of your forecasts for overall PCE inflation during 2008:H2 (the right column of the third panel) is now about 1½ to 2¼ percent, a drop of about 2 percentage points from June.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In this regard, a number of you noted the implications of recent sharp declines in energy and commodity prices that were apparently triggered by the worldwide slowdown in economic activity.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In contrast, your projections for core PCE inflation in 2008:H2 (the right column of the bottom panel) are a notch higher than in June.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Exhibit 2 reports your projections for the next three calendar years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you anticipate little or no GDP growth during 2009; as with your implicit forecasts for the second half of 2008, these projections are about 2 percentage points lower than in June.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A few of you are projecting even weaker outcomes, with output declining about 1 percent, whereas a few others are projecting stronger economic growth of about 1½ to 1¾ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The width of both the ranges and the central tendencies of your projections for real GDP growth for 2009 and 2010 has increased noticeably.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Still, all of you anticipate that economic expansion will resume by 2010, and most of you expect a further pickup in growth during 2011.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the narratives accompanying these projections, a number of you said that you expect the pace of recovery to be damped by persistent credit market strains, ongoing adjustment in the housing market, and economic weakness abroad.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Apparently, only a few of you assumed that additional fiscal stimulus would be enacted.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you project that the unemployment rate will peak at around 7 to 7½ percent in 2009 and decline gradually over the subsequent two years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, you generally expect that, even by the end of 2011, the unemployment rate will still be at or above 5½ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, most of you anticipate that the unemployment rate in 2011 will remain well above your own projections of the longer-run unemployment rate that were provided in your trial-run submissions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendency of your projections for overall PCE inflation is about 1¼ to 2 percent for 2009 and about 1½ to 1¾ percent for 2010 and 2011—roughly the same as for your forecasts of core PCE inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: About half of you projected inflation rates in 2011 close or identical to your own individual assessments of the rate of inflation consistent with Federal Reserve’s dual mandate for promoting price stability and maximum employment, where we have again judged the latter from your longer- term trial-run submissions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But half of you are projecting that inflation in 2011 will be below your own individual assessments of the mandate-consistent inflation rate by about ¼ to ½ percentage point, and in one case, by more than 1 percentage point, mainly reflecting the lagged effects of weak economic activity and the relatively sluggish pace of recovery.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In your forecast submissions, several of you indicated that the appropriate path of monetary policy would involve less near-term easing than assumed in the Greenbook, and more than half of you expressed the view that policy tightening would need to occur several quarters earlier and at a substantially more rapid pace than in the Greenbook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Exhibit 3 presents your views on the risks and uncertainties in the outlook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the top left-hand panel, all of you now see uncertainty about growth as elevated relative to historical norms.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown to the right, most of you continue to perceive the risks to growth as weighted to the downside even with the downward revision in your modal projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Several of you pointed to the possibility that financial market turmoil might not subside as quickly as anticipated and to significant risks of an increasingly negative feedback loop between credit markets and economic activity.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the bottom left-hand panel, most of you also continue to see an elevated degree of uncertainty about inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In June, most of you judged the risks to the inflation outlook as skewed to the upside, but as shown to the right, nearly all of you now see the risks to the inflation outlook as either balanced or tilted to the downside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Exhibit 4 summarizes the results of the trial run on longer-term projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: These projections were intended to represent values to which variables would converge over time, say five to six years ahead, under the assumption of appropriate monetary policy and in the absence of any further shocks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For real GDP growth, your longer-term projections have a central tendency of 2½ to 2¾ percent and a range of about 2 to 3 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For the unemployment rate, your longer-run projections have a central tendency of 4¾ to 5 percent and a range of about 4½ to 5¾ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For both variables, the central tendencies are very similar to those of the projections for 2010 that you made in October 2007, shown in the bottom panel, a point at which many of you viewed the modal outlook for 2010 as being fairly close to the balanced growth path of the economy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For PCE inflation, your longer-run projections have a central tendency of about 1¾ percent and a range of 1½ to 2 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The range of these projections is identical to the range of two-year-ahead inflation projections that you made last October; the minutes from that meeting indicated that those projections were influenced importantly by your judgments about the measured rates of inflation consistent with the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate of promoting price stability and maximum employment.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The request for the trial-run projections suggested that convergence might typically occur over a period of five to six years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One of you noted that the convergence process this time will likely occur over an even longer period because of the severity of the economic crisis.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, apparently most of you thought that convergence would occur sooner than that, suggesting that the configuration of this trial run produces a good representation of FOMC participants’ views of the steady state values of GDP growth, unemployment, and inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As usual, the staff will be preparing a summary of economic projections (SEP) and will be circulating drafts to you over the next few weeks along with drafts of the minutes.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The published SEP, and hence the drafts, will not incorporate the longer- term projections from the trial run.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The staff will provide to you separately a version of the SEP that has been modified to incorporate the longer-term projections generated by the trial run.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The subcommittee will consult with the Chairman about next steps.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One possibility would be for the Committee to discuss experience with the trial run at its December meeting and make a provisional decision at that time as to whether to proceed in January with regular longer-term projections; a final decision could be made in January.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Before we go too long, we’ll take a coffee break, but now let’s take some questions.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the forecast, the federal funds rate goes to 50 basis points, and I take it that’s essentially as low as you think it can go.

speaker: LACKER
text: You treat that as sort of the lower bound on nominal interest rates.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That’s how we were thinking of it.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The 50 basis points, however, was not done on the basis of any deep analytical analysis of whether that, in fact, is the zero bound, and I think that’s an issue that the staff will need to address pronto.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the message in the forecast with that funds rate path was that we think this shock is large enough that you will need to lower the funds rate as low as you think it can feasibly go.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, whatever that lower bound is, I have a question that’s kind of hypothetical.

speaker: LACKER
text: I wasn’t a member of the Committee five years ago.

speaker: LACKER
text: My understanding, though, is that much thought was given to how we would conduct monetary policy if we needed to reduce the nominal federal funds rate to zero or its effective equivalent.

speaker: LACKER
text: My understanding is that the general conclusion—and my understanding is that this is mainstream economists’ general view as well—is that the way we would do that would be to expand the monetary base, perhaps by buying assets outside the normal range of assets that we would buy.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, the first question is, Is that correct?

speaker: LACKER
text: Then I have a follow-up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You can answer, but let me just make a suggestion, which is that there were a number of memos and studies done in 2003.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we ought to look at them, update them, and circulate them fairly soon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we’ll do this in some detail; but by all means, let’s hear the answer.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: President Lacker, I would say that there are a number of strategies that the Committee could think about if it were at the point that it felt it couldn’t lower the federal funds rate any further, be that zero or some higher level.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One would be communications that suggest to market participants a willingness to hold short-term rates at very low levels for a very long period of time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, one could view the 2003 experience as implementing that strategy with the “considerable period” language.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But obviously the idea is to try to hold down the longer-term rates that matter for spending to a larger degree than might be implied by market participants’ views that you might instead begin to firm monetary policy sooner.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: There are a number of other possibilities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As you suggest, one would be simply to expand the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet further—engage in a sort of quantitative easing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The effectiveness of that could be debated.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Another possibility that was discussed, at least in the period in which the studies were done, would be to change the composition of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, we’ve already done a lot of that with the various lending facilities, and so the scope for additional expansion there would need to be thought through.

speaker: LACKER
text: The reason I ask is that my understanding is that the strategy of expanding the monetary base would work through increasing inflation or reducing deflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That’s not how I would think about it.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I would think about it as giving, if it works, depository institutions increased incentives to expand their lending by providing them with a great deal more funding than they actually need and thereby increasing spending propensities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I would see this more as part of a package of various ways to stimulate spending by reducing real interest rates but not as something that would feed through directly to inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Rather this would more properly be viewed, at least in the way I think about things, as fighting deflation rather than trying to cause a higher positive rate of inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: My understanding is that economists such as Woodford and others who have studied this believe that, by using monetary assets to purchase other assets, we can make the price level and thus the inflation rate higher than it otherwise would be.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is that a fair understanding?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think that’s right.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the thrust of the elementary approach to quantitative easing is the old Milton Friedman idea—that changing the composition of money and other assets changes relative returns.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it’s a way to bring down returns on other assets and create stimulus even if the policy rate is down to zero.

speaker: LACKER
text: The mechanism Friedman sketched ultimately produces a proportionate increase in the price level, doesn’t it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Eventually, but through the aggregate demand mechanism.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should look at the Woodford thing, but I don’t think that’s quite the right characterization of his view.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, the reason I ask all of this is that, with an interest rate on reserves above zero, that’s effectively equivalent to a zero lower bound on nominal interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: So we are effectively doing this quantitative easing.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the thought that sparks is that, if the mechanism involves creating inflation, then I’d wonder what checks we have on the scale of open market operations now to ensure that we’re not, by expanding our balance sheet as much as we have, risking an increase in inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think that’s the right characterization, but I’d be happy to talk about it off line.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As you characterized the forecast in the Greenbook, it is really the result of very large adjustments to the financial constraints piece—in fact, they’re about double what they were in the September Greenbook—and those adjustments or factors really account for a large portion, maybe not all, of the downward revision in the forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, one of the inputs in the financial factors are spreads of various kinds in the VARs that you used to estimate those.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But those spreads we’ve learned are very, very volatile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They can rise very quickly, as we’ve seen.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They also can fall very quickly sometimes.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Spreads have actually come down a little in the last few days, which is the good news.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If our facilities are successful, they actually may fall further—knock on wood; that would be very nice.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I get a little nervous making our forecast be driven so much by something that’s potentially very, very volatile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, we get a bit of a picture of this—and I want to applaud the staff—in I guess it was exhibit 5, where you were comparing the baseline forecast and the two alternative scenarios, particularly the one in which you get quicker recovery in the financial sector.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I thought that was a very useful exercise, and I really appreciate it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My interpretation or intuition is that the “more rapid financial recovery” scenario is what the forecast would look like had we not done the additional add factors in October and instead held them to what they were in September.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That suggests that the real data, whether on spending or other things, have driven the forecast down a little, but not a whole lot.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, in that scenario, you imply that the funds rate would actually be held constant at 1½ percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So, in looking at those two scenarios and trying to parse out how much risk or how much probability to attach to them, what is the staff’s view?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Obviously here’s what you thought the baseline would be, but if I ask you what you think the probabilities are on some of these different scenarios—in particular, I’m interested in this sort of faster recovery—do you have any sense of what the probabilities of these two different outcomes might be and how one might think about that?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They imply very different paths for the funds rate and very different forecast profiles, but their differences depend on variables that are very, very volatile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So can you give me some probabilities of how you think about those two scenarios?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I can give you some probabilities, but I don’t know how seriously you should take them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You can give me a distribution.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: What we wanted to convey in the alternative scenarios that we showed this time—and we reduced the number because we thought the possible little risks that you might be facing were being swamped by some really big ones—was our sense that the likelihood function is pretty flat around the baseline and the two alternative scenarios that we show here in exhibit 5.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As I was telling President Evans at lunch today, I feel a bit as though the forecast is going to depend a lot on when the clock stopped, given how much volatility there has been in the stock market and in corporate spreads.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: When the clock stopped, we had close to a 25 percent weaker level on the stock market, 200 basis points higher on the Baa spread, and a 7 percent higher dollar.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There were a whole lot of negative forces operating on this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, both the conventional wealth effect and cost-of-capital channels account for about one-third of the downward revision we made.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The special nonconventional credit channel effects account for a third, and a third of the downward revision really is a combination of the stronger dollar and the weaker foreign outlook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The part that I feel most comfortable with in this forecast is that there has been a very significant negative shock to the economy and that it is difficult to imagine that activity will not be affected importantly by that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The part that I feel most uncertain about—and, as you point out, is relevant to the policy decisions that you are going to make over the next several meetings—is that I have no idea about the timing or the manner in which this will fade away.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So we have it fading away gradually over the next two years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think that a more rapid recovery is certainly a possibility.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you noted, even that scenario doesn’t go back to where we were in September.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One, the incoming data suggest that the underlying economy is starting out at a weaker place, and even if conditions were to improve very rapidly over the next quarter or two, you have still sustained a hit that is going to take some time to play out through the system.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: By the same token, I don’t think that you can discount the more extended and deeper financial fallout here.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have certainly been surprised over the past year in many ways by just how virulent and persistent this shock has been.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Two, looking at the current state of aggregate demand and aggregate activity, I think we are probably still just at the front edge of the credit constraint effects on actual spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So you could still be faced with some very substantial restraint on spending—and more than we have built into the baseline forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So, and as you noted, the difference in the policy prescriptions there—the worse scenario is that the funds rate stays as low as it can stay for several years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other would be—putting too fine a point on it—that optimal control, even with the more rapid recovery, goes down to 1 percent on the funds rate and then starts recovering to 1½ percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But that is obviously a very different policy picture.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I just don’t think that, at this point, science is going to allow us to put a lot of probability mass on one of those scenarios versus the other two.

speaker: MORIN
text: In exhibit 3, in the middle left panel, if you look at our financial turmoil effects, with the gray shading, the bulk of the markdown in 2008 actually is what we’re labeling the financial turmoil.

speaker: MORIN
text: But those are data we pretty much already have in hand.

speaker: MORIN
text: We are calling much of the shortfall in consumption that we expect to see in the third quarter as “financial turmoil.” So much of the weakness in the second half of this year isn’t just taking a flyer on what we think turmoil is going to do; some of it is already in the data.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was looking at the table in the Greenbook, at the bottom.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That’s where I was trying to back out some of this.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have a question and a statement disguised as a question.

speaker: FISHER
text: A quick question on fiscal policy, both domestic and international.

speaker: FISHER
text: Being struck, Ms. Kole, by your verbs “whacked” and “disintegrated”—very forceful language—what are your assumptions about fiscal policy in terms of staff projections, first, for the domestic economy and, second, for other economies?

speaker: MORIN
text: Right now, although the odds are that there will be a fiscal package next year, it is not a feature of the baseline forecast.

speaker: MORIN
text: We discussed two alternative simulations for different packages, but additional fiscal stimulus is not a feature of the baseline.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We made a deliberate decision in constructing the forecast, given the enormous uncertainty about both the size and the composition of those fiscal packages.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We had so many moving parts in our baseline forecast that we wanted to present you with that and then show you what the consequences might be, first, of a stimulus package that looks a lot like the one we had this year—which we think probably gave a shock, but a very short-lived shock, to aggregate demand and then faded away.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That doesn’t really have many important consequences for the outlook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The second was a much larger package that delivered some stimulus over the next two years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That had a bit of an effect in terms of raising GDP growth and lowering the unemployment rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But even that $300 billion fiscal package wasn’t enough, in our baseline forecast, to lift the funds rate assumption off the floor.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I think one of the messages would be that, to have a fiscal package that would actually influence your current policy discussion, you have to think both that it would be extremely large and that it would deliver stimulus over an extended period of time to be effective that way.

speaker: KOLE
text: I think that in many of the major foreign countries there is room for fiscal stimulus.

speaker: KOLE
text: That may be a bit of an upside risk to our forecast because, for example, China has already put some things in place.

speaker: KOLE
text: They have increased exporter rebates, and they are also putting more money into homebuilding and trying to prop up the construction industry.

speaker: KOLE
text: Japan just announced a bigger package.

speaker: KOLE
text: I’m not so sure if it will go through.

speaker: KOLE
text: Korea has announced—and even some of the oil producers are announcing—plans to put money into the system.

speaker: KOLE
text: I don’t think we have fully incorporated that.

speaker: KOLE
text: Maybe we have thought about it in China’s case because we think that they will do everything they need to do to keep that economy growing at a—

speaker: FISHER
text: So it’s possible that we might have marginally higher rates of growth than—

speaker: KOLE
text: I think that the United Kingdom, too, is expanding fiscal policy.

speaker: KOLE
text: Europe hasn’t really announced much yet, but perhaps they will do more as well.

speaker: FISHER
text: The second thing goes back to this business of the judgmental effects of financial market turmoil.

speaker: FISHER
text: Do you have any concern that the financial turmoil may have reduced the marginal effectiveness of changes in the funds rate?

speaker: FISHER
text: In other words, if you think in my simple way of a patient on the operating table, we have an IV tube into them, we titrate the fed funds rate—we have been cutting rates—but the tube has been crimped.

speaker: FISHER
text: The flow, I would suggest may not be as full as it would have been before.

speaker: FISHER
text: Is it possible that we haven’t felt the full effects or, all things being equal, we haven’t felt the same effects that we would have felt if the pipes hadn’t been crimped?

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m curious as to your view on that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The answer to that is “yes”—it is certainly possible.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, it is very difficult to separate things that might actually have changed the transmission channel of monetary policy from just big financial developments that have offset the beneficial effects of easing policy.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We built an assumption into the baseline forecast that GDP responds close to the average response to a fed funds rate reduction, as would normally be the case.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The one small technical area in which it seems as though the effect almost certainly would be smaller is that, with the equity premium so high right now, any given change in the funds rate is likely to result in a smaller change in the required return on equity and probably a smaller stock market response than you would normally get.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So I think, basically, it is certainly possible, but in our forecast we have assumed that the additional reductions will have GDP consequences along the lines of the normal response.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take fifteen minutes for coffee, and then we’ll do part of the go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, why don’t we turn part of our dinner period to the go- round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s start with President Lockhart.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Most of the anecdotal information from the Sixth District is consistent with the downbeat picture that has been emerging in the national data.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The sentiment of directors and their contacts has turned decidedly more pessimistic regarding current economic conditions and the near-term outlook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Banking contacts indicate a further tightening of credit standards, while stresses on household and small business finances have resulted in increased credit card usage.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A state economic-development official noted that some banks have halted their 90/10 SBA lending.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Bankers active in the VRDN (variable rate demand note) market noted that municipalities are under pressure with declining revenues and higher financing costs.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Nonresidential building contractors noted a large increase in the number of canceled projects.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Advisory council members described a substantial decline in domestic shipping and transport activity for most goods, other than energy products, and some slowing of export volumes through regional ports.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Finally, retail contacts, in anticipation of the coming holiday season, noted that orders are down, and heavy price discounting has begun already.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Thematically, Atlanta’s forecast is consistent with the Greenbook, but we are projecting a slightly more severe and protracted downturn in business activity than the Greenbook baseline.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My assumption is that the cascading dynamic at work in the financial markets may take longer than projected in the Greenbook to come to an end.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As a consequence, I view the Greenbook’s scenario entitled “more financial fallout” as the most plausible storyline among the likely range of outcomes.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I should acknowledge that we’re in an interval between the announcement of the TARP and its full implementation.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The encouraging improvement in credit spreads and term funding we have seen in recent days may accelerate once the TARP is operational.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: With inflation abating more or less as expected and with such uncertainty surrounding the playing out of continuing and recently worsening turmoil in the financial markets, I have to view the balance of risks as more negative for growth than upside for inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I think it is clear that inflation has been rolled over by the steamroller of the credit crisis.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am not going to belabor what I have heard from the CEOs I have spoken to.

speaker: FISHER
text: Basically, the best summary is that things have gone from interesting to unbelievable.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have had an implosion of economic activity.

speaker: FISHER
text: Business women and men, not having any pricing power, are doing what you would expect them to do: They are cutting their costs of goods sold, which means they are shedding head count dramatically.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are stretching out their ROI assumptions, and they are cutting back on cap-ex and, basically, assuming pro-cyclical behavior on the downside.

speaker: FISHER
text: I doubt that any of us are going to report anything different, particularly since I think I am in a District that, relatively speaking, is still strong.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would hope that during our discussions today we would each take the time, or at least ask, for some response.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would like some response from you in particular.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is no question about that.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are in dire straits.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is no inflationary tail, or if there is, it is completely flattened in terms of the foreseeable future.

speaker: FISHER
text: The risks are to the downside on economic growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: A question I have is, What do we do next?

speaker: FISHER
text: Actually, I should address the issue of what we do first.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t think doing dribbles and drabs is an answer.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we just do nothing—and I could make that case because we’ve done an awful lot—or we do something that is a firm statement.

speaker: FISHER
text: But in response to that statement, the question has to be, What do we do as next steps?

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m particularly curious about whether or not we address during this meeting, and tonight and tomorrow, not only next steps but what the end game is.

speaker: FISHER
text: Where do we want to be?

speaker: FISHER
text: How long are we going to be there, and eventually, how do we exit?

speaker: FISHER
text: But that is, of course, the ultimate question that I think we can delay.

speaker: FISHER
text: So, Mr. Chairman, I’d like to suggest that we not go through our standard ritual of reading about our Districts and so on because I don’t think there is going to be a whole lot of difference.

speaker: FISHER
text: The real question is, What do we do about it, and what’s the cognitive road map from here?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, I for one will certainly give my response to that at the appropriate time, and we need to hear from everybody.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But everyone is obviously free to talk about whatever they want to talk about.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In the run-up to Halloween, we have had a witch’s brew of news.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The downward trajectory of economic data has been hair-raising—with employment, consumer sentiment, spending and orders for capital goods, and homebuilding all contracting—and conditions in financial and credit markets have taken a ghastly turn for the worse.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is becoming abundantly clear that we are in the midst of a serious global meltdown.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Like the Board staff, I have slashed my forecast for economic activity and now foresee a recession with four straight quarters of negative growth starting last quarter.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I wish that I could claim that I place a lot of confidence in the sobering forecast, but I am sorry to say I can’t.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In fact, I think we will be lucky if the adverse feedback loop that is under way doesn’t wrench us into a much more pronounced and more protracted downturn.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The outlook for inflation has shifted markedly, too, with the days of heightened upside inflation risks behind us.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In fact, I am concerned that beyond next year we run the risk of inflation falling below the level consistent with price stability.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even before the extraordinary deterioration in financial market conditions over the past few weeks, there were numerous signs that the economy had weakened dramatically.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I won’t recite the litany of disappointing data but instead try to touch upon some high, or I guess I should say low, notes based on what my contacts tell me.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They are consistent with President Fisher’s observations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Consumer purchases of durable goods, especially motor vehicles, have been particularly hard hit by the one–two punch of tight credit and reeling consumer confidence.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The mood on showroom floors is downright grim.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One auto dealer in my District reports that he is now experiencing the worst period in his thirty-plus years in the business.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A home appliance retailer adds that he has never seen more uncertainty and gloom from both the retailers and the vendors.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This sentiment is echoed by a large retailer who says simply, “The holiday shopping season is going to stink.” Businesses are under siege from weak demand, high costs of borrowing, curtailed credit availability, and pervasive uncertainty about how long such conditions will last.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Our contacts report that bank lines of credit are more difficult to negotiate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Many have become more cautious in managing liquidity and in committing to capital spending projects that can be deferred.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They are even cutting back trade credit to customers.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even firms that are currently in good shape report that they are hunkering down, cutting back on all but essential spending, and preparing for the worst.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Our venture capital and private equity contacts tell us that they are instructing their portfolio companies to cut costs, put expansion plans on hold, and draw down existing credit lines.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The market for commercial mortgage-backed securities has all but dried up, and lenders have also become less willing to extend funding.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With financing unavailable, I am hearing talk about substantial cutbacks on new projects and planned improvements on existing buildings, as well as the potential for distress sales of properties whose owners will be unable to roll over debt as it matures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The deterioration in overall financial conditions since the September FOMC meeting is truly shocking.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even with today’s 900-point increase in the Dow, broad indexes are still down about 20 percent, and the latest data suggest house prices in a freefall.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Baa corporate bonds are up about 200 basis points since our last meeting, low-grade corporate bonds are up a staggering 700 basis points, and to top it all, the dollar has appreciated nearly 10 percent against the currencies of our trading partners.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The sharp deterioration in financial and credit conditions will weigh heavily on economic activity for some time.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition, prospects for the one remaining cylinder in the engine of growth—namely, net exports—are bleak owing to the slowdown in global demand and the appreciation of the dollar.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We now expect real GDP to decline at an annual rate of 1¼ percent in the second half of this year and to register two more negative quarters in the first half of next year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That forecast is predicated on cutting the funds rate to ½ percent by January, as assumed in the Greenbook, and also is premised on another fiscal package.

speaker: YELLEN
text: An absolutely critical pre-condition for the economy to recover next year is for the financial system to get back on its feet.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In that regard, I have been greatly heartened by the important actions that the Treasury, the FDIC, the Fed, foreign governments, and other central banks have taken in recent weeks to improve liquidity and inject capital into the financial systems.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But we are fighting an uphill battle against falling home prices, an economy in recession, and collapsing confidence.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is not clear whether these steps will reopen credit flows to households and businesses, especially those with less than sterling credit.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Under the Greenbook forecast we will see further large declines in housing prices over the next two years.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Banks and other financial institutions will likely suffer larger losses than many had anticipated, and that will mute the impact of recent capital injections.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The interaction of higher unemployment and rising delinquencies raises the potential for even greater losses by banks and other financial institutions and for an intensification of the adverse feedback loop we have worried about and are now experiencing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Such a sequence of events plausibly could lead to outcomes described in the “more financial fallout” alternative scenario in the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There are considerable downside risks to the near-term outlook as well.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I mentioned, the most recent economic data have consistently surprised on the downside, and I see a real risk that the data may continue to come in weaker in the near term than the Greenbook has assumed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, a dynamic factor model that my staff regularly uses is much more pessimistic in the near term than is the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This model aggregates the information contained in more than 140 data series.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Based on the most recent economic and financial data available, this model predicts that real GDP will fall 2½ percent in the fourth quarter.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The model’s pessimism reflects the combination of the recent weak data releases for the month of September, followed by the abysmal data that we have available so far for October, including financial market prices, regional business surveys, and consumer sentiment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Turning to inflation, the most recent data have been encouraging.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Looking forward, the sharp decline in commodity prices, especially oil prices, will bring headline inflation down relatively quickly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: More fundamentally, the considerable slack in labor and product markets will put downward pressure on the underlying rate of inflation over the next few years.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A number of my contacts already report that their businesses are working on lower margins in the more challenging economic environment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I expect headline PCE price inflation to decline to about 1½ percent in 2009 and core PCE price inflation to be 1¾ percent next year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I expect both inflation rates to edge down to 1¼ percent in 2010.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the sizable downside risk to the forecast for growth, the risks to the inflation forecast are likewise weighted to the downside.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In conclusion, I think the present situation obviously calls for an easing of policy, as I assumed in my forecast.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the seriousness of the situation, I believe that we should put as much stimulus into the system as we can as soon as we can.

speaker: EVANS
text: In spite of the fact that I am going to validate what President Fisher said in terms of content, I am reminded of what candidate Ronald Reagan said in 1980 against George Bush.

speaker: EVANS
text: To paraphrase, “I paid for the plane ticket down here.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m going to tell you what I learned.” Pessimism is running deep, and no one I spoke with this round was immune to the current economic and financial turmoil.

speaker: EVANS
text: Even contacts who have sworn for months that their prudent financial management had insulated them from funding difficulties now report being stressed.

speaker: EVANS
text: The speed of the turnaround in sentiment has been breathtaking.

speaker: EVANS
text: Some of these new reports about changes in financing conditions came from large manufacturing firms that had been doing well this cycle.

speaker: EVANS
text: For example, John Deere noted that its financing subsidiary was having difficulty rolling medium-term notes that fund their customer leases.

speaker: EVANS
text: This seems symptomatic of financial stress because the subsidiary has a large capital cushion with high-value collateral backing the leases.

speaker: EVANS
text: Caterpillar did have better luck getting such funding but only because it went to the market during a very brief window when lenders were actively seeking customers with high credit quality.

speaker: EVANS
text: I also heard numerous reports of businesses having difficulty renewing long- standing lending arrangements with their banks; and for those who were able to get new loans, the terms were typically viewed as unattractive—at least they felt so.

speaker: EVANS
text: Several Chicago directors indicated that businesses were successfully tapping existing loan commitments and revolving credit, much along the lines that President Yellen just mentioned.

speaker: EVANS
text: However, this was not greeted enthusiastically by their bankers.

speaker: EVANS
text: In fact, I heard a very interesting story about a major New York bank CEO who spent some time in Chicago a couple of years ago.

speaker: EVANS
text: He was calling a large customer to assure him that their credit lines were good and that they didn’t need to be taken down preemptively.

speaker: EVANS
text: The customer, who is our chairman, listened politely and then tapped the line anyway.

speaker: EVANS
text: No wonder banks are worried about their liquidity position.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to nonfinancial developments, reports on both current and expected real activity have turned uniformly more negative.

speaker: EVANS
text: An abrupt change occurred in September.

speaker: EVANS
text: People are spooked—sorry—[laughter] and it is showing through to spending.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have grown accustomed to the inherent pessimism of one of my retail contacts.

speaker: EVANS
text: He has often said that business has never been weaker in 40 years, but this time he said never in 46 years.

speaker: EVANS
text: I also heard many reports about how the slowing in demand is worldwide.

speaker: EVANS
text: In my District, the sharp slowdown is evident in the Chicago purchasing managers’ index.

speaker: EVANS
text: In October, it plunged nearly 20 points, to 37.8, the lowest level since the last recession in May 2001.

speaker: EVANS
text: This index will be publicly released on Friday.

speaker: EVANS
text: Businesses appear to be responding to the drop in demand by doing anything and everything they can to cut back spending.

speaker: EVANS
text: Labor demand is way off.

speaker: EVANS
text: My Manpower contact indicated that even companies that are doing well had turned cautious about hiring and are trying to squeeze out more productivity.

speaker: EVANS
text: He thought that the drop in sentiment could have some extra impact, given that it was occurring during the annual planning cycle for corporations.

speaker: EVANS
text: The idea was that a lot of harder-to-sell structural adjustments were being implemented anyway and that CEOs wanted to get these moves done quickly and have them behind them by early 2009.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is consistent with a range of reports we have heard that new capital spending is dead in the water or that planned expansions are being canceled.

speaker: EVANS
text: On a positive note, I think we are seeing the benefits of the structural improvement and inventory management that has occurred over the last 25 years.

speaker: EVANS
text: My contacts are reporting some increases in inventories, but they think that so far they have kept stocks under relatively good control.

speaker: EVANS
text: With prompt production cuts, we may not get the additional downside of a big inventory swing later in the cycle, perhaps when it is more painful.

speaker: EVANS
text: Turning to the national outlook, our forecast envisions a full-blown recession, roughly on the scale of the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: But like everyone else, I have a great deal of uncertainty about this projection.

speaker: EVANS
text: Things could turn out a lot worse.

speaker: EVANS
text: In contemplating the transmission from recent financial events to the real economy, there seem to be at least two channels to note.

speaker: EVANS
text: First, there is the dramatically reduced availability and higher cost of credit.

speaker: EVANS
text: Second, a recessionary psychology has emerged strongly in households and businesses.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to the psychology, I haven’t spoken with anyone this round who thought there was a good reason to undertake any kind of discretionary expenditure.

speaker: EVANS
text: Clearly, the self-reinforcing dynamics implied by these and other reports could generate a deeper downturn than I have written down in my forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to the credit channel, the hit to the nonfinancial sector has intensified a good bit.

speaker: EVANS
text: We clearly are sailing in uncharted waters when it comes to quantifying these effects.

speaker: EVANS
text: The factors identified in the Greenbook highlight the unprecedented nature of the financial impulses to the economy.

speaker: EVANS
text: Looking ahead, I expect that the improvement in financial conditions will be somewhat faster than in the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: That is my cautious optimism.

speaker: EVANS
text: Still, in our forecast, financial headwinds weigh substantially on growth throughout 2009 and continue, to a degree, into 2010.

speaker: EVANS
text: Accordingly, substantial resource gaps remain open throughout the projection period.

speaker: EVANS
text: Also, I expect inflation expectations to decline in this depressed environment.

speaker: EVANS
text: With greater slack, lower inflation expectations, the reduction in energy and other commodity prices, and the higher value of the dollar, we are projecting core inflation to move under 2 percent by 2010.

speaker: EVANS
text: And I won’t be shocked if the Greenbook projection for this to happen in 2009 actually happens.

speaker: EVANS
text: So, on balance, I think that inflationary risks are low but the downside risks to the economy are very high.

speaker: EVANS
text: Much as President Fisher indicated, it is much in line with the reports so far.

speaker: LACKER
text: Business and consumer sentiment in the Fifth District has deteriorated markedly.

speaker: LACKER
text: Even though economic conditions were already decelerating heading into our September meeting, a discrete shift in outlook seems to have occurred.

speaker: LACKER
text: It seems to me to have originated during the week of September 15 or shortly thereafter.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our business contacts express anxiety about the national economy, and they express uncertainty about the meaning for their firms’ prospects of the astonishing sequence of events that began unfolding that week.

speaker: LACKER
text: Both consumers and firms have been increasingly unwilling to make long-term commitments and engage in discretionary expenditures.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consumers are delaying large and discretionary expenditures.

speaker: LACKER
text: Firms have adopted a wait-and-see attitude on investments.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our regional survey released this morning shows a substantial drop in business conditions as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our business survey respondents report that obtaining business loans is more difficult than three months ago, and there are widespread reports of lenders tightening credit terms and seeking to reduce exposures.

speaker: LACKER
text: Most respondents, however, also indicated that they would still be able to satisfy their borrowing needs.

speaker: LACKER
text: When you listen to bankers, they will tell you that they are tightening standards, but they also report that they are still extending credit to solid borrowers with high-quality deals.

speaker: LACKER
text: I find it difficult right now to pin down the real effects of the financial market turmoil of the last few weeks.

speaker: LACKER
text: As the Greenbook notes, assessing such effects “poses significant identification challenges.” Specifically, it is hard to disentangle the effects of the increased cost of bank capital from those of the deterioration in the economic environment facing borrowers.

speaker: LACKER
text: Personally, I suspect the latter are playing the more prominent role in the tightening of credit terms right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: Looking on the bright side, the near-term inflation picture has eased noticeably since our September meeting, mainly because of the decline in oil and other commodity prices.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Greenbook carries this moderation into its long-term forecast, where PCE inflation now converges to 1 percent in 2013.

speaker: LACKER
text: I did a double-take when I saw that—it had me wondering whether the Greenbook was ghost-written this month by President Plosser.

speaker: LACKER
text: Whoever’s forecast it is, the longer-term projected moderation in inflation relies heavily on the opening-up of a large and persistent output gap.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the current circumstances, I am not sure how plausible that story is.

speaker: LACKER
text: In particular, I have been struggling with how to think about the effect of credit market disruptions on the concept of potential output.

speaker: LACKER
text: To the extent that we think of these disruptions as analogous to shocks to intermediation technology—and that is what the models of these kinds of credit channel effects generally tell you to do—it seems to me that we should see them as pulling down potential as well as actual output.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe this point has been made at previous meetings.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have also talked before about the tenuous nature of the Phillips curve relationship, and it is difficult to forecast.

speaker: LACKER
text: The slope is sort of flat.

speaker: LACKER
text: We had been scheduled to discuss inflation dynamics, and we postponed that, for good reasons I believe.

speaker: LACKER
text: I hope we can get back to it soon because I think it’s going to be relevant to how we see our way through this.

speaker: LACKER
text: In any event, I think we should be careful not to be overly optimistic about the forecast of an inflation decline driven by a large output gap.

speaker: LACKER
text: The shift in the Greenbook’s long-term inflation projection is noteworthy for another reason, I believe.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are getting closer to a 1 percent target federal funds rate, and we may actually reach 1 percent at some meeting soon.

speaker: LACKER
text: The last time this happened it sparked a widespread discussion of and concern about the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to make a couple of related observations.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, a key to conducting monetary policy at the zero bound is being able to keep inflation expectations from falling and thereby increasing real interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: From this perspective, the revision of the Greenbook’s forecast from 1.7 percent one meeting ago to 1.0 percent for five-year-ahead inflation implies that we run a monetary policy regime in which five-year-ahead expected inflation varies pretty significantly in response to contemporaneous shocks.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think that variability in long-run inflation projections can help our ability to manage inflation expectations at the zero bound.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’d be better if we ran a policy in which long-run expected inflation was more anchored, more stable.

speaker: LACKER
text: You can tell where I’m going with this, I’m sure.

speaker: LACKER
text: This highlights the value of an explicit inflation objective as well as the value of being able to communicate clearly about how we view the functioning of monetary policy at the zero bound.

speaker: LACKER
text: Second, I will just note briefly that the economics of monetary policy at the zero bound are closely related to the economics of paying interest on reserves at close to the target rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, if I’m not mistaken, they are virtually identical.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think progress on both fronts would be useful right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: Finally, let me just comment on financial market conditions.

speaker: LACKER
text: My sense is that what the public has seen—the large failures, the variety of resolution techniques, the deliberations leading up to the Congress’s adoption of the bill it adopted—taken together have added up to significant pessimism on people’s parts and have altered optimal strategy for a lot of financial institutions.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I think that is altering how people allocate portfolios and has led to further volatility in certain markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: It has led some institutions to adopt a wait-and-see attitude, to see how particular programs are going to be implemented.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that we are seeing at least some dead-weight loss associated with the burdens of shifting financial flows between things that are covered and things that aren’t and we are seeing a good deal of rent-seeking behavior as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: What we are seeing is going to have the effect of masking the evolution of underlying fundamentals.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is going to make it harder to see our way through this and understand just what is happening.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that is going to be a thicket that we will need to cut through in the months ahead.

speaker: LACKER
text: That concludes my comments, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While the LIBOR–OIS spread has narrowed somewhat, the mutual fund industry is no longer experiencing waves of redemptions, and commercial paper market conditions have improved, we’re still not back to the short-term credit conditions that prevailed before the failure of Lehman Brothers.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This outcome is striking considering the historic interventions that have occurred in the past month.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With all of the new government guarantees and equity infusions here and abroad, the limited improvement in short-term credit markets attests to the degree of concern and risk aversion prevailing in financial markets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: These concerns are likely to become even more elevated if the economy slows to the degree expected in most forecasts.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Like the Greenbook, our forecast anticipates a significant recession.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The Boston forecast includes three consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth and results in an unemployment rate peaking above 7½ percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The weakening labor market and the large losses in housing and stock wealth make it quite likely that consumption will shrink in the second half of this year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While we need housing to reach bottom, mortgage rates relative to federal funds rates remain quite high, and further job losses are likely to aggravate the upward trend in foreclosures and add to the downward pressure on housing prices.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With limited new home purchases and demand for vehicles weak, consumption of consumer durables is unlikely to recover until next year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Commercial real estate, which has held up reasonably well, all things considered, is likely to be much weaker next year as new and rollover financing is difficult to obtain and staff cuts and hiring freezes affect the space needed by businesses.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: More generally, firms are likely to have little incentive to make new investments until the severity of the downturn becomes much clearer.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Unfortunately, many of our trading partners are likely to face an even more severe downturn, aggravated by their slow fiscal and monetary response to deteriorating economic and financial conditions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While the Greenbook assumes the stock market will rise by 8 percent for the remainder of this year—it looks as though that happened today—

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think that just offset the decline that had happened since the time we finished the Greenbook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: —I would say that I’d be surprised by that outcome.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There are several looming financial problems that are likely to affect financial markets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Bill Dudley highlighted the one that I think is the biggest for me, which is that the NAV (net asset value) triggers for hedge funds will be a significant problem in the fourth quarter.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Without comprehensive information on hedge funds, it’s difficult to know the extent of the problems they are facing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, since the stock market remains one of the few markets available for the disposing of assets in bulk without a significant liquidity haircut, I’d expect significant selling in the fourth quarter.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My second big concern is that rollover financing will become more problematic as financial problems persist.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Particularly exposed are real estate developers and highly leveraged private equity firms.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My third worry is that neither insurance companies nor commercial banks have reserved for the economic outcome in our baseline forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Under-reserving and high payout ratios are likely to limit the amount of additional lending that banks are willing to take on.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: These financial problems place additional downside risk to our forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Our forecast, like the Greenbook forecast, expects the rate of inflation to slow as a result of falling food and energy prices and significant excess capacity emerging in the economy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In fact, our equations indicate there is a non-negligible risk that deflation will be a problem in the outyears of our forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Unlike President Lacker, I was surprised that it stayed as high as 1 rather than as low as 1.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The outlook for a weak real economy and falling inflation highlights the need for both monetary and fiscal policy to offset some of the financial and economic problems that we are likely to experience.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Let me just briefly say that, in our region, we have continued to do actually better than the national average, but that is beginning to wane.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We are seeing, obviously, the energy effect show itself as rigs are being put out of production and you see a slowing there.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We are seeing some concerns being raised about agricultural prices and the boom that has been going on in that part of the economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That said, there’s still a reasonable amount of business going on that they haven’t frozen up.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We asked our directors and our other advisers how they were seeing things, and it varies.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There were some organizations that say that our non-investment-grade borrowers from the banks, if they had credit already, are still able to access those lines.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If they lost some portion because of a bank problem or something like that, they cannot get new credit, so it is cut off in that way.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that’s important to keep in mind.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Businesses themselves are beginning to pull back on their capital plans.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Their balance sheets—obviously outside the auto industry—are still decent, but they’re saying, “We’re looking at this, and we’re pulling back until we see how it plays out.” You are beginning to hear more of that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They feel that they can get credit.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Some of them are talking about actually trying to pull down their lines to make sure they have the money, and the only thing keeping them from doing that is they don’t know what to do with it once they get it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They’re afraid of losing their credit, but they also know that it costs if they pull it down.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So the dynamics there are interesting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the national outlook, I’ll be brief.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that obviously the projections for recession are in place.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Down is where we’re going.

speaker: HOENIG
text: How much, though, is speculation right now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I don’t know that anyone does until we begin to see things settle out.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Inflation should be down as well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Obviously, when you have a recession, you will back off from that, but how much?

speaker: HOENIG
text: That’s not clear at this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There is a lot in play, and that’s why we don’t know the answers to those questions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have these liquidity facilities and an enormous amount of liquidity out.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have the TARP that is now in process but not completed.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That’s going to have an impact, and I think those are very important.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As we discuss our own policy, we are very close to the point of the quantitative easing discussion that we had, as you said, in 2003.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Pulling that material out and taking a look at that is important as we decide what we’re going to put our money into as we try to stimulate this economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Right now we’re subject to waiting and seeing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There’s been a lot done, and attitudes are a critical part of this now, and we just have to wait to see how those change over the next quarter or two.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not going to say much about the District conditions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the Third District, as many of you have noted, they’ve weakened considerably.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I will make just a couple of observations that I think might be pertinent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our last Business Outlook Survey, the one that was released a week ago, had actually gone into positive territory in September to 3.8, which was the first positive reading we had had since January—since, I guess, last December, actually.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And it dropped from that plus 3.8 to minus 37.5 in one month.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, it’s relevant to know the timing of this a bit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our survey is done during the first 2 weeks or the first 10 or 12 days of each month—which meant that the September survey was closed on September 12, 4 days before that weekend.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So what we see is a very precipitous, dramatic change in the tone that had as much to do with events and perhaps policy actions as with what was actually going on in the economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I share a bit of President Lacker’s concern to try to disentangle a little the tone and feel of the economy, which really did feel as though it fell off a cliff in September, unlike any other month that I’ve seen during this episode.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have to think carefully about disentangling that effect not just because something fundamental happened to the economy but also to see to what extent policies, whether our policies or Treasury’s policies, have contributed to a change in tone and increased uncertainty and aggravated what might be the real fundamentals going on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t know the answer to that question, but it suggests something that many of us have argued over time—that more- consistent and more-predictable policies can help us avoid some of that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One special question that was asked in this survey in October was whether firms had trouble getting credit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Interestingly enough, only 14 percent of the respondents reported that they had trouble obtaining credit, but twice that number, almost 30 percent, reported that they believed that their customers were having trouble getting credit, which was an interesting dynamic going on that leads to a bit of uncertainty.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess the best thing I can say about the Third District right now is “Go Phillies!” Maybe that will turn things around in the Third District.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Anyway, let me turn briefly to the national outlook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It has deteriorated, certainly more than I expected, from what I thought in June.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In our conference call on October 7, I indicated that I was revising my forecast downward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I expect the economy to contract during the second half of this year and perhaps in the first quarter of next year—but that’s less clear to me—and then gradually approach what I would consider trend growth over 2009, so that by the end of 2009 we’re getting back toward what might be considered trend growth, which I consider to be about 2.5 to 2.7 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In essence, for 2010-11, I pushed out my recovery of the economy by somewhere between six and nine months because of the current turmoil.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I expect the unemployment rate to peak around mid- ’09 at about 7¼ and then to decline gradually to its long-run rate of about 5 percent by the end of 2010.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation pressures have subsided somewhat since June, and inflation expectations have remained contained.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I expect core inflation to decline gradually from the current levels to my goal of about 1.7 percent by 2010.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, my overall forecast is considerably better than the Greenbook baseline forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, it’s similar to what we talked about as the “more rapid financial recovery” scenario, which makes some of the adjustment for the financial turmoil somewhat quicker and somewhat less dramatic than in the baseline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The fed funds rate path underlying my forecast is less accommodative than the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I assume that the fed funds rate remains at 1½ percent through the spring of next year and then gradually begins to rise, reaching 4¼ percent by the end of 2010.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, there are certainly risks around that forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Somebody at this table has to be a little more optimistic after all, and we have risks around all forecasts in this environment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Certainly mine is no exception.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In particular, the effect of the financial markets, as we’ve all been talking about, remains highly uncertain and highly risky, and I am not trying to disregard that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Every day it seems as though there’s a new development, usually negative, although I guess 900 points on the Dow today should be considered good news.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But in fact, I believe that the risks around the Greenbook baseline forecast are to the upside, as I have alluded to.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, the baseline entails a sizable downward adjustment based at least partly on the volatile financial data, especially spreads.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Spreads can fall dramatically, although they don’t always do so.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But they can rise and fall very quickly, and I think it’s very risky to base monetary policy, which ought to be taking a longer-term perspective, on week-to-week movements in such volatile variables.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If spreads do continue to fall over the next quarter or two as they have in recent days and if the financial market tools we’ve put in place have the desired effect, we could see the economy becoming much stronger than the Greenbook’s baseline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Second, in the Greenbook, inflation falls and remains low despite a very low fed funds rate path.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, it’s reminiscent of the funds rate path in 2003-04.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This apparently is due to the sizable output gaps that open up in the forecast period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, these output gaps arise in the forecast because the effects of the financial turmoil show up mainly in aggregate demand.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, as I’ve suggested in previous meetings and as President Lacker alluded to, I think a plausible alternative view is that the financial market disturbances we’ve experienced—resulting in a restructuring of the financial system and a lowering of the efficiency of financial intermediation—act on the supply side as well, much like a somewhat persistent productivity shock with an associated damping effect on measures of potential GDP for some period of time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If so, we’ll see much smaller output gaps opening up, and that means the risk of higher inflation than in the Greenbook, especially if the baseline funds rate path is followed as they lay out.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In thinking about the appropriate monetary policy going forward, it’s important that we not let our policy be whipsawed by volatile market data.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have been lowering the funds rate since January, largely in anticipation of a recession or to mitigate the chances of one occurring.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, it may finally have arrived.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Does that mean we have to lower more?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The level of the funds rate is always a difficult question.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Clearly, if we experience a sustained slowdown in real economic activity, which suggests a lower equilibrium in the real rate of interest, policy needs to allow the funds rate to fall with the equilibrium rate, and I based my recommendations throughout the year on such a forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I think it’s a mistake to overreact to volatile data, especially when it’s the stock market.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although there has always been the desire and much pressure from markets to do something when we see such swings in the market, in my view, the economy is better served if monetary policy is a steadying hand, taking appropriate action when the intermediate-term view dictates, but not overreacting to fluctuations in the market with an inappropriate tool.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a question about the potential output view.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So you would also have to argue that the natural rate of unemployment is higher because of this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I mean, I understand why productive capacity would be affected, but why do you—

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, I don’t like the NAIRU, but in my baseline forecast, my natural rate of unemployment is higher than what the Greenbook has.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it rises because of the financial situation.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I could, Mr. Chairman, in the dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models, one of which I understand has been adopted by the staff for use in forecasting, employment fluctuates with shocks to productivity, and it’s the natural correspondent to that.

speaker: LACKER
text: So in some sense the unemployment rate rises because the natural rate rises, but that’s a way of saying that the natural rate goes up in recessions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not sure if proponents of the natural rate view that as consistent with that old model, but that’s what happens in these models.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Employment fluctuates, but to get unemployment you need a richer picture of matching, or something like that.

speaker: LACKER
text: You need some matching model, and you get intersectoral flows.

speaker: LACKER
text: You get the same thing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But even in my steady state, if I view this as a permanent inefficiency in financial intermediation that changes things, the unemployment rate is a little higher.

speaker: STERN
text: I’ll start with a few comments about the District economy, which will sound pretty familiar by now.

speaker: STERN
text: The preponderance of the anecdotes from business contacts that I’ve talked with since our last meeting have been distinctly negative.

speaker: STERN
text: It’s not just a slowing of activity or some deterioration but a sharp contraction in activity, particularly with regard to discretionary spending or discretionary projects, beginning in the middle of September.

speaker: STERN
text: The one exception to that is commercial construction, where there are enough things under way that business remains pretty good.

speaker: STERN
text: But the backlogs are dropping, and so weakness certainly is anticipated next year.

speaker: STERN
text: I thought another possible exception to the negative tone was the housing market in the Twin Cities—not that the housing market in the Twin Cities is in and of itself so important but that it might be representative of some middle-of-the-road markets across the country.

speaker: STERN
text: Clearly, it’s not indicative of what’s going on in Florida, California, or places like those because sales volumes in the Twin Cities had been up distinctly.

speaker: STERN
text: Some of that is no doubt due to short sales and foreclosures; nevertheless, there were some other signs that were favorable.

speaker: STERN
text: The affordability index has really improved a lot.

speaker: STERN
text: It is back to levels of 2002-03, which Realtors call very comfortable.

speaker: STERN
text: The ratio of housing prices to rent has moved back to the levels of 2002-03, and that’s also encouraging.

speaker: STERN
text: I already mentioned the higher sales volumes.

speaker: STERN
text: Unfortunately, when you get beyond those statistics and look at other things, it’s too early to declare stability in the housing market or anything resembling underlying improvement.

speaker: STERN
text: Part of the problem is something that we’ve talked about before.

speaker: STERN
text: The inventory of unsold, unoccupied properties remains very substantial—by historical experience way above anything resembling normal.

speaker: STERN
text: Second, even though the price-to-rent ratio has come down, it’s still elevated relative to the longer-term historical experience.

speaker: STERN
text: So it looks to me as though, even in that market, there are some further price declines to come and it’s going to take some more time to get through all of this— probably well into next year.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as the national economy is concerned, I, too, have marked down my outlook for real growth for the balance of this year, for all of next year, and into early 2010 as well.

speaker: STERN
text: This reflects to some extent the nature of the incoming data but also the intensification of the financial problems and associated headwinds, the impact of the negative wealth effect, and so on.

speaker: STERN
text: When I looked at my June forecast, back then the forecast obviously looked better, although there were a number of what I called “identifiable negatives.” They have proven, for worse rather than for better, to be relevant.

speaker: STERN
text: I already talked about some of them.

speaker: STERN
text: In addition, we still have the problem in housing with excess inventories.

speaker: STERN
text: We have steady declines in employment, which obviously have negative implications for consumer spending, and the credit headwinds as well.

speaker: STERN
text: So now I have the economy contracting through the middle of next year, modest growth resuming thereafter, and robust growth beginning with the second quarter of 2010—quite some distance off.

speaker: STERN
