text: On the inflation outlook, I have for some time been thinking that inflation would begin to slow this quarter.

speaker: STERN
text: With the decline in commodity prices, the evolution of the economic outlook, and so forth, my confidence in that forecast has increased, and I do expect inflation to diminish over the forecast period.

speaker: STERN
text: So I think I’ll conclude with that.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I concur with the view that we face a very serious situation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In most respects I agree with the Greenbook baseline projection, with the reasoning that the Board staff used to arrive at the projection, and with their view that the risks to growth are to the downside.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like the Greenbook projection, my projection is heavily influenced by judgments that we are bringing to the projection from forces that are not captured by our models.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The magnitude of the judgmental adjustment has become strikingly large, as we talked about earlier, and I realize that, if one wanted to be a skeptic about the Greenbook baseline, one would have to look no further than these assumptions and question their significant influence on the outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But I am not a skeptic.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: During the past few weeks, in our Bank we have stepped up our contacts with business people from large, medium, and smaller businesses, bankers, and local government officials.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We have been asking them to tell us not so much what they think and feel but what has actually happened to their order books, production runs, and account receivables and what actions they are taking as a result.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: It suffices to say that the feedback about the environment was overwhelmingly negative.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Respondents say that their situation has gone either from good to bad or from bad to worse, and I want to share just two anecdotes that I think capture the essence of what we are facing—one of them from a business perspective and the other from a consumer perspective.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: One of my directors is the CEO of a company that produces and sells forklift trucks all over the world.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: He reported last week that his sales are down and orders have fallen off dramatically, and he expects to be announcing some layoffs soon.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But what was making a greater impression on him is the fact that orders for the forklift parts have fallen off as well, and this tells him that the warehouse operators have cut back on the use of trucks that they already own.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My second story concerns the owner of a body shop that is located in a solid, middle class community.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: He told us that he was doing record business all year until last month, when business just went dead.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: He said it is not that people suddenly don’t need auto repairs, but in fact, they are collecting the insurance money and not fixing their cars.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: They want the cash and they don’t want to pay out the deductible.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Stories like these convince me that the Greenbook baseline is on the right track.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do part company with the Greenbook in one respect—namely, the longer-term inflation outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think it is quite likely that we are going to experience some costly reallocation of resources across some sectors of the economy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Finance and construction are two obvious examples.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Going forward, I think there is reason to think that fewer workers and less capital are going to be employed in these sectors.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The costly adjustment is going to be characterized by slower productivity growth, higher trend unit labor costs, and a smaller output gap than would otherwise occur, leading to somewhat less disinflation in the outyears in my projection.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Nevertheless, with output and inflation expected to decline sharply over the coming quarters, I think it is essential for us to be thinking about the zero bound in conducting monetary policy in a low inflation environment, and I will address the magnitude, timing, and communication aspects of our monetary policy in tomorrow’s go-round.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Economic conditions in the Eighth District have deteriorated since the September Beige Book.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Citing weak demand and higher input costs, a variety of manufacturing firms throughout the District reported job cuts and plant closings.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The decline in manufacturing activity has been concentrated in firms producing durable goods.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Service sector activity also continues to decline.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In particular, recent layoffs have been reported in business, medical, and financial services.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Two large auto dealers have closed and filed for bankruptcy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Retail sales are steady, but contacts have noticed that consumers are trading down to lower-priced products.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The residential real estate sector continues to decline across the District.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As lending standards have tightened for commercial building projects, industrial construction has slowed.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Payroll employment numbers continue to vary across the Bank’s Branch cities.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The most recent figures suggest that Memphis and St. Louis continue to lose jobs at a pace faster than at the national level.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Louisville has moved from two consecutive months of positive year-over-year employment growth to negative growth in the most recent month.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Little Rock continues to experience positive year-over-year employment growth.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Unemployment rates in St. Louis and Memphis remain above 7 percent—that’s 7.2 percent and 7.1 percent, respectively.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Louisville’s unemployment rate is 6.6 percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In opposition to the national trend, Little Rock’s unemployment rate has fallen to just 4 percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The national outlook is clouded by dramatically increased uncertainty fueled by the financial market turmoil.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The explosion of uncertainty is driven in part by speculation about the nature of the government response to the turmoil, both in the United States and abroad.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We know from past experience that, when economic actors—investors, businesses, and consumers—are faced with new and substantial uncertainty, they tend to adopt a “wait and see” approach, during which they make as few commitments as possible.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This seems to be a reasonable expectation in the current environment, so we should expect to see many types of important economic decisions being deferred.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Anecdotal evidence seems to support this idea.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Most likely, this means we will experience an important deterioration in economic activity during the second half of 2008 and into 2009.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In times of increased uncertainty, it can be useful to consider distinct alternative scenarios instead of considering a baseline scenario with many possible offshoots.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The financial sector crisis that we are experiencing has some admittedly inexact parallels with the banking crises that occurred in Japan since 1990 and in the Nordic countries in the early 1990s.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The general tenor of the literature on these events is that the Nordic countries dealt forthrightly with their financial sector problems, suffered through recessions, but were well positioned to grow once the crisis had been addressed.

speaker: BULLARD
text: For Japan, real economic performance was subpar for a long time, and it is the Japanese outcome that is a looming risk for the U.S. economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Part of the Japanese experience was the lowering of nominal interest rates to zero.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This was done, no doubt, in the name of doing everything possible to help the economy recover.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It was not very successful and, in fact, may have been counterproductive.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Recent academic work—I’m thinking of Jess Benhabib here—has emphasized the possibility of a low nominal interest rate, low inflation rate, steady state equilibrium, and a trap at very low or zero nominal interest rates.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This steady state coexists with the targeted steady state, the one we know and love, which has inflation at our specified target and relatively high nominal interest rates.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So there are two possible focal points for the economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Markets clear at both of these focal points.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My main concern is that if we choose to continue to flirt with the trap steady state, we should think clearly about the possible implications given the current environment.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The trap steady state is associated with very low inflation expectations, actually deflation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is, in fact, what happened to Japan.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They experienced deflation of about 1 percent for a number of years.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Since our core problems are in the housing market, which is dominated by nominal contracting, deflation could sharply exacerbate our problems and lead to further difficulties.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am, frankly, not sure that this is a wise route for the Committee or for the nation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My preferred approach would be to maintain rates at the current low level and to use alternative fiscal policy actions to address the particular concerns in financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, it’s a little after 6:00 p.m., a long afternoon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we recess the meeting until tomorrow morning?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s a reception and a dinner up on the terrace, which is for your convenience.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s no business being conducted, and we’ll see you in the morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have some data this morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Dave, would you like to discuss this?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: You have at your place a table on orders and shipments of durable goods, one of the more inscrutable releases to actually make sense of, but the bottom line is very little effect on our basic outlook here.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you can see in that second set of numbers, the shipments area excluding the aircraft line was up 2 percent in September.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That was actually a little stronger than we had penciled in, but only enough to add a few basis points to GDP growth in the third quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Then you can see that it has basically been averaging flat for the last two months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This is a September figure, so it’s fairly dated at this point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The orders figures, the set of numbers above—again looking at the “excluding aircraft” line—have been coming down.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I wouldn’t say that they’re collapsing, but they’re certainly weakening some.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So this really has no appreciable effect on our outlook for a small decline in equipment spending in the third quarter and a more appreciable decline in the fourth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Does the resolution of the Boeing strike have any macro implications?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We actually predicted that the strike would end this week.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It wasn’t looking too good last week.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we’re expecting that it would provide a small rebound effect on first-quarter GDP growth.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It’s going to take a little while to get production back on track here.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: 6 The materials used by Mr. Stockton are appended to this transcript (appendix 6).

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let’s continue with our go-round.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We expect a recession at least as bad as the 1990–91 recession, with a significant risk of a deeper, more protracted downturn worse than the ’80s, and a very substantial rise in the unemployment rate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Inflation is decelerating quickly, and deflationary forces are ascendant around the globe.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The huge decline in energy and commodity prices will add to a very substantial downward pressure on core inflation from increased economic slack around the world.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We could see an abrupt change in inflation expectations into deflationary territory.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We’ve seen a lot of policy action over the past few weeks.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One question is whether policymakers should wait to measure the effects of these measures before going further, and I want to talk a little about that question.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: My view is that I don’t think so.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The outlook has been deteriorating ahead of the policy response.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is true both here and around the world.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The magnitude and speed of the tightening financial conditions, the erosion in business and consumer confidence, the fall in actual spending, and the shift in inflation risk together present very grave risks to growth and to the financial system.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mitigating these risks is going to require more monetary policy here but even more so in the other major economies.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But in addition to the very substantial easing in the global stance of monetary policy ahead, the substantial damage that has already happened to financial intermediation globally suggests that a broad-based and quite large fiscal stimulus will be critical to prevent an excessive fall in aggregate demand.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: How quickly and how far should we reduce the federal funds rate in the United States?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The Greenbook and the Bluebook present a very strong case for moving down another 100 basis points quickly.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: In fact, if I read the pictures in the Bluebook correctly, they might imply a need to get real rates to the negative 3 to negative 5 percent territory relatively quickly, if we could do that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we don’t move another 50 today, we’ll be behind again.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Monetary policy has effectively tightened substantially since the summer, of course, because of the intensification of financial pressures and because of the rise in forward real interest rates that have come with the rapid deceleration in expected future inflation.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Beyond this meeting and this choice, our choices are harder.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think we need to get real rates lower and, to make sure we get them there, we need to keep them low enough long enough.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This requires that we get the nominal fed funds rate as low as possible as soon as possible.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t see a good case for monetary policy gradualism in the current context.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The risks are too great.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we’re too tentative, the damage to the financial system and to the real economy could be much greater and much harder to correct.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we end up doing too much, we can always adjust.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That’s an easier problem to solve.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: With global financial markets placing progressively more weight on a very severe global recession, the “keep our powder dry” and “reserve our remaining ammunition” arguments don’t seem that compelling to me.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We don’t have much ammunition left in the fed funds rate anyway.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If we hold that back, it will likely be less effective when we ultimately use it.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The more powerful escalation options we have left will probably involve communications, such as continued commitments to keep rates low enough long enough that we avert creeping expectations of deflation and can be confident that inflation will come in around our target level over the forecast period.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t have a strong view now about how low we can go with the nominal fed funds rate without causing too much risk of damage to the functioning of financial systems.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We need to look at all possible options, though.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the principal focus of our staff’s work in the coming weeks will be to put together a set of alternative policy options going forward along with the analysis of their benefits and risks so that we’re in a position to act quickly enough to be effective.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Just a few final points.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think this basic risk-management choice really involves three dimensions of judgment.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One is about the relative probability of alternative outcomes.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The second is about the relative consequences of or the damage caused by those alternative scenarios.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Importantly, it also involves a judgment about the ease of correcting, adjusting, or mitigating the consequences of being wrong.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This is just a stylized presentation, but in the staff notes yesterday, there was a nice way to think about those choices.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just wanted to point out one thing about this stylized framework of those choices, which is the consequence.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If you look at exhibit 5, the bottom left panel, which shows the inflation outcome associated with the “more rapid recovery” scenario, in this presentation you don’t have much risk of a very bad inflation outcome in the event that we end up doing too much with too much policy and have to take that back.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Again, it’s important to recognize that it’s not just about the probability that we attach to the alternative scenarios.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s not just about the relative impact of the consequences of those scenarios.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s about the ease with which we can correct for a judgment that was wrong—in this case, a judgment that we did too much.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: This may understate the complications in correcting for that error and may make it look easier than it may ultimately be, but I think it’s a nice framework.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Finally, I just want to point out, just to underscore the basic point: This is not going to be principally about monetary policy going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: If you look at the broad framework of policies that are now in place, both here and globally, and the instruments we have to play with, along with the fiscal authorities: we have monetary policy; we have the liquidity arrangements and what we do with our balance sheet over time; we, the collectively integrated government, have the broad fiscal policy questions and the scope for either a broad-based substantial fiscal package or more-targeted fiscal measures, as the Chairman suggested, to focus on the credit markets; and we have the capacity to alter the framework of capital and guarantees that is now in place.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Beyond that, the government here also has the ability to change what the GSEs, the FHA, and the FHLB can do.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So when we think about escalating going forward, to go to President Fisher’s question from yesterday, we have the ability on all these fronts to do more if that’s necessary and prudent.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think the mix has already changed substantially.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It was probably mostly fiscal nine months ago.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It is certainly mostly fiscal now in a broader sense, except that many of the major economies going forward will have to move monetary policy very substantially.

speaker: KOHN
text: A number of the presentations yesterday talked about falling off a cliff in the middle of September.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we need to remind ourselves that we were sliding downhill pretty fast before we hit that cliff.

speaker: KOHN
text: The third-quarter data, which aren’t really affected by what happened in the last two weeks of September, indicate that the economy was weaker than we thought at the time of the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think Dave Stockton or Norm Morin noted that about a third of their downward revision reflected incoming data rather than the credit tightening.

speaker: KOHN
text: That was especially true for consumption, with real consumption spending falling through the summer, responding to lower employment and tighter credit.

speaker: KOHN
text: Private domestic final purchases were revised down to a decline of 3½ percent in the third quarter after being flat in the first half.

speaker: KOHN
text: Housing price declines picked up in August, and I think the deteriorating economy and concerns about the economy were reflected in increased nervousness in financial markets over the summer into the first half of September.

speaker: KOHN
text: It was really those worries about what the losses were going to be and how they would spread from mortgages to loan books generally—that deepening pessimism—that doomed the marginal institutions like AIG and Lehman and the GSEs.

speaker: KOHN
text: They just didn’t have a chance to recapitalize or stabilize themselves when so many of the other market participants were worried about what their own positions would be.

speaker: KOHN
text: The resulting flight to liquidity and safety, the loss of confidence that followed, the deepening gloom, and the failures and near failures and associated losses triggered a tremendous tightening of financial conditions over the intermeeting period—President Yellen and others discussed this—despite the 50 basis points of easing.

speaker: KOHN
text: Even after the 900 point increase yesterday, equity prices are down about 20 or 22 percent over the intermeeting period.

speaker: KOHN
text: The dollar is up 10 percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: Corporate borrowing rates are up for investment-grade corporations 200 to 250 basis points.

speaker: KOHN
text: Banks tell us that they’re tightening across every dimension of their lending; and other lenders, like finance companies, are also cutting back very, very sharply.

speaker: KOHN
text: You can see this in autos clearly, but the stress is much broader than just the auto finance companies.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have good programs in place to deal with many of these problems—the capital, the FDIC guarantees, and the Federal Reserve balance sheet facilities—and they are having some effects relative to the freezing up of markets that we had in mid-September.

speaker: KOHN
text: We can see that interbank spreads and LIBOR have come down some.

speaker: KOHN
text: Commercial paper rose, I guess, on Monday with the introduction of our facility.

speaker: KOHN
text: Declines in money market mutual funds have abated, though they’re still there, and there are some signs that maturities are beginning to lengthen in funding markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: As these programs are more fully implemented, we’ll see some greater effects—including, I hope, some greater willingness to extend credit.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also assume that the fiscal package is necessary, as in the Greenbook “fiscal stimulus” alternative.

speaker: KOHN
text: But we need to remember that the improvement we’ve seen over the last couple of days is relative to a situation in which funding markets were in effect frozen beyond a very short term, and although a sharp snapback is possible, as President Plosser was noting yesterday, I think further gains are more likely to be gradual.

speaker: KOHN
text: In the past few days, the declines in LIBOR have seemed very grudging and gradual, and LIBOR remains quite high—I think close to 75 basis points higher— relative to what it was in mid-August, before we even cut rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: This was three-month LIBOR that I looked at this morning.

speaker: KOHN
text: In an environment of economic weakness, spreading credit problems, falling house prices, a number of false dawns in this episode so far, and death and near-death experiences, lenders and investors are going to continue to be very cautious and conserve their liquidity and capital.

speaker: KOHN
text: So despite further improvements, financial conditions will remain quite tight.

speaker: KOHN
text: The effects of lower wealth, higher borrowing costs, the stronger dollar, and tighter nonprice terms of credit will play out over the next few quarters, putting downward pressure on an economy that was already in recession.

speaker: KOHN
text: At the same time, heightened uncertainty and fear of future problems caused a sharp deterioration in attitudes and spending even apart from the effects of credit.

speaker: KOHN
text: Judging from the Conference Board index, regional purchasing manager surveys, and anecdotes—including what we heard around the table yesterday—it feels like a recessionary psychology, as I think Charlie Evans called it.

speaker: KOHN
text: Others talked about pulling back and curtailment of discretionary spending in train, and this is not just caused by credit effects.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we’ve had a downward shift in aggregate demand as well as a movement along the aggregate demand curve, and this downward shift in aggregate demand will propagate through multiplier–accelerator effects even if attitudes begin to improve some.

speaker: KOHN
text: The global dimensions of the shock are important.

speaker: KOHN
text: As we talked about yesterday, heightened risk aversion has had a pronounced effect on emerging market economies as well as on industrial economies.

speaker: KOHN
text: Net exports cushioned domestic weakness in the first half of the year, but with the dollar strong, if anything we’ll be absorbing weakness from abroad, not exporting it, as the rest of the year goes on and we get into next year.

speaker: KOHN
text: Growing credit problems abroad will only add to pressures on many large global lenders who might have thought they were diversified geographically.

speaker: KOHN
text: But a little like our U.S. housing market, they will find that diversification doesn’t really work when there’s a global recession.

speaker: KOHN
text: The net effect of all of this is a much weaker growth path for the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: In my forecast, I had a somewhat steeper near-term decline in economic activity and a slightly sharper bounceback than the staff, including my fiscal assumption, but I also have the unemployment rate peaking at over 7 percent, as the Greenbook did.

speaker: KOHN
text: With commodity prices plunging, the added slack maintained through several years, and declines in inflation expectations, inflation will be on a clear downward track.

speaker: KOHN
text: In the Greenbook, this downward track for inflation obtained even with the assumption of some rebound in commodity prices and the resumption of dollar weakness.

speaker: KOHN
text: In my forecast for inflation from next year on, inflation was at or below the 1½ to 2 percent rate I would like to see as a steady state consistent with avoiding the zero bound when adverse shocks hit.

speaker: KOHN
text: Critically, the downside risks around activity forecasts are huge and tilted to the downside.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think they’re huge because we’ve never seen a situation like this before, certainly not in my experience dating all the way back to 1970, and have only the vaguest notion of how it will play out in financial markets and spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think they’re tilted to the downside because I, like the staff, assumed a gradual improvement in financial markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: That could be delayed or even go in the wrong direction for a time, further tightening financial conditions.

speaker: KOHN
text: In addition, the effect on spending of the heightened concerns and tighter credit conditions could be larger and longer lasting than I assumed.

speaker: KOHN
text: For some time an important downside risk to the forecast has been a sharp upward revision to household saving as wealth, job availability, and borrowing capacity eroded.

speaker: KOHN
text: I assumed a moderate increase in the saving rate, but I can definitely see the possibility that adverse developments will galvanize a more thorough rethinking by the household sector of what saving is needed, and that will affect investment as well as consumption.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’ll get to the policy implications of all of this in the next round.

speaker: WARSH
text: The first sentence of the Greenbook said that “recent economic and financial news has been dismal”; and the last sentence on page 1 of the Bluebook said that “markets generally remain extremely illiquid and volatile.” I can’t do better than that, but I can certainly do worse; so let me give that a try.

speaker: WARSH
text: Market prices and official and corporate data confirm an additional leg down in mid- September, which has been much discussed.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think it is going to become increasingly clear that October, particularly the first 20 days of the month, was materially worse.

speaker: WARSH
text: So if we fell off the cliff in the middle of September, I think that once the data come out and find their way into the marketplace in October, the Greenbook forecast might look a bit more positive than the facts on the ground would suggest.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a result, my own forecast is less optimistic than the Greenbook, but there is plenty of uncertainty, as I think Dave Stockton talked about yesterday.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me make a few comments about financial markets before turning to the broader economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: I expect a prolonged period of significantly strained credit markets, and that strain is likely to be exacerbated between now and year-end and I suspect even well into 2009.

speaker: WARSH
text: The credit intermediation process that we’ve talked about is fundamentally broken.

speaker: WARSH
text: I talked six months ago about the financial architecture that was fundamentally being changed.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that has all happened faster than I could have anticipated.

speaker: WARSH
text: Confidence, not just in counterparties but in basic rules of doing business across financial markets, has been lost, and my own sense is that loss of confidence is not easily fixed, even by well-intended government programs.

speaker: WARSH
text: We should all be quite patient in terms of seeing the benefits of the rather dramatic actions taken by the official sector, both here in the United States and overseas.

speaker: WARSH
text: Corporate bond rates and other risk spreads may well fall from their recent peaks, as suggested in the Greenbook, but spreads across asset classes are likely to stay far wider than historical norms throughout the forecast period.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think these new spread relationships are uncertain.

speaker: WARSH
text: So what we thought would be sort of normal spreads of LIBOR and normal spreads of corporate bonds, all have to be reassessed not just by us but also by market participants.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even if credit is now made more available to businesses through some of these new Treasury and other programs, I suspect the all-in cost of capital is likely to materially impede business investment, particularly given expectations by businesses for a weaker economy in the upcoming period.

speaker: WARSH
text: As Vice Chairman Geithner suggested, monetary policy might be able to do a bit about this, but it is not going to be able to change it very much.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn to three points on the economy before closing.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, in the near term, given my sense of how October is tracking, it’s likely to be extraordinarily weak.

speaker: WARSH
text: I expect weaker fourth- quarter consumption than the Greenbook, weaker labor markets going into 2009, and a materially weaker fourth-quarter GDP print.

speaker: WARSH
text: Some labor surveys—including some of my own preferred measures, like the JOLTS—seem to be holding up; but I’m not sure that that’s going to hold for another couple of months.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I’d expect the labor markets to trend more materially in the direction that I’ve discussed.

speaker: WARSH
text: Well, what about beyond the near term?

speaker: WARSH
text: What about 2009 and beyond?

speaker: WARSH
text: It strikes me that the catalysts for marked improvement are lacking.

speaker: WARSH
text: When I think about fiscal policy, regulatory policy, tax policy, and trade policy, which I talked about previously, it’s not obvious to me that any of those are going to provide some kind of catalyst for a marked change in the contour of the economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the fiscal front, I assume that the fiscal stimulus is likely to be larger, maybe even materially larger, than in the Greenbook alternative simulation, but my own conclusions are similar to the Greenbook’s, which is that I’m not sure it’s going to be terribly effective.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m not sure it’s going to be constructed in that way, and I’m not sure it will do nearly as much as it will inevitably be advertised to do.

speaker: WARSH
text: A more disturbing trend probably even than the efficacy of a fiscal package— which in my own view is absolutely necessary, but again I query whether it’s going to be structured in a way to do what it needs to do—is that potential output in the forecast period is likely to fall.

speaker: WARSH
text: Trend growth rates are coming down, and I expect productivity to fall perhaps even more than in the Greenbook projection.

speaker: WARSH
text: The vaunted resilience of the U.S. economy, which I’ve talked about for a long time, is certainly going to be tested during this period.

speaker: WARSH
text: Business investment, it strikes me, will be a useful gauge as we get into the first quarter of 2009 to see how tough an economic period we have in front of us, and I worry about the decisions that business people will be making.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now, of course, against all of this, markets could snap back, as we saw a little yesterday—2009 could look better.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have to remain open minded about the possibility that the economy will continue, as it has over the past ten or fifteen years, to outperform model-based expectations.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn to foreign growth.

speaker: WARSH
text: These decouplers, which were so prominent for so long, are somehow hard to find these days.

speaker: WARSH
text: Foreign growth strikes me as likely to fall faster and stay lower than in the Greenbook projection.

speaker: WARSH
text: The road back is not likely to begin as early as the first quarter of 2009 for our major trading partners.

speaker: WARSH
text: The “more financial fallout” alternative simulation strikes me as significantly more likely for foreign growth.

speaker: WARSH
text: In light of a growth trajectory that is better here in the United States than outside the United States, at least relative to current market expectations, I’d expect the foreign exchange value of the dollar on balance to strengthen against a basket of foreign currencies.

speaker: WARSH
text: So let me turn finally to inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: The trend on import prices, the broad measures of commodity prices, and the expected dollar strength all suggest that inflation problems are abating markedly.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think an open question, which isn’t likely to be dispositive but is likely to be interesting, is how sticky prices are, particularly from the consumer product companies during this period—how long the various surcharges and increases in prices we’ve seen can stay high and the companies attempt to keep profit margins.

speaker: WARSH
text: My guess is that they can make profit margins look decent for another quarter or two; but beyond that, prices across a broad set of products and services are likely to retrace some of the gains in recent periods.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’ll save the balance of my remarks for the next round.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, the autumnal bonfires have really sort of heated up since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we have evidence in the United States and now worldwide of what emerging market literature calls “sudden stops”—a sudden stopping of the flow of capital, the so-called flow of hot money, into Latin America or other countries and the devastating impact that could have when suddenly credit is no longer available.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I’ve been talking about the slow burn of the problems in the credit markets, but I think we saw that move up to a different level globally over the past six weeks.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This is the concern that we had earlier in the year about a regime shift.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We seem to have moved from a growth regime to a sliding-by-with-some-growth regime and now to a contractionary one and the nonlinear effects that we had been concerned about.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As we always say, it’s particularly difficult to predict where the economy is going to go.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But there’s evidence of why it’s so difficult because almost any measure of volatility is up dramatically.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That’s true on the financial market side, on the real side, as well as just in movements of consumer confidence.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I think that we can say with some confidence that it is particularly difficult to predict which way things are going to go.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As many people have said before, a few spreads have come down, but given the extent of our actions and those of other governments around the world—central banks, fiscal authorities, et cetera—it is surprising that there has been so little effect.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now, maybe it’s just because so much is going on that there’s a fair amount of confusion and uncertainty about what the programs mean, how they will actually be implemented, and to whom they will be applied.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that’s perhaps part of the reason for some of the spreads not coming down with respect to interbank borrowing—there is a lack of clarity about exactly how the FDIC program will operate and exactly how the TARP will operate.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’ll hear more about that in a bit, but I think it’s going to take time for people to feel confident about how that will work.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, I think there is real uncertainty because after thirty days some banks may not get the guarantees or may have the guarantees pulled back.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think there is also a lot of uncertainty about who will get TARP funding and who is qualified for TARP funding.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As information comes out about people not being qualified or markets being concerned that individual institutions are not going to be qualified, that could put on a lot of pressure.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Unfortunately, that’s going to be coming in addition to the end- of-the-year pressures.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I see a number of looming risks, particularly in the financial services sector, as we fully implement and clarify some of the programs that I think on balance can be helpful but that can actually cause some uncertainty at individual institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Others have also mentioned broader challenges in the emerging markets and the insurance companies and certainly we have the hedge fund redemptions that are looming.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I’m very concerned about trying to get over the end of the year with so many different pieces putting additional pressure on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Even some of the pieces that we thought would be helpful potentially have a lot of downside risk to them.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But even if we get through this—and the government guarantee programs, the special liquidity facilities, and the negative real rates that we have and potentially may make even more negative would provide some support—the fundamental uncertainty is not going to be resolved until we see what is going to work in the financial sector, what’s going to be the successful business model, and what are going to be the new sets of activities that can be undertaken.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Will certain funding markets come back and at what spread once you take away all these special programs?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Until that is worked out, I don’t see how the markets can figure out who will survive and who won’t, who is going to be there in three months and who isn’t.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that the programs are very valuable in providing a time out—a time for people to reassess.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But until there’s greater clarity in those financing markets going forward, I don’t think the markets will actually be able to recover.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That why the alternative simulation that puts things off a bit more seems quite sensible to me.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As I often do, I talked with some of the largest providers of consumer credit in the United States.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They are reporting, exactly as Governor Kohn said, that consumption or spending growth was decelerating through the summer, but it did seem to get much more rapid in September and October.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One of the large companies actually reported significant contraction on the consumer side of spending.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On the small business side, it was still positive but down from double-digit growth in the second quarter to basically flat.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They also looked across income categories.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This is not a phenomenon of just the people at one or the other end of the spectrum.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It seemed to be across the board for what they looked at.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: All of them have reported, just as the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey did, a significant reduction of credit lines.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So even if we’re not seeing credit in and of itself having contracted yet, the ability to get credit down the line is going to be much, much more difficult.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also the funding markets for the credit card companies have effectively closed.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Things may come back, but I think it’s going to take time for that to happen, and they were certainly not optimistic about that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As virtually everyone has mentioned, inflationary pressures for a variety of reasons are much lower, and I think that fits into what the Vice Chairman said about thinking about the costs of moving now and perhaps moving “too quickly.” There seem to be lower costs now in being a bit more aggressive than, let’s say, six months ago because much less inflationary pressure seems to be out there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think a prudent risk-management point of view would certainly take into account those costs and benefits.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We need to use our monetary policy tools as effectively as we can and then work with the other tools that a number of others have mentioned to try to get the markets to be more comfortable with where things will go and then be able to lend to each other—to have the unlocking of the credit markets without government guarantees, without negative interest rates, and without extraordinary liquidity facilities.

speaker: DUKE
text: I focused on the “more rapid financial recovery” scenario, not so much because I thought it was the most likely but just trying to think what it would take to bring that about.

speaker: DUKE
text: I’m not sure that the policy changes we have done recently will do that, but I am fairly certain that we are going to keep at it until we find something that restores confidence.

speaker: DUKE
text: I was shocked when I was looking at the Bluebook at how short a time has passed since the meltdown of all these major financial institutions—Fannie, Freddie, Lehman, AIG, WaMu, and Wachovia.

speaker: DUKE
text: There is a sense among those who were affected, who lost from it, that they just really didn’t see it coming, at least not at this speed, and that all of them had adequate regulatory capital, and the bankers at least were used to watching a sort of gradual burndown of that capital before institutions failed.

speaker: DUKE
text: They had a sense of being unable to predict who was going to be saved, who was going to get whacked, and who would be the winners and the losers.

speaker: DUKE
text: So subsequently both the banks and their customers froze, and there has been very little activity since then.

speaker: DUKE
text: All the banks I talked to reported having stopped doing business with one or more counterparties and that one or more counterparties had stopped doing business with them, and they were shocked by both of those things.

speaker: DUKE
text: So, first and foremost, it is clear that we need to restore confidence and predictability.

speaker: DUKE
text: In this sense, the recent moves to increase deposit insurance, to guarantee interbank short-term debt, and to provide capital on the same terms to banks of all sizes should be helpful—but only as long as we can do this without creating new uncertainty about who is going to benefit and who is not.

speaker: DUKE
text: Without being too subjective or too cute, we need at this point just to create confidence in our entire system.

speaker: DUKE
text: The demonstrable and preemptive support of the nine largest financial institutions; our public support of AIG; similar support of globally important banks by their home countries; and the resolution of Wachovia and National City, the two largest troubled institutions, without loss should help us avoid shocking surprises while everybody calms down.

speaker: DUKE
text: In this light, my conversation with the banks centered mostly on their reactions to the recent policy changes.

speaker: DUKE
text: All thought the deposit insurance increase was helpful.

speaker: DUKE
text: They varied in their estimates of the importance of the increase to $250,000, with a lot of them pointing out that for consumers they had already really restructured deposits to insure fairly large amounts, and several were using the CDARS (Certificate of Deposit Account Registry Service) program for larger depositors.

speaker: DUKE
text: They were even more enthusiastic about the coverage of transaction accounts, although one banker felt as though this coverage really hadn’t gotten as much visibility as it should, particularly with corporate treasurers, and many had already seen corporate and institutional deposits move into Treasuries and felt as though it was going to be difficult to get those back.

speaker: DUKE
text: There was even much more confusion about the guarantee of short-term debt.

speaker: DUKE
text: One banker questioned how they would know whether the fed funds sold to another bank actually fell inside the 125 percent cap.

speaker: DUKE
text: Another one thought that the all-or-nothing structure of the guarantee was a little difficult to work with.

speaker: DUKE
text: Interestingly, and as I pointed out yesterday when I asked about interest on reserves, nobody had even focused on it.

speaker: DUKE
text: They had bigger fish to fry.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I wouldn’t read anything into those early results.

speaker: DUKE
text: As for capital injections, most were taking a hard look at it.

speaker: DUKE
text: Two large community banks had just issued private capital to support growth that had been attracted from competitors, but they thought that they could profitably deploy the new capital.

speaker: DUKE
text: Other banks were interested in having the capital just in case they had the opportunity to buy weaker competitors, particularly deposits or branches in problem resolutions.

speaker: DUKE
text: None was really concerned about the announced restrictions, but a number of them were somewhat suspicious of the possible restrictions that might come later.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some small banks with already high levels of capital somehow felt pressured to apply anyway just to show that they would qualify, although they didn’t think it would give them much growth.

speaker: DUKE
text: In all cases, capital is only part of the story.

speaker: DUKE
text: They also need reliable funding if they are going to expand lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: This will have to come either from reliable deposit growth or from the reopening of secondary markets because all of them were reluctant to increase borrowing from any source.

speaker: DUKE
text: The loan-to-deposit ratio is growing new fans.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of lending, all reported that they were still lending to their relationship customers, and they were cutting back on credit to credit-only customers.

speaker: DUKE
text: As one defined it, if 90 percent of the revenue is coming from credit, then that was a customer relationship they wanted to exit.

speaker: DUKE
text: They still report no significant deterioration in the C&I book.

speaker: DUKE
text: I asked about drawdowns from companies, and across the board they said they had seen it in a couple of instances but really they had not seen an awful lot of that, so that might be some posturing rather than actual drawdowns on the credit.

speaker: DUKE
text: They are, however, exercising strong pricing discipline, and the pricing decisions, more than credit decisions, are being escalated up the approval chain, actively outreaching to customers that they want to keep and assuring them of credit availability.

speaker: DUKE
text: But because they have no pricing power on the funding side and pricing became very skinny on loans in recent years, there is a high level of sticker shock going on, which might explain some of the complaints about unreasonable terms.

speaker: DUKE
text: They also report very high levels of caution from their customers, with the descriptions ranging from “hunkering down” to “wait and see.” There were more anecdotal reports of companies riding trade credit by trying to accelerate receivables or extend payables.

speaker: DUKE
text: Now, whether this is due to the actual or to the perceived unavailability of credit from banks is not yet clear.

speaker: DUKE
text: Real pressure is on commercial real estate lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: They are very selective in new projects.

speaker: DUKE
text: They are processing renewals for only one year, using the opportunity to shore up pricing and underwriting, and no longer writing mini-perms.

speaker: DUKE
text: So far, the performance is holding up on commercial properties, with strong performance on apartments and weakness showing up in retail.

speaker: DUKE
text: Residential construction and land development continues to be a problem.

speaker: DUKE
text: In visiting the San Francisco and the Kansas City Banks, I was shocked to hear the same story from large builders about land sales.

speaker: DUKE
text: One builder had a 300-acre parcel with a cost of $75,000 an acre, listed it for $15,000 an acre, and sold it for $10,700.

speaker: DUKE
text: Another reported a property with a cost basis of $120 million selling for $12 million.

speaker: DUKE
text: Apparently, the impetus for both of these transactions was a judgment that the cash received from tax refunds was more advantageous than holding out for better pricing.

speaker: DUKE
text: So the outlook for lending in residential construction or commercial real estate is dim far into the future, and I would say the same thing for syndicated or participated lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: However, to the extent that banks can exit those segments, it should free up funds for normal lending for businesses and consumers.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask Governor Duke a question.

speaker: FISHER
text: Do you sense in this deep dive into the institutions that you talked to that they are benefiting from cuts in the fed funds rate?

speaker: FISHER
text: Are they enthusiastic or not about the prospect for a lower fed funds rate?

speaker: DUKE
text: Actually, I have heard a couple of reports that, when we did that last 50 basis point cut, banks did not lower their prime.

speaker: DUKE
text: A lot of banks still have prime-related credits.

speaker: DUKE
text: As we lower the rates, whether it makes a difference on anything else, it affects the prime, and there are still an awful lot of 5 percent CDs out there.

speaker: DUKE
text: So as we lower rates, we are cutting into those margins, and it is likely to turn some of them negative.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would just echo that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have heard the same thing from bankers in our District—just vociferous complaints about lowering rates because their loan rates go down but their cost of funds doesn’t.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, if I could just add one other thing.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are hearing more and more about people switching to LIBOR, trying to shift their lending contracts to LIBOR rather aggressively, obviously, because they are higher rates.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I’m wondering if you’re picking that up as well.

speaker: DUKE
text: But just as soon as they get them switched over there, maybe we’ll be successful at bringing LIBOR down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me try to summarize all that I heard today and yesterday, and then I’ll try to add some new comments to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The outlook for economic growth appears to have deteriorated quite significantly since the last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Data on consumer spending, production, and employment had weakened more than expected even before the recent intensification of the financial crisis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Over the past six weeks or so, however, financial conditions have greatly worsened, and risk aversion has increased, despite actions here and abroad to stabilize the banking system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Equity values have declined sharply amid conditions of low liquidity and extraordinary volatility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit market conditions have improved modestly since the global actions to recapitalize banks and guarantee their deposits, assisted also by additional central bank liquidity actions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, in almost all credit markets, spreads remain much wider, maturities shorter, and availability more constrained than was the case before the intensification of the crisis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Firms face continued funding risk and rollover risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Banks have probably not reserved sufficiently for the credit losses to come, and hedge funds will be hitting their net asset value triggers in greater numbers, forcing them to liquidate assets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The duration of future financial turmoil is hard to judge, but it could be lengthy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The worst thing is that financial conditions appear already to have had a significant and remarkably quick effect on activity and consumer and business expectations and plans.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most Committee participants see us in or entering a recession and have marked down significantly their expectations for near-term growth or for the pace of the recovery.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The difficulty of predicting the course of the crisis or its effects on the economy has also increased forecast uncertainty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, the ultimate effects of some major policy actions, such as the creation of the TARP and the bank guarantee, are not yet known.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Uncertainty about future policy actions, as well as uncertainty about the economy, has affected behavior in markets and the broader economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumer spending has weakened considerably and probably fell sharply in the third quarter, reflecting in part a recessionary psychology.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumer durables, such as automobiles and discretionary expenditures, have been particularly hard hit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This weakness reflects the same set of negative influences on consumption that we have been seeing for a while, now compounded by losses of equity wealth and confidence effects on prices, although lower oil prices may provide some relief.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The labor market continues to decline, with many firms reporting that they are cutting back workers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The housing sector has not been noticeably worse than expected, and reports are somewhat mixed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But on a national basis, the contraction is continuing, and recent developments in the economy and credit markets are likely to have adverse effects.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inventories of unsold new homes remain high, putting pressure on prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nonresidential construction continues at a moderate pace; but backlogs are falling, and the sector is looking increasingly vulnerable to weakening fundamentals and tighter credit conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Whether a new fiscal stimulus package will be passed and to what extent such a package would be helpful remain open questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Manufacturing production has weakened significantly as have expectations of demand, including export demand.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit is becoming more of a problem for many firms and their customers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Spending on equipment and software appears to have slowed, reflecting greater pessimism and uncertainty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Falling commodity prices may reduce mining activity and cool the boom in agriculture.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the plus side, firms are reporting fewer cost pressures, and inventories do not appear excessive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Deterioration in global growth expectations has been marked.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Industrial economies had already shown signs of slowing, and they have been hit hard by recent financial developments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Emerging market economies, until recently evidently not much affected by the U.S. slowdown, have in recent weeks also been hit hard by the spreading financial crisis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Together with the stronger dollar, these developments are likely to restrain future growth of U.S. exports.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inflation risks have declined materially, reflecting the fall in the prices of energy and other commodities, the stronger dollar, and the prospect of considerable economic slack.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Firms report much reduced pricing power and lower markups.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inflation expectations have come down, both in the surveys and in the TIPS market, though it wasn’t noted—but I will note—that the TIPS market is distorted by illiquidity and other problems there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most participants see both overall and core inflation moderating in the coming quarters toward levels consistent with price stability, with some seeing a risk of undesirably low rates of inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some note, however, that financial dislocations affect aggregate supply as well as aggregate demand and may reduce the extent to which slower growth damps inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s just my sense.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me make just a few additional comments, none of which will be radically different from what we have already discussed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think it is overwhelmingly clear that we are now in a recession and that it is going to be a severe one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To give some sense of perspective, the postwar record for duration is 16 months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If the NBER sets this experience as having begun early this year, I think we have a reasonable chance to break that record.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The largest increase from peak to trough in unemployment rate was in 1981.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It was 3.6 percentage points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Starting from 4.4 percent, I think we have a chance to come close to that number.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yesterday’s drop in consumer confidence in one month from 61 to 38 shattered the previous low of 43 in December 1975.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think we are talking about an episode here that could easily be among the largest postwar recessions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t know how things would have evolved without the developments in September, but obviously we have to deal with that reality.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It was just a few weeks ago that we were dealing with what might have been a true systemic crisis, in the week leading up to the G-7 and IMF meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it has been very fortunate that Europe, the United States, and other countries have adopted vigorous responses to that, including bank capitalization, bank guarantees, and other measures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That has been very important in calming the situation somewhat and reducing the systemic aspects of investor concerns.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That being said, concern about counterparties remains very strong.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Risk aversion is intense, spreads remain high, and I think that this has now become really pervasive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It isn’t just a question of junk bonds and weak borrowers or weak credit histories.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The spreads on GSE debt, on high-grade corporate debt, and other areas have also widened, leading to a very broad based tightening in credit conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that, overall, any reasonable reading of financial conditions suggests that the tightening of credit or financial conditions in the last six weeks or so has been quite substantial and overwhelms the effects of our coordinated rate cut.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, normally you would expect to see a tightening of credit conditions affect the economy with some lag.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It takes time for people to borrow money and to use the money they borrow to make expenditures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But compared with that prediction, we have instead seen a sudden stop—a remarkable and very rapid effect on economic activity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is possible this is due less to the direct effects of credit availability and more to the psychological impact of these events.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One possible analogy is the 1980 Carter credit controls, when the government announced what seemed to be a tightening of credit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was a very sharp response in economic activity, probably based more on expectations than on actual credit availability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unfortunately, the credit controls could be removed by government fiat; we are not able to do that today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One interesting development is that the labor market has not yet shown as much weakness as one would expect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unemployment insurance claims and other indicators do not yet show a marked deterioration.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I expect that we will see more deterioration of the labor market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Besides the intensification of the financial crisis that has markedly increased the restrictiveness of financial conditions, I think the other very important development since our last meeting has been the internationalization of the crisis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We had already seen weakening in Europe before the most recent intensification, but it has become much more severe.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is little doubt that the United Kingdom and Europe are in or about to enter recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My sense is that their monetary policy responses will be stronger than what the Greenbook anticipates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I believe they will be very aggressive in responding to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A new and particularly worrying development is the fact that the crisis has now spread beyond the industrial countries to the emerging markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The G-7 weekend was quite an interesting one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It was a striking experience.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I heard over and over again from the Indians, from the Brazilians, and from all over the world that, until the middle of September we were fine, we were not being much affected, we didn’t see much effect on our trade flows, and suddenly everything changed; and now we are under severe stress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are seeing tremendous outflows.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Commodity price declines are hurting many countries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that is going to be a very significant development as we go forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just to give some data, in just a few weeks the EMBI spread, the emerging market sovereign debt spread, went from 280 basis points to 850 basis points; and the emerging market equity index has fallen about 40 percent since the last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is not obvious that these changes were justified by economic fundamentals.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Many of these countries are very well run and had shown a lot of progress in their domestic policies and their domestic economies.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Instead, I think they are suffering contagion from us mostly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unfortunately, the implications of this will be not only the usual trade and commodity price type of implications but also, and even more important, financial implications.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are now seeing that the adverse feedback loop, which we’ve been talking about for a long time in the United States, is becoming a global phenomenon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, European banks are very heavily exposed to emerging market debt.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we are going to see yet more of this interaction between the financial markets and the broader economy, except at a global rather than a national level.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: These developments, obviously, are very disturbing and don’t bode well for U.S. growth or now for global growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Somewhat ironically, all of this deterioration in the global outlook has led the dollar to appreciate very sharply, which is interesting to say the least.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For us that obviously also has important implications for inflation, and as Governor Kohn mentioned, it means that we will be less a recipient of foreign strength and more a supporter of foreign weakness than we have been until now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On inflation, I know there is some discomfort in talking about a 1 percent policy rate and promising to keep it low for a protracted period—and all those things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have seen this movie before, and I think we all have to recognize the importance of watching the implications of that for our economy and for asset prices and to take quite seriously the responsibility for removing accommodation in a timely fashion once the crisis has begun to moderate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That being said, I don’t think that there is really any case in the near term to be worrying very much about inflation—or, perhaps even less so, the dollar—as we look at our policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And given what is happening in the global economy, I don’t see a commodity price boom any time soon, although I think as the economies do begin to recover in the next year or so that we might see some recovery in commodity prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that, as everyone has indicated, this is a very worrisome situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think we have control of it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think we know what the bottom is, so we have to remain very flexible and very open to new initiatives as they become necessary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There has been some comparison of this to the Japanese situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m beginning to wonder if that might not be a good outcome.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The advantage of the Japanese was, first of all, that they were isolated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The rest of the world was doing okay, and they were able to draw strength from their exports and the rest of the global economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although they had very slow growth, they never really had a deep recession or big increases in unemployment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we are looking at perhaps a much sharper episode, and our challenge will be to make sure that it doesn’t persist longer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think that one lesson of both Japan and the 1930s as well as other experiences is that passivity is not a good answer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We do have to continue to be aggressive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have to continue to look for solutions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some of them are not going to work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some of them are going to add to uncertainty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I realize it’s a valid critique.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I don’t think that this is going to be a self-correcting thing anytime soon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we are going to have to continue to provide support of all kinds to the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me stop there and, unless there is any question or comment, ask Brian to introduce the policy round.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 7 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will be referring to the version of table 1 that was distributed to you on Monday.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is reproduced in the package before you labeled “Material for Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” Changes in the language relative to the Bluebook version are shown in blue.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Starting on the right-hand side of the table, even though members saw the economic and financial information that became available over the intermeeting period as worse than expected, they might be inclined to leave the stance of policy unchanged at today’s meeting, as in alternative C. As noted yesterday, your 7 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 7).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: economic projections reveal that many of you anticipate that inflation pressures will diminish less quickly than the staff anticipates, and several of you noted explicitly that you thought less easing would be appropriate than was assumed in the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, the Committee already reduced rates in early October, responding to at least some of the adverse economic news.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, the Federal Reserve has put in place additional facilities to support credit intermediation, and the Treasury and the FDIC are moving quickly with the implementation of other programs that should, with time, help stabilize financial institutions and markets and enhance the flow of credit to households and businesses.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, you might believe that the Congress is likely to enact a second fiscal stimulus package, possibly reducing the need for additional monetary policy accommodation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The rationale section of the statement suggested for alternative C would acknowledge the intensification of financial turmoil and the weakening of the economic outlook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, it would also cite the range of policy actions taken in recent weeks as factors that should help over time to improve credit conditions and promote a return to moderate economic growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The language on inflation would be essentially identical to that used in the Committee’s statement earlier this month, noting that the upside risks to inflation have been reduced.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The risk assessment would state explicitly that the Committee’s primary concern is the downside risks to growth, suggesting a predilection for lowering rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Nonetheless, with market participants anticipating an easing today—a 50 basis point move is seen as most likely—an announcement along the lines of alternative C would point to a much higher trajectory for the federal funds rate over the next few months than investors had expected.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Short- and intermediate-term Treasury yields would likely jump, credit spreads probably would increase further, and equity prices might decline sharply.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If the Committee is of the view that further policy accommodation is appropriate at this time but is also quite uncertain about the extent of rate reductions that will ultimately be required, it might be attracted to the 25 basis point easing of alternative B at this meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Members might have a less pessimistic outlook for the economy than that presented as the baseline in the Greenbook or might at least be quite uncertain as to the extent of the negative forces at work in the economy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: At the same time, you may view the incoming information as suggesting that the 50 basis point easing earlier this month is unlikely to be sufficient to adequately balance the risks to economic activity and inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Given these considerations, you might see modest further easing today as appropriate and be prepared to cut rates again in coming months should developments warrant.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement proposed for alternative B would note that the pace of economic activity appears to have slowed markedly, and it would repeat language from your early October statement indicating that the financial market turmoil is likely to exert additional restraint on spending.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The announcement would also indicate that, in light of the decline in the prices of energy and other commodities, the Committee expects inflation to moderate in coming quarters to levels consistent with price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As noted in a box in the Bluebook, we think that, in view of your previous policy communications, outside analysts would interpret such a statement on the inflation outlook as indicating that the Committee anticipates that overall inflation will drop to around 1½ percent to 1¾ percent before long, a indication that would be consistent with the central tendency of your inflation projections for 2009.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The risk assessment in alternative B, paragraph 4, would cite the same broad range of policy actions that was proposed in alternative C, paragraph 2.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would indicate that the predominant concern of the Committee is the downside risks to economic growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Market participants see a 25 basis point easing at this meeting as possible, but at this point they seem to place significantly higher odds on a 50 basis point reduction.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The explicit citation of downside risks to growth would suggest that further easing could be forthcoming after this meeting, but this announcement still would suggest a higher path for the federal funds rate than they anticipate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Consequently, short- and intermediate-term rates might tend to edge up after such an announcement, credit spreads might widen somewhat further, and equity prices might decline.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative A, the Committee would ease policy 50 basis points at this meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: An economic outlook along the lines of the Greenbook forecast would provide one rationale for choosing this alternative.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Greenbook forecast for aggregate demand has been slashed dramatically, importantly reflecting a sharp decline in equity prices, a steep rise in credit risk premiums, and a considerable climb in the foreign exchange value of the dollar.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One metric for this revision is the Greenbook-consistent measure of the short-run equilibrium real interest rate, r*, which has been cut nearly 3 percentage points since the September meeting to a level of about minus 3 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That level is about 2 percentage points below the actual real funds rate defined on a consistent basis.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The staff outlook for a protracted period of substantial economic slack, together with the recent plunge in energy prices, points to a considerable diminution of inflation pressures, with overall inflation falling to 1½ percent next year in the Greenbook forecast—even with the Greenbook’s assumption of 100 basis points of further easing by early next year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But even those who are somewhat less pessimistic about the outlook than the Board staff might view the modal outlook as having deteriorated enough, or the downside risks as having increased enough, to warrant a 50 basis point rate cut today.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The rationale language for alternative A in the revised version of table 1 is similar to that for alternative B, but alternative A, paragraph 2, notes additional factors that are restraining growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The risk assessment, too, is similar to that for alternative B, but it references the rate reduction that would be implemented today under this alternative and notes that downside risks to growth remain, without saying that the downside risks are the Committee’s predominant concern.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: An announcement along these lines seems largely consistent with market participants’ expectations, and the market reaction would likely be relatively small.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no questions, why don’t we begin our go-round.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think that this is a tough call.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I support alternative B, with the statement wording as presented.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my thinking, a 25 basis point cut today is part of a total 75 basis point action, including the October 8 move.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I believe the deterioration we have seen in September and October and the resulting downward revision of the outlook merit a cumulative response of this magnitude.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That said, I am sympathetic to the view that we would be well advised to keep some powder dry to respond to shocks or developments ahead.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I anticipate that, because a number of the dynamics in the markets have not really played out, we will have more shocks and they could come from further financial institution failures, corporate failures, a sovereign debt crisis, and market disarray; and in other markets, such as the municipal market, there is always a chance of a geopolitical event.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In all likelihood these things come in combination or in rapid fire.

speaker: LOCKHART
