text: So, as I said, I am sympathetic to the “powder dry” view, but I see the powder dry objective as being in conflict with responding to the recent deterioration.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Therefore I come to 25 basis points or alternative B to some extent as a compromise, combined with the 50 basis points of October 8.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I favor alternative A, a 50 basis point cut in the funds rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This action, and even more, is justified by the dramatic developments since our last meeting—a deepening of the recessionary outlook worldwide, the near meltdown of the global financial system, and the abatement of inflationary pressures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Frankly, it is time for all hands on deck when it comes to our policy tools, and the fed funds rate should be no exception.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although we cut the funds rate 50 basis points a few weeks ago, the Greenbook inflation projection was revised down more than that, so the ex ante real funds rate actually edged up over the intermeeting period.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We need to do much more and the sooner, the better.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One might argue against such a policy move in favor of a wait-and-see approach to better gauge if the recent flurry of policy initiatives will turn things around.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In normal times, I would have some sympathy for this argument, but these are about as far from normal times as we can get.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We are in the midst of a global economic and financial freefall, and the confidence of households, businesses, and investors is in shambles.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The adverse feedback loop is playing out with a vengeance.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Lenders continue to ratchet up terms and standards, sapping the ability of households and businesses to spend.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As the economy weakens, further loan defaults will mushroom.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think strong, clear action is needed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Historical precedents, such as the case of Japan, teach us that it is a mistake to act cautiously as the economy unravels.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the clear lesson from both economic theory and real-world experience is to lower rates as quickly as possible to avoid a deeper and more protracted recession, not to keep our powder dry or to wait to use tools until later if they are available to us now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The more medicine we give and the sooner we give it, the better.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The Bluebook optimal policy simulations tell us that, absent the zero bound, the funds rate should be lowered well below zero next year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Since that is not an option, we should do the most with what we’ve got and cut the funds rate aggressively now.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like President Yellen, I support alternative A, the 50 basis point cut.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it’s the right response to the very, very substantial change in the economic outlook since the last meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: We would have cut the nominal federal funds rate by 1 percentage point and real federal funds rates by something less than 1 percentage point depending on what you think is happening to inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: But surely inflation expectations are coming down—and coming down substantially.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the incoming information, the weakness before the shock hit in mid-September (which to me suggests that we didn’t have any insurance against that weakness at the time), the extraordinary tightening of financial conditions, and the downshift in spending that we’ve seen since mid-September all suggest that a 1 percentage point cut in the real rate, and even a little less than a 1 percentage point cut, would seem a very modest and moderate response to the shock.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s probably a down payment.

speaker: KOHN
text: If the staff is right, we will need more.

speaker: KOHN
text: I built more into my own forecast.

speaker: KOHN
text: But even if the economy is not as weak as the staff has built into the Greenbook, I think a substantial cut in the federal funds rate is entirely appropriate.

speaker: KOHN
text: All of us—without exception, I think—said that there were downside risks to their forecasts, and a number of us have cited the possibility of a very deep recession here.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think we need to take action.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are starting with a situation in which the economy is declining.

speaker: KOHN
text: The unemployment rate is rising.

speaker: KOHN
text: There is a global recession in train.

speaker: KOHN
text: It seems to me, from a risk-management perspective, that the costs of not doing enough—the costs of being reluctant to lower rates and making that situation worse—are far larger than the costs of going a little too far because things turn around faster.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we are in a situation in which it is almost impossible at this point to go too far.

speaker: KOHN
text: Mr. Chairman, we may have to take it back at some point in the future, but right now I think the 50 basis points is absolutely justified by the conditions in which we find ourselves.

speaker: KOHN
text: I was drawn, as the Vice Chairman was, to the staff simulation having to do with a more rapid financial recovery.

speaker: KOHN
text: I myself think that’s a very small probability.

speaker: KOHN
text: But even if that’s what happens, we’ll know by December whether the financial markets are recovering faster.

speaker: KOHN
text: We can stop at 1 percent, if we’re getting that recovery; and the outcomes, as the Vice Chairman noted, really aren’t that bad in that recovery.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think that even the small probability of a very sharp turnaround in the markets is still consistent with cutting rates another 50 basis points at this meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: The fact that we are already low is not a reason to hold back.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t agree with the “keeping the powder dry” kind of argument.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the lessons of history, including from Japan, are that the closer you get to the zero lower bound the more aggressive you should be.

speaker: KOHN
text: If you let weakness build, that weakness will overwhelm your policy tools.

speaker: KOHN
text: The most effective use of the limited scope for policy easing is to be preemptive and stop weaknesses from building.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think a 50 basis point easing will have beneficial effects.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think that the markets will react very much.

speaker: KOHN
text: We won’t see those beneficial effects.

speaker: KOHN
text: But if I can compare it with doing 25 or nothing at all, I think doing 25 or nothing at all would have adverse effects.

speaker: KOHN
text: With 25 or nothing, you’ll get longer-term rates up, you’ll get stock prices down, and you’ll get an erosion of confidence at a time when we don’t need it—that the central bank doesn’t get how serious this situation is.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that the last easing was largely offset by the loss of confidence and the rise in uncertainty.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also agree that it might not feed through as directly and completely as it often does because banks are trying to rebuild and lenders are trying to rebuild profit margins.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I still think it will be effective.

speaker: KOHN
text: As I say, I convinced myself of that by asking about what would happen with the alternatives, and I think the alternatives would be far worse.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to keep fine-tuning the TARP and the liquidity provision.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with all of that.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to move on lots of dimensions.

speaker: KOHN
text: But these things will not be sufficient in and of themselves to counter this.

speaker: KOHN
text: Monetary policy is a fairly blunt instrument, but we need to stimulate the spending wherever we can to do this.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some have expressed concern about circumstances forcing us to ease between meetings.

speaker: KOHN
text: Will that take us further?

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we need to make clear in our statement and our minutes—particularly in our minutes—that we do expect a weak economy going forward, at least a moderately softer economy, and that the process may call for further easing.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it will call for further easing at the next FOMC meeting, but we can get to the next FOMC meeting and see.

speaker: KOHN
text: But it should take a substantial and unexpected deterioration relative to that path to justify an intermeeting action.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think we are absolutely right to have a prejudice toward taking actions at meetings, when we can sit around and discuss things.

speaker: KOHN
text: The odds are high that we will need to go further, but we should do that at a meeting if we can.

speaker: KOHN
text: If we do have a very strong and substantial deterioration even relative to our weak outlook and we do end up moving between meetings, surely that move would not put us at a level that is unjustified by the circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think we can deal with the intermeeting situation and not have the pressures of the market, the pressures of expectations, get us to a level at which we’re ultimately uncomfortable.

speaker: KOHN
text: In short, I think it’s a very serious situation.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to do all we can to counter this situation.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now is not the time to hold back.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Like the Greenbook forecast, our forecast predicts a significant recession.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Further easing will likely help mitigate the severity of the recession.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Coupled with improvements in short-term credit spreads, a reduction in the federal funds rate should lower rates on home equity lines of credit as well as business and consumer rates tied to LIBOR, easing cash flow for consumers and businesses.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We are facing problems of historic proportions, both here and abroad.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A 50 basis point easing, as in alternative A, is both necessary and appropriate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Even with the easing assumed in the Greenbook, the unemployment rate remains too high for too long.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The inflation rate falls enough to be well below my target.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: To avoid a severe and prolonged recession, we will very likely need further monetary easing and a significant fiscal package, even after this 50 basis point reduction in the federal funds rate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would just note in terms of the language that, although I am comfortable with the alternative A language, my actual views would be closer to saying “the predominant concern of the Committee is the downside risk to growth” rather than “nevertheless, downside risks to growth remain.”

speaker: EVANS
text: After thinking about this for quite some time, I cannot convince myself that alternative A is not the right way to go.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Let the transcript reflect that.

speaker: EVANS
text: You were very effective in listing a number of dire circumstances.

speaker: EVANS
text: The fact that we may challenge the maximum duration of a recession in the postwar period, any mention of the 1981-82 recession is very frightening, you even mentioned 1975 in terms of the reduction in confidence, and the 1980 credit crunch also—you were able to do that without any mention of the 1930s, and that’s quite compelling, I would say.

speaker: EVANS
text: So for the reasons that have been already discussed, the outlook is quite unfavorable, and I think that this will help improve matters.

speaker: EVANS
text: But as I thought about the concerns that I have, one concern is whether this will actually be viewed as effective today.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m not sure about that.

speaker: EVANS
text: The last time we cut rates, financial stress intervened to swamp any beneficial interpretation of that.

speaker: EVANS
text: Whether that affects our credibility, I think that Don Kohn was very effective in mentioning that there will be credibility hits in the other direction if we don’t take some action like that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I do think that eventually things will subside and the beneficial effects of lower policy will be seen.

speaker: EVANS
text: About the dry powder argument, we are not going to have many more actions left after this, but I don’t see what the alternatives are other than to go ahead and put this in place.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t subscribe to the view that inflation is likely to be too low, although that is a risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: Inflation concerns, the financial stress, all of those issues, even taking into account the risk that President Bullard mentioned the other day, I think speak strongly to the fact that we’re running out of normal monetary policy options and that fiscal actions are going to be strongly important.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I do favor alternative A.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Well, Mr. Chairman, I certainly understand how serious this matter is, and I guess I am of the view that alternative A is not going to solve much.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There is a psychology, I understand, in the market that is going on, and I am not convinced that our continuing to take these actions and then having adverse outcomes is necessarily going to inspire confidence.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think we need to let our actions work their way through.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Part of the problem is that the credit mechanism is stuck right now because of the tremendous uncertainties.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Then I look at all of the things we have done over the last month, and the ramping up of the liquidity facilities has really exceeded even our ability to sterilize.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So we have had, in effect, a funds rate that is well below our target.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have excess reserves in that period that were over $280 billion when they are normally $2 billion, and that was before we added more swap lines and more liquidity into the market.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Frankly, I think we are at a point now where the liquidity mechanisms that we’re trying to use, not our interest rate targeting, are really our monetary policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As we go forward, perhaps we need to think about how we are going to conduct monetary policy under a quantitative easing environment.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is what I think we will effectively be at if we move again today.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So how we think about liquidity and about the credit mechanisms is really where more of our attention will have to be spent.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Lowering the rate may have some positive effects, but I doubt it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I would just stay where we are, let some of these past actions begin to work through, and see what the effects of those are before we then take another move because I think the market would just appreciate some stability over time in our actions so that they can see these things begin to work.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It isn’t a problem of the interest rate level right now, in my opinion, so that’s why I would wait and see.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Clearly, forecasts have been marked down since our September meeting—mine included.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This reflects the weaker data that we have obtained on the real side, especially consumer spending and manufacturing, but also worsening conditions in the financial markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Accordingly, in an intermeeting move on October 8, we cut the funds rate 50 basis points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yet the additional effect on the economy of financial turmoil during the last month remains highly uncertain.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Spreads in many markets remain higher than at the time of our September meeting, but some have started to decline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If our new facilities have the desired impact, we may well see spreads continue to fall back to September or lower levels.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is very difficult to say at this time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although I dislike intermeeting rate cuts, I supported the October 8 cut because it was part of a coordinated effort among central banks around the world and it seemed justified given that our growth outlook had deteriorated and inflation expectations had remained stable.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We may well have to do more, but I think we are near the end of what we can do with monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, it’s difficult to determine the appropriate level of the funds rate, and I want to draw your attention to the Greenbook, which showed that, whether we cut today or don’t cut today, the paths of GDP, employment, and inflation over the next year or two are not much different.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, in most models, cuts of that magnitude do not show up very heavily in real variables.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would also note that, according to the Greenbook, we could cut the rate to zero and have no effect on inflation, apparently, for the next four years.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, given the fact that rate cuts don’t have much effect, even in the Greenbook simulations, we have cut rates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It may not make much difference, as President Hoenig was saying.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My preference at this meeting would be to stand pat and see how the data and financial markets improve.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We are already engaged in extraordinary quantitative easing, even at this point, and we are hearing from bankers that the funds rate will do little to stimulate lending on their part or improve their balance sheets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, delaying necessary rate cuts is not desirable.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But given the considerable uncertainty around our forecast, it is not clear that further cuts are either necessary or desirable or are going to be effective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And doing so for purely psychological reasons, from my standpoint, is a dubious way to conduct policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A comparison of the baseline Greenbook forecast with the alternative scenario involving more-rapid improvement in financial conditions suggests that the appropriate policy path is very much dependent on knowing whether the increase in financial stress in September will be lasting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If conditions deteriorate further, which they might, we may want to cut in December.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If conditions improve, this may not be necessary.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given the decline in confidence in our markets and institutions, I think the Fed can play a positive role by being a steadying hand.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That’s another reason to wait a bit longer before moving again.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do not believe that we inspire confidence by appearing to react to market fluctuations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Even though that’s not what we’re doing, I fear that we often give that appearance.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, although we have gotten positive reactions to the creativity of our liquidity programs, I think we have missed opportunities for raising confidence by rolling out our liquidity facilities in a piecemeal fashion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We had announcements made every day between Monday and Wednesday, on October 6, 7, and 8.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it would have been far better to announce these actions as a well- thought-out package, explaining the intention of the individual pieces and how they related to one another.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: For example, we now have three different lending programs designed in whole or in part to support money market mutual funds.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have concern that we have been looking reactive rather than proactive, even though I know that some of these programs had been in the works for a while.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have argued that it is important that we think about our policy choices in terms of policy paths—that is, a dynamic path.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The principles of dynamic programming suggest that we think about our policies in a backward-looking way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This, I believe, applies not only to monetary policy but to our liquidity programs as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In this spirit, I believe that we must think hard about our exit strategies both from the liquidity programs and from our very low funds rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we have dug ourselves a very deep hole in terms of the breadth and depth of our lending to the private sector.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We seem, at times, to be the lender of first resort as well as the lender of last resort.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We must make sure that we have a sturdy ladder that will enable us to climb our way out of this hole.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is especially important given the interaction between the programs and the differences across the programs in their current expiration dates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the monetary policy side, we have added significantly to liquidity in the economy, as I alluded to earlier.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given the uncertainty surrounding our forecast, we may very well find ourselves in a position of having to reverse those injections sooner than expected.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am even more concerned with this planning process than I have been when I have raised this point before.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The baseline funds path in the Greenbook is quite extraordinary from my perspective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It suggests that we can keep the funds rate low, below 1 and even close to zero, throughout most of the forecast period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, in 2011 the funds rate is still below 2 percent, even though the economy is growing at 4.4 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We may disagree somewhat on the magnitude of the contributions of our low interest rate policies in the 2003–05 period to the current problems, but I don’t think many of us want to repeat that episode.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yet looking at the baseline forecast and where the funds rate remains—below 1 percent or certainly below 2 percent for the next four years—it strikes me as a risky strategy at best and perhaps even a dangerous one.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have previously expressed views around this table that this Committee historically has been reluctant to raise rates in a timely fashion, and I believe that fear is reinforced by what I see in the baseline forecast in the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That projection worries me a great deal.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We must not act in a way that sows the seeds of the next crisis.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Despite the pressure of the here and now, we cannot and should not ignore the consequences of our actions in the intermediate term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Managing our way from point to point, dealing with immediate problems, can very easily lead us to a place in which we do not wish to be—thus the importance of thinking in terms of a path.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it would also serve us well to think about the process we will follow to unwind our liquidity programs in advance, so that we avoid unintended consequences across markets, and about the communication strategy that will ease the transition back to a more market based provision of liquidity.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In sum, Mr. Chairman, although I would prefer not to move today, I recognize that my forecast is more optimistic than most.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, I also accept the notion that there is a great deal of uncertainty about the outcomes and fragility in the marketplace, and your concerns are well noted.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, I will not dissent against a 50 basis point cut.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I would like to remind the Committee of our earlier discussions and the general agreement I thought I heard that, when the time comes, we will have to raise rates and we may have to do so aggressively.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In all likelihood, that will occur before lagging indicators, such as the unemployment rate, are firmly on the decline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is not the projection offered in the Greenbook baseline.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Bullard, you have a handout?

speaker: BULLARD
text: I do have a handout.

speaker: BULLARD
text: 8 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I guess before I start, I just want to say that I generally agree with everything everyone is saying.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is a dire situation, and I am perfectly comfortable with that assessment.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What I want to do with my comment here is just put on the table one idea about why a rate reduction might be counterproductive.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is what I’m trying to do here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The U.S. economy now appears to be in recession.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Intensified financial market turmoil and very fluid expectations have created a very difficult situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A key question for the Committee is what to do with the monetary policy piece of the policy response to the situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We know that monetary policy is a blunt instrument that does not directly address fundamental problems in financial markets.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We have other programs in place to try to address those problems more directly.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We also have important fiscal actions, which are probably having the largest effect in trying to stabilize the current situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Unlike the ECB, we already lowered nominal interest rates aggressively earlier this year in anticipation of the possibility of weak macroeconomic performance.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We are now in the middle of a further round of easing, which is threatening to send nominal interest rates to zero, given the force of events.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is this the optimal policy, or could it backfire on the Committee?

speaker: BULLARD
text: I want to at least lay out the possibility that a very low nominal interest rate policy may be counterproductive.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My key worry is that housing markets remain at the core of the current turmoil.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Mortgage markets— 8 The materials used by Mr. Bullard are attached to this transcript (appendix 8).

speaker: BULLARD
text: $14 trillion or so, about one GDP—are based on nominal contracts.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Deflation tends to be very destructive in an environment of nominal contracting.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I want to stress that macroeconomic expectations are very important for the way the economy actually evolves and will evolve going forward and that those expectations are very fluid in the current environment.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The Japanese experience, while it is not an exact parallel, represents an important reference point for the current situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Japan’s problems were very real.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Some have described the outcome as a lost decade.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So let’s turn to the graph here for just a second.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is what I was talking about yesterday.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is an argument put forward by Jess Benhabib, Stephanie Schmitt-Grohé, and Martín Uribe.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the vertical axis is the nominal interest rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the horizontal axis are the inflation rate and inflation expectations, which in this graph are going to be the same thing.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The diagonal line labeled “Fisher” is just a Fisher relationship.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The nominal interest rate is the real interest rate, r, plus inflation expectations.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Then policy is described by the line with the kink in it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The policy line means that, when medium-term inflation expectations are above target, we raise the nominal interest rate and, when medium-term inflation expectations are below target, we lower the nominal interest rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That works beautifully around the targeted equilibrium, the π* in this environment, and all goes well.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s just that, when you go to low nominal interest rates, strange things start to happen because you have to do something with policy as you come to very low nominal interest rates.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You could just go to zero, and then you would have the horizontal line labeled “policy” that would go across all the way to the minus r there.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Or you could stop at some earlier level.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I chose something here to illustrate what the Greenbook seems to have in mind, say ½ percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But any way you cut it, this is going to create another crossing of the Fisher relation and create a second steady state.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is the main point of the Benhabib analysis.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You can layer on top all kinds of other stuff that you would like to include in your model, but most models are going to have a Fisher relationship, and most models are going to have the policymaker reacting by adjusting the nominal interest rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So this other steady state, the steady state with low nominal interest rates, has deflation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If you get stuck there, in our current environment, this would exacerbate the housing problem a lot and make our problems much more severe.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So this is just one caution about going to a very low nominal interest rate environment.

speaker: BULLARD
text: When I saw this six or seven years ago, it had some influence on me.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Before this, I was not worried about any of the zero bound issues.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But then, this does make me a little nervous, given the core problem in our situation, which is the housing problem.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So let me set that aside then.

speaker: BULLARD
text: One thing this line of research pointed out—and a whole bunch of papers have been written since this paper—is the existence of this second steady state and that the deflation associated with the trap steady state is a worrisome phenomenon.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There are two steady states here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You can just argue that you don’t think the lower one is going to be the one the economy coordinates on and that eventually we are going to go back to the high one and that is perfectly fine.

speaker: BULLARD
text: However, the Japanese case seemed to be zero nominal interest rates and a moderately low rate of deflation for quite some time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You could say that, if we coordinate on this low nominal interest rate steady state, we can somehow take fiscal policy actions to move off that to the other steady state.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is a more complicated issue.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That has been addressed in the literature, and that is also a reasonable thing to say.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I guess my main concern about this is, since it is a very dire situation and I think we are going to go very close to zero very soon, I want us to do it with our eyes open.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It has some possibility of creating a worse environment.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is the only thing I wanted to say here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So my preference based on this would be to leave rates alone and say, “Let’s use fiscal policy.” I don’t think what we have now is an interest rate problem.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What we have now are problems in credit markets, and I think they are being fairly well addressed by the most recent fiscal actions, including capital injections into the banking sector.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So that would be my preference at this point.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, if you had kicked around in the streets of Hong Kong in 1997, then you would have wandered into elementary schools and seen what we called at that time “Quotrons”—children trading stocks on the lunchroom floor.

speaker: FISHER
text: It was the surest indicator that the market was out of control.

speaker: FISHER
text: This morning I opened the Wall Street Journal, and on the front page they describe an exercise run by the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, which you know is Wall Street’s biggest trade group, with a similar program in American schools.

speaker: FISHER
text: It says that a 13-year old in Wilmington, Delaware—Michael Ashworth—is slumped by his computer, weary from another rough day in the stock market with all his favorite picks—Domino’s Pizza, the Hershey Company, and Gap—surprise!

speaker: FISHER
text: “I’ll be honest with you,” he confided, “before all this I asked my Mom to give me stocks for Christmas.

speaker: FISHER
text: But then, I told her not to do it.

speaker: FISHER
text: I asked for a parakeet instead.” Now, this is not as exotic or thoughtful a handout as the one from my colleague from St. Louis, but here’s the point.

speaker: FISHER
text: He may not get that parakeet because the pet store may not have access to credit.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is, to me, the fundamental issue that I think President Plosser—and I won’t repeat his arguments—and President Hoenig were referring to.

speaker: FISHER
text: The concern I have is not about the price of money.

speaker: FISHER
text: In fact, I think we are not seeing that kind of transmission mechanism—Governor Duke gave testimony to that earlier.

speaker: FISHER
text: All of us are aware that it is not moving as quickly through the IV tube as we would like it to because of the crimped nature of the tube.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have no problem with the language in alternative A, except for the first paragraph, and the phrase “including today’s rate reduction.” I have an open mind.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do think the issue in terms of restoring the system comes back to credibility and predictability.

speaker: FISHER
text: You cannot have a functioning capitalist system if you have total uncertainty.

speaker: FISHER
text: These are the issues that I believe President Plosser, President Hoenig, earlier President Lacker, and others were referring to in the first intervention.

speaker: FISHER
text: I thank President Geithner in particular for addressing the questions I asked yesterday, and there was reference to them earlier.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have done so much so quickly.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are in a quantitative easing period.

speaker: FISHER
text: The question is whether it actually makes a difference if we cut rates or not and whether the price of money is actually the issue or the fact that money is not flowing, that there are counterparty risks and rollover risks, and all the things we have talked about at this table and each of us has articulated in our public speeches.

speaker: FISHER
text: To be very honest with you, Mr. Chairman, I am open-minded about this because I could make that argument both ways.

speaker: FISHER
text: If it doesn’t matter, why not cut 50 basis points?

speaker: FISHER
text: I am not convinced yet—and I’d like to listen to the rest of the arguments— that alternative A, in terms of the action, is the right way to go.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do think it’s very important that we be very clear and articulate in laying out how we see the world, and I do believe that the language in alternative A does the best job of all the columns that have been presented.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I come back to the question I asked before.

speaker: FISHER
text: What are the next steps?

speaker: FISHER
text: What is the end game?

speaker: FISHER
text: I’d like to know before I cast my vote.

speaker: FISHER
text: I will conclude with actually once again agreeing with President Yellen, as I think I have done twice in history.

speaker: FISHER
text: The last time was at the last meeting.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it’s very important that we have all hands on deck, that we have a unanimous decision.

speaker: FISHER
text: But, still, I would like answers to my questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Fisher, I promised you answers, and I will deliver them.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I strongly favor alternative A, a 50 basis point cut in our fed funds target rate today.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think it is important for us to move aggressively and quickly to offset the strong forces that are acting to depress economic activity.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I know that some prefer a more measured response, especially as we move closer to the zero bound, but the lesson I take from history is that more and sooner is better than taking smaller steps over time.

speaker: LACKER
text: The economic outlook has definitely deteriorated.

speaker: LACKER
text: On top of the slowing at the beginning of the third quarter, a sequence of policy actions and statements has spread an inchoate fear.

speaker: LACKER
text: In response to that, a wide variety of economic agents have delayed outlays.

speaker: LACKER
text: The breathtaking credit market interventions that we have undertaken in the last several weeks are going to make it hard to judge whether those markets are stabilized.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is going to make it even harder to judge how and when to withdraw.

speaker: LACKER
text: Governor Duke asked rhetorically what it would take for recovery to begin.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it is not going to be a very healthy recovery unless we have made substantial progress toward withdrawing these interventions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I know it’s probably premature in the midst of a crisis to be talking about the recovery, but a number of people did, and I think it makes sense on the grounds that President Plosser advanced for us to be thinking ahead.

speaker: LACKER
text: President Geithner talked about the will and the desire and that it amounts to a matter of will to reverse course later on.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that in withdrawing these subsidies and these credit market interventions is where we are going to need the will.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is going to be really hard to disenfranchise somebody who now has access to one of these programs.

speaker: LACKER
text: The inflation outlook has improved.

speaker: LACKER
text: Expected inflation has come down.

speaker: LACKER
text: A couple of people have noted that.

speaker: LACKER
text: That brings the real rate where the interest rate is now—to about zero.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I can favor a 50 point reduction in the federal funds rate target at this meeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think a funds rate that is, in real terms as best as we can measure it, about minus 1 percent is how we should see our way through here, at least in the near term.

speaker: LACKER
text: Like President Evans, I will mention the 1930s.

speaker: LACKER
text: What I take from my reading of the Great Depression is that this is what central banks should do in times like this—keep real interest rates low.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me make a couple of brief observations.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I mentioned yesterday, I think we are going to face a challenge communicating about our strategy.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we need to reduce interest rates to the lowest practical level to which we feel we can reduce them, I think yesterday’s discussion suggests that the Committee could use a refresher course on the monetary economics of the zero bound.

speaker: LACKER
text: I applaud President Bullard for his breaking new ground by providing a figure from the Journal of Economic Theory.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to put something on the table about the federal funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are voting today on the target for the federal funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: The way our operations are conducted now, we are leaving so many excess reserves in the system that we are driving the federal funds rate down to the interest rate on reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: The interbank risk premium is likely to become small as the FDIC guarantee becomes well understood and more broadly effective.

speaker: LACKER
text: The GSEs are likely to catch on that they deserve more on their funds.

speaker: LACKER
text: Small banks, as Governor Duke says, that haven’t really paid attention to what this new regime is about are going to find that brokers are going to be able to find them placements at closer to the interest rate on reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I think that the sloppy trading below the interest rate on reserves is going to fade over time.

speaker: LACKER
text: As long as we have excess reserves at the scale that we do, as long as the Desk has added that many reserves, we are going to have the effective federal funds rate at the interest rate on reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: Because we are voting on the federal funds target rate, I think that the Committee ought to have some understanding from the staff that either excess reserves are going to be drawn down to the point that the effective rate is lifted off the interest rate on the reserves floor or—and this would be my preferable course of action—we raise the interest rate on reserves to equal the target rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Otherwise, we are voting on something, but we are actually doing something else.

speaker: LACKER
text: I can understand the desire to err on the side of soft rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is what we did in August 2007.

speaker: LACKER
text: But as rates go down, we need to be more and more careful about what the Committee is actually voting on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just to support what you said, we are obviously still trying to find our way in how to use this in the new regime with the excess reserves interest rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is possible that at some point we might decide to target that interest rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That might be the most straightforward thing to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But as I understand it—and, in fact, I’m quite confident—the intention of the staff and the Board is to try to figure out what the relationship is between the excess reserves interest rate and the federal funds rate as normally measured.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we can establish a reliable relationship, then we should try to—and we will—use that to hit the target.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s coming close to it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We certainly are not trying intentionally to come under the target.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If that fails, then we will go to what you are suggesting, which is effectively what I’m saying, and make them the same.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then, effectively, there is no difference between targeting the interest rate on excess reserves and targeting the federal funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are certainly open to that, and there is no intention to do anything other than to try to figure out a way to take the FOMC’s decision and put it into practice in the money markets.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, financial headwinds continue to be a major part of my thinking about the economic outlook.

speaker: STERN
text: Reasonable people can differ about that issue, but it seems to me that the headwinds are significant and they are likely to persist.

speaker: STERN
text: Partially as a consequence and partially for other reasons, the economic outlook has deteriorated, and the inflation outlook, fortunately, has improved.

speaker: STERN
text: So I favor alternative A, and I am satisfied with the language associated with it.

speaker: STERN
text: Let me make just one additional comment.

speaker: STERN
text: One way of thinking about lowering rates at this juncture and its potential effectiveness is that it is important to reduce the price of liquidity in this environment.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that’s what lowering the target would do.

speaker: STERN
text: That said, if I think about policy a bit beyond this meeting, I start with an observation that Governor Kohn made.

speaker: STERN
text: We are probably going to receive a batch of pretty negative economic news over the next several months.

speaker: STERN
text: At the same time, a lot of programs are in place, as everybody is aware; and perhaps my optimism is ill-conceived, but I actually think that they have the promise of being effective over time.

speaker: STERN
text: So it’s not just a question in my mind of the nature of the news we get, but are we also seeing signs that all these programs are getting some traction and being effective?

speaker: STERN
text: If they are, that ought to temper our desire to go further.

speaker: STERN
text: Obviously, a lot of things are in play, and a great deal of uncertainty is present here and abroad.

speaker: STERN
text: But we will simply have to assess all these developments as best we can as time passes.

speaker: STERN
text: I think I’ll end my remarks there.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me begin by agreeing with Don Kohn on two things.

speaker: WARSH
text: This is the toughest economic period I can remember in his lifetime, [laughter] and I support alternative A. I think the inflation trends and the trends in the global economy give us flexibility, which six months or so ago I did not think we would have.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that gives us some degree of freedom that, given all of the negative tone, including my own, around the table, gives us at least some source of comfort.

speaker: WARSH
text: Next I would say that I agree with the consensus around the table, which is that these problems are not principally about monetary policy.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I also think that monetary policy isn’t irrelevant to this, and all agencies of governments around the world are making tough decisions, and the marginal benefits of further monetary policy changes strike me as not high but not irrelevant.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think President Plosser talked a bit about the alternative policy paths in the Greenbook that range from keeping the fed funds rate constant where it is to taking it to zero percent and the surprisingly small differences in output, employment, and core inflation there.

speaker: WARSH
text: In some ways, in the discussion that we’re having about 25 or 50 or moving or not, it would not be fair for any of us to overstate the importance in terms of directly affecting the economy in the short term.

speaker: WARSH
text: That goes to my final point, which is that the most valuable asset that we have isn’t what at the end of this meeting might be 100 basis points left of monetary policy.

speaker: WARSH
text: Frankly, it is the credibility of the institution and the credibility of the FOMC.

speaker: WARSH
text: If I compare our credibility now to virtually any other organization in the United States or maybe even globally, I think our credibility is holding up quite well, particularly relative to the degree of difficulty we have in front of us, relative to the trauma in financial markets and the weaknesses in the economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: So it is that asset, that credibility, that we need to continue to protect more than incremental basis point moves on the fed funds rate.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that credibility will be tested over this period as it will for our counterparts.

speaker: WARSH
text: We don’t want to find ourselves in a corner come December or come a couple of brutal days in the markets where we feel compelled to continue to act and make 50 basis point moves unless and until we know where we want to end up on this.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I’m sympathetic to that point of view.

speaker: WARSH
text: We need to tell the story before the story is told for us of what our lower bound is, why it’s there, and what our diagnosis of the economy is.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that the Chairman and the rest of us will have ample opportunity to do that between now and December and that it is quite important to make sure we come out of this as strong as we have been through this period so far.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Well, I’ve not been able to convince myself not to agree with President Evans.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As everyone has said, we have this very significant global shift that has stepped down real activity and financial activity.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The inflation environment has changed dramatically from a number of months ago with the change in commodity prices, the change in the value of the dollar, and the change in not just U.S. but also global resource utilization.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we’ve seen just an enormous change there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, when you look at the expected federal funds rate path— we have to be careful in looking at anything in the markets these days because of liquidity, risk premiums, or term premiums that we’re not quite sure about—the markets are expecting significant cuts from us.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They are not expecting any immediate or near-term significant increases in inflation, and I think all of the indications are that it will be going down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In a cost–benefit analysis, the costs seem relatively low in terms of the potential for inflation of doing this.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Now, we have to think about it in terms of benefits, and a number of people have touched on the transmission mechanism.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I do think that there are forces that mute the extent to which a 50 basis point cut translates into 50 basis points or lower on costs, but I don’t think they completely offset it.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It still has the effect of reducing the cost of liquidity, reducing many people’s borrowing costs.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it still does have an effect even if there’s an offsetting risk spread and even if there’s an offsetting bank action that affects that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So in terms of costs and benefits, at this time it seems that the costs are relatively low or muted, and the benefits are positive and potentially high.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In particular, as I mentioned before, I’m concerned about the confluence of forces that may make things very difficult around the end of the year.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If you look at a lot of these LIBOR or forward markets, they’re not coming down either in the United States or around the world.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have a lot of uncertainties with hedge funds, with the potential for other institutions getting into trouble, and with just the implementation of our policies—in particular, as I mentioned, the way the FDIC guarantee program and the TARP program work may end up singling out institutions and bringing them down more quickly than otherwise.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I think it makes sense in terms of cost–benefit analysis, even more so given the tail risk around the end of the year, to act now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have another opportunity to act in December and obviously an opportunity to act at any point if we do see a dramatic change.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We are getting near as much as we can do, but I don’t see the costs of acting more aggressively and more quickly here outweighing the benefits.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I support alternative A with the language as drafted.

speaker: DUKE
text: I confess I find myself torn between the position of President Plosser and the equally compelling arguments of Governor Kohn, and that makes alternative B quite attractive as a way, not because of any optimism about the economic outcome, but I really do question the effectiveness of any move in the fed funds target given the actual trading of the fed funds rate right now.

speaker: DUKE
text: When we set the interest rate on reserves, at that point I was concerned that our interest on reserves would disrupt the market for fed funds between banks because of the risk premium.

speaker: DUKE
text: With the FDIC insurance, I think that goes away, and so probably President Lacker’s suggestion deserves some strong consideration.

speaker: DUKE
text: I am also painfully aware of the operational and financial difficulties that banks experience at a 1 percent fed funds rate and the likely difficulties of other intermediaries as the absolute level of rates falls further.

speaker: DUKE
text: As I stated in my earlier remarks, I’m also most concerned about the importance of predictability in returning confidence to the markets, and in that light, I am concerned about market expectations.

speaker: DUKE
text: But having recently been an expecter rather than a decider, I’m going to suggest that most of those doing the expecting don’t understand at all the issues that we’ve discussed here today.

speaker: DUKE
text: There’s a thought that, if the fed funds rate just comes down, it would maybe make this pain go away.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I agree with Governor Warsh that the public statements in the intermeeting period and as we approach the point where we simply can’t meet market expectations anymore are critically important to shape market expectations.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I do think it’s important that the markets focus on the other efforts, and with that I would support alternative A.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Mr. Chairman, I support alternative A, both the action and the language for the reasons I said earlier.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I just want to make a couple of other points.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think the only way to be predictable in a crisis like this is to be predictably inert or to be late.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I don’t understand the basic argument that you add to confidence by being inert or by being late or, as the Chairman said, by being passive despite overwhelming evidence about changes in the outlook and risks to financial stability.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The argument that makes me most uncomfortable here around the table today is the suggestion several of you have made—I’m not sure you meant it this way—which is that the actions by this Committee contributed to the erosion of confidence—a deeply unfair suggestion.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Now, a lot of things happened over the last three months and the last year, and a lot of things happened in terms of policy over the last six weeks.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is no doubt that communication about policy by all the arms of the U.S. government and the uncertainty created by the actions by all the arms of the U.S. government contributed in ways to uncertainty about the policy response going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: There is also no doubt that inevitably in a crisis like this, when policy moves forcefully, it is scary because a lot of people are not yet at the point of assessing or understanding the forces driving our decisions.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think it’s just unfair to suggest that the actions by the Chairman and this Committee were a substantial contributor to the erosion in confidence and to uncertainty about further policy actions, even though it’s true that when we move with force and drama it has the risk of adding to uncertainty.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I’d be very careful to look more broadly at the full range of other things that happened in that period of time, including, for example, the confusion established by the range of different choices for interventions in Lehman, AIG, the GSEs, WaMu in particular, and Wachovia and what that meant.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Look particularly at the damage to confidence created by the Congress’s actions in the weeks after the legislation was first proposed.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Compare that, for example, with the announcement effect of the initial thing.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Look also at the uncertainty created around what the package was designed to do and how it was designed.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But please be very careful, certainly outside this room, about adding to the perception that the actions by this body were a substantial contributor to the erosion in confidence.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think that Don Kohn said it best.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The whole framing, which seems to have hardened now, that the world ended with the Lehman bankruptcy is just deeply unfair to the basic truth.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Independent of whether there was an option available at the time, the erosion in underlying economic conditions and in confidence in the future outlook was powerful and substantial going into August and early September.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: So I just offer that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: You know, everyone wants to quote FDR.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: FDR said at one point, “If I judge the mood of the country right, what this calls for is bold experimentation.” I do not believe that this Chairman and this Committee have been irresponsibly experimenting at the cost of predictability and confidence going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: What we have done is a relatively well designed series of escalations in monetary policy and liquidity intended to be preemptive against what we knew was substantial risk of a very adverse economic and financial outcome.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The risks were not broadly shared, not just in this room but outside.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I think the judgments by the Chairman were largely correct in weighing those risks appropriately at that time, and I think we all owe him a substantial amount of deference for the judgments he made and his wisdom.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: Both here in this room and in the effect he had on the policy choices that the fiscal authorities also ultimately made look very good now and will look even better over time as people understand how grave and substantial the risks were that we were facing in the economy and the financial system.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: One last point to President Fisher’s question.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: President Fisher asked the obvious question, which is, What next?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I think a very good approach to decisionmaking is to say, “I don’t want to know so much about this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I want to know about the next three things.” I know the Chairman is going to give a nice, thoughtful, and complete answer to this.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I would just say the following: We don’t need to know today what is next on the monetary policy front.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We know there may be some arguments for going lower than 1 percent.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have to think through very carefully the collateral damage consequence in terms of what that does to market functioning and behavior.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: We have to look at the alternatives to that, including in communication.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: A range of other policy options are within our capacity to influence and effect that will give us the ability to minimize downside risk going forward.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: But I don’t think that we need to know—and we cannot know with precision—what the optimal mix of those things is now before deciding what to do, although I’m very sympathetic to the basic judgment.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The question really is, In moving today, are we going to do more harm than good to our ultimate objective?

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It’s very hard to make the case that we do damage to any of our basic fundamental objectives and mandate.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I can see a much stronger case that we do a lot of damage to those if we don’t act today, even though we all recognize that ultimately this is going to require more than monetary policy to address the risk here.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’d just like to just take a moment to react.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not sure whom you heard saying that the result was primarily a result of this Committee’s actions or the Chairman’s actions or anyone else’s actions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If those were words you were putting in my mouth, that was not what I said, President Geithner.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do think I have been supportive of almost all the actions in terms of liquidity facilities; I supported the actions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also was supportive of the Lehman Brothers decision.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I think it’s a far cry from saying that uncertainty about policies contributes to uncertainty—which you agreed to—it’s a far cry from that to saying we lay the blame at the feet of this Committee or the Chairman.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I don’t know what straw man you were setting up, but it certainly didn’t apply to this member of the Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just offer some thoughts that may be somewhat more expansive than usual in response to the questions that have been raised.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some of this is extemporaneous, so you’ll have to bear with me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me first talk about the strategy we pursued thus far and where we are and then think about where we might go as a country as well as an institution going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Without going through all of the familiar discussion about how the crisis began, what the sources of it were, I think that the Federal Reserve’s responses are essentially three.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, we were relatively early and aggressive in our monetary policy easing, particularly compared with other countries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, we have been creative and expansive in our use of liquidity tools, including a wide variety of lending programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Third, we have used our available, but not always adequate, tools to try to stabilize systemically critical failing institutions and to try to mitigate systemic risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Without sounding too defensive, I will try to argue that I think on all three of these we have been more or less in the right direction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, on the early and aggressive monetary policy easing, obviously there was a lot of concern—a lot expressed abroad that we were going to create a stagflationary 1970s type of situation and that we were going to destroy the dollar and its role as an international currency.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our response essentially was that we thought that the increases in commodity prices were mostly a relative price change induced by changes in real demand for commodities and in the supply of commodities across the globe and that, at some point, those commodity price increases would stabilize, which would lead to a moderation of the inflationary effects and concerns.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It took longer than we had expected; but once it began, it was more pronounced than we had expected.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inflation has not become the problem that was anticipated by many early on, and the dollar, of course, is now stronger than it was before we began our cutting of interest rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in retrospect, I think our monetary policy, although not perfect certainly—and our communication was not always perfect—broadly speaking was appropriate given what has turned out to be a very severe economic situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Liquidity expansion also received some criticism early on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was a view that this was inducing moral hazard.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was also some question of whether this was an effective approach.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We were helped in this respect by the fact that the ECB joined us very early in this type of aggressive policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know the counterfactual.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has obviously not solved all of the problems.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I think there’s a strong perception in the markets and in the general public that these actions have been supportive, and they helped mitigate the effects of the crisis on the functioning of the financial system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I feel comfortable also with that approach.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The attempts to stabilize failing systemically critical institutions, beginning with Bear Stearns, have obviously been very controversial.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There have been criticisms from the right and from the left.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: From the right, the initial criticism was that we have no business interfering with the market process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should let them fail.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The market will take care of it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We heard this as recently as Jackson Hole.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I never took this seriously.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just don’t believe that you can allow systemically critical institutions to fail in the middle of financial crises and expect it to be not a problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t want to get into the issue about the inconsistency.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s true that we treated senior debt differently between Fannie and Freddie and WaMu and Wachovia, but I don’t think that that is the reason we are having the financial crisis we’re having.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there was a panic brought about by the underlying concerns about the solvency of our financial institutions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That panic essentially turned into a run.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Companies like Wachovia that had adequate Basel capital faced a run on their deposits, which was self-fulfilling.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The investment banks essentially faced runs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We did our best to stabilize them, but I think that it was that run, that panic, and then the impact the panic had on these major institutions that was the source of the intensification of financial crisis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I don’t buy the argument that we should stay out of the business of protecting the financial system, and I think that the major factor was, in fact, the panic that was generated by the underlying uncertainties and the effect that had on critical institutions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also more recently we have heard more of a critique from the left, which is, What in the heck were you guys doing letting Lehman fail?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is interesting given that the critique had been the other one for quite a while.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that critique is unfair at a narrow level in that, first, Lehman was a symptom as well as a cause of the recent crisis and, second, the Fed and the Treasury simply had no tools to address both Lehman and the other companies that were under stress at that time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that criticism is appropriate, though, as directed toward the United States as a whole.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We did not have—as the Europeans have or as we have FDICIA for banks—a system that was set up to allow a reasonable and responsible orderly resolution of nonbank systemically critical institutions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we now have made a lot of progress there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The TARP will provide a good interim solution.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is very important that in the future we address the too-big-to-fail problem that we have, that we find ways to reduce that problem, and that we find ways to deal systematically with firms that are in crisis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So given the fog of war—which has, of course, been intense going back for more than a year—I would defend what we’ve done in terms of the general direction, acknowledging that execution is not always perfect and that communication is not always perfect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, what about the future?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: History suggests that, whenever a financial crisis becomes sufficiently severe, ultimately the only solution is a fiscal solution, and we will have a fiscal solution.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that the financial system will muddle through, in which case the fiscal solution will be of the sort we’ve already seen: injections of capital, support for critical firms, support for the credit markets in general; Keynesian-style demand support.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I hope that’s where we’re going to be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In my own testimony, I argued that we should try to focus whatever stimulus we have in solving the underlying problems rather than simply handing out money and that we could do that, again, by addressing credit markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would add, foreclosure, homeownership, and some of those issues as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I hope that’s where the fiscal policy will be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I hope that will take the lead from us going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, we’ll have to continue to play a supporting role in a lot of different ways.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other possibility, of course, is that things get much worse and that we are in the same situation as Sweden or Japan, in which case a massive recapitalization of the banking system will be necessary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That will eventually happen, but I just note that, in all of these fiscal dynamics, there is a political economy overlay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You have to get to the point that it is not only the right policy to induce fiscal support but also that it is politically possible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s one reason that I think the TARP was not possible before the most recent period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In fact, it was barely possible recently.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, again, I believe that fiscal policy will have to be a critical part of the solution going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Another part that we should not forget about is the international response, which is now just beginning really to become serious.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The responses after the G7 weekend on banks and bank guarantees were important and suggested a commitment by other countries to stabilize the system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we will see aggressive monetary policy going forward, and I think we’ll see increasingly aggressive fiscal policy in other countries because they recognize that the decoupling is no longer a realistic story.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s going to be important as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to the Federal Reserve, just generally speaking—and I’ll come back to the specific recommendation for today—again, I think that our liquidity provision has been constructive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has allowed the use of our balance sheet to help push in the deleveraging process that’s been going on now for more than a year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My guess is it will probably expand some more, but I don’t see it expanding a lot more, if for no other reason than we are reaching the limits of our operational capacity as well as balance sheet capacity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we have been reasonably successful in staying on the side of liquidity provision and not straying into credit or taking credit risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to stay on that side of the line both for legal reasons and because that’s the way monetary policy and lender-of-last-resort policy are supposed to work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I hope that the fiscal interventions will now be able to take away some of these responsibilities from us, but we’ll have to see how they play out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I confess that I hear President Plosser’s concerns about reversing these programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I recognize that it’s something we’ll have to do carefully.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I just don’t see it as being something that will be a huge problem if the economy begins to recover and credit markets begin to function more normally.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we’ll be able to do it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Japan was able to get out the quantitative easing without too much difficulty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I acknowledge the point that it is something we’re going to have to plan for and think about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On monetary policy, I think it is important for us to be responsive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Even if we stipulate for the moment that the interest rate changes we might make today have a minimal effect on the cost of capital—and I don’t necessarily agree with that, but let me stipulate it—there is still the importance of the signaling and what we’re trying to tell the markets about what we plan to do in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Frankly, I don’t think that we should try to signal that we are going to stand pat, that we are reluctant or refuse to move lower.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have to be prepared to move as low as makes sense.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: By that I mean in part that there are institutional factors that affect the efficacy of monetary policy at very low interest rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re all aware of that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I asked yesterday, and I’ll ask again, for the staff to go back to the 2003 work, to update it, and to think it through and help us understand what I would call the effective zero.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What is the real zero?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is it 50 basis points?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is it 75 basis points?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have to recognize that if we do go to literal zero, it would have very substantial effects on a number of financial markets, and we would have to ask ourselves whether the benefits from that are worth the dislocations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Japanese thought they were, and for example, they did shut down the interbank market for a long time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Maybe doing it is worth that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those are decisions that we need to make before the next meeting, and we will have opportunities to talk about this together and in public as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I do think that monetary policy needs to be proactive and to continue to be part of the solution here going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I essentially accept the general change in outlook as proposed by the Greenbook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Since our last meeting there has been an effective tightening in financial conditions, which has overwhelmed the 50 basis point cut that we did with the other central banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The outlook has become much worse.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is important for us to act aggressively and to signal essentially that we’re willing to do whatever is necessary to support the recovery of this economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There has been a lot of talk about confidence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the best thing we can do for confidence is to say that we’re going to do whatever it takes, even if it involves extraordinary actions, to get this economy back onto a path where it can begin to grow in a reasonable way again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Signaling coyness, being cute, is not a safe strategy right now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We just need to be straightforward and say that we’re going to do what it takes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In my view, just to be specific, 50 basis points is the right step today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, a number of concerns and objections have been raised.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me address just a few of them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is President Bullard’s very interesting presentation on the inflation trap, and intuitively it’s clear that, for a given real interest rate, you can have an equilibrium at which you have a high nominal rate and a high expected inflation rate or you can have a low nominal rate and deflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Both of those things are possible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was the trap that Japan got into.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We obviously want to avoid the deflation trap.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The question is, How do you avoid it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As far as I can see—obviously we can get further into this—the best two ways to avoid it are, first, as President Lacker suggested, reaffirm our commitment to price stability defined as 1½ to 2 percent or whatever our Committee’s general view is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re going to try to do that with our projections and potentially with the trial projection that we’re doing, and I think we can continue to strengthen our commitment to maintaining a positive inflation rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other thing, in terms of the dynamics, is to be aggressive in trying to avoid getting to a deflationary situation, where those expectations move in that direction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think deflation expectations will arise spontaneously because we’re cutting interest rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think they’ll arise because the economy is expected to be extremely weak, and anything we can do to eliminate that expectation in my view would be helpful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second objection I’ve heard is the question of whether or not these actions are effective.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think they are effective.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Maybe they’re not as effective as under normal circumstances, but let me put it to you this way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we cut 50 basis points today and the LIBOR–OIS spread rises 50 basis points tomorrow, I will accept that there’s a problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But if the LIBOR spread doesn’t move much and the overall LIBOR drops 50 basis points, then I think that we’re having an effect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you look at LIBOR over the past year, you’ll see a dramatic decline even though the spreads have widened.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think you can argue that we’re not having any effect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To the extent that we’re having a muted effect, you can just as well argue that we should be more aggressive because you need to do more to get the same impact.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I understand those concerns, and I reiterate, responding to Governor Duke and others, that as we get very low, there are side effects on certain institutions and financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to understand those, and that’s part of our decision process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I don’t think it’s the case that monetary policy has zero impact.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The third argument I’ve heard is the “keep the power dry” argument.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unless you think that movements in the rate are entirely psychological in their effect, I don’t think that that’s a strong argument in this particular circumstance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, we analyzed this quite a bit in the 2003 episode, and the general outcome from the literature and from simulations done by our own staff—Dave Reifschneider, John Williams, and others have published research on this—is that the best way to avoid the zero bound is to be more aggressive than normal to try to avoid the accumulation of weakness and try to avoid getting into that trap.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So more-preemptive strategies are, in fact, consistent with what we’ve done for the last year.

speaker: BERNANKE
