text: My recommendation for today is 50 basis points and the language in alternative A. I do think that it will be at least moderately beneficial both in terms of psychology and in terms of reducing the cost of funding and giving some additional support to funding markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I hope that in these remarks, which again are somewhat extemporaneous, I have addressed to some extent the future steps.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We ought, again, to think very hard in the next six weeks about what the real zero is and what the implications are of going below, say, 75 basis points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then we ought to make a determination, and it may be that we can sit still in December.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It may be that things improve quite a bit in the markets, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One advantage of doing 50 today is that we almost certainly will not have to do anything intermeeting because we will have done this significant step today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in December we’ll be able to look at the situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We may be able to do little or nothing—it is possible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But if we decide that further action is needed, at that point we should be prepared to decide what the regime is going to be, how far we’re going to go, and what the effective zero is, and I think that we shouldn’t hesitate to do that if that’s what the situation calls for.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think there is a way forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I understand the need to withdraw all these policy actions at an appropriate time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I don’t think that focusing on the near term for the moment is at all inconsistent with the fact that at some point these things will have to be reversed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, any further questions or comments?

speaker: FISHER
text: First, I would like to thank you, Mr. Chairman, for that very thorough and clear elucidation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I meant to mention earlier that I actually agree with President Evans.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s worthwhile now and then evoking Ronald Reagan.

speaker: FISHER
text: What I mean by that is not his “Where’s the pony?” comment, but more important, the reason he was so successful as a leader was that he had clear objectives, they were limited, and they were well articulated.

speaker: FISHER
text: It doesn’t matter if you’re a Democrat or a Republican.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it’s very important for us to understand what our objectives are in order for us to be fully supportive.

speaker: FISHER
text: By the way, Tim, as Mr. Plosser has been, I have been fully supportive of all of these initiatives.

speaker: FISHER
text: Again, I want to thank you, Mr. Chairman, for helping us understand better the cognitive road map because it is critical for all of us to do what Janet suggested, which is have all hands on deck and make sure we’re all fully supportive.

speaker: FISHER
text: Against that background I would support alternative A.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Just a question or thought.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As the staff prepares the review of the 2003 studies and memos and thinks about what zero effectively means and how we might operate in those circumstances, one thing I think would be useful to include is a discussion of whether or not when that time comes we announce that publicly and say, “Okay.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: From now on we have to do X, Y, or Z,” and make it part of the communication strategy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But if we get to the point where we now as a group have some concerns that, well, effectively we really don’t want to go below X, we will have to do some other operational actions as a substitute for that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there’s no problem doing that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is not a problem.

speaker: LACKER
text: Yes, I also strongly support your charge and direction to the staff to assemble with all due haste updated information for the Committee about what the effective lower bound on nominal interest rates is.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I’d urge you, along the lines of what President Plosser suggested, to include in that charge what we would do once we got there, what we could do, and what would be open to us.

speaker: LACKER
text: I emphasize again the relevance even if we don’t get there because analytically we’re effectively doing that right now with interest on reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: The classic economics of this is that, when you get down to effective equivalence between a monetary asset and a government bond of one-day duration or whatever, to be effective monetary policy needs to be fiscal policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: It needs to acquire other assets that we wouldn’t normally otherwise acquire.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’re doing that right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’d emphasize the importance and relevance of that.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: I also think it would be helpful, as the staff looks at the policy options going forward, that they do other parts of the communication options, too—not just those but also other ways to think about how to make policy for looking at and communicating a path that are different from what we did in 2003.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: It would be good to look at options for how we talk about policy going forward in that context along with just the operational choices and the policy choices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Just to follow up on that—I think that’s a very excellent suggestion, President Geithner.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To be very specific about that, in our trial run, one thing that we did was to look at what we thought was the steady state.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One way to engender some communication about the longer run might be to include what the Committee thought the steady-state neutral level of the funds rate would be in that environment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’d describe the path by which we got there; it would convey some sense to the marketplace of what we thought would be in some normal world a reasonable level of the funds rate consistent with those targets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just throw that on the table as something to think about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would you call the roll, please, Debbie?

speaker: DANKER
text: This vote encompasses the language of alternative A that was in the package passed out earlier today as well as the directive from the Bluebook, which states the following: “The Federal Open Market Committee seeks monetary and financial conditions that will foster price stability and promote sustainable growth in output.

speaker: DANKER
text: To further its long-run objectives, the Committee in the immediate future seeks conditions in reserve markets consistent with reducing the federal funds rate to an average of around 1 percent.” Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Geithner Yes Governor Duke Yes President Fisher Yes Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes President Pianalto Yes President Plosser Yes President Stern Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll need the governors to join me in my office for just a moment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Everyone else, let’s all take a twenty-minute coffee break.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When we come back, maybe we can start at that point with your briefing, David, on the TARP, and around 12:15 we’ll break and get lunch and hear the end of the briefing, if that all works for everybody.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The expected duration of the next part of our meeting is four hours, three hours?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should be done by 1:00.

speaker: DANKER
text: It’s not part of the meeting.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: The nonmeeting part of the meeting?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s only a briefing, not a meeting, once we come back.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A twenty-minute break now and then we’ll have a briefing and lunch.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, let me officially get to the point of adjourning the FOMC meeting just by first noting that the next meeting is Tuesday, December 16.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Put that on your calendar.

speaker: GEITHNER
text: That’s a long way away.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Can’t we meet before then?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d like to remind you that you have until 5:00 p.m. on Thursday to submit revisions to your economic projections, in case the markets change your views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Sorry—using information only through the end of today’s meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All right, the FOMC meeting is adjourned.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We welcome Chris Cumming, who is sitting in for New York.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As you know, under the extraordinary circumstances we added an extra day to the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The purpose of the meeting taking place today is to discuss the zero lower bound and related policy and governance issues, and I hope that the discussion today will set up our policy decision for tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just for preview purposes, the program today will start with Bill Dudley and Q&A.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll then have a staff presentation on the zero lower bound and alternative policies.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll have a go- round on those issues, including nontraditional policies and communications associated with it and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just mention that on the agenda for tomorrow, after the policy decision, we have the subcommittee’s report on long-run projections and the quarterly projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We put that there to save time and to make sure that we met our deadlines; but obviously there’s some linkage between that and the discussion today, and if anyone wants to bring that up today, please feel free to do so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, if we’re very efficient—as I hope we will be—I’d like to get to the staff economic briefing at the end of today, if possible—if not, not—and then there’s dinner afterwards.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So without further ado, let me turn to Bill Dudley.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Unfortunately this package is a little thicker than usual, but that’s the way it goes, I guess.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The stimulus provided by monetary policy to the real economy depends not only on the level of the federal funds rate but also on the health of the financial system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The ability of market participants to intermediate and act effectively as the transmission channel between the change in the federal funds rate target and financial asset prices is critical.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When bank and dealer balance sheets are constrained as they are now, this transmission mechanism is impaired, and traditional monetary policy instruments become limited in their ability to support economic activity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: 1 The materials used by Mr. Dudley are attached to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The recent sharp deterioration in the macroeconomic outlook and the forced deleveraging of the nonbank portion of the financial sector have led to sharp declines in asset values during the past few months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The consequence will be further big mark-to-market losses for investment and commercial bank trading books and a significant increase in loan-loss provisions on commercial bank loan books.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: These losses are likely to intensify the vise on financial firm balance sheets, and that is likely to further impede the Federal Reserve’s efforts to ease financial conditions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a consequence, a broadening of our suite of liquidity facilities that bypass banks and dealers may prove to be necessary.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Equities, corporate debt, and securitized assets—especially commercial- mortgage-backed securities (CMBS)—have all been hard hit, and the commodity sector, the preferred asset class of choice earlier in the year, has been clobbered.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 1 of the handout, U.S. equity prices fell sharply beginning in September.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the aggregate indexes have bounced off their low points, the S&P 500 index had still fallen 30 percent between the end of August and the end of November.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is the relevant quarter for Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, which report this week.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the current calendar quarter, despite the rebound, the S&P 500 index has declined about 25 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The carnage has also been evident abroad, especially in emerging markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The corporate debt market has scarcely been more hospitable.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The high-yield corporate bond yield for some broad indexes has climbed above 20 percent (exhibit 2).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Assuming a 20 percent recovery rate on defaults, yield levels in this sector appear to fully discount a default experience consistent with the peak reached in the Great Depression.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The securitization markets have performed little better.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Not only are most securitized markets shut to new issuance, but also the yields on even the highest-rated outstanding tranches have climbed sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 3 illustrates the current spreads for different types of AAA-rated consumer securitizations—credit cards, auto loans, and student loans.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 4 illustrates the sharp deterioration in valuations in the CMBS market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The left panel shows spreads on a basket of post-2003 vintages.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The right panel shows the price performance of particular AAA-rated CMBS tranches.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Most have fallen about 20 points in the past quarter.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Commodity prices also continue to plummet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 5, the declines have been particularly pronounced in the energy and industrial metals sectors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In contrast, gold prices have held up quite well (exhibit 6), especially since the October FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Gold prices presumably have been supported by the drop in global short-term interest rates, which reduces the carrying cost of owning gold.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is also possible that gold is viewed as a hedge against the risk that central bank policy actions could ultimately prove inflationary.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Presumably, the fear may be that the exit from these policies could be delayed or prove more difficult to engineer than generally anticipated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This poor performance of financial and real assets has a number of important implications.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, the earnings of most major financial intermediaries will be very poor this quarter.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, the two investment banks that report this week are almost certainly likely to record large mark-to-market losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that Goldman Sachs will report a loss of around $2 billion when it reports tomorrow morning.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This may actually understate the carnage because compensation booked for previous quarters can be reversed and the reversal of income taxes paid will reduce the size of the loss.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Commercial banks will also not be spared when they report next month.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Not only will they have significant losses on their trading books, but also loan-loss provisions are likely to climb sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: JPMorgan indicated last week that the current quarter has been terrible, and they have been one of the best-performing commercial banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The sharp decline in asset prices is also likely to reinforce the deleveraging process that is occurring throughout the financial sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although hedge fund performance in November was better than in the previous months, preliminary figures show that the aggregate index continues to slide (exhibit 7).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We’re down about 17 or 18 percent so far this year, and that’s the worst performance in hedge fund history in the aggregate by a significant margin.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although the redemption deadlines for year- end have generally passed, this pressure will persist into the first quarter and beyond for two reasons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, many fund-of-funds managers will get another round of redemption requests before year-end, which will cause them to ask for monies from the hedge funds that are part of their fund-of-funds families in the first quarter.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, some hedge funds restrict or “gate” the rate of withdrawals.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, Citadel suspended all redemptions for their two biggest funds through March 31.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This means that there will be a backlog in unfulfilled requests that will take time to satisfy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Bernard Madoff scandal may also lead to additional redemption requests.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The losses suffered by dealers and banks mean that their balance sheet constraints will continue to stymie the Federal Reserve’s efforts to supply liquidity to prospective borrowers.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 8, recent TAF auctions have been undersubscribed, and as shown in exhibit 9, the amount of dollar liquidity supplied via our swap lines has stabilized even though term LIBOR remains elevated well above the minimum bid rate that we charge on those auctions and the fact that swaps are open-ended in size.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problem is no longer one of supplying sufficient liquidity to the banks and dealers.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problem is getting these intermediaries to pass the liquidity onward to their clients.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Balance sheet constraints reveal themselves in many guises.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although LIBOR- OIS spreads have narrowed somewhat, they remain very elevated relative to historical levels (exhibits 10 and 11); jumbo mortgage rate spreads remain wide relative to conforming mortgage rates (exhibit 12); and cash instruments that take balance sheet room trade at significantly higher spreads than the corresponding derivatives that don’t.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 13 illustrates the spread between high-yield cash bonds and the corresponding CDX high-yield derivatives index.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This widening in that basis is one reason that some banks have taken large losses in the fourth quarter.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Evidence that balance sheet constraints are impeding the availability and cost of credit continues to proliferate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is obviously important because, if credit is not available on reasonable terms, this is likely to exacerbate the downward pressure on the economy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A darker economic outlook, in turn, threatens to lead to more losses and balance sheet pressures, reinforcing the downward dynamic.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of credit availability, the commercial mortgage area appears to be particularly vulnerable.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: According to industry sources, about $400 billion of mortgage debt—most put on five to seven years ago—needs to be refinanced when it comes due in 2009.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In recent years, commercial banks and the CMBS market provided the major source of funds for the commercial mortgage market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The owners of this commercial real estate are worried that, without new Federal Reserve and Treasury initiatives, funding will not be available to refinance this mortgage debt in 2009 on virtually any terms.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Investment-grade and high-yield corporate debt will also have to be refinanced.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 14 illustrates that more than $600 billion of term investment-grade corporate debt will need to be refinanced in 2009.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So far, this market still looks open for business, but it may become less so if the macroeconomic environment continues to deteriorate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the credit markets, are there any areas that have shown improvement?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The answer, of course, is “yes.” In those areas in which the federal government, including the Federal Reserve, has applied the most force, the situation has generally stabilized or improved.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Let me briefly give a few examples.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, the FDIC funding guarantee, the Citigroup intervention, and the $250 billion of TARP money allocated for bank capital seem to have stabilized the banking sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 15 and 16, CDS spreads have been pretty stable recently despite the deterioration in the macroeconomic outlook.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the commercial paper funding facility (CPFF) has led to significant improvement in the commercial paper market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 17, the yields on highly rated commercial paper have declined.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As this has occurred, the CPFF has become less attractive, and the number of issuers and the amount of commercial paper purchased each day by the CPFF have moderated sharply (exhibit 18).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Just as important, after an initial surge in which the CPFF represented virtually all of the long-dated maturity issuance, the CPFF share of long-dated issuance has fallen significantly (exhibit 19).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So far, the CPFF has worked pretty much as designed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, our announcement and purchases of agency debt have brought in agency debt spreads relative to Treasuries.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, in the five-year sector, debt spreads for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have narrowed more than 50 basis points since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fourth, our announcement that the Federal Reserve would purchase up to $500 billion in GSE mortgage-backed securities has caused the spread between conforming mortgages and Treasuries to narrow sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Coupled with the fall in Treasury yields—encouraged somewhat by the Chairman’s suggestion in a speech that the Federal Reserve might buy long-dated Treasuries for the SOMA—this has caused conforming mortgage rates to drop sharply (exhibits 20, 21, and 22).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As a result, mortgage refinancing activity has climbed sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 23 illustrates the spike upward in the Mortgage Bankers Association mortgage applications to refinance index that has occurred in the past two weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibits 24 and 25 contrast the performance in markets with federal government intervention to those markets without.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Spreads have generally narrowed where there has been intervention and widened elsewhere.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The contrast in the behavior of spreads suggests that one might wish to expand our existing facilities further.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The TALF is an obvious potential candidate given that it could conceivably be extended in multiple dimensions—including the scope of asset classes, vintage, and credit quality.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In my opinion, the liquidity facilities should be viewed as part of our suite of monetary policy tools.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The impulse of monetary policy to the real economy depends not just on the level of the federal funds rate but, more important, also on the impact on financial conditions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In normal times, movements in the federal funds rate result in moves in financial conditions in the same direction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Markets do the work, and financial conditions ease as the federal funds rate is cut.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But in extraordinary times such as the present, in which banks and dealers are unwilling to on-lend liquidity because of balance sheet constraints, federal funds rate reductions alone may be ineffective in easing financial conditions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In such an environment, special liquidity facilities that bypass the banks and dealers may prove necessary to ease financial conditions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, expansion of our liquidity tools does blow up our balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Exhibit 26 shows the growth of the balance sheet and the changes in its composition over time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Since late September, the balance sheet has grown sharply mainly because of the expansion of our foreign-exchange swap program (shown in light blue), the CPFF (shown in brown), and the TAF program (shown in purple).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibit 27, which is a snapshot of our balance sheet late last week, this has caused excess reserves to rise sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The growth in excess reserves has been exacerbated by the rolling off of the Treasury SFP (supplementary finance program) bills.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We peaked at about $500 billion earlier, and now we have $364 billion of SFP bills on our balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Treasury was unwilling to continue this program at its earlier level because of worries about reaching the debt limit ceiling in the first quarter and because they would have had to notify the Congress 60 days before that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Turning now to the Desk’s efforts to implement monetary policy and the FOMC’s directive, the effective federal funds rate has continued to trade soft relative to the target rate (exhibit 28).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The interest rate paid on excess reserves (IOER rate) has not been a perfect substitute for the Treasury SFP program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because the IOER rate for the two-week reserve maintenance period is set at the lowest level that occurred anytime during that period, the sharp drop last Thursday evident in the exhibit occurred because banks anticipate a substantial cut in the federal funds rate target and the IOER rate at this FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The drop in the effective rate has occurred even though we have increased the rate paid on excess reserves to equal the federal funds rate target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although some of this softness in the effective rate relative to the target reflects the sales of federal funds by GSEs that are not eligible to be paid interest on excess reserves, this is by no means the whole story.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The unwillingness of major banks to bid more aggressively for these funds is an important factor.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This unwillingness to fully arbitrage the gap between the IOER rate and the effective federal funds rate is another consequence of the lack of balance sheet capacity in the banking sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although we are exploring ways to remove most of the GSE effect from the picture, even if we were to be successful in doing this, we expect that the balance sheet constraints would still be powerful enough to cause the effective federal funds rate to trade soft relative to the target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, if the GSE federal funds volumes were removed, it is not clear what the effective target would represent because trading volumes could then turn out to be very, very low.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The drop in the effective federal funds rate has been accompanied by a corresponding drop in other short-term interest rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, general collateral repo rates have collapsed almost all the way to zero (exhibit 29).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is likely to lead to a rise in Treasury fails because, when general collateral repo rates are very low, the cost of shorting Treasury securities becomes negligible.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As fails climb, in turn, this erodes market function in the Treasury market and reduces the usefulness of the Treasury market as a hedging vehicle for other fixed-income assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The effect of fails on Treasury market function can be seen in exhibit 30, which shows how errors in our Treasury yield curve model have increased as short-term interest rates have fallen close to zero.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of monetary policy expectations, the federal funds rate futures curves (exhibit 31) and the Eurodollar futures curves (exhibit 32) continue to shift lower.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, with the effective federal funds rate persistently trading below the target rate, it is unclear how much of this shift represents a change in expectations about what the Committee will do with respect to the target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The primary dealer credit survey sheds considerably more light here.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As shown in exhibits 33 and 34, rate expectations have shifted lower since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: All 16 respondents to our most recent survey expect the FOMC to reduce the target, with most (13 out of 16) calling for a 50 basis point reduction in the target rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: No dealer expects a 25 basis point cut at this meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Two are at a 75 basis point cut, and one anticipates a 100 basis point reduction in the target rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A slim majority—9 out of 16—expect a 50 basis point target to be the trough for the target rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Most expect that the FOMC will not cut the target at future meetings, and no rate hikes are expected by anyone until the second half of 2009 at the earliest.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Comparing exhibits 33 and 34, the most recent survey shows considerably less dispersion in the four-quarters-ahead federal funds rate forecasts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, for completeness, I include our standard chart on inflation expectations as measured by the Board’s and Barclays’ measures of the five-year, five-year-forward breakeven inflation rate (exhibit 35).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think these breakeven rates provide much information right now because the TIPS market has been heavily influenced by the sharp fall in CPI inflation that will accrue to TIPS over the next few months and by the growing illiquidity of TIPS versus nominal Treasuries.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Interestingly, the most recent primary dealer survey shows no change in five-year, five-year-forward expectations for CPI inflation, with the average of the group remaining at 2.4 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There is, however, somewhat greater dispersion on both sides indicating uncertainty about how successful the Federal Reserve will be in keeping core PCE inflation in the “comfort zone” of 1½ to 2 percent on a longer-term basis (exhibit 36).

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There were no foreign operations during this period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I request a vote as always to ratify the operations conducted by the System Open Market Account since the October FOMC meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, I am very happy to take questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was a sharp decline in the spike in the fails recently?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There are two potential explanations, and it’s really hard to sort out what’s driving it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One is just that trading volumes have come down, and as trading volumes have come down, fails have come down.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So that’s part of it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s just tied to trading volume.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second explanation is that the Treasury Market Practices Group published a best practices report basically arguing that a penalty rate should be put on fails, and it is going to design a road map to show how that might be implemented in practice.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It may be that, given that publication, people who before might have been more cavalier about shorting Treasury securities at very low interest rates are now somewhat less inclined to do so just because of the moral suasion of that report that it is not a good thing to do.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it is some combination of those two, I think.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Bill, in your discussion on exhibit 13 and around the idea that a number of resets are coming for mortgages—the earlier seven-year ARMs and so forth—and as you also look forward to where mortgage rates are, why are you anticipating trouble with the ability to refinance, given the outlook for mortgages rates?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think you have to distinguish between conforming mortgage markets and everything else.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The conforming mortgage market is doing fine.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Some spreads are a little wider than they have been historically, but our actions seem to have been pretty successful in bringing those spreads in a bit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the conforming mortgage market rate is fine.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problem is in commercial-mortgage-backed securities and nonconforming mortgages.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The appetite to provide financing there is very, very much impaired, especially in the commercial mortgage market.

speaker: FISHER
text: Bill, has the FDIC’s temporary liquidity guarantee program interfered with or added to the confusion in the purchase and sales of fed funds, or has our excluding sales under one month changed the picture?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think it has created much confusion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The biggest confusion is who is guaranteed and who is not and which instruments are guaranteed and which instruments are not.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think people will have trouble sorting that out.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Most of the issuance has been long term—three years.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: People say, “Well, if I’m paying 75 basis points, let me get the most value for that.” So there hasn’t really been much channel conflict with the very short end, and I think that the fact that one month and in is not covered also has reduced that potential channel conflict.

speaker: FISHER
text: Is that pretty well understood in the marketplace?

speaker: FISHER
text: Then speaking of guarantees, I have just one more question, if I may, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: FISHER
text: In chart 14, are these net of credits that might have some kind of government guarantee?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In fact, when you look at the issuance of investment-grade corporate debt recently, there’s quite a bit of it, but most of it is the guaranteed stuff.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So excluding the guaranteed stuff, the issuance volumes do not look as robust as the aggregate number suggests because so much of that is the guaranteed stuff.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t have the number off the top of my head.

speaker: BULLARD
text: At the beginning of your comments, you said that you expected further big mark-to-market losses.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Do you mean over and above what markets anticipate now?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I mean that in the fourth quarter they will reflect the decline that occurred from August 30 to November 30 for the investment banks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: September 30 to December 30 just hasn’t been yet recorded on their balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They haven’t announced it yet.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You cited that Goldman number of $2 billion, but that’s been widely reported.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That has been widely reported.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Morgan Stanley is also going to report this week, and it is highly likely they will have similar losses.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Then I just want to understand—on exhibit 2 you said something about a fully discounted default rate last seen in the Great Depression.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What did you mean by that?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, if you basically take that 21 percent and compare it with the default rates in the Great Depression and write down some numbers for recoveries, if you had a default rate equal to the Great Depression default rate and you had a 20 percent recovery, you’d actually do pretty well owning high-yield debt at these levels right now.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the level of yields fully discounts horrific default rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In fairness, these are junk bonds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is possible that we could have default rates greater than those of the Great Depression.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’m just saying that these levels discount that kind of outcome.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, the high-yield debt market today is different from general default rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yeah, I think that’s a fair point.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Was there something like a junk market in the Great Depression that we can compare this with?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, there were certain leveraged utility companies that you could argue were pretty junky.

speaker: FISHER
text: Corporate grade became junk in the Great Depression.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Michael Milken hadn’t been born yet.

speaker: LACKER
text: That’s a calculation that embeds risk neutrality into the extrapolation?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, you could solve for the risk premium that was left over, and we did a back-of-the-envelope calculation in New York on that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It was an excess return of about 600 basis points.

speaker: LACKER
text: Doesn’t that depend on the assumption about the correlation between—

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is back of the envelope.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, you’d have to dig down pretty deeply to try to separate what’s the default rate and what’s the risk premium.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the point here is that the market is discounting very adverse outcomes.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I just want to follow up on that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Would you say that that represents a tremendous amount of pessimism out there, or are you saying that you think we’re going to get default rates like the Great Depression?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: No, I think it’s some combination.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think you can really separate how much of it is default rate versus how much of it is risk premium.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The point is that there’s probably a considerable amount of both.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Clearly the risk premiums are high because we see risk premiums on safe assets being very, very high.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The classic example is the student loan, which is 97 percent guaranteed by the federal government, trading at LIBOR plus 350 or LIBOR plus 400.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That’s probably a pretty good measure of risk premium—that’s your underlying risk premium on all assets, maybe a few hundred basis points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker has a two-hander.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, about the risk premium, it’s either a lot of pessimism or a lot of correlation between defaults and bad states of the world and essentially low growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: The second thing, I took a look at the student-loan-asset-backed securities that you talked about—FFELP.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think you have a chart here.

speaker: LACKER
text: It turns out that the trusts are guaranteed a rate of return equal to the commercial paper rate, and any excess over that they have to return to the Department of Education.

speaker: LACKER
text: They get a payment if the return is below that.

speaker: LACKER
text: Your coupon is 200 points above LIBOR, and LIBOR is trading a bit above commercial paper rates, right?

speaker: LACKER
text: So there’s a negative spread built into the trust documents.

speaker: LACKER
text: They’re paying 300 basis points more than they’re earning on the trust.

speaker: LACKER
text: So a little extra premium seems pretty reasonable.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is my understanding of that security correct, Bill?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think what you’re describing is the perspective from the issuer of the obligation.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The issuer of the obligation has a problem because on one side they get commercial paper and on the other side they get LIBOR, and so they have a mismatch.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They have essentially a basis risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But about where securities are trading in the market or what end-investors can invest in the securities—I think you’re referring more to the issuers of the securities, and the chart I showed is what investors in the AAA tranches get.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think it’s a slightly different thing.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, wouldn’t investors want to discount or take into account the fact that the trust, which is their only source of payment, is earning about 300 basis points less than the coupon?

speaker: LACKER
text: Wouldn’t that show up in a higher premium on what the investor is willing to pay?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t see it that way.

speaker: WILCOX
text: President Lacker, it’s a complicated security, but it’s wrapped by a guarantee that ultimately the Department of Education will make good on to the tune of 97 cents on the dollar.

speaker: WILCOX
text: There’s one little detail that is causing another piece of friction in the market, and that is that, if the servicer doesn’t perform on the loan, then the Department of Education has the right to not make good on the guarantee.

speaker: WILCOX
text: But other than that, it’s about 97 percent guaranteed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We think they’re pretty safe—not perfectly safe, but pretty safe.

speaker: WILCOX
text: Apparently the ability of the Department of Education not to make good on the guarantee is very rarely exercised.

speaker: LACKER
text: But the Department of Education doesn’t guarantee LIBOR plus a 200 basis point coupon.

speaker: LACKER
text: It guarantees the commercial paper rate.

speaker: WILCOX
text: I believe Bill’s point is that it guarantees a return to the investor.

speaker: LACKER
text: That still doesn’t seem that irrationally priced.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, we need a motion to ratify domestic open market operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s turn now to Brian, and we’ll have a staff presentation on the zero lower bound.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m being reminded that this is a joint Board–FOMC meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m reconvening a Board meeting that began this morning.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As the Committee requested at your last meeting, the staff has provided background for your discussion today of issues related to the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Ten days ago, we sent you 21 notes covering lessons from the U.S. and Japanese experiences in disinflationary or deflationary environments; the possible costs to financial markets and institutions of very low interest rates; the potential benefits of further rate reductions; and the advantages and disadvantages of nonstandard approaches to providing macroeconomic stimulus that could be employed when the federal funds rate cannot be reduced further.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Numerous staff members contributed to these notes—too many to recognize individually right now.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But I would nevertheless like to thank them collectively for their intensive efforts on this project when many were already quite busy with other important assignments.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Steve Meyer will now summarize the key conclusions from the staff work, and then I will review the suggested questions for discussion that we sent to you last week.

speaker: MEYER
text: By way of background, the Greenbook and many private forecasters project a sizable drop in real GDP from mid-2008 to mid- 2009, followed by sluggish growth into 2010, even with short-term interest rates barely above zero and with substantial fiscal stimulus.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Board staff and the median forecaster in the December Blue Chip survey predict that unemployment will peak around 8.25 percent in 2010.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Greenbook forecast shows core PCE inflation dropping below 1 percent in 2010; many private forecasters envision similar disinflation.

speaker: MEYER
text: Moreover, responses to a special question in the latest Blue Chip survey indicate that private forecasters see a sizable risk of deflation, and stochastic simulations of FRB/US that take the Greenbook forecast as the baseline suggest a roughly 1-in-4 chance that the core PCE price index will decline over one or more of the next five years.

speaker: MEYER
text: In short, forecasts generally suggest that additional stimulus would be desirable.

speaker: MEYER
text: With the target federal funds rate at 1 percent and the effective rate significantly lower, the Committee has little scope for using conventional monetary policy to stimulate the economy.

speaker: MEYER
text: As a practical matter, the System’s large liquidity-providing operations and the Treasury’s decision to scale back the supplementary financing program make it likely that the effective federal funds rate will remain quite low into the new year.

speaker: MEYER
text: Even so, the Committee could choose to apply some additional stimulus by reducing its target federal funds rate and pushing the effective funds rate closer to zero.

speaker: MEYER
text: The research literature strongly suggests that a central bank should quickly cut its target rate to zero when it faces a substantial probability that conventional monetary policy will, in a few quarters, be constrained by the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates.

speaker: MEYER
text: But as discussed in several of the notes you received on December 5, driving short-term interest rates to zero would have costs as well as benefits.

speaker: MEYER
text: Zero or near-zero rates cause a high volume of fails in the Treasury securities market, leading to decreased liquidity in that market and potentially in other fixed-income markets.

speaker: MEYER
text: And if short-term rates remain very close to zero, some money market funds probably will close.

speaker: MEYER
text: Such costs may argue against cutting the target funds rate to zero and driving the effective rate closer to zero.

speaker: MEYER
text: Whether or not the Committee chooses to cut its target rate to zero, policymakers may find it helpful to expand the use of nonstandard monetary tools.

speaker: MEYER
text: In the current environment, using such tools has two potential benefits.

speaker: MEYER
text: First, they may help the Federal Reserve achieve better expected outcomes on both parts of the dual mandate.

speaker: MEYER
text: Second, nonstandard tools could help mitigate the risk of an even more negative outcome.

speaker: MEYER
text: It may prove useful to group nonstandard tools into four broad categories and treat each category in turn.

speaker: MEYER
text: The first category is simple quantitative easing.

speaker: MEYER
text: This approach uses conventional open market operations such as buying short-term government debt and conducting repurchase agreements to raise excess reserves in the banking system to a level well beyond that required to drive short-term interbank rates to zero.

speaker: MEYER
text: The objective is to spur bank lending by ensuring that banks have ample funding at very low cost.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Japanese experience suggests that greatly expanding excess reserves, per se, has limited success in spurring bank lending, and thus has modest macroeconomic effects, when banks and borrowers have weak balance sheets.

speaker: MEYER
text: The second category of nonstandard policy tools is targeted open-market purchases of longer-term securities.

speaker: MEYER
text: The objective here would be to reduce term spreads or credit spreads and thus reduce the longer-term interest rates that are relevant for many investment decisions.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Committee could, for example, direct the Desk to buy a large amount of longer-term Treasuries.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Bank of Japan bought sizable quantities of Japanese government bonds; its purchases are thought to have lowered yields.

speaker: MEYER
text: The available evidence for the United States suggests that adding $50 billion of longer-term Treasury securities to the SOMA portfolio (a bit less than 1 percent of publicly held Treasury debt) probably would lower yields on such securities somewhere between 2 and 10 basis points; a substantially bigger purchase could have a disproportionately larger effect as longer-term Treasuries became scarce.

speaker: MEYER
text: Of course, what matters for the macroeconomy is the effect on private agents’ borrowing costs and wealth.

speaker: MEYER
text: Those effects are difficult to predict.

speaker: MEYER
text: Corporate bond yields should decline with Treasury bond yields, though perhaps less if supply effects are the main reason Treasury yields fall.

speaker: MEYER
text: But corporate bond yields could decline more than yields on Treasuries if the Committee’s action reduces investors’ concerns about downside risks and thus reduces credit risk premiums.

speaker: MEYER
text: Such a boost to confidence could also lift stock prices and household wealth.

speaker: MEYER
text: Another possibility is to instruct the Desk to buy a large quantity of GSE debt and mortgage-backed securities to reduce their yields and thus drive down mortgage rates.

speaker: MEYER
text: As Bill noted, markets reacted positively to the November 25 announcement that the Federal Reserve will buy $100 billion of GSE debt and up to $500 billion of agency-backed MBS; yields on 10-year GSE debt and option-adjusted MBS yields fell about 60 basis points that day, and the spread over 10-year Treasury yields narrowed about 40 basis points.

speaker: MEYER
text: Quoted rates on conventional conforming mortgages declined a similar amount in subsequent days.

speaker: MEYER
text: The magnitude of the announcement effect, which is consistent with estimates from the research literature, suggests that additional targeted purchases of agency debt and MBS could provide further macroeconomic stimulus.

speaker: MEYER
text: The third major category of nonstandard tools encompasses special liquidity and lending facilities.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Board could choose to expand current facilities or create new ones.

speaker: MEYER
text: Special liquidity facilities for banks and other financial firms are intended to help them meet their customers’ needs for credit by providing a reliable source of funding even if the markets in which those lenders usually raise funds are disrupted or if their depositors withdraw funds.

speaker: MEYER
text: Indeed, these facilities seem to be meeting these needs effectively.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Term Auction Facility, or TAF, is one example; the Asset- Backed Commercial Paper Money Market Mutual Fund Lending Facility, or AMLF, is another.

speaker: MEYER
text: Liquidity facilities may also support specific funding markets.

speaker: MEYER
text: The idea is that such markets are more likely to function if borrowers are confident that they will be able to issue and roll over debt and if lenders are assured that they will be able to fund purchases of debt instruments or reduce their holdings of such instruments when necessary.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Commercial Paper Funding Facility, or CPFF, is an example of this sort of program.

speaker: MEYER
text: Although the commercial paper market has not returned to normal, the CPFF has been helpful in supporting overall credit flows and reducing some credit spreads.

speaker: MEYER
text: Direct discount window lending to creditworthy nonfinancial firms is another potential tool for supporting economic activity.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Federal Reserve Act allows such lending, on a secured basis, if the borrower is unable to obtain adequate credit from banking institutions during unusual and exigent circumstances.

speaker: MEYER
text: Significant further expansion of the System’s lending programs would raise a host of issues.

speaker: MEYER
text: New facilities that lend directly to individuals, partnerships, or corporations would have to meet the requirements in section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Reserve Banks would take on more credit risk unless the Treasury or other parties took substantial first-loss positions.

speaker: MEYER
text: Moral hazard would become a larger issue.

speaker: MEYER
text: The resulting increase in reserve balances would further complicate the implementation of monetary policy unless the FOMC were willing to accept a federal funds rate of essentially zero.

speaker: MEYER
text: Developing satisfactory exit strategies would be challenging.

speaker: MEYER
text: And the practical burdens of designing and operating a sizable number of new liquidity facilities would be substantial.

speaker: MEYER
text: Even so, some expansion might prove useful if credit conditions do not improve.

speaker: MEYER
text: Communication and commitment strategies are the fourth and final category of nonstandard policy tools.

speaker: MEYER
text: In current circumstances, the Committee might use such strategies in an effort to lower market expectations of future short-term interest rates and thus reduce long-term rates, or it might wish to prevent expectations of deflation from taking hold.

speaker: MEYER
text: I will mention three strategies that the Committee might pursue.

speaker: MEYER
text: First, research suggests that it would be helpful for the Committee to be explicit about its longer-term goals, particularly about its goal for inflation.

speaker: MEYER
text: Foreign experience supports the theoretical prediction that an explicit and credible inflation objective helps anchor longer-run inflation expectations and thus can help prevent a downward drift in expected inflation and an upward drift in real interest rates during a protracted period of high unemployment and slowing inflation.

speaker: MEYER
text: That is, an explicit longer-run inflation target can prevent the public from thinking that the Federal Reserve will allow inflation to remain persistently below rates that the Committee has previously said are desirable.

speaker: MEYER
text: The Committee has discussed the pros and cons of a numerical objective for inflation several times.

speaker: MEYER
text: You may wish to consider whether the significant risk of deflation and the near certainty that the zero lower bound will constrain conventional monetary policy have changed the cost–benefit calculus.

speaker: MEYER
text: Second, the Committee could announce that it will seek to run a somewhat higher rate of inflation for a number of years than it will seek in the long run.

speaker: MEYER
text: Such a promise, if deemed credible, would stimulate real activity by raising inflation expectations and reducing medium- and long-term real interest rates.

speaker: MEYER
text: Researchers have proposed several approaches for dealing with the zero lower bound that would operate in this fashion, including targeting a slowly rising price level.

speaker: MEYER
text: These approaches would be a significant departure from historical practice, and so their pros and cons would need to be evaluated carefully.

speaker: MEYER
text: Third, research suggests that it would be helpful for the Committee to provide more-explicit information about its views on the likely future path of the federal funds rate.

speaker: MEYER
text: Suppose, for example, that the Committee concludes that it most likely will need to keep the federal funds rate close to zero for some time to spur an economic recovery and to prevent a persistent decline in inflation.

speaker: MEYER
text: In the current environment, an announcement to that effect might lead market participants to expect the funds rate to remain near zero for a longer time than they now think likely; the announcement might also lead to an increase in expected inflation.

speaker: MEYER
text: Those changes in expectations would lower nominal and real bond yields, providing some stimulus to economic activity.

speaker: MEYER
text: Theory suggests that it would be important to make clear that the Committee’s current view about the likely future path of policy is conditional on current information and the current outlook and to spell out how the actual policy path would depend on a range of possible future outcomes.

speaker: MEYER
text: Communicating this conditionality could be difficult.

speaker: MEYER
text: The bottom line from the staff’s analysis is that unconventional monetary policy tools can be useful complements to well-designed fiscal stimulus and to steps to recapitalize and strengthen the financial system.

speaker: MEYER
text: Additional purchases of longer-term securities, expansion of targeted lending facilities, and explicit statements of policymakers’ goals and intentions all seem likely to be useful when conventional monetary policy is constrained by the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates.

speaker: MEYER
text: Our limited experience with these tools makes it difficult to estimate the amount of macroeconomic stimulus that would be generated by each and thus makes it difficult to calibrate their application.

speaker: MEYER
text: If the Committee and the Board choose to make greater use of nonstandard tools now or in the near future, it may be appropriate to deal with the uncertainty by using the tools in combination.

speaker: MEYER
text: Finally, the Bank of Japan's experience suggests that nonstandard tools are more likely to be effective if they are used aggressively.

speaker: MEYER
text: I’ll now turn back to Brian.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2 The staff provided eight questions to help frame your discussion, and those questions are included in the package we have placed before you—a single page with a blue cover sheet.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I would like to comment briefly on each of them.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The first question deals with the issue of whether policy adjustments should be accelerated when the zero bound looms, as the research literature indicates, or whether the Committee should “keep its powder dry”—for example, if it believes that the announcements of rate cuts have some special ability to buoy confidence.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In present circumstances, a key practical consideration is that the System’s liquidity programs have already resulted in a very low effective federal funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Absent a very substantial unwinding of those facilities, the effective funds rate will remain close to zero for the foreseeable future even if the Committee adopts a significantly positive target for the federal funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Still, the announcement of cuts in the target rate probably would trigger further reductions in the prime rate and thus in rates paid by a sizable fraction of debtors.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternatively, the Committee might set a target rate significantly above zero to convey its intentions for the stance of monetary policy over a period longer than the intermeeting period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The second question concerns your views of the costs of very low interest rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the financial markets, very low short-term rates are likely to erode liquidity; fails will increase, and the returns available on some short-term investments simply will not overcome the transaction costs.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The staff research concluded that certain financial intermediaries, such as Treasury-only money market funds, will clearly be adversely affected by very low interest rates, and those adverse effects could have spillover effects into other markets, such as the repo market.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But not all financial institutions will be hurt by low rates; there will be winners and losers, depending partly on their asset–liability mix.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, our work suggested that financial institutions in the aggregate tend to benefit from the macroeconomic stimulus of monetary policy easing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Overall, judging the point at which the marginal costs of rate reductions exceed the marginal benefits is quite difficult.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The third question asks whether you see a net benefit from communicating your intentions for inflation beyond the next few years or your views about the likely stance of monetary policy over some period longer than the intermeeting period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Specifically, we suggested that you comment on the desirability of stating (1) that you intend to hold the funds rate at very low levels until specified conditions prevail, (2) that the Committee is concerned about the risks of excessive disinflation and will act to mitigate that risk, or (3) that the Committee will be willing to temporarily accept higher rates of inflation in the next few years in order to limit the economic downturn 2 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are attached to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The draft statements presented in the “Policy Alternatives” section of the Bluebook include language that you might consider if you decide to pursue one or more of these possibilities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Questions 4 through 8 cover nonstandard policy tools.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Question 4 asks your views about the benefits of large open market operations in agency debt, agency MBS, and Treasury securities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Such purchases are clearly within the authority of the FOMC, and the staff research suggests that they have definite potential to stimulate economic activity by lowering longer-term interest rates, although calibrating those effects is difficult.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, members could be troubled by the fact that purchases of agency debt and MBS could be regarded as steering funds to the GSEs and to particular economic sectors.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In your responses to this question, you may want to comment on whether you are concerned by the credit-allocation aspects of such purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You may also want to provide your views on the channels through which purchases of Treasuries or agency securities would have a beneficial effect.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In particular, do you see the power of such tools as arising from their effects in reducing long-term yields and spreads and supporting aggregate demand through those channels?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Or would you emphasize the increase in excess reserves and the monetary base that would accompany such purchases and the possible effects on bank lending?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Question 5 relates to liquidity facilities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As Steve noted, the creation of additional lending facilities is another potentially powerful policy tool for the Federal Reserve— particularly in current circumstances, in which credit flows in some markets are severely disrupted.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Some of those facilities appear to have been successful in supporting credit flows and thus economic activity.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But even though further additions or expansions could be helpful to credit intermediation, taking these steps would involve a number of substantive issues.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, the design, implementation, and ongoing operation of such facilities pose real resource challenges to the System.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, these programs raise governance issues.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Because such programs generally rely on the section 13(3) lending authority, authorization of these programs is the responsibility of the Board, and the decision to lend is made by the Reserve Bank.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: At the same time, these programs create reserves and thus potentially affect the FOMC’s ability to influence the funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Question 6 is open-ended: Do you see other nonstandard policy tools besides open market purchases and liquidity facilities as likely to be particularly helpful in current circumstances?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If so, what are those tools?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Question 7 returns to governance issues: Given that the Desk has begun to purchase agency debt and MBS, how should the FOMC specify its directive to the Desk?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If the Committee instructed the Desk to undertake purchases in order to attain specific objectives for interest rate levels or rate spreads, serious practical issues could arise.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Longer-term yields are heavily affected by expectations of future policy rates, which are in turn importantly driven by incoming economic news as well as by various risk premiums.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Experience indicates that our operations have an effect on longer-term yields, but to have an effect that is economically significant, the operations may need to be very large.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even then, given the substantial effects of the other factors that affect yields, it might be very difficult or impossible to achieve specified rate levels or spreads.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As an alternative, the Committee could instruct the Desk to purchase specific quantities of particular types of obligations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Such an approach is clearly feasible, but its potential benefits may be harder to communicate to the public except in qualitative terms.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Another issue is whether the directive should be conditional on market developments.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Bluebook provided drafts of directives in which the basic approach is to specify quantities of purchases over specified periods of time but with some allowance for qualitative judgments about market conditions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Question 8 comes back to communication issues.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If the Committee embarks on the use of unconventional policy tools, clearly communicating the nature of the policy and the intended objectives will be challenging.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, once the Committee has formally brought its target for the federal funds rate to around zero or otherwise has signaled that further rate reductions will not be forthcoming, there will surely be press stories asserting that the Committee has “run out of ammunition,” potentially undermining the Committee’s message that monetary policy still can provide considerable stimulus.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Overcoming these communication challenges will be somewhat easier if the Committee is able to agree on the substance of what it is trying to accomplish and a broad approach to explaining it to the public.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But achieving such agreement is complicated by significant remaining uncertainties about the effectiveness of the various unconventional policy tools, a very uncertain economic outlook, and other factors.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In your remarks, you may wish to provide your views of the best practical means for the Committee to address these communication challenges.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We would be happy to respond to your questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to give special thanks to the staff, some of whom are here and some of whom are not, for an extraordinary amount of work on these difficult topics over a short period of time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We very much appreciate those efforts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Brian or Steve or anyone else?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no questions, we’re ready for the go-round on this topic.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d like to ask your indulgence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s an awful lot here, and I’d like to go first this time and try to clear out some underbrush and to lay down some issues in the hope that it will perhaps focus our discussion a bit more.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As you know, we are at a historic juncture—both for the U.S. economy and for the Federal Reserve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The financial and economic crisis is severe despite extraordinary efforts not only by the Federal Reserve but also by other policymakers here and around the world.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to monetary policy, we are at this point moving away from the standard interest rate targeting approach and, of necessity, moving toward new approaches.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, these are very deep and difficult issues that we are going to have to address collectively today and tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to say that, although we are certainly moving in a new direction and the outlines of that new direction are not yet clear, this is a work in progress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The discussion we’re having today is a beginning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Everyone can rest assured that this conversation is going to continue for additional meetings, and today we’re not going to be setting in stone an approach that will be used indefinitely.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In fact, it would be hubristic to do so, given all the uncertainties and changes that we face.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m not going to try to address all of these questions, but I thought it would be useful for me to talk a bit, first, about nontraditional policies and then, second, about the important issue of governance, which I know a lot of people are concerned about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me start, first, with nontraditional policies.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to note that we are working and we should continue to work to improve our control of the effective funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The interest rate paid on reserves is not currently sufficient to keep the rate at the target.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s for a lot of reasons with which you are all familiar.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would just note that the staff is still working.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should not give up on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The interest rate on reserves may be more effective as people get used to it, as balance sheet constraints ease, and as the rate gets higher if we decide to raise rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that is still a tool that we should keep and be aware of.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are other strategies—opening term accounts of various kinds, taking steps to encourage arbitrage, using Treasury bills, or perhaps issuing our own bills.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In fact, we have had a lengthy discussion in this Committee of alternative structures for implementing monetary policy that involve different ways of setting up reserve requirements.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So first of all, let’s just acknowledge that, although we are not keeping the effective funds rate at the target currently, we should not assume that that’s always going to be the case.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We do have some optionality in that direction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That being said, it’s obvious that the effective funds rate now is quite low, and given the amount of excess reserves in the system, we’re going to have to find other ways at least in the near term to address the economic crisis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One approach, as was discussed by Steve and others, is communications.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Here, in particular, I think, we are at early stages.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think we’re going to come to any conclusions today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a lot of interest in terms of possibilities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The one thing I would say is that, if we do use communications as a way of providing information about future policy moves, we should be very careful to make those interest rate forecasts, if you will, conditional on the state of the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It should be very clear, if we give forward guidance of some kind, that the evolution of the policy rate will depend on how the economy evolves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The more clarity we can provide in that direction, the more effective our policy will be and the less problem we will have exiting from that strategy in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The statements that were circulated in the Bluebook gave two examples just for discussion, both of them in alternative A.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In paragraph 2, there was some suggested language for using an inflation target as a way of managing expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just read the sentence: “In support of its dual mandate, the Committee will seek to achieve a rate of inflation, as measured by the price index for personal consumption expenditures, of about 2 percent in the medium term.” The idea there would be to try to stabilize inflation expectations, avert deflationary expectations, and keep real rates lower than they otherwise would be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The 2 percent in that statement is a placeholder.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously if we do this, we would have to talk more about what 2 percent means.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is it a permanent level?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is it a temporary number?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But that is one strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would add that, of course, as we have discussed, adopting what might be a de facto inflation target is a pretty big deal, and if we decide to do that, I would like to have some opportunity to consult with the Congress appropriately.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But if we decide to go in this direction, I do think that this might be a good time because it is certainly not a negative as far as employment growth is concerned in this context, and so it might be easier to explain.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other example of communication, also in alternative A, ties policy to economic forecasts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “The Committee anticipates that weak economic conditions are likely to warrant federal funds rates near zero for some time.” I note that this is a forecast of policy rather than a commitment to policy, but it does provide some information about the Committee’s expectations and should affect market rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, again, I think we’re at early stages of this particular approach, but it may be promising, and I hope today’s discussion will provide some insight.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second general approach to conducting nontraditional monetary policy is by use of the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have already begun to do this to some extent, as you know.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In some respects our policies are similar to the quantitative easing of the Japanese, but I would argue that, when you look at it more carefully, what we’re doing is fundamentally different from the Japanese approach.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me talk about that a bit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Japanese approach, the quantitative easing approach, was focused on the liability side of the balance sheet—specifically the quantity of bank reserves, the monetary base, or however you want to put it, in the system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The theory behind quantitative easing was that providing enormous amounts of very cheap liquidity to banks, as Steve discussed, would encourage them to lend and that lending, in turn, would increase the broader measures of the money supply, which in turn would raise prices and stimulate asset prices, and so on, and that would suffice to stimulate the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, the focus of the quantitative easing was on the liability side, and indeed, there were targets, as you know, for the amount of excess reserves or reserves in the system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the verdict on quantitative easing is fairly negative.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It didn’t seem to have a great deal of effect, mostly because banks would not lend out the reserves that they were holding.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The one thing that it did seem to do was affect expectations of policy rates because everyone understood it would take some time to unwind the quantitative easing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, that pushed out into the future the increase in the policy rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I would argue that what we are doing is different from quantitative easing because, unlike the Japanese focus on the liability side of the balance sheet, we are focused on the asset side of the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, we have adopted a series of programs, all of which involve some type of lending or asset purchase, which has brought onto our balance sheet securities other than the typical Treasuries that we usually transact in.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You are all aware of the lending facilities for banks and dealers, the swaps with foreign central banks, the promised purchases of MBS, the various credit facilities for which even I do not know all the acronyms anymore.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In this case, rather than being a target of policy, the quantity of excess reserves in the system is a byproduct of the decisions to make these various types of credit available.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that’s a very different strategy, and Bill gave some evidence—we can debate it further—that these different policies have had some effects on the markets at which they’re aimed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, to distinguish between the balance-sheet, quantitative-easing, liability-side approach and the asset-side approach that we have been using, I do not think—and I feel this quite strongly— that it makes any sense for us to have or try to describe monetary policy with a single number, which is the size of the balance sheet or the size of our liabilities, as the Japanese did.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are a number of reasons for this, but the least important reason is probably just the fact that many of our programs don’t have fixed sizes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They are open-ended—like the swap programs, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also, many of the programs have different timing, different durations, maturities, beginning points, ending points, and the like, and so in that respect I think it would be difficult to put in a single number.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: More important, the programs on the asset side of our balance sheet serve different purposes and have different structures, and aggregating a dollar of MBS purchase, a dollar of commercial paper purchase, and a dollar of swaps to make three dollars strikes me as being apples and oranges.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do not think that is the right way to think about it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Furthermore, and finally, these programs obviously have different operational costs and risks, different risks of losses, different maturities, and most important, they present different issues with respect to the exit strategy, which we will want to talk about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Rather than looking at this as a single number, as a measure of the liability side of the balance sheet, I think we ought to think about it as a portfolio of assets, a combination of things that we are doing on the asset side of our balance sheet, that have specific purposes and that may or may not be effective; but we can look at them individually.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me turn now quickly to the governance issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Before getting into them, let me just say that, whatever difficulties we may have finding appropriate governance, it is certainly the case that the Federal Reserve Act did not exactly contemplate the situation in which we find ourselves today.

speaker: BERNANKE
