text: I think we all agree that getting the right policies for the U.S. economy is the top priority and, whatever we do, we need to find a way to get the right policies in place.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Frankly, I think the best way to achieve that—I am going to talk about some details—is through operating in good faith.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we work together and keep each other apprised of developments and our views, we will be able to make this work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we take too narrow an approach, too legalistic an approach, I think it will be much more difficult.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me make a few comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I can focus this best by simply answering the question: If the federal funds rate is at zero and the FOMC no longer sets the target, then what is the role of the FOMC in monetary policy?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have four answers to that question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first is that the Federal Reserve’s outlook is the FOMC’s outlook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is, the FOMC’s views about the evolution of the economy, of prices, and of financial conditions will govern our policy decisions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, it is the FOMC’s outlook that appears in the minutes, it is the FOMC’s outlook that appears in the projections, and it is the FOMC’s outlook that appears in our communications.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, if your board members ask you with respect to monetary policy, “Well, what are we doing now?” the answer is, “Keep telling us what you are seeing in the economy and financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will transmit that to the full FOMC because the FOMC’s outlook is the perspective that governs the policy actions that we take.” The second role of the FOMC, I believe, is in the communication policy, both in the narrow and in the large.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the narrow, if we decide to adopt a target, make a commitment about the length of time in which we hold rates low, or make any other kind of verbal promise in our statements or in other contexts, that is obviously the FOMC’s prerogative, and I think we understand that that’s how it would work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The third area is the most difficult one, and that has to do with the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The law provides a kind of odd co-dependence, if you will, between the Board and the FOMC with respect to the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Both the Board and the FOMC are enjoined by the Federal Reserve Act to pursue the dual mandate, and both the Board and the FOMC have powers that affect the size and composition of the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, the FOMC has authority over Treasuries, agency purchases, and swaps, whereas the Board has, in particular, the 13(3) authority, which has been utilized a lot lately for credit programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we have dual authority, and we have dual or joint responsibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the only way to deal with that essentially is through close consultation and collaboration.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My commitment to you is that we will work together even more closely, even more collegially, going forward to make sure that everyone is on board and understands what we are doing with respect to our various programs on the asset side of our balance sheet and that each person on this Committee is well informed and is able to give views and input into the discussions that we have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The legal authorities are what they are, but I do think that a collective and cooperative effort can help us solve this problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, I understand that the briefing sessions that I have provided have been useful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am willing to commit to do those as frequently as necessary, and I am willing to make them into meetings if we need to have two-way discussions and input from the Committee with respect to policy actions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is a bit awkward, but I hope that cooperation will allow us to work together on the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, there is a special issue here, though, which is the unwind issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One way in which the balance sheet affects the responsibilities of the FOMC is that, if the FOMC is going to be raising interest rates at some point in the future, clearly, it needs to have information and understanding about the constraints being placed on policy by the size and composition of the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that keeping the FOMC as a whole informed about the balance sheet, about the programs, about the constraints that may be placed on the unwind, and about alternative strategies for raising rates once the time comes, is incumbent upon me and the rest of the Board to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As a down payment on that, I have asked Bill Dudley, if there is time tomorrow, to give you a bit of an update on the TALF, the asset-backed securities loan facility, and talk to you about some issues that it raises for the unwind and for future interest rate policies.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Fourth, and finally, with respect to the FOMC responsibilities, is communication to the public.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The public doesn’t make the distinction between the Board of Governors and the FOMC.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The public understands the Federal Reserve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What we need to do is to come together and decide what policies we want to pursue and then collectively take responsibility for those policies and communicate them in a coherent and consistent way to the broad public.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is the responsibility of all of us, and I hope we can work together to provide everybody with the information that they need to do that effectively.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, I am going to say that, given the state of confidence in the markets and in the economy, I hope whatever disagreements we may have that as much as possible we can keep them within these walls.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to the public, we need, as much as possible, to communicate a clear strategy going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So those are just some thoughts on governance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am eager to hear your views about how to do it better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am also interested in knowing how you think these governance issues should translate into the statements and into the directives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we have thrown out some suggestions there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are not in any way wedded to them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If other people have other ideas, we are very open to adopting those ideas.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But at least I want to say that I am fully aware of these issues, and I think that however many structures we may impose, nothing is going to substitute for a good faith, collaborative effort in making this work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me stop there and begin the go-round with President Lacker.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me echo your comments about the staff’s work.

speaker: LACKER
text: They have provided us with a very comprehensive compendium of research and experiences relevant to the policy problems that we are facing now.

speaker: LACKER
text: And they have presented it in a surprisingly digestible form, all things considered.

speaker: LACKER
text: This was no small feat, as you and Brian noted, given the other demands on the staff’s time over the past few months.

speaker: LACKER
text: Clearly, as you said, Mr. Chairman, this is a critical moment for the Fed and the economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: Whatever we do and say at this meeting is going to mark a discrete change in the way we have conducted policy and communicated about it to the public in recent years.

speaker: LACKER
text: Some of this change, as has been noted, is already under way.

speaker: LACKER
text: We exhausted our ability to sterilize the additional reserves created through credit expansion at about the same time we implemented interest on excess reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: Beginning with this meeting, we have to articulate how we would intend to conduct monetary policy and pursue the goals of our dual mandate with the funds rate at a very, very low level, perhaps zero, and perhaps for a very extended period of time.

speaker: LACKER
text: Before addressing specifically the questions that Brian has laid out for us, I want to make clear what I think is one of the central issues at hand, and that is the Committee’s control over the monetary base and its conduct of monetary policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: When we target the fed funds rate at any rate above zero, we instruct the Desk to manage reserves or, equivalently, the monetary base so as to keep the effective funds rate at our target.

speaker: LACKER
text: Monetary policy has always been about controlling the base, and this continues to be true at the zero lower bound on interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, the path of the monetary base is even more critical at the zero bound because that is how we prevent deflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: By managing the public’s expectations about future base growth and future inflation, we manage current real rates and influence real activity.

speaker: LACKER
text: In essence, we prevent deflation by convincing the public that future base growth will be inconsistent with a falling price level.

speaker: LACKER
text: Just as a thought experiment, imagine that we commit to keeping interest rates at the zero bound for an extremely long time period, say infinitely.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we do that—this is a clear result from the literature—it does not prevent a deflationary equilibrium.

speaker: LACKER
text: But if we can commit to keeping the monetary base at a finite level, not falling, then that does rule out a deflationary equilibrium.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it is key that expectations about the base, not just nominal interest rates, are vital for our ability to prevent a deflationary equilibrium.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that focusing on the monetary base is going to help communication, and the reason is that a lot of people out there might not understand the relationship between credit spreads and growth or inflation or various other things that we are doing.

speaker: LACKER
text: But in almost everyone’s mind is the phrase “too much money chasing too few goods.” It provides, for a lot of people, an intuitive link between money and inflation, and I think we—for all the warts of our policy in the early 1980s under Chairman Volcker—exploited that well, to convey to the public that we were committed to bringing inflation down in a simple, intuitive way.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that can help us now, analogously, in convincing the public that we are going to be able to prevent deflation because we control money.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Committee’s management of the base or bank reserves is distinct, in my view—as you noted, Mr. Chairman—from the initiatives that use our balance sheet to target specific financial market spreads.

speaker: LACKER
text: Credit market programs may have macroeconomic effects.

speaker: LACKER
text: Indeed, that is their intended effect—to have beneficial macroeconomic effects on growth and inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is the same as other fiscal policy initiatives that also may have macroeconomic effects.

speaker: LACKER
text: But they are not monetary policy, and I think that is fairly clear.

speaker: LACKER
text: This Committee, I take it as given, is responsible for monetary policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the end of the day, monetary policy is about controlling the monetary base or bank reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: From the point of view of FOMC policy, what is important about the nonstandard tools and credit market programs is their effect on the monetary base.

speaker: LACKER
text: Again, to make this contrast stark, a policymaker controlling spreads cannot prevent deflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: A monetary policy maker controlling the base can.

speaker: LACKER
text: I should note that the ability to pay interest on reserves means that we face this issue generically, whether or not the funds rate is zero, because now, with interest on reserves, we can vary the monetary base independently of how we vary the federal funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: This makes it even more important that we make this transition in a way that clarifies the Committee’s role.

speaker: LACKER
text: Turning now to Brian’s questions, I think the most important one is number 7, the one about the directive to the Desk.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe that, if the directive is not going to specify a numerical target for the funds rate, then we need to find a way to specify some numerical target or range for the growth in the monetary base or the growth in bank reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, I realize that the directive is to the Desk, which has control over the SOMA account, and under a strict constructionist interpretation, that doesn’t necessarily equal the quantity of the monetary base.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, the discrepancy has gotten fairly large now with all of these credit programs.

speaker: LACKER
text: But if the Committee doesn’t provide direction about the interest rate, that is fixed at a floor, and if the Committee doesn’t provide direction about a monetary aggregate, the Committee really isn’t doing monetary policy, in my view.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Committee can also choose specific asset categories for the Desk to buy for the System Open Market Account, but that shouldn’t be confused with monetary policy as long as the monetary base is being determined at the margin by our credit programs.

speaker: LACKER
text: To put it slightly differently, individual Reserve Banks can propose their own credit programs, subject to the Board of Governors’ approval.

speaker: LACKER
text: But if they want to monetize those assets, then I would expect that the Committee’s prior approval would be required if an alteration in the base target were needed.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is what I would propose for the directives.

speaker: LACKER
text: Question 8 flows directly from question 7.

speaker: LACKER
text: What we should communicate is that we are targeting a quantity of the monetary base or bank reserves, and this communication should be made in a way that is broadly similar to the way we talk about interest rate policy, stating that our goals are for growth in the monetary base that supports the achievement of sustainable real growth and our medium-term goal for inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Question 3 also deals with communication, but more from the point of view of the funds rate path.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think in the present environment we should communicate that we anticipate that it will be near zero for some time—or something to that effect.

speaker: LACKER
text: Regarding part B of question 3, instead of citing the risk of deflation, I think we should presume some measure of success and communicate that we intend to use the growth of reserves to minimize the risk of inflation running below our medium-term inflation goal.

speaker: LACKER
text: Regarding part C, I think we should stick to communicating our goals for inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Questions 4 and 5 are about the means by which we grow our balance sheet and the monetary base, and I think the Committee should strive to maintain as much distance as possible from credit allocation.

speaker: LACKER
text: To me that means trying to have as little effect as possible on relative prices among nonmonetary assets, and I say that because I don’t think we really know enough to second-guess those outcomes.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I would like to see us focus on long-term Treasuries.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me close with a few remarks about the Committee.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the 1920s, each individual Reserve Bank made open market operation decisions on its own, in an uncoordinated way.

speaker: LACKER
text: That proved ineffective, and at times we were operating at cross-purposes, one Reserve Bank selling while another was buying.

speaker: LACKER
text: In response, the Conference of Presidents formed the Open Market Investment Committee to coordinate our decisions and make all the purchases through the good offices of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

speaker: LACKER
text: But the role of the Board of Governors in that Committee was unclear.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, the Board at times tried to order the Open Market Investment Committee to do things that the presidents didn’t want it to do, and they came to an impasse.

speaker: LACKER
text: This was remedied with the legislation of the 1930s that created the Federal Open Market Committee.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now we do things that weren’t envisioned then, that’s for sure.

speaker: LACKER
text: But, surely, the guiding principle there was that they wanted one single governance body in the Federal Reserve System to be responsible for the monetary conditions in our country, and I take that to be the guiding spirit of the FOMC as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is the only body in the Federal Reserve System in which we all come together as one and subject ourselves to the discipline of listening to each other’s different views and forming a workable consensus on the way forward.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree, Mr. Chairman, that we shouldn’t be splitting hairs about legal niceties about who is responsible for what.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree wholeheartedly that we should work toward consensus for that, and that is why I think the Committee has to have a serious role in monetary policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think that focusing the Committee’s decisions on just what the System Open Market Account does and leaving all these other programs to have whatever affect they might on the base is the right way forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I won’t try to respond, but I do want to ask you what your interpretation of the Japanese experience is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They had enormous increases in the base, no increase in M1, and no inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, let me say that there are models and sets of policy rules under which in the short run there is an irrelevance proposition, a kind of Modigliani–Miller theorem, about exchanges of monetary assets for short-term liquid securities that are virtually perfect substitutes and at the zero lower bound are definitely perfect substitutes.

speaker: LACKER
text: So that is definitely true.

speaker: LACKER
text: The point I made about the base in the long run is true as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: It has to do with eliminating certain possible conjectures that the public might make about our willingness to tolerate deflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the Japanese case, they were widely known to be quite eager to lift interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: It was known that they viewed the problems in the banking sector as exacerbated by low interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: They thought that raising real interest rates would provide more discipline and force more restructuring in the banking system.

speaker: LACKER
text: So they continually had to fight to keep the long end of the yield curve down.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t view that experience as providing the best evidence about what a firm commitment to preventing deflation could be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Fisher, you had a two-hander.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just want to ask a question—again acknowledging that I am the least well educated on this subject matter and not as erudite in my understanding.

speaker: FISHER
text: So this is a tutorial question.

speaker: FISHER
text: What we have been doing is implicitly acknowledging that standard monetary tools are not as effective as they could be because of the financial frictions that we have encountered in the marketplace.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we have been targeting dealing with those financial frictions.

speaker: FISHER
text: My question, President Lacker, is just from an educational standpoint: Do we know how much monetary base or balance sheet expansion would be needed to bring credit spreads back into normal order or to deal with these financial frictions?

speaker: FISHER
text: If we are going to target the monetary base, I worry about the operational consequences of doing so, since it seems to me that is an open-ended question.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is a very good question.

speaker: LACKER
text: We don’t have any models to draw on because we don’t have any data that would allow us to uncover a structural relationship between spreads and the quantity of the base.

speaker: LACKER
text: In any event, even were we to focus solely on our primary objectives for growth and inflation, I think we would have trouble there.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we would have a great deal of difficulty figuring out a quantitative relationship between the monetary base at the zero bound and our objectives.

speaker: LACKER
text: But we started the way we usually do things—without a serious quantitative understanding of the relationship between the funds rate and growth and inflation, and we groped and groped and found our way.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are going to grope and try to find our way in this new regime, and we are going to have to think hard about it and make some guesses—by trial and error—just the way we learned how to do funds rate targeting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I, too, want to add my praise to the staff.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It was an extraordinary set of memos, as Jeff indicated, making reasonably clear very difficult literature on a complex topic.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I want to thank them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Reading through them was very helpful to me in trying to sort out some of my own views as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As we know, the nominal funds rate has been trading well below our target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The real funds rate is about minus 2 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The outlook for growth is now even weaker than it was before.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In that case, we would want our policy rates to decline with the equilibrium real rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But the zero bound, of course, may constrain us, and our ability to do that is complicated by the prospect of declining inflation expectations, which make more difficult our ability to let the funds rate fall.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Once we are in the situation in which our policy rate is effectively zero, it does become a constraint on monetary policy—as has been well explained.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In that case, theory suggests that our policy strategy must focus on ways of raising expectations of inflation, so that, near the zero bound, real rates can decline while nominal rates remain close to zero.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One way to implement such a strategy is to credibly commit to keeping policy accommodative for some period of time after the funds rate is no longer constrained by the zero bound and before moving policy back to more neutral rates, thereby raising expectations of inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Eventually, however, we would need to bring policy rates back up in line with economic conditions, to avoid a permanent increase in long-run inflation expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That will be a tricky task to be sure.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What we promise to do with policy in the future is of overriding importance in this framework.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, I am sympathetic to this theoretical analysis, but I have some concerns as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The models that deliver these results are models of full commitment and thus presume that policymakers have already in some sense credibly committed to deliver on an inflation target and to deliver this strategy in the event that the near-zero bound becomes binding, which in these models amounts to having a price-level target as opposed to an inflation target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would like to think that we are committed and credible policymakers as far as the public is concerned, but, frankly, I have my doubts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would feel more comfortable if this Committee had agreed to a well-articulated inflation target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Had we done so, the current task before us might have had a greater chance of success.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Unfortunately, we do not have that luxury.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Consequently, I am somewhat less confident of how the public and the marketplace will react to our efforts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The trick we face now is how to make these promises understandable and credible.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One difficulty is that the optimal policy for many models in these circumstances is very complicated and very difficult to understand, much less communicate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we hope to affect expectations, we need to explain our policies in a way that the public can understand.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Even approximation of optimal policy in these circumstances would involve price-level targeting, as I said, and it would be very difficult to explain, particularly since the FOMC has never formalized its inflation target, let alone a price-level target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we would be better off trying to communicate something simpler.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, we need to tell the public that we have lowered the funds rate as low as we think it is beneficial to go.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do have some concerns about lowering the target rate all the way to zero.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We still do not understand why having interest rates on reserves isn’t working to keep the funds rate at its target, and there may well be unintended consequences of moving our target to zero, beyond those well articulated in the Board’s staff notes.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Whether that lowest rate is 100 basis points, 75 basis points, 50 basis points, or 25 basis points is very hard to say.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, given the law of unintended consequences and our lack of experience at the lower bound in this country, I do not want to go all the way to zero.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I think we do need to communicate clearly to the public that, when we reach whatever that effective zero rate is, we are done.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A way of communicating that might be by giving a funds rate target or range, say, between zero and some percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There are two additional practical advantages I see that argue for bounding our target rate above zero.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, it will allow additional time for banks to become more proficient at managing their reserves, so that our interest-rate-on-reserves regime can become effective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: By going to zero, we will effectively shut out that learning process.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Second, I believe that when the time comes to raise rates, even by modest amounts, we will be in a better position to do so from a non-zero position than from a zero position.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Next, we need to communicate that the FOMC desires inflation rates that are higher than perhaps our long-run target and communicate an inflation range we are aiming for.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is somewhat difficult because we have refused to communicate such a target in the past.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We certainly need to communicate that we do not wish deflation in a very weak economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We also may wish to convey that we are going to keep the nominal funds rate low for some period of time because we desire higher inflation, and that currently seems to be expected.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Communicating this serves to increase commitment, and it also limits misunderstanding when inflation rates might temporarily be above a longer-run target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, I think we need to say ex ante that we desire higher inflation rates than currently.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As suggested earlier, this would be easier to communicate had we adopted a target earlier.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Regarding the use of nonstandard policy tools—in my view, we are already there.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: With the funds rate trading below target, we are effectively conducting monetary policy through quantitative easing, which I define as increases in reserves either by open market operations or by any other means.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, expansion of our balance sheet, including unsterilized lending, is monetary policy, as it is monetizing the debt, either public or private.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As an aside, I find the description of such a policy as nonstandard a bit peculiar since using balance sheet quantities as instruments of policy has had a long tradition in monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, even the Federal Reserve has targeted nonborrowed reserves at various points in its history.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In principle, I have no objections to quantitative easings of this form.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But if that is how we view the new regime, then we need to publicly acknowledge that we have changed—that we have a new instrument— and communicate how monetary policy will be determined going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Internally, we also need to resolve, as has been pointed out, how decisions about our lending and liquidity facilities will be made, particularly now that these have become the main instrument of monetary policy as opposed to being the mechanism for providing liquidity to improve market functioning, which is then sterilized.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The FOMC, and not only the Board of Governors, needs to be involved in decisions about the magnitude of such lending and the choice of assets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In effect, these are choices about the extent of the Fed’s balance sheet and its expansion or contraction.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There are a number of ways in which one might proceed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, I believe we need to publicly convey that we have entered a new regime.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Otherwise, it may look as though we have lost control of monetary policy or that the FOMC, which sets the target funds rate, and the Board of Governors, which largely is controlling the liquidity provisioning, are at odds.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One obvious step would be to change the directive to the Desk, which is released in the minutes, in a way that clearly indicates that the new regime is now operative and that the FOMC has deliberately chosen to be in that regime.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We would then have to communicate something about the size of the balance sheet going forward in terms of limits, ranges, or maximums of some form, such as President Lacker was suggesting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My preference is for the directive to specify objectives in terms of asset quantities rather than the level of non-funds-rate interest rates or interest rate spreads.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is question 7 of the staff memo.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: These latter two are not under our control and, even more so than before, reflect counterparty risk not liquidity impairments.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, the transmission mechanism from reserve quantities to rates and spreads is not precise enough for these to be operational objectives.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Setting a quantity limit on the size of the balance sheet is more familiar—similar to our experience with operating a reserves-based target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In this quantitative regime, it means that the Board of Governors wishes to implement new lending programs that expand the balance sheet— that is, that are not sterilized.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Board of Governors would have to seek approval of the FOMC to get such an expansion but not necessarily for the composition of the assets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I have articulated before, I believe we need to remain cognizant of the line between monetary policy and fiscal policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would prefer to see us purchasing Treasuries rather than riskier assets, as I would favor the purchases of long-term Treasuries over new 13(3) facilities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This refers to questions 4 and 5.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To the extent that some of our lending programs are targeted at aiding specific markets, my preference would be to shift those assets from the Fed’s balance sheet to the Treasury and substitute Treasury securities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This would help distinguish monetary policy from credit policy and preserve our ability to conduct independent monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We also need to recognize that, as the economy begins to recover, these programs will need to be unwound, and this may occur before all financial institutions are fully recovered.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some of our facilities have termination dates and will shrink naturally as those dates are reached; but others, like the agency MBS programs or the TALF, will complicate the problem.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Under a well-functioning corridor system, should we get there, the target rate will be somewhere between the upper and lower bounds, and we will have to shrink the balance sheet if we expect to hit our target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The reduction may be quite significant if it is accompanied by a general fall in the demand for reserves by banks.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Even if we imagine going to a floor system in which, in principle, we can raise the target rate without shrinking the balance sheet, we need to be concerned about the health of our balance sheet so that we can ensure that we can finance the interest rates on reserves and pay them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Note that if we do go to a floor system, the rate paid on excess reserves will become our instrument, and we will need to agree on how to set that rate going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my view, that rate should be decided by the FOMC.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In summary, under a quantitative easing regime, the magnitude of the quantitative easing should be an FOMC decision.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To the extent that the quality of assets on our balance sheet complicates future monetary policy decisions, the asset makeup of the Fed’s balance sheet should also be in the FOMC’s purview.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One option that has been discussed is for the Fed to issue its own debt—other than Federal Reserve notes, I assume.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am uncomfortable with this proposal.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is likely to require congressional approval, and oversight will no doubt be sought since the Fed’s securities will be public debt.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This potentially generates opportunities for the Congress to control our debt ceiling and perhaps the pricing of our securities, in ways that may limit our ability to conduct independent monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, I am very skeptical that this would be a good path to follow.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This is an extremely important discussion, and I am glad that you have arranged a special session.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I very much appreciate the comprehensive and outstanding memos from the staff.

speaker: YELLEN
text: At our October meeting, we agreed to take whatever steps were necessary to support the recovery of the economy, and that principle guides my thinking on monetary policy at the zero bound.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In most circumstances, I see few advantages to gradualism, and certainly whenever we approach the zero bound, I think the funds rate target should be quickly reduced toward zero.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As to the level of the lower bound, my default position is that we should move the target funds rate all the way to zero because that would provide the most macroeconomic stimulus.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, every 25 basis point cut in the target typically takes about 25 basis points off the prime rate and associated borrowing rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The institutional concerns about Treasury fails and Treasury-only money market funds merit consideration, but I don’t consider them serious enough to ban lowering the target to a very low level.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Still, the surprising results we obtained from paying interest on reserves should make us chary about predicting the reactions of financial markets to new circumstances, so there may be some benefits from allowing the funds rate to trade between zero and, say, 25 basis points.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Let me now turn to the third set of questions on communication strategies.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Looking ahead, I believe that there could be significant benefits to communicating effectively the FOMC’s intentions to hold the target funds rate at a very low level.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The Japanese experience at the zero bound suggests that this is one channel that can work, and the evidence suggests that our own guidance that began in 2003 similarly influenced longer-term rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We learned then, though, that it is hard to convey the conditionality of such intentions and the multiple influences on the optimal setting of the funds rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Still, I favor trying to include forward-looking communication on policy expectations in future FOMC statements.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We could also consider using the FOMC minutes to provide quantitative information on our expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, we could reveal the funds rate projections that implicitly accompany our quarterly economic projections, publishing ranges and central tendencies of the federal funds rate along with those for GDP growth, unemployment, and inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The advantage of this approach is that it would provide a clear future path to the funds rate that is conditional on the economic environment pertaining to output and inflation relative to our goals.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We did discuss this approach before, and I remember that a number of you were uncomfortable with it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But circumstances have changed, and there could be particular value now in adding the federal funds rate to our projections, and in fact, we could consider a trial run.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I believe that, in addition to providing guidance on the likely path of future interest rates, we should become more communicative about our longer-term inflation objective to avoid a decline in inflation expectations as inflation drops over the next few years below desirable levels.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One way to accomplish this is to include quantitative information on our longer-term projections in the Summary of Economic Projections (SEP), as the Subcommittee on Communications has recommended.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We could go even further to endorse a Committee-wide long-term inflation objective, although that is something that we would have to further consider carefully.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We could supplement including longer-term projections in the SEP with language in the FOMC statement that is akin to that used in 2003, when the Committee referred to an unwelcome decline in inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Alternative B does take a step in that direction.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The bracketed language in alternative A goes further by specifying a medium-term Committee inflation target.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This is a big step, and one that deserves thorough debate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There are theoretical papers demonstrating the potential benefits in a liquidity trap of committing to an inflation rate after the economy recovers that is higher than we would actually want ex post because raising inflation expectations lowers real rates, thereby stimulating the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In theory, by committing to more inflation than we actually want later on, we could generate extra stimulus now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But this strategy requires a strong commitment device because the Committee will have an incentive to renege later on when the economy has recovered.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I do understand the attractions of such a strategy in theory, but I am not at all convinced that the benefits would exceed the costs in practice.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It would be enormously difficult to explain and could harm the Fed’s overall credibility as an institution.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Moreover, it is not only real rates but also nominal rates that influence housing demand, and any increase in longer-term nominal rates triggered by higher inflation expectations could adversely affect this key sector.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Let me now turn to the nonstandard policy tools that the FOMC and the Board have authorized.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I wholeheartedly support the many actions that have been taken to increase liquidity in the financial system, as well as those designed to increase credit availability and lower borrowing costs.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Going forward, I support both the purchase of agency debt and MBS by the System Open Market Account and purchases of long-term Treasury debt.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Both existing evidence and the market response we just saw to the recent announcements and comments concerning such programs suggest to me that such purchases can push longer-term borrowing rates down.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Other new programs—for example, to improve credit market functioning in A2/P2 commercial paper and in commercial and private-label residential-mortgage-backed securities—are well worthy of consideration.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Naturally, the potential benefits and costs of each new facility or program need to be assessed before adoption.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Formulating the guidance from the FOMC to the Desk regarding how these new programs should be described remains a challenge.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think a possible formulation could have the FOMC setting some objectives for levels or movements in Treasury yields or MBS spreads, but those open up thorny issues, and I think that this is something we really have to study further.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to the FOMC’s operating regime going forward, I oppose switching from a regime based on targeting of the fed funds rate to one based on a quantitative target for the monetary base, excess reserves, or the overall size of our balance sheet.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The Board or the FOMC or both, in my view, should consider the merits of each program on its own, without any presumption of PAYGO.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Most of you probably recall that PAYGO was a budget device employed by the Congress to constrain the federal deficit to a target level.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In our case, an overarching decision by the FOMC about the size of our balance sheet or the monetary base would force tradeoffs among our various programs to hit that total, similar to PAYGO.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Imagine, however, that the commercial paper market were to revive, allowing us to terminate the CPFF.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Excess reserves would decline, but that decline would have no negative effect on economic activity, so there should be no presumption that some other program should be expanded to restore the monetary base to its previous level.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Theory suggests that when the monetary base is increased by purchasing conventional SOMA assets, its expansion should have little or no effect on the behavior of banks or asset prices more generally after the zero bound has been reached.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Abstracting from expectational effects, the evidence generally supports this view.

speaker: YELLEN
text: While the quantity of money is surely linked to the price level in the very long run, most evidence suggests that variations in the base have only insignificant economic effects in the short or medium term under liquidity trap conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This makes the base an inappropriate operating instrument for monetary policy in a zero bound regime.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As Japan found during its quantitative easing program, increasing the size of the monetary base above levels needed to provide ample liquidity to the banking system had no discernible economic effects aside from those associated with communicating the Bank of Japan’s commitment to the zero interest rate policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think my views on this mirror those that you expressed in your opening comments, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to the directive, the version proposed in the current Bluebook specifies the types and amounts of mortgage-related assets that the Desk should buy and the objective of these purchases—namely, to boost activity in the mortgage and housing markets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Language of this type is consistent with the policy approach I support, in which each credit facility program and asset purchase decision is judged on its own merits, according to whether it improves the availability of credit or lowers its cost, thus stimulating the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I support this approach to drafting the directive going forward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is one way in which the Committee communicates the logic of monetary policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I think we do need to go further—as you emphasized, Mr. Chairman—in providing clear explanations to the public about the objectives of the various facilities, how they work, and why they are part of a coherent monetary policy strategy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to governance, I endorse the suggestion that you made, Mr. Chairman, about how we should proceed—that is, to work together collectively to forge and communicate a consensus view of the entire Committee to the public, while adhering to the particular responsibilities that the Board and the FOMC each have according to our governing legal document, which is the Federal Reserve Act.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I also want to thank the staff for preparing these memos.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They are very stimulating, a great discussion of a very difficult topic, and I know it was a lot of work.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I also want to agree with the Chairman that all comments in this arena are in the spirit of optimal monetary policy, which is the only way I would make any comments here at the table.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What is the best policy?

speaker: BULLARD
text: What will get the economy back on track soonest?

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is always what we are trying to think about here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The truth is that there are lots of ways that you might think about what the optimal policy is, so that is what the debate is about.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Let me begin with the first part of the memo asking for comments saying whether we should go quickly or gradually to zero.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think the most important element is somehow to switch away from nominal interest rate targeting once the target approaches zero because at that point the target just ceases to make any sense and you leave the private sector in the dark about any signals that they might be receiving about where the Committee intends inflation and monetary policy more generally to be going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: To go quickly to zero is effectively what we have already done with respect to the federal funds rate, at least in terms of the actual federal funds rate, and if I am reading the Greenbook appropriately, according to the staff Greenbook forecast, it is evidently not going to help very much going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think we did go to zero fairly quickly here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I do not find the Reifschneider–Williams paper, which I know carries some weight around here, very compelling, so let me give the brief reasons behind that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: For one thing, you are taking a model and you are extrapolating far outside the experience on which the model is based.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That might be a first pass, but that is probably not a good way to make policy, and I wouldn’t base policy on something like that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There are also important nonlinearities.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This whole debate is about nonlinearities as you get to the zero bound, and in my view, they are not taken into account appropriately in this analysis.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You have households and businesses that are going to understand very well that there is a zero bound.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It has been widely discussed for the past year.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They are going to take this into account when they are making their decisions, so you have to incorporate that into the analysis.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is a tall order—there are papers around that try to do that, and many other assumptions have to go into that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The third thing I think is important is that, in other contexts, gradualism or policy inertia is actually celebrated as an important part of a successful, optimal monetary policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Mike Woodford, in particular, has papers on optimal monetary policy inertia, and many others have worked on it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In those papers, it is all about making your actions gradual and making sure that they convey some benefit to the equilibrium that you will get.

speaker: BULLARD
text: All of a sudden, in this particular analysis, when you are facing a zero bound, that goes out the window, and I don’t think that it is taken into account appropriately in the analysis.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, it is thrown out the window exactly at a time when you might think that the inertia and the gradualism are most important, which would be in time of crisis when you want to steer the ship in a steady way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I think that we have a long way to go to understand exactly how to behave near a zero bound, and I would not make policy based on that particular analysis or the subsequent work.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But as I stated at the beginning, I think it is a moot point anyway because the effective fed funds rate is trading near zero.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Does the zero bound impose significant costs on financial institutions?

speaker: BULLARD
text: In general, to this I would say “no,” as the markets can adjust.

speaker: BULLARD
text: More important, markets should be expected to adjust to the optimal monetary policy that we set.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We are not in the business of keeping particular markets working in the particular ways that they have worked in the past.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t want to disrupt things so rapidly that we upset the apple cart.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the other hand, I think the attitude should be that, given enough time, we should expect markets to adjust appropriately.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I guess that is what I think about that issue of going quickly or not.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We talked for a minute about communication strategies.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Three were mentioned in the memo.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The first was to hold the federal funds rate at zero until specified conditions obtain.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The second one was the FOMC will act to counter inflation below target, and the third one was to accept higher inflation later.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In general, I think that the communication idea is important and valuable to think about in this situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is because it plays to the rational expectations, forward-looking aspect of the behavior of households and businesses.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My sense is that the benchmark forecasting models embodied in the Greenbook or in a prominent private-sector forecast such as Macroeconomic Advisers may understate these kinds of effects because they don’t completely incorporate the forward-looking elements probably as much as we would like.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is because it is very difficult to do.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I think that the communication thing is the right idea.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But I do not think that communicating that we intend to hold the federal funds rate at zero until specified conditions obtain will have much effect because the market already expects that we will maintain the rate at zero until conditions improve.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That strikes me as a way of saying that we have hit our constraint, we are bound by our constraint, and so we are effectively doing nothing further.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I wouldn’t want to get into that kind of message in the communication game, and the communication game is a tricky one.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If we went that route, I think deflation would develop.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The economy would become mired in a deflationary trap similar to Japan’s, which I illustrated last time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In general, my feeling is that understanding the Japanese situation as something like a steady state is more how we need to think of it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In a steady state, the markets are clearing, the expectations are consistent with outcomes, and there is no pretense of returning to the previous situation unless you eliminate that steady state or somehow shock the system out of that steady state.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In Japan the policy rate has not been above 1 percent for fourteen years.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That starts to sound to me as though the best way to think about this is that there may be multiple steady states out there, and you may be at risk that the dynamics will send you to the deflationary trap.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Our understanding about the dynamics of those—I know because I have worked on them myself—is very poor.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Exactly how they would work and how you would get coordination on one versus the other is a very difficult question.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That research is in its infancy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But the concept that you might think about the possibilities in the situation as being multiple steady states should perhaps be entertained more seriously around the table here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It is much better to say, as far as a communication strategy, that we are constrained on interest rates and therefore we are switching to something else.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think a monetary base, reserves, or some kind of quantity measure would be fine.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The reason you want to do this is that you want to remind the private sector that we control inflation and that we intend to keep inflation close to our target.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is a way to tell a story about how you are going to do that—a way to signal to the private sector.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So to get the intended effect in the minds of the private sector, you eliminate references to the federal funds target and force them to rethink their views of monetary policy and rethink what we are doing.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Of course, this has to be done in a reasonable way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It can’t be done in a willy-nilly way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, all the issues that have ever come up around this table about monetary targeting and reserves and all the difficulties with that would come up again.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But I think it is a great way to make the switch, much as Volcker did in 1979, and get the private sector to reorient to the new reality.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So, yes, it is very important to stress that we will counter inflation below target—I guess that is the second part of this question—and the idea of, well, you could say we are going to accept higher inflation later, perhaps much later.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Although being a theory guy I like that because you are playing on rational expectations, it doesn’t seem as credible to me with the private sector.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The way we are looking at it now, you would be talking far into the future, promising some more inflation—you know, in 2013 we will do 5 percent or something like that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It just seems too far away to have a lot of effect on our situation right now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Let me talk briefly about purchases of agencies and longer-term Treasuries.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In general, I think this is okay, but I do not think we should expect a lot of impact from this.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think the effect will be marginal.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I might remind the Committee that the famous Operation Twist from the 1960s was generally judged to be ineffective, and that is why I think the central banks did not, generally speaking, play games on the yield curve in the past.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I guess I would prefer agencies to the longer-term Treasuries because of the more direct correlation with the mortgage markets.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that might help our case a little in this current situation, but I wouldn’t expect a lot out of that policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Expansion of 13(3) credit backstops—I see this as likely, the way policy is going.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it is helpful in some circumstances.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would like to see us work harder, maybe much harder, on the metrics for success of these facilities and perhaps rework or discontinue facilities that may not be meeting expectations.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We saw some justification here earlier in the report by Bill Dudley, which I interpret as saying that the goal is to reduce risk premiums from what markets say they should otherwise be.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Frankly, I am not sure in all cases what the purpose of the programs is.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We have a lot of them out there.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We should be assessing, and then we should turn around and say, “This one is working.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This one is not working.” I would like to see a lot more in that direction.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I understand that we haven’t done it so far because, obviously, we are running on all cylinders.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We are fighting very hard here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But going forward, that is something we should be thinking about.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Our other nonstandard tools are useful.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Again, I think we need to reestablish with the private sector that the central bank controls the medium-term inflation rate, even in environments where the nominal interest rate is zero.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A simple way to communicate this is to start talking more about reserves, the monetary base, and the monetary aggregates.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Again, this has to be done in a reasonable way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We understand that taking out a program is going to change things, and we need to communicate that effectively.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We understand that the links between money growth and inflation may not be exactly what we would like them to be, but this is the situation we are in because our interest rate channel has turned off.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So in normal times, I would prefer to communicate in terms of interest rates, but that is not the situation that we are in right now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Let me talk a bit about the directive to the Desk.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In my opinion, the directive should be in terms of the quantity of reserves, letting the level of the federal funds rate trade as necessary— again, not unlike the Volcker situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Presumably, the federal funds rate would trade close to zero on average.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The prescription to express the directive in terms of reserve quantities has a long tradition here on the Committee.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That language was used at least through 1994, if I have it correct.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I remember when I was first in the Federal Reserve System we would talk about the degree of pressure on reserve positions, and so there is ample precedent inside the System to work this way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that would keep everything working smoothly in terms of governance.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I see no reason not to go in that direction.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The introduction of new programs that are intended to have a minimal effect on the level of reserves, as occurred before September of this year, would not interfere with the reserves objective of the Committee.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Others do interfere with that objective, and in that case they would need to be approved here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But my sense of the Committee here, though I can’t speak for everybody, is that I don’t think we would have any pushback on that, and we would keep the governance thing very clear if we did it that way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So that would be my preference.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I agree with the Chairman that we want the best policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We want to work in a cooperative manner, and I think that is one way to do it here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: When the market turmoil abates, then we should begin setting target ranges for reserves or monetary base growth.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Once the crisis is past, then we can begin setting a federal funds target again, maybe coming back with a range initially for the federal funds rate and then gradually moving back into the targeting regime, which I agree in normal times is a much better way to communicate policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Let me talk just for thirty seconds on the communication of alternative tools.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Above all, we have to communicate that we control medium-term inflation even when nominal interest rates are zero and that we intend to keep inflation near target.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is the overriding objective in this situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Otherwise, you are going to let inflation probably drift far below target, and the market will be scratching its head about, well, what are you going to do about it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take fifteen minutes for coffee and then come back and continue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Hoenig, whenever you are ready.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would like to start off also by saying how much I appreciate this.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think it is an important opportunity for us not necessarily to agree—because committees are designed to bring different views together and, one hopes, to come to consensus—but to hear one another and to feel more comfortable knowing where we are as we move from here.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I really do appreciate this opportunity.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am going to go through the questions in somewhat the order they were given, and let me begin by discussing the first two questions on policy strategy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The key issues here are how low to move the fed funds rate target and at what speed.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I agree with the view that keeping your powder dry is no argument for not going immediately to zero.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, I think that there are other good reasons for not going to zero at this time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In fact, the condition of the financial markets is a strong argument for being especially cautious at this juncture about going toward zero and about how fast if we were to choose to do that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It is clear from the studies, at least the way I read the studies that were provided—which I would also add were just excellent—that the market dysfunction in some very important markets, including the Treasury market, increases substantially as you move toward the zero bound.

speaker: HOENIG
text: At what precise level this occurs is not defined, but evidence does suggest that it is a genuine issue.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Indeed, markets are clearly showing signs of impairment in that the effective federal funds rate is trading well below the current target of 100 basis points.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It would be unfortunate if our monetary policy actions were to cause major and avoidable effects on the functioning of these markets, especially with the current fragile state of the financial system and when the benefits, as I interpret them, are not obviously significant.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I believe we can minimize the damage, so to speak, in these markets by maintaining the fed funds target above 50 basis points—I prefer 100—and by taking actions to ensure that the effective funds rate trades closer to the target over time, recognizing where we are starting from.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The way to do this, of course, is to put limits on the size of the current swaps and liquidity programs—I suppose that is, as others have said, a size limit on the balance sheet—to the point that the Desk can begin to sterilize the reserve injections of these other programs.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We are not there, I realize, but I would like to see that as the goal.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to question 3 on communication strategies, there is evidence that communications about the future policy path may have measurable effects on interest rates and other asset prices, especially in circumstances where the markets and the central bank have different views about the future policy path that need to be reconciled.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Especially in the United States, a statement about the policy path is likely to be more influential on market expectations than a statement on inflation right now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As to the statement about the policy path, it is possible to have a significant effect on longer-term rates when market views about the policy path differ significantly from our views and there is credible commitment to keep the target rate low for a very long period of time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In general, I think that it is difficult to construct a very specific statement that is credible to markets and does not unduly tie the hands of this Committee.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Consequently, if the Committee decides to adopt language about future policy actions, I would prefer more-general rather than more-specific condition statements.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would note that the more- general language we used in ’03 through ’05 appears to have been more effective than the Bank of Japan’s more-specific conditioning statements during the period of quantitative easing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As to the inflation communications, I would be opposed to a statement that suggests that inflation risks have threatened the dual mandate and that the Committee will act to mitigate this risk.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I also expect inflation to come down over the next few months, but this reflects considerable unwinding of temporary factors, as we noted elsewhere, and the risk of deflation is modest at this time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I also would be strongly opposed to a statement that suggests that we would accept higher-than-normal inflation rates in the next few years.

speaker: HOENIG
text: While such a statement might be appropriate in a deflationary environment, the U.S. economy is not yet at that point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Instead, our inflation rate has been higher than acceptable for the past five years, I believe in part because of our willingness—understandably, but still our willingness—to err on the side of accommodation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In the future, should inflation come in very low for a sustained period of time, such a statement about accepting higher inflation might have some benefit in preventing a sharp decline in inflationary expectations.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But in today’s circumstances, such a statement could lead markets again to conclude that we would respond very slowly to higher inflation pressure in the future.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think it would confuse and not actually clarify.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On nonstandard policy tools, I am okay with expanding the purchase of agency debt and mortgage-backed securities and longer-term Treasuries.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Right now, all, in my view, are government guaranteed.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, I am not in favor of direct support of private securities through backstop credit facilities or other procedures.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am of the view that we have stepped far in the direction of credit allocation and have undertaken actions that are fiscal measures and not appropriate for a central bank, even in a crisis like this.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In my opinion, the long-run costs to the economy and the Federal Reserve of engaging in credit allocation exceed the near-term benefits of supporting limited segments of the market.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There is a relative price effect.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In terms of agency and Treasury purchases, I agree that the immediate focus should be on reducing the agency spreads over comparable Treasuries.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Treasury rates have come down a good deal, but agency spreads have widened.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Normally, private yields move with the Treasury rates, as we know.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, the current crisis has largely broken the usual connection.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Therefore, I don’t think that actions to lower Treasury rates further will have much effect on other rates, and I would concentrate more on bringing other rates down.

speaker: HOENIG
text: However, in the coming months, as the economy begins to recover, Treasury rates will likely come under upward pressure.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To the extent that markets begin to incorporate a view of the policy path that differs from ours, I think we might want to consider purchases, as discussed here, of longer-term Treasuries at that time or perhaps altering our communication strategy then.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the form of the directives, I would generally favor quantitative targets for Desk purchases.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Although it will be somewhat difficult for this Committee to determine appropriate quantitative targets, I don’t think we want to move in the direction of specifying targets for interest rates or spreads for these other instruments because the exit strategy for these approaches could be very disruptive for the financial markets.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In terms of communicating our use of nonstandard tools, if we go that way, I think that the more we say, the better for everyone.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It is important to articulate the range of options under discussion; and when they are announced, it is important to discuss not only how they will be implemented but also how they would be expected to help in achieving our objectives.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Right now confidence is quite fragile, as we all know, and so it is important that we send positive and constructive messages and not unduly surprise the markets with our actions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Two other issues not directly related: As we talk about our policies going forward, I think we really do need to spend a little more time talking about what it means in terms of the deleveraging process that is going on.

speaker: HOENIG
text: People talk about it freely, but I don’t think it is clear in anyone’s mind and would perhaps affect our actions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Also we need to talk about the potential effects of the fiscal policies that will be unveiled soon.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I add my thanks to the staff for the excellent summaries, particularly those that covered the Japanese experience.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My reading of that experience argues for acting aggressively and moving directly to whatever lower bound we consider the effective minimum.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The economic outlook has deteriorated sharply, and as I look at the incoming data and our near-term forecasts, I find it reasonable to expect that we will see more troubling data by the time of our January meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I concur with the Greenbook assessment that the outlook calls for a cumulative reduction of 75 basis points over the next two meetings.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: At the risk of jumping ahead a little, my preference is to get there at this meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: If there is an argument for a more gradual two-step approach, it is that more communication is needed to explain the Committee’s strategy and condition the markets for a zero lower bound policy regime.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I was on the receiving end of this argument at my Atlanta board meeting last week—which Don Kohn witnessed as a guest—at which some directors strongly resisted moving to the lower bound without, in their view, a clearly articulated statement about how policy will operate going forward.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Mr. Chairman, in your speech two weeks ago you made a good effort to prepare the public for the possibility that the Committee may soon have to operate with policy targets that are unfamiliar.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But it strikes me that there is a chicken–egg problem of when it is appropriate to lay out the new approach.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Again, I read the Japanese lesson as move aggressively but at the same time communicate very clearly the whys and hows of the policy course.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: President Plosser pointed out in his memo circulated last week—and I believe President Lacker noted last meeting—that we have at least implicitly entered into a quantitative easing regime already.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The fed funds rate has been trading for some weeks near the level that we are likely to find as the lower bound.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think we must move to a decision at this meeting on communication strategy, independent of whether or not we move to the lower bound in one step.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I don’t see that this need is significantly reduced by delaying the move to the lower bound, especially if that destination is inevitable, as I believe it to be.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On the question of costs of the zero lower bound policy to markets and financial institutions, in my reading of the analysis and the background memos taken as a whole, maintaining the effective funds rate at a level somewhere near 25 basis points may help avoid problems in some markets that would otherwise arrive at zero.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think we have to be concerned that at absolute zero the infrastructure of some markets might atrophy as market participants shift resources in the direction of operations where profits are more attainable.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: These concerns might argue for stating the federal funds rate target in terms of a range, and I would support a lower bound in the range of 0 to 25 basis points.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As regards communication strategies, to state the obvious, financial market participants would prefer to know as much as possible about the level of rates in a zero lower bound regime, the duration of adherence to that policy, and when and on what basis the policy will change.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The Committee can’t fully satisfy those needs, but we can provide assurances that equip market participants with a clear framework for planning and anticipating change of policy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think it is important to communicate that we intend to stay the course with this policy until some combination of materially improved conditions obtain in both financial markets and the general economy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That is to say, we should indicate that the policy is not short-term shock treatment to be quickly reversed, unless, of course, conditions dictate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As regards indicating specific conditions that would inform a change of policy or a change of course, I favor an approach that addresses conditionality in general terms using language such as “the Committee intends to hold the federal funds rate target at this level until such time that it judges conditions are present for material and sustained improvements in financial market functioning and economic growth.” I prefer to reference general economic conditions rather than to use phrases like “near zero for some time” as in Bluebook alternative B.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Further, I think it is appropriate to reinforce that our policy will be calibrated based on our longer-term inflation objectives.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am not comfortable with formal statements indicating that the Committee is willing to accept higher rates of inflation than it normally would find desirable.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my view, the goal is to avoid entrenching expectations that deviate too much from our explicit or implicit price stability objectives in both inflationary and deflationary directions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think this goal is best pursued by stating our commitment to medium-term price stability.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This statement can be in general terms, but I would also support the more explicit numerical reference in Bluebook alternative A.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As regards more purchases of agency debt, agency MBS, and long-dated Treasuries, my view is that open market operations should be conducted in the manner that enhances overall market liquidity in the most efficient and least disruptive way.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This may well be by purchases of agency debt and MBS beyond the level announced.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, to the extent that enhancing overall market liquidity requires efforts to directly manipulate prices in particular markets beyond the federal funds market, I think we may be better served by developing specifically targeted facilities to do so.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As regards the further expansion of liquidity facilities, to date we have attacked dysfunctional market conditions in the interbank funding market, the Treasuries market, the commercial paper market, the mortgage market, and, shortly, the asset-backed securities market.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The more we migrate with these facilities in the direction of general corporate debt and other nonfinancial issuers’ markets, the more our policy actions involve contentious issues of moral hazard, possible distortion of the necessary process of relative price discovery, and the appropriate division of labor between the central bank and the Treasury.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think that we just need to keep this in mind as new facilities are considered.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The extension and broadening of existing facilities, and possibly new facilities, may be necessary.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I judge that the broad policy of targeted facilities has been successful to date.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding nonstandard tools, I find myself in agreement with the thrust of President Plosser’s suggestions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In a quantitative easing regime, it makes most sense to express our directive in terms of a quantitative target.

speaker: LOCKHART
