text: And as regards your comments earlier, Mr. Chairman, I tend to look at this target question as a tradeoff between targeting quantities versus prices or rates, and I believe that the quantitative target approach is the correct approach, even if we decide to operate with the common understanding that our short-term objective is, for example, to generate a particular path for long-term Treasuries or agency debt.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Based on my reading of the literature and history as well as on my own experience, I have doubts about our capacity to reliably control specific relative asset prices, at least in markets unlike the federal funds market, where we are the monopoly supplier of the asset being traded.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But that does not preclude setting quantitative targets for the purchase of particular assets and evaluating the appropriateness of those targets against a variety of outcomes, including the interest rates that emerge in those markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am, however, predisposed toward the line of thinking expressed by President Lacker in his pre-meeting memo.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: By choosing to express the directive in terms of the monetary base or some measure of reserves, the decisions of the Committee remain in the range of traditional monetary policy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My conjecture is that a reserve base quantitative directive would help to draw a clear line between traditional monetary policy decisions in the purview of the FOMC and the enhanced credit policies implemented under 13(3) authority.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Let me move to the communication approaches.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Again, internalizing the Japanese experience, we will be well served by a significant and coordinated communication effort.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Our press statement might be supplemented by an additional explanation of whatever new operational procedures we adopt, followed by a public statement, perhaps even a press conference, by the Chairman.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Throughout this crisis, we have been provided excellent support in the form of talking points.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: These have been a great help to me and my staff in providing accurate and timely information on the various policy actions taken by the Federal Reserve.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: With similar assistance in this case, I think we can collectively commit to providing the sort of common voice on the facts that will promote public understanding of the direction in which we decide to head.

speaker: EVANS
text: I, too, would like to add my thanks to the staff for an excellent set of memos—very good analysis.

speaker: EVANS
text: I would agree with pretty much everyone that the economic outlook and financial stress warrant further relief for financial conditions, so I am going to be supporting, ultimately, further quantitative easing as needed.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have to admit that I am not quite sure what the most effective form of that easing is.

speaker: EVANS
text: It just doesn’t seem obvious to me.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I certainly embrace your suggestion, Mr. Chairman, of continuing the regular briefings, and when necessary, those should be meetings to affirm certain programs that are on the table.

speaker: EVANS
text: I agree with all of your comments about how important confidence is.

speaker: EVANS
text: Let me turn to some of the specifics of the questions about the standard policy issues with the fed funds target.

speaker: EVANS
text: With a deep recession looming and inflation receding, I see no reason to keep our fed funds powder dry.

speaker: EVANS
text: There is no reasonable uncertainty at this point about the deepness of the recession or the financial stress, and I think the economy would benefit from further financial accommodation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Because we can’t really hit our fed funds target because of the breadth of our lending programs that are on our balance sheet today, I think the damage to the Treasury repo and money market mutual funds is unavoidable at this point.

speaker: EVANS
text: For our policy actions, I think that we should continue to communicate in terms of our objectives.

speaker: EVANS
text: In my opinion, this strategy covers most of the issues asked of us.

speaker: EVANS
text: The fed funds rate will be low for some time under our forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t think there is much doubt about that, and our forecast helped with that.

speaker: EVANS
text: Disinflation risks are part of this outlook, and I think that should be well understood.

speaker: EVANS
text: We can communicate that in our speaking.

speaker: EVANS
text: If our inflation target were explicit and we talked about it more—higher future inflation expectations than just, if it were the case, ½ percent or lower—that would be part of the communication calculus.

speaker: EVANS
text: As things stand, our long-term projections may be adequate here, but more explicitness in general would be helpful.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is interesting to me that alternative A encompasses all of these in relatively muted language.

speaker: EVANS
text: Frankly, if we are expecting a big impact from that statement, I think we need to include a bold font typeface, [laughter] because I don’t think it will be picked up necessarily.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I think it is really well done.

speaker: EVANS
text: In terms of the questions on particular interventions, the memos brought forward pretty clearly that the effect of the interventions depends on the size of the operations and where the markets are.

speaker: EVANS
text: The memos were very good about talking about individual markets and making me aware of a number of details, but they were often pretty much in isolation of how they would flow through to other markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is not exactly clear to me how important that segmentation or separation is to achieve the goals that we are hoping for from those interventions.

speaker: EVANS
text: I suppose in well-functioning markets you might expect more of those funds to be flowing across those markets, and so you would be generally providing market liquidity.

speaker: EVANS
text: In the current situation, with more stress, there probably is more separation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is that ultimately going to mean we are more effective?

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not even sure because there is the added stress that has to be dealt with.

speaker: EVANS
text: So the particular interventions are not exactly obvious to me, and portfolio rebalancing could have implications.

speaker: EVANS
text: In one of them, there was a correlation matrix—for a particular size of operation, where agencies are influenced in one way or Treasuries are influenced—about when we would see other prices move around.

speaker: EVANS
text: That is possibly a guide to this leakage.

speaker: EVANS
text: But, of course, those are unconditional correlations, as I understood them, and I am not exactly sure how the exogenous interventions that we are talking about would translate from those correlations.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is really an identification problem at some level.

speaker: EVANS
text: My takeaway from that is that I find most comforting the quantitative easing additions that improve total market liquidity.

speaker: EVANS
text: It seems to me that the Treasury and agency purchases are the safest.

speaker: EVANS
text: When we get into credit allocation, we have these facilities in place, and we will probably need to do more.

speaker: EVANS
text: Mr. Chairman, you talked about the unwinding consequences that the Committee will have to worry about, and I think that they are also pretty important.

speaker: EVANS
text: Last, on the nonstandard approaches for quantitative easing and what that means for the Desk, I guess this is a harder problem with the dual governance issues than I had really anticipated.

speaker: EVANS
text: I would have thought that it was relatively straightforward—once we hit the zero bound on the funds rate that we would identify that we need to expand the balance sheet.

speaker: EVANS
text: I kind of like it in terms of the asset side.

speaker: EVANS
text: The Committee could authorize a broad range of what that would mean.

speaker: EVANS
text: We could reaffirm the existing lending programs—not approve them, for that is the role of the Board—and point to the important role that they are playing.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our statement could provide guidance on the sizes, which would pretty much just be a restatement of the existing sizes of the programs.

speaker: EVANS
text: But we could provide ranges of how the Committee might expect that to be conducted over the intermeeting period if something arose that required an addition, or we were being briefed on new programs as they were rolled out, that could be part of it.

speaker: EVANS
text: All of that said, I accept your good faith approach—the more we talk and the more that we understand this and are consulted, it should be adequate.

speaker: EVANS
text: In terms of communicating to the public, under the approach that I just mentioned we would basically state that the fed funds target is essentially zero because of all of the lending facilities.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’d have some statement about the range of the balance sheet, something that is not supposed to be so constraining but that would be somewhat helpful.

speaker: EVANS
text: The descriptions of the Fed lending programs would be part of that—they are well done—and the term sheets, and we would reinforce our commitment to the policy mandates that we have in our statements and our forecasts.

speaker: EVANS
text: So, just to conclude, I think we can go further down the quantitative easing policy path.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not really convinced that this is going to do everything that we are hoping, and I am a little concerned as we get to the point where we have an intense desire to effect more that we might tend to disagree a little more.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I am confident that we will think it through very carefully.

speaker: KOHN
text: I want to join the others in thanking the staff for their work.

speaker: KOHN
text: These are very difficult issues, and I think you have brought to bear a lot of what little information we have on these subjects and have kind of kept me out of trouble for the last week.

speaker: KOHN
text: My wife thanks you as well.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the questions in the first set are largely moot, as a number of people have said.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are already close to the zero bound, and because I think moving there aggressively under the current circumstances is the right thing to do, I don’t have any regrets about that.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like President Yellen, I came into this situation, at least a couple of months ago, wondering why zero wasn’t the right lower bound.

speaker: KOHN
text: I recognize the market issues that might obtain—sort of as President Bullard said, I wonder whether markets won’t adjust as we go on—but so close to zero, the difference between 6½ basis points and zero isn’t going to matter very much.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think we ought to keep our eye on how markets are functioning, whether they adjust, and where we should be.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, once we are at a minimum—and I think we ought to get wherever we are going at this meeting, as soon as possible (a number of people have said that, and I agree)—we can’t influence actual expected short-term rates with our actions.

speaker: KOHN
text: We do need to rely on other methods to change relative asset prices—longer-term rates relative to short-term rates, private rates relative to government rates, nominal rates relative to expected inflation—and that is where the communications and the size and the composition of the asset portfolio come in.

speaker: KOHN
text: Both the communications and the portfolio actions can be effective and influential, but I think we need to recognize that we are losing our most powerful policy instrument.

speaker: KOHN
text: The effects of these other aspects of our policies are uncertain, and it will require some trial and error to figure out where we are going.

speaker: KOHN
text: With respect to communications, I do think it would be useful to tell people the conditions under which we expect to keep rates low and the conditions under which we would be prepared to raise interest rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we can tell them if we think it is going to be soon or if it is going to take some time.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I agree with your point at the beginning, Mr. Chairman—and President Plosser and others said this—we should emphasize the conditions rather than the time period.

speaker: KOHN
text: We shouldn’t commit to a time path.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think something like this should help long-term nominal rates better reflect our expectations for the path of policy and could be especially important if markets come to anticipate a firming before we actually anticipate firming.

speaker: KOHN
text: It could come into play, particularly in the context of some massive fiscal stimulus, which seems to be coming.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think we want the effects of that fiscal stimulus diminished or crowded out by increases in long-term rates that are based on a false assumption about the effect of the fiscal stimulus on monetary policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think being clear about where we want inflation to be over the long run will probably help anchor inflation expectations a bit better—keep them from drifting down when inflation itself is very low and keep real interest rates from rising—and thereby reduce the odds of persistent deflation taking hold.

speaker: KOHN
text: We will have an important opportunity to take a step in that direction if we agree to our longer-term forecasts in January.

speaker: KOHN
text: As President Yellen noted, the Subcommittee on Communications is recommending that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think voting on an inflation target would be a substantially bigger step.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is, we would have to reach agreement on that.

speaker: KOHN
text: It could be a more powerful signal of our intentions, and it might become necessary.

speaker: KOHN
text: I certainly think we ought to discuss it.

speaker: KOHN
text: It has a lot of implications that we need to look at, including where we will be in a couple of years.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we need to be careful.

speaker: KOHN
text: A number of people—outside commentators, anyhow—have noted that they thought that we kept our eye too much on macro variables in the low inflation period and that gave rise to these asset-price increases.

speaker: KOHN
text: I disagree, but I think it is an open question.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have seen comments from other members of the FOMC wondering whether we should look at more than just the path for consumer prices when we are setting monetary policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: But let’s not do something now without thinking about how it is going to play five or ten years down the road.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also agree with your point, Mr. Chairman, about congressional consultation.

speaker: KOHN
text: Having an inflation target won’t have any effect if it is repudiated by the Congress.

speaker: KOHN
text: As soon as we make it, it could have a negative effect.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think changes in the size and composition of our portfolio can affect relative asset prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: I guess I think, President Evans, that changes are more likely to be effective at times like these, when markets are illiquid and participants have very, very strong preferences for one sector or another.

speaker: KOHN
text: When private parties seem unwilling to lend to each other, substituting Federal Reserve credit for private credit can be quite effective.

speaker: KOHN
text: Carefully designed programs can reduce the cost of credit and increase the availability of capital to households and businesses.

speaker: KOHN
text: I see where we are as a natural extension of where we have been.

speaker: KOHN
text: Really since August 2007, we have been using our balance sheet to try to stimulate credit markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: At first we sterilized that by selling Treasury securities.

speaker: KOHN
text: Then we sterilized it by the Treasury selling Treasury securities.

speaker: KOHN
text: Then that program ran out, and we thought we could sterilize it by interest on excess reserves, and it didn’t work.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I don’t think we have crossed a sudden barrier in the last month or two.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is true that the base has begun to rise because we have run out of the other sterilization options.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I do think it is a natural extension of where we have been for a while.

speaker: KOHN
text: That brings me to the monetary base.

speaker: KOHN
text: I find myself more skeptical about the effect of increases in the monetary base per se than what I hear around the room.

speaker: KOHN
text: Such increases I think are supposed to affect asset prices by inducing banks to substitute into higher-yielding assets.

speaker: KOHN
text: Give them a bunch of reserves, and they substitute into higher-yielding assets like loans.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I wonder how effective that is when short-term rates don’t decline with the increase in the base because we are pinned at zero—that is, we are in a liquidity trap—and when banks are reluctant to expand portfolios because they are concerned about capital and their leverage ratio.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I don’t really understand the channels through which an increase in the monetary base, under these circumstances, is supposed to affect economic activity.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have seen a huge increase in the base over the last couple of months and no effect on the money supply.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, that is very short term, I agree.

speaker: KOHN
text: Your observation, Mr. Chairman, was that we saw a big increase in the base in Japan.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with President Lacker that they weren’t as dedicated to that as they might have been, but I just don’t see any evidence that the base isn’t going to be absorbed in a declining money multiplier rather than an expanding money supply and increased activity.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t understand the channels.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the base, as we are setting this out, is determined by the people who use our credit facilities.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that is very important, and I don’t want to upset that.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I would be very, very hesitant to restructure the directive in terms of the quantity of reserves or the monetary base.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would have to understand much better what that means, and I wouldn’t want to constrain the use of liquidity facilities with such a restraint.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the situation in the 1970s and early 1980s was very different.

speaker: KOHN
text: First of all, the October 6, 1979, meeting that went to monetary targeting was a natural evolution of a lot of work that had relied more and more on the money supply as a way of communicating about policy over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: Second, it was about constraining inflation, holding it down.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do agree, Jeff, that “too much money chasing too few goods” is something that people kind of understand.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am not sure that they understand the opposite—too little money chasing too many goods, or whatever, as a cause for deflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it would be very, very difficult to communicate what that meant and how that was supposed to work.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it is a very different situation than we had back then.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think we can help by increasing and directing our asset expansion in particular directions.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have seen evidence, as Bill showed us in the MBS and GSE purchases and the commercial paper facility.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also I favor the consideration of purchases of long-term Treasury bonds.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that will help to lower longer-term rates in an environment of large liquidity and term premiums.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would consider expanding our purchases of MBS and GSE debt, if it looks as though they might help bring down mortgage rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with others who have said that they would be very reluctant to specify such operations with a rate target because I don’t think we can really control that.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think that talking about quantities would be much better, as we have done with the MBS.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would also continue to look for other ways to use our discount window to help restart credit markets or substitute for private markets in which the functioning is impaired, and I would be open to a variety of possibilities.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that credit allocation is very uncomfortable for the central bank.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have been into that for a while.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wish we didn’t have to be there.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I don’t see any evidence that the private sector is going to start lending anytime soon on its own.

speaker: KOHN
text: If I saw that some of those other markets with which we weren’t involved and weren’t likely to get involved—like the junk bond market that Bill showed us in that chart—were beginning to open up without our help, that would be fine.

speaker: KOHN
text: But nothing is happening out there in the markets that we are not touching.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think that is only because everybody is waiting for us to intervene in those particular markets, because there are a bunch of them that they know we can’t or won’t intervene in.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we need to remain open to possible further credit market interventions.

speaker: KOHN
text: This raises very difficult governance issues.

speaker: KOHN
text: Our inability to sterilize and the huge increase in our balance sheet raise very difficult questions about how the Board and the Reserve Banks together carry out their shared responsibility for achieving the objectives of the Federal Reserve Act.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is not so much about legalities as it is about how to reach the best decisions and how best to explain those decisions to the world at large.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have always worked in a collaborative and cooperative way, and I think we need to continue to do that.

speaker: KOHN
text: Crisis management strains the normal collaborative and deliberative mode of Federal Reserve operations.

speaker: KOHN
text: Decisions get made on short notice, often over a weekend, but as you said, Mr. Chairman, we can work at improving our collaboration.

speaker: KOHN
text: The FOMC, as a body, will continue to have the major influence on our communications about the outlook, the likely path of rates, and the acceptability of the inflation outcome.

speaker: KOHN
text: The key elements in our communications have always been and will remain under the control of this group, and that is a large part of what we will be doing.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that we should, when consistent with fulfilling our obligations to protect financial stability, consult more and earlier on liquidity facilities.

speaker: KOHN
text: I hope that we can emerge from this discussion and subsequent ones with an agreed-upon framework for what we are doing and what motivates it under these unusual circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we—the Federal Reserve System, the FOMC, all of us—should consider issuing an explanatory document on these matters that we can all agree to.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wrote this before this meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now that I have heard the meeting, I am not sure it is possible.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think it might be worth the effort.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are you in charge of drafting it?

speaker: STERN
text: Let me make some comments, first about nonstandard policies, then about communication, and finally a bit about the balance sheet, governance, and so forth.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to the nonstandard policies, Bill Dudley’s charts 24 and 25 showing the spreads narrowing with intervention and spreads tending to widen elsewhere seem to make a pretty compelling starting point at least, not only for the value of the programs in place but perhaps for considering additional ones.

speaker: STERN
text: I guess I am kind of wary about that at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: A sentence in one of the staff papers that pertains to this—let me also compliment the staff for the quality and the volume of what they have produced here—caught my attention: “It is difficult to provide specific recommendations for further intervention at this time, in part because facilities that are most obviously valuable to address current conditions have already been put in place or are in train.” That is one concern I have—that we may be heading toward diminishing returns.

speaker: STERN
text: In addition, as I think somebody has already observed, there is a possibility that, if we carry this too far, we interfere with what would otherwise be normal and healthy market adjustments.

speaker: STERN
text: Some of that is going to have to work its way through.

speaker: STERN
text: Finally, one thing from the Japanese experience is the so-called preservation of zombies, which, whatever you might say about its short-run value, clearly wasn’t of value to the long-run health of the economy.

speaker: STERN
text: So my preference as far as nonstandard tools would be to emphasize purchases of longer-term Treasuries and of GSEs and mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: STERN
text: At least at this point, that is where I would want to put my emphasis.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to communication, as I think President Evans said, reiterating our longer-run objectives, indicating—given conditions as we perceive and expect them—that the funds rate is likely to remain low for a considerable period of time or, alternatively, that reserve provision is going to remain generous, however we want to say it, is acceptable.

speaker: STERN
text: There could be some value, if we can get there, in specifying an inflation target, and certainly the effort to provide longer- term steady-state forecasts will work in that direction.

speaker: STERN
text: I think we need to be a little careful, though, as Governor Kohn suggested, to think through a variety of issues that are associated with this.

speaker: STERN
text: I can even imagine that, even if we were to agree on an inflation target and even if the Congress had no objection, it might be a bit of a distraction at this point and there could be a lot of debate external to the System whether it is the right target and why or why not, and so on and so forth.

speaker: STERN
text: Of course, that is not our principal concern at the moment.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to the balance sheet and governance issues, I certainly can get comfortable with the consultative, collaborative approach you described.

speaker: STERN
text: There might be some value from a credibility point of view—I put this more as a question than a conclusion—in trying to specify some numerical range for the base, reserves, or something in that the public could monitor whether in fact we are doing what we say we are doing.

speaker: STERN
text: To the extent that we are concerned about the possibility of excessive disinflation or of deflation, this would be a way for the public not only to take our word for it but also to monitor that in fact we were conducting policy in a way consistent with that.

speaker: STERN
text: President Lacker, in his discussion, indicated that emphasizing the base was a way to emphasize, at least in the longer run, that we weren’t intending to let inflation get too low.

speaker: STERN
text: I put this as a question—this could be a way of helping credibility because the public could monitor it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would also like to join the chorus of people thanking the staff, in particular the staff members who were working on the memos on Japan.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Having done some work on Japan myself, I know that getting the institutional details right is far from easy, particularly when you are not a native speaker.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I much appreciated the work in that area.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The probability of a severe economic downturn accompanied by deflation is too high, and the effective fed funds rate is already very close to zero.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This combination calls for aggressive, nontraditional policies.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My reading of the parallel Japanese experience highlights two general principles.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The first is one that President Stern highlighted.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There is a macroeconomic impact from what we do in bank supervision.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Banking problems should be addressed expeditiously, with realistic write-downs of problem assets and recapitalization of problem banks.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In particular, we should prevent perverse incentives where problem borrowers are supported while healthier borrowers are starved for credit as banks try to satisfy balance sheet constraints and avoid further loss recognition.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, monetary and macroeconomic policies to address financial dislocations should be proactive and forceful rather than released gradually over an extended period of time.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In the context of the questions that we have been asked to address, I’d like to encourage us to take three actions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, I would explicitly state that the Committee seeks to achieve a core PCE inflation rate of 2 percent in the medium term.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: For the second time this decade we are approaching the zero nominal interest rate bound.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Setting too low an inflation target threatens to place us in our current predicament too often.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In contrast, by setting an explicit target at 2 percent, we will indicate our resolve to take nontraditional policies necessary to achieve that goal.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Because the inflation target adopted under the current circumstances would be designed to raise inflation expectations and stimulate the economy, this may be a particularly propitious time to adopt such an explicit target.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A 2 percent target would also be consistent with our own revealed preference as the core PCE inflation rate has averaged 1.94 percent, very close to 2 percent, over the past ten years.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, during the past recession, 30-year conventional mortgage rates reached 5¼ percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The current rate has been hovering at 5½ percent and has reached that level only since we announced our program to purchase $600 billion in GSE debt and mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The housing sector remains the epicenter of our problems.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given the current outlook, I would suggest using facilities to move toward an interest rate target, for example, by reducing by 100 basis points from current levels the conventional 30-year mortgage rate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Lowering the 30-year conventional mortgage rate would reduce the cost of purchasing new homes, encourage refinancing by those with sufficiently high credit scores and equity in their homes, and support fiscal policies that are targeted at more-troubled homebuyers.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It would help troubled and healthy homeowners, stimulate the most distressed area of our economy, and help financial institutions exposed to problems in housing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Such a target would be understandable to the general public, and actions already taken have made some progress in this area and serve as an example.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would focus on the mortgage rates rather than the Treasury yield curve because lower Treasury rates seem to be having little effect on rates paid by households and businesses, and the desire to avoid credit risk has already brought 10-year Treasury rates to lows not seen in most recent recessions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Third, our facilities for short-term credit have been successful.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Short-term commercial paper rates have fallen as a result of our programs, as was highlighted by Bill Dudley, and the rollover risk at the end of the year has been mitigated by the commercial paper program.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Increasingly, however, I have been hearing complaints about banks pulling lines of credit when they are up for renewal primarily because the banks are facing balance sheet issues.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: One possible remedy might be to extend our commercial paper facility to highly rated firms for longer maturities than are covered by the commercial paper market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: All three suggestions would be easily communicated and understood by the public, would address directly the areas of the economy in which financing has become particularly difficult, and would highlight our resolve to avoid a deflationary economy, such as Japan experienced for over a decade.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would just end with the note that I agree with the Governor Kohn on the monetary base for two reasons.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The first is that I do not think our facilities have been particularly well designed to set a quantitative target.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Many of the facilities are open ended.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Go through the following thought experiment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Suppose a money market fund once again breaks the buck.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The AMLF will probably go up $150 billion or $200 billion.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would expect the commercial paper facility to go up.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would expect that most of the bank facilities would also go up.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we were limited by a quantitative target at the very time that we actually want those facilities to be expanding, we would be constrained.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I do not think that is a good idea in the current situation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The second reason comes from my reading of what happened in Japan, and this goes to some of the remarks that the Chairman made.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The monetary base in Japan did expand very rapidly.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: When banks are capital constrained, expanding reserves very rapidly does not translate into an expansion of the broader balance sheet.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So we could very easily see a situation in the United States in which banks continue to be capital constrained for some time.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Despite increasing the monetary base, we might not see an expansion in terms of other assets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That is exactly why I agree with the Chairman that we should be focused on the asset, not the liability, side of the balance sheet.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also want to start by thanking the staff for the excellent background materials they provided.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: While I certainly wish we were not in this circumstance, I do think that this is a critical conversation for us to be having at this meeting, and the background materials were extremely helpful.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am going to proceed directly to the questions that Brian provided as I believe they cover the major issues well.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I have some general answers to the questions, but I think that we are going to be learning a lot in the process of implementing policies into ever more uncharted waters.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: On the question of whether the Committee should quickly move the target fed funds rate toward the zero bound or get there more gradually, I strongly support moving quickly.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I agree with the memos that the Japanese experience points to the value of moving aggressively.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Also, we have already moved beyond the targeted fed funds rate as many have commented, and so we are merely confirming a reality.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: On the questions pertaining to the costs to financial markets or institutions and the limits to our rate reduction, I think the notes covered very well the costs to some money market funds.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Bankers in my District have also expressed concerns about additional margin squeezing that they will face with a lower fed funds rate.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So, yes, there are significant costs to financial markets and institutions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, I believe that the current environment and our need to allow the fed funds rate to trade close to zero trumps these costs, and in my view a 25 basis point fed funds rate is an appropriate minimum.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Regarding the question about the communication strategy, I think another lesson that we have learned from the Japanese experience is the role of effective communication and the role of anchoring inflation expectations.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I do see the benefit in communicating that the Federal Reserve intends to hold the target fed funds rate at a very low level until specified conditions are obtained, and that the Committee sees a sizable risk that inflation in the coming quarters could be appreciably lower than is consistent with price stability.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also see that there may be some value to communicating that our policies might result in a temporarily higher inflation rate in the future, both to indicate this possibility and to signal a willingness to make sure that the risk of deflation dissipates before we alter our course.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Although we have not adopted a formal inflation target, I do believe that the release of our longer-term projections as suggested by the Subcommittee on Communications will be helpful in managing inflation expectations.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Moving to questions 4 and 5 regarding nonstandard policy tools, my own preference is for a mixed strategy—that is, some direct Treasury and agency purchases and some expansion of our private asset purchases using the TALF.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I support your view, Mr. Chairman, that we should keep our focus on expanding the asset side of our balance sheet.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think we should consider increasing the purchase of agency debt and mortgage-backed securities beyond the levels that we have already announced.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also see advantages in initiating large-scale purchases of longer-term Treasury securities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: These actions should help to lower interest rates across a broad spectrum of longer-term assets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As we have talked about, direct purchases also fit more naturally into the FOMC’s governance structure, whereas the TALF-like approach is more awkward to fit into the FOMC’s purview.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As some have commented, direct purchases might expose our System Open Market Account to some capital losses, but that seems an acceptable risk for monetary policy in such a challenging environment.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do think that the focus of our FOMC meetings next year should be on evaluating and adjusting the composition and size of our purchase of securities in response to changing economic conditions so that the directive need not build in explicit conditioning on market and economic circumstances.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Further expansion of our credit backstop facilities under section 13(3) is also likely to be beneficial in current circumstances.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think the CPFF has been a helpful addition to our facilities, and I am hopeful that the TALF will be equally effective.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So, in summary, I favor applying all of these approaches and remaining flexible.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also believe that a clear starting point on how the Committee would formulate its directive would be to direct the Desk to purchase specific quantities of assets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As a formal matter, we might need to include “up to” in our directive language, but we should anticipate that the Desk would be successful in meeting that objective.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think that the uncertainty surrounding the effects of our actions makes longer-term interest rates or spreads too unreliable to be communicated as targets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Finally, on the question of effectively communicating nonstandard policy tools, I liked the language in some of the Bluebook alternatives for our policy options.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, because of the historic nature of implementing nonstandard policy tools, I think that a good communication plan should also include a formal press conference or a speech in which, Mr. Chairman, you announce the changes.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: That would serve to emphasize the change in our procedure and eliminate some of the uncertainties about the role of the fed funds rate target.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Again, I’d also like to thank the staff for the excellent notes.

speaker: CUMMING
text: It’s useful to start out with our near-term goals, as most of us have done, to provide stimulus and support for the economic recovery and to prevent too large a fall in inflation.

speaker: CUMMING
text: The root problems, I think, are worth focusing on for a second: insufficient global demand, hurdles to economic activity from a severely impaired financial system, and as I’ll report tomorrow, behavior that is influenced by confusion and fear among businesses and households that are tending to reinforce the downward trend of the economy.

speaker: CUMMING
text: That environment, I think, gives us some goalposts to look for in terms of framing the strategy.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I find very appealing Marvin Goodfriend’s characterization of the duality of the central bank’s policy.

speaker: CUMMING
text: We have a monetary and what he calls a credit policy at the same time.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In normal times setting the fed funds rate influences financial conditions, especially credit markets, in a fairly predictable manner, and this Committee from time to time has discussed where overnight rates and financial conditions have diverged.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In these times, we’re observing a major disconnect between overnight rates and financial conditions that is reflected in huge spreads but also in a lack of transactions and in nonprice rationing in markets.

speaker: CUMMING
text: So coming back to the question of what some of our goals are: To address the problems that we see, communication is really the essential element, and we should be aiming for maximum impact in whatever actions we take and also in our communications.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I think, therefore, that we should bring rates down now as far as we think we can take them.

speaker: CUMMING
text: But the more important decision is articulating what we are going to do going forward, why we are doing it, how long we are planning to do it, and under what conditions we would stop doing it.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Some of the confusion that is out there about what the Federal Reserve has been doing reflects the fact that our operations really cover two very different kinds of things.

speaker: CUMMING
text: On one side we are expanding liquidity and supporting the recovery of financial markets by the CPFF, the MBS purchases, and the upcoming TALF.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In other facilities we are preventing catastrophic market outcomes through asset disposition, such as the Bear Stearns transaction, AIG, and the recent transaction we’ve had with Citi.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In addition, there are a lot of technicalities and legalities to these facilities that make it hard for the general public to understand what we are doing.

speaker: CUMMING
text: So more fundamentally we need to communicate what we want to accomplish, and that importantly involves our commitment to price stability, as many have said here in the sense of keeping prices in the medium term rising in line with our 1½ to 2 percent preference, and our commitment to a resumption of sustainable economic activity.

speaker: CUMMING
text: When I turn to look at what kind of facilities we should be thinking about going forward, once interest rates are down to their minimum level, there are really a few things that I would highlight.

speaker: CUMMING
text: First, in many ways we could influence expectations about short-term policy rates through our long-term debt purchases, as many have said.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In particular, when we try to lean against expectations expressed in the yield curve that rates are going to rise soon, and we’re seeing some of that today, we can intervene in markets that directly affect major elements of aggregate demand, and I would see that as a very important role of our agency MBS program and also the CPFF to address where firms are really being starved of working capital.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Because of its structure, the TALF provides a very broad umbrella under which we could do intervention, again, where we see credit markets failing and economic activity impeded by the lack of finance of a wide variety.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I think that we should look at the CPFF and the TALF more as backstop facilities that provide the credit we need but also build in a kind of exit strategy so that, when spreads come down, there is an opportunity for the market basically to tell us, “You can wind this down now.” We need to communicate the criteria by which we are choosing these markets.

speaker: CUMMING
text: We have mentioned these three big market segments.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I think simpler is much better than having something that’s very complicated or having many, many facilities.

speaker: CUMMING
text: As part of this, the crucial thing is to provide to the marketplace some kind of conditional commitment.

speaker: CUMMING
text: If we don’t feel that we’re ready yet for the inflation target, certainly between this meeting and the next we really need to think about what kind of conditional commitment we could make—what conditions in the marketplace would lead us to feel that our work was largely done.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I would also note, though, that the historical notes made the excellent point that the risk is that we withdraw stimulus too quickly—that we believe the patient is healing when, in fact, the patient is merely stabilized.

speaker: CUMMING
text: So our commitment must be both ambitious in its level and compelling as it is communicated to the public.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I think we need to return to the expository approach that the Fed and then-Governor Bernanke took during 2002 and 2003, by which we carefully laid out the elements, the foundation, and the expected outcomes of our approach in that period.

speaker: CUMMING
text: As valuable as it was in 2002-03, it is even more valuable today, when confusion and anxiety are shaping behaviors that will amplify the downward forces in the economy.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I also endorse the recommendation that many have made to think about a press conference.

speaker: CUMMING
text: The need for reassuring communication to the public is, I think, very great.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I would add two more thoughts.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Of course, it is really crucial that we are coordinating our policy with Treasury, and there are many ways in which we do that today—certainly, we need coordination of fiscal and monetary policy.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I frankly would like to see more of our asset-disposition activities taken on by the U.S. government so that it would be easier for us to describe the facilities that we have as supporting the market and restoring market functioning.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I also believe, as I’m sure that many of you do, that we will probably need some kind of agreement with the Treasury vis-à-vis our exit strategy.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I particularly underline the real possibility, which several have mentioned here, that we may want to raise interest rates well before the markets are really fully healed or fully sustainable by themselves.

speaker: CUMMING
text: We’ll need to be able to negotiate that in the sense of both the path we take and the understanding we have with the fiscal authorities.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Then just to conclude here, I also very much want to endorse the point that President Rosengren made about needing to fix the banking system and doing it sooner rather than later.

speaker: CUMMING
text: There really is no ability for the economy to function without a strong banking system.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Certainly I believe that you are hearing, as I am, of many instances in which the rationing that is going on through the banking system right now is reaching a destructive potential.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In that kind of world, I think we need to turn our attention to that.

speaker: CUMMING
text: The Federal Reserve is one of the most important supervisors in our country and in the world, and I think we can do a lot to lead to the very tough actions that need to be taken there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Several people have mentioned press conferences.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I should say that we’re looking very carefully at the idea of doing quarterly press conferences with the release of the projections, along the lines of the Bank of England.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we decide to do that—and input from the Committee is welcome—the first one would be in February.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It would coincide in this case with the Humphrey-Hawkins additional presentation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a speech at the London School of Economics in mid-January in which I will be able to lay out a lot of these issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know if that’s soon enough, but I don’t know whether we think we should do more communication or not.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s something we can talk about tomorrow perhaps, but I did want you to know that we are looking at the quarterly press conference model.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, my colleague Harvey Rosenblum made an interesting point the other day that we’re at risk of being perceived as migrating from the patron saints of Milton Friedman and John Taylor to a new patron saint—Rube Goldberg.

speaker: FISHER
text: By the way, I’m going to give a speech on Rube Goldberg next Thursday—I do think that it is important not to make it needlessly complicated.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I think it’s very important that we have this discussion.

speaker: FISHER
text: I welcome the discussion and welcome the papers so that we can not only have a cognitive road map for ourselves but also figure out how we’re going to clearly articulate a deliberate change in regimes to the public.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to underscore what you said at the beginning of this conversation, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: FISHER
text: We should be guided by what’s best for the country—period—and not get into internecine concerns about governance.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s what’s best for our economy and what’s best for the world economy.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’d like to talk about three points.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to talk about the current predicament in very general terms.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to touch on governance and then on communications.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, with regard to our current situation, it’s pretty clear that purchases and sales of fed funds have been distorted by risk aversion, distrust of counterparties, and fear of pending bank insolvencies.

speaker: FISHER
text: Quantitative easing resulting in massive excess reserves, we’ve talked about that; complications arising from the transition to paying interest on required and excess reserves—as you pointed out earlier, this is a regime shift that we’re still trying to effect and perfect; the need for GSEs to invest overnight money at any positive rate; bank capital shortages that prevent the GSE funds from being arbitraged; and quite possibly the FDIC’s temporary liquidity guarantee, although that seems to be a minor factor—in these circumstances, focusing on the fed funds target seems to me to be a diversion of our focus and energy, and I sent around a memo to that effect.

speaker: FISHER
text: Moreover, the short- term riskless rate, the T-bill rate, is virtually zero.

speaker: FISHER
text: Reductions in the targeted fed funds rate cannot lower the riskless rate any further.

speaker: FISHER
text: Adding to our difficulties is the fact that we simply do not know how financial intermediaries or money and capital markets will behave and function when interest rates get this low.

speaker: FISHER
text: We do have the Japanese example.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have worked and lived in Japan, and we have learned from what they’ve done.

speaker: FISHER
text: But the fact is that we have no sustained experience in the modern era in the United States with T-bill rates and the effective fed funds rate trading near zero.

speaker: FISHER
text: We do know that money market funds will become unprofitable if rates get much lower.

speaker: FISHER
text: Let me just say to those who sort of dismiss that, I think we might look a little foolish if we drove some of them out of business, especially after creating two special facilities to support their continued intermediation functions on the basis that they were critically needed for their roles in the commercial paper market.

speaker: FISHER
text: Furthermore, I’ve spoken with several community bankers, and I subjected Governor Duke to some of that during her visit to Dallas.

speaker: FISHER
text: Their unanimous response to a further reduction in the targeted fed funds rate would be to set a floor for their prime rate at its current 4 percent level or some of them are suggesting that they would switch to a lending rate based off LIBOR—again, with a floor to protect their margins, which are being severely tested.

speaker: FISHER
text: To the extent that larger banks depend on deposits as a source of funding, reductions in the fed funds target rate from current levels could damage their profitability also, and this goes to one of the points made by President Rosengren and First Vice President Cumming.

speaker: FISHER
text: We do have to bear in mind that it’s important to have a vibrant and healthy banking system across the country.

speaker: FISHER
text: In this new and untested interest rate environment, it is, in my opinion, tenuous to assume that the fed funds target rate is the marginal cost of funds to a bank and that all of the usual and customary costs in pricing relationships will hold.

speaker: FISHER
text: If deposit rates approach zero, as they are likely to do for all but the zombie banks, it’s probable that the demand for currency will increase, a prospect that I would prefer to avoid.

speaker: FISHER
text: To sum up, we’re in an interest rate environment in which the linear properties of our model are likely breaking down.

speaker: FISHER
text: So where does this leave us?

speaker: FISHER
text: It leaves us with the critical need to refocus our strategy and communication efforts on what we have been doing and will continue to do—namely, restore the public’s confidence and trust in financial intermediaries and financial markets, reduce term liquidity and credit spreads to something approaching more-normal levels, improve the flow of credit through financial intermediaries and financial markets, and restore economic growth and reverse the spillover of inflationary pressures from asset markets to the markets for goods and services.

speaker: FISHER
text: Operationally it seems to me that we need to shift our focus away from the fed funds rate target—parenthetically, which we cannot control—to something that we might better influence—namely, the reduction, or perhaps a better phrase, the normalization of liquidity and credit spreads.

speaker: FISHER
text: The fact is that we have already entered this domain, and by stating it that way—that is, approaching the normalization of liquidity and credit spreads— we would have a clear exit strategy, and we could discontinue this focus when spreads return to something approaching normal.

speaker: FISHER
text: This has the additional advantage that it is a conditional commitment.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would avoid any reference to specific targeting for the monetary base or the size of our balance sheet.

speaker: FISHER
text: We simply do not know in current circumstances how fast or how far, as I referenced earlier in my question to President Lacker, we need to expand our balance sheet to restore normal spreads or normal credit flows.

speaker: FISHER
text: Some of our facilities—for example, the MMIFF—have worked with almost no usage.

speaker: FISHER
text: Others have acquired extensive usage.

speaker: FISHER
text: In sum, it seems clear to me that focus on the target fed funds rate is misplaced in the current environment.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we are to restore the functioning of the credit markets, we need to address that objective explicitly.

speaker: FISHER
text: With regard to governance, in addition to reading the 21 papers that were sent out and the Bluebook, this last week I read a novel called World without End written by Ken Follett.

speaker: FISHER
text: It should have been called A Book without End because it goes on for 1,000 pages.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s about the plague in the fourteenth century.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of the interesting lessons from reading that book is that the monks in that period, who dominated society, reverted to the old orthodoxy learned from the Greeks.

speaker: FISHER
text: They were the best educated.

speaker: FISHER
text: They were the Oxford-educated intelligentsia.

speaker: FISHER
text: But by reverting to the old orthodoxy, they did not learn what the nuns learned, which is what you learn from practice.

speaker: FISHER
text: The reason I mention this, Mr. Chairman, is that I think there is great value, as we try to figure out and articulate the new regime, to have these shared discussions at the table.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to thank you in that sense for your comments, not only about good faith but also about the need to have this discussed broadly within the FOMC and not just adhere to the old orthodoxy.

speaker: FISHER
text: All of us have different levels of experience and backgrounds, and we learn from those different levels of experience and backgrounds.

speaker: FISHER
text: Finally, on the issue of communications, one of my colleagues often says that, if you’re Elton John, you are expected to sing “Bennie and the Jets” every single time and at every single concert.

speaker: FISHER
text: It seems to me that, once we get and hone our message, we must repeat it incessantly and stay on message in order to have it penetrate.

speaker: FISHER
text: In Austin, you gave what I consider to be a hallmark and—not trying to flatter you—for monetary policy a historic speech.

speaker: FISHER
text: What was Bloomberg’s first reaction?

speaker: FISHER
text: The Fed may cut rates further.

speaker: FISHER
text: We all need to stay on message.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I think it’s very important, whether we have press conferences or whether you give speeches, that we need to hammer the theme of the new regime that we are about to embrace over and over and over again.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I didn’t pick “Bennie and the Jets” just because of your name, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I do hope you remember that we must have that constant refrain.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we’re going to sell something, we have to sell it by repeating it, not asking the press to interpret it for us but to get the message out in—excuse me, Governor Kohn—full frontal view.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m in awe of a presentation that has Rube Goldberg, the Black Death, “Bennie and the Jets,” and full frontal view all in it.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I’ll begin where Governor Fisher ended his remarks.

speaker: WARSH
text: To thank Brian, David, and Nathan for two reasons: First, obviously I thought you did a great job, and second, I didn’t want to be the first jerk around this table not to acknowledge you.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I felt some burden now to be 15 for 15 and thank you for the work.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me make three background points and then try to answer some of the questions that Brian asked of us.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, I think we have two risks in the zero lower bound discussion.

speaker: WARSH
text: One is overstating the importance of our judgments today in helping the economy get back to potential.

speaker: WARSH
text: The second risk is understating the importance of prospective Fed actions given our frustration that our policy accommodation to this point has only partially offset the deterioration and credit weakness in the real economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: The first trick is getting that balance right, recognizing that our actions are important but probably not determinative, at least solely determinative of the outcomes, given what markets will end up doing with the messages we send and given the need for fiscal and other policies.

speaker: WARSH
text: The second trick is that, notwithstanding our announcements or what we take to be our target, the effective rate is likely to be very close to zero for quite some time.

speaker: WARSH
text: So maybe more precisely in this context, the zero lower bound problem could be understood to mean that the expected protracted period of weakness will come because monetary policy is unable to provide enough stimulus to generate a robust recovery.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is true as far as it goes, but we shouldn’t assign more import to this problem than it deserves.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is, the protracted period of weakness is not simply or largely about monetary stimulus.

speaker: WARSH
text: It’s about a broken financial architecture of which the official sector response, including monetary policy, is only one piece.

speaker: WARSH
text: At the same time, monetary policy can’t be as efficacious as desired and is constrained by these zero lower bound problems.

speaker: WARSH
text: Thus, we don’t have a free pass to stand idle.

speaker: WARSH
text: Incremental interest rate policy may be of limited value, but it’s still relevant in stimulating demand.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second point—the judgments today are made harder by the degree of market discontinuity and market dysfunction.

speaker: WARSH
text: I take very seriously the risk that reducing the fed funds rate to zero could further degrade the functioning of financial markets and do so at a very inauspicious moment.

speaker: WARSH
text: Getting that market functioning is our way out of this mess, and though we would in normal markets expect money market mutual funds and regulated and unregulated financial institutions to adjust, there’s a lot about their behavior in the past six months that hasn’t followed normal custom.

speaker: WARSH
text: I worry at this time, when we’re trying to get markets to respond, about putting an incremental burden on their reaction function.

speaker: WARSH
text: The current period is distinguished from 2003 and other antecedents by the broader systemic fears about our system of credit intermediation, and I agree strongly with the idea advanced in the materials that were presented last week that the level of the Treasury repo rate is more critical to Treasury market functioning and the functioning of other markets than the target rate or the effective fed funds rate.

speaker: WARSH
text: The deterioration in repo market liquidity that Bill and others spoke about correlates strongly with lots of other bad things—fails in Treasury markets, the inability to predict market clearing prices, and the inability to hedge other assets.

speaker: WARSH
text: During this period, in which we have seen this unfortunate behavior, everything else seems to have gone wrong as well, so it is hard to draw any causation here.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I do worry about those market effects.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a third point, on balance I’m inclined to believe that the macroeconomic benefits of pushing the envelope to get to zero may be outweighed, particularly now, by additional financial market problems.

speaker: WARSH
text: In more normal circumstances, disruptions in these markets could be addressed quickly by changes in market practices.

speaker: WARSH
text: But there is reason to worry this time how quickly they could come.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn now to some of the questions that Brian raised.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, on the question of whether we should move or keep our powder dry, I think it’s clear that, once we decide and we know where we want to go, we should move as swiftly as possible to get there.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I think the key word there is “readiness.” So when we want to make this final move, we need to be ready in three respects.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, the Board and the FOMC have to be ready in terms of what our consensus is.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, the markets must really understand why we are making this change in regime—they need to comprehend fully what is driving our policies.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, we have to have an operational ability to perform and execute, and that’s really a question for Bill and his colleagues as we continue to expand our facilities.

speaker: WARSH
text: The second question was about the cost of reducing the fed funds rate target to zero.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would put it simply that the zero lower bound in my opinion isn’t zero, but it is lower than 1 percent.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m not sure if it’s 25 or 50, but I would be probably cautious about pushing beyond the point of our comfort.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, in terms of the benefits of communications, we are judged by our actions far more than our words, and I think the markets have gathered a view of what our reaction function is.

speaker: WARSH
text: So when we talk about the need for our communication language to emphasize the conditionality of it, I think that’s quite consistent with how we’ve talked previously about our forecast.

speaker: WARSH
text: Our judgments on policy are dictated by our forecasts.

speaker: WARSH
text: As our forecasts change, so too might our decisions.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think I’d put our communications in that regard.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of introducing or reintroducing an inflation target at this point, I’m not sure that it would, at least in the short and medium term, drive the kind of market reaction that we would expect.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think markets would be wondering, after long discussions over the previous eighteen months about subcommittees and communication policies and inflation targets: Why now?

speaker: WARSH
text: Is it that we’re actually now more concerned about inflation expectations and the medium-term view of what’s consistent with price stability than we were during much of that period in which we were talking about inflation that was higher than our expected range?

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m not sure I have been able to internalize and conclude why that would be appropriate at this very moment to introduce into our statements.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of nonstandard policy tools and the purchase of large amounts of agencies and Treasuries, I think that the Chairman’s point about the composition of the asset side of our balance sheet is key.

speaker: WARSH
text: In a different regime, I would have been uncomfortable about agencies.

speaker: WARSH
text: But my view is that they are wards of the state at this time.

speaker: WARSH
text: The U.S. government has said so.

speaker: WARSH
text: To the extent that we can provide our fire power to both the Treasury market and the agency market, it is probably worthwhile to do both.

speaker: WARSH
text: We probably have an opportunity to test the importance of some of these nonstandard policy tools in executing the timing and process and making public our announcement to this point of providing up to $600 billion in aid to this market.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would prefer to avoid setting a ceiling on conventional rates—that’s not the role of the Fed.

speaker: WARSH
text: Better to leave that announcement to others.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think it is also critically important with respect to agencies that we make sure we understand the posture and policies of the new Administration.

speaker: WARSH
text: If they think that the agencies are effectively going to be treated like wards of the state, I’d feel more comfortable.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of the expansion of credit backstop facilities, my first concern would be that I’d defer to Bill and his colleagues about operational bandwidth.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, I think we probably have an opportunity—and you do, Mr. Chairman, in your speech early next year—in announcing what our criteria are and what our framework is for expanding our credit backstop facilities.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, I’d say that we do need to address, probably in that same period, our exit strategy and clean up any edge problems that might have developed during this period.

speaker: WARSH
text: The CMBS market is in lousy shape.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that’s not largely because of what we’ve done, but there is a gravitational pull on the bit of liquidity that is out there to the residential market and away from the CMBS market.

speaker: WARSH
text: There’s probably an opportunity for us to try to clarify that in the context of the TALF program.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, in terms of other nonstandard tools that would be particularly useful, again, I think it would be important to state publicly in all of our discussions the need for the fiscal authorities to be taking first losses and ensuring that the new Administration, the new Treasury, is prepared to support the Fed in that so that they’re in the credit-loss business and we are really just using our facilities and knowledge to put that into place.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I thank you very much.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I will make it 16 out of 16 on the excellent work of the staff, but I think also something that comes through from that is that we have to have a great deal of humility given the situation that we’re in.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We can use analogies from Japan.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We can use analogies from other parts of history or from Sweden, but there are a lot of parts that are unique, and a lot of what we’re doing is, as I think President Bullard said, outside where some of the data have been in the past.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So we do have to come at this with a little humility.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Actually, the Japanese experience weighs very heavily on me because that’s perhaps one that I know well and in which I see perhaps the closest analogies.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: One of the facts that President Bullard mentioned is extremely important and weighs heavily on me—they have had their target rate at less than 1 percent for almost a decade and a half.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But something that President Bullard didn’t focus on is how little growth they have had in that period.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We are moving into an era of very low interest rates, and we want to revive growth and think about how we can do that, and that gets to the overall objective.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we also want to avoid the problems that Japan has had because it would probably not be a good idea to be in a regime in which we feel forced to have the fed funds rate at less than 1 percent for a decade and a half.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Clearly, there are theoretical, empirical, and practical reasons for moving rapidly.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The Japanese example is very clear on that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Practically, we are largely already there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, I simply can’t imagine that over the next 6 or even 12 weeks we’re going to get data that would make us think that we shouldn’t be moving interest rates down or that we aren’t in a state of the economy in which we have to do something fairly aggressively.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We already see some disruptions in the markets because of the low effective rates.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have to be mindful of these consequences and monitor them closely.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As has been mentioned a couple of times, we have the comparison of the markets in which we’ve intervened that seem to be working a bit better and the markets in which we didn’t intervene that aren’t working as well.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Although I actually do agree with that interpretation, we have to be a bit careful about that in going forward because there could be some unintended consequences, such as in commercial paper.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: A1/P1 interventions can help that market out, but they could have some unintended consequences for A2/P2.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Just because the other markets are not improving as these are, we have to be careful about drawing conclusions that it must mean that we need to intervene in market Y and market Z and A, B, C down the line.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That’s not to say that I think that what we’ve done so far has not been helpful.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I do believe that it has been, but I think we just have to be very, very careful about those unintended consequences.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Communication strategy, as so many people have said, is crucial because we’re stepping into a new world.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We basically have a lot of explaining to do, and one of the key things to explain is that we have not gotten to the end of our tether, that there’s still a lot more that we can do, even though a lot of the world thinks that, once we have “given up” on interest rates or gotten down to our lower bound, we can’t be that effective.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have to be very effective in arguing that, no, that’s not the case.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In the discussion, a number of people mentioned that trying to provide a framework for understanding this is really, really crucial.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Explaining that we may need to keep interest rates at a low level for a while based on the conditions in the economy is important, but that doesn’t mean that low interest rates are not helping economic recovery.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We should be expressing concerns that inflation could fall below the level that we consider consistent with our dual mandate.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that’s something that is also very important to talk about—methods that we could use to attack that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think this does in the broad sense raise the value of an inflation target.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I would be very concerned, as I think President Stern and some others mentioned, at this point about getting into that debate because, even if we did go to the Congress and a few members of the Congress said that’s okay, that still would be a very big debate and I think a distraction from exactly where we want to go.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we need to think about that over the long run, particularly if we start to see the inflation rate going down or if we see that we’re not being effective at fighting expectations of deflation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I think for the moment that it would be too much of a burden on our communications and would perhaps cause too much confusion in the market.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: They have gotten all of these new facilities.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’re stepping into a new world potentially depending on our decision tomorrow.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we also then introduce an inflation target at this time, it may just be a lot to digest.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I think it is a discussion that we need to continue to have.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In terms of the specifics of the actions that we need to take moving forward, once again, I think the lessons of Japan are important.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We want to focus a little more on the asset side than on the liability side.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The Chairman characterized things in a very effective way to argue that we’re not doing precisely the same thing and that we potentially can be more effective.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think it’s not just about some particular reserves level.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The example that President Rosengren gave is one that weighs on me.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We need to be nimble in responding to different problems.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We may have new facilities.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We may purchase more or fewer securities.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Being constrained by or picking out a particular number for reserves doesn’t seem to be the most effective way to build our credibility that we will fight these problems.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Although there is a long history in the Fed of looking at things like the monetary base, nonborrowed reserves, and such, I think there are good reasons that we moved away from them.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Of course, I’m from the University of Chicago, and so Milton Friedman is spinning right now, [laughter] but money demand has not proved to be a very stable function over time, particularly now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The money multiplier has certainly been anything but stable, making it more difficult for us to focus credibly on a particular reserves level to see what the ramifications are for the rest of the economy.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That is not to say that we shouldn’t have an eye on those issues.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But given the uncertainties, I would be reluctant to focus on that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think a focus on the asset side is much more effective.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Ultimately in all the programs and actions that we undertake, we have to think about the exit strategy, as a number of people have mentioned.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that’s very important for us both with longer-run expectations and in just making sure that, as we do intervene, we minimize the amount of distortion.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: In some sense we are purposefully distorting what the market is doing now, but in some sense we think of the market as being distorted from where it normally would operate.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So we have to be at peace with that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We need to do that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we also want to make sure that as much as possible we try to restore that functioning.

speaker: KROSZNER
