text: Making clear that we do these things with reluctance and do want to get out of them to restore the normal market functioning will again be a very important part of our communication strategy to make this all work.

speaker: DUKE
text: I’d like to make it unanimous in thanking the staff.

speaker: DUKE
text: For me, particularly, you have extended the process by which every hour that I’ve been here has been deeply educational and have helped put the things I’ve been doing since I got here in some sort of a context.

speaker: DUKE
text: Along those lines, the one thing I thought I might address is the economics of the world from whence I came—and that is the economics that bank managers are facing today— because I think that’s an important part of this discussion.

speaker: DUKE
text: I’m sure most of you have heard from bankers really pleading not to lower the rates, and there’s a very good reason for that.

speaker: DUKE
text: I actually expanded the number of banks that I normally talk to—in addition to Federal Advisory Committee, the North Carolina bankers and some of the Texas bankers—and the plea was unanimous: Please don’t lower the rates.

speaker: DUKE
text: The reason for that really goes to the prime rate, not the fed funds rate.

speaker: DUKE
text: If the prime rate moves down, I do believe that dollar for dollar it’s going to reduce bank profitability.

speaker: DUKE
text: If we were to go to zero, if prime were to go to 3 percent, I think it would take our entire banking system on an operating basis to an unprofitable level.

speaker: DUKE
text: To give you an idea, the non-interest operating costs of banks have not changed an awful lot over the last seven or eight years.

speaker: DUKE
text: They fluctuate about 5 basis points, but it’s a little over 3 percent of assets in non-interest operating costs.

speaker: DUKE
text: The non-interest income that offsets that may be 60 basis points.

speaker: DUKE
text: So you are looking at a 240 basis point hurdle that margins have to get over.

speaker: DUKE
text: The interest yields right now are 40 basis points lower than they were in 2002, going into the 1 percent fed funds rate.

speaker: DUKE
text: Credit costs are certainly higher.

speaker: DUKE
text: They’re higher by 10 to 18 basis points.

speaker: DUKE
text: Fee income is lower by 10 to 16 basis points.

speaker: DUKE
text: If you put all of that together, profitability is already lower by 60 to 75 basis points.

speaker: DUKE
text: On a marginal basis, deposit competition is fierce.

speaker: DUKE
text: CD rates are in the 3½ to 4½ percent range.

speaker: DUKE
text: Money market accounts are around 3 percent.

speaker: DUKE
text: New entrants into the insured deposit arena are intensifying this competition still further, and the banks are incredibly bitter about nonbanks coming into that arena.

speaker: DUKE
text: Lower-cost funding is available from some nondeposit sources, but the banks are feeling pressure from their examiners to limit usage of noncore funds, including discount window borrowings.

speaker: DUKE
text: A bank issued the FDIC-guaranteed debt last week, three years at a cost of 2 percent plus the 100 basis points that they pay the FDIC.

speaker: DUKE
text: So that cost is 3 percent.

speaker: DUKE
text: All of these costs are in excess of the prime rate.

speaker: DUKE
text: On the asset side, the banks are shying away from purchases of securities because of mark- to-market concerns.

speaker: DUKE
text: The new loans that are being booked are being tied to prime, but they’re tied to prime with floors, with those floors generally in the 5 to 5½ percent range.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some existing loans have floors, although many do not.

speaker: DUKE
text: Home equity loans, credit card loans, and smaller bank commercial loans are typically tied to prime.

speaker: DUKE
text: Prime might reference that bank’s own prime—and some banks did not lower their prime or were slower to lower their prime the last time we changed the fed funds target—but more commonly it will reference New York or Wall Street prime.

speaker: DUKE
text: Larger loans and mortgages are more likely to be tied to LIBOR, although I understand that competition in recent years has moved toward contracts that give the borrower the option at any time of using a prime-based rate or a LIBOR-based rate.

speaker: DUKE
text: With pressure on both sides of the interest margin, credit costs are sure to rise, and with the prospects for fee income down, the banks are uniformly begging for no change.

speaker: DUKE
text: When asked how they might manage with lower rates, most said that the only choice they would have at this point would be to shrink their balance sheets rather than compete for business at a negative spread.

speaker: DUKE
text: The other rates that affect bank profitability have not moved with the fed funds rate, and so in this case it is about spreads, not rates.

speaker: DUKE
text: Now, it’s certainly possible that individual banks are exaggerating the effects that lower rates will have on their institutions and that their reactions will not be as strong as they claim.

speaker: DUKE
text: However, my question is, What if they are right?

speaker: DUKE
text: If we get down to a 25 basis point regime and we find out that it simply puts our banking system out of business, how do we then reverse that and move back up, and how do we explain that change?

speaker: DUKE
text: I’m not as familiar with the economics of money market funds, but I have to assume that their pressures are similar, and the note indicates that they might be willing to operate at a loss for a time.

speaker: DUKE
text: But the more we communicate that this would be an extended amount of time, how long would they be willing to operate at a loss?

speaker: DUKE
text: No matter where we set our fed funds target, there’s really very little that we can do differently, as in starting tomorrow.

speaker: DUKE
text: The current actual rate reflects a broken market.

speaker: DUKE
text: There are much lower volumes in the fed funds market right now, and a much higher percentage of those are with institutions that can’t earn interest on reserves.

speaker: DUKE
text: So, Bill, I still see some hope for the fed funds market coming back.

speaker: DUKE
text: Over time, as banks get more comfortable with each other, the opportunities to get a little higher yield as well as to open up an unsecured borrowing source will lead banks back into the fed funds market.

speaker: DUKE
text: But if that market did start to revive a bit, I would hate for us to be in a regime in which, at that point, we had to pressure it again to bring the rates back down.

speaker: DUKE
text: For this reason I think suspending the fed funds target as a policy tool rather than lowering it might be the safer course because it would let prime find its own level and the banks might not necessarily feel pushed to lower prime if we did not change our target.

speaker: DUKE
text: I had a number of notes on communication, most of which have been said.

speaker: DUKE
text: But the one point I’d like to make is that, when I think of communication, I think of it on a retail level.

speaker: DUKE
text: I think about our communication to consumers and to business owners rather than to the more sophisticated audiences that the notes tend to refer to.

speaker: DUKE
text: I think we have to be sure that we do communicate on a retail level—that we communicate on the nightly news, local newspaper level.

speaker: DUKE
text: Many of you have backgrounds in education, and I think at this point it’s our job to teach and explain what we’re doing and how it might affect individual consumers and individual businesses.

speaker: DUKE
text: In that sense, it’s important that we stay on message and that we have very clear terminology that we use over and over again.

speaker: DUKE
text: Even in the conversation today, the term “quantitative easing” was used differently by different speakers.

speaker: DUKE
text: I do think we have to be careful, again, on the fed funds rate target.

speaker: DUKE
text: I noticed the same thing that President Fisher did as far as the Chairman’s December 1 speech.

speaker: DUKE
text: Any time we talk about the fed funds rate, it is the only thing that’s going to be reported.

speaker: DUKE
text: Finally, I also think we have to be careful about references to the experience in Japan.

speaker: DUKE
text: We should emphasize the differences and the reasons that we expect to be successful because, in many places, references to the experience in Japan lead people to believe that we’re in for a very, very dismal future, and I don’t think that’s what we want to communicate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I actually would like to try to distill some impressions from our discussion and, going even a step further, maybe draw some very tentative conclusions for the statement and decision tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do that in the spirit of fairness because tomorrow you have a chance to rebut what I say now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me just draw some tentative conclusions, and if you disagree or if there are multiple options, perhaps you can respond in our go- rounds tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, with respect to the level of the fed funds rate, I think generally speaking people want to be aggressive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They recognize the difficulty, the severity, of the situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some were somewhat fatalistic, saying, well, we can’t really keep the rate much above zero anyway, so it’s somewhat of a moot question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With that said, Governor Duke was just the last of a number of people who did point out that there are various institutional, market, and other considerations that would suggest trying to keep the rate above zero if possible, although she had a very interesting alternative, which is just not to have a target, which might be helpful in at least a few contexts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me ask Bill about feasibility here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Suppose for the sake of argument that we had a range of 25 to 50 and we set the interest rate on reserves at 50.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It might work eventually, but right now I would guess the spread between the effective funds rate and the target would be bigger than that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We’re sort of running that experiment right now.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The market consensus is that the Fed is going to reduce the target 50 basis points at this meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That’s incorporated in the current federal funds rate trading because it’s the lowest interest on excess reserves during the two-week maintenance period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We’re trading in a range of about 10 to 15 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We don’t have that much information, but right now that spread is probably 35 to 40 basis points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think we probably couldn’t do what you said.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If we worked on it—you know, took the GSEs and made it so that they couldn’t sell fed funds and did a few other things—maybe we could get that spread down to 25 basis points over time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Brian, do you have anything?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it may be that our options are a range of 0 to 25 or no target, but those are two options that I would point to.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I should also say, as I discuss the statement here, I think that in a very real sense this is a transitional meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I mean, we can’t go from 0 to 60 in one meeting, and I think we have to allow for the possibility that there will be further refinement as we go forward into January.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I raise, as the first point, exactly how we state the policy decision.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do we make reference to the funds rate?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are we okay with a 0 to 25 range?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I hear and recognize the concerns about too low a rate, and it’s just a question of feasibility in the short term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One advantage about having a range is that we could indicate that over time we’re trying to get to 25.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would be at least slightly helpful, I think.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second issue I want to mention is communication.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I thought there was actually a good bit of consensus.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A number of people spoke somewhat approvingly of an inflation target or some broader inflation objective, but I didn’t hear much sentiment for doing it immediately or in the very near term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it is something that we ought to take very seriously, particularly if inflation starts to drop further.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should do it in a prepared way, and I need to consult and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I agree with the comment that this is a long-term objective that we have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This may be an excellent opportunity to do it because not only is there no tradeoff between growth and inflation in this context but also there won’t be any suspicion that we’re choosing a rate that’s convenient.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I mean, we are probably below the rate that we would choose as a target.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it might be worth considering in the longer term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For tomorrow, though, I did hear quite a bit of interest in conditionality in terms of the ZIRP (zero interest rate policy) type of strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We had—I think it was in alternative A, paragraph 3—a statement that said, “The Committee anticipates that weak economic conditions are likely to warrant a federal funds rate near zero for some time.” I wonder if that meets what people were talking about, or were there people who wanted to express it more explicitly in terms of our qualitative objectives or otherwise?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I hear a willingness to have at least a qualitative conditionality for our policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would invite overnight or tomorrow any alternative phrasing that people think might be more effective.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is an important decision to make.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The third issue—and I’m just making very high level comments here; I have a whole bunch of notes that I’m not going to repeat at this point—has to do with our various programs and purchases.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the great majority of the Committee is comfortable with MBS and Treasury purchases.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At least that’s what I heard.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I took a majority to be in favor of, or at least accepting, the credit facilities that we have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There were requests for more metrics, more explanation, more criteria, more exit strategies, and so on, and I think those were all valid points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I take from this is that these asset-side programs, the credit facilities as well as the MBS and other programs, are part of our new regime, that most people view them as part of our new regime, and that the inclusion in our statement of some reference to these kinds of programs, as in the variants that were circulated in the Bluebook, would probably be desirable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A point of considerable discussion and some contention, with respect to both governance and communication, was the use of a measure of the base or excess reserves as a quantitative indicator of monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With those who advocated it, I think there were really two objectives, if I may.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One was to have a measure of monetary policy that would influence expectations and, if effective, would raise inflation expectations and the like.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But another function of that, I believe, was the desire to have, from a governance perspective, the FOMC setting some kind of indicator of monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to the use of, say, the base as a measure of monetary policy, I would say that for tomorrow we’re pretty far from being able to feel comfortable doing that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We haven’t done the work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We haven’t done the analysis of the transmission mechanisms.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We haven’t looked at what monitoring ranges and how they might work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it would be a radical step to take in one meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I leave that open as we continue to think about what the right indicators of policy are.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I understand the desire for governance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think what I would propose—and again, by all means, respond tomorrow—would be, at least in our directive, that we have, as somewhat suggested already, the Committee affirm or otherwise indicate its approval of quantitative programs— $500 billion MBS; $100 billion GSE debt; $200 billion for TALF, if you are willing; et cetera—and pursuant to that, that the Board make a regular practice of bringing any new program or any expansion of existing programs to the FOMC for review and discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That may not be entirely satisfactory, but it would certainly indicate to the public that the FOMC has reviewed it from a monetary policy perspective, and it would appear in the directive, the minutes, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I put that out as just a possible compromise on that issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think those are the main elements of the statement and the directive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I heard a lot about a desire for an explanatory document, talking points, other supporting material, speeches, and press conferences.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We hear that, and it will be very important for us to try to develop such materials.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I said at the beginning that I think it’s unusually important for us to try to speak in a unified way externally, not because I want to avoid dissent—and of course, everyone’s views can be expressed—but as Governor Duke pointed out, because I think we have an educational mission here that needs to be taken seriously.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the more consistent we can be in our explanations and our discussion, the better it will be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those are just some things that I drew from the discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, you’ll have an opportunity tomorrow, at least one go-round or maybe two go-rounds, to agree or disagree.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first question is, What time do we begin tomorrow?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are scheduled for 9:00 a.m.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that would be adequate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Does everyone feel comfortable keeping their economic go-round remarks reasonably short?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If everyone is game for that, we’ll start tomorrow morning at 9:00 and now adjourn the Board meeting—you didn’t notice that—and also just remind you that there’s a reception and dinner available for your convenience.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be no business conducted at that dinner.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: See you in the morning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s start off today with the economic outlook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Dan, will you be taking the lead?

speaker: COVITZ
text: I will be using the packet of charts that starts with the staff presentation on financial markets.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The charts for the other two presentations are included in this packet and follow mine.

speaker: COVITZ
text: As shown in the top left panel of your first exhibit, long-term nominal Treasury yields posted their largest intermeeting decline in over twenty years.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The primary explanation for this decline, outlined to the right, is that investors markedly revised down their economic outlook, leading both to a lower expected path of monetary policy and to continued flight to high-quality assets and away from securities with credit and liquidity risk.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Yields also fell following Fed communications regarding alternative monetary policy tools, such as the purchase of long-term Treasury securities, agency debt, and mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: COVITZ
text: One measure of flight to quality, shown in the middle left panel, is the covariance of percent changes in stock prices and Treasury yields.

speaker: COVITZ
text: When investors pull back from risk-taking, stock prices fall, and so do Treasury yields, resulting in a positive covariance between the two.

speaker: COVITZ
text: When flight-to-quality effects are substantial, prices in both markets are volatile, making the covariance particularly large.

speaker: COVITZ
text: In recent months, the covariance soared to well beyond its 2002 peak.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Since the October FOMC, it has come down somewhat but remains extremely elevated, an indication of continued and substantial flight to quality.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Another perspective on investor perceptions is provided by the equity risk premium, shown by the red shaded region in the panel to the right and measured as the difference between a trend year-ahead earnings-to-price ratio on S&P 500 stocks and a real long-run Treasury yield.

speaker: COVITZ
text: This measure ballooned in mid- November as stock prices and Treasury yields fell and then narrowed a bit over the past month, as indicated by the plus signs.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Even so, the risk premium remains extraordinarily wide.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Yield spreads on 10-year corporate bonds, shown in the bottom left panel, increased further over the intermeeting period.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The spread on high-yield bonds (the red line) topped 1,600 basis points, and the spread on BBB-rated bonds (the black line) exceeded 600 basis points.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The BBB spread is now comparable to average levels recorded on similarly rated bonds during the Great Depression.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Changes in corporate bond spreads can be decomposed into changes in one-year forward spreads.

speaker: COVITZ
text: As shown in the panel to the right, the 117 basis point intermeeting increase in the 10- year BBB spread reflects increases in forward spreads across the term structure, consistent with investor flight to quality and away from risk.

speaker: COVITZ
text: In addition, the forward spreads ending in two years and five years increased more than the spread ending in 10 years, suggesting that investors have become more concerned about credit risk in 3 The materials used by Mr. Covitz, Ms. Aaronson, and Mr. Ahmed are attached to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: COVITZ
text: the medium term—that is, more concerned about the possibility of a protracted economic downturn.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Your next exhibit examines recent conditions in the commercial paper market.

speaker: COVITZ
text: As shown in the top left panel, outstanding financial CP and ABCP (the black and red lines) dropped in September and October but since then have partially rebounded.

speaker: COVITZ
text: In contrast, nonfinancial commercial paper outstanding (the blue line) has been relatively flat, although nonfinancial programs rated A2/P2 (not shown) have contracted roughly 40 percent since early September.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The noticeable increases in financial CP and ABCP around the time of the last FOMC meeting reflect the implementation of the Federal Reserve’s commercial paper funding facility (CPFF), which ramped up quickly and now holds roughly $300 billion of highly rated commercial paper.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The recent stability is also likely due to flows back into prime money market funds since early November (shown by the red bars above the zero line in the panel to the right).

speaker: COVITZ
text: According to recent surveys of money-fund managers, prime funds have substantially increased their holdings of ABCP, reportedly reflecting the confidence provided by the asset-backed commercial paper money market mutual fund liquidity facility (AMLF), which stands ready to provide banking organizations with nonrecourse loans to fund purchases of highly rated ABCP from 2a-7 money funds.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Turning to pricing, the middle left panel shows that the spread on overnight A2/P2-rated nonfinancial CP (the blue line) trended down over the intermeeting period.

speaker: COVITZ
text: About half of the reduction in A2/P2 spreads reflects a sample shift toward higher quality overnight issuers, while the other half of the spread reduction is due to improvements in pricing for a constant sample of issuers, suggesting a positive spillover from sectors of the market directly affected by the Fed liquidity programs.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The overnight ABCP spread (the red line) also declined, on net, over the intermeeting period.

speaker: COVITZ
text: In contrast, overnight yields on CP from highly rated nonfinancial and financial programs (not shown) have traded at levels close to the effective federal funds rate for the past several weeks.

speaker: COVITZ
text: To examine year-end pressures, the panel to the right shows the gap between thirty-day and overnight A2/P2 yields.

speaker: COVITZ
text: This gap has been volatile but has trended up since late November, when the 30-day rate from our smoothed yield curve began to reflect trades that crossed year-end.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Year-end funding pressures are explored further in the bottom left panel.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The red bars show average percentages of paper that were placed over year-end as of mid-December from 2003 to 2007.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The corresponding percentages for 2008 are denoted in blue.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The first two bars indicate that, with respect to getting past year-end, programs rated above A2/P2 as a group are ahead of their average pace over the previous five years.

speaker: COVITZ
text: In contrast, the second two bars show that lower-rated programs are behind.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Overall, as outlined in the bullet points to the right, conditions in the commercial paper market appear to have been stabilized by the various policy interventions in this market.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Even conditions in the nonfinancial A2/P2 sector, which falls outside the government liquidity and guarantee programs, have improved, but the sector remains strained.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Year-end pressures appear substantial for lower-rated programs.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The remainder of my briefing reviews funding flows in longer-term markets, starting with financing for nonfinancial businesses.

speaker: COVITZ
text: As shown by the red portions of the bars in the top left panel of exhibit 3, investment-grade bond issuance has held up fairly well in recent months, while speculative-grade issuance, shown by the blue portions of the bars, has dwindled to nothing.

speaker: COVITZ
text: This pace of financing does not appear to pose substantial near-term funding pressures for the nonfinancial corporate sector as a whole.

speaker: COVITZ
text: As shown by the blue bars to the right, the volume of speculative-grade bonds due to mature is relatively light in 2009 and 2010 before it moves up somewhat in 2011.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Moreover, the pace of investment-grade bonds that will mature in coming years, denoted by the red bars, is comparable to recent issuance levels.

speaker: COVITZ
text: In addition, as shown in the middle left panel, liquid asset ratios for firms rated speculative- and investment-grade remain relatively high.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Perhaps more troubling for nonfinancial businesses is that funding from banks has slowed.

speaker: COVITZ
text: As shown in the middle right panel, C&I loans expanded rapidly in September and October reportedly reflecting, to a substantial extent, a wave of drawdowns on existing lines of credit.

speaker: COVITZ
text: However, the expansion of C&I loans halted in November.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Equally striking, the plot in the bottom left panel shows that the change in commercial mortgage debt, based on flow of funds data, turned substantially negative in the third quarter, as the outstanding amounts both at banks and in securitizations fell.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Overall, nonfinancial business borrowing, shown on the bottom right, has slowed sharply this year, and with financial conditions expected to remain tight and investment projected to be weak, the staff forecast calls for borrowing to remain very tepid through at least 2010.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Household credit is the subject of my final exhibit.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Mortgage debt, shown by the blue line in the top left panel, is estimated to have contracted in the second and third quarters, in combination with the continued decline in house prices, shown by the thin black line.

speaker: COVITZ
text: We have very little data for mortgage debt in the fourth quarter, but MBS issuance in October, shown to the right, was somewhat below the already low third- quarter level.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Other types of household debt have also begun to contract.

speaker: COVITZ
text: As shown in the middle left panel, revolving and nonrevolving consumer credit rose only a bit in the third quarter and then fell in October.

speaker: COVITZ
text: While the slowdown in consumer credit likely reflects, in part, a reduction in demand, the secondary market for such credit has also become substantially impaired.

speaker: COVITZ
text: As shown to the right, issuance of ABS backed by auto and credit card loans slowed markedly in the third quarter and was near zero in October and November, as quoted spreads on BBB and AAA ABS (not shown) soared.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Results from the Michigan survey, shown in the bottom left panel, suggest that the contraction in household debt reflects both the reduced supply of credit and weak demand.

speaker: COVITZ
text: As shown by the black line, an unprecedented share of households has pointed in recent months to tighter credit as the reason that it has not been a good time to purchase an automobile.

speaker: COVITZ
text: At the same time, the percentage citing concerns about the economy, plotted in red, has increased to the top of its historical range and remains the reason mentioned most often by respondents as a deterrent to purchasing an automobile.

speaker: COVITZ
text: With financial markets under stress, consumer credit likely will need to be funded mainly on bank balance sheets in coming quarters.

speaker: COVITZ
text: However, as shown in the panel to the right, banks’ unused loan commitments for both households and businesses have declined substantially this year, as net new commitments have not kept up with drawdowns on existing lines—another indication of the tighter supply of bank credit.

speaker: COVITZ
text: Stephanie will now continue with our presentation.

speaker: AARONSON
text: I will be referring to the exhibits that follow the green nonfinancial cover page.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The indicators that we have received since the last FOMC meeting suggest that real activity has been contracting rapidly, and as Dan has described, financial conditions have continued to deteriorate.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Starting with the labor market, private payroll employment (the inset box in the top panel) plunged 540,000 in November, and the figures for September and October were revised down noticeably.

speaker: AARONSON
text: All told, November’s drop brought the three-month decline in private employment (the black line in the top panel) to an annual rate of 4.2 percent—a much steeper pace of job loss than we were expecting in the previous Greenbook.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The retrenchment in November was pervasive across both goods- and service-producing industries.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As shown in the middle left panel, initial claims for unemployment insurance have continued their steep climb since the November survey week, consistent with a further large drop in employment in December.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Meanwhile, in the household sector, nominal sales at the retail control grouping of stores (the inset box in the middle right panel) declined 1.5 percent in November, which given a large energy-driven price decline, translates into an increase in real spending for the month.

speaker: AARONSON
text: We had been expecting real outlays in this category to fall further.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As shown by the rightmost blue bar, with the latest retail sales number, we now think that real PCE on goods other than motor vehicles is on track to fall at an annual rate of 5¼ percent, not as bad as the 9¼ percent decline we projected in the Greenbook but still very weak.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Near-term indicators of consumer spending point to further weakness in the coming months.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Notably, the Reuters/University of Michigan survey index of consumer sentiment, plotted in the bottom left panel, remained at recessionary low levels in the first part of December.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Sales of light vehicles (the bottom right panel), which slumped in October, fell further in November, to an annual rate of 10.1 million units, a much slower pace than we had anticipated.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Anecdotal reports suggest that sales are soft again this month.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Given the weak fundamentals for demand and tight credit, we project vehicle sales to remain depressed over the next several months.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As shown in the top left panel of exhibit 2, residential construction has continued to slide.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Single family starts fell further, to 441,000 units—somewhat lower than our expectations—and permits continued to move down last month.

speaker: AARONSON
text: In the business sector, new orders for nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft (the red line in the top right panel) dropped for a third straight month in October; and with orders falling below shipments for a second consecutive month, the backlog of unfilled orders shrank further.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Yesterday, the Board released data on industrial production in November.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Total IP (the inset box in the middle panel) fell 0.6 percent in November.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Excluding the effects of rebounds from the Boeing strike and September hurricanes, IP moved down 1.6 percent last month.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The black line in the panel plots the three- month diffusion index of manufacturing IP, a measure reflecting the net fraction of industries that experienced an increase in production.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As you can see, over the past few months that number has plummeted to 21, indicating that the contraction in industrial activity has been remarkably widespread.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Overall, the incoming data led us to steepen significantly the contraction in real GDP that we are forecasting for the current quarter and the first quarter of next year.

speaker: AARONSON
text: In these two quarters, we expect output to decline at an average annual rate of nearly 5 percent.

speaker: AARONSON
text: In both quarters, a significant chunk of the revisions has come in private domestic final purchases (lines 3 and 4 of the table).

speaker: AARONSON
text: In addition, the available indicators suggest that firms are acting aggressively to limit unwanted increases in their inventories.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As shown in line 5, firms have been drawing down inventories at a moderate pace in the second half, and we expect even faster liquidation next quarter in response to the sizable contraction under way in final sales.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Your next exhibit focuses on the medium-term outlook, starting with some of the key background factors that have influenced our thinking about the outlook since the October Greenbook.

speaker: AARONSON
text: On the downside, as noted earlier, financial conditions have deteriorated further in recent weeks.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As can be seen in the top left panel, the index of financial stress that we track continued to rise sharply.

speaker: AARONSON
text: One important component of that increase in stress has been the further widening of corporate bond spreads for investment-grade issues (shown by the gray shaded area in the top right panel).

speaker: AARONSON
text: In addition, equity prices are lower than we projected, taking an even bigger bite out of household resources.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Meanwhile, in the external sector, the path of the dollar (shown in the middle right panel) is somewhat stronger than in our October forecast, and the outlook for foreign economic activity has weakened further.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Shaghil Ahmed will have more to say about these developments shortly.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As you know from reading Part 1 of the Greenbook, in light of the intensification of recessionary forces that emerged over the intermeeting period, we based this forecast on the assumption of a lower level of the federal funds rate than in our previous projection (not shown).

speaker: AARONSON
text: In addition, we now assume that $500 billion in new fiscal stimulus actions will be enacted early next year, on top of the roughly $165 billion in the stimulus package enacted earlier this year.

speaker: AARONSON
text: These assumed fiscal actions include permanent tax cuts for most individuals, higher transfer payments, grants to state and local governments, and support for housing.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As shown in the bottom left panel, these new federal programs boost the impetus to GDP growth from fiscal policy considerably relative to our assumptions in the October Greenbook.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Two other factors also provide more support to real activity in this forecast.

speaker: AARONSON
text: First, mortgage rates (the bottom right panel) have fallen about ½ percentage point since the October Greenbook.

speaker: AARONSON
text: With the spread over the 10-year Treasury yield still quite wide, we project that mortgage rates will fall further over the projection period.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Second, oil prices (not shown) have fallen more in recent weeks than we anticipated in the October Greenbook; the lagged effects of these declines provide a greater lift to spending in 2009.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The top left panel of your next exhibit summarizes our medium-term projection.

speaker: AARONSON
text: On balance, we expect that the factors restraining activity will far outweigh the supportive influences, with real GDP falling at an annual rate of 3 percent in the first half of next year.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The decline is led by a steep drop in business fixed investment (lines 5 and 6).

speaker: AARONSON
text: In the second half of the year, real activity begins a slow recovery as PCE (line 3) picks up and residential investment (line 4) begins to stabilize.

speaker: AARONSON
text: In 2010, the recovery is projected to gain momentum as household spending strengthens further and business purchases of equipment and software begin to rise.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As is typical, the recovery in nonresidential investment is expected to lag.

speaker: AARONSON
text: By postwar standards, we are projecting a deep, prolonged recession and a very sluggish recovery.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The middle left panel provides some perspective.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The black line shows the level of real GDP, indexed to its own peak, in the second quarter of 2008.

speaker: AARONSON
text: By way of comparison, the red and blue lines show the paths of real GDP during the recessions that started in November 1973 and July 1981, respectively.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As can be seen, the projected contraction in real GDP in the current episode is about in line with that experienced during those two earlier “big” recessions, but our projected recovery is noticeably more prolonged.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The box to the right summarizes some of the important factors that impede the projected recovery.

speaker: AARONSON
text: First, we think that the economy will continue to face significant (albeit moderating) financial headwinds over the next two years, with elevated risk premiums, restrictive lending conditions, and general uncertainty restraining real activity for some time to come.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Second, tight monetary policy did not help generate the current recession, and we don’t see monetary ease as likely to generate as much impetus to recovery.

speaker: AARONSON
text: In fact, as the third bullet point notes, the federal funds rate is already close to the zero lower bound, greatly limiting the scope for conventional monetary policy to provide further stimulus to real activity.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The importance of this last factor is illustrated by the bottom set of panels.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The exercise is similar to the simulations presented in the Bluebook, except that this one allows the federal funds rate to turn negative.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The green line in the bottom left panel shows the simulated federal funds rate path.

speaker: AARONSON
text: If unconstrained, the optimal funds rate would fall below zero in early 2009 and drop to negative 5½ percent in the third quarter of 2010.

speaker: AARONSON
text: In this scenario, the unemployment rate, shown in the middle panel, peaks at 7¾ percent in 2009—about ½ percentage point lower and a year earlier than in the Greenbook projection.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The four-quarter change in core PCE prices, shown at the right, bottoms out at just over 1¼ percent in mid-2010 and then turns up, in contrast with the continued deceleration in the extended staff forecast.

speaker: AARONSON
text: In the context of the zero bound, achieving an outcome for real activity and inflation consistent with the unconstrained optimal control exercise would likely require some combination of greater fiscal stimulus and nontraditional monetary actions than we have built into the current projection.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Your final exhibit summarizes the outlook for inflation.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As shown in line 1 of the top left panel, we now project that total PCE price inflation will slow to about 1 percent in 2010, while the core rate (line 7) falls to 0.8 percent.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The decline in inflation reflects a combination of widening slack in resource utilization, reduced energy and materials prices, and a net decline in core import prices; these factors also push down long-run inflation expectations.

speaker: AARONSON
text: I should note that we received data on the November CPI this morning.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The total CPI fell 1.7 percent, driven by a sharp drop in energy prices.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The core CPI was unchanged last month.

speaker: AARONSON
text: We had been expecting an increase of 0.1 percent.

speaker: AARONSON
text: One measure of resource utilization, the unemployment rate, is projected to reach 8¼ percent in 2010.

speaker: AARONSON
text: In our forecast, the wide unemployment rate gap puts substantial downward pressure on costs and prices.

speaker: AARONSON
text: However, as suggested in the middle left panel, we may be overstating the downward pressure on inflation caused by slack.

speaker: AARONSON
text: In particular, the current cycle has been associated with especially large employment declines in several industries, notably construction and finance.

speaker: AARONSON
text: If these declines are leading to an unusual amount of employment reallocation across industries, structural unemployment would increase, which in turn would raise the NAIRU.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The remaining panels present some analysis of the issue using a measure of sectoral reallocation and a set of Beveridge curves.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The middle right panel depicts an index of sectoral employment reallocation across industries.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The index is based on the growth rates of employment in 15 industries relative to the growth rate of total employment, adjusted at the industry level for typical cyclical movements in employment shares and is similar in spirit to a measure constructed at the Chicago Fed.

speaker: AARONSON
text: As can be seen, even after removing the typical cyclical behavior, increases in sectoral reallocation often occur around recessions, which is not surprising since each business cycle produces a unique set of imbalances.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Indeed, the amount of sectoral reallocation indicated by this measure has been rising over the past year or so.

speaker: AARONSON
text: However, to date it remains low relative to previous spikes in reallocation.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Another way to determine whether there has been a rise in structural unemployment is through the so-called Beveridge curve, two versions of which are shown in the bottom panels.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The version at the bottom left plots the unemployment rate, adjusted for the Emergency Unemployment Compensation program, on the horizontal axis against the job openings rate, measured by the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS), on the vertical axis.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The bottom right panel shows a Beveridge curve calculated using the Help-Wanted Index as the measure of job openings.

speaker: AARONSON
text: If there has been a significant increase in structural unemployment, then one would expect that for a given level of the job openings rate, the unemployment rate would be unusually high—that is, to the right of the plotted Beveridge curve.

speaker: AARONSON
text: This might occur, for example, if many of the job openings were for nurses but a disproportionate number of the unemployed were bond traders, who are not qualified for the job openings.

speaker: AARONSON
text: So, what do these Beveridge curves say about structural unemployment?

speaker: AARONSON
text: The blue and red circles in the two panels show the data points for the third quarter of 2008 and for the most recent months available.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The latest readings from the JOLTS do stand to the right of the estimated curve, while the latest readings from the Help- Wanted Index are closely in line with past experience.

speaker: AARONSON
text: At this point we are reluctant to draw strong conclusions from just a couple of observations from either measure, and we read the evidence as consistent with at most a small increase in structural unemployment thus far.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Of course, these data do not tell us what will happen in the coming quarters, when we anticipate further job losses in financial services and continued weakness in construction and manufacturing.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Shaghil will continue our presentation.

speaker: AHMED
text: I will be referring to the exhibits that follow the blue International Outlook cover page.

speaker: AHMED
text: Financial markets in foreign economies remain stressed but have not suffered further pronounced deterioration since the October FOMC meeting.

speaker: AHMED
text: As shown at the top of your first exhibit, government bond yields in major industrial economies have dropped, likely reflecting further expected monetary policy easing, lower inflation expectations, and a firming of the belief that economic recoveries are not around the corner.

speaker: AHMED
text: Equity markets, shown in the middle left, have changed only moderately, on net, since your last meeting, compared with large declines in previous months.

speaker: AHMED
text: The emerging-market aggregate CDS spread, shown in the middle, has been volatile but remains elevated.

speaker: AHMED
text: As shown to the right, gross private capital inflows to emerging markets through debt and syndicated loans have continued to trend downward.

speaker: AHMED
text: The exchange value of the dollar against the major foreign currencies (the black line in the bottom left panel) has moved down a little since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: AHMED
text: Some bilateral exchange rate movements were substantial, however, with the dollar appreciating markedly against the pound and depreciating against the yen.

speaker: AHMED
text: As shown to the right, the dollar has appreciated somewhat against the currencies of our other important trading partners, driven by movements in the Mexican peso and the Brazilian real.

speaker: AHMED
text: Earlier this month, the dollar registered one of its biggest daily increases against the Chinese renminbi in recent years, although this shows up only as a tiny blip in the chart.

speaker: AHMED
text: We believe that Chinese authorities will allow the renminbi to depreciate somewhat in the coming months; NDF (nondeliverable forward) contracts also imply an expected depreciation of the renminbi against the dollar over the next year or so.

speaker: AHMED
text: Incoming evidence on economic activity abroad continues to be grim.

speaker: AHMED
text: As shown in line 1 of the table in exhibit 2, we now estimate that foreign economic growth was below 1 percent in the third quarter.

speaker: AHMED
text: Although growth in Canada (line 7) and Mexico (line 12) surprised on the upside, readings elsewhere were generally weaker than expected, with real GDP contracting in the United Kingdom, the euro area, and Japan (lines 4 through 6).

speaker: AHMED
text: As shown by the red bars in the middle left panel, net exports made significant negative contributions to growth in these three economies.

speaker: AHMED
text: Domestic demand (the blue bars) was also soft.

speaker: AHMED
text: Growth in emerging Asia (line 9) was barely positive in the third quarter, reflecting subdued growth in China (line 10) and substantial contractions in most of the newly industrialized economies (shown in the middle right).

speaker: AHMED
text: With data from the current quarter pointing to greater weakness than we expected and a substantially more pessimistic U.S. outlook, we have further slashed our forecast for total foreign growth to minus 1½ percent in the current quarter and minus 1¼ percent in the next, before a recovery to a positive but still relatively weak average pace of about 1 percent through the remainder of next year.

speaker: AHMED
text: The widespread nature of the economic slowdown in large part seems to reflect trade linkages.

speaker: AHMED
text: As depicted at the bottom, in recent years U.S. economic growth (the black line) and the growth of total real exports of our major trading partners (the green line) have been significantly related.

speaker: AHMED
text: Although foreign exports are affected by many factors in addition to U.S. GDP, the relationship shown and the gloomy outlook for U.S. economic activity through next year paint a bleak near-term picture for foreign exports.

speaker: AHMED
text: Your next exhibit focuses on the advanced foreign economies in more detail.

speaker: AHMED
text: Data from Europe point to a sharp slowing in the current quarter.

speaker: AHMED
text: The timeliest indicators are PMIs (purchasing managers’ indexes), which, as shown in the top left panel, have plummeted in recent months in both the United Kingdom and the euro area, reaching levels well below those observed during the 2001 downturn.

speaker: AHMED
text: As depicted to the right, in Japan, exports (the black line) and industrial production (the blue line) have contracted during the current quarter, and conditions in the labor market have deteriorated further, as manifested by the decline in the ratio of job openings to applicants (the red line).

speaker: AHMED
text: Indicators from the current quarter in Canada, shown in the middle left, point to weakness in real exports and a continued drop in housing starts.

speaker: AHMED
text: Authorities in advanced foreign economies are attempting to shore up aggregate demand through fiscal stimulus.

speaker: AHMED
text: As listed in the middle right panel, many countries have announced stimulus packages, including Germany, France, and the United Kingdom.

speaker: AHMED
text: We estimate that the actual stimulative content of the packages announced so far is likely to be small but expect that additional measures will be introduced next year.

speaker: AHMED
text: The total fiscal stimulus that we are assuming should boost growth in the advanced foreign economies by ¼ to ½ percentage point at an annual rate from mid-2009 through 2010.

speaker: AHMED
text: The possibility of bigger fiscal initiatives is an upside risk to our outlook for foreign growth.

speaker: AHMED
text: Many of the foreign central banks have become more aggressive in easing monetary policy, as can be seen at the bottom left.

speaker: AHMED
text: Since the last FOMC meeting, the Bank of England and the ECB have slashed policy rates by a total of 250 basis points and 125 basis points, respectively, and the Bank of Canada and the Bank of Japan have lowered rates by smaller amounts.

speaker: AHMED
text: More rate cuts are expected in all of these economies, which could bring rates in Japan back down to the zero lower bound.

speaker: AHMED
text: As shown on the bottom right, inflation in the advanced foreign economies is now expected to recede at a faster rate than previously projected, reflecting sharp declines in commodity prices as well as diminished resource utilization.

speaker: AHMED
text: Turning to emerging-market economies, as shown in the top left panel of exhibit 4, the recent behavior of Chinese industrial production, total exports, and imports from Asia is now reminiscent of developments during the year 2001.

speaker: AHMED
text: The plunge in imports from Asia casts doubt on the notion that China has become an independent engine of growth in the region.

speaker: AHMED
text: As depicted to the right, Korean exports and aggregate industrial production in Korea, Singapore, and Taiwan are plummeting.

speaker: AHMED
text: In Mexico, third-quarter output was bolstered by expansion in the agricultural sector, but as shown in the middle left, exports have moved down sharply, and consumer confidence has dropped below 2001-02 levels.

speaker: AHMED
text: In Brazil, too, shown on the right, there has been some softening in exports (the black line), which had been supported by high commodity prices, although industrial production (the blue line) has held up a bit better.

speaker: AHMED
text: With prospects for exports in the doldrums, policy stimulus has become all the more important to the outlook for emerging-market economies.

speaker: AHMED
text: As noted in the bottom left, monetary easing has continued, with interest rate cuts in many emerging Asian economies, including China and Korea.

speaker: AHMED
text: China, Malaysia, and Brazil have also lowered bank reserve requirements.

speaker: AHMED
text: In addition, fiscal stimulus packages have been announced in a number of economies, most notably China.

speaker: AHMED
text: China’s 16 percent of GDP spending package considerably overstates the ultimate effects on growth as it includes some previously announced projects, its implementation may take longer than announced, and the federal government is slated to pay for only 30 percent.

speaker: AHMED
text: Discounting the headline number, we estimate that the Chinese package could boost growth 1 to 1½ percentage points per year.

speaker: AHMED
text: Other countries, such as Korea and Mexico, have introduced smaller but still sizable packages, which we expect will give some impetus to growth.

speaker: AHMED
text: In sum, our near-term forecast calls for total foreign growth to be the weakest since 1982, and as sketched out in our alternative simulation in the Greenbook, there would appear to be downside risks even to this forecast.

speaker: AHMED
text: Your final exhibit focuses on the U.S. trade outlook.

speaker: AHMED
text: Weak global demand has contributed to falling prices for food and metals, which have led a sharp decline in nonfuel commodity prices (the blue line in the top left panel).

speaker: AHMED
text: Oil prices (the black line) also have continued to move down rapidly, but futures prices project some recovery ahead.

speaker: AHMED
text: The fall in commodity prices has exerted downward pressure on U.S. trade prices (shown in the top middle panel); both core import prices and core export prices dropped markedly in October and November, which for import prices were the largest monthly declines in the fourteen-year history of the index.

speaker: AHMED
text: A sense of the extent of weakness in global demand can also be seen in shipping rates (shown to the right), which have taken a nosedive.

speaker: AHMED
text: As in the 2001 recession, U.S. real exports and imports of goods (shown in the middle left) are now trending down.

speaker: AHMED
text: Imports (the red line) have been moving down all year.

speaker: AHMED
text: The falloff in exports (the black line) is a more recent development and, in part, reflects hurricane-related disruptions and the strike at Boeing.

speaker: AHMED
text: As shown in the table, growth of both real exports of goods and services (line 1) and real imports (line 3) was noticeably weaker in the third quarter than we had previously estimated.

speaker: AHMED
text: For the current quarter, we see both real exports and real imports contracting sharply, reflecting the slowdown in global demand.

speaker: AHMED
text: Looking ahead, our projections for a stronger broad real dollar (shown in the middle right) along with our weaker outlook for foreign growth have led us to revise down sharply our forecasts for exports, especially in 2009.

speaker: AHMED
text: In the near term, our projections for imports have also been marked down considerably.

speaker: AHMED
text: As shown in line 5, the contribution of net exports to U.S. growth is expected to swing slightly negative in the current quarter, following large positive contributions earlier this year.

speaker: AHMED
text: The current quarter’s contribution is considerably weaker than projected in both the October and the December Greenbooks, as last week’s export data surprised us on the downside.

speaker: AHMED
text: Next quarter, with a substantially greater step-down in imports than in exports, we expect the contribution of net exports to U.S. growth to jump back up, before returning to negative territory for the remainder of the forecast period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Remind me what your anticipation of the current account deficit is for next year.

speaker: AHMED
text: I think the deficit goes down to about 3 percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We see the current account deficit, as Shaghil said, bouncing between 3 and 3½ percent of GDP through 2009 and 2010.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the near term, you have much weaker foreign growth and a stronger dollar, but that is offset by the lower level of oil prices, so that keeps the current account deficit around the 3 to 3½ percent range.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I was just looking at the policy rates abroad here—this is the picture in exhibit 3, I guess.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It shows the ECB, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England all leveling out before they get to zero.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Do you have a sense of what the plans are there, or what they are saying about that, or are we going to see a sort of global move to zero?

speaker: BULLARD
text: What is your sense of that?

speaker: AHMED
text: Looking at the policy that is going forward, first of all, we are forecasting here what we think they will do, not necessarily what we think they should do.

speaker: AHMED
text: Given their past behavior, we think that they will be ratcheting up the rates the first chance they get.

speaker: AHMED
text: The timing is a bit different, but the rates are broadly in line with market participants’ expectations.

speaker: AHMED
text: In the case of the euro area, for example, at the end we are even a little lower than the market participants are expecting.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So this is from surveys of market participants?

speaker: BULLARD
text: But you are getting the information from surveys and other things.

speaker: AHMED
text: It is informed by surveys, yes.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I would add that I think the ECB in particular has a real aversion to policy activism.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In fact, Trichet was on the wires this morning indicating that they are not really comfortable with where they are right now.

speaker: SHEETS
text: They may pause in January, and I think it really would take a more severe outcome for activity in the euro area than what we have incorporated in our forecast to get the ECB down to zero.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, that is a risk.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I would say that there are downside risks here.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I would put a higher probability on seeing the Bank of England or the Bank of Canada go to zero.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But as Shaghil emphasized, here we are basically just writing down what we think they are going to do, and we generally follow the futures markets fairly closely.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But it certainly would be a surprise to me if, over the next six months, we saw other major central banks in the proximity of zero.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just a comment on the projections for China—these numbers seem to be less than what they are saying officially.

speaker: FISHER
text: That sort of jibes with the reports that I am hearing back from the CEOs doing business in China.

speaker: FISHER
text: In fact, the cutback has been much more dramatic than they expected.

speaker: FISHER
text: Semiconductor firms, for example, have put ship-stop orders, meaning they are stopping for lack of payment, and the retailers are seeing a noticeable drop in attendance at their stores.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I think that our numbers are more fitting.

speaker: AHMED
text: I think the latest official numbers don’t incorporate the November data, which just came out—actually, they came out yesterday—and some trade data since the Greenbook.

speaker: FISHER
text: But you are saying that we do expect further currency depreciation.

speaker: AHMED
text: In the near term, yes, through the first half of next year.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have three questions, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: FISHER
text: One on the commercial paper market.

speaker: FISHER
text: What is the spread between A1/P1 and A2/P2 right now?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For term, it is a huge spread, probably 300 basis points or so, but overnight it is much smaller.

speaker: COVITZ
text: As you go out the term, it is even more.

speaker: FISHER
text: So the incentive for A1/P1 borrowers is to do everything they can to keep that status, obviously.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is a much more attractive proposition.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Which leads to more-conservative financial management and business management.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You do everything you can not to become an A2/P2 borrower, to slip off the A1/P1 ladder.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Historically BBB was the sweet spot of the corporate capital structure, and that was associated with A2/P2 commercial paper borrowing, which people thought was safe.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It turned out not to be quite as attractive as they had thought.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think over history this isn’t the only time when A2/P2s have come under stress.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Whenever there were disruptions in the market—for example, after the California utilities defaulted in the early part of the decade—A2/P2 outstandings plummeted, and A2/P2 spreads rose, though not nearly to this magnitude.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But that is a portion of the market that is under stress because this market in general tends to be very, very skittish.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the first sign of trouble, there is quantity rationing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I didn’t show the outstandings of the A2/P2s, but they have gone down—as I think I mentioned—40 percent in the last couple of months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So quantity rationing is already taking place, and they are having trouble getting over year-end.

speaker: FISHER
text: I guess my point is that the way in which it works is that it gives people incentives to be even more conservative in the financial management of their operations.

speaker: FISHER
text: On household credit, do we have a sense of how much shift is taking place between credit card usage and debit card usage?

speaker: FISHER
text: Under these conditions of duress, has that been a noticeable change, or is it just marginal?

speaker: COVITZ
text: I don’t know those data.

speaker: FISHER
text: It might be something to look at next time.

speaker: FISHER
text: Finally, on the inflation table in exhibit 5—and you have talked about the numbers that were released this morning—do you see additional monthly deflationary numbers on the headline CPI, or could you see this happening for a prolonged period, say for a quarter?

speaker: FISHER
text: We have a table here for 2008, 2009, and 2010.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the top line, the PCE price index, do we envision monthly or perhaps quarterly extensions of deflationary headline numbers?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have another two months of small declines anticipated as the energy prices continue to pass through and then, beyond that, some small increases.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So we don’t see this as an extended period of negative headline.

speaker: FISHER
text: And what is the order of magnitude?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are looking for about minus 0.5 percent in December and minus 0.1 in January.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are also not expecting the core figures to remain as low as they have been running for the past month or two.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We do think that they have been held down by some very significant declines in air fares.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That could continue for another month or two—again, as the energy price pass-through works.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: They have also been held down by some very large declines in lodging away from home, which is a volatile series, and it is not likely to sustain this level.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Despite the fact that we don’t see them as low as they have been the past two months—that is, declining to flat—we are expecting some fairly small increases going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have core inflation heading down, and all of these exhibits have shown a significant reduction in price pressures coming from import prices, from energy prices, and from broader commodity prices as well as the increase in slack that, as Stephanie pointed out, is keeping a real lid on labor costs.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our staff does such a fine job.

speaker: LACKER

speaker: LACKER

speaker: LACKER
text: I have a question for Stephanie.

speaker: LACKER
text: You know, they do such a great job.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Jeff, are you feeling okay?

speaker: LACKER
text: The sectoral reallocation is really intriguing, and it is something that I have been curious about in this whole episode.

speaker: LACKER
text: The measure is not one I am familiar with.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is one for which you count each industry as a unit, right?

speaker: AARONSON
text: It is a Lilien type of dispersion index.

speaker: AARONSON
text: This isn’t actually how we calculate it, but it is essentially how the industry’s share of employment changes relative to total employment.

speaker: AARONSON
text: So it is the growth in that industry’s employment relative to total employment.

speaker: AARONSON
text: What we do is that we know that over the business cycle each industry has a typical pattern—durables employment goes down a lot during recessions whereas, say, health care doesn’t go down that much.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Those types of changes aren’t typically associated with sectoral reallocation.

speaker: AARONSON
text: That is, we don’t really think of those things that are typical over the cycle as being associated with an increase in the NAIRU.

speaker: AARONSON
text: We want to take those out, so we take out the typical cyclical movements, such as manufacturing always goes down in a recession and finance is acyclical.

speaker: LACKER
text: And housing always goes down in a recession.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Housing and construction always go down, so we take that out, and then we say, okay, so now there are these atypical movements that are greater than we usually see.

speaker: AARONSON
text: That is what we would consider the sectoral reallocation.

speaker: AARONSON
text: That is what is left over.

speaker: AARONSON
text: You can see, as I mentioned in the briefing, that actually during recessions there is a lot of sectoral reallocation, even once you take out the usual declines in employment that differ across industries.

speaker: AARONSON
text: That is because each recession has different causes.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Different industries have grown a lot during the boom—like finance recently or, say, communications during the late 1990s—and those sectors are going to shrink more than usual during the recessions and get back to more of an equilibrium state.

speaker: AARONSON
text: That is what is going on here.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it is sort of a bummer that these go up in the recession if you are trying to measure what is happening to the NAIRU.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I always thought of the phrase “sectoral reallocation” as having to do with the theories of the business cycle in which cyclical downturns are caused by an unexpected decline in a given industry that causes resources to shift out of that industry and that it takes time for them to be absorbed into some other industry.

speaker: LACKER
text: From that point of view—if you are trying to measure that component as opposed to policy-induced, widespread declines in activity—I would think you would want not to take out the cyclical part.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am thinking about housing.

speaker: LACKER
text: We devoted a lot of resources to housing in 2005, much less now.

speaker: LACKER
text: Those resources thrown on the market, in fact, are the proximal cause of the initial downturn in employment growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: A lot of ancillary industries are related, so I would think that, if we didn’t take out the usual housing cyclical thing, which is really sharp in the early periods, you would see a bigger rise here.

speaker: AARONSON
text: I have looked at that, and actually, it doesn’t make that much of a difference.

speaker: AARONSON
text: Construction goes down in every recession, and so by that measure sectoral reallocation is higher in every recession.

speaker: AARONSON
text: I mean, construction is contributing more to sectoral reallocation here than in previous recessions because the declines have been larger.

speaker: AARONSON
text: So that fact is captured.

speaker: AARONSON
text: The fact that construction is having a larger-than-typical decline is precisely what is captured here.

speaker: AARONSON
text: But even if you said, okay, well, maybe in every recession industries shrink and that is associated with some sectoral reallocation, the measure actually looks very similar—not just across the current episode but across all the episodes.

speaker: LACKER
text: I guess it is also related to how you think about the NAIRU.

speaker: LACKER
text: To some extent, if unemployment goes up in recessions, then what unemployment is supposed to be goes up in recessions as well, it seems.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have a question about the first exhibit.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is the first set of exhibits.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is also about commercial paper.

speaker: LACKER
text: Would you folks encourage us to view the improvement that has taken place in the A2/P2 market as a measure of how the A1/P1 market might have improved had we not intervened?

speaker: LACKER
text: It is sort of a baseline, right?

speaker: LACKER
text: It is like the control group.

speaker: COVITZ
text: I think it is very difficult to interpret it that way because the intervention did happen and the bulk of the improvements happened subsequent to the intervention.

speaker: LACKER
text: What sort of spillovers from our intervention in A1/P1 do we expect perhaps to have influenced or to have led to an improvement in A2/P2?

speaker: COVITZ
text: I think that the decline in the A2/P2 overnight suggests improvement.

speaker: COVITZ
text: But there is some concern about sample selection, and you have to worry about that at the same time.

speaker: COVITZ
text: It could be just that you are getting higher-quality issuers in the A2/P2 sector.

speaker: COVITZ
text: But it turns out you’re not.

speaker: COVITZ
text: It turns out that it explains only about half of that decline.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You know, it also may have helped the money market fund industry to keep its money knowing that there was a facility outstanding that could provide liquidity for that sector because we did see inflows back into the money market mutual funds.

speaker: LACKER
text: So their willingness to buy A2/P2 may have been affected by another program, not the CP one.

speaker: LACKER
text: You are saying the money market fund program—

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They provided more stability to the system as a whole.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: To the prime money funds.

speaker: LACKER
text: So we can’t separate the individual programs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There is a second factor.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There has been discussion of extending the A1/P1 program to A2/P2, which the industry is certainly aware of, but I would highlight with the A2/P2 that a lot of the mutual funds do not want to hold it over the end of the year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Most of the A2/P2 borrowers are having trouble rolling over year-end.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There is a real risk that that market will have to rely on backup lines of credit, and it’s not clear whether the A2/P2 market comes back after the New Year, if that happens, or in what capacity it does.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I think the real test will be to look at this chart in January or February.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, you wouldn’t expect speculation about imminent extension of the program to A2/P2 to support the overnight rate for A2/P2 unless they expect it to be implemented overnight.

speaker: LACKER
text: A question about strains: To what extent are we able to disentangle whether the market is strained or the issuers are strained?

speaker: COVITZ
text: In the CP market itself?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You can look at credit ratings, for example, or what’s happening to their profitability.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is highly likely that the strains in the CP market are more dramatic than any change in the underlying financial condition of the A2/P2 borrowers.

speaker: COVITZ
text: You could think about what the default risk is, say, for the corporate sector.

speaker: COVITZ
text: You could break down a pretty simple model of defaults conditional upon our outlook for the economy, and that would have the default rate rising.

speaker: LACKER
text: But you don’t observe investors’ expected defaults themselves.

speaker: COVITZ
text: You don’t, but you can take a guess at what you think that is, and it is higher.

speaker: COVITZ
text: It is not at Great Depression levels under any of the models I’ve looked at.

speaker: COVITZ
text: It’s not even at the levels of default rates in 2002.

speaker: LACKER
text: So you are saying that this paper is underpriced.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is that how you measure strains?

speaker: LACKER
text: I am always curious as to what strains mean.

speaker: COVITZ
text: The way that I’m referring to it is just that risk premiums are really, really large.

speaker: COVITZ
text: I’m not saying that they are necessarily irrational.

speaker: COVITZ
text: I am just saying that they are really, really large.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have a question or observation, which is of the optimistic variety although it presents sort of a challenge.

speaker: EVANS
text: In the medium-term outlook in exhibit 4, if you focus on 2010, the Greenbook projection has real GDP growing at 2.4 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’re beginning to come out of this.

speaker: EVANS
text: The unemployment rate is peaking.

speaker: EVANS
text: If you could implement the optimal control federal funds rate, it would be bottoming out.

speaker: EVANS
text: Maybe that would mean whatever quantitative easing credit programs we would be doing would be at their peak and maybe would be coming off.

speaker: EVANS
text: But it is also the time that the inflation rate is low and continuing to fall.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is going to be a tension for us as we start thinking about, and we are about to engage in mentioning, the possibility that inflation could be—well, whatever—lower than ideal.

speaker: EVANS
text: What would you guess the risks might be around that inflation forecast?

speaker: EVANS
text: How hard is it going to be for us not to continue to worry about inflation being low or to communicate that inflation is going to continue to be low even though things are improving?

speaker: EVANS
text: Just any kind of advice would be helpful.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: My guess is that, if our baseline forecast evolves in the way we are expecting here, you are still going to be worried about the downside risk to inflation even if, in fact, we were in the process of bottoming out because there will still be a very substantial output gap.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the commodity price side, things are fairly stable, and at least in our forecast, inflation expectations are probably drifting down some.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the other hand, there are upside risks to that inflation forecast as well.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I do actually think that our baseline forecast, on the assumptions that we have had to make in constructing it, is reasonably well balanced because another possibility is, in contrast to the gradual downtrend that we’re expecting in inflation expectations, that inflation expectations will be stickier, you will be able to convey a greater sense that you wouldn’t want inflation over the longer haul moving down below 1 percent, we won’t get as much disinflation into inflation expectations or into labor costs, and you’ll get greater stability there than we’re expecting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So to my mind, looking ahead, monitoring how those inflation expectations evolve in the context of an economy where things are weakening will be very important.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the same topic—the medium-term outlook and, in particular, the optimal control exercise at the bottom, which is showing us how we’re constrained—is there some quantitative policy that we could undertake that would get us to the green lines here, maybe by creating more inflation than we would think desirable in the long run?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The point of constructing this optimal control is to say that, gee, if you weren’t constrained, here is how we thought optimal behavior—the sort of optimal outcome— would be, given the shocks.

speaker: STOCKTON
