text: You’re asking me whether or not there are quantitative policies that you could put in place.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I was actually hoping that you folks were going to be able to tell me.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: You face a challenge in constructing policy, but we have collectively a challenge in understanding how whatever policies you implement are actually going to show through into our longer-term outlook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The point here is that, in the absence of some nonconventional monetary policy actions or substantial fiscal stimulus, we see a very extended period of weak activity, high output gap, and declining inflation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Sometimes what people do is they say, okay, suppose you could just control inflation directly, which we know is hard, but suppose then you just trace out an optimal path for inflation that would get you to the green line.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Obviously, if you could levitate inflation expectations, that would be one thing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other thing is that note 21 in the package we sent you included some exercises that suggested, if you took actions that could significantly reduce the long-term Treasury rate and compress mortgage spreads, there would be ways in which you’d be able to provide more stimulus for the economy.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, all those things we suggested, at least the ones that we showed in that note, weren’t sufficient to get you back to equilibrium quickly.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But there are policies, obviously, that we think will be able to provide some stimulus.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This optimal control exercise then would have an objective that would be a quadratic objective in some real output or unemployment—

speaker: AARONSON
text: Minimizing the unemployment rate and the deviations of inflation from its target.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s saying that you wouldn’t be willing to suspend your inflation target for a while to improve things on the real side.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that might be helpful as well because then the Committee could think about what those tradeoffs are.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In ordinary times, you might have a certain weight on the two objectives, but you might shift that in other situations.

speaker: AARONSON
text: If I can also just put this in a little more context—by the end of 2010, the gap on the unemployment rate between the baseline and the optimal control is about 1 percentage point.

speaker: AARONSON
text: So if you use a simple rule of thumb from an Okun’s law type of model, that would be a couple of percentage points on the level of GDP.

speaker: AARONSON
text: GDP would have to grow a couple of percentage points faster over 2009 and 2010 to close that 1 percentage point gap in the unemployment rate between the baseline and the optimal control.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In an earlier meeting, if I recall correctly, there was mention of the European banks’ exposure to emerging-market sovereign debt—a concern about the trend lines in that sovereign debt.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Are you tracking that in any sense?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My concern is that there could be another full-blown debt crisis of some kind coming.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is not covered in these charts, but do you have a sense of default risk on the part of emerging-market sovereigns?

speaker: SHEETS
text: The European banks are particularly exposed, much more so than U.S. banks or Japanese banks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: A big chunk of that exposure is to central and eastern Europe, and as you suggest, we see significant risks to the European banks as a result of that exposure.

speaker: SHEETS
text: What makes it even a little dicier is that exposure is concentrated in several countries, particularly Sweden, Austria, and to a slightly lesser extent Italy.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Recently there has been significant economic turmoil in Hungary and Ukraine.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Fund has stepped in, and the EU has helped as well with large financing packages.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The latest one we’re watching very closely is the situation in Latvia, where the exchange rate is significantly overvalued.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The external position looks very, very dicey.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Fund is in there negotiating a program.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There has been a lot of back and forth about what should be done with the exchange rate regime.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The banking system also looks vulnerable—so what should be done with the banks?

speaker: SHEETS
text: It is not exactly clear how all that is going to be resolved.

speaker: SHEETS
text: My personal feeling is that, given the risks—and the Europeans recognize the extent of the risks—if Latvia goes, it could blow out the rest of the Baltics and then sweep around into Central and Eastern Europe and then feed back into Western Europe.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So I see the risks there as being of first order for the Europeans.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given that recognition, I think that the EU and major European governments are going to do what’s necessary to make sure that the situation in Latvia stabilizes at least for a while.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The end game over the next several years is very much an open issue for a lot of these economies that were in ERM-II and evolving into hoping to adopt the euro.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think that there are potentially some very pronounced vulnerabilities and some painful adjustment that will need to happen in some of those Central and Eastern European countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So absolutely that is a major risk.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It’s one we’re watching as closely as we can.

speaker: FISHER
text: Nathan, you would probably have been arrested for treason if you had said that in Latvia—literally.

speaker: FISHER
text: The economist who gives a negative forecast is arrested for treason.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let’s start our go-round with First Vice President Cumming.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I thought I would make a couple of points that underscore the substantial increase in the downside risks that we incorporated into the forecast that you all received on Friday.

speaker: CUMMING
text: That change was really encouraged by our economic advisory panel, which suggested that the downside risks were much larger than we were estimating at the end of November.

speaker: CUMMING
text: First, we have been meeting, as of course all of you do, with small business people.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Bill Dudley put a panel of investors together, too, and I have a couple observations out of that and our discussions with community bankers.

speaker: CUMMING
text: One is that the cutbacks in financing are very real.

speaker: CUMMING
text: There is a lot of evidence that the banks are going in and looking at lines and cutting them back to both investors and the small-business community.

speaker: CUMMING
text: The small business community is also on the receiving end of much tighter financial management at their larger customers—that is, the people they’re supplying—as those firms are not paying their bills or are extending the terms on which they pay their bills to a much greater number of days.

speaker: CUMMING
text: That has induced a hunkering-down mentality on the part of the small business owners.

speaker: CUMMING
text: The other sobering thing they pointed out to us—and this is very much in line with Governor Duke’s comments about the community banks yesterday; we hear the same thing—is that small businesses and the community banks can hold out for a while but not forever; margins are getting squeezed, and financing is getting squeezed.

speaker: CUMMING
text: The precautionary actions that the small businesses are taking will help them for a while, but they can’t hold out for more than six or nine months.

speaker: CUMMING
text: That is a particularly sobering statement for us in the Second District because, despite the fact that we are at the epicenter of the financial industry in New York—a major driver for the Second District economy—we have only just barely started to feel the effects of layoffs and reductions in activity in the city.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Our regional leading indicator index went down very, very sharply in the month of October, but that is still to be realized in the economy.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In particular, when we have looked at past episodes, the declines in incomes that we have suffered in the region have ranged between 4 percent and 10 percent in the financial industry when we actually get into one of these adverse periods.

speaker: CUMMING
text: That decline is usually spread over three or four years, so we are really talking about something that could last a good bit longer than six to nine months in our District.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Second, we do a survey of inflation expectations that is in many ways similar to the Michigan survey, and our survey results are almost completed and are very similar to those of the Michigan survey.

speaker: CUMMING
text: But we do ask one question that isn’t asked there, and that is about the longer run—that is, the 2010-11 outlook for prices and inflation.

speaker: CUMMING
text: From that we can impute a risk of deflation, which was 6 or 7 percent in early October and is now 12 percent.

speaker: CUMMING
text: So that risk of deflation seems to be growing even in the kind of population that is surveyed by the Michigan folks.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As requested, I will be brief.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Like the Greenbook, we see an economy in which the unemployment rate remains very elevated, and inflation is below my target for several years.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Our own equations would indicate that these elevated unemployment rates are likely to put even more downward pressure on the inflation rate than forecast in the Greenbook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The labor market is extremely weak, and there is a significant risk of deflation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I believe that greater use of nontraditional policies will be needed to mitigate more-severe outcomes than encompassed in the baseline forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: On the financial side I would just highlight two points.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, many banks are placing interest rate floors on home equity loans and on commercial loans.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Pervasive use of floors may make the choice of which low federal funds target to pick of little relevance to actual borrowing costs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We may want to consider surveying banks to get a better understanding of where these floors are currently being set.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, many firms are reporting that their lines are not being renewed and are asserting that it reflects problems with the bank not the borrower.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Discussions with community banks indicate that, for smaller borrowers, community banks are benefiting from this trend.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, it may be useful to understand better how the reductions in lines, particularly at troubled banks, are affecting the overall economy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think bank micro behavior is going to be very important for macroeconomic outcomes, and we might want to increase the amount of effort that we are putting into understanding both their financial condition and how their behaviors may be changing over the next six to nine months.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Whether that’s done through the bank supervision process or the loan officer survey or which mechanism we use, I think we need to probably get a little more intelligence on exactly what those trends are.

speaker: LACKER
text: The economic news since the last meeting has certainly been grim, and our presentation today bore that out.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our directors and other District contacts are quite gloomy, and their reports are also consistent with a broad-based pullback in discretionary outlays by consumers and firms.

speaker: LACKER
text: In these circumstances with the funds rate around 1/ percent, it is hard to see a benefit of 8 prolonging any further reduction.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree with the staff analysis that any potential dislocation in money market institutions is likely to be minor, and I observe that, to the extent that money market institutions provide value to the economy in the form of circumvention of prohibitions on interest and other legal restrictions on financial arrangements, the traditional welfare analysis would count their demise as a benefit rather than a cost.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I have to admit I haven’t tried explaining that to a money market fund manager.

speaker: LACKER
text: The hard question now, I think, concerns the possibility of deflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have seen negative overall inflation since energy prices peaked in July—it was 1.8 percent for the PCE at an annual rate since then and 4½ percent before today’s release for the CPI—and the core indexes have softened notably as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: I still think we are going to be able to avoid this fairly easily, but I do not think the risk is negligible.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is one of the most dangerous prospects we face right now, and we have to pay very close attention to it.

speaker: LACKER
text: The reason I think it is going to be easy to avoid is that we have seen declines in core inflation before when energy prices fell—mid-2005 and late 2006 are recent examples.

speaker: LACKER
text: Further, compensation growth does not yet appear to be slowing rapidly, although those data are fairly dated and so it is hard to sense what the last couple of months are going to look like.

speaker: LACKER
text: The key to avoiding deflation, of course, is our ability to shape expectations about the future course of monetary policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I had a spirited discussion about this last night over salad with Governor Kohn and Mr. Eggertsson.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is essentially what all the models tell you—that staying out of a deflationary equilibrium requires commitment to paths for the monetary base that are inconsistent with a steadily falling price level and that commitment to keeping the nominal interest rate low is not sufficient.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, it is sort of hard to get a handle on this.

speaker: LACKER
text: It took me a while, but the key to thinking about this is that models with Taylor-type rules embed within them the perfect credibility of inflation returning in the long run or over a medium term to the targeted rate that is built into the Taylor reaction function.

speaker: LACKER
text: If instead you take those models and just allow arbitrary fiscal and monetary policy rules, that is when you are forced to face the result that committing to an infinite series of zero nominal rates is not sufficient and that you have to keep a monetary aggregate from declining along with the price level.

speaker: LACKER
text: One way to think about this is that it is just like preventing inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: To prevent inflation, we have to prevent expectations that the value of money will fall in the future.

speaker: LACKER
text: To rule that out, we have to rule out expectations that the quantity of money is going to rise continually, and we do that with interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: This line of reasoning is different from the reasoning you get in a Phillips curve with purely backward-looking expectations, where you have a recursive relationship between real growth and inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Instead, in any model with a little forward-looking stuff, you have expectations driving things.

speaker: LACKER
text: Preventing deflation is the same thing—preventing expectations that the value of money will rise indefinitely.

speaker: LACKER
text: To do that you need to prevent expectations that the quantity of money will fall indefinitely, and you would like to do that with low interest rates, but you cannot at the zero bound.

speaker: LACKER
text: So you have to influence expectations about the future course of the base.

speaker: LACKER
text: This to me is the simple intuition for that.

speaker: LACKER
text: All of this is just to suggest that our ability to communicate is going to be crucial.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All of these strategies are time-inconsistent, of course.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we have to be willing as a Committee to sit here and accept higher-than-normal inflation ex post.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just point that out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have to ask ourselves if we would be willing and if the public would be willing to accept that.

speaker: LACKER
text: “Time-inconsistent” is another way to say that they require commitment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m just saying that there are also different ways to do it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We could also just target a higher inflation rate, which is probably another way of doing it.

speaker: LACKER
text: You could target the inflation rate not falling.

speaker: LACKER
text: I mean, we don’t have to go all the way.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is the subtle thing about this.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the pure Taylor rule overstates our credibility, but people do not think that we are going to follow it perfectly.

speaker: LACKER
text: They don’t have very diffuse priors over what policies.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are somewhere in-between, and I think bolstering that credibility is important.

speaker: LACKER
text: Something I was going to say in the policy round—given that we haven’t announced a target, we ought to try that first.

speaker: LACKER
text: That comes first, before saying that we are going to move our target up for a little while.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would just comment—and I think that your point is a good one—as we go forward, we are going to be thinking hard about how to influence expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Your point is also right, as we discussed earlier, about why we need additional policies besides our zero rate policy, either other kinds of quantitative policies that are obviously linked to base movements or fiscal or other policies as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I don’t think there is that much disagreement on the analysis.

speaker: LACKER
text: No, I do not think so.

speaker: LACKER
text: The point I was making about the base is that none of those is sufficient to rule out deflation without specifying what the base is.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The reports from my contacts have been very weak for several weeks now.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Sadly, I feel as though the data have been catching up with the anecdotal comments that I have been receiving for a while.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I have been hearing a lot of comments along the lines of “orders have fallen off a sheer cliff,” “the lights were suddenly switched off,” and “my business is dead in the water.” One thing I have noticed is that the negative outlook has spread to more and more corners of the economy, even those corners that had remained robust for a relatively longer period.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: For example, one of my directors, who runs a manufacturing company and exports 70 percent of his products, is a producer of highly specialized equipment that is used in steel production.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: He has few competitors and no debt, and until recently he was feeling very comfortable with a two and a half year backlog.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Last week he reported that the backlog has essentially vanished.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: His customers’ problems have now become his problems.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This has become a typical refrain.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We had become used to hearing companies talk about their desire to hold onto liquidity.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Now businesses are also focused on how they are going to protect themselves in this weakening economy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Even businesses with a healthy amount of cash are cutting back sharply on investment, hiring, and production plans.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In this environment, it is clear that forecasts need to be revised down sharply.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like the Greenbook, my own projection, which seemed pretty dire just a month ago, has also been revised down sharply with the incoming data and anecdotes.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The question now is how long and how deep a decline we will experience.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At the same time, it also remains difficult to judge how far disinflation will go.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My projection sees substantial output gaps and energy prices that are likely to remain low.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: That has caused me to lower my inflation projection further as well.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My inflation forecast now is clearly below desirable levels for much of 2009.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Still, it looks as though the risks remain very much to the downside for output and inflation, if only because further downside misses are getting more and more problematic.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The insurance metaphor, I think, has been exhausted.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We are now more in a situation of treating mass trauma.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Perhaps some of our actions will later be judged as having gone too far.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But in my view, right now it clearly is better to ensure that the treatment is large enough rather than risk falling short.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Third District economic news is similar to the national news.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our December business outlook survey, which remains confidential until Thursday, will post another very weak number.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In November the number was minus 39.3.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The December reading will be released, and it will be minus 32.9—somewhat better but still deeply in negative territory.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: New orders, shipments, and employment are all very weak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Price indexes on the survey have fallen appreciably below zero for the past two months and are near their lowest levels since we began the survey in 1969.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is after being at nearly their highest levels over the same interval just a few months ago.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, firms are expecting prices to continue to decline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: November’s reading marked the first time that the future prices-paid index has been negative.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The mood is generally quite grim.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Greenbook also paints a very bleak picture.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would like to think that this isn’t the most likely outcome, but it is increasingly difficult to argue against that based on recent economic data.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have revised down my own forecast, of course.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although I’m still not quite as pessimistic as the Greenbook, I admit that the Greenbook is no longer an outlier as I am used to thinking about it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The forecasts for output are nearly as bad as or are worse than the economy experienced in 1974-75.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Inflation has moderated significantly, and near-term inflationary expectations have also moderated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our December Livingston survey participants see CPI inflation averaging just ½ percent in 2009.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the Greenbook, forecasted core inflation will be just over 1 percent next year and will decelerate to ¾ percent in 2010.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: With the growth prospects so weak and inflation expectations decelerating, the appropriate real funds rate obviously will probably decline, raising the possibility as we discussed yesterday that the zero bound on nominal rates will pose a problem for us.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At the same time, since mid-September the effective funds rate has been trading well below the FOMC’s target of 1 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As we discussed yesterday, we are effectively conducting monetary policy through quantitative easing—by which I mean an expansion of the Fed’s balance sheet by both conventional and nonconventional means.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have no objections in principle to this easing process; but as I discussed yesterday, I believe that we need to acknowledge publicly that we are now in a new regime, with a new way of implementing monetary policy, and that it is a deliberate choice of this Committee.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Otherwise we risk confusing market participants or implying that we are no longer in control of monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But in doing so, we need to communicate how this policy will be conducted going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Board of Governors and the FOMC will have to decide how they will handle the governance issues surrounding this new regime.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It seems clear to me that monetary policy determinations should remain in the purview of the FOMC regardless of whether we are using standard or nonstandard policy tools.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, I think we have to come to grips with three very important policy issues at this juncture.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They include (1) how to implement monetary policy via an expansion of our balance sheets for standard fed funds targeting; (2) what decisionmaking process the FOMC and the Board should use in implementing these policies via the balance sheet expansion; and (3) how to communicate all of these to the public in a transparent and, most important, credible fashion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I agree with the Chairman that we need to maintain and embrace the collaborative process between the Board of Governors and the FOMC, which has been our method of moving forward during this crisis.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I remain convinced that in these times of uncertainty we need to be explicit and to communicate that monetary policy remains under the purview of the FOMC.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As we discussed yesterday, our primary goal is to set policy that yields the best economic outcomes for the economy, consistent with our dual mandate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think our history demonstrates that the institutional structure of the FOMC and clearly articulated goals and methods yield the best policy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think President Fisher at the last meeting actually proposed that, since we all knew where the economy was, we just suspend discussion and get on to what to do about it.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Forgive me for a six-week reaction function here, President Fisher, but I tend to agree with that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I will be very brief.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The points I will make have either been made or will be made, I am sure.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We are facing dysfunctional financial markets, a rapidly weakening real economy, and a very negative psychology, a darkening mood.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In addition, I am picking up in my contacts uncertainty or even questioning of what can be done and what good anything close to conventional monetary policy will do.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My board of directors, advisory councils, and other contacts reflect deepening pessimism, and many of those contacts confirm the view that consumer activity and the economy in general pulled back dramatically in September and October.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I have adjusted my forecast similarly to the Greenbook and commercial forecasters.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think it is very difficult at this point to forecast with any confidence that conditions will gel in a way necessary for a recovery.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The Greenbook sees a somewhat sharper snapback by midyear, reflecting the influence of a fiscal stimulus, than I am prepared at this time to project.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Our forecast assumes a protracted period of weakness through all of 2009, somewhat more along the lines of the “more financial stress” scenario in the Greenbook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding financial markets, I would just comment that the pressures on the hedge fund sector have clearly not abated and may be intensifying.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Over the weekend we picked up rumors of a Fed intervention that has not been discussed here, so I presume that it was just a rumor.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Nonetheless, rumors were circulating that a major hedge fund group was about to collapse and that our people were “in,” so to speak, over the weekend.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As Bill mentioned yesterday, the Madoff scandal certainly has not helped the picture regarding hedge funds.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding risks, it is not my baseline scenario, but the risk of deflation obviously cannot be ignored, and the apparent speed of disinflation is quite a concern.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The Atlanta staff prepared several forecast scenarios, and there were some plausible downside scenarios that really were quite ugly.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So to preview later comments, I think the balance of risks at this point is decidedly to the downside and justifies a trauma-management approach—or, in more normal terms, a risk-management approach—of acting aggressively at this meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you, and if there has been any intervention in hedge funds, the Chairman is unaware of it.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am relieved to hear that.

speaker: FISHER
text: He just wanted you to know about it, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The Tenth District’s economy, like the others, has systematically worsened.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our retail sales are down.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The housing market is certainly not improving, and manufacturing has weakened.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In our two stronger areas, energy is showing a pretty good slowdown with these falloffs in prices, and rigs are being stacked; the agricultural sector is also feeling the pressure as commodity prices fall.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So it is uniformly poor.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As far as the national economy and outlook go, I have no major differences with the outlook that has been presented by others.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would tell you that we have done different projections ourselves.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think a lot depends on what will be developed on the fiscal side as we move from here, and I am kind of waiting to see about that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I do have one other comment and perhaps request as we think about this, and it follows on yesterday’s conversation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It strikes me, as I look broadly and see what’s happening in our own region, that the intermediation process is broken as it goes through the banking industry and then more broadly than that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The deleveraging process that is under way is actually accelerating—it is worsening and complicating our ability to fix the intermediation process.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As a result, we as the central bank are going around that process as we try to get credit working, and I understand that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But it does have consequences—some good for those particular markets where we’re bringing intermediation forward but also perhaps some not so good as other sectors are left behind in that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: My point is that we really do have to focus, in working on the fiscal side with the Treasury or whomever, on fixing the broken intermediation process, and that is the banking industry.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I know we are working with the TARP.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It needs some additional work.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But out of that comes my request.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We spent a fair amount of time yesterday talking about the Japanese experience.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I wonder if we wouldn’t benefit if we looked at the Nordic experience of the early ’90s—how you go in, take a look at that, and how you conduct policy around that—and have a discussion among ourselves because I think there are some lessons there that we might learn to our benefit as we move forward from here.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That’s a suggestion I have, not just my report on the District.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It was a good suggestion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have looked at that example and had a chance to talk with Stefan Ingves, who is the Governor of the Central Bank of Sweden and was very much involved in that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It was a very good and prompt response, but it was different from our current situation in that the banks were already mostly insolvent and no longer functioning when the government intervened.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They took the standard steps of taking off nonperforming loans—so the usual process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They still had a significant recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the basic lessons are there, but we have some characteristics in this particular episode—banks still functioning, the complexity of the assets, and so on—that make it even more difficult.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I agree with that, but at the same time, I see the similarity.

speaker: HOENIG
text: When you don’t go in and try to drive it back quickly, you get the Japanese outcome of prolonging it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I don’t know where the banks are yet, but I know that things are getting worse and that the intermediation process is broken.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So just maybe there is something in-between—something that can be done that forces outcomes for some of these banks.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Even though they are not insolvent as such, we have poured a ton of equity into those institutions, and I am not sure if we shouldn’t have added some other elements to that that might have helped on the other side.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you can indulge just one more observation, which is that one thing we learn from these episodes is that the political economy matters tremendously.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The public is very reluctant to get involved in putting money into banks, and only when they become persuaded that doing so is essential do you get that result.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In Japan it took a long time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In Sweden it was much quicker, and that’s an important element.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A two-hander from President Bullard.

speaker: BULLARD
text: May I just make one comment on that?

speaker: BULLARD
text: For those of you who have not read about the Nordic experience, Seppo Honkapohja, who is a member of the Board of the Bank of Finland, has given a speech within the last two months.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You can probably go to the Bank of Finland web page.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There may be other information, but that is just one summary from a person who lived through it and has been involved in policy for a long time.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In my view, cumulative recessionary dynamics are deeply entrenched, with mounting job losses leading to weaker consumer spending, tighter credit, more job losses, and so on; and this nasty set of economic linkages is gaining momentum.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Like the Greenbook, I anticipate a long period of decline, and in fact, the consensus forecast is that we’re now in the longest and one of the deepest postwar recessions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I hope that a recovery will begin in the middle of next year, but the risks seem skewed to the downside for several reasons.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, compared with the average recession, we face unusually difficult financial conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My contacts complain bitterly that even firms with sterling credit ratings have difficulty securing credit.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Some banks appear reluctant to lend because financial markets are skeptical about the quality of their assets and their reported net worth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: An accounting joke concerning the balance sheets of many financial institutions is now making the rounds, and it summarizes the situation as follows: On the left-hand side, nothing is right; and on the right-hand side, nothing is left.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The second factor skewing risk to the downside is the unusually fearful and pessimistic psychology that’s developed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One director, who heads a national department chain, predicts carnage in the retail sector after year-end, as stores close after trying to hold on through the holidays.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although some stores have been able to keep sales up to reasonable levels, heavy price discounting will translate into huge losses.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Businesses have also generally turned very cautious, hoarding cash and slashing capital spending.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A third factor that worries me is that, in contrast to many past recessions, this one is global in nature, and the fact that it’s a worldwide slowdown—while lowering commodity prices, which is good—is also going to make it harder for us to pull out.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Turning just very briefly to the labor market, the Beveridge curve chart that Stephanie presented during her briefing suggests that we have seen an unusually large increase in the unemployment rate recently in comparison with the decline in job openings, at least in the JOLTS data.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think one interpretation might be that the unemployment rate has risen in part because we have had an unusual rise in labor force participation during this recession.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Labor force participation has been higher than would be expected, particularly for three demographic groups: young adults, married women, and older workers nearing retirement.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Analysis by my staff estimates that this rise in participation could reflect behavioral responses to unusual credit constraints and wealth declines.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Specifically, young adults aged 20 to 24 years appear to be entering the labor force in unusual numbers, and that might reflect diminished access to student loans.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Similarly, more married women are entering the labor force, and that’s a possible reflection of diminished access to home equity and credit card loans.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Finally, an unusually large number of older workers are in the labor market, and that may reflect the negative wealth shock associated with the collapse of housing values and the plummeting stock market.

speaker: YELLEN
text: All in all, I expect the anomalous increase in labor force participation to put continued upward pressure on the unemployment rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to inflation, developments since our October meeting have again lowered the outlook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’m particularly concerned about the disinflationary effect of actual and prospective economic slack.

speaker: YELLEN
text: During the postwar period, core PCE inflation has actually fallen at least ¾ percentage point in every single year in which unemployment has averaged 7½ percent or more.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given that in each of the next two years the unemployment rate is predicted to average at least 8 percent, it seems quite likely that by the end of 2010 core inflation will have fallen at least 1½ percentage points.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That creates a very real risk of deflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So under these circumstances, I definitely believe that we should do everything in our power to stimulate aggregate demand.

speaker: EVANS
text: As gloomy as our last meeting was, conditions have deteriorated substantially further since then.

speaker: EVANS
text: Practically all of my contacts reported that economic events had turned sharply lower once again in the last three to five weeks.

speaker: EVANS
text: This goes well beyond the auto sector and other parts of the District that have been struggling for some time.

speaker: EVANS
text: The most optimistic comment from my directors was this, “At least Iowa is going to hell slower than everywhere else.” It is tough to follow that accounting joke, you know—that was good.

speaker: EVANS
text: More seriously, the most optimistic theme I heard from a number of business contacts went something like this, “We are conserving cash and furiously cutting costs by year-end.

speaker: EVANS
text: But we hope to pause in the first quarter and take stock of where conditions appear to be heading.

speaker: EVANS
text: Then, we will act accordingly.” Frankly, I doubt such a wait-and-see pause in cost-cutting will occur that soon.

speaker: EVANS
text: For the purposes of this meeting and our actions over the next few months, I agree with the main thrust of the Greenbook projection.

speaker: EVANS
text: We are facing large contractions in the next two quarters, and I don’t expect to see meaningfully positive growth before the fourth quarter.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think we need substantial further accommodation after today’s meeting.

speaker: EVANS
text: I see the timing and the size of those actions for the most part being shaped by the large recessionary forces in train and the enormous financial headwinds.

speaker: EVANS
text: The disinflationary forces in play clearly are strong, but currently I do not expect that they will prove large enough to generate outright deflation.

speaker: EVANS
text: In terms of my earlier question about the Greenbook forecast—as I understand the way it was put together—if the quantitative easing helps, monetary policy would be somewhere between the funds rate at zero and the optimal control.

speaker: EVANS
text: So, in fact, it would be a little better than I first suspected.

speaker: EVANS
text: Inflation would be somewhat above that path.

speaker: EVANS
text: That might be a useful benchmark to watch for if we are fortunate enough for the forecast to be that stable, but time will tell.

speaker: EVANS
text: Quantitative easing should also lead to an increase in the monetary base.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t know if there was any lasting conflict between your comments and President Lacker’s, but I think that what we have contemplated will lead to the base increasing and that will generate expectations about inflation beyond just Taylor-rule dynamics, I would guess.

speaker: EVANS
text: In fact, there is certainly a lot of discussion and criticism out there that our balance sheet is going to lead to large inflationary risks.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t share that, given how I think we will unwind the programs.

speaker: EVANS
text: But that certainly would help, and it would move us in that direction.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I will keep an open mind on deflationary risk.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, as just about everyone has said—and I certainly agree—the near-term outlook is grim.

speaker: STERN
text: Virtually all the anecdotes of any consequence that I have received recently have been negative.

speaker: STERN
text: Payroll employment has been, obviously, dropping significantly; and if you look at the trajectory, if that kind of trajectory continues for any length of time beyond the next month or so, it will surpass the declines in employment that we typically have seen, certainly in the last three recessions.

speaker: STERN
text: My outlook for the real economy for the next five or six quarters has essentially the same profile as the current Greenbook.

speaker: STERN
text: I do have a somewhat better recovery starting in the second or third quarter of 2010, but at this point I have to admit that it is more hope than conviction.

speaker: STERN
text: It is based on a diminution of many of the factors that are currently restraining the economy and producing the significant contraction that is under way.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as the inflation outlook is concerned, I don’t have quite as much disinflation as the Greenbook does, but I wouldn’t say that we are all that far apart at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: One footnote to that: I do get a lot of comments and questions along the lines that President Evans mentioned— “Gee, with that expansion in your balance sheet, with all those reserves, aren’t we going to have a lot of inflation in the future?” Maybe I ought to say “yes” to that question.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In the Eighth District, there is a clear and sharp downturn, as in the national picture.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There is a clear turn to survival strategies, and you really see that when key CEOs and other figures start talking about lower capital expenditures for 2009, cutting the lower levels in 2008 in half or more.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that’s very consistent with the Greenbook.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The effects on our District from any auto restructuring may be substantial, and that is something I have ratcheted up here in the last few months.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A common theme among all contacts—and it echoes some of what has been said around the table here—is that rate cuts at this point will have no effect on the macroeconomy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Their thinking is, well, of course, since short-term Treasuries are trading at zero—I think one-month Treasuries actually hit zero here a bit ago—they are not going to have any effect.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But as Governor Duke pointed out yesterday, and I think this is an important concern, the impact on bank profitability may be substantial, exactly at the wrong time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: First Vice President Cumming picked that up, too.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that is a concern.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it suggests favoring an option of de-emphasizing the federal funds rate as a target at this meeting, as we will get to in the policy discussion.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But then you might not trigger this prime rate cut that would otherwise normally accompany a major move by the Fed.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the national picture, I expect a sharp downturn in the fourth quarter and the first quarter.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Expectations are extremely negative now and extremely fluid.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that is probably the biggest factor facing us going forward into 2009.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The expectations are so fluid that they portend a deflationary environment if we do not control the situation very soon.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am also very concerned about the global aspect because we haven’t really seen this kind of coordination across the globe in the rapid movement to probably zero interest rates.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t think we really know what that means going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We are going to be looking at bad news coming in at least until summer, and we have no way at this point to signal a reaction to that bad news via normal policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is the gravity of the situation, and in some ways it is the downside of a preemptive policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Had I been on the Committee earlier this year, I would have supported the preemptive policy to try to avoid this situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But one downside of it is that you do not have the ability to continually react as bad news comes in.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In sum, I think we are moving to a Japanese-style deflationary, zero nominal interest rate, situation at an alarming pace.

speaker: BULLARD
text: To stay in the game and control expectations, we need a Volcker- like transformation, something like—although the situation is different—the ’79 announcement, which knocked private-sector priors off the idea that they should trigger all reactions to announcements on nominal interest rates.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You need a dramatic move that emphasizes this new reality.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Continued focus on the federal funds rate at this point would not face that reality.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Above all, we have to establish in the minds of the private sector—and maybe in our own minds as well—that we control medium-term inflation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We should take the attitude that we can create the inflation we need to stay near target by one means or another.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think, actually, this may be an excellent time to set the inflation target, although it sounds as though we are drifting away from that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But if I can argue for it for a few minutes here, I think it might have an important effect on the navigation through the recession during 2009.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Of course, in normal times, to undertake some action like that, we would want a lot of study, and we would want to have time to talk it through with the Congress and other interested parties, as we would for interest on reserves.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But we don’t have that luxury right now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We want to take the action now to help control the situation, and I think we could sell that as a work in progress, which can be modified later.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But we do want to keep these expectations under control in this very fluid situation.

speaker: FISHER
text: President Rosengren talked about micro behavior, and at the beginning, First Vice President Cumming talked about the hunkering-down mentality.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have been focused on the microeconomic behavioral responses to our current situation.

speaker: FISHER
text: As one of my CEO contacts outside my region said, we are basically all, in his words, “chasing the anvil down the stairs,” and that is that the behavioral responses of both businesses and consumers are driving us into a slow-growth cul-de-sac and a deflationary trap.

speaker: FISHER
text: One CEO I talked with was quite pleased that he could borrow $40 million over the weekend for a total of $250.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is great from a commercial paper standpoint; he is an A1/P1 issuer.

speaker: FISHER
text: However, were he to go to the longer-term debt markets, it would cost him 7½ percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: So they can finance their daily operations easily.

speaker: FISHER
text: But in terms of their long-term planning, they and others are responding—and I see this uniformly across my contacts—out of concern about the high cost of debt and the spreads over Treasuries, by doing what any businesswoman or businessman would do.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are planning on less cap-ex, and they are cutting back on their plans for acquisitions of the weak, which they would like to take advantage of under the current circumstances.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are also responding to the situation by cutting back on head count.

speaker: FISHER
text: So, Chris, there is very much a hunkering-down mentality, not just in my District but across the country.

speaker: FISHER
text: That leads to further economic weakness—that plus the fact that they are chary about issuing and paying for things with shares in a very weak market.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am hearing more and more worries about their pension liabilities and how they are going to be able to finance those.

speaker: FISHER
text: Obviously this is leading to the kind of economic behavior that none of us would like to see.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the consumer side, you see a similar behavioral pattern.

speaker: FISHER
text: It seems that after Black Friday, according to my sources, there was weaker behavior than one had expected.

speaker: FISHER
text: The spending pulse data that I get from one of the large credit card companies reflect what one would expect under these circumstances—that is, a shift to nonbranded products, smaller purchases of items, a rotation out of credit cards to debit cards and cash payments according to the pay cycle, and overall an expectation, on both the business and the consumer side, that things will get cheaper if they wait longer and they postpone either their cap-ex or their consumer purchases.

speaker: FISHER
text: The one ray of sunshine that I was able to find is that one large law firm, Cravath, has announced that it is not increasing its billing rates in 2009, [laughter] and other law firms are actually planning to respond by cutting their billing rates.

speaker: FISHER
text: One woman whom I know summarized it this way: “This is the divorce from hell.

speaker: FISHER
text: My net worth has been cut in half, but I am still stuck with my husband.”

speaker: KOHN
text: I am not going to even try to top either of those anecdotes or jokes.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree certainly with the thrust of the comments around the room.

speaker: KOHN
text: The economy is in a steep decline.

speaker: KOHN
text: There was a break in confidence somewhere in September that took what had been a gradual decline in employment, production, and output and made it much, much, much, much steeper.

speaker: KOHN
text: The feedback loop between the financial markets and the real economy just intensified—turned up many, many notches at that time.

speaker: KOHN
text: Households and businesses, as President Fisher was remarking, are very worried, and they are acting in a way to protect themselves.

speaker: KOHN
text: They have cut back on spending, and they have cut back on lending.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the response of businesses is particularly interesting.

speaker: KOHN
text: They responded very, very rapidly to the falloff in demand with cuts in employment and production.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we are not even getting the sort of automatic stabilizer effect that we usually get from a buildup in inventories and a bit of labor hoarding as demand drops.

speaker: KOHN
text: Thus businesses’ actions are just accentuating the weakness.

speaker: KOHN
text: As many have remarked, the weakness is global, everywhere, including in emerging- market economies where, as Shaghil showed us, the inflow of capital has slowed substantially.

speaker: KOHN
text: There is no real region to lead the globe out of this swamp we are in.

speaker: KOHN
text: Financial markets remain very strained.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think of particular concern are the securitization markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: When they are not operating, a lot of credit to households and businesses won’t be available at the same time that the banks are tightening up very sharply.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have seen in these charts that household and business borrowers with anything less than very high credit scores are just finding credit either extraordinarily expensive or unavailable.

speaker: KOHN
text: As a consequence, a very sizable output gap has opened up.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we can see that the decline is going to remain steep for some time.

speaker: KOHN
text: The multiplier–accelerator effects of the drop in demand we have seen over the last couple of months have to feed back through consumption and investment.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think we have seen the full effect of the tightening in credit conditions and the decline in wealth from the end of September on.

speaker: KOHN
text: You can see the continuing economic decline in the initial claims data, the weekly IP, and the anecdotes we heard around the table on sales; and financial markets are going to remain impaired for a while despite our best efforts to open them up.

speaker: KOHN
text: There are huge losses in the capital of intermediaries to absorb, so folks will be very cautious about making loans.

speaker: KOHN
text: As long as investors, savers, households, and businesses see the economy in steep decline, the fear that is gripping the financial markets and the economy isn’t going to abate very rapidly.

speaker: KOHN
text: Inflation is decelerating across a broad front, and that is going to continue.

speaker: KOHN
text: Economic slack will be increasing, cost pressures will be abating, and the ability to pass through cost increases will be highly constrained.

speaker: KOHN
text: So far, longer-term inflation expectations seem to have been reasonably well anchored, though they are very hard to measure.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I agree with President Bullard that we are going to need to watch this very, very closely for signs of a disinflationary dynamic taking hold.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think what happens to the economy and inflation over the latter part of next year is extremely uncertain.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have huge changes in forecasts in very short periods of time, and I suspect, like the staff, that the improvement in financial markets and the rebound in the economy will be gradual, in part reflecting the limited power of monetary policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: But even if we thought that a sharper rebound next year was a distinct possibility, I don’t think it would matter very much for our policy purposes here today.

speaker: KOHN
text: The trajectory, the economic decline, the extent of the output gap, and the degree of disinflation in train all imply that our task at this time is to try to limit economic weakness.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, the latest leg of deterioration, which began in mid-September, is showing few signs of abating, as Governor Kohn suggested.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the November retail sales data look like a head fake.

speaker: WARSH
text: Revisions to September and October, as the Greenbook suggested, make us think that November was probably worse and December worse still.

speaker: WARSH
text: So in some ways I think our job is difficult because the weakness seems to be accelerating.

speaker: WARSH
text: Globally, the deterioration is found everywhere.

speaker: WARSH
text: The data are playing catch-up.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am less optimistic that foreign activity will perform as well as the Greenbook suggests and that foreign activity will respond in 2010 because of lags in policy response and less flexibility in their labor markets, their product markets, and their political markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: The depth and the degree of the fall in data and policymakers’ expectations overseas, particularly in Asia, are remarkable, shocking even, and I think we are likely to see policy responses there that are hard to judge but are likely to be changing pretty quickly.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of U.S. households, real household net worth has collapsed about 15 percent or so through the end of the third quarter—more than in 2001 and more than in 1974.

speaker: WARSH
text: Ongoing declines in financial markets and house prices are likely to depress wealth further in the fourth quarter and beyond.

speaker: WARSH
text: So-called savings from lower energy prices look as though they pale in comparison to what else is happening to U.S. household balance sheets.

speaker: WARSH
text: As we have discussed before, every asset everywhere in the world is being revalued, and households are feeling it.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of financial markets, I will underscore what Dan suggested and what Bill suggested yesterday—the significant overall deterioration in conditions.

speaker: WARSH
text: We all have a tendency at this point in the year to say, “Well, there are a lot of year-end effects, and we are not going to really know until we get through this period.” We have had baby versions of year-end effects in the quarter-end effects in almost every meeting that we have had, and I have been a little dismissive of those.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say that there does appear to be more year-end stuff going on in these markets than there has been since this period of weakness began.

speaker: WARSH
text: If you think about the two former investment banks that have balance sheets and year- ends that close at the end of November, this is the last quarter in which they will have that.

speaker: WARSH
text: They have had more demands and more interest in, in effect, renting out their balance sheet as their customers’ balance sheets end in December than they ever have had.

speaker: WARSH
text: The prices that are being paid for them to rent their balance sheets—to take exposures off the balance sheets of their clients—suggest that maybe, just maybe, the year-end effects are more significant this time than they were in the previous six or seven quarters.

speaker: WARSH
text: It doesn’t give me a ton of optimism, but in January, market functioning could look a little better, and I think that would be the best news we have seen for a while.

speaker: WARSH
text: You have heard me say before that, until we see market functioning improving and until we see these markets clearing, it is unrealistic to expect the real economy to turn.

speaker: WARSH
text: I still think that is true.

speaker: WARSH
text: Turning to two final items, inflation and the fiscal package—on the inflation front, although there are risks in this environment for prices to fall below those consistent with price stability, I still believe that these risks are not likely to materialize in the medium term.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I take stock of, but ultimately discount, the Greenbook’s deflation alternative simulation.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the fiscal front, more, bigger, faster is what is going to happen inevitably to what I would describe as the first fiscal package of 2009.

speaker: WARSH
text: The trillion dollar number over two years, which is now being bandied about, is larger than the Greenbook forecast and looks almost assured, with a greater share going to the states in my view than in the Greenbook forecast, more toward public infrastructure, perhaps less toward tax cuts on a relative basis than in the Greenbook, but bigger.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would be surprised if that initial package isn’t supplemented through larger annual appropriations and another stimulus package, if not by the end of 2009 then by 2010.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a result, my own sense would be that the 2010 deficit is likely to be significantly larger than the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now, knowing the precise contours of this fiscal package is tough.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say the only good news is that the duration of the slowdown is likely to suggest that the fiscal package may end up being somewhat more permanent in its incentives and somewhat more permanent in its effects; and I suspect, because of that, it is likely to provide some good news to the economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I wouldn’t expect that to happen in the next twelve or eighteen months, other than perhaps a bit of benefit on the arithmetic.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of changing the overall contour, pace, and strength of the resilient economy, I would say that is still quite a way off.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: President Lockhart’s forecast about what members would say about the forecasts I think has turned out to be right, and I certainly don’t want to disappoint.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I agree with what others have said, and I think most everything has been said about the intensification of the recessionary flames around the world.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: What I will do is just quickly look at it from the perspective of part of the banks’ balance sheets and the things that may not be left on those balance sheets, to just underscore how I think this is going to be protracted for the financial services sector for a while.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On the consumer side, as many people have mentioned, the very sharp step down in employment, the very large job losses, the increases in the unemployment rate, and the decreases in wealth have been leading to very significant increases in consumer delinquencies and very high roll rates—that is, people who become delinquent rolling directly into charge-off.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: This is happening not only on the credit card side and on a lot of different parts of the consumer side but also in mortgages, for which we are seeing exactly the same kind of thing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Although the most recent numbers that came out from the Mortgage Bankers Association suggested some stabilization in foreclosure starts, that actually had more to do with the laws in various states slowing down that process rather than any real change in the underlying economics.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Of course, we still have a lot of option ARM types of resets that will be coming through in 2009.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So a lot of pressure is there, and as was mentioned, housing prices are still going down.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We haven’t yet seen as much of an actual downturn in commercial real estate, but undoubtedly that will occur as fewer people are shopping in shopping malls and as a lot of other commercial real estate projects don’t have the payoffs that people expect.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Also, an enormous amount of refinancing is going to be necessary during the next few months, and having to pay an additional 600 or 800 basis points really changes the economics of a lot of these projects, if they can even get the refinancing at an additional 600 to 800 basis points.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: For leveraged loans, another piece of the balance sheet, as people have said, there is very little activity going on in takeovers.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The only positive there is that the failure of certain deals has taken some of the pressure off certain banks’ balance sheets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On the commercial and industrial side, as we have noted, the investment-grade market for debt issuance seems to have maintained itself, but that is really one of the few markets that is there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If any challenges come in there, it could be very, very difficult for firms to finance investment.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We certainly have seen the spreads going up recently, even if the volume has come back a bit.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But as we have seen in the non-investment-grade part, the spreads have blown out, and the financing is not there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That tends to be a little more of what many banks have on their balance sheets, and so I think that is representative of the challenges that the banks are going to have.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That suggests that we have a lot of challenges in banking and financial institutions’ balance sheets to come that have nothing to do with any particular level of assets or accounting issues but just real economic factors that are going to be affecting the balance sheets.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So the credit headwinds are going to be very, very strong for a number of quarters going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The points that President Rosengren made are extremely important ones.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have to think about, as we move to the zero lower bound, how that is going to affect behavior of financial institutions.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Certainly, the staff memos were good on addressing some issues, but I think that other things that have been mentioned, like imposing minimums or floors on interest rates on loans, we have not carefully analyzed or really understand well.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There may be a variety of other responses that we don’t understand well that we really do need to get a better handle on, both to see how the effects of traditional monetary policy change—the transmission mechanism—and to think about the nontraditional aspects of monetary policy that we would be undertaking by using our balance sheet.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So where can we use it most effectively?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If the financial institutions are changing their behavior, we need to be cognizant of that and think about where we need to try to unfreeze markets if we are going to be using our balance sheet in that way, and I think it is very important that we do so.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I will underscore also what other people have said about the great importance of clearly articulating what we are doing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is not that we have given up and that the Fed is impotent but that, through changes in our balance sheet, we can be quite potent in particular markets and in general.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That then brings us to whether we can be too potent and raise inflation concerns.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Exactly as President Stern said, we should be so lucky to have that as our problem.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We do need to make sure that we maintain credibility and show that we feel that we can and do act to offset concerns about deflation.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is very difficult to tell what the price-level evolution is likely to be over the next year, but I do think that there is a real concern about that, and we have to take that very, very seriously going forward.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we would, obviously, be able to get out of these different programs, and we need to think about getting out of them at some point.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But right now the key is getting into the programs, using the nontraditional approaches, to make sure that we offset a deflationary psychology that could develop.

speaker: DUKE
text: Yesterday I talked about the income statement of the banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: I would like to talk a bit about the balance sheets now.

speaker: DUKE
text: Up to this point, for the small and medium-sized community banks, it has been pretty much business as usual.

speaker: DUKE
text: But now even those banks are finding it increasingly difficult to lend.

speaker: DUKE
text: Community banks and regional banks are trying, but it is tough.

speaker: DUKE
text: Funding is tight and expensive.

speaker: DUKE
text: It costs 3½ percent to keep a CD and 4 percent and up to attract one.

speaker: DUKE
text: The smaller banks are especially bitter about pricing against Citi and those nonbanks that have recently converted to bank holding company and thrift holding company charters.

speaker: DUKE
text: For a bank to qualify for TARP funding, the examiners are raising the bar on noncore funding.

speaker: DUKE
text: One bank reported a meeting with both the OCC and the Fed in which the OCC criticized, and the Fed defended, the bank’s use of the discount window.

speaker: DUKE
text: Examiners are raising the bar on capital: 12 is the new 10 on risk-based capital.

speaker: DUKE
text: Borrowers are not in nearly as good shape as they were.

speaker: DUKE
text: The best credits are choosing not to borrow, and they are adjusting their plans so that they get through on their own cash flow.

speaker: DUKE
text: So the requests coming into the banks are more and more likely to be desperation requests—loans to cover operating losses or to meet payroll.

speaker: DUKE
text: Cracks are appearing in C&I loans.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some banks are exiting loans to entire industries, especially auto dealers, marine and construction trades, and retail.

speaker: DUKE
text: The performance of commercial real estate, especially retail properties, is deteriorating.

speaker: DUKE
text: Hospitality is falling off rapidly, and office buildings are expected to be next.

speaker: DUKE
text: Apartments are still okay, and all of this is in addition to problems with construction loans.

speaker: DUKE
text: Lower mortgage rates are helping refinance, but it is not the best time of the year to judge what it is going to happen with purchase activity.

speaker: DUKE
text: There are still issues with jumbos, with down payments, and with requirements for very high credit scores.

speaker: DUKE
text: As we have talked here, it occurs to me that perhaps the traditional tools of monetary policy are all directed at bank credit, and the strongest nontraditional tools that we have are addressed more to the securitization markets—the TALF and the purchase of GSEs.

speaker: DUKE
text: In this instance, most of the problems are not really caused by a cutback in bank lending but a complete collapse of the securitization markets, and so that is why these tools may be more necessary.

speaker: DUKE
text: I asked questions also about the TARP capital and got different reactions.

speaker: DUKE
text: Several bankers said that they didn’t need it, they were scared off by the ability of the Congress to change the terms at any time, and they had elected not to take it.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some took it because they thought they could leverage it into good business.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some took it as cheap insurance.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some took it to be in a position to acquire in what they see as the necessary weeding out of weaker players, and they think that should happen sooner rather than later.

speaker: DUKE
text: Several complained about delays in providing terms for smaller banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: Every single bank was adamant about the evils of mark-to- market accounting and other-than-temporary impairment.

speaker: DUKE
text: There is a big diversion between market losses and credit losses, so that leads to bankers who are afraid to buy securities because they are worried about further marks as the markets go down.

speaker: DUKE
text: But they are also unwilling to sell securities because they don’t believe that the current market price adequately reflects the potential credit losses.

speaker: DUKE
text: There is some speculation that the mark-to-market losses will absorb all of the TARP capital that was just injected, and I think that is something we might want to calculate as fourth-quarter reports come out.

speaker: DUKE
text: Then, the next big writedown is on servicing portfolios as lower rates spur refinancing activities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And thanks, everyone, for a very concise but also very informative roundtable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a coffee break until 11:30.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we reconvene, have a brief summary of our go- round, and then I will make just a few additional comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The participants noted that the economic downturn has intensified sharply recently with significant downside risks to the outlook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Recessionary dynamics have set in, with interplays among real and financial variables.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The economy is likely to contract through early next year, with considerable uncertainty about subsequent developments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumption, employment, and production indicators have weakened further.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial conditions remain very strained, with improvement in some areas, but many the same or worse.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The global economy has also slowed markedly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Looking more specifically at different sectors, credit conditions continue to tighten, with credit lines not being renewed and banks, including smaller banks, hunkering down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Securitization markets are still largely dysfunctional.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The overall deleveraging process continues to be a powerful drag on activity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Delinquencies are increasing, implying greater credit losses for banks and other lenders, with small businesses being among the borrowers facing tighter conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Banks continue to face intense balance sheet pressures and are reluctant to lend or make markets, and feedback effects from worsening credit quality to the balance sheets of financial institutions are evident.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Regarding the consumer, spending continues to contract, as households face ongoing pressures with respect to wealth, income, credit availability, and job security.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Psychology is very negative, and luxury and discretionary expenditures are being cut back.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Labor market developments have been negative as well, with accelerating job losses and participation finally declining after remaining high for a period of time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The latest housing numbers suggest a continued contraction in that sector.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The fall in mortgage rates has sparked some refinancing and purchase mortgage applications, but the longer-term impact on housing demand is not yet evident.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nonresidential construction is projected to fall significantly, reflecting poor fundamentals and tight credit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Federal fiscal policy will likely provide aid to states, including funds for infrastructure, but the size and the timing of the economic impact of that policy remain uncertain.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Manufacturing production continues to slow, along with new orders, capital spending, and business expectations; mining and drilling activities have been reacting to the decline in commodity prices, as has agricultural activity to some extent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Export demand has weakened with the sharp slowing in the global economy of recent months and the strengthening of the dollar since the summer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The sharp global slowdown, including emerging markets, will make recovery more difficult.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Manufacturing surveys show that firms expect considerable near-term weakness and declining pricing power.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, inflation looks set to decline significantly, reflecting falling commodity prices, rising slack, limited pricing power, and falling inflation expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Participants cited the risk that inflation could fall below desired levels.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is just a very quick summary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me make just a few additional comments, but I won’t add, I think, a great deal of insight to our discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will just note for the record here that the NBER has finally recognized that a recession began in December 2007.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I said in the Christmas tree lighting ceremony that they also recognized that Christmas was on December 25 last year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Committee was a little more forward-thinking.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We began cutting rates, of course, in September 2007 and did 100 basis points of cuts in January 2008.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Despite our efforts, this recession, in terms of duration and depth, is likely to be equal to or greater than the two largest previous postwar recessions, those in 1974-75 and 1981-82.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are a number of reasons that may be the case, and some of them were already discussed by the staff.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The financial conditions are the most obvious difference between this recession and the earlier ones.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A number of previous recessions have had financial headwinds of one type or another.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, the current financial crisis and housing correction bear some family relationship to the stock market decline and the capital overhang in the 2001 recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But overall, the financial aspects of this episode are, I think, much more serious than in previous cases.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To cite two aspects: One, as Governor Warsh noted, there has been a big impact on household wealth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The flow of funds accounts show a decline in nominal wealth of about 11 percent in the last year or, as he said, a decline in real wealth of about 15 percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is going to lead to an increase in saving, which would be desirable in the longer term but in the short term is going to create dislocation.

speaker: BERNANKE
