text: Two, this financial crisis has affected the intermediation of credit far more severely than any other episode since the 1930s.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have already seen a big impact on intermediary capital and bank activity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The deleveraging process is continuing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, reduced risk-taking, deleveraging, all of those things are not necessarily bad, but the adjustment process is a very difficult one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A second reason that this recession could well be more severe than the previous ones has to do with the cyclical position of monetary policy, a fact also noted by the staff.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The 1974-75 and 1981-82 recessions were basically generated by a tightening of monetary policy, and when the Federal Reserve decided to let up, essentially conditions began to rebound.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, in this case, other factors have driven the downturn.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Monetary policy was proactive in trying to promote recovery.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But given where we are today, at the zero lower bound, we are unable to ease policy in the way that we saw in those previous episodes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This suggests, as others have noted, the need for additional policy actions, either on our part or by the fiscal authorities, to get the economy moving again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, a third reason that I think this episode is particularly severe is the global nature of the downturn, which a number of people have also noted.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has always been said that, if the United States sneezes, the rest of the world catches cold.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there has always been a certain amount of coherence or synchronicity between U.S. downturns and those around the world.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the extent of the global downturn this time is really quite exceptional.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is striking that global growth over the past few years has been between 4 and 5 percent, and now the Greenbook is looking at a 1.6 percent decline for global activity in the fourth quarter and a decline of about 0.6 percent in the first quarter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is quite a big difference between what we might think of as potential and actual growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, as I said, there are a number of reasons to think that this is going to be a very severe episode and that we are far from being at the turning point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I won’t go through the sectors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have all discussed consumption, employment, housing, commercial real estate, and financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: These are all aspects of the downturn that continue to be exceptional and very worrisome as we look forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will make just a couple of comments about inflation or disinflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The forecast is for significant disinflation—perhaps not deflation, although deflation is easily within the standard errors of the forecast.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A number of factors may affect this forecast or create risks on both sides.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Stephanie talked about structural unemployment perhaps being a factor that might make the effect of slack less than otherwise.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, there may be some evidence that the Phillips curve is steeper when unemployment is high—that is, recessions tend to have a greater impact on inflation than do small changes in growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That only goes to say that there is a lot of uncertainty about exactly how far the inflation rate will fall.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although we might reach a technical deflation, I guess it is worth pointing out here that there is nothing special about zero.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is, from this point on, any further disinflation will have the effects of making a given nominal interest rate a higher real interest rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is making monetary policy de facto tighter and perhaps having debt deflation effects as the real value of debts and debt payments becomes greater as inflation falls.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Because we are already at the zero lower bound, obviously that constraint is already in play.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think we shouldn’t focus too much or focus the public too much on the deflation line, on that zero number.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is not all that consequential.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Rather, the disinflation process—and a very low rate of inflation—is a source of concern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just to summarize, I don’t think my outlook differs very significantly from what I have heard around the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the issues are what we do about it, and in that spirit, we should turn now to the policy round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me turn to Brian to introduce the monetary policy alternatives.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 4 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will be referring to the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” This package includes the October policy statement, draft policy statements for this meeting, and associated draft directives to the Desk.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternatives A and B have been revised somewhat relative to the versions that were distributed in the Bluebook, partly reflecting yesterday’s discussion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In addition, as shown in bold in paragraph 1 of alternative A, it seemed appropriate in current circumstances to incorporate a sentence on financial conditions, as the Committee has done in its recent statements; the same sentence has also been included in alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We have presented a total of four policy alternatives for your consideration.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Given the unusual circumstances, 4 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 4).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: the statements associated with all four alternatives depart to some degree from the statements that have typically been issued by the Committee in recent years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative A represents the sharpest departure.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Rather than starting with the policy action, the statement would begin by describing the economic situation, noting that the economic outlook has weakened further.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It goes on to say that inflation pressures have diminished quickly and that inflation could decline for a time below the rates that best foster economic growth and price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Reflecting what seemed to be a consensus yesterday, the sentence in brackets articulating a medium-term inflation objective has been dropped.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We have also bracketed the clause indicating that inflation could drop for a time to very low levels, partly because some Committee members might not yet be convinced that such an outcome is a serious risk at this time and to avoid raising such concerns prematurely.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The third paragraph would indicate that the Committee judges that it is not useful to set a specific target for the funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would explain that judgment by noting that, as a result of the large volume of reserves provided through liquidity programs, the federal funds rate has already declined to very low levels.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would also note that economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate for some time, avoiding the use of the “near zero” phrase.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The clause “weak economic conditions are likely to warrant” implies some conditionality, but the conditions under which rates would be raised are not spelled out.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The fourth paragraph would set out a general plan for implementing unconventional policy to support the functioning of financial markets and stimulate the economy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It reiterates that the Federal Reserve will be buying agency debt and mortgage-backed securities and indicates that those purchases could be ramped up if conditions warrant.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It indicates further that the FOMC is evaluating the potential benefits of buying longer-term Treasuries.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It also indicates that the Federal Reserve will be considering other ways of using its balance sheet to support credit markets and economic activity.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We suggested dropping the word “actively” to avoid a suggestion that a new facility will be announced imminently.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Over recent months, the discount rate has moved in lockstep with the target federal funds rate, at a level ¼ percentage point above that rate, and very recently the rates on required and excess reserves have been set essentially by formula equal to the target federal funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Because a target federal funds rate would not be established under this alternative, those formulas could not be used.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We have suggested that, under this alternative, the Board act to lower the discount rate 75 basis points, to ½ percent, and that the interest rates on required and excess reserve balances be reduced to ¼ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The positive interest rates on reserves would maintain some upward pressure, albeit perhaps modest, on the federal funds rate, consistent with a view that there are some costs in terms of financial market performance of driving the funds rate literally to zero.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The discount rate of ½ percent would maintain a fairly small penalty for borrowing at the window.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In certain substantive respects, alternative B, the next page, is similar to alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most important, federal funds would trade at about the same very low rates as in alternative A, partly because the discount and reserves interest rates, discussed in paragraph 5, would be set at the same levels as in alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, the wording of the rationale section of the statement—paragraphs 2 and 3—is essentially identical to the corresponding paragraphs for alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, alternative B differs from alternative A by explicitly setting a target range for the federal funds rate of 0 to ¼ percent, as shown in paragraph 1.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We have restructured the introduction to the discussion of unconventional policy measures in paragraph 5 so that it is generally similar to the corresponding paragraph in alterative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, the final sentence of alternative A, paragraph 4, has been substituted as the last sentence of alternative B, paragraph 5.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Both alternatives A and B would put the Committee clearly in the realm of unconventional policymaking going forward.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The various policy interest rates would be reduced to very low levels, several unconventional policy tools will already have been implemented, and the statements would indicate clearly that further unconventional tools could be deployed.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee might choose either of these alternatives if members had an outlook similar to that of the Greenbook or if they were especially concerned about the downside risks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Both alternatives would constitute somewhat more vigorous policy action than market participants anticipate for this meeting, and accordingly it is possible that financial markets would respond favorably.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On the other hand, there is some risk that confidence could be undermined if the main message that comes through is that the Federal Reserve is out of ammunition.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As was noted yesterday, such alternatives place a premium on Fed communications that convincingly indicate that the Federal Reserve can still provide monetary stimulus.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative C, on the next page, the Committee would reduce the federal funds target rate 50 basis points today.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee might choose this option if it agreed that further monetary stimulus is warranted by the evolving economic outlook but was unsure that it would be necessary, or desirable, to reduce the target federal funds rate to around zero.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The rationale for the action presented in paragraphs 2 and 3 would be fairly similar to those of alternatives A and B. Paragraph 4 notes the downside risks to the outlook and indicates that the Committee will use all available tools to promote its dual objectives, suggesting that the Committee will consider further reductions in the target federal funds rate and that further liquidity measures could be forthcoming.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You could fine-tune the message regarding the federal funds rate by explicitly indicating that you are willing to or not willing to cut the funds rate further.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under this alternative, we have assumed that the discount rate would be lowered in line with the target federal funds rate to 75 basis points; the draft included in the Bluebook erroneously indicated that the rate would be lowered to 50 basis points.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Because the FOMC would set a target rate under this alternative, we have assumed that the reserves interest rates would continue to be set via the existing formulas, so that those rates would move down to ½ percent absent further changes to the target funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As Bill noted yesterday, although these interest rates on reserves would provide some upward pressure on the funds rate, that pressure is likely to be more than offset by the large supply of reserves, and paragraph 7 notes that federal funds are likely to trade below ½ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although this approach provides a straightforward expectation for the funds rate, it has an unappealing aspect in that the Committee would be changing its target while simultaneously admitting that the target will not be hit, implicitly raising the question of the meaning of the target.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Nonetheless, this statement is likely consistent overall with market expectations, and a pronounced market reaction one way or the other seems unlikely.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative D, the Committee would keep the target federal funds rate at 1 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The rationale portion of the statement would acknowledge that the near- term outlook has deteriorated and that significant downside risks are present.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, the statement would note that the broad range of policy actions taken in recent months should help, over time, to improve credit conditions and support a return to moderate growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement would recognize that the federal funds rate would likely average significantly below the target for some time, but it would not imply that a further reduction of the target rate is being contemplated.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It thus suggests that the Committee would seek to return the actual federal funds rate to 1 percent over time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Overall, this statement would surprise market participants considerably, both in terms of the decision regarding the target funds rate and in suggesting that further monetary policy stimulus, through conventional or unconventional policy, is unlikely.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The final two pages of the package provide draft directives to the Desk that incorporate some changes relative to the versions that were included in the Bluebook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The directive for alternative A would provide some quantitative guidance for the Desk’s open market operations while reserving some role for an assessment of evolving market conditions, specifically the language that “the Committee directs the Desk to purchase GSE debt and agency-guaranteed MBS, with the aim of providing support to the mortgage and housing markets.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The timing and pace of these purchases should depend on conditions in the markets for such securities and on a broader assessment of conditions in primary mortgage markets and the housing sector.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: By the end of the second quarter of next year, the Desk is expected to purchase up to $100 billion in housing-related GSE debt and up to $500 billion in agency-guaranteed MBS.” The directive would not specify a target range for the federal funds rate, while that for alternative B would.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The directive for alternative A would state explicitly that the Committee has suspended setting a target for the federal funds rate and that it expects federal funds to trade at exceptionally low levels.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The directive for B establishes the fed funds range of 0 to ¼ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In line with one of the points raised yesterday, that the size and the composition of our entire balance sheet affect the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy stance, the final sentence of the revised directives for alternatives A and B states an expectation that the SOMA Manager and the Committee’s Secretary will keep the Committee informed of ongoing developments regarding the System’s balance sheet that could affect the attainment over time of the Committee’s objectives of maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The directive for alternative C, on the next page, is generally similar to that for alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But it would acknowledge that federal funds are likely to trade below the ½ percent target rate set under this alternative.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The directive for alternative D would include a similar recognition but with a target federal funds rate of 1 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In addition, this alternative would not provide specific guidance on open market purchases.

speaker: LACKER
text: Brian, the first sentence in alternative B says, “The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to establish a target range for the federal funds rate of 0 to ¼ percent.” In the staff analysis of various options for implementing interest on excess reserves, I think option 4 was the one that is closest to the reality of what we are implementing now—just a straight interest rate on excess reserves and an overprovision of reserves to drive it down to the floor.

speaker: LACKER
text: In that analysis, the staff anticipated that it would be a floor, which it turned out not to be.

speaker: LACKER
text: But it anticipated that, with that floor in place, the effective funds rate would generally be above the floor, and it envisioned choosing a rate on excess reserves ¼ point below our target rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: So do you envision in this that we would have to take any measures if suddenly the downward forces on the effective rate would bring the funds rate above ¼?

speaker: LACKER
text: Or is this just under the supposition that it would take a while and that it is unlikely to get above ¼?

speaker: LACKER
text: You see, back in the early analysis there were forces that you believed would lead it above ¼, so I am wondering how you are thinking about it.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: President Lacker, the forces that we were thinking would bring it above ¼ were largely a risk premium—the difference between federal funds, which have some amount of credit risk, and deposits at the Federal Reserve, which of course do not.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think we would not anticipate that we would need to do anything very different from what we have been doing—just continue to provide a very large amount of reserves, which is a byproduct of our liquidity provisions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With the interest rate on balances set at ¼ percent, that configuration of balances and rates would result in a federal funds rate somewhere in the range of 0 to ¼.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, the reason I ask is that I am a little hesitant to set an upper bound on a range without understanding what sort of mechanism we would have for making that credible.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is why I asked about that.

speaker: LACKER
text: One, the word “zero”—can you help me understand the thinking about why we should be a little averse to using that word?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, one reason might be that, if you gave some weight to the view that very low interest rates do have costs in financial markets and you wanted to preserve some rhetorical or substantive leeway, you would want to have a somewhat positive interest rate, to the degree that you could achieve one, but still a low level.

speaker: LACKER
text: We, in the late 1970s, adopted a set of guidelines regarding agency debt and modified that in the late 1990s.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t have a copy with me.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the latest adoption of that was January 2003, and I believe it is permanent.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it is still in effect.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it states that our purchases are not intended to channel funds to any specific sector.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am wondering about the staff’s interpretation of the consistency between our GSE debt and agency-guaranteed MBS purchases, and that guidance.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I do have that guideline here, and you are correct, President Lacker.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The first paragraph of the guideline says that System open market operations in agency issues are an integral part of open market operations, designed to influence bank reserves, money market conditions, and monetary aggregates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The second paragraph says that open market operations in those issues are not designed to support individual sectors of the market or to channel funds into issues of particular agencies.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As you remembered, in my briefing yesterday I did raise the question as to Committee members’ views of the allocation of funds to particular firms or sectors.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is possible that the Committee may want to modify, suspend, or repeal this guideline at some point.

speaker: LACKER
text: They do seem inconsistent, though, and I think it is something, Mr. Chairman, that we ought to consider.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I am somewhat at fault here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I did consult with everyone on the Committee and discussed what we were going to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would say that, going forward, we should probably bring all such plans to the Committee.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would be good to have that public.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is a public document, is it not?

speaker: LACKER
text: Or it is not a public document yet.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is on the Committee records, right?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I believe it is public.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would be nice to have that in conformance with what we are actually doing.

speaker: FISHER
text: May I ask two questions, please?

speaker: FISHER
text: With regard to alternative A, I am curious, Brian, as to how you think the bankers would respond to that in terms of their pricing behavior and loans and prime.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, our friend from the New York Desk, how do you think the markets might respond to alternative A—not overnight, by the way, which I couldn’t care less about, but over the longer term.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On the former, just a guess, I would think that without any target federal funds rate—and given the well-known issues that we have been discussing about pressures on banks—it is possible that the prime rate would not be reduced by the full extent of the implicit reduction in the money market conditions that the FOMC would be targeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But I don’t really have a good sense as to what would happen quantitatively.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the market will be slightly confused, but I think they will figure it out quite quickly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They will scan the document and figure out, well, what does this really mean?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They will be surprised by the magnitude of the interest rate reduction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As I said yesterday, most of the dealers are clustered around a 50 basis point reduction in the target.

speaker: FISHER
text: Even though we are not stating a specific target, it would be implicit in the change in the level of the discount rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are saying here that we are at exceptionally low levels of the funds rate for some time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think they will understand that this is it and that the funds rate is going to be very, very low.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, the next day you will probably observe a federal funds rate that is no more than a couple of basis points, would be my guess.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Just a follow-up on that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am a little confused that we don’t set a target but we are operating under an interest on reserves scheme by which we pay a deposit rate, which in fact we just lowered.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is there some kind of disconnect between what is in alternative A, paragraph 5—lowering the discount rate and the interest rates on reserves—and not noting a change in the target rate when, in fact, we have already established that the deposit rate is going to be the target rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Maybe the markets will see through this, but I don’t know.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am not quite sure I understand what is going on and how this would work, in terms of communications or interpretations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the markets would look at this as saying it is a substantial rate cut.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The funds rate has been trading soft to the interest rate on excess reserves by a considerable margin.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The interest rate on excess reserves was cut considerably, so they will figure out that, therefore, the funds rate is going to trade at an exceptionally low level.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But you are right—it will not be quite as straightforward as putting it out there right up front.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess my trouble is that the Committee judged that it is not useful to set a specific target for the funds rate and yet this will be interpreted as that we reduced the target in effect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We can discuss this in the go-round.

speaker: EVANS
text: May I just ask Bill Dudley if he could describe how he anticipates his operations would differ between alternative A and alternative B?

speaker: EVANS
text: How would you do things differently?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we wouldn’t do things differently to any meaningful degree.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it might be helpful to flag just a few things about which I would particularly appreciate the Committee’s advice.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first is the issue that President Plosser was discussing, which is alternative A—not specifying a range or a target—or alternative B—specifying a range.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the argument for specifying a range is that it seems a little clearer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you look at, for example, the Japanese experience, even when they were in quantitative easing, they still had a target for the call rate, as I understand it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are some counter-arguments, which Governor Duke and others have raised, about the impact on banks and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is question number 1.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Question number 2—and this doesn’t preclude other points, of course—is that in paragraph 3 of alternative B, for example, we have bracketed just for your reference the risk of inflation’s declining below optimal levels.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would be interested to know your views on whether or not to include that bracketed phrase.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Third—again looking at alternative B—in paragraph 4 we have the conditional statement that “weak economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate.” A little informal polling suggested that people were sort of okay with this way of stating the conditionality.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But if there are any concerns about that or, alternatively, if you would like to include a reference to disinflation as one of the conditions, that is just something I want to flag as a question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A fourth and final point I want to flag—and President Yellen pointed this out to me—in paragraph 5 we have a sentence saying that “the Committee is also evaluating the potential benefits of purchasing longer-term Treasury securities.” I think to put that in there we should feel that sometime in the next few meetings there is a significant chance that we would in fact engage in some kind of a program.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t want to put it in there if it is a complete red herring.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So those are four points that I have, but of course, you may have other questions or issues that you want to raise.

speaker: DUKE
text: Mr. Chairman, just one response to President Lacker’s and President Plosser’s observations, which I think are related.

speaker: DUKE
text: If you set the rate that we are going to pay for interest on reserves the same as the target rate for fed funds and the market does repair itself and resume, then you would expect there to be some risk spread over the rate that we are paying on interest on reserves.

speaker: DUKE
text: So if we don’t set a target or we set the target something higher than the rate that we are paying, at least if the markets do start to resume, then the Desk isn’t in a position of then having to try to drive the rate back down again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll begin with President Rosengren.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The bleak outlook calls for aggressive action.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With the effective federal funds rate already well below our target, there is a logic to moving to the floor at this meeting and redirecting attention to nontraditional policies.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Thus, I am comfortable with alternative B and would reduce the interest rates on required and excess reserves to 25 basis points.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the questions that the Chairman just posed, I am comfortable specifying the range of 0 to ¼ percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would actually keep the bracketed information.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I am okay with the conditionality.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would remove the reference to the Treasury securities, and for the future I would certainly want to think about expanding the purchase of GSE and agency mortgage- backed securities beyond $600 billion.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Also I would support, at a future date, setting a target of 2 percent for the core PCE inflation rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I support alternative A, so let me just talk for a few minutes about what I like about it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I like the language “not useful to set a specific target for the federal funds rate” in alternative A because I think this will begin the process of getting the private sector to think in alternative terms about monetary policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That would be similar to the moves made during the 1979-82 period.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Let me just stress that I think the whole process is going to be very difficult.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We have an entire generation of private-sector financial market participants who are conditioned to think only in terms of a federal funds rate target as the whole definition of what monetary policy is.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I might remind the Committee—if it needs reminding, and it probably doesn’t—that it is a big country out there.

speaker: BULLARD
text: When you start talking to others outside the particular participants in financial markets, the level of understanding of monetary policy is very limited.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The subtleties get lost, and so it is going to take a lot of time and effort to convince everyone and to explain to everyone that we are switching to new policies.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I expect, in fact, that it will probably be a three-year period that will be marked by controversy over headlines that are of the form, “What is the Fed doing?”—much like the 1979-82 period, when there was continuing controversy and continuing efforts to explain.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I also like the paragraph that places emphasis on alternative policies.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would keep the bracketed information.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I thought the conditionality was okay.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I will say about the alternative policies, those policies have unknown impact, and so we don’t want to be too detailed here because they may have to evolve in the future.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would take out the part about the longer-term Treasury securities.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would put in the inflation target.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I said before that I think it is an important point to be able to reassure and anchor expectations in this very fluid situation, which may rapidly unravel on us.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is a good opportunity to do this, and I would go ahead with that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t think it is that different from our longer-term projections, but it is much more direct and communicates much more clearly to markets that we have a medium-term inflation target.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the question of what should be in the directive, I will say this: I see it as somewhat dangerous for this Committee and for the nation to say nothing about the level of reserves or the monetary base.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It is true that it may not be inflationary now or in normal times, and it may not have been inflationary in Japan.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But there are many examples around the world where money supplies got out of control and inflation was a very serious problem.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It could be explosive in some parts of the world, especially if there were a large loss of confidence in the U.S. government or in the performance of this Committee.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I think we want to reassure the world that we are carefully monitoring that situation, that we have our eye on it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As several people have commented around here, a common refrain among business leaders we talk to is, “What the hell is going on?

speaker: BULLARD
text: You know, your balance sheet is way up.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Isn’t that going to be inflationary?” And we are saying “no,” but I think we need to give continual reassurance that we are monitoring that situation, we have it under control, and we are thinking about it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I also think, as President Stern said yesterday, that it would help signal our intention to keep inflation near target, other than simply promising to do so, which is just pure reliance on our credibility.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You have something quantitative that you can point to.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Obviously, it has to be done in a sensible way that allows us to bring in other programs and expand the balance sheet in other ways.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it is just a matter of making a statement that we are keeping our eye on the whole situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As far as the other alternatives, let me disparage them for a minute.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t know—we haven’t gone all around the table here—but I don’t want to be naming targets that we don’t intend to hit.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I don’t want to say that we have a target but we are not actually going to do it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If we are going to do that, then we have to change the language somehow that whatever the number that we are naming is not really a target.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would be very averse to doing anything like that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In alternative B, the first sentence states a target range for the federal funds rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My feeling about this is that effectively, in the big picture, no one will read past that first sentence.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They will just say, “Oh, yes, the Fed lowered interest rates.” The idea that we are switching to some new regime or that markets have to start thinking in alternative ways about monetary policy is going to be lost.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If you wanted to put a more aggressive spin on this, this is the do- nothing option.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The effective federal funds rate is near zero anyway, so this is just saying, “Well, this is business as usual.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We are going to sit on our hands.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We are constrained by the zero bound, and we are not going to really change anything.” So I see it as important to get the markets off this, and I see alternative A as one way to do that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But maybe you all will convince me otherwise.

speaker: LACKER
text: Given the dismal state of the economy, and with the funds rate averaging around 1/ percent anyway, I don’t see any reason to wait to bring 8 the fed funds rate down to effectively zero.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree with the staff analysis that any dislocation of the money funds is likely to be minor.

speaker: LACKER
text: My board put in for a 75 basis point cut in the discount rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: When I looked over at my small bankers, I was afraid one of them was going to throw a shoe at me.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I support alternative A. I think it makes sense to deemphasize the funds rate target.

speaker: LACKER
text: For reasons that were illuminated by Brian earlier and reasons that Governor Duke alluded to as well, I don’t think a target range is useful.

speaker: LACKER
text: We don’t want to discourage hope among our community bankers that we might get above ¼ percent should conditions normalize to some degree.

speaker: LACKER
text: We do set an interest rate on excess reserve balances, or more precisely, the Committee’s reduction in the federal funds rate target reduces the rate on excess reserves, given the Board’s adopted formula for setting the excess reserves rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have a similar sort of governance disconnect between the discount rate approval decisions of the Board of Governors and the federal funds rate decisions taken by the Federal Open Market Committee.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have managed to coordinate those very effectively, with cohesion and with consensus.

speaker: LACKER
text: It seems to me to make sense to take the same approach to the excess reserves rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: I like the language in alternative A, paragraph 3, where we abandon the target and indicate that the funds rate is likely to be near zero for a while.

speaker: LACKER
text: The conditionality, the way it is expressed there or in B4, is fine with me.

speaker: LACKER
text: I like the idea of shifting attention to the interest rate on reserves by including the statement in the related actions sentence of A5; that further cements the governance coordination that we have in mind there.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it makes eminent sense to be very explicit very soon about our numerical objective for inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Monetary policy at the zero bound is all about discouraging expectations of deflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we haven’t tried first announcing an explicit objective for inflation, we don’t have any excuses if we fail to prevent a fall into a deflationary equilibrium.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I am sympathetic to the notion that it might not be best to slip it in the statement in the dead of night without any fanfare.

speaker: LACKER
text: It might encourage the view that it is a temporary expedient and that we might abandon this language in some future statement, should we find it convenient.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it would be better to do this and issue a separate statement very clearly articulating that the Committee has adopted a numerical inflation objective, here is what it means, here is how we interpret it, and here is why we do it.

speaker: LACKER
text: Perhaps January would be the right time to do that, and we could, between now and then, lay the groundwork for a clearer and more forceful communication.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it is likely to have a bigger effect on financial market participants and the public should we do so.

speaker: LACKER
text: Without that statement about an objective, the sentence that precedes it—specifically the phrase that is in brackets in A2—is a little scary.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I would prefer to leave that bracketed thing out if we are not going to include the inflation objective.

speaker: LACKER
text: The fourth paragraph in alternative A and the corresponding paragraphs in B and C discuss how we are going to conduct monetary policy while the funds rate is at zero.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think they are intended to signal a shift toward quantitative measures, but I found the language ambiguous and confusing.

speaker: LACKER
text: None says anything about the monetary base.

speaker: LACKER
text: None says anything about the size of our balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: In other words, they don’t indicate that the credit programs wouldn’t be sterilized.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the phrase “use our balance sheet” is ambiguous.

speaker: LACKER
text: It doesn’t necessarily mean expand the size; it could mean put some stuff on it.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I would like to see us find a way to improve the clarity of the language in paragraph 4 regarding the quantitative measures that I think it is intended to communicate.

speaker: LACKER
text: That paragraph also mentions two programs: the agency debt purchases, which we talked about earlier—let me set that aside—and the TALF, which the Committee has not been asked to formally consider and approve.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, I can appreciate the strict constructionist governance view of who gets to approve them; it is not important that we vote on them.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I have been thinking about this in terms of the ideal—the vision you portrayed and described for us yesterday of a cohesive consensus-building decisionmaking process.

speaker: LACKER
text: I compared the TALF and what the Committee has heard about it.

speaker: LACKER
text: Contrast that with the deliberations we gave to the extension of foreign exchange swap lines to emerging-market countries.

speaker: LACKER
text: There were fairly extensive briefing memorandums provided to the Committee, and there was a fairly lengthy discussion of that step.

speaker: LACKER
text: In contrast, we were basically informed about the TALF rather than consulted in any meaningful sense.

speaker: LACKER
text: Part of the problem here is that this paragraph conflates the use of our balance sheet with expansions of the base, and these are two distinct policy actions.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the current circumstance, unsterilized lending does increase the base.

speaker: LACKER
text: But we have been doing these programs since before that was true, and the distinction doesn’t come through clearly in the language here.

speaker: LACKER
text: There is a tension here because a couple of different plausible theories are floating around about how this stuff affects the economy and our objectives and how things are going to work at the zero bound.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am not sure that we are going to settle on a single theory.

speaker: LACKER
text: In fact, I am sure that we are not going to settle on a single theory.

speaker: LACKER
text: But we should strive, in the interest of consensus, for a statement that encompasses a range of plausible views.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have done that in the past in finessing things like different views of the Phillips curve and the like, and I would urge us to try to do that here rather than take a monolithic approach.

speaker: LACKER
text: Finally, let me say something about the directive.

speaker: LACKER
text: The new drafts of A, B, and C add a sentence, the operative words of which are “keep the Committee informed,” and it is that the Secretary and the System Open Market Account Manager would keep the Committee informed.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is somewhat short of the language you used yesterday, which admittedly might not be appropriate for the directive.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I wrote the language down, and it is that the Board would bring programs to the FOMC for review and discussion.

speaker: LACKER
text: I like the sentence that is added in the sense that it is a step in the right direction toward your vision of a collaborative body seeking consensus on these issues.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I am afraid that this language won’t do much to dispel questions that have arisen in the press about our governance cohesion and decisionmaking.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I personally would prefer to go as far as we could in that direction.

speaker: LACKER
text: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Jeff, I just want to make a couple of comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A very small one is that, in an early draft, instead of saying “entail the use of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet” we had “entail increasing the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet.” We thought that might not be appropriate because things go on and off.

speaker: LACKER
text: Other things pull it down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We were probably going to do that as a trend, maybe not day to day, but it has some of the flavor of increasing the base.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is one just observation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the TALF, we have added a presentation today from Bill Dudley and Pat Parkinson.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, on the directive, there is a bit of a difference, which is that I do think we need to bring new programs, et cetera, for your information, as I said before.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But this is actually a stronger statement in that it also means that we should report to you on the ongoing implications of existing programs for the base and for the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there is a bit of a difference in those two concepts.

speaker: LACKER
text: Mr. Chairman, I do like the “increase” statement, and I think we could easily explain that we are looking at a partial differential effect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One possibility is “entail increasing the size.” There is some risk there, but I think that would be the general trend that we are considering.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the real issue is what happens to the CPFF, what happens to the swap programs, and the take-up of the TAF.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Those are the three big elements, and they conceivably could run down in the first quarter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You could say “increasing over time the size” or something like that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was the reason we switched.

speaker: LACKER
text: The statement doesn’t have to stand for the whole first quarter, does it?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think the issue is that, because we have open facilities, we just can’t guarantee what their take-up is going to be relative to what they are today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The swap lines are roughly $600 billion; those could come down.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, each facility makes the balance sheet bigger than it otherwise would be.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: A lot of these could go down quite substantially if conditions improve, and we wouldn’t control that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was the concern we had—that it wouldn’t necessarily be a monotonic increase, that it could have ups and downs depending on usage and so on.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, I have in mind here the confusion that some around this table have reported hearing from the public about what we are doing with our balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think acknowledging that it is expanding in size would be an important feature.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we can hear from others about that as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: I certainly agree that more accommodation is needed.

speaker: EVANS
text: We need to take actions to provide, as best we can, the quantitative easing equivalent of the optimal control path as discussed in the briefing.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not sure ultimately how feasible that will be, but it is a good goal for us over the next few months.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, in terms of the differences between alternative A and alternative B, as I understood Bill Dudley, there is no operational difference in these two options.

speaker: EVANS
text: It really comes down to how we want to communicate with ourselves and also the public.

speaker: EVANS
text: I tend to favor alternative B, certainly for now, and maybe alternative A later.

speaker: EVANS
text: After all, if the funds rate is going to go to zero in reality, then alternative A might be the right language.

speaker: EVANS
text: But we will have time to see that.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is a reasonable sequencing.

speaker: EVANS
text: The action today that we are dropping the funds rate target range 75 to 100 basis points is big, and certainly that will be the first thing that they see in the first line.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think they will continue reading.

speaker: EVANS
text: The language on the conditionality about the funds rate being exceptionally low is certainly okay today.

speaker: EVANS
text: The language says, “The Committee anticipates that weak economic conditions are likely to warrant.” I guess there is some question as to whether or not we should include the dual mandate here—that disinflationary forces are also part of that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I could go with the consensus there, but I would just raise that as a question.

speaker: EVANS
text: Regarding the bracketed risk that inflation could decline for a time below optimal rates— the rates that we think are best—back in 2003 this is what got a tremendous amount of attention.

speaker: EVANS
text: That is another reason that, as people read further, it could have a very large effect.

speaker: EVANS
text: It seems to be accurate.

speaker: EVANS
text: One way to deal with that would be to allow the minutes to capture that discussion, at least this time, and perhaps to put it in next time.

speaker: EVANS
text: It depends on the accumulation of how many of these large noteworthy developments we want in the statement here.

speaker: EVANS
text: I would be even more comfortable if that type of statement were accompanied by a context such as that we would be seeking conditions of inflation being around 2 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: I realize that this may not be the ideal time to include that without a more extended discussion.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I would be okay with the bracketed information, if that is the consensus.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think we should probably omit the Treasury purchases if we don’t think that we are going to do that by March.

speaker: EVANS
text: Certainly, omitting it today is low cost.

speaker: EVANS
text: Given all the information, it is probably overload.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am okay with the language in the directive.

speaker: EVANS
text: Accompanying the language is all of the discussion about the collaboration that we have between the Board and the Committee generally, and so I have a very good feeling about that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that it will tend to evolve as this goes on, whether or not it is maximum thresholds or just changing the composition of all of this.

speaker: EVANS
text: So those are my preferences.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like the others who have spoken before me, I think this situation is very serious.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to do all we can, and I think we need to recognize the reality of where we are.

speaker: KOHN
text: So either alternative A or alternative B does that to a significant extent.

speaker: KOHN
text: I guess I have a slight preference for alternative A as a better recognition that we are not really controlling the federal funds rate in here.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have these other balance sheet things going on, and to me alternative B has a little of the flavor of drawing your target around the hole we have already made in the barn door, or whatever, and pretending that you have some control that you don’t really have.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think A is better.

speaker: KOHN
text: President Bullard made a very good point that A tends to refocus attention on these alternative policies that we all agree will be the focus of our attention going forward.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I could live with either A or B.

speaker: KOHN
text: In terms of some of the issues you raised—so going down alternative A—in paragraph 2, the bracketed language, here I agree with President Lacker.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think my slight preference would be to wait until January to do this.

speaker: KOHN
text: Whether or not we have an explicit inflation target as we come out of the January meeting, we can debate in January.

speaker: KOHN
text: We will, I hope, have at least these long-run projections, and this bracketed language can be explained in terms of those long-run projections.

speaker: KOHN
text: Right now, it kind of sits out there.

speaker: KOHN
text: We haven’t yet explained what we think the rates are that best foster economic growth and price stability in the longer term.

speaker: KOHN
text: By the end of the January meeting, we can do that.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think I would wait for that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the conditional language in the third paragraph is helpful, and I would favor keeping it in.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is appropriately conditioned on weak economic conditions.

speaker: KOHN
text: If other people wanted to add “the disinflationary forces,” which I think come primarily from the weak economic conditions, that would be okay with me, too.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I am fine with this.

speaker: KOHN
text: In the first sentence of paragraph 4—this is a small point—I would take out the “to continue”: “The focus of policy going forward will be to support the functioning .

speaker: KOHN
text: ..” When I first read the “to continue,” it sounded as though we are just going to continue what we are doing now.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I would take that out, but that is a small point.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the discussion about whether we should put the size in, I am a little worried about putting it in because the balance sheet has grown so rapidly.

speaker: KOHN
text: If it came down because year-end pressures abated and because the swaps with all of those foreign central banks might tend to come down after the end of the year, I don’t think that the Committee would necessarily want Bill to be replacing every dollar of Eurodollar swaps that came down with something else.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we are talking about a long-run trend in the base, and we need to be careful about not trying to leave the impression that in every intermeeting period we would expect the base to increase, especially when we don’t control that size.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I would be a little cautious about that.

speaker: KOHN
text: Certainly, if we did include “increase the size of the balance sheet,” I also would say something about the composition.

speaker: KOHN
text: In my view, it is actually the composition more than the size that is going to influence relative asset prices, even though I do recognize that over very long periods, if we keep the base from declining, it would be hard to have prices decline.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I am not sure that is really an effective way to deal with expectations in the short or intermediate run.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would include the purchases of longer-term Treasury securities.

speaker: KOHN
text: Among other things, I think we ought to do it sometime in the next few months.

speaker: KOHN
text: The fact that you have already talked about it, if we omit it—I guess I disagree with President Evans here—I don’t think that will be low cost.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have a series of things we are doing, and that is not part of it.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think there could be an adverse market reaction.

speaker: KOHN
text: Going back to the base for a second, I agree that we need to do a better job of explaining, as I said yesterday, what this new framework is, how the increase in reserves and the base fits into it—if we can come to some conclusion on that—and why under these circumstances a very large increase in the base isn’t inflationary and how that comes about.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to do a much better job of explaining these kinds of things.

speaker: KOHN
text: But, again, I would be hesitant to put an explicit target in terms of the level of reserves or the base in there because I don’t really understand the channels through which they influence prices or activity in the short and intermediate terms.

speaker: KOHN
text: Finally, on bank profits and the effects there, ordinarily I wouldn’t worry about bank profits.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is just a transfer between the owners of banks and households and businesses, and quite frankly, transferring some income to households and businesses seems like a pretty good idea most of the time in these circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that it is more ambiguous than usual, given the worries about the financial sector.

speaker: KOHN
text: Still, we are doing a lot for the banks.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are giving them capital.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are guaranteeing their liabilities—we, the government, that is.

speaker: KOHN
text: This will reduce the rates at which they borrow from the discount window and from each other, so they are getting something there.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think banks are going to need to figure out how to operate at these really low interest rates, so I wouldn’t let my concern about bank profits stop me from doing either alternative A or alternative B.

speaker: LACKER
text: Just a thought in response to Governor Kohn’s comments: Would the phrase “add to” do a better job than “increase the size of” in conveying the sense that these programs are going to make the balance sheet bigger than it otherwise would be, rather than lead to an absolute increase in the size of the balance sheet?

speaker: KOHN
text: I am not sure those words help me, actually.

speaker: KOHN
text: “Add to” sounds the same as “increase” to me.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have missed the subtlety here.

speaker: KOHN
text: We could put that in there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is already Greek anyway.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My preference is to move in this meeting to the consensus lower-bound range for the funds target, and I prefer the range of 0 to 25.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I believe either alternative A or alternative B will work as serviceable options, and I can live with either one.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But I actually lean toward alternative B. I think it is the clearest, and with the inclusion of the language related to deflation, it is also internally more consistent.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In particular, my preference is to indicate that the FOMC intends to keep the policy rate low until economic and credit conditions improve, and I think it is appropriate to emphasize that our policies will be calibrated based on longer-term inflation objectives.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I said yesterday, I am thinking that the conditionality language could be stronger.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Specifically, I have in mind something along the lines of a statement that reads that “the Committee intends to maintain this range for the federal funds rate until such time that it judges conditions are present for material and sustained improvements in financial market functioning and economic growth, and the Committee believes that this policy course is consistent with its medium-term price stability objective.” I think that kind of language could fit at the beginning of paragraph 4, around that area, in alternative B. I think that is stronger than the implicit conditionality that is already in the statement.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my rounds of contacts before the meeting, one conversation did resonate with me.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It was a call from a financial market participant for hearing what the plan is and what the strategy is and affirming that there is a plan.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think stronger conditionality language would respond to that need in the marketplace.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As regards the questions, I think I have already covered some of them.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I would prefer the specifying of a range in alternative B. I would lean toward including the language “and sees some risk that inflation could decline” because it ties in with the “all available tools” language at the beginning of paragraph 4.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In other words, I think, if we include that language in paragraph 3, we are setting up a risk and the “employ all available tools” responds strongly to that risk.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding the inclusion of the long-term Treasury securities, I am persuaded by Governor Kohn’s comment that we should include it.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is consistent with whatever public discussion we have had to date, including your speech of two weeks ago.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think, at the end of the day, alternatives A and B really amount to the same thing in terms of policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I could live with either, but on communication grounds, my own strong preference would be for B. I think it is important at this juncture for the FOMC to state very clearly what it wants the federal funds rate to be, that we want it to remain close to zero, and I think we best do that by specifying explicitly a rate or, as it is, a range.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Both A and B eliminate the gap we have had between the target and the reality of where the funds rate is actually trading, but B eliminates that gap by embracing the current reality as desirable.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In contrast, it seems to me that A is saying that the Committee is all but helpless to affect the funds rate, so, after all, it would be a charade to set a target.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Then it kind of acknowledges, well, but, you know, the funds rate trading near zero is really not such a bad thing, given the weakness in the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we have greater command over the funds rate’s destiny than alternative A suggests.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If the Board and the FOMC really wanted to push the effective funds rate up above zero, say to 50 or to 100 basis points, the Board could choose to raise the rates paid on reserves and the discount rate, and we could get it up, even though we have all of this enormous quantity of excess reserves and even though interest on reserves isn’t working in quite the way we expected.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I agree that it would be a bit odd to be setting the interest on reserves and discount rates above our target for the federal funds rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But it seems to me it could be done, and we are not powerless to accomplish it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I don’t like the suggestion that we are just helpless to move the funds rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we should say that we don’t want to move the funds rate up.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t want it to trade above the 0 to 25 basis point errange.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I certainly don’t want that.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the forecast is grim.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we should go as low as we can as fast as we can without harming the functioning of money markets, so keeping the funds rate trading in the 0 to 25 range is desirable.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If it were to be the case, following President Lacker’s earlier question, that we suddenly saw the interest on reserves floor working better and fed funds started trading above 25—the funds rate could, for example, move up to 50 or so—I would hope that the Board would actually lower the interest rate paid on reserves to hold the funds rate in the 0 to 25 range.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I think we should go down and do it decisively in one step today.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the other matters, in alternative B, paragraph 3, I favor including the bracketed language suggesting that we expect and are not happy to see inflation declining below levels we consider consistent with price stability.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I agree with President Evans on the merits of doing that.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I like the forward-looking language from A that has been added in bold to B concerning the odds that we will keep the funds rate low for some time.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the Treasuries, I am worried about making an announcement or giving a hint that we are not going to follow through on them pretty quickly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am personally in favor of and support buying longer-term Treasuries, and I haven’t heard a lot of opposition to it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If we really are going to do it and do it pretty soon, I have no problem with including language to that effect.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I don’t think we should throw a hint out there unless we intend to follow through.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to the wording of the directive, I am happy with it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to the issue about the monetary base and increasing the size of our balance sheet, I would endorse Governor Kohn’s remarks on that topic.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we were still working with the framework of targeting the fed funds rate, I would prefer D, and I would accept C, and I would vote accordingly.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But I think what I’ve heard in the past two days is that we have really abandoned that framework, and this is kind of a ratification of that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that our framework now is actually in A and B in the statement that we are going to “expand its purchases .

speaker: HOENIG
text: as conditions warrant.” If that’s the case, then going with A, in which you don’t set a fed funds rate or talk about it, is probably preferred.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I also think that we’re now in a credit policy type of framework, and it bothers me.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I have a lot of sympathy for what Presidents Lacker and Bullard said.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would prefer, rather than a statement that says “as conditions warrant,” that we have some kind of a monetary base criterion for the future.

speaker: HOENIG
text: This is something that we ought to think about.

speaker: HOENIG
text: At the same time, I do not think that we should have inflation below optimal in this statement.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I don’t think we’re there, and, at this point, I think it should not be hinted at.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that “purchasing longer-term Treasury securities” goes with the conditionality statement anyway.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We’ll do what it takes, and if it takes purchasing longer-term Treasuries, that’s it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is what we have unless we go back and look at a new framework that we need to get out and talk about with the public, and I hope that as our meetings and our discussions progress, we begin to focus on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, as I said yesterday, this is a work in progress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll keep working on it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I didn’t quite get your proposal.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you propose leaving in the sentence about Treasuries at this meeting?

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we’re going to have statements that say we’re going to purchase mortgage-backed securities as conditions warrant, I don’t think “purchasing longer-term Treasury securities” is a much different step from that, so we can leave it in.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Obviously, for us to counteract the powerful forces that are weakening our economy and financial markets, we should provide maximum monetary policy stimulus as quickly as possible, and conducting monetary policy on the basis of a fed funds rate target is no longer the best strategy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do think it is time and it would be helpful to begin focusing the public’s attention on the unconventional approach to monetary policy, and I think alternative A does a better job of doing that.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: What I like about alternative A is its straightforward characterization of the policy situation and how we plan to respond to it.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I support leaving in the language that is bracketed in alternative A, paragraph 2, about the risk that inflation could decline for some time below rates that best foster economic growth and price stability.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The reason I say that is that we have been using the language that the Committee expects inflation to moderate for some time now, and given the discussion, I think we expect that situation to be getting worse.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I would support leaving that in.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I would also leave in paragraph 3 the more forward-looking language about keeping the low level of the fed funds rate for some time.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also would keep in the language on the potential benefits of purchasing longer-term Treasury securities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I assume that the minutes that are released in three weeks are going to say that we discussed it and that we will be evaluating it.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I would just leave it in.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Also, given the dire economic outlook that we are talking about and the aggressive response that we think monetary policy should take, I think just saying merely that we stand ready to expand the purchase of agency debt and mortgage-backed securities isn’t aggressive enough.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do realize that there are a lot of important questions that are left unanswered, such as determining the mix of assets to purchase and how to know when enough is enough, and then how to shrink our balance sheet when the time comes.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But I do think that adopting alternative A is taking a big step in the direction of giving the public some indication of what we plan to do.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Finally, I know you just said that we will come up with some language and some framework around what we are doing.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But as discussed in yesterday’s conversation, having some talking points even in the near term so that we are consistent in our language on what we are doing would be helpful.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At a time when there is a lot of confusion out there and markets are as fragile as they are, having us all talk about this in the same way would be helpful.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, as several people have observed—and I agree—I don’t think there’s any significant policy difference between A and B. That’s certainly where I am.

speaker: STERN
text: From a communication point of view, I have a mild preference for B. I think it’s a little clearer on the margin and would be helpful in that regard.

speaker: STERN
text: So I would work off B as to some of the issues and suggestions that have been raised.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to the first issue, I would not include the information in brackets in paragraph 3 at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: I think Governor Kohn made a good point that we’re likely to be much better positioned to do that in January in conjunction with the SEP and the longer-term projections.

speaker: STERN
text: I am in favor of inflation targeting, but I think exactly how and when we get to that is important.

speaker: STERN
text: So I wouldn’t want to do that simply in a casual way and do it too rapidly.

speaker: STERN
text: As I look at paragraph 3, I have a couple of other questions.

speaker: STERN
text: The first sentence says that “inflationary pressures have diminished quickly,” which is certainly true, but I think it may be more important that they have diminished appreciably.

speaker: STERN
text: So I would just make that point.

speaker: STERN
text: I might also say, rather than “the Committee expects inflation to moderate in coming quarters,” which I think is probably true, that you might just say “the Committee expects modest inflation in coming quarters.” The reason I’m putting it that way is that I’m trying to get out of this point precisely about whether it is or isn’t going to run below what we think might be consistent with the dual objectives.

speaker: STERN
text: I think the conditionality in paragraph 4 is fine.

speaker: STERN
text: If there’s a good way to strengthen it, doing so would also be fine with me.

speaker: STERN
text: But trying to modify these things on the fly is always difficult.

speaker: STERN
text: Finally, I would include the thought about purchasing longer-term Treasuries.

speaker: STERN
text: I think we should, and because I think we should, I think we should say that.

speaker: STERN
text: So I guess that covers the topics I want to cover.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Maybe I should ask Bill.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you see any purely operational issues in the next few months if we decide to purchase longer-term Treasuries?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We can do it, but we’re under a strain.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As long as we don’t start until sometime in January, I think we could manage, as long as you don’t ask us to do it every day.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: How about once every couple of weeks?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: These are, indeed, troubling times, and I think in troubling times it’s even more important that we be as transparent and clear as possible.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it’s time that we publicly convey that we have entered a new monetary policy regime.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To do otherwise perpetuates the view that we are no longer in control of monetary policy rather than that we have opted to implement policy through a different means, particularly our balance sheet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There’s ample room for judgment here and disagreement, but, Mr. Chairman, with all due respect, I’m deeply troubled by elements of the steps that we are taking today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In effect, I interpret our proposed actions as substituting credit-allocation policies for monetary policies.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Both the expansion of our balance sheet and the fed funds rate are now determined or will be now determined by decisions about which markets or firms are deemed worthy of our intervention and support and some assessment of how much money we want to throw at them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we all agree that we are looking for the best policies.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that it’s also true that best policies are based on clearly articulated goals and objectives and in credible and systematic actions to achieve those goals and objectives, and they can also be credibly communicated to the public.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I feel that our approach to credit policy comes up lacking in each of these dimensions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our goal may be to prevent systemic risk, but we haven’t clearly defined what that is or the criteria that we’re using to decide whom to lend to and when to lend to them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s very important for both clarity and transparency that we rectify this deficiency, or we may continue to create moral hazard and to see market after market after market seek our help.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The message from the literature we discussed yesterday is that near the zero bound our credibility and our commitment to generate inflation and prevent expectations of deflation to develop are paramount.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My reading of the proposed language is that it does little to signal that commitment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, it seems to suggest that our primary objectives are and will continue to be credit interventions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Confusing our monetary policy objectives with our credit policies is not the kind of message that I’m comfortable with.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we need to be careful not to convey to the market that monetary policy has become ineffective, and I don’t think anyone at this table wishes to do that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: President Lacker articulated the importance in the current environment of keeping inflation expectations well anchored, and measures of the base—or if you would rather, look at the asset side of the balance sheet, either way they’re both measuring the balance sheet—are a means of anchoring those expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t think the language of the directive or the statement is clear enough in addressing either the effectiveness of monetary policy or the credible commitment to avoid deflation or even to maintain inflation near our target, which is clearly not deflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not quite as fearful of deflation as President Bullard or some others, but I think we need to be mindful and reinforce our commitment to low but stable inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the governance side, I continue to believe that the FOMC is the appropriate body for making monetary policy decisions and that replacing monetary policy with credit policies that are unconstrained by this Committee is to violate both good governance and the spirit of the operating understanding of the FOMC.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yesterday and in my memo to the Committee earlier this week, I argued that the directive and the statement should clearly state that we are in a new regime and should articulate how that new regime will operate going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My interpretation is that the proposed language, particularly alternative A, does help indicate that we are moving to a new regime.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That’s important, and therefore, I lean in that direction.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But that language fails to articulate how that new regime will operate, except to say that the Board of Governors will continue credit market interventions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It says nothing about the terms and strategies that we’ll employ to do so.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The implicit message is—and I think the market will clearly interpret it this way—that the FOMC has ceded monetary policy decisions to the Board of Governors, and I think that will be damaging.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Such a step, in my view, is not good policy, nor is it good governance, and it may have political ramifications as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Once the Committee sets the precedent that the Board of Governors can assume sole responsibility for monetary policy, we run the risk of losing the strength and the diversity of views that the System has always brought.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My sense is that this Committee’s setting some kind of cap on the size of the balance sheet was an effort to clarify the role of monetary policy in contrast to credit policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
