text: I think the reaction I heard yesterday around the table was a litany of reasons why setting base growth targets is not appropriate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While that might be an interesting debate to have, that was not the point I was proposing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was requesting that we have a debt ceiling, if you will, and that the FOMC would review and adjust that debt ceiling as it deemed appropriate—not targets for balance sheets per se.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Such a debt ceiling would not prevent the Board of Governors from managing the asset side of the balance sheet via 13(3) lending.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Only when unsterilized lending exceeded the debt ceiling might formal approval be required from the FOMC.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Mr. Chairman, my discomfort is not a matter simply of good governance.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is more fundamentally about the lack of clarity, discipline, and transparency that the strategy is offering, and I have deep concerns.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’d like to offer a couple of suggestions for the Committee to consider about language, and I’m working off alternative A, which I think is probably the working hypothesis here.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So to answer your questions, Mr. Chairman, I have been and continue to be in favor of an explicit inflation target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Most of you are aware of that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am sympathetic to the view, as I think President Lacker said, that slipping it in in the dead of night is probably not the right way to go about it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would add that I do not like the bracketed phrase regarding the Committee’s seeing some risk of inflation coming in too low.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As President Lacker suggested, it might cause fear in the marketplace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I do think we could change the second bracketed statement, which was struck out: “In support of its dual mandate, the Committee will seek .

speaker: PLOSSER
text: a rate of inflation .

speaker: PLOSSER
text: of about 2 percent.” I think we could change that and heighten the importance of inflation to us and our dual mandate by saying something to the effect of “in support of its dual mandate, the Committee will seek a low and stable inflation rate over the intermediate term.” That would be short of specifying an inflation target but would reinforce the notion that we are still committed to achieving a low but stable inflation rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My biggest problem is with paragraph 4, which I think could be simplified greatly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would like to emphasize that monetary policy remains in the purview of the FOMC and that we have entered a new regime.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would propose, just for the sake of getting it on the table, that paragraph 4 be simplified to say that “the focus of the FOMC’s monetary policy going forward will be to continue to support the dual mandate and the functioning of a financial market to stimulate the economy through open market operations and other measures that entail the use of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet.” Then I would say, “Today the FOMC affirms the expansion of the Fed’s balance sheet up to $3 trillion and will periodically review and adjust that in the pursuit of our dual mandate.” Repeating the litany of credit-market interventions that we have engaged in seems just repeating what we’ve already done.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not sure that serves much purpose in the context of monetary policy making at this point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not opposed to buying GSEs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not opposed to buying longer-term Treasuries.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we need to modify Brian Madigan’s statement about the conditions under which we should purchase GSEs so that we are being internally consistent, but I don’t have any objection to it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think we could be clearer.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We could be less confusing in our policies by emphasizing again our commitment to keep inflation stable and at a positive level and clearly indicating that quantities do matter and that this Committee is responsible for those quantities and will interact with the Board of Governors and our credit policies to see that we can achieve the goals that we all decide on.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, before I get started, I do think that President Plosser has raised good issues on the governance matter.

speaker: FISHER
text: I hope that we will continue to discuss this, bearing in mind that there may be changes in the composition of the governors with a new President and given the faith that we built up with the existing governors, so that we have to get at least our lines of understanding clear as we go through time.

speaker: FISHER
text: As to the alternatives that we face, the problem with the economy isn’t the interbank lending rate or even the riskless rate.

speaker: FISHER
text: The problem with the economy and with the financial markets is that intermediation has broken down.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think our actions should forcefully be directed toward the clearing of blockages in the financial plumbing and not just fiddling with the faucet.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s the availability and distribution of credit that is problematic.

speaker: FISHER
text: In that sense I like alternative A.

speaker: FISHER
text: In fact, President Stern, I like its ambiguity, and I’ll tell you why.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am quite worried that stating zero to 25 basis points will bring down upon us the wrath of bankers.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do think it’s important that community banks be profitable and that they be healthy.

speaker: FISHER
text: First Vice President Cumming pointed this out in her comments, and to me this alternative gives us substantial wiggle room, as it were, in its ambiguity.

speaker: FISHER
text: Vice Chairman Kohn pointed out that paragraph 5 is good for the bankers.

speaker: FISHER
text: Without stating a specific target fed funds rate, it allows them to price their loans according to how they see fit.

speaker: FISHER
text: That appears to be taking place anyway.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is a separation between the fed funds rate and the prime loan rate.

speaker: FISHER
text: So unless I’m missing something, bankers should positively interpret both paragraph 1 and paragraph 5 in terms of their operating leeway.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would suggest that this is an important step forward in making clear the way we’re going to operate henceforth.

speaker: FISHER
text: It does indicate a regime change, and as President Bullard pointed out, I think we have to be forceful in doing so.

speaker: FISHER
text: I could diddle with the language, but to be even more forceful I would transpose paragraph 4 and paragraph 3.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is, the first two paragraphs strike me as fine.

speaker: FISHER
text: At this juncture I would not put in an inflation target because I don’t think we’re prepared for it as a Committee.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m comfortable leaving in paragraph 2 that we see some risk that inflation could decline below optimal rates for a time.

speaker: FISHER
text: After all, we just got the number that makes that very clear—minus 1.7 on the headline rate.

speaker: FISHER
text: But then I would go immediately into what our focus is going to be.

speaker: FISHER
text: I rather like President Plosser’s one edit to make clear that it’s the focus of the FOMC’s policy.

speaker: FISHER
text: After we have laid that clear—and if, indeed, just parenthetically we are going to make some Treasury purchases, we should include that in there; if we are not, we should not—then in what would be paragraph 4, strike “in current circumstances” and say that “the Committee judged that it was not useful to set a specific target for the fed funds rate.” You’re making it very clear that we have a regime change.

speaker: FISHER
text: As to the content of paragraph 4, assuming we are going to be purchasing longer-term Treasuries, I’d leave it as it is.

speaker: FISHER
text: Repeat it over and over and over again.

speaker: FISHER
text: You started with your speech in Austin, and that makes it operative.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have no problem with it, and I would urge it be included as written.

speaker: FISHER
text: So my suggestions, in summary, are that we embrace alternative A; we transpose paragraphs 4 and 3; we take out the wording “in current circumstances” because obviously we’re judging things in current circumstances; and we not include an inflation target at this juncture but do include the rest of the bracketed language in paragraph 2.

speaker: FISHER
text: I believe this is sellable to our bankers, and I believe it’s a good way to proceed.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Like others, I see the circumstances as requiring the most action we can take.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Therefore, I would favor alternative A somewhat over alternative B, but I could live with either.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I think that alternative A has the advantage, which President Bullard described and others have referred to, that it does signal a significant change in what we’re doing and draws attention to it.

speaker: CUMMING
text: If anything, it probably provokes more dialogue with us as a central bank, which I think at this point is a good thing.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Turning to the next paragraph, I’m a bit concerned that inflation is, in fact, moderating very quickly.

speaker: CUMMING
text: This morning’s number for the total CPI is 1.1 percent.

speaker: CUMMING
text: That would lead me to ask whether we are expecting inflation to moderate or are, in fact, seeing inflation moderating.

speaker: CUMMING
text: This point is similar to President Stern’s.

speaker: CUMMING
text: That would also lead me to leave in the bracketed point about the future and the concern there because I think it’s better if we put it on the table than have people say, “Don’t they see that as a problem?” To that end, I also want to endorse the kind of broad strategy statement that President Lockhart put forward.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I actually came into the meeting with a very similar sentence from my staff, really talking about what our goal is.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I think it does help to set the stage for what follows here, and this was a focus on improving conditions in financial markets or financial intermediation and ensuring a recovery in output and maintaining low inflation.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I think that President Lockhart was proposing that it follow paragraph 2, perhaps in its own paragraph.

speaker: CUMMING
text: We would raise the question of the risk of too low inflation but then have the next paragraph really speak to what our goals would be, and I thought the sentence that you had sounded good.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I can confuse the matter by saying that I was thinking of it in alternative B, and Ms. Cumming has it in alternative A.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Then continuing with this, I would comment on the next paragraph.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I’m very sympathetic to the idea that President Lacker was putting forward—that we somehow need to talk about our expectations about the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I was going to offer one suggestion: Perhaps for the “entail the use of” phrase in the first sentence of paragraph 4 we could substitute “sustain the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet at very high levels”—something that would indicate that we expect the balance sheet to remain really large but doesn’t talk about whether we’re increasing it from today.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I would leave in the sentence on the longer-term Treasuries in large part because we have already talked about it publicly and the language here gives us the opportunity to evaluate and does not necessarily commit us to those purchases in the future.

speaker: CUMMING
text: In any case, we would need to explain whether or not we’re going to purchase longer-term Treasuries, having raised it already.

speaker: CUMMING
text: On the directive, I would say that I am comfortable with the directives as written.

speaker: CUMMING
text: There might be room, if we found the right language for the size of the balance sheet, for inserting that sentence in here, for example, whatever we take from the first sentence of paragraph 4.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I also think that, as part of this monitoring that the System Open Market Account Manager and the Secretary will provide for the Committee, there really is the opportunity to develop much better disclosure of what the Committee is doing, what our balance sheet looks like, and what actions we’re taking— some kind of ongoing monitoring that could be shared with the public that I think would also be very helpful in explaining what the Federal Reserve is actually pursuing in the near term and what it is doing with the balance sheet.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I was really impressed by something that President Lacker said yesterday, which is that— and I paraphrase—we are in uncharted waters but we are groping our way forward.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I think that it is a great metaphor for where, in fact, we are.

speaker: CUMMING
text: Some of these questions—such as what specific forward-leaning language we’d like to put in our statement over time and how we think about the monetary base versus the credit policy type of actions that we’re taking—are all things that I think we will continue to learn about and explore.

speaker: CUMMING
text: What I had put forward is that, as we come to understand them better, we have an opportunity to communicate with the public and help them understand better what we are, in fact, doing.

speaker: WARSH
text: As others have said, the choice among these alternatives, particularly A, B, and C, is not really a choice about the effective rate.

speaker: WARSH
text: It’s a choice about our clarity, our conviction, and maybe most important, our readiness in announcing a new regime.

speaker: WARSH
text: As I described yesterday, I think the zero lower bound is not zero, and so there are risks particularly in these markets of going there or threatening to go there.

speaker: WARSH
text: So the balance of my suggestions and edits come from the zero phobia.

speaker: WARSH
text: First let me talk about C briefly.

speaker: WARSH
text: Alternative C is a sort of way station.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is our last chance to describe the old regime and to pivot to a new regime, whether the new targeted rate was 25 or 50 basis points.

speaker: WARSH
text: But seeing that there doesn’t seem to be much interest in that, I won’t try to reconcile the music and lyrics of C, which announces a target and then says we’re going to miss it; but I had a couple of suggestions to try to bring that together.

speaker: WARSH
text: So let me confine the balance of my remarks to the choice between A and B. I think in alternative A we are all-in.

speaker: WARSH
text: It makes the new regime explicit.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is likely to be somewhat of a surprise to markets and puts a large burden on all of us—particularly you, Mr. Chairman—not only in the next few hours but really for the next days and weeks in describing with great rigor what the new regime is.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we’re up to that, but it is certainly a tall task at a time of great uncertainty in markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: The way I would try to make that task a little easier is through various channels—suggesting that we are in some ways revealing the new target in paragraph 5 by suggesting that the implied effective target is 25 basis points, given what our change is on the discount rate and the interest rate on reserves.

speaker: WARSH
text: So that, I think, has a way of making the transition to the new regime less massive than it might be and reinforces my zero phobia point.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that’s one way in which the bold, new regime with a lot of explanation in the next few weeks can at least be not as scary to the markets in the next couple of days.

speaker: WARSH
text: If we were to go in that direction, I’d make one modest suggestion.

speaker: WARSH
text: In the first paragraph, I would insert the word “between”—so “the Federal Open Market Committee decided today to establish a target range for the federal funds rate between zero and ¼ percent”—to suggest that you’re not going to be at that endpoint.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now, I’ll admit that’s not a massive change, but it makes me feel a bit better about my phobia and about how markets, banks, and others might react knowing that that is a point you do not want to cross.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now, on your open question, setting a range in terms of the optimal level of inflation or not, I’m not crazy about a range.

speaker: WARSH
text: But if we have a range, I think it is scary, lurchy, to include it today, and so I wouldn’t do it.

speaker: WARSH
text: Conditionality, I think, is fine.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t feel strongly about our considering Treasury securities.

speaker: WARSH
text: I do like Governor Kohn’s suggestion about deleting “to continue” because bold new regimes aren’t continuations of what we’ve done.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think that’s an important change by Governor Kohn.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Obviously you have a bleak outlook.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It’s very important to act quickly and decisively, and I think it’s clear from the discussion that our choice is between A and B.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But as a number of people have mentioned, the economic substance is probably nearly identical in alternatives A and B.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Our exposition of it, though, can make a very big difference.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: There are an enormous number of moving parts, and there is a lot to digest.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We potentially have here, as I count them, seven new things that people have brought up.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That’s just an enormous amount to deal with, and I think some of them we want to delay.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The inflation target is very important, but it brings up issues here, and I’m not sure that we want to talk about something like that now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So let me just quickly run through these.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We have to think about the dynamic of what we are going to say next time.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: What is this committing us to talk about?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: First, the rate cut is one very big issue—75 versus 50 basis points.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Although some market participants think it will be 75, I think that will still be news, but I think it’s very important for us to move there.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Second, just moving to a range is something new; I think that is something that is actually quite newsworthy in and of itself.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Going to no target at all is extremely newsworthy, maybe too newsworthy to include with all these other things.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think of this and the discussions that we’ve had as setting up an extremely valuable template for how we should be thinking about the statement and what we need to be explaining today as well as over the next few meetings.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So I would actually say that, given all of the moving parts and all of the changes, talking about a range either “between” or “of” zero to ¼ percent would make a lot of sense.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t think we’re introducing any more ambiguity.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we’re introducing a bit of ambiguity especially for people who are not that well informed by saying that we don’t have a target anymore.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: What President Yellen said was that it could easily be misinterpreted as “gosh, we don’t really have control over these things anymore anyway.” I don’t think any of us believes that, and I think there’s more of a chance of that misinterpretation, which I don’t want us to have, if we do that today with all the other changes than if we waited a little.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I still think the range is a pretty big shift.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Expressing concerns about inflation being less than the level fostering economic growth— again, I think that’s something that I would prefer to wait on.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I like President Stern’s edit about talking about the appreciable diminution of inflationary pressures, but I would wait on putting in the phrase about whether the level is too low to be consistent with fostering economic growth.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I mentioned the inflation target.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think we should wait on that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’re introducing conditionality, which I think is valuable to do, and I think the phrase there is fine.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: We’re talking about old and new programs as well as balance sheet issues.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: As a number of people have mentioned, we have already talked about standing ready to expand the purchases of agency securities as conditions warrant.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So that’s forward leaning already.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we are committed to doing the Treasury securities fairly soon, I think we should just go along with that and feel comfortable with that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But we do have to think a bit about the precedent of making concrete new policies that we’ve generally talked about in this statement.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Is it something that we want to do going forward?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Does this commit us to doing that?

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I don’t think so, but I think we should just think about that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Then I think it’s very important that we talk about the use of the balance sheet.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I agree with Governor Warsh that to be bold you don’t say “continue to.” But we are talking about some existing programs, so in some sense we are continuing.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I’m not quite sure exactly where we want to go on this, but I just wanted to raise that ambiguity.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: On the balance sheet, though, I go back to the Chairman’s remarks from yesterday.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: It is important to think about the composition of the balance sheet, not just the size in and of itself—Governor Kohn also made reference to this—so I would be very wary of focusing on the size here.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I think that just talking about ways to use the balance sheet is the appropriate way to go now.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we have more experience and understand better how the size might evolve over time, how the different programs we have might fluctuate, I’d feel more comfortable with that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: If we talk about the size or commitment to growth of that size or expecting it to be large, just as a number of people said, it could suddenly shrink, and we don’t want people to think that we’re changing monetary policy because of that.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: Some of these things would just be changing over time.

speaker: DUKE
text: I do favor alternative A.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of what will happen with the prime rate, I frankly don’t know, but I think it will leave the banks to determine their own prime rate and floors as they wish.

speaker: DUKE
text: I would not minimize the fact that we are actually still setting a rate for the interest on excess reserves as well as the discount rate.

speaker: DUKE
text: This experience with interest on reserves is brand new for us, and I don’t think we’ve had enough experience to know how it is actually going to work.

speaker: DUKE
text: It does leave room for the spread to establish itself as the fed funds market regenerates, and I think it gives us some room to have some experience with that regime.

speaker: DUKE
text: I think this communicates the regime change better than any of the other alternatives, and at the end of the day, this is a communication document.

speaker: DUKE
text: I would strongly echo President Pianalto’s comments that, in this new regime, we really need to stay on the same page to avoid total confusion in the marketplace.

speaker: DUKE
text: I know that independence of thought is one of the strengths of this body, but if we could for a time set that aside at least in public and all speak from the same talking points, it would make all of our policies more effective.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of the specifics of the statement, I would defer to another day the language in brackets in paragraph 2 of alternative A.

speaker: DUKE
text: The conditional language I would keep in.

speaker: DUKE
text: About the phrase “to continue” and really all of paragraph 4, to my mind, although we are continuing some of the things that the Board has done, it has not necessarily been clear that all of these have been considered by the FOMC.

speaker: DUKE
text: To me this takes everything we are doing and puts it in the middle of this table and gives us time to discuss which of them we like, what we might use or not use, and how we might express the degree to which we would use all of these tools.

speaker: DUKE
text: We’ve made a lot of progress in a very short time in coming to the broad outlines of the things that we might do going forward, and in coming meetings we’ll actually contour those more and make them more specific.

speaker: DUKE
text: I would include that as well.

speaker: DUKE
text: As to whether or not we “use” our balance sheet or “expand” our balance sheet, I would leave it at this point as “use our balance sheet” and have further discussion on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Boy, you’ve left me a simple task.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yes, a two- hander from President Fisher.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I just want to come back to a point I suggested.

speaker: FISHER
text: Is there any sense in transposing paragraphs 3 and 4 to emphasize the new regime?

speaker: LACKER
text: In light of our discussion of “use of” in this balance sheet quantitative, I was going to point out that President Plosser’s suggestion about a specific number for an upper bound on the size of our balance sheet would remedy the problem that we were discussing there.

speaker: LACKER
text: In addition, it would greatly alleviate the deep discomfort I and perhaps others may have about our governance practices and the extent to which they’re publicly known.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would also emphasize that there are two theories about the effect of our balance sheet and that this is written from the credit- spreads point of view, and it would be useful to encompass both.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just say, generally speaking, that we are making a lot of changes here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d like to suggest that we move gradually.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But one suggestion I did like and would propose to see if it helps you is First Vice President Cumming’s suggestion of saying that we’ll provide support with measures that sustain the size of the Federal Reserve balance sheet at a high level.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That makes it very explicit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Later we can go further about quantitative guidelines and so forth, but for the moment we’re saying that the balance sheet size itself is of importance.

speaker: LACKER
text: Because the word “size” is a quantitative word, it does a lot better than “use of,” which is ambiguous about sterilization.

speaker: LACKER
text: So to that extent I view First Vice President Cumming’s suggestion as very positive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser, does that satisfy you for today?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Would you read that again, please?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just for today, “the focus of policy going forward will be to support the functioning of financial markets and stimulate the economy through open market operations and other measures that sustain the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet at a high level.”

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it is the focus of the FOMC’s monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The focus of the Committee’s policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in the spirit of trying to move gradually and not just overwhelm the market, I would like, as I say, to move halfway to where we want to be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was a slight majority in favor of alternative A, but I’m very concerned that, if we don’t say anything about the funds rate, there is just going to be confusion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am also concerned about the view that President Yellen, Governor Kroszner, and others raised if we sort of say that we’re not targeting it anymore.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It suggests that we’re indifferent to the rate or that we have no ability to raise it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What does it mean to say that rates will be kept low for a long time, if we don’t have some view on that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I would cite the Japanese precedent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I understand the concerns about community banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think that’s not a reason that should control our policy, and they certainly can change their pricing policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me make some suggestions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Brian, will someone take notes?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then we can come back.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In order to be conservative and avoid risk, I would like to propose alternative B.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the first paragraph, I would take Governor Warsh’s suggestion and say “target range for the federal funds rate between 0 and ¼ percent.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “Target range for the federal funds rate of between 0 and ¼ percent.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Not “of between” but “a target for the federal funds rate between 0 and ¼ percent.”

speaker: LACKER
text: So the target is between.

speaker: KOHN
text: A target or a target range?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “The target range for the federal funds rate between 0 and ¼ percent.”

speaker: LACKER
text: So the target range is to be between those two numbers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Paragraph 1 is the same.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Paragraph 2 is the same, including the additional sentence about financial markets, no longer bolded.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Paragraph 3, President Stern was right about “quickly.” Why don’t we say “appreciably”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, a lot of people have talked about inflation targets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we should look at that very seriously.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Today is not the day to do it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Maybe that should be introduced simultaneously with concerns about deflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I propose that we strike the bracketed material but put the word “further” after “moderate”: “The Committee expects inflation to moderate further in coming quarters.” The fourth paragraph as is—most people were okay with the conditionality there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the fifth paragraph, strike “continue to”: “The focus of the Committee’s policy going forward will be to support the functioning of financial markets and stimulate the economy through open market operations and other measures that sustain the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet at a high level.” You know, I get the sense from the Committee that they will entertain purchases of Treasury securities in the next quarter or so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In order not to jerk the market around too much, I think we should therefore mention it and leave it where it is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the only change in paragraph 5 that I’m proposing is in the first sentence.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: So the last sentence will have “continue to” or not?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yes, I think it has to be there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “The Federal Reserve will continue to consider ways of using its balance sheet.” I think we have to say that because we have used it.

speaker: DUKE
text: Would that say “the Committee”?

speaker: DUKE
text: Would that say the “Committee will” or “the Federal Reserve will”?

speaker: DUKE
text: Perhaps “the Committee will continue to consider ways to use the Federal Reserve balance sheet.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “The Committee will continue to consider ways of using the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet.” I think we should leave it where it is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just leave it ambiguous for now, if that’s okay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So those are the changes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Brian, would you like just to read that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are you able to read it that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you have the information?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would you go ahead and read the thing?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to establish a target range for the federal funds rate of 0 to ¼ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Since the Committee’s last meeting, labor market conditions have deteriorated, and the available data indicate that consumer spending, business investment, and industrial production have declined.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Financial markets remain quite strained and credit conditions tight.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Overall, the outlook for economic activity has weakened further.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Meanwhile, inflationary pressures have diminished appreciably.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In light of the declines in the prices of energy and other commodities and the weaker prospects for economic activity, the Committee expects inflation to moderate further in coming quarters.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Federal Reserve will employ all available tools to promote the resumption of sustainable economic growth and to preserve price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In particular, the Committee anticipates that weak economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate for some time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The focus of the Committee’s policy going forward will be to support the functioning of financial markets and stimulate the economy through open market operations and other measures that sustain the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet at a high level.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As previously announced, over the next few quarters the Federal Reserve will purchase large quantities of agency debt and mortgage-backed securities to provide support to the mortgage and housing markets, and it stands ready to expand its purchases of agency debt and mortgage-backed securities as conditions warrant.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee is also evaluating the potential benefits of purchasing longer-term Treasuries securities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Early next year, the Federal Reserve will also implement the term asset- backed securities loan facility to facilitate the extension of credit to households and small businesses.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Federal Reserve will continue to consider ways of using its balance sheet to further support credit markets and economic activity.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And then the related action.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is a clarification, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I hate to be difficult, but in thinking about this as a step, we talked about an inflation target.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What other steps do you see that we need to clarify as we try to make this process more—I’m looking for some forward-looking language here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we need to talk about it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there are two promising directions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is to have an inflation target or something close to an inflation target, depending on how the Committee decides, what we think is feasible, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other would be to develop a more formalized structure for discussing the integrated responsibilities we have with respect to the balance sheet, and that could involve quantitative ranges, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I didn’t quite like your ceiling because I think in some cases you might want to have a floor.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I don’t think, as I said yesterday, that we can describe our policies in a single number, and I don’t think that a target for the overall size of the balance sheet is a sufficient statistic for what we’re doing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I do think that, for governance and other reasons, we can talk about ranges, consultation, and so on, about the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I apologize that this is an imperfect document.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Given the many moving parts, as I said, I wanted to try to keep it from being too overwhelming.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is going to be a big enough step as it is.

speaker: KOHN
text: By sustaining the balance sheet at a high level, we’re not promising that it won’t fall from here, right?

speaker: KOHN
text: Just that it will be higher than it ordinarily would be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That it’s going to be above $800 billion for some time I would think is a fair statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Does anyone else have a comment?

speaker: WARSH
text: I apologize for the bad English that I offered before, but an alternative to the first sentence that you read that would, I think, be English to Jeff’s fair point—it would be to delete the word “target.” So it says, “To establish a range for the federal funds rate between zero and ¼ percent.” So those are your two options.

speaker: LACKER
text: But it’s the same issue.

speaker: LACKER
text: “Range” is the noun, and you’re saying that the range lies between those things, and you’re not telling everyone what the range is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It would be a range of 0 to ¼ percent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that would be right.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I can’t support that, and I’ll tell you why.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do feel that we had an elegant solution in alternative A. I firmly believe that if we target 0 to 25 basis points—the effective funds rate we all know is trading at 1/ —it is going to create enormous backlash.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is 16 unacceptable to me to say that the bankers will figure out how to deal with this.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, as far as money market funds are concerned, the expense load is usually 30 basis points.

speaker: FISHER
text: So for whatever it is worth, I will be a minority of one, but I cannot support that.

speaker: FISHER
text: Alternative A was elegant in that it made no statement.

speaker: FISHER
text: Then, and I think very important, by dwelling on this business of what our target rate is, we diminish what we’re doing, and what we’re doing is changing things fundamentally, which I fully support.

speaker: FISHER
text: So for whatever it’s worth, I understand all the counter-arguments.

speaker: FISHER
text: Janet and I have talked about this.

speaker: FISHER
text: I know what people are going to say.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think (a) it is an unnecessary distraction, (b) it creates a potential political backlash, and (c) it is counterproductive.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I just want to state it myself straightforwardly and honestly—I may be the only person at this table, but I’ll vote against that.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you give us alternative A, I’ll vote for it.

speaker: FISHER
text: I know I’m one of 17 at this table—there are more than 17 people at this table.

speaker: FISHER
text: I apologize, but I don’t think it’s necessary to make the funds rate clear.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s implied in what we’re doing, but alternative A gives people enough ambiguity to steer around it, and that’s my opinion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think confusion is an extraordinarily dangerous thing for us.

speaker: FISHER
text: The key is paragraph 4 in alternative A—that is what we’re doing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: No, I agree with that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What B says is that this is the end of one regime and the beginning of another.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first one says that this is the end, and then we say what are we doing going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that clarity is needed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we did what you’re suggesting, I don’t know for sure what would happen, but I think there would be a lot of commentary and questions: “What are they saying?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What do they mean?” That would be much more than what B does.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I thought hard about it, and I know that there was a mixture of views.

speaker: DUKE
text: I’d like to ask one question just, again, about going forward.

speaker: DUKE
text: We talked about what you would do differently tomorrow under alternatives A and B and determined that it was nothing.

speaker: DUKE
text: What would you do going forward if federal funds started to trade above 25 basis points under alternative B?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I guess we would stop doing reverse repos to signal our protesting of the fact that the fed funds rate is trading soft to its targets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That’s the first thing we’d do.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I have to say that I think the probability of this happening is extremely remote because banks are balance sheet constrained and therefore aren’t going to do that perfect arbitrage.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Maybe in a normal world it would be possible to get fed funds to trade above the interest on excess reserves, but in this world it’s just extraordinarily unlikely.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But if it were to happen, we would signal our unhappiness with that, and the first thing we would do is we’d stop doing the reverses that we’ve been doing every day to protest the softness in the funds rate.

speaker: DUKE
text: But you would be able to pull it back down.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t know how quickly we could pull it back down.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think that this is going to happen under almost any conceivable circumstance, but if it were to happen, we would basically add reserves to protest what we’re seeing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We’d have another FOMC meeting, and we would make an adjustment to the framework.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think this is an extremely remote possibility.

speaker: CUMMING
text: I think that, if we see the risk of institutional factors, like the way the prime rate is linked to rates, really getting in the way of good policy, we have an obligation to work with the banking community, work with other regulators if necessary, and work with the SEC if necessary to clear those institutional obstacles.

speaker: CUMMING
text: So I wouldn’t let the institutional things be something that gets in our way, rather they would be something that we can really help overcome where we see problems.

speaker: CUMMING
text: That link could be changed, and we may want to work actively with the banking community to make sure that it happens.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: No, clearly the banks are not required to move their prime rate with anything in particular.

speaker: FISHER
text: They can always have their markup, but you can also reverse the argument and say, so why do you want to cut rates?

speaker: FISHER
text: Again, I think we’re pushing on a string here, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: FISHER
text: Forgive me for speaking, but the guts of what we’re doing and the importance of what we’re doing, which I fully support, are in paragraph 4, and I believe we’re distracting from that by focusing on the fed funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with what you’re saying about the important part, but it is nevertheless the case that—as President Yellen pointed out—if we wanted to, we could raise the funds rate if we put on enough pressure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, in an important sense a decision is being made here to end this particular policy approach and to move clearly to another one with the words “the focus of the Committee’s policies going forward will be” and that is described in a lengthy paragraph.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am just so concerned about what will happen if we say we’re not going to target it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is it going to be 5 percent tomorrow?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just fear the confusion.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In terms of what we’re going to be speaking about regarding the new regime, I think it was easier when we had alternative A and we were going to a new regime than when we’re saying, “Well, okay, we’re going to end this regime here.” I’m giving this speech; I get questions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We’re going to end this regime, and we’re going to go to this.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So now I’m in the middle of a transition, and I’m trying to explain it, but other than, “Yes, we left this behind, and here we are going forward.” So that’s my concern about the middle step here.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I guess in your opinion it’s easier to explain going from “Here’s the old regime; we’re going to stick to it for a little while longer and then .

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Today is the end of the old regime.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Going forward, this is what we’re going to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I’m just concerned about not saying what we’re doing with the funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are we going to let it do whatever it wants to do from today?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that’s just going to create volatility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I’m sorry for those who are in disagreement.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For what it’s worth, Mr. Chairman, I agree with you.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the market will be more confused about alternative A than alternative B.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If that’s important, then that should be part of the decision.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I asked you that during the question period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I said substantively we’re not going to conduct policy any differently, but the market will be more confused about A than about B in terms of having to process what this means.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, it will get to the right answer eventually, but it will be more confused in terms of processing information, in my opinion.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: I just want to underscore that, because that was my concern in moving toward B rather than A because I certainly agree that the economic substance is the same.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But I do think there’s much more of an opportunity for misinterpretation by the market, and for us to say that we don’t have control of the fed funds rate is the main concern that I have with A. I think B is very clear.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: The idea of talking about a range, including zero, is something that at least as far as I know the Fed has never done before, and I think that’s an enormous shift.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: That will be seen as a real shift.

speaker: KROSZNER
text: But to go to A would have ambiguity and would be very difficult to explain to people who are not real aficionados that we’re not saying, “Gosh, we really don’t have the opportunity to fix the federal funds rate anymore.

speaker: FISHER
text: I heard eleven people argue the case for alternative A. I counted them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most of them said it was pretty close, and it’s a matter of communication.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s my judgment that we are just going to cause a lot of criticism and a lot of concern and confusion if we do it now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I also agree that it’s fairly close.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But my feeling is that the concern of clarity is more important to me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would you call the roll, please?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: There is also the issue of the directive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The directive would stand as we’ve written it, with the additional sentence at the end?

speaker: DANKER
text: The vote will encompass the statement as Brian Madigan read it and the draft directive for alternative B as was shown in the handout.

speaker: DANKER
text: Since it is longer this time and we are short of time, I won’t read it.

speaker: DANKER
text: Chairman Bernanke Yes First Vice President Cumming Yes Governor Duke Yes President Fisher No Governor Kohn Yes Governor Kroszner Yes President Pianalto Yes President Plosser With some reluctance, I will vote yes.

speaker: DANKER
text: President Stern Yes Governor Warsh Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Could we bring lunch back?

speaker: DANKER
text: That doesn’t usually work well in a recorded session.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s have half an hour for lunch.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Board meeting, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Board meeting is adjourned.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Board will go into my office.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will take a half hour break, and then we have just a few short items afterwards to complete.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s reconvene briefly for a couple of other items.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On consideration, in order to maintain a united front with the Committee, President Fisher changed his vote to vote “yes” on the resolution.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, Governor Kohn is going to talk a bit about our longer-term projection, and then we would like just to hear a bit from Bill Dudley and Pat Parkinson about the TALF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have had several previous briefings on this, but we will update this and talk a bit about its implications for balance sheet management.

speaker: KOHN
text: You should have gotten memos from the Subcommittee on Communications having to do with the longer-term projections.

speaker: KOHN
text: In considering the trial run and also the current situation, in which the ’09, ’10, and ’11 projections really weren’t settling down and didn’t look as though they would soon settle down into what would be consistent with where we would want things to be in the long term.

speaker: KOHN
text: In these circumstances, the subcommittee thought it would be a good idea to go ahead with a quarterly extension of the projections to give the public a better idea of where we thought output, growth, employment, and inflation were expected to be over the longer run.

speaker: KOHN
text: We made four recommendations within that overall recommendation.

speaker: KOHN
text: We recommended that we do it quarterly, not just once a year, and that the discussion be integrated with the rest of the quarterly projection process in the Summary of Economic Projections.

speaker: KOHN
text: We also recommended that we continue to do this for total PCE inflation but, as we did in the trial run, not do it for core PCE to emphasize to the public that it was the total we were looking at over the long run and not the core.

speaker: KOHN
text: We thought that the questionnaire should ask each participant to provide “your best assessment of the rate to which each variable would converge over the longer term (say, five to six years from now) in the absence of shocks and assuming appropriate monetary policy.” This would be something that didn’t emphasize the fact that it was five or six years but where things would settle down and it might take five or six years to settle down.

speaker: KOHN
text: So those are our recommendations.

speaker: KOHN
text: Did I missing anything—I’m looking at the subcommittee members?

speaker: KOHN
text: After today’s and yesterday’s discussions, I think the subcommittee will also take another look at whether the Committee should move further in the direction of an inflation target and get some material to the Committee before the January meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we are not looking for a vote on this today, but if anybody has any views about whether this is the appropriate direction in which to go, I would like to hear them.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the subcommittee ought to consider whether, if the Committee adopts a 2 percent or whatever inflation objective, it might be more confusing than clarifying for us to also be issuing these long-range convergence projections.

speaker: LACKER
text: My first cut at thinking this through—I haven’t given this a lot of thought—is that, if we are going to say our target is X, I don’t see why we would even need these.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is why they need to look at it now because I think they really are substitutes.

speaker: LACKER
text: Yes, I think they are substitutes.

speaker: KOHN
text: You might still need the output and unemployment.

speaker: LACKER
text: We don’t control—well, you know that—sorry.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any other comments or questions?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess, given the zero lower bound issues that we have been discussing and some of the consequences of being there, the difficulty of dealing with policy in that environment, in previous meetings on this topic we have talked about the prospects of specifying the funds rate path or the range of the funds rate paths of Committee members and their projections.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It was suggested earlier that, had we done that previously, we might be in a position to signal to the markets more about our commitment to inflation or something like that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I guess what I’m saying, in the context of both inflation targeting and its projections, giving that a second round of thought, in terms of how it might fit in with that, would be useful under some circumstances.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me turn to Bill, who very kindly learned that he was on the program about fifteen hours ago.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is better than the time I found out I had to discuss a Stiglitz paper in grad school about 12 hours ahead of time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I read the Stiglitz paper three times, and then I started to understand it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: What I thought I would do, if I could, is invert the order and start with the balance sheet issues and then go into the TALF because I think that there is a broader question of our exit from all our liquidity programs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is a very legitimate issue.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You can imagine a circumstance that sometime in the future we still have an inflated balance sheet, and we actually want to raise the federal funds rate target.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The question is, Would we be able to do so?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The good news, of course, is that a lot of our facilities are going to go away pretty naturally—the swaps, the CPFF, and the TAF.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We may have to give it a bit of a nudge, but those programs should downsize pretty automatically.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Even after that, we are still going to have on our books a lot more agency debt and a lot more agency mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We’re going to have loans outstanding that are associated with Bear Stearns and AIG.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are going to have longer-term Treasuries.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have potentially a very large funding obligation to Citigroup, if its losses go through the FDIC and TARP money.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Then, of course, the TALF could also still be on our balance sheet, depending on what the terms of those TALF loans are.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am going to come back to that a little later.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Generally, I am not worried about our ability to raise the level of interest rates, even if our balance sheet is still inflated at the time, for a number of reasons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, I think the interest rate on excess reserves does work, just not quite as well as we had hoped.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The gap between the interest on excess reserves and the effective funds rate has been running in the 40 to 50 basis point range.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That means that, if we were to raise the interest rate on excess reserves, we would raise the whole complex of interest rates, including the effective fed funds rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The gap is as large as it is because, when balance sheet capacity is scarce, people have to be paid to use their balance sheet to arbitrage that difference.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think that gap today is pretty stable, and we can expect that, as the balance sheets return to a more normal condition, over time that gap might actually narrow as people say, “Well, gee, I have more balance sheet capacity to do this arbitrage.” So that would be point number 1.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Point number 2 is that we can probably take active steps that reduce the cost of that arbitrage to banks today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We can limit the GSEs in terms of their fed funds sales, and we can also reduce the balance sheet consequence of the arbitrage by potentially removing those purchases from the leverage ratio, giving them a little regulatory relief, which actually makes some sense because there is really no risk to a bank that is buying fed funds from another bank and putting them on deposit with the Fed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There is no interest rate risk overnight.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So that is something that we might want to consider.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Another thing that I think is important to recognize is that there may be other means of addressing our excess reserves problems.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The first point is that interest on excess reserves is probably good enough to do a reasonable, if somewhat sloppy, job in pushing up interest rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In addition to that, we have other ways of addressing excess reserves in the system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have the ability to change our monetary policy framework.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We had a meeting earlier this year in which we discussed some of the potential places we might want to go.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To drain excess reserves, if we decided that was necessary to get better control of the federal funds rate, we could do reverse repos with a broader set of counterparties, like money market mutual funds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We could do that using the agency debt on our balance sheet and using the Treasury debt on our balance sheet, and we could probably do that in size, since the money market funds would be very happy to be our counterparts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, we could also change the monetary framework in a more radical way.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One can imagine a system by which we set voluntary reserve targets for banks at pretty high levels, where the rate they got if they were above the target dropped off considerably and the rate they got below the target dropped off considerably.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So we could basically give the banks incentives to hold the amount of their excess reserves that actually are in the banking system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, the Treasury could help us, as it was helping us for a while.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The SFP bills actually did work.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problem was that, as the Treasury’s borrowing needs skyrocketed, it started to worry about running into the debt limit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: What actually happened—it was a political issue—it didn’t want to notify the Congress 60 days ahead of time that it might hit the debt limit, and that is really why it started backing away from the SFPs.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, we could resolve this in a couple of different ways.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One, if the debt limit were raised enough, you would have plenty of room.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Or you could potentially exempt the SFPs from the debt limit, and you could argue that doing so makes sense because there is debt here and there is cash on the Federal Reserve balance sheet, so no real net debt is created.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Last, you could gain legislative authority to issue Fed bills, which I think is actually a little more radical step.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the attractiveness of that, of course, is then we have complete control over our destiny, and you don’t have the mushing together of church and state, where we are at least somewhat dependent on the Treasury for managing our monetary policy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the bottom line for me is that I don’t think we should be concerned about the large size of our balance sheet constraining our ability to manage our interest rate policy going forward.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That should not be a driver of what we decide about our liquidity facilities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So why is this important?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, the TALF, just to recap, is a program in which we would basically lend funds against AAA-rated consumer asset-backed securities on a nonrecourse basis to basically anyone—not quite anyone, not foreigners, but pretty much anyone who wants to do it—and we would conduct these transactions through the dealer community.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the TALF program we would be offering three things to investors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, they would be offered more leverage than they can get today because the haircuts that we would put on the securities would not be the 50 percent type of haircuts that the market is putting in place today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They might be 10 percent, 20 percent, or 30 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are still negotiating, determining that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So investors could get a lot more leverage than they can get today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second thing that would be offered is protection against tail risk, and that is something that investors very definitely can’t get today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because the loan would be nonrecourse, the investor could lose only the amount of the haircut, and that is really important in a world where prices are very volatile.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So that would significantly reduce the mark-to-market risk of investing in the securities from the perspective of investors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, probably the most important thing, we would be providing term funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: People could buy these securities, which are of relatively long duration.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It depends on what security you are looking at, but the securities probably range in duration from two years to seven or eight years, if you are looking at student loans.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So this facility would not work if the term were very, very short.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have been in the process of going out and talking quite extensively to issuers and investors over the past couple of weeks.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Board staff has been involved.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The New York Fed staff has been involved.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Basically what we found out is that they like the program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The leverage is not quite as important as we thought.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They said they could live with less leverage rather than more leverage.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They like the protection against the tail risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The nonrecourse nature of the loans, of course, is very attractive.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the main thing on which they focused and that they said was most important for the success of the program was the length of the term of the loans.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: When we went forward with the initial term sheet, we were talking about a one-year term, and the investors have come back quite forcefully and said that a one-year term is not sufficient.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The program will not work with a one-year term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Now, maybe they are exaggerating the degree to which it wouldn’t work, but it does seem fairly credible that there is no reassurance that one year from now we are going to be completely out of the situation that we are in today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So, certainly, it is completely legitimate to be worried as an investor about the rollover risk one year from now, given that these are assets of longer durations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Where I come out on all of this is that I think we really do need to be attentive to that concern, and we should try to make the term of the TALF loans as long as possible, subject to protecting the Fed, obviously, from credit losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If we were to make it short term, I think there is a high probability that the program would fail.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that would be a huge blow to our credibility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Up to now we have done pretty well in wheeling out programs that have done what we said they were going to do.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think this is a particularly important program because of its ability to be expanded in multiple directions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Treasury is very, very interested in this program as a way of using TARP capital efficiently.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So to wheel this out on terms that are too short and that make the program unattractive would be very, very damaging to our credibility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: My view is that we should be willing to offer these loans at term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would favor three years.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think if we do that, this program will be successful.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, if we do that, we are going to have more balances on our books.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This program was originally conceived of as about a $200 billion program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is probably as big as it would get for consumer ABS, but obviously, if we expand it to CMBS and other things, it could be considerably larger than that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So that is sort of where we are.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Pat, do you have anything you want to add?

speaker: PARKINSON
text: No, I don’t think so.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Again, I think the message, as Bill is saying, from the investors and the issuers was that a three-year term would greatly enhance the chances of success.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Indeed, I think our friends in the Treasury Department, at least in the case of government-guaranteed loans, would like to go even longer than that.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But both the Board staff and the New York staff thought that it would work best at three years.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Three years gets you far enough along that reasonable people will believe that three years from now you might actually be able to get private-sector financing for this stuff.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am going to need to consult on an informal basis with the other Board members on this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But in the spirit of our discussion yesterday, I invite questions or comments, which will inform our thinking on this as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Does anyone have any questions or thoughts on this?

speaker: LACKER
text: You said that investors who bought this and put this and got the lending would have the haircut at risk, right?

speaker: LACKER
text: They would get all of the upside?

speaker: LACKER
text: So if spreads close in the marketplace, then they get the upside—so we are essentially lending to them to make a leveraged bet on the securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The purpose of this facility is not to give investors profits.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The purpose of this facility is to address the fact that lending spreads on AAA-rated securities are extremely wide right now and the securitization market is closed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The idea is that, if you offer more- attractive terms than those available in the market, the demand for these securities will increase, issuers will be able to sell these securities at better prices and lower spreads, and the consequences of that will be lower lending rates and improved credit availability to households.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The goal at the end of the day is not to do anything for investors.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The goal is to harness investors’ profit motivation to drive down spreads in the AAA market.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, why are spreads high?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Our view is that spreads are high mainly because people can’t get leverage—that is number 1.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Number 2, the traditional buyers of these AAA-rated assets either have disappeared completely, like SIVs and bank conduits, or have balance sheet constraints.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the risk capital hasn’t really been willing to come in because they can’t get the financing to make it worth their while.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You know, LIBOR plus 300 is not an attractive proposition for someone who is using capital on an unleveraged basis.

speaker: LACKER
text: When I think about leverage and the demand for a given security, if I, as an investor, am going to make a leveraged purchase, then whoever is giving me a loan to make that is also taking a risk position in the security.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the demand that leveraged investors make is really a joint demand by them and the lenders.

speaker: LACKER
text: Everything you have said sounds as if demand is low.

speaker: LACKER
text: Am I missing something here?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The demand is low for these securities today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is low because of lack of leverage.

speaker: LACKER
text: In other words, I’m saying that people who would provide funding also have a low demand or a low evaluation of the value of those securities.

speaker: LACKER
text: This all amounts to a bunch of people out there putting a low value on these securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: No, I don’t think that is quite right.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are in basically a market disequilibrium, where the traditional buyers of these securities have vanished.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In a normal market environment, it would be completely reasonable to lend against these securities on a leveraged basis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the people who would do that lending—banks and dealers—are balance sheet constrained, and that is why they are not willing to make those loans.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If we had a normal banking and dealer situation today in which they were willing to extend loans to their counterparties, they would be providing the leverage.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But that is just not happening.

speaker: LACKER
text: Do you mean they are not making purchases?

speaker: LACKER
text: They still exist—right?— you said buyers vanished.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: The lenders, I think he was saying.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Some of the buyers vanished in the sense that they were SIVs or a lot of them were actually securities lenders who were reinvesting their cash collateral in this, and they have learned a lesson about doing that.

speaker: LACKER
text: What evidence do you have that their absence from the market doesn’t reflect just adverse views about the value of the securities that we should treat the way we treat all other security evaluation decisions that market participants make?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I think the counterfactual is what the investors tell us.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They tell us that that is not the case.

speaker: LACKER
text: These are the ones who would be aided by this program, right?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If you look at AAA-rated assets, the historical credit risk on these assets is very, very low.

speaker: LACKER
text: Over the cycle or in a recession?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yesterday we talked about AAA tranches of student loans, which are 97 percent backed by the Department of Education.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They are selling at LIBOR plus 300 or LIBOR plus 400.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is hard to say that those securities are priced there because of credit risk.

speaker: LACKER
text: What would a security like that have sold for in 1974 or 1981?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would be very surprised if you saw anything similar to what we are seeing today.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, they didn’t exist them, so we can’t look it up, for one.

speaker: LACKER
text: So how do we know these are out of bounds with what they would have traded at?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Jeff, this is all a judgment call.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have been making lots of judgment calls.

speaker: LACKER
text: But you are not giving us any evidence about this, Bill.

speaker: LACKER
text: You are not bringing anything coherent that is—

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is an ongoing discussion about whether prices in markets are in some sense Pareto optimal prices or whether there is liquidity risk, other premiums, that the central bank could do something about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know any way to resolve it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have the same discussion each time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So we are going to give them a three-year term to give them assurances that they don’t have to worry about rolling over.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am assuming that, as the market improves—and it should over the next year or 18 months—this would be almost self-liquidating because it would then become attractive to these parties to leave now and that would be taking it off our balance sheet.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Is that the operating assumption?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, it really depends on what rate we are charging for the loan.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Presumably we are going to charge for the loan at a rate that is attractive in times of extremis and somewhat expensive in normal times.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the question really is, Will the market financing improve quickly enough to make the market a cheaper source of funds?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think we can count on all of these loans going away before the end of the term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we have to presume that the term could actually be three years because we just don’t know whether the financing will be available from the private sector sooner.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That puts us at risk of taking a loss, then, if we should decide to reverse the policy action.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But we could accelerate that process by raising the minimum rate at which we would lend and so make it a higher spread above LIBOR.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: If we are going to do it through an auction—there are still some questions about how to allocate the credit within this program—and if there is a minimum rate at which we would make funds available in the auction (that would be the spread over LIBOR) and we adjust that spread upward, we’re giving them more of a push to go back to relying on market financing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That would be the ideal—to push them back out as quickly as possible when the market straightens out.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I think the idea would be that the window for this program would not be three years.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It would be a shorter period of time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the program would come to an end by the end of 2009 perhaps, but the loans that we had made during that period could be outstanding for some time beyond that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But we’re talking about a lot of assets on our books.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The other thing that we should talk a bit about is credit risk to the Fed in all of this.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the important thing to recognize here is that the credit risk to the Fed is quite low because the Federal Reserve is protected by two things.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One, it is protected by the haircuts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Fed’s risk is a credit risk not a mark-to-market risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Two, the Fed is also protected by the TARP money.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The way this will work is that, to the extent that people put securities to us, we take those securities and we place them in a disposition SPV (special purpose vehicle) that’s capitalized by TARP money.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We’ve been doing a lot of work recently about how risky these assets are and what the risk of loss is to the Fed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It turns out that it’s very hard to generate scenarios in which the Fed has any meaningful risk of loss.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I have no problem with that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: What I’m thinking about is, if we do define a new regime, how we conduct policy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: How are we tying ourselves down now relative to what we might want to do in the future in moving these assets on and off our balance sheet?

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that the more flexibility we have in moving them out, the more flexibility we have in any new regime we put forward, and to me that’s important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Kohn, did you have a comment?

speaker: KOHN
text: A comment and a question.

speaker: KOHN
text: One comment, to follow up on your comment, Mr. Chairman, to President Lacker—I think there’s pretty good evidence that there are liquidity strains in the market, beyond just credit strains, impinging on the price of these securities.

speaker: KOHN
text: One piece of evidence I would cite is the difference between on-the-run and the off-the-run Treasury security rates, which have gapped out by 40 or 50 basis points even from—well, I’m not even sure where they are relative to ’98, but I think they’re at record levels.

speaker: KOHN
text: The unwillingness of people—by “people” I mean market makers—to take positions and to do trades—their caution—is affecting the pricing of all kinds of securities well beyond the credit risk, and obviously there’s no difference in the credit risk in on-the-run and off-the-run Treasury securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Cash bonds versus derivatives, for example.

speaker: KOHN
text: The point that Bill made yesterday was that the equivalent things are selling at very different rates and no one is doing the arbitrage.

speaker: KOHN
text: Second, I like the model that Bill just described in which the Federal Reserve supplies liquidity but the private sector plus the Treasury takes the credit risk.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that puts us in the right place and puts the taxpayer in the right place.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think it’s a good idea to get this thing working and look for other opportunities to use it with the agreement of the Treasury.

speaker: KOHN
text: We can’t do it by ourselves.

speaker: KOHN
text: My questions are that I thought we had some feedback along two lines I’d like to hear your comment on.

speaker: KOHN
text: One is that AAA wasn’t enough, that when we started this we thought doing just AAA tranches would restart the markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: The other question is about the nonleveraged purchasers of this paper.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’re not really catering to them, and will it be successful soon?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the AAA—it is really for specific classes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we’ve heard that somehow the AAA would not be sufficient mostly from the auto loan area.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s hard to judge how credible that is, given that the AAA is the big bulk of the capital structure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So if you’re getting good financing for most of the capital structure, it’s hard to believe that you can’t pay people at the bottom of the capital structure a high enough rate to induce them to do that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think I’m a little skeptical that this is true.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that this program will be successful even if we confine it to just AAA.

speaker: PARKINSON
