text: Even of those who are saying that today they’re having trouble not only placing the AAA but also placing the other tranches, a number say that, if you could start pricing the AAA tranche, that would make placing the others a lot easier.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Basically you’d be determining how much of the spread income from the underlying assets has to go to the AAA, and that tells you how much you have left to compensate the lower rated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You can figure out the economics better once you know how much you have to pay for that 75 percent of the capital structure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think this program addresses the nonleveraged, but I think there’s not much nonleveraged interest in this sector at this point.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Well, that’s the fundamental problem.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Again, some of them were these classes of investors, who are no longer around.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Even if they were around, I don’t think we’d want them around—the SIV and securities lenders et cetera.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But then you have the pension funds, the insurance companies, and so forth that are not in the market, and this really doesn’t do anything at least initially to bring them back to the market.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: We have scratched our heads at some length trying to figure out a program that the Federal Reserve could develop that would entice them into the market.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But I think the fundamental problem is that our tool is the ability to lend, and if we’re lending, there has to be a borrower.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: If you’re talking about pension funds or life insurance companies that are not leveraged investors, it’s just not clear how we can do much to help them get enthusiastic again about buying these securities.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: In the longer run, the agenda of providing liquidity to markets has to be joined with the reform agenda and figuring out what we can do to bring back confidence in structured credit products by those types of investors.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: There are lots of recommendations out there—from the President’s Working Group and the Financial Stability Forum—and SIFMA came out with a long study about restoring confidence in the securitization markets.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: All of that, unfortunately, is going to take a while to implement, and as with so many other things these days, we’re in uncharted territory.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Nobody knows for sure, I think, whether any of those things, even though they make sense, will really be sufficient to bring those investors back.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But as much as we try to come up with programs to address that, it seems at the moment to be beyond our power.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: May I add just one thing to that?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s also not clear to me that the private sector won’t be clever enough to take these things and package them into securities that have the equity and the leverage embedded in them and sell them to people who want to get high rates of return.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It might be a pretty interesting proposition.

speaker: LACKER
text: So are there any other constraints of a legal or regulatory nature on participants in this market?

speaker: LACKER
text: Is there anything that keeps any hedge fund in the world from buying these things?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, we’re still working on—

speaker: LACKER
text: No, no, no, not the program—the underlying securities.

speaker: LACKER
text: Anyone could buy them, right?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The issuers have to basically conform with the TARP executive comp restrictions.

speaker: LACKER
text: Even not participating in the program.

speaker: LACKER
text: There are no limitations on the investors who can participate, for example, in the market for asset-backed student loans.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, there is in this program, in that we’re trying to figure out the right way of restricting it to U.S. investors.

speaker: LACKER
text: The program doesn’t exist yet.

speaker: LACKER
text: Right now, today, is there anything that restricts a hedge fund in London from buying an asset-backed security.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think so—not that I’m aware of.

speaker: LACKER
text: The reason I ask—the point that I’m making—is that you can reference theories but, at the end of the day, it’s not just those predictions.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s the whole range of things about the theory.

speaker: LACKER
text: We haven’t, in this, seen many theories put on the table, and the ones that have been—things like cash-in-the-market pricing—just don’t seem to match up well with the facts.

speaker: LACKER
text: There’s a gigantic, billions of dollars worth of investors out there who have the capability of buying any of this stuff.

speaker: LACKER
text: In Treasuries, people are capable of arbitraging that on-the-run and off-the-run thing.

speaker: LACKER
text: To explain this by appealing to some market segmentation seems really weak in this environment.

speaker: LACKER
text: You know, I welcome discussing theories under which these are Pareto improving programs, but I haven’t seen one that’s convincing yet.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I think it comes back to the point that Bill made earlier.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: If you’re a hedge fund, even LIBOR plus 500 is still not a rich enough return to that hedge fund unless you can borrow against those securities and leverage it up into a higher return.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: And until 18 months ago you could have gotten the financing from Deutsche Bank, the Swiss banks, or any of our fine U.S. banks; but it doesn’t appear at the moment that any of them are terribly interested in lending on a secured basis even to the strongest of hedge funds.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we’re in disequilibrium.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We’re in a disequilibrium in which the dealers and banks that used to do this lending are in the process of dramatically shrinking their balance sheets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Goldman announced their fourth quarter today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They shrank their balance sheet by 18 percent from the end of their third quarter to the end of their fourth quarter.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That’s certainly not any notion of equilibrium in the marketplace, and I think that is what’s causing the stresses in the securities markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: I mean, what are we doing?

speaker: LACKER
text: We’re in the middle of an adjustment process, it takes some time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The way I look at it, President Lacker, is that the deleveraging process is happening at a very rapid rate, and that speed can cause quite a bit of damage to financial conditions and, therefore, to the real economy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To the extent that we intervene and slow down the pace of that deleveraging, we can probably mitigate the degree of damage to financial conditions and to the real economy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That’s how I think about it.

speaker: LACKER
text: I look forward to seeing the model.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, I guess there are at least a couple of theories you could have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One of them has to do with capital.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you think that certain types of intermediaries have specialized knowledge and their ability to lend depends on their capital, then there are informational asymmetries in which clearly exogenous destruction of part of that capital is going to affect equilibrium outcomes in the market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other class of models has to do with liquidity, where you have thick or thin markets depending on “I trade if you trade” and so on and you have markets in which nobody is trading and so no one wants to be the first to enter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: By becoming a marketmaker, you can perhaps generate more activity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there are some interesting perspectives out there.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m familiar with those models.

speaker: LACKER
text: We don’t have time to discuss them now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: No, we should discuss them off line.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The loss of the securitization market is really important, so I think this facility is a very important innovation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My question is, How important were the conduits to this market, and how confident are we that there will be structures to bring back the securitization market?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Or are we basically bridging to these things going on bank balance sheets or other types of financial intermediaries?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: How do you see this?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I guess the question is, From your perspective, what is this a bridge to?

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I think the conduits were more important in some asset classes than others.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: In credit cards, for example, the conduits were pretty important.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But even there they were important in recent years.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: I think they were important in recent years because spreads kept on coming down and down and deterred the real money investors that traditionally invested in these products—they were no longer interested.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Yet the underwriters were able to keep the game going at those low spreads by resorting to selling to conduits and securities lenders and those sorts of things.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: So over time, if we could deal with some of the issues around confidence and ratings and the other things that may be deterring the real money investors from entering the market, there is a hope of bringing them back and going back not to 2007, when it was conduits and that kind of stuff, but to, say, 2002, when you had real money investors buying these securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also how you go through the cycle and what the loss experiences on these securities are going to be are hugely important.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If this is the worst recession in 30 years, that’s going to be a very interesting data point in terms of what the credit losses on the securities are.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If it turns out that the credit losses are low and the securities are robust, I think that will create more demand for these securities over time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You have to weigh that, of course, in terms of what leverage we are going to require financial institutions to carry and how leveraged they can be, and where we set those two standards will determine what goes through the capital markets versus what goes through depository institutions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Do we have in mind a limit as to how broadly we would make the credit facility available?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Currently we have the class of securities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re looking at consumer and small-business ABS.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The Treasury has basically committed $20 billion of TARP, and we think that’s going to fund a program of roughly $200 billion of credit cards and auto loans and so on.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I ask that question because there are some very important industrial companies that have been financing at fairly attractive rates and are now going to have to refinance that at far less attractive rates.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that will have every bit as significant an impact on the economy as the mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So unless we think through how we limit this, I think there’s a legitimate case for just about anything.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, I’m sympathetic with your view that broader is better than narrower because of all the boundary issues that one creates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we all are sympathetic with that.

speaker: FISHER
text: For example, would you consider AAA industrial-grade credits?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we would consider it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The real issue is the Treasury’s willingness to use TARP money.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We can’t do any of this without the Treasury’s commitment, so we’re somewhat constrained in our ability to broaden it in the dimensions that we might want to broaden it.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: We’ve heard from practically everyone that’s not within the class of consumer ABS and SBA loans.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: We have heard from the commercial real estate people and from the auto dealers about their floor plan loans; we have heard from the banks that would like to get the motorcycles and leases.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But also corporate loans—the CLO (collateralized loan obligation) market also is shut down.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: So there is no question.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: Again, we’re in a hard place because, if we weren’t constrained in part by the TARP capital and our concerns about our balance sheet, we would maybe be able to have a much broader program in which we didn’t have to make these kinds of decisions.

speaker: PARKINSON
text: But given that there’s only $20 billion of TARP capital and we’re willing at this point to go only to $200 billion, you can’t really say we’ll take all these different asset classes.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We really have to focus on fixing the intermediary process in the United States.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There’s no limit to this.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The refinancings coming due are huge.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, the limits include the TARP capital, our own willingness with respect to the balance sheet, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There really are limits to what this can accomplish.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But in some sense, just to follow up on this point, the limits are what is really important here because, as long as we don’t define some limits and we just say limited by TARP capital, well, that doesn’t really answer the question.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As long as the markets act as if we or someone else is going to step in and rescue them from any more lending arrangements they happen to be facing, the incentives for the intermediary system to repair itself or to gradually adjust are going to be limited.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m worried about the lack of definition about what constitutes a legitimate market or instrument or firm that we wouldn’t save.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s a good point, and I think one thing that is a problem now is the transition between Administrations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll soon have a new Treasury Secretary and a new Administration.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it’s very important—I’ve discussed this with Tim Geithner and others—that as soon as possible we lay out a broad strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What are the components of our strategy?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What are we going to do going forward?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And what are the limits to it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, implicitly, what are the limits to it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: How are we going to approach the banking issue?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What are we going to do about failing firms?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: How are we going to try to address the securitization markets?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the more clarity we can provide—I fully agree with the critique that lurching is very bad, and we need to provide an overview.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a lot of sympathy from the new Treasury to do that, and we just have to overcome the fact that we’re in a transition at the moment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I take that point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s a very good point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: By the way, Mr. Chairman, I want to thank you.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I thought your exchange of letters with Senator Dodd, I guess it was, over the automobile issues was well done.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think you read it, though.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Excuse me, I read about it.

speaker: LACKER
text: I just want to raise two things that worry me.

speaker: LACKER
text: One is that, when these programs are small, you subsidize X percent of the credit market.

speaker: LACKER
text: The other 1 minus X percent, the effect on their rate of return, their borrowing costs, probably is small.

speaker: LACKER
text: But when X gets near—I don’t know where it is now—⅓ or ½, then our subsidization is raising borrowing costs for everyone who doesn’t get money.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The commercial paper market might be a counter-example to that.

speaker: LACKER
text: There are some models in which that is the case.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s not obvious how we rule them out.

speaker: LACKER
text: The second thing is—I don’t know how you evaluate this—you must be thinking whether this means that in every moderate-sized recession henceforth we’ll view the Federal Reserve’s best policy as extending—

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not a moderate recession, and it’s not a normal financial downturn.

speaker: LACKER
text: Every recession of the size we’ve now seen 3 of in the last 50 years.

speaker: LACKER
text: So every recession of that size?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You have to have a deep recession and a financial crisis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Twice a century, or once a century so far.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’ll give you an example—the VIX has never been this elevated this long since the Great Depression.

speaker: LACKER
text: So you’re saying that you’re not concerned about setting up expectations for the next recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I’m also concerned about getting through this recession.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So those are the tradeoffs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other questions about the program?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let me just tell you that I’m going to be doing a call with the press at 3:15 in the Special Library.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any FOMC member who has nothing else to do and would like to join is welcome.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Michelle has given your Public Affairs people the phone number so that they can listen in, and we’ll see how that goes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next meeting is Tuesday-Wednesday, January 27-28.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Last night Michelle Smith and I attended the swearing in of Tim Geithner by Vice President Biden, with President Obama in attendance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we now have a new Treasury Secretary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be a dinner tonight after the meeting at which we will honor Tim and say good-bye from this post as he goes into another.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is a new year and new things, and so this morning the Federal Reserve Bank of New York announced their new President—Bill Dudley.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You made it all the way across the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: [Laughter, followed by applause] We welcome you and look forward to working with you in your new capacity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As you know, Governor Kroszner resigned in anticipation of the appointment of the new Governor, Dan Tarullo.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But Dan has not yet cleared the Senate, so obviously he won’t be attending the meeting, which leaves the Governors here as an embattled few, [laughter] and I think the lowest number of sitting Governors probably in a very long time.

speaker: LACKER
text: We will go easy on you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me also welcome the new members cycling into the FOMC as voting members—Jeff Lacker, Charlie Evans, Dennis Lockhart, and Janet Yellen.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first part of the meeting is the annual organizational part for the FOMC, so we will be just in FOMC mode for the next few minutes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: After we do that business, we will go into a joint Board–FOMC meeting, as earlier I discussed and we talked about this new way of operating.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to begin with the election of Committee officers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I need a motion for appointment of the Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure and an honor to recommend Ben Bernanke to be Chairman of this Committee.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am not sure what sins you committed in an earlier life, but I sure hope you had fun.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It’s the first nomination I’ve heard like that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you all very much.

speaker: KOHN
text: You need to recognize me again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I need to recognize you again, Governor Kohn.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is a particular pleasure to nominate Bill Dudley as the Vice Chairman of this Committee.

speaker: KOHN
text: I join you in welcoming him.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now the staff officers of the FOMC.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Debbie, would you please read the list?

speaker: DANKER
text: For Secretary and Economist, Brian Madigan; Deputy Secretary, Debbie Danker; Assistant Secretaries, Matt Luecke, Dave Skidmore, and Michelle Smith; General Counsel, Scott Alvarez; Deputy General Counsel, Tom Baxter; Assistant General Counsel, Rich Ashton; Economists, Nathan Sheets and Dave Stockton; Associate Economists from the Board, Jim Clouse, Tom Connors, Steve Kamin, Larry Slifman, and David Wilcox; and from the Banks, Dave Altig, Dan Sullivan, Joe Tracy, John Weinberg, and John Williams.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: May I have a motion?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next item on the agenda is the selection of a Federal Reserve Bank to execute transactions for the System Open Market Account.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Sorry, am I on the wrong item here?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is that a different order?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m sorry, I missed an item.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Item 2 is a proposed revision to the program for security of FOMC information.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You received a memo from Scott Alvarez and Debbie Danker.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This appeared to be mostly minor procedural changes to the rules.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The most substantive change was a rule affecting the access to confidential information of people who are not regular employees—i.e., consultants.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any questions for Scott or Debbie or any comments?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now we go on to item 3, selection of a Federal Reserve Bank to operate the SOMA.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In a shocking development, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York has again expressed willingness to serve in this capacity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In this context, I would like to take note of a memo that was sent to the Committee by Louise Roseman and the Division of Reserve Bank Operations about their assessment of the controls and procedures related to the SOMA and the management of the various new facilities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They found that those controls were effective and that the SOMA activities complied with established directives, guidelines, and procedures.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think the report we have is that New York is doing a fine job and should continue to carry out this function.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: May I have a motion, please?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Item 4 is the selection of the manager of the System Open Market Account.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We now have changing leadership in New York, and therefore we are not quite ready to select a permanent manager or to vote.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Prior to the meeting, I appointed Trish Mosser as temporary manager of the Open Market Desk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will come back to the Committee for a vote when a permanent position is established.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now that Trish is here, she gets to do some work, I guess.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have three items— 5, 6, and 7: a proposed revision to the authorization for domestic open market operations, a proposed revision to the authorization for foreign-currency operations, and a proposed treatment of the guidelines for the conduct of system open market operations in federal agency issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Trish, could you talk about all three of those briefly, please?

speaker: MOSSER
text: I would be happy to.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The proposed changes were discussed in a memo that went out to the Committee last week as well as in a memo that proposed a slight amendment to the domestic authorization that was circulated yesterday.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Let me start with the foreign-currency area, for which there are three distinct parts to consider.

speaker: MOSSER
text: With respect to the authorization for foreign-currency operations, we propose keeping the 2008 authorization mostly unchanged.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We have one modest alteration.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We propose adding four additional currencies to the list of permissible foreign exchange purchases and sales—the Australian dollar, the Brazilian real, the Korean won, and the New Zealand dollar.

speaker: MOSSER
text: This is being done to reflect the foreign exchange swap agreements that were put in place in 2008 with the central banks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: On the foreign-currency directive, we are currently recommending no changes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Regarding the procedural instructions with respect to foreign-currency operations, we are proposing a slight modification to the introductory paragraph, adding the words “unless otherwise directed by the Committee,” to recognize explicitly that the instructions can be superseded by the Committee.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I can pause now for a vote on the foreign side, or I can continue on and talk about the rest.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Could you go through all three, please?

speaker: MOSSER
text: I would be happy to.

speaker: MOSSER
text: With respect to the authorization for domestic open market operations, we are proposing several amendments.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The specific changes include, first, minor changes to consolidate language for repo and reverse repo operations into a single paragraph; second, the addition of a new paragraph 2 that codifies the New York Fed’s authority to transact in agency mortgage-backed securities for the SOMA portfolio using agents, such as asset managers and a custodial bank.

speaker: MOSSER
text: This paragraph also allows the custodial agent to engage in repo transactions in order to manage the cash balances that are generated by agency MBS holdings.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Third, we are adding language in the final paragraph, as suggested by a Reserve Bank President, that makes explicit the authority of the SOMA manager, following instructions from the Chairman, to take actions that “result in material changes in the composition and size of the assets in the System Open Market Account.” This authority, however, would be subject to the requirements, set out in the last sentence of the paragraph, that the Chairman consult with the Committee, if feasible.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It would also make clear that “any such adjustment shall be made in the context of the Committee’s discussion and decision at its most recent meeting.” The intended effect of the proposed revisions is to place the governance of intermeeting changes by the Chairman in the size and the composition of the SOMA portfolio on the same footing as changes in the degree of pressure on reserve positions and the fed funds rate.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Last, in light of the Federal Reserve’s current program of purchases of agency debt and agency MBS, the staff recommends that the guidelines for agency debt and agency MBS purchases be temporarily suspended.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The status of the guidelines will then be reviewed at next year’s January FOMC meeting.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I should note that there is a precedent for this.

speaker: MOSSER
text: For example, paragraphs 3 through 6 of this document were temporarily suspended by the Committee in August 1999.

speaker: MOSSER
text: At the time, the SOMA manager was concerned about the Desk’s capacity to respond to any Y2K year-end effects and sought the authority to accept agency debt and agency MBS collateral.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would like to comment on the implications of items 5 and 7, in particular for our GSE purchase program.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In late November, as you know, I directed the Open Market Desk to begin a program of purchasing MBS and agency debt, based on the authorizations to do that and a consultation by phone that Don and I had with all the members of the FOMC.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At the time, I felt comfortable with that decision.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Since then, given how central the MBS purchase program has become to our policy and given the issues of governance that have been raised and we have all discussed, I now believe that I made a mistake in doing that—I should have consulted more closely and then taken a vote of the FOMC.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I want to pledge to you that I will not take any similar actions in the future without a formal consultation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, the effect of item 5 is essentially to make that part of the rules.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Item 5 puts the substantial changes in the portfolio on the same footing as a change in the federal funds rate—i.e., the strong presumption is that this will be done in formal consultation with the Committee and that the Chairman retains the right to make intermeeting adjustments but only in situations where consultation is not feasible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I believe this is the right direction in which to go, and I support making that change.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On item 7, on the guidelines for purchases of agencies, I think this is a useful clarification.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I would like to at least record that, in my own view, I don’t think that our MBS purchase program is credit allocation in the sense that this guideline was intended to address—for several reasons.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, to my mind, credit allocation involves a preference for a certain class of borrowers relative to what normally functioning markets would throw up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In this case, the issue is not an attempt to distort allocations away from some efficient outcome; rather, it is our intention to try to make markets work better and to bring us closer to a normal market outcome.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, I view the MBS purchase program as being really very close to monetary policy in spirit and intent in that we are trying to address broad issues of macroeconomic stability by stimulating an important component of aggregate demand.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we are using this particular tool not because we have a preference for housing but because we are trying to stimulate overall aggregate demand.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Indeed, as you know, we are in fact looking at various types of credit in order to achieve that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think this is similar to the normal use of monetary policy, which affects different sectors differently, not because we have a preference for one sector or another but because our tools allow us to address different components of aggregate demand with different force.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am saying all of this because I do have this view, and I want to get it out on the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nevertheless, I think it is a clarification and useful for us to formally suspend these guidelines for the time being.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me open the floor for comments and questions on any of these three items.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, Mr. Chairman, I think this may be the first time that a Wellesley woman has had responsibility for the Trading Desk.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am married to a Wellesley woman.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am used to being tutored by a Wellesley woman.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I have two questions that I would like to ask, just out of ignorance.

speaker: FISHER
text: The first is about the 65-day rule, particularly—and I may not understand this—but in paragraph 1(B) and then paragraph 4, the requirement to resell after 65 days or less, does that apply in the case of MBS or not?

speaker: FISHER
text: Then the second: Is the limit on $25 billion of an open position in all foreign currencies still current?

speaker: FISHER
text: Is that appropriate under current circumstances?

speaker: MOSSER
text: However, based on a previous vote, we have exempted the fluctuations in the value of foreign portfolios due to changes in the exchange rates.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We do nothing at this point but passively invest both our yen and our euro portfolios.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But given the size of exchange rate movements that we have, it would be possible at some point for us inadvertently to exceed a $25 billion limit.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So we are assuming that we fixed an exchange rate at a time when we were under $25 billion, and we determined that, if we happen to go over inadvertently, it would not be a good idea then to go into the market and actively buy or sell foreign exchange to undo that.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So other than that exemption, yes, we are abiding by that, and that is in force right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: First of all, I applaud the changes in item 5 to the domestic authorization.

speaker: LACKER
text: I will note here that it has been a triennial tradition for the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond President to dissent on the foreign-currency-related directives.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am going to break with tradition and support them.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our opposition in the past had to do with their use and the implications in foreign exchange operations that struck us as off-balance-sheet fiscal policy that was more properly done by the Treasury.

speaker: LACKER
text: However, I would like to share a couple of comments on the Guidelines for the Conduct of System Operations in Federal Agency Issues.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me just state at the outset that, in my view, they conflict with what we are doing now with agencies.

speaker: LACKER
text: “Credit allocation” is a term of art, and I think there is room for reasonable people, in good faith, to take different positions on what that means, as is the case with terms like “normal market functioning” as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think of the term in this context by comparing purchasing agency securities with some broader-based purchase of a similar quantity.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we will have an opportunity to discuss this later in agenda item 8, but that thought experiment leads me to believe that these operations must, compared with a broader- based purchase of Treasuries, lower particular market sectors’ interest rates relative to others and leave others higher than they otherwise would be.

speaker: LACKER
text: I recognize that there are members—in fact, the broad majority here—who probably want to continue with the program and not suspend the guidelines.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I had my choice, I would not suspend the guidelines; I would suspend the program.

speaker: LACKER
text: So what I would like to do is respectfully register a negative vote on this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we are ready to vote, then, why don’t we do them separately, beginning first with the revision to the Authorization for Domestic Open Market Operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do we have a motion?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I take that as unanimous.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, the revision to the Authorization for Foreign Currency Operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Third, the proposed treatment of the Guidelines for the Conduct of System Operations in Federal Agency Issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Given what President Lacker said, why don’t we call the roll on this one.

speaker: DANKER
text: Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Dudley Yes Governor Duke Yes President Evans Yes Governor Kohn Yes President Lacker No President Lockhart Yes Governor Warsh Yes President Yellen Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That covers the organizational items.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At this point I would like to convene a Board meeting joint with the FOMC.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I need a motion to close the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So now for the rest of today and tomorrow, we will be in joint session.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s turn now to our regular Desk reports, starting with Trish, and these reports will include not only our regular financial updates but also the broader discussion of balance sheet issues and so on that we talked about at our videoconference.

speaker: MOSSER
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Spence and I will be referring to the financial conditions and facilities handout in front of you.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Stress in financial markets has eased somewhat in recent weeks, but very unevenly.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Markets directly supported by the Federal Reserve or government actions have seen declines in spreads, improved liquidity, and modest increases in trading and lending activity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But markets beyond the reach of Fed and government programs remain very strained.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Moreover, the economic and financial downturn is very rapidly depleting banks’ capital cushions.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Let me start with markets in which the Fed has intervened.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Interbank lending spreads, shown in exhibit 1, have continued to narrow.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The sharpest declines in LIBOR–OIS spreads actually occurred before year-end, and at present, one-week and one-month spreads are below their early September levels.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The declines in spreads occurred at the same time that private lending among banks increased modestly— particularly at the one-week and one-month tenors.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But almost no one is willing to take the risk of lending on an unsecured basis to a bank for more than a month.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As a result, LIBOR spreads three months and beyond remain elevated.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As Spence will discuss in more detail, declining spreads and increased private-sector lending have been reflected in reduced demand for term liquidity at our facilities.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Similarly, in commercial paper markets, activity is up, and spreads are down.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Rates on all types of A1-rated paper have declined—you can see this in the second exhibit—since the announcements of the various Fed facilities for commercial paper and money market funds.

speaker: MOSSER
text: After year-end, even A2/P2 commercial paper spreads, which are not eligible for the CPFF, fell sharply.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In exhibit 3, consumer mortgage rates, as well as mortgage and agency spreads have declined notably since the announcement of the Fed purchase programs in November.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In addition, secondary mortgage market spreads to Treasuries fell again during the first week of the purchase program in early January.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Retail conforming mortgage rates have increased somewhat from very low levels in early January, moving up with long-term Treasury yields, but they remain well below the levels that prevailed before the Fed’s purchase program was announced.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Spence will be talking in more detail about the MBS purchase program in a few minutes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The FDIC guarantee of financial debt has had an indirect effect on the corporate bond market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Corporate bond spreads, pictured in exhibit 4, widened throughout the fall, but since December these spreads—which do not include FDIC guaranteed debt—have declined.

speaker: MOSSER
text: At the same time, the nonguaranteed portion of new issuance, seen in exhibit 5, has actually increased; in just the first two weeks of January, it accounted for more than half of new issuance.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Apparently, guaranteed debt is not attractive to traditional corporate bond investors, so they have shifted into obligations of nonfinancial issuers.

speaker: MOSSER
text: This has effectively increased demand for a small pool of corporate bond issuers, causing spreads to decline.

speaker: MOSSER
text: 1 The materials used by Ms. Mosser and Mr. Hilton are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: MOSSER
text: In contrast, markets without Fed or government backstop—such as consumer­ asset-backed securities, commercial-mortgage-backed securities, and leveraged loans—have shown little or no improvement.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Consumer ABS spreads (exhibit 6) have narrowed a bit since the passing of year-end but remain very elevated despite expectations for the beginning of the TALF program in late February or early March.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Activity is at a standstill, and according to both the packagers and the buyers of securitized products, it is likely to remain so until the TALF is up and running and market participants have a sense that it will “work.” CMBS and leveraged-loan prices, shown in the next exhibit, seemed to stabilize late last year but recently have fallen even further as the macroeconomic outlook has continued to worsen more sharply than expected.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The outlook for nonagency mortgage securities continues to deteriorate.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Recently the rating agencies projected even larger losses, which will cause formerly AAA super senior tranches to be downgraded to default-level ratings.

speaker: MOSSER
text: All of this is, of course, more bad news for holders of these securities—including banks, insurers, and the GSEs—which are likely to face larger write-downs on mark-to-market assets and significantly larger impairment charges.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Recent headlines about capital impairments at several of the Federal Home Loan Banks reflect these ongoing write-downs.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Despite the modest improvements in some markets, one should not underestimate how remarkably fragile financial markets are right now.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The process of deleveraging, asset sales, and overall reduction in the risk profile of large financial institutions continues unabated—although in a somewhat more orderly way than a couple of months ago.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Lack of liquidity is one symptom of this fragility.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Although liquidity has improved since the beginning of the year, for most markets this improvement can be characterized as moving from “nonexistent” to “very poor.” Even core benchmark markets such as Treasuries and foreign exchange have exceptionally strained liquidity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Volumes are at multiyear lows.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Bid-asked spreads in euro–dollar foreign exchange trading (exhibit 8) have more than doubled.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In benchmark Treasury markets, the amount traders will buy or sell at a given price—the trade quote size shown in exhibit 9—is 0.1 of normal.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Volatility has remained correspondingly high across nearly all markets, even with the improved conditions in the last few weeks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: High volatility and poor liquidity can be self-reinforcing.

speaker: MOSSER
text: They raise the cost of making and underwriting markets, which leads to less trading, higher spreads, less credit formation, and in general a lot less risk-taking.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The lack of liquidity across markets has led to some obvious unexploited profit opportunities.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibits 10 and 11 give a couple of examples.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibit 10 shows the average error between the yield on 10-year Treasury securities and the predicted yield for those securities based on the Board’s model.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In normal market conditions, a host of market participants—trading desks, institutional investors, and hedge funds—trade constantly each day to exploit such large gaps and arbitrage them away.

speaker: MOSSER
text: At present, a combination of balance sheet constraints and high volatility has caused a pullback in this activity, which, again, is self-reinforcing.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibit 11 has a second example of an unexploited profit opportunity—namely, the spread between yields on corporate credit default swaps (CDS) and corporate bonds.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Even in normal market conditions, the corporate CDS market is the more liquid (because it requires less balance sheet and is a more standardized product), but the difference amounts to a few basis points.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Currently the spread between CDS and corporate bonds is more than 200 basis points for “liquid” investment-grade bonds and nearly 450 basis points for high yield.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Large losses and associated balance sheet constraints of banks and dealers are major reasons for the drying up of liquidity across markets.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But also important is the lack of arbitrageurs—most notably hedge funds.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Hedge fund losses in the last few months have been enormous.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As exhibit 12 shows, 2008 was the worst year on record for the hedge fund industry, with losses of 20 to 40 percent for the group.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Almost every type of hedge fund had double-digit losses (except short equity, and they were shut out of the market for some time).

speaker: MOSSER
text: Losses were concentrated in the second half of the year, with about two-thirds of them in the last quarter.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The poor performance provoked record redemptions, estimated to be at least $150 billion and as much as $400 billion.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Of course, redemptions would have been much larger if many—particularly large—hedge funds had not shut their gates.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In response, hedge funds have deleveraged very quickly, adding more downward pressure to asset prices and further undermining liquidity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In short, the capacity of the financial system to absorb and mitigate shocks is small—as small as it has been during this crisis.

speaker: MOSSER
text: At present, there are two closely linked risks to the fragile equilibrium in markets.

speaker: MOSSER
text: One, of course, is the continued rapid deterioration in the macroeconomic outlook, both in the United States and globally.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The second is the truly precarious financial condition of many of the largest financial institutions, particularly the global banks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Fourth-quarter bank earnings, which we are in the midst of receiving, were expected to be very bad, and in fact have been even worse for the major U.S. banks, as exhibit 13 shows.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Earnings expectations for large European banks are even worse than for U.S. banks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If they disappoint to the same degree, the Q4 losses just for the banks in the table could easily be above $70 billion.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Adding in the hedge fund losses and the large expected losses at the GSEs and insurance companies, Q4 losses in the hundreds of billions seem likely.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The outlook for banks is hugely uncertain.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Simply put, investors are worried about the size of the “hole” in banks’ balance sheets—that is, the size of the additional asset write-downs and reserving that will be necessary.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If the hole is large, as anticipated, or worse, enormous, how will banks be able to fill it?

speaker: MOSSER
text: As exhibit 14 shows, banks’ regulatory capital ratios look fairly robust, but for large banks, the ratio of tangible common equity to tangible assets—a metric that investors and rating agencies follow closely—looks much more precarious.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Most important, losses come first out of common equity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Replacing those losses at current share prices implies potentially massive dilution for current shareholders.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As a result, bank equity prices remain under severe pressure—as can be seen in exhibits 15, 16, and 17.

speaker: MOSSER
text: To scale just how far bank equity prices have fallen, the market cap of all U.S. banks (including investment banks) is now about the same as the market cap of the soft drink industry.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The downward pressure on U.S. and European bank stocks is reinforced by uncertainty about the form and size of government intervention, particularly for the weakest players, which are viewed as closer to insolvency or government assistance.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Even if some investors view banks as having significant long-term value, the possibility of government dilution or even nationalization discourages capital injections from the private sector.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In contrast, government support of banks has capped their credit spreads, which you can see in exhibits 18, 19, and 20.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Although credit tiering is evident in CDS spreads, the level of bank CDS for both U.S. and foreign banks has remained in the high end of the investment-grade range.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Equity holders may expect to be wiped out, but debt holders clearly view the probability of losses as fairly low.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Market expectations that large-scale fiscal action will need to be taken in support of the economy and the financial system have had a significant effect on sovereign credit default swap spreads.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The CDS spreads in exhibit 21 have risen because the expected fiscal cost has soared and because of uncertainty about the ultimate size of the bill—which will depend critically on global economic growth and on the magnitude of government assistance to financial institutions.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Not surprisingly, CDS spreads for small countries with relatively large financial services sector—such as the United Kingdom, Spain, and Ireland—have increased proportionally the most.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In recent weeks, movements in sovereign CDS spreads have mirrored movements in the countries’ bank CDS spreads.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Accompanying the increase in sovereign CDS spreads has been a pronounced steepening of yield curves in the major economies.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibit 22 shows that in recent weeks Treasury yields in the United States are up at all maturities, but the increases in longer-term yields are particularly large—the 30-year is up about 40 basis points in the last week and a half or so.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Part of this increase is likely due to short-run supply increases.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the next few weeks, $150 billion of new Treasury coupon securities will be auctioned, and this week alone, we are auctioning $200 billion of Treasury bills, notes, and bonds.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Given illiquid market conditions, we shouldn’t be surprised to see a rise in yields that is somewhat exaggerated.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Nonetheless, with large and sustained fiscal deficits on the horizon, somewhat higher borrowing rates are not too surprising.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Finally, a few words about monetary policy expectations.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The results of the Desk’s latest dealer survey are shown in exhibit 23.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Neither the dealers nor the futures markets expect any change in the target fed funds range in the near term.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Dealer economists expect the current fed funds target range to be maintained well into 2010, reflecting widespread views that the combination of a deep recession and continued financial crisis will require easy monetary conditions for some time to come.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Spence will now discuss the balance sheet and the use of facilities.

speaker: HILTON
text: Assets on the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet, as of last Friday, totaled $2.04 trillion, as shown in exhibit 24.

speaker: HILTON
text: The total has declined about $250 billion from its recent peak on December 17, with most of that decline coming since the year-end.

speaker: HILTON
text: I should note that most of the data in these charts are as of last Friday, and just within the last day there have been some fairly significant developments at some of the facilities.

speaker: HILTON
text: For example, at the CPFF, borrowing came down as much as $50 billion yesterday and another $21 billion just today, and we’re learning today about large declines in swap facilities that will take effect on this Thursday.

speaker: HILTON
text: But before I get into some discussion of the individual facilities, let me give the general picture of what we’ve been seeing.

speaker: HILTON
text: In general, demand at several of the special liquidity facilities has fallen to one degree or another in recent weeks, reflecting a relaxation of stressful conditions in some of the money markets, as suggested by the downward movement in money market yields, which is shown in exhibit 25.

speaker: HILTON
text: Some of the key term funding rates that are linked to several of our liquidity facilities are shown here.

speaker: HILTON
text: The direct support offered by various Federal Reserve programs, which since October have provided a large amount of term funding to banks, dealers, and other financial institutions—as well as the support offered by various government initiatives—has been behind much of the easing of conditions in these funding markets and also helps explain why the year-end passed fairly uneventfully.

speaker: HILTON
text: Lower rates in these financing markets in turn affect the economic incentives to use some of the facilities, and that is being reflected in the more recent experience.

speaker: HILTON
text: But other factors, such as an ongoing deleveraging of positions, have also contributed to falling usage in some cases.

speaker: HILTON
text: Looking ahead, we anticipate that the net size of the balance sheet is likely to continue to fall for a time, but by how much is difficult to say.

speaker: HILTON
text: Even if reported market rates remain at levels that suggest cheaper funding could now be secured in the market, the liquidity behind those quotes is not always deep.

speaker: HILTON
text: Any net decline that we see in coming weeks will also likely prove to be temporary.

speaker: HILTON
text: The agency mortgage-backed security and agency debt purchase programs are really just getting under way, and the TALF program starts only later this winter.

speaker: HILTON
text: Moreover, as we have already experienced, the usage of many of these facilities could change quickly and substantially should conditions in financial markets again deteriorate.

speaker: HILTON
text: Now I’ll tell about some of the recent experiences at individual facilities in more detail.

speaker: HILTON
text: The term securities lending facility (TSLF), which is illustrated in exhibits 26 and 27, does not affect the size of our balance sheet but does alter the composition of assets that must be financed in the marketplace.

speaker: HILTON
text: TSLF loans outstanding are just around $125 billion, and that’s off a level of about $200 billion in post-September.

speaker: HILTON
text: The auctions continue to be undersubscribed, and stop-out rates have regularly been at the minimum bid rates.

speaker: HILTON
text: Even over the year-end, only a small quantity of the options on loans sold under the TSLF options program were exercised.

speaker: HILTON
text: The downward trend in participation here is consistent with the narrowing in spreads between the term repo rates on the collateral that we accept and those on the Treasury securities that we lend.

speaker: HILTON
text: In rough order of magnitude, these spreads are now in line with the minimum bid rates at both the schedule 1 and the schedule 2 TSLF auctions.

speaker: HILTON
text: Dealers have also indicated that their holdings of some private securities that are eligible under schedule 2 continue to shrink and that money market funds and other investors are now more willing to finance the agency debt and agency MBS that we accept on schedule 1.

speaker: HILTON
text: On that last observation, I’ll note that today we let our last outstanding 28-day single-tranche repo mature, bringing to closure the initiative begun last March under which we arranged term repos against agency mortgage- backed securities as collateral.

speaker: HILTON
text: As recently as one month ago, the outstanding value of these operations was still at its peak of $80 billion.

speaker: HILTON
text: Net draws by foreign central banks under our swap agreements have come off a peak of $586 billion in early December, and as of last Friday, they stand $120 billion below that, as shown in exhibit 28.

speaker: HILTON
text: Declines in LIBOR and foreign exchange swap funding costs seem to be having a direct effect on participation levels.

speaker: HILTON
text: Most of the dollars made available by the participating foreign central banks are allocated at a rate of OIS plus 100 basis points, across one-week, one-month, and three-month tenors.

speaker: HILTON
text: Recently, OIS rates out to three months have been standing at about 20 basis points.

speaker: HILTON
text: There have been considerable reductions in draws at the shorter maturities, where LIBOR rates are now well below these allocation rates.

speaker: HILTON
text: Some of the decline in the shorter maturities has been offset by increases in draws at the three-month maturity, where three-month LIBOR rates are now very close to the OIS plus 100 basis point threshold.

speaker: HILTON
text: But just this morning we learned of an $80 billion decline in net draws on some of the 84-day allotments, about $50 billion at the ECB.

speaker: HILTON
text: Term auction facility loans outstanding have come off their peak level of $450 billion reached over the year-end and now total $416 billion (exhibit 29).

speaker: HILTON
text: Most of this decline reflects the run-off of some of the special forward-settling operations arranged last November that spanned the year-end.

speaker: HILTON
text: Although propositions have been below the offered amounts since last October, when the auction sizes were raised to $150 billion, the quantities borrowed remain large, as seen at the last several auctions, including yesterday’s 84-day operation (exhibit 30).

speaker: HILTON
text: Improvement in the term interbank market has not so far translated into a significant decrease in participation at our TAF auctions.

speaker: HILTON
text: That may reflect the fact that the minimum bid rate is set equal to the interest rate paid on excess reserves, which is just 25 basis points, and that most banks have ample collateral available to secure such loans.

speaker: HILTON
text: In line with the more general trends, borrowing at the PCF and the PDCF has been falling as well, as indicated in exhibit 31.

speaker: HILTON
text: PCF borrowing has been running around $60 billion, and PDCF borrowing has been about $30 billion.

speaker: HILTON
text: The commercial paper funding facility passed a major milestone yesterday—its three-month anniversary.

speaker: HILTON
text: As shown in exhibit 32, much of the $350 billion of commercial paper purchased through last Friday under the program was acquired in the first days of operations, beginning on October 27.

speaker: HILTON
text: Since then, increases have continued at a steady but much slower pace.

speaker: HILTON
text: The CPFF purchases only 90-day paper, and reflecting the heavy concentration of purchases at the outset exactly three months ago, $88 billion matured yesterday.

speaker: HILTON
text: Of yesterday’s maturing paper, only $33 billion was replaced with new issuance at the CPFF; the remaining $55 billion of the maturing total was not.

speaker: HILTON
text: Today another $57 billion was maturing, of which about $20 billion to $25 billion rolled off.

speaker: HILTON
text: This is pretty much what we would expect and what several of the participants in the program had indicated that they would likely do, given that CP rates in the market are now well below the CPFF loan rates.

speaker: HILTON
text: These rates are set at OIS plus 200 basis points for unsecured paper (100 basis points less for paper with a guarantee) and OIS plus 300 basis points for asset-backed CP.

speaker: HILTON
text: Issuers that did not roll over their maturing CP at the CPFF covered themselves in one of several ways.

speaker: HILTON
text: Some had pre-funded themselves in the CP market, were funding themselves elsewhere, or had reduced their overall funding need.

speaker: HILTON
text: Short-term funding markets were able to absorb the increased issuance with no apparent problem yesterday, although some backup in CP rates has been seen in recent days and a large amount of CP issued to the CPFF, about another $130 billion, matures over the coming week or so.

speaker: HILTON
text: The use of two facilities targeted at money market funds reflects the continuing improvement in the position of these funds.

speaker: HILTON
text: AMLF (ABCP money market mutual fund liquidity facility) loans continue to run off and are now just about $15 billion (exhibit 33).

speaker: HILTON
text: Still there has been no borrowing at the MMIFF (money market investor funding facility).

speaker: HILTON
text: Inflows into prime money market funds and funds that invest in agency paper remain on a steady uptrend (exhibit 34).

speaker: HILTON
text: There have been, however, some areas of growth in the assets on the balance sheet.

speaker: HILTON
text: Purchases of agency MBS, being made through our four investment managers, have continued at a fairly steady daily pace since these operations commenced on January 5 (exhibit 35).

speaker: HILTON
text: Cumulative commitments total $58 billion (through January 23).

speaker: HILTON
text: This puts us on a pace to accumulate as much as $500 billion by the end of the second quarter.

speaker: HILTON
text: Few of the purchases arranged so far have actually settled—so far about $7 billion.

speaker: HILTON
text: This reflects the considerable delays between purchase and settlement that characterize this market.

speaker: HILTON
text: Of the contracted purchases so far, the vast majority have been for MBS for 30-year maturities, most with coupons ranging from 4.5 percent to 5.5 percent.

speaker: HILTON
text: The option-adjusted spread to Treasury rates narrowed almost 50 basis points after the announcement of the program in November.

speaker: HILTON
text: On balance, spreads have tightened somewhat further since purchases began in early January, but there have also been periods of modest backup amid strong selling pressure.

speaker: HILTON
text: Some of the selling pressure reportedly reflects a lack of clarity among market participants about the Fed’s commitment to this market after the second quarter and the $500 billion purchase objective has been met.

speaker: HILTON
text: Investors are worried that there may be a “cliff,” with purchases ending abruptly at the end of the second quarter.

speaker: HILTON
text: This uncertainty could be lessened if, for example, the Committee stated that the program will continue beyond midyear as market conditions warrant.

speaker: HILTON
text: Conforming mortgage rates had been about 6 percent just before the program announcement.

speaker: HILTON
text: Shortly after we began our purchases, they were being posted by the same banks at rates as low as just under 5 percent, but they have more recently moved back up closer to 5.5 percent as originators struggle to process the wave of refinancings that has ensued.

speaker: HILTON
text: Working with the investment managers, we have been confronting the challenges of both building up a large portfolio of agency MBS and trying to be supportive of smooth market function.

speaker: HILTON
text: This has provided some perspective about the potential value of our being sellers at times or of participating in the dollar-roll market, even as part of a strategy oriented toward building and maintaining a large portfolio.

speaker: HILTON
text: Likewise, the rise in mortgage applications, shown in exhibit 36, indicates that the supply of new agency MBS may increase sharply in coming months, which may be a factor that we need to consider in determining the appropriate pace for MBS purchases going forward.

speaker: HILTON
text: Meanwhile, we have continued to purchase agency coupon securities, arranging about one operation per week.

speaker: HILTON
text: Since purchases began in early December, we have bought a total of $23 billion (exhibit 37).

speaker: HILTON
text: So far at least, most of the narrowing in spreads of agency debt to Treasury securities realized since this initiative was announced in late November has been maintained.

speaker: HILTON
text: The purchases reportedly have contributed to the market’s receptive response to the renewal of debt issuance by the agencies this month.

speaker: HILTON
text: Trish noted the relative lack of improvement in those markets not directly targeted by any of the Federal Reserve’s newer liquidity facilities.

speaker: HILTON
text: With that as background, let me provide a brief update on the term asset-backed securities loan facility (TALF).

speaker: HILTON
text: Just as a quick reminder, through the TALF, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York will lend as much as $200 billion on a nonrecourse basis for up to three years against certain AAA-rated consumer ABS as collateral.

speaker: HILTON
text: The U.S. Treasury Department will provide $20 billion of credit protection to the New York Fed in connection with the TALF, and further protection will be provided by haircuts on the loans.

speaker: HILTON
text: In recent weeks, staff members at the New York Fed, the Board, and the Treasury have made significant progress in finalizing several aspects of the program that are critical to its success.

speaker: HILTON
text: These include working out a host of operational details.

speaker: HILTON
text: The aim is to post the terms and conditions for the facility and to provide frequently asked questions by the end of this week, with the goal of being operational maybe even as soon as late February or early March.

speaker: HILTON
text: I’ll conclude my review of the financial assets on the balance sheet by noting that we last ran off a small portion of our remaining bill holdings last September and have arranged no outright operations in Treasury securities since then.

speaker: HILTON
text: We now hold around $475 billion.

speaker: HILTON
text: We have no conventional repo agreements outstanding and have not arranged any such operations in the market since October.

speaker: HILTON
text: On the liability side of the balance sheet, the offset to net swings in total assets has mostly been in excess reserves, which are now in the neighborhood of $800 billion—maybe now closer to $700 billion.

speaker: HILTON
text: The Treasury had built up its balances held at the Fed under its supplementary financing program to a level of $560 billion in November.

speaker: HILTON
text: Since then, it has been running down these balances because of debt ceiling considerations, and they now total $175 billion.

speaker: HILTON
text: Brian will now continue our presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The staff is recommending that the Board and the FOMC act to extend the various liquidity facilities that are scheduled to expire on April 30.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The PDCF, the TSLF, the AMLF, the CPFF, the MMIFF, and the temporary reciprocal foreign-currency arrangements are all currently scheduled to expire at the end of April.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As Trish noted, conditions in some financial markets have improved somewhat in recent months, but those improvements have been limited.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With the macroeconomic situation and the condition of financial institutions both deteriorating significantly, the recent improvements would seem to be attributable not to any strengthening of the fundamentals but rather to the range of actions taken by the Federal Reserve, the Treasury, the FDIC, the Congress, and foreign central banks and governments to stabilize the financial system as well as to the passage of year- end.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As Spence has noted, even though the usage of some facilities has declined, amounts outstanding under some programs, such as the CPFF, remain substantial.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, the level of usage is by no means an adequate metric for assessing the contributions of these programs to stabilizing markets.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In many cases, market participants continue to look to the facilities as important backstops for their funding.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In these circumstances, it would seem premature to consider terminating any of the existing liquidity facilities at this time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although the facilities do not expire for three months, the staff believes that the Board and the FOMC should act now to extend them.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Absent an action to extend the programs, market participants and analysts are likely to speculate increasingly about the Federal Reserve’s intentions for the facilities, which probably would add unhelpfully to market jitters.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, lenders may increasingly become concerned that borrowers will not have access to backup funding facilities to repay currently extended loans when those credits mature in a few weeks and hence could become more chary about lending now.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The staff recommends that the Board and the FOMC extend the expiring facilities through October 30.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This six-month extension from April 30 should be sufficient for now to assure market participants that the lending programs will be available for the period of time relevant for money market transactions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A case could be made for an even longer extension to take the programs over year-end—say through January 30, 2010—but you may be concerned that such a very long extension could signal a view that the financial crisis will be quite protracted.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, for the programs that depend on the Board’s section 13(3) authority, the requirement to find that unusual and exigent circumstances are present may be interpreted as making it difficult to extend these programs for a full year from now.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If you do extend the facilities through October, as recommended, you may wish to plan informally on revisiting the expiration dates of these programs around the time of your June or August meeting so that you will be able to provide advance notice to market participants about whether or not the programs will be extended beyond October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Some of the Federal Reserve’s special programs—for example, the TAF—do not have a set expiration date and hence do not need to be extended.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, the TALF is not set to expire until year-end.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Thus, under the staff proposal to extend the other expiring facilities through October 30, the TALF would not need to be extended at this time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If the Board and the FOMC act at this meeting to extend the programs, the staff anticipates that the extensions would be announced to the public on Thursday at 10:00 a.m. Because the swap lines are among the items proposed for extension, part of the press release would be joint with our foreign central bank counterparties.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Draft resolutions for consideration by the Board and the FOMC were included in the staff memo on this matter.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Trish will now continue our presentation.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I am going to discuss long-term Treasury purchases by the SOMA for a few minutes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Last week, we circulated a memo outlining four options with respect to the long-term Treasury purchase program.

speaker: MOSSER
text: To summarize: Option 1 is to retain purchases as an option but not to implement at this time; option 2 is to implement a pilot program; option 3 is to implement a large-scale purchase program; and option 4 is to purchase illiquid long-term Treasuries not with the explicit goal of bringing down longer-term yields but to improve Treasury market functioning.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In addition, of course, there was an implicit option of announcing that a long-term Treasury purchase program was completely off the table.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The staff recommended option 1—retain the program as an option that continues to be evaluated but don’t implement at the current time.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The staff demurred from implementing such a program at this time for five reasons.

speaker: MOSSER
text: First, for the further expansion of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet that would be needed, this program was viewed as likely to be less effective dollar for dollar in easing financial conditions than programs more directly linked to credit formation and to markets with more impaired liquidity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Second, it was unclear how big such a program would need to be to push down yields significantly from their current quite low levels.

speaker: MOSSER
text: A large program might not do much at these levels.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In that case, the program would be an especially inefficient use of balance sheet capacity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Third, such a program could potentially distort the relationship between Treasury and private-sector yields, affecting Treasury yields while having little effect on private rates.

speaker: MOSSER
text: This could potentially undermine the value of Treasuries as a hedging vehicle.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Fourth, such a program might even have adverse effects.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In particular, some commentators would almost certainly argue that such purchases amounted simply to “monetizing the federal deficit.” Although it is difficult to assess what effect such arguments would have on financial markets, worries on this score could conceivably lead to higher risk premiums, which could undermine the program’s effectiveness.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Fifth, the program would increase the interest rate risk inherent in the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet because the long-term Treasuries would be funded by excess reserves—an overnight obligation.

speaker: MOSSER
text: This means that, if short-term rates rose in the future, the Fed’s net interest margin could be squeezed, potentially generating losses for taxpayers.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The staff does recommend, however, keeping the program alive as an option.

speaker: MOSSER
text: After all, some of the decline in Treasury yields since early December may be due to expectations of such a program in the future.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If the Committee endorses the staff’s recommendation, to retain it as an option but not implement it at this time, will long­ term Treasury yields rise significantly—say more than 10 or 20 basis points?

speaker: MOSSER
text: That does not seem likely.

speaker: MOSSER
text: First, most market participants, even those that believe the FOMC will purchase long-term Treasuries eventually, do not anticipate that the Federal Reserve will necessarily begin purchases right away.

speaker: MOSSER
text: They generally believe that, with Treasury yields as low as they are currently, there is no need to commence such a purchase program immediately.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Second, market participants are placing a probability of only about 50 percent that such a program will be implemented at all.

speaker: MOSSER
text: That’s based on our latest primary dealer survey.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If the program is kept on the shelf and remains a part of the tool kit and that is clearly communicated to the market via the FOMC statement, we would anticipate that this would generate at most only a modest backup in Treasury yields.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Finally, the note distributed last week also contained some observations about some of the other options for moving ahead with purchases at this point and discussed some of the execution issues raised by the purchase program.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I’ll now turn to Nathan, who will continue our presentation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given ongoing stresses in the global financial system and the vulnerability of some key U.S. institutions to foreign-currency funding pressures, the staff has begun to assess the pros and cons of establishing temporary liquidity swap lines that would allow the Federal Reserve to lend euro, yen, sterling, and Swiss francs to U.S. institutions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These lines would be the mirror image of our existing swap lines and would allow the Federal Reserve to respond to eventualities ranging from a foreign-currency liquidity squeeze faced by a single U.S. bank all the way to a systemic shortage of foreign-currency funding among U.S. institutions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We raise this issue in today’s meeting in the spirit of bringing to your attention an issue that we see emerging on the horizon.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That said, we are still sorting through and evaluating a number of considerations that bear on this initiative, and we would very much appreciate your thoughts and guidance.

speaker: SHEETS
text: One major money center bank has recently shown particular vulnerability to foreign-currency funding pressure.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This institution’s huge presence in foreign markets is reliant on secured and unsecured foreign-currency funding.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The vulnerability of its foreign deposit base and limited foreign-currency collateral has been apparent on a number of occasions over the past several months.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indeed, just last Monday, when U.S. markets were closed, our bank supervisors had significant concerns regarding the institution’s ability to access sufficient foreign-currency funding.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There were similar worries during a particularly stressful period in November.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In each instance, the necessary financing was obtained, but the situation nevertheless remains fragile.

speaker: SHEETS
text: While this one institution is a focus of concern at present, we cannot rule out scenarios in which other large U.S. institutions also run into trouble meeting their foreign-currency funding needs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There is a related risk that, once one U.S. institution showed pronounced vulnerability in this regard, other U.S. institutions might also then be viewed as vulnerable and that a broader foreign- currency liquidity crunch could develop.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These observations suggest that it would be prudent for the Federal Reserve to have the capacity to backstop the foreign-currency funding needs of U.S. institutions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Establishing temporary swap lines with foreign central banks strikes us as a straightforward way to achieve this objective.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Such swap lines would ensure that the Federal Reserve could serve as a lender of last resort in foreign currencies for U.S. institutions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In particular, these lines would offer a reliable vehicle for providing foreign-currency funding to U.S. banks during times when U.S. markets were closed because of either time zone differences or U.S. holidays.

speaker: SHEETS
