text: Our expectation is that these new swap lines would be signed and implemented only if funding conditions clearly warranted.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We do not recommend putting them in place on a precautionary basis, largely because we are not certain how the markets would receive the announcement of such facilities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Rather, the features of these lines could be negotiated with our central bank counterparties, with the draft agreements then put on the shelf to be approved and executed as needed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: To ensure that these lines could be rapidly implemented in deteriorating conditions, we recommend that the FOMC consider delegating authority to the Foreign Currency Subcommittee to conclude such arrangements.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There might still be some announcement effect created by the reporting of such a vote in the FOMC minutes, but it would probably not be seen as signaling the same urgency as an announcement that the facilities themselves had been established.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The authority granted to the subcommittee in this regard would be symmetric to that already delegated to the subcommittee to negotiate swap arrangements to allow major foreign central banks to lend dollars.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Three further issues are worth mentioning briefly.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First, the legal structure of our existing swap lines requires the Federal Reserve to deposit the foreign currency it receives as part of the swap in an account at the foreign central bank.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These new swap lines would be symmetric to our existing lines, but they would allow the Federal Reserve to lend the foreign currency to U.S. financial institutions and require foreign central banks to deposit the dollars they receive at the Federal Reserve.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In principle, our existing swap arrangements could be amended to allow us to lend foreign currency.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But we would prefer implementing these new swap lines through a separate and parallel set of agreements in order to reduce similarities to the old-style swap lines that were used to fund foreign exchange intervention in previous decades.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Second, there are other means that could, in principle, be used to get foreign-currency funding to U.S. institutions under stress.

speaker: SHEETS
text: One alternative would be striking agreements with foreign central banks for them to lend against high-quality dollar collateral.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But central banks have been working on these procedures for some time, and although progress has been made, not enough of these arrangements are in place to address the existing vulnerabilities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, foreign central banks may be hesitant to lend to a troubled U.S. institution during a period of stress, particularly on the basis of collateral held outside their jurisdictions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As another approach, we could simply require U.S. institutions to sell their dollar collateral and obtain foreign currency themselves in the foreign exchange spot or forward market.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, this might be difficult or disruptive during periods of market stress and would leave institutions vulnerable during times when foreign markets are open and U.S. markets are closed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Third, the provision of foreign-currency denominated liquidity to the foreign branch of a U.S. depository institution would rely on the discount window authority of the Reserve Banks, and some technical issues would need to be worked through in implementing a lending arrangement along these lines.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The staff is not proposing that you vote today to establish these new swap arrangements, but we are highlighting this as an issue meriting your attention.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We also note that, if stresses in foreign-currency funding conditions persist, we may be back to you—perhaps very soon (and perhaps even in the middle of the night)— [laughter] with a request to move forward with these arrangements and the corresponding delegation to the subcommittee.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That concludes our presentation, and we are very happy to take your questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was very informative and a lot to digest as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just remind the Committee that the only action item in the list, other than the ratification of domestic open market operations, is the proposal to extend the programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The discussions of Treasury purchases and foreign-currency swaps are just for information at this point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will have an opportunity in a few minutes to have a discussion on these issues, but before we do that, let me first see if there are any questions for our colleagues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any questions for Trish or her colleagues?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So the TALF is scheduled to end in January, but all the other programs with this vote will be scheduled to end in October, is that right?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Yes, and for the other ones that have a maturity date, the extension would be through October 30.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It seems a little peculiar to have different dates.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It seems particularly peculiar to have it end at the end of the year when that is likely to be a problematic time, regardless of whether things settle down.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So, actually, I would have a preference to go to January.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But if we are not going to go to January, I do think that we should discuss it at the June meeting, not the August meeting, because I know that there has been some uncertainty in the markets about which programs would be extended.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I don’t think the speculation has been particularly healthy, so it is better to have a little more clarity.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It might be worthwhile, if we are going to have it end in October, actually to include that it would be discussed in June so that people know that it will come up again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a tradeoff between giving people the assurance of a long period, and flexibility—not committing our balance sheet for an extended period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I agree with you that, if we do this, we ought to revisit it earlier rather than close to the date.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The August meeting seems a little late, given that there is likely to be speculation about year-end by August.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is it too early to ask for a few more details on the swap description that you were talking about?

speaker: EVANS
text: In the following sense—there was nothing distributed on this, right?

speaker: EVANS
text: Because the question that I asked before about the swaps—and I had been comforted by the answer—is what our loss exposure is when we provide swaps to foreign central banks.

speaker: EVANS
text: They stand behind them, so that is about as good as we have.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is sounding a little different.

speaker: EVANS
text: If I understood what you were talking about, it is that we will be using them as an agent to provide funding to our troubled institutions, and some discussion about what guarantees and whatnot would be very helpful.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The risk profile would be different for exactly the reason you suggest.

speaker: SHEETS
text: A lot of the analysis on this particular proposal has been done just over the past few days, and that is one reason that we are not presenting it with a fuller description and more detail.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But we certainly intend to continue to do that work, and as we make progress on some of these issues, we certainly plan to circulate a memo to the Committee describing some of the other issues.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is it too early to have some idea what the order of magnitude of the funding requirements might look like?

speaker: SHEETS
text: We haven’t thought systematically about that issue.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I mean, I could guess—

speaker: EVANS
text: I wouldn’t hold you to it, if you are willing to.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But I think it would probably be better not to guess.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Maybe Trish wants to guess.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have noticed that the astute responders don’t go for that line.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Potentially fairly large—particularly if we are considering more than one large institution.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the scenario that Nathan laid out, which is the risk that we are considering, we think it is somewhat less likely that we would use these lines for the sort of operations that most of our foreign central bank counterparties are using to distribute dollars, which are operations and tenders that are open to all.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We don’t see that kind of need across a broad group of institutions and a broad group of banks around the United States.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But there is certainly a subset of institutions, many of them quite large with very sizable foreign exchange funding, that fund themselves in Asia, Europe, and South America.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Should those institutions end up being in worse financial shape, many of them actually have quite substantial collateral with us at the discount windows in the various Districts.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But they would not need funding in dollars.

speaker: MOSSER
text: They would want to come to us instead and, for example, take out a discount loan—they could do it through other mechanisms—in a foreign currency rather than in dollars.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The way that we would then finance it—given the relatively modest size of our foreign exchange reserves and the fact that the reserves are only in two currencies—would be to establish swap lines and fund them that way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vice Chairman, did you have an intervention?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, just a very brief one to reinforce Nathan’s point.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We began discussions with the foreign central banks literally last week on this issue, and it was really begun because of the vulnerability that we felt on Martin Luther King’s Birthday with our being closed and what would happen in that environment—how we could get liquidity to a U.S. bank that might have difficulties abroad.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of President Evans’s questions about risk, this is really no different from our lending domestically to a domestic institution against collateral that we hold, except that we are basically using that collateral to fund the foreign exchange swap.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So you can just think of it as equivalent to our lending to a domestic institution against the collateral they hold here in the United States.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, do you have an intervention?

speaker: LACKER
text: You may have mentioned this, but who bears the foreign exchange risk in this?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Maybe Vice Chairman Dudley and Trish have some thoughts on this.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The way that we structure the foreign exchange swaps now is at a fixed exchange rate for both the front and the back leg, so that we don’t have—

speaker: LACKER
text: So the other central bank bears it.

speaker: LACKER
text: So in this case, who would bear it?

speaker: MOSSER
text: We would basically get back the dollars that we gave to them.

speaker: LACKER
text: So we would bear the foreign exchange risk of the swap.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Details have not been addressed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There is a new dimension to think through—that is, who is bearing the foreign exchange risk vis-à-vis our central bank counterparty?

speaker: SHEETS
text: And I don’t think the terms there are going to be different.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But then, when we go on to lend that foreign exchange to our commercial bank, there is a new dimension in thinking about foreign exchange risk.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That is a credit risk.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That is not a foreign exchange risk.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Well, it depends on which currency it is being booked in.

speaker: LACKER
text: When you say it would be the same, it depends on whose point of view it is.

speaker: LACKER
text: The way Trish described it, we would bear the foreign exchange risk vis-à-vis the other central banks.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is that what you are saying?

speaker: SHEETS
text: We are still thinking through that point.

speaker: MOSSER
text: That is the part that is still being worked out.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I am sorry—I misunderstood your question.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We would bear, for example, through the discount window the risk of lending in yen and euro.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Obviously, the collateral would be in dollars, and the foreign exchange risk would be—

speaker: LACKER
text: Obviously, it is a lending risk.

speaker: LACKER
text: But before you do the loan, you swap with the foreign central bank.

speaker: LACKER
text: The way we do it now, the foreign central bank bears the currency risk, and in this one, we would.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The way that works is, when we do that swap, we agree to unwind that swap at the exchange rate that prevailed at the time the swap was made.

speaker: SHEETS
text: My preference in these negotiations is that, for these other swaps, we would do exactly the same thing vis-à-vis our foreign central bank counterparties.

speaker: LACKER
text: To make them bear it?

speaker: SHEETS
text: So they would still be bearing the foreign exchange risk.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But in some sense we are promising that we get back the dollars we put in and they get back the foreign currency they put in.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is risk in that the currency is going to be worth less in dollars, but it is not risk in that you are getting back anything different than what you actually extended.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In some sense, the Federal Reserve and they don’t really care because they get back their currency and we get back our currency.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s an element of hedging here.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, actually, President Evans asked one of the questions that I was going to ask.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mine is a lot more generic, of Trish: To what degree do you sense that this credit default swap market is helping or hindering efficient markets and the equilibration of these distortions that we are seeing?

speaker: FISHER
text: Because there is some debate about this.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am talking about the speculative CDS positions.

speaker: MOSSER
text: My view is that the credit default swap market has taken a lot of abuse for many things that would have happened even if it didn’t exist.

speaker: MOSSER
text: There have been a few times, certainly, that the peculiarities of the structure of the CDS market have led to more-volatile changes in spreads from one day to the next.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But, quite honestly, it is a more liquid market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It probably gives you a truer price signal for the vast majority of credits out there, particularly large corporations, both financial and nonfinancial, than the corporate bond market does.

speaker: MOSSER
text: When market liquidity goes away and it is harder to discern fundamental movements in asset prices, the less liquid market—and that is definitely corporate bonds—gives you the worst signal, and the CDS market probably gives you a better signal.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Given the size of the CDS market, the rapidity with which it grew, the size to which it grew, and the fact that it is a little the dog that didn’t bark and that there were certainly problems with the Lehman bankruptcy and a lot of technical issues, my view is that, frankly, it has been one of the markets that has continued to function—not wonderfully, but it still functions—and some liquidity is still there.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Others may have a slightly different view, but that has been our experience.

speaker: FISHER
text: That actually is the basis of my question.

speaker: FISHER
text: The point is whether we are getting good information from the CDS spreads, not a distorted version.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think they are probably less distorted—certainly in the case of corporates.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: First, since we are beginning the year, a broad appeal to speak to the furthest person in the room rather than to the person next to you.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is very hard to follow many of these answers because I can’t hear you down at this end of the table, and I can imagine our colleagues here in the back of the room have no idea what is being discussed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is probably a little premature to be thinking in this detail, but the institution that Nathan described I think we can all guess because of their foreign operations.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: They have funding needs in many, many currencies.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Charlie, can you hear me at the end of the table?

speaker: EVANS
text: I was just trying to guess whom you were talking about.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Would we be using hard currency swap facilities to deal with softer currency funding problems when the crisis could begin in a minor currency?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Is there that kind of linkage conceivably in how we structure and address this?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That is the first question.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The second question is, If this is an institution for which we have already had an intervention with a significant and very public amount of money involved, would we be offsetting this against that intervention facility, or is this incremental?

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the first question, you are absolutely correct that this particular institution does have significant foreign-currency funding needs in some of the minor Asian currencies, for example, and has experienced stresses in those.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think that is an issue that we would need to ponder as to how to proceed on, and it was in the back of my mind in the sense that in our presentation we emphasized euro, yen, sterling, and Swiss francs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Suppose it is a minor Asian currency.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Would we want to think about swap lines with some minor central bank to allow them to have that currency, or is getting them yen enough?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Given market differences, time zones, and everything else, is getting them yen going to be sufficient to be able to provide the funding in some of the other Asian currencies?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Those are issues that we are going to have to spend a fair amount of time thinking hard about.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think maybe the second question is more for New York.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t think we are nearly far enough along in this process, nor have we spoken in sufficient detail to either our bank supervisory or our discount window colleagues to make that judgment, frankly.

speaker: MOSSER
text: At this point, the fact that I know is that quite a significant amount of collateral is posted within the Federal Reserve System at the discount window that is not currently being borrowed against.

speaker: MOSSER
text: That is, honestly, probably as much as we can say at this stage.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But, clearly, that would be a set of conversations we would have to have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, we can go to a Committee discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are going to have two more go-rounds in which everybody gets to state their views, so I was hoping that instead of a go-round we could have a more interactive, unstructured discussion of the issues that have been raised by the presentations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you allow me, I would like to start by just posting you on a few items and making a few comments, and then we will open the floor for discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it is important to understand that the calls on our balance sheet and our programs will be very much conditioned by the decisions being made in the Administration and the Congress about the kinds of support they are intending to provide and the approach they are going to take.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As you know, Tim Geithner, who was sworn in just yesterday, is overseeing the work with the remainder of the TARP and perhaps an expansion of the TARP, depending on how things go.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Staff members at the Board and the Federal Reserve Banks have been working very extensively on programs with our fellow bank regulators and have provided a great deal of support and information to the Treasury as they have been trying to think about how to go about stabilizing the banking system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It seems clear at this point that any solution they are going to come up with is going to have at least two components.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One would be the removal of bad assets in some way from the balance sheets of the banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For that purpose, there has been discussion, as you know, of an aggregator bank, ring-fencing, or some kind of insurance program that would allow banks to purchase insurance against tail risk for their assets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second component that is almost certain to be involved would be capital.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But there are a lot of open issues: What is the appropriate instrument, what control rights would be associated with it, should the capital be put in just in time or should it be put in preemptively to make sure that there is coverage for subsequent losses, and what would be the ultimate cost?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, will the remaining monies in the TARP be sufficient?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the smart money is betting no.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, the Treasury is working on the foreclosure programs, which will probably involve up to $50 billion to $100 billion of the TARP, and is looking to support credit markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I assume that the TALF would be part of that program.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have had a few very preliminary discussions with Tim Geithner about the consequences for these programs, for the Federal Reserve, and tried to talk about our priorities and our concerns.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it is a bit strong to say that I am looking for a new Fed–Treasury accord here, but maybe not that strong.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is a good opportunity, the next couple of months, as planning is done and as the Administration goes to the Congress and makes requests, to try to clarify as much as possible what role the Fed is expected to play.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, I think we should be as allergic as possible to (a) long-term commitments of our balance sheet because of the difficulty of unwinding and (b) credit risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those are the two things that concern us.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, if we do an aggregator bank, it would be important to make sure that it is financed not by long-term Federal Reserve liquidity but by, as one option, private financing guaranteed by the FDIC, although I think the Fed should be open to doing short-term collateralized lending, as it would for any bank, as part of that process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Likewise, if ring-fencing becomes part of the plan, I would defend our actions with respect to two large banks, where we have taken tail risk positions as being necessary for financial stability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But going forward, I hope that we will find solutions that don’t involve that kind of glitchy approach.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that the top priority is to try to get the bank resolution program done in a way that is consistent with good practices on our part.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a couple of other requests for Tim, and I should just emphasize this is very, very preliminary.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Ideally, one would be that, if the government at some point does develop a resolution trust company or an aggregator bank, they should consider, for example, taking off our balance sheet some of the assets that we have acquired at our Maiden Lane facilities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, an important issue for us would be the management of the exit strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Treasury has already requested from us some memorandums on the supplementary financing bills and on the Fed bills idea, and I believe that they will give serious consideration as to how they can assist us in the exit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The lowest priority for me at this point would be the TALF-like approach, for two reasons at least.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that it is an effective approach that will not happen unless the Fed is involved, because of the TARP scoring method—the fact that the TARP is scored in terms of the full amount that is lent or purchased rather than in terms of some measure of credit risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, it is extremely unlikely that the Congress would give any kind of authorization that would allow for the TALF to continue, absent some kind of Fed cooperation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would also argue that the TALF is much closer to conventional central bank activity than some of the other things that we are concerned about—i.e., it is given the capital support from the Treasury, it is protected from credit risk, and it is mostly short-term lending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For those reasons, I would put that as lowest priority.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, I think that, as much as possible, we need to cooperate and work with the Treasury to try to get the banking system and the economy stabilized.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But this is an opportunity, and I will do what I can to try to get assurances from the Treasury about how things will evolve in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In my view, the main constraint will be certainly not the goodwill of the Treasury or of the Administration but rather the constraints that they face in dealing with the Congress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As you know, the TARP and the bank stabilization programs are extremely unpopular.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is going to take a certain amount of political capital to get additional resources.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, they are going to have to dole out their political capital in a quite sparing way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I will continue to work on these issues, and I understand that they are important to the Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I support the extension of the programs to October.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We did discuss going over year-end.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The tradeoff is the commitment to a longer outstanding funding, but I do think that we ought to revisit that in a timely way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On Treasury purchases, I would like to reiterate what Trish said.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that there is good reason to keep this on the table, that it is not really a good idea to throw away this option at this point, but that it is probably not an efficient way to use those balance sheet capacities at this juncture.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I would agree with the recommendation of the staff on that, and I think part of our discussion certainly tomorrow in the policy round would be exactly how to express that in our statement language.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just a couple of other comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, one of the issues, which you can see in the press commentary—“murky new territory,” “unknown, uncharted waters,” et cetera, et cetera—is that, clearly, for us to be successful with our current set of policies, it is important for us to be as open and transparent as possible and to provide as much information as possible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want you to know that we have here at the Board, in cooperation with the Reserve Banks, a new transparency initiative which has at least two parts, maybe three.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that Governor Kohn has consented to head a committee that is going to review all of the information associated with our balance sheet, the programs, collateral, and all of those things and ask the question, for information that we do not release, whether we have a good, strong policy justification for not releasing it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, then we should be as forthcoming as possible about providing the public with information about the collateral, about the programs, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will have a hearing on February 10, when I will discuss these issues in front of Barney Frank’s committee, and I have a speech at the National Press Club the week after that, when I will address the press and let them ask questions about these issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other part of the transparency initiative is to try to make our programs more accessible to the general public, including the media, congressional staffers, and the like.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have an effort under way to develop a website, essentially, that will link to all of the information that we have and that will provide overall discussion and education about our various programs, which we hope to get going within a month at the latest.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the educational aspect of this is very important in trying to get people more comfortable with the regime that we are operating in, given the constraint on the federal funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, going along with our discussion about extending the various facilities, I should tell you that, using the authority vested in me, I extended the TAF—the auction facility—until the end of the quarter at the current level of $150 billion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that particular item goes to the end of March.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But that is an authority, as I understand it, that we can use here at the Board.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have taken a good bit of time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me stop and turn to President Lacker for comment or discussion on the issues of the balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m happy to kick off our first go-round in this format.

speaker: LACKER
text: Obviously, we established a new interest rate regime at the last meeting and have some knotty issues—a lot of challenges—ahead of us.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to borrow a bit of time from my remarks later in the meeting and use them here, if I could.

speaker: LACKER
text: I respect your appeal for disorganized interaction, but I have organized my thoughts.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am happy to give a disorganized version, if you would like, but— PARTICIPANT.

speaker: LACKER
text: There is an observational equivalence here, I am sure.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, let me applaud the discussions you have initiated with the Treasury.

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to comment a bit on that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think they are very important right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: What I would like to talk a bit about, first, is just the two schools of thought that we have been contending with here about how to use our tools—how we should conduct policy in this new framework.

speaker: LACKER
text: One, obviously, is using our balance sheet to influence the size of our monetary liabilities in an attempt to influence the growth of the public’s nominal expenditures, and the other is to use our balance sheet to intervene in market segments that seem particularly strained and where consequences for the broader economy appear to be particularly significant.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that the term asset-backed securities loan facility, which is our next program to be implemented, is illuminating here and raises significant questions about these two schools of thought.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I want to explore it for just a couple of minutes.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is aimed at improving conditions in the market for securitizations of credit card, auto, and small business loans, with the hope of improving the securitization markets’ functioning and thus increasing the flow of credit to consumers and small businesses.

speaker: LACKER
text: Quarterly interest rates on such securitizations have been exorbitantly high of late—I think Ms. Mosser’s presentation had them up about 500 to 600 basis points over LIBOR—and new issuance fell to virtually zero in the last quarter, as I understand it.

speaker: LACKER
text: Expected loss rates on the underlying loan portfolios have risen significantly since September, but there are some who argue that the spreads on AAA tranches are far too high to be explained by increasing loss rates alone.

speaker: LACKER
text: Another relevant factor is that there has been a widespread pullback from structured finance.

speaker: LACKER
text: Investors have lost confidence in some of the inputs into the securitization process—rating agency assessments would be an obvious one—so investors are not willing to pay nearly as much now for consumer loan securitizations as they once were.

speaker: LACKER
text: In addition, one hears other reports that some investors in this class of securitization are more reluctant to hold these securities now because of mark-to-market volatility, which for this class of investors passes through their income statement, in contrast with some of the issuers who, if they hold the same securitizations on their own balance sheet, don’t have to run mark-to-market changes through their balance sheets.

speaker: LACKER
text: So there is a certain comparative advantage in accounting treatment to the issuers holding these.

speaker: LACKER
text: This leads me to the next thing.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the other side of these securitization markets bears a careful look.

speaker: LACKER
text: We happen to have two of the largest credit card ABS issuers in our District.

speaker: LACKER
text: Both of these firms have simply declined to issue securitizations because it is cheaper to use their balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: Their funding costs—there was one issue, 2¼ percent, year and a half money—some of them quote 1½ percent for brokered deposits.

speaker: LACKER
text: In comparison with that, the spreads in the secondary market that Ms. Mosser quoted are something like 5 or 6 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: So there is no way in which it makes sense for them to actually do the securitization.

speaker: LACKER
text: Instead, they just hold it on the balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: In essence, their demand for securitization funding is very elastic because the closest substitute is not much more costly.

speaker: LACKER
text: As a result, the increase in funding costs hasn’t been nearly as much for them as the increase in these spreads would indicate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, you might think that the pressure this puts on these banks’ balance sheets would lead them to cut back credit extension at the margin as a result of this.

speaker: LACKER
text: But both of these institutions report quite clearly and emphatically that their lending terms—that is to say, the decision algorithms for what to grant an individual consumer—have not changed as a result of this.

speaker: LACKER
text: They are still chasing consumers who are creditworthy.

speaker: LACKER
text: These are getting harder to find because consumers are generally riskier now.

speaker: LACKER
text: But these banks’ policies have not changed because of what has happened in the securitization markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: This suggests that the disruption in securitization markets has had little effect on consumer credit availability.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is consistent with evidence that I found in the back of the Greenbook that interest rates on credit cards and auto loans have fallen, not risen, over the past several months despite the increase in the ABS spreads, which would make you think that they would be rising.

speaker: LACKER
text: More broadly, securitization is a mechanism for reallocating risk.

speaker: LACKER
text: But more fundamentally, it is a mechanism for arbitraging capital requirements and getting a more favorable regulatory treatment, capital treatment, by moving things off balance sheets.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the question is, Do we have a policy interest in further subsidizing regulatory capital arbitrage?

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think the answer is “yes,” and I don’t think we have a broader interest in subsidizing securitization markets compared with on-balance-sheet lending.

speaker: LACKER
text: Moreover, at the end of the year, banks are going to have to consolidate these securitizations on their balance sheets anyway, under FAS 140.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I am led to wonder: Do we have a policy interest in reversing the steps they have taken already to adjust to this new accounting regime?

speaker: LACKER
text: Again, I don’t think the answer is “yes.” So the bottom line about the TALF is that I don’t think it addresses a demonstrable market failure.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I will speak about in a minute, I think doing this would channel credit away from other worthy borrowers.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it exacerbates moral hazard, and I think it sets bad fiscal precedence.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we are going to expand our balance sheet—and I do think it makes sense to do so right now—I believe we should do so in a way that is as neutral as possible across market segments.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the best way to do this is to purchase U.S. Treasuries.

speaker: LACKER
text: What effect would this have?

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, the natural benchmark, the simplest model you would write down—and there are more- complicated models in which something else would happen—is one in which the presumption would be that risky financial assets are priced off risk-free Treasuries based on the standard risk considerations, the standard asset-pricing considerations.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t see any particular reason to believe that those spreads would move one way or another in response to a change in medium- and long-term Treasury yields.

speaker: LACKER
text: The staff memo on purchasing long-term securities gives a number of reasons that they recommend against the idea, and frankly, I don’t find them very compelling because most of them apply with equal force to a targeted credit program like the TALF.

speaker: LACKER
text: The risk of increasing inflation by monetizing debt applies to both public and private debt, I think.

speaker: LACKER
text: The risk of taxpayer loss would seem to be even more of an issue if we take on credit risk in addition to interest rate risk.

speaker: LACKER
text: We heard earlier about our purchases of 30-year mortgage-backed securities and agency bonds.

speaker: LACKER
text: The deleterious effects of distorting relationships among various interest rates would seem to be more of a problem for targeted credit programs than buying U.S. Treasuries.

speaker: LACKER
text: On this last point, the thought experiment I carry around in my head about this is to compare a targeted credit program such as TALF with a same dollar amount purchase of U.S. Treasuries.

speaker: LACKER
text: The effect on the monetary base is going to be the same, by assumption.

speaker: LACKER
text: But buying Treasuries is likely to lower rates across the board in the private sector, whereas the credit program is just going to lower the target rates, leaving rates in non-targeted market segments higher than they would be if we bought Treasuries.

speaker: LACKER
text: In other words, choosing a targeted credit program over buying Treasuries is like deciding to lower rates for borrowers in the targeted segment by drawing away funds from other sectors and raising rates in other sectors, compared with a program of buying a risk-free security like Treasuries.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t see a compelling reason to raise some borrowers’ interest rates in order to lower some other borrowers’ interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: In particular, it is hard for me to see how we know this would have a positive effect on aggregate demand, on net.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, obviously, we have a collection of credit programs on our books already, and we have been discussing the fundamental problem that these are likely to pose when the time comes for us to withdraw monetary stimulus.

speaker: LACKER
text: The solution that I think you are right to pursue with the Treasury—and I would like to propose and I would advocate—is that we transfer financing of our credit programs wholesale to the U.S. Treasury and that we work to establish a new understanding—call it a Treasury–Fed credit accord, if you want—under which we would agree that, henceforth, intervention in credit markets, apart from our usual peacetime-like discount window functioning, will be the responsibility of the U.S. Treasury.

speaker: LACKER
text: This would give us back control of the monetary liabilities on our balance sheet and would make it much simpler to find an exit strategy.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would reduce the risk of loss to our capital accounts and the attendant reputational risk.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would reduce the risk perceived by market participants that we might abruptly terminate some credit programs in order to reduce the monetary base.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would reduce the risk perceived by market participants that we might compromise inflation in order to sustain credit programs.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would also reduce our vulnerability to the charge that we are using federal monies outside the constitutional appropriations process and that we have abused our powers by disguising asset purchases and credit guarantees, for which we do not have explicit authority, as loans.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is what we have done in the Citigroup and Bank of America case, and it is one thing that makes me very uncomfortable about those programs and would lead me to favor proposing that the Treasury take on those guarantees as well, because there is nothing in principle that limits their ability or the FDIC’s ability to have taken on all of the risk in both of those cases.

speaker: LACKER
text: In short, my view is that, no matter how you feel about our credit programs—whether you are for them or “agin” them—it would be better for the Treasury to finance them.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t see any operational impediment to transferring our credit programs to the Treasury.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our expertise is very critical to them, of course, but we have been lending our expertise to the Treasury for decades by performing fiscal functions for them and helping them run their debt auctions, and we have recently lent our people to staff the TARP, and I don’t see any reason that our people couldn’t continue to be involved in the administration of programs.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Treasury would, obviously, have to issue additional debt to finance the programs, but the Fed would, in the first instance, have an equal demand for U.S. Treasury debt.

speaker: LACKER
text: From the public’s point of view, the initial implementation would leave their balance sheets unaffected.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then, over time, we could vary the size of our balance sheet, independently of the size of the credit programs.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think you are right, Mr. Chairman, that this would be an uphill climb.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would require broad agreement with the Administration and the Congress and perhaps even legislation.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I think you are also right to note that this is an excellent opportunity in this regard.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are on the cusp of sweeping revisions of decades-old laws governing financial regulation.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consideration is being given, as you noted, to forming a so-called aggregator bank.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I think it is a very good time to initiate a new understanding of the appropriate roles of the central bank and the fiscal authority.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I applaud your efforts to pursue those discussions.

speaker: LACKER
text: There may be an aversion to spending our political capital—and I know we marshal that very carefully here in the System— on such a request.

speaker: LACKER
text: But we were willing to spend political capital in 1951 to gain control of the liability side of our balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is what the original Treasury–Fed accord did, and that has been essential to the independent conduct of monetary policy since then.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I think we are entitled to exert ourselves politically on this one.

speaker: LACKER
text: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think, in principle, that we agree that it would be better to have all of this done by the Treasury.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we have to accept political realities, prioritize, and try to address the most important issues first and see how far we can get.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On Treasuries versus other purchases, I don’t want to get deeply into it, but any kind of model without perfect, complete markets has to recognize the existence of liquidity premiums, which can differ across markets and which affect the effect of a given amount of demand on a purchase of a given asset.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it isn’t evident that applying our purchasing power on assets where markets are deep and liquid and liquidity premiums are low would have the same effect as on other markets where liquidity premiums are high.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I am just addressing that there is a reason that it is not a purely neutral operation.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t want to go deeply into technical details either, but a certain presumption with regard to credit risk is that there are potentially adverse consequences of distorting relative credit risks across markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t see why the same thing shouldn’t apply to liquidity risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would say that the markets are already distorted.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are starting from a point of the market not in equilibrium in the sense of normal long-time functioning.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are starting with markets that are very out of joint relative to where they have been historically.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So to say that you are distorting markets by the intervention, in fact we are actually trying to push markets back to something closer toward normality.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: About your point whether there is a market failure in the securitization market, I think there is absolutely a market failure in the securitization market, and you basically cited what it was.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The very fact that securitization rates are well above the rates that the banks would demand to hold it on their own balance sheet tells you that the market is fundamentally broken down.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is certainly true that those particular banks that you cited may not be balance sheet constrained, but the banking system as a whole is clearly balance sheet constrained.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: What the TALF does is basically provide balance sheet capacity to the private sector that the banking system today cannot provide.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, even if the ABS market is functional for those two banks that you note, there are a whole bunch of other problem areas in the securitization market that the TALF could be used to address in the future.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For example, the commercial real estate market is an area about which lots of people have been coming to us and saying, “We are going to have a real problem refinancing the commercial mortgage loans that come due in 2009 because there is no balance sheet capacity in the commercial banking sector.” So although it may be true for the two particular banks that you described, I don’t think it is true for the banking system as a whole.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that the TALF can address a real market failure because it provides a number of things that the market can’t get right now, which are balance sheet capacity, protection against downside risk, and term funding.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Those three things are not available in the market right now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Fisher, you had a two-handed intervention?

speaker: FISHER
text: I do want just to jump in.

speaker: FISHER
text: I thought your response was appropriate and correct, and obviously ultimately we would like to put as much of this back to the Treasury as possible.

speaker: FISHER
text: The ultimate objective is to insulate ourselves as a central bank as much as possible from political pressures, so we can do what central bankers do.

speaker: FISHER
text: I might also add as much as possible from market pressures, but that is another matter.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I disagree with the point made— and I agree with the staff conclusion—with regard to the purchase of Treasuries.

speaker: FISHER
text: It strikes me that there is enormous fear in the marketplace about the potential for open-ended stimulus in fiscal policy and there is great concern that we will acquiesce by monetizing fiscal policy.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am very reluctant to go down that road.

speaker: FISHER
text: That strikes me as one of the strongest arguments that the staff made.

speaker: FISHER
text: At any rate, at this point I don’t think it is necessary.

speaker: FISHER
text: Rates are quite low as they are.

speaker: FISHER
text: I disagree, Jeffrey, in ideal market situations, as the Vice Chairman just pointed out—whatever you are of this Committee— [laughter]

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am still trying to figure that out myself.

speaker: FISHER
text: As one of our many Vice Chairmen pointed out, this is a highly distorted market, and I would suggest—I was listening to what you said—in fact, the effort may lower Treasury rates at the price of raising other rates that you might crowd out perversely by supporting the Treasury market at this juncture.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I would support the staff’s recommendations.

speaker: FISHER
text: Because we have so many things on the table, I did have a question with regard to Brian’s point.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is, when would we consider closing a facility?

speaker: FISHER
text: As long as we have these different facilities open—and we haven’t shoved everything over to the Treasury—might it not send a good signal to the market—and I know President Plosser is probably going to talk about this a little, too, because we talked about it at lunch, just to be open—to close down one of these facilities that was not being utilized.

speaker: FISHER
text: For example, the AMLF or the MMIFF—all of these “initialisms” are getting confusing—if they are not active, do we want to give to all of them the same time extension?

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, you might respond that we don’t know yet but they might be utilized.

speaker: FISHER
text: I haven’t read through the specifics of your language proposition, but might we not at least make it clear that, if we feel that we have leeway, we could close down any one of these facilities while we extend their ultimate maturity?

speaker: FISHER
text: So the real question is, Can we find something that we might actually close to demonstrate that we don’t just have an open- ended book, until we reach the point that you wish to reach, Mr. Chairman, as you articulated and as President Lacker argued, where we shove this onto the Treasury?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think that general principle is right.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In fact, in the open market area we have wound down one program—the long-term RPs.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But right now I think that simply extending the facilities does not mean that they will necessarily be in place for the entire period of time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The FOMC and the Board could evaluate, as time goes on, whether these programs are needed.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I do think that closing down any of these programs at this time does run the risk of sending a signal that you think you are pretty far along in this process and you are going to start closing things down relatively quickly.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So I think it carries a risk.

speaker: MOSSER
text: For what it is worth, I think that the signal to markets of closing even the dormant facilities, given my obvious view about how fragile things are, could actually have a pretty serious, significant, adverse effect, even though they are not being used.

speaker: MOSSER
text: They are viewed very much—particularly the two facilities you mentioned and particularly the MMIFF—as a backstop.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We don’t need it now.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It is not priced attractively, frankly, given the spreads in markets.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But should we go through another period, heaven forbid, like September and October, it would be used, according to market participants.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser has been very patient.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: May I turn to you?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, some of my remarks were in fact going to be exactly this point— that we need an opportunity to bolster our credibility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As President Fisher said, I think we have an opportunity.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The AMLF, in particular, is winding down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is not being used very heavily, and indeed it is a facility that is almost redundant given that we have the commercial paper facility and the MMIFF and all of those three programs are intimately related to one another.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It doesn’t appear to me at all obvious that we need all of them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Whatever the AMLF is providing could also be provided as backstop through the CP program and through the MMIFF.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think we could do ourselves a real favor and signal to the market that we are judicious, careful, and wise about our choice of programs—that when we believe we have redundancies in the programs we don’t just let them run on and on and on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it would do a lot for our credibility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There is another program that we haven’t really talked about in a while and that I think we could also eliminate without much consequence and have, again, a credibility issue with the distinction between us and the Treasury.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In August, we had an agreement with the Treasury to allow the GSEs to borrow from the discount window.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The argument in that case was that we were doing that because the Treasury did not yet have the appropriations to do the lending and they needed to get that worked out.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They certainly now have that, and indeed, the GSEs are wards of the state.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To the best of my knowledge, we have never lent to the GSEs through the discount window.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t anticipate that there is any prospect that we will.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The fact is that we are buying agency debt as it is.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To the best of my knowledge, we haven’t rescinded that authorization—or at least the Board hasn’t rescinded that authorization.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think these are two examples in which programs are actually not doing anything particularly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have other means of backstopping the markets that we are worried about.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: By beginning to show that we can be thoughtful in how we unwind some of this stuff, it could actually be a credibility-building device.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To the extent that there are very, very fuzzy lines out there in the world among the political classes, including the public, about where the boundaries are drawn between fiscal policy and monetary policy—which I believe is the case—these two actions might help us draw back and gain a little more clarity about what we are about and what we are not about.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would just say, Mr. Chairman, that I applaud your efforts with the Treasury on this, and I support them 100 percent and will do anything I can to help that along because I think it is a very, very important step.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that we could have an opportunity by extending some of the programs but not extending those that aren’t really doing anything.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As long as I have the floor, Mr. Chairman, I would like to comment on a couple of other things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we need to work harder on developing the specific information—that is, both data and qualitative information—that we need to make our decisions exactly about extending or exiting from these facilities and any new ones that we might create.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This would help our own policy deliberations, making us more systematic in our approach, and would be beneficial to market participants, helping them learn what to expect from us.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although the decision today for many of you may seem obvious that we should extend all of these facilities for fear of disrupting something or other, I think that, as we get closer in time to a situation in which we really do want to exit these programs, the decision process will become more difficult.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Having a more systematic, data-driven approach to making that decision in advance will do a lot to help us as we move forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We presumably want to look at metrics to gauge the efficiency of these facilities in improving the functioning of particular markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the past, we saw a great deal of information on spreads, but, as I have said before, I don’t consider spreads as sufficient information.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Volumes are important as well, as I have stressed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I appreciate the work of Spence and the staff.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I thought that the detailed discussions of the different programs were very helpful, and I applaud the staff for that effort.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But we also need to know what to do with those data and how we interpret and analyze the information.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As has been alluded to already, if trading is thin, for example, some spread measures may be completely irrelevant to thinking about some of this information.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It may be a demand problem as opposed to a market liquidity problem.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, I think we need an idea of what level of spreads and volumes we will be satisfied with when the time comes.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The memo from Vice Chairman Dudley on Desk authorizations talks about reducing spread levels more in line with historical norms.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is that the right level?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Does it mean that we have spread levels similar to those in July 2007?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I very much doubt that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Shouldn’t we be thinking that these spreads will be elevated perhaps for some time to come given the real credit risks that have been revealed in the current episode?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If so, how much higher?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And shouldn’t we be thinking about spread levels consistent with weak or recessionary economic periods as a more proper benchmark in this environment?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is certainly true that spreads on some consumer-type loans are very high.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But many are not out of line with what we have witnessed in other recessionary periods.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How do we tell the difference, and how do we think about that?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In addition, to the extent that private-sector intermediation is broken and the Fed’s lending facilities are substituting for some of that role, it seems to me that you want to look at metrics to gauge the degree of private-sector intermediation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that we need to focus more on the health of the banking sector itself, such things as loan growth and the use of reserves in the banking sector.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I discussed last time, I think quantities of these various measures on our balance sheet will be relevant for those sorts of discussions as to how we think that intermediation process is functioning.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We need to pay attention to how we set prices in these facilities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We want to ensure that our lending facilities don’t crowd out private-sector intermediaries when they are healthy enough to return to the market.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Otherwise, of course, we risk distorting the real price signals and potentially delaying the recovery of credit-market functioning.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: More discussion of price-setting in our facilities would be welcome.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We heard some of that today, and I applaud that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Do we have the right penalty rates built in?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are the auctions set at the right minimums?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Referring to these on a regular basis and discussing the implications they have on volumes would help us be alert to changes in markets and their functioning and help ensure that we are not delaying the markets from healing themselves.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So, overall, I think we should have a much more systematic analysis and discussion of these sorts of issues if we are to properly assess the effectiveness and necessity of these facilities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have already talked about terminating some of these programs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: By letting programs like the authorization of the GSEs and the AMLF expire—I think they are redundant—and canceling this emergency access to the discount window, we can strengthen our credibility, we can further delineate the line between fiscal policy and monetary policy or between the Treasury and the central bank, and we will strengthen the belief that we in fact will withdraw from these special arrangements at the appropriate time and do so in a thoughtful way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would like to talk just a bit about the purchases of long-term Treasuries.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The staff recommends keeping this program at bay for now or at least not implementing it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t really have any strong objections to that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think the staff’s memo, though, omitted one reason that buying Treasuries, in fact, might be desirable, and I really didn’t find its arguments for not doing it terribly compelling either.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I see some benefits to having more Treasuries in our portfolio, regardless of how one assesses the magnitude of the real economic effect on borrowing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It might prove easier—and I think this gets back to the accord, Mr. Chairman, in your discussion—for us to unwind from some of these things if, in fact, we have Treasuries rather than MBS.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think our credit programs do carry risks.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Aside from the moral hazard problems we have created, we face challenges when we attempt to liquidate particularly non-Treasury assets from our portfolio.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We will get pressure from various interest groups to retain certain assets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We will certainly, in all likelihood, get calls from consumers, builders, and Congressmen if we start to sell mortgage- backed securities out of our portfolio in order to reduce its size.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We will hear fears that the mortgage rates may rise.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We will have some market participants resisting our desire to pull back from our credit programs, fearing that markets remain too fragile or the economy’s headwinds are too strong.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we will make every effort to resist such pressures, but they could make it difficult for us to conduct monetary policy in a way that is consistent with our mandate, particularly our mandate for price stability.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, given that we have crossed the bridge on credit allocation schemes to specific markets, it will be much easier in the future for special interest groups to ask us to repeat such actions, especially if they can’t get the answers they want from the political process.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, I think—and I realize this view isn’t shared by all—that the credit allocation schemes we are pursuing run a real risk of impinging on our independence and our ability to control our balance sheet and, hence, monetary policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Again, drawing back from the AMLF and perhaps the GSE discount window lending facility may help us begin to reassert a bit of that independence.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: For that reason, I am not uncomfortable with buying long-term Treasuries, partly because of their portfolio effect as a substitute for buying MBS.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Mr. Chairman, I think that your comments about moving more of this to the Treasury are exactly right, and it certainly applies to Maiden Lane.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it would apply to the CPFF in some respects and perhaps to the TALF, as President Lacker was suggesting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I didn’t find the staff’s arguments against purchasing long­ term Treasuries particularly compelling.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess I share President Lacker’s view that, if we are blowing up our balance sheet—whether we are blowing it up with MBS or with Treasuries—it is still expansionary monetary policy as far as I am concerned, and I don’t think it should make that much difference on inflationary expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The staff also raised the problem of interest rate risks inherent in longer-term Treasuries.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Again, I don’t see this as a particular problem distinct from our purchases of mortgage-backed securities, which also contain interest rate risk at the end of the day, if we have to sell them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Both of these programs increase the maturity mismatch on our balance sheet in very similar ways.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am a little puzzled—maybe I will save this for the policy go-round—about why we should leave the door open in the statement.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The estimated reduction in longer-term yields, as the staff suggested, is somewhere between 10 and 30 basis points, which is, at best, quite uncertain based on the empirical evidence.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Putting aside my concern for portfolio composition and my preferring Treasuries, I don’t find buying long-term Treasuries that compelling, except for this portfolio reason.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, a better reason for leaving the door open may be this portfolio argument, but I don’t think we could explain that very well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We could simply say that we continue to weigh the costs and benefits.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I do have some reservations about continuing to discuss in our statement programs or actions that we might or might not take.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that there are certain risks to that in terms of making markets believe that we may do something, and then, if we don’t do it, we lose some credibility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But we can talk about that in the policy go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, you had a quick two-hander?

speaker: LACKER
text: In the interest of your interest in informal exchange, I was interested in responding to our new Vice Chairman.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t understand in what sense the observation that prices are low and that quantities are very low constitutes a demonstration that the consumer-backed ABS market is broken down.

speaker: LACKER
text: Can you think of a model in which that results?

speaker: LACKER
text: Yes, demand is low, and supply is elastic.

speaker: LACKER
text: What we are talking about, it is important to remember here, is the interaction, the rivalry, between the balance sheet channel of credit flows and the securitization channel.

speaker: LACKER
text: A broad array of contractual features are important to the relative attractiveness for market participants of those two channels—covenants, risk allocation, regulatory and accounting treatments, and the like.

speaker: LACKER
text: On balance sheet constraints—would some firms prefer that the demand for securitization be higher, high enough that securitization was less costly for them than holding it on balance sheet?

speaker: LACKER
text: Yes, I am sure that is true.

speaker: LACKER
text: But if that is the criterion for whether or not a market is broken down, then it is hard to see the difference between a market being broken down and just regulatory capture in some broad sense.

speaker: LACKER
text: You talked about markets being distorted already.

speaker: LACKER
text: I can picture information constraints, verification costs, asymmetries, and the like that would lead market outcomes to be less felicitous for all concerned than they otherwise would be.

speaker: LACKER
text: But, yes, information constraints constrain achievable outcomes, but so do technology constraints.

speaker: LACKER
text: Would we be better off if we could get more output with the same amount of labor and capital?

speaker: LACKER
text: But I don’t think you would call the market distorted because that is the case.

speaker: LACKER
text: The question is why it is distorted.

speaker: LACKER
text: If you come to me with a model—with some story, not even a model—that sketches out the interaction of information with technologies and with market participants’ incentives that convinces me that markets are distorted in a way that government intervention can remedy, I am all ears, and I would be happy to talk about it.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have been asking for that for a year and a half.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have been even doing the work for you.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have been even bringing models to the table.

speaker: LACKER
text: I haven’t gotten any information or any market observations that seem consistent with one story or another.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am not sure that this request has been taken seriously.

speaker: LACKER
text: So, yes, if markets are distorted by something or other, fine, but that is hardly an answer for justifying the TALF in my view.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I guess this deserves an answer.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, first of all, I think we have a fundamental disagreement about how we are looking at the current set of events.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we are in the middle of a disequilibrium, not an equilibrium.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You are looking for models that describe equilibrium outcomes, and I think we are in the middle of a disequilibrium caused by the massive deleveraging of the nonbank balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As that process unfolds, we are not where your model wants to describe.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Number two, what we are observing is well outside the realm of historical experience.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think that to be able to produce a model that describes what we are seeing is very, very difficult because we have never been here before.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are just generating the empirical data now to develop the model that we can actually test.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of this issue—is the securitization market evidence of market failure?—I think my example is just a very simple one.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The fact that the bank, as you describe it, would rather hold these assets on its balance sheet than securitize them and AAA yields are higher than the net return to the bank of holding them on its balance sheet is telling you that there is a lack of arbitrage between the bank market and the nonbank market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think fundamentally we have a disagreement about what the process is that we are describing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You say, “Show me a model.” I certainly want to see your model that describes what has happened over the past 18 months because I think it is very, very difficult to show that model as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am going to regret this, but I am going to ask you a question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you think the United States economy is at a Pareto efficient point at this moment?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With the best position we can be at right now?

speaker: LACKER
text: All constraints taken on board.

speaker: LACKER
text: What was the question again?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The question was, Is the United States economy at a Pareto efficient point at this moment?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And the answer was “yes.” Okay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is obviously a different view.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, that is a fundamental basis of the disagreement.

speaker: EVANS
text: May I ask an information question?

speaker: EVANS
text: President Lacker alluded to two banks that funded their operations at a very low rate.

speaker: EVANS
text: Was that with the FDIC senior guarantee on their debt?

speaker: EVANS
text: That is a distortion that is helping them, right?

speaker: EVANS
text: I am running into that when I talk to a lot of people.

speaker: EVANS
text: I will come back to that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am fine with that, but—

speaker: EVANS
text: Well, that is a distortion.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is a government intervention.

speaker: LACKER
text: Are we intervening to make securitization just as subsidized as bank balance sheets?

speaker: EVANS
text: Our problem is that there is one distortion here, and then there is something else, and then they don’t offset or they do offset, and people are inside or they are not.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we are in a world of second best, I understand that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are in that world.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, then, what is it that unfairly tilts the playing field toward bank balance sheets?

speaker: LACKER
text: I mean, you have this regulatory tax, and it tilts in the other direction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You are exactly right that historically the securitization market has had elements of regulatory arbitrage.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that is true.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think, in this particular case, it is not really the reason that AAA ABS assets are still selling at such high yields right now.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The reason that they are selling at high yields right now is that the borrowers who would love to invest in these assets on a leveraged basis can’t get leverage.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Their inability to get leverage is being driven by the balance sheet constraints of the dealer and bank community, which is a disequilibrium event caused by their historically large mark-to-market losses and loan-loss provisions, which are depleting their capital and constraining their ability to lend.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So this is a disequilibrium.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Five years from now, we won’t be here, and banks will have the ability to lend, they will be able to lend on AAA assets on a leveraged based, and AAA yields will be much lower.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just say in response to President Plosser, I should tell everyone that, assuming that we extend these programs and the swaps, we will not announce anything until Thursday morning because we want to coordinate with the foreign central banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, first of all, obviously, please keep it confidential.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But could I ask the Board and the New York staff to have at least a discussion about the two programs that President Plosser mentioned, the GSE approval and the AMLF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I would propose to extend the AMLF today as part of the package, but the Board would have the ability to reverse that tomorrow by notation vote if we decide that we get some kind of support.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The AMLF is not the FOMC; it is the Board.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I understand that, but what I am saying is that I am hearing what you are saying, and I think we ought to look at that particular program.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have to be a little careful because we don’t have a lot of advance time here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we should look at that.

speaker: LACKER
text: Disequilibrium, in this context, is a non sequitur.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is a conversation stopper.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is like appealing to astrology—it is the equivalent of that.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we are out of equilibrium, what happens out of equilibrium?

speaker: LACKER
text: What is determining what happens?

speaker: LACKER
text: People make choices on their way to making adjustments.

speaker: LACKER
text: They were in equilibrium when they made the choices that resulted in the losses, and now that equilibrium is playing out, obviously.

speaker: LACKER
text: Would these leveraged borrowers like there to be a greater demand for their liabilities?

speaker: LACKER
text: This all looks as though demand is low.

speaker: LACKER
text: I will ask you a question.

speaker: LACKER
text: The buggy whip industry—is that sector broken?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Hoenig, on that note—

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Can you answer the buggy whip question?

speaker: HOENIG
text: I have heard that story, and I don’t need to review it again.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I have just a couple of things that I want to comment on here.

speaker: HOENIG
text: First of all, I do appreciate this, because we are thinking about where we are and we are thinking about how we might exit this, even though we have a lot of turmoil ahead of us.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that part of President Lacker’s point and the Vice Chairman’s point may be that we are in an adjustment process.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We are deleveraging like crazy in this economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That resulted from an excess at an earlier point, and we are going to find a new equilibrium.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is the process we are going through, and it is very difficult.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Much of what we have done I wish had been done in the Treasury to begin with.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I still think that would have been the right call.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But it wasn’t, so we are where we are.

speaker: HOENIG
text: How do we get where we are going, and how do we do this transition?

speaker: HOENIG
text: What we have are these facilities, and I hope that we use them temporarily.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I hope we do take advantage of working with the Treasury to move as much of it out as we can.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Some of it is self-liquidating, and I think we will get out of it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But some of it is not, and that is the part I would like to be able to push toward the Treasury, and that would be part of our plan.

speaker: HOENIG
