text: I would also say that I am reluctant to go with long-term Treasuries, not because I don’t necessarily agree with some of what you are saying but because I am worried about some of the consequences of the perception that we are directly funding the Treasury and monetizing debt immediately.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I want to think that through before I get on that bandwagon, given where we have already come at this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: To change just a bit, Mr. Chairman, I want to talk about the TARP and the future as we go forward, as you have these discussions coming up.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think there is no confidence in it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It has been inequitably administered across the United States, and that is why you have such bitterness about it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So in looking forward, we have an opportunity to do that better.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The way we outline how we are going to deal with financial institutions and banks in the future is extremely important now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I want to thank Nathan for the summary report on the Swedish experience or the Nordic model and so forth because, as we talk about aggregator banks or RTCs or some approach to the problem, I think that is a very good model to look at.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It offers us opportunities to deal with this problem as it gets worse because I think the problems across a broader base of banks are getting worse.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Commercial real estate is now feeling a little pressure.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think we are beginning to see a turn in agriculture again and a turn related to energy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: These problems are going to become more difficult, and how we go forward with the next iteration—and I wouldn’t call it the TARP any longer—of this banking problem is important.

speaker: HOENIG
text: One thing that I have some disagreement with regarding Nathan’s conclusions is whether we have the mechanisms to do a kind of Swedish model, given the more-complex institutions and the size of this country.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But I suggest that we do.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have a cadre of experienced people across the United States—in the Comptroller’s office, the FDIC’s office, and the Federal Reserve’s offices—so that when this comes, if we think about it now and plan, we can begin to say which banks should be looked at.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Part of the problem with the last issue of the TARP was that we went in and looked at a lot of these institutions and they were on the margin.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But we were changing the criteria as we went along instead of having the criteria set and going in and looking at these institutions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Which ones are solvent at the moment, and for which ones would capital help maintain solvency?

speaker: HOENIG
text: You can’t have any guarantees on this, given the trends in the economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But we ought to have a systematic, equitably applied solution for the next wave that is coming our way.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That would be very important to have set up because it would help keep a lot of commercial real estate loans off our balance sheets.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we handle the next section as we have the past around asset-backed securities, we are going to have a lot more assets on our balance sheet, and that does worry me.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So that is something for us to think about going forward.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First of all, Mr. Chairman, I agree with your prioritization that, to the extent possible, it makes sense for the programs that have substantial credit risk to be borne by the Treasury.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Obviously certain circumstances forced other decisions along the way, but I think that is a good prioritization.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Then the second prioritization is that ideally we would be focused on markets and not individual names, and that’s consistent with moving the Maiden Lane facilities over to the Treasury to the extent possible.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think both of those prioritizations make sense.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: On the AMLF, I actually was roughly at the same point in November, and its size has come down since then.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I have had a number of discussions with a variety of mutual funds about winding down the AMLF.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: They don’t view the AMLF as being the same animal as the other money market facility, and I have been told that it will take severe duress before they use the other facility because they are worried about stigmatizing themselves.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As for the AMLF, because it is the sale of asset-backed securities, there is not the same stigma attached.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So actually we had $800 million come in today.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It was a money market fund that has experienced very substantial runoffs that are not occurring with other organizations.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I have been told that, even if it goes down to a small number, money market funds’ willingness not to hold extensive cash balances or very short term maturities is, in part, due to the fact that they can liquidate their positions in asset-backed securities relatively quickly.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The AMLF is not ideally structured—I definitely agree with that—but I am not sure that the other facilities are perfect substitutes.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we were not to extend it, I would want to do that only after some discussion with a number of money market fund families because I think we might find that it would have an effect on their willingness (a) to hold asset-backed commercial paper and (b) to hold a variety of other assets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think that they would look for other ways to get much more liquid because, as has been highlighted, the financial markets are very fragile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: May I just ask about that?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The asset-backed paper that actually comes through the AMLF, is it mostly commercial paper?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It is all asset-backed commercial paper.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It’s all A1/P1 asset-backed commercial paper.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So they could also sell that into our commercial paper facility, could they not?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This is a money market fund.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The commercial paper facility is for issuers of commercial paper.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The AMLF is for money market funds.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So they are not the same.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The issuer, in principle, could buy it back from the money market fund and then potentially issue into the CPFF, but that is not an obligation that the issuer would necessarily have.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There has been an unwillingness to do that actually.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It has been the experience of the money market funds.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In a more general sense, I think that, since the end of the third quarter, we have been in a situation in which both the securitization market has broken down and bank balance sheets are quite constrained, which is why we have seen spreads that are very, very large.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I do think that the various short-term credit facilities that we have established have both brought the spread down and brought more liquidity to the market more generally.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So in a general context, those facilities have been quite beneficial.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I have just a couple of short comments.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, in the earlier presentation, I noted that tangible common equity was highlighted in the slides, and I would say that a lot of our programs have been tied to preferred equity, and the markets, Moody’s, and the rating agencies are focused on tangible equity.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So whatever we do going forward, I think we need to spend a lot more time thinking about tangible common equity because we are seeing in supervision presentations that institutions that have substantial excess capital by regulatory ratios are also sometimes institutions that the market is running away from because, when they do the tangible equity calculation, it’s a problem.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So we ought to give a little more thought to common shares going forward.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, I come out in a different place related to our purchase of mortgage-backed securities and GSEs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Mortgage rates have been around 6 percent for a year and a half.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: After the announcement of the program, they went down to 5 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The housing market has been the epicenter of this problem.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It is a problem both for the housing market and for financial institutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Rather than cutting back on that program, if we are trying to have an effect on borrowing costs that affect the economy, that program would be the one I would expand.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would expand that program and not do Treasury securities because Treasury securities are the one asset that everybody wants to buy now.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I am not sure that we have to get in line with everybody else to buy the same thing that everybody else wants and push down a rate that is already low.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The problem is not that Treasury securities are too high.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The problem is that everything else is high relative to Treasury securities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So if we want to lower borrowing costs, that is exactly what some of these facilities are designed to do, and that is what I think we need to do.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I am supportive of doing more actually for the mortgage market, and that is for discussion tomorrow.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The TALF is of the same nature, and I think it actually is quite beneficial.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would hope that we could get it operational as quickly as possible.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I know that dealing with accountants, lawyers, and others becomes very complicated, but I think that the sooner we get that up and running, the better.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I do question whether the size is going to be appropriate if we really want to have a significant effect.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We are going to have to look at both the size of that facility and the assets that we are thinking about—particularly the CMBS market that was alluded to.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It is designed to deal primarily with original issuers of these securities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Another question that is similar to the problem asset—for holders of those securities, you could have a TALF-like program that deals with people who are holding those assets rather than issuing those assets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That gets more at the financial institutions’ issues rather than at the issuers’ issues, but I think that is another program that we should at least think about as an alternative.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I agree with you, President Rosengren, about the objective of trying to lower the spread on the MBS, and the mortgage market is important.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, another way of expressing one of my concerns is that, as we continue to focus on one asset class at a time— mortgage-backed securities, asset-backed credit card debt, auto loans—I worry that we are gradually being drawn into an ever-wider array of private credit markets and private asset classes and instruments that we will just gradually expand.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Where is the limit to this, and how do we define what those limits are?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How do we decide what the criteria are that constitute something important enough for us to intervene in that way?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I see this creep broadening our balance sheet in ever-greater dimensions in these private credit markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I worry that, in its doing so, the implication is that, almost in a negative feedback loop, each market is going to become dysfunctional by something so that it will drag us in.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My desire is to have better objective criteria that help us decide when it is appropriate and when it is not, because I think that we are just going down a slope here that is broadening the scope, which is not helpful for the institution.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser, we do have a shadow value on our balance sheet constraint, right?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we do have limits to what we can do, and so we have to make choices about where the impact will be most effective and where it will be the best for the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vice Chairman Dudley and then President Rosengren, and then I am going to go without hesitation to President Evans, who has been waiting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There is a presumption in President Plosser’s remarks and President Lacker’s remarks earlier that, if we intervene in one market, we are going to make these other markets that are adjacent to those markets somehow worse.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In fact, we have seen in several cases that it actually does not work that way.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It works in just the opposite way.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One good example is the commercial paper market in which the A2/P2 market has actually improved probably in part because of the commercial paper funding facility’s taking some of the strain off the commercial paper market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it might work that way sometimes, and improving one market may make another market worse.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But it also may be that improving the function of one market by providing balance sheet eases the aggregate balance sheet constraint, which then leads to improvement in other, adjacent markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it is not necessarily true that doing something in one market makes other markets in which we are not intervening worse.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I may just comment on that, the important thing is to keep track of what sort of thought experiment you have in mind.

speaker: LACKER
text: A sterilized intervention, or an intervention in which you are intervening in a market and comparing that with intervening more broadly in Treasuries, is one thing.

speaker: LACKER
text: Another thing is an intervention that is unsterilized and that does not pull some other assets out of the market.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would just point to Ms. Mosser’s presentation, which she opened with characterizing markets as that rates in markets in which we have intervened have broadly improved and rates in markets in which we have not intervened have broadly deteriorated.

speaker: LACKER
text: To me that has the flavor of consistency with the notion that our issue of liabilities and sale of Treasuries is pulling funds out of other markets and increasing rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But did they deteriorate because of our intervention?

speaker: LACKER
text: We have to fund it somehow, and the funding is going to pull money from somebody, right?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Did they deteriorate because of our intervention, or did they deteriorate because the macroeconomy was deteriorating at a very rapid rate?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would argue that they deteriorated because the macroeconomy was deteriorating at a very rapid rate, not because of our intervention.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just very quickly, in terms of the allocation, housing is an interest- sensitive component of GDP.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Every time we change interest rates, we are in effect going to have an impact on housing, and it is going to be disproportionately borne by housing than other sectors of the economy because of its interest-sensitivity.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I view what we are doing with the MBS and GSEs as dealing with the one area that we can actually change.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think it is going to have a much bigger effect.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In the Greenbook charts that we will be looking at tomorrow, if we had a fed funds rate that we could lower, I do not doubt that we would be lowering the fed funds rate if we had that possibility.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We don’t have that possibility.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So we have to look to an alternative asset.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Where is the biggest bang for the buck?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It’s probably in housing right now.

speaker: EVANS
text: I will just make a couple of comments based on the discussion today.

speaker: EVANS
text: When it comes to the TALF, I find that I am of two minds.

speaker: EVANS
text: I do think it will ultimately be useful for deploying important central bank liquidity in an attempt to provide more-accommodative conditions.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I am concerned that we are picking winners throughout this process.

speaker: EVANS
text: When you mention that we are going to consider CMBS, I am reminded of the fellow who came to my office and gave me a presentation.

speaker: EVANS
text: He owns shopping malls, and last fall he desperately needed funding and still does, but they are not worth very much at the moment.

speaker: EVANS
text: He wanted a program like this, but it wasn’t available—I do not know that it was, anyway.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have also received phone calls from heavy equipment manufacturers in my District.

speaker: EVANS
text: I know you have gotten a letter from at least one of them about their finance company financing.

speaker: EVANS
text: For them the issue is that they are unlucky enough not to have a thrift through the OTS.

speaker: EVANS
text: So they cannot get the FDIC unsecured-funding temporary guarantee on that, and their assets cannot be funded that way.

speaker: EVANS
text: There are some competitors that have access to this, and they have done very well, and others that haven’t.

speaker: EVANS
text: As we get into this allocation type of decisionmaking, I am not quite sure how we are going about doing it.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is CMBS selected because it is an important market that we need to keep functioning or because it is going to have a particular macroeconomic effect that is beneficial?

speaker: EVANS
text: How does that compare with other sectors and whether they are on our radar screen or not?

speaker: EVANS
text: Maybe that was the right decision, but when we select certain types of asset-backed securities to buy—it is just very difficult.

speaker: EVANS
text: I also want to agree with many of the comments that President Plosser made with regard to the programs that we have.

speaker: EVANS
text: The briefing today was very helpful in describing the various programs.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think we need some additional metrics along the lines of just routine types of statistics so that we can see and have a better idea.

speaker: EVANS
text: Your familiarity is very great with these, and ours is not as great.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have to admit, as I look at it more, I find that, although I am very concerned about exit strategy in general, at the moment our balance sheet doesn’t worry me quite so much.

speaker: EVANS
text: Finally, I want to applaud your comments at the beginning, Mr. Chairman, about discussions with the Treasury and that we, as best we can be, should be allergic to any attempts to use our balance sheet for long-term financing.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that is exactly right.

speaker: EVANS
text: I wish you all the best for all of us.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have tried to grapple with the very vague discussions of aggregator banks, and when I talk to academics, they do not always help me because they resist the fact that public funds are going to be put into this—they think that it really should be something that public funding is not a part of.

speaker: EVANS
text: If you pick a very large number that is required to take assets off the balance sheet of banks—I do not know what the number is, but it is in trillions—and then you think about how the Treasury is going to fund this, the only way they can do that is by issuing Treasury bonds.

speaker: EVANS
text: Ms. Mosser was talking about how $150 billion puts strains on yields.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think you very quickly come to our balance sheet and how we are able to leverage up, and it even makes sense— because why do the gross funding through bonds when it is really a net kind of funding against assets?

speaker: EVANS
text: So it makes a lot of sense, but it causes a lot of trouble.

speaker: EVANS
text: I hope that I am wrong in thinking about that and that there are very easy ways out of it.

speaker: EVANS
text: But those are some of our concerns, and they will be very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I certainly agree that you cannot trust academics.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Just a couple of curiosity questions really for the staff.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: If we were to convey assets to the Treasury and mark them to market at that time, let us say, Maiden Lane or AIG, what losses would we be recognizing at that point?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we have a mark-to-market loss on the Bear Stearns assets in Maiden Lane I.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t have mark-to-market losses in anything else.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What would be ideal would be to work out some arrangement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It would take some accounting work, but at Maiden Lane I, we have a letter from the Treasury saying that the Treasury will bear those losses through seigniorage, and there should be some way to arrange an asset called future reductions of seigniorage or something like that that would make us whole.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that those things can be worked through, but obviously there is a lot of technical work to be done on that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The second question—nobody has mentioned any particular markets on our radar screen that, if we had criteria, we might intervene in.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But the one on which I get feedback is the municipal market, and we have a legal issue that we cannot lend to municipalities unless they happen to be corporations.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Presuming for the moment that there was some legislative treatment of that, what is the status in discussing with the Treasury an intervention in that particular market?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is a broken market as far as I can tell at this stage.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That has not come up.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would say that the market is not doing well, but it is doing better than it was a month ago.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it is improving, but I am not aware of the Treasury having this on the front burner.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The fiscal package has a great deal of money for states and localities, which would probably be the primary source of support for those.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In principle, you could set up an SPV that the municipality issued out of.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That would be the corporate entity that we would lend to.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You could do that, but it is not clear whether this problem isn’t going to gradually resolve itself.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do want to pick up on what President Evans and President Rosengren said, which is that I think it is possible to set criteria, but there is a constraint on how much we can do in terms of both size and duration and, of course, limits on credit risk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Given those constraints, we have to make choices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although I do not think that this is actually science here, I do think we can try to think about, for example, interest-sensitive sectors or sectors in which our interventions will have particularly strong effects on liquidity premiums and the like.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is not science, but I do think there is a sense in which we can make those choices and in which we are constrained.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I recognize that this is a whole new field.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would make the comment that I have had recent conversations with foreign leaders, including Prime Minister Brown—all of whom said that the Federal Reserve is leading the way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The United Kingdom is undertaking these programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Japan is undertaking these programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is becoming a new approach.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When you hit zero, you have to think about other ways to affect the economy, and so at least in that respect we are not the outlier anymore.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A lot of ground has been covered, and I do not want to rehash things that have already been said.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In general, I would just associate myself with President Rosengren’s remarks and say that, with respect to choices that we have to make, I very much agree with the idea that a focus on mortgage-backed security markets is something that can be effective, is working, and deserves priority.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I also want to support the point that Bill Dudley and others have made about commercial-mortgage-backed securities and the notion that this is something that was announced in connection with the TALF, that we were studying the possibility of extending this facility to commercial-mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have been following this quite closely, and I would like to agree with the points that Bill made about this.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This seems to me like something that could be the next very serious problem for the banking system and for property prices in general.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There is huge rollover risk here, where we have hundreds of billions of dollars of loans that are coming due on commercial properties for which the underwriting was originally pretty solid.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am very concerned that the underlying economics is now deteriorating largely because of the economy, and banks obviously have very high concentrations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A lot of banks in this area are very loath to lend.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The commercial- mortgage-backed securities market seems to be completely dead.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am really very concerned that, without the ability to refinance these loans, we are going to have properties dumped on the market and we will begin to see exactly the same thing happen with commercial real estate that we are seeing with housing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It could lead to a further wave of unnecessary bank failures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So although I am sensitive to the idea that, yes, we are making decisions about what sectors are deserving or are of priority in terms of credit allocations and there are counterarguments against our doing that, we do have choices to make, and I would focus a lot of serious attention on proceeding in that area.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me turn to Governor Kohn and then take a coffee break.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then we can continue if people are so inclined.

speaker: KOHN
text: Just a few quick points, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with those who say that it is very uncomfortable picking which markets to intervene in.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wish we weren’t here, but we are.

speaker: KOHN
text: I just do not see an alternative to it.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we have been here since August ’07 really, when balance sheets constraints—people were hoarding capital and liquidity—impaired the arbitrage among markets, and central banks had to use their balance sheets to step between private parties increasingly to take risks where the public was not willing to take risks.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now governments are going to have to step in to spend where the public isn’t willing to spend.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we have this withdrawal from risk-taking, this hoarding of capital, not spending, and the government’s role here is to step into that breach to keep the economy from shrinking even further.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think there are balance sheet constraints.

speaker: KOHN
text: Jeff’s banks in the Richmond District may say that they have not changed criteria, but certainly the answers to the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey suggest that banks in other Districts have tightened terms and standards for making consumer loans.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is really hard to judge which markets, I agree.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think they should be important markets with systemic effects and ones where our intervention can make a difference.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is really hard to say ahead of time, but we ought to be looking for those.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that we need to be thinking about exit strategies and balance sheet constraints, but I sure hope we do not put emphasis on that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think our problem right now, given where we are, is not how we are going to get out of this but how we can ameliorate the decline in the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: The more we talk about how we want to get out and the constraints, the less effective our policies will be.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that is what happened to Japan.

speaker: KOHN
text: The Japanese central bank kept talking about how they did not really want to be here, they could not wait till they got out, this was uncomfortable, and they did not want to be doing this.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it undermined that aspect of the credibility of what the central bank was doing.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to have this conversation internally.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to keep three chess moves ahead in what we are doing.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I wouldn’t want worries about the size of our balance sheet and our exit strategies to importantly constrain our ability to make a difference in credit markets going forward.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the buying of Treasuries, I would keep that on the table.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think rates are already low, as President Rosengren and others have pointed out.

speaker: KOHN
text: We do not really need to intervene there, whereas for mortgage-backed securities I think the interest rate risk is low because some of us might argue that those rates were too high relative to Treasuries and we are not taking the same kind of risk buying at that low price versus the high price that we might be with a Treasury.

speaker: KOHN
text: But it is not really about the risk on our balance sheet.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is about the effects we can have.

speaker: KOHN
text: Those rates are already low.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do not think we need to buy Treasuries at this point.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would keep that option on the table to see what happens to those rates going forward and where we think we can be most effective.

speaker: KOHN
text: In terms of worries about monetizing the debt, here I do agree with President Lacker.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think this is about inflation and inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are, I hope, going to take some steps to make our inflation objectives a little clearer tomorrow.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we need to keep that in mind, and we should not have to worry about people accusing us of monetizing the debt.

speaker: KOHN
text: We should keep our focus on the macroeconomic variables.

speaker: KOHN
text: Finally, on transparency, we have started up, as the Chairman said, a little working group to see what more we can do.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are concentrating in part on the collateral side.

speaker: KOHN
text: Can we say more about collateral without impairing the functionality of our windows?

speaker: KOHN
text: We are thinking about things we might add and publish quarterly instead of weekly and whether there is more we could do on that basis.

speaker: KOHN
text: Any suggestions that Reserve Banks have would be gratefully received.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a coffee break until 4:30, and then if anyone else would like to enter in when we come back, that would be fine.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do not want to cut anyone off.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would anyone else like to comment?

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am going to play the role of provocateur here and ask a couple of questions that are in the spirit of having a wide-ranging and strategic discussion, as we are having here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Here is something that people said to me recently.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is a question for Mr.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Sheets about swap lines, one of our favorite topics.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Here is the statement: These swap lines are giving control of the U.S. monetary base to foreign governments, especially through persistent and large usage by the foreign central banks.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I will stop on that one and see what you think about that.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In each one of the disbursements under these lines, the Federal Reserve and the FOMC have the prerogative to determine whether or not it is in our interest to go forward with the swaps.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So I think that we maintain a crucial governance role.

speaker: SHEETS
text: If we come to the conclusion that at some point the costs of this program or the costs of extending that dollar liquidity outweigh the benefits, then we can start winding up the program.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So I don’t think that is right.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So what is the magnitude right now of the swap lines that are outstanding?

speaker: SHEETS
text: The total outstandings are around $465 billion.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So a scenario would be that you go over the next five years, with zero nominal interest rates and an ongoing financial crisis, and these things stay out there because of needs for dollar funding in Europe.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Now you had a permanent one-time increase of, say, $500 billion in the monetary base.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Isn’t this what we are looking at?

speaker: SHEETS
text: Well, for what it is worth, our forecasts of the European economy and European interest rates are not consistent with that scenario.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Market expectations are not consistent with that scenario.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I hope that is not what we are looking at.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am just trying to ask a series of provocative questions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: You are doing a good job.

speaker: MOSSER
text: May I add one parenthetical point to that?

speaker: MOSSER
text: The swaps—unlike the TALF, for example—are priced at a penalty to market rates, and to the extent that market spreads do come down, as we have seen in the past two months, swap lines do self-liquidate.

speaker: MOSSER
text: They have declined very noticeably—they were nearly $600 billion at one point.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As the spreads come in, effectively the private sector comes in and undercuts the central bank, which was by design.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So now I am going to try to reconcile Presidents Lacker and Rosengren [laughter] and get your and our new Vice Chairman Dudley’s reactions.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My experience in economics is that it is not that helpful to talk about equilibrium and disequilibrium.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I am going to talk about it in a different way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You have firms and people who do the best they can, given the constraints that they face.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There are frictions out there, and we know what the friction is here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It is a very severe information friction in certain financial markets.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It is a crisis of financial engineering in which, when the new financial instruments were created, they were thought to be good devices, but they turned out to have serious transparency issues and that created information problems.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So now you say that, given that friction, I am going to let everybody optimize.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Jeff will say, well, that is a Pareto optimum given the friction and, if there is nothing you can do about the friction, then that is the best you can do.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But if there is some policy you can do to ameliorate the friction and pull that out, you will get a better solution.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would say that that is Mr. Dudley’s position.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The position that it is just technology and there is probably nothing we can do about the crisis in financial engineering would be the Lacker position.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I was wondering if you guys would react to that and see if that reflects your views.

speaker: LACKER
text: I will say “yes,” [laughter] with the additional note that with that answer alone you might wonder why I get so exercised, but it is that withdrawing that friction does not seem to be what any of our programs have been designed to accomplish.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Yes, and I agree with that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There seem to be a lot of things that are being done in many parts of the government and maybe parts of the Fed that are not really getting at that information friction.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I am going to ask the most provocative question of all.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The Chairman said at the beginning that we should obviously be allergic to taking on credit risk, and normally, I think everyone here agrees with that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But maybe now is the time to rethink that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You have a serious information problem out there.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You have a lot of reactions to that that are tangential to the core problem, and we are talking about doing open market operations, which used to be always in Treasuries, now in MBS.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It would not be that hard to say let’s just do the open market operation swap of money for a financial instrument using the toxic assets that are such a problem in this economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Normally I would not say things like this, so I am stepping out of character.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But in the interest of provoking discussion, maybe now is the time to at least start thinking about something like that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That would get to the heart of the matter.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If you try to go through the Congress, they are wonderful people and everything, but the process gets politicized—and we know this; we are seeing that already—and so all kinds of other things get done.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This would get at the core of the problem.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You would be taking on risk, but you take on some interest rate risk even when you buy Treasuries.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The whole idea would be to price these at the right price, which I understand is very tricky, but who better to do it than the 500 economists that hang out at the Fed?

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I don’t know—should it necessarily be a 100 percent benchmark that we do not want to take on credit risk, or should it be only a 95 percent benchmark or something like that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me say something about these frictions and why we can affect them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are two frictions that I think are important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One of them relates to the friction of illiquidity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is a tradition of central banking that we lend against illiquid assets when there is a panic run, and we know that panic runs are equilibrium phenomena and they can occur even though the assets are worth more than the liabilities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would argue that that kind of phenomenon has generalized into a lot of aspects of our economy—for example, the funding of various kinds of off-balance-sheet instruments, the commercial paper market, the money market mutual funds, and lots of other vehicles—and a lot of what we are doing is very much consistent in spirit with the idea of providing backup liquidity to allow firms to meet redemption demands without having to sell off assets into illiquid markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that is the thrust of a lot of what we are trying to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other type of friction that I think is important has to do with information capital.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a sense in which the capital of the banking system is the most important wealth in the world because it supports the information gathering and other institutional activities that banks can do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When, for whatever reason, there is a loss of bank capital and their activities are restrained and they are not able to make full use of the information and other skills that they have; that is a problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would argue that in a world where there are other frictions—sticky prices or wages, for example—the inability of the banks to fully use their information capital to extend credit and make loans and make markets will lead to a bad outcome for the economy as a whole.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The intellectual argument then is that there is a social benefit, a social externality, to providing more capital, and that is what a lot of the TARP and these other things involve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, traditionally in your comment about credit, it is not easy to make a clear distinction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is always the issue of liquidity versus solvency and so on, but it is not easy to make a clear distinction between lending against solvent but illiquid assets versus providing capital for informationally intensive agents, like banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that line is not completely clear.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But by history and tradition, the central bank has always leaned toward liquidity provision.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The government has always leaned toward credit allocation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that is a distinction that is worth trying to preserve, although admittedly we are not always going to do it perfectly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think we can specify what the frictions are, make coherent sense of them, and try to explain how our actions are related to them.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We do not want to maintain that if it is going to send us into an even more prolonged downturn.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I mean, it might be nice if we always did liquidity and Treasury always did credit, but I am saying—

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we have taken on credit risk in emergency situations, as you know.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But as I promised at the beginning, I think to the extent that we can use the opportunity of a new Administration and so on to clarify responsibilities in a better way, then we ought to do so.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we all appreciate what an extraordinary situation we are in and have experienced for the last eighteen months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A lot of what we are doing is requiring our good sense and historical knowledge and our intuition.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But as I think maybe the Vice Chairman mentioned, we do not really have the historical basis for all of the things that we are having to deal with here.

speaker: LACKER
text: That was a very clear and lucid description of what the core crystallized issues are regarding frictions—regarding the thing that in my fogged state I was not able to articulate to Vice Chairman Dudley a minute ago.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is what I think we have been struggling to get our hands around, and so I appreciate your clear articulation of that.

speaker: LACKER
text: As you know, these are sort of classic problems in banking economics.

speaker: LACKER
text: About liquidity, I am struck by the hedge funds.

speaker: LACKER
text: To date as far as I know—maybe New York knows about one that is about to blow up—we have not been challenged by them.

speaker: LACKER
text: Here is a set of participants not viewed as likely to benefit from the safety net that, over the past couple of years, have structured their liabilities in a way that makes them relatively insulated from run-like phenomena.

speaker: LACKER
text: That illustrates the broader point about models of panic-stricken runs—the extent to which you issue a contract that makes you vulnerable to that is endogenous and leads me toward wondering if the safety net has really been what is driving the instances of run-like behavior not only in the banking system.

speaker: LACKER
text: On informational capital, I think you are right on target there.

speaker: LACKER
text: Obviously, it was the subject of your very seminal research, inspiring to all of us.

speaker: LACKER
text: There I think about a lot of the pulling away—people taking their loan accounts—from Wachovia and Governor Duke’s bank a year ago telling me that they were picking up customers that were uncomfortable working with Wachovia or B of A.

speaker: LACKER
text: Switching costs are there for sure.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I struggle with how hard they are and, again, appreciate that you have crystallized genuine scientific issues to clarify the discussion.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, I was just going to comment on Jeff’s comment.

speaker: STERN
text: I think the hedge fund industry for the most part has weathered this remarkably well, but of course, the five biggest hedge funds, Goldman, Merrill, et cetera, et cetera, are gone.

speaker: STERN
text: What is left is a good deal smaller and presumably a lot less consequential than the ones we have seen.

speaker: STERN
text: Let me just add, Mr. Chairman, that I agree 100 percent with what you just said.

speaker: STERN
text: We have long had a system in which the commercial banking system has been a backup source of liquidity to other financial institutions and the nonfinancial sector as well.

speaker: STERN
text: For a variety of reasons, partially because of what has happened to capital and partially because the shadow banking system is growing so rapidly relative to the banking system, even though I would say banks in the aggregate are continuing to play that role, it has become increasingly difficult for them to function effectively as the backup source of liquidity.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that is an important justification for the actions we have taken.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Just to respond, Jeff, to the comment that the hedge funds haven’t faced a run-like phenomenon.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One of my contact conversations with a hedge fund manager effectively said, “We are in a run.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This period is a run.” It is a run that has episodes at the end of quarters and so forth, so it operates a bit differently, but the effect is the same.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, if I could, Mr. Chairman, just to be clear—it is not that they are not subject to runs; it is that runs don’t bring them down the way an institution like a classic bank in 1932 would have been brought down by a retail run.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As you point out, an important point is that institutional structures, contracts, and so on are endogenous, and policy affects them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we are in a situation at this point where past is past and what is sunk is sunk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have to deal with the situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And it is very, very important for us to go forward to try to change the legal structure, the regulatory structure, and even Federal Reserve operating procedures in ways that will encourage more-stable systems in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But at the moment, the fire is burning, and we have to think about that.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I could, that is a very important insight.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is part of the classic tension between healing now versus looking at what we are doing as part of a repeatable process from which people are going to be forming expectations about our future behavior.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is the inevitable tension.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unless there is anyone else, let me thank you for a very useful discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am sure that we will have more in the future, but this really sets the parameters and the issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I took many things away from this discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One of them is that we need to keep thinking about our metrics regarding the efficiency and efficacy of our programs—in particular, how the shadow value of duration or illiquidity in our balance sheet is matched against the benefits of a particular program that has certain implications for our balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would challenge the staff—as all the hard tasks go to the staff—to think more about how we can evaluate the efficacy of our programs, in particular, and the opportunity costs as well, in terms of the space they take up or the duration that we create in our balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One useful exercise that we ought to be thinking about is, if we were to go another step, where would it be and on what criteria would it be decided.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would perhaps answer the question about there being no plan, no control, and no delimiting factors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that we can make progress on trying to answer these questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is not going to happen immediately, but I hope over time it will help.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have a request, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: LACKER
text: I asked the System Open Market Account manager a couple of days ago, but now he is not the manager anymore.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I did that on purpose.

speaker: LACKER
text: You just didn’t want to do it.

speaker: LACKER
text: Tomorrow or maybe today we will hear about a forecast for the path of the federal funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: In creating that, it is endogenous.

speaker: LACKER
text: It depends on the economy, but it also affects the economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was wondering if we could get one for our balance sheet, subject to uncertainty of all the obvious kinds.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would be useful to help us think about the capacity of programs and extending them.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it would be useful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with that, and I thought we would have done more of that today, in fact.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But what we can do—and what we ought to think about for future reference—is maybe scenarios as opposed to forecasts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That might be a better way to think about it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was going to ask exactly the same question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we are ready, we still have some votes to take here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me first ask the FOMC to do the routine ratification of domestic open market operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do I have a motion?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Hearing no objection, thank you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Now, to approve the extension of the programs, I would like to propose that we extend the list of programs through October 30, as proposed by the staff.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should have some discussion about the AMLF and others, recognizing that, even if we announce an extension, rationalization down the road or restructuring is always a possibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So this would be a motion for the Board to extend the 13(3) programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All Board members okay with this?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Hearing no objection, thank you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need from the FOMC a resolution to extend the swap arrangements through October 30.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Not hearing any objections, the motion is approved.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need a separate resolution from the FOMC to extend the TSLF through October 30.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any concerns, objections, or comments?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Hearing no objections, thank you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me remind you again that this is all confidential until Thursday morning because we want to coordinate our announcements with other central banks, and we will take the opportunity to at least look at the two programs that President Plosser mentioned.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me turn now to the economic situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Boy, I think it has been a while since we were three and a half hours into the meeting before we got to the staff forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The GDP is a little smaller than it was at the start of the meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Actually I do not want to give President Lacker any concerns about whom he is listening to.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I want to introduce Dan Sichel, Karen Dynan, and Trevor Reeve, who will be presenting the outlook.

speaker: SICHEL
text: 2 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: SICHEL
text: I’ll be referring to the material labeled “Staff Presentation on the Economic Outlook.” The incoming data largely have ratified the bleak near-term outlook we projected in the December Greenbook; the spending data have painted a gloomy picture, and readings on employment and production were even weaker than we had expected.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Starting first with the employment data, the top left panel of exhibit 1 shows the dramatic worsening of the labor market in recent months.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Private payrolls declined almost 520,000 per month on average in the fourth quarter.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The panel to the right shows manufacturing industrial production excluding motor vehicles.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Factory output has been plummeting as manufacturers are responding aggressively to declines in both domestic and foreign demand.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The motor vehicle sector has been hit particularly hard.

speaker: SICHEL
text: With extremely sluggish sales, automakers have been slashing production—plotted in the middle left panel—and we anticipate a sizable further reduction in assemblies this quarter.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Turning to households, the latest data confirm that consumers continue to retrench.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As shown by the blue bars, real PCE for goods other than motor vehicles appears headed for a very large drop in the fourth quarter, and we anticipate a further decline this quarter.

speaker: SICHEL
text: These projections are similar to those in the last Greenbook.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In the housing sector, starts (the black line in the bottom left panel) declined further last month and now are less than one-quarter of their peak level in 2006.

speaker: SICHEL
text: With the level of permits (the red line) still below starts, we expect further declines in starts in the next few months.

speaker: SICHEL
text: All told, as shown to the right, we project that real GDP contracted at an annual rate of about 5 percent last quarter.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Given the greater weakness in the employment and production data, we have lowered our forecast for the first-quarter change in real GDP to minus 5½ percent.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In the second quarter, the rate of decline in real GDP moderates as the new fiscal package—discussed more in a minute—boosts demand.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The top left panel of exhibit 2 summarizes the medium-term outlook for real activity.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We anticipate that recovery will begin, albeit slowly, in the second half of this year, with real GDP projected to increase at an annual rate of about 2 percent; next year, output is expected to rise about 2½ percent.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The box to the right lists key factors contributing to the onset of recovery: Financial stress begins to recede, housing begins to stabilize, monetary and fiscal stimulus provide a boost to demand, and inventory liquidation comes to an end.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Regarding fiscal stimulus, although the precise composition of what will be passed remains a moving target, we now assume a package of $800 billion, $300 billion more than what we penciled into the December Greenbook.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The larger size of the package is an important source of our slightly stronger outlook for economic growth than in the last Greenbook.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The bullets in the middle left panel highlight our estimates of the response to the various provisions of the plan.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Households begin spending the tax cuts of $180 billion and transfers of $90 billion when received.

speaker: SICHEL
text: On the other hand, we expect the investment response to the business tax cuts to be limited.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In addition, of the total new funding for state and local governments, we project that only 40 percent will be spent by the 2 The materials used by Mr. Sichel, Ms. Dynan, and Mr. Reeve are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: SICHEL
text: end of 2010 as infrastructure projects take some time to get under way and as the spending of other grants is smoothed out somewhat.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The panel to the right puts the pieces together.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We estimate that the fiscal package will boost real GDP growth by a bit less than 1½ percentage points this year and almost 1 percentage point next year.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Our estimates of the GDP effects are smaller than those of some other analysts, with the discrepancy mostly reflecting our assumption of slower spend-out rates by state and local governments.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Inventory dynamics—the subject of the bottom panels—are another element importantly shaping the recession and recovery.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The table in the bottom left reports the contributions of inventories to real GDP growth in key periods over the business cycle.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The first column shows the contributions in the current episode, and the second column shows averages for the postwar period.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As can be seen on line 1, in the year before the peak in real GDP in 2008:Q2, inventories were already being liquidated aggressively, in contrast to the usual positive contribution.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As shown on line 2 of the table, from the peak to the trough, inventories hold down real GDP growth only a little.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Because inventory liquidation was already quite rapid before the peak, once the contraction in sales got under way, the rate of liquidation needed to steepen only a bit more.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In contrast, during many past episodes, the drag from inventories was much larger as manufacturers had to play catch-up once sales turned down.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In the year after the trough (line 3 of the table) liquidation comes to an end, and the swing in inventories boosts real GDP growth 1 percentage point, about in line with historical averages.

speaker: SICHEL
text: This increase in the inventory contribution is an important feature of the projected recovery in real GDP.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Karen will now discuss developments shaping the outlook for households and businesses.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Exhibit 3 covers the housing sector.

speaker: DYNAN
text: As can be seen in the top left panel, our forecast calls for single-family housing starts to bottom out in the first half of this year and to move up gradually thereafter.

speaker: DYNAN
text: One factor behind the projected improvement in housing demand is the interest rate on 30-year fixed-rate conforming mortgages, shown in the top right panel.

speaker: DYNAN
text: This rate fell sharply following the November 25 announcement of the Federal Reserve’s MBS purchase program, and we expect it to remain low over the next two years.

speaker: DYNAN
text: That said, our projected pickup in housing activity is quite modest, as mortgage credit remains more difficult and more expensive to obtain than might be implied by the conforming mortgage rate alone.

speaker: DYNAN
text: As summarized in the middle left panel, the disappearance of nonprime mortgages from private sources makes it much more difficult to obtain mortgages for households lacking solid credit histories, unable to make significant down payments, or in need of low introductory interest rates.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Part of the gap has been filled by an increase in originations associated with Federal Housing Administration programs, but such originations remain far below the level of private nonprime originations at their peak.

speaker: DYNAN
text: In addition, lending is now more restrictive than in the past to those seeking to finance an amount above the conforming limit.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Housing demand is likely also being damped by an expectation that house prices have not reached their trough.

speaker: DYNAN
text: We project that house prices will decline significantly further before flattening out at the end of 2010.

speaker: DYNAN
text: As shown in the middle right panel, this decline pushes one measure of the overvaluation of housing that we monitor well into negative territory.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Prices typically overcorrect at the end of housing cycles, but this correction is amplified by the extent of the earlier overvaluation and by the excess supply of unsold new and existing homes that we foresee over the forecast period.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The bottom left panel shows one implication of the bust in house prices—a rise in the share of prime and subprime mortgages with low current equity.

speaker: DYNAN
text: As shown on lines 1 and 2, the recent declines in house prices have led to considerable increases in the shares of mortgages with equity below 20 percent.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Moreover, as indicated on lines 3 and 4, the share with negative equity has also increased rapidly.

speaker: DYNAN
text: These low levels of home equity, along with greater job losses, have pushed foreclosures— shown in the bottom right panel—to very high levels.

speaker: DYNAN
text: In 2008, lenders initiated more than twice as many foreclosures as in 2006.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Notwithstanding the government foreclosure mitigation efforts embedded in our forecast, we expect prime foreclosures (the red portions of the bars) to remain high this year before diminishing somewhat in 2010.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Subprime foreclosures (the blue portions) are projected to show a more pronounced decline largely because the stock of outstanding subprime loans is shrinking in response to the cessation of new loans and the termination, through default or refinancing, of existing loans.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Exhibit 4 features our outlook for consumer spending.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Real disposable personal income (the blue bars in the top left panel) fell in the second half of last year, but real consumer spending (in red) declined even more sharply.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Disposable income is projected to step up early this year as a result of the sizable personal tax cuts and increases in transfer spending built into our forecast.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Despite the support from fiscal measures, consumer spending is projected to increase only weakly this year and moderately next year.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The saving rate (the black line in the panel at the right) is projected to move up sharply in early 2009 as the tax cuts are only gradually spent.

speaker: DYNAN
text: We expect saving to remain elevated over the next two years, in part because of the sharp drop in household wealth relative to income (the red line) and because of households’ greater uncertainty about their income prospects.

speaker: DYNAN
text: We think that spending will be damped in coming quarters as well by difficult borrowing conditions.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The middle left panel shows two important sources of the credit available to finance consumer spending.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The blue portions of the bars correspond to housing equity tapped through home equity loans and cash-out refinancings; surveys suggest that households traditionally put perhaps one-fifth of such funds toward consumer purchases.

speaker: DYNAN
text: As can be seen, mortgage equity withdrawal declined sharply last year.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Consumer credit (the red portions of the bars) also fell off over the year, turning negative by the fourth quarter.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The declines in household borrowing reflect, to some extent, reduced demand for loans, as the weaker economy has led households to defer spending.

speaker: DYNAN
text: However, as illustrated in the middle right panel, a reduction in supply is clearly playing a role as well, with banks continuing to tighten standards on consumer loans.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Developments in the consumer ABS market are contributing to the tighter credit conditions for households.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The market has seen very little issuance since October, and spreads have been very high.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The commercial banks that make most credit card loans have access to alternative sources of funding, such as deposits and various new forms of support from the government.

speaker: DYNAN
text: In contrast, the finance companies affiliated with auto manufacturers, which traditionally have been an important source of auto loans have not (for the most part) had access to these alternative sources.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The bottom right panel shows the dollar volume of new loans per vehicle sold—one metric of the extent to which the finance companies support sales.

speaker: DYNAN
text: This indicator had been fluctuating around $5,000 per vehicle, but dropped to less than $3,500 in November.

speaker: DYNAN
text: That said, loan originations should pick up this year, with the expected implementation of the TALF, and GMAC, now a bank holding company, having announced that it will resume lending to some consumers with weaker credit records.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The next two exhibits focus on business investment and finance.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The top left panel of exhibit 5 depicts a key underpinning of our investment forecast—the accelerator mechanism.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Business fixed investment as a share of output (shown in red) tends to track the lagged growth rate of output (in black).

speaker: DYNAN
text: The sharp deceleration that we have seen in output is expected to exert a significant drag on investment this year and next.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Indeed, as shown by the red bars in the panel to the right, we estimate that business spending on equipment and software fell nearly 10 percent last year, and we project it to decline by an even larger amount this year before making a moderate recovery in 2010.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Investment in nonresidential structures held up better in 2008, but we expect a sharp decline this year and a further decline in 2010, due in part to the lags in planning and implementing new structures projects.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Spending in the business sector is also held down by credit market conditions.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Firms are finding credit expensive and more difficult to obtain because investors are demanding extremely high returns for holding risky assets.

speaker: DYNAN
text: In the stock market, the dramatic decline in equity values over the past year has pushed the trend earnings-to­ price ratio (the red line in the middle left panel) well above the range seen over the past quarter century.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The gap between this ratio and the real Treasury perpetuity yield (shaded in turquoise in the left panel and plotted as a line on the right) is a rough measure of the equity risk premium.

speaker: DYNAN
text: At more than 10 percentage points, the gap is extraordinarily high by historical standards.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Spreads on corporate bonds are also extremely elevated, keeping yields relatively high despite substantial declines in long­ term risk-free rates.

speaker: DYNAN
text: As can be seen in the bottom left panel, yields on 10-year BBB- rated bonds have fallen since the December FOMC meeting but remain at the high end of their range since 2002.

speaker: DYNAN
text: That said, issuance of nonfinancial investment-grade bonds, shown in the inset box, moved up in the fourth quarter and has held up in at a solid pace in January.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Yields on speculative-grade bonds, shown in the bottom right panel, also remain unusually high, and speculative-grade issuance, though up somewhat in January, is still fairly weak.

speaker: DYNAN
text: C&I loans from commercial banks represent another important source of funding for businesses.

speaker: DYNAN
text: As shown in the top left panel of exhibit 6, C&I lending fell off sharply at the end of last year, and we expect it to remain weak this year.

speaker: DYNAN
text: We believe that the downswing partly reflected reduced demand for loans as businesses trimmed plans to invest and, after relying heavily on bank lines while credit markets were disrupted in the fall, turned back to other sources of funds, such as corporate bonds.

speaker: DYNAN
text: However, the supply of credit has also been reduced.

speaker: DYNAN
text: As shown in the top right panel, most of the senior loan officers we just surveyed reported having tightened standards on C&I loans further and having increased the spreads of loan rates over their cost of funds.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The next four panels turn to some of the factors that have exacerbated the credit problems in the commercial real estate sector.

speaker: DYNAN
text: As can be seen in the middle left panel, rents (the red line) have decelerated sharply over the past two years, and vacancy rates (the black line) are on the rise.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Prices for commercial properties, shown on the right, turned down sharply in late 2007 after soaring over the preceding three years.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Our forecast calls for a significant further price decline.

speaker: DYNAN
text: These weaker conditions have contributed to rising delinquencies among commercial real estate loans, as seen in the bottom left panel.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The delinquency rate on such loans held by commercial banks (the turquoise line) climbed further in the third quarter.

speaker: DYNAN
text: As shown in red, the delinquency rate on loans in commercial-mortgage-backed securities (or CMBS) has been rising as well.

speaker: DYNAN
text: The box to the right summarizes key implications of the shutdown in the CMBS market.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Although the market traditionally has provided very little construction financing, the inability to issue should add to the pressures on banks’ balance sheets and thereby indirectly damp structures spending.

speaker: DYNAN
text: In particular, if it remains closed, the CMBS market will not be able to help refinance the large amount of bank construction loans expected to come due this year, as it would in normal times.

speaker: DYNAN
text: In addition, a smaller amount of loans currently within CMBS will come due this year and will need new financing from alternative sources such as banks.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Dan will pick up the discussion from here.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The top left panel of exhibit 7 provides some longer-term context for the deep recession and sluggish recovery that we are projecting.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The red line shows the level of real GDP, indexed to its own peak in the second quarter of last year.

speaker: SICHEL
text: By way of comparison, the green and blue lines show the paths of real GDP during the recessions that started in 1973 and 1981, respectively.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As noted to the right, the projected contraction in real GDP in the current episode is broadly in line with those two earlier big postwar recessions, but the projected recovery is noticeably more sluggish.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In part, this pattern reflects the influence of financial turmoil on the macroeconomy.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Gauging the hit to the economy from the recent financial stress is, to put it mildly, an inexact science.

speaker: SICHEL
text: One benchmark is the typical pattern experienced by economies during and after the onset of financial crises.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As noted in the bullets in the middle left panel, research on this topic—most notably the work by Carmen Reinhart and Ken Rogoff—indicates that downturns linked to major financial crises in advanced economies tend to be severe.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Reinhart and Rogoff identify five major financial crises in advanced economies in the postwar period; these include Spain in 1977, Norway in 1987, Finland and Sweden in 1991, and Japan in 1992.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The panel to the right shows one possible metric for gauging the magnitude of output loss in these episodes.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The first blue bar shows average growth in real GDP in these five countries during the four years prior to the crisis.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The red bar shows average growth in the worst two consecutive years after the onset of the crisis.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The average step-down in real GDP growth after these financial crises was about 5 percentage points.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The right-hand side of the bar chart shows figures for the current episode in the United States.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The blue bar shows average growth in the four years before 2007, the date used as the onset of the crisis.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The red bar shows our projection for average growth in the worst two years following the onset, 2008 and 2009.

speaker: SICHEL
text: On this metric, we are projecting a pattern similar to, though not as severe, as these other episodes.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Still, we see the evidence from past financial crises as suggesting that the risks to activity are tilted to the downside.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The bottom three panels highlight the alternative simulation in the Greenbook that explores that possibility.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As you know, in the baseline forecast we anticipate that financial market strains will gradually wane over the next two years.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In contrast, in the “more financial stress” scenario, we assume that risk premiums on a variety of securities move up significantly from their current levels and then come down more slowly than in the baseline.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As shown to the left, real GDP in this scenario contracts considerably in 2009 and increases only a little in 2010.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The unemployment rate (the middle panel) peaks at 9¼ percent, and core inflation (the panel on the right) moves below zero.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The top panels of exhibit 8 examine the cyclical properties of labor productivity, plotting the level around the staff’s estimate of trend.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As noted in the first bullet in the middle left panel, in some earlier recessions—such as those that started in 1973 and in 1981—labor productivity was pro-cyclical.

speaker: SICHEL
text: That is, labor productivity fell below trend during the recession—likely reflecting some labor hoarding—and then rose fairly quickly thereafter.

speaker: SICHEL
text: During the 1990 recession this pattern was barely evident, while it was not observed at all during the 2001 recession.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In the current episode, shown in the top right with a magnified scale, we expect that labor productivity will exhibit a mild pro-cyclical pattern.

speaker: SICHEL
text: With this recession anticipated to be quite deep, we expect many businesses to find that deeper job cuts would require shedding core personnel, leading to some labor hoarding in the near term.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Later this year, firms in recovering sectors expand production without initially adding to payrolls.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Accordingly, job losses in the private sector continue in the second half, and the unemployment rate (the black line in the middle right panel) rises further.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Given the additional near-term weakness in our outlook for activity, the unemployment rate now is expected to peak at 8½ percent early next year, a bit higher than in the last Greenbook.

speaker: SICHEL
text: This slack in resource utilization puts considerable downward pressure on inflation.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In addition, the sharp drop in energy prices (the bottom left panel), along with declines in import and commodity prices, also restrains our forecast of core inflation.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As shown to the right on line 3 in the table, we project that these factors will push core PCE inflation down to 1 percent this year and to 0.8 percent next year.

speaker: SICHEL
text: With the decline in energy prices, total PCE inflation (line 1) dips a little below core this year but then rises a little above core next year as energy prices increase a bit.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Shifting gears, exhibit 9 reprises material from the pre-FOMC briefing that Bob Tetlow delivered yesterday; it takes a closer look at an unconventional policy action included as an alternative simulation in the Greenbook.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As you know, in our baseline scenario, the zero lower bound constraint on the federal funds rate is binding until 2013.

speaker: SICHEL
text: This constraint partly explains our pessimistic baseline forecasts for unemployment and inflation, which are shown as the black lines in the panels at the top of the exhibit.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We can demonstrate the implications of the lower-bound constraint for the economic outlook using an unconstrained optimal control simulation, much like the one you saw in the December Bluebook, which would prescribe lowering the funds rate to about negative 4¼ percent by the end of this year.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The effects of such a monetary policy, if it were feasible, are shown by the green lines in the panels.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As you can see in the top left panel, by 2011 the unemployment rate would be more than 1 percentage point below the baseline path, and the top right panel shows that inflation would be ¾ percentage point above baseline at that point.

speaker: SICHEL
text: A large-scale asset purchase program—or LSAP program, for short—of mortgage-backed securities and longer-term Treasury securities is one of a variety of the unconventional monetary policies that could, in principle, combat this problem.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The efficacy of such a program depends on several assumptions, summarized in the middle left panel.

speaker: SICHEL
text: First, these assets must be imperfect substitutes for short-term debt—an assumption most economists would find reasonable; otherwise, actions intended to affect their returns could be undone through arbitrage with short-term securities.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Second, Treasury bonds and MBS must remain good substitutes for other types of long-term debt, as they are thought to be under normal conditions, so that reductions in yields on the targeted securities spill over to other private interest rates.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Third, movements in long-term rates should ideally continue to favorably influence stock prices, the exchange rate, and other financial markets, thereby boosting the program’s stimulative effect.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As noted in the middle right panel, the LSAP program we used for the alternative simulation assumes purchasing $500 billion in Treasury securities as well as further purchases of $500 billion in agency MBS beyond those already announced.
