speaker: SICHEL
text: These purchases are assumed to be carried out over the next year and a half and are eventually unwound over 2012 and 2013.

speaker: SICHEL
text: As indicated by the next set of bullets, we assume that these purchases reduce various long-term interest rates between 75 and 125 basis points over the next few months; these estimated effects are consistent with the analysis in the notes completed in December that dealt with various zero lower bound issues.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Using these estimates, the macroeconomic effects of the program are shown by the red lines in the panels at the top.

speaker: SICHEL
text: According to the FRB/US model, the unemployment rate follows a path only modestly above the theoretical unconstrained optimum, and inflation is closer to the unconstrained trajectory.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Moreover, the federal funds rate (not shown) rises above the lower bound at the beginning of 2012, one year earlier than in the baseline projection.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The potential benefits of this particular LSAP program notwithstanding, some important caveats are laid out in the bottom panel.

speaker: SICHEL
text: On the financial end, the direct interest rate effects of the program are highly uncertain, if only because we have so little experience with this sort of program.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Second, the current dysfunction in some financial markets could limit the magnitude of indirect effects—that is, the spillovers into markets other than those in which purchase activity takes place.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Third, the size of the program may be subject to economies—or dis-economies—of scale.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Fourth, LSAP programs, and unconventional policies more generally, introduce tricky “exit issues” regarding how to unwind the program without disrupting markets, incurring large losses on the Federal Reserve’s portfolio, or sparking a longer-run inflation problem.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Regarding macroeconomic issues, with credit availability so constrained at the moment and uncertainty so high, the model may understate—or overstate—the size of the response of consumption and investment to changes in financial conditions of a given magnitude.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In addition, possible heavy reliance on mortgage rates and housing to drive economic recovery entails some risks, particularly if spillovers from mortgage rates into other asset prices are limited.

speaker: SICHEL
text: All told, as this discussion makes clear, some significant potential benefits and costs need to be weighed when considering the possible implementation of large-scale asset purchase programs.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Trevor will now continue the presentation.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the top left panel of your first international exhibit, equity prices in the advanced foreign and emerging-market economies have turned down over the past couple of weeks amid very gloomy economic indicators and intensified concerns about financial institutions.

speaker: REEVE
text: Bank stock prices, in the next panel, have been especially hard hit.

speaker: REEVE
text: As Trish and Spence noted earlier, strains in interbank funding markets have eased on balance since your last meeting, despite deepening concerns about the banking sector.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the middle left panel, three-month LIBOR–OIS spreads have continued their gradual descent.

speaker: REEVE
text: Demand for dollar funding abroad appears to have eased following the turn of the year, as evidenced by recent declines in outstanding draws from central bank liquidity swap facilities.

speaker: REEVE
text: With a good chunk of these swaps currently having an original maturity of three months, it will take some time for these draws to roll off even if funding pressures ease further.

speaker: REEVE
text: In foreign exchange markets (the bottom panels), the dollar dropped sharply following the December cut in the federal funds rate target.

speaker: REEVE
text: But since that time, as it has become increasingly clear that deteriorating conditions would lead foreign central banks also to ease policy further, the dollar has reversed course and has appreciated slightly on net over the intermeeting period.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the bottom right, we continue to project a modest depreciation of the dollar over the next couple of years, but this reverses only a little of the late-2008 appreciation.

speaker: REEVE
text: The table at the top of your next exhibit summarizes our outlook for foreign growth.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown on line 1, we estimate that total foreign GDP contracted at a pace of 3¾ percent in the fourth quarter, the weakest quarterly reading in our thirty-eight­ year history of this series.

speaker: REEVE
text: We expect foreign output to fall sharply again in the current quarter.

speaker: REEVE
text: These figures are considerably weaker than in the December projection, as incoming data, which we had expected to be grim, nonetheless surprised us on the downside.

speaker: REEVE
text: We continue to project foreign GDP to stabilize toward the middle of the year and then to begin to recover as financial conditions gradually improve, fiscal and monetary stimulus supports activity, and the U.S. economy regains its footing.

speaker: REEVE
text: Of course, there are downside risks to this view, and data received in the past few days suggest that we may make additional downward revisions to our near-term outlook.

speaker: REEVE
text: One of the most striking recent developments has been the very sharp drop in global manufacturing and international trade, as shown by the plummeting purchasing managers indexes in the middle left panel.

speaker: REEVE
text: As manufacturing is pro-cyclical, steep declines in output and trade should be expected given the broader downturn.

speaker: REEVE
text: That said, for many countries the recent movements have been breathtaking.

speaker: REEVE
text: The Japanese economy has been particularly hard hit.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the middle right panel, real exports have plummeted with the decline in foreign demand and the appreciation of the yen.

speaker: REEVE
text: Real household spending, while far from a source of strength, has held up better.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown on line 4 of the table, we estimate that Japanese GDP contracted at a 5¼ percent pace in the fourth quarter and expect that GDP will keep shrinking until late this year.

speaker: REEVE
text: The euro area (line 5) is not faring much better, with GDP contracting at a 2 percent pace in the fourth and first quarters.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown on the bottom left, industrial production in the euro area, as elsewhere, has fallen sharply.

speaker: REEVE
text: Retail sales have slumped but have not collapsed.

speaker: REEVE
text: The emerging Asian economies (line 9) are taking a severe beating, with output contracting at a 6½ percent pace in the fourth quarter amid widespread declines in exports.

speaker: REEVE
text: Real GDP in Korea and Singapore (not shown) plunged 21 percent and 16 percent, respectively, and growth in China (line 10) came to a standstill.

speaker: REEVE
text: As indicated in the bottom right panel, continued strength in Chinese retail sales has countered some of the weakness in external demand, but growth in industrial production has fallen considerably.

speaker: REEVE
text: With Chinese authorities taking strong measures to support the economy, we see growth strengthening in the quarters ahead but remaining well below the 10 percent average over the past decade.

speaker: REEVE
text: The weakness in the U.S. and foreign economies has shown through to U.S. trade flows, the subject of your next exhibit.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown by the green line in the first panel, our exports have dropped sharply.

speaker: REEVE
text: Imports, however, have dropped even more, leading to a marked narrowing of the trade deficit in November, as indicated to the right.

speaker: REEVE
text: Much of this narrowing is attributable to the value of oil imports, which has plummeted with the fall in oil prices.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown on the middle left, imports have also been held down by the decline in motor vehicle sales, which has led to a sharp slide in automotive imports.

speaker: REEVE
text: Although we expect overall imports and exports to continue to fall in the current quarter (as indicated by the dots), the drop in exports is tempered somewhat by a projected rebound in aircraft exports.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the middle right, last autumn’s strike at Boeing and subsequent production delays resulted in a notable drop in aircraft exports, which should be reversed.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown on line 1 of the table, we estimate that real exports plummeted at a 20 percent pace in the fourth quarter, a much steeper rate of decline than previously projected and a very sharp reversal from the strong performance seen earlier in the year.

speaker: REEVE
text: Our markdown to real import growth has been nearly as large, resulting in a contribution of net exports to GDP (line 3) that is down only about ½ percentage point in the fourth quarter from our December projection, bringing it close to zero.

speaker: REEVE
text: We see trade continuing to contract in the current quarter; but with the fall in imports exceeding that for exports, the net contribution is projected to be positive.

speaker: REEVE
text: Thereafter, however, the contribution of net exports turns negative.

speaker: REEVE
text: Your next exhibit provides some historical context for this projection.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown by the red line in the top panel, the downturn in foreign growth that we anticipate is similar in magnitude to the 1982 and 2001 episodes but is somewhat more persistent.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown by the solid red bars in the middle panel, exports subtracted about 1 percentage point from U.S. GDP growth in 1982 and 2001.

speaker: REEVE
text: Thus far in the current episode, however, the contribution of exports to GDP is less negative, as the plunge in exports at the end of last year followed robust growth in previous quarters.

speaker: REEVE
text: One key difference in the current recession is the real value of the dollar.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the bottom panel, the dollar was relatively strong and on an upward trajectory heading into the 1982 and 2001 downturns, providing additional restraint to exports.

speaker: REEVE
text: Leading into the recent period, in contrast, the dollar was notably weaker and thus provided a boost to exports.

speaker: REEVE
text: But with the dollar recently taking back some of its previous decline and with foreign demand remaining depressed, exports are projected to decline again this year, marking the first two-year consecutive decline in 50 years.

speaker: REEVE
text: Your next exhibit turns to commodity prices.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the first panel, oil and other commodity prices have plunged from their July peaks.

speaker: REEVE
text: These dramatic movements have led some observers to conclude that speculators played a key role in these price dynamics, particularly for oil.

speaker: REEVE
text: Evidence for this hypothesis, however, remains elusive.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the top right, the two main villains in this story, noncommercial traders (mainly hedge funds) and index investors, were reducing their exposure to crude oil over the first half of 2008, when oil prices were surging.

speaker: REEVE
text: Over the past couple of months, noncommercial traders have rebuilt their positions, even as oil prices have continued to decline.

speaker: REEVE
text: Moreover, the pattern of observed inventories is not consistent with the speculation hypothesis.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the middle left, U.S. crude oil inventories declined well below typical levels as prices were rising and hit a low right as the oil price peaked.

speaker: REEVE
text: Since then, inventories have moved up sharply, reflecting the collapse in oil demand.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown to the right, the growth of world oil demand turned negative around the middle of last year.

speaker: REEVE
text: Emerging-market demand decelerated sharply late in the year, leading to the biggest annual decline in global oil use since the early 1980s.

speaker: REEVE
text: In response to the downturn in demand, OPEC has announced several production cuts in an effort to support prices.

speaker: REEVE
text: As indicated on the bottom left, OPEC production (the red line) moved lower in the second half of last year and will fall considerably further if the cartel complies with its January target.

speaker: REEVE
text: These production cuts are unlikely to lead to a quick turnaround in oil prices given the large shock to demand.

speaker: REEVE
text: But over time (as shown on the bottom right), lower production along with firming demand should contribute to higher oil prices, as reflected in futures market quotes and our projections.

speaker: REEVE
text: Nonfuel commodity prices are also expected to move up going forward, albeit more slowly than oil prices.

speaker: REEVE
text: Commodity price fluctuations have been a key driver of broader price movements.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the top left panel of your next exhibit, we project consumer price inflation in the advanced foreign economies to continue to drop sharply from elevated levels, largely reflecting swings in food and energy prices, although increasing slack also plays a role.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown in the middle left, inflation excluding food and energy in the advanced foreign economies has moved in a much narrower range.

speaker: REEVE
text: At this point, the risks of a prolonged period of deflation appear small for these economies, with Japan being the clear exception.

speaker: REEVE
text: As shown below, the central banks of the advanced foreign economies have cut policy rates sharply in recent months, and we expect a little additional easing going forward.

speaker: REEVE
text: Inflationary pressures have also diminished sharply for the emerging Asian economies, as shown in the middle right.

speaker: REEVE
text: For Latin America, however, inflation has remained elevated, partly as a result of currency depreciation.

speaker: REEVE
text: Consequently, monetary authorities have been reluctant to ease policy while inflation concerns persist.

speaker: REEVE
text: Within the past two weeks, however, both Brazil and Mexico have begun to lower policy rates, and we expect additional easing in the coming months.

speaker: REEVE
text: Brian will now continue our presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 3 I will be referring to the separate package labeled “Material for Briefing on FOMC Participants’ Economic Projections.” Exhibit 1 depicts the central tendencies and ranges of your current forecasts for 2009 to 2011 and over the longer run, following the integrated approach to the inclusion of longer-run projections that was recommended by the Subcommittee on Communications and discussed at the December FOMC meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The likely severity of the current recession is clearly evident in this exhibit: Nearly all of you expect real GDP to shrink this year, the unemployment rate to climb to at least 8½ percent by the fourth quarter, and total PCE inflation to be less than 1 percent on a fourth-quarter over fourth-quarter basis.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This figure also highlights your expectations that a period of three years is likely to be insufficient for the economy to return to a balanced-growth path following the current economic shock.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, although the benchmark horizon for the longer-run projections was specified as about five to six years, several of you noted that the convergence process might well take even longer than that.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Exhibit 2 tabulates the central tendencies and ranges of your latest projections; corresponding information about the Committee’s previous projections—those from last October—is indicated in italics, and Greenbook projections are included as a memo item.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the left column of the top panel, your forecasts for real GDP growth in 2009 have a central tendency of minus 1¼ to minus ½ percent, as most of you expect output to contract further during the first half of this year—at an annual rate of about 3 to 4 percent—before resuming positive growth, albeit at a low rate, during the second half.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, you generally anticipate a relatively sluggish recovery that reflects the gradual waning of financial stresses, continued weakness in the housing sector, and poor growth prospects abroad.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As a result, most of you see 3 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: GDP growth as only gradually reaching a faster pace that eventually brings the economy back to its balanced-growth path.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Nearly all of you estimate that real GDP will grow over the longer run (the right-hand column) at an annual rate of 2½ to 2¾ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendency of these longer-run growth projections is the same as for the trial run that was conducted last October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the second panel, your forecasts of the unemployment rate in the fourth quarter of 2009 fall in a range of 8 to 9¼ percent, more than a percentage point higher than for the projections that you made last October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In explaining these revisions to your near-term outlook, many of you pointed to the weakness of incoming data on consumer spending and labor market conditions and to the rapid slowdown in global economic activity.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your unemployment projections further ahead also underscore the anticipated slow pace of recovery: Most of you expect that, even in 2011, the unemployment rate will be about 6¾ to 7½ percent, well above your estimates of about 4¾ to 5 percent for the unemployment rate that will prevail over the longer run in the absence of further shocks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your longer-run projections for the unemployment rate have the same central tendency as in October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your forecasts for inflation in 2009 have also shifted markedly since last October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your forecasts for overall PCE inflation in 2009 (the first column of the third panel) now have a central tendency of 0.3 to 1 percent, a full percentage point lower than the central tendency of your October projections; and most of you now expect a core PCE inflation rate of about 1 percent this year (the first column of the bottom panel), compared with the central tendency of 1½ to 2 percent for your October projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Looking further ahead, the width of the central tendencies and ranges of your inflation projections has increased considerably.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, the range of your overall PCE inflation projections for 2011 spans an interval of nearly 2 percentage points—about twice as wide as the range of your projections last October.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: From your accompanying narratives, it is evident that these differences reflect the diversity of your views about the pace of economic recovery, the sensitivity of inflation to economic activity, the prevalence of downward nominal wage rigidity, and the degree to which you see longer-run inflation expectations as likely to remain firmly anchored over the next several years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Many of you anticipate that inflation in 2011 will still be well below your individual assessments of the mandate-consistent inflation rate—that is, the longer-run rate of inflation that each of you sees as most consistent with the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate for promoting price stability and maximum employment.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your assessments of the mandate-consistent inflation rate have a central tendency of about 1¾ to 2 percent and a range of 1½ to 2 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This central tendency is noticeably higher than in October; at that time, your assessments were tightly clustered around a value of 1¾ percent, whereas 2 percent is now the median and the mode of the distribution.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In your forecast submissions, many of you indicated that your views regarding the appropriate path of monetary policy are roughly similar to those of the Greenbook, which assumes that the federal funds rate will remain close to the zero bound through late 2012.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, a number of you noted that policy tightening would commence somewhat sooner than that, and a couple of you expressed the view that the federal funds rate will need to be raised substantially above current levels during the second half of this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Exhibit 3 presents your views on the risks and uncertainties in the outlook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the top left-hand panel, all of you see uncertainty about growth as elevated relative to historical norms; and as shown to the right, most of you continue to perceive the risks to growth as weighted to the downside, even with the downward revision in your modal projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the accompanying narratives, many of you emphasized the uncertainties in gauging the evolution and implications of the global financial turmoil, the effects of nontraditional monetary policy tools, and the size and effect of the fiscal stimulus package.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the bottom left-hand panel, nearly all of you see an elevated degree of uncertainty about the inflation outlook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown to the right, a majority view the risks to that outlook as roughly balanced, whereas the rest of you see the risks as tilted to the downside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Some of you noted that the degree of uncertainty about the inflation outlook reflects uncertainty about the evolution of resource slack and the path of commodity prices, which are highly sensitive to global economic conditions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Others mentioned that the risks to the inflation outlook could eventually become tilted to the upside if stimulative policy measures are not unwound in a timely fashion once the economy begins to recover.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As you know, your agenda reserves time for a decision tomorrow as to whether to proceed with regular publication of longer-run projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You may wish to indicate your general views on that issue in the economic go-round.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As usual, the staff will be preparing a Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) and will be circulating drafts to you over the next few weeks along with drafts of the minutes.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Should you decide to proceed with longer-term projections, these projections from this cycle would be included in the SEP to be released along with the minutes of this meeting in mid- February.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do we have questions for the staff?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have a few questions, two really short ones—just clarifying ones—and two longer ones.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the presentation, I have a question on exhibit 7, the recovery across different recessions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I note that you say you started it at the second quarter of ’08 as being the trough.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Everything else starts that at the NBER trough, which would have been the fourth quarter of ’07.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Why did you do that and not do it elsewhere?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is there any reason for it?

speaker: SICHEL
text: You could do these types of cyclical comparison charts either way, dating from the NBER peak or dating from the series-specific peak.

speaker: SICHEL
text: What is done here is to index to the series-specific peak so that you look at each of the path cycles and say when GDP turned down in that cycle.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In many cycles, that is the same as the NBER peak, but in some cycles it is not.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In this cycle, in particular, it came a couple of quarters later.

speaker: SICHEL
text: You could do it the other way—in which case you would see the red line rising first and then coming down.

speaker: SICHEL
text: It is just a different way of presenting the same information.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was just curious what the rationale for using that peak in some cases, but in other parts of the presentation you used the fourth quarter.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Arguably, it really just comes down to that it is a different way of presenting the same information.

speaker: SICHEL
text: You get a cleaner comparison because every business cycle has some unique features and the timing differs in some particular ways.

speaker: SICHEL
text: This is trying to abstract from those differences in timing.

speaker: SICHEL
text: But one could do it the other way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The second clarifying question—I’m curious about tightening standards on consumer loans, particularly credit cards, in exhibit 4.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: When you asked a banker in the survey about tightening credit card lending, how am I supposed to interpret that?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Does that mean that they have reduced physically or technically the credit limits on credit cards?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Does it mean that they are offering fewer credit cards?

speaker: DYNAN
text: Brian can correct me if I am wrong, but I believe it is more the latter— offering fewer credit cards.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It has been great that I get much fewer requests to apply for credit cards.

speaker: DYNAN
text: We have asked separately about what they are doing to credit lines.

speaker: DYNAN
text: In fact, more than half are saying that they are reducing credit lines as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess the issue there for me is, if they are reducing excess credit lines—for example, on credit cards that were not being exercised anyway—or just not offering as many cards, how I interpret that in terms of really tightening credit is a bit loose there compared with some other things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I just wanted some clarification.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, I have two more-substantive questions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, about inflation forecasting: The best way I can describe forecasting in this environment is guesswork, and certainly my staff and I have struggled with the inflation forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In a lot of models, the approach to inflation forecasting both depends on and is very sensitive to varying degrees of incorporating forward- looking expectations and how much looking backward you do.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In this environment, when you have big swings up and down in inflation, looking backward may or may not be very helpful or very good.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It also depends a lot on how much credibility you think the central bank has.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is further complicated because we are at the zero bound, and that is difficult to incorporate into the models.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would like a little discussion from you about how you came up with your forecast for inflation in this model—how much of the path that you got is really dependent on the model because, frankly, it is really hard to figure out what to do, given all those things I just mentioned.

speaker: SICHEL
text: So I share your pain.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Regarding how we put this together, we are not looking at any particular model.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We are looking at a range of models and trying to make the best judgment that we can about how the various forces that affect inflation are likely to come into play over the next couple of years.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In terms of frameworks, we look at some pretty standard, backward-looking models that do not have any forward-looking components, just traditional measures of resource slack.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We also look at some forward-looking models in which we incorporate various measures of inflation expectations to try to avail ourselves of the information in some of the survey-based measures of inflation expectations that have a more forward looking component.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In terms of the factors that are particularly important for this contour, the very large amount of resource slack shown in that picture as captured by the unemployment rate—although one could measure that in many ways—is one important feature in the considerable slowdown of inflation.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We think that a lot of slack will be putting downward pressure on wages and prices.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Then we add to that the movements in energy and other commodities and materials prices and the movements in import prices, which have all been quite dramatic recently in the direction of pushing inflation down.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We think that all those things in terms of the forward-looking component are also going to be weighing on inflation expectations and that, as businesses and households in the economy see all of those factors and see headline inflation numbers coming down, inflation expectations themselves will be coming down some.

speaker: SICHEL
text: So we do the best we can with a range of models and try to bring the best judgment we can, and this is where we land.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it is very difficult

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The thing that we are having the greatest difficulty with is trying to think about the evolution of inflation expectations in this current environment, in which monetary policy has the fed funds rate pinned at zero, and that shows through in other places.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In this forecast, we are assuming that, because actual inflation is going to run as low as it is for the reasons that Dan said, there will be some downdrift in inflation expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is implicit in this forecast, maybe on the order of ½ percentage point over the next few years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are uncertain enough about that that we obviously wanted to show some alternative simulations because a reasonable case could be made that, in fact, we are not going to get as much downdrift in inflation expectations as we have implicitly built into this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We showed a simulation with anchored expectations running at about 2 percent, and I could see that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Even though we have already entered a period of extreme weakness, as we showed in the briefing yesterday, the Michigan survey, with 5-to-10-year-ahead inflation expectations, has not really shown any discernible movement yet.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We might have expected that we would already have seen that if the effect was going to be large.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the other hand, just taking a look at historical evidence on sacrifice ratios would suggest a great deal more disinflation than we have built into this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If you just used average sacrifice ratios of 4, you would come up with something similar to what we had in the deflation scenario that we showed.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Though I am skeptical about that particular sort of pure backward-looking model, I do not think you could write off the possibility that, given that we think we are going to be in an extended period of extreme weakness with large output gaps and declining price pressures coming from commodities and oil, you could see a more significant movement in inflation expectations and even lower inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So we are struggling with all of the exact issues that you laid out.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This is our best guess at this point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So just two observations about that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One is that we spent a lot of the past year, as we had the run-up in headline inflation due to oil on the upside, and most of us stressed the importance of anchored expectations and believed that expectations remained fairly well anchored.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Consistent with that ongoing view, my outlook looked more like your “anchored inflation expectations” framework.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess I’d also just comment that a lot of the empirical evidence on, let me call it, the new-Keynesian Phillips curves with output gaps suggests that the sensitivity of inflation to some of those gap measures is certainly not as large as the sacrifice ratio of 4 that you would put in.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think there might be reason to diminish that effect, particularly if you thought, as we have discussed before, that some of these shocks might, in fact, be shocks where you actually have a new, lower equilibrium.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So the gap is maybe not as large as it appears to be.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Just to be clear: In our forecast, we are assuming a much flatter Phillips curve than has been the traditionally estimated one and a higher sacrifice ratio.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My last question is about fiscal stimulus and your estimates there.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is hard not to read the commentary, and there is a huge debate going on about the effects of stimulus.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Look at the empirical evidence, the theoretical evidence—the empirical work by Blanchard, and Valerie Ramey’s stuff, and you have Christina Romer’s work on the different estimates of multipliers and all that sort of stuff.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the discussion, you highlighted two pieces in particular: The first was the consumer tax cut and the debates about whether or not that is going to be saved or spent, and the second one, which I thought was somewhat more interesting, was that you thought that the business tax cuts would not have much effect.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess I had two questions about that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One, my reading of the empirical evidence is that those business tax cuts often do have some very short run stimulative effects, but the empirical evidence also says that large spending increases oftentimes have a negative effect on business investment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is where the substitution comes from.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I just would like a little insight in terms of the model or the assessment of the pieces of this stimulus and how it plays into what you’re assuming about some of those multipliers and so forth.

speaker: SICHEL
text: To pick up on the business side of that first—we looked at the experience from the 2002–04 business tax cuts, and our best reading of that was that we just did not see much effect.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In terms of the empirical work that we did, we just don’t think that there is a big kick there, perhaps particularly in a period when many businesses are in tough times and taking losses.

speaker: SICHEL
text: It just may not be enough or the right kind of thing to get them to start investing.

speaker: SICHEL
text: So our reading of the evidence is that on the business side there just will not be much.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If that is true, it would suggest that the other relevant piece of evidence for this is that, if large increases in expenditures as opposed to tax cuts act as a negative on business investment, as some of the empirical evidence suggests, your forecast for business investment may be worse than what you have in your model—or not?

speaker: SICHEL
text: I guess that channel would come through a user-cost effect on large expenditures and so on pushing up interest rates and generating crowding-out through that sort of a channel.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We do have a modest increase in Treasury rates in this forecast for a variety of reasons, but we also have quite a dramatic decrease in, say, Baa bond rates and those spreads coming in during this period, when we think, as the macro risk diminishes, we are going to see some declines in credit spreads.

speaker: SICHEL
text: I think that decline in credit spreads going forward is likely to more than offset whatever forces there might be from the kind of expenditure-based crowding- out.

speaker: SICHEL
text: On the household side, we are looking at the proposed tax cuts as being permanent.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We are treating them as permanent tax cuts, so we are treating those the way that we would typically treat a change in income in the usual model.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We have a marginal propensity to consume of about 0.7.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We have some lags by which about 60 percent of the spending that is going to happen happens in the first year and about 85 percent by the end of the second year, and we are doing a pretty standard sort of analysis there with the types of numbers that we are getting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, the key is that you were treating them as permanent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That answers the question there.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We are interpreting this proposal as a down payment on a permanent change.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other questions for the staff?

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am comparing exhibit 3 with exhibit 6 here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In exhibit 3 you have the middle panel on the right, “Overvaluation of Single-Family Homes,” and in exhibit 6, the middle right panel, you have “Prices of Commercial Properties.” On exhibit 3, I guess this is a judgment call: a reduction in home values of about 25 percent—am I reading this right?—from where they are now.

speaker: DYNAN
text: You have to remember that rents are also rising in this calculation.

speaker: DYNAN
text: But just in terms of the price component, we have seen a decline of about 15 percent so far, and we are going to see another 15 percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Another 15 percent on homes.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I have done pictures like this, too, because I think it shows that the bubble part is out, and whatever else is remaining is overreaction, which is what you are saying.

speaker: DYNAN
text: That is consistent with our view, yes.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But on commercial properties and then in exhibit 6, you have maybe a different story, a more moderated downturn there, if I am reading this right.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is there a reason that we should think commercial properties are not as susceptible to the overcorrection as housing is?

speaker: DYNAN
text: We do not have a model—or we have not really found a robust model— for overvaluation of commercial property, so it has been more difficult to analyze formally.

speaker: DYNAN
text: But more generally, the reason we think that there will be such a large overcorrection on the residential side is that, with our forecast for the huge numbers of foreclosures, we think we are going to see a lot of supply dumped on the market and that it will perhaps lead sellers to aggressively cut prices.

speaker: DYNAN
text: So far that has not happened in the commercial area, although we certainly think it is a risk.

speaker: DYNAN
text: We agree with President Yellen’s view that, depending on what happens in the CMBS market, it could be something that would happen.

speaker: DYNAN
text: But your reading is correct—we are not foreseeing a massive overcorrection on the commercial side at this point.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I guess I will interpret that as there might be some downside risk in this area.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the assessment of fiscal policy, what is the effect of the deficit program on longer-term Treasury rates?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That is a hard question to answer with any precision, but here goes.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have implicit in this forecast a rise in the ratio of federal debt to GDP of about 15 percentage points over the next two or three years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: You may recall that there was a whole cottage industry several years ago trying to estimate the effects on long-term interest rates of that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One study done by Glenn Hubbard and Eric Engen, one done by Thomas Laubach, and I’m forgetting the third one now, but they all came up with effects.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Some were in the range of 2 to 3 basis points per percentage point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If you used those estimates to get a rough idea of how much you might be holding up Treasury yields from what they otherwise would be, you would get something between ¼ and ½ percentage point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I am not really sure in the current circumstances how relevant some of that empirical evidence is, in that we don’t think we are going to be in a situation where there will, as Dan noted, be very much crowding-out because the output gap is so large over this period.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It is not quite as though the federal government is going to be competing with the private sector for the resources.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There are going to be a lot of slack resources available, in our estimate of the output gap.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is that a global output gap or just the United States?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I am not sure whether I would venture a guess as high as the upper end of that range, but clearly we are starting to hear some stories about Treasury yields being affected by anticipation of a very significant rise in debt here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I just have one more thing.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It is exhibit 9, which is “An Unconventional Policy.” We have two graphs at the top, on the unemployment rate and core PCE prices.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I guess I would interpret these to say that, if you were serious about putting confidence bounds around these estimates, you probably could not tell these apart statistically.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Do you think that is a fair assessment, or are they more tightly estimated than that?

speaker: SICHEL
text: If you look at the picture in Part 1 of the Greenbook, we have some confidence bands based on Greenbook errors.

speaker: SICHEL
text: If you compare the large-scale asset purchases line in that picture with the baseline, the large-scale asset purchases line is near the edge of the 70 percent confidence interval.

speaker: SICHEL
text: It is important to acknowledge that there is a tremendous amount of uncertainty, particularly in thinking about these types of programs and the effect of these types of programs.

speaker: SICHEL
text: If you think about all the steps as you go through the exercise of trying to gauge what the effect of these programs is and you go through all the steps of the purchase of securities—what is the effect on interest rates in the market where the securities are purchased; what is the spillover to other markets; and then in this environment, what are the implications for economic outcomes?—there are many places to be very uncertain.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So there is a lot of additional uncertainty that may not be properly captured in those confidence bounds?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is that what you are saying?

speaker: SICHEL
text: Well, the confidence bounds are based on a draw of errors over the past 20-plus years.

speaker: SICHEL
text: That may not correctly capture the environment that we are in now.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think we can safely say that the confidence intervals are wide here, I think wider than we show in those estimates, probably wider than you can get on a legal size piece of paper.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We start out with our normal simulations that have all of the uncertainty about the shocks to the economy and even about the structure of the model of the economy.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: These simulations have the tremendous added uncertainty of what these purchase programs will actually do to private interest rates, and as the note that was circulated to the Committee indicated, there is just a lot of uncertainty about how any particular program would affect mortgage rates, Treasury rates, the Baa rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are doing our best here.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In some sense, this was a response to a question that you posed last time: What would it take to fill the gap between the unconstrained and the baseline forecasts?

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But I think it is extremely uncertain.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We didn’t get lines that went like this or where it would have a huge effect but it would be very bad for other elements of the economy or something like that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We did not really get that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We got things that are close to baseline.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are doing Bayesian decision analysis and not classical hypothesis testing here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is a very different proposition.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I decided to withdraw my question.

speaker: STERN
text: I want to get back to commercial real estate for a second.

speaker: STERN
text: As I recall, we had a very significant correction in commercial real estate in the late ’80s, early ’90s.

speaker: STERN
text: I wonder if you have looked at what you are anticipating for the next couple of years relative to that experience and whether it was similar, more severe, less severe, or whatever.

speaker: DYNAN
text: Actually, at this point, the rise in delinquency rates is—

speaker: STERN
text: You are going to get some help from Steve.

speaker: OLINER
text: I am just going to add a few words.

speaker: OLINER
text: I think we are expecting problems in that sector that will not be as severe as the downturn in the late ’80s and the early ’90s in large part because we did not have the massive amount of overbuilding in this cycle that we had then.

speaker: OLINER
text: It is true that we have had a tremendous drop in demand for space, but we are coming into this cycle in a much better supply position.

speaker: STERN
text: The second question: Did you calculate an implicit fiscal multiplier for the next couple of years?

speaker: STERN
text: If so, what is it?

speaker: SICHEL
text: Those numbers are hard to interpret, but we did a calculation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I tried to get an answer on that, and they would not give it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Maybe they will answer it for you.

speaker: SICHEL
text: In the sorts of calculations we talked about of figuring out what the impulse is, we have a multiplier of about 1.3.

speaker: SICHEL
text: If you compare that with others, though, it is very important to be careful because those multiplier calculations include all sorts of different things.

speaker: SICHEL
text: What are you assuming is endogenous or exogenous?

speaker: SICHEL
text: What other things move, and when you do that calculation, what of those things that move are you including or not including?

speaker: SICHEL
text: So we think that is very much in the range of the numbers that other analysts looking at this type of program are using.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We do not think we are doing anything particularly different there.

speaker: SICHEL
text: You might see a number that looks different, but if you dig under the surface and you do an apples-to-apples comparison, I think we are very much in the range of what others are doing there.

speaker: FISHER
text: Real quick, a domestic question and an international question.

speaker: FISHER
text: The domestic question, which is just a data question: What do we expect the Treasury issuance to be in fiscal year 2009?

speaker: FISHER
text: The numbers I have seen go up to $2½ trillion.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We are projecting a deficit for fiscal 2009 of about $1.8 trillion.

speaker: FISHER
text: But my question is new issuance.

speaker: SICHEL
text: I do not have those numbers.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have an answer to that question, but I do not have it right in front of me.

speaker: FISHER
text: Could you get it to me sometime?

speaker: FISHER
text: On the international side—maybe this is a question for Nathan—I am curious.

speaker: FISHER
text: As I understand it, the Exchequer has given the Bank of England permission to purchase outright high-quality corporate bonds.

speaker: FISHER
text: I presume that they have had the same kind of discussion that we have had about moral hazard, how far they want to go, which securities they wish to purchase, and so on.

speaker: FISHER
text: I was thinking about that looking at this table in exhibit 11 and the United Kingdom’s predicament, but do you know who has some insight into that decision and how perverse or how wise it is?

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think it is fair to say that, of the major central banks, the Bank of England has been particularly concerned about the moral hazard sorts of issues and has moved into these kinds of programs with great reluctance.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The major feature that I see of this announcement by the Bank of England is that now they can purchase outright stuff that they were taking only as collateral.

speaker: SHEETS
text: My understanding is that this program is limited to AAA-rated assets, and I don’t see them taking on as a result of this a huge amount, or really any, credit risk under their balance sheet.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So I interpreted this as a relative modest step down the road toward balance sheet expansion.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That’s my reading of it.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We can look at it again more carefully and see if we have different views at that point.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The U.K. program more generally had some really aggressive features that didn’t involve the Bank of England.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For instance, the government is now going to be guaranteeing the asset side of the balance sheet as well as the liabilities side of the balance sheet for institutions and those sorts of things that were part of the announcement.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But I saw the Bank of England step as more incremental, rather than some sort of significant quantum shift in the orientation of their policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m looking at exhibit 9.

speaker: LACKER
text: I note that the program involved half MBS, half Treasury and that mortgage rates fell 125 basis points and Baa rates fell 75.

speaker: LACKER
text: What if it was all Treasury?

speaker: LACKER
text: What would the fall in mortgage rates be, and what would the fall in the Baa rates be?

speaker: LACKER
text: Would the effect on growth be larger or smaller?

speaker: SICHEL
text: I can tell you a little about that.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We did unpack the simulation and think about what if it was just $500 billion in MBS.

speaker: SICHEL
text: What does that look like?

speaker: SICHEL
text: What if it was just $500 billion in Treasuries?

speaker: SICHEL
text: What does that look like?

speaker: SICHEL
text: It is very important to highlight the uncertainties that Dave Stockton just mentioned with these estimates being incredibly uncertain.

speaker: SICHEL
text: We are trying to do something consistent with what was in those zero lower bound notes, but boy, there is a lot of tough stuff going on.

speaker: SICHEL
text: So when we do that and we think about a $500 billion Treasury package, we would see Treasuries coming down about 50 basis points and Baa yields and mortgage rates coming down about 30 basis points.

speaker: SICHEL
text: The assumption there is that you get a hit on Treasuries and then a somewhat smaller spillover into other markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: Did you say 30 for both mortgage rates and Baa?

speaker: SICHEL
text: Yes, and there is no great science here.

speaker: SICHEL
text: It is looking at correlations of rates and how these rates have moved historically and so on.

speaker: SICHEL
text: If you look just at MBS, you find that you would get a bigger effect on mortgage rates, maybe something on the order of 90 basis points on mortgage rates, 50 on Baa, and maybe 30 on Treasuries.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Then when we take all of that and we run it through FRB/US and think about $500 billion of this and $500 billion of that, what are the output effects?

speaker: SICHEL
text: In FRB/US, the output effects are pretty similar for those two programs.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Now, there are many channels through which these programs would affect the economy that are not captured in FRB/US.

speaker: SICHEL
text: One could make very plausible arguments for why, in fact, those two effects might not be the same, so let me just leave it there.

speaker: LACKER
text: When you say “same,” you mean at the aggregate level.

speaker: SICHEL
text: At the aggregate level, right.

speaker: LACKER
text: Presumably the fraction that is houses is different.

speaker: SICHEL
text: But if you look at what the change is in the unemployment rate relative to the baseline, it is about the same.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Right, the composition is different.

speaker: LACKER
text: So this implies that, if you did $1 trillion in Treasuries, the Baa rate would be lower.

speaker: SICHEL
text: What is the comparison that you are doing?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: He is multiplying by two.

speaker: SICHEL
text: Yes, and then comparing it is lower than what?

speaker: LACKER
text: I guess I am confused.

speaker: LACKER
text: I see—the Treasuries have a smaller overall multiplier.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it would be just 30.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it would just be 60 on that and 60 on the—

speaker: SICHEL
text: These numbers are very rough.

speaker: SICHEL
text: I feel like I am being tortured, giving these out here.

speaker: LACKER
text: In exhibit 6, the projections, bottom panel, longer-run inflation forecast, the dotted line is our October projections, and the solid lines are our January projections.

speaker: LACKER
text: If our intent was to find an inflation number that we all report that had some stability from forecast to forecast, we seem to have failed.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, it could be that the Committee’s views have changed in the last several months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You mean, for example, where you want to anchor long­ term inflation expectations?

speaker: LACKER
text: So one interpretation is that the implicit longer-run inflation objective of the Committee has changed over this quarter.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: And one plausible reason for that is that the Committee is now experiencing the actuality of a very large negative demand shock and maybe it now believes that it needs a larger inflation buffer than it previously thought would be best.

speaker: LACKER
text: But this exact variability is what led us to be unhappy with the third year of the forecast mechanism for revealing an implicit inflation target.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It could go the other way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You could say that the trouble with the fixed target is that it doesn’t allow for knowledge to accumulate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I mean, there really has been another deflation scare, and it may affect our views.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, we’ll discuss this more.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think I saw Governor Duke try to intervene during the conversation about the responses to the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey, which was something I was discussing with Governor Kohn a minute ago.

speaker: LACKER
text: You know, when I think about what people say about credit constraints, the idea of a consumer with given characteristics—FICO score, income, and everything—with GDP growth of plus 3 versus GDP growth of minus 5, the identical consumer is going to be riskier in the second situation.

speaker: LACKER
text: If a bank is not willing to lend in the second situation and is willing to lend in the first situation, I assert that they would say they are tightening their standards.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would also assert that it does not seem like a credit-channel, credit-constraint type of thing, as you might otherwise think.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It would be interesting to compare the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey over different cycles, for example.

speaker: LACKER
text: Right, it would, but I was going to ask Governor Duke because she is probably actually—

speaker: DUKE
text: I will speak for myself.

speaker: DUKE
text: When bankers talk about credit terms, that is typically going to be something like the credit score, the debt-to-income ratio, or some metric of underwriting with the most obvious example being GMAC’s announcement right after becoming a bank holding company that they were going to reduce their minimum credit score from somewhere in the low 700s to somewhere in the mid-600s, which would obviously mean that they would approve a larger number of applications.

speaker: DUKE
text: Sometimes a change in terms is done to reduce the number of accounts or the volume; sometimes it’s done to increase the quality.

speaker: DUKE
text: A couple of things are going on.

speaker: DUKE
text: Right now you have the same consumers’ credit metrics deteriorating very rapidly.

speaker: DUKE
text: So even if you did not change the metrics you were using, you would still approve a much smaller proportion of the applications.

speaker: DUKE
text: So that is going on.

speaker: DUKE
text: The other thing I will be interested to see the next time we do this survey is that the banks are feeling a tremendous amount of political pressure on their lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: I am not sure that they want to report that they have tightened their terms for consumer lending or even particularly that they are going to change those terms.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I think we might see some pretty drastic reports of at least not tightening terms on consumer lending in the next survey.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Seeing no other questions, why don’t we adjourn for today, and we will begin tomorrow the first thing—9:00 a.m.—with the go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a reception across the way and dinner.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the announcement of the extension of our various programs, we have had additional communication with the European Central Bank, and they are well disposed toward extending the swap arrangement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it turns out that they need a few more days to get formal approval from the Governing Council.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Their proposal is that we announce next Tuesday morning so that they can get the approval on Monday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have had some discussions about communication strategy, and the view appears to be that putting all of our programs in one announcement is probably the best way to go because otherwise you create questions about why this and not that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So although it puts some pressure on our confidentiality and all the other things, I think the plan—and I would be happy to take comments or advice—would be to hold off until next Tuesday morning to announce both the swap extensions and the credit programs that we voted on yesterday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser, we did inquire about the AMLF and had some discussions—talked with President Rosengren and his staff.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The view is that there are some complications and difficulties with ending it in a peremptory way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will continue to discuss that, but we think for the moment we should not cancel it immediately.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Rosengren, would you like to comment on that?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As I said yesterday, I talked to the money market funds.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: They do think that the backup facility, while they hope they don’t have to use it, has been serving a different purpose from some of the other facilities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There is some concern that, if we were to announce the closure, we would get inundated with asset-backed commercial paper right before we closed down the facility.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: And the money market funds would have to do other things to try to remain more liquid, so we might create issues that we are not trying to create at this time.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I would be in favor of extending it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With the understanding that we will continue to look at all these programs and review them and that we always have the option to restructure and rationalize what we do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any thoughts or comments on the communication issue?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, it is time for the economic go-round, and we will start with President Lockhart.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In Atlanta, we just completed a full cycle of our Branch board meetings and the Atlanta board discussions, as well as quite a number of pre-FOMC calls.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: No surprise, sentiment about the economy continues to worsen as more parties are feeling the effect of the downturn.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Fallout from financial market stress and the contracting economy continues to spread and is affecting sectors previously thought to be insulated—for example, hospitals and universities.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Consumer retrenchment has significantly affected restaurants, the travel industry, and a wide variety of personal services.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The anecdotes I am hearing on consumer behavior are quite colorful.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Describing the popular culture, one director said, “It is cool not to spend.” A director who is a chief financial officer of a large national home-improvement retailer described the recent shifts in consumer purchases within their stores in the direction of paint (if I am out of work, I might as well paint those walls), snow blowers (no longer willing to pay for service in the snow belt), and zero-radius lawnmowers (not to mow one’s lawn but to hire oneself out to mow others’ lawns).

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Anecdotal feedback also supports the Greenbook view that house prices continue to feel downward pressure.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In some parts of the Sixth District—for example, South Florida and metro Atlanta—I am advised that prices may yet decline another 10 to 20 percent over the year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There is widespread frustration over the inability to make longer-term plans in such a highly uncertain environment.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This seems the case across the spectrum of economic actors, including banks, large and smaller businesses, and households.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Investment decisions are being indefinitely postponed.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We are hearing from business and consumer borrowers that they can’t get loans or that lending terms for new or existing loans have tightened to an extent that they perceive as unreasonable.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Bankers are telling me that there is little loan demand from qualified borrowers.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Our S&R examiners noted a migration to asset-collateralized secured loan structures for previously unsecured cash flow-based C&I loans.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Prompted by the question that we sent out in advance, much of the discussion at our recent board meeting centered on Fed communication strategy and execution.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Atlanta directors were uniform in their call for intensified and simplified communication aimed at the general public to treat confusion, anxiety, and a deficit of confidence.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Saying much the same thing, financial market contacts emphasized the heightened importance at this time of a clear and credible framework and plan for improving financial conditions and the avoidance of the appearance of one-off emergency policies.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: This theme reflects a context of deep concerns about the financial sector in general and some very large institutions in particular.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Turning to the national economy and my forecast, the broad strokes of my forecast haven’t changed materially since October.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Then I was, on balance, rather pessimistic, and I remain skeptical of a more V-shaped recovery developing in the second half of 2009 and 2010, as projected in the Greenbook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Now, I acknowledge that the Greenbook narrative used the words “gradually strengthening,” but it did depict 2 percent growth in the second half and 2½ percent next year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In contrast, I continue to anticipate a flatter, more protracted, L-shaped recovery moving through 2011.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is my sense that the rebuilding—or “rearchitecting,” to use Governor Warsh’s term—of the financial system and the rebuilding of business and household balance sheets will take a long time, restraining growth in the process.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Similar to the “more financial stress” alternative scenario, I think the dysfunction in the ordinary channels of credit intermediation is likely to linger; and as in the “more cautious spending” alternative, I think rates of business and household saving could rise significantly and remain elevated after the recovery takes hold.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One Wall Street firm calls this their “frugal future hypothesis.” One of my financial contacts argued that the context of any recovery would be one of working through structural issues that are deep and wide.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The referenced structural issues include the balance of saving versus consumption, with the obvious implication for consumer demand.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The potential for a longer period of more-intractable disinflation could obviously complicate progress toward recovery, and this possibility weighs heavily on my assessment of the risks we face.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Also, I find it hard to think of an “appropriate” policy that anticipates core PCE inflation remaining under 1 percent through 2013, as in the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Again, of course, the Greenbook forecast is not conditioned on appropriate policy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I have, therefore, conditioned my assumption about the path of policy on adequately addressing the risk of further unwelcome disinflation that threatens deflation.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My longer-run outlook, assuming no further adverse shocks, has inflation returning to a 2 percent trend, and my growth projection converging to a 2½ percent potential.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Let me add that I support the subcommittee’s proposal on the long­ term forecast.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, since the last FOMC meeting, our District’s economy has continued to weaken, and this weakness is widespread and is taking on more of the complexion of the national economy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Led by a sharp decline in manufacturing and slower export growth, year-over-year private employment growth slipped into negative territory in November for the first time in our region since ’04.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Consumer spending weakened in December despite heavy discounting, and residential real estate activity remains quite depressed.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Conditions in commercial real estate have deteriorated markedly, and financing in this sector has become extremely difficult.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I might add a footnote here: In discussions of this with some of the folks involved in commercial real estate, they are concerned about a couple of years from now because in 2002, 2003, and 2004 there were a lot of commercial real estate projects put into play at very low cap rates and very good interest rates, with a 10-year balloon.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So those are all turning now with obviously less value because they are assuming that the cap rates will be higher.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They are also assuming that the buildings will not be as new, and therefore the values will be under pressure.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So they feel that the problems in commercial real estate are only beginning.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Those parts of the District that depend on energy and agriculture continue to be somewhat better, but these areas are expected to show—and are, in fact, showing—declines, and we expect pretty sharp declines in ’09 due to the falloff in commodity prices.

speaker: HOENIG
text: District businesses are moving rapidly to address the sharp slowdown.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Many have instituted hiring and wage freezes, and layoffs have risen considerably.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Many businesses have significantly curtailed current production and future capital spending plans.

speaker: HOENIG
text: For example, our energy industry contacts expect a 30 to 50 percent reduction in drilling activity and a 35 to 60 percent reduction in capital expenditures in ’09.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The fiscal situation for states and local governments has also deteriorated very rapidly.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Most District states are now looking at significant budget shortfalls over the next two years.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Most states plan to address these deficits through spending reductions rather than tax increases.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The situation for local governments is somewhat mixed, depending on whether they rely on property taxes or on sales taxes for the revenue base.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Many states and localities are looking for assistance from the federal stimulus package to avoid more draconian cutbacks in spending.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Banking conditions are deteriorating within the region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Nonperforming loans are increasing, and losses are mounting as well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Turning to the national economy, recent economic data have been worse than expected, leading me, like others, to revise down the forecast for growth this year.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I now think we could see negative growth into the third quarter before the economy picks up as the fiscal stimulus begins to take hold later.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In the near term, I see considerable downside risk to growth due to the pervasive weakness in the U.S. and foreign economies and the substantial financial headwinds that remain in place.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Indeed, I fully expect banking conditions to deteriorate further, even as financial markets begin to stabilize.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I am especially concerned that commercial real estate, as I mentioned earlier, could be the next shoe to drop, with broad implications for banks and insurance companies across the country.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Consequently, the strength and the timing of the recovery appear, obviously, very uncertain at this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In terms of inflation, the significant decline in energy and commodity prices, along with a weaker economy, has obviously put considerable downward pressure on overall and core inflation, as a cyclical effect of this recession.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think it would not necessarily be timely to start projecting deflationary pressures, and although I get more questions about that, at this point I don’t consider that the highest risk we have.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Like everybody’s District, our District has slowed and continues to look very weak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The business outlook survey actually rose a little last month, but it is still measured deeply in recessionary territory.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our banks continue to lend—to households, in particular.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They have cut back on commercial lending, and credit quality continues to deteriorate across all loan categories in the District.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Housing sales are down, but prices have not fallen to the degree that they have in some parts of the country, probably on average—the declines have been more modest.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And the housing problems are not quite as bad as in some parts of the nation, but everything has deteriorated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So, basically, in the Third District, the current economy and its outlook look largely like those of the nation as a whole, and all indications are that this recession will certainly be one of the worst in the postwar period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There are lots of reasons for doom and gloom.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As we have just heard, there are lots of reasons that we think that this recession and this weakness will continue, perhaps for some time to come.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But somebody has to take a somewhat more optimistic view—just to make the distribution complete, if for no other reason, right?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think there are common elements to many business cycles.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also find that one thing people have focused on a lot regarding the press and other things is that business sentiment, consumer confidence, and how people feel about the future appear to be very sensitive in this particular phase of the cycle.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Those things are pretty gloomy right now, but I would suggest that many economic cycles do have some commonalities, and one of those commonalities that often appear—not every time, but often—is that sentiment can turn around very quickly and it can change for reasons that sometimes we don’t understand or can’t easily predict.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is also true that financial markets can move very quickly in various directions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have seen them move very quickly to the bad.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Once markets begin to heal, they could move very quickly in the other direction.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So for the sake of optimism, I think there is still a possibility that at some point—maybe not in the first half of this year and maybe not even in the second, but there is still the hope—things could turn fairly quickly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am not basing a lot on that, but I do feel somewhat more optimistic than a lot of people—including my staff, by the way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They forced me to say that they take no responsibility for this, [laughter] and so I am letting them completely off the hook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do anticipate the growth path to look somewhat like that in the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I am basically a little more optimistic than they are—a very weak first half, maybe some positive growth in the second half, which may just balance each other out, but that may be an optimistic perspective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I expect the economy to gain some steam in 2010, to about 3 percent, and settle into something closer to a steady state or at least to a long-run trend in 2011.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have less overshooting in my forecast than some of the models do—and I think than the Greenbook—because, as I explained yesterday, I have less of an output gap than they do.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think some of the productivity shock on financial intermediation is showing up in less of a gap, and therefore there is less of a closure and pushback on the other side.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Unemployment rates will clearly rise this year above 8 percent, but I hope that by the end of the year they will begin to stabilize or perhaps come down a bit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On fiscal policy, as I was asking the staff yesterday, I am not very optimistic that the fiscal package will do much for the economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A multiplier of 1.3 is probably pretty optimistic, from my perspective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I haven’t built in much effect from fiscal stimulus.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I hope the fiscal package is constructed to give its best shot at helping, but I am not entirely optimistic about what its shape will actually look like or whether it will actually be very much help.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Obviously, because I am on the more optimistic side, the risks to my forecasts are clearly to the downside.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My inflation forecast is less deflationary than the Greenbook’s baseline, and it is similar, as I said yesterday, to the alternative simulation labeled “anchored inflation expectations.” In that sense, I am relying more on forward-looking expectational models than on distributed lags of past inflation, which heavily affect both the output gap and the forecast of inflation going forward, given the wild swings in relative prices that we have seen.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think more in terms of estimated new-Keynesian Phillips curves, in which the output gaps both are smaller and have less effect on inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Again, those lead me to a little less dire scenario in terms of the deflationary pressure of output gaps going forward.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I put a lot more weight on our credibility for keeping inflation near 2 percent than on the past behavior of prices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There is some risk to this inflation forecast, as I alluded to.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Near term, we will not see much inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am not concerned about that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nor do I think that deflation is going to be very persistent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some of it is already in train because of the way oil prices are behaving.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do think that, in the longer term, there are inflation risks unless we manage our balance sheet appropriately.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am encouraged by our discussion yesterday and some of the language that we talked about in terms of thinking about how we manage that in a careful way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Finally, I would just repeat my request—I think it was at our January meeting on inflation targeting—that it would be useful in our forecast summaries actually to forecast and report out, as we do with other measures, our assumed policy paths that each of us are using for our projections.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the internal summary, you give a verbal description of people saying what their assumed policy path is.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I do think that it would be useful to summarize those in terms of both ranges and central tendencies because, as we move—assuming that we can and do—to a more explicit inflation-targeting regime, that range of central tendencies for the assumed policy paths should be added.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it will both help for transparency reasons and help anchor expectations as to what we are doing, and that would be good.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would encourage us to continue to pursue that effort, and, of course, I am in favor of the longer-term projections.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We are in the midst of a very deep and protracted downturn, and I have to squint really hard to see any light at the end of the tunnel.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is a sad commentary that the one glimmer of light during this intermeeting period has been that economic developments have been roughly in line with our expectations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In other words, we were braced for the bad news we received.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For example, we had expected a dreadful holiday retail season, and that is precisely what we got.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One of my directors, the head of a national department store chain, reported that his company posted its worst season since it was founded in 1901.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We had anticipated severe hemorrhaging in jobs and a sizable jump in the unemployment rate, and that, too, is what we got.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Many of my business contacts are reporting layoffs and wage freezes.

speaker: YELLEN
