text: One unpleasant surprise among the economic data was last week’s 15 percent drop in housing starts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The residential housing sector has now shrunk so much that the only real assurance that it will ever stabilize seems to be the fact that construction spending cannot go negative.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This is just about the only zero lower bound that is working on our side.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Turning to financial markets, it is comforting that lending terms eased in a few markets, notably money and mortgage markets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But equity markets continue to sink, and credit spreads remain breathtakingly large.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Another of my directors, the chairman of a large, well-known apparel company, reported that his company, which is rated BB, looked hard for additional financing and the best they could come up with was a loan rate of 18 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have also heard many reports concerning the tightening of trade credit.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, a particularly severe shortage of credit to finance international trade flows may conceivably help explain why both exports and imports are shrinking by abnormally large amounts relative to the decline in GDP.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Looking ahead, I expect that, as in the Greenbook, high borrowing costs and the continuing credit crunch will help prolong the recession for at least a couple more quarters.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Accordingly, I project that real GDP will decline ½ percent this year, and the unemployment rate will rise to 8½ percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, I am hopeful that a large and timely fiscal stimulus will help kick-start a recovery by the end of the year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In particular, based partly on our situation in California, I think the Greenbook’s assessment of the impetus provided by the proposed federal fiscal stimulus directed toward state and local governments is on the pessimistic side.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The Greenbook assumes that such spending will roll out slowly over the next several years, providing little near-term stimulus.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, my contacts told me that in California a lack of funds has already halted construction on a number of public infrastructure projects, and these projects could be quickly restarted if federal funds help the state close its huge budget gap.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Outside California, the data suggest that most of the country is facing near-term cuts in state spending in areas ranging from education to construction, and it appears that the fiscal stimulus will allocate money largely to those states that could most use it to avoid immediate spending cuts and finance shovel-ready infrastructure projects.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Still, even with a large fiscal stimulus, it will take many years before the economy returns to potential and economic slack is eliminated.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Unfortunately, over the intermeeting period, I have become much more pessimistic about the downside risk to my modal growth forecast owing to the rapidly deteriorating condition of the banking system.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For much of the past year, it was the financial sector that was constricting the real economy, but now the slowing economy is returning the favor.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The sharp decline in equity prices and increases in CDS spreads for bank holding companies since our last meeting presumably reflect the market’s concern about the likely magnitude of losses that will hit the banking sector.

speaker: YELLEN
text: These losses now reflect a broad-based deterioration in performance across the whole spectrum of consumer and corporate lending.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I mentioned yesterday, I share President Hoenig’s concern about commercial real estate over the next few years.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I fear a cycle in which rising vacancies and falling valuations make it impossible for owners to refinance loans that will be coming due, leading to forced selling and intensifying downward price pressures.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Such a development may undermine the soundness of many regional and community banks, whose exposures to this asset class are substantial.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Let me conclude with some discussion of the outlook for inflation, for which there are also sizable risks.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I expect core PCE price inflation to come in at about 1 percent this year and then edge down a bit more in 2010 and 2011.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the sizable downside risks to the forecast for economic growth, the risks to inflation also appear tilted to the downside.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As in several of the Greenbook alternative scenarios, it is not hard to imagine a situation with excessive declines in inflation and a long-lasting deflationary trap, much like Japan’s experience and perhaps even complete with zombie banks.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, I am reminded that the last time we were concerned about the possibility of deflation in 2003 we were head-faked.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The deceleration in prices during that period was not sustained, and it was actually concentrated in a few categories of goods, particularly used cars with very flexible prices and owners’ equivalent rent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My staff has taken a first look at the current episode in order to see how widespread deflationary pressures are across various categories of goods and services.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the available data, they find in this preliminary look that the recent deflationary pressures are more prevalent now than during the 2003 deflationary scare.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Just as in 2003, some recent price declines are in categories of goods with highly flexible prices, like used cars and apparel, where price cuts could reflect a temporary response by retailers to sell off excess inventory.

speaker: YELLEN
text: However, disinflationary pressures are somewhat more prevalent now than in 2003 in categories of goods and services characterized by sticky prices.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We will be analyzing these data in greater depth going forward and monitoring them, but we think they raise the risk that we could see a prolonged period in which inflation falls well below the level consistent with our dual goals of price stability and maximum sustainable employment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That leads me, especially now, to favor going ahead with the publication of our longer-term projections, especially given that inflation over the next three years, our standard horizon, looks as though it is unlikely to converge to the levels that we think most desirable in the longer term.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it makes going ahead with the extended forecast particularly appropriate now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The Eighth District economy is clearly in recession.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There has been recent significant deterioration in labor markets.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The only comment I would have on that is that the pace of decline may be somewhat less rapid than in the nation as a whole.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Other parts of the country appear to be deteriorating faster, but certainly the Eighth District is not immune, and anecdotal information from many, many sources suggests that credit market frictions continue to be a substantial drag on economic activity.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In the national outlook, of course, we are in the midst of probably the worst of a sharp and significant downturn.

speaker: BULLARD
text: For the shorter term, like 2009, I think the Greenbook assessment seems plausible.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Longer term, I don’t think that the Greenbook assessment is plausible.

speaker: BULLARD
text: According to the Greenbook baseline, the federal funds rate remains at zero into 2013, even though, according to the table in Part 1, page 19, real GDP at that point will have grown at rates of 2.6 percent, 4.9 percent, and 5.3 percent for the previous three years, and we would still be sitting at zero according to the forecast.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Unemployment would have dropped 300 basis points, and we still would not have moved.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That doesn’t seem very plausible to me as a longer-term forecast.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Core PCE inflation remains below 1 percent according to the baseline forecast.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So this strikes me as a little implausible, and I think it might color our thinking from a strategic perspective.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It strikes me as implausible, especially if we pursue some reasonably aggressive quantitative policies.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Then I would expect that that forecast would not materialize.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So one reading of the baseline forecast would be that, under current planning, the FOMC is not going to be aggressive enough to keep inflation at target over a reasonable time frame, like five years.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is one way to look at it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: To do that, you would have to be more aggressive with the quantitative policies.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am going to have more to say about that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Like President Yellen, I am concerned, as some of you know, about a deflationary trap, and I just want to stress here for a few minutes the global aspect of this.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We are not going to get any good news globally over the next six to nine months on the economy, anywhere.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A baseline assessment would be that this will force the Bank of England, the ECB, and the Bank of Canada to zero nominal interest rates.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They are saying maybe not, but I think that they will all be forced to zero.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Of course, the Bank of Japan is at 10 basis points right now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So you will have the G-7 economies all at zero.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is a lot of time to be getting bad news on the economy worldwide.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is why I am very concerned about deflationary expectations possibly taking hold, and I would regard expectations as being the main determinant of actual inflation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If that is what transpires, we will face many years in this deflationary trap outcome, and that will be a global outcome.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am very concerned about that, and so I say the key near- term goal is just to avoid that outcome.

speaker: BULLARD
text: How can we do that?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Well, much of the analysis that we have remains in terms of the federal funds rate, and much of our own thinking around the table remains in terms of the federal funds rate as defining what monetary policy is.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If we are not planning to move off zero for five years, I think that we have to change our thinking and we need even greater focus on quantitative measures in future analysis.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Like it or not, we need to see our policy more in quantitative terms so that we can assess possible paths and what is going to be effective.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am afraid that is going to mean talking more about the monetary base, monetary aggregates, reserves, and the balance sheet.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The key thing is how much balance sheet expansion we can accomplish before we run into inflation troubles.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There has to be some kind of answer to this.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is it $1 trillion—in which case we are already over and are in inflation danger?

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t know where that is right now, and I think we need some kind of quantitative assessment of that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We did get some of that in a simulation from the staff—a $1 trillion outright purchase of Treasuries and MBS, with minor effects on inflation according to the baseline model.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That would suggest that we have a lot of room to maneuver.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am sure that we could have a long debate about how accurate that is and everything, but that would suggest that we have a lot of room to maneuver, and we could be much more aggressive if we want to avoid this deflationary outcome, which is the real danger over the next twelve months.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I see that as the key to our policy choices.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Again, if it is not inflationary, then we can do a lot more.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If it is inflationary—if it is going to translate into inflation—then we have to be very careful about it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But we need to get better metrics of where we are on that, and right now it just seems wide open.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am going to close with the mystery of the round numbers.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Proposed expansions of programs seem to come in suspiciously round numbers.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Some of them are like $500 billion; another number is $250 billion.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Contrast this with the accuracy of the federal funds rate, where we will talk about small increments and out many years into the future.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This just shows how much we are used to thinking in terms of the fed funds rate, and we are used to doing the analysis in terms of the fed funds rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We have lots of mechanisms in place.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We have a lot of inexperience when we are thinking on the quantitative side, so we are very rough in our characterization.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is perfectly understandable, but we need to move more and quickly in that direction.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It seems to me that we would like to think maybe in increments of $25 billion or maybe a little larger increment than that and then have some kind of quantitative assessment about why the numbers are what they are and what we think that they will do.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That will inform our choices going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: When we have done quantitative policy in the past, it has often been in terms of growth rates.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You would think in terms of money, reserves, or whatever you wanted to think about, and you would talk about a certain pace of expansion, maybe moderating later in the future or something like that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That seems like a very logical thing to do in this situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So those are some thoughts on the economy and on policy.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, Mr. Plosser said he would take a more optimistic view to make the distribution complete.

speaker: FISHER
text: I was going to say that I am going to take the opposite tack, but President Yellen pretty much summarized what I was about to say.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do want to comment on my District, and second, I want to talk very briefly about microeconomic behavior based on my discussions with various CEOs around the country—26 this time.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, you have the list of who they are outside my District.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, with regard to our District, like President Hoenig’s, our two Districts, I believe, are the only ones that had positive employment growth last year.

speaker: FISHER
text: In the Eleventh District, we created 192,400 jobs, according to our adjusted data, all in the private sector.

speaker: FISHER
text: That machine has stopped; in fact, we would have a straight line downward if we were to chart it.

speaker: FISHER
text: Manufacturing, chemicals, commercial construction, energy, and transportation services have reported significant drops in demand.

speaker: FISHER
text: Oil and gas prices have fallen, as I think we are all well aware.

speaker: FISHER
text: The rig count has come down accordingly.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just for clarification purposes, the oil and gas industry accounts for 10 percent of our employment; nonetheless, it is a significant factor.

speaker: FISHER
text: Our high-tech industry is under pressure.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think anybody who read the newspaper saw Texas Instruments’ recent numbers.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are reflective of what is going on in that sector.

speaker: FISHER
text: Exports, which are important, have been particularly hit hard by declining growth in external markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are the largest exporting state.

speaker: FISHER
text: Our exports have declined—interestingly, because of the stronger dollar but also because of the weakness overseas that you mentioned, President Bullard.

speaker: FISHER
text: Our largest industry in terms of employment, our medical industry, is suffering in terms of foreigners who come to be repaired in Houston, Dallas, and elsewhere.

speaker: FISHER
text: So our District, like President Hoenig’s District, has now fallen into recession, and we are like everybody else—for the most part (we still are Texans).

speaker: FISHER
text: I will refrain this time around, Mr. Chairman, from referring to Rube Goldberg, Bennie and the Jets, and Elton John.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I do want to recall what I consider to be a prescient insight of James Madison, who said, “The circulation of confidence is better than the circulation of money.” When I speak to CEOs around the country, I would say that confidence is not just waning, it is in a freefall.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is leading me to conclude that, obviously, their behavior is becoming hard-over pro-cyclical, and the consequences are the kind of serious recessionary scenario that President Yellen pointed out and significantly higher deflationary risks.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that negative outlook, particularly the outlook for deflation, is the 800-pound gorilla or, my having just come back from the Galapagos, the 800-pound blue-footed booby in the room.

speaker: FISHER
text: And I don’t think we should be shy to talk about it.

speaker: FISHER
text: Businesses are doing what they should be doing—what you and I would do or what any woman or any man who runs a business would do under the circumstances.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are aggressively cutting head count.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of the CEOs I talked to, who employs one of the largest workforces in the country, said he had three drawers.

speaker: FISHER
text: In the one drawer he plans to cut 17,000 jobs, unannounced as yet; in a drawer to the right of that, a still higher number; and in a drawer to the right of that, a still higher number.

speaker: FISHER
text: I asked about the drawers to the left, and he said, “There are none.” Even businesses that are well run and well capitalized are doing, again, what any businesswoman or businessman would do under the circumstances.

speaker: FISHER
text: If they are in good shape, which are few, they are using this as a chance to cull out the kind of legacy middle management they have been waiting to get rid of for some time.

speaker: FISHER
text: Therefore, the bias is to lower head counts.

speaker: FISHER
text: We saw pretty dramatic numbers announced one day or two days ago, and I think that is intensifying, not lessening.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are implementing pay and merit freezes.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are stretching out their payables.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t know if this is public or not, but GE has gone around to their major suppliers and asked for forbearance on payables—GE, AAA-rated credit, whom we are assisting at this time.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are aggressively pursuing their receivables, particularly the law firms and other service-sector firms.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are running their plant and equipment at the lowest levels in some time.

speaker: FISHER
text: TI is running its factories at 33½ percent of capacity.

speaker: FISHER
text: The Eastman chemical plant in Tennessee is running at the lowest capacity utilization in over 100 years.

speaker: FISHER
text: You see this, again, across the board.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the rails, there are 100,000 cars that are unutilized.

speaker: FISHER
text: And to go back to my favorite metric of the 70-foot-long lumber-carrying cars, there are 285 miles of unutilized cars of that nature across the rail industry.

speaker: FISHER
text: Very critically, they are cutting back dramatically on cap-ex.

speaker: FISHER
text: Not a single CEO I spoke to, from Disney to the large manufacturers, is doing anything but.

speaker: FISHER
text: The least amount of cutback that I heard was 12 percent, and the average, I would say, is up to a third.

speaker: FISHER
text: So, in my view, the Greenbook base case has understated the effect of this dynamic.

speaker: FISHER
text: My outlook is probably the most pessimistic of all of the Banks.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am line number 8, for those of you who are guessing.

speaker: FISHER
text: We all know, by the way, who line number 18 is, because it says, “New York says this; New York says that; New York says this.” Mr. Chairman, basically my conclusion is that the instrument panel we are using—and I say this with enormous respect for the people who do this wonderful work for us—is almost inappropriate to the cockpit of the airplane that we are flying.

speaker: FISHER
text: You mentioned yesterday, Mr. Chairman, that we are dealing with these extraordinary circumstances.

speaker: FISHER
text: I believe that the only way we can proceed is to be as deft as we possibly can be with the kind of programs that we put forward.

speaker: FISHER
text: As concerned as I am about their long-term inflationary consequences, my concern right now is that we are underestimating the potential deflationary consequence to microeconomic behavior and the macroeconomic numbers that President Yellen mentioned.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would like to conclude with just a comment about the TARP.

speaker: FISHER
text: Every banker I speak to who has taken money from the TARP regrets it.

speaker: FISHER
text: They feel that they have been taken, in the words of a borrower of almost $3 billion from the TARP.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are worried about government interference.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is conditioning them to take actions that, again, are pro-cyclical in a perverse way—disincentivizing management and demoralizing the people who work for those firms.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t know what we can do about that, but I am deeply concerned about this drumbeat now of negativism about the TARP and regret for having participated.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I will comment on policy later.

speaker: FISHER
text: I thank you for including my suggestions in the reworded statements that we have, and I look forward to that debate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think greater clarity on the TARP and the bank rescue programs is essential, and it is obviously a very high priority for the Treasury and for the government.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just want to comment that the animal spirit theory of the business cycle seems to be getting some resuscitation here.

speaker: EVANS
text: I will resist the temptation to mark down my forecast right now.

speaker: EVANS
text: Conversations with my business contacts indicate that the economic contraction is proceeding with full force.

speaker: EVANS
text: These discussions were very consistent with the near-term outlook of the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: There were two noteworthy recurrent themes that I would like to elaborate on—the rapid pace of job destruction and the large uncertainties that private-sector decisionmakers face.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to job destruction, consistent with the national data, all CEOs I spoke with indicated that they are in the process of large-scale layoffs and are studying further job cuts.

speaker: EVANS
text: Much as President Fisher referred to with his three drawers, I did not find a left drawer either.

speaker: EVANS
text: The uniformity of these reports is striking.

speaker: EVANS
text: The best economic report I received was from John Deere that agriculture was still holding up well enough that they are going to do okay, they thought.

speaker: EVANS
text: They are cutting only hundreds of jobs.

speaker: EVANS
text: Everybody else is cutting way more.

speaker: EVANS
text: All of my contacts also say that the easy job eliminations have already been made or are in train.

speaker: EVANS
text: Everyone is now contemplating making more-difficult cuts of valuable core staff.

speaker: EVANS
text: These cutbacks, if they go through with them, will adversely influence firms’ ability to respond when we do eventually see the signs of economic recovery.

speaker: EVANS
text: I had a story about how replacement garbage disposals are down 20 percent, which must mean that people are now washing dishes when their disposal breaks down.

speaker: EVANS
text: Anxiety is the second recurrent theme.

speaker: EVANS
text: Uncertainty and risk aversion are inhibiting economic and financial activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: Obviously, much of this reflects the inevitable uncertainty regarding the depth and persistence of the downturn.

speaker: EVANS
text: But as President Lockhart mentioned, I am also hearing from all quarters that businesses cannot understand the rationale used to undertake government policy interventions.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is not just businesses.

speaker: EVANS
text: A political leader in Illinois, the Mayor of Chicago, whom I will quote, tells me that when he runs into homeowners in the city, a number of them have mentioned that they are wondering where their mortgage relief is coming from.

speaker: EVANS
text: They are thinking about not paying their mortgage.

speaker: EVANS
text: Without a clearer understanding of the rules of the game, they will be more cautious and sit on the sidelines, and they are clamoring for greater clarity.

speaker: EVANS
text: When I tried to ask my directors about what they preferred most—we can’t do more with the funds rate—more policy accommodation or more clarity, they clearly chose clarity over policy.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, in spite of what I am going to say, I do support our current programs, but I am reporting on our environment and the challenges that we are facing here.

speaker: EVANS
text: With regard to banks, relatively healthy banks that took TARP money are concerned that they will be subjected to future government restrictions.

speaker: EVANS
text: Again, as President Fisher mentioned, I think there is some regret.

speaker: EVANS
text: Many bankers who could have gotten by without TARP injections took the money because they feared that nonparticipation might be inferred as a signal of weakness.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now they are concerned that the costs could be considerably higher than advertised, in part because of political pressure for lending mandates in an economic environment that makes credit quality challenging.

speaker: EVANS
text: Another uncertainty relates to the configuration of credit policies and potential changes in them.

speaker: EVANS
text: I talked about this just briefly yesterday.

speaker: EVANS
text: In many cases, our lending facilities and government guarantees restore funding sources to some parties but disadvantage others who are outside the safety net protection.

speaker: EVANS
text: For example, I have heard from several durable goods manufacturers who have captive finance companies that provide funding for dealers or customers.

speaker: EVANS
text: Those who owned a bank or had previously utilized commercial paper funding thought that the CPFF and the Treasury guarantees have been helpful.

speaker: EVANS
text: But not everyone is in this position.

speaker: EVANS
text: According to those who were excluded, the separating equilibrium imposes higher costs on them than the previous pooling equilibrium, in which the high costs were shared more by all of them.

speaker: EVANS
text: Similarly, the TALF is expected to be very helpful to some but not others under the current plans.

speaker: EVANS
text: Though our lending programs have been helpful on balance, their differential effects, unfortunately, open us up to political risks.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is difficult to do the cost–benefit calculations at the moment, because the TALF hasn’t gotten under way.

speaker: EVANS
text: Once we see how well that is going, I think we will have a better idea of that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I also hear repeatedly that uncertainty is boosting lending rates and keeping capital sitting idle on the sidelines.

speaker: EVANS
text: Bankers I talked to who have balance sheet capacity are charging higher credit spreads.

speaker: EVANS
text: They all tell me that this change is a return to more normal and prudent consideration of risk and underwriting.

speaker: EVANS
text: So some of that could be what President Yellen’s borrowers are experiencing as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: In fact, in reading through the first report to the Congress of the Financial Stability Oversight Board, I saw many of these arguments mentioned there as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: So everyone is obviously dealing with this issue.

speaker: EVANS
text: A private equity contact mentioned that he raised a fund of $5 billion this summer—I think it was supposed to be higher than that—but has not made a single investment yet.

speaker: EVANS
text: Given the scarcity of capital and the high level of risk, he says expected returns must be much higher than before.

speaker: EVANS
text: This obviously implies that capital injections from these private sources will be very expensive when they are finally deployed.

speaker: EVANS
text: Furthermore, some are concerned that government actions are hard to predict and add to uncertainty.

speaker: EVANS
text: They bring up what happened to WaMu’s debt holders.

speaker: EVANS
text: One of our directors explicitly mentioned Governor Kohn’s testimony about our hopes for private capital injections alongside public injections.

speaker: EVANS
text: I went back, and it is written very well, but no one could envision that happening without greater clarity on the rules guiding those interventions.

speaker: EVANS
text: All of these stories feed into our outlook for the national economy.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our forecast for growth is very similar to the Greenbook’s.

speaker: EVANS
text: Although my gut instinct is now conditioned to reflexively mark down every forecast I see, cool-headed analysis suggests that risks are a bit more two-sided around pessimistic outlooks.

speaker: EVANS
text: One reason is that the risks surrounding our expectations for growth over the next year or two depend a good deal on the effect of the fiscal stimulus.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think in our forecast we have this helping a bit more than most around the table in the second half.

speaker: EVANS
text: Although I favor fiscal stimulus, I do continue to wonder about the effectiveness of such large programs and the ability to efficiently target large sums to the intended projects in a full and timely fashion.

speaker: EVANS
text: Still, I thought we were a bit conservative in estimating their GDP effects, so the risks to growth over the next couple of years have some upside possibilities.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our inflation outlook is a bit more sanguine than the Greenbook’s.

speaker: EVANS
text: We see inflation falling only to about 1¼ percent in 2011.

speaker: EVANS
text: We are on the high side.

speaker: EVANS
text: Of course, resource gaps are expected to be very large and could pull inflation lower than in our forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: But predicting inflation expectations seems harder than usual right now.

speaker: EVANS
text: Indeed, there is a remarkable diversity of views about where inflation is headed.

speaker: EVANS
text: As many of my academic colleagues are quick to point out, the substantial liquidity injections and large government deficits pose an important upside risk to the longer-run inflation outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: Not only have academics brought up the enormous liquidity and unpleasant monetarist arithmetic, but so have some of my directors and other business contacts.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the other hand, if agents’ expectations of inflation focus more heavily on the large resource gaps, we could face significant downside risks as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: So there is a lot to balance out here.

speaker: EVANS
text: President Plosser and President Bullard mentioned this, too.

speaker: EVANS
text: Even Dave Stockton sort of gave us a pass on the fact that we have a lot to chew through here as to what could be a reasonable argument.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is hard to know where expectations balance out, but our base case is that inflation expectations will not decline as much as envisioned in the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t think this really changes the policy implications.

speaker: EVANS
text: We still need the useful monetary policy accommodation that is really called for in this outlook.

speaker: EVANS
text: Finally, I do support the long-term forecasts.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I wish I could report some improvement in the outlook from my contacts, but sentiment in my District has not shifted.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Everyone is anticipating more bad news on the output front, and they are much less confident about when the turnaround is going to occur.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Importantly, this is increasingly translating into reduced investment plans.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My business contacts who were previously uncertain about the outlook but had not yet reduced their planned investments now seem to be joining the tide of other businesses that are scaling back.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Those who had already lowered their investment plans seem to be accelerating their reductions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I focused my conversations with my business contacts on investment decisions because it seems to be a critical factor separating the relatively optimistic private forecasters from the pessimists, and my contacts’ investment plans are keeping me very much in the pessimists’ camp.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I guess I am balancing out this end of the table.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In particular, I have revised down business fixed investment in my forecast.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am now anticipating a steep decline of just over 20 percent in the second quarter, and this is the aspect of my forecast that changed the most during this intermeeting period.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am now expecting to see a reduction in real GDP of 0.8 percent for 2009, the same as the Greenbook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Potential growth in the medium term might be damped by some of these investment reductions, but I have not yet revised down my estimate for potential over the five-to-six-year period, which I put at 2.7 percent.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do see disinflation pressures continuing, and the gap remains elevated in my forecast.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But the pricing reports from my business contacts remain uncertain.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This uncertainty does not surprise me, given that the volatility we have seen in prices has been quite large.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But at this point, some people are just as worried about inflation as they are about deflation, despite the latest headline inflation data.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Obviously, they are looking at some of our longer-term policy decisions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Long-term inflation expectations in the Michigan surveys that we discussed yesterday, though, do not seem to be shifting either up or down yet.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Nevertheless, I do expect weak demand to gradually lower inflation rates to levels that are going to require further monetary policy actions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But with inflation expectations in my projection unchanged, unlike the Greenbook, the decline in core inflation in my projection is less persistent than the Greenbook, and my outlook for core inflation in 2011 rises to 1.4 percent.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In my view, our monetary policy needs to remain accommodative for a time to better insulate us from deflation and zero bound problems.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am one of those participants who did change their perspective on the longer-term PCE inflation objective.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I had been in the 1¾ percent camp for some time, but because of my concern about deflation and zero bound problems, I have raised that longer-term projection to 2 percent for PCE inflation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: It is difficult to feel very confident, as others have said today, about characterizing the balance of risks to the outlook in this extremely abnormal environment.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, I cannot help but think that the risks to both economic growth and inflation are unbalanced to the downside.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Without data revealing some stability, it is hard to argue against more downside risks, as others have commented this morning.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Businesses are far more focused on survival than they are on new opportunities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: On the inflation front, the stability of businesses’ and households’ inflation expectations, as we currently see them, may not remain, and so the downside risk to inflation remains.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Regarding the longer-term projections, they were proposed by the subcommittee to help us with our communication with the public, and I have enthusiastically supported all of the recommendations and the steps in this direction.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also support releasing our long-term projections from this meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: These projections should help the public solidify their expectations for economic performance, especially when our current troubles have abated.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am also encouraged that there is strong agreement among the participants, as Brian reported yesterday, about our expectations for economic performance five to six years out.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I think releasing them will be helpful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Anticipating for a moment the statement in the policy round, there is a proposed sentence that says that the Committee anticipates a gradual recovery later this year with downside risks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am listening to the discussion about near-term pessimism and concern and uncertainty, but then you mentioned your forecast of minus 0.8 percent for 2009, which arithmetically suggests that you do think there will be positive economic growth later in the year, and I think many of the projections that we got were in the same general ballpark.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just want to flag that as an issue for the next round, which is whether we are comfortable talking about positive growth later in the year or whether we think we should just remain agnostic on that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Like the Greenbook, the Boston Fed forecast has the unemployment rate well above the NAIRU and the inflation rate uncomfortably low throughout the forecast period.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Because our view is that inflation is more sensitive to significant excess capacity, our forecast implies an even greater risk of deflation than the Greenbook’s forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Even with the substantial fiscal stimulus and recent monetary policy actions done to date, our outlook implies that it will take more than five years to return to full employment and an inflation rate of 2 percent or more.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Housing continues to be a key component of the problems.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Falling housing prices reduce the wealth of consumers, contribute to problems at financial institutions, and provide little incentive for residential investment to improve and so are a significant contributing factor to our dire outlook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Until housing starts stabilize, I am skeptical that equity prices will show the improvement embedded in the Greenbook forecast.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The rising unemployment rate will be placing further pressure on housing but will also be a contributing factor in weakening commercial real estate, which a number of people around the table have highlighted.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Commercial real estate has held up better in some locations, such as Boston, but even those locations are beginning to soften.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: With little credit available and vacancy rates climbing, my contacts with real estate developers have become increasingly depressing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In Boston, commercial real estate has also been buoyed by building by hospitals, colleges, and universities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, losses experienced in endowments have caused the construction to be halted unless it was fully funded and already started.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Banking continues to be stressed.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Large banks are experiencing large losses in their investment portfolios as highly-rated securities continue to sell at very steep discounts, if they sell at all.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: They are also likely to experience substantial increases in loan-loss reserves, which appear to be lagging the problems.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The economy and financial markets remain susceptible to further bad news emanating from the banks.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Despite monetary and fiscal actions taken or likely to be taken soon, our forecast indicates that, without more-significant actions, unemployment rates will remain too high and inflation will remain too low for an uncomfortably long period of time.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Regarding the long-term projections, I do support publishing those.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would note, as President Pianalto did, that there does seem to be an increase as to where people are targeting inflation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It might be good to update some of the staff work that was done on what the probability of hitting the zero lower bound is and what the probability of deflation is.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It does seem that our targets have been somewhat based on taste rather than focusing on the tails of the distribution.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think we have learned something about the tails of the distribution, and it might lead to a more informed discussion if we discussed in more depth what the probability is now that we have had some recent evidence of those two outcomes.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, I think there is little question that the immediate prospects for the economy are negative.

speaker: STERN
text: It is going to contract in this quarter; certainly my guess is the second quarter and possibly into the third.

speaker: STERN
text: But in response to your question, I do think there will be beginnings of the recovery in the second half of the year, precisely for the reasons spelled out in yesterday’s presentation: the dynamics of the inventory- adjustment process, a gradual further improvement in financial conditions, the ebbing of weakness in housing activity, and the consequences of stimulative policies, both monetary and fiscal.

speaker: STERN
text: So I do think that there is a reasonable probability—I guess this is going to make me the optimist at the table—that something like the Greenbook forecast is going to be realized over that time frame.

speaker: STERN
text: I know there is a lot of negative sentiment around right now and a lot of negative rhetoric.

speaker: STERN
text: You know, that is part and parcel of a recession.

speaker: STERN
text: I am not suggesting that we take a lot of comfort from that, but I do think we should keep it in perspective that it goes with every recession that I have observed.

speaker: STERN
text: They can say, “Well, this time we really mean it,” [laughter] but somebody gave me an article from Time magazine back in 1991, and they were describing that recession just like this one.

speaker: STERN
text: So we should try to bear that in mind.

speaker: STERN
text: That said, of the alternative simulations, the one that really caught my attention was the “more financial stress” scenario.

speaker: STERN
text: I do think some risks are there.

speaker: STERN
text: They are associated mostly with uncertainty about programs and prospects.

speaker: STERN
text: I do think that the establishment and operation of an aggregator bank, assuming it is done effectively, would be a good idea.

speaker: STERN
text: I think it might even be advisable to go further than that, using the Swedish example, and close down some large, insolvent institutions.

speaker: STERN
text: I realize that is probably very, very difficult and possibly risky, but the benefits could be very high as well in reducing the uncertainty that seems to be plaguing the financial sector and a good number of its customers.

speaker: STERN
text: Finally, I do support the release of the longer-term forecasts.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that they provide additional information of value and that they will help to anchor expectations.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our indicators and the anecdotal reports from the Fifth District are quite consistent with the national picture and the picture that emerges from the reports that we have heard around the table from the Reserve Bank Presidents so far today.

speaker: LACKER
text: There are only three nuances that I would take note of.

speaker: LACKER
text: One is recent declines in the wage indexes in the manufacturing and services areas in our District—just a couple of months of decline but potentially meaningful.

speaker: LACKER
text: Second, on the other side, expected prices received in manufacturing have swung decisively from negative territory in November, more than minus 1 percent, to positive territory, above 1½ percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: Third, a fairly significant decline has occurred in the last two months in the index for expected capital spending in manufacturing.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the national level, our outlook is basically aligned with the Greenbook, with a couple of exceptions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am a bit more optimistic about the pace of growth when the recovery begins.

speaker: LACKER
text: I expect inflation to return above 1 percent later this year and to get to about 1½ percent rather than sag in the out years.

speaker: LACKER
text: I do not think we are going to want to keep the nominal rate at the floor for nearly as long as the Greenbook expects.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am thinking liftoff is likely sometime in 2010 rather than in 2012.

speaker: LACKER
text: I endorse the statements made by Presidents Evans and Stern and others about the depressing effect of the lack of clarity around government credit policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: Capital injections that have occurred so far and prospects for future capital injections seem to have induced a tipping dynamic by which we are at a corner solution—there is no private equity coming in for fear of what future capital injections might do to them, and so we are left with the public sector being the only source of prospective capital.

speaker: LACKER
text: Looking ahead at the strategy, I think we want to get to a point where the banks are healthy, which means they can raise equity privately.

speaker: LACKER
text: That transition is the hard one to solve, and I endorse the ideas that President Stern just alluded to.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would also say that I think public statements about our potential future credit programs and the expansion of our programs to asset classes could well be a drawback in that they add uncertainty about where we are going to come in next.

speaker: LACKER
text: I will cede the rest of my time to my past self.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As noted around the table, the economy continues to contract at a rapid rate, and there are few signs that the pace of decline has slowed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That said, clearly there are some positive elements in aspects of financial conditions, such as interbank funding rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Corporate bond and mortgage rates have eased somewhat since our last meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Oil prices have fallen a lot over the last few months, and that has bolstered household real income.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the political uncertainty about what is next should lessen now that the Obama Administration has assumed power.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Over the next few weeks, the Administration is likely to pass its fiscal program and announce how it plans to utilize the second tranche of TARP monies.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That should lessen some of the uncertainty in financial markets about the public policy response.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But these developments should not comfort us much, if at all.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In my view, the risks to the New York Fed forecast and the Greenbook forecast, which don’t differ very much, remain very much to the downside, and we should emphasize that when we motivate our response to the crisis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, in addition to the labor market woes already cited, the banking system is probably in worse shape today than it was last fall, despite the injection of hundreds of billions of dollars of government capital.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the ability of the federal government to adequately recapitalize the banks as loan-loss provisions mount is in question, impaired by the question of whether the size of the second TARP tranche will be big enough to do the job.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A good portion of this is going to be used for other areas, such as mortgage foreclosure mitigation, and there are exceedingly poor politics associated with giving more resources to aid the banks, making it problematic whether a third TARP installment, which might be needed, can actually be secured politically.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Inadequate bank capital is at the core of our problems, and I am not sure we are going to be able to solve this problem quickly or definitively.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It would be much better to do too much in terms of capital injection, taking back that excess later, than being a day late and many billions of dollars short as we have often seemed to be throughout this financial crisis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Adequate capital in the form of tangible common equity is essential to restore confidence, improve credit availability, and restore good market function.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second issue I would like to talk about is household net worth.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is contracting at a rate exceeded only in the Great Depression.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We should not understate the size of the blow to U.S. households, for households’ wealth has been evaporating at an alarming rate at a time when the personal saving rate has been unusually low and the safety net had been whittled back.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That is not a good combination.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is the first big economic downturn in which defined- contribution plans, which are immediately affected by changes in financial asset value, are the dominant source of retirement income for many households beyond Social Security.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In the past, defined-benefit plans with a fixed monthly payment insulated retirees and their families from changes in financial asset values.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, the decline in wealth may not be over.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although I will not predict the equity market, the Greenbook forecast of a 12 percent annualized return over the next two years could turn out to be optimistic.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: After all, if bank balance sheet constraints are causing risk premiums to be unusually high, couldn’t this also translate into the risk premium for the U.S. equity market remaining high with lower equity prices at least over the near term?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, even if equity prices do better, it certainly looks as though housing prices will continue to fall for another year or so, until housing inventories are brought down to more-normal levels.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, the U.S. recession is occurring in the context of global weakness.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This means that the trade sector is not likely to provide any significant degree of support here or anywhere else.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think this is very important, especially in the context of the staff’s analysis of the Reinhart– Rogoff consequences of past crises.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The staff forecast showed a lesser decline relative to past crises and what has happened historically.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yet in those past crises, individual countries had the out of depreciating their currencies and having trade improvement.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We do not have that out this time, and I think that just makes me a bit more nervous about whether our experience will be more in line with those historical experiences.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I know the Greenbook and our own modal forecast assume that the recovery will begin in the second half of the year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I hope that is true.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But it strikes me that, until our banking system is repaired, the risks lie clearly to the downside of such a traditional-recovery, V-shaped forecast.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At a minimum, the degree of uncertainty about the outlook is unusually wide, as described in the Greenbook and illustrated by the width of our fan charts.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are well outside the range of normal experience.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In such circumstances, model-based forecasts probably should be viewed with somewhat greater skepticism, and the Greenbook acknowledges that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Under these circumstances, the Federal Reserve needs to continue to be aggressive in providing liquidity and balance sheet capacity to the private sector.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The goal should be to ease financial conditions as much as possible in the current environment, subject to the constraints imposed by our legal authority, subject to protecting ourselves against credit risk and the issues posed by further rapid balance sheet expansion on our exit from our current suite of special liquidity facilities.

speaker: KOHN
text: I find myself within the central tendency of Committee projections, maybe including the Philadelphia staff in that central tendency.

speaker: KOHN
text: But there is not much comfort in numbers, is there?

speaker: KOHN
text: I think I agree with everyone that data since the last meeting indicate that the steep decline in spending and production is ongoing.

speaker: KOHN
text: Employment and production have been cut back especially sharply as businesses are adjusting to the collapse in demand that we saw last fall by reducing inventories and head count very, very aggressively.

speaker: KOHN
text: Final demand is also continuing to contract.

speaker: KOHN
text: Consumption, business equipment spending, and housing are all falling rapidly, and commercial construction is on the cusp of pulling back in a major way.

speaker: KOHN
text: There is really no sign that the pace of decline in final demand is slowing.

speaker: KOHN
text: To some extent, the ongoing drop in final demand reflects the playing out of the downward shift in demand and the tightening of financial conditions that we saw last fall.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is, we are seeing the kind of multiplier–accelerator effects that we saw before on consumption, working through declines in jobs and income, now on business capital spending, working through expectations of weaker sales going forward.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think I saw an accelerator chart yesterday.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are also feeling the lagged effects of tighter credit in the fourth quarter and sharp declines in equity and housing markets then.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, presumably these sorts of downward pressures on spending from past real and financial shocks would diminish over time, though it could be quite some time before they play out.

speaker: KOHN
text: Unfortunately, I think that, on top of the playing out of those effects, there are some further new pressures on spending coming into play.

speaker: KOHN
text: Further declines in prices of housing and equity in the first quarter will weigh on consumption going forward, and equity prices were lower than what the Greenbook had assumed.

speaker: KOHN
text: The Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey suggests that the tightening of credit by banks is continuing, and I am sure that the mounting layoffs are increasing the fear of job loss and continuing to depress, if not depressing even further, consumer confidence and sparking pullbacks in spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have also heard many reports this morning about businesses becoming much more cautious.

speaker: KOHN
text: Finally, as the Chairman and others have remarked, the remarkable widespread decline in economic activity abroad is just holding down demand all over.

speaker: KOHN
text: It is reducing our exports.

speaker: KOHN
text: No part of the world economy is providing support to global demand.

speaker: KOHN
text: Despite some signs of improvement, financial markets remain severely disrupted and fragile.

speaker: KOHN
text: Outside the GSEs, securitization markets remain virtually shut down.

speaker: KOHN
text: Credit to any but high-quality borrowers is still very expensive.

speaker: KOHN
text: For example, the yield on BBB corporate bonds, which would cover the median business, is about 2 percentage points higher than it was in the first half of September.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is a pretty sharp increase in the cost of capital.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have been especially worried, as others have remarked, about some of the developments in the last few weeks, some sort of backsliding in markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have seen a further drop in equity prices and a strengthening of the dollar pointing to somewhat firmer financial conditions at a time when we need financial conditions to be easier.

speaker: KOHN
text: The further evidence of the vulnerability of banks and other intermediaries has been especially concerning.

speaker: KOHN
text: Losses by these guys were much larger than people anticipated, even people with pessimistic views.

speaker: KOHN
text: CDS spreads have risen in response to the sizable drop in stock prices.

speaker: KOHN
text: LIBOR has backed up again a bit.

speaker: KOHN
text: We have said all along that part of the adjustment to the new steady state in financial markets will involve more credit flowing through intermediaries and less through securities markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: But intermediaries remain under substantial pressure to deleverage, shrink assets, and conserve capital and liquidity, and there are lots of losses to come even under the moderate recession scenario of the Greenbook.

speaker: KOHN
text: The staff estimates that there are about $1 trillion of losses coming from the third quarter on, with about half of those at U.S. banks and thrifts.

speaker: KOHN
text: So there is much more pain to come.

speaker: KOHN
text: In this environment, both perceptions of risk and aversion to risk will remain heightened.

speaker: KOHN
text: Banks will be capital-constrained and worried about their survival, and credit will be tight for some time, even with a well-designed TARP that has taxpayers taking tail risks from lenders through capital insurance and asset purchases.

speaker: KOHN
text: Still, I do have a rebound in the second half of the year.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do not know exactly what quarter it will occur in, but I do think there is a reasonable hope.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is my modal forecast, and I think it is reasonable.

speaker: KOHN
text: There are a couple of reasons for that part of it.

speaker: KOHN
text: It depends on government actions.

speaker: KOHN
text: This massive fiscal stimulus is one obvious thing, but I also think a well- designed support package for banks that does reduce uncertainty and builds capital and further Federal Reserve actions that work to ease financial conditions will at least help to stabilize markets and stop the continued erosion of credit availability and perhaps begin to turn things around with slow improvement.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that at least we can stabilize things.

speaker: KOHN
text: There are some natural market mechanisms in play as well that will help to bring the economy back.

speaker: KOHN
text: The drop in energy prices is certainly building real incomes, and the fall in house prices and lower interest rates are increasing affordability and, I think, will ultimately spur purchases.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think demand curves do slope downward and to the right eventually—at least that is what I learned in Economics 101.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am waiting for it to work in the housing market.

speaker: KOHN
text: The initial negative effects of that initial pullback in spending, the multiplier–accelerator effects, and the tightening of the fourth quarter will eventually fade.

speaker: KOHN
text: Businesses did come into this downdraft with inventories under good control, and their prompt responses in cutting production and employment mean that inventory and staffing levels will soon be comfortable even for very low levels of demand, and production and hiring can be raised promptly in line with demand.

speaker: KOHN
text: In my forecast the unemployment rate did get to 8½ percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: With that slack, inflation continues to drop, and even with long-run inflation expectations well anchored, I had total and core PCE in the 1 to 1¼ percent range in 2010–11, well below my objective of 2 percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think that risks remain to the downside, mainly from financial fragility and the possibility of tighter credit conditions, lower equity prices, steeper declines in house prices, et cetera.

speaker: KOHN
text: It could take longer than I have assumed for the financial situation to stabilize.

speaker: KOHN
text: In that environment, there is a risk—and not a trivial risk—of a deflationary spiral taking hold with even lower inflation expectations feeding high real interest rates with policy stuck at the lower bound.

speaker: KOHN
text: In that regard, I, like others, support proceeding with our long-run projections.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think they will help to clarify where we want things to go in terms of inflation and could be especially useful in our communication about inflation when it seems to be getting below where we want it to go.

speaker: KOHN
text: They might help a little around the edge to anchor inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would not expect a huge effect, but they could help a little when we really need it.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me begin with financial markets before turning to the economy.

speaker: WARSH
text: On financial markets, I will give a few points that I have described in my notes as “tenuous improvements in market functioning,” but I really think that I will describe them as feigning optimism.

speaker: WARSH
text: So let me feign optimism with three points on financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, bridge financings: We saw earlier this week a very large bridge financing to fund an acquisition.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say that bridge financing by its very terms probably could not have come together 30 or 45 days ago.

speaker: WARSH
text: There are a couple of other very large deals being contemplated that require bridge financing, and I would say this bridge looks different from bridges of the last cycle.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would not call it a new equilibrium, but I would say that neither the acquirers nor the lenders/underwriters would have been prepared to agree to terms like this.

speaker: WARSH
text: This is a bridge that is not very good.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is a bridge that gets expensive in a hurry.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is a bridge that could give way.

speaker: WARSH
text: But buyer, seller, and underwriter came to terms here; and whether or not this is a new equilibrium in funding transactions with some assurance that there will be cash for a period of time if the acquirer does not lose its rating, this and other factors suggest that at least there is a new negotiation happening.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I would say that it is a positive sign.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, trading businesses: The firms that are left and that still have meaningful trading businesses had fantastic Januaries.

speaker: WARSH
text: Why did they have such good Januaries?

speaker: WARSH
text: There is just not a lot of competition left.

speaker: WARSH
text: A lot of volatility is now presumed to be built into the models and into traders’ behavior.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say that, if you are still in the trading business and you are looking for sources of profit and good news to get you through this cycle, some are there.

speaker: WARSH
text: The capital intensity of these trading businesses is lower than it was before.

speaker: WARSH
text: The necessity for firms to commit capital to be profitable in trading is lower.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I would say, again, that this is some, tenuous, improvement and may be a new equilibrium there, which is good news for some of the survivors that are in trading.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, and I think probably the most essential point, is about the prospects for large, internationally active financial institutions to raise capital.

speaker: WARSH
text: There is a good chance that in the next week there will be a large non-U.S. internationally active financial institution that tests the capital markets for a very large capital raise.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is likely to be a rights offering.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is likely to be at a very significant discount to its current share price, but I would guess that it gets done.

speaker: WARSH
text: If it gets done, that says that there still is private capital at some price.

speaker: WARSH
text: Maybe it is a price that existing shareholders don’t like.

speaker: WARSH
text: Maybe it is a price that companies don’t want.

speaker: WARSH
text: But if those private markets are open for the relatively strong outside the United States, I would say that is encouraging and we need it.

speaker: WARSH
text: The last 30 capital raises by financial institutions aren’t just losers.

speaker: WARSH
text: They are big losers, and it is hard for investors and others to be opportunistic when they see that track record.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think the success or failure of these financial institutions might well be tested in the next week—when we see a pretty good institution give it a real shot.

speaker: WARSH
text: So that’s my optimistic pitch.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now words of caution: As Trish said yesterday, I think that we are back at maybe the most precarious state in financial markets that we have been at, at least in a regularly scheduled FOMC meeting, and I think that this is going to be an awfully consequential few weeks.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is true that risk aversion has been reduced, but only a bit.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have seen a bit of an unwind in the flight to quality and a bit of an unwind in the flight to the most liquid securities, but, boy, I would be hesitant to overstate the improvement here.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even if we look at high-yield markets and we note that they are off their peaks, there are still expectations of defaults that are near Depression levels.

speaker: WARSH
text: I want to take comfort in some of these data, but I think it is probably just a bit of a bump from the darkest, scariest days that we had in the prior period.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, I would note that share prices of large financial institutions broadly and regional financial institutions have all gotten crushed in 2009 so far, and that has raised real questions about the solvency and durability of their franchises as publicly held entities.

speaker: WARSH
text: So the question remains: How have credit markets seemed to improve along the lines that Trish and Bill have mentioned, while we have had this huge markdown in the valuation of these companies?

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, as Trish noted yesterday, I think the answer is us, the Fed.

speaker: WARSH
text: Sure, we have seen some improvements in markets that we haven’t been directly involved in, like A2/P2.

speaker: WARSH
text: But the Fed’s facilities have been primary in support and have been a partial bulwark against broader financial institution weakness.

speaker: WARSH
text: So in some ways I use that to reconcile the discrepancy between improvements in market functioning, at least in the very short term, and the miserable news that we have had on broad financial institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, a note of caution and concern: There are still a lot of 50-cent dollars out there, and no one seems to want to buy them.

speaker: WARSH
text: That these arbitrage opportunities are still available in markets that don’t require great sophistication and that people are not taking them up should tell us that something is very, very wrong.

speaker: WARSH
text: Only those buyers who have longer-term horizons, risk neutrality, and balance sheet capacity can participate in these markets, and those are criteria that are not found among most folks that could partake.

speaker: WARSH
text: So these 50-cent dollars might be 60-cent dollars, but they are still out there, and that should be telling us that things are in pretty tough shape.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, and maybe of most concern about the state of financial markets, is the large and increasing number of financial institutions, including many that are most systemically important, that are perceived by markets to be effectively insolvent or nearly so.

speaker: WARSH
text: Single-digit share prices for a large class of financial institutions do not strike me as a new equilibrium.

speaker: WARSH
text: And to avoid the theological argument that we had a bit of yesterday on whether this is an equilibrium or disequilibrium, I will tell you that I do not think it is going to stick around for long.

speaker: WARSH
text: If you think about these financial institutions that are trading at $3, $5, or $7, I am not sure I understand how they can continue to get through the next 12 months in that state.

speaker: WARSH
text: I do not know how they can run their businesses, how they can incentivize their employees, or how governance will hold with the specter of continued losses and possible nationalization.

speaker: WARSH
text: My sense is that this is not a sustainable equilibrium, and I fear which way it breaks.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the specter of nationalization may delay public market recapitalization of many of these firms, though I expect that the new Administration will do all it can to provide clarity.

speaker: WARSH
text: As the real economy continues to deteriorate, I suspect that it will take a couple of shots at this to “get it right.” And this single-digit share price might well continue to limit the efficient provision of credit to the real economy and continue to hinder financial flows.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I am skeptical in a tumultuous world that these single- digit share prices are sustainable for financial institutions, and, again, the way in which they are likely to break is pretty disturbing.

speaker: WARSH
text: So what does all of this mean for the real economy?

speaker: WARSH
text: Others said it more extensively than I will, but the economy is in terrible shape.

speaker: WARSH
text: Activity is falling fast with little indication of stabilization even at new lower levels.

speaker: WARSH
text: As I think Dan described yesterday, the nature of this turmoil, which I define more as a breakdown of the global financial architecture than some housing-led recession, is likely to have a recovery period that is slower, bumpier, and tougher than most recent recessions would suggest.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a result of all that, I am more negative on GDP and employment prospects than the Greenbook forecast is, in both the near term and the medium term.

speaker: WARSH
text: Mr. Chairman, with respect to your question about the second half, I think we should see, arithmetically and because of the inventory issue, a slowdown in weakness, but it does not look to me anything like a real recovery.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am also skeptical of near-term GDP growth that is expected from the stimulus package.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t expect foreign economies to perform as well as the Greenbook says or to recover even as quickly as the United States will, as it no doubt ultimately will.

speaker: WARSH
text: I expect net exports to be less supportive of GDP growth than the Greenbook suggests, and I read foreign exchange markets as being supportive of the view that advanced foreign economies will actually underperform the United States in the period ahead.

speaker: WARSH
text: A couple of final concerns before I turn to inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: In a world like this, where the model of capitalism that has come from the United States is now being doubted—maybe even ridiculed in some corners of the world—the risk of big policy errors everywhere, not just here but everywhere, is higher.

speaker: WARSH
text: The U.S. weakness in the story line—that somehow this started in the United States and this is the fault of the United States—makes it harder for us to stop bad policies from being undertaken outside the United States.

speaker: WARSH
text: So with all of that, I am quite uncertain about the timing of improvement in financial conditions.

speaker: WARSH
text: The decision on the use of TARP funding is thus likely to be critically important, and this solvency overhang is likely to be harmful to GDP in the balance of 2009.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that the framing question for the new Administration should and might be what the official sector can do to help reopen capital markets so that real common equity that these institutions need can come to bear.

speaker: WARSH
text: What sorts of risk insurance do we need to provide?

speaker: WARSH
text: I am not sure how the real economy can get traction until some of those things are answered.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, on the inflation front, I will be brief.

speaker: WARSH
text: The inflation picture, of course, bears watching, but I am still skeptical that deflation risks rank as high as many of the other risks that I and others have described today.

speaker: WARSH
text: Inflation expectations remain key and obviously should be a focus of our continued discussions here.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the long-term projections and the recommendation that comes from the subcommittee, I support it.

speaker: WARSH
text: The benefits, at least in my view, will be felt more inside this room.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think it does help us communicate and understand one another’s views.

speaker: WARSH
text: The idea that somehow that is going to have anything more than a modest near-term effect on how the world thinks about inflation and thinks about our behavior probably overstates, but I do think it is, on balance, a step in the right direction.

speaker: DUKE
text: In looking at the banks and talking to the bankers, I started with the fourth-quarter earnings announcements.

speaker: DUKE
text: The first part is what they consider to be real, which is the higher loan-loss provisions.

speaker: DUKE
text: In this, unemployment has led to an acceleration in delinquencies that goes across all consumer products.

speaker: DUKE
text: The reduced activity in the cash flow of businesses has resulted in higher C&I delinquencies.

speaker: DUKE
text: Vacancy rates and the lack of takeout financing are creating problems in commercial real estate, but I am still not sure that is as big a problem as maybe it looks, certainly not as much as in residential, with the ability to renegotiate those loans and to continue the cash flow on them being better than it has been in residential.

speaker: DUKE
text: Appraisals took another leg down, which has heightened loss severities.

speaker: DUKE
text: When you combine that with lengthening real estate marketing times, particularly for home equity loans, there is less willingness to buy through the first mortgage, and so the junior liens are becoming total loss rather than partial recoveries.

speaker: DUKE
text: I would point out that the same pessimism about future conditions that drives the reserving also drives the underwriting conditions for future loans, and that is why they are continuing to tighten.

speaker: DUKE
text: Not so real in terms of the numbers that showed up in the fourth-quarter loss are the model losses and goodwill impairment in other than temporary impairment, particularly on trust preferred securities; there is something just deep in the DNA of bankers that they do not believe.

speaker: DUKE
text: They are used to marks on credit, and they believe in marks on credit, but they do not believe in the marks based on market conditions.

speaker: DUKE
text: So if you look at these securities, if they were accounted for as a troubled debt, they would be written down to 90.

speaker: DUKE
text: If they are accounted for under market conditions, they are written down to somewhere between 30 and 50.

speaker: DUKE
text: In the minds of the bankers, this is a portion of their capital that will return when ultimately their projections of future cash flows are proved to be correct, if they can live that long.

speaker: DUKE
text: The loan charge-offs would be tax deductible, but the security write-downs are not tax deductible.

speaker: DUKE
text: So when asking them about whether or not they would sell these securities at their current marks, only those who thought they might get some tax advantage would be willing to sell them at the current marks.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of goodwill and these write-downs, I really had not focused on how the goodwill-impairment process works.

speaker: DUKE
text: It is a two-step process, and it appears that now, if the current fair value of an acquisition does not equal the goodwill amount—which means that the market conditions for bank equities are causing the goodwill to be written down—they are not really concerned about analysts because the analysts are, as we all know, focusing on tangible capital.

speaker: DUKE
text: But they are concerned about the headline risk as their customers and potential customers read about huge losses in the institutions.

speaker: DUKE
text: Finally, mortgage-servicing rights—the one negative consequence of lower rates is that the expected refinance then reduces the value of mortgage-servicing rights.

speaker: DUKE
text: A number of you have mentioned the TARP money.

speaker: DUKE
text: In this case, there were several who were approved for capital but elected not to take it, much to the annoyance of the Treasury.

speaker: DUKE
text: Their reasons were that their capital levels were high or adequate already.

speaker: DUKE
text: They could not see the loan demand in the future and were concerned about additional conditions that might be imposed by the Congress.

speaker: DUKE
