text: Many of these had time to actually see the introduction of the Frank bill before they had to make a final decision, and that definitely informed the decision.

speaker: DUKE
text: Their concerns are what you would expect—that lending quotas would be imposed and that would actually increase their risk; that the dividend restrictions would make it more difficult for them ultimately to raise private equity; and that compensation restrictions would affect what they view as strategically important incentive plans.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I do not think that any of them would be particularly inclined to take another voluntary program.

speaker: DUKE
text: With the smaller banks, the mutual and the subchapter S banks just saw a posting of the terms for them for CPP.

speaker: DUKE
text: This process is taking a lot longer to work through all the different parts of the system than we might have realized.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some have been approved but haven’t yet received their money.

speaker: DUKE
text: Even on the TLGP, the FDIC temporary liquidity guarantee program, many of them are reporting that they are getting slow to no response from FDIC.

speaker: DUKE
text: They were planning to use these guarantees for lines from upstream correspondents, and they are just not getting any answer.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of liquidity, all the banks are seeing good deposit growth.

speaker: DUKE
text: However, some of this growth has to be viewed as temporary, given that there is a year-end expiration of the unlimited demand deposit insurance.

speaker: DUKE
text: In normal times, you have a parking of risk-averse assets in bank deposits, and those can move out just as quickly as they came in.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some are still concerned about additional funding, as well as the examiner expectations or the FDIC additional charges based on expanding nondeposit sources, such as Home Loan Bank advances or brokered funds.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some are holding large amounts of excess reserves as an actual or perceived cushion against funding sources pulling away, as well as a demonstration of both liquidity and capital strength.

speaker: DUKE
text: In lending, most of them do report weak loan demand, and those that are reporting stronger loan demand seem to be in markets in which the larger players are pulling back or are involved in mergers.

speaker: DUKE
text: Those that are seeing loan growth don’t initially even see the income boost from that as they have to establish initial reserves on the net growth.

speaker: DUKE
text: To counteract the angry political climate, banks are actively highlighting in their press releases all of their new loan fundings, even the gross fundings.

speaker: DUKE
text: Advertising for consumer and small business loans has improved application volume, but the quality is low, which leads to lower approval rates on all types of credit.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of construction lending, the projects that aren’t in trouble are simply finishing out the current phase and stopping, and this applies even vertically.

speaker: DUKE
text: One banker reported a high-rise condo project that the builder just capped off at ten stories and decided that was the end of the project.

speaker: DUKE
text: There is a bit of lending to take over distressed projects of others.

speaker: DUKE
text: There is significant deterioration in the creditworthiness of businesses and consumers, with at least one banker expressing concern about the predictive capability and the stability of credit scores in the current environment: Businesses that are being affected by rapidly changing asset prices go from positive earnings through the third quarter to chapter 11 by the end of the fourth quarter.

speaker: DUKE
text: All new loans are priced to higher spreads with floors in them.

speaker: DUKE
text: The range that I heard is 4 to 6 percent.

speaker: DUKE
text: So as we look at what is happening to prime, I don’t think that is necessarily what is happening to rates at which anyone is actually borrowing.

speaker: DUKE
text: The big exception to weak demand is in mortgage applications, which are at record levels.

speaker: DUKE
text: There aren’t as many competitors out there, and as with other credit types, the approval rates are lower.

speaker: DUKE
text: Appraisals may be a problem, and it is mostly refinance, but there is a trickle of purchase activity.

speaker: DUKE
text: They tend to believe that the purchase activity is currently being deterred by a fear of job loss and expectations for more government incentives down the road.

speaker: DUKE
text: The rate drop also came at a seasonally low time for purchasers.

speaker: DUKE
text: Then the last piece is the need to sell an existing home, and they may be upside down in the existing mortgage.

speaker: DUKE
text: There are reports of contracts sometimes five deep, of the contract waiting for sale of an existing home that is waiting for sale that is waiting for sale.

speaker: DUKE
text: So if at some point the first sale can occur, it will actually multiply itself in many cases.

speaker: DUKE
text: Finally, banks are actually getting quite creative in growing or strengthening their loan portfolios.

speaker: DUKE
text: There is a network of banks in Nebraska that are actually co-underwriting as well as participating in larger credits.

speaker: DUKE
text: There was a bank that had offered a 7-year or 10-year fully amortizing mortgage, trying to take advantage of the new propensity to save, and actually has seen great take-up on it from borrowers who want to use the lower rates to pay off their mortgages sooner rather than to lower their payments.

speaker: DUKE
text: Another one is using the sales force to go out and offer proactively to restructure business and commercial real estate loans, say, for twelve to twenty-four months of interest only to improve the cash flow and at the same time increase the rate on the loan.

speaker: DUKE
text: Another bank is using half of its production teams to go out and sell problem assets to private-market investors who are in their market and familiar with the projects.

speaker: DUKE
text: The bottom line—the community and regional banks are finding ways to survive; in fact, three of the banks had record years on the upside for 2008.

speaker: DUKE
text: But it is really ugly out there.

speaker: DUKE
text: So while there are some signs of recovery in markets, they are outside the banking system.

speaker: DUKE
text: I think that it is going to be incredibly difficult to stimulate the economy through the programs that involve bank lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: It is going to take more-direct programs, such as mortgage-backed security purchases or the TALF to act as stand-ins for the securitization markets.

speaker: DUKE
text: In fact, I believe this is the time to expand the range of mortgages that are eligible for GSE guarantees to include jumbo and higher loan-to-value mortgages as a way to replace the currently closed private-label markets.

speaker: DUKE
text: Even if the government takes the problem loans off bank balance sheets, we will still ultimately need to liquidate much of the underlying collateral, and that is going to require more lending than the banks can currently fund.

speaker: DUKE
text: We could also find ourselves at some point using the discount window in more and more of a Home Loan Bank way for core funding rather than as a lender of last resort to fund the nonmortgage lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: I know that all of these suggestions go against the grain of almost everyone here, but frankly, capital alone just will not restart bank lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: I think the banks are going to pull back, repair as best they can, and create the earnings to rebuild their own capital until they can begin to attract private equity.

speaker: DUKE
text: President Bullard yesterday used a phrase.

speaker: DUKE
text: He said that people do the best they can given the constraints they face, and that is how I would title my remarks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you all very much.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Debbie informs me that coffee is ready.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a 20-minute break.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I can start by offering a summary of the discussion around the table, which was informative as always but fairly uniform this time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The intermeeting data, as we have seen, indicate a very sharp contraction, both domestically and abroad, which reflects in large part the effects of the intensification of the financial crisis but also the increasingly powerful feedback loop from the economy to financial conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Many people noted that the financial conditions remain very fragile.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumption, employment, and production indicators suggest that the pronounced contraction in activity in the fourth quarter is likely to continue through the first part of 2009.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Participants noted that the slowdown is very widespread across sectors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some participants expect a return to positive economic growth later this year, citing such factors as fiscal policy, lower oil prices, inventory adjustments, government efforts to stabilize the financial sector, and the possibility of improving confidence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, uncertainty remains high, and risks are to the downside as sentiment is currently very depressed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Moreover, based on experiences with other financial crises, the possibility of a protracted slump or L-shaped recovery remains significant.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some financial markets, including markets that have received Fed support, such as the money and mortgage markets, have shown modest signs of improvement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, bank losses for the fourth quarter were greater than markets anticipated, and many institutions remain under substantial stress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Bank loans are declining with tighter terms, falling credit demand, and a lack of creditworthy borrowers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Very tight credit conditions are, in turn, affecting both households and firms.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Declining asset values are also affecting wealth and confidence, including declines in defined-contribution pension plans.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Whether the new government initiatives to stabilize banking are successful will be an important factor in the outlook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumers continue to retrench, cutting back as balance sheets are repaired and precautionary saving rises in an uncertain environment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Employment declines have been large, with firms projecting further job cuts ahead, and there are wage and salary freezes occurring.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Fiscal stimulus could also provide a boost to consumer income and support state and local spending, which is currently contracted.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There has been little indication of stabilization in the housing sector as house prices and building activity continue to decline.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nonresidential construction is likely to fall as financing dries up and fundamentals weaken.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A number of participants expressed concern that commercial real estate could follow the path of residential real estate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other investment has also contracted in light of prevailing uncertainties, including uncertainties about government policy, tight credit, and low capacity utilization.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Lower commodity prices have affected drilling and mining activity and to a lesser extent agriculture.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Exports and imports have both fallen sharply, reflecting both domestic and global slowdowns and possibly lessened availability of trade finance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inflation has fallen significantly and looks likely to be low in the medium term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is some risk that inflation could fall below levels consistent with good economic performance, and some expressed concern about a deflationary trap possibly at the global level.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, maintaining stable inflation expectations remains very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Currently there appears to be quite a bit of diversity in the public’s inflation expectations, including concerns about both deflationary and inflationary outcomes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is just a summary of comments I heard.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do not have a great deal to add on my own.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me make just a few remarks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, I share with everyone the observation that activity has fallen very rapidly, perhaps not much more quickly than expected at our last meeting but still confirming the very substantial effects of the financial crisis and the overall tightening in the credit markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A somewhat bigger surprise is the decline in global economies, which has been more severe than anticipated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On a global basis, this seems very likely to be the worst postwar recession, and the global declines will make it more difficult for the U.S. economy to recover.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As others have noted, there have been some marginal improvements in a few financial markets, and the Fed’s programs, at least in those markets, seem to have had some benefits.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have seen a little improvement in corporate bond markets as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The most important news on the financial side since the last meeting, though, has been the worse-than-expected results in the banking system, the fact that we have had to go back and address instability in two of our largest four banking organizations, despite the large injections of TARP capital.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is indicative of the tremendous concerns about the stability of the banking system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The continuing credit losses pose a real challenge both to the banking system and to efforts by the government and the Treasury to restore stability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My general view is that, although fiscal policy could be helpful and will probably provide some impetus later this year and next year, we may see something similar to what we saw in the spring, which was a temporary boost and then very little sustained recovery unless we can get substantial improvement in the banking situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I share the same uncertainties about the prospects of recovery or at least the beginning of positive economic growth later this year that others have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Greenbook case relies fairly heavily on inventory dynamics.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Currently inventory liquidation is subtracting from growth, and so stabilizing final sales at zero by midyear, which seems like an easy task, would be sufficient to give us some positive growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That said, it is probably not such an easy thing to ensure that final sales stabilize.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should expect to see continued declines in investment and in trade.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We may see some growth in government, obviously with the fiscal programs; but even so, to get to zero growth in final sales, the Greenbook needs to forecast growth of about 2 percent in real consumption in the second half of the year, which given current developments may not be so easy to obtain.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So like many of you, I guess that we will see a stabilization, perhaps some modest positive growth, in the latter part of this year, but this is by no means a certainty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It will depend very substantially and perhaps most fundamentally on achieving some stabilization in the banking sector.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think that other financial improvements will compensate for continued deterioration in bank balance sheets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next intermeeting period will be very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is of great significance that we have now made it through the political transition period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it did create additional uncertainty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is interesting that the implications of the March inauguration in 1933 were the reason we pushed it back to January, and we may make it November 5 next time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I think it is good that we do have—political views notwithstanding one way or the other—a new Administration with some political capital and with a mandate to take action, and we ought to know a lot more by the next meeting about what those plans are and how the Federal Reserve fits into the overall program for stabilization.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think that this intermeeting period will be critical.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On inflation, I tend to take the conventional view that the extent of slack and declining commodity prices, because of both domestic and foreign slow growth, will lead to declining inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I recognize the issues about expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think on the whole, though, that they will move down rather than up.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is important to note that, given that we are already at zero in terms of the policy rate, the dividing line between deflation and inflation is not really that significant.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s disinflation at this point, which both raises real interest rates and creates the debt deflation mechanism that moves wealth from debtors to creditors, which for good reasons is probably not a neutral transfer because of the effects it has on financial stability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I do think that disinflation is a concern, but that is probably a relatively slow moving process, and we can keep our eye on it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do hope that improving our communication with respect to our inflation objectives will, on the margin, be beneficial.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Of course, inflation expectations are important both in financial markets and in the general public.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I imagine our communications are more effective on the financial side, but we can also try to have a more aggressive communication strategy with respect to the broader public.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will make just one comment anticipating policy a bit, which is that I think we ought to recognize that we could be at zero for quite a long time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There were a few comments that, with economic growth expected beginning in the second half, we might be coming out of zero relatively soon, and it could be the case.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we have to be prepared to do that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But even aside from the Greenbook’s very long term projection of zero rates, I noted that, if you take the central tendencies of this Committee for 2011 and stick them into a Taylor rule, you still get minus interest rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I still think, based on the median and modal views of this Committee, it is likely that rates will be low for some time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore I agree with President Bullard that we do have to think very hard about our quantitative approaches and, as we discussed yesterday, find ways to make them more effective, to communicate them more accurately, and to assess them quantitatively.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those are all critical steps, and that will be a challenge for us as we go forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So even if we are not moving the federal funds rate around, there is still going to be a great deal to do and a great deal to think about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me stop there and turn now to Brian Madigan to introduce the policy round.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 4 I will be referring to the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” This package includes the revised versions of the draft statements that were distributed on Monday.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: By lowering the target federal funds rate essentially to zero at its last meeting, the Committee entered the realm of unconventional monetary policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Given our limited experience operating in this regime, I thought it might be helpful to begin my remarks by reviewing the various tools you might employ if you decide that further monetary policy stimulus is appropriate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: First, the Committee can communicate its intentions in ways designed to influence the expectations of private-sector decisionmakers.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, as President Plosser noted, the Committee could provide additional information to the market about its expectation for the path of the federal funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In its December statement, the Committee offered some information about its intentions by indicating that it “anticipates that weak economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate for some time.” The Committee’s action to lower the federal funds rate target nearly to zero was greater than market participants generally expected, and its message about short-term rates remaining low for some time further conditioned expectations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Interest rates moved noticeably lower across the entire yield curve, indicating that the combination of the action and the statement provided additional monetary stimulus.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee could be more specific about the future path of the funds rate— for example, by being more explicit about how long the target rate is likely to remain close to zero or even by providing your expectations to the market for the trajectory of rates after liftoff.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, just as you provide ranges and central tendencies for real GDP growth, the unemployment rate, and inflation, you could likewise do for 4 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 4).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, given the enormous uncertainties about the financial and economic outlook, you might be uncomfortable providing such specificity, and you may be concerned about the implications for the Federal Reserve’s credibility if those expectations proved to be far off the mark.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Varying your qualitative descriptions of the path of the funds rate in light of incoming data is another possibility.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: At some point you might also wish to consider articulating the conditions that would prompt you to begin raising rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: At a minimum, though, as the Chairman noted, the Committee could continue to reiterate that interest rates are likely to remain low for some time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Unless the evolving economic outlook strengthens considerably relative to your economic forecasts, delivering this message continuously seems likely to be an essential component of the Committee’s communications for a while.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee could also communicate its views regarding other policy tools.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, it could be explicit about the amounts of open market purchases that it intends to undertake, the types of securities it intends to buy, and the time frame for those purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee’s December statement followed this principle regarding mortgage-backed securities and agency debt.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee could also expand its communications about inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, the Committee could make clear that any near-term declines in inflation below its optimal level will be strongly resisted in the medium to long term.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With nominal short-term rates now pinned at zero, measures that support inflation expectations may reduce the upward pressure on real interest rates that develops as actual inflation declines, thus limiting the extent of restraint on aggregate demand that emanates from that source.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In this regard, you have several communication approaches at your disposal.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For example, as discussed earlier this month, the Committee could establish and publish a numerical longer-term inflation objective.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Or the Committee could decide to proceed with collecting and publishing participants’ longer-term projections for inflation, growth, and unemployment—an approach that most of you evidently support.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, you could implement both approaches, with the longer-term projections explaining how you envision that inflation will approach your longer-run objective over time and how growth and unemployment will converge toward their steady-state values.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A decision on the longer-term projections is included later in the agenda for today’s meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A third possibility is that the Committee could use its statement to make clear that it recognizes the risk that inflation could fall persistently below its optimal level.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: By explicitly identifying that possibility, the Committee would suggest that it is prepared to take actions to counteract such an outcome.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The ability to further expand the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet to apply additional economic stimulus—or at least to offset some of the restraint coming from developments in financial markets—offers another set of unconventional policy tools.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In particular, the Federal Reserve can expand its use of what the Chairman has called “credit policies” by implementing programs designed to facilitate flows of credit to borrowers who normally obtain funds through markets that have become dysfunctional.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To an important degree, the opportunities for exercising these tools will be driven by ongoing market developments: Apart from expansions of existing facilities, either in terms of amounts or in terms of coverage, it is difficult to predict exactly how such credit policies might be augmented—or even whether it would be desirable to create new facilities—without advance knowledge of where market conditions might deteriorate next.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, as discussed yesterday and today, the Federal Reserve has already indicated the possibility of expanding the TALF to include commercial-mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In assessing whether expansion of such facilities is warranted, the Federal Reserve will need to take careful account not only of the possible efficacy of the programs but also of a range of other considerations, including moral hazard and the implications for the System’s exit strategy in returning to a normal framework for conducting monetary policy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Other aspects of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet, such as the reciprocal swap arrangements and the System’s portfolio of Treasury and agency securities, offer a third set of opportunities for providing greater stimulus.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: At the moment, there would not seem to be much motivation for increasing the authorized amounts of swap lines, as conditions in global interbank funding markets have generally improved somewhat over recent months.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, expanding the System’s purchases of agency debt and mortgage-backed securities might represent a more compelling possibility for applying further monetary stimulus.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Purchases of longer-term Treasury securities are another possibility.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The System’s MBS purchases have already had a notable effect in lowering mortgage rates, and the Committee might see further action in this direction as likely to be productive.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As discussed by the Committee yesterday, purchases of Treasury securities might help improve conditions in private credit markets, but engaging in such purchases would also have some disadvantages.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative A for this meeting, the draft statement for which is shown on the next page of the exhibits, would exercise several of the options for applying more stimulus.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The decision to apply additional stimulus under this alternative would be explained by the indication in the first sentence of paragraph 2 that the economy has weakened somewhat more than anticipated.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would also be supported by the statement in the last sentence of the paragraph that the downside risks to the outlook are “significant”—an adjective that, as President Fisher noted, might be seen as less alarming than “sizable” while still getting the point across.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Paragraph 3 would indicate that the Committee expects inflation pressures to remain subdued, and it would reveal a concern that inflation could persist for a time below rates that best foster economic growth and price stability in the longer run.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As I noted previously, identifying this risk explicitly could help reduce the extent to which market participants lower their assessment of the FOMC’s inflation expectations in response to near-term declines in inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Paragraph 4 reiterates the point made in December that the Federal Reserve will employ all available tools to promote the resumption of sustainable economic growth and again notes that these measures are likely to keep the size of the balance sheet at a high level.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The next two paragraphs provide language to explain the choice of an expanded program of purchasing mortgage-backed securities or a new program to purchase Treasury securities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative 1 would increase the planned purchases of MBS to $750 billion; the current pace of purchases would be maintained, and the additional amounts would be purchased in the third quarter.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Market participants have already expressed some concern about what happens when the currently authorized program concludes at midyear, and an announcement of additional purchases of MBS seems likely to at least maintain, if not increase, the downward pressure on mortgage rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative 2 would entail the purchase of up to $250 billion in Treasury securities this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The final paragraph of the statement for alternative A notes that the Federal Reserve will soon implement the TALF.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It also indicates that the Committee will be monitoring the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet and assessing whether expansion of or modifications to the lending facilities would serve to further support credit markets and economic activity and help to preserve price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: All in all, alternative A would be most consistent with a view that the economic outlook is unsatisfactory, that the Committee has several tools that it can employ to improve that outlook, and that the benefits entailed in using these tools outweigh the costs.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative B, shown on the next page, would also express the view that the federal funds rate is likely to remain low for some time, but it differs in some notable respects from alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The first sentence in the second paragraph cites evidence that the outlook remains weak but does not state that the economy has deteriorated further.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, like alternative A, it notes that the downside risks to the outlook are significant.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The inflation paragraph also points to subdued inflation pressures, but it omits any indication of concern about the downside risks to inflation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The final paragraph notes that the FOMC stands ready to expand the quantity of its MBS purchases and the duration of the program as conditions warrant; this indication would also help address market concerns about the end of the program at midyear.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The draft indicates that the Committee is prepared to purchase longer-term Treasury securities if evolving circumstances indicate that such transactions would be particularly effective in improving conditions in private credit markets.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This wording is intended, first, to indicate that the Committee has reached a decision—it is not still “evaluating” possible purchases; second, to suggest that the Committee does not see such purchases as the most beneficial action the Federal Reserve can take in current circumstances; and third, to note that conditions could change in a way that would prompt the Committee to initiate purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Overall, alternative B does not entail additional action at this meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee would indicate a possible expansion of its MBS program without taking such action now.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But the statement would suggest that the FOMC is unlikely to purchase Treasury securities, at least absent a significant change in circumstances.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With market participants evidently building in significant odds of Fed purchases, it seems likely that such a statement could spur a noticeable backup in longer-term Treasury yields—perhaps as much as 20 basis points or so.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee might be inclined toward alternative B if it sees the economic outlook as not having deteriorated materially since the last meeting.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It might be encouraged by the tentative signs of improvement in some financial markets and believe that further improvements are possible as the TALF comes on line.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It also might think that the passage of a large fiscal stimulus package is likely and that further significant legislation to provide support to financial markets and institutions could be forthcoming from the Congress.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In these circumstances, and with the Federal Reserve already having applied considerable monetary and financial stimulus, the Committee might think it most reasonable at this time to monitor the effects of the actions taken to date, assess the likely effects of further policy actions, and be prepared to implement additional measures such as expanded purchases of mortgage- backed securities, if needed.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative C, shown on the next page of the handout, also would express the view that the federal funds rate is likely to remain low for some time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would note that the Federal Reserve continues to purchase large quantities of agency debt and mortgage-backed securities and would note the imminent implementation of the TALF.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, this alternative would be silent on further Federal Reserve actions to support credit markets and stimulate the economy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With no mention at all of possible purchases of Treasury securities, market participants would likely conclude that the Federal Reserve had dropped the idea, and Treasury note and bond yields could jump appreciably.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: More generally, analysts would infer that the Federal Reserve was unlikely to take further stimulative policy actions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative C is most consistent with a view that considerable monetary and financial stimulus has already been applied and that the potential costs of further stimulative actions by the Federal Reserve outweigh the potential benefits.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement released after the December meeting is included as the last page for your reference.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no questions, why don’t we begin our policy and statement go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s start with President Rosengren.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The current outlook envisions an inflation rate below 2 percent throughout the forecast period.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We have judgmentally adjusted our inflation forecast upward relative to the straight model outlook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Thus, our forecast entails a significant risk of deflation occurring in 2010 unless additional actions are taken.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I see little harm in expanding our program of purchases of mortgage-backed securities and GSE securities to lower mortgage rates further.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While this alone is unlikely to be sufficient, it will help stabilize housing and the financial sector.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would prefer this policy to purchasing long-term Treasury securities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Rates on long-term Treasury securities remain quite low as many investors prefer to hold government securities of all maturities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Trying to reduce the spreads relative to Treasuries is likely to be more effective as it more directly attacks the elevated borrowing costs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would note that, in our own projections over the three-year period, not a single one of us had an unemployment rate back below 5½ percent, and I would note that only one of us thought that we would get to 2 percent if that was our inflation goal over the three-year period.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The difference between alternative A and alternative B is whether we say we might do something versus doing something.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It does seem that, if all of us think that we are not going to get to where we want to go within three years, this would be the time to actually do something.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, obviously, as we have said, the downside risks to the economy are quite large, in part because we are involved in very serious banking conditions that probably also will worsen significantly over the next several months.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In particular, the exposures of the banking system and insurance industries to commercial real estate, as we have said, represent a significant risk both to financial stability and to economic activity.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There has been some improvement in financial market functioning in recent weeks, but most of the improvement is tied to the significant support from our programs and other government programs and not from the markets repairing themselves.

speaker: HOENIG
text: These repairs still lie ahead, I suspect, and this will absorb increasing amounts of our time as we try to deal with that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Second, over the next several months, fiscal policy will take center stage.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think this is the first phase that we are hearing all the discussions about now, and this Committee will need to decide how it should position itself relative to a potentially large amount of new fiscal stimulus that has really not all been defined at this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I suggest it would be prudent then to wait to see more about the form, timing, and likely effect of the fiscal stimulus before firmly committing to new expansionary policy programs that would be defined in alternative A.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition, fiscal steps to deal with toxic assets and thereby improve the functioning of the financial system may alter our approach to supporting the financial system and market stability.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think there are some pretty significant issues around these institutions that will be discussed in the very near future.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Consequently, I favor alternative B rather than alternative A at this time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Also, as to additional nontraditional monetary policy measures that we might employ, I agree with the Board staff’s recommendation that we retain the option of purchasing long-term Treasury securities at a future date but not engage in these purchases now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I do agree with what President Rosengren had to say about that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Treasury purchases would send a clear signal.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In addition to what President Rosengren said, they would clearly begin to acknowledge the monetizing of our deficit.

speaker: HOENIG
text: At this juncture, I would prefer that we continue with our previously announced efforts to reduce the spreads of agency and private securities over Treasuries.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would also like to recommend that we think ahead as to how we might provide support to institutions and markets that provide financing to commercial real estate, should conditions in that sector continue to deteriorate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It would be helpful to try to outline a process that does not force us to again go around the intermediation process or find ourselves in a kind of very quick, over-the-weekend approach to things.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I also favor the inflation risk discussion in alternative B.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As I indicated earlier, the decline in overall and core inflation in the last couple of months and during the recession is to be expected and represents really no surprise, although it is significant.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Although I expect inflation to remain low for some time, I do not feel that deflationary risks have increased to the point that we need to reflect them in our communications.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In fact, I think that to do so could only lower inflation expectations and put pressure on real interest rates.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I’ll stop at that point.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I favor alternative B. I think it’s important to reiterate that we will likely maintain our target range of 0 to ¼ percent for some time.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am certainly open to the idea of buying longer-term Treasuries, but I would not go forward with such a policy today, and I like the wording in B concerning our attitude toward that.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am certainly also very open to the idea of expanding our purchases of mortgage-backed securities and supportive of President Rosengren’s views on this.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think I would not go forward with it today, however, given that we have only just begun to buy these securities.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have a long way to go before we ramp up to anything close to our commitment, and right now it makes sense to wait to see what the Administration puts forward in terms of their program to support the banking system, to see if they are willing to collaborate with us in expanding the TALF facility, and in what directions they plan to go and in what ways they may proceed to support the housing market.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So just in terms of the timing of a further commitment there, I think I would be tempted to wait.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The one suggestion I would make concerning alternative B is that I would like to add to it the sentence from the end of paragraph 3 in alternative A that concerns the inflation risk assessment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The additional sentence reads, “Moreover, the Committee sees some risk that inflation could persist for a time below rates that best foster economic growth and price stability in the longer term.” I would add that to B because I think it is an accurate assessment of the situation, and commenting on the risk makes our discussion of inflation comparable to our discussion of growth, where we also comment on the risks.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As you noted, we all agree that the outlook for economic growth is bleak.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: To be sure, our policy actions so far have been aggressive; but even so, I have a predisposition to provide further monetary stimulus.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: From a risk-management perspective, there are very few scenarios I can think of that would suggest that further monetary stimulus would be a mistake.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But despite my bias for action, I am hesitant about how to proceed.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As I was putting my thoughts together for this portion of the meeting, I recalled the many conversations that we have had around this table about our communication policy.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Even when we were operating in a well-defined policy regime, we often experienced great difficulty in determining how best to express our decision and our intentions publicly.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Now we are operating in a new policy regime—credit easing—that we understand conceptually but for which no operational handbook yet exists.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We don’t know how to write down the policy rule for this environment, and we surely don’t have any empirical estimates to guide our decisions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Our discussion yesterday about what the effect is of a $250 billion purchase of MBS or a $250 billion purchase of longer-term Treasury securities demonstrates that we just do not have certainty around the effects of those actions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Before this crisis began, the public had a fairly good grasp of our policy rule.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Now they are trying to find the new rule, and I hope they do not find one before we figure out exactly what it is.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I certainly hope that we find it before John Taylor does.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The serious issue is how we can best manage expectations in this policy regime when we are so uncertain about so many things.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Alternative A, in my view, conveys a stronger degree of certainty to the public than I have at the moment about our policy rule.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I don’t know the basis for selecting $250 billion more of mortgage-backed securities or $250 billion additional in the longer-term Treasuries.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do not want to convey or set up the expectations that, by wanting to ease more, we are now going to use the $250 billion increase in our announcement of purchases, whether they are mortgage-backed securities or longer-term Treasuries, just as the ¼ percentage point change in the fed funds rate had been viewed in our prior policy regime.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Alternative B doesn’t cite specific quantities, but it does communicate a willingness to step up the pace and to extend the duration of our credit programs, and I think that is the appropriate action for today.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The alternative also reminds the public that additional credit easing in the form of the TALF and mortgage-backed security purchases is on the horizon, and I think we will be well served to tell the public as much as we can and then update them frequently as our own views evolve.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think alternative B does that without overstating what we know.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In favoring alternative B—and I am now the fourth person in this go-round—I am going to offer a fourth alternative in terms of the language.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I, like President Yellen, would add paragraph 3 from alternative A regarding our inflation outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Then given our go-round today and your comments about how you heard the go-round, Mr. Chairman, I think paragraph 2 in alternative A more accurately describes the view that we have had more weakening than we thought.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So those changes—paragraphs 2 and 3 out of alternative A but paragraph 4 out of alternative B—are what I would recommend for today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just to clarify, I think what Brian says is right.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The only difference between alternative A, paragraph 2, and alternative B, paragraph 2 is that in A(2) it says “weakened somewhat more than anticipated” whereas in B(2) it says just “remains weak.”

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Right, and we were commenting that many of us said that things had gotten weaker.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: That is the only observation I would make.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am going to counsel essentially a wait- and-see attitude, and then I am going to confuse you by arguing that later we should be very aggressive.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think the wait-and-see attitude would echo a lot of what President Yellen said.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We have a new Administration coming in.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They are promising to be very aggressive on many dimensions.

speaker: BULLARD
text: One of them is a fiscal stimulus package.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think we want to see what that turns out to be and what the provisions of that are at the end of the day.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There we have some fairly good expectations, but I think I would still want to see how it pans out.

speaker: BULLARD
text: More critical are the discussions about direct approaches to try to mitigate problems in financial markets, possibly through an aggregator bank.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I see this as absolutely critical as to how we might proceed going forward, so I would want to hear more about what is going to happen on that dimension.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I do think we will get a lot of information over the next several weeks along that dimension, so that is an argument to wait and see what happens.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, we have our program of outright purchases of MBS, which is generally regarded as successful, but we are only a bit along on that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We are not up to our $500 billion target, and so we can let that continue while we try to get information about what the new Administration has in mind.

speaker: BULLARD
text: For these reasons, I think my position is most consistent with alternative B, but I do have several comments on the alternatives.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My first comment—and I was talking about this last time—is that I would prefer to get the federal funds rate off the top of the statement.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would move it to the end.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is not projected to change for a long time, maybe four years.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What you learn in English class about writing is that you put your main message first.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Your main message is, Here are the things that are different from where we were last time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Obviously the interest rate is not going to change for a long time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You want to be stressing right off the bat that here is the key decision that we made today, and so I would try to rearrange this to put that first.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I do not have specific suggestions on this.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that would go a long way to communicate the nature of monetary policy during 2009, 2010, and 2011.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Again, I want to stress that we really have to work hard to get the private sector off the idea that the federal funds rate is the definition of monetary policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There are many things that we have been discussing that can be done, and we are doing them, so we have to design our statement to reflect that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that even our own thinking has not evolved away from the federal funds rate as the definition of monetary policy as much as it needs to.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A central bank that refuses to talk openly about money creation is suspect.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If we refuse to discuss the matter or discuss the matter only euphemistically, we will lose credibility.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Furthermore, others will discuss it for us, and the private sector will define who we are and what we are doing.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I think we should be more open in talking about our policy, which is direct open market purchases by reserve creation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We should think harder about that, and we should talk more about that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that I have quantitative measures.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I know we do not like to talk about money here, but let’s talk about money for just a minute.

speaker: BULLARD
text: M2 growth was quite rapid in the fourth quarter, and that seems promising to me given the situation globally.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But it seems that the staff expects M2 growth actually to moderate in 2009 down to 3 percent.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That seems counterproductive to me.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We should be more aggressive if we want to get something like a broad measure of money growing rapidly enough that we’re sure that we’re going to be able to avoid a global deflation trap.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That gives you something to shoot for.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We recognize that the old debates on money pointed out that linkages are not tied to ultimate outcomes.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We know that, but still, in an environment of zero nominal interest rates, this might be a reasonable way to go.

speaker: BULLARD
text: People would understand what we’re talking about and would understand that we have our inflation objectives in mind as we are trying to ease here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So that is just a little comment on M2.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I have also come to the conclusion—and maybe all of you were ahead of me—that time may not be a healer here as far as financial market problems.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There were a lot of comments around the table that, well, we’ll give the financial markets more time—six months—to adjust and so on.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Well, we are 18 months into this crisis, and I actually thought when we were a year into the crisis that markets had had enough time to adjust.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It did not prove to be the case.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So the thing is that these information problems do not go away with the passage of time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that is the key thing that we have learned here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Eighteen months along, and this is as bad as ever—this is in the last couple of weeks.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So direct approaches to solve market information problems are going to be essential, and that’s one reason that we need to see what the new Treasury and the new Administration have in mind on that dimension.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But to the extent that a direct solution does not materialize—and it is certainly very possible that something gets proposed, and something gets done, and then it does not work very well—then that may dictate our policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We may have to be all the more aggressive in that scenario, but I want to wait and see how this stacks up in the next few weeks.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Explicit numbers in the alternatives, as in Alternative A, seem crude and suspect to me.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What we would like to be talking about is the growth rate of the balance sheet net of the temporary components or the easily reversible components.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We would like to cull out the lender-of-last-resort programs, the ones that we think will go away in a reasonable time frame or will naturally go away if market conditions improve.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But we also have more-persistent or more­ permanent components of the balance sheet, such as MBS purchases, which I do not think we will be in a position to reverse anytime soon.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That to me is just an increase in the money supply.

speaker: BULLARD
text: These individual numbers might also create option values to waiting in the market.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You might think that mortgage rates are low today, but maybe the Fed will come out in the spring and announce another $500 billion, and so you will wait because you think mortgage rates are going to be even lower in the future.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In the past when we have talked about quantitative things, it has always been in growth rate terms or some kind of growth rate strategy that extended over the whole projection period, so the explicit numbers at this point seem crude to me.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My sense is that we may have room to do much more in open market purchases than we have right now based on what the Greenbook is telling us.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Five years from now we still do not have inflation up at 2 percent, as President Rosengren pointed out.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If that is really what we think—and one of the simulations added $1 trillion to that and we still did not hit our inflation target after five years—possibly we have room to do a lot more and could be a lot more aggressive.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But I just do not think at this point we have the right metrics in place, so I just cannot be sure at this point.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that is where we can improve in the next couple of meetings.

speaker: KOHN
text: I certainly think the economic outlook is unsatisfactory, and it sure has not gotten any better over the intermeeting period.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am not sure it has gotten materially worse.

speaker: KOHN
text: If I look at the Greenbook forecast, the revisions to Q4 and Q1 are to the right of the decimal point, and we have a lot more fiscal stimulus coming.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am not totally comfortable with President Pianalto’s suggestion to emphasize that it has gotten worse, but certainly the outlook remains quite weak.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we are in a situation where we need to be looking for everything we can do to ease financial conditions.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would encourage you, Mr. Chairman, to pursue an understanding with the Treasury, which you talked about yesterday, about the division of responsibilities on risk-taking and also about reserve sterilization over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: In particular, if we can get legislation and understanding on the latter that enables the Treasury or, even better, the Federal Reserve to issue bills without debt limits and congressional controls, what you called yesterday the shadow price of our balance sheet space would diminish very, very considerably, and we could play the more aggressive role that President Bullard was talking about.

speaker: KOHN
text: We wouldn’t have to worry about how we are going to take it back.

speaker: KOHN
text: If we have another tool to take it back, we would be much more aggressive on our activities.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think right now the constraints on the financial system are more about capital and worries about future capital, downside risk, than they are about liquidity.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do like the division of labor in the TALF—that the Treasury takes the risk and we supply the liquidity.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think I am uncertain now whether it will be effective.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think there is a good chance, but as we get experience with that, we should be looking very hard at other markets like CMBS that might also be helpful.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also, we should be looking at how we could be useful in other aspects of TARP 2, subject to the constraints about risk-taking and balance sheet space that you had noted yesterday, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think lifting and ring-fencing assets may be very, very valuable to reducing risk and stabilizing the system.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the Treasury security purchases, I think it is correct not to do that now.

speaker: KOHN
text: I guess I would keep it a little more on the front burner than what I am hearing from some other people.

speaker: KOHN
text: Rates are pretty low now.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would keep my eye on those forward rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: If they look as though they are coming up, I would give it some serious consideration if we thought that the market was building expectations about future rates that were inconsistent with returning the economy to high levels of employment over time.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would be more in favor of it.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think we have a number of things in train right now.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to see how the Administration is working out.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with the others who have said that we are temporarily in wait-and-see mode.

speaker: KOHN
text: I am comfortable with not doing anything now, as we have under alternative B, but working very, very hard on new initiatives as we see where we can be useful.

speaker: KOHN
text: With regard to other wording issues on alternative B, I agree with President Yellen and President Pianalto that taking that sentence from A about inflation being too low and putting it in paragraph 3 here would be good, especially in conjunction with that “help to preserve price stability” that President Fisher suggested we put in the last paragraph because now we are helping to preserve it from below.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think those two things would work together, and I hope we have the long-term projections coming out, which will reinforce that message.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I agree with that.

speaker: KOHN
text: President Bullard yesterday and again today emphasized whether the monetary aggregates or reserve aggregates can be useful to us.

speaker: KOHN
text: I guess I start somewhat skeptical about that, but I think we should be doing very hard research about whether broad measures of money or narrow measures of reserves have some relationship to spending even at the zero bound.

speaker: KOHN
text: President Bullard, you said that M2 growth looks a little low to you this year.

speaker: KOHN
text: Under these circumstances, how are we going to raise that?

speaker: KOHN
text: Will putting in more reserves do anything?

speaker: KOHN
text: I am not sure, but I would encourage you and your staff and others around the System to work hard on whether these quantitative measures are more useful to us right now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Two or three people have mentioned the last sentence in paragraph 3.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would just like to get a bit of reaction from Governor Kohn or President Yellen.

speaker: HOENIG
text: My concern with putting that sentence in is that you change expectations toward the thing you are trying to avoid.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we suddenly start saying that we are thinking inflation is getting too low and it is not consistent, people then are going to be convinced that it is getting too low and we are going to put more pressure on it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We ought at least to think about that before we get on a bandwagon here.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I do not know if anyone wants to comment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would just reiterate that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I worry about that phrase for exactly that reason.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We potentially shape the expectations in a way that we do not want to have them shaped by going too far in that direction.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I share your view.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is a very difficult question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, it also suggests that our policy will be more aggressive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it is a bit hard.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I honestly do not know.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Or, in fact, it may suggest that, if we believe it, our policies aren’t going to be enough to prevent it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is in our longer-term forecasts.

speaker: KOHN
text: Well, we will be publishing forecasts that have those inflation numbers in them.

speaker: LACKER
text: The spread of views on this is likely to be related to the extent to which we believe our credibility is complete—in other words, if we think that expectations about inflation are so fragile and so changeable that our statement highlighting the possibility of deflation could move them around.

speaker: LACKER
text: On the other hand, you could take the point of view that they are so well anchored that it will not move them around.

speaker: LACKER
text: I find myself in the Hoenig and Plosser camp on this—not viewing them as as well established as we want.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, that is consistent with my statement.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The tension here is that this is probably factually correct, and so the question is whether or not you want to say what is factually correct because you are afraid that it will influence expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, there are a lot of things that are factually correct that we don’t say.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is also factually correct.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Others can comment on this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I must admit to not having a strong view myself.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the coward’s way out is to say that we do not know yet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would be one reason, President Yellen, to delay a meeting or two before putting that in.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But, of course, I understand exactly what you are saying, and it may well be the case that this is yet another way of signaling a long-term, aggressive policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But, President Evans, you are next, so why don’t we just go straight to you?

speaker: EVANS
text: Let me ask a question.

speaker: EVANS
text: Has anybody conveyed that thought in speeches or testimony either from you or Governor Kohn, in which case it would be less newsworthy?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do not think so, and that is why I am a little leery.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have certainly said it in speeches.

speaker: EVANS
text: I may have said something like that, too; I’m not quite sure.

speaker: EVANS
text: I do find myself largely in agreement with the emerging consensus here.

speaker: EVANS
text: In fact, as I was listening to President Yellen’s comments, I found them to be wholly satisfactory from my viewpoint.

speaker: EVANS
text: I do have a preference for alternative A today.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think obviously what we would like to do is to lower the funds rate, but we cannot do that.

speaker: EVANS
text: So we are struggling for the best way to do that, and we do not have a great way to understand exactly the influence of our credit programs on that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I ask myself what the value of waiting and seeing is right now.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the one hand, we have not implemented the TALF, although we have been talking about it for quite some time, and so it will be useful to have some experience with that and see what the signals are coming from that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I find myself in agreement with Governor Kohn on this, but I am unsure how it is going to work out, and so there will probably be some adjustments.

speaker: EVANS
text: Then I ask myself whether we can afford to wait, given what we are looking at.

speaker: EVANS
text: It does seem as if there is a lot of uncertainty as to fiscal policy—exactly what the size of it will be and how it will play out.

speaker: EVANS
text: In our own forecast we have a stronger role than some others, but uncertainty is there.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I looked at alternative A with the MBS, it mentions that we are not going to complete this until the end of the third quarter, and that by itself has a great amount of delay.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that is very pragmatic, and that is the way it would actually occur.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not quite sure whether the cost of putting that off and announcing it at our next meeting, if that is the right way to do it, would be that high.

speaker: EVANS
text: There is also the uncertainty of what the Administration will pursue.

speaker: EVANS
text: As President Bullard and others mentioned, if there is a proposal for a large aggregator bank coming forward from the Administration, what will be the size of that?

speaker: EVANS
text: What are the dimensions of that, and would we need a big action now or how would that play into it?

speaker: EVANS
text: There are a lot of uncertainties, and so I just cannot say I know for sure on that.

speaker: EVANS
text: In terms of the specifics, I did find myself okay with the language on inflation perhaps as “below rates that best foster economic growth.” But I agree—there is a lot of uncertainty as to how that will be perceived, but it does seem factually correct that there is some risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I would be okay with that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I suppose we have not really discussed—or have we?—your question, Mr. Chairman, about the sentence whether we anticipate a gradual recovery later this year.

speaker: EVANS
text: It does seem to me as though in almost every forecast we see economic growth certainly being positive by the fourth quarter and we hope by the third quarter.

speaker: EVANS
text: I worry a bit that, if we are more pessimistic in our statement about that, it would seem to be some type of vote of no confidence in fiscal actions that are forthcoming.

speaker: EVANS
text: It doesn’t seem to be factually incorrect that we are expecting this, and so I would favor leaving that.

speaker: LACKER
text: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: LACKER
text: I fully support the expansion that we have engineered in our monetary liabilities.

speaker: LACKER
text: I view our strategy as having expanded them fairly dramatically to provide stimulus now that we are at the zero bound.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think our strategy going forward is going to be focused on maintaining them at a high level and, while the economy is in distress, perhaps varying the quantity and perhaps increasing it should distress increase, and that seems productive.

speaker: LACKER
text: When the economy recovers, begin withdrawing that stimulus; then at some time in the future, lift the funds rate off the floor.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am cognizant that assessing the appropriate magnitude of that expansion is terribly difficult, for reasons that President Bullard and Governor Kohn discussed.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are, in fact, at the limit of our professional understanding of the transmission mechanism, although I think there is a lot that is known that we could fruitfully review and discuss in the Committee on this issue.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am less supportive of the way in which we brought about this expansion in our monetary liabilities, as you all know.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I said yesterday and on many other occasions, I think the case for targeted credit programs is weak, briefly put.

speaker: LACKER
text: They do not address any demonstrable market failure.

speaker: LACKER
text: They channel credit away from other worthy borrowers, exacerbate moral hazard, and set bad fiscal precedents.

speaker: LACKER
text: Regarding the exit strategy, I do not see anything inherent in the economics that has motivated our intervention into these programs or that links that to the state of the business cycle and where the funds rate needs to be.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I do not see why it would necessarily be the case that, when we want to lift the funds rate, the perceived needs in any of these dysfunctional credit markets will have necessarily gone away.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that is clear just from the way the case has been made and the fact that credit markets can dysfunction in the way they have been claimed to dysfunction in peacetime, in any part of the business cycle.

speaker: LACKER
text: The TALF is our next new targeted credit program to be introduced.

speaker: LACKER
text: It is on deck to be implemented in February.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe that it would be better policy for us not to implement the TALF but instead to expand our balance sheet by buying U.S. Treasury securities.

speaker: LACKER
text: The effect on credit markets will be more neutral.

speaker: LACKER
text: It will avoid distorting credit flows across private borrowing segments.

speaker: LACKER
text: Adverse incentive effects would be minimized, and I think it would maintain more distance between us and redistributional fiscal policies.

speaker: LACKER
text: Concerning buying Treasuries, I think that monetization is something that I am less concerned with because the way I view it is that the choice should be what we buy, in which case we are monetizing the same amount of stuff.

speaker: LACKER
text: I can appreciate the concern that, coming at a juncture in time in which a large fiscal stimulus is being enacted, there would be a natural risk—and I think it is a risk—that the public would make the inference that our increase in the balance sheet was at the behest of the Administration.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we should strive to avoid that.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we maintain our monetary liabilities flat across this episode for the next quarter or so, we would be able to do that, but I will admit that is a risk.

speaker: LACKER
text: You have had conversations and will have conversations with the Administration about the idea of a new accord.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I said yesterday, I applaud those.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that is another reason to hold off introducing any new program that we might ultimately be considering—and I think we ought to consider—transferring wholesale to the Treasury.

speaker: LACKER
text: For all of these reasons, Mr. Chairman, unless we decide at this meeting to defer the TALF, I would respectfully dissent because I would prefer to expand the monetary base by purchasing U.S. Treasury securities rather than through targeted credit programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would view it as unlikely that conditions would be unusual and exigent across a wide span of credit markets simultaneously when we were having a significant recovery in the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But of course, that is an empirical issue.

speaker: LACKER
text: Excuse me, if I could just reply—in the TALF as it is envisioned, we are to declare that for three years it is going to be unusual and exigent, as I understand it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The term funding lasts for three years, but the actual program ends at the end of this year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Right, which is similar, for example, to what the FDIC is doing with the systemic risk exception with the 10-year bond issuance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also, from a monetary policy point of view, our plan for these programs is to create terms that will automatically extinguish interest at some point as conditions normalize.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the interpretation is that circumstances have to be unusual and exigent at the time it is entered into.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, there are some legal niceties here that we can get to another time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it is clear that we will be keeping the funds rate between zero and 25 basis points for some time to come, although “some time to come” is a bit vague, which obviously has some desirability.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I recall last time that we had a significant discussion about making sure that our statements about the fed funds rate had some conditionality to them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do not know whether the statement the way it is worded is actually sufficiently conditional or conveys that message or not, but I just raise that as an important aspect of communicating.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our plans are, in fact, conditional, and we need to make sure that is included.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Actually, I can live with the language in alternative B. I think it does seem to characterize the current state of the economy, which is clearly quite weak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I expressed earlier, I am really not inclined to put in the additional sentence that President Yellen suggested for the reasons that I worry about the fragility of expectations, and I think we need to maintain our credibility and our firmness with our view that we are going to maintain those.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am also a little worried.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have two problems with alternative A.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One, it sounds too panicky to me.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Chairman and actually Governor Kohn mentioned the fact that things look pretty bleak.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But if you look at the Greenbook forecast, it is really not that much different from the one in December.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: December was a clear shocker, if you want to think in terms of changing people’s expectations about our forecast profile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: From December to now, it is not entirely obvious to me that the bad news we have received was that much unanticipated—maybe a little, but not hugely.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would hate our statement or the minutes to reflect such a gloomy view that the markets read it as another big downward shift in the forecast because I think it may do more to damage the markets and cause concern.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would like to have the minutes and even the statement reflect a little more that this was not entirely unanticipated, which is why I like alternative B.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is not that big a change in our view, which was pretty gloomy to begin with.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I have argued before, and others have mentioned, anchoring inflation expectations, as I alluded to, is central to both our credibility and our success going forward in this environment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I agree with President Bullard, as he said in the earlier go-round, that the Greenbook path—and I alluded to this as well—of a zero fed funds rate for the next four years paired with a 3 to 4 percent real growth rate and essentially no inflation to me seems highly implausible both as a positive statement in terms of a forecast and as a normative one.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Somehow those three pieces do not fit together real well in the way I think about the world, in part because I am not sure I understand entirely how the expansion of our balance sheet actually fits into that forecast and perhaps how that affects inflation as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I do not find that terribly, terribly plausible.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: More important, if we are to retain our credibility to maintain stability of inflation expectations, we must develop or offer a more transparent discussion of the link between our current policy actions and that objective or those expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do not think we have done that yet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In this regard, we do need to think more about sizes, quantities, and evolutions of our balance sheet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I stressed at our last meeting, and as President Bullard suggested, there are ways to begin doing that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t claim to know what those right quantitative measures are.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we need to do some research.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But just because we don’t know what the right measures are doesn’t mean that they don’t matter or that we should ignore them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The clarity of policy demanded by the public for the TARP and the pattern of interventions applies not just to the Treasury but also to our bailouts and our interventions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we need to continue to work on transparency in this regard and the way all of these pieces fit together.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Otherwise, I do fear that we would be further contributing to a delay in the recovery, as institutions sit on the sidelines and investors wait to see what next intervention or bailout is likely to come.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I am not terribly comfortable with alternative A. I don’t like naming quantities for some programs and not others.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that is not a good strategy—it singles out some programs as being more important.

speaker: PLOSSER
