text: I don’t think we know enough about the quantities to be able to mention them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also agree with President Hoenig and others who have suggested that we really don’t know how the fiscal policy bailout, the aggregator bank, and our roles in these various things might evolve.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We need to wait and see before we make commitments to specific numbers of things in which we are not sure what role we will play.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Finally, and related to this, I do have some concerns about continuing to discuss programs or actions that we might choose to pursue.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While I understand the intent of that may be to manage expectations and signal our commitment to explore every possible avenue to support the economy, such statements are speculative in some sense and may at times do more to confuse the market than to settle it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, if we were to talk about things we might do and then decide not to take these actions, how would that affect our credibility and the message that we are sending?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In his discussion, Brian talked about how the phrase about longer-term securities might be interpreted—and this is really what I am referring to.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t know how it is going to be interpreted, to tell you the truth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have a lot of uncertainty.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I do worry about our talking, in a statement of policy actions, about speculative actions that we don’t know whether we are going to do or not.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I worry about what that is going to do to the markets, particularly if at some future time we drop it, and that we may have gotten ourselves into a bind by putting it in there.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We need to think very carefully going forward in this regime when we really haven’t decided yet what policy instruments we are going to be using and how we are going to be using them— speculating about that in our statement seems to me to be a bit risky.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I can support alternative B, Mr. Chairman, pretty much as it stands, with the caveats about not being more negative than we were last time and some caveats about both the conditionality and the forward-looking statements.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my view, the worrisome recent developments in the financial markets, combined with the current self-reinforcing interplay of bank news, economic data, and deteriorating public confidence, call for another increment of action in advance of the Administration’s proposals with their inherent unpredictability—that is, the unpredictability of the political process.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I could or I will accept alternative B, but I support alternative A, which I would characterize as signaling that things are a bit worse, take out some insurance, and do a little more.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think the characterizations of the state of the economy in sections 2 and 3 are appropriate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I actually, to some extent, supported the use of the word “sizable,” but I am certainly okay with the change back to “significant” as a safer term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I also interpret section 3 as saying that at least continued disinflation is a real risk, and I think that is a realistic statement at this time.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I support alternative 1 in section 4 with its action of adding $250 billion to the MBS program.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am persuaded by the staff argument, which is supported by my own staff, to defer but keep on the table the introduction of a longer-term Treasury securities purchase program.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, I would tinker a little with the words “prepared to” for reasons somewhat similar to President Plosser’s.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think “prepared to” may convey too much intentionality.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It could be interpreted as “absolutely ready but holding off,” or conceivably someone else might interpret it as “inclined to but with some hesitancy at this stage.” I think it is, therefore, too ambiguous.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I would prefer signaling that the Committee “holds open the option” of such a program, and I would prefer those words over something like “still evaluating.” Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: STERN
text: I favor alternative B, as written.

speaker: STERN
text: I think it does accurately capture the sense of the discussion here.

speaker: STERN
text: There are probably other ways of capturing that sense, but for me that does the trick reasonably well.

speaker: STERN
text: I do think it provides us with ample flexibility—ample leeway in the short run—to pursue our objectives.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t worry much that it is going to unnecessarily constrain us in the next few months to do what we think we need to do.

speaker: STERN
text: So I find that all positive.

speaker: STERN
text: Finally, I would avoid associating quantities with purchases of mortgage-backed securities and other things.

speaker: STERN
text: They seem arbitrary at this point, and I think paragraph 4, as written, conveys the message without putting in the numbers.

speaker: STERN
text: So I am pretty happy with it as it stands.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I submitted my recommendations in writing.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am pleased with the way they were included.

speaker: FISHER
text: Basically, what I am hearing is that we should take alternative A and append paragraph 4 of alternative B and most parties would seem to be satisfied, at least those that are most worried and expressed themselves.

speaker: FISHER
text: I will use President Yellen as an example, but as others did as well.

speaker: FISHER
text: With regard to that one sentence that is at the end of paragraph 3—“Moreover, the Committee sees some of risk that inflation could persist for a time below rates that best foster economic growth,” et cetera—I think we offset that by the reference to “help to preserve price stability” at the very end.

speaker: FISHER
text: The reason I wanted that included—and I thank you for its being included—is that it speaks from both sides of this.

speaker: FISHER
text: We are not going to tolerate deflation, and we are aware of the fact that there are concerns that we are setting the stage for an inflationary backlash.

speaker: FISHER
text: So my recommendation is to use those first three paragraphs in alternative A and the last paragraph in alternative B. I agree with the majority of the sentiment at this table.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would not have specific numbers.

speaker: FISHER
text: My colleague to my left refers to that as crude.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would say that it just puts a target on our chest, meaning that it gives the markets something to shoot at.

speaker: FISHER
text: But if we don’t deliver or somehow we are not interested in finally getting those numbers, we have basically set ourselves up for disappointing the marketplace.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would also, in the interest of being provocative but at the same time sensible, take President Bullard’s suggestion with a full heart.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would take that first sentence and change it: “The Federal Open Market Committee will keep its target range for the federal funds rate at 0 to ¼ percent,” and I would put it as the second sentence in paragraph 4.

speaker: FISHER
text: The fact is that we are focused on all of the rest.

speaker: FISHER
text: So it would read, “The Federal Reserve will employ all available tools to promote the resumption of sustainable economic growth and to preserve price stability.

speaker: FISHER
text: The FOMC will keep its target range for the federal funds rate at 0 to ¼ percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: The focus”—and the operative word is “focus”—“of the Committee’s policies,” et cetera, et cetera, et cetera.

speaker: FISHER
text: So those are my recommendations there.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would like to add one other point, Mr. Chairman, and that is when we talk about waiting to see what happens.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that is a very good point.

speaker: FISHER
text: We don’t know what is going to come out from the fiscal side.

speaker: FISHER
text: We don’t know what is going to be proposed in terms of the Treasury.

speaker: FISHER
text: President Stern made what I thought a sensible reference today not only to the aggregator bank but also perhaps to the need to close down some operations.

speaker: FISHER
text: I hope that we will bear that in mind.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would like to leave you with just a simple analogy.

speaker: FISHER
text: In the medical field, the greatest costs are at the very end of life, the last year of life.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is, certain that the sting of death will strike, we spend most of our medical expenses keeping someone alive, knowing that they are going to die.

speaker: FISHER
text: It seems to me that we are doing that with too many institutions.

speaker: FISHER
text: You made a comment in our last conference call that you drew the line at the failure of Bank of America.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think I understand you.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I would not draw the line at letting somebody fail, and I think we need to begin to work our way toward that in order to clear the air and deal with the issues in a forthright manner.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is a separate subject.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have strayed too far.

speaker: FISHER
text: In summary, alternative A, the first three paragraphs, with paragraph 4 from B, and consider President Bullard’s grammatical change as sensible English.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My remark about Bank of America referred to a disorderly or uncontrolled failure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously an orderly wind-down that preserves stability is a different matter.

speaker: WARSH
text: Maybe I will start with a note on the political economy before turning to the statement.

speaker: WARSH
text: I had thought that we would know the situation was improved when the Fed was off the front pages.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we have been off the front pages not because the situation has improved but because the Treasury is taking over the front pages, and that is a good thing.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I feel pretty comfortable that we are finding ourselves slowly but surely into this week’s headlines that we are murky and they don’t know.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am not that encouraged, as I think about this statement for us, to try to make news if we don’t have it.

speaker: WARSH
text: The baton has been passed to a new Administration, and we should be cautious about stepping up before we know exactly where they are and before we know where we are.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is just an instinct, which maybe pervades and suggests a preference for alternative B.

speaker: WARSH
text: With respect to a couple of the items that have been debated on alternative B, Mr. Chairman, I would resist the suggestion that we import the sentence in section 3 of alternative A. I prefer to keep it as is.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would rather not, to the point made at the other end of the table, add on additional risk at this point in the public square.

speaker: WARSH
text: My own sense is that the risks haven’t changed materially since we last met.

speaker: WARSH
text: But adding that sentence suggests that somehow we are now acknowledging that they have, and at least to my mind it is not quite there.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even though sometimes I also have an instinct to make the statement a confessional of sorts, I think it is dangerous for us to do that until the lust is outside our hearts, so to speak.

speaker: WARSH
text: I had always been accused by someone who very recently sat at this table of temporizing.

speaker: WARSH
text: But with his recent absence, I suggest that we temporize here on paragraph 3.

speaker: WARSH
text: Though I think it is quite possible that we will include a sentence along the lines that President Yellen suggested, put me in the temporizing camp, but please don’t tell him.

speaker: WARSH
text: So what does that mean?

speaker: WARSH
text: I like alternative B as written.

speaker: WARSH
text: Not to add to your burdens, but I am also uncomfortable with the way the sentence reads on the purchase of longer-term Treasury securities.

speaker: WARSH
text: I read it and I think the markets would read it as that we have reached a decision.

speaker: WARSH
text: The way it is written now is that we have reached the decision that we are likely to do it later.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that is not quite where we are.

speaker: WARSH
text: So given the position we are in, I would make the following minor edits, which I think change it a little.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say, “The Committee also is prepared to purchase longer-term Treasury securities”—now I change a few words here—“if circumstances were to evolve in a way that such transactions would be particularly effective,” because, again, I think as written it says “if evolving circumstances indicate.” I think they read that to say, “We presume circumstances will be evolving, and we will take these actions.” I guess it may be more conditional and take us slightly out of the box in which we find ourselves.

speaker: WARSH
text: So, again, my suggestion would be, “If circumstances were to evolve in a way that indicates that such transactions would be particularly effective,” though I think it is ideal that we not find ourselves in the situation of pondering and debating in the public square.

speaker: WARSH
text: Given where we are, I think that is the best alternative we can do at this moment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I just want to make an observation that, if we are going to have the economic projections come out at the same time, the public doesn’t read the Greenbook, but it does look at our projections.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Between now and October the inflation forecast will dramatically change.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we are doing the long-run projections at the same time, the biggest bar is going to be at 2 percent, and our forecast is going to say that virtually none of us thinks we will get there in three years.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So in terms of being factually accurate, we should at least think about the implications of our economic projections coming out at the same time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To complicate this even further, on the one hand this would be a change from December, and there has not been a big change, in our view, since December.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, Debbie points out to me that the minutes from the December meeting had exactly this sentence about inflation—that some members saw significant risks that inflation could decline and persist for a time at uncomfortably low levels, and then similar language that relates to being below the sustainable level, and so on.

speaker: LACKER
text: I had a friendly amendment to Governor Warsh.

speaker: LACKER
text: “If evolving circumstances were to indicate” seems more parsimonious.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are going to have to review all of these things in the end here.

speaker: DUKE
text: I think I am marginally favoring A with B4 or B with A2 and 3.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s go through that again.

speaker: DUKE
text: I could be perfectly happy with B. I think the difference is that it is not so much that we don’t know yet that we are going to have to do something more.

speaker: DUKE
text: It is that we don’t know yet what that something more is likely to be.

speaker: DUKE
text: The uncertainties that are in my mind and those that have been expressed are likely to be resolved by the time of our next meeting, such as the shape and the effect of the fiscal stimulus; the strategy for dealing with weaknesses in the banking system, including whether it is going to be additional capital injections, an aggregator bank, or nationalization; the pace of bank closures; and the strategy for dealing with distressed mortgages and foreclosures and, more important, our role in whatever that strategy is likely to be.

speaker: DUKE
text: If our balance sheet is not required to take problem assets from the bank balance sheets, it may very well be required to provide loans for the subsequent purchases of either those assets or the underlying collateral.

speaker: DUKE
text: Finally, with respect to commercial real estate, I think that we still need to investigate the structure of the commercial MBS and their relationship with servicers to see if we are going to have the same modification issues that we have had with residential mortgages.

speaker: DUKE
text: So with all of those unknowns that are likely to be resolved in the short term, again, I am marginally happier with conveying the rationale for greater action but not yet identifying that action.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have been discussing whether we should embark on a long-term Treasury purchase program or whether we should engage in a greater magnitude or duration of agency MBS purchases.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am not sure these really are the next and best escalation options.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Not surprisingly, I agree with the staff memo on long­ term Treasuries, since I helped write it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the TALF expansion really is probably our next and best escalation option, but we are not prepared to do that quite at this time because we have to do that hand in hand with the Treasury.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I want to agree with Governor Warsh that this is probably a time for temporizing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It seems clear to me that we do want to continue to expand our liquidity facilities, but to do so we have to satisfy a number of criteria.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would argue that there are five criteria that any liquidity expansion should satisfy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, the market in question needs to be dysfunctional, and we might measure that by lack of liquidity, higher spreads, and lower volumes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Two, the dysfunction has to be tightening financial conditions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There needs to be a fairly direct link between the market in which we are intervening and economic activity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Also, if there is a clear alternative source of funds, then intervention may not be warranted.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, we need to be confident that our facilities are likely to be helpful in improving market function and easing financial conditions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The goal should not be to displace markets but instead to provide support that primes markets to function better.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the CPFF is a good example in that respect.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fourth, we need to be comfortable that we will indeed be secure to our satisfaction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fifth, we have to be comfortable that exit from these programs can be managed to avoid any conflict with our dual mandate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The TALF program, especially if the Treasury provides us with some support on the balance sheet exit issue, appears to fit best with these criteria.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If the TALF works as anticipated in restarting the consumer ABS market and bringing down AAA-rated ABS spreads, then we may wish, with the Treasury as partner adding additional TARP capital, to broaden it to other asset classes that are also in distress.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In particular, the CMBS market and the nonconforming RMBS market appear to be very good candidates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is not just the financing related to new activity that matters but also the ability for maturing debt to be refinanced.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is a particularly important issue in both commercial real estate and nonconforming residential mortgage markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I believe the TALF program is very important because it provides three elements that are not broadly available to private investors right now—(1) term funding, (2) leverage and balance sheet capacity, and (3) protection against tail risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The TALF would bypass banks and dealers and provide balance sheet capacity directly to risk capital—capacity that today is unavailable because of the deleveraging that is taking place among banks and dealers and making them much less willing to extend such credit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It also provides protection against tail risk.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because the financing is done on a nonrecourse basis, the most an investor can lose is the size of the haircut.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In this sense, although the TALF program is a lending program, one can also consider it to be a contingent purchase program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In very bad states of the world in which AAA-rated consumer ABS tranches decline sharply in value, these securities will be put to the Federal Reserve and placed in an SPV capitalized by TALF money.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second issue I want to talk about is the exit issue.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Although I agree that this is a very important topic, I wonder how helpful it is to worry about this publicly, for two reasons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, anxiety expressed by us about the exit issue may fan fears that we will not be able to exit smoothly and avoid an inflation problem.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If market participants were broadly to share this opinion, the result could be higher risk premiums and tighter financial market conditions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the more we express concern with exit and our balance sheet, the more we may alter expectations about how much we are willing to do to support the economy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we should err on the side of reinforcing the message that the FOMC will do all it can to ease financial conditions and stimulate the economy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Worrying publicly about the balance sheet seems to undercut that goal to some degree.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At the same time, we should work aggressively to make sure that our balance sheet will not interfere with the appropriate conduct of monetary policy later, and we should clearly explain to the public our ability to do so.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of the statement, I prefer alternative B language generally, but I would suggest two alterations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In paragraph 2, the language that “the outlook for the economy remains weak” seems too mild to me and could be taken by market participants as sounding complacent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I prefer the language from alternative A, which states that “the economy has weakened somewhat more than anticipated,” which I believe is factually correct and provides greater information about how the data are coming in relative to our forecast.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I also think it signals greater concern by the Committee about the outlook, which is where the Committee actually is in terms of thinking about policy going forward.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second alteration I would suggest in alternative B is where we are talking about the implementation of the TALF.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We say “next month” in alternative B.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Given that our ability to enact this program is subject to some degree to the Treasury’s coming along with us in a timely fashion, I think it would be better to change “next month” to “later this winter,” which will give us until March 21, giving us a few more weeks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That last thing worries me quite a bit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What did we have in December?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Another possibility might be just to say “soon.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I thought of that as well, but does that satisfy you there, Vice Chairman?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think “later this winter” does provide an endpoint.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am not sure how long “soon” is.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is always winter somewhere.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have a lot to go through here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So just to get factual information here, my understanding from the staff was that we were well on track to implement during February, and I have heard nothing from the Treasury to indicate anything other than support for this program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, I think that is correct, although the Treasury right now is scrambling to get their new staff up and running.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So there is some risk that what had been agreed to by the old Treasury now needs to be sort of relitigated with the new Treasury.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That could delay our putting out a term sheet to market participants, which they really need to have several weeks ahead of time for this program to get up and operational.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think there is a good chance that we are still going to be able to make February or certainly early March, but we probably want a bit of wiggle room there because we don’t have complete control of the process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are you okay with “will soon implement”?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would prefer “winter,” but I can live with that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If we take a broad view of what “soon” means—yes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Brian, let’s accept that one, unless— President Fisher.

speaker: FISHER
text: Can’t we just say, “The Federal Reserve will be implementing”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is that okay with everybody?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “The Federal Reserve will be implementing.” Thank you, and thanks, everyone, for the useful comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me try to address a few other things here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we are very much in agreement on the substance—that we want to maintain an aggressive stance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I also would just say, as a general point, that I fully agree—and I am sure everyone does—that we want to look for better metrics and better ways of communicating and expressing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As a general invitation to all of you and your staffs, you don’t have to wait until the next meeting, and you don’t have to wait until the week before the next meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are delighted to hear explicit proposals for metrics or communication or statements that you would like to circulate, and we can discuss throughout the entire intermeeting period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is no need for us to wait until the last minute.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me just encourage you to follow through with that, and let us see your proposals.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There have been a number of suggestions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the spirit of temporizing, I do believe that, although we want to convey our concern about the economy and our willingness to be aggressive with policy, there really is a high likelihood that we will learn a great deal in the next intermeeting period about what the Treasury will be proposing, what the Congress will be proposing, and what our role will best be fitting into those overall ideas.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, hearing you, I am a bit reluctant to commit at this moment to a specific increase in either our GSE or our Treasury purchase program.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Perhaps we should have made more explicit yesterday what our plan was going to be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I would prefer to maintain the optionality of alternative B, which talks about standing ready both to expand the GSE program and to purchase Treasuries under the appropriate circumstances, and I will come back to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second set of suggestions had to do with the characterization of the economy and inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are two in particular.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One was whether to characterize the economy as weak or weakened somewhat more than anticipated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am actually a little surprised to hear the support for “weaker than anticipated” in that the Greenbook has not really changed much since December and the thrust of the commentary was that things were weak but not much weaker than anticipated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am in your hands.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am going to be taking some straw votes in a few minutes, so this is just a question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My sense on that one is that I could consider different language, but it seems as though “the outlook remains weak” conveys our view.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am not sure that I have heard that the outlook itself has changed significantly since our last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was my sense, but I am willing to be instructed on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the statement about inflation being below the level consistent with economic growth and price stability, a number of people suggested that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think I am okay with that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It was introduced in the minutes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I am going to do in a minute—let me just warn you—is take a couple of straw votes, and I will ask all participants to tell me whether you would like to add that sentence or not.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know any other way to resolve this, since I personally think we could go either way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other issues—I think it is a very interesting suggestion to move the material about the federal funds rate into paragraph 4.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I wish that you had sent that in a week ago so we could have thought about it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it makes sense, but I guess at the last minute here I am a bit anxious about making that big a change in the structure of our statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I reiterate our interest in hearing proposals for statements throughout the intermeeting period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the issue about Treasuries—it is difficult in both directions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser raises the question about raising a possibility and then not doing it, which is certainly an issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, we have also been criticized for calling audibles on the line at the last minute and surprising people.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Based on the discussion and on things that President Lacker said, and so on, I think it is in fact a possibility that we would take this route.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I personally think that we shouldn’t rule it out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is not something we want to undertake yet because we certainly want to find out what the other options are going to be in terms of the other things that the Treasury is proposing and so on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Mr. Chairman, on that point—it does concern me that this is a bit of a conundrum about how we do the statements, but I would be more comfortable with the language that Governor Warsh suggested, which gives a little more conditionality to it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, I was diagramming that sentence.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I didn’t even write it down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, as simplified by President Lacker, it was “is prepared to purchase longer-term Treasury securities, if evolving circumstances were to indicate that such transactions would be particularly effective.” I think that’s three subjunctives.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the Lacker suggestion is “if circumstances were to indicate that.”

speaker: LACKER
text: Oh, I didn’t take out “evolving,” but I am indifferent on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But see, the purpose of “evolving” is the sense that—don’t you want to convey the optionality that this is going to take place and will be evaluated over time?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The word “evolving” suggests an ongoing process.

speaker: WARSH
text: The delta is, Are the evolving circumstances going to evolve as we presume, in which case we have pre-committed to it?

speaker: WARSH
text: Or is our decision going to be based on whether the evolving circumstances change in one way, which then triggers our “yes”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, Governor Warsh, there is an “if” here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I mean, that certainly implies that our action is conditional on certain things happening that may or may not happen.

speaker: WARSH
text: May I use a life line?

speaker: WARSH
text: Brian, do you read it, as written, to say that we have reached a decision and our decision is contingent upon facts of the world in the future or that we have reached a decision and, if the world proceeds as we expect it will, then we will do this?

speaker: WARSH
text: I am not sure I picked up from your introduction which you think you and markets would read.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I read this as saying that we don’t know how the circumstances will evolve, but if they evolve in the way that indicates that this would be particularly helpful, then we are prepared to purchase.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, for example, one possible theory would be that we will respond only if there is a big backup in rates and that seems to be an effective approach.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would be an example of evolving circumstances.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My guess is—though it is always foolish to make guesses—that this will be viewed as slightly negative news, not positive news, for the Treasury market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will have to see.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say that Treasury markets are sort of 50/50 on when we are going to go forward.

speaker: WARSH
text: So this is really the question: Does it go 55/45 or vice versa?

speaker: WARSH
text: It is hard to know.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the sense is that the more they read the “if” to be an “if,” the more conditional it is and the more consensus there is around the table, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: WARSH
text: So it is really just whether we think that there is sufficient conditionality as written or whether the Lacker–Warsh thing adds to the conditionality.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, I fear that taking out “evolving” actually reduces the clarity because “evolving” implies an ongoing process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Without the word “evolving,” it suggests that we are still evaluating the current situation and then trying to assess whether the conditions are met to take the action.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, the action words are “prepared to purchase.” Are we going to maintain those in there, or would we change it, keep “evolving,” and put “will consider purchasing”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, we already have a number of subjunctives.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it is the “prepared to purchase” that indicates a decision made, and that is the phrase that bothers me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One reason that I was comfortable with this language was that I do think that we will not be maintaining the world in suspended animation indefinitely.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will have much more clarity, I believe, by the next meeting, and at the next meeting we would be able to say something like “the Federal Reserve will be focusing its attention on X, Y, or Z.”

speaker: KOHN
text: Mr. Chairman, I think putting the “particularly” in there actually steps us back a little, despite the “is prepared to.” It is an “if” clause already.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t see how “if circumstances were to indicate” is different from “if evolving circumstances indicate,” particularly with the “particularly” in there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I don’t want to pull back completely because I do think there is a realistic possibility—and I realize that there are different views—that it is going to evolve over time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We still have a lot of discussion and further thinking to do, not only about the specific types of purchases and programs but also about how we are going to evaluate the overall thrust of policy, and so on.

speaker: WARSH
text: To conflate game shows, I don’t want to be voted off the island.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Have I addressed the major questions?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I would like to do is propose alternative B with two issues that we will now take a straw vote on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The one change we have agreed on so far is “the Federal Reserve will be implementing the TALF.” The other two possible changes have to do with the characterization of the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first one would be in B2, to replace the first sentence with the first sentence from A2, “suggests that the economy has weakened somewhat more than anticipated.”

speaker: EVANS
text: Mr. Chairman, it is the “anticipated.” Couldn’t we just say, “The economy has weakened further”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, there is a distinction between the outlook and the economy itself.

speaker: EVANS
text: In this case, it doesn’t say “outlook.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, do you want to say, “The economy has weakened somewhat further”?

speaker: EVANS
text: That would be okay with me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Pianalto, do you have a view?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: How about “suggests that the economy has weakened further”?

speaker: KOHN
text: What do we have about the outlook then?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: No one seemed to object to the last sentence, which gives a recovery but with downside risks.

speaker: KOHN
text: But it doesn’t have a sense that the outlook is weak until that recovery.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have to think about this.

speaker: KOHN
text: The outlook remains weak, and there is—

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think “weakened further” is not dangerous.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it’s the economy rather than the outlook that has weakened further.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is as mild as saying we have stepped from the fourth quarter into the first quarter, which is going to be a contraction.

speaker: LACKER
text: I missed what’s on the table.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is it that the economy has weakened further or that the outlook has weakened further?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I hear a slight preference for—okay, Brian— “suggests that the economy has weakened further.” All right.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The last question, then, is whether or not to add or replace B3 with A3.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would add the sentence that “the Committee sees some risk that inflation could persist for a time below rates that best foster economic growth and price stability.” I propose to take a straw vote of all of the participants—not just members but participants.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All those in favor of making the change?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One, two, three, four, five, six.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it is a reasonable change.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think it is dramatic.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess we have made three changes now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I propose alternative B. I think it conveys the sense of the Committee.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It maintains, as much as possible, our optionality while suggesting that we are going to be aggressive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, we will be looking both to the Treasury and to the government for their actions over the next intermeeting period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Once again, I invite members and other participants to submit their suggestions for communication and measurement over the intermeeting period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I probably should mention that there will be opportunities for us to communicate about our views further.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, I have a testimony on February 10 on our transparency and our communication.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a speech at the National Press Club, which will have more of a press conference type of flavor, sort of between a speech and a press conference, on February 18.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then, I have the Humphrey-Hawkins hearings, followed by Budget Committee hearings, so you will be seeing a lot of me on television.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My complexion is not usually green but probably will be by then.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we will have a chance to communicate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I hope that each of you, in your own speeches and other interactions with the public, will take as much of the opportunity as you can to try to explain what we are doing, how we are thinking about the economy, and how we are thinking about our policy in this unusual environment.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just want to thank you, Mr. Chairman, for the spirit in which we have conducted these conversations in this meeting.

speaker: FISHER
text: As you know, at least of some of us felt that we might be disenfranchised.

speaker: FISHER
text: You may be enfranchising us too much.

speaker: FISHER
text: At least speaking for myself, I want to thank you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we are ready for a roll call vote.

speaker: DANKER
text: Would you like me to read the statement, as amended?

speaker: DANKER
text: “The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to keep its target range for the federal funds rate at 0 to ¼ percent.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Committee continues to anticipate that economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate for some time.

speaker: DANKER
text: Information received since the Committee met in December suggests that the economy has weakened further.

speaker: DANKER
text: Industrial production, housing starts, and employment have continued to decline steeply, as consumers and businesses have cut back spending.

speaker: DANKER
text: Furthermore, global demand appears to be slowing significantly.

speaker: DANKER
text: Conditions in some financial markets have improved, in part reflecting government efforts to provide liquidity and strengthen financial institutions; nevertheless, credit conditions for households and firms remain extremely tight.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Committee anticipates that a gradual recovery in economy activity will begin later this year, but the downside risks to that outlook are significant.

speaker: DANKER
text: In light of the declines in the prices of energy and other commodities in recent months and the prospects for considerable economic slack, the Committee expects that inflation pressures will remain subdued in coming quarters.

speaker: DANKER
text: Moreover, the Committee sees some risk that inflation could persist for a time below rates that best foster economic growth and price stability in the longer term.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Federal Reserve will employ all available tools to promote the resumption of sustainable economic growth and to preserve price stability.

speaker: DANKER
text: The focus of the Committee’s policy is to support the functioning of financial markets and stimulate the economy through open market operations and other measures that are likely to keep the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet at a high level.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Federal Reserve continues to purchase large quantities of agency debt and mortgage-backed securities to provide support to the mortgage and housing markets, and it stands ready to expand the quantity of such purchases and the duration of the purchase program as conditions warrant.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Committee also is prepared to purchase longer- term Treasury securities if evolving circumstances indicate that such transactions would be particularly effective in improving conditions in private credit markets.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Federal Reserve will be implementing the term asset-backed securities loan facility to facilitate the extension of credit to households and small businesses.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Committee will continue to monitor carefully the size and composition of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet in light of evolving financial market developments and to assess whether expansions of or modifications to lending facilities would serve to further support credit markets and economic activity and help to preserve price stability.” This vote will also encompass the directive from page 48 of the Bluebook.

speaker: BERNANKE

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Item 11 is the longer-run projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I heard no concerns about it, so why don’t we go ahead and—President Lacker.

speaker: LACKER
text: I pointed out yesterday that the distribution of the numbers for inflation had shifted notably.

speaker: LACKER
text: I understand that people’s views about the appropriate inflation rate—the steady-state inflation rate that they would put in a Taylor rule or some other reaction function— might change from quarter to quarter.

speaker: LACKER
text: I also pointed out that I thought the motivation for doing that was dissatisfaction with the extent to which the third year of our forecast inflation changed from quarter to quarter and that it diminished the extent to which that report of our forecasts served as a proxy for our Committee’s agreed-upon numerical inflation objectives.

speaker: LACKER
text: At our last meeting, we discussed adopting an explicit numerical inflation objective.

speaker: LACKER
text: That hasn’t appeared on the agenda today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I was about to report.

speaker: LACKER
text: I guess my attitude toward the longer-run projections is that I remain unconvinced, as I was in our October discussion, that the benefits exceed the costs, and I wanted to use the opportunity here to ask about the status of adopting a numerical objective for inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I agree with you that this has disadvantages and advantages relative to a formal target.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I wanted to thank everybody for the very useful discussion that we had in the videoconference, and I promise not to have a full discussion of inflation targets any time soon because I do think we do have a pretty good sense of people’s views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I took from the conference call, among other things, was that the Committee was willing to grant me some discretion to try to discuss with the political bodies what their views would be on going forward with an explicit objective.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I mentioned to you even before the meeting, I had spoken to the Administration, and I have had some follow-up discussions there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My sense is that there would not be any serious opposition from that side, although I need to continue to talk with them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the more difficult question is on the congressional side, and I have a meeting with Barney Frank on Monday, in which I will raise this issue among other issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My sense of the meeting was that it was worth doing some socializing and some exploring of these issues but that we wanted to be very careful and very sensitive at this difficult juncture about not creating new political problems for ourselves but only if we can persuade the leaders of the country that this is something constructive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I will continue to try to do that and continue to work on this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think, frankly, that this continued expansion of our projections actually makes it much easier to sell because it creates a context in which the Congress can see that this is only part of a program that involves meeting both parts of our mandate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Mr. Chairman, do you view it as feasible, likely, or very unlikely that consultations could result in your Monetary Policy Report to the Congress this season involving a revelation of an objective?

speaker: LACKER
text: Or is that too much to hope for?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will have to see.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It will depend a lot on the reaction I get from a few key people.

speaker: LACKER
text: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vice Chairman, did you have a comment?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I guess I am somewhat less than fully enthusiastic about publishing long-term projections at this time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I could support it, but I just want to make a couple of points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, I think it is a somewhat awkward time to introduce long-term projections.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Our forecasts are almost certainly going to be very wrong, given the level of uncertainty.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Moreover, long-term projections may be viewed by market participants as off point.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The economy is sinking rapidly, yet the FOMC is spending its time constructing forecasts for 2011 and beyond.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, if the goal is to introduce long-term projections to communicate the Committee’s views about parameters such as the NAIRU, the potential growth rate, and the desired level of inflation, wouldn’t it be better to simply proceed and publish those measures rather than long­ term projections, which are just an approximation of those parameters?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, I think the individual long-term projections are difficult to link back to the projections for 2011.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If one of the primary objectives of the long-term projections is to provide some background for how the projections past 2011 will converge to the Committee’s goals, you might want to consider different ways of constructing the central tendency forecast.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Fourth, I worry a little about what happens when the composition of the FOMC changes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The long-term projections that result might change because of changes in the composition, not because of an underlying change in view by individual members.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think it would be hard for market participants to know how to judge those changes over time, quarter to quarter, as the projections evolve.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I can support it, but I am not enthusiastic.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I think we see that there are both advantages and disadvantages of doing this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess I would disagree only slightly on the issue of timing in that, to the extent that this does give some sense of what the Committee’s preferences are on appropriate monetary policy over the longer term, certainly an issue that has come around the table quite a bit is the need to stabilize inflation expectations in a situation where they might be quite potentially unstable in either direction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is one consideration.

speaker: EVANS
text: May I make just one quick point?

speaker: EVANS
text: President Lacker mentioned that there was some concern about changes in the inflation long-term projection on a quarter-to-quarter basis.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t interpret the distribution that way.

speaker: EVANS
text: It seems to me as though it was probably importantly influenced by our discussion at the videoconference, and it was a one-off type of change.

speaker: EVANS
text: I know I changed my forecast from 1¾ to 2 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: I had previously felt constrained that 1¾ was pretty much a Committee consensus midpoint, and so I figured we would be acting that way.

speaker: EVANS
text: But now, with more people thinking it was 2, that was how I changed it.

speaker: EVANS
text: I get a sense that others around the table may have done the same thing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It seemed to be noted that the mode is 2, and so the majority believe that 2 is the right number, and there are arguments for allowing a slightly higher target given the recent experience.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other comments about the projections or inflation targets?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, with the caveats that were raised, I still believe that there was a general view that we ought to go ahead with the longer-term projections as part of the summary that will be published along with the minutes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So why don’t we do that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have updated you on inflation targets, which is still really at just the discussion stage.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just ask you quickly—this was our first experiment with the somewhat modified meeting structure—either now or in the intermeeting period, give us your feedback or comments about the effectiveness of this structure.

speaker: BERNANKE

speaker: BERNANKE

speaker: ROSENGREN

speaker: ROSENGREN

speaker: ROSENGREN

speaker: BERNANKE

speaker: BERNANKE

speaker: BERNANKE

speaker: BERNANKE

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me turn it over now to Trish Mosser.

speaker: MOSSER
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Financial market developments during the intermeeting period have been driven largely by three factors: continued sharp deterioration in global economic conditions, uncertainty and pessimism about the health of financial firms, particularly commercial banks, and reactions to a wide range of unconventional policy measures by many central banks and governments.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Despite last week’s rally, as exhibit 1 shows, global equity prices are sharply lower.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The S&P 500 has fallen 16 percent since the beginning of the year.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Of course this is much better than a week ago; as of last Monday, the S&P 500 was down 1 Materials used by Ms. Mosser are appended to this document (appendix 1).

speaker: MOSSER
text: 25 percent for the year.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Foreign stock markets, which had fallen 15 percent to 25 percent from the beginning of the year to a week ago Monday, are now down “only” 5 percent to 17 percent for the year.

speaker: MOSSER
text: This, of course, reflects the deep, nearly global recession which has occurred in response to the financial crisis.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The sharp contraction in credit is now a global phenomenon, resulting in credit losses, write-downs, and financial deleveraging occurring nearly everywhere.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Financial firms also had a bit of a respite last week, in part based on predictions of better first quarter earnings, but overall they remain very distressed.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The continued uncertainty regarding both the health of financial firms as well as the nature of government assistance programs has weighed on their capital structures.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As can be seen in exhibit 2, both common and preferred equity indexes for financial firms are down sharply during the intermeeting period.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In fact, preferred equity of financials has fallen more than 20 percent since late January, while common equity prices are down less than 10 percent, reflecting increased risk of suspended dividends or conversion of preferred equity to common.

speaker: MOSSER
text: This trend is even more pronounced for those firms that have already received government capital and, thus, for which the possibility of losses further up the capital structure is perceived to be largest.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Perhaps more jarring is the very large widening of financial firms’ CDS spreads in recent weeks, which can be seen in exhibits 3 through 5.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Bank CDS spreads are now significantly wider than they were during the height of the financial turmoil last fall, following the Lehman bankruptcy.

speaker: MOSSER
text: This is truly extraordinary in light of the government programs that have been announced or expanded in recent weeks: the FDIC guarantee program, the announcement of the Administration’s stabilization plan, and several public statements that systemically important firms will not be allowed to fail during the current crisis.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The widening of CDS spreads reflects several factors.

speaker: MOSSER
text: First, in the U.S., there is deep concern that the current bank stress assessment will result in actual or de facto nationalization of some institutions; this raises the possibility that debt holders as well as equity holders will take a hit.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Second, financial firms with more opaque balance sheets—commercial banks, insurance companies, and some finance companies, such as GE Capital—have experienced larger increases in CDS spreads.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The lack of clarity about the size of “toxic” assets and how legacy accrual assets will be marked has led to questions about their viability.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In fact it’s notable that the CDS spreads of the two former investment banks, which largely mark their balance sheets to market, have not widened in recent weeks, although they remain at very high levels.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Third, market liquidity continues to deteriorate in nearly every market where the Fed has not intervened, including CDS.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Thus, the price impact of even small CDS trades and small positions can move spreads sharply; for example, a relatively small number of investors continuing to take short positions in financial CDS may be responsible for the bulk of the price action in recent weeks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Finally, and perhaps most importantly, investors are very concerned about whether the “strings” attached to government assistance for financial institutions or markets will be changed in the future.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In particular, the risk that the “rules of the game” for debt investors will be changed— after investments have been made—has risen sharply in recent weeks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: To quote a member of our Treasury Market Practices Group, “the rules coming from Washington change every other day; no one is willing to invest in anything.” It’s worth noting that this risk extends beyond investments in banks and is a reason that some investors are not planning to use the TALF, no matter how attractive the economics of the program may be.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In response to continued deterioration in both economic and financial conditions, central banks around the world have eased monetary policy conditions to an unprecedented degree in recent weeks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Of the G-20 central banks, eighteen have eased monetary policy since the beginning of the year.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In addition, exhibit 6 shows that most of the major central banks have lowered interest rates to near zero and embarked on programs to expand their balance sheets through additional liquidity programs as well as credit-easing and quantitative-easing programs.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Credit-easing programs have generally focused on purchases of commercial paper and corporate bonds outside of the U.S.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the U.S., the investment-grade corporate bond market is the rare credit market that is operating fairly normally, but this is not the case in many countries.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The local market responses to these new programs—some of which I will discuss in a moment—have generally been positive, but their relative impact globally is harder to discern.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In particular, movements in major dollar FX rates (exhibit 7) do not appear to be closely related to changes in policy stance, the degree of central bank balance sheet expansion, or relative economic prospects.

speaker: MOSSER
text: For example, one might expect the euro, or at least the Canadian dollar, to have appreciated relative to the U.S. dollar since the beginning of the year, given the euro area’s higher policy rates and the Canadian economy’s relative stability.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But, in fact, the dollar has appreciated against nearly every major currency since the beginning of the year.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Certainly, the dollar’s position as a reserve currency and its continued status as a safe haven have contributed to its appreciation.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Last week’s intervention by the Swiss National Bank to weaken the Swiss franc relative to the euro (exhibit 8) is one reflection of concern over the deflationary impact of an appreciating currency.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The SNB’s intervention last Thursday pushed the Swiss franc down nearly 3½ percent relative to the euro in a matter of minutes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: While the SNB does not plan to engage in ongoing competitive devaluations, preventing a sharp appreciation of the currency, particularly vis-à-vis the euro, is a key component in its quantitative-easing plan to prevent deflation.

speaker: MOSSER
text: However, the United Kingdom probably wins the prize for the most aggressive quantitative-easing plan, at least in terms of its timetable.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Two weeks ago, the Bank of England announced an asset-purchase program focused on commercial paper, corporate bonds, and government securities.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Given the limited size of U.K. credit markets, the BOE announced that the majority of the purchases will be of government bonds, and specifically over the next three months they will purchase as much as £75 billion of gilts in the 5- to 25-year maturity range.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The planned BOE gilt purchases amount to 5 percent of U.K. GDP, nearly 12 percent of total gilts, and 18 percent of nominal gilts held by the public.

speaker: MOSSER
text: To put this in some perspective, a similar-sized program in the United States, by these metrics, would entail purchases of U.S. Treasuries ranging from $585 billion up to nearly $750 billion over a three-month period.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Since the announcement, gilt yields have fallen 19, 53, and 79 basis points in the 5-, 10-, and 20-year maturities, respectively, but 2-year yields have risen 38 basis points—they are not buying 2-year gilts.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As shown in exhibit 9, most of this was an announcement effect.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Interestingly, the spread between the policy rate and the 10-year yield in the U.K. (exhibit 10) did not decline.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In other words, long-term yields have fallen in parallel with the policy rate.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Finally, private credit yields did decline with the policy action, particularly corporate bonds, which the Bank of England will also purchase.

speaker: MOSSER
text: However, as noted in exhibit 11, other yields, notably swaps, fell significantly less than government yields, leading to an increase in swap spreads.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Turning now to our own asset-purchase programs, we have continued to purchase both agency MBS and debt at a steady pace.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Agency debt purchases now amount to nearly $47 billion and MBS outright purchases total $219 billion, as well as an additional $69 billion in dollar rolls, which I will discuss in a moment.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibit 12 shows that the spreads of both agency debt and MBS to Treasury yields have been fairly stable since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Notably, however, the conforming mortgage rate to households has continued to decline to about 5⅛ percent.

speaker: MOSSER
text: There are several reasons for this, including the introduction of our dollar roll program in early March.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the first week of March, there was a nearly 100 basis point drop in the forward financing rate for MBS relative to the MBS cash repo rate (exhibit 13).

speaker: MOSSER
text: You may recall that the dollar roll market is like a “repo” market for forward delivery of agency MBS.

speaker: MOSSER
text: To give an example, the March–April dollar roll transaction, which is what we’re purchasing now, is a transaction that simultaneously purchases MBS for delivery in March and sells identical MBS to be delivered in April.

speaker: MOSSER
text: By participating in the dollar roll market, we have lowered the cost of managing mortgage inventory and moved forward financing spreads back to levels that prevailed before last fall’s turmoil.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In addition, as the refinancing wave from January abates, mortgage lenders’ ability to process new mortgages has increased, and they have tended to lower rates to borrowers.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Finally, retail spreads, while high, have come down because of the improved liquidity and predictability of conditions in the secondary mortgage market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Since our purchase program began in January, other investors and arbitrageurs have “followed” us into the MBS market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Not only are bid-asked spreads lower, but, as shown in exhibit 14, the daily price volatility of new MBS has declined steadily, reducing uncertainty about prices at which new mortgages can be sold.

speaker: MOSSER
text: While our MBS purchase program has helped to lower MBS spreads from the exceptional levels seen last fall, they remain very high by historical standards, as shown in exhibit 15.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In contrast to the Treasury yield curve, which is shown in exhibit 16, mortgage spreads do not appear to have a predictable relationship to the business cycle.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The Treasury curve, while steep, seems consistent with past episodes of economic weakness.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In anticipation of Dave’s and Joe’s discussion of large-scale asset purchases, exhibit 17 scales our asset purchases so far relative to upcoming new issuance.

speaker: MOSSER
text: To date, the MBS program purchases are very close in size to the overall new issuance in the MBS market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: However, market expectations are for a large refinancing wave during 2009 (the result of low rates and mortgage relief programs).

speaker: MOSSER
text: The median estimate is for $1.8 trillion in new issuance, but estimates vary widely—from under $1 trillion to $3 trillion.

speaker: MOSSER
text: For comparison, a median estimate of long-term Treasury issuance is also shown.

speaker: MOSSER
text: At our current pace of purchasing, we will not keep up with expected new MBS issuance.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Finally, I want to say a few words about policy expectations and the impact of our programs.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibit 18 shows the results of the Desk’s latest survey of dealer economists along with market-implied expectations for the future policy rate.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Most dealers continue to expect policy rates to stay close to zero until at least the second quarter of 2010 and to remain below 1 percent into 2011.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Market-implied expectations continue to be skewed upward, but we believe this probably reflects the high risk premiums in future Eurodollar rates rather than an accurate reading of policy expectations.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Markets directly supported by Fed programs continued to function reasonably well.

speaker: MOSSER
text: However, as seen in exhibit 19, both secured and unsecured money market rates have increased modestly in recent weeks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The increase in LIBOR rates largely reflects increased credit risk of banks and is consistent with the rise in bank CDS spreads.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The rise in Treasury repo rates, in contrast, reflects the large Treasury issuance and associated ample supply of Treasury collateral for lending.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Spreads on consumer-asset-backed securities have narrowed somewhat since the last FOMC meeting in anticipation of the first TALF subscription, which opened today.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Our expectations for the first TALF subscription are modest, with a few billion dollars of lending against ABS, most likely backed by auto and credit card lending.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Bill will be saying more about the TALF in a few minutes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Spence will discuss various aspects of the balance sheet in more detail.

speaker: MOSSER
text: However, I would like to point out in exhibit 20 the continued decline in the size of our balance sheet, as the liquidity programs shrink at a faster rate than our purchase programs increase.

speaker: MOSSER
text: On a related operational note: Demand for borrowing Treasury securities from our term securities lending facility has continued to decline, with operations for both Schedule 1 and 2 collateral consistently undersubscribed.

speaker: MOSSER
text: TSLF operations are very staff-intensive, so we are proposing to reduce the frequency of Schedule 2 auctions from the biweekly schedule that was implemented during the market turmoil last fall back to the original weekly schedule.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We plan to maintain the overall size of the TSLF program for the present but will continue to assess whether changes may be appropriate in the future.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I’ll now turn it over to Bill Nelson who will discuss the TALF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Trish, does that proposal require any approval?

speaker: MOSSER
text: It does not, according to the authorization—but I’ll bow to Debbie for greater wisdom on that.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, may I ask just one question on exhibit 17?

speaker: FISHER
text: This is calendar year 2009?

speaker: NELSON
text: As Trish noted, the subscription for the first TALF operation begins today.

speaker: NELSON
text: The loans requested between now and Thursday will settle on March 25, exactly four months after we first announced the program.

speaker: NELSON
text: Those months were spent canvassing potential ABS issuers and investors to determine the program design characteristics that would be most successful, evaluating the risks of the program and developing the associated controls, and working out the back-office arrangements.

speaker: NELSON
text: Nevertheless, the size of the initial TALF subscription is going to be modest, in part because potential borrowers are uneasy using the TALF to finance ABS purchases.

speaker: NELSON
text: Potential borrowers and primary dealers have largely been unable to work out mutually acceptable customer arrangements.

speaker: NELSON
text: A particular sticking point seems to be assigning responsibility for the risk that a potential borrower is determined to be ineligible for the program at the eleventh hour, leaving the primary dealer, who is typically the underwriter, responsible for funding the issue.

speaker: NELSON
text: Investors are also reportedly concerned that participation in the program will expose them to government interference in their business, a fear apparently confirmed on Friday when it became more widely understood that recipients of 13(3) loans will be subject to tighter restrictions when hiring noncitizens.

speaker: NELSON
text: We are trying to facilitate agreements between potential borrowers and primary dealers, we are seeking to provide as much clarity as possible on the issue of hiring noncitizens, and we are addressing other issues as they arise.

speaker: NELSON
text: We continue to hope that participants will grow more comfortable with the program over time.

speaker: NELSON
text: I note that revisions to the FAQs to help clarify some issues are going on right now.

speaker: NELSON
text: The subscription that starts today is for the TALF program as initially announced.

speaker: NELSON
text: The New York Fed will be extending three-year nonrecourse loans against newly issued triple-A-rated auto, credit card, and student loan ABS and ABS guaranteed by the Small Business Administration.

speaker: NELSON
text: The monthly operations will continue through this December unless extended by the Board.

speaker: NELSON
text: The program has a $200 billion ceiling and is supported by $20 billion in credit protection from the Treasury.

speaker: NELSON
text: As you all know, the Board is prepared to consider increasing the size of the program up to $1 trillion, supported by up to $100 billion in credit protection from the Treasury.

speaker: NELSON
text: The expansion would entail widening the list of eligible collateral to encompass much of the universe of newly issued triple-A-rated collateralized obligations, for the most part backed by newly and recently issued loans.

speaker: NELSON
text: Staff at the Board, New York Fed, Chicago Fed, Atlanta Fed, and the Treasury have been evaluating specific asset classes for possible inclusion in the program and have been developing prospective terms and conditions.

speaker: NELSON
text: We are concentrating first on the largest asset classes and will recommend specific categories of securities for inclusion on a flow basis as we complete our reviews.

speaker: NELSON
text: As a first step in that expansion, we recommend that the Board approve adding four categories of ABS to the list of eligible collateral, starting with the April operation.

speaker: NELSON
text: The four categories are the first to be recommended because they have relatively straightforward structures similar to those already taken, allowing us to evaluate them quickly.

speaker: NELSON
text: Although they are smaller asset classes than the consumer ABS already accepted, they are the largest among the securities that can be evaluated quickly.

speaker: NELSON
text: The first three are the principal types of ABS that were excluded from the initial program because they are not backed by consumer loans: ABS backed by loans or leases relating to business equipment, ABS backed by leases of vehicle fleets, and ABS backed by revolving lines of credit used to finance showroom inventories.

speaker: NELSON
text: The fourth is ABS backed by the credit provided by residential mortgage servicers when homeowners miss payments.

speaker: NELSON
text: Mortgage servicers have found credit increasingly difficult and expensive to obtain.

speaker: NELSON
text: Accepting the ABS at the TALF should improve the servicers’ ability to work with homeowners to prevent avoidable foreclosures.

speaker: NELSON
text: All the assets proposed to be accepted will have maturities of three years or less, resulting in a good fit for the three-year term of the TALF loans.

speaker: NELSON
text: The proposed new collateral classes are of roughly equivalent risk to the types already accepted.

speaker: NELSON
text: After applying the recommended haircuts, which range from 8 to 13 percent, the risk to the Federal Reserve should be similar to the de minimis risk associated with the types of ABS already accepted as TALF collateral.

speaker: NELSON
text: We estimate that accepting the new categories of ABS would increase demand for TALF loans through December by $30 billion to $130 billion.

speaker: NELSON
text: If the Board approves the additions, we would release revised terms and conditions and FAQs for the program on Thursday.

speaker: NELSON
text: We are also evaluating the other remaining major collateralized asset classes for inclusion under the TALF, for example, CMBS and non-agency RMBS.

speaker: NELSON
text: Subject to Board approval, terms and conditions for these asset classes could be announced as early as mid-April.

speaker: NELSON
text: Staff members have held extensive discussions with issuers, investors, and rating agencies about several asset categories and have narrowed down the scope of securities that we might recommend accepting.

speaker: NELSON
text: For instance, CMBS would likely include those backed by solidly underwritten existing mortgages and by mortgages that are being refinanced, and RMBS would likely include those backed by mortgages exceeding the conforming loan limit and possibly mortgages to near-prime borrowers.

speaker: NELSON
text: Because a number of the assets envisioned for the expansion are more complicated than those currently taken or thus far proposed to be taken at the TALF, staff members are planning to recommend that a collateral agent be hired to assist with underwriting and that a portfolio manager be hired to monitor the assets accepted.

speaker: NELSON
text: Staff members are also evaluating the use of the TALF to address the legacy asset problem.

speaker: NELSON
text: The Treasury has proposed that the Federal Reserve accept at the TALF older securities that were rated triple-A when issued but that may or may not still be rated triple-A.

speaker: NELSON
text: One reason to expand the TALF to legacy assets would be to increase demand for, and hence the prices of, the eligible assets, thereby bolstering the balance sheets of financial institutions.

speaker: NELSON
text: Another reason would be to remove the eligible assets from the balance sheets of their current holders, leaving those firms with cleaner, more transparent balance sheets and an improved capacity to attract new equity from private sources.

speaker: NELSON
text: In the Treasury’s proposed structure, the legacy TALF loans have five-year terms, but in other ways the facility resembles the existing TALF.

speaker: NELSON
text: Staff members have analyzed the feasibility of the legacy TALF proposal for a few asset classes, specifically 2005- to 2008-vintage CMBS still rated triple-A and subprime and Alt-A RMBS rated triple-A at origination.

speaker: NELSON
text: Our preliminary assessment is that, for many of these securities, haircuts and other terms could be set that would adequately protect the Federal Reserve and the Treasury but would nevertheless elicit sufficient investor demand to be helpful.

speaker: NELSON
text: We have concluded, though, that it would be necessary in some cases to set haircuts on a security-by-security basis.

speaker: NELSON
text: Nevertheless, we believe that we could operate the program at sufficient scale and with sufficient speed by hiring an outside contractor.

speaker: NELSON
text: Joe Gagnon and Dave Reifschneider will now discuss large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Before you start, let me just say that I’ll give a briefing on the Treasury’s plans and all of these issues after the presentations here.

speaker: GAGNON
text: 2 Dave Reifschneider and I will review the papers on large-scale asset purchases (LSAPs) that were sent to the Committee last week.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Considerable evidence indicates that policy-induced changes in the supply of long-term bonds affect bond yields.

speaker: GAGNON
text: As noted in the top panel of your first exhibit, a memo circulated to the FOMC last December reviewed the economic literature on this question and 2 Materials used by Messrs. Gagnon and Reifschneider are appended to this document (appendix 2).

speaker: GAGNON
text: reported that a Federal Reserve purchase of $500 billion of long-term Treasury securities could plausibly reduce the 10-year Treasury yield by 20 to 100 basis points.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Such a purchase would also be expected to lower long-term private yields.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Generally speaking, public and private long-term debt markets are closely linked, and correlations of changes in yields across these markets have historically been very high.

speaker: GAGNON
text: However, in recent months these correlations have declined noticeably, raising the possibility that spillovers across markets may currently be lower than normal.

speaker: GAGNON
text: The middle panel presents evidence on the effects of recent central bank communications on bond yields.

speaker: GAGNON
text: On November 25 (the first column) the Federal Reserve announced a program to purchase $600 billion of agency debt and agency MBS.

speaker: GAGNON
text: On December 1 (the second column) Chairman Bernanke stated that the Federal Reserve was considering purchasing substantial quantities of long-term Treasury securities.

speaker: GAGNON
