text: On December 16, the FOMC stated that it stood ready to expand its purchases of agency securities and confirmed that it was considering large-scale purchases of Treasuries.

speaker: GAGNON
text: On each of these occasions, the 10-year Treasury yield and long-term private yields fell substantially.

speaker: GAGNON
text: On January 28, the FOMC did not indicate any change in its stance toward purchasing long-term Treasuries, whereas market participants reportedly attributed a significant probability to such a move.

speaker: GAGNON
text: None of these moves appears to be attributable to economic news.

speaker: GAGNON
text: As Trish mentioned, on March 5, the Bank of England announced that it plans to purchase £75 billion of mainly long-term sterling Treasury securities.

speaker: GAGNON
text: The final column shows that a range of public and private long-term yields fell sharply after the Bank of England’s announcement.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Household mortgage rates are quite a bit stickier than yields on traded securities, which makes them unsuitable for inclusion in the table.

speaker: GAGNON
text: However, as shown in the bottom panel, most of the decline in Treasury yields since mid-November (the red line) has passed through to conforming 30-year mortgage rates (the black line).

speaker: GAGNON
text: I’ll now turn the presentation over to Dave.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The top panel of your next exhibit reviews the basic channels through which buying agency MBS or long-term Treasury securities potentially influences the real economy.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The primary mechanism is through a broad improvement in financial conditions.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As Joe discussed, such purchases reduce yields on the targeted securities.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In addition, the evidence suggests that these reductions spill over to yields on corporate bonds and other long-term instruments; if so, these interest rate movements should spark higher equity prices and a lower real exchange rate.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In turn, household spending, business investment, and net exports should strengthen in response to lower borrowing costs, higher wealth, and greater international price competitiveness.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As illustrated in the middle panel, the stimulus from an LSAP program hinges on the extent of financial spillover.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The table shows a sequence of predictions from the FRB/US model for the response of real GDP to purchasing a further $500 billion in agency MBS, assuming successively greater spillovers.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As shown in line 1, even though the program is assumed to lower MBS yields and mortgage rates by 75 basis points, the boost to the level of real GDP would be small in the absence of any spillover to other financial markets.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But if, as in line 2, the fall in MBS yields leads to lower corporate bond yields and other interest rates, the boost to the level of real GDP climbs to ½ percent by 2011.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Expanding the spillovers yet further to the stock market (line 3) and the real exchange rate (line 4) more than doubles the amount of stimulus, to roughly 1 percent by 2011.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Other simulations, not shown here, suggest that the stimulus provided by purchases of long-term Treasury securities also is highly sensitive to the extent of financial spillover.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But if such purchases were to reduce the general level of interest rates, boost equity prices, and lower the dollar, then the resultant stimulus to real activity would be only modestly lower than that provided by an MBS-only program, as indicated in the memo line of the table.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As noted in the bottom left panel, these FRB/US simulations do not capture all the potential ways in which an LSAP program could stimulate real activity.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: For example, lower mortgage rates could boost home prices, thereby stimulating household wealth and spending.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Theoretical calculations suggest that a percentage point decline in interest rates could boost house prices as much as 15 percent; however, empirical estimates suggest that the increase might be closer to 2½ percent.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In addition, lower interest rates might, via mortgage refinancing, transfer income to cash-strapped borrowers from more affluent households who are net lenders.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Calculations suggest that such income transfers could provide a modest boost to consumption.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As indicated by the red line in the figure to the right, when refi effects and 2½ percent higher house prices are incorporated into the FRB/US simulations, the stimulus from a $1 trillion LSAP program—evenly divided between Treasuries and MBS—rises noticeably.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Effects are larger yet if house prices increase by the theoretical 15 percent (the green line).

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Turning to your next exhibit, these results imply that asset purchases have the potential to compensate for the inability of conventional monetary policy to ease further.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As noted to the left, the staff assumes that the federal funds rate will remain essentially at the zero bound for several years, as illustrated by the black line to the right.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But unconstrained “optimal” monetary policy would call for the fed funds rate to fall even lower, were that possible (the red line).

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: To overcome this shortfall in conventional monetary policy would require additional fiscal and unconventional monetary actions.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The middle panels illustrate how the Greenbook outlook for unemployment and inflation might change if the Committee opted to expand the current program of buying agency debt and MBS by either $500 billion (the red line) or $1 trillion (the green line).

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Under the smaller program, all the additional purchases are MBS; under the larger program, purchases are evenly divided between MBS and long-term Treasury securities.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Both programs are assumed to generate a full range of financial spillovers but no boost to home prices or any increase in consumption from refi-related income transfers; in addition, monetary policy in both cases is set “optimally,” subject to the zero lower bound constraint.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As shown to the left, both programs limit the rise in the unemployment rate and cause it to fall more quickly than in the baseline (the black line).

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: All told, the larger program fills roughly half of the gap between the staff forecast and what hypothetically would occur under unconstrained monetary policy (the blue line).

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: As shown to the right, both programs would also mitigate the fall in inflation that is projected in the baseline.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The bullet points at the bottom offer a few caveats to this analysis.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: First, these results depend importantly on extensive financial spillover effects; unfortunately, empirical evidence on the size of stock market and exchange rate effects is slim.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Second, gauging the economic effects of further asset purchases is quite difficult under current conditions, even if extensive financial spillovers do occur.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: In particular, households and firms may be reluctant to increase spending in the face of so much uncertainty, and credit constraints may limit their ability to respond to improved financial conditions; alternatively, cash-strapped households may be more responsive than normal to any boost to income provided by an LSAP program.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Finally, the effectiveness of an LSAP program in stopping an unwelcome disinflation might be greater than the simulations indicate if large-scale asset purchases directly bolster the Fed’s credibility.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I’ll now turn the presentation back to Joe.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Exhibit 4 presents some risks that might arise from expanding LSAP programs.

speaker: GAGNON
text: The most important risk, which is covered in the upper panel, is whether large asset holdings might threaten the Federal Reserve’s ability in the future to achieve its monetary policy objectives.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Spence Hilton will be discussing this issue in the context of the overall balance sheet of the Federal Reserve, and Brian Madigan will discuss potential new policy tools to ameliorate this risk.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Large-scale holdings of marketable assets are not likely to constrain the Federal Reserve’s policy stance in the future.

speaker: GAGNON
text: With short-term interest rates pinned at the zero bound, asset purchases provide macroeconomic stimulus, and asset sales provide macroeconomic restraint.

speaker: GAGNON
text: If it were deemed necessary to raise short-term interest rates, and holdings of long­ term assets appeared to conflict with this goal, these assets could be sold off or potentially used as collateral for reserve-draining short-term operations.

speaker: GAGNON
text: However, outright sales of long-term assets could lead to a financial loss; and some of the tools that could be used to drain reserves without engaging in outright sales are still under development.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Moving to the lower panel, even though fiscal revenue is not an objective of monetary policy, it may be of interest to note that LSAPs are significantly increasing the income generated by the Federal Reserve.

speaker: GAGNON
text: This is because the interest rate earned on long-term assets is much greater than the marginal interest rate paid on liabilities.

speaker: GAGNON
text: However, by increasing the leverage and maturity mismatch of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet, LSAPs increase the volatility of future income.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Your final exhibit discusses strategies for pursuing LSAPs.

speaker: GAGNON
text: The upper panel reviews three classes of long-term security that the Federal Reserve is authorized to purchase: Treasuries, agency debt, and agency MBS.

speaker: GAGNON
text: As Dave discussed, under current market conditions, we believe that MBS purchases provide a somewhat greater macroeconomic stimulus than equivalent purchases of the other two classes.

speaker: GAGNON
text: This primarily reflects our view that MBS purchases will reduce private interest rates more than an equivalent volume of Treasury purchases.

speaker: GAGNON
text: However, in light of the considerable uncertainty surrounding our estimates of the spillover effects across asset markets, including a significant share of Treasury securities and a modest share of agency debt in any expansion of Federal Reserve purchases may be a prudent strategy.

speaker: GAGNON
text: The lower left panel shows that the spread of mortgage rates over MBS yields rose in December with the surge of refinancing applications.

speaker: GAGNON
text: These two series have been highly correlated in the past.

speaker: GAGNON
text: The staff projects that current low mortgage rates and the Administration’s new Making Home Affordable program are likely to create another, more sustained, surge in refinancing applications in coming weeks.

speaker: GAGNON
text: As discussed in the panel to the right, there are some potential actions the Federal Reserve could take to hold down the spread of mortgage rates over MBS yields and thus enhance the macroeconomic impact of its policies.

speaker: GAGNON
text: These include focusing purchases on new-production MBS to support new loans rather than seasoned loans.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Another possibility, if it were determined to be consistent with the Federal Reserve’s statutory authority, is selling put options on forward MBS to help mortgage originators hedge the uncertainty of their application pipelines.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Perhaps even more unconventionally, the Federal Reserve could provide some assurance through its communications to the market that low mortgage rates are likely to persist for several months or more.

speaker: GAGNON
text: This might reduce volatility in rates and thus reduce originator hedging costs.

speaker: GAGNON
text: It might also ease the crush of homeowners trying to refinance at the same time, which strains the currently reduced capacity of mortgage originators and puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Nathan Sheets will now discuss foreign currency liquidity swaps.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The staff recommends that the FOMC establish swap lines with major foreign central banks that would allow the Federal Reserve to backstop the foreign currency funding needs of U.S. institutions operating abroad.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These lines would give the Federal Reserve the same capacity to act as a lender of last resort that our existing dollar swap lines provide foreign central banks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This proposal involves two components.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First, the FOMC would create a new set of swap lines with foreign central banks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These new swap lines would be designed to provide the Federal Reserve access to foreign currency liquidity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We suggest establishing such lines with the Bank of England, the European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan, and the Swiss National Bank.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We envision that the lines with the BoJ and ECB would be set at roughly $100 billion equivalent, and the lines with the BoE and the SNB would be a little less than half as large.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These central banks have indicated that they are open to establishing such lines with us.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Second, the FOMC would need to create a mechanism to transfer the foreign currency received in the swap with the foreign central bank to a U.S. financial institution.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We propose that you authorize use of the System Open Market Account to conduct swap transactions for this purpose.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This transaction would be structured as follows.

speaker: SHEETS
text: An institution that was facing severe foreign currency funding pressures would approach its Federal Reserve Bank.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Reserve Bank would then assess the financial position of the institution and the extent of the foreign currency funding need.

speaker: SHEETS
text: If in the Reserve Bank’s judgment a swap was appropriate, the Reserve Bank would initiate a request with the Foreign Currency Subcommittee, which would have delegated authority to approve swap draws.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Requests for rollovers would also be initiated through the Reserve Bank.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Federal Reserve would swap foreign currency to a U.S. institution in exchange for dollars.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Federal Reserve would charge the institution a fee (which would be equal to the foreign central bank’s policy target plus an additional charge) and would also take a 3 to 5 percent security deposit in cash.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This deposit would protect against a scenario in which an institution failed to unwind the swap and in which the dollars that were received in the swap proved insufficient to extinguish our foreign currency obligation to the foreign central bank.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We anticipate that such swaps would be conducted at very short tenors, primarily overnight through one week.

speaker: SHEETS
text: While we would expect a U.S. institution that faced difficulties obtaining sufficient foreign currency funding in a market abroad to turn first to the foreign central bank, we see three scenarios in which that option might not be available.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First, an institution might have insufficient collateral at the foreign central bank to meet the drain on its funding and be unable to mobilize sufficient resources on its own, perhaps because the U.S. payment system was closed or because the institution was experiencing broader funding pressures.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Second, the foreign central bank might choose not to lend to an institution even in the presence of acceptable collateral; this might reflect concerns about the institution’s underlying financial condition or political pressures.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Third, the Federal Reserve might wish to provide foreign currency funding as part of an effort, presumably coordinated with other U.S. authorities, to prevent a disorderly unwinding of an insolvent institution’s balance sheet.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Such lending, of course, would be done in a manner consistent with the constraints of FDICIA and other legal protocols.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As I noted at the January meeting, one major U.S. institution has shown particular vulnerabilities regarding its foreign currency funding, but we cannot rule out scenarios in which other large U.S. institutions might run into similar trouble.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There is a related risk that once one U.S. institution shows vulnerability in this regard, other U.S. institutions might also then be viewed as vulnerable and that a broader foreign currency liquidity squeeze could develop.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In our view, roughly half a dozen major U.S. institutions have sufficient foreign operations to be vulnerable in this respect.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These observations suggest that it would be prudent for the Federal Reserve to have the capacity to backstop the foreign currency funding needs of U.S. institutions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Establishing temporary swap lines with foreign central banks strikes us as a straightforward way to do this.

speaker: SHEETS
text: While there is a good possibility that these lines would never actually be drawn on, they nevertheless would provide valuable insurance against the risk of severe stress.

speaker: SHEETS
text: One important issue that we have grappled with is whether the transaction with a U.S. financial institution should be structured as a swap using SOMA or as a foreign currency denominated loan from the discount window.

speaker: SHEETS
text: After considerable deliberation and reflection, we were persuaded that the back-to-back swap structure is the way to go.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Federal Reserve traditionally conducts its foreign currency transactions out of SOMA, and there is no precedent for discount window lending in foreign currencies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: A key complication with the discount window approach is getting the foreign currency from SOMA to the appropriate Reserve Bank, since only the Federal Reserve Bank of New York has accounts at foreign central banks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, systems to record and manage discount window operations were not designed to track loans in foreign currencies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: By putting these swap lines in place, we would signal our intention to pursue best practice in home–host relations.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We would be prepared to provide liquidity support to a U.S. institution if the foreign central bank were reluctant to step in.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This could also give us increased negotiating leverage to expect foreign central banks to provide similar support to their institutions operating in the United States.

speaker: SHEETS
text: What risks do these transactions pose to the Federal Reserve?

speaker: SHEETS
text: The risks attending the swap with the foreign central bank would be nil.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As with our dollar liquidity swaps, there is no exchange rate or interest rate risk, because these parameters are specified upfront.

speaker: SHEETS
text: And the foreign central bank is required to deposit the dollars it receives in the swap at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, so there is no credit risk.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As for the transaction with the U.S. financial institution, the Federal Reserve is protected first by the short tenor of the transaction.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Second, the dollar holdings received in the swap could be used to acquire foreign currency if the institution fails to unwind the transaction.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Third, if these dollars prove inadequate to repay the foreign central bank fully—either because the dollar has depreciated or because of transactions costs—the Federal Reserve will draw on the cash security deposit that the institution has provided.

speaker: SHEETS
text: All told, we judge that Federal Reserve resources would be well protected against any financial risks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We also note the possibility of moral hazard—institutions may come to depend on the Federal Reserve to meet their foreign currency funding needs, rather than arranging for sufficient funding in the market or mobilizing their collateral for use at a foreign central bank.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, we have structured these swaps to minimize this risk to the extent possible.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In particular, the size of the fee and the cash deposit should help ensure that the swaps are attractive only as a last resort.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Establishing these foreign currency swap lines requires FOMC approval—either directly or through delegation to the Subcommittee.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We envision that approval by the full Committee would be followed by a press release within 10 days or so and, in any event, would be reported in the minutes.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As such, the establishment of these lines would quickly become public knowledge.

speaker: SHEETS
text: While the staff had previously feared that a public announcement could generate a negative reaction from the markets, the current weakness of confidence toward the banks may diminish this concern.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indeed, an announcement that this backstop had been put in place could even enhance confidence.

speaker: SHEETS
text: If in the Committee’s judgment the announcement effects associated with these facilities would be manageable, then you could authorize these foreign currency swap lines at the meeting today.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, if you remain concerned about negative announcement effects, then we recommend that the Committee delegate authority to the Foreign Currency Subcommittee to approve these swap lines.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This would enable the announcement to be deferred, pending a time when draws on the lines would actually be made.

speaker: SHEETS
text: There might still be some announcement effects created by reports of an FOMC vote to delegate this authority to the Subcommittee, but it would probably not be seen as signaling the same urgency as an announcement that the facilities themselves had been established.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The authority granted to the Subcommittee in this regard would be symmetric to that already delegated to the Subcommittee to negotiate dollar liquidity swap lines.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I conclude by noting that the Bank of Mexico has recently expressed interest in drawing on its dollar swap line with the Federal Reserve.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We are currently working with our Mexican counterparts to better understand the situation in their economy and how they would use the dollars.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These discussions are ongoing, and we will keep you posted as they proceed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Spence Hilton will now continue our presentation.

speaker: HILTON
text: I’m going to review major changes on the Federal Reserve balance sheet since the last FOMC meeting and then summarize some long-run balance sheet analysis that was in the memo distributed last week.

speaker: HILTON
text: Last week, the Markets Group distributed its first comprehensive report on developments at the various lending facilities and purchase programs over the past intermeeting period, with a discussion of related financial market developments.

speaker: HILTON
text: That report offers much more detail than I will provide in my remarks.

speaker: HILTON
text: Just ahead of the last FOMC meeting in late January, the total size of the balance sheet was $2.04 trillion, a bit off levels reached just ahead of the year-end.

speaker: HILTON
text: As shown in exhibit 2, over the course of that last week in January, which included the FOMC meeting dates, assets fell almost $200 billion.

speaker: HILTON
text: Declines were widespread among the various short-term lending facilities, with the steepest drop-offs in total draws on the swap lines used to fund dollar lending by foreign central banks, and in the commercial paper funding facility.

speaker: HILTON
text: As shown in exhibit 3, for the past several months now, interest rates on alternative market sources of financing available to many borrowers have been below the rates on the facilities themselves.

speaker: HILTON
text: Ongoing deleveraging of balance sheets has been cited as a factor contributing to reduced borrowing.

speaker: HILTON
text: 3 Materials used by Mr. Hilton are appended to this document (appendix 3).

speaker: HILTON
text: As shown in exhibits 4 through 9 on the following two pages, since early February, lending through many of the short-term liquidity facilities has declined further to one degree or another.

speaker: HILTON
text: Still, these facilities remain a crucial source of funding for some borrowers, despite rate quotes that suggest cheaper market sources of funding.

speaker: HILTON
text: A notable exception to the general trend is the term auction facility, shown in exhibit 7.

speaker: HILTON
text: The volume of propositions at the TAF auctions at the minimum bid rate of 25 basis points has increased some in recent weeks, although total propositions have remained below the total offering amounts.

speaker: HILTON
text: As Trish noted, purchases of agency MBS and agency debt have been steadily rising.

speaker: HILTON
text: Purchases of agency MBS show up in a very lumpy way on the balance sheet, because of market practice to concentrate settlements on select dates, often with a considerable lag.

speaker: HILTON
text: Last Thursday alone, the size of the balance sheet jumped, as about $160 billion of purchase commitments settled, which now leaves the total balance sheet about unchanged from its level just ahead of the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: HILTON
text: In coming weeks, we anticipate that recent patterns in different components of the balance sheet will continue.

speaker: HILTON
text: There is potential for increased lending through some of the short-term liquidity facilities ahead of the March quarter-end date as a possible stress point.

speaker: HILTON
text: But apart from the aforementioned increase in TAF auctions, we have not seen this so far.

speaker: HILTON
text: Meanwhile, our outright purchase programs are set to proceed on a steady upward path.

speaker: HILTON
text: Turning to longer-term prospects for the balance sheet, the memo distributed last week presents illustrative forecasts of the balance sheet out to 2016.

speaker: HILTON
text: Projections were constructed based on certain economic assumptions, varying degrees of financial stress assumed over the next couple of years, and on policy assumptions motivated by the economic and financial conditions.

speaker: HILTON
text: For simplicity in estimation, the various liquidity facilities, purchase programs, and other balance sheet initiatives are grouped into just a handful of broad asset categories.

speaker: HILTON
text: A baseline scenario was developed using economic conditions similar to those of the March Greenbook, and an optimistic scenario and a stress scenario were built around this case.

speaker: HILTON
text: The methodology was kept very simple given the obvious uncertainties.

speaker: HILTON
text: But the broad contours of the asset projections are thought to be illustrative of different orders of magnitude for the size of the balance sheet that could be realized under several plausible sets of assumptions.

speaker: HILTON
text: Projections for the balance sheet and the asset components for each of the three scenarios are shown in exhibits 10-12.

speaker: HILTON
text: In the stress case shown in the bottom panel, solid growth only takes hold in 2011, another financial market stress period is assumed to occur later this year, and there is a significant total expansion in outright purchase programs.

speaker: HILTON
text: In this case, the balance sheet peaks at $4.6 trillion in 2010, although most of the growth occurs this year.

speaker: HILTON
text: In the outyears—2011 and beyond—in all scenarios we assume a natural runoff of assets.

speaker: HILTON
text: Short-term lending at liquidity facilities dissipates relatively quickly.

speaker: HILTON
text: TALF loans mature on schedule.

speaker: HILTON
text: And the gradual declines in outright holdings reflect either maturities or prepayments of agency mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: HILTON
text: On the liability side of the balance sheet, apart from some assumed nominal growth in Federal Reserve note liabilities, the offset to asset movements is the level of reserve balances held by depository institutions.

speaker: HILTON
text: The reserve estimates can provide a sense of the possible size of any need either to drain reserves or to increase reserve demand should the Federal Reserve wish to target short-term interest rates—the federal funds rate—using conventional operating procedures that are typically associated with keeping excess reserve levels near zero.

speaker: HILTON
text: Exhibit 13 shows reserve levels for all three scenarios.

speaker: HILTON
text: Peak reserve levels reach $3.7 trillion in 2010 in the stress scenario.

speaker: HILTON
text: While it is unlikely that a return to a positive interest rate target would coincide with when reserve levels were at their maximum, that occasion could come unexpectedly quickly nonetheless.

speaker: HILTON
text: The memo concludes by presenting the various options available to the Federal Reserve for accomplishing this.

speaker: HILTON
text: From October to December 2008, excess reserves were left high, and market rates were considerably below the interest rate paid on excess reserves.

speaker: HILTON
text: There are good reasons to believe that experience may not represent the normal relation between market rates and the rate of interest paid on excess reserves.

speaker: HILTON
text: Nonetheless, policymakers might be uncomfortable at this point adopting a framework to control market rates by setting the interest rate paid on excess reserves alone while leaving excess reserves at high levels.

speaker: HILTON
text: The Treasury’s supplementary financing program or authority for the Federal Reserve to issue its own debt would provide considerable capacity to drain reserves, and little additional operational infrastructure would be needed.

speaker: HILTON
text: Traditional monetary policy tools, sales of assets and reverse RPs, could be developed to support reserve draining operations on a much larger scale than ever used in the past.

speaker: HILTON
text: These could take some time to develop to their full potential, and there is some question about the scale on which these tools could be deployed.

speaker: HILTON
text: Finally, the broad authority to pay interest on reserves that the Federal Reserve now has could be utilized in other ways to shape demand for reserves so as to effectively reduce excess reserves to levels that would allow the Fed to target positive short-term interest rates within a more conventional operating framework.

speaker: HILTON
text: Here, too, some period of time would be needed to develop an effective operating framework using interest-on-reserves authority.

speaker: HILTON
text: Now I’ll turn it over to Brian to conclude.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As Spence Hilton noted, it could be very useful to have an additional tool for draining substantial volumes of reserves from the banking system and shrinking the monetary base.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Either the issuance of Fed bills or an enhanced supplementary financing program run by the Treasury on behalf of the Federal Reserve could be particularly helpful.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The staff has drafted legislative language that would authorize these tools.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Because the Treasury would have a substantial interest in such programs, and because we would need the Treasury’s support in advancing such legislation, we have been discussing this subject with the Treasury.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Our presumption is that we would not seek legislation both for Fed bills and for an enhanced SFP.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Rather, we and the Treasury together would raise both possibilities with the relevant congressional committees to discuss the substance and the political prospects for each.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On the basis of those discussions, one approach or the other would be advanced.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To give adequate assurance to the Federal Reserve and to the markets that these tools will provide the capability to tighten monetary policy as necessary and when necessary, the tools would have to be effectively under the Federal Reserve’s control.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Two possible constraints are of particular concern: the public debt ceiling, and possible interference by a future Treasury.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To ensure that a binding debt ceiling does not disrupt the conduct of monetary policy, Fed bills or Treasury bills issued under an enhanced SFP program would have to be excluded from the debt ceiling.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: And to ensure that a future Treasury could not block the implementation of appropriate monetary policy, the Federal Reserve either will need to be able to issue its own obligations as it sees fit to carry out its statutory mandate, or it will need to be able to direct the Treasury to do so as its proxy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, the Congress may see the exclusion of Fed bills or SFP obligations from the debt ceiling as an unwarranted dilution of the congressional responsibility to appropriate government monies and to authorize the issuance of federal debt.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: And we recognize that the Treasury is concerned about the potential for issuance of such securities to interfere with the Treasury’s responsibility for managing the public debt.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Draft legislation prepared by the staff would assign the primary responsibility within the Federal Reserve for the issuance of Fed bills or SFP bills to the Federal Open Market Committee.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This seems appropriate because the main purpose of the tool, as we see it, is to ensure the capability of the FOMC to tighten monetary policy when appropriate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We see Fed bills as a tool on the liabilities side of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet that would essentially be symmetric with our asset-side open market operations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The legislation should also address several other key issues.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In that regard, we have included the following specific elements in the draft legislation we sent to the Treasury:  First, Fed bills would be full faith and credit obligations of the United States in order to maximize their acceptability to investors, to make them as close substitutes as possible for Treasury securities, and to minimize the interest expense of such obligations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text:  Second, for similar reasons, Fed bills should not be subject to state and local income taxes.

speaker: MADIGAN
text:  Third, the Treasury has suggested a statutory maximum maturity of Fed bills in order to limit interference with Treasury debt management.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We have recommended a maximum maturity of one year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Treasury staff members prefer a shorter maximum term.

speaker: MADIGAN
text:  Finally, we have recommended that the Fed not be required to notify the Treasury a fixed number of days before issuing Fed bills or scheduling issuance of SFP bills, but rather that the legislation indicate qualitatively that issuance of Fed bills or SFP bills should minimize interference with the conduct of the Treasury’s regular debt management responsibilities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As President Plosser and others have noted, there are pros and cons to the Fed bills and expanded SFP proposals.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: And even with the support of the Administration, the political prospects for such legislation are not clear at this stage.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is possible that the Federal Reserve may need to accept some changes to the draft legislation to obtain passage.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One possible change that might help make the program acceptable to all interested parties would be a sunset provision under which the authority to issue such obligations expires after, say, five years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you for a very thorough set of reports.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Out of those reports, there was, I believe, one action item we’ll come back to—besides ratifying the open market operations—which is the swap proposal that Nathan discussed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But let’s open now for questions to any of the staff.

speaker: FISHER
text: If I can go back to the beginning, or almost the beginning, and ask some questions about the TALF in terms of lessons learned—I understand that Barclays has put together a pass-through certificate program that seems to have some acceptance, at least in the hedge fund community.

speaker: FISHER
text: Could you bring us up to date on that and what it means in terms of the functioning of the TALF?

speaker: FISHER
text: Does it make it more complicated?

speaker: FISHER
text: And is it something that’s going forward?

speaker: NELSON
text: I’ll do the best I can.

speaker: NELSON
text: First of all, this is something that we’ve been allowing the private sector to develop.

speaker: NELSON
text: It’s not like some of these other instances where we’ve worked with the private sector to develop special purpose vehicles like the MMIFF.

speaker: NELSON
text: These are private sector efforts.

speaker: NELSON
text: These things first came up in discussions when we were trying to think of ways to make the program useful for real money investors.

speaker: NELSON
text: Part of the challenge in the TALF is that the objective is to encourage an investor class that normally hasn’t invested in asset-backed securities to move into that space, namely, leveraged investors.

speaker: NELSON
text: Traditionally, asset-backed securities have been held by real money investors, like pension funds and insurance companies.

speaker: NELSON
text: So we were trying to think of ways that the program could be made more attractive for those investors.

speaker: NELSON
text: One way to do that would be to have a special purpose vehicle purchase the asset- backed securities and take the loan and raise the haircut part of that transaction by issuing equity.

speaker: NELSON
text: That equity could conceivably be a tradable security which could be invested in by real money investors.

speaker: NELSON
text: When we looked at that a month or so ago, it didn’t necessarily seem as if it was going to be successful, though my understanding is that it has gotten more momentum in recent weeks.

speaker: NELSON
text: In particular, the one thing that I think would really make it take off would be if those equity tranches could be rated by the credit rating agencies, and I am not sure where that effort stands.

speaker: NELSON
text: Another reason these special purpose vehicles came up was our requirement that we only lend to U.S. entities.

speaker: NELSON
text: Many hedge funds are actually foreign entities, but we viewed it as acceptable (and I may not get this exactly right) if there was a U.S. arm of that entity with a U.S. operation—an actual person, a manager there—that would be a U.S. entity that we could lend to.

speaker: NELSON
text: So to some extent there was an effort to set up vehicles along those lines.

speaker: NELSON
text: Then, lastly, there has been interest in potentially insulating the financial institution from some things like the H-1B visa issue that I just mentioned or some other consequences of the program itself.

speaker: NELSON
text: I don’t think any of these things are likely to be moving forward for this subscription, but rather they are continuing to be reviewed by the private sector and being developed.

speaker: FISHER
text: But just so I understand this, let’s assume that this proceeds.

speaker: FISHER
text: I perceive it as having significant momentum in the investment community.

speaker: FISHER
text: The SPVs would be performing basically a clearing function.

speaker: FISHER
text: They create a CUSIP-identified tradable security.

speaker: FISHER
text: The people that could buy those securities would not have to worry about all the ramifications of the TARP in terms of the political ramifications that seem to be spooking the hedge fund and other communities—is that correct?

speaker: NELSON
text: Well, it’s not clear, and I think that’s the rub right now.

speaker: NELSON
text: The folks that are concerned about compliance, I think, have written our regulations to say we will look through such structures to the ownership entity to make sure that the compliance protocols have been followed.

speaker: NELSON
text: On the other hand, when we say whom we’re actually lending to, I think that language has been more along the lines of—in particular, say, for whether or not it’s a U.S. entity—“it’s okay to set up one of these entities.” And because those two efforts are not yet completely lined up, that’s why I believe these things are still under development and there are still open questions that need to be answered before it’s clear that they will be able to go forward.

speaker: FISHER
text: Would you say that this search for new engineering is a function of the discomfort of the hedge fund community and the investment community with the TALF, given the TARP restrictions that are placed on top?

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m just trying to understand where this came from.

speaker: NELSON
text: I think it came up for several of these reasons.

speaker: NELSON
text: That’s certainly one of them.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I can see where this could also certainly be suspicious politically.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m just trying to understand how this TALF thing is going to unfold, because there seems to be some momentum in this direction, at least from the standpoint of Simpson Thacher, who are the lawyers behind it.

speaker: FISHER
text: Forget about the dealer relationship to the Fed—it’s between the dealers and the investment community where there’s still this odd linkage here.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of the order, I think the SPV was initially a device so that real money investors could get involved in the TALF.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But then, as all the political considerations became more severe over the last couple of weeks, people thought, “well, hey, we could also use it for this second purpose—to provide some distance from the government and the TARP restrictions.” But the original impetus was for real money accounts.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of the reasons I’m raising it is that I think we’ve got to be careful not to get the cart before the horse here, and in the presentation, I realized, just looking down the path, we’re talking about legacy assets.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’re going to have to get the first setup correct before we go further down the path.

speaker: FISHER
text: At least I would recommend that to the Committee.

speaker: NELSON
text: Yes, and we have remained very focused on that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Can you quickly give me a matrix that says what TALF issuance we’re talking about and how much, starting with the original $200 billion and then the various add-ons, up to the total—just so I understand what we’re talking about in each issuance or expansion of the TALF program?

speaker: NELSON
text: At this time, our estimate is that, over the life of the program, the collateral that was approved initially—that’s beginning today, and that’s consumer ABS and Small Business Administration ABS—that should amount, we think, to $100 billion.

speaker: NELSON
text: So we won’t make it to $200 billion unless the program is expanded.

speaker: NELSON
text: The additional asset classes that we’ve proposed to the Board for inclusion, which would largely complete the asset-backed securities space, as well as mortgage servicer advances, would add another $30 billion.

speaker: NELSON
text: So those combined would still not bring us to $200 billion.

speaker: NELSON
text: The rest of the analysis is really very tentative.

speaker: NELSON
text: So our effort is to be as inclusive as possible, and we’re looking at the major collateralized high-quality asset classes.

speaker: HOENIG
text: This would go all the way to legacy commercial-mortgage-backed securities?

speaker: NELSON
text: At this point I was thinking in terms of newly issued securities.

speaker: NELSON
text: The range that the teams have provided goes from $50 to $500 billion depending on a number of issues, including whether or not warehouse financing is available, whether or not investors can grow comfortable with the rather extreme mismatch between the maturity of the TALF loans and the maturity of the underlying securities.

speaker: NELSON
text: So that last step conceivably would still not take us to the $1 trillion.

speaker: NELSON
text: But it is, I must say, very uncertain because they’re still just scoping out those securities.

speaker: NELSON
text: Now, legacy assets would then add on to that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have several questions and a comment at the end.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, a compliment to the New York staff: I thought that the material distributed ahead of time outlining all of the asset programs was very informative, very well laid out, and very succinct.

speaker: LACKER
text: My compliments to you on that work.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have a question for Ms. Mosser.

speaker: LACKER
text: This has to do with the comparison between a program of agency and MBS purchases like we’ve been pursuing and what a program of U.S. Treasury purchases would look like.

speaker: LACKER
text: My understanding is that you plan your announcements and the size of your purchases a little bit in advance.

speaker: LACKER
text: Would we get any more flexibility by using Treasuries rather than MBS or are they pretty much the same?

speaker: LACKER
text: Would you get a little more flexibility to vary the size of the purchases week to week?

speaker: MOSSER
text: It’s a different kind of flexibility.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the mortgage-backed securities program, although we do buy across the curve in all coupons, we are focused very much on the TBA, or the forward delivery market, which trades weeks and months in advance of delivery.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If that’s the market that you’re trading and buying in, you have a huge amount of flexibility from day to day to respond to prices in that market and just to buy more forward contracts or fewer or do a dollar roll and offset some of those if you have to.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But then on delivery day you get, as we did last week, $160 billion of securities.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So in that sense of flexibility—can you respond daily to market events, for example, tighter spreads, narrower spreads?—it’s very easy to do.

speaker: MOSSER
text: That’s a very deep, liquid market; it’s a very homogeneous market, even though what you get delivered is fairly heterogeneous.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the Treasury market, it’s a different kind of flexibility.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We can buy in various parts of the Treasury curve.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the mortgage market, it’s very hard to move around the mortgage yield curve easily, but it’s easy to do that in the Treasury curve.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So I’m not quite sure what you mean by flexibility.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If you mean sheer quantity, they’re probably about the same.

speaker: LACKER
text: When you buy Treasuries, when you do a coupon pass, do you settle the same day or next day?

speaker: LACKER
text: These MBS and agency securities—they settle once a month?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Several times a month, but yes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It depends on the type of security, but yes, basically once a month.

speaker: LACKER
text: So if I looked at it from the point of view of what happens to bank reserves, it’s just a once-a-month hit.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Well, it’s once a month per type of security.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So there are actually several days a month.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But it’s very periodic and very, very predictable when they’re going to settle.

speaker: LACKER
text: For Spence, I was very interested in the forecast of the balance sheet, and we’ve been talking about that for the last couple of meetings.

speaker: LACKER
text: You have the forecast going up in a straight line to the end of the year, and I take it that’s just because you forecasted the end-of-year balance sheet, right?

speaker: LACKER
text: Do you have a sense of what it’s going to do between now and the next meeting?

speaker: LACKER
text: Have you done that exercise?

speaker: HILTON
text: Not really systematically in the way this is put together.

speaker: HILTON
text: Our sense, though, between now and the next meeting, is that what we’re going to be buying is fairly predictable.

speaker: HILTON
text: I’m not sure what the settlement dates are, but if the settlement dates were smooth, we would be expanding pretty much at the same pace.

speaker: HILTON
text: I’d expect the liquidity facilities, though, to hang out where they are and maybe, on balance, come off a little bit further, barring some sort of a stress period.

speaker: HILTON
text: So I would anticipate that we’re predominantly in an expansion phase right now.

speaker: LACKER
text: So, in principle, if I asked you to write down numerically, as you did for the end of the year, a forecast for the monetary base at the next meeting, say, you could do that?

speaker: HILTON
text: Yeah—with a nice confidence interval.

speaker: LACKER
text: Subject to the usual caveats.

speaker: LACKER
text: A question for Mr. Nelson.

speaker: LACKER
text: You named a bunch of asset categories that you’re considering for the TALF.

speaker: LACKER
text: What criteria are you using to pick those asset classes?

speaker: LACKER
text: I mean, what sort of principle or objective is driving those choices?

speaker: NELSON
text: Our objective is to take as broad a set of assets as possible, consistent with choosing ones that can be taken efficiently, that we can figure out ways to take with acceptable risk to the Federal Reserve System and to the government.

speaker: NELSON
text: But of relatively simple, straightforward structures, so that we can manage and understand the risk—but, nevertheless, as wide a group as possible.

speaker: NELSON
text: We’re just on the way to that at this stage.

speaker: LACKER
text: The original impetus involved certain securitization markets, where I thought we were motivated by particular observations that suggested distress.

speaker: LACKER
text: Are the problems we see in markets widespread across securitization?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Separate from conforming mortgage markets, where we have a different program, all other ABS markets, to my knowledge, are pretty much shut down.

speaker: LACKER
text: And then a question for Mr.

speaker: LACKER
text: You talked about moral hazard.

speaker: LACKER
text: This institution that you talked about—or any institution in this category—presumably has overseas operations in which they have liquid liabilities and less liquid assets?

speaker: LACKER
text: And I think we talked about this at the last meeting, right?

speaker: LACKER
text: That’s where you first briefed us on this.

speaker: LACKER
text: So, over that period—it’s been almost two months now—could an institution like that have reduced its vulnerability to the possibility of having a funding problem in another currency?

speaker: LACKER
text: Could it have let its deposits run off, maybe sell the assets upstream to the parent?

speaker: LACKER
text: And if that’s true, then wouldn’t the presence of this program influence an institution’s incentives to take steps in the weeks ahead to protect against potential funding problems?

speaker: SHEETS
text: That’s obviously a profoundly important question, and let me just address it at several different levels.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In terms of the specifics of that particular institution, one of the things that’s been a challenge for us is to get good data—for a range of such institutions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So it’s hard to state categorically what this institution or other institutions have done with their balance sheets over the last couple of months.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But I do think it’s very telling that in mid-February the stresses on the financial sector and the banks were, if anything, even more pronounced than they were in mid-January.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Yet we didn’t hear the same kinds of reports, and we didn’t observe the same stresses as in January, which may very well point to exactly the phenomenon that you’re indicating here—that the institution did things to reduce its vulnerability to these sorts of pressures.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So I think that is going on, absolutely.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That raises the question of whether this sort of a facility would dull those sorts of incentives.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As I said in my remarks, we’ve done everything we possibly can to structure this in such a way that it would be attractive to an institution only as a very last resort—the fees that we’re charging, the additional collateral, and so on and so forth.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Nevertheless, we can imagine instances where the drain on the foreign currency funding might be very intense, and even a well-managed institution might have problems raising sufficient collateral and resources on its own.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We can also imagine instances where the foreign central bank is not enthusiastic about lending against even good collateral for an institution.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Bank of Japan, in particular, remembers an instance from the late ‘90s when the Federal Reserve was not enthusiastic about lending to Japanese institutions because of what were perceived as political pressures in the United States, and they’ve asked us to consider the possibility that something similar might happen to them, and they wouldn’t be able to lend to U.S. institutions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So notwithstanding the moral hazard risk, which, as I said, we’ve done everything we can in this proposal to attenuate, we still see that there would be plausible states of nature where it would be prudent to have these foreign currency swap lines in place.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I could just follow up, Mr. Chairman, I take it that the institutions, the half dozen you referred to, are bank holding companies in the United States.

speaker: LACKER
text: What steps have we taken—particularly regarding the one you referred to as being especially vulnerable—to encourage them to reduce their vulnerability to funding risks in foreign currencies?

speaker: SHEETS
text: I would have to defer to the regulators.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I don’t know if Trish has some information.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I also would defer to the supervisors on this.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But we have had conversations with the supervisory teams of a couple of these institutions (not just the one) since we decided that it was worth investigating, and nearly all of them are deleveraging abroad as they are deleveraging here and attempting to reduce their liquidity risk.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think that eliminating that risk in a really short period of time is probably unrealistic, considering the size and scope of operations, including very traditional banking operations—which, we all know, are subject to runs—that several of these institutions have in many countries.

speaker: MOSSER
text: And many of those countries do not have, for example, the deposit insurance schemes that the United States does, which means the institutions are more vulnerable there.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think the possibility of completely shutting down and eliminating the risk in a short period of time is probably unrealistic, although movement in that direction is a good idea.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is it our sense that they’re doing all they could?

speaker: MOSSER
text: My impression is that they are moving in that direction.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I wouldn’t superimpose my views over the supervisors’ about whether they’re doing everything they can.

speaker: BAILEY
text: I’m not quite sure how to frame “all they can.” I think the supervisors— particularly with the company that’s probably the most international of all—have clearly gone through their funding.

speaker: BAILEY
text: It has set up appropriate funding mechanisms within those countries where they are being looked at, and they have taken good significant steps to try to address some of the vulnerabilities.

speaker: BAILEY
text: They’ve had outreach meetings with the different central banks.

speaker: BAILEY
text: So during the last year, they have actually been taking a lot of aggressive steps to try to minimize the vulnerability associated with that.

speaker: BAILEY
text: But some of the organizations are big purchasers in foreign currencies.

speaker: BAILEY
text: We just can’t shut that down that quickly, nor do we expect to.

speaker: BAILEY
text: It’s just not a believable strategy for that funding mechanism.

speaker: BAILEY
text: But they’re looking more broadly both at the U.S. and abroad.

speaker: LACKER
text: I guess I’m looking not for shutting them down, but for measures that could reduce the funding vulnerability, the liability–asset mismatch that gives rise to the risk.

speaker: BAILEY
text: They absolutely have been not only looking at those strategies, but also executing those strategies.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are we just going to do questions for now?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are we going to have an opportunity to do a sort of go-around?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There will be a discussion period as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is just for questions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just wanted to go by the rules.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the large-scale asset purchases, I have a couple of questions about some of the underlying assumptions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was struck by the fact that the assumption was that, under an MBS purchase of $500 billion, the rates on corporates and Treasuries also go down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But the net effect of that, given the assumptions you made, was that corporate spreads rise by 20 basis points, whereas under a Treasury bill purchase, corporate spreads fall by 20 basis points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m puzzled about what model generates that kind of differential effect, and how much that might be driving some of the stimulation results that you’ve got.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m a little puzzled about what drives—well, I know what drives it; the numbers you put down drove it—but I didn’t know whether you thought that was internally consistent or whether there were economic mechanisms that you thought that was consistent with.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The second question I had was about the assumptions about the elasticities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You’ve got a mortgage-backed security market that’s $7 or $8 trillion, somewhere in that neighborhood, you’ve got a $500 billion purchase—so that’s a little less than 10 percent of the marketplace— and you get a 75 basis point effect, whereas for long-term Treasuries you’ve got less than $2 trillion total and you do a $500 billion operation, and you only get a 30 or 50 basis point effect.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So there you’re participating in almost a third of the market, and in the other case only about 10 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It may be true that those are the right elasticities, but I’m wondering where those came from.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: To get any effect in some of this stuff, you’ve got to have some sort of market segmentation going on so that you can play the yield curve game a little bit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The other question on that topic was related to President Lacker’s question.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The presumption of these programs, particularly the mortgage-backed purchases, is that there’s something amiss in the markets, that we’re trying to fix some intermediation problems, or there are some dysfunctions in those markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And yet it seemed to me that, as you expanded the so- called spillover effects and they got bigger and bigger and bigger, it goes against the very presumption of why you wanted to be in these markets in the first place—to try to promote intermediation and liquidity.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I didn’t know how these two assumptions connected or reconciled with one another—how you could get both large spillover effects and maintain the presumption that these markets were dysfunctional.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wasn’t quite sure how those two pieces fit together.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the swaps, following President Lacker’s comments, I had some of the same questions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It seems to me that you offered three reasons why these swaps might be needed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One was this issue of not having enough collateral in the foreign country for the central bank to do the lending it wanted to do, and the second reason was the foreign central bank maybe wouldn’t accept the U.S. bank’s collateral.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But the other reasons really had to do with the solvency of that institution.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It seems to me that, from an operational point of view, if a bank is insolvent, it’s not clear we ought to be lending to them in the first place, so I’m not sure that’s a reason to be in this business.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And given that it only applies to perhaps four or five banks, if it’s really a liquidity problem, it seems to me that doing this through the discount window is a much more natural way to think about what it is we’re doing and the problem we’re trying to solve.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You offered some concerns about how difficult that would be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess none of those seemed insurmountable to me.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And the fact of the matter is that we would probably be doing most of this lending out of New York anyway, so it’s not as if you’re going to have to worry about lots of the Reserve Banks necessarily having to get foreign currency.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It just seemed to me that it might be a better way to go because (a) we do not want to lend to insolvent institutions and (b) the discount window seems appropriate for exactly that liquidity problem rather than designing another facility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The last question I have is about the announcement effects.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I worry that this is going to be interpreted by the markets as a veiled or not-so-veiled attempt to support one institution.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think the markets will see through that very quickly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t know how to mitigate that if we decide to do it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It could be viewed as a less than transparent effort on the part of this institution to support a particular institution, and I think that, in turn, may damage our credibility and damage our reputation in the marketplace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think if an institution is in trouble and we make the decision to help it in some way, then we ought to do it on its merits and not try to “back door” that solution through another mechanism.

speaker: GAGNON
text: If I could start with the first couple of questions, I think our views have been evolving somewhat as we’ve been working on this.

speaker: GAGNON
text: When I looked at the literature while I was working on the December memo, there wasn’t an agreed-upon way to normalize or scale purchases like this.

speaker: GAGNON
text: So what I did at the time was to take the most common approach, which was to look at the total size of the market across all maturities—and that was about $5 trillion for U.S. Treasuries.

speaker: GAGNON
text: The idea was to consider a purchase over a broad range of maturities at the long end, say, maturities of more than three years, but I didn’t fine-tune it to segments or look at just the long end per se.

speaker: GAGNON
text: You might want to do that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If you want to get a lot of response, it seems to me you’ve got to think about it as a segmented market of some kind.

speaker: GAGNON
text: I have been moving in the direction that you’re thinking of about whether there are differential effects, but there’s just not an accepted view in the literature on how to do this—it isn’t even really discussed very much.

speaker: GAGNON
text: On the MBS market, if you take MBS and agency debt together and then net out the agency holdings of MBS, you get about $7 trillion.

speaker: GAGNON
text: But it’s not clear you should merge them in that way; if they were each treated separately, as two separate markets—agencies and MBS—those would each be smaller.

speaker: GAGNON
text: I wasn’t sure, I threw up my hands and said, “well, it’s roughly the same size.” That’s how we got the $500 billion treated that way in each market.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Since we wrote the December memo, Treasury debt has gone up a lot; and it’s noted in our latest memo that, in fact, the range we get, which is quite large— 20 to 100 basis points—would need to be shifted down some, given that about $1 trillion of Treasuries have been issued just since we wrote the earlier memo.

speaker: GAGNON
text: So the ground is shifting beneath our feet.

speaker: GAGNON
text: And I didn’t really pay attention to that until quite late in the process.

speaker: GAGNON
text: But these ranges are quite large.

speaker: GAGNON
text: We just don’t know within a big range where the answer is.

speaker: GAGNON
text: One final thing before I let Dave jump in is, given all of that, we still thought purchases of MBS, especially initially, would have a bigger effect on MBS yields than purchases of Treasuries would have on Treasury yields, because the MBS market was strained and spreads were unusually high.

speaker: GAGNON
text: We thought we could push the spreads down.

speaker: GAGNON
text: And they’re still on the high side historically, so there is still, I think, some scope to do that.

speaker: GAGNON
text: And if you keep going down that road, presumably, the scope to do further improvements of spreads does diminish.

speaker: GAGNON
text: In terms of your question, we have the effect of MBS purchases lowering the corporate spread to Treasuries.

speaker: GAGNON
text: And we have Treasury purchases raising the corporate spread.

speaker: GAGNON
text: So, again, we thought buying private assets would reduce private spreads generally to some extent, whereas buying Treasuries, which are the favored asset, actually might widen spreads.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Because the market would anticipate that we may go in and buy those other private assets, such as corporate bonds?

speaker: GAGNON
text: The thought was that the Treasury purchases would be taking a safe haven out of the market and then that would lower Treasury yields more than other assets, so it would widen spreads.

speaker: GAGNON
text: For MBS purchases, it seemed to us that just generally you’re helping remove private sector assets, so it should help all private sector assets relative to Treasuries.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s just a funny distortion, it seems to me.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: There is a funny distortion, but I think in some sense it can almost be a distraction.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: One of the problems we had was—and we talked about this when we wrote this down—whether we should stick with this bigger own-yield effect on MBS than on Treasuries.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: And our sense is—I hope it came out in the memos—we don’t really know what the direct own-yield effects will be.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We had sort of an experiment on the first $500 billion—what’s the second $500 billion going to be?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So there’s this issue of scale that could change quite a bit as you go through time.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Whether there are spillover effects from MBS into Treasuries or into high- grade corporates—there’s a huge uncertainty about that.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: And for that reason, I think you shouldn’t interpret the model simulation evidence—to the extent it is evidence—as suggesting, “oh, MBS is the way to go because you get a much bigger bang for your buck on that than you would for Treasuries.” I don’t think that’s the way to interpret it at all.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I think the way to interpret the model simulation results is that buying large amounts of these securities, whether it’s Treasuries or MBS, has at least a fighting chance of bringing down the general level of long-term interest rates.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: And if you can do that, and if that spills over into the stock market, the exchange rate, that sort of thing, then you potentially get a major stimulus to the real economy.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: If the program just becomes narrow on one particular market—suppose you just drive down MBS—then you might not get very much for that.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Maybe you would get a little bit more—maybe—in the case of MBS, because then you’re affecting mortgage rates and refi effects and house prices—maybe—but it’s not really where the big payoff comes from, at least as far as these particular stimulations go.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The big payoff comes from general reductions in the level of all long-term rates, and then these other things follow.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So we thought that was important.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: That’s really the main way to think about the program.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What I was trying to get at was this issue that the payoff is lowering all long-term interest rates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And your assumption is that you’ve got this differential spread effect.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is that driving this notion that buying MBS might be differentially better?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Why wouldn’t you just buy Treasuries and get the spillover?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Joe and I may part company here, but I don’t think there’s a strong case that buying MBS is definitely more advantageous than Treasuries.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I think we just don’t know enough about what size the effect is.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: There are reasons to think that it might be bigger in the case of MBS, but it’s very difficult to say.

speaker: GAGNON
text: I would just note that MBS yields have come down a lot more than Treasury yields over this period, so that would support our view.

speaker: GAGNON
text: Whether that would continue for the next $500 billion or the $500 billion after that—maybe not.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, that really prompts the other question: What’s the appropriate way to think about the scales of these operations?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How do we think about diminishing returns in these markets?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: It’s anyone’s guess, and it’s also the case, as Joe said in his remarks, that the more you focus on one market, the more you’re not really taking a diverse strategy on something in which it’s not quite clear how this is going to play out.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Also, the more you focus on one market, the more the question arises at some point: Do you just decouple that market from everything else?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I think the second question that you raised had to do with this issue of fixing market dysfunction and whether that was a potential conflict if you were getting this better economy.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Although we thought of the bigger MBS effect as maybe having potentially a somewhat bigger bang for the buck, because it might be helping to ease certain market strains, we thought in all cases that the reason for this policy is not to deal with the strains of financial markets per se.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: It may have that effect by strengthening the economy and so on and so forth—an indirect effect— but the main purpose was to get around the zero bound by driving down the average level of long-term interest rates and getting other general financial conditions to improve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Trish, did you have a comment?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Yes, I had a comment about how long this goes on.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It seems—both from our MBS purchase program and from the U.K.’s announcement—that a huge amount of the interest rate effect happens on announcement, not on execution.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It doesn’t grow over time as the purchases get bigger and bigger and bigger.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Discerning spread changes from the purchase levels is very tricky business, and so is the macro effect—I wouldn’t venture there.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But that announcement effect happens because of the assumption that the central banks are going to keep buying for a while, not that they’re just going to do it for a month or two and then stop the program and go away.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I am fairly certain that in the U.S. we’ll see that reaction in mortgage spreads—if the determination was made to stop in July, the forward rates in July would pop right up and we’d be back to approximately where we were in January.

speaker: MOSSER
text: There’s a question already arising about what the Bank of England is going to do after three months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, uncertainty about our policies really creates a lot of problems.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’d like to congratulate you on being a tough taskmaster, with having us sit and listen to an hour’s worth of briefings without any questions.

speaker: EVANS
text: I had seven, but I’m down to three now.

speaker: EVANS
text: And I’ll be jumping around, too, because of that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’d like to ask a question of Dave Reifschneider first, having to do with exhibit 3 on the inflation forecast under large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: EVANS
text: Let me mention at the outset that I’ll reveal later on in this meeting that I’m not overly concerned about inflation, but having seen this chart, I’m suspicious of this, and it’s in the way that the analysis is done.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I read the Bluebook, it seems that the unconstrained optimal policy has inflation rising because inflation expectations rise, and you have inflation expectations depend on errors in the Taylor rule, as I understand it.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I’m guessing that the model is seeing very accommodative monetary policy and translating that into increases in inflation expectations, and that’s why inflation is up.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, I’m going to guess that you do not have that same effect in these other forecasts.

speaker: EVANS
text: And that makes no sense to me because the whole point is to replicate an accommodative monetary policy.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I would have come up with some translation of how accommodative and unusual this is and tried to feed this into it.

speaker: EVANS
text: Success would be when you come up with a nontraditional policy that matches that the unconstrained outcome, because that’s what we’re trying to do with the optimal policy.

speaker: EVANS
text: My guess is that, if you went back and were successful, this inflation outlook would have more overshooting, right?

speaker: EVANS
text: So I don’t think we can rely too much on that chart.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: When we were doing the Bluebook box, we had this discussion.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We saw that this is a real limitation of the model—that in one case it gets to learn off of what the fed funds rate is doing relative to the rest of the economy, and in the other case it doesn’t know how to learn off of these large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So we said, what are we going to do about it?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Do we just write something down?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Do we try to come up with the correct fix?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: And the answer was, we had ideas for how to fix it correctly, but there is no way we’re going to figure out the right way to do this in a week.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So you are exactly correct.

speaker: EVANS
text: I like the model analysis.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think it’s very useful, and I think this is just a limitation, and that’s how everybody should interpret it, because you’re doing a great job on the unemployment rate here.

speaker: EVANS
text: That sort of tips you off.

speaker: EVANS
text: Let me jump to the balance sheet scenarios, because I looked at those scenarios, but didn’t see one that, in light of disinflation risk, I would like to see.

speaker: EVANS
text: If it were costly to have one more, I would drop one of the others instead.

speaker: EVANS
text: The ones that I’d like to see are where the Committee finds itself in a position where we need to raise rates, but we have a lot of sticky assets on our balance sheet, we’re not quite sure how to address that, and we don’t get legislative relief.

speaker: EVANS
text: While I do not put a high probability on this scenario, I think it’s important to understand it.

speaker: EVANS
text: What if inflation expectations rose?

speaker: EVANS
text: I think it would have to be an exogenous increase— something that is not currently imbedded in my thinking and in the model analysis here—but, what if?

speaker: EVANS
text: Certainly a lot of people are out there looking at our balance sheet—I think incorrectly—but they’re looking at it and saying “something’s going to get out of hand.” So if we could see a scenario like that, including how we would have to grapple with balancing the conflicts, it would be very informative.

speaker: EVANS
text: That’s more of a suggestion.

speaker: EVANS
text: Finally, I have a relatively elementary question about the TALF: What is the value- added of the investor in the middle in this entire transaction?

speaker: EVANS
text: We’re bringing hedge funds to the table, and I’ve thought, well, they’re going to help with price discovery to make sure that this issuance is really right, but I don’t know that that’s really a strong role.

speaker: EVANS
text: There’s a lot of private capital on the sidelines—according to what everybody tells us—and they’re going to bring a very small part of it to the transaction.

speaker: EVANS
