text: But what they are demanding—I hear from everybody I talk to—are very high levered rates of return, which hedge funds are typically associated with delivering.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is going to be in relatively low-risk transactions—triple-A.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’re not expecting to lose on them, but we could.

speaker: EVANS
text: But what does this mean?

speaker: EVANS
text: We’re hoping this will kick-start a secondary market.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s that kick start—I don’t know where that comes from.

speaker: EVANS
text: There’s capital on the sidelines.

speaker: EVANS
text: What will bring it to the table?

speaker: EVANS
text: I would guess that they would start by looking at this and saying, “Well, the safest investment has 20 percent rates of return.

speaker: EVANS
text: So from here on out the risk curve, the rates should be higher.” I’m already hearing from a lot of contacts that this is very expensive, that they have to deliver this, and they’re not sure if they are going to participate very much.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is the risk–return frontier in some sense being moved up by this program?

speaker: EVANS
text: Will competition really bring these returns down?

speaker: EVANS
text: That’s what we always think, but I don’t know where competition is going to come from, because it’s on the sidelines.

speaker: EVANS
text: I really have to understand why it’s on the sidelines and why it will now be forthcoming.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you think there’s an aggregation externality in liquidity—getting activity going again so that people issue and so on?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would be one reason why it would stimulate additional activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: It seems like a hope at the moment.

speaker: EVANS
text: And I’m not opposed to hoping a lot.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that’s our best tool right now.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’ve followed a few international liquidity crises over the years, and they often start in strange places, and my question is: Do we need to think about exotic currencies—currencies in which there is not really a dollar swap or foreign currency swap market that could provide funding, but where the institution in mind may have pretty sizable book?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The idea would be to try to nip something in the bud before it gets to a hard currency.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This is an issue I’ve actually spent a fair amount of time thinking about.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For instance, one of these major institutions has a fair amount of exposure to some of the secondary and tertiary emerging Asian currencies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But the staff simply didn’t feel comfortable recommending the establishment of, say, 30 or 40 or 50 swap lines with foreign central banks.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We see this proposal as providing a foreign currency backstop for these institutions—a safety net of some stripe—which, hopefully, between giving them access to yen or euro or whatever the case may be, and their dollar holdings, would enable them to respond to stresses in some of these secondary markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I note that there is a risk.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We don’t see it as being significant, but there’s a risk that these institutions might mobilize collateral from some of these markets where there is liquidity support into some of these secondary markets; hence becoming more dependent on our liquidity facilities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But we didn’t see any way around leaving some residual liquidity risk.

speaker: SHEETS
text: It’s a thorny, thorny issue.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Mr. Chairman, President Plosser asked several questions about the swap lines.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Could I go ahead and answer those?

speaker: SHEETS
text: First of all, let me underscore that we see these lines as being focused primarily and exclusively on liquidity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: What we have in mind in that third case is that an institution has been declared dead and is out of business; we’re suggesting in that sort of a scenario, it might be useful for the authorities to have access to foreign currency liquidity in the process of winding up the balance sheet and ensuring an orderly wrap-up, consistent with all of the legal protocols and so on.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We’re not advocating a loan to an institution that’s actually insolvent as if it were a solvent institution.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Your second question was on the discount window versus the SOMA approach or the swap approach.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As I said in my remarks, it’s something we spent a lot of time deliberating.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the one hand, there are certain aspects of this that have a discount window flavor.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the other hand, there’s no history of the discount window doing foreign currency operations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We’ve done a lot of things without much history.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the other hand, SOMA is where we’ve done all of those foreign currency operations, and at the end of the day, operationally, we just saw the discount window approach as adding another layer of complexity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We had to figure out how to get the resources from SOMA to the individual Reserve Banks in order to make the discount window loan.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But this was a very close call, and it really was an issue of zigging rather than zagging.

speaker: SHEETS
text: From an operational standpoint, we felt that SOMA was the better approach.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Trish, do you want to expand on that?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Not to be too technical here, but because this swap would be cash collateral, in that sense there’s not a loan actually.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The institution would have to produce cash dollars and get cash yen, or whatever, on the other side.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If they’re in the middle of a distress situation, where do they get that cash?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Well, they’re probably going to be getting it from the discount window, honestly, or perhaps from the PDCF or somewhere else in order to execute this transaction.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So if there’s lending going on to an institution like this, it would be lending in dollars.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We don’t want to impose where the cash dollars come from, as a practical matter.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We don’t know quite where their collateral might be.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It might be in the PDCF.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It might be in their bank.

speaker: MOSSER
text: And it seemed, therefore, that to separate the liquidity swap part out from the lending part might actually have a few virtues.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On your third question about the announcement effects, we freely admit that there are uncertainties surrounding the nature of those announcement effects.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the one hand, as you described, there’s a possible adverse reaction.

speaker: SHEETS
text: On the other hand, at present it’s really no secret that major U.S. financial institutions are experiencing a range of stresses, so moves by the central banking community to further bulletproof liquidity in the global economy could be seen as a very positive thing.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But I grant that there is uncertainty.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We don’t know exactly how it would be received.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That is why we gave you this “proposal A versus proposal B” structure.

speaker: SHEETS
text: And if the Committee is concerned about the possibility of an adverse announcement effect or concerned that the announcement wouldn’t have manageable effects, then maybe the best approach would be a delegation to the Subcommittee; the Subcommittee could establish these lines closer to a time when it looked like they were actually going to be drawn on.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The other thought I have in response to your comments is, even though we’re likely talking about only a half a dozen institutions that have these sorts of vulnerabilities, if adverse circumstances arose, the implications could be very severe.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So I think it behooves us to think through the possibilities beforehand, and, as necessary, put in place mechanisms to address those sorts of vulnerabilities to the extent that we can.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nathan, would you address an elementary question?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we delegate the authority to the Foreign Currency Subcommittee, why wouldn’t that appear in the minutes, for example?

speaker: SHEETS
text: It would appear in the minutes.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But draft resolution B, which is the delegation to the Subcommittee, is not nearly as specific as draft resolution A.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This is just saying that the FOMC delegated to the Foreign Currency Subcommittee the capacity to negotiate these foreign currency swap lines—it doesn’t delineate the lines with the same degree of specificity that the other resolution does.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, it’s not saying that these lines are established—it’s only saying that the Subcommittee has the capacity to establish them if it so chooses.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So it’s not as specific, and our view, at least, is that it wouldn’t be seen by the markets or by the world as indicating the same degree of urgency as an actual approval of the lines would.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I have a couple of questions, and both of them have been answered indirectly through our give and take, but I wanted to make sure I was clear in my understanding of these issues.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Both President Hoenig and President Lacker have asked my first question, but I’m going to ask it in a third way, just to make sure I’m clear.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As we’re contemplating the extension of the TALF into these other, more narrow, categories, is it because there are critical problems in these markets?

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Or is it also a supply issue?

speaker: PIANALTO
text: That is, we can’t reach even the currently announced $200 billion if we are purchasing securities only in the categories that we’ve already announced.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The second question is somewhat related, and, again, I think you’ve already answered this.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Do we know who is purchasing the lower-rated tranches of the securities, and what price are they paying for them?

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I know, Mr. Chairman, you said that the securitization market isn’t even existent, but a lot of my contacts have been saying that it is important to the functioning of the ABS market to also get those lower-rated securities purchased and trading.

speaker: NELSON
text: Let me distinguish in my answer between those assets which we requested the Board to add this week and the completion of TALF 2.0.

speaker: NELSON
text: For the assets that are being added this week, the objective is to fill out the ABS space, largely.

speaker: NELSON
text: That’s the market that, in fact, shut down in the fourth quarter.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So that means that there are both critical problems in that market and that, in order to get the dollar amount that we’re trying to put into that market, we need to expand the asset classes.

speaker: NELSON
text: These asset classes themselves are smaller than the ones that have already been approved, but they are, nevertheless, relatively large in size.

speaker: NELSON
text: But it won’t get us meaningfully closer to the ceiling.

speaker: NELSON
text: We’re addressing it at this point because the assets are quite similar to the ones that we’ve already added, so that we were able to review their risks and bring them on board quickly.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: President Pianalto, the reason for doing this is because those markets, like the other ABS markets are not functioning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re not trying to fill up the bucket.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: If we wanted to take on less risk, we could stay in the one market.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: There are enough of those securities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This is more about addressing the critical issues in those other markets.

speaker: NELSON
text: And, in fact, some of the sectors that we’re proposing for inclusion were harmed by the initial announcement because they are near substitutes to those things that we announced we were including.

speaker: NELSON
text: So it was very desirable to finish that phase.

speaker: NELSON
text: I think that the answer is relatively similar in the next stage—it’s just that there’s much more review that needs to be done.

speaker: NELSON
text: Perhaps it will be done within a month, but it then moves to the larger space of markets that are also impaired but are similar in that they are the securitized, high-quality space of newly originated securities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Is there any activity on the lower-rated paper?

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We are taking the triple-A.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Is there any activity in the lower-rated securities?

speaker: NELSON
text: In many cases, the lower-rated tranches are retained by the issuers, so that they’re able to issue the triple-A securities by retaining the lower rated.

speaker: NELSON
text: I don’t have any specific information about other lower-rated tranches that have been issued in conjunction with, admittedly, just a handful of ABS that are being issued at this subscription, and who is purchasing those.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The first one follows up on President Evans’s earlier question.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have been somewhat concerned about exit strategies.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it’s probably going to be quite a while before we have to worry about it, but I think I’d feel better about expanding some of these programs if we did have that worked out.

speaker: YELLEN
text: When I read the balance sheet scenarios, I was comforted at first to see that it’s going to be a very long time before we need to deal with this at all.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But then I looked at it a little bit more carefully.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I thought maybe there was something in the scenario you laid out that was inconsistent, because it was based on the March Greenbook forecast, but that assumed no additional unconventional policies.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Then, in your baseline you added $500 billion in purchases of MBS, which, in the staff memos on that program, has quite a bit of macro impact.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It seemed to me that, with the likely impact of a $500 billion program, we would have a stronger economy than in the baseline.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We would probably want to be raising rates in 2012 rather than 2014.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I guess that would be about the same time that the TALF was building up and might be difficult to unwind.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So my question is: Have I misunderstood that, or have I taken too sanguine a message from your scenario about exit strategies?

speaker: YELLEN
text: My second question is for Bill, and it concerns the extension of the TALF from newly originated asset-backed securities to legacy assets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I recall, there were just a couple of paragraphs in the memo on that.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But it seems to me to be a very big step, and I’m not sure I really understood it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Is this considered the PPIF program?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Yellen, in just a few minutes I will brief on all of the developments in the Treasury program, including this and the PPIF, and the FDIC role.

speaker: HILTON
text: Well, it’s a good observation.

speaker: HILTON
text: The assumptions we took for the baseline were just purely the economic ones.

speaker: HILTON
text: We did have an extension built into the outright purchase program in the baseline of $500 billion, as you’ve noted, but we did not try to calibrate a feedback effect, as you suggest, which would be a reasonable thing to do.

speaker: HILTON
text: That could move up a bit the period in which you might want to be otherwise raising the target rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Some of my questions are for David and Joe.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’m looking at exhibit 3 again.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think the overall analysis is beautiful, but this unconstrained policy with the negative nominal rates is not really a feasible outcome.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The truth is, you don’t know what would happen, because it’s not feasible.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But then, to put that on here as where we’d like to be in these pictures, I think, gives a little bit of a misleading idea about how we should think about these large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Would it be possible to say, “If I could pursue an optimal unconstrained policy just on asset purchases, here’s how much I’d do, and here’s how I’d let it unwind”?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Maybe that should be the baseline and we should skip the negative fed funds rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What would that look like?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Would that get you all the way to the funds rate line, or throw that line out?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Or where would it take us?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Unfortunately, I haven’t run it, and I’m kicking myself because we did talk about whether we ought to run it.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So I don’t know what the answer is.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I do know that if you had a $2 trillion program and you went by our assumptions, you’d replicate the hypothetical and completely unattainable and maybe completely unrealistic unconstrained optimal policy line.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: One question would be: What’s the cost of buying all of these long-term securities?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I’m not sure what that is.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: This is part of the reason we hesitated on running this.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But if you were completely unconstrained, you’d probably buy everything you could get your hands on in an attempt to drive long-term rates right to zero.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But presumably there’d be some balance sheet costs—I’m not sure how to calibrate or describe exactly what those costs are.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Presumably, there’d be a shadow cost, so you wouldn’t buy everything you could get your hands on.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But the basic proposition that “buy a lot” would be a good thing to do—yes, that would flow from that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So we have a baseline, which is just to stick with our zero nominal interest rate, conventional stuff, and not do anything else, just let the economy play out.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Then we say, “Well, we can improve on that with some asset purchases.” But we don’t want to go too far, because you just get too far out of bounds.

speaker: GAGNON
text: One of the costs might be fiscal, in some sense.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The natural thing to ask is: Why are there limits on this?

speaker: BULLARD
text: As I’ve said before, there’s the mystery of round numbers.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it’s the problem President Yellen raised, which is the exit strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is there a cost to exiting?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that’s the main constraint.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also, there are probably some costs associated with having banks holding enormous amounts of excess reserves.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I think the staff decided that buying a trillion was feasible and buying $2 trillion may be feasible.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But at some point, it’s more of a question for you.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: And what point is it just not feasible to go beyond, between the market problems you potentially create and the potential problems in setting up for exiting?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I don’t know what the limit is, but I think the gist of your question is: Whatever that limit is, would it make sense to go to it?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: On this kind of analysis, the answer is “yes,” whatever that feasible limit is.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Our job as policymakers is to somehow trade those off.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And I guess the model just doesn’t help us with that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But the question is: Wouldn’t it be useful to try to get some handle on it?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Suppose that limit’s not $2 trillion, suppose it’s $750 billion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How do I think about what that number looks like, even within some ballpark?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it would just be very helpful for us to think about when those diminishing returns on the types of costs that the Chairman alluded to begin to kick in.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And how do we think about that?

speaker: MOSSER
text: There’s a completely different set of limitations, namely, how much the payment and settlement system can handle, depending on how compressed we make these purchases.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We have not done this yet for Treasuries, but for mortgage-backed securities, we think that if we tried to buy $1½ to $2 trillion more this year, we would come close to breaking it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s great to know these kinds of constraints.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It’s possible there’s a workaround for those sorts of things.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But if there is, we’d have to start it tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We could just acquire Fannie and Freddie directly.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I can’t give up the floor without tormenting Mr.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In your report, and in some of the questions, we’ve talked about moral hazard problems.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Your response, which I thought was a good one, was that you were going to do the pricing in a way that made it a backstop facility, so that you gave the proper incentives to financial firms to stay out of this facility unless it was absolutely necessary.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is your sense that that’s going on with the other swaps, especially in Europe?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Are we pushing them so that they are avoiding the same problem on the other side?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Or do you think we run the risk of becoming a permanent part of the market for dollar funding elsewhere in the world, just sort of a routine thing?

speaker: SHEETS
text: My sense is that the pricing of our dollar swap facilities globally, and particularly in Europe, is such that they had been attractive during times of stress.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But as the market has healed a little bit, they’re less attractive.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Let me just be really concrete here.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The outstandings to the ECB, as of early December, were about $314 billion under the swaps program.

speaker: SHEETS
text: At the end of last week, those outstandings were down to $168 billion.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So we have seen a sizable—slightly less than 50 percent—drop in those outstandings.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Similarly, global swaps outstanding in early December were $582 billion, and at the end of last week they were at $330 billion.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So I think we’re seeing the program and the pricing work the way that we want it to.

speaker: SHEETS
text: During those year-end pressures and with exceedingly high stress, this liquidity was very attractive.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As the situation seems to ease a little bit, it’s not as attractive.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I know that a number of our counterparties have had auctions where they’ve seen significant declines in participation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Some that don’t have unlimited lines have actually seen some of their auctions undersubscribed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Here’s another example of the decline on a much smaller swap line: Australia was running about $27 billion outstanding in late November and is now below $10 billion.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So I think the pricing of these facilities—and Trish may want to expand on this—has been done so that the incentives are the way we want them to be.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think where the LIBOR rates are well inside, for example, one week and one month, those are the operations that are most undersubscribed and least used.

speaker: MOSSER
text: There’s more in three-month, where the market rates are still more elevated—again, this is reflecting credit risk and balance sheet constraints at institutions and how long they’re willing to lend to each other.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think the ultimate question is: If things continue to improve, will the swaps ultimately wind all the way down to zero?

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think there’s probably a risk that there would still be a few institutions that would like to continue to borrow, and we’ll just have to take away the punch bowl when the time comes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But, like Nathan, I’m encouraged that, as rates come down, and in particular, as we basically get underbid by the market, the facility usage drops off pretty quickly.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So as long as that trend continues, I think we’re fine.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Whether, in the end, we have to take it away is a possibility—we’ve had those discussions with the other central banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Speaking of facility usage—[laughter]—why don’t we take a coffee break for about 15 minutes, and then we will recommence around 4:30.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next item on the agenda is billed as a discussion of the balance sheet and lending program issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I’d like to do, with your indulgence, is to start off by posting you on a number of developments that pertain to these programs, and then make some comments on some policy issues, and then we can have an open discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just want to remind everyone, of course, that we have two full go-rounds subsequent to this discussion, so let’s make this part of it more informal, and then everyone will have an opportunity, of course, in the go-rounds to give their views if they haven’t had a chance in the discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me begin with some postings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, a relatively minor point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s time to announce the amounts and schedules for the term auction facility for the second quarter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unless there are objections, I propose to follow the recommendation of the staff and approve $150 billion per auction in April.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would be the same as we’ve had for some time now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second thing I wanted to talk about is the accord discussions with the Treasury, which I have mentioned a few times.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that we are getting somewhat close to a possible agreement, and I want to update you on where that’s going, and it’s going to be relevant to some of the other points I want to make.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The subject of the accord will be a potential conflict between the Fed’s role as a monetary authority and as a financial stability authority, the point being: How do we define the role of the Fed in such a way as to minimize the conflicts between those two functions?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Currently what we have in mind is a short document that would have—besides an introduction stating the motivation—four key general points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first point would be a positive statement of the need for Treasury–Federal Reserve co-equal cooperation during this financial crisis, so that is a positive good and something that we want to continue to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second point is that, although the Fed may provide liquidity in its role of pursuing financial stability, the Fed must be insulated from credit risk and must not undertake credit allocation, which the accord will state are within the province of the fiscal authorities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What is meant by “credit allocation”—and this relates to some of the discussion about the TALF—is that, to the extent that the Federal Reserve gets involved in credit markets, we should try to do so in a broad way that addresses the macroeconomic situation as opposed to picking winners and losers within small categories of credit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The third of the four principles is the need to protect the Fed’s monetary stability function from the financial stability function, if you will.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, the Fed and the Treasury have agreed on the need for sterilization tools that will allow the Fed to prevent any increases in its balance sheet from affecting its ability to conduct normal monetary policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As Brian already said, we have developed legislative language, and I have promises from the Administration of the highest level of effort to go to the Congress immediately—today—to try to get reactions, try to get some approval of either Fed bills or the SFP program, and that would be attached to legislation that is currently being contemplated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll say more about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As Brian mentioned, I think we would prefer Fed bills, but we are putting both out there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other thing that we are prepared to do, if we get resistance, and which I think a few people around the table might prefer, is to put a sunset on Fed bills or on this provision, so that it’s only for the current situation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The fourth element of the accord would be an agreement between us on the need for a comprehensive resolution regime for systemically critical nonbank financial institutions, which we do not have, and which I have called for and others have called for—a way to wind down nonbanks in a safe and orderly way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, we would want to say that a key element of any such regime would be a careful definition of what role would be expected of the central bank.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We might have a role—we might have a liquidity provision role, we might have other roles, depending on what the Congress wants to do—but it should be carefully defined.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As part of this, sort of aspirationally, the Treasury at this point—and we’ll just have to see how the negotiation comes out—will state its intention that when it is able to do so it will remove from our balance sheet the Maiden Lanes and the other residuals from our various rescue operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I believe that these are the main elements that we need.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: From my perspective, it preserves our ability to do what we’re doing now, which is to continue to support credit market functioning and to address the macroeconomic situation, even though the interest rate is at the zero bound.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I realize it doesn’t go as far as some perhaps might like, but I do think that it will be an important step, a historic step, towards defining an appropriate line between our various functions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It should be clear that a principal reason that the Treasury is being so cooperative is that they would like us to support them in their bank rescue program.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So what I’d like to do now is tell you where that is and what’s going on there, and talk to you about what the Fed’s role, if any, would be in that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I should say that we have not approved anything.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But they are looking for some kind of answer from us very quickly, and, therefore, this would be an opportunity for people to make comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The original bank proposal of the Treasury had five elements, of which four have now been laid out to the public: the supervisory assessment, with the stress scenario; the equity instrument—the mandatory convertible preferred—that would be given to banks that need it; the TALF—the joint TALF—which, of course, is already, as of this week, in operation; and the foreclosure mitigation plan.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The last element, which has not yet been described and that we want to get to, is a public–private partnership for dealing with what they now call “legacy assets.” I guess it’s like “legacy systems”—and the word “legacy” used to be a good word.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have to say that I agree with the objective.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I supported the original TARP motivation, and a big part of that was to remove opaque and damaged assets from bank balance sheets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I believe that is part of any successful bank cleanup program, because it will allow banks to attract private capital and give them balance sheet space to go back to normal lending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I do think that’s an important element of the plan.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Currently, this fifth element has, in turn, three parts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first part, which has nothing to do with the Fed, is an FDIC facility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The purpose of the FDIC facility would be to take damaged portfolios directly off of the balance sheets of banks; this would happen after the conclusion of our supervisory assessment, during the six-month period in which banks are supposed to be raising capital or otherwise taking action to stabilize themselves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A bank would offer an asset pool, and a third-party valuation agent would estimate an expected price on the pool.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then, the supervisor and the bank would discuss implications for pro forma valuations and the stability of the bank—capital needs, and the like.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there would be some preliminary discussion about whether or not the bank should actually engage in making this offer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If the bank decides to offer the asset pool, then the FDIC would dispose of it in the same way that it currently disposes of assets of failing banks: It would have an auction, and the price that the bank receives for the pool would be determined by the winning bidder.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is going to be highly leveraged, which is the reason that they hope to attract bidders who will pay more than fire-sale prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The leverage will come in two forms.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that there will be an 80/20 partnership between the U.S. government and the private participant, with 80 percent of the capital from the government.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And then, there is leverage provided by the FDIC, which is supported by FDIC guarantees, to attract funding.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: An example of the leverage is that given a $19.5 billion portfolio, a private investor could have a 20 percent interest in it for $557 million— obviously, this is a very highly leveraged position.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why would banks want to do this?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not clear that they will, but there are some possible reasons.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is that we are looking in our supervisory assessment at embedded losses that go beyond one year, beyond the provisions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So banks may make the determination that it’s in their interest to sell some portfolios, even if they’re in the accrual book.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second is the proposition that, by selling off assets, a bank can make itself attractive to private equity and thereby, perhaps, avoid a capital injection from the U.S. government.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Of course, typically, the sale of assets, if they’re marked down, would create a bigger capital hole than initially, and so the U.S. government will have to stand ready to provide enough capital in case the private sector is not forthcoming.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s the FDIC part of the plan.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It covers only portfolios sold directly by banks and possibly bank holding companies.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The FDIC is not willing, or says it doesn’t have the authority, to deal with assets that are not taken directly from banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other two parts of the plan involve creating facilities to buy various classes of troubled or legacy assets, essentially from anybody in the market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And the question is: How would they work?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s where the Fed would be involved under the Treasury’s proposal.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Before I talk about them, let me just say one word about process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Fed has been a full participant in all of these discussions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ve done the lion’s share of the work on a number of these issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And we have, in general, tried to resist the Treasury’s strong demand for precipitant action, and tried to slow them down, and tried to make sure that we get this right, if at all possible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ve also been very careful throughout this process in trying to ensure necessary protections for the Fed—that’s what the accord is about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Another example is that we essentially vetoed a ring-fencing proposal, because we didn’t like the way the Fed was involved in those types of operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I should also say that I did have the opportunity to meet with the President on these issues; of course, we talked about a wide variety of things, but we spent about 20 minutes talking about the Fed’s role and our concerns and our issues, and he was very receptive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, he promised his full support for sterilization tools.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I’ll mention parenthetically that I have talked to him about inflation targets as well, and he said, “That sounds really good.” I’m sure his advisers will get to him before long—[laughter]—but he was interested in that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So what are these two last parts of the plan?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One part is public–private partnerships, which are basically hedge funds that have 80 percent government ownership and 20 percent private ownership.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You could have the U.S. government in partnership with PIMCO, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those hedge funds will be able to buy assets essentially from anybody; there may be some restrictions on the type of asset, but not restrictions on whom they can buy them from.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There would be a 20/80 share in terms of returns, because the private sector is putting up 20 percent of the capital.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The final part is TALF financing—that is, the Fed would allow these legacy assets to be financed in the TALF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s a little hard to see at first, but if you look at it carefully, you’ll see that the combination of the public–private partnership—where the equity share gives shares in the assets—with the financing facility is really economically equivalent to the FDIC facility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And what appears to be a difference—the put option in the TALF and the haircuts having to differ according to the asset risk—is actually paralleled in the FDIC program, because there they’re going to have to set leverage according to asset class in more or less the same way.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the combination of the two is essentially the same kind of thing, but it works for any type of asset.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are a number of issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is certainly the viability and workability of the program.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have to say that our initial reactions were negative, and we told the Treasury that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our concern was that it would be very, very difficult to deal with these very heterogeneous assets and to find haircuts that would work for each asset.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, we have looked at it more carefully.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A team that included Mike Gibson from the Board, and people from New York as well, has done what they called a “proof of concept” analysis to ask whether this could be made to work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They looked at some representative asset classes, and their conclusion is that it is workable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But they think that, if we’re going to do this, it would be necessary to get outside contractors to recommend to us what the haircuts ought to be, what the risk profiles ought to be, and what capital we should require for safety.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, they think we should have asset managers to take care of these things, so that we don’t have to burden our staff further.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second issue is what it implies for the size of the Fed balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We had previously discussed this when Secretary Geithner first put out the bank plan.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: He announced, with our agreement, that the $200 billion TALF program could be expanded “up to”—a very cautious set of words—“up to” $1 trillion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At that time, we thought that the extra money would go into CMBS and RMBS.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The idea here is that we would not have a change in that—that even if legacy assets are included, we would still be “up to” $1 trillion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, in that sense, we would not be changing the rules of the game.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My own view is that we will not get to $1 trillion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First of all, the Treasury is very short of capital.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It has to fund not only the capital of the banks, but it also has to fund the FDIC program and the public–private funds, as well as the TALF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s going to be a significant barrier to expansion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then, I think that, practically, as we’ve seen, the process is just very difficult.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It requires a lot of analysis, and what we’ve seen in the initial work on some of the simpler assets is that we may not get the demand that we thought.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And, in any case, it’s not going to happen for some months down the road.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there are implications for the balance sheet, but they’re not different from what they were prior to this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to assurances, I’ve already talked about the accord.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And, particularly with regard to the Fed bills work, we will maintain the “no credit risk” principle by insisting that we be fully protected if we do this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll mention one other thing, which has not been explored, but which seems to me to be a very live possibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The senior debt obligations of the TALF would be very safe assets, because they would be senior not only to the Fed and the Treasury, but also to the haircuts, so it seems possible to me that one other way to mitigate the effects of this on the Fed’s balance sheet would be to sell debt to the private sector to finance part of the TALF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I should say that we had at least one presentation on this to the Board.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Board has not taken a decision.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We wanted to bring this up here and hear comments from the FOMC.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are not fully persuaded that it’s workable and viable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In any case, we’re going to have to come to some conclusion pretty soon, because the Treasury is very eager to get going.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we did want to bring this to you and tell you what was going on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll be happy to answer questions about this in a moment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Before I give up the floor, though, I want to talk just a bit about the policy decision for this meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The most likely direction that we would go, as suggested by the alternative statements, would be to increase our asset purchases.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m concerned—I don’t want us to be making that decision in the last five minutes tomorrow when we’re trying to work on the statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I’d like to encourage at least some discussion of that today, because it fits in with the presentations that we heard.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although we don’t have to make a final decision until tomorrow, at least I’d like to know where people are, roughly speaking, on this topic.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will tell you what I think, because I’m fairly open on the subject.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do think that, as we will discuss, the economy has deteriorated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our balance sheet has shrunk over the last few months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s true that we’ll continue to buy MBS, but our TALF activities, even if we get into the legacy TALF, are not likely to scale up for some time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So my own view—again, I want to hear everybody’s views—is that at this meeting, we ought to approve an additional asset purchase.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One possibility, which is probably the minimum we ought to do, would be to double the agency program from $500 billion MBS and $100 billion debt by midyear, to $1 trillion and $200 billion by the end of the year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This would essentially do for the second six months what we’re doing for the first six months of 2009.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That certainly would be a possibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just say that I’m very interested to hear views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We might want to go bigger than that, if we think that we want to be more aggressive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other possibility, of course, as we’ve discussed, is also or alternatively to buy Treasury securities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: People will express their views on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that’s a potentially useful direction to go in, and I’m very open to that, if that’s what people want to do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the U.K. example is promising.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It does show that there can be benefits not only to the Treasury market but also to the broader private markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I’m not that concerned about adverse implications, say, for inflation expectations, because we’ve all seen Treasury purchases in many other contexts; besides the British context, the Japanese have done a lot of this, the Swiss, the Canadians are going to start doing this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It would be potentially in conjunction with MBS purchases.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think there are issues there, but I’m open to this possibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to say that I would like to hear some discussion today and in the go-round tomorrow, so that when we get to the final policy decision we won’t be making a spur-of-the­ moment decision.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll have a sense of where everybody is and what the best outcome might be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me stop there and open it up for general discussion or questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s try to maintain an informal format, and, remember, we have two go-rounds ahead of us.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have just a clarifying question.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: When you say this stuff merges into the TALF, I’m just not quite sure I understood how this would work.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Could you explain that again?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Basically, what happens now is that an investor buys a security and leaves that security with the Fed and gets 90 percent financing—or 10 to 1 leverage—against that security.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s a put option, because it’s nonrecourse lending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it would be the same thing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In this case, the public–private hedge fund—80 percent Treasury, 20 percent private sector—would purchase some RMBS, and it would finance that RMBS—get leverage on that RMBS—by depositing it at the TALF in the same way that an investor does currently.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The main difference is that the haircuts would have to adjust according to the risk characteristics of the assets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So we would have to set a new schedule of haircuts for these securities, because presumably they would be the much riskier and perhaps toxic assets of the banking system.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And we’d have to make sure we had sufficient capital from the Treasury.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that what might be going on is that these might happen in one-off deals where portfolios are being presented, and that would require us to hire investment banks or asset analysts to do the work for us and give us their assessments of the risk characteristics.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Back to the accord issue for the moment—you talked about Maiden Lane going back to the Treasury at some point or under certain conditions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Would these assets in the TALF be candidates for that same sort of transfer?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In one indirect sense—if we find that we can no longer finance them because of monetary policy considerations, then, under the SFP model, Treasury financing would replace Fed financing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the difference between this and Maiden Lane is that Maiden Lane involves very long-term assets, and the TALF program is a three-year program, and presumably it would be winding down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A two-hander from President Evans.

speaker: EVANS
text: Just to clarify—the legacy-asset aspect of this would be within the currently envisioned $1 trillion?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Within the current limits, yes.

speaker: LACKER
text: You said something that confused me.

speaker: LACKER
text: You said we would be protected against risk because we would be senior to the Treasury.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then you said “and the haircuts”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I was talking about the possibility of getting private debt as a substitute for Fed financing in the TALF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s a hypothetical possibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But, in general, the way the TALF works is that we have a haircut to protect us, and, if there are any further losses, then the Treasury is the first to take them.

speaker: LACKER
text: But the haircut and the Treasury capital aren’t two separate things, right?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: No, they are two separate things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But the Treasury capital is the same.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The ratio hasn’t gone up for these assets relative to the TALF assets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ve got to figure out two parameters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Probably the simplest thing would be to pick a single ratio of Treasury capital to leverage, because we don’t want to do that asset by asset.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the haircuts will have to vary, and the combination of the haircut and the Treasury capital will protect the Fed against loss.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Or we could take the Treasury capital and apply it against all of the assets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s what I’m saying, yes.

speaker: LACKER
text: So that’s separate from the Treasury capital invested alongside the private sector in the partnerships?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s separate from it, yes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Treasury capital comes in in two places—one to give leverage and the other to protect the Fed.

speaker: LACKER
text: Back to Maiden Lane—would that include the two ring-fence guarantees?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not going to happen in the next six weeks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not going to happen in the current political atmosphere.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it would be a stated intention of the Treasury that, at some point, they would be looking to take these things off our hands, and that would, in my mind, include those things as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: I may be pressing you for things that haven’t been put on the table, but do you envision a public statement with all of these elements in it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yes, within a week or two.

speaker: LACKER
text: And would it lay out a timetable on any of this, or the transfer?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It will state that we are actively engaged on the Fed bills-SFP front.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It will state the principle that the Fed is not to take credit risk, which we will enforce.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It will state our intention, which is a strong intention on both sides, to undertake the negotiation on a resolution regime that will define what role the Fed might have in those kinds of contexts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And it will state the aspirational goal of the Treasury taking Maiden Lane off our balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: Help me understand the statement about the Fed not taking credit risk, because we do, and it’s just a matter of degree.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, we take credit risk—even the CDS spreads on Treasuries are not zero.

speaker: LACKER
text: Would we have an understanding with the Treasury about what “de minimis” means?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the case of the TALF, we have worked out criteria where very extreme—very extreme—loss outcomes do not touch the Fed, and probably don’t even touch the Treasury; but they don’t touch the Fed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Bill, do you want to talk about that?

speaker: NELSON
text: In the risk analysis for TALF 2.1, we looked at a scenario which we considered to have a 1 percent probability.

speaker: NELSON
text: And even in those scenarios, all of the credit costs were covered by the risk spread itself, so not only the Fed but also the Treasury did not take any losses.

speaker: NELSON
text: Our objective is basically to follow that principle with the legacy TALF, I think the principle would be that under our stress scenario neither the Treasury nor the Fed would be expected to take losses.

speaker: NELSON
text: So losses, in order to come to the Fed, would first have to eat through the Treasury protection, which we don’t expect to happen at all in the stress scenario.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I’m trying to understand this.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The TALF is for three years, and the way I see it, we’re taking the assets they put into this organization, which you expect to liquidate and recover at least enough to the point where we’re protected.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But how confident are you that we can roll this stuff off our balance sheet in three years?

speaker: HOENIG
text: So we might have to turn them over later, or the market would have to change so much that you could sell them, and whoever has the 20 percent risk would take any write-off.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I see us as taking the “bad bank” position in a “good bank–bad bank” scenario.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re financing the bad banks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We aren’t the capital in the bad bank.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As long as in the liquidation we don’t go past the capital that’s placed into it, right?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But in terms of your other question, we’ll have to be very careful about maturities, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For a three-year loan, when the three years are up, if the value of the asset has fallen by more than the haircut, they will put the asset to the bad bank, and the asset managers of the bad bank will sell it or dispose of it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If the value of the asset has not fallen as much as the haircut, then there will be a strong incentive for the public– private partners—and, of course, for the government, because the Treasury will be the dominant partner—to find other financing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In your exploration of this, have you thought about the Congress setting up a good bank–bad bank facility?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Are they resistant to that?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Or do we just think that’s not a good option?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the Administration is weighing the possibility of legislation to get additional authorities, for example, considering whether it would be possible to change the scoring on the TARP, which is very unfavorable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If they can get appropriate authorities, I think they would do that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the politics is just unbelievably bad, and it’s very difficult to get anything done.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it’s their intention to try.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think they believe that they may not have enough resources to do all they need to do, in which case they will pursue other resources, and we can see what happens.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My own guess is that, one way or another, we’re probably not going to end up taking very much stuff, either because there won’t be that much interest, or because there will be other facilities, or because some other arrangement will develop.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is in order to have something that’s part of the bigger program in the short term.

speaker: FISHER
text: I didn’t understand you there for a second.

speaker: FISHER
text: When you say “would not take much stuff,” are you saying the bad bank would not take some of these assets?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I was just conjecturing that, in the end, this legacy TALF would probably not do very much business.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is that because of the pricing?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Because of the pricing and the difficulty of finding private sector participants.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s only a bad asset at a high price.

speaker: EVANS
text: If the third-party assessment comes out at a reasonable price—

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we have to mark it down to a market price which we’d lend against, and then there’s a haircut on top of that, of course.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, the question is: Is that attractive?

speaker: FISHER
text: Can I come back to the Treasury’s quid pro quo, particularly the third key element, the public–private partnership?

speaker: FISHER
text: You mentioned that there was discussion within the Board—what are the concerns as the Board views it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The complexity is one issue: Would we be able to figure out how to do haircuts in a way that would be meaningful—that is, so that, on the one hand, the haircuts would be not so conservative as to imply no business, and, on the other hand, they’d be conservative enough to provide enough safety?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Another issue that we and the FOMC are considering more broadly is: What are the implications for our balance sheet, and management of our balance sheet?

speaker: FISHER
text: This may be for later discussion.

speaker: FISHER
text: Maybe I’m a little confused.

speaker: FISHER
text: If I go back to our previous discussion and a comment that I think Mr. Nelson made—did you say that we were looking at this, the legacy assets into the TALF, as a way to take some bad assets off the balance sheets of banks?

speaker: NELSON
text: Is the legacy TALF a means to try to take the bad assets off bank balance sheets?

speaker: NELSON
text: Yes, that’s one of the objectives.

speaker: FISHER
text: Could you clarify that please?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The way it is now conceived, the FDIC would be responsible for taking portfolios directly from banks and probably bank holding companies.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the answer to that question I guess is, “no.” The intent would be to try to create more liquidity and pricing discovery, and so on, in these markets generally.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we would use the public–private hedge fund, as you described it, as a way to end up with some kind of pricing mechanism for legacy assets that trade on the market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I suppose if they wanted to buy from a bank, I don’t think there would be any restriction on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But that’s not the point of it.

speaker: FISHER
text: It just seems to me we are going through—this is a comment, and it, again, may be based on ignorance—a lot of jujitsu here to get around the issue of creating a good bank–bad bank, taking the toxic assets in the bad bank and clearing it in that way.

speaker: FISHER
text: The TALF is becoming inordinately complicated.

speaker: FISHER
text: And I guess, if you’ll forgive a horrible pun, I’m worried TALF is getting too clever by HALF.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’re adding one segment on top of another, just as we’re beginning to figure out how this thing is going to work.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I said, I’m sure this will not be operational for months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s one reason that I think that we can’t wait for it in terms of our broader policy objectives.

speaker: FISHER
text: But you are talking about moving very quickly on this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s still going to be months, I am sure.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Mr. Chairman, just a two-hander.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was going to ask a question about the difference between the FDIC program and the TALF-related program.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How would I think about what type of assets would go to the FDIC program and which ones would come in to us through the hedge funds?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Based on the relative pricing of those two mechanisms and how they would work, which vehicle would attract what types of assets?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I said, economically they’re very similar.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The FDIC, though, would deal directly with banks and could take a whole portfolio—it could be a completely heterogeneous portfolio—and there would be a bid on that portfolio, just the same way as when you wind down a failed bank.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would imagine that the remit for these hedge funds would be “buy RMBS on the market.” I think it would be less heterogeneous than the portfolios that the FDIC would be taking.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The FDIC would be a much more classic bad bank type of structure.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Would the design of the heterogeneous portfolios be up to the seller or up to the FDIC?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There’s a sort of RTC analogue here: In the RTC period, assets were put together to make the package attractive enough to bid on, knowing there was some terrible stuff, but also some not-so-bad stuff in it.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Who is going to design those portfolios?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If I’m incorrect on anything, please, staff members, don’t hesitate to correct me, but my understanding is that the supervisors and the bank together would determine the portfolio.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in many cases there would presumably be a mixture of accrual and marked-to-market assets, a mixture of different kinds of assets, derivatives, and other things that are hard to break off but can be part of a portfolio.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I just wanted to ask a few questions about the accord.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What kind of legal standing does an accord have?

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is this a gentleman’s agreement, or what is it?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we’re one step ahead of the 1951 accord, which wasn’t even written down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To my knowledge, there is no document representing the 1951 accord.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So it’s a genuine agreement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This would be an agreement signed by me and by the Treasury Secretary and approved also by the President and the Administration.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We would share it with congressional leaders as well.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The ’51 case held for a long time because there were no attempts to change it subsequently, and that’s the hope here as well, I guess.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But it’s really just an agreement between the Administration and the Fed for now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Two of the provisions are really “asks” from the Congress.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Do I have that right?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They are asks from the Congress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Treasury and the Fed agree they are needed and will cooperate in trying to get those things passed.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The Congress may or may not agree to them.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, that’s always, of course, a risk.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So the accord in ’51 was about how the Fed and the Treasury were actually going to interact.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It did not involve this part about what we’re going to get the Congress to do or not do.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’m just trying to understand what the object is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, it will formalize the understanding that the Fed will take no credit risk in the TALF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m happy to answer as many questions as people want to ask, but, again, I also hope to hear something about asset purchases before we close today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On asset purchases, [laughter] I think there are lots of good reasons to escalate: The economy is weaker; financial conditions are tighter; in addition, the TALF is off to a slow start because of all of the stuff that’s swirling around on AIG and TARP.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The broader TALF, I think, is going to come much later.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: While there might be an announcement on legacy TALF relatively soon, the actual operationalization of that, I think, is going to take many months—just given that the TALF 1.0, which we’re enacting today, took four months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And the PPIF—it’s not even clear whether banks are going to be willing to sell assets to the PPIF.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Are they going to get a high enough price to engage in those transactions?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it seems to me that right now it’s on us.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And it’s more on us than it was even a few weeks ago, because I think the political climate has deteriorated significantly, so the ability of the Administration to go back to the Congress and get more TARP money is significantly less than it was even a few weeks ago.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Then the question is: What should we escalate to?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The lines in David’s graph suggest that $2 trillion would put us roughly on top of the unconstrained line.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And, conveniently, the numbers I was going to advocate total $2 trillion, by coincidence rather than by design.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We did not talk beforehand, as David can attest.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that I’d want to escalate the agency MBS program to more than $1 trillion, because escalating to $1 trillion through year-end is basically keeping the run rate exactly the same as the program is doing right now, which is essentially $500 billion every six months.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think we should escalate the program, and I would suggest $1½ trillion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The market will not give us much credit for just extending the program another six months at the same purchase rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the market generally expects us to extend the program, so I don’t think that’s really going to have a lot of benefit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would increase the agency debt from $100 billion to $200 billion, so I’m at $2.2 trillion, to be honest.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I’m not counting that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think the agency debt is really very important or that effective, but I think leaving it out raises more questions than it’s worth raising at this juncture.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And I would engage in a Treasury purchase program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The last time I was here, I argued mostly against it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think the stakes are pretty high right now.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We don’t know exactly how much a Treasury purchase program would do, but, if we start one, we’ll be able to answer that question.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There’s a lot of information that we really just don’t have right now.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I would suggest engaging in a Treasury purchase program, starting immediately, up to $500 billion, concentrating in 2-year to 10-year maturities and buying both nominals and TIPS.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We can also purchase things outside of those maturities to avoid distortions to the shape of the yield curve.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But that’s what I would do.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One other thing before I give up the floor—I just want to stress what the point of the reverse swaps is.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The point is to prevent some bad piece of news that creates a liquidity run in some foreign market from putting us in a very difficult position in which a foreign central bank is unwilling to lend to a U.S.-owned company because it doesn’t have enough collateral, and we don’t have the ability to get them the money quickly enough to prevent a default.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that we want to do this.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’m not sure whether we want to delegate it to the Subcommittee or actually enact it in the FOMC; but it would be really unfortunate if we didn’t do this, and then something happened that caused the exact problem that this reverse swap will address, and then we’d say, “Why didn’t we do what we could have done to avert it?” So it’s a belt-and-suspenders approach, but I think we’re in an environment where we need both a belt and suspenders.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the asset purchases, my view is that the hole in aggregate demand is really quite large, and as I look at the figure on the gap between the optimal policy and the zero bound, I think it’s really stunning, so I’m open to proposals for substantial purchases.

speaker: EVANS
text: In fact, I’m not totally confident in any particular program that we have proposed, so I favor diversifying: Both MBS and Treasuries sounds like a pretty attractive option from my standpoint.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m not quite sure how to evaluate the numbers that the Vice Chair just laid out.

speaker: EVANS
text: I know I can’t disagree with him, but I don’t quite know how to calibrate these other policy measures like in the Greenbook and Bluebook figure.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I’d like to hear more about that tomorrow, but I’m open-minded.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the accord, it sounds good.

speaker: EVANS
text: The way we’ve talked about it is that it’s a long-term accord.

speaker: EVANS
text: Right now we have a lot of assets on our balance sheet that we would like to be able to get rid of.

speaker: EVANS
text: If issuing Fed bills is the way to go, that would be fine.

speaker: EVANS
text: You mentioned that some might favor a sunset provision.

speaker: EVANS
text: Would that be on the order of three or four years, or 20 years?

speaker: EVANS
text: It sounds like it’s aimed at getting us out of the current situation, and I think that’s a good idea.

speaker: EVANS
text: But over the next 30 years, our ability to have that authority might be a problem.

speaker: EVANS
text: In reading your testimony on the 13(3) authority and the grilling that you got, I don’t recall anybody who thought it was a great idea that the Fed had the authority to undertake this on their own, and they wouldn’t admit that they knew that this was possible, at least according to what I had read.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I just wonder, would a future accord be a 13(3)-type of activity that causes us to acquire these assets, and then we’d need to issue bills?

speaker: EVANS
text: I guess I’m just wondering under what circumstances we would issue bills.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think the lasting lesson from all of this is that we don’t want to get here again, that we ought to conduct policy in a way to avoid this.

speaker: EVANS
text: Future regulatory changes that might help out are obviously one way, market discipline is another, and responding to large changes in asset prices that we don’t understand very well might be another.

speaker: EVANS
text: But keeping the average level of the fed funds rate at a place where we don’t expect to hit the zero bound again might be much more attractive now, having gone through this, so that might be something we should talk about at some point.

speaker: EVANS
text: If along the way you could get an explicit numerical price objective out of this, that would be quite good.

speaker: EVANS
text: And then, lastly, let me ask another question.

speaker: EVANS
text: If the likely take-up on our TALF for the legacy assets is low, and given the prudent central bank lending that we are doing (at least according to the people I talk to in the marketplace; they don’t find this very attractive), is the Treasury going to be satisfied with that?

speaker: EVANS
text: How are we going to respond to them?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, my assumption is that they would move on to other strategies, which would involve perhaps the Congress, not us.

speaker: EVANS
text: That would be more desirable from a public policy standpoint.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: On the swap lines, I do think that we could put in the minutes that it’s basically procedural—it’s symmetric with what other foreign central banks have done with us.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would argue for being transparent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We need to be prepared for foreign funding problems, and I think it just makes sense to be clear on it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the resolution of holding companies, which ties into the foreign swap lines, I think that’s as important an issue as the Fed bills, and I think trying to find a way to push resolution makes sense.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If you could argue that, if we had the resolution powers now we could be doing much more effective things with AIG, there may be a hook to actually move things along more quickly.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I don’t know where our thinking is, but I see this as a chance to try to push that, particularly if it would give us an opportunity to abrogate contracts in the event that we or somebody else had resolution power.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But I think we should try to move that just as quickly as the Fed bills.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the removal of problem assets, I agree that’s a critical component.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I strongly agree that we shouldn’t be doing ring-fencing institution by institution, so I’m glad we’re moving away from that strategy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think the first-best solution would be more aggressive write-downs of assets, creating a bad bank for the most troubled banks.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think it’s a much more straightforward solution, and I realize that it does mean much more capital for some banks because we will be taking aggressive action.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But I think that, just as we shouldn’t have banks deferring losses, we, as the central bank and the Treasury, shouldn’t defer losses if they’re really on the balance sheet.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The first-best solution, I think, is to try to work with the bad bank solution.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The TALF for problem legacy assets—I think we shouldn’t make these programs particularly voluntary.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we’re going in and forcing write-downs, and the write-downs are fairly significant, the banks are going to want to participate in the program, because they will have already taken the losses.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So, instead of trying to make it voluntary, I think we should have the write-downs be severe enough that they’re going to want to get the assets off their balance sheets because they’ve already taken the losses and they’re not trying to defer additional losses.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Thinking about how we can have a supervisory strategy that guarantees that outcome might make it much easier than hoping that people volunteer their portfolios.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: To the extent that we can do that, that would be my preferred option.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the policy, I think this is the time to be very aggressive.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I strongly prefer option A in the Bluebook, or possibly even a little bit larger, as Vice Chairman Dudley has suggested—I’d be open to that as well.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We’re far from reaching either element of the dual mandate over the forecast horizon.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This is the time to push rates down.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We have a new program from Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae that’s going to include refinancing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The refinancing involves paying closing costs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Now is the time to push the rates down, so that the people who are refinancing and participate in that program only have to pay the closing costs one time.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It will also square us with some of the other issues in terms of encouraging servicers to come up with solutions.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It’s also spring—the right time for the housing sector, and we do need the housing sector to start bottoming out, getting people back into the market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we push rates down significantly right now, I think many people will start coming off the sidelines, because even if they don’t think prices have hit bottom, they will probably think interest rates are at an all-time low and they may want to take advantage of that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I think it’s a very good time to be doing that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I do have concerns that the TALF is off to a slow start.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: When I talk to hedge funds, they’re quite skeptical about how successful that program is going to be.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We’ve been kind of relying on that as possibly being a successful policy tool.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Because I’m a little more skeptical about either the TALF or the public–private fund working, it calls all the more for more aggressive policy, which is embedded in option A.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I think option A, which has both the Treasuries and the mortgage-backed securities, is the way to go.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the resolution authority, Board staff has been working on legislative language, and Governor Tarullo and others are reviewing it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think, frankly, that the Congress will be looking to the Fed and the Treasury to come up with the language, because it’s a very complex set of issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And we are working on it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I was just going to talk about asset purchases a little bit.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What I’m concerned about is these one-off moves, and I’ve been concerned about round numbers— $1 trillion, $500 billion, and so on.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think all of the things that we do in interest rate targeting should also come in when we’re doing our asset-purchase program.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In interest rate targeting, as it has developed over the last 20 years, it’s all about the whole path of interest rates over a long horizon in the future.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s all part of the policy: How credible you are about letting the private sector know how you’re going to behave and how you’re going to react to things in the future.

speaker: BULLARD
text: When we hit the zero bound, that all went out the window.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Now we’re taking one-time actions, with the private sector very uncertain about how we’re going to frame that in the future.

speaker: BULLARD
