text: And we know that, no matter what model you have, that’s not the right way to do policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I think we want to get back to something like policy paths for asset purchases.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Even if we don’t say it in our statements, the private sector is already imputing what they think that’s going to be.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They just have bigger confidence bands around it than they would otherwise have.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So what I was going to talk about during the policy go-round is somehow to get to where you can announce continuations of purchases at some rate, or something like that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My intuition is that that’s the right way to do these policies, instead of saying, “I’m going to come in with $500 billion to this particular market on this particular day, and I may or may not do any of this in the future.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is why I wanted to hear some of this today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you have a specific suggestion, you could bring it tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I would comment that we have been pretty clear about what the timeframe is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ve said $500 billion by midyear, and the proposal would be a trillion by the end of the year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we are effectively giving monthly rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But then, what happens after that is the problem.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Yes, what happens after that?

speaker: BULLARD
text: And, I think, on the Treasury purchases, we have vacillated a little.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think as a Committee that we want the whole path out there for the policy tools.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also it might be good to indicate a little bit of contingency about buying at a certain pace; for example, “we’re looking at the data as they come in—if they come in a little stronger in the fall than we think, maybe we’ll tamp down a little bit,” that kind of thing.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s what I’d also have in mind.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Otherwise, you commit all the way to the next year, or beyond next year, and it turns out something else happens that you didn’t expect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Taylor rule, and so on, emerged essentially from historical experience.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It wasn’t ever stated in advance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s a problem: We don’t really have a reaction function out there, we’re sort of just starting the rational expectations process.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need a way to think about that, and suggestions are welcome.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We should feed back the conditions.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We don’t know what the rule looks like, I agree.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We could say something like, “We will continue as long as,” or something.

speaker: BULLARD
text: “We’re going to monitor conditions.” “We’re going to buy at this pace.” “We give ourselves the option of buying at a slower pace if things come out better than expected,” or something like that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I appreciate that, and suggestions are welcome.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me confine my remarks to the large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: WARSH
text: I must admit, I am quite uncomfortable with the idea of purchasing long-term Treasuries in size.

speaker: WARSH
text: As the papers described to us, the benefits could well be quite small.

speaker: WARSH
text: My sense is the costs might not be.

speaker: WARSH
text: This is an idea that we’ve been discussing for a few months, and as I think about the need that we all feel to escalate, my sense is it has gotten more attractive now because we have run out of some very good alternatives.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me highlight some of these concerns.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, I think the nature of the Treasury market is, frankly, quite different from the nature of the GSE markets that we’ve already entertained— and I think I’d be comfortable entertaining those more.

speaker: WARSH
text: The long-term Treasury markets are functioning reasonably well; they’re highly liquid and the desire for risk-free assets is still quite high.

speaker: WARSH
text: My sense is, notwithstanding those facts, at this particular moment in time, Mr. Chairman, there are serious questions being raised by market participants and market commentators about the government’s ability to fund new higher expected levels of Treasury issuance—that is, they may or may not, in the market’s view, be able to find buyers at market-clearing prices.

speaker: WARSH
text: Then if the Fed is perceived to be monetizing debt and serving as a buyer of last resort in the name of lowering risk-free rates, we could end up with higher rates and less credibility as a central bank.

speaker: WARSH
text: My own sense is this could be self-defeating.

speaker: WARSH
text: Very recent discussions that Nathan Sheets and I had with certain large non-U.S. buyers of Treasury securities confirmed these suspicions.

speaker: WARSH
text: They note that at times like this we are one government, and if the Treasury and the Federal Reserve have to collude to somehow solve the issuance problem, it could be signaling greater problems about our ability to fund ourselves.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I would say my concerns are particularly pronounced at a time like this.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now, of course, all central banks are struggling with arrangements between the fiscal authorities and the monetary authorities, as we are.

speaker: WARSH
text: There’s no easy way around it.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the accord is certainly a step in the right direction.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I fear that if we are perceived to be colluding with the Treasury around this idea, in the name of saving 25 or 30 or 40 basis points in the short term, we’re running serious risks.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even if our actions lowered long-term risk-free rates for a time, and we got a pop—and I suspect we would get a pop—it does strike me the spillover benefits to lower rates on a broader range of securities are likely to be small, probably smaller than the models would suggest.

speaker: WARSH
text: The availability of financing is unlikely to change by virtue of our actions.

speaker: WARSH
text: Our actions don’t appear to me to change the universe of institutions or the universe of assets that are financeable, and credit markets would not open to anyone or anything new.

speaker: WARSH
text: The best that could be said is that we are lowering rates on riskier securities by a very small fraction, and that amount is likely to be overwhelmed by daily moves in risk premiums, as has been evidenced in the last few days, with costs that, as I mentioned, could be quite large.

speaker: WARSH
text: With respect to the U.K. example, which has gotten quite a bit of attention overseas, I think there’s a little less there than meets the eye.

speaker: WARSH
text: My own sense is, this is more a story of liquidity, by virtue of the government entering markets that are considerably less liquid than Treasuries, and it’s also a bit of a story of a much more activist central bank in the U.K. than the markets had become accustomed to.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think that’s probably playing some role as well.

speaker: WARSH
text: In light of the choices we have, I think it would be preferable at this point to increase our emphasis on mortgage-backed securities, as has been described.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we could continue to argue that that is solving a very serious problem, which is that market functioning is still more impaired in that market than we think is ideal.

speaker: WARSH
text: They are wards of the state, yet they are trading as very poor, imperfect substitutes for the Treasuries.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that would be a better option to take at this time.

speaker: LACKER
text: About asset purchases, I agree we should do more now.

speaker: LACKER
text: The monetary base has declined by $200 billion in the last couple of months.

speaker: LACKER
text: That was unanticipated, at least on my part, and the outlook seems to have worsened.

speaker: LACKER
text: So, if anything, we should be moving in the other direction.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have a concern I’d like to discuss first about how we go about this.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have these demand-driven credit programs that are having a big influence on the base.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve talked for two meetings now about different points of view about whether it’s credit programs and our asset side or whether it’s our liability side and the monetary base.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve talked about credit frictions, and we’ve talked about the demand for bank reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think if we’re honest with ourselves, we admit that we as a group don’t have a clear view—we haven’t decided between these two theories.

speaker: LACKER
text: Policy robustness suggests acting as if either could be true.

speaker: LACKER
text: In this instance, the two don’t conflict; they coincide.

speaker: LACKER
text: Both a focus on the base and a focus on the credit programs suggest we do more now because the economy has weakened in the last couple of months.

speaker: LACKER
text: What that perspective suggests to me is two things.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, that in the materials we distribute before the meeting (this is something I have discussed with our secretary) it’s hard for me to evaluate alternatives that differ in the size of one program on our balance sheet—the SOMA—without having a sense of what’s happening to the rest of our balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: There’s a substantial amount of uncertainty about the TALF, about the CPFF rolling off, and so on.

speaker: LACKER
text: It would make more sense, at least to me, for us to evaluate alternatives in terms of where the base is going to be.

speaker: LACKER
text: And this perspective of thinking that the base matters is one that leads me to think that maybe we should specify policy in terms of the base.

speaker: LACKER
text: The second implication that it suggests to me is that we might want to direct the Desk to ensure that the base does at least something—that it at least achieves a certain level or that it doesn’t go down in the intermeeting period.

speaker: LACKER
text: We could set an objective and say, “By the next meeting the base goes up by at least X.” Such a line in the directive wouldn’t conflict with any credit programs, but it would direct the Desk to offset any unanticipated falls in the base due to a running off of the credit programs.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is something I’d like to see us consider and talk about tomorrow.

speaker: LACKER
text: More broadly, I like President Bullard’s idea—and I think that’s the way we ought to think about this—that we’ve got to vary what we plan to do with the base in response to economic conditions, as in a sort of a reaction function.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we’re kind of groping toward this.

speaker: LACKER
text: What the New York staff did in forecasting the base is a great start, but it’s a little hard to get a handle on such a large aggregate number so far ahead.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not looking for daily or weekly forecasts of the base—that would be a little overkill.

speaker: LACKER
text: But something with a bit more granularity on the time scale might be useful.

speaker: LACKER
text: I recognize there’s a lot of uncertainty about what these other contributors to fluctuations in the base are going to do in the near term, and we ought to take that into account.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I think setting a floor for the path for the base in the near term has some usefulness to it.

speaker: LACKER
text: About mortgage-backed securities versus Treasuries, I have a preference for Treasuries.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was asking Ms. Mosser about flexibility, and I thought that maybe intervening in Treasuries would be a little more flexible than in agencies.

speaker: LACKER
text: But, more broadly, I worry about the exit problem, and I worry about the optics of a situation in which, when the recovery begins, we’re holding a huge portion of the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac securities, and we’re contemplating selling it off in order to tighten monetary policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I worry about what elected political officials will have to say about that and what pressure they might bring to bear on us to forestall selling off a big agency portfolio.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we’d face much less pressure with regard to Treasuries, appealing as we would to the 1951 accord.

speaker: LACKER
text: About FX swaps, I have very mixed feelings for live institutions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m very concerned that the presence of it, which the banks would obviously come to be aware of, would diminish their incentive to inoculate themselves against the circumstances that would give rise to their need for it, despite the best efforts of our supervisory staff to ensure they pursue those inoculations.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think Case 3 is persuasive in conjunction with the closedown or windup of a large institution.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’m willing to reluctantly support it.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we ought to be transparent about it, as President Rosengren said.

speaker: LACKER
text: About an accord, what you’ve outlined is not my ideal accord.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think that the credit-risk-free line you’ve sketched is a bright one.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that the price that we’re paying is pretty high in terms of using the TALF to fund what in early February was announced as something that would be funded by the FDIC.

speaker: LACKER
text: Bank rescues, I think, are worthwhile; buying toxic assets is very worthwhile.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it’s very important that it gets done.

speaker: LACKER
text: Something clean and simple and uncomplicated has much to recommend it, so I find myself supporting President Rosengren on this, for some straightforward program.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the last meeting, we talked a lot about the TALF.

speaker: LACKER
text: I won’t rehearse the things I said then about it, but I’ll note now that to some extent what we’re doing is recreating leverage.

speaker: LACKER
text: I thought that there’s at least a case that a lot of what went wrong in the last decade was excessive leverage.

speaker: LACKER
text: And if you think too-big-to-fail is a problem, it’s a problem because it leads to excessive leverage.

speaker: LACKER
text: We seem to be trying to restore the status quo ex ante conditions in credit markets by restoring the same extent of leverage, and I’m not sure that that’s the right philosophy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not sure that we can have a lot of confidence about the incentives of the private participants in the partnership.

speaker: LACKER
text: Are their incentives going to be to price it cleanly or to overpay because they have the downside put to us?

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not sure I see analytically how that works out.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d like to get rid of the ring fences very soon.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think New York has executed theirs.

speaker: LACKER
text: We in Richmond have not executed ours.

speaker: LACKER
text: If there’s any chance of relieving us of having to execute that legal document, I’d really appreciate it.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I’m not getting my hopes up, obviously.

speaker: LACKER
text: I take it that this would require congressional action to authorize the Treasury to take this?

speaker: LACKER
text: About Fed bills, I agree with President Plosser that it’s something that would weaken our ability in the future to resist entreaties to provide funding for something that the Administration would rather not go to the Congress for.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is not a comment on our current political independence.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m confident that you’ve undertaken everything that we have discussed in making a full independent judgment about what was worthwhile for the Federal Reserve.

speaker: LACKER
text: I just worry about future political leaders and the situation we could find ourselves in one day.

speaker: LACKER
text: About resolution techniques, it has always struck me that there are two things that get talked about there in one bundle: One is technical legal provisions of conservatorship authority and the laws around resolving them, and the other is funding.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have a model that works with banks, and the funding of that is pretty transparent.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d rather not get us involved in similar resolution funding for some other types of institutions.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me just point out that the original accord gave us independent control over our balance sheet, and I’m not sure this really restores that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, let me give my comments on expanding our balance sheet by first saying that I agree with those who have said, and I think you have said, that we cannot get the economy going until we get the banking and intermediation process fixed.

speaker: HOENIG
text: And I think that’s an important premise for going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That means we need to focus on resolution, and I think this proposal that’s being worked on using the TALF and using us to help finance a bad bank is actually going to delay dealing with this very serious problem.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Given the comments that President Rosengren and others have made, I think we have an opportunity to get this done with some legislation that would create the ability to put some of these holding companies in receivership and move forward, so that we can get the banking system fixed on a sustained basis.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that’s important, because I am very concerned about the TALF and growing our balance sheet, even at this meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think we should pause, because we have the TAF, we have other means to provide liquidity, should it be needed, and we have excess reserves that are sizable.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think we should focus on fixing the banking system and conserve our balance sheet carefully.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I wouldn’t want it necessarily to decline dramatically, but I don’t think it would with the TAF, and so forth; we have the mechanisms to provide liquidity.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But if the majority decides to go forward with it, then I do prefer mortgage-backeds to Treasuries.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I disagree in a sense with President Lacker because I think it would just open us up to charges of monetizing Treasury debt.

speaker: HOENIG
text: And my experience is that it doesn’t matter if you’re holding mortgage-backeds or Treasuries; when you try to sell them off your balance sheet, interest rates go up—it doesn’t matter; people are going to be upset.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So we’re better off with mortgage-backeds because it makes a cleaner line for us to say we are not in that business.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I also want to talk about excess reserves and Fed bills.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that, as the banking industry itself has learned about excess reserves and the payment of interest, it is learning to arbitrage.

speaker: HOENIG
text: From a governance point of view and from a simplicity point of view going forward, if the FOMC were made the party responsible for setting the interest rate on excess reserves, we would set the floor and control the fed funds rate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: You don’t need Fed bills if, in fact, the banking industry has learned how to arbitrage it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I agree with President Plosser—getting us into issuing bills or in a so-called cooperative relationship with the Treasury, where we’re taking Treasury bills, is a very tenuous path for us to go down, and I’d stay away from it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think paying interest on excess reserves would go a long ways to managing our balance sheet, or, I should say, our ability to control the fed funds rate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the swaps, I understand where they’re coming from on that, and I take that pretty much as a given, but hopefully it will be carefully managed and not easily accessed by the institution that needs it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the interest rate on excess reserves, I think it’s coming to play the same role as the discount rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If the FOMC set a target for the federal funds rate, that would essentially determine where the interest rate on excess reserves would be, analogous to the discount rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that analogy will hold up pretty well in the future.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I want to comment on the additional asset purchases, principally.

speaker: FISHER
text: I fully agree with Governor Warsh—in fact, I think he understated the case, and that is that I don’t think it’s advisable to purchase Treasuries here.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’ve sent a note around about that.

speaker: FISHER
text: For the record, I just want to repeat some of the arguments in there.

speaker: FISHER
text: To my knowledge, there is no liquidity problem in the Treasury market.

speaker: FISHER
text: There are no obvious signs of a breakdown in arbitrage across maturities, unless Trish tells us differently.

speaker: FISHER
text: The spreads between high-grade private issues and Treasuries do indicate that the markets are not functioning normally—I take that for granted, and you can see it every day—but that doesn’t mean that lowering long-term Treasury rates will affect private sector rates.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do worry about the perception—and it’s palpable—that we will be succumbing to political pressure to monetize the exploding borrowing needs of the Treasury.

speaker: FISHER
text: Trish, you gave us some numbers today—if I add them correctly for the fiscal year 2009, it’s around $2 trillion.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s an inordinately large number.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m preparing for a trip I am about to make to Asia, and I do think that there’s a lot of sensitivity about this there.

speaker: FISHER
text: (I’m not sure if that is whom you were referring to in your reference, Governor Warsh.)

speaker: FISHER
text: If we are viewed as the handmaiden of the Treasury here, I believe you might have a negative reaction, not a positive reaction.

speaker: FISHER
text: If the majority decides in favor of increased purchases, I support respecting President Hoenig’s view.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would prefer that we purchase GSE securities—the number is somewhat arbitrary, Bill, as you pointed out.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would do it by size, or at least announce that we could go up to a size.

speaker: FISHER
text: The one thing I would caution against is giving a specific date, unless we are absolutely certain we can meet that date.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to make a general point here.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is a lack of confidence in the marketplace.

speaker: FISHER
text: There was reference to that before; we see it with everybody we talk to.

speaker: FISHER
text: Confidence is a function of competence, and I think we should exercise our muscle where we have proven ourselves quite competent.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have proven ourselves quite competent, for example, in the commercial paper market, and we are proving ourselves quite competent in the mortgage-backed securities market.

speaker: FISHER
text: There’s a question mark out there on the TALF—we’re not quite sure.

speaker: FISHER
text: And it’s not because the staff isn’t making a great effort—we’re just going through this new process, and it has become enormously complicated.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to play to our comparative advantage.

speaker: FISHER
text: No question we could buy Treasuries—I don’t think that’s the issue—but I disagree with that for other reasons.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I would support an expanded program on mortgage-backed securities, because we are competent in performing in that area.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the issue of the swap lines, I agree with the comment that this is procedural.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we have to be very clear in expressing this.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do worry that it may become quite evident to some that we’re doing this for one particular institution, and I think you could have retribution in terms of price reaction vis-à-vis that institution and the rumors about others.

speaker: FISHER
text: But as long as we keep that in mind and express it clearly, then, were I a voter, I would vote to proceed.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the issue of Fed bills and special Treasury issuance, initially I indicated that I would be against the issuance of Fed bills.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m somewhat more enlightened now that the maturity that you described is in terms of one year or less.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have been worried that a CDS market would develop around the Fed, which would be a negative development, particularly if there was a long maturity.

speaker: FISHER
text: I still have doubts about the concept.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m not as clear in my own mind, as President Hoenig just expressed, as to the alternative, but I do worry about the eventual assumption that we might grow that program rather than rein it back in.

speaker: FISHER
text: Therefore, if we were to proceed with issuing Fed bills or an alternative, I would want to have a clear sense of provision.

speaker: FISHER
text: Otherwise, I think the expectation would be that we would continue to expand the program, and, therefore, give rise to these doubts about the further purchase of Treasuries.

speaker: STERN
text: Let me just comment on three or maybe four issues.

speaker: STERN
text: First, with regard to asset purchases, I don’t have a conviction about the magnitudes, but I would diversify the purchases by adding Treasuries.

speaker: STERN
text: I suspect that the preponderance of our purchases would still be mortgage-backed securities, but both because it puts us in a better position when it comes time to unwind and because it may turn out to be effective, I would certainly start to purchase long-term Treasuries.

speaker: STERN
text: I’m not worried—I could be dead wrong about this—about great concerns about collusion or funding exploding federal debt.

speaker: STERN
text: These are unusual and exigent circumstances.

speaker: STERN
text: People would understand what the intent of the program is, in my judgment.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to the TALF—as initially described, I thought, and I think, it has some promise.

speaker: STERN
text: The way I saw it, you have some markets that are not working—there are no prices.

speaker: STERN
text: One of the things we learned from the Japanese experience, the Depression of the ’30s, and some other episodes is that you need to have resource reallocation occur.

speaker: STERN
text: We’ve got to move resources from places where they’re no longer needed to where they are needed, and you can’t have that happen without prices.

speaker: STERN
text: So we need to get those markets restarted, and I’m in favor of the TALF as described.

speaker: STERN
text: I would stay away from legacy TALF; funding the bad bank is a close cousin to being the bad bank.

speaker: STERN
text: That’s the job of the Congress and the Administration, and of course, they’re not going to be quick to pick that up if we’re willing to do it.

speaker: STERN
text: But it seems to me we’ve got to make a stand somewhere with regard to this, and this seems to me to be a very clear and direct place where we ought to do that.

speaker: STERN
text: Finally, with regard to Fed bills or SFP, what troubles me about that is that from one perspective it could be viewed as circumventing the debt ceiling, and I don’t think we want to put ourselves in that position.

speaker: STERN
text: If we say to the Congress, “Understand that this is one of the effects of passing this legislation,” so that everything is on the table, then I’m not troubled by it.

speaker: STERN
text: But if we’re not that transparent, then I would also stay away from that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The legislation explicitly says it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It makes no sense to have the SFP, in particular, if it’s subject to the debt ceiling, because then we would not be able to use it.

speaker: STERN
text: So long as that’s understood.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have a few brief comments on the various issues.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Starting with the swaps, I support the staff recommendation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it’s a prudent step.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There were two possible draft resolutions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think I would favor the greater transparency of A, but I don’t feel strongly about it and could support either.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Then just a brief comment on the banking system.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it’s essential to fix the banking system for exactly the reason that President Hoenig and others emphasized.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we will not get recovery until we have a strong, healthy banking system with good banks that can attract capital.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would really love to see this done in the most transparent and straightforward way, namely, creating a good bank–bad bank type of framework.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I agree fully with President Rosengren’s comments—I would not make this a matter of optional sales of some portfolios of assets by banks that wanted to do it into a facility.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would go in and much more aggressively, as he suggested, force write-downs on the value of these assets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have a great opportunity to do it after the stress test is over, and I would push these institutions into spinning off their operations, in the cases where it is needed, into a good bank–bad bank structure.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If we had legislation that allowed for the resolution of systemically important financial firms that aren’t banks, that would be much easier—to give us the power to push firms without necessarily having to put them into a conservatorship, but to take those steps.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So that’s what I think would be ideal, and I think it’s important for economic recovery.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I understand it’s expensive, and I understand it’s hard to go to the Congress to get the amount of capital that’s needed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the FDIC facility is a move in the right direction.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I prefer it to what we’re doing now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It’s not ideal, but I think it’s a step in the right direction.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the legacy TALF, I have issues similar to those that President Stern enunciated.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’m not dead set against it, but I do have qualms about our becoming involved in that business.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the purchase options, I certainly see the benefits of additional purchases of MBS, especially given that there’s going to be a step-up in issuance over the next couple of months in connection with refinancing of mortgages.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The spreads are still high, although they’ve come down, and it seems to me that the expansion of that program could have a beneficial effect on the housing market and the economy and on bringing long-term yields down more generally, since other long-term assets are substitutes for mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I worry a little bit that they’re harder to unwind than Treasuries, but, still, it’s something that I would be very supportive of going ahead with now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Bill mentioned a number much higher than I had envisioned.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I don’t know what the right number is, so I’m quite open on that.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would be supportive of going ahead with purchases of Treasuries at this point, as well, on various grounds.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One is that the economy is just a disaster area.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The economic outlook is utterly dreadful, and we have said we stand ready to do absolutely everything that’s needed to support the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We have let some time pass without doing anything, and in light of the outlook I would want to do everything we can.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I thought the staff memos made a good case for the idea that the Treasuries and MBS purchases would have favorable macro effects, and I understand the concern about “what are we doing monetizing the debt?” That’s quite a legitimate concern, but, on balance, I come out in the same place as President Stern—I don’t think we’ve lost our independence, I think people realize these are unusual and exigent circumstances, and taking a step like that now is a favorable thing for the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I am supportive of A and am very open-minded about magnitudes.

speaker: KOHN
text: Let me hit some of these subjects as well.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’re in a position where doing the right thing is not obvious.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’re in a second-, third-, or fourth-best situation, and I think we’ve got to make the best of what we’re doing, given all of the constraints.

speaker: KOHN
text: It puts us in a very difficult situation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would include the swaps in that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would be in favor of going ahead because I think we need to have this in our arsenal.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I do worry about the announcement effect and whether, as several people have pointed out, markets will figure out this is really about one institution— otherwise, why are we doing this now?

speaker: KOHN
text: We don’t have the situation we had when we put the other swaps into play, in which there was generalized pressure on the markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I guess the head of your transparency subcommittee is for being a little less transparent.

speaker: KOHN
text: I could go either way on it, but I would prefer alternative B in that case, just to downplay it a little more because of the announcement effects.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we need to put it into play either way.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the Fed bills and SFP, I wish I believed that the rate on excess reserves would work, but I don’t, and I think we’ve seen evidence that it doesn’t work.

speaker: KOHN
text: Banks are capital-constrained, and all of us are talking about further substantial increases in our balance sheet.

speaker: KOHN
text: Some people are concerned about whether those increases in the balance sheet and, in effect, monetizing the debt, will have inflationary effects, and I’m concerned that all of these assets end up being excess reserves in a banking system that’s capital-constrained (and I know there’s no risk weight on these reserves, but they are part of the leverage ratio).

speaker: KOHN
text: I think having Fed bills or SFP will alleviate those concerns and will reduce some of the constraints on our actions now because it will take the funding of those actions outside the banking system and will give us a clear framework for an exit when we need to exit.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I’m strongly in favor of pursuing those.

speaker: KOHN
text: I recognize the political potential here, but I think in this situation, that’s a lesser risk than the risk that we don’t do everything that we should be doing because we’re worried about the exit.

speaker: KOHN
text: On legacy assets, I agree that a clean, simple program would be much better than these three complicated, interrelated things that are hard to explain.

speaker: KOHN
text: You did a great job, Mr. Chairman, but it’s hard to understand how they relate to each other.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we’re hung up on two issues.

speaker: KOHN
text: One is pricing the assets for a going concern.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is unlike the S&Ls, where the RTC just got the assets because the S&Ls collapsed.

speaker: KOHN
text: All the RTC had to do was worry about auctioning them into the market.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now we’ve got to worry about the price at which we’re taking them from banks that are going concerns and, partly because we don’t have a resolution regime, from bank holding companies that are going concerns.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we really have no choice—we don’t have a legal way of putting them out of business in a controlled kind of way.

speaker: KOHN
text: Related to that is the second issue, the amount of TARP capital available.

speaker: KOHN
text: When we write these assets down, it’s going to leave huge holes in the balance sheets of some banks, and there’s the TARP capital constraint.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wish neither of these were constraints, but they are.

speaker: KOHN
text: So, I think, given those constraints, we should probably go ahead with the legacy TALF as long as the total TALF doesn’t go over that $1 trillion mark.

speaker: KOHN
text: On asset purchases, I agree with the others who have said the economy is very weak.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is a serious situation.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s not obvious that the TALF and these other indirect ways are having that big an effect—I think they’ll have some effect.

speaker: KOHN
text: What we do know is that direct purchases of assets from the market have been very effective in the commercial paper area and in the MBS area.

speaker: KOHN
text: Where we do not fool around with all of the indirect SPVs, we can have an effect, and we need to do that.

speaker: KOHN
text: Apologies to Bill Nelson—he’s doing a great job.

speaker: KOHN
text: But it would be much easier if we just bought the securities, even at market prices, rather than going through all of this circular financing.

speaker: KOHN
text: Particularly with the constraint on the funds rate at the zero bound, we need to use all of our tools, and asset purchases are the most effective tool we have right now, so I would definitely buy some more MBS.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like President Yellen, I’m not sure exactly what amount, but I would certainly at least continue at the current rate you were talking about, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I would buy Treasuries also.

speaker: KOHN
text: It really concerned me over the intermeeting period that there was this generalized tightening of financial conditions at a time when the economy was weak: Among the things that tightened was the risk-free rate, and corporate rates went up pari passu, more or less, with the risk-free rate.

speaker: KOHN
text: Having seen Treasury rates rise while the economy was sinking was a very troublesome thing to me.

speaker: KOHN
text: It felt like financial conditions were tightening at exactly the wrong time.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think we need to lean against that tendency in a very visible, transparent way.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think buying longer-term Treasuries is the way to do that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it will work in the sense of lowering interest rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the table that Joe showed us was telling, where all of these announcements have had the expected effects on interest rates—it’s not basis point for basis point.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like President Plosser, I’m a little surprised that these announcements would have that effect, given that the markets are very, very liquid.

speaker: KOHN
text: But that’s what the data show.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also, in every case the exchange rate moved in the expected direction.

speaker: KOHN
text: So buying Treasury bonds would not only lower Treasury and corporate rates, but I think it also would take some of the pressure off the appreciation of the dollar, which has been part of the tightening of financial conditions.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the Treasury will issue securities across the maturity spectrum, because they’re concerned about their debt management over the long run.

speaker: KOHN
text: So, in effect, I think by buying Treasury debt, we’re financing the deficit with either reserves or Fed bills.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’re changing the relative supply of long- and short-term assets, and that’s one of the limited tools we have when the federal funds rate is at the zero bound.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we ought to be using that tool.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think right now we need to make sure that fiscal policy is as effective as it can be.

speaker: KOHN
text: So monetizing the debt to me is not a negative under the current situation, because it’s helping fiscal policy be effective—provided we can do it in the context of not having rising inflation expectations and not having concerns about our independence.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think these announcements haven’t had an adverse effect on people’s perceptions of our independence.

speaker: KOHN
text: In the context of pursuing a framework for Fed bills and SFP—so we’re actively thinking about the exit strategy at the same time we’re buying the bonds—and in the context of our longer-term projections and strengthening what we say about inflation expectations, I think we can buy the bonds without concerns about raising inflation expectations.

speaker: KOHN
text: The program will underline in a very visible way our expectation that interest rates are going to be low for a while.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vice Chairman, did you have a two-hander?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I just had a question about the liquidity of the Treasury market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: People have said a couple of times that the Treasury market is really liquid.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t really think it’s all that liquid.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Trish, did you have a comment?

speaker: MOSSER
text: It’s more liquid than anything else.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But that’s a pretty sad statement at this stage.

speaker: MOSSER
text: There are, in fact, huge price gaps between the different pieces of the Treasury curve.

speaker: MOSSER
text: One of the things we do by going in is actually to improve liquidity, particularly at the long end, and hopefully help to bring down yields that way as well.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It is interesting—and this is a point I made in my presentation—that our presence in the mortgage-backed securities market, particularly the large presence in the TBA market, which is the forward liquid part of the market, has improved liquidity tremendously, according to the asset managers we’ve been using.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think our buying Treasuries would hopefully have some effect there, too.

speaker: FISHER
text: Can I ask a question about that, Mr. Chairman?

speaker: FISHER
text: The 10-year rate has sort of altered between 2.70 and 3.00 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: And when we talk about buying Treasuries to bring rates down, give me an order of magnitude.

speaker: FISHER
text: Are we talking about going back to 2.70?

speaker: FISHER
text: Are we talking about 2.50?

speaker: FISHER
text: Let’s say we did something in size.

speaker: FISHER
text: What would your expectations be, just so we have a reference point for this discussion?

speaker: MOSSER
text: It partly depends on where we would buy.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t want to get too technical here, but I think we’d probably start not with the rates you see every day—the on-the­ runs—we’d probably start with the off-the-runs where we can improve liquidity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Normally as the off-the-runs come down, part of that would be the spread to the on-the-runs that would come down as well—hopefully it’s low.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We would move across the curve.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think the strategy—which we’re in the process of working out, because we weren’t so sure that we were going to be doing this—would be to start there, but to go to recently issued securities, where there’s a little bit of liquidity but not a lot.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In terms of the size of the effect, honestly, I don’t think we have any better estimates than the ones that Joe gave you.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We’re guessing there would be a very large announcement effect, of the order of magnitude that Joe said.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Once we got going—let’s say it’s $500 billion, and people figure out how much per week approximately we were going to do—we’d move back and forth across the curve.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We would announce in advance approximately over a course of weeks what tenors of the curve we would be buying—not exact days and exact amounts, because we don’t want to get front-run that badly, but we’d want to give folks a sense of where we were going.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If we thought there were particular distortions in one part of the curve, we would focus more there.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So we’re doing something somewhat analogous to the way we are managing the MBS program: We don’t have an explicit target, but when both retail rates get high and mortgage spreads get high, the investment managers know to buy more, and we would take the same approach.

speaker: FISHER
text: But we would expect we’d still have a positive-shaped yield curve, obviously.

speaker: FISHER
text: It would still be fairly steep.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It would still be steep, but not as steep as it is now.

speaker: FISHER
text: If my memory is correct, it does help bankers to have a positive relationship.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d like to ask what you mean by “improved liquidity” in this context because we use that term a lot.

speaker: LACKER
text: There’s a market, there are some sales, there’s a bid and there’s an asked, there’s a certain flow.

speaker: LACKER
text: We come in and we buy a lot.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then afterwards, the price is presumably higher.

speaker: LACKER
text: When you say “liquidity is improved,” do you mean there’s increased the volume because we added volume by purchasing a bunch, or do you mean the bid-asked spreads are lower?

speaker: LACKER
text: Or do you mean the price is higher?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Bid-asked spreads, trade depth, how much size of a trade you could put through, how easy it is to hedge.

speaker: LACKER
text: So even apart from our volume, other people’s volume is higher.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We want other people to follow us in.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Our volume alone is not going to do it.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If others don’t follow us in, it won’t work.

speaker: MOSSER
text: What’s interesting about the MBS market is that volumes were low, bid-askeds were very wide, and daily price volatility bounced all over the place.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So if you actually wanted to sell any mortgages, it was very hard to figure out where they were going to price.

speaker: MOSSER
text: What has happened since we have come in is that others have come in after us, because our managers add a little stability—if the price gets too high, they buy a little more that day; they buy less if it’s a little low.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So they temper their purchases on a day-to-day basis.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t know if we’d do it literally day to day for Treasuries, but we would do it over time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Think about it as: Volatility comes down, therefore the risk premiums will come down as a function of lower volatility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And that’s what brings rates down.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given the deterioration in the outlook, I do believe that aggressive policy action is needed.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I came to the meeting prepared to support alternative B, primarily because the simulations that the staff provided indicated that purchasing mortgage-backed securities gave us a bigger bang for our buck than the purchase of Treasury securities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, I am willing to consider the purchase of Treasury securities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I listened to Vice Chairman Dudley’s comments about the fact that the TALF is slow to get up and running and that we don’t have experience in the purchase of long-term Treasury securities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I do support the expansion of the purchase of mortgage-backed securities and the increase in agency debt purchases, but I am also willing to be open-minded about the purchase of Treasury securities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Regarding the extension of the TALF, I am concerned that we are not being clear about our objectives.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Some of the questions we had around the table today indicate that.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I don’t want our periodic announcement of additional classes of securities to be interpreted as if we are just being reactive.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think that if we do move ahead with the expansion of the program, then making our objectives clearer will help the public understanding and help build confidence around the program.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There are two sorts of questions I’d like to address and tell you where I think I am and where I might be tomorrow or the next day after that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The questions are, first of all, the expansion of the balance sheet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Should it be bigger than it is?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not opposed to expanding the balance sheet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’ve never expressed much opposition to it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What’s not clear to me is whether we have the right set of metrics to help us judge how much expansion we need and what the right tradeoffs are as we do it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In that regard, before I go any further, I want to thank the staff.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’ve been raising some of these questions off and on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The New York staff and the Board staff have presented an incredible set of memos for us this time, and I just want to thank them a lot for their efforts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They’re really working hard to try to address these questions, which are very challenging because they do not have easy answers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s much easier to ask them than it is answer them, and I appreciate that fact.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do think, though, that we need some better metrics to think about what it means to expand the balance sheet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m very sympathetic to President Lacker’s view that maybe we ought to think about what’s the size of the monetary base or the size of the balance sheet and set some bounds on it and how we think of measuring that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Improving on metrics in that regard would be very useful.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Also, in terms of the size of the balance sheet, thinking about why it ought to be bigger or smaller and what the appropriate magnitudes would be may help us think about what the composition of that balance sheet is going to look like.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think we need to think about the size first of all.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The second issue is, if we agree to increase the balance sheet to whatever size we want it to be, then we need to think about its composition.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Should the increase be in Treasuries?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Should it be in mortgage-backed securities?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Should it be more TALF?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And here I’m a little frustrated because I find myself, as I’ve said before, worried about credit programs and fiscal policy issues and other things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But even stepping away from that, it seems to me that we do these various programs on almost a one-off basis.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think one of the challenges we face is getting some grasp of how these programs are benefiting us at the margin.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We’re always taught that you do things at the margin.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So you want to equate the marginal benefits of the different programs that we’re trying to be involved in, regardless of our debates on other points about them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One of the things that I think we should also think hard about is how the different programs interact with each other.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I raised the question last time, when we talked about extending them, whether maybe we could get rid of some of them, whether maybe they’re not doing what we thought they would do.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How does the commercial paper program interact with the Treasury’s guarantee program, which interacts with the AMLF, which interacts with the MMIFF?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In trying to get, as I think the Chairman said last time, some rationalization of these programs, I’d ask where at the margin we’re trying to get some benefit from each of these and how do we equate them across that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I worry a little about the consequences of our pursuing programs where we become the lender of first resort rather than the lender of last resort.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One of the things we want is to have our benefits spread across, or marginally equated across, programs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I worry about the consequences of our participation in some markets, where we either are the market or we’re making ourselves the market by what we do.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that’s something that we have to be concerned about.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have to worry about the anticipation that other players won’t be in the market, as long as we’re there.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Looking a bit beyond just the direct impact: Are we discouraging participation?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are we trying to revive markets that maybe shouldn’t be revived?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, by trying to keep certain specific markets in place, are we impeding the marketplace’s search for other credit-allocation or capital-raising mechanisms?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think we have to worry about the endogeneity of the performance of these markets with respect to the decisions and plans we make.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That brings me back to President Bullard’s point about having a plan and having a path.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it’s very important, and it interacts with this notion of the degree to which we’re creating problems for markets or solving problems in some of these markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Not knowing what our path of actions is going to be over the future, I think, is a source of uncertainty in the marketplace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The way I think about it is by trying to get to answers for questions like: What do we think the size of our balance sheet ought to be or what should its path be?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How do we equate the marginal benefits from each of these programs to achieving that growth, knowing full well that if we don’t articulate what our strategy is and how we’re going to end when we enter markets, then we can actually increase uncertainty and volatility rather than reduce it?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have to think about those choices.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How does that play against the TALF and Treasury bills?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we’re going to expand our balance sheet—and, again, I’m not convinced that we need to, but I’m not necessarily opposed to it—I do lean towards Treasury bills for a couple of reasons.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I worry about the knock-on effects that I was just alluding to about TALF programs at the margin and the various other programs that we have.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m uncomfortable with not having more Treasuries on our balance sheet; I think Treasuries would help our exit strategy at the end of the day.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My view of buying Treasuries, though, is really about the composition of our balance sheet and not about trying to drive down long-term Treasury rates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, in this environment, where it’s essentially a zero interest rate bound, buying short-term Treasuries is sort of a swap, and economic theory tells us that’s not going to help us very much.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So we end up being forced into buying longer-term assets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But my first concern is getting a better balance of Treasuries versus all this other stuff on our balance sheet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I’d be inclined in favor of buying Treasuries.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It doesn’t mean I’d be opposed to buying more MBS at some point in the future, but we haven’t gotten to the $500 billion level yet, and we haven’t articulated a path.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I’d wait until we got a plan together to articulate this path before we announced additional purchases of those types of assets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Like President Stern, I’m not a big fan of doing the legacy ABS through the TALF.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’ll treat the bad bank model separately.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But expanding the TALF to legacy stuff is going a little too far.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Again, I worry about us becoming the lender of first resort, and I’m just not sure that’s where we want to be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the bad bank/good bank—President Stern made this point—I’m not sure that ought to be our business or that we ought to be funding it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that should be a Treasury issue, and if we can avoid being in that business, I would prefer it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re not funding the bad bank.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But we’re taking on the assets in support and providing the liquidity through the TALF to do that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’d rather let the FDIC program work than have us augment it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But let me move on to the other two issues.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the resolution mechanism, Mr. Chairman, I think you’ve been very clear about it; in fact, people in this room, myself included, have been talking about this for almost a year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We need to get on with that, and it’s very critical.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that’s going to help us a lot, so I support that effort.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As to the accord, I shared a memo about it with the Committee.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My views there are pretty clear.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do think that it’s important that the accord as I proposed it be about keeping our balance sheet much more pristine and about the exit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It had its antecedents in Al Broaddus’s and Marvin Goodfriend’s work and even was a recommendation of the financial stability group of the G–30.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I do think that it’s a form of constrained discretion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we don’t want to be in the business of doing fiscal policy and we want to discourage the Congress from coming to us to engage in fiscal policy, then we want to make it easier for us to say “no” in those circumstances.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think, Mr. Chairman, you’ve done a terrific job in this; in the example of the Congress talking about funding the automobile companies, you were very clear that that was not our business.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We want to discourage those kinds of requests, and my concern is raising the threshold for saying “yes.” What worries me about the Fed bills option, as opposed to the supplemental financing securities, is that the Fed bills option is going to make it easier for them to ask us to do things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think of it as giving us an almost incredibly unconstrained discretion to do fiscal policy or to be asked to do fiscal policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And that may ultimately become a lack of independence, not a source of independence.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That worries me, because, at some point down the road—maybe ten years, fifteen years, whatever—if the Federal Reserve became more politicized than it has been in the past, it might be much more susceptible or much more responsive to a claim that “we have to coordinate monetary and fiscal policies, and therefore, Federal Reserve, you should issue some Treasury bills on our behalf and do some things to help coordinate policies.” That probability may not be large, but it would be a very bad outcome for the institution, and I think we should do all we can to resist being in that spot.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The sunset provision, Mr. Chairman, as you suggested, may provide us some protection against that, but if the sunset provision comes along and we’ve issued Fed bills in the past, then it might be easy for them to want us to do it again.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So my current feeling is, if I cannot get a true accord, as I advocated in my memo, I’d prefer the supplemental financing program to be conducted as needed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we think we need that sterilization capability, I’d rather go that route.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The time is late, and in the interest of time and in response to the body language I see around the room, I’m going to limit myself to talking about the asset-purchase question.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I came here favoring growing the balance sheet with more asset purchases principally because of the deteriorating outlook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A lot of good arguments have been made on both sides, whether it be Treasuries or an MBS program.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I, on balance, favor the MBS approach for reasons a number of you have articulated, particularly Governor Warsh.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But I would like to focus my remarks on a dimension that has been touched on, but perhaps not explicitly addressed, and that’s the communications challenges.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In lots of conversations over the last few weeks, particularly with directors and so forth, I get the increasing sense that we have big communication challenges, and they are part of the problem.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There’s a lot of confusion and uncertainty regarding how we’re making our decisions, what comes next, and how it all fits together as a total policy set.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think we need to consider favoring programs that are already in place.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Simplicity, I think, counts in these circumstances.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I would argue that it may be better to err on the side of “no new stuff” if we can, to be as concrete as we can, to try to explain the decision framework that we are using, and to try to repeat a holistic explanation of policy going forward.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I think a consideration in the decision is the question of communication.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: President Fisher used the term “confidence.” President Bullard talked about “path.” President Plosser used the word “uncertainty.” This all comes together to me as one more element to take into consideration, which is: How do we communicate it clearly, so the public, particularly the business public, understands?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For those who have talked about rates, would expressing purchases in terms of monthly rates be of any help?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I haven’t yet heard a specific suggestion about how to do that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Something like, say, “the Desk will aim to buy $80 billion a month of mortgage-backed securities.”

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You’d want it conditional on the financial conditions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In other words, if things got worse, you’d want to accelerate the rate, and similarly, if things got better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m looking for a concrete example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d be more than happy to try to accommodate this kind of language if we can figure out how to do it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Brian is already worried about missing dinner, I’m sure.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: He’s worried about missing going to bed today.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Let me think about the question overnight, and I’ll come back with an answer tomorrow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll discuss that in the morning.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Mindful of the fact that I’m now the major impediment between the Federal Open Market Committee and dinner, I will follow President Lockhart’s lead and confine myself to comments on the large-scale asset-purchase issue.

speaker: TARULLO
text: But could I ask Trish a couple of quick questions beforehand?

speaker: TARULLO
text: One, Trish, you said earlier something about the equivalent of absorption capacity, or I guess it’s actually going in the other direction, the effective limit on MBS purchases.

speaker: MOSSER
text: And the number was—this is our best guess—an additional $2 trillion of mortgage-backed securities, that might strain it.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Second, you were working with the half trillion figure for government securities, which had been put in the Bluebook.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Is there a minimum figure below which a palpable impact wouldn’t be felt?

speaker: MOSSER
text: That’s a very hard question to answer.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I am concerned that a very small quantity would be seen as ineffective, and part of this is about the announcement effect, not to mention the liquidity effect.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Could it be less than $500 billion?

speaker: MOSSER
text: We calculated about how much we would have to buy every week, and we’d go in two or three times a week with several billion dollars every time.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So these would be sizable transactions from our perspective.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It could be scaled back a bit, but I wouldn’t want to put it at $100 billion or $200 billion, not over a nine- month period.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I’m afraid it wouldn’t be effective.

speaker: TARULLO
text: So, somewhat informed by those helpful answers, here are my views as they now stand.

speaker: TARULLO
text: First, it seems to me that under current circumstances, for the reasons many of you have stated, the risks for us are in doing too little, not in doing too much.

speaker: TARULLO
text: That leads me to the predisposition towards a large figure, at least as large as the Option A total that was included in the Bluebook, and, as Vice Chairman Dudley has suggested, perhaps larger than that as well.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Second, it seems to me with respect to the issue of the proper number—how do we know where we are going, how do we know how much is enough—you all have for some time been, and now I’m joining you, navigating in waters in which there’s not a particularly good map to follow, so it’s necessarily a matter of making judgments based upon what appear to be still seriously dysfunctional credit markets and a serious absence of liquidity and a seriously underperforming real economy.

speaker: TARULLO
text: In those circumstances, I feel pushed towards the larger end of the ranges that have been identified as appropriate.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Third, for the reason that President Evans stated earlier in the afternoon, my inclination is towards multiple instruments.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I’ve been struck just in my first six weeks here how many times people have commented that correlations or predictions that people might have expected in normal times are now breaking down a bit.

speaker: TARULLO
text: We’re not entirely sure of the effects of the application of a particular policy instrument, and it seems to me that, under those circumstances, it would be wise to mix instruments that are essentially directed towards the same end.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Having said that, my instinct, if it is possible—and this is why I asked Trish the question about minimum purchases of government securities—is for an asymmetric number and an asymmetric emphasis upon the MBS rather than the Treasury securities.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Here I’d echo—or steal—some of the points that Vice Chairman Dudley made a moment ago.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Finally, on communications, I have a slightly different, but I think complementary, point to the one that President Lockhart made: If we go this route of including both MBS and Treasuries, I hope we could at least consider giving some explanation in the Committee’s statement about why we’re pursuing both rather than simply stating “here is the amount of each which we’ve instructed the Desk to purchase.” Thank you.

speaker: DUKE
text: Now I’m the one standing in the way of dinner.

speaker: DUKE
text: I just want to talk a bit about expansion of the TALF and then also about asset purchases.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of expanding the TALF, my concern is about some of the asset classes, for instance, commercial-mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: DUKE
text: I don’t know a lot about how those are put together, but I do know a lot about commercial mortgages, and they’re much closer to business loans than they are to real estate loans.

speaker: DUKE
text: They’re entirely dependent on cash flows of different types of businesses.

speaker: DUKE
text: So if we get into those kinds of purchases and we start to determine the haircuts, we’re going to be looking at credit allocation, because we’re going to be looking at differences in conditions in different industries and the real estate that supports those industries.

speaker: DUKE
text: The second thing is that I don’t think you can make a bad asset into a good one by taking a larger haircut.

speaker: DUKE
text: If we’re going to be taking assets not from banks, but from anybody who wants to disgorge them, then what would keep us from simply moving assets from one hedge fund to another?

speaker: DUKE
text: And I really get concerned that the Fed ends up getting stuck trying to digest every hairball that’s out there in the marketplace.

speaker: DUKE
text: That’s a technical term, “hairball.” I also worry that when we originally talked about expanding the TALF up to $1 trillion, it was with the understanding that that was conditional upon our getting the ability to issue either Fed bills or the supplemental Treasury securities.

speaker: DUKE
text: That has gotten lost in the discussion of it, and I worry that with a quick announcement on this other facility, the notion would again get lost, namely, that it’s dependent upon other things happening.

speaker: DUKE
text: Finally, I don’t see this as a good bank–bad bank situation, and I worry whether we’d have enough left to deal with emergencies if they came up.

speaker: DUKE
text: I’ll talk more about this tomorrow, but the more I keep going around and around considering all the things we’re trying to do to fix the banking system—while I think it’s important—I’m not nearly as confident as everyone else that it’s something that we can do.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I keep coming back to thinking that the only thing we can do is to put a floor under house prices.

speaker: DUKE
text: If we could put a floor under house prices, that would also put a floor under bank losses, and I think it’s our best chance to get moving in the right direction.

speaker: DUKE
text: Before I move to asset purchases, I’d like to start with the story of an elderly wealthy gentleman who had taken a young bride and begun to spend money like crazy.

speaker: DUKE
text: His friends got very concerned that he was going to go through his entire fortune, and they elected one of their number to go and talk to him about it.

speaker: DUKE
text: He said, “Sam, we’re really concerned.

speaker: DUKE
text: We want to make sure that you know that you can’t buy love.” Sam said, “I know you can’t buy love, but if you spend enough money, you can buy something that looks so close you can hardly tell the difference.” So I think if we spent enough money, got enough of a hit right now, it would look like a floor on house prices, and we might have something every bit as good as a floor on house prices.

speaker: DUKE
text: It seems like the best time, when we have the synergies with the housing program, which should reduce foreclosures and should increase the ability to refinance.

speaker: DUKE
text: Both borrowers and purchasers are so incredibly hair-trigger sensitive to what goes on with mortgage interest rates.

speaker: DUKE
text: Mortgage interest rates went down when we made the announcement before, but that was in November, and that was not the season when people buy houses.

speaker: DUKE
text: If we do this in the spring, when there are other programs that would support it and when it’s pretty obvious that there’s not going to be any fiscal stimulus coming along that would also further support house purchases, then maybe we’ve got a window of opportunity where we can go in there and put a floor under house prices, and that will start to move some of these other things.

speaker: DUKE
text: And with that, Mr. Chairman, I believe I’m the last one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, I’m certainly glad we avoided a go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Before we leave, we have a little bit of business.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have to ratify domestic open market operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We do have to vote on the temporary liquidity swap lines.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I heard most people proposing A, which was the more transparent alternative, understanding that there were perhaps some risks to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Kohn, are you okay with that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would anyone else like to speak on that question?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, do you want to take the roll on the swap lines?

speaker: DANKER
text: On resolution A from the memo.

speaker: DANKER
text: Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Dudley Yes Governor Duke Yes President Evans Yes Governor Kohn Yes President Lacker Yes President Lockhart Yes Governor Tarullo Yes Governor Warsh Yes President Yellen Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At dinner tonight we’ll celebrate Governor Kroszner’s return, and we’ll begin tomorrow morning at 9:00 a.m.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess we’re ready now, finally, for the economic review.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me turn it over to Dave Stockton.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In looking at the myriad ways in which we were surprised by the incoming data and forced by evolving economic and financial circumstances to revise our forecast, I began to think that maybe my wife was on to something when she recently gave me a T-shirt that reads “Mind of an Athlete – Body of a Genius.” Well, as you know from reading the Greenbook, we did mark down substantially our forecast this round.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We are now projecting that real GDP will fall 2¼ percent this year and increase just 1½ percent next year; those are downward revisions of about 1½ and 1 percentage point, respectively, from our January projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Given that weaker outlook for activity, we expect that the unemployment rate will rise to 9½ percent in early 2010, where it will remain through the end of the year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Three principal factors were behind the sizable downward revision that we made to our forecast: first, much weaker foreign activity and a stronger exchange value of the dollar; second, weaker incoming data on employment, production, and spending for the domestic economy; and third, at least as of last Wednesday, a drop in the stock market of about 15 percent relative to our January forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Steve will have more to say about the foreign outlook, but in sum, the projected deterioration in foreign activity and the higher value of the dollar account for about one-third of the downward revision that we have made to our forecast of GDP.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the incoming data on the domestic economy have been dismal as well.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Starting with the labor market, private payrolls have been dropping at an average monthly pace of 650,000 since November, surprising us to the downside.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, the level of payroll employment in February was 550,000 lower than was anticipated in our January forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: And since the February reference week, initial claims have moved up further, as has the level of insured unemployment, suggesting that job losses likely remained appreciable this month.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The household survey has shown a similar deterioration.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The unemployment rate rose to 8.1 percent in February, nearly ½ percentage point above the level that we expected in our previous forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Measures of manufacturing production also point to a steep contraction in activity.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: After falling at a 17 percent annual rate in the fourth quarter, further widespread declines in factory output in January and February put us on track for an even steeper drop in the current quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, national and regional purchasing managers’ indexes suggest that declines will continue in the coming months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Plummeting output left the capacity utilization rate in the manufacturing sector at about 67 percent in February, its lowest level since we began publishing that series in 1948.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, the motor vehicle sector has been especially hard-hit.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In response to the steady weakening of demand over the past year, automakers have slashed production.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Assemblies of light vehicles fell to a 3.7 million unit pace in January, the lowest level since the 1950s, and that includes months in which there have been UAW strikes.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Production increased to a still meager 4½ million unit pace in February, and we expect a further increase to about 5½ million units in March.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But for the current quarter as a whole, the average level of production is low enough to lop 2 percentage points off the change in real GDP.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have motor vehicle sales bottoming out in the next couple of months at levels just a bit below those seen in February.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If that occurs, some further modest increase in production seems likely, as inventories will have been brought into substantially better alignment with sales.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That said, production in the second quarter is only expected to move up to what we previously would have considered a deep recession level of 5¾ million units.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In addition to significant downside surprises in the labor market and in industrial production, the incoming spending data have been much weaker than we had expected seven weeks ago.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Starting with some ancient history, we lowered our estimate of fourth-quarter real GDP by 2 percentage points to show a decline of 6¾ percent at an annual rate, with much weaker final sales more than accounting for the downward revision.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, the incoming data early this year have led us to revise down our estimate of output for the first quarter as well.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, the ink had barely dried on the Greenbook when we received weaker-than-expected trade data last Friday.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Taking on board those data, we would probably mark down a bit further our projected decline in real GDP closer to minus 7 percent, about 1¼ percentage points below our January forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Aside from net exports, some of the biggest negative surprises have been in capital spending, which is contracting more sharply than we had expected.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Business fixed investment fell at an annual rate of 22 percent in the fourth quarter and is projected to drop at a 25 percent pace this quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
