text: Large cutbacks are being made in outlays for both equipment and structures.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The pullback in capital spending has been greater than can be explained by business sales and interest rates alone, suggesting that financing constraints and heightened economic uncertainty are part of the story.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Spending by state and local governments has fallen noticeably as well; we had been expecting these governments to hold outlays roughly steady while waiting for greater clarity on potential relief from the federal government.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Instead, mounting budget pressures led these entities to cut employment and spending late last year and early this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We still think fiscal stimulus will provide a boost to state and local spending, but from a lower underlying base than we had expected in January.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The one notable positive innovation has come from retail sales, which posted increases in both January and February.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Given the stronger recent numbers and the imminent support from fiscal stimulus, we now expect some stabilization in consumer spending in the near term, rather than the declines we had projected in the last forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Still, with mounting job losses, deteriorating household balance sheets, and sour sentiment, we don’t think a sustained upturn in consumer spending will occur until late this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: All told, the large downward revisions we have made to employment, production, and sales in the near term have important implications for the dynamics of the forecast going forward.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The weaker labor market implies lower incomes and lower consumer outlays.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: And with the stock market down from our previous projection, those multiplier consequences for spending are amplified by more negative wealth effects.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The accompanying weaker spending and business sales, in turn, feed back into lower capital outlays through the accelerator effect.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Another key element in the downward revision that we made to our forecast was housing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It has seemed, no matter how low we set the forecast, the data surprise us to the downside.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Sales, starts, and permits all fell more than we expected in January, and we revised down the projected trajectory of housing starts significantly over the forecast period.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As for the timing of when we expect to reach the bottom in starts, with a dogged persistence that is beginning to resemble that of Chicago Cubs fans, our motto remains, “Wait until next quarter.” Yesterday’s data on housing starts for February provide a glimmer of hope.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Both starts and permits moved up, rather than declining as we had expected.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But just as a few wins in spring training don’t portend a World Series, it would be premature to read the starts figures for February as suggesting that we have reached a bottom in this sector.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The deeper declines that have occurred in final sales have left firms facing a larger inventory problem than we had earlier thought.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In addition to the overhangs of unsold houses and motor vehicles that have been with us for some time, inventory- sales ratios now appear elevated in a wide range of industries.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As a consequence, the production adjustment in our current forecast is larger and more protracted than the one incorporated in the January Greenbook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: While our projected recession is deeper and longer than in our previous forecast, we do see a variety of forces capable of braking the decline in activity and promoting an eventual recovery.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For one, the most negative multiplier-accelerator effects associated with last year’s shock are expected to fade out over the course of this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, fiscal stimulus should provide a sizable boost to demand and production in coming months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: And, we expect financial conditions to gradually improve over the balance of this year and in 2010, with the stock market turning up, bond spreads narrowing, and credit restrictions easing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This broad improvement in financial conditions is an important element in our projected recovery.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On this point, we take some limited comfort from the lack of further deterioration in recent months in some of our summary measures of financial stress—indicators that we have used to help gauge the unusual restraint on spending created by the disruptions in financial markets.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: All told, an anemic recovery gets under way in 2010 and then gathers further momentum in 2011 and beyond.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One notable feature of our forecast is that we have a downturn that in magnitude equals or exceeds those of 1970s and 1980s, but is followed by a recovery that looks like the gradual ones of the early 1990s and early 2000s.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We think this makes sense for several reasons.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: First, the deterioration in household wealth has been enormous, and even with our projected increase in the stock market, the wealth-to-income ratio remains much lower than it has been for the past 20 years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The adjustment of household spending to that reduction in wealth seems likely to occur slowly, holding down spending for some time.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Second, and perhaps more speculatively, we don’t think sizable pent-up demand is developing in either the household or business sector.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Admittedly, it is awfully difficult to estimate target capital stocks for either sector, but our rough estimates suggest that we should not expect a big boost from efforts to rebuild depressed capital stocks.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Third, conventional monetary policy actions have been exhausted, and we did not assume any additional nonconventional actions in this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nor have we assumed any additional fiscal stimulus.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: And finally, as we noted in the January chart show, we read the evidence as suggesting that recoveries from financial crises tend to be more sluggish than those from other recessions.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Turning to inflation, the CPI for February was released this morning.4 The headline CPI increased 0.4 percent, in line with our expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Although food prices edged down 0.1 percent, higher gasoline prices boosted the energy component by 3.3 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Core CPI increased 0.2 percent, which was 0.1 percentage point above our forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Our miss was, at least in part, attributable to a jump in motor vehicle prices—an event which I am prepared to claim, with uncharacteristic confidence, either didn’t happen or will be reversed in the next few months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Beyond the near term, we have marked down further our inflation projection, in response to the weaker outlook for economic activity, a stronger dollar, and lower oil prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: After increasing 2 percent in 2008, total PCE prices are now projected to increase ½ percent over the four quarters of this year and to increase ¾ percent next year, with the projection for both years about ¼ percentage point below our January forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We expect a smoother deceleration in core PCE prices, from 2 percent last year to 1 percent this year and ½ percent in 2010.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There are sizable risks to both sides of our inflation projection.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the one hand, many of our models are projecting a more pronounced deceleration of prices and a move into outright deflation by next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Those models appear to be expecting an appreciable decline in inflation expectations in response to wide margins of slack in resource utilization and low rates of headline inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the other hand, it is very difficult to discern any noticeable shift down in longer-term inflation expectations since last summer, even as headline inflation has come down in the wake of the 4 A table distributed by Mr. Stockton is appended to this document (appendix 4).

speaker: STOCKTON
text: collapse of energy prices and the unemployment rate has jumped up.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have taken the middle ground here and assumed that expectations will drift lower but by less than some of our models are projecting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Steve will complete our presentation.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Following on Dave’s litany of woes about the U.S. economy, I can offer little comfort from the international arena except to say that we’re not alone in our troubles.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Data we’ve received since your last meeting indicate that foreign GDP declined at a 7¼ percent annual rate in the fourth quarter, much faster than we estimated in January and the sharpest quarterly decline—by far—since the start of our series in 1970.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Of course, while the phrase “misery loves company” rings true from a psychological standpoint, it doesn’t work so well in economics.

speaker: KAMIN
text: As I’ll discuss later on in my remarks, U.S. exports plunged in the fourth quarter and were a significant drag on U.S. growth.

speaker: KAMIN
text: The fact that the rest of the world has joined the United States in recession is not all that surprising.

speaker: KAMIN
text: With the United States accounting for about a quarter of global GDP, and with the world’s major economies tightly linked through trade and finance, downturns in the U.S. economy historically have coincided with downturns in foreign growth.

speaker: KAMIN
text: The big surprise has been which countries have been hit the hardest.

speaker: KAMIN
text: The United States, the United Kingdom, and the euro area, which have been at the epicenter of the financial crisis, registered fourth-quarter declines in GDP of “merely” 6 to 7 percent.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Conversely, in many economies whose banking and housing sectors were less affected by the initial turmoil, output dropped much more sharply: by 10 percent in Mexico, 12 percent in Japan, 13 percent in Brazil, and more than 20 percent in Korea, Taiwan, and Thailand.

speaker: KAMIN
text: What accounts for the seemingly outsized response of many economies to the financial crisis?

speaker: KAMIN
text: Clearly, one factor at work here is that, as is typically the case in recessions, the demand for manufactures has fallen more sharply than demand for total goods and services—this has led to unusually sharp falloffs in exports by many Asian economies.

speaker: KAMIN
text: A second factor has been the collapse in commodity prices, which has weighed heavily on economies in Latin America and the Middle East.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Finally, since the intensification of the global crisis last fall, investors have been pulling out of many emerging market economies, disrupting the flow of credit to households and firms.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Indicators for the current quarter are pointing to another 7 percent drop in foreign GDP, with activity declining at a similar pace in both the advanced and emerging market economies.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Industrial production, purchasing managers’ surveys, and business and consumer sentiment have either continued to fall in the past few months or are holding at the extraordinarily depressed levels reached late last year.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Our forecast has foreign output declining more gradually in the second quarter before bottoming out later this year and accelerating to nearly 3 percent by the end of 2010.

speaker: KAMIN
text: If our forecast materializes, the foreign economy will have endured four quarters of contraction, the same as in the 1981–1982 recession, but much longer than the slowdowns of 1974 and 2001.

speaker: KAMIN
text: By the time the foreign economy touches bottom late this year, real GDP will have declined a record 4¼ percent, and we are projecting a weaker rebound thereafter than occurred following the prior downturns.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Accordingly, although it seems premature to be predicting the recovery when economies are still in free fall, our outlook does not seem entirely fanciful.

speaker: KAMIN
text: It does, however, depend importantly on a number of factors that remain up in the air, including a stabilization of financial conditions and the recovery of the U.S. economy.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Given the difficult outlook, strong support from the public sector will be critical.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Foreign governments will be providing a substantial amount of monetary and fiscal stimulus over the next few quarters.

speaker: KAMIN
text: However, given the pace at which private demand is contracting and our uncertainties over its prospects, we judge this stimulus to be just adequate to secure the tepid recovery we are projecting, but insufficient to insure against any future negative shocks.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Starting with monetary policy, Japan, Canada, and the United Kingdom already have cut policy rates to 50 basis points or below.

speaker: KAMIN
text: And although the ECB’s target remains at a lofty 1½ percent, the market rate itself has been trading in the neighborhood of 85 basis points.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Accordingly, any significant further monetary support will have to come from balance-sheet expansions.

speaker: KAMIN
text: The Bank of England, Bank of Japan, and Swiss National Bank have moved forward on such measures in recent weeks, and we expect them to be followed by other major foreign central banks, but to what extent and with what ultimate effect on their economies remain open questions.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In the emerging market economies, notwithstanding the pace at which output is contracting, we expect only moderate further policy loosening.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Central banks in Asia have already eased considerably, and a number of policy rates in the region are now at 2 percent or below.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In Latin America, interest rates remain much further above the zero lower bound, but the falloff in capital inflows, associated sharp currency depreciations, and continued high inflation will likely restrain further rate cuts.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Given the uncertainties associated with monetary policy, the need for fiscal support is all the more pressing.

speaker: KAMIN
text: By our estimates, recently announced fiscal plans should add about 1 percentage point to foreign growth, both in the advanced and emerging market economies, in 2009.

speaker: KAMIN
text: This represents considerable stimulus, roughly similar to that projected for the United States this year.

speaker: KAMIN
text: But as only the U.S. and Chinese plans provide significant additional stimulus in 2010, more effort will be required should the global recession prove more persistent than expected.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Moreover, many countries with high public debt or deficits—such as Greece, Ireland, Hungary, and Turkey, to name just a few—are constrained from substantial fiscal support and may even have to cut their budgets.

speaker: KAMIN
text: If financial conditions ease enough to allow freer access to international capital markets, a number of governments may loosen monetary and fiscal policies further.

speaker: KAMIN
text: However, rather than stabilizing, there is a distinct risk that financial conditions could take a turn for the worse.

speaker: KAMIN
text: We are particularly concerned that the fragile situation in Eastern Europe could deteriorate into a full-fledged banking and balance-of-payments crisis, jeopardizing the condition of many western European banks and potentially triggering a global emerging markets meltdown.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Such a crisis would not only deepen contractionary pressures in the world economy, but would prompt many governments to tighten their monetary and fiscal stance, just when accommodative policies were most needed.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Even without an emerging markets meltdown, the global recession is having a profound effect on international trade and on the U.S. economy.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In the fourth quarter, U.S. real exports plunged at an annual rate of 25 percent.

speaker: KAMIN
text: This, by itself, would have subtracted more than 3½ percentage points from U.S. GDP growth.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Because U.S. imports plunged as well, net exports subtracted a little under a half percentage point from GDP growth, but this is still a far cry from the nearly 2 percentage point positive contribution registered in the first half of 2008.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Going forward, we expect both imports and exports to drop off further this quarter and next as the recession here and abroad continues, with the contribution of net exports hovering around zero.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In the remainder of the forecast period, however, imports start picking up along with the U.S. economy, while exports remain moribund.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Although we see the economies of our trading partners recovering a bit faster than the U.S. economy, another outcome of the global financial crisis—the nearly 20 percent rise in the dollar since last summer—helps support imports and restrain exports.

speaker: KAMIN
text: As a result, we predict net exports will subtract a half percentage point from U.S. GDP growth during the remainder of the forecast period, adding yet another headwind to a long and growing list.

speaker: LACKER
text: Mr. Stockton, what did you say about auto prices?

speaker: LACKER
text: I didn’t quite catch what made you believe they were going to reverse.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: New vehicles prices were up nearly a percentage point, 0.8 percent, for February.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I guess it was just more a hunch, given the incredible weakness in demand currently, and the fact that there still is a very high days’ supply.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It seems unlikely to me that we are on the verge of a turnaround in motor vehicle prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So we had actually been expecting a decline.

speaker: STERN
text: Dave, the Administration has asserted that the fiscal policy package will preserve and/or increase jobs by 3 to 4 million in the next couple of years.

speaker: STERN
text: I was trying to figure out from your fiscal policy analysis what the comparable number was.

speaker: STERN
text: I couldn’t quite get there, although my rough calculation was maybe 2 or 2½ million.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It centers on about 2 million, somewhere between 1¾ to 2¼ million jobs implicit in our package over the course of the next two years.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On the international side, you talked about and our focus seems to be on Eastern Europe and the European banks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But I’m hearing a lot of concern about Mexico, both political meltdown—really serious civil disorder problems— and, obviously, some economic implications.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Do you have any comments on the Mexican economy?

speaker: KAMIN
text: From an overall economic standpoint, the situation in Mexico is quite serious.

speaker: KAMIN
text: First of all, for the past three or four years, Mexican growth has probably been less than we might have expected, given its proximity to the United States and our markets and given how much potential there was for the economy to grow if the right structural reforms were implemented.

speaker: KAMIN
text: In fact, a lot of those reforms have not been implemented.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Mexican growth has been sort of moribund.

speaker: KAMIN
text: It has depended on the United States as a source of both external demand and jobs for its people.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Now that the U.S. economy is going down, the Mexican economy is suffering pretty badly, as evidenced by the 10 percent annual rate of decline in GDP in the fourth quarter.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Let me just add that obviously it is facing very serious political problems as well.

speaker: KAMIN
text: There have been a lot of reports in the paper about drug problems and the violence associated with that.

speaker: KAMIN
text: So, clearly, on a wide range of issues, Mexico has got problems.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Balance of payments and banking sector issues were of course front and center in Mexico’s crisis of ’94 and ’95, and we would be hesitant to discount that possibility entirely now, but, interestingly, the banking system in Mexico seems to pose less risk than it might— certainly less than the banking system in Eastern Europe and probably less than those in other emerging market economies.

speaker: KAMIN
text: First of all, a large share of its banks are foreign-owned, and that represents some source of stability.

speaker: KAMIN
text: On top of that, the banks that are operating there appear to be less dependent on short-term wholesale sources of financing.

speaker: KAMIN
text: So their situation is a little better.

speaker: KAMIN
text: Obviously, the situation could take a turn for the worse in the coming year if the decline in output is sufficiently large that nonperforming loans go up a lot.

speaker: KAMIN
text: But for right now, as I say, while Mexico has got a lot of problems on the balance of payments and on the banking fronts, the issues don’t seem as pronounced.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then, we’re ready to begin our economic go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m going to start with President Bullard.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The Eighth District economy is in recession.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s possibly somewhat less severe than in some parts of the country, but still a very sharp recession.

speaker: BULLARD
text: All of the problems that we see nationally are certainly apparent in the Eighth District, including credit market problems, deeply depressed auto sales, declining house prices, and so on.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The national economy appears to have weakened further relative to January expectations.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think there’s further downside risk, and I agree with many here that the main risk is some kind of failure to get the financial sector on track toward recovery.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The global aspect of the downturn continues unabated.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think this is a very worrisome factor.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s largely outside our historical experience in the modern era.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It may be that we’re not fully comprehending the meaning of global events because they haven’t really been part of our experience.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And I’m worried about that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think expectations remain very fluid, both for the course of the real economy and for inflation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We know that expectations have a huge influence on macroeconomic outcomes.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That influence is partially masked in normal times: In normal times, expectations are very stable; in normal times, for output, the private sector would expect something close to the balanced growth path; in normal times, for inflation, the private sector would expect something close to the implicit inflation target pursued by the central bank.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So, in normal times, it appears that expectations don’t move that much, and, perhaps, therefore, are not so important to how the economy is going to function.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But these are not normal times.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As a result, expectations are very fluid and can be significantly influenced by just a few events.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s as if the private sector is throwing out all of the old data, because the old data come from a different regime that doesn’t apply anymore, and they’re looking at the most recent developments, just a few things that are happening, and deciding which direction the economy is likely to go and which direction inflation is likely to go.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is what makes me especially worried about the economy and the inflation path during 2009.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In particular, I think further disinflation and possible deflation is a clear near-term risk.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Deflationary expectations could become entrenched during 2009, especially given the downside risks to the forecast, including the global nature of the very sharp downturn and the possibility that the financial sector problems won’t be addressed in an appropriate way or quickly enough.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Deflation would exacerbate problems in the housing sector and credit markets generally because of the prevalence of nominal contracting in the economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I think a near-term goal for monetary policy is to avoid this outcome.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In the medium term, we actually face inflation risk, because the expansion of the balance sheet would suggest lots of inflation possibilities out there.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I call this a two-headed dragon.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But if we get stuck in a deflationary trap, you’re never going to see that materialize.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And, again, a deflationary trap is, to my thinking, a steady state: You get stuck there, and you cannot get out.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is a deflationary trap a real possibility?

speaker: BULLARD
text: We have the clear example of Japan.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We have foreign central banks sending their policy rates to zero globally.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Our own model and our own baseline forecast have core PCE inflation at 1 percent in 2009, and below 1 percent for 2010, 2011, 2012, and 2013.

speaker: BULLARD
text: With an economy in that kind of state for that long, suppose you get another negative shock at some point; then, you do go down to the deflation trap equilibrium and get stuck there.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I really think it’s a problem for the near term—that we could get stuck in that trap.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Policy should attempt to avoid letting deflationary expectations take hold.

speaker: BULLARD
text: How should we do this?

speaker: BULLARD
text: I really liked the Bank of England’s announcement during the intermeeting period.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They said that they were planning to expand the balance sheet to increase the monetary base.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They said that they expected that to feed through to the broader money stock measures and that the growth in the money stock would help them to maintain their medium-term inflation target.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I thought that was a crystal-clear piece of communication, and the markets understand exactly what it means and what the intent of policy is.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I thought that that was a good example to follow.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Those are my comments on the economy.

speaker: FISHER
text: I was first going to say to Dave Stockton that our wives have an affinity for T-shirts.

speaker: FISHER
text: My wife, a smart Wellesley woman who spent most of her time at MIT, arrived at Oxford noting that the ratio of women to men was 1 to 11.

speaker: FISHER
text: She had a T-shirt for other women which she sold briskly, and it said, “Come to Oxford where the odds are good, but the goods are odd.” Mr. Chairman, I want to report on the microeconomic input I received from my corporate contacts, which numbered some 29 CEOs around the country whom I talked to before this meeting.

speaker: FISHER
text: Unfortunately, it confirms what Dave and Steve presented.

speaker: FISHER
text: In fact, one actually called me and said, “Do you want some good news?” And I said, “Please.” He said, “Call somebody else.” As to our District, we have fallen finally into recession.

speaker: FISHER
text: We created jobs last year.

speaker: FISHER
text: I believe we are the only District that did create jobs last year, or had jobs created in the District.

speaker: FISHER
text: The cut is less severe—it will take fewer stitches to mend—but, nonetheless, we have been cut.

speaker: FISHER
text: As to the national economy, my favorite indicators are all negative.

speaker: FISHER
text: There are 175,000 railcars that are out of commission.

speaker: FISHER
text: There has been some improvement in bulk shipping rates, but that is a head fake according to shippers I have talked to, because of the extraordinary purchase of iron ore that China undertook recently—in fact, record amounts.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you look at containers and other shipping indicators, these are all flat to negative.

speaker: FISHER
text: Of the world’s large aircraft fleet, 20 percent—that’s 2,800 airplanes—are now sitting unused in the desert.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you look at Boeing’s numbers, it received only four orders for new aircraft versus several hundred last February.

speaker: FISHER
text: And I’m told by my contacts in the airline industry that the Chinese government has ordered all of their carriers not to take the liberty of buying a single plane in 2009.

speaker: FISHER
text: That from one of the largest net new buyers of aircraft in the world.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is very little cap-ex taking place.

speaker: FISHER
text: In fact, every corporate contact I spoke to, from the large manufacturers to even Disney, is cutting back on cap-ex and displaying all kinds of microeconomic behavioral patterns that indicate the kind of deflationary trap that my colleague just spoke about.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’ve talked about them before, but the essence is they are withholding decisions.

speaker: FISHER
text: They’re withholding decisions because they hope to get it done cheaper later.

speaker: FISHER
text: They’re also withholding decisions because they are confused.

speaker: FISHER
text: And you see this in some of the data from those that touch many consumers in the country, as well.

speaker: FISHER
text: For example, according to AT&T, its large enterprise business has just stopped; its small business demand is in decline; its 800 services are down.

speaker: FISHER
text: And, very interestingly, overall minutes are declining significantly.

speaker: FISHER
text: One of the indications of movement of people is roaming minutes.

speaker: FISHER
text: Roaming minutes domestically and internationally, according to the CEO of AT&T, have come to a screeching halt.

speaker: FISHER
text: The picture is similar if you talk to people in the travel and entertainment business, which I do like to look at.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you aggregate it properly, not just airline travel, not just hotels, but sports and entertainment and all that derives from it, it’s a significantly sized industry.

speaker: FISHER
text: According to Disney’s CEO, travel and entertainment is down 46 percent year-over-year in February.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s confirmed by the number of credit card transactions, which are up, but the total amount is down.

speaker: FISHER
text: According to the CEO of JCPenney, whom I’m fortunate to have on my board, this is going to manifest itself in further contraction, with particular risk in the commercial real estate area.

speaker: FISHER
text: The chairman of the retail federation estimates that, of 1,100 major malls in the United States, a third will fail over the course of the next three years.

speaker: FISHER
text: This is not happy news.

speaker: FISHER
text: Part of it has to do with the lack of debtor-in-possession financing.

speaker: FISHER
text: Without DIP financing, you accelerate the process.

speaker: FISHER
text: And I don’t know how we are ever going to deal with that situation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I couldn’t find any silver linings.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is, I suppose, a pewter lining, as I like to call it.

speaker: FISHER
text: And, Governor Tarullo, without any insult to your industry, one of the virtues is that the legal industry is also contracting [laughter]; 6,000 people were laid off from major law firms year to date.

speaker: FISHER
text: There’s a website that actually tracks this.

speaker: FISHER
text: What’s interesting about it is that the transaction business has dried up and is not being compensated for by the bankruptcy business.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think the reason the bankruptcy business is not proceeding is because debtor-in-possession financing is very hard to come by and remains a problem.

speaker: FISHER
text: There’s also another pewter lining in the Wal-Mart reports: Gas price declines have added $120 to $130 per customer per month.

speaker: FISHER
text: The CEO, however, noted some inflation in apparel prices thus far this year, but they believe that is also a head fake, because they can tell from their own inventory that eventually those prices will have to come down.

speaker: FISHER
text: So overall, Mr. Chairman, the situation is bleak.

speaker: FISHER
text: The key underlying weak factor that I hear about from CEO after CEO, from microeconomic operator after microeconomic operator, big or small, is a lack of confidence.

speaker: FISHER
text: When I first walked onto the training floors of Brown Brothers 37 years ago, Robert Roosa gave me a quote that I haven’t forgotten, which came from James Madison: “The circulation of confidence is better than the circulation of money.” There is no confidence.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to come back to a statement I made yesterday, and I’ll withhold my comments on policy until the next round.

speaker: FISHER
text: In order to instill confidence, first, it takes time and, second, you have to exhibit competence.

speaker: FISHER
text: And in order to exhibit competence, I think you have to keep things simple.

speaker: FISHER
text: I came away from yesterday’s session deeply concerned about our conversation about the TALF and the complexity with which we’re engaging in policy.

speaker: FISHER
text: And I hope we can figure out a way to do what we do in the simplest, most communicative manner possible.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m worried that we are turning to the shadow banking system to solve problems that they put us into in the first place.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’ll just conclude with an analogy as a teaser for what I expect to say in the next round, and that’s the following.

speaker: FISHER
text: We have to be very, very careful that we don’t give a steam shovel and a case of Red Bull to the people who dug us into the hole we are in and who have undermined confidence and have put us in a predicament that’s extremely difficult to get out of.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Let me start by congratulating you on having a highway interchange named after you.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’m sure we all envy you having your own off-ramp.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Conditions in the Sixth District remain very weak, and our contacts expect worsening conditions in the near term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Businesses have made significant workforce reductions and tell us they are prepared to make additional cuts if economic conditions worsen.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The end of the first quarter was seen by some as being a key milestone.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: If business conditions have not improved by then, they will move further to put their businesses in survival mode, so more layoffs could be forthcoming in April.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: All sectors of commercial real estate are under pressure from growing vacancy rates and upward adjustment of cap rates.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’m concerned that growing problems in commercial real estate are likely to further complicate efforts to stabilize the banking system and credit markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There’s anecdotal evidence of alarm being expressed about and by the local government sector.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Some jurisdictions and authorities are pinched not only by falling revenues but also by borrowing conditions in the municipal finance market.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One large city mayor estimated several thousand private sector job losses from projects not helped by the stimulus package that will shut down in the near term due to financing difficulties.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Our directors and their contacts, as well as financial market contacts, are becoming increasingly vocal over the lack of specificity regarding economic policy and their inability to understand what we would call our decision rules.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A major source of confusion is uncertainty about what policy actions will come next and under what circumstances expansions of current policy will be decided.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Turning to the national economic conditions in the outlook, the numbers indicate we remain in serious recession, with most data coming in worse than Atlanta’s already downbeat expectations.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: If we were to submit a formal forecast for this meeting, we would adjust our trajectory for the economy downward and push the timing of the beginning of a recovery further out.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As mentioned earlier by Dave Stockton, one positive in the recent data is retail sales numbers.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, the CFO of the country’s second largest retailer advised a cautious interpretation of sales numbers.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Consumer purchases are occurring in an environment of deep price discounts and may not be a very solid indicator of improving economic health.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Also, retailers are consolidating their inventories as they prepare for store closures.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We believe the risks remain to the downside for both economic growth and inflation.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my conversations this time with a few financial market participants and bankers, there was acknowledgement of improved conditions in a number of markets, particularly where the Fed continues to intervene.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Also, progress of investment-grade corporate funding markets was noted.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: At the same time, there was sentiment that the Fed’s credit programs may have to stay in place for quite some time, well into 2010.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On the subject of the housing and home mortgage market, I heard the view that the magic rate threshold for qualifying mortgage applications volume is 5 percent.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: When rates drop below 5 percent, refinancing volume especially has picked up markedly.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: To repeat what I said yesterday, most of the sharpest comments dealt with the perceived policy ambiguity and the effect of this on markets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We are more than a year into this recession, and yet the decline in GDP and deterioration in labor markets continue unabated and, indeed, continue to surprise on the downside.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While I’m hopeful that our actions and the fiscal stimulus package will help to stabilize the economy in the second half of the year, the downside risks to our forecast remain my primary concern.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Like the Greenbook, the Boston Fed forecast expects that the unemployment rate will remain well above full employment, and inflation will remain well below my target throughout the forecast horizon.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Indeed, the Boston Fed forecast implies a high probability of a deflationary period if aggressive action is not taken.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Concerns with credit availability continue to be a dominant theme when I talk to businesses of all sizes.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Lenders are looking for opportunities to tighten terms of lending agreements, and rollover of financing agreements remains problematic.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In anticipation of continuing financing difficulties, firms report that they are restricting operations.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Even organizations that normally would build through a downturn, such as hospitals and major universities, have halted projects, leaving holes and half-finished buildings at many construction sites in Boston.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I see several worrisome near-term concerns that are likely to impede more-normal financial market functioning.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, once we have reworked the initial submissions of the stress tests, the results for several major banks are unlikely to be consistent with public pronouncements by some major banks that additional capital is not necessary.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As our baseline forecast is quickly converging to the stress scenario used in the exercise, there is a real risk of loss of public credibility as it becomes apparent that some large banks will need substantially more capital, which in the current environment can only be supplied by the government.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I am concerned that stock prices and credit markets may suffer additional setbacks and make some of our forecasts for the stock market going forward a little more problematic.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, the delays in removing problem assets will continue to cast a shadow on many asset prices.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We may need to move to simpler, more straightforward solutions for removal of problem assets, possibly in conjunction with the additional equity infusions at the end of the stress tests.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Third, like President Lockhart, I’m very worried about the commercial real estate sector, which is rapidly deteriorating.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Neither the CMBS market nor banks are likely to provide much support for the rollover of commercial real estate financing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: And I’m increasingly concerned about life insurance companies, which have traditionally been significant investors in commercial real estate, as share prices of the major publicly held life insurers are now for the most part selling at less than one-fifth of what they were six months ago, likely resulting in a limited financial capacity to provide commercial real estate financing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In addition, the decline in commercial real estate prices is putting many commercial properties under water, adding to financing constraints.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While we normally do not consider life insurers to be a source of systemic concerns that would have significant impacts on markets, that assumption may be tested over the course of this year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Finally, stabilizing the housing sector is critically important.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While a small component of GDP, the impact of housing problems has been disproportionate to its weight in GDP.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Declines in housing prices continue to limit borrowing capacity for households, cause large losses in household wealth that slow future consumption, and contribute to the significant losses embedded in mortgage instruments and related derivative products for a variety of financial intermediaries.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While recently announced federal programs should help, those programs may not fully reflect the new reality that job losses are likely to be the primary reason that borrowers cannot make payments.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We held a mortgage foreclosure event in Hartford, Connecticut last month, attended by roughly 900 borrowers.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Discussions with the borrowers at the event, and subsequent survey results, indicate that job losses among one or more family members were already a key driver in pushing borrowers to foreclosure.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Taking aggressive action to stabilize housing and employment may be particularly important at this juncture.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Mr. Chairman, I would say that the Tenth District is going to reflect very much what you have heard in the national briefing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It was doing better than the nation as a whole but is now quickly deteriorating into the national average.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our labor markets have continued to deteriorate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Unemployment rates are going up in each of our states.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our manufacturing activity has actually plummeted, importantly because of the weakening of the export market that was mentioned earlier.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our agricultural sector is still holding its own, but it, too, is showing signs of weakening, as is our energy industry.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Commercial real estate is showing signs of weakening because of some of the refinancing that’s now required and because of the increasing vacancies that are affecting the cash flows off these and, therefore, affecting some of the parties holding these notes.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would point out, too, that financing in the region has deteriorated, I’d say “badly” almost, and I’ll give you one anecdote.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I understand that it’s not hard data, but it gives you a sense of the situation.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We have an insurance company that does premium financing, about $1 billion financed out of a major New York bank.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It went back to refinance a portion of the loan, and the bank wanted LIBOR plus 500.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The CEO of this company said, “You know, I understand I have to help recapitalize that industry, but this is taking all my profit.” So it is trying to get other types of financing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: And that kind of pressure is, of course, trickling down and affects how they do business as well.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So it is a pretty daunting task for businesses in this type of environment, I realize.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Finally, when we look across the District, we’re seeing increasing numbers of problem banks, as well as banks that we would put on a watch list because of the concentrations in, say, real estate or some sectors of agriculture.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So, overall, the District is reflecting the deteriorating conditions in the nation as a whole, and, that is, of course, a concern to us as well as to everyone else here.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Third District economy remains very weak, and there are few signs that this weakness will lessen any time soon.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The three-state region hit its employment peak in January 2008.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Since then, it has lost 1.8 percent of its jobs, and 60 percent of that loss has come just in the last three months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You might step back and say, “Well, maybe this is the darkness before the dawn.” I wish I had confidence in that, but I’m not sure that’s what’s going on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our Business Outlook Survey is set to be released at 10:00 tomorrow morning, so it’s confidential until then.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Last month’s reading was near a record of minus 41.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The reading that will be reported tomorrow morning is minus 35, so it’s some improvement.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We usually take about five points as being statistically significant, so this is just at that margin.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A few months ago, the index went up and just fell back down again.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I don’t know that there’s a whole lot of comfort in the most recent number; I take it to mean things are about the same as they were.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Survey participants do expect the outlook to improve in the next six months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But many of the forward-looking indicators suggest that before that comes about there will be further cutbacks in employment and further retrenchment in capital investment at our regional manufacturers.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although banks in the Third District are in somewhat better shape than the national average—they tend to be doing pretty well—they do report consumer loan volume is down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And many of them also report that companies don’t want to invest and don’t want to borrow money at this point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So it’s demand retrenchment rather than just supply retrenchment, from their perspective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Bankers in general in our District are angry—they’re mad, they’re furious at the government.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m getting requests to give TARP money back at an increasing pace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They’re not being allowed to do it, or nobody at the Treasury is helping them do that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They are, as President Lockhart said, frustrated with the lack of clarity about where policy is going and what it’s going to be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They’re angry about the changes in the rules of the game, the ground shifting beneath their feet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And they’re frustrated that some of the programs aren’t doing what they’re supposed to be doing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have one major player in the student loan industry saying that the TALF is not going to do anything for student loans, which, by and large, are 7- to 10-year loans in view of the time it takes to get through college.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So buying new issues of three-year loans won’t help them, because they don’t offer many student loans for three years.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I can go down the list of many other industries who feel the same way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Whom are we going to bail out, whom are we going to protect, and whom are we going to support going forward?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think there’s a lot of angst, a lot of uncertainty, and a lot of frustration out there in the business community and the financial community in particular.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So our District economy’s outlook looks largely in line with that of the national economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As President Bullard suggested, one of the things that has been most worrying in the recent episode is the dramatic decline in foreign countries and the impact that’s having.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That’s something we can’t do much about directly, but it is worrying, and, again, it’s causing more angst and more fear and more problems.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, amidst this downpour of bad news and numbers, there is a possible ray of sunshine.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I note—as Dave Stockton did—that the consumption numbers seem to suggest that the free fall in consumption may have come to an end.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I hope that’s the case; that would be encouraging.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Both retail sales and disposable income numbers have held up in the last couple of months, and personal consumption expenditures have as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The last two months of consumer price inflation data suggest to me that the risk of a sustained deflation, at least in the near term, is somewhat abated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I’m not as concerned as some are—President Bullard, for example—about the shift to sustained deflationary expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although I think we have to worry about it, that’s not my number one concern at this point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Overall, my outlook for the national economy is pessimistic for the near term, although I continue to have a lot of belief that markets eventually will recover, so I may be a little more optimistic on a recovery than the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The economic and financial news has been grim.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Things are now so bad that I actually open the Greenbook with greater trepidation than my 401(k).

speaker: YELLEN
text: The awful employment and spending data have not been much of a surprise, but they do dispel remaining hopes that we might see a turnaround any time soon.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This conclusion is reinforced by what I’m hearing from my business contacts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Their already sour mood is taking another sharp turn for the worse.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One director reported that businesses were so shaken that it would take a sustained period of positive data, on the order of six to nine months, before they would begin to consider expanding production and employment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Another disturbing sign of how tough things are getting is that people appear to be breaking into their piggybanks to make ends meet—the Cash Product Office reports huge increases in the amount of coins being brought into our inventory.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The December inventories of quarters and dollar coins were up more than 50 percent from 2007, and even pennies were up nearly 25 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Looking ahead, some more-optimistic forecasters have argued that we’re likely to see a rapid V-shaped recovery similar to the ones that followed several past severe postwar recessions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The case for such an outcome is that housing construction and purchases of durable goods, especially cars, have been running way below trend for some time.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Over time, these capital stocks will fall well below desired levels, and eventually investment must rise to bring stocks back in line with fundamentals.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The resulting pent-up demand may lead to a surge in spending once the financial system regains its health and uncertainty is diminished.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But my fear is that we may not even get a modest U-shaped recovery, much less a V- shaped one.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have three reasons for this pessimism.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, the global nature of the recession means we can’t rely on foreign demand to provide support for our economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Instead, a sharp downturn abroad and recent dollar appreciation have driven down our exports and exacerbated our downturn.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, given the high degree of synchronization among all of the major economies of the world, this is the first truly global recession since the Depression.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Furthermore, as the downturn has spread to more countries, new cracks have developed in the already strained banking system.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Steve discussed the situation in Eastern Europe, and we share his concerns.

speaker: YELLEN
text: These countries have an estimated $1½ trillion of debt to Western European banks, and it’s fortunate that U.S. banks have little exposure in this region.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But loans from Austrian banks to Eastern Europe exceed 80 percent of Austria’s GDP, and the exposure of banks in Sweden and Belgium exceeds 30 percent of GDP.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Severe losses on these loans do pose significant threats to the banking systems in these countries.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My second concern is that, despite our best efforts at using both traditional and nontraditional monetary tools, the stance of credit market conditions has only improved modestly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In past recessions, the Fed has been able to fuel a turnaround rapidly by stepping on the accelerator through sharp rate cuts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But in the current crisis, it feels more like we are desperately trying to power a bicycle uphill rather than pressing an accelerator on a high- powered sports car.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This conclusion is supported by work by my staff that aims to gauge the stance of credit market conditions.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In particular, we use principal components analysis on a set of private sector interest rates to construct a metric of credit conditions that in normal times moves very closely with the real federal funds rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: According to this metric, we were basically treading water during much of the last year, with our policy actions roughly neutralizing the effects of the credit crisis on private rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Since September and the introduction of more aggressive policy actions by the Fed, the FDIC, and the Treasury, this metric of credit market conditions has improved somewhat and is now at a level consistent with a modest degree of accommodation, but nowhere near as much accommodation as implied by the level of the real fed funds rate or called for by the stance of the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: And, of course, this analysis abstracts from non-price terms of credit, and those continue to tighten as well.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We see that in the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey.

speaker: YELLEN
text: And one community banker on my board mentioned that he finds it now difficult to summon the emotional energy to make loans to anybody at all.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A third reason to doubt that we will enjoy a V-shaped recovery is the huge damage that has been done to balance sheets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Household wealth has plummeted: It fell more than $5 trillion in the fourth quarter alone.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Unfortunately, households were not well positioned for such a shot to wealth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Instead, many had leveraged up to the hilt, and the combination of the dramatic loss in wealth and the massive household debt overhang portends years of subdued spending as households go through an extended period of deleveraging.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I see worrisome parallels to the Japanese corporate sector during the 1990s.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In that case, the attempt of firms to pay down debt produced a decade of weak investment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The downward pressure on household leverage will come both from lenders and from households.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Lenders are likely to demand more collateral for loans going forward, and that collateral has been devastated by the collapse of housing and other wealth; and households are likely to recognize the benefits of stronger balance sheets for precautionary reasons and meeting longer-term goals, such as down-payment requirements and retirement.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As one of my directors quipped, people may come to realize that they don’t need three cars—they can get by with two and maybe even just one.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The outlook for inflation is worrisome as well.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it’s fair to say it is no longer a risk that inflation will persist for a time below the preferred rate—instead, it’s our expectation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: What’s more, the probability of outright deflation is significant.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In that regard, I’m closely monitoring wage developments, as I view the outbreak of sizable wage cuts to be a crucial step leading to sustained deflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have heard scattered reports of such cuts, but so far the majority of my directors say they’re reluctant to cut wages for fear that it would undermine employee morale.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Nonetheless, many of them cautioned that if the economy continues to deteriorate, they will have no choice but to cut wages and salaries.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So, to summarize, I don’t see forces at work that will propel our economy into sustained robust recovery any time soon.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even though the Greenbook forecast is hardly upbeat, I see substantial downside risk to that forecast, both for economic activity and inflation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The reports from my contacts have been very weak for months now.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In order to get a better sense of the outlook, I asked some of my contacts some questions focused on whether their responses thus far to the recession have been enough to prepare them for the weakness that they are anticipating in their markets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Unfortunately, the vast majority of them said that they had not done enough and that they continue to curtail their activities and investments at a very quick pace.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: And their confidence in a recovery later on this year is dwindling.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am concerned that this lack of confidence is translating into actions that will further dampen our prospects in coming months.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I was surprised that even some of the more successful manufacturers in my District, such as Eaton, Lincoln Electric, and Parker-Hannifin, are all implementing further cutbacks in investments, hiring, and production plans.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In several cases, these further cutbacks have been motivated by this deepening retrenchment that we are seeing with our foreign partners.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But some of my contacts are losing confidence in the policy responses to the recession.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Several of my directors noted last week at our meeting that public confidence is obviously critical to our recovery plans, yet the public is increasingly finding the government’s response confusing and incomplete.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This lack of confidence is weighing on their expectations for growth this year and even next year.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Now, my directors are certainly supportive of the actions that the Federal Reserve has taken, particularly the stress-testing that we are doing of banks and the long-term asset purchases.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, they are concerned that the communications about some of the other government programs—some of the Treasury plans—have been unclear, and, therefore, are hampering the recovery.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Mr. Chairman, I think that your interview on 60 Minutes played a helpful role in clarifying some of these programs, and I did receive many calls from directors and business contacts saying that they thought the interview was well received.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Like the staff, I revised down my projection for output and inflation based on the incoming data, and, obviously, the weakening global outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My projection is very much in line with the Greenbook baseline, although in my projection the unemployment rate peaks at 10 percent, because I don’t anticipate as much of a cutback in the participation rate as the Greenbook does.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Also, I do think that the outlook calls for a larger policy response.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In my baseline, I’ve incorporated the simulations on additional nontraditional policies.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I know the Greenbook hasn’t, because they are obviously difficult to include in a numeric projection.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But at this point, I have included some of that policy response in my outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In my view, the risks remain very much weighted to the downside for both output and inflation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given the repeated markdowns that we’ve made to our projections, I think more downside misses are likely to make it more difficult to restore confidence that we are dealing with the economic crisis appropriately.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At this point, neither the projections nor any of the anecdotal reports that I have received are likely to make a difference in or shift our policy response.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We are in the midst of an economic decline that doesn’t have concrete signs of a developing recovery.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I think we need to react to the current crisis thoroughly, but also with as much as clarity as possible.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I know we’ve talked a lot about the focus on our communications of what we are doing.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I do think that is critical at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: I fully agree we are certainly in the midst of a significant contraction.

speaker: STERN
text: Back in January when I submitted my forecast for the first half of the year, I had the economy declining at an annual rate of 4 percent, which is now quite close to the Greenbook number.

speaker: STERN
text: The question I’ve been asking myself is: Should I mark the forecast down further and push the recovery off further?

speaker: STERN
text: So far, I’m not fully convinced that that’s the right response, in part because, as Dave Stockton noted, the basic case for recovery is the same as it has been—stimulative monetary and fiscal policy, gradual further improvement in financial market conditions, and the internal dynamics associated with the corrections that occur during a recession; that is, production and employment decline, an inventory correction process occurs, ultimately aggregate supply falls below even diminished aggregate demand, and then you have set the stage for the expansion.

speaker: STERN
text: Moreover, as a veteran of many, many forecasting exercises, I’ve seen some of this phenomenon before.

speaker: STERN
text: There’s a tendency in the midst of a serious recession, especially if you’re doing bottom-up forecasting and going through the various components of aggregate demand— consumer spending on durables, nondurables, services—to take a look at each component and say to yourself, “Well, that can’t get better any time soon.” And by the time you’ve gone through that, you’ve eliminated all possibilities of any component getting better any time soon.

speaker: STERN
text: So you wind up with a forecast with a very extended recession.

speaker: STERN
text: Finally, there’s only one other point I’d make.

speaker: STERN
text: It’s not meant to provide a lot of comfort but just to suggest that it wouldn’t take all that much for the recovery to get under way in the third quarter, albeit initially quite sluggishly.

speaker: STERN
text: I just did an arithmetic exercise—that’s all it is— and if consumer spending in the aggregate grew at 1½ to 2 percent rate in the third and fourth quarters, that would turn those negative GDP numbers in the Greenbook into slightly positive GDP numbers.

speaker: STERN
text: The only reason I make that point is that it wouldn’t take all that much.

speaker: STERN
text: Consumer spending has shown some signs of leveling off, so it may be that there’s some silver lining there.

speaker: LACKER
text: The clear deterioration in the real economic outlook since our last meeting is consistent with the information we had from the Fifth District.

speaker: LACKER
text: All our survey indexes remained at very low levels.

speaker: LACKER
text: The forward-looking components of most weakened as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Carolinas have been particularly hard-hit in recent months.

speaker: LACKER
text: Their economy is manufacturing-intensive and export-oriented, more so than the rest of the country, and their housing markets, which had lagged the national cycle, have weakened substantially in the last year.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was pleasantly surprised by the retail sales numbers and the Greenbook’s improved outlook for consumption expenditures, which suggest that diminishing marginal returns to cutbacks in discretionary spending may be setting in.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m a little wary about making too much of it.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the weak labor market is going to weaken further, and the possibility of further declines in wealth could easily drive household spending down another step.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d note though that in more normal times a significant deterioration in the forecast from one Greenbook to the next would bring with it a revision in the assumed policy path for the fed funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now that we’re at zero, I’d expect a commensurate revision in the path for our balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I’m reading the Greenbook correctly, the staff hasn’t made any change to their baseline policy assumptions, and I would have thought the Greenbook would have built in more expansion of credit programs or the monetary base or both.

speaker: LACKER
text: In this context, it’s striking that, as I mentioned yesterday, the monetary base has declined by $200 billion since the beginning of the year.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m looking at daily averages over the first two weeks of January versus the period ending, I think, March 11.

speaker: LACKER
text: I understand some big MBS transactions settled on March 12, so there’s a tiny little spike in the figures.

speaker: LACKER
text: But, still, that was striking.

speaker: LACKER
text: The base obviously remains at a very high level, consistent with our statements, but I wonder if that $200 billion decline means that we tightened policy since the beginning of the year.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think we know one way or the other, but I’d think we would want to make sure we increase the base whenever the outlook deteriorates significantly.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is why I think it would be useful for us to begin outright purchases of Treasuries, and moreover, I’d like to suggest that we explicitly direct the Desk to make sure that the monetary base expands by a significant amount during the policy period—maybe even put the number into the directive for the intermeeting period.

speaker: EVANS
text: The executive summary for my business reports this round is: Things have never been so bad.

speaker: EVANS
text: This view is essentially unchanged from January; they weren’t happy then either.

speaker: EVANS
text: These reports seem to represent a continuation of the severe contraction rather than additional negative impulses.

speaker: EVANS
text: But that’s not especially comforting, as this is shaping up to be the worst economic downturn since the 1930s.

speaker: EVANS
text: But President Stern’s comments did make me feel better about the outlook, so I certainly hope I’m wrong there.

speaker: EVANS
text: The Greenbook’s presentation of an unconstrained optimal monetary policy response was striking in my opinion.

speaker: EVANS
text: The size of the policy gap is so large that quibbling over differences in model specifications and the like seems beside the point.

speaker: EVANS
text: I was contemplating asking Dave Stockton what it would take to generate inflation—maybe if potential output was less favorable than we think, that’s how it would happen.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I couldn’t imagine that the answer would change my opinion because they had one scenario that went some ways towards that already.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think this gap is representative of the tremendous amount of economic slack that we are facing.

speaker: EVANS
text: If adequate policy actions are not forthcoming or are not feasible, then larger and longer-lasting economic costs may be looming.

speaker: EVANS
text: Many of my contacts noted that if the economy did not find a bottom soon, they would be in for another round of major reductions in productive capacity.

speaker: EVANS
text: They specifically noted the likelihood of cuts in core labor forces and capital infrastructures.

speaker: EVANS
text: These adjustments would be very costly to undo when the economy eventually recovers.

speaker: EVANS
text: The commentary I heard on financial market difficulties suggests that our credit policies are now fighting against even greater headwinds than before, but it’s unclear how we might counteract this additional deterioration directly.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition to continuing concerns about credit supply, more contacts are noting that the severe contraction is causing the credit quality of borrowers to deteriorate.

speaker: EVANS
text: Ford said that when they’re making auto loans, the banks seemed to be getting the better-credit-quality buyers at the moment, but they said that their rejections on retail financing were 50 percent now, which is up 10 percentage points.

speaker: EVANS
text: Federal Reserve, Treasury, and FDIC programs have eased credit supply conditions somewhat and hopefully will lead to more improvement, but the reduced creditworthiness looms as a potentially even larger problem than restrictive credit supply.

speaker: EVANS
text: In terms of the likely effectiveness of the TALF, I heard a number of different perspectives from my contacts.

speaker: EVANS
text: Discover Financial said the current TALF spreads were too wide to be attractive.

speaker: EVANS
text: Nonetheless, they thought the TALF would be a useful backstop.

speaker: EVANS
text: They also said they would consider using it, especially if investors became willing to accept somewhat smaller rates of return, that is, low double-digit returns.

speaker: EVANS
text: Investors in the middle of this transaction seem to be doing very well without really accepting a lot of risk—I’m not sure they’re bringing a lot to the table, frankly.

speaker: EVANS
text: Ford was expecting to place several billion dollars of securities backed by consumer auto loans with TALF borrowers.

speaker: EVANS
text: They thought this would be quite helpful, but on the other hand, both Ford and GM indicated that they would like to use the TALF to finance dealer inventories.

speaker: EVANS
text: However, the high cost for credit enhancements to secure a triple-A rating would make it uneconomical for them to do so.

speaker: EVANS
text: As a central bank, our credit policies are necessarily conservative.

speaker: EVANS
text: They are aimed primarily at improving credit supply conditions by lending on prudent terms.

speaker: EVANS
text: But what makes the terms prudent to us results in many issuers seeing the TALF as being too restrictive and on unattractive terms.

speaker: EVANS
text: I said to one CEO who was complaining of this that, if we were a private financial company with this pricing policy, we wouldn’t last a week.

speaker: EVANS
text: Indeed, those firms with access to the TLGP were unanimous in preferring that source of funding to the TALF.

speaker: EVANS
text: Several of these also advocated expanding the borrowing capacity under the TLGP, and firms without access to the TLGP were lobbying to get in.

speaker: EVANS
text: Such are the benefits and distortions of our public programs.

speaker: EVANS
text: So my reading is that the prudent terms for the TALF make it less attractive and suggest its take-up rate and effectiveness may be limited.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m not advocating changes necessarily—I’m just reporting that its macroeconomic effectiveness may be smaller than the economy needs.

speaker: EVANS
text: Framing the monetary policy discussion with a viewpoint on the national economic outlook is fairly simple this time.

speaker: EVANS
text: Although I could cite some differences between my forecast and the Greenbook’s projections, these differences do not change three material observations.

speaker: EVANS
text: First, enormous resource gaps through 2010 for sure will continue to require aggressive monetary accommodation with nonstandard tools.

speaker: EVANS
text: Second, for the foreseeable future, disinflationary forces seem strong enough that aggressive monetary policy accommodation would not impose undue risk to our price stability goal.

speaker: EVANS
text: Third, to offset these disinflationary forces, a sharp rise in inflation expectations would be necessary.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think it would have to be exogenous.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s not in my forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: The circumstances by which this would occur are hard to predict, although commentators point to risks from the expansion of our balance sheet and future fiscal deficits.

speaker: EVANS
text: I do not expect these will have a quantitatively important impact on inflation expectations over the next couple of years.

speaker: EVANS
text: Finally, the Greenbook’s baseline is so dismal that, with the unemployment rate headed to 9½ percent and a substantial disinflation in train, even the most optimistic alternative scenarios do not see an increase in the fed funds rate before 2013.

speaker: EVANS
text: None of us are accustomed to thinking that a prolonged period of zero short-term interest rates will be associated with a lack of inflationary pressures.

speaker: EVANS
text: For virtually all of our contemporary monetary memories, inflation has been above desirable levels in the U.S.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is an enormous challenge to our thinking and to our typical approaches to monetary policy strategy.

speaker: EVANS
text: Indeed, the FRB/US calculations where inflation did overshoot were premised on the idea that these Taylor shocks would lead to an increase in inflationary expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: That is, that they are very accommodative.

speaker: EVANS
text: But we don’t see that in our analysis at the moment.

speaker: EVANS
text: I began to think about the policymaker who equally weights his or her displeasure on either NAIRU or output and inflation gaps, which are the underpinnings for the optimal policy in the Bluebook.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’re looking at an output gap in the Greenbook of 8 percentage points, so with equally weighted displeasure, you ought to be willing to accept inflation that is somewhat higher than your target.

speaker: EVANS
text: Given these large expected output gaps, even a borderline inflation nutter would be willing to accept a substantial risk of overshooting in the inflation target.

speaker: EVANS
text: So the bottom line, in my opinion, is that a well-designed program of substantial nontraditional monetary accommodation, in concert with clearly specified dual mandate goals and reasonable safeguards, will keep long-term inflation expectations anchored.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In general, I think the Greenbook baseline forecast is pretty sensible.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The New York Fed view is not much different, but, echoing President Stern’s comments, I can also tell a credible story of why the rate of economic contraction first slows, then the economy reverses direction as we move into the second half of 2009: The inventory cycle turns from negative to positive, the decline in housing activity ends, mainly because there’s no room to fall further, and fiscal stimulus provides support to consumer spending and cushions the downward adjustment in state and local government outlays.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Unfortunately that doesn’t tell us much about 2010 and beyond.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In my view, the longer-term outlook rests on the answers to two key questions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, what is the desired household saving rate?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Where is it headed, and how rapidly will we get there?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Or to put it somewhat differently, echoing President Yellen, where is the household sector in its deleveraging process?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And, second, will the financial system stabilize and credit availability steadily improve over the next couple of quarters?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, these two interact.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If we don’t get an improvement in credit availability, asset prices will go down further, and that will feed back into the household saving rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The fourth-quarter flow of funds data were, I think, as expected.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They’re going to show this 9 percent drop in household net worth, which brings the ratio of household net worth to income back to levels not seen since the mid-1990s.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That would seem to imply that the household saving rate, which is currently around 5 percent, will likely need to rise even further.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And the question is: To what level?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There has to be quite a bit of uncertainty about that both in terms of where we are going and how fast we are going to get there.

speaker: DUDLEY
