text: One possible benchmark would be the household saving rate of the early 1990s, which was slightly below 8 percent.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If that’s where we’re headed, I’d say that’s probably doable while still having an economic recovery, although it is considerably higher than the Greenbook forecast of 5¼ percent this year and next.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: An 8 percent rate does not seem too high a bar, given that we have a lot of fiscal stimulus coming.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The fact that most of the stimulus will be saved does not mean that the stimulus has been ineffective, since the counterfactual in this case might be that the households would have had to reduce their spending in order to achieve their new desired level of savings.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: However, one could argue that there’s a risk that an 8 percent household saving rate may be too low.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Demographics may imply the need for a higher saving rate now, given that the working-age population is much older now than it was in the 1990s; in other words, if we adjust for the age mix of the population today, an 8 percent figure back then might map into a 9 percent or 10 percent figure today.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If that’s the case, obviously the task is a bit more daunting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But the bottom line is, we simply do not know how older households are going to react to the wealth losses that they’ve experienced in terms of how much they’re going to raise their saving rate, whether they’re going to delay their retirement, whether they’ll have the opportunity to delay their retirement and keep their jobs, and whether they’ll accept lower standards of living in retirement.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s just a huge open question.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Some commentators have set the bar much higher.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: They argue that the ratio of household debt to income needs to fall back to levels of the mid-1980s.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That’s a very high bar, implying the ratio would have to decline by more than half.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It would suggest that the deleveraging process of households has only just begun and that we have many, many years of deleveraging ahead of us.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that’s a bit too pessimistic a view for several reasons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Over time, the cost of financial intermediation has fallen; that implies to me a higher debt-to-income ratio and a higher asset-to­ income ratio, as well.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, some of the changes in tax policy do encourage you to hold more assets and more liabilities; for example, earlier, you might have paid off your mortgage, and now you refinance your mortgage and instead fund your 401(k) plan.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In that case your assets and liabilities are both higher now relative to your income, but you are not worse off.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I expect we’ll see some further decline in the household debt-to-income ratio, but because I think the longer- term secular trend has been upward, I don’t think we’re going to need to see decades-long household deleveraging.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At least I hope not.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Of course, the difficulty in deleveraging will depend on the inflation outlook.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If we do fall into a debt–deflation dynamic, then, as income drops, real debt burdens will increase, and it will become even more difficult for households to deleverage even if they want to.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So that just underscores why we need to do everything we can to minimize the risk of a deflation outcome.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second key issue is, of course, the stability of the financial system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Without this, I don’t think we can have a sustainable recovery.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Yes, the economy could improve a little bit during the second half of 2009, but if we don’t fix the financial system and its ability to intermediate between savers and borrowers, I suspect 2010 will be very disappointing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is why the downside risks to the forecast still are predominant in our views at the New York Fed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The FOMC and the Board should concentrate on taking whatever steps are needed to improve market functioning and the viability of the large banks, which lie at the core of the financial system.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This implies expansion of our liquidity programs, such as the TALF, and, at minimum, increased purchases of agency mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It also implies support for the Treasury’s CAP, which is designed to get additional capital into the banking system, as well as a willingness to extend our suite of 13(3) activities and our foreign exchange swap programs.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with the general sentiments around the table.

speaker: KOHN
text: The economy is falling further and faster than we thought it would.

speaker: KOHN
text: We see some signs of stability, as President Plosser pointed out, in consumption and even in housing, but these are very tentative and at a very low level; I think even if household spending were to level out and get a little boost from fiscal policy in coming quarters, the economy would continue to fall further, at least for a little while.

speaker: KOHN
text: Business investment is very weak and will continue to decline in response to previous downshifts in sales through the multiplier-accelerator effects and in response to tight credit and very constrained credit availability.

speaker: KOHN
text: I was surprised in looking at the investment chart in Greenbook Part 2 to see that the cost of credit has actually risen substantially for businesses at a time when that’s obviously counterproductive.

speaker: KOHN
text: Global demand shows no signs of stabilizing and will continue to depress exports, as Steve was telling us, especially in light of the stronger dollar, which just adds further downward pressure there.

speaker: KOHN
text: To me, perhaps the most troubling developments have been in the financial sector.

speaker: KOHN
text: Maybe that’s because I’m spending my days and nights worrying about them.

speaker: KOHN
text: There has been a tightening of financial conditions over the intermeeting period, even as the economy has weakened: The dollar has increased, equity markets have fallen, and interest rates, including the risk-free rate, have risen in recent weeks.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think there’s a growing lack of confidence in financial institutions.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is not just a U.S. phenomenon, it’s a global phenomenal; Trish’s chart showed increases in CDS spreads everywhere—Europe, U.K., U.S., Asia—everywhere.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the recession is spreading more and more into the loan books of these banks globally, and that’s undermining confidence, despite government efforts everywhere to try to shore up confidence.

speaker: KOHN
text: We used to talk about resilience in the economy—that was part of President Stern’s discussion of why economies bounce back—but I think part of the natural equilibrating mechanisms involves expectations that things will get better, that is, people spend based on that expectation.

speaker: KOHN
text: As President Bullard pointed out, expectations about the future are very depressed, and I agree.

speaker: KOHN
text: Uncertainty is extremely high, and people don’t know what to expect, so they’re not taking risks, and that’s impeding the bounce-back in the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: Government’s responses to the difficulties are certainly contributing to this uncertainty.

speaker: KOHN
text: Again, this is not a U.S. phenomenon.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think governments everywhere are having trouble finding their footing about what to do here.

speaker: KOHN
text: These are very difficult issues without obviously correct answers and responses, and, therefore, you see changes in approaches in various jurisdictions, not just in the U.S.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we’ve got a difficult witch’s brew here.

speaker: KOHN
text: There’s populist anger constraining policy options.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need the smartest people in the country in our troubled financial institutions and in our government working on solutions, and we’re driving them away from both of those institutions every day.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the set of circumstances implies that improvement in the financial sector is likely to be quite slow and halting, at a minimum.

speaker: KOHN
text: Lenders and investors are becoming more wary and less confident.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’ve got the risk of a further major deterioration in the financial sector, where the failure of several large institutions is a nontrivial risk and could be brought on by government policies.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the projection of stabilization of demand in the second half and recovery next year is reasonable as fiscal policy kicks in and assuming financial stability, but the downside economic and financial risks are very, very large.

speaker: KOHN
text: And even if the economy stabilizes in the second half of the year, we’re starting at a much lower level, with a very high output gap.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I agree with others who have pointed to the risk of deflation and the interaction of that risk with the high levels of debt in the household sector as a very grave danger going forward.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me discuss four points: first, the economy in the near term with an emphasis on non-U.S.; second, medium-term implications of all these policy responses for the trend growth in productivity; third, financial markets; and fourth, briefly, financial institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the economy, the real economy is deteriorating globally, as everyone has said.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the hard question is whether the pace of deterioration is slowing, and I suspect the answer is, “no, it’s not.” National capitals, including our own, do not seem to be capable in times like this, for many of the reasons Don has described, of slowing that deterioration.

speaker: WARSH
text: If anything, some actions seem to be giving rise to more uncertainty and greater weakness.

speaker: WARSH
text: Dave Stockton talked in detail about the data on spending and production, which continue to be poor, revealing the weakness in our economy and labor markets to be broad and deep.

speaker: WARSH
text: In the rest of the world, the deterioration, as has been discussed, is probably broader, probably deeper, and, more troubling still, probably even less likely to receive effective responses.

speaker: WARSH
text: The second-derivative question there is clear.

speaker: WARSH
text: If anything, the problems overseas are accelerating.

speaker: WARSH
text: The total collapse in global trade is well understood at this point.

speaker: WARSH
text: The hard piece for me to get my arms around is: What are the second- and third-order effects of this weakness in global markets, in global economies, and what could lead in the near term to significant political, policy, and balance-of-power challenges around the world?

speaker: WARSH
text: Are we entering a period of instability that makes the rest of the world’s economies even more vulnerable than they have been in recent years to exogenous shocks?

speaker: WARSH
text: And I don’t think it takes an incredible imagination to think about what those could be.

speaker: WARSH
text: The unwinding of fiscal imbalances is happening fast, but the deterioration across our economies is happening even faster.

speaker: WARSH
text: The delta, I suspect, is a breakdown in confidence and the risk of policy failures which are exacerbating the situation.

speaker: WARSH
text: Perhaps it’s true that the current account surplus countries are at greater risk than the deficit countries.

speaker: WARSH
text: The G-20 meetings of this last weekend were, I would say, different in a couple respects from prior international meetings.

speaker: WARSH
text: For example, six months ago there continued to be a sort of schadenfreude about the U.S., some sense that people think the U.S. is getting what it deserves.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is nowhere in the room at this point.

speaker: WARSH
text: There is a worldwide need for U.S. leadership, a need for the U.S. economy to recover with great strength, and a rooting for the U.S.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think most of the other G-20 members were of the view that if the U.S. does not get this thing turned around, they are going to be in a very dire situation, even more dire than under current prospects.

speaker: WARSH
text: In addition, I thought that the most interesting topic was what was discussed only in the most hushed tones at these meetings, and that was Eastern Europe.

speaker: WARSH
text: It was still not allowed to be discussed broadly because I think the fears were so, so significant.

speaker: WARSH
text: Almost every other issue was put squarely on the table for a broad discussion, but the banking problems in Eastern Europe were hidden from public view, and that was more troubling than I had thought even before I went into the meeting.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, in terms of the medium-term economy here in the U.S., I thought that the adverse supply condition scenario in the Greenbook was quite indicative of more damaging risks.

speaker: WARSH
text: The misallocation of labor and capital across the economy merits some responsibility for this recession, and getting that allocation back to equilibrium is what recessions are all about.

speaker: WARSH
text: It’s not obvious that is happening, at least at this point.

speaker: WARSH
text: Capital is not finding its way to anything close to its most efficient uses.

speaker: WARSH
text: Labor markets are not able to dynamically adjust.

speaker: WARSH
text: And these problems are likely to be particularly pervasive as the path to a new architecture for credit intermediation remains unclear.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think over time the real risk is that we are going to end up with less trend productivity, less growth, and a higher NAIRU.

speaker: WARSH
text: Policy actions seem unconducive to restoration of the growth rates that we have come to expect in recent years.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, let me talk about financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think financial market functioning is as poor as Governor Kohn described.

speaker: WARSH
text: Policy uncertainty has become the watchword, not just for the real economy, but for financial markets; and I suspect that when we look at CDS spreads for large financial institutions, notwithstanding the commitments that this institution and the Treasury have given, what markets have come to determine is that the Congress will be calling the shots, and that is a problem.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think markets are very uncertain, when there are 435 leaders in one body and 100 in another, about exactly what might come out of that, and the idea that there might be one party in control of government does not seem to be enough to drive leadership in a single direction.

speaker: WARSH
text: Thus, I’m not taking too much signal from the improvement in markets in recent days.

speaker: WARSH
text: Backlogs around financings are perhaps better than they were a week or two ago, and, in fact, a large pharmaceutical company last night priced a range of debt securities at impressive spreads.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m really suspicious about whether a deal like that will be able to be done in the next couple of weeks, and so I think the backlogs are a big question.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn then finally to financial institutions as they relate to financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: I concur wholeheartedly with what President Rosengren said earlier.

speaker: WARSH
text: I worry very much that the policy response that’s going to come from Washington in the next several days and weeks will not be well received, will require another pivot, and there might well be litigation around that.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that is very, very damaging.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we are entering a period in the next couple of weeks that could well determine the strength in the economy in the next couple of quarters, and I think, as Governor Kohn said, expectations in the real economy are confused because government actions in the name of boldness seem to be quite ambiguous.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is a very, very difficult combination.

speaker: DUKE
text: I’m going to talk again about the banks, and as a reminder, these are the traditional commercial banks, and it’s a variety of them just below the top four across the country in varying conditions and of different sizes.

speaker: DUKE
text: Of that group, four are subject to the stress test, and in talking to them this time, I’d note that I’ve never, ever talked to bankers where the conversation was so much about government and so little about the banking business, particularly given what they’re facing right now.

speaker: DUKE
text: With the four banks that are subject to the stress test, I first asked them what the process was, and I got three different answers—so they didn’t even quite understand what it was they were being asked to do.

speaker: DUKE
text: Two of them were convinced that it’s a Trojan horse for nationalization.

speaker: DUKE
text: Several of them questioned whether this test is even going to have credibility in the marketplace once it gets done, thinking it’s possible that those who are shown to be weak will simply have confirmed suspicions, but those who are shown to be strong will not get any boost in confidence from that.

speaker: DUKE
text: Also, there’s a concern that they’ll be at a standstill for the six months that have been given in order to raise private capital, because, even if they pass—even if they’re not to get any government capital—if they go out to get private capital, then it looks like they are doing that only to avoid getting the public capital, so basically they cannot go to the capital market.

speaker: DUKE
text: Private capital is absolutely unwilling to come in until their status is assured and is not willing at this point to be a minority partner with the United States government.

speaker: DUKE
text: We’ve talked a lot about confidence, and one issue is that we have no confidence in our banks ourselves as a government, so it’s very hard to engender public confidence in those banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: Politics and bonuses, particularly with respect to the original TARP I capital: That capital now feels completely stigmatized.

speaker: DUKE
text: Banks thought it would be a sign of strength.

speaker: DUKE
text: The public perception is that they’ve been bailed out.

speaker: DUKE
text: The nondeductible dividend, the political strings attached, and the unknown future combine to make many of them, as President Plosser said, want to give it back.

speaker: DUKE
text: Given the events of this week, I think AIG first nearly took out the financial system and now may make it impossible for us to do any form of financial rescue.

speaker: DUKE
text: There was a letter from the Special Inspector General for TARP that went to all of the banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: It was a prosecutorial-sounding letter demanding to know exactly what they had done with every dollar that they had received from the government.

speaker: DUKE
text: They found that almost impossible to respond to, but all of them are working on it.

speaker: DUKE
text: The executive compensation restrictions: The CEOs are not concerned about their own pay, and they’re not concerned about that of their top lieutenants.

speaker: DUKE
text: What they are concerned about is their top revenue-producers who are being actively recruited by nonbanks and in some cases larger banks; these people might be in the top 25 in a small bank, but if they go to a larger bank, they would no longer be part of the top 25.

speaker: DUKE
text: At another bank, the chief of credit is retiring and the CEO does not think that he can find a replacement under the executive compensation restrictions.

speaker: DUKE
text: They’re still waiting for the Treasury to publish the regulations, and they don’t know, for example, what the effective date is.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some of them wonder whether they’re going to have to take back the 2008 bonuses already paid.

speaker: DUKE
text: There are questions about vesting: If the vesting cannot occur until the TARP money is paid back, does that mean they cannot vest 100 percent, or does that mean they can only partially vest?

speaker: DUKE
text: If they vest 100 percent once the capital is paid out, what is that going to do to the income statements?

speaker: DUKE
text: Two of them were deferring their stockholders meeting until the proxy rules became clearer.

speaker: DUKE
text: The removal of requirements for paying the TARP capital back, which was part of the last fiscal recovery plan: Investors already viewed this as temporary, and therefore they were treating it as a loan rather than capital—hence the focus on tangible common equity.

speaker: DUKE
text: Now it’s clearly temporary, clearly a loan, and clearly not capital.

speaker: DUKE
text: One of the banks said that they were getting calls from numerous private equity firms, which they originally would never have talked to, saying, “Once you get through the stress test, if you want to give the TARP capital back, we will come in.” Ordinarily they would not have taken it, but now they’re looking at that as an option.

speaker: DUKE
text: The Chairman said in his interview on 60 Minutes that a sign of the economy recovering would be a major institution getting private capital—you may get that wish.

speaker: DUKE
text: All but one expressed the absolute desire to repay, and that is what they’re focused on.

speaker: DUKE
text: The one that was not going to repay is going to put itself in a position to repay and just simply not pay it back until, as he said, “the clouds part and the sun shines.” So no banks are willing to leverage it further and get into a position of needing to keep it.

speaker: DUKE
text: So it’s not doing any good.

speaker: DUKE
text: It is not performing any function except sitting there as a standby.

speaker: DUKE
text: Capital stories: One bank was contacted by another—both were fairly good-sized banks and they talked for a good amount of time.

speaker: DUKE
text: It was a good strategic fit.

speaker: DUKE
text: There was no issue with price.

speaker: DUKE
text: There were no social issues.

speaker: DUKE
text: However, it required additional capital, and they turned it down.

speaker: DUKE
text: Another one had been in detailed talks with the FDIC about taking over a problem bank.

speaker: DUKE
text: The deal included taking additional TARP in order to make the deal work.

speaker: DUKE
text: They notified the FDIC that they were standing down; they no longer wanted to have anything to do with that.

speaker: DUKE
text: And finally, a bank that had not taken any of the government capital had sold trust preferred and common with just a few phone calls last year.

speaker: DUKE
text: This year, the only buyers are the nonpublic investors, because they’re worried about mark to market and OTTI, and they will not invest if TARP capital is present.

speaker: DUKE
text: Now the trust preferred will be priced at 11 to 12 percent fixed with warrants; last year that price was LIBOR plus 375.

speaker: DUKE
text: The bottom line is that the political and public perception right now precludes the use of government capital for healthy banks, and the presence of public capital has put private capital further out of reach.

speaker: DUKE
text: All of that being said, I still believe, when we look back on this episode, we will determine that the injection of capital into the banks kept us from a meltdown.

speaker: DUKE
text: But we’ll also conclude that the public outcry forced the capital back out again.

speaker: DUKE
text: My most optimistic projection is that it will be replaced sooner than anticipated with internal and private sources and that banks will then learn to work with the capital that’s available to them.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of the FDIC, the restriction and higher fees for issuance of the TLGP are causing banks to speed up issuance.

speaker: DUKE
text: They originally thought they had a period of time, and the investment bankers were feeding these issues out in sort of a measured way.

speaker: DUKE
text: Now they all feel like they have to issue before April 1, before the price goes up.

speaker: DUKE
text: Banks did not see the FDIC increase in the premiums and the special assessment coming.

speaker: DUKE
text: Most of them, of course, believe that they’re paying for the bailouts of large banks in some way, and it wipes out a significant portion, if not all, of quarterly earnings.

speaker: DUKE
text: Now to the bankruptcy cram-down for prime, jumbo, and all types of securitizations: The bankruptcy cram-down will alter the order of payments, so that the losses are then shared equally by all tranches rather than in order.

speaker: DUKE
text: This is going to further reduce the value of triple-A tranches of those, and the staff estimates that’s a market of about $600 billion in securities.

speaker: DUKE
text: The Federal Home Loan Banks: The Seattle bank became the first to exhaust its retained earnings.

speaker: DUKE
text: They’re primarily mark-to-market losses, and it’s making the case that they’re not real losses.

speaker: DUKE
text: But the question is: What does this mean for valuation of the stock that the banks hold?

speaker: DUKE
text: Stock ownership is a requirement for borrowing, so anybody who’s borrowing from Federal Home Loan Banks also owns that stock.

speaker: DUKE
text: The advances are getting significantly more expensive.

speaker: DUKE
text: This is not an issue just for small banks—the top 10 banks have 20 percent of the advances from Federal Home Loan Banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: Bankers’ banks and corporate credit unions, I think, pose similar risks for smaller institutions.

speaker: DUKE
text: Fair value accounting is still the number one concern in the industry.

speaker: DUKE
text: I would look to see what happens with the impact of the revised standards on the first quarter.

speaker: DUKE
text: That could be very helpful, although banks that took big losses in the fourth quarter don’t get to reverse them.

speaker: DUKE
text: Let’s switch just a minute now and talk about what’s actually going on in the banking book.

speaker: DUKE
text: Deposits are growing, in some cases significantly.

speaker: DUKE
text: Transactions, as consumers change their behavior, are down significantly, as are overdrafts.

speaker: DUKE
text: In the loan area, demand is down sharply.

speaker: DUKE
text: Consumer and small business applications are up a bit, but the approval rates are down about 10 percent, as you said.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of home equity loans, the reasons for the denials are primarily issues with debt-to-income ratios and appraisals.

speaker: DUKE
text: One thing that consumer groups in here in last week reminded me of—which I had forgotten and shouldn’t have—is that home equity is a primary funding source for small businesses, not SBA loans.

speaker: DUKE
text: We tend to look at home equity as a consumer loan, but it is really small business financing.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of business loans, they are down from lack of income and in many cases actually outright losses.

speaker: DUKE
text: In the construction loan area, they are still working through the existing residential construction loans and dealing with lots and lots of lots.

speaker: DUKE
text: There’s not much new commercial construction—it’s primarily medical or educational facilities.

speaker: DUKE
text: And there is no takeout for completed construction.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some banks are pulling away from loan products, segments, industries, or geographic areas.

speaker: DUKE
text: Others are taking the best of the deals and underwriting them individually.

speaker: DUKE
text: For example, if somebody says, “I’m getting out of all deals to a given segment,” a smaller bank will come in and underwrite them individually and take the best of those deals.

speaker: DUKE
text: Those are the ones that are growing their loans.

speaker: DUKE
text: Student loans: They were already low margin due to a mismatch in reference rates.

speaker: DUKE
text: The banks are currently doing more volume than they want, and they seem delighted to hear that the federal budget is taking them out of the student loan business.

speaker: DUKE
text: Mortgages: The application volume slowed when rates picked up, and it’s still primarily refinancings.

speaker: DUKE
text: Loan modifications: The GSE and service portfolios were modified, but they are concerned about the long-term effect of the very low rates with the ceiling for their own book.

speaker: DUKE
text: Credit quality: Delinquencies continue to rise.

speaker: DUKE
text: They’re starting to sell properties at the same rate they’re bringing in new ones.

speaker: DUKE
text: The growth in loans that are ninety days past due are primarily loans that are in the process of modification.

speaker: DUKE
text: The commercial loans are the ones showing real trouble right now, and as I said yesterday, commercial real estate loans are really just business loans.

speaker: DUKE
text: The repayment and the collateral value of those loans depend on the business cash flows, and the appraisals right now are stunningly low.

speaker: DUKE
text: Many retail stores are closing.

speaker: DUKE
text: Others are on percentage rent, so that cash flows do drop with sales.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some centers are one tenant away from disaster.

speaker: DUKE
text: Hospitality is suffering from not only the recession but the stigma.

speaker: DUKE
text: In Hawaii they are having $10 million a week in cancellations.

speaker: DUKE
text: The banks, though, are not foreclosing.

speaker: DUKE
text: In this case, they are modifying, offering reduced payments, and putting on nonaccrual as long as the operator will continue to operate, because they don’t want those properties back.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some banks are actually incentivizing their loan officers to move loans out rather than to bring loans in.

speaker: DUKE
text: Some banks are offering to settle performing loans at a discount in order to get them off the books.

speaker: DUKE
text: One bank is considering making jumbo loans at conforming rates on its own books to diversify its borrower risk and reduce the inventory of construction loans.

speaker: DUKE
text: With the residential construction loans, you almost get an impression of a store that’s getting ready to go out of business and hasn’t been able to buy new inventory: The inventory they have is not the inventory that’s selling, and it’s just sitting there on the shelves.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of auto loans, there are lower losses on cars that are coming off lease.

speaker: DUKE
text: The wholesale inventories are firming up, and I think that would show through to new cars by the third quarter.

speaker: DUKE
text: Rental agencies are trimming their fleets by about 20 percent.

speaker: DUKE
text: Dealers can’t sell, so they are looking to manufacturers to repurchase the inventory.

speaker: DUKE
text: A Lexus dealer said he has customers who normally would buy on a regular basis and can afford to buy, but are worried about the appearance of buying in a situation where people are losing their jobs.

speaker: DUKE
text: The boat inventory is aging.

speaker: DUKE
text: It’s now three years old, and G.E.

speaker: DUKE
text: Capital is the only company financing boats.

speaker: DUKE
text: Borrowers do not expect to have to pay.

speaker: DUKE
text: One CEO was at his neighbor’s house, which she had just purchased for $1.6 million.

speaker: DUKE
text: The neighbor showed the improvements that she was making and then asked who the modification officer at the bank was because she wanted to modify the mortgage on her vacation home.

speaker: DUKE
text: Another CEO had a private banking client come in who had purchased a home with a private banking loan for $2 million in 2005.

speaker: DUKE
text: The loan was interest only for a million and a half.

speaker: DUKE
text: At one point, the client got a $3 million offer and turned it down.

speaker: DUKE
text: Now the property is for sale at $1 million, and the client said he would continue to make the payments if they reduced the loan to $750,000.

speaker: DUKE
text: There’s a huge increase in fraud.

speaker: DUKE
text: Floor plan and wire transfer were the two that were mentioned.

speaker: DUKE
text: In summary, right now I’m really not hearing much about bank-specific issues that are impediments to lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: Government liquidity is cheap and plentiful.

speaker: DUKE
text: The primary reasons for not lending are related to creditworthiness and concern about economic conditions and collateral values.

speaker: DUKE
text: Banks are reducing credit line availability, but it is due to concerns about credit and collateral.

speaker: DUKE
text: Loans are difficult for larger amounts, for credit-only customers, for those with high debt-to-income ratios or weak credit histories, for those who have little equity, and for any construction loan.

speaker: DUKE
text: I don’t think the banks will ever go back to lending at the spreads typical before this episode, so many of those who think that they can’t get credit are concerned more about the cost of credit, and I think those high loan spreads are here to stay.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Not surprisingly, my assessment of the economy and the financial sector converges with those that have already been expressed.

speaker: TARULLO
text: So let me just quickly make a few additional observations that support the hypothesis of an even longer period for stabilization and recovery than reflected in the Greenbook forecast and, thus, even greater vulnerability for the economy for some time to come.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I begin with an admittedly speculative point about the domestic labor market, but one that complements some earlier comments by Presidents Yellen and Evans.

speaker: TARULLO
text: It appears to me that an unusual number of industries will be undergoing major structural adjustments during the course of this downturn and, as a result, may not rehire at the rate that might be expected in a cyclical rebound.

speaker: TARULLO
text: These industries are two groups.

speaker: TARULLO
text: One consists of industries like construction and financial services that were directly involved in the asset bubbles associated with the financial crisis.

speaker: TARULLO
text: It seems likely that overcapacity in those industries so far exceeded sustainable demand that the post-recession employment profile will be substantially, rather than just moderately, below pre-crisis levels.

speaker: TARULLO
text: A second group consists of industries that, even in the middle part of the decade, had seen significant pressure on their business models.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Companies and sectors as diverse as autos, media, legal services, and retail were already in the process of consolidation and/or downsizing.

speaker: TARULLO
text: This process has clearly accelerated under the weight of the contraction in real GDP.

speaker: TARULLO
text: There are good reasons—anecdotal, I admit, but good reasons, nonetheless—to believe that, to a greater or lesser degree, each of these industries will emerge from this recession permanently leaner than they were, and some may be fundamentally changed.

speaker: TARULLO
text: This observation is, as I noted, to date unsupported by even raw data, much less by systematic comparison with earlier severe recessions.

speaker: TARULLO
text: But if my intuition is buttressed by such an analysis, elevated unemployment levels may be stickier for a longer time than we now anticipate.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The emergence of new firms and industries that might normally be expected to pick up some of the slack will, at the same time, be hindered by continuing dysfunction in financial markets.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I have some very different observations about the international economy, but, I’m afraid, with similar implications for the shape of the GDP growth curve.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The downward revisions of economic performance abroad do not seem to have been met with a sense of policy urgency in many countries, particularly with respect to non-monetary policy measures in the advanced foreign economies.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Indeed, my conclusion from my week in Europe was not dissimilar to that of Governor Warsh.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I observed, in addition, that there has been a kind of collective decision among policymakers to put on a relatively happy face publicly, while being unable privately to offer any grounds for optimism.

speaker: TARULLO
text: In formal comments and public utterances, a number of policymakers made reference to wholly adequate stimulus measures.

speaker: TARULLO
text: They discounted the significance of increased bank CDS spreads, or, in at least one case, commented on the wonderful bargains available to those who still had jobs.

speaker: TARULLO
text: This attitude is of particular concern because, as Steve Kamin mentioned, the effects of stimulus measures in many advanced foreign economies are substantially front-loaded into 2009.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Whether because of policy paralysis in the face of daunting challenges or, in some cases, because of the weak political circumstances of incumbent governments, too many countries seem unable or unwilling to elevate their responses to rapidly deteriorating conditions.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I worry that a similar hesitancy to take forceful steps could lead to inadequate responses to contingencies, such as widespread banking problems in emerging markets.

speaker: TARULLO
text: An absence of confidence in the political strength of the government can also push officials towards more serious consideration of measures, such as shifts in foreign exchange policies, which may relieve a certain amount of domestic pain by shifting it elsewhere in a neutral or even negative-sum fashion.

speaker: TARULLO
text: My concerns about this issue have increased dramatically in the last week.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Many emerging markets have limited capacity to help themselves, given their own fiscal and monetary constraints.

speaker: TARULLO
text: One major exception, of course, is China.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Yet even China seems to be relying in the medium term on a rebound in advanced foreign economies that would restore many of the exports lost in recent months.

speaker: TARULLO
text: While that approach worked well for countries coming out of the Asian financial crisis in 1999, it was built on the strength of largely unaffected American and European economies.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Obviously, demand in our economies will be weak for quite some time.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Moreover, the continued problems in our financial sectors imply that capital flows to emerging markets are unlikely to pick up, as they did following the Asian financial crisis.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Despite these impediments to a reasonably fast-paced return to conditions promoting rapid emerging market growth, there’s little indication in China or elsewhere that policymakers have used the crisis to accelerate shifts in their own growth models away from a high level of export dependence.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Coupled with what is, at least for the present, a somewhat passive policy instinct in some advanced economies, international developments may, like our domestic employment situation, suggest a more prolonged and shaky recovery period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I understand coffee is ready.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a 20-minute break?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me start by trying to summarize the discussion around the table, and then I’ll give a few additional comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The group agreed that the economic outlook has worsened significantly, and although it wasn’t noted, we have seen very sharp declines in both the fourth and the first quarters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The slowdown is widespread across sectors and has included not only such areas as construction, manufacturing, and retail, but also hospitality, shipping, and to some extent energy, agriculture, and other areas.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A notable development has been declines abroad, which have been exceptionally severe, and which, together with the stronger dollar, are hurting U.S. exports.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was a view on the part of some that there might be some stabilization later this year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Factors that might promote a weak recovery later this year or in 2010 include fiscal policy, monetary stimulus, improvements of financial markets, slower declines in housing, and working out of the inventory cycle.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, I have to say that there wasn’t much conviction behind this view, and some saw at best an L-shaped recovery.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Risks clearly remain to the downside, and a protracted period of economic weakness remains a significant possibility, reflecting factors such as an ongoing lack of confidence in government policy, general uncertainty, need for economic restructuring, and the ongoing deleveraging process by both financial institutions and households.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: International prospects may not be much better, as other countries also face needs for restructuring and many are having inadequate policy responses.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumption data improved slightly in January and February, but consumption fundamentals remain quite weak.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Declines in wealth have been sharp and have led consumers to attempt to repair balance sheets by increasing their saving.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The labor market is shedding jobs rapidly, and substantial job losses may continue for a while.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing starts and permits have increased a bit, and the Administration’s foreclosure mitigation plan may also be of some help in the housing market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nevertheless, housing continues to disappoint to the downside in general, and house prices continue to fall.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It was noted that declines in house prices affect not only the rates of residential construction but also consumer wealth, as well as the quality of assets that are held by financial institutions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the financial sector, many credit markets, especially those in which the Fed has intervened, remained fairly stable in the intermeeting period, despite worsening economic news, and some highly rated corporations have issued debt.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, confidence in the banking system has deteriorated, as reflected, for example, in widening CDS spreads.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Lending is down, reflecting in part credit supply constraints, as well as lower loan demand and bank concerns about credit quality and about the economy in general.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Participants remain concerned about the effects of lack of financing on the commercial real estate sector in particular.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The success of government actions to stabilize the banking system remains an important factor in the outlook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s a great deal of public skepticism about government efforts in this regard, as well as populist reaction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Industrial production has fallen sharply both here and abroad as global trade declines.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Managers remain pessimistic and uncertain about prospects for sales, prices, and employment and are prepared to cut employment and investment further if improvement does not materialize.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Demand for new capital goods remains weak, as capacity utilization has set a postwar low.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit constraints are perceived to be an important problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most participants expect inflation to remain very low for a time, and some are concerned about the risk for deflation, including falling wages.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Deflationary trends could result in a deflation trap or a debt–deflation dynamic.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Expectations of inflation, but also general economic conditions, will clearly play an important role going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those are some of the things I took away from the discussion—I’m sure I left out many points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: [No response] Let me just add a bit to that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t have a great deal to say.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As everyone noted, the intermeeting news was generally disappointing—below expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s notable that in December we thought things were bad enough to cut rates to zero, and in the last two meetings the changes in the outlook both times have been quite negative.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, like the rest of the world, the U.S. economy experienced very sharp declines in the fourth quarter and apparently now in the first quarter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Perhaps the most striking development since the last meeting is the weakening of the global economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s really quite remarkable how quickly that happened.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Many of you have experienced being abroad and hearing people say that on Tuesday things looked okay and on Thursday a sudden chill hit the atmosphere and there’s been a tremendous decline since then.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think one interpretation of the worsening of our outlook is that, in fact, the shock that hit the world economy in September and October was a truly enormous shock and that we have been slow in understanding how big it was and how persistent it was.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, in some sense, it’s not that we’ve had new shocks, but rather that we are just coming to the point of understanding how bad that shock was.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There were, of course, a few glimmers of positive news, and President Stern and others made note of that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There were some indications of stabilization in consumption in January and February, and that is before the actual fiscal stimulus kicks in, which may be of some help unless you think people are anticipating it, which is possible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That seemed to happen last spring actually.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also, we saw a bit of improvement in the housing starts and the permits yesterday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there’s a little good news there, but, like most people, I wouldn’t want to take too much of a signal from that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First of all, both of these data sets are very volatile month to month, and they suffer from a great deal of seasonality and other factors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But more importantly, given the size of the shock that the world economy apparently was hit with in the fall, there’s going to be an unavoidable cyclical dynamic that’s just going to have to work its way out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s almost nothing that can be done at this point to avoid it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, consumer spending may stabilize, but it’s going to be facing very substantial headwinds, including the familiar list of further stock price declines, house price declines, ongoing job losses, confidence declines, and the same factors that we’ve talked about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d reiterate also the point that the Vice Chairman made about the saving rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have a recent reading of about 5 percent in the household saving rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That was possibly, to some extent, exaggerated by temporary increases in income.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If the consumer wants to maintain that saving rate or go higher, it suggests a relatively weak consumption profile going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Moreover, even if consumption stabilizes, the rest of the dynamic is still very powerful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inventories, for example—the inventory profile looks worse than it did at the last meeting, in the sense that the overhang seems to be greater than we thought it might have been and, therefore, the cycle will take longer to work its way through.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I talked about this at the last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At the last meeting we had inventory dynamics leading possibly to slightly positive economic growth by the third quarter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those dynamics now look distinctly less favorable.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inventory investment is likely to be negative throughout the rest of the year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It may add to growth in the sense it will be less negative going forward, but, certainly, that dynamic is going to be a very powerful one for some time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other dynamics that have been talked about around the table include investment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We could hardly expect strong investment in the context of declining output, a postwar low in capacity utilization, credit constraints, uncertainty, et cetera.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With investment continuing to be quite weak, final sales will be weak, and therefore, the inventory dynamic will be stretched out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s also, of course, an employment dynamic to the extent that the employment levels are above the sustainable levels from the perspective of individual firms.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As the continued economic weakness is perceived, we’ll see further job losses and further dynamic adjustment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would reiterate the importance of the global decline.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Steve talked about the implications for contributions to GDP of the swing in exports from early last year until now, and there obviously is not going to be major change in that in the near term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And finally, there was a lot of discussion around the table, which I would reiterate, about financial conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is some improvement, or at least some stabilization, in some credit markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that we’re certainly better off than we were at the beginning of the shock in September and October, but banks are under exceptional stress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The CDS spreads were mentioned.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The political situation is very adverse in terms of ensuring that the government will have the resources and support to take the necessary action to get the banking system stabilized.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thinking about the alternative simulations in the Greenbook, I think delayed financial repair might well be one that we would want to consider.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The experience of other countries and other episodes is that that leads, at best, to a period of stagnation, if not to further decline.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t want to be completely bleak.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Like others, I saw a few positive signs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There’s some indication that the free fall of the fourth quarter and first quarter might be moderating to some extent, particularly in consumer spending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If that’s so and if fears of a depression or some extreme event begin to wane, we may see some stabilization of final demand, which then will feed into the inventory and investment dynamic over time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But under any circumstances, and particularly if the banking situation is not resolved in a favorable way, I think we can expect to see very large output gaps develop and a very sustained, weak condition for the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That obviously has implications for inflation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I mentioned last time, deflation per se is not necessarily the issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The fact is that, as disinflation progresses, that itself will raise real interest rates and exacerbate to some extent the debt issues and the housing-valuation issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So putting that all together, as many people discussed yesterday, I do think that some aggressive policies may be called for today, and with that I’ll stop and turn to Brian to introduce the policy round.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 5 As indicated by the Greenbook and by your discussion this morning, the economic outlook has deteriorated markedly over the intermeeting period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: At the same time, the options for applying additional stimulus quickly appear limited.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It now seems likely that the TALF will lift off only slowly.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: And prospects for the enactment of additional fiscal stimulus, at least in the near term, appear dim.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In these circumstances, consideration of further monetary stimulus through large- scale asset purchases would seem to be warranted.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Bluebook presented two policy alternatives, A and B, that involved additional asset purchases and one, alternative C, that would not involve further stimulative measures.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will focus my remarks this morning on alternatives A and B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This morning, we have proposed revisions to the draft statements; the revised statements are provided in the package that was distributed to you earlier labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” I will begin with alternative A, on page 2.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under this alternative, the rationale section—paragraphs 1 and 2—would note that the economy is undergoing a severe contraction and that the near-term economic outlook has worsened.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It would point to a number of indicators of the economic weakness.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Paragraph 1 would end on a note of some optimism by stating that the policy actions taken to stabilize financial markets and institutions, together with fiscal and monetary stimulus, will contribute to a gradual resumption of sustainable economic growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Paragraph 2 would note the Committee’s expectation that inflation will remain subdued, dropping the phrase “in coming quarters” that was used in the January statement, consistent with a view that inflation could be low for some time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, it would again cite “some risk that inflation could persist for a time below rates that best foster economic growth and price stability in the longer term.” As President Fisher noted, the rationale section provides a rather downbeat reading on the economy, but perhaps one that is realistic.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the policy paragraph, alternative A would again indicate the Committee’s intention to employ all available tools.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It says that the Committee will hold the federal funds rate range at 0 to ¼ percent and indicates an expectation that economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate “for an extended period.” This phrase would suggest a longer interval than the phrase “for 5 Materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this document (appendix 5).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: some time” used in January and suggested for alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To provide additional economic stimulus, the Committee would take three policy actions under alternative A: increasing the amount of its agency MBS purchases by $500 billion to a total of $1 trillion this year; increasing the amount of its purchases of agency debt securities by $100 billion to a total of $200 billion this year (the boost to agency debt purchases is an addition relative to the alternative presented in the Bluebook); and initiating purchases of longer-term Treasury securities that are to total $300 billion over the next six months.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This paragraph would also note that the TALF has been launched.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement would conclude by indicating that the Committee will be carefully monitoring the System’s balance sheet and by suggesting some predilection toward stepping up its balance sheet expansion by noting that “it will be assessing whether a faster pace of asset purchases would be helpful in improving credit market conditions and supporting economic activity.” A possible downside of including such language is that it suggests a possible course of action that the Committee may end up not pursuing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative B, on the next page, begins with a rationale section, paragraphs 1 and 2, that is identical to that proposed for alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, under alternative B, the Committee would not initiate purchases of Treasury securities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Rather, it would more than double its purchases of agency MBS securities, to a total of $1.25 trillion this year, and double its purchases of agency debt securities to $200 billion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This alternative would not include anything comparable with the final clause of alternative A indicating that the Committee was inclined to further step up its asset purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In summary, alternative A would constitute a somewhat more aggressive expansion of the FOMC’s asset purchases than alternative B.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The differences in terms of total asset purchases are small: Alternative A would commit to an expansion of your asset purchases by a total of $900 billion, whereas the increase under alternative B would be just slightly less, at $850 billion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, as I noted, the language of alternative A would be more forward-leaning with respect to possible future increases in asset purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: And the initiation of Treasury purchases might suggest to market participants that the Committee’s operations could be expanded particularly in that direction in the future.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The key difference between alternative A and alternative B really is whether or not to purchase Treasury securities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To review the arguments for and against such purchases, you might be inclined to proceed with purchases of longer-term Treasury securities if you: believe that the economic situation had deteriorated so substantially that you did want to apply “all available tools” as indicated in your previous statement; feel that it might be helpful to diversify the tools that you are applying to the situation; believe that purchasing Treasury securities rather than private securities is preferable to minimize the Federal Reserve’s involvement in credit allocation; or think it might be easier to unwind in the future holdings of Treasury securities than holdings of private securities such as MBS, which might be less liquid or might be seen in the future as tied particularly to primary mortgage market conditions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On the other hand, you might be inclined not to purchase longer-term Treasury securities if: you think that purchases of private securities such as MBS would more effectively improve conditions in private credit markets and thus provide better support to private spending; or you are concerned that market participants might believe that you are monetizing the federal debt, a perception that might lead to adverse effects on term premiums or, perhaps, on inflation expectations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative C, page 4, the Committee would make no adjustment to the policy tools that it is already implementing, and it would not reference any modification to the Federal Reserve’s liquidity programs other than those that have been previously announced.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Instead, the statement would indicate that the Committee decided to keep its target range for the federal funds rate at 0 to ¼ percent and indicate that it continues to anticipate that economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate for some time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The second paragraph would note that the near-term economic outlook is poor but indicate that the Committee anticipates that a gradual recovery in economic activity will begin later this year, subject to significant downside risks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The final paragraph of the announcement would note the range of policy actions that are already in train.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Bluebook also presented an alternative structure for the FOMC statement, based on a suggestion provided by President Bullard.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Applying that structure to alternative A, and incorporating this morning’s suggested revisions to the policy actions, is shown on page 5 as alternative A′.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A′ is substantively the same as A, but it reorders the statement such that the Committee’s actions are presented first.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In particular, the first sentence of the statement indicates that “The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to increase the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet further by purchasing $300 billion of longer-term Treasury securities over the next six months and by acquiring an additional $500 billion of agency MBS and $100 billion of agency debt securities this year.” Obviously, this approach gives greater prominence not only to the actions themselves but also to their effect on the Committee’s balance sheet.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Conversely, this approach gives less prominence to the very downbeat summary of the economic situation in paragraphs 2 and 3, a possible advantage of this approach.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, the flow of the statement may be seen as a bit less logical, in that it presents the Committee’s actions before discussing the economic conditions that motivated them.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternatives B′ and C′, pages 6 and 7, apply the same structure to alternatives B and C. The final three sections of the package provide draft directives for the three basic alternatives and their primed variants.

speaker: EVANS
text: Brian, in the Bluebook and yesterday we saw a chart of how the unemployment rate and the inflation rate would play out under these different strategies.

speaker: EVANS
text: My question is about alternative A, the largest program that we’re considering.

speaker: EVANS
text: Is it plausible/likely/possible that what we’re looking at here would be enough?

speaker: EVANS
text: Would the markets look at this and think that the FOMC has taken actions that it believes, if the outlook doesn’t deteriorate further, would be enough?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You’re asking about how the markets would interpret this?

speaker: EVANS
text: Is it likely that the Committee would be willing to see this as large enough to put us in a good position and we’d just wait for confirmation of the outlook?

speaker: EVANS
text: Are we even close to that?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Judging by the simulations that were presented in the Bluebook, I would say that this alternative A is roughly comparable to the green dash-dotted line on page 32, if you happen to have that in front of you.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It’s roughly the same size, with a slightly different composition.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So the effects on interest rates might be similar.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, that would not get the Committee, on this analysis, to something comparable to the unconstrained policy.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A quick question: The directives have “up to,” and the statements do not have “up to.” Is that important?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A question from President Fisher.

speaker: FISHER
text: May I just ask, Mr. Chairman, a question of Ms. Mosser?

speaker: FISHER
text: Every one of these statements says that we’ve launched the term asset-backed securities loan facility.

speaker: FISHER
text: Could you just give us a quick update of where we stand on that, because the wording here might be questioned?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Because the deadline is tomorrow, not surprisingly, we have no one who has signed on the dotted line.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We have, however, three very serious issues—two of them auto- related, one of them credit card-related—that appear at this stage pretty likely to go through.

speaker: MOSSER
text: There do seem to be at least enough customer-to-dealer contracts signed, or in the process of being signed.

speaker: MOSSER
text: My ballpark guesstimate, based on the numbers I’ve seen, is $5 billion—could be $8 billion—total.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Quite frankly, before the machinations of the last week and a half, I don’t think we truly anticipated more than $5 to $10 billion in the first subscription.

speaker: MOSSER
text: There’s been no price discovery in this market for several months.

speaker: MOSSER
text: And just on those grounds alone, many issuers and investors might be somewhat reluctant to be first in the TALF.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we can’t say it has launched.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Well, we’ve launched it in the sense that the subscription is open and that lending has happened.

speaker: DUKE
text: I just want to make sure my math is correct and my understanding is correct.

speaker: DUKE
text: When we do the additional $500 billion in mortgage-backed securities, does that increase the pace at which we buy them, or does it extend the time from June until the end of the year?

speaker: MOSSER
text: The $500 billion would largely extend the buying through the end of the year.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If the Committee has a preference that those be front-loaded, that would be possible for us to do from an operational standpoint.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As a matter of fact, if the Committee would be interested in giving us direction on that, we’d be happy to take it.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Honestly, the additional $500 billion would not be a huge surprise to the market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think the expectation of most is that $500 billion at the same pace through the end of the year is a likely outcome of today’s meeting.

speaker: DUKE
text: Under alternative A, by my count it’s $500 billion in MBS, $300 billion in Treasuries, and $100 billion in agencies, for a total of $900 billion.

speaker: DUKE
text: Would we expect that to have a similar result as in the note on $1 trillion in a combination of mortgage-backed securities and Treasuries?

speaker: DUKE
text: Is that the result we would be looking for from alternative A?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think we consider it to be roughly the same.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Our ability to discriminate between effects on one market or another is pretty limited.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: There’s lots of uncertainty around these estimates.

speaker: DUKE
text: For alternative B—which is $750 billion plus $100 billion, I get $850 billion.

speaker: DUKE
text: Would we also expect that to have similar impact?

speaker: DUKE
text: In other words, would the fact that there’s no Treasury component matter?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Given our ability to distinguish between them, we wouldn’t be able to say that that made a material difference from any other one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There was a two-hander from President Rosengren.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It would seem that, if the goal is to push rates down and cause a wave of refinancing, then we’d want to be doing the bulk of the purchasing during the period where the refinancing would occur, which presumably would be over the next quarter.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If everybody refinances over the next quarter or two, the ability to purchase new mortgages in the second half of the year would probably be pretty limited, if we’re actually successful in doing it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It does seem that the goal is not to have an even flow over the course of the year, but to enable rates to get low enough that we facilitate a wave of refinancings and new home purchases.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I think it would be good if we can provide some clarification that the goal is not to spread it out, but to push the rates down and get the refinancings going, which would imply front-loading, assuming the program is successful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you think the front-loading is more important than the announcement effect?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I wouldn’t want to be constrained to do only a limited amount and have the refinancings cause rates not to go down very much.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You don’t necessarily want to save the $500 billion for the second half of the year is what you’re saying?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If it’s appropriate, I’d rather do it sooner than later.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I want to get as much bang for the buck in the next two quarters as we can.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Can we find a phrase that would be added that would say something like “with the greater portion to be done in the first—”?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: “Over the next several months.”

speaker: WARSH
text: “Increasing the rate of purchases.” I think that’s what you are trying to get the markets to gather.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Except it’s a little bit uncertain, because if we front-load it, then later there’s less.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Brian, I just want to make sure I understand the numbers as well, and it comes down to a difference in wording between A and B.

speaker: TARULLO
text: In B, you have “increase its purchases of agency debt this year by $100 billion to a total of $200 billion.” In A, it just says, “boost its purchases” and “now anticipates purchasing $200 billion.” I guess that makes the headline number in alternative A $1 trillion.

speaker: TARULLO
text: But, if I understand correctly, it’s really an additional $900 billion of authorized purchases.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Why is the alternative A today $100 billion less than the alternative A in the Bluebook, which was $500 billion additional MBS and $500 billion Treasuries?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Could I interject something here for just a moment?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I asked yesterday, everyone gave their views, and I listened very carefully to what the options were.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What was suggested here today was two approaches.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One expanded on the MBS front, going from $1 trillion for this year to $1¼ trillion, with a concomitant small increase in agency debt, but no Treasuries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other approach was to maintain the same pace of MBS purchases through the second half of the year—subject to a bit of language about timing, in response to the point that was raised—and to open a new front on the Treasuries side; there I was responding to concerns that a number of people raised about monetization and the independence perception, and so on, trying to make it seem more like a step into this arena rather than a big-scale, new intervention.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that was the thinking on those two approaches.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me now add, having heard the discussion around the table today, I think I would like to raise a third option, which is the union of the two, which would be the $750 billion of MBS, plus the $300 billion of Treasuries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d be open to that as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m trying to avoid the proliferation of too many alternatives, but what I heard today suggests that some people at least might be interested in yet a more aggressive approach, while still attentive to the costs and benefits of expanding our balance sheet faster and further.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do I have clarity on sort of what the options are now?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any other questions for Brian?

speaker: LACKER
text: My question is actually for Ms. Mosser.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we adopted either B′ or the schedule that the Chairman suggested, and you were to pace it the way you would, what are the chances that the monetary base will shrink in the next intermeeting period?

speaker: LACKER
text: You’ve got the TAF, CPFF, AMLF, and foreign exchange swap lines.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is there a significant chance that you won’t make enough purchases in the intermeeting period to offset other declines in our assets and leave the monetary base shrunken rather than expanded over the period?

speaker: MOSSER
text: If we accelerate, particularly on the mortgage side, and front-load those, I would view it as very unlikely.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Spence probably has a better feel on the liquidity programs.

speaker: MOSSER
text: A little shrinkage there might occur, but, particularly if we add Treasuries and we are more aggressive on the mortgage side, I would view it as very unlikely that the base would shrink.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You have this one question of the settlement of mortgage securities, though, which might not actually occur by then.

speaker: HILTON
text: You really have to look at what the settlement date is almost.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In thinking about the base, because the settlements are so lumpy we probably have to switch a week forward and note that even though the base might shrink one week, it will jump up a lot the next when all of the MBS settle.

speaker: LACKER
text: Do you think the base is likely to increase?

speaker: LACKER
text: Would that be your expectation?

speaker: LACKER
text: A couple hundred billion, would you guess?

speaker: HILTON
text: It’s not a long intermeeting period, so a couple hundred billion might be a little bit larger than is realistic.

speaker: HILTON
text: It is hard to anticipate where the liquidity facilities are going, but the fact that they have been relatively stable on balance for a couple of months—since late January—makes me think that, without some fundamental change in liquidity conditions, they’re probably not going to break in a substantial way one direction or another.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’m sorry, if I could just add a point.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: With the CPFF, you had this big refinancing wave that happened late January.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You’re not going to have another one until late April, and there’s going to be less coming due at that time.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So that’s probably not going to change dramatically.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The big question is on the foreign exchange swap side.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But that has already come down a lot.

speaker: LACKER
text: The current size is around 400 or 500 billion?

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think I can say with some confidence that, if we buy a lot of mortgages, by the middle of May it’s very unlikely that the monetary base will be shrinking, and it will grow fairly aggressively, because the big settlements in mortgage-backed securities tend to happen in the middle of the month.

speaker: LACKER
text: Just to pursue this a little more, what’s sketched out here is $1¼ trillion of increases in our assets above what they otherwise would be.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we were interested in assuring that a certain portion of that passed through to the base, that might call for even more offsetting increases.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me ask something operational.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we wanted to be sure that the base expanded, or that it expanded by a certain amount, could you vary Treasury purchases within the intermeeting period in a way that would react to incoming information on the foreign exchange swap usage, and the like, to achieve that?

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think there might be better tools for doing that, though.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Honestly, if that were the guidance given, we would probably go back to doing repos.

speaker: HILTON
text: The other element is our involvement in the dollar roll market as well, which we probably could scale up at a relatively fast pace, if we wanted to.

speaker: HILTON
text: Again, though, we would have to look at the calendar, because those also settle on a discrete date.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, President Lacker, just to reiterate the options quickly: The “all MBS” option would be $850 billion—that’s $750 billion plus $100 billion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What I will call the “Treasury” option is $900 billion—that’s $500 billion MBS plus $100 billion agency debt plus $300 billion Treasuries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The “combined” option is $1.15 trillion—that’s $750 billion MBS, $100 billion debt, and $300 billion Treasuries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My reaction to your question is that, particularly if we front-load the MBS, even though there might be some weekly variation in the base, the very strong trend of the base will be clearly up for the rest of the year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This will certainly make it very clear to everybody that that’s the intention, and that will be the result.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, you understand my concern.

speaker: LACKER
text: There is $1 trillion on our balance sheet that is demand-driven and could roll off in very uncertain circumstances.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not quite sure whether that will happen or not.

speaker: LACKER
text: So you can understand why this leaves a fair amount of uncertainty about where the base is going to be at the end of the year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It would all have to roll off.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It certainly would be very unlikely, but okay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Anyone else have a question for Brian?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just in terms of parameters, we have the three substantive options.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to remind you that there are also two statement options.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is more similar to what we’ve had before, which states the economic situation first, and then goes through the paragraph on policy actions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We also have proposed an alternative suggested by some comments that President Bullard made that in some ways would be analogous to our old structure in that it would put the policy actions first.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For the sake of convenience, let’s call that the “inverted” structure—without any derogation implied.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me now go to President Plosser, if you’re ready.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I raised some issues yesterday about asset purchases and policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think some of the things that remain questions for our policies going forward include, for example: How do we evaluate the merits of the various programs we have?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: How do we equate the programs at the margin to get the most bang for the buck as we use our balance sheet?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think a lot of the discussion yesterday about Treasuries versus MBS had a mixed tone to it, in the sense that part of it was a desire to use monetary expansion to support the economy at large, while some people wanted to use the asset purchases for liquidity purposes or to bring mortgage rates down or to target credit market interventions in certain markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
