text: Certainly, part of the debate about whether to use Treasuries or MBS depended on which side of that fence you were on.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think we still have some work to do about deciding the policy mix.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I’m going to throw a monkey wrench in the works.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Yesterday the Chairman asked for alternative ways of saying some of this.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One of the issues we discussed, and it came out, I think, loud and clear, was that there’s a lot of concern about the path of policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: When we announce policy actions—whether they be the TALF, MBS, or what have you—we tend to announce them as quantities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As a result, it’s not very clear what happens when that quantity is reached.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What will be the next market?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What will happen going forward?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think there’s an argument that conducting policy in that manner creates a lot of uncertainty in the marketplace about what’s going to come next.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Are they going to do it again?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And, if so, how big would that be?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Another issue when we target specific volumes is that the conditionality of those interventions doesn’t come through very clearly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It may seem that we are going to do the $500 billion no matter what else happens.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So President Bullard and I—I’m going to implicate him as well—wondered, “Well, is there another way to do this that might be helpful?” We put together a new version of the statement, with the idea that we want to get beyond just announcing one-off programs that we may or may not do again and move toward thinking about saying that we’re going to have a plan to increase the size of the balance sheet or increase the size of certain components of the balance sheet over a period of time, and that we’ll adjust those growth rates, if you will, as needed, as the economy either worsens or improves.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The proposed wording was passed around—we’ve called it alternative B′′.6 The idea here was to address the question, “Okay, how else could we communicate to the markets about what our plan is?” Paragraph 1 basically becomes, “The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to continue to increase the Federal Reserve balance sheet through the purchase of agency MBS and Treasury securities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Committee expects the growth rate of the MBS and Treasury components of the balance sheet combined to average about 10 percent a month.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Committee will carefully monitor macroeconomic and financial conditions and adjust this rate of expansion as warranted.” 6 The statement distributed by Mr. Plosser is appended to this document (appendix 6).

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, we came up with 10 percent a month.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Basically, that would get us to the $1 trillion over the course of the year, which we were talking about yesterday.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s ambiguous about whether it ends up being Treasuries or MBS.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It then says we will carefully monitor this expansion at each meeting and adjust it as we deem appropriate—if we need to ramp it up, we can do that, and if we want to bring it down, we can bring it down.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The rest of the statement is pretty much the same as the original.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We took the rest of what was paragraph 1 and made it paragraph 2, which is basically a discussion of the TALF and the other programs that we’ve initiated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So it is the same there, and the rest of the statement basically follows B.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Again, our view is that we were looking for a way to get us out of thinking about one-off programs or volumes of purchases that we’re going to make, and instead we were trying to set a target or objective for a growth rate of some set of quantities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think there can be debate about whether it should be Treasuries plus MBS.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think President Lacker would probably prefer it to be targeting the base to get the same outcome.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But we wanted to put this on a table as kind of a straw man to get the Committee thinking a little bit about different ways to help us manage expectations better.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s also contingent on economic conditions, which we think is important.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So, Mr. Chairman, I know we surprised you with this, but you asked us this question, so we thought we’d try to come up with an alternative that’s worth discussing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s interesting, and some may view the lack of specificity between MBS and Treasury as a plus, and some might view it as a minus.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it’s an interesting alternative, so I appreciate your doing that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Did you want to talk at all about the choice of the substantive alternatives?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have a preference for Treasuries in general, as I discussed yesterday.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My preference for Treasuries is not particularly driven by a desire to push down long-term interest rates so much as it is by a desire to help manage the composition of our balance sheet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not as worried about the effect on inflation expectations of buying Treasuries, in part because, if there is a concern about expectations of inflation, it’s that I really don’t want them to fall.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I am not too worried about that aspect of it, and I do prefer Treasuries.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In terms of the magnitudes, I’m sympathetic to expanding, but I don’t have strong opinions about how much we should expand.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, to state the obvious: We’re at the zero bound, we’re resorting to extraordinary tools to offset the deflationary and other consequences of overly tight monetary policy, and we have to deploy that extraordinary tool kit effectively, deliberately, and with clarity.

speaker: FISHER
text: President Lockhart injected a little humor by congratulating you on your having an interchange named after you and pointing out there is an off-ramp.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is no off-ramp right now, unfortunately.

speaker: FISHER
text: And President Pianalto pointed to your 60 Minutes performance, which I also wanted to applaud, except to point out there was one weakness: You were opposite George Clooney in that time slot.

speaker: FISHER
text: I mention these things because I’m sympathetic to what President Plosser mentioned, in that, (a) there is no off-ramp, and (b) we have to think way ahead.

speaker: FISHER
text: I talked two years ago about decision trees.

speaker: FISHER
text: We at least have to think of where this highway is possibly going to take us.

speaker: FISHER
text: The ad hocery of what we are doing is a bit of a concern to all of us at the table; but let’s acknowledge the fact that we are in extraordinary circumstances, and we have to play ball according to what’s on the field.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do have a preference, as I stated yesterday, to focus on where we have demonstrated extraordinarily well our capacity to play, which is in the mortgage-backed securities market.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m very sympathetic to President Rosengren’s argument, particularly as to timing.

speaker: FISHER
text: Although I don’t have a vote in this matter in this cycle, I would support alternative B. I still have concerns about being viewed as monetizing deficits.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think there’s a possibility that the political class—that is, the legislature—will ask for still more.

speaker: FISHER
text: But it’s not clear to me whether buying Treasuries might be interpreted as our accommodating fiscal profligacy, although I understand the circumstances of the moment, which are certainly trying.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think Governor Tarullo offered a very sophisticated approach to this yesterday, which is to do things in proportion; and I could live with the alternative that that has the lesser weighting on Treasuries.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do think it is important to exercise our muscle in the mortgage-backed securities market.

speaker: FISHER
text: My contacts tell me that when you get to the 4½ percent level, you do have some effectiveness, and I think that’s clearly an area where we want to have extraordinary effectiveness.

speaker: FISHER
text: As to the statement itself, Mr. Chairman, I’m not sure why we’re emphasizing the job losses and all of the things that, as I said in my note, you’re aware of even if you live on Mars.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do worry about that, given the fact that we are the institution that everybody’s looking to—in part because we did get out ahead of the rest of the world.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’re viewed as a precious institution with, I think, superior credibility compared to all of the other institutions of government at present.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m not sure it’s helpful to keep pounding on the negative.

speaker: FISHER
text: The economy is contracting, and it continues to contract.

speaker: FISHER
text: The important thing is that we say what we’re going to do about it, and we do so with clarity.

speaker: FISHER
text: Let me add parenthetically that I appreciate your moving the fed funds decision down to where it should be, which I believe both of us asked for last time—that is, moving it down in terms of order of priority.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to conclude with one last statement.

speaker: FISHER
text: My greatest concern is the TALF.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think I made that obvious.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would caution you to be very careful on this public–private partnership.

speaker: FISHER
text: I made my living doing extraordinarily complex transactions—taking distressed companies, restructuring them, and taking the equity out—and I was confused yesterday by what was described.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I’m more worried about the politics of it.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we have to be very careful with our precious franchise in dealing with an embattled opposite, particularly on the Administration side, so that we don’t jeopardize our special standing in the community by appearing to accommodate political necessity and exigency.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would urge you, and this Committee, to stay away from the legacy assets for now.

speaker: FISHER
text: And I would urge you to be very careful about any commitment to the public–private partnership concept.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I missed one point I wanted to make in my comments.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: President Fisher reminded me of it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In our B′′, one of the things we changed was the description of the economy, which, Jim and I both agreed with President Fisher, sounded panicky.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We changed what I think was in paragraph 2 to take out a lot of the detailed description and wrote, “The decision reflects the Committee’s view that the economy is undergoing a severe contraction,” which it is.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And we said “the near-term outlook is weak.” The other change in the same spirit is in the rest of that sentence: “the Committee anticipates that market forces and policy actions will contribute to a gradual resumption of sustainable economic growth.” I think in the original it says that policy actions alone will stabilize the world.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And, frankly, I think creating an impression that the only game in town is policy actions and that market economies have no contribution to make in this stabilization is setting us up for failure and a credibility problem.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So we added the reference to market forces.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’m going to talk a little more about this B′′ option.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Let me just follow up on some of President Plosser’s and some of President Fisher’s comments.

speaker: BULLARD
text: When we think about optimal policy under interest rate targeting, which is what we’re all used to, we decide what we’re going to do and we communicate it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It has a path because you’ve got a rule in mind about how you’re going to operate policy in the future, so that gives you a projected path, and that allows the private sector to coordinate on that path.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s all part of how the equilibrium works and how the optimal policy works.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What I’m concerned about right now, and in the last couple of meetings, is that we’re not doing that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Because we hit the zero bound, the interest rate targeting regime was taken off the table by events, so we’re ending up with these one-time announcements, with round numbers, and that makes the future path of policy unclear.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The private sector, as I said yesterday, will try to guess what the FOMC will do, regardless of whether we say anything or not.

speaker: BULLARD
text: For years and years we didn’t say anything.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But we can do a lot better, I think, by reducing that uncertainty and by laying out some kind of a path—“here’s what we’re thinking”—and making it contingent, of course, on macroeconomic events.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So that’s what we are trying to get at here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Clearly, the focus is on asset purchases around the table, so this B′′ certainly talks in those terms.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A problem that I’m concerned about is that pre-committing to a particular number without making it contingent on macroeconomic developments may not be wise.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Incoming data may not match up with the commitment that you made.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It would be the same thing under interest rate targeting.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You would say, “we’re going to go somewhere today, there’s a projected path out there,” but, of course, it’s always dependent on incoming data.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Alternative B′′ tries to address these issues, and I might say it’s equally well called A′′, because it’s not really tied to particular amounts.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In fact, you might end up with a little more in total here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s very aggressive, let’s put it that way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: First, the form of the statement: You say the main thrust of policy at the beginning of the statement, which is something I’d like to see us do, and we certainly did that under the interest rate targeting regime—we would say right away what we did with the fed funds rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The fed funds rate at zero is not news right now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Even the fact that it’s going to stay at zero for a long time is not news right now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I just moved that part down in the statement.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Most of these statements have that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There are three principles behind this B′′, so let me just talk about them.

speaker: BULLARD
text: First of all, there is the agency MBS plus Treasuries as a group.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Second, there’s a growth rate feature to it, so you talk in terms of growth rates instead of specific numbers.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And the third principle is that you adjust in response to economic developments, so you have this policy rule aspect.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Let me address all three of these.

speaker: BULLARD
text: First, the agency MBS plus Treasuries: This is certainly the type of large-scale asset purchases that we’ve been talking about.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It avoids mention of balance sheet growth as a whole, because you’ve got volatile aspects of the balance sheet that are under what I would call liquidity provision.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There you’ve got the TAF in particular (it’s whoever shows up for the auctions), you’ve got the swaps, and you’ve got the commercial paper facilities.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s now about $1 trillion, as President Lacker was pointing out.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Our own projections expect that to run off as financial conditions improve.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So this version just sets those programs aside and thinks about managing them separately.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The agency MBS plus Treasuries as a group provides some flexibility.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As Trish has pointed out, MBS can be lumpy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You’ve got this refi wave coming in.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So you could do more MBS at certain points, and you could do more Treasuries later, and you don’t have to specify it at the level of the Committee.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There are good arguments on all sides about the choice between MBS or Treasuries, and demerits on both sides, so I think maybe the thing to do is just mix them together and provide some flexibility.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, my own view on this is that they’re both backed by the Treasury effectively, anyway, so I don’t see a lot of difference.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Now you’ve got this persistent component of the balance sheet, which is the MBS plus Treasuries, and that’s going to grow at this 10 percent approximate rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Frankly, it’s an extremely rapid rate, but that’s what we want because we’re in a very sharp downturn here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Then, you’ve got these temporary components of a balance sheet, which are going to run off, hopefully, when the financial market turmoil abates.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And it’s this underlying trend that you want to get the markets to focus on, as the Chairman was saying a minute ago.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So this is a plan for expansion in the persistent components of the balance sheet, and it helps coordinate private sector expectations and reduce uncertainty about policy going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This has been a key private sector concern, as we’ve heard around the table.

speaker: BULLARD
text: All of the contacts are saying to us, “What are you guys doing?

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t understand the policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There are all these announcements.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I can’t figure it out.” So maybe this is a simpler and more transparent approach, without getting into a lot of specifics about particular asset categories.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The biggest thing for me, and perhaps for President Plosser, is that you’re not pre­ committing.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You can adjust as you go along.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is a plan, but, like an interest rate path, it would be contingent on macroeconomic developments, and you’re not stuck with a particular number going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s the third part: You’d be able to adjust this in response to economic developments.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Again, we’re going to be at zero nominal interest rates for a long time, probably globally.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it’s important to try to lead globally and give a signal to other central banks about how they might implement their policies.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is a kind of a feedback rule.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Obviously, we don’t know what the rule is at this point, and we don’t know how much we will react to incoming developments.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s something we have to learn over time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Hopefully, we can figure that out as we go along.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But this would get us going in that direction and provide a credible replacement for our interest rate rules that were taken away from us by events.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s my case for the main part of it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’ll talk just briefly about the other parts of the statement.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The description of the economy, paragraph 3, is whittled down from the text in some of the other statements.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s in response to President Fisher’s comments.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We can certainly say that the economy is in bad shape, but I don’t think we have to say too much more than that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Obviously, because we put convenient numbers on here, you can mix and match with your other favorite descriptions of the economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I agree completely that we should be very aggressive in this situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But we need to be aggressive in an organized way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, we’re taking unprecedented actions.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You have to be careful about going too far in a direction without a plan.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We don’t know what the effects really will be; our models really don’t tell us too much about it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So this alternative holds out options for adjustment as data arrive.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Hopefully it would provide better communication to the private sector, and hopefully you’d get a more effective policy out of that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A lot of communication is not just us talking, but it is saying “I’ve got a clear path for future policy.” I’m very concerned about deflation near term.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’m concerned about a deflation trap in which you go to this new steady state and get stuck there.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But a medium-term risk is that the economy behaves sort of like normal, and if a normal recovery takes hold, then you’ve got a possibly explosive inflationary situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But that’s down the road.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You have to avoid the deflation trap outcome first.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Maybe if we did get to that medium-term stage, this would set us up to be able to react to that situation a little better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you again for constructive suggestions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a couple of questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I do want to point out we did try in alternative A to create a reaction function element in the very last sentence, where we say, “We will be assessing whether a faster pace would be helpful.” Essentially, the pace will be varying as conditions change—it’s hard to be more specific than that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess I have one question for you and one for Trish.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For Trish, maybe you can help me.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What do you think would be the effect of not specifying the breakdown between Treasuries and MBS?

speaker: MOSSER
text: We’d immediately get the question: What’s the breakdown between Treasuries and MBS?

speaker: MOSSER
text: And what are you going to do about agencies?

speaker: MOSSER
text: But the agency debt market is the simple part to answer, because that’s a much smaller market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think we’d end up having to give a hint, or they would take away from our first two operations what your preferences were, whether that was correct or not.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I took it from the discussion that people would like to front-load MBS to the extent that’s feasible.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But this formulation would let you still have growth later on, if you want.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a question for Presidents Plosser and Bullard about the flexibility you get by saying just “per month” without any specification of timeframe.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I imagine you would, therefore, have less of an announcement effect, and it would be more difficult to do a persuasive front-load in that case.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t know why the announcement effect would be any different.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It adds up to the same amount.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, one thing you could say—I’m just trying to be helpful—would be “a combined average of about 10 percent per month in the next few quarters,” or something like that, to give a bit of a horizon.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This also relies on people being able to do geometric calculations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll put that aside for now.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, actually, Mr. Chairman, we did debate whether or not there ought to be horizon on it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I think you could give a horizon if you wanted to, as long as you kept the conditionality that we will monitor this going forward and that it’s subject to economic and financial conditions.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am not sure I understand one point about this.

speaker: LACKER
text: Presidents Bullard and Plosser propose a geometric path.

speaker: LACKER
text: But why not pick an endpoint and go linearly to that?

speaker: LACKER
text: That is what we are doing with the MBS so far.

speaker: LACKER
text: Doesn’t that make more sense?

speaker: LACKER
text: We could still call that 10 percent per month.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I would say in fact, to President Rosengren’s point, one might actually want it to be front-loaded.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we say an “average” of 10 percent a month.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s go on, if I might.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This was the most depressing go-round in a year and a half, and this was a really bad year and a half, so it highlights that we’re far away from where we want to be, both in inflation and in unemployment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: And in terms of communicating with the public, I think that’s what we’re communicating to the public: We’re not where we want to be, and we want to get there as quickly as we can.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I don’t think simple rules on the balance sheet or the monetary base are appropriate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: These are different programs for different problems.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If the interbank market is disrupted, I would expect swaps and TAF to go up.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we have a real problem in other areas, I’d want to do significant asset purchases.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: These are not substitutes, and just having either a balance sheet or a monetary base rule is assuming that these programs are substitutes for each other.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: They’re dealing with different problems.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think this is an opportune time to push down rates as significantly as we can.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think we should be very aggressive.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think everybody’s discussion around the table indicated we should be aggressive.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I like the idea of heavily weighting on MBS purchases; I think that will be the most effective.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I also like the idea that, if we’re going to try to get the most bang for the buck, given that these are experimental programs, we ought to try at least to see what happens with the Treasuries as well.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So my preference would be to do the combination of A and B, which is the $1.15 trillion total, to try to have as big an effect as possible.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: And I would try to front-load it so we get as much impact in the spring as we can.

speaker: LACKER
text: Obviously, sentiment is pretty gloomy around the table, and there’s a fair amount of consensus that we want to make monetary policy more aggressively stimulative with our actions at this meeting, and we’re grappling with how to structure that shift.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it makes sense to embark on a fairly aggressive asset purchase program, but I think we ought to admit that we’re fairly uncertain about how our actions are going to go about affecting the economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: This isn’t different in principle from four years ago— then we were unsure about how another quarter point one way or another was going to affect the economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: But the magnitude of the uncertainty is quite significant here.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve talked around this table for a year and a half about different theories of how these programs and our actions are affecting the economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve talked about credit market frictions, asymmetric information, and other frictions that might inhibit certain markets’ ability to respond adequately to disruptions.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’re not going to settle that debate here.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve also talked about the effect of changes in the monetary base.

speaker: LACKER
text: Banks appear to have absorbed a humongous amount of reserve holdings without a readily discernible effect on a lot of other aspects of their behavior.

speaker: LACKER
text: It suggests banks are more or less indifferent between holding reserve balances and other assets that function as very liquid reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: And, if so, that rationalizes the view I’ve heard some express that increasing the supply of bank reserves is generally going to be ineffective at the margin.

speaker: LACKER
text: And there are some readings of historical episodes of very low interest rates that are consistent with that as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: But this logic has its limits.

speaker: LACKER
text: Commercial banks hold only about $1.3 trillion in Treasury and agency securities, so if there’s a flat spot in the demand curve by banks for bank reserves, it might not take that much more of an increase in our balance sheet to get past that flat spot.

speaker: LACKER
text: And if we do that, I think there’s bound to be some effect; there just has to be a finite upper limit on this flat spot of the demand curve for reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: And even before that, I’d expect some rates of return to have to change.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have a bank in my District that held $136 billion in reserves a couple of days ago.

speaker: LACKER
text: Surely the configuration of repo rates and the other instruments they operate in must have an effect on their willingness to hold that much in reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s really hard to know where that upper bound is—where the end of the flat spot is—because we don’t have much data to draw on; but I think it must be there.

speaker: LACKER
text: So, as I argued yesterday, I think we need to recognize some uncertainty about which theories are the right ones to rely on and how to think about what we do.

speaker: LACKER
text: I take the credit easing we’ve done—program by program, aimed market by market—as arguing that more of those programs in more of those markets is more stimulative than fewer in lower dollar amounts.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that the logic of this focus on the monetary base also suggests that more monetary base is more stimulative than less.

speaker: LACKER
text: So, in the current setting, I think trying to ensure that we at least achieve a certain amount of growth in the base is consistent with both views and worth pursuing.

speaker: LACKER
text: That’s what has motivated my line of questioning for Patricia Mosser, and it motivates why I’d like to suggest that we put a clause in the directive, at the end of sentence four, that says, “but should ensure that the monetary base expands by at least X billion dollars during the intermeeting period.” I don’t think we should conduct policy by slapping 47 constraints on the Desk at every meeting, but it strikes me as a small thing to ask in order to be sure that the stimulus that might be withdrawn as some of these programs roll off is offset as we go forward.

speaker: LACKER
text: I would favor the larger program that you outlined, Mr. Chairman, with the $300 billion, the $750 billion, and the $100 billion increases.

speaker: LACKER
text: I like the idea behind the suggestion of Presidents Plosser and Bullard about putting a commitment to a pattern of purchases in the statement.

speaker: LACKER
text: But for the reasons I just outlined, I’m not sure that gets us where we want to be.

speaker: LACKER
text: It seems to me that if we did that, and yet the balance sheet went down by the end of the year because of a bunch of other stuff rolling off, I’m not sure we’d be persuaded that we had made monetary policy more stimulative or eased credit.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’d like to see us focus on the overall size of our balance sheet and our programs and the base.

speaker: LACKER
text: That would provide as well with an overarching framework, a kind of coherence to what we do, to convey the sense that we’re not just responding market by market, but that we have an overarching conception of how we’re providing stimulus and how we’re going to get through this.

speaker: LACKER
text: And I share the view of Presidents Fisher, Plosser, and Bullard that toning down the language would be useful.

speaker: LACKER
text: It has always been the case that there’s a mapping from words we use, like “somewhat adverse,” to people’s interpretations, which are much scarier than “somewhat adverse.” I think we’re stepping outside that mapping when we go as far as we did in the statement as it’s drafted.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, Trish and Spence, would you folks think about a sentence that could be added to one of the directives, to the effect that “The Desk will strive to ensure that the monetary base” or “the size of the portfolio,” or something like that, “has a positive monthly growth rate,” or whatever you think would be realistic or manageable?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t want to put in something that, just for operational reasons, doesn’t work.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’ve been listening to this, and I’m sympathetic to the different ways we’d like to try to characterize a path.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think it’s very difficult.

speaker: EVANS
text: “Ensure” is a strong word.

speaker: EVANS
text: I had been thinking about maybe something weaker like, “We would expect to see the base grow,” which is sort of an indicator of how we think things are going, but not the policy rule itself.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “It is the expectation of the Committee that the base will be growing over time,” or something like that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m just making this assignment, and they’ll come up with a suggestion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll discuss it at the end, okay?

speaker: EVANS
text: Perhaps with a clause “conditional on stability in certain lending facilities.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll make some kind of attempt.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s just a good faith effort, that’s all.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I could suggest, because of the possibility of SFP or Fed bills, you might want to try both the base and the balance sheet, rather than choose one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we’ll worry about SFP when we get it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me address this issue about pessimism.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just want to point out that the January statement was isomorphic to what we’re proposing to say in this one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s not exactly the same, but it’s very similar.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The only difference is that the last sentence in January was that the “downside risks are significant,” and we leave that out of this one.

speaker: FISHER
text: We did state it before.

speaker: FISHER
text: Therefore, why don’t we just say “continues to contract” or “contract severely?” Again, we’re hammering this point, and I believe we are beginning to be scary.

speaker: FISHER
text: Just for a moment, I want to go back to your 60 Minutes show.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that was a positive.

speaker: FISHER
text: It was a lift, and we engendered some confidence.

speaker: FISHER
text: Here we are just pulling the rug out again.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s the “severe contraction” phrase, I think, that gets attention.

speaker: KOHN
text: Let’s see if I can hit some of the highlights here.

speaker: KOHN
text: I certainly agree with everybody else that we need to be going in with everything we can under the current circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: And the question is: What can we do, and how can we explain it?

speaker: KOHN
text: I favor your combined alternative A plus B. I think that qualifies within the limits of what we can do as a good effort under the current circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: As we discussed yesterday, what we do know is that asset purchases seem to be the most effective thing we can do.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’ve seen the MBS purchases be effective.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it’s a good idea to use all of the tools, and buying Treasuries is one of the tools, so I think we ought to include Treasuries.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think there’s enough evidence from the event studies that that will have a positive effect on financial conditions.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m not worried about the issues of monetizing the debt or inflation expectations, given the size of the output gap and given the fact that we’re working on exit frameworks at the same time and we’ve strengthened our discussion of the long-term inflation objectives.

speaker: KOHN
text: In terms of shifting the emphasis to the base, President Lacker, you talked about uncertainty in linking our portfolio to the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that goes for the base as well.

speaker: KOHN
text: I actually asked a senior official at the Bank of England how he would explain how increasing the base and increasing the money supply were supposed to affect the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I got kind of a shrug of the shoulders and “Well, we’ve run out of this other stuff, so we’re going to talk about this stuff now,” rather than a really coherent explanation of how the transmission channels run from the base to the money supply to the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I guess I’m not ready to put my marbles entirely in that particular basket yet.

speaker: KOHN
text: In particular, I can’t quite link the short-run fluctuations in the base—the meeting-to-meeting or week-to-week fluctuations—to what we’re trying to accomplish.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it depends a lot on why the base would go down.

speaker: KOHN
text: If it went down because the whole demand for credit was going down and the economy was weakening, then we ought to be leaning against that and trying to increase the base.

speaker: KOHN
text: But if it went down because markets were working better or because, for example, Europeans had better access to dollar funding, I don’t think that’s something we necessarily have to lean against.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think, under the current circumstances, seeing a long-term upward trend in the base is useful and useful discipline on the Committee.

speaker: KOHN
text: But linking to a month-to-month growth rate or meeting-to-meeting fluctuations within that long-term trend—I don’t think that will help market confidence, I don’t think that’s really going to be useful to us, and I don’t think it will be seen as putting a new framework that everybody understands around monetary policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: Broad money growth actually has been quite strong in the United States.

speaker: KOHN
text: It was at 14 percent plus in the fourth quarter, and 10 percent in the first two months of the year, so we’re not seeing that kind of tightness.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with President Fisher that the TALF is complex and difficult.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is a difficult situation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we’re constrained, as I said yesterday, by various laws and regulations about what we can do and what’s politically possible in this situation.

speaker: KOHN
text: So it’s very uncomfortable, but I’m not sure we have any alternatives other than the asset purchases on the credit side of the balance sheet.

speaker: KOHN
text: And I think we ought to just push ahead and make the best of a difficult situation.

speaker: KOHN
text: Certainly doing something about legacy assets is very critical to the health of the banking system.

speaker: KOHN
text: If we can contribute, I think we ought to do so, without jeopardizing our ability to carry out monetary policy over the long term or taking credit risk on the balance sheet.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the various wording issues, I’d prefer alternative A or A plus, or whatever it would be in your combined alternative, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: As you can tell from my previous comments, I’m not sure that saying something about the growth in the base on a month-by-month basis or the growth in assets on a month-by-month basis would actually reduce uncertainty.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the markets would kind of wonder what that was about.

speaker: KOHN
text: Maybe we could prepare the way.

speaker: KOHN
text: Maybe we should do some research to look at how these things are linked together.

speaker: KOHN
text: But right now, what they expect us to do is talk about the amount we’re going to buy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the fact that we’re leaning towards MBS is important.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I’d go with the wording of alternative A.

speaker: KOHN
text: My problem with A′ is that I’m imagining what it might be like if we didn’t take any additional actions at the next meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: Suppose at the next meeting we just decided to continue with what we’re doing, then I don’t know what A′ would say.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I’m more comfortable with the ordering of the paragraphs in A than I am with A′.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the first paragraph, I did think the end of the first sentence, “…the economy is undergoing a severe contraction and that the outlook for the next several quarters has worsened,” could be read as suggesting we expect a sharp decline in the economy for several quarters.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I certainly would cross that out.

speaker: KOHN
text: On the rest of it, I wondered, as you did, Mr. Chairman, about cutting back on all of the detail as compared with last time, whether people would notice that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m kind of indifferent and will go along with wherever the Committee wants to come out on that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think we need to say that we’re in a contraction, the near-term outlook is weak, and we expect things to stabilize later.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I can respond very briefly to Governor Kohn, I agree with everything you said about uncertainty, about the mechanisms by which changes in the monetary base are transmitted to economic conditions, and about the difficulty of articulating how those mechanisms would work.

speaker: LACKER
text: I wouldn’t advocate putting all of our marbles in that policy transmission mechanism.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d just note that it’s a viable contender, and we ought to act as if that might be how we’re affecting the economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: Hitting a target for monetary base growth, plus or minus, isn’t what I was advocating.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was just thinking about making sure it’s at least as stimulative as we think it ought to be.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As we talk about this statement, I think it’s sadly ironic that, after we’ve doubled the size of our balance sheet, we’re having a conversation about being worried that it may shrink a little bit.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It’s incredible to me that we would have that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: And I agree with what Governor Kohn said in that I don’t think we should start talking 10 percent monthly growth or whatever it is.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We’re trying to deal with a broken intermediation and banking system at the same time, and I don’t think we can turn it into a monetary policy instrument in terms of how much we expect the balance sheet to grow at this point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: With that, I would say I am much more in favor of statement B as we had it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would admit that the banking system is broken.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That’s part of the reason we’re doing the TALF.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we’re going to expand and we’re going to address the broken intermediation process, we should focus on mortgage-backeds.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That’s what the idea was to begin with.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we now introduce Treasuries into that (1) I think it’s only going to be confusing, and (2) I think we do have to look long term.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our introducing purchases of longer-term securities farther along the yield curve sets a precedent, and I don’t think it’s easy to back off from that once we get through this mess we’re in right now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So that’s why I prefer B. I also want to take just a minute and talk about the legacy TALF.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There’s reference to populist reaction to this, and I actually think that this reaction is justified in important ways.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We ought to think about that, because people are now confused between TARP and TALF, and I think when we add the legacy TALF, it’s going to confuse things even more.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The reason that they’re reacting to it is TARP.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I agree that it was necessary to keep from having a meltdown, but the execution of it was so confusing and so inequitable across the system that it created great backlash.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Some of the backlash was very justified—for example, when you have some banks being told, “You’re going to take it,” and a thousand other banks being told, “You can beg for it,” and following that up with changing the rules, you’re not going to get anything but a backlash.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that’s important to keep in mind.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So as we think about going forward, I come back to President Fisher’s point about needing a decision tree on how we’re going to deal with these legacy assets.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our getting involved in the legacy TALF, as I’ve heard it described to this point, is, I think, very risky—very dangerous, almost—in terms of what the outcomes might be, because there aren’t clear, defined decision trees indicating who’s really going to be accountable for what.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We need to get that clarified before we have another reaction like the one we had recently.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Finally, I do want to come back to something Governor Kohn mentioned yesterday in reference to my comment about using excess reserves to help manage the balance sheet and set the rate floor.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I know that it got off to a rough start, but I think we are getting our sea legs and the industry is getting their sea legs.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we start issuing Fed bills, I think we are introducing another tool that will start out with the best intentions, but expectations will be raised, how we use it will be brought into account, questions will arise about trying to get around debt ceilings and so forth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think we should try to avoid that if we can and see if we can use our interest on excess reserves as a management tool.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So with those comments, I’ll again say I’d go with B.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As I said, I think we’re in the midst of a very severe recession—it’s unlikely to end any time soon.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The optimal policy simulations would take the fed funds rate to negative 6 percent if it could, and because it can’t, I think we have to do everything we possibly can to use our other tools to compensate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to what we should do today, my preference is for the combined alternative that would combine $750 billion of mortgage-backed securities, $100 billion of extra agency debt, and the $300 billion of Treasuries.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I certainly support the MBS purchases.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think they’re likely to have a very positive effect on the housing market, particularly now, and I certainly agree with President Rosengren’s suggestion that we should front-load the purchases for the reasons he gave.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I said yesterday that I would also support purchases of Treasuries.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it would be useful to begin that now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I favor diversification of what we do, given the uncertainties about the impacts of any of these programs.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There’s a principle elucidated by William Brainard 30 years ago that, when policy actions have uncertain effects, you should simultaneously use all of your instruments, and I think that’s a worthwhile principle for us now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A couple of things on language.

speaker: YELLEN
text: One of the differences between A and B concerns the characterization of how long we plan to keep the fed funds rate low.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A states “for an extended period,” while B uses the phrase “for some time.” The fed funds futures market at this point seems to expect rate hikes next year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That’s not our own expectation, and to try to align market expectations better with ours, I would like to see the switch to “an extended period” as in A.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to A or A′—that issue of what goes first—I could certainly accept either.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I was positively inclined toward A′ on the principle that it makes sense—and we’ve always done this— to state right away what the policy decisions are.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Now the focus is not on the fed funds rate, so it makes sense to state that we’ve decided to do such-and-such with respect to programs.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I think that Governor Kohn has made an excellent point, raising the question, “What will we do if we don’t have any action on a particular day?” It may be difficult; we don’t want to keep shifting from one thing to another if we can’t envision how we’re going to write that on the day we don’t do anything new.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I guess I would agree that it’s better to stick with the A formulation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to alternative B′′ that Presidents Bullard and Plosser proposed, I really thought it was a very worthwhile and constructive idea.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There are aspects of it that I liked and that I thought were quite sensible, such as suggesting some conditionality of what we might do relating to economic and financial conditions and having some flexibility in the composition of what we do.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I thought that was very interesting and useful.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But I would emphasize that I don’t agree with the underlying theory that says that there is a relationship between the size of the monetary base and our impact on the economy, and I would associate myself with the comments of President Rosengren and Governor Kohn on this.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I don’t like the language that suggests an emphasis on the size of our balance sheet and the size of the base.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we have a real theoretical disagreement among ourselves as to exactly how our policy works, and I just wouldn’t endorse going in that direction.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Just to respond a little bit, this doesn’t say anything about the monetary base.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This says large-scale asset purchase done in a certain way, which, I guess, is what our model has said.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is just a way to set the asset purchases—that’s my intent.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I said yesterday, I think that it’s important that we do something big, so your combined proposal is closer to that for sure, and I definitely think that we should diversify our actions.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m a little concerned that we’re not going to have a lot of good evidence on how effective these programs are for a few quarters.

speaker: EVANS
text: Maybe we’ll be able to interpret something from how the yields move around, but they also move around a lot anyway.

speaker: EVANS
text: We like to take credit when they move in the right direction.

speaker: EVANS
text: And then other things happen.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t know—it’s very difficult.

speaker: EVANS
text: The delays are: It takes time to implement, it takes time to have an impact, and it takes time to assess.

speaker: EVANS
text: So as President Yellen indicated, we don’t have enough confidence to bank on a single nontraditional channel, I prefer doing more of these.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am a little sympathetic both to the discussion about the usefulness of indicating something about the timing and to the way that Presidents Plosser and Bullard characterized this in terms of growth rates.

speaker: EVANS
text: What did seem to come out in the discussion that I, at least, was not aware of, was how we intend to play these purchases out.

speaker: EVANS
text: There are good market reasons for the way they’re done, and the markets understand that.

speaker: EVANS
text: So finding some way to provide that information, I think, would be useful.

speaker: EVANS
text: I can see why the growth rate is attractive, but indicating front-loading or something about the time element seems to be important.

speaker: EVANS
text: We do have an awful lot of programs in place that are intended to be stimulative.

speaker: EVANS
text: There’s everything that we’ve done, with the TALF increasing, and there’s what the FDIC has done, with the TLGP.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t believe that we’ve seen anything in terms of the outlook for what the FDIC part of this new program, with the Treasury purchasing bad bank assets, would be either, but presumably that would be stimulative as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: By the time we put all of this in place, we’ve got a lot that should be helping out.

speaker: EVANS
text: So the question I have is how to quantify what is enough.

speaker: EVANS
text: As Governor Kohn mentioned, we should be doing everything we can do, so I think the combined proposal is better.

speaker: EVANS
text: Frankly, I don’t understand why we couldn’t improve this to $500 billion in Treasuries, too.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’re a little arbitrary, it seems to me, in terms of the total magnitude.

speaker: EVANS
text: I would like to be able to point to something like our Bluebook analysis—an analysis where we think that this is as close as possible to our best model-based thinking, on what the optimal policy response would be to reach the best we can achieve for the unemployment rate, recognizing that there are outcomes we cannot achieve.

speaker: EVANS
text: The reason for wanting something like this is, I would like it to be big enough now so that we can shift the hurdle for additional action at the next meeting more toward “the outlook has now deteriorated further, and we need some type of action.” Because, at the next meeting, we’re still going to have calls for “What’s next?

speaker: EVANS
text: What’s next?” We know how to think about responding in terms of the fed funds rate and where the target is, but the target for asset purchases is less clear, so that’s why my preference is for more now so that we can shift that burden.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’d be willing to expand the Treasury purchases to $500 billion, but nobody else has indicated that.

speaker: EVANS
text: Finally, I think that we can spend an awful lot of time trying to get the wording exactly right so that we’re all happy with it.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think it’s going to be incumbent upon all of us to make some public comment.

speaker: EVANS
text: When we talk in public, some of these issues will come up, and I think some of it will naturally be fleshed out if there are residual uncertainties.

speaker: EVANS
text: Obviously, when you speak, Mr. Chairman, you clarify things quite a bit, but there might be some things for the rest of us to say.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The rationale for a slightly smaller purchase of Treasuries is that we don’t know what the effect will be, and it’s kind of a “toe in the water” thing.

speaker: EVANS
text: I guess I didn’t indicate that I do prefer alternative A the way it’s written.

speaker: EVANS
text: In terms of the next meeting, the alternative A′ issue could be dealt with by saying something like “the Committee decided not to change its policies or its programs.” In order to shift the burden, I would like to consider whether there is some language such that “with today’s action we anticipate” this better outcome in the last sentence.

speaker: EVANS
text: That would help a little bit there, but it’s just a suggestion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am informed, President Fisher, that you have to leave for a plane.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am also informed that today is your 60th birthday.

speaker: FISHER
text: What a nice way to celebrate my birthday.

speaker: FISHER
text: With people I greatly respect, and I just want to say I hope I live to be as old as Don Kohn.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We do have to move along here.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think the case for increased asset purchases is pretty compelling.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It’s the sense of the Committee, and certainly I agree with that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I have to think through a series of other decisions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The first one has to do with scale, and my thinking coming in was that the scale needed to be proportionate to the deterioration in the outlook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Speaking at least for myself and the Atlanta analysis, clearly, there has been deterioration since January, but it’s within the range that I would have assumed at that time was plausible.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I’m a little concerned about overreacting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: When we first got the alternatives, alternative B was $500 billion, and that, of course, was entirely in mortgage-backed securities and agency notes.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Yesterday we learned that the TALF is likely to roll out slowly.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That’s information that, I assume, is not going to be understood by the public.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It would probably undermine the program if we said that we expected that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I had factored the TALF into my sense of proportional response.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I favor the alternatives that are below $1 trillion dollars.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I don’t want to overstate this, but I think we don’t have good guideposts for how to size the action, so I think it’s reasonable to ask: Will the public infer from our actions that we know something that they don’t, and is this response of over $1 trillion—which will probably get some headlines— really a signal that things are even worse than they actually are and in that sense could dig us a little bit deeper?

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding timing: if we go with the mortgage-backed securities alternative, I do favor the views of President Rosengren that there’s a chance of accelerating that and making it have high impact in the near term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I can support the Treasury idea.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But I actually think the central question is the choice between Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I can support Treasuries, but my bias really is to favor the mortgage-backed securities option, so that would be one of the option Bs.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I like that for its certainty, its impact on housing, and its clarity in communications.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I mentioned yesterday in my comments about communications, certainly what I’m hearing is that many of our constituencies would prefer simplicity and not a lot of new programs, so I’m leaning against the Treasury purchases because it adds complicating factors.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But if we are going to support the Treasury purchases, I endorse Governor Tarullo’s suggestion that we explain why we did it very clearly.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: For example, if we are doing it for liquidity reasons, then we should explain that; if we’re doing it for the purpose of scaling up the balance sheet, we should explain that; if we believe that there are spillover effects, we should be explicit about that in our rationale.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding statement content, I have some sympathy for the version offered by Presidents Plosser and Bullard, but I’m not sure we can avoid quantities.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think the logical question that the press is going to ask, having been conditioned to hearing quantities, is: “How much does this add up to?” It’s very hard for us not to provide at least some estimate of that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Conceivably there is some way of crafting language that would address both the pace of purchases as well as the ultimate quantity.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I don’t know how specific we have to be in the directive to make it a workable directive.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I’d leave that up to the Desk.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’m also okay with toning down “severe contraction”—that was my original reaction when I read the alternatives a few days ago—to something that’s not quite as stark as that.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding statement structure, I don’t have a strong feeling.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think we have two options.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: You either have a structure that builds up to the action, which has been our traditional approach, or the action followed by the rationale.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I have a slight preference for building up to the action, based on Governor Kohn’s comment, namely, what happens if we don’t, in fact, have an action.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: We certainly want to be consistent going forward, as much as we can, on how these things are put together.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So given all of that, where I come out is in support of alternative B, but, when it comes down to the vote, I will support A, A′, or A plus or B [laughter], or B′.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Yes, I’ll end with a reference to Charlie Brown: You know, sometimes I’m wishy-washy and sometimes I’m not.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My definitive support is for alternative B.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lockhart, on the issue of explaining the Treasury purchases in alternative A, if we do the combination, we’d want to import the sentence from alternative A that starts with, “Moreover, to help improve conditions in private credit markets, the Committee decided....” So that follows up the previous language and explains that we’re not monetizing the debt and so on.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: It is clear to me from our discussion of the outlook that more action is needed, but as I said earlier, I also think we need to focus on the clarity of our communications in order to build public confidence.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Looking over the options that were presented today, I do prefer alternative B. I am clearly in favor of aggressive action, and as I noted yesterday I am open to the purchase of longer-term Treasuries, but as President Lockhart just mentioned, in the interest of effective communications, I think we need to better explain why we decided to engage in the purchase of Treasury securities at this time.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Brian gave us four reasons why we might want to consider that, and as you know, Mr. Chairman, in our statement in January we did say that we would do that in order to improve conditions in private credit markets, but I still think that may be a little too vague.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: While the staff comments yesterday indicated a little less certainty that we get a larger bang for the buck if we purchase MBS versus Treasuries, I think we do have evidence that purchases of MBS have generated significant interest rate reductions just through their announcement effects.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Also, the staff simulations highlighted yesterday the economic importance of stabilizing housing prices and the effects on household wealth.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So, with the larger purchase of MBS along with some of the Treasury initiatives working in tandem, I think alternative B is a preferred way to go.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In terms of the statement language, the option of B′ or B, I slightly favor putting our actions in the front line or the first paragraph.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: There is some premium, I think, on clear and easily verifiable actions in these difficult and confusing times, although, after listening to Governor Kohn’s comments about “what do we do when we don’t take actions,” I see that that might be a little confusing.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But overall, B′ is my preference at this meeting.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, it seems like almost everything is fair game.

speaker: STERN
text: So let me just make a few comments.

speaker: STERN
text: I expressed my reservations about legacy TALF yesterday, so I won’t reiterate those.

speaker: STERN
text: I hope I was clear.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to purchasing assets, I do favor including purchases of Treasuries.

speaker: STERN
text: I did back in December, I think, when we first talked about it.

speaker: STERN
text: So I would certainly go down that path.

speaker: STERN
text: That leads me to alternative A and the language, and I’m willing to go with the larger quantity that you proposed.

speaker: STERN
text: All of the quantities are around $1 trillion—quite honestly, I’m not sure we’re going to get a big difference in terms of market or macroeconomic effects at the end of the day, but I can certainly go with that.

speaker: STERN
text: I would start with the language in alternative A.

speaker: STERN
text: Just a couple of comments about that.

speaker: STERN
text: I think I would be in favor of abbreviating the litany of the economic conditions.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t know that it adds all that much at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: If we say “severe contraction,” I think that gets the message across.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to A versus A′, you could probably take care of Governor Kohn’s concern at the next meeting by just saying, if we didn’t do anything new, that the Committee reiterated its intention, and I think that would probably take care of it.

speaker: STERN
text: But I don’t see any great advantage, quite honestly, to reworking it, at least at this point.

speaker: STERN
text: So I have a mild preference for A as written.

speaker: STERN
text: Having said that, I do think the Plosser-Bullard approach has merit, if we can get over some of these questions that have arisen, such as, “What will people in the market make of it?” and “Will people still want quantities?” and “Is there a way of integrating that approach with some quantities, if that would help clarify things?” I think those are all worth serious consideration.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t have the answers today, so I’m not proposing that we adopt that.

speaker: STERN
text: But I do think that perhaps there are at least the beginnings of a framework there that we ought to be thinking about at future meetings and that may serve to help our communication and help people in the markets understand better than they do right now where we intend to go.

speaker: WARSH
text: Just a few points first.

speaker: WARSH
text: Given the policy uncertainty that we’ve all described that is out there in the world, it strikes me our preferences here in this room should be putting a greater emphasis on things that are clear and purposeful versus those that are big and bold and more.

speaker: WARSH
text: Clear, purposeful, big, bold, and more—if you could pull it all together in one fell swoop, that would be fine, but absent that, I would put the preference on clear and purposeful.

speaker: WARSH
text: We’ve talked a lot about the makeup of our balance sheet.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would just reiterate a truism which I think still has merit—our biggest asset here is our credibility, which is a function of a lot of things, including clarity, success, and trying to speak as much as we practicably can with one voice; and that will obviously govern my vote in support of the consensus emerging from this discussion.

speaker: WARSH
text: Having said that, I continue to have a strong preference for avoiding Treasuries for reasons I described yesterday and given that, since December, markets seem to see us as alternately having some affection and disaffection for purchasing Treasuries for reasons that have been hard to understand.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we need to be prepared to address that issue if, as I expect, we include Treasury purchases in our statement today.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of the size of these various elements, I think the only thing worse than buying Treasuries is to buy them in such a tepid way that we don’t have any effect.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think if we’re in, we’re in.

speaker: WARSH
text: And I take very little comfort from the idea that we would be somehow testing this out just a bit.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think, in effect, what we’re really all saying, Mr. Chairman, is we are balance-sheet-constrained.

speaker: WARSH
text: There is only so much of these new assets, whether they be mortgage-backed or Treasuries, that we are comfortable with, given the risks to our flexibility.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I am troubled that the $300 billion will be perceived to be relatively light.

speaker: WARSH
text: But given people’s preferences around here, I won’t spend more time on that.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of some of the language, I concur with the emerging consensus that we should delete some of the carnage in describing the economy on the grounds that it is well understood.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’ve got next to nothing to offer on style between prime and nonprime.

speaker: WARSH
text: And on the Plosser–Bullard proposals, I think that it’s a pretty interesting framework.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t think it’s ready for prime time, so I’d associate myself with what President Stern said, that it would be a useful way in which we could start to think in anticipation of our next meeting.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I don’t think at this moment we can easily capture that in a way which goes back to first principles of being clear and precise.

speaker: DUKE
text: I am actually in favor of the largest amount that we can all agree on.

speaker: DUKE
text: My objective, as I stated yesterday, is to have the biggest effect on housing that we possibly can.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of how we explain that, I do like the prime version, because it puts the action first.

speaker: DUKE
text: Having spent more of my time reading the statements than issuing them, it seems to me the first paragraph was always the action paragraph.

speaker: DUKE
text: And I think for a good time to come this will be our action.

speaker: DUKE
text: In addition, I think the easier we can make this to report, the better off we are.

speaker: DUKE
text: If you get reporters, particularly third- and fourth-level reporters, on a deadline and all they read is the first part and skim through the rest, they may not necessarily pick up the size of this action.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I have a pretty strong preference for the prime version.

speaker: DUKE
text: Also, while I find it interesting to put it on a percent-growth basis, we’ve already started down the path with the dollar amounts, and I think continuing with the way we’ve been communicating it already has some certainty and some simplicity.

speaker: DUKE
text: To me it feels like announcing a stock repurchase in the private sector.

speaker: DUKE
text: In that case, you size your stock repurchase in relation to the amount of outstanding shares that you have, and it’s perceived that way and tends to impact your price that way.

speaker: DUKE
text: Finally, on measuring effectiveness, I think the questions at this point would be: How big an effect does it have immediately on housing, on the stock market, and on things that create wealth, and how quickly do we see whether or not it has spillover effects?

speaker: DUKE
text: The last piece is this sentence that says we “will be assessing whether a faster pace of asset purchases would be helpful in improving credit market conditions.” I originally liked that, because it implied that we were willing to do even more.

speaker: DUKE
text: On thinking about it, though, there’s something to be said for creating a little bit of fear in the housing markets that this is a window of opportunity to refinance or purchase.

speaker: DUKE
text: So if it doesn’t look like rates may go down further if you wait, then I think that’s got some real value.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I suppose ultimately I come down in favor of A plus′.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I must find new nomenclature, I’m afraid.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Of the options on the table right now, I favor the combined option.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Like Governor Duke, I would have been receptive to a higher number, and I guess President Evans would have been as well.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The reason for that is twofold: (1) just because of my understanding of the magnitude of the challenge right now, and (2), as President Evans said, I think, it’s really very important for us to be able to project a strong but adaptable approach to monetary policy, not just until the next meeting, but over the course of the next year.

speaker: TARULLO
text: It seems to me that by rolling out a bigger, more ambitious headline number, if you will, but then saying we’re going to implement that over an extended period of time, it gives us the opportunity at each of the next several Open Market Committee meetings to say “we are staying with an aggressive policy.” In contrast to when you’re working with the fed funds rate and you either have to stay where you are or reduce it another 25 or 50 basis points, here one could say that the Desk is continuing in an aggressive fashion to make purchases.

speaker: TARULLO
text: That leads into the issue of communication more generally, and like President Lockhart, I think the maximum amount of explanation of what we’re doing and why we’re doing it is important.

speaker: TARULLO
text: There is and has been over the last several days a near obsession among markets about whether or not we are going to engage in large-scale purchases of Treasuries.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I will predict that there’s going to be a lot of speculation about why we’re doing it.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I will also predict that the explanation that it’s “helping improve conditions in private credit markets” will not seem to most commentators to be a complete explanation.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Thus, in an effort to respond to Governor Warsh’s concerns—which I don’t share to the extent of being unwilling to do securities purchases, but do think are important—I would hope that in the delicate but important arena of communications outside of the formal statement, we will be able to find a way quite quickly to clarify why we’re doing this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think one argument that’s been made here is that we want to diversify in different markets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, there’s a need for more stimulus, and it looks like less support is going to be coming from other quarters, so a substantial escalation is appropriate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, given what I said yesterday, I favor doing both.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would favor scaling up the Treasuries’ size to $500 billion from $300 billion, per Governor Warsh’s comment that, if you’re going to do this, you might as well do it in size.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think the balance sheet constraint here is really meaningful, because we can sell or repo the Treasuries at a future date.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I just don’t think that’s a reason to make the distinction between $300 billion and $500 billion, and I think we’ll have a more definitive test of how the market perceives this if we do $500 billion rather than $300 billion.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: At $300 billion, if we don’t get much response, we’re not going to know if it was because the market thought the scale was small.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think $500 billion is a more appropriate metric.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I favor A over A′ just because I think it’s simpler and it’s more consistent with what we’ve been doing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And I agree that we should not be quite so scary in reminding people of how badly the economy is doing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s try to put this all together.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most importantly, I think there’s a pretty strong consensus for the combined package, the total of $1.15 trillion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I heard the point about doing even more in Treasuries.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess I think that just crossing the Rubicon will have a significant announcement effect, because it will signal our willingness to do more if necessary in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am a little concerned about misinterpretation of what we’re doing, so I guess I would like to propose to stay where we are for the moment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We can always change it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I very much appreciate the contribution from Presidents Plosser and Bullard.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think we’re quite ready to go there, but I do think we can start communicating in that way and start trying to talk about percentages as we talk in speeches and other contexts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think, in particular, since we want to front-load, it’s hard to put it in percentage terms at the moment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I think that to get the maximum effect in the short run that Governor Duke talked about, it would be better to have a headline number.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I think it’s actually a very constructive point, and we should think about ways to move in that direction if we can.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So what I propose is to start from alternative B. I think it’s reasonable to do either B or B′, but I didn’t hear a huge amount of demand to go to B′.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I heard the concerns about the first paragraph.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What if we say that “the economy continues to contract,” as some suggested?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “Information received since the Federal Open Market Committee met in January indicates the economy continues to contract,” period, and we’d drop “the outlook has worsened” as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then, if you like, we could drop, say, the sentence that starts with “Weaker sales prospects,” but I think that is consistent with our previous style in trying to describe elements of the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then I would note that we have a somewhat optimistic ending in this paragraph.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I don’t think that it’s going to be a huge shocker to anybody, and we do have to motivate why we’re taking such a strong action.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I had suggested this notion of putting in market forces in terms of returning to stability.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I didn’t know whether you had forgotten that, but nobody ever commented on it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I was trying to keep life as simple as I can, but let’s see here.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: “The Committee anticipates that market forces and policy actions will contribute to …”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are people okay with substituting that sentence?

speaker: TARULLO
text: To what market forces are you referring?

speaker: KOHN
text: I think what I heard around the table, Mr. Chairman, was not much confidence that market forces are moving in that direction and might even be moving in the other direction.

speaker: PLOSSER
