text: There’s not much confidence that government forces are going to fix it either.

speaker: LACKER
text: Surely, if the economy recovers, it’s going to be a combination of policy actions and market forces.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, all we’re saying here is that these things will contribute.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re not saying that they’re the only reason.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I just want to press on that a bit.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It gives the impression that we’re hanging on a thread as to what the Congress does or what we do or something like that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t think you want to leave that impression.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Despite what the government does, you might recover faster or you might recover slower, and I think you should leave that thought in the minds of private citizens.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, I think what we’re saying here is that we anticipate that these things will contribute to an overall dynamic.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In B, in the third paragraph, we have the sentence about the “additional $750 billion of agency mortgage-backed securities, bringing its total purchases of these securities to $1.25 trillion this year, and to increase its purchases of agency debt this year by $100 billion to a total of $200 billion.” So that’s exactly as in B.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Can we say something like, “the Desk has been instructed to…”?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I have a possible sentence, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: “The timing of these purchases will be determined, in part, by conditions in primary and secondary mortgage markets.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think that’s what people wanted to say, though.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think it’s fine for the Desk just to accelerate its purchases, and the market is going to see it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is it okay to do it that way and not put it in the statement?

speaker: MOSSER
text: I had something very similar to Brian’s.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I actually stole the last sentence from alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Part of the issue, Mr. Chairman, is that we don’t know exactly when the bulge in issuance is going to happen.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll come to that one.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s back up a second.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is the question of “federal funds rate for some time.” President Yellen suggested going to “for an extended period.”

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think that’s more accurate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are we okay with that?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Can somebody explain to me how I am supposed to interpret that change?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Because conditions have worsened, our expected liftoff time is probably longer than it was.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then we have the sentence on the agency debt—that’s okay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then the next sentence about “prepared to purchase long-term Treasuries” is to be replaced by the sentence in alternative A: “Moreover, to help improve conditions in private credit markets, the Committee decided to purchase $300 billion of longer-term Treasury securities over the next six months.”

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Are we putting “up to’s” in front of all of these numbers?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do we have “up to’s” in the original announcements?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think they are always “up to.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let’s make sure we have consistency with that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As Governor Duke and some others noted, there were questions about the last part.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We should end the last sentence, “The Committee will continue to monitor carefully the size and composition of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet in light of evolving financial market developments,” period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we say “in light of evolving financial and economic developments” instead?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I’m dropping all the stuff about assessing our lending programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At this point we’re in an assessment mode.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the only question remaining, Brian, is the “up to.”

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think that may be actually difficult to work in here quickly in some cases just as a grammatical issue.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the one issue, though, is to make sure it’s not quite so definitive that you are committing to purchase exactly that number.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we put “up to” in front of each?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it’s “up to an additional $750 billion.”

speaker: KOHN
text: “…agency debt this year by up to $100 billion.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And then on Treasuries, “purchase up to $300 billion.” Brian, are you ready to try to read?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: From the top, “Information received since the Federal Open Market Committee met in January indicates that the economy continues to contract.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The rest is the same, and the second paragraph is the same.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So the third paragraph: “In these circumstances, the Federal Reserve will employ all available tools to promote economic recovery and to preserve price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee will maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 0 to ¼ percent and anticipates that economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate for an extended period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To provide greater support to mortgage lending and the housing markets, the Committee decided today to increase the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet further by purchasing up to an additional $750 billion of agency mortgage-backed securities, bringing its total purchases of these securities to up to $1.25 trillion this year, and to increase its purchases of agency debt this year by up to $100 billion to a total of up to $200 billion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, to help improve conditions in private credit markets, the Committee decided to purchase up to $300 billion of longer-term Treasury securities over the next six months” Then there is the TALF sentence.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Then, “The Committee will continue to monitor carefully the size and composition of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet in light of evolving financial and economic developments.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do we have something, Trish?

speaker: MOSSER
text: About either the pace of purchases or the size of the balance sheet?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The directive is to be made consistent, and we said something along the lines that—

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have to put the Treasury sentence in the directive.

speaker: LACKER
text: Can we use Directive A?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t issue the directive at 2:15, do we?

speaker: DANKER
text: But we vote on it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll put in the Treasury part.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then, can you include a sentence like, “The Desk will endeavor to ensure that the size of the portfolio rose”?

speaker: MOSSER
text: We could say, “The Committee anticipates that the combination of outright purchases and various liquidity facilities outstanding will cause the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet to expand in the coming months.” We’re a little hesitant to pick the next intermeeting period because of the lumpiness of mortgages, honestly.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But if that would suffice, we think that would work best from our perspective.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are we ready for a vote now?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Debbie, would you call the roll, please?

speaker: DANKER
text: Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Dudley Yes Governor Duke Yes President Evans Yes Governor Kohn Yes President Lacker Yes President Lockhart Yes Governor Tarullo Yes Governor Warsh Yes President Yellen Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next meeting is April 28 and 29.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Lunch will be available, and over lunch, Laricke Blanchard will provide us with an update on congressional activities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is a joint meeting of the FOMC and the Board, so I need a motion to close the Board meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our first item of business is to get reports on Desk operations, liquidity programs, and balance sheet developments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me turn first to Trish Mosser.

speaker: MOSSER
text: 1 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Financial conditions have improved modestly in the last month and a half, reacting to aggressive policy actions in many countries, some improvement in the near-term outlook for the largest financial firms, and tentative signs that the free fall in global economic activity may be leveling off a bit.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Equities are up, credit spreads are narrower, the dollar is weaker (that’s probably a good sign in this environment), volatility is down, and liquidity in many markets has improved.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Despite these modest improvements, financial markets and institutions, by any normal measure, are very stressed.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In short, the calm in markets is very uneasy, and continued improvement will depend critically on upcoming policy initiatives—particularly the outcome of the capital assessment program (CAP)—and of course, on the evolution of the macroeconomy.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The May 4 release of the CAP results is a major risk event for financial markets, probably the largest since the passage of the TARP legislation last fall.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Importantly, the risk surrounds not so much the disclosure of which large banks are likely to need additional capital in a stressed environment or even how much capital they might need.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The important new information in the CAP release is the plan for how those capital holes will be filled, including what next steps banks will need to take, how and when government capital may be used, and what conditions will be imposed upon the banks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Lack of clarity about standards and future actions is likely to lead to even greater uncertainty about the future viability of large banks, and it increases significantly the risk of bank runs—in either wholesale or retail markets.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As exhibit 1 shows, credit default swap spreads have narrowed in recent weeks, as macro news has been less dire and equity markets have rallied.

speaker: MOSSER
text: High-yield spreads have fallen more than 500 basis points since early March, and notably cash bond spreads of both investment-grade and high-yield corporates have fallen even more than CDS spreads, signaling some improvement in corporate bond market liquidity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Credit spreads of financial firms have also narrowed—by more than 100 basis points 1 The materials used by Ms. Mosser are appended to this transcript (appendix 1).

speaker: MOSSER
text: since early March—but much of the narrowing has occurred outside the U.S. banking sector.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Concern about the nature of government intervention in the banking industry has prevented a significant narrowing in spreads, despite stronger equity prices.

speaker: MOSSER
text: A comparison of exhibits 2 and 3 makes this clear.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Despite rising stock prices and declining volatility, most U.S. bank CDS spreads have widened in the last month and a half.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In contrast, European banks, whose equity price performance is similar to that of U.S. banks, have had a narrowing of CDS spreads.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Setting the CAP and the political environment aside for the moment, exhibit 4 shows that banks’ first-quarter performance surprised to the upside, with most large global banks beating the Q1 earnings expectations, in some cases by wide margins.

speaker: MOSSER
text: That said, however, the quality and the sustainability of these earnings have been questioned, and the uncertainty about banks’ ability to absorb future losses— particularly related to consumers, leveraged loans, and commercial real estate— remains high.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As you can see in the last column, regulatory capital ratios for most large U.S. banks exceed requirements, but their ratios of common equity to capital (in the third column) remain quite low.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Tangible common equity relative to assets has become the de facto measure of bank health for most market participants, for a couple of reasons.

speaker: MOSSER
text: First, losses have to be covered by revenue and common equity, and given market uncertainty about the future size of bank losses, more common equity is viewed as a sign of health regardless of other types of capital.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Second, the public policy focus on potential needs for additional common equity (directly or through convertible preferred equity) has increased the market’s focus on that measure.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It is particularly interesting to note that European banks, in the bottom half of the table, have significantly lower tangible common equity ratios (and regulatory ratios) than U.S. firms.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Moreover, most analysts believe that European banks are not as far along in writing down their assets as their U.S. counterparts, and they have proportionally more recession-related losses ahead of them.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Nonetheless, European bank equity performance has been about the same as that for U.S. banks; and as I noted earlier, European bank credit spreads have narrowed, whereas those of U.S. banks have widened.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Another measure of the near-term uncertainty regarding U.S. banks can be seen in the term structure of bank CDS spreads in exhibit 5.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Normally CDS term structures slope up slightly.

speaker: MOSSER
text: However, currently banks’ CDS spreads are inverted, suggesting that if banks can survive the next two years, then the probability that senior debt holders will face losses is significantly diminished.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Despite the hand-wringing over the near-term future of the banks, liquidity conditions in many markets have improved.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In particular, some of the unexploited profit opportunities that we have noted in the past are now actually being exploited.

speaker: MOSSER
text: For example, in exhibit 6, the spread between three-month funding in the foreign exchange swap market relative to LIBOR has narrowed to pre-crisis levels.

speaker: MOSSER
text: This reflects better liquidity and trading conditions as well as a willingness of banks and others to take some additional risk onto their balance sheets.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Similarly, exhibit 7 shows a decline in the average absolute difference between actual and modeled Treasury yields, reflecting an increased willingness by market participants—banks, dealers, hedge funds, and so forth—to commit balance sheets and to arbitrage away the price differences in the Treasury market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: At the bottom of the page, exhibit 8 shows jumbo and conforming 30-year mortgage rates.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Not only have both mortgage rates come down, but the spread between them (in orange) has actually narrowed since the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: MOSSER
text: You might well be surprised at this.

speaker: MOSSER
text: After all, the secondary market for securitizing jumbo mortgages remains closed, and the Fed purchase program is focused solely on conforming mortgages.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So one might expect that, whatever effect the Fed’s program has had in lowering conforming rates, this progress could well be to the detriment of the jumbo market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But that is not what has happened.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Jumbo rates appear to have fallen about 50 basis points in response to the decline in Treasury yields after the March FOMC meeting and notably have remained at those levels since then.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I have already highlighted one market response to our Treasury purchase program; let me turn there next.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As you can see in exhibit 9, the FOMC’s program to purchase $300 billion in long-term Treasuries by September had an immediate announcement impact on long-term Treasury yields.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But since then, long yields have drifted higher and are now just 10 to 15 basis points below the pre-March FOMC levels.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Of course, it’s hard to know the counterfactual here.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Given the large quantity of new Treasury issuance and less dismal macro news, Treasury yields might be well above their mid-March levels in the absence of Fed purchases.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We are more encouraged by the effect of the purchase program on volatility and liquidity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibit 10 shows that implied volatility in both Treasury and swaps markets fell sharply on the announcement and have remained low.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Actual volatility has fallen as well.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Market participants tell us that, although our purchases may not prevent long­ term Treasury yields from rising, they expect that such increases will be more orderly because of our regular presence in the market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Market participants are already discussing (and pricing) what may happen when the Treasury purchase program ends.

speaker: MOSSER
text: At present, most expect that the Treasury purchase program will be expanded and extended beyond September.

speaker: MOSSER
text: However, the risk that the program may expire in September is reflected in options prices.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Implied volatility over the next six months has fallen, but volatility over the subsequent six months has been rising in recent weeks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The Desk is focusing its purchases in the 2-to-10-year segment of the Treasury curve, consistent with the FOMC’s directive to help improve conditions in private credit markets.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As you can see from exhibit 11, we are making smaller purchases outside this target range—to the disappointment of some market participants—but will continue to concentrate most of the $300 billion in purchases between two and ten years.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Somewhat to our surprise, we are purchasing a sizable amount of on-the-run Treasuries.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Because of the very large amount of new Treasury supply and the continued pressure on dealers to keep their balance sheets small, on­ the-runs are being offered to us in large sizes and at quite competitive prices relative to the market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: One last note about the Treasury market: This Friday a new market standard of charging for failures to deliver in the Treasury market will go into effect.

speaker: MOSSER
text: While we wholeheartedly believe that this will improve Treasury market liquidity when interest rates are low by reducing the incentives to deliberately fail, there may be some anomalous Treasury movements in upcoming weeks as market participants adjust to the new standard.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Turning to the mortgage-backed-securities purchase program, exhibit 12 shows the daily pattern of our agency MBS purchases, including the step-up in average size after the March FOMC meeting.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Our purchases have been a little smoother in recent weeks largely because volatility is lower.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Early on we bought more on days when MBS prices were low and less on days when prices were high.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As volatility has declined, there are fewer of those days.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In addition, because volatility is lower, originators are selling more forward and at a steady pace, which is reflected in our purchases.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We are purchasing TBAs (the forward MBS) at about $135 billion per month, although we anticipate that delivery will be lumpy and that June deliveries of MBS, in particular, may be very large.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibit 13 shows a limited announcement effect on agency MBS and mortgage rates after the March FOMC.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Since then, however, primary rates have drifted lower, and secondary MBS yields have been stable, despite the rise in Treasury yields.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Given the size of our MBS purchase program, we are not surprised at our ability to influence secondary-market MBS yields, but we have a more limited ability to influence primary mortgage rates.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The good news is that the primary–secondary mortgage spread has not widened with the recent large refinancing wave (unlike earlier this year), but overall the spread remains quite wide by historical standards.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The spread is affected by a number of other factors, including fees charged by the GSEs; the costs of hedging mortgage inventories, servicing spreads, and valuations; and the pricing power and capacity constraints of the originators.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Unfortunately, our purchases can help to influence only some of these factors—specifically, hedging and pipeline costs—and the Administration’s housing program can help to lower GSE costs and servicer costs, but the other factors (in particular, pricing power and capacity constraints) may, in the future, work to push spreads higher.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibit 14 makes clear why our ability to influence MBS yields is larger than our ability to move Treasury yields.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Our MBS purchase program—both to date and as planned through the end of 2009—represents a sizable portion of expected new MBS supply this year.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In contrast, our announced Treasury purchases amount to less than a third of expected issuance over the life of the program.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Although the TALF subscription in April was even smaller than we had anticipated, we are somewhat encouraged by the price response and the fact that non- TALF securitizations have come to market as well.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibit 15 shows that secondary- market spreads on triple-A-rated ABS continued to narrow after both TALF subscriptions.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Moreover, the yields on new securitizations have been at least 100 basis points tighter (and in some cases, as much as 700 basis points tighter) than the spreads in exhibit 15.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Much of this drop in yield is due to better liquidity conditions and the fact that TALF subscriptions have provided the market with some price transparency for the first time in months.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As shown in exhibit 16, better liquidity and pricing have encouraged non-TALF securitizations as well—particularly in auto loans and credit cards, where activity had effectively ground to a halt last fall.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As in our purchase programs, one measure of success for the TALF is whether other market participants follow us in.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If the TALF, even in small sizes, can provide some price discovery and a bit of liquidity to the ABS market, it could be a catalyst for improving credit conditions.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In short, the economics of the TALF work.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But the program continues to be dogged by the slow take-up by borrowers, particularly by political baggage, including repeated contradictory statements by various public officials regarding the TARP-related “rules of the road” for borrowers on issues such as executive compensation.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The outlook for the upcoming May 5 subscription is for six to eight consumer securitizations for an estimated $7 billion to $9 billion.

speaker: MOSSER
text: On the supply side, as many as 14 TALF-eligible deals could come to the May subscription and 12 additional deals in June; but given the uncertainties on the demand side of the market, we are hesitant to predict a sizable subscription at this point.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The liquidity facilities—the TAF, the swaps, the commercial paper and money fund facilities, the TSLF, the PDCF, and the PCF—continue to shrink as conditions in money markets have improved.

speaker: MOSSER
text: LIBOR, foreign-exchange swap, and financial CP spreads are all narrower since the March FOMC meeting.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Some of this is due to reduced demand for funding as financial firms delever and term out their debt, particularly through the FDIC guarantee program.

speaker: MOSSER
text: However, market participants do report some increase in the availability of term funding.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Although most of the programs are slowly winding down, the CPFF—shown in exhibit 17—is lumpy.

speaker: MOSSER
text: This week about $150 billion in CPFF paper is maturing.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Since yesterday, $85 billion of this paper has matured, but less than half of that—about $40 billion—has been reissued to the facility.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If this trend continues for the week, CPFF outstandings could fall below $175 billion.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Exhibit 18 summarizes the overall trends in the balance sheet, most notably the step-up in purchase programs and the continued shrinking of liquidity programs.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The balance sheet grew more than 8 percent in March and 5½ percent in April (at monthly rates).

speaker: MOSSER
text: This has been accompanied by similarly impressive growth rates in the monetary base.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The lumpiness of several of the programs—CPFF and MBS purchases, in particular—makes it unlikely that we will achieve steady growth of the balance sheet from week to week or even month to month; however, the balance sheet and the monetary base will almost certainly continue to expand at a rapid pace in the near term.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Our outright purchases are now on the order of $200 billion per month—a much faster pace than we anticipate (or almost anyone does) for the rolloff of the liquidity programs even if market conditions continue to improve.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So we expect robust balance sheet growth—on the order of 6 percent per month—in the near-term.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Seth and Chris will be discussing long-term balance sheet trends in a few minutes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As a prelude to that, our latest primary dealer survey suggests that few expect changes to our purchase programs at this meeting but many place higher odds on program expansion as the year proceeds.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Dealer economists expect that by mid-2010 the Fed will have purchased more than $1.3 trillion in MBS, $500 billion in Treasuries, and over $200 billion in agency debt.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In other words, nearly everyone expects significant expansion of the Treasury purchase program, and some expect expansions of the agency and MBS programs.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Longer term, the expected path for the fed funds rate, shown in exhibit 19, actually moved up somewhat.

speaker: MOSSER
text: On average, dealers now expect the fed funds rate to rise to about 1 percent by the end of 2011.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The continued rapid expansion of the balance sheet as well as the shift in composition away from near-term liquidity facilities and to long-term lending and purchases naturally raises a number of questions regarding how the Desk is going to conduct monetary policy in the future when the FOMC would like to target a higher policy rate.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Although the Committee may feel that that particular policy decision is well down the road, the staff has already begun work on how the Desk could achieve a significantly higher policy rate with a balance sheet that is very large and composed mainly of long-duration securities and loans.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We are preparing an extended briefing and discussion of this issue for the June meeting.

speaker: MOSSER
text: To preview some of the tools and instruments that we are considering: First, if we are granted legislative authority to issue central bank bills, how could that authority best be used?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Second, how might our current legal authority to pay interest on excess reserves be used to allow better control of the policy rate—for example, through the use of a redeposit facility?

speaker: MOSSER
text: There are a number of legal and operational complexities to work through on this topic.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Third, to what extent can we sterilize excess reserves by lending out our portfolio of securities via the repo markets and the MBS dollar roll market?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Given the very large size of our holdings, it is unlikely that we could feasibly lend out the entire portfolio, but even lending out a portion of our Treasuries, agencies, and MBS might be helpful in targeting a higher policy rate.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Fourth, how feasible will it be for the Desk to sell securities in order to shrink the portfolio, including the potential impact on interest rates, financial market liquidity, and the Fed’s income?

speaker: MOSSER
text: We doubt that there is a single magic bullet in this list, but we will continue to work through the legal, operational, and accounting—not to mention policy—issues and will report back to you at the June meeting.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Finally, I would like to request a vote to renew our long-standing bilateral swap lines of $2 billion with the Bank of Canada and $3 billion with the Banco de México.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The Committee received a memo from Nathan and me recommending the annual renewal of the lines now, although we are well aware that our recent experience with liquidity swaps warrants a wholesale rethinking of these facilities.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We will do that, and we plan to come back to the Committee in the not-too-distant future with a more thoughtful discussion of the role of swap facilities across central banks.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the meantime, we recommend the renewal of these smaller lines.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I also request a vote ratifying domestic operations since the last meeting.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Seth will now continue the presentation.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: For this meeting, the Bluebook included a new section that presented projections for the Fed’s balance sheet, and I’ll be referring to the exhibits in the handout entitled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Projections of the Balance Sheet and Monetary Base.” The projections 2 The materials used by Messrs. Carpenter and Burke are appended to this transcript (appendix 2).

speaker: CARPENTER
text: that we put into the Bluebook were linked directly to the policy alternatives presented in the Bluebook.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Chris and I will briefly explain the assumptions that underlie those projections, caveats associated with the exercises, and the projections themselves.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Under the current policy approach, the scale of asset purchases and demand for Federal Reserve liquidity and credit facilities, given their terms and conditions and the evolving financial and economic conditions, will drive the size and composition of the Federal Reserve’s assets and the quantity of liabilities.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The composition of those liabilities will be determined primarily by the evolution of currency demand and other factors on the liability side of the balance sheet, with reserve balances determined largely as a residual.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The balance sheet projections are “bottom up” forecasts based on assumptions about the various components of the balance sheet.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: We should emphasize at the outset that all of our assumptions, and therefore the resulting projections, are subject to significant error.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The significant uncertainty surrounding the outlook for the economy, the uncertain response of users of Federal Reserve credit to the state of financial markets and the economy, and the fact that some elements of the balance sheet are policy choices make these projections more judgmental than typical forecasts.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The charts in exhibit 1 illustrate the assumptions that the staff has made.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: As suggested in the top set of graphs, we assume that the Board extends at least some of the section 13(3) lending facilities beyond their current expiration dates later this year and that the FOMC extends the horizon for the foreign central bank liquidity swaps.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The recent improvements in functioning in some markets, however, have led to decreased usage of several facilities, as Trish noted.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: For example, draws on the foreign central bank swap lines and borrowing from the TAF have fallen so far this year.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Consistent with this development, we assume that demand for credit from all of the facilities, with the exception of the TALF, falls to zero over the next couple of years as markets recover.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The assets held by Maiden Lane, Maiden Lane II, and Maiden Lane III are assumed to mature or eventually be sold over time; they reach zero in 2015.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: In light of the slow initial uptake of the TALF, under the baseline projection the facility is assumed to peak at $500 billion at the end of 2010, half of the announced $1 trillion limit.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: For the baseline, we also assume that all TALF loans have a three-year maturity and that none defaults.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: As shown in the next set of graphs labeled “Securities,” in the baseline scenario (denoted by the blue lines) the Desk purchases $300 billion of Treasury securities, $200 billion of agency debt, and $1¼ trillion of agency mortgage-backed securities this year as directed by the FOMC in March.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: We assume that the agency debt and Treasury securities are held to maturity.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: MBS are held to maturity as well but are subject to prepayment.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Given the historically low coupon on the securities that the Desk has purchased, we assume a slower-than-average path for the prepayment of MBS that implies that approximately half of the MBS purchases remain on the balance sheet in 2016.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Of course, the Committee may consider other possible courses for policy.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Consistent with alternative A in the Bluebook, one alternative scenario is based on an additional $450 billion in purchases of Treasury debt (the red line in the graph).

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Another scenario includes the additional Treasury securities as well as a TALF that reaches $1 trillion, with a second wave of loans that have a five-year maturity, shown by the red lines in the middle row of the top set of charts.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: On the liability side of the balance sheet, we assume that Federal Reserve notes, shown in the bottom set of charts, expand at the same rate as money stock currency as projected by the staff under the Greenbook forecast through 2010 and at the rate of nominal GDP growth thereafter.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The Treasury’s accounts at the Federal Reserve return to historically normal levels from their current total of roughly $300 billion; specifically, the supplementary financing account falls to zero, and the general account returns to the $5 billion target by the end of 2009.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Taken together, these assumptions plus additional assumptions for miscellaneous assets and liabilities imply a path for reserve balances.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Chris will now discuss the projections.

speaker: BURKE
text: I will now review the baseline balance sheet projections, which are shown in exhibit 2.

speaker: BURKE
text: As Seth noted, assets determine the size of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet over the next several years.

speaker: BURKE
text: If credit extended under 13(3) programs and through the liquidity swaps evolves as assumed, the long-term asset purchases and TALF loans will be the dominant factors driving balance sheet growth.

speaker: BURKE
text: The baseline projection sees these programs expanding rapidly over the remainder of this year, and consequently, total assets surge and eventually peak at $3.4 trillion at year-end, an increase of about $1.2 trillion from current levels.

speaker: BURKE
text: At that point, agency debt and agency MBS make up over 40 percent of total assets, whereas Treasury securities represent less than a quarter of total assets, much less than the roughly 90 percent share that Treasury debt represented in 2007.

speaker: BURKE
text: The increase in TALF loans also contributes to the very rapid expansion of the balance sheet in 2009.

speaker: BURKE
text: Subsequently, however, with asset purchases having ceased and TALF loans no longer being extended, the maturation and the prepayment of assets cause a gradual contraction in assets until the end of 2015.

speaker: BURKE
text: At that point, the Desk resumes open market operations to maintain reserve balances around the $25 billion level.

speaker: BURKE
text: Because balance sheets balance, total liabilities increase along with assets this year.

speaker: BURKE
text: Given our assumptions for steady and moderate currency growth, the level of reserve balances largely parallels the path of assets, although the substantial reserve- adding decline in Treasury account balances at the Fed further increases reserve balances this year.

speaker: BURKE
text: In the baseline scenario, reserve balances peak at $2.4 trillion at the end of this year.

speaker: BURKE
text: Thereafter, reserve balances decline, following the contraction in assets, and approach zero in 2015.

speaker: BURKE
text: Because some positive level of balances is needed for the implementation of policy, as noted above, we assume that the Desk resumes its historical practice of open market operations to offset drains of reserve balances caused by currency growth and maturing assets.

speaker: BURKE
text: We calculate the monetary base as the sum of currency and reserve balances.

speaker: BURKE
text: As presented in exhibit 3, in the baseline scenario the monetary base grows rapidly in 2009 and into 2010.

speaker: BURKE
text: After the first quarter of 2010, however, the monetary base begins to contract as the liquidity facilities are winding down, new asset purchases cease, and previously purchased assets begin to mature.

speaker: BURKE
text: The base continues to contract until 2015, at which point the expansion of currency and the stabilization of reserve balances lead to a resumption of growth.

speaker: BURKE
text: If economic conditions worsen or the Committee judges that greater stimulus is warranted, an even greater expansion of the balance sheet would result.

speaker: BURKE
text: A more aggressive path for asset purchases, like alternative A in the Bluebook, assumes an additional $450 billion in purchases of Treasury debt in 2009.

speaker: BURKE
text: An even greater escalation—along the lines of that assumed in the Desk memo of April 24, 2009, to the Committee—assumes the same $450 billion in new Treasury debt purchases and also assumes that TALF loans reach the $1 trillion limit.

speaker: BURKE
text: Moreover, for illustrative purposes, the second wave of TALF loans is assumed to have a five-year maturity.

speaker: BURKE
text: The resulting path for the Federal Reserve’s assets is shown in exhibits 4 and 5.

speaker: BURKE
text: Under these alternative scenarios, assets peak at $3.7 trillion and $4.2 trillion, respectively.

speaker: BURKE
text: Similar to the baseline, after asset purchases stop and TALF loans reach their limit, assets begin to decline.

speaker: BURKE
text: Under both alternative scenarios, the balance sheet shrinks to the same size as in the baseline scenario in 2015.

speaker: BURKE
text: Given the greater amount of assets, reserve balances are also larger in these two expansion scenarios.

speaker: BURKE
text: They peak at the end of this year at $2.9 trillion and $3.2 trillion, respectively, but decline in a manner similar to the baseline until the end of 2015.

speaker: BURKE
text: As was shown in exhibit 3, the growth in the monetary base is qualitatively similar to that in the baseline.

speaker: BURKE
text: Under the Greenbook projection, the Committee is assumed to begin raising the federal funds rate in 2013.

speaker: BURKE
text: At that point in the baseline, there is more than $400 billion in reserve balances, and balances are even higher under the two expansion scenarios.

speaker: BURKE
text: Thus, these projections implicitly assume that alternative tools and operating procedures can be put in place to achieve the path for the federal funds rate consistent with the goals of monetary policy even with elevated reserve balances.

speaker: BURKE
text: As Trish noted, these issues are under study by the staff and will be discussed at the next meeting.

speaker: NELSON
text: As indicated in the memo circulated to the FOMC on Friday, we are recommending that the Board expand the list of TALF-eligible collateral to include commercial-mortgage-backed securities and insurance premium finance ABS.

speaker: NELSON
text: We are also recommending that the New York Fed offer five-year maturities on loans collateralized by CMBS and certain other long-lived assets.

speaker: NELSON
text: The TALF documentation has from the outset signaled a likely expansion to CMBS.

speaker: NELSON
text: We are currently proposing that the TALF accept newly issued CMBS.

speaker: NELSON
text: We expect to have a proposal for legacy CMBS in a week or two.

speaker: NELSON
text: Today, we propose accepting newly issued, fixed-rate, triple-A-rated CMBS that are not subordinated to any other bonds in a given CMBS pool.

speaker: NELSON
text: The loans in the pool must all be on income-generating properties.

speaker: NELSON
text: We anticipate that the TALF-eligible CMBS will be used to refinance maturing loans that had been conservatively underwritten (and therefore retain significant positive equity) and to purchase distressed properties—those in or at risk of default.

speaker: NELSON
text: Providing liquidity for refinancing would help prevent an increase in defaults on economically viable commercial properties, prevent further stress on current holders of the maturing mortgages, and free up their balance sheets for additional lending.

speaker: NELSON
text: Providing liquidity to finance the purchase of distressed properties will help facilitate the price discovery process and reduce the high levels of uncertainty about property values.

speaker: NELSON
text: When evaluating the appropriate haircuts, we tried to take account of credit losses, the likelihood that the TALF loans would not be repaid, and mark-to-market losses.

speaker: NELSON
text: We propose haircuts of 15 percent for CMBS with an expected life of 5 years or less, rising to 20 percent for CMBS with an expected life of 10 years.

speaker: NELSON
text: The haircuts would then be boosted by a projected 6 to 8 percentage points on average by the diversion of interest carry to repay the loan, which I will discuss in a minute.

speaker: NELSON
text: In addition, in contrast to our procedure for TALF 1.0 assets, we will have a collateral gatekeeper that will review the deals and exclude those that appear unacceptable.

speaker: NELSON
text: In the current economic environment, loss predictions are especially uncertain, but we did our best.

speaker: NELSON
text: Using these haircuts, we anticipate that in a stress scenario, defined as a 1-in-10 event, about 10 percent of the loans would default and that the collateral at the time of default would be about 20 percent below the loan values.

speaker: NELSON
text: Thus, for the entire portfolio of CMBS loans, we project losses in a stress scenario of 2 percent.

speaker: NELSON
text: At the same time, we would be charging the five-year swap rate plus 100 basis points on the loans.

speaker: NELSON
text: The excess spread on the loans accumulates as a first loss position.

speaker: NELSON
text: Over the life of the five-year loans, that buffer will amount to about 5 percent of the loan portfolio.

speaker: NELSON
text: Because the accumulated excess spread is more than double the expected losses, we expect that, even in a stress scenario, neither the Treasury, which is in the second loss position, nor the Federal Reserve, which is in the third loss position, would experience losses on the TALF loans backed by new- issue CMBS.

speaker: NELSON
text: We anticipate that the New York Fed will accept a different set of NRSROs for CMBS.

speaker: NELSON
text: Currently, we take Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch ratings on the collateral accepted for all Federal Reserve lending.

speaker: NELSON
text: A Systemwide project is under way to develop procedures for evaluating rating agencies for each collateral type, but the full project will take many months to conduct.

speaker: NELSON
text: We accelerated the review of NRSROs for CMBS.

speaker: NELSON
text: The results are not quite complete, but we anticipate that the list of recommended NRSROs for CMBS will differ from the list we have used in other lending programs.

speaker: NELSON
text: The other asset class we propose adding to the program is insurance premium finance ABS.

speaker: NELSON
text: Insurance premium finance ABS are backed by loans to small businesses to pay for property and casualty insurance.

speaker: NELSON
text: Unlike households, businesses pay for such insurance upfront.

speaker: NELSON
text: More than 1½ million of these loans are extended to small businesses each year.

speaker: NELSON
text: When we asked market participants what remaining ABS categories we should have accepted under TALF 1.0, we were unanimously told “insurance premium finance ABS.” The ABS bear very little credit risk because the underlying loans are collateralized by the residual unused insurance premium.

speaker: NELSON
text: Nonetheless, spreads on these ABS have ballooned along with other ABS spreads.

speaker: NELSON
text: We spoke to the four largest premium finance companies.

speaker: NELSON
text: Three of them are enthusiastic about the possibility that these ABS might be TALF-eligible.

speaker: NELSON
text: One of those three is AIG Credit, a subsidiary of AIG.

speaker: NELSON
text: The unenthusiastic company is BB&T, which is benefiting from its funding advantage as a bank.

speaker: NELSON
text: We are also proposing that the TALF begin to offer 5-year loans.

speaker: NELSON
text: All TALF loans currently have 3-year maturities.

speaker: NELSON
text: CMBS generally have 10-year terms.

speaker: NELSON
text: Market participants were uniformly of the view that the TALF would not be very helpful for CMBS unless the loan maturity is lengthened.

speaker: NELSON
text: The maturity mismatch is also a significant negative for student loan ABS and SBA ABS, which have even longer maturities than CMBS.

speaker: NELSON
text: We propose offering TALF loans with 5-year maturities for CMBS, student loan ABS, and SBA ABS.

speaker: NELSON
text: We would also propose that 5-year loans be offered for newly issued RMBS and legacy CMBS and RMBS if these assets are eventually added as eligible collateral.

speaker: NELSON
text: A 5-year loan term reduces the maturity mismatch and extends the refinancing problem well beyond the expected end of the recession.

speaker: NELSON
text: In order to reduce the risk that this program might impede your ability to raise the funds rate above zero when the time comes, we would limit the total amount of TALF loans with 5-year maturities to $100 billion.

speaker: NELSON
text: For now, we propose extending 5-year loans to all who request them and otherwise qualify, but we would develop and put in place an auction mechanism in the future if it appears to be necessary.

speaker: NELSON
text: As an incentive to encourage investors to choose a 3-year loan or to repay a 5-year loan early, we propose diverting some of the interest payments on the collateral backing 5-year loans toward accelerated repayment of the TALF loan, with a significantly greater amount diverted in the fourth and fifth year.

speaker: NELSON
text: We expect that this early repayment will equal about 8 percent of outstanding CMBS loans, resulting in the extra haircut I mentioned earlier.

speaker: NELSON
text: If the proposed changes to the program are adopted, we anticipate that about $30 billion in TALF loans collateralized by newly issued CMBS and about $2 billion in loans backed by insurance premium finance ABS will be extended by December 31 of this year, when the program is scheduled to end.

speaker: NELSON
text: If the changes are adopted, we anticipate making a public announcement this Friday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will have an opportunity shortly to have a general discussion of these issues, but for right now let’s just take any questions that might be for the staff.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I have a question on the mortgage-backed-security purchase program, in particular looking at figure 13 and figure 14.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Figure 13 shows that the mortgage rates have come down as you discussed, and what’s striking to me is that it looks as though we accounted for roughly 80 percent of the issuance of mortgage-backed securities over the first four months of the year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we had been willing to buy 100 percent of the issuance, I assume that we would have been a price setter in that market and we would have had the ability to push rates even further down.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So my question is, (A) Is that accurate, and (B) if our guidance to the Desk was to try to get the retail rate between 4 and 4¼ percent, do you think we would be able to do that for the new issuance?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As you’ve highlighted, we account for most of the coupon purchases between 4 and 5 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So if, instead, we had instructions that we’re really intending to try to get that rate down, would you be able to hit it?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Probably, but at a cost.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Right now, even though we are buying a significant proportion of the new issuance, there are others who are buying new issuance as well—fixed-income money managers and a few banks and so forth.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In addition to that, there is a fair amount of trading activity in what I will call “off-the-run TBAs”—the higher-coupon TBAs—as well as in the forward market, both for hedging purposes and for speculation purposes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If we followed that strategy, we would effectively wipe everybody else out of the market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: There wouldn’t be any secondary trading.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We would be the only purchaser, and we could probably continue to drive down at least the secondary spreads.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: What does “wipe out” mean?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Does “wipe out” mean that they leave the market temporarily and come back in once rates go back up, (if they go back up)?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It’s not a wipe-out financially; it is just that they are not active in the market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the short run, they probably take some capital gains, in point of fact.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The big question is when they would come back and how quickly.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The experience of central banks completely taking over markets to the point that the market is effectively shut except for what the central bank is buying is not so pretty from a liquidity standpoint.

speaker: MOSSER
text: For example, in Japan it took a year and a half to get their money market to work again in any kind of normal way, and that was a money market, not a relatively complex product like MBS.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I think the big question is, if we completely dominate the trading in this market, we can probably set whatever price we want, but if there are no other buyers that will complicate things for the originators in the following sense.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Originators will have to be very certain about how much we’re going to buy, the price, and the point at which we’re going to exit.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As long as they’re very certain about the price and we buy absolutely everything, they’ll have no problem originating at low rates.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But the minute there’s any hint that we’re not going to buy every last dollar, there’s uncertainty about what they can sell to someone else.

speaker: MOSSER
text: At that point it’s going to be much harder for them to hedge their pipeline, and the spread between the secondary rate and the primary rate may be wider.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So I think there’s a concern that perhaps the spread could widen out despite our best efforts to drag the secondary rate down.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The short story is that there is a bit of a tradeoff between how low we can push the secondary-market rate and how much we want to preserve some liquidity in the market so that we have an exit strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Could I just follow up on that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Looking at it from the other side, we’re focused mostly on new issues.

speaker: MOSSER
text: About 85 percent of the TBAs that we buy are between 4 and 5 percent coupons, which is nearly all of the new issuance.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So, yes, we’re very focused on the new issuance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why are we doing that instead of mixing new issues and seasoned mortgages?

speaker: MOSSER
text: We are buying some seasoned.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t know if I have a maturity breakdown in this chart pack, but there is one, I believe, in the balance sheet briefing that we sent around.

speaker: MOSSER
text: About 10 percent is off the run.

speaker: MOSSER
text: With the two refinancing waves, that part of the market is actually shrinking.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Our purchases of high-coupon MBS may not be so big as a share of outstandings, but our market share keeps rising every day because those are exactly the loans that are being prepaid into 4s, 4½s, and 5s.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So by the end of this refi process, a huge proportion of the market is going to be concentrated between 4 and 5½ percent—perhaps not 80 percent but we would guess 60 to 70 percent of the market—at which point our numbers will not look so out of line.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We’re just a little ahead of the curve.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Just to follow up one more time.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we had given instructions that our goal was to try to get the retail rate between 4 and 4¼ percent, which is what some of the projections had indicated we might get to, how much more do you think you would have had to purchase to achieve that goal?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: And would it have had the undesirable effects that you were talking about?

speaker: MOSSER
text: If we had started out purchasing absolutely everything, the answer is that it would have had the undesirable effects.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We could have gotten the rate down.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t know if I could quantify buying absolutely everything.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It’s probably not, shall we say, a nice, linear relationship between how much we buy and how far we could have gotten the rate down.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I’m guessing that, if we really wanted to get the rate down another 100 basis points, which is what you’re talking about here—50 to 100 basis points on the retail mortgage rate—we would have had to buy all the new issuance and quite a substantial amount of the outstanding 5s as well.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So we would have had to buy at least 40 to 50 percent more than we did.

speaker: FISHER
text: And this is independent of what happens in the Treasury market?

speaker: MOSSER
text: The narrower we make the secondary spread to Treasuries, the more everybody else is going to exit the market because nobody else has our funding advantage, shall we say, or our ability to just magically create the dollars to purchase these assets.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If the Treasury yields did not come down—and if we focused more on mortgages, presumably they would not— then the spreads would get so compressed that they would not be attractive to anyone else.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to come back to exhibit 14, about which President Rosengren asked a question.

speaker: FISHER
text: Are these the most up-to-date numbers, including the ones that were reported in the press in the last two days, regarding the budget situation and the likely Treasury issuance?

speaker: FISHER
text: Then I have a question on the last presentation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I may have missed something, but you added that we would have a collateral gatekeeper.

speaker: NELSON
text: We’re in the process of hiring at this time.

speaker: NELSON
text: We don’t have someone now, but we are hiring two sorts of vendors right now.

speaker: NELSON
text: The process is under way, and we anticipate hiring someone next week, I think.

speaker: NELSON
text: We’re looking at what’s called a “collateral monitor,” which will be a number of firms that will help us value collateral that is pledged to us.

speaker: NELSON
text: We need those professionals in particular for valuing legacy RMBS pledges of collateral, but they will also be able to help us evaluate other collateral, including CMBS, that’s brought to us.

speaker: NELSON
text: Then another function that we’re hiring for is an expanded collateral custodian.

speaker: FISHER
text: So this isn’t just for the CMBS market.

speaker: FISHER
text: I was a little confused.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The staff memo on the recommendations for the expansion of the TALF mentions on page 3, in the paragraph on the TALF ceiling and credit support, that you project that the New York Fed will make less than $150 billion in TALF loans through December 31; and in the Bluebook baseline, it looks as though it is about $100 billion at the end of 2009.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: How confident are you that we can then do $400 billion in 2010, and how important are CMBS to the successful expansion of the TALF?

speaker: CARPENTER
text: There are a couple of parts to that question, so I suppose a couple of people will have to answer.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: For just the baseline projections, we wanted to be illustrative, first and foremost, to give you all a chance to understand what sort of impact different sizes of TALF programs would have on the balance sheet and what that would mean down the line in terms of levels of reserve balances and potential exit strategies.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: We intentionally, therefore, did not try to tie it to the operational details that Bill and colleagues are going through in seeing how quickly they would actually be able to arrange deals with specific borrowers for specific types of collateral.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Bill, in terms of the detail, I don’t know if you or Trish want to comment.

speaker: NELSON
text: I would just highlight that this really illustrates the incredible uncertainty about forecasting things like this.

speaker: NELSON
text: Several months ago we thought that this program would ramp up relatively quickly.

speaker: NELSON
text: We are now observing that it is not doing so, in large part because of things that are themselves hard to predict: the ability of the primary dealers and the customers to work out their legal disagreements and the political concerns of the investors.

speaker: NELSON
text: If those things were to clear up, this program could move up really quickly, but they may not.

speaker: MOSSER
text: On CMBS, our understanding, in talking to the investors and the syndicators, is that the new-issue CMBS are obviously a substantially smaller pool of possible loans and securitizations than the legacy.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Opening it up to legacy actually makes the larger number seem, at least relative to take-up so far, more possible.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If for some reason we would stop with just the current-sized TALF, I think I at least would be surprised if we got to $400 billion.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But if it is opened up to legacy assets, then the possibility of getting the larger numbers is more likely.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Mr. Chairman, this obviously may be an issue for discussion in the policy go-round.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: But if there is a lack of confidence that we can expand our balance sheet with the TALF program, at what point do we talk about other ways to accomplish this?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I just want to thank Trish Mosser as acting SOMA manager for dispensing her duties with such élan and skill.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As you know, Brian Sack will be joining us as the head of the Markets Group and, subject to the Committee’s vote, will become the SOMA manager going forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d like to interject my thanks also, Trish, for a wonderful job, and to the staff in general.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our whole system has changed from interest rates to balance sheets and from money supply to lending programs, and I have been very impressed.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think our colleagues would share my view that the material you’ve provided to us on the various programs and the analysis that the Board staff has done on their effects have been extremely helpful, and I just want to express my appreciation for that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Just a question on the maturity on the TALF.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We want to go from three to five years.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That, of course, means that rolling off our balance sheet will be slower.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Is the five years determined by conditions that they told us about or the length of the assets being brought on?

speaker: HOENIG
text: What caused us to move from three to five years?

speaker: NELSON
text: I guess it’s a compromise between what we’ve heard from market participants about the effectiveness of the program and the feedback from you and others and from the Board on their preferences that the maturity of the loans be kept as short as possible.

speaker: NELSON
text: So we have discussed in particular whether or not a five-year loan would be more effective than a three-year loan, and we have heard back that it would be appreciably more effective.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So the maturity they are really looking for is 10 years.

speaker: NELSON
text: They would like for the maturity to be as long as possible.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Right, because that is what they are turning over now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So this would help them.

speaker: HOENIG
text: When they come toward the five years, then they would be pressed pretty hard because they would still have these assets to deal with—to refinance and so forth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We will see future pressure as they come against the five years because they need the ten-year length?

speaker: LACKER
text: I want to express my appreciation to the staff for the comprehensive and voluminous information that they have presented this time about balance sheet projections, breaking out the components and doing a thorough job of presenting the implications for the base, all the components, and the liabilities.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it’s an excellent, comprehensive, and much better framework for the Committee.

speaker: LACKER
text: Mr. Chairman, the staff material presented included a memo that I think Brian Madigan distributed about the simulations.

speaker: LACKER
text: There was one about the interest rate effects, large-scale asset purchases, and other work about the effects of different things.

speaker: LACKER
text: Would it be safe to assume that there’s a later part of our program in which the staff will be discussing that?

speaker: LACKER
text: If I had questions about the economic effects of changes in our balance sheet for the staff, would that be a more appropriate time to bring it up?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Will you be able to take questions on that after your presentation?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yes, after the economic presentation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, I’d like to open the floor for a brief interactive discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have two go-rounds to come, and so there’s no need for everyone necessarily to state their views.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I did want to leave open the opportunity so that we can address any issues that are on people’s minds.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to make just a few preliminary comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I will, in fact, be repeating some things that Trish said, which is that, as we look at the time profile of the balance sheet even under our current plan, it is evident that we are going to need various exit strategies.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is going to be very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to reiterate that we are working very hard—and I will talk specifically in a moment—to bring some specifics to the Committee in June.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First of all, as I think Brian may discuss, one set of issues relates to winding down or extending existing programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Winding down could mean either letting them expire—many of them are slated to end in October—or changing the terms over time so that they become less attractive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in June we will bring to you a set of recommendations from the staff about which programs might be extended over year-end and which might be either allowed to expire or modified in some way so that they will naturally shut down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, as Trish was discussing, we have a set of work streams looking at different ways of sterilizing the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want to begin by saying that, although I think it would be prudent for us to assume that we do not have Fed bills or the supplemental financing program from the Treasury, I think in fact there’s a reasonable chance that we will get one or the other at least.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Administration and the Treasury are strongly supportive of Fed bills, and I have gotten some good responses from some key congressmen.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So although it may not be the appropriate moment right now to do that, we will continue to pursue that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If that doesn’t come through, then of course we can go back also to the SFP, which I think under your assumption was not included in the analysis.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that’s a direction in which to go.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In addition, the staff will continue to work on interest on reserves to make that more effective.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that there are things we can do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Trish mentioned a redeposit facility or a term deposit facility, changing the structure of reserve requirements, and other things that we can do to make that more effective.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Another thing we can perhaps do is work with the Treasury to manage GSE balances in a better way so that they don’t get dumped into the market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The issue of reverse repos has come up, which would be a way to essentially fund our holdings in the markets other than via excess reserves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Utilizing the repo markets has the advantage of putting upward pressure on short-term interest rates at the same time that we’re trying to raise the federal funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it will have, in some sense, a double effect—both a market effect and an effect on reserve balances.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The TALF doesn’t look to be likely to go to $1 trillion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll see how it evolves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In any case, we have limited at this point the longer-term commitments to $100 billion, and we are looking at possible options for finding different ways to finance the TALF, which also might relieve our balance sheet to some extent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Then, if necessary, we can sell assets, which in turn would be tightening.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think these are extraordinarily important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need to have a good sense of what our exit strategy is as soon as possible, both because we want to be able to reassure markets and ourselves that we are comfortable with where we are and because, if we do decide to become more aggressive and do additional purchases, we would obviously be much more willing to do that if we were quite confident about our ability to exit in a timely manner.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just wanted to assure everyone that we are working on those things, and we plan more-extensive presentations in June on all those issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me now just ask: Does anyone want to comment or raise any issues on this whole set of topics?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I, too, want to extend my appreciation to the staff and to you, Mr. Chairman, as well, for your comments just now about the extensive work that’s being done.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think it’s really terrific, and I know that it has been a lot of work and a lot of new ideas on the table, and I just want to extend my appreciation for all the efforts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Mr. Chairman, I do have two questions that I’d like to raise.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One is in regard to Fed bills.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I’ve expressed before, I have some trepidation about Fed bills, not because of their economic effect but because of the political ramifications that they may have in terms of a potential invitation for the Congress to express more opinions about what we do with our Fed bills and how we use them.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One way to describe this is to suppose that we propose Fed bills to the Congress, and of course, as we’ve discussed, your preference would be to have those Fed bills with no strings attached—not subject to debt limits, not subject to oversight by the Congress, and so forth.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s not an unreasonable possibility, for example, that the Congress might come back and say, “We’re going to give you this, but here are the strings that are going to be attached.” My question is, What would we do in that circumstance?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Would we be forced then to take Fed bills with the strings attached, or would we then turn around and say, “Oh, on those terms we don’t want it”?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we broach it that way and they come back and say, “Well, you’ve got it,” then from a political standpoint they have potentially a lever to call the Federal Reserve before them to talk about either debt ceiling limits or uses of Fed debt in replacing other kinds of public debt.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I’m just wondering if we have a strategy or if we thought about the consequences.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Would we be forced to take it on their terms as opposed to our terms?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s a very good question.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would first like to make the observation that Fed bills are not an exotic instrument.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We are about the only major central bank that doesn’t have this capacity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I was having a very entertaining conversation with Governor Shirakawa of the Bank of Japan, and he was explaining to me the subtleties.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They have the ability both to take interest on reserves and to issue their own bills and he was saying, “Well, it depends whether it’s two o’clock or four o’clock in the afternoon, which one is better for fine tuning;” and I was saying that I wish I had exactly that kind of flexibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But what I perceive—and of course, politics are always difficult to assess—is that the resistance that we might get would be less a desire to force us to use Fed bills to support certain credit programs but rather the opposite.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the concern of the Congress is that it might give us too much unchecked authority, and they might be resistant to doing that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So one possible compromise that might come up, which might answer your concerns to some extent, would be to put a strict time limit in terms of allowing this for the exit strategy but not after that, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: About strings being attached, obviously strings that compromise monetary policy independence would not be acceptable, and I do think that we have the Administration’s support on that issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, if they involved disclosures about programs and things of that sort, if we felt that they were consistent with the effectiveness of those programs and monetary policy independence, those would be the kinds of things we could discuss.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At the end of the meeting tomorrow, Governor Kohn is going to talk about some of our transparency initiatives, things we’re trying to do that will make us more open in the information we disclose—again, without compromising either the effectiveness of our lending programs or monetary policy independence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that would clearly be my set of criteria.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I appreciate your point, and I understand that Fed bills are not necessarily an unadulterated blessing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The political environments of other central banks that have those aren’t necessarily the same as our political environment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: No, but things are tough all over.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My second question, which you haven’t mentioned, is that I’d appreciate any update or thought you have on the inflation-targeting issues that we talked about recently.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is that a continuing discussion?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And if so, what is its status?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yes, we’ve decided that we would like the Administration to affirmatively say, “We think this is a good idea.” We think that’s a possibility, but there’s an awful lot going on right now, and that doesn’t seem to be the top priority.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it certainly is on the agenda.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It is still quite alive, and one of the issues would be just when the right time is.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You and I would probably agree that there would be advantages to doing it at some point relatively soon, given the uncertainties about exit strategies, Fed policies, et cetera.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But we’re going to have to let the crush of events to some extent determine what is the optimal point in doing that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the Administration has considerable interest in supporting this, and as I said, I got fairly good responses from a couple of key congressional people as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think it is alive, but we should not be too impatient and should wait for it to mature in the fullness of time.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would like to go back to President Plosser’s first question, just to understand the politics here.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we pursue getting approval for Fed bills, which committee do we go through to do that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would imagine it would be the oversight committees—the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs in the Senate and the Financial Services Committee in the House.

speaker: FISHER
text: For which there is also a lot on their plate.

speaker: FISHER
text: I mean, look at the Dodd–Shelby committee, for example.

speaker: FISHER
text: Having talked with Governor Shirakawa about this just two weeks ago—there’s enormous political interference in his operations, as you know—I share President Plosser’s concern—not that it’s not a good idea, but again, this is enormously complicated, given the other things that are involved.

speaker: FISHER
text: From a banker’s standpoint, I’m particularly sensitive given some of the language that’s in there.

speaker: FISHER
text: That, too, is complicated—that is the point I want to make.

speaker: FISHER
text: I assume that we are aware of that and are trying to maneuver our way through it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I understand that, and as I said, I think we have to plan.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We may have this tool, but we should plan as if we will not have it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no other comments, we have a couple of votes to take.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first is to ratify domestic open market operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, Trish mentioned very quickly—and you did receive a memo—the annual renewal of the swap lines with Mexico and Canada.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This has been going on for many years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that they are somewhat redundant at this point, given the other swap lines that we have, but we have maintained this relationship for some time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is there any discussion or are there questions about that?

speaker: LACKER
text: In the past, the Richmond Bank and I, myself, have had a tradition of voting against these.

speaker: LACKER
text: Earlier this year I did vote in favor of the swap lines that were introduced as part of our management of this crisis.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m willing to support these, given that a reexamination of these is under way.

speaker: LACKER
text: The distinction in my mind is the association of these particular swap lines with the history of foreign exchange intervention, which has been thought of as fiscal policy and outside the bounds of this institution, quaint as that notion may seem these days.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’m happy to support this now.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Could I have a motion?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s turn now to the economic situation and Dave Stockton.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: 3 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan and I are going to be referring to the two exhibits entitled “Recent Economic Indicators.” The question everyone seems to be asking is whether, in the parlance of our Chairman, we are now seeing “green shoots” in economic developments both here and abroad.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan and I thought that we would take a crack at addressing that question this afternoon.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I should note right up front that my track record for spotting green shoots is not inspiring.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: While in high school, I had a brief job with a lawn service.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One day while I was riding my tractor, a woman came running out her back door gesticulating wildly.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: It turns out that the patch of unruly weeds I had just mowed down were, in 3 The materials used by Messrs. Stockton and Sheets are appended to this transcript (appendix 3).

speaker: STOCKTON
text: fact, the green shoots of her emerging asparagus garden.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Two weeks later, I was working in a local slaughterhouse.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That life lesson taught me that an inability to distinguish the green shoots from the weeds can have unpleasant consequences for one’s career path.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Unfortunately, I have found that, over time, the job of making those kinds of distinctions hasn’t gotten any easier.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Case in point: The economic data that we have received over the past six weeks have presented a decidedly mixed bag.

speaker: STOCKTON
