text: To be sure, they stand in sharp contrast to the preceding six months of data that were unrelentingly awful.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One area in which the incoming data suggest that contraction may be giving way to stabilization is consumer spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As shown in the top left panel of the first exhibit, real outlays for consumer goods other than motor vehicles plummeted in the second half of last year, knocking more than 2½ percentage points off the change in real GDP.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: More recently, spending appears to have flattened out.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The data are noisy on a monthly basis and subject to sizable revisions, so any conclusion that declines here have ended would be premature.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Still, the consumer sector is looking better today than it did earlier this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Housing also may be stabilizing, or at least not falling as rapidly as it had been earlier.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Sales have steadied a bit in recent months, and single-family starts and permits—shown in the panel to the right—have flattened out thus far this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But as this chart makes clear, there have been other instances of relative stability over the past couple of years that proved not to be durable.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Similarly, the steep declines in motor vehicle production that occurred last fall and into this winter may be over, and a small uptick in production seems to be under way.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As seen in the middle left chart, the automakers slashed production in the fourth and first quarters in response to the weakening of sales and excess inventories.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Production moved up some in February and March and was scheduled at a pace of about 6 million units for the second quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Given the lingering inventory overhang in this sector, we had assumed in the Greenbook an underbuild of about 0.5 million units.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The announcement of production cuts by GM after we closed our forecast suggests that we were leaning in the right direction.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, given that announcement, we would be inclined to take another 400,000 units off the forecast of motor vehicle production in the second quarter.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That, in turn, would lower our current-quarter GDP forecast about ¼ percentage point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But as can be seen by the red dot, even with that adjustment, motor vehicle production is likely to be a small positive for current-quarter growth rather than being a substantial subtraction, as it had been in the preceding two quarters.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As shown in the panel to the right, outside motor vehicles, manufacturing output continued to contract sharply through March, with the declines widespread.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At this point, we have a few regional purchasing managers’ surveys that are pointing to some lessening in the rate of decline in the factory sector.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But with inventory–sales ratios high, our expectation is that manufacturing IP will continue to drop appreciably in coming months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We received orders and shipments for nondefense capital goods (plotted in the bottom left panel) after we completed the Greenbook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Those data were very close to our expectations and consistent with our view that equipment spending will continue to decline rapidly this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Likewise, the available information suggests activity in the nonresidential construction sector remains on a steep downtrend.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In brief, there are few green shoots among the indicators of capital spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But the biggest single challenge to our view that the pace of contraction in aggregate activity is lessening comes from the labor market.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Initial claims for unemployment insurance (plotted in the bottom right panel) have moved up further on net since the last employment report, pointing to another sizable decline in payroll employment this month.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Other labor market indicators are similarly bleak.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Undaunted, we are forecasting some gradual lessening in the pace of job loss in coming months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But that is pure forecast, based on our assessment that the decline in aggregate output is, in fact, abating.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I should note that, even if we are right and the rate of decline in aggregate output is diminishing—or, in another of the day’s favorite phrases, the second derivative of activity is turning positive—that isn’t setting the bar very high.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We could be correct about the sign of the second derivative, but if we are in the process of shifting from a 6 percent rate of contraction to, say, a 4 percent rate of contraction, then the look and feel of this economy will not be much different in coming months than it has been over the past six months.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For now, we read the balance of the data as suggesting that the intensity of the recession is letting up some and that, indeed, activity has been a bit firmer than we had projected in March.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Some of the modest upward revision that we made to the forecast of activity in the first half of this year reflected the upward surprises in consumption and housing that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But as Nathan will discuss shortly, we have also been surprised by a plunge in imports.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: While it would be hard to chalk that up as “good news,” it does imply that the weakness in domestic demand that we observed in recent months has fallen more on foreign producers and less on domestic producers than we had previously estimated.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: If the modest upward surprises in the economic data were the only information that we had received over the intermeeting period, the revisions to our forecast beyond the current quarter would have been small, and we would likely have continued to project a contraction in aggregate activity through the end of the year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But as you know from reading the Greenbook, we revised up our projection of real GDP growth in the second half of this year and in 2010 about 1 percentage point at an annual rate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That upward adjustment reflects almost entirely the improvement in financial conditions of late.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Equity prices in this forecast are nearly 20 percent above the levels anticipated at the time of the March Greenbook.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The 30-year fixed-rate conventional mortgage is about 35 basis points lower than we had been expecting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The triple-B corporate bond yield is down about 50 basis points, and junk bond yields are down considerably more.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At the same time, since the March Greenbook the broad nominal dollar has fallen roughly 3½ percent, providing additional impetus to demand for domestic production.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, we have been monitoring measures of financial stress and the results of the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey to gauge changes in financial conditions that operate outside the normal interest rate, asset price, and exchange rate channels captured by our models.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: These measures also have improved of late and have led us to make some additional upward adjustment to our projection this round.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The improvement in financial conditions in recent weeks is unquestionably good news.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But we are uneasy that a forecast revision of this dimension rests so heavily on readings from financial markets, which at several points over the past two and half years have shown signs of stabilization that proved short-lived.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: And principally because there are no signs of improvement in the labor market, we still view the risks to our forecast has more heavily weighted to the downside.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: That said, for the first time in a long while, we are experiencing developments that give some shape to the upside risks to the forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Better economic news and improving financial conditions, such as we’ve seen in recent weeks, could feed back on each other more powerfully than we have allowed for in the baseline forecast, producing a stronger recovery.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For now, our best guess is that the contraction in activity will continue through midyear, that output will roughly stabilize in the second half, and that something that begins to feel like a recovery will get under way by the middle of next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The basic factors influencing this trajectory will be familiar.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The inventory cycle plays out, with the liquidation of stocks lessening over this year and turning to a small accumulation next year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Housing bottoms out in response to improving affordability.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Fiscal stimulus provides support to consumer spending and to cash-strapped state and local governments.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Monetary policy remains accommodative, and financial markets and institutions continue to heal gradually, providing support to household and business spending.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As Nathan will discuss, similar improvements are expected to become evident in foreign economies.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Turning to the inflation forecast, after three consecutive months in which core PCE prices were unchanged, we have now had three months in which those prices rose about 0.2 percent per month.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We think there are some good reasons to average across this period, and that is close to what we have done in this forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: For one, the price changes late last year were especially low for goods prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: There were widespread reports that the exceptional weakness in sales last fall had led to deep discounting by retailers.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As sales firmed early this year and merchandisers made some progress in working off inventories, those discounts have reportedly been reduced.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: This may be one of the rare instances in which the anecdotes and the data are in reasonable accord.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: A second factor helping to explain the pattern has been the behavior of nonmarket prices, which posted very small increases late last year and larger increases of late.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, we don’t attach much signal to the movements in these prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Our basic take on the data is that there has been some deceleration in core consumer prices over the past year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On a 12-month change basis, the change in core PCE prices appears to have slowed from a pace of about 2¼ percent a year ago to a pace of just under 2 percent by March of this year.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Looking ahead, we expect some further deceleration in core inflation, to 1¼ percent for 2009 as a whole and ¾ percent in 2010.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Sizable economic slack and reduced cost pressures associated with the earlier declines in the prices of energy and other commodities should put downward pressure on price inflation over the next two years.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have a little less disinflation in this forecast than in March owing to the somewhat stronger economy, the weaker dollar, and higher oil prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But for the most part, the trajectory remains the same.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We continue to see large risks on both sides of our projection of inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: On the downside, most of the econometric models that we follow project greater disinflation, with many forecasting inflation to move below zero.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Even if the slope of the aggregate supply curve is relatively shallow, an output gap of 6 to 7 percent can exert noticeable downward pressure on price inflation.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Moreover, these models expect an extended period of low actual price inflation to result in a downward movement in inflation expectations.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: These mechanisms are at work in the baseline forecast, but more faintly than in the models.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The chief reason is that we are skeptical that inflation expectations will drop as much as suggested by most of these models.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We have seen little movement in measures of longer-term inflation expectations over the past six months despite rising unemployment and declining commodity prices.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Indeed, an important upside risk to our forecast is that there is no material retreat in inflation expectations and, consequently, less disinflation going forward than we currently project.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Nathan will continue our presentation.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Like the domestic forecast, our outlook for growth in the foreign economies is a little stronger than in the previous Greenbook—up about ½ percentage point on average throughout the forecast period.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We estimate that output abroad contracted sharply in the first quarter of this year, matching the fourth quarter’s 7 percent drop.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We expect real GDP in the second quarter to contract a further 2½ percent at an annual rate—which, although representing some moderation in the pace of decline, would still be the worst quarterly outcome in four decades were it not for the plunges recorded in the two previous quarters.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Our working hypothesis is that foreign growth will gradually rebound, turning slightly positive in the second half of this year before recovering more earnestly next year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Consistent with this forecast, we believe that some early signs of stabilization around the world are starting to emerge, although the evidence on this score is admittedly mixed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Your international exhibit shows some data that have informed our thinking.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As in the United States, equity prices around the world (the top left panel) have moved up since the time of your last meeting, potentially suggesting that some severe outcomes may now be seen as less likely.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These gains in stock prices were led by a rebound in financial sector equities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: More broadly, global financial stress appears to have receded some: LIBOR–OIS spreads, CDS premiums, and corporate bonds spreads have all posted declines.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The spot price of WTI has risen to around $50 per barrel, up about $7 per barrel since the March Greenbook.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Other commodity prices have also increased, albeit by smaller amounts.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the case of oil, the rise likely reflects OPEC’s aggressive production cuts of 3½ million barrels a day since September.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But with a broad array of commodity prices showing increases, the rise may also signal a stronger outlook for global demand for commodities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the advanced foreign economies, the recent news on activity has been mixed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Industrial production, shown in the middle left panel, has continued to sink, and unemployment rates have moved up more.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Japanese economy experienced a particularly sharp decline in the first quarter, with GDP plummeting an estimated 18 percent at an annual rate, an even steeper drop than in the fourth quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For other advanced foreign economies, the rate of contraction is estimated to have also steepened in the first quarter, albeit less dramatically.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, some recent survey data show signs of an incipient slowing in the rate of contraction.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Purchasing managers’ indexes and some other surveys have tended to edge up over the last month or two.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These surveys remain below 50 and thus indicate further contraction but at a slower pace.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That said, the picture is far from uniform; for example, Japan’s Tankan survey (not shown) sank in the first quarter to its lowest level on record.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In emerging Asia and Latin America, we see a little more evidence that the sharp drop in activity may be letting up.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As in the advanced economies, most purchasing managers’ index surveys suggest some abating in the rate of contraction, and China’s PMI indicates that the expansion has resumed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Many of the sharpest declines in output were in economies that were heavily exposed to the collapse in world trade.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The bottom middle panel shows that exports in some countries have ticked up somewhat or flattened out, although they are still at very low levels.

speaker: SHEETS
text: To varying degrees, industrial production has also bottomed out in China, Korea, Brazil, and Mexico.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Perhaps most notably, China’s GDP release for the first quarter surprised us on the upside, with growth rebounding—by our reckoning—to roughly 6½ percent at an annual rate, up from just 1½ percent in the fourth quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We see this bounceback as suggesting that the substantial stimulus that the authorities have put in place may be working more quickly than we had anticipated.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But we underscore our standard disclaimers about the reliability of the Chinese data.

speaker: SHEETS
text: At the time of the last Greenbook, our decision to write down a forecast that called for the pace of contraction to ease during the second quarter was largely an act of faith.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We are now a little more confident in this regard.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition to the early glimmers of hope in the data, governments and central banks around the world continue to actively combat the weakness in demand with fiscal and monetary stimulus.

speaker: SHEETS
text: More central banks in the advanced economies have neared the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates, and others have maintained or expanded their unconventional measures.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Central banks in emerging-market economies have been able to lower their policy rates as well.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Moreover, the recent commitment by the G-20 leaders to increase the IMF’s lending capacity and the introduction of the Fund’s new flexible credit line appear to have diminished the downside risks facing the emerging-market economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Based on these developments, the overall tone of our international forecast has notched up from one of unmitigated terror in March to just very deep anxiety at present.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Suffice it to say that we still see many risks: The recent data have been mixed—with those ticking up only having done so for a month or two; financial market conditions are still fragile; and it remains to be seen whether the macro policy responses that have been put in place will be sufficient to stem the ongoing declines in private spending.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Moreover, the recent outbreak of swine flu poses potentially serious downside risks to economic activity, particularly in Mexico.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The global recession is having a profound effect on U.S. trade.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We now estimate that both exports and imports dropped an astonishing annual rate of 31 percent in the first quarter, with imports more than 11 percentage points weaker than projected in March.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Together these changes add 1 percentage point to U.S. GDP growth in the first quarter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: February imports were held down partly by production disruptions associated with the Lunar New Year in Asia, but West Coast port data for March suggest a rebound.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Auto trade, especially imports, should bounce back some following North American production shutdowns earlier this year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: That said, the ongoing disruptions in the auto sector are likely to generate further fluctuations in trade flows in coming months.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Also, notably, the ISM series for export orders has inched up from its December low.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Since the March Greenbook, the broad nominal dollar has fallen roughly 3½ percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This depreciation has come in response to a number of developments, including the FOMC’s March announcement that it would ramp up asset purchases, the smaller-than-expected cut in the ECB’s policy rate early this month, and signs of diminished risk aversion—which have tended to support EME currencies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Despite this depreciation over the past six weeks or so, the broad dollar is still up more than 2½ percent since the end of last year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Going forward, the decline in the dollar and higher foreign growth have raised our projection for exports, and the stronger outlook for the United States has lifted our forecast for imports as well.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But even after these upward revisions, the outlook for trade is still quite weak, with exports continuing to contract through the third quarter and import growth remaining soft.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Net exports, after adding a little more than ½ percentage point to the change in GDP in the second quarter, are projected to subtract ½ percentage point on average in the second half of this year and in 2010.

speaker: SHEETS
text: All told, while signs of stabilization might very well be appearing, they do not change our view that the global recovery will most likely be slow and tentative.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the realm of green shoots, our forecast is much more like a small potted plant or a vulnerable asparagus garden than a large leafy tree.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Brian will now continue our presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 4 I will be referring to the separate package labeled “Material for Briefing on FOMC Participants’ Economic Projections.” Exhibit 1 tabulates the central tendencies and ranges of your latest projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Corresponding information about your January projections is indicated in italics, and April Greenbook projections are included as memo items.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the top left portion of the table, your forecasts for real GDP growth in 2009 have a central tendency of minus 2 to minus 1¼ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That is a downward shift of about ¾ percentage point from 4 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 4).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: January, reflecting markdowns to your forecasts for both the first and the second halves of this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you now anticipate that output will contract at an annual rate of 3½ to 4 percent during the first half of this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Almost all of you see positive growth during the second half, albeit generally at a low rate, reflecting slow and uneven improvement in financial conditions, some stabilization in the housing sector, and stimulative monetary and fiscal policies.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Consistent with the downward revision to near-term GDP growth, each of you revised up your projection of the unemployment rate for late this year; the central tendency of your forecasts for unemployment in the fourth quarter of 2009 is now 9.2 to 9.6 percent, an upward shift of about ¾ percentage point from your January projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Looking further ahead, all of you project a pickup in economic growth in 2010, as financial conditions continue to normalize, and robust growth in 2011.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Consequently, you expect that the unemployment rate will be trending down during those years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But each of you indicates that the unemployment rate in the fourth quarter of 2011 is likely to be well above your estimate of the long-run equilibrium unemployment rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the exhibit, the central tendency of your projections for unemployment in late 2011 is 7¾ to 8½ percent, whereas the central tendency for the longer-run equilibrium unemployment rate, just to the right of the dotted line, is 4¾ to 5¼ percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Turning to inflation, shown in the lower half of the table, all of you see slower headline and core inflation this year than in recent years; the central tendency of your projections for headline PCE inflation in 2009 is 0.6 to 0.9 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: About three- quarters of you project that inflation will remain at or below your view of “mandate consistent” inflation through 2011.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But reflecting the diversity of models of inflation dynamics in use among economists and central bankers, some of you see inflation slowing through 2011 in response to a persistently high degree of economic slack, whereas several of you see inflation rising above your estimate of “mandate consistent” inflation in 2011 or even in 2010 as inflation expectations respond to rapid expansion of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendency of your projections for headline inflation in 2011 is 1.0 to 1.9 percent; the range, at 0.5 to 2.5 percent, is much wider.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your views on the outlook for this year and next are broadly similar to the staff’s view: Greenbook projections for real GDP growth, unemployment, and inflation for 2009 and 2010 are all within the central tendencies of your projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That similarity breaks down in 2011: About two-thirds of you predict both higher unemployment and noticeably higher inflation in that year than does the Greenbook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Indeed, several of you noted explicitly that you do not share the staff’s view of inflation dynamics.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That divergence in views may help explain why about half of you anticipate that it will be necessary to begin moving the federal funds rate up in 2011 or even in 2010, appreciably earlier than envisioned by the Greenbook, which assumes that the federal funds rate will remain close to the zero bound through 2012.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: None of you changed your views on the “mandate consistent” inflation rate in this round: The central tendency remains 1¾ to 2 percent, and the range remains 1½ to 2 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Three of you are at 1½ percent, two are at 1¾ percent, and twelve are at 2 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown by exhibit 2, your views on the uncertainties and risks in your projections have not changed appreciably since January.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Almost all of you again see greater-than-usual uncertainty in your projections of both growth and inflation, reflecting the unusual nature of the shocks that triggered the current recession and our limited experience with unconventional policy tools.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you continue to judge that the risks to growth are tilted to the downside (and those to unemployment tilted to the upside) but that risks to inflation are roughly balanced.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Some of you note that you see the near-term risks as tilted to the downside but see the risks to growth in your outyear forecasts as roughly balanced, whereas several of you stated that the rapid expansion of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet will shift inflation risks to the upside going forward.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In short, your current projections show a deeper recession in 2009 than did your January projections but not a longer recession.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your projections continue to show a recovery starting later this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you still expect the recovery to be sluggish initially but to gain traction in 2010 and to pick up steam in 2011.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even so, none of you thinks that the economy will have returned to full employment by the end of 2011.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you expect inflation to remain subdued, but the range of views on the outlook for inflation in 2011 remains wide.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Dave, Nathan, or Brian?

speaker: LACKER
text: I would like to ask a question about the effect of our balance sheet expansion on the economy.

speaker: LACKER
text: I notice that the staff has come around to the view that purchases of Treasuries or MBS are likely to have roughly equal, similar magnitude, effects on a range of interest rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I have argued, that is the natural place to start.

speaker: LACKER
text: A couple of points in some of the staff material mentioned that the amount of reserves on bank balance sheets could crowd out private lending.

speaker: LACKER
text: I wanted to explore that a bit because it is at the core of our struggles to figure out just how the stimulus of a larger balance sheet works.

speaker: LACKER
text: I take it that the way your analysis works is that microeconomically, market by market, Treasuries do this and MBS do that, based on the ratios that you calculate, and you estimate the effects that way.

speaker: LACKER
text: But on bank lending, wouldn’t it be the case that the Treasuries or the MBS that we purchased would free up space on private-sector balance sheets that would crowd in private lending in an amount equal to the amount that the increase in reserves on bank balance sheets would crowd out private lending?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think to some degree that would be true.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The question is, to some degree, where the Treasuries come from, at least in terms of focusing on your question about the leverage ratio.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If they are coming predominantly from the banking sector, that may have the effect you are talking about.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But if they are coming from outside the banking sector, where capital ratios are less important, that won’t have the effect relative to the leverage ratio that you mentioned.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, let me follow that up.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let’s say it all comes from outside the banking sector.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then you have all these folks outside the banking sector, and they all have bank deposits because we buy these through banks.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the liability side of all the banks has gone up.

speaker: LACKER
text: As a first step, that doesn’t change the capital ratio, but the traditional sort of money market buyer’s story, that traditional mechanism, has banks, when they have more reserves relative to deposits than they want, lending it out and scaling up their balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: And while the standard money-and-banking textbook leaves bank capital aside, the natural extension is that they are able to bid for capital in the appropriate ratio to the size of their balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: Granted, some banks are currently holding lots of these reserves and are having difficulty raising private- sector capital now and are not in a strong position to increase the balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: But there is the rest of the banking sector, and the reserves can easily be lent to them and find their way through the usual mechanism.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it seems as though there ought to be the opportunity for that inflow of deposits to finance itself.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is just a one-for-one effect.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then, on top of that, you have the potential for a multiplier effect.

speaker: LACKER
text: The reason I ask about this is that the usual prediction would have been that this amount of reserves would have just led to an explosion in M2, an explosion of lending, and a burst of inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: You mentioned at the beginning that one way to think about this is, well, we are buying Treasuries from banks, so they are holding more reserves, but we are on the flat part of the demand curve because of interest on reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: So what we are adding in reserves is a perfect substitute for what we are taking out—short-term Treasury bills.

speaker: LACKER
text: But banks’ holdings of Treasuries, agencies, and MBS, which are all presumably perfect substitutes, have gone up $200 billion.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it doesn’t seem as though it is the case that we are just engineering a substitution of reserves for debt on bank balance sheets.

speaker: LACKER
text: It seems as though banks have substantially increased their demand for liquid assets.

speaker: LACKER
text: That seems to explain why we aren’t getting this money multiplier effect.

speaker: LACKER
text: But, then, we are going to run up reserves to $2¼ trillion, $2½ trillion.

speaker: LACKER
text: What if we take this baseline assumption that reserves are a perfect substitute, at the interest rate on reserves—for short-term Treasuries, agency debt, and MBS, say—and we run up reserves to $2½ trillion?

speaker: LACKER
text: Aren’t we going to run through banks?

speaker: LACKER
text: I mean, unless their demand for liquid assets rises, aren’t we going to just push through that?

speaker: LACKER
text: And how are we going to think about what happens to bank balance sheets?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I don’t know what you mean by “push through.”

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, they are holding reserve balances of $800 billion, $900 billion, plus $1.2 trillion in the stuff that is kind of a perfect substitute for it.

speaker: LACKER
text: We are going to make reserves bigger than that sum.

speaker: LACKER
text: So something has to give, and we struggle with what that is going to be and what kind of stimulative effect that might have.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Part of the experience from Japan is that the Bank of Japan had a hope that that would happen—that in effect at some point you pile up enough excess reserves that banks just don’t want them anymore and they begin to lend them.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So it begins to operate the way that you say.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But it didn’t in Japan.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: The experience—at least the way we have read it—was that it never happened.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: So if we go back a few months, when we started thinking about how expanding the balance sheet might work, and go back to the list of things that we sent the Committee in December, the mechanism you just described was on the list of “Could it work this way?” We’ve learned a lot from the experience of Japan and have taken a lesson from it—that it seems as though you can run up excess reserves to a tremendous amount and the banks will just accept it.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: What came up this time was a twist that I had never thought of before—I’m definitely not the expert in this room on this; Brian can speak to it—the sense of how it actually could begin to work in the other direction.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Because of the way leverage ratios, for example, are calculated, the banks might actually get so uncomfortable with so many reserves that they would actually begin to cut back on lending.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I don’t know that we’ve seen that either.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We haven’t, but that was a sort of perverse effect like this that the Japanese began to worry about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Couldn’t you just as well argue that, if they ran into that constraint, they’d want to get rid of the reserves and lend them out?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But then the problem is that it doesn’t help.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But that’s a problem in the capital position.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think the question is whether the banking system as a whole is acting as though it’s constrained by capital and whether we expect that it will continue.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Now, we certainly think that that’s the case.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Bank credit overall is contracting pretty markedly, and of course, we all know about very low bank share prices and the difficulties in raising capital.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So I think the implicit assumption here is that, at least for some time going forward, the banking sector as a whole will remain capital constrained.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I agree that there is some scope for shifting credit around among banks, but at least the current experience with the behavior of banks strongly suggests that the system as a whole is constrained.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, the runoff of bank credit by itself doesn’t speak to whether or not they are capital constrained.

speaker: LACKER
text: I mean, lots of people report a decline in demand.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most people are not wanting the assets.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve discussed this before at a few meetings: Nobody is as creditworthy as they were two years ago, and there have been widespread reports of declining demand for credit, even in the Greenbook this time as well.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It’s both demand and supply for bank credit, but we have very strong experience that the supply of bank credit is contracting.

speaker: LACKER
text: But the Japan experience—I mean, there must be some limit to this, right?

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Well, they took it a long way.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Now, it could be that demand for credit was imploding enough that the Bank of Japan just never took it far enough, but the Bank of Japan took it an awfully long way.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We thought that a distinction between what they did and what we have been doing is that we are targeting liquidity support operations toward particular sectors—markets that are having severe problems—or, alternatively, trying to do a major twist on the yield curve to drive down long rates—so two things that they didn’t really try at the scale that we’re trying.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have two-handers from Governor Kohn and President Yellen.

speaker: KOHN
text: Of course, if the banks lend it out, it doesn’t destroy the reserves.

speaker: KOHN
text: If they started lending it out, which would be great, their whole balance sheet would rise, and an individual bank might see that it had substituted one asset for another.

speaker: KOHN
text: But the banking system can’t get rid of the reserves.

speaker: KOHN
text: My question is whether lowering the interest rate on excess reserves would help the process that President Lacker was talking about.

speaker: KOHN
text: Part of the problem—well, maybe it is not a problem—so part of the phenomenon is that they can earn 25 basis points on a totally risk-free asset, so the incentive for them to look for alternative assets and set in motion the sort of traditional transmission mechanism that President Lacker was talking about is somewhat damped by that.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think the question is how much.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Surely it goes in that direction.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In evaluating the risk–return tradeoff from holding reserves or making a commercial loan at LIBOR plus 200 or some other basis, there’s a big difference between those returns.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You wonder whether lowering the relevant rate of either 25 basis points on excess reserves or the federal funds rate from 15 basis points further down really is going to make a very big difference.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One of the costs you have to trade off in making that judgment is whether you are concerned at all about the market effects that would surely come about on the federal funds rate amid all the things we talked about previously regarding the possible impairment of market function.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Now, there are possible offsets to that.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Trish already mentioned the change in the new fails penalty, for instance, which might help deal with at least one of those issues.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’ve also been worried about the leverage ratio issue and whether or not it might mean that our long-term asset purchases have a perverse effect.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Looking at leverage ratios for various large banking organizations, they don’t seem very close to the regulatory minimums.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the other hand, I thought you had reported to us that the major reason that interest on reserves had failed to provide a floor for the federal funds rate—after all, the question is why banking organizations don’t borrow at the federal funds rate and then hold them and earn a higher return by keeping it in their accounts and earning interest on reserves— was concern about leverage ratios and leverage ratios beginning to bind.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I thought that perhaps you mentioned—I can’t recall where I heard this—that large banks have been asked why they aren’t doing that.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If I’m right that concerns about leverage was their answer, then it gives me greater concern about this issue.

speaker: MOSSER
text: One change in behavior, though, from the very first implementation of interest rates on excess reserves back in the fall, whether it was a learning curve, getting our systems up to date, or whatever—Chris can correct me if I’m wrong on this—the major downward pressure on the funds rate now is due to the trading by the GSEs, which don’t get the 25 basis points.

speaker: MOSSER
text: They’re not eligible for it.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In fact, the trading between banks is actually quite small right now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Why can’t the large banks borrow in the funds market from the GSEs and hold the proceeds in their account and arbitrage that out?

speaker: YELLEN
text: I understand that the GSEs can’t earn interest on reserves, but it seems like a pure arbitrage opportunity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: They can simply buy it and hold it, but that doesn’t show up in the reported funds rate.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The reported federal funds rate that you see every day is on the broker trading volume, and the vast majority of the people who bother to trade are the GSEs.

speaker: BURKE
text: The GSEs are selling fed funds, and banks are buying them, holding them, and arbitraging the rate as you’re suggesting.

speaker: BURKE
text: But roughly speaking, 80 percent of the brokered volume that we’re seeing in fed funds is GSE sales.

speaker: BURKE
text: So in terms of what we’re seeing as actual rates being reported and why those rates are where they are, I believe it’s a function of GSEs selling and banks buying, where banks buy at 15 and hold at 25 and make that arbitrage.

speaker: BURKE
text: But that doesn’t answer the question of why more banks aren’t buying more and then lending and making an even bigger spread.

speaker: BURKE
text: The anecdotal evidence that the Desk has gotten from the banks is that it’s a leverage ratio constraint.

speaker: YELLEN
text: And that’s what’s feeding my concern about this leverage issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is a good issue for us to look at more carefully.

speaker: LACKER
text: If I could just comment on this—just two things.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, President Yellen, the way I’d reconcile it in my mind is that the first part of your question sounded as though you were thinking about the leverage ratio with a fixed amount of capital as constraining your balance sheet and what I think Chris Burke replied was that the gist of what we’ve heard from banks is that they act as if there’s a shadow value that they have to earn on that arbitrage.

speaker: LACKER
text: Imposed internally on their trading desk is the shadow price on their capital, and I don’t think that those two are inconsistent.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then Governor Kohn talked about lowering the interest rate on reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: I guess I think about banks as choosing, taking the interest rate on reserves and a bunch of other interest rates as given, how much they want to hold; and for us to put more out there is going to require some interest rate other than the interest rate on reserves to adjust.

speaker: LACKER
text: That’s different from the usual situation in which, when we increase reserves, you go down this demand curve, and the federal funds rate itself changes.

speaker: LACKER
text: Here it’s essentially the price of substitutes.

speaker: LACKER
text: So repo rates, reverse repo rates, and the yields on agency debt would be the first things that ought to change to induce them to want to meet their demand for liquid assets via reserve balances rather than agencies or what have you.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that more insight into that would be really useful.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me just point out that your work on the effect of large-scale asset purchases entirely ignores all of this.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s as if it doesn’t matter how we finance these purchases, whether by bank reserves, Fed bills, or what have you.

speaker: LACKER
text: That makes me a little uncomfortable in placing too much weight on them in these simulations.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me finally mention that what motivates all of this is how we know we’re going to be doing enough—President Pianalto’s question.

speaker: LACKER
text: How do we know if we’ve done too much?

speaker: LACKER
text: How do we know, looking at this, when to reverse course?

speaker: LACKER
text: And how do we know when demand by banks for reserves is pulling back and they’re about to try to lend them out to get rid of them and set off an expansion in M2 in lending?

speaker: LACKER
text: These are tough questions, and I think, Mr. Chairman, supplementing your outline of work going forward with some analytical work on this issue that uses our insight into bank balance sheets and bank balance sheet management would be useful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think those are solvable problems.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Evans, you’ve been waiting.

speaker: EVANS
text: I have two questions, but first, I want to thank the staff for a very careful, thorough investigation of the role of inflation expectations in the simulations, and the simulations in general.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t think this is a very important issue for today, but in terms of the modeling strategy, I was somewhat surprised about the way that you came out in favor of the adaptive expectations for modeling medium- or long-term inflation expectations.

speaker: EVANS
text: Especially at a time when we’re concerned about the possibilities that our extraordinary monetary expansions might make some people uncomfortable with the expectations, I thought that you would at least have a channel in there that we could activate and see how that affects things.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I say, I don’t think it’s really very important for discussion today, but it will be as we start going forward on that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t know if you want to comment.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I think we made a change, as you’ve said, this time.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We also said in the memo that we were continuing to work on it.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We are definitely leaving it open.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: I hope it was clear from the memo where we are.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: We’re very uncertain about it, and at the moment we have a number of people working on trying to figure out a new way.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: There are a couple of things.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: First, I suspect that you probably will be changing things over time.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Where we locked it in this time is just for the moment.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Second, I assume that, as we go forward, we will continue to do the sort of thing we’ve done in the past, which is to present you with alternative ways of thinking and alternative ways of how this might play out.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: Even when we’re through the episode, we probably won’t be able to tell exactly what truth is.

speaker: REIFSCHNEIDER
text: But certainly as we’re going through the episode and we definitely don’t know what truth is, we’re going to provide alternatives.

speaker: EVANS
text: I appreciate the effort, and I thought it was very well done, very careful.

speaker: EVANS
text: The second question, in terms of the Greenbook analysis—well, the forecast—is if you could clarify a bit the way that you make assumptions about the credit environment.

speaker: EVANS
text: I know that you have special factors during this period—you have the principal components from a few different surveys—and I think that that’s very helpful.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s not a surprise that I would favor something like that.

speaker: EVANS
text: I guess the question is, coming through the bank stress test and if there are concerns that the banks that are going to have to take the additional capital and they’re unhappy about this and they’d like to get out from under it, it’s not quite clear to me that they will try to lend a great deal on the basis of the additional capital.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s sort of insurance against future losses.

speaker: EVANS
text: So we might be facing additional credit squeeze conditions.

speaker: EVANS
text: How important is that for this Greenbook forecast?

speaker: EVANS
text: How is it incorporated as a potential risk?

speaker: EVANS
text: In thinking about the financial factors, I know the forecast has exogenous and endogenous components as to how they’ll run off, but I doubt that it incorporates that type of risk factor.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’re using several imperfect measures of financial stress to fix a misspecified model.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So the exact kinds of concern that you have about the bank channel into overall lending and spending are really missing from the staff’s large-scale model.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: What we’re trying to do is gauge some of these imperfect measures—first, from some measures from the capital markets and principal components of various measures of volatility, spreads, and so forth and, second, from the principal components of the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’re still going to have to apply a lot of additional judgment to the forecast going forward as we see bank lending conditions changing in ways that maybe those measures are not capturing.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I just think this is just one additional area that we’re going to be struggling with going forward.

speaker: EVANS
text: But it does seems likely that, if there were a less-than-positive reaction and the various spreads started to back up, we would see this in the indicators that you’re looking at, and that would have a natural type of damping effect on the forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: So some of it would be accommodated, and then some would be more judgmental.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’d be capturing more as it was happening, but I think that our ability to forecast what is going to happen is severely limited.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, my question is on a different part of the credit markets, and that’s the bond markets—private debt.

speaker: FISHER
text: If I recall correctly in the Bluebook, we have had an impact—there has been a response or at least an action—and the spreads have narrowed somewhat.

speaker: FISHER
text: Issuance is “robust” or such, relatively speaking.

speaker: FISHER
text: My question is, Where do we think it’s going?

speaker: FISHER
text: Obviously it’s not going to cap-ex.

speaker: FISHER
text: I presume this is the question.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s going into paying down bank debt or replacing short-term debt.

speaker: FISHER
text: And if that’s correct, do we have a sense whether this is significant in terms of the impact on the economy?

speaker: MOSSER
text: To the extent that it’s paying down higher-cost debt—

speaker: MOSSER
text: Aside from paying down short-term debt, it’s reducing their liquidity risk and taking pressure off money markets.

speaker: MOSSER
text: To the extent that it is replacing more-expensive bank debt and loans with corporate debt that less expensive and long-term and so less expensive in the duration sense—then that’s additional cash for the corporation.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So it’s a pretty classic recession shift in composition in the corporate bond market, when cap-ex is usually declining.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t know that what they’re doing now is particularly atypical given how slow economic activity is.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If and when the economy turns the corner, the composition of the corporate bond market will tend to be a follower, not a leader.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So cap-ex will determine the way out, rather than the ability to get funds determining cap-ex, at least at this point in the business cycle.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But in terms of the changes that we’ve made in the forecast, that lower cost of capital is implicit in the decline in corporate bond yields and is an important factor that we built in here.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Now, that doesn’t prevent capital spending from continuing to contract, but it’s contracting more slowly because the cost of capital is lower than it otherwise would have been.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So it is leaving an imprint in our outlook.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, it’s 4:00 p.m.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I understand that coffee is ready.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a 20-minute break.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’re ready to begin with our economic go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me start with President Rosengren.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There have been some initial signs that the recession may be approaching a trough.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It is too soon to tell whether the trough of the recession has truly been reached.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Whenever we do reach the trough, the economic recovery is likely to be anemic.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Consumers have experienced significant wealth loss despite the rebound in the stock market since March, and consumption is likely to be restrained by further job losses.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The rising fraction of homeowners who find themselves underwater makes it difficult for them to move around, and unless job prospects improve, they are going to have a difficult time moving.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: These continued constraints in the recovery have influenced my forecast for the economy.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I expect unemployment to peak somewhat higher than in the Greenbook and improvements in the labor market to be more gradual than in the Greenbook.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The significant slack in the labor markets will continue to place a lot of downward pressure on inflation, and there remains a significant risk that deflation will not be avoided.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I continue to believe that the risks around this outlook remain on the downside.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: My primary concerns are that the reaction to the stress test is unpredictable.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Contacts through the AMLF have noted that they are concerned that the stress test could lead to downgrades in asset- backed commercial paper to below the A1/P1, rendering them ineligible for the AMLF program.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In addition, they note that money market funds have been more transparent with their public holdings so that there could be another surge in redemptions for money market funds that hold paper and for banks that perform poorly on the stress test.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, I have my own concerns about the results of the stress test.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: President Evans’s question highlighted that institutions undergoing the stress test may behave more as if they are capital constrained than they would in the absence of the stress test.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think there is a very strong desire right now to avoid government capital infusions, and that desire seems to only be growing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Even banks that do not have the mandatory convertible preferred (MCP) are likely to be affected.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Banks outside the 19 banks undergoing the stress test will pursue the same conservative asset-producing strategies, concerned that the same criteria might be applied to them.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Among the 19 that will not need the MCP, it may be rational to slow their own organic growth so that they can take advantage of asset sales or acquisition opportunities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If I am right and the structure of the stress-test program discourages the expansion of lending, all business lending, particularly commercial real estate lending, could be adversely affected.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Contacts with insurance firms note that insurance regulators have not made clear how they will react to FASB rules on valuing illiquid assets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This uncertainty may cause insurance companies to further shrink their balance sheets at the same time that banks are doing the same thing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Thus, although there have been some positive signs on the economy since the last FOMC meeting, I remain concerned that the financial headwinds may not have abated yet.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Third District’s economy remains very weak, and the Philadelphia staff’s state and coincident indicators and leading indicators suggest continuing weakness, especially in the labor markets both in our District and in the nation as a whole.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although unemployment in our District is currently slightly below the national average, there is little reason to believe that we won’t catch up at some point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our business outlook survey improved a bit in April, rising to minus 24.4 from a minus 35 in March, but obviously this is still a very low reading.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The survey does offer some glimmers of hope—“green shoots,” as I guess is the wisdom now—and firms’ expectations about activities six months from now have improved considerably.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: They rose more than 20 points last month, to a plus 36.2, which is the highest reading since October 2007.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In general, our business contacts and our staff forecast suggest that the contraction will continue for a while in the District.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One piece of anecdotal evidence that is worth noting, however, comes from one of our board members, who is the CEO of a leading manufacturer of residential and commercial flooring.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: For some time now he has been quite pessimistic, as you can imagine, and for the first time in well over a year he said something positive last week—that he is beginning to see a bottoming in the housing market.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I take this as significant because he has been one of our most pessimistic commentators over the last year and a half—of course, understandably so.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: His information is consistent with other signs in the data of some stability beginning in the housing market, like the news of the upward revision of February new home sales that we received last Friday.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Let’s hope that such welcome signs continue, but it is not a sure thing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would also note that my contacts from the credit card industry have told me that non-auto consumer purchases for the month of April seem to be tracking at a fairly modest pace of plus 0.4 percent on a month-over-month basis.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Though not a great number, it is encouraging that the stabilization in consumption and spending seems to be continuing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So the Third District’s economy looks largely in line with the national economy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, I have never been one to go easily along with the crowd, and in that regard I continue to be somewhat more optimistic than President Rosengren about economic growth, particularly in the second half of this year and in the next year, and even more so than the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, based on incoming data, I did revise down my GDP forecast for 2009 from the January forecast and revised upward the unemployment forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The revision reflects the fact that the contraction in the first quarter of this year seems to have been much steeper than I had anticipated in early January.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I expect positive but modest growth in the second half, making the fourth-quarter-over-fourth-quarter change in real GDP modestly negative.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have not changed my growth forecast for 2010 or 2011.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I expect the economy to gain traction in 2010, picking up to about 3 percent in 2010 and settling into something closer to about 2.7 percent for the long-run trend in 2011.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I see less of a growth rebound than many forecasts because I view the financial market shock with which we have been hit acting much like a negative and somewhat persistent productivity shock to the financial intermediation sector.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One implication of that view is that the equilibrium real output has fallen, and thus the output gaps as usually measured would be overstated.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The very weak labor market data during the first quarter have led me to revise up my path for the unemployment rate almost 1 percentage point throughout my forecast period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Obviously there are risks to this forecast, and I share President Rosengren’s concern about the fragility of the financial markets and the potential for the stress-test announcement to have unfavorable reactions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My downwardly revised projections are roughly balanced, but with perhaps more than the usual amount of uncertainty.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now I realize that my forecast is more optimistic than many, but I don’t think we should discount the economic dynamics suggested by the historical data, even though I realize that the current episode might be a significant outlier from prior experiences.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This view is shaped, in part, by forecasts from a New Keynesian DSGE forecasting model that we are developing, whose virtue is that it runs solely off historical correlations in the data as reflected both in its estimated parameters and in the model shock processes.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This type of model produces a forecast with significant recovery under way by the end of the year.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While I see somewhat more growth than the Greenbook, I also see less deflationary pressure than the Greenbook baseline and greater risk of higher inflation in the outyears.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There are several reasons for this less optimistic view on inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, my forecast relies more on forward-looking expectations of inflation compared with FRB/US, in which backward-looking elements are more heavily weighted in forming expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Second, I put less weight on output gaps as predictors of inflation as seems to be called for by the empirical estimates of New Keynesian Phillips curves.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And third, I’m not convinced that the size of the output gap is nearly as big as suggested in the Greenbook for the reasons I have already mentioned regarding the nature of the shocks we faced.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This perspective also seems appropriate and is consistent with the work of Orphanides and some others indicating the pitfalls of depending too much on output gap measures, which it shows cannot be reliably measured in real time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, Orphanides finds that the ex post revisions of output gaps are of the same order of magnitude as the output gap itself.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is particularly hard to measure gaps at business cycle turning points.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My skepticism of the empirical relevance and measurability of output gaps and my view that forward-looking expectations of economic agents dominate lead me to be highly suspicious of the Greenbook’s inflation outlook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Indeed, if we look at inflation forecasts from a DSGE model, we find inflation rising over the forecast period, with headline PCE inflation rising above 3 percent in 2010 and exceeding 4 percent by 2012.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, I understand that the current situation and the nature of the current shocks suggest that sizable error bands are around the forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Still, I find that it is a useful exercise to examine these kinds of forecasts from alternative models, which are informative and helpful in thinking about the overall outlook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus my view is that there is a growing risk of higher-than-desired inflation in the outyears of the forecast.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: With the funds rate at the zero bound and the concern for some near- term deflation, having inflation in the near term run a little higher than our long-term goal might be desirable.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I don’t think that we should be willing to accept inflation outcomes above our goal once the expansion is well under way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I see that the longer-term inflation risk is tilted to the upside because I have grown more dubious of our ability to correctly time the withdrawal of the significant liquidity injections we have undertaken.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, for 2009 I am forecasting inflation in excess of 1 percent—1½ percent and rising through the forecast period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now, this forecast is based on my assumption that, as the financial markets and conditions improve and housing markets stabilize, the FOMC will begin to contract its balance sheet and raise the funds rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Appropriate monetary policy in this forecast requires that we begin raising the funds rate by the end of this year, certainly by early next year, and then continue to raise it throughout the forecast period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have it reaching 3½ percent by the fourth quarter of 2011.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, this is a much steeper path than that in the Greenbook, which wouldn’t be surprising since the Greenbook is zero from here on out; but it is consistent with my more optimistic forecast and my view that we cannot keep the funds rate at zero for the next three years and expect to achieve anything close to our inflation objective.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My forecast would show considerably more acceleration if I assumed the Greenbook’s baseline forecast.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I want to start out talking about the Texas manufacturing report.

speaker: FISHER
text: As you know, I don’t often talk about my District.

speaker: FISHER
text: Because we do produce a large share of total manufacturing goods in the United States, I want to point out that the report we released yesterday indicated pretty much what I am hearing from CEOs around the country.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is, the indexes for production, capacity utilization, and volume of new orders and shipments edged upward for the second consecutive month, but our firms are reporting that job cuts exceed hires by a 10 to 1 margin, and 36 percent of the firms noted a decline in work hours.

speaker: FISHER
text: That said, the six-month outlook turned positive for the first time since June 2008, reflecting either wishful thinking or quite probably a sense that firms have battened down the hatches, have a better sense of their vulnerabilities, and have a better sense of visibility vis-à-vis the budgeting that they have now ratcheted down, and I think that may account for some of this optimism.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I would not point to a silver lining.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is what I call a pewter lining, slightly better than it was before.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is confirmed by the comments I received from the CEOs to whom I talked after I got back from China—not very many, but hopefully indicative.

speaker: FISHER
text: But here are the lukewarm responses that I got in talking to some of them.

speaker: FISHER
text: For example, the head of the National Retail Federation, who sits on my board and runs JCPenney—I love this one: “I never thought flat would look so good” was his comment.

speaker: FISHER
text: “Still negative, but a slightly better tone.” From the CEO of Wal-Mart, seeing a little more discretionary spending, “It’s soft but not accelerating.” Shifting over to an entirely different sector, the CEO of Disney: “Early signs that deterioration is starting to slow.” And from the CEO of Exxon looking, as I like to do, at the chemicals, lubricants, asphalt, and other possible leading indicators—or at least indicators in terms of where the stimulus package may be hitting the road: “There weren’t any places where things got worse.” The only place where I could find that things had gotten worse was in the rails.

speaker: FISHER
text: Shipments are down 19 percent year to date.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that reflects mainly coal and a shift to natural gas at these cheap prices for electricity consumption.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do note, if you look at the Edison Electric data through April 18, that weekly electricity output is still declining.

speaker: FISHER
text: So there may be some green shoots, but I’d like to say that there are no sparks in terms of that kind of indicator activity.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am going to focus the remainder of my remarks on the impressions gained from my trip from April 6 to April 22 to Tokyo, Singapore, Beijing, Shanghai, and Seoul, with a focus on China.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, I would like to preface it by saying that here at home all of the Bank Presidents have their views, but I’m not sure that’s understood by the public.

speaker: FISHER
text: We always say it, but abroad nobody understands that distinction.

speaker: FISHER
text: As I told you, Mr. Chairman, before I left for the trip, I stuck to the party line, remembering the old definition that a diplomat is someone who is sent abroad to lie for their country.

speaker: FISHER
text: I was just extremely diplomatic, faithfully toed the line, and just basically listened very carefully.

speaker: FISHER
text: Here is what I heard.

speaker: FISHER
text: With regard to Japan, we have seen their latest projections for the fiscal year that has started—down 3.1 percent following an equally awful year last year.

speaker: FISHER
text: In addition to visiting at length with the Commissioner of the FSA and Governor Shirakawa, as I mentioned earlier, and the staff, I met with several CEOs.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have been going there since ’79.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would say that I had never seen them this pessimistic, I think largely because 22 percent of the economy is manufacturing and 40 percent of that is the auto industry in one form or another.

speaker: FISHER
text: And their demographics are awful.

speaker: FISHER
text: Industrial production is down 30 percent.

speaker: FISHER
text: The last time that happened—I think I may have mentioned this at the last meeting—was when Godzilla destroyed Tokyo in a movie in 1954.

speaker: FISHER
text: So there is definitely a mood of extreme pessimism in Japan, and I found that very discouraging.

speaker: FISHER
text: The situation in Singapore is different.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is worse in terms of the short term.

speaker: FISHER
text: The first- quarter performance is down 19 percent for GDP.

speaker: FISHER
text: But Lee Kuan Yew and his successors are planning for tapping into China.

speaker: FISHER
text: And quickly to skip over to Korea—that was the one place in which I didn’t feel like a dartboard or receiver of spears in that the timeliness of our foreign exchange swap really was helpful, and they are most grateful.

speaker: FISHER
text: Their own ship seems to be floating a little better, and the economy seems to be stabilizing somewhat.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to focus on China.

speaker: FISHER
text: I met with the requisite what they call “barbarian handlers,” which includes Yi Gang and the CBRC Commissioner and the China Investment Corporation people.

speaker: FISHER
text: I also met with the nonbarbarian handlers, quite a few who are just purely internal, both in politics and in business.

speaker: FISHER
text: Here is the take-home: They reported 6.1 percent economic growth for the first quarter.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am always amazed at the alacrity with which they report their numbers.

speaker: FISHER
text: Kind of like Radar on MASH, they seem to know the number before the quarter is over.

speaker: FISHER
text: I did find out, Mr. Chairman, where the 8 percent came from.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is that Deng Xiaoping asked in 1980 what it would take to quadruple the economy by the year 2000, and the answer was 8 percent compounded.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is where the 8 percent comes from.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is reported all the way up—from the governors on up.

speaker: FISHER
text: But as far as this 6.1 percent figure, Nathan, if you look at their import–export activity for the first quarter, exports were down 18 percent, imports were down 70 percent on an arithmetic measured basis.

speaker: FISHER
text: And their electrical output is continuing to decline.

speaker: FISHER
text: It declined 5 percent in the first quarter—our fourth quarter and through the first quarter—and there just is no correlation currently, although it has been very high historically, between GDP growth and electricity consumption and output.

speaker: FISHER
text: But currently their electricity output is significantly lagging the numbers they are reporting for economic growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, with regard to the People’s Bank of China and the CBRC, they reported that lending has focused on squeezing out excess capacity.

speaker: FISHER
text: That seems to be their objective, and this was repeated by several of the business leaders.

speaker: FISHER
text: They also feel that the budgeted amount they had planned for this calendar year all has been lent out in January and February, with some excess floating into the securities markets, particularly the equity market.

speaker: FISHER
text: The concern that we picked up was, for the third quarter, fourth quarter, and into next year, that basically the thrust of the fiscal package and the guidance they have given for lending, which is extending beyond the formal banking system to the trust banks and these new private banks, is basically taking place currently and might not have the kind of follow-through that they hope to see.

speaker: FISHER
text: The bottom line is that they cannot re-gear their economy very quickly.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are still dependent on the United States—significantly—and on Europe.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is 42 percent of their export activity.

speaker: FISHER
text: The bottom line of that is that their reserves will build more slowly.

speaker: FISHER
text: Still, they have no choice but to focus on U.S. dollars and Treasuries in terms of their investment and a small amount of mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: FISHER
text: They are seeking a greater role for their currency through their swap lines and through their trade invoicing in Hong Kong and some of the other major cities.

speaker: FISHER
text: So it is unremarkable that (a) they have deep concerns about the value of their Treasury debt and (b) fewer concerns about their agency holdings.

speaker: FISHER
text: I could have told them that we decided to purchase $5 trillion in mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: FISHER
text: It didn’t seem that it would have had much impact.

speaker: FISHER
text: But their concerns were constant.

speaker: FISHER
text: In every single meeting, in more than 40 meetings, they did not once fail to mention that they were concerned about our purchasing Treasuries and that they were skeptical about our ability to pull off a successful withdrawal of liquidity when the time comes.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to conclude by reading from the April 20 issue of the China Daily.

speaker: FISHER
text: The same article appeared in the People’s Daily in Chinese.

speaker: FISHER
text: The former Vice Premier Zeng Peiyan said, “The U.S. Federal Reserve’s recent purchase of its Treasury bonds, which effectively prints new money, is likely to turn the budget deficit into inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: That will lead to the depreciation of the U.S. dollar and cause a major loss in China’s foreign exchange reserves.

speaker: FISHER
text: And “the depreciation of the dollar has become an inevitable historical trend.” So it is a frisky place, and they are booming relative to everybody else.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I basically would put that message under a subtitle of what I call “Malice in Wonderland.” They seem to be eager to underscore this particular issue in order to protect the value of their investment.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I didn’t, frankly, find anything different from the kind of concerns I hear expressed here at home and by others who are invested in Treasuries.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would say that basically China’s economy is not performing as well as it is reported, that they still are dependent on us, and that they confirm, Nathan, what you mentioned earlier, which is that the global economy may be picking up a bit but it still is in basically bad shape.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is a welcome relief to say for the first time in recent memory that the economic data since our last meeting have not been uniformly disappointing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The pace of contraction in aggregate spending appears to have slowed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Consumer spending and housing show welcome signs of stabilization.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Overall, financial conditions have improved, and I have seen no indication that a dangerous deflationary dynamic has thus far taken hold.

speaker: YELLEN
text: These are encouraging signs, but we should be careful not to overreact to developments that may yet prove to be will-o’-the-wisps.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The economic outlook remains fraught with peril.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am particularly concerned about the labor market, where the data are appalling.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Not only has the unemployment rate risen 1.7 percentage points over the past four months, but recent readings on initial claims point to another dismal labor report for April.

speaker: YELLEN
text: What is worse, the unemployment rate appears to understate the true magnitude of the labor market deterioration.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For one thing, the incidence of permanent, as opposed to temporary, layoffs is high in comparison with past downturns.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Another, and probably more important, point is that there has been an unprecedented increase in involuntary part-time work.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It far exceeds what would be expected given the rise in unemployment.

speaker: YELLEN
