text: My staff’s analysis of CPS data confirms what we hear from our business contacts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The use of furloughs is widespread, and the surge in part-time work for economic reasons is broadly based across occupations.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The associated reduction in hours is nontrivial.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Our expectation is that the underemployment rate—a broad measure that adds individuals working part-time for economic reasons to those unemployed—will top the level reached in 1982 by year-end.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We expect it to climb from its current rate of about 14½ percent to over 16 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Turning to growth, my forecast is similar to that in the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I expect the unemployment rate to peak at 9.6 percent late this year, a tad higher than the Greenbook, reflecting in part a somewhat more optimistic view of potential output growth compared with the Board staff’s view.

speaker: YELLEN
text: And, like the Greenbook, I anticipate a slow recovery in subsequent years, not the rapid V-shaped recovery we have frequently seen following deep recessions in the past.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Several factors underlie my view that the recovery will be slow.

speaker: YELLEN
text: First, as I mentioned at our March meeting, I anticipate that the process of balance sheet repair that households are undergoing will result in subdued consumer spending for an extended period.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Second, monetary policy both here and abroad is severely constrained by the zero lower bound on interest rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, the optimal policy simulation indicates that we should lower the funds rate to negative 7½ percent, if that were feasible.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, it isn’t, so we have turned to unconventional monetary policy tools, but these are imperfect substitutes for standard monetary policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: According to the Bluebook simulations, even if we more than double the large-scale asset purchases we have put into motion, we are nowhere near the desirable outcome in terms of unemployment and inflation, which might be within reach if the zero bound were not constraining policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In addition, the slow start of the TALF program raises doubts about whether this tool will provide a great deal of lift to the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Third, I am concerned that the banking system is not really strong enough to expand credit in the manner that is required for a rapid economic rebound.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The new capital that is slated for injection following the stress test should be helpful, but I think it will likely prove insufficient.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Thanks to the Herculean efforts of staff members across the Federal Reserve System and other agencies, we now have a much clearer picture of the potential losses confronting our major banks.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My personal interpretation of the data—and I think my assessment is consistent with market views as revealed in CDS spreads and the prices of bank shares—is that there remains a nontrivial probability that the existing common shareholders of a number of the major banks will be wiped out in an adverse economic scenario.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This possibility diminishes their incentive to raise new capital to support additional lending.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The problem is that the benefits of the extra capital would accrue disproportionately to debt holders and preferred shareholders, including the U.S. government, who are more senior in the capital structure.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A separate problem is that banks with government capital appear heavily focused on getting out from the restrictions and stigma associated with the TARP.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They insist that it is impossible to raise new private equity when it will sit side by side with money from the government, and this creates an incentive for them to devote their earnings to pay off TARP capital rather than to use the retained earnings to support increased lending.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have enumerated several reasons why I project a sluggish recovery.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Additionally, I remain concerned about downside risks.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I am particularly concerned that another shoe may drop.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Confidence in global financial markets is extremely fragile, and more bad news could trigger another panic and run on the financial system.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Unfortunately, the road ahead is littered with headlines of defaults, bankruptcies, and rising unemployment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: While a big chunk of the losses associated with residential mortgages may have been realized already, we are only at the beginning of that process for consumer and commercial real estate loans, and the magnitude of the likely losses has risen dramatically as the economy has deteriorated.

speaker: YELLEN
text: European banks face a similar situation with mounting losses and a sizable exposure to Eastern Europe.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If another shoe drops, risk premiums are likely to spike again, and a further pullback in lending and spending seems likely.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My staff has been examining the effects of tighter lending standards and measures of uncertainty on consumer spending.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They find that these two factors explain a sizable share of the weakness in consumption growth in the second half of last year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In our baseline forecast, these negative influences are expected to dissipate over the next year, contributing to a revival of consumer spending.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But a real risk is that further bad news could reverse this process.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The false dawn scenario in the Greenbook illustrates one potential outcome.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Let me, finally, comment on inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have been struck by the resilience in wages and core inflation despite sharply declining commodity prices and a dramatic increase in slack in the labor and goods markets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Measures of long-run inflation expectations have also been reasonably stable, and that is very reassuring.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Looking forward, I expect inflation expectations to remain well anchored.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I expect core inflation to dip down to 1½ percent this year and 1 percent next year, about ¼ percentage point above the Greenbook forecast and similar to the well-anchored expectations scenario reported in the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Of course, given the very somber outlook for the global economy and the downside risks to this forecast, there is considerable chance of a more sizable fall in inflation, and such a scenario represents another downside risk to the outlook for economic activity as well.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In summary, despite the recent bits of good news, the economy remains in very bad shape.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I expect at best a gradual recovery starting late this year, with core inflation remaining below my preferred 2 percent rate for the next few years, and I see substantial downside risk to that forecast for both economic activity and inflation.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Mr. Chairman, I agree with the staff assessment that—to use their words—hints of stabilization in the incoming data and some favorable financial developments since the time of the March meeting have occurred.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But I also agree with their words that the evidence on this issue is by no means decisive.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I see the situation as quite ambiguous.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I note a positive turn in business sentiment in my District.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think it is best described as a waning of extreme pessimism rather than growing optimism.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Like President Fisher’s CEO, one of my directors said that “flat is the new up.” My retail contacts advise that the weak retail spending numbers of March are more characteristic of what to expect in the second quarter than the strengths seen in January and February.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The nation’s largest home improvement chain announced that March sales are down sharply year over year, and they are further marking down their modest sales projections for the balance of 2009.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Home sales have shown greater stability—around low levels, of course—in most parts of the Sixth District and are up year over year in Florida.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: By most accounts, new home inventories continue to creep lower.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But there is still considerable downward pressure on prices, and builders do not anticipate any sustained increase in construction activity anytime soon.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A large backlog of foreclosures and other home inventory is likely to enter the pipeline soon.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A comment on condominiums, which represent a significant portion of my District’s real estate market: They are under increasing pressure.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That pressure has been exacerbated by the fragile financial condition of homeowner associations, further distancing some otherwise creditworthy buyers from access to adequate credit.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In addition, serious concerns continue to be expressed about commercial real estate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One contact said that there is almost no financing available.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Even after accounting for weakening fundamentals, this source indicated that there is a serious lack of liquidity and predicted that commercial real estate will put major stress on financial institutions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On balance, the attitude that the economy would bump along the bottom for some time is common among my business contacts and continues to be a factor affecting my outlook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The forecast I submitted is similar in some respects to President Yellen’s.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is similar to the Greenbook over the balance of the year.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Although I, too, see a recovery under way toward the end of the year, I expect that the expansion will be considerably slower than in the Greenbook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my view, a slow restoration of credit market function, constrained consumer activity, and lingering economic uncertainty that restrains investment spending are likely to retard the recovery process.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The general perception of improving financial and credit markets presented in the Greenbook was supported by my financial market contacts.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Like the Greenbook, I am hearing positive reports of improved access to capital markets for investment-grade nonfinancial corporations, and this has extended down to triple-B firms as well as some improvement in the high-yield and convertible bond markets.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But my contacts continue to describe financial markets as quite fragile.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As President Rosengren commented on extensively, the bank stress tests are, unsurprisingly, seen as a critical event, and opinions on the subject were varied.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One contact predicted that the results are likely to be quite contentious and disruptive.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In contrast, another argued that tough and aggressive tests would be a positive sign that problems are being confronted.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Concern was also expressed in some of these conversations about the state of the insurance sector.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The insurance sector is more than triple the size of the investment banking sector, which in many respects was the source of some of our problems, and the view was expressed that the sector could deteriorate further if capital restrictions begin to bite.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As to the restoration of the financial markets, we did a poll of some of our directors regarding the TALF, which they said was generating very little interest.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: They cited a lack of demand from borrowers, insufficient detail about the program, uncertainty over future business conditions, and some community banks saying that the minimum of $10 million was too steep to participate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Regarding the balance of risks, my assessment of the risk to economic growth remains weighted to the downside.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: However, I have revised my assessment of the risk to inflation to being broadly balanced.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Consistent with the ambiguous state of the outlook at this juncture, I remain concerned about and attentive to deflation risk while recognizing that our various actions to grow the balance sheet may stoke inflation expectations and bear upside inflation risk.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The Eighth District economy, like the national economy, is mired in recession.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it is somewhat less severe than some other areas, but it is still a very sharp recession.

speaker: BULLARD
text: One winner in the District, and in the nation, is Wal-Mart, which has benefited from trade-down by consumers during the recession.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This has also mitigated some problems in an otherwise overbuilt northwest Arkansas.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Some contacts— not all, not even most—see very tentative signs of a bottoming out.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But at least one contact who has been very pessimistic—this is like President Plosser’s contact—felt that sales volume and revenue numbers had flattened out and that, therefore, the firm had found the bottom.

speaker: BULLARD
text: More important, this particular CEO was actually acting on that idea going forward and developing business strategies based on the idea that they were at the bottom.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is in the transportation industry.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Nationally, this is one of the worst recessions in the postwar era, according to a number of metrics.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My judgment is that, at this point, we will just need to have more data before we can see what is going to happen here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am not particularly convinced that we have seen signs of bottoming out.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Turning points are notoriously hard to predict.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You could easily turn down again, given the situation that we are in.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As President Yellen has stressed, we are susceptible to further shocks from unknown quarters.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In my view, we have lots of issues that are really not resolved at this point, especially the financial market turmoil but also issues in the auto sector and the prospects for global recovery.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Measures of financial market stress are showing only modest improvement, and that is relative to very high peaks, so I would not find this very convincing.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If we were seeing these kinds of numbers before the crisis began, we’d be saying that these are horrible numbers.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So it is only modest improvement relative to a very bad situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Time has not been a healer for financial markets.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If you would have told me at the beginning, in August 2007, that these would still be lingering this long, I would have been very surprised.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would have expected them to heal.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The FRB/US model is probably not a good guide for policymaking in this environment.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I base this on the brilliant figure provided in the memo by Robert Tetlow and Peter Tulip.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It is their figure 1, which shows 90 percent confidence intervals for key forecast variables as of June 2007.

speaker: BULLARD
text: No doubt, many of you read it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Actual events have far outstripped these measures of uncertainty, so we are way outside the confidence bands that were put around forecasts at that time except for inflation, and my interpretation of that is that we are quasi-inflation targeting and inflation stays close to the target.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The memo does a great job of summarizing issues about thinking about uncertainty in our models.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We often talk about uncertainty around the table, but it is hard to internalize the extent to which it is true and what the magnitudes really are.

speaker: BULLARD
text: One way to think about how much uncertainty we face is to consider not just what has happened in the United States in the last 20 years or even the last 4 years but to consider what happens sometimes in foreign economies.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You have lots of experiences internationally—many different countries, many different times and places, and many different policies that have been pursued, some of them with disastrous effects.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Of course, we always say, “Well, those are foreign countries.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That didn’t happen here.” But getting a range of experience and a range of the kinds of things that can happen in what is a very explosive situation that is marked by panics, runs, and huge expectational effects might give you a better idea of the kinds of outcomes that might materialize going forward and how much uncertainty is really out there, as opposed to what has happened just in the United States over a relatively benign period until recently.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We know that macro expectations are critical for the behavior of the economy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is probably not the FRB/US model’s strong suit.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The model is great at tracking the evolution of the U.S. economy in ordinary, relatively tranquil circumstances.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It is not designed to capture the types of dramatic global signaling effects that we have witnessed during the last nine months.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I would downplay the predictions from the model at this juncture, and I think implicitly we all say that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that is also the recommendation of the staff—if you work with the model every day, you understand what the limitations are, where the assumptions are, and what other kinds of effects are not part of the design of the model.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I just want to mention the memo by Eileen Mauskopf and Jae Sim, which I thought was also quite good.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They also stressed the uncertainty about their estimates, which is certainly dramatic.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But at the same time, this memo begins to lay out the ideas about an optimal plan for the Committee and for monetary policy going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Whatever policies we decide on, we do need a reason that we think a particular path is the optimal one.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As I have said before, I would like to get away from the one-time announcements that tend to surprise the market.

speaker: BULLARD
text: When the market is surprised by what we do, that is not necessarily a very good sign.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is a sign that they are not understanding what we are up to, and that they are surprised at the time that the announcement is made.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is not usually a signal that the policy is close to optimal.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Current policy in the United States is trading heavily on U.S. credibility.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If we were a small developing country pursuing our current policies, I do not think we could get away with it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Expectations of inflation would rise rapidly, in my opinion.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So this shows how much credibility and expectations will influence U.S. outcomes going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We are leaning very hard on this aspect, and the rest of the world is counting on our credibility.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Our models are not good at dealing with these issues.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The model, as I said before, is designed to track in tranquil times.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If we push too hard, we may again get surprised by outcomes that are not potential outcomes that the model can describe.

speaker: BULLARD
text: One possibility would be a sharp rise in longer-term Treasury yields, such as that which the Chinese officials described to President Fisher.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am concerned at this juncture about the potential for large mistakes.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We have an output gap, which is yawning by traditional measures.

speaker: BULLARD
text: However, like President Plosser, I would emphasize the New Keynesian concept of an output gap, which is probably far smaller.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The New Keynesian model is the leading theory on the table today in academia.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In it, the economy has to react to a very large and very real shock.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The gap is then not the difference between what happens on average and actual output but the difference between a flexible price concept of output and the actual output that you get on sticky prices.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That gap is likely to be much smaller than what is described in our FRB/US model, and this has the potential, at this juncture, to be a huge policy error.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If you consider the description by Athanasios Orphanides, the rise of inflation during the 1970s was all based on poor estimation of output gaps and maybe poor concepts of output gaps.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it is a clear and very pronounced risk in the current circumstances.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If you think that the economy had to react to this real shock and then the flexible price level of output is a little different from the sticky price level of output, that’s your output gap.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Otherwise, you think that the output gap is way up here and so it is very different.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A key medium-term risk for the Committee is that we think about that concept in the right way.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I will finish up with a few comments on the balance sheet.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I have advocated splitting the balance sheet into two components, and much of the analysis is doing that in various ways.

speaker: BULLARD
text: There is a lot more discussion in terms of seeing certain programs as transitory, lender-of-last­ resort programs, so-called liquidity programs, as opposed to the persistent outright purchase programs of MBS, Treasuries, and agency debt.

speaker: BULLARD
text: One idea I would have going forward for the lender-of-last-resort programs, one thing the Committee and the Board could consider, is trying to price those programs so that they are all backstops.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This means that especially the TAF, the CPFF, and the swaps would all continue to exist, but we would arrange the pricing to make them just outside what would be available through market channels.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am not sure exactly how this could be done, but I think it could be done.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My sense is that we are closer to that right now than we have been in the last nine months.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If we could do that, you could take the volumes in those programs down to zero, but the programs would remain in place with the backstop pricing in case financial market turmoil again intensifies.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This would provide the benefits of these programs without clouding up the balance sheet with large volume, which might be helpful for monetary policy going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It is close to what a lot of people have talked about here—that the programs would fade away.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But we could make them fade away by doing the pricing in just the right way, so that they would be backstops, but they would not have much volume in them.

speaker: EVANS
text: Much as President Yellen said, I think the best news today seems to be that, for once, the forecast has not deteriorated between FOMC meetings.

speaker: EVANS
text: In fact, looking at, in the Greenbook, the evolution of the staff forecast, this is about the only noticeable time that the forecast has improved in the past year.

speaker: EVANS
text: So thanks very much, Dave and your staff, for that.

speaker: EVANS
text: President Bullard just made a number of very interesting and stimulating comments, and I want to take just a slight exception.

speaker: EVANS
text: I thought that the rap on FRB/US was a bit too tough on the forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I understand it, it is really more the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: I agree with you that you have to know what you are trying to use the model for—the question that is being asked.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I am hard- pressed to think of any model that would predict well during this period.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that these models are helpful for verifying our intuition in a disciplined fashion in response to a number of these issues.

speaker: EVANS
text: You pointed out that the Mauskopf–Sim paper was useful, and that used FRB/US as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I just wanted to mention that.

speaker: EVANS
text: We have nudged up our forecast a bit, and there is not much distance between our projections and the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: The broad contours of that outlook seem consistent with what I am hearing from my directors and other business contacts.

speaker: EVANS
text: They say that the pace of deterioration is slowing and report that the most dire scenarios now seem less likely.

speaker: EVANS
text: Some of them had been close to making some major structural cutbacks but are now postponing those plans in the hope that they can be avoided completely.

speaker: EVANS
text: A couple of factors seem to underlie the modest improvement in the outlook of business people.

speaker: EVANS
text: One is that credit conditions are somewhat better.

speaker: EVANS
text: This is evident in the spreads and other data that we looked at earlier—the Greenbook’s financial factors indexes—and in the rebound in equity markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: Another factor is that, after all the cutting, the economy’s natural cyclical adjustment process is finally becoming evident.

speaker: EVANS
text: Inventories have been slashed, and although many firms say that they have more cutting to do, they are at least to the point where they can imagine having stocks under control.

speaker: EVANS
text: After that, they will need to increase production to keep up with demand.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, in sectors, such as housing, that have had the most excess capacity, falling prices may be finally helping to stabilize demand.

speaker: EVANS
text: That said, the improvement in tone is a relative one.

speaker: EVANS
text: As President Bullard said, my conversations with business people are still dominated by reports of further declines in activity and extremely difficult business environments.

speaker: EVANS
text: Whereas previously they talked as if the bottom was unimaginably far in the future, now they can see faint signs of its emergence.

speaker: EVANS
text: I suppose in the Washington area this goes as green shoots.

speaker: EVANS
text: Perhaps in Minneapolis it is referred to as the spring thaw.

speaker: EVANS
text: In Chicago, the Cubs are playing baseball, and it won’t be long before they are thinking about next year.

speaker: EVANS
text: Anyway, nobody seems to think the bottom is here yet.

speaker: EVANS
text: While businesses feel that the risk may be lower, many still feel as though they are in a battle for survival, and they are acting accordingly.

speaker: EVANS
text: In our District, with autos and steel and heavily weighted toward manufacturing, that seems to be the case.

speaker: EVANS
text: This all seems consistent with our forecast, which, like the Greenbook, projects further declines in output this spring before fiscal stimulus and the change in inventory dynamics lead to positive growth in the second half of the year.

speaker: EVANS
text: Absent another round of contracting credit conditions, this is a reasonable expectation.

speaker: EVANS
text: I hope these forecasts rely on modest credit market improvements and are not premised on outright rebounds in credit conditions.

speaker: EVANS
text: That seems less likely, especially given the commentary from Dave Stockton in the question and answer period.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not especially optimistic that the stress-test results and whatever public capital injections they necessitate will boost appreciably the supply of bank lending.

speaker: EVANS
text: After all, additional injections are insurance against higher possible losses.

speaker: EVANS
text: I worry that bankers will spend more time trying to right-size their balance sheet in order to repay their TARP money, and this has been mentioned by others as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the TALF, we are off to a slow start.

speaker: EVANS
text: There are fears of further government-imposed restrictions.

speaker: EVANS
text: Clearly, this is a useful backstop for some impaired ABS markets.

speaker: EVANS
text: It seems less likely to be a stimulus for robust expansion of aggregate demand, but less of a headwind is a plus at this point.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our inflation forecast has not changed much.

speaker: EVANS
text: We have revised up 2009 a bit to reflect the incoming data, but we continue to see core PCE inflation coming in at about 1¼ percent in 2010 and 2011.

speaker: EVANS
text: The risks to the inflation outlook have not changed and continue to be significant in both directions, it seems.

speaker: EVANS
text: The large and persistent resource gaps justify some worry about more- marked disinflation, but it is not possible to speak in public and avoid hearing that inflation and inflation expectations are about to increase greatly because of the explosion of our balance sheet and concerns about monetizing the rising government debt.

speaker: EVANS
text: Perceptions of previous episodes, in which policy reversed course tentatively, slowly, and even late, haunt these critics; and issues like the Orphanides gap are also a possible reason for that concern.

speaker: EVANS
text: Everyone has carefully discussed the need for a prudent exit strategy to avoid these risks, and I appreciate all the commentary about more discussion at our June meeting to look at our balance sheet and possible exit strategies.

speaker: EVANS
text: So there is little more that we can do on this score at the moment, but maintaining our current policy trajectory might help a bit, given the improved situation today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We can add to the statement, “Wait until next year.” President Pianalto.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: During the intermeeting period, I heard from an encouraging number of contacts that business conditions were showing some initial signs of stabilizing at very low levels.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Relatively large companies with deep pockets and access to credit seem prepared to wait out the recession, although many have to make some painful adjustments.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Others, especially small businesses, worry openly about running out of cash and time.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Some employers are still considering reductions in staffing, and it is rare to find companies engaged in any net hiring.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Even hospitals, which are traditionally very stable employers, have been reducing staff where possible in response to declines in demand.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Public-sector and nonprofit employment continues to be under pressure as well.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Although most of the employment declines we are observing result from cyclical forces, I think that more than the usual share of employment losses also stem from structural factors.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: After reviewing the declining pattern of job openings reported in the JOLTS data, as well as the relatively low levels of temporary layoffs that President Yellen commented on, my staff concludes that labor market reallocations are likely to be quite large and prolonged during this business cycle.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Regarding inflation, I appreciate the concern about a continuing deceleration in our price measures.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, I am struck by the number of people I speak with who worry that our policy actions will cause inflation to accelerate in the future.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In fact, the people who worry about accelerating inflation far outnumber those who express concerns about future deflation.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I am not overly concerned at this point about deteriorating inflation expectations.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My view is that, with clear communication about our inflation objectives, our large-scale asset purchase will damp the decline of long-term inflation expectations, something that the Reifschneider–Roberts memo tells us is not captured in FRB/US.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In my projection, core PCE inflation remains in the range of 1 percent to 1½ percent through 2011, whereas in the Greenbook baseline, inflation falls below 1 percent.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The anecdotal information that we collected, along with the data that we received, hasn’t led me to make any material changes to my outlook for employment and output since our March meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My current output projection has some differences in timing of the recovery compared with the Greenbook baseline; however, I don’t consider them to be material.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My forecast for the unemployment rate does deviate more substantially from the Greenbook as a result of my interpretation of the persistent weakness that we are seeing in labor markets.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My baseline projection has more labor reallocation taking place than the Greenbook does, and that drives my forecast for unemployment to peak at a bit over 10 percent before it begins to decline.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The additional labor reallocation embedded in my outlook is another factor that puts my core inflation forecast on a higher path than that in the Greenbook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: That is, I see a somewhat smaller output gap than the Greenbook does because I see a somewhat lower level of potential output in my projection coming from the labor market reallocations that I commented on.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: It goes without saying that the level of uncertainty around my projection is unusually great, and there are many risk factors that could render it inaccurate.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: One of the risks that looms large in my mind—and it has already been mentioned by several others around the table today— is that announcing the results of the stress test could add to the fragility of the banking system, and it could result in a further pullback in bank lending, as others have commented.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: At least that was the gut reaction I got from the bankers that I talked to as I was presenting the preliminary results of the test.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I hope that we will fully consider these concerns as we decide what information to release publicly.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Many of us are on record as saying that, in order to restore confidence in the banking system, we have to see private capital go back into that system.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am concerned that announcing that a majority of the 19 bank holding companies need additional capital and that the additional capital can come from the government is going to scare private investors away.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So, on balance, I regard the risk to my outlook for both output and inflation to be weighted to the downside, especially taking into consideration some of the announcement effect of our stress test.

speaker: LACKER
text: A bit of a shift in our District information is discernible over the last month or two.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our Fifth District manufacturing survey, which you will recall is released a few days later than the New York and Philadelphia indexes, but covers more manufacturing activity than both of those indexes combined—

speaker: FISHER
text: But not as much as my District.

speaker: LACKER
text: I believe more than the Dallas District as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: The survey has moved sharply back to neutral over the last two months from the exceptionally negative readings we were seeing earlier, and the shipments and orders components have increased from around minus 50 in February to around zero now.

speaker: LACKER
text: Interestingly, the six-months-ahead expectation measures for shipments and orders are solidly in positive territory, but the index for capital expenditures remains negative, suggesting that excess capacity will be restraining business investment for a while.

speaker: LACKER
text: So far we have not seen similar moves in our service sector survey.

speaker: LACKER
text: Overall our surveys suggest a bottoming out in goods production but continued decline in services.

speaker: LACKER
text: Qualitative information from our directors and other contacts also suggests a shift in tone from uniformly dismal to mixed.

speaker: LACKER
text: Some directors see signs of life for building lot transactions in some markets—North Carolina and central Maryland were mentioned.

speaker: LACKER
text: There are scattered reports of an increase in residential real estate traffic, although contacts are not yet saying that this has translated into increased sales.

speaker: LACKER
text: Even though this may just be the seasonal pickup you’d normally expect, people seem to be treating a normal seasonal pickup in real estate traffic as positive news, given the experience of the past few years.

speaker: LACKER
text: The Fifth District hospitality sector seems to have been hurt by a fear of adverse publicity.

speaker: LACKER
text: One director whose firm stages trade shows says that “fun” appears to be the new F word.

speaker: LACKER
text: A contact who runs a resort on the South Carolina coast reports corporations canceling bookings for which they have already paid in full.

speaker: LACKER
text: People apparently don’t want to risk the bad publicity of showing up, which is puzzling because critics presumably object to the expenditure not the utility derived.

speaker: LACKER
text: In West Virginia, the coal industry is described as somewhat shell-shocked because of falling coal prices, although drilling rigs from western states have been moving east to take advantage of increased drilling activity in the Marcellus shale formation.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the national level, there have been some signals consistent with a business cycle trough sometime in the middle of the year, I think.

speaker: LACKER
text: I put the tentative signs of stabilization in the housing sector chief among these since the return of some confidence on that front seems important for restoring a broader willingness by households to resume discretionary spending.

speaker: LACKER
text: Of course, we have been fooled by hints of housing market bottoms before.

speaker: LACKER
text: So it is not hard for me to curb my enthusiasm.

speaker: LACKER
text: Still, the recent consumer spending numbers also suggest that a broader household resilience may be emerging.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consumers seem to have been cutting back in response to the general erosion in their confidence about future income and wealth; and the fact that consumer spending was relatively stable in the first quarter, despite ending on a down note, might reflect some households looking through the recession toward a return to sustained growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: Similarly, I think the weakness in business spending has been driven mainly by a dearth of foreseeable profit opportunities as opposed to being held back by credit constraints.

speaker: LACKER
text: The tentative signs of stabilization on the durable goods front are welcome news, but I think it will take some evidence of a sustained improvement in consumer spending and, thus, revenue growth to bring business spending back to the table in a major way.

speaker: LACKER
text: Regarding inflation, the stability of long-term expectations has been notable and stands in contrast to the Greenbook’s forecasted expectations that inflation will drift steadily downward over the next few years.

speaker: LACKER
text: Personally, my outlook for inflation expectations is centered near 2 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the inherent difficulties in projecting inflation expectations are significant, but there’s also at least as much of a chance that they will increase significantly during the recovery rather than decrease.

speaker: LACKER
text: I continue to worry about how we are going to know whether we are doing enough, too little, or too much and how we are going to know when to begin unwinding the expansion of our balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: It seems like a daunting problem for us.

speaker: LACKER
text: My sense is that credit spreads are going to be too ambiguous to act on, and I am leery of taking too much comfort from Japan’s experience.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I believe we could use a better understanding of the effect of our large reserve balances on the banking system.

speaker: LACKER
text: Finally, Mr. Chairman, down in North Carolina the bankers are distributing these lapel pins.

speaker: LACKER
text: They’re little round green things and they say “EGBAR.” Now I am not going to be able to do justice to a North Carolina drawl, but it comes out something like this: “Everything’s going to be all right.” I don’t know whether they believe it or whether they just want their customers to believe it.

speaker: LACKER
text: But in any event, they don’t say when it’s going to be all right, so I’m not sure that we should put much faith in this either.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any charge for the pins?

speaker: LACKER
text: I got this one for free, and that means it is worth less than $20.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Your drawl will be reflected in the transcript.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, I’m in substantial agreement with the Greenbook forecast, for the next four or five quarters anyway.

speaker: STERN
text: As several people have noted, certainly there is a lot of uncertainty around, but it seems to me that there is a reasonable chance that recovery will get under way around midyear—June, July, or thereabouts.

speaker: STERN
text: I think it is worth bearing in mind that, if that happens, we probably won’t discern it for at least several months thereafter—August, September, or October—partially because of data flows and partially because, as I expect, initially the recovery will be quite modest, which means that the incoming data are going to be mixed at best and it will be possible to read some of it positively and some of it negatively.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that this level of uncertainty is simply going to be part of what we’re going to experience.

speaker: STERN
text: I do agree, as I said earlier, that the recovery will initially be quite modest.

speaker: STERN
text: President Yellen and others have done a good job of elucidating the reasons for that.

speaker: STERN
text: Nevertheless, I didn’t really revise my forecast from January, so I have almost all the same numbers.

speaker: STERN
text: If I were going to revise the forecast, I’d probably revise it up rather than down at this point—not by a lot and not trying to get to the typical recovery alternative in the Greenbook, which would be extraordinary if the economy produced something like that.

speaker: STERN
text: But it does seem to me that the variety of data that have come in have been better than anticipated, including improvement in credit market conditions.

speaker: STERN
text: None of that may turn out to be durable, but on the other hand, I think we have been anticipating that some of this was going to improve and some healing would occur over time.

speaker: STERN
text: I guess I don’t expect the stress test to lead to an increase in bank lending.

speaker: STERN
text: I thought the stress test was trying to address uncertainty about the conditions of banks, and I think it’s going to come down to whether the report is credible with regard to two large and very sick institutions.

speaker: STERN
text: But I don’t think the rest of it is going to matter very much.

speaker: STERN
text: It is really whether the numbers associated with those institutions strike people in the financial markets as sensible, appropriate, and so forth.

speaker: STERN
text: If they do, I think the stress test will probably have helped.

speaker: STERN
text: If not, I think we’re going to have potential chaos—I guess that’s the way I would put it.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as inflation goes, I expect inflation to be low, but certainly the second-most-asked question I get when I’m out talking to people is, “Aren’t we going to see a burst of inflation with the expansion in your balance sheet and with the stance of fiscal policy?” So it seems to me that discussing exit strategies, sterilization, and so forth in June is going to be important, and communicating with the public about this is going to be important, recognizing that we might have a bit of a timing issue on our hands.

speaker: STERN
text: I guess the way that I would put it is that we first want to make sure the fire is out.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Let me start with the District, and I’ll be brief.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I have talked to several dozen people in the region, and I have not had a single one tell me that they think things are improving.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But what I do hear is that things are not getting any worse except for a couple of areas.

speaker: HOENIG
text: One of those areas is natural gas production, which if those rigs are moving your way, I’d look at them pretty carefully before I put them in production, given the price of natural gas right now.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The other is commercial real estate.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There is a lot of angst about commercial real estate in the region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Projects are on hold and have been stopped.

speaker: HOENIG
text: A lot of banks are holding this stuff, and a lot of them have pretty heavy concentrations of it, which gives me pause.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the other hand, when they say things are not getting worse, there are some indications of manufacturing beginning to stabilize, some retail sales beginning to stabilize, and even some of the housing, even though it is down from a year ago, in the last couple of months has shown some stability as well in the region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: About the national outlook—I think that, as we go through the rest of this year and into next year, we will see things improve.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There are a couple of positive forces and then one thing that I consider a real negative.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The two positives are that, as we see inventories and values adjust, people then will begin to move forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Complementing that is the fact that the stimulus package is starting to flow.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We’re seeing a lot of highway projects really getting going, especially in our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The one thing that I find interesting is the value of subsidies because, as the ethanol industry is collapsing, we are now in the wind tunnel—seeing enormous amounts of investment on wind energy being placed there.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There is no way to get it out yet, but they are building these towers by the thousands, and that is adding a lot of activity in the rural areas, particularly of our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The negative is the credit and banking conditions.

speaker: HOENIG
text: There is a fair amount of capital in these banks, but when you see their asset issues and their uncertainty around those assets, they are conserving that capital and they are holding back on lending.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Another part of this is, as we have introduced each new plan—whether it was the PPIP or whatever—money has gone to the sidelines to see how that is going to evolve.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That has made things slower than they might have otherwise been, and I think we need to be aware of that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As you boil all of this down, I think the stimulus will be a big plus as we move through this year and into next.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As we stabilize, there’s a real upside, but the credit market banking level is a big risk going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I don’t think we’ve begun at all to address the commercial real estate problems that are just wreaking havoc.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the economy is going to do somewhat better over the next few months and, I hope, quarters.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A big swing in the rate of inventory liquidation is certainly going to help, and we have seen in the past that it can be very, very powerful quarter to quarter.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A good example is the fourth quarter of 2001 to the first quarter of 2002—which was probably the worst forecast I ever made in my life—but I’m not going to be very impressed by that for several reasons.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, we still do not have the banking system on a sound footing, and that’s pretty damning, frankly, 20 months into this crisis.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If we can do a good job with the supervisory capital assessment program and get more capital into the banking system, then we have a fighting chance.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In this regard, I think it is important for us all to be on message about this.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Next week is going to be really, really important.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The announcement will generate lots of criticism: The stress test is not severe enough, the estimated losses are too low, and so on.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I believe that we should emphasize three points.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: First, what is the purpose of the exercise?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To get more capital into the banking system and thereby to make the adverse outcome less likely.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is important not to get lost in the fine print.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Second, the adverse scenario that was assumed is still considerably worse than the base forecast; and in the adverse scenario, banks would still be well capitalized.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We need to emphasize that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Third, in assessing the loss figures, we need to make it clear that the losses that matter for commercial banks are credit losses, not liquidation losses.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because banks have deposits, they can hold their assets to maturity.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This means that the liquidation value is mostly irrelevant.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is particularly important in the current environment, of course, because the illiquidity discount is unusually high.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This makes the value of the assets to those, such as banks, that are leveraged and have deposits that can fund and hold those assets much greater than the value of the assets to those, such as hedge funds, that have difficulties in this environment obtaining leverage.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second thing that I would stress about the economic outlook is that a lot of pain is still ahead, and I’ll echo some of President Hoenig’s comments.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Commercial mortgages and highly leveraged loans appear particularly vulnerable.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Commercial mortgages are suffering from a double whammy—a higher capitalization rate on mortgages and lower income.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is pushing down commercial real estate values sharply.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The John Hancock Tower sold for half the price at which it was purchased in 2005, and that’s considered a prime property rather than a not very attractive property.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t see this ending very quickly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the corporate side, highly leveraged businesses are going to have trouble refinancing for the same reason.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rise in the risk- adjusted return demanded by investors will significantly drive down the value of the underlying enterprises.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: For many private equity deals, covenant-lite loans and PIK toggles will delay the day of reckoning, but that just means that the resulting hole that must be filled will be bigger as a consequence.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The third thing I’d say on the economy is that the big news is the large adjustment that households are going to have to make in terms of deleveraging and the offsetting shift that we’re going to have to see in foreign economies toward stimulating domestic demand and away from exports.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That’s going to take quite a bit of time, and to my mind that process is just starting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: This is one more reason that I think the risks to the economic outlook, even expecting that GDP growth may resume by the second half of this year, are still very much to the downside.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like the others, I’m encouraged by some of the signs of stability in household spending and consumption and of housing demand leveling out in the first quarter, albeit at very low levels.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it is an especially hopeful sign that the stability occurred when jobs and production were declining very rapidly, and at least for the first two months of the quarter, the financial markets were getting worse, not better.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also encouraging, as others have pointed out, is the stability and slight improvement in financial conditions over the last month or so.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think perceptions that the downside risks have abated are in the financial markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: This is a necessary condition for economic recovery and is indicative that confidence has stabilized and may be beginning to increase.

speaker: KOHN
text: You see a bit of this in household consumer confidence in the past month or two.

speaker: KOHN
text: Production is below even the weak level of demand; so as long as demand doesn’t fall off further, conditions are in place for working through the inventory cycles in goods and houses with a gradual rise in production as the negative inventory dynamics of the past few quarters ebb and reverse.

speaker: KOHN
text: And there are good reasons to think that final demand will continue to stabilize.

speaker: KOHN
text: Consumption behavior in the first quarter does suggest perhaps a more gradual upward drift in the saving rate after a very sharp adjustment in the level of consumption in the second half of last year due to declining wealth, greater uncertainty, and very, very poor job prospects—so maybe a slower increase in the saving rate from here on out.

speaker: KOHN
text: Housing demand is at frictional levels.

speaker: KOHN
text: Of course, I thought that several quarters ago, but maybe it really is at frictional levels now and is perhaps being bolstered by low prices and interest rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: I take some encouragement from the firming in commodity prices, which I think suggests that global weakness is beginning to abate somewhat.

speaker: KOHN
text: Certainly the conversations I had with G-20 emerging-market central bankers over the last weekend were that, like some of the anecdotes we’re hearing around the table, they see less weakness and some signs of improvement and the commodity markets were an important sign of that.

speaker: KOHN
text: As consumption demand stabilizes, the decline in capital investment should abate as the capital stock comes in line with the lower level of sales.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I agree with the basic shape of the staff forecast for the next few quarters: a slower decline and then stability.

speaker: KOHN
text: Still, I do think there are downside risks for the near term, especially from an accident in the financial sector.

speaker: KOHN
text: Signs of improvement are tentative.

speaker: KOHN
text: Lots of people have addressed the stress-test risk, and I think it’s very, very large both for an accident in the near term, over the next week or two, and for damping.

speaker: KOHN
text: If confidence isn’t restored through the injection of capital and banks get even more cautious about not wanting to convert the convertible preferred into government common, or if they have to take that convertible preferred, they’re going to damp their lending.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think there are near-term and long-term risks here.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with what the Vice Chairman said: The idea here was to build confidence.

speaker: KOHN
text: If we handle it right, I think it is possible; but the risks are huge.

speaker: KOHN
text: Even though I see downside risks, I think they’re smaller than I thought they were a meeting or two ago.

speaker: KOHN
text: The end of the recession is still a forecast, but at least we have some tentative evidence that the elements are falling into place.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also agree with the staff expectation that the subsequent recovery will be gradual, more gradual than in past recessions, with a large output gap persisting for some time.

speaker: KOHN
text: My reasons are the same that many others have cited.

speaker: KOHN
text: Financial repair will be slow.

speaker: KOHN
text: As President Bullard pointed out, borrowing rates, terms, and conditions for many private borrowers are still very tight, and we would have considered them very tight at any other time even if they have improved some.

speaker: KOHN
text: A return to more-normal financial markets and easier financial conditions will take time.

speaker: KOHN
text: The financial system is adjusting to reduced leverage and better liquidity protection, and that will be good in the long run.

speaker: KOHN
text: But that adjustment is going to take time, and it implies tight credit for a while.

speaker: KOHN
text: More intermediation is going to have to flow through banks, and banks will need to rebuild capital.

speaker: KOHN
text: Though the government capital might be helpful in that regard, it’s not clear that it will be.

speaker: KOHN
text: And lenders are still worried about the economic outlook and credit losses, and I think that concern is likely to dissipate slowly.

speaker: KOHN
text: As others have pointed out, household balance sheets also need repair.

speaker: KOHN
text: Saving rates will be high relative to recent history and could trend higher as households rebuild wealth.

speaker: KOHN
text: Confidence is likely to recover slowly after recent events.

speaker: KOHN
text: Animal-spirit-damped expectations will remain a restraint on spending.

speaker: KOHN
text: Businesses and households, given the shocks that they have been through, are likely to remain cautious.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the global character of the downturn also suggests that the upturn is going to be restrained.

speaker: KOHN
text: There are policy constraints on fiscal policy in lots of places because of concerns about long-term fiscal sustainability, and of course, monetary policy almost everywhere including the United States is constrained by the zero lower bound.

speaker: KOHN
text: No country is really going to pull the others out of the recession, and I am concerned over the intermediate to the longer run about what is going to substitute for consumption.

speaker: KOHN
text: The U.S. household demand for houses and for goods and services has really been an engine of growth for the global economy, and it’s not obvious to me where the substitute for that is going to come from.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I do think a slow, gradual recovery is the most likely outcome.

speaker: KOHN
text: I had something like the staff’s forecast—a little faster at the end, but still quite slow.

speaker: KOHN
text: The inflation implications of this are that inflation should continue to drift down.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the gap is high and will be high for some time.

speaker: KOHN
text: That will put downward pressure on inflation, although inflation expectations are anchored and the downward drift should be limited.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with President Plosser and others that you can’t really measure the output gap.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s a concept, not a thing you can ever measure, and it’s risky to put a lot of weight on it.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I do think the gap is large enough right now, and the information we have from which we can infer what’s going on suggests that it’s still large.

speaker: KOHN
text: If you look at 12-month inflation rates—PCE, CPI—they are all drifting down, which is what you would kind of expect if you had an output gap, although the last three months were higher than we anticipated, so maybe you need to keep an eye on that.

speaker: KOHN
text: We don’t have much in the way of compensation data.

speaker: KOHN
text: The last compensation data we had were for the fourth quarter.

speaker: KOHN
text: One measure—the productivity and cost measure—was kind of flat, had been flat through the year, and didn’t show any trend; but the ECI, which is a measure on which we’ve put more emphasis in previous analyses, did show a distinct deceleration through the fourth quarter, which would suggest to me that there was an output gap.

speaker: KOHN
text: Average hourly earnings, which is a very flawed measure of labor costs, that we have through March, showed a very, very definite deceleration.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think the price and wage data, imperfect as they are, suggest that there is a considerable output gap putting downward pressure on increases in those things.

speaker: WARSH
text: After the despair at our last meeting, we may have expected to find ourselves with locusts, floods, and plagues.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I suspect the swine flu pandemic and the leaked stress-test results do seem like veritable green shoots in comparison.

speaker: WARSH
text: May that be the ninth and last reference to green shoots today, unless my colleagues choose to reference that as well.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think, as the Greenbook and Dave suggested, that the most significant change since the last time we met is in the tone, tenor, and level of financial markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I hesitate to take too much definitive comfort from these improvements and recognize, of course, that the financial markets and the real economy are relating to one another.

speaker: WARSH
text: But, again, a lot seems to be hinging on continued improvements in these markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: So let me talk first about financial market developments; second, briefly about financial firms and stress tests; third, about the economy; and, fourth, briefly about inflation.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, on the financial market side, we have seen since the lows on March 9 a $3 trillion addition to the net worth of U.S. households.

speaker: WARSH
text: Globally, the addition to net worth is probably around $9 trillion.

speaker: WARSH
text: I tend to think that that is more constructive, more important to outcomes, than stimulus packages that we and others could have constructed.

speaker: WARSH
text: If that trend continues, then the Greenbook might end up looking calm in comparison, but I am probably not as bullish as that.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that the change in net worth, the change in market cap, is indicative of principally an unwinding of some fear, an unwinding of some risk premium, and maybe a little better, the market’s view of improved economic prospects.

speaker: WARSH
text: But the benefits of the equity market improvements aren’t confined to wealth.

speaker: WARSH
text: We see second-order improvements in confidence, even though it is at low levels.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is coming back slowly, but seemingly surely, to various measures of business confidence and consumer confidence.

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, if that trend holds, we will be in awfully good shape.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me look, after the equity markets, to a market that I haven’t referenced for some time, which is the convertible market.

speaker: WARSH
text: The convertible markets are booming.

speaker: WARSH
text: Keep in mind, as Trish and others probably discussed previously, convertible markets are a very hot or a very cold market.

speaker: WARSH
text: The market right now is exceptionally hot.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think it tells us something about investor preferences.

speaker: WARSH
text: Investors have seen markets move 20, 25, 30 percent in equity.

speaker: WARSH
text: They say, “Well, I want a bit of an equity appreciation.” At the same time, they are still a little risk averse, so they want that downside protection, all of which is making the convertible market the market of choice.

speaker: WARSH
text: We see a range of companies, both high-quality names and lesser names, using the convertible market to raise meaningful capital.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would say that the pipelines in the convertible market are as large as they have been in eighteen months or two years, and those markets are robust, even in this upcoming week.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the Greenbook talked in detail about the fixed-income markets, which continue to show some improvement, making all-in financing costs lower than I think many, including myself, would have expected them to have been when we last met.

speaker: WARSH
text: I also see renewed interest in financial institutions issuing non-TLGP paper, which I think is a good sign, first, to try to prove that they are okay, different, and better, but also they are starting to feel more comfortable that the government backstops won’t be around forever, and they want to differentiate themselves.

speaker: WARSH
text: With that, let me turn to financial firms and stress tests, my second point of focus.

speaker: WARSH
text: Prior to the stress-test results, we have seen a race by the relatively strong to access these markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: The capital that Goldman Sachs raised some weeks ago was much discussed, and just this morning Northern Trust raised $750 million of equity capital.

speaker: WARSH
text: After a greenshoe option is triggered by the underwriter, it will be something closer to $900 million.

speaker: WARSH
text: Now, the book at Northern Trust—which markets perceive to be a relatively strong mix between a recurring revenue business and an old-fashioned bank but maybe still a bit more the former—was good, healthy, but not massively oversubscribed.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think they raised this capital at around $50 a share, trading a couple of dollars higher going into the pricing this morning.

speaker: WARSH
text: That does tell me that there are markets—that is, there is demand for high-quality names, but it is not an insatiable demand.

speaker: WARSH
text: Given Northern Trust’s success, we should feel that, if what we do is effective on the stress tests, the markets will be open for some, but not all, of the names that are seeking private capital.

speaker: WARSH
text: In addition, Northern Trust, Credit Suisse, and BB&T are in the market today raising debt at yield spreads that are remarkable—275 to 325 over 5-year and 10-year money.

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, this is very encouraging, probably more encouraging than I would have suspected at the last FOMC meeting.

speaker: WARSH
text: Let me turn to the aptly named stress tests.

speaker: WARSH
text: Depending on execution, they could undermine some of the progress that is at the center of the improvements over the past several weeks.

speaker: WARSH
text: I say that because, historically, financial firms are a higher beta move on broader markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: They have tended to track the S&P historically, at least over the last 20 years, with higher peaks and lower valleys.

speaker: WARSH
text: But they tend to be related to it.

speaker: WARSH
text: In fact, in the last six weeks, bank stocks and financial firms generally have outperformed the broader markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: To the extent that the financial firms suffer, I would expect them to bring down a lot of firms—or at least bring down their market capital—that are unrelated to the banking business.

speaker: WARSH
text: I will highlight several key issues on the stress tests, just asking the questions, but I think we have all debated them at some length.

speaker: WARSH
text: One, will regulators or markets be the predominant determinants of the fate of these 19 firms?

speaker: WARSH
text: Two, will the firms in need of capital have six months to raise private capital or six days?

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, is the specter of government capital confidence inducing or panic inducing?

speaker: WARSH
text: Fourth, and probably most meaningful for the broader economy, what is the resulting competitive landscape, and what is the impact of that landscape on the real economy?

speaker: WARSH
text: With that, let me turn to a third point, which is the real economy itself.

speaker: WARSH
text: I am probably a little more anxious than the Greenbook about the economy and would leave in some of Dave’s and the team’s add factors that made the judgmental forecast a little darker than model predictions for just a bit longer because of the uncertainty that is in store for us over the next few weeks.

speaker: WARSH
text: In addition, I would expect the cap-ex downside risks to be greater than the Greenbook estimates.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would expect the turn in inventories from liquidation to modest growth to perhaps help the arithmetic of second-half growth but provide very little comfort beyond that.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would also expect less improvement in PCE than the Greenbook, but I will have to admit that it is hard to judge.

speaker: WARSH
text: Over the long term, I continue to expect weaker GDP than the Greenbook and higher unemployment, and I suspect that is mostly because I expect a higher NAIRU and lower potential GDP in the outyears for a whole range of reasons, but maybe most simply said, because articles of faith of how this economy works have been up-ended or are in the process of being undermined.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I am just not sure how quickly we get back to trend or whether the old trend is at all indicative of the new.

speaker: WARSH
text: On foreign growth, I think that the forecast from Nathan and his team, though encouraging, likely overstates the return of these non-U.S. economies to growth.

speaker: WARSH
text: Whatever the path is for the United States, I expect the path for the advanced foreign economies overseas to be slower and the return to be less pronounced.

speaker: WARSH
text: In the back of my mind, the problems facing the United Kingdom, Japan, and some other countries—and I hesitate to think that we would ever want to be trading places or seats with them—are fundamental and much harder to get out of after a period like this.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, on inflation, I continue to be more worried about upside risks to inflation than downside risks.

speaker: WARSH
text: As a result, I would expect the removal of the extraordinary policy accommodation to be at a rate faster than the Greenbook suggests and be at slower-than-current market expectations.

speaker: WARSH
text: And I expect that core inflation will remain somewhat higher than in the Greenbook over the forecast period.

speaker: DUKE
text: In looking at the false dawn scenario, I was sobered by the degree to which the Greenbook forecast depends on the reduction in financial sector turmoil.

speaker: DUKE
text: And I share President Rosengren’s concern about the potential destabilization resulting from the announcement of the stress-test results.

speaker: DUKE
text: I am, similarly, skeptical that government capital would spur any additional lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: Instead, it seems that lending is going to be constrained by the private capital positions, which will then be evaluated in light of capital standards that have been implied by the stress tests.

speaker: DUKE
text: I suspect that the most important confidence-building aspect of the stress tests may be actually the degree to which government stands ready to provide absolute support in terms of both capital and liquidity to firms in case there is a destabilizing event.

speaker: DUKE
text: In my talking to the banks that were subject to the stress test and were awaiting their results, they reported that they were surrounded by lawyers and that they had developed communication plans A, B, and C for all of their expected scenarios in terms of the results.

speaker: DUKE
text: I emphasize communication plans—no capital plans.

speaker: DUKE
text: The reason for this is that they simply did not believe that they had any ability to raise private capital alongside government capital, and so that exercise seemed futile.

speaker: DUKE
text: I was struck by one banker to whom I talked who went on at length about his preparations for his stress-test results, to the point that, when I hung up, I went back and checked and determined that, no, he was not covered by the stress test.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I called him back and said, “You know you are not covered by this.” And he said, “I know, but we will be.” He was absolutely convinced and had been encouraged in that belief by his regulators.

speaker: DUKE
text: I did talk to one who was not going to need additional capital, who was getting a strong amount of interest from private equity to repay his government capital but felt as though he would really prefer to wait about six months to separate the stress-test results from the original TARP capital injections.

speaker: DUKE
text: Also, there were some concerns as to what might unfold in the next six months.

speaker: DUKE
text: I don’t think that is unique to him.

speaker: DUKE
text: I think that a number of companies, although they may have talked about wanting to get out of the original capital, are going to be a little less anxious than they might appear.

speaker: DUKE
text: One bank that did give back the TARP capital has seen no improvement in its stock price and no discernible improvement anywhere else.

speaker: DUKE
text: However, I heard from a smaller bank that did give back the capital, and the contact reported much rejoicing in his community, a surge in new customers, and congratulations all around.

speaker: DUKE
text: But the scariest part is that his mother cried in joy and pride when he returned his government capital.

speaker: DUKE
text: The amount of uncertainty about the rules and the changing of the rules are certainly limiting the effectiveness of the TARP, the TLGP, and the PPIP.

speaker: DUKE
text: A number of firms reported that they were trying to work down their government funding but that private funding is still scarce, and no matter who their primary regulator is right now, they are dealing with multiple regulators for multiple programs, all with differing priorities and requirements—the FDIC for the TLGP, the Fed for the TAF, and the Treasury for the TARP.

speaker: DUKE
text: They also said that they can’t rely on traditional correspondents.

speaker: DUKE
text: They have been jerked around by the Home Loan Banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: As one bank put it, at least the Fed won’t redline Michigan.

speaker: DUKE
text: OTTI rules have made a difference for some of the banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: One of them reported 44 basis points on tier 1 capital, 17 basis points for first-quarter write-downs that would have occurred, and 27 basis points in the true-ups.

speaker: DUKE
text: So the OTTI has really made a substantial difference.

speaker: DUKE
text: Earnings, obviously, were better than expected.

speaker: DUKE
text: There are record mortgage originations that are primarily refinance, but some reports of increasing purchase activity.

speaker: DUKE
text: Interestingly, Florida was reported to be 50/50 between refi and purchase, with the reason that the prices have dropped too much for refis to be able to take place and the low prices on foreclosures are actually attracting buyers.

speaker: DUKE
text: Mortgage income is probably sustainable through the year.

speaker: DUKE
text: Good trust and investment income.

speaker: DUKE
text: Loan pricing is much better than it has been historically; the deposit pricing pressure, which had been very strong in the fall, is easing a bit; and prices seem a bit more rational.

speaker: DUKE
text: For smaller banks, the margins are down 100 to 160 basis points since the start of the easing, and all banks are worried about the special FDIC assessment.

speaker: DUKE
text: Demand is weak for new lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: They are pricing for risk.

speaker: DUKE
text: Term tightening is primarily in the higher loan-to-value.

speaker: DUKE
text: There is a big demand for floor plan lending.

speaker: DUKE
text: In fact, the SBA is trying to figure out how to be helpful, but the problem is that nobody has any expertise anymore.

speaker: DUKE
text: As the captives took over that business, the expertise atrophied in the other banks.

speaker: DUKE
text: The smaller banks are still seeing demand from large bank customers, but their ability to meet that demand is becoming more and more strained by their liquidity and capital availability.

speaker: DUKE
text: Deposit growth continues, although the rate of growth seems to be slowing.

speaker: DUKE
text: Transaction accounts within deposits are down almost 10 percent, and overdraft income is down more than 12 percent.

speaker: DUKE
text: Regarding credit quality, delinquencies are still growing, but they are actually more predictable and are coming up as models are predicting.

speaker: DUKE
text: The states that are heavily affected by the auto business are seeing bigger deterioration.

speaker: DUKE
text: The loans that are coming into collection at least now have something to work with.

speaker: DUKE
text: Severity is growing, although some report that home prices are stabilizing.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of nonperforming-loan levels, a couple of banks pointed out that the nonperforming level is not necessarily the best indicator of losses because consumer loans go from delinquent or even not delinquent to charge-off.

speaker: DUKE
text: Only the real estate loans go through the non-accrual process.

speaker: DUKE
text: Nonperformers are increasing even at those banks with low levels of problems.

speaker: DUKE
text: As one bank president put it, if the loan officer had actually looked at the property, he would never have made the loan.

speaker: DUKE
text: The traditional workout activity is going on, deciding which ones they can work with and which ones they need to dispose of.

speaker: DUKE
text: Non-accruals also are growing because of the length of time for judicial foreclosures.

speaker: DUKE
text: It now apparently takes 24 months to complete a foreclosure in the State of Florida because they are so backed up on judicial.

speaker: DUKE
text: It used to take 12 months; now it is up to 24.

speaker: DUKE
text: Then, some banks are holding their ORE for a better market.

speaker: DUKE
