text: I will focus a bit on commercial real estate and the extent to which the use of CMBS and the TALF might be helpful.

speaker: DUKE
text: Eighty percent of maturities in commercial real estate are held in banks, and the CMBS targeted by the TALF actually won’t take out the construction loans and is likely to affect about 20 percent of the rest.

speaker: DUKE
text: As the Vice Chairman pointed out, vacancies are up, rents are down, and cap rates are up.

speaker: DUKE
text: Multifamily is holding up the best, then office.

speaker: DUKE
text: Retail is very weak, and hospitality properties are a disaster.

speaker: DUKE
text: Take-out commitments are being honored, but there are no new commitments.

speaker: DUKE
text: So they are converting the maturities to a three-to-five-year mini-perm, but the appraisals are running 50 to 55 percent of those appraisals done even a year or two years ago.

speaker: DUKE
text: Once the appraisal comes in that low, it breaks the covenants, and then they have to request a paydown and actually put the loans on non-accrual.

speaker: DUKE
text: They are not necessarily moving to foreclosure.

speaker: DUKE
text: They said the Street will worry about the increase in the level of non- accruals, which makes it optically expensive.

speaker: DUKE
text: But they feel that over the long term they are much better served by waiting through this cycle in the real estate market and that the reduction in value in this cycle is not necessarily due to overbuilding but is actually due just to issues going on in the regular economy.

speaker: DUKE
text: The medium-risk properties are the ones that really need to come out of the system.

speaker: DUKE
text: One bank reported that 40 percent of non-accruals are SBA 504 program loans, which means that they are only 50 percent loan-to-value, because the next 40 percent is actually protected by SBA guarantees, but they still have to show them in non-accrual.

speaker: DUKE
text: They are also getting mixed signals from regulators on loans in process of collection.

speaker: DUKE
text: So as we look at issues with commercial real estate, we may be able to address some of this in the supervision and examination standards rather than necessarily trying to do anything specifically with those loans.

speaker: DUKE
text: And that is my report, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: TARULLO
text: While anchoring the last spot in the go- round has the disadvantage of addressing an audience that is weary, if not catatonic, [laughter] it does have the advantage of allowing me to endorse a consensus without having to repeat all of the reasoning that has generated it.

speaker: TARULLO
text: So let me begin by agreeing with what I hear to be the prevailing view.

speaker: TARULLO
text: First, the pace of decline in the economy has slowed significantly since our last meeting.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Second, since our last meeting, we have seen some encouraging indications in the data, but, Mr. Chairman, I have to say here that the one thing you may regret from your “60 Minutes” appearance is the use of this phrase.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Third, there is considerable uncertainty whether these are green shoots promising blossoms to come or a school of red herring swimming across the sea of death.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Within this broadly shared frame of reference, I would make two observations.

speaker: TARULLO
text: One, with an eye to history, relates to the uncertainty that I just noted.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The other relates to the likely duration of a recovery period once the bottom has in fact been reached.

speaker: TARULLO
text: As to history, we all know that serious recessions have their own idiosyncratic origins and run their own course.

speaker: TARULLO
text: However, in light of the mildly hopeful data in the intermeeting period, I thought it useful to ask the question whether similar signs have in the past converged in what turned out to be a false dawn and, if so, whether we can distinguish between signs of a false dawn and signs of true recovery.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Looking at the last two serious economic downturns in the United States—the 1973–75 and the1981–82 recessions—staff members from Dave Stockton’s division provided some interesting answers.

speaker: TARULLO
text: First, in both instances there was indeed a period during which hopeful signs converged that in retrospect were not harbingers of imminent stabilization and recovery but were instead followed by further deterioration.

speaker: TARULLO
text: In each case, housing starts, initial claims, PCE growth, industrial production, and equity markets all improved noticeably at approximately the same time.

speaker: TARULLO
text: That is, the signs were even more uniformly tilted toward the upside than they are at present.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Second, a review of Greenbooks from the relevant periods reveals that the staff interpreted these data as indicating the end of cyclical declines.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Third, what we now know to be the actual beginnings of recovery, however, were characterized by improvements in these same indicators at a pace not unlike that which had been seen in the earlier false dawn.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Needless to say, two cases do not a pattern make.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Moreover, further analysis of these and other examples might yield more finely grained conclusions.

speaker: TARULLO
text: For the present, though, this modest inquiry helps explain and, indeed, excuse our collective low levels of assurance in our assessments of current conditions.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Let me now rehearse some reasons that I continue to tend toward the view that, even when a true turning point is reached, recovery may be much more gradual—even halting at times—than has been our experience with economic downturns since the Second World War.

speaker: TARULLO
text: First, as noted in a number of recent studies, most recently Rogoff and Reinhart, economic downturns that begin with a financial crisis can be expected to be more painful and to have longer recovery periods than other serious recessions.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Although it is very difficult to disaggregate the effects of reduced demand, asset value uncertainty, and capital impairment, it seems probable that this last factor is both important and unlikely to be remedied soon, the TARP notwithstanding.

speaker: TARULLO
text: With some notable exceptions, improvements in credit markets still seem generally associated, directly or indirectly, with government support.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Indeed, to a considerable extent, our financial institutions are all still fundamentally tethered to government guarantees or support.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Second, as I suggested at the last FOMC meeting, in an unusual number of industries, structural changes that were insipient even before the onset of the financial crisis, have been accelerated with the potential for extended negative effects on employment.

speaker: TARULLO
text: At the same time, sources of financing for new businesses are likely to remain constrained for some time to come.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Third, as many of you have already noted, there are significant headwinds that may partially offset any positive momentum that develops.

speaker: TARULLO
text: For example, again, as you have noted, it seems likely that the considerable damage to commercial real estate markets has only begun working its way through the financial system, with attendant negative implications for the balance sheets of many regional banking organizations.

speaker: TARULLO
text: A somewhat different example is suggested by the possibility that many foreign economies may be lagging the U.S. downturn.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Particularly with respect to the euro area, lags in employment reduction, bank balance sheet repair, and other factors lead me to a somewhat more pessimistic view of economic performance in the coming quarters than was suggested in the Greenbook, whose alternative scenario of lower foreign economic growth produces materially negative effects on U.S. economic performance.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Fourth, and finally, the likely continued fragility of the economy makes it unusually vulnerable to shocks, which could, in effect, set the reset button on the recovery effort.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Some of these potential shocks are classically economic, such as a crisis in an Eastern European country or a former Soviet Republic.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Others, such as a swine flu pandemic or adverse geopolitical developments, are truly exogenous.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Neither individually, nor as a whole, do these factors have salience for our decisions at this meeting.

speaker: TARULLO
text: However, they do suggest that policy challenges may extend for a considerable period—policy challenges, I should say, beyond that of the unwinding of our balance sheet.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Even when dawn truly breaks, it promises to be a very slowly clearing day.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And thank you all for a very interesting set of comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is a good time for us to break.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a reception and dinner upstairs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: No business will be conducted, just for your convenience.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will begin tomorrow at 9:00 a.m.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we have some data to begin with.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I think folks should find the little GDP scorecard at their seats.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The advance estimate for first-quarter GDP was released this morning.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The top-line GDP figure that the BEA is currently estimating, minus 6.1 percent, is very close to our estimate of minus 6.3 percent.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As usual, the offsetting errors were our friends.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I would point to two on the domestic spending side.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Personal consumption, as you can see, was stronger than we had estimated—2.2 percent versus the 1.1 percent we had projected.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: At this point, we will have to see the details to know whether there is any signal that we should take from that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The other area that I would note is nonresidential structures, which came in at minus 44.2 percent versus the minus 26.4 percent that we were forecasting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I guess that won’t come as much of a surprise to many of you who reported incredible weakness in that area yesterday.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Some of that unexpected weakness came in the drilling and mining activity, so maybe some of those rigs that are making their way from Kansas City to Richmond got lost somewhere along the way.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We hope so for Richmond’s sake.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: As you know, there are areas of missing data in this advance estimate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In two areas, the BEA wrote down assumptions for the March missing data that are different from ours.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: One is imports, for which it wrote down a weaker figure for March than we are, and the other is inventories, for which it wrote down a weaker March figure than we are.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: The GDP consequences of those two different assumptions, in fact, are just about offsetting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We would be inclined to stick with our estimate at this point.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We don’t really think that the BEA 5 The materials used by Mr. Stockton are appended to this transcript (appendix 5).

speaker: STOCKTON
text: knows anything more than we do about those particular pieces of data.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: But, sticking with our assumptions, the consequences for the top line would be roughly offsetting.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Finally, on prices, you can see that the BEA is a little lower on core prices—0.2 percentage point lower—than our Greenbook estimate.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I don’t think we would have any reason to second-guess them on that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So that is the end of the report, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have the rare advantage of having had overnight to work out my summary of the discussion so it may be somewhat more coherent than usual.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me start with that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The intermeeting period saw some tentative evidence of stabilization of real activity, or at least a slower decline relative to the earlier sharp contraction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Indicators of possible stabilization appeared in data on consumption, housing, durable goods, regional manufacturing reports, and other areas.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Surveys and some anecdotal reports suggested a slightly greater confidence on the part of households and businesses.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial markets also generally improved.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inventory decumulation has been brisk, suggesting possible increases in production in the medium term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, labor markets remained weak and global economic and financial conditions, adverse.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Overall, participants were very cautious about taking too much signal from the incoming data, noting its tentative nature, particularly the improvement in the financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: False dawns have occurred in previous recessions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: To the extent that participants saw an upturn materializing, most thought that it would be relatively anemic because of factors such as financial headwinds, including ongoing deleveraging; the need for economic restructuring; slow global economic growth that may be lagging the U.S. cycle; and the high vulnerability of the fragile economy and financial system to shocks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Further policy support, both in the United States and abroad, would be constrained by the zero lower bound on interest rates and by the already high level of fiscal borrowing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumer spending shows some signs of bottoming out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Fiscal stimulus will support consumer income going forward, and the rising stock market and possibly slower declines in house prices imply that wealth is no longer dropping so sharply.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are at best, however, only the slightest indications of improvement in labor markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unemployment claims and job losses remain high; firms are undertaking permanent reductions in labor force; and involuntary part- time work is unusually elevated.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing activity is giving some indications of stabilizing at a very low level, with affordability and buyer traffic up and inventories down.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, prices are likely to continue to fall, in part because of the additions to supply from high rates of foreclosure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Production and investment remain weak, although firms’ attitudes are not quite as negative as they recently were.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Drilling and mining have been affected by commodity prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Industrial production has continued to fall both here and abroad, and growth rates in both advanced and emerging-market economies have fallen significantly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: China is somewhat stronger than other Asian countries, but perhaps not as strong as its official statistics imply; and like many other countries, it remains dependent on export demand.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Europe faces slow growth and potentially serious banking problems, including exposures to Eastern Europe.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial market conditions generally had a better tone.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Stock prices rose, money markets exhibited better liquidity and lower spreads, corporate issuance of bonds and convertible securities is healthy, volatility is down, and other indicators of market functioning have improved.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Better financial conditions have helped confidence, even as indications of economic improvement have reduced risk aversion in markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, financial markets had shown signs of improvement on several previous occasions before worsening again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Moreover, although banks generally reported good earnings in the first quarter and their share prices rose, confidence in banks—as shown in CDS spreads, for example—remains tenuous.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A number of people observed that the disclosure of the capital assessment results on Monday will be a stress test in itself for the banks and the markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit continues to contract because of declining credit quality and loan demand, capital constraints on banks that don’t want to base increased lending on government capital, and the unavailability of financing through securitization markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Lack of financing for commercial real estate remains a particularly serious issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most see inflation as remaining low for the foreseeable future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Slack looks to be high and increasing, as reflected in high unemployment and low capacity utilization.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Wages are growing more slowly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With the slight improvement in the outlook and the incoming inflation data not particularly low, deflation risks have moderated but remain a worry for some participants.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the other hand, some expressed concerns about upside inflation risks, reflecting the possibility that the output gap is being overestimated and that forward-looking expectations may react to factors such as the Fed’s rapid balance sheet expansion and its purchases of Treasury securities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Effective exit strategies from Fed policies and good communication are necessary to maintain confidence that price stability will be achieved.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is my overview.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, let me make just a few comments, as usual.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am after Governor Tarullo, and so it is even more difficult for me than for him to come up with something new.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the proverbial green shoots, [laughter] we all want to be cautious, but it is nevertheless better to see good news than to see bad news, and we have seen some nascent signs of improvement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although they are small, subject to revision, and so on, they do occur across a number of areas, and so that is a positive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But, of course, I agree that we need to be very cautious about overinterpreting what are still relatively modest changes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am reminded of a comment I heard on MSNBC while I was watching Tim Geithner’s press conference after the G–7.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Tim had said something to the effect that the rate of decline had slowed, and the commentator said, “Well, if you close all the factories in the first quarter, the rate of growth will stop declining.” I think one area that we all do feel somewhat better about is the financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There has been a range of improvements in areas where the Fed has been involved but also in other areas like the corporate markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A wide range of volatility and stress measures have also looked a bit better, and we saw a bit of improvement in the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It could be that we are seeing a bit of the adverse feedback loop working in the other direction, which is, of course, good.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The markets, in turn, have responded to some extent to improved news, and higher stock markets, for example, have helped confidence and probably spurred some extra consumer spending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But, again, back to the theme of not overinterpreting or overextrapolating, we have seen how quickly those gains can be lost.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As we look at the economy and try to think about where it is going, it is useful to have on two sets of glasses—both a short-term cyclical-dynamic set of glasses and a medium-term adjustment set of glasses.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the short-run cyclical dynamics, we are seeing what may be the working-through of a classic inventory cycle.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The GDP data just shown were a striking contrast between the fourth quarter and the first quarter in terms of the composition of final demand versus inventory decumulation.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In that respect, it is encouraging that inventories are moving back toward balance.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Greenbook sees that process as ongoing, with inventory decumulation in the second quarter being about as large as in the first quarter.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Nevertheless, obviously, as that cycle proceeds, we will perhaps see some improvement in production.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Of course that depends on seeing stabilization in final demand, which ultimately drives the short-run cycle, and there are a lot of risks here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: People have talked about the risks to commercial real estate, other construction, trade, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The key element, as usual, will be the consumer, and I do think that the improvement in the first quarter is not entirely a fluke.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there are some signs of improvement in that area, notably that wealth is not declining as quickly—the stock market and housing prices are not falling as much.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We saw a rather marked increase in sentiment yesterday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Fiscal policy is going to be supportive of consumer spending.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Credit is tight but probably not getting worse.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The main uncertainty there, as a number of you pointed out, is the labor market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Until we see a bit of improvement there, that will remain a major source of uncertainty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But in the surveys and so on, we have seen just a bit of indication that consumers see strengthening in the labor market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the combination of some potential stabilization in final demand and the working- through of the inventory dynamics does give some hope—again, with all the caveats that everyone has expressed—that we will see somewhat better economic growth performance in the next couple of quarters and possibly even the end of the technical recession by the fall.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In thinking about that, though, we should also keep in mind not just the short-run growth dynamics but also the amplitude of this whole episode.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Burns and Mitchell, in their original classic work, divided the business cycle into six stages, which were of indeterminate length.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And the bigger the recession, the longer each of the cycle’s six stages was.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, the shock that hit the economy in the fall of last year was enormous, and it was global.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So even if we see the usual inventory–final demand dynamics working through, that combined with the restraining effects of financial stress and the like suggests that this will be a slower, deeper cyclical pattern than is normal.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, to summarize, on the cyclical side, while Governor Tarullo’s examples of false dawns are very instructive, I think there is a decent chance that we will see some improvement in the near term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other perspective, however, which I think is very important and a number of people pointed out, is the medium-term constraints and dynamics that affect the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unfortunately, our economy still has a significant number of very serious imbalances that need to be resolved before it can grow at a healthy pace.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, the leverage issue of both the financial and the household sectors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, wealth–income ratios are well below normal, and therefore more saving is needed to rebuild those ratios.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Third, we have dramatic fiscal imbalances, which have to be reconciled at some point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Fourth, we have current account imbalances, which are at least temporarily down, but the Greenbook forecast for the medium term is that there is probably some worsening in that dimension.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And fifth, as a number of people mentioned, the unemployment we are seeing is probably not mostly a temporary-layoff type of unemployment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There is a lot of reallocation going on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The financial and the construction sectors are probably not going to be as big in the future as they have been recently, so there will need to be that readjustment across sectors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you put all of those imbalances together and you think about what is going to support sustainable economic growth, it is a little hard to see where a robust recovery is going to come from.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In particular, consumption is unlikely to be dynamic, as President Trichet would put it, because of leverage and the need to build wealth and because of lower employment and those factors.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The government sector is unlikely to be a major support indefinitely because of the need to rebalance the fiscal budget.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Therefore, by arithmetic, that leaves only two categories, which are investment and net exports.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A capital boom would be very good news.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Among other things, it would help solve some of these reallocation problems and allow new industries to expand or to grow.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it is not obvious where that is going to come from, and the financial constraints are also a drag on that direction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, what we really and truly need, as we have been saying for many years, is a rebalancing of global demand that would allow the United States to have better external demand.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, there are some preliminary steps in that direction, notably in China and a few other countries that are beginning to understand that full reliance on exports is not necessarily a safe strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But that is not likely to be a near-term solution.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So when you look at the economy from both of these short-term dynamic and medium- term dynamic approaches, the conclusion is that we may have some improvement this year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That, of course, is hostage to financial conditions and to consumer behavior and attitudes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I don’t see much scope for a stronger recovery.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are things going in that direction, such as the depth of the recession, which may at some point mean a stronger recovery.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it is difficult to see the underlying factors that will lead to a powerful recovery in the near term, and so we will have to deal with that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The implications for policy, as people have pointed out, are not entirely unambiguous because, to the extent that slow growth reflects things like reallocation and changes in the structure of the economy, it is as much a potential growth issue as it is an aggregate demand issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that is my assessment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unless there is any comment or question, let me turn now to the policy round, and I will call on Brian.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 6 Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I will be referring to the package labeled “Material for Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.” The April Bluebook presented two basic policy alternatives for your consideration.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative A, the Committee would buy an additional $450 billion of Treasury securities on top of its already announced plans to purchase up to $1.75 trillion of Treasury, agency, and mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative B, the Committee would maintain its previously announced plans.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Bluebook also offered a variant of alternative B, dubbed B′, which translates the announced total purchases of securities and time frames into monthly dollar amounts and monthly 6 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 6).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: growth rates of the System’s securities portfolio.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Turning to page 2, this morning we have proposed a change to the first paragraph of all the alternatives (shown in red) in order to be more consistent with the economic data released this morning and with the general sense that household spending could be leveling out.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That proposed change is applied to all of the alternatives in the packet.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Committee might adopt the further expansion of its securities portfolio proposed in alternative A if it thinks that the economic outlook under its current policy path is unacceptably weak and believes that the advantages of providing additional monetary policy stimulus through expanded large-scale asset purchases would outweigh the disadvantages.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under the staff’s analysis, the outlook is indeed quite weak.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although economic activity bottoms out around the middle of this year, the recovery remains tepid until mid-2010.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The staff sees the economy expanding at a pace below that of potential GDP through the first quarter of next year—even though potential growth is temporarily held down by financial strains and the need to reallocate resources—so the unemployment rate rises to 9¼ percent by the end of this year and only edges lower next year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the extended Greenbook baseline forecast, the Committee is assumed to hold the federal funds rate at its effective lower bound until 2013.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Those very low short-term interest rates, together with the lagged effects of the Committee’s large-scale asset purchases and other policies to support financial markets, strengthen financial institutions, and boost spending eventually produce sufficient repair of balance sheets in the financial and household sectors and enough aggregate demand to spur growth to 4½ percent in 2011 and tilt the trajectory of unemployment down more noticeably.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But the staff projects that, even with these policies, the economy does not return to full employment until late 2013, four-and-a­ half years from now.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In the staff forecast, core PCE prices rise at an average annual rate of less than 1 percent over the next five years, well below the 2 percent rate that the majority of you view as consistent with your dual mandate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: While your own forecasts generally point to somewhat higher inflation than foreseen by the staff, you still anticipate inflation to be below 2 percent over the next three years.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If you judge that the outlook for economic activity is excessively sluggish and inflation is likely to be on the low side of its optimal level, you might be inclined to provide additional monetary stimulus by expanding your large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Market participants appear to put only small odds on an expansion of your securities purchases today, so the announcement of an additional $450 billion of Treasury purchases might lower longer-term interest rates, including private rates, by 20 to 45 basis points.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Although these estimates are subject to great uncertainty, such a reduction might raise the level of real GDP after three years by ¼ percent to 1 percent relative to baseline and lower the unemployment rate 0.1 to 0.5 percentage point in 2011.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The language proposed for alternative A does not differ markedly from that used by the Committee in its March statement, but as I noted, the material shown in red is less downbeat than both the March language and that proposed in the Bluebook.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, relative to March, the reference to declining equity wealth has been dropped in view of the rebound in stock prices over the intermeeting period, and the sentence on the slump in U.S. exports and recession abroad has been omitted.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, to explain the motivation for undertaking the additional policy action of alternative A, the final sentence of the first paragraph would indicate the Committee’s anticipation that economic activity will continue to contract in the near term and that the subsequent recovery could be sluggish.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The second paragraph, on inflation, is essentially the same as in March, but it uses a slight variant of the language to refer to inflation rates that are “most consistent with sustainable economic growth.” That revised wording is employed to avoid suggesting that inflation fosters economic growth, but this improvement may not be worth the costs in terms of market analysts wondering what subtle message the Committee is sending by making the change.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The third paragraph of alternative A modifies the corresponding paragraph of the March statement to indicate the expansion in the asset purchases but otherwise explains the Committee’s intentions in essentially the same way, referring to a total quantity of asset purchases spread out over specified time periods this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Another change in language is to note explicitly that asset purchases will be state contingent by indicating that “the Committee is prepared to make further adjustments to the timing and overall amounts of these purchases of Treasury, agency, and mortgage- backed securities as appropriate in view of the evolving economic outlook and conditions in financial markets.” The penultimate sentence now references the Fed’s liquidity programs generally rather than specifically citing the TALF, as in the most recent three statements; this change might be desirable in view of the TALF’s slow start.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In considering whether to expand asset purchases, the Committee would need to balance a number of factors, including the baseline outlook for both economic growth and inflation, the risks around that outlook, and the benefits, costs, and uncertainties of a further expansion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In your forecast submissions, several of you indicated that you were concerned that the Committee’s large-scale asset purchases and other programs that expand the System’s balance sheet could unanchor inflation expectations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: More generally, as I noted yesterday, many of you projected noticeably higher inflation in 2011 than does the staff, even with somewhat less economic growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A sense that the risks to inflation relative to the Committee’s objectives were more nearly balanced than suggested by the staff forecast might incline the Committee to pause at this meeting, as under alternative B, on page 3.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A decision to stand pat might also be supported by a judgment that the Federal Reserve and the government have now put in place a range of effective programs to support credit flows and economic activity—programs whose effects on the real economy and inflation will be evident only with a considerable lag.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, the Committee may be encouraged by recent information suggesting that the deterioration in the economy may be slowing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Paragraph 1 for alternative B is largely the same as that for alternative A, including the reference to some easing in financial conditions and the modified passage shown in red, but the final sentences do not express an expectation that the recovery will be sluggish.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As in March, the final clause refers to a gradual resumption of sustainable economic growth.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The paragraph on inflation is identical to that in the March statement.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The third paragraph, on policy actions, is substantively similar to that used in March; in particular, the Committee would make no change to its program of large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The third sentence from the end would note that the timing and overall amounts of its asset purchases may be adjusted in view of the evolving economic outlook and conditions in financial markets, as in alternative A.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Unless that sentence is interpreted as suggesting that the Committee is leaning toward expanding or contracting its asset purchases, an announcement along the lines of alternative B seems unlikely to prompt much market reaction.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative B′, page 4, is identical to alternative B except that, in response to suggestions from Presidents Bullard and Plosser, we included text (highlighted in yellow) that translates the dollar amounts and time frames of future asset purchases into monthly average dollar amounts and monthly average growth rates of the System’s securities portfolio.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Some readers may find the additional information helpful; others may find confusing the proliferation of numbers that results from expressing the Committee’s unchanged plans for asset purchases in three different ways.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also attached for your reference on pages 5 and 6 are alternatives B′′ and B′′′ as proposed by Presidents Bullard and Plosser.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: These alternatives are, again, substantively the same as B and B′.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But they provide the material in a different order by beginning with a paragraph on the Committee’s policy decision, then presenting the two paragraphs on the rationale, and concluding with various points, including the Committee’s intention to monitor the size and composition of the balance sheet.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is worth noting that B′′ and B′′′ cover the federal funds rate target in this final paragraph rather than in the introductory paragraph.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A key difference from B and B′ is the way that B′′ and B′′′ quantify the plans for asset purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under alternative B′′, the Committee would specify numerically only a monthly growth rate of 18 to 20 percent for its security holdings, rather than the total dollar stock of planned purchases; the announcement states that that the specified growth rate is consistent with the Committee’s already announced plans.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative B′′′ would take a similar approach but would articulate the growth of the securities portfolio in dollar terms rather than percentage terms.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Finally, let me note that we distributed to you this morning a corrected exhibit from my briefing yesterday on your economic projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: No central tendencies or ranges that I discussed were affected.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Brian?

speaker: EVANS
text: Brian, listening to your presentation and some of the discussions yesterday, I am a little confused about the way the policy options are presented.

speaker: EVANS
text: I know there will be a discussion about the rate of purchases, but it does seem as though the policies that we are implementing, as I was talking about with Vice Chairman Dudley beforehand, have a cliff-like nature to them in the sense that we have a pace for purchases and then we’re just going to stop under the current implementation by the Desk.

speaker: EVANS
text: The Desk, I suppose, is charged with the responsibility of inferring a path that the Committee hasn’t really specified, and it feels very incomplete.

speaker: EVANS
text: We are almost surely locking ourselves into a future action in order to smooth that cliff-like purchase behavior, which we just haven’t discussed.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am not saying that I disagree with any of that, but it feels different from the way we have always talked about the funds rate policy in the past, when we could take an action and choose to not do that the next time.

speaker: EVANS
text: There seem to be future ramifications from these actions.

speaker: EVANS
text: So do we leave it to the Desk to infer how to implement the additional, say, $300 billion of Treasury purchases as opposed to telling them that, in addition, there is a plan that, if this is the entire amount to be done, it should tail off in some smooth fashion?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, of course, the Committee issues a directive to the Desk, and my understanding of the directive—and Trish may want to comment on this—is that the Committee has essentially instructed the Desk to carry out the purchases that are specified at rates that roughly average the amounts specified by the Committee but that also potentially take into account market conditions.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Now, you are raising a separate issue, which relates to the questions that Presidents Bullard and Plosser have raised.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is, What’s the longer-run path or the longer-run plan for the Committee’s open market purchases?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I agree that, in an ideal world, the Committee would articulate a fully blown plan for its monetary policy settings over the indefinite future.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think that is difficult to do in practice.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One way to look at this is that the world will surely turn out differently, either better or worse, from the way we currently see it in terms of the baseline projection, and eventually the Committee will need to adjust its plans for large-scale asset purchases and other monetary policy settings like the federal funds rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That could conceivably mean that later this year, for instance, the Committee scales back its large-scale asset purchases or expands them.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: So I do not think that the way that the Committee has already expressed its statement or its directive to the Desk rules out those adjustments at some point in the future.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It just doesn’t make clear at this point what those will be in the absence of information about how the economy and the outlook will progress.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I would agree with that.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The first is that there really is no cliff-like expectation in the market right now.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The good news is that we have a lot of credibility that we’re not going to stop abruptly one day.

speaker: EVANS
text: But we get all of that from your presentation.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Right, and in fact, if you look at the latest primary dealer survey, to a firm practically, there is an expectation, regardless of the level effect, that the wind-down will be smooth.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The timing of that varies from respondent to respondent, but the expectation is that we will not all of a sudden stop buying on December 30 or 31 of this year, particularly in Treasuries on September 30.

speaker: MOSSER
text: My second comment has to do more with the actual implementation.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Is “steady as she goes” the right approach versus some another approach to purchasing, given that we are uncertain about the endpoint and how slowly we might wind these down?

speaker: MOSSER
text: My comments here are really dependent upon the program we’re talking about.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The MBS program—purchasing MBS, the issuance of MBS—is very lumpy.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We could very well be well ahead of a steady-as­ she-goes plan in purchasing MBS, given the current directive we have, in the next two or three months because there is a huge refinancing wave coming through and, if we don’t purchase, mortgage rates will rise or rise more than we want them to.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If that is the way the market dynamics turn out, that is the Desk’s intent in terms of instructing our investment managers.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So we’re well prepared to be very flexible there and perhaps come back to the Committee with a warning at some point to say that we are well ahead of a steady pace, but our expectation is that purchases will taper off.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Or we could come back and say, if we want to keep this program going, then what is the Committee’s view about increasing the size?

speaker: MOSSER
text: As Brian noted, we don’t know which of those scenarios we may face, but those are the scenarios.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The agency debt purchase program similarly, honestly, is very dependent upon the financing needs of the GSEs.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It is possible that the program might actually pull back early, if their portfolios shrink and there is less debt out there and less need to support the market in order to support the agency market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Then again, if the GSEs’ portfolios grow and our mandate is still to purchase, we may be lumpier in how we purchase those securities.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Treasuries are different because of the steady issuance.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Because we know that the Treasury Department is going to be issuing just a huge amount of debt at a steady pace and we also know, particularly for Treasuries, that the announcement effect may be as important as anything else in terms of lowering the level of interest rates, we are more inclined toward “steady as she goes” in purchasing there.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So the problem that you’re worried about and the cliff effect may perhaps be more relevant from an operational standpoint to the Treasury purchase program than to the other two programs.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Brian, I am sure that this is covered in some of the write-ups, but could you walk through how the number 450 billion was selected and what other numbers were considered?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I would see this in the context of the overall set of materials that the staff has provided to the Committee, especially at the last meeting and this meeting, and the various attempts that we’ve made to calibrate the different amounts of asset purchases to evolving economic conditions and their effects on the economy.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We didn’t look carefully or specifically at a whole range of options.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Basically these would be viewed as linear, and if the Committee were inclined to go with the smaller number, then the effects on the economy and interest rates would be correspondingly smaller, and vice versa for larger purchases.

speaker: FISHER
text: Part of the cliff nature is that we’ve stated specific end dates, originally six months and now by autumn, and with regard to the mortgage-backed securities, we stated by the end of the year.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would just like some clarification on the comment you made, Trish, about understanding the lumpy nature of the mortgage-backed securities market and whether or not the agencies need more financing.

speaker: FISHER
text: What caught my ear was your comment about Treasuries and that that is what the community expects.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’re going to even this out since there’s constant issuance over the time frame that we articulated.

speaker: FISHER
text: In creating that cliff, we’re committed to that.

speaker: FISHER
text: But was your comment that they expect us to do more when this is over?

speaker: MOSSER
text: The market expectation is absolutely—

speaker: FISHER
text: It will continue to grow this over time after we have run the course of what we previously stated.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the Treasury program, yes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Our dealer survey had an average of the program that the sizes total to approximately $500 billion, but their estimates there are quite skewed.

speaker: MOSSER
text: A number of individuals expect that the program will be $750 billion, along the lines of what it is in alternative A.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In fact, I would also say that, in the dealer survey, we asked economists for their opinions.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If we asked the Treasury traders for their opinions, I think we would probably get an average or a median expectation that the Treasury program would be even larger than $500 billion.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But it is the one program that all market participants say will be both extended, partly because its terminal date is earlier than the mortgage and agency one, and expanded by a sizable amount.

speaker: FISHER
text: And that larger number would be what percentage of the expected issuance?

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t have your charts from yesterday.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It would still be only about half.

speaker: FISHER
text: In terms of the larger number that you gave?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Yes, even the larger number would be about half.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If I understand your comments correctly, the Committee has effectively committed to more than what we said, according to the private sector’s view of what we’re going to do, and probably more than what the Committee is going to do—because, if we don’t believe our own cliff, it’s just not credible.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s not a credible commitment to say we’re just going to stop all at once at a point in time.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In terms of cliff effects, because of the lumpiness, if the market conditions are appropriate, it will be easier, for example, to slow down quickly the purchases of MBS and, to a degree, the purchases of agency debt.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The Treasury piece will be the part for which, because of the smooth issuance and the expectations, from an operational standpoint, we would guess that a smoother slowdown would be a more advisable implementation strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’d like to say, though, that I don’t see any reason that you couldn’t say that we’re going to extend this three months but we’re going to have a tapering off.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Our recommendation would be that, if the Committee has been clear about their intentions that it’s not needed, we would put on a timetable—we’re now publishing a schedule two weeks in advance; we don’t put in the quantities, but we put in the section of the curve—and we would make clear that we’re going to diminish our purchases over time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, we are ready for our policy go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me start with President Plosser.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Committee has embarked on a strategy of working on all fronts to combat the severe economic downturn and continuing problems in our financial intermediation sector.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The recent return of some relative stability in financial markets is, of course, welcome.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I believe it remains fragile.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In particular, as many noted yesterday, I think that the pending release of the bank’s supervisory stress tests has the potential to be very disruptive to markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Let’s hope that doesn’t happen.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Like many of you, I agree that the type of recovery we are likely to see is going to be modest, but my reasoning and my view of that modest recovery is somewhat different from those perhaps expressed through the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I tried to articulate yesterday, my view of the decline in equilibrium output is driven by a severe shock to the financial intermediation sector.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It might be not only large but also fairly persistent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What that does is manifest itself in higher­ than-normal unemployment rates—sectoral reallocations as the Chairman is referring to—and perhaps imbalances that the economy must work through in response to that shock.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus, GDP will be lower and unemployment rates will be higher.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The main difference such a view has for the outlook, compared with the Greenbook view, is the model’s implications for output gaps, inflation, and policy paths.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In this equilibrium story, the real allocations must occur, but it is dubious that the policy actions can do much to prevent those costs from occurring.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This view also implies that gaps are smaller and less downward pressure on inflation is present, and thus the appropriate policy paths under consideration would be less expansive in order to constrain inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Turning to policy, I think we face some very big challenges and uncertainties.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Board has now approved another expansion in eligible collateral for the TALF, with the previous expansion announced just a month ago.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And the staff is considering even further collateral expansions, including legacy assets, with recommendations expected in the next few weeks.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It seems as though we are in a cycle in which we announce interventions in one market or asset type and then almost immediately turn around and consider other interventions in other markets and other asset types.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Clearly, our intention is to improve market functioning in these sectors.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I am increasingly uncomfortable with the practice, and I am concerned that our announcements—and indeed the whole strategy of gradually expanding the breadth and scope of our interventions across both asset classes and maturities—are another source of instability in the marketplace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am not certain that we have adequately evaluated the interactions among all of these programs or that we have an adequate sense of the marginal benefit of the incremental actions that we are undertaking.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Moreover, can we be sure that our programs are not distorting markets, discouraging the return of participants who are waiting on the sidelines for the next great deal or subsidy from the Federal Reserve policies, and hampering the development of new, sustainable market mechanisms for raising capital and allocating credit, thus actually delaying financial market recovery?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I have said before, I am not against expanding our balance sheet, given the current economic conditions and outlook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do prefer that expansion be done with more-liquid government securities, such as Treasuries rather than MBS, relative to illiquid private securities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am troubled by our difficulty in quantitatively determining what might be the right amount of expansion that is appropriate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nevertheless, given our current commitments, I am against announcing any further increases today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The change in the forecast, and certainly in the Greenbook and many people’s forecasts since March, doesn’t seem to warrant further expansions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we need to give our actions time to work.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thus I favor some version of B, B′, B′′, or B′′′.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That narrows it down quite a bit.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would also prefer, in general, that we be more explicit about the linkage between our policy actions and our inflation goals.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We mention in paragraph 1 that our policy actions will contribute to a gradual resumption of sustainable economic growth, yet in paragraph 2 we give only a forecast for inflation with no mention of our related policy actions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This seems to me oddly asymmetric.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: By failing to link our balance sheet expansion with our inflation goals, we fail to communicate an important and explicit aspect of our policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We don’t say, for example, that we are taking these actions in part to help ensure that we avoid deflation or, given that we are operating at an effective lower bound, having inflation slightly higher would not be unwelcome.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: By failing to make this link to our policy actions and our inflation goal, we are not being as transparent as we could be, and I think we risk the public’s breaking the link between our actions and inflation, thus potentially weakening our credibility and our ability to maintain those well-anchored expectations.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Short of being explicit about adopting an inflation target, we could, for example, create more of a link by slightly modifying paragraphs 2 and 3.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am working off of B rather than B′ for now.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We could strike the second sentence in paragraph 2 on inflation—if I’m looking at the right one—where we say, “Moreover, the Committee sees some risk that inflation could persist for a time below rates that best foster economic growth and price stability in the longer term.” We could strike that sentence and change the first sentence of paragraph 3 to read, “In these circumstances, the Federal Reserve will employ all available tools to promote economic recovery and to forestall any risk that inflation could persist for a sustained period of time below rates consistent with price stability.” In other words, I think we need to make sure that the actions we take link to our inflation objectives more directly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I suggested yesterday, I think we are at risk of generating substantial inflation in the not-too-distant future, and that is particularly so in the policy path described in the Greenbook.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s useful to remind ourselves that the high inflation episode in the 1970s is a case study of a rapid monetary expansion in the context of an apparently substantial output gap, and the overreliance on and overstatement of poorly measured estimates of an output gap and a reluctance to make the difficult decision to reverse accommodation in a timely fashion contributed to very bad economic outcomes in that episode.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe the current situation poses an eerily similar set of circumstances and conditions, and we must be careful not to repeat that unpleasant experience.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m troubled by the challenge that we face in determining how we will decide when we’ve done enough.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: As I’ve noted several times, I’m skeptical of relying too heavily on interest rate spreads as the sole criterion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: More generally, I’m uncomfortable with the communication of our actions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The memo that President Bullard and I circulated last Friday tries to address some of these concerns.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have proposed language that reinforces the notion that our policy is state contingent and that we are on a policy path rather than focused on one-time announcements for the purchase of some class of securities, be they MBS or Treasuries, of some magnitude usually expressed in some round number of billions of dollars without any explanation as to where those numbers come from, much as President Lockhart’s question is about where the $450 billion came from.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think our recent statements may be creating more uncertainty than necessary about what the FOMC will do next in terms of announcing new quantities or new purchases of assets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The current approach will leave the impression, as was just discussed, that we will stop purchasing assets suddenly, cold turkey, and perhaps face the cliff problem that was just discussed.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I’d like to spend just another minute, Mr. Chairman, to make some comments about B′′ and B′′′ from my standpoint just so the Committee understands a little where we are coming from.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We did two or three things that we think are pertinent and important.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: First, we moved the action up to the first paragraph, which is more consistent, we believe, with the traditional way in which we’ve structured our policy statements.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We also took seriously the notion that we have made commitments.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Rather than providing a litany of numbers, we think that we would just say in the first sentence, “Treasury securities.” We purchased “Treasury securities, agency debt, and MBS in a manner consistent with our previous announcements.” That suggests two things.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One, in our previous announcements the Committee was explicit about saying that we would purchase up to a certain amount.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It doesn’t guarantee either that we would get there or that we might not exceed it, but it does say “up to.” I think it is important that we maintain that flexibility, and we think that our language helps ensure that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We also chose to focus on the asset side of the balance sheet, as the Chairman has many times discussed the issue of focusing on assets rather than on the liabilities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We also note that we retain flexibility as to how the Desk would actually implement this.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Trish just gave us an example of the lumpiness of some of this thing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This does not say that we would purchase every asset at the same pace, but it talks about the general pace of expansion of the balance sheet, and the Desk would have some flexibility to implement that depending on the nature of the securities that they were purchasing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the staff’s B′ version, we were troubled by the expression “20 percent per month” for a given period of time, which ignores compounding problems.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If you did follow 20 percent per month literally, we would actually far exceed the purchases that we announced.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So we chose to focus on growing the balance sheet and the total purchase of these securities by, we said, 18 to 20 percent per month over the near term because as, the balance sheet grows, the growth rate would actually start to decline.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We thought it would be better to express it that way than over a longer period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The log of 1 plus r approaches r when r is small, but when r is 20 percent, those approximations don’t work very well anymore.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Finally, in the first paragraph we make very explicit, as Brian suggested, that the Committee stands ready to adjust both the timing and the overall amounts of its purchases as the economy evolves, and that’s the important conditionality.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We believe that trying to move to a statement that looks like this will not only help us communicate to the markets that we are on a path—an important path, we think—but also preserve our flexibility in terms of conditionality.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We also believe that having a statement structured more like this will help us when the time comes to start an exit strategy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This gives us more flexibility in expressing what we believe the policy path may be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I will leave it at that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Thank you for the extra time, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: By the way, I also want to compliment and thank the staff.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Brian and I had several conversations over the last several weeks talking about how to do this, and the staff were very helpful and very accommodating, and I just want to express my appreciation for the interactions that led to these suggestions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have just one small comment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I appreciate your doing what I asked, which is to work in advance and provide a concrete alternative, which I think is very helpful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a question about B′′ versus B′′′—the 18 to 20 percent versus the $160 billion per month.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think a problem with the 18 to 20 percent is, of course, that if we follow our plan, a week from now we’ll be announcing 15 to 18 percent or something, and that could be misconstrued as a change in our strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It isn’t quite as transparent in that respect.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So in doing this, my inclination would be to go with the dollar number.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I just raise that point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, that’s why the B′′′ was there.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That was part of the discussion, to figure out what’s the best way to express that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But, again, I think that’s a point worth discussing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t feel as strongly about that as I do some other pieces.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I guess as we consider all the options, I do prefer alternative B and not the primes.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I guess I’m more concerned about and more interested in the fact that we are increasing our balance sheet by the extent that we are, and I’m not enamored of the idea of doing that and saying, “Here’s the path that we’re going to take.” I’m more concerned about the amount than I am whether we have a path, because that’s the striking point.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I also like the wording in the sense that the Committee under any of these is prepared to adjust the timing and the amounts.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If you think about how much the projections have changed in the Greenbook, for example, from the last meeting to this meeting and if we are near the bottom, things could change, and I think the Committee would need to reconsider even the amounts at another meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The wording in the B alternative allows us to do this.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I did note and am very much appreciative of the work that the staff did on the projections on the balance sheet because I think it does point out that, if we go to these sizes, we have some real challenges ahead of us.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think the June meeting is extremely important in terms of thinking about an exit strategy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That’s very important because, if we do achieve the total amount under the mortgage-backed securities, our holdings will be larger than those of either Fannie or Freddie, and that’s a striking statement as far as our role in the economy goes.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That gives me some pause.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I hope that the next meeting will show even more positive news and we can adjust these numbers going forward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The Greenbook projection, with which I broadly concur, assumes no change from our announced asset purchases.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It foresees unemployment remaining above 9 percent through the end of 2010 and inflation well below our preferred rate for even longer.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I consider this unacceptable in light of our mandates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think we need to do more to get the economy moving forward.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think our actions at the last meeting provided compelling evidence that purchases of longer-term Treasury securities worked to bring down borrowing rates and improved financial conditions more broadly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Now that we’ve tested the waters, it’s time to wade in by substantially increasing our purchases of Treasury securities.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In fact, I could support increasing the amount beyond $750 billion and would consider including securities of durations down to one year.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The latter step would be aimed at bringing down one-year and two-year rates that are well above those consistent with our expectations for the future path of policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Now, we could wait until our June meeting to take this step, but the question to my mind is why we would wait.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As with the funds rate, I don’t see a reason to keep our powder dry.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I prefer to take appropriate, bold action to stimulate the economy sooner rather than later.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Regarding the best way to communicate our asset purchases to the public, I strongly support the approach that we have taken so far and see no reason to change it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Our statements provide clear information on the expected size and duration of each of our asset purchase programs.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Economic theory suggests that it is the size of the cumulative asset purchase relative to the size of the market that affects the yield and, therefore, the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In other words, it is aggregate purchases, not the growth rate, that matters.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This is an important point because it implies that our communications should focus on levels or, alternatively, on the shares of the outstanding stock that we hold and not on changes or growth rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A focus on growth rates or changes would confuse our message, and I therefore would consider it a mistake.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I also think it’s important to report the various types of asset purchases separately rather than as a sum because their effects on financial conditions and the economy may differ.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Our statements do leave open the question of what we will do once the announced purchases have been completed, but this ambiguity is appropriate given the high degree of uncertainty about the outlook and the effectiveness of the asset purchases.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indeed, we’re already far clearer about our projections of asset purchases than we have ever been about the future path of the funds rate.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So perhaps the change we should be considering is how to better communicate the funds rate path we think is most likely.

speaker: EVANS
text: Just to ask a question—would the Desk interpret alternative A as a greater pace of purchases or just pushing it out to the end of the plan?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Given this size, it would be a greater pace as well.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It would be like the mortgage program.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We’re purchasing Treasuries at $50 billion per month.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The $500 billion that was in the dealer survey would be a steady pace, so to go to $750 billion would be increasing the pace.

speaker: EVANS
text: Would it be over the entire currently envisioned purchase time, or would some of it be pushed beyond that?

speaker: MOSSER
text: It would depend on what the Committee asked us to do.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If the directive is to extend it through December, then we would spread it out over whatever time frame the Committee gives us.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am just asking whether or not further clarification would be required.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Trish, on President Yellen’s suggestion of shortening maturities, that has the other benefit of making our exit strategy easier.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do you see similar market benefits of mixing in more one­ to-three-year maturities, for example?

speaker: MOSSER
text: There would probably be some market benefits at the front end of the curve.

speaker: MOSSER
text: There’s no question that the one-to-two-year section of the curve reacted less than the section further out.

speaker: MOSSER
text: That’s probably because a lot more issuance is there, and so the quantity we’re buying relative to supply is a little smaller.

speaker: MOSSER
text: And if we did it pretty explicitly, particularly between one and two years, we’re guessing that it would steepen the yield curve; but we hope that, if it was announced, that additional purchases across the curve would have an announcement effect of bringing the whole curve down.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So for that portion of the curve we think that it would be useful in bringing yields down.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It would do less, though, to bring down mortgage rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it really depends a little on why you are purchasing the Treasuries.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Are you purchasing the Treasuries to bring down mortgage rates, or are you purchasing Treasuries to steepen the yield curve?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The same logic could apply to mortgage-backed securities, though, because you could do 3-, 5-, and 7-year mortgage-backed securities, and that has the opposite story.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Those would not be as deep, and so you might have a bigger impact if you did the shorter maturities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Unlike changing the maturity on the Treasuries, arguably you’d have a bigger impact if you changed the maturities and bought ARMs rather than the 15- and 30-year fixed.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That’s also something that might be worth thinking about because the ARM rates haven’t come down very much.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So if you’re looking at a 30-year fixed, a 15-year fixed, and a 7-year ARM, the 7-year ARM hasn’t moved all that much, for example.

speaker: LACKER
text: Yes, but the relative depth of the market matters in only a habitat kind of view, in which case the spillover to other markets is commensurately lower even if you’re having a higher effect.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that is what was troubling Governor Kohn.

speaker: STERN
text: I’m sort of lost as to how this might work.

speaker: STERN
text: I thought you said earlier that the people in the marketplace anticipate that we’re going to buy more Treasuries than we’ve announced so far anyway.

speaker: FISHER
text: After the time frame is over or during the time frame, just for clarification?

speaker: MOSSER
text: They are expecting both an extension and an expansion.

speaker: STERN
text: So if we officially announce an expansion, are they simply going to mark everything up from here, or are they going to say, “That’s what we expected—end of story”?

speaker: MOSSER
text: That depends upon the size.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The size they’re expecting now is smaller than what has been proposed in alternative A.

speaker: STERN
text: So if we do something bigger, presumably they’re going to say that’s probably it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: No, I don’t think that’s right.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think doing it means that you like what you’ve done.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You want to do more, and it opens the door for doing even more at subsequent meetings.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just say that, although we have to manage expectations, we’ve made a commitment to what we’ve made a commitment to, and with the federal funds rate, we have surprised markets, and if we have to surprise markets, we’ll do it again.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there is no commitment to do anything other than what we’ve said.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have the right, as we say explicitly in the statement, to adjust the timing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We could, for example, phase out by extending the period but not the amount in order to go out more slowly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There are other things we can do.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let’s not jump the gun here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I do want to ask you—just because this came up earlier—to think for the next meeting a bit about the idea of whether shorter maturity MBS would have benefits because it would, in addition, have some exit benefits.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Yes, and we are going to study purchasing ARMs, which we had not purchased.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Not just ARMs but also seasoned MBS with shorter duration.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t want to leave the impression that we’re not buying any seasoned MBS.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In fact, the purchases that we’re making in the dollar roll market are actually exclusively the higher coupons because that’s where the liquidity in the market was most affected.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So from a balance sheet, month-to-month perspective, we actually are purchasing them.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We’re simply then rolling those purchases for the following month and lending them out, if you like, through the financing market.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But we could definitely investigate increasing the share of higher coupon MBS as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: Well, I’m at a loss to understand how to interpret the market’s expectation.

speaker: EVANS
text: You talk to people in the markets quite a lot.

speaker: EVANS
text: During that conversation, do they understand this path better than everyone else?

speaker: EVANS
text: I mean, we don’t communicate this in our statement.

speaker: EVANS
text: I guess the question is, If in our own commentaries we go out in public, would you be relatively indifferent toward our describing it?

speaker: EVANS
text: We said we would do $300 billion, and I have interpreted this that, as we get closer to $300 billion, we would smooth this down and finish up.

speaker: EVANS
text: That is how this reads.

speaker: EVANS
text: It’s a $300 billion program.

speaker: EVANS
text: But others in the market have an expectation that it’s going to go on to another $100 billion or something like that.

speaker: EVANS
text: What is the right amount of information to communicate?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It says we will adjust our magnitude and timing according to the information as it comes in.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we could expand the program, we could reduce it, or we could spread it out.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: All of those things are options.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t think it’s fundamentally different from other monetary policy decisions, which involve both communication and responding to new information that comes across the transom.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t think the communication challenge is any different than it is with discussing the swap lines or the 13(3) programs.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Markets participants understand that it is path dependent.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Their view is that, if the economy gets significantly worse, the probability that the Board of Governors will extend the 13(3) programs and that the FOMC will extend the swap lines and the purchase programs is much higher.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The better that things get, the less likely that is.

speaker: EVANS
text: That dependence suggests a change in the path other than what we’re currently expecting.

speaker: EVANS
text: So as I think about this, there’s an outlook; there’s an option chosen.

speaker: EVANS
text: If the outlook stays the same, then we’ve said $300 billion, and it could be closed down, not just a recurrence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A two-hander from the Vice Chairman.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think part of the confusion here is that we do a program and the market is also evaluating whether the program is effective, and then how are we going to react to the perception of the effectiveness of the program?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So if we do a program and the market responds in the way that we want the market to respond, the market participants are going to assume that, gee, it worked pretty well for the Federal Reserve, so of course the Federal Reserve is likely to want to do more of it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Their view is conditioned not just on the macroeconomic outlook but also on how the markets respond to the program.

speaker: DUDLEY
