text: In this particular case of the Treasury securities, I think that the market expects that the program is going to be expanded because (1) we did expand the MBS purchase program and so they’ve already seen that, when the market seems to get the desired response, the Fed has responded by increasing the size of the program and (2) they’ve seen that the Treasury program seems to have worked in the desired way that we intended.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So all of those things point to an expectation that they expect the program to be expanded.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But it also depends on the economic outlook.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But it’s not just the economic outlook; it’s also how the program seems to work in practice because we don’t have any track record on this.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: By emphasizing, as the Chairman just did, the ability to increase, slow down, extend, and so forth, it sounds to me like a very tactical approach.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The directives that come every six or seven weeks from the Committee, are they a mode of guidance to the Desk that’s going to be enough for you to interpret how to make those adjustments, or are we talking about a more frequent consultation with the Committee in order to be able to respond tactically?

speaker: MOSSER
text: From a tactical standpoint—and I’m using the word “tactical” literally— I think we have plenty of direction from the Committee.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We obviously need, particularly given how unusual and new these programs are, to communicate back to you to let you know what our tactics are, and we’ve tried to be clear with you.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In fact, particularly in the case of the Treasury program, we’ve tried to be very clear with the market what our tactics are because transparency seems to make it more effective rather than less.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Now, if I can re-interpret your question just a bit, should either financial or macroeconomic conditions change dramatically, would we like to have more strategic instruction from the Committee?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Yes, on a more frequent basis.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But barring that, I don’t see that we need a lot more direction on the day-to-day tactics, which I think we tried to lay out for you in broad terms.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The fact that the private sector has some expectation about what we’re going to do doesn’t tell you anything.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They’re always going to have an expectation about what we are going to do, even if we’re a completely silent Committee.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The point is that it is not optimal policy as we’ve come to understand it over the last 25 years.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You want to be in sync with the markets, and a lot of that is that the measure of success is not announcement effects.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If you say that you’re going to buy a new category of assets that you have not talked about before, you’re going to surprise the market.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You’re going to get some effect on that day.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It might have nothing to do with optimal policy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s go back to our regularly scheduled program.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m comfortable with continuing on the path that we laid out at the last meeting—expanding our balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: We did pretty well against objectives over the intermeeting period.

speaker: LACKER
text: Asset purchases added $215 billion, and the net runoffs in other lending, the reduction in the Treasury’s general account, and some other miscellaneous wiggles in our balance sheet meant that currency plus reserves increased by $146 billion, virtually all of that in reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’m happy with how we did over the last intermeeting period.

speaker: LACKER
text: This last discussion has been fascinating against the backdrop of our not having a clear sense of exactly why and how expanding our balance sheet affects the world.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think about all the experience we’ve had with tracing the course of the fed funds rate through a recovery and out again, and I look at the graphs of our balance sheet and the timing of the recession, and I’m thinking, Why should our balance sheet peak in December or whenever it does?

speaker: LACKER
text: Do we have an analytical sense that that’s the right timing for the magnitude of the stimulus?

speaker: LACKER
text: Maybe it’s just the time path cumulatively summed.

speaker: LACKER
text: But this habitat theory doesn’t say that there are announcement effects; I’m not sure you get any announcement effects in that.

speaker: LACKER
text: And is it the assets or the liabilities?

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we’re really groping in the dark here.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we need to recognize that.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’d like to see the Desk pay some attention to the base and accelerate its pace of purchases a little if the credit programs are running off faster than we seek.

speaker: LACKER
text: Similarly, if the credit programs don’t run off as fast as we think, maybe the Desk could lighten the pace and respond accordingly.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it’s going to be really hard to think about adjusting this over the year.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I said yesterday, it’s not likely to happen next week, for sure, but what if banks’ demand for liquidity, protection against adverse market events, falls or rises?

speaker: LACKER
text: That could shift the effect of what we’re doing.

speaker: LACKER
text: It could shift us toward a much more stimulative effect or a much less stimulative effect pretty suddenly, and I think we need to be alert for that.

speaker: LACKER
text: As for the statement, something B-ish would be good for me.

speaker: LACKER
text: I guess I like the general structure of B′′′, as it’s being called here—it’s simple.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I could go with any of them.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m in favor of the action and language of alternative B with no primes.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we don’t need to take additional action today.

speaker: KOHN
text: We need to get further along in implementing what we’ve done.

speaker: KOHN
text: With a less negative outlook, I think the need for an additional, immediate reaction is less pressing and, given the high level of uncertainty, it argues for being a little more gradual in our actions.

speaker: KOHN
text: Having said all that, I agree with many of the points that President Yellen made.

speaker: KOHN
text: The outcomes we predicted are just not satisfactory from the perspective of the objectives that the Congress has given us.

speaker: KOHN
text: The lowest unemployment rate we have in 2011 is 6½ percent.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, I think the NAIRU may have risen in the structural changes, but whether it has risen 2 full percentage points, I think even President Plosser—let the transcript show that President Plosser shook his head “no.” So even at the end of 2011, we have an output gap.

speaker: KOHN
text: We can discuss how big it might be, but something is there.

speaker: KOHN
text: And inflation in most of our forecasts—not all of them, but most of them—is still on its way down.

speaker: KOHN
text: So this is not a satisfactory outcome, and we need to think carefully about what we can do about it, consistent with what the Congress has told us to do as the objectives of monetary policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: There are a number of potential things we could do.

speaker: KOHN
text: One is more purchases of long-term securities, as President Yellen suggested.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m not comfortable at this point with the suggestion that President Rosengren was making yesterday—that we set a long-term interest rate and aim for that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that would complicate the exit strategy tremendously.

speaker: KOHN
text: But my mind is open to these things.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’d like to hear further arguments on this, and if the situation does fail to improve, I think we ought to be open to all those alternatives.

speaker: KOHN
text: As I said yesterday, I would consider lowering the rate on excess reserves.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s not a big deal, but it moves in the right direction at some point.

speaker: KOHN
text: And we’re talking about possibly being more explicit on two kinds of paths.

speaker: KOHN
text: One is the path for future purchases, and the other would be the path for the federal funds rate.

speaker: KOHN
text: So President Bullard is right.

speaker: KOHN
text: Optimal policy kinds of discussions say that you ought to tell people what you’re going to do in the future.

speaker: KOHN
text: The Canadians have now moved to that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think the uncertainty about the future path of purchases is any different qualitatively from the uncertainty about the future interest rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: So if we’re going to start specifying the future path of purchases, we need to think about whether we should also be specifying future interest rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: The Committee has had trouble with doing that because of the sense of commitment, but it needs a thorough discussion before we go down that path.

speaker: KOHN
text: I also have an issue with the cliff effect.

speaker: KOHN
text: I, too, thought that the major effect came from reducing the stock of debt in the hands of the private sector, not necessarily the pace at which we do it.

speaker: KOHN
text: I can imagine that the pace matters some, but it’s mostly a stock thing.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t know how important the cliff effect is.

speaker: KOHN
text: How do we know when we’ve done enough?

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s going to be really hard, and as President Lacker said, we are in territory that we’ve not been in before.

speaker: KOHN
text: We don’t know what the metrics are.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’re just going to have to factor everything through the forecast, discuss where the path of financial conditions is going and what the implications for the forecast are, and decide when we need to tighten.

speaker: KOHN
text: It isn’t going to be easy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I hope that President Plosser is right and we come to that decision sooner rather than later.

speaker: KOHN
text: But my expectation right now, looking at the projections that we submitted today, is that we are not going to be there any time soon.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Just to clarify the unemployment rate discussion, Governor Kohn, I think the difference in the language that you and I would use on this particular issue has to do with the fact that, even at 6½ percent unemployment, which was my forecast for the outyears, is above what I would consider the steady state.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But that does not necessarily mean that monetary policy has some ability either to speed up that convergence or to alter it, and that’s the difference between the models and the assumptions that we’re talking about.

speaker: LACKER
text: Governor Kohn, you described the forecast as unsatisfactory with respect to our mandated objectives.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is it unsatisfactory because a preferable outcome is feasible or because the feasible outcomes make us really unhappy?

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we could move.

speaker: KOHN
text: There are actions we can take to move us toward preferable outcomes.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that monetary policy at the zero bound is really difficult, and we’re not quite sure what the outcomes are for the levers we push.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’re never sure when we push the federal funds rate lever, what the outcome is going to be.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I haven’t given up on the possibility that monetary policy, even at the zero bound, can favorably affect the outcomes and get us closer to our legislative objectives.

speaker: KOHN
text: That is basically what we’ve been trying to do since December, and I think more of the same and maybe some innovations along several lines might be helpful.

speaker: KOHN
text: But, no, I think there are feasible actions we could take that would at least move us in the right direction.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As I was saying yesterday on the economic outlook, my judgment is just that we’re going to have to see more data at this point.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As many people around the table noted, turning points are notoriously hard to predict.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And when the economy is down, as Governor Tarullo and others noted, it is vulnerable to further shocks, which might come from directions that are not contemplated right now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’m also probably more pessimistic about financial markets than most here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think they probably have not improved all that much, and I guess I would not put too much weight on stock price movements.

speaker: BULLARD
text: These are the guys that brought us the tech bubble, remember?

speaker: BULLARD
text: They just fluctuate way too much to take them as much of a signal in the short term.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I think the basic mode for this meeting is that we probably need more information.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As many people, including President Pianalto and others, emphasized, we’d like to see how these stress tests come out.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is a big near-term issue for the Fed, and we’d like to see what happens there.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A critical issue for this Committee is how the Fed bills are going to go and how they are going to move through the Congress, as the Chairman was talking about yesterday.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’d also like to hear more about interest on reserves and related issues—possible sterilization techniques—to be discussed at the June meeting.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That may change the framework of discussion around here dramatically if we can think about those things and make more progress on those issues.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On policy, we were very aggressive last time—appropriately so, I think.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Part of the argument around the table was that it was a timing issue with respect to housing and mortgage markets.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I agree with Governor Kohn.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We’d like to learn more about the effects of those actions as we go through the spring here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Any further commitments that we would make on asset purchases at this point would seem to apply mostly to a date in the future—say, the October– December time frame.

speaker: BULLARD
text: To me it seems unclear why we would make that commitment based on the information we have today.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We could make that commitment at a future meeting when we have better information on how the economy is progressing.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, alternative A, as I’ve been arguing, does something I haven’t liked—it contains what seem to me to be arbitrary round numbers of asset purchases.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I do agree with President Yellen that outcomes are certainly bad; and the fact is, as the Chairman was noting, in September–October this economy experienced a very large, very real shock, and the economy is going to have to adjust to that shock.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Optimal policy can mitigate and help that adjustment, but it cannot offset it completely.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So our job is to figure out how much and what is the optimal path that we can calculate that will help as much as we can help.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But I think there are probably limits to what monetary policy can do in the face of a very large and global shock.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Of the many B alternatives, I like B′′, but I’m willing to entertain the discussion around the table here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: A lot of good ideas are being mentioned here on this.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So as I said before, I would like to see policy expressed as a state-contingent rule to the extent possible.

speaker: BULLARD
text: What we should have in our heads is a Taylor-type rule for asset purchases.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In a Taylor-type rule you do not say what you are going to do with the funds rate in the future.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You say, “Here’s the rule; here’s how we react to developments in the economy.” Everyone understands this, this informs the entire equilibrium, and that’s how the equilibrium works.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We could maybe do the same kind of thing for asset purchases and say that this is how we are going to react to incoming events and on inflation, the output gap, and maybe other variables that we think are important, and that will inform the entire equilibrium and this is how we go forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Inside models, that is actually the optimal way to proceed.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would like to try to get—and we have been doing a lot, and the staff has done a lot, which I appreciate—more in that direction in a difficult environment when we have a lot of challenges in front of us.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So that would be one way to implement what I would interpret as the key lesson from optimal monetary policy in the past 20 or 25 years in academic circles, as President Plosser and others have talked about.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I like the emphasis that the Committee has adopted in a lot of the discussion here that we’re concerned mainly about the persistent components of balance sheet expansion—agency MBS, Treasuries, and agency debt—and that it is the key issue going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I like thinking of those as one group, which some of the staff memos did—it’s a great way to think about it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I also have the idea that I floated a bit yesterday that, for the more temporary programs—the liquidity programs—to price them all as backstops just a little outside what would make all the volumes fall to zero.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Those programs would stay in place, but then they would all get off the balance sheet, and you would not be clouding up your balance sheet with these temporary liquidity programs.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They would still be there as a backstop; and if financial turmoil intensified, they’d be there to be used.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But you’d have the idea that these things are used in time increments of weeks, not months or years.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think we should think about that, but maybe I’m the only one who thinks that we should.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The temporary expansion of the balance sheet or the monetary base or asset purchases even over many months is unlikely to have a meaningful effect on inflation in the medium term.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We know that the effect of any policy depends importantly on the private-sector expectations of that policy—that is, on the whole policy path.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If we do not define a policy path, the market will form expectations anyway and define a path for us, and so I think we should be clear in our own heads about what we are trying to do, what we think the optimal policy path looks like, and why.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As I stressed yesterday, surprise announcements are not a characteristic of optimal policy as I understand it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Good policy is a state-contingent plan that is well understood by the private sector.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Most announcement effects tend to go away and might mislead us on what the impact of policy really is.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I think the bottom line is that we should stand pat for today.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We should get more information on the economy, on the stress tests, on the Fed bills possibility, and on other sterilization techniques.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’d also like to look into the backstop pricing for liquidity programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just for clarity, backstop pricing is part of our thinking on exit that we’ll be talking about, Brian?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I had hoped that the actions taken at the last meeting would have had a larger impact on long-term rates, particularly the 30-year fixed mortgage rate.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Our rates may fall further as the backlogs at mortgage brokers subside.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I’d like to encourage the Desk to consider what additional institutional feature might facilitate pushing mortgage rates down further faster using markets in which we don’t have much experience.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As Trish highlighted in yesterday’s discussion, there are a number of things that we don’t directly affect, but we may be able to affect them indirectly.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In fact, that may be more efficient than increasing purchases—to think about some of those institutional features and whether we can help adjust them.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the policy options, I prefer alternative B. I’d like to understand better the effect of existing programs before deciding what additional actions are necessary.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If our mortgage-backed-security purchase program is successful in significantly lowering mortgage rates, that may have the stimulative effect we desire.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, even if that program is successful, the Bluebook simulations as well as those done by my staff make it clear that the optimal policy simulation would indicate that further actions are necessary.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Like President Yellen’s, my forecast remains far from the goal for either inflation or unemployment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So the question for me is, What is the most effective way to try to get closer to achieving those goals?

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It’s not clear to me right now what the most effective use of our balance sheet is if the goal is to reduce borrowing costs to consumers and businesses.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I’m a little uncertain whether that’s through more large Treasury purchases, whether that’s more actions in the TALF, or whether that’s doing something different in the mortgage market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Thinking that through might be more useful than expanding our balance sheet further at this time.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I’m going to argue for alternative B, with only two minor editorial suggestions.

speaker: FISHER
text: But first I want to turn to the papers and suggestions of Presidents Plosser and Bullard and append what President Rosengren just said.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do think that Presidents Plosser and Bullard have identified a real weakness in our current formulation of communication of monetary policy, but I would respectfully submit that they failed to identify the solution.

speaker: FISHER
text: What the public had before when we operated in simpler times and is now missing seems to me to be a sense of how we will adjust policy in response to shocks of various kinds.

speaker: FISHER
text: With the transmission of monetary policy to the real economy disrupted by the disarray in financial markets, the funds rate up against the zero bound, and our taking policy in new directions, I sense that the public—whether it’s the public here, in China, or anywhere else that has invested in our markets—is still confused about what has been driving our decisions and what our next moves are likely to be, conditional on the evolution of the economy.

speaker: FISHER
text: The sense of confusion isn’t so bad for our liquidity programs, as was implied by Presidents Plosser and Bullard.

speaker: FISHER
text: It has often been noted that these are a natural extension of our discount window function, and I think that’s understandable.

speaker: FISHER
text: They’ll tend to unwind themselves as financial conditions improve or normalize.

speaker: FISHER
text: But things get messy with our purchase of mortgage-backed securities and especially our purchase of longer-term Treasuries.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that there is still a lack of clarity in understanding our intent here.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, maybe it’s just that I’m the only one who doesn’t understand the clarity.

speaker: FISHER
text: I may be the only one confused, but I don’t think that’s the case.

speaker: FISHER
text: For example, what should the public expect?

speaker: FISHER
text: Should the public expect that the purchases of MBS will continue until the residential construction situation bottoms out, until home prices bottom out, until foreclosures stop rising, or until one or another of these economic variables actually turns around and starts moving in the other direction?

speaker: FISHER
text: Or should the public be told to expect that the purchases will continue until spreads between mortgage rates and Treasuries rates normalize?

speaker: FISHER
text: Vice Chairman Dudley just now raised the issue of how we want the market to respond.

speaker: FISHER
text: Well, with regard to large-scale purchases of longer-term Treasuries, the hope apparently is that they will put some downward pressure on long-term private rates.

speaker: FISHER
text: That’s the way we’ve stated what we’ve inferred.

speaker: FISHER
text: But how do we judge whether our efforts have been helpful, given that many other factors affect the rates we hope to influence?

speaker: FISHER
text: What interest rate spread are we supposed to be looking at?

speaker: FISHER
text: In this case, that’s not clear to me.

speaker: FISHER
text: Do we just keep doing more and more until there’s some unmistakable evidence that a recovery is under way?

speaker: FISHER
text: Again, I respect very much what Presidents Plosser and Bullard have put on the table, but it doesn’t say very much to resolve the questions and the uncertainty that I’ve just raised.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is not clear to me what difference it will make whether we say our intention is to buy X billion by the end of the year or to purchase X billion per month or to increase our holdings at Y percent annual interest rate.

speaker: FISHER
text: The lesson of history is that it’s extraordinarily dangerous for a central bank to target any measure of real activity in setting its policy.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we certainly ought not to say that we’re going to pursue action A until home sales rebound, for example.

speaker: FISHER
text: It has also been proven dangerous for central banks to try to target longer-term interest rates.

speaker: FISHER
text: At least that’s my reading of history.

speaker: FISHER
text: As Milton Friedman pointed out a long time ago, such attempts can all too easily lead to inflation or deflationary consequences.

speaker: FISHER
text: So that leaves spreads and/or a price and/or a price times a quantity and nominal values as an intermediate target.

speaker: FISHER
text: For MBS, as noted above, a spread might make sense, but what about longer-term Treasuries?

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s not clear to me.

speaker: FISHER
text: And the Reifschneider– Roberts memo makes abundantly clear how little we understand the links between Fed purchases of longer-term Treasuries and inflation.

speaker: FISHER
text: We still need a good deal of clarity in our ability to state our exit strategy, and I know we’re going to be talking about that later.

speaker: FISHER
text: For the time being, given the questions I have, despite the good efforts of the Presidents from Philadelphia and St. Louis, I would strongly argue for alternative B. I think it would confuse the markets if we took the course outlined in alternative A.

speaker: FISHER
text: One thing that was pretty clear around the table yesterday, I counted eight people who mentioned the fact that, every time we go out to speak, people are worried about the long-term inflationary consequences of what we’re doing with our balance sheet—again, whether it’s in Beijing or someplace in Minnesota, because I remember Gary mentioned it as well.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we were at the point to expand our purchase of Treasuries, I think it would confirm suspicions that we’re just hell-bent on monetizing government deficits.

speaker: FISHER
text: That is not our intention, but I think it would confirm those who have such suspicions.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, I don’t think it’s necessary.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’re only partially way through the program that we’re trying to execute and we’ve agreed to execute now through autumn, previously over a period of six months.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we’ve changed that wording slightly.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it would be a mistake, Mr. Chairman, despite sensitivity to President Yellen’s arguments, to argue for alternative A.

speaker: FISHER
text: With regard to two minor editorial suggestions, first, Brian, I appreciate the changes that were made.

speaker: FISHER
text: But just to be accurate and given what we’ve been hearing, I would add “and staffing” to the end of the sentence that begins, “Weak sales prospects.” “Weak sales prospects and difficulties in obtaining credit have led businesses to cut back on inventories, fixed investment, and staffing.” Indeed, that is what they’ve been doing.

speaker: FISHER
text: Then with regard to President Plosser’s concern—and I think the concern of all of us—about anchoring inflation expectations and anchoring inflation, we could accomplish that by appending to the end of the very last sentence of that first paragraph, because we’re talking about our policy actions, “will contribute to a gradual resumption of sustainable economic growth without sacrificing the Committee’s long-term commitment to price stability.” (A) That’s true.

speaker: FISHER
text: (B) It would provide comfort to those who wonder if we are sacrificing our long-term commitment to price stability.

speaker: FISHER
text: The operative words in that sentence are that we continue to anticipate that our policy actions will contribute to a gradual resumption of sustainable economic growth.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would add “without sacrificing our longstanding commitment to price stability.” That would address the concerns that I heard from many, many people, and I think, President Plosser, that would address your concern as well.

speaker: EVANS
text: At our last meeting, I favored the large-scale asset purchase option that was offered to the Committee.

speaker: EVANS
text: In fact, I asked for a little more.

speaker: EVANS
text: The reason was that I thought that we should get to the most appropriate policy and provide the support to the economy and the outlook so that we could plausibly stand pat if the outlook stabilized.

speaker: EVANS
text: I thought we should get to the best feasible outcome that we could support, and so at that time I understood $300 billion to be $300 billion unless the outlook or the markets changed or something like that.

speaker: EVANS
text: Coming in, I thought that our action in March was close enough.

speaker: EVANS
text: We also have the TALF expanding and other support.

speaker: EVANS
text: With those actions, I thought that this pushed the burden for future policy actions to be based upon something in the outlook that was not currently anticipated, and in fact, I think the current Greenbook outlook is pretty stable.

speaker: EVANS
text: It has improved a bit and is consistent with this view.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I favor alternative B, which I interpret as no change in our policy.

speaker: EVANS
text: If we decided that we thought we could do more to improve the outcome and we wanted to do more, I think that we should find the right level as quickly as possible today on the basis of what we know so that we can stand pat.

speaker: EVANS
text: I worry that meandering policy is not confidence inspiring.

speaker: EVANS
text: When we trigger a policy action, it should be on the basis of something we have learned about how the economy is evolving differently than we thought or there is actually news that normally would be interpreted as requiring that type of action.

speaker: EVANS
text: I am just concerned about how the public is going to gauge our policy changes in this most complicated environment.

speaker: EVANS
text: Lastly, I do think there is a difference between our large-scale asset purchases as a policy instrument and our funds rate changes.

speaker: EVANS
text: It is not just future expectations of the fed funds rate.

speaker: EVANS
text: With the funds rate action, when we could do that, we could do it today or tomorrow.

speaker: EVANS
text: Markets understood that to be implemented by the Desk, and we were in that environment.

speaker: EVANS
text: Markets had more experience with that, and so they knew how to form expectations about policy, our response function.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now it’s more difficult when it’s unclear and there are reasons that it’s unclear.

speaker: EVANS
text: We don’t always agree exactly on how the transmission mechanism works in general and especially now.

speaker: EVANS
text: But with large-scale asset purchases, it takes up to six months for the action to be implemented because it takes place over a period of time.

speaker: EVANS
text: We ourselves don’t really have good expectations of how those programs might change, and the public is even more challenged in that way.

speaker: EVANS
text: The faster that we can get to the position that we think is best to support the best outcome that is feasible, the better off we are.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I think that alternative B at the moment is the right choice.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’ll ask President Pianalto to go ahead, but then maybe we can take a coffee break.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given the high degree of uncertainty about the outlook and the uncertainty around how to size the quantity and composition of our asset purchases, I think the best course of action today is not to add any more uncertainty to this environment.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I hope that our meeting in June will be helpful in reducing some of the uncertainty around our asset purchase program.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So today I prefer making only minor changes to our statement, and I support alternative B.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Why don’t we take a 20-minute coffee break.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lockhart, whenever you are ready.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It is a challenge to be as succinct as President Pianalto.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Actually, I am a little bit ambivalent, quite frankly, coming into this decision.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I said yesterday, I think that the economy is in an ambiguous state and there is a lot of uncertainty.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I have sympathy for the arguments that President Yellen made that alternative A could actually tip the balance to better outcomes and improve on the forecast, which really isn’t acceptable over the longer term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: A negative, which President Fisher mentioned, is the likelihood that alternative A would be interpreted as closer to deliberate monetization.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So, as I said, I am supporting alternative B, and I favor adopting the language that helps establish a clearer understanding of policy conditionality over time.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I thank Presidents Plosser and Bullard for all their efforts because I think they drove that point home very strongly.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So I strongly support the alternative B language that says that the Committee is prepared to make further adjustments in timing and overall amounts “as appropriate, in view of the evolving economic outlook and conditions in financial markets.” The full impact of March’s policy decision on real economic activity hasn’t yet been realized, and there is fiscal stimulus in train that is yet to be fully reflected.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: So as many others have stated, I would like to wait and see how the financial and economic environment evolves.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, on the consideration of A versus B, I prefer B for several reasons, which I will try to summarize quickly.

speaker: STERN
text: First of all, I do think the economic outlook has improved a bit.

speaker: STERN
text: Maybe it will turn out to be a false dawn, but maybe it will continue to improve.

speaker: STERN
text: We will just have to see how that goes.

speaker: STERN
text: More important, I think that policy has already done a lot, if you take a broad range of things that we have been engaged in and have introduced since the fall of ’07.

speaker: STERN
text: That is not to say that we can’t or shouldn’t do more, if appropriate, but I think we need to bear in mind that we have been aggressive and reasonably timely, certainly over the last year or more.

speaker: STERN
text: And I am not sure that there is all that much more we can do with regard to the outcomes associated with the dual mandate between now and the end of 2011—two and a half years.

speaker: STERN
text: I am just not persuaded that a lot more activity on our part is going to have a major effect on how those numbers are going to look over that time frame.

speaker: STERN
text: I also am a little concerned, or I wonder, whether we would continue to get a lot of bang from increased asset purchases along the lines that we seem to think we have had so far.

speaker: STERN
text: This can’t be a free lunch.

speaker: STERN
text: At some point, there have to be both a diminishing response in the market and increasing risks of adverse consequences for inflation or other things going forward.

speaker: STERN
text: I think we need to bear that in mind, if and when we decide that we want to scale these things up even further.

speaker: STERN
text: So for those reasons, at this time, I favor alternative B.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as language is concerned, I would be equally happy with B or B′′′.

speaker: STERN
text: I think either of those is fine, and I do think that tying our policy more explicitly to our inflation objective, along the lines that President Fisher or President Plosser suggested, would be constructive for the reasons they suggested.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, I was extremely uncomfortable with the Treasury purchases when we last met.

speaker: WARSH
text: I continue to be extremely uncomfortable with them.

speaker: WARSH
text: I won’t relitigate that here for the reasons I articulated last time; plus, I don’t like losing.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t want to lose again.

speaker: WARSH
text: So as Sun Tzu said, I will step back from that.

speaker: WARSH
text: It is no surprise, then, that I oppose an increase in our Treasury purchases beyond what we did last time.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of the discussion about markets and their expectations that we had earlier in this round, Mr. Chairman, I think we should not be surprised that markets want more; and the more we give, the more they will want.

speaker: WARSH
text: Having a strong, large, and credible buyer of Treasury securities is all to the good for a Treasury desk, and so I don’t think we should be surprised by that at all.

speaker: WARSH
text: With that large caveat, I favor alternative B. I think that we should be patient.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we should be the adults in town.

speaker: WARSH
text: We should favor as much policy certainty as we possibly can have.

speaker: WARSH
text: We have an opportunity here not to be lurchy, not to be jumpy, and I think alternative B captures that.

speaker: WARSH
text: I have one other area of discomfort with alternative B that I would raise.

speaker: WARSH
text: In paragraph 3, Mr. Chairman, after we denote in detail the numbers of our purchases, which really are just a restatement of what we did previously, we then go on to say, “The Committee stands ready to adjust the timing and overall amounts of its purchases .

speaker: WARSH
text: in view of the evolving economic outlook.” I think that the markets are unlikely to view that language neutrally.

speaker: WARSH
text: The sentence is new from what we said in March, and it looks to me as though, when last time we said that we stood ready to do something, we were standing ready to buy Treasuries if circumstances evolved, which we ultimately did.

speaker: WARSH
text: I view that as being quite forward leaning.

speaker: WARSH
text: In fact, it probably does match market expectations, which Trish rightly described.

speaker: WARSH
text: But it tends to pre-judge that outcome.

speaker: WARSH
text: At least if I am properly hearing our colleagues around the table, it is not a judgment that we want to make.

speaker: WARSH
text: And I continue to think that the last sentence in paragraph 3—where we say, “The Committee will continue to carefully monitor the size and composition”—certainly gives us that flexibility.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is the same sentence that we used in March, which gave us that flexibility.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I must say that I don’t really understand the rationale for including this new sentence about standing ready, particularly the reference to overall amounts of those purchases, until we have gone much further.

speaker: WARSH
text: So that is a particular area of discomfort on alternative B.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, in the debate that is brewing about the limits of monetary policy in this cycle, I think I would associate myself with President Stern and suggest that we have accomplished much.

speaker: WARSH
text: On balance, what we have done over these past 18 months has been remarkable.

speaker: WARSH
text: If the next 18 months force the same kind of innovation and creativity by the Federal Reserve, we can almost guarantee that those projections we have submitted here in April aren’t coming to pass.

speaker: WARSH
text: So this might be a proper time for us to be a bit more patient and to be a bit more hesitant to continue to push the envelope, and we will see whether or not the projections come to pass.

speaker: DUKE
text: I am going to support alternative B.

speaker: DUKE
text: Although I agree with President Yellen that the forecast outcome is not desirable, I also agree with a number of others that I am not sure I understand right now the effectiveness of which programs.

speaker: DUKE
text: We are also in a situation where we are dealing with numerous programs, some of which we control the size and others of which we do not control the size, particularly if we look at the TALF and the expectation of the TALF going anywhere from $100 billion to $1 trillion, depending on what the take-up is.

speaker: DUKE
text: Right now, as we add the CMBS and we put it out there at five-year terms, we are going to limit the five-year terms to $100 billion.

speaker: DUKE
text: It is not clear whether we would get additional growth on the three-year terms, so I would rather wait and see how that works out.

speaker: DUKE
text: On the language, I think it is very difficult to come up with language that indicates a steady set of purchases for very different programs.

speaker: DUKE
text: If you look at the lumpiness that Trish pointed out in the mortgage markets—but even if you look at our statements—the $300 billion purchases going to autumn versus the mortgage-backed securities going to the end of the year don’t translate into even purchases from now until the end of the year.

speaker: DUKE
text: So, for those reasons, I would prefer the language in alternative B.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I believe the problem with which we are confronted, as many of you have already noted, is fundamentally one of communication.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I would elaborate that a bit to say that I think the problem may be in no small part our ability to communicate to ourselves, individually and collectively, why we are doing what we are doing.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I regard that as important because of what I said yesterday and what the Chairman mentioned this morning in the conclusion to his wrap-up, which is that we may be faced with a suboptimally performing economy for some time to come in which the policy challenges will extend beyond the challenge of readjusting our balance sheet over a number of years.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Under these circumstances, it becomes more important that we have a clear sense of what policy instruments we think are available and why and how we are going to deploy them in response to a given set of conditions.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Based on listening to the March meeting discussion and this meeting’s discussion, I do not feel that we are actually in a position to articulate a standard that is roughly comparable to what is articulated when normal monetary policy is being done.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Under those circumstances, I favor saying the least because my concern is that saying more will lead to inferences that we don’t actually want people to draw.

speaker: TARULLO
text: So, for example, by adopting a more forward-leaning strategy such as alternative A this morning, I fear that a message would be sent as to how exactly we are reading the green shoots versus the red herrings debate.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I fear that there would be an inference drawn that we have concluded that we know how the Treasury purchases are actually functioning and we have some reason to believe that they will respond to what we think the most important problems in the economy are.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Like Governor Warsh, I do fear a bit that an inference will be drawn as to our being more willing to accommodate the fiscal policies that are being pursued right now, which I think is not something that any of us has decided we want to communicate.

speaker: TARULLO
text: This is not to say that I would be opposed to increased purchases of Treasuries or, indeed, any other number of policy instruments, but only once we are in a position to communicate with enough specificity, either in our statements or through other means of communication, so as to guard against those kinds of inferences being drawn.

speaker: TARULLO
text: On the merits, I think that President Yellen stated the economic conditions better than I could, and I subscribe to her analysis.

speaker: TARULLO
text: On the outcomes, I favor alternative B, and I should say I guess that I favor alternative B with as little change from the March policy statement as is possible, given that we are now in a later month, precisely to avoid any of the inferences that I suggested could be wrongly drawn being in fact drawn.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I have some sympathy with President Yellen’s case for expanded purchases, but I think that we have to recognize that these purchase programs have costs as well as benefits.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Speaking for myself, I would really feel more comfortable if we had a more formal evaluation of what those costs and benefits were regarding what we have done up to now.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One cost that I don’t think we have ruminated on very much is the interest rate risk that we are actually taking on the Fed’s portfolio.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One thing I have wondered about is, if the balance sheet were to get $6 trillion and most of that was Treasuries and MBS, what would happen if short-term rates rose above the yield on our portfolio?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: What would happen if we were asking the Treasury to pay us money because we had negative interest?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In a way, we are turning ourselves into a kind of S&L in terms of our balance sheet structure, and we really need to think about what the implications of that are for the medium and longer term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I would encourage the staff to do analysis on those kinds of issues for the June meeting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The second reason that I don’t think it is appropriate to do it right now is that it would send an odd signal to the market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are saying that things are better, yet we feel the need to expand our purchase programs in a way in which the market was not anticipating us to do.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think it would be a little confusing to the market.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the market is expecting us to do something in June about Treasuries because of the cliff question.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In other words, what happened?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is a six-month program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The market is going to start looking ahead to what happens at the end.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We need to do more to get clear on how we think about these cliff effects.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is not quite the same as the federal funds rate because you could argue that ending the purchase program is de facto tightening.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You are taking away something that is pushing down rates, so I don’t think it is quite the same as specifying the federal funds rate path.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It is a lot different, too, because there is so little experience with it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We have had many, many economic cycles in which to get a sense of the federal funds rate—you know, market prices, futures expectations, et cetera—but I think we need to do some more work on this whole cliff effect.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the market implicitly assumes that we are going to taper off and smooth the rough edges.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I notice that, in the balance sheet simulations that were put forward yesterday, it went to the end and just ended abruptly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t think that is really what the market expectation is.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think they expect us to round those off.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But we haven’t really discussed that formally as a group, and we need to come to some conclusions on that.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: As far as the choices for the statement, I favor the B alternatives—you know, B′, B′′, and B′′′.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I am not sure what is gained by the added details.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The market participants can already calculate the monthly purchase rates by just taking what we have announced about duration and magnitude.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I also think that writing down specific monthly purchase rates implies that the growth rate of the balance sheet is the prime metric driving our thought process.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I don’t really think that is right.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We are really thinking more about the effect on financial conditions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And I don’t think a dollar of Treasury purchases is necessarily the same as a dollar of agency purchases or agency MBS or some other things that we are doing with our balance sheet.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I don’t want to suggest that a dollar of the balance sheet is created equal across all our different facilities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Finally, if we added some more detail, it would be a little confusing to people because they would say, “Well, why are they telling us this now?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Why didn’t they tell us this a meeting ago, two meetings ago, or three meetings ago?” So I think it would be more confusing than illuminating to the markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, I again have benefited from a good discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the policy discussions—don’t take this the wrong way—are getting better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think they are getting more informative and more interesting as we go along.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I do appreciate it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the substance there is a good bit of consensus—not complete consensus—on standing pat.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have seen a bit of improvement, but it is very tentative, and other factors, like the bank assessment program and fiscal policy, are in train.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So there is some benefit in watchful waiting for a time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have, of course, taken very strong actions in the last few meetings, including a December move to zero and the large asset purchases that we announced last time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also, before substantial increases in our balance sheet, I think many of us—certainly, I—feel that we need to get further advanced in our understanding of the exit strategy and the tools we will have and what we will be doing as we go forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So understanding that more stimulus would be good, as suggested by the Taylor rule, for example, I think that it would be better to stand pat on the purchases this time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With respect to the statement, I appreciate very much the discussion on alternative B′′′ and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the consensus for the group was to stay with what we have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The issue here is that we haven’t quite figured out how to express the state contingency.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we had a Taylor rule that would tie the monthly purchases to observables, as President Bullard was suggesting, I think that would be right and good.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Unfortunately, the only way to establish such a rule is through a long period of experience, unless we are prepared to write it down, which I am not quite sure we are.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Another issue related to that is—the analogy is not perfect—whether it is the flow of purchases or the stock of purchases that matters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Given our inability to write down a contemporaneous Taylor rule, another alternative approach that one might use in an interest rate context would be to specify a path and then to change that path as new information comes in.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is part of the debate between instruments and target rules, for example.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So as I said, I very much appreciate the insight and discussion of this issue, and I hope we will continue to make progress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would take some exception to the view that we are making up numbers entirely, because we have done our best—and the staff has certainly done its best—to try to assess the market and interest rate effects of these actions and feed them into the model.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, there is a lot of uncertainty, but being uncertain doesn’t mean you do nothing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It means you do the best you can, given the information that you have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On state contingency, Governor Warsh raised the concern about the new sentence, three from the bottom, that “the Committee stands ready to adjust the timing and overall amounts of its purchases of securities.” Governor Warsh, is your concern that this signals that we are going to increase?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: My thought about this was that it would in fact signal that we are being state-contingent and that this would be equally likely to induce us to decrease as to increase.

speaker: WARSH
text: In light of our behavior and the language around our behavior historically, I think that markets would read this as going in one direction and the one direction is far more likely up.

speaker: WARSH
text: Again, I think the overall amount certainly triggers it.

speaker: WARSH
text: And I must say that I don’t understand what that sentence does that isn’t accomplished in the final sentence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, the way I thought the two sentences were different is that the first one speaks specifically to the securities purchases, which is the topic immediately before it, and it creates for us the flexibility to adjust the timing, for example, to taper off or, for that matter, to adjust the size of the program.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I view the last sentence as addressing the static overall size and also, when we say “composition,” as implying that we are looking at the mix of programs and so on as well as the securities purchases.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So that was the intent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are others uncomfortable with that sentence?

speaker: LACKER
text: I made the mistake, when I initially read it, of reading the plain language version as symmetrically contingent.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I think Kevin is fairly persuasive that, in the context of our statement, it is likely to be read as pointing toward the possibility of expansion.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, there are times in which the appropriate contingency ought to be asymmetric, but I don’t think we intend to communicate that here.

speaker: KOHN
text: Governor Warsh had a point about the words “stands ready,” which we did use before.

speaker: KOHN
text: Suppose we soften those words a little and say, “The Committee will consider adjusting the timing and overall” so that it sounds like something we will consider in the future rather than we are poised to do it.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t know whether that would help, Governor Warsh.

speaker: WARSH
text: Yes, I do think that helps.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “Will consider”—was that what you said?

speaker: KOHN
text: That is what I said, and President Plosser said “will evaluate”—“the timing and overall amounts of its purchases.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But get rid of “as appropriate.” “The Committee will evaluate the timing and overall amounts of its purchases in view of the evolving economic outlook.”

speaker: KOHN
text: Everything we do is appropriate.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think that is an improvement, but I still think—and I regret not mentioning this myself—that Governor Warsh makes a key point.

speaker: FISHER
text: Given what Trish told us in terms of expectations, even though I don’t like being driven because, as it was pointed out earlier, the markets and the dealers are never satisfied.

speaker: FISHER
text: But even with softening language like that, it is new, and you are opening up the door.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t think you should put it in here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there any defenders of that sentence?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I kind of like it.

speaker: EVANS
text: I kind of like it, too.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, I am prepared to strike it, if that is the will of the group.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I kind of like it as well, but I thought it gave us some flexibility to say, “We won’t go as far.” If this doesn’t serve that purpose—and I think I would defer to you, Kevin, on this, because I hope that conditions evolve so that we don’t have to go to the total— then I would back away.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I agree with Governor Warsh that the market thinks that the prospect of taking down the size of the facilities is extremely low.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So then I would strike it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Mr. Chairman, I liked your explanation that you thought you had two bases covered here.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That is the way I read it.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I didn’t read it the way Governor Warsh did.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am going to propose a modification, and then we are going to take a straw vote.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The modification is, “The Committee will continue to evaluate the timing and overall amounts of its purchase of securities,”—get rid of “as appropriate”—“in light of the evolving economic outlook and conditions in financial markets.” Is that an improvement, Governor Warsh?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So let me ask all participants, all 1 people, for a “yes” or “no”—or feel free not to vote.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So how many would like to retain that sentence as amended?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, that is a majority then.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the sentence will be changed to, “The Committee will continue to evaluate the timing and overall amounts of its purchases of securities in light of the evolving outlook and conditions in financial markets.” As for the other suggestions that were made for paragraph 1, President Fisher made a suggestion close to this, and I was thinking how to respond to President Plosser’s concern about balancing our concerns about growth and price stability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am not quite sure that President Fisher’s suggestion of saying “without sacrificing” quite works because the causal factors in that last sentence in paragraph 1 include not only the Fed but also fiscal and monetary stimulus, market forces, and a whole variety of things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What if we add to the end of alternative B, paragraph 1, the words “in a context of price stability”?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So it would say, “The Committee continues to anticipate that these various factors will contribute to a gradual resumption of sustainable economic growth in a context of price stability”?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My concern was that we wanted to link our policy actions that we believe are consistent with our objective of price stability.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Mr. Chairman, your suggestion doesn’t link the two necessarily.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It just places it in a context.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am struggling a bit with what the right language might be.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But the first sentence of paragraph 3, though, says, “Will employ all available tools to promote economic recovery and to preserve price stability.” So that links our tools.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is this last phrase helpful to you, President Fisher?

speaker: FISHER
text: I agree with your point because it does talk about fiscal and monetary stimulus.

speaker: FISHER
text: I appreciate the fact that we at least make some reference to price stability, and I think that is the important point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So you are going to add that sentence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am going to add the phrase at the very end of paragraph B1, the words, “in a context of price stability.” All right.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The last thing that came up, President Fisher suggested in the third sentence of alternative B, “Weak sales have led businesses to cut back on” then, instead of “inventories and fixed investment,” have “inventories, fixed investment, and staffing.” I think that is fine substantively.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The only thing I would note is that we do reference job losses in the previous sentence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So does anyone have a view on that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I am happy to make the change.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Shall we go ahead and make the change?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So “inventories, fixed investment, and staffing.” Do you have all of those changes now?

speaker: LACKER
text: The word “somewhat” in the first sentence just snags my brain.

speaker: LACKER
text: “Somewhat” is great the way we usually use it—you know, somewhat higher, somewhat lower.

speaker: LACKER
text: That is a long and honored tradition in central banking.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: How about “appears to be somewhat slower”?

speaker: LACKER
text: That would be much more direct.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess that pace requires an adjective—appears to be somewhat slower, the pace is slower.

speaker: LACKER
text: I am not a good enough writer to know why.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: “The pace of contraction appears to be somewhat slower.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You know, this is actually kind of fun here.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have always enjoyed it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Debbie, do you think you are able now to read the statement?

speaker: DANKER
text: I will give it a shot, and the eventual vote will be on both the alternative B directive from the Bluebook—I don’t think it is affected by this language change— and the statement that I am about to read.

speaker: DANKER
text: Please correct me if I don’t have it right.

speaker: DANKER
text: “Information received since the Federal Open Market Committee met in March indicates that the economy has continued to contract, though the pace of contraction appears to be somewhat slower.

speaker: DANKER
text: Household spending has shown signs of stabilizing but remains constrained by ongoing job losses, lower housing wealth, and tight credit.

speaker: DANKER
text: Weak sales prospects and difficulties in obtaining credit have led businesses to cut back on inventories, fixed investment, and staffing.

speaker: DANKER
text: Although the economic outlook has improved modestly since the March meeting, partly reflecting some easing of financial market conditions, economic activity is likely to remain weak for a time.

speaker: DANKER
text: Nonetheless, the Committee continues to anticipate that policy actions to stabilize financial markets and institutions, fiscal and monetary stimulus, and market forces will contribute to a gradual resumption of sustainable economic growth in a context of price stability.

speaker: DANKER
text: In light of increasing economic slack here and abroad, the Committee expects that inflation will remain subdued.

speaker: DANKER
text: Moreover, the Committee sees some risk that inflation could persist for a time below rates that best foster economic growth and price stability in the longer term.

speaker: DANKER
text: In these circumstances, the Federal Reserve will employ all available tools to promote economic recovery and to preserve price stability.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Committee will maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 0 to ¼ percent and anticipates that economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate for an extended period.

speaker: DANKER
text: As previously announced, to provide support to mortgage lending and housing markets and to improve overall conditions in private credit markets, the Federal Reserve will purchase a total of up to $1.25 trillion of agency mortgage-backed securities and up to $200 billion of agency debt by the end of the year.

speaker: DANKER
text: In addition, the Federal Reserve will buy up to $300 billion of Treasury securities by autumn.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Committee will continue to evaluate the timing and overall amounts of its purchases of securities in light of the evolving economic outlook and conditions in financial markets.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Federal Reserve is facilitating the extension of credit to households and businesses and supporting the functioning of financial markets through a range of liquidity programs.

speaker: DANKER
text: The Committee will continue to carefully monitor the size and composition of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet in light of financial and economic developments.”

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That is what I have as well.

speaker: DANKER
text: Chairman Bernanke Yes Vice Chairman Dudley Yes Governor Duke Yes President Evans Yes Governor Kohn Yes President Lacker Yes President Lockhart Yes Governor Tarullo Yes Governor Warsh Yes President Yellen Yes

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have a couple of other items here—one substantive item.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have, as you know, a Transparency Committee, which has been very actively investigating all aspects of our programs, our institutional structure, and everything else to try to find whether there are opportunities to provide more information to the public about our activities that would not compromise our legitimate need for confidentiality of our policy objectives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I asked Governor Kohn to report to us briefly on progress in that committee.

speaker: KOHN
text: Let me begin with a bit of a sidebar, which is that the work of the Transparency Committee of this group is to decide what should be public and what needs to be confidential.

speaker: KOHN
text: In that regard, I found an article in the Financial Times, in which somebody seemed to have seen a staff paper, to be troubling.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think we need to decide as a group what information gets out and what doesn’t and preserve that confidentiality.

speaker: KOHN
text: What we’ve been doing is considering a number of possible steps to improve transparency for our liquidity programs.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’ve been concentrating on the collateral side.

speaker: KOHN
text: What can we say to reassure people that we are behaving in a responsible way and that we are not putting the public’s money at risk?

speaker: KOHN
text: We were embarked on this for a couple of weeks, but I would say that congressional pressure on this issue has stepped up.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also in recent weeks we have had requests for detailed data on individual borrowers, and the budget resolution had two amendments related to us.

speaker: KOHN
text: One was a Dodd–Shelby amendment, which called on the transparency side for the reporting of the amount and nature of collateral in the liquidity facility; the extent of losses on the Maiden Lanes and other special purpose vehicles due to collateral revaluations; information on the number of borrowers under various programs, including measures of concentration; and then information on contracts that we have with private-sector firms involved in design, pricing, management, and accounting of the lending programs.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are addressing all of those points, and I think our proposal, when it finally gets done, will satisfy the Dodd–Shelby amendment.

speaker: KOHN
text: In addition, Senator Sanders asked for the identity of firms receiving liquidity assistance and the value of the assistance each firm had gotten and what they were doing with the assistance.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are less inclined to do that because our view is that it will undermine the effect of the program.

speaker: KOHN
text: So we can come back.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would be interested in the views of other members of the FOMC on that.

speaker: KOHN
text: We are preparing tables on the number of borrowers and the amounts of discount window borrowing by type of institution at the discount window for banks divided by banks (and maybe by size) and then thrifts as a separate line—for example; the number of borrowers and amounts borrowed under the other facilities, PDCF, TSLF, all of that sort of thing.

speaker: KOHN
text: Trying to get some sense of the concentration and those things, like the top five borrowers, the top ten borrowers, what proportion of the total they account for, a table showing the percentage of the collateral pledge by depository institutions being used to secure loans by different types of institutions.

speaker: KOHN
text: We do have a breakout of the types of collateral now, but we would break out things a bit further, particularly on the security side, where we will give the ratings of the securities that are used as collateral.

speaker: KOHN
text: And we’re working on this business of how much we spend on the private- sector firms.

speaker: KOHN
text: We published a lot of information about the Maiden Lanes and the commercial paper facility in the annual report that just came out a couple of weeks ago, and one thing we’re looking into is whether we could update that information quarterly.

speaker: KOHN
text: So when the Maiden Lanes are marked to market on a quarterly basis, perhaps some of the additional information that appeared in the annual report could also be done on a quarterly basis.

speaker: KOHN
text: It wouldn’t be subject to the oversight of an outside auditor, but we could generate it in the same way we generate that.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, as I said, we’ve discussed the congressional request about detailed information on individual borrowers, and we looked at different ways of cutting that.

speaker: KOHN
text: So could we not do it for the discount window for banks but do it for the unusual—the 13(3)—facilities?

speaker: KOHN
text: Could we not do it for the regular discount window but do it for any unusual facility, which might include the TAF?

speaker: KOHN
text: Could we do it for some facilities but not for others because of our concerns about stigma, particularly for the TALF, for example?

speaker: KOHN
text: It just seemed impossible to cut this thing in a clean way that would satisfy the people who want information and wouldn’t discourage the use of the facilities in such a way as to undermine the effectiveness in promoting financial stability.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I would be very interested in other people’s views on this.

speaker: KOHN
text: Another problem that we saw was that most people, especially banks and probably others, have used our facilities under the assumption that their names wouldn’t be released to the public.

speaker: KOHN
text: So going back and releasing those names struck me as particularly problematic.

speaker: KOHN
text: If we were going to release any names and we decided that was okay, I think I would advocate doing it prospectively and giving people warning.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’re aiming at getting something done that the Chairman can talk about in his JEC testimony next week.

speaker: KOHN
text: So at least have an outline of what we’re trying to do—we are getting close; we’ve been mocking up tables—and then get those tables out within the next week or two after your testimony, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: That’s the summary of where we are.

speaker: KOHN
text: One idea that the Chairman had was whether, instead of just adding all of this stuff to our web site, we could embody it in a report to the Congress on a monthly basis.

speaker: KOHN
text: Our web site is sort of by function.

speaker: KOHN
text: So there’s a risk-management function, and then there are some other, different functions.

speaker: KOHN
text: We could re-cut it so that it was by facility instead of by function.

speaker: KOHN
text: Under each facility we could talk about the risk-management characteristics, how we value the collateral marked to market, do the margins, and then give all the information on that.

speaker: KOHN
text: That might be a more user-friendly way to present things to the Congress.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have time now for questions and comments.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we elect not to reveal names, would these tables be constructed the way that the Census does it, where if there are fewer than n firms, where n is a number like—

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the way that we have generally released data in the past, if there were three or fewer, we would consolidate that category with another category.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am concerned about the releasing of names and Don’s point, that you can’t renege on assumptions and promises made earlier.

speaker: FISHER
text: Tactically, I don’t know what you’re planning to say next week, but I would rather be viewed as being forced to do this rather than suggesting it terms of releasing names prospectively going forward because one of the great concerns is—we’ve seen this with the TALF and with the PPIP and everything else—the rules keep changing.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t want to be viewed as one of the agents of changing the rules in a way that upsets people who have banked on us to be a steady institution.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would just suggest that we be very careful about that and think that through.

speaker: FISHER
text: Now, the Congress has its prerogatives.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m not sure we want to feed that one.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would rather almost be in a responsive mode.

speaker: FISHER
text: I am a little worried that, if we don’t respond sufficiently, they could be extremely harsh, and maybe—Don, you summarized an awful lot there.

speaker: FISHER
text: We were talking about feeding the monsters of the market earlier.

speaker: FISHER
text: Feeding the monsters of the Congress is also saying that you can never really satisfy them.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m not calling them monsters for the record, but they have a voracious appetite.

speaker: FISHER
text: I would be really careful on this business of suggesting that we release names.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we’re viewed as the one who suggested it, it might upset the people whom we serve and who are important to our ability to function.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I’d just ask you to consider that.

speaker: FISHER
text: The other obvious trap—and I saw this on the visiting committee overseeing Harvard’s investment debacle—whenever you talk about what you’re spending on something in the private sector, it’s always going to be too much.

speaker: FISHER
text: So just get ready for that one because you can’t satisfy people very easily on that.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is always too big a dollar amount.

speaker: STERN
text: But some of those fees are in the annual report, aren’t they?

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think they’re aggregated.

speaker: KOHN
text: I mean, they must be implicit in the expense categories, right?

speaker: KOHN
text: But they’re not broken out by the fees that we’re paying for servicing these special facilities.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think except for the audit fees.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Except for the audit fees.

speaker: LACKER
text: I thought they were for the Maiden Lanes.

speaker: STERN
text: Yes, I thought they were for the Maiden Lanes.

speaker: LACKER
text: Not individually, but for each Maiden Lane I thought there was an expense line.

speaker: KOHN
text: But we’ve hired outside help—right, Bill—for a lot of the other facilities?

speaker: HOENIG
text: Just to add to that, we should not release the individual names.

speaker: HOENIG
text: You will undo half of what you have tried to do so far.

speaker: HOENIG
text: As open as we should be, we also have a responsibility to make sure this thing is managed in an orderly way, and if we release names, I think the stigma will be back in a flash and lots of issues around it.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I agree with those comments.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Stern, did you have your opportunity?

speaker: LACKER
text: If the Congress wants to make us release names, we could insist that the names of Home Loan Bank borrowers also be released.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other comments or questions for Don?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, we appreciate your taking this on in your voluminous spare time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our approach, it was suggested, is to do as much as we reasonably can and then try to draw the line at that point.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s how we‘re going to try to approach this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just have a few announcements, and then we will be free.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, you have until tomorrow at 5:00 p.m. to submit your revisions, if you have any, to your projections.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, you’ll see an SDS transmission on your BlackBerry because we are putting up links to the 2003 transcripts—a very interesting set of transcripts of the FOMC meetings—which will be released publicly on Friday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So they are confidential until Friday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, I know there are ongoing conversations about the stress test, the capital supervisory program, but we have already scheduled a video meeting on Friday for an update and how we’re going to manage things on Monday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That doesn’t mean that’s the only opportunity if you have particular banks that you are concerned about or you want to hear more about what is going on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Please don’t hesitate to get in touch with us, but we thought Friday would be a good time to bring everybody up to date.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, lunch will be available in about five minutes for those who can stay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The next meeting will be on Tuesday and Wednesday, June 23 and 24, and the meeting is adjourned.

speaker: BERNANKE
