text: However, the staff subsequently learned that the Treasury is concerned about possible adverse effects of a rescission of the authority at this time; a legislative proposal for restructuring the GSEs has not yet been put forward, and in these circumstances a rescission could prompt questions about the strength of government support for the GSEs and hence be destabilizing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Board might consider it prudent to defer action on this recommendation for the time being.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Drafts of Board and FOMC resolutions to implement these proposals were provided to you last week.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That concludes the staff presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: We would be happy to respond to your questions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you very much, and thanks again to the staff for the extraordinary amount of very useful work behind these presentations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We will go over specifically what resolutions will be needed to address the program recommendations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But before we go into Q&A, I just want to ask Trish and Brian what you’re asking for today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You’re asking for a vote, I understand, on the securities lending for GSEs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The other things that you mentioned, Trish—like the portfolio approach, tapering, hybrid ARMs—are you just looking for input at this point, or are you looking for a decision?

speaker: MOSSER
text: For the hybrid ARMs, we are looking for input.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It’s currently authorized, but we’d like the Committee’s views.

speaker: MOSSER
text: For the portfolio approach, if it goes across asset classes, it’s going to require very substantial communication by the Committee, I believe, so that’s really much more in the realm of the policy discussion, because it would be effectively making sizes flexible and fungible.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Regarding more flexibility within asset classes, again, under the current authorization, we have that authority, but we’d be interested in the Committee’s input.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’d like to start with Brian.

speaker: FISHER
text: First, in your presentation, you did not mention—or maybe I missed it—that the pace of corporate bond issuance picked up.

speaker: FISHER
text: The spreads have come down—that was well covered—but tell us a little bit about the tone and the pace of the market.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, have rates themselves come down along with the narrowing of spreads?

speaker: SACK
text: The pace of corporate bond issuance has picked up.

speaker: SACK
text: May was a very heavy month, about $40 billion of issuance.

speaker: SACK
text: That strength seemed to spill into June.

speaker: SACK
text: Anecdotally we’re seeing this bond issuance used for a variety of purposes.

speaker: SACK
text: In part it’s being used to pay down bank loans and pay down CP.

speaker: SACK
text: We are also seeing lots of holding of liquid assets.

speaker: SACK
text: This activity may just be some rotation or substitution on corporate balance sheets, but the pace of bond issuance certainly has picked up in response to the more favorable borrowing rates.

speaker: SACK
text: As your question suggested, certainly the collapse in spreads has been sufficient to outweigh the increase in Treasury yields.

speaker: SACK
text: So, yes, corporate bond costs have declined.

speaker: FISHER
text: Trish, our stated objective was to lower private credit rates and to increase credit availability, and further in your presentation you mentioned two specifics on that.

speaker: FISHER
text: One was obviously mortgages and the other was corporate credits.

speaker: FISHER
text: So we might conclude that we have been successful on the corporate credit front.

speaker: FISHER
text: Is that a fair assessment, or is it too early to tell?

speaker: FISHER
text: When you talk about lowering rates in your presentation, Trish, I’m a little confused.

speaker: FISHER
text: Our objective as I understood it was never to seek to lower rates on Treasuries deliberately.

speaker: FISHER
text: It was to have an effect on the private credit markets.

speaker: FISHER
text: Do I understand that correctly?

speaker: MOSSER
text: For corporate bonds, clearly, both yields and spreads have come way down, not just because of our actions presumably, but particularly because of the recovery in equity markets.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I guess we can take credit for some of that.

speaker: MOSSER
text: On the mortgage side, however, the spreads are or became effectively as low as we reasonably believe that we could push them with both the agency debt and the agency MBS program.

speaker: MOSSER
text: That means that additional purchases are going to have very large side effects; as we have discussed in the past, that makes us very concerned about exit and about market functioning and keeping the market healthy.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So at this stage our ability to lower private credit rates in the mortgage sphere is extremely limited unless our impact in the Treasury market directly is bigger.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I don’t know if you want to stick to that subject with other questions, or may I go ahead and ask the other?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If you have other questions, go ahead.

speaker: FISHER
text: If I could quickly ask Jim and Spence—on the demand side, am I missing something here?

speaker: FISHER
text: Wouldn’t the simplest solution be to seek an increase in reserve requirements?

speaker: FISHER
text: The paper outlines the pros, but it wasn’t clear to me what the cons are.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Spence may have some other points.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: The existing regime for reserve requirements is very hard to rationalize.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: It’s based on the monetary policy implementation of the early 1980s and very much focused on transactions deposits.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: I think that using that kind of creaky, old structure to generate a huge increase in required reserves would be a little awkward.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: And then there are the communications challenges associated with why we would be raising reserve requirements by a huge amount, even though they are being remunerated—it still might be awkward to explain.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: Spence may have some further comments.

speaker: HILTON
text: I would also point out the inflexibility to change the level and the inflexibility in terms of the scope that it provides the reserve requirement structure in banks in managing their reserve accounts.

speaker: HILTON
text: I would agree that, yes, it would work in the technical sense of giving us some leverage over short-term interest rates, but I would say that, with the authority that we have to pay interest on reserves, we could do a lot better and come up with something that’s more flexible.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Vice Chairman has a two-hander.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think another issue is, of course, that the reserve requirements wouldn’t fall precisely on those who have the excess reserves.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So you’d be creating a lot of frictional cost by doing it that way.

speaker: KOHN
text: When we had reserve requirements on nonpersonal time deposits, it was kind of a nightmare administratively—there were too many ways around it, and it was very hard to define what was inside and outside.

speaker: KOHN
text: Now, we don’t have the tax on reserves that we used to have, but I still think it would be very, very cumbersome, and I’m not sure what the advantage would be relative to just paying interest on term deposits.

speaker: FISHER
text: So the answer is no.

speaker: FISHER
text: And then a question for Brian Madigan.

speaker: FISHER
text: When we talk about an increase in the primary credit spread—and I realize you’re not recommending that currently—have you considered the effect it would have on smaller and regional banks?

speaker: FISHER
text: At least through our discount window, we see some increased activity there, and we’re just a small part of the System.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I wonder if we’ve taken that into account in that recommendation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Very much so, I would say.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m just wondering if we’ve thought about the politics of this, now when they’re a little bit sensitive about a new consumer protection agency and so on.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Well, not so much the politics, but the economics.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It’s not just the 11th District.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think there has been a fairly broad-based increase in terms of usage of primary credit by small institutions because they find the rate attractive.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The question is whether that’s a good thing or a bad thing.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think from the point of view of central banking, our general perspective in redesigning the discount window facility some years ago was to set up the primary credit program as a Lombard facility that institutions wouldn’t find attractive in routine circumstances but would turn to only as a backup.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Pricing the primary credit rate at a level that is consistent with that was one of the challenges in designing the primary credit program initially.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It surely seems to be the case that as that spread narrows, exactly as you would expect, banks increasingly tend to use that as an ongoing source of funding, and that is, I think, the consideration that needs to be balanced.

speaker: FISHER
text: At the same time, we would be maintaining the TAF, but increasing the rate so that there would more of a penalty associated with it.

speaker: FISHER
text: Did I understand that correctly?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think that is open for discussion at this point.

speaker: FISHER
text: And who are the most active users of the TAF?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It’s used by some large domestic U.S. banks as well as by foreign branches.

speaker: FISHER
text: That would be one of my concerns—the optics of having a facility, which we, at least, have seen used by foreign branches, and maintaining it even though you might make it a little bit more difficult, while at the same time phasing out something that helps smaller and regional banks.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just wonder if there isn’t a conflict there.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: My assumption is that the TAF would largely be wound down over roughly the same period of time.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Federal Reserve might ultimately choose to maintain a TAF in the steady state, but at a very low level.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It wouldn’t be a significant source of funding for large banks, foreign banks, or anybody.

speaker: FISHER
text: If I may just ask one more question, Mr. Chairman, of Brian, which is on the FX swaps.

speaker: FISHER
text: In your judgment, to what degree have the comparable ECB facilities and the IMF lending program substituted for or buttressed or deterred the effectiveness of our program?

speaker: FISHER
text: In other words, we see less demand currently.

speaker: FISHER
text: Is it because of those two facilities?

speaker: FISHER
text: Maybe your colleague to your right might have a view.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We have seen a dramatic decline in the outstandings under our swap facilities—from about $250 billion at the last meeting to about $120 billion now; and just one other historical data point is that the peak was around $580 billion in December.

speaker: SHEETS
text: My sense is that this sharp reduction really is a reflection of healing in global dollar funding markets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think the policies that have been put in place with respect to IMF lending capacity have been important in soothing nerves of investors globally, but I think that’s more for the emerging market economies than, say, European markets, where the swap lines have been so important.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, the ECB has some small swap lines with a number of European countries, but, again, I don’t see them as playing significantly into the demand for dollar funding.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The bottom line is that healing in the dollar funding markets has been the key driver there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, did you have a two-hander?

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, I was going to say that we tried increasing reserve requirements when excess reserve holdings were really large once in the late 1930s, and it didn’t turn out so well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It did sop up the excess reserves, though.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I have a question for Brian and Trish about your figure 5 on the large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It’s interesting what a straight line that is.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Over the last six months, obviously, the economic forecast has changed—interest rates have moved, financial conditions have changed—and yet our program has been invariant to all of those changes.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So my first question is whether you think that you’re restricted from being able to do anything other than a straight line program.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I thought you had more flexibility, but I want to get your sense of whether you have the flexibility currently to be able to vary the amount that you’re purchasing or not.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would say that, in talking to people in the financial community in Boston, one of the surprises was that the purchase program was invariant to the rise in interest rates that we’ve recently experienced, which certainly sent quite a message.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Did you debate whether you had the flexibility to do anything to, in effect, resist some of that increase, both in the Treasuries and the mortgage-backed securities?

speaker: SACK
text: We have interpreted the directive as having some flexibility, but it is relatively limited, in that we varied the approach that we take to purchases and the pace of purchases to respond to problems with market functioning.

speaker: SACK
text: So we do vary the purchases to ensure that markets can continue to function and that we’re not causing too much strain in the markets.

speaker: SACK
text: One concrete example of this is that the approach to agency debt purchases has moved to a somewhat more flexible one that has reduced the pace and that raises the possibility of not getting all the way to the $200 billion because of what we’ve seen in the development of the functioning of that market.

speaker: SACK
text: So we’ve taken some limited flexibility in terms of responding to how markets function.

speaker: SACK
text: I think the more difficult issue is whether to exercise any flexibility in response to changes in market interest rates—that is, beyond the reaction to market functioning, whether the Desk should respond and try to resist increases in, say, MBS rates or Treasury rates.

speaker: SACK
text: There I think our view is that we certainly don’t have enough guidance from the Committee about the extent to which that responsiveness should be implemented or the yield levels at which purchases would ramp up.

speaker: SACK
text: We have not taken a dynamic market-responsive approach in that regard, and that’s why this is one of the issues that Trish raised in her briefing, namely, whether the Committee would like to consider moving to a more flexible approach.

speaker: SACK
text: She raised the issue of doing that across asset classes, but she also raised the issue of doing that within an asset class to be more responsive to interest rates.

speaker: MOSSER
text: One follow-up remark to that: On a daily basis in implementing the MBS purchase program, particularly during the refinancing wave, we were sensitive to supply and spreads, and we would buy somewhat more on certain days and a little less on other days.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But, to be honest, that shows up as a very tiny bump in the overall pace of purchases.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As long as spreads were continuing to narrow overall, we did not make very large changes from week to week and month to month in quantities.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Even though there was some daily movement, the changes we made were small ones.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In the Treasury program, quite honestly, given its relatively small size, we didn’t feel that we had the flexibility nor that flexibility was necessarily a wise approach, since, frankly, it would not be credible, given chart 7—the size of it is just too small to have an appreciable effect on the level of yields.

speaker: MOSSER
text: When we were being flexible in agency MBS, it tended to be in response to spreads more than to the level of yields.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Vice Chairman, you had a two-hander?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the agency MBS, I think there is some notion that the rate of purchases will somehow be loosely linked to the amount of originations and the effect on spreads.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So we are a little bit ahead of schedule in terms of doing the $1.25 trillion, but that’s also because originations were very, very strong, and they’ll probably be weaker in the second half of the year.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So the purchases will probably slow down a little bit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To your point, President Rosengren, it would be really hard to accelerate purchases in response to a backup in yields, because that would then run into the conflict of having only so much authority over such-and-such a time period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I mean, talk about potentially having severe cliff effects: I’m going to buy more as rates go up?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: What happens if rates go up more?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Then I’m going to buy more, and then I’m also going to be out of ammunition.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think actually putting that in practice without the FOMC sort of dynamically altering the limits of how much the Desk could do would, I think, be very, very difficult.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Well, we could always reload.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So there is an option.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Right, but the Desk does not want to make a presumption that you’re necessarily going to reload, and it’s probably inappropriate for the Desk to make that presumption.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think it’s a pretty complicated thing to do in practice.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We do have a long tradition of leaning against the wind, and this program seems not to be very interested in leaning against the wind.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I thought you had enough flexibility to do that.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Personally I would hope that you would have the flexibility to do that and that we might do a little bit more of it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of your hybrid, I think it’s a very good proposal.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: You did note it’s a very small part of the market, and, looking at data from McDash confirms that it’s an extremely small part of the market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: That is a part of the market where, if we wanted to push rates down more aggressively, we could do so with relatively low costs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It seems that $1¼ trillion in mortgages is a lot to support market functioning.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I actually have a broader goal than market functioning, which is to get the cost of housing down for people who might want to purchase houses.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If we’re worried about market functioning in the 15- and 30-year area, it does seem that the 5- and 7-year area is one where there’s virtually no activity now; earlier this decade you could get a 7-year ARM for 4½ percent, no points, no closing costs.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We haven’t hit anything close to that in this period.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Given where the economy is, I don’t quite understand why those ARMs haven’t come down and why they’re not priced more favorably.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It may be reputational effects from the subprime market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There might be a reason to stay away from 3-year ARMs, because the “3-27” has some connotations.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The 5-year and 7-year ARMs have the advantage of being longer term while still meeting some of our balance sheet issues.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So you might want to give some thought to the politics of the choice between 3-year and 5- or 7-year.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But it would seem with the 5- or 7-year, we could lean against the wind and actually do more—we could actually try to push the rate low enough so that, if the 30-year mortgage were very high because of what was happening in the Treasuries, it would actually encourage housing purchases in that market without changing the magnitude of what you’re doing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I would like you to have a lot more flexibility to do that and possibly to push those rates down more aggressively than we’ve been willing to do with the 15- and 30-year rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let’s stay in question mode for a while, and then we’ll have an opportunity for free discussion.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have a couple of things I want to ask about.

speaker: LACKER
text: First, let me compliment the staff on providing us with a special abundance of interesting analytical reading over the weekend.

speaker: LACKER
text: Obviously a lot of work and thought went into it.

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me first check something and then ask a question.

speaker: LACKER
text: In the projections of the balance sheet, there are two scenarios, but your projections for the use of credit facilities and liquidity facilities are the same in both.

speaker: LACKER
text: Am I correct about that?

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The difference between the two is not very big, partly because the liquidity and credit facilities are starting to wind down fairly quickly now over the next year or so.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: So we didn’t see that much reason to make significantly different assumptions about them.

speaker: LACKER
text: So you made the same assumptions?

speaker: LACKER
text: I was thinking about it a different way, and I wanted to get your thoughts on this.

speaker: LACKER
text: The basic scheme here is, you write down our asset purchases, and then program by program you have a sense of what you are going to project for usage, and then you add those up, and then you subtract currency, and you get reserves, right?

speaker: LACKER
text: In the old days we did it the other way, right?

speaker: LACKER
text: We used to think that if we drained reserves, for example, that would force banks to the window to borrow.

speaker: LACKER
text: So we used to think that you would take our assets, subtract currency, and there would be a certain demand for reserves, and the residual would be met by borrowing.

speaker: LACKER
text: So you guys have turned it around.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: I would slightly prefer to think of it as that you guys have turned it around.

speaker: LACKER
text: This is the economics of the market.

speaker: LACKER
text: I mean, we’re just changing policy here, right?

speaker: LACKER
text: Let me explain why I’m thinking about it.

speaker: LACKER
text: We monitor pretty closely the institution that leads your league table for holdings, and we monitor the liquidity management function particularly closely.

speaker: LACKER
text: They have $150 billion in balances with us.

speaker: LACKER
text: They also hold a sizable portfolio—$70 or $80 billion—in general collateral Treasuries and agency MBS.

speaker: LACKER
text: They view those two as really close substitutes as liquid assets.

speaker: LACKER
text: By the way, I was a little puzzled that in one of the papers that talked about banks and lending, liquid assets never made an appearance and was sort of the residual, I guess.

speaker: LACKER
text: The institution is undergoing a review now.

speaker: LACKER
text: What we hear is that they’re thinking of reducing their Fed balance now and increasing their holdings of agency MBS and Treasuries in order to get a higher yield.

speaker: LACKER
text: That suggests a demand for reserves that’s determined by the relative yields of things.

speaker: LACKER
text: Another observation I had is that over the last couple of months, we’ve ramped up asset purchases, liquidity programs have come in below expectations, and reserve holdings seem to have been sort of flat, all of which is kind of striking and also has the flavor of this other direction that I talked about.

speaker: LACKER
text: Do you see what I’m saying?

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The logic underlying it, such as it was, was that the use of the facilities by depository institutions is by and large determined by economic and financial market conditions; that is, while financial markets are under strain, depository institutions will continue to borrow and other institutions will continue to borrow, and when things get better, they’ll borrow less.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: We’ve thought of that aspect of it as being roughly independent, and, for most cases, that seems to be borne out by the anecdotal information we get from markets.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The particular institution you’re talking about, I agree, is quite different from a lot of the other institutions.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: That bank has a very large amount of reserve balances that it owns outright in some sense.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: In addition, it’s also borrowing a reasonably large amount from the Federal Reserve.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: To me, that says that it’s choosing, as I think you characterized it accurately, its level of reserve balances as a specific target—this is how much it wants to hold, and it has some latitude to go up or down.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Our reading on the rest of the banking system—the banking system in the aggregate—is not quite that way.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The bulk of the activity in lending facilities involves not depository institutions but other institutions.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Their borrowing through the commercial paper funding facility, for example, shows up as a quantity of reserve balances, but it’s not a depository institution that has done that borrowing.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: If we wanted to get that set of reserve balances out of the banking system, there’s not a bank that would intentionally repay that borrowing to reduce their reserve holdings—it’s the CP issuer that’s doing it.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: So, in that sense, we’ve separated most of the borrowing as a response to financial market conditions and economic conditions in constructing the reserve balances.

speaker: LACKER
text: In some of these programs, like the CPFF, counterparties are outside the banking system, but in the TAF, the primary credit facility, and to some extent the foreign currency swap lines, those are all inside now.

speaker: LACKER
text: Wouldn’t you think that how much a bank wants to borrow is determined in part by how much reserves they want to hold?

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, to some extent, it’s an unfair question.

speaker: LACKER
text: We all recognize that in reality it’s a simultaneous thing—given the yields they see, they decide how much reserves to hold, and given their funding opportunities, they decide where to get the funds.

speaker: LACKER
text: But it seems plausible to me that they choose reserves, we buy assets, and that results in inflow of reserves to them; they don’t need to borrow them from anybody, they’ve got somebody else funding them essentially, and so they run off the borrowings.

speaker: LACKER
text: The reason I ask is that in the analytics you have shown us about that, you haven’t shown us anything about this link through reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: When we’ve had this big discussion for several months now about the effect of these large-scale asset purchases, it has all been sort of microeconomic, financial market by financial market.

speaker: LACKER
text: If this picture I’m drawing is right, then I wonder if there’s a channel that’s missing from your analysis.

speaker: LACKER
text: For example, for Bank of America to hold more reserves, that means they’d have to want to hold less Treasuries and MBS, which means the yields on those would have to go down.

speaker: LACKER
text: So we could be buying peanuts and Crackerjacks, and it would drive yields down.

speaker: LACKER
text: Do you see what I am saying?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: President Lacker, I think we subscribe to pretty much all of the points you’ve made, but our ability to quantify the elasticities that you’re talking about, I think, is essentially nil.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: This is a good area for research and further thought, but this is what we could do in the limited time we had available.

speaker: LACKER
text: Well, the reason I ask about this is that the focus is all supposed to be about exit strategy.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve come through SCAP, and financial market conditions seem to be on the mend.

speaker: LACKER
text: Admittedly there’s a lot of downside risk and a lot of uncertainty—is the economy going to find its footing?—but it’s also conceivable that something like the Greenbook forecast comes about later this year and we get positive growth.

speaker: LACKER
text: And it’s conceivable that banks’ ability to raise equity improves—this was left out of your analysis; you took equity as sort of an exogenous parameter.

speaker: LACKER
text: But if banks find that, because of an increase in economic growth, there are some borrowers that they are interested in lending to, they could ramp up lending and expand equity.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we continue to buy assets and their need for funding collapses, so that the borrowing through our facilities collapses, we could get to the point where they’re holding all the reserves they want.

speaker: LACKER
text: Then there’s sort of a discrete change, where we’re pushing reserves up in a way that can’t be absorbed by changes in their borrowing.

speaker: LACKER
text: So the concern I have is the possibility that our programs could get very stimulative very quickly.

speaker: LACKER
text: That’s why I’m thinking about what the effect would be if they weren’t borrowing anything but we kept pumping reserves out there by buying assets.

speaker: LACKER
text: Do you see what I am saying?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Don’t we have the ability to affect the rate at which people can borrow through the interest on excess reserves?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If that really became a problem, we would be able to affect that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If that happened, the low short-term rates would be transmitted to longer-term rates, and you would see a decline in rates across the board, which would, of course, be stimulative.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But presumably the economy doesn’t respond immediately, and we’d be able to offset that by interest rate policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: Would we want to add reserves at $100 billion a month or so and raise the interest rate on reserves at the same time?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I assume that if we came to an exit point and started raising rates, we would no longer be buying assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: All of the asset purchase programs are “up to.” They do depend on the conditions at the time.

speaker: LACKER
text: Banking is sort of sitting there with a certain amount of borrowers.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m worried about a flip back to the classic model in which we pump in reserves and they lend it, and it’s stimulative.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The other problem is that they’re still balance sheet constrained in terms of the amount of capital they have relative to their assets.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You can see that in a wide variety of areas; for example, the spread of jumbo mortgages relative to conforming mortgages is still very elevated.

speaker: LACKER
text: But presumably their ability to access equity markets is going to improve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We hope we’re successful in this regard.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Hoenig has a two-hander.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Thank you, and this is a question for you, just to clarify.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I understand where Jeff is coming from, but when I read these papers and I listen to these presentations, I think we have more than an exit strategy discussion going on here.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Eric has kind of drifted onto one discussion about managing rates.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Another is around managing the portfolio—how we adjust.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Then there is the exit strategy, which has two dimensions, but I think we are only discussing one.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The first dimension is the traditional monetary one of how you get the fed funds rate up.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The second is around large-scale asset purchases, which we’re not really talking about today, since we still have this line showing our holdings going up and the only thing is how we are going to adjust the line going up, but that is not an exit strategy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is about how we are going to manage going up that line; that is the concern, I think.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I wonder if it would help to split these up when we are talking.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I mean part of this is about managing the rate, which is different than exit strategy, and it would help clarify when we get into the discussion part of the meeting to say which one we are going to focus on first.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Right now I think we are focusing on all three intermittently here and back and forth, and I think that will cause maybe more confusion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, were you finished?

speaker: LACKER
text: I had two smaller things to ask about.

speaker: LACKER
text: One had to do with MBS spreads.

speaker: LACKER
text: This past intermeeting period is one of those episodes where convexity-related hedging, that is, selling in the Treasury market, was a widespread feature of commentary, and it has happened many times before in the last decade or so.

speaker: LACKER
text: The picture you get, and let me check this, is that there are a lot of holders of mortgage-backed securities who hold a lot of Treasuries.

speaker: LACKER
text: So they’re active in the Treasury market and they’re active in the MBS market.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is that a good picture, a fair picture?

speaker: MOSSER
text: They may have Treasury securities that they could sell.

speaker: MOSSER
text: They also have the ability to short them.

speaker: MOSSER
text: They can also do similar portfolio adjustments in the swaps market, which, through follow-on effects, through other trading mechanisms, will affect Treasury yields.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So they can pay fixed on swaps.

speaker: LACKER
text: So this is broadly speaking a set of financial market participants very active in MBS markets and very active in Treasuries as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: They would seem to have the ability to look at the spread and make decisions at the margin about buying and selling Treasuries or MBS based on their view of the proper level of the spread or where the spread is headed, right?

speaker: MOSSER
text: Well, the convexity hedging phenomenon, particularly in the current episode, was actually more concentrated in servicers and not so much in MBS investors themselves, although I’m sure there were a few of those that were selling convexity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Servicing portfolios have even more convexity than mortgages, so, dollar for dollar, it doesn’t take a big change in their duration to cause someone who is hedging to sell either a lot of swaps or a lot of Treasuries.

speaker: MOSSER
text: One reason for the speed is that there are many servicers, they have really, really similar portfolios, and they all go in on the same day or two and conduct the same sorts of trades in the same direction.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m less interested in convexity-related trading per se than the linkages between the MBS and the Treasury markets.

speaker: LACKER
text: There are a lot of players taking a position on the spread, and I’m wondering what we know that they don’t know about where the spread should be.

speaker: LACKER
text: So, analytically, on what basis would we make a judgment that the spread is too low or too high?

speaker: LACKER
text: This is history they can see, right?

speaker: MOSSER
text: But we used the long history of spreads to Treasuries to make a judgment about how narrow they were.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We also considered whether there was anyone else who was buying for investment purposes, in other words, anyone else who was willing to come in and actually purchase them to hold besides us.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If we were the only long-term purchaser, we took that as a signal that we had lowered spreads to the point that they were not attractive to other investors.

speaker: MOSSER
text: That was the place that we were before the convexity hedging episode, and it’s one of the reasons that we were already beginning to slow down.

speaker: LACKER
text: A related question: One of the memos was pretty eloquent about the need for greater clarity and better communication about our strategy.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is there any chance that providing the Desk with more flexibility about the composition of our asset purchases could diminish rather than enhance market understanding of our strategy?

speaker: MOSSER
text: I believe that flexibility could be a very successful strategy, but it would need substantially more clarity about the Committee’s views and literally its reaction function, for lack of a better term, which may be very difficult to do, given how far out we are in uncharted territory.

speaker: LACKER
text: One final question about the interest rate on reserves and the reserve management tools: Does the staff think it’s at all likely that the effective funds rate would not be brought up pretty much in tandem if we raised the interest rate on reserves under current arrangements?

speaker: CLOUSE
text: I think there’s an excellent chance that it would rise.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: We just don’t know whether it would go up by an 80 percent factor or a 90 percent factor—that remains to be seen.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: So I think it’s very prudent to examine all of these other tools.

speaker: CLOUSE
text: We just really are in uncharted territory, especially with hundreds of billions of dollars in reserve balances outstanding.

speaker: LACKER
text: Have you thought about whether we care about the federal funds rate per se, that is, if the interest rate on reserves is more relevant than the weighted average you calculate every day?

speaker: HILTON
text: I think it’s a good question.

speaker: HILTON
text: What does the rate represent?

speaker: HILTON
text: What does the gap represent?

speaker: HILTON
text: Does it represent a rent that banks are extracting, or does it represent their own spread aligned with their borrowing rates and their lending rates?

speaker: HILTON
text: I think that’s a legitimate question, and in my mind it’s an open one.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The experience last fall, though, gives you some reason to think that the fed funds rate is relevant.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The fact that the substantial spread between the interest rate on excess reserves and the fed funds rate seems to be reflected in other market interest rates like LIBOR, CP, and so on, suggests that it’s not solely the IOER rate that’s the relevant margin.

speaker: KOHN
text: I have a couple of questions.

speaker: KOHN
text: On this strategy for dealing with the large-scale asset purchases, what are other central banks doing?

speaker: KOHN
text: I notice the Bank of Japan is doing just a certain amount per month.

speaker: KOHN
text: And the Bank of England just did what we did—they announced a total.

speaker: KOHN
text: But are they varying within that total?

speaker: KOHN
text: Are they exercising flexibility or is the process pretty mechanical?

speaker: KOHN
text: Are there any lessons for us from what they’re doing?

speaker: MOSSER
text: It’s our understanding that it’s fairly mechanical.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Now, a couple of times the Bank of England has bought so much that they were afraid that they were reducing liquidity in the market, and they have slowed down again from a market functioning standpoint.

speaker: KOHN
text: Sort of like what we have done with the MBS.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But they absolutely are much more focused on a reserves or a money target than the SOMA purchases have been.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Bank of England has moved at a pretty regular pace of about £25 billion a month.

speaker: SHEETS
text: One place where I think they do have a little bit of flexibility that they have chosen not to utilize is in the composition of the purchases; they have the gilts approved, but they could also buy corporates and commercial paper, yet the vast majority of their purchases have been in the gilts.

speaker: KOHN
text: Other central banks have found it difficult, as have we, to specify the reaction function, I suspect.

speaker: KOHN
text: Brian, you mentioned that Treasury supply is driving up Treasury rates, but my impression is there has been no news on Treasury supply.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s a very common thing to hear, but I wondered.

speaker: SACK
text: I think for this intermeeting period, most estimates of borrowing needs of the Treasury didn’t rise.

speaker: SACK
text: So I would say that’s more of a “backdrop” condition, not the main driver of the rising yields over this intermeeting period.

speaker: SACK
text: But it’s certainly a very important factor over a broader time period.

speaker: KOHN
text: And finally for Seth, are there any consequences of not covering our expenses?

speaker: KOHN
text: Do we continue to pay salaries?

speaker: KOHN
text: For the Governors we can do that out of spare change—the vending machine receipts will pay the Governors’ salaries—but what about for the rest of you?

speaker: SACK
text: If you’re going to go down that road, you should make the salaries responsive to the upside as well.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: That sounds like a profit-sharing plan for the Fed employees.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The accounting treatment is that once there’s no net income after paying dividends and that sort of thing, we stop remitting money to the Treasury.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: What happens if we can’t even make the dividend payments to the member banks?

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The Reserve Banks would not pay their dividends to the member banks, but they would have to make that up in subsequent years.

speaker: KOHN
text: Are they forced not to pay dividends, or is that a choice?

speaker: CARPENTER
text: My recollection is that it’s a choice, and part of it comes from Board direction to the Reserve Banks.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Then the question becomes how long this goes on; it ends up accumulating through time, and then in subsequent years it just takes that much longer before we start getting back to normal.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: We have to save up earnings.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The accounting for it is still being evaluated.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: There’s some view that some of the remittances that have already been paid to the Treasury could be recouped by booking an asset that’s essentially a prepayment, and then that might be able to be pushed back an extra year; the accountants in the System are working on the actual treatment of that.

speaker: KOHN
text: If we get into this situation, there’s nothing mechanical about it that would impinge on our independence?

speaker: KOHN
text: We could continue to meet our responsibilities?

speaker: KOHN
text: President Bullard and I were at a conference where a lot of academics were worried, I think, that if we didn’t meet our expenses, something awful would happen.

speaker: KOHN
text: Something awful may happen, but--

speaker: BULLARD
text: Just to follow up on that, are there examples of foreign central banks that have been in a position like this?

speaker: SHEETS
text: There have been a number, I think, that have had to turn to their treasuries to be recapitalized.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I don’t have a lot of details about those experiences at my fingertips, but it’s something that has happened before, and there are some precedents we could look into.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My sense of this, then, is that you are at the mercy of the Treasury.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If they’re merciful, then they recapitalize you.

speaker: KOHN
text: What I was getting at was that I didn’t think you were at the mercy of the Treasury, but rather that it was our choice.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s not the foreign experience.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, the dividends are one buffer.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Beyond the dividends, presumably, and the capital, then you would be at the mercy, I would imagine.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I don’t think that’s clear.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I mean, there’s nothing that says necessarily that a central bank can’t operate with negative capital.

speaker: SHEETS
text: And I would bet that we could also find some examples of foreign central banks that did have negative capital.

speaker: SHEETS
text: You know, it can be a little uncomfortable.

speaker: SHEETS
text: For the cases that I can think of, they have eventually gone to their treasuries to seek recapitalization, but I think there’s a range of experiences out there with this that we can look at.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There’s nothing that says they can’t operate, but do you think the political environment is such that something dramatic might happen in response to that, given what has gone on in this episode?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would think that would be the bigger risk, not the accounting treatment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is not going to happen in the intermeeting period.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The issue from my perspective is that it’s political.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In other words, the day that you find out that you’re no longer remitting positive balances to the Treasury, there’s a nice, juicy news story, and then they go evaluate: Why did this come about?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Because the Fed engaged in these large-scale asset programs and because of asset–liability mismatch.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Was that prudent for the Federal Reserve to do?

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Just to clarify a bit, what we sidestepped in the analysis was the fact that the remittances are actually made currently by individual Reserve Banks, and it is very, very common for an individual Reserve Bank not to have sufficient capital to equate with surplus and to make a remittance to the Treasury.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Over the past decade or so, it’s been something like 40 weeks per year that at least one Reserve Bank hasn’t made a remittance to the Treasury.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: So it’s not as though this is something that is completely unprecedented for the Federal Reserve.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: What would be very different here is that it would happen for the Federal Reserve System as a whole.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Evans, do you have a two-hander on this?

speaker: EVANS
text: Well, I had a question that was related to Governor Kohn’s question on this.

speaker: EVANS
text: Do we have a particular attitude towards mark-to-market losses, that is, capital losses, versus having our net income go to zero?

speaker: EVANS
text: That was one of the more striking graphs, a very extreme example.

speaker: EVANS
text: I would have thought that there would be an accounting entry that would allow us to continue to fund whatever we needed to do, but the political issue seems to be an important one.

speaker: EVANS
text: It would be well known along the way, so that people would see it coming, but some of these tools would involve capital losses right away.

speaker: EVANS
text: Would that raise a similar red flag in terms of our balance sheet?

speaker: EVANS
text: Would we be worried about that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it’s a consideration.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First of all, you wouldn’t want to be selling huge amounts.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Second, you probably could mix different assets of different vintages and do things of that sort.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I think it is a consideration that we should pay attention to.

speaker: EVANS
text: My question was really: Do any of the reserve management tools have better attributes than others?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most of them—like reverse repurchases, things that don’t involve actually selling the assets, but rather involve financing them in different ways—don’t have the capital loss component.

speaker: EVANS
text: We will lose money on them, though, right?

speaker: EVANS
text: Because presumably the interest rate we have to pay on the repo is going to be higher than the income that it’s earning.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If it gets to 8 percent, then we’re in a loss position.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Kohn, were you finished?

speaker: STERN
text: I’ve got a couple of questions.

speaker: STERN
text: The first one is on the exit strategy, and the second one is a little more tangential.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to the expiration dates for these liquidity facilities, if we extend them to February 1, 2010, what kind of commitment and communication are you thinking about so that they actually do end then?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There would be a press release Thursday, which we’ve been working on, and we can show you a draft.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Here are the proposed final sentences of the introduction: “The Board and the FOMC will continue to monitor closely the condition of financial markets and the need for and effectiveness of the Federal Reserve’s special liquidity facilities and arrangements.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Should the recent improvements in market conditions continue, the Board and the FOMC currently anticipate that a number of these facilities may not need to be extended beyond February 1.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, if financial stresses do not moderate as expected, the Board and the FOMC are prepared to extend the terms of some or all of the facilities as needed to promote financial stability and economic growth.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The public will receive timely notice of planned extensions, discontinuations, or modifications of Federal Reserve programs.” That’s the kind of language that we were trying to communicate—not too definitive, but clearly raising the possibility there won’t be any further renewals.

speaker: STERN
text: The second question is about the TALF and the quantities.

speaker: STERN
text: I gather we now think TALF volumes might go to $175 billion whereas heretofore we were up around $500 billion, and I think earlier we even had a larger number.

speaker: STERN
text: Is all of that consistent with the objectives of this program?

speaker: STERN
text: Where is this coming from?

speaker: NELSON
text: I think partly it’s experience as we work with the program.

speaker: NELSON
text: It’s an awareness that as ABS markets improve, we’re not going to need as much TALF activity to support them.

speaker: NELSON
text: It’s becoming consistent with what we’re seeing in CMBS markets.

speaker: NELSON
text: Right now the numbers we’re putting down for TALF 2.0 peak at $50 billion, which is about what we think is going to be needed for CMBS, and with TALF 1.0 it’s—I forget the numbers that we actually put down—but it’s a more modest $125 billion, which is where we see activity at its current pace ending in the first quarter.

speaker: NELSON
text: So it’s consistent with the policy objectives.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Just quickly, I want to go back to Governor Kohn’s original question on the accounting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In this document there is a discussion about investments held in consolidated variable-interest entities, with a conservative assumption that we could take a $5 billion hit and then no more losses after that, even if interest rates went up pretty significantly.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Is that a conservative assumption?

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is, if interest rates went up significantly, wouldn’t you expect more losses out of that?

speaker: CARPENTER
text: It has been the stated policy that it’s expected that these assets will be managed through time to recover everything, so in that sense the official view is that there will be no losses.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Given that, the estimate is conservative—it’s taking on more losses than was originally expected by the policy itself.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: The other part that’s not obvious to me is the effect if, for example, interest rates rose.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: If that increasing rate was because the economy as a whole was getting better and financial markets were healing and everyone thought the outlook was very, very rosy, then the underlying value of some of those assets may no longer be distressed.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Some of the write-downs are because of the strains in financial markets.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: You could imagine cases where some of those assets increase in value because the economy is turning around and the outlook is brighter, and it’s exactly those sorts of multivalent influences that caused us to throw up our hands somewhat and take the coward’s way out.

speaker: HOENIG
text: The second question is also related to the earlier discussion.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In some of the accounting that I’ve seen and what I believe I saw discussed in here was the establishment of a prepaid account to the Treasury to go back and, therefore, bring your surplus up so you could continue to pay your dividends and so forth.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Are those only allowed under special circumstances, or would those be allowed in any kind of a loss circumstance, so they would enable us to continue to pay dividends?

speaker: CARPENTER
text: Right now what’s envisioned is the case where losses were sufficiently large that capital would go negative.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: What has been written into Reserve Bank accounting policy is the ability to create a prepaid asset for things that have happened year to date.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: They are currently working on ways of going back not just year to date, but the prior year as well, so that would be used in the event of losses where you wouldn’t have enough retained earnings to equate surplus with capital paid in.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That would address part of Governor Kohn’s concerns about continuing to pay for operating expenses and continuing to pay dividends.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have a few questions.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Some of them have been touched on already, but let me just see if I can get some clarifications.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One question is for Brian, and it’s related to your conversation with Eric about SOMA lending of agency debt and the liquidity in the market.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: You said that one of your reactions so far has been that you have kind of slowed down the purchases.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, if you’re worried about the liquidity of that market and we’re soaking up all of the liquidity, what’s wrong with another option, namely, to stop buying?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Why create a program where we’re buying them and lending them back out again?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Why not just not buy them in the first place and let the liquidity of the market deepen as we move forward?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is there something wrong with that strategy?

speaker: SACK
text: Well, I think it’s quite possible that we will exercise the “up to” part of the mandate regardless of whether we’re lending the agency securities or not.

speaker: SACK
text: I think the desire to lend the agency securities is in response to concerns about market function, which would be there whether the program ended at $100 billion or $150 billion or $200 billion.

speaker: SACK
text: In either case, SOMA holdings are going to be a sizable portion of the benchmark GSE market, and, as I said, we’re already hearing reports from the market about concerns about shorting and not enough floating supply of these issues.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That’s because we are buying them, right?

speaker: SACK
text: That’s because we are buying them, right.

speaker: SACK
text: It’s a matter of degree.

speaker: SACK
text: If you don’t get to $200 billion, you lessen the problem, but I think we would pursue the authority to lend our agency holdings regardless of whether we thought the program was going to end before $200 billion or get all the way to $200 billion.

speaker: SACK
text: We’re already seeing these strains.

speaker: SACK
text: We think making these holdings available to the market makes sense in terms of supporting market functioning, treating these assets the way we treat other SOMA holdings, and, as I said, posing little risk to the Federal Reserve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is about making sure that you can deliver a specific issue.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It doesn’t affect reserves or the stance of monetary policy, I don’t think.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: No, I was thinking purely in terms of the liquidity of the market, which I thought you were concerned about.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we are heavily into buying in these markets and taking those assets out of the market, and there are some liquidity problems for some of these issues, then all we’re doing is turning around and lending them back out again to help liquidity.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It seems like we’re giving with one hand and taking away with the other.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m just trying to understand a little bit about it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: You might not know ex ante which things are going to have liquidity issues in the future.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m not necessarily opposed to the program.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Having a lending program allows you to accommodate those shortages that might occur ex post.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the winding down of some of the liquidity procedures, there are some specific recommendations that are made about the TAF auctions and some others about mixtures of extending the dates, cutting back auction sizes, and/or changing prices in some form.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m curious about how the staff thinks about the right mixture of controlling prices versus quantities, the tradeoffs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I mean, October is still what, five months away.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In thinking about when is the right time if we thought we wanted to extend, how much in advance do we need to do that?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is there an option of continuing to sort of just proceed with gradually ramping up prices or costs of these programs to encourage the users to wean themselves off of this and go back to the market?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Then we would not make the decision to extend maybe for—I don’t know—a little longer or wait a little while to see whether or not we can wean these players off and into the market.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So thinking about the mix of both price and quantity controls, I guess I was looking for some insight as to how do you pick between those two and the tradeoff versus extensions or not.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think it is, unfortunately, a fairly complicated situation, so it’s difficult to give a simple answer to your question.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For one thing, we have both standing facilities and auction facilities, and they’re really very different in terms of their philosophy and what you might think their purpose is and how to unwind them.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: An auction facility, pretty much by construction, can be unwound primarily just by reducing the amounts offered, whereas to make a standing facility less attractive, obviously you’d increase the interest rates or otherwise make the terms less attractive.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: To some degree what we’ve proposed here has included elements of both of those—for instance, making the terms less attractive in the case of the AMLF by requiring the redemption threshold, and reducing the auction amounts in the case of the TAF.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: They’re just two very different facilities that require different approaches.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As we noted in the memo, it’s not really feasible to scale back the AMLF by raising the interest rate on that particular program.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On the timing, that’s a difficult question.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I think one consideration is that, as we get closer to the termination dates of programs, market participants will be deciding whether or not to lend to particular counterparties, depending on whether that counterparty is going to have the option of turning to the Federal Reserve to repay the investor or the lender.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That argues at least for a significant lead time in notifying the market as to when these facilities are likely to go away.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: What I was thinking about was the pace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Take the TAF, for example— the recommendation is to cut from $150 billion to $125 billion, and maybe or maybe not to raise the minimum bid rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Why don’t we cut to $100 billion immediately?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s undersubscribed by a substantial amount.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Why not move the minimum bid to something closer to the interest rate on excess reserves rather than making it so far below it that we’re subsidizing, at least in the current environment.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We’re sort of mixing those two things up, trying to figure out what the right balance and strategy are, or how aggressive one wants to be in this process.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: It is very much a matter of judgment, I think, including how aggressive you think is appropriate at this point, given circumstances that arguably remain very fragile, with the banking system still under a lot of strain.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Well, I worry particularly about the TAF—it’s so dominated by a couple of banks, and I don’t want to confuse supporting a couple of banks with the broader purpose of sort of what these bank programs might be doing.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I wanted to make a couple of other points—and Jeff made both of these in a different form.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: One is the communication issue.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If you provide more flexibility to the Desk to do some of this stuff, communication is going to be really, really, really difficult, and we may be accused of being less transparent rather than more transparent about that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I think that’s going to be a very tough task.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The other point is on the interest on excess reserves.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s certainly true that there’s a possibility that as the markets and the economy begin to recover, we’ll have a lot of excess reserves sitting out there.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And the opportunity cost to banks may be, “Okay, when can I make a good business loan at 8 percent or 7 percent?” And they view the risk tradeoffs for that as the right ones.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We may be faced with a situation, even if we thought interest on excess reserves worked perfectly, where we would have to raise the IOER very aggressively to choke off that massive amount of liquidity that may be just sort of running out into the marketplace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If interest on excess reserves isn’t working as we’d like to see it work, then we are going to have to combine that with some other mechanism for draining those excess reserves.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The question is: What’s the relevant interest rate that’s going to guide us in some of those moves?

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And I think that’s very difficult to sort out, even with the tremendous job the staff has done—there’s a lot of forest and a lot of weeds here in trying to sort through the details.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I do think it’s important that we try to make sure that if Plan A doesn’t work, we have a Plan B.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That is, we need to make sure that if IOER doesn’t work as we hoped it would, we have other mechanisms to drain the reserves.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But we may have to do that at a very rapid pace, which may mean some of these mechanisms that you suggest may operate more quickly and are more easily implemented than others, and that might be a consideration that we have to think about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Plosser, I think there are two mechanisms that prevent this thing that you’re worried about from happening overnight.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t think overnight, but it may be a period of months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first one is that, assuming that we have the power to raise interest rates, which is what this whole discussion is about, then rates on longer-term securities will reflect the expected path of future policy rates and, therefore, will not go to zero.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So to the extent that there’s an expectation over the next three years the Fed will be raising rates at a reasonable pace, that will limit the amount that the supply price of credit can fall.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And then, the second point is, of course, that, although financial markets move quickly, all of our models tell us that the economy itself moves somewhat more slowly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: With a large output gap, it’s going to take some time certainly for the economy to reach its full potential.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I understand all of the issues with the output gap, and so on, but I don’t want to leave the impression that this is something that’s going to require a turnaround within a matter of weeks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I just don’t think that’s a real concern.

speaker: EVANS
text: First, I’d like to compliment everyone on the new audio system, although it picks up the Blackberry noise pretty well, too.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the reserve management tools, I’ve read your speeches and heard you describe them with quite a lot of energy.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’re looking at quite a number of tools, and yet I wonder how different they are in terms of their ability to achieve what we want.

speaker: EVANS
text: What I have in mind is that the interest on reserves tool by itself—especially with the elements that are designed to help the GSEs somehow earn interest on their reserves—seems powerful enough, so that that should work.

speaker: EVANS
text: But what if, for some reason, it doesn’t work?

speaker: EVANS
text: Maybe somebody could describe the elements of the other markets that we’re expecting to take advantage of that somehow would provide an independent channel that would help out.

speaker: EVANS
text: For example, would the reverse repo market really work very well in an environment where the banks seem not to be arbitraging the interest on reserves?

speaker: HILTON
text: If we are seeing a gap between the rate that banks are earning on excess reserves and what they are paying, I think that I would approach that situation as really an arbitrage opportunity for us.

speaker: HILTON
text: If we’re talking about reverse repos as the tool, as long as we have the collateral and we can basically get to those depositors directly or even indirectly, then that would be the mechanism that we would use to grow the reverse repo market.

speaker: HILTON
text: But in contemplating the potential scale for the operations, I don’t think we should believe that we are necessarily limited by measures we currently have of the size of that market.

speaker: HILTON
text: Rather, it’s a matter of how many reserves we want to drain and who it is that is earning a rate from the banks that’s well below the interest on excess reserves and therefore would be interested in lending to us at a slightly higher rate.

speaker: HILTON
text: So that’s how we would simultaneously lift rates and manage down the size of the banks’ balance sheets, that is, bring down excess reserves and some of their liabilities.

speaker: EVANS
text: As I was thinking about this, it seemed that one attractive feature is that the money market mutual funds would be potential customers here.

speaker: HILTON
text: We have thought of them.

speaker: HILTON
text: We haven’t approached them about it.

speaker: HILTON
text: But in terms of thinking of a pool of liquidity, that might fit the kind of description I provided, yes.

speaker: EVANS
text: So there’s no obvious reason to think that, when the banks are not taking up these arbitrage opportunities, there’s some underlying feature that also would make the money market mutual funds somehow reluctant?

speaker: EVANS
text: Well, they’re not designed to.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’m just trying to think in terms of the risks that we might face.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: One extra bit of data that might help with that specific question is that, even in the past couple of days, and in the past months, when the effective federal funds rate has been right at the top of the zero to 25 basis point band—or we would just say right up against the rate on excess—it has been associated with the repo rate being above the excess rate, that is, at 27, 28, 29 basis points.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: And we’ve been hearing that that has been causing some of this shifting of funds that might have been lent unsecured into the secured funding markets.

speaker: CARPENTER
text: So I think that is very much in line with Spence’s point about the repo market being a way for us to take care of some of that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I just wanted to see if I have this right about exit strategies.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And I have to say Brian Madigan’s memo here on liquidity facilities is a masterpiece of clarity, so thank you for that, Brian.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s super clear what we’re going to do and what we’re thinking about with each program, why we’re thinking about it, why we’re thinking of the different options.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And when I look at large-scale asset purchases, it’s much less about exiting, and maybe it’s a little bit about coping.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But I expected to see more about what we could do if we wanted to reduce our holdings, and all I see is that we’re going to have to sell.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So my question for Trish is this: Is the bottom line that the plan is basically buy and hold?

speaker: BULLARD
text: In other words, when we’re buying now, we’re basically committing to a very large balance sheet for a very long period of time, and then the other stuff is all a question mark about what that means in terms of macroeconomics, that is, whether it’s worrisome or dangerous or not.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But as far as the balance sheet itself, it’s ramping up, and we don’t see good ways to mitigate that.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I have two responses—at least two.

speaker: MOSSER
text: The first is that certainly “buy and hold” has been the staff’s maintained hypothesis when we do Seth’s pictures of the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: MOSSER
text: And if we’re going to be reducing excess reserves in the future, while we could do it through selling, probably our first step—and I think this would be the staff’s bias—would be to use the reverse repo market in order to manage to a higher federal funds rate.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So that’s my first response—as a baseline, probably yes.

speaker: MOSSER
text: However, there are a couple of caveats to that.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It does very much depend on how the Committee wants to react to whatever the macro and financial conditions are at the time we are exiting.

speaker: MOSSER
text: One can imagine a scenario, the really high-inflation scenario that Seth played out, where the Committee might very much want to tighten financial conditions in the broad economy very quickly.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Selling a really large quantity of assets very quickly would probably achieve that for you, no matter how we manage the short-term interest rate.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So I think it’s very dependent on the Committee’s views at the time that exit comes around.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It’s possible to do, but the question is: Will that be what the Committee wants to do, both with the size of the balance sheet and in terms of influencing financial conditions?

speaker: BULLARD
text: If you get into a high-inflation environment, it’s too late.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We’ve already failed at that point.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I can believe at that point you might want to take more radical action, but the idea is to get this optimal path.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We have been purchasing these securities on the upside very quickly, with the intent of influencing private credit rates.

speaker: MOSSER
text: On the exit side, at the point we would decide to sell, we have been going with the assumption that we would exit much more slowly in the optimal case.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We would sell very slowly and in small quantities—this is not built into Seth’s baseline, but we could do this—in the way that we have been purchasing Treasury securities for decades, which is to buy regularly, in tiny amounts, being as market-neutral as humanly possible.

speaker: MOSSER
text: That can be achieved, but that’s a slow unwinding.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It’s faster than what’s built into Seth’s pictures, but it’s quite small.

speaker: MOSSER
text: A big year would be $50 billion or $70 billion on the purchase side, on the upside, in the old days.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So we would assume that size on the downside.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So it’s not a rapid way to bring down the balance sheet.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Earlier this spring we were thinking of having Fed bills or a Treasury program that would mitigate this problem.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But those are now politically off the table.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Is it correct to think that now that they’re off the table we have basically committed to a large balance sheet?

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s the way I read these memos.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They wouldn’t affect the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They’re just alternative ways of financing, which is what we are talking about.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Fed bills, or doing reverse repos for that matter, wouldn’t shrink the balance sheet, they would simply shrink reserves; that is, they would affect the liability side of our balance sheet, but not the asset side—the assets would still be just as big.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have a very brief intervention, because it’s related exactly to this point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Brian, a little earlier when I asked you the question about agency debt, you said that you presumed we were going to go to the limit on that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Is it the expectation of the Desk and the markets that the operative words of “up to” certain amounts in our policy statements are basically irrelevant, and that, in fact, we’re viewed as committed to going to those amounts and we wouldn’t consider doing less?

speaker: SACK
text: Actually, what I said before was that the Desk may exercise the “up to” part of the directive.

speaker: SACK
text: And what I meant by that is that we may not get to the entire $200 billion on account of these concerns.

speaker: SACK
text: Now, the question is: What does the market expect?

speaker: SACK
text: We actually changed our procedures for accepting tenders on agency debt in a way that we think is going to taper off the pace and perhaps leave us short.

speaker: SACK
text: I would say this hasn’t garnered a ton of market attention.

speaker: SACK
text: There may be a period during which they have to learn and adjust to that, or it may just not be that big of a deal.

speaker: SACK
text: So I think the markets understand we have some flexibility.

speaker: SACK
text: They haven’t reached a definitive conclusion that the SOMA holdings may fall well short of $200 billion.

speaker: SACK
text: But presumably over the next several months there will be increasing inference in that direction, if things evolve the way we expect.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Do you think the same is true for the MBS and Treasuries?

speaker: SACK
text: I think the purchases of the Treasuries have been regular and steady and nonresponsive to market conditions, and that’s very well understood at this point in the markets.

speaker: SACK
text: For MBS, I think what happened is that, over this intermeeting period, the markets learned that the Desk was less responsive than they anticipated.

speaker: SACK
text: The current MBS secondary rates reflect that understanding.

speaker: SACK
text: It’s just that the adjustment of how they got there was perhaps lumpier because of that learning.

speaker: SACK
text: I think the secondary MBS rates stayed lower for longer, because there was this assumption about more Desk responsiveness, and they then had to adjust up more abruptly.

speaker: SACK
text: But on net, it’s at a point where the markets seem to understand that the Desk is exercising only limited discretion in terms of making those purchases.

speaker: MOSSER
text: One comment: On the primary dealer survey that we do before every meeting, we did ask this question about probabilities of increasing versus decreasing.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We didn’t really ask the “up to” part, we just asked whether the sizes might be decreased.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In all three categories, there was some weight put on decreasing the size of the programs.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If I’m recalling the numbers correctly, it was smallest for the Treasury program, but that’s partly because it’s scheduled to end in September, and it’s closer to being done.

speaker: MOSSER
text: But there is some weight being put on decreases in size, meaning not getting all the way.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: To continue the grilling of Brian and Trish, my interpretation in sort of street terms of what you said earlier is that the directive has been a problem for the Desk for last few weeks.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: And we’re in somewhat extraordinary times where you may have been uncomfortable—I’m putting words in your mouth—that you were making policy as opposed to interpreting the wishes of the Committee.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Can you be more explicit about what you’d like to see in a directive that would work, and yet at the same time deal with the external communication sensitivities?

speaker: MOSSER
text: I’ll take a stab at that one.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t know that it is so much that we didn’t have a sense of what the Committee wanted, although there were times when perhaps we didn’t have perfect clarity, but rather it’s that I don’t think the public and the markets always understood.

speaker: MOSSER
text: For example, there was discussion in the market that the Treasury purchase program was going to be immediately expanded in the middle of May—in an intermeeting period—and extended and enlarged substantially as Treasury rates continued to rise.

speaker: MOSSER
text: In fact, this was a shockingly widely held opinion, despite the Chairman’s public statements that were close to being to the contrary.

speaker: MOSSER
