text: So, on the communication issue, everyone understands that these are very unusual programs, but it would be good to clarify what your expectations are in terms of the direction of what the programs are likely or not likely to do.

speaker: MOSSER
text: For the Treasury purchase program, in particular, there’s a bit less clarity.

speaker: MOSSER
text: For the MBS program and the agency program, the markets have now figured out that, up to a point, narrowing spreads was the goal.

speaker: MOSSER
text: As for going further than that, the Desk is likely to step back and say, “We’re not going to become the 100 percent only investor.” But they learned that by watching what we were doing as opposed to getting a communication from the Committee.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If your preference is “steady as she goes” through the end of the programs, subject to the caveat that if conditions improve the Committee may use the “up to” option, then that would help as sort of a basic starting point.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Beyond that, it depends on what the Committee’s true views are about the ultimate goals of the programs and whether they should be enlarged or kept the same size.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I can build on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Could you imagine language like, “…will respond to market conditions, spreads, and the pace of issuance,” or something like that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would you recommend something like that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would you propose something like that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If so, you need to think about that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is that what you had in mind, President Lockhart?

speaker: MOSSER
text: If the Committee is comfortable with the option that I spoke about in my presentation for flexibility within asset classes and agrees with our assessment that, subject to this sort of communication, it would be useful, then that would be the right kind of clarifying statement.

speaker: SACK
text: I would say that, if the Committee is comfortable with the degree of flexibility that the Desk has been exercising, then I would leave it alone, in terms of public communications at least.

speaker: SACK
text: To the extent that you start to change the directive, it’s going to involve a lot of guessing about what has changed and what’s going to happen now.

speaker: SACK
text: I think the market has gone through a learning process that may have caused some abrupt movements here and there, but it has gotten to a point where it pretty much understands that the general approach is slow and steady, with some flexibility around that in response to market functioning.

speaker: SACK
text: And if that’s what the Committee is comfortable with, we’re at a point where we don’t need any kind of public clarification.

speaker: SACK
text: If the Committee wanted the Desk to be more responsive to market interest rates, then that would require some kind of communication to the market, so that they didn’t have to infer it over time just from our actions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think many of us on the Committee would be looking to you to tell us if you think there’s a strategy that, for a given amount of purchases, would achieve better results, and, if so, what that is and how you would recommend communicating about it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we have to rely on your market knowledge to do that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if you do believe that’s the case, perhaps for the next meeting or before then, you could present us with some alternatives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But if you think where we are now is fine, that’s good, too.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But let’s not fail to take advantage of some improved operating process, if it gives us better results.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Assuming the “up to” sizes stay where they are, I think I agree completely with Brian, particularly regarding the Treasury program, where we simply don’t think anything other than “slow and steady” is probably the appropriate implementation strategy given its current size and its current expiration date.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We are already, frankly, moving in the direction of more flexibility, as Brian described, on the agency debt program, and we’ll continue to move that way, assuming that the spreads don’t widen and we don’t get dislocations in the opposite direction.

speaker: MOSSER
text: If flexibility is going to be useful, it would be in the MBS program, and, obviously, we’d be happy to write down a couple of alternatives for the next meeting.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It might help clarify the language.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Another alternative may just be to clarify in the Humphrey-Hawkins report, rather than coming up with a whole new vehicle.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It could just provide a bit more language about what the intent of the programs is and about our thought processes.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: From my perspective, the statement and the minutes are not great vehicles for communicating about this.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But if we’re departing from what we’ve been doing, we want the Committee to—

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’m assuming that we’re going to stay on the same path.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I still think it would be useful to have something in the Humphrey-Hawkins report that explains what this is.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And then, if we depart, I agree, I think we’d have a different directive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, did you have a comment?

speaker: LACKER
text: I think you are right, Mr. Chairman, to ask the Desk for their suggestions as to language that would help them achieve the results we desire.

speaker: LACKER
text: A corollary to that is that they understand the results we desire.

speaker: LACKER
text: My interpretation of what we decided when we embarked on this was to achieve whatever improvement in MBS yields would result from the quantity we sketched out, not to peg yields at a given level, not to dampen fluctuations in yields, not to reduce the dispersion of future yield outcomes, and not to respond in the way the markets seem to expect us to respond.

speaker: LACKER
text: We didn’t put that in the directive, obviously, and we didn’t put that in the statement either.

speaker: LACKER
text: In preparing for this meeting, I looked at the statements and read them from the perspective of the intermeeting period, and it strikes me that there are things in the statements that markets could have latched onto that led them to misinterpret what results we desired to achieve.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that’s useful to keep in mind.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s fair enough, but there may even be technical issues, like not wanting to be the only buyer, and things of that sort, that we would want to communicate.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Mr. Chairman, really a question for you, not for this side of the table.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The Treasury proposed that it would have the last call in approving 13(3) authorizations.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Have we developed a view on that and communicated that in any way?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As I mentioned, I would like to defer that to lunch tomorrow, but I will present all of these issues and tell you about the report and the other aspects that we’ll start undertaking, and then cover it at that time.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I thought someone might ask this, which is why I didn’t get in the queue.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Brian, what kind of reaction do you expect from markets and economic commentators to the press release the Chairman is working on?

speaker: TARULLO
text: He read us part of the draft on the modifications to the various liquidity facilities.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Specifically, do you think there’s much of a chance that it will be read as, if not the beginning of tightening, the lifting up of the screwdriver and placing it against the screw?

speaker: TARULLO
text: I’d also be interested in what Brian Sack and Trish think about that.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: First of all, it is complicated, and I think it will take a while for people to understand all of the elements, assuming the Board and the FOMC follow the staff recommendation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A second point, though, is that it will be read very much in the context of the announcement tomorrow and what that says about your intentions with respect to the federal funds rate, the asset purchases, and so on.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In some sense that will really very much condition the reaction, because, among other things, that will give the economic backdrop, the rationale, for how the Committee is approaching monetary policy at this stage.

speaker: SACK
text: I would add that without the sentences that the Chairman read, it’s a somewhat mixed release.

speaker: SACK
text: At least one program is being scaled down, but others are being extended, so the direction is not really clear.

speaker: SACK
text: I think the focal point of the markets would be the sentences that were read about the extended date being the expected terminal date, and I do think there’s some risk that that will be seen as the first step—as you said, “lifting the screwdriver.” So it is a risk.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I would agree with that.

speaker: MOSSER
text: It is a small risk.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Because of this renewal, the swap partners are aware of at least that portion of the press release, although not of the rest of the liquidity facilities, obviously.

speaker: MOSSER
text: We informed them that some language along the lines of what the Chairman read would likely be in the press release.

speaker: MOSSER
text: Their reaction in a number of cases was: “Oh, well, we’re not going to put anything like that in our press release,” and a couple of them were outright concerned about it.

speaker: MOSSER
text: So there was a dispersion—some thought it was fine, and others not.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I would agree with Brian—I think there is a risk.

speaker: MOSSER
text: I don’t know that it’s large, but there is a small risk that it would be viewed as a bit of tightening.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I presume that, if you had thought of this, you would have already suggested it, but does anything come to mind that would allow us to mitigate that risk?

speaker: MOSSER
text: The last sentence that was added to the press release, which says the Board and the Committee would also consider expanding if things get worse, helps to mitigate that risk quite a bit.

speaker: SACK
text: The statement is conditioned on anticipated further improvement that hasn’t really been defined.

speaker: SACK
text: So I think it leaves open some issues.

speaker: SACK
text: If conditions just stay where they are, does that mean the programs will be extended?

speaker: SACK
text: How much improvement is expected?

speaker: SACK
text: I would just say it’s complicated to signal that so far in advance.

speaker: LACKER
text: Is the risk all to the downside?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it’s mixed—there are extensions going on as well as some trimming back.

speaker: LACKER
text: But is termination also potentially a signal of the confidence we have in the economy and financial conditions?

speaker: LACKER
text: Is there a chance they’d interpret it that way?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m not sure I want to litigate this here, although I’d be happy to have discussions with people.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If I could once more read just part of it: “Should the recent improvements in market conditions continue, the Board and the FOMC currently anticipate that a number of these facilities may not need to be extended beyond February 1.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, if financial stresses do not moderate as expected, the Board and the FOMC are prepared to extend…” and so on.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I have a clarifying question on the discussions around exit strategy and the LSAP.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Would there be, then, a discussion at each meeting as to whether we should go to the “up to” limit?

speaker: HOENIG
text: In other words, should there be a specific decision whether to go forward?

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think you have to address that before you start talking more generally about raising the fed funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s part of the policy strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In just a minute we can take a coffee break, if that is okay.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: When we come back, we will have a bit more discussion among the group on the issues that were raised by the presentations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just try to identify three topics that we might want to talk about.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The first one is Brian’s recommendations on trimming back the various facilities or extending facilities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll have to take some Board and FOMC votes on that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You have Brian’s handout that shows the recommendations of the staff.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So if anyone has thoughts on any of those, that would be the first issue that I would suggest.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second is the set of issues related to exiting from our expanded balance sheet and raising interest rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just say that many people have called for us to communicate more about this, and I think that’s very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The current plan is for the Monetary Policy Report, which will be issued in a few weeks, to have a section which will describe, in some more detail than we’ve given so far, the tools we’d be looking at to achieve the exit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We don’t want to put in things that are very speculative.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But to the extent that the Committee is comfortable with things like reverse repos, and so on, we’d want to describe those in that section.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So any thoughts or comments about the relative value of different methods or concerns would be useful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And then, the third topic would be just the things that Trish and Brian were raising and that President Hoenig alluded to, which is thinking about the asset purchase strategy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Even if we don’t change our position at this meeting, do we want to begin thinking about a tapering strategy?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Do we want to advise the Desk to change its reaction function?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we can discuss things related to that set of issues.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Of course, whatever else you want to bring up is fine, but I thought those three areas might be worth comments in the free discussion period.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Before we do that, why don’t we refresh ourselves with about a fifteen-minute coffee break?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The floor is now open for people who’d like to make comments on the three topics I mentioned before the break or anything else that the presentations brought to mind.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I want everyone to have a chance to speak, but I do hope we can get to the economic presentation today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we can do this in 45 minutes or so, that would be very helpful.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Would anyone like to start off?

speaker: WARSH
text: Mr. Chairman, let me try to be brief but address a couple of the topics that were raised in the so-called question part of the discussion.

speaker: WARSH
text: And then I’ll try to go through the topics that you mentioned briefly.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, the remittance discussion, where I think we put that in legal terms—Seth was asked for decided legal judgments—and we put it in political terms.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think most of the remittance discussion actually is about credibility.

speaker: WARSH
text: In the event bad things happen and we end up with losses that are enduring, what does that do to the credibility of Fed actions?

speaker: WARSH
text: The Fed’s ability to affect these markets typically comes not because of the size of the actions, but because of who is taking them.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I think that credibility could suffer in those circumstances, and I’ll try to use that credibility idea to consider whether we are crowding in other investors to these markets or crowding out other investors for the balance of my discussion on your third point on asset purchases.

speaker: WARSH
text: The Desk asked for our views on several topics.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, on the policy objectives of the asset purchases, I think markets have heard us say different things about what our objective function is.

speaker: WARSH
text: Mine would be to improve market functioning, to bring liquidity to markets that are not trading, to narrow bid–asked spreads, and the like.

speaker: WARSH
text: This would suggest having the Desk devote its resources to securities, such as off-the-run securities, that are less liquid.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think markets have heard other objectives from us, although not explicit objectives, such as to set price levels across Treasuries or MBS.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we have rightly steered away from it.

speaker: WARSH
text: But they think that we are still cognizant of prices at some level and that we are trying to move rates lower.

speaker: WARSH
text: So the first question the Desk asked is: Could we collectively be clear on an objective function?

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we could, and I would suggest that your Humphrey-Hawkins testimony and Monetary Policy Report might be the best means of doing so.

speaker: WARSH
text: The second question raised by the Desk was about expanding asset purchases.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m exceptionally uncomfortable with expanding asset purchases, particularly now.

speaker: WARSH
text: The Desk, I think, had a preference, understandably, for increasing Treasuries.

speaker: WARSH
text: That doesn’t fit my preferred objective, which is that we’re entering markets to improve market functioning.

speaker: WARSH
text: So, on that basis, I think that market was working well before we got in it, and I’d say it’s still working well.

speaker: WARSH
text: But if we got into it in significant size, I could see it actually working less well.

speaker: WARSH
text: Had risk-free rates fallen markedly since we started purchasing Treasuries, Mr. Chairman, I would have expected some to say: “Well, then we should do more of it.” But risk-free rates have increased since we started purchasing, yet I hear some say, “Well, we should do more of it.” So I’m not sure what fact scenario would have suggested doing less of it, and it makes me a little uncomfortable.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think Brian Sack did a great job of explaining how all-in costs of capital for real private companies in this market have come down, and meaningfully so.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t think that has much, if anything, to do with our Treasury purchases.

speaker: WARSH
text: It could have much to do with the suite of things that we’ve done in the last 20 months, but I think it gives too much credit to suggest that somehow that’s related to the purchases of Treasuries.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t think that our science is so good that we know that increasing the size of our Treasury purchases to $450 billion, but not to $750 billion, would have a modest, marginally positive effect.

speaker: WARSH
text: It’s not at all obvious to me where risk-free rates would be had we avoided buying Treasuries; they might have been higher or they might have been lower.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I must say I’m not convinced, and as a result, not at all comfortable expanding further.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of the expanding purchases of agencies, I think the Desk rightly warns us that doing so could actually do some harm to that market.

speaker: WARSH
text: Given how big we are to the new issuance market there, I think we might well have already done some harm.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is, we entered that market when it wasn’t functioning, and we helped improve market functioning.

speaker: WARSH
text: But to the extent that we’re 70 or 80 percent of certain classes of securities, I would say that that two-sided market is not forming well, and I would be very hesitant to go further there.

speaker: WARSH
text: The third question raised by the Desk: What about flexibility between and among asset classes, that is, what if we just pool all of this stuff together and say we’re smart and we’re going to use the following criteria?

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that would be read by markets to mean that we’re increasing potentially the purchases of Treasuries.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that would risk crowding out those investors who would think that there are strange things afoot, so I don’t think that’s a prudent idea.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of flexibility within asset classes, I think markets have learned that we’re not as responsive to changes in rates as they would like, and my own sense would be it’s a noble goal to have flexibility, but flexibility in a vacuum will lead to continued ambiguity or accentuated ambiguity.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I don’t think that that’s a great way forward.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of increasing flexibility to be more responsive to market rates, I just don’t think we should be fighting against the tape here.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m not sure we know what the real market-clearing rates are for some of these things.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of securities lending, which I think has been much abused outside of the Federal Reserve and poorly understood by market participants, I share Brian’s view that our being in the securities lending business could actually be useful to solve what I would consider to be the preeminent policy objective of helping market functioning improve.

speaker: WARSH
text: So that’s just a quick list of some of the things that you asked us to address, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: WARSH
text: On Brian Madigan’s modifications of various liquidity facilities, I think it is confidence-inducing, not risk-inducing, for the world to know that we are thinking about exits.

speaker: WARSH
text: Even those market participants who think that the economy could well unwind again will believe that we can be more comfortable improvising in a forward-leaning way if we can at the same time be thinking about how we get out of this when conditions warrant.

speaker: WARSH
text: Without going into detail on Brian’s list, I think it’s constructive, and I think that the Thursday press release is likely to be in some ways more impactful to market’s understanding of our way forward than our FOMC statement on Wednesday.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On your three questions, I agree with much of what Governor Warsh just said.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In terms of exit strategies, I think the staff did a terrific job in thinking through this and in the very elegant way they laid out the options.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In my own personal view, I think we could be a little more aggressive in either cutting quantities or moving minimum bids up in some combination, particularly for the TAF and even for some of the others, in terms of the haircuts.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In general, I’m very supportive of the strategy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The only thing I was very disappointed in was the GSE facility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That facility came on not quite a year ago.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It has never been used.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The Treasury got funding to support the GSEs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would have liked to have seen that facility rescinded back in September or October after the Treasury got funding.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I still think it ought to be rescinded.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t think that is a place we ought to be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I do think the announcement of these modifications to the facilities and particularly the language in the press release that the Chairman read will, in fact, be positive for the economy as a whole.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: There may be some places in the markets that will lose the subsidies that some of these things might be providing, but on net I think it will be a good signal to the marketplace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the tools for managing the balance sheet, again, there were a lot of interesting ideas.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think many of them could work.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would just like to reiterate how strongly I feel about not wanting to have Fed bills.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It is a bad idea, not because it can’t manage the balance sheet, but because I fear that it poses incredible political risks to the System.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s an opportunity for interference, an opportunity for the Congress and the political parties to view this as another way to intrude on Federal Reserve policymaking.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Although we may ask for the autonomy to make those decisions, that doesn’t necessarily guarantee that they will grant it.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I have expressed this view before.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I feel very strongly about Fed bills as not a good way to go in this environment; many of the other tools, though, such as reverse repos and others, could accomplish much the same thing, and I would encourage us to continue to work on those and the other options, because they entail much less potential political risk.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: On the LSAP issues, I agree with almost everything Kevin just said.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our objectives, I thought, were fairly clear; that is, we’re not targeting a price or a yield.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The markets seemed to believe that we were.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we would be well served, as was suggested, by clarifying it, perhaps in the Chairman’s testimony in July, to try to reinforce that and disabuse the markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I was struck by some of the other things that the Desk was talking about.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I want to read a couple of sentences, and I quote: “Staff sees evidence of both stock and flow impacts from our experience so far, although we cannot be certain of the precise mechanism by which they work, or if the effects are permanent or transitory.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That leaves a considerable degree of uncertainty in designing and implementing the LSAP programs.” That suggests to me we don’t know exactly what we’re doing or how it’s working, and so that argues against flexibility and the notion that we’re going to go in there and play some game to raise this yield or lower that spread when, in fact, we don’t know how these mechanisms are working.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I guess I would steer away from the flexibility.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that the “slow but steady” path is just fine, and that we can clarify that we are not targeting a particular yield or price, but rather we’re encouraging market functioning and liquidity, and leave it at that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In terms of the expansion, we still have a lot of purchases we could make if we wanted to.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m opposed to going out and authorizing more purchases of agency debt, MBS, or Treasuries at this point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t think we need to make that decision right now.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And if anything, things are looking somewhat better.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I would oppose that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would also be against this notion of going in and buying hybrid ARMs or creating options.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we do that because we can.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It’s not clear to me what the objective is.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We have been pretty unclear as to exactly how effective we have been in some of these markets on some of these prices and yields and what exactly the impacts are going to be.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think the evidence is pretty mixed on our ability to go in and sort of micromanage various subsectors of these markets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So I don’t see any particular reason to expand into hybrid ARMs or to sell put options on longer-term assets.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I just do not think that is going to help us very much.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, you’re going to hear some similarity to what you just heard from Governor Warsh and President Plosser.

speaker: FISHER
text: I agree with most of the statements that were made.

speaker: FISHER
text: I feel particularly strongly about the issue of the Treasuries.

speaker: FISHER
text: As Governor Warsh mentioned, I’m beyond particularly uncomfortable, I am especially uncomfortable.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think there’s no evidence that it has a positive impact.

speaker: FISHER
text: We can tell ourselves and we can tell the marketplace that, indeed, the corporate debt market has improved.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m rather pleased with that; obviously, we all are.

speaker: FISHER
text: I’m not sure there’s direct causality, but I do think the risk-return tradeoff is way too negative.

speaker: FISHER
text: Even if we figure out a cute way to say it, there still is a suspicion that we’re monetizing deficits, although we’ve been much firmer in our public statements on that.

speaker: FISHER
text: And I realize that in chart 4 that’s just a somewhat important factor, but it is a factor, and I worry about that.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to come back to Brian’s recommendations.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think we have to be very careful that we’re not perceived as basically providing facilities to prop up institutions that are too big to fail at the expense of other institutions that desire to grow.

speaker: FISHER
text: In my earlier remarks, I used the wrong term.

speaker: FISHER
text: I said “political,” and I meant “optical”—I think the optics are rather poor.

speaker: FISHER
text: If TAF is being used, as was pointed out in the staff paper, principally or significantly by two institutions that are too big to fail, I think we have to be careful about that.

speaker: FISHER
text: President Plosser made a suggestion that we might limit it even more severely in terms of the amounts; I think he was suggesting a pricing impact there.

speaker: FISHER
text: Obviously, classical central banking is to lend at a penalty rate.

speaker: FISHER
text: But that penalty rate is a gift compared to what we would be charging smaller and regional banks.

speaker: FISHER
text: Therefore, I would ask you to go through the list and think of which of these facilities are really in place to prop up institutions that are too big to fail.

speaker: FISHER
text: And I would be curious as to which of those facilities you consider as actually having an impact there and as helpful on that front and which are not.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I reiterate my concerns about the optics of TAF and the primary credit recommendations.

speaker: FISHER
text: On the issue of exiting, obviously the market is asking for it.

speaker: FISHER
text: I do think the Monetary Policy Report, Mr. Chairman, is the appropriate vehicle, and, perhaps, your Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.

speaker: FISHER
text: Like President Plosser, I personally am uncomfortable with Fed bills.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t think it is politically feasible.

speaker: FISHER
text: The staff points that out.

speaker: FISHER
text: I worry about the market that would be made in those and the derivatives that would be written from them.

speaker: FISHER
text: I have spoken to that before, but I don’t think that is a particularly wise recommendation to make.

speaker: FISHER
text: I will make one last recommendation, only half in jest, which is that we get rid of the TALF program and we call that the Bill Nelson Relief Act.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If we got rid of it, it would be a relief for Bill Nelson, I’m sure.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I’m now a little confused.

speaker: TARULLO
text: It sounds to me as though we’re now having the monetary policy discussion, and if that’s what we’re going to do, that’s fine.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I just want to know if that’s what we’re actually doing.

speaker: FISHER
text: I was just reacting to the three points that were raised.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I think we’re now getting to the substance of what I thought was going to be tomorrow’s discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Well, I’ll leave it to people to do what they want.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the issues that we were discussing were the exit tools, the tactics for the Desk in dealing with large-scale asset purchases, and the winding down of the programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Those were the things that I asked people to talk about, so perhaps we could focus on those.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’ll try to be brief and confine my remarks to the three things that you asked about.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With respect to the credit and liquidity facilities and the timing of trimming them back, I thought that Brian and the staff put forward a very well thought out proposal, and it’s a proposal I completely support.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it is important to include language of the type that you read from the draft that you’re preparing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’ll say this again in the policy round, but I want to emphasize that we have to be very careful not to signal an early end to policy stimulus, and while I see a good reason to withdraw the facilities in the manner that you set out, I think it’s very important to put in place language that leans against the idea that we’re looking for an early end to policy stimulus.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I support the proposal and the language you read.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On exit strategies, I do think you indicated that you might discuss this in detail in the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think that’s absolutely the right place to do it, and I think it’s important to indicate that we have complete confidence in our ability to withdraw stimulus when we need to do so, that we have the tools to do it, and that when the time comes, which is not now or soon, that we will proceed to do it.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The wording for monetary policy alternative B has been changed, but the phrasing in the original draft of B is the type of thing I think we have to be very careful to avoid.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It suggests that we’re not sure if we have the ability to exit and, therefore, we will carefully consider whether we should expand our balance sheet further.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I believe we do have the tools.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I thought the staff did a wonderful job of preparing the memo on exit strategies.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It convinced me that, if the only thing we had to work with was interest on reserves, it probably would be sufficient.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I thought this idea of strengthening it through collateralized accounts was really clever, was implementable, and was almost foolproof.

speaker: YELLEN
text: And I would love to see the staff do the further work that would be necessary to confirm that that is a foolproof technique, adding to the arsenal of tools, such as triparty reverse repos, and making sure that that is entirely workable.

speaker: YELLEN
text: To me, it seems that package, if we do nothing else, is sufficient for us to assert confidently that we can do what is needed when the time comes.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But that time is not now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the LSAPs, they obviously do get into policy issues, and let me try to leave some of the policy issues around this until tomorrow.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Initially I was an enthusiast for long-term Treasury purchases.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I thought the purpose of it was not only to improve liquidity and market functioning, but also to influence yields to push them down.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Now, I didn’t see it as a commitment to a particular rate, which would be very dangerous; but, other things equal, and depending on our assessment of overall financial conditions and the outlook, I saw it as an attempt to push rates lower than they would otherwise be.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On theoretical grounds, I believe there’s a very strong case that they should have some effect, but it has been awfully hard to identify exactly what that effect is, and I think that we’re beginning to run into costs of pursuing that further.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think our reputation for independence is suffering, and the public is obviously concerned that we’re monetizing the debt and that it’s going to lead to an outbreak of inflation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I have to say that I completely disagree with these views, but I can’t say they’re not prevalent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I encounter them day in and day out.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So at the present time, I would say the benefits don’t merit the costs, but I wouldn’t want to see Treasuries taken off the table if conditions were to deteriorate and attitudes were to change.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think our communications around this have really been a problem, and as I consider the concrete proposals the staff put forward in their memo, it seems to me that improving our communications is important.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The thing that most concerns me is the autumn expiration date for our long-term Treasury purchase program.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We either have to decide now or we’ll have to decide in August.

speaker: YELLEN
text: There will be a lot of market speculation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In the meantime if we could do something at this meeting to clarify rather than keep the market guessing, I think it would be desirable.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This brings me to the suggestion—which is a policy decision, but to my mind, in some sense, a relatively small one—to add a sentence that says something like “to align the end dates (or the timing) of the three asset purchase programs, we’ve extended the current pace of Treasury purchases through the end of the year, bringing the total size of the program to $450 billion.” That would say they are all aligned at the end of the year and that we’re going to decide what to do with these programs.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I would like to see us take that off the table.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Quickly, on other issues, I could see some merit in flexibility in terms of the allocation of our purchases between MBS and Treasuries.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We didn’t have a concrete proposal, but assuming that we’re not going to expand the overall level of our Treasury purchases, except perhaps extending the program at the current pace to the end of the year, then I agree that this isn’t the right time to go in that direction.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The idea of leaning against the wind—I could see some merit in it, but it will be incredibly complicated to reach agreement and communicate to the Desk or to the outside world what we’re doing, and I wouldn’t go there now at all.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’d just maintain steady as you go.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I do think the idea of adding hybrid ARMs to the program is very constructive, given what’s happening in the housing market and given that mortgage rates have backed up so much, so if that’s a viable, practical possibility, I would move in that direction, too.

speaker: STERN
text: In thinking about the three issues you raised, I start from the presumption that we don’t need to convince market participants at this stage that we will do what it takes to, if possible, restore stability and to encourage financial and economic health.

speaker: STERN
text: I think we need to convince them that we have an exit strategy and that we are prepared to execute it in a timely way.

speaker: STERN
text: So against that background, with regard to the trimming and extending of the liquidity facilities, I’m generally fine with the proposal that Brian described and the language that you put forward.

speaker: STERN
text: If it were my nickel, I might tighten up that language and make the commitment to end the programs a little more forcefully, but the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony might be a better place to elaborate on that whole set of issues.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to the LSAP, those suggestions strike me as solutions in search of a problem.

speaker: STERN
text: What I mean by that is that financial market conditions have been getting better.

speaker: STERN
text: Now, maybe interest rates have backed up, but there are a number of explanations for that, and it’s very difficult to sort through exactly which might be responsible.

speaker: STERN
text: If conditions hadn’t been improving, I might be interested in trying to fine-tune the LSAP, but because they have been improving, I don’t see any great value—in fact, I don’t see any value whatsoever—in going down that path, and I would avoid it.

speaker: STERN
text: With regard to exiting and raising interest rates when the time comes, I guess I think there are a variety of tools that would enable us to address the situation.

speaker: STERN
text: I am not terribly concerned about this.

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t quite understand the issue about having committed ourselves to a permanently large balance sheet.

speaker: STERN
text: The size of the balance sheet is up to the Committee ultimately, and if we decide that we want to shrink it, then we simply give the directive to the Desk that it should be shrunk, and they will have to execute that.

speaker: STERN
text: So I don’t see that as a problem.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I would start with Brian’s description, and I’m generally supportive of this proposal.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It does give an end date, and I agree with President Stern—I think the firmer that end date is, of course, the better.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the TAF issue that President Fisher brought up, I think he has valid points, but I do think we need to look at that pretty carefully, and I know you are going to do some follow-up on that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: And because we’re talking about exit strategies, and these liquidity facilities are part of it, it does extend to the LSAP.

speaker: HOENIG
text: From my perspective, the most unusual thing that we have is the LSAP, and I think that’s where we need to focus when we think about exit strategy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think at each meeting we should first make a decision about whether we even want to go to where we have said the “up to” figure is.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It becomes very important that we make a rational choice around that, because the first step of exiting is not going any further.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that’s critical and takes time and effort.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I also think having the equivalent of GSE assets on our balance sheet with these MBS is questionable in terms of the role of the central bank, if we have, in fact, stabilized the markets.

speaker: HOENIG
text: And I am very uneasy about purchasing long-term Treasuries.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Perhaps it is optics, but I think in some sense it’s also reality—you are monetizing the debt.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So that’s how I think about our exit strategy across all the actions we’ve taken.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In terms of the flexibility on how to administer this, I think we should not have flexibility.

speaker: HOENIG
text: If we met the needs of the MBS that we put on, and now our additional purchases are causing other issues, then that’s a sign, perhaps, that we shouldn’t be going to the limit.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think we should be aware of this and take note of it and not just say, “Well, we’ve got to get to the total.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Let’s shift over to long-term Treasuries.” There’s information in the feedback we are getting from the market that we ought to use and not ignore.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That’s how I look at your three questions, and less flexibility in the third is better than more.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’ll take the points in the sequence that you mentioned.

speaker: EVANS
text: On Brian’s and the staff’s facility recommendations, although I long for the day when we are comfortable with markets to the point of ending 13(3) authority, I’m not bothered by the individual programs.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think they’re well put together, and I think the plan, as stated, is a good one.

speaker: EVANS
text: Frankly, I think markets will see the conditional statements in the release as indicating our willingness to keep the 13(3) authority for a time.

speaker: EVANS
text: I wouldn’t think that they would think we’re about to ramp it down, but we’ll see.

speaker: EVANS
text: And I do think that ending 13(3) will be done appropriately, it will be positive, it will be a boost, much like the SCAP.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the exit strategies and the reserve management tools, much as President Yellen indicated, I tend to favor the tools that strengthen the interest on excess reserves mechanism, and there are a number of those that, put together, should strengthen the arbitrage.

speaker: EVANS
text: Reverse RPs, I think, are also a good tool.

speaker: EVANS
text: If we’re looking to the money market funds as one source of liquidity, that’s going to sort of alter the commercial paper market, since they’re a big source of funding there.

speaker: EVANS
text: And I just don’t know what the implications are.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’d want to understand expected dysfunction in that market—as opposed to unexpected dysfunction—to see what we’d be doing there.

speaker: EVANS
text: But reverse RPs are quite good, I think.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the comment that we should try to project complete confidence in our ability to do this, mostly I agree with that.

speaker: EVANS
text: My first reaction is that you’ve actually talked quite a lot about exit strategies already.

speaker: EVANS
text: And in your Q&A with the Congress, I’m not exactly sure how much of what you intend to say will be new.

speaker: EVANS
text: Just your saying it is newsworthy of course.

speaker: EVANS
text: But I’m not quite sure how that will play out.

speaker: EVANS
text: I was very struck by the extreme scenario on net income which indicated that the balance sheet would be so large that we could find ourselves in a situation where we are challenged by it—challenged in an optics sense, not in our ability to create new reserves to pay and fund what we need to do.

speaker: EVANS
text: As we’ve learned through the introduction of all of our facilities and in using our authorities, there is a risk to the institution at some level that we should be mindful of.

speaker: EVANS
text: I should add that I think it is being handled very well so far.

speaker: EVANS
text: Finally, on the large-scale asset purchases—and I’ll try to be true to not talking about policy on this.

speaker: EVANS
text: The Committee selected a number, for example, for Treasury purchases, of $300 billion, and I thought that it would be implemented to that number.

speaker: EVANS
text: So if tapering effects are important for a given time frame, then I would have envisioned going at X dollars per month for a time, and then within the last one or two months tapering to half of that.

speaker: EVANS
text: That allows the Committee to revisit it in a timely fashion to say, “Should we extend it?” as President Yellen suggested, or it could be tapered on to $300 billion.

speaker: EVANS
text: But it would be a policy decision that the Committee makes.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’ll leave it at that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think I agree with everyone else.

speaker: KOHN
text: We absolutely need a framework that people can have confidence in for how we’re going to exit the current balance sheet and raise interest rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: But as we’ll discuss tomorrow, I think it’s way too early to begin that exit, and I do worry about signaling an exit before the economy is really ready for it.

speaker: KOHN
text: But we do need to have the framework.

speaker: KOHN
text: In that regard, I’m comfortable with the liquidity facilities proposals in Brian’s memo.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think basically they recognize and validate what’s already happening in the market, and that’s fine.

speaker: KOHN
text: And I was comfortable with the sentence you read, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it was sufficiently conditional, and I wouldn’t strengthen it.

speaker: KOHN
text: My concern is that, if we find ourselves in a position where we don’t want to wind down, we haven’t already told people we are going to wind down, but rather we have told people we are going to be looking at things.

speaker: KOHN
text: I came in a little like President Fisher, looking for perhaps raising that TAF minimum bid rate, thinking that, unlike all the other facilities we have, that’s one that doesn’t quite wind down as automatically as markets improve.

speaker: KOHN
text: My mind is still open on that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I haven’t heard a lot of support for that, but I thought raising that would reinforce the winding down.

speaker: KOHN
text: I appreciate Brian’s point that it’s an auction facility—they can always cut the amounts rather than raise the price; but raising the price would reinforce that.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I guess, on balance, I would be slightly in favor of raising the TAF penalty rates.

speaker: KOHN
text: On exit tools, I was actually encouraged by the presentations by the staff—Spence, Trish, and others—which indicated that we do have a lot of tools.

speaker: KOHN
text: And, like President Evans, I see these tools for sterilizing or reducing reserves working together with interest on reserves, and I feel more confident than before I read the memo that we can accomplish a lot.

speaker: KOHN
text: I guess you’re going to have to work on these reverse RPs—who the counterparties are (including the GSEs) and whether you need to diversify past the dealers.

speaker: KOHN
text: I’m not totally convinced you do need to; the dealers are there to be intermediaries, and they can play that role.

speaker: KOHN
text: Anyhow, that would be a good thing.

speaker: KOHN
text: And the time deposits I thought also were a good thing.

speaker: KOHN
text: I wouldn’t rule out selling assets quite as much as some of you would.

speaker: KOHN
text: We took these special actions to lower rates—I will come to that next—but if we’re in a situation where we are worried about inflation, we can undo them, although maybe not in huge size.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would think selling some of the portfolios, depending on the circumstances, might not be a bad idea.

speaker: KOHN
text: That brings me to the LSAPs.

speaker: KOHN
text: My objectives were different from yours, Governor Warsh.

speaker: KOHN
text: I voted for this in order to lower interest rates, or at least to make interest rates lower than they otherwise would be.

speaker: KOHN
text: It was keyed to the macroeconomic outlook last March, which was pretty dire and getting worse all the time, and we had run out of fed funds ammunition in December.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I was not uncomfortable.

speaker: KOHN
text: I was in favor of diversifying our portfolio of purchases into Treasuries.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the monetizing problem is keyed to the fiscal deficit outlook.

speaker: KOHN
text: If that weren’t so uncertain and looking so unsustainable, I don’t think people would be worried about us.

speaker: KOHN
text: But it is uncertain and looking unsustainable, so I think we need to be careful about the interaction of monetary and fiscal policy.

speaker: KOHN
text: Therefore, I would not be in favor of increasing those purchases at this time.

speaker: KOHN
text: I came into the meeting thinking about some flexibility across instruments within the total amount and across time.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I’ve been discouraged by the discussion at the meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we can set a price or we can set a quantity, but setting the relationships of price and quantity in a clear way is just very, very hard.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think I’d stick with what we are doing now.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would be okay with small purchases of hybrid ARMs.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it might encourage that market a little bit and help the mortgage market, which has been adversely affected by the uptick in Treasury rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we have to be really careful about our communications in terms of discriminating between our ability to exit smoothly and implying that we’re about to exit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I will probably come back to this point tomorrow.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The anxiety that I have about inadvertently implying to the market that we are exiting soon is particularly high now, because the market has already priced in a lot more tightening than most of us think is likely over the next year or two.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That said, of course, we have to be prepared for exit, and I think being prepared for exit and articulating that is really, really important in keeping inflation expectations well anchored, and also in keeping the dispersion of inflation expectations compact.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think we definitely have to do that, but I think it’s tricky to do one without implying the other.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of Brian’s recommendations on the facilities, I’m pretty comfortable with all of it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I do want to make sure the language stays where it is, though, and doesn’t get more definitive about what happens in February.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think February is a long time away, and I wouldn’t want to prejudge what we’re going to want to do or not want to do in February.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think where we are right now in terms of the language is about right.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It basically says there’s a possibility that we might not extend it, so the market is put on notice.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But it doesn’t necessarily commit us to ending the facilities.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the TAF, I am on the other side of that issue from Don on the rate rise.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s not a big deal for me, but let me just explain why I am on the other side.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think raising the rate on TAF will be seized upon by some as the beginning of raising interest rates.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it’s not the TAF rate rise that bothers me per se.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I can certainly understand the argument for doing that in the small, but I’m a little worried that if we do it, people will say, “Oh, look, this is the very beginning of the rate hikes, because they have now raised the rate on the TAF.” There’s also a second, more subtle issue on the TAF, if we are actually going to go to the sporadic TAF auctions over the longer term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We probably can’t really do that in a normal environment with a penalty rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If you think of the transition on the TAF, we’d have to move to a penalty rate, and then later on, as we go to the sporadic auctions, we’d actually have to lower the rate again.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That just seems a little confusing to me.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But my main concern is the signal in terms of monetary policy that people might draw from raising the rate.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the LSAP, I don’t feel very defensive about what we’ve been doing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: After all, we did get a really good mortgage refinancing wave—that was the point of the exercise.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s hard to know how much of it was MBS versus Treasuries, and we’ll never really know for certain.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I feel pretty good about basically having achieved that objective.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of Treasuries, I don’t think there’s any appetite for going much larger.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the choice is really between standing pat and going to, as President Yellen said, $450 billion and extending it through year-end.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The advantage of the latter is that you don’t have to make up your mind quite so soon, but the disadvantage is that it seems like a pretty weak response.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It shows a lack of sort of confidence in what the Fed is doing with this facility.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I guess I’m slightly leaning toward standing pat, because I worry that the other option would be viewed as too little to be significant.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think the suggestion about hybrid ARMs makes a lot of sense.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In some ways, if we don’t do that, we’re basically distorting the relationship between the fixed-rate agency MBS and the hybrid ARMs, and it’s not really clear why we would want to do that.

speaker: DUKE
text: On the question of extensions and modifications on liquidity facilities, I’m generally in favor of the proposal, but I wonder if one option might be to raise the minimum rate for TAF at the same time we increase the spread on the primary credit, so that we’d be treating the two different types of borrowers the same way.

speaker: DUKE
text: On the exit strategies, it strikes me that the whole discussion is incredibly similar to a normal exercise in asset-liability management that goes on in banks all the time and that we should probably be paying attention to the same kind of tools that are used in banks to simulate various possibilities.

speaker: DUKE
text: Regarding these tools, I don’t think they’re mutually exclusive, so some modeling of an optimum mix—a funding mix if you will—of all of the various tools, taking into account some of the different barriers that we might run into in different markets, might make some sense.

speaker: DUKE
text: Also, I’d be interested in some sort of regular reporting, whether it is in Notes or the Bluebook or one of the other books, so that we keep an eye on the potential costs of the exit strategies in a number of different environments.

speaker: DUKE
text: As a banker, I have been in a situation where I have looked into the future and have seen losses that would arise from unwinding positions that I had taken.

speaker: DUKE
text: Of course, at that time, I was never able to adjust my cost of funds absolutely.

speaker: DUKE
text: So it occurs to me this could involve an incredibly magnified political risk.

speaker: DUKE
text: There’s a huge temptation not to take those losses when the risk associated with taking the losses is very high.

speaker: DUKE
text: So we need to make sure that we’re paying attention to those costs, particularly if they would bring us under political pressure at the same time that we’re doing something that’s politically unpopular to begin with.

speaker: DUKE
text: So, again, I think modeling those out is important.

speaker: DUKE
text: I guess the statement that struck me the most is that the banking organizations have not discussed with System staff the possible effects of increased Systemwide reserves.

speaker: DUKE
text: I haven’t seen any indication that anybody anywhere in the banking industry has thought about the implications of these very high reserves in the system.

speaker: DUKE
text: I’ve been trying to think what that effect might be, and, frankly, I don’t know.

speaker: DUKE
text: But it strikes me that this level of reserves is going to have some sort of effect, so we should start to think about that, too.

speaker: DUKE
text: Hopefully, some of our researchers can come up with some possible impacts.

speaker: DUKE
text: Finally, on flexibility, I’m probably, again, headed dangerously close to the policy round discussion.

speaker: DUKE
text: When we first started these programs, I wasn’t entirely sure how much we would need, so it strikes me that, if a given purchase amount is beginning to impair functioning in any market that we are in, we have to wonder if that purchase amount minus one is also doing anything positive in that market.

speaker: DUKE
text: That would seem to indicate that certainly we’re getting close to an exit for agency debt.

speaker: DUKE
text: And I wonder, as originations go down, whether we end up in the same place with the MBS.

speaker: DUKE
text: Those are my comments, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I agree with Brian’s recommendations.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the TAF option of raising the minimum bid rate, I come out where Governor Kohn does.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There are several large institutions that are borrowing heavily from the TAF that are just holding them as excess reserves.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think having a 10 basis point charge and making it a little bit costly actually does make sense; it will probably bring down the TAF borrowing somewhat, which, given the size of our balance sheet, probably also makes sense.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the tools for exit, I agree with virtually everything that President Yellen said, so I’m not going to repeat it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of the asset purchase strategy, we don’t need to buy $1¼ trillion just for market function and liquidity in mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We weren’t trying to set interest rates, but we were certainly trying to influence interest rates.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There’s no reason to do something of that magnitude unless we’re going to influence interest rates.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So I do think that there’s still a little bit of difference around the table about exactly what we think these programs are intended to do.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But we made a distinction between quantitative easing and the asset side of the balance sheet.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: To me, that meant that we’re trying to get the financing costs lower.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: It’s hard to break this out from the discussion for tomorrow.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But if we’re not happy with where we are on our dual mandate, this is the only tool we have.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: And the way it operates has to be through the cost of financing.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: So, it’s a topic for discussion for tomorrow, but I think we have to make that link.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We can’t talk about it separately.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I just have a few quick comments.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I agree with all the points in the Madigan memo.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it does recognize what is happening with our liquidity facilities.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I have advocated before that we get them all priced as backstops and not that they actually need to be used at every point in time.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would also announce a rescission date for GSE lending.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Couldn’t we make that February 1, 2010, as well?

speaker: BULLARD
text: That would push it off into the future and would line it up with the other dates as opposed to doing it immediately.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I would go ahead and raise the minimum bid rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t feel strongly on that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I guess I come out where Governor Kohn and President Fisher have.

speaker: BULLARD
text: My thinking on that was that we could encourage more-normal market functioning there.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Vice Chairman Dudley brings up a good point, namely, that it sounds like raising an interest rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that’s a communication issue, and that would have to be handled appropriately.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the issues related to exiting, my overall reading is that there are some very promising but unproven ideas here, mostly to do with interest on reserves and reverse repos.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We think they’ll work, but at this point they’re not really proven.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I guess I’m reluctant to go further with asset purchases without more concrete ideas on how we’ll manage this going forward, although I do admit that these are promising.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The current policy response to the crisis has been to lower nominal interest rates to zero and more than double the monetary base.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think this discussion indicates that that increase in the monetary base will be very persistent, which is unprecedented in post-war U.S. history.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I am worried that we don’t really know what the implications of that might be, and we don’t really have tools in place to manage that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So we’re not really exiting from that increase in the base, we’re just saying: “That was our response.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We’re going to more than double the monetary base, and we’re going to see what happens.” On asset purchases strategy, I’d be fine with the tapering off.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t feel really strongly on that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think if we stick with our dates, the exit might go fine on the Treasuries.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In the current environment of large fiscal deficits, as several people have mentioned, including Governor Kohn, there’s always going to be talk about monetizing the debt.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I just don’t think we can get away from it in this environment.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Anything we do that smacks of buying up more Treasuries is going to be problematic.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So even though I have advocated in the past for treating MBS and Treasuries and debt all as one package and letting the Desk manage it, now I think it may not be the best thing to do.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’m also sympathetic with President Rosengren, who spoke earlier this afternoon about a state-contingent reaction function.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I have advocated for this before here, and though I know we are a long way from that, that’s really what you want.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You want to be able to communicate to the public that if the data come in a little bit worse, then we’re going to do a little bit more, and if the data come in a little bit better, we’re going to do a little bit less.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s the kind of thing that you want.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You have that in something like a Taylor Rule for interest rate policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You’d like that for asset purchases.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We just haven’t been able to formulate something like that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’d like to encourage us to keep thinking in that direction.

speaker: BULLARD
text: After all, zero interest rates might go on for several years, so it’s not as if this situation is about to end.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I think we should still keep thinking about that, but I know that we’re a long way from that at this point.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also support Brian’s recommendations on our credit and liquidity facilities.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In regards to tools for exiting, I am also very appreciative to the staff for the excellent work that they did.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am now more confident that we have the tools.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am also very much in favor of using the Monetary Policy Report to describe the tools that are available to us.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: And I prefer focusing on those tools that we currently have available to us that don’t require any legislation or other changes.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I also agree with Governor Kohn’s comments that it’s too soon to consider a change in policy, but I also agree that it’s not too soon for the Committee to start talking about a framework—or the process that we’re going to be using—to decide how we are going to apply these tools.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In addition, I think it would be helpful for the staff and this Committee to start looking at some alternative language for use in statements that will describe this environment that we are going to be in, where we are simultaneously adjusting our fed funds target and managing the size of our balance sheet.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As President Yellen stated, I think that getting prepared to communicate is just as important as getting ready to use the tools.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’ll start with our instructions to the Desk on asset purchases.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree with Governor Kohn, and I was going to express it the same way—for clarity of instructions, fixing a price or fixing a quantity really can’t be beat.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree with President Bullard that a reaction function would be preferable on some grounds, and if we were able to communicate a well-understood one, that would be great.

speaker: LACKER
text: But in this instance I just don’t think we have the time to communicate that in a way that does not add uncertainty about the exact way in which we’re likely to react to incoming data.

speaker: LACKER
text: Moreover, I want to emphasize that I think we should give the Desk less discretion, and I do that without any lack of respect for the tremendous acumen and skill of the people on the Desk.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s just that it places an impossible burden on them to operationalize our terms of art in the directive and to communicate that coherently to markets in a way that doesn’t add chatter that we don’t need and that distracts us from what we’re doing.

speaker: LACKER
text: As for monetizing debt, we’re monetizing mortgage-backed securities just as much as we’re monetizing debt.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the danger—and this has been the danger this spring—is conveying that the amount we monetize might vary with the amount the government issues.

speaker: LACKER
text: That’s something we have to stay away from, and it’s another reason not to go down the path of seeking to adopt a kind of a reaction function that tries to skin a bunch of cats.

speaker: LACKER
text: As to our exit strategy, I think we’re likely to be in this situation with zero interest rates for a while.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I have a hard time ruling out the possibility that, if the Greenbook’s expectation comes true, towards the end of the year there will be another gigantic sigh of relief, much as we experienced after the bottom in March—maybe not euphoria, but a turn in expectations and sentiment that makes the world look different and makes us at least want to think about backing away from stimulus before the end of the year.

speaker: LACKER
text: I have no idea how likely that is, but I think we need to pay attention to the amount of stimulus we’re providing and the effects we’re having.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we need to pay attention to the banking system, in particular, and to monitor bank asset holdings and their liquid liabilities and that channel for policy.

speaker: LACKER
text: Sure, we were intervening in order to reduce MBS rates and to reduce Treasury yields below what they otherwise would have been.

speaker: LACKER
text: Granting that, it’s not clear which of those two channels had the bigger effect.

speaker: LACKER
text: But we need to be thinking about the timing—what it’s going to look like when it’s going to be the right time.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that it’s too early to signal that we’re thinking about exiting, but it’s not too early to explain in the Monetary Policy Report that we are thinking about what it would be like.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’re not thinking about doing it yet, but we’re planning and thinking carefully about the mechanics of it.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that raising the interest rate on reserves seems quite likely to succeed.

speaker: LACKER
text: To my mind, the most logical and natural path forward on this issue of reserve management is to use this opportunity to back away from federal funds rate targeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve backed away from nonborrowed reserves targeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: If historically, by some fluke, we had been targeting RP rates over the last three decades, I don’t think we would have known the difference, and yet RP rates never equaled the fed funds rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I don’t think we have a real strong reason to tie ourselves to the federal funds rate as opposed to the RP rate.

speaker: LACKER
text: The interest rate on reserves in this regime is going to be the relevant marginal rate for banks.

speaker: LACKER
text: So when the time comes, I think we just back away from the target, explain that, “here’s our policy rate, the interest on reserves,” and let it go at that.

speaker: LACKER
text: As a result—and this is sort of related—I think we should be really hesitant to engage in clever tinkering to try to get around problems with this, as good as we seem to have been at clever tinkering recently.

speaker: LACKER
text: So to my mind, reserve collateral accounts are just not worth the bother.

speaker: LACKER
text: In terms of changing the leverage ratio and exempting some institutions, I don’t think we should tinker with supervision and regulation just to solve a monetary policy problem.

speaker: LACKER
text: I find the guidance thing to be even murkier.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t want us to have that ability.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t want to make us a target for those who would want us to finance stuff.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve gotten involved in housing finance, and I think one of our biggest political problems in the next couple of years is going to be backing away from housing finance, the way we had to back away from it in the 1970s.

speaker: LACKER
text: That transition out, I think, would be made more difficult if we have this off-balance-sheet thing.

speaker: LACKER
text: I was stunned to learn in the staff memos that if this had full faith and credit, our books would be consolidated with the U.S. government.

speaker: LACKER
text: To me, that has some optical characteristics that I think are dangerous for us as an institution.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’d be seen as on balance sheet and yet outside of appropriations.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I just don’t think we should go down that road.

speaker: LACKER
text: Hybrid ARMs—again, sort of clever tinkering.

speaker: LACKER
text: For us to go to these little markets and kind of try to pick up some effect just opens us to rent-seeking.

speaker: LACKER
text: Maybe we’ve gotten good at handling it, but it just doesn’t seem worth it to me.

speaker: LACKER
text: As for the facilities, I would have terminated them all.

speaker: LACKER
text: I wouldn’t have initiated any of them anyway, but given the Board’s decision, I’m willing to go along with the foreign central bank swap arrangement.

speaker: LACKER
text: But let me say about rescinding the GSE facility that I am wildly enthusiastic.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I’ll help you with your time, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Everything I believe has already been said by one person or another.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Just very quickly, let me summarize a few things.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there was a lot of support for Brian’s recommendations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The only issue I heard was some discussion about raising the bid rate on the TAF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: You can raise the rate by cutting the quantity or by raising the rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think the optics are a little bit risky to be raising the rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I would be inclined to go with the recommendation that the staff has put forward.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: On the exit strategy, I guess I disagree with President Lacker.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think it’s important for us to have these other tools to diversify our ability to sterilize reserves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: A number of things are very interesting—reverse repos, collateralized lending, term deposits.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And we didn’t talk about redemptions, but redemptions actually are part of this, too.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s going to be significant over the next couple of years.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think most people agree that it would be very valuable to have as detailed as possible a discussion of the exit strategy in the Monetary Policy Report.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And I think there was good support for that, and we should proceed with that.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, on the Desk and flexibility, there didn’t seem to be much interest in giving you a great deal of flexibility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I want to make a couple of points.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One is, clearly, we don’t want purchases to be counterproductive, so if you are overwhelming the market, or something like that, you should either adjust or let the Committee know about it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think there was also a good bit of interest in your promoting liquidity and, in that respect, considering off-the-run securities, things of that sort.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I personally also would support lending securities.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that just adds to the liquidity in the market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll talk more tomorrow about asset purchases as a strategy, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just say to President Plosser and President Lacker, that we should close the GSE lending authority.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It turned out to be an inconvenient moment, but we will do that as soon as we can find an appropriate time.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Mr. Chairman, I think we should say for the record that Brian should draw no negative inferences from the fact that at his very first meeting President Lacker suggests that we should withdraw discretion from the Desk.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is the latest we’ve ever ratified the open market operations, I’m sure, in the history of the Federal Reserve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If there are no other comments, we need to take a few votes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, by the FOMC to ratify domestic open market operations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Next, by the FOMC to modify the authorization to allow the lending of agency debt.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there those who would like to be recorded in opposition to that?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The remaining votes are on the program extensions or modifications.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Mr. Chairman, could I recommend one change to the recommended resolutions?

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The draft that was circulated indicated that the New York Fed is directed “to suspend operations of” the TSLF options program.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I recommend substituting “to suspend auctions under” the TSLF options program.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The reason for the change is that there are options outstanding, and I don’t think the intent would be to prevent those options from being exercised.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We need a motion to extend the swap agreements.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is there anyone who objects?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The FOMC needs to extend the TSLF until February 1, understanding that the schedule 1 auctions will be suspended and the schedule 2 auctions reduced in size and that the options program will be suspended along the lines that Brian mentioned.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For the Board, we are asked to extend the AMLF, the commercial paper funding facility, the primary dealer credit facility, and the TSLF.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This includes the additional restrictions on the AMLF, which Boston will take care of, the reduced offerings under the TSLF, and the tightening of collateral conditions for the primary dealer credit facility.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And we will not extend the MMIFF, the money market facility.

speaker: MADIGAN
