text: On the tightening of the collateral restrictions, it’s likely that that will not be implemented immediately but some time in the next several months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That will be clear in the statement tomorrow?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Any objection from the Board?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Finally, from the Board, the resolution to scale back the TAF according to the schedule that Brian suggested.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Again, we’ll provide you with a press release as soon as possible, and it will go out on Thursday, at noon, I believe.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let us go on now to the staff presentation on the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Michael Kiley and Nathan Sheets will make the presentation.

speaker: KILEY
text: 6 I will be referring to the materials that were just distributed.

speaker: KILEY
text: Recent data suggest that economic activity has continued to contract, but at a more moderate pace than the breathtaking declines registered around the turn of the year.

speaker: KILEY
text: As shown in the top left panel of your first exhibit, job losses remained sizable through May, albeit smaller than those recorded earlier in the year; despite the moderation in job losses, the unemployment rate jumped another ½ percentage point last month, to 9.4 percent.

speaker: KILEY
text: In manufacturing, the rate of decline of industrial production (shown in the top right panel) has lessened somewhat in recent months, with the moderation in production cuts broad-based.

speaker: KILEY
text: We expect that real GDP will rise a bit in the third quarter.

speaker: KILEY
text: While the most significant factor behind the expected near-term pickup is the progress firms— especially automakers— have made on adjusting inventories (a topic I will return to shortly), the stabilization in household demand since late last year also plays an important role.

speaker: KILEY
text: As shown in the middle left panel, real consumer spending has been roughly stable since January.

speaker: KILEY
text: The stabilization in household demand is also apparent in the housing market.

speaker: KILEY
text: As shown in the middle right panel, sales of existing homes 6 The materials used by Messrs. Kiley and Sheets are appended to this transcript (appendix 6).

speaker: KILEY
text: through May, released earlier today, and sales of new homes through April have been roughly flat since late last year.

speaker: KILEY
text: In contrast to the stabilization in household demand, recent data suggest that business outlays have continued to contract.

speaker: KILEY
text: As shown in the bottom left, shipments of nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft (the red line) continued to trend down through April.

speaker: KILEY
text: And, with new orders well below shipments, we expect further near- term declines.

speaker: KILEY
text: We will receive information on orders and shipments through May tomorrow morning.

speaker: KILEY
text: As shown to the right, we expect real GDP to fall at an annual rate of 1 percent this quarter, and to rise ¾ percent in the third quarter.

speaker: KILEY
text: The top panel of exhibit 2 lists some of the key factors shaping our medium-term outlook.

speaker: KILEY
text: The outlook for inventories drives much of the contour over the second half of this year.

speaker: KILEY
text: As shown by the blue bars in the middle left panel, firms’ efforts to trim bloated inventories in the first half of the year were a sizable drag on GDP.

speaker: KILEY
text: In the second half, the slowing in the rate of liquidation provides an arithmetic boost to GDP growth.

speaker: KILEY
text: Next year, as inventories come into better balance, the advance in GDP is driven primarily by final sales.

speaker: KILEY
text: Returning to the box at the top, several factors shape our expectation that final demand will begin to improve next year.

speaker: KILEY
text: First, the stabilization in the housing market brings about an end to the drag from residential investment by early next year, and we expect housing construction to turn up modestly thereafter.

speaker: KILEY
text: More broadly, we expect risk premiums on corporate bonds and equities to decline further, which, in conjunction with the declines we have already seen and support from monetary policy, contribute to gains in household wealth and a lower cost of capital.

speaker: KILEY
text: The middle right panel provides some perspective on the impact of wealth on household outlays: The declines in household wealth associated with falling house and equity prices are estimated to have placed a substantial drag on consumption expenditures both last year and this year.

speaker: KILEY
text: We expect this drag to ebb by a percentage point next year, which, in conjunction with improved access to credit and the effect of stabilization in the labor market on household incomes, helps consumption expenditures to advance 2¾ percent in 2010.

speaker: KILEY
text: The bottom left panel presents the familiar accelerator mechanism, where business fixed investment as a share of output (shown in red) tends to track, with a lag, the growth rate of output (shown in black).

speaker: KILEY
text: We expect the deceleration in output over the past year to damp business investment through early next year; thereafter, equipment and software spending is expected to pick up.

speaker: KILEY
text: However, spending on nonresidential structures is likely to continue to decline for some time, reflecting high vacancy rates, falling prices of commercial real estate, and persistently tight credit conditions in that sector.

speaker: KILEY
text: Putting the pieces together, we project that real GDP will advance a bit more than 1 percent at an annual rate over the second half of this year and about 3 percent next year, both higher than in the April Greenbook.

speaker: KILEY
text: The somewhat faster pace of growth relative to April reflects the positive effects of lower risk premiums on corporate debt and equity, a lower exchange value of the dollar, and a modestly better outlook for foreign activity, which together outweigh the heightened drag from higher mortgage rates and oil prices.

speaker: KILEY
text: Your next exhibit summarizes the inflation outlook.

speaker: KILEY
text: The readings on core PCE price inflation in March and April averaged ¼ percent; these gains were boosted by the response of producers to the increase in federal excise taxes on tobacco.

speaker: KILEY
text: Given the news in the May CPI report, we estimate that core PCE prices advanced a more moderate 0.1 percent in May.

speaker: KILEY
text: Turning to the panel at the right, we project the unemployment rate to rise to 10 percent by the end of this year and to edge down a bit in the second half of 2010.

speaker: KILEY
text: We have also boosted our estimate of the NAIRU a touch, to 5 percent, reflecting the accumulation of evidence that the high rates of permanent job losses in this recession will raise the level of frictional unemployment for a time.

speaker: KILEY
text: Our energy price forecast is shown in the middle left panel.

speaker: KILEY
text: With the price of oil projected to be about $15 a barrel higher, on average, over the projection period, we anticipate somewhat more acceleration in energy prices through the middle of next year than in the previous projection.

speaker: KILEY
text: Finally, we expect core import price inflation (shown at the middle right) to pick up over the second half of this year, reflecting, in part, the run up in non-oil commodity prices and the decline in the exchange value of the dollar.

speaker: KILEY
text: As shown by the green line in the bottom panel, we expect overall PCE inflation to slow from 1.4 percent this year to 1.1 percent in 2010.

speaker: KILEY
text: Core inflation is projected to slow a bit more.

speaker: KILEY
text: The projected deceleration in core inflation reflects the substantial drag induced by economic slack.

speaker: KILEY
text: Given the central role of economic slack in our projection, the next exhibit discusses uncertainty regarding our estimates of resource utilization.

speaker: KILEY
text: The upper two panels focus on the differences in the degree of slack signaled by our current estimates of the output gap and the unemployment gap—that is, the deviation of the unemployment rate from the staff estimate of the NAIRU.

speaker: KILEY
text: The panel to the left plots the output gap (the black line) and the unemployment gap (the red line, plotted on an inverted scale).

speaker: KILEY
text: As highlighted to the right, the output and unemployment gaps typically provide similar signals; this similarity is largely by construction, as we use information from developments in both product and labor markets to jointly inform our estimates of potential GDP and the NAIRU.

speaker: KILEY
text: However, a sizable discrepancy has opened up during this recession—with the unemployment gap suggesting an even greater degree of slack than suggested by the output gap.

speaker: KILEY
text: In the Greenbook, we highlighted several possible explanations for the discrepancy.

speaker: KILEY
text: First, the GDP data, as currently published, may understate the contraction in real activity; indeed, the data on Gross Domestic Income, which in principle estimate overall economic activity as does GDP, have been significantly weaker than GDP since 2007.

speaker: KILEY
text: Second, labor force participation may currently be boosted to an unusual degree by the Extended Unemployment Compensation (or EUC) program, by the declines in wealth and their effect on the labor supply of near- retirees or other workers, or by other factors, such as an unusual concentration of job losses among individuals with strong labor force attachment; such unusual boosts to participation would have a large influence on the unemployment gap but not much effect on the estimated GDP gap.

speaker: KILEY
text: Finally, we may currently have underestimated the size of shifts in the NAIRU or other elements of potential, possibly contributing to mismeasurement of slack.

speaker: KILEY
text: Indeed, we often change our estimate of output gaps with hindsight.

speaker: KILEY
text: The panel at the middle left shows how our current estimates of the output gap (the black line) differ from the initial estimates we made over the history of the last 20 years (the green line); such differences may reflect revisions to data, changes in the staff’s methodology, and the fact that underlying trends are more easily detected looking backward than looking forward.

speaker: KILEY
text: Nonetheless, the revisions over the past two decades are not especially large: The root-mean-squared error from the initial to current estimate is less than one percentage point over this period.

speaker: KILEY
text: This size of revision is much smaller than that found in some academic studies that focused on the 1970s or early 1980s.

speaker: KILEY
text: Another way to assess uncertainty regarding resource utilization is to compare estimates of slack derived from different methods.

speaker: KILEY
text: As highlighted in the box at the middle right, different methods will imply different estimates of potential GDP.

speaker: KILEY
text: I consider estimates from three methods.

speaker: KILEY
text: The first is the staff estimate, which is loosely based on a growth accounting approach along with a number of underlying models (related to productivity dynamics, Okun’s law, and the Phillips curve, for example).

speaker: KILEY
text: The second is a trend-cycle decomposition of GDP using a simple Phillips curve in which inflation is a function of the output gap, a model that has been used in many academic studies.

speaker: KILEY
text: The third is derived from a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (or DSGE) model developed at the Board.

speaker: KILEY
text: This model, called EDO for Estimated, Dynamic, Optimization-based model, consists of a set of equations for the spending, production, and wage and price decisions of households and firms that are derived from utility- and profit-maximization under model-consistent expectations.

speaker: KILEY
text: The bottom panel presents the range of estimates generated by these methods, the 90 percent confidence interval around this range, and the staff’s estimate of the output gap.

speaker: KILEY
text: First, uncertainty is significant: the 90 percent confidence interval for the second quarter of this year spans from about -2 percent of potential GDP to about -8 percent of potential GDP.

speaker: KILEY
text: Second, the staff’s estimate of the output gap is in the lower half of the confidence interval, but it is not the most negative estimate; the estimate from the DSGE model is more negative, at a bit below -7 percent.

speaker: KILEY
text: Finally, the entire confidence interval for the output gap is below zero, by the largest margin seen over the past two decades.

speaker: KILEY
text: In summary, it seems highly likely that the economy currently is operating with considerable slack.

speaker: KILEY
text: Your final exhibit focuses on two other risks to the inflation outlook.

speaker: KILEY
text: As discussed in the top left box and shown in the upper right, long-run inflation expectations have been reasonably well anchored for some time.

speaker: KILEY
text: In our projection, this prevents a sharper deceleration in inflation.

speaker: KILEY
text: However, an unmooring of expectations is a risk: For example, expectations could shift down markedly in response to the weak economy and decelerating wage gains; alternatively, expectations could ramp up, perhaps in response to our expanding balance sheet.

speaker: KILEY
text: Another important risk surrounding our inflation projection relates to the links between resource utilization and inflation, discussed in the middle panels.

speaker: KILEY
text: Inflation appears less sensitive to resource utilization than in the past; for example, the middle right panel presents estimates of the slope of a simple Phillips curve using rolling 20-year samples; these show a lower sensitivity of inflation to utilization in the most recent data.

speaker: KILEY
text: This apparent reduction in sensitivity is one factor that contributed to our projection that inflation will decelerate by less than it did during earlier periods of substantial slack.

speaker: KILEY
text: But it is possible that the recent data are leading us astray, because reliable identification of the slope of the Phillips curve may require large movements in utilization.

speaker: KILEY
text: The post-2003 estimates plotted in the chart are based on sample periods that exclude the early 1980s, and they may not be a reliable guide now that we have reentered a period of high unemployment.

speaker: KILEY
text: If the effect of utilization on inflation were similar to that apparent during the early 1980s disinflation, we could see deflation.

speaker: KILEY
text: The bottom panels illustrate these risks using two alternative simulations from the Greenbook.

speaker: KILEY
text: In the first, we assume that long-run inflation expectations (corresponding to the PCE price index) rise 1 percentage point, to 3 percent, by early next year.

speaker: KILEY
text: This increase becomes partially self-fulfilling, and core PCE inflation averages 1½ percent in 2010 and then climbs steadily, reaching 2½ percent by 2013.

speaker: KILEY
text: Given the stronger price outlook, the federal funds rate lifts off from zero a year earlier than in the baseline.

speaker: KILEY
text: The second simulation (labeled deflation) assumes an effect of slack on inflation and an accelerationist structure to the Phillips curve more consistent with models estimated over sample periods including the 1970s and early 1980s.

speaker: KILEY
text: As a result, core prices are flat or falling through 2011, and only rising slowly thereafter.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Although a wide array of asset prices plays a role in our forecast, the dollar holds a special place in the hearts of those of us in the International Finance Division.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the top left panel, the broad real dollar has moved down significantly since its peak in March.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As displayed in the middle panel, the dollar has posted large declines in recent months against many currencies of the advanced foreign economies, or AFEs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The dollar has also depreciated significantly against emerging market, or EME, currencies (shown on the right), which has prompted a number of these countries, including Brazil, Russia, and several in emerging Asia, to intervene in foreign exchange markets to temper the pace of their currency’s rebound.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, however, the dollar has essentially moved sideways since the U.S. payrolls release on June 5, as the less-grim-than-expected report pushed up the path of short- term U.S. interest rates relative to those abroad.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Although the dollar has declined substantially over the past few months, it still has not reversed the sharp rise posted in the second half of 2008 and early this year, as financial market participants sought refuge in U.S. Treasuries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We believe that the primary reason for the dollar’s recent depreciation is an unwinding of this flight to safety, partly predicated on an improving outlook for the global economy.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The marked rebound in some previously distressed EME currencies is consistent with this hypothesis.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, as shown in the middle left, the spreads on BBB corporate bonds have declined, most steeply in the United States, but elsewhere as well.

speaker: SHEETS
text: And global equity prices (shown on the middle right), despite retreating some in recent sessions, have rebounded significantly on balance in recent months.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition to an increase in risk appetite, some currencies—such as the Canadian and Australian dollars and the Brazilian real—have been supported by a rise in commodity prices.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The spot price of WTI oil (the black line in the bottom left panel) has jumped to nearly $70 per barrel, up $15 per barrel since your last meeting, and nonfuel commodity prices have increased about 10 percent on average.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These rises seem to signal an incipient increase in the demand for commodities, in light of recent—and expected future—improvements in global economic conditions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Notably, the International Energy Agency and the U.S. Department of Energy have revised up their forecasts of global oil demand.

speaker: SHEETS
text: And, as shown on the bottom right, the Baltic Dry Index—a measure of bulk shipping rates—has recently moved up, in line with a rebound in Chinese purchases of iron ore and other commodities.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Some market commentary has also linked the dollar’s recent decline to concerns about the U.S. fiscal outlook and the extent of Treasury issuance.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As seen in the first panel of your next exhibit, U.S. Treasury yields have recently moved up more than sovereign yields abroad, but we see this difference as largely reflecting an unwinding of flight-to-safety flows.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Moreover, although sovereign CDS premiums (the top right panel) have increased some of late, they have not risen disproportionately in the United States relative to other countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Indeed, the dollar continued to depreciate against the pound even after the United Kingdom was put on a credit watch by S&P in mid-May.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Other observers have attributed the dollar’s decline to anxieties about future U.S. inflation, but it is difficult to square this view with various measures of inflation expectations, which seem reasonably well anchored—as Michael Kiley has shown.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Your next panels focus on the U.S. external sector.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the table, we see net exports adding about 1 percentage point to U.S. economic growth in the current quarter, with the decline in imports continuing to outpace that of exports.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Thereafter, net exports should subtract about ½ percentage point from growth in the second half of this year and a ¼ percentage point in 2010, as the recovery of imports is seen to be somewhat stronger than that of exports.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The relative strength of imports reflects several factors.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First, notwithstanding the dollar’s recent depreciation, it is still up about 10 percent over the past year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In light of the long lags in our trade equations, the exchange rate is likely to be a net source of stimulus for imports and drag on exports for some time.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, as shown on the right, with U.S. and foreign GDP growth expected to proceed at roughly comparable paces through the forecast period, the persistently higher income elasticity of U.S. imports—the so-called Houthakker-Magee asymmetry—should also boost import growth relative to export growth.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As seen in the bottom left panel, the current account deficit in the first quarter narrowed to less than 3 percent of GDP, the lowest reading in a decade.

speaker: SHEETS
text: However, our forecast calls for the deficit to widen again, to about 4 percent of GDP by the end of next year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition to the relative strength of real imports, which I just discussed, the run-up in oil prices plays a key role in this projection.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown on the right panel, the oil import balance—which had improved by $300 billion in recent quarters—is poised to deteriorate.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Your next exhibit examines the outlook for foreign activity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Aggregate GDP growth abroad (line 1 of the table) contracted at an 8½ percent annual rate in the first quarter, the sharpest decline on record.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But recent data have signaled that the pace of contraction slowed significantly in the second quarter and, indeed, have prompted us to mark up our forecast.

speaker: SHEETS
text: We now expect foreign growth to rise to roughly 1¾ percent during the second half of this year and to around 3 percent in 2010.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The recovery is expected to be rather lackluster, as households and firms around the globe remain conservative in their spending decisions and the flow of credit remains anemic as financial institutions repair their balance sheets.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the advanced foreign economies, recent survey data, such as purchasing managers’ indexes, are well off their recent lows and are now close to levels that signal a stabilization of activity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In addition, a few pieces of so-called hard data for these countries, including retail sales (the right panel) and industrial production (not shown), seem to be flattening out.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Consistent with these admittedly fledgling signs of stabilization, our forecast for the AFEs (line 3 in the table) calls for economic growth to rise slowly from the first quarter’s 7½ percent plunge to roughly zero in the second half of this year and to nearly 2 percent next year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This forecast is a few tenths higher than in April, in line with recent data and the improvement in financial conditions.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The trajectory of our forecast is also helped by a swing in the contribution from inventories in some countries, as firms have quickly drawn down their stocks in recent quarters.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Monetary policy is another supportive factor.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As you know, central banks in these economies have cut rates to very low levels and are implementing unconventional policy measures in an effort to stimulate economic activity.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Fiscal stimulus—the bottom left panel—should also bolster activity this year.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But the fiscal boost falls off markedly next year in the AFEs, highlighting a risk that their recoveries may stall if a rebound in private demand is not well entrenched.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Moreover, labor market conditions in these economies are likely to worsen for a while.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The middle panel shows projections of unemployment rates for the foreign economies from a simple model that regresses the unemployment rate on GDP growth and lags of both variables.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This framework indicates that unemployment rates abroad are likely to continue rising until well into 2010 or even later, and European policymakers themselves have expressed deep concerns about the near-term trajectory of the labor market.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Consistent with these observations, our forecast sees activity in the advanced foreign economies remaining quite soft, with their output gaps (the right panel) only stabilizing next year and generally lagging the U.S. recovery.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As shown in the table at the top of your next exhibit, GDP in the emerging market economies (line 1) plunged at a 9¾ percent rate in the first quarter, including a 21½ percent drop in Mexico (line 4).

speaker: SHEETS
text: GDP in these economies is projected to decline slightly in the current quarter and then gradually accelerate, with growth reaching 4½ percent in 2010.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This recovery is supported by a projected further recovery in capital flows, continued stimulus from macroeconomic policies, and strengthening global demand.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The Mexican economy again contracted sharply in the second quarter, depressed by the flu outbreak, but we see those effects as being quickly reversed.

speaker: SHEETS
text: The EMEs are showing some marked signs of improvement, especially China.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As seen in the middle left panel, China’s PMI has moved up to a reading that our empirical work indicates is consistent with GDP growth of above 5 percent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As for harder data, the 12-month growth of Chinese retail sales has continued to hold up well, and that of fixed investment has risen to almost 40 percent, fueled by fiscal stimulus and rapid bank lending.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Also, as shown on the right, electricity production and imports—two indicators that had shown marked weakness—have rebounded vigorously of late.

speaker: SHEETS
text: All told, our sense is that the Chinese economy is in the midst of a moderate recovery, but the extent to which China will become an engine of growth for the region, or for the global economy more generally, remains to be seen.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In other emerging market economies, signs of stabilization are also becoming more apparent.

speaker: SHEETS
text: As in China, PMIs (the bottom left) have bounced back from their lows in a number of emerging Asian and Latin American economies.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Industrial production (the middle panel) has decreased at a slower pace or even moved back up, and retail sales (not shown) have righted themselves.

speaker: SHEETS
text: This strengthening performance appears to stem in part from an improvement in exports (the right panel), which have bottomed out or rebounded in many EMEs.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Brian Madigan will conclude our presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 7 I will be referring to the separate package labeled “Material for Briefing on FOMC Participants’ Economic Projections.” Exhibit 1 tabulates the central tendencies and ranges of your latest projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Corresponding information about your April projections is indicated in italics, and June Greenbook projections are included as memo items.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the upper left portion of the table, your forecasts for real GDP growth in 2009 have a central tendency of -1.5 to -1 percent.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That is an upward shift of about ¼ to ½ percentage point from April, reflecting increases to your projections for both halves of this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You indicated that the upward revision was in response to the better tone of the data releases and improvements in financial conditions over the intermeeting period.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your growth forecasts for 2010 and 2011 are similar to those you provided in April.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even though you project higher real GDP growth over the near term, all of you raised your forecasts of the unemployment rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendency in the fourth quarter of 2009 is now 9.8 to 10.1 percent, about ½ percentage point above your April projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You still expect that the unemployment rate will trend down during 2010 and 2011, but the levels remain about ½ percentage point above your April projections.

speaker: MADIGAN

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, each of you indicated that the unemployment rate in the fourth quarter of 2011 is likely to be well above your estimate of the long- run equilibrium unemployment rate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown in the lower half of the table, recent information has led you to raise your forecasts for headline and core inflation from those in April.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The central tendency of your projections for headline PCE inflation in 2009 is 1.0 to 1.4 percent, about ½ percentage point above that of April, and you made small upward revisions in 2010 and 2011.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Many of you noted that these upward revisions reflect the influence of higher-than-expected core inflation data and higher energy prices, and some pointed to higher inflation expectations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Most of you still project that inflation will stay around or below your view of “mandate-consistent” inflation through 2011, but your expectations for inflation continue to span a wide range.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Some see inflation slowing through 2011 in response to persistently high economic slack, while others see inflation rising above “mandate-consistent” inflation because of the influence of the rapid expansion of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet on inflation expectations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Over the near term, your views on the outlook are broadly similar to those of the staff.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Greenbook projections for real GDP growth, unemployment, and inflation for 7 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 7).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 2009 are within the central tendencies of your projections.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, by 2011 noticeable differences are evident.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The Greenbook’s real GDP growth forecast for that year is above the central tendency of your projections, while the staff forecasts for the unemployment rate and core inflation are below the central tendencies.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Several of you again noted explicitly that you do not share the staff’s view of inflation dynamics.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: That divergence in views helps explain why more than half of you anticipate that it will be necessary to begin moving the fed funds rate up appreciably earlier than envisioned by the Greenbook, which assumes that the federal funds rate will remain close to the zero bound through 2011.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: As shown by the left panels of exhibit 2, your views on the degree of uncertainty surrounding your projections have not changed appreciably since April.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Almost all of you see greater-than-usual uncertainty regarding your projections of both economic growth and inflation, reflecting the unusual nature of the shocks that triggered the current recession and our limited experience with nontraditional policy tools.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, as shown in the right-hand panels, more of you now judge that the risks to growth and inflation are roughly balanced.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: For economic growth, many of you see the recent economic and financial developments as having reduced downside risks.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Fewer of you now judge that inflation risks are skewed to the downside, and a large majority of you see inflation risks as balanced overall.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Mr. Chairman, that concludes our presentation.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But while I have the floor, could I note that I misspoke earlier when I said that the timing of the PDCF haircuts would be announced in the press release on Thursday.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Those haircuts aren’t published, so it wouldn’t make sense to put them in the press release.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But the Desk will inform the dealers at the appropriate time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you for the presentation.

speaker: FISHER
text: I just have some questions of Nathan.

speaker: FISHER
text: You mentioned the Baltic Dry Index in the context of Chinese iron ore imports.

speaker: FISHER
text: Chinese iron ore imports are far exceeding steel production, as you know.

speaker: FISHER
text: So my question is: How sustainable, in your opinion, is this recovery?

speaker: SHEETS
text: We have reason to believe that these Chinese purchases are playing a very special role here.

speaker: SHEETS
text: What is China doing with all of these commodities that they’re purchasing?

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think the answer has three parts.

speaker: SHEETS
text: First, some of these commodities are actually being consumed by Chinese firms in association with the fiscal stimulus that’s being put in place.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Second, some are being used to replenish inventory levels.

speaker: SHEETS
text: In the fall, when the Chinese and global economy hit something of a wall, many firms just backed away entirely from commodity purchases, and that is one of the reasons why the bottom fell out of the commodity market.

speaker: SHEETS
text: So those inventory levels are low, and they’re being brought back to normal levels.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Third, I think that there is some strategic purchasing going on in the Chinese economy right now.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Commodities are cheap, and they’re pretty confident that at some point they’re going to need to use them, so they’re buying things and stockpiling them.

speaker: SHEETS
text: My sense is that, of those three causes, the first one is indicative of early stages of a recovery in the Chinese economy.

speaker: SHEETS
text: I think that’s probably sustainable.

speaker: SHEETS
text: These inventory-based explanations are less sustainable, so it wouldn’t surprise me if, over time, Chinese purchases flattened out, or even came back from where they are today.

speaker: SHEETS
text: Now, if that happens in the context of a broader global recovery, less demand for basic materials from China would be offset by increased demand from other countries.

speaker: SHEETS
text: But I think there is a risk that the commodity markets have gotten ahead of themselves and that the Chinese will stop buying at this furious pace, and we’ll see a little bit of unwinding of the increases in commodity prices that we’ve seen over the last few months.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The PCE energy prices seem to be coming off in the forecast into 2010, while the oil commodity price continues to rise slightly, suggesting it’s non-oil energy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Can you explain what the thinking is there?

speaker: KILEY
text: I think that’s mainly just looking at rates of changes versus levels.

speaker: KILEY
text: It’s true that the level in 2010 is picking up, but the rate of change is decelerating, because we’ve seen a big run-up right now in oil prices, and that will be passed through over the second half of this year.

speaker: EVANS
text: Brian, I just wanted to ask you a question.

speaker: EVANS
text: Taking note of the extremely large range on the inflation forecast for core PCE, is this outside of historical experience?

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t mean the history of our projections—we haven’t been doing it that long.

speaker: EVANS
text: But have we seen this kind of range among professional forecasters, even taking note of the fact that they might want to market their forecasts in a particular way because they’ve got different jobs than we do?

speaker: EVANS
text: It seems very large, and, frankly, it challenges your ability to listen to all of the commentary around the room in an even-keeled way, it seems to me.

speaker: EVANS
text: Well, that’s my reaction—speaking of shipping.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: I don’t know the answer to your question, President Evans, but it is, as I noted in my remarks, fairly striking.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: Just relative to the Greenbook stochastic simulations or the confidence intervals, even that wide range in 2011 is within the 70 percent confidence interval of the forecast.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: So it’s a sad statement on forecasting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I appreciate the discussion about measures of slack and output gaps, and I was particularly struck by the measures that were produced by the EDO model.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the Bluebook, your description of the construction of the output gap is not the way I normally think of it—it looks like some long-run trend or steady-state model.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Most of these stochastic, general equilibrium models think about equilibrium output being at a point in time, and then you get shocked away from that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The difference between what might be produced by a sticky price model versus a flexible price model gives you some measure of the difference between what’s feasible and what you actually get.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But you’ve defined the output gap in a much different way, using what looks like some concept of steady state, and I was a little puzzled by that choice.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Of course, in your discussion you highlighted the fact that that actually led to the EDO model having a very large output gap rather than a somewhat smaller one.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Most of these DSGE models lead to much more volatile measures of what you might think of as equilibrium or potential output at a point in time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If you sort of rethink, then, the range of where potential output might be in terms of what different models give you, I guess I wouldn’t have selected that subset, I would have selected a little different subset.

speaker: KILEY
text: A lot of that is jargon, terminology.

speaker: KILEY
text: We were trying to create some definitions that could be consistently applied across many models.

speaker: KILEY
text: So certainly in our model there’s a natural rate of output or an equilibrium rate of output that would be consistent with economic efficiency according to that model or with the absence of wage and price rigidities according to that model.

speaker: KILEY
text: Those two wouldn’t necessarily be the same.

speaker: KILEY
text: But one could have many different definitions of the natural rate of output or the equilibrium rate of output.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It depends on your model.

speaker: KILEY
text: We’ve published papers on using that model and constructing those measures.

speaker: KILEY
text: Those measures depend upon a set of assumptions regarding certain elements in the structure of the economy that many models don’t even make assumptions about.

speaker: KILEY
text: So we couldn’t compare that concept with a time-series model, like the trend-cycle decomposition of GDP.

speaker: KILEY
text: Nor could we compare that necessarily with the staff’s estimate; in putting together potential output, the staff takes a long-run growth accounting view and doesn’t think about what would happen if, for example, it removed all price and wage rigidities for the economy.

speaker: KILEY
text: We wanted to place all of our models on an equal footing, so we took a very standard definition of potential output for this exercise for the EDO model—the Beveridge–Nelson definition.

speaker: KILEY
text: The model has a representation of the economy that has stochastic trends and unit roots and all of these things in it, and we can crank through all of that machinery and generate a long-run forecast for output, just as you could in a time-series model, or in the FRB/US model, or in basically any model.

speaker: KILEY
text: We considered that to be a really good thing, because we can actually use the same idea across models—we’re not mixing apples and oranges.

speaker: KILEY
text: When we do that in this model, there’s a lot of slack right now.

speaker: KILEY
text: Other models of a similar type could give you a different answer—it could be that the natural rate of output gives you a very different answer.

speaker: KILEY
text: So you have to think about why you want to look at all of these concepts, and think about what you’re comparing across different models.

speaker: KILEY
text: This seemed like the simplest way to compare across models.

speaker: KILEY
text: In response to a different question, you might want to use a different concept.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I guess I don’t disagree with anything you’ve just said, except that I think it’s important to note that the concept of potential output is not model-free.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Therefore, we have to think hard about what this construct looks like.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: At some level, you’re making some assumptions about what that concept means, and that concept can differ quite a bit across models that one might choose from.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That’s what makes all of this hard in sort of figuring out what the interpretation might be.

speaker: KILEY
text: That’s absolutely right, and I just want to clarify one thing.

speaker: KILEY
text: The definition of “potential” here is a statistical definition that’s consistent with the model.

speaker: KILEY
text: We didn’t say, “Okay, we’re going to use this statistical method for the output gap,” and then put it in the model, and a bunch of Phillips curves, or a bunch of other things.

speaker: KILEY
text: The model is completely independent of that statistical machinery, and wages and prices and everything are being driven by all of the things that are appropriate in a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model.

speaker: KILEY
text: It’s trying to match the data, so when you generate a statistical measure of the output gap from this model, that statistical measure will forecast low inflation, because statistically that’s what it thinks happens in the data.

speaker: KILEY
text: That theoretical concept plays no role in the model—it’s a statistical concept.

speaker: LACKER
text: The version of the output gap that President Plosser was referring to, as opposed to this other statistical one—that’s the one that governs inflation dynamics in that model, isn’t it?

speaker: KILEY
text: In a simple three-equation model that’s true.

speaker: KILEY
text: But once you have sticky prices and sticky wages, monopoly power, other sources of distorting shocks, there is no simple relationship between what would happen in the absence of wage and price rigidities and what would happen to inflation.

speaker: KILEY
text: You could write down a model—a very simple model—where that would be true.

speaker: KILEY
text: But it need not be the case.

speaker: LACKER
text: But that one is related, somehow, in a complicated way, and the one you display is not, right?

speaker: KILEY
text: We forecast inflation with the model I’ve displayed.

speaker: KILEY
text: It forecasts very low inflation, because the output gap is so big.

speaker: KILEY
text: That’s not a behavioral relationship, that’s a statistical regularity.

speaker: LACKER
text: I thought you said the model stood apart.

speaker: LACKER
text: What does this gap measured from EDO have to do with inflation dynamics in the model?

speaker: KILEY
text: In the model, it doesn’t.

speaker: KILEY
text: But the model is trying to capture the data.

speaker: KILEY
text: You can simulate the model a million times, generate data, and then regress anything against anything and you find reduced-form relationships.

speaker: KILEY
text: The reduced-form relationships, consistent with the model and the data, are that output gaps predict low inflation.

speaker: KILEY
text: And that’s a reduced-form characteristic of the model that comes from its structure.

speaker: KILEY
text: It’s a pretty big and complicated model, as many are these days.

speaker: KILEY
text: But, because it tries to capture the data, and because it looks like that’s a regularity in the data, it’s generating that prediction.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Thank you for a very productive discussion.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Dinner tonight is purely social at the British Embassy at 7:30.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll begin tomorrow at 9:00 a.m. with the go-round.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we have a report on some data from Dave Stockton.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: First, Mr. Chairman, I think yesterday I broke my own record.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I said one thing at the meeting, and it was wrong.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: I would like to correct that.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: In response to President Evans’s observation about the wide dispersion of the inflation forecast in 2011, I think I said that the range of those forecasts was within the 70 percent confidence interval that we generate using stochastic stimulations.

text: Now, it is still the case that orders remain well below shipments and that overall equipment spending is still contracting, but I think we’d view these data as at least being supportive of our view that the pace of that contraction in equipment spending is lessening.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We’re going to get new home sales data later this morning.

speaker: STOCKTON
text: We don’t have those yet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ll begin our economic go-round with President Plosser.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: 8 The materials used by Mr. Stockton are appended to this transcript (appendix 8).

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Business conditions in the Third District remained relatively soft in May and early June.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nevertheless, the steepness of the decline appears to have eased rather dramatically, and the tone from our business contacts has noticeably improved.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: While our contacts don’t expect a strong upturn in business activity, they clearly see signs of stabilization in the near term.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The most positive indicator from our Business Outlook Survey, which was released last week, is manufacturing, and that index said that general activity improved from a minus 22.6 in May to a minus 2.2 percent in June—a 20-point swing, which is rather significant as these standards go.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This indicates essentially flat activity in the District now.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is considerably stronger than some of the national industrial production numbers, but consistent with some of the other regional manufacturing surveys.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our survey has a fairly long history—a little longer than Richmond’s, I believe, but I’m not sure.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And a movement above zero in this index likely marks the recession’s trough, based on past relationships between this index and NBER recession dates.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The future activity index moved up quite sharply in June to levels we haven’t seen in several years.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The most negative factor in the District was the unemployment report.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The unemployment rate in our three states rose another 0.4 percentage point and now stands at 8.4 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Payrolls have continued to fall, and, even in our surveys, the employment picture does not look terribly bright.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Based primarily on the expected labor market data, I’ve revised downward slightly my near-term forecast for 2009 and upped my unemployment rate forecast compared with April.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I have to confess that my forecast in April was on the outlier side of positive compared with many others.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: The basic shape of my forecast, however, remains very similar: A return to positive economic growth in the second half of this year and recovery gaining traction in 2010, picking up to about 3 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: This is actually similar to the Greenbook’s forecast, which has been revised up since our last meeting, so maybe we are converging here at some point.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: However, our inflation forecast continued to differ.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I see less deflationary pressures than the Greenbook baseline, and, even with its upward revision to inflation, I see greater risk of higher inflation not in the near term, but in the outyears.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I continue to be skeptical of putting too much weight on output gaps as predictors of inflation.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My reading of the literature suggests that gaps are difficult to measure with any precision, and this may be one reason that gap measures get little weight in empirical estimations of New Keynesian Phillips curve models.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: From the staff discussion yesterday on the range of gap measures, it appears we may have very different perceptions about how to go about constructing the appropriate measure of potential output.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Nevertheless, I think it was interesting.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, the estimates reported yesterday showed a very wide range of views of what the output gap may be—from something like minus 7 or 8 percent to minus 2 or 3 percent.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We view that as being a range of uncertainty about the magnitude of the gap.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In a simple Phillips curve model, that may imply a difference of between 200 and 300 basis points in what a Taylor rule might imply about the fed funds rate.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: That’s a pretty large difference in policy stance, so that may suggest very different policies.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we are closer to the smaller measure of the output gap than to the larger measure, it also means that we may have to raise rates sooner than we might think.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In Philadelphia’s own DSGE forecasting model, we actually get considerably higher inflation pressures going forward than the Greenbook baseline shows, particularly if the fed funds rate stays at zero through 2012.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given the difficulties in estimating and forecasting inflation, I do think we need to consider alternative forecasts seriously.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: With the aggressive monetary policy actions we have taken, I think this means looking at the possibility that our own inflation forecast possesses clear risks to the upside and preparing ourselves and the public for the possibility that we may have to act sooner rather than later.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In addition, the size of our balance sheet might complicate our ability to respond as rapidly as necessary to curtail inflation pressures.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And while inflation expectations have so far remained anchored, I think we have to be cognizant of the fact that this might change if agents become convinced that projected fiscal deficits will be monetized or if we fail to act in a timely manner.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: For these reasons, I think we should be very cautious of being overly confident that we can leave monetary policy accommodation in place as long as the Greenbook suggests without some very bad consequences on the inflation front.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Needless to say, with that perspective in mind, the fed funds rate path embedded in my forecast is considerably steeper than the Greenbook’s, which holds rates at zero through 2011.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe we will need to begin raising rates by early next year at the latest and throughout the forecast horizon, to at least 3½ or 4 percent by the fourth quarter of 2011.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t believe we can keep the fed funds rate at zero and expect to achieve anything close to our inflation objective or maintain our credibility in achieving that objective over the longer run.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We can say what we please, but it cannot substitute for action.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Our assessment of the output gap will be central to how the Committee thinks about the appropriate time to change course and begin to tighten, and we may have to do so in a fairly rapid way.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we dramatically overestimate the size and persistence of the output gap and wait, we will be too late to stem significant inflation risk.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we also will need to monitor carefully quantities of various kinds, whether it be bank lending or other measures.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In the past, our operating procedures have constrained reserves deliberately through our control of the fed funds rate and through limiting reserves to the marketplace.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Now those reserves are already out there, in the form of excess reserves in the banking system.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: When banks decide it’s time to start lending again, those reserves can move from excess reserves into bank lending very quickly, and they will not need to be supplied by us as in the old operating regime.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Therefore, I think this transition might be very quick—I don’t mean days, but certainly over a series of months.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Depending on what we view as the appropriate equilibrium interest rate, our setting for the fed funds rate or the IOER may have to move up quite rapidly, because the opportunity cost of funds in terms of bank lending may move up fairly rapidly in the process.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we’re going to face some severe challenges at the turning point when we have to make the decision to move.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: It may come sooner than we think, and it may have to be more rapid than we think.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we have to prepare ourselves for that possibility, and through our communications, prepare the public for that eventuality as well.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I want to add my thanks to those of President Evans for the improved amplification.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I could hear President Plosser here very well.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the last two weeks, because of the possible gap between reports of increasingly optimistic sentiment and underlying reality, the Atlanta Bank took great care to collect a lot of input from directors’ business and financial contacts.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Reports from the business community clearly indicate greater stability.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: That said, the tone of these reports suggests an economy that is still exceptionally fragile.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: There is not much optimism among my contacts for a strong recovery.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Business capital spending is being indefinitely postponed, and there is little appetite for hiring, even for seasonal or temporary positions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: One Atlanta director, a partner in a top management consulting firm, stated that they are doing very little growth work and that most of their large corporate strategy assignments relate to positioning for subdued business conditions for the next five years.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the financial sector, banks are still very cautious in credit extension.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: C&I loan demand remains quite soft, and mortgage demand fell sharply when mortgage rates rose above 5 percent.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The outlook I submitted is little changed from late April.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I expect this will be an exceptionally slow recovery.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I find the alternative simulations presented in this meeting’s Greenbook to be quite pertinent.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: My outlook has elements of the scenarios for both the slower recovery and labor market damage.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In my view, a slow restoration of financial markets will limit credit availability well into 2010, and the rebuilding of wealth is likely to be spread over several years.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: These influences will inhibit the usual forces of recovery.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: The significant reorganization of the economy could keep the unemployment rate elevated for years into the recovery.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As regards prices, the recent rise in oil and some other commodity prices could raise inflation statistics this summer, but we’ve also seen downward price pressure elsewhere in the data.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Overall, I’m in the camp that is not overly concerned about inflation for the medium term.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I continue to think the prospect for deflation is roughly balanced against the likelihood that inflation will accelerate above a rate consistent with price stability.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But even if I am somewhat sanguine about inflation, I acknowledge a high level of uncertainty about the inflation outlook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I also note that concern about inflation expressed anecdotally on the part of my business contacts is clearly rising; this concern seems to be connected to apprehension about how the Fed will manage its balance sheet going forward.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I see it, the context of our policy discussion involves the potential of a widening separation in public and market sentiment between the expectation of policy reversal and exit and a more uncertain and fragile underlying reality.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am concerned that too much talk of exit could get ahead of reality.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As several said yesterday, this presents a particularly delicate communication challenge coming out of this meeting.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The reports from my District have revealed lingering concerns about how the economy will evolve over the rest of this year.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Most of my contacts agree that their worst fears for the economy seem less likely to be realized now, but they are still far from optimistic.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Expectations for the remainder of the year varied from further reduction in activity levels to a very moderate resumption in economic growth.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Reports of hiring are still rare, and several contacts from larger companies suggest that they are working on another round of layoffs.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: From my District vantage point, it still looks like a very gradual recovery process.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The inflation picture is mixed.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I am hearing a growing number of contacts expressing fears of inflation driven by rising commodity prices and ballooning fiscal deficits, but I am also hearing widespread reports of downward pressures on wages and benefits.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Synthesizing these reports and the incoming data into an outlook continues to be challenging.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I have revised up slightly my output forecast from the April meeting, as business fixed investment, although still a considerable drag on growth, declines less steeply than in my previous outlook.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: While business spending on equipment is likely to pick up in the second half of the year, spending on structures, as was mentioned yesterday, will probably take longer to recover.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Some recent favorable readings from the housing indicators have also attenuated the near-term decline in residential investment in my outlook and have raised the prospect for a turnaround in housing in the second half of the year.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My forecast still has the unemployment rate peaking at just over 10 percent in early 2010.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: The continued rapid rise in unemployment certainly remains an important drag on the economy as new jobs are hard to find for many of the workers who were laid off.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: I revised up my inflation forecast for 2009, but I left my longer-term inflation projection on a gradual path towards 2 percent.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As we discussed yesterday, the latest Survey of Professional Forecasters has a broader variance around the longer-term inflation trend, but the median inflation projection is largely unchanged.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: And, as we said yesterday, we have seen an unusually wide range of inflation projections in this round of the Committee’s submissions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We know that the liquidity problems in the TIPS market have made that a more difficult indicator to use to deem where inflation expectations are.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: We have done some work at the Cleveland Fed using a different method of looking at the TIPS data, and those results suggest that inflation expectations have returned to pre-crisis levels.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Apparently, these results have been confirmed by the staff of the San Francisco Fed, who used a different methodology but came to the same conclusion.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Consequently, although inflation expectations are still volatile, I do think that it is reasonable to characterize them as anchored.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In my view, the risks to the forecast remain to the downside for output, because the improvements in the real economy that we are seeing remain nascent and, I think, fragile.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: However, I did revise my views of the risks around the inflation forecast to “balanced”—they are large but symmetric.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: This remains a very challenging period to evaluate the incoming data, and even a smaller gap doesn’t mitigate the fact that the economy is still contracting in the current quarter, and most projections show limited growth for a considerable period.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Despite my forecast for higher inflation compared with the Greenbook, my overall outlook leaves the economy a fair distance from needing a tighter monetary policy.

speaker: EVANS
text: Over the past several weeks, my key concern about the outlook has been whether the improvements in the forecast would be sustained.

speaker: EVANS
text: Were the green shoots hardy enough to survive adverse weather?

speaker: EVANS
text: The news I’m hearing from my directors and other business contacts seems tentatively consistent with this improved forecast now being on a somewhat more solid footing.

speaker: EVANS
text: Before the last meeting, my contacts reported that activity was still declining, but that the pace of deterioration was slowing.

speaker: EVANS
text: Now, two months later, they characterize this as a stabilization that is in train.

speaker: EVANS
text: I see these comments as being in broad agreement with the Greenbook’s assessment of economic activity.

speaker: EVANS
text: My discussion with the U.S. CEO of ArcelorMittal is a good summary of how things are likely improving in a number of industrial segments.

speaker: EVANS
text: The parent company is the largest steel producer in the world.

speaker: EVANS
text: Last summer, steel prices peaked at over $1,000 a ton, and inventories were relatively lean throughout the industry.

speaker: EVANS
text: As the recession intensified, inventories climbed and prices fell.

speaker: EVANS
text: Just recently, prices were down to $380 a ton, which, I’m told, just covered variable costs.

speaker: EVANS
text: Since late last year, the firm has cut production sharply and repeatedly.

speaker: EVANS
text: Today their capacity utilization is about 40 percent, and they are running only two of their nine blast furnace facilities.

speaker: EVANS
text: During this period, steel service centers, which compete by buying steel and distributing from inventories, have been running down their stocks.

speaker: EVANS
text: About three weeks ago, their de-stocking process seemed to end, and prices have risen modestly, by about $20 a ton.

speaker: EVANS
text: Currently Mittal sees production, shipments, and inventories all stabilizing.

speaker: EVANS
text: Looking to the summer, their order books for July are full, and they’re now deciding whether to fire up a third blast furnace in the middle of July for August production and delivery.

speaker: EVANS
text: To justify this increase to 55 percent capacity, they need sustainable future orders—today’s report seems helpful, perhaps—not just the end of de-stocking.

speaker: EVANS
text: Making this judgment about sustainability is difficult, in part because Mittal’s chief customers today are the non-bankrupt auto companies and other durable goods producers whose order flow can be chunky.

speaker: EVANS
text: So if GM and Chrysler improve, that would further support production decisions like this.

speaker: EVANS
text: I’ve heard stories similar to Mittal’s from other contacts.

speaker: EVANS
text: For example, a large, diversified tool and parts manufacturer said that some of its major customers have completed their de-stocking cycles, although they have not yet relayed plans to begin rebuilding inventory levels, so it’s not showing up in higher production yet.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, the continued restructuring process at Chrysler and GM is a positive factor for manufacturing output and particularly in our District.

speaker: EVANS
text: These reports seem consistent with our forecast of slow to modest GDP growth in the second half of 2009.

speaker: EVANS
text: Still, few businesses are reporting increasing activity, and the decision to raise production will be a close call for many firms for some time.

speaker: EVANS
text: Another important element solidifying the outlook is the improvement in credit conditions.

speaker: EVANS
text: Clearly, conditions continue to be challenging.

speaker: EVANS
text: Many businesses report that lines of credit are being reduced and borrowing rates are being adjusted upwards.

speaker: EVANS
text: But even businesses who say that access to credit is still a problem acknowledge that conditions are not as restrictive as they were a couple of months ago.

speaker: EVANS
text: High-quality firms have found that debt and equity markets have become quite receptive to new issuances, and the TALF appears to have been both directly and indirectly beneficial for credit markets, according to participants whom I have talked to.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the inflation front, I have been somewhat surprised that there has not been more downward momentum so far.

speaker: EVANS
text: As the Greenbook points out, inflation expectations have not moved down as expected.

speaker: EVANS
text: I did ask my staff to investigate quantitatively what the size of a labor reallocation story might be for the natural rate of unemployment.

speaker: EVANS
text: There’s a member of my staff who has some papers on reallocation, sort of a David Lilien-style measure of dispersion and how that translates into higher NAIRUs, and she updated that unobserved components model.

speaker: EVANS
text: The bottom line is that you can get the natural rate to move upwards of about 6 percent, but it’s really hard to get much more out of that.

speaker: EVANS
text: Even if you went as far as 7 percent, which the data do not indicate, that’s still quite a large resource gap.

speaker: EVANS
text: I continue to hear a great deal of concern that our expansive provision of liquidity, large-scale asset purchases, and future federal deficits pose medium- and longer-term risks on the inflation front.

speaker: EVANS
text: I know we can deal with these issues in a variety of ways, as we discussed yesterday.

speaker: EVANS
text: However, many of these programs do have exit costs that are somewhat larger than I previously thought.

speaker: EVANS
text: Our forecast continues to assume that resource slack and contained inflation expectations will result in a decline in inflation over the projection period.

speaker: EVANS
text: I do thank Dave for his clarification this morning.

speaker: EVANS
text: Frankly, I think he was more right than not.

speaker: EVANS
text: I didn’t realize, looking at the distribution, that there’s a cherry-picking to this—if you take out just the high and just the low, the range is about ½ to 2 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I think that’s closer to inside the 70 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’re not expecting as large a decline as is in the Greenbook.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’re looking for core PCE inflation to be closer to 1½ percent in 2010.

speaker: EVANS
text: Finally, from our January–March meetings to today, there has been a marked reduction in uncertainty and downside economic risks as I see it, especially downside skews.

speaker: EVANS
text: In March the abyss scenario weighed heavily on my list of concerns.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I favored what I will refer to as a robust control approach to policymaking, specifically: Try many programs in substantial size; give strong credence to their possible success in spite of their uncertain impacts; and hope that some or all would provide needed accommodation.

speaker: EVANS
text: Of course, we’re not out of the woods yet, but the likelihood of the abyss scenario has declined notably.

speaker: EVANS
text: In addition, I’ve been surprised by the reduction in disinflationary risks.

speaker: EVANS
text: So to my mind, these are very important developments.

speaker: EVANS
text: They lead me to put less weight on this robust control approach and move more towards the conventional weighing of the expected effectiveness and cost of these programs, and I do find myself moving back towards more balanced assessments of the necessary magnitudes for various nontraditional policies.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Like the Greenbook, the Boston Fed forecast now expects that we will reach an unemployment rate of 10 percent.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Unfortunately, this statistic probably understates the degree of weakness in labor markets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In discussion with small and medium-sized businesses in New England, it is striking how many firms have placed workers on part-time schedules and how many firms have reported reducing nominal wages to avoid further job cuts.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If New England’s firms are representative of the wider economy, these practices may have implications for the recovery.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: First, firms are likely to defer hiring not only until they are confident that the recovery has firmly taken root, but also until they have restored hours to those workers whose hours they have already reduced.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Second, wage pressures on inflation are likely to continue to be subdued, as firms in weak sectors of the economy defer wage increases until demand for their products increases.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In my forecast, the recovery is quite restrained, making it unlikely that we reach full employment during the forecast horizon.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The recovery will be slower if mortgage rates do not encourage buyers back into the market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While the 30-year mortgage rates have come down somewhat from the recent spike, they remain well above the rates earlier this spring.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Not surprisingly, loan applications have slowed, and Realtors report diminished foot traffic after the rates increased.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But higher rates may slow the recovery even further.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Higher rates will likely put downward pressure on housing prices.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: This, in turn, will further diminish household wealth, reducing consumption as households seek to recover from already large wealth losses.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In addition, lower house prices will likely add to the many households who struggle with the potential of home foreclosure.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: As I discussed briefly yesterday, an interesting aspect of the mortgage market during this recession is that five- and seven-year ARMs are not priced as attractively as they were earlier in this decade.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: If longer-term mortgage rates remain high, improved pricing of longer-term ARMs does have the potential to bring some borrowers back into the market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While financial markets have improved, they remain fragile.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The municipal bond market could still be roiled by the lack of political will by some states and municipalities to address their financial problems.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Bank lending could be affected if commercial real estate and consumer loans continue to deteriorate, forcing higher loan loss reserves, which, for many banks, are still moving slowly relative to the growth of nonperforming loans.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While the securitization market appears to have improved somewhat as a result of the TALF, it is unclear how the eventual removal of TALF financing and the possible legislation on securitization are likely to affect the recovery in this market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Overall, my forecast is not much different from the last FOMC meeting, and, frankly, that forecast implies uncomfortable outcomes for both unemployment and inflation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Higher mortgage rates have caused me to push out the housing recovery, and the recent labor report has raised my path of unemployment.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Many banks remain capital constrained, and I expect many more to be constrained as they need to increase loan loss reserves.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Thus, I place a low probability on rapid expansion of bank lending over the next two years.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Even by the end of 2011, I expect that the unemployment rate will be well above full employment and inflation will be well below my target.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In the Eighth Federal Reserve District, the decline in economic activity is slowing or stopped.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Still, there are no immediate signs of improvement during the summer or fall.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Business contacts are definitely subdued.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I might even describe them as resigned to sluggish economic performance for the foreseeable future.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In recent calls that I made, there were some reports of slower activity in the second half of May and into June, so we’ll see if that shows up in the numbers going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That worried me a little bit.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the national scene, my sense is that markets may have jumped ahead of the reality of the economy during the last 60 or 90 days.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That said, I am hoping for some improvement in the second half, but I think there’s a tremendous amount of uncertainty about where the economy will be going forward.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think we’re vulnerable to further shocks.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Shocks are unpredictable, so I don’t know where they would come from.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But when you’re down, other things can happen.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I also think that the longer that the recession drags on, the greater the likelihood that new problems can arise that would not have been problems if the economy had turned around sooner.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And I just wanted to say I remain concerned about the global nature of this recession, which I think is largely unprecedented in the postwar era.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’ve been concerned about possible deflation and a deflationary trap, that is, a steady state that we could actually get stuck in.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If we were to enter such a trap in 2009 or 2010, we would have a very hard time getting out.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The first priority for me has been to avoid this outcome, and that means building up inflation expectations.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think the probability that this will happen has fallen some.

speaker: BULLARD
text: For instance, the five-year TIPS inflation compensation has increased—it’s about 125 basis points now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I know there’s a lot of analysis about exactly how to look at that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: If you just take it at face value, it has improved a lot from very negative values in December and January, but it’s still not a lot of inflation over the next five years.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s below our inflation target, and you’d like to see it higher, I think.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, the Greenbook forecast has inflation declining further, so I don’t think we’re out of the woods on the deflation threat, although the outlook has improved a lot from what it was in the December-January time frame.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think we’re entering a period of volatile expectations in markets.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The markets are just not sure what to think about the unprecedented policy environment.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They’re looking at numbers that they have not seen before, and they’re not sure what to think—large budget deficits where the longer-term outlook is very unclear.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Given that, I think our purchase program looks like— and I put that in quotes: “looks like”—debt monetization.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t think anybody involved wants to go there, but that’s the appearance.

speaker: BULLARD
text: And you’ve got legislation pending that may appear to threaten Fed independence.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think the hard thing about our debt markets is that they’re global markets, so especially for those outside the U.S. who may not understand the subtleties of our politics, this just looks like a lot of debt issuance by the Treasury and some purchases by the central bank.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s just very hard to get away from that perception, and that has made me pessimistic about further expansion of our large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think current policies are pushing very hard on our credibility.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As I mentioned before, I don’t think we could get away with these policies if we were a smaller developing country.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Fortunately, we do have a large stock of credibility to draw upon, but we need to be careful.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Just because everything has gone well for a long time in the U.S. doesn’t mean it will continue to do so this time around.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Again, the policy response to this crisis has been unprecedented, so the current situation may not produce the outcomes that we hope for.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’m also concerned, along with President Plosser and others, about the emphasis in the narrative on a large output gap keeping inflation at bay into the indefinite future.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I don’t think inflation is a near-term problem, but it could be a medium-term problem.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I also think there are conceptual difficulties with the traditional output gap measures.

speaker: BULLARD
text: The empirical relationships are not that great.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So the moment is really ripe for a possible policy mistake along this dimension, since we’re coupling that with our unprecedented policy action.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that’s going to remain an issue for the FOMC for some time to come.

speaker: HOENIG
