text: Well, Mr. Chairman, in our District, clearly conditions do remain weak, but the information we are receiving suggests the contraction has lessened, and expectations for future growth have actually improved.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We are seeing some reductions in residential real estate inventories in the lower-priced housing sector, partly because house prices have adjusted and partly because of some credits for first-time home buyers.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Manufacturing continues to contract, but there are signs that the decline has moderated noticeably.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our May manufacturing survey showed that the pace of decline in production has actually reversed and in employment and capital spending it has stabilized.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Preliminary results from our June survey further indicate that we are close to almost recovery levels in terms of District manufacturing.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our energy sector, having fallen pretty significantly, has stabilized, but we are primarily producers of natural gas, so stabilizing is about as good as we expect for any time soon.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Commercial real estate remains a source of pretty considerable weakness.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Our directors and District business contacts indicate that a combination of higher vacancy rates and some difficulties in obtaining financing are really limiting that market in our region.

speaker: HOENIG
text: On the national front, our outlook isn’t a whole lot different from that of the Greenbook, except in one important way, and that is that we have a more aggressive policy path for interest rates.

speaker: HOENIG
text: They increase almost a year sooner than some outlined in the Greenbook.

speaker: HOENIG
text: In terms of the inflation outlook, we are not seeing any pressures towards deflation and, actually, not seeing any signs at this point towards inflation either.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So I see the risks as fairly balanced as we go forward.

speaker: STERN
text: Broadly speaking, District economic conditions continue to track the national economy for the most part, as is typically the case.

speaker: STERN
text: There’s pronounced weakness in business investment (both in commercial construction and in spending on equipment and software), signs of stabilization in consumer spending, and continued deterioration in the labor market, although recent declines in employment have not been as severe as those at the national level.

speaker: STERN
text: There are some encouraging signs in terms of sales activity in the residential real estate market not related to foreclosures or short sales.

speaker: STERN
text: And we do have a reasonably healthy agricultural sector and a reasonably healthy energy sector.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as the national outlook is concerned, my forecast is quite similar in most respects to the latest version of the Greenbook outlook.

speaker: STERN
text: I expect positive economic growth to resume momentarily and to be quite subdued initially for the reasons that have been previously well identified—continued strained credit conditions, negative wealth effects, significant job losses, and lots of excess capacity both in the services sector and in a variety of goods-producing industries, as well.

speaker: STERN
text: But given the pace and depth of the downturn, I’ve been asking myself, shouldn’t we expect perhaps a more typical recovery?

speaker: STERN
text: I haven’t been able to quite talk myself into that scenario yet, but I guess I wouldn’t entirely dismiss it.

speaker: STERN
text: In any event, I do expect momentum to build and growth to accelerate as we get further into 2010, and to accelerate further in 2011, basically because the problems that I just alluded to should be diminishing over time, and we’re in an environment of expansionary policies.

speaker: STERN
text: As far as inflation is concerned, I continue to expect inflation to remain relatively low, given appropriate policy.

speaker: STERN
text: And in this regard, I expect that the federal funds rate will have to start moving up in the latter half of next year, or early 2011 at the latest, in order to achieve that outcome.

speaker: LACKER
text: Fifth District economic conditions are pretty well aligned with the national situation, with activity stabilizing in some areas, though at a level that’s still pretty depressed.

speaker: LACKER
text: Our manufacturing index has risen above zero from deep into negative territory, and there are encouraging signs for orders, shipments, and, to a lesser extent, capital expenditures.

speaker: LACKER
text: Nevertheless, services, residential construction, and the labor market all remain depressed.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think it does appear that the real economy is reaching something of an inflection point.

speaker: LACKER
text: Since the turn of the year, real PCE, light motor vehicle sales, and single-family home sales, starts, and permits have leveled out and, in some cases, eked out small gains.

speaker: LACKER
text: Initial unemployment claims have steadied and have come off their early peak.

speaker: LACKER
text: Consumer sentiment indexes have bounced back from their lows.

speaker: LACKER
text: The ISM manufacturing survey rallied, as did many regional surveys.

speaker: LACKER
text: Encouragingly, the new orders component poked its head above 50, and, moreover, this morning’s durable goods report seems pretty positive.

speaker: LACKER
text: Equally heartening has been the improvement in financial market conditions.

speaker: LACKER
text: Equity prices for financial institutions are up significantly from their lows in early March.

speaker: LACKER
text: Bank CDS spreads have declined.

speaker: LACKER
text: A wide range of large banks have successfully issued equity and non-FDIC guaranteed debt.

speaker: LACKER
text: Three-month dollar LIBOR rates are below 1 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: Triple-B corporate bond yields are just below 8 percent, off from their 2008 year-end highs of 10 percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think all of this suggests a substantial reduction in risk premiums.

speaker: LACKER
text: And because the extent to which bank liabilities are government supported hasn’t changed materially over the horizon, the improvement is probably due to a better outlook for fundamentals.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the same time, these signs of stabilization do not by any means guarantee vigorous economic growth any time soon, and I don’t think they will prevent unexpected shocks, obviously.

speaker: LACKER
text: The stabilization in housing starts and auto sales is encouraging, but it’s occurring at extraordinarily low levels.

speaker: LACKER
text: The outlook for commercial real estate is not good—further increases in vacancies, delinquencies, and loan losses are in store.

speaker: LACKER
text: And many banks face further increases in credit card losses and commercial real estate losses as well.

speaker: LACKER
text: While, at this point, it looks as if these familiar features of cyclical downturns are going to prove manageable, they do suggest that we have a ways to go before the downturn is over and growth may be slow for a while.

speaker: LACKER
text: Since December, core PCE inflation, excluding tobacco, has come in fairly close to 1½ percent.

speaker: LACKER
text: But even though energy prices helped us late last year, gasoline prices have been increasing steadily over the last few months.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve seen a consistent pattern over the last several years of increases in energy prices followed by smaller but noticeable increases in core inflation with a lag of a couple of months.

speaker: LACKER
text: This pattern makes me skeptical of the Greenbook’s forecast that core PCE inflation is going to fall significantly over the next couple of months and quarters.

speaker: LACKER
text: And it leads me to expect core inflation to remain where it is, or, if anything, to rise over the next few months.

speaker: LACKER
text: Core inflation has been reasonably well behaved so far this year.

speaker: LACKER
text: Worries about future inflation have become disappointingly common over the last few months among financial market participants and among my contacts—people raise it independently.

speaker: LACKER
text: And a couple of Presidents have cited concerns that link that to what people see happening to our balance sheet.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think concerns about sustained deflation have evaporated more or less, and measures of inflation expectations have increased noticeably, obviously, since our last meeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: They’re back to levels consistent with those we saw before the middle of last year, levels we associated with price stability.

speaker: LACKER
text: Market commentary speculated about the possibility—we talked about this a lot yesterday—that the Fed will come under pressure to monetize future deficits, given the currently unsustainable upward path they seem to be on.

speaker: LACKER
text: We’ve been reasonably clear about our planned purchases, but we provided much less information, I think, about our reaction function.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think that’s an inevitable byproduct of the urge to preserve discretion, and this is an example of the extent to which discretion can be the enemy of clarity.

speaker: LACKER
text: That lack of clarity, I think, contributed to the belief—and maybe it’s not a predominant belief, but it is something you hear—that we might be setting a ceiling on long-term interest rates, kind of the way we did before the 1951 Accord, a period when monetary policy was very inflationary.

speaker: LACKER
text: In this context, the signs of stabilization in the real economy and financial markets make it unlikely that we could announce additional open market purchases without aggravating market concerns about inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: But, more broadly, whatever we do with the statement at this meeting, I think we should strive to add clarity.

speaker: LACKER
text: About exit, I think it’s too soon to hint that it’s imminent, but at the same time I think there would be a great benefit in clarifying the extent to which we believe we know how it would work and how we could accomplish that.

speaker: LACKER
text: And that’s sort of the delicate balance to strike in the Monetary Policy Report, I think.

speaker: LACKER
text: Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: YELLEN
text: At our meeting in late April, we had begun to see hopeful signs of impending economic recovery, and subsequent economic and financial developments have strengthened the view that the economy is bottoming out.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even so, the outlook over the next several years remains disturbing.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My modal forecast shows economic growth resuming next quarter, but I expect the recovery to be quite gradual.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The output and employment gaps are, at a minimum, quite large, so it will take a long time to regain full employment under current monetary and fiscal policy settings.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although downside risks have diminished, I remain concerned that the recovery is still fragile.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The news on housing has been good.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A broad array of data shows signs of stabilization, but the recent sharp rise in mortgage rates makes me worry about the future.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Several of my directors and advisory council members who are connected with the housing sector stress that the improved outlook for housing remains precariously tied to mortgage rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Recent data on consumer sentiment and spending show improvement due in part to the fiscal stimulus.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Even so, I continue to hear a flood of downbeat anecdotes on household buying patterns.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My contacts tell me that demand remains weak and that firms are cutting prices to generate sales, putting profit margins under tremendous pressure.

speaker: YELLEN
text: They note that consumers are continuing to shift from higher-cost discretionary items to lower-cost necessities.

speaker: YELLEN
text: A major discount retailer reports that for the first time in his memory consumers are passing up bulk purchases of food and other staples at discount prices in favor of smaller packages with higher unit prices, because they can’t come up with the money to carry the associated inventory.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This suggests very tight liquidity constraints.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Consumers seem particularly concerned about the tightening of credit card limits.

speaker: YELLEN
text: And, of course, labor markets continue to deteriorate badly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It’s a sign of how bad things really are that near euphoria broke out with the announcement of 345,000 nonfarm jobs lost in May.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The unemployment rate is soaring month by month, and, even worse, it appears to understate the true extent of the deterioration, given the unusually high incidence of permanent, as opposed to temporary, layoffs, and the unprecedented increase in involuntary part-time work.

speaker: YELLEN
text: On the bright side, overall financial conditions have certainly improved since we last met.

speaker: YELLEN
text: That bodes well for recovery.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It’s encouraging that so many banks have been able to raise private capital, and in many respects market stress has subsided.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The combination of falling risk spreads on bonds, higher stock prices, higher Treasury rates, and a lower dollar seems consistent with a greater appetite for risk, probably stemming from the positive tone of emerging economic data.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This development should be constructive for growth overall, but, as I said, I hope that the associated rise in mortgage interest rates doesn’t reverberate too strongly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With foreclosures on the rise, and house prices still falling, higher borrowing costs could stall the emerging rebound in residential construction, further impairing financial institutions and markets and, thereby, hampering the recovery more broadly.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My forecasts for output and employment are similar to the Greenbook’s, so I won’t go into the details.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I do want to emphasize that I anticipate a rather sluggish recovery, not the rapid V-shaped recovery we have frequently seen following deep recessions in the past.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The process of balance sheet repair that households and financial institutions are undergoing will result in subdued spending for an extended period, and monetary policies here and abroad are not able to play as big a role as usual in promoting recovery because of the constraint of the zero lower bound on short-term interest rates.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Given the uncertainties in the outlook, I very much appreciated the range of well- designed alternative simulations presented in the Greenbook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I noticed that even under the typical recovery simulation, which has much stronger growth than in the baseline, the unemployment rate remains well above the 5 percent NAIRU by the end of 2011, and inflation hovers around 1 percent.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This outcome reflects the large unemployment and GDP gaps estimated for the first quarter.

speaker: YELLEN
text: With a GDP gap of about 5½ percent, the economy is in a deep hole, and it will take a long time to climb out, even if growth is rapid.

speaker: YELLEN
text: This is a key consideration in designing optimal policy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: My forecast contains an estimate of the output gap similar to the Greenbook’s, but I’m well aware that the size of the gap is uncertain and sensitive to the precise methodology that’s used.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So for this forecast round, we assessed the level of the gap from a variety of different perspectives to see if any central tendency emerged.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The analysis that we carried out turns out to be very close to what Mike Kiley described in yesterday’s briefing and what the Board heard in the briefings that you had on Monday.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Obviously, great minds think alike, and I know President Evans and his staff in Chicago were doing exactly the same things that we did and the Board did.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I won’t go into all of the details.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’ll just say we reverse engineered wage and price Phillips curves to estimate the level of the GDP gap that would produce the inflation rates now being observed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We used a variety of wage and price measures to assess sensitivity.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We investigated whether a possible decline in the efficiency of the job-matching process might be raising the NAIRU by comparing cross-industry dispersion of employment growth in this cycle with earlier ones.

speaker: YELLEN
text: And we, too, assessed the evidence relating to the Beveridge curve and possible shifts.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I simply want to second or third the conclusions that Board staff reached and that President Evans described.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is possible to find reasonable methodologies that would lead to a short-run NAIRU higher than that used by the Board, or to output gaps that are somewhat smaller than those that are embodied in the Greenbook or in our forecast.

speaker: YELLEN
text: But no matter what methodology is used, in every case we find very substantial slack in labor and product markets.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I’d like to discuss briefly one thing that we did.

speaker: YELLEN
text: We looked at whether the financial crisis and the large sectoral reallocations away from housing finance and autos may have slowed underlying total factor productivity growth and thereby the pace of potential output growth.

speaker: YELLEN
text: If so, our forecast of output growth going forward could be too large.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Although measured TFP has declined over the past year or so, which is typical of past recessions, we find that, adjusted for the utilization of labor and capital, it has actually risen strongly during the recession.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The conclusion that underlying productivity growth has remained on or actually above trend is confirmed using an alternative approach of estimating permanent technology shocks from the productivity data.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So, to conclude, if the recovery is as slow as the Greenbook and I expect, it will take quite a number of years to get back to potential output.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As a result, I expect core inflation to drift lower over the next few years, falling below the 2 percent rate that seems best to me.

speaker: FISHER
text: I recently accompanied my wife to a board meeting of the American Film Institute, of which she is a director, in President Yellen’s District in Hollywood, and to prepare for that trip I read Evelyn Waugh’s wonderful novel The Loved One: An Anglo-American Tragedy.

speaker: FISHER
text: The plot line is about a minor British poet who goes to write the greatest movie of all time about the life of Percy Shelley and settles for employment at a pet cemetery called The Happy Hunting Ground.

speaker: FISHER
text: There’s a precious scene in that novel where the tough head of the film studio is surrounded by people around a table and in the back benches.

speaker: FISHER
text: The people around the table are described as “yes men” and those on the back benches as “nodders.” I find myself nodding and saying yes—[laughter]—to everything that has been said by my predecessors at this table.

speaker: FISHER
text: There is a unanimity of view, it seems to me, that, as President Yellen just pointed out, the economy is bottoming out, but it is a gradual and fragile recovery, and it will take a long time to regain employment.

speaker: FISHER
text: I forecast an almost checkmark-shaped recovery, which is a long recovery, as President Rosengren stated, with the unemployment rate masking some of the problems we have with our workforce, and I do not foresee a very quick recovery.

speaker: FISHER
text: What concerns me is that the people that I talk to, the CEO list that I give you, and even the people we talked to in that part of the country, which is not known for being plugged into reality, also have a unanimous view.

speaker: FISHER
text: I want to touch on two aspects that were mentioned by my predecessors here.

speaker: FISHER
text: The first is with regard to President Rosengren’s point that unemployment may be masking deeper problems.

speaker: FISHER
text: Even in your District, President Rosengren, I noticed that Harvard Law School just sent out a letter recommending that their graduating class seek employment in other fields—perhaps at pet cemeteries; I’m not quite sure.

speaker: FISHER
text: If you look at Skadden, Arps or Cravath, Swaine, & Moore, people that I talk to, they have deferred an entire class in terms of their hiring.

speaker: FISHER
text: So here’s the point: I think we also need to be cognizant of the fact that the service sector is going to have a very slow recovery in the process.

speaker: FISHER
text: This was underscored by the CEO of AT&T, who said, “If it isn’t life or death, we’re not hiring anybody or investing in anything.” And I think that’s pretty much a unanimous view around the table of CEOs that I spoke to.

speaker: FISHER
text: Second, President Lockhart mentioned cap-ex.

speaker: FISHER
text: When you have excess slack, you’re going to have less commitment to cap-ex.

speaker: FISHER
text: But here’s the point I want to mention: Among the CEOs that I speak to, and even people that you would never expect to be critical—I’ll drop a name, because it was absolutely shocking, Warren Beatty, for example— there’s a unanimous worry that, “The plethora of programs coming out of Washington is creating enormous uncertainty.” Uncertainty is the enemy of decisionmaking, the enemy of capitalism.

speaker: FISHER
text: We’ve talked about this before.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s not that changes are being proposed.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s that no one knows when they will stop, and I find that this has heightened uncertainty in the business sector and is retarding cap-ex.

speaker: FISHER
text: And that won’t change until there is resolution about the enormous changes that have been proposed by the Congress, by the Administration, and so on.

speaker: FISHER
text: It’s not that the business community and others are against the proposals, it’s that there are so many coming so quickly that it’s creating enormous uncertainty.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is this the Warren Beatty who starred in Reds?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Well, hopefully heaven can’t wait too long.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I just want to amplify what President Fisher said about the uncertainty created by all of the Obama Administration initiatives.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We heard from one large firm that this is really important, especially in health care: Why would you build a new wing of a hospital if you don’t know what the reimbursement rates are going to be?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Generally, I think the economy is still very weak.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we’re probably at or very close to a cyclical bottom.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The market reaction, though, is really mostly, to my mind, about pricing out the tail risk of a depression rather than pricing in a strong recovery, and I think the market over the last week or two has sort of been rethinking its reaction.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: What has been going on in the labor market is pretty striking.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The rise in the participation rate may be indicative of stress in terms of balance sheets and people being forced back into the labor market, even though the prospects aren’t very good.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Past credit crises certainly suggest that the dynamics of recovery this time will be very different.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The wealth shock is unprecedented.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Credit availability is going to be constrained for quite a while.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There are significant rollover risks for large groups of borrowers—the commercial mortgage market is probably the most significant one.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And it’s going to take several years, I think, for the financial system to get back to more normal functioning.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One thing that struck me in looking at the macro data is how we’ve been benefiting from unusually favorable income dynamics up to now.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If you look at the trend of income relative to hours worked and wages, real disposable income growth has been very, very strong—6½ percent at an annual rate in the first quarter and on pace by the New York Fed forecast for a 4.2 percent annual rise in the second quarter.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That has allowed the saving rate to rise sharply without triggering a big fall in consumer spending.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The problem is that the factors underlying the sharp rise are all behind us: the big increase in transfer payments, automatic stabilizers, the large COLA for Social Security caused by the big run-up in energy prices last year, the tax cuts, changes in withholding rates in April, and payments made to Social Security recipients in May and June.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Looking forward, the trend in real disposable income is going to be much worse in the second half of the year—we’re probably going to see actual declines.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So we’re assuming that consumption will rise despite the fact that disposable personal income is falling, and the saving rate will fall as a consequence.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But I think there is a risk to the downside, because maybe the saving rate won’t fall and consumption will just be weaker than we anticipated.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The other thing I am worried about is this: I think it’s very premature to rule out further financial market disruptions.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: A couple of times in the crisis we’ve thought that things were getting better, and then there was another shock.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Obviously, when Lehman failed, we had no idea what the macroeconomic consequences of that were going to be.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: One thing I am worried about is that the TLGP is almost certainly going to end September 30, so that means financial institutions are going to face more rollover risk for all the debt that’s coming due after September 30.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And we still have several very large, systemically important institutions that are very fragile and that have broad international operations.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We don’t have a resolution mechanism to deal with them if they get into difficulties.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: And the political will to help these firms if they do get into trouble, I think, is quite a bit subdued compared to what it was a year ago.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So I think that’s something to be concerned about.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On inflation, I think the near-term outlook is that core inflation is going to moderate from where it has been.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The tobacco taxes are sort of a funny anomaly—how you raise taxes shouldn’t really affect the inflation numbers, but it does in certain cases.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Inflation expectations seem to be well anchored despite some worries about monetization of the debt, and we have a very large output gap.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: To make sure that we keep inflation expectations well anchored, I think we need to do more in articulating why will be able to exit smoothly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The biggest upside risk on inflation to me would be a broad loss of confidence in the U.S. abroad caused by worries about fiscal sustainability and the independence of the Fed.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The only way I can see getting a big inflation problem any time soon is if the dollar were to collapse.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: There’s probably some risk of that, but I think it should be very low as long as we communicate clearly that we have the tools to manage our exit smoothly and that we are committed to long-term price stability, regardless of what the fiscal authorities do.

speaker: KOHN
text: Data since the last meeting, along with what we have heard around this table, and reports from the Reserve Bank Districts, should give us much more confidence that the economy is indeed in the process of bottoming out.

speaker: KOHN
text: And I think basically what we’re seeing is that the sources of weakness are abating.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’ve got consumption leveling out, housing demand leveling out, and eventually investment should follow that process.

speaker: KOHN
text: Maybe we’re seeing a little bit of that in today’s meeting.

speaker: KOHN
text: The inventory cycle is further along, with stocks being reduced—not as much today, Dave, I guess, as we might have anticipated, but they’re still being reduced—and they’ll come into better alignment with sales.

speaker: KOHN
text: At that point, more of current sales and any increase in sales will need to be met from increases in production and ultimately increases in employment, setting in motion a positive accelerator multiplier process.

speaker: KOHN
text: Commodity prices are rising, anticipating increasing demand, and sentiment has come back from a very, very weak level.

speaker: KOHN
text: Of course, as many have pointed out, importantly, in financial markets, we see narrowing spreads, rising equity prices, access to markets for banks raising equity, and access to bond markets for businesses.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I think there’s a lot of news that suggests that the economy is, indeed, stabilizing.

speaker: KOHN
text: But, like many others around the table, I don’t see many signs that there’s a rebound in economic activity yet, nor do I see signs that the rebound, when it comes, will be other than quite moderate.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I have strengthened my outlook a little bit relative to April, but not by much, and it has still got the same basic pattern, which is very similar to the Greenbook.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think there are a couple of forces that will be holding back the recovery.

speaker: KOHN
text: As a number of you have mentioned, one of them is in the financial sector.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’ve had encouraging news on financial conditions and financial repair over the intermeeting period.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I think the underlying problems are severe and structural.

speaker: KOHN
text: Further improvement is likely to be gradual.

speaker: KOHN
text: The markets that seem to be working well are the plain vanilla markets, like corporate bonds, where risks are more easily judged.

speaker: KOHN
text: But even there, risk premiums remain quite high by historical standards.

speaker: KOHN
text: The costs of debt and equity capital are elevated.

speaker: KOHN
text: Securitization markets away from government support are still held back by uncertainty both about the legal regulatory framework—and I think that uncertainty has probably been increasing in recent weeks with various proposals—and about the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the securitization markets are particularly sensitive to economic uncertainty, because the risk characteristics of securitized debt are more complicated.

speaker: KOHN
text: Those problems aren’t going to go away quickly.

speaker: KOHN
text: More credit is going to have to flow through banks.

speaker: KOHN
text: Banks continue to face constraints on balance sheet capacity—they’re using the capital they raise to repay the government, not to expand loans.

speaker: KOHN
text: Losses will be mounting in coming quarters on commercial real estate and consumer loans, and I think credit supply will be slow to ease and spreads of bank lending rates relative to cost of funds will remain elevated as earnings and capital are restored.

speaker: KOHN
text: Many of the innovations that enabled households to shift consumption over time, particularly to bring consumption forward when wealth rose, will be much more limited in availability—home equity lines of credit, subprime credit of all types—and markets remain fragile.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the tentative positive interactions between financial conditions and economic conditions that we’ve seen over the last few days and months can be easily disrupted by some bad news.

speaker: KOHN
text: So credit supplies will be limited and risk spreads will shrink gradually, only slowly reflecting the full effects of the low federal funds rate and our credit-easing actions.

speaker: KOHN
text: Even aside from the credit effects, I think global aggregate demand is likely to recover gradually.

speaker: KOHN
text: Like President Bullard, I’m really struck by the global nature of this downturn.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think households and businesses will remain very cautious everywhere following the unpleasant surprises of recent quarters.

speaker: KOHN
text: President Fisher’s comments about uncertainty holding back both consumption and investment are well taken.

speaker: KOHN
text: And uncertainty about the course of the economy, about the availability of jobs and business earnings, will abate slowly.

speaker: KOHN
text: Many areas of the world are lagging our cycle.

speaker: KOHN
text: I worry especially about Europe, which faces very sharp increases in unemployment and problems in the banking sector that they’re only beginning to acknowledge and confront.

speaker: KOHN
text: Also, there are issues about where the global demand is going to come from over the medium term.

speaker: KOHN
text: U.S. households will not be the engine of global demand, as they have been for the last fifteen years, as those households rebuild wealth.

speaker: KOHN
text: Staff has roughly stable saving rates for the U.S.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think they’re more likely to trend higher than lower after the recent experience.

speaker: KOHN
text: And even with stable but higher saving rates in the U.S., it is not clear what will fill the global aggregate demand gap.

speaker: KOHN
text: The lack of domestic demand in Asia—the Chairman’s global saving glut—has been holding down equilibrium real rates in recent years, and that’s not going to change very rapidly.

speaker: KOHN
text: Stronger demand in Asia ultimately depends on structural reforms in the Chinese economy especially, and especially in its financial sector.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I don’t expect any rapid reduction in the dependence on export-led growth from Asian countries.

speaker: KOHN
text: And we’re reaching the limits of fiscal policy to fill demand gaps—demographics and entitlement concerns everywhere are raising questions about fiscal sustainability and will constrain fiscal impetus.

speaker: KOHN
text: It’s always hard to see what will spark a recovery at the bottom of a recession, and we could be pleasantly surprised this time, too.

speaker: KOHN
text: But my best judgment is that these factors are holding down the equilibrium real interest rates to very low, perhaps negative, levels at a time when the ability of monetary policy around the world to lower rates well below equilibrium is severely limited by the zero nominal bound and by low inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: In these circumstances, I see a large output gap persisting and putting downward pressure on inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree that the gap is unobservable and that we can make mistakes in gauging it.

speaker: KOHN
text: There are also important points about resource-shifting, which raises the NAIRU temporarily.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I was very impressed by Mike Kiley’s charts and by President Evans’s and President Yellen’s comments.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we’ve got a sizable output gap right now by almost any measure, both in the labor market and in the product market.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think a lot of indirect evidence is consistent with that sizable gap, especially in the labor market.

speaker: KOHN
text: Most measures of labor compensation have decelerated sharply in recent months and quarters.

speaker: KOHN
text: To be sure, inflation hasn’t come down as fast as expected, reflecting in part higher energy prices and special factors.

speaker: KOHN
text: The tendency for some inflation expectation measures to edge higher is troubling, and we need to pay very careful attention to that in our policymaking.

speaker: KOHN
text: Productivity growth has been surprisingly rapid.

speaker: KOHN
text: The staff doesn’t interpret the very rapid growth in productivity in the first half of this year as a pickup in the underlying trend, but rather as a change in cyclical characteristics.

speaker: KOHN
text: But surely the rapid productivity growth we seem to be experiencing doesn’t suggest a slowdown in trend growth, and cost pressures from unit labor costs should remain subdued.

speaker: KOHN
text: With the global output gap large, competition will be intense and there will be little pricing power for business or labor.

speaker: KOHN
text: So like many others, I forecast a slowing in inflation, albeit not as much as in the staff forecast.

speaker: KOHN
text: So, on balance, I see persistent output gaps and inflation falling below my 2 percent objective over the next few years.

speaker: KOHN
text: My forecast, like that of the Greenbook, is that we don’t do very well against either of our dual objectives.

speaker: WARSH
text: I thought I would talk briefly about the real economy, then financial markets, and then inflation, in that order.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the real economy, in terms of near-term growth and employment prospects, like many of you, I think GDP growth looks shaky through year-end.

speaker: WARSH
text: The arithmetic of GDP may yield a positive quarter or two, but I see very little evidence that that will be enduring, or at least something that is a strong foundation on which to build.

speaker: WARSH
text: President Fisher was much chagrined yesterday to park his shiny new car next to what he described as my clunker, and he suggested that I take the government up on its generous $4,500 voucher.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’ve decided my answer is “yes,” so I’ll do my part, I think, in the third quarter.

speaker: WARSH
text: Unemployment is walking, if not running, away, as Presidents Rosengren and Yellen suggested.

speaker: WARSH
text: I suspect that the trend in unemployment is likely to create a political demand for consideration of a new fiscal package.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think the debate on that will be hugely consequential, not necessarily in terms of the economy, but in terms of getting further market attention on fiscal sustainability.

speaker: WARSH
text: Downside risks to this rather weak forecast, I think, are in place, both with respect to non-U.S. growth and non-U.S. financial market improvements, to which I think President Dudley made good reference.

speaker: WARSH
text: In terms of medium-term growth prospects, I also see downside risks as pro-stability policies proliferate.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think unemployment is likely to be more determinative of the shape of this recovery than the path of housing prices or other asset prices, and I share the views expressed by many that NAIRU looks as if it’s trending higher.

speaker: WARSH
text: I raise that not really to quibble about the size of the output gap, but rather to suggest that the reallocation between capital and labor is likely to last longer and that the incomes in this economy in the medium term are probably less reliable, given the emerging mix of macroeconomic policies.

speaker: WARSH
text: I compliment Dave and his staff for continued work on the labor market damage scenario, which, I think, is more real than we wish to imagine.

speaker: WARSH
text: Internationally, it strikes me that there is much more complacency about where things stand on the global economy than I would have expected.

speaker: WARSH
text: When we talk to bank regulators and large banks elsewhere around the world, there’s almost a nostalgia about the events of last fall.

speaker: WARSH
text: And many of them have not gone through the capital-raising that our banks have.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we are rightly uncertain, as both Bill and Don suggested, about the risks to U.S. institutions.

speaker: WARSH
text: But I think the risks look to me at least as high, if not higher, for banks elsewhere in the world, and I’m really struck by the fact that they are seeming to race back to the good old days at capital levels that look to me quite low, with expectations for GDP growth in their home countries which, I think, are likely to disappoint.

speaker: WARSH
text: Decoupling, which, I thought, we had proved over the course of the last year was a myth proliferated by Wall Street, seems to have found its way back into financial markets and to economists traveling around the world.

speaker: WARSH
text: There is a view that, well, even if the U.S. bumbles along, China has figured out how to be a strong growth engine for Asia, and Europe is getting traction in and of itself.

speaker: WARSH
text: In my view, we have one global integrated economy, and those who think that somehow these other engines of growth are sufficient to get us through this near-term weakness, I think, are likely to be disappointed.

speaker: WARSH
text: On the financial market side, the capital-raising that came out of the stress test results is nothing short of impressive.

speaker: WARSH
text: That is $75 billion to keep us away from Sunday night meetings, so that has got to make us feel a little bit better.

speaker: WARSH
text: The capital and corporate equity and debt markets are as open as they’ve been since this crisis began.

speaker: WARSH
text: But having said all of that, I must say I’m a little troubled that markets don’t seem to be discriminating.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’d be more confident if there were more differentiation between and among assets in the U.S. or between U.S. assets and non-U.S. assets.

speaker: WARSH
text: It looks to me as though the kind of market discipline, which I have described as being back and punitive, seems to have stepped back for a while.

speaker: WARSH
text: And there are a whole lot of lemmings that seem to be chasing indexes and buying into everything.

speaker: WARSH
text: So I’m not as comfortable as I wish I were about this bounce off the bottom in asset prices everywhere around the world since the March 9 lows.

speaker: WARSH
text: As I think was described by Bill and others, what we’re seeing in these markets I would rationalize as an abatement of the panic, rather than a sign of robust recovery.

speaker: WARSH
text: These asset prices strike me as not yet having found a new sustainable equilibrium, so the summer could test the value of these asset prices.

speaker: WARSH
text: I put a little emphasis on this, because it does strike me that the increase of, say, 30 percent on average in asset values from spring until now might be more consequential than all of the fiscal stimulus packages in trying to help get this economy going again.

speaker: WARSH
text: And to the extent that those wealth effects are reversed, I think that’s likely to be hugely consequential.

speaker: WARSH
text: We talked a little bit yesterday about Treasury markets.

speaker: WARSH
text: I would only say that in the intermeeting period I think the move up in Treasury yields is for both benign and less benign reasons—it’s hard for me to differentiate exactly which carries the day.

speaker: WARSH
text: Finally, on the inflation front, as many have suggested, I think the dashboard indicates some normalization of inflation readings consistent with marking down prospects of deflation, rightly in my view.

speaker: WARSH
text: We can see higher inflation compensation in the TIPS market and elsewhere.

speaker: WARSH
text: Still, inflation expectations remain seemingly well anchored, even though we have now seen in markets both inflation and deflation scares that have gotten their attention and maybe gotten some of ours, too.

speaker: WARSH
text: I’d just end with a sort of thought experiment, much of which we could carry on in Round 2.

speaker: WARSH
text: If we had this weak current economy and this set of projections that we’ve all forwarded for consideration and public disclosure, but had not had the panic and the extraordinary fear-inducing moments of the last year, where would policy be?

speaker: WARSH
text: Would our prospects for policy be different?

speaker: WARSH
text: Or are we keeping our policy accommodation at the extraordinary levels in part because of what we’ve endured?

speaker: WARSH
text: I’m not sure I know the answers to those questions, but they are things I will continue to think about.

speaker: DUKE
text: The banks have settled down a little bit since the stress test.

speaker: DUKE
text: They report the stress tests were not all that terrible, and they were as surprised as I was at the ease of the capital raise.

speaker: DUKE
text: They’re looking for opportunities now to raise debt.

speaker: DUKE
text: There’s no trust preferred available, and a couple were issuing investment units; one had a common equity and a convertible bond component, and another reported having to add warrants to debt in order to attract investors.

speaker: DUKE
text: All would like to pay back the TARP, and they’re divided into those who most likely will not be able to soon and those who can.

speaker: DUKE
text: For those who will not soon, they’re not sure that they’re out of the woods, and they acknowledge that they wouldn’t survive being wrong.

speaker: DUKE
text: Those who have or will soon pay back cite worries about losing their top revenue producers, the cost of the government capital, the fact that new investors who are providing capital want them to get out, and—probably the most honest response—“Because everybody else is getting out.” In terms of liquidity, they are moving down to or up to 100 percent loan-deposit ratios— those with higher ratios are shedding credit and those with lower ratios are the beneficiaries of that.

speaker: DUKE
text: Deposits are still growing, but at a much slower rate, and, interestingly, in discussing their liquidity, they all pointed to their excess funds on deposit with the Federal Reserve.

speaker: DUKE
text: So, again, I don’t see any indication that bankers are concerned about excess reserves right now.

speaker: DUKE
text: In fact, they think they’re creating them.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of profitability, margins are finally improving.

speaker: DUKE
text: Expenses are down except for FDIC assessments.

speaker: DUKE
text: Mortgage income was huge in the first two quarters, but refinance activity, in particular, has slowed dramatically with the higher rates.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of credit management, the long process of working through residential problems continues.

speaker: DUKE
text: Construction lending has plateaued or a little bit better.

speaker: DUKE
text: OREO properties are moving, although there are still problem areas, such as lots in Arizona and condos in Florida.

speaker: DUKE
text: C&I is actually holding up.

speaker: DUKE
text: A few banks mention noticeable problems with small businesses and said that mom-and-pop stores are simply giving up.

speaker: DUKE
text: Their classifications are growing as the financial statements come in and show the expected lower profitability, but they’re still not showing up in delinquencies.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of commercial real estate, it’s getting worse, but it still seems manageable.

speaker: DUKE
text: The bottom is not falling out.

speaker: DUKE
text: Loans are classified, but not yet charging off.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of office buildings, as the leases renew, rents are being negotiated down, and one banker who had just worked through his residential construction was dismayed to find that the offices he had financed were full of real estate companies.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of retail, there’s a lot of fallout among the smaller tenants, and there are problems with the anchors; the anchor tenants can renegotiate because there’s a clause that gives all of the smaller tenants an out if they lose the anchor tenants.

speaker: DUKE
text: So the anchor tenants are absolutely taking advantage of the ability to negotiate down.

speaker: DUKE
text: And then finally we asked about the auto dealers, and they are, I think, pretty successful at moving the inventory, but they are left with debt on special use properties.

speaker: DUKE
text: In terms of new lending, high-quality credits are paying down, and demand is all from low-quality credits.

speaker: DUKE
text: One banker said he was willing to battle the examiners over his own weaker credits, but he was not willing to take on someone else’s, so if someone is turned down at their primary bank, they’re unlike to find a home anywhere else.

speaker: DUKE
text: There are lots of problems with appraisals.

speaker: DUKE
text: In particular, there are not enough recent comparables.

speaker: DUKE
text: Many banks are exiting some products, some geographies, some industries, as well as credit-only relationships, although risk pricing is the best in ten years.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I’m left to wonder how we finance this recovery.

speaker: DUKE
text: Staff recently helped me use the flow-of-funds data to look for the drop in credit so far, and we found that the drop in credit up to this point has not been nearly what you might have expected and has actually been in the middle to the upper range of past credit crunch recessions.

speaker: DUKE
text: I believe that the support provided to the financial system kept it from dropping, but that support is now steadily being withdrawn, if not intentionally, then through stigmatization.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I believe the credit crunch is still to come.

speaker: DUKE
text: Many, many bank balance sheets are still supported by government capital and liquidity.

speaker: DUKE
text: This credit cycle also will leave plenty of credit impairment wreckage behind.

speaker: DUKE
text: The bankers and their examiners are very, very risk-averse.

speaker: DUKE
text: I think business credit is going to hold up better as profitability will probably come back with the improvement of sales as well as the fallout of competitors, but consumer credit is going to be impaired for a long while.

speaker: DUKE
text: The number of bankruptcies, delinquencies, foreclosures, and charge-offs, the fact that the same credit score now equates to a much higher risk, and the fact that collateral values are significantly lower will all contribute to less credit available to consumers.

speaker: DUKE
text: Most importantly, there are a number of broken business models.

speaker: DUKE
text: While I do believe that we need new business models in these times, the transition is likely to be much more painful than we currently anticipate, and I see it in two areas.

speaker: DUKE
text: The first area is mortgage lending, where there’s no visibility on what is going to happen with the GSE system, and there is yet no securitization 2.0 on the horizon—so I don’t see what happens in terms of housing finance.

speaker: DUKE
text: The second area is credit cards.

speaker: DUKE
text: This may be a second, smaller wave of problems similar to the subprime mortgage crisis.

speaker: DUKE
text: As I hear anecdotes of people who are in trouble on their mortgages, I am struck by the number of stories that include phenomenal amounts of credit card debt— $30,000, $50,000, $100,000—built up by taking on more and more cards with increasing lines, then reloading by refinancing a first mortgage or an equity line and starting again.

speaker: DUKE
text: Just as the subprime market failed when refinance stopped, credit charge-offs are going to grow as the availability of larger lines, additional cards, and debt consolidation loans disappears.

speaker: DUKE
text: This is fed by the current business model for credit cards, which was a land grant model.

speaker: DUKE
text: The issuers would cast a wide net, trolling for new customers using teaser rates and additional lines, and then they would underwrite and price after acquisition of those customers, pricing for profitability by testing price increases on a sample of customers with similar characteristics and then increasing the profit by balancing the higher interest income with lost customers and write-offs.

speaker: DUKE
text: Line management included a discovery that the highest limit becomes the primary card, so line increases were based primarily on propensity to spend and propensity to carry balances, offset by the higher credit risk.

speaker: DUKE
text: New restrictions both in our regulations and in legislation now will require that they underwrite in advance, and I’m not quite sure whether this means underwrite the ability to carry the interest or the ability to pay off in the traditional three- to five-year time frame.

speaker: DUKE
text: I don’t know what “capacity to repay” will do.

speaker: DUKE
text: Combined with record charge-off levels, estimates are for a reduction of 25 to 30 percent in availability.

speaker: DUKE
text: If we have nearly $1 trillion in outstanding, this could be a reduction in credit available of $200 to $250 billion, combined with an inability to reload through equity loans or home refinance.

speaker: DUKE
text: Indeed, the second most cited reason for home equity was to refinance credit card debt.

speaker: DUKE
text: So what does this do to the saving rate if those most likely to finance deficit spending can no longer do so?

speaker: DUKE
text: I had written down here that I don’t know yet, but fortunately, Governor Kohn, President Yellen, and the Vice Chairman have all suggested the possible impact of this reduction in credit.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Listening to the 15 of you who have preceded me this morning, I am struck by the fact that the central tendency of our economic analyses may be even narrower than that suggested in the projections that were gathered in advance of this meeting.

speaker: TARULLO
text: So although, Mr. Chairman, it’s your job and not mine to summarize, I think much of what I’m going to say necessarily reiterates much of what has already been said.

speaker: TARULLO
text: First, the recent hopeful signs of stabilization cannot obscure the fact that economic conditions remain poor.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Even some of the hopeful signs themselves reveal how bad things are.

speaker: TARULLO
text: As many of you have noted, improvements in financial market conditions are still quite dependent on government-provided liquidity facilities and guarantees.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The recent rise in housing starts follows a precipitous multiyear decline, and it could yet be blunted by rising mortgage rates.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Recent developments in the labor market have also been cited as cause for guarded optimism, but again, as many of you have noted, the news is not all good.

speaker: TARULLO
text: In fact, the news is not good at all, it’s just less bad.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The decline in initial unemployment claims and the reduction in job losses over the last couple of months are surely welcome, but unemployment claims are still at very high levels, and we are still losing jobs in the economy, just at a reduced rate.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Meanwhile, the unemployment rate continues its apparently inexorable rise towards double digits.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The rate of involuntary non-full-time employment has more than doubled in the last eighteen months, and the level of aggregate hours worked continues to decline.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Since December 2007, the ranks of unemployed Americans have swelled by seven million.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Analogous points could be made about industrial production, retail sales, or just about any other economic indicator.

speaker: TARULLO
text: So let me end this first point by noting that, whatever the merits of the protagonists in the great debate on the correct measure of the output gap, the number is clearly large.

speaker: TARULLO
text: My second point, again, I think, reflecting what many of you have already said, is that there continue to be many reasons to believe that recovery, when it does come, will be slow and fragile.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I have now been tutored by Governor Duke to listen to the words that recur the most during a conversation, and this morning “sluggish” was high among them.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Although this is not a particularly controversial observation, I think it’s one that bears repeating as we consider our policy trajectories going forward.

speaker: TARULLO
text: As many of us have noted previously, background circumstances suggest an elongated recovery.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Economic downturns that begin with a financial crisis have historically been more painful and with longer recovery periods than other serious recessions.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Households, financial institutions, and other firms are all repairing their balance sheets in reaction to big reductions in asset values and large debt overhangs.

speaker: TARULLO
text: This response, while understandable and in many respects necessary, leans against the stimulus provided by increased government spending.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Some headwinds are even more apparent than at our last meeting.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Even as we’re heartened by market reception of the SCAP process and by the significant capital raises of many of the SCAP institutions, we must also note that, overall, bank lending is still declining.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Moreover, the list of banks slated for closure grows longer each week, as does the list of problem banks that I receive once a week.

speaker: TARULLO
text: As some of you around this table have been predicting, the difficulties in commercial real estate markets are growing and may soon be felt with a vengeance at many regional and smaller banks.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Expectations of an uneven and gradual recovery are reinforced when one looks abroad.

speaker: TARULLO
text: As in the United States, signals from Europe are mixed, albeit on a somewhat lagged basis, but there are, as here, drags upon renewed growth when growth does come.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The effects of the smaller stimulus programs in Europe will dissipate more quickly than in the U.S. Also, conditions within a number of European banking systems are still not well known.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The apparent reluctance of many countries to conduct and report publicly on their own stress tests has stoked concerns that weakness in real estate, Eastern Europe, and other exposures are weighing heavily upon some of these institutions.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Several of you have already mentioned China.

speaker: TARULLO
text: China is frequently cited as one bright spot in a world economic canvas that is otherwise dark gray, but it, too, actually presents a more ambiguous case.

speaker: TARULLO
text: While the size and speed of China’s stimulus package has produced impressive results in bringing its GDP growth above 7 percent, there is little evidence that China or for that matter other East Asian nations are adjusting their growth models toward greater emphasis on domestic consumption.

speaker: TARULLO
text: They seem to be using infrastructure and other stimulus spending as a kind of holding pattern, apparently expecting a significant rebound of consumption in the United States and Europe.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Thus, even the Chinese recovery may have limited self-sustaining momentum.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The continued and, I fear, misplaced faith in the resurgence of the old export-led growth model is captured in the image of about 400 empty container ships parked in Singapore awaiting a return to the old normalcy.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Like everyone, I welcome the indications of stabilization and in some areas bottoming out.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Few would deny that we are significantly better situated than just a couple of months ago.

speaker: TARULLO
text: However, we should not be carried away with optimism or too hastily moved towards the exits.

speaker: TARULLO
text: In the current circumstances of a significant output gap, rising unemployment, uneven improvement in financial markets and firms, and uncertain prospects abroad, inflationary pressures are neither evident nor likely to be generated within the U.S. economy any time soon.

speaker: TARULLO
text: While I do not expect to double dip, I don’t think it can be ruled out entirely either.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The economy remains unusually vulnerable to exogenous shocks or to renewed stress at one or more significant financial firms.

speaker: TARULLO
text: This is the most serious economic slump since the Depression, and it is far from over.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: This is a good time for a coffee break of about 20 minutes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a summary, which I will read to you.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most participants saw a slowing contraction and tentative signs of stabilization in economic activity.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Business and household confidence has improved some, and surveys show improved expectations for the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inventory liquidation continues, which is a positive for growth later this year, and financial markets have continued to improve.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Despite this relatively good news, though, most saw the economy as still quite weak and fragile and vulnerable to new shocks.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Labor markets are extremely soft, and financial markets may be ahead of themselves.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: While output should begin to grow again, the pace is likely to be quite slow and tentative.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although downside risks have been mitigated somewhat, they still exist.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Likewise, recovery abroad seems likely to be uneven and gradual, with Europe still facing financial problems and East Asia still too reliant on exports.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumer spending, though no longer declining, is not robust either, reflecting the weak labor market, sharp wealth reductions, and higher oil prices.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Real income growth is likely to slow for the remainder of the year.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Consumers continue to focus on necessities and appear liquidity constrained.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Housing has shown a few signs of life but is vulnerable to the effects of the rising mortgage rates and continuing high rates of foreclosure.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Capital investment remains very soft, reflecting unused capacity and uncertainty about the economy and about the policy environment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Across industries, weakness is widespread and includes service industries, although some areas, such as energy and agriculture, are doing better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Labor markets remain a particular area of concern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Despite some improvement in new and continuing UI claims, and a less bad payroll report for May, the unemployment rate and the rate of job loss remained high, with little near-term prospect for improvement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Total hours of work have fallen significantly.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: More layoffs are permanent, and the amount of involuntary part-time work is high.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I should add that participation rates have risen also because of wealth effects.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Slow wage growth is reflecting this weakness.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The NAIRU may have risen somewhat, but a significant unemployment gap still probably exists.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Financial markets continue to show improvement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The banking stress tests were perceived to be successful and resulted in capital raises and improved funding conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Loan volumes are not falling especially dramatically, but in part this reflects government support, which may be withdrawn.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Reduced lending and tighter terms also reflect worsening credit quality, and banks still face substantial credit losses in coming quarters.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Other credit markets also continue to improve, including the corporate market and the ABS market.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The financing of commercial real estate remains problematic, however, and fundamentals for the sector are weakening.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Improvements in financial markets support the stabilization of the broader economy but could prove fleeting if the projected strengthening in growth and profits does not materialize.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Higher oil and commodity prices will raise headline inflation in the near term, while core inflation seems likely to be low.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As noted, wages continue to remain nearly flat, and productivity has been surprisingly high, so that the growth in unit labor costs is moderate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Overall, inflation seems likely to be well controlled in the near term, and most see deflation risks as now relatively small.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Some were concerned about inflation expectations in the medium term.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As measured by TIPS breakevens and by most household and business surveys, inflation expectations seem to be stable at reasonable levels.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: However, publicity about fiscal deficits and the Fed’s balance sheet has concerned many in the public and may be reflected in inflation risk premiums and longer-term interest rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Communication about the exit strategy and the Fed’s commitment to price stability is an important tool for managing expectations.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: At the same time, some suggest that it is important not to signal that the unwinding of the Fed’s extraordinary measures is imminent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That’s my summary of what I heard, which I do think was a fairly consistent message around the table today.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just add a few thoughts, which will not be particularly novel, given all that has been said.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: First, I think one can’t help but be at least somewhat encouraged by the developments in financial markets since our last meeting.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The Federal Reserve staff and leadership, I think, deserve some credit for the assessment of the banking system, and the results that that had.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s very encouraging that banks can raise equity and that their funding has improved—CDS spreads have declined.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that, although systemic risk is still around, it is much less now than it was a few months ago, and the reduced probability of a major calamity in the financial system is, in itself, I think, a positive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We’ve also seen improvements, as I mentioned, in other credit markets as well, partly because of government support, including Fed programs.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Obviously, an important development in the financial markets in the intermeeting period was the increase in long-term interest rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Yesterday when the staff showed the changes in government rates across a number of industrial countries, I thought it was interesting that the increase in the U.K. rate was about the same as the increase in the German rate, both of which were much less than the U.S. rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Since the U.K. is viewed as having many of the same problems in terms of fiscal sustainability and the balance sheet that we have, the fact that those rates had risen no more than rates in Germany suggests to me that a lot of what’s happening in the U.S. is the result of a stronger outlook and a reversal of the flight-to-quality flows, which in itself is, I think, encouraging.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, again, I think one of the better developments of the intermeeting period is the broad- based improvement in financial markets.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Having said that, as someone already mentioned, we’ve been head-faked on this before.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I recall October 2007 when our statement essentially declared the financial crisis to be over, and again, in the summer of 2008 when we were expecting growth and recovery, and then we got hit with calamities in September and October.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I do think we need to be very cautious and recognize that the financial improvements are, in some sense, discounting progress that is expected in the future.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And until we see concrete evidence of that progress, we shouldn’t overreact to the financial improvements.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As many people have noted, the explicit evidence even for stabilization, much less for recovery, is not really at hand yet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, consumption growth in the second quarter is still likely to have been negative, and there are a number of drags that continue to be an issue there.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In the labor markets, many have noted very severe conditions.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Although UI claims have come down a bit, they’re still at extraordinarily high levels, and we would expect to see continuing job losses for some time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In housing, mortgage rates and foreclosures are going to be a drag on the very tentative improvement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think my message is that we should be encouraged by the financial improvements but note that they are very contingent.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: They depend on the realization of actual improvement in the economy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We have seen some stabilization, but the evidence of solid stabilization or the beginnings of growth is certainly not here yet, and we should not overestimate that evidence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s also important to keep in mind that, although we’re accustomed to thinking about the stages of the cycle and to think about growth rates, the amplitude of the shock was extraordinarily large.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So we are very far away by any measure, I think, from normalcy.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Even if the economy does begin to grow at a slow pace, we’ll be very far from full employment for some time, which has implications.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The longer you’re away from full employment, the worse credit losses will be, the worse hysteresis will be in the labor market, the worse income effects will be on consumers, and so on.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So the size of the decline also will have effects that could lead to a longer persistence as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So, again, I think we should be somewhat cautious about declaring victory.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inflation—I heard both sides of this argument.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I guess the standard view would be that core inflation, at least, is likely to continue to moderate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There were a number of special factors besides the tobacco taxes.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: There were some unusual aspects of the change in model year for automobiles, which probably raised inflation in the last few months.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I would expect that to be relatively soft.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It’s consistent with very slow growth in nominal wages.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Also, there’s productivity growth, which keeps unit labor costs under control.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Inflation expectations are a somewhat different matter, as others have mentioned.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: What has happened so far—namely, that inflation has come back up to more normal levels—I take as a success, not a problem.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Deflation risks were a concern.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Within reason, an increase in inflation expectations reduces real interest rates and reduces debt burdens and is actually positive.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Of course, as many people have noted, we don’t want too much of a good thing—we don’t want to go further.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Higher inflation rates, besides being a problem for price stability, probably have negative effects on growth as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: For example, higher nominal mortgage rates tend to raise nominal payments, which could have effects on the demand for housing.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I agree with President Plosser and others that we do have to pay very close attention to inflation expectations and that our communication will be very important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In that respect, I think that the careful description of our exit strategy in the Monetary Policy Report and the Humphrey-Hawkins will be important.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And all of us should continue to emphasize our ability to withdraw the stimulus and to maintain our focus on price stability.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me stop there and ask Brian to turn to the policy round.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Before I begin, let me note that Carol Low has available a corrected version of the chart from yesterday that had the date axis labeled incorrectly.9 The Bluebook presented three monetary policy alternatives for your consideration—alternatives A, B, and C—as well as a variant of alternative B, labeled B´.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: On Monday, we provided revised drafts of the accompanying statements.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Those drafts, along with the Committee’s April statement, are included in the package labeled “Material for FOMC Briefing on Monetary Policy Alternatives.”10 A choice of alternative A, page 2, could be motivated by a view that the current settings of policy instruments—a near zero fed funds rate for an extended period, the current specification of the Committee’s large-scale asset purchases, and the terms and conditions of the Federal Reserve’s credit and liquidity programs—are unlikely to produce an outcome consistent with the dual mandate, especially given the recent backup in long rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Your projections indicate that many of you anticipate economic weakness persisting for several years; the central tendency of your unemployment projections at the end of 2011 is 8½ to 8¾ percent, and most of you see inflation in 2011 below rates that you consider to be consistent with price stability.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, many of you see very slow convergence beyond that, with at least five Committee participants anticipating that it will take the economy more than five to six years to return to a balanced growth path.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Furthermore, a substantial minority consider the risks to economic growth to be skewed to the downside.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With both a modal outlook for weak growth and low inflation, and downside risks around the outlook for activity, macroeconomic considerations would seem to argue for providing additional monetary policy stimulus at this juncture.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, with the federal funds rate at the zero bound, the Committee has limited policy options at its disposal.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: One of those options is to step up its large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: But as discussed yesterday, the Committee’s scope for increasing its large-scale asset purchases is also somewhat constrained: The Desk judges that purchases of agency debt securities, if anything, should be cut back from the currently specified amount of up to $200 billion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: And the Committee could encounter increasing difficulties in buying agency mortgage-backed securities without distorting interest rate spreads, particularly if the recent backup in long rates persists and reduces the volume of mortgage refinancing and gross MBS issuance.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In these circumstances, the Committee might be left with Treasury securities as the only asset readily available for increased purchase.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative A specifies that the Committee would increase its purchases of Treasury securities by $450 billion.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: 9 The corrected materials for Mr. Carpenter’s briefing are appended to this transcript (appendix 9) 10 The materials used by Mr. Madigan are appended to this transcript (appendix 10).

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With market participants, according to the Desk’s primary dealer survey, putting only small odds on an increase in purchases, staff estimates suggest that such an announcement might reduce longer-term interest rates by ¼ to ½ percentage point.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The staff further estimates that, by the end of 2011, a reduction in long-term rates by this amount could be sufficient to lower the unemployment rate by 0.2 to 0.4 percentage point.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, in its consideration of expanded asset purchases, the Committee would need to weigh certain other factors.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: First, despite the staff’s estimates, you might be skeptical about the effects of asset purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Or you may simply be quite uncertain about those effects and prefer to wait for further evidence.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Also, market perceptions of debt monetization and risks to inflation expectations that could accompany such an expansion are a worry.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: If the projections made by many of you turn out to be correct, inflation will remain quite subdued and any inflation scare should subside; but at this point, with the economic outlook improved, you may see appropriate risk management as calling for waiting before considering further action.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A related concern is that you yourselves might not be completely confident that the Federal Reserve will have the technical tools to execute an exit strategy at the appropriate time, particularly with an even larger balance sheet than is expected under the current program of asset purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In addition, as noted yesterday, the Federal Reserve could also experience reduced income and diminished remittances to the Treasury or capital losses even with currently planned asset purchases, and an expansion of these purchases could amplify such losses.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Alternative A incorporates another option for providing additional policy stimulus: The Committee could be more explicit about the period of time over which it expects to hold short-term interest rates at exceptionally low levels; this might be an alternative means of putting downward pressure on longer-term interest rates and spurring aggregate demand that would not involve further asset purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
