text: In particular, the bracketed language in paragraph 3 notes that, rather than simply reiterating the April indication that the Committee “anticipates that economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate for an extended period,” you could instead indicate that “economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate at least through mid-2010.” This more specific formulation might help limit the extent to which markets price in an earlier start to firming than the Committee currently sees as likely.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Such a statement would take the Committee in a direction that several other central banks—the Bank of Canada, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, and the Riksbank— have already taken.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Two notes provided to the Committee by the International Finance Division explored the experience of those central banks with these more explicitly contingent commitments.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The staff concluded that, at least on balance in these three cases, the commitments seemed to have had limited effects on market pricing, in part because they were perceived as providing little new information to the market.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The first and second paragraphs of the statement language for alternative A would set forth the motivation for further action at this meeting, particularly by citing the recent backup in bond yields.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The first paragraph would note that “Although conditions in financial markets have generally improved, the Committee judges that further monetary policy stimulus is warranted to help ensure that the sharp rise in some longer-term interest rates over recent months does not undermine a recovery in overall economic activity.” And the second paragraph would indicate that “the Committee still sees some risk that inflation could persist for a time below rates that best foster economic growth and price stability in the longer term,” repeating language used in its last three policy statements.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, if you see the current stance of policy as suitably balancing the various risks facing the Committee, you instead might be inclined to issue a statement along the lines of alternative B, page 3.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under this alternative, the Committee would continue to indicate that it expects the fed funds rate to remain exceptionally low for an extended period, and it would retain the existing limits on its large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The language in the first paragraph would be somewhat more upbeat than in April, noting that the pace of economic contraction is slowing, that financial market conditions have improved, that sentiment has risen, and that the inventory correction is proceeding.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, the Committee would temper that optimism by noting that “economic activity is likely to remain weak for a time.” The second paragraph would reiterate the Committee’s expectation that inflation will remain subdued, but it would omit the sentence citing the risk that inflation could persist at suboptimally low rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The third paragraph of the revised version of alternative B is mostly similar to the corresponding paragraph in the April statement.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, the second sentence indicates that the Committee “continues to” anticipate exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate, thus pushing back slightly on the expectation among some market participants of an early increase in the fed funds rate target.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Toward the end of the paragraph, the statement no longer includes the indication that “The Federal Reserve is facilitating the extension of credit to households and businesses and supporting the functioning of financial markets through a range of liquidity programs;” repeating that point no longer seems necessary.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The statement continues to note that policymakers are monitoring the size and composition of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet, but it adds the thought that the Federal Reserve “will make adjustments to its credit and liquidity programs as warranted,” consistent with tomorrow’s announcement of extensions and modifications to various liquidity programs.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The final sentence, in brackets, would signal that the Committee is factoring exit issues into its current policy decisions by noting that “The Committee will take careful account of the necessity of assuring that policy accommodation can ultimately be withdrawn smoothly and at the appropriate time.” Market participants reportedly expect little change in today’s FOMC statement, apart from a somewhat more optimistic assessment of the economic outlook than in April.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: In most respects, the draft statement for alternative B is consistent with those expectations.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: However, analysts will take note that the sentence expressing concern about downside inflation risks has been dropped.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, even with the emphasis in the third paragraph that the Committee “continues to” expect the fed funds rate to remain exceptionally low, the bracketed final sentence, if included, could give the impression that the Committee is preparing to remove policy accommodation sooner than markets currently expect, and it is possible that this sentence in particular could prompt a noticeable backup in interest rates.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: You may want to express your judgments about the desirability of including this point in the upcoming go-round.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: With the revisions to the language of alternative B since the Bluebook was published, the message of alternative B has become closer to that in the Bluebook’s alternative B´.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: And if the bracketed sentence in the revised version of alternative B were dropped, that alternative and alternative B´ would be substantively similar, so we have dropped alternative B´ as a separate option.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The version of alternative B without the bracketed sentence seems unlikely to prompt much market reaction.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Should you believe that the Committee ought to prepare to reduce the degree of monetary accommodation before long, you might see selection of alternative C, page 4, as appropriate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Of course, that view would be difficult to motivate under either the Greenbook forecast or the central tendency of your projections, but you might see the economy as likely to be more resilient than implied by these forecasts.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Even more pertinently, some of you have expressed concerns that the System’s enlarged balance sheet, its purchases of Treasury securities, and the extremely low federal funds rate might unmoor inflation expectations; the increase in inflation compensation and in survey measures of inflation expectations over the intermeeting period might be viewed as worrisome in this regard.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Against this backdrop, you might see a relatively near-term exit from the very accommodative policy stance as appropriate.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Under this alternative, the end of paragraph 1 would note explicitly the Committee’s expectation that a gradual recovery in economic activity is likely to begin later this year.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: The inflation paragraph would indicate a view that inflation will remain subdued but would leave out the phrase “for some time.” As in the current draft of alternative B, this alternative would drop the recent reference to downside inflation risk.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Importantly, in paragraph 3, the Committee’s expectation of the likely time frame for “exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate” would be changed to “until late this year.” This language would suggest that the Committee anticipates raising the federal funds rate beginning around year-end.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: Moreover, further down in paragraph 3, the statement would now indicate that “The Committee anticipates that the pace of purchases of securities will taper off gradually by the end of the year.” This sentence would convey a clear sense that the Committee does not intend to increase its asset purchases and, in fact, will begin to wind down its purchases of Treasury securities before long.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: All in all, such an announcement would be quite surprising to market participants, and in all likelihood it would prompt a considerable backup in interest rates and substantial market volatility.

speaker: MADIGAN
text: A table that compares the three statements is included on the final page for your reference.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Are there questions for Brian?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Not seeing any questions, let’s start with President Plosser.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’ve already highlighted some of my views on policy yesterday and earlier today.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Let me just sort of clarify.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My view of the outlook for the real economy is really not much different from most people’s around the table—near-term weakness, with modest growth returning in 2010.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: In fact, my own forecast is for less growth in 2011 than the Greenbook’s—a slow recovery in the economy in many respects.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t disagree with that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Where I disagree has more to do with the nature and the specification of the Phillips curve and how that guides both our inflation forecast and its implications for policy.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I don’t believe that the empirical relationship with gaps or slack is nearly as tight and predictable and reliable as oftentimes we think it is, so my concern is that we have to be careful about that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would remind the Committee that, between 1991 and 1996, the staff, according to the chart they handed out yesterday, had substantial output gaps ranging from 2 to 4 percent for most of that period, and inflation hardly budged—it remained between 2½ and 3 percent during that whole period.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So while I don’t want to rely on anecdotal information, it is true that this link between output gaps and inflation is not a very strong one.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we have to be cautious about relying too heavily on that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: My skepticism about the measurement of those gaps and the relationships with inflation is most relevant for the deliberations we will have about when it’s time to reverse course and how we decide when that time is.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think that’s going to be a very difficult choice, given the uncertainty surrounding these relationships.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A tightening cycle will inevitably occur, and choosing the right time to do it is going to be important for our future ability to achieve price stability.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I also think that, historically, this institution has been somewhat slow on the uptake many times.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we rely too heavily on measures of slack in labor markets or unemployment rate gaps, we will inevitably find ourselves behind the curve, because we know unemployment rates take a long time to turn around, and the economy will turn around before that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: If we wait until the unemployment rate becomes an unacceptable level to reverse course, I’m fairly confident that we will be well behind the curve.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: So my point is really about the nature of the Phillips curve, and about the reliability of those estimates, and about our ability to rely on them for policy decisions during this critical time.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I believe the economy is in this sort of bumpy transition from dramatic contraction hopefully to expansion.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I agree with everyone that there are substantial risks to that forecast, and we need to be conscious of those risks and those concerns.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I’m very supportive, as I said yesterday, of the staff’s proposals on winding down the facilities.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I am opposed to increasing our large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we need to be very cautious in that effort.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We still have a ways to go, so we still could increase purchases if we chose to do so.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: And I don’t believe we ought to make decisions about adding to that volume very precipitously or quickly.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would also hope that the argument is symmetric; that is, if the economy improves and evolves in the way that many of us are hoping it will over the course of the fall, then we may not necessarily have to go to the full limit on some of these programs.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we have to make that clear to the public as well.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: A major issue I see in the policy decision today has to do with language—I think it’s the communication effort that’s going to be so difficult.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think ultimately we are going to have to find a way to extract ourselves from the current language of “exceptionally low levels of the federal funds rate for an extended period.” That’s why I am somewhat sympathetic to the first part of paragraph 3 in alternative C, although I wouldn’t be nearly as explicit about the timing in that paragraph: “until late this year.” I would sort of strike that and just say, “for some time.” Even if we raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points, it’s still exceptionally low, so I’m not sure that the difference between level and changes here is important.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: Given my hesitancy and skepticism about tying our inflation forecast too tightly to slack measures, I actually am happier with paragraph 2 in alternative B than I was before, in the sense that both the persistence and size of the output gap become somewhat less dominant.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I would prefer C in that regard, but I think paragraph 2 is better than the version in the Bluebook that we saw, so I’m happy with that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I think we have some difficult choices before us in the coming quarters, and it would be helpful if we could continue to push for our inflation targeting goals.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: I hope that that is not off the table and will continue to be pursued.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: But I do think that in the coming months and coming quarters we are going to have to make some very difficult economic decisions, and we could face considerable political pressure in the face of that.

speaker: PLOSSER
text: We need to prepare ourselves for that and prepare the markets for it.

speaker: LACKER
text: I think we should continue now with the announced schedule of asset purchases.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t think expanding our purchases makes any sense now, given the stabilization of the economy, the diminution of concerns about deflation, and the emergence of some scattered concerns about inflation.

speaker: LACKER
text: I agree with you that we’ve sort of normalized inflation and inflation expectations at this point, and we’re okay where we are.

speaker: LACKER
text: But given that, I don’t think it makes sense to provide more stimulus.

speaker: LACKER
text: It’s true that our credit programs have run off more rapidly than we expected as of the last meeting.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I discussed yesterday, it means our balance sheet is smaller, so you might think that it provides less stimulus than you would otherwise expect.

speaker: LACKER
text: I outlined another perspective, where some components of borrowing respond endogenously, as sort of a residual.

speaker: LACKER
text: This perspective is based on the notion that the demand for reserves isn’t perfectly elastic at current rates.

speaker: LACKER
text: That would suggest that the degree of stimulus hasn’t turned out to be much different from what we expected it to have been.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m happy that the Desk didn’t attempt to offset the shortfall in the balance sheet, as the discussion at our last meeting might have led them to think I would have desired.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m broadly apprehensive about the increases in reserves implied by completing the path of asset purchases we’re on.

speaker: LACKER
text: As I’ve indicated, I think the impact depends on the nature of the demand for bank reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: If what I outlined yesterday has some validity, then, at some point, all that buffer of borrowing from us goes away, and then the nature of the impact of our balance sheet expansion shifts qualitatively.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, whether it’s quantitatively important or not, I don’t think we know.

speaker: LACKER
text: We have all known that we’re sort of groping in the dark here as to what the exact analytics are of this balance sheet expansion as monetary stimulus.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I think the kind of thing I outlined yesterday deserves some consideration, and it makes me apprehensive about following all the way through on the purchases.

speaker: LACKER
text: Now, I’m not saying I have any idea about when we’re going to want to withdraw stimulus, or how the economy will play out.

speaker: LACKER
text: It just strikes me as plausible that we get to a state where we need to think about exit.

speaker: LACKER
text: I don’t know when that is, and I can’t pretend that I do.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I think that, when we do get there, we’re going to need to be cognizant of the elasticity of demand for reserves.

speaker: LACKER
text: In consequence, I think we ought to give some consideration at the next few meetings to lower paths for our asset purchases.

speaker: LACKER
text: If we get outcomes that are on the good side of what we are expecting, in the fourth quarter we could find ourselves in a situation where we want to pull back on what we’ve planned.

speaker: LACKER
text: I also think maybe a less gradual unwinding of the assets ought to be on the table.

speaker: LACKER
text: I applaud the staff again, by the way, for all of the good work they’ve done so far on our exit strategy.

speaker: LACKER
text: But I think we’d all admit we have a little more to do.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m happy with alternative B. I’m happy omitting the bracketed sentence at the end.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not quite sure what it means.

speaker: LACKER
text: I’m not quite sure about the extent to which we have taken account of ensuring that our policy accommodation can be withdrawn smoothly and at the appropriate time.

speaker: LACKER
text: So I’m not sure how we’d explain it to people.

speaker: LACKER
text: And, besides, I think it’s a little too soon to convey, as I think the sentence would, that we think of exit as likely to be imminent enough to warrant our mentioning it in the statement.

speaker: LACKER
text: At the same time, I do think it’s important, as I said earlier, to convey in the Monetary Policy Report, or elsewhere, that we have a grasp on this and we’re working hard on it.

speaker: LACKER
text: Also, I’m happy omitting the statement in paragraph 2 about inflation being at low levels—I think it’s important to acknowledge the shift in inflation outlook.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Like President Lacker, I favor alternative B in both substance and wording.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think the staff captured my view with their description of alternative B, which said the slow pace of recovery is largely unavoidable in light of the nature and severity of the global financial crisis and the time required for healing and other structural adjustments.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think alternative B also recognizes the tentative nature of improvement in the economy, so I see it as a “stay the course” policy.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As mentioned yesterday, the balance sheet is expected to grow to approximately $2.8 trillion, so I think the playing out of programs as currently designed should represent sufficient stimulus to sustain the progress we’ve seen.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I am sympathetic to the view that was expressed by both Presidents Plosser and Lacker that if we see better results, we should consider scaling back the LSAP programs.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: At the same time, I think it would be a mistake to react too early and strongly to the signs of stabilization and better financial market conditions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As many said yesterday and today, we have a particularly subtle communication task coming out of this meeting.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think we need to encourage positive views that can be self-reinforcing to stabilization and ultimately to recovery.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: But I also think we have to present a sober characterization of the state of and outlook for the economy, and we should be signaling that we’re not withdrawing stimulus and support for the economy at this time.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: It’s okay, I believe, to signal that we’re thinking and planning for an eventual exit, but not initiating an exit.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: Yesterday, I supported—though I didn’t speak for it—the plan presented by Brian Madigan for the expiration of the facilities, and I agree that the press release should and does emphasize the conditionality of that plan.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think much of the communication task, as discussed yesterday afternoon, should be accomplished after today’s statement, for example, in the Chairman’s Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: On the statement itself, I can support it as it’s presented.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: In the revised proposal, I favored B′ before it was eliminated.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think it is continuous with the April statement and gives a “stay the course” message.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: As I said earlier, it accurately captures the economic conditions.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: I think the inflation language is a logical update to the April language, and since my forecast does not assume an increase in the policy rate this year or next, I’m comfortable for the time being with the “extended period” language.

speaker: LOCKHART
text: And finally, I do not support the bracketed statement that was appended.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I can support alternative B, although on purely policy grounds I think that a strong case exists for further monetary stimulus.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The economy appears to be stabilizing and downside risk has declined, but it will be many years before the economy is close to operating at full employment.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Not surprisingly, the Bluebook optimal policy simulation shows that the stance of policy is not even close to the optimal degree of accommodation.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As the Bluebook points out, unemployment is anticipated to run around 1½ percentage points higher on the constrained path than on the unconstrained path for the next three to four years, and this translates into a cumulative loss on the order of 10 percent of GDP, or $1½ trillion, and creates a very strong case for doing everything possible to stimulate the economy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The problem is that the obvious remaining tool, large-scale Treasury purchases, may be less effective than hoped and may entail a variety of unquantifiable costs, as we have discussed.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I wouldn’t want to take an expansion of this program off the table if the economy were to worsen, but I wouldn’t push for an expansion now.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The bottom line for me is that we likely will need to maintain the current stance of policy for a very long time to get back to full employment, and my main concern is that markets will anticipate and we may be tempted to withdraw our accommodation too soon, thereby aborting the recovery.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Christina Romer recently wrote a pertinent essay for The Economist on “The Lessons of 1937” that you may have read.

speaker: YELLEN
text: As many of you know, in that year, following two years of robust recovery, the Federal Reserve tightened policy too soon because it was worried about large quantities of excess reserves in the banking system.

speaker: YELLEN
text: The economy plunged back into depression, and I believe that a parallel can be found in Japan’s experience of the 1990s as well.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So I think we need to do all that we can to avoid creating the impression that we intend to raise the federal funds rate any time soon.

speaker: YELLEN
text: For this reason I definitely prefer to drop the final sentence in brackets in B concerning exit strategy.

speaker: YELLEN
text: By bringing this issue up in the policy statement, I am afraid we will reinforce the market’s impression that we may begin to tighten policy sooner rather than later.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think discussions of exit strategy would be better handled in testimony or speeches by the Chairman.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In the event that a reference is included in this statement, I have a very small wording change to propose.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Currently the statement refers to taking “careful account of the necessity of ensuring that policy accommodation can ultimately be withdrawn.” The phrase “can ultimately be withdrawn” sounds to me like we’re not sure we can do it or that we may refrain from easing policy in particular ways later on because of our concern about our ability to withdraw.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So if it is included, I would prefer a more confident wording, namely, “ensuring that policy accommodation is ultimately withdrawn smoothly and at the appropriate time.” So I would essentially change “can be” to “is.” I also have a wording suggestion to make in paragraph 1 concerning the outlook, and my objective here, again, is to make the statement slightly less optimistic, slightly less able to be interpreted as saying that we are anywhere close to withdrawing stimulus, and, in my view, slightly more balanced.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I propose adding to a sentence in paragraph 1 of B to recognize that even though financial conditions have improved on balance, which is a net positive for the outlook, the increase in mortgage rates we have seen has the potential to impede recovery in the housing market.

speaker: YELLEN
text: In particular, I would propose the following language: “Conditions in financial markets have generally improved in recent months, although the sharp rise in mortgage rates has the potential to impede recovery in the housing market.

speaker: YELLEN
text: Indicators of consumer and business sentiment…” and so on.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think the increase in mortgage rates has been substantial.

speaker: YELLEN
text: It is one of the most important and most discussed developments since our last meeting, and it does create a risk to the outlook.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it deserves mention in the statement as a negative factor that partially offsets what is a net improvement.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I also would argue for including it for the sake of balance.

speaker: YELLEN
text: I think it parallels our discussion in the very next sentence that says that there are some factors restraining household spending, and again, in the inflation section where we mention increases in the prices of energy and commodities as an offset to our view that inflation will remain generally subdued.

speaker: YELLEN
text: So that’s a concrete suggestion.

speaker: EVANS
text: I took some comfort from our discussion yesterday on reserve management tools, although we had discussions about these before.

speaker: EVANS
text: It does seem as if these tools are likely to be enough to allow tightening when we need it.

speaker: EVANS
text: Previously I would have thought that we would have to grapple with the problem of getting our balance sheet in better shape and that markets would see that coming well before we ever got to a positive federal funds rate.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I guess I’m more persuaded—although the continued staff analysis will be helpful on this—that it’s likely to be more contemporaneous; that is, when we decide that we need to tighten, we can bring these tools to bear quickly and may not have to signal very much in advance.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think that’s very helpful, because part of what we’re grappling with right now is how to position ourselves for doing the tightening a few meetings or several meetings into the future.

speaker: EVANS
text: I don’t have a firm opinion really on when it’s likely to be the case that we’ll need to tighten.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think it’s pretty far in the future, 2010 maybe.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the large-scale asset purchases, I guess I prefer leaving them the way they are, given the improvement in the economy.

speaker: EVANS
text: If at the next meeting we think it’s going to be important to communicate about a tapering-off strategy—if we are worried about the cliff—I think we probably need to decide now about how to communicate that.

speaker: EVANS
text: If we wait, then the cliff is going to be that much closer, and you’re not really going to be able to do this with the existing size.

speaker: EVANS
text: So if you want to maintain the existing size, I think you would need to do that soon, like today probably.

speaker: EVANS
text: But it’s not in the statement.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the inflation forecast, it does seem to me that there’s a pretty wide dispersion of forecasts for core PCE in 2011, which is not that far away—so the dispersion is a bit unusual.

speaker: EVANS
text: If you take out the high and the low, then it’s ½ to 2 percent.

speaker: EVANS
text: I hope that the minutes will reflect this diversity of opinion in a slightly robust fashion, because that debate is taking place out in the public.

speaker: EVANS
text: We all go out and face very difficult questions, and even though we might feel pretty confident about our outlook for inflation, this dispersion of views is sort of a reality check as to how we deal with that.

speaker: EVANS
text: On inflation forecasts, it does seem like there is substantial resource slack now.

speaker: EVANS
text: It has been a very deep contraction, and so my own forecast is relatively low.

speaker: EVANS
text: Even if you allow for differences of NAIRUs, it’s a big amount of slack.

speaker: EVANS
text: But there are risks, and we know the theory says that inflation expectations can “take off.” That would be a key element in inflation determination and our forecast.

speaker: EVANS
text: Events somewhat beyond our control—fiscal pressures and how they are dealt with in the large number of programs that are coming down the pike, as President Fisher reminded us—and our balance sheet size are adding to this risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: I think what we’ve been doing is appropriate, but it does add to the risk.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I think a lot of it comes down to how much confidence we have in a particular forecast, and some people are inclined to write a larger number for 2011, and others are inclined to write down a much smaller number.

speaker: EVANS
text: I kind of prefer to take the middle course, but in this particular bimodal situation, these opposing forces are difficult.

speaker: EVANS
text: So normally in a situation like this, we can fall back on timing: We don’t have to do this today, and in the worst case, we’re several meetings before the pressure erupts, and, Mr. Chairman, you will be providing testimony soon in your Monetary Policy Report, and that would be a natural way to communicate that.

speaker: EVANS
text: But it does seem as though these issues have been out there, you’ve been out front in talking about them.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I just don’t know exactly what the likely impact is going to be from delivering that message again.

speaker: EVANS
text: So even though the bimodal beliefs are quite different, I prefer the middle course, and so I do prefer alternative B.

speaker: EVANS
text: On the particular issues for the statement, I’m not bothered by the bracketed statement at the end.

speaker: EVANS
text: I guess if I were going to make the best case, it is that it seems accurate that we will continue to take careful account of this.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’ve got the reserve management tools.

speaker: EVANS
text: We’ve just had a meeting where we talked an awful lot about it.

speaker: EVANS
text: So it’s not inappropriate to raise this now.

speaker: EVANS
text: The Chairman and others have talked about exactly this issue, and probably have used words very similar to this.

speaker: EVANS
text: We say it in public.

speaker: EVANS
text: So what does it mean if we don’t say it here in the statement but we say it in public?

speaker: EVANS
text: Well, we can always ask that question because that’s not an uncommon type of omission.

speaker: EVANS
text: It does seem as if the language in the second paragraph gets at this middle ground for inflation, because we took out the part saying something like “inflation could be uncomfortably low,” or whatever the language was indicating that it could be suboptimal.

speaker: EVANS
text: So I’m comfortable with alternative B.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The forecast has high unemployment rates and low inflation rates through 2011, and the Greenbook forecast expects an undesirably low inflation rate even at the end of 2013.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Missing both elements of the dual mandate through 2011 and possibly beyond strongly suggests to me that we should attempt to provide more stimulus both to avoid a multiyear elevated unemployment rate and to avoid a prolonged period of lower than desired inflation.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Mortgage and Treasury rates have risen despite our large-scale asset purchase program.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: The increase in Treasury rates likely reflects the reduced precautionary demand for that asset as financial markets have improved.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: However, the increase in mortgage rates is likely to slow both residential investment and consumption relative to what they would be if we were pushing rates lower.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: There has been a reluctance to intervene more aggressively in the thirty-year mortgage market because it is felt that this would disrupt market functioning.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: But if our LSAPs cannot produce mortgage rates that are low enough to spur refinancing and new construction, then we have dramatically expanded our balance sheet with little to show for it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I believe we can and should do more.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: While I support alternative B, I would encourage the Desk to further reduce mortgage rates relative to Treasury rates.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Furthermore, since the market for five- and seven-year ARMs is already quite limited, aggressive activity in ARMs would restore the market and provide a low-cost alternative for some homebuyers willing to float after five or seven years.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Because of the lack of activity, setting a low rate in this market and increasing volume would not disrupt market functioning.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In fact, it would resuscitate the market.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: These ARMs also have some appeal for our balance sheet since they mature relatively quickly, making the exit strategy easier for these assets.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: Acting more aggressively to restore the ARM market and to further reduce the spread relative to Treasuries for longer-maturity mortgages seem like appropriate steps to gain greater confidence that we will achieve both elements of our dual mandate within a reasonable time horizon.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I would emphasize that the experience of the past seven years has taught us that conducting monetary policy in a very low-inflation environment is not as straightforward as we might have wished.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: At some point, we should have a fuller discussion of our inflation goal in light of the probability of reaching the zero lower bound in the future and the difficulty in conducting monetary policy when we are at the zero bound.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: In terms of what’s in the statement, I actually would not be for having the final sentence.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: We have not been communicating the path of the LSAP program.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I think we can taper as appropriate without necessarily having to discuss how we’re going to taper it.

speaker: ROSENGREN
text: I do prefer President Yellen’s language—I do think it’s appropriate to mention the rise in rates, because it has been quite appreciable, and it has been probably the biggest news that we’ve had in the last month in terms of what has been going on in the financial markets.

speaker: STERN
text: Well, I don’t know if we’re at a turning point in economic activity, although I don’t think we’re far away.

speaker: STERN
text: But one thing I do know is that when you’re close to or at turning points, there’s always a tremendous amount of uncertainty: It’s very difficult to read the state of the economy; it’s very difficult to come to a conclusion with confidence as to how the economy is going to perform going forward in this kind of environment.

speaker: STERN
text: The reason I mention that is that I think decisionmaking isn’t going to get any easier any time soon.

speaker: STERN
text: I think this is going to characterize things probably for the next year and perhaps more.

speaker: STERN
text: In this environment with all of this uncertainty, one nice rule of thumb might be to do no harm, especially since recent trends, while certainly not great, are better than they had been and in some ways better than we had anticipated just a few months ago.

speaker: STERN
text: So I wouldn’t change any policy parameters at this point with regard to purchases of longer-term assets or other parameters that we might think about.

speaker: STERN
text: Yesterday I commented that I didn’t think we had a problem convincing market participants that we were prepared to do what it would take to restore financial stability and ultimately economic health.

speaker: STERN
text: I think people believe that and understand that.

speaker: STERN
text: I’m a little less convinced that they understand that we do have an exit strategy and will execute it appropriately.

speaker: STERN
text: Against that background, and to begin to address that concern, I can favor either President Plosser’s alternative C—the one he described in the material he distributed late last week—or alternative B as presented here with that last sentence in brackets included.

speaker: STERN
text: (It’s okay with me if it’s modified along the lines that President Yellen suggested.)

speaker: STERN
text: I don’t think that sentence will be read as if we’re about to change policy any time soon.

speaker: STERN
text: As President Evans commented, people have been talking about that publicly.

speaker: STERN
text: I think that would provide reassurance to people in the marketplace and people in the economy more generally that we are aware of the challenge and we’re prepared to address it: We know we’re in an environment where our balance sheet has expanded tremendously and is likely to expand further, given our plans, and where there’s a very expansionary fiscal policy in place with no end in sight.

speaker: STERN
text: I think it would be appropriate to make that point clear.

speaker: KOHN
text: As I noted at the end of my remarks, I don’t think the central tendency that we’ve submitted is really a satisfactory outcome for the economy.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’re looking at an unemployment rate—just considering the center of the central tendency—of about 8½ percent in two and a half years and an inflation rate of 1½ percent, which is below the 2 percent that most of us have favored; and that’s probably headed lower unless the economy picks up steam very, very fast after that.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that’s why most Taylor rules and the optimal control simulations that President Yellen mentioned call for negative nominal interest rates now.

speaker: KOHN
text: Moreover, I think from a risk-management perspective, which we used to talk about around here, even though the risks are more balanced on either side of this sluggish recovery now than they were, I think the cost of a shortfall is greater than the cost of an overshoot.

speaker: KOHN
text: We know how to counter inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: We’ve done it before and we can do it again.

speaker: KOHN
text: But this central tendency tells me that, given the size of the shock, we’re having trouble getting satisfactory outcomes for output and inflation.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think the risk, as President Bullard pointed out, is that we could be caught in a high-output-gap, low-inflation or even deflationary environment.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think that’s going to happen, but I think there’s a risk there, and if we get caught in that, I think it’s very, very difficult to figure out how to get out of it.

speaker: KOHN
text: This seemed to be much easier, Mr. Chairman, when we were lecturing Japan than when we’re doing it ourselves.

speaker: KOHN
text: Everybody had a solution for them, and somehow when you’re there, there are a lot of complications, aren’t there?

speaker: KOHN
text: So of the two possible policy errors—moving toward tightening too soon and moving too late—I’m more worried that we’ll move too soon than that we’ll move too late.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we can correct that latter one.

speaker: KOHN
text: I don’t think there is anything we can do about this now, despite the lack of satisfactory outcome.

speaker: KOHN
text: Because of inflation sensitivity, because of exit worries, because of concerns about monetization of the debt in the presence of a large and uncertain fiscal path, I’m not advocating more policy action today.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we should continue with our purchases.

speaker: KOHN
text: I would go up to the limits that we’ve set, and I would include the ARMs—at least a small amount of the ARMs—in those purchases, hoping to have a positive effect on mortgage markets.

speaker: KOHN
text: I hope our next decision is how and when to remove accommodation, to remove the quantitative and interest rate accommodation, but I don’t rule out the possibility that we could take future easing actions if circumstances called for it—that would be more large-scale asset purchases, possibly, and, to my mind, lowering the interest rate on excess reserves would help as well.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I would be careful not to say something that rules out the possibility of doing something more later.

speaker: KOHN
text: In response to President Stern, I’d be concerned that putting that sentence in here would cast doubt on whether we’re willing to use all of the tools available under the circumstances.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think that it’s far too soon to signal that the exit is drawing closer; furthermore, if we’re seen as worried about the exit and looking carefully at it, it will undermine our effect.

speaker: KOHN
text: I agree with everyone else—we need to be very, very clear that we will be able to exit when we decide to exit.

speaker: KOHN
text: But I don’t think we’re anywhere close to making that decision.

speaker: KOHN
text: So I support the language of alternative B without the bracketed sentence.

speaker: KOHN
text: I do think removing this sentence about inflation being less than desirable from the second paragraph will be seen as a little bit more hawkish, a little bit more worried about inflation than we were before.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we could justify keeping the sentence based on the forecasts that we have from the Committee, but the forecasts have been revised up and certainly the degree to which the Committee expects inflation to be less than it ideally should be has been reduced to some extent.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think it’s especially important to keep in the sentence about continuing to anticipate that economic conditions are likely to warrant exceptionally low levels of the fed funds rate for a time.

speaker: KOHN
text: I think we need to signal to the market that, even if they’ve changed their expectations for future interest rates, we have not, at least not appreciably.

speaker: KOHN
text: And finally, on President Yellen’s point, I guess I’d be concerned that putting in her whole sentence would really undermine the sense that financial conditions had improved and that the economy was in the process of bottoming out.

speaker: KOHN
text: If we did anything, I would just add something like, “Although mortgage interest rates have risen, conditions in financial markets have improved on balance in recent months.” Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think alternative B is sensible at this juncture.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In this situation, I’m going to argue here that it’s a good time to take stock and get more information—we’d like to see how this recovery develops over the summer.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, I think we’re able to retain alternatives for future meetings, and I agree with Governor Kohn that we may want to move at future meetings.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I’ll talk about several aspects of alternative B.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On the bracketed last sentence concerning the exit strategy, I agree with some of the comments that have been made that this may be more confusing than helpful with respect to the LSAP program.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We will discuss exit, and, as President Yellen said, it’s better discussed in testimony.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This is an inherently technical, complicated thing—it just will not come across in a simple way to the general public.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It takes a lot of explaining, and I think it will be hard to figure out from this sentence what is meant in terms of exit strategy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I also prefer the “as warranted” language.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I want to talk for just a minute about forward guidance and naming specific dates for when we might make future interest rate moves, as are contemplated in alternatives A and C. First of all, I think everyone has said that we need the conditionality—you need to know how the economy is evolving in order to know when you’re going to make a move.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Naming a specific date seems to undermine that, and in fact, I think it might go the wrong direction.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You might essentially be pre-announcing a rate increase far ahead of when you actually have the information to decide whether you want to do that or not.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Of course, you could always move later and get the market to move off that, but you’re kind of drawing this line in the sand, and I’m not sure that’s what the Committee wants to do.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I know other countries have done this.

speaker: BULLARD
text: One thing I will say about that is, when you do that, you do get announcement effects, but that’s because you surprised the markets.

speaker: BULLARD
text: That’s not necessarily good policy or a good thing to do.

speaker: BULLARD
text: This business of promising to keep rates lower for longer works well in models, but you’re pushing very hard on this rational expectations assumption inside the models—everybody has great foresight about the future, everybody understands, there’s a lot of credibility—and I’m not sure that that maps into the reality of our situation.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Also, when you say “lower for longer,” you mean relative to what would otherwise be the optimal policy rule, and I’m not sure that we actually have that embedded out there in the market.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think the effects that we might get from further strengthening our commitment to low rates further out in the future are probably lost in the reality of the situation that we face.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I also think there are limits, just because of discounting in the future—if you promise to keep rates low far into the future, then that gets discounted by the markets the farther you go into the future.

speaker: BULLARD
text: In summary, I would just keep the “for an extended period” language at this meeting and at future meetings.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think that taps into the amount that we can get out of that future commitment, and it’s doing as much as we can on that dimension.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Let me just make a few brief comments here about expanding the LSAP.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I’ve characterized this as increasing the persistent components of the balance sheet, so I would ignore the components that are running off, such as the TAF.

speaker: BULLARD
text: They are going up at a rapid rate.

speaker: BULLARD
text: As I said earlier, you know, there are concerns about monetizing the debt, and I won’t go into those again—I think that’s an appearance issue, not an intention on anybody’s part.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Those perceptions are very hard to control outside the U.S.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I guess what I think about LSAP is that we are only about halfway through the current program.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We don’t really need to commit to further purchases at this time, but we have the optionality to do that later.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I may be sympathetic with that later on.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So right now I think it’s better to wait and gather information over the summer.

speaker: BULLARD
text: On cliff effects, I’m convinced now that we can just let the program expire as scheduled, and it won’t have a major market disruption.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Again, we have conditionality to do more if we want or if it seems necessary.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Let me just regale you with policy rules for large-scale asset purchases.

speaker: BULLARD
text: President Lacker said earlier that discretion is the enemy of clarity, which I thought was Shakespearesque of him.

speaker: BULLARD
text: But we’ve not been clear about our reaction function with respect to these programs, and that makes it hard not just for the public, but also for ourselves.

speaker: BULLARD
text: You make a one-time announcement and the market is wondering, well, will they make another announcement in six months and another announcement six months after that?

speaker: BULLARD
text: It’s very hard to know.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it’s the Committee’s job—I should add, not the Desk’s job—to get a reaction function so that, if unemployment or output gaps deteriorated in a certain way, that would be the case when we would do more.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Or the Committee could set some kind of mapping for how much we would want to do in various situations.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I actually think that would help us and allow us to do more if necessary, because you’d be conveying this understanding of a state-contingent path out there in the future, which is the object that we don’t have right now.

speaker: BULLARD
text: Finally, this is a lost cause, but I would advocate moving the federal funds rate later in the statement.

speaker: BULLARD
text: I think it reduces emphasis on the federal funds rate as the key tool of policy.

speaker: BULLARD
text: We’re seeing now that—everybody’s wondering, “Oh, maybe you’ll raise rates later this year or next year” or something like that.

speaker: BULLARD
text: It may be that, the way things are evolving, the fed funds rate will turn out not to be our primary policy tool on the other side of this.

speaker: BULLARD
text: So I think we should think more about de-emphasizing the federal funds rate.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Bullard, we already moved it from the top of the statement all the way down to paragraph 3.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I thought that was a fair compromise, by the way.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: My outlook assumes that our policy accommodation is going to continue for some time, and yet the recovery is still quite prolonged.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: As has been noted, financial market conditions have improved somewhat during the intermeeting period, but those improvements have taken place alongside of continuing significant public policy interventions.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So a little progress has been made, but I think the economy needs a considerable amount of time to cement that progress.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: In this environment, I think we have room to continue to evaluate the outlook and the effects of our current programs.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: So I support alternative B.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given Brian’s comments about the uncertainty on how the language in the bracketed sentence would be received, I would just leave it out.

speaker: PIANALTO
text: Given that we are going to have a Monetary Policy Report and that you are going to give testimony in the near future, I would just rely on those vehicles to address some of these issues more fully.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I’m fine with alternative B, and I would at some point—not today, but in the future—have a preference for C. I could work with the language that’s in the brackets, but it’s not essential to me.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Obviously, the economy remains weak.

speaker: HOENIG
text: But, as the discussion and as the projections have indicated, it’s also true that economic and financial conditions have improved.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We expect to see some modest improvement in economic growth, perhaps in the latter part of this year and even next year, as we’ve discussed.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We’re now in a situation where the data are changing, and we are beginning to talk about the possibility of a turning point, and in that regard, I agree with President Stern—the data are mixed, and they will be mixed for some time.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Looking toward the decisions ahead of us, I think that, given the mixed data and given the experiences that we had in the fall of 2007 and in the summer of 2008, there will be an enormous power of inertia at this table not to make that downward mistake.

speaker: HOENIG
text: It’s hard to perceive that the monetary and fiscal stimulus that’s in place, as significant it is, will really carry the day forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We’re going to resist that until we actually see the data.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Furthermore, this period of low inflation is going to kind of reinforce our view that we should wait and we should make sure that the recovery is strong.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think that’s where we do risk the other side of this, and that’s how we create inflationary issues or bubbles four or five years down the road because of this extended period of accommodation, and we shouldn’t lose sight of that.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I think it’s extremely important.

speaker: HOENIG
text: With that in mind, I was pleased that we had the conversation yesterday about our exit strategy.

speaker: HOENIG
text: My goals around that are that we find ourselves in a position where we can talk about our policy rate being moved back towards neutral and we can talk about the fact that we’re shrinking our balance sheet and the degree of excess reserves.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I agree that we don’t want to repeat the experience of the late 1930s, but that was a very blunt movement up in reserve requirements.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Hopefully we’ve learned that lesson and would be much more sensitive and much more gradual.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Given the degree of stimulus, I think it will take us years to even get back close to neutral.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So the economy is going to be growing slowly, but our moves back toward neutral also will be very slow.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Another goal, besides shrinking our balance sheet, should be restoring the composition of our balance sheet.

speaker: HOENIG
text: We are now in the credit allocation business towards the housing market, and that, of course, gives me some pause.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I do think that a case can be made for scaling back our asset purchase program, doing less than is currently authorized.

speaker: HOENIG
text: When we originally began these purchases some months ago, the outlook was considerably weaker.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Deflation was a possibility, although a small one, and financial stress was, in fact, elevated.

speaker: HOENIG
text: With the improving economic and financial conditions, with the very significant fiscal stimulus beginning to kick in, and with deflation even less of a threat, I think it would be prudent to reevaluate these purchases and determine whether we need to go up to the total amount.

speaker: HOENIG
text: That is what I mentioned yesterday about carefully reviewing that at each meeting.

speaker: HOENIG
text: I also would be very reluctant to expand the Treasury purchase program.

speaker: HOENIG
text: Given the size of the debt that is being issued, the optics on that can be nothing but harmful going forward.

speaker: HOENIG
text: So we have lots to think about in the long term, and I want to begin to raise the need for that long-term perspective today, even though some decisions along those lines are still in the future.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Chairman, I’m in favor of alternative B. I appreciate some of the restructuring that was made from the previous draft.

speaker: FISHER
text: I agree with President Yellen that we ought to change the wording in that last bracketed sentence, because I’m in favor of including that sentence, and here’s why.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think the market is asking us to at least clarify that we have thought about an exit strategy.

speaker: FISHER
text: With all due respect to Brian, whose work I admire enormously—both Brians, by the way—I think we might actually get a negative market reaction unless we clarify, at least in the very general terms in which this has been described.

speaker: FISHER
text: “The Committee will continue to take careful account of the necessity of ensuring that policy accommodation,” as Janet said, “is (or will be) ultimately withdrawn smoothly and at the appropriate time.” It doesn’t say too much.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think it tees up your congressional testimony.

speaker: FISHER
text: I agree in this sense with President Evans and President Stern; I certainly am not opposed to including it, and, in fact, I think we should include it.

speaker: FISHER
text: If we did, and I would urge us to consider it, then I don’t think we need to say “continues to anticipate.” That’s a little bit too conditional.

speaker: FISHER
text: Mr. Vice Chairman, I get your point—we are “continuing to,” but the fact is we do anticipate.

speaker: FISHER
text: Plus, we use the word “continue” twice in one paragraph.

speaker: FISHER
text: So I would urge you to consider, Mr. Chairman, including that last sentence.

speaker: FISHER
text: It is, indeed, a fact that we are taking account of the necessity of ensuring that policy accommodation is or will be ultimately withdrawn smoothly and at an appropriate time.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t see what it costs us, and I do think there is a general explicit and implicit expectation that we do so.

speaker: FISHER
text: One other comment: I haven’t thought this through tremendously, but I don’t necessarily disagree with President Rosengren’s suggestion, because I think the Desk ought to have some leeway with regard to the mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: FISHER
text: As everybody in this room knows, I thought the Treasury purchase program was a mistake.

speaker: FISHER
text: It was a very expensive mistake.

speaker: FISHER
text: I don’t think it has helped.

speaker: FISHER
text: I think has actually set us back a little bit, and obviously I wouldn’t be in favor of extending it any further.

speaker: FISHER
text: But now that we’re there, we might continue the program until it’s done.

speaker: FISHER
text: But I think the Desk might have some discretion, and we might so instruct the Desk— not in this statement—but they might work their way around the yield curve a bit for mortgage- backed securities and into certain types of mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: WARSH
text: First, I think it is likely we’ll need to remove our policy accommodation sooner than the Greenbook indicates, but I think it’s unlikely we’ll begin to remove it as quickly as markets currently suggest.

speaker: WARSH
text: Second, given the commitments that we have made, notwithstanding the “up to” language, on the asset purchases, while I’m not in favor of extending that obligation, I do think we should work to achieve that existing commitment, for credibility purposes.

speaker: WARSH
text: Third, I support alternative B and will just make a few comments on language.

speaker: WARSH
text: With respect to the last sentence, I think it is essential that markets understand that we are taking these exit considerations seriously.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think that is good both for actions that we could take that are even more aggressive—that they know we’re taking it with full understanding and confidence that we can exit—and for actions that we have already undertaken.

speaker: WARSH
text: Having said that, I don’t think this is the right place to be making that argument.

speaker: WARSH
text: I don’t think our experience in the last few years in using this statement for nuance or for volume control has proven to be the most effective way of doing so.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think we have ample opportunities through you, Mr. Chairman, to be very clear about the need for exit and these considerations.

speaker: WARSH
text: So, on balance, though I’m sympathetic to the truth of it, I think it would be more prudent for you to make this point clear and consistent in your Monetary Policy Report and other speaking opportunities.

speaker: WARSH
text: If the bracketed sentence were in, we’d be proving a little too much.

speaker: WARSH
text: To me, the fact that we’re now entering this into the statement does have the feel of sort of protesting.

speaker: WARSH
text: So on balance, I would favor not doing it, though I am, of course, comfortable with the substance.

speaker: WARSH
text: I just want to flag the penultimate sentence.

speaker: WARSH
text: “The Federal Reserve is monitoring the size and composition of its balance sheet.” I like it, and I think it helps for the announcement that we make on Thursday, about Brian Madigan’s recommendations, which is pretty important.

speaker: WARSH
text: I think it’s nice that we have a bridge to that, so that market participants and reporters alike don’t think that we have, in their view, yet again surprised them on what the substance is.

speaker: DUKE
text: I’m going to be quite repetitive, so I’ll be very brief.

speaker: DUKE
text: I, too, am troubled by the projections not being consistent with our dual mandate.

speaker: DUKE
text: However, with Treasuries as the only option for expansion, I’m not at all convinced that a modest increase in our Treasury purchases brings us that much closer to our objective.

speaker: DUKE
text: And I am concerned about the difficulties with exiting an even larger balance sheet.

speaker: DUKE
text: So I support alternative B, and I would omit the final sentence in light of the risk that the interpretation would be that our exit is imminent.

speaker: DUKE
text: Finally, I would echo President Rosengren’s and Governor Kohn’s support of option ARMs.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I must confess to being somewhat discomfited by what I see as a disconnect between the analyses of the economy, which I alluded to in the earlier go-round, and the fact that when it comes to policy there seems to be more concern about the potential for inflation some years out than there is with the serious underperformance of the economy today and for the foreseeable future.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I understood our action in March to be an effort to provide further accommodation in the circumstance of zero-bound rates.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I think it’s very difficult to make a judgment now as to exactly what effect that has had.

speaker: TARULLO
text: It does seem, as President Yellen mentioned earlier, that there is a strong theoretical case, that the counterfactual is difficult to come by, and that it is, other than statements of future intentions, really the only policy tool available to us.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I was somewhat attracted by not an option in the Bluebook, but an option included in the June 16 memo from the two Brians, which was to modestly stretch out the Treasury purchase program until the end of the year.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I was attracted to that for a variety of reasons.

speaker: TARULLO
text: One is that it just created a certain time symmetry in our decisionmaking, because the MBS and agency debt programs go through the end of the year.

speaker: TARULLO
text: That, in turn, avoided what I fear is now going to be an enormous spotlight placed upon us at the August meeting, which is going to be interpreted as the moment of truth in deciding what happens now with the large-scale asset purchase programs.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I also thought that it might offset, to some degree, what I continue to fear is going to be the interpretation of market actors and economic observers more generally—not simply that we failed to expand today, but, within the context of the announcement to come tomorrow, the announcement likely to come from the FDIC, and, precisely as President Fisher has noted, because there seems to be a demand that we talk about scaling back the program, that this inaction will be seen as a beginning response to those demands, which, for obvious reasons, I think is misplaced as a policy matter.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Having said all of that, I note that there is little or no appetite in the rest of the Open Market Committee for even this action and certainly not for what was included in the Bluebook as alternative A, which I actually wouldn’t favor at this point either.

speaker: TARULLO
text: So I would be prepared to go along with alternative B.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Let me now turn to the language issues in alternative B, which, as you can imagine, also reflect some of my concerns.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Like some of the earlier speakers, I find that the first paragraph is a bit too upbeat, not just for the way that I read the economy, but, again, for the conversation we had around this table earlier this morning.

speaker: TARULLO
text: It’s not that there’s anything in there that’s wrong or that I disagree with.

speaker: TARULLO
text: It’s not what is said—I guess it’s more what was left unsaid.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I was trying to figure that out overnight following dinner at the embassy and the baseball game later on in the evening.

speaker: TARULLO
text: It lacks a reference to what so many of us commented on, which is our expectation of just how slow the recovery will be when it comes.

speaker: TARULLO
text: You see gradual resumption of sustainable growth in there, but the likelihood of a long period, and a rather halting one at that, is what came through in much of what all seventeen of us said earlier in the day.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I would welcome any suggestions from anybody else as to how we might add that idea.

speaker: TARULLO
text: The more important issue to me is the potential inclusion of the final bracketed sentence, which I think would be a significant policy mistake.

speaker: TARULLO
text: And I think that for several reasons.

speaker: TARULLO
text: One is my substantive policy views, which I described earlier.

speaker: TARULLO
text: But, probably more importantly for the rest of you, I think it would be a mistake precisely because of the way these statements are read, so I’m elaborating a bit on what Governor Warsh has said.

speaker: TARULLO
text: As everybody knows, anything regarded as new in these statements is invested with enormous significance.

speaker: TARULLO
text: By and large, the statement goes a little bit by increment—a word is dropped here, a phrase is added there, and people kind of masticate those changes.

speaker: TARULLO
text: If you’ve got something that is brand new, something that appears to be satisfying a demand from a certain group of market actors, I think that will be invested with enormous significance.

speaker: TARULLO
text: Under the circumstances, I don’t see that the policy position of the Open Market Committee is there, and I, for one, don’t think that we’re going to actually get there anytime soon.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I also agree with President Lacker in that I have difficulty understanding what that sentence actually means.

speaker: TARULLO
text: It’s either a tautology, in which case it’s not particularly helpful, or it’s suggesting something that I don’t think we’ve actually done in a policy sense.

speaker: TARULLO
text: So I think it’s both appropriate and important for the Chairman and others, either in public testimony or on background, to explicate the various considerations that were reflected in the very useful memos distributed by the staff.

speaker: TARULLO
text: But I do think that this would be the story of this Open Market Committee meeting if it were included.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Lacker, you had a comment?

speaker: LACKER
text: Governor Tarullo, you mentioned an imminent announcement by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation?

speaker: TARULLO
text: I think they’re likely to ramp back the guarantees that they’ve been providing.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The statement is one way we communicate, but we also communicate in speeches.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I just want to reemphasize one more time that it’s really important in our communications to distinguish between stressing how well prepared we are to exit, in the sense of having the necessary tools, and actually exiting.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we have to be really clear on that, or else we are going to confuse people into thinking we’re about to exit because we’re talking about our ability to exit.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We obviously need to demonstrate that we have the ability to exit to keep inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: But we don’t want them to think that we’re going to exit soon, or sooner than we actually think, because that will boost the expected path of short-term rates, which will raise long-term interest rates, and, therefore, choke off recovery.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If you think of long-term rates as having three major components—the expected path of real short-term rates, inflation expectations, and risk premiums—you can sort of put it in that context.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Making it clear that the economy is pretty weak and that we don’t think there’s any meaningful inflation risk, so we can keep short-term rates low for an extended period, should put the focus on that first component, keeping the real rate path expectations well contained.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: Making clear that we have the tools to exit smoothly, so we can keep inflation in check over the longer term, should work on that second component by keeping inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It also should work on the third component, because if we keep inflation expectations well anchored, there will be less dispersion in terms of inflation expectations, and that presumably will result in a lower risk premium.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: That’s sort of how I think about it conceptually in terms of the task at hand.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s not easy, but I think we have to be very, very careful in how we go forward communicating.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of the LSAP program, I think the tapering is not as big an issue for Treasuries, because the amount of Treasuries that were purchased is not that large relative to the flow of issuance.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think we can do it without actually saying it explicitly.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: We can just purchase Treasuries at a little faster rate than the $300 billion rate over six months, and so at the end we won’t have quite as much left, so it will just taper off.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The other problem with talking about tapering is that it implies that you’re done.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: If we start talking about tapering, people say, “Oh, they’re done.” I think it’s premature at this stage to make strong statements about what we want to do or not do with the purchase programs going forward, especially if the environment turns out to be worse than we expect.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the first paragraph, I agree with Governor Tarullo.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: The first paragraph does sound sort of upbeat.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I’m not really sure how you would fix it—maybe you could try to have some language that suggests that none of this is a real surprise.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In other words, the economy is evolving pretty closely to the forecast that we actually had, so the improvement is not a shock to us.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s just that there are lots of other issues still outstanding that make us worry about the strength of the recovery over the longer term.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: So it’s a little bit upbeat relative to what I think we really think around the table.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: In terms of the statement, I’m in favor of B.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: On the last, bracketed sentence, my question is really: does it reassure, or does it make the market more worried about our ability to exit and about the timing of exit?

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think you could argue it both ways, as people around the table have done.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: My view is, if we’re not sure, we probably shouldn’t include it, because I go back to what Governor Warsh said: This is not the greatest medium of communication.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I think I would exclude the last sentence, just because I’m not sure how the market will react to it.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: It’s probably better to take that up in the Chairman’s testimony or in the Monetary Policy Report or in speeches.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that most of us are agreed that, given the improvement in the economy, there’s not much need to change our policy stance today, so we should keep our programs in place on the schedule that we have already announced.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: That would bring us to alternative B, which I think is the right choice.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Most of you were in favor of striking the last sentence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that’s the right decision.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I’m reminded of an experience I had when I first took this job, when we were still raising interest rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I told a congressional committee that the time would come, eventually, when we would have to stop raising interest rates.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Of course, the expectation of an immediate rate change went right through the market, and I was completely flabbergasted by the inability of the markets to understand plain English.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I think there would be a risk of suggesting that we were preparing to exit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: In this case, we are taking very substantial steps to address this particular issue, not just in testimony.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Our current plan is to have a significant description of exit strategy, tools, and so on, in the Monetary Policy Report, which would obviously be available to everyone in more detail than I could give in a short testimony.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So I would recommend dropping the last sentence.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We had some original language on tapering, and I think the problem that we were having with it was there’s no way to describe our plans to taper without essentially determining at this point that we are almost certainly going to stop.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We may well do that, but I think if we can maintain that optionality for one more meeting it would probably be a good idea.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think we could stop the Treasury program flat, or we could say we are doing $30 billion a month the rest of the year, or whatever, but I don’t think that we need to take that decision yet.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Yellen, supported by President Rosengren, brought up the mortgage rate issue, and I think she had two objectives.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: One was to point to an important factor; the other was to kind of tone down the cheeriness of the first paragraph.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I have a specific concern with the mortgage rate sentence—if we say that mortgage rates are a big problem, that’s going to signal something about our asset purchase program, I’m afraid, so that’s a concern that I would have.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: But I do understand the issue about general tone.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Let me just raise this for consideration.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: The second sentence in alternative B, “Conditions in financial markets have generally improved in recent months, and indicators of consumer and business sentiment have risen,” is obviously a very positive sentence and one that has no parallel in the April statement.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: We could, if people like, either strike the sentence entirely, or, perhaps to recognize that there has been general improvement in financial markets, strike the second part about consumer and business sentiment, which would change the tone a bit.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I don’t know if that would satisfy the need.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Governor Tarullo mentioned this as well.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Is there any response to that thought?

speaker: TARULLO
text: I would find striking the sentence useful.

speaker: TARULLO
text: I think it would balance it a little bit better.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Striking the whole sentence, is everyone okay with that?

speaker: LACKER
text: I think the “financial conditions have improved” is worth having.

speaker: DUDLEY
text: I would cut that second half of the sentence.

speaker: STERN
text: I would drop the second part of it.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: So what I’m hearing is drop the second half, is that okay?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: President Yellen, does that sound okay?

speaker: BERNANKE
text: Brian will end the sentence after “in recent months” and strike the part about sentiment.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: I think that is all that was on the table.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: As noted, it is somewhat more upbeat.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: It does drop the concern about deflation, although it does say “subdued for some time,” which is a strengthening of what we said last time.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: And, of course, it does refer appropriately to the adjustments—the credit and liquidity programs—which will be followed up on Thursday.

speaker: BERNANKE
text: If not, Debbie, would you take the roll?

speaker: DANKER
text: The vote covers the statement that’s in the packet that was handed out today, with two changes.

speaker: DANKER
text: One is dropping the phrase “and indicators of consumer and business sentiment have risen.” The other is dropping the bracketed sentence at the bottom.

speaker: DANKER
