speaker: Warsh
text: Detractors have argued that this end-of-history thesis is a "mirage" (Kagan, 2007).
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Intervening geopolitical events appear to have upended the notion that History is all but written, that ideological conflicts will inexorably abate.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: At the very least, the experience of the past dozen years suggests that the hopes and aspirations for a less confrontational political and ideological era may be delayed.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: But even as the geopolitical situation has become more complex, and as conflicts among ideologies become more obvious, I wonder whether we are seeing--in certain other spheres of social interaction--some coalescing of views, some mutual understanding of what makes for a strong and enduring system.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Here, befitting an audience of business leaders and economists, I am thinking of economic policy and, in particular, monetary policy in market-based economies.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: As recently as several months ago, some may have been tempted to believe that, in the realm of economic policy, we were on the precipice of the end of history.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: The seemingly benign financial and economic conditions of the past few years may have appeared to be approaching this nirvana.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: If the end of economic history were at hand, what would it look like?
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: You would almost assuredly find strong, synchronized global economic growth; favorable inflation readings and anchored inflation expectations; low global risk premiums and low term premiums; muted volatility across asset markets; a relatively free flow of products and services across national boundaries; interconnected financial markets; deep, robust, and highly liquid secondary trading; the democratization of credit and growing access to capital; and, finally, a stance of monetary policy approximating its natural equilibrium.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Think of the economic environment of several months ago, prior to the more recent financial turmoil.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: The appearance of these sorts of benign indicators could have provided useful testimony in support of the end-of-history thesis in the economic realm.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: But then what is to be made of the global liquidity shock that crested in August and continues to manifest itself to this day?
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: In my view, recent financial turmoil should not be considered an accident of history.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Rather, it is History's latest reminder to policymakers and market participants alike that we ought to be humble in our convictions and cautious in our deeds as we seek a better understanding of what makes a strong and stable economic and financial system.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: The lessons learned from natural experiments in economics during recent decades offer great promise that macroeconomic performance can be improved.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: But as empiricists outside of our "dismal science" would remind us, there are few control groups in economics.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: As a result, the definitive account has not been written.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Nor has the practical conduct of policy yet evolved to the point at which financial crises and economic downturns can be wholly avoided.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: As a result, I will argue, the end of history may have to wait awhile.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Let me first discuss the evolution of financial markets.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Next, I will highlight the evolution of monetary policy and financial stability.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Finally, I will turn to more recent financial and monetary events.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Evolution of Financial Markets During the past several years, the cause of economic freedom and the culture of capitalism have appeared firmly on the march.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Founding ideologies aside, countries' economies are more connected by virtue of increased trade of products and services.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Free markets, technological innovation, and instant communications are the watchwords of the global economy.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: And the dissemination of financial innovation has gained new converts.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: London, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Shanghai increasingly seek to challenge New York as the center of global financial markets.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Competitive national ambitions, perhaps, have demanded an embrace of economic liberalism to build wealth even among those regimes that may prefer something closer to autocracy in their non-economic dealings.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Democratizing credit to enlarge the global middle class, efficiently allocating capital, and dispersing risk exposures--these remain compelling practices for private market participants throughout the world.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: These financial market tailwinds bolstered worldwide economic growth, which is near record levels.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: In 2006, the U.S. economy grew 3 percent, while growth outside the United States averaged nearly 4 percent as all major regions racked up solid gains.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: So far this year (through the third quarter in the United States and through the second quarter elsewhere), U.S. output growth managed to continue apace, while growth for the rest of the world picked up to more than 4 percent.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Clearly the global economy has been firing on all cylinders, with emerging Asia taking the lead.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: There can be little doubt that this macroeconomic performance is due, at least in part, to the increased adoption of liberal economic practices around the globe.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Perhaps, then, the case for the end of economic history is not without some evidentiary backing and persuasive appeal.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Evolution of Monetary Policy and Financial Stability In a recent survey paper, David Laidler identifies three tenets that embody the current consensus on the conduct of monetary policy in advanced economies (Laidler, 2007).
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: First, market economies are inherently self-righting; second, open economies perform best under flexible exchange rates; and third, central bankers should focus on price stability as their long-run objective.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Monetary policy in the past couple of decades can, almost assuredly, claim far more successes than failures.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Look no further than measures of consumer price inflation in the advanced economies.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Median inflation (as defined by the International Monetary Fund) has held near 2 percent for the decade.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: This performance has helped anchor inflation expectations, which, in turn, has helped damp the pass-through of supply-related price shocks.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: The low inflation rate has also permitted central banks to respond more forcefully to output fluctuations and more opportunistically to ensure low and stable prices.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: The improved inflation performance has come not at the expense of, but in conjunction with, output stability.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Researchers have documented the so-called Great Moderation, in which the U.S. economy has achieved a marked reduction in the volatility of both real gross domestic product and core inflation over the past twenty years or so.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Most economists would probably attribute at least some portion of the Great Moderation in the growth of real output to monetary policy.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Despite the record of steadier economic performance, bouts of financial market instability continue to arise.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Indeed, in my judgment, the inexorable march of technological change and creative destruction in a market economy all but assures the occurrence of such episodes (Schumpeter, 1942).
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: To be sure, it is the recurrence of such episodes that supplies kindling to the debate on the appropriate balance between flexible, competitive financial markets and regulations that could limit the exuberance of market responses, irrational or otherwise.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: In the episode at hand, early-cycle increases in housing prices, escalating returns of leveraged buyouts, and lower all-in financing costs made possible by structured-finance products highlighted new profit-making opportunities for providers and users of capital.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: As economic historians remind us, more entities are thus drawn into the activity until competition pushes its boundaries beyond the point of positive returns (Kindleberger, 1996).
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Eventually, some shock to the system exposes the fragility, and the shock is often followed by fear and overreaction before a new equilibrium is established.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: In these circumstances, financial markets often suffer from episodes of widespread illiquidity amid a rise in risk aversion among investors.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Policymakers and market participants know with certainty that investors' risk perceptions and preferences will change and that stresses will recur, but predicting their onset, scope, or duration is exceedingly difficult.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Surely, policymakers and market participants have advanced in their knowledge and in the adaptability of their tools to help mitigate these negative effects on real economic activity.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: But as the events of 2007 make clear, the latest chapter in economic history should remind us of the habitual, but perhaps not immutable, drivers of human behavior in financial markets.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Recent Financial Developments The consequences of the liquidity shock of 2007 on the financial markets and the real economy are still playing out in real time.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: It is premature to delineate lessons learned with complete assurance.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: The facts, nonetheless, can perhaps be placed in some narrative context, drawing on the experience of prior bouts of financial instability.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: History, of course, is far from a perfect teacher.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: After all, history does not repeat itself; it only appears to do so.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: In that regard, the causes and consequences of market turmoil are still insufficiently understood for the end of history to be declared.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: And as I briefly discuss the phases often accompanying financial market turmoil--retrenchment, reliquification, revaluation, review and refinement--you will recognize that these phases are neither discrete nor complete as year-end approaches.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: After several years of strong domestic and global growth, financial markets appeared highly accommodative for issuers and investors.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Many willing investors purchased complex financial products convinced that they would achieve outsized returns because the future would look like the recent past.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: On the other side of the trade, originators operated under the presumption that secondary markets would remain liquid.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: And the resulting market-clearing prices across a range of asset classes were predicated on a world of modest risk premiums, low credit spreads, and plentiful liquidity.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Market confidence ultimately begot complacency (Warsh, 2007).
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: By mid-summer, complacency was upended.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: What followed was a rapid period of retrenchment, the first phase of financial market turmoil.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: As concerns about losses on subprime mortgages and securitized products intensified, investors withdrew liquidity and markets became impaired.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Investors revisited, almost anew, the quality of the information about their assets.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Financial intermediaries also pulled back from making markets in many products, and the engines of financial innovation were all but turned off.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: As the strains in financial markets intensified, many of the largest financial institutions became jealously protective of their liquidity and balance sheet capacity.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Amid heightened volatility and diminished market functioning, they became more concerned about the risk exposures of their counterparties and other potential contingent liabilities.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: For some, that process lasted days and weeks; for others, it may yet continue for many months.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: In the second phase--reliquification--financial institutions decided on the new liquidity levels and capital ratios at which they were prepared to conduct business.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Many banks became markedly less willing to provide funding to customers, including other banks.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Given reduced confidence in their ability to quantify and price risks, balance sheet capital remained a scarce commodity.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: As a result, both overnight and term interbank-funding markets were pressured considerably.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Even today, some banks face potentially large needs for dollar funding, and their efforts to manage their liquidity may be contributing to pressures in global money markets and foreign exchange swap markets.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: More broadly, many financial institutions appear hesitant to put opportunistic capital to work.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: The next phase--revaluation--requires that the new prices be established in accordance with the new financial environment.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: The process of price discovery appears to be quicker and more assured among corporate credits.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Think, for example, of the markets for high-yield and leveraged loans, in which risk spreads have returned to more moderate levels.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: We have seen significant evidence that the process of revaluation in other previously disrupted markets is also under way.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Investors are differentiating risks, for example, among asset-backed commercial paper programs, and many spreads have moderated.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Revaluation, however, may be a slower, tougher slog in the mortgage markets for those vintages in which the underlying asset quality is less certain.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: How quickly asset markets substantially complete the revaluation phase depends on the speed with which stakeholders regain comfort in their ability to value these assets.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Financial markets rarely normalize in a steady, linear fashion.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: More often, as market sentiments sway between fear and greed, asset prices fluctuate and seek support (volume) before establishing new trading ranges.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: That pattern is particularly pronounced when the underlying economic fundamentals are less certain.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Hence, the next phases--review and refinement--are the hardest to predict with precision.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: As circumstances dictate, some financial institutions will review and refine their capital ratios, risk metrics, and business imperatives and proceed forward.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Others may find that, in the course of review, they return to the phases of retrenchment and reliquification.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Central bankers are prudent to stay alert to these changes.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Without a doubt, then, this is a time of testing.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Stakeholders will need to discern whether they are witnessing some impairment of the financial sector, or merely a realignment of the competitive landscape.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Moreover, I suspect that some of the more complex structured products and investment strategies will be substantially modified; others will die.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: But, in the end, an improved understanding of how to create, bundle, distribute, and assess risk will not be forgotten, at least not for a cycle.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Recent Monetary Policy Actions The financial shock of 2007 and its potential threat to the economy changed the view held by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) of the most appropriate stance of monetary policy.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: The stresses led to greater financial restraint on economic growth.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Impaired price discovery impeded the flow of capital.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: At the time of our September meeting, the downside risks to the real economy appeared to have increased; greater uncertainty could have led lenders and investors to pull back further.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Moreover, data on inflation were relatively stable, and inflation expectations appeared to remain anchored.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: From a risk-management perspective, these circumstances warranted a strong policy action.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: By doing more and sooner, the FOMC intended its policy action to counterbalance the tighter financial conditions and help forestall some potentially adverse effects of financial market disruptions on the real economy.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: To that end, the FOMC cut its target for the federal funds rate 50 basis points at its September meeting.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Subsequent economic information received suggests that activity in the third quarter expanded at a solid pace, even though housing activity subtracted about 1 percentage point from real activity.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Some indicators, however, suggest that activity may have slowed in the current quarter, and the prospect that such perceived softness may prove real and enduring is understood.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: In addition, stresses remain evident in certain asset and credit markets, even though financial market conditions today appear much improved from their August nadir.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: There are also important reasons to be concerned about the outlook for inflation.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Although recent readings on core inflation have been favorable, prices of crude oil and other commodities have increased.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: These changes most likely will put upward pressure on overall inflation in the short run.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Moreover, the decline in the foreign exchange value of the dollar could lead to higher prices for imported goods.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: If these same forces cause inflation expectations to become less reliably anchored, then inflation could increase in the longer run as well.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: As you know, last week, the FOMC reduced its target rate an additional 25 basis points, to 4-1/2 percent.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Combined with the action of the September meeting, the FOMC judged that the cumulative policy easing of 75 basis points reduced the downside risks to growth, and that these risks were now roughly balanced by the upside risks to inflation.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Should incoming data materially change our forecast, or risks to our forecast, for growth and inflation, so too would our view on the appropriate stance of monetary policy.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Conclusion Ultimately the ability of the economy to withstand shocks is a function of the flexibility and resiliency of labor, product, and capital markets; strong and resilient market infrastructures; and good macroeconomic policies, not the least of which is monetary policy.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Much progress has been made in our understanding of monetary policy in market-based economies.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Indeed the economic trends of the past generation show great promise, albeit interrupted by periods of genuine distress.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: In my view, we almost invariably end up with better macroeconomic outcomes than if we viewed stability as the sine qua non of policy.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Recent events serve as an important reminder that the next chapter of history is still being written.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Perhaps, that is always the case.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: As in the political realm, the path to the end of history may well prove to be prone to advance, overshoot, and correct.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: We must continue to deepen our understanding of financial markets and monetary policy, equipped with ample humility on a long, productive, and admittedly uneven path.
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

text: Francis Fukuyama advanced an affirmative view of this question when he published "The End of History?"
speech_title: The End of History?
speech_venue: To the New York Association for Business Economics, New York, New York

speaker: Warsh
text: Noting that the historical origins of the phrase can be found in the writings of Hegel and, later, Marx, Fukuyama wrote that "what we may be witnessing is not just the end of the Cold War, or the passing of a particular period of postwar history, but the end of history as such: that is, the end point of mankind's ideological evolution and the universalization of Western liberal democracy as the final form of human government" (p. 4).

speaker: Kroszner
text: I would also like to offer thanks and extend congratulations to all the parties involved in the successful adoption of Basel II.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: This includes staff at each of the U.S. banking agencies, who worked tirelessly and with incredible determination and patience to see this rulemaking to its completion, as well as the principals at the other agencies, who worked very hard to find common ground and develop a rule that would serve the public interest and satisfy each of our agencies' objectives.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Of course, I would also like to thank the many industry participants--some of whom may be here today--who spent considerable time and effort providing valuable comments on our proposals over the past several years.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Your contributions made the final rule a much better product.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Developing Basel II was like running a marathon, and even though some of us may have hit the wall and wanted to drop out at mile 20, we persevered and successfully reached the finish line.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: I am proud of what we have all accomplished.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Final Rule In the banking industry, most of the innovation and evolution in risk-management practices occur on a continuous basis, generally in small steps.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Updates to banking regulations, on the other hand, typically occur in large jumps.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As was the case with Basel I nearly twenty years ago, I consider the adoption of Basel II to be a major step forward in banking regulation in the United States.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Importantly, we are also working on an additional proposal, known as the standardized approach, to offer non-core banks a set of regulatory capital requirements that have more risk sensitivity than the current Basel I rules, but less complexity than the advanced approaches in the Basel II final rule.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: One of the main reasons we were able to complete the Basel II final rule successfully, I believe, was our renewed focus on the fundamental rationale for developing Basel II: enhancing the safety and soundness of the U.S. banking system by providing more-risk-sensitive capital requirements for our largest, most complex banks and improving risk management practices at those institutions.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Moreover, we endorsed the notion that the U.S. rule would foster international consistency and be less burdensome on banks if it adhered more closely to the international Basel II framework finalized in 2006--and if it also aligned as closely as possible with what banks themselves were doing for risk management.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: These were principles that I emphasized as I represented the Federal Reserve in interagency discussions, and I believe my counterparts shared these views.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Perhaps our ability to refocus stemmed from a fresh set of comments received on our proposals, our renewed commitment to getting things right, and the infusion of some new approaches brought to the table.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Regardless, we of course owe a huge debt of gratitude to our predecessors, who broke the hard ground in the long U.S. rulemaking process.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Reasons for Adopting Basel II I would like to return briefly to our reasons for adopting Basel II, since it is useful to remember why we undertook so much effort to see it through.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: While the existing Basel I capital regime was a major step forward when introduced in 1988, it has become outdated for large, complex banking organizations.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Retaining Basel I for these institutions would have widened the gap between their regulatory capital requirements and their actual risk profiles, generating further incentives for regulatory arbitrage to take advantage of that gap.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In contrast to the simple risk-bucketing approach of Basel I, in which exposures to obligors of varying creditworthiness were given the same capital treatment, the new Basel II rules require banks to distinguish among the credit quality of individual borrowers.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: For example, under Basel I almost all first-lien residential mortgage exposures are subject to the same risk weight regardless of the borrower's creditworthiness, whereas Basel II provides for a more refined differentiation of low- versus high-credit-quality mortgage borrowers.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Likewise, Basel I is inadequate for dealing with capital markets transactions such as highly structured asset-backed securities.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Basel II, on the other hand, provides a much more refined approach by requiring banks to hold capital commensurate with the actual risks of such transactions.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Recent market events highlight why a robust and independent assessment of risk on the part of banks is so important.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The enhanced risk-sensitivity of the Basel II advanced approaches creates positive incentives for banks to lend to more-creditworthy counterparties and to lend against good collateral, by requiring banks to hold more capital against higher-risk exposures.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The Federal Reserve's role as the nation's central bank reinforces our belief in the importance of maintaining prudent and risk-sensitive capital requirements for financial institutions.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Financial stability is enhanced when banks' regulatory capital measures adequately reflect risk, as well as when banks continually improve their risk-management practices.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Since the Basel II regime is far superior to the current Basel I regime in aligning regulatory capital requirements with risk and fostering continual improvements in risk management for our largest and most complex banking organizations, I believe it will contribute to a more resilient financial system as a whole.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In addition, let me emphasize that the Basel II regulatory capital framework establishes a more coherent relationship between regulatory measures of capital adequacy and the day-to-day risk management conducted by banks.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: That is, it builds on risk-management tools, such as credit-risk rating systems and economic capital, that are already in use at sophisticated financial institutions.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As a result, Basel II will be better able than the current system to adapt over time to innovations in banking and financial markets and will reduce incentives for arbitrage that arise from the gap between what the regulators require and what sound economic risk management requires.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Moving Ahead with Basel II Implementation Next Steps for Supervisors I used the analogy of running a marathon earlier, describing how the final rule represented a finish line of sorts for the U.S. banking agencies.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Alas, I'm afraid that we cannot rest because in fact we have simply passed the baton from the runner in the first stage of the race--rule finalization--to the runner in the next stage--implementation.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Successful implementation of Basel II will require additional hard work and determination.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As most of you know, the agencies have for some time been preparing for Basel II implementation by working to integrate Basel II into our day-to-day supervisory processes.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: With completion of the final rule, we must now be ready to pace ourselves through another long, intensive, but ultimately rewarding, effort.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The agencies are already working hard to foster consistency across banks and across the agencies.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We are building upon the cooperation already established through our work on the final rule and our efforts to prepare supervisory staff for the Basel II qualification process.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Our supervisory staffs have been meeting regularly for some time to align qualification approaches, iron out any differences, and ensure that each bank subject to Basel II is treated appropriately and consistently.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We also remain attentive to the way in which the framework is implemented in other countries, so that we can minimize the burden placed on banks by having to meet multiple national rules.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: I hope our decision to align the definition of default for wholesale exposures more closely with the definition used internationally, for example, sends a positive signal about our intentions to increase cross-border consistency and reduce unnecessary burdens that can distract banks from one of the fundamental goals of Basel II--improving risk management.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Of course, the agencies need to move ahead with Basel II implementation carefully and with our eyes wide open.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The advanced approaches are a significant change from our current, time-tested, risk-based capital rules, and we have therefore embedded the transitional safeguards set forth in the agencies' 2006 proposal into the U.S. Basel II rule.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: These safeguards will help ensure that capital levels remain strong and that we have sufficient opportunity to assess the framework before full implementation.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Importantly, we also are retaining the leverage ratio and our existing prompt-corrective-action framework.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As noted in the agencies' July press release, we are committed to a robust and transparent study of the framework during the transitional phase to assess its overall effectiveness, and we will address any material deficiencies that we identify.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: This study should include active and meaningful dialogue among the agencies, the industry, market participants, Congress, and other interested parties.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: This is consistent with my view that whenever regulators undertake a major regulatory change, a careful and thorough empirical review of the effectiveness of the regulation is extremely valuable.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Such a review can help assess whether the goals for the rule are being met, whether the benefits of the rule exceed the costs, and how the rule can be made more effective and less burdensome.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In addition to this study, during and after the transitional phase we will be relying upon ongoing, detailed analyses to evaluate continuously the results of the new framework in operation.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: A primary objective of this ongoing review will be to ensure that capital levels remain prudent.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: For example, we will respond if we see unreasonable declines in capital requirements at individual institutions that do not appear to be supported by either those banks' own internal capital-adequacy assessments or by our supervisory view of those institutions' risks and how well those risks are managed.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As has long been the case with our capital rules, we expect that adjustments to the capital framework will be made over time to address industry and market developments, any potential shortcomings in the rule identified in our review and analysis during implementation, and new and improved techniques of risk management.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Next Steps for Bankers Completion of the Basel II rulemaking process means that banks adopting the new rule must also gear up their efforts.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Of course we recognize the substantial work that bankers have undertaken over the past several years to prepare themselves for Basel II.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: But, understandably, they have had to wait for completion of the final rule to see how the agencies would articulate certain requirements--some of them quite detailed.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Therefore, it would seem that bankers need to read the rule very carefully and take time to understand how their own bank will be able to meet its requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As stated in the final rule, and as the U.S. agencies articulated several years ago, the key instrument in the qualification process is a bank's implementation plan.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: This written implementation plan, approved by a bank's board of directors, must describe in detail how the bank complies, or intends to comply, with the rule's qualification requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Specifically, the plan must describe how the bank intends to address the gaps it has identified between its existing practices and the qualification requirements set forth in the rule for the advanced approaches, covering all consolidated subsidiaries.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The implementation plan also must include objective, measurable milestones--including delivery dates--and a target date when the bank expects its advanced approaches to be fully operational.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The bank must establish and maintain a comprehensive and sound planning and governance process to oversee implementation efforts, and must demonstrate to its supervisor that it meets the qualification requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Banks subject to the final rule on a mandatory basis, the core banks, have up to six months to adopt an implementation plan.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Of course, banks may always submit their plans earlier, and I understand that a number of core banks are working toward that goal.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: This deadline for submission of plans by core banks is intended to prevent delays in starting implementation efforts.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: However, the final rule provides flexibility and gives banks adopting Basel II ample time to fully meet the qualification requirements once they have adopted an implementation plan.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Specifically, a bank's plan may include developmental goals for full implementation for up to thirty-six months from the effective date of the final rule.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As supervisors, we will take the qualification requirements seriously, expecting banks to meet both the letter and the spirit of those requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Thus, we strongly recommend that banks undertake their own sober and frank appraisal of their ability to meet the final rule.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Systems development can take time, for example, and it is important to make sure that these systems function appropriately.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: While I believe that expeditious adoption of Basel II will have significant benefits, it is of the utmost importance that the implementation not be rushed but be undertaken thoughtfully and deliberately.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: After a bank has submitted a credible implementation plan to its primary supervisor, it must then begin a parallel run lasting at least four consecutive calendar quarters, during which the bank's supervisor must determine the bank's compliance with the qualification requirements to be satisfactory.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: During the parallel run, a bank remains subject to the Basel I risk-based capital rules for all applicable regulatory and supervisory purposes, but the bank also must calculate its capital ratios using the advanced approaches and report pertinent information to its supervisor.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: It is only upon notification from its supervisor that a bank can move into a series of three transitional periods (each lasting at least one year), during which the cumulative reductions of the bank's risk-based capital requirements are limited.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Supervisory approval is needed to move to a subsequent transitional floor-level and then to move from the transitional floors to stand-alone use of the Basel II rules.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Importantly, as bankers move forward with implementation, they should not lose sight of Pillars 2 and 3, which may ultimately be more important to the success of Basel II than Pillar 1, which has received the bulk of the attention so far.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Under Pillar 2, banks are required to have an internal process--which will be subject to rigorous supervisory review--for ensuring that they are holding enough overall capital to support their entire risk profile.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Thus, Pillar 2 should be a key area of focus for banks implementing Basel II.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The preamble to the final rule describes the steps that supervisors will take under Pillar 2, namely that supervisors will take into account a bank's internal capital-adequacy assessment process--known as its ICAAP--as well as the bank's compliance with the minimum capital requirements set forth in this rule, and all other relevant information.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The agencies expect banks to implement and continually update the fundamental elements of a sound ICAAP--identifying and measuring material risks, setting capital-adequacy goals that relate to risk, and ensuring the integrity of internal capital-adequacy assessments.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: A bank is expected to hold adequate capital against all of its material risks, particularly those risks not covered or not adequately quantified in the risk-based capital requirements--such as liquidity risk or interest-rate risk in the banking book.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In general, a bank's ICAAP should reflect an appropriate level of conservatism to account for uncertainty in risk identification, risk mitigation or control, quantitative processes, and any use of modeling.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In most cases, this conservatism will result in levels of capital or capital ratios above minimum regulatory requirements to be regarded as adequate.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Pillar 3 is a key mechanism for banks to communicate to market participants about their risk profiles, their associated levels of capital, and the manner in which they are meeting the requirements in the final rule.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In addition to providing information about its various components of regulatory capital and its minimum capital requirements and ratios, a bank must disclose information about how it measures and manages credit risk, operational risk, equity risk, and interest-rate risk in non-trading activities, as well as the range of risks related to securitizations.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: For example, a bank has to describe the operation of its credit risk rating system as well as the data used in parameter estimates for credit losses.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Some of these disclosure requirements will be new for banks but others are already required by, or are consistent with, existing U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, Securities and Exchange Commission disclosure requirements, or bank regulatory reporting requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As a strong believer in market discipline and the importance of information in market transactions, I believe Pillar 3 will improve bank disclosures about risk profiles and enhance discussions between bankers and market participants about risk-management practices.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Of course, while we want to promote consistency, we must also allow bankers some flexibility in meeting the Basel II requirements and permit a reasonable amount of diversity of practices across banking organizations.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Such flexibility will allow banks to use and readily improve their existing risk-measurement and risk-management practices.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: More to the point, as supervisors we should actively encourage such improvements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As we move forward, we encourage banks to raise issues as they try to meet the rule's requirements; in other words, we want banks to maintain an ongoing dialogue about implementation with their supervisors, who stand ready to answer questions and assist banks in interpreting Basel II requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Standardized Approach Proposal for Non-Core Banks Before concluding, I would like to discuss the agencies' additional plans for revising capital rules, specifically plans for those banks not subject to the advanced approaches of Basel II.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Some commentators on the earlier Basel II and Basel IA proposals voiced concerns that adoption of a new capital framework for the largest and most complex U.S. banking organizations could disadvantage other U.S. banking organizations, particularly the smaller banks.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We understand that banks not required to adopt Basel II are facing a choice about whether to opt-in to the advanced approaches.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Some of these banks may be sophisticated institutions that exhibit sound risk management but do not quite meet the criteria to be core banks.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The agencies recognize that such institutions should be afforded an alternative for more-risk-sensitive capital requirements, but one that is not as complex as the advanced approaches.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In this regard, the agencies have responded by committing to proposing a "standardized" approach instead of Basel IA.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Specifically, the staffs are currently working on a notice of proposed rulemaking that would implement some of the simpler approaches for both credit risk and operational risk from the Basel II framework--referred to as the standardized approach.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The proposal is being developed as an optional risk-based capital framework for all banking organizations that are not required to adopt the advanced approaches.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We also expect to retain our existing Basel I-based regulatory capital framework for those smaller banks that would prefer to remain under that regime.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The proposal for the standardized approach will take into consideration relevant commentary received in response to the Basel IA and Basel II proposed rules that were published in late 2006 and should, in essence, modernize the Basel I-based rules without imposing a substantial implementation burden.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Among other things, the proposal is being designed both to provide greater differentiation across corporate exposures based on borrowers' underlying credit quality and to recognize a broader spectrum of credit-risk mitigation techniques.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The agencies are also considering how to implement Pillars 2 and 3 of the Basel II framework in the standardized proposal in a manner that is commensurate with banks' complexity and risk profiles.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Our goal is to realize the benefits of these two pillars without imposing excessive regulatory burden and without creating competitive advantages or disadvantages for different types of banks.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: I expect this proposal to be presented to the Board for consideration within the next several months, and I encourage all interested parties to review and comment on this proposal once it has been issued.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We are keenly aware of the need for capital requirements to make sense from the standpoint of both safety-and-soundness and competitiveness; we recognize that a one-size-fits-all approach is probably not the best for our banking system, in light of our wide range of institutions.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We remain sensitive to the principle that if we have multiple regulatory capital frameworks, they must work together to improve the safety and soundness of our entire banking system without artificially creating competitive inequalities.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Our goal is to have the standardized approach ready for implementation concurrently with the start of the first Basel II transition phase.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Conclusion The U.S. banking agencies have reached an important milestone in adopting the final rule for Basel II.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Our focus on the fundamentals of improving risk management consistent with safety and soundness, and on international consistency, has been key to achieving this success.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Obviously, however, effective implementation of Basel II is as important as, if not more important than, the rulemaking process.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: It is imperative that we observe how the new rule works in practice--assessing carefully both its advantages and its limitations.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: I am confident that both banking organizations and the supervisory community are up to the challenge.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: It is also important to modernize the existing Basel I-based regulatory capital framework to improve the risk sensitivity of capital requirements at the non-core banks, by offering a standardized option.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Finally, we should all bear in mind that implementation of Basel II--and, more significantly, the improvements in risk measurement and management that will be required--will not be a one-time event, but rather an ongoing process.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Basel II is designed to accommodate innovation and change as markets and risk-measurement and -management evolve over time.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As one marathon is completed, yet another begins.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Final Rule In the banking industry, most of the innovation and evolution in risk-management practices occur on a continuous basis, generally in small steps.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Updates to banking regulations, on the other hand, typically occur in large jumps.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As was the case with Basel I nearly twenty years ago, I consider the adoption of Basel II to be a major step forward in banking regulation in the United States.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Importantly, we are also working on an additional proposal, known as the standardized approach, to offer non-core banks a set of regulatory capital requirements that have more risk sensitivity than the current Basel I rules, but less complexity than the advanced approaches in the Basel II final rule.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: One of the main reasons we were able to complete the Basel II final rule successfully, I believe, was our renewed focus on the fundamental rationale for developing Basel II: enhancing the safety and soundness of the U.S. banking system by providing more-risk-sensitive capital requirements for our largest, most complex banks and improving risk management practices at those institutions.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Moreover, we endorsed the notion that the U.S. rule would foster international consistency and be less burdensome on banks if it adhered more closely to the international Basel II framework finalized in 2006--and if it also aligned as closely as possible with what banks themselves were doing for risk management.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
