text: These were principles that I emphasized as I represented the Federal Reserve in interagency discussions, and I believe my counterparts shared these views.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Perhaps our ability to refocus stemmed from a fresh set of comments received on our proposals, our renewed commitment to getting things right, and the infusion of some new approaches brought to the table.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Regardless, we of course owe a huge debt of gratitude to our predecessors, who broke the hard ground in the long U.S. rulemaking process.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Reasons for Adopting Basel II I would like to return briefly to our reasons for adopting Basel II, since it is useful to remember why we undertook so much effort to see it through.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: While the existing Basel I capital regime was a major step forward when introduced in 1988, it has become outdated for large, complex banking organizations.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Retaining Basel I for these institutions would have widened the gap between their regulatory capital requirements and their actual risk profiles, generating further incentives for regulatory arbitrage to take advantage of that gap.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In contrast to the simple risk-bucketing approach of Basel I, in which exposures to obligors of varying creditworthiness were given the same capital treatment, the new Basel II rules require banks to distinguish among the credit quality of individual borrowers.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: For example, under Basel I almost all first-lien residential mortgage exposures are subject to the same risk weight regardless of the borrower's creditworthiness, whereas Basel II provides for a more refined differentiation of low- versus high-credit-quality mortgage borrowers.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Likewise, Basel I is inadequate for dealing with capital markets transactions such as highly structured asset-backed securities.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Basel II, on the other hand, provides a much more refined approach by requiring banks to hold capital commensurate with the actual risks of such transactions.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Recent market events highlight why a robust and independent assessment of risk on the part of banks is so important.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The enhanced risk-sensitivity of the Basel II advanced approaches creates positive incentives for banks to lend to more-creditworthy counterparties and to lend against good collateral, by requiring banks to hold more capital against higher-risk exposures.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The Federal Reserve's role as the nation's central bank reinforces our belief in the importance of maintaining prudent and risk-sensitive capital requirements for financial institutions.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Financial stability is enhanced when banks' regulatory capital measures adequately reflect risk, as well as when banks continually improve their risk-management practices.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Since the Basel II regime is far superior to the current Basel I regime in aligning regulatory capital requirements with risk and fostering continual improvements in risk management for our largest and most complex banking organizations, I believe it will contribute to a more resilient financial system as a whole.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In addition, let me emphasize that the Basel II regulatory capital framework establishes a more coherent relationship between regulatory measures of capital adequacy and the day-to-day risk management conducted by banks.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: That is, it builds on risk-management tools, such as credit-risk rating systems and economic capital, that are already in use at sophisticated financial institutions.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As a result, Basel II will be better able than the current system to adapt over time to innovations in banking and financial markets and will reduce incentives for arbitrage that arise from the gap between what the regulators require and what sound economic risk management requires.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Moving Ahead with Basel II Implementation Next Steps for Supervisors I used the analogy of running a marathon earlier, describing how the final rule represented a finish line of sorts for the U.S. banking agencies.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Alas, I'm afraid that we cannot rest because in fact we have simply passed the baton from the runner in the first stage of the race--rule finalization--to the runner in the next stage--implementation.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Successful implementation of Basel II will require additional hard work and determination.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As most of you know, the agencies have for some time been preparing for Basel II implementation by working to integrate Basel II into our day-to-day supervisory processes.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: With completion of the final rule, we must now be ready to pace ourselves through another long, intensive, but ultimately rewarding, effort.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The agencies are already working hard to foster consistency across banks and across the agencies.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We are building upon the cooperation already established through our work on the final rule and our efforts to prepare supervisory staff for the Basel II qualification process.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Our supervisory staffs have been meeting regularly for some time to align qualification approaches, iron out any differences, and ensure that each bank subject to Basel II is treated appropriately and consistently.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We also remain attentive to the way in which the framework is implemented in other countries, so that we can minimize the burden placed on banks by having to meet multiple national rules.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: I hope our decision to align the definition of default for wholesale exposures more closely with the definition used internationally, for example, sends a positive signal about our intentions to increase cross-border consistency and reduce unnecessary burdens that can distract banks from one of the fundamental goals of Basel II--improving risk management.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Of course, the agencies need to move ahead with Basel II implementation carefully and with our eyes wide open.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The advanced approaches are a significant change from our current, time-tested, risk-based capital rules, and we have therefore embedded the transitional safeguards set forth in the agencies' 2006 proposal into the U.S. Basel II rule.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: These safeguards will help ensure that capital levels remain strong and that we have sufficient opportunity to assess the framework before full implementation.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Importantly, we also are retaining the leverage ratio and our existing prompt-corrective-action framework.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As noted in the agencies' July press release, we are committed to a robust and transparent study of the framework during the transitional phase to assess its overall effectiveness, and we will address any material deficiencies that we identify.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: This study should include active and meaningful dialogue among the agencies, the industry, market participants, Congress, and other interested parties.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: This is consistent with my view that whenever regulators undertake a major regulatory change, a careful and thorough empirical review of the effectiveness of the regulation is extremely valuable.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Such a review can help assess whether the goals for the rule are being met, whether the benefits of the rule exceed the costs, and how the rule can be made more effective and less burdensome.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In addition to this study, during and after the transitional phase we will be relying upon ongoing, detailed analyses to evaluate continuously the results of the new framework in operation.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: A primary objective of this ongoing review will be to ensure that capital levels remain prudent.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: For example, we will respond if we see unreasonable declines in capital requirements at individual institutions that do not appear to be supported by either those banks' own internal capital-adequacy assessments or by our supervisory view of those institutions' risks and how well those risks are managed.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As has long been the case with our capital rules, we expect that adjustments to the capital framework will be made over time to address industry and market developments, any potential shortcomings in the rule identified in our review and analysis during implementation, and new and improved techniques of risk management.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Next Steps for Bankers Completion of the Basel II rulemaking process means that banks adopting the new rule must also gear up their efforts.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Of course we recognize the substantial work that bankers have undertaken over the past several years to prepare themselves for Basel II.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: But, understandably, they have had to wait for completion of the final rule to see how the agencies would articulate certain requirements--some of them quite detailed.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Therefore, it would seem that bankers need to read the rule very carefully and take time to understand how their own bank will be able to meet its requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As stated in the final rule, and as the U.S. agencies articulated several years ago, the key instrument in the qualification process is a bank's implementation plan.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: This written implementation plan, approved by a bank's board of directors, must describe in detail how the bank complies, or intends to comply, with the rule's qualification requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Specifically, the plan must describe how the bank intends to address the gaps it has identified between its existing practices and the qualification requirements set forth in the rule for the advanced approaches, covering all consolidated subsidiaries.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The implementation plan also must include objective, measurable milestones--including delivery dates--and a target date when the bank expects its advanced approaches to be fully operational.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The bank must establish and maintain a comprehensive and sound planning and governance process to oversee implementation efforts, and must demonstrate to its supervisor that it meets the qualification requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Banks subject to the final rule on a mandatory basis, the core banks, have up to six months to adopt an implementation plan.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Of course, banks may always submit their plans earlier, and I understand that a number of core banks are working toward that goal.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: This deadline for submission of plans by core banks is intended to prevent delays in starting implementation efforts.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: However, the final rule provides flexibility and gives banks adopting Basel II ample time to fully meet the qualification requirements once they have adopted an implementation plan.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Specifically, a bank's plan may include developmental goals for full implementation for up to thirty-six months from the effective date of the final rule.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As supervisors, we will take the qualification requirements seriously, expecting banks to meet both the letter and the spirit of those requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Thus, we strongly recommend that banks undertake their own sober and frank appraisal of their ability to meet the final rule.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Systems development can take time, for example, and it is important to make sure that these systems function appropriately.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: While I believe that expeditious adoption of Basel II will have significant benefits, it is of the utmost importance that the implementation not be rushed but be undertaken thoughtfully and deliberately.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: After a bank has submitted a credible implementation plan to its primary supervisor, it must then begin a parallel run lasting at least four consecutive calendar quarters, during which the bank's supervisor must determine the bank's compliance with the qualification requirements to be satisfactory.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: During the parallel run, a bank remains subject to the Basel I risk-based capital rules for all applicable regulatory and supervisory purposes, but the bank also must calculate its capital ratios using the advanced approaches and report pertinent information to its supervisor.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: It is only upon notification from its supervisor that a bank can move into a series of three transitional periods (each lasting at least one year), during which the cumulative reductions of the bank's risk-based capital requirements are limited.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Supervisory approval is needed to move to a subsequent transitional floor-level and then to move from the transitional floors to stand-alone use of the Basel II rules.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Importantly, as bankers move forward with implementation, they should not lose sight of Pillars 2 and 3, which may ultimately be more important to the success of Basel II than Pillar 1, which has received the bulk of the attention so far.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Under Pillar 2, banks are required to have an internal process--which will be subject to rigorous supervisory review--for ensuring that they are holding enough overall capital to support their entire risk profile.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Thus, Pillar 2 should be a key area of focus for banks implementing Basel II.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The preamble to the final rule describes the steps that supervisors will take under Pillar 2, namely that supervisors will take into account a bank's internal capital-adequacy assessment process--known as its ICAAP--as well as the bank's compliance with the minimum capital requirements set forth in this rule, and all other relevant information.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The agencies expect banks to implement and continually update the fundamental elements of a sound ICAAP--identifying and measuring material risks, setting capital-adequacy goals that relate to risk, and ensuring the integrity of internal capital-adequacy assessments.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: A bank is expected to hold adequate capital against all of its material risks, particularly those risks not covered or not adequately quantified in the risk-based capital requirements--such as liquidity risk or interest-rate risk in the banking book.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In general, a bank's ICAAP should reflect an appropriate level of conservatism to account for uncertainty in risk identification, risk mitigation or control, quantitative processes, and any use of modeling.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In most cases, this conservatism will result in levels of capital or capital ratios above minimum regulatory requirements to be regarded as adequate.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Pillar 3 is a key mechanism for banks to communicate to market participants about their risk profiles, their associated levels of capital, and the manner in which they are meeting the requirements in the final rule.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In addition to providing information about its various components of regulatory capital and its minimum capital requirements and ratios, a bank must disclose information about how it measures and manages credit risk, operational risk, equity risk, and interest-rate risk in non-trading activities, as well as the range of risks related to securitizations.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: For example, a bank has to describe the operation of its credit risk rating system as well as the data used in parameter estimates for credit losses.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Some of these disclosure requirements will be new for banks but others are already required by, or are consistent with, existing U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, Securities and Exchange Commission disclosure requirements, or bank regulatory reporting requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As a strong believer in market discipline and the importance of information in market transactions, I believe Pillar 3 will improve bank disclosures about risk profiles and enhance discussions between bankers and market participants about risk-management practices.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Of course, while we want to promote consistency, we must also allow bankers some flexibility in meeting the Basel II requirements and permit a reasonable amount of diversity of practices across banking organizations.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Such flexibility will allow banks to use and readily improve their existing risk-measurement and risk-management practices.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: More to the point, as supervisors we should actively encourage such improvements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As we move forward, we encourage banks to raise issues as they try to meet the rule's requirements; in other words, we want banks to maintain an ongoing dialogue about implementation with their supervisors, who stand ready to answer questions and assist banks in interpreting Basel II requirements.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Standardized Approach Proposal for Non-Core Banks Before concluding, I would like to discuss the agencies' additional plans for revising capital rules, specifically plans for those banks not subject to the advanced approaches of Basel II.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Some commentators on the earlier Basel II and Basel IA proposals voiced concerns that adoption of a new capital framework for the largest and most complex U.S. banking organizations could disadvantage other U.S. banking organizations, particularly the smaller banks.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We understand that banks not required to adopt Basel II are facing a choice about whether to opt-in to the advanced approaches.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Some of these banks may be sophisticated institutions that exhibit sound risk management but do not quite meet the criteria to be core banks.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The agencies recognize that such institutions should be afforded an alternative for more-risk-sensitive capital requirements, but one that is not as complex as the advanced approaches.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: In this regard, the agencies have responded by committing to proposing a "standardized" approach instead of Basel IA.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Specifically, the staffs are currently working on a notice of proposed rulemaking that would implement some of the simpler approaches for both credit risk and operational risk from the Basel II framework--referred to as the standardized approach.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The proposal is being developed as an optional risk-based capital framework for all banking organizations that are not required to adopt the advanced approaches.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We also expect to retain our existing Basel I-based regulatory capital framework for those smaller banks that would prefer to remain under that regime.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The proposal for the standardized approach will take into consideration relevant commentary received in response to the Basel IA and Basel II proposed rules that were published in late 2006 and should, in essence, modernize the Basel I-based rules without imposing a substantial implementation burden.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Among other things, the proposal is being designed both to provide greater differentiation across corporate exposures based on borrowers' underlying credit quality and to recognize a broader spectrum of credit-risk mitigation techniques.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: The agencies are also considering how to implement Pillars 2 and 3 of the Basel II framework in the standardized proposal in a manner that is commensurate with banks' complexity and risk profiles.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Our goal is to realize the benefits of these two pillars without imposing excessive regulatory burden and without creating competitive advantages or disadvantages for different types of banks.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: I expect this proposal to be presented to the Board for consideration within the next several months, and I encourage all interested parties to review and comment on this proposal once it has been issued.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We are keenly aware of the need for capital requirements to make sense from the standpoint of both safety-and-soundness and competitiveness; we recognize that a one-size-fits-all approach is probably not the best for our banking system, in light of our wide range of institutions.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: We remain sensitive to the principle that if we have multiple regulatory capital frameworks, they must work together to improve the safety and soundness of our entire banking system without artificially creating competitive inequalities.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Our goal is to have the standardized approach ready for implementation concurrently with the start of the first Basel II transition phase.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Conclusion The U.S. banking agencies have reached an important milestone in adopting the final rule for Basel II.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Our focus on the fundamentals of improving risk management consistent with safety and soundness, and on international consistency, has been key to achieving this success.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Obviously, however, effective implementation of Basel II is as important as, if not more important than, the rulemaking process.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: It is imperative that we observe how the new rule works in practice--assessing carefully both its advantages and its limitations.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: I am confident that both banking organizations and the supervisory community are up to the challenge.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: It is also important to modernize the existing Basel I-based regulatory capital framework to improve the risk sensitivity of capital requirements at the non-core banks, by offering a standardized option.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Finally, we should all bear in mind that implementation of Basel II--and, more significantly, the improvements in risk measurement and management that will be required--will not be a one-time event, but rather an ongoing process.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: Basel II is designed to accommodate innovation and change as markets and risk-measurement and -management evolve over time.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Kroszner
text: As one marathon is completed, yet another begins.
speech_title: Implementing Basel II in the United States
speech_venue: At the Standard & Poor's Bank Conference 2007, New York, New York

speaker: Bernanke
text: Montagu Norman, the Governor of the Bank of England from 1921 to 1944, reputedly took as his personal motto, "Never explain, never excuse."
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Norman's aphorism exemplified how he and many of his contemporaries viewed the making of monetary policy--as an arcane and esoteric art, best practiced out of public view.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Many central bankers of Norman's time (and, indeed, well into the postwar period) believed that a certain mystique attached to their activities and that allowing the public a glimpse of the inner workings would only usurp the prerogatives of insiders and reduce, if not grievously damage, the effectiveness of policy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Norman's perspective on central banking now seems decidedly quaint.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Over the past few decades, central banks around the world have worked assiduously to become more open about their activities.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In fact, Norman's own institution, the Bank of England, has in recent years been a leading exponent of increased transparency in central banking.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Monetary policy makers have adopted a range of methods to improve their communication with the public, including timely announcements of policy actions, expanded testimony before members of the legislature, the release of minutes of policy meetings, frequent public speeches, and the regular publication of reports about the economy and monetary policy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: This increased openness is a welcome development for several reasons.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Most importantly, monetary policy makers are public servants whose decisions affect the life of every citizen; consequently, in a democratic society, they have a responsibility to give the people and their elected representatives a full and compelling rationale for the decisions they make.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Good communications are a prerequisite if central banks are to maintain the democratic legitimacy and independence that are essential to sound monetary policy making.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, a considerable amount of evidence indicates that central bank transparency increases the effectiveness of monetary policy and enhances economic and financial performance in several ways.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: First, improving the public's understanding of the central bank's objectives and policy strategies reduces economic and financial uncertainty and thereby allows businesses and households to make more-informed decisions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Second, if practitioners in financial markets gain a better understanding of how policy is likely to respond to incoming information, asset prices and bond yields will tend to respond to economic data in ways that further the central bank's policy objectives.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, if market participants understand that arriving information about the economy increases the likelihood of certain policy actions, then market interest rates will tend to move in a way that reinforces the expected actions, effectively supporting the goals of the central bank.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Third, clarity about the central bank's policy objectives and strategy may help anchor the public's long-term inflation expectations, which can substantially improve the efficacy of policy and the overall functioning of the economy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Finally, open discussion of the central bank's analyses and forecasts invites valuable input and feedback from the public.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The benefits of an open and accountable policymaking process have spurred the Federal Reserve, along with other major central banks, to take a number of actions over the years to increase its transparency.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Appropriately, given the unique position of the Federal Reserve and the sensitivity of financial markets to its communications, these steps have generally been incremental in nature; but, taken together, they have substantially increased the ability of the American public to understand and to anticipate monetary policy decisions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Congress has also long been aware of the importance of Federal Reserve transparency and accountability; in particular, a series of resolutions and laws passed in the 1970s set clear policy objectives for the Federal Reserve and required it to provide regular reports and testimony to the Congress.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 1 Since 1975, the Federal Reserve has presented testimony twice each year to the Congress on the conduct of monetary policy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: These semiannual presentations have become an important vehicle for the U.S. central bank to make known its views on the outlook and on the appropriate stance of policy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Other notable milestones in the Federal Reserve's progress toward greater openness include:  in 1979, the first release of semiannual economic projections; in 1983, the first publication of the Beige Book, which summarizes information about economic conditions received from the Federal Reserve System's business contacts; in 1994, the decision to release a postmeeting statement when policy actions had been taken; in 2000, the beginning of the practice of issuing a statement after each meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and including in the statement an assessment of the balance of risks to the Committee's objectives; in 2002, adding the FOMC roll call vote to the postmeeting statement; and in 2005, the speeding up of the release of the minutes of FOMC meetings, from a delay of some six or seven weeks to just three weeks.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In testimony to the Congress at the time of my nomination as Chairman, in 2005, I pledged to continue the trend toward greater openness sustained under Chairman Greenspan.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In so doing, I stressed the importance of continuity with the policies and strategies that have served the American economy well.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Any further changes, I promised, would come only pursuant to a consensus within the FOMC that those changes would enhance the Committee's ability to pursue its dual mandate of achieving maximum employment and price stability.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Toward that end, the FOMC has engaged in extensive deliberations over the past year or so to consider further steps toward greater transparency.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Guided by a subcommittee chaired by Board Vice Chairman Donald Kohn, the FOMC reviewed the full range of our communications with the public.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 2 As indicated in a statement issued by the FOMC today, these discussions have led to a decision to increase the frequency and expand the content of the publicly released economic projections that are made by Federal Reserve Board members and Reserve Bank presidents.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I mentioned, the Federal Reserve has published economic projections for almost thirty years, and, indeed, the Federal Reserve was the first major central bank to release such projections.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 3 Today's announcement builds on that foundation.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the remainder of my remarks I will describe the changes that we plan to make, and then explain why I believe that, collectively, they represent an important further step toward greater transparency.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Toward More Informative Economic Projections Because monetary policy affects spending and inflation with a lag, policy decisions must be based on an assessment of medium-term economic prospects.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Thus, the Committee cannot fully explain its policy decisions without sharing its economic outlook with the public and the Congress.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: To provide more-timely information about the evolving outlook, the Federal Reserve will release FOMC participants' economic projections four times each year, rather than twice each year as we have done previously.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Projections will continue to be released in February and July of each year to coincide with the semiannual Monetary Policy Report and the associated testimony to the Congress.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Two additional sets of projections will be published in conjunction with the minutes of the FOMC meetings held around the beginnings of the second quarter and the fourth quarter of the year (in 2008, the April and October meetings).
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The first expanded set of projections will be released next week, on November 20, together with the minutes of the October FOMC meeting.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The horizon of the projections will be extended from two years to three.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The projections released next week will extend through 2010.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Each of the participants in the FOMC meeting--including the Federal Reserve Board members and all the Reserve Bank presidentsââwill, as in the past, provide projections for the growth of real gross domestic product (GDP), the unemployment rate, and core inflation (that is, inflation excluding the prices of food and energy items).
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, participants will now provide their projections for overall inflation.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Both overall and core inflation will continue to be based on the price index for personal consumption expenditures (PCE).
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Projections will continue to be made independently by each FOMC participant under the assumption of "appropriate" monetary policy, that is, the future evolution of the federal funds rate judged by that participant to be the one most likely to foster economic outcomes that satisfy the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Following past practice, we will publish the central tendency and the range of the projections for each variable and each year.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 6 We will also publish a comparison with the previous set of quarterly projections; a chart showing central tendencies and ranges for each variable; and charts showing the distribution of participants' projections and how that distribution has changed since the previous release.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Accompanying the numerical projections will be a discussion--a projections "narrative" if you will--that summarizes participants' views of the major forces shaping the outlook, discusses the sources of risk to that outlook, and describes the dispersion of views among policymakers.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: By providing a medium-term perspective, the narrative will complement the discussion of shorter-term developments contained in the minutes.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: We will also provide qualitative information about participants' views on both the uncertainty and the balance of risks surrounding the outlook, together with quantitative historical information on the typical range of projection errors.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 7 Of course, the specific material provided and its form of presentation may change over time as we gain experience and receive feedback.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Benefits of the Enhanced Projections The enhanced projections will provide the public with several types of useful information.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, I find it helpful to think of the projections as functioning in three different ways:  as a forecast, as a provisional plan, and as an evaluation of certain long-run features of the economy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Most obviously, the projections reflect the economic forecasts of FOMC participants and as such should provide the public with greater and more-timely insight into the Committee's views of the economic outlook and the risks to that outlook.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Of course, because our knowledge of the structure of the economy is incomplete and future economic disturbances are often unforeseeable, economic forecasting is a highly uncertain enterprise.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 8 The only economic forecast in which I have complete confidence is that the economy will not evolve along the precise path implied by our projections.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Nevertheless, as I have already noted, because policy affects spending and inflation with a lag, Committee members have no choice other than to make medium-term forecasts--provisional and subject to uncertainty though they may be.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Providing more information about these forecasts, including discussions of the factors underlying the forecasts and of FOMC participants' assessments of the risks to the Committee's objectives, should improve the public's understanding of the rationale for the current stance of monetary policy and any changes to that stance.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The public will also be better able to judge the extent to which the Committee's rationale is reasonable and persuasive.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The projections also function as a plan for policy--albeit as a rough and highly provisional one.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I mentioned earlier, FOMC participants will continue to base their projections on the assumption of "appropriate" monetary policy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Consequently, the extended projections will provide a sense of the economic trajectory that Committee participants see as best fulfilling the Federal Reserve's dual mandate, given the initial conditions and the constraints posed by the structure of the economy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: To illustrate, consider the question of the length of time over which a central bank should aim to restore price stability following an unwanted increase in inflation.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: A central bank that places weight on both employment and price stability, like the Federal Reserve, would not attempt to disinflate immediately or establish a fixed time frame for the restoration of price stability.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Rather, the optimal expected time required for completing the disinflation would depend on a host of factors, including the size of the initial deviation from price stability, the initial state of the real economy (for example, the level of unemployment), whether the rise in inflation resulted from transitory or more persistent sources, the extent to which inflation expectations are well anchored, and so on.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In circumstances in which disinflationary policy is necessary, the extended economic projections would make clear that the Federal Reserve is committed to maintaining price stability, but they would also provide some indications about what the Committee views as the most appropriate pace of disinflation, given the state of the economy and the requirements of the dual mandate.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In like fashion, the speed at which policy aims to return the economy to its sustainable rates of growth and employment following a period of resource slack should depend in part on the nature and extent of inflation risks, among other considerations.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: More generally, the extended projections will convey additional information about the Committee's policy strategies and thus help augment the Committee's transparency, predictability, and accountability.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Finally, the extended projections will embody information about FOMC participants' evaluations of certain long-run features of the economy, evaluations determined both by the economy's structure and by the Committee's policy objectives.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Because of the extension of the projection horizon to three years, participants' inflation projections will convey more information regarding their views about the measured rate of inflation that, in the long run, is consistent with the Committee's dual objectives of maximum employment and price stability.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Were price stability the only objective mandated for the Federal Reserve, the FOMC presumably would strive to achieve zero inflation, properly measured--that is, the optimal measured inflation rate would deviate from zero on average only by the amount of the estimated measurement error in the preferred inflation index.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: But under the Federal Reserve's dual mandate, the determination of the appropriate long-run inflation rate must take account of factors that may affect the efficient functioning of the economy at very low rates of inflation, such as the risk that the zero lower bound on nominal interest rates might hinder the effectiveness of monetary policy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Thus, the (properly measured) long-run inflation rate that best promotes the dual mandate is likely to be low but not zero.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Ultimately, households and businesses care about the overall, or "headline," rate of inflation; therefore, the FOMC should refer to an overall inflation rate when evaluating whether the Committee has met its mandated objectives over the long run.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: For that reason, the Committee has decided to publish projections for overall inflation as well as core inflation.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In its policy statements and elsewhere, the Committee makes frequent reference to core inflation because, in light of the volatility of food and energy prices, core inflation can be a useful short-run indicator of the underlying trend in inflation.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, at longer horizons, where monetary policy has the greatest control over inflation, the overall inflation rate is the appropriate gauge of whether inflation is at a rate consistent with the dual mandate.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: FOMC participants will continue to couch their inflation projections in terms of PCE inflation, rather than, say, inflation as measured by the consumer price index, because the PCE index is generally thought to provide the single most comprehensive and theoretically compelling measure of consumer prices.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: That said, no single measure of inflation is perfect, and the Committee will continue to monitor a range of measures when forming its view about inflation prospects.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The lengthening of the projection horizon will also allow the public to infer more about FOMC participants' current judgments about the rate of GDP growth and the unemployment rate that the economy can sustain in the long run.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Over time, effective monetary policies foster rates of growth and unemployment close to their long-run sustainable rates.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, in contrast to inflation, which in the long run is determined by monetary policy, the rates of economic growth and unemployment that can be sustained in the long run are determined by many factors outside the control of central banks.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Among these factors are the advance of technology, entrepreneurial activities, the growth in the size of the labor force, the rate at which workers acquire new skills, tax and regulatory policies, and the efficiency of labor markets in matching workers with positions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Consequently, the long-run sustainable rates of economic growth and unemployment should be viewed as constraints on what monetary policy can achieve and not as variables that policymakers can freely choose.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, estimates of sustainable rates of growth and unemployment have been shown to be highly uncertain at any point in time; and they may vary significantly over time in light of new information and changes in the structure of the economy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Thus, the longer-run projections of growth and unemployment should be treated with considerable caution.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Relationship to Inflation Targeting As you may know, I have been an advocate of the monetary policy strategy known as inflation targeting, used in many countries around the world.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Inflation targeting is characterized by two features:  an explicit numerical target or target range for inflation and a high degree of transparency about forecasts and policy plans.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The steps being taken by the Federal Reserve, I must emphasize, are intended only to improve our communication with the public; the conduct of policy itself will not change.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Nonetheless, in light of the changes to communications we are undertaking, one might fairly ask how the Federal Reserve's approach relates to inflation targeting.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: A superficial drawback of inflation targeting is its very name, which suggests a single-minded focus on inflation to the exclusion of other goals.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In fact, the practice of monetary policy in an inflation-targeting regime is not necessarily inconsistent with a dual mandate such as that given to the Federal Reserve; indeed, most if not all inflation-targeting central banks today practice "flexible" inflation targeting, meaning that they take account of other economic goals besides price stability--notably economic growth, employment, and financial stability--when making policy decisions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, a broad consensus exists among central banks, whether they have an explicit numerical target for inflation or not, that maintaining low and stable inflation over time is the best means by which monetary policy can promote economic efficiency and maximize the nation's economic welfare.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Thus, at least since the stabilization of U.S. inflation in the 1980s, the Federal Reserve's approach to monetary policy has had much in common with that of central banks that describe themselves as inflation targeters.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Nevertheless, some aspects of inflation targeting may be less well suited to the Federal Reserve's mandate and policy practice.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, although inflation-targeting central banks certainly pay attention to economic growth and employment, their formal accountability is often largely couched only in terms of a price-stability objective.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Likewise, the communication strategies of inflation-targeting central banks tend to be focused on the formal inflation objective and the horizon over which that objective will be achieved.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I have emphasized today, the Federal Reserve is legally accountable to the Congress for two objectives, maximum employment and price stability, on an equal footing.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: My colleagues and I strongly support the dual mandate and the equal weighting of objectives that it implies.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Of course, as I have discussed, the Federal Reserve's influence over these objectives differs importantly in the long run:  Monetary policy determines the long-run inflation rate, whereas the factors that influence the sustainable rates of growth and employment in the long run are largely outside the central bank's control.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Still, over time, monetary policy must strive to foster rates of growth and employment close to their long-run sustainable rates.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve must thus be accountable for the effects of its policies on the real economy as well as on inflation.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The enhanced projections that I have described today will provide additional information pertinent to both halves of the Federal Reserve's mandate.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: At a more technical level, the Federal Reserve differs from most inflation-targeting central banks in that it provides information about the independent projections of Committee members rather than a single collective forecast.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: To some extent, that difference reflects the relatively large size of the FOMC and the geographic dispersion of Committee participants; those factors would make the development of a detailed consensus forecast quite difficult as a practical matter.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: But, as I will discuss briefly, such a diversity of viewpoints can enhance the quality of policy decisions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Diversity of the Committee An important strength of the Federal Open Market Committee is its diversity.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Board members and Reserve Bank presidents who sit around the table at each meeting of the FOMC bring a wide range of perspectives to the deliberations that reflect the participants' professional backgrounds, the regions of the country with which they are most familiar, and their differing approaches to economic and policy analysis.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The task participants face at each meeting is to forge a rough consensus regarding the outlook, the risks to the Committee's objectives, and the appropriate policy response.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Of course, it is not always possible--indeed, it would be rather unusual--to come to a set of conclusions that fully represent the views of every participant.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: But the process of searching for common ground is itself an important aspect of how the Committee operates.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Diversity of views drives the Committee to adopt an eclectic approach and thus serves to limit the risk that a single viewpoint or analytical framework might become unduly dominant.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The changes to the projections process announced today preserve the important role played by this diversity of perspectives.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I have noted, Committee participants will continue to produce individual projections that reflect their judgments about the state of the economy and their approaches to policy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: From the internal perspective, I expect the more frequent sharing of projections and the additional information they contain will improve our discussions and policy debates.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: From the external perspective, the public will gain additional and more frequent information about both the central tendencies and diversity of participants' views.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, the additional narrative material that will accompany the numerical projections will illuminate both the consensus of opinion and the differences in judgments that may emerge.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Conclusion The communications strategy of the Federal Reserve is a work in progress.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: I believe that the changes announced by the FOMC today are an important advance:  The changes will provide a more-timely insight into the Committee's outlook, will help households and businesses better understand and anticipate how our policy decisions respond to incoming information, and will enhance our accountability for the decisions we make.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: But the changes are also evolutionary, in that they build on long-established practices; in that respect, they represent just one more step on the road toward greater transparency at the Federal Reserve.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute 25th Annual Monetary Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Committee will continue to look for ways to improve the accountability and public understanding of U.S. monetary policy making.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Communications
