speaker: Bernanke
text: It seems to me, paradoxically, that both long ago and only yesterday I attended my own Class Day in 1975.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: I am pleased and honored to be invited back by the students of Harvard.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Our speaker in 1975 was Dick Gregory, the social critic and comedian, who was inclined toward the sharp-edged and satiric.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Central bankers don't do satire as a rule, so I am going to have to strive for "kind of interesting."
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: When I attended Class Day as a graduating senior, Gerald Ford was President, and an up-and-coming fellow named Alan Greenspan was his chief economic adviser.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Just weeks earlier, the last Americans remaining in Saigon had been evacuated by helicopters.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: On a happier note, the Red Sox were on their way to winning the American League pennant.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: I skipped classes to attend a World Series game against the Cincinnati Reds.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: As was their wont in those days, the Sox came agonizingly close to a championship but ended up snatching defeat from the jaws of victory.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: On that score, as on others--disco music and Pet Rocks come to mind--many things are better today than they were then.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In fact, that will be a theme of my remarks today.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although 1975 was a pretty good year for the Red Sox, it was not a good one for the U.S. economy.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Then as now, we were experiencing a serious oil price shock, sharply rising prices for food and other commodities, and subpar economic growth.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: But I see the differences between the economy of 1975 and the economy of 2008 as more telling than the similarities.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Today's situation differs from that of 33 years ago in large part because our economy and society have become much more flexible and able to adapt to difficult situations and new challenges.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Economic policymaking has improved as well, I believe, partly because we have learned well some of the hard lessons of the past.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Of course, I do not want to minimize the challenges we currently face, and I will come back to a few of these.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: But I do think that our demonstrated ability to respond constructively and effectively to past economic problems provides a basis for optimism about the future.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: I will focus my remarks today on two economic issues that challenged us in the 1970s and that still do so today--energy and productivity.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: These, obviously, are not the kind of topics chosen by many recent Class Day speakers--Will Farrell, Ali G, or Seth MacFarlane, to name a few.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: But, then, the Class Marshals presumably knew what they were getting when they invited an economist.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Because the members of today's graduating class--and some of your professors--were not yet born in 1975, let me begin by briefly surveying the economic landscape in the mid-1970s.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The economy had just gone through a severe recession, during which output, income, and employment fell sharply and the unemployment rate rose to 9 percent.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Meanwhile, consumer price inflation, which had been around 3 percent to 4 percent earlier in the decade, soared to more than 10 percent during my senior year.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The oil price shock of the 1970s began in October 1973 when, in response to the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil producers imposed an embargo on exports.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Before the embargo, in 1972, the price of imported oil was about $3.20 per barrel; by 1975, the average price was nearly $14 per barrel, more than four times greater.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: President Nixon had imposed economy-wide controls on wages and prices in 1971, including prices of petroleum products; in November 1973, in the wake of the embargo, the President placed additional controls on petroleum prices.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: As basic economics predicts, when a scarce resource cannot be allocated by market-determined prices, it will be allocated some other way--in this case, in what was to become an iconic symbol of the times, by long lines at gasoline stations.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In 1974, in an attempt to overcome the unintended consequences of price controls, drivers in many places were permitted to buy gasoline only on odd or even days of the month, depending on the last digit of their license plate number.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, with the controlled price of U.S. crude oil well below world prices, growth in domestic exploration slowed and production was curtailed--which, of course, only made things worse.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition to creating long lines at gasoline stations, the oil price shock exacerbated what was already an intensifying buildup of inflation and inflation expectations.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In another echo of today, the inflationary situation was further worsened by rapidly rising prices of agricultural products and other commodities.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Economists generally agree that monetary policy performed poorly during this period.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In part, this was because policymakers, in choosing what they believed to be the appropriate setting for monetary policy, overestimated the productive capacity of the economy.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: I'll have more to say about this shortly.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Federal Reserve policymakers also underestimated both their own contributions to the inflationary problems of the time and their ability to curb that inflation.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, on occasion they blamed inflation on so-called cost-push factors such as union wage pressures and price increases by large, market-dominating firms; however, the abilities of unions and firms to push through inflationary wage and price increases were symptoms of the problem, not the underlying cause.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Several years passed before the Federal Reserve gained a new leadership that better understood the central bank's role in the inflation process and that sustained anti-inflationary monetary policies would actually work.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Beginning in 1979, such policies were implemented successfully--although not without significant cost in terms of lost output and employment--under Fed Chairman Paul Volcker.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: For the Federal Reserve, two crucial lessons from this experience were, first, that high inflation can seriously destabilize the economy and, second, that the central bank must take responsibility for achieving price stability over the medium term.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In that year, crude oil cost a little more than $30 per barrel.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: 3 Since then, crude oil prices have increased more than fourfold, proportionally about as much as in the 1970s.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Now, as in 1975, adjusting to such high prices for crude oil has been painful.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Gas prices around $4 a gallon are a huge burden for many households, as well as for truckers, manufacturers, farmers, and others.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: But, in many other ways, the economic consequences have been quite different from those of the 1970s.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: One obvious difference is what you don't see: drivers lining up on odd or even days to buy gasoline because of price controls or signs at gas stations that say "No gas."
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: And until the recent slowdown--which is more the result of conditions in the residential housing market and in financial markets than of higher oil prices--economic growth was solid and unemployment remained low, unlike what we saw following oil price increases in the '70s.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: For a central banker, a particularly critical difference between then and now is what has happened to inflation and inflation expectations.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The overall inflation rate has averaged about 3-1/2 percent over the past four quarters, significantly higher than we would like but much less than the double-digit rates that inflation reached in the mid-1970s and then again in 1980.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, the increase in inflation has been milder this time--on the order of 1 percentage point over the past year as compared with the 6 percentage point jump that followed the 1973 oil price shock.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: 4 From the perspective of monetary policy, just as important as the behavior of actual inflation is what households and businesses expect to happen to inflation in the future, particularly over the longer term.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: If people expect an increase in inflation to be temporary and do not build it into their longer-term plans for setting wages and prices, then the inflation created by a shock to oil prices will tend to fade relatively quickly.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Some indicators of longer-term inflation expectations have risen in recent months, which is a significant concern for the Federal Reserve.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: We will need to monitor that situation closely.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, changes in long-term inflation expectations have been measured in tenths of a percentage point this time around rather than in whole percentage points, as appeared to be the case in the mid-1970s.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Importantly, we see little indication today of the beginnings of a 1970s-style wage-price spiral, in which wages and prices chased each other ever upward.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: A good deal of economic research has looked at the question of why the inflation response to the oil shock has been relatively muted in the current instance.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: 5 One factor, which illustrates my point about the adaptability and flexibility of the U.S. economy, is the pronounced decline in the energy intensity of the economy since the 1970s.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Since 1975, the energy required to produce a given amount of output in the United States has fallen by about half.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: 6 This great improvement in energy efficiency was less the result of government programs than of steps taken by households and businesses in response to higher energy prices, including substantial investments in more energy-efficient equipment and means of transportation.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: This improvement in energy efficiency is one of the reasons why a given increase in crude oil prices does less damage to the U.S. economy today than it did in the 1970s.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Another reason is the performance of monetary policy.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve and other central banks have learned the lessons of the 1970s.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Because monetary policy works with a lag, the short-term inflationary effects of a sharp increase in oil prices can generally not be fully offset.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, since Paul Volcker's time, the Federal Reserve has been firmly committed to maintaining a low and stable rate of inflation over the longer term.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: And we recognize that keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored is essential to achieving the goal of low and stable inflation.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Maintaining confidence in the Fed's commitment to price stability remains a top priority as the central bank navigates the current complex situation.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although our economy has thus far dealt with the current oil price shock comparatively well, the United States and the rest of the world still face significant challenges in dealing with the rising global demand for energy, especially if continued demand growth and constrained supplies maintain intense pressure on prices.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The silver lining of high energy prices is that they provide a powerful incentive for action--for conservation, including investment in energy-saving technologies; for the investment needed to bring new oil supplies to market; and for the development of alternative conventional and nonconventional energy sources.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The government, in addition to the market, can usefully address energy concerns, for example, by supporting basic research and adopting well-designed regulatory policies to promote important social objectives such as protecting the environment.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: As we saw after the oil price shock of the 1970s, given some time, the economy can become much more energy-efficient even as it continues to grow and living standards improve.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Let me turn now to the other economic challenge that I want to highlight today--the productivity performance of our economy.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: At this point you may be saying to yourself, "Is it too late to book Ali G?"
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, anyone who stayed awake through EC 10 understands why this issue is so important.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: 7 As Adam Smith pointed out in 1776, in the long run, more than any other factor, the productivity of the workforce determines a nation's standard of living.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The decades following the end of World War II were remarkable for their industrial innovation and creativity.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: From 1948 to 1973, output per hour of work grew by nearly 3 percent per year, on average.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: 8 But then, for the next 20 years or so, productivity growth averaged only about 1-1/2 percent per year, barely half its previous rate.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Predictably, the rate of increase in the standard of living slowed as well, and to about the same extent.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The difference between 3 percent and 1-1/2 percent may sound small.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: But at 3 percent per year, the standard of living would double about every 23 years, or once every generation; by contrast, at 1-1/2 percent, a doubling would occur only roughly every 47 years, or once every other generation.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Among the many consequences of the productivity slowdown was a further complication for the monetary policy makers of the 1970s.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Detecting shifts in economic trends is difficult in real time, and most economists and policymakers did not fully appreciate the extent of the productivity slowdown until the late 1970s.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: This further influenced the policymakers of the time toward running a monetary policy that was too accommodative.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The resulting overheating of the economy probably exacerbated the inflation problem of that decade.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Productivity growth revived in the mid-1990s, as I mentioned, illustrating once again the resilience of the American economy.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: 10 Since 1995, productivity has increased at about a 2-1/2 percent annual rate.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: A great deal of intellectual effort has been expended in trying to explain the recent performance and to forecast the future evolution of productivity.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Much very good work has been conducted here at Harvard by Dale Jorgenson (my senior thesis adviser in 1975, by the way) and his colleagues, and other important research in the area has been done at the Federal Reserve Board.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: 11 One key finding of that research is that, to have an economic impact, technological innovations must be translated into successful commercial applications.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: This country's competitive, market-based system, its flexible capital and labor markets, its tradition of entrepreneurship, and its technological strengths--to which Harvard and other universities make a critical contribution--help ensure that that happens on an ongoing basis.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: While private-sector initiative was the key ingredient in generating the pickup in productivity growth, government policy was constructive, in part through support of basic research but also to a substantial degree by promoting economic competition.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Beginning in the late 1970s, the federal government deregulated a number of key industries, including air travel, trucking, telecommunications, and energy.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The resulting increase in competition promoted cost reductions and innovation, leading in turn to new products and industries.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: It is difficult to imagine that we would have online retailing today if the transportation and telecommunications industries had not been deregulated.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, the lowering of trade barriers promoted productivity gains by increasing competition, expanding markets, and increasing the pace of technology transfer.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Finally, as a central banker, I would be remiss if I failed to mention the contribution of monetary policy to the improved productivity performance.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: By damping business cycles and by keeping inflation under control, a sound monetary policy improves the ability of households and firms to plan and increases their willingness to undertake the investments in skills, research, and physical capital needed to support continuing gains in productivity.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Just as the productivity slowdown was associated with a slower growth of real per capita income, the productivity resurgence since the mid-1990s has been accompanied by a pickup in real income growth.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: One measure of average living standards, real consumption per capita, is nearly 35 percent higher today than in 1995.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, the flood of innovation that helped spur the productivity resurgence has created many new job opportunities, and more than a few fortunes.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: But changing technology has also reduced job opportunities for some others--bank tellers and assembly-line workers, for example.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: And that is the crux of a whole new set of challenges.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Even though average economic well-being has increased considerably over time, the degree of inequality in economic outcomes over the past three decades has increased as well.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Economists continue to grapple with the reasons for this trend.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: But as best we can tell, the increase in inequality probably is due to a number of factors, notably including technological change that seems to have favored higher-skilled workers more than lower-skilled ones.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, some economists point to increased international trade and the declining role of labor unions as other, probably lesser contributing factors.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: What should we do about rising economic inequality?
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Answering this question inevitably involves difficult value judgments and tradeoffs.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: But approaches that inhibit the dynamism of our economy would clearly be a step in the wrong direction.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: To be sure, new technologies and increased international trade can lead to painful dislocations as some workers lose their jobs or see the demand for their particular skills decline.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, hindering the adoption of new technologies or inhibiting trade flows would do far more harm than good over the longer haul.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the short term, the better approach is to adopt policies that help those who are displaced by economic change.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: By doing so, we not only provide assistance to those who need it but help to secure public support for the economic flexibility that is essential for prosperity.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the long term, however, the best way by far to improve economic opportunity and to reduce inequality is to increase the educational attainment and skills of American workers.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The productivity surge in the decades after World War II corresponded to a period in which educational attainment was increasing rapidly; in recent decades, progress on that front has been far slower.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, inequalities in education and in access to education remain high.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: As we think about improving education and skills, we should also look beyond the traditional K-12 and 4-year-college system--as important as it is--to recognize that education should be lifelong and can come in many forms.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Early childhood education, community colleges, vocational schools, on-the-job training, online courses, adult education--all of these are vehicles of demonstrated value in increasing skills and lifetime earning power.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The use of a wide range of methods to address the pressing problems of inadequate skills and economic inequality would be entirely consistent with the themes of economic adaptability and flexibility that I have emphasized in my remarks.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: I will close by shifting from the topic of education in general to your education specifically.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Through effort, talent, and doubtless some luck, you have succeeded in acquiring an excellent education.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Your education--more precisely, your ability to think critically and creatively--is your greatest asset.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: And unlike many assets, the more you draw on it, the faster it grows.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Put it to good use.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: The poor forecasting record of economists is legendary, but I will make a forecast in which I am very confident: Whatever you expect your life and work to be like 10, 20, or 30 years from now, the reality will be quite different.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: In looking over the 30th anniversary report on my own class, I was struck by the great diversity of vocations and avocations that have engaged my classmates.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: To be sure, the volume was full of attorneys and physicians and professors as well as architects, engineers, editors, bankers, and even a few economists.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Many listed the title "vice president," and, not a few, "president."
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: But the class of 1975 also includes those who listed their occupations as composer, environmental advocate, musician, playwright, rabbi, conflict resolution coach, painter, community organizer, and essayist.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: And even for those of us with the more conventional job descriptions, the nature of our daily work and its relationship to the economy and society is, I am sure, very different from what we might have guessed in 1975.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: My point is only that you cannot predict your path.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: You can only try to be as prepared as possible for the opportunities, as well as the disappointments, that will come your way.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: For people, as for economies, adaptability and flexibility count for a great deal.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Wherever your path leads, I hope you use your considerable talents and energy in endeavors that engage and excite you and benefit not only yourselves, but also in some measure your country and your world.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts

speaker: Bernanke
text: Today, I wish you and your families a day of joyous celebration.
speech_title: Remarks on Class Day 2008
speech_venue: At Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts
