text: 4 Clearly, the industry needs to better understand the link between compensation and risk management, as in the past those two areas have usually been addressed in isolation.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Generally, investors analyze financial institutions on a risk-adjusted basis, interpreting profits based on the amount of risk taken.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Management at financial firms should do the same thing with regard to their business units and their employees.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: A risk-sensitive compensation framework will help provide the right incentives for employees, and establish a better link between the actions of those employees and the firm's overall risk profile.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Institutions should be particularly sensitive to employee activities that could either directly or indirectly impair access to funding or disrupt liquidity.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Clearly, bank directors have an influential role to play in setting compensation, and they should exercise their authority to establish a more risk-sensitive compensation framework while embedding it in the broader strategic risk management framework of the institution.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Directors should understand the consequences of providing too many short-term and one-sided incentives.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: There are many ways that this risk sensitivity could be accomplished, and it is up to the firms themselves to arrive at solutions.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: One possibility, for example, is to include more types of deferred compensation, since the risks of certain investments or trades may not manifest themselves in the near term.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: It makes sense to try to match the tenor of compensation with the tenor of the risk profile and, thus explicitly, take into account the longer-run performance of the portfolio or division in which the employee operates.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: A good risk-sensitive compensation regime, properly embedded in a strong strategic risk management framework, can bring about changes in behavior so that the firm's employees refrain from taking on risk beyond the firm's stated risk appetite.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Perhaps most importantly, such a compensation regime must give the appropriate incentives to take risks fully into account during good times, when many often underestimate longer-term risks.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Conclusion I have tried to lay out the importance for banking institutions to develop and maintain a strategic risk management framework that fully incorporates all the risks they face--both internal and external--when making choices about what activities and markets in which they will operate.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Indeed, having a corporate strategy that does not include risk management at its core is not really a strategy at all.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Market infrastructure, which affects not only the ways in which firms are connected to each other but also the types of shocks to confidence that they may encounter, is an important external factor that should be taken into account in strategic risk management.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: As a concluding point, I will offer a few comments on one additional area to which banking institutions must pay particular attention: the regulatory and supervisory structure in which banks operate.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Banking is an industry that is subject both to market competition and considerable regulation.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Therefore, banking institutions must not only evaluate potential changes in the competitive financial landscape (as I noted earlier), but must also pay attention to potential changes on the regulatory side.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Over the past year, there have been a number of suggestions for possible statutory changes in U.S. financial services regulation, so bank directors must be prepared for whichever outcomes such changes might imply for the regulatory structure in the United States.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: For example, the Congress may wish to undertake legislative action to effect regulatory changes, or there may be changes to the existing authority and responsibility of certain regulatory bodies.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: In any event, there will likely be some type of adjustments in regulatory structure simply given the changes in the financial services landscape.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Given the fluid situation in which we find ourselves today, bank directors and senior management in their strategic planning have to anticipate a range of potential outcomes in the regulatory sphere in both the short and long term.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Since banking and financial markets are so interconnected, the fundamental transformation in financial services is affecting all types of financial institutions, even those less directly affected by recent events.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: Importantly, in developing strategic risk management frameworks, institutions must not only understand the direct consequences to their own firms of such shifts, but must also recognize that consequences to other firms can have effects on the broader market.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: The heightened importance of funding and liquidity is a clear example of a major change that has far-reaching ramifications and, thus, has to be appropriately addressed in assembling any credible strategic risk management framework in an interconnected world.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner
text: In my remarks, I will use the terms "banks," "banking institutions," and "banking organizations" interchangeably.
speech_title: Strategic Risk Management in an Interconnected World
speech_venue: At the Risk Management Association Annual Risk Management Conference, Baltimore, Maryland

speaker: Kroszner

speaker: Bernanke
text: I appreciate the opportunity to speak at this symposium.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: My remarks will focus on the mortgage securitization process, how it has been affected by the financial crisis, and how it may evolve in response to this crisis.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the United States, as you know, mortgage securitization has been dominated by two government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs), Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, as well as by the combination of the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) and Ginnie Mae.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: By contrast, private-label securitization became a significant presence in mortgage securitization only during the past decade, motivated in part by developments in financial engineering.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The financial crisis has upset the linkage between mortgage borrowers and capital markets and has revealed a number of important problems in our system of mortgage finance, including weaknesses in the structure and oversight of the GSEs and perhaps in the originate-to-distribute model of credit provision itself.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Private-label securitization has largely stopped, and Fannie and Freddie were placed into conservatorship by their regulator after they were judged to be operating in an unsafe and unsound manner.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Our task now is to begin thinking about how to best reestablish a link between homebuyers and capital markets in a way that addresses the weaknesses of the old system.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In light of the central role that the GSEs played, and still play, any such analysis must pay particular attention to how those institutions should evolve.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Mortgage Market and Mortgage Securitization in the Financial Crisis The financial crisis that began in August 2007 has entered its second year.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Its proximate cause was the end of the U.S. housing boom, which revealed serious deficiencies in the underwriting and credit rating of some mortgages, particularly subprime mortgages with adjustable interest rates.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: As subsequent events demonstrated, however, the boom in subprime mortgage lending was only a part of a much broader credit boom characterized by an underpricing of risk, excessive leverage, and the creation of complex and opaque financial instruments that proved fragile under stress.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The unwinding of these developments is the source of the severe financial strain and tight credit that now damp economic growth.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although problems with mortgage origination were not the only cause of the crisis, mortgage markets have been deeply affected.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Banks and thrifts are still making new mortgage loans, but they have tightened terms considerably, essentially closing the private market to borrowers with weaker credit histories.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Importantly, with the securitization market for private-label mortgage-backed securities shut down, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae currently are the only conduits through which mortgages can be securitized and sold to investors.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: By contrast, in 2005, these three entities represented only about 50 percent of the securitization market.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The ability of Fannie, Freddie, and Ginnie to continue to securitize mortgages has largely depended on the confidence of investors that the government stands behind these organizations.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: As such, it was very significant when signs emerged in midsummer that investors were beginning to lose confidence in Fannie and Freddie.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: As investors became increasingly concerned about the capital positions of these companies, the risk increased that they would not be able to roll over their debt as needed to finance their portfolios and purchase new loans.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Eroding investor confidence in the GSEs endangered not only the U.S. mortgage market but the financial system more generally, given the enormous quantities of the companies' debt outstanding in private and public portfolios around the world.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: At the recommendation of the Administration, the Congress subsequently passed a bill that, among other things, created a new and stronger regulator for the GSEs, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), and provided the Treasury with powers to purchase GSE debt and equity.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve worked closely with the FHFA, the Treasury, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to assess the financial condition of Fannie and Freddie, including assessing the capacity of the firms to absorb potential losses stemming from the rapid deterioration evident in single-family mortgages and mortgage-related private-label securities.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The observations of Federal Reserve and OCC staff supported the view of the director of the FHFA that both firms were operating in an unsafe and unsound condition.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In light of these findings, the director of the FHFA placed Fannie and Freddie into conservatorship on September 7.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: At the same time, the Treasury committed to making significant capital and liquidity support available to the GSEs to ensure the continued safety of their senior and subordinated debt and their mortgage-backed securities.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve endorsed those actions as consistent with maintaining financial stability, supporting the housing market, and protecting the taxpayer.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The initial market reactions were positive.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Funding costs for the GSEs declined sharply, as did spreads related to mortgage pricing.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, the process of securitizing conforming mortgages remained robust, and the tens of thousands of investors in GSE debt and mortgage-backed securities have been reassured that their investments are safe.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: More recently, however, markets for GSE debt and mortgages have again come under some stress because of the widespread dislocations in financial markets generally.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Looking beyond the immediate concerns, I agree with Secretary Paulson that the conservatorships of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can usefully be viewed as a "time out"ââone that will give everyone involved, especially the Congress, the opportunity to reconsider the appropriate roles of Fannie and Freddie in the U.S. mortgage market.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Key objectives of that reconsideration include both minimizing systemic risk and putting in place the most efficient mechanism possible for providing the mortgage credit necessary to sustain homeownership and a healthy housing sector.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: To address these issues, we must consider both the part played by securitization in the mortgage market and the role of the government and government-sponsored entities in facilitating securitization.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The ability of financial intermediaries to sell the mortgages they originate into the broader capital market by means of the securitization process serves two important purposes:  First, it provides originators much wider sources of funding than they could obtain through conventional sources, such as retail deposits; second, it substantially reduces the originator's exposure to interest rate, credit, prepayment, and other risks associated with holding mortgages to maturity, thereby reducing the overall costs of providing mortgage credit.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Developing an effective securitization model is not easy--according to one economic historian, mortgage securitization schemes were tried and abandoned at least six times between 1870 and 1940.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: 1 Eventually, experience provided three principles for successful mortgage securitization.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: First, for the ultimate investors to be willing to acquire and trade mortgage-backed securities, they must be persuaded that the credit quality of the underlying mortgages is high and that the origination-to-distribution process is managed so that originators, such as mortgage brokers and bankers, have an incentive to undertake careful underwriting.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Second, because the pools of assets underlying mortgage-backed securities have highly correlated risks, including interest rate, prepayment, and credit risks, the institutions and other investors that hold these securities must have the capacity to manage their risks carefully.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Finally, because mortgage-backed securities are complex amalgamations of underlying mortgages that may themselves be complex to price, transparency about both the underlying assets and the mortgage-backed security itself is essential.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: During the early phases of the development of the subprime mortgage market, most lenders and investors followed these principles.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Investors readily understood the simple senior/subordinated structure, and substantial useful information was provided about the subprime pools.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, during the credit boom period in the United States, worldwide demand for assets of perceived high quality became intense.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Incentives to properly underwrite and evaluate new mortgage credit weakened, and many investors became over-reliant on credit ratings.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: To meet investor demand for customized products, the securities became increasingly complex.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although highly sophisticated methods for sharing risk were developed, not enough attention was paid to the risk that housing markets might turn down sharply across a range of geographical areas.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The rapid rise in early payment defaults in the fall of 2006 signaled that something had gone wrong.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: As investors lost confidence, significant flaws in the securitization process, including inadequate risk management and disclosure as well as excessive complexity, became apparent.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Perhaps the recent mortgage cycle will be remembered as just another failed episode of financial innovation.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: But one feature that makes it different from previous episodes was the relative success of government-sponsored securitization.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac continued to produce and sell significant quantities of mortgage-backed securities to secondary-market investors throughout the period of turmoil.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Their ability to continue to securitize when private firms could not did not appear to result from superior business models or management.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Instead, investors remained willing to accept GSE mortgage-backed securities because they continued to believe that the government stood behind them.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: That experience suggests that, at least under the most stressed conditions, some form of government backstop may be necessary to ensure continued securitization of mortgages.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, as I will discuss, that government support can take many forms.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Future of the GSEs:  Improving Upon the Existing Model?
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: How can we ensure that, in the future, mortgage securitization will be feasible even during highly stressed financial conditions?
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the remainder of my remarks, I will consider some alternative approaches that focus largely, but not exclusively, on the potential role of the GSEs.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: One approach would be to try to return Fannie and Freddie to their pre-conservatorship status.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In considering this possibility, we should remind ourselves of the problems that have surfaced with the traditional GSE structure.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: First, the existing GSE model involves an inherent conflict between the objectives of the companies' private shareholders and the objectives of public policy.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, the GSEs were reluctant earlier this year to raise capital and to expand their operations, even though this would have helped financial and macroeconomic stability at a time of much-reduced mortgage availability.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The GSEs' disinclination to support the mortgage market was motivated by the fact that raising additional capital would have diluted the values of the holdings of the existing private shareholders.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Second, during the past 15 years or so, the GSEs have operated with high leverage compared with other large financial institutions.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: This relative lack of capital ultimately proved their downfall.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Of course, to the extent that the debt of the GSEs is perceived to be guaranteed by the government, it is in the shareholders' interest for the companies to increase leverage whenever possible.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Third, it is also in the shareholders' interest for the GSEs to maximize the size of their portfolios to take advantage of the differential between the returns to mortgage-backed securities and the low GSE funding costs arising from the perceived guarantee.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, as the Federal Reserve has argued for many years, the enormous GSE portfolios pose risks to financial stability.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: As a result of the concerns I just outlined, the Federal Reserve Board in the past has advocated a three-part approach to GSE oversight:  a strong regulator, capital standards adequate for the risks the GSEs assume, and an explicit and measurable public purpose for the GSEs' portfolios.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: 2 Progress has been made in meeting some of these conditions.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 established a strong regulator with the power to establish more-robust capital standards and with some authority over the size of GSE portfolios.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, the law directs the new regulator to establish criteria to ensure that the portfolios are consistent with the mission and safe and sound operations of the enterprises.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, the public purpose of the GSE portfolios, at least during times when financial conditions are relatively normal, has not been fully clarified, and systemic risks will remain as long as the portfolios remain large.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, the recent legislation does not fully resolve the fundamental conflict between private shareholders and public purpose that is the source of many concerns about the GSEs.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Considering some alternative forms for the GSEs (or for mortgage securitization generally) during this "time out" thus seems worthwhile.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Needless to say, however, even if alternative organizational structures are considered for the future, the U.S. government's strong and effective guarantee of the obligations issued under the current GSE structure must be maintained.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Linking the Mortgage Market and the Capital Markets:  Some Alternative Approaches How might the GSEs be reorganized in the future to address the problems that have been revealed with their traditional structure?
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Are there approaches that do not rely on GSEs to create a robust mortgage securitization market that will function in bad times as well as good?
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: One option that has been discussed is to privatize the GSEs and let them compete in the market as private mortgage insurers and securitizers.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: To eliminate the presumption of government support and to stimulate competition, some proposals advocating privatization call for breaking up the companies into smaller units before privatizing them.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Privatization would solve several problems associated with the current GSE model.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: It would eliminate the conflict between private shareholders and public policy and likely diminish the systemic risks as well.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Other benefits are that private entities presumably would be more innovative and efficient than a government agency, and that they could operate with less interference from political interests.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, whether the GSE model is viable without at least implicit government support is an open question.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: From a public policy perspective, a greater concern with fully privatized GSEs is whether mortgage securitization would continue under highly stressed financial conditions.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I have noted, almost no mortgage securitization is occurring today in the absence of a government guarantee.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: So, if the GSEs were privatized, it would seem advisable to retain some means of providing government support to the mortgage securitization process during times of turmoil.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke

speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Incentives to properly underwrite and evaluate new mortgage credit weakened, and many investors became over-reliant on credit ratings.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: To meet investor demand for customized products, the securities became increasingly complex.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although highly sophisticated methods for sharing risk were developed, not enough attention was paid to the risk that housing markets might turn down sharply across a range of geographical areas.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The rapid rise in early payment defaults in the fall of 2006 signaled that something had gone wrong.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: As investors lost confidence, significant flaws in the securitization process, including inadequate risk management and disclosure as well as excessive complexity, became apparent.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Perhaps the recent mortgage cycle will be remembered as just another failed episode of financial innovation.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: But one feature that makes it different from previous episodes was the relative success of government-sponsored securitization.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac continued to produce and sell significant quantities of mortgage-backed securities to secondary-market investors throughout the period of turmoil.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Their ability to continue to securitize when private firms could not did not appear to result from superior business models or management.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Instead, investors remained willing to accept GSE mortgage-backed securities because they continued to believe that the government stood behind them.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: That experience suggests that, at least under the most stressed conditions, some form of government backstop may be necessary to ensure continued securitization of mortgages.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, as I will discuss, that government support can take many forms.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Future of the GSEs:  Improving Upon the Existing Model?
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: How can we ensure that, in the future, mortgage securitization will be feasible even during highly stressed financial conditions?
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the remainder of my remarks, I will consider some alternative approaches that focus largely, but not exclusively, on the potential role of the GSEs.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: One approach would be to try to return Fannie and Freddie to their pre-conservatorship status.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In considering this possibility, we should remind ourselves of the problems that have surfaced with the traditional GSE structure.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: First, the existing GSE model involves an inherent conflict between the objectives of the companies' private shareholders and the objectives of public policy.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, the GSEs were reluctant earlier this year to raise capital and to expand their operations, even though this would have helped financial and macroeconomic stability at a time of much-reduced mortgage availability.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The GSEs' disinclination to support the mortgage market was motivated by the fact that raising additional capital would have diluted the values of the holdings of the existing private shareholders.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Second, during the past 15 years or so, the GSEs have operated with high leverage compared with other large financial institutions.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: This relative lack of capital ultimately proved their downfall.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Of course, to the extent that the debt of the GSEs is perceived to be guaranteed by the government, it is in the shareholders' interest for the companies to increase leverage whenever possible.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Third, it is also in the shareholders' interest for the GSEs to maximize the size of their portfolios to take advantage of the differential between the returns to mortgage-backed securities and the low GSE funding costs arising from the perceived guarantee.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, as the Federal Reserve has argued for many years, the enormous GSE portfolios pose risks to financial stability.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: As a result of the concerns I just outlined, the Federal Reserve Board in the past has advocated a three-part approach to GSE oversight:  a strong regulator, capital standards adequate for the risks the GSEs assume, and an explicit and measurable public purpose for the GSEs' portfolios.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: 2 Progress has been made in meeting some of these conditions.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 established a strong regulator with the power to establish more-robust capital standards and with some authority over the size of GSE portfolios.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, the law directs the new regulator to establish criteria to ensure that the portfolios are consistent with the mission and safe and sound operations of the enterprises.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, the public purpose of the GSE portfolios, at least during times when financial conditions are relatively normal, has not been fully clarified, and systemic risks will remain as long as the portfolios remain large.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, the recent legislation does not fully resolve the fundamental conflict between private shareholders and public purpose that is the source of many concerns about the GSEs.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Considering some alternative forms for the GSEs (or for mortgage securitization generally) during this "time out" thus seems worthwhile.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Needless to say, however, even if alternative organizational structures are considered for the future, the U.S. government's strong and effective guarantee of the obligations issued under the current GSE structure must be maintained.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Linking the Mortgage Market and the Capital Markets:  Some Alternative Approaches How might the GSEs be reorganized in the future to address the problems that have been revealed with their traditional structure?
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Are there approaches that do not rely on GSEs to create a robust mortgage securitization market that will function in bad times as well as good?
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: One option that has been discussed is to privatize the GSEs and let them compete in the market as private mortgage insurers and securitizers.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: To eliminate the presumption of government support and to stimulate competition, some proposals advocating privatization call for breaking up the companies into smaller units before privatizing them.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Privatization would solve several problems associated with the current GSE model.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: It would eliminate the conflict between private shareholders and public policy and likely diminish the systemic risks as well.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Other benefits are that private entities presumably would be more innovative and efficient than a government agency, and that they could operate with less interference from political interests.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, whether the GSE model is viable without at least implicit government support is an open question.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: From a public policy perspective, a greater concern with fully privatized GSEs is whether mortgage securitization would continue under highly stressed financial conditions.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I have noted, almost no mortgage securitization is occurring today in the absence of a government guarantee.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: So, if the GSEs were privatized, it would seem advisable to retain some means of providing government support to the mortgage securitization process during times of turmoil.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: One possible approach, suggested by Federal Reserve Board economists Diana Hancock and Wayne Passmore, is to create a government bond insurer, analogous to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: 3 This new agency would offer, for a premium, government-backed insurance for any form of bond financing used to provide funding to mortgage markets.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, debt and mortgage-backed securities issued by the (privatized) GSEs as well as mortgage-backed bonds issued by banks would be eligible for the guarantee.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: That approach would clearly limit the government's exposure while making the benefits of explicit government support available to the market.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: GSE-type organizations are not essential to successful mortgage financing; indeed, many other industrial countries without GSEs have achieved homeownership rates comparable to that of the United States.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: One device that has been widely used is covered bonds.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Covered bonds are debt obligations issued by financial institutions and secured by a pool of high-quality mortgages or other assets.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Today, covered bonds are the primary source of mortgage funding for European banks, with about $3 trillion outstanding.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: These instruments are subject to extensive statutory and supervisory regulation designed to protect the interests of covered bond investors from the risks of insolvency of the issuing bank.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Legislation typically specifies the types of collateral permitted in the cover pool, defines a minimum over-collateralization level, provides certainty of principal and interest payments to investors in the case of insolvency, and requires disclosures to regulators or investors or both.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, the government generally provides strong assurances to investors by having bank supervisors ensure that the cover pool assets that back the bonds are of high quality and that the cover pool is well managed.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Issuance of covered bonds in Europe has not been unaffected by the financial turmoil, and at times the interest rate spreads relative to government debt have risen.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: But generally speaking, European banks have been able to find buyers for these bonds.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, issuance of covered bonds totaled more than $16 billion in September 2008, although this amount represents a decline of 45 percent from a year earlier.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, interest rate spreads on covered bonds have typically been much narrower than the comparable spreads on senior unsecured debt and mortgage-backed securities.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: This relationship has continued to hold throughout the market turmoil, perhaps because of the comprehensive regulatory and statutory frameworks associated with covered bonds in most European countries.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: To date, not many covered bonds have been issued in the United States, for several reasons.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: First, the Federal Home Loan Banks (FHLB) can tap capital markets and provide cost-effective funding for mortgage assets.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, as a source of financing, covered bond issuance today is not generally competitive with FHLB advances.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Second, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have traditionally securitized U.S. prime mortgage assets.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The GSEs' implicit government backing and their scale of securitization operations have made it difficult for banks to use covered bonds to finance their own prime mortgages.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Third, the United States does not have the extensive statutory and supervisory regulation designed to protect the interests of covered bond investors that exists in European countries.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: To this end, the recent introduction of the FDIC policy statement on covered bonds and the Treasury covered bond framework were constructive steps.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Finally, the cost disadvantage of covered bonds relative to securitization through Fannie and Freddie is increased by the greater capital requirements associated with covered bond issuance.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Covered bonds do help to resolve some of the difficulties associated with the originate-to-distribute model.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The on-balance-sheet nature of covered bonds means that the issuing banks are exposed to the credit quality of the underlying assets, a feature that better aligns the incentives of investors and mortgage lenders than does the originate-to-distribute model of mortgage securitization.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The cover pool assets are typically actively managed--non-performing assets are replaced with similar, but performing assets--ensuring that high-quality assets are in the cover pool at all times and providing a mechanism for loan modifications and workouts.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: The structure used for such bonds tends to be fairly simple and transparent.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: These features, together with the demonstrated success of covered bonds in other countries, make this approach attractive.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: That said, given longstanding features of the U.S. system such as the prominent role of the Federal Home Loan Banks, covered bonds may remain an unattractive option to U.S. banks.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Even closer ties to the government, with or without shareholders.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: A third approach, besides privatization and covered bonds, is to tie the government-sponsored enterprises even more closely to the government.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In doing so, the choice must be made whether to continue to allow an element of private ownership in these organizations.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: A public utility model offers one possibility for incorporating private ownership.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: In such a model, the GSE remains a corporation with shareholders but is overseen by a public board.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Beyond simply monitoring safety and soundness, the regulator would also establish pricing and other rules consistent with a promised rate of return to shareholders.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Public utility regulation itself, of course, has numerous challenges and drawbacks, such as reduced incentives to control costs.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Nor does this model completely eliminate the private-public conflict of the current GSE structure.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: But a public utility model might allow the enterprise to retain some of the flexibility and innovation associated with private-sector enterprises in which management is accountable to its shareholders.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: And, although I have noted the problems associated with private-public conflict, that conflict is not always counterproductive; an entity with private shareholders may be better able to resist political influences, which, under some circumstances, may lead to better market outcomes.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: If private shareholders are excluded, several possibilities worth exploring remain.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: One approach would be to structure a quasi-public corporation without shareholders that would engage in the provision of mortgage insurance generally.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Here, perhaps, one might envision the consolidation of the GSEs and the FHA, with all securitization undertaken by a Ginnie Mae-type organization.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Private mortgage insurers could still participate in this framework, though the role of the government in supporting mortgage insurance and securitization would become more explicit than it is today.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Finally, one might consider cooperative ownership structures, where the originators of mortgages must hold the capital in the government-sponsored enterprises, analogous to the current structure of the Federal Home Loan Banks.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Conclusion Regardless of the organizational form, we must strive to design a housing financing system that ensures the successful funding and securitization of mortgages during times of financial stress but that does not create institutions that pose systemic risks to our financial markets and the economy.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Government likely has a role to play in supporting mortgage securitization, at least during periods of high financial stress.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: But once government guarantees are involved, the problems of systemic risks and contingent taxpayer involvement must be dealt with clearly and credibly.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
speech_venue: At the UC Berkeley/UCLA Symposium: The Mortgage Meltdown, the Economy, and Public Policy, Berkeley, California

speaker: Bernanke
text: Achieving the appropriate balance among these design challenges will be difficult, but it nevertheless must be high on the policy agenda for financial reform.
speech_title: The Future of Mortgage Finance in the United States
