speaker: Kohn
text: As you know, we are in the midst of a global financial crisis that is now weighing heavily on economies around the world.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Although the outlook remains extremely uncertain, both the fragility of the financial system and the weakness in real activity seem likely to persist for a while.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: To promote maximum sustainable economic growth and price stability, the Federal Reserve has responded to this crisis by easing monetary policy markedly, and we have greatly expanded our liquidity facilities to keep credit flowing when private lenders have become reluctant or unable to do so.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Other central banks have also cut policy rates significantly and expanded their lending.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In addition, the federal government and governments around the world have taken extraordinary actions to strengthen financial systems to preserve the ability of households and businesses to borrow and spend.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: The current situation is so severe that it calls for careful review of how such a crisis evolved and how we can prevent a similar situation from happening again.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: This conference is a welcome step in that review, as it asks about the lessons we have learned, particularly for monetary policy, from the collapse of subprime lending and the preceding house-price bubble--developments that contributed importantly to the present financial crisis.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: This morning I would like to reflect on some of what I, in my role as a monetary policy maker, have learned from recent developments in the housing sector and, more broadly, in financial markets as a whole.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In doing so, I will revisit the remarks I made in 2006 in Frankfurt at a festschrift for Otmar Issing.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: 2 There I argued that a central bank facing a possible asset bubble would have to surmount some high hurdles before it would be justified in tightening policy beyond what the outlook for output and inflation would require, after taking into account past and projected asset price developments.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In the aftermath of the collapse of the housing market and in the midst of the ensuing financial and economic turmoil, does that conclusion still hold?
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: More time and study will be needed before we can be confident about the lessons of the current crisis.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: But to foreshadow the remainder of these remarks, based on what we know today, I still have serious questions about whether trying to use monetary policy to check speculative activity on a regular, systematic basis would yield benefits that outweigh its costs.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: I hasten to add that it is evident from the current crisis that much has to change on the regulatory front.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Governments around the world face the challenge of revamping the regulatory structure governing financial markets.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: And changes in this area, I believe, will prove to be the most necessary and effective at reducing the odds on another severe financial crisis.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Today, however, I will focus on some of the lessons of the current crisis for monetary policy.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Alternative Strategies for Addressing Asset Price Bubbles In my 2006 speech, I discussed two different strategies for monetary policy to deal with a possible asset price bubble--the "conventional strategy" and "extra action."
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: A central bank following the conventional strategy does not attempt to use monetary policy to influence the speculative component of asset prices, on the assumption that it has little ability to do so and that any attempt will only result in sub-optimal economic performance in the medium run.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Instead, the central bank responds to asset price movements, whether driven by fundamentals or not, only to the degree that those movements have implications for future output and inflation.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: This conventional strategy conforms to the Federal Reserve's dual mandate under the law and it has been our policy strategy; it also has been consistent with the practices of most inflation-targeting central banks.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: However, some observers have argued for a more activist policy than this one.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Specifically, they have urged central banks, upon perceiving the development of an asset bubble, to take extra action by tightening policy beyond what the conventional strategy would suggest, with the hope of limiting the size of the bubble and thus the fallout from its deflation.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Such a strategy, if successful, could deliver substantial benefits, and a number of central bankers have talked about the need to consider a policy of extra action on occasion, and perhaps have even implemented such a strategy.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: However, taking extra action also would entail some costs, such as creating, for a time, higher unemployment and lower inflation than would otherwise be desired.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In assessing these two alternatives for monetary policy, in the 2006 speech I concluded that a strategy of extra action might be justified if three tough conditions were met.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: First, policymakers must be able to identify bubbles in a timely fashion with reasonable confidence.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Second, a somewhat tighter monetary policy must have a high probability that it will help to check at least some of the speculative activity.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: And third, the expected improvement in future economic performance that would result from the curtailment of the bubble must be sufficiently great.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Of course, we live in an uncertain world, and accordingly policymakers should always be open to the possibility that these conditions might be satisfied and that extra action would be appropriate.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: But my thought at the time was that, in practice, the likelihood of ever meeting the three conditions seemed remote.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In the aftermath of the bursting of the housing bubble, however, the severity of the fallout might seem to call this judgment into question.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: So let's re-examine each of the three conditions and see what the current crisis has taught us.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Potential Gain from Limiting Bubbles Let me start with my third condition, the potential gain from limiting bubbles, because this is where my views have changed the most.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Although I was concerned about the potential fallout from a collapse of the housing market, I think it is fair to say that these costs have turned out to be much greater than I and many other observers imagined.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In particular, I and other observers underestimated the potential for house prices to decline substantially, the degree to which such a decline would create difficulties for homeowners, and, most important, the vulnerability of the broader financial system to these events.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In retrospect, I may have been unduly comforted by the resilience of the U.S. economy to the collapse of the high-tech bubble, to the earlier Russian debt default and failure of Long-Term Capital Management, and even to the commercial and residential real estate debacles of the late 1980s and early 1990s (as difficult as that recovery was).
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: But mopping up after this asset price bubble has turned out to be much harder because of its greater magnitude, the centrality of residential housing and finance to our economy and financial system, and the surprising ways obscure and complex financial transactions have exposed banks and other financial institutions to heavy losses.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In addition, financial and economic linkages across countries have made this crisis truly global in scope, affecting both developed and developing economies.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: As a result of all these factors, the economic disruption here and abroad is likely to be considerably more severe than in past episodes.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: The severe fallout may indicate a larger potential gain than I had anticipated to leaning against excess exuberance in asset markets.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: However, realizing that potential rests on meeting my two other conditions as well--the timely identification of the bubble, and the ability of a central bank to materially influence the trajectory of the speculative component of asset prices.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Identifying Bubbles in a Timely Manner As for the first of the three conditions, events of the past few years, coupled with advances in our understanding of how bubbles form and persist, have made me a little less dubious that policymakers can reliably identify a serious bubble before it bursts.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: However, I am still skeptical about our ability to detect bubbles early enough to make a general policy of leaning against them successful on average.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: The identification of bubbles in real time is tricky because not all the fundamental factors driving asset prices are directly observable; thus, any judgment by a central bank that an asset is overpriced is by nature uncertain.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: My views on this aspect of the identification problem have been reinforced by my experience during the inflation of the housing bubble.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Over the first half of the decade, we saw a sustained, rapid rise in both home values and mortgage debt.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: As this process continued, concern about its sustainability grew and many observers started speculating that a bubble was in place.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: During this period, staff throughout the Federal Reserve System examined whether house prices were overvalued and arrived at a wide range of answers.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: For example, one set of models that linked rental rates and house prices indicated as early as the start of 2004 that the market was significantly overvalued, while another set of models suggested, even as late as December 2005, that house prices could be justified by fundamentals.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: 3 Thus, controversy over the existence of a bubble persisted almost right up to the actual peak in the housing market.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Because the economic consequences of mistakenly responding to a misidentified bubble are substantial, central bankers may be reluctant to take extra action in the face of such uncertainty, especially if they are risk-averse.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Policymakers may also be reluctant to act because a bubble "call" might seem to require them to be more knowledgeable than market participants.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: After all, if at least some market participants perceive the emergence of a bubble, wouldn't they arbitrage that mispricing away?
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Recent research, however, suggests reasons for why market participants who think they know that a bubble exists still may not trade to eliminate it.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: For example, if some market participants recognize the presence of a bubble but do not know how common their knowledge is, they might reasonably expect to make the most profits by riding the bubble for as long as possible, with the goal of trying to sell the asset just before it collapses.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: 4 Other research emphasizes that certain institutional structures--such as secured lending and delegated portfolio management--can create substantial costs in trading against an asset price bubble, so that even market participants who are conscious of the bubble will not find it profitable to trade against it.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: 5 Together, these studies suggest that policymakers may be able to detect bubbles that will not be quickly arbitraged away, thus strengthening the argument for considering extra action.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Nonetheless, even if policymakers are confident that a bubble has emerged, the question of the timeliness of the call remains.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: The essential problem is the timing of the detection of the bubble relative to the timing of its collapse.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: The risk is that the detection and subsequent policy response occur not long before the bubble collapses on its own.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Given the lags associated with monetary policy, the resulting contractionary effects on the economy of the monetary tightening would occur just when the adverse effects of the bubble's collapse are being realized, worsening rather than mitigating the effects of the bubble's collapse.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: And the inevitable lags in detecting bubbles increase the likelihood that, by the time action is taken, speculative activity will have progressed to the point that its collapse is not far off.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Thus, even if we could have known for sure that a housing bubble existed, and that tighter monetary policy would have significantly checked the unwarranted rise in home prices, policymakers would have had to make this call early on--at least a year and probably more before the peak in the real estate market in 2006--for such an action to have been beneficial.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Ability of Monetary Policy to Influence Bubbles This brings me to the remaining condition--the requirement that monetary policy be able to materially check expansions in asset bubbles.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Clearly, interest rates play an important role in determining the fundamental value of corporate equity, houses, and other assets.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: However, I noted in my earlier speech that the influence of interest rates on the speculative component of asset prices is unclear from both a theoretical and empirical standpoint.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: My views on this issue have not changed much, largely because of the still-murky role that monetary policy played in promoting the surge in house prices and the accompanying run-up in both conventional and subprime mortgage debt.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Although tighter monetary policy might have succeeded in shifting down the path of house prices, it is still not clear to what extent small or even moderate policy actions would have discouraged the broader speculative developments that have characterized the current episode:  overly optimistic expectations of price appreciation, excessive leveraging, and a marked increase in risk-taking by homeowners and investors.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Of course, a substantial tightening of policy, leading to a significant slowing in the economy and rise in unemployment, might have had a marked effect on housing price gains.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: But undertaking such a policy course on a regular basis whenever asset price misalignments are detected would likely prove to be a relatively poor strategy on average, especially given the possibility of false positives in identifying these misalignments, and the existence of other potential remedies.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In general, taking more-targeted steps--for example, regulatory changes intended to strengthen the financial system--would seem a better course of action under such circumstances.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: To be sure, some observers contend that the low level of the federal funds rate in 2003 and 2004 was clearly a primary cause of the housing bubble, and that a significantly tighter stance of monetary policy would have been warranted.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: As you know, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), after having sharply lowered its policy rate during the 2001 recession, further lowered the federal funds rate in late 2002 and 2003 in response to an outlook for continued tepid real growth and a possible unwelcome disinflation.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: This accommodative stance helped set the stage for a more robust recovery, and as the expansion took hold in 2004, the FOMC began to tighten in a gradual manner that was publicly signaled in advance.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: How might these monetary policy actions have fueled speculation?
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Perhaps a low policy rate early in the decade, by stimulating housing demand and pushing up the level of home prices, incorrectly led households and lenders to extrapolate these price increases into the indefinite future.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Overly optimistic expectations may have had an unusually stimulative effect on the housing market after 2003 because borrowing constraints were being eased by new financial developments, such as the growth of subprime lending and other nontraditional mortgages, fueled in part by investor demands for the higher yields on complex structured products.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: 7 In addition, the increased use of adjustable-rate mortgages--which are more closely tied to short-term policy rates--may have initially boosted the stimulus from a lower federal funds rate.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: These stories have a certain plausibility, but a closer examination raises questions about monetary policy and the housing and credit bubbles.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Although low short-term interest rates probably supported housing demand and home prices for a time--an effect that helped offset the negative effects on economic growth and employment of the steep decline in business investment--the role of monetary policy in fueling the speculation in real estate is still not clear.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Studies that have tried to address how much monetary policy contributed to the increase in house prices during this period are inconclusive.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: 8 And in general, the channel from interest rates to house prices has not been strongly established empirically, suggesting it might take a very large hike in the federal funds rate to have a substantial effect on real estate values.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: 9 Moreover, if accommodative monetary policy engendered extrapolative expectations and speculation starting in 2003, why did it not restrain these factors after mid-2004 as the federal funds rate was increased?
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Tightening should have limited the extent to which households (especially those using variable-rate mortgages) were able to borrow, thereby slowing the pace of house price appreciation.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Furthermore, many of the worst subprime loans were made after the federal funds rate had normalized, and reflected a wide array of deficiencies in the financial markets.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: The contrasting movement of short-run and long-term interest rates over this period further complicates any assessment of the link between monetary policy and the housing market.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Housing demand and home prices are, presumably, most closely linked to the 30-year fixed mortgage rate and the expected average borrowing rate to be paid over the life of adjustable-rate mortgages.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: That these actual and expected loan rates moved sideways even as the federal funds rate rose suggests that other factors besides monetary policy were at work, especially since the FOMC clearly signaled that it would be returning the funds rate to a normal level over time (albeit at a "measured pace").
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: A good portion of the appreciation in house prices probably is due to the structural changes that were taking place in mortgage financing--specifically, the opening up of subprime lending and the expansion in associated securitization markets with its strong demand for mortgages from investors.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Gauging the effects of expanded subprime lending on house prices is complicated by two-way causality--more lending can drive up house prices, but expected house price increases can also induce more lending.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Undoubtedly, causality did indeed run both directions.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: But studies do indicate that an expansion in credit leads to increased house prices, and suggest that structural changes in mortgage finance likely boosted the rate of house price appreciation.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Another key observation that must be reconciled with any explanation of recent events is that the run-up and subsequent decline in house prices was not limited to the United States; indeed, some countries have experienced even larger swings in house prices.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: 11 In most countries during this period, long-term interest rates were low despite the fact that their central banks did not ease monetary policy as markedly as the Federal Reserve.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: A common factor behind these low rates, and perhaps in part behind the shared increase in house prices as well, is the "global saving glut" identified by Chairman Bernanke--the large amounts of savings, both official and private, from Asian and oil-exporting nations that tended to lower neutral interest rates globally.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In a broader sense, perhaps the underlying cause of the current crisis was complacency.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: With the onset of the "Great Moderation" back in the mid-1980s, households and firms in the United States and elsewhere have enjoyed a long period of reduced output volatility and low and stable inflation.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: These calm conditions may have led many private agents to become less prudent and to underestimate the risks associated with their actions.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: While we cannot be sure about the ultimate sources of the moderation, many observers believe better monetary policy here and abroad was one factor; if so, central banks may have accidentally contributed to the current crisis.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: But would a somewhat tighter stance of policy in recent years have reversed this complacency?
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Central banks would likely have needed to produce recessions of some consequence in order to force agents to reevaluate the costs of taking on risk--an outcome unlikely to improve societal welfare.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Rather than using the blunt tool of monetary policy to induce prudence, we should examine more closely the possibility of using regulation and prudential supervision to address concerns about overleveraging and other risk-taking behavior.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In short, we still do not fully know what caused the run-up in house prices and over-building.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Short-term rates were low in 2002-04 as the Federal Reserve countered the risks it saw to good economic performance, and these low rates  probably had some effect on housing markets at the time.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: But the problems largely built up after policy rates were well on their way to neutral, and other factors appear to have played major roles.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: We have learned little about the likely effect that a somewhat higher funds rate would have had on the speculative element of prices.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Of course, it is important to keep an open mind about the relationship of short-term interest rates and speculative activity.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: If it becomes clear that monetary policy can predictably influence the evolution of bubbles, central banks should take that ability into account when crafting policies intended to keep output rising in line with its potential and inflation low and stable.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Conclusion In sum, I am not convinced that the events of the past few years and the current crisis demonstrate that central banks should switch to trying to check speculative activity through tighter monetary policy whenever they perceive a bubble forming.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: The recent experience may have made us a bit more confident about detecting bubbles, but it has not resolved the problem of doing so in a timely manner.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Nor has it shown that small-to-modest policy actions will reliably and materially damp speculation.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: For these reasons, the case for extra action still remains questionable, despite our having learned that the aftermath of a bubble can be far more painful than we imagined.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Some may object to this assessment, arguing that the current crisis is so bad that, in retrospect, monetary policy should have been appreciably tighter to deflate or forestall the housing boom earlier in the decade, even if that meant a substantially weaker economy.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: This argument has two defects.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: First, monetary policy is made in real time, not with the benefit of hindsight, and any evaluation of competing strategies for the systematic conduct of policy must be grounded in that fact.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Although we must learn from history, we cannot implement policy strategies that assume more information about the future than we can ever have.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Second, even if we ignore the fact that policymakers at the time could not have known what the future held in store if the funds rate followed the path it actually did, we also need to recognize that we cannot be sure what would have happened if policy had taken a different course.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: If policy had tightened appreciably at an early stage of the housing boom, say in mid-2003, it would have done so when the unemployment rate was still rising and inflation seemed poised to move to an undesirably low level.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Such a course of action might well have created its own unforeseen consequences that we might now be ruing.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: This assessment aside, recent events would seem to have some implications for the conduct of monetary policy.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: For example, in light of the demonstrated importance to the real economy of speculative booms and busts (which can take years to play out), central banks probably should always try to look out over a long horizon when evaluating the economic outlook and deliberating about the appropriate accompanying path of the policy rate.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: The Federal Reserve staff has for sometime regularly provided the FOMC with this sort of extended-horizon analysis.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In particular, the staff regularly generates likely paths for the economy over the next five years or so under different economic and policy assumptions; these scenarios often highlight different possibilities for the evolution of prices for homes and other assets.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Note that the focus here is not a single baseline outlook; rather, the emphasis is on exploring the various ways events could play out and the implications for monetary policy.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Another lesson of the current crisis is that central banks need to improve their understanding of the workings of the financial system, its vulnerabilities, and its links to the real economy.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: We must try to find ways to discern more quickly if financial innovation and other factors are leading to a buildup of destabilizing forces, such as rapidly rising asset prices or excessive leverage.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Moreover, the unexpectedly rapid resonance of financial turmoil through global markets signals a need for further study of the complex cross-country linkages among lenders and borrowers, and the ways in which those linkages are influenced by such factors as leverage, interdependent counterparty relationships, and backup liquidity agreements.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Finally, more effort needs to be spent on further investigation of the financial accelerator and other credit-channel effects, given the accumulating evidence that such effects can give rise to an adverse feedback loop between financial markets and the real economy.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn

speaker: Kohn
text: Some of the literature in this area would seem to imply that small policy moves explicitly motivated by a potential bubble, or similarly motivated public statements and regulatory changes, could effectively signal or induce market participants who know about the bubble to trade against it.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Whether such actions would be able to limit the expansion of asset price bubbles merits further research.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Kohn and Sack (2003) did not find that statements by then-Chairman Greenspan on valuations affected misaligned asset prices, but the many warnings from central bankers in financial stability reports and speeches about mispriced risk and even housing bubbles in some countries would seem to provide material for much needed further research on this topic.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: For example, Cardarelli, Igan, and Rebucci (2008) found evidence that house prices have become more sensitive to monetary policy in countries with more mortgage deregulation.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Del Negro and Otrok (2007) find little influence on the national component of house price appreciation from 2001 to 2005.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In contrast, Iacoviello and Neri (2008) contend that monetary policy accounted for more than a quarter of the run-up.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: However, both of these papers only look at the effects of the non-systematic component of monetary policy.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In addition, Iacoviello and Neri include the Regulation Q period in their estimation sample, likely increasing the effect of monetary policy on the housing sector.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Studies of the relationship between house prices, interest rates, and other factors find only a weak interest-sensitivity of home prices to both short-term and long-term interest rates when estimated using aggregate time-series data over the past 25 years, as documented by Gallin (2004) and Campbell, Davis, Gallin, and Martin (2006).
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Mian and Sufi (2008) found that Zip code areas with high latent credit demand prior to the bubble's emergence experienced larger expansions in the supply of mortgage credit and larger increases in house prices, despite being subject to weaker economic conditions; this result also held for Zip codes that, because of inelastic housing supply, would not be expected to see price increases above the inflation rate for construction costs.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Overall, this study attributed 40 percent of the national rise in house prices to increased subprime lending.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Leamer (2007) noted that house price increases occurred in some of the lowest-priced Zip codes.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Wheaton and Nechayev (2008), using results obtained from time series regressions for a number of different housing markets over the period from 1975 to 1998, found a correlation between measures of credit availability and unexplained movements in house prices, which suggests that structural changes in mortgage finance may have contributed to the increase in house prices.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: Finally, Cardarelli, Igan, and Rebucci (2008) found evidence that countries with the most advanced housing finance systems are more exposed to housing sector shocks.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Kohn
text: In addition, housing credit in several other countries appears to have expanded beyond the traditional pool of households in recent years, although probably (comparable data are scarce) to a lesser degree than in the United States.
speech_title: Monetary Policy and Asset Prices Revisited
speech_venue: At the Cato Institute's 26th Annual Monetary Policy Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: It is a privilege for me to be here in Texas, and I would like to thank the Austin Chamber for hosting this luncheon.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Texas economy is strong and diversified, accounting for more than a trillion dollars of output last year.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, our nation, and Texas too, is being tested by economic and financial challenges.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Those challenges and the Federal Reserve's policy responses are the topic of my remarks today.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Federal Reserve Policies during the Crisis As you know, this extraordinary period of financial turbulence is now well into its second year.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Triggered by the contraction of the U.S. housing market that began in 2006 and the associated rise in delinquencies on subprime mortgages, the crisis has become global and is now affecting a wide range of financial institutions, asset classes, and markets.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Constraints on credit availability and slumping asset values have in turn helped to generate a substantial slowing in economic activity.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve's strategy for dealing with the financial crisis and its economic consequences has had three components.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: First, to offset to the extent possible the effects of the crisis on credit conditions and the broader economy, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) has aggressively eased monetary policy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The easing campaign began in September 2007, shortly after the turbulence began, with a cut of 50 basis points in the target for the federal funds rate.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The cumulative reductions in the target rate reached 100 basis points--that is, a full percentage point--by the end of 2007.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: As indications of economic weakness proliferated, the Committee continued to respond, reducing the target rate by an additional 225 basis points by the spring of this year.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: By way of historical comparison, this policy response stands out as exceptionally rapid and proactive.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In taking these actions, we aimed not only to cushion the direct effects of the financial turbulence on the economy, but also to reduce the risk of a so-called adverse feedback loop in which economic weakness exacerbates financial stress, which, in turn, leads to further economic damage.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Unfortunately, despite the support provided by monetary policy, the intensification of the financial turbulence this fall has led to a further deterioration in the economic outlook.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Committee again responded by cutting the target for the federal funds rate an additional 100 basis points in October.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Half of that reduction came as part of an unprecedented coordinated interest rate cut by six major central banks on October 8.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Committee's rapid monetary easing was not without risks.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Some observers expressed concern at the time that these policies would stoke inflation, and, indeed, inflation reached high levels earlier this year, mostly as the result of a surge in the prices of oil and other commodities.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Throughout this period, the Committee remained closely attuned to inflation developments.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Because control of inflation requires that the public's longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored, we paid particularly close attention to indicators of those expectations, as inferred, for example, from financial markets and from surveys of households and businesses.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, the Committee maintained the view that the rapid rise in commodity prices primarily reflected sharply increased demand for raw materials in emerging market economies, in combination with constraints on the supply of these materials, rather than general inflationary pressures.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: We expected that, at some point, global economic growth and the associated growth in the demand for commodities would moderate, which would result in a leveling out of commodity prices, consistent with the predictions of futures markets.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: As you know, commodity prices peaked during the summer and, rather than leveling out, have actually fallen dramatically with the weakening in global economic activity.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: As a consequence, overall inflation appears set to decline significantly over the next year toward levels consistent with price stability.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although monetary easing likely offset some part of the economic effects of the financial turmoil, that offset has been incomplete, as widening credit spreads and more restrictive lending standards have contributed to tight overall financial conditions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, many traditional funding sources for financial institutions and markets have dried up, and banks and other lenders have found their ability to securitize mortgages, auto loans, credit card receivables, student loans, and other forms of credit greatly curtailed.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Consequently, the second component of the Federal Reserve's strategy has been to support the functioning of credit markets and to reduce financial strains by providing liquidity to the private sector--that is, by lending cash or its equivalent secured with relatively illiquid assets.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: To ensure that adequate liquidity is available, consistent with the central bank's traditional role as the liquidity provider of last resort, the Federal Reserve has taken a number of extraordinary steps.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: For instance, to provide banks and other depositories easier access to liquidity, we narrowed the spread of the primary credit rate (the rate at which banks borrow from the Fed's discount window) over the target federal funds rate from 100 basis points to 25 basis points; extended the term for which banks can borrow from the discount window to up to 90 days; and developed a program, called the Term Auction Facility, under which predetermined amounts of credit are auctioned to depository institutions for terms of up to 84 days.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: These innovations resulted in large increases in the amount of Federal Reserve credit extended to the banking system.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Following the funding crises faced by Bear Stearns and other institutions this past spring, we also expanded our liquidity programs to include primary dealers in the government securities market.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: It should be emphasized that the loans that we make to banks and primary dealers through our standing facilities are both overcollateralized and made with recourse to the borrowing firm, which serves to minimize the Federal Reserve's exposure to credit risk.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: To further improve funding conditions, the Federal Reserve has also recently introduced facilities to purchase highly rated commercial paper at a term of three months and to provide backup liquidity for money market mutual funds.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In our globalized financial markets, the provision of dollar liquidity has international as well as domestic aspects.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: To improve dollar funding conditions in important foreign markets, the Federal Reserve has approved bilateral currency swap agreements with 14 foreign central banks.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Swap facilities allow each of the central banks involved to borrow foreign currency from the other; in this case, foreign central banks such as the Bank of Japan, the European Central Bank, the Bank of England, and the Swiss National Bank have borrowed dollars from the Federal Reserve to re-lend to banks in their jurisdictions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Because short-term funding markets are interconnected, the provision of dollar liquidity in major foreign markets eases conditions in dollar funding markets globally, including here in the United States.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Importantly, these swap arrangements pose essentially no credit risk because our counterparties are the foreign central banks themselves, which take responsibility for the extension of dollar credit within their jurisdictions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Judging the effectiveness of the Federal Reserve's liquidity programs is difficult.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Obviously, they have not yet returned private credit markets to normal functioning.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: But I am confident that market functioning would have been more seriously impaired in the absence of our actions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: My reading of the evidence and the reports we have received is that these programs have been helpful in lowering spreads in certain short-term funding markets, enabling financial and nonfinancial businesses to obtain credit that would have been costly or difficult to obtain elsewhere, and allowing a more orderly process of asset sales and the necessary deleveraging by financial institutions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Ultimately, however, market participants themselves must address the fundamental sources of financial strains by raising new capital, restructuring balance sheets, and improving risk management.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: This process is likely to take some time.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve's various liquidity measures should help facilitate that process indirectly by boosting investor confidence and by reducing the risk of severe disruption during the period of adjustment.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Once financial conditions become more normal, the extraordinary provision of liquidity by the Federal Reserve will no longer be needed, and financial institutions will again look to private counterparties, and not central banks, as a source of ongoing funding.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Consistent with the historical mission of the Federal Reserve, the third component of our policy response has been to use all our available tools to promote financial stability, which is essential for healthy economic growth.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: At times, this has required working to preserve the stability of systemically critical financial institutions, so as to avoid further costly disruptions to both the financial system and the broader economy during this extraordinary period.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, the Federal Reserve collaborated with the Treasury to facilitate the acquisition of the investment bank Bear Stearns by JPMorgan Chase and to stabilize the large insurer, American International Group (AIG).
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: We worked with the Treasury and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to put together a package of guarantees, liquidity access, and capital for Citigroup.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Other efforts include our support of the actions by the Federal Housing Finance Agency and the Treasury to place the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac into conservatorship and our work with the FDIC and other bank regulators to assist in the resolution of troubled depositories, such as Wachovia.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In each case, we judged that the failure of the institution in question would have posed substantial risks to the financial system and thus to the economy.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve has worked to promote financial stability through other means as well, such as strengthening the financial infrastructure.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York has led cooperative efforts to improve the clearing and settlement procedures for credit default swaps and other over-the-counter derivatives.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, the Federal Reserve is collaborating with the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to facilitate the development of central counterparties for the trading of credit default swaps.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Properly managed, central counterparties can mitigate the counterparty risk that has proved a source of contagion in the past year.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve's efforts in conjunction with other agencies to prevent the failure of systemically important firms have been controversial at times.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: One view holds that intervening to prevent the failure of a financial firm is counterproductive, because it leads to erosion of market discipline and creates moral hazard.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: As a general matter, I agree that preserving market discipline is extremely important, and, accordingly, the government should intervene in markets only in exceptional circumstances.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, in my view, the failure of a major financial institution at a time when financial markets are already quite fragile poses too great a threat to financial and economic stability to be ignored.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In such cases, intervention is necessary to protect the public interest.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The problems of moral hazard and the existence of institutions that are "too big to fail" must certainly be addressed, but the right way to do this is through regulatory changes, improvements in the financial infrastructure, and other measures that will prevent a situation like this from recurring.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Going forward, reforming the system to enhance stability and to address the problem of "too big to fail" should be a top priority for lawmakers and regulators.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, recent events have revealed a serious weakness of our system: the absence of well-defined procedures and authorities for dealing with the potential failure of a systemically important nonbank financial institution.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the case of federally insured depository institutions, the FDIC has the necessary authority to resolve failing firms; indeed, in situations in which the failure of a firm is judged to pose a systemic risk, the FDIC's powers are quite broad and flexible.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: No comparable framework exists for nondepository financial institutions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve is authorized to lend to nondepositories under unusual and exigent circumstances, but such loans must be backed by collateral sufficient to provide reasonable assurance that they will be repaid; if such collateral is not available, the Fed cannot lend.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: And until recently, the Treasury also did not have the authority to inject capital to prevent the disorderly failure of systemically significant private institutions.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the absence of an appropriate, comprehensive legal or regulatory framework, the Federal Reserve and the Treasury dealt with the cases of Bear Stearns and AIG using the tools available.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: To avoid the failure of Bear Stearns, we facilitated the purchase of Bear Stearns by JPMorgan Chase by means of a Federal Reserve loan, backed by assets of Bear Stearns and a partial guarantee from JPMorgan.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the case of AIG, we judged that emergency Federal Reserve credit would be adequately secured by AIG's assets.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, neither route proved feasible in the case of the investment bank Lehman Brothers.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: No buyer for the firm was forthcoming, and the available collateral fell well short of the amount needed to secure a Federal Reserve loan sufficient to pay off the firm's counterparties and continue operations.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The firm's failure was thus unavoidable, given the legal constraints, and the Federal Reserve and the Treasury had no choice but to try instead to mitigate the fallout from that event.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: Fortunately, we now have tools to address any similar situation that might arise in the future.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: The intensification of the financial crisis this fall made clear that a comprehensive approach involving the fiscal authorities was needed to address more effectively the problems of the financial system.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Greater Austin Chamber of Commerce, Austin, Texas

speaker: Bernanke
text: On that basis, the Administration, with the support of the Federal Reserve, asked the Congress for a new program aimed at stabilizing our financial markets.
speech_title: Federal Reserve Policies in the Financial Crisis
