speaker: Bernanke
text: For almost a year and a half the global financial system has been under extraordinary stress--stress that has now decisively spilled over to the global economy more broadly.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The proximate cause of the crisis was the turn of the housing cycle in the United States and the associated rise in delinquencies on subprime mortgages, which imposed substantial losses on many financial institutions and shook investor confidence in credit markets.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, although the subprime debacle triggered the crisis, the developments in the U.S. mortgage market were only one aspect of a much larger and more encompassing credit boom whose impact transcended the mortgage market to affect many other forms of credit.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Aspects of this broader credit boom included widespread declines in underwriting standards, breakdowns in lending oversight by investors and rating agencies, increased reliance on complex and opaque credit instruments that proved fragile under stress, and unusually low compensation for risk-taking.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The abrupt end of the credit boom has had widespread financial and economic ramifications.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Financial institutions have seen their capital depleted by losses and writedowns and their balance sheets clogged by complex credit products and other illiquid assets of uncertain value.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Rising credit risks and intense risk aversion have pushed credit spreads to unprecedented levels, and markets for securitized assets, except for mortgage securities with government guarantees, have shut down.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Heightened systemic risks, falling asset values, and tightening credit have in turn taken a heavy toll on business and consumer confidence and precipitated a sharp slowing in global economic activity.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The damage, in terms of lost output, lost jobs, and lost wealth, is already substantial.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The global economy will recover, but the timing and strength of the recovery are highly uncertain.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Government policy responses around the world will be critical determinants of the speed and vigor of the recovery.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Today I will offer some thoughts on current and prospective policy responses to the crisis in the United States, with a particular emphasis on actions by the Federal Reserve.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In doing so, I will outline the framework that has guided the Federal Reserve's responses to date.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: I will also explain why I believe that the Fed still has powerful tools at its disposal to fight the financial crisis and the economic downturn, even though the overnight federal funds rate cannot be reduced meaningfully further.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve's Response to the Crisis The Federal Reserve has responded aggressively to the crisis since its emergence in the summer of 2007.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Following a cut in the discount rate (the rate at which the Federal Reserve lends to depository institutions) in August of that year, the Federal Open Market Committee began to ease monetary policy in September 2007, reducing the target for the federal funds rate by 50 basis points.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: 1 As indications of economic weakness proliferated, the Committee continued to respond, bringing down its target for the federal funds rate by a cumulative 325 basis points by the spring of 2008.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In historical comparison, this policy response stands out as exceptionally rapid and proactive.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In taking these actions, we aimed both to cushion the direct effects of the financial turbulence on the economy and to reduce the virulence of the so-called adverse feedback loop, in which economic weakness and financial stress become mutually reinforcing.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: These policy actions helped to support employment and incomes during the first year of the crisis.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Unfortunately, the intensification of the financial turbulence last fall led to further deterioration in the economic outlook.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Committee responded by cutting the target for the federal funds rate an additional 100 basis points last October, with half of that reduction coming as part of an unprecedented coordinated interest rate cut by six major central banks on October 8.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In December the Committee reduced its target further, setting a range of 0 to 25 basis points for the target federal funds rate.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Committee's aggressive monetary easing was not without risks.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: During the early phase of rate reductions, some observers expressed concern that these policy actions would stoke inflation.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: These concerns intensified as inflation reached high levels in mid-2008, mostly reflecting a surge in the prices of oil and other commodities.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Committee takes its responsibility to ensure price stability extremely seriously, and throughout this period it remained closely attuned to developments in inflation and inflation expectations.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, the Committee also maintained the view that the rapid rise in commodity prices in 2008 primarily reflected sharply increased demand for raw materials in emerging market economies, in combination with constraints on the supply of these materials, rather than general inflationary pressures.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Committee members expected that, at some point, global economic growth would moderate, resulting in slower increases in the demand for commodities and a leveling out in their prices--as reflected, for example, in the pattern of futures market prices.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: As you know, commodity prices peaked during the summer and, rather than leveling out, have actually fallen dramatically with the weakening in global economic activity.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: As a consequence, overall inflation has already declined significantly and appears likely to moderate further.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Fed's monetary easing has been reflected in significant declines in a number of lending rates, especially shorter-term rates, thus offsetting to some degree the effects of the financial turmoil on financial conditions.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, that offset has been incomplete, as widening credit spreads, more restrictive lending standards, and credit market dysfunction have worked against the monetary easing and led to tighter financial conditions overall.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, many traditional funding sources for financial institutions and markets have dried up, and banks and other lenders have found their ability to securitize mortgages, auto loans, credit card receivables, student loans, and other forms of credit greatly curtailed.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Thus, in addition to easing monetary policy, the Federal Reserve has worked to support the functioning of credit markets and to reduce financial strains by providing liquidity to the private sector.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In doing so, as I will discuss shortly, the Fed has deployed a number of additional policy tools, some of which were previously in our toolkit and some of which have been created as the need arose.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Beyond the Federal Funds Rate:  The Fed's Policy Toolkit Although the federal funds rate is now close to zero, the Federal Reserve retains a number of policy tools that can be deployed against the crisis.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: One important tool is policy communication.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Even if the overnight rate is close to zero, the Committee should be able to influence longer-term interest rates by informing the public's expectations about the future course of monetary policy.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: To illustrate, in its statement after its December meeting, the Committee expressed the view that economic conditions are likely to warrant an unusually low federal funds rate for some time.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: 2 To the extent that such statements cause the public to lengthen the horizon over which they expect short-term rates to be held at very low levels, they will exert downward pressure on longer-term rates, stimulating aggregate demand.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: It is important, however, that statements of this sort be expressed in conditional fashion--that is, that they link policy expectations to the evolving economic outlook.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: If the public were to perceive a statement about future policy to be unconditional, then long-term rates might fail to respond in the desired fashion should the economic outlook change materially.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Other than policies tied to current and expected future values of the overnight interest rate, the Federal Reserve has--and indeed, has been actively using--a range of policy tools to provide direct support to credit markets and thus to the broader economy.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I will elaborate, I find it useful to divide these tools into three groups.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although these sets of tools differ in important respects, they have one aspect in common:  They all make use of the asset side of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: That is, each involves the Fed's authorities to extend credit or purchase securities.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The first set of tools, which are closely tied to the central bank's traditional role as the lender of last resort, involve the provision of short-term liquidity to sound financial institutions.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Over the course of the crisis, the Fed has taken a number of extraordinary actions to ensure that financial institutions have adequate access to short-term credit.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: These actions include creating new facilities for auctioning credit and making primary securities dealers, as well as banks, eligible to borrow at the Fed's discount window.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: 3 For example, since August 2007 we have lowered the spread between the discount rate and the federal funds rate target from 100 basis points to 25 basis points; increased the term of discount window loans from overnight to 90 days; created the Term Auction Facility, which auctions credit to depository institutions for terms up to three months; put into place the Term Securities Lending Facility, which allows primary dealers to borrow Treasury securities from the Fed against less-liquid collateral; and initiated the Primary Dealer Credit Facility as a source of liquidity for those firms, among other actions.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Because interbank markets are global in scope, the Federal Reserve has also approved bilateral currency swap agreements with 14 foreign central banks.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The swap facilities have allowed these central banks to acquire dollars from the Federal Reserve to lend to banks in their jurisdictions, which has served to ease conditions in dollar funding markets globally.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In most cases, the provision of this dollar liquidity abroad was conducted in tight coordination with the Federal Reserve's own funding auctions.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Importantly, the provision of credit to financial institutions exposes the Federal Reserve to only minimal credit risk; the loans that we make to banks and primary dealers through our various facilities are generally overcollateralized and made with recourse to the borrowing firm.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve has never suffered any losses in the course of its normal lending to banks and, now, to primary dealers.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the case of currency swaps, the foreign central banks are responsible for repayment, not the financial institutions that ultimately receive the funds; moreover, as further security, the Federal Reserve receives an equivalent amount of foreign currency in exchange for the dollars it provides to foreign central banks.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Liquidity provision by the central bank reduces systemic risk by assuring market participants that, should short-term investors begin to lose confidence, financial institutions will be able to meet the resulting demands for cash without resorting to potentially destabilizing fire sales of assets.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, backstopping the liquidity needs of financial institutions reduces funding stresses and, all else equal, should increase the willingness of those institutions to lend and make markets.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: On the other hand, the provision of ample liquidity to banks and primary dealers is no panacea.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Today, concerns about capital, asset quality, and credit risk continue to limit the willingness of many intermediaries to extend credit, even when liquidity is ample.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, providing liquidity to financial institutions does not address directly instability or declining credit availability in critical nonbank markets, such as the commercial paper market or the market for asset-backed securities, both of which normally play major roles in the extension of credit in the United States.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: To address these issues, the Federal Reserve has developed a second set of policy tools, which involve the provision of liquidity directly to borrowers and investors in key credit markets.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Notably, we have introduced facilities to purchase highly rated commercial paper at a term of three months and to provide backup liquidity for money market mutual funds.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, the Federal Reserve and the Treasury have jointly announced a facility that will lend against AAA-rated asset-backed securities collateralized by student loans, auto loans, credit card loans, and loans guaranteed by the Small Business Administration.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve's credit risk exposure in the latter facility will be minimal, because the collateral will be subject to a "haircut" and the Treasury is providing $20 billion of capital as supplementary loss protection.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: We expect this facility to be operational next month.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The rationales and objectives of our various facilities differ, according to the nature of the problem being addressed.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In some cases, as in our programs to backstop money market mutual funds, the purpose of the facility is to serve, once again in classic central bank fashion, as liquidity provider of last resort.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Following a prominent fund's "breaking of the buck"--that is, a decline in its net asset value below par--in September, investors began to withdraw funds in large amounts from money market mutual funds that invest in private instruments such as commercial paper and certificates of deposit.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Fund managers responded by liquidating assets and investing at only the shortest of maturities.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: As the pace of withdrawals increased, both the stability of the money market mutual fund industry and the functioning of the commercial paper market were threatened.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve responded with several programs, including a facility to finance bank purchases of high-quality asset-backed commercial paper from money market mutual funds.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: This facility effectively channeled liquidity to the funds, helping them to meet redemption demands without having to sell assets indiscriminately.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Together with a Treasury program that provided partial insurance to investors in money market mutual funds, these efforts helped stanch the cash outflows from those funds and stabilize the industry.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve's facility to buy high-quality (A1-P1) commercial paper at a term of three months was likewise designed to provide a liquidity backstop, in this case for investors and borrowers in the commercial paper market.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I mentioned, the functioning of that market deteriorated significantly in September, with borrowers finding financing difficult to obtain, and then only at high rates and very short (usually overnight) maturities.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: By serving as a backup source of liquidity for borrowers, the Fed's commercial paper facility was aimed at reducing investor and borrower concerns about "rollover risk," the risk that a borrower could not raise new funds to repay maturing commercial paper.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The reduction of rollover risk, in turn, should increase the willingness of private investors to lend, particularly for terms longer than overnight.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: These various actions appear to have improved the functioning of the commercial paper market, as rates and risk spreads have come down and the average maturities of issuance have increased.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In contrast, our forthcoming asset-backed securities program, a joint effort with the Treasury, is not purely for liquidity provision.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: This facility will provide three-year term loans to investors against AAA-rated securities backed by recently originated consumer and small-business loans.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Unlike our other lending programs, this facility combines Federal Reserve liquidity with capital provided by the Treasury, which allows it to accept some credit risk.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: By providing a combination of capital and liquidity, this facility will effectively substitute public for private balance sheet capacity, in a period of sharp deleveraging and risk aversion in which such capacity appears very short.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: If the program works as planned, it should lead to lower rates and greater availability of consumer and small business credit.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Over time, by increasing market liquidity and stimulating market activity, this facility should also help to revive private lending.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Importantly, if the facility for asset-backed securities proves successful, its basic framework can be expanded to accommodate higher volumes or additional classes of securities as circumstances warrant.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve's third set of policy tools for supporting the functioning of credit markets involves the purchase of longer-term securities for the Fed's portfolio.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, we recently announced plans to purchase up to $100 billion in government-sponsored enterprise (GSE) debt and up to $500 billion in GSE mortgage-backed securities over the next few quarters.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Notably, mortgage rates dropped significantly on the announcement of this program and have fallen further since it went into operation.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Lower mortgage rates should support the housing sector.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Committee is also evaluating the possibility of purchasing longer-term Treasury securities.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In determining whether to proceed with such purchases, the Committee will focus on their potential to improve conditions in private credit markets, such as mortgage markets.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: These three sets of policy tools--lending to financial institutions, providing liquidity directly to key credit markets, and buying longer-term securities--have the common feature that each represents a use of the asset side of the Fed's balance sheet, that is, they all involve lending or the purchase of securities.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The virtue of these policies in the current context is that they allow the Federal Reserve to continue to push down interest rates and ease credit conditions in a range of markets, despite the fact that the federal funds rate is close to its zero lower bound.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Credit Easing versus Quantitative Easing The Federal Reserve's approach to supporting credit markets is conceptually distinct from quantitative easing (QE), the policy approach used by the Bank of Japan from 2001 to 2006.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Our approach--which could be described as "credit easing"--resembles quantitative easing in one respect:  It involves an expansion of the central bank's balance sheet.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, in a pure QE regime, the focus of policy is the quantity of bank reserves, which are liabilities of the central bank; the composition of loans and securities on the asset side of the central bank's balance sheet is incidental.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Indeed, although the Bank of Japan's policy approach during the QE period was quite multifaceted, the overall stance of its policy was gauged primarily in terms of its target for bank reserves.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In contrast, the Federal Reserve's credit easing approach focuses on the mix of loans and securities that it holds and on how this composition of assets affects credit conditions for households and businesses.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: This difference does not reflect any doctrinal disagreement with the Japanese approach, but rather the differences in financial and economic conditions between the two episodes.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, credit spreads are much wider and credit markets more dysfunctional in the United States today than was the case during the Japanese experiment with quantitative easing.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: To stimulate aggregate demand in the current environment, the Federal Reserve must focus its policies on reducing those spreads and improving the functioning of private credit markets more generally.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The stimulative effect of the Federal Reserve's credit easing policies depends sensitively on the particular mix of lending programs and securities purchases that it undertakes.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: When markets are illiquid and private arbitrage is impaired by balance sheet constraints and other factors, as at present, one dollar of longer-term securities purchases is unlikely to have the same impact on financial markets and the economy as a dollar of lending to banks, which has in turn a different effect than a dollar of lending to support the commercial paper market.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Because various types of lending have heterogeneous effects, the stance of Fed policy in the current regime--in contrast to a QE regime--is not easily summarized by a single number, such as the quantity of excess reserves or the size of the monetary base.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, the usage of Federal Reserve credit is determined in large part by borrower needs and thus will tend to increase when market conditions worsen and decline when market conditions improve.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Setting a target for the size of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet, as in a QE regime, could thus have the perverse effect of forcing the Fed to tighten the terms and availability of its lending at times when market conditions were worsening, and vice versa.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The lack of a simple summary measure or policy target poses an important communications challenge.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: To minimize market uncertainty and achieve the maximum effect of its policies, the Federal Reserve is committed to providing the public as much information as possible about the uses of its balance sheet, plans regarding future uses of its balance sheet, and the criteria on which the relevant decisions are based.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Exit Strategy Some observers have expressed the concern that, by expanding its balance sheet, the Federal Reserve is effectively printing money, an action that will ultimately be inflationary.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Fed's lending activities have indeed resulted in a large increase in the excess reserves held by banks.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Bank reserves, together with currency, make up the narrowest definition of money, the monetary base; as you would expect, this measure of money has risen significantly as the Fed's balance sheet has expanded.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, banks are choosing to leave the great bulk of their excess reserves idle, in most cases on deposit with the Fed.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Consequently, the rates of growth of broader monetary aggregates, such as M1 and M2, have been much lower than that of the monetary base.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: At this point, with global economic activity weak and commodity prices at low levels, we see little risk of inflation in the near term; indeed, we expect inflation to continue to moderate.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, at some point, when credit markets and the economy have begun to recover, the Federal Reserve will have to unwind its various lending programs.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: To some extent, this unwinding will happen automatically, as improvements in credit markets should reduce the need to use Fed facilities.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Indeed, where possible we have tried to set lending rates and margins at levels that are likely to be increasingly unattractive to borrowers as financial conditions normalize.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, some programs--those authorized under the Federal Reserve's so-called 13(3) authority, which requires a finding that conditions in financial markets are "unusual and exigent"--will by law have to be eliminated once credit market conditions substantially normalize.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, as the unwinding of the Fed's various programs effectively constitutes a tightening of policy, the principal factor determining the timing and pace of that process will be the Committee's assessment of the condition of credit markets and the prospects for the economy.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: As lending programs are scaled back, the size of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet will decline, implying a reduction in excess reserves and the monetary base.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: A significant shrinking of the balance sheet can be accomplished relatively quickly, as a substantial portion of the assets that the Federal Reserve holds--including loans to financial institutions, currency swaps, and purchases of commercial paper--are short-term in nature and can simply be allowed to run off as the various programs and facilities are scaled back or shut down.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: As the size of the balance sheet and the quantity of excess reserves in the system decline, the Federal Reserve will be able to return to its traditional means of making monetary policy--namely, by setting a target for the federal funds rate.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although a large portion of Federal Reserve assets are short-term in nature, we do hold or expect to hold significant quantities of longer-term assets, such as the mortgage-backed securities that we will buy over the next two quarters.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although longer-term securities can also be sold, of course, we would not anticipate disposing of more than a small portion of these assets in the near term, which will slow the rate at which our balance sheet can shrink.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: We are monitoring the maturity composition of our balance sheet closely and do not expect a significant problem in reducing our balance sheet to the extent necessary at the appropriate time.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Importantly, the management of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet and the conduct of monetary policy in the future will be made easier by the recent congressional action to give the Fed the authority to pay interest on bank reserves.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In principle, the interest rate the Fed pays on bank reserves should set a floor on the overnight interest rate, as banks should be unwilling to lend reserves at a rate lower than they can receive from the Fed.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In practice, the federal funds rate has fallen somewhat below the interest rate on reserves in recent months, reflecting the very high volume of excess reserves, the inexperience of banks with the new regime, and other factors.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, as excess reserves decline, financial conditions normalize, and banks adapt to the new regime, we expect the interest rate paid on reserves to become an effective instrument for controlling the federal funds rate.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, other tools are available or can be developed to improve control of the federal funds rate during the exit stage.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, the Treasury could resume its recent practice of issuing supplementary financing bills and placing the funds with the Federal Reserve; the issuance of these bills effectively drains reserves from the banking system, improving monetary control.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Longer-term assets can be financed through repurchase agreements and other methods, which also drain reserves from the system.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In considering whether to create or expand its programs, the Federal Reserve will carefully weigh the implications for the exit strategy.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: And we will take all necessary actions to ensure that the unwinding of our programs is accomplished smoothly and in a timely way, consistent with meeting our obligation to foster full employment and price stability.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Stabilizing the Financial System The Federal Reserve will do its part to promote economic recovery, but other policy measures will be needed as well.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The incoming Administration and the Congress are currently discussing a substantial fiscal package that, if enacted, could provide a significant boost to economic activity.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In my view, however, fiscal actions are unlikely to promote a lasting recovery unless they are accompanied by strong measures to further stabilize and strengthen the financial system.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: History demonstrates conclusively that a modern economy cannot grow if its financial system is not operating effectively.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the United States, a number of important steps have already been taken to promote financial stability, including the Treasury's injection of about $250 billion of capital into banking organizations, a substantial expansion of guarantees for bank liabilities by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Fed's various liquidity programs.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Those measures, together with analogous actions in many other countries, likely prevented a global financial meltdown in the fall that, had it occurred, would have left the global economy in far worse condition than it is in today.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, with the worsening of the economy's growth prospects, continued credit losses and asset markdowns may maintain for a time the pressure on the capital and balance sheet capacities of financial institutions.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Consequently, more capital injections and guarantees may become necessary to ensure stability and the normalization of credit markets.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: A continuing barrier to private investment in financial institutions is the large quantity of troubled, hard-to-value assets that remain on institutions' balance sheets.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The presence of these assets significantly increases uncertainty about the underlying value of these institutions and may inhibit both new private investment and new lending.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Should the Treasury decide to supplement injections of capital by removing troubled assets from institutions' balance sheets, as was initially proposed for the U.S. financial rescue plan, several approaches might be considered.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Public purchases of troubled assets are one possibility.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Another is to provide asset guarantees, under which the government would agree to absorb, presumably in exchange for warrants or some other form of compensation, part of the prospective losses on specified portfolios of troubled assets held by banks.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Yet another approach would be to set up and capitalize so-called bad banks, which would purchase assets from financial institutions in exchange for cash and equity in the bad bank.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: These methods are similar from an economic perspective, though they would have somewhat different operational and accounting implications.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, efforts to reduce preventable foreclosures, among other benefits, could strengthen the housing market and reduce mortgage losses, thereby increasing financial stability.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The public in many countries is understandably concerned by the commitment of substantial government resources to aid the financial industry when other industries receive little or no assistance.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: This disparate treatment, unappealing as it is, appears unavoidable.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Our economic system is critically dependent on the free flow of credit, and the consequences for the broader economy of financial instability are thus powerful and quickly felt.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Indeed, the destructive effects of financial instability on jobs and growth are already evident worldwide.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Responsible policymakers must therefore do what they can to communicate to their constituencies why financial stabilization is essential for economic recovery and is therefore in the broader public interest.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Even as we strive to stabilize financial markets and institutions worldwide, however, we also owe the public near-term, concrete actions to limit the probability and severity of future crises.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: We need stronger supervisory and regulatory systems under which gaps and unnecessary duplication in coverage are eliminated, lines of supervisory authority and responsibility are clarified, and oversight powers are adequate to curb excessive leverage and risk-taking.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In light of the multinational character of the largest financial firms and the globalization of financial markets more generally, regulatory oversight should be coordinated internationally to the greatest extent possible.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: We must continue our ongoing work to strengthen the financial infrastructure--for example, by encouraging the migration of trading in credit default swaps and other derivatives to central counterparties and exchanges.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The supervisory authorities should develop the capacity for increased surveillance of the financial system as a whole, rather than focusing excessively on the condition of individual firms in isolation; and we should revisit capital regulations, accounting rules, and other aspects of the regulatory regime to ensure that they do not induce excessive procyclicality in the financial system and the economy.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: As we proceed with regulatory reform, however, we must take care not to take actions that forfeit the economic benefits of financial innovation and market discipline.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Particularly pressing is the need to address the problem of financial institutions that are deemed "too big to fail."
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: It is unacceptable that large firms that the government is now compelled to support to preserve financial stability were among the greatest risk-takers during the boom period.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The existence of too-big-to-fail firms also violates the presumption of a level playing field among financial institutions.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the future, financial firms of any type whose failure would pose a systemic risk must accept especially close regulatory scrutiny of their risk-taking.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Also urgently needed in the United States is a new set of procedures for resolving failing nonbank institutions deemed systemically critical, analogous to the rules and powers that currently exist for resolving banks under the so-called systemic risk exception.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Conclusion The world today faces both short-term and long-term challenges.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the near term, the highest priority is to promote a global economic recovery.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve retains powerful policy tools and will use them aggressively to help achieve this objective.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Fiscal policy can stimulate economic activity, but a sustained recovery will also require a comprehensive plan to stabilize the financial system and restore normal flows of credit.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Despite the understandable focus on the near term, we do not have the luxury of postponing work on longer-term issues.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: High on the list, in light of recent events, are strengthening regulatory oversight and improving the capacity of both the private sector and regulators to detect and manage risk.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: Finally, a clear lesson of the recent period is that the world is too interconnected for nations to go it alone in their economic, financial, and regulatory policies.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: International cooperation is thus essential if we are to address the crisis successfully and provide the basis for a healthy, sustained recovery.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speaker: Bernanke
text: A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point.
speech_title: The Crisis and the Policy Response
speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England

speech_venue: At the Stamp Lecture, London School of Economics, London, England
