speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Community banks serve businesses and consumers throughout the country, in both rural and urban areas.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: They are a leading provider of credit to small businesses, a key source of job creation in this country.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the decades leading up to the current crisis, the nature of lending had changed dramatically, with greater industry consolidation, increased economies of scale and scope, and a larger portion of credit being supplied by nonbanks.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: While such changes challenged community bankers, your institutions have remained vitally important.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Indeed, during the current crisis, some data show recent increases in loan and deposit balances at community banks, while such balances are generally flat or even decreasing at the largest banks.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: The various efforts that the Federal Reserve has taken to provide backup liquidity to financial firms and to improve the functioning of financial markets have, I believe, helped all segments of the financial system, including the community banking sector, and the economy more generally.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Helping community banks also helps the local communities that they serve.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: One important way that community banks may assist their communities is by working with at-risk homeowners to avoid preventable foreclosures.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Foreclosures can result in clusters of vacant properties, which in turn can foster crime, stretch municipal resources at a time of weakening revenue, and lead to lower house prices throughout the neighborhood.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: These are some of the reasons why the Federal Reserve, along with the other U.S. banking agencies, has encouraged banks to participate in the Making Home Affordable loan modification program established by the Treasury.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: While continuing challenges remain, opportunities also exist for community banks.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: In some instances, community banks are able to step in at crucial moments when local businesses or consumers have been unable to find credit elsewhere.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Indeed, as some banks have chosen to cut back on lending to conserve capital and liquidity, community banks in strong financial condition may find that they can gain creditworthy customers even in today's economic environment.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Such community banks also may find opportunities to reclaim customers and business from nonbank lenders who have drawn back as the securitization markets have encountered difficulties.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Community banks are able to respond promptly in such cases because of their in-depth knowledge of their markets, their locally focused management teams and boards, and their commitment to tailoring unique credit products for individual borrowers and businesses.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Addressing the "Too Big to Fail" Problem Many of you likely are frustrated, and rightfully so, by the impact that the financial crisis and economic downturn has had on your banks, as well as on the reputation of bankers more generally.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: You may well have built your reputations and institutions through responsible lending and community-focused operations, but nonetheless, you now find yourselves facing higher deposit insurance assessments and increasing public skepticism about the behavior of bankers--outcomes that you perceive were largely caused by the actions of larger financial institutions.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Many of you managed your businesses prudently and shunned more exotic instruments and activities.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: And many of your customers--households and businesses--avoided excesses and are able to meet their financial commitments on a timely basis.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: No doubt this frustration has been heightened by the problems caused by financial firms that are too big or too interconnected to fail.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Indeed, the too-big-to-fail issue has emerged as an enormous problem, both for policymakers and for financial institutions generally.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Creditors of a firm perceived as too big to fail have less incentive to monitor and restrict the firm's risk-taking through adjustments to the price at which they lend money to the firm.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: If left unaddressed, this weakening of market discipline creates an unlevel playing field for smaller institutions, which may not be able to raise funds as cheaply, even if their individual risk profiles are better, or at least no worse, than those of their larger competitors.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: The erosion in market discipline distorts market behavior and can give firms an incentive to grow--either internally or through acquisitions--in order to be perceived as too big to fail.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Government rescues to prevent the failure of major financial institutions also have required large amounts of public resources.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: These actions have involved extremely unpleasant and difficult choices, but given the interconnected nature of our financial system and the potentially devastating effects on confidence, financial markets, and the broader economy that would likely arise from the disorderly failure of a major financial firm in the current environment, I do not think we have had a realistic alternative to preventing such failures.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: That said, these episodes have shown clearly that the problem of too-big-to-fail is extremely serious.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: To address this issue, which should be a top priority for financial reform, policymakers will need to act on several fronts.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: First, supervisors--as we are already doing--must vigorously address the weaknesses at major financial institutions with regard to capital adequacy, liquidity management, and risk management.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Firms whose failure would pose a systemic risk must receive especially close supervisory oversight and be held to the highest prudential standards.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Aside from its direct benefits for the safety and soundness of these large institutions, such an approach also would help offset financial firms' incentive to grow until they are perceived to be too big to fail.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Second, supervisors must pay close attention to compensation practices that can create mismatches between the rewards and risks borne by institutions or their managers.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: As the Federal Reserve and other banking agencies have noted, poorly designed compensation policies can create perverse incentives that can ultimately jeopardize the health of the banking organization.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Management compensation policies should be aligned with the long-term prudential interests of the institution, be tied to the risks being borne by the organization, provide appropriate incentives for safe and sound behavior, and avoid short-term payments for transactions with long-term horizons.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Third, as the recent financial crisis has highlighted, risks to the financial system may arise not only in the banking sector, but also from financial firms that traditionally have been outside the regulatory and supervisory framework applied to banking organizations.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Under federal law, all banking organizations--regardless of size--are subject to consolidated supervision for safety and soundness purposes.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: At a minimum, policymakers must ensure that a similar statutory framework is put in place for all systemically important financial firms organized as holding companies.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: The agencies responsible for implementing this framework also must vigorously exercise their authority to help ensure the safety and soundness of nonbank firms whose failure could threaten the stability of the financial system.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Broad-based application of the principle of consolidated supervision would also serve to eliminate gaps in oversight that would otherwise allow risk-taking to migrate from more-regulated to less-regulated sectors.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Fourth, continued strong and concerted efforts are needed to improve the financial infrastructure--or "plumbing"--that supports the trading, payments, clearing, and settlement activities that are so critical to the functioning of the financial system.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: I have described elsewhere the various steps that the Federal Reserve is taking in coordination with other supervisors and market participants to improve the resiliency of over-the-counter derivative markets and the market for triparty repurchase agreements.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: 4 Improvements in these areas should reduce the likelihood that the failure of any individual institution would have substantial spillover effects on other financial institutions or the broader markets, and thereby make it less likely that the government would need to intervene.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Finally, an important element of addressing the too-big-to-fail problem is the development of an improved resolution regime in the United States that permits the orderly resolution of a systemically important nonbank financial firm.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: We have such a regime for insured depository institutions, but it is clear we need something similar for systemically important nonbank financial entities.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Improved resolution procedures for these firms would help reduce the too-big-to-fail problem by giving the government the option of safely winding down a systemically important firm rather than keeping it operating.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Reducing Procyclicality in the Financial System In the current environment, financial institutions of all sizes are trying to meet the needs of creditworthy borrowers while at the same time maintaining sufficient capital and other resources to weather the ongoing crisis.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Capital rules, accounting policies, and other regulatory standards should not make this job even more difficult by encouraging excessively procyclical behavior by financial institutions--that is, behavior that causes financial institutions to tighten credit in downturns and ease credit in booms more than is justified by changes in the creditworthiness of borrowers.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: No one questions the underlying objectives of capital rules and accounting standards, which are to ensure the safety and soundness of financial institutions and to accurately and transparently disclose an institution's financial condition, respectively.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, some aspects of existing capital rules and accounting standards may unduly magnify the ups and downs in the financial system and the economy.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, the capital rules require banks to maintain capital ratios that meet or exceed fixed minimum standards.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Because banks typically find raising capital to be difficult in economic downturns or periods of financial stress, their best means of boosting regulatory capital ratios during difficult periods may be to reduce new lending, perhaps more so than is justified by the credit environment.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, as many institutions and auditors will attest, determining the appropriate valuation of illiquid or idiosyncratic assets can be very challenging, especially in highly strained market conditions.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: The economic downturn also has renewed the debate concerning the appropriate levels of loan loss reserves over the cycle.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Institutions themselves often try to offset the potential for procyclicality in capital levels by maintaining strong capital buffers to absorb swings in regulatory capital requirements.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: This type of action is in line with supervisory expectations that call for banking organizations to be able to assess their overall capital needs and hold capital commensurate with their individual risk profiles--beyond complying with minimum regulatory capital requirements.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Most community bankers understand this point.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Your institutions generally hold capital in excess of minimum regulatory requirements--sometimes well in excess.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Nonetheless, the issues surrounding procyclicality are not easy, and their consideration will require a careful balancing of important public policy interests.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Policymakers should review existing capital rules and accounting standards to determine whether these rules and standards could be modified to reduce their potential to have unduly procyclical effects without weakening their ability to achieve their fundamental objectives.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: I'm pleased to note that the Basel Committee and the Financial Stability Forum already have work under way to address excessive procyclicality in capital regulations, and that the Financial Accounting Standards Board is issuing new guidance that relates to mark-to-market accounting in inactive markets and other-than-temporary impairments.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Conclusion I want to conclude by encouraging you as community bankers to operate prudently in the current environment, but not to let fear drive your decisions.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: You should all continue to exercise good risk management--including strong underwriting for individual exposures and proper management of credit concentrations in your portfolios.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: You should also be certain that any deterioration in asset quality and borrowers' conditions are accurately identified, measured, and managed.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: And you should take steps to maintain a strong financial condition with sufficient capital and liquidity levels as preparation for any future economic and financial uncertainty.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: By doing so, you can ensure that your institutions can continue to provide a steady and consistent source of credit to businesses and borrowers for years to come.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: If community banks are prudent but opportunistic in extending credit to strong borrowers, they will help the economy recover while benefiting from that recovery themselves.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: Primary dealers are broker-dealers that trade in U.S. government securities with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Bernanke
text: The New York Fed's Open Market Desk engages in trades on behalf of the Federal Reserve System to implement monetary policy.
speech_title: The Financial Crisis and Community Banking
speech_venue: At the Independent Community Bankers of America's National Convention and Techworld, Phoenix, Arizona

speaker: Duke
text: My time as a commercial banker spanned numerous business cycles.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: It also encompassed at least one severe financial system crisis, in the late 1980s through the early 1990s, albeit one that was not as severe as the current one.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: From my time as a commercial banker, I already understood the factors considered by bankers in the initial lending decision as well as those in loss mitigation when collecting those same loans.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: As a central banker, I have come to appreciate even more fully the role of credit in our economic well-being.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: So I thought it would be appropriate for me to provide my perspective on credit conditions in our economy and the current crisis.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Today, I would like to discuss a three-dimensional view of the flow of credit to households and businesses and describe the evolving role of banks in the U.S. economy.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: I will begin by taking a look at recent trends in aggregate borrowing by households and by the nonfinancial business sector.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: These trends will be placed in a historical context by looking back at previous booms and busts in the credit cycle.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: One might call this the "macroeconomic view" of credit.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: When looking at aggregate borrowing, it is important to remember that a change in debt outstanding can be driven by any one of three factors or, more commonly, a combination of all three.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In the macroeconomic view of credit, I will discuss indicators related to changes in demand for credit.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: I will also examine two determinants of the supply of credit.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The first determinant relates to lenders' assessment of the creditworthiness of borrowers given future economic conditions.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The second relates to credit constraints caused by the financial condition of the lenders.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Although fiscal and monetary policies that improve macroeconomic conditions will also boost the demand for credit and improve the creditworthiness of borrowers, if credit is constrained by the balance sheets of the banks, only programs to relieve such strain will improve credit availability.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: This condition is the reason for the injections of capital into banks through the Troubled Asset Relief Program, or TARP, and the financing provisions offered through the Public-Private Investment Program, or PPIP, as well as the expansion of Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) deposit and nondeposit guarantee programs.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Next, I will consider the providers of credit.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Using the Federal Reserve's flow of funds data, I will look at the evolution from 1950 to 2008 in the market shares of financial intermediation for banks, thrifts, insurance companies, and "other" firms, which range from finance companies to the entities that issue asset-backed securities (ABS).
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Although these data could suggest that the importance of banks has significantly diminished, I will argue that it matters how we measure what banks have been doing.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In particular, it is important to take into account the off-balance-sheet activities of banks when securitization became more pervasive and when it abruptly stopped.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: This "financial intermediation view" of credit, in my opinion, illustrates the importance of supporting the availability of all forms of lending, whether it be on-balance-sheet lending by banks, credit originated by banks and securitized and sold to investors, or credit supplied by nonbank lenders.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The Federal Reserve has long served as a lender to banks, providing them with liquidity to maintain lending in times of stress.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Over the past year and a half, however, the Federal Reserve has greatly expanded its provision of liquidity, establishing facilities under which we auction term funding to banks on a secured basis, provide liquidity to primary dealers and money market mutual funds, and supply credit to issuers of commercial paper.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In addition, through our purchases of agency debt and mortgage-backed securities, the Federal Reserve is lowering the cost of borrowing for mortgages as well as creating an outlet for loans that are originated by banks and nonbanks and securitized by the agencies.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: 1 Most recently, the Federal Reserve, in conjunction with the Treasury, has established the Term Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility, or TALF, which uses capital provided by the Treasury in combination with liquidity provided by the Federal Reserve to enhance the availability of credit to households and businesses.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Because banks remain central to financial intermediation, they deserve a closer look, particularly during this time of financial-sector turmoil.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In my discussion of the "banking view" of credit, I will summarize the current state of the banking industry.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: As you know, banks play a special role in just about every economy in the world, and the United States is no exception.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Banks' liabilities are generally more liquid than their assets.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: They are also the main repositories of deposits, which provide immediately available liquidity to households and businesses and are used to undertake transactions for goods and services.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In addition, banks provide intermediation between borrowers and savers.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Indeed, banks remain the principal source of finance for a large part of the economy.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Given these important and distinctive functions, it is, perhaps, obvious that adverse shocks to the financial system and the banking industry can have detrimental effects on economic activity.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The current financial turbulence, like several similar events in the past, has placed severe strains on the U.S. banking system with serious repercussions for the economy as a whole.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The "Macroeconomic View" of Credit Looking back over the past 50 years or so, credit extended to households and businesses has almost always declined just before, and during, economic downturns.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: And almost as often, a debate has ensued about whether the nation was in a "credit crunch."
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: 2 According to the White House Council of Economic Advisers, "a credit crunch occurs when the supply of credit is restricted below the range usually identified with prevailing market interest rates and the profitability of investment projects."
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: 3 Judging whether a credit crunch is happening in real time is not easy.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: It is extremely difficult to sort out the relative importance on the flow of credit of reduced demand due to weaker economic activity, reduced supply because borrowers appear less creditworthy, or reduced supply because lenders face pressures, such as a shortage of capital, that restrain them from extending credit.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In other words, while demand considerations could certainly result in a decline in credit flows, a reduction in the supply of credit--caused either by bank balance sheet pressures or by banks reluctant to lend to less-creditworthy borrowers--could produce the same result.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Figure 1 presents annualized quarterly percent changes in debt growth for home mortgages in the United States from 1952 to 2008, with shaded areas denoting National Bureau of Economic Research recession periods.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Strikingly, the quarterly rate of growth for home mortgage debt, which includes mortgages and drawn-upon home equity lines, has typically declined before and during each recession and then picked up when economic conditions improved.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: What is different this time around is the runoff in home mortgage debt: It declined in the fourth quarter for the first time in more than 50 years.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The recent decline in mortgage debt was likely partly driven by weaker demand for housing amid rising unemployment and rapidly falling home prices.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: It is equally likely that supply-side considerations have played a role.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: First, the run-up in mortgage delinquency rates and the higher loss rates associated with reductions in collateral values indicate that the creditworthiness of borrowers has declined.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The unprecedented increase in mortgage defaults has resulted in more foreclosures and tighter mortgage lending terms, which are shown from 1990 onward in figure 2 .
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Although the net fraction of banks tightening lending standards on mortgage loans was about 50 percent in our most recent Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey on Bank Lending Practices, it should be noted that most banks had already tightened their lending standards substantially in 2008.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Second, the shutdown of the private mortgage-backed securities market has placed greater pressures on bank balance sheets not only to provide credit to borrowers with damaged credit histories, but also to provide so-called jumbo mortgages that are originated in amounts that are over the conforming loan limits applicable to loans sold to or guaranteed by the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and by Ginnie Mae.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Of course, credit provision to some borrowers was helped through mortgage insurance programs offered by the Federal Housing Administration, which were recently expanded by the Congress through increases in coverage levels.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Similarly, other borrowers have been able to qualify for mortgages that became eligible for securitizations by the GSEs because of increases in conforming loan limits.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Indeed, as the non-agency mortgage-backed security market contracted by roughly 15 percent in 2008, Ginnie Mae increased its outstanding supply of single-family mortgage-backed securities by roughly 33 percent.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Even with the growth of such securitizations, banks still needed to expend some balance sheet capacity to warehouse loans on their books prior to securitization.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In response to these supply-side developments, the Treasury, the FDIC, and the Federal Reserve have encouraged banks to work with existing borrowers to avoid preventable foreclosures.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: 5 The Federal Reserve and the other banking agencies also have encouraged banking organizations to participate in the Treasury's Home Affordable Modification Program.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: 6 Doing so should help to stem the runoff in mortgage debt and to damp the added downward pressure on house prices that can occur when neighborhoods have clusters of foreclosed properties.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In addition, the Treasury's Capital Assistance Program, the FDIC's Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program, and the Federal Reserve's programs to provide liquidity are intended to help ease the funding and balance sheet pressures banking organizations face, thereby allowing them to undertake responsible lending activities, including new mortgage originations.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: I will now turn to nonmortgage consumer credit, which is shown in figure 3 .
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The growth rate for consumer credit has been trending down, on balance, for years, but it remained quite robust until the latter half of last year.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Indeed, consumer credit fell quite sharply in the fourth quarter.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Looking back over the past 50 years, nonmortgage consumer credit typically weakens throughout a recession as labor markets deteriorate and often turns down even after the recession ends.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Thus, history suggests that consumer credit growth will likely slow further in the near term; in addition, many banks have tightened terms and standards for nonmortgage consumer loans.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Turning to the business sector, and in particular the corporate sector, the major components of borrowing are bonds, commercial paper, commercial mortgages, and commercial and industrial bank loans.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: As shown in the left panel of figure 4 , gross bond issuance for investment-grade firms increased in the fourth quarter of last year from a very weak third quarter and seems to have increased further in the first quarter of this year as firms appear to have strengthened their balance sheets by shifting toward longer-term debt.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In contrast, speculative-grade bond issuance has remained sluggish.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In September 2008, nonfinancial corporations' commercial paper outstanding contracted (the black solid line in the right panel of figure 4, as money market mutual funds--ordinarily major investors in commercial paper--faced significant strains.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Losses on Lehman Brothers paper led one prominent fund to "break the buck"--that is, to fail to maintain a net asset value of $1.00 a share--which undermined investor confidence in such funds and triggered significant withdrawals from funds that typically invest in private-sector debt.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In response, the Treasury established an insurance program for money market mutual fund investors, and the Federal Reserve introduced new programs to provide liquidity to money market mutual funds.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In addition, the Federal Reserve authorized the Commercial Paper Funding Facility to provide a liquidity backstop for U.S. issuers of commercial paper.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: 7 These programs helped to restore confidence in money market mutual funds and improve the functioning of the commercial paper market.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: By early this year, the strains in the commercial paper market had eased notably.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The volume of bank lending in 2008 mirrored developments in the commercial paper market.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In the fall, bank commercial and industrial lending surged for a time (the red dotted line in the right panel of figure 4, reportedly reflecting, in part, substantial draws on previously existing long-term lending commitments; then such lending contracted sharply as access to other sources of funding, such as commercial paper, improved.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In this manner, bank loans provided at least a partial substitute for market-based funding until market functioning improved.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: That said, the growth rate for debt of nonfinancial businesses decreased sharply in 2008.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: As shown in figure 5 , debt growth for nonfinancial corporate businesses reached almost 15 percent at the peak of the business cycle in December 2007, but it was less than 3 percent by the end of 2008.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Looking back, it is apparent that debt growth for nonfinancial corporate businesses can, and often does, decline sharply as the economy slows.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: During recessions, which are indicated in the figure by shading, debt growth has typically decreased and sometimes even become negative, such as during 1990-91.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In part, such declines in debt growth are derived from declines in demand for the goods and services produced by nonfinancial firms.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In addition, such declines reflect the ongoing tightening of lending standards that can result from the deterioration of the fundamentals that support lending.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Turning to commercial mortgage growth, figure 6 presents such data from the 1950s through 2008.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: As with the debt series plotted in previous charts, commercial mortgage growth typically drops off during a recession as retail sales slow and less office space is needed for workers.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Especially striking is the prolonged contraction in commercial mortgages outstanding after the 1990-91 recession.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Since the peak of the recent business cycle, commercial mortgage growth has slowed with each passing quarter.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: By the fourth quarter of 2008, its annualized growth was only about 1 percent.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The "Financial Intermediation View" of Credit The commercial paper market example, which I briefly described earlier, highlights the fact that financial intermediaries can play an important safety-valve role for the financial system.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: When the commercial paper market suddenly dried up, financial intermediaries were able to fund firms that had unused lines of credit or other commitments.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: 8 Moreover, the Federal Reserve, through its lending programs, contributed to improved conditions in the commercial paper market so that issuance of these short-term funding instruments could resume.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In today's economy, much of the flow of credit comes from lending that occurs outside of the banking system.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Here again, it is useful to take a historical look at financial intermediation to better understand the potential effect on the availability of credit to households and businesses from the recent shutdowns in the securitization and commercial paper markets and to get a first glimpse at how financial intermediation markets responded.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Consider, for example, the shares of commercial mortgages outstanding--funded by depositories, insurance companies, other financial institution, and commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS)--presented in figure 7 .
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: The share funded by CMBS (the orange line) increased from almost nothing in 1990 to almost 30 percent in 2008.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In an accounting sense, most of this increase in funding from the capital markets came at the expense of direct holdings of whole loans by insurance companies (the dashed green line) and other intermediaries (the black line), whose funding shares fell by half between 2000 and 2008.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In contrast, depositories' share of commercial mortgages outstanding (the purple line) held steady from 1990 through 2007.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In 2008, the decrease in the commercial mortgages funded by CMBS--the downtick of the orange line at the end of the sample--was offset by an increase in commercial mortgages funded by depositories--the uptick of the purple line.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

text: These data suggest that depositories increased their share of commercial mortgages as securitization markets stalled in 2008.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: Again, banks and other depositories served an important safety-valve function for the commercial mortgage market.

speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: In figure 8 , Federal Reserve flow of funds data are used to construct market shares of all financial intermediation provided by four major classes of institutions: banks, thrifts, insurance companies, and "other financial intermediaries," which range from finance companies to the entities that issue ABS.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke
text: 9 In 1950, banks' share of financial intermediation (the red line) was about 50 percent; it declined and then rose to about 48 percent in the mid-1970s, then it trended down to about 33 percent at the turn of the century.
speech_title: A Framework for Analyzing Bank Lending
speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Duke

speech_venue: At the 13th Annual University of North Carolina Banking Institute, Charlotte, North Carolina

text: The "Banking View" of Credit Even though the total provision of financial intermediation services by banks remained high relative to other financial intermediaries and their on-balance-sheet financial intermediation services increased in the fourth quarter of 2008, it must be recognized that there are many types of banks in the United States with different specializations, geographic concentrations, and comparative advantages.

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I will discuss, we no longer live in a world in which central bank policies are confined to adjusting the short-term interest rate.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Instead, by using their balance sheets, the Federal Reserve and other central banks are developing new tools to ease financial conditions and support economic growth.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Some Principles for Balance Sheet Policy Before I get into the details of our balance sheet and how it reflects various Federal Reserve initiatives, I would like to note some general considerations that have been important in shaping our policy approach.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: As you know, financial markets and institutions both in the United States and globally have been under extraordinary stress for more than a year and a half.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Relieving the disruptions in credit markets and restoring the flow of credit to households and businesses are essential if we are to see, as I expect, the gradual resumption of sustainable economic growth.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: To achieve this critical objective, the Federal Reserve has worked closely and cooperatively with the Treasury and other agencies.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Such collaboration is not unusual.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: We have traditionally worked in close concert with other agencies in fostering stable financial conditions, even as we have maintained independent responsibility for making monetary policy.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Though we have been creative in deploying our balance sheet, using a multiplicity of new programs (and coining a multiplicity of new acronyms, I might add), we have done so prudently.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: As much as possible, we have sought to avoid both credit risk and credit allocation in our lending and securities purchase programs.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I will discuss further today, the great majority of our lending is extremely well secured.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: And our programs have been aimed at improving financial and credit conditions broadly, with an eye toward restoring overall economic growth, rather than toward supporting narrowly defined sectors or classes of borrowers.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: In pursuing our strategy, which I have called "credit easing," we have also taken care to design our programs so that they can be unwound as markets and the economy revive.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, these activities must not constrain the exercise of monetary policy as needed to meet our congressional mandate to foster maximum sustainable employment and stable prices.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: We are also committed to working with the Administration and the Congress to develop a new resolution regime that would allow the U.S. government to effectively address, at an early stage, the potential failure of systemically critical nonbank financial institutions.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: As this audience well knows, the lack of such a regime greatly hampered our flexibility in dealing with the failure or near-failure of such institutions as Bear Stearns, Lehman Brothers, and American International Group (AIG).
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: The principles I have just noted were recently formalized in a joint Federal Reserve-Treasury statement.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: 1 Those principles are: (1) that the Fed will cooperate closely with the Treasury and other agencies in addressing the financial crisis; (2) that the Fed in its lending activities should avoid taking credit risk or allocating credit to narrowly defined sectors or classes of borrowers; (3) that the Fed's independent ability to manage monetary policy must not be constrained by its programs to ease credit conditions; and (4) that there is a pressing need for a new resolution regime for nonbanks that, among other things, will better define the Fed's role in preventing the disorderly failure of systemically critical financial institutions.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: I welcome the clarity that this public statement brings to the principles underlying our policy strategy during this very difficult period.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Balance Sheet as a Tool of Monetary Policy The severe disruption of credit markets that began late in the summer of 2007 and the associated tightening in credit conditions and declines in asset prices have weighed heavily on economic activity here and abroad.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve has responded by aggressively easing short-term interest rates, beginning in September 2007.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: In October 2008, as the financial crisis intensified, the Federal Reserve participated in an unprecedented coordinated rate cut with other major central banks.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: At its December 2008 meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) reduced its target for the federal funds rate close to its lower bound, setting a target range between 0 and 1/4 percent.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: And, with inflation expected to remain subdued for some time, the Committee has indicated that short-term interest rates are likely to remain low for an extended period.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: With conventional monetary policy having reached its limit, any further policy stimulus requires a different set of tools.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve has been a global leader in developing such tools.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: In particular, to further improve the functioning of credit markets and provide additional support to the economy, the Fed has established and expanded a number of liquidity programs and recently initiated a large-scale program of asset purchases.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: These actions have had significant effects on both the size and composition of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Notably, the balance sheet has more than doubled, from roughly $870 billion before the crisis to roughly $2 trillion now.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the remainder of my remarks, I will walk you through the major components of the Fed's balance sheet, which is a convenient way to discuss the range of policy tools the Fed is employing and some of the issues we are confronting in our policy decisions.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: An excellent source of information on our balance sheet, by the way, is a new section of the Board's website, entitled Credit and Liquidity Programs and the Balance Sheet.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: 2 This section brings together much diverse information about the Fed's balance sheet, including some only recently made available, as well as detailed explanations and analyses.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Serious Fed watchers should add this link to their online favorites list.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Let me begin with the asset side of our balance sheet.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: For decades, the Federal Reserve's assets consisted almost exclusively of Treasury securities.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Since late 2007, however, our holdings of Treasury securities have declined, while our holdings of other financial assets have expanded dramatically.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: It is useful to group the Federal Reserve's assets into three broad categories: (1) short-term credit extended to support the liquidity of financial firms such as depository institutions, broker-dealers, and money market mutual funds; (2) assets related to programs focused on broader credit conditions; and (3) holdings of high-quality securities, notably Treasury securities, agency debt, and agency-backed mortgage-backed securities (MBS).
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: 3 As I will discuss later, the Federal Reserve also has provided support directly to specific institutions in cases when a disorderly failure would have threatened the financial system.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Liquidity Programs for Financial Firms The first of these categories of assets--short-term liquidity provided to financial institutions--totals almost $860 billion and today represents nearly 45 percent of the assets on our balance sheet.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: These loans are made to sound institutions, are fully secured, and are for maturities no greater than 90 days, usually less.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: Thus, they are very safe.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: The main components of this category are lending to commercial banks and primary dealers, as well as currency swaps with other central banks to support interconnected global dollar funding markets.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: From its beginning, the Federal Reserve, through its discount window, has provided credit to depository institutions to meet unexpected liquidity needs, usually in the form of overnight loans.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: The provision of short-term liquidity is, of course, a long-standing function of central banks.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: In August 2007, conditions in short-term bank funding markets deteriorated abruptly, and bank funding needs intensified sharply.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: In response to these developments, the Federal Reserve reduced the spread of the primary credit rate--the rate at which most institutions borrow at the discount window--relative to the target federal funds rate, and also made it easier for banks to borrow at term.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, as in some past episodes of financial distress, banks were reluctant to rely on discount window credit to address their funding needs.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond 2009 Credit Markets Symposium, Charlotte, North Carolina

speaker: Bernanke
text: The banks' concern was that their recourse to the discount window, if it became known, might lead market participants to infer weakness--the so-called stigma problem.
speech_title: The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet
