speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Capital for the funds will be provided jointly by private investors and the Treasury.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: In addition, the government will provide the funds with leverage (through Federal Reserve lending or FDIC guarantees) that currently cannot be raised from market sources, allowing the funds to increase their purchases of legacy assets.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: These facilities are structured to give the government a share of any gains in the value of assets purchased while protecting the private-sector investors from some of the downside risks inherent in real estate credit at present.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: By providing such protection along with leverage that is unavailable in markets today, the government hopes to bolster demand for these assets and restart markets in them.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Taken together, these financial repair programs are a comprehensive and substantial effort to help financial institutions resume lending and so support economic activity.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Banks worried about the adequacy of their capital have been reassured by the capital provided by the Treasury, and they may also be more optimistic about their ability to raise private capital once they have shed legacy assets.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: At the same time, concerns about the availability of funding should be eased by access to government-guaranteed funding options.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Moreover, as I noted at the outset, these programs need to be viewed as complementing the monetary, fiscal, and other policies put in place to alleviate financial strains and support aggregate demand.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Indeed, when I think back to the exceedingly perilous financial situation last September and October, I judge the efforts at financial repair as at least a qualified success.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Risk spreads in bank funding markets have narrowed, and the liquidity positions of many institutions have improved.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Despite significant pressures on many financial firms, we have generally avoided fire sales of assets by institutions that were troubled or were anticipating trouble.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Despite this progress, financial markets remain very fragile, lenders are still very protective of their capital and liquidity, risk spreads remain elevated, and many segments--especially securitization markets--continue to be impaired.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: However, some of the government programs I have discussed--those to restart markets, provide additional capital buffers, and open outlets for legacy assets--are just now being implemented.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: While these programs are quite promising, we will not be able to judge their success at restarting lending for a time.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Foreclosure Mitigation Another way that the government has intervened to limit the spillovers of financial problems to the real economy, and vice versa, is by taking steps to reduce unnecessary foreclosures.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Most notably, the Treasury recently announced the Making Home Affordable program that will provide financial incentives to encourage lenders and servicers to refinance existing mortgages with new mortgages having lower payments, thereby helping at-risk homeowners to avoid foreclosure.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: The large supply of foreclosed-upon houses coming onto the market has placed added downward pressure on house prices, and clusters of vacant properties can lead to higher crime rates and strains on municipal budgets as well.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Thus, in addition to helping homeowners stay in their houses, limiting foreclosures should benefit lenders, mitigate adverse impacts on affected communities, and, by limiting the decline in overall home prices, help support the macroeconomy.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Fiscal Policy In addition to the wide range of policies to bolster financial firms and markets and so damp the adverse feedback loop of the past year and a half, the government has put in place fiscal stimulus that will support spending and economic activity directly.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: The fiscal package includes tax cuts to bolster household incomes, new infrastructure investments, and financial assistance to state and local governments, many of which would otherwise have had to cut spending in light of declining revenues.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: The economy is very weak and is likely to remain so for a while despite strong application of both conventional and unconventional monetary policy actions; as such, this point in time would seem to be a textbook moment for substantial fiscal stimulus.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: With monetary policy likely to be quite accommodative for an extended period and the margin of unused capacity extraordinarily large, crowding out of private-sector spending by the fiscal expansion should be limited.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Potential Policy Risks The policies that we have pursued have been targeted to the problems we face--strains in funding markets, tight credit conditions, balance sheet weaknesses at some banking institutions, rising foreclosures, and weak overall economic activity.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: By taking this broad approach to the situation, we allow for positive interactions among the policies we put in place and have the best chance of countering the adverse feedback loop that has been an important driver of economic and financial developments since the outbreak of the crisis.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Nonetheless, the success of these policies is subject to a number of risks.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Protectionism and Financial Nationalism One risk is that the crisis and the accompanying deterioration in economic conditions will lead to increases in protectionism and financial nationalism.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: In hard times countries may turn inward, focusing on the difficulties facing their own financial firms and the dislocations in their own economies.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: And taxpayers may conclude that commitments of government money should be devoted primarily to policies that will directly benefit their nations' citizens.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Although these reactions are natural, we need to recognize that if all countries react in this way, the result will be great inefficiency and a worse outcome for all.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: For example, as is well known, international trade benefits all nations by allowing for the more efficient production of goods and services.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: The current system of relatively open international trade has been gradually built up over many years and has contributed substantially to global prosperity.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: To backtrack now would be a tremendous setback that likely could not be reversed for a very long time.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: And if governments responded to problems at financial institutions in their countries by attempting to protect only domestic investors, the result would be a rapid, and likely very disruptive, unwinding of the international capital flows that run through the global banking system, resulting in greater strains on financial institutions and so on the economy.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Re-creating the Problems That Got Us Here?
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: A second risk that we should consider is whether in our efforts to deal with the financial crisis, we are inadvertently re-creating many of the structures and behaviors that contributed to the crisis.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: For example, the government is providing increased leverage even as markets are calling for deleveraging; some of the government programs make use of credit ratings from the same agencies that so evidently fell short in their assessments of structured financial instruments; some of these programs employ financial structures similar to the off-balance-sheet entities that proved unstable in the crisis; we are trying to keep interest rates very low to support asset prices and spending after an episode in which low long-term rates probably contributed to unsustainable housing prices; and, finally, we are supporting economic activity by further increasing government deficits at a time when the longer-term fiscal outlook is already troubling.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: So are we just perpetuating the errors and misjudgments that led to the crisis, and thus sowing the seeds of a new crisis in the years to come?
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: The steps we have taken need to be seen as part of an effort by the government to smooth the transition of our financial sector and economy to a more sustainable situation.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Both markets and regulators are going to press financial firms to employ less leverage.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Similarly, households will need to save more of their income over time, and in that process domestic spending will be brought more into line with our nation's potential to produce, thus reducing our dependence on foreign savings.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: However, the speed and force of the private-sector adjustments risk overshooting.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Investors, badly surprised by the performance of some structured instruments and also by the extent of the economic downturn, have--at least for the time being--pulled back sharply from risk-taking.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: But they will regain confidence over time and return to markets that are now at a standstill.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Government programs, like the TALF, can help rebuild that confidence.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Similarly, the prices of some assets may be in the process of overshooting their long-run levels, reflecting heightened risk aversion and the very weak economic outlook.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: And low asset prices could lead to a prolonged period of depressed consumer and business confidence and what will ultimately prove to be an excessive shortfall in consumer spending and business capital outlays.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: While these adjustments are playing out, we are, in effect, temporarily substituting the government's balance sheet and spending for their private-sector counterparts.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: However, while near-term stability seems to require slowing these adjustment processes, we must put in place frameworks for exiting these programs if we are to end up with a market-based economy that is more balanced and more resilient.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Over time, the Federal Reserve must reduce its lending; the government must put its deficits on a distinct downward track; financial institutions must retire government assistance and operate on their own.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Dealing with the Government The success of these policies requires that they be utilized.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Because the government must protect the taxpayer, it needs to be sure that institutions taking taxpayer money are using the resources efficiently to address the intended problem.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: To ensure that government money is used appropriately, the government must monitor how it is used and impose conditions on those receiving it.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: However, the conditions for government assistance need to be carefully calibrated to protect the taxpayer while still allowing the policy objectives to be accomplished.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Firms might hold back on accepting government help if they saw the cost of meeting the conditions as greater than the benefit of the assistance or if they were concerned that the conditions might change in an undesirable way after the assistance had been accepted.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Such hesitance could impede the effectiveness of government programs and slow the recovery of jobs and income.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Will We Need to Do More?
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: My final issue is the hardest: Are the policies we have put in place sufficient to restart the flow of credit, or will the government need to do more?
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: The answer, of course, is that we don't know--we have no reliable precedents for the current situation.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Policymakers are operating in a highly uncertain environment--one marked by a huge amount of unquantifiable risks.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Most people, including policymakers, did not anticipate the depth, breadth, and severity of the financial meltdown and economic downturn.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: We have had to remain very flexible and open to policy actions that had no precedent.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: And all of us--the Federal Reserve, the Administration, and the Congress--must continue in this posture.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: We must keep our ultimate objectives for the economy firmly in mind--sustained recovery to high levels of output and employment with price stability.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: We will continue to adapt our policies as necessary to accomplish these objectives.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: The views are my own and not necessarily those of other members of the Federal Open Market Committee.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: William English of the Board's staff contributed to these remarks.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Kohn
text: Primary dealers are broker-dealers that trade in U.S. government securities with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
speech_title: Policies to Bring Us Out of the Financial Crisis and Recession
speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speech_venue: At the Forum on Great Decisions in the Economic Crisis, College of Wooster, Wooster, Ohio

speaker: Warsh
text: These measures are objective, all-too-familiar indicators of recessions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: They emerge during periodic troughs in our economic history.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: They are thought by most observers to be part of the business cycle.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The decennial recessions of 1981-82, 1991-92, and 2001-02 were of differing causes and consequences.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: But they were alike in one key respect: They were extremely disruptive to countless workers, businesses, and communities.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In the case of the United States, these periods were endured, and growth resumed apace, matched by new opportunities.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The march of growing prosperity, however imperfect and interrupted, continued.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: These words are different, not just in degree but also in kind.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: They are more normative, but no less consequential to the real economy.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: They are indicative of panic conditions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In panics, once firmly held truths are no longer relied upon.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Articles of faith are upended.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And the very foundations of economies and markets are called into question.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Some economists, market participants, and historians--not so long ago--were prepared to relegate these highly charged descriptions of despair to the dustbin of history.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Government policies improved, understanding of economics deepened, and markets found a more sustainable equilibrium, or so it was thought.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The period of the past 16 months is already well chronicled in the popular lexicon as a recession.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The recent data are consistent with the view that this recession will endure longer and be deeper and broader than most.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Characterizing the current period as a "recession" is still wanting, insufficient in some important respects.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In my view, this period should equally be considered a panic, one that preceded, if not made more pronounced, the official recession.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Hence, the Panic of 2008, which preceded the calendar year, is a more revealing description of the recent economic and financial travails.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: As I will describe, panics involve generalized fears--often related to financial firms--that magnify economic weakness.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The encouraging news, I should note, is that panics end.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And this panic is showing meaningful signs of abating.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The storied panics in U.S. economic history were generally marked by widespread bank runs as depositors lost confidence in large segments of the banking system.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: 2 Such was the case in the Panics of 1837, 1857, 1873, 1893, and 1907.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Depositors withdrew funds and hoarded cash, generating increases in currency holdings relative to deposits.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: 3 This loss of confidence was not limited to individual depositors.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: 4 During these panics, banks lost confidence in one another.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Banks withdrew funds in interbank deposits held at money center banks--then the central repositories for the reserves of the country's banking system.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Increased withdrawals of interbank deposits exceeded the money center banks' ability to meet demand, and payments were suspended to other banks.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The scramble for funds spilled over into the money markets, where rates on call loans to brokerage houses, considered at the time to be very liquid investments, soared to extreme levels.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: This series of events from a century earlier echoes the events of our time.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Panic manifested itself in the summer of 2007.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Asset-backed commercial paper markets seized up in the United States and abroad.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Commercial banks lost confidence in each other, putting pressure on overnight London interbank offered rates.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Strains intensified in the spring of 2008 when Bear Stearns could not borrow even on a secured basis.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And then the panic intensified further in the fall of 2008, as interbank funding markets stopped functioning and overnight rates soared to extraordinary levels.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: When one money market mutual fund "broke the buck," fears were raised about others.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Fund outflows escalated rapidly, threatening the stability of short-term funding to businesses and municipalities.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Confidence in money center banks plummeted, as was the case a century before.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And market participants lost trust in their counterparties.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Extraordinary actions, however, have been taken--with some notable success--to lessen panic conditions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Panics involve losses of confidence in the financial system, when even sound firms find it difficult to borrow.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Panics are threatening to economic well-being.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Panics take even less kindly to, and often result from, uncertainty.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And panics place a greater burden on the deftness of policy responses than recessions alone.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Our economic history contains many contractions in output--and losses in wealth--that were unconnected to panics.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: 5 In the Panic of 2008, however, the breakdown in the financial sector has contributed to, and exacerbated, the economic downturn.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Economic and Financial Conditions The current financial and economic turmoil is marked by indicia of both recession and panic conditions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: By official measures, the current recession is already significant in scale, scope, and duration.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And the deterioration in employment conditions in the current episode already ranks comparably to the recession of 1981-82.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The unemployment rate is 8.5 percent and likely, in my view, to increase steadily through the balance of the year.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Economic output, as measured by gross domestic product, contracted at a rate of about 6-1/4 percent in the fourth quarter of 2008 and is on track to contract sharply again in the first quarter, which would put the current contraction among the most severe post-World War II recessions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Though the pace of decline is likely to abate, I am decidedly uncomfortable forecasting a sharp and determined resumption of growth in the coming quarters.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The panic conditions that have marked this period may also have long-run implications.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: I suspect that the process of an efficient reallocation of capital and labor will prove slower and more difficult than is typical after recessions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Policymakers should be wary of policies that make the economy still less capable of the growth, productivity, and employment trends that have marked the postwar period.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In the United States, average stock prices have fallen by 40 percent in 2008 and another 6 percent this year.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The average market capitalization of large banking firms plummeted 50 percent in 2008 and continued to fluctuate significantly this year as uncertainty about their earnings prospects, potential balance sheet impairments, and sustainability of business models intensified.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Greater clarity as to policymakers' objectives for financial intermediation would likely prove very constructive to financial markets.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: More consequentially, in my view, it would improve the prospects for economic performance.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In the household sector, Federal Reserve data indicate that household net worth fell $11 trillion in 2008, or about 18 percent, the largest annual decline recorded.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: 6 Relative to disposable income, household net worth fell from a ratio of about 6 to one to less than 5 to one, erasing about a full year's worth of income in wealth.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: For the median household, net worth is estimated to have decreased at a greater rate--23 percent in 2008.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: 7 Household balance sheets may have contracted about another 7 percent in the first quarter, and I am watching keenly for that trend to change in subsequent quarters as part of the recovery.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: House price declines accounted for much of the decline in net worth for the median household.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: But, more than in previous periods, household wealth was harmed by declining share prices through direct equity exposure and retirement plan holdings.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Households are thus confronting the risks of income statement shocks through job losses and more significantly correlated changes in the value of virtually all other assets.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The heightened concern about these risks is indicated by the extremely high equity risk premiums, which reflect, among other factors, the risk that investors who suffered a loss in income may also be forced to sell their stocks when valuations are low.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Traditional rules of income and asset diversification appear to offer scarcer protection than generally advertised.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: As a result, households are questioning the route to financial security.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Homeownership is no longer perceived to ensure low-risk capital appreciation.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And assurances by investment managers to invest in "stocks for the long haul" are being subjected to intense scrutiny.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Investors of all stripes--sovereign wealth funds, large long-only institutional investors, private equity sponsors, hedge funds, and retail investors--are searching for new rules of asset allocation and appropriate risk premiums in an uncertain and unusual economic environment.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In a typical recession, the mix of balance sheet contraction by households and businesses and of trends on employment and production would pose meaningful challenges for policymakers.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: I would argue that the challenge is exacerbated when recessionary dynamics are compounded by panic conditions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Fundamental Reassessment Previously, I argued that we were witnessing a fundamental reassessment of the value of every asset everywhere in the world.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: 8 This diagnosis seems truer, and still more troubling, today.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The trading of legacy loans and securities continues to reveal systematic underpricing at issuance of once seemingly benign risks--credit, liquidity, counterparty, and even sovereign risks--which are demanding continued reassessment and recalibration.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Until these assessments are more cleanly refined and more broadly understood, we are likely to observe elevated levels of volatility and unwillingness by many investors to participate in certain asset markets at virtually any price.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The ongoing reassessment of these risks continued through the first quarter of 2009.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Some financial markets and economic actors are still searching for a new equilibrium; others appear to have called off the search teams altogether until the new equilibrium arrives.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Since the beginning of 2009, global equity markets have fallen about 15 percent, and the global market capitalization of financial institutions generally underperformed the broader indexes.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: 9 Few sanctuaries appear to exist from the recession and corresponding global asset revaluation.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: These real-time economic and financial market indicators surely describe recessionary conditions, a period of significant economic weakness and a global revaluation of asset values.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: But the depth and severity of this downturn are due, I believe, to a more profound panic phenomenon.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Market participants wonder whether the forms of financial intermediation and functions of financial institutions--long connecting savers with investors--will be implemented in a manner that will enhance, or reduce, economic well-being.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Some are questioning the efficacy of the remaining vestiges of the existing financial architecture and remain uncertain of the timing, efficacy, and policy preferences for the financial architecture that will ultimately emerge.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Surely, they applaud the goal of policymakers to reform the financial system to make it more durable through the cycle and less susceptible to shocks.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: But some query whether policy actions are, on balance, lessening or stoking panic conditions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Articles of Faith Headlines have been dominated in recent weeks by the legal rules that govern contracts.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: To be sure, markets function best when economic actors comport themselves in a manner consistent with the rule of law.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: 10 Fidelity to the rule of law is not just some aphorism for a judicial system to protect property right disputes among private parties.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Nor should it be just some preachy truism of economic development for emerging economies.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Rather, it is the linchpin of modern market economies like ours.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And it suffers its greatest blow when the governing authorities are unwilling to uphold their end of the bargain.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Nonetheless, despite some highly publicized suggestions to the contrary, I remain highly confident that the government will work tirelessly to uphold its obligations.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Hewing to the rule of law, however, may be the easier part.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The panic bred by the loss of confidence in the underlying financial architecture is difficult to remedy beyond the purview of statutes and regulations.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: A weighty accumulation of unwritten, but no less critical, practices and understandings governs behavior and establishes expectations in market economies.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Over time, these informal understandings attract deep and loyal followings by economic actors.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: They become articles of faith.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Deviations from them tend not to be illegal, but they can markedly change perceptions of risk and return.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: When that happens, the resulting expectations are unmoored, with significant and often highly detrimental consequences for market functioning and economic progress.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Panics can thus be understood as periods in which key articles of faith are cast in doubt.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: After long periods of economic prosperity--in the most recent case, the so-called Great Moderation--articles of faith accumulate.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Some of these understandings are strong and enduring and well grounded; others, more problematic or misplaced; others still, properly and promptly discarded.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Some of these articles of faith are rooted in government policies; others develop as a matter of private practice.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Regardless of their cause and contour, when faith is undermined, the resulting fear and ambiguity can accelerate the deterioration in economic performance.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Some key articles of faith have been undermined with respect to some financial institutions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And that is as it should be.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Risk-management failures at some large, systemically significant financial institutions are now legendary.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In some cases, investors and counterparties came to rely to their detriment on these entities and their financial wherewithal.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: As wholesale funding markets became tougher to navigate, many financial institutions suffered, some rightly so.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: But their stronger peers with significantly more robust risk-management practices also appear to be paying a heavy price.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: It is difficult for the strong to thrive, let alone survive, when they reside in a neighborhood that is being decimated.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And when panic conditions persist and long-held articles of faith lose their following, markets often react indiscriminately.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Government policies, in my view, should encourage differentiation among firms, even those in seemingly close proximity.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: For policymakers to act otherwise is to risk their own credibility and risk undermining the pace of economic recovery.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Market participants appear equally uncertain about the nature, objective, and duration of the relationship between the government and financial institutions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Given the choices available to policymakers during the past 24 months, some uncertainty is unavoidable.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Consider the saga of the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs).
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In my judgment, the story of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac exposes perhaps the most consequential negative shock to the financial system during this period.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: For about a generation, the GSEs issued debt that was thought by virtually all market participants to be backed de facto by the U.S. government.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The GSEs traveled the world, selling debt at rates and terms and funding schedules that were largely comparable to Treasury securities.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Some loud protestations aside, government policy--broadly defined--tended to countenance investor expectations.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: At year-end 2007, the outstanding public debt of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac totaled about $5.0 trillion, roughly comparable with the publicly held Treasury debt of $5.1 trillion, and spreads to Treasuries on their senior debt amounted to about 30 to 50 basis points, even though the institutions were thinly capitalized relative to their asset composition and risk characteristics.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In the fall of 2008, however, GSE senior debt spreads widened significantly to more than 500 basis points.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Market participants grew increasingly skeptical of the GSEs' financial and operational wherewithal and were uncertain of the depth of government support.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: When markets decided to test policymakers, as markets are especially wont to do during panics, the Treasury was forced to intercede, effectively taking control of the entities.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Congress authorized successive Administrations to take forceful actions, including appropriations of up to $200 billion to-date, to assure investors and counterparties that the institutions would remain solvent.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: These efforts, while necessary and well intended, have not completely resolved the uncertainty around the GSEs to market participants.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Indeed, even after extraordinary actions most recently by the Federal Reserve to improve liquidity and market functioning in the agency debt markets, confidence in the GSEs is less than markets were long accustomed to before this period began.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: When presumptively risk-free, highly liquid assets backed by the highest-grade sovereign are subject to large swings in value, the risk-return profile of virtually all other assets becomes highly uncertain.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The resulting portfolio reallocation boosts demand for Treasury securities, and reduces demand for assets that are genuinely riskier, placing upward pressure on risk premiums across a wide range of markets.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In addition, financial firms that had assumed that their holdings of GSE debt were as good as cash were forced to reassess the adequacy of their liquidity positions, adding to balance sheet pressures and leading to even greater safe-haven demands for Treasury securities.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Across a broad range of financial institutions and financial markets, an unhealthy mix of recession dynamics and panic conditions appear at work.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: But, in my view, it is predominantly the latter--the uncertainty with respect to financial intermediation and the corresponding breach of articles of faith--that have exacerbated the downturn.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Conclusion Let me offer several concluding observations that may help frame a new foundation for growth and ensure that discarded articles of faith are repaired, reformed, or replaced.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The Panic began before the recession and will assuredly end before it.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Getting the financial intermediation process to function with greater efficacy--even before a new financial architecture is firmly established--is a necessary condition to a sustained recovery.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The Panic is the result of both faulty private practices and flawed public policies.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: To place blame either exclusively on private financial firms or chiefly at the doorstep of the official sector is incorrect.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Financial stability demands policy stability.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The official sector's policy preferences must be communicated clearly, credibly, and consistently and backed by concrete action.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: To accelerate the formation of a new financial architecture, the official sector should outline and defend a positive vision for financial firms and welcome private capital's return.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The nature and terms of the relationship between financial firms and the official sector should not be left in limbo.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Finally, and perhaps most important, policymakers across the government must be ever mindful of the long-term consequences of their actions.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Fluctuations in economic output and employment are unavoidable.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: As a result, policymakers' objective should be more humble: Maximize sustainable economic growth while reducing the incidence, severity, and economic fallout of future shocks.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: And we must ensure that the long-heralded strengths of the U.S. economy--the resiliency and dynamism in our labor markets, product markets, and, yes, our financial markets--are allowed to flourish.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In so doing, trust will continue to displace panic in our markets, and our economy will ultimately rebound with great vigor and even greater promise.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: The views expressed herein are my own and do not necessarily reflect the views of other members of the Board of Governors or of the Federal Open Market Committee.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: I am grateful for the assistance of Mark Carlson , Daniel Covitz , and Nellie Liang of the Board staff, who contributed to these remarks.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Economic historians disagree on the distinction between financial panics and financial crises.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In my view, a panic involves a more insidious set of events in which risk aversion rapidly displaces confidence and individuals and institutions are forced to reexamine fundamentally their world views.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: Financial crises, by comparison, are more episodic, more localized, and less fundamental to the structure and functioning of the financial and economic system.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Warsh
text: In the case of a financial crisis, confidence may be lost by an institution, or even a class of institutions, but faith in the financial and economic system remains largely intact.
speech_title: The Panic of 2008
speech_venue: At the Council of Institutional Investors 2009 Spring Meeting, Washington, D.C.

speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis

speaker: Bernanke
text: My remarks today will focus on the ongoing turmoil in financial markets and its consequence, the global economic recession.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The financial crisis, the worst since the Great Depression, has severely affected the cost and availability of credit to both households and businesses.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Credit is the lifeblood of market economies, and the damage to our economy resulting from the constraints on the flow of credit has already been extensive.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: With recent job losses exceeding half a million per month, this year's college graduates are facing the toughest labor market in 25 years.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the communities in which you and I grew up, many families are trying to cope with lost employment and depleted savings or are facing foreclosure on their homes.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Firms have shut factories and cancelled construction projects.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: States and municipalities are scrambling to find the funding to provide critical services.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: And although we naturally tend to be most aware of conditions in the United States, we should not overlook the impact that the crisis is having virtually everywhere in the world, particularly on many citizens of countries that struggle economically even when the global economy is doing well.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the midst of all of these concerns, many Americans have recently celebrated Easter or Passover.

speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: As you may know, a highlight of the traditional Passover meal occurs when the youngest child asks four questions, the answers to which tell the history of the Jews when they were slaves in Egypt and during their exodus to the Promised Land.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the spirit of the holiday, today I will pose and answer four important questions about the financial crisis.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Of course, my answers will have to be brief, but we will have more time for additional questions at the conclusion of my prepared remarks.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: How Did We Get Here?
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The first question I would like to address is: How did we get here?
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: What caused our financial and economic system to break down to the extent it has?
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Not surprisingly, the answer to this question is complex, and experts disagree on how much weight to give various explanations.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In my view, however, to tell the story fully--and, in particular, to understand its international scope--we need to consider how global patterns of saving and investment have evolved over the past decade or more, and how those changes affected credit markets in the United States and some other countries.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: At the most basic level, the role of banks and other financial institutions is to take the savings generated by households and businesses and put them to use by making loans and investments.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, financial institutions use the funds they receive from savers to provide loans that help families buy homes or allow businesses to finance inventories and payrolls.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Financial markets, such as the stock and bond markets, perform a similar function, as when a firm raises funds for a new factory by selling a bond directly to investors.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: When the financial system is working as it should, it allocates funds both prudently (that is, with proper attention to risk) and efficiently (to the most productive uses).
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Importantly, in our global financial system, saving need not be generated in the country in which it is put to work but can come from foreign as well as domestic sources.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the past 10 to 15 years, the United States and some other industrial countries have been the recipients of a great deal of foreign saving.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Much of this foreign saving came from fast-growing emerging market countries in Asia and other places where consumption has lagged behind rising incomes, as well as from oil-exporting nations that could not profitably invest all their revenue at home and thus looked abroad for investment opportunities.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Indeed, the net inflow of foreign saving to the United States, which was about 1-1/2 percent of our national output in 1995, reached about 6 percent of national output in 2006, an amount equal to about $825 billion in today's dollars.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Saving inflows from abroad can be beneficial if the country that receives those inflows invests them well.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Unfortunately, that was not always the case in the United States and some other countries.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Financial institutions reacted to the surplus of available funds by competing aggressively for borrowers, and, in the years leading up to the crisis, credit to both households and businesses became relatively cheap and easy to obtain.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: One important consequence was a housing boom in the United States, a boom that was fueled in large part by a rapid expansion of mortgage lending.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Unfortunately, much of this lending was poorly done, involving, for example, little or no down payment by the borrower or insufficient consideration by the lender of the borrower's ability to make the monthly payments.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Lenders may have become careless because they, like many people at the time, expected that house prices would continue to rise--thereby allowing borrowers to build up equity in their homes--and that credit would remain easily available, so that borrowers would be able to refinance if necessary.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Regulators did not do enough to prevent poor lending, in part because many of the worst loans were made by firms subject to little or no federal regulation.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Mortgage markets were not the only ones caught up in the credit boom.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The large flows of global saving into the United States drove down the returns available on many traditional long-term investments, such as Treasury bonds, leading investors to search for alternatives.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: To satisfy the enormous demand for investments both perceived as safe and promising higher returns, the financial industry designed securities that combined many individual loans in complex, hard-to-understand ways.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
