text: These new securities later proved to involve substantial risks--risks that neither the investors nor the firms that designed the securities adequately understood at the outset.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The credit boom began to unravel in early 2007 when problems surfaced with subprime mortgages--mortgages offered to less-creditworthy borrowers--and house prices in parts of the country began to fall.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Mortgage delinquencies and defaults rose, and the downturn in house prices intensified, trends that continue today.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Investors, stunned by losses on assets they had believed to be safe, began to pull back from a wide range of credit markets, and financial institutions--reeling from severe losses on mortgages and other loans--cut back their lending.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The crisis deepened last September, when the failure or near-failure of several major financial firms caused many financial and credit markets to freeze up.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Stock prices fell sharply as investors lost confidence in the financial sector and became gloomy about economic prospects.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Declining stock values, a teetering financial system, and difficulties in obtaining credit triggered a remarkably rapid and deep contraction in global economic activity and employment, a contraction that has persisted through the first months of 2009.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Both the ongoing financial crisis and economic contraction have posed major challenges to economic policymakers.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: What Is the Fed Doing to Address the Situation?
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Those challenges bring me to my second question: What has the Federal Reserve been doing to address the economic and financial crisis?
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Fed's mandate from the Congress is to promote maximum sustainable employment and stable prices.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, the Fed is expected to contribute to financial stability by acting to contain financial disruptions and prevent their spread outside of the financial sector.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Thus, we have been serving as a first responder to the crisis.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Fed's basic policy tool for influencing economic activity and inflation is its ability to control very short-term interest rates--specifically, the federal funds rate, which is the rate that banks pay each other for overnight loans.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Lower interest rates can be used to stimulate private-sector borrowing and spending at times like the present when the economy is suffering from a lack of demand.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In September 2007, shortly after the turbulence in financial markets began and signs of economic weakness started to appear, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the body that determines the Federal Reserve's monetary policy, began to aggressively reduce the federal funds rate.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: By the spring of 2008, we had cut that interest rate from 5-1/4 percent to 2 percent, a highly proactive policy that helped to cushion the economy from some of the effects of the financial turmoil.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: But, as I mentioned a moment ago, the intensification of the financial crisis in the fall of 2008 led to a further significant deterioration in the economic outlook.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The FOMC responded with additional interest rate cuts, and since December, our policy interest rate has been essentially zero.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, the FOMC has made clear that it expects economic conditions to warrant holding the federal funds rate low for an extended period.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, given the ongoing problems in credit markets, conventional monetary policy alone is not adequate to provide all the support that the economy needs.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Fed has therefore taken a number of steps to help the economy by unclogging the flow of credit to households and businesses.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In doing so, we have demonstrated that the Fed's toolkit remains potent, even though the federal funds rate is close to zero and thus cannot be reduced further.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: We have taken a wide range of actions to help restore the flow of credit, of which I will only mention a few of the most important.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: One set of actions involves making short-term loans to banks and other financial institutions.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Banks and other financial intermediaries normally make longer-term commitments--such as residential mortgages and business loans--yet rely on funding that may be relatively short-term, such as customer deposits that can be withdrawn at any time.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: To have the confidence to commit to longer-term loans and investments, banks must be sure that they will have ample access to funding when necessary.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: To give this assurance to banks, the Federal Reserve has made clear that it will provide short-term credit to sound financial institutions as needed.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Indeed, serving as a lender of last resort to financial institutions is a method that central banks have used for centuries to try to calm financial crises.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: To underscore our commitment to providing short-term funding to banks when they need it, we have lowered the interest rate we charge for short-term loans and extended the term of the loans to up to three months.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: We have also begun to auction funds to financial institutions, thereby allowing the interest rate paid to depend on the level of demand.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Importantly, this lending is extremely safe from the point of view of both the Fed and the taxpayer.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Not only is our lending short-term and restricted to healthy institutions, but we require that the borrowers pledge, as security, collateral whose value exceeds the amount we are lending.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Fed's lending to financial institutions has helped to ease conditions in a number of key financial markets, reduced important benchmark interest rates (such as the London interbank offered rate, or Libor, to which payments on some mortgages and other types of loans are tied), and increased the willingness of banks to make credit available.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: A second strategy the Fed has employed is to use targeted lending to help free up critical credit markets outside of the banking system.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: A good example of targeted lending is our efforts in the commercial paper market.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Commercial paper is a form of short-term debt issued by a variety of businesses to finance their operations; paychecks and payments to suppliers can depend on it.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Among the largest investors in commercial paper are money market mutual funds.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: At the peak of the crisis last fall, many people who had invested in money market mutual funds lost confidence in those funds and withdrew their money; this loss of funding forced money market mutual funds to reduce their own investments, which in turn caused serious problems in the commercial paper market.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Through a series of lending programs, and in coordination with steps taken by the Treasury, the Federal Reserve helped restore confidence in both money market mutual funds and the commercial paper market.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Over time, withdrawals from money market mutual funds have been replaced by modest net inflows, and borrowers in the commercial paper market have seen significant improvements in the cost and availability of funding.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: More recently, the Federal Reserve has also initiated a lending program, with the cooperation of the Treasury, designed to free up the flow of credit to households and small businesses.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Among the forms of credit on which the program is currently focused are auto loans, credit card loans, student loans, and loans guaranteed by the Small Business Administration.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: We are currently reviewing other types of credit for possible inclusion in this program.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In all cases, we will be taking the appropriate measures to minimize the risk of loss to the Federal Reserve.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Restoring stability to the market for housing and home mortgages has been a particular area of concern.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: To address this problem, the Fed has employed a third type of policy tool--namely, buying securities in the open market.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The FOMC has approved purchases of well over $1 trillion this year of mortgage-related securities guaranteed by the government-sponsored mortgage companies, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Buying mortgage-related securities helps to drive down the interest rates that consumers pay on mortgages, and, indeed, the rate on a traditional 30-year fixed-rate mortgage has recently fallen to less than 5 percent, the lowest level since the 1940s.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Certainly, the housing market remains depressed, but lower interest rates and house prices are making houses more affordable.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, two years ago, when mortgage rates were higher than 6percent, payments on a mortgage covering 80 percent of the cost of a $215,000 home would have been more than $1,000 per month; today, the price of that same house may have fallen to $170,000, and, at today's mortgage interest rates, the monthly payment would be about $700.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Lower mortgage rates are also helping some homeowners refinance their mortgages to reduce their monthly payments.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve will continue to take the necessary steps to unclog the credit markets and strengthen the economy.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: We will also continue to work closely with other agencies, such as the Treasury and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), each of which has also taken a variety of actions to help stabilize financial markets, as well as with other central banks around the world.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Does the Fed's Aggressive Response Risk Inflation Down the Road?
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The multifaceted policy response that I've described has been aggressive.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: I am confident that such a proactive policy response is well justified by the serious ongoing problems in financial markets and the economy.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, some have raised the third question I will address: Could the Fed's aggressive actions to stabilize the economy today lead to an inflation problem down the road?
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: I mentioned earlier that the Fed's mandate from the Congress is to foster price stability as well as maximum sustainable employment.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The FOMC treats its obligation to ensure price stability extremely seriously.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Price stability supports healthy economic growth, for example, by making it easier for households and businesses to plan for the future.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In practice, price stability does not require that inflation be literally zero; indeed, although inflation can certainly be too high, it can also be too low.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Experience suggests that inflation rates that are close to zero or even negative (corresponding to deflation, or falling prices) can at times be associated with poor economic performance.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Cases in point include the United States in the 1930s and the more recent experience of Japan.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In their latest quarterly projections of the economy, most members of the FOMC indicated that they would like to see an annual inflation rate of about 2 percent in the longer term.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Right now, because of the weakness in economic conditions here and around the world, inflation has been running less than that, and our best forecast is that inflation will remain quite low for some time.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Thus, the Fed's proactive policy approach is not at all inconsistent with the goal of price stability in the medium term.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although inflation seems set to be low for a while, the time will come when the economy has begun to strengthen, financial markets are healing, and the demand for goods and services, which is currently very weak, begins to increase again.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: At that point, the liquidity that the Fed has put into the system could begin to pose an inflationary threat unless the FOMC acts to remove some of that liquidity and raise the federal funds rate.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: We have a number of effective tools that will allow us to drain excess liquidity and begin to raise rates at the appropriate time; that said, unwinding or scaling down some of our special lending programs will almost certainly have to be part of our strategy for reducing policy stimulus once the recovery is under way.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: We are thinking carefully about these issues; indeed, they have occupied a significant portion of recent FOMC meetings.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: I can assure you that monetary policy makers are fully committed to acting as needed to withdraw on a timely basis the extraordinary support now being provided to the economy, and we are confident in our ability to do so.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: To be sure, decisions about when and how quickly to proceed will require a careful balancing of the risk of withdrawing support before the recovery is firmly established versus the risk of allowing inflation to rise above its preferred level in the medium term.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, this delicate balancing of risks is a challenge that central banks face in the early stages of every economic recovery.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: I believe that we are well equipped to make those judgments appropriately.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, when the time comes, our ability to clearly communicate our policy goals and our assessment of the outlook will be crucial to minimizing public uncertainty about our policy decisions.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Why Did the Fed and the Treasury Act to Prevent the Bankruptcy of Some Major Financial Firms?
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The final question is as difficult as it is important: Why did the Fed and the Treasury act to prevent the bankruptcy of some major financial firms, such as the investment bank Bear Stearns and the insurance company American International Group, or AIG?
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: We must answer that question not only because the decisions have been controversial, but also because it bears on the steps we need to take as a country if we are to avert a repetition of the crisis.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: As a general rule, my strong preference is that any firm that cannot meet its obligations should bear the consequences of the marketplace.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: But recent circumstances have been truly extraordinary.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Consider the situation on September 16 of last year, when the insurance conglomerate AIG faced pressures that threatened to force it imminently into bankruptcy.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: At that time, the strains in the global financial system were unprecedented and extreme, and the confidence of financial market participants in the system was rapidly eroding.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The investment bank Lehman Brothers had filed for bankruptcy the day before, and the mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, after suffering losses that threatened their solvency, had effectively been taken over by the government just two weeks earlier.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: As waves of panic and fear washed over the markets, the Fed and the Treasury became very concerned about the stability of a number of other major financial firms.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Large, complex financial institutions tend to be highly interconnected with other firms and markets, and AIG was more interconnected than most.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, AIG had insured many billions of dollars of loans and securities held by banks around the world, and its failure would have rendered those insurance contracts worthless, imposing large losses on the global banking system.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, banks had extended more than $50 billion in credit to the company, much of which would have been lost.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Many other serious consequences would have followed from a default by AIG: Insurance policyholders would have faced considerable uncertainty about the status of their policies; state and local governments, which had lent more than $10 billion to AIG, would have suffered losses; workers whose 401(k) plans had purchased $40 billion of insurance from AIG against the risk of loss would have seen that insurance disappear; and holders of AIG's substantial quantities of commercial paper would have also borne serious losses.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: But much more important, the disorderly failure of AIG would have put at risk not only the company's own customers and creditors but the entire global financial system.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Historical experience shows that, once begun, a financial panic can spread rapidly and unpredictably; indeed, the failure of Lehman Brothers a day earlier, which the Fed and the Treasury unsuccessfully tried to prevent, resulted in the freezing up of a wide range of credit markets, with extremely serious consequences for the world economy.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The financial and economic risks posed by a collapse of AIG would have been at least as great as those created by the demise of Lehman.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the case of AIG, financial market participants were keenly aware that many major financial institutions around the world were insured by or had lent funds to the company.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The company's failure would thus likely have led to a further sharp decline in confidence in the global banking system and possibly to the collapse of other major financial institutions.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: At best, the consequences of AIG's failure would have been a significant intensification of an already severe financial crisis and a further worsening of economic conditions.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Conceivably, its failure could have triggered a 1930s-style global financial and economic meltdown, with catastrophic implications for production, incomes, and jobs.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve and the Treasury agreed that in the environment then prevailing, AIG's failure would have posed unacceptable risks for the global financial system and for our economy.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Accordingly, the Federal Reserve, with the full support of the Treasury, made a loan to AIG to prevent its failure.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The loan imposed tough terms; in addition, senior management was replaced, and shareholders lost almost all of their investments.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, because the firm avoided a declaration of bankruptcy, creditors of AIG were protected.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: In my view, preventing the failure of AIG was the best of the very bad options available, but it nevertheless involved major costs, including financial risks to the taxpayer.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The American people also quite correctly see as unfair that AIG was saved from bankruptcy because of the dangers to the system that its failure would have posed, even as many other companies, including nonfinancial and smaller financial firms, have not received the same treatment.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Allowing AIG to at least partly avoid the discipline of the marketplace also sets a bad precedent.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: For these reasons, it is essential that we make changes to the financial rules of the game to prevent a similar episode from occurring in the future.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: First, we must ensure that all types of financial institutions, especially large and interconnected ones like AIG, receive strong and effective government oversight.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: AIG's regulatory oversight was limited, which allowed it to take dangerous risks largely out of sight of federal regulators.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Second, the AIG experience demonstrates that federal regulators urgently need a new set of procedures for dealing with a complex, systemically important financial institution on the brink of failure.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Such rules already exists for banks: If a bank approaches insolvency, the FDIC is empowered to intervene as needed to protect depositors, sell the bank's assets, and take any necessary steps to prevent broader consequences to the financial system.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, for an insurance conglomerate like AIG, or for a large financial holding company that owns many subsidiary companies, these rules do not apply.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Among other things, a good system for resolving nonbank financial institutions would allow federal regulators to unwind a failing company in ways that minimize disruptions in financial markets.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: An effective regime would also provide the authorities greater latitude to negotiate with creditors and to modify contracts entered into by the company, including contracts that set bonuses and other compensation for management.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: More generally, we need significant reforms to financial regulation and financial practices that will reduce the risk of future financial crises like the one we are currently experiencing.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve strongly supports such reform efforts.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Conclusion The current crisis has been one of the most difficult financial and economic episodes in modern history.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Recently we have seen tentative signs that the sharp decline in economic activity may be slowing, for example, in data on home sales, homebuilding, and consumer spending, including sales of new motor vehicles.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: A leveling out of economic activity is the first step toward recovery.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: To be sure, we will not have a sustainable recovery without a stabilization of our financial system and credit markets.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: We are making progress on that front as well, and the Federal Reserve is committed to working to restore financial stability as a necessary step toward full economic recovery.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: I am fundamentally optimistic about our economy.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Among its many intrinsic strengths are universities and colleges like Morehouse, which help talented students gain not only a command of a body of knowledge but also the capacity to think creatively and independently.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Institutions like this one train the professionals, entrepreneurs, and leaders who will shape our economy in the future.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: Today's economic conditions are difficult, but the foundations of our economy are strong, and we face no problems that cannot be overcome with insight, patience, and persistence.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve will certainly do its part to help restore prosperity and opportunity to our economy.
speech_title: Four Questions about the Financial Crisis
speech_venue: At the Morehouse College, Atlanta, Georgia

speaker: Bernanke
text: The concept of financial innovation, it seems, has fallen on hard times.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Subprime mortgage loans, credit default swaps, structured investment vehicles, and other more-recently developed financial products have become emblematic of our present financial crisis.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Indeed, innovation, once held up as the solution, is now more often than not perceived as the problem.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: I think that perception goes too far, and innovation, at its best, has been and will continue to be a tool for making our financial system more efficient and more inclusive.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: But, as we have seen only too clearly during the past two years, innovation that is inappropriately implemented can be positively harmful.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In short, it would be unwise to try to stop financial innovation, but we must be more alert to its risks and the need to manage those risks properly.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: My remarks today will focus on the consumer protection issues raised by financial innovation.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: First, though, I want to say how pleased I am to join you for the sixth biennial Federal Reserve System Community Affairs Research Conference.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: We all want to see our communities grow and thrive, especially those that have been traditionally underserved.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: But the people in this room know as well as anyone that, when it comes to consumer protection and community development, good intentions are not enough.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Hard-won knowledge, as exemplified by the empirical work presented here during the past two days, is required.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: I applaud your diligent and tough-minded research in analyzing what works and what doesn't.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Only with such knowledge can efforts to spread prosperity more widely become increasingly effective.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Sources of Financial Innovation Where does financial innovation come from?
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the United States in recent decades, three particularly important sources of innovation have been financial deregulation, public policies toward credit markets, and broader technological change.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: I'll talk briefly about each of these sources.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The process of financial deregulation began in earnest in the 1970s, a period when stringent regulations limited competition and the range of product offerings in the markets for consumer credit.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, Regulation Q, which capped interest rates on deposits, hampered the ability of depository institutions to attract funding and thus to extend credit.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Restrictions on branching were a particularly significant constraint, as they limited the size of the market that individual depository institutions could service and thus their scope to reduce costs through economies of scale.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 1 The lifting of these regulations, especially branching restrictions, allowed the development of national banking networks.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: With national networks, the fixed costs of product innovation could be spread over larger markets, making the development and marketing of new products more profitable.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Many public policy decisions have affected the evolution of financial products and lending practices.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: One particularly important example was the Community Reinvestment Act of 1977 (CRA), which induced lenders to find ways to extend credit and provide services in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Another important set of policies was the government's support for the development of secondary mortgage markets, particularly through the government-sponsored enterprises, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Secondary mortgage markets were rudimentary and thin in the 1970s; indeed, the Federal Reserve's Flow of Funds accounts do not even record private securitization activity until the early 1980s.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: As secondary mortgage markets--an important innovation in themselves--grew, they gave lenders both greater access to funding and better ability to diversify, providing further impetus to expansion into new markets and new products.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: On the technological front, advances in information technology made possible the low-cost collection, processing, and dissemination of household and business financial data, functions that were once highly localized and, by today's standards, inefficiently managed.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 2 As credit reporting advanced, models for credit scoring gradually emerged, allowing for ever-faster evaluation of creditworthiness, identification of prospective borrowers, and management of existing accounts.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: All these developments had their positive aspects, including for people in low- and moderate-income communities.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Prior to the introduction of the CRA, as you know, many of these communities had limited access to mortgages and other forms of consumer credit.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Subsequent innovations in financial products and services, processes, and technology helped at least some underserved consumers more fully enter the financial mainstream, save money, invest, and build wealth, and homeownership rates rose significantly.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Yet with hindsight, we can see that something went wrong in recent years, as evidenced by the currently high rates of mortgage delinquency and foreclosure, especially in minority and lower-income neighborhoods.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Indeed, we have come almost full circle, with credit availability increasingly restricted for low- and moderate-income borrowers.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: And the damage from this turn in the credit cycle--in terms of lost wealth, lost homes, and blemished credit histories--is likely to be long-lasting.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: One would be forgiven for concluding that the assumed benefits of financial innovation are not all they were cracked up to be.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: A number of factors explain the recent credit boom and bust, including problems stemming from financial innovation.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: From a consumer protection point of view, a particular concern has been the sharp increase in the complexity of the financial products offered to consumers, complexity which has been a side effect of innovation but which also has in many cases been associated with reduced transparency and clarity in the products being offered.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: I will illustrate the issue in the context of some familiar forms of consumer credit: credit cards, mortgages, and overdraft protection.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Credit Cards, Mortgages, and Overdrafts: Some Instructive Examples The credit card is an example of financial innovation driven by technological advance, including improvements in communications, data management, and credit scoring.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: When the first general-purpose credit card was issued in 1952, it represented a way to make small loans more quickly and at a lower cost than the closed-end installment loans offered by retailers and finance companies at the time.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, this form of credit doubled as a means of payment.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Card issuers benefited by spreading fixed costs over multiple advances of credit, over larger customer bases, across geographic areas, and among many merchants.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 3 From the consumer's perspective, credit cards provided convenience, facilitated recordkeeping, and offered security from loss (by theft, for example).
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 4 Their use gradually expanded among American families, rising to 43 percent in 1983 and to 70 percent by 2007.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Among lower-income families, usage increased from 11 percent in 1983 to 37 percent in 2007.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Mortgage markets saw similar product innovations.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, in the early 1990s, automated underwriting systems helped open new opportunities for underserved consumers to obtain traditional forms of mortgage credit.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: This innovation was followed by an expansion of lending to borrowers perceived to have high credit risk, which became known as the subprime market.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Lenders developed new techniques for using credit information to determine underwriting standards, set interest rates, and manage their risks.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: As I have already mentioned, the ongoing growth and development of the secondary mortgage market reinforced the effect of these innovations, giving mortgage lenders greater access to the capital markets, lowering transaction costs, and spreading risk more broadly.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Subprime lending rose dramatically from 5 percent of total mortgage originations in 1994 to about 20 percent in 2005 and 2006.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Innovation thus laid the groundwork for the expansion of credit card and mortgage lending that has taken place over the past 15 years or so, as well as some other forms of credit like auto loans.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, while innovation often brought consumers improved access to credit, it also brought increased complexity and an array of choices that consumers have often found difficult to evaluate properly.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Take the case of credit cards.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the early days, a card may have allowed the user to make purchases or obtain cash advances, with a single, unchanging annual percentage rate, or APR, applied to each feature.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Card fees were typically limited to an annual fee, a charge for cash advances, and perhaps fees for making a late payment or exceeding the credit limit.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In contrast, today's more-complex products offer balance transfers and treat different classes of purchases and cash advances as different features, each with its own APR.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In addition, interest rates adjust much more frequently than they once did, and the array of fees charged for various features, requirements, or services has grown.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: More-complex plans may benefit some consumers; for example, pricing that varies according to consumers' credit risk and preferences for certain services may improve access to credit and allow for more-customized products.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Growing complexity, however, has increased the probability that even the most diligent consumers will not understand or notice key terms that affect a plan's cost in important ways.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: When complexity reaches the point of reducing transparency, it impedes competition and leads consumers to make poor choices.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: And, in some cases, complexity simply serves to disguise practices that are unfair and deceptive.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Mortgage products have likewise become much more complex.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Moreover, in recent years, the increased complexity has sometimes interacted with weakened incentives for good underwriting, to the detriment of the borrower.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The practice of securitization, notwithstanding its benefits, appears to have been one source of the decline in underwriting standards during the recent episode.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Depending on the terms of the sale, originators who sold mortgage loans passed much of the risk--including the risks of poor underwriting--on to investors.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Compensation structures for originators also caused problems in some cases.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, some incentive schemes linked originator revenue to particular loan features and to volume rather than to the quality of the loan.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Complexity made the problem worse, as the wide array of specialized products made consumer choices more difficult.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, some originators offered what were once niche products--such as interest-only mortgages or no-documentation loans--to a wider group of consumers.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: And, we have learned, loan features matter.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Some studies of mortgage lending outcomes, after controlling for borrower characteristics, have found elevated levels of default associated with certain loan features, including adjustable rates and prepayment penalties, as well as with certain origination channels, including broker originations.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 7 Although these results are not conclusive, they suggest that complexity may diminish consumers' ability to identify products appropriate to their circumstances.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The vulnerabilities created by misaligned incentives and product complexity in the mortgage market were largely disguised so long as home prices continued to appreciate, allowing troubled borrowers to refinance or sell their properties.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Once housing prices began to flatten and then decline, however, the problems became apparent.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Mortgage delinquencies and foreclosure starts for subprime mortgages increased dramatically beginning in 2006 and spread to near-prime (alt-A) loans soon thereafter.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: By the fourth quarter of 2008, the percentages of loans 60 days past due, 90 days or more past due, and in foreclosure were at record highs.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Credit cards and mortgages are not the only product classes for which innovation has been associated with increased complexity and reduced transparency.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: I will cite one more example: overdraft protection.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Historically, financial institutions used their discretion to determine whether to pay checks that would overdraw a consumer's account.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In recent years, institutions automated that process with predetermined thresholds.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Although institutions usually charged the same amount when they paid an overdraft as when they returned the check unpaid, many consumers appreciated this service because it saved them from additional merchant fees and the embarrassment of a bounced check.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: However, technological innovations allowed institutions to extend the service, often without consumers' understanding or approval, to non-check transactions such as ATM withdrawals and debit card transactions.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: As a result, consumers who used their debit cards at point-of-sale terminals to make retail purchases, for instance, could inadvertently incur hundreds of dollars in overdraft fees for small purchases.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In response to this problem, the Board last December proposed regulatory changes that would give consumers a meaningful choice regarding the payment of these kinds of overdraft fees, and we expect to issue a final rule later this year.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Protecting Consumers in an Era of Innovation and Complexity In light of this experience, how should policymakers ensure that consumers are protected without stifling innovation that improves product choice and expands access to sustainable credit?
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The first line of defense undoubtedly is a well-informed consumer.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Federal Reserve System has a long-standing commitment to promoting financial literacy, and we devote considerable resources to helping consumers educate themselves about their financial options.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: 9 Consumers who know what questions to ask are considerably better able to find the financial products and services that are right for them.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The capacity of any consumer, including the best informed, to make good choices among financial products is enhanced by clear and well-organized disclosures.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The Board has a number of responsibilities and authorities with respect to consumer disclosures, responsibilities we take very seriously.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In the past year or so, the Board has developed extensive new disclosures for a variety of financial products, most notably credit cards, and we are currently in the midst of a major overhaul of mortgage disclosures.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In designing new disclosures, we have increased our use of consumer testing.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: The process of exploring how consumers process information and come to understand--or sometimes misunderstand--important features of financial products has proven eye-opening.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: We have used what we learned from consumer testing to make our required disclosures better.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, our recently released rules on credit card disclosures require certain key terms to be included in a conspicuous table provided at account opening; we took this route because our field testing indicated that consumers were often already familiar with and able to interpret such tables on applications and solicitations, but that they were unlikely to read densely written account agreements.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: We have also learned from consumer testing, however, that not even the best disclosures are always adequate.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: According to our testing, some aspects of increasingly complex products simply cannot be adequately understood or evaluated by most consumers, no matter how clear the disclosure.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In those cases, direct regulation, including the prohibition of certain practices, may be the only way to provide appropriate protections.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: An example that came up in our recent rulemaking was the allocation of payments by credit card issuers.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: As creditors began offering different interest rates for purchases, cash advances, and balance transfers, they were also able to increase their revenues through their policies for allocating consumer payments.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, a consumer might be charged 12 percent on purchases but 20 percent for cash advances.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Under the old rules, if the consumer made a payment greater than the minimum required payment, most creditors would apply the payment to the purchase balance, the portion with the lower rate, thus extending the period that the consumer would be paying the higher rate.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Under these circumstances, the consumer is effectively prevented from paying off the cash advance balance unless the purchase balance is first paid in full.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In an attempt to help consumers understand this practice and its implications, the Federal Reserve Board twice designed model disclosures that were intended to inform consumers about payment allocation.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: But extensive testing indicated that, when asked to review and interpret our best attempts at clear disclosures, many consumers did not demonstrate an understanding of payment allocation practices sufficient to make informed decisions.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In light of the apparent inadequacy of disclosures alone in this case, and because the methods of payment allocation used by creditors were clearly structured to produce the maximum cost to the consumer, last year we put rules in place that will limit the discretion of creditors to allocate consumers' payments made above the minimum amount required.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: We banned so-called double-cycle billing--in which a bank calculates interest based not only on the current balance, but also on the prior month's balance--on similar grounds; we found from testing that the complexity of this billing method served only to reduce transparency to the consumer without producing any reasonable benefit.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: These actions were part of the most comprehensive change to credit card regulations ever adopted by the Board.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Similar issues have arisen in the mortgage arena.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Many of the poor underwriting practices in the subprime market were also potentially unfair and deceptive to consumers.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: For example, the failure to include an escrow account for homeowners' insurance and property taxes in many cases led borrowers to underestimate the costs of homeownership.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: In this case, allowing greater optionality--which we usually think of as a benefit--had the adverse effects of increasing complexity and reducing transparency.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Restricting this practice was one of the new protections in the residential mortgage market that the Board established in a comprehensive set of rules released in July.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Banning or limiting certain underwriting practices, which the new rules do for the entire mortgage market, also helps to address the incentive problems I discussed earlier.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: For institutions that we supervise, these incentive issues can also be addressed by requiring that lenders set up compensation plans for originators that induce behavior consistent with safety and soundness.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: Where does all this leave us?
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
text: It seems clear that the difficulty of managing financial innovation in the period leading up to the crisis was underestimated, and not just in the case of consumer lending.
speech_title: Financial Innovation and Consumer Protection
speech_venue: At the Federal Reserve System's Sixth Biennial Community Affairs Research Conference, Washington, D.C.

speaker: Bernanke
